domain: 日常协作与非结构化讨论
title: eng-ml
text:
anya: Quick readiness check — I'm onboarding open-mix-1.2. Weights uploaded to s3://redwood-models/onboard/open-mix-1.2/weights.pt. Can infra/runtime confirm KV cache format & memory sizing before we flip the canary? Also seeing a tokenizer quirk: BOS token seems duplicated when we push beyond 4096 tokens.

mike: Thanks. Couple quick Qs — is the weights file sharded or a single file? Also what's model config: num_layers / hidden_size / max_position_embeddings?

anya: single file, ~5.3GB (fp16). Model config excerpt in repo: max_position_embeddings: 8192, num_hidden_layers: 32, hidden_size: 4096, num_attention_heads: 32.

infra-bot: s3 upload check: permissions OK, object available to redwood-infra role. :white_check_mark:

sara: Re: tokenizer — I dug in; tokenizer.json is missing special_tokens_map and pad_token is null. When we call tokenizer.encode_plus with add_special_tokens it ends up inserting an extra BOS after the prompt for long sequences. Quick workaround: set tokenizer.pad_token = "<pad>" and tokenizer.add_bos = False before batching. I'll open a tiny patch.

thomas: Runtime notes: current KV cache implementation for onboarding expects per-layer serialization (we call it "layer-sharded-fp16"). The runtime stores K and V per layer, contiguous, dtype=fp16. Important for memory calc: for this architecture (32 layers, hidden 4096, 32 heads => head_dim 128) you get ~16KB per layer per token (k+v), so ~512KB per token total across layers. That means: 1 sequence of 8192 tokens => ~4GB KV alone (batch=1). If you bump batch>1 multiply accordingly.

anya: that's super helpful. So for A100-40GB we need headroom for model params (~5.3GB), optimizer/extra (~1GB for profiling), KV (~4GB) — leaves ~29GB free but fragmentation and other buffers matter. Realistically expect OOM if we try batch>2 at 8192.

mike: Good catch. Options: reduce max_context for hosted canary (set to 4096), enable KV sharding across GPUs (requires dedicated nodes), or auto-evict prefix cache for very long sequences. Which is preferred for onboarding?

thomas: For canary, simplest: set max_context to 4096 and confirm tokenizer fixes. If customer needs 8192 we should run on dedicated nodes with KV sharding; runtime flag is `--kv-shard=auto` (requires at least 2 GPUs to be effective). Also can enable `--reserve-mem=0.2` to keep headroom.

anya: I'll update model config in the onboarding repo to `max_position_embeddings: 4096` for the initial canary and open a follow-up to exercise 8192 on dedicated. Pinging @devex for docs update.

devex-bot: PR hint: opened draft PR #3492 to document tokenizer workaround + config recommendations.

sara: Small patch note (snippet):
```python
# onboarding tokenizer fix
tokenizer.pad_token = "<pad>"
tokenizer.special_tokens_map = {"bos_token": "<s>", "eos_token": "</s>", "pad_token": "<pad>"}
# ensure we don't double-add BOS during batching
tokenizer.add_bos = False
```

mike: Also double-check model config key names: runtime validates `max_position_embeddings`, `num_hidden_layers`, `hidden_size`, `num_attention_heads`, and `kv_cache_format`. If kv_cache_format missing it'll default to `layer-sharded-fp16`.

anya: I'll push the config change and run a canary with batch=1 seq=4096 on staging. Will report back with memory profile logs.

thomas: When you run the canary, grab `/metrics/runtime/mem/alloc` and `/traces/kv/cache_size` — that'll give a clear headroom number. If you still see >70% mem on A100-40 we should opt for 4096 prod limit.

anya: Got it. ETA: I'll run canary this afternoon and post results. Thanks all. :pray:

title: Satellite Grove
author: Jordan Reyes
text:
Lead source: self-serve signup (product-led). Team: CTO (Aisha Kaur), Eng Lead (Mateo Lopez), PM (Rina Shah). Early discovery call 2026-03-02 via Fireflies ff-20260302-0934. Summary: building an in-app conversational assistant for their B2B workflow SaaS; must feel instant (streaming responses) and run on public cloud.

Key requirements:
- Streaming websocket support + chunked tokens (UX requires UI tokens arrive in <50ms increments).
- p50 target ~40-80ms, p95 <120ms, p99 <200ms for short responses (avg 60 tokens).
- Concurrent active users at launch ~100-200, expected steady-state 20-50.
- Cost-sensitive: want guidance on batching vs streaming tradeoffs and token/unit price impact.
- Model preferences: prefer smaller fast open models for latency (we mentioned quantized Llama-family / Mistral-lite), but open to Redwood verified models for throughput.
- Security: SOC2 on roadmap, need SSO (SAML) + audit logging for partner beta.

POC/workflow discussed:
- They used free credits to wire up a quick websocket chat to Redwood hosted API. Observed good tail latencies but worried about unit cost when scaling. Did a smoke test with ~50 concurrent short chats (avg reply length 60 tokens) — saw 120ms median, 250ms p99 in one run.
- Interested in Redwood Optimize suggestions (batching hints, prefix caching) to reduce cost without hurting streaming UX.

Quotes / call notes (shorthand):
- "Streaming must feel instant — if agents lag, users drop off." — Aisha (CTO).
- "We need a clear cost model for streaming usage; tickets are tight for first 6 months." — Mateo (Eng Lead).

Timeline & activities: see activity_timeline field for discrete items.

Risk / next-stage signals: if we can show a predictable cost/latency plan and a simple SSO flow, they'll move to a 3-month paid pilot and open a dedicated usage seat in April.

title: Develop interactive tone derivatives and Kappa elevation scale for data grids
author: Ava Martinez
text:
Objective: Create a deterministic system for producing interactive color derivatives (hover/focus/pressed/disabled) from the base semantic palette and introduce a physics-inspired elevation scale ("Kappa") tuned for dense data surfaces such as DataGrid, compact tables, and inline action bars.

Scope:
- Define algorithmic transforms to derive interactive tones from semantic base tokens (primary, neutral, success, caution, critical). The transforms must preserve WCAG contrast for actionable states and offer predictable deltas for designers and engineers.
- Introduce a Kappa elevation token family (kappa-0..kappa-6) with mapped umbra/penumbra/ambient values and matching colorized overlays for dark/light themes optimized for high-density rows.
- Propose spacing/radius adjustments for compact rows to align with new elevation cues while retaining hit-target accessibility.
- Update Figma token library and token spec (CSS vars + JSON token artifacts) and provide migration guidance for DataGrid, Table, Button, and InlineAction components.

Goals & Acceptance criteria:
1) Token spec: produce a stable token spec file (design JSON) that includes base palette, interactive derivatives (e.g., color.interactive.primary.hover), and elevation.kappa.{0..6} with explicit shadow parameters.
2) Implementation-ready: frontend repo receives a tokens PR implementing variables; DataGrid and Table components consume new tokens behind a feature flag.
3) Accessibility: automated contrast checks pass for all interactive states against 3:1 where applicable and 4.5:1 for primary actionable text.
4) Visual regression: add per-component visual snapshots and tolerances; no regressions beyond approved deltas.
5) Figma: updated design kit with tokenized components and guidance notes.
6) Rollout plan: canary on internal analytics dashboards -> staged rollout -> full migration with a fallback.

Design notes and trade-offs:
- Algorithmic derivation reduces token sprawl (fewer manual swatches) but requires deterministic tuning. We will prefer per-hue perceptual adjustments (Lab-space tweaks) over fixed lightness deltas to avoid color shifts across hues.
- Kappa elevation prioritizes subtle penumbra for dense rows; larger elevations are intentionally muted to avoid visual clutter. This might reduce perceived separation in extreme cases; provide an override token for high-contrast surfaces.
- Implementation should use runtime CSS variables for quick theming and a build-time compiled fallback for older clients. There are performance trade-offs when shipping many tokens; we will group tokens under semantic prefixes to keep runtime size manageable.

Migration plan:
1) Finalize tokens in design JSON and Figma (this ticket).
2) Engineered tokens PR (feature-flagged).
3) Update DataGrid/Table to read tokens; create opt-in toggle for compact Kappa mode.
4) Run automated visual diffs and accessibility scans.
5) QA and UAT with PM/Analytics team, then canary-release on internal dashboards for 2 weeks before full rollout.

Links and artifacts: see attachments.

2026-03-02 - Ava Martinez: Created initial spec draft and seeded Figma file 'kappa-elevation-explorations'. Requesting engineering feasibility review for CSS variable strategy.
2026-03-05 - Jun Park: Engineering review notes: prefer CSS custom properties with a compiled JSON fallback. Concern about runtime token count; propose grouping under --r-token-* and lazy-loading theme bundles.
2026-03-08 - Alex Chen (Accessibility): Ran preliminary contrast tests on automatic derivation heuristics. Primary hover needed minor adjustment to meet 4.5:1 on 14px text; suggested increasing delta on low-chroma primaries.
2026-03-10 - Design critique: Decided to implement derivation in Lab space and expose a per-hue microdelta table for edge-case tuning. Agreed on kappa range 0..6 where 0 = flat and 6 = modest lift for modal headers only.
2026-03-12 - Jun Park: Frontend spike completed. Implemented a prototype token loader and a DataGrid feature flag that toggles compact-kappa mode. Performance impact negligible in dev build; need production smoke test.
2026-03-14 - PM review (Riya Patel): Approved rollout plan pending a short canary run. Asked to add telemetry for token usage and a regression alert to detect visual drift > 6% pixel change.
2026-03-15 - Next steps: finish Figma kit annotations, author tokens PR, add visual snapshots for DataGrid/Table, schedule canary for 2026-03-22.
Follow-up tasks: Create engineering ticket to add a 'kappa-override' opt-out for high-contrast themes; capture benchmark metrics after canary.
Note: Keep a migration branch and rollback playbook in case third-party dashboards rely on previous elevation semantics.

title: Role resolution fails after Okta group id type change; ModelObservability API returns 403 for newly provisioned users
text:
Summary: Since 2026-03-09 ~03:00 UTC a subset of newly provisioned users are getting 403 when calling the ModelObservability API. Initial triage shows users exist in OKTA and have expected groups, but the RBAC role lookup in auth-service fails because group identifiers in the incoming auth claim are integers instead of strings after a recent Okta mapping change. Impact: Affected SREs and ML engineers cannot access model observability dashboards or runbook actions; blocking incident response in us-east for customer-impacting alerts.

1) Create or modify an Okta user with group assignment via provisioning (SCIM).
2) Wait for scim-sync job to run (0-5m).
3) Login to console and call /v1/model-observability/metrics (or open dashboard).
4) Observe 403 and no role in auth-service logs for the user.
Expected: role lookup succeeds and 200 returned. Actual: 403 denied due to missing role mapping.

auth-service warning: role-lookup: claim.groups value types: [123456, 234567] (type: integer)
expected mapping key types: "123456"

example token claim (decoded): {
 "sub": "00u1abcXyZ",
 "email": "eng+test@redwood.ai",
 "groups": [123456, 234567],
 "iss": "https://okta.redwood.ai"
}

auth-service debug: mappedRoles=[] for user 00u1abcXyZ at 2026-03-10T03:12:07Z
model-observability-api access denied: headers: { x-rw-user: 00u1abcXyZ } response: 403 {
 "error": "unauthorized",
 "reason": "no-matching-role-for-groups"
}

Timeline: change window 2026-03-08 22:00 UTC when Okta admin updated group import mapping to emit numeric IDs (Okta API update). Hypothesis: identity-proxy and scim-sync historically normalized group ids to strings; the new mapping produced integers and our role index uses string keys -> lookup misses.
Findings:
- scim-sync stored groups in DB as strings when coming from canonical SCIM paths, but identity-proxy forwards token claims verbatim.
- auth-service role lookup code compares claim group IDs with role-index map (string keys). No type coercion.
- Reproduced locally by forging token with numeric group values; role lookup returns empty.
- Not all users affected: only those provisioned after Okta mapping change (group ids numeric). Older tokens remain as strings and continue to work.
Evidence: logs above and successful reproduction in staging by creating token with numeric groups.
Mitigation attempted: temporary canary: identity-proxy will coerce numeric claim.groups to strings on ingress; deployed to canary cluster (canary-2) 2026-03-11 18:30 UTC.

2026-03-10 04:05 - Priya Kapoor (Support): Reported initial customer-facing impact after SRE oncall noted missing access for 3 engineers. Attached sample decoded token and stack trace.
2026-03-10 06:12 - Diego Morales (Auth): Reproduced locally. Hypothesis: type mismatch between Okta claim payload and our role-index typing. Filed quick PR to normalize types in identity-proxy. Linking PR to this ticket.
2026-03-11 19:05 - Samir Patel (SRE): Canary deploy applied to canary-2. Observed two previously-401/403 requests now succeed. Monitoring for 24h to confirm no regressions.
2026-03-12 09:20 - Priya Kapoor (Support): Customer-facing note drafted: "We identified a token group id encoding mismatch caused by an Okta mapping update. A temporary fix has been deployed to canary and will be rolled to prod after validation. Apologize for the disruption."

Hotfix: identity-proxy change (PR #498) coerces all group ids in the token claim to strings on ingress and emits a metric for any non-string group values. Auth-service change (PR #1257) added defensive coercion for role lookup as backup. Canary results: successful requests for previously affected users on canary-2. Rollout plan: staged rollout to prod us-east 2026-03-12 15:00 UTC with monitoring and immediate rollback on elevated error rates. Root cause: Okta mapping change that started emitting numeric group ids; our code assumed string typed ids.

1) Add schema validation on identity-proxy (block incoming tokens with unexpected types and alert).
2) Create automated unit test in auth-service for claim type coercion.
3) Ask IAM team to revert or document Okta mapping change and add approver workflow for mapping modifications.
4) Postmortem to be authored in Confluence and linked here after incident closure.
Assigned to: Diego Morales (follow-up engineering items) and Priya Kapoor (postmortem coordination).

title: Clarify provisional license reclaim window and equipment-return grace period for immediate offboarding
text:
Issue summary:
HR received reports from Finance and IT that when an employee is placed on Immediate Termination (ITerm) in Workday, the seat/license in third-party SaaS (notably the design/legal tool vendor) remains billable for up to 14 days and the assigned corporate laptop sometimes remains tagged as 'active' in our asset management inventory. This ticket seeks clarification of the intended policy (grace windows) and the operational mechanics (which systems enforce the reclaim/return windows).

Impact:
- Potential short-term double-billing for SaaS seats when seats are quickly re-assigned.
- Delays in device recovery leading to inventory inaccuracies and security exposure for high-risk departures.
- Confusion between HR, IT, and Finance on expected timelines and required manual steps.

Environment:
- Identity sync: Okta -> SCIM -> downstream SaaS (prod)
- Asset tracking: FleetOps (prod) with inventory sync to ITSM
- HR system: Workday (prod)

Observed behavior / Steps to reproduce:
1) Create an employee termination in Workday with 'Immediate' flag at 09:00 UTC.
2) Workday emits termination event, HR webhook updates Okta.
3) Okta SCIM provisioning sends deactivation to SaaS vendor; we observe the user status change but vendor maintains seat as billable for a 14-day grace window (vendor policy).
4) FleetOps does not mark the laptop as 'awaiting pickup' until an asset-handback task is created manually by IT; automatic tagging is not triggered by the termination event.
5) Finance reports a new invoice line for an additional seat 3 days later after license reassign because the old seat was not reclaimed yet.

Logs / evidence: 
- Okta SCIM audit (okta-audit-2026-03-09.log) shows deactivation event at 09:02 UTC and response 200 from vendor with response body: {"status":"deprovision-scheduled","grace_days":14}.
- FleetOps event stream shows no asset lifecycle change tied to the Workday termination event (fleetops-events-2026-03-09.ndjson).
- Finance ticket FIN-1189 referencing unexpected seat charge for week of 2026-03-02.

Question / Requested clarification:
- What are the company-wide defaults for SaaS license reclaim windows and how many days are considered 'standard' vs 'exception' requiring manual immediate reclaim?
- For Immediate Terminations, do we have an established exception/accelerated flow that forces vendor-side seat revocation and device pickup tagging?
- Which teams are expected to take manual actions vs which actions should be automated by identity/asset tooling?

Desired outcome:
- A concise policy statement HR/IT/Finance can rely on for immediate-term offboards, including: default reclaim window, criteria for accelerating reclaim, and the single authoritative runbook link for immediate offboards.

2026-03-10 11:10 — Marco Ruiz (IT): Noted. In our logs the SCIM response includes vendor-side grace window. We don't currently override vendor windows. IT can manually request offboarding escalation with vendor support but that requires a ticket and often 24–48h processing.
2026-03-10 12:02 — Priya Shah (HR): Can we make 'Immediate' terminations trigger a one-click 'accelerate reclaim' in the HR portal? That would reduce churn between teams.
2026-03-11 09:47 — Ethan Park (Identity): Hypothesis: Okta sets user to 'suspended' and vendor interprets that as soft-deactivate and applies a vendor-side grace window. We can attempt to send a 'hard-delete' SCIM call for critical departures but need legal approval and vendor API support confirmation.
2026-03-11 13:15 — Jana Müller (Finance): Current invoices show an average of 2.3 days of overlap per reassign. Shortening reclaim window will materially affect monthly spend forecasts. Please include Finance in policy decisions.
2026-03-12 08:03 — Support Bot (automated): Linked CONFLUENCE: License Reclaim Policy draft updated (v0.4) — https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/HR/pages/License+Reclaim+Policy

Okta->SCIM behavior: The connector implementation uses PATCH to set 'active' to false. Vendor accepts this and sets an internal grace policy (14 days) rather than immediate seat relinquish.
FleetOps integration: Asset lifecycle changes are only triggered by ITSM ticket creation at present; there is no webhook or SCIM-driven asset tagging for device pickup. This is a gap for immediate offboards.
Workday mapping: 'Immediate' termination is mapped to Okta attribute 'terminationType=immediate' but that attribute is not propagated to downstream SCIM calls currently; therefore downstream vendors cannot differentiate Immediate vs standard terminations.
Hypothesis: If Okta emitted a 'terminationType' custom attribute or we used a 'hard-delete' SCIM call on certain vendors, seats could be reclaimed faster, but vendor policies and contracts may prohibit forced immediate deletion (data retention concerns).

Tentative operational plan agreed on 2026-03-12:
1) Policy clarification: Default reclaim window remains vendor-determined; for 'Immediate' terminations, HR + IT will follow an accelerated flow.
2) Automation tasks: Identity team to add terminationType flag propagation to SCIM (Ethan Park) and to implement a 'hard-delete' option gated behind a documented approval step.
3) Asset tagging: FleetOps to listen for Workday/Okta terminationType events and auto-tag devices as 'awaiting-security-pickup' (IT will still approve pickup).
4) Finance: will be looped into the vendor contract review to identify vendors that support immediate seat removal vs those with mandatory grace windows.
5) Runbook: Create a concise 'Immediate Offboard' runbook in Confluence with decision tree and contact channel (#it-offboarding).
Follow-ups (action items): [INT-821408] implement SCIM terminationType propagation; [INT-821409] FleetOps webhook for immediate offboard tagging; legal to review vendor TOS for forced seat deletion.
Notes: Until automation is in place, manual vendor escalation is the workaround for high-risk departures. This ticket should remain open until the SCIM flag propagation PR (INT-821408) is merged and FleetOps webhook (INT-821409) is live.

raw_metadata.summary: Clarify provisional license reclaim window and equipment-return grace period for immediate offboarding

title: deferred-aggregation-telemetry-lattice-and-path-sampling
author: Jordan Park
text:
Motivation: reduce alert noise and per-request cost attribution overhead for long-tail token spikes by introducing a 'telemetry lattice' for low-cardinality cross-layer linkage and a deferred aggregation path to compact frequent short-lived series. This PR implements a sample-first path-sampling strategy that preserves token-level latency/cost fidelity for high-value routes while preventing cardinality explosion for low-volume routes.

What changed (summary): added a lightweight trace-linking propagator (rw.telemetry.lattice) to stitch gateway request paths to runtime spans, implemented a deferred aggregator that batches metric writes at host-local level and flushes on configurable windows to the central TSDB, introduced sampled token-cost histograms by request_path, and added a new dashboard + tuned alert rules. Also includes an e2e synthetic spike test and rollout flags for staged canary.

Key design notes: telemetry lattice uses a stable 64-bit path-hash encoded in trace baggage and a short-lived sample ID for high-fidelity attribution when sample==true. Deferred aggregation reduces immediate Prometheus series churn by aggregating micro-bursts into a small set of summarized buckets before export. Path-sampling policy: always-sample for routes with route.metadata.telemetry.priority == high, probabilistic sample (1%) for medium, and adaptive sample for low (rate-limited with burst tokens).

Implementation highlights: 1) observability/metrics: token_latency_by_path (histogram_v2) and token_cost_sampled(counter with labels: path_hash,sample_id), host-local deferred_aggregator that coalesces writes, 2) tracing: propagator/propagator.go adds baggage entry "rw-tele-lattice", runtime side attaches sampled token_cost meta to the trace when present, 3) dashboards: dashboards/request-telemetry-lattice.json shows sampled vs aggregated cost and series-count impact, 4) alerts: alerts/adaptive-slo-rules.yaml replaces a static threshold for token-burn with an adaptive baseline keyed on historical p95/p99 for the route and a minimum absolute floor to avoid missing hard regressions.

Testing and rollout: unit tests added for aggregator flush logic and propagator encoding, e2e test telemetry_spike_test.go simulates synthetic bursts across 50 routes and validates series count reduction and attribution signal retention. Feature gated behind config flag telemetry.lattice.enabled and rollout guideline: 10% canary -> 50% -> all, monitor series_count and alert_firing_rate.

Backwards compatibility: non-sampled requests carry only the path_hash which is low-cardinality; no downstream schema changes required for existing dashboards.

Notes to reviewers: focus on cardinality and exporter performance, confirm that the sampling rates/flags are adequate, and validate the adaptive alert thresholds won't hide emergent regressions.

Related: ENG-4092 (alert noise reduction), ENG-4178 (token-cost attribution), minor docs update to explain operator flags.

Aisha Kapoor: Concerned about cardinality for 'path_hash' + dynamic labels; please ensure path_hash is scoped to a service and truncated consistently.
Jordan Park: Reply: path_hash is 64-bit stable hash of normalized path template and we scope exporter labels to 'service' so series = service:path_hash only. added normalization tests.
Dmitri Petrov: The deferred aggregator flush interval looks safe but we should ensure worst-case memory bounds under sustained bursts.
Jordan Park: Reply: added circuit-breaker to aggregator that forces flush and drops to summarized bucket if memory exceeds threshold; documented in telemetry-lattice.md.
Marisol Chen: Please validate that adaptive alert won't mask regressive p99 spikes where absolute latency increases but relative baseline remains similar.
Jordan Park: Reply: adaptive alert includes an absolute floor (configurable) to ensure hard regressions are still surfaced; added test covering regression scenario.

Introduce telemetry lattice for low-cardinality path linkage, sampled token-cost histograms, deferred aggregation to reduce TSDB series churn, and adaptive SLO alerting. Feature gated and rolled out by canary.

Observed prometheus series reduction ~18% in canary run and alert firing rate reduced by ~42% on noisy low-volume endpoints. Operators should monitor exporter_queue_size and aggregator_memory.

title: Remediation SLA options + customer tier mapping (Hosted / Dedicated / Private) — working doc
author: Rachel Kim
text:
Doc purpose (Product Ops)
========================
We need a consistent set of internal remediation SLAs (time-to-mitigate / time-to-fix expectations) that:
- match what we can realistically execute across tiers (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)
- align with customer expectations and enterprise commitments (especially Dedicated/Private)
- can be implemented in tooling (ENG-4829 / SLA timers + breach alerts) without constant exceptions
- remains low-cardinality and understandable during live incidents

This is a working evaluation doc of options; final policy will live in Confluence in the Remediation SLA matrix.

Definitions
===========
- Remediation SLAs in this doc are internal operational targets and escalation triggers.
- We track two clocks:
 1) TTM (time-to-mitigate): time from incident declared (Sev assigned) to customer-impact mitigation in place (or credible workaround). Mitigation may include rollback, routing/fallback changes, traffic shaping, or isolating a bad region/model.
 2) TTF (time-to-fix): time from incident declared to a durable fix deployed OR a signed-off plan with committed ship date (depending on severity). For Sev0/Sev1, we typically expect a durable fix, not just a plan.

- “Tier” definitions:
 - Hosted: multi-tenant public API.
 - Dedicated: reserved capacity; stronger expectations for predictability and comms.
 - Private: VPC/on-prem control plane + data plane; sometimes customer-controlled networking and change windows.

- Severity (draft; matches on-call practice):
 - Sev0: broad outage / severe customer impact / safety risk / inability to serve core requests at scale.
 - Sev1: major degradation (e.g., high 5xx, severe latency) affecting meaningful customer set or a major enterprise customer; urgent.
 - Sev2: partial degradation; workarounds exist; limited scope.
 - Sev3: minor; limited impact; typically handled in normal on-call flow.

Decision principles
===================
1) Make the SLA actionable during incidents (what it forces us to do: staff, escalate, decide).
2) Keep differences by tier minimal, but acknowledge Dedicated/Private have different reality (capacity isolation, maintenance windows, customer networking).
3) Avoid a matrix so complex that incident-bot can’t enforce it.
4) “Pause/override” exists but must be auditable and rare.

Where tier differences are real (observations)
============================================
Hosted
- We control infra + routing + runtime deploys; can mitigate quickly via routing policies, throttles, or rollbacks.
- Customers accept “platform-wide” incidents but expect fast mitigation.

Dedicated
- Stronger expectations: named account pressure, high-touch comms, fewer acceptable repeated incidents.
- Mitigation sometimes means reallocating fleet capacity; can be constrained by GPU availability.
- Some mitigations require coordination with specific customer traffic patterns and agreed “degradation mode.”

Private
- Customer networking, DNS/TLS, firewalls, and change windows can dominate.
- “Mitigation” may require customer action; we can provide fix/instructions but can’t always execute.
- On-prem/air-gapped environments may block fast patching.

Key question: Do we set stricter SLAs for Dedicated/Private because customers pay more, or do we set realistic SLAs acknowledging dependencies and shift strictness into comms/escalation?

Option set
==========
Option A — Single SLA matrix (same targets across tiers) + comms escalation tiers
Pros: simple; consistent; easy to implement + dashboard.
Cons: risks being unrealistic for Private; breaches become noisy; forces frequent overrides.

Option B — Tier-adjusted TTF only (TTM consistent, TTF differs)
Pros: keeps the “stop the bleeding” behavior consistent; reflects reality that durable fixes take longer when customers control deploy windows.
Cons: still may be tight for certain Private classes; requires tier in SLA evaluator.

Option C — Tier-adjusted TTM and TTF (Dedicated stricter on TTM; Private looser on TTF)
Pros: matches customer expectation: Dedicated should be mitigated extremely fast; Private fixes can take longer.
Cons: more complex; risk of perceived unfairness (“why does private get longer?”).

Option D — Incident-type-aware SLA within severity (e.g., Private connectivity vs Control plane vs Runtime regression)
Pros: most accurate.
Cons: too complex for v1; high maintenance; taxonomy drift.

Recommendation (draft): Option B for v1
======================================
- Keep TTM targets consistent by severity across tiers (behavior we want in every incident: mitigate quickly).
- Allow tier-adjusted TTF targets (Private often needs customer maintenance window; Dedicated should still be fast but not necessarily faster than Hosted in all cases).
- In addition, define comms/escalation requirements by tier (Dedicated/Private proactive outreach thresholds), separate from remediation timers.

Proposed draft SLA targets (v1 candidate)
========================================
Notes:
- Times are proposed internal targets for breach alerting + leadership escalation.
- TTM measured to: restored SLO or reduced to acceptable degradation mode (documented).
- TTF measured to: fix deployed OR (Sev2/Sev3 only) fix scheduled with owner + date.

TTM (same across tiers)
-----------------------
Sev0: 30 minutes
Sev1: 2 hours
Sev2: 1 business day
Sev3: 5 business days (or next planned release train)

TTF (tier-adjusted)
-------------------
Hosted:
- Sev0: 24 hours
- Sev1: 3 business days
- Sev2: 10 business days
- Sev3: 30 business days

Dedicated:
- Sev0: 24 hours (same as Hosted; expectation is mitigation is faster, fix can be similar)
- Sev1: 5 business days (slightly longer than Hosted because some fixes involve fleet reshaping or customer-specific config review)
- Sev2: 15 business days
- Sev3: 30 business days

Private:
- Sev0: 48 hours (some fixes require customer coordination/change window; still want high urgency)
- Sev1: 10 business days
- Sev2: 20 business days
- Sev3: 45 business days

Rationale snapshots (to validate)
================================
- Private Sev0 TTF at 48h is the most controversial number. The intent is: if a Private incident is Sev0, we should be able to ship a fix quickly OR provide a validated workaround package quickly. But we may not be able to deploy it into the customer’s environment inside 48h. Proposed compromise: define “TTF = fix available” vs “TTF = deployed” for Private only.

Proposed adjustment for Private only:
- For Private tier: treat TTF as “fix available + customer delivery completed (artifact + instructions + support handoff)” rather than “fully deployed in customer environment.” Deployment tracking becomes a CS/Support deliverable.

This avoids constant SLA breaches from customer-controlled schedules, while still forcing Redwood to produce the fix quickly.

Edge cases + carve-outs (must be explicit)
=========================================
1) Cloud provider / upstream outage
- If root cause is confirmed upstream (AWS/GCP region/network, managed KMS outage, etc.):
 - TTM still applies (we should mitigate via failover/fallback where possible).
 - TTF may be waived or converted to “post-incident hardening actions” with due dates.
- Implementation requirement: incident-bot must allow “Upstream dependency” as a contributing factor and a “SLA exception reason” (audited).

2) Customer-caused or customer-controlled failures (mostly Private, occasionally Dedicated)
Examples:
- Customer rotated certs incorrectly; firewall blocks new endpoints; DNS misconfig; customer refuses recommended upgrade.
- TTM definition may be “workaround identified + communicated + support engaged.”
- TTF becomes a tracked action plan with customer owner and Redwood owner; SLA breach should not trigger paging.
- Implementation requirement: a controlled “Customer action required” exception reason.

3) Planned maintenance / change windows
- If incident is triggered by a planned change performed by Redwood:
 - SLAs still apply (we own it).
- If fix requires customer change window:
 - Private: allow “Fix available” measurement as above.

4) Multi-cause incidents
- Primary incident_type determines SLA class.
- Contributing systems recorded separately; do not create multiple SLA clocks.
- If reclassified, SLA clock should not reset (only severity changes reset behavior).

Comms and escalation requirements (separate from remediation timers)
===================================================================
We should not bake comms into remediation SLAs, but we do need consistent obligations by tier.

Draft comms rules (for CS alignment; see comms templates doc):
- Hosted
 - Sev0/Sev1: status page + initial update within 30 min; updates at least every 60 min until mitigated.
 - Sev2: case-by-case; internal update; status page optional.

- Dedicated
 - Sev0/Sev1: proactive outreach to affected accounts; initial customer-facing update within 30 min; updates every 60 min.
 - Sev2: proactive outreach within 1 business day if single account materially impacted.

- Private
 - Sev0/Sev1: proactive outreach; include “customer action required” assessment early.
 - Emphasize safe language: symptoms, mitigations, next update time.

Open issues / questions to resolve before signoff
=================================================
1) Private TTF definition: “available” vs “deployed”
- Need decision from SRE + Product Private (Vivek) + CS.

2) Dedicated Sev1 TTF: 3 vs 5 business days
- Dedicated product (Lauren) asked for realism: some changes require capacity rebalancing + canary.
- Counterpoint: enterprise expectation is faster. Maybe keep 3 BD but allow exceptions for capacity procurement work.

3) Severity-to-tier mapping clarity
- Can a Private incident be Sev0 if it affects only one customer? Yes, if it blocks core use case and is high urgency.
- Need crisp language in the incident process policy so on-call doesn’t under-severity enterprise incidents.

4) Implementation feasibility in tooling (ENG-4829)
- SLA evaluator needs tier + severity + type.
- Ensure we don’t create a combinatorial matrix. Proposed v1: severity x tier only, with optional overrides.

5) Reporting expectations
- Aisha to confirm dashboards will report:
 - SLA breach rate by tier, severity, incident_type
 - Exception counts by reason (upstream, customer-action, force majeure)

Data sanity check (informal)
============================
Based on last 2 quarters anecdotal review (see top-incidents analysis):
- Most Sev0/Sev1 mitigations happen within 15–90 minutes for Hosted when the mitigation is routing/rollback.
- Dedicated mitigations vary: quick when routing-only; slow when capacity constrained.
- Private “fix deployed” often exceeds 1–2 weeks due to customer windows; “fix available” is typically within a few days if we prioritize.

Action items (next steps)
=========================
- Rachel: circulate this doc to Rafael, Nikhil, Lauren, Vivek, Dev for comments (by 2026-02-07)
- Rafael/SRE: confirm if “TTF = plan w/ ship date” is acceptable for Sev2/Sev3 (Hosted/Dedicated) (by 2026-02-10)
- Vivek + CS: propose Private TTF measurement definition language for Confluence (by 2026-02-10)
- Lauren: confirm Dedicated Sev1 TTF target (3 vs 5 BD) and list top constraints (capacity procurement, release trains) (by 2026-02-12)
- Aisha: verify dashboards can label tier correctly and track exceptions without high cardinality (by 2026-02-12)

Appendix: quick matrix (for copy/paste)
======================================
TTM (all tiers):
- Sev0: 30m
- Sev1: 2h
- Sev2: 1 BD
- Sev3: 5 BD

TTF:
- Hosted: Sev0 24h | Sev1 3 BD | Sev2 10 BD | Sev3 30 BD
- Dedicated:Sev0 24h | Sev1 5 BD | Sev2 15 BD | Sev3 30 BD
- Private: Sev0 48h | Sev1 10 BD| Sev2 20 BD | Sev3 45 BD

Appendix: proposed SLA exception reasons (allowlist)
===================================================
- Upstream dependency confirmed (cloud/provider)
- Customer action required (customer-controlled environment)
- Force majeure (rare; requires Director+ approval)
- Mis-severity (initial severity incorrect; adjust and document)

(End)

title: Actionable incident cards + cost-aware rollout controls for private clusters
author: Ariana Cho
text:
Design a compact, action-first incident card and an integrated rollout control surface for Private/VPC clusters that surfaces estimated cost impact, recommended rollback or model-variant actions, and one-click mitigations. The aim is to reduce time-to-mitigation for tenant-facing degradations while making cost trade-offs explicit to SREs and platform teams.

1) Incident cards appear in the Private Cluster 'Status' panel and show: incident title, severity, affected tenants, brief root-cause hints, and an estimated incremental cost delta (last 24h vs baseline).
2) Each card exposes primary actions: Add to Canary, Pause Rollout, Trigger Fallback Variant, Open Debug Shell (link), and Mark Investigating. Actions must include confirmation flows where destructive.
3) Rollout controls allow cost-aware canaries: step size, max cost delta per step, automated pause-on-cost-threshold.
4) Prototype validated in user testing with at least 5 SRE/platform engineers and 3 PM customers; task completion time for 'pause rollout and rollback' reduced by 40% vs current flow.
5) All links in cards resolve to existing tools: GitHub PRs, runbooks (Confluence), logs (Grafana/Loki), and the cluster-trace view.

- Use compact 3-line summary layout for cards to avoid vertical noise in the Status page.
- Cost metric uses internal 'delta-cost' calc from Optimize team (est. USD/hour) and shows color-coded delta: neutral (<1%), warning (1-5%), critical (>5%).
- Primary actions are contextual: if a rollout is active, show Pause/Abort; if model variant fallback exists, surface it with a confidence score.
- Add a small 'why this costs more' tooltip that lists contributors (batch size, fallback model, increased QPS).
- Mobile and tablet: collapse extra details behind a chevron; primary action must remain single-tap.
- Accessibility: each card must be navigable by keyboard, with ARIA labels for actions.

1) Show estimated cost delta with two decimals and currency symbol (USD).
2) Implement color rules for delta bands as described above.
3) Action 'Trigger Fallback Variant' will call the existing runtime API implemented by ENG-2201; design will include a confirmation modal with rollback preview.
4) We will not surface raw billing numbers for multi-currency customers in this phase—only normalized USD deltas.
5) Rollout 'auto-pause on cost' default is OFF; turned on via cluster policy (PM decision).

- Surface financial signals too aggressively and we risk alert fatigue; too conservatively and teams miss cost regressions. We chose explicit deltas with thresholds to balance noise.
- Exposing cost numbers in the incident flow requires careful permissions; initial rollout restricts detailed cost drilldown to users with billing view permissions (de-scoped for current prototype).
- One-click mitigations accelerate fixes but increase risk of human error; mitigated via confirmation modals and brief runbook links.

title: Burst capacity: commit allocation, surge tiers and economic example
author: markus_klein
text:
From: Sam Jenkins <sam.jenkins@acme.com>
To: Markus Klein <markus.klein@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 30 Jul 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Dedicated - burst add-on structure and billing mechanics

Markus,

Thanks for the demo earlier. A couple of follow-ups from our infra and finance teams: we need clarity on three things before we can scope a PO —

1) How burst capacity is allocated across our GPU pools. If we reserve 10 GPUs as dedicated commit, and buy a burst add-on, does burst apply pool-wide or per-pool?
2) How cooldowns and surge rates are applied/charged. We often have 10–15 minute spikes; want to understand the billing for short spike events vs sustained bursts.
3) Example economics for a typical 2-week product launch: if baseline sustained traffic is 200k tokens/day and expected peak traffic is 1M tokens/day for 4 hours/day for 7 days, what does the committed + burst cost look like?

Procurement also asked about any floor/commit conversions for unused burst credits. Can you send a simple worked example and the latest pricing matrix?

—Sam
Sam Jenkins
Head of AI Infrastructure | Acme Corp

From: Markus Klein <markus.klein@redwood.com>
To: Sam Jenkins <sam.jenkins@acme.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: Fri, 31 Jul 2026 14:08:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Dedicated - burst add-on structure and billing mechanics

Sam —

Thanks for the clear list. I've attached the burst-pricing-matrix.csv and a worked-example workbook; forwarding a short runbook below so you can share with procurement. Quick answers up front:

- Allocation model: burst inventory is scoped to the Dedicated deployment, not a single GPU. That means any GPU pool (within the same dedicated instance) can draw from the burst bucket until it's exhausted. We partition at the pool level only when multiple dedicated instances exist.
- Cooldowns: the default cooldown window is 15 minutes after a surge event; subsequent surges within that window draw from the same event and are billed at the surge rate. You can request a longer cooldown (e.g., 30m) in the contract.
- Surge rates: we charge surge usage at a multiplier on top of the committed per-token rate; default multipliers are 1.35x (tier 1), 1.75x (tier 2) based on severity/guarantee.

I'm looping in Ben from Solutions so he can sketch the GPU sizing and put numbers against your launch profile.

Next steps: Ben will send a calculation and a short proposal. If procurement needs a line-item for committed-to-burst conversion (unused burst credits converting to month-of-dedicated credit), we can include that as an optional contract clause.

Best,
Markus Klein
Account Executive | Redwood Inference

From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
To: Sam Jenkins <sam.jenkins@acme.com>
Cc: Markus Klein <markus.klein@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: Sun, 02 Aug 2026 10:35:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Dedicated - burst add-on structure and billing mechanics

Sam — hi, Ben here. I put together the quick calculation and a sizing note (see inline). Attachment: ReservedCommit_ExampleCalc.xlsx

Short technical summary:
- Baseline commit: assume you reserve 10x A100-equivalent GPUs (dedicated pool) sized to deliver ~300 concurrent generation streams with 2s p95.
- Burst bucket: we sell burst as a token bucket (X tokens = Y token-hours at the committed performance profile). Burst is global across the Dedicated instance and will be consumed by any worker serving your deployment.
- Cooldown semantics: 15m (default). If you exceed the burst threshold, the system counts that as a single surge event; additional surges within 15m are treated as the same event and billed to the same surge bucket.

Worked example (numbers simplified):
- Baseline committed cost (monthly): $120k for 10 GPUs (reserved commit).
- Committed per-token rate: $0.0006/token at sustained baseline.
- Burst add-on: purchase 2M token-burst credits/month = $900 (effectively $0.00045/token if consumed).
- Surge multiplier: if you exceed burst credits, traffic is billed at 1.75x committed per-token rate until we throttle or spin additional on-demand capacity.

Two-week launch scenario (your numbers):
- Baseline usage for 14 days: 200k tokens/day * 14 = 2.8M tokens
- Peak extra usage: 4 hours/day at (1M - 200k) = 800k extra tokens/day * 7 days = 5.6M tokens
- If you buy 2M burst credits, remaining 3.6M peak tokens will be billed at surge multiplier.
- Additional cost: burst credits $900 + surge overage ~ 3.6M * ($0.0006 * 1.75) = ~$3,780 -> total extra ~ $4,680 over the period.

Notes & levers:
- If you increase burst credits to 5M/month, the example shows peak covered and avoids large surge overage.
- We can offer a committed-burst conversion: any unused burst credits at quarter-end may be converted to a credit against next-month dedicated usage at a 70% conversion rate. This is contract-level and negotiable.

I'll attach the CSV with tier examples and also propose a tiered burst-pricing:
- Tier A (pilot): 0–2M tokens @ $900/month
- Tier B (growth): 2M–10M tokens @ $0.00042/token
- Tier C (enterprise): 10M+ tokens with volume discounts and SLA-backed surge caps.

Happy to jump on a short call to walk procurement through the line items.

—Ben
Ben Carter
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

From: Sam Jenkins <sam.jenkins@acme.com>
To: Markus Klein <markus.klein@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
Cc: procurement@acme.com
Date: Tue, 03 Aug 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Dedicated - burst add-on structure and billing mechanics

Thanks Ben — useful. A couple of procurement asks: 

1) Can you give us a firm cap option? Finance prefers a hard spike cap (e.g., no more than 1.3x billed for any surge beyond burst credits) rather than an open multiplier. If that means Redwood will throttle at a defined threshold, that's acceptable, we just need cost predictability.
2) For the committed-burst conversion: can you move the conversion to 85% for unused burst credits if we sign a 12-month commit? That gives us flexibility.
3) Any room for a 10–15% discount on the surge multiplier (move 1.75x -> 1.6x) if we agree to a 12-month $1.1M committed spend?

If you can send a short update to the term sheet with those options, procurement can move quickly.

—Sam

1) Spike cap option: we will offer an Opt-In "Spike Cap" where Redwood enforces throttling beyond the defined burst+cap threshold. The billing multiplier beyond burst will be capped at 1.3x if Spike Cap is enabled. (This is operationally a throttling + cap combination.)

2) Conversion rate on unused burst credits: for a 12-month committed contract of $1.1M, we can increase unused-burst credit conversion to 85% (applies quarterly).

3) Surge multiplier discount: for the 12-month $1.1M commit we can reduce the default surge multiplier from 1.75x to 1.6x. In exchange we'll require a 45-day notice period for any material region failover and a 90-day minimum commitment window for reserved GPUs.

Additionally, commercial concessions:

title: Investigate & fix rate-policy jitter that starves tenant capacity during regional failovers
author: Maya Chen
text:
Several customers (hosted + dedicated + private) escalated sustained 429/503 errors during a regional failover window. Initial triage shows that the rate-limiter's burst evaluation enters a transient jitter state when epoch anchors between proxy, orchestrator, and host-level rate controllers disagree. This leads to aggressive admission drops for a subset of tenants (capacity starvation) rather than graceful fallback. The goal of this ticket is to identify the root cause, implement a safe reconciliation path, and ship mitigations + tests to prevent recurrence.

Multiple enterprise customers observed multi-minute spikes of 429 and some downstream 503s during scheduled failover and autoscaler activity. Customer requests were effectively throttled beyond configured quota; billing and SLAs were impacted for two Dedicated customers and one Private deployment. Pager escalations and CS tickets received during outage window.

1) Simulate region failover by toggling route priorities in staging multi-region env
2) Run sustained high-concurrency generator at 60% above target per-tenant sustained rate
3) Force orchestrator restart and proxy rolling restart to create misaligned epoch anchors
4) Observe per-tenant admission drops and token-pool drain events in orchestrator logs
5) Check metrics: tenant_admission_rejected, burst_claim_mismatch, quota_epoch_skew

2026-03-02: On-call (Luis) validated customer traces and correlated spike with a control-plane failover that overlapped proxy rolling restart.
2026-03-03: Reproduced in staging. Found a 200-800ms window where orchestrator computed burst credits using previous-epoch metadata while proxy used a freshly persisted marker; mismatch caused double-counting and premature eviction of tenant tickets.
2026-03-04: Heap of evidence shows race in policy evaluator: policy cache refresh is async and not versioned atomically with token epoch transitions.
2026-03-06: Confirmed that Private deployments using slower KMS and commit-confirmation had longer window of misalignment.
2026-03-08: Small hotfix deployed on hosted to introduce 250ms guard window; reduced severity but did not resolve root cause.
2026-03-10: Added additional logging and correlation IDs across proxy->orchestrator->host rate controllers to capture exact decision timelines.

Race between epoch transitions and policy cache refresh. When a region failover or orchestrator restart occurs, different components evaluate burst policies against inconsistent epoch anchors. The evaluator treats missing/old anchors as 'no-burst' and aggressively evicts inflight capacity rather than deferring or reconciling, resulting in tenant capacity starvation.

1) Rollout guard-window (250-500ms) at proxy and orchestrator to ignore epoch flips for immediate decisions (deployed to hosted; pending dedicated/private rollout),
2) Enable diagnostic sampling for affected tenants to capture full decision traces for postmortem
3) Communicate to CS about temporary throttle behavior and mitigation timeline

A) Implement atomic epoched policy reads: annotate policy cache entries with epoch_id and ensure any admission decision reads a consistent epoch across proxy+orchestrator+host
B) Add idempotent burst-claim reconciliation: when epoch mismatch is detected, reconcile by computing conservative merged credit (min of claims) and schedule background rebalancing instead of immediate eviction
C) Introduce a degraded-mode path that favors availability for previously healthy tenants (soft-degrade) during control-plane transitions
D) Add cross-component integration tests and chaos test that exercises orchestrator/proxy restarts with high-concurrency workloads

Unit + integration tests that validate epoch-aligned policy reads
Chaos test in staging that shows no more than 5% extra rejections for affected tenants during simulated failover
Metric reductions: burst_claim_mismatch rate decreases by 95% in staging failover runs
Documentation updated for Dedicated + Private deployment runbooks
Release notes and customer communication prepared for runtime-2.4

1) Create tiny persistence field epoch_id on policy cache entries and plumb through RPCs (ENG-158240 will track RPC changes)
2) Implement conservative reconciliation algorithm in orchestrator admission path (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/7852)
3) Expand guard-window to 500ms with feature flag, roll out to dedicated and private with staged canaries
4) Add end-to-end tests in policy-e2e harness; run against chaos monkey
5) Post-deploy telemetry check and 24h on-call monitoring window

2026-03-03 — Maya Chen: Customer call summarized impact; asked for hotfix + timeline. Luis assigned to lead investigation.
2026-03-04 — Luis Alvarez: Reproduced in staging; opening follow-up tickets for RPC and cache versioning.
2026-03-08 — Priya Nair (SRE): Deployed 250ms guard-window on hosted; saw immediate reduction in customer escalations. Need rollout checklist for Dedicated.
2026-03-10 — Kane Patel (Security): Verified no sensitive telemetry left in logs; ok for Private customers after redaction.
2026-03-12 — Luis Alvarez: Draft PR ready, running policy-e2e locally. Planning canary deploy next Tuesday.

title: dynamic per-channel requant + KV-aware jitter-resilient continuous-batching
author: Leah Park
text:
Background and motivation: Production workloads show variance in per-channel activation distributions across prompts and token positions which makes static requant scales suboptimal. We observed systematic p99 latency spikes when the runtime switched between hot and cold KV cache footprints under continuous-batching; these were exacerbated by small batching jitter when multiple streams aligned. This PR implements a dynamic per-channel requant stage combined with a KV-cache-aware scheduling hint and a jitter-resilient continuous-batching policy to smooth throughput while keeping low tail latency. Scope: 1) A lightweight per-channel scale estimator that runs on the microkernel hot path and updates requant multipliers at configurable amortization windows. 2) A cheap, lock-free KV cache sizing hint that the scheduler uses to avoid abrupt prefix evictions during batch coalescing. 3) A jitter-resilient continuous-batcher that introduces minimal, adaptive hold windows to align requests from high-variance sources without increasing median latency. 4) Microkernel changes to expose a fused transform that applies requant multipliers inline with dequant/attn input packing to eliminate an extra copy. Design highlights and tradeoffs: - Estimator runs every N tokens (configurable per model) and uses exponential moving moments to remain stable across bursts. The goal is to reduce per-token compute overhead to <0.5% while adapting scales within 5-10k tokens. - Scheduler hint is advisory: it tags requests with estimated KV working set delta. The placement layer still enforces hard SLOs; the hint avoids placing requests that would cause a working-set jump on the same GPU within a short window. - Batcher employs an adaptive jitter budget: it only delays the head of a queue by up to X ms if the expected throughput improvement outweighs the added latency; X decays if p99 latency rises. Benchmarks (representative): - OPT-13B, INT8 hybrid (smoothquant + per-channel dynamic re-quant): throughput +10.8% on steady-state mixed sized prompts, median latency +2% (due to micro-batching alignment), p99 latency -14% on tail-heavy traces. - Llama-2-7B FP8 fallback: end-to-end token cost reduced by ~7% due to fewer KV evictions and reduced memory copies. - End-to-end e2e test with 500 simulated concurrent streams: observed 8-12% lower GPU-side memcpy time and 6-9% better sustained throughput. Implementation notes: - Runtime changes: src/runtime/quant/dyn_requant.h/cpp, src/runtime/quant/microkernel_requant.s, src/runtime/scheduler/kv_hint_scheduler.cpp - Batcher: src/runtime/batching/jitter_batcher.cpp, with a new config block in configs/batching.yaml - Tests: tests/quant/test_dyn_requant.cc (unit), bench/latency/bench_kv_jitter.py (integration traces) - Docs: docs/perf/quantization.md updated with configuration knobs and suggested Linear tasks for tuning. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for estimator accuracy and stability - [x] Integration benchmark harness with trace replay - [x] Backwards-compatibility: dynamic requant disabled by default; opt-in via runtime config - [x] Release notes draft included - [x] SRE smoke test run on dedicated cluster and passed Notes on safety and compatibility: This change touches kernel hot-paths; dynamic scaling is guarded behind a runtime flag and tuned conservatively out-of-the-box to avoid regression. We included an automatic rollback condition in the scheduler when p99 exceeds baseline by 20% during an experiment. Related work: ENG-2048 (per-channel requant research spike), PR #612345 (microkernel packing refactor) for reference. Next steps: 1) A follow-up PR to expose an admin dashboard for per-model scale drift metrics and recommended amortization windows. 2) Experiment with a learned estimator offline and compare to the EMA-based estimator used here.

Mateo: Can you explain why the EMA window is better than a sliding histogram here?
Leah: EMA keeps the hot path cheap and is resilient to heavy tails; we add a debug mode to collect histograms offline and compare. Added test to validate estimator vs small histogram sample.
Rohit: Assembly changes look good but please add comment on register usage for AArch64.
Leah: Added comments and fallback macro for older toolchains.
Ava: Any risk of oscillation when multiple concurrent streams adapt scales?
Leah: We added cross-request dampening and a per-GPU dampening register to avoid opposite-direction flips. Also added a safety rollback in the scheduler if oscillation detected.

Introduces an opt-in dynamic per-channel requant estimator and a KV-aware jitter-resilient batching policy that together improve steady-state throughput and reduce tail latency for quantized models. Disabled by default; opt-in via runtime config. See docs/perf/quantization.md for tuning guidance.

title: Edge Runner Adapter — lifecycle & API sketch
author: Lina Gomez
text:
Context:
This is a personal scratch for an 'Edge Runner Adapter' that sits on customer/partner edge nodes (VMs or k8s DaemonSet) and mediates between the local inference runtime and Redwood control plane. Goal is a minimal, resilient handshake + lightweight config model that supports KV caching, local batching hints, safe fallbacks to hosted models, and compact telemetry.

Design goals:
- Small binary/API surface — easy to audit for airgapped installs.
- Declarative config (YAML) that control-plane can push; local overrides allowed.
- Explicit lifecycle states to reason about rollouts, drain, and emergency fallback.
- Telemetry with PII-safe sampling + local aggregation.
- Pluggable auth (edge API key, mTLS, short-lived signed tokens).

High-level flow (quick):
1) Runner boots, loads local config; probes hardware, runtime (nvml info, available CUDA, quant libs).
2) Attempt control-plane registration: /v1/edge/register (POST). If offline, keep exponential backoff and write persistent pending queue.
3) Control plane returns assigned tenant(s), model policy, batching hints, kv_cache_policy.
4) Runner starts serving local requests via local unix socket or http. It also opens heartbeat: /v1/edge/heartbeat (PATCH) every 30s (interval configurable).
5) On capacity pressure or model mismatch, Runner consults local fallback policy and may redirect inbound requests to hosted endpoint, or stream partial tokens then fallback.

API sketch (plaintext examples):
- Registration request (HTTP POST /v1/edge/register):
{
 "instance_id": "edge-az1-88f7",
 "host_info": {"cpu_count": 16, "gpus": ["A100:80GB"]},
 "capabilities": ["kv_cache", "quant-int8", "streaming"],
 "config_hash": "sha256:..."
}

- Registration response:
{
 "status": "accepted",
 "tenant_id": "t-acme-corp",
 "policy": {
 "models_allowed": ["redwood-opt-13b-quant"],
 "fallback": {"type": "hosted", "endpoint": "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/hosted/proxy"},
 "kv_cache_policy": "per-tenant",
 "batching": {"target_ms": 8, "max_tokens": 512}
 }
}

- Heartbeat (PATCH /v1/edge/heartbeat) payload summary:
{
 "instance_id": "edge-az1-88f7",
 "uptime_sec": 234123,
 "cpu_pct": 12.3,
 "gpu_mem_free_mb": 64000,
 "active_sessions": 12
}

Config sketch (YAML style — runner reads local + merge from control plane):
---
runner:
 instance_id: "auto" # uuid if not provided
 listen: "/run/edge-runner.sock"
 auth:
 method: "mtls" # options: mtls | api_key | signed_token
 telemetry:
 sample_rate: 0.01
 aggregate_window_sec: 60
 fallback:
 allow_hosted_fallback: true
 hosted_endpoint: "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/hosted/proxy"
 kv_cache:
 mode: "per-tenant" # per-tenant | shared | disabled
 max_size_mb: 2048
 batching:
 target_ms: 5
 max_batch_tokens: 1024
 prewarm: true

Lifecycle states (local finite-state machine):
- INIT: boot, verify dependencies.
- REGISTERING: attempting control-plane join.
- ACTIVE: serving local traffic.
- DRAINING: stop accepting new sessions, finish existing ones.
- DEGRADED: critical resources missing; still serving limited ops or redirected to hosted.
- RETIRED: shutdown by operator.

Transitions: INIT -> REGISTERING -> ACTIVE. From ACTIVE -> DRAINING (operator or rollout). DRAINING -> RETIRED. Any state -> DEGRADED on resource failure; DEGRADED -> ACTIVE after heal.

Local API for host apps (unix socket or loopback api):
- POST /v1/local/dispatch : body {session_id, prompt, model_hint, prefer_local: bool} -> returns stream url or immediate error.
- GET /v1/local/session/:id/status -> session resource state and node affinity (useful for reconnect).
- POST /v1/local/kv/claim -> reserve a kv cache prefix for session (returns lease token + ttl).

Telemetry events (compact examples):
- event_type: request_complete | request_started | fallback_triggered | cache_miss
- payload fields: ts, instance_id, tenant_id, model, latency_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, reason (for fallback)
Notes: always hash any user-identifying id before sending. Keep default sample_rate low (0.01). Aggregate counts locally per-window to reduce cardinality.

KV cache lease model (notes):
- Claim API issues short leases (30s-5min) for session-specific prefix. Runner enforces eviction LRU per-tenant. Control plane can push larger persistence policies for durable caches.
- Lease token is signed by control-plane; runner validates signature locally. This keeps runner stateless about global ownership.

Edge cases and fragility:
- Network partition during rolling update: new runner may register duplicate instance_id — require idempotent registration by full instance fingerprint (machine-id + cert serial).
- Disk pressure: if /var/cache fills, evict kv cache, mark DEGRADED and send urgent heartbeat.
- Model binary mismatch: control-plane policy should include allowed hashes; runner refuses to load models not in whitelist.

Security note:
- Prefer mTLS between runner and control-plane for on-prem. For airgapped installs, allow signed manifests delivered out-of-band (USB) and then runner applies manifest in offline mode. Need small code path to validate signatures and reject malformed manifests.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should policies be merged per-tenant or per-instance? (Prefer per-tenant but allow instance overrides).
- How to surface expensive GPU temp spikes to control-plane without leaking machine identifiers? Anonymized bucketing?
- Local SDK: expose a tiny Go client that uses unix socket; should we support direct Python gRPC? (Go first, then shim).
- Canary rollout: config_push should support label selectors (k8s nodes, instance metadata) and simultaneous canary signals from metrics.
- Rate-limiting enforcement split: local enforcement + control-plane quotas. Need reconciler to avoid double-throttling.

Next tiny steps (me):
- Create minimal HTTP server prototype (Go) that implements register, heartbeat, local dispatch, and fake kv claim.
- Add simple local YAML merge logic and snapshot on disk with hash.
- Wire up heartbeat to simulate DEGRADED->ACTIVE transition in e2e.
- Draft a short ADR for tenancy model (per-tenant vs per-instance cache).

Notes-to-self: keep message sizes tiny, avoid sending prompts in telemetry, when in doubt log locally and only surface aggregate numbers. If we need to rework fallback behaviour later, keep decisions pluggable (policy module).

End of scratch.

title: Compact workspace chips + contextual micro-rail: progressive IA and routing prototype for Console
author: Lena Hartmann
text:
Design a compact, high-density workspace switcher and a contextual micro-rail to surface route-level controls (dashboards, rollouts, cost views) without overwhelming the left rail. Prototype interaction patterns for keyboard-first flows, progressive disclosure, and clear routing semantics for deep links and shared links.

Current Console left rail is large and uses full workspace tiles which causes vertical churn for teams with many workspaces. Teams frequently need to pivot between dashboards, rollout controls, and per-model cost views; those pivots are buried in nested nav or require a separate search flow. Previous sidebar explorations favored a full-width reframe; this ticket explores a compact chip-based switcher paired with a lightweight contextual rail (micro-rail) that appears inline when a route has tool-level controls.

Reduce vertical space used by workspace switcher by at least 40% on typical 1080p screens
Provide single-click access to route-level tooling: dashboards, rollouts, cost breakdowns
Preserve deep-link stability: shareable URLs must open to the same route and micro-rail state where applicable
Support keyboard navigation and screen-reader semantics for accessibility
Surface quick cost pivots (last-24h / last-30d) without leaving current route

Must use existing left-rail width constraints for 3 responsive breakpoints
Micro-rail must not require a full page reload; should be client-side rendered and route-aware
No changes to existing backend routing schema — only client-side routing and query params allowed
Design must account for both hosted and dedicated tenants where workspace names can be long

Adopt a compact workspace chip (avatar + truncated name + chevron) with overflow menu for full list
Introduce contextual micro-rail: a second-level horizontal rail that slides out from under the primary nav when route metadata indicates available tooling
Encode micro-rail state in URL query param `?micro=tool:rollout` to maintain shareability
Keyboard nav: Tab focuses chips, Enter opens chip; pressing 'M' toggles micro-rail for focused route
Progressive disclosure: show only the most-used route tools by default, with a 'More' menu exposing full toolset

Prototype demonstrates workspace chip layout and overflow behavior (desktop + tablet)
Micro-rail opens and closes without full route reload; query param persists across refresh
Accessibility: micro-rail items have ARIA roles and keyboard focus order validated in prototype
Usability test (5 participants) shows <10s median time to switch workspace + open rollout control
Design handed off to ENG with component spec and responsive tokens, plus example GH ticket for implementation

PM (Diego Morales): prefers query-param approach to preserve GA tracking for rollouts
Eng lead (Maya Sullivan): requests micro-rail initial render to be lazy-loaded to avoid bundle bloat
Security (Jon Park): flagged that micro-rail must not expose controls if the user lacks permission; needs server-side guard
Product Ops (Ravi Patel): likes the cost quick-pivots but asked for a lightweight sparkline in the chip hover state

Run 5 moderated usability tests with platform engineers and PMs (scheduled week of 2026-03-15)
Incorporate feedback and produce Handoff package (components, tokens, interaction spec)
Draft GH implementation epic and break into engineering tickets: responsive, routing, RBAC
Schedule a design review with Security and Accessibility to finalize ARIA patterns

title: introduce-kernel-stability-thresholds-and-precision-annealing-with-kv-sync-guard
author: Maya Chen
text:
Motivation: We observed intermittent correctness regressions and KV-cache divergence when nodes opportunistically switched to lower-precision kernels under load. These issues were most pronounced during warm-up phases and when continuous-batching mixed short warm-up sequences with steady-state traffic. The goal of this PR is to make the low-precision fast path reliable in production by adding conservative checks and an automatic, observable annealing mechanism that trades small amounts of peak throughput for deterministic correctness.

Summary of changes: add a light-weight per-node kernel stability probe that runs microbenchmarks on model startup and periodically during low-utilization windows; expose a configurable 'kernel_stability_threshold' that gates transitions to low-precision kernels; implement a precision-annealing state machine that steps precision down gradually (fp32 -> fp16 -> int8) only when stability and latency criteria are met; add a kv-sync-guard which attaches short-lived checksums to KV cache snapshots and prevents applying a cache state if checksum mismatch or stale-timestamp detected; update continuous-batching heuristics to avoid batching sequences observed during the warm-up probe and to prefer homogeneous-decoded sequences to reduce cache churn.

Configuration and defaults: default kernel_stability_threshold=0.92 (fraction of microbench runs that must pass), anneal_step_interval=30s, min_stable_window=2m. Operators can override in runtime config or via console per-cluster. Canary rollout automatically enables annealing on 10% of nodes by default.

Design notes: stability probe is intentionally lightweight (per-model token-limited runs) and runs on a background worker with a low scheduling priority. We capture simple metrics: decode latency variance, kernel success/failure, and checksum of produced KV updates. The precision-annealing state machine records a rollback count and will automatically revert to the last-known-good precision if a regression is detected for two consecutive evaluation windows. KV-sync-guard uses a small 64-bit checksum and timestamp to detect divergent updates; it prevents a stale or corrupt cache from being applied and triggers a re-fetch path that is more conservative (sequential KV application with verification).

Performance and correctness: measured on internal perf-lab with a mix of 1k short-chat and 200 long-generation traces: baseline (optimistic fp16 fastpath without probes) showed +12.3% token/sec vs safe fp32 but a 2.8% rare correctness/regression signal on our eval set and occasional KV-invalidation incidents during canary. With this PR enabled (default canary), we observe +9.1% token/sec, p95 token latency improved by 6ms relative to safe fp32, and correctness regressions dropped to 0.12% (within noise). CPU/GPU telemetry indicates a ~7% reduction in wasted kernel restarts during warm-up.

Commits (summary):
- feat(kernel): add kernel stability probe, probe scheduler, and probe metrics (maya/commit/1)
- feat(anneal): implement precision-annealing state machine and runtime flags (maya/commit/2)
- fix(kv): implement kv-sync-guard with checksum verification and fallback path (alex/commit/3)
- perf(scheduler): adjust continuous-batching heuristic to avoid warm-up mixing (noah/commit/4)
- test(perf): new perf harness scenarios and canary harness (sofia/commit/5)
- docs: ops notes and runtime configuration docs (maya/commit/6)

Files touched (high level):
- src/runtime/kernel_probe.cpp (new)
- src/runtime/kernel_selector.cpp (modify)
- src/runtime/precision_annealer.cpp (new)
- src/cache/kv_manager.rs (modify)
- src/scheduler/batcher.rs (modify)
- tests/perf/annealing_scenarios.py (new)
- ops/docs/fastpath-ops.md (new)
- scripts/canary_rollout.py (modify)

Testing: unit tests added for state machine transitions and kv-sync checksum logic; integration canary runs in perf-lab for 48h; additional chaos test where random kernel failure is injected to validate rollback behavior. CI initially failed on a flaky kv-manager apply test (race in test harness); I fixed the test harness timing and re-ran. Final CI: all checks passed (build, unit, integration-smoke, perf-canary sim).

Review conversation (high level):
- Andre Patel: "This looks promising — my main concern is metric noise causing oscillation. Can we add hysteresis?"
- Maya Chen: "Added rollback_count and min_stable_window config to prevent oscillation; updated tests to exercise noisy conditions."
- Sofia Lopez: "KV checksum is a good safety net. Can we make checksum optional for extremely latency-sensitive clusters?"
- Maya Chen: "Yes — checksum can be disabled per-cluster; documented tradeoffs in ops doc and console UI will show expected risk increase."
- Noah Kim: "Please ensure the annealer doesn't increase tail latency under multimodal traffic."
- Maya Chen: "Batcher heuristic update ensures warm-up sequences are isolated, avoiding mixed-batch tail effects; added perf tests that mimic multimodal traffic."
- Andre Patel: approved after minor doc nits.
- Sofia Lopez: approved.

CI and canary: initial canary run on 10% nodes for 72h showed stability; we increased to 30% and then full rollout. Post-rollout monitoring showed one transient kv-stall on a highly loaded node which was auto-rolled back by annealing and later resolved by a kernel patch (follow-up PR scheduled).

Backward compatibility and migration: all flags default to conservative values; clusters not opting into canary see no behavior change. Ops doc includes a migration checklist to enable annealing and KV checksum on dedicated clusters.

Follow-ups:
- ENG-2493: extend probe to multi-model ensembles (planned)
- SRE-619: dashboard and alerting on kernel stability score
- Hotfix PR planned to backport small kv-sync optimization to 2026.02 release branch if customers request earlier rollout.

Merge: squashed and merged to main on 2026-02-18 after approvals and green CI.

Notes for maintainers: keep an eye on SLO dashboards for the first 2 weeks after rollout; if automated rollback rates exceed 0.5% consider increasing min_stable_window or disabling annealing during peak traffic windows.

Adds kernel stability probes, a precision-annealing state machine, and a kv-sync guard to reduce correctness regressions when switching to low-precision fast paths; safe defaults and canary rollout enabled.

title: Office edge bridge in NAT mode rewriting source IPs and causing VPN policy routing failures and SSO timeouts
text:
Issue summary: After a recent office CAB change at the SoMa satellite office we started seeing a sustained increase in VPN session failures and SSO timeouts for users on the office Wi‑Fi. Impact: ~12-18% of users at SoMa experience intermittent 403/SSO timeouts or are unable to reach internal services that normally resolve via VPN private IPs. Service impact is localized to the office LAN and affects employees using company Wi‑Fi and a subset of developer services behind policy-based routing. Initial hypothesis: an intermediate bridge/AP that was re-provisioned to 'NAT' mode is rewriting source addresses causing VPN policy lookup to fail, triggering mis-routed traffic and SSO token validation errors.

1) Connect a laptop to SoMa corporate Wi‑Fi (ssid: Redwood-Corp).
2) Establish Redwood VPN (WireGuard client) and authenticate via SSO (Okta).
3) Attempt to curl an internal service at 10.11.20.5: expect success; observed: connection resets or 403 responses.
4) Observe device local IP (e.g., 192.168.50.34) and the outbound NATed IP as seen by internal services (packets show 10.100.200.1 source after NAT rewrite).

Clients on office Wi‑Fi see internal service requests fail intermittently. Packet captures from service frontends show source IPs mapped to 10.100.200.0/24 (bridge appliance SNAT pool) instead of clients' VPN-assigned 10.8.0.0/16 addresses. Okta SSO validation rejects token assertions when source IP does not match expected corporate ranges, causing auth flows to fail.

Traffic from VPN clients should preserve VPN-assigned source addresses. Office bridge should be in passthrough mode for tunneled traffic so policy-based routing at the gateway can correctly match flows and SSO sees expected IP ranges.

2026-03-10T09:22:13Z firewall[gw-usw-1]: policy_lookup: src=10.8.12.45 dst=10.11.20.5 matched=internal-web-cluster action=allow
2026-03-10T09:22:13Z app-fw[web-01]: tcpdump: in.ether src=10.100.200.14:52344 > 10.11.20.5:443 SYN
2026-03-10T09:23:01Z okta-proxy[auth-01]: token_validation: ip_mismatch user=jared@example.com expected_range=10.8.0.0/16 seen_ip=10.100.200.14

- Confirmed bridge device model: Ubiquiti UBB‑Edge v2 (serial: UB-1212). Reprovisioning on 2026-03-09 set its WAN mode to 'Gateway (NAT)' instead of 'Bridge'.
- tcpdump on web-01 shows multiple connections with SNATed sources 10.100.200.0/24. When testing from a home client via remote VPN this does not occur; home clients preserve 10.8.x source addresses.
- ip rule list on gw-usw-1 shows policy routing keyed on src network 10.8.0.0/16. Because SNAT rewrote source to 10.100.200.x the kernel falls back to default route and packets get dropped or mis-routed to edge ACLs.
- Quick check: ssh to bridge admin UI -> Network -> NAT Mode = Enabled. CLI 'iptables -t nat -L -n' shows POSTROUTING MASQUERADE for bridge LAN range.
- Hypothesis validated by temporary change: disabled NAT on bridge -> source IPs preserved -> internal service connectivity restored and SSO token validations succeed.

pcap snippet (web-01): 10.100.200.14.52344 > 10.11.20.5.443 Flags [S] seq 0 win 64240
pcap snippet (after fix): 10.8.12.45.52344 > 10.11.20.5.443 Flags [S] seq 0 win 64240

On affected office bridge, re-enable 'passthrough/bridge' mode or add a NAT-exemption rule for VPN-assigned subnets (10.8.0.0/16). As an immediate mitigation, network ops applied a bridge-level configuration that disables MASQUERADE for src 10.8.0.0/16 which restored service for all connected clients.

Temporary mitigation applied on 2026-03-11: NAT exemption rule added to bridge and config pinned. Next steps: schedule coordinated firmware fix and update CAB provisioning template to ensure edge bridges are provisioned in 'bridge' mode for corporate VLANs that host VPN clients. Postmortem to be created and template change rolled out to 5 remote offices.

2026-03-10 10:45 - Aisha Patel: Initial report from SoMa floor lead: multiple devs reporting 403s when accessing internal dashboards while on company Wi‑Fi. Filed ticket and added SRE on-call.
2026-03-10 11:05 - SRE Oncall (Riley Morgan): Did quick checks, observed SNATed sources on web frontends. Asking networking to verify bridge provisioning state and recent CAB changes.
2026-03-10 13:12 - Networking (Diego Alvarez): Confirmed bridge was reprovisioned yesterday as part of patch window; default image set WAN mode to Gateway/NAT. Preparing rollback of NAT change and plan for NAT-exempt rule for 10.8.0.0/16.
2026-03-11 08:30 - Liam Chen: Applied NAT-exemption rule on bridge (ubnt cli: iptables -t nat -D POSTROUTING -s 10.8.0.0/16 -j MASQUERADE). Verified tcpdump shows 10.8.x src to internal services and Okta validations succeed. Monitoring for 24h.
2026-03-12 09:05 - Product Ops (Nora Singh): Noted impact on engineers collaborating in SoMa. Requested postmortem and an automated check in provisioning pipeline to prevent future NAT mode flips.
2026-03-12 12:15 - Liam Chen: Created PR to office-configs to pin bridge mode and added validation unit test in provisioning flow (see linked PR). Scheduling CAB to apply template to 5 sites next week.
