title: SSE stream cuts final whitespace and punctuation after HTTP/2 priority preemption behind customer's edge proxy
text:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that SSE streams delivered to their web clients occasionally arrive with the final characters (trailing whitespace and punctuation) missing. The content is syntactically complete but the last sentence sometimes loses a trailing space or final period, which breaks downstream client-side heuristics that expect a newline/terminator.

Impact:
- Affects BrightDocs' production readers in us-east (enterprise account).
- Visible as malformed final paragraphs in ~0.2% of long streaming responses for a subset of sessions; higher during bursts.
- Customer considers this a data-integrity issue for document export pipelines and flagged it as high priority.

Environment:
- Customer located behind an enterprise edge proxy that uses HTTP/2 with priority and stream preemption enabled.
- Requests from browser -> edge proxy (h2) -> Redwood API Gateway (h1/h2) -> serving runtime.
- Observed on models: gpt-large-v2, redwood-compat-1.0.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Client opens SSE connection to /v1/stream with long completion (>512 tokens) over HTTP/2 through their edge proxy.
2) Under simulated burst (20 concurrent streams from same client IP) the client sees the SSE session finish normally but the last token is missing trailing whitespace/punctuation in ~1/500 sessions.
3) Replaying the same request bypassing the edge proxy (direct to Redwood) does not reproduce.

Logs / evidence provided by customer (sanitized):
- Edge proxy debug: "PRIORITY_UPDATE stream=124 preempted-by=86" followed by "STREAM_HALF_CLOSED" at the same timestamp.
- Client observations: final SSE data event contained valid JSON but missing final space and ".".
- Server access log: upstream 200 OK and Content-Length reported matches payload; socket close shows short write on last segment.
- Customer captured wireshark/pcap that shows small 0-length data frame sequence around stream termination coincident with priority frames.

Requested outcome:
- Prevent loss of final characters so downstream tools consuming SSE do not get malformed last tokens.
- Understand whether this is a customer edge proxy bug, a compatibility issue with our gateway, or an intermediary interaction that needs mitigation in the platform.

2026-03-12 11:02 - Aisha Patel (Support): Acknowledged. Assigned to SRE for triage. Requested pcap and edge proxy config from customer. First response: asked for sample request id and timestamps.
2026-03-12 14:30 - Marco Ruiz (SRE): Initial triage — reproduced a very similar symptom in our internal lab by enabling HTTP/2 priority preemption on an nginx-based proxy and streaming a long response. Observed truncated final whitespace in ~1/1000 runs. Filed hypothesis that priority reordering can steal the final chunk if socket-level write coalescing occurs at the proxy boundary.
2026-03-12 16:05 - Marco Ruiz (SRE): Collected traces: linked span IDs to trace in observability: https://obs.redwood.ai/trace/abc123 (sensitive view). Upstream responded with full body and normal end-of-stream; the proxy sent a PRIORITY_UPDATE and then a half-close before flush completed.
2026-03-13 09:18 - Dev (Evan Chen): Reviewed reproduction notes. Hypothesis: our gateway writes final SSE delimiter as a very small write ("\n\n") and some HTTP/2 proxies with aggressive priority handling or write coalescing may drop trailing bytes when a stream is preempted or RST_STREAM races with end-of-stream. Proposed temporary mitigation: coalesce final delimiter into same buffer as last token to ensure single write syscall at gateway.
2026-03-13 11:46 - Marco Ruiz (SRE): Tested Dev's coalescing patch in staging (serving-runtime PR #1820). Results: no occurrences in 50k long-stream requests behind nginx-priority emulation. Pushed patch to canary for customer-specific route.
2026-03-14 08:05 - BrightDocs support contact (Helen Zhou): Confirmed that after canary route applied they no longer see trimmed final characters in the last 48 hours in their smoke tests. Planning to disable priority on their edge proxy as an extra precaution while platform mitigation rolls out cluster-wide.
2026-03-14 10:12 - Marco Ruiz (SRE): Next steps — schedule global rollout of coalescing fix, add observability metric to detect SSE-final-byte-loss (heuristic comparing last-token checksums), and create KB article recommending websocket fallback or proxy priority disable while using SSE for very long streams.
2026-03-14 12:00 - Evan Chen (Dev): Opened PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1820 (coalesce final SSE delimiter into last write) and added unit test covering http2-proxy preemption path.
2026-03-14 12:22 - Aisha Patel (Support): Customer notified of canary success and given recommended mitigations. Keeping ticket open until patch is rolled out and automated detection is in place.

Workaround applied: coalescing final SSE delimiter into last write (canary) + customer disabled HTTP/2 priority on their proxy. Temporary mitigation confirmed by customer. Long-term: global rollout of coalescing fix and add detection metric. Follow-up task INT-800901 created for rollout automation.

1) Customer disabled HTTP/2 priority on their edge proxy for routes to Redwood OR 2) Use websocket streaming fallback for sessions that must preserve trailing whitespace until the global fix is rolled out.

title: Span Beacon — Anchored Thread Navigator & Correlation Lens
author: Aisha Kaur
text:
Introduce an anchor-first drilldown workspace for request sessions: a lightweight, left-anchored 'Span Beacon' panel that pins a chosen span or correlation ID and surfaces related threads, sibling spans, and filtered timeline tracks. The goal is to let engineers and SREs maintain focus on a single causal anchor while exploring related requests, latency anomalies, and KV-cache hot-paths without losing context. This feature complements existing session search by enabling persistent anchors, quick comparisons across spans, and inline metric overlays (token counts, GPU time, retry counts).

MVP will support a single anchored span or correlation ID per workspace to reduce complexity.
Timeline will prioritize 'snap-to-anchor' + compare-overlay instead of full multi-anchor viewport for first release.
Lazy-load deep-span children with a server cursor; client will provide 'expand all' hint but not fetch by default.
Metric overlays (token count, model name, GPU-ms) are included as lightweight badges and optional toggles.
Expose a compact 'copy correlation ID' action in the anchor header for easy cross-tool navigation.
Hide any sensitive payload fields by default; show a redacted preview with an explicit 'reveal' action that logs access for audit.

2026-02-20 — Kickoff: scoped initial hypothesis and primary use-cases with PM and Eng (investigate slow tail, correlation drift, cross-model fallbacks). Decided to prioritize single-anchor UX over multi-anchor for MVP to reduce cognitive overhead.
2026-02-24 — Early sketches: two-pane layout (left anchor lane + right timeline canvas) tested internally. PM prefers compact anchor header that survives navigation; Eng flagged concerns around rendering large span trees at 200ms polling.
2026-02-28 — Prototype v0.1 created in Figma; added affordances: 'pin span', 'snap to child', correlation badge with copy-to-clipboard, and heat-strip for per-span latency. UX research session scheduled.
2026-03-03 — Usability feedback: developers appreciated anchor persistence and the compare-to-anchor overlay. Observability team asked for an optional toggle to show raw trace IDs and to integrate with current waterfall view.
2026-03-07 — Engineering review: recommended lazy-loading deep spans, virtualized span list, and server-side correlation indexing. Noted requirement for API changes (trace API: include parent pointer and KV-cache annotations).
2026-03-11 — Accessibility pass: ensured keyboard focus flows for anchor pin/unpin, aria-labels for timeline markers, and color-contrast adjustments for heat-strip.

PM (Diego Martinez) — strong alignment on SLO debugging flow; ask to add 'compare to baseline' toggle that overlays median latency for selected service.
Eng (Priya Shah) — prefer server-side pagination for sibling spans; flag: avoid client-side rehydration of massive KV caches.
Observability lead (Marcus Chen) — request ability to pin multiple correlation badges for cross-session stitching in future iterations.
Security (Olivia Park) — reminder to hide plaintext user tokens in span metadata and to surface KMS-protected fields with a lock icon; recommend a threat model review if we include payload snippets.

Finalize high-fidelity screens for anchor header and compare-overlay (owner: design, due 2026-03-14).
Eng to prototype server-side cursor and correlation index endpoints (owner: ENG, dependency ticket ENG-33450).
Add telemetry events spec for anchor interactions and compare toggles to instrumentation backlog (owner: Observability).
Run two 90-minute follow-up usability sessions with backend engineers and SREs to validate navigation and keyboard flows (scheduled 2026-03-16).
Prepare release notes blurb and in-app tour outline for rollout (owner: PM).

title: Modernize CI by replacing legacy bash pipelines with composite actions and plugin hooks
author: Asha Mehta
text:
Motivation: The monolithic bash pipelines under .github/workflows and scripts/legacy-ci.sh have become brittle and hard to iterate on across services. This PR modernizes the pipeline by introducing reusable GitHub composite actions, a plugin hook system for per-repo policy, and a small cross-platform ci-toolbox binary to compute robust cache keys and talk to the remote cache store. Scope: 1) Add .github/actions/checkout-composite, test-shard-composite, lint-runner-composite. 2) Replace repo-level shell orchestration with composite action calls and a dynamic matrix generator (tools/ci/matrix-gen.js). 3) Remove scripts/legacy-ci.sh and in-repo Docker-in-Docker usage; use buildah/kind where needed. 4) Add ci-toolbox (tools/ci-toolbox/main.go) used by composite actions for cache keying and fast retries. 5) Add .github/ci-config.yml with opt-in staged rollout flags for teams to adopt incrementally. Checklist: - [x] Add composite actions and document inputs/outputs - [x] Implement matrix generator and update matrix shapes - [x] Port lint/test usages to new composites - [x] Add ci-toolbox with basic cache key and remote fetch - [x] Add integration CI job that runs composites end-to-end on a canary subset - [x] Remove legacy script invocations and update README-ci.md Migration notes: The new composites are backward-compatible by default and live alongside legacy workflows during a 2-week canary. Owners can enable ci-config.yml flags to opt into new flows. Rollback is as simple as switching the workflow reference back to legacy scripts if an issue is detected. Risks and mitigations: Cache-key changes may cause cache misses on first runs; ci-toolbox includes a dry-run mode to preview keys. Matrix reshaping can increase pipeline concurrency; we added a default concurrency limit and a dynamic shard sizing heuristic. Future work: Add telemetry hooks to Redwood Console for per-route CI latency and cost, and introduce a GH App to enforce team opt-ins.

Diego Ramos: Nice move away from brittle bash. Please add a unit test for matrix-gen edge cases.
Asha Mehta: Added unit tests for empty-service-lists and large-shard heuristics in commit 4.
Maya Chen: We need an opt-out flag for repos that still depend on Docker-in-Docker; can you add an explicit allow-dind: true in ci-config.yml?
Asha Mehta: ci-config.yml now supports allow_dind and a canary_percentage. Default is false.
Evan Liu: CI runs flaked once on macOS runners in step 'install-tools' — reworked tool install order and pinned go:1.20 image in composite; reran and green.
Maya Chen: Approving pending green CI and docs update.
Diego Ramos: Approved. Squash-merge when ready.

Internal: Replace legacy bash CI with composable GitHub composite actions and a lightweight ci-toolbox binary. No user-facing behavior changes.

7 commits: initial composite action skeleton, matrix generator, ci-toolbox CLI and unit tests, workflows switched to composites for core services, removed legacy scripts, docs and README updates, pinned minimal action SHAs.

title: Field-level redaction mapping and legal-basis tagging for EU banking audit - evidence & export profile request
text:
Issue summary: Customer (EuroBank Holdings, enterprise) requests a signed evidence package and SIEM export profile that demonstrates per-field redaction decisions together with attached legal-basis tags (e.g., consent, contract, legitimate_interest) and consent timestamps for EU-region tenant activity. Impact: This is a compliance block for an upcoming regulator audit (scheduled 2026-03-20) — customer needs proof of how PII was redacted, which legal basis applied to each record, and a cryptographically signed manifest for delivered artifacts. Environment: prod, eu-west region, single-tenant on Redwood Dedicated. Request: 1) A sample export (CSV and Parquet) for a 7-day slice (2026-02-28 to 2026-03-06) showing pseudonymized identifiers and the redaction_reason field per event; 2) A mapping document describing the redaction rules applied (field name -> rule id -> redaction level); 3) Per-record legal_basis tags and consent timestamps where available; 4) Signed delivery manifest (SHA256) and an RFC3161 timestamp of manifest creation; 5) A short runbook describing how to reproduce the same export via the Console or API, including parameter names and recommended query filters.

Customer reproduction intent: query audit stream for tenant eurobank-prod between 2026-02-28T00:00:00Z and 2026-03-06T23:59:59Z with fields: event_id, timestamp, actor_id, resource_id, changes, redaction_reason, legal_basis, consent_timestamp.
Support suggested API call: GET /v1/audit/exports?tenant=eurobank-prod&start=2026-02-28T00:00:00Z&end=2026-03-06T23:59:59Z&format=parquet&redaction=include_metadata
If export fails: capture exporter logs and console export job id, share with Support for investigation.

Customer-provided sample (anonymized): event_id=evt_01ab, timestamp=2026-03-02T14:12:03Z, actor_id=usr_xxxxx, resource_id=doc_9a8b, redaction_reason=phone_mask, legal_basis=consent, consent_timestamp=2025-11-12T09:22:11Z
Support collector note: export job 2026-03-11T08:45:22Z -> job_id=exp-7890 returned 206 partial content (missing redaction_reason column)
Exporter debug: 2026-03-11T08:45:21Z INFO starting export slice tenant=eurobank-prod start=2026-02-28 end=2026-03-06 format=parquet include_meta=true
Redaction engine trace: 2026-03-11T08:45:25Z WARN rule_lookup_timeout for field 'consent_timestamp' fallback=empty

Aisha Patel (Customer Success) 2026-03-10: Received audit request from EuroBank compliance lead (Sofia Lind). They specifically require legal_basis per event and proof that consent timestamps are retained when present. Audit date is 2026-03-20, asking for deliverables by 2026-03-13.
Evelyn Chen (Support) 2026-03-10: Acknowledged. Started triage to verify export feature flags and whether redaction metadata is included by default. Investigating exporter job behaviour in eu-west cluster.
SRE on-call (Marcus Lee) 2026-03-11: Confirmed exporter runs in dedicated pool for eurobank-prod. Found recent rollout of redaction-engine v1.9.2 on 2026-03-09 — noting a change that can omit optional metadata fields when rule backend times out.
Evelyn Chen 2026-03-11: Requested permission to run a controlled re-export and provide a signed manifest. Proposed approach: create export snapshot, pseudonymize actor_id/resource_id with salted HMAC, include redaction_reason and legal_basis columns, sign manifest with platform signing key and attach RFC3161 timestamp. Asked customer to confirm acceptance of salted HMAC pseudonymization as proof artifact.
Sofia Lind (Customer) 2026-03-11: Confirmed salted HMAC pseudonymization is acceptable provided we include mapping of hashing salt fingerprint and that the legal_basis and consent_timestamp are present as separate columns. Also asked for a short statement of chain-of-custody for the delivered artifact.

Hypothesis 1: Recent redaction-engine update introduced a race condition with the rule backend (rules-service) leading to missing redaction_reason/legal_basis values when rule lookup exceeds 250ms timeout.
Hypothesis 2: Exporter configuration for dedicated tenants had include_meta defaulted to false for performance; need to verify tenant config override for eurobank-prod.
Checks performed: 1) Reviewed export job logs (job_id=exp-7890) and saw WARN for rule_lookup_timeout. 2) Checked tenant config: export.include_meta = false (inherited from global defaults) for eurobank-prod. 3) Validated rules-service latency spikes around 2026-03-09 due to cache miss after rollout.
Partial finding: When rules-service returns late, exporter records an empty value for redaction metadata instead of retrying or marking record for manual review. This explains missing column in customer sample export.

Planned immediate workaround: run a controlled replay export with exporter param include_meta=true and increased rule_lookup_timeout=1000ms for the requested 7-day slice; pseudonymize identifiers via HMAC-salt provided by Support; generate SHA256 manifest and request RFC3161 timestamp from our timestamping service.
Planned follow-up engineering fix: create a patch to make exporter tolerate rule lookup timeouts by queueing records for async metadata enrichment and include a manifest flag 'metadata_partial=false' to fail exports that would otherwise omit redaction metadata. Triage ticket created: INT-33421.
Deliverable timeline: Controlled export + signed manifest to customer by 2026-03-13. Engineering patch targeted for 2026-03-20 with rollout to prod-eu after validation.

title: Neon-orchestrated attention: hybrid Flash + kernel tiler with lazy-KV streaming
author: Evan Chen
text:
Summary: Introduces a neon-orchestrated hybrid attention path that combines a lightweight FlashAttention-style fast path with a tiled microkernel fallback. The patch adds a tiler that decides at runtime between (1) the optimized Flash micro-path for dense short sequences and (2) a new neon-prefetch tiled kernel for long contexts and odd sequence-lengths. Additionally this PR implements a lazy-KV streaming integration: instead of allocating/evicting large KV pages eagerly, the runtime streams KV slabs on demand and performs background prefetch with priority hints from the batcher. Motivation: our production traces show two dominant sources of per-token latency and cost: kernel selection overhead for mixed-length workloads and expensive full-KV swaps on long-context workloads. The hybrid path reduces kernel dispatch overhead and keeps the fast Flash path density benefits while the tiler maintains throughput on longer sequences. Design notes: - Kernel Tiler: a lightweight heuristic that computes tile sizes based on seq_len, k/v cache hits, and device utilization. Tiler exposes hints to the scheduler (tile_size, prefetch_priority, use_flash_path). - Flash micro-path: minimal changes to the existing Flash bridge to support neon-friendly memory layout and allow partial-row processing for non-4x head dims. - Neon tiled kernel: a new microkernel optimized for moderate tile sizes (32..256) with streaming prefetch and FP16 accumulation; includes an in-kernel rotary index remap to avoid extra memory passes. - Lazy-KV streaming: KV is broken into logically contiguous slabs. When a request needs a slab not present, we schedule an async prefetch and continue with partial KV (best-effort) to maintain tail latency. Background prefetching uses LRU+priority hints from the tiler. - Scheduler integration: continuous-batcher emits per-request hints (hot_token_prefix, expected_future_tokens) so the runtime favors coalescing requests that share KV slabs. - Fallback semantics: graceful fallback to the tiled kernel if flash_path fails or when the tiler estimates minimal benefit. Implementation touches: serving/runtime/tiler/* (core tiler & heuristics), serving/runtime/kvcache/streamer.* (lazy slab manager + prefetch worker), serving/runtime/kernels/neon_tiled_attn.* (new kernel), serving/runtime/kernels/flash_bridge adjustments, tests/perf/bench_attn_tiler.py, docs/attn_tiler.md. Testing & benchmarks: - Microbenchmarks across sequence lengths 8..16384, heads 8..64, model dims 1024..6144. - Canary on dedicated pools (pool-attn-4g). Results (canary): p50 latency -6%, p95 latency -12% on mixed-length workloads (avg seq ~512), throughput +18% on long-context workloads, token-cost -9% (due to fewer KV churns). Rollout plan: canary to 5% dedicated capacity for 48h, monitor tail latency, KV cache miss rate, memory OOMs. If no regressions, gradual increase over 7 days. Migration notes: no API changes. Config flags: runtime.tiler.enabled (default: true), kvcache.lazy_streaming (default: false) — kvcache.lazy_streaming off by default during initial rollout. Checklist: - [x] Design doc (ENG-1842) - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Perf harness runs - [x] Canary plan - [x] Docs update - [x] Security review (no new surface) Known limitations: streaming introduces additional background IO which can increase memory churn under extreme concurrency; tiler heuristics are intentionally conservative and will be tuned as we gather telemetry. Backwards compatibility: existing model pins and rollouts remain unaffected.

Maya Singh: Nice approach. Can you add a short unit test that simulates partial-KV availability so we exercise the partial-forward path?
Evan Chen: Added a test in tests/unit/partial_kv_sim.cc and a perf harness scenario to the bench suite. Also added metrics 'kvcache.partial_forward_count'
Liam O'Rourke: Two nits: (1) rename prefetch_priority -> slab_priority (2) add a short comment on why rotary remap is in-kernel. Otherwise LGTM.
Evan Chen: Renamed per request and expanded the kernel comment to explain avoiding extra memcpy during remap.
Ravi Iyer: Observability: add an exported trace span around tiler decisions and the async prefetch edge. Please ensure spans include tile_size and slab_id.
Evan Chen: Added spans and unit tests for trace fields. Verified with local Jaeger that spans are emitted.
Maya Singh: Approving after CI pass.
Liam O'Rourke: Approved. Good microbench wins are convincing.

Introduce neon-orchestrated hybrid attention tiler and lazy-KV streaming: reduces p95 latency on mixed workloads and improves throughput for long-context models. Config flags introduced: runtime.tiler.enabled, kvcache.lazy_streaming. Backwards-compatible.

title: Introduce Batch-Cache Policy Synthesizer for automated batching, cache TTLs, and quant profiles
author: Sofia Martinez
text:
Motivation: Production teams increasingly ask for safe, explainable defaults for batching, cache TTLs, and quantization profiles tuned to their unit-econ targets. Manual tuning is slow and error-prone; naive defaults either leave money on the table or cause latency regressions. This PR introduces the 'Batch-Cache Policy Synthesizer' — a small service and integration that synthesizes conservative, runbook-driven defaults and optional suggestions for aggressive cost-saving profiles, backed by workload traces and unit-econ objectives.

What this changes:
- New service: internal/optimizer/policy_synthesizer that consumes sampled request traces, cost/latency SLO goals, and historical model perf profiles to output a ranked set of policy candidates (batching window, max batch size, prefix cache TTL, kv-cache-hotlist-size, quantization profile id).
- CLI: tools/cost-synthesizer/bin/rcs (runbook-config-synth) for operators to generate profiles locally from a trace file and preview expected token-cost and p50/p95 latency deltas.
- API: /v1/internal/policy_synthesizer/generate (protected) to request on-demand policy suggestions for a customer or model route.
- Redwood Console integration: Add a lightweight Recommendations drawer that surfaces the top-3 candidates along with estimated saving, expected latency impact, and confidence score.
- Safeguards: Every suggestion includes a conservative fallback policy and an automatic canary rollout plan (10% traffic -> 50% -> 100%) with automatic rollback on latency or quality regressions.
- Tests: unit tests for candidate scoring, integration tests for the CLI path, and e2e smoke that runs a small synthetic trace through the service and validates metrics emitted to metrics.redwood (new metric: optimizer.synthesized_policy.{applied,rolled_back}).

Design notes (short):
- Scoring model: multi-objective heuristic that combines estimated per-token cost delta, expected p95 latency delta (from per-op instrumentation), and an uncertainty penalty derived from sample size. Operators can pick a unit-econ target multiplier (e.g., 0.8x cost target) and the synthesizer returns candidates that meet the target while keeping p95 within a user-configured latency window.
- Quant profiles: the synthesizer references the model-registry quant profiles and recommends the lightest quant that has a validated quality delta < configured threshold (default 1% BLEU/ROUGE-style surrogate). If no profile passes, quant recommendations are omitted.
- Safety floor: all policies include a required minimal TTL and max_batch safeguards to avoid excessive batching for latency-sensitive routes.

Files changed (high level):
- internal/optimizer/policy_synthesizer/service.go (core synthesizer)
- internal/optimizer/policy_synthesizer/score.go (scoring heuristics + unit-econ logic)
- tools/cost-synthesizer/cli.go (trace -> suggestion path)
- api/internal_routes.go (new internal endpoint + auth guard)
- console/src/components/RecommendationsDrawer.tsx (UI surface)
- docs/operator/runbooks/policy-synthesizer.md (runbook + rollout playbook)
- tests/integration/synth_cli_test.go
- tests/e2e/synth_smoke_test.yaml

Short commit summary: 
- feat(synthesizer): initial synthesizer and scoring heuristics
- feat(cli): rcs tool and local trace parsing
- feat(api): internal endpoint and auth scope
- feat(console): recommendations drawer and telemetry hooks
- test: integration + e2e smoke coverage and CI job
- docs: runbook and operator guidance

Backwards compatibility: The synthesizer produces policy JSON that is fully compatible with the existing /configs/policy schema. There are no default changes to runtime behavior unless an operator explicitly applies a synthesized policy or accepts a Console recommendation.

Rollout plan: Merge to main -> feature flag guarded release for 48h to internal canary orgs -> open beta for customers with opt-in flag in Console -> enable for customer accounts with automated guardrails after 30 days if telemetry shows safe behavior.

Notes on CI: Initial CI run showed a flaky timing-dependent test in synth_cli_test.go (race with metrics exporter). I added a deterministic fake exporter and re-ran. The final CI run passed: all unit, integration, and e2e smoke checks green.

Aiden Park: Nice work — can you clarify how uncertainty is estimated?
Sofia Martinez: We use bootstrap sampling on trace segments; explained in score.go comments and added a unit test. Uncertainty is expressed as a multiplicative penalty on cost savings.
Maya Singh: Would like a conservative default for cache TTL to avoid cold-start storms after deploy. Add a minimal ttl of 100ms?
Sofia Martinez: Agreed, added safety_floor_min_ttl=100ms with a test and documented in runbook.
Ravi Desai: CI failed on the first run due to a race in the fake exporter; approving once that flake was fixed and metrics stabilized.
Maya Singh: Approved (+1) — good to go behind feature flag.
Aiden Park: Merged with squash commit; follow-up: add telemetry dashboard for analyzed routes (ENG-5523).

Added a new policy synthesizer to suggest conservative and aggressive batching/caching/quant profiles based on sampled traces and unit-econ targets. Operator CLI and Console recommendations included. Feature is opt-in and guarded by feature flags; includes automatic canary rollout and rollback guardrails.

This PR intentionally does not change defaults at runtime. Operators must apply generated policies via the Console or API. The synthesizer will be iterated on during the beta to tighten scoring and quality checks.

title: Cohort Comparator & Trace Linker for Deployment Health
author: Aisha Kapoor
text:
Build a combined Cohort Comparator and Request Trace Linker inside the Console to make canary/A-B/shadow rollouts diagnosable end-to-end. The feature surfaces per-route metric diffs between cohorts, links anomalous metric deltas to sampled request traces, and exposes suggested rollback signals (automated and manual) backed by thresholded telemetry. This is intended to reduce MTTI for rollout regressions and make auto-rollback decisions transparent to product and platform teams.

Comparator UI shows side-by-side cohort-level charts for latency (p50/p95), error rate, token cost, and request throughput for a selected time window
Diff view highlights statistically significant deltas and annotates percentage change with confidence intervals
User can click a diff to see sampled traces from both cohorts with request-level metadata (route, model version, routing policy, input hash)
Trace Linker pins causal spans and shows top 3 signal contributors (e.g., model variant, batch size, region) derived from instrumentation
Auto-rollback triggers are visible per-rollout and can be toggled; Console records the reason and suggested fallback model
All telemetry queries are reproducible (copyable query) and dashboards exportable as PNG/CSV
Feature is behind a Console feature flag and gated to Dedicated/Hosted customers in beta

Product: finalize comparator UX flows and error states (mockups)
Design: high-fidelity mockups for comparator panel, trace overlay, and diff heatmap
Engineering: instrument cohort labels in request pipeline and add trace sampling hook for cohort comparison
Engineering: build backend telemetry aggregator service to compute per-route deltas and significance tests
Engineering: expose API endpoints for cohort queries and trace joins
SRE: validate query performance and set retention defaults for cohort metrics
QA: e2e tests for trace linking across canary/A-B/shadow traffic scenarios
Docs: write Console help guide and rollout observability playbook

Alpha: enable feature flag for internal Redwood tenants only (1 week)
Beta: open to selected customers on Dedicated and Hosted with opt-in (4 weeks)
GA: enabled by default for all Console users with feature rollout controls (post-beta)

High cardinality of route/model/version labels could make diff computations slow
Trace sampling bias between cohorts may create false-positive causes
Auto-rollback without clear human-readable rationale could erode trust
Data retention costs if coarse-grained sampling is insufficient for forensic analysis

Aggressive trace sampling increases root-cause fidelity but raises cost — start with adaptive sampling tied to metric deltas
Pre-computing cohort diffs reduces UI latency but increases storage/compute; prefer on-demand with short cache window initially
Expose simple auto-rollback toggles first; defer fully automated ML-driven rollback recommendations to later cycle

Engineering spike 2026-03-13 showed ClickHouse aggregation of cohort diffs at 5m windows is 3x cheaper than per-request joins

title: Mini-dashboard widgets: keyboard-first flow, RTL mirroring, and adaptive contrast audit
author: Ava Chen
text:
Audit and prototype updates for compact dashboard widgets used in Cost Explorer and Rollouts pages. title: Security review - Private upgrades: audit logs, backup encryption, rollback evidence (Cascade)
author: Markus Klein
text:
Cascade walked through audit/compliance evidence requirements for Private upgrades (VPC) with an eye toward SOX-ish controls and internal auditability. Redwood reviewed planned upgrade lifecycle events (upgrade started, prechecks pass/fail, backup started/completed, migration start/end, rollback invoked/completed), and discussed required fields to make logs useful in Splunk (who, what version, where, correlation IDs). Open questions centered on retention/tamper-evidence, and how customer-managed KMS keys apply to backups and upgrade state. Redwood committed to sharing the audit event schema draft + an example Splunk mapping, and confirming support bundle contents (upgrade plan JSON, last-run logs, checksum list for artifacts).

Redwood to share draft audit event schema + sample payloads for upgrade/rollback lifecycle events.
Redwood to confirm backup encryption behavior in VPC Private (EBS/CSI snapshots vs logical dumps) and what is encrypted with customer CMK.
Cascade to provide their minimum audit log retention requirement and whether WORM storage is mandated internally.
Redwood to send a one-pager on how to forward Private audit logs to Splunk (HTTP Event Collector) and what fields are indexed by default.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up focused on evidence for rollback drills and how to document 'successful rollback' for auditors.

Naomi Feldman - Send audit log event list + required fields (actor, source IP, cluster ID, from/to versions, plan_id, result) to Cascade. Due: 2025-06-18
Kevin Osei - Confirm SIEM integration story (Splunk HEC + syslog) and recommended retention defaults for Private. Due: 2025-06-20
Irene Choi - Provide details on backup encryption: snapshot types supported, key ownership, and how restore verification is logged. Due: 2025-06-20
Connor O'Brien - Share redacted example 'upgrade evidence packet' (plan JSON + logs + checksums) from staging. Due: 2025-06-21
Elena Petrova - Share Cascade constraints on maintenance windows and who is allowed to execute upgrades (RBAC roles). Due: 2025-06-19

Meeting header
Date: 2025-06-12
Time: 09:03 AM PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Title: Security review - Private upgrades: audit logs, backup encryption, rollback evidence (Cascade)

Attendees (Redwood): Markus Klein, Naomi Feldman, Marcus Lin, Kevin Osei, Irene Choi, Connor O'Brien
Attendees (Cascade Financial Group): Priya Nair, Daniel Cho, Elena Petrova, Samir Gupta, Mei Tan

---

[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool, okay, I think we’re at time. Thanks everyone for joining. This is the security and compliance review specifically on the Private upgrade and rollback work we’ve been doing. Priya, Daniel, Elena, Samir, Mei—thanks for making time.

[00:13] Priya Nair: Thanks Markus. Yep, we want to go deep on audit logging and evidence. We’ve had… painful audits around change control and we don’t want upgrades to be a blind spot.

[00:24] Markus Klein: Totally. Quick intros on our side—Naomi leads security product review, Marcus is security engineering, Kevin works on audit/SIEM requirements, Irene is infra lead for Private, and Connor runs release engineering.

[00:38] Daniel Cho: Great. I’m Daniel, security engineering. Elena runs the k8s platform. Samir internal audit. Mei is ops.

[00:46] Markus Klein: Awesome. Naomi, do you wanna set context?

[00:50] Naomi Feldman: Yep. So the new upgrade flow for Redwood Private is moving to a more deterministic, plan-based approach. The auditability piece is: we emit upgrade lifecycle events, we persist the executed plan and step results, and we make sure backups/rollback are traceable. Today we want to validate what fields you need for evidence and how we plug into Splunk.

[01:15] Priya Nair: And just to be clear, this is for Private in a VPC, right? Not on-prem.

[01:20] Irene Choi: Correct for you, yes. But we’re building it in a way that also works for on-prem/air-gapped, so some of the artifact signing and checksum stuff will show up.

[01:32] Elena Petrova: Okay. We also have a question on whether your backups are encrypted with our KMS keys or yours.

[01:38] Naomi Feldman: Yep, that’s on the agenda.

[01:42] Markus Klein: Maybe we start with the audit log events and then do backup encryption, then talk about “evidence packets” for your auditors.

[01:51] Samir Gupta: That order works.

[01:54] Naomi Feldman: Cool. So for upgrade/rollback we’re defining a set of audit events. Think: upgrade.started, upgrade.precheck.completed, upgrade.backup.started, upgrade.backup.completed, upgrade.apply.started, and then sub-events like migration.started, migration.completed. If rollback happens: rollback.invoked, rollback.step.completed, rollback.completed.

[02:19] Daniel Cho: When you say audit events, is this in your control plane or in the Private cluster?

[02:24] Kevin Osei: In Private deployments we treat audit logs as first-class in the customer environment. So the events are emitted by the Private control-plane components running in your cluster, and they can be forwarded out to your SIEM. For VPC, you can also mirror to your logging stack—CloudWatch or Splunk.

[02:41] Daniel Cho: That’s good. We need logs to stay inside our account. Forwarding is fine as long as we control the destination.

[02:48] Priya Nair: We also need actor attribution. Like, “who” triggered the upgrade.

[02:54] Naomi Feldman: 100%. For each event we’re capturing actor.type and actor.id. Actor can be a human principal coming via SSO (SAML/OIDC), or a service account. We’ll also include the initiating client—CLI vs UI—and the request ID.

[03:11] Elena Petrova: So if Mei runs “redwood private upgrade apply” from her laptop, you’ll capture her identity from SSO? Or is it just Kubernetes RBAC?

[03:22] Connor O'Brien: It’s both, kind of. The installer authenticates against the Private API using your configured SSO. Once authorized, the actual jobs run in-cluster under service accounts, but the events keep the “initiated_by” identity from the API call.

[03:39] Mei Tan: That’s important because auditors will ask. The Kubernetes service account is not enough.

[03:44] Naomi Feldman: Exactly. We’ll also log the “approved_by” field if you choose to require an approval gate. That’s optional and depends on your process. But we can log that an approval was recorded.

[03:58] Priya Nair: We do require approvals for production changes. If you can log “change_ticket_id” that would help.

[04:05] Markus Klein: Like linking to your ServiceNow or Jira ticket?

[04:08] Priya Nair: Yes. Even if it’s just a free text field the operator passes in.

[04:14] Connor O'Brien: That’s in scope. In the plan generation step we can accept metadata—ticket ID, maintenance window ID—and persist it into the plan artifact and emit it with each audit event.

[04:27] Daniel Cho: What about source IP and device info?

[04:30] Marcus Lin: We can log source IP of the API call, user agent, and if mutual TLS is enabled, we can include the client cert fingerprint. Device posture beyond that we don’t do.

[04:42] Elena Petrova: Okay.

[04:44] Naomi Feldman: Another key thing is correlation. So events include: upgrade_id (UUID), plan_id, cluster_id, environment (prod/stage), and component scope (control plane vs data plane). Then each step has step_id.

[05:04] Samir Gupta: Can I ask, will you log failures in a way that’s intelligible? Not just “exit code 1”.

[05:10] Naomi Feldman: We’re trying. We log result=success|failure|skipped, a reason code, and an error_class. Full stack traces can be noisy; we put detailed logs in the component logs, but audit events will have a summarized failure reason.

[05:26] Samir Gupta: For evidence, summarized is better, as long as we can show a control worked. Example: precheck failed because insufficient storage, upgrade aborted.

[05:36] Irene Choi: Exactly that. Storage headroom precheck is blocking. So if it fails, apply doesn’t start, and you get an audit event showing “precheck.blocking_failed” and which precheck.

[05:49] Daniel Cho: Are you also logging “what versions”? Like from 1.8.2 to 1.9.0.

[05:54] Connor O'Brien: Yes. from_version, to_version, and chart/runtime artifact digests. Specifically we’ll include the Helm chart version, installer version, and image digests (sha256). For air-gapped bundles, also the bundle manifest checksum.

[06:13] Elena Petrova: Nice.

[06:15] Priya Nair: Okay. Now about retention and tamper evidence. We have requirements that audit logs be retained for 400 days and ideally immutable.

[06:25] Kevin Osei: So on our side, we don’t provide WORM storage in your environment. What we do is: emit structured JSON logs to stdout / file, and make it easy to forward to your immutable log store. In AWS that could be CloudWatch + retention + export to S3 object lock, or directly into Splunk with an index retention policy.

[06:46] Daniel Cho: That’s fine; we can do that. But we need you to not overwrite logs in-cluster before shipping.

[06:53] Irene Choi: Default is log rotation at the node level, but we recommend a log agent (Fluent Bit) shipping in near real-time. For upgrade events specifically, we also persist the plan + results in a Kubernetes secret/configmap-like store, but we can talk about where.

[07:09] Elena Petrova: Wait, you store upgrade state in Secrets? That raises flags.

[07:13] Irene Choi: Great catch. We don’t store sensitive material there. The “upgrade state” is mostly IDs, timestamps, versions, step status. Any credentials are referenced, not stored. For example, “backup_location_ref” not actual keys.

[07:28] Marcus Lin: And we can configure encryption at rest on etcd for Secrets, which you probably already have.

[07:34] Elena Petrova: We do have etcd encryption.

[07:36] Priya Nair: Still, we’d want a clear statement: what exactly is stored, and for how long.

[07:43] Naomi Feldman: Understood. We can share the data classification: upgrade plan artifact (non-secret), execution results, pointers to backups, and the audit events. Retention configurable; default maybe 30 days in-cluster, but you’d forward to Splunk for 400 days.

[08:02] Samir Gupta: For evidence, we need at minimum: who initiated, what changed, when, was it approved, and what was the outcome. Rollback also needs the same.

[08:12] Naomi Feldman: Makes sense.

[08:14] Markus Klein: Can we switch to rollback traceability? That’s been a big topic.

[08:19] Daniel Cho: Yes. Specifically: if you rollback, how do we prove we rolled back fully? And if there was a partial upgrade, how do we know what state we’re in.

[08:29] Connor O'Brien: The plan-based approach helps. Upgrade apply writes a state machine record: stage started/completed. Rollback consumes that state and emits rollback events per stage. After rollback, we run post-rollback health checks, and we emit rollback.completed with health=pass/fail and references to checks.

[08:50] Mei Tan: What are the checks?

[08:52] Irene Choi: For control plane: API ready, controller reconciles, DB connectivity. For data plane: model runtime pods ready, service endpoints healthy. Plus we can run a simple synthetic request if configured.

[09:06] Elena Petrova: Is synthetic request mandatory? Some environments don’t allow outbound.

[09:11] Irene Choi: Not mandatory. It can be purely internal to the cluster.

[09:15] Daniel Cho: And the DB migrations—this is the scary part. If the upgrade runs a migration that’s not reversible, rollback might not fully restore.

[09:26] Marcus Lin: Right. We’re adding guardrails to require backward-compatible migrations for N-1 to N where possible. But we also rely on backups as the ultimate escape hatch.

[09:38] Priya Nair: So for audit, you need to log “migration started”, “migration finished”, and also whether it was “forward-only” or reversible.

[09:46] Connor O'Brien: We can log migration version and whether rollback would require restore-from-backup. But “reversible” is tricky—depends on the schema.

[09:56] Naomi Feldman: We can at least log a “rollback_mode”: in-place rollback vs restore-required, determined by the plan. The plan generation step can mark certain transitions.

[10:09] Samir Gupta: That would help. Auditors like explicit declarations.

[10:13] Markus Klein: Good feedback.

[10:16] Naomi Feldman: Let’s talk backups now. Elena asked the key question: encryption and key ownership.

[10:22] Elena Petrova: Yep. We will not accept backups encrypted with a vendor-owned key. It must be our CMK.

[10:30] Irene Choi: For VPC deployments, backups can be snapshots (EBS/CSI) or logical dumps, depending on component. For EBS snapshots, encryption uses your AWS KMS key if the volume is encrypted with your CMK. Snapshots inherit encryption. For logical dumps, we can encrypt with a key you provide via KMS envelope encryption.

[10:55] Daniel Cho: Wait, you do logical dumps of what, Postgres?

[10:58] Irene Choi: Postgres for control plane DB, yes, if you choose that mode. Default is snapshot-based for speed, but we support logical as an option.

[11:09] Daniel Cho: And where are those dumps stored?

[11:12] Irene Choi: S3 in your account, typically. Or an internal object store you provide. For on-prem it could be an NFS or object store endpoint.

[11:24] Priya Nair: For us, S3 with bucket policies and object lock, ideally.

[11:29] Kevin Osei: That’s a good pattern. We’ll provide guidance and can log the backup location reference (bucket name is probably okay) but we’ll avoid logging paths with sensitive info.

[11:40] Samir Gupta: Do you log backup success? And how do you verify restore?

[11:45] Irene Choi: Yes: backup.started, backup.completed, backup.failed. For verification, we can run a restore validation step in non-prod or as a dry-run. In prod, verification is typically checking snapshot completion and DB consistency checks. We can log “backup_verification=skipped|passed|failed” with why.

[12:06] Mei Tan: If you can do a checksum verification for the dump artifact, that’s useful.

[12:10] Irene Choi: For logical dumps we can generate a checksum and store it alongside. For snapshots it’s trickier; AWS handles integrity, but we can log snapshot IDs.

[12:23] Daniel Cho: For audit we need: snapshot IDs, KMS key ID (at least reference), timestamps.

[12:30] Irene Choi: We can log KMS key ARN in a redacted form, like last 6 chars, or full—depends on your preference.

[12:38] Priya Nair: Full ARN is okay, it’s not secret.

[12:41] Marcus Lin: Agreed, it’s not a secret.

[12:44] Naomi Feldman: Another item: who can access backups. We’ll recommend IAM least privilege and separate roles for backup vs restore.

[12:53] Daniel Cho: Good.

[12:55] Markus Klein: On evidence expectations, Samir, what are you typically asked to present?

[13:01] Samir Gupta: For a change: a ticket, approval evidence, time window, proof the change was applied, and monitoring evidence that it didn’t degrade controls. For rollback drills, proof we tested rollback and it worked.

[13:15] Naomi Feldman: Okay. Our idea is an “upgrade evidence packet” that includes: the plan JSON (what was intended), the execution report (what happened), the audit log event timeline, and links to backup IDs. Plus a hash of the plan. Connor, right?

[13:32] Connor O'Brien: Yeah. Also, the installer can output a summary at the end: from/to version, prechecks, backup ID, migrations, duration. That can be attached to the change ticket.

[13:46] Priya Nair: That would be ideal if it includes a unique ID that matches the audit events.

[13:51] Connor O'Brien: That’s the upgrade_id.

[13:53] Elena Petrova: Can we query the system later for the last upgrade? Like API endpoint.

[13:59] Irene Choi: Yes, we’ll have something like “/admin/upgrades/history” returning last N upgrades. You can also just read from stored plan artifacts.

[14:11] Daniel Cho: Are those endpoints authenticated via SSO? We don’t want anonymous.

[14:15] Marcus Lin: Yes, same auth, plus RBAC. Read-only “auditor” role is an option.

[14:22] Priya Nair: That’s helpful for internal audit.

[14:26] Naomi Feldman: Okay, switching gears slightly: log forwarding. Kevin, can you speak to Splunk specifically?

[14:33] Kevin Osei: Sure. We emit audit events as JSON. For Splunk, you’d run a forwarder or use Fluent Bit output plugin to Splunk HEC. We’ll provide a sourcetype recommendation like “redwood:private:audit”. Fields: event_type, event_time, actor_id, actor_email, cluster_id, upgrade_id, from_version, to_version, result, reason_code.

[14:58] Daniel Cho: Will you include request_id? We correlate with API logs.

[15:02] Kevin Osei: Yes. request_id and trace_id where applicable.

[15:07] Elena Petrova: We use Datadog for metrics and Splunk for logs. If you emit metrics about upgrades, that’s also good.

[15:15] Irene Choi: We do. We’re adding upgrade metrics: precheck failure count by category, migration duration, rollback frequency. Those go to Prometheus by default.

[15:27] Mei Tan: Perfect.

[15:29] Priya Nair: Can you confirm that rollback invocation is always logged, even if rollback fails mid-way?

[15:36] Naomi Feldman: Yes. rollback.invoked is emitted at start, then rollback.step events. If it fails, rollback.failed with reason. That’s the intention.

[15:48] Daniel Cho: Okay.

[15:50] Samir Gupta: On tamper evidence: do you sign the logs?

[15:54] Marcus Lin: We do not cryptographically sign every log event today. In practice customers rely on their centralized log pipeline with access controls and immutability. For on-prem, we’re exploring signing the upgrade plan artifact itself (manifest signature). But per-event log signing is heavy.

[16:16] Priya Nair: That’s acceptable if we have object lock in S3 or Splunk retention. But we might ask for plan artifact signing.

[16:24] Connor O'Brien: The air-gapped bundle verification work includes signature and checksum verification. We can reuse that for plan artifacts: hash + optionally sign with a key you control or our release key.

[16:39] Daniel Cho: I’d prefer customer-controlled signing if possible, but even a hash is better than nothing.

[16:45] Naomi Feldman: Noted.

[16:47] Markus Klein: Elena, what about your maintenance window practices? Might impact what we log.

[16:52] Elena Petrova: We have a defined window, 2 hours, and only Platform Ops can execute. We also want “dry run” prechecks earlier in the week.

[17:02] Irene Choi: That’s supported. Precheck can run without applying. It emits an audit event too: precheck.completed (dry_run=true).

[17:12] Mei Tan: Great.

[17:14] Daniel Cho: Can we talk about what’s included in the support bundle? In incidents we often need to prove what happened without giving you full cluster logs.

[17:23] Markus Klein: Yes, good question.

[17:25] Connor O'Brien: Support bundle includes: upgrade plan JSON, last execution report, precheck output (sanitized), and references to artifact digests. It can redact secrets. You choose what to include.

[17:40] Priya Nair: We will want to redact names sometimes.

[17:43] Naomi Feldman: Understood. We can allow “pseudonymize user” options, but for audit you might actually want the real actor. For sharing with Redwood support, you can redact.

[17:56] Samir Gupta: For audit we need real actor. For vendor support, we can redact.

[18:01] Daniel Cho: Makes sense.

[18:03] Elena Petrova: Also: where do the backups live relative to the upgrade state? I don’t want upgrade state to point to a backup that got GC’ed.

[18:12] Irene Choi: That’s addressed by retention policies. We’ll set backup retention default to, say, 7 days or 14 days; you can set higher. The plan will include “minimum_retention_until” timestamp. And we can block deletion until after upgrade success is confirmed.

[18:30] Mei Tan: Is backup optional? Like can someone skip it.

[18:34] Irene Choi: In the safe-by-default flow, it’s required unless you explicitly set a flag “--no-backup” and you need elevated permission. And that choice is logged.

[18:46] Priya Nair: Great. That’s a control.

[18:48] Samir Gupta: Log “backup_skipped=true” with actor.

[18:52] Naomi Feldman: Yep.

[18:55] Daniel Cho: On encryption: for logical dumps, you said envelope encryption. Can you explain quickly.

[19:01] Irene Choi: Sure. We generate a data key via KMS, encrypt the dump locally, store encrypted blob in S3, and store the encrypted data key with it. To decrypt, you need access to KMS to unwrap. So Redwood never needs your key.

[19:19] Daniel Cho: Good.

[19:20] Priya Nair: And in on-prem, if there’s no KMS?

[19:24] Irene Choi: For on-prem we support external KMS or HSM integrations where possible, or customer-provided key material. But that’s a separate track.

[19:33] Markus Klein: For Cascade we’ll stick to AWS KMS.

[19:37] Naomi Feldman: Another compliance question: audit event fields and PII. Actor email is PII in some jurisdictions. Do you have constraints?

[19:46] Priya Nair: In our policy, it’s okay in internal logs with access controls. We’d rather have email for unambiguous identity.

[19:54] Daniel Cho: Yeah.

[19:55] Samir Gupta: Agreed.

[19:58] Naomi Feldman: Okay.

[20:01] [crosstalk]

[20:02] Markus Klein: Sorry, go ahead Daniel.

[20:04] Daniel Cho: One more: do you log RBAC changes during upgrade? Sometimes upgrades adjust roles.

[20:10] Marcus Lin: We don’t automatically change your RBAC unless required. But if the chart applies new ClusterRoles, Kubernetes audit logs would capture it. On our side, we can emit an audit event “rbac.resources.applied” with counts, not full YAML.

[20:27] Elena Petrova: That would help. Kubernetes audit logs are huge.

[20:31] Naomi Feldman: We’ll consider it.

[20:34] Markus Klein: I want to make sure we capture your “must have” list. Priya, if you had to pick top 5 fields/events.

[20:42] Priya Nair: 1) upgrade started with actor identity and ticket ID. 2) prechecks with pass/fail and blocking reasons. 3) backup completed with snapshot IDs and key reference. 4) migration start/end and whether restore required for rollback. 5) upgrade/rollback completed with health checks.

[21:06] Naomi Feldman: That’s aligned.

[21:08] Samir Gupta: Also approvals if you support them.

[21:12] Connor O'Brien: Yes.

[21:14] Markus Klein: Great.

[21:16] Kevin Osei: One more: we should confirm how you want timestamps. We use RFC3339 with timezone. Splunk ingests okay.

[21:24] Daniel Cho: RFC3339 is fine.

[21:27] Elena Petrova: Also include monotonic sequence? Sometimes logs arrive out of order.

[21:33] Kevin Osei: We can include sequence_number per upgrade_id, yes. That helps ordering.

[21:41] Elena Petrova: Great.

[21:43] Naomi Feldman: Nice catch.

[21:46] Markus Klein: We have about 10 minutes left. Anything else on evidence expectations? Or questions on our SOC2 posture etc.

[21:54] Priya Nair: We already have your SOC 2 report, that’s fine. This is more about operational controls. If you can provide a sample “upgrade evidence packet” that we can show auditors, that’s huge.

[22:07] Connor O'Brien: We can provide a redacted sample from staging. It will show the plan JSON and event timeline.

[22:15] Samir Gupta: Include an example where prechecks fail and upgrade is blocked. That demonstrates control.

[22:22] Naomi Feldman: Good idea.

[22:24] Mei Tan: And maybe one where rollback happens.

[22:28] Connor O'Brien: We can do that too.

[22:31] Daniel Cho: One more question: do you have an “upgrade window” config that prevents upgrades outside a time range?

[22:39] Irene Choi: Terraform changes are adding an upgrade window variable. The system can enforce “apply only within window” and log attempts outside window.

[22:51] Priya Nair: Great. Log denied attempts too.

[22:54] Naomi Feldman: Yes.

[22:56] Markus Klein: Okay, let’s recap actions. Naomi will send the audit event schema draft. Kevin will send Splunk forwarding guidance and retention recommendations. Irene will write up encryption behavior for backups. Connor will share the evidence packet sample. And Elena you’ll send your RBAC constraints and who can run upgrades.

[23:16] Elena Petrova: Yes.

[23:18] Daniel Cho: Sounds good.

[23:20] Priya Nair: Thanks all. This was very productive.

[23:23] Markus Klein: Great. We’ll schedule a follow-up in about two weeks focused on rollback drills and auditor language.

[23:30] Naomi Feldman: Thanks everyone.

[23:32] [meeting ends / recording stops]

Note: Fireflies transcript truncation — audio continued with scheduling logistics and small talk for ~2 minutes; not captured cleanly.

title: SOC2 ↔ ISO control translation — 1:1 dry-run scratchpad
author: Paulina Rivera
text:
Purpose / context:
- Prep notes for 1:1 with Alex before auditor dry-run (external audit team scheduled in 3 weeks).
- Goal: confirm control owners, evidence locations, and call script that maps SOC2 CC controls to ISO clauses so we don't fumble translations.
- Keep this messy — checklist + phrases I can read verbatim during the dry-run.

High-level agenda for 1:1 (15–20m):
1) Quick readout: where we are (GAP summary). 2) Walk control mapping for the 8 controls flagged as higher-risk. 3) Agree owners + evidence links. 4) Decide dry-run script + escalation path.

What I want from Alex:
- Buy-in on proposed owner changes for CC6 (change management) and CC7 (logical access).
- Approval on using the packaged KMS docs as primary evidence for CC3 (confidentiality).
- Clarity on which vendor risk exceptions we can carry forward and which need mitigation before auditor arrival.

Quick gap snapshot (top items to speak to):
- CC6 (Change mgmt): missing formal rollback evidence for two infra rollouts (2025-07, 2025-09). Proposed: ask release-eng to produce postmortem + rollback runbook. Owner: Devon. ETA: 2026-02-28.
- CC7 (Logical access): temporary contractors in SSO audit log flagged; need attestation from Hiring/People Ops for contractual access end dates. Owner: Maya. ETA: 2026-02-24.
- CC3 (Confidentiality/encryption): KMS rotation procedure written but not in Confluence section expected by auditor. Action: move docs -> confluence/crypto and attach key rotation logs from S3. Owner: Paulina (me) + infra. ETA: 2026-02-21.
- Vendor risk: two vendors (third-party observability, external model hosting) have incomplete questionnaires. We have compensating controls but need final sign-off. Owner: Alex to escalate to procurement. ETA: 2026-03-05.

Control translation notes (short mapping phrases to say aloud):
- "SOC2 CC3 maps to ISO A.8/A.10/A.13 territory — highlight our KMS + network segmentation as the primary artifacts."
- "CC6 change control: correlate ISO A.12 change management records with our Jira release tags + rollout policies in the release playbook."
- "CC7 logical access: show SSO audit export + RBAC matrix; link to employee offboarding checklist and artifact in HR."

Evidence checklist (short form) — call these out, confirm link and owner in 1:1:
- KMS key rotation logs — owner: Infra (Devon). Location: S3 /confluence link. Format: CSV + screenshot. Status: partial.
- SSO audit export (last 12 months) + RBAC matrix — owner: Identity (Maya). Location: internal vault link. Status: missing contractor attestation.
- Release postmortems for Jul/Sep infra rollouts — owner: Release Eng (Devon). Location: Jira SEC-2345 sub-tasks. Status: missing rollback runbook.
- Vendor questionnaires (observability + model host) — owner: Procurement (Alex). Location: procurement drive. Status: incomplete.
- Encryption architecture diagram + network segmentation — owner: Infra (Paulina + Devon). Location: confluence/arch. Status: draft, needs tidy.

Questions to confirm with Alex (concrete ask lines):
- "Can procurement expedite the outstanding vendor questionnaires and add an attestation field for data-handling?"
- "For the contractor SSO issue: is an HR attestation acceptable as evidence or do we need signed termination records?"
- "Do we want to surface KMS rotation logs directly in Confluence or keep them in S3 with a signed pointer? Which is auditor-friendly?"

Dry-run script / phrases for the auditor call (keeps me on track):
- Intro: "Hi — I'm Paulina, security ops. For this control area we will show the mapping between Redwood's operational practices and the SOC2 criteria; we can also crosswalk to ISO clauses where helpful."
- For change mgmt: "We use Jira for change requests, tagged release pipelines for deployment, and a post-deploy verification checklist. Here's a sample ticket + the deployment tag that rolled the change into production."
- For access control: "SSO centralizes access; offboarding is automated with HR triggers. Shared here is the last 12 months of SSO logs plus the RBAC matrix."
- For KMS/encryption: "Encryption is enforced at rest and in transit; our key rotation schedule and cloud KMS configuration are attached. We can provide logs for the last two rotations."

Potential small talk / placemats (notes to self):
- Mention how Private deployments use customer-managed keys (good to show flexibility).
- Emphasize rollout fallback policies (reduces concern about missing rollback runbook).
- If auditor pushes on vendor incomplete questionnaires, propose compensating control: contractual right-to-audit clause + perimeter isolation evidence.

Follow-up action items (concrete, assignable):
- Paulina: Copy KMS rotation logs into confluence/crypto + add readme linking to S3 snapshot. Due 2026-02-21.
- Devon: Produce rollback runbook and attach to the two postmortems (Jul/Sep). Due 2026-02-28.
- Maya: Get contractor access attestation from People Ops (signed). Due 2026-02-24.
- Alex: Escalate vendor questionnaires to procurement and confirm remediation plan. Due 2026-03-05.
- Paulina + Alex: Draft 10-min dry-run script and rehearse 1:1 (schedule 30m). Suggested time: week of 2026-02-22.

Notes re: evidence formats auditor prefers (from last year's notes):
- Prefer consolidated PDFs with a short executive summary rather than raw CSVs. I'll generate 2–3 "executive evidence packets" for each control.
- Annotated screenshots with timestamps help; I'll add brief annotations showing search filters used.

Risk statements to have ready (short):
- If vendor questionnaires remain open, residual risk = medium (limited access to vendor personnel). Compensating control: network ACLs + data minimization.
- Missing rollback runbook increases incident recovery time; mitigated by automated canary rollouts currently in place.

Reminder: things I can't promise in 1:1 (call-outs to avoid):
- Don't commit to rewriting the entire network diagram — propose incremental edits and a designated reviewer.
- Don't promise vendor remediation timelines beyond procurement's scope.

Quick template email to send after 1:1 (to paste into Slack/email):
"Alex / team — thanks for the run-through. Per our discussion, I'm going to: 1) add KMS logs to confluence, 2) create the rollback runbook PR, 3) collect contractor attestations. Please confirm when procurement has updated the vendor questionnaires. I'll circulate the dry-run script once it's ready"

Stuff to log in Jira after 1:1 (immediate tickets):
- SEC-XXXX: Add KMS evidence to Confluence (link). -> Paulina.
- SEC-XXXX: Rollback runbook for Jul/Sep rollouts -> Devon.
- SEC-XXXX: Contractor access attestation -> Maya.

Open questions I still have (to research before 1:1):
- Does the auditor accept HR attestations as primary evidence for contractor offboarding? (check past audit notes)
- Exact retention window preference for KMS logs (12 vs 24 months).
- Which Confluence space auditors prefer — security vs infra?

Endnotes (personal):
- Keep script short and repeat the mapping line: "here's the policy, here's the artifact, here's the timestamped evidence."
- Bring printed evidence packets to the audit interview — auditors sometimes like physical PDFs.

-- Paulina
(scratchpad: will clean into a confluence short checklist once items nailed down)

title: Tethys Systems - SI Channel & Cloud GPU Fit Discovery
author: Maya Patel
text:
Introductory discovery between Redwood and Tethys Systems to evaluate a channel+SI partnership. Discussed integration options (hosted API vs. dedicated vs. private), expected customer use-cases (real-time chat, high-throughput batch embeddings), Tethys go-to-market model (reseller + managed services), rough commercial assumptions, and an initial pilot framework. Action items: share partner packet, provide VPC/private deploy checklist, run a short perf baseline with Tethys sample workload, and schedule executive alignment next week.

Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-03-27
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE); Jonas Reed (Redwood SE); Sofia Alvarez (Tethys); Ravi Menon (Tethys); Diane Cho (Tethys)

Optional autogenerated sections:
- Topics: partner GTM, technical fit, pilot scope
- Action items: listed below

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood partnerships team. Uh, quick round of intros?
[00:10] Sofia Alvarez: Hi, Sofia here, Head of Partnerships at Tethys. We focus on integrating cloud GPU capacity into managed SI offerings, so we resell + manage for enterprise.
[00:19] Ravi Menon: Ravi, lead cloud architect. We'll be responsible for the technical validation and ops side.
[00:24] Diane Cho: Diane, biz dev — I'm here to map channel motions and commercials.
[00:29] Jonas Reed: Jonas, SE, Redwood. I'll dig into perf, deploy modes, and what a POC would look like.
[00:35] Maya Patel: Great. High level — today's goal is to see whether there's a clean channel + SI fit: whether Tethys can package Redwood's inference runtime and Dedicated/Private options into your managed offering.
[00:46] Sofia Alvarez: Yes. A couple things — our customers care about latency for chat apps and throughput for embedding pipelines. We also need to understand margining and how we can white-label or resell.
[00:58] Jonas Reed: Understood. Just to frame technical options quickly: Redwood offers Hosted API (fastest), Dedicated reserved capacity for predictable throughput, and Private (VPC or on-prem) for regulated customers. Each has tradeoffs — Hosted is easiest but less isolated; Private gives you full network control but longer lead time.
[01:14] Ravi Menon: On privacy — we have a few customers in finance and healthcare. They require customer-managed KMS, audit logs, and usually a VPC peering option. Can Redwood support customer KMS and HSM integrations?
[01:28] Maya Patel: Yes, we integrate with customer KMS and support HSM-based key wraps for Private deployments; audit logs and SSO/SAML are supported. We can share the security checklist.
[01:36] Diane Cho: For the reseller economics, do you have a partner margin sheet or channel pricing?
[01:42] Maya Patel: We do — I'll share the one-pager and a suggested margin structure. Typical is a reseller discount on usage + fixed fee for Dedicated commitments. We can also support marketplace listings if that's part of the go-to-market.
[01:55] Sofia Alvarez: Marketplace would be helpful. For Dedicated, how does autoscaling and burst capacity work? Our customers sometimes have spiky loads.
[02:04] Jonas Reed: Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling policies and burst into spare capacity tiers. We also have routing policies that can fall back to cheaper variants — e.g., quantized models — when capacity constrains. Note: for tight latency SLOs we tend to pin to guaranteed capacity.
[02:19] Sofia Alvarez: Okay. On the integration side — do you expose an SDK or is it just REST? Our engineering teams usually want an SDK and a lightweight operator integration for deployment.
[02:28] Jonas Reed: We have a REST API + SDKs. For Private, we provide a helm chart and an operator for on-prem installs; for VPC we do a customer-managed control plane. There might be some missing words in the transcript — the ops artifact is basically a deploy pack with kube manifests.
[02:45] Ravi Menon: Sounds promising. For the POC, we want to run a sample workload: 50 QPS for chat with 32-token avg latencies and a weekly batch of 2 million embeddings. Can Redwood give us cost/latency projections for that?
[02:58] Jonas Reed: Yes. We can run a short benchmark — two paths: lightweight hosted baseline (fastest to start) and a Dedicated profile to show predictable throughput and unit economics. We'll need your prompt/embedding input and sequence length distribution to model cost.
[03:13] Diane Cho: Timeline-wise, we typically want a demo to our sales engineering, then an internal pilot with 2 target customers over 6–8 weeks. Is that a feasible pilot window?
[03:24] Maya Patel: Absolutely feasible. We usually do a 4–8 week pilot depending on access to data and environment. If we start with hosted, it's quicker. For Private it adds provisioning lead time.
[03:33] Sofia Alvarez: One question: can Redwood support white-labeling the UI or at least allow us to own the billing of end customers? Some of our deals require billing under our contract.
[03:43] Maya Patel: We can support partner billing via reseller arrangements and marketplace flows; white-label UI is trickier on hosted but for Dedicated/Private you can host your own control plane and integrate our runtime under your branding. We'll need legal to sign off on reseller terms.
[03:55] Ravi Menon: On networking, what does VPC peering look like? Do you do transit VPC or direct peering? We need to document the exact traffic flow and egress implications for our customers.
[04:06] Jonas Reed: For VPC/private we support direct VPC peering and private link equivalents depending on cloud provider. We'll provide a network topology diagram and egress guidelines — there's some variability by region and provider.
[04:18] Sofia Alvarez: Do you have any channel co-sell incentives or lead credits?
[04:22] Maya Patel: Yes, we have lead credits and co-sell arrangements; we also provide joint marketing support for priority partners. We'll include GTM enablement materials in the partner packet.
[04:32] Diane Cho: Any limitations on model catalog? We often onboard customers wanting Llama variants and some proprietary small models.
[04:38] Jonas Reed: We support a curated model catalog and can onboard partner-requested models. For private/pinned models there's a validation phase around licensing and compatibility. Also note: in transcript the product name Redwood Optimize got spelled as 'Redwood Optimise' earlier in doc, minor discrepancy.
[04:56] Maya Patel: Let's talk about success criteria for a pilot: SLOs, cost targets, and customer acceptance. Typical metrics: 95th percentile latency under X ms, embedding cost per 1k under Y dollars, and integration work less than Z engineering-weeks.
[05:10] Ravi Menon: Those metrics are fine; we will provide a target customer and sample telemetry to measure. Also need to check SOC2/ISO reports; can you share SOC2 Type II?
[05:20] Maya Patel: Yes, SOC2 Type II and ISO summaries available. We'll share redacted reports under an NDA.
[05:26] Sofia Alvarez: Good. On board ops: what's the provisioning time for a Private deployment in our EU region? Our customers need EU data residency.
[05:36] Jonas Reed: For Private VPC in EU, provisioning is typically 2–4 weeks depending on customer infra readiness and KMS/HSM setup. Hosted in an EU region is immediate, but note hosted data residency guarantees vary by contract.
[05:50] Diane Cho: Commercially, if we commit to a Dedicated reserve on behalf of a customer, can Tethys get a volume discount?
[05:57] Maya Patel: Yes, Partner/Reseller volume discounts can be structured as an addendum to the Dedicated contract. We'll outline tiers in the margin sheet.
[06:05] Ravi Menon: A technical nit: KV cache behavior — if we run large context chains, how does Redwood handle KV eviction and batching? We've had trouble with other systems reloading the kv too often.
[06:14] Jonas Reed: Good question. Our runtime does continuous batching and manages KV cache across requests; behavior depends on sequence length distribution and model variant. We have caching strategies and an option for a sticky session pin to keep KV warm for certain flows. I'll share a short technical note on cache heuristics.
[06:30] Sofia Alvarez: Any constraints on model quantization for specific accuracy needs? Some customers need high fidelity for legal text generation.
[06:36] Jonas Reed: Right — quantization reduces memory and cost but can affect output quality. We recommend A/B testing with your prompt sets; Redwood Optimize provides recommended quantization profiles per workload. We'll include that in the perf deliverable.
[06:48] Maya Patel: Ok, let's recap next steps (quick): Maya share partner packet and margin sheet; Jonas run baseline and share perf notes; Ravi provide sample workload and residency constraints; Sofia coordinate executive sync. Any other asks?
[07:01] Diane Cho: Please include a sample SLA for Dedicated + support tiers.
[07:05] Maya Patel: Will do.
[07:08] Sofia Alvarez: Also, if possible, include an example reseller contract term sheet.
[07:12] Maya Patel: We'll include a term sheet template.
[07:15] Jonas Reed: I'll start a lightweight bench run on hosted using your embeddings and chat traces once Ravi shares. Expect initial numbers in 5 business days.
[07:25] Ravi Menon: Sounds good. One minor point: any known outages or fallbacks for regional capacity? Customers fear sudden capacity loss.
[07:33] Maya Patel: We have routing and fallback policies — we can route to model variants or alternate regions, and Dedicated has SLA-backed capacity. We'll include our fallback playbook.
[07:42] Diane Cho: Great. That covers most things. Thanks all.
[07:46] Maya Patel: Thank you — Maya to follow up with materials.
[07:50] Sofia Alvarez: Thanks. We'll aim to share sample by end of week.

(Transcript contains occasional transcription noise and mislabels; some product names spelled slightly differently in conversation.)

title: Strip compat-proxy and unify persisted flag schemas
author: Marina Alvarez
text:
Summary: A legacy compatibility proxy and an ad-hoc legacy-flag-mapper were introduced in early rollout phases to accept old client configs and route traffic to fallback handlers. Over time these have become maintenance burden: duplicated telemetry, increased tail latency variance, and brittle conditional logic that blocks safe schema evolution. This ticket removes the compat-proxy and migrates persisted flag keys/configs to a single canonical config-schema v2. The work includes safe migration tooling, operator controls, and a staged rollout with clear observability.

Legacy compat-proxy binary and all HTTP/gRPC routes removed from the runtime and service mesh
Config-schema v2 is the sole accepted on-disk format; v1 reader deprecated and gated behind operator toggle
Migration scripts can perform idempotent dry-runs and produce a migration report listing changed keys
No customer-facing errors attributable to missing legacy keys during a 72h full-ramp window
Telemetry shows no net increase in P99 latency or error-rate > 0.5% vs baseline after full rollout

Create operator-only toggle 'allow_v1_configs' default=false
Run discovery job across S3/DB to enumerate v1 configs and generate migration plan
Execute idempotent migration in dry-run mode and publish report to migration-bucket
Perform controlled migration on a small set of non-critical Dedicated clusters
Flip runtime to reject v1 payloads only after all persisted configs migrated
Remove v1 reader code and compat-proxy from runtime in the final release

Phase 0: Nightly dry-runs for 3 days and manual review of reports
Phase 1 Canary: Migrate 1-2 canary clusters (approx 3% traffic) for 6 hours
Phase 2 Staged: Expand to 20% traffic over 24h if canary stable
Phase 3 Ramp: 60% for 24h with automated health checks and human-on-call
Phase 4 Full: 100% with deprecation notice and archive of v1 artifacts

Unit tests for config parser and migration utilities covering edge cases
Integration tests simulating old-client requests against migrated configs
Contract tests for public API to ensure no behavioural deltas after migration
Load tests at 2x expected peak with traffic shapes that previously hit compat-proxy
Chaos test: kill compat-proxy in staging to validate graceful degradation path

Dedicated customers using custom config loaders may experience failures if not coordinated
Silent behavioural regressions for rare request shapes due to flag-key renames
Alert noise from duplicated metrics during partial rollout could mask true regressions
Edge-case malformed v1 entries may require manual remediation and slow migration

If significant regressions: 1) Pause migration jobs and set 'allow_v1_configs'=true; 2) redeploy previous runtime release to affected shards; 3) run remediation to restore original keys for impacted configs; 4) communicate to customers and schedule follow-up fixes; 5) reopen canary after fixes.

2026-02-16: Architecture review — agreed to consolidate mapping logic into config service
2026-02-22: Discovery job run in staging found ~1.3K v1 configs; 12 clusters with custom loaders detected
2026-03-01: Security requested verification for KMS-wrapped keys during migration; added key-rotation checklist
2026-03-08: Dry-run migration executed on two non-customer clusters; small number of malformed v1 entries reported
2026-03-12: Oncall approved canary window; Derek to execute canary on 2026-03-13

Notify Dedicated customers and Solutions Engineering 72 hours before any migration affecting their clusters. Ensure logs include 'compat_migration' trace ids for at least 30 days. Post-migration, run an analytics job to validate feature-usage metrics and reconcile with pre-migration baseline.
