title: ChatPlay onboarding sandbox demo — streaming, params, retries
author: Alex Mercer
text:
Intro demo of Redwood Hosted Chat/text generation for NimbusApps. Covered streaming behavior, parameter tuning (temperature/top_p/max_tokens), and retry/backoff strategies. Discussed SSO/KMS concerns and criteria for a pilot. Agreed on sandbox access, security docs, and a perf benchmark next week.

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Vega (Redwood Product), Samir Patel (NimbusApps CTO), Jordan Lee (NimbusApps Lead Eng), Maya Chen (NimbusApps Security), Terry Huang (NimbusApps PM)

Auto-generated sections (may be imperfect):
Summary: quick hosted demo, show streaming, show params, answer latency/cost questions, clarify security and data flows.
Action items: see metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: alright hi everyone, thanks for taking time, this is Alex from Redwood Inference, I'm an AE, with me is Priya our SE and Carlos product, uh hi team
[00:08] Samir: hey thanks Alex, Samir here, quick note we have about 40 minutes, we'd like to see a live sandbox run and understand retry behavior, and also want to confirm we can meet our data residency needs
[00:18] Alex: yep perfect, we'll start with a quick orientation to the hosted API and console, then Priya will run a live sandbox demo showing streaming and parameter tweaks, and we'll finish with security stuff and next steps
[00:29] Jordan: cool, high level our use case is an in-app assistant with short back-and-forth conversations, sub 300ms median latency ideal, but we care about cost — we might favor smaller models if quality is good enough
[00:40] Priya: sounds good, thanks Jordan. quick housekeeping, the sandbox we'll use is rate-limited but mirrors prod behavior for streaming and retries. i'll open the playground now — one sec
[00:52] Speaker 1: (typing sounds)
[01:04] Priya: okay loading, i pasted an example chat payload. first thing — streaming: you'll see tokens arrive incrementally over a single SSE stream, that's what we call streaming; it reduces perceived latency since the client sees tokens earlier even if final generation takes longer
[01:18] Terry: question, does streaming hold any extra state on our side? like session cookies or KV cache?
[01:24] Priya: good question, streaming is just the output transport. the runtime still manages the KV cache per conversation if you enable it; that cache lives on the server side (redwood-managed for hosted) unless you run private. you can pin cache ttl or disable prefix caching if you need strict data controls
[01:39] Maya: when you say cache lives on server side — is it encrypted and is it surfaced in logs?
[01:45] Carlos: short answer: cache is encrypted at rest with KMS, and we do not persist raw user PII in audit logs; you can configure retention windows and we have an option to disable certain debugging logs. we'll follow up with the security docs
[01:58] Jordan: nice. back to streaming — can we do chunking instead? we have a websocket-based client that prefers discrete messages
[02:05] Priya: yes, you can consume via websockets or SSE and you can buffer into logical chunks client-side. the responses are the same, it's just transport. we also support callback webhooks if you want server-to-server delivery for completed outputs
[02:18] Samir: ok demo time if that's cool
[02:20] Priya: yep starting with a simple prompt: "You are an assistant that summarizes user messages in one sentence." i'll set temperature to 0.2 and max_tokens to 60. watch the stream
[02:34] [02:34] Priya: (sends request)
[02:38] [02:38] STREAM OUTPUT BEGIN
[02:38] Priya: "User asks for concise summary of meeting notes — assistant provides one-line recap with action items."
[02:44] [02:44] STREAM OUTPUT END
[02:45] Jordan: that was immediate, was it actually streaming or just small output?
[02:50] Priya: small output but still streaming. for longer outputs you'll see partial sentences come through every, say, 50-150 tokens depending on model and batch timing. the runtime tries to flush tokens frequently to reduce tail latency
[03:03] Terry: curious — how do you tune for cost? is temperature tied to cost?
[03:09] Priya: temperature affects randomness not cost. cost is primarily tokens (input + output) and the model choice/size. we recommend smaller quantized variants for high-volume assistant tasks. also prefix caching and batching help amortize cost across similar requests
[03:22] Alex: quick interjection, for your use case — if you have short back-and-forths, enabling conversation-level KV cache and a compact model often gives a good cost/latency tradeoff
[03:33] Samir: what's your recommended retry/backoff pattern if we see transient 503 or timeouts? we want to avoid duplicate messages in the app
[03:40] Priya: typical pattern: idempotency key per user-turn, exponential backoff with jitter, and use the request status endpoints to reconcile if you need strong exactly-once semantics. Redwood returns partial tokens on timeouts if the runtime was able to produce them; we document best-effort semantics — for critical flows we recommend server-side dedupe and using model-side stop tokens to mark completeness
[03:59] Jordan: can you show an example of a retry where the first attempt times out and we resume without double-processing?
[04:06] Priya: sure — i'll simulate a transient by throttling the sandbox to cause a timeout. i'll include an idempotency key in the header and then re-call. watch the IDs
[04:18] [04:18] Priya: (runs simulated request — network hiccup)
[04:28] Priya: first call returned 504 after 10s (sandbox threshold). our client then waited 1s + jitter and retried, the second call found a cached KV snapshot and continued, returning the missing tail tokens — you can avoid showing the duplicate prefix by reconciling using the last received token id or sequence number
[04:46] Samir: that makes sense. what about streaming partials — if a client disconnects mid-stream, do you keep the generation alive server-side?
[04:54] Priya: for hosted with default settings the generation continues for a short grace window and if the client reconnects with the same idempotency key you can resume; otherwise it may be GC'd. in private deployments customers can tune grace windows and longer-term retention policies
[05:10] Maya: from a security lens we need to make sure session data isn't kept longer than 24 hours — is that configurable?
[05:16] Carlos: yes retention is configurable per account and we can set a 24-hour TTL for KV and logs in the pilot. we'll include the configuration snippet in the security docs we share
[05:28] Terry: can you show the Console briefly — how we inspect per-route latency and cost?
[05:33] Alex: sure i'll switch to the console, give me a sec
[05:38] [05:38] Speaker 2: (screen share)
[05:44] Alex: here is the requests dashboard, you can filter by model, route, and time. per-route breakdown shows median/95p latency, token counts, and cost per 1k tokens. there's also a trace we can pull for a single request to see kernel selection and batching behavior
[05:58] Jordan: kernel selection? like GPU kernel?
[06:01] Carlos: yeah, that's an internal detail — the runtime picks optimized kernels based on sequence length and model profile, and you can see a label saying quant_fast or long-seq optimized. it's mostly for our internal tuning but helpful during perf debugging
[06:16] Samir: any hard guarantees on latency for hosted? we may need a 200ms p95 for short queries
[06:22] Priya: hosted has best-effort SLAs; for firm latency SLOs we recommend Dedicated with reserved capacity and pinned model variants. hosted usually hits low latency for small models but can't guarantee a fixed 200ms p95 under heavy bursty traffic
[06:36] Jordan: what about regional routing? can we force traffic to eu-west?
[06:40] Alex: yes you can set routing policy per API key to prefer a region; we also have fallback to nearest region if capacity is full. for strict data residency we offer Private (VPC) deployments
[06:50] Maya: does hosted support customer-managed KMS?
[06:53] Carlos: hosted supports customer-managed KMS integrations for encrypting customer keys, and you can bring your own key in Dedicated or Private as well
[07:02] Terry: any competitors we should know about? we evaluated OtherCloudAI; they had simpler pricing but not the same KV features
[07:09] Alex: yep OtherCloudAI was mentioned earlier, and OpenHost; our differentiator is the production-first controls and observability for inference economics
[07:18] Samir: let's return to parameters — show me how to tune for more deterministic replies, e.g., for legal-sounding copy
[07:24] Priya: set temperature to ~0, top_p can be left at 1.0 or reduced to 0.7 for tighter sampling. also control length with max_tokens and use stop sequences to prevent run-ons. i'll demonstrate with an example: prompt: "Draft a one-paragraph legal-style summary" temp 0.0, top_p 0.7
[07:42] [07:42] Priya: (sends request)
[07:46] [07:46] STREAM OUTPUT BEGIN
[07:46] Priya: "Pursuant to the agreement, the party shall..."
[07:52] [07:52] STREAM OUTPUT END
[07:53] Jordan: looks good — do you have built-in safety filters for hallucinations or PII redaction?
[07:59] Priya: we have content safety checks and optional PII detectors that can redact or flag outputs. for high-sensitivity workloads you can enable stricter filters and human-in-the-loop review hooks
[08:11] Maya: what's in the audit logs? do they include token-level content?
[08:15] Carlos: audit logs include metadata and request hashes by default; you can choose to enable full payload logging for debugging, but it's off by default and auditable. retention configurable
[08:25] Samir: any example of how retries affect cost? if we retry often won't we pay double tokens?
[08:31] Priya: yes retries can increase tokens if the model re-generates the same output; that's why idempotency keys and partial-token reconciliation help. we also recommend short client-side timeouts and backoff so retries occur only when truly necessary
[08:46] Terry: on the SDK side, how do we do streaming in our React native app? we use websockets already
[08:52] Priya: we'll share example snippets; basically open a websocket to /v1/streams with the api key, send the chat messages and read incremental events. SDKs have helper abstractions for reconciling streaming fragments and deduping duplicates
[09:05] [09:05] Speaker 1: (crosstalk)
[09:10] Alex: quick recap before we dive into a short benchmark — agreed next steps are: send sandbox creds, share security docs, run perf test and meet again; any other asks?
[09:20] Samir: can you include cost estimates for 5M tokens/month with a compact model vs large one?
[09:26] Alex: yes we'll include a cost comparison sheet and a recommended profile for your workload
[09:31] Jordan: ok let's run the perf — Priya can you run a 1-min 50-concurrency chat generator against the compact model so we can see latency and error rate?
[09:38] Priya: starting now — this is simulated load using the perf harness, note sandbox throttle may create some retry noise so results are conservative
[09:48] [09:48] (perf run in progress; noise: repeating short logs)
[10:05] Priya: results: median latency 230ms, p95 420ms, error rate 2.5% (mostly induced by sandbox throttle). tokens per response avg 34. i'll capture the full CSV and upload to your CRM note
[10:22] Jordan: thanks, those numbers are promising
[10:25] Maya: security follow-up: I'll validate that the sandbox uses encrypted transit and request that we see an example KMS config; if ok we'll proceed to pilot
[10:35] Alex: great, we'll send the KMS snippet and SOC2 summary today. Priya will run the larger 100-concurrency test and share results by next Friday
[10:45] Terry: one last quick question: if we want model rollouts and canary — can you do percentage-based rollouts?
[10:51] Carlos: yes console supports canary rollouts per route with percentage traffic splits and automatic fallback rules if error > threshold. we'll include a short doc on rollouts
[11:02] Samir: perfect, thanks everyone. feel free to send invites for the pilot kickoff next week
[11:06] Alex: thanks all, we'll follow up. bye
[11:10] End of meeting

Notes on transcription: occasional mislabels (Speaker 1/2) where attendees interjected. Some technical nouns may be transcribed imperfectly (e.g., "KV cache" as "K V cache" or "kernel" as "kernal") — see security docs for canonical terms.

title: Risk-thread notes — SOC2 prep (scratch)
author: Aisha Khan
text:
Quick brain dump while mapping controls to actual product touchpoints — messy. Intended to be a running diary of open questions, small experiments, and what I need to hand off to ENG/SRE/Product later.

Context and goal:
- Prep for SOC2 readiness review (targeting initial readiness check in April).
- Focus: evidence collection for A.1 (access control), A.3 (change management), and A.5 (monitoring/logging) — mapping existing artifacts to common control statements.
- Keep notes about how Hosted/Dedicated/Private deployments differ for evidence (esp. on private where customer-managed KMS comes in).

Things I observed (raw):
- Access control: console uses Okta SSO; service-to-service auth uses mTLS and signed tokens. Need explicit docs for service token rotation frequency and how we revoke (is it in infra-runbook?). Ticket: INF-2345 references token rotation work but not runbook.
- KMS: Hosted uses Redwood KMS (AWS KMS CMKs). Private offering points to customer KMS; evidence trail inconsistent across private installs. Ask PS: what artifacts do we get from on-prem install? (audit logs, KMS policy snapshots).
- Logs: central ELK cluster for hosted, but Dedicated customers may have separate logging sinks; need a matrix of where logs live per deployment type.

Open questions (prioritized):
1) Evidence for user access reviews: who signs off, cadence? Product says quarterly but can't find signed review artifacts for last two quarters. Who owns exec signoff? (ping Lena)
2) Change control: PR approvals exist but change window approvals for infra changes (cluster upgrades) are not consistently captured. Is there a single ticket tag we can query? Maybe use label "maintenance-window" — check with release-eng.
3) Incident response timelines: we have PagerDuty playbooks, but the post-incident review (PIR) template isn't standardized. Need a minimal PIR template for SOC2 evidence.

Quick mapping sketch (control -> artifact examples):
- Logical access: Okta audit export (CSV), identity provider config screenshots, HR termination sync logs (workday -> Okta sync).
- Provisioning/deprovisioning: GitHub org membership change logs, jira tickets for access requests (JIRA-SEC-90), ad-hoc slack approvals — need to capture those in a ticketed workflow or copy of message archived.
- Change management: PR + changelog + deployment runbook (deploy traces from CI). For major infra changes: meeting minutes (release notes) + rollback plan.
- Monitoring: CloudWatch alarms + pager logs + SLI dashboards (console path: Console -> Observability -> Per-route dashboards). Take screenshots with timestamps.

Small checklist (things I can do now):
- [ ] Export Okta org logs for Oct 2025–Mar 2026 (request via SC-ops).
- [ ] Pull list of KMS keys in Hosted account and attach key policy snapshots.
- [ ] Create a minimal PIR template and share in #trust-ops for feedback.
- [ ] Draft a short one-pager on how Private deployments differ for auditors (3 bullets).
- [ ] Tag PRs that included infra changes with "infra-change" and create a saved filter in GitHub.

Notes to self / heuristics:
- For auditors, snapshots/screenshots with timestamps + export files are usually accepted. Keep raw exports though (CSV/JSON) not just screenshots.
- When in doubt, capture both: short explanatory note + primary evidence.
- Lean on PS for private-deploy evidence — they have install checklists but not retained in central repo. Ask to start copying artifact manifest to shared s3.

Potential risks / escalations:
- Private deployments: gaps in centralized evidence (risk: inability to show uniform control implementation). Mitigation: require a minimal evidence kit as part of every private deploy.
- Service tokens: unclear rotation/revocation process — medium risk for access control.
- Audit trail retention: logs are kept for 90 days in some envs; SOC2 reviewers might expect 12 months for certain records. Need policy alignment.

Random fragments / links to stitch into final doc:
- "confluence: CON-SEC-1122" (policy draft for logical access)
- "jira: JIRA-SEC-90" (access review request)
- GH PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/1024 (infra change with deploy notes)
- slack convo (trust-ops #) TS=1679900000 — save permalink

Who to loop in next: Lena (access reviews), Ramon (dedicated/private onboarding evidence), Jaime from release-eng (change window tagging), PS lead (for private installs).

Draft paragraph for auditors (very rough):
"Redwood enforces role-based access through SSO (Okta) and automated provisioning linked to HR. All infrastructure changes are executed through our CI/CD pipeline with PR approvals and documented runbooks; major changes use scheduled maintenance windows and rollback plans. For Private deployments, a standardized evidence kit is produced during on-boarding to demonstrate parity of controls despite customer-managed infrastructure."

Final notes: keep this file informal. I'll convert to a formal control mapping table next sprint. Save TODOs and open Qs as tickets so we don't lose them in Slack.

title: PearlGate Embed Labs
author: Sofia Martinez
text:
CRM snippets + rep notes. Mid-market SaaS, product team building a contextual search layer for their docs + support chat. Current stack: Postgres for metadata, S3 for raw docs, they plan to use Pinecone (trial) but open to integrating Redwood's routing + batch embed generation. Key ask: reliable nightly batch job (5M documents/month, incremental delta) + on-demand embeddings for user queries. Throughput targets: embedding throughput ~400 qps peak during batch windows (they plan parallel workers), semantic search end-to-end latency target <150ms for top-10 retrieval + re-rank. Cost-sensitive: prefer a Dedicated committed capacity plan if unit economics beat hosted at scale. Want clear per-route token cost breakdowns in Console. Security: SOC2 required, SSO/SAML for engineering/admins, KMS for key management, audit logs retained 1 year (customer-facing compliance). Data residency: majority NA but 15% EU customers — asks whether Dedicated can pin region or require VPC peering to EU region. title: Zero-to-POC Canvas + 30/60/90 Facilitation Notes
author: Ethan Rivera
text:
Purpose:
Run a tightly-scoped customer workshop that produces a validated Zero-to-POC Canvas, draft success criteria, and a concrete 30/60/90 rollout plan. Designed for mid-sized product teams evaluating Redwood Dedicated or Private deployments.

Format options (choose one):
- Rapid (90 minutes): high-level alignment + tech spike plan. Use when customer already has stakeholder alignment but needs a quick validation roadmap.
- Standard (3 hours): full canvas, slide walkthrough, interactive mapping wall, and breakout spike design. Recommended for first full-day engagement.
- Deep Dive (half-day): adds architecture whiteboarding and performance acceptance tests. For technically heavy customers.

Prework (send 4 days ahead):
- Short questionnaire (team, primary use case, expected QPS, latency SLO, data residency constraints).
- Ask for one representative prompt set or a sample conversation flow (for chat use cases) and a small dataset for embedding/retrieval tests.

Agenda (3-hour, standard):
- 0:00–0:10 — Welcome + goals (Facilitator): set expectations; confirm outcomes.
- 0:10–0:30 — Customer context & constraints (Customer leads): product goals, users, privacy/regulatory must-haves. Capture on the canvas.
- 0:30–0:50 — Success Criteria workshop (Group): define 3 measurable success metrics (e.g., 95th p99 latency < 300ms, inference cost <$0.03/token, end-user satisfaction > 4/5). Prioritize.
- 0:50–1:20 — Architecture options & tradeoffs (Facilitator + Eng): hosted vs dedicated vs private; routing/fallback policies; data flow diagram. Use whiteboard.
- 1:20–1:35 — Break (short)
- 1:35–2:05 — Hands-on mapping wall (Interactive): map data sources, privacy touchpoints, and model artifacts to deployment options. Dot-vote risks and unknowns.
- 2:05–2:35 — Experiment design & quick wins (Breakouts): design 2 small validation spikes (one functional correctness, one performance/cost). Document acceptance criteria and estimated effort.
- 2:35–2:50 — 30/60/90 draft plan (Facilitator): align owners and milestones, dependencies, and go/no-go gates.
- 2:50–3:00 — Next steps & commitments (Wrap): agree on deliverables, dates, and communication cadence.

Zero-to-POC Canvas (one-page deliverable — fill during session):
- Use case summary: 1–2 lines.
- Primary personas & business KPIs: list.
- Must-have compliance/controls: list.
- Traffic profile: expected QPS, peak concurrency, avg sequence length.
- Latency & cost targets: hard SLOs and soft targets.
- Recommended deployment mode: hosted | dedicated | private (with rationale).
- Minimal viable model and fallback: model family, quantization/size recommendation, fallback policy.
- Data path & residency: inbound sources, logging, PII handling, retention.
- Success metrics & acceptance criteria (3 items).
- 2 validation spikes (title, owner, success criteria, estimated effort in days).
- 30/60/90 milestones (see below).

Sample slide outline (10–12 slides, short deck to leave with customer):
1) Title + objective (one sentence). Speaker note: what problem we solve together.
2) Agenda & deliverables from today.
3) Customer context snapshot (pulled from prework).
4) Zero-to-POC Canvas (visual one-pager).
5) Deployment tradeoffs (hosted/dedicated/private) — pros/cons table.
6) Measurement & acceptance strategy (latency, cost, quality).
7) Validation spikes (two experiments with owners & timelines).
8) 30/60/90 rollout plan (milestones).
9) Risk register & mitigation (top 5).
10) Operational considerations (observability, rollouts, fallback).
11) Pricing/commitment ask (if applicable).
12) Next steps & owners.

Facilitation notes (tips and micro-scripts):
- Opening: "We’ll leave today with a one-page POC plan and two experiments you can run within 2–4 weeks."
- When getting stuck on scope: use the "no-more-than-3" rule — at most 3 KPIs, 3 stakeholders, 3 technical unknowns for the POC.
- Dot-vote technique: give each participant 3 dots to allocate across risks/unknowns. Use top-3 as spike focus.
- Timeboxing: call out remaining time at 5-minute marks; assign someone as timekeeper.
- Handling disagreements on deployment: refocus on acceptance criteria. Ask "Which deployment lets us test the primary success metric fastest?"

Breakout templates (copy into a doc during workshop):
- Spike title
- Hypothesis (one sentence)
- Data required
- Steps (1–5 bullets)
- Success criteria (explicit measurement)
- Owner & estimate (days)

30/60/90 Example plan (deliverable to leave with customer):
- Day 0–30 (Discovery & fast validation):
 - Finalize POC scope, run spike 1 (functional) and spike 2 (performance), deliver sample outputs.
 - Deliverable: working notebook + perf report (p95/p99, token cost).
 - Owner: Solutions Eng (initial), Customer Eng.
- Day 31–60 (Integration & ops):
 - Integrate model into staging path, add tracing/cost telemetry, run canary with subset of traffic.
 - Deliverable: staging endpoint, alerts, dashboard.
 - Owner: Customer infra + Redwood SRE/Eng.
- Day 61–90 (Scale & handoff):
 - Scale tests to expected QPS, finalize security controls, sign-off on go/no-go gates.
 - Deliverable: runbook, SLA checklist, go-live date recommendation.
 - Owner: Product + Customer Ops.

Acceptance gates (go/no-go):
- Quality gate: model meets baseline precision/recall or user satisfaction target on representative dataset.
- Performance gate: meets latency SLOs at target load with acceptable cost.
- Compliance gate: data handling and encryption meet stated requirements.

Top risks & mitigations (to capture on mapping wall):
- Unknown: sample data incompatibility. Mitigation: sample ingestion spike day 1.
- Unknown: auth/integration complexity (SAML, internal proxies). Mitigation: early security sync and integration checklist.
- Risk: cost overrun on inference. Mitigation: use smaller quantized model for canary + Redwood Optimize recommendations.

Deliverables to produce within 5 business days after workshop:
- Filled Zero-to-POC Canvas (single page).
- Two spike runbooks and owners.
- Draft 30/60/90 with milestones and owners.
- Shared slide deck (10–12 slides) and a short summary email template to reach execs.

Checklist for SE before running the workshop:
- Send prework and collect responses.
- Build a starter canvas and pre-populate known fields.
- Provision a lightweight test harness (notebook + token) to demo quick model outputs.
- Prepare mapping wall materials (virtual Miro board or physical sticky notes).
- Confirm attendees include 1 exec sponsor, 1 engineering lead, 1 product owner, 1 security/infra contact.

Follow-up email skeleton (one-paragraph + attachments):
- Opening line: thank you + one-sentence outcome.
- Attachments: canvas, slides, spike runbooks, 30/60/90 plan.
- Call to action: confirm owners and two-week check-in date.

Notes from recent customer run (lessons learned):
- Customers often under-estimate the cost variance between dev and production traffic patterns — show a cost band example early.
- Early encryption/key management conversations avoid late delays for Private deployments.
- Small, high-confidence spikes build trust faster than large, ambiguous proofs.

Outcomes (intended):
- A signed-off POC scope and timeline.
- Two rapid validation spikes with owners and explicit success metrics.
- A clear 30/60/90 roadmap that ties to business KPIs.

Quick reference (one-liners):
- If asked about latency vs cost: "We trade latency for cost via batching/quantization and routing policies — measure both on your sample workload."
- If asked about model drift: "Schedule a quality regression checkpoint in the 60-day milestone tied to production prompts."

End of document.

title: HyperOnboard: Role Launch Snapshot and 30-90 Activation Template
author: Maya Patel
text:
Purpose: quick, reusable working template to take a candidate through offer acceptance to contribution in 30/60/90 days. Combine a compact hiring plan, a measurable interview rubric, and a pragmatic onboarding checklist that managers and POs can copy-edit for specific roles.

Status and intent: working draft for FY26 hiring sprints (early trials with infra and platform-engineering hiring waves). This is intentionally opinionated about signals we care about (ramp speed, cross-team communication, test-driven ownership). Use as a baseline; annotate with role-specific tasks and replace TODOs.

Quick orientation (one-liner): HyperOnboard is a "launch packet"—a short, shareable checklist + rubric to align hiring, the hiring manager, mentor/buddy, and recruiting operations on acceptance -> day 90 outcomes.

Scope: ICs (IC2–IC5) across engineering, product, and SRE. Not a replacement for full People Ops handbook; intended to accelerate first-90 days and instrument early quality signals for hiring calibration.

Hiring plan snapshot (for manager + recruiter):
- Hiring signal: 2–3 concrete deliverables expected in first 90 days (choose 1 fast win in month 1, 1 impact work in month 2, 1 cross-team deliverable by month 3).
- Timeline: Week 0: offer & logistics; Week 1: shadow + infra access; Week 2–4: small shipable task; Month 2: feature/infra milestone; Month 3: cross-team rollout + owner handoff.
- Interview loop (baseline for eng roles): Recruit screen (30m) -> Hiring manager (45m) -> Two technical rounds (60m each: system design + code pairing) -> Collaboration/communication round (30–45m) -> Exec/skip-level if IC4+ (30m). Total on-site loop time 3.5–4.5 hours.
- Comms: recruiting to post-offer email should include role launch snapshot (this doc), buddy assignment, first-week calendar skeleton, and links to requisite access checklists.

Offer packet checklist (ops items to complete before start):
- Signed offer + I-9 (if applicable)
- Manager assigned, buddy assigned, and initial 1:1 scheduled for day 1
- Infra access requests issued (jira access + repo perms + cloud console)
- Workstation shipped or on-site booking confirmed
- Security & compliance onboarding assigned (if private deployment/regulatory customer)
- Prestart reading pack shared (team RFCs, relevant incidents, current PRs)

Interview rubric (single-page, numerical scale 1–5, with anchor examples). Use for calibration and debrief notes. Keep score fields in ATS but capture qualitative: examples, gaps, and evidence.
- Areas and anchors:
 - Technical correctness (1–5): Can the candidate implement correct, maintainable code during pairing and explain tradeoffs? Anchors: 5 = correct and robust solution with edge cases and tests; 3 = correct but brittle or missing edge cases; 1 = incorrect or major misconceptions.
 - System design (1–5): Ability to decompose requirements, propose measurable SLAs, identify bottlenecks, and consider operational costs. Anchors: 5 = clear architecture + failure modes + rollout plan; 2 = vague tradeoffs, misses core ops concerns.
 - Product sense & impact orientation (1–5): Prioritization, outcome-thinking, ability to tie technical choices to user/business impact. Anchors: 5 = identifies measurable metrics and tradeoffs; 1 = overly academic solutions with no product tie.
 - Collaboration & communication (1–5): Clarity of explanations, receptive to feedback, cross-functional mindset. Anchors: 5 = proactive clarifying, invites feedback; 2 = closed off or unclear.
 - Ownership & learning velocity (1–5): Evidence of shipping end-to-end, learning new domains quickly. Anchors: 5 = repeated examples of shipping and improving systems; 1 = no evidence of ownership.
 - Cultural/values fit (1–5): Evidence of glue work, candidate’s ability to operate in high-performance, ambiguous environments. Anchors: 5 = pragmatic, bias for action, clear examples; 1 = passive.
- Interview debrief template (copy into ATS notes): "Top strengths (2–3): ...
 Top risks (2–3): ...
 Required onboarding supports if hired: ...
 Recommended 30/60/90 milestones: ..."

Onboarding checklist (practical, manager-first):
- Pre-day-1 (recruiting + manager): welcome doc + first-week calendar sent; Slack invite; send buddy intro email; create required infra tickets; create first-ticket for fast-win task (estimate <3 days).
- Day 1: 1:1 with manager (30–60m) covering role context + 30/60/90 goals; team lunch (virtual/in-person); buddy walkthrough of repos and dev flow; confirm access to ticketing and CI.
- Day 2–5: environment setup validation (local dev, tests pass), complete required security trainings, pair on the fast-win task with buddy, first-week retrospective on Friday (30m).
- Week 2–4: ship fast-win (owner signs off), start second deliverable (mentor-guided), scheduled sync with adjacent team leads.
- Month 1 manager check (end of month): evidence review of fast-win, signal check on documentation contributions, feedback conversation and adjustments to 30/60/90.
- Month 2: take ownership of a mid-scale deliverable, lead a small design doc, participate in oncall rotation shadow if applicable.
- Month 3: lead cross-team rollout or ship major milestone; provide retrospective + proposal for ongoing ownership.

Manager checklist and risk mitigations:
- Before start: confirm buddy and first-ticket exist.
- Weekly 1:1 agenda template: 5m personal check-in, 10m blockers, 20m skill-building or project planning, 10m feedback loop.
- Escalation triggers (email to p-ops + hiring manager): not shipping a measurable artifact by day 30, ongoing access blockers >48h, repeated missing meetings.

Buddy playbook (short):
- First 2 weeks: pair 3x for 90–120m on dev flow and codebase.
- Provide curated list of 6–8 reading items (design docs, incidents, coding standards).
- Shadowing: 2 oncall tickets, 1 deploy cycle.

Evaluation signals (early):
- Technical: able to run test suite locally and fix one failing test in week 1.
- Product: articulates impact metric for a fast-win by end of week 1.
- Collaboration: schedules and leads at least one cross-team sync by week 4.
- Ownership: closes owner-assigned ticket with PR and reviewer responses in <2 weeks.

Template: 30/60/90 milestones (copyable):
- 30 days (learn & ship): complete environment, ship small bug/feature, present learnings to team.
- 60 days (own & expand): own a component or endpoint, reduce latency/bug rate or deliver feature scope, mentor newcomer pairing.
- 90 days (integrate & lead): lead a cross-team launch or own SLA for a subservice, propose roadmap items.

Recruiting playbook notes (ops & interviewer hints):
- Recruiter checklist: send role launch snapshot with offer email; collect candidate prestart constraints (visa, hardware needs); confirm buddy availability.
- Interviewers: focus on concrete examples. Ask for "past 2–3 months shipped work" and one code example. Rate on evidence, not potential.
- Calibration: every hiring round should include at least one calibrated interviewer (eng lead who has completed calibration exercise in last 6 months).

Open questions / TODOs (working):
- Define explicit ramp metrics per org (platform vs. product eng) — who owns this? action: Priya to draft baseline by 2026-02-12.
- Should we require a documented 90-day plan in the offer packet for IC4+? pros/cons noted (clarity vs. inflexibility).
- Add a short checklist for Private deployments hires (HSM/KMS onboarding).

Sample email snippets (copyable):
- Pre-start welcome: "Congrats and welcome — attached is a short launch snapshot with your first-week calendar, your assigned buddy (NAME), and a link to our quick-start repo. Please complete the short security training before day 3."
- Manager day-1 note: "Hi NAME — excited to have you. Today we'll cover role context and your first-week goals. Please bring questions about accounts/access. Expect a walking tour of current work and an intro to the fast-win ticket."

Notes-to-self / working artifacts:
- Keep this doc <2 pages for offer attachments. Expanded examples belong in Role Launch Library (linked_artifacts).
- Run a pilot with 6 hires in Q1 2026 and collect manager/buddy NPS at day 30 and day 90.

Version history: 0.1 draft — initial template compiled from hiring interviews, manager feedback, and recent onboarding retros (nov 2025–feb 2026).

Appendix (quick checklist for recruiter to paste into ATS notes):
- OfferStatus: signed/unsigned
- BuddyAssigned: yes/no
- FirstTicketCreated: ticket-id
- WorkstationShipped: yes/no
- SecurityTrainingAssigned: yes/no

End of HyperOnboard template. Copy, edit, and iterate.

title: Staggered canary burst: pin inconsistency causes subset of requests to reroute to legacy variant
text:
Issue summary:
During a staggered canary rollout for rw-instruct-7b-v3 in us-east-1, NimbleApps reported ~12% of their requests being served by an older model variant despite an explicit tenant-level model pin. The behavior lasted for ~45 minutes and coincided with an autoscaler prewarm burst triggered by a traffic spike.

Impact:
- Customer reported mixed outputs and downstream feature regressions for active users (measured anomalous quality score increase and user complaints).
- Approximately 11k requests affected for the customer across the incident window.

Environment:
- Production, us-east-1, Dedicated pool for NimbleApps (reserved capacity pool id: ded-342)

2025-11-02 Priya Singh (Support): Customer opened chat reporting that a portion of requests are returning legacy responses after we started the canary. They provided request IDs and timestamps. Asked to triage asap.
2025-11-02 Liam Chen (SRE): Acknowledged; collecting edge logs and routing snapshots. Initial hypothesis: pin commit race between orchestrator commit and edge cookie rotation during prewarm handoff.
2025-11-03 SRE-team (Liam Chen): Found routing mesh epochs where cohort snapshot contained mixed variant entries for tenant nimbleapps-17. Edge logs show affinity cookie TTL renewal at the same second as prewarm probe success; some flows lost pin before orchestrator snapshot completed.
2025-11-04 Support (Priya Singh) -> Customer: Confirmed we are rolling a targeted hotfix that changes prewarm handshake ordering to commit pins before edge cookie rotation. Asked customer for traffic window to cutover safely.
2025-11-05 NimbleApps (Customer): Verified behaviour has ceased after cutover; provided sampling confirming no legacy outputs in a 1h window post-fix. Thanked on call for quick turnaround.

What we observed:
- Autoscaler prewarm created N new prewarm nodes at t0+12s in response to surge.
- Prewarm handshake had a non-atomic ordering: node marked healthy -> edge cookie rotation -> orchestrator snapshot commit.
- In ~9% of sampled requests, edge rotated tenant affinity cookie just before orchestrator committed the new pin mapping, causing requests to land on edge shards that still resolved the tenant to the legacy variant.
- Orchestrator snapshots showed an overlapping epoch where two different routing tables were readable by different edge shards for ~18s.
- No GPU OOMs or serving runtime crashes found. Latency remained within SLO except for slight tail increase during the handoff window.

Hypotheses considered and eliminated:
- Tokenization mismatch in the model: rejected after verifying request payloads and embeddings.
- Customer-side pinned version misconfiguration: rejected; tenant manifest showed explicit pin to rw-instruct-7b-v3 prior to rollout.

Contributing factors:
- Prewarm handshake ordering (health -> rotate cookie -> commit) is non-atomic across control-plane and edge.
- Edge cookie rotation TTL is short and coincided with the commit window during a burst.
- Canary scheduling used staggered slice times (0s, +10s, +20s) which increased overlap surface for commit windows across shards.

Immediate mitigations applied:
1) Rolled a hotfix to orchestrator to change prewarm handshake ordering: commit pin mapping before issuing edge cookie rotation. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/orchestrator/pull/3184. Deployed to us-east-1 dedicated pools at 2025-11-04T04:00Z.
2) Increased health-probe smoothing for prewarm nodes to reduce transient epoch changes during bursts.
3) Added a guard in edge-proxy to prefer orchestrator pin mapping when epoch differences detected within a 30s window.

Rollout notes:
- Hotfix applied via canary (5% -> 25% -> 100%) over a 3-hour window for dedicated pools; monitored cohort pins and customer telemetry.
- Post-deployment checks (logs + sampling from NimbleApps) showed 0% legacy-routed requests in the 1h stable window.

Follow-ups and action items:
- Engineering to add an orchestrator unit test that asserts prewarm handshake atomicity across control-plane and edge (owner: Liam Chen, target: 2025-11-12).
- Create a capacity-surge playbook to avoid staggered slice overlap during autoscaler prewarm (owner: Product, target: 2025-11-20).
- Postmortem scheduled and linked: https://confluence.redwood.ai/postmortems/SUP-209876-postmortem

Customer communication:
- Notified NimbleApps via support and scheduled an incident review call. Customer confirmed remediation and accepted workaround as final resolution.

title: Evidence-driven offer evaluation and onboarding trigger playbook
author: Nina R. Shah
text:
Summary:
This playbook defines a measurable, evidence-driven process for offer evaluation and the automated triggering of role-specific onboarding pathways at Redwood Inference. It replaces ad-hoc offer decisions and fragmented onboarding handoffs with a single decision matrix, a negotiation and risk log, and concrete onboarding triggers tied to role risk, compliance needs, and ramp objectives.

Who this is for:
- Hiring managers
- Recruiters and Talent Acquisition
- HR Business Partners (HRBPs)
- People Ops specialists who build onboarding curricula
- Legal and Finance for offer approvals

Goals and principles:
- Make offer decisions transparent and auditable using a standardized scorecard.
- Reduce time-to-offer while preserving quality of decision-making (target: 48-hour typical offer SLA from verbal approval).
- Trigger onboarding pathways automatically based on objective signals (role, clearance, vendor status, critical deliverables).
- Record negotiation outcomes and commitments centrally for manager and HR ownership.

Key owners and roles:
- Recruiter: manage candidate communications, prepare initial offer package, populate scorecard.
- Hiring Manager: complete technical/cultural evaluation, set ramp objectives, confirm L4/L5+ approvals.
- HRBP: ensure compliance with compensation bands and local labor law; finalize benefits language.
- Finance: sign-off on salary above band midpoint + 15% (approval threshold).
- Legal: review for contractor/consultant engagements and NDAs.

Offer evaluation process (step-by-step):
1) Populate Offer Scorecard (required before verbal offer)
 - Responsible: Recruiter + Hiring Manager
 - Required fields: role level, base salary proposed, equity award, bonus eligibility, reason for hire, candidate score (0–5) across: technical fit, problem-solving, role-specific skills, team fit, ramp risk.
 - Attach: interview scorecards, reference-check notes, and compensation benchmarking snapshot.

2) Automated Decision Matrix applies
 - If candidate_score >= 4.0 AND proposed_comp <= band_midpoint + 10% -> auto-approve (Recruiter/HRBP finalize).
 - If candidate_score between 3.0–4.0 OR proposed_comp between band_midpoint + 10% and +25% -> HRBP + Hiring Manager sign-off required.
 - If candidate_score < 3.0 OR proposed_comp > band_midpoint + 25% OR offer contains atypical clauses -> Finance + Legal review and exec sponsor.

3) Negotiation and Risk Log (template)
 - Fields to capture: candidate_request (text), impact_on_budget (Y/N), manager_commitments (Y/N), date, negotiator name, final decision.
 - All negotiated deviations from the standard package must be recorded and stored in the candidate dossier.

4) Offer SLA targets
 - Verbal offer: within 48 hours of decision to hire.
 - Written offer (signed by HRBP/Legal): within 72 hours of verbal acceptance.
 - Exception path: roles requiring external contractor conversion, export control, or security clearance: review window up to 10 business days.

Offer Scorecard (required fields — flat table representation)
- candidate_name | role | level | technical_score (0-5) | problem_solving (0-5) | team_fit (0-5) | ramp_risk (low/med/high) | aggregate_score (0-5) | proposed_comp_pct_vs_band_mid | approvals_required

Decision and approval thresholds (examples)
- Aggregate score >= 4.0 and comp <= +10% => Recruiter + HRBP sign.
- Aggregate score 3.0–3.9 or comp +10%–+25% => Hiring Manager + HRBP required.
- Aggregate score < 3.0 or comp > +25% => Finance + Legal + Exec sponsor.

Onboarding trigger taxonomy
This section maps objective signals in the scorecard and offer to an onboarding pathway. Triggers are evaluated automatically by the People Ops intake system when the candidate signs the offer.
- Role risk triggers (immediately escalate): access to PII/PHI, admin network access, SOC2 high-impact role. => Trigger: Restricted onboarding pathway (security clearance checklist, 1:1 with Security engineer before first day).
- Compliance triggers: EEA employment, contractor vs. employee conversion, background check flags. => Trigger: Extended HR/Legal onboarding (pre-hire paperwork, local labor compliance steps).
- Ramp-critical triggers: role with measurable Q1 deliverables or cross-team dependencies. => Trigger: accelerated immersion track (prestart reading list, assigned buddy, condensed 30-day objectives).
- Remote/new-country triggers: candidate located outside primary region or requiring relocation. => Trigger: remote-localization packet and payroll/accounting enrollment steps.

Onboarding pathways (short descriptions)
- Core Standard Onboarding: baseline 90-day plan with security training, benefits enrollment, manager 30/60/90 goals and weekly 1:1 cadence.
- Restricted Onboarding: additional security orientation, expedited IAM provisioning, elevated audit logging for first 30 days.
- Accelerated Immersion: preboarding reading checklist, assigned project with narrow scope, daily standups first 2 weeks, weekly deliverable reviews.
- Compliance-Extended: staged paperwork, legal sign-offs, delayed access to production until checks complete.

Manager checklist (first 30/60/90 — condensed)
- Day 0–7: complete role-specific equipment and access; schedule 30/60/90 goal alignment; introduce to buddy; assign first-week small deliverable.
- Day 8–30: weekly check-ins; confirm completion of security and compliance training; evaluate initial pass/fail on deliverable; adjust ramp plan.
- Day 31–90: bi-weekly checkpoints; evaluate against three core KPIs defined at offer; formal 90-day calibration with HRBP.

Metrics and reporting:
- Offer conversion rate (verbal -> signed) target: >= 85%.
- Time-to-offer median: <= 4 days.
- Offer approval exceptions: logged and reviewed monthly; target fewer than 5% of hires.
- Onboarding pathway accuracy: measure after 90 days if assigned pathway matched actual risk/need; target >= 90% correct routing.

Escalation and exceptions:
- Use the Hiring Exception queue for unusual packages. Exception requests must include business justification, alternate candidates considered, and an ROI statement.
- Exceptions older than 7 days without approval auto-escalate to People Ops Director.

Templates and artifacts (examples to copy into ATS or People Ops system):
1) Negotiation log CSV header: date, negotiator, field_changed, candidate_request, decision, cost_delta_to_budget, manager_comment
2) Offer email snippet: "We are excited to extend the role of <ROLE> at Redwood Inference. Your base salary will be <AMOUNT>, equity <DETAILS>, and benefits <LINK>. Please review the attached offer and return a signed copy by <DATE>."
3) 30/60/90 Goals template: three objectives per period, success criteria, owner, and measurement method.

Related playbooks and references:
- Structured hiring committee protocol (link in related_pages).
- Manager 30/60/90 templates (People Ops templates library).

Revision history and governance:
- This playbook is maintained by People Ops (owner: Nina R. Shah).
- Review cycle: annually or after any significant comp band or legal change.
- Change approvals: HRBP + Head of People for policy changes; People Ops Director for process changes.

Appendix: example offer approval email subject
- Subject: "Approval Request: Offer for <Candidate Name> — Role <Role> — Level <L#> — Compensation uplift <+X%>"

End of document.

title: Pillarhaven Insightworks
author: Ethan Brooks
text:
Run 2-week Hosted API POC with parity test suite; prepare Dedicated pricing proposal and capacity options; schedule security QA kickoff.

Context: Pillarhaven is a mid-market B2B SaaS (product analytics + in-app help). Currently on OpenAI for chat & embeddings; runs ~120k monthly tokens (prod), expect growth to 700k within 12 months. Primary driver: lower inference unit costs + predictable latency for in-app assistant and automated summarization. Secondary driver: regulatory requirement for stronger audit trails and ability to isolate data in a VPC when migrating to Dedicated.

Key quotes / call highlights:
- "We need output parity for top-5 prompts before we flip traffic; customers notice tone changes." (Head of Product)
- "Pricing predictability matters more than absolute lowest cost — committed capacity + burst are attractive." (VP Eng)

Technical / evaluation details (POC scope):
- Workloads: multi-turn chat (support assistant), long-doc summarization (1k-10k tokens), embeddings for semantic search and reranking.
- Latency targets: 95th percentile < 250ms for <512 token chat responses in Dedicated; Hosted POC target < 300ms at test QPS.
- Throughput: baseline 50 qps peak for chat, 200 qps for bulk embedding jobs (batching acceptable).
- Migration needs: OpenAI-compat API behavior (messages schema, streaming semantics, stop sequences), token counting parity, and identical temperature/penalty mapping.
- Parity testing: run 2k representative prompts through Redwood hosted API with compat layer; compare semantic similarity (embeddings), ROUGE/BLEU and human review for summarization; target regressions <3% on critical prompts.

2026-01-12: Inbound lead from product blog; initial qualification by AE Ethan Brooks.
2026-01-20: Hosted API demo (chat+embeddings) - AE + SE (Priya). Fireflies ff_20260120_9b3f.
2026-02-05: Security call - infra asks about KMS, VPC peering, retention; provided SOC2 evidence.
2026-02-12: Pricing sync - asked for committed throughput tiers and burst allowances; discussed committed-discount model.
2026-02-20: POC kickoff approved - 2-week hosted POC, dataset = 5k historical support chats + 1k long-docs for summarization.
2026-02-26: Parity test run 1 - embeddings parity OK, summarization shows style/regression differences on ~8% samples.
2026-02-28: Internal Redwood follow-up: propose mapping rules for prompt compatibility + regression mitigation plan.

openai_compat_layer
prompt_parity_suite
evals_integration
latency_95p<250ms
throughput_200qps
kv_cache_support

Interested in committed Dedicated tier with monthly commit. Key negotiation items: commit size that covers peak QPS + 20% burst, overage pricing, migration credit for Hosted POC months, and transition timeline (30-60 days). Asked for blended ARR estimate and TCO comparison vs current vendor.

Phase 1: Hosted POC using OpenAI-compat shim + prompt parity tests. Phase 2: Pilot on Dedicated (small reserved pool) with VPC peering and KMS. Phase 3: Cutover using blue/green traffic split and regression monitor; fall back to original provider for 14 days if regressions exceed threshold.

Medium. Biggest risks: subtle prompt-output drift on summarization and code-like responses; SSO/SAML timing for enterprise SSO; contract terms for data residency. Mitigations: run human-in-the-loop comparisons during POC, tune quantization/profile recommendations from Redwood Optimize, schedule SAML integration early.

1) Upload canonical prompt set & 2k sample chats to POC sandbox (engineering to provide). 2) SE to deliver parity-run plan + baseline metrics by 2026-03-04. 3) Redwood to send Dedicated term sheet and committed tier options by 2026-03-10. 4) Schedule security QA with Pillarhaven infra week of 2026-03-08.

title: Bounded-window KV cache with adaptive backpressure and graceful GPU-OOM fallback
author: Leah Morgan
text:
Context: We're seeing tail-latency spikes and intermittent GPU OOMs in multi-tenant serving when long sequences lead to large KV residency. Current paged/blocked KV designs reduce average memory but cause sudden allocation pressure and head-of-line stalls when many long-context requests overlap.

Problem statement: We need a practical runtime-level strategy that: 1) bounds per-request KV working set growth using a windowed retention model, 2) signals and smooths load to upstream scheduling to avoid synchronous OOM cascades, and 3) provides a deterministic fallback path that preserves latency SLOs for short requests while allowing long requests to continue with degraded throughput.

Proposal summary: Implement a "bounded-window KV" mode that splits KV residency into fixed-duration windows (logical time slices of attention history) with the following features: 
- Soft retention limits per-request (N windows) with an LRU-like priority inside each window.
- Adaptive backpressure signals exposed to the scheduler: soft_shed and holdback tokens that throttle batching and admission for requests that would push resident set above a dynamic high-water mark.
- Graceful OOM fallback: when hard limit is reached, use a prioritized partial-eviction strategy (drop older windows for low-priority requests while preserving most-recent window + KV prefix cache for high-priority/latency-sensitive traffic).

Why different from existing approaches: Unlike slab-only or chunked allocators, windowed retention encodes temporal locality at a coarse granularity that simplifies eviction math and gives predictable worst-case resident set sizes. Combining this with explicit backpressure tokens reduces synchronous eviction storms that previously caused cascading tail latency.

Design links and artifacts: 
- Design doc (internal Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Bounded-Window-KV-Design
- Simulation notebooks (Drive): https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/1-window-sim
- Microbench harness (GitHub): https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra-kv-sim/pull/67

Implementation plan: 
1) Runtime data structure: implement per-request window table metadata (compact 16B entries per window pointer) and a global residency counter that tracks resident bytes per-window-weighted.
2) Admission controller: expose tokens from an admission service that inspects current residency vs. dynamic target and returns admit / delay / shed directives. Integrate with batching pipeline to delay low-priority requests before they enter KV allocations.
3) Eviction policy: prioritized window eviction with per-request priority and age heuristics. Implement fast path that can drop entire oldest windows without touching inner-page structures to keep CPU costs minimal.
4) Fallback path: for requests delayed or partially-evicted, route to a best-effort streaming execution that sacrifices throughput (smaller KV context, truncated attention) but keeps token latency within SLO for the top-k critical requests.

Performance targets: 
- Keep P95 token-level latency increase < 10% for latency-tier traffic under memory pressure test harness.
- Reduce frequency of GPU OOM events to < 1 per 10M tokens in stress tests.
- Maintain aggregate throughput > 75% of baseline for mixed workload in degraded mode.

Trade-offs and open questions: 
- Granularity of window: 64-token windows vs 256-token windows — larger windows give higher retention efficiency but coarser eviction control. Simulation suggests 128-token windows hit a good sweet spot for typical request distributions.
- Admission latency vs batching benefits: delaying requests to avoid OOM can reduce batch sizes and hurt throughput for some workloads. We plan conservative holdback thresholds tuned per-customer tier.
- Memory accounting complexity: per-window accounting gives predictable bounds but increases meta-data overhead; we aim for <0.6% memory overhead at 1M concurrent windows.

Acceptance criteria:

Runtime exposes bounded-window mode toggled by config flag and defaults to off
Admission controller returns admit/delay/shed and integrates with existing batching pipeline
Eviction path can drop whole windows atomically without per-token ops
Benchmarks: P95 token latency delta < 10% for latency-tier traffic under stress
OOMs reduced to <1 per 10M tokens in stress harness
Documentation: Design doc, runbook, and operator dashboard tile for resident set and token holdback metrics

ENG-48961-1: implement per-request window metadata and residency counters
ENG-48961-2: admission controller API and scheduler integration
ENG-48961-3: prioritized window eviction fast-path
ENG-48961-4: fallback streaming execution path for truncated KV context
ENG-48961-5: end-to-end benchmarks and fault-injection tests
ENG-48961-6: docs, runbook, and dashboard

13-Feb: initial spike analysis — long tails caused by overlapping long-context interactive sessions from internal partner. Traces attached in Confluence.
02-Mar: simulation shows 128-token windows reduced peak resident set by ~38% for mixed workload; see sim notebook.
05-Mar: design review with SRE and Runtime teams — agreed on token-based admission and prioritized eviction. Follow-up: refine holdback thresholds per-customer tier.
09-Mar: prototype PR merged (partial): https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/2345 — includes window metadata and basic eviction. Next: admission controller integration.
12-Mar: stress run with prototype produced 3 OOMs over 50M tokens; failure analysis points to race when admission delayed batches are re-inserted. Plan: add epoch-based admission tokens to avoid double-allocation.

Amit: Started implementation of the window table. Need review for atomic updates pattern to avoid contention on high qps paths.
Rosa (SRE): Please add metrics for 'holdback_count' and 'shed_count' and a histogram of delay durations. We'll hook alerts to those metrics.
Kyle (PM): Prioritize fallbacks for enterprise tier to preserve interactive UX; lower tiers can accept higher shed rates.
Leah: I'll schedule a follow-up demo after admission controller integration — aiming 2026-03-22.
PR links: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/2345, https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra-kv-sim/pull/67

title: Trailing silence and incomplete final JSON when re-establishing SSE after iOS connection warm-up behind Apple HTTP proxy
text:
Issue summary: Customer reports SSE streaming sessions ending with a trailing silence and an incomplete final JSON object after an iOS client (managed device) reconnects. The client receives a partial JSON payload (closing bracket missing or truncated final text) but the stream does not emit an explicit terminal event. Impact: Customer's app shows 'incomplete' responses for ~5-15% of long-running streams on iOS 15/16 devices behind the Apple HTTP proxy used in their MDM. This affects Generation and Chat endpoints and causes user-visible corruption in message endings. Environment: prod-us-west, customer using our hosted API via SDK v1.12.0, mobile network: corporate Wi-Fi with Apple HTTP proxy/transparent caching. Observed: - Session logs show a short idle period then a socket rebind/hand-off from device path manager. - Edge logs include: "connection: id=sk-8765 partial_close=true late_fin=true" and serving-runtime logs show "stalled-flush: true" for the stream session. - Client-side: SDK reports reconnect, normal resume handshake, then receives no explicit "[DONE]"-like event or end-of-stream marker; final JSON block is truncated. Steps to reproduce (customer-provided): 1) Start a long streaming generation (>120s) on iOS device on corp Wi-Fi. 2) Background the app for ~10s then bring it to foreground. 3) Observe stream reconnect and final payload missing trailing characters. Expected: stream resumes and emits final terminal event or complete JSON. Observed: trailing silence and truncated final object. Additional notes: Issue more frequent when device OS performs a connection warm-up (path negotiation) or when Apple HTTP proxy inserts an intermediary probe. This appears different from standard proxy chunking issues we've seen previously because the connection close code sequence is unusual (delayed FIN coalesced with keepalive).

[edge-2026-03-12T14:02:11Z] x-request-id=7f9c2a session=ss-04f3
[edge-2026-03-12T14:02:12Z] connection: id=ss-04f3 partial_close=true reason=idle_probe_coalesce code=SOCKET_MIGRATE
[serve-2026-03-12T14:02:12Z] stream_id=ss-04f3 stalled-flush=true kvcache-primed=true last-frame-offset=18432
[client-logs] sdk.v1.12.0: reconnecting, resumeToken present
[client-logs] received chunk: "{\"choices\": [{\"text\": \"...and finally we recommend\"}\n\n(EOF)\n"

Initial hypothesis: Apple HTTP proxy on managed networks sometimes coalesces an idle-probe FIN with a subsequent TCP migration, which the edge treats as a definitive stream close before the serving-runtime has flushed the trailing buffered tokens. Differences vs known issues: not classic proxy truncation or chunk reordering; here the edge emits partial_close marker and we see a stalled flush rather than an explicit RST. Reproducer verification: Support able to reproduce locally using an iOS device simulator + a transparent proxy that delays ACKs. Correlation: request ids with partial_close show higher incidence when keepalive interval on client > 20s. Temporary mitigation: instruct customer to enable websocket fallback in SDK or set keepalive to 15s. Observed workaround success: websocket fallback avoided truncation in 30 test runs (0/30 truncations).

2026-03-10 09:12 - Aisha Patel (Support): Customer provided traces, SDK logs, and curl reproduction. Assigned to Eng for deeper analysis.
2026-03-11 11:04 - Liam Chen (SRE): I reproduced a reproducible case with a transparent proxy that delays ACKs and triggers a socket migration event. Observed serving-runtime stall while flush queue had ~120 bytes pending. Attaching sample pcap to internal ticket.
2026-03-11 16:30 - ScribeNow (Customer): We can enable websocket fallback in our app, but would prefer SSE to be robust. We rely on SSE for analytics pipeline compatibility.
2026-03-12 08:45 - Ingrid Müller (Edge Eng): Hypothesis: edge-proxy currently converts unusual FIN+probe sequences to partial_close and notifies upstream synchronously. Proposing instrumentation to defer terminal event emission by 250ms to allow flush. Preparing a small spike PR to toggle via runtime flag.
2026-03-13 10:00 - Liam Chen (SRE): Deployed a canary flag that delays terminal emission by 250ms for sessions matching apple-http-proxy UA heuristics. Ran 100 synthetic sessions; truncation rate dropped from 12% to 0.8% on the canary pool. Need Eng signoff for rollout plan.
2026-03-13 14:10 - Aisha Patel (Support): Customer confirmed they'd accept a server-side mitigation if it doesn't conflict with SLAs. Asked for ETA on patch rollout and whether there are any side effects.
2026-03-13 15:45 - Ingrid Müller (Edge Eng): Preparing PR with flag gated by label 'defer-terminal-on-coalesced-fin'. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/1423. Plan: deploy to canary for 48h then progressive rollout if no regression in connection counts or memory use.

Workaround: customer enabled websocket fallback in their app (short-term). Engineering created a canary server-side mitigation (defer terminal emission by 250ms for sessions that match Apple HTTP proxy heuristics). PR opened and canary shows significant reduction. Follow-ups: - Monitor canary for 48h (Liam/Edge team). - Add more robust detection for coalesced FIN patterns and extend test harness to include Apple HTTP proxy behavior (Ingrid). - Postmortem if rollout proceeds to prod to capture metrics and potential regressions.

title: Private Console: Network Path Storyboard & Upgrade Rehearsal (prototype)
author: Asha Patel
text:
Design and prototype an interactive ‘Network Path Storyboard’ for the Private/VPC Console that helps tenants rehearse cluster upgrades and connectivity changes before they are applied. The storyboard surface should let operators: 1) narrate a connectivity scenario across logical layers (tenant app -> VPC route -> cluster node -> egress), 2) step through simulated events (maintenance window, node drain, route failover) with visualized latency and cost delta annotations, 3) surface automated risk flags derived from recent health metrics and policy guardrails, and 4) emit a shareable checklist and rollout plan (canary steps + rollback). Goal: reduce upgrade fear and on-call churn by making network impacts explicit and actionable for SREs and tenant owners. Prototype scope for this ticket covers the storyboard interaction patterns, a compact risk summary card, and a cost-annotation overlay tied to the batching/throughput estimate model. Does not include backend simulation engine integration (separate ENG ticket).

title: Surface Pro (ARM) dual-radio metric flip during roam causes WireGuard split-tunnel to lose internal routes
text:
Issue summary: Multiple Surface Pro (ARM) devices reporting sudden loss of access to internal services immediately after roaming between 2.4GHz and 5GHz SSIDs. VPN (WireGuard) remains 'connected' but traffic to internal subnets (10.10.0.0/16) no longer flows. Impact: several engineers working on private repos and internal dashboards were blocked. Scope: 6 confirmed machines in SF office, same Wi-Fi AP cluster, mixed OS build 22H2 on ARM.

Expected behaviour: roam completes, VPN stays connected and internal routes remain pinned via split-tunnel rules.

Observed behaviour: after roam, Windows chooses different physical adapter and flips interface metrics; WireGuard continues with handshake but system route table places default for internal subnets via physical adapter that has no corporate VLAN reachability, causing traffic to leave on guest VLAN and be dropped by edge firewall.

1) Start WireGuard client connected to corporate split-tunnel config (internal subnets pinned).
2) On Surface Pro ARM device, trigger 2.4GHz->5GHz roam (walk between APs or toggle radio to force handoff).
3) Observe Windows network interface metric and route table immediately after roam (use `Get-NetIPInterface` / `route print`).
4) Attempt to reach internal service (e.g., git.redwood.internal:22 or 10.10.5.12) — connect fails despite WireGuard reported as connected.
5) Compare traffic path with packet capture on client (Wireshark) and AP logs.
6) Reboot or manually set interface metric back and confirm connectivity returns.

Selected excerpts: 
- WireGuard status: peer=corp-peer latest-handshake=0s transfer=12.4 MiB/1.2 MiB
- Windows Event Log (NetworkProfile) 2026-02-24 09:18:12: Interface metric changed: InterfaceIndex=23 old=25 new=2
- netsh interface ip show config (post-roam): Ethernet 23 (Wi-Fi-5G): Metric 2, IPv4 DHCP, DNS suffix not set
- route print (post-roam): 10.10.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0 192.168.50.1 if 23 metric 2
- AP Controller logs: client A: roam success to AP-B bssid=aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff, assigned VLAN guest (300) due to NDP mismatch

2026-02-24 09:40 - Triage: Confirmed 3 devices reproducing sequence in SF office. WireGuard shows active encryption, but system route points to wrong gateway (guest VLAN). Hypothesis: driver or Windows automatic metric change after roam causing routes to prefer a non-corporate interface.
2026-02-24 11:15 - Network Eng (Diego): AP controller performed VLAN reassignment for those client sessions on roam due to sticky client policy; observed DHCP lease refresh mapping client to guest VLAN for short window (30s) before corporate VLAN restored.
2026-02-24 14:05 - Windows sysadmin (Liam): Verified Windows behavior: on ARM build 22H2 with specific Qualcomm driver v4.2.0.13, `Automatic metric` flag toggles on roam, recalculating interface metric and reordering route table. Confirmed that persistent split-tunnel routes remain but traffic egresses via interface with lower metric to non-corporate gateway.
2026-02-25 09:12 - Repro test: Disabled 'EnableReassociation' on AP and forced roam — metric flip still occurs but VLAN remains corporate; suggests dual contribution: both AP transient VLAN assignment and client metric recalculation necessary to cause outage.
2026-02-26 10:00 - Vendor engagement: Opened ticket with Qualcomm driver team; they acknowledged a known issue where NDIS 6.70 events trigger metric recalculation on 802.11r handoff for certain NIC firmware. Vendor provided a beta driver that pins interface metric.
2026-02-27 16:30 - Mitigation test: Applied local Group Policy (script) to set interface metrics to higher priority for corporate SSID; confirmed successful mitigation on 5 test devices.
2026-03-01 08:00 - Rollout: Deployed updated WireGuard client (1.2.3) which ignores ephemeral route replacements for pinned subnets, and pushed GPO to fleet to set explicit interface metrics for corporate SSIDs. Monitoring shows no recurrences in SF cluster after change.

Asha Patel (2026-02-24 09:25): Reported by eng team after losing access to internal dashboards post-meeting roam. Attached Wireshark capture and `route print`.
Support - Liam O'Connor (2026-02-24 09:35): Acknowledged, investigating. Asking for affected device model list and timestamps.
Network - Diego Ramos (2026-02-24 11:20): Looked into AP controller logs; saw transient VLAN assignment during reassoc. Noted sticky-client policy triggered on AP-B.
QA - Mei Chen (2026-02-25 10:10): Reproduced with debug build; metric flips observed only on Qualcomm NICs on ARM Surface. Intel x86 devices unaffected.
Qualcomm Vendor Rep (2026-02-26 13:04): Confirmed similar reports; provided driver beta and will include long-term fix in upcoming firmware.
Liam O'Connor (2026-02-27 17:00): Deployed GPO with interface metric script to 200-device pilot (SF office + remote ARM devices). Please validate if anyone still sees issue.
Asha Patel (2026-03-01 08:12): Confirmed fixed for previously impacted machines. Thanks for the quick turnaround.

Root cause: Interaction between AP controller transient VLAN reassignment during roam and Qualcomm Wi-Fi NDIS driver behavior on ARM devices that triggers automatic interface metric recalculation. This allowed split-tunnel routes to be overshadowed by a lower-metric gateway on the guest VLAN.

Immediate remediation: 1) Deployed a client-side mitigation: Group Policy to set explicit interface metric for corporate SSID and a PowerShell script to re-assert routes for 10.10.0.0/16 on network change. 2) Updated WireGuard client to 1.2.3 which rejects ephemeral route replacements for pinned subnets. 3) Adjusted AP controller sticky-client policy to avoid transient VLAN flips during 802.11r handoffs on the affected AP cluster.

Permanent fix / follow-up: Qualcomm to release driver firmware with NDIS fix (vendor ticket QC-29812). IT will monitor and schedule driver rollout after vendor QA. Created follow-up internal task INT-356802 to track vendor driver validation and fleet upgrade.

title: NorthPoint Signalworks
author: Maya Chen
text:
Mid-market B2B SaaS product team evaluating Redwood for chat-first workflows plus semantic search. Started on hosted API; moving to Dedicated POC to validate latency, cost, and secure deployment (VPC + KMS). POC will exercise canary rollouts and fallback routing between model variants and regions, and must demonstrate automated rollback rules tied to eval/regression checks.

2024-08-05 - inbound trial signup (hosted API). Product team ran smoke tests.
2024-09-10 - hosted API demo with Maya. Primary ask: p95 latency <200ms for chat flows.
2024-10-22 - cost/throughput workshop. Customer requested Dedicated options for predictable SLA.
2024-11-12 - security review kickoff with SecOps; requested SOC2 evidence + KMS diagram (see Drive)
2024-11-15 - SE Jamal performed throughput sim (concurrent chat workload). Proposed canary + fallback blueprint.
2024-11-18 - verbal approval to run 4-week Dedicated POC. Signed NDA; awaiting SOW/pricing doc.

POC objective: validate Dedicated pool for interactive chat + embeddings at mid-market scale (200-400 daily concurrent users).
Latency targets: p95 <180ms for short chat (<=512 tokens); p50 <80ms. Product lead: "We can't accept >150ms 95p for primary flows" (sourced earlier).
Throughput & cost: target token unit cost < $0.0009 during POC; acceptable burst behavior with autoscaling up to 2x baseline.
Model strategy: baseline = Llama-2-70B quantized (fast kernels); canary variant = Llama-2-13B quantized; fallback to 13B under heavy load or degraded perf.
Routing plan agreed for POC: primary region = us-east-1, secondary = eu-west-1. Failover preference = region failover (warm standby) over throttling.
Canary rollout plan: 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% over 4 days. Automatic rollback triggers: quality regression (eval suite), latency breach >200ms p95, or error rate >0.5%.
Security constraints: customer requires SAML SSO, customer-managed KMS for key wrapping, audit logs with 12-month retention, and US-only residency for PII flows.
Networking: must complete VPC peering + egress allowlist; team flagged requirement for stable static egress IPs for compliance.
Open ask: provide example quantization profiles and recommended kernel settings for customer inference budget; sample config in Drive link.
Quote from CTO on call: "We like the routing/fallback idea — want clear SLAs on rollback automation and model parity metrics."
Decision criteria for purchase: meets latency SLAs in POC, passes security checklist, and forecasted TCO within estimated range.
Internal stakeholders: Product (Emily R), Infra Lead (David H), SecOps (Rina S), Finance (Alex P).
Sales notes: pricing sensitivity — prefer annual committed capacity if 10–20% discount off list, will consider Dedicated reserved pool if SLOs match.

4-week Dedicated POC: reserved pool (4x A100 equiv), canary plan (5/25/50/100), primary us-east, secondary eu-west, model variants: 70B-quant and 13B-quant, success metrics: p95 latency <180ms, token cost < $0.0009, error rate <0.5%.

11/12 SecOps: asked for SOC2 in-scope list + KMS architecture
11/15 Perf review: Jamal suggested dynamic prefix caching for common prompts
11/18 Exec: greenlight for POC provided, budget contingent on SOW

Finalize Dedicated POC SOW & pricing; infra kickoff w/ SecOps; provide model variant list and canary config

internal budget sign-off (Finance)
VPC peering & egress IP allowlist pending
SAML integration details from IdP team

Pricing deck shared; awaiting Finance approval. Legal asked for data residency addendum. Expect SOW signature in 6-8 weeks after POC if successful.

title: Supplier credit note posted to wrong cost center causing GL variance during March close
text:
Issue summary:
A supplier (Aurelio Systems) submitted a credit note on 2026-03-02 for invoice INV-2026-117. The credit note was processed by AP on 2026-03-03 but was posted to cost center 700-DEV instead of 720-OPS. This caused a negative adjustment to the DEV OPEX for March and a corresponding GL variance in the monthly close reconciliation.

Impact:
- Finance month-end close for March shows a -$24,312 variance in cost center 700-DEV.
- Internal P&L for Product shows incorrect OPEX allocations affecting headcount budgeting.
- Potential downstream impact on chargebacks to product teams if not corrected before close.

Environment:
- ERP: AcmeLedger v4.9 (production)
- AP workflow: AP-Portal v2.1 -> Batch posting service (ap-posting-svc)
- Region: us-east accounting cluster

Steps to reproduce / verify:
1) Search ERP for supplier Aurelio Systems, document CN-2026-03-02 (credit note).
2) Inspect GL posting for that document: journal JRN-2026-533 shows cost center 700-DEV.
3) Compare vendor ledger vs invoice INV-2026-117 and original PO PO-4412; original PO cost center is 720-OPS.
4) Review ap-posting-svc logs for 2026-03-03 02:10-03:00 UTC window.

Logs / evidence attached in ticket (references below).

03-10: Initial triage - confirmed credit note exists and GL posted to 700-DEV instead of 720-OPS (JRN-2026-533).
03-10: Pulled ap-posting-svc logs: job 2026-03-03T02:12 processed CN-2026-03-02; mapping table lookup returned cost_center=700 due to stale mapping row (mapping_id=mc_map_02) that was not refreshed after PO migration on 2026-02-28.
03-11: Confirmed mapping table in AcmeLedger was updated in staging but not promoted to production. The promotion job failed with timeout and left the old mapping in place.
03-11: Cross-checked with Procurement: PO PO-4412 was migrated and assigned 720-OPS on 2026-02-27. Procurement confirmed no change to supplier Aurelio settings.
Hypothesis: deployment rollback timeout prevented mapping promotion which led ap-posting-svc to use legacy mapping during batch post.

2026-03-10 | Liam Chen (Assignee): Assigned to myself. Reproduced posting in ERP and extracted JRN-2026-533. Raising with infra to inspect deployment logs for mapping promotion.
2026-03-10 | Priya Rao (Infra): ap-deploy job #998 timed out on 2026-02-28 due to DB migration lock. We retried but promotion step was not applied to the production mapping table.
2026-03-11 | Elena Ortiz (Procurement): Confirmed PO cost center should be 720-OPS; vendor sent credit note referencing INV-2026-117. Procurement requests corrective journal and vendor notification.
2026-03-12 | Liam Chen: Created corrective journal CJ-2026-041 to reallocate $24,312 from 700-DEV -> 720-OPS pending approval. Finance approval requested from Head of Finance (Markus Engel).

Workaround/fix in progress: Created corrective journal CJ-2026-041 to move the credit amount to 720-OPS. Requested expedited approval from Head of Finance. Infra applied the missing mapping promotion and scheduled a verification run against recent AP batch posts to ensure no other mis-postings. Follow-ups: (1) run full reconciliation of March AP posts for mappings; (2) add a pre-deploy validation check to prevent mapping promotions from being skipped; (3) notify affected product finance leads after journals are posted.

Obtain Head of Finance approval for CJ-2026-041 (Liam to chase).
Run reconciliation for March AP batch to identify other mis-postings (Finance Ops).
Implement pre-deploy validation in infra pipeline and add an alert when mapping promotion step fails (Infra/Platform).
Notify Procurement and affected cost center owners once CJ posts are complete and reconciliation cleared.
