title: Traffic escrow and rehearse proxy for staged promotes
author: Priya Desai
text:
Motivation:
We frequently observe that promotes that look good on telemetry during a short canary window still cause edge-case regressions once given full traffic. This PR introduces two complementary primitives: (1) a traffic_escrow service that holds routing decisions and only releases commits once a rehearse pass and smoke policy succeed, and (2) a rehearse_proxy that can inject synthetic canary traffic and replay recorded request traces into candidate serving revisions without affecting production state.

Goals:
- Allow operators to stage promotes with a commit escrow lease that requires an endorsement from rehearse results before full cutover.
- Provide a reproducible, auditable rehearse run that exercises session affinity, header routing, and KV cache warmup without serving user writes to production.
- Reduce time-to-revert via an escrow ledger that records the include/exclude criteria, lease owner, and rehearse outcomes per promote.

What this PR contains (single-string description):
Implemented a TrafficEscrow controller, a RehearseProxy sidecar + router middleware, a small replay harness for synthetic canaries (replay driver + sampler), and related observability (metrics, traces, and a prometheus scrape target). Included an admin API to grant/revoke escrow leases and an operator CLI hook to trigger a rehearse run. The rehearsals are configurable with smoke policies and timeout/rollback thresholds.

Checklist:
- [x] TrafficEscrow controller + database-backed ledger (sqlite for dev, Postgres migration script included)
- [x] RehearseProxy middleware for routing and replay isolation
- [x] Replay driver and synthetic canary harness with pluggable samplers
- [x] Feature flag gating (rollout.traffic_escrow) and integration tests
- [x] Prometheus metrics + tracing spans for rehearse runs
- [x] Operator CLI commands and docs stub

High-level commits:
- commit 1: controller: add TrafficEscrow CRD and schema, controller reconciliation loop with lease lifecycle
- commit 2: middleware: rehearse proxy router and headers + session-affinity passthrough
- commit 3: replay: synthetic canary driver and reservoir sampler, smoke policy evaluator
- commit 4: telemetry: metrics, traces, and prometheus target
- commit 5: migrations: add escrow ledger table and migration script
- commit 6: tests: e2e rehearse integration tests + unit tests for policy evaluator

Changed files (high level):
- services/traffic-escrow/controller.go (new)
- services/traffic-escrow/ledger/migrations/0001_create_escrow_table.sql (new)
- services/traffic-escrow/api/escrow.proto (new)
- runtime/middleware/rehearse_proxy.go (new)
- runtime/replay/driver.go (new)
- runtime/replay/sampler.go (new)
- deploy/helm/templates/escrow-deployment.yaml (mod)
- observability/metrics/escrow_metrics.go (new)
- cli/ops/escrow_cli.go (new)
- docs/ops/traffic-escrow.md (new)
- tests/e2e/rehearse_integration_test.go (new)

Small illustrative snippet (rehearse proxy header handling):

func (rp *RehearseProxy) ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
 if rp.isRehearseRun(r) {
 // tag and route to candidate revision; keep responses sandboxed
 r.Header.Set("X-Rehearse-Run", rp.currentLeaseID)
 rp.routeToCandidate(w, r)
 return
 }
 rp.routeNormal(w, r)
}

(Full diffs are intentionally small here; implementation files are focused and mostly additive.)

Operational notes:
- Default behavior is a no-op until rollout.traffic_escrow is enabled.
- The escrow ledger keeps soft TTLs for leases; expired leases auto-fail after the configured grace period.
- Rehearse runs can be run in parallel for non-overlapping cohorts; controller rejects overlapping leases by default to avoid double-warmup.

Review thread summary (single string):
See reviewers list for full thread. Key points from review: Liam asked for stronger invariants around overlapping leases; addressed by adding overlap detection in the controller and a unit test. Maya requested clearer observability for rehearse runs; added metrics and traces and a prometheus scrape target with labels rehearse_run and cohort_id. Diego recommended a Postgres migration rather than sqlite for staging; added migration and a readme about storage backends. CI flakes on the first run due to a timing issue in the replay sampler; fixed by adding deterministic seeding in tests.

Selected review comments and replies:
- Liam O'Connor (2026-02-16): "Controller needs deterministic behavior when two promotes touch the same cohort. How does reclamation work?"
 - Author reply (Priya): "Added overlap checks and a ReclaimLease method; controller now serializes conflicting lease requests and exposes a metric escrow_conflicts_total."

- Maya Li (2026-02-18): "Can we get a top-level metric that shows rehearse run pass/fail ratio over the last 24h?"
 - Author reply: "Added rehearse_run_result_total{outcome=\"pass\"|\"fail\"} and example dashboard panels in docs/ops."

- Diego Alvarez (2026-02-19): "DB choice: use Postgres in staging. Please include migration and docs."
 - Author reply: "Included migration script and a small switch in config to pick sqlite for dev, postgres for staging/prod."

CI and test summary:
- CI pipeline: unit (go test), linters (golangci-lint), integration (docker-compose rehearse harness), e2e (k8s kind).
- Run 1: unit/lint passed, integration timed out (race in replay sampler), rerun tests after deterministic seeding.
- Run 2: all checks passed.

Post-merge actions:
- Enable rollout.traffic_escrow behind a canary flag for SRE on a single cluster for two weeks (ENG-2401).
- Run a handful of rehearses using recorded traces to validate session-affinity and cache warmups.
- Add a small playbook to run a fast revert if rehearse failures exceed threshold.

Why this is different from existing rollout features:
This PR focuses on the concept of escrowed commits plus a rehearse proxy that allows routing and replay isolation so that candidate revisions can be exercised end-to-end without touching production state. Existing staged promote primitives at Redwood emphasize traffic phasing and shadowing; traffic escrow gives an operator-level commit gating primitive with a ledger and rehearsals that are auditable and replayable.

Risk assessment:
- Low to medium risk: mostly additive components behind feature flags. The largest surface is the rehearse proxy which touches routing; we've guarded it with feature flag gating and unit tests.

Notes for on-call and SRE:
- Metric to watch: escrow_conflicts_total, rehearse_run_result_total, rehearse_run_duration_seconds_bucket, rehearsal_sandbox_errors_total.
- CLI: redwood ops escrow grant --lease-id=<id> --cohort=<name> --owner=<user>

If any follow-ups are requested, they will be tracked in ENG-1024 and ENG-2401.

Adds a traffic escrow component and a rehearse-proxy to allow dry-run rehearsals of staged promotes. No API changes for external customers; operational feature behind feature flag. Improves safety for deferred promotes and reduces blast radius of bad promotes by enabling synthetic canary replays and commit-escrow leases.

Liam O'Connor: Controller needs deterministic behavior for overlapping leases; suggested serialization + metric for conflicts.
Maya Li: Request to add rehearse_run_result_total metric and dashboard panels.
Diego Alvarez: Use Postgres in staging; add migration and docs for storage backends.
SRE: Flag gating and rollout plan required before enabling in prod; recommended a canary cluster run.

title: Observability agent service-account impersonation denied due to cross-cloud IAM conditional mismatch
text:
Issue summary:
A subset of observability agents (metrics/traces collectors) running in the Dedicated fleet are failing to push telemetry because they cannot impersonate the GCP service account when routed via the AWS STS->GCP broker. This started after a recent org-policy/IAM cleanup that added attribute-based conditionals on serviceAccount impersonation roles.

Impact:
- Production metrics and traces missing for ~6 Dedicated customers in us-east and eu-west regions for ~36 hours.
- Alerts suppressed for affected tenant routes; engineering oncall escalations generated.
- No customer-facing requests reported yet, but internal SLAs for observability were violated.

Environment:
- prod | us-east, eu-west
- Dedicated fleet (redwood-dedicated-prod), STS identity broker between AWS account A and GCP org.
- Affected component: observability-agent container image: redwood/obs-agent:v2.1.4

1) From an affected dedicated node, run: gcloud auth print-access-token --impersonate-service-account=sa-observability@customer-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com
2) Observe IAM denial: 'Request had insufficient authentication scopes' or 'Permission iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken denied'.
3) Trace path through STS broker: aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/redwood-sts-broker -> broker uses workload identity federation to exchange credentials for GCP impersonation.
4) Reproduce intermittently depending on which broker instance and GCP org policy evaluation path is used.

2026-03-10T02:12:14Z obs-agent[pid=4378]: ERROR: impersonation failed: iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken denied for sa-observability@customer-project.
 (requestor: sts-broker-arn:aws:sts::ACCOUNT:assumed-role/redwood-sts-broker/session)
2026-03-10T02:12:14Z broker[info]: federated token exchange success -> attempting gcloud impersonate -> IAM DENY response: 'Permission denied. Condition "resource.name.startsWith('projects/_/serviceAccounts/')" not satisfied'
2026-03-10T02:45:01Z gce-audit[warning]: orgPolicy: constraint 'iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains' enforced; conditional binding present on roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator

Support (Rajesh Patel) 2026-03-10: Triage - observed spike in obs-agent 'impersonation failed' errors. Opening cross-team Slack #infra-iam and paging SRE.
SRE (Marta Alvarez) 2026-03-10: Initial hypothesis - recent org-level conditional binding added to service account token creator role; may be matching on resource.name vs resource.service. Asking Cloud Infra to export binding conditions.
Cloud Infra (Tobias Nguyen) 2026-03-11: Confirmed conditional exists on project-level role binding applied by terraform module 'iam/roles-v2'. Condition expression uses request.auth.aud and resource.name mismatch when using federation via STS broker. Working on repro and mitigation plan.
Support (Emily Chen) 2026-03-12: Working mitigation - temporarily relax conditional on dedicated broker principal in staging, then apply to prod after validation. Will coordinate a short maintenance window and notify customers if needed.

- Root cause: Org-level IAM conditional added to restrict iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator to calls where resource.name matches 'projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/serviceAccounts/*' exactly. Workload identity broker exchanges credentials via federated principal path that results in a slightly different resource.name evaluation path, causing condition to fail.
- Reproduced locally by using the broker's federated token with alterted audience claim -> condition evaluation fails only for broker-issued tokens.
- Also observed a related org-policy enforcement that denies certain federated principals unless an attribute 'broker_id' is present in the condition. The broker did not add this attribute in its token exchange flow.
- Affected customers: dedicated tenants on redwood-dedicated-prod whose telemetry pipeline uses broker instance group a/b. Not all instances affected because some broker instances include additional claims.

Mitigation applied 2026-03-12 03:40 UTC: Temporarily updated terraform 'iam/roles-v2' module to add an exception for arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/redwood-sts-broker with a condition that matches the broker's token attributes.
Follow-up permanent fix: (1) Update STS broker to include 'broker_id' and stable audience claim during federation exchange; (2) Add unit/integration test to terraform module to validate conditional expressions against broker tokens; (3) Roll out a policy-change runbook for cross-cloud IAM condition updates.
Post-action: Verified metrics ingestion resumed for affected tenants within 15 minutes of mitigation. Created proposaland PRs for infra and broker changes.

title: Tenant Observability & Evidence Contract for Regulated VPC Deploys
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Summary:
This document defines the observability, telemetry, and evidence requirements Redwood expects for regulated customers deploying the Private (VPC) product. It is an operational contract that outlines the metrics, traces, logs, retention, and artifacts required for customer acceptance, ongoing compliance, and post-incident audits.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Provide a concrete, testable checklist that field engineers, SREs, and customer infra teams can use during private VPC deployments to satisfy regulatory evidence requests (PCI/ISO/SOC-style) and internal Redwood SLAs.
- Scope: Applies to all Private VPC deployments for customers with regulated workloads (PHI, PCI, PII-sensitive). This covers control-plane connectivity, runtime agents, telemetry pipelines, and secure artifact handoff.

Key objectives:
1) Ensure visibility to support 99.95% tenant-facing availability SLO and latency SLOs (see SLOs section).
2) Collect and preserve evidence for security and compliance audits with tamper-evident retention controls.
3) Standardize acceptance tests and artifacts to reduce delivery time and avoid rework.

SLOs and performance thresholds (tenant-facing):
- Availability: 99.95% monthly for tenant inference endpoint (measurement: synthetic probes from customer region + control-plane logs).
- Latency: p95 < 120ms for 256-token synchronous calls; p95 < 250ms for 1024-token calls (measured at ingress for successful 2xx responses).
- Error budget: 0.05% of requests may return 5xx or timeouts; any breach requires incident runbook and customer notification within 1 hour.

Observability categories and minimums:
1) Metrics (Prometheus-format):
 - Required metrics exported by runtime-agent and control-plane: redwood.runtime.requests_total, redwood.runtime.requests_failures_total, redwood.runtime.latency_seconds_bucket (histogram), redwood.runtime.kv_cache_hit_ratio, redwood.controlplane.sync_latency_seconds, redwood.controlplane.config_version{tenant}, redwood.controlplane.fallback_count.
 - Scrape frequency: 15s for runtime-agent critical metrics, 60s for control-plane aggregated metrics.
 - Retention: raw metrics retained in customer-visible TSDB for 90 days; aggregated rollups (1h) for 2 years.

2) Traces (OpenTelemetry):
 - Required spans: request ingress, runtime decode/encode, model kernel exec, kv-cache lookup, control-plane routing decision.
 - Sampling: adaptive sampling with minimum 5% global sample and 100% sampling for any request flagged as failed (>5xx) or taking >p99 latency.
 - Retention: traces retained for 90 days in a tamper-evident store (customer-managed or agreed third-party like Tempo+S3 with signed manifests).

3) Logs (structured JSON):
 - Required logs: access logs (per-request), runtime-agent system logs, control-plane audit logs, key rotations, and storage access attempts.
 - Format: JSON with at minimum {timestamp, tenant_id, request_id, route, model, status_code, latency_ms, node_id}.
 - Retention: 365 days for audit logs; 90 days for operational logs unless regulatory requirement dictates more.

4) Telemetry integrity and chain-of-custody:
 - All telemetry bundles delivered for audits must include salted hashes (SHA256) and a signed manifest from the control-plane operator.
 - For air-gapped customers, manifests must be exportable via signed tarball and verified with customer-provided key.

Evidence artifacts (deliverables for acceptance and compliance):
- Live SLO dashboard link (Grafana) scoped to tenant with view-only credentials.
- A 30-day extract of: metrics (Prometheus export), traces (OTLP export), and logs (JSON NDJSON) for the agreed window.
- Signed telemetry manifest and hash list (SHA256) with timestamped signatures.
- Configuration snapshot: control-plane config_version, model versions, container images with image digests, and quantization/precision profile.
- Access & audit log slice showing KMS/HSM key uses during install and initial 7 days.

Acceptance tests and checklist (field delivery):
1) Pre-install (customer infra):
 - Validate VPC CIDR and routing per network readiness checklist.
 - Confirm KMS/HSM integration and that customer can accept signed manifests.
2) Installation validation (engineer run):
 - Synthetic probe checklist: 5 probes from each customer region to runtime SNI endpoint. All probes must return 200 within latency SLO for initial acceptance.
 - Metrics ingestion validation: Verify runtime-agent metrics scraped at 15s and visible in Grafana panels.
 - Traces: Generate 100 synthetic requests with varied sizes; confirm 5% sampled traces + all failures sampled; spans contain model and kv-cache annotations.
 - Logs: Export last 24 hours of structured logs and validate JSON schema and presence of required fields.
3) Compliance artifact handoff:
 - Produce the signed telemetry manifest and initial 30-day artifact bundle (or since-boot) and deliver via agreed channel (secure S3, signed USB for air-gap).

Example telemetry ingestion config (YAML snippet for runtime-agent):
telemetry:
 metrics_scrape_interval: 15s
 otlp_endpoint: https://collector.customer-vpc.example:4317
 trace_sampling:
 default_rate: 0.05
 spike_capture_threshold_ms: 1500
 log_format: json
 log_shipper: fluent-bit

Evidence export command examples:
- Metrics (Prometheus TSDB block export): curl -u readonly:token "https://prom.customer-vpc.example/api/v1/export?range=30d" -o metrics-30d.tar.gz
- Traces (OTLP export): otelcli export --endpoint https://collector.customer-vpc.example:4317 --from=2025-09-01 --to=2025-10-01 --out traces-30d.ndjson

Operational runbook pointers (post-acceptance):
- Alerting: Must configure the following alerts at customer and Redwood side: runtime_errors_rate > 0.5% for 5m; p95_latency > 140ms for 10m; telemetry_pipeline_lag > 2m for 5m.
- Incident evidence protocol: When an incident is created for a regulated tenant, the on-call engineer must capture: 1) A zipped telemetry bundle (metrics + traces + logs) covering incident window +/- 60 minutes. 2) Signed manifest and chain-of-custody note stored in customer evidence bucket. 3) Post-incident RCA attached with references to artifact hashes.

Upgrade & rollback evidence expectations:
- For any runtime upgrade affecting model execution (kernel/quantization changes), the delivery packet must include: pre-upgrade baseline metrics/traces (7 days), smoke test results, and canary traffic plan; post-upgrade artifact bundle (first 24 hours) and a signed rollback-ready image digest list.
- Rollback procedure must preserve telemetry artifacts from the failed upgrade window and mark them immutable for the duration of the investigation.

Acceptance signoff template (required fields):
- Tenant ID: 
- Deployment ID: 
- Control-plane config_version: 
- SLO verification: pass/fail with measured values
- Evidence artifacts delivered: list of file paths and manifest hash
- Signatures: Field engineer / Customer security lead / Redwood delivery lead (email + timestamp)

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary owner: Private Deployments Delivery - delivery-oncall@redwood.ai
- Observability owner: Eng Platform Metrics team - metrics@redwood.ai
- Escalation matrix: see /confluence/eng-oncall/incident-process (must be mirrored into customer handoff docs).

Security and privacy notes:
- Telemetry exports MUST be filtered for tenant PII unless customer explicitly requests full payload capture and provides documented legal approval.
- KMS keys used to sign manifests must be rotated per customer policy; Redwood will provide rotation proof (signed key rotation log) as part of audit artifacts.

FAQ (short):
Q: What if a customer cannot host a Prometheus/OTLP endpoint?
A: Redwood can host a collector in a dedicated ingress VPC peered to the customer per the hybrid-control-plane model; in that case additional network ACLs and data residency controls are required and documented in the network appendix.

References and related docs:
- Private deploy acceptance and smoke validation (linked), post-install telemetry checklist (linked), and control-plane manifest format specification (internal doc).

Appendix A - Minimal evidence table (human readable):
Artifact | Minimum window | Format | Retention | Delivery method
Metrics export | 30 days | Prometheus TSDB / csv | 90 days raw, 2y rollups | secure S3 / scp
Traces | 30 days | OTLP -> ndjson | 90 days | signed tarball / s3
Audit logs (KMS/Install) | 365 days | JSON NDJSON | 365 days | s3 w/ bucket policy

Appendix B - Contact matrix and escalation SLA:
- Tier 1 response: Delivery engineer within 1 hour
- Tier 2 escalation: Platform SRE within 4 hours
- Tier 3 legal/compliance engagement: within 24 hours

Revision history:
- 2025-10-15: initial draft (Aisha Patel)
- 2026-02-20: expanded trace sampling policy and added signed manifest requirements (Lena Fischer)

title: eng-platform
text:
Maria Chen: Morning — quick async standup for eng-platform. What I did: merged the small change to auth middleware that preserves x-forwarded-user, verified with unit tests. Blockers: noticed some 401 spikes against the API gateway in the staging trace; digging into routing fallback behavior. Today: finish a canary rollout for the routing policy changes and follow up on the spike.
Ajay Patel: /what I did: added per-route rate-limit config to the yaml schema, and stubbed the planner to read it. Blockers: need an integration test harness that simulates bursty traffic for the quota refactor. Today: wire the simulator and push a test run to CI.
Liam O'Connor: Did code review on Maria's auth change — left one comment about header normalization. Also pushed a small perf patch to continuous-batching. No blockers. Today: will help Ajay with the simulator and run a couple of load scenarios.
Sophia Rivera: I ran the staging traffic replay overnight (route: /v1/generate) — saw the same 401 spikes around 03:12 UTC. Trace looks like requests hitting fallthrough-route which has auth disabled. Not sure why the policy match didn't pick the primary route. Blocker: need a dump of the policy table at the time of the replay. @Maria can you dump the policy state from staging?

Maria Chen: Yup, grabbing it now — running `./admin dump-policy --env=staging --since=1714998000` (will paste output).

deploy-bot: Deployment started: gateway-service v2.18 -> v2.19 (canary=10%) by @maria
Maria Chen: Pasting relevant excerpt from dump (sanitized):
```
routes:
 - id: generate-primary
 match: path_prefix: /v1/generate
 auth_required: true
 predicates:
 - header: x-client-type == "web"
 - id: generate-fallback
 match: path_prefix: /v1/generate
 auth_required: false
 predicates:
 - header: x-client-type == "internal"
```
Maria Chen: Hmm — staging replay requests have x-client-type: "web-prod" which doesn't match either predicate. That's why fallthrough is triggered. I'll add a predicate that handles wildcard prefixes.

Ajay Patel: Good catch. For routing policy language, would `header_prefix: x-client-type starts_with "web"` be ok? We should avoid too many predicate types.

Liam O'Connor: Agree — prefer `starts_with` vs regex for perf. If we add a small normalizer that maps "web-prod" -> "web" at ingress, that also fixes auth mapping. But might hide client-versioning.

Sophia Rivera: For next steps — Maria, can you: 1) add starts_with predicate to the policy and canary to 20%? 2) attach the staging policy dump as a gist or paste here? 3) Ajay/Liam can help with simulator runs after change.

Maria Chen: Plan: will open a tiny PR for policy change + tests, increment canary to 20% after deploy passes smoke, and paste the policy dump link. ETA ~2h. @Ajay @Liam please stand by for pairing on simulator.

Ajay Patel: I'll queue the simulator job once PR is merged. Also leaving a note to add a unit test for rate-limit fallback when a route match fails (we had no test for that edge case).

Liam O'Connor: Ping me when you merge, I'll run the replay with 10k qps burst and forward the metrics. Also watching for latency tail increase due to auth normalization. :eyes:
deploy-bot: Deployment succeeded: gateway-service v2.19 (canary=20%) — rolling.

Maria Chen: Thanks. No other blockers from me, except coordinating the simulator. Will post PR link when ready. :thumbsup:

Sophia Rivera: Great — I'll monitor the staging dashboard and alert if 401s reappear. If anything else, post here.

Ajay Patel: Quick follow-up: which config key did we pick for per-route rate limits? I used `limits.per_minute` in the schema; confirm and I'll add CI validation.

Maria Chen: `rate_limit.per_minute` is what the runtime expects (we documented this in the schema notes). Ajay, please keep `limits.` as an alias for backward compatibility and add a deprecation warning in the validator.

Liam O'Connor: all good. small note: if rate-limit config is missing, runtime should fall back to global default (10k/min) — we should add a test asserting that.

Maria Chen: Noted. I'll include tests for fallback and predicate matching. Closing my standup — will update with PR link.

title: eng-oncall
text:
Jordan H: taking over APAC primary for tonight. quick summary: INC-2026-98 is still active in ap-southeast-1, errors on the embeddings pipeline (model-cache / kv-store path). paging started ~20:10 UTC, current status: degraded but customers only seeing intermittent 5xxs. handing off with actions-in-progress and a short plan.

Sam C: +1. I flipped the circuit-breaker for the model-cache service to 'soft' at 20:35 UTC to reduce fanout to downstream p99-slow nodes. command used: `curl -X POST $ADMIN/api/v1/cb/model-cache -d '{"state":"soft"}'` (logged in ops vault). This has cut the retry storm but error_rate still ~3.8%.

sre-bot: Incident INC-2026-98 created by pagerduty at 2026-02-14T20:12:03Z. Tags: embeddings, ap-southeast-1, customer-impact:partial. Priority: P2.

Nisha R: metrics snapshot at 20:40 UTC: embeddings-serve p50=220ms (baseline 110ms), p95=3.7s (baseline 1.2s), error_rate=3.8% (baseline 0.2%). Traffic skew: top customer calls from APAC increased due to customer batch jobs. KV-cache hit rate dropped from 92% -> 74% on retry-heavy keys.

Jordan H: noted. Is this correlated with the nightly cache warm job?

Sam C: yes — we saw overlap with the cache-warm cron at 20:08 UTC. The cron triggered a full prefix scan which amplified writes to kv-store. I suppressed the cron (`kubectl patch cronjob cache-warm -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}'`) at 20:22 UTC. But node-level pressure persisted because of retries.

Alex P: trying a controlled rollback: routing 15% of embeddings traffic to quantized-2 (smaller) model to relieve memory pressure on large-hosts. Applied weighted route via routing service: `POST /routes/embeddings/weight { "quantized-2": 0.15 }`. Initial results: requests routed fine, lower mem usage on a subset of hosts.

Sam C: also kicked a targeted rolling restart of 3 kv-store pods (pods a,b,c) to clear stuck file descriptors — `kubectl rollout restart statefulset/kv-store -n infra --selector=kv-group=hot --max-unavailable=1`. Restarts finished by 20:50 UTC. Some short 502 spikes during pod cycling.

Nisha R: after restarts + routing changes: p95 trending down to 2.1s, error_rate down to 1.6% at 20:58 UTC. Still above baseline, but heading in right direction.

Jordan H: customer impact: a small subset of enterprise customers experienced 20-40% failed embeddings between 20:10-20:45 UTC. CS alerted major customers and provided workaround (retry with backoff). No data loss reported. Logging shows most failures were timeouts from downstream kv-store.

Alex P: FYI — I've opened a ticket with storage team to investigate compaction/backpressure on the shards involved (ST-721). Mentioned hot keys and cron overlap.

Sam C: current mitigations in place: circuit-breaker=soft, cache-warm cron suspended, 15% routing to quantized-2, 3 pod restarts, rate limiter increased for embed service to 150rps -> `scale config` change, and temporary request-level backoff enforced at gateway.

sre-bot: Runbook automation: step 4 (drain problematic hosts) marked IN_PROGRESS by Sam C at 20:46 UTC. Step 6 (notify account owners) marked COMPLETE.

Jordan H: handoff checklist for incoming primary/secondary:
- Primary (me): keep monitoring p95 and error_rate for embeddings-service and kv-store metrics.
- Secondary (Sam): owns rolling restarts / scaling actions, eligible to escalate to infra lead (Alex) if shard compaction suspected.
- Coverage gap: APAC midnight window (00:00-02:00 local) — no SRE on-site; I'll be available but would like someone to be ready to hand back by 02:30 UTC.

Jordan H: runbook pointers: https://redwood.internal/runbooks/embeddings-kv-throttling (use the 'soft cb' pattern), and emergency fallback routing: https://redwood.internal/runbooks/fallback-routing. Use the 'notify-customers' template under playbooks.

Nisha R: monitoring to watch (dashboards): `infra/kv-store/latency`, `models/embeddings/p95`, `routing/weighting-breakdown`, `alerts/error-rate-embeddings`. Alerts: Sev2 if error_rate > 3% sustained 5m, Sev1 if >6% or data-loss flags.

Sam C: immediate next actions I will take after handoff: 1) confirm there are no more warm-cron triggers scheduled, 2) watch the throttle logs (`/var/logs/throttle.log`) for retry patterns, 3) keep the rolling restart plan ready if error_rate climbs back.

Jordan H: escalation contacts: infra lead @Alex P, product oncall @maria-p (if customer SLA breach), and exec notify if >30min widespread customer impact.

Alex P: follow-up items for post-incident: 1) change cron to staged-warm that pads over low traffic windows, 2) add shard-level circuit-breakers, 3) capacity plan for APAC rebalancing. I'll open RFCs after incident closure.

Nisha R: tagging expected recovery target: p95 <1.5s and error_rate <0.5% by 02:00 UTC. If not met, escalate for dedicated capacity in region.

Jordan H: handing over primary duty now. I'll stay on for 45m of overlap. If anything spikes, @Sam C please ping me on pager and post brief note in this thread. Leaving the current mitigations documented above.

Sam C: ack. I'll be on watch. Leaving a short run command snippet for incoming oncall:

```bash
# quick healthchecks
curl -sS $METRICS/api/embeddings/p95 | jq .value
kubectl get pods -l app=kv-store -n infra -o wide
curl -sS $ADMIN/api/v1/cb/model-cache | jq .state
```

Jordan H: thanks all. Signing off primary handoff at 21:00 UTC — will be reachable for 45m.

sre-bot: Thread archived: no further automated updates.

title: eng-infra
text:
maya: seeing intermittent 1-3% packet loss between rack-4a and rack-4b since ~03:05 UTC, spikes line up with LB healthcheck failures. GPUs in pool-gpu-2 getting preempted more often :grimacing:
netops-bot: detected interface flaps on tor-04 (phys port 12) 03:04:58 -> 03:09:03; flap count 5 in 5m
aj: ok grabbing pcap and stats, can you post the LB logs and which VIPs were impacted? :eyes:
maya: VIPs: gen-infer-01 and gen-infer-02, both fronted by internal L4 LB. LB logs show backend conn resets and higher RTTs to backends in rack-4b. snippet:
```
[03:06:12] backend 10.2.132.45 failed healthcheck: tcp timeout
[03:06:12] backend 10.2.132.47 failed healthcheck: tcp timeout
[03:06:12] failed backends 2/8
```
simon: can you run ethtool on tor-04 uplinks and also check MTU/ECN counters on host side? suspected ECN/MTU truncation issues from previous incidents.
maya: putting commands here, running now:
```
# on host gpu-node-27
ip link show eth0
ethtool -S eth0 | egrep 'rx_errors|tx_errors|rx_no_buffer'
# on tor
show interface te0/12 counters
```
nicole: also check for RDMA QP resets on the affected hosts, those can be sensitive to packet drops.
aj: results: ethtool shows small rx_drops and rx_crc errors bumping during spike window, MTU=9216 on hosts, tor ports report large 'fragmented' counters increasing. pcap shows TCP MSS negotiation ok but we see occasional IP fragments with DF set and don’t get proper reassembly.
maya: weird, hosts have jumbo MTU but ToR may be truncating due to intermediate device or misconfigured VLAN translation. could be ECN bits being cleared/tripping hardware bug.
simon: paste of tor counters and pcap md5:
```
Tor counters (partial): rx_errors: 0 tx_errors: 0 fragmented: 42
pcap md5: 9a3b...edf2
```
aj: next step: run iperf3 across racks with -M (set MSS) and also test with different MTU sizes to reproduce. can someone schedule quick netns iperf?
maya: running iperf now from gpu-27 -> gpu-46 (rack-4a -> rack-4b)
```
iperf3 -c 10.2.132.46 -P 4 -t 30
[summary] retransmits: 120 (bad)
iperf3 -M 1400 -> retransmits 3
```
nicole: that pretty strongly indicates path MTU blackhole or fragmentation handling issue. lowering MSS fixes it.
simon: is this only TCP? RDMA/payloads over RoCE also saw increased CQ errors earlier today. RDMA likely hit by packet drops.
maya: yes, RoCE counters showed QP resets correlated to same timestamps.
netops-bot: ticket created NET-1983: ToR tor-04 suspected hardware ECN/fragment handling bug. owner=@aj oncall=@simon
aj: temporary mitigations: 1) disable ECN on internal LB-to-backend connections 2) push mtu clamp on LB frontends to 1500 3) schedule trunk reconfig to preserve jumbo across leafs
maya: applied LB MTU clamp on gen-infer VIPs at 03:40 UTC, immediate drop in retransmits in 15m window.
```
iperf3 summary after clamp: retransmits 2, jitter low, latency stable
RoCE CQ errors dropped to baseline
```
simon: good. we should still replace tor-04 SFP or linecard during maintenance; hardware vendor has a firmware note about ECN+jumbo interplay on this ASIC family. filing FR to infra-planning.
nicole: also recommend running path MTU discovery tests from orchestrator to nodes and adding alert for fragmented counter > 10/min.
aj: created followup infra ticket INFRA-447 to replace tor-04 linecard and to test with vendor patch in staging.
maya: Thanks all — rolling monitoring rule and leaving LB clamp until hardware fix. will update INFRA-447 when vendor schedules. :thumbsup:

title: Adoption Velocity Radar — Customer Implementation Compact
author: Priya Singh
text:
One-page compact tracker designed for weekly check-ins with customers running inference rollouts. Focuses on milestone velocity, single-line owner responsibilities, active blockers with mitigation proposals, and suggested next steps. Intentionally terse so CSMs can paste to Slack or QBR notes.

Priya Singh — CSM lead for Nimbus Health — weekly sync, go-live coordinator, exec update owner
Ethan Zhao — Solutions Eng — integration triage, prompt/schema liaison, test harness owner
Maya Patel — Performance Eng — responsible for load profile, latency regression signoff
Liam O'Connor — Dedicated Ops — capacity commit, GPU sizing, autoscale policy owner
Escalation path: Priya -> CS Manager (Ava Martinez) -> Solutions Eng Lead (Diego Ramos)

M1: Baseline integration tested — Target date 2025-12-05 — Current: complete (smoke only) — Owner: Priya
M2: Tokenization & prompt schema locked — Target date 2026-01-15 — Current: in_progress — Owner: Ethan
M3: Latency & cost SLOs defined for production routes — Target date 2026-02-10 — Current: blocked (load tests queued) — Owner: Maya
M4: Dedicated pool config (reserved) approved — Target date 2026-02-28 — Current: in_progress — Owner: Liam
M5: Canary rollout to 10% traffic — Target date 2026-03-10 — Current: planned — Owner: Priya

M1: 9/10 — done but needs end-to-end validation in staging
M2: 6/10 — progress steady, pending schema signoff
M3: 3/10 — blocked on load environment access
M4: 5/10 — procurement signoff pending internal finance approval
M5: 2/10 — dependent on upstream unblock (M3 + M4)

B1: Load test environment access pending customer IAM approval — Severity: high — Impact: blocks latency SLO validation — Proposed mitigation: escalate via customer security lead, temporary token-based access window
B2: Prompt schema disagreement between product and legal (PII handling) — Severity: medium — Impact: delays final prompt set — Proposed mitigation: sticky note doc + 2pm alignment call, convene Legal + Product
B3: Model quantization profile not validated on customer's on-prem hardware — Severity: medium — Impact: cost/latency estimate uncertain — Proposed mitigation: schedule short remote bench session with ops team; share trimmed test model

Priya: Send IAM checklist and escalation note to customer by 2026-03-02
Ethan: Produce canonical prompt-schema doc with examples (cut 1-pager) by 2026-02-28
Maya: Reserve 2h bench slot and run quantization smoke tests; capture perf metrics by 2026-03-04
Liam: Draft dedicated pool config options and cost delta table for customer review by 2026-03-05
All: Prepare 10 minute executive summary slide for upcoming QBR (key risks, ask)

2026-02-25: Customer granted tokenized access to subset of staging for smoke tests (temporary)
2026-02-20: Product raised legal question about redaction patterns — meeting scheduled 2026-02-27
2026-02-18: Solutions Eng delivered initial prompt latency matrix (p50/p95) for open model variant

Weekly stand: Mon 10:30 PST. Run format: 5m quick wins, 10m blockers, 10m decisions. Bring short ask cards. Capture decisions in thread and update tracker immediately.

1) Get IAM approval window scheduled w/ customer security (Priya lead)
2) Lock prompt schema v0.2 and publish to Confluence (Ethan)
3) Run quantized model bench and post results in Slack #cs-nimbus (Maya)
4) Present dedicated vs hosted cost delta in next customer sync (Liam + Priya)

title: FluentForge Mediaworks
author: Jordan Kim
text:
Inbound from content marketing vertical — demo requested after whitepaper CTA. Primary ask: scale templates and batch generate large sets of SEO articles (daily jobs ~10k+ completions).
- Source: inbound MQL via webinar 'Scaling Content Ops' (2026-02-20).
- Quote from CTO: "We need predictable cost per article and low tail latency for short templates."
- Prefers open/quantized models to control cost; willing to test Redwood hosted if unit economics beat current provider.
- Interested in batching and prefix/KV caching to amortize prompt overhead across thousands of similar templates.
- No immediate enterprise compliance requirement beyond SOC2; will accept public-cloud SaaS.
- Wants a short POC: 72h run, measure tokens per article, avg latency, cost per 1k completions, cache hit rate.
- Pricing deck sent (drive link). Security questionnaire partially answered; SOC2 attestation requested.
- AE notes: good fit for Hosted API self-serve -> convert by showing 30-40% cost saving with batching+cache.
- Typical content length: 200-800 tokens; many repeated prefixes (title, brand boilerplate).
- Rate expectations: sustained bursts, ~800-1200 reqs/sec for 5-10 minute windows; typical steady-state 50-200 reqs/sec.
- Engineering concerns: tokenization differences across models, sample quality for SEO, deterministic output for templates.

Workload: high-volume templated article generation + social posts. Latency target: median <200ms for template fills; tail <1s on bursts. Throughput: ability to handle brief bursts of ~1k rps. Cost sensitivity: priority #1 — goal to reduce per-article cost by 30% vs current provider. Model preferences: open weights preferred, support for quantized runtimes and smaller model variants acceptable if quality is preserved. Routing/fallback: single-region public cloud is fine, automatic fallback to cheaper model variant acceptable under quality guardrails. Observability: token-level cost and per-route latency analytics required. Security: SOC2 attestation and audit logs. POC success metrics: cost per 1k completions, avg latency, cache hit rate, quality sample pass rate >= 90%.

Offer: Hosted API sandbox, recommended config: batching enabled (adaptive), prefix KV caching for templates, suggest model family X (quantized). Estimated cost scenario modeled in deck. 72h POC to gather real metrics. Can enable rate limits and burst quotas in account. No dedicated/private ask at this stage.

title: Tideway Shipping integration - inference evaluation kit
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Customer-specific evaluation kit for Tideway Shipping: pinned prompt set, private dataset manifest, acceptance thresholds for generation and extraction tasks, regression checks and sign-off steps for model deployment into Dedicated or Private environments.

1) ETA normalization - 
Prompt: 'User: Shipment 99342 from Port of LA to Seattle, expected departure 2025-01-02 08:00 PST. Provide normalized ETA in ISO8601 with timezone and 95% confidence interval. Field outputs: eta_iso, ci_lower_iso, ci_upper_iso.
System constraints: if no exact time, return best-effort estimate and include 'confidence_note'.'
2) Incident summary extraction - 
Prompt: 'Input: user-submitted incident notes (free text). Task: extract fields - incident_type, affected_legs, root_cause_hypothesis, estimated_delay_minutes, followup_required (yes/no). Return JSON only.
Edge guidance: if multiple causes, return top2 ranked by likelihood.'
3) Customs document classification - 
Prompt: 'Given OCR text from a shipping manifest, classify whether customs_form is complete: {complete|missing_required_fields|unreadable}. If missing_required_fields, list the missing keys from [HS_code, consignee_tax_id, item_value_currency]. Provide short rationale (<30 words).'
4) Conversational assistant - short answer policy - 
Prompt: 'User asks about port congestion. Provide concise answer (<=3 sentences), cite data source id if available in dataset (source_id), and include clear next-step action (contact carrier / check ETA / escalate) when applicable.'

tideway_shipments_q4_2024.csv (2.1M rows) - structured: shipment_id, origin_port, dest_port, depart_ts, arrival_ts, carrier, mode, recorded_delay_min, annotations (json)
tideway_incident_notes_anon_2024.ndjson (42k records) - free-text incident reports with anonymized PII; includes severity_label from ops team
tideway_manifests_ocr_samples/ - 1200 OCR outputs (txt) & paired ground-truth manifests (gold_json) for customs fields extraction
sla_latency_trace_samples.zip - 10k request traces with token counts, model_variant, and end-to-end latency measured in ms (labels for synthetic load scenarios)
tideway_customer_faqs_redacted.md - curated FAQ pairs used for conversational quality checks

Extraction F1 (incident fields) - target >= 0.88 on hold-out private set
ETA absolute error - median <= 3.5 hours, P95 <= 18 hours for route class 'domestic-short'
Classification accuracy (customs completeness) - target >= 0.95 precision for class 'missing_required_fields'
Conciseness score (assistant) - >= 0.9 judged by length and relevance heuristic
Regression safety checks - hallucination rate <= 1% on sensitivity prompt subset

All primary metrics met on private hold-out within +/- 5% of baseline model (baseline: rwi-1.2b-v2)
No single test-case in critical-regression-suite degrades by >5 absolute points in extraction F1
Latency SLO: 95th percentile end-to-end < 600ms for small requests (<256 tokens) on Dedicated configuration (c4-large), validated with sla_latency_trace_samples
Determinism: pinned prompt outputs stable across 3 cold-starts and 5 warm-starts (string-level equivalence for structured fields), except for explicit stochastic fields documented in prompts
Privacy/PII: no raw PII present in model outputs for the private dataset samples (spot-check 200 records by data-ops)

Critical-regression-suite.csv includes 480 items: 200 extraction-critical, 120 ETA-critical, 100 classification, 60 conversational. All must be rerun for every model bump.
Automated nightly run on dedicated-ci: compare new candidate vs pinned baseline; auto-fail if any extraction F1 drop > 3% on any sub-slice (route, carrier)
Manual review gate triggered if hallucination rate on 'safety-phrases' subset > 0.5%
Randomized re-run for OCR pairs with seed variations to check stability of character-level extraction

Top failure modes observed in exploratory tests: 1) numeric normalization across timezones, 2) truncated OCR leading to 'unreadable' false positives, 3) multi-cause incidents confused by pronoun resolution
Representative failing example included in linked_artifacts: github issue #142 (ocr-truncation-edgecase)
Recommended mitigations: add timezone canonicalization helper at transform stage, increase OCR sampling diversity, inject synthetic multi-cause templates into training prompts

rwi-1.2b-v2 (baseline) - recommended for initial Dedicated rollout
rwi-3.8b-quant (candidate) - lower cost path; evaluate extraction F1 tradeoffs
rwi-1.2b-v2+context-window-4k (experimental) - for long-manifest OCR aggregation tests

Projected steady-state qps: 35 req/s for Tideway production traffic profile (80% small requests <256 tokens)
Burst capacity: support up to 120 req/s for 2 minutes without queue growth using dedicated burst pool
Target latency SLOs: median < 120ms generation, P95 < 600ms for small requests on dedicated hardware; measured under synthetic load in sla_latency_trace_samples

1) Automated metric pass in CI (all acceptance_criteria met)
2) SRE smoke test in staging (5k synthetic requests, validate latency and error budget)
3) Applied ML sign-off: review regression report and manual spot-checks (owner + collaborators)
4) Security & privacy review confirmation from security team (artifact: security-review-TIDEWAY-2024-11)
5) PM and Tideway ops acceptance (email thread archived: tideway-onboard-approval@redwood.corp)
6) Canary: 5% traffic on Dedicated for 48 hours, automated rollback if error rate or key metrics drift > threshold
7) Full rollout and post-rollout 72-hour monitoring handoff

Key open questions: (a) Should we expand ETA evaluation to include sea-vs-rail routing logic? (b) Confirm anonymization rubric with data-ops before any public sample sharing. Please check linked PR for synthetic templates and leave comments on corner-case handling.

For internal evaluation runs, use balanced_sample.py to draw 5k records stratified by route class and carrier. For privacy checks, use the pii_spotcheck notebook and mark reviewed entries with tag 'pii-checked'.

Keep evaluation logs, model_shas, and dataset_manifest versioned in the tideway-integration repo. Provide table: model_sha, dataset_manifest_sha, run_timestamp, metrics_csv_link (store in private S3).

Aisha Patel (applied-ml)
SRE Lead: Lucas Mendes
Security: Marta Novak
Tideway Ops contact: Hugo Liang (tideway-ops@tideway.com)

title: Microbench notelet: small quant runs & prompt seeds
author: Anika Rao
text:
Goal: quick, messy notes for few-shot microbench and quant experiments. Keep ephemeral.

Top-line findings so far (quick):
- NF4 PTQ on 7B gives ~1.8x token throughput improvement vs fp16 at batch=1 on A100, loss ~+0.6 ppl for story prompts (small sample).
- GPTQ-ish 4-bit (per-channel) seems better on longer contexts (seq=1024) vs row-wise; NV memory savings noticeable, kernel warmup cost visible.
- KV cache prefix reuse: for repeated system prompts + shared prefix, observed 6-9% end-to-end latency reduction when cache hits are warm. Need more runs.

Loose todo (next 48h):
- [ ] Re-run nf4 vs gptq 7B with seeds 7, 23, 59 (three runs) for two prompt families (roleplay, summarization). Save logs to bench-run-20260313.
- [ ] Add latency traces (tiny) with --trace-kernel and collect p50/p95 for token generation step (not total).
- [ ] Try static vs dynamic KV caching: script bench/cache_experiments.py (flag --static-prefix-size).
- [ ] Perf ticket to infra: request smaller CUDA persistent pool for short-lived containers (INF-xxxx).

Prompt sets (quick copy):
- roleplay-short: 
 "You are an expert editor. Improve the clarity: 
 
 INPUT: {text}
 OUTPUT:"
- summarization-long: 
 "Condense the passage into 3 bullets, keep facts, remove filler. PASSAGE: {text}
 SUMMARY:"
- retrieval-qa seed example: 
 "You are a search assistant. Given snippets, pick the most relevant sentence and explain why in one line. SNIPPETS: {snips}
 ANSWER:"

Experiment commands (local bench machine):
- baseline fp16 run: python bench/run_microbench.py --model redwood/7B --dtype fp16 --batch 1 --seq 512 --out ./runs/fp16_s512_b1.log
- nf4 ptq: python bench/run_microbench.py --model redwood/7B --dtype nf4 --ptq yes --batch 1 --seq 512 --out ./runs/nf4_s512_b1.log
- gptq-ish: python bench/run_microbench.py --model redwood/7B --dtype int4 --gptq yes --batch 1 --seq 1024 --out ./runs/gptq_s1024_b1.log

Quick metrics to capture in run summary (one-line):
- tokens/sec (inference step), p50_latency_token_ms, p95_latency_token_ms, perplexity / ppl (on small eval set), MRR@10 (if retrieval).

Notes-to-self about quantization artifacts:
- watch for odd tokenization artifacts: sometimes nf4 conversion introduced increased repetition on early tokens in interactive prompts. Could be KL drift in distribution.
- layerwise outliers: layer 12 and 18 show larger quantization error (run per-layer MSE script). Consider per-layer bit allocation or outlier-aware folding.

Unresolved questions / hypotheses:
- H1: For short chats (<128 tokens), nf4 wins on latency + cost, but for longer sequences (>512) GPTQ 4-bit with better outlier handling might maintain quality — test.
- H2: KV cache warm-start benefits are function of prefix length distribution; need to synthesize synthetic prefixes and measure cache hit rate impact on end-to-end.

Notes on eval set (tiny):
- 40 prompts: 10 roleplay-short, 15 summarization-long, 15 retrieval-qa. Keep random seed fixed (seed=42). Small eval but fast.
- Save eval artifacts: runs/eval-seed42/ (log, generated outputs, token-level latencies).

Housekeeping / where to stash outputs:
- small run artifacts -> s3://redwood-playground/microbench/2026-03/ (ask Jordan for temporary write creds)
- larger runs -> bench-nfs1:/mnt/bench-archive/quarter1/2026

Slack notes to self: ping @jordan if run > 3h; mention issues in #infra-bench.

Rough next-day plan:
- morning: re-run nf4/gptq seeds; collect traces; quick summary in PR description for benchmark PR.
- afternoon: try smaller batch sizes (0.5? sim) and one warmup experiment (5 warm tokens) to see kernel warmup shape.

Random micro-things I noticed:
- small model conversion script conv/quantize_v2.py prints a warning about "outlier clamp" defaulting to 2.5 — try lowering to 2.0 to see quality tradeoff.
- GPU mem fragmentation: restart container between runs if mem footprint drifts +2%.

If time: run a tiny AB test where prompts include an extra system instruction and measure change in MRR and repetition.

End of notelet. Keep ephemeral.

-- Anika

title: Unit cost investigation - Zephyrus Labs
author: Jordan Lee
text:
Intro discovery to map Zephyrus' usage patterns, target latency and strict monthly budget. Main discussion focused on per-token unit economics, batching and KV/prefix caching tradeoffs, hosted vs dedicated cost and private deployment compliance (VPC/KMS/SOC2). Agreed next steps: pilot scope and micro-benchmarks.

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-25 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Zephyrus Head of ML), Lina Morales (Platform Eng), Rafael Hu (Finance), Amara Singh (CTO)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, Jordan from Redwood. Thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Ethan: Ethan here.
[00:10] Lina: Lina.
[00:12] Rafael: Rafael.
[00:14] Amara: Amara.
[00:16] Priya: Priya from the solutions eng side. Happy to dig into benchmarks.

[00:28] Jordan: High level agenda — understand Zephyrus workloads (qps, typical prompt/response lengths), budget constraints, latency SLOs, and tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated, and private. Then outline a pilot. Sound good?
[00:36] Amara: Yep that's perfect. We're specifically worried about token burn — our legal and finance team are nervous about runaway costs if we spike.

[01:05] Ethan: Quick context: we run an assistant that summarizes internal docs and generates code suggestions. Average request is 750 tokens input, 600 tokens output, peak qps around 8 but most of the day it's 1-2 qps. We want sub-400ms latency for short assistant flows but 1-2s is okay for longer generation. Budget ceiling per month for inference is $45k.

[01:47] Rafael: And just to be explicit — we need predictable unit economics. If we do hosted, how do we cap spend or get alerts? If dedicated, what's the break-even?

[02:12] Priya: Great, those are the right levers. A few concepts to set expectations: per-token pricing (hosted), reserved GPU cost for Dedicated (committed monthly), and private / VPC which adds a platform fee. Then there are runtime levers — batching, prefix/KV cache, and quantization which materially change cost per token.

[02:50] Lina: Can you quantify — like if we enable KV cache and batch to 8 requests, does cost drop 30%? 50%?

[03:12] Priya: It depends on request distribution. For a lot of small repeated queries, prefix/KV caching can be 40-70% savings on recurrent tokens. For our serving runtime with continuous batching, you typically see 20-45% effective token-cost reduction vs naive single-request inference when batching to sizes of 4-8 and keeping latency SLOs. But for long outputs (600 tokens) batching often helps amortize overhead so savings can be smaller per token but large in throughput terms. Those are rough numbers; we'll run a micro-benchmark on your prompt set.

[04:05] Ethan: When you say prefix cache — does that store user context in KV on GPUs? We're concerned about PII persistence and retention.

[04:22] Priya: Good point. We let customers configure cache policies. For hosted we can do ephemeral KV cache not logged to persistent storage; for Dedicated/Private you can point cache to your own managed store or disable it entirely. We also support TTLs and zero-retention modes. We'll include KMS details in the security pack.

[05:10] Rafael: From finance perspective — show us break-even for dedicated. If our peak qps is 8 but steady is 1-2, committed capacity might be wasteful unless autoscaling with burst works.

[05:32] Jordan: Exactly. Dedicated has a committed GPU pool and predictable throughput. We have automatic burst options and routing policies — fall back to hosted variants when reserved capacity is saturated. The break-even is driven by utilization: if you use >~65% of a reserved token throughput for the month, dedicated typically becomes cheaper. But again depends heavily on model size, quantization, and batching.

[06:10] Amara: Can you explain quantization here? We have some internal concerns about quality regressions.

[06:21] Priya: We offer QC profiles — 8-bit and mixed-precision quantization paths. For many of the open models we onboard, 8-bit gives near-parity for most generation tasks, but we'll run evaluations on your eval set to measure delta. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization profiles per workload and flag regressions.

[07:00] Ethan: Ok so pilot looks like: run our representative small/medium/large prompts, measure latency, tokens, and quality under three modes: hosted (standard), dedicated reserved pool with autoscale/burst, and private VPC. Also measure with/without KV cache and batching.

[07:28] Priya: That's our usual micro-benchmark. We'll need sample prompts, sample traffic shape (qps histogram), and expected SLOs per route. Also any blocked tokens or redaction rules.

[08:00] Lina: On the private/VPC side — will Redwood manage the control plane or do we need to run anything on-prem?

[08:18] Jordan: For Private we offer a customer-managed data plane, optional on-prem pack, and a private control plane. You can choose the model — VPC peered control plane or fully air-gapped. KMS/HSM integrations are supported. We'll surface the architecture diagram in the security docs.

[08:45] Rafael: SOC2 and audit logs are non-negotiable. We need API-level audit for token lineage and RBAC.

[08:58] Priya: We have per-token tracing and token-level cost attribution in the Console. Audit logs and SSO/SAML with SCIM are supported; we'll attach our SOC2 report and the logging sample.

[09:22] Ethan: Competitor question — how do you compare to Anthropic/openai on pricing?

[09:30] Jordan: On raw hosted per-token, we're competitive on open models, and for dedicated we can beat managed endpoints when utilization is high due to GPU amortization and batching optimizations. Also our routing and fallback gives predictable latency during spikes. We'll include a competitor compsheet.

[10:02] Lina: About throttles and spend controls — can we enforce hard monthly caps or per-route budgets?

[10:12] Priya: Yes — we support per-route quotas, alerts, and hard limits. For hosted we can set quota thresholds and soft limits; for Dedicated we can add caps in the control plane and also route to lower-cost model variants when thresholds are hit.

[10:45] Amara: For our planning, can you give an example calculation? Say 1.5 qps steady, 45k budget, average total tokens per call 1350, what do we look at?

[11:00] Jordan: Quick back-of-envelope: steady 1.5 qps is ~129,600 requests/month (1.5 * 3600 * 24 * 30). At 1,350 tokens per request that's ~175M tokens/month. If hosted per-token = $0.00003 per token (example), that would be about $5.25k — but that per-token number varies by model and context — embedding vs gen different. If using larger model and higher per-token rates, it scales up. The key is batching, caching and model choice can drop effective cost per served token considerably. We'll produce scenarios with realistic per-token rates for the models you want.

[12:10] Rafael: That example number seems low — are you counting both input and output?

[12:18] Priya: Yes both. But remember per-token rates differ for input vs output on some pricing plans; we'll annotate that. Also for long outputs, batching helps less for tail latency so effective cost per user request might be higher; that's why we do the benchmark.

[13:00] Speaker 6 (mumble): question on caching architecture — how is cache invalidation handled?

[13:10] Priya: Cache invalidation is TTL-based and explicit API calls to clear prefix keys. For shared contexts we recommend a short TTL and user-scope keys. We'll document recommended policies.

[14:05] Ethan: On measurement — we want to be able to attribute cost to features and products internally. Can Redwood break down cost per route and per token type?

[14:18] Jordan: Yes the Console provides token-level cost breakdown, route-level dashboards, and traceable request IDs. You can export CSVs for cost allocation.

[15:00] Lina: Any limitations on model pinning across hosted and dedicated? We want consistent behavior when we roll from hosted to dedicated.

[15:12] Priya: You can pin model versions and rollout policies. The same model artifact can be used across hosted and dedicated; kernel selection and quantization may vary but we try to keep behavior consistent. We recommend a canary rollout to validate outputs.

[16:00] Rafael: Inventory question — what's the minimal committed term for Dedicated? Monthly? Annual?

[16:12] Jordan: We have monthly and annual reserved options. Monthly reserves give flexibility; annual reserves give pricing advantages. We'll include a few reserved capacity price points in the pilot materials.

[16:40] Ethan: Tuning question — will Redwood suggest batching configs automatically?

[16:48] Priya: Redwood Optimize recommends batch sizes and cache policies based on observed latency distribution and usage patterns. You can also set hard latency SLOs and it will suggest conservative batch sizes to meet them.

[17:20] Amara: Ok, quality. We need to run our eval set for rouge/bleu and also human spot checks. If quantization drops accuracy for our code suggestions, we need a rollback plan.

[17:33] Priya: Absolutely — we'll run model regression evals and tie alerts to quality thresholds. Rollback is supported and we suggest progressive rollouts.

[18:00] Jordan: Quick risks — unpredictable spikes, long-tail requests that blow up tokens, and data residency/compliance. How important is region residency?

[18:12] Amara: Strongly prefer EU residency for certain customers. We need logs and data at rest in EU for some cases.

[18:28] Jordan: We support region pinning and private deployments in selected regions. We'll note the regions available for Private.

[19:05] Rafael: Financial ask — show a 12-month spend plan for hosted vs dedicated with scenarios Low/Med/High usage.

[19:18] Jordan: We'll prepare a 12-month spreadsheet with break-even points and sensitivity to avg tokens, qps, and batch sizes.

[20:00] Ethan: For the pilot telemetry — what logs do you need from our side?

[20:08] Priya: Representative prompt set, qps histogram, target eval queries, and any per-request metadata you want to propogate like tenant-id so we can show cost attribution. Also a sample of blocked tokens/redaction rules.

[20:45] Lina: How long does a typical pilot take?

[20:52] Jordan: Micro-benchmarking can start in a week and results in 5-7 business days. A fuller pilot with regression evals and dedicated capacity tests is typically 3-4 weeks.

[21:20] Rafael: On procurement — any security questionnaires we can pre-fill?

[21:27] Jordan: We'll send an NDA/security packet, SOC2, and a standardized security questionnaire. We can also fill customer security questionnaires as part of the enterprise process.

[22:00] Ethan: Wanted to raise a potential blocker — our legal might force us to avoid sending PII to hosted endpoints. If so, private on-prem is likely. How much overhead for private?

[22:14] Priya: Private incurs an onboarding and platform fee and possibly on-prem infra. We can give a cost delta and implementation plan. For many customers we do a VPC/private control plane which reduces friction versus full on-prem.

[23:05] Amara: Any quick wins we should try first to reduce token-cost before changing architecture?

[23:12] Priya: Prompt engineering: truncation, instruction tuning to shorten outputs, caching repeated prefixes, and aggressive batching for non-latency-critical routes. Also using a smaller model variant for lower-cost routes.

[24:00] Lina: Are you able to run a quick sim for our 1.5 qps baseline during the pilot to validate queueing/latency under burst?

[24:12] Priya: Yes — we'll simulate steady and burst patterns, and show latency percentiles and cost.

[25:00] Ethan: On reporting — we want monthly alerts if any route goes > 20% above forecast.

[25:08] Jordan: That's doable. We'll configure cost monitors and Slack/webhook alerts.

[26:00] Rafael: Curious — for auditing token lineage, do you store raw tokens? How is redaction handled?

[26:12] Priya: By default we do not persist raw input tokens for hosted customers unless explicitly enabled for debugging. For Dedicated/Private you control persistence. Redaction hooks can filter PII before logs.

[27:20] Ethan: Ok final thing — show us a sample SLA for Dedicated latency targets.

[27:30] Jordan: Dedicated SLA typically commits to P99 latency targets for a class of requests and uptime. We'll send the SLA draft.

[28:00] Amara: Good. Let's summarize next steps so everyone is aligned.

[28:06] Jordan: Summary recap: 1) Jordan sends pilot scope including hosted/dedicated/private cost scenarios and 12-month spend model 2) Priya runs micro-benchmark on the sample prompts with/without KV cache and batching and shares results 3) Customer provides prompt set, qps histogram, and compliance contacts. Any additions?

[28:36] Ethan: Add security docs and SOC2.

[28:40] Rafael: And a finance-specific break-even table comparing monthly vs annual Dedicated reserves.

[28:50] Jordan: Got it. We'll aim to deliver pilot materials by next Tuesday.

[29:05] Amara: Timeline-wise, procurement review will take ~2-3 weeks once we have security pack.

[29:15] Jordan: Great — we'll be responsive. Any other blockers?

[29:22] Lina: One small one — we may need a short demo of Console cost breakdown during the next meeting.

[29:30] Jordan: We can do a 30-minute walkthrough of Console.

[29:40] Priya: I'll also include the micro-benchmark runbook and scripts so you can reproduce locally.

[30:00] Ethan: Thanks, this is productive.

[30:05] Jordan: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the documents and schedule the bench run.

[30:12] (end call)

Notes on transcript quality: Some speaker tags are generic or approximate, occasional words mis-transcribed (e.g., "K V cache" vs "KV cache", "quantize" vs "quantization"), filler words and overlaps present.

Recap (as spoken):
- Customer profile: Zephyrus runs doc summarization and code suggestions; average request ~1,350 tokens; steady qps ~1-2, peak ~8; budget $45k/mo.
- Key concerns: predictable unit economics, token lineage and compliance (SOC2/KMS), dedicated vs hosted break-even, caching and batching impact, quantization quality.
- Agreed pilot: micro-benchmark across hosted/dedicated/private, with/without caching/batching, regression evals, and a 12-month spend model.

Attachments referenced: pilot-scope-template (link in chat), SOC2-summary.pdf (will be sent), example cost model spreadsheet (will be sent).

End of transcript.

title: Cohort signal loss during synchronized canary flip caused unpinned routing to quantized variant
text:
Issue summary: During a synchronized canary roll for redwood-v1-large we observed that a small customer cohort lost explicit model pin state and was routed to the quantized variant (redwood-v1-large-q4). Impact: ~1400 requests over a 12m window returned lower-quality outputs and tokenization deltas; customer observed increased hallucination in 18% of affected responses (reported by customer and confirmed by telemetry). Environment: Dedicated tenant on prod:us-east-1. Steps to reproduce: 1) Start a weighted canary (10%) for redwood-v1-large across us-east-1 with prewarm enabled. 2) Trigger an orchestrator snapshot merge (scheduled merge job). 3) Send steady tenant traffic that relies on explicit version pin headers. Observed behaviour: A cohort of sessions lost model pin during the snapshot merge and were routed to redwood-v1-large-q4 (fallback path) instead of honoring tenant pin. Token counts and tokenizer fingerprints differed, leading to evaluation regression triggers from customer QA set. Expected behaviour: Tenant pin must be preserved across orchestrator snapshot merge; fallback routing should not select a different tokenizer family variant when pin is present. Relevant logs (trimmed): "2026-03-10T18:12:02Z control-plane: commit-snapshot nid=8792 merging epoch 412 -> 413" "2026-03-10T18:12:02Z orchestrator: cohort-signals: cohort=tn-998 lost-pin during merge window (prewarm=true)" "2026-03-10T18:12:03Z edge: route-resolver: selected target=redwood-v1-large-q4 weight=0.0->0.10" "2026-03-10T18:12:08Z serving-runtime: tokenization: tokenizer-hash mismatch from request header - expected 0x3b9f, got 0x8a2c" Additional notes: No 5xx spike, no autoscaler activity; issue correlates with coordinated snapshot/commit and edge prewarm probe timing jitter.

2026-03-10 18:25 - Ethan Park (Support): Customer Narrative Labs opened ticket after noticing quality regression. Provided initial logs and sample request IDs: req-82391, req-82402.
2026-03-10 18:40 - Priya Nair (SRE): Reproduced cohort loss in staging by forcing orchestrator snapshot merge during a prewarm window. Observed same edge route decision to q4 variant when pin header missing for ~12s.
2026-03-10 19:05 - Maya Chen (Customer Success): Confirmed with customer that they set explicit 'X-Model-Pin: redwood-v1-large' header; customer reports intermittent loss, not all requests affected.
2026-03-11 09:12 - Jordan Lee (Runtime): Tokenizer hashes differ between v1-large and v1-large-q4; should never be selected when pin present. Working on guard in route-resolver.
2026-03-12 11:30 - Priya Nair (SRE): Temporary mitigation deployed: route-resolver now verifies pin header at selection time and rejects fallback variants with differing tokenizer-family. Monitoring for false positives.

Hypothesis A: Orchestrator snapshot merge briefly cleared in-memory cohort pin map while control-plane applied new routing epoch, creating a window where edge route-resolver could not find a pinned mapping.
Hypothesis B: Edge prewarm probe timing (probe jitter ~30-50ms) caused a transient routing decision to include lower-cost q4 variant due to a race with weight application (weight transition 0.0->0.10).
Telemetry: Cohort loss aligns at 2026-03-10T18:12:02Z +/- 2s with snapshot commit event and prewarm probe spikes. No autoscaler preempt or GPU eviction recorded.
Control-plane review: commit-snapshot flow holds pin-delta writes, but a bug allowed a short-lived read-before-write window during epoch increments when prewarm flag true.
Edge analysis: route-resolver prioritizes explicit pin but falls back to best-available variant when lookup fails; it did not verify tokenizer-family equivalence before routing to quantized variant.
Repro: Deterministic in staging by inducing orchestrator merge while toggling prewarm and sending pinned header; reproduces cohort loss consistently when merge and first prewarm probe align within 60ms.
Customer impact: A subset of streaming chat sessions observed mixed-variant outputs; not all tenants affected because most flows had longer-lived pin leases (>30s).

Mitigation steps taken: 1) Edge route-resolver patch rolled to prod (hotfix) that enforces: if a requested pin exists in header, reject candidate fallback variants where tokenizer-family != pinned model. 2) Control-plane commit-snapshot flow patched to serialize pin-map flush before epoch activation (PR merged: orchestrator#2147). 3) Deployed a short-term canary throttle to delay weight transitions by 200ms during snapshot commits to avoid the probe/merge race. Outcome: Customer reports quality metrics returned to baseline within 1 hour after hotfix. Follow-ups: add end-to-end unit test for pin-map visibility during snapshot commit, add telemetry to count pin-resolve-failures, update canary playbook to include snapshot coordination.

raw_metadata.summary: Cohort signal loss during synchronized canary flip caused unpinned routing to quantized variant
