title: routing-and-controlplane-runbook-architecture-notes
author: Maya Chen
text:
Purpose
This doc is a combined architecture + operational runbook for our routing policy engine and control-plane components across multi-region deployments. It is intentionally practical: short diagnostics, commands, and mitigations embedded in architecture context so on-call engineers can both reason about root cause and act quickly.

Scope
- Components: routing-policy-service (RPS), control-plane-api, policy-store (etcd/consul), route-agent (edge sidecar), regional health aggregator, and the global policy router.
- Cross-region concerns: affinity, KV replication lag, split-brain on leader election, and fallback model variant routing.
- Not included: serving-runtime GPU node-level debugging (see serving-runtime/sre-runbooks).

Architecture notes (brief)
- Control plane (control-plane-api + policy-store) is the single source of truth for routing policies, rollout stages, and region weightings. It exposes a versioned API used by route-agents to fetch policies on startup and at policy-change webhooks.
- Route-agents run in each region and maintain an in-memory policy cache and local evaluation engine for low-latency routing decisions. Agents watch the policy-store via streaming endpoints and apply delta updates.
- Policy evaluation order: explicit-route (customer pin) -> canary -> weighted-routing -> geo-affinity -> fallback. Policies are deterministic and evaluated top-to-bottom.
- Rollouts: canaries are enabled by rollout rules stored in the policy-store. Each rollout has a name, window, and metric criteria (latency and error thresholds).
- Health checks: agents report region-level health via health-aggregator which updates a region-status index used by global router.

Common incident scenarios + runbooks
1) Control plane API unresponsive (HTTP 5xx or timeouts)
- Symptom: config change fails; route-agents show repeated fetch retries; recent deploy of control-plane-api; alerts: PLAT-CONTROL-API-ERR.
- Quick checks:
 - Check SLOs/dashboard: control_plane_api_request_latency_p50/p95, control_plane_api_error_rate (Dash: Platform / Control Plane / API)
 - kubectl -n platform get pods -l app=control-plane-api; kubectl logs -f deployment/control-plane-api -c api --tail 200
 - curl -v https://control-plane-api.internal/healthz || echo "down"
- Quick mitigations:
 - If pods are CrashLoopBackOff: kubectl describe pod <pod> to see OOM or config errors. Revert recent config change (kubectl rollout undo deployment/control-plane-api) if deploy timestamp aligns with incident.
 - If high CPU due to policy-store scan: scale up replicas temporarily: kubectl scale deploy/control-plane-api --replicas=4 (notify infra).
 - If external dependency (auth/KMS) failing: flip maintained feature-flag to allow unauthenticated local reads for emergency: POST to admin toggle endpoint (requires infra approval).
- Recovery steps:
 - Redeploy last known-good image: kubectl set image deployment/control-plane-api control-plane-api=registry.redwood/internal/control-plane-api:stable-20260201
 - Validate route-agents reconnected: check route-agent logs and policy version: kubectl logs -l app=route-agent -c agent | grep "policy_version="
- Post-incident:
 - Open PLAT JIRA ticket, attach timeline and last deploy id (PLAT-CONTROL-API-ERR-YYYYMMDD), run postmortem template, update changelog.

2) Policy drift or incorrect evaluation order deployed (bad rollout rules)
- Symptom: certain traffic unexpectedly hits a fallback model; regression alerts on quality (Rerank/quality evals) or sudden cost increase.
- Quick checks:
 - Check policy versions: curl https://control-plane-api.internal/v1/policies/versions last_3
 - Search for recent policy changes: git log --since="48 hours" -- platform-configs/policies
 - Query route-agent logs for "policy-eval" traces and decision path: kubectl logs -l app=route-agent | egrep "policy_eval|decision_path"
- Quick mitigations:
 - Push emergency policy patch that restores previous rule ordering. Use the policy-store admin UI to revert version or use API: POST /v1/policies/revert {"version":"v123"}
 - If automatic rollouts continue to apply bad policy, disable rollout engine: PATCH /v1/admin/settings {"rollout_enabled":false} (only for <30m).
- Recovery steps:
 - Validate behavior in canary region and run synthetic tests (see linked_artifacts). Promote fix to all regions after 30 minutes of stable metrics.

3) Regional split-brain / KV replication lag causing inconsistent policies across regions
- Symptom: region A has new policies, region B still uses older policies -> inconsistent routing; alerts: PLAT-POLICY-REPL-LAG.
- Quick checks:
 - Check policy-store replication status: kubectl -n platform exec -it statefulset/policy-store -- /bin/psql -c "SELECT * FROM replication_status;"
 - Check agent-sync metrics: route_agent_policy_sync_lag_seconds{region="us-east-1"}
 - Look for leader-election warnings in logs: kubectl logs -l app=policy-store | egrep "leader|raft|election"
- Quick mitigations:
 - If leader elected incorrectly, force leader stepdown to trigger re-election: kubectl exec -it pod/policy-store-0 -- /bin/consul operator raft remove-peer <peer-id> (follow infra runbook) or use etcdctl to promote leader.
 - Temporarily set global routing to prefer region with majority policy consistency: POST /v1/admin/routing/override {"global_prefer":"us-west-2"}
- Recovery steps:
 - Reconcile KV store: run the replication repair script from git (scripts/repair-kv-replication.sh) with oncall approval. Monitor sync lag and then lift routing override.

4) Route-agent high-latency evaluation causing end-to-end latency spikes
- Symptom: route-agent CPU usage high, p99 eval latency elevated, affecting latency SLOs.
- Quick checks:
 - route_agent_eval_latency_p50/p95/p99, route_agent_cpu_usage
 - Check rule set size: POST /v1/admin/policies/size for region to see number of rules loaded
- Quick mitigations:
 - Reduce policy complexity: enable emergency-compact policy set: POST /v1/admin/policies/compact {"reason":"latency_immediate"} to temporarily apply simplified ruleset.
 - Scale route-agent horizontally: kubectl scale deployment/route-agent --replicas=<current*2>
- Recovery steps:
 - Run policy pruning process to remove obsolete legacy rules (ticket PLAT-3120). Re-introduce full rule set gradually via canary.

Investigations / diagnostics cheat-sheet
- Verify control-plane health: curl https://control-plane-api.internal/metrics | egrep "control_plane_api|policy_store"
- Agent status per region: curl https://health-aggregator.internal/regions | jq . (look for last_synced_ts)
- Policy version reported to router: curl https://global-router.internal/status | jq '.policy_version'
- Example kubectl debugging commands:
 - kubectl -n platform exec -it deploy/control-plane-api -- curl -sS localhost:8080/debug/vars | jq .
 - kubectl logs -l app=route-agent -c agent --since=30m | egrep "warn|error|policy_eval"

Escalation and ownership
- First responder: oncall-platform (rotation). If control-plane API >15m, escalate to platform-sre lead and platform eng owner.
- Pager escalation policy: see PLAT-SOP-ESCL (Confluence link in linked_artifacts). Provide timeline, last_playbook_steps, and any admin toggles we exercised.

Safety knobs and feature flags (where to flip things)
- rollout_enabled (boolean) - disables automated rollouts when false. Admin API path: /v1/admin/settings
- policy_store_read_fallback - allows route-agents to use cached policies for longer TTL when set.
- global_routing_override - temporarily forces traffic to a single region or traffic tier. Use only for short windows and record justification.

Templates / quick commands
- Revert control-plane deployment: kubectl rollout undo deployment/control-plane-api -n platform
- Scale route-agent: kubectl scale deploy/route-agent -n platform --replicas=6
- Force policy-store leader election: kubectl exec statefulset/policy-store-0 -n platform -- /usr/local/bin/raftctl transfer-leader --target-id=<id>
- Emergency compact policy (API): curl -XPOST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://control-plane-api.internal/v1/admin/policies/compact -d '{"reason":"latency_immediate"}'

Post-incident checklist
- Create JIRA ticket with affected regions, start/end times, deploy ids, and mitigations taken (labels: incident, control-plane).
- Add timeline to ticket and link to this doc.
- Run policy audit: ensure no manual emergency edits remain. Archive emergency policy versions to policy-store/history.
- Update runbook with any new commands, gotchas, or learned metrics.

Known gaps / follow-ups
- No safe automated rollback from policy migrations that touch more than 500 rules. Action: implement transactional policy-apply with preflight dry-run (PLAT-4010).
- No RBAC approval flow for emergency admin toggles. Action: short-term Slack approval step required; long-term: implement approval queue.

Appendix: useful dashboards and tests
- Dashboards: Platform / Control Plane / Policy Store Replication; Platform / Routing / Agent Latency; Platform / Global Router Health.
- Synthetic tests: per-region policy-eval synthetic (synthetic/policy-eval) that runs every 30s; endpoint: https://synthetic.internal/policy-eval?test=basic-route

Contact list (oncall rotation owners)
- platform-oncall: @platform-oncall (pager), lead: Arjun Patel <arjun@redwood.com>, eng-owner: Maya Chen <maya.chen@redwood.com>

Notes to self (working area)
- Need to add TLS cert rotation steps for policy-store replication (deferred to infra).
- Double-check rollback image tags used in last 3 control-plane deploys.
- Follow up: add example logs for policy-eval decision_path so new oncall can grep them quicker.

End of doc.

title: openai-compat: responses-v3 deterministic-seed routing + metadata passthrough and streaming reassembly
author: Marisol Vega
text:
Motivation: the OpenAI Responses API v3 introduces a seed/determinism flag and richer per-response metadata fields. Customers expecting parity through our OpenAI compatibility layer were hitting two classes of issues: 1) requests with deterministic seeds sometimes routed to fallback model variants causing non-deterministic behavior, and 2) streaming reassembly and function/tool-calling events lost user-supplied metadata (e.g., trace ids) on intermediate fragments. This PR: - Propagates the new 'seed' and 'determinism' fields from OpenAI-style Requests through our compatibility translation layer so upstream callers can control RNG determinism when we map to compatible model variants. - Adds per-request metadata passthrough: preserves and forwards top-level metadata and nested response-level metadata (user supplied) through streaming frames and the final assembled Response object. - Stabilizes streaming reassembly for mixed partials (text chunks, tool call fragments, structured JSON outputs) by introducing a sequence/frame id and last-frame markers in the compat layer; this avoids interleaving when a single call fan-outs to auxiliary model variants. - Ensures function/tool-calling events are emitted with the original 'metadata' and 'seed' fields intact so SDKs relying on tool traceability continue to work. - Adds exhaustive integration tests against the Responses v3 contract and extends streaming unit tests to emulate packet reorder and intermittent delivery. Implementation notes: - New compatibility translator: redwood/openai_compat/responses_v3_translator.py maps OpenAI fields to internal inference request flags (seed->rng_seed, determinism->sampling_profile). Translator is intentionally minimal: we preserve unknown fields in a passthrough map under compat_metadata for future extensions. - Streaming layer changes: redwood/api/streaming.py: implement frame_sequence_id and final_fragment bool. Reassembly uses (request_id, frame_sequence_id) ordering plus a small re-sequencing buffer gated by latency_slo to avoid head-of-line blocking. - Routing: routing/policy.py updated to prefer exact-architecture variants when determinism is requested; fallback still allowed if pinned variant unavailable. - Tests: tests/integration/test_responses_v3_compat.py includes deterministic-seed repeatability checks, metadata round-trip assertions, and simulated packet reordering scenarios. - Docs: docs/openai_compat.md updated with Responses v3 mapping and guidance for determinism semantics. Backwards compatibility: default behavior unchanged if seed/determinism not provided. We intentionally do not make determinism true by default because it impacts throughput. Checklist: - [x] Translator for seed/determinism fields - [x] Metadata passthrough in streaming frames - [x] Stable reassembly and ordering buffer - [x] Routing preference when determinism requested - [x] Integration + unit tests - [x] Docs update - [x] CI passing on rerun Rollout/rollback notes: feature gated behind a compatibility flag (OPENAI_COMPAT_V3=true) and an experiment toggle for routing. If customer issues are observed around tail latency with deterministic requests, the routing policy can be relaxed to fallback earlier while preserving seed values in logs for replay/diagnosis.

Amit Patel: The translator looks good overall. One open question: if the requested seed exceeds 64 bits, how should we normalize? Suggest we hash down with siphash and record the original in compat_metadata. Can you add a test for large seeds?
Marisol Vega: Responding to Amit: added normalization using siphash64 in translator and test case in tests/integration/test_responses_v3_compat.py line ~120. Original seed preserved in compat_metadata.seed_raw for auditability.
Claire Nguyen: Reassembly buffer hardens well but we should be conservative with the latency_slo default. Recommend 20ms default or tie it to per-customer SLO config. Also noted minor lint issues in streaming.py.
Marisol Vega: Reduced default re-sequence buffer to 20ms and moved config to per-customer tunables. Fixed lint comments and added comments describing tradeoffs.
Benji Rosen: Verified end-to-end locally including tool call round-trips; approved after Marisol pushed the siphash change and the docs clarification.
CI Bot: Build #2245: lint failed on first run; second run passed (all checks green).

On rollback semantics (what we can say today):

- Supported upgrade path is N-1 → N for Redwood Private. We do not currently support skipping major versions without a review.
- Rollback is supported to the previously running version provided:
 (a) the upgrade hasn’t crossed a non-reversible schema boundary, and
 (b) the recommended backups/snapshots were taken before applying migrations.
- Our current guidance: take a pre-upgrade backup of the control-plane DB + config state; if on EBS/CSI, take a volume snapshot; if managed DB, take a point-in-time snapshot.
- For migration failures: we run migrations with guardrails (lock timeouts, idempotent steps), but in the event of a failure we can roll back application components immediately and then restore DB to the pre-upgrade snapshot.

What I’d like to avoid: “guaranteeing” a fixed rollback time without knowing their storage/backend. We can give a typical range and define prerequisites (snapshot ready, prechecks clean, artifacts available).

title: Introduce "safelock" fast-path gating + precision toggle and KV-eviction safety for runtime
author: Aisha Kumar
text:
Context and motivation:
This PR addresses a recurring class of incidents where aggressive fast-path kernel selection and lower-precision execution (fp16 / int8) produced rare but hard-to-detect correctness deviations for edge prompts. At the same time, customers expect throughput and lower cost. We need a runtime mechanism that lets us enable high-performance paths without risking silent correctness regressions in production.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds a 'safelock' gating layer in the kernel selection path. The safelock prevents switching to a fast path unless a set of runtime validators pass (numerical consistency, kv-cache integrity checks, and recent success window).
- Introduces a precision toggle API (per-model, per-deployment) with three modes: strict (fp32 only), balanced (fp16 with strict validators), aggressive (fp16/int8 allowed once warmed).
- Adds a lightweight runtime validator harness: stochastic correctness probes run as background requests against canary inputs to compute divergence metrics (token-level mismatch rate, logit-delta distribution). Validators are cheap and attach metadata to requests that triggered path selection failures.
- Changes KV cache eviction policy to be conservative when cache-warmness is below threshold; combined with safelock it avoids invalidating cached KV frames that fast kernels rely on.
- Integrates safelock signals with the continuous-batching scheduler: until a deployment's validators reach a success threshold, scheduler prefers conservative batching and disables cross-model micro-batching that can expose interleaving bugs.
- Adds observability hooks: metrics (safelock.blocked_count, validator.mismatch_rate, precision.switch_count, kv.eviction_suppressed) and a dashboard stub.
- Adds a feature flag runtime.enable_safelock (default true for new deploys) and model config fields precision_mode and validator_policy.

Design notes and rationale:
- The safelock is intentionally conservative: it is designed to minimize customer-visible regressions at the cost of initial throughput until a model warms. We prefer false negatives (staying on slow path) over false positives (silent incorrect outputs).
- Validators are probabilistic and run only on a small fraction of traffic (configurable). We do not rely on end-user prompts alone; the system feeds a small canary corpus that includes known edge cases and adversarial tokens used in previous incidents.
- KV-cache eviction suppression is implemented as an additional guard in the eviction worker: if cache_warmness < 0.7 and safelock.enabled, eviction respects a soft TTL and only evicts when memory pressure exceeds a higher threshold. This prevents state churn that invalidates prefix caching assumptions used by some kernels.

Commits (high-level):
- feat(runtime): add safelock kernel gating and validator harness (A. Kumar)
- feat(config): model precision_mode and validator_policy proto + defaulting (A. Kumar)
- fix(kv): conservative eviction path and warmness estimator (R. Patel)
- perf(scheduler): integrate safelock signal into batching decisioning (L. O'Connor)
- test: end-to-end validator integration tests and canary job (E. Tan)
- docs: runtime safelock/precision-mode doc, migration notes (doc team)

Files touched (high-level):
- runtime/kernel_selector.cpp/h (safelock implementation, gating checks)
- runtime/precision_policy.proto (new model-level config)
- runtime/validator/ (background probe harness, small canary corpus)
- serving/scheduler/continuous_batcher.cpp (respect safelock signals)
- serving/kvcache/eviction_worker.cpp (suppressed eviction path)
- metrics/registry (new metrics added)
- tests/e2e/validators_integration_test.cc (new suite)
- docs/runtime/safelock.md (operator-facing guide and flags)

Small illustrative snippet included in the patch (non-executable):
"""
if (safelock.enabled() && !validators.passed_recently(dep)) {
 // force fallback to conservative kernel + fp32 path
 selectKernel = KernelSelector::conservative(model, seq_len);
} else {
 selectKernel = KernelSelector::fastpath(model, seq_len, precision_mode);
}
"""

Benchmarks / numbers:
- Baseline (main, before PR) on rtx-a100-80gb, long-tail tests: median latency 48ms, p99 180ms, throughput 2200 tok/s.
- With safelock enabled (default config) immediately after deploy: median latency +6% (51ms), throughput -8% (2024 tok/s) while validators warm.
- After 30m of live traffic and validator success: median latency +1% (48.5ms), throughput -2% (2160 tok/s).
- Aggressive mode (opt-in, warm): throughput +12% over baseline; we see a measurable cost win.
- We ran a correctness sweep against our regression corpus (n=1200 prompts) showing token-level mismatch reduced to <0.02% for balanced mode; in aggressive mode mismatch rises to ~0.6% on the corpus (expected, opt-in).

Testing and CI:
- Added unit + integration tests for validator harness and eviction behavior.
- Added synthetic stochastic tests that simulate rare floating-point edgecases.
- CI: initial pipeline had one flaky test (eviction_worker race) failing on Linux-asan; fixed in second commit. Final CI: all checks passed (build, unit, integration, perf-smoke).

Review discussion (highlights):
- Marco: "I like the safelock abstraction; can we ensure the validator corpus is editable by SREs without code changes?"
- Aisha: "Yes — validators read a canary file from /etc/redwood/validators/corpus.json and we added operator docs. SRE can update via configmap for k8s deploys."
- Eve: "Concerned about metric cardinality when we annotate every request with validator metadata."
- Aisha: "We emit aggregated counters and histograms; only a small sampling logs request-level debug traces behind a flag."
- Liam: "Scheduler changes look sane. Need additional canary rollout plan for enterprise customers with strict SLAs."
- Aisha: "Added rollout doc and an opt-out label on deployment config; default for existing deployments is unchanged (safe-mode learned)."

Edge cases / known tradeoffs:
- There is an initial throughput hit until validators warm. We mitigate by sampling only a small portion of traffic for validators and allowing manual warm-up (canary traffic injection).
- Aggressive precision_mode is opt-in; customers should enable only after verifying on internal test prompts. We include a CLI tool for running the validator corpus locally against a deployment.
- The KV eviction suppression increases memory use under some failure modes; we documented emergency knobs and introduced an automatic disable threshold if memory pressure remains high for 10s.

Migration / operator guidance:
- New deploys: safelock enabled by default. Operators can set runtime.enable_safelock=false to revert (not recommended).
- To opt into aggressive precision: update model config: precision_mode=aggressive and monitor validator.mismatch_rate.
- Dashboards: added a starter Grafana dashboard (docs link) and alerts for validator.mismatch_rate > 0.1% and safelock.blocked_count being unexpectedly high.

Backward compatibility:
- All config fields default to conservative behavior; no breaking changes. Models without precision_mode set continue to use fp32 until they pass validators.

Post-merge actions / follow-ups (linear):
- ENG-4983: add automated warmup job to inject synthetic canary traffic during deploy windows (follow-up).
- ENG-5122: add per-customer precision analytics and billing impact report.

Merge outcome:
- Final status: merged via squash. Branch merged to main after approvals from Marco, Eve, and Liam. CI green at merge.

If you want to test locally: run tools/runtime_cli --run-validators --config test/configs/precision_local.yaml against a dev deployment; run scripts/kv_warmup.sh to pre-fill the kvcache with the canary prefix set.

Thanks to Rohan Patel for eviction work, and the QA team for extended regression runs.

Patch size: moderate; favors safety and observability over aggressive micro-optimizations up front.


Added a runtime 'safelock' gating mechanism to avoid correctness regressions when enabling fast-path kernels and lower-precision execution. New precision toggle with runtime validators. KV-cache eviction made conservative under uncertain cache-warmness. Backwards-compatible; opt-in via config.

title: Partial final output missing after SSE reconnect during TLS renegotiation behind edge proxy
text:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that when a streaming SSE connection briefly drops during a TLS renegotiation event at the edge, the client receives a truncated final output: the last sentence or final punctuation is missing and no explicit end marker arrives. The server logs show the completion event emitted, but the client-side stream terminates early after reconnect.

Impact:
- Affects Inkling Health's production inference pipelines in eu-west.
- Partial outputs break downstream post-processing and fail schema validation for their clinical note ingestion (automated).
- Observed on ~3% of long-running streaming sessions during peak load windows.

Environment:
- prod (eu-west) behind vendor edge proxy (CloudEdge) + vendor CDN.
- Clients use SSE long-polling from browser and also a Node.js backend that implements reconnect/resume.
- Model: rw-instruct-large-v1, typical max_tokens ~1024, average response length ~600 tokens.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start a long streaming generation from eu-west with prefix that yields a long final sentence.
2) Simulate TLS renegotiation at the edge by triggering a short RST/reconnect (they used their synthetic traffic tool to flip the client IP and trigger a rehandshake).
3) Observe returned stream on client: most of the time it resumes fine, but in a subset the final sentence is cut off and no terminal event arrives.

Expected behavior:
- Client should receive full streamed tokens including terminal metadata (choice completion). Reconnect/resume should either stitch output seamlessly or include an explicit end marker.

Actual behavior:
- Server emits completion and logs show terminal event for the request id, but the client sees an abrupt stop after an earlier chunk. No explicit "[DONE]" or terminal JSON arrives. Reconnect handshake shows success, but resumed stream never emits the missing trailing tokens.

Workaround (customer):
- Increase client-side post-reconnect polling window and re-request tail tokens using non-streaming completion API; this recovers text but adds latency and cost.

Attachments:
- customer provided curl and Node.js reproducer, sample client traces, and a HAR file (attached separately in support portal).

Open SSE stream to /v1/stream with a long prompt that generates a long final sentence
From a test machine behind the same edge, flip IP or trigger short RST to force TLS rehandshake at the edge
Allow reconnect to occur and observe client-side stream events and final terminal event presence
Repeat under load to increase probability of occurrence

2026-03-12T08:23:45Z api-gateway: proxy_write returned 0 bytes to edge worker (code=EPIPE) connection_id=conn_9b
2026-03-12T08:23:46Z edge-proxy: TLS renegotiate start connection_id=conn_9b client_ip=203.0.113.45
2026-03-12T08:23:46Z edge-proxy: coalesced-keepalive zero-length write observed, buffering=true
2026-03-12T08:23:46Z serving-runtime: request=req_6f3a connection_lost_event=true, terminal_delivery_confirmed=false

Initial hypothesis: edge proxy zero-length write or buffering during TLS renegotiation causes downstream client to interpret stream as complete. Reproduced in lab by enabling 'edge-worker buffering' and forcing a TLS rehandshake; observed identical symptom. Further narrowed to case where proxy coalesces an SSI keepalive packet with the final JSON boundary, then performs connection migration and the client-side SSE parser treats the next boundary as a new stream rather than continuation.

What we checked:
- Server emits final JSON and exits stream (confirmed).
- Gateway recorded a 0-byte write to the edge worker immediately prior to client disconnect.
- Client reconnects and requests resume token, but resume offset points to earlier chunk (off-by-one) because the proxy suppressed the terminal delimiter during buffering.

Immediate mitigation tried:
- Applied an API-gateway config to insert an explicit "event: end" / "data: [DONE]" line before flushing final chunk for eu-west. Reduced occurrence rate from ~3% to ~0.1% in canary traffic.

Next steps:
- Collaborate with edge-proxy vendor to disable coalescing of zero-length keepalives for SSE endpoints, or to preserve final JSON boundaries across renegotiation.
- Add extra server-side terminal marker for SSE (backport to stable) to make client reconcilers robust to proxy buffering.
- Add more robust resume offset verification on server to ensure resume doesn't skip final tokens.

Mitigation applied: gateway now injects an explicit SSE end marker before connection handoff in eu-west canary. Customer workaround documented. Root cause vendor coordination required for permanent fix.

Applied canary change 2026-03-13 21:12 UTC to eu-west API-gateway fleet: insert explicit terminal SSE event prior to drain. Monitoring shows reduced error rate. Opening a vendor support ticket with CloudEdge (ticket CE-5542) to request fix for zero-length coalescing during TLS renegotiate. Engineering to prepare backport for streaming runtime to include optional double-terminal marker.

2026-03-12 10:12 - Aisha Patel (Support): Customer reports truncated final sentence on SSE resumes when client TLS renegotiates at the edge. Attaching reproducer and HAR.
2026-03-12 11:05 - Daniel Park (SRE): Reproduced in staging with edge-worker buffering enabled. See logs. Hypothesis: proxy coalescing zero-length keepalive into stream boundary.
2026-03-13 09:20 - Inkling Health (Customer): We can confirm workaround of re-requesting tail tokens; production impact is reduced but not acceptable for latency-sensitive processing.
2026-03-13 22:00 - Daniel Park (SRE): Deployed canary gateway change to inject explicit SSE terminal event prior to handoff to edge. Monitoring in progress.
2026-03-14 07:30 - Priya Mehta (Platform Eng): Suggest adding server-side resume offset validation and an idempotent terminal marker — preparing a small patch for review (PR referenced).

title: Graceful batching backpressure and latency isolation for continuous prefill/decode
author: Asha Patel
text:
Motivation: Our continuous-batching pipeline currently prioritizes throughput, but under certain request mixes (short chat turns mixed with long-prefills) we see tail latency spikes and unfair slowdown of latency-sensitive routes. This ticket implements a graceful backpressure and latency isolation layer in admission control plus lightweight batch shaping hints so kernel selection and attention optimizations remain performant at the tail. The goal is to reduce 99.9th token latency for latency-sensitive routes by 35-50% without losing >10% aggregate throughput on heavy mixed workloads.

Scope: admission scoring, soft priority queues, prefill-aware shape hints emitted to the batcher, and a small runtime admission policy that can trigger compact kernels or decode-only fast paths. This work should be orthogonal to autoscaling and focused on per-GPU runtime scheduling and request admission.

Non-goals: changing global QoS for Dedicated customers, implementing persistent per-customer reservations, or adding billing changes. Those are follow-ups managed under Reserved Capacity roadmap.

1) End-to-end e2e test shows 99.9th token latency improvement >= 35% for latency-tagged route under mixed synthetic workload (short chat probe + long prefill).
2) P99 and P99.9 for throughput-only benchmarks degrade by <10% vs baseline.
3) No regressions in unit tests; integration tests for kernel fallback exercised.
4) Feature flag gated and can be toggled per-cluster; rollout doc merged.
5) Github PR with runtime + admission unit tests merged and performance dashboard linked.

High-level design: add an admission scorer computed at request enqueue time: score = alpha * latency_sensitivity + beta * prefill_length_norm + gamma * cache_hit_priority. Requests with score above threshold go to a fast-path soft-queue with small max batch size and strict latency timer; lower scored requests enter throughput queue where the batcher shapes larger batches. The scoring is additive and configurable by route.

Kernel interaction: fast-path queues trigger compact-kernel selection (fewer fused attention kernels, minimal KV routing) to reduce per-token latency; throughput queues prefer wide-kernels and aggressive batching. We will expose a 'batch_hint' metadata field from admission to the kernel selector runtime that can be used to prefer FP16-fused kernels for latency peers and quantized kernels for throughput peers.

Attention optimization: for latency-tagged requests we will enable early-attention pruning (heuristic based on prefix similarity) to reduce attention compute for long prefills when safe. This is implemented as a costed decision that falls back if model logits change above a threshold.

Trade-offs considered:
- Setting too-small fast-path batch sizes reduces throughput; choose conservative defaults and tune via canary.
- Kernel switching adds overhead; amortize by caching kernel choices per (model, seq_len_bucket, batch_hint).
- Attention pruning can change outputs; limited to routes with regression guards and eval prompt sets.

Configuration: all knobs behind feature flag runtime.batching.latency_isolation; defaults off in Prod, enabled in canary clusters.

1) Merge feature-flagged implementation behind runtime.batching.latency_isolation.
2) Unit + perf tests in CI: run existing perf harness with mixed workload (link to test harness below).
3) Canary: enable on 2 non-critical prod clusters for 48h and monitor p50/p95/p99/p99.9 token latencies and throughput.
4) Sweep tuning: adjust alpha/beta/gamma and fast-path max-batch size based on canary telemetry.
5) Full rollout across all clusters if canary metrics meet acceptance criteria.

Artifacts: design doc https://confluence.internal.redwood/runtime/latency-isolation, perf harness dashboard https://dashboards.internal.redwood/runtime/batching/ENG-23109, draft PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1892

Primary: token-level p99.9 latency for latency-tagged routes; Secondary: overall tokens/sec, p99 latency, decode tokens/sec, kernel-switch counts, attention-prune hit-rate, model output regression rate on eval set. Alert if p99.9 increases >10% for non-latency routes. Dashboard linked in rollout plan.

2026-03-10: Ticket created. Initial design sketched and sync with SE + SRE done. Linked perf harness and design doc.
2026-03-11: Prototype admission scorer implemented (alpha=0.7, beta=0.2, gamma=0.1). Unit tests added. Local microbenchmarks show 20% p99.9 reduction on toy workload. PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1892
2026-03-12: Security/Privacy review not required per checklist but product reviewed attention-prune regression risk. Added eval gating to ensure prune disabled for routes with failing evals. Discussed kernel cache TTL to avoid jitter (decision: 5min).
2026-03-13: Canary plan approved by SRE. Canary clusters identified (prod-canary-2a, prod-canary-2b). Instrumentation added: kernel_switch.counter, attention_prune.hit_rate gauge. Scheduled canary toggle for 2026-03-15 02:00 UTC; SLO runbook drafted and attached in Confluence.

title: GPU CI credential rotation and image promotion safety kit
author: Asha Patel
text:
Summary

Purpose
This document defines a safety-first pattern for: (1) rotating CI credentials used by GPU provisioning and image-promotion pipelines, and (2) promoting GPU runtime images (golden bundles) to production pools with provable checks and fast rollback paths. The kit bundles Terraform/IaC patterns, CI job templates, runtime verification checks, SLO-driven gating, and an operator runbook for emergency credential revocation.

Why this matters
- Credential rotation without careful orchestration can leave running inference pools unable to pull images, causing degraded capacity and failed deployments.
- Image promotion (CI -> staging -> prod) must be atomic and verifiable: a mismatched image in a GPU pool can produce model-regression incidents.
- Past incidents show the majority of image-promotion outages occur during key rotation + cross-account image copy windows. This doc reduces blast radius.

Scope
Applies to: all CI pipelines that build GPU runtime images, the Terraform modules that provision tenant GPU hosts and warm pools, and the image-signing/attestation services used by Redwood Inference.

Owner and contacts
- Owner team: engineering (Infra Reliability)
- Primary oncall for rollout windows: infra-oncall@redwood.com
- Escalation: Diego Ramos (Lead - GPU Infra), Priya Shah (Security), Evan Liu (CI/CD)

Terminology
- Golden image: signed OCI image bundle used for production inference nodes.
- Image promoter: CI job that signs, copies, and tags artifacts into the production registry.
- Promotion window: the short period where an image transitions from staging to prod and cross-account copies may be in-flight.

Safety principles (high level)
1) Always sign images with key versioning (KMS key alias + key-id). Verification must include key version metadata.
2) Use a promotion plan that stages in-region canaries before full fleet promotion.
3) Make credential rotation a two-phase operation: preflight (test) then swap (cutover) with automatic rollback on failure.
4) Prefer short-lived credentials (ephemeral IAM role / signed cert) for CI agents; store long-term secrets only in HSM-backed KMS.
5) Maintain an explicit PROMOTION SAFETY MATRIX mapping signals to actions (below).

Promotion safety matrix\
| Signal | Threshold | Action | Rollback trigger |
|--------|-----------:|--------|-----------------|
| Canary 99th latency increase | +40% vs baseline | Halt promotion, mark image suspect, run deeper perf trace | Auto-revert to previous tag in 15m if >2 buckets exceed threshold |
| Error rate (5xx) | >0.5% absolute | Re-route 100% traffic off canary nodes, abort promotion | Full fleet rollback if persisted for 10m |
| Tokenization mismatch (new tokenizer failure) | any runtime error | Halt; capture failing prompt, block image | Manual rollback after investigation |
| Image signature verification failures | any | Stop promotion, alert security, revoke CI key version | Block until signature chain validated |
| Pull auth errors across >=2 regions | >=3% pull failures | Pause promotion; force ephemeral credential refresh | If persists 10m, automated rollback and revoke ephemeral role |

Preflight checklist (CI + Terraform)
1) CI builds image and signs with signing service (key alias: kms/gpu-image-signer). Artifact metadata must include key-version and build-id.
2) CI runs integration smoke: small inference harness against a staging warm pool (tag: staging-smoke). Verify latency and correctness metrics.
3) Terraform plan for registry permissions and cross-account roles is generated and reviewed via tfsec/gate. Module names referenced: tf-modules/registry-crosscopy, tf-modules/ephemeral-ci-role, tf-modules/warm-pool-provisioner.
4) Register promotion intent in the promotion ledger (tagged Git commit + promotion ticket).

CI pipeline example (GitHub Actions / Buildkite style)
- name: build-and-sign-gpu-image
 runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
 steps:
 - checkout
 - run: |
 docker build -t staging-gpu:${{GIT_SHA}} -f infra/Dockerfile .
 docker push staging-gpu:${{GIT_SHA}}
 - uses: redwood/sign-image-action@v1
 with:
 image: staging-gpu:${{GIT_SHA}}
 kms-key: projects/redwood/locations/global/keyRings/gpu/cryptoKeys/gpu-image-signer
 - run: |
 curl -X POST https://signing.redwood.internal/attest -d '{"image":"staging-gpu:${{GIT_SHA}}","key_version":"v3"}'

Promotion job (partial)
- name: promote-to-canary
 env:
 EPHEMERAL_ROLE_ARN: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ci-ephemeral-publisher
 steps:
 - assume-role $EPHEMERAL_ROLE_ARN --duration 900
 - run: |
 ./scripts/cross-account-copy --src staging-gpu:${{GIT_SHA}} --dst prod-gpu:${{PROMOTION_TAG}} --regions us-west-2,eu-west-1
 - run: |
 terraform -chdir=infra/promotion apply -auto-approve -var='image_tag=${PROMOTION_TAG}'

Terraform patterns and recommendations
- Module: registry-crosscopy
 - Purpose: declaratively model cross-account ECR/GCR copy permissions and a short-lived promotion task.
 - Inputs: src_repo, dst_repo, allowed_regions, promotion_role_arn
 - Outputs: promotion_task_id, crosscopy_logs_s3
- Module: ephemeral-ci-role
 - Purpose: create an IAM role the CI system assumes for promotion. Short-lived session only; require MFA for manual triggers. Use OPA policy to prevent wide-scoped permissions.
- Remote state gating: the promotion apply must assert a remote state lock and include a semaphore key in a central tfstate bucket to avoid concurrent promotions.

Credential rotation protocol (two-phase)
Phase A: Preflight (no live swap)
1) Provision new KMS key version and create alias kms/gpu-image-signer -> key-vN.
2) Deploy CI adapters (sign-image-action) to use key-vN in a feature-flagged mode and run 100% test-signings that do not change promotion ledger. Verify that attestation services accept key-vN signatures.
3) Run shadow cross-account copy with ephemeral role using new signing metadata. Confirm copies succeed across all target regions.
4) Monitor for 24h (or 3 release windows) for any unexpected pull auth regressions.

Phase B: Cutover (the swap)
1) Schedule change window (SLO: <30m blind window).
2) Update alias kms/gpu-image-signer -> key-vN (atomic alias swap).
3) Revoke short-lived CI credentials associated with key-v(N-1) after 5m grace. Rotate ephemeral role sessions.
4) Promote a canary image signed with key-vN. Verify canary health for 20m across latency/error metrics.
5) Proceed to full fleet promotion if no triggers fired; otherwise, revert alias to key-v(N-1) and mark key-vN as revocation-pending for forensic review.

Emergency rollback runbook (oncall steps)
1) Detect: Pager fires for pull auth failures or mass pod CrashLoopBackOff when pulling prod images.
2) Immediate action (within first 5 minutes):
 - Confirm via cross-region registry metrics whether pull auth errors are present and their percentage.
 - If pull auth failures >=3% across >=2 regions, run: ./scripts/revoke-ci-ephemeral-sessions --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ci-ephemeral-publisher
 - If image signature mismatch reported, quarantine the image tag: mark in the promotion ledger as blocked.
3) If problems persist >10m:
 - Revert registry image tag on affected warm pools to previous production tag via terraform apply -var='image_tag=${PREV_TAG}'
 - Recreate node groups (if nodes are stuck) by triggering warm-pool rolling-replace job.
4) Post-incident: open an incident review, attach promotion ledger entries, CI logs, KMS audit trail, and the short-lived session token logs.

Observability and SLOs to enforce
- Canary latency delta SLO: canary 99th must stay within +25% of baseline during canary window.
- Image pull success: >=99.5% successful pulls within 1m of request at steady state.
- Promotion lead time: preflight checks must finish within 90 minutes for standard releases; emergencies may use expedited path with manual approver.

Telemetry dashboards (must include)
- Registry pull success rate by region and account (1m and 5m windows)
- Image signature verification failures by key-version
- Promotion job success/failure histogram (by commit)
- Canary latency and error rate trends vs baseline (auto-annotate promotion events)

Automation safety checks (required CI gates)
- Signatures must be validated by attestation service and include key-version metadata. Job fails on mismatches.
- OPA admission check in promotion Terraform that asserts promotion_task_id is unique and no concurrent promotions are in progress.
- Pre-promotion smoke harness that runs 100 inference prompts and validates outputs against a golden-response set (fuzzy matching allowed; threshold 95% similarity).

FAQ and edge cases
Q: What if a region's image copy lags by more than 30 minutes?
A: Pause promotion and trigger a manual crosscopy re-run. If unable to copy within 60 minutes, postpone full promotion and continue with a limited regional promotion strategy.

Q: Who can manually trigger expedited promotions?
A: CI admins with MFA + a signed approval from the Release Lead and Security. The ephemeral role requires an MFA assertion to be assumed for manual flows.

Appendix A — Example Terraform stub for ephemeral role
resource "aws_iam_role" "ci_ephemeral_publisher" {
 name = "ci-ephemeral-publisher-${var.env}"
 assume_role_policy = data.aws_iam_policy_document.assume.json
 tags = { team = "gpu-infra", created_by = "ci-pipeline" }
}

# OPA policy (promotion gate) — high level
# deny if concurrent_promotion == true
package promotion.gate

default allow = false

allow {
 not input.concurrent_promotion
}

Change log
- 2024-02-15: Initial draft (Asha Patel)
- 2024-04-10: Added KMS two-phase rotation guidance and example CI snippets (review: Diego Ramos)
- 2024-06-03: Updated safety thresholds and rollback timing after postmortem lessons (review: Priya Shah)

Related resources
- tf-modules/registry-crosscopy README in repo infra/modules (link internal)
- signing.redwood.internal (image attestation service)
- infra/runbooks/warm-pool-rolling-replace-runbook.json

Acknowledgements
Thanks to Diego Ramos, Priya Shah, Evan Liu, and the Release Engineering rotation team for review and early testing.

title: Quickstarts Adoption KPIs (Hosted API) — draft sheet
author: Nikhil Sharma
text:
TAB: Summary
Last updated: 2025-03-14 (Nikhil)

Goal
Define a KPI + telemetry spec to measure whether Quickstart Templates (RAG + Agents) improve Hosted API activation, conversion, and reduce support load, without collecting sensitive content.

Scope
- Hosted API self-serve + sales-assisted (but metrics primarily PLG).
- Template-originated traffic only (tagged / identifiable).
- Initial templates: rag-agent-python, rag-agent-typescript.

North Star (v1)
- Time-to-First-Success (TTFS): from first API key created to first successful template-run request (200 + stream completed OR non-stream response completed) within 60 minutes.

Primary KPIs
1) Activation
- TTFS (p50/p90) for template users vs non-template new users
- Activation rate: % of new accounts reaching “First Success” within D0 (same day) / D7

2) Conversion
- % of activated template users converting to paid within 14/30 days
- $: first 30-day revenue per activated template account (median)

3) Retention / quality of adoption
- D7/D30 retention: % of activated template accounts with >= X tokens / >= Y requests
- Share of traffic tagged as template-originated for first 7 days (proxy for “stuck with it”)

4) Support deflection
- Support tickets per 1k new accounts (template cohort vs baseline)
- Template troubleshooting page engagement vs ticket creation (proxy)

Guardrails
- Opt-in telemetry by default for non-essential headers; templates must still function if telemetry is disabled.
- No prompts, completions, retrieved documents, or tool outputs in analytics events.
- Avoid high-cardinality dimensions (don’t log raw request IDs, customer IDs in metrics tags; use internal joins).

Owners
- KPI definitions + targets: Nikhil (Hosted API PM), Henry (Hosted API PM)
- Telemetry platform + analytics plumbing: Logan Wright
- Template implementation: Monica Patel (DevEx)
- Docs funnel + troubleshooting instrumentation: Elliot Price (Docs), Wei Chen (Tech writer)
- Support deflection measurement: Priya Shah (Support feedback loop), Dev Patel (Support ops)

TAB: KPI Definitions

KPI 1 — Time-to-First-Success (TTFS)
Definition
- Start: timestamp of first API key created OR first successful auth handshake (whichever is available reliably in data warehouse).
- End: timestamp of first “template_success” event OR first “api_request_success” with template tag + completion/stream end.

Inclusion criteria
- Accounts created after template launch date.
- Template cohort identified by either:
 (a) CLI init event (qs.cli.init)
 (b) template app event (qs.app.start) with template metadata
 (c) API traffic containing template tag header (see telemetry section)

Success condition
- Any generation/embedding request that returns 200 AND is not immediately followed by a client-abort flagged error. For streaming:
 - Success = stream completed (client received end-of-stream) OR server sent a final chunk.

Reporting
- p50/p90 TTFS by: template_name, language, sdk (py/ts), region (bucketed), and plan type (free/paid)

KPI 2 — Activation rate
Definition
- Activation event: first_success
- Rate D0: % of new accounts that reach first_success within 24 hours of signup.
- Rate D7: % within 7 days.

Activation funnel stages (see “Funnel Events” tab)
- signup_created
- api_key_created
- template_scaffolded
- local_run_started
- first_success
- deployed_success (optional, later)

KPI 3 — Conversion to paid
Definition
- % of accounts in template cohort converting to paid plan within 14 and 30 days of signup.
- Also track: time from first_success -> paid conversion (p50/p90).

Notes
- Separate self-serve paid vs sales-assisted contract conversions.
- For sales-assisted, treat “opportunity created” as intermediate metric.

KPI 4 — Retention / sustained usage
Definition
- D7 retention: activated accounts with >= 10 successful requests OR >= 200k tokens by day 7.
- D30 retention: activated accounts with >= 50 successful requests OR >= 1M tokens by day 30.

Rationale
- We want to avoid counting “one-and-done” template runs as success.
- Thresholds should be revisited after internal beta baselines.

KPI 5 — Support deflection
Definition
- Ticket rate: (# support tickets created by accounts in cohort within first 14 days) / (# accounts in cohort) * 1000
- Compare to baseline cohort (new accounts same time window, non-template identified).

Ticket taxonomy (initial)
- auth (401)
- quota/rate limit (429)
- networking/timeout
- streaming disconnect
- otel exporter/config
- tool schema validation
- retrieval empty/poor relevance

Success metric
- Reduce ticket rate by 15–25% for template cohort vs baseline within 60 days of public launch.

TAB: Funnel Events (Event dictionary)

Conventions
- Prefix “qs.” = template/quickstart specific events
- Prefix “api.” = already-existing API traffic events, with added template tags/dimensions

Required fields for qs.* events
- template_name (enum; e.g., rag-agent)
- template_language (python|typescript)
- template_version (semver string)
- distribution (cli|github)
- telemetry_opt_in (true|false)
- environment (local|ci|prod) — keep as small enum

Event table

| Event name | When fired | Source | Required properties | Optional properties (bounded) | Owner | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| qs.cli.install | CLI installed | CLI | os (mac|linux|windows), arch (x64|arm64) | shell (zsh|bash|fish) | Monica | If we can’t reliably capture, drop. Useful to debug install friction. |
| qs.cli.init | Template scaffolded | CLI | template_name, template_language, template_version, distribution=cli | git_init (true|false) | Monica | Writes a local “version stamp” file; event only if telemetry_opt_in=true. |
| qs.cli.doctor | Doctor run | CLI | template_name, template_language, template_version | checks_failed_count (0-10), primary_failure (enum) | Monica | primary_failure: missing_api_key|bad_model|collector_unreachable|dns|other |
| qs.app.start | App started | App | template_name, template_language, template_version, environment=local | runtime (node|python), framework (fastapi|express|other) | Monica | Used to measure “got it running”. |
| qs.app.first_request | First user request made in app | App | template_name, template_language, template_version | request_kind (chat|embed|rerank), used_retrieval (true|false) | Monica | Avoid logging user input. Just the action category. |
| qs.app.first_success | First successful completion/stream | App | template_name, template_language, template_version | streaming (true|false), used_tools (true|false) | Monica | This is preferred “First Success” marker; fallback to api.request success if missing. |
| qs.app.error | Template error surfaced to user | App | template_name, template_language, template_version, error_category (enum) | http_status (200/400/401/429/5xx), retry_attempted (true|false) | Monica + Priya | error_category aligns with template error taxonomy; keep stable for support. |
| api.request | Any API request | Gateway/SDK | request_id (internal), customer_account_id (internal) | template_tag (string), template_version (string) | Logan | Template tag should be join key for cohorting; do not create high-cardinality metrics tags. |
| api.request.success | Successful API request | Gateway/SDK | status=200 | latency_bucket (enum), tokens_in_bucket (enum), tokens_out_bucket (enum) | Logan | Use buckets to avoid cardinality issues. |
| api.request.error | Failed API request | Gateway/SDK | status (401|429|5xx|timeout) | error_type (enum), retryable (true|false) | Logan | Align with SDK error types. |

Template tag header proposal (for api.* attribution)
- Header: X-Redwood-Template
 - Value: <template_name>@<template_version>;<language>
 - Example: rag-agent@1.1.0;python
- Header: X-Redwood-Template-Opt-In
 - Value: true|false

Notes
- Headers must be optional. Some corporate proxies reject unknown headers; templates should support disabling via env.
- Gateway allowlist required (see linked PRs). If blocked, templates should still work and fall back to qs.* events only (if any).

TAB: Dashboard Spec (What we want in Console/Analytics)

Dashboard 1: Quickstarts Overview
- New accounts (daily)
- Template cohort size (daily)
- Activation rate D0/D7 (template vs baseline)
- TTFS p50/p90 (template vs baseline)
- Top failure categories (qs.app.error) by count

Dashboard 2: Funnel (Template cohort)
- api_key_created -> qs.cli.init -> qs.app.start -> first_success
- Drop-off % at each step
- Median time between steps

Dashboard 3: Reliability + cost signals (Template-tagged traffic)
- 401 rate, 429 rate, 5xx rate
- streaming disconnect rate (if detectable via SDK / client abort signals)
- Latency p50/p95 (bucketed)
- Tokens out per request (bucketed)

Dashboard 4: Support deflection
- Tickets per 1k new accounts (template vs baseline)
- Ticket breakdown by category
- Link-outs: troubleshooting docs views, “helpfulness” votes (if available)

Operational view (internal)
- Filter in Console for template-tagged traffic (required for triage + demos)
- Ability to pivot by template_name + version (low cardinality only)

TAB: Targets (initial strawman; to revisit post-internal beta)

Assumptions
- Templates are production-minded; primary value is reducing onboarding entropy and failure loops.

Targets (first 60–90 days post public launch)
- TTFS p50 <= 20 minutes for template cohort (from api_key_created)
- Activation D0: +10–15pp vs baseline
- Activation D7: +5–10pp vs baseline
- Conversion to paid (30d): +2–4pp vs baseline (small early expectation)
- Support tickets per 1k new accounts: -15% vs baseline

What “baseline” means
- New accounts in same time window that do not have template tags or qs.* events.

TAB: Implementation Notes / Constraints

Privacy
- Do not log prompts, retrieved text, tool inputs/outputs, file paths.
- For error events, include category + short stable error_code only (no full stack traces in analytics).

Cardinality constraints
- Allowed dimensions for dashboards: template_name, template_version (top N only), language, environment, status code, error_category.
- Not allowed as metric labels: account_id, request_id, raw model name if too granular (use “model_family” bucket where needed).

Data quality concerns (known)
- Some users scaffold via GitHub template without CLI; we need API-level attribution via headers.
- Some proxies block headers; telemetry should be resilient/optional.
- Streaming “success” is tricky; we need consistent detection (SDK improvements in flight).

Dependencies
- CLI emits qs.cli.init / qs.cli.doctor (DevEx)
- SDK/gateway header allowlist + safe handling (Platform)
- Console filter for template-tagged traffic (Console/Analytics)
- Support ticket tagging alignment with taxonomy (Support Ops)

TAB: Open Questions
1) TTFS start timestamp source
- API key created is best but not always tied to “first attempt”. Alternative: first 401/200 request timestamp.

2) Opt-in defaults
- Do we default telemetry_opt_in=true for template events but make header tagging opt-in? (current leaning: yes; reduce proxy issues)

3) GitHub template attribution
- If user clones repo, we can still set X-Redwood-Template by default from app config. But we need an obvious “turn off telemetry” switch.

4) Defining “paid conversion” for sales-assisted
- Use opportunity created + stage progression? Or strict paid contract signature only?

5) Support deflection attribution window
- 14 days vs 30 days. Support suggests 14 days captures most onboarding tickets; keep both in reporting.

6) Regions / deployment modes
- For hosted API metrics, we can bucket by region. For Dedicated/Private, separate dashboards later.

Change log
- 2025-02-07: Added support deflection definitions + ticket taxonomy mapping.
- 2025-02-21: Updated template header proposal to be optional due to proxy/header issues found in early trials.
- 2025-03-14: Added funnel step definitions (qs.app.first_success preferred over api.request.success for streaming correctness).

title: Runbook Writing and Telemetry Bootcamp Curriculum — Operator Training
author: Priya Kapoor
text:
Summary

This page documents a repeatable, instructor-led bootcamp to train platform operators and engineers to write high-quality runbooks that are telemetry-driven, testable, and maintainable. The curriculum is designed for new operators, service owners, and incident responders who will author or own runbooks for platform services (prefix cache, allocator, tenant-slicing, model-variant router).

Audience

- Platform operators and SREs
- Service owners in eng-platform and eng-serving-runtime
- Oncall engineers who respond to latency/cost incidents

Learning objectives (measurable)

1. Produce a runbook that contains a clear escalation path, data-driven detection predicates, and an operator checklist.
2. Write two telemetry queries (one metric-based, one log-based) that reliably surface the condition the runbook describes.
3. Create a synthetic verification (unit) that validates the runbook’s detection predicates against a small replay dataset.
4. Implement a post-incident update cycle and link to the action in the runbook so it can be closed by the owner.

Curriculum overview (3-day instructor-led)

Day 0 — Prework (self-paced)
- Read: "Runbook authoring and maintenance guidelines" (required).
- Complete a short quiz on SLO definitions and common platform failure modes.
- Setup: access to Grafana/Tempo, Kibana, and a sandbox tenant. Confirm permissions with infra-oncall.

Day 1 — Foundations and detection
- Morning: Lecture (1.5 hr) — Runbook structure and the telemetry-first principle.
 - Sections: Summary, Impact, Detection (metric + log predicates), Immediate actions, Escalation, Rollback, Postmortem link.
 - Example services: kv-prefix-cache, dynamic-allocator, model-variant-router.
- Lab (2.5 hr): Write detection predicates for a synthetic latency spike:
 1) Metric predicate: p95 latency > 300ms for 5m AND error rate > 1% for 2m.
 2) Log predicate: queries that include "kv-cache:miss" and "eviction-reason=reshuffle" for >50 events in 10m.
- Homework: Author a first draft runbook for a provided scenario.

Day 2 — Triage, actions, and testability
- Morning: Workshop (2 hr) — Mapping telemetry to operator actions.
 - Instrumentation checklist: SLI names, tag conventions (region, tenant_id, model_variant), and minimum retention expectations (30 days for alerts, 90 days for postmortem traces).
 - Ownership patterns: primary, secondary, oncall-runbook-maintainer.
- Lab (3 hr): Implement a synthetic verification for the runbook detection predicates using the synthetic-replay harness.
 - Deliverable: three test cases (baseline, transient spike, persistent degradation).
- Evening: Peer review session — teams exchange runbooks and provide 3 actionable comments.

Day 3 — Escalation, de-escalation, and lifecycle
- Morning: Tabletop simulation (2 hr) — live incident with operator rotation. Measured outcomes: time to detection, time to mitigate, number of escalations, checklist completeness.
- Afternoon: Retrospective (1.5 hr) — calibrate SLOs and adjust detection thresholds.
- Closing: Runbook merge checklist and post-incident update procedure.

Assessment and certification

- Pass criteria: runbook accepted in repo (PR merged), synthetic verification green, and at least one successful tabletop participation.
- Certificate: "Telemetry-Driven Runbook Author (Redwood)" valid for 18 months. Re-certification: 2-hour refresher + one tabletop.

Delivery model and resourcing

- Instructor: Platform training lead (approx. 1 dedicated trainer per cohort of 12).
- Duration: 3 days (24 total hours including pre/post work).
- Environment: sandbox cluster with one copy of kv-prefix-cache and dynamic-allocator seeded with synthetic load.
- Tools: Grafana (dashboards pre-built), Loki/Kibana, Tempo (trace slices), synthetic-replay harness (repo: infra/synthetic-replay).

Runbook template (required fields)

1) Title (single line)
2) Summary (1–2 sentences) — short impact statement
3) Owner (primary, secondary) — team and pager alias
4) Impact and user-visible symptoms — list
5) Detection
 - Metric predicate (exact expression)
 - Log predicate (example query)
 - Trace pattern (optional)
6) Immediate mitigation steps (numbered)
7) Escalation path (names/roles and contact method)
8) Safe rollback / service-level de-escalation (how to revert changes)
9) Diagnostics checklist (commands, queries, dashboard links)
10) Post-incident required actions (TTR SLA for update: 7 days)
11) Verification tests (links to synthetic tests)
12) Related runbooks and runbook-ids

Required telemetry examples (copyable)

- Metric predicate (PromQL):
 sum(rate(request_duration_ms_bucket{job="kv-prefix-cache",le="0.3"}[5m])) by (region) / sum(rate(request_duration_ms_count{job="kv-prefix-cache"}[5m])) by (region) > 0.95
- Log predicate (Loki):
 {app="kv-prefix-cache",env="prod"} |= "kv-cache:miss" | json | tenant_id!="" | count_over_time(10m) > 50
- Trace predicate (Tempo/trace): search for spans with operation.name =~ "kv-prefix-cache.*evict" and duration > 100ms, aggregated by tenant_id.

Synthetic verification example (bash)

- Reproduce a persistent-degradation case with synthetic-replay:
 1) ./synthetic-replay --scenario=kv-cache-eviction-heavy --duration=15m --tenants=10
 2) Wait for PromQL predicate to evaluate true in the sandbox (check metrics-exporter).
 3) Run owner diagnostics script: tools/diagnostics/kv-cache-inspect.sh --tenant <id>

Tabletop scenarios (catalog)

- KV cache shard reshuffle during black-box warmup
- Region-specific allocator starvation (spot preemption cascade)
- Model-variant fallback thrash causing token-cost spikes
- Multi-tenant cold-cache cold-start causing onboarding failures

Retention and SLO guidance for runbooks

- Telemetry retention required for runbook validation: metrics 30d, logs 90d, traces 90d.
- Alert SLO: detection-to-acknowledge median <= 3m for SEV2, median <= 1m for SEV1 during business hours.
- Escalation target: oncall primary owns initial mitigation within 15m of alert for SEV1.

Merge checklist (PR to runbook repo)

1) Runbook filled using template and linked to service metadata (service ID, repo).
2) At least one synthetic verification included and green in CI.
3) Two reviewers from different teams approved (one operator, one service owner).
4) Dashboard links present and dashboards annotated with threshold panels.

Ownership and follow-up

- Course owner: Priya Kapoor (eng-platform training). Contact: priya@redwood.ai (internal).
- Curriculum reviewers: see metadata above.
- Quarterly review: curriculum and scenario catalog reviewed each quarter; runbook templates updated at least annually.

Appendix A — Example telemetry queries and dashboard panels

- Grafana panel: "kv-prefix-cache p95 by region"
 - PromQL: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_ms_bucket{job=\"kv-prefix-cache\"}[5m])) by (le, region))
- Alert rule: "kv-cache-p95-region-high"
 - Expression: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_ms_bucket{job=\"kv-prefix-cache\"}[5m])) by (le, region)) > 0.3
 - For: 5m, Labels: severity=SEV2, owner=kv-cache-team

- Example debug command (operator):
 - kubectl -n platform logs -l app=kv-prefix-cache --since=15m | jq -r '.message' | grep eviction

Related pages and templates

- Runbook authoring guidelines (required pre-read) — /confluence/eng-platform/how-tos/runbook-authoring-and-maintenance-guidelines-2025
- Synthetic-replay repository — infra/synthetic-replay (internal git)

Revision history

- 2025-09-10: Created by Priya Kapoor (initial curriculum draft).
- 2025-11-02: Added PromQL examples and tabletop scenarios (reviewers: Ethan, Marta).
- 2026-02-15: Adjusted assessment criteria and certification validity (finalized).

title: Fewshot attenuation heuristics — lab notes
author: Maya Patel
text:
Purpose
Quick personal scratchpad capturing experiments and heuristics for reducing exemplar overdominance in few-shot prompt sets (what I call 'attenuation') — aim: keep exemplar signal useful but avoid literal copying, brittle token-level overfit, and instruction hijacking.

Background / rationale
- Problem: when small numbers of exemplars are highly similar or strongly formatted, model tends to: copy exact phrasing, overfit label tokens, or treat examples as hard rules instead of cues. This shows up as hallucinated metadata, hallucinated reasoning steps, or brittle failures on paraphrase inputs.
- Goal: heuristics that are cheap to test in hosted/Dedicated flows; prefer prompt-side fixes (no fine-tuning) that interact well with Redwood runtime features: prefix caching, batching, and token-budget SLOs.

Experiment log (chronological)
1) baseline 3-shot (A)
- Template: \"Instructions: Paraphrase to plain English. Example 1 -> Q: \"What is the meaning of life?\" A: \"Life means...\"\" (simple exact format)
- Observed: 36% verbatim reuse for unique phrases, 18% hallucinated numeric claims.

2) example-noise (B) — tiny perturbations
- Apply light paraphrase to exemplars (tense swap, synonym replace). Keep labels same.
- Observed: small reduction in verbatim copying (~22%) but occasional polarity flips (because paraphrase introduced negation in two examples).

3) anchor-token dilution (C)
- Insert neutral anchor sentence before each example: \"(Example for style only; ignore facts.)\"
- Observed: Large drop in factual hallucination (13%), but model ignored label formatting more frequently -> answer brevity decreased.

4) exemplar-weighting via explicit meta cues (D)
- Prefix: \"Examples are guides, not rules. Provide your own phrasing.\" and add \"EXAMPLE_START\" tokens between examples (unique sequence).
- Observed: Better paraphrase diversity; lower exact-match. Slight latency + token usage increase (anchor tokens counted).

5) negative-exemplar (E)
- Include 1 negative example showing what *not* to do.
- Observed: helped on structure errors but introduced confusion when negative example had contradictory label tokens.

Quick takeaway: combination of paraphrase augmentation + explicit \"guidance\" prefix seems promising. Anchors reduce hallucination but cost tokens.

Prototype heuristics (to test systematically)
- ShotRotation: rotate order of exemplars per request to avoid position bias (cheap, interacts badly with caching — needs route-aware cache bypass).
- SoftParaphrasePool: maintain pool of 5 paraphrase variants per exemplar; sample 1–2 per prompt. Reduces verbatim reuse.
- AnchorLite: single short anchor token phrase (\"Style guide: be original.\") vs full sentence; measure delta/loss ratio.
- ExampleContrast: for categorical tasks, include 1 borderline example to widen model boundary; for generative tasks include 1 counterexample to show failure modes.
- TokenBudget-aware truncation: if request close to budget, automatically switch to AnchorLite + 1-shot.

Failure modes observed / notes
- Instruction hijacking: too many meta-cues cause model to treat prompt like a multi-step instruction list and follow the wrong step. Keep meta-language short.
- Contradictory anchors: negative examples that contradict label vocabulary can flip final labels. Use neutral phrasing for negatives (show format, not content).
- Caching/cold-start interaction: rotating exemplars defeats prefix caching; for high-QPS routes, prefer static exemplar unless you have hot cache invalidation.

Sample prompt prototypes (short)
1) SoftParaphrase 3-shot (compact)
\"GUIDE: Use your own words. \nExample 1:\nQ: How to reset my router?\nA: Turn it off, wait 30s, turn on.\n--\nExample 2:\nQ: Steps to cancel subscription?\nA: Sign in, go to billing, click cancel.\n--\nNow answer:\nQ: {{user_q}}\n\"

2) AnchorLite + negative (compact)
\"Style: concise, do not echo examples exactly.\nBAD EXAMPLE:\nQ: What is pi?\nA: 3.14159 EXACT (do not mirror)\nGOOD EXAMPLES:\n... (2 positive paraphrased examples)\nAnswer: {{user_q}}\n\"

Measurement plan (automated)
- Metrics: exact-token overlap rate, n-gram reuse, paraphrase-similarity (embedding cosine to exemplars), faithfulness score (task-specific), token cost delta, 95th pct latency.
- Dataset: 400 eval queries per template; include paraphrase + adversarial variants.
- Compare across: baseline static-3shot, SoftParaphrase, AnchorLite, Rotation-once-per-1000, Negative-example. Use Redwood Dedicated for consistent latency measurement.

Open questions / TODOs
- Q1: How much does exemplar diversity interact with model size/quantization? run small-medium-large (ggml/FP16/8-bit) matrix.
- Q2: Should we expose attenuation knobs in the SDK (e.g., sample_paraphrase_count, anchor_level)? sketch API surface.
- Q3: Best practice doc: one-pager for Solutions team summarizing heuristics + when to prefer server-side cache bypass. Draft outline needed.

Action items (short)
- [ ] Run 5k evaluation across two models and log metrics (owner: Jonas) — Linear-4821
- [ ] Prototype SDK flags for AnchorLite and ShotRotation (owner: me) — drop-in param: attenuation: {none, lite, full}
- [ ] Short internal note for Solutions with examples and recommended defaults (owner: Priya)

Rough notes to self (messy)
- prefer 1–2 short anchors instead of long meta paragraphs; long ones break model flow
- negative exemplars should not reuse label tokens; use neutral markers like \"LABEL:X\" to show format only
- consider embedding-cluster sampling to pick exemplars that are diverse w.r.t. user query (but cost is extra lookup)
- remember: batching + shared prompt templates can accidentally leak anchoring if not per-request randomized

Snippets / quick experiments to copy into test harness
- bash pseudo: \nfor MODEL in rwd-xl rwd-medium; do run_eval --template softparaphrase --paraphrases 3 --samples 1; done

References / links for myself
- internal: RFC: fewshot-guidance-patterns (confluence id: 8743)
- external: paper on instruction induction: \"When Prompts Collude\" (noted in reading list)

End of pad.

(Notes intentionally rough — keep evolving. Will move to a more polished playbook if evaluation results look promising.)
