title: Deployment sterile window and fallback choreography
author: Avery Chen
text:
Planning session to finalize deployment sterile-window policy, coordinated fallback choreography across regions, and align on runbook triggers + telemetry gating for launch. Focus on minimizing blast radius during model rollout and ensuring fast automatic fallback to edge model variants. Discussed A/B gating, canary thresholds, and required dashboards and runbook edits.

Header: 2027-01-19 10:00 PST / Duration 62 minutes / Attendees: Avery Chen, Sofia Ramos, Jonah Park, Priya Nair, Marco Li, Ellen Graves, Tomás Rivera

00:00 Avery Chen: ok let's kick off, thanks for carving the time, I want to get to one clear sterile deployment window policy and the fallback choreography so we can ship the optimizer bits this sprint
00:12 Marco Li: yep morning, we've got exec eyes on this, timeline hasn't changed, go-no-go is end of next week
00:18 Sofia Ramos: quick note, the runtime team pushed the KV cache optimization which reduces cold-starts but it flips some timings, so we need to adjust canary thresholds
00:30 Jonah Park: (murmur) uh and the dedicated pools behave differently under prefix caching
00:34 Priya Nair: agreed, we've seen the metric skew on P50 vs P95 when prefix hits rise
00:40 Ellen Graves: just so we're aligned, sterile window means no schema or infra changes during the seventy-two hour window around rollout? how strict
00:52 Avery Chen: yeah, strict. we want only immediate rollback-safe toggles during the window. No infra merges unless critical. Also, all canary traffic routes must be reproducible and reversible
01:06 Tomas Rivera: question on region routing — if a region is degraded do we fail-over to nearest region or to a cheaper model variant in same region
01:18 Sofia Ramos: we prefer same-region fallback when possible to reduce latency impact; if capacity is exhausted then route to variant-small which is quantized
01:30 Marco Li: is variant-small acceptable for early customers? it changes token quality
01:36 Jonah Park: quick comment — quality drop is measurable but for 60% of edge cases it's fine, we need a customer-facing SLA note
01:48 Priya Nair: and KMS keys for the private deployments — do we need a different key rotation window during sterile
01:55 Avery Chen: good catch, Priya. no key rotations during sterile unless emergency key compromise, add to runbook
02:03 Ellen Graves: action: runbook edit, add key rotation policy
02:10 Tomas Rivera: (crosstalk) telemetry — we need a composite gating signal, not just error rate. latency spikes + request entropy + model perplexity
02:22 Sofia Ramos: agreed. propose composite health score: [latency P95, token drop rate, perplexity regression]. Thresholds: green<0.6, amber 0.6-0.8, red>0.8
02:36 Jonah Park: how do we compute perplexity in prod cheaply? approximations only
02:42 Sofia Ramos: we can use sampled evaluation on 1% traffic plus the light-weight perplex proxy we prototyped
02:51 Marco Li: (interrupts) sampling might miss edge regressions during high load
02:54 Priya Nair: we can bias sampling towards failed routes and new prompt templates
03:02 Avery Chen: ok, let's settle on sampling plus error-biased sampling. Jonah, you'll put the sampling config in the canary spec
03:12 Jonah Park: yep, I'll own that
03:14 timestamp 03:14
03:16 Ellen Graves: about rollback — automatic vs manual? we discussed auto fallback to variant-small for red>0.8, but manual for perplexity regressions that exceed delta 0.15
03:30 Sofia Ramos: auto fallback to variant-small for infra or latency-only incidents; require manual for quality regressions because of business impact
03:40 Tomas Rivera: manual decisions add latency to mitigation — we should define a fast path for high-severity quality degradation with a dedicated runbook step
03:52 Priya Nair: create a 'fast fallback' runbook where on-call can trigger emergency auto-fallback given an approval token — two clicks pattern
04:03 Avery Chen: good, and require postmortem within 48 hours for any fallback event
04:12 Ellen Graves: agree, and include retrospectives with product and customer success for external communication
04:20 Jonah Park: can we simulate a fallback during the staging window? like a chaos injection that forces a region degrade
04:28 Sofia Ramos: yes, we have a chaos script. needs permission to touch routing tables; schedule with infra
04:36 Marco Li: schedule the simulation in the two weeks before launch, coordinate with SRE page rotation
04:43 Priya Nair: SRE will need a runbook dry run and oncall brief, add to schedule
04:49 timestamp 05:00
05:00 Tomas Rivera: on observability — dashboard checklist: model quality panel, composite health score, canary histogram, latency tail waterfall, KV cache hit-rate
05:12 Sofia Ramos: also add token-level cost meter per route so we can detect cost regressions early
05:18 Jonah Park: note: batcher config changes can affect cost dramatically; include batcher version in telemetry
05:24 Ellen Graves: who owns the dashboard build
05:27 Priya Nair: SRE owns infra panels, runtime owns model panels, product owns the narrative and acceptance criteria
05:34 Avery Chen: assign owners: Tomas dashboard infra, Sofia model panels, Jonah canary specs and sampling, Priya runbook edits, Ellen communications
05:45 Jonah Park: (soft laugh) and me for the sampling, yeah
05:48 timestamp 06:00
06:00 Marco Li: quick discussion on canary schedule — 2% traffic for 30m, 5% for 1h, 20% for 3h then ramp to 100% over 12h if green
06:12 Sofia Ramos: those windows are fine but P95 baseline must be within 10% of baseline or abort
06:18 Priya Nair: also add a hard abort if error rate increases by 50% vs baseline in any window
06:25 Ellen Graves: document the exact metrics and rollback steps in the canary spec and confluence
06:30 Avery Chen: on-call runbook must include checklist: pre-deploy health scan, post-deploy smoke, canary health checks, rollback steps, communication template
06:40 Tomas Rivera: dependency freeze — we need a two-day freeze on runtime-critical libraries and driver updates
06:46 Sofia Ramos: agree. no quant kernels merges 48h before sterile window
06:51 Jonah Park: and mark emergency exemptions for security fixes only
06:55 timestamp 07:15
07:15 Priya Nair: discussion: private deploy customers — we need to surface the fallback behavior in the contract and in customer docs; some customers won't accept cross-region fallback
07:28 Marco Li: yes, legal/product will need an appendix for fallback policies per deployment mode (hosted/dedicated/private)
07:36 Ellen Graves: action: legal to draft fallback appendix and SLO note, product to review

07:48 Jonah Park: also add a technical verification for on-prem: KMS behavior during fallback and if we can gracefully use local model artifacts
07:56 Sofia Ramos: on-prem has latency but we can support model variant in same rack; document the artifact sync behavior
08:03 timestamp 08:30

08:40 Priya Nair: timeline for tests — run 1: next Tuesday, run 2: two days later, dry run for runbook one week before release
08:50 Marco Li: make sure we have SRE rotation aligned that week
08:55 Ellen Graves: communications plan — runbook owners to draft customer comms and release notes two days before rollout
09:02 Jonah Park: small point, quant skew — if quantized variant differs more than 0.12 BLEU-ish equivalent then flag
09:10 Sofia Ramos: we'll map BLEU to our surrogate quality metric
09:15 Avery Chen: ok time check, 12 minutes left. let's recap owners and immediate deliverables

09:24 Avery Chen: Jonah — canary spec + sampling config (due 2027-01-22)
09:31 Jonah Park: got it

09:40 Sofia Ramos: noted

09:49 Priya Nair: noted

09:58 Ellen Graves: i'll get legal synced

10:07 Marco Li: confirmed

10:24 Sofia Ramos: good KPI

title: Access approved but console permissions not provisioned after Okta issuer domain swap
text:
Issue summary:
Users report that Access Request approvals show as 'Granted' in the Support Console but the target internal service (runbook/console) still returns 403. Happens after the recent Okta issuer domain swap (okta-old.redwood -> okta-new.redwood).

Impact:
- Internal engineers cannot escalate to runbooks or use the console automation tooling after approvals.
- Blocks oncall workflows during testing; affects ~12 engineers across multiple teams.

Environment:
- prod (us-east) - internal console + identity-proxy + okta-new.redwood

Steps to reproduce:
1) Submit Access Request for runbook elevation in Support Console using existing flow.
2) Approver approves the request (shows Granted in UI).
3) Attempt to open runbook — receives 403 with 'missing RBAC grant'.
4) Inspect auth logs on identity-proxy and console-service.

Observed logs/snippets:
- identity-proxy: "ERROR auth: issuer mismatch: token_iss=https://okta-old.redwood/oauth2/default, expected=https://okta-new.redwood/oauth2/default"
- console-service: "RBAC: no matching grants for principal: user:12345 issuer=https://okta-old.redwood"

Notes: This started after the Okta issuer domain migration rolled earlier this week; some tokens/approval links still carry the old issuer in their assertion/redirect flow.

2026-03-10 09:12 - Priya Shah: Reported by SRE oncall after two engineers couldn't escalate. Assigned to Ethan for initial triage.
2026-03-10 10:05 - Ethan Cole: Reproduced in prod. Token issuer mismatch seen in proxy logs. Hypothesis: approval tokens generated before migration still referencing old issuer; console and proxy validate against new issuer only.
2026-03-11 14:22 - Claire Wu (Identity): Confirmed Okta org swap completed; legacy issuer still active for 24h. We thought token exchange would normalize issuer during exchange but logs disagree.
2026-03-12 08:30 - Ethan Cole: Implemented temporary auth-layer allowance to accept old issuer for access-request assertion path. Rolling to prod canary (10%). Monitoring for unintended acceptance of stale tokens.
2026-03-12 12:00 - SRE oncall: Canary at 10% shows successful provisioning for previously-failing users. No obvious regression in other flows after 3h.
2026-03-12 15:40 - Priya Shah: Customer-facing note not required (internal only). Tracking follow-up to rotate any long-lived tokens that may contain old issuer references.

Initial hypothesis: RBAC grant lookup keys include issuer, so any token with old issuer won't match grants issued under new issuer mapping.
Checked audit logs: Access Request approval events authored at 2026-03-09 23:xx still contain 'iss' set to https://okta-old.redwood. Approvals created after 2026-03-10 02:00 have new issuer.
Identity-proxy currently rejects tokens whose 'iss' does not match configured accepted_issuers list (single value).
Support Console's approval token generator signs a short-lived JWT with an 'iss' claim set to the Okta issuer configured at time of generation. Some queued approvals were created before migration and delivered post-migration.
RBAC datastore keys: grants are indexed by (principal_id, issuer). When issuer changes, previously-created grants are still stored under old issuer namespace; provisioning call attempts to read grants using issuer from assertion.
Attempted local repro by forging approval JWT with old issuer and calling provisioning endpoint — repro'd 403 with same logs as production.

Short term mitigation: Deployed identity-proxy update to accept both https://okta-new.redwood and https://okta-old.redwood on the access-request/provisioning endpoint only. This allowed in-flight approvals to complete normally without touching global token acceptance.
Medium term fix: Backfilled RBAC grants for recently-approved requests by running migration job that normalizes grant keys from old issuer to new issuer for approvals in the migration window (2026-03-09 22:00 -> 2026-03-10 04:00). PR: github.com/redwood-inference/rbac-tools/pull/57
Long term: Update approval token generation to include an 'orig_iss' claim and update provisioning to canonicalize issuer during lookup. Add explicit migration step to retirement playbook for future issuer changes. Added unit tests for multi-issuer acceptance in identity-proxy.
Follow-ups:
- Security to review acceptance window (Ethan & Claire).
- Rotate any long-lived service tokens that may embed old issuer references.
- Run additional audit to ensure no external tokens accepted accidentally.

title: Orbital Networks — GTM co-sell sprint & operational risk triage
author: Alex Chen
text:
Meeting header: 2026-12-20 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~62 minutes | Record: Yes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood Partnerships); Marta Rojas (Orbital VP Partnerships), Daniel Cho (Orbital Head of Cloud), Samir Patel (Orbital Solutions Architect), Erika Nguyen (Orbital Legal)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- Purpose: align on co-sell motion, risk areas for pilot, and next steps for a joint GTM sprint.
- Key concerns: customer compliance (data residency, KMS), deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private), pricing splits, and target account lists.
- Agreed: Redwood to produce a benchmark/cost spreadsheet; Orbital to provide topology and target accounts; legal to align on procurement timeline.

Topics detected: Co-sell GTM timeline; pilot scoping; Private deployment constraints; SLA and procurement; competitive positioning.

[00:00:05] Alex (Redwood AE): ok uh good afternoon everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Alex Chen from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. We're joined by Priya, our solutions engineer, and Liam from partnerships. Can we do a quick round of intros from Orbital?
[00:00:18] Marta (Orbital): yeah hi, Marta Rojas, VP Partnerships, thanks for setting this up. We're keen to figure out how we run a quick co-sell sprint and what the operational risk looks like.
[00:00:25] Daniel (Orbital): Daniel Cho, I run cloud engineering, so I'll own the infra questions.
[00:00:29] Samir (Orbital): Samir Patel, solutions architect, I'll drive the integration with our partner portal and mapping to account teams.
[00:00:33] Priya (Redwood SE): hey, Priya here, hi everyone. Quick note—I'll try to keep the deep-dive focused to your asks so we can land next steps.

[00:01:05] Alex: objective for today is threefold: one, agree a one-page co-sell plan; two, identify any blockers for a pilot (esp around VPC/KMS/SOC2); three, pick a target set to go after in Q1. Does that sound right?
[00:01:20] Marta: yep that sounds right. also want to make sure we don't step on your current vendor agreements, we have a couple of channel exclusivities to watch for.

[00:01:45] Priya: ok jumping into tech-- we usually recommend starting hosted for fast time-to-value unless you have strong regulatory needs. For enterprise pilots though, Dedicated or Private (VPC) is common. Quick question: do you have a hard requirement for on-prem or is it just preference?
[00:02:02] Daniel: currently it's preference for some of our customers in telco/defense verticals. We have two pilot accounts that require data residency in EU and at least customer-managed KMS. So Private/VPC is likely for those two.
[00:02:18] Alex: good callout. That leans us toward a Private deployment for the pilot but we can still demo hosted for internal stakeholders.

[00:03:12] Samir: can you explain the dif between Redwood Dedicated and Redwood Private? sometimes our sales folks confuse them.
[00:03:20] Priya: sure—Dedicated is reserved GPU capacity in Redwood's managed pool with predictable throughput and SLA; Private is a VPC or on-prem deployment where you control the network and key management. Private gives you full control over KMS/HSM and audit logging in your environment. There's also hybrid where we can route sensitive requests to Private and less-sensitive to Hosted to save cost.
[00:03:45] Marta: ok hybrid sounds interesting for a phased approach.

[00:04:10] Daniel: latency is a concern for one pilot; they expect sub-150ms for short chat flows at P95. Is that achievable on Dedicated?
[00:04:23] Priya: depends on model choice and quantization. For base Llama-like open models we're routinely hitting P95 <120ms with our Dedicated configs for 8k context on A100-equivalent. For Private, latency benchmarks depend on customer infra—if you have NVLink and colocated inference nodes, even better. We should run a sample workload to be sure.

[00:05:05] Alex: question on commercial—Orbital, how do you usually structure partner rev splits? Are you open to a lead-gen plus referral fee or do you prefer multi-touch co-sell deals?
[00:05:19] Marta: our standard is 60/40 on ARR for co-sells but we can be flexible based on account motion and who owns the procurement. For pilot/demo leads we sometimes do flat referral fees.

[00:05:45] Alex: we can model both. I'll send a simple spreadsheet with two scenarios.

[00:06:30] [00:06:30] Priya: on compliance—SOC 2 Type II is available, we also support SAML/SSO and SSO integrations, audit logs, and KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and HSM options for Private. Any must-haves?
[00:06:50] Erika (Orbital Legal): Erika here, procurement note: we'll need a data processing addendum and clarity on data retention and delete APIs. Also want to flag a couple of our enterprise customers require subprocessor info and EU processing guarantees.
[00:07:05] Alex: understood. We have a security pack (SOC2, infra diagrams, subprocessors) we'll share. We'll also note our retention delete APIs.

[00:07:45] Samir: integration flow—Orbital's partner portal calls a third-party function that runs an LLM step for re-ranking leads. We can point that at Redwood via an API key but we'd rather not send full PII to hosted endpoints. So we want tokenization + prefix-caching on your side, or route the PII to Private. Thoughts?
[00:08:10] Priya: yeah, two patterns: 1) partial obfuscation/tokenization before hitting Hosted or 2) Private where the data never leaves your VPC. We also support prefix/KV caching to speed repeated queries and reduce cost. If PII is a blocker, Private is the cleanest approach.

[00:09:00] Daniel: curious about fallbacks—if dedicated capacity is saturated, will requests fail or route to hosted? we need graceful degradation.
[00:09:12] Priya: we have smart routing and fallback policies—can route to a lower-cost model variant or to hosted, with circuit-breaker thresholds. We can set strict policy to avoid sending PII to hosted variants.

[00:09:45] Marta: on sales ops—we want a joint one-pager for SDRs and AE playbooks. Included should be value props, target ICP, a simple flow for handing leads, and a swimlane of responsibilities. Can Redwood help with that?
[00:10:00] Alex: yes we'll produce a co-sell playbook draft. Liam from our partnerships team will help with enablement materials.

[00:11:15] Liam (Redwood): quick note from partnerships—we've done similar co-sells with three ISVs this year, typical close time is 3-6 months, but with a strong pilot we can accelerate to 45-60 days. Key is clearly signed pilot scope and able champion in the account.

[00:11:50] Marta: ideal timeline for us is a pilot kickoff in mid-Jan, with GTM in March. Is that feasible?
[00:12:01] Alex: yes that aligns with Redwood capacity planning; we'll need commitments on target accounts and legal constraints by late December to hit that.

[00:12:40] Samir: technical ask—can Priya show a quick high-level runbook for a Private bring-up? Steps, network ports, certs, KMS handshake?
[00:12:52] Priya: absolutely—(high-level) step 1: exchange network egress/IP allowlist and firewall rules; step 2: KMS integration via customer-managed keys with MFA HSM interop; step 3: deploy inference nodes with our agent (container) and register with Private control plane; step 4: set routing policies and test canary. We have a runbook we'll share.

[00:14:05] Daniel: what's the expected ops touch for Private? we don't want a 6-month integration.
[00:14:12] Priya: typical Private bring-up is 2-4 weeks with a small infra team if you have infra templates; our ops team handles most orchestration and we provide the agent. If on-prem air-gapped, that takes longer.

[00:15:00] Alex: let's talk pilot measurement—what success metrics should we agree on?
[00:15:06] Marta: pipeline influenced, SQLs generated, latency SLA met, and no data residency breaches.
[00:15:12] Samir: also operator lift—ease of deployment and maintenance.

[00:15:40] Priya: ok for the benchmark I'll use your sample prompt set, run cost/latency across Hosted and Dedicated estimates, and show 3 model variants (quality/cost tradeoffs). That will give a clear recommendation for pilot.

[00:16:20] [00:16:20] Alex: on pricing—if Orbital wants to pilot with us on Private, we can do a reduced pilot rate for 3 months to validate. After pilot we transition to committed Dedicated or Private pricing. I'll capture a pilot offer in the spreadsheet.

[00:17:10] Erika: legal ask—if pilot data is considered customer data, we need to see the DPA and confirm delete APIs. Also want an indemnity clause for data breaches.
[00:17:22] Alex: we'll attach the DPA and highlight delete endpoints. For indemnity we'll have legal follow up—I'll loop our legal counsel into the thread.

[00:18:10] Marta: competitive question—how do we position vs Anthropic and OpenAI for regulated customers?
[00:18:18] Priya: differentiate on deployment flexibility and observability—our Private offering plus token-level cost/latency dashboards is a good selling point. Also our rollouts and automatic fallback policies help customers feel safe in production.

[00:18:50] Samir: can Redwood join our customer QBR call during the pilot? it'd be helpful for the account team to have a technical presence.
[00:18:59] Alex: yes, we're happy to join QBRs and co-present customer wins.

[00:19:35] [00:19:35] -- brief cross talk/overlap; some audio glitch --

[00:20:05] Priya: a couple of technical caveats—quantization reduces memory and can affect some rare token completions; we recommend a small eval set to ensure no quality regressions. Also continuous batching and KV cache interacts with prompt engineering; we can help craft prompts to be cache-friendly.

[00:21:00] Daniel: about observability—we need traces per request and token-level cost attribution for our finance team. Can Redwood provide that?
[00:21:08] Priya: yes, Console includes token-level breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and tracing hooks you can link to your observability backend. We'll demo a console snapshot in the next call.

[00:22:10] Marta: on GTM enablement—we want a joint webinar in March. Who owns the content?
[00:22:18] Liam: partnerships can co-produce; Redwood marketing will own registration and creatives but Orbital subject matter experts should present the customer POV. We'll draft a proposed agenda.

[00:23:05] Alex: ok let's recap decisions so far: 1) pilot scope will include two target accounts (one EU-residency with Private deployment, one US with Dedicated), 2) Redwood will run benchmarks and provide a pilot pricing sheet, 3) Orbital will share network/topology and procurement constraints. Anything missing?
[00:23:24] Marta: include the referral / rev split options in the spreadsheet.
[00:23:28] Alex: noted.

[00:24:10] [00:24:10] Short silence / background noise

[00:24:35] Priya: quick risk triage—listed technical risks: data exfil risk (mitigation: Private or tokenization), latency risk (mitigation: benchmark + Dedicated), quality regression on quantized models (mitigation: eval set + canary), procurement delay (mitigation: pilot SOW and short-term commercial).

[00:25:22] Samir: do you have standard pilot SOW templates for co-sell?
[00:25:28] Alex: yes we'll attach a lean SOW that includes success criteria, timelines, deliverables, and a short 30/60/90 review cadence.

[00:26:00] Erika: procurement windows—we typically have ELA reviews take 3 weeks internally; if there's partner momentum we sometimes expedite. We'll confirm.

[00:26:40] Daniel: question—does Redwood require any specific egress ports or protocols for Private agent?
[00:26:48] Priya: mostly standard HTTPS outbound to control plane endpoints, plus a TCP port for agent metrics if you want direct collection. We'll send the exact allowlist.

[00:27:30] Alex: ok I'm going to open the co-sell playbook doc we start from—(Alex shares link) this is a skeleton with messaging, ICP, and a basic handoff flow.
[00:27:45] Marta: perfect, we'll review and add our account mapping.

[00:28:30] [00:28:30] Technical tangent—discussion of model variants and quantization choices; some incomplete sentences and filler: "...so if you go 4-bit it tends to, uh, reduce GPU memory but you might see slight acceptance on rare tokens..."

[00:30:05] Priya: we will run three model variants: 1) high quality (larger model), 2) balanced (quantized medium), 3) cost-optimized (small quantized). We'll show expected token costs and latency for each.

[00:31:20] Samir: network compliance—for EU account we need data never to cross into US datacenters. Can you pin processing to EU region in Private?
[00:31:28] Priya: yes Private can be hosted in EU region only and our control plane supports region pinning. For Hosted we also have EU regions but for strict residency Private is the preferred route.

[00:32:10] Alex: what's the minimal data we need from Orbital to run the initial benchmark?
[00:32:16] Samir: a 100 prompt sample set, expected tokens per call, and traffic profile (concurrency & peak TPS).

[00:32:28] Alex: great. Can you share that by Tuesday?
[00:32:32] Samir: yes we can—I'll upload to the shared drive.

[00:33:00] Priya: we'll also need a small golden set for quality checks; ideally 20-30 edge-case prompts.

[00:33:20] Marta: anything on pricing transparency? our finance folks will want NRE, pilot discounts, committed spend tiers.
[00:33:30] Alex: we'll surface those in the spreadsheet. We'll show pilot discount, committed tier pricing, and an ops uplift for Private.

[00:34:05] [00:34:05] brief audio glitch, one participant reconnects

[00:35:00] Daniel: for the POC, who will be the day-to-day technical lead on Redwood's side?
[00:35:06] Priya: that'll be me; Priya Desai, and I'll be supported by our onboarding ops team.

[00:35:40] Alex: I'll handle commercial and partner enablement. Liam will support GTM.

[00:36:10] Samir: regarding co-sell motion—do you have a recommended lead handing mechanism? SFDC or shared spreadsheet?
[00:36:20] Liam: we can do SFDC shared records or a lightweight partner portal intake. For pilots a shared spreadsheet is simplest. For scaled co-sell we'd push SFDC integration.

[00:36:55] Marta: ok shared spreadsheet for pilot; we'll coordinate SSO invites for the account team.

[00:37:40] Priya: last tech note—if you want strict data segregation, we can enable query-level encryption where only your KMS decrypts tokens. It's slightly more complex but feasible.

[00:38:10] Samir: that might be necessary for one of the accounts. Let's plan on that as a risk mitigation.

[00:39:05] [00:39:05] quick side convo about market messaging; filler words, laughter

[00:40:00] Alex: time check—we're about 40 minutes in. Are people ok to keep going 20 more minutes?
[00:40:05] Marta: yep good.

[00:40:25] Priya: I'll summarize the technical deliverables: benchmark spreadsheet for three variants, runbook for Private bring-up, list of allowlist ports, and console demo snapshot.

[00:41:10] Alex: and commercial deliverables: co-sell one-pager, pilot SOW template, pricing spreadsheet, rev-split scenarios.

title: Sandstone Corp — Search prototype: embeddings + rerank walkthrough
author: Maya Chen
text:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-29
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rafael Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Sandstone), Tom Becker (Sandstone), Ellen Yu (Sandstone)

Summary: Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on embeddings + reranking pipeline for a lightweight search prototype. We demonstrated the embeddings endpoint, then the rerank endpoint and console insights. Discussed tradeoffs: latency vs cost, batch sizes, and caching. Agreed next steps to share a notebook and sample dataset.

Topics: Hosted embeddings, reranker endpoint, Redwood Console quick metrics, Optimize suggestions (batching/quant), security notes (data retention, SSO/KMS), benchmarking plan.

Transcript (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect):
00:00 Maya: Ok, hi everyone thanks for joining, we got about 45 minutes, quick intros?
00:05 Priya: Hi I'm Priya Nair, I run search at Sandstone, we have a small team working on QA and product search, excited to see a hosted flow.
00:12 Tom: Tom Becker, principal ML eng, mainly focused on retrieval pipelines and infra.
00:17 Ellen: Ellen Yu, product, I'll be looking at metrics and user impact.
00:21 Rafael: Rafael here, Redwood SE, i'll do the technical demo, show embeddings + rerank calls and a console peek.
00:29 Maya: Perfect, i'll jump in with context, why we think Redwood fits, but Rafael hands off to you.

02:10 Rafael: Alright, i'm sharing my screen — apologies if bandwidth is a bit laggy — first slide very quickly: hosted API — embeddings endpoint returns 1k-d vectors, we support batching, streaming not necessary for embeddings.
02:27 Tom: Quick q, what dimensionalities are available? we currently use 768 from our model.
02:33 Rafael: We can host models at 512, 768, 1024 depending on model variant, and we auto-normalize. There was that note in the onboarding docs, link I'll paste after.

05:00 Rafael: Now i'll call the embeddings endpoint — note this is the hosted Redwood API key tied to the demo tenant — code snippet: POST /v1/embeddings with payload, you get back base64 floats, or we also provide numpy-friendly JSON.
05:24 Priya: The response looks fine, does it include request latency per item?
05:28 Rafael: It returns overall latency header and token-level timing on gen endpoints, for embeddings we return a timing_ms field; you can see on the console we also break down cost per-k token equivalent for comparables.

07:10 Rafael: Next step is retrieval: vector search against their index — for the demo i preloaded a tiny index of 1200 product docs — i run an ANN query — here's cosine scoring then top-k.
07:39 Ellen: Is the vector index managed by Redwood or do we need to host separately?
07:43 Rafael: For hosted search we provide an optional vector index managed layer (like a managed ANN cache) — for customers who want full control you can use your own index and call Redwood reranker only.

10:02 Rafael: Ok reranker — this is the main differentiator for quality — we pass candidate set + query to /v1/rerank with model param, and you get re-scored list; reranker takes advantage of context tokens and often improves MRR significantly.
10:27 Tom: Does reranker pay per-token? i'm thinking about cost.
10:31 Rafael: Yes rerank is per-token plus a small candidate fee, but we have Optimize suggestions to trade off batch sizes, or use a cheaper rerank model for production. We also support fallback policies — if Dedicated capacity is busy we route to compatible variant.

13:55 Priya: Our latency target is P95 < 200ms for web search. How realistic is that for embeddings + rerank?
14:04 Rafael: For small candidate sets (top-10) and optimized models you'll be sub-200ms on Dedicated or regional hosted if sequence lengths are small; on standard hosted tier P95 can be higher depending on concurrency. The console shows token latency histograms so you can pinpoint tail latencies.

16:20 Maya: Can we quickly show the Console — just want Priya to see cost/latency per route.
16:25 Rafael: Yep switching to console — this dashboard is per-route, per-model breakdown, here's an example of a search route showing avg latency, p95, and token spend. Notice the predictive Optimize suggestions panel — it recommended batch size 8 for their load and quantization profile x4.

18:40 Tom: About caching — do you support prefix or KV cache for rerank scenarios?
18:46 Rafael: We have KV cache primarily for generation workflows; for search we do prefix caching of repeated queries and can cache rerank results for identical candidate+query pairs, but TTLs are configurable in the route config. There is an edge case where user queries are near-identical and caching improves unit cost a lot.

21:10 Priya: Security question, we need SOC2 and customer-managed keys, plus SSO.
21:20 Maya: Yes we support SOC 2, you can integrate KMS/HSM for Private deployments; for hosted we offer encrypted-at-rest and offer bring-your-own-key for Dedicated in certain tiers, SAML SSO for console access. We'll send the security pack.

24:00 Rafael: Now i'll demo a full pipeline: 1) call embeddings, 2) ANN lookup, 3) call rerank with top-12 candidates, 4) return top-5. I'll run it with two rerank models so you see difference.
24:22 [code run noises]
24:38 Priya: Oh interesting the newer reranker bumps a different doc to top — can you show the token breakdown?
24:41 Rafael: Yep token breakdown panel — see how the prompt and doc contexts consume tokens; this is where Optimize suggests a lower-context prompt to reduce cost.

28:15 Tom: What about throughput? our peak qps is ~1200, burst to 3k.
28:23 Rafael: For those volumes you tend to want Dedicated capacity with autoscale pools; we can create a commitment that matches 1200 steady qps and brief burst headroom. We'll size GPUs based on model latency.

31:00 Ellen: If we wanted to run an A/B — reranker A vs reranker B — what's the best Redwood approach?
31:08 Rafael: Console supports rollout policies per-route: canary, weighted A/B, automatic fallback. We also capture per-variant metrics and you can tie quality alerts to evaluation prompts.

33:40 Priya: A practical question — we have an existing OpenSearch pipeline, can Redwood just slot in as a rerank service?
33:50 Rafael: Absolutely, many customers keep their ANN/index and call Redwood reranker for re-scoring only. You pass candidate IDs and texts or references, credentials are simple API call with request-scoped metadata for audit logs.

36:12 Tom: How do we handle private data — e.g., internal docs with PII? retention policy?
36:20 Maya: You can set data retention to zero for hosted, or use Dedicated/Private where logs are kept in your VPC and you control retention. We also support redaction at ingest in the SDK layer.

38:40 Rafael: Quick note on costs — for the demo tenant I ran rerank on a mid-size model; rough numbers show campaign per-query cost, but Optimize tab has suggestions if you want to switch candidate generation to an embedding cluster offline and only rerank top-5 online.

41:15 Priya: We're also evaluating index refresh cadence — how quick to re-embed new content?
41:21 Rafael: You can do streaming embedders or batch reindex; we provide a jobs API and can trigger background re-embeds; recommended is nearline for catalog updates, real-time for user generated content.

43:30 Ellen: Ok let's recap next steps.
43:33 Maya: Recap: Rafael sends notebook and code, Maya sends pricing and security pack, Sandstone shares a sample of query logs and target SLOs.
43:45 Priya: Sounds good, i'll coordinate with Tom and upload logs.
43:50 Tom: We'll also push a small anonymized dataset.
43:55 Maya: Great thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites for a bench run next week.
44:01 Rafael: Thanks, bye.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-heard words, speaker overlaps, names sometimes appear as first name only. Links referenced: https://redwood.ai/docs/embeddings, internal benchmarking sheet (link shared post-call).

End of transcript.

title: eng-platform
text:
anna: Quick sync — thinking about introducing a cost-aware routing layer that prefers cheaper model variants for lower customer tiers and by region. It should also have automatic fallback to higher-quality variants if we detect quality regressions. High-level idea, not details yet.

mike: +1 on the idea. Two engineering concerns: 1) model compatibility (tokenization, output format) 2) how we estimate token cost before routing. We need cheap per-request cost estimate in the routing path. :thinking:

jess: For telemetry we should emit: route_decision, estimated_token_cost, chosen_variant, quality_score, fallback_trigger, and token_counts. That lets us correlate cost savings vs quality regressions.

oliver: UX note — console needs a simple toggle per-customer and a rollout slider. Folks should be able to opt-out / pin to expensive variant. Also show expected savings and recent fallback rate in the UI.

sam: Quotas/limits angle: if we route free-tier customers to cheaper variant we should also enforce a per-customer token_budget so they can't blow past cost forecasts. If budget exceeded, either degrade to a lower-rate limit or surface upsell.

mike: Implementation sketch: routing policy lives in the control plane. At request time we compute a cheap estimate: tokens_est = ceil(prompt_len / avg_chunk) + ceil(max_output_len / avg_chunk) then cost_est = tokens_est * variant_unit_cost. If cost_est <= tier_max we pick the cheaper variant, else default. Need to cache avg_chunk per model.

anna: Example policy snippet I mocked up for discussion:```json
{
 "policy": "tier_based_variant",
 "rules": [
 {"tier": "free", "preferred": "open-medium-q4", "max_token_cost": "0.0005"},
 {"tier": "pro", "preferred": "redwood-base-q2", "max_token_cost": "0.0015"}
 ],
 "fallback": "redwood-base-q2",
 "health_check": {"quality_window": 1000, "min_quality_score": 0.84}
}
```oliver: Love the JSON. Two UX asks: a) show historical quality_score for the preferred variant in the rollout modal b) expose an override button to pin per-customer or per-route.

jess: On the quality side we need a lightweight signal for immediate feedback: use a mix of synthetic prompt set evaluations (nightly) + sampled in-prod metrics: perplexity delta proxy, rerate rejects, user-supplied flags. We shouldn't wait hours to detect regressions.

mike: For fallback behavior we can implement a fast failure detector: if fallback_count > 0.5% over last 1k requests OR average quality_score < threshold, start routing X% to fallback variant immediately and escalate to full failover after N minutes. Implement as a rolling window in the routing service.

sam: How about token cost controls enforcement? Suggest adding a per-request pre-check that returns a routing_decision with estimated_cost and a flag allow_fallback. If allow_fallback=false then we either 1) reject with 402-like (insufficient budget) or 2) route but with strict rate limit. Need product to decide.

anna: Good point — product: prefer soft-fallback (rate limit + upsell message) for free tier, hard block only if explicit budget exhausted.

title: entitlements-and-purchase-pathways-playbook-2030
author: Maya Chen
text:
Overview
=======

Purpose: This playbook consolidates company-wide procedures for entitlements (access and permissions), change governance, data handling expectations, procurement and expense approvals, vendor lifecycle management, and travel approvals. It is intended for all Redwood employees and contractors who request or approve resources, commit changes to production, or manage third-party relationships.

Scope: Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployment teams, platform and infra teams, procurement interactions, people-ops travel arrangements, and any third party that will access Redwood systems or customer data.

Quick links: Access Portal (Okta + Access Request), VendorHub (procurement back-end), ExpenseFlow (employee expenses), Legal intake form, Security questionnaire (security.redwood.local).

Roles and responsibilities
--------------------------

- Requestor: person initiating an access, change, purchase, vendor relationship, or travel booking. Responsible for completeness and business justification.
- Manager/Approver: direct manager who validates business need and budget availability.
- Approving Officer (Finance/Procurement): validates procurement thresholds, tax, and vendor classification.
- Security Reviewer: evaluates data access risk and mandatory controls (SOC2, encryption, contract clauses).
- Legal Reviewer: reviews contract terms for vendor agreements above threshold or with custom IP/data terms.
- Proc Ops (Vendor Onboarding): completes supplier setup, obtains W-9/COI as applicable.

Principles
----------

- Least privilege: grant minimal entitlements required for the job and set automatic expiration where practical.
- Segregation of duties: approval and provisioning paths must not be owned by the same individual for medium/high risk requests.
- Evidence-first approvals: all approvals must be attached to the request in VendorHub or Access Portal.
- Risk proportionality: stricter controls for vendors with data access, privileged infra access, or requests above financial thresholds.

Access & permissions (entitlement lifecycle)
-------------------------------------------

1) Request process

- Use the Access Portal (accessible from the Redwood Console > Tools > Access Request).
- Provide: justification, target systems (service name and environment), requested role (exact RBAC role), duration, and manager approval.
- For long-lived roles (>90 days), supply quarterly business justification and add reviewer in Access Portal.

2) Approval matrix (summary)

- Day-to-day access to non-prod systems: manager approval.
- Prod read-only access: manager + security notification.
- Prod privileged/infra access (SSH, K8s-admin, DB write): manager + security + infra-owner approval.
- Emergency elevated access: break-glass procedure (see Runbook ID: RG-2026-breakglass).

3) Provisioning and deprovisioning

- Provisioning is automated via Okta + Terraform runbooks (Infra-IAC). On approval, provisioning SLA is 2 business days for standard requests, 8 hours for emergency sprints.
- Access expirations are enforced: default 30 days for contractor requests, 90 days for internal hires unless renewed.

4) Periodic review

- Quarterly access attestation: team owners must validate active entitlements and remove stale accounts. Failure to respond triggers automated revocation notices.

Change management
-----------------

Scope: Any modification to production services, infra provisioning, IAM policies, or customer-facing configuration.

Change categories and approval paths:

- Standard change: pre-approved, repeatable changes (e.g., routine OS patching via controlled pipeline). Requires change ticket and notification to SRE runbook subscribers.
- Normal change: requires Change Review Board (CRB) approval for higher impact (planned releases that affect SLAs). CRB meets twice weekly.
- Emergency change: immediate fixes that must follow the emergency roll-forward checklist and be retroactively documented in the change ticket.

Change windows and freezes:

- Quarterly freeze: last two business days of each quarter are freeze windows for major releases unless exception approved by CTO and SRE lead.
- High-risk releases: require canary rollout and 30% traffic validation for 24 hours before full rollout.

Change request minimum content (ticket):

1. Change owner and contact
2. Rollout and rollback plan with automation steps
3. Expected impact and post-deploy validation steps
4. Backout criteria and timeline
5. Stakeholder notification list

SLOs and audit

- All normal changes must have an associated ticket and be auditable for 12 months.
- Emergency changes must be documented within 48 hours.

Data management and classification
--------------------------------

Classification levels:

- Public: content intended for public consumption.
- Internal: operational information not intended for external distribution.
- Confidential: employee, business, or customer information that requires access controls.
- Restricted: regulated or highly sensitive data (PII, payment data, health data) that requires encryption at rest and in transit, strict access controls, and audit logging.

Handling rules (summary):

- Confidential & Restricted: store only in approved systems (Redwood Console vaults, encrypted S3 with KMS). No vendor transfer without security and legal sign-off.
- Data retention: default retention for logs is 90 days; for customer-facing telemetry retention follows contractual obligations.
- Data deletion: use Data Erasure Request form and verify via automated deletion job.

Procurement and expenses
------------------------

Purchase approval thresholds (effective):

| Amount (USD) | Approvals required | Notes |
|--------------|-------------------|-------|
| < 2,500 | Manager | Auto-approval in VendorHub if budget tag present |
| 2,500 – 50,000 | Manager + Finance | Finance checks budget and tax classification |
| > 50,000 | Manager + Finance + Procurement + Legal | Requires exec sponsor and procurement intake form |

Procurement steps (numbered):

1. Create a request in VendorHub including business justification, vendor name, SOW/quote, and budget tag.
2. Attach vendor compliance docs (SOC2, ISO, insurance certificate) when available.
3. Finance validates budgets and tax treatment within 3 business days.
4. Procurement routes to Legal for >50k or non-standard T&Cs.
5. Once approved, Procurement issues purchase order and coordinates supplier setup.

Expense reimbursement:

- Use ExpenseFlow, attach receipts within 30 days of expense. Per diem caps: domestic $150/day, international $250/day unless pre-approved. Card use: corporate cards are preferred for travel; personal card reimbursements require manager approval.

Vendor management lifecycle
--------------------------

Onboarding checklist (timeline expectations):

- Initial intake: vendor submitted via VendorHub, 1 business day acknowledgement.
- Risk assessment: Security performs questionnaire review; expect 5-7 business days for standard vendors, 15-20 days for those handling Restricted data.
- Contracting: Legal drafts/negotiates terms; standard NDA/SOW templates for low-risk vendors. Time: 5–15 business days depending on terms.
- Procurement & finance: vendor setup (W-9/COI), tax classification, payment terms.

Minimum vendor requirements by risk tier:

- Low risk (no data access): PO, standard SOE, vendor contact, invoice cadence.
- Medium risk (limited data access): PO, signed DPA, security questionnaire, SOC2 Type II preferred.
- High risk (customer data or privileged infra access): PO, DPA, SOC2 Type II or penetration test report, system access plan, contractual breach notification clause, indemnity terms.

Offboarding and termination:

- Termination checklist: revoke credentials, recover assets, enforce data return/deletion, final invoice reconciliation, and a post-termination confirmation from vendor. Procurement must retain termination evidence for 7 years.

Travel policy (high level)
-------------------------

Booking: Use Travel Portal (linked from Redwood Console). Lowest reasonable fare policy applies for economy class. Business class requires exec-level pre-approval for travel over 8 hours.

Approvals: Manager approves travel requests in Travel Portal. International travel must include security and people-ops notification if travel is to high-risk countries listed by People Ops.

Per diems and expenses: See ExpenseFlow caps. Receipts required for all items >$25.

Safety and incident reporting:

- In case of an incident while traveling, contact People Ops emergency line and Security: security@redwood.com. All incidents must be reported within 24 hours.

Templates and forms (where to find)
----------------------------------

- Procurement intake form: VendorHub > New Request > Procurement Intake (use template 'Procurement-Intake-v2').
- Data Erasure Request: Redwood Console > Data Requests.
- Change request template: CRB ticket template in Jira (project: RED-CHANGES).
- Access request template: Access Portal (select role and environment).

Example procurement JSON payload (for VendorHub API)

{
 "requestor": "alice@example.com",
 "vendor": "Acme Analytics",
 "amount_usd": "7500",
 "justification": "Production observability for dedicated clusters",
 "budget_tag": "infra-monitoring",
 "required_by": "2027-02-15"
}

Appendix: enforcement and exceptions
-----------------------------------

- Exceptions: Managers may request a documented exception for short-lived needs; exceptions require a written business case and a compliance review.
- Enforcement: Repeated policy violations (e.g., unmanaged vendor engagements or expired privileged access) will be escalated to the employee's manager and may trigger procurement suspension or disciplinary review.

Contacts and ownership
----------------------

- Policy owner: Finance-Legal (policy owner contact: procurement@redwood.com).
- Security contact for vendor risk: security@redwood.com.
- People Ops travel & benefits: people-ops@redwood.com.

Revision history
----------------

- 2026-11-12: Initial draft published by Maya Chen.
- 2026-12-03: Updated procurement thresholds and added emergency change SLA (reviewed by Luis Alvarez and Priya Nair).

Related artifacts and references
-------------------------------

- Runbook RG-2026-breakglass (eng-sre/runbooks).
- VendorHub API docs (internal link).
- Security questionnaire template (security-and-compliance/audit-logging).

End of document

title: Tenant Telemetry Consent and Redaction Playbook for Private Deploys
author: Asha Patel
text:
Summary

This playbook defines the consent model, telemetry categories, mandatory redaction/minimization pipeline, and operator runbooks for tenant telemetry in Redwood private deployments (VPC and on‑prem variants). It is intended for field operators, customer success, and security stakeholders responsible for evidence artifacts required by regulated customers.

Applicability

- Applies to all private deployments managed by Redwood (VPC-private and on‑prem packages).
- Scope: runtime telemetry (service metrics, request traces, model metadata), operational telemetry (container metrics, host telemetry), and optional diagnostic dumps (heap, core, model weights metadata).
- Does NOT apply to customer application payloads that are explicitly forwarded through service proxies; those are covered by the customer data contract and separate redaction templates.

Telemetry Categories and Examples

1) Essential operational telemetry (always-on, low-cardinality)
 - Examples: instance_cpu_pct, gpu_util_pct, disk_iops_95, process_up
 - Purpose: SLO monitoring, alerting, capacity planning

2) Request-level telemetry (controlled sample rate / hashed identifiers)
 - Examples: request_latency_ms, tokens_generated, model_variant, route_name
 - Note: fields that could be PII/PHI must be redacted or hashed.

3) Diagnostic payloads (customer opt-in)
 - Examples: full request/response payloads, model KV cache snapshots, internal debug stacks
 - Must be opt-in and time-limited; stored in restricted buckets with customer approval.

Consent Model and Customer Controls

- Default mode: minimal telemetry (category 1 + aggregated request-level metrics with strict hashing and no payloads).
- Optional modes (customer selects during onboarding):
 1) "diagnostic-opt-in" (retains full request/response for T days)
 2) "enhanced-sampling" (higher sample rate for request-level metrics only)
 3) "no-external-telemetry" (local-only telemetry; no telemetry leaves VPC except for aggregated SLO telemetry if contract allows)

- Consent artifacts: a customer must sign the Telemetry Consent Form (template in Appendix) and specify: retention_days, sample_rate, redaction_profile_id. This metadata is stored in the deployment manifest under /etc/redwood/telemetry/consent.json and is surfaced in the control-plane UI.

Data Redaction & Minimization Pipeline

Overview:
1) Ingest filter (node-level): rejects known high-sensitivity fields before serialization.
2) Redaction transform (service-level): applies JSON path redactors, regex scrubbers, and structured PII detectors.
3) Hashing/Tokenization (metric-level): deterministic hashing of tenant identifiers using HMAC-SHA256 with tenant-specific key (rotated per policy).
4) Sink selector: routes telemetry to correct storage class (aggregated metrics store, restricted object store, local-only storage).

Redaction Profiles:
- profile-basic: remove keys named ["password", "ssn", "credit_card", "medical_record"], mask 80% of long strings, remove attachments > 128KB
- profile-strict: profile-basic + remove any field matching regex patterns for emails, phone numbers, and base64 blobs
- profile-none (diagnostic-opt-in only): no redaction beyond size caps

Sample redaction table (in prose):
- Field: request.user.name -> Action: drop
- Field: request.user.email -> Action: redact local-part, keep domain (e.g., xxxxx@company.com)
- Field: request.prompt -> Action: truncate to first 512 characters, then apply NER PII scrubber

Operator Runbook: Toggle, Audit, and Emergency Redaction

1) Verify consent manifest
 - Command: sudo cat /etc/redwood/telemetry/consent.json\ - Expected: valid JSON with keys: tenant_id, profile_id, retention_days, sample_rate, approved_by
\2) Switch deployment to 'local-only' for a tenant (example, safe mode for regulatory hold)\ - Steps:
 a) In the control plane: open tenant config -> Telemetry -> select 'no-external-telemetry' -> apply
 b) CLI fallback: redwoodctl tenant update --id <TENANT> --telemetry-mode local-only
 c) Validate: curl -sS http://localhost:9100/telemetry/status?tenant=<TENANT> | jq '.mode' should return "local-only"

3) Enforce emergency redaction for a window
 - Purpose: immediate purge or redaction when a customer requests removal for an incident
 - Steps (operator):
 1) Create a redaction job: redwoodctl telemetry redact --tenant <TENANT> --pattern "/request/payload" --mode truncate --reason "DSAR" --until 2026-07-01
 2) Monitor job: redwoodctl telemetry jobs get --id <JOB_ID>
 3) Generate evidence bundle: redwoodctl telemetry jobs export --id <JOB_ID> --output /tmp/evidence-<TENANT>.tar.gz

4) Audit logs and evidence retention
 - All toggle and redaction operations must be logged to the restricted audit log (immutable) with fields: operator_id, action, tenant_id, timestamp, justification_id.

Acceptance Tests & Evidence Requirements

Before handoff to customer, run the following checks and attach evidence to the onboarding package:

- Acceptance checklist (automated):
 1) consent.json present and schema-valid
 2) sample_rate applied (verify by synthetic trace generator with 1K requests)
 3) redaction profile enforced (submit synthetic PII and assert it is removed)
 4) local-only mode test (if requested)

- Evidence bundle contents:
 - consent.json (signed copy)
 - telemetry-config.yaml at deploy time
 - sample sanitized trace (redacted)
 - audit log entries showing operator approval

Upgrade & Rollback Considerations

- Upgrades that change redaction behavior must be treated as a migration: any profile changes require (A) migration script that reprocesses retained diagnostic payloads or (B) documented customer opt-in to reprocessing.
- Backward compatibility: new profiles must include a compatibility mapping and a migration tool: redwoodctl telemetry migrate-profiles --from old-id --to new-id --dry-run
- Rollback CPs: If a control-plane upgrade introduces a bug that lifts redaction rules, initiate emergency rollback and run the emergency redaction steps above. Preserve an evidence bundle that shows the rollback window and actions taken.

SLOs and Monitoring

- Telemetry integrity SLO: 99.9% of agent heartbeats per minute.
- Redaction correctness target: 100% synthetic-PII detection in test harness within 24 hours of deployment.
- Audit latency: toggles and redaction jobs appear in immutable audit log within 10s.

Operator Playbook Examples (Appendix)

Example consent.json (stored on node):
{
 "tenant_id": "tenant-1234",
 "profile_id": "profile-strict",
 "retention_days": 30,
 "sample_rate": 0.01,
 "approved_by": "legal@customer.com"
}

Sample CLI snippets:
- Switch to diagnostic opt-in for troubleshooting:
 redwoodctl tenant update --id tenant-1234 --telemetry-mode diagnostic-opt-in --retention 7 --profile profile-none

- Start a redaction job and monitor:
 JOB=$(redwoodctl telemetry redact --tenant tenant-1234 --pattern '/request/payload' --mode truncate --reason 'DSAR')
 redwoodctl telemetry jobs get --id $JOB

- Validate redaction locally (operator):
 curl -sS http://localhost:9101/debug/last-redacted?tenant=tenant-1234 | jq '.'

Owner & Contacts

- Document owner: Security (Asha Patel) – ascs@redwood.ai
- Oncall (telemetry-sre): pager: #telemetry-oncall (Slack) and schedule in the SRE rota
- Legal and Compliance: Maya Chen (reviewer)

Change History

- 2026-01-12: Created (Asha Patel)
- 2026-03-02: Added emergency redaction procedure (Ethan Brooks)
- 2026-06-15: Clarified profile mapping and added CLI validation steps (Maya Chen)

Appendix: Templates and Quick Reference

- Telemetry Consent Template (to be attached to onboarding package)
- Redaction profile mapping matrix (CSV)
- Synthetic PII test harness: runs 10K synthetic requests to validate redaction profile at sandbox rate

If you need an executable checklist or migration scripts, open a ticket to infra-sre with the tag "telemetry-redaction" and include tenant_id and deployment_id.

title: Fractured Context: Session Anchoring & Context Interleaves - Notes
author: Derek Shaw
text:
Purpose and scope:
This is a lightweight scratchpad for thinking about 'fractured context' strategies: when a long session is assembled from multiple interleaved short interactions (multi-document chat, task switching, user sessions with gaps) and how to keep latency and cost predictable while preserving retrieval/continuity quality.

Motivation (quick):
- Users expect context continuity across ephemeral turns and across background tasks (e.g., user edits doc A, then does a quick search, comes back).
- Full prefix replay is expensive at 1k+ tokens per turn; naive KV cache growth or repeated retrievals blow cost/latency.
- Need heuristics or micro-protocols to anchor session state cheaply and recover context when needed.

Reading roundup (notes + immediate takeaways):
1) "Session Anchors for Long Conversational State" (arXiv:2403.01234) - skimed
 - idea: create compact anchor vectors at decision points (every N tokens or after topic change).
 - anchors are small (128–512 dims), stored per-session; on context switch, retrieve nearest anchors and rehydrate partial KV cache via learned projector.
 - takeaway: anchor projection noise likely high for factual detail; works better for topical continuity + procedural cues.

2) "KV-summarize: fragment summarization to compress attention state" (internal notes + related work)
 - offline summarization of stale KV segments to 1–2 sentence summaries that are kept in prompt context rather than expanding KV cache.
 - tradeoff: lossy summaries reduce token cost but can break exact retrieval for code/legal stuff.

3) "Interleaved Context Scheduling (ICLR workshop slides)"
 - scheduling requests by urgency: low-urgency turns can be batched and served with cached summaries; high urgency uses full KV rehydration.
 - practical: annotate requests with "urgency" metadata from client SDK.

Open questions / hypotheses:
- H1: Anchors + light projection will preserve >80% topical coherence while cutting rehydration tokens by 60%.
- H2: For factual fidelity (exact names, code), anchors will fail; need hybrid: anchors for discourse, fetch original KV for critical segments indicated by metadata.
- H3: User-visible latency SLO improves if we precompute anchors on idle CPU/GPU cycles and keep a small LRU of recent anchor->KV mappings.

Experiment sketch (priority ordering):
A) Benchmark anchor retrieval vs full KV rehydration (toy dataset)
 - Dataset: 200 synthetic sessions (mix edits, searches, code) assembled from public chatlogs + internal anonymized sessions.
 - Metrics: continuity_score (human-rated 1-5), token_cost, average_latency, factual_precision@k for retrievals.
 - Implementation notes: reuse kv-playground repo branch from linked PR; add anchor projector model (2-layer MLP) and serialization format.
B) Urgency-based scheduler prototype (client + server hooks)
 - Add "urgency" header in SDK, default low. Server policy: if low and session > N tokens, return summary placeholder and queue background rehydration.
 - Measure user-perceived latency and number of follow-up rehydrations.

Edge cases to capture:
- Multi-document merges (two docs referenced across a session) -> anchors need multi-anchor composition, or metadata indicating document ids to pull exact KV when necessary.
- Hallucination risk when relying on compressed anchors for facts; include fallback that detects high-entropy model outputs (logprob heuristics) and triggers full fetch.

Implementation details & quick notes to self:
- Anchor format: {session_id, t_offset, vec_dim=256, topics=[top-3-lda], token_span=[start,end], doc_ids=[...]} but in Drive scratchpad keep minimal: session_id, t_offset, vec (base64) and token_span.
- Storage: per-customer LRU store (Redis) for hot sessions; long-term anchors in S3 with TTL 30d.
- Rehydration pipeline: projector on CPU -> small KV patch assembled and injected to runtime via runtime API (use existing cold-fill path in serving-runtime).
- Metrics to log: anchor_hit_rate, rehydrate_count, rehydrate_tokens, anchor_project_error (cosine diff vs full-KV-embedding).

Acceptance criteria for prototype:
- end-to-end: anchor generation + rehydration path that adds <50ms extra server-side on top of normal inference.
- experiments: demonstrate >=40% token cost savings with continuity_score drop <=0.5 points on 1-5 scale for non-factual tasks.

Notes from sync with Maya (2024-08-27):
- Maya: prefer starting with a purely synthetic corpus to avoid privacy headaches; she will generate 500 sessions with annotated topic boundaries.
- Action: Maya will push dataset to s3://redwood-experiments/anchors/synth-500 by 2024-09-02.

Immediate TODOs (short):
- [ ] Fork kv-playground branch and wire anchor projector (Derek) - target 2024-09-01.
- [ ] Add urgency header to SDK stub (Ivy) - target 2024-08-30.
- [ ] Create evaluation rubric and small Mechanical Turk instructions for continuity scoring (Derek + Maya) - target 2024-09-05.
- [ ] Draft Confluence page describing anchor format + policies (Derek) - link to draft when ready.

Risks / constraints:
- Privacy: anchors derived from user text could leak PII if not filtered; need deterministic redaction before anchor projection.
- Cost: extra storage overhead and CPU for projectors; mitigate by low-dim anchors and LRU eviction.
- Ops complexity: introduces second-tier state (anchors) to manage; require clear TTLs and graceful degradation.

Random brainstorms (loose):
- Use hashed-document-ids in anchors so they are opaque to ops team; store decryption keys per-customer.
- Hybrid anchor+gap-fill: anchors point to compressed diffs; when user asks factual queries, gap-fill is fetched on-demand and stored for future anchors.
- Explore learned gating net (tiny classifier) that predicts when anchors are safe vs need full rehydration based on recent prompt tokens.

References to revisit (read fully):
- arXiv:2403.01234 (session anchors) - deep read
- GitHub PR: kv-playground/pull/72 - runtime hooks for cold-fill
- ICLR slides: "Interleaved Context Scheduling" - follow up author questions

End of notes.

title: wavefront-collective-scheduler-compact-kernel-selector
author: Asha Patel
text:
Motivation: multi-GPU tensor-parallel workloads show sporadic tail latency spikes when collectives are scheduled naively at layer boundaries. This PR introduces a wavefront-style collective scheduler that groups nearby collective ops into a compact execution wave and a compact_kernel_selector that prefers smaller, lower-latency kernels for short-sequence invocations. The goal is to reduce communication stalls, improve KV cache prefetch alignment with collectives, and give the runtime a low-overhead heuristic to pick kernels that minimize per-token latency for short and mixed-length batches. Work items: - implement wavefront scheduler with layer-aware grouping and interleaved compute/comm launch windows - add compact_kernel_selector with device-query and sequence-length histogram input - introduce a KV-shard prompter that prefetches KV shards for upcoming wavefronts (heuristic-based) - NCCL launch param autotuner that records performance fingerprints and falls back to conservative settings on regression - unit + integration tests and perf-canary workload validation Checklist: [x] scheduler core implementation and unit tests [x] kernel selector + device query [x] KV prefetch heuristic + metrics hooks [x] NCCL autotuner prototype [x] perf benchmarks against baseline [x] documentation and release note entry Context and motivation: customers running TP-4/8 models reported 10-30% 95/99 latency regressions after a recent batching change; root cause was misaligned collective launches interleaving with KV cache fills. This PR aims to reduce that variance without sacrificing throughput on large continuous-batching workloads.

+// wavefront_scheduler: group nearby collectives into a compact launch window
+void WavefrontScheduler::schedule_layer_group(...) { /* heuristics */ }
+// choose compact kernels for short sequences to reduce per-token overhead
+KernelProfile select_compact_kernel(const DeviceCaps& d, int seq_len) { ... }
+// KV prompter triggers async prefetch for shards that next wavefront will need
+kv_prompter->prime_shards(predicted_shard_list);

Marco Rivera (2025-11-18): Great direction. Two asks: (1) add a toggle to disable prefetch at runtime for memory-constrained nodes, (2) add a short writeup on how the NCCL autotuner decides to roll back parameters.
Asha Patel (2025-11-19): Added runtime toggle `wavefront.kv_prefetch.enabled=false` and documented the autotuner rollback policy in nccl_autotuner.cpp comments.
Riley Chen (2025-11-24): Found a flake in the canary when TP=8 and batch_size=1; looks like a race between the prompter and KV-commit. Please add a microlock around the shard-state transition.
Asha Patel (2025-11-26): Added microlock and reworked the prompter to use versioned shard tokens. Re-ran canary, flake resolved.
Devon Liu (2025-12-01): Approved after perf numbers look solid and tests are green. Left a suggestion to add a diagnostic metric for 'wavefront_gap_ms' to the console dashboards.
CI Bot (2025-11-20): build failed (unit tests) — failing test: SchedulerTest.GroupingBoundaries — fixed by 2025-11-21 commit b2c4f7a.

Introduce wavefront collective scheduler and compact kernel selection heuristics to reduce TP tail latency and stabilize continuous-batching workloads; opt-in KV-shard prefetching and NCCL autotuner. Expected impact: ~12% 99th latency reduction on mixed-length serving and up to 18% throughput improvement on short-sequence micro-batches.

TP-4 mixed-length canary: 99p latency down 12% (from 210ms to 185ms)
TP-8 short-seq micro-batch: throughput +18% (tokens/s), p95 latency stable
Cont-batching steady-state: <2% throughput variance vs baseline, improved tail stability

Feature gated: wavefront scheduling and kv_prefetch are off by default for existing clusters. Ops can enable via runtime flags or console toggles per pool. NCCL autotuner writes small fingerprint files to /var/lib/redwood/nccl-fingerprints; rotate/backup as part of cluster upgrades.

Medium. Introduces new concurrency surface (prompter <-> shard state) and autotuner state. Thoroughly tested on perf canary; rollout recommended via canary then gradual percentage rollout with metrics watch (wavefront_gap_ms, kv_prefetch_bytes, nccl_fallback_count).

title: Crypto hierarchy, rotation, and SIEM export — runbook
author: Asha Patel
text:
Purpose and scope:
This runbook captures the operational design and step-by-step procedures for key lifecycle management (cloud KMS, HSM-backed keys, and customer BYOK), rotation patterns, and formatted audit export to the SIEM. It is intended for security engineers, platform engineers (private/dedicated), and on-call SREs who will perform rotations, evidence collection, and incident responses related to encryption-at-rest.

Non-goals:
- Specifying vendor-specific API docs (those are linked in the artifacts section).
- Replacing the Verified KMS onboarding checklist — this complements it with operational playbook material.

Overview of crypto hierarchy (recommended model):
- Root/Signer (offline or HSM-protected root key): only used to sign intermediate keys and for bootstrapping. Extremely high entropy, stored in FIPS-validated HSM or offline guard.
- Master Key (MK): KMS-managed single-purpose key used to encrypt/unwrap key-encryption-keys (KEKs). Rotated infrequently; stored in cloud KMS or HSM with strict RBAC.
- Key-Encryption Keys (KEKs): Per- tenancy (customer or environment) keys used to wrap Data Encryption Keys (DEKs). KEKs live in KMS/HSM and are subject to rotation policies independent of DEKs.
- Data Encryption Keys (DEKs): Short-lived keys used for envelope encryption of object data (S3, blockstore, DB column encryption). DEKs are generated by the service, encrypted with KEK, and stored alongside ciphertext.

Why envelope encryption: improved rotation and small blast radius — DEKs are cheap to rotate and do not require re-encrypting blobs when KEK rotates (only rewrap operation).

RBAC v2 for keys (mapping to roles):
- key-admin: create/delete/grant/revoke KEKs and manage key policy metadata. Should be restricted to Security Eng and Platform Admins. (Granting on a per-key resource basis.)
- key-operator: initiate rotate/rewrap operations, request key usage metrics, and run emergency revocations. Intended for SRE on-call + rotation automation service accounts.
- kms-viewer: read-only access to key metadata, audit entries, and rotation history; used by auditors and compliance reviewers.
- crypto-service (machine/account): service principal used by runtime to perform encrypt/decrypt operations — scoped to specific KEKs via least privilege.

Access controls and constraints:
- No human accounts with direct encrypt/decrypt rights on production KEKs unless explicitly approved and logged.
- All changes to key policy must require multi-approver workflow via ticket (JIRA-SEC or ServiceNow) with a signed justification field.

Rotation policy matrix (recommended default):
- Root/Signer: rotate only on explicit key compromise or re-keying cycle every 5+ years (with offline ceremony).
- Master Key (MK): 18–36 months, or immediately on suspected compromise.
- KEK (per-tenant): 6–12 months; automated rewrap of DEKs recommended during low-traffic windows.
- DEK: TTL 24 hours to 90 days based on workload sensitivity; for high-volume object stores, prefer short TTL (7–30 days) and frequent rewraps.

Rotation step-by-step (KEK rotation, automated):
1) Pre-checks:
 - Confirm current KEK metadata and last_rotation in KMS.
 - Verify successful snapshot/backup of key metadata snapshot (S3 location: s3://redwood-sec-key-metadata/yyyymmdd).
 - Check outstanding re-wrap tasks and in-flight writes; consult per-route write-latency dashboard.
 - Ensure automation runbook is in a healthy state (CI job green).
2) Create new KEK version in KMS/HSM using secure API. Tag version with rotation-correlation-id and timestamp.
3) Update service principal grants for the new key version (if using explicit version grants).
4) Enqueue rewrap job that will read ciphertext metadata, call KMS unwrap with old KEK -> DEK, then wrap DEK with new KEK, and write back wrapped value. Jobs are sharded and rate-limited to preserve latency SLOs.
5) Monitor rewrap progress, look for rewrap-failure counts and backoffs. Failures trigger automatic re-try with exponential backoff and eventual pager escalation to on-call.
6) After >= 95% rewrap completion, update key policy primary-version pointer to new KEK version. Keep old version alive for 30–90 days for rollback and emergency decrypt.
7) Post-ops: generate evidence bundle (audit logs, job run IDs, manifest of rewrapped object IDs) and export to secure evidence store.

Manual emergency rotation (compromise suspected):
- Immediate steps: set KEK to disabled state for new wraps (maintain unwrap to allow decrypts if needed), create incident ticket, notify CS/Legal if customer keys involved. For BYOK, escalate to customer contact according to contract.

BYOK specific flows and customer-supplied HSMs:
- Onboarding requires: customer intent form, key rollover policy acceptance, and KMS import key ceremony recorded in Confluence page.
- BYOK keys are treated as external-key IDs — Redwood stores only wrapped DEKs. Key operations with external HSM require dedicated connector host in customer VPC or HSM proxy with mutual-auth TLS.
- Rotation for BYOK: coordinate schedule with customer; do not perform unilateral rotation of a customer-supplied root. Documented SLA window must be observed.

Audit log schema (key events) — canonical fields (JSON log entry):
- timestamp: ISO8601 string
- event_type: one of [KEY_CREATE, KEY_ROTATE, KEY_VERSION_CREATE, KEY_DISABLE, KEY_ENABLE, KEY_DELETE, KEY_UNWRAP, KEY_WRAP, KEY_POLICY_CHANGE]
- resource_id: kms://<region>/<key-id>
- actor: <principal-id or service-account>
- actor_type: human|service|external-customer
- action_id: UUID (correlation across services)
- request_id: cloud-kms-request-id (if available)
- outcome: success|failure|partial
- reason: free text (failure reason / policy change note)
- correlation_tags: list of tags (rotation-correlation-id, ticket-id)
- old_version: version-id (if rotation)
- new_version: version-id (if rotation)
- rewrap_manifest_loc: s3://... or null
- sampled_trace: diagnostic trace id or null
- raw_event: raw provider event (if available)

Example log (single-line JSON):
{
 "timestamp": "2024-11-05T22:14:31Z",
 "event_type": "KEY_ROTATE",
 "resource_id": "kms://us-east1/ke-abc123",
 "actor": "svc-key-rotation@redwood-infra",
 "actor_type": "service",
 "action_id": "b3a85d6f-4c2b-4a9d-8e1c-3d9f7a9d2fbb",
 "request_id": "cloudreq-9922",
 "outcome": "success",
 "reason": "scheduled-rotation",
 "correlation_tags": ["rotation-20241105", "JIRA-SEC-1290"],
 "old_version": "v1",
 "new_version": "v2",
 "rewrap_manifest_loc": "s3://redwood-sec-key-manifests/rewrap-20241105.json",
 "sampled_trace": "trace-7a9e",
 "raw_event": null
}

SIEM export mapping guidance:
- Ingest each canonical audit log into the SIEM as a single event with the following mapped fields: time, src_principal (actor), event_type, resource, correlation_id (action_id), outcome, tags, message.
- Enrich events with identity attributes from IAM (team, manager, risk_score) and with customer ids for tenant-scoped keys.
- Create SIEM detection rules for abnormal activity patterns:
 - Multiple KEY_UNWRAP calls from different service principals for the same resource within a short window.
 - New key-version creation without a preceding JIRA ticket tag.
 - KEK rotates outside maintenance window.
 - Unexpected external-customer key access from internal VMs.

Evidence automation (post-rotation evidence bundle):
- Components to collect automatically after a rotation or emergency action:
 - Audit log slice covering action_id and +/- 24 hours.
 - Rewrap manifest (list of objects rewrapped and shard ids).
 - KMS provider raw response payloads and request IDs.
 - CI/CD job run ids and artifacts (automation run logs).
 - Signed PDF of rotation approvers (if manual approvals present).
- Automation job will package the above into a signed tarball, compute a SHA256, upload to s3://redwood-sec-evidence/<action_id>/evidence.tar.gz and emit an evidence-created audit event.

Testing, validation and rollback:
- Canary run: pick a low-traffic tenant and perform a KEK rotate + rewrap. Validate decrypt success on sampled objects for 48 hours. Use automated smoke tests (github.com/redwood-infra/tests/key-rotate-canary).
- Rollback: if rewrap fails en masse, revert primary-version pointer to previous version and abort further wrap jobs. Keep failure manifest for investigation.

Monitoring and observability:
- Key metrics to publish: rewrap_progress_percent, rewrap_error_rate, key_usage_per_minute, key_latency_p50/p90/p99 for wrap/unwrap calls, key_policy_change_count.
- Dashboards: per-region key counters, tenant-impact view, and a security incidents dashboard that surfaces any disabled keys or rapid version churn.

Operational playbook checklist (pre-rotation):
- [ ] Confirm maintenance window and customer notifications (if tenant scoped).
- [ ] Snapshot key metadata.
- [ ] Ensure rewrap jobs have capacity and throttles configured.
- [ ] Backup evidence store writable.

Post-rotation checklist:
- [ ] Rewrap >= 95% completed or documented exception list.
- [ ] Evidence tarball produced and verified.
- [ ] Post-rotation smoke tests green.
- [ ] Update key inventory and rotation calendar.

Compromise handling (short runbook):
1) Immediately mark key as disabled for new wraps and log action.
2) Create incident ticket with correlation_id and contact list.
3) If customer key (BYOK), notify customer per contract and follow agreed escalation.
4) Start forensic capture: full audit slice, host traces, and rewrap manifest.
5) If necessary, perform emergency rewrap to new KEK and reject old version; expedite evidence export for compliance.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Do we require HSM for all MKs by default or only high-sensitivity tenants? (propose: high-sensitivity and enterprise with SLA >$Xk/month)
- Retention policy for old key versions beyond rollback window (30/90/365 days?)
- Integration point for RBAC v2 authorization checks in the KMS proxy — pre-check or delegated to provider?

Next steps (action items):
- Lina: draft BYOK onboarding form for customer agreements (due 2024-11-20).
- Diego: implement SIEM enrichment pipeline prototype (P0) and push PR.
- Samir: add rotation canary to infra tests and schedule monthly runs.

References and links:
- KMS provider docs (internal vault): CONFLUENCE-SEC/KMS-Provider-APIs
- Rewrap job implementation: github.com/redwood-infra/rewrap-service (PR-487 linked above)
- Evidence automation template: CONFLUENCE-SEC/Evidence-Automation-Template
- Incident escalation contact list: CONFLUENCE-SEC/Incident-Contacts

Notes and contextual snippets (working):
- Consider adding rate-limit bucketing per-tenant to rewrap workers to avoid noisy-tenant storms.
- We should index rewrap-manifests by tenant and time for quick e-discovery.
- Long-term: explore native HSM signing for root key ceremonies and publish an offline attestation record.

Document history:
- 2024-11-08 created (initial draft) — Asha
- 2024-12-02 major edits: added audit-schema, SIEM mapping — Diego
- 2025-01-14: added BYOK coordination language and evidence automation details — Lina

Great to meet today — thanks for walking us through the triage flow and the latency constraints for short, clinician-facing prompts. Quick recap and proposed next steps so everyone is aligned: 

1) Primary goals we heard
- Clinical triage responses should be accurate and concise for short prompts (~20–80 tokens)
- Streaming UX must avoid partial incoherent fragments and respect stop sequences for list-style outputs
- Latency target: ideally <= 300ms for initial tokens on short responses; < 700ms tail for longer follow-ups (we discussed getting you stronger SLOs once we baseline)

2) Recommended model candidates to evaluate (initial):
- redwood-44b-int8 (balanced quality / throughput)
