- Stop-sequence enforcement: verify EOS/stop-token handling when prompts include explicit delimiters
- Partial output coherence: stress tests with incremental decoding — ensure the partial tokens emitted are syntactically coherent and not deceptive mid-sentence
- KV/prefix cache behavior for short-turn dialogs: measure cold vs warm latency
- Sampling settings for clinical tone control (temp, top-p / top-k) and their impact on hallucination risk

5) Next steps / asks for you
- Please confirm the sample prompts are representative and send any additional high-priority prompt batches (preferably <100 examples to start)
- Grant the eval folder access to evals@medbench.ai and procurement@clearpathhealth.com so we can share artifacts
- Confirm procurement timeline (procurement@clearpathhealth.com copied) if you want pricing/commit options in parallel

6) Our immediate internal plan: run streaming bench across the three model candidates with the sample prompts, capture per-token latencies and a coherence score (automated metric + small human pass). I’ll loop Ben and Marissa in for execution and follow-up.

Attachments: CPH-PromptSamples.csv, initial-bench-summary.pdf

Thanks — talk soon.

title: Intermittent 429s from signed-cookie refresh loop in ephemeral worker pool during bulk ingest
text:
Issue summary:
Customer reports repeated 429 responses during a nightly bulk ingest run that stages objects via signed cookies. Failures started after a safe restart of their ingest fleet and coincide with a scheduled canary of a proxy-side keepalive change. BrightFleet uses ephemeral worker pools that refresh signed cookies frequently (~every 90s).

Impact:
- ~20% of ingest batch requests receiving 429s intermittently across a 2 hour window (2026-03-09 03:00–05:00 UTC).
- Customer sees backlog and retry storms causing delayed downstream processing and SLA risk for enterprise tier.

Environment:
- Customer tier: enterprise, VPC peering to prod us-west-2, using pooled edge proxy IPs and signed-cookie approach for pre-signed uploads.
- Ingest orchestrator uses 200 concurrent ephemeral workers per region; each worker refreshes cookies from control-plane every ~90s.

Steps to reproduce (reported by customer):
1) Start parallel uploader with 200 workers using signed-cookie refresh schedule identical to production.
2) Observe steady-state for 10 minutes, then trigger a restart of a subset of workers (simulates canary).
3) Measure HTTP 429s from /upload endpoint and ambiguous throttle headers.

Observed logs / telemetry (customer-provided):
- Repeated 429s with X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 and X-RateLimit-Reset drifting between 10–60s.
- Ingest orchestrator logs show bursts of signed-cookie refresh requests to the auth service clustered at restart time.
- Edge proxy traces show keepalive connections sticky to pooled IPs; some cookie refresh POSTs get routed through a small subset of origin instances.

Hypothesis / initial triage notes (Support):
- Likely interaction between signed-cookie refresh fanout and token-bucket accounting at the route layer. Ephemeral workers renewing cookies simultaneously can concentrate accounting at the ingress proxy and momentarily exhaust per-route refill credits.
- Proxy keepalive change may have reduced upstream affinity churn, inadvertently concentrating refresh requests to fewer rate-limiter partitions.

Immediate mitigation requested:
- BrightFleet asked for guidance to avoid enqueueing large simultaneous cookie refreshes and whether a server-side smoothing/fanout backoff is possible.

Requested action items:
- SRE: check proxy partitioning/affinity metrics around 2026-03-09 03:00 UTC and correlate with rate-limiter partitions and refill windows.
- Auth team: inspect signed-cookie issuance logs to confirm refresh clustering and whether refresh endpoints are rebalanced across origins.
- Support: provide customer with recommended client-side jitter/backoff pattern and short-term bypass options (e.g., stagger refreshes, use slightly longer cookie TTL while testing).

Notes on customer posture: BrightFleet is sensitive to any required code changes but can deploy a staggered refresh patch to their ingest agents if recommended by Support.

Expected next updates: SRE to post partition metrics and a short tracer link; Support to propose a safe stagger pattern and verify whether an infra-side fast fix (refill smoothing) can be staged for canary revert.

2026-03-10 | Sofia Martin (Support): Acknowledged. Escalating to SRE and Auth. Please attach raw trace ids if available. First response ETA within 1 hour.
2026-03-10 | Riley Tan (SRE): Looking at proxy partitioning metrics for us-west-2. Initial signal: 3 proxy upstreams received ~85% of cookie-refresh traffic during the restart window. Adding router traces to this ticket.
2026-03-10 | Elena Park (Auth): We see a cluster of POST /auth/signed-cookie that align with the worker restart time. Origin distribution skewed; investigating why load balancer didn't round-robin across auth pool.
2026-03-11 | Riley Tan (SRE): Confirmed refill window exhaustion on route weight 42. Rate-limiter partitions used by those 3 upstreams had aligned refill epochs; recommend changing client jitter and scheduling a short-term refill smoothing flag. Filing INT-3315 for infra rollout path.
2026-03-11 | Sofia Martin (Support): Recommended client workaround to BrightFleet: add randomized jitter 30–120s to their refresh schedule and increase ephemeral cookie TTL to 5 minutes when running bulk ingest. Customer accepted and will deploy patch to canary tonight.
2026-03-12 | BrightFleet (Customer): Applied jitter patch to their canary; observed 99.8% successful uploads during the 2 hour test window. Will keep monitoring and requests follow-up on permanent infra mitigation.
2026-03-12 | Riley Tan (SRE): Scheduling infra action: enable 'refill-smoothing' experiment on affected rate-limiter partitions during next maintenance window. Linked INT-3315 and related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rate-limiter/pull/221

Workaround applied by customer (staggered refresh + temporary longer TTL). SRE confirmed refill-window exhaustion as root cause due to partitioned accounting and proxy affinity. Infra mitigation planned (refill-smoothing experiment) and tracked via INT-3315. Customer to monitor; follow-up in 72h to confirm closure.

title: CI agent sudoers rule change prevents nightly artifact upload step
text:
Issue summary: During the 03:00 nightly release pipeline, CI jobs that push build artifacts to the internal S3-compatible store are failing at the upload step. Impact: All nightly release artifacts (docker layers, tarballs) are not being published which blocks downstream canaries and nightly retention jobs. Affected pipelines: release/nightly, release/nightly-e2e. The failure started immediately after a tenant-wide sudoers policy change pushed by Security on 2026-03-09.

Observed behavior: ci-agent attempts to run the upload helper (/usr/local/bin/artifact-uploader) via sudo to set up ephemeral credentials; sudo returns "permission denied" for the ci-agent user, causing the step to exit 126. No change was made to the pipeline or uploader by Release Eng sinds 2026-03-08.

Environment details: CI runners are fleet of ephemeral GCP VMs (image: rwinf-ci-runner-202601), using systemd unit to spawn runner processes as user 'ci-agent'. Artifact storage is S3-compatible objectstore behind internal gateway (artifacts.redwood.local).

Required outcome: Restore artifact uploads for nightly pipelines ASAP and prevent similar permission regressions during security policy rollouts.

Checkout release/nightly pipeline manifest
Trigger a job on an ephemeral runner using image rwinf-ci-runner-202601
Run step: sudo /usr/local/bin/artifact-uploader --push --dest artifacts/redwood/nightly/<build-id>
Observe sudo error: 'ci-agent is not in sudoers file' and exit code 126

Mar 10 03:01:13 runner-54 systemd[1]: Started job release-nightly-artifact-upload.
Mar 10 03:01:14 artifact-uploader[8421]: Starting upload to artifacts.redwood.local
Mar 10 03:01:14 sudo: ci-agent : user NOT in sudoers ; TTY=unknown ; PWD=/home/ci-agent ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/local/bin/artifact-uploader --push --dest artifacts/redwood/nightly/2026-03-10-03
Mar 10 03:01:14 artifact-uploader[8421]: exited with code 126

title: chat v1: parameter normalizer, role aliasing, stop dedupe and streaming backpressure improvements for /v1/chat.completions parity
author: Evelyn Chen
text:
Motivation: Close a set of subtle incompatibilities between our /v1/chat.completions adapter and OpenAI's behavior that have been causing developer friction in streaming function-call flows and stop/logprobs handling. This PR implements a compact 'parameter normalizer' layer and a streaming framing/backpressure handshake to make the adapter tolerant of real-world clients and OpenAI-style payloads. Summary of changes: - Parameter normalizer: unify and sanitize incoming params (max_tokens, temperature, top_p, n, presence_penalty) and map them to our internal API consistently; accept both string and numeric encodings, preserve explicit nulls, and prefer client-provided values for edge cases. - Role aliasing: accept and normalize role names coming from clients ("assistant", "system", "user", "tool", and legacy aliases like "ai" or "bot"); ensure role is preserved in both final and streaming envelopes. - Stop sequence deduplication: support stop as string or array; expand single-string stops into an array; dedupe overlapping sequences (e.g. ["\n\n", "\n\n\n"]) and maintain order stability to match OpenAI semantics. - Sparse logprobs: add an opt-in sparse_logprobs mode that mirrors OpenAI's sparse token-level logprob structure when requested; keep heavy-weight computation behind an explicit flag to avoid perf regressions. - Streaming framing & backpressure: introduce a light handshake in the stream start (sent as first SSE/delta) that communicates our token framing and heartbeat expectations; implement backpressure signaling for HTTP/2 clients to avoid partial JSON objects when a client pauses mid-stream. - Function-call streaming support: improve chunking for function_call.name/arguments so that streaming deltas assemble deterministically into valid JSON payloads even across reconnects; final chunk action inserts a stable end-of-function marker to make reconstruction robust. - Response envelope parity: normalize streaming deltas to include a minimal structured 'choice' envelope (id, index, finish_reason) so downstream OpenAI-compat consumers don't need ad-hoc heuristics. - Tests & docs: add unit and integration tests for the normalizer, streaming handshake scenarios, and a new example in the docs showing a robust client reconnection strategy. Checklist: - [x] Parameter mapping implemented and unit-tested - [x] Streaming handshake and backpressure implemented with integration tests - [x] Role aliasing covered by parser tests - [x] Stop dedupe logic covered and fuzz-tested - [x] Sparse logprobs gating and tests - [x] Docs updated (compatibility section + example client) - [x] Runtime perf smoke tests run on canary cluster Notable design decisions: - We intentionally do not try to replicate obscure historical OpenAI quirks; instead the normalizer applies conservative, well-documented rules and exposes a strict compatibility flag for customers who really need historical behavior. - The streaming handshake is opt-out via a client header (X-Redwood-Compat: openai-v1) to avoid breaking existing non-OpenAI clients. - Sparse logprobs are computed on-demand and annotated in the response metadata to allow downstream billing/observability. Related: ENG-4321 (parameter normalization epic), SUP-2107 (customer-reported toolcall truncation).

Samir: Can you clarify how explicit null values are treated vs missing keys? There was a customer case where max_tokens=null meant 'use default' rather than '0'.
Author (Evelyn): Normalizer treats explicit null as 'unset' and falls back to model defaults; added a unit test for that scenario.
Asha: The backpressure header naming looks fine, but please add a short blurb in the docs about HTTP/1 clients where we emulate the behavior over SSE.
Author (Evelyn): Added docs section and an SSE emulation implementation for older clients.
Leo: Sparse logprobs look good; make sure we annotate toggles in telemetry so customers can track extra compute costs.
Author (Evelyn): Telemetry annotation added (adapter.openai_v1.sparse_logprobs=true) and documented cost footnote.

title: SLO Cadence Bootcamp & Cross-functional Rehearsal Notebook
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Purpose:
This is a working notebook for a compact, operational-first SLO cadence bootcamp aimed at product, infra, platform, and support partners. The goal is not to write another policy doc — its to rehearse precise handoffs, validate signals, and train responders on the SLO rhythm we expect teams to run for model-serving features (hosted API, dedicated, private).

Objective (measurable):
- Run a 10-person cross-team rehearsal and complete 3 tabletop-to-live escalation handoffs within 2 weeks.
- Validate the SLO signal chain end-to-end (client metric -> aggregators -> alert -> incident bridge -> postmortem starter).
- Produce 5 small, actionable changes to the SLO observability checklist and 2 quick configuration changes (alert thresholds, runbook links).

Audience:
- SREs, Feature Engineers owning model endpoints, Platform Engineers, Customer Success on-call leads, Product PMs for priority features.

High-level bootcamp plan (2 weeks):
Week 0 (prep)
- Day -7: Invite list, pre-reading, attach current SLOs + incident runbooks, mapping doc.
- Day -5: Data sanity check run: make sure metrics exporter, rollups, and alerting queries are returning expected values.
- Day -3: Quick sync with observability infra to enable synthetic tests and a short-lived alert channel for the rehearsal.

Week 1 (rehearsals)
- Day 1: Orientation (1 hour): cadence overview, roles, how to read SLO dashboards.
- Day 2-3: Tabletop sessions (2x 90m) focused on: slow tail latency (P95->P99 divergence) and token-cost regression. Use incident-sculpting templates (see exercises section).
- Day 4: Live mini-sim (4 hours): inject synthetic latency to a staging model pool and exercise automated fallback routing. Observe system kinetics, KV cache warm-up effects, request batching shifts.
- Day 5: Debrief and quick fixes (2 hours): triage suggested changes and apply 2 configuration items in staging.

Week 2 (handoff & measurement)
- Day 8: Canary failure escalation (full replay): simulate a sustained GPU pool failure in a single region and route traffic to fallback variant. Walk the oncall rota through the escalation.
- Day 10: Customer-impact tabletop (90m): product PM and CS run prioritization decisions (who to call, customer comms).
- Day 12: Postmortem starter & metrics audit (2 hours): ensure the postmortem stub has required SLO evidence and signal artifacts.

Session roles and responsibilities (short form):
- Incident Commander (IC): SRE oncall (primary). Starts bridge, drives tl;dr, ensures runbook steps executed.
- Observability Lead: platform-observability engineer. Owns dashboards, ensures alerts fired and screenshots are captured.
- Feature Owner: product/feature engineer for the affected endpoint. Executes rollback/fallback if required, decision authority for product trade-offs.
- Routing/Fallback Engineer: serving-runtime engineer. Validates model variant/fallback routing and capacity changes.
- CS Rep: customer-success oncall lead. Prepares communication template and customer impact assessment.
- Recorder/PM: takes notes, timestamps key signal artifacts for postmortem.

Exercises (unique, repeatable):
1) Incident Sculpting: P95->P99 Divergence
- Scenario: After a model update, P95 stays stable but P99 latency spikes for long-tail queries. No immediate request drop, but error budgets are bleeding.
- Steps:
 - Observability Lead runs the "tail-sampler" query (provided snippet) to collect full-request histograms.
 - IC declares SLO burn threshold; Feature Owner decides between throttling long queries or rolling back.
 - Routing Engineer toggles prefix-KV caching to test mitigation; measure 15-minute impact.
- Learning targets: how quickly can teams identify root-cause (model complexity vs batching behavior), and can fallback routing prevent escalation within 20 minutes.

2) Model Serving Cost Spike (token-cost regression)
- Scenario: A change increases token churn for a set of prompts causing 2x cost on a mid-tier route and a steady SLO burn on latency under load.
- Steps:
 - Use recorded traffic replay in a staging pool for 30 minutes.
 - Observability Lead shows token-cost attribution per route; CS flags customers at risk.
 - Quick mitigations: reduce max_tokens, enable quantized variant for that route, or apply rate limiting.
- Learning targets: map cost signal to SLO choices and runbook entries.

3) Partial-region GPU Failure + Fallback Validation
- Scenario: One region's dedicated pool loses 60% capacity over 10 minutes (simulated), autoscaler triggers but not fast enough.
- Steps:
 - Routing/Fallback Engineer force-routes 20% traffic to secondary region/model variant.
 - IC checks latency and errors on radar; if customer-impacting, CS drafts comms.
- Learning targets: time-to-fallback, warm-up cost, and customer impact communication template timing.

Rehearsal scripts (short snippets you can read out):
- "Bridge open. We see P99 at 2.4s for route X, error rate stable. Token cost has increased 2.1x for the last 10m. IC asks: Feature owner, do you own rollback or do we throttle?"
- "Observability: attaching dashboard snapshot and flame graph link. Routing, can you confirm fallback candidate is ready?"

Artifacts to capture during runs (must be saved to the incident folder):
- Dashboard screenshots with timestamped queries.
- Alert firing history (raw JSON).
- Sampling of raw traces and the input prompts that caused the tail.
- Command history for any toggles (rolling back, routing changes).

Success metrics and acceptance criteria:
- All alert-to-bridge times <= 5 minutes for synthetic tests.
- At least 1 successful automated fallback during live mini-sim with < 15% customer-impact traffic diverted.
- Post-bootcamp: 80% of participants can list the SLO signal chain in a 3-point checklist test.

Quick runbook checklist (bite-sized items):
- Is the correct SLO policy attached to the route? (yes/no)
- Can synthetic tests be triggered in < 10m? (who owns it)
- Alert severity mapping set: P99 latency -> page; error-rate -> page; cost-spike -> slack only.
- Postmortem stub created with links to dashboards, alert JSONs, and timeline.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self):
- TODO: Get explicit buy-in from Product for automated rollback on canary model updates (Marco).
- TODO: Validate synthetic load harness for token-cost tests (Lina).
- Question: should cost-spike alerts page SRE or only alert CS+product first? (discuss in debrief).
- TODO: Add a short "customer-impact rubric" to runbooks so CS can rapidly classify impacted tenants.

Debrief template (use after every rehearsal):
- What worked? (top 3)
- What blocked the run? (top 3)
- Quick fixes applied during the run (list + owner)
- Follow-ups and owners (JIRA tickets recommended)

Appendix: handy queries & snippets (copy-paste friendly)
- Tail-sampler (pseudo):
 SELECT bucket, count FROM request_latency_histogram WHERE route = 'api/model-x' SINCE -15m
- Token-cost attribution (pseudo):
 SELECT sum(tokens*cost_per_token) BY route WHERE time > -1h
- Bridge start template (slack):
 "Bridge open: slo-bootcamp: route X, P99 2.4s, error-rate 0.12%. IC: @oncall-sre. Observability: @obs-lead. Feature: @feature-owner. Recording on."

Appendix B: short rehearsal checklist for participants (one-pager to print):
- Bring laptop, ensure VPN access to staging project.
- Confirm you have access to incident folder and alert logs.
- Read the SLO one-pager (2 minutes).
- Be ready to be assigned IC or Observability roles during a run.

Revision history (quick):
- 2026-01-15 created initial bootcamp notebook (Aisha).
- 2026-01-22 added fallback validation exercise and success metrics (Marco).
- 2026-02-10 updated linked artifact references and added debrief template (Aisha).

Notes (informal):
- This is intentionally lean: emphasize runs over long design debates. Keep scripts short and actionable.
- If product is uncomfortable with automated rollback, focus on fast throttles and explicit customer comm windows.
- Keep the incident folder tidy: attach a single JSON timeline and up to 5 representative traces.

End of notebook.

title: Private Console — Mesh Connectivity Inspector (compact tenant panel)
author: Priya Desai
text:
Goal: Design a compact, information-dense inspector panel for the Private Console that surfaces tenant-level mesh connectivity, recent path health, and safe rollback actions. This panel should live as a collapsible strip in the tenant overview and expand into a transient overlay when operators need details. It must be usable by SREs and Platform Engineers to make fast triage decisions (isolate region, trigger rollback, estimate cost impact) without drilling into multiple screens.

Scope: initial MVP for single-tenant view, covers cross-region connectivity map (simplified), last-5-heartbeats visualization, top-3 failure signals (e.g., packet loss, high retransmit rate, control-plane lag), suggested mitigations (restart agent, reroute traffic to region B, initiate rolling upgrade rollback), and a compact cost delta estimator showing estimated additional egress and reserved capacity cost for failover.

Out-of-scope: full multi-tenant graph, packet-level trace replay, deep topology editor. Those will be follow-ups if MVP is validated.

Compact panel fits within 340px height in tenant overview in collapsed state
Panel expands to overlay with per-path details and last-5-heartbeat sparkline
Top-3 signals are algorithmically ranked and human-readable (label + severity color)
Quick actions available: Open runbook, Trigger safe rollback (requires two-step confirm), Route traffic to alternate region (preview cost delta)
Design handoff artifacts (Figma frames, interaction spec) provided and validated by ENG lead
Analytics events defined for expand/collapse, action clicks, and confirm steps

Show only top-3 signals by default to keep surface scannable — full list accessible in expanded overlay
Cost estimator shows a conservative 95th-percentile delta pulled from cost-service rather than live billing to avoid surprising numbers
Rollback action will be a controlled two-step flow that triggers a canary first (safety requirement from Eng) — design includes both canary and global rollback options
Compact visual language uses small sparklines + status pill (green/amber/red) rather than large heatmaps to preserve density
Panel will default to collapsed in tenant overview; tenants with active incidents auto-expand up to 30 seconds after page load

Backend needs new summary API (ENG-28901) to drive top-3 signals and cost estimate — latency and rate limits need to be validated
Security teams require audit logs for rollback and routing actions — UI must surface confirmation and note that actions are audited
Mobile and very narrow viewports will show only the status pill and an overflow menu linking to full overlay
Cost estimator accuracy limited until cost-service supports per-tenant reserved-capacity breakdown (work in separate ENG ticket)

Export Figma components: InspectorStrip, SignalRow, CostDeltaFlyout, ConfirmRollbackModal
Provide CSS token mapping and accessibility text for each actionable element
Include interactions: hover states, keyboard focus order, aria labels for screen reader support
Tracked implementation tasks: client-side expand/collapse animation, API integration for /v1/tenants/{id}/mesh-summary, telemetry events (analytics)
Suggested implementation priority: render skeleton first, then populate signals, then cost delta (cost call can be delayed)

UX review with PM + Eng (scheduled 2026-03-05) — get sign-off on compact vs. expanded affordances
Sync with ENG-28901 to confirm API contract and fallback payload shape (2026-03-04)
Prototype validation session with two SRE customers (2026-03-09) and collect usability notes
Prepare design tokens and export assets for dev handoff by 2026-03-12

title: aggregate artifact origins into release index for private-installer
author: Maya Patel
text:
Add cross-repo artifact origin aggregation to release index used by private-installer; includes pipeline changes, index schema extension, signature/verification cross-checks, and docs for operator consumption.

Context and motivation: Private-installer releases consume artifacts produced by multiple build pipelines (core runtime, helm charts, terraform modules, third-party vendor artifacts). Existing release index entries pointed to single build blobs but lost origin metadata (repo/build-job/container image digest). This PR extends the release index generation to aggregate origin provenance across repos/pipelines so operators can inspect where each artifact came from and verify chain-of-custody at install time.

What this PR does: - Adds an `origins` aggregate block to the release index JSON that lists source repository, pipeline job id, build commit, and optional SBOM/cosign references per artifact. - Modifies the private-installer indexer job to query multiple artifact registries and cross-reference artifact digests to upstream build metadata (via the new origin-mapper service). - Adds origin-mapper microservice (lightweight Go lambda) that merges build metadata across internal buildkite/jenkins/job-run APIs and returns a normalized origin statement for an artifact digest. - Updates CI/CD pipelines: new step in release pipeline to call origin-mapper and attach signed origin blobs to TUF/manifest staging area. - Enhances verification: indexer validates cosign signatures on origin blobs (if present) and records signature verification result in the index. - Adds operator docs and an index API example in private-installer docs for auditors to query artifact origins during upgrades/rollbacks.

Checklist (implemented): - [x] Extend release index schema (index-schema/v2) with `origins` field and verification metadata - [x] Origin-mapper service implementation and unit tests - [x] Release pipeline changes (buildkite/jenkins) to emit origin blobs - [x] Indexer changes in private-installer repo to consume origin blobs - [x] Add integration test that replays multi-repo build metadata into staging index - [x] Docs: private-installer operator guide section on origin queries - [x] Security review: minimal privileges for origin-mapper to query job metadata APIs

Commits (high-level): - feat(indexer): add origin mapping hooks and schema v2 metadata - feat(origin-mapper): initial service with buildkite and jenkins adapters - ci(release): add origin-stage and sign-origin steps, upload to staging TUF area - docs(installer): add operator guide and example queries - test(integration): multi-repo origin aggregation smoke test - fix(ci): tolerate missing SBOM references for third-party mirrored artifacts

Files/areas changed (high-level): - private-installer/cmd/indexer: indexer changed to call origin-mapper and persist origins into index JSON - private-installer/internal/index/schema_v2.go: new schema and JSON marshaling changes - tools/origin-mapper/: new Go service and adapters for buildkite/jenkins - infra/ci/pipelines/release.yml: added origin-stage, sign-origin and upload steps - docs/private-installer/origins.md: operator documentation and API examples - charts/private-installer/values.yaml: small annotation for chart provenance - scripts/dev/replay-origins.sh: local dev helper to simulate upstream metadata

Review conversation (summary): - Lina: "Nice; can we guarantee origin-mapper rate limits won't blow up during a large release?" Author: "Origin-mapper queues queries and caches job metadata for 24h; added circuit-breaker and bulk query path. See origin-mapper/README for eviction rules." - Ethan: "Add tests for mirrored artifacts where upstream job metadata is absent." Author: "Added integration test that marks missing upstream metadata and attaches best-effort origin assertion with source:mirror and mirror-ref." - Zoe: "Signature verification path looks good, but require operator flag to enforce failed verification as hard-fail for critical releases." Author: "Added CLI flag `--enforce-origin-verification` to indexer and documented recommended usage in docs." - Security review (internal): "Ensure origin-mapper tokens scoped read-only and short lived." Author: "Confirmed; CI injects ephemeral tokens, and service uses read-only tokens with minimal TTL. Details in infra/ci/README-security.md."

CI summary: - Initial run: integration tests failed due to missing adapter for legacy Jenkins job API (fixed in second commit). - Second run: unit + integration + lint passed. - E2E staging run: origin blobs uploaded and cosign verification passed for signed artifacts; unsigned third-party artifacts recorded with `verified:false`. Final ci_status: pass.

Edge cases and limitations: - For artifacts mirrored from external vendors we may not retrieve upstream build job metadata; index will include `source: mirror` and a pointer to mirror provenance where available. - This PR does not change TUF signing policy; origin blobs themselves are uploaded to staging and signed with cosign in the release pipeline. TUF package signing remains the authoritative release signature. - Performance: origin-mapper adds an extra ~200-400ms per artifact during index generation in current staging; indexer runs concurrently and batching mitigates impact in typical releases.

Migration and rollout plan: - Index schema v2 is backward-compatible: indexer writes `schema_version: 2` and tooling falls back to v1 when v2 entry not present. - Rollout: release pipeline will emit v2 indexes to a staging bucket for two release cycles; operator tooling supports reading v1 and v2. - Post-merge action: update release-runbooks and notify SRE and compliance teams to start auditing origin queries on next private-installer release.

Merge outcome: Approved by Lina and Zoe after two rounds of review and tests; merged via squash on 2025-11-12.

Notes for future work: - Consider adding signed SBOM references into origin blobs for deeper attestation. - Explore offloading origin metadata to a dedicated provenance catalog service with search capabilities.

title: Optimize Conductor 4.0 release notes and migration guide
author: Priya Ramakrishnan
text:
Overview

This document describes the Optimize Conductor 4.0 release: feature highlights, API and UX changes, SLO and cost implications, a step-by-step migration and rollout checklist for customers and internal teams, and known issues and rollback procedures. Optimize Conductor 4.0 ships a new multi-tenant optimization engine, deep integration with the Fidelity Advisor, and kernel-aware scheduling to reduce per-token cost while preserving observed fidelity.

Goals of the release

- Reduce average per-token inference cost for mixed conversational workloads by 15–35% depending on traffic shape.
- Enable live fidelity negotiation between the Optimize Advisor and the serving runtime for dynamic, SLO-aware routing.
- Provide robust, telemetry-first migration paths for existing Conductor 2.x/3.x customers with minimal service disruption.
- Expose a stable API and a migration shim to preserve backwards compatibility for SDKs and partner integrations.

What’s new in 4.0 (high level)

1) Multi-tenant optimization engine
- A federated optimizer that maintains per-tenant batching and caching policies with a global capacity-aware admission controller.
- Benefits: better cross-tenant utilization, fewer cold-start penalties for low-volume tenants.

2) Kernel-aware scheduling and quantization profiles
- Scheduler now uses model architecture and target hardware metadata (kernel fingerprints) to select quantization and execution paths per-batch.
- Benefits: improved throughput for quantized variants, automatic fallbacks to safe execution paths under load.

3) Fidelity Advisor v2 integration
- Live API that negotiates fidelity targets per-request with the serving runtime. Fidelity policies are evaluated against real-time telemetry and historical customer thresholds.
- Benefits: observable, auditable fidelity decisions and automated crediting adjustments.

4) Hybrid KV-prefetch cache coordinator
- Local-prefetch proxy and a cloud-coordinated KV cache eviction protocol reduce repeated KV misses for session-heavy conversational workloads.

5) Telemetry and cost-normalization changes
- New per-route cost attribution fields (cost_estimate, cost_adjuster_id).
- Streaming telemetry schema v3 (see Observability section below).

6) Console UX and API changes
- New Optimize Conductor UI: per-tenant policy editor, rollout simulator, and a migration dashboard.
- API: /optimize/v4/policies, /optimize/v4/migrate, /optimize/v4/simulate

Compatibility and deprecations

- Backwards compatibility: SDKs calling /optimize/v3 will be routed to a compatibility shim which preserves prior semantics for 12 months post-release. We recommend migrating to v4 within 90 days for full performance benefits.
- Deprecated: legacy batch policy fields 'batch_target_ms' and 'kv_strategy: legacy' are deprecated and will be removed in 2029-10-01.

Important SLO and performance notes

- Expected latency impact: median generation latency unchanged for steady-state traffic; p95 may improve for quantized-optimized paths but can increase during initial migration windows by ~5–10% while batchers warm.
- Cost impact: measured 15–35% savings in mixed chat + embeddings workloads in beta; savings are sensitive to session affinity and average prompt length.
- Telemetry SLO: optimize-conductor ingestion should achieve 99.9% delivery for telemetry events; customers relying on fidelity negotiation should ensure <500ms telemetry propagation to meet tight latency SLOs.

Release compatibility matrix (summary)

- Conductor 2.x -> 4.0: Must run migration shim; recommended staged canary rollout (see checklist).
- Conductor 3.0 -> 4.0: Direct upgrade supported; run the compatibility tests in the migration playbook.

Migration plan and checklist (recommended approach)

Ownership: product -> release manager; eng-platform -> rollout; eng-serving-runtime -> runtime compatibility; customer-success -> customer comms.

Phases:
1) Preparation (2 weeks before canary)
- Identify tenants for staged rollout; prefer 5–10% of traffic slice for initial canary.
- Verify that the customer has telemetry-forwarding >= 99% and healthchecks for /v1/health of local-prefetch proxies.
- Run preflight simulator: curl -X POST /optimize/v4/simulate -d '{"traffic_profile":"tenant-sample"}' and confirm cost_estimate delta.

2) Canary (1 week)
- Deploy Optimize Conductor 4.0 to a single region and enable only non-critical tenants.
- Monitor p50/p95 latency, KV miss rate, policy decision error rates, and fidelity negotiation failures.
- Keep compatibility shim active for any SDKs hitting /v3.

3) Gradual rollout (2–6 weeks)
- Increase traffic in doubling increments (10% -> 20% -> 40% -> 80% -> 100%), waiting for stable telemetry after each step (minimum 24 hours).
- Validate cost and quality metrics against baseline.

4) Post-rollout verification (2 weeks)
- Run fidelity regression suites (PRD test harness) and collect customer-reported regressions.
- Disable compatibility shim after confirming zero critical regressions for 14 days.

Migration checklist (detailed)

- [ ] Run preflight simulation and capture cost_estimate baseline.
- [ ] Ensure customers have updated SDKs supporting v4 or confirm compatibility fallback is acceptable.
- [ ] Confirm telemetry schema v3 ingestion is enabled for the tenant.
- [ ] Validate KMS/HSM policies for any encrypted KV prefetch state.
- [ ] Coordinate canary window with customer success for high-value accounts.
- [ ] Record rollback points (cluster snapshots, config versions).

API changes and examples

New endpoints (examples):
- POST /optimize/v4/policies
 payload: {"tenant_id":"t-123","policy":{"fidelity_target":"balanced","batch_budget_ms":60}}
- POST /optimize/v4/migrate
 payload: {"tenant_id":"t-123","target_version":"4.0","dry_run":true}
- POST /optimize/v4/simulate
 payload: {"traffic_profile":"conversational-heavy","seed":42}

Sample migration CLI (internal):
- rwdctl optimize migrate --tenant t-123 --target 4.0 --dry-run

Console changes and operator guidance

- New migration dashboard: shows per-tenant cost delta, fidelity regression flags, and a staged rollout controller.
- Operators should use the simulator to sanity-check policy updates before committing to tenant production.

Observability and telemetry details

Telemetry schema v3 highlights: new fields
- cost_estimate (float): in USD per 1000 tokens estimated by optimizer
- cost_adjuster_id (string): id of the cost normalization rule applied
- fidelity_decision_id (string): cross-reference to Fidelity Advisor decision traces

Recommended dashboards and alerts
- Dashboards: Optimize Conductor 4.0 -> Per-tenant cost trends, Batch utilization heatmap, Fidelity decision trace viewer.
- Alerts (examples):
 - fidelity.negotiation.failures > 1% in 5m -> Sev2 (owner: eng-serving-runtime)
 - kv.miss_rate increase > 2x baseline in 10m -> Sev2 (owner: eng-platform)
 - telemetry.ingestion.failures > 0.1% in 15m -> Sev1 (owner: eng-sre)

Quality and evaluation guidance

- Run the packaged regression harness: tests/regression/optimize_v4/ which includes synthetic traffic shapes: conversational-heavy, short-prompt-burst, embedding-only, mixed-transactional.
- Evaluation metrics to track: response_consistency, hallucination_rate (if available), latency_p95, per_token_cost.

Known issues and limitations

- During heavy partitioning events the hybrid KV-prefetch coordinator may temporarily increase tail latency by up to 40% until evictions stabilize. Workaround: toggle prefetch:fallback_to_local = true.
- Some edge model variants with custom CUDA kernels may not yet benefit from kernel-aware scheduling; consult the compatibility matrix.
- Console migration dashboard can display stale cost deltas for tenants with infrequent traffic; use the simulate endpoint for accurate dry runs.

Rollback plan

- If p95 latency or fidelity regressions exceed defined thresholds during canary:
 1) Pause rollout and revert policy updates via /optimize/v4/policies rollback API.
 2) If regression persists, scale back to previous conductor image using cluster snapshot and disable multi-tenant optimizer feature flag.
 3) Notify customer-success and schedule a hotfix window.

Security and compliance notes

- Conductor 4.0 requires that any prefetch cache state persisted to disk is encrypted with customer KMS keys for customers with restricted confidentiality settings.
- Audit logging: all fidelity negotiation decisions are written to the audit log stream with retention consistent with customer's compliance tier.

Customer communication and enablement

- Outbound comms: send migration playbook and preflight checklist to customers 10 business days before planned migration.
- Include an optional 30-minute technical review call for enterprise customers during canary.

Appendix A: Backwards compatibility shim behavior

- The compat shim translates /optimize/v3 semantics to v4 with the following rules:
 - Legacy batch_target_ms -> batch_budget_ms mapping with normalization factor 0.8.
 - Explicitly disables kernel-aware scheduling for shimmed requests to preserve latency characteristics.
 - Returns a deprecation header: X-Optimize-Deprecation: v3-compat; replacement: /optimize/v4

Appendix B: Telemetry migration sample

- Example event (schema v3):
 {
 "timestamp":"2028-09-15T14:32:05Z",
 "tenant_id":"t-123",
 "route":"/v1/generate",
 "cost_estimate":0.0024,
 "fidelity_decision_id":"fd-789",
 "batch_id":"b-456"
 }

Contacts and ownership

- Release owner: Priya Ramakrishnan (product)
- Runtime compatibility: Anika Patel (eng-serving-runtime)
- Rollout and infra: Marcus Liu (eng-platform)
- Customer enablement: Diego Alvarez (customer-success)

Document history

- 2028-09-15: Draft created by Priya Ramakrishnan
- 2028-09-18: Internal review and expanded migration checklist (reviewers: Diego, Maya)
- 2028-09-20: Published after resolving compatibility shim behavior notes

title: refactor-thoughtstream-kiran
author: Kiran Patel
text:
Context:
This is my late-night thoughtstream after skimming the large PR that touched batching, KV cache boundaries, and a few public SDK changes. Not a finished doc; more of a sequence of heuristics, micro-checks, and follow-ups I want to remember and possibly turn into a tidy checklist for the team.

High-level concerns (gut):
- Backwards compatibility: SDK surface was changed for that optional `batch_hint` param. Need to confirm SDKs are tolerant for older clients.
- Performance regression risk: the new batching warm-up path may alter latency p50/p95 during short-burst workloads.
- Cache safety: cross-tenant KV-cache key normalization looked subtly different (strip-vs-preserve trailing slashes). That can lead to cache poisoning or silent correctness issues.

Quick manual checks I did (and outcomes):
- Read the new unit tests: they cover happy paths but not the case where sequence_length >> batch window. Missing.
- Ran a small local benchmark (dev machine) with sample trace: p50 unchanged, p95 increased ~12%. Likely due to more aggressive group aggregation.
- Searched for usages of `batch_hint` in repo: only internal tests + one example in docs updated.

Immediate TODOs (short actionable items):
- Add test for long-sequence integration: `tests/integration/batching/large_sequence_stress.py` (simulate seq_len 8k, N=20).
- Add a unit test ensuring KV-cache key canonicalization preserves leading/trailing hashes used by legacy clients.
- Add a wavy note to CHANGELOG for SDK param change + migration note.
- Ask docs to verify examples and SDK compatibility across Python/TS clients.

Review checklist I want to formalize (use for future PRs):
- API/SDK safety:
 - Did author add a migration note? (CHANGELOG + SDK quickstart updated)
 - Are default values non-breaking? If not, provide a compatibility shim.
- Tests:
 - Unit tests for edge cases (very short, typical, very long sequences).
 - Integration that exercises batching under bursty arrival patterns.
 - Property test for KV cache key normalization (idempotent canonicalization).
- Performance:
 - Benchmark script included or CI benchmark job triggered.
 - Baseline comparison attached (script + raw numbers).
- Observability/telemetry:
 - New metrics introduced have docs and tags (e.g., `batch.window_size`, `cache.miss_reason`).
 - Logging at appropriate level for anomalous states (not spammy).
- Security:
 - No sensitive data logged by default (check `str()` of request objects).

Edge-case ideas and hypotheses to test:
- Hypothesis A: aggressive grouping merges heterogeneous sequence lengths that cause KV-cache eviction thrash. Repro: create interleaved traffic with seq_len 16 and seq_len 2048 and observe KV cache churn metrics.
- Hypothesis B: changed key normalization causes multi-tenant collisions when tenant id is omitted in the cache key. Repro: synthetic two-tenant simulation and assert cache separation.

Refactor smells I noticed (possible follow-ups):
- The batching code has three nested `if` trees controlling timers. Suggest extracting a `BatchPolicy` enum and strategy object to make behavior explicit (warm-up, steady, drain).
- Several functions in `batching.py` mutate a shared `BatchState` in place; prefer immutable snapshots for easier reasoning in tests. Might be a bigger change but would simplify property-based tests.
- Duplicate small helper `normalize_key` in two modules — consolidate into `utils/cache.py`.

Proposed small, low-risk quick wins (good for rollback):
- Add a short e2e test that runs in CI (smoke) to assert p95 < baseline + 20% for a synthetic load. Not perfect but catches large regressions.
- Add logging when cache key normalization causes a hash-collision fallback (log at debug with stack context).
- Re-introduce an opt-in feature flag for the new warm-up logic so we can doserver-side toggles during canary.

Questions for author (to include in PR comment):
1) Are there any documented breaking changes for SDKs? If not, can you add a line in the PR description and CHANGELOG?
2) Where do you expect the p95 regression to be mitigated in production — will autoscaling smooth this, or is it an algorithmic change?
3) For key normalization: was the intent to canonicalize across tenants or to preserve raw input?
4) Can you add a small benchmark script that runs in ~2 minutes and outputs p50/p95 so we can run quickly in CI?

Notes to self (mental checklist before approving):
- If tests and small e2e are added and `batch_hint` preserves defaults, I'm comfortable approving and gating the rollout via feature-flag canary.
- If key normalization remains ambiguous, request a small design doc (1 page) and hold merge until clarified.
- If p95 reg grows >25% in CI, block and ask for rollback or more conservative rollout.

Commands / snippets I ran (for reproduction):
- local: `python tools/bench.py --profile batching --clients 10 --seq-len 2048 --duration 60`
- inspect: `rg "normalize_key" -n src | sed -n '1,120p'`
- quick-gc: `python -m pytest tests/unit/test_cache_normalization.py -q -k long_sequence`

Longer-term ideas (parking lot):
- Provide a small property-testing harness for batching properties (using Hypothesis) so we fuzz arrival orders and sequence-length distributions.
- Consider exposing a runtime hint API for customers to suggest batching priorities for latency-sensitive requests.
- Explore using sampled tracing of KV cache hits to build a heatmap for eviction hotspots — would help tuning cache sizes per model.

Closing/Next steps:
- Post the above checklist as a lightweight PR review template in the review docs repo.
- Ping @Soren and @Maya with quick notes and ask the author for the three immediate test additions.
- If author pushes tests and benchmark, re-run quick CI smoke and re-evaluate p95.

---
Personal: this feels like a ~2-3 day follow-up (mostly adding tests, a short note in CHANGELOG, and a canary flag). If the author is responsive, I can shepherd the quick follow-ups tomorrow morning.

title: Adaptive Degradation Safety & Verification Manual
author: Sanjay Rao
text:
Summary:

This manual defines the safety contracts, verification checks, benchmarking protocols, and operational runbooks we use to validate adaptive degradation and fallback behavior in the Redwood serving runtime. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and release owners who gate runtime and scheduler changes. The document consolidates architecture contracts, test harnesses, profiling playbooks, measurable acceptance criteria, and incident response steps into a single reference.

Scope:
- Covers adaptive degradation (fidelity staircases, model-variant fallback, burst shedding) and scheduler/kernel interactions.
- Includes verification checks executed in CI, pre-release staging, and canary phases.
- Prescribes profiling and benchmark procedures for SLO verification and performance regressions.
- Provides runbooks for on-call and release owners for graceful rollback and mitigation.

Principles and safety goals:
1) Observable and measurable: every degradation path must have a minimal observable signal (metrics, traces, events) and a single source-of-truth trace ID for forensic replay.
2) Fail open vs fail closed rationale: correctness-critical requests (enterprise-configured) should prefer fail-closed; non-critical/latency-sensitive requests can fail open to preserved throughput.
3) Bounded fidelity loss: fidelity steps should degrade quality predictably (quantified by eval sets) and be reversible.
4) Deterministic rollback: any automated fallback must expose a deterministic rollback path and human-confirmable guardrails.

Architecture contracts (high-level):
- Degradation tiers: primary (full model), degraded-1 (quantized), degraded-2 (short-context variant), fallback (smaller model / cached-embeddings). Each tier has an SLO budget and cost profile.
- Kernel scheduling contract: the scheduler must maintain per-request kernel affinity for the first N tokens and preserve KV cache affinity during tier transition windows (default N=16).
- Eviction and warmup contract: when a session is evicted from KV cache, a warmup window of configurable length (default 60s) is reserved to rehydrate frequently-seen prompts without degrading SLOs.

Verification matrix (summary table):
| Check ID | Purpose | Where executed | Acceptance threshold | Action on fail | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VD-01 | End-to-end tail latency under 95th percentile SLO | CI staging + canary | p95 < 1200ms for interactive path | block release, auto-rollback in canary | runtime-sre |
| VD-02 | Kernel latency jitter for hot kernels | perf-lab | 95th/50th ratio < 3.0 | schedule throttling + revert kernel flags | runtime-kernel-team |
| VD-03 | Fidelity regression on golden prompt set | automated evals | task-specific metric delta < 1.5% | fail gating | applied-ml |
| VD-04 | KV cache hitrate during warmup | synthetic replay | hitrate > 70% after 120s | degrade to cached-response fallback | runtime-sre |
| VD-05 | Correctness of fallback routing (no request loss) | chaos lab | 0 dropped requests during routing switch | incident | runtime-oncall |

Verifiable artifacts for each check:
- Synthetic replay corpus snapshot (sha256) used in CI.
- Expected telemetry schemas (metric names, tags) and trace samples.
- Baseline benchmark outputs (binary artifacts) for diff-based gating.

CI and pre-release harnesses:
1) CI unit stage: microbenchmarks for individual kernels (latency, occupancy, memory). Thresholds are enforced as fast-fail rules.
2) Staging perf run: full-stack replay of production traffic sampled (1:1000) with degraded-tier injection. Output artifacts: histogram dumps, kernel traces, KV cache heatmaps.
3) Canary: traffic ramp with A/B model variants and automated rollback on VD-* failures. Canary policy: 1% -> 5% -> 20% over 30m windows with automated health checks every 5m.

Benchmarking protocol (detailed):
- Workloads to run:
 - Interactive short-chat (mean tokens=40, 90th=128) — target low-latency SLOs.
 - Streaming long-output (mean tokens=800) — target throughput and memory stability.
 - Embeddings burst (large batch sizes) — target batching efficiency and memory footprint.
- Metrics collected:
 - end_to_end_latency_ms (p50/p90/p95/p99), kernel_exec_time_ms per-kernel, gpu_mem_used_mb, kv_cache_hitrate_pct, tokens_per_second_per_gpu.
- Tooling & commands (examples):
 - Run synthetic replay: 
 ./perf-runner --profile=replay --corpus=sha256:abcd1234 --duration=15m --out=artifacts/replay-$(date +%s).tgz
 - Microbenchmark kernel: 
 python tools/microbench.py --kernel matmul --batch 1 --seq 128 --out json --repeat 50
 - Collect trace samples for a request: 
 curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $CI_TOKEN" https://staging.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -d '{"prompt":"<<golden>>"}' -o /tmp/trace.json
- Acceptance criteria pattern:
 - No p95 regression > 8% vs baseline.
 - Kernel jitter (95/50) <= 3.0.
 - KV cache delta < 5% hitrate loss after warmup period.

Profiling playbook snippets (how-to):
1) Latency fingerprint collection (on perf-lab machine):
 - Start full instrumentation: export PERF_SAMPLER=on; ./runtime --enable-tracing --trace-sample-rate=0.01
 - Run workload for 10 minutes and collect traces: tar -czf traces.tgz /var/tmp/traces/*
 - Post-process: python tools/trace-aggregate.py --input traces.tgz --output traces-summary.json
2) Kernel causality mapping:
 - Use kernel-hint exporter to annotate kernels with request-id and token-index. Example PromQL to find kernel hotpaths: sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms_bucket[5m])) by (kernel_name)
3) Latency attribution checklist:
 - Confirm p95 skew aligns with a specific kernel or queue time via trace waterfall.
 - Check GPU utilization and eviction events within the window.
 - Validate KV cache hit/miss correlation with session affinity changes.

Runbook: Adaptive Degradation incident triage (short):
1) Detection: Alert triggers if p95 or error-rate breaches gating thresholds (see Verification matrix).
2) Initial triage (first 10 min):
 - Owner: oncall-runtime.
 - Query: run the baseline PromQL dashboards (listed below) and capture current vs baseline.
 - Commands:
 - promql: rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket[5m]) by (route)
 - runtime CLI: runtimectl list-sessions --filter=evicted=true --since=10m
3) Containment (10–30 min):
 - If caused by kernel regression: flip kernel rollout gate to previous stable tag (runtimectl kernel-set active:stable-<tag>) and pause canaries.
 - If caused by cache warmup regression: enable elevated pre-warm (config: prewarm_multiplier=2) and route new sessions to degraded-1 temporarily.
4) Remediation (30–90 min):
 - Roll back flagged config or kernel. Run perf-runner quick replay to validate.
 - If degradation persists, scale dedicated pool capacity for 15 minutes to reduce pressure and collect artifacts.
5) Post-incident verification: Ensure all VD-* checks pass in staging before re-enabling automated rollouts.

Release gating checklist (for runtime and scheduler changes):
- Code owner review and ADR reference.
- Automated CI checks: unit tests, lint, kernel microbenchmarks.
- Perf artifacts present: replay corpus, baseline histograms, and guard thresholds.
- Canary policy configured and health checks defined (list health checks and thresholds attached).
- Rollback plan and human approvers designated in the release ticket.

Instrumentation and metrics schema (quick reference):
- metric names: runtime.request.latency_ms, runtime.kernel.exec_ms, runtime.kv.hits, runtime.fidelity.tier, runtime.eviction.count
- required tags: service, model_name, model_variant, route, region, canary_id
- recommended tracing fields: request_id, session_id, token_index, kernel_name, warmup_phase

Ownership and escalation:
- Runtime architecture owner: runtime-arch@redwood.ai (primary: Sanjay Rao).
- Kernel scheduling owner: kernel-team@redwood.ai.
- Oncall rota: runtime-sre (see internal roster).
- Escalation path: oncall -> SRE lead -> runtime-arch -> Eng Director (timed escalation at 45m).

Appendices:
A) YAML example: adaptive degradation policy (example config to be applied via runtime fleet config)

 degradation_policy:
 tiers:
 - name: primary
 model_variant: v2-full
 slos:
 p95_latency_ms: 900
 - name: degraded-1
 model_variant: v2-quantized
 slos:
 p95_latency_ms: 700
 - name: degraded-2
 model_variant: v2-shortctx
 slos:
 p95_latency_ms: 350
 warmup:
 kv_cache_warmup_seconds: 120
 prewarm_multiplier: 1.5
 fallback:
 strategy: route-to-smaller-model
 max_inflight_fallback: 250

B) PromQL examples (quick):
- p95 latency for route: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
- kernel jitter index: (histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le, kernel)))/(histogram_quantile(0.5, sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le, kernel)))

C) Minimal reproduction recipe for regressions:
1) Snapshot failing commit and baseline artifacts.
2) Run perf-runner with the failing kernel flag enabled and the baseline corpus.
3) Collect traces (traces.tgz) and microbench outputs.
4) Upload artifacts to /artifacts/regressions/<ticket-id>.

Related reading and references:
- See routing and fallback architecture ADR (link in related_pages).
- Profiling playbooks and telemetry contract (links in related_pages).

Notes and change log:
- 2026-01-15: Initial draft and adoption of verification matrix (S. Rao).
- 2026-03-10: Added canary ramp policy and refined kernel warmup contract; added runbook remediation steps (E. Hart, D. Alvarez).

If you are implementing a new scheduler or kernel change, follow this manual start-to-finish: 1) add microbench checks, 2) register threshold baselines, 3) run staging replay, 4) validate VD-* checks, 5) enable canary with the configured ramp, 6) monitor and be ready to rollback.

title: Cross-role Tool Access Governance and Self-Service Handbook
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Summary:

This handbook defines the governance model, operational runbook, and self-service flows for granting, reviewing, and revoking access to Redwood’s internal tools across roles and teams. It is intended for people-ops, engineering managers, security reviewers, and tool maintainers. The goal is to make tool access predictable, auditable, and fast while minimizing over-permissioning.

Key Principles:
- Least privilege by default: users receive the minimum role required to do their job.
- Role-driven access: we prefer role-based assignments with ephemeral exceptions.
- Self-service first, manual oversight when necessary: automate safe, common grants.
- Clear ownership: every tool has an owner and an escalation path.
- Auditable lifecycle: provisioning, reviews and deprovisioning are tracked centrally.

1) Scope and Definitions
- Tool: any internal SaaS, self-hosted service, or repo that requires explicit credentials or permissions (examples: AWS consoles, Jira admin groups, prod Grafana, CI pipelines).
- Role: a named collection of permissions (e.g., developer-readonly, infra-operator).
- Access Request: a request submitted to the Access Portal for a role or tool-specific permission.
- Exception: temporary access outside standard roles; must have an expiration and approver.

2) Ownership and Responsibilities
- Tool Owner (team-specified): maintains the role catalog, documents required permissions, defines safe self-service gates, and responds to escalations.
- People Ops: owns onboarding/offboarding orchestration, periodic review cadence, and highest-level policy.
- Security: defines acceptable exception policies, approves high-risk tools, and performs audits.
- Manager (requester approver): verifies business need and ties access to role/mission.

3) Access Model (high level)
- Role Catalog: canonical list of roles for common tools; stored in the Access Portal.
- Self-Service Roles: low-risk roles that can be assigned instantly (examples: docs-edit, ci-reader)
- Request-and-Approve Roles: medium-risk roles requiring manager approval (examples: staging-deploy, metrics-writer)
- Manual Approval Roles: high-risk roles requiring security review (examples: prod-admin, billing-admin)

4) Standard Provisioning Flow (Self-Service preferred)
1. User initiates request via Access Portal (or CLI).
2. For self-service roles: immediate grant recorded in audit log; user notified.
3. For manager-approval roles: manager receives approval email and must respond within 48 business hours; if approved, provisioning executes automatically.
4. For security-approval roles: security reviewer staged; expected SLA is 3 business days.
5. All grants include metadata: requester, approver, justification, expiration (if exception), and ticket ID.

5) Approval Matrix (sample)
| Tool Category | Example Tools | Typical Role Name | Approval Path | Max SLA for Approval | Expiration Policy |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Low risk | Docs, Internal Wiki | docs-edit | Self-service | Instant | Persistent (attached to employment) |
| Medium risk | Staging CI, Dev DB | staging-deploy | Manager | 48 business hours | 90 days (auto-renew) |
| High risk | Production infra, Billing | prod-admin | Manager + Security | 3 business days | 7 days (explicit extension only) |

6) Exception and Emergency Access
- Emergency access (e.g., incident mitigation) uses the Fast-Track Exception flow:
 1) Requester files an incident-tagged access request with justification and incident ID.
 2) On-call approver (manager or designated incident commander) may grant a 4-hour temporary token via the Access Portal.
 3) Security must be notified within 1 hour and will follow up to convert to a formal exception or revoke.
- All emergency grants are logged and retroactively reviewed as part of the incident postmortem.

7) Deprovisioning and Offboarding
- Standard offboarding timeline:
 - Day 0: account disabled for interactive access within 4 hours of HR offboarding signal.
 - Day 1: short-lived API tokens invalidated; persistent service accounts rotated if necessary.
 - Day 7: cloud console roles removed; scheduled backup of any outstanding owner responsibilities.
- Manager responsibility: reassign ownership before final removal.
- Audit: people-ops runs weekly deprovisioning reports, security runs monthly verification.

8) Periodic Access Reviews
- Quarterly review for all high-risk roles.
- Biannual review for medium-risk.
- Annual review for low-risk.
- Review process: automated report produced by Access Portal -> owner validates or initiates deprovisioning -> people-ops enforces changes within 7 business days.

9) Tool Onboarding Checklist (for Tool Owners)
1. Identify required roles and map to least-privilege sets.
2. Document roles in the Role Catalog section of the owner page.
3. Define which roles are self-service vs require approval.
4. Provide an onboarding runbook with contact points and SLOs.
5. Register tool owner and escalation email in the Access Portal.
6. Provide a test account and verification steps for the access flow.

10) Technical Integration Patterns
- Recommended: integrate tool with SSO and SCIM for group sync.
- Fallback: if SCIM unavailable, implement an API-based provisioning endpoint with scoped tokens and change tracking.
- Example access request payload (JSON):
{
 "requester": "user@redwood.com",
 "tool": "grafana-prod",
 "role": "viewer",
 "justification": "Oncall rotation",
 "expires_at": "2026-02-28T23:59:00Z"
}
- Example CLI (Access Portal CLI):
$ rwd-access request --tool grafana-prod --role viewer --justification "oncall"

11) Monitoring, Auditing and KPIs
- KPIs to track: time-to-provision (median), percent self-service, number of active exceptions, time-to-deprovision after offboard.
- Reporting cadence: weekly provisioning dashboard, monthly audit exports (CSV) to security vault.
- Audit checks: verify no more than 5% of production-admin grants are older than 30 days without re-approval.

12) De-Escalation and Dispute Resolution
- If a manager or user disputes a grant or removal, escalate to people-ops with the ticket ID. People-ops will convene: manager, tool owner, and security to adjudicate within 5 business days.

13) Sample Runbook: Granting Prod-Read Access (Manager-Approved)
1. Manager submits request in Access Portal with business justification.
2. Portal routes to tool owner notification and manager approval.
3. On approval, provisioning job runs (SCIM or API).
4. Access granted; audit log written; notification sent to requester and manager.
5. After 90 days, system creates a renewal task for the manager.

14) Implementation Roadmap (next 18 months)
- Q2 2026: Complete SCIM integrations for top 10 tools.
- Q3 2026: Launch delegated team-admin roles for large product groups.
- Q4 2026: Build exception analytics dashboard and automatic expiration nudges.

15) Appendix: Common Role Examples
- developer-readonly: view-only GitHub repos, dev dashboards.
- ci-builder: CI pipeline trigger and artifact write to staging buckets.
- infra-operator: deploy to staging, manage infra-as-code prs.
- prod-admin: full production console access (high-risk).

Contact and Escalation
- People Ops team: people-ops@redwood.com
- Security on-call: security-oncall@redwood.com
- Tool owner contact: listed on each tool owner page in the Access Portal

Change Log
- 2025-03-18: Created by Aisha Patel (initial policy and flows).
- 2025-09-10: Added emergency fast-track and SLA clarifications (reviewers: Marcus Liu).
- 2026-01-14: Extended roadmap and clarified offboarding SLAs (reviewers: Sofia Ramirez, Ethan Morales).

title: Ops daybook: GPU rebalance + network flaps
author: Ethan Park
text:
Quick morning brain-dump and running todo for the day (ops daybook).

Context / summary:
- Overnight low-priority rebalance started to move some >80% slot pools off node-g8-17 to reduce tail latency for <32 token requests.
- Observed two short network flaps in us-west-2 between 03:10–03:14 that coincided with streaming p99 spikes for several hosted model routes.
- Node g8-17 shows rising ECC error counters on GPU1 (nvme logs?). Need to check hardware monitoring + open RMA if persistent.

Top priorities (today):
1) Finish manual drain of g8-17 if ECC doesn't reset after a restart (safety window: 2 hours).
 - Quick commands: kubectl cordon node/g8-17; drain with --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data (confirm running batch jobs first).
 - Verify running pods: kubectl get pods -o wide | grep g8-17 ; check model-serving pods with label app=runtime.
 - Notify SRE channel before drain (give 5m heads up).

2) Rebalance plan follow-up and capacity validation (post-drain):
 - Confirm slot counts: infra/slot-metrics dashboard -> target pool size for hosted-small = 4200 slots. Current after overnight = ~4120. Need to spin up two extra pools (s1/s2) if below 4100.
 - If autoscaler doesn't trigger after 15m, run: terraform apply -var="extra_pools=2" modules/pools ; coordinate with release-eng if pool images are changing.

3) Network flap triage (root cause hunting):
 - Look at edges: vpc flow logs + cloud provider incident page for us-west-2 between 03:05–03:20.
 - Check BGP flaps on backbone nodes (infra-bgp-*) and link stats on cr0 switches (metrics: ifInErrors / ifOutErrors spiking).
 - Correlate with streaming client errors (route /v1/streaming) – grep logs for connection reset errors around timestamps.

4) Hotfixes and immediate mitigations:
 - Add temporary routing fallback: promote model-variant small-latency-1 for critical routes (hosted-api: /v1/generate) to avoid cross-node KV cache misses.
 - Increase short-term burst capacity on dedicated pools if p99 remains >350ms for more than 20m (see runbook threshold).

Daily checklist / run notes (tick when done):
- [ ] Check ECC counter on g8-17 GPU1 and GPU2 (nvidia-smi -q).
- [ ] Post to #platform-alerts: "Starting drain on g8-17 in 5m for ECC investigation".
- [ ] Run pod drain and validate rollout (watch logs for OOM/killed LRU).
- [ ] Confirm slot pool counts across regions (us-west-2, us-east-1, eu-west-1).
- [ ] Validate autoscaler logs for pool creation (grep: autoscaler INFO created pool).
- [ ] Review BGP / cr0 metrics for error spikes.
- [ ] Follow up with hardware vendor if ECC persists; open RMA case and attach nvml logs.

Notes to self / debugging hints:
- If drain causes sudden downstream latency: scale up a warm pool (warm-pool-ephemeral) rather than immediate global autoscale to reduce model cold-starts.
- KV cache miss pattern shows up as repeated full-context loads in logs: search for 'kv-cache-miss' tag.
- For network flaps, look at syn/fin reset counts per AZ in telemetry dashboards (important signal).

Retrospective items to log after incident:
- Was the autoscaler tuning conservative for burst workloads? (check scaling cooldowns; consider lowering to 60s for critical pools).
- Can we add synthetic health checks that detect ECC trends earlier (anomaly alert when ECC++ for same GPU 3x in 24h)?
- Add an automated playbook entry to automatically pin critical routes to low-latency variants during cross-AZ jitter.

Questions / unresolved:
- Did Maya's patch to the serving-runtime batching policy land in prod? If so, was it rolled to us-west-2 early March? (linked GH PR above).
- Are we still using the old nvml-exporter for ECC metrics or has infra switched to the new hw-telemetry pipeline? Need to confirm to avoid blind spots.

Handoff notes for evening shift:
- If drain completed: leave node as cordoned and tag with 'pending-rma' in inventory; do not recommission until hardware team confirms.
- If network flaps resumed after 10pm, escalate to on-call network lead and open INC ticket with provider.
- Summary to paste in handoff: short bullet list with actions taken, current slot counts, any in-flight pool creations, hardware RMA status.

Commands / snippets to keep handy:
- kubectl cordon node/g8-17
- kubectl drain node/g8-17 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force
- nvidia-smi -q | grep -i ecc -A4
- prometheus query: increase(errors_total{job=\"cr0\"}[15m]) > 0

Random notes / brain dump (for later cleanup):
- Might be worth adding a small agent that watches nvml counters and posts to slack when threshold hit (very low-ceremony webhook).
- Look into cross-region KV cache replication idea: warm a minimal prefix across two AZs for most-frequent short requests.

End of day: write quick summary and paste to #platform-handoff including links to PR/Tickets.

-- Ethan
