title: Employee Lifecycle Operating Manual
author: Aisha Kapoor
text:
Summary:
This operating manual describes the end-to-end employee lifecycle at Redwood Inference: candidate sourcing and hiring, pre-boarding and first-week onboarding, role expectations and promotion pathways, benefits and perks, internal tooling access, lateral moves, and offboarding. It is intended for hiring managers, people-ops partners, new hires, and engineering managers who run rotations.

Purpose and scope:
- Provide a single, practical reference that combines process, templates, ownership, and tooling for the full employee lifecycle.
- Apply to all US, EMEA, and APAC hires unless a regional policy overrides a specific benefit or compliance rule.

Owners and escalation:
- Primary owner: People Ops (people-ops).
- Secondary owners: Hiring Managers (owner_team: engineering/product), IT & Security for access provisioning.
- Escalation path: People Ops -> Head of People Ops -> COO.

1) Hiring and candidate experience
Intro: Use Greenhouse as the single source of truth for candidate workflow and scorecards. Follow the interview loop below to ensure consistent evaluation.

Interview loop (standard for IC / engineering):
1. Recruiter screen (30 min) – cultural fit, motivation, logistics.
2. Technical screen (45 min) – system design or coding depending on level.
3. Take-home or paired exercise (where applicable).
4. Onsite / loop (4–5 interviews, 60 min each): design, deep dive, product sense, manager, and bar-raiser.
5. Debrief and hire decision.

Hiring checklist (pre-offer):
- Background checks scheduled (if required by role/region).
- Compensation calibration with People Ops and Finance.
- Offer letter drafted using standard template (GH: /templates/offer-standard).
- Manager confirms onboarding buddy and first-week schedule.

Offer and acceptance: Send offer via Greenhouse-generated PDF and include: start date, manager, team orientation details, first-week agenda, remote equipment plan, 30/60/90 expectations.

2) Pre-boarding (2–4 weeks before start)
- People Ops creates HR record (Workday) and triggers Okta provision.
- IT orders laptop & peripherals; procurement SLA: 7 business days for US, 14 business days EMEA/APAC.
- Manager sends welcome packet with first-week agenda and buddy assignment.
- New hire completes required e-learning (security basics, code of conduct) before day 1.

3) Day 1 and first week: sample schedule
- Day 1: 09:30 welcome (People Ops), 10:30 accounts & SSO setup (IT), 13:00 team lunch (virtual/in-person), 15:00 product overview.
- Week 1: role-specific onboarding sessions, compliance training, assigned small starter task (<= 8 hrs) to land productive ramp.

Quick access checklist (Day 1):
- Okta / single sign-on configured
- Email and Slack active
- Miro/Jira/Confluence permissions verified
- Github repo access granted and PAT guidance provided

Sample CLI for engineering access request (manager-initiated):
- Create an internal access ticket: "ops-tool create-access --user a.kapoor --roles coder,ci-runner --reason 'onboarding'"
- For cloud project access (example):
 gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding redwood-inference-prod \
 --member='user:alice@example.com' \
 --role='roles/viewer'

4) Role expectations and career ladders
Overview: Each function maintains a leveled ladder (IC and managerial tracks). Managers must publish role-specific rubrics during hiring and at promotion time.

Promotion rubric (summary):
- Required artifacts:
 - Updated competency self-assessment
 - 360 feedback collected via People Ops template
 - Evidence of impact (PRs, release notes, customer outcomes)
- Criteria to evaluate:
 1. Scope increase: impact beyond current team or feature area.
 2. Technical/functional depth: demonstrates craft and tradeoffs.
 3. Influence: mentorship, cross-team coordination, shaping product direction.
 4. Consistency: contributions sustained over 6–12 months.

Competency snapshot (example table):
| Level | Scope | Expected outcomes | Promotion signal |
|-------|-------|-------------------|------------------|
| IC2 | Owns single feature | Delivers on feature roadmap, clear tickets | Repeated reliably across 6 months |
| IC3 | Multi-feature / small service | Leads design, mentors peers, measurable KPIs | Significant impact on product metric; scales work |
| IC4 | Cross-team area | Shapes architecture, leads cross-team projects | Recognized as a subject matter expert |

Manager training and expectations:
- All managers complete Manager Essentials within 60 days of assuming role.
- Managers must set clear 30/60/90 plans with employees and review progress monthly.

5) Benefits and perks (high level)
Summary: Redwood offers competitive benefits that include health coverage, 401(k) or local equivalent, parental leave, flexible time off, learning stipend, home-office stipend, and commuter benefits where applicable. Specific eligibility and plan details are in Workday.

Benefits quick table:
| Program | Eligibility | Notes |
|---------|-------------|-------|
| Health insurance | Full-time, post-probation | Multiple plans; enrollment in first 30 days |
| Parental leave | Full-time | 16 weeks primary, 8 weeks secondary (US policy) |
| Learning stipend | All employees | $1,200/year for conferences/courses |
| Home-office stipend | New hires | $500 one-time; additional ergonomic budget via People Ops |

Perk highlights:
- Monthly wellness stipend (local currency equivalent)
- Quarterly hackday and team offsite support
- Referral bonus paid after 90 days of hire

6) Internal tools and access patterns
Primary tooling matrix (ownership and notes):
- HRIS: Workday (People Ops)
- ATS: Greenhouse (People Ops/Recruiting)
- SSO: Okta (IT/Security)
- Password manager: 1Password (IT/Security)
- Communication: Slack (All)
- Code repo: Github Enterprise (Eng)
- Ticketing: Jira (Eng/Product)
- Documentation: Confluence (All)
- Cloud console: GCP (Infra team manages project namespace)

Access request lifecycle:
1. Manager opens access request ticket in ServiceNow/IT portal with role code and justification.
2. IT verifies procurement and assigns hardware.
3. Okta group sync grants access to tooling within 24 business hours (priority: 48 hours during ramps).

Common templates (copy into ticket):
- Subject: "New hire access request: [Name] – [Team] – [Start Date]"
- Body: "Name: 
Role: 
Start date: 
Required groups: github:coder, jira:team-X, gcp:dev-project-A"

7) Lateral moves, rotations, and sabbaticals
- Lateral moves should be notified to People Ops at least 30 days before the target start.
- Rotation duration: typically 3–6 months; sponsoring manager defines clear goals.
- Sabbatical policy: Eligible after 3 years of continuous service; reference People Ops policy for approval workflow.

8) Offboarding and knowledge handover
Offboarding checklist (manager + People Ops):
1. Confirm final date and communicate to payroll and benefits.
2. Knowledge transfer plan: at least one shadow week and written runbook for critical responsibilities.
3. Revoke access: trigger automated Okta deprovisioning (day-of) and rotate shared credentials.
4. Exit interview scheduled by People Ops.

Data retention and security notes:
- Managers must ensure ownership transfer of any customer accounts or keys before offboard.
- For Private deployment engineers, rotate production creds and report to Security within 24 hours.

9) Metrics and SLAs for People Ops services
- New hire full provisioning SLA: 5 business days (US), 10 business days (EMEA/APAC).
- Offer-to-accept cycle time target: median 7 days.
- First-week enablement rate: target 95% of hires meet Quick access checklist by EOD Day 1.

10) Templates and quick examples
Manager 30/60/90 outline (paste into calendar invite):
- 30 days: learn codebase, ship a small ticket, meet cross-functional partners.
- 60 days: lead a small design, mentor another engineer, improve a CI/CD flow.
- 90 days: own a feature end-to-end with metrics and post-mortem.

Sample welcome Slack message:
"Please welcome @new-hire (Role, Team). Start date: 2025-04-01. Buddy: @buddy. First 1:1 with manager scheduled on Day 2. Please say hi and share any docs that will help them get up to speed."

FAQ (selection):
Q: Who signs off on promotions?
A: Manager + peer review + People Ops calibration committee.

Q: How do I request a laptop upgrade?
A: Submit hardware request with manager approval; upgrades are reviewed quarterly.

Appendix: Templates, links, and references
- Offer templates: /templates/offer-standard
- Promotion packet checklist: /templates/promotion-packet
- Manager training: /learning/manager-essentials
- Security onboarding: /security/new-joiner

Revision history:
- 2024-09-15: created by Aisha Kapoor (People Ops)
- 2025-03-10: updated procurement SLAs, added CLI example and rotation policy

If anything in this manual conflicts with a legal or regional policy, the regional policy supersedes. For questions or suggested edits, contact people-ops@redwood.com.

title: Causal Regression Investigation Handbook
author: Asha Menon
text:
## Summary

This handbook defines a causal-first process for investigating model regressions (quality, latency, and cost) observed after a change (model version, quantization profile, infra, or prompt). It combines signals from the eval harness, production telemetry, and unit-level artifacts to form testable causal hypotheses and rapidly converge on root cause. This doc is intended for ML engineers, SREs, and applied ML owners performing triage on regression alerts.

## Scope

- Applies to regressions discovered via: continuous eval pipelines, production quality alerts, customer escalations, or automated regression bisect results.
- Covers causal graph design, hypothesis generation, experiment design, statistical testing, and actionable rollback/fix patterns.
- Not a replacement for the automated-bisect playbook; rather, this is the manual/analyst layer for ambiguous or cross-cutting regressions.

## Ownership and Escalation

- Primary owner: Applied ML - Model Quality team
- On-call SRE: for runtime/latency regressions
- Escalation: if causal analysis points to infra/serving runtime, escalate to Eng-Serving-Runtime within 4 hours.

## Definitions

- Regression: measurable degradation in an SLO or metric compared to baseline (pre-change).
- Change event: deploy, quantization profile change, router policy update, prompt set modification, or model promotion.
- Primary signals: evaluation harness results, production cost/latency/quality telemetry, example traces, token-level diffs.

## Signals and Data Sources (ordered by priority)

1. Eval harness: stable test-set metrics, per-slice breakdowns, and seed-fixed reruns.
2. Production telemetry: per-route token latency, error rates, kv-cache hit rates, and token counts.
3. Shadow traffic and A/B results (if available).
4. Client traces / transcript samples (anonymized).
5. Deployment metadata: model SHA, quantization profile ID, kernel selection log, GPU type, and routing policy.

## Causal DAG Templates

Use these canonical Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) templates to structure thinking. Draw the DAG and explicitly list assumed causal links before testing. Example templates (textual):

- Template A (Model-change-driven): ChangeEvent -> Weights/Quantization -> ModelBehavior -> OutputQuality
- Template B (Runtime-interaction): ChangeEvent -> KernelSelection/Batching -> Latency -> TimeoutErrors -> Quality
- Template C (Prompt/Context): ChangeEvent -> PromptSet/ContextTruncation -> KV-CacheHits -> EffectiveContext -> OutputQuality

Always annotate nodes that are observable vs latent and list available instrumentation for each node.

## Investigation Checklist (step-by-step)

1. Record the alert context: metric, threshold, time window, impacted slices (routes, languages, long vs short prompts).
2. Snapshot deployment metadata for the time window: model_id, model_sha, quant_profile, runtime_version, host region, and GPU type.
3. Replicate the failure in the eval harness with the same model and quantization profile, using the failing prompt slices. Use deterministic seeds where applicable.

 Example CLI to re-run a failing slice locally:
 
 curl -X POST https://eval-harness.internal/run -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"slice_id":"lang-en-long-context", "model_id":"m-v42", "quant_profile":"q8_4", "seed":42}'

4. Construct a concise causal DAG and list 2–3 competing hypotheses (e.g., quantization introduced a tokenization-sensitive bias; kernel fallback increased latency and triggered truncation).
5. Prioritize hypotheses by plausibility and ease-of-test. Run targeted ablations:
 - A/B run with float32 weights vs quantized profile on the same hardware.
 - Run with and without KV-cache enabled.
 - Run with controlled batch sizes to reproduce kernel selection differences.

6. Apply causal tests: difference-in-differences, regression adjustment, and when appropriate, causal-impact or DoWhy-style causal estimation.

 Minimal SQL snippet to prepare test/control cohorts:

 SELECT request_id, model_tag, quant_profile, prompt_slice, quality_score, latency_ms, kv_cache_hit
 FROM production_prompts
 WHERE event_time BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-02'
 AND prompt_slice IN ('lang-en-long-context', 'lang-en-short')

7. If initial tests are inconclusive, schedule targeted shadow traffic or a canary with enhanced telemetry for 2 hours covering the failing slices.
8. When confident in root cause, prepare remediation: rollback plan, targeted quantization tweak, kernel configuration change, or prompt update. Document the fix in the incident tracker.
9. Close the loop: add failing prompts to the prompt-sets-and-benchmarks suite and create a new quant-eval slice if quantization was causal.

## Statistical Decision Rules

- Minimum sample size: 500 requests per slice for high-variance tasks (chat/long-context); 100 for low-variance embeddings or deterministic reranks.
- Significance: two-sided p < 0.01 for primary SLOs. Use bootstrap CIs for non-normal metrics (BLEU-like or token-level fidelity).
- Effect size threshold: absolute quality-drop >= 2% or relative latency increase >= 20% is actionable by default. Adjust per-SLO tier.

## Example Causal Test (Python pseudocode)

# Example: Use DoWhy to estimate effect of quantization on quality_score

from dowhy import CausalModel
import pandas as pd

# load prepared cohort dataframe
df = pd.read_csv('cohort.csv')
model = CausalModel(data=df, treatment='quant_profile_q8_4', outcome='quality_score', common_causes=['prompt_length', 'route', 'seed'])
identified_estimand = model.identify_effect()
estimate = model.estimate_effect(identified_estimand, method_name='backdoor.propensity_score_matching')
print(estimate)

Note: include diagnostics and sensitivity analysis for unobserved confounding.

## Integrations with Automated Bisect and Eval Harness

- When bisect returns candidate change windows, attach a causal-analysis job that:
 - Replays failing trace samples across candidate model variants.
 - Runs the lightweight DoWhy/DiD tests on per-slice cohorts.
 - Produces a short causal report in the bisect output (delta metrics, p-values, suggested root causes).

- Hook names: eval-harness/replay, bisect/causal-report, telemetry/query-cohort.

## Required Instrumentation and Data Schema

Minimum columns for any cohort extract (plain text table):

| column_name | type | description |
| request_id | string | unique request identifier |
| event_time | timestamp | request time |
| model_tag | string | model identifier (e.g., m-v42) |
| quant_profile | string | quant profile id |
| route | string | API route or product feature |
| prompt_slice | string | slice label from prompt catalog |
| quality_score | float | chosen quality metric (0-1 normalized) |
| latency_ms | float | end-to-end token latency |
| kv_cache_hit | bool | cache hit flag |

Ensure all datasets are (a) anonymized, (b) token counts and sample prompts excluded from exported CSVs by default.

## Common Root Causes and Recommended Fixes

- Quantization-precision-bias: Re-run quant profile with per-layer fallback, raise precision on sensitive layers, add per-slice quant-tune.
- Kernel-fallback-latency: Pin kernel to earlier stable runtime for affected model length range; increase timeout SLOs temporarily.
- KV-cache-eviction-regression: Investigate policy, add explicit cache hold for long contexts or move to a larger shard.
- Prompt-truncation-shift: Add guardrail in prompt pipeline to preserve critical prefix tokens; add unit tests in prompt-sets.

## Playbook for Live Mitigation (fast timeline)

1. Within 30 minutes: if customer-facing degradations, enable fallback model variant (float or previous release).
2. Within 2 hours: collect reproducer examples and run targeted canary with enhanced telemetry.
3. Within 24 hours: implement permanent fix or schedule rollback.

## Post-Incident Actions

- Add failing prompts to permanent prompt regression suite.
- Create a quant-eval slice and add to nightly eval for that profile.
- Update the causal DAG library with the final root cause and evidence.
- Run a retrospective with owners (Applied ML, Serving Runtime, SRE) and record action items.

## Templates and Reporting

Use the following one-page template for causal-report attachments to incidents:

- Title: (short)
- Summary: 2–3 sentences
- Candidate hypotheses tested (list)
- Data used (cohort sizes, time windows)
- Statistical tests and results (p-values, CIs)
- Root cause (with confidence: low/medium/high)
- Action taken and follow-ups

## Related Pages

- eval-harness/serving-simulation-eval-harness-2026
- quantization-profiles/kv-cache-quant-stability-audit-playbook-2025
- regression-triage/automated-regression-bisect-and-blame-assistant-2026

## References

- DoWhy documentation and examples
- Google: CausalImpact R package
- Redwood internal: prompt-sets-and-benchmarks/prompt-coverage-matrix-and-annotated-drift-repair-guide-2024

---

title: per-route function-call telemetry and JSONL output tagging
author: Maya Patel
text:
Motivation: customers using function/tool-calling and structured output have limited ability to correlate tool calls to per-route metrics, and streaming JSONL outputs lack stable tags for downstream log processors. This PR attaches per-route metric tags to function-call events, enriches JSONL streaming output with consistent telemetry headers, and adds trace propagation across the OpenAI-compat adapter layer. Changes aim to improve observability without changing public API semantics. Summary of changes: 1) Add per-route "route.tags" metadata to function-call events emitted by the gateway and runtime; 2) Emit a compact telemetry header ("rwid, srv, route, call_idx") at the start of streaming JSONL chunks to enable log reassembly; 3) Propagate distributed trace context and span IDs into function-call instrumentation and structured logs; 4) Update openai-compat adapter to translate OpenAI-style "request_id" into rwid and include route tags for compatibility; 5) Add unit and integration tests covering streaming reassembly and metric label cardinality limits; 6) Add doc comments and console notes for admins about limiting custom route tags. Checklist: - [x] Add telemetry header and tests - [x] Preserve streaming shape for openai-compat clients - [x] Ensure route tag cardinality cap (100) enforced - [x] Add end-to-end smoke test against mock tool runner - [x] Update docs and changelog Impact: no user-facing API change; observability improvements are additive. Rollout plan: feature gated behind experiment flag "obs.route_tags_tool_calls" for three days in canary, then staged rollout to 25% traffic, then full rollout assuming no regressions. Monitoring: added alerts for spike in unique route tags and increased rate of incomplete streams.

Jon Liu: Can you confirm the added telemetry header is at most 256 bytes to avoid proxy truncation?
Maya Patel: Confirmed, header is compacted and base64-encoded; tests include a 256-byte boundary case.
Sofia Ramirez: We should cap unique per-route tags to avoid high-cardinality metrics - where is that enforced?
Maya Patel: Cap enforced in runtime/instrumentation/serializer.go with a hard limit of 100 tags and metrics emitted when limit hit.
Evan Brooks: Integration tests flaked once on CI due to a timing window in the mock tool runner, please add retry/wait up to 500ms.
Maya Patel: Added small retry and fixed race; CI rerun included below.
Sofia Ramirez: Approving pending a short note in docs about tag cardinality and cost implications.
Sofia Ramirez: Approved after doc update.
Release-Manager (auto): No conflicts with main; merge allowed.

Add per-route telemetry tags for function/tool calls and compact streaming JSONL telemetry header (rwid, srv, route, call_idx). This improves ability to correlate tool calls with per-endpoint metrics and enables downstream log reassembly. Feature rolled out behind experiment flag obs.route_tags_tool_calls.

title: Reconcile Stripe/NetSuite exports and fix proration edge-case billing deltas
author: Aarav Patel
text:
Summary:
There are persistent mismatches between exported Stripe invoices (and invoice items) and the downstream NetSuite import. The largest diffs occur when subscriptions change mid-cycle (plan upgrades/downgrades) where Stripe creates prorated invoice items and our NetSuite mapping either drops lines or aggregates them incorrectly, causing invoice amount deltas and customer disputes.

Symptoms observed:
- NetSuite totals for March invoices were ~0.7% higher than Stripe exported totals for 120 customers; variance concentrated on prorated subscriptions.
- Reconciliation job flags group A (proration) as 'unmatched' because our export job only exports top-level invoice totals for subscription changes, not individual invoice_item entries with prorations and negative adjustments.
- Rounding behavior: Stripe sends amounts in cents, but our aggregator applied float rounding then re-converted leading to off-by-one-cent errors across many lines.
- Edge case: when rate-limit throttles usage-export worker, duplicate usage submissions have been collapsed incorrectly and subsequently cause net-new invoice items in Stripe not reflected in nightly export snapshot.

Impact:
- Customer billing disputes and support tickets (5 escalations last week).
- Revenue recognition mismatches for finance; manual adjustments required.

Goal:
Fix export/reconciliation pipeline to ensure one-to-one mapping between Stripe invoice items and NetSuite import rows, handle proration line items precisely, harden rounding to cents, and eliminate duplicate-usage collapse errors caused by rate-limited exporters. Ship migration/backfill for prior month mismatches and add monitoring to detect regressions.

Nightly Stripe export contains invoice_item_id-level lines for all invoices including prorations
NetSuite import mapping accepts invoice_item_id as primary key and preserves sign and cents exactly
Reconciliation job diff rate reduced to <0.05% for prorations over a 7-day baseline
Backfill job runs to correct March mismatches and creates audit log entries for manual finance review
Unit + integration tests for rounding and proration edge cases included in CI
Runbook updated; Slack alert channel & dashboard tile for proration diffs

Create subscription S on plan A on 2026-02-01
Upgrade subscription S to plan B on 2026-02-16 via the customer portal (creates prorated invoice items in Stripe)
Run nightly exporter job (billing-exporter) to produce Stripe CSVs; observe if invoice_item_id rows are present
Import exported CSV into NetSuite staging import; verify sign and cents preservation
If mismatch occurs, inspect exporter log for rounding warnings and usage-export worker retry events

Exporter: switch all amount math to integer cents and avoid float conversions. Add explicit invoice_item_id, subscription_id, invoice_id, and currency columns to the CSV export.
NetSuite mapping: adjust import template to use invoice_item_id as natural key. Preserve original Stripe amount and a 'proration_flag' when quantity != 1 or when invoice_item.description contains 'proration'.
Reconciliation: add matching by invoice_item_id then fallback to (invoice_id + description + amount_cents) with strict tie-breaker rules.
Backfill: use Stripe API pagination to collect historical invoice_item list for the afflicted date range (2026-02-01 -> 2026-03-31). Produce an audit CSV with reconciliation_reason column.
Monitoring: add Grafana panel to show percent of invoices with unmatched prorations, alert at 0.2% for 6h sustained.
Rate limiting: adjust usage-export worker to persist interim events to S3 before dedupe so transient rate-limit retries don't collapse distinct events. Add idempotency key generation per usage_event_id + sequence.
Tests: create integration harness that spins up a local Stripe-mock and NetSuite-import-simulator for CI smoke tests; include edge-case fixtures (negative prorations, cents rounding).

2026-02-16: Initial report from Finance showing March/Stripe vs NetSuite discrepancy (ticket FIN-184). Assigned to billing reliability squad.
2026-02-18: Repro steps saved: reproduce using subscription fixtures: plan-small -> upgrade mid-cycle to plan-medium (see ./fixtures/proration-upgrade.json in billing repo).
2026-02-22: Investigated Stripe export: found export job aggregated invoice-level totals for subscription updates rather than emitting invoice_items. Patch proposed to include invoice_item rows (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/billing/pull/312).
2026-02-25: Discovered rounding bug: intermediate float sum used in exporter. Switched to integer cents arithmetic in local branch. Added unit tests for fractional cent flows.
2026-02-28: Rate-limit related duplicate usage collapse: traced to usage-export worker where retry/backoff collapsed two near-identical usage events into one aggregate with wrong quantity. Filed ENG-4818 to harden usage dedupe logic.
2026-03-03: Sync with Finance & PM. Decided on two-phase rollout: 1) Export change + tests 2) NetSuite mapping update + backfill. Document link: https://confluence.redwood.ai/billing/recon-proration-plan
2026-03-05: NetSuite mapping patch prepared (internal import mapping sheet version v2). Spreadsheet: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/billing/netsuite-mapping-v2.xlsx
2026-03-07: PR review feedback from Lydia (Finance) requesting invoice_item_id present as the last column and original_stripe_amount_cents retained; updated PR accordingly.
2026-03-09: Deployed exporter patch to staging. Nightly reconciliation ran: proration diffs dropped from 0.7% to 0.12% for staging dataset. Observed two remaining classes of failures: legacy invoices with manual adjustments and very old subscriptions using legacy meter. Preparing backfill plan.
2026-03-10: Started writing backfill job to reconcile March mismatches. Backfill will: export historical invoice_item rows from Stripe API, compute expected NetSuite rows, and create CSV for Finance to import with audit metadata.

- In-scope: request/response logging for user-facing inference calls; headers and associated metadata (trace IDs, request IDs); diagnostic/audit streams.
- Primary requirements you flagged: PII removal (names, emails, phone numbers, SSNs), redaction of sensitive headers (cookies, auth headers), deterministic handling of trace/request IDs (preserve correlation but not raw values), data residency within US regions, and strongly-limited access to raw logs.
- Retention preferences you mentioned: 90 days for request/response logs by default; 365 days for audit logs (security/infra).

Open questions we flagged on the call (please confirm):
1) Should trace/request IDs be pseudonymized (same input -> same pseudonym) or hashed + salted per-tenant so correlation works only within your account?
2) Which endpoints do you want excluded from request logging entirely (health, metrics, certain admin endpoints)?
3) Any regulatory constraints requiring immutable archival vs reversible redaction for audit purposes?

Proposed immediate next steps from our side:
- Share a short technical spec for our redaction pipeline (regex + ML-based PII classifier + token-level masking), with examples of sanitized output. (I’ll attach a spec and sample sanitized logs.)
- Provide a diagram of where logs are stored, encryption-at-rest details, and the access control model.
- Prepare a scoped POC for MedSecure in us-east-1 (we can also propose us-west-2 if you prefer), timeline: 3 weeks to POC, sample sanitized logs delivered within 5 business days of POC kickoff.
- Deliverables: Pseudonymization approach (options), retention configuration settings, and an access-control runbook for your SOC team.

Action items for you:
- Confirm whether pseudonymization should be deterministic across customers or strictly per-tenant salted.
- Share any logging exclusions and the list of internal contacts who must be able to read audit logs.

Attachments: I’m attaching the proposed spec and an anonymized sample we’ll use for the POC.

If that aligns, I’ll schedule a technical deep-dive with engineering and your security lead next week.

Thanks Dylan — useful recap. A few clarifications from our side so the POC scope is tight:

1) Trace/request IDs: we need to preserve the ability to correlate across microservices but cannot accept raw IDs. Preferred approach is deterministic pseudonymization that is stable within our tenant but not reversible by Redwood engineering. We explicitly prefer a per-tenant salt.

2) Retention: we need 365 days for security/audit logs; for request/response logs a default of 90 days is acceptable, but we may request a 180-day option during trials.

3) Residency: this must be hosted in a US region (us-east-1 preferred). If the POC includes backups, we need assurance backups remain within the same region.

4) Redaction proof: our auditors will want a sample of both raw -> redacted pairs (privileged view) and a sanitized version for the app team. Can you provide a sanitized sample plus a privileged sample under an NDA or secure transfer?

Subject: Re: MedSecure — follow-up: log controls, PII redaction, residency

Alex — great questions. Answers below and what we can commit to for the POC.

1) Pseudonymization approach
- We propose per-tenant deterministic pseudonymization: each tenant gets a unique KMS-wrapped salt. Inputs (trace/request ID) are hashed with HMAC-SHA256 + salt and then truncated to 16 bytes (base64) for storage. This preserves correlation in your account while preventing cross-tenant correlation by Redwood. Keys can be customer-managed (BYOK) if required.

2) PII redaction pipeline
- Multi-stage: (a) lightweight regex stripping for obvious patterns (SSN, credit card, phone), (b) ML-based PII classifier for contextual detection (names, free-text emails), (c) token-level masking for user message content.
- Failure mode: If both regex and ML confidence are below threshold, the pipeline will: redact the suspect span with a deterministic pseudonym and emit a high-severity alert to your security webhook (configurable). No unmasked value will be persisted.

3) Retention & storage
- Configurable retention per stream: request_logs (default 90d), audit_logs (default 365d). We can support a 180d option for request_logs for the trial period.
- Backups will be region-locked to the POC region (us-east-1) and marked with the same retention policy.

4) Access & key management
- KMS integration: support for customer-managed keys (AWS KMS CMKs), Redwood-managed KMS with strict IAM roles, or HSM-backed keys for enterprise customers.
- Decryption/pseudonymization privileges: by default, only a Red team service account has access to re-identify for support with an auditable workflow (ticket required). For MedSecure we recommend BYOK so only your SREs hold re-identification capability.

5) Deliverables & timeline
- Tech spec (attached): Proposed_Log_Pseudonymization_Spec.pdf
- Sample sanitized logs: sample_sanitized_logs_example.txt (will provide both sanitized and privileged pairs under an NDA channel)
- POC plan: kickoff week of 6/21, 3-week POC, internal milestone for sanitized sample within 5 business days of kickoff.

6) Diagram & failure behavior
- We’ll include a dataflow diagram showing collection -> preprocessor -> pseudonymization -> storage + audit stream. If masking fails, entries are pseudonymized and the raw value is not stored; an alert webhook will fire and the event will be tracked in an audit-only stream.

title: Operational Flows and Policy Gallery
author: Maya Chen
text:
Purpose and scope:

This page consolidates company-wide operational flows and reusable policy artifacts relating to access and permissions, change management, data lifecycle, procurement & expenses, vendor onboarding, travel policy, and internal templates. It is intended as a single-entry reference for teams to discover the canonical process, required approvals, and the standard templates used by Redwood Inference.

Audience:
- Engineering, Product, Security, Finance, People Ops, and Procurement partners.
- Team leads and managers who approve access, spend, or changes.

Summary (quick reference):
| Area | Owner | Target SLA / Thresholds | Key system | Approval path |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Access & Permissions | Security + IT | Standard request: 48 hours; Elevated: 5 business days; Emergency: <4 hours | IdentityHub (IAM) | Manager -> Security reviewer -> IAM admin |
| Change Management | Eng-Platform | Standard change window: 02:00–05:00 PST; Emergency changes: immediate runbook | OpsChange | Change owner -> CAB -> Release manager |
| Data Management | Security + Data Platform | Retention: 1y/3y/7y by classification; Backup RPO 24h | DataLake / Vault | Data owner -> Security review |
| Procurement & Expenses | Finance-Legal | < $5k: manager; $5k–$75k: procurement; > $75k: exec | ProcureFlow, Spendly | Req -> Procurement -> Finance -> Exec (if needed) |
| Vendor Management | Procurement | Onboarding: 7–14 days | Vendor Portal | Security review -> Procurement -> Contracting |
| Travel & Expenses | People Ops + Finance | Per-diem and policy; pre-approval for > $2k | Spendly | Traveler -> Manager -> Finance |

Note: See "Templates" section at the end for direct links to request and approval forms.

1) Access & Permissions (Identity lifecycle)

Overview:
Redwood centralizes identity and access control to IdentityHub. All access must follow least-privilege principles and be tied to an owner and business justification. Temporary elevated access must have an expiration.

Roles and responsibilities:
- Requester: submits request in IdentityHub with justification and business owner.
- Manager: approves role change and validates business need.
- Security reviewer: performs risk review for privileged access (SRE/infra, customer data, KMS/HSM).
- IAM admin: applies the change and documents in the audit log.

Standard process (step-by-step):
1. Requester files an Access Request in IdentityHub with resource, role, justification, and requested duration.
2. Manager approves or rejects within 48 hours. If no response, escalate to manager's skip-level.
3. If the role is privileged, Security reviewer has 2 business days to respond; may place conditions (MFA, limited scope).
4. IAM admin provisions access. Provisioning events must include ticket ID and expiration.

SLOs and monitoring:
- 90% of standard requests fulfilled within 48 hours.
- Emergency access (investigations, P1 incidents): target same-day (4 hours) turnaround via on-call IAM admin and Security Pager.
- Monthly audit: all privileged roles reviewed quarterly.

Exceptions and emergency process:
- Emergency access uses the Emergency Access Runbook (link: OpsChange/Emergency-Access-Runbook). Every emergency grant must be accompanied by an audit ticket and post-incident access review within 7 days.

2) Change Management (Services & Infra)

Purpose:
To minimize risk from configuration and code changes by standardizing assessment, scheduling, and rollouts.

Change categories:
- Standard changes: pre-approved, low-risk, follow templated rollout (e.g., dependency bumps, non-prod config changes).
- Normal changes: require CAB review; typically feature deploys, infra patches.
- Emergency changes: require immediate action; follow Emergency Change runbook and postmortem.

Approval matrix and windows:
- Standard changes: no CAB if they match the Standard Change Catalogue and use a validated automation playbook.
- Normal changes: submit in OpsChange 72 hours before planned window. CAB meets daily for fast lanes and weekly for large changes.
- Change window: default maintenance window 02:00–05:00 PST; services with global usage must consult SRE before scheduling.

Rollback policy:
- All normal and emergency changes must include a rollback plan and a success metric (SLO delta or error rate).
- If errors exceed alert threshold (error rate > 0.5% or latency > 2x baseline), trigger rollback and incident response.

Post-change verification:
- Owner must run the Post-Change Checklist in OpsChange within 4 hours of completion and mark the change as successful or failed.

3) Data Management (Classification, Retention, Access)

Classification table:
| Classification | Examples | Default retention | Access controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Public | Marketing assets | 0 | Read-only public URLs |
| Internal | Documentation, non-sensitive logs | 3 years | Corporate SSO with RBAC |
| Confidential | Customer PII, analytics with identifiers | 7 years | Justified access, strict logging, DLP |
| Restricted | KMS keys, secrets, regulated customer data | As required by contract | Restricted to named individuals, HSM/KMS controls |

Data handling requirements:
- PII and Confidential datasets require a documented Data Processing Agreement and must be stored only in Vault-backed buckets with encryption at rest.
- Backups: daily snapshot with retention according to classification. Restore drills: annually for Restricted data, bi-annually for Confidential.

Retention and deletion:
- Automated retention policies are enforced via DataLife jobs. Data owners must declare retention period at onboarding.
- Deletion requests use the Data Deletion Template and are tracked in the Data Deletion Register.

Data change control:
- Schema migrations that touch production must be submitted to Data Platform and follow the Migration Review workflow (submit migration PR, canary run, monitoring).

4) Procurement & Expenses

Procurement thresholds and approvals:
- <$5,000: Manager approval via ProcureFlow (Spendly card optional).
- $5,000–$75,000: Procurement team approval + Finance-Legal review (Supplier terms assessment).
- >$75,000: Procurement + Finance-Legal + Executive approval (SVP or CFO).
- Capital spend: follow Capitalization policy; enter requisition with finance tag.

Competitive sourcing and vendor evaluation:
- For purchases > $50k, obtain at least 2 competitive quotes and document selection rationale in ProcureFlow.
- Risk scoring: Procurement assigns a Vendor Risk Score (1–10). Any vendor with score >=7 triggers Security review and may require SOC2/ISO evidence.

Expense reimbursement rules (high level):
- Use Spendly to submit expense reports. Receipts required for all items > $25.
- Per-diem for domestic travel: $75/day lodging cap: $250/night without pre-approval.
- International travel: pre-approval required for trips exceeding $2,000.

Audit and controls:
- Monthly reconciliation between ProcureFlow and accounting.
- Random sample expense audits quarterly (finance + internal audit).

5) Vendor Management

Onboarding checklist (7–14 day target):
1. Vendor request created in Vendor Portal (ProcureFlow) with SOW/quote.
2. Procurement performs commercial review and risk scoring.
3. Security runs technical and compliance review (SOC2/penetration test evidence as required).
4. Legal reviews contract terms and data processing clauses.
5. Finance provisions payment terms and payment method.
6. Account team verifies go/no-go.

Contractual controls and SLAs:
- Standard contract must include: data residency clause, breach notification timeline (<=72 hours), liability caps, and SLA definitions (uptime, support response).
- For production services that affect customer traffic, require 99.9% uptime SLA and a runbook integration.

Offboarding and termination:
- On contract end, Procurement triggers Offboarding Checklist: license termination, access revocation in IdentityHub, data return or secure deletion, final invoice settlement.

6) Travel policy (concise)

Pre-approval:
- Any trip expected to exceed $2,000 requires manager & finance pre-approval via Spendly.

Travel safety and insurance:
- All employees traveling on business automatically receive Redwood travel insurance and are covered under the company incident response procedures.

Booking and allowable expenses:
- Use company preferred vendors where available. Personal upgrades should not be charged to company cards without explicit manager approval.

Expense timelines:
- Submit expense reports within 10 business days of trip completion. Late submissions may delay reimbursement.

7) Templates and artifacts (canonical)

Available templates (ProcureFlow / Confluence Templates):
- Access Request Template (IdentityHub Request Form) -> /confluence/templates/access-request-template
- Change Request Template (OpsChange Change Form) -> /confluence/templates/change-request-template
- Data Deletion Request -> /confluence/templates/data-deletion-request
- Vendor Onboarding Checklist -> /confluence/templates/vendor-onboarding-checklist
- Low-value Purchase Requisition (<$5k) -> /confluence/templates/requisition-lowvalue
- Expense Report Template (Spendly) -> /confluence/templates/expense-report-template

Example JSON/YAML snippets:
- Minimal change request example (YAML):
---
title: "Upgrade dependency X"
components: [service-a, service-b]
window: "2026-09-01T02:00:00-07:00 to 2026-09-01T05:00:00-07:00"
rollback: "helm rollback v1"
owner: "team-service-owner@example.com"
---

Audit and enforcement:
- Policy exceptions must be recorded using the Exception Request Template and approved by the policy owner. Exceptions are logged and reviewed quarterly.
- Non-compliance (unapproved access, unauthorized spend) escalates to the owner_team and may be subject to disciplinary action per HR policy.

Operational readiness and playbooks:
- Each area above has an associated runbook stored in OpsChange and linked from this page. Runbooks include command snippets, contact on-call rotation, and verification checks.

Change log for this page:
- 2026-02-10: Created by Maya Chen (initial gallery and templates).
- 2026-05-12: Procurement thresholds updated; added vendor risk scoring (Diego Alvarez).
- 2026-08-01: Added emergency access SLA details and retention clarifications (Samira Patel).

Contact and ownership:
- Primary owner: Finance-Legal (policy lead: Maya Chen, maya.chen@redwood.com).
- For operational questions: security@redwood.com, procurement@redwood.com, people-ops@redwood.com.

Related resources and links:
- Central Policy Index: /confluence/policies-and-process/central-policy-index-and-core-processes-2025.json
- OpsChange runbooks: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/
- IdentityHub operator docs: /confluence/eng-infra/iam/

How to request updates to this gallery:
- Submit a PR against this page via the internal docs workflow or email the policy lead. All updates must list reviewers and a summary of change.

title: GCP Marketplace onboarding + billing review (Redwood Inference)
author: Stephanie Nguyen
text:
Redwood and the GCP Marketplace team reviewed how Redwood’s new marketplace SKUs map to GCP billing dimensions (usage-based token/embedding meters vs subscription/commit dimensions), and what identifiers must be carried end-to-end (consumerId/entitlement) to ensure correct metering. GCP emphasized keeping dimension names stable, ensuring aggregation and rounding are consistent, and making the onboarding flow resilient to entitlement propagation delays. The group aligned on a staging test plan: subscribe with a test buyer account, validate entitlement lookup, provision/link a Redwood org, generate an API key, send test inference traffic, confirm metering events appear with the expected dimensions, and verify cancellation/plan change behavior. Redwood will send a proposed dimension list and sample metering payloads for review.

GCP Marketplace SKU dimensions and Cloud Commerce metering
Entitlement + account linking expectations
Onboarding UX expectations (subscription -> entitlement -> Redwood org provisioning)
Testing plan in staging before listing submission

Redwood to share final proposed GCP dimension names/IDs per SKU (Hosted/Dedicated/Private + add-ons) for partner review.
GCP to confirm any naming/length constraints and whether multiple dimensions per offer are acceptable for Redwood’s packaging.
Redwood to run the staging procurement test end-to-end (subscribe -> entitlement -> org link -> first API call -> metering verification) and report results + logs.
Schedule a follow-up 30-min review focused on cancellation, plan change, and delayed entitlement propagation edge cases.

Cole Summers: Send GCP partner team a draft mapping table (internal meter -> GCP dimension) and 2–3 example metering payloads by 2026-01-18.
Ben Carter: Provide screenshots/wireframe of the marketplace onboarding entrypoint and error states (entitlement not found, pending propagation, wrong org) by 2026-01-19.
Anika Desai: Confirm recommended aggregation interval + rounding guidance for token-based meters and any API quotas to plan around by 2026-01-20.
Miguel Alvarez: Share a reference link / checklist for Cloud Commerce metering validation and how to verify events in the partner console by 2026-01-20.
Chris Osei: Set up a follow-up session and circulate the staging test plan checklist by 2026-01-17.

Meeting header
Date: 2026-01-16
Time: 10:03 AM PT
Duration: 54 min
Title: GCP Marketplace onboarding + billing review (Redwood Inference)
Attendees:
- Redwood Inference: Stephanie Nguyen, Chris Osei, Cole Summers, Nadia Rahman, Ben Carter
- Google Cloud Marketplace: Priya Shah, Anika Desai, Miguel Alvarez

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool, thanks everyone for making time. This is Stephanie from Redwood, I run a lot of the enterprise motion, and we’ve got Cole and Nadia on billing and metering, Ben on onboarding funnel. We wanted to do a sanity pass on the GCP marketplace requirements, specifically billing dimensions and the onboarding UX expectations before we submit.

[00:18] Priya Shah: Sounds good. Thanks Stephanie. Priya here, partner dev manager. Anika and Miguel are the experts on the technical billing side. We saw your email about new SKUs, so today is basically make sure it’s compatible with Cloud Marketplace and Cloud Commerce.

[00:33] Chris Osei: Yep, and I’m Chris, program lead on our side for the marketplace refresh. I’ll keep us on agenda and capture action items.

[00:41] Anika Desai: Hi all. Anika, partner engineering. I can talk through entitlement, procurement IDs, and the typical “gotchas” we see when SaaS vendors wire up the onboarding.

[00:50] Miguel Alvarez: Miguel here. Cloud Commerce metering / billing integrations. Happy to go deep on dimensions, aggregation, rounding, and what reviewers will look for.

[01:01] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Quick context: we’re replacing legacy listings. We now have Hosted API usage-based, Dedicated capacity, and Private deployment. We want the marketplace SKUs to map cleanly to our internal billing meters. The primary issues we want to avoid are dimension mismatches and the buyer gets invoiced for something weird.

[01:20] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah. The big thing is consistency. Dimension names and IDs in the offer need to match what you’re sending in metering events. And be careful if you’re changing them later—customers don’t like it and it can break reporting.

[01:35] Cole Summers: That’s exactly what we’re trying to nail. Let me outline what we were thinking and you can tell us what’s realistic. For Hosted, we meter “tokens generated” and “input tokens” internally, but we can expose it as “tokens” total if that’s simpler. We also have embeddings measured as “embedding units” (basically per 1K tokens equivalent). For Dedicated, we have reserved GPU capacity, which internally is monthly commit + overage. Private is more of a platform fee plus support tier.

[02:05] Miguel Alvarez: Okay. So in Cloud Marketplace, you can do usage-based dimensions and you can do subscription pricing models, and you can also do committed-use style constructs depending on the product type. Most SaaS partners keep it simple: one or a small number of usage dimensions, like “1K tokens” or “1M tokens”, and then for a base subscription you do a seat or a flat monthly fee.

[02:29] Nadia Rahman: Quick question on granularity. If we do “1K tokens” as the unit, do you see partners reporting fractional quantities? Like 123.456 units? Or is it recommended to round?

[02:41] Miguel Alvarez: You can send decimal quantities, but you should document how you compute it and be consistent. The most common pattern is you aggregate per hour or per day and send integer quantities. But for token meters, lots of folks send decimals, just be explicit. Rounding differences between your UI and the invoice is where support tickets come from.

[03:02] Ben Carter: On the onboarding side, we have this subscription -> entitlement -> Redwood org provisioning. One issue we see on AWS is entitlements sometimes take a few minutes to show up. Is that also a thing on GCP?

[03:14] Anika Desai: Yep. It’s not usually super long, but there can be propagation delay. The UX expectation is you handle “pending” gracefully. Like, don’t show a scary error that says “you are not entitled.” Instead say “we’re still syncing your subscription, retry in a few minutes” and maybe a refresh button.

[03:32] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s helpful. We’ve got an entitlement verification endpoint and a sync job; we can make sure the UI does the “pending” messaging.

[03:41] Priya Shah: Also important: the marketplace reviewers will click through the onboarding. If they hit a dead end, that’s friction during review. Provide a support link and clear instructions.

[03:53] Chris Osei: Got it. Maybe we jump into identifiers. Anika, can you talk about what we should store and what we can expect to receive? We’ve seen “consumer ID” in docs but there are like multiple names for it.

[04:07] Anika Desai: Yeah. So, you’ll have a procurement account / buyer account. When a customer subscribes, there’s an entitlement created. Depending on your integration, you’ll get a consumerId and entitlement name or resource. Your system should treat that as the source of truth for “is this customer subscribed” and also for mapping metering events to the right buyer.

[04:30] Cole Summers: For metering, we need a stable key to associate usage to the marketplace customer. We also have our internal “org_id”. So our thought was: marketplace entitlement maps to Redwood org, and then that org has one or more projects / API keys. Usage is aggregated at org level and then billed.

[04:49] Miguel Alvarez: That’s typical. Just ensure you don’t mix multiple entitlements into a single org without clear logic. If a customer buys two subscriptions, you need to decide whether that’s two entitlements attached to one org or two orgs. Reviewers will look for correct allocation.

[05:06] Ben Carter: We have an edge case: existing Redwood customers may subscribe later through marketplace for procurement reasons. So they want to link the marketplace subscription to an already-existing org.

[05:17] Anika Desai: That’s also common. UX expectation: you allow linking to an existing account. But ensure authentication is done. And avoid a scenario where someone can claim an entitlement that isn’t theirs.

[05:31] Stephanie Nguyen: Right. We require sign-in, then they paste an entitlement or we detect via login? We were thinking detect via a “claim token” page in our console.

[05:42] Anika Desai: Either works. Most partners do a redirect back with parameters, or they ask the user to input the entitlement ID. Redirect flows are nicer but more work. For review, either is acceptable as long as it’s documented.

[06:00] Chris Osei: For this phase we’re doing a marketplace-specific entrypoint in our console. It will prompt for “GCP marketplace subscription” and then run entitlement verification.

[06:10] Miguel Alvarez: That’s fine. On billing: I want to zoom in on the dimension list. Can you share what you propose?

[06:18] Cole Summers: We don’t have final IDs yet, but draft is something like:
- Hosted: “hosted_tokens_1k” and “hosted_embeddings_1k”
- Rerank: “rerank_requests_1k” (maybe)
- Dedicated: “dedicated_gpu_hour” or “dedicated_capacity_unit”
- Private: “private_platform_month”
- Add-ons: “compliance_pack_month”, “extended_audit_log_retention_month”
The big question is whether “Dedicated” should be a usage dimension or a subscription SKU.

[06:55] Miguel Alvarez: Dedicated capacity tends to fit better as subscription / contract. Usage metering for “gpu hours” works, but you need to align it with what you’re actually providing. If it’s truly reserved, then a monthly subscription fee is clearer. If there’s burst/overage, you can meter overage separately.

[07:16] Nadia Rahman: We can do either. Internally we track reserved pool size and then tokens anyway, but the contract is the key. If you recommend subscription for reserved, then our metering is mostly for overage.

[07:29] Priya Shah: From a procurement standpoint, enterprise buyers usually prefer a predictable subscription line item. Then usage-based Hosted is more PLG.

[07:41] Stephanie Nguyen: That matches what we’re seeing. One thing we’re worried about: we want three clear “paths” in the listing—Hosted, Dedicated, Private. But under the hood GCP constructs are not always “three products.” It’s one listing with plans, right?

[07:57] Priya Shah: Exactly. You typically have one product listing and multiple plans. You can describe the three modes in the copy, but technically it’s one product with pricing plans.

[08:12] Ben Carter: On the onboarding, would you expect different landing pages for different plans? Like, if someone buys Private, they shouldn’t be dropped into “create API key and call the hosted endpoint” because their next step is networking and deployment.

[08:26] Anika Desai: That’s a good point. Ideally yes: after entitlement, route them to the appropriate next steps. But you can also have a general landing page that asks “what did you purchase?” or reads the plan from the entitlement.

[08:43] Cole Summers: Reading the plan from entitlement is doable if the entitlement includes plan name. We just need to be careful with plan rename.

[08:52] Miguel Alvarez: Plan rename is okay if you keep the underlying plan ID stable. Don’t key logic off display name.

[09:01] Chris Osei: Noted. We’ll key off ID.

[09:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s talk about reviewer expectations on the metering payload. Miguel, can you share what they check?

[09:14] Miguel Alvarez: Sure. They’ll check: (1) you’re using the correct API endpoints, (2) the consumerId or entitlement is valid, (3) the dimension is a valid one configured in your offer, (4) the quantity is non-negative and within reason, (5) timestamps are sane (not future by a day), (6) idempotency—you don’t double bill on retry.

[09:40] Nadia Rahman: On idempotency: we have an internal “usage_event_id” and we can keep a ledger. If we retry, we send the same event id. Is that a pattern you like to see?

[09:52] Miguel Alvarez: Yes. Exactly. Store the request ID and mark it as sent. Most of the “billing mismatch” issues are duplicate sends during outages.

[10:05] Ben Carter: Do you have any advice on how to validate end-to-end that metering is going to show up for the customer? Like, in AWS we can see it in the buyer account pretty quickly.

[10:15] Miguel Alvarez: On GCP, you can see metering records in the partner console and via reports, but it’s not always instant. For testing, you want to confirm your API calls succeed and then use the console to verify the usage events are recorded. Anika can share the checklist.

[10:33] Anika Desai: Yeah, I can send a link. There’s a “test buyer” flow too. You procure with a test account, then you validate that entitlement is created and your backend can resolve it.

[10:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Another question: dimension naming constraints. We saw some limitations around character length and allowed characters.

[10:56] Miguel Alvarez: Keep it short, alphanumeric plus underscore usually. Avoid spaces. If you have to include a version, don’t. Better to keep the same dimension and change the price model rather than changing the dimension name.

[11:13] Cole Summers: That’s helpful. We were going to do “hosted_tokens_1k” rather than “hosted_input_tokens_1k” and “hosted_output_tokens_1k” to keep it one dimension. We can still show the breakdown in our console for observability, but bill as total tokens.

[11:32] Miguel Alvarez: That’s a good compromise.

[11:35] Stephanie Nguyen: And embeddings we can keep separate.

[11:38] Miguel Alvarez: Yes.

[11:40] Chris Osei: I want to make sure we cover onboarding UX expectations. Ben, can you describe what we’re building and get GCP feedback?

[11:49] Ben Carter: Sure. So in our console, when you click “Get started”, there will be a “Purchased via marketplace?” path. If they choose GCP marketplace, we ask them to sign in. Then we try to auto-detect entitlements tied to that user, and if we can’t, we allow them to paste an entitlement ID. If entitlement is found, we show “link to existing org” or “create new org.” After that, we prompt them to create first API key for Hosted, or if the plan is Dedicated/Private, we route to request provisioning steps.

[12:24] Anika Desai: That’s pretty aligned with what we like to see. Two things: (1) make it very clear what to do if they’re not the person who purchased. Sometimes procurement buys and engineering uses. So include instructions like “ask the billing admin to invite you” or “forward this entitlement ID.” (2) include a retry experience for pending entitlements.

[12:50] Ben Carter: Yep. We have an error state “Entitlement not found” that currently suggests contacting support. We can change that to “may take a few minutes” and include refresh.

[13:02] Priya Shah: Also include support SLA information and the right support channel for marketplace customers. It doesn’t have to be complex, but the listing should say how to get help.

[13:12] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll incorporate that into listing FAQs. On testing: we need a clear test plan. Chris, we have some draft steps; can we align with GCP?

[13:22] Chris Osei: Yeah. Proposed test checklist:
1) Subscribe to plan in GCP Marketplace using test buyer
2) Verify entitlement exists (via API/console)
3) In Redwood console, run entitlement verification and link/create org
4) Generate an API key
5) Send a small set of inference requests (chat/text and embeddings)
6) Verify metering calls succeed and appear under correct dimension
7) Cancel subscription and verify access behavior (grace period?)
8) Re-subscribe / plan change and verify entitlements update
9) Negative tests: wrong entitlement, cross-org linking, delayed propagation

[14:03] Miguel Alvarez: That’s good. On cancellation: define your policy. Some partners cut off immediately, some allow a grace period. But it needs to match your listing terms and how you interpret the entitlement state.

[14:18] Cole Summers: Our default is to stop accepting billable traffic if entitlement is inactive, but we may allow a short grace if the cancellation is accidental. For marketplace we probably keep it strict.

[14:31] Anika Desai: During review, they’ll test cancel and see if your UI reflects it. If there’s a grace, document it.

[14:40] Nadia Rahman: On entitlement state changes, how quickly do we see “active -> cancelled”? That’s a potential race.

[14:49] Anika Desai: It’s usually quick, but again, you should poll or have a scheduled sync. Don’t assume immediate.

[15:00] Ben Carter: We have a sync job that runs every few minutes and on-demand verification. We can tighten it during onboarding.

[15:08] Miguel Alvarez: Just be careful with rate limits. If you have everyone spamming “verify entitlement” you might hit quotas. But for normal scale it’s okay.

[15:19] Stephanie Nguyen: One more thing: our SKUs include compliance add-ons (like extended audit log retention, compliance pack). Is it common to have add-ons as separate dimensions or separate plans?

[15:34] Priya Shah: It depends. If it’s truly an add-on, separate plan can be complicated. Some do “bundle plans” (base + add-on). Others handle add-ons off-marketplace. If you want it procured via marketplace, bundling plans is usually easiest.

[15:54] Miguel Alvarez: If you do it as a usage dimension, that’s weird for a monthly compliance pack. Better as subscription line item. But you can create a plan called “Hosted + Compliance” and so on.

[16:09] Cole Summers: That increases plan combinatorics. We were trying to keep it minimal.

[16:14] Stephanie Nguyen: For enterprise procurement, it might be okay. We can do a small number: Hosted, Hosted+Compliance, Dedicated, Dedicated+Compliance, Private. Something like that.

[16:26] Priya Shah: Exactly. Keep it manageable.

[16:29] Chris Osei: Let’s capture that as an open decision: add-ons as bundles vs separate plans.

[16:35] Ben Carter: If it’s bundled, onboarding can still read plan ID and show the right “features enabled” banner.

[16:42] Anika Desai: Yep.

[16:44] Miguel Alvarez: For dimensions, fewer is better. If you have too many, it’s harder to validate.

[16:52] Nadia Rahman: Another metering nuance: we do streaming responses. Tokens get generated over time. We aggregate at end of request. That means we may emit one usage record per request or per batch. Is that okay?

[17:07] Miguel Alvarez: That’s okay. The marketplace doesn’t care if you batch, as long as it’s accurate and you can explain your aggregation. Many partners aggregate per hour to reduce volume.

[17:19] Cole Summers: We can aggregate per hour per org per dimension. That’s probably a good default.

[17:26] Miguel Alvarez: Yes.

[17:28] Stephanie Nguyen: Any pitfalls with multi-region? Our hosted API runs in multiple regions. If a GCP marketplace buyer uses us in EU, does billing care?

[17:39] Priya Shah: Billing doesn’t care, but listing and security docs might. If you claim data residency, make sure it’s accurate. The marketplace reviewers may look at your data handling statements.

[17:52] Chris Osei: We’re preparing a security packet; we’ll align wording.

[17:57] Anika Desai: From onboarding side, if you route them to a region selection, ensure it’s clear. Some customers think marketplace implies region-specific. It doesn’t necessarily.

[18:10] Ben Carter: We plan to ask region at org creation and default to the closest region, but allow override.

[18:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[18:20] (brief crosstalk)

[18:22] Stephanie Nguyen: Miguel, can we ask about “dimension mismatch” issues you’ve seen? We had one on AWS where our internal meter name didn’t match the marketplace dimension and we billed wrong. We’re trying to prevent it.

[18:37] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah, common. It’s usually one of: using display name instead of dimension ID, or typos, or changing the offer and not updating code. The best practice: keep a single source config file for mapping, version it, and add automated tests that validate the dimension list against what’s configured in marketplace.

[18:57] Cole Summers: We have a billing catalog config in code. We can add a test that asserts “these dimensions are the only allowed ones.” But we can’t programmatically query the marketplace config easily.

[19:10] Miguel Alvarez: You can still do a manual gate before launch: export the dimension list and compare. And once stable, don’t change often.

[19:21] Nadia Rahman: We also emit telemetry events in our pipeline. We can alert on unknown dimension errors.

[19:28] Miguel Alvarez: Perfect. Set alerts on 4xx responses from metering API.

[19:35] Chris Osei: Okay. Let’s do a quick pass on what GCP needs for submission beyond billing: screenshots, support, security docs, etc. Priya?

[19:46] Priya Shah: You’ll need: final listing copy, pricing plans configured, support contact info, a privacy policy link, and security documentation depending on the category. For enterprise oriented products, we often see SOC 2 statements, encryption, retention, audit logging. You don’t need to paste the whole report, but your claims must be accurate.

[20:10] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. We’ll provide a marketplace security overview and pointers to evidence under NDA.

[20:18] Anika Desai: Reviewers like diagrams. Even a simple data flow diagram helps.

[20:23] Ben Carter: We have a diagram showing subscription -> entitlement -> Redwood control plane -> inference runtime. We’ll use it.

[20:31] Chris Osei: Back to testing. Anika, you mentioned a test buyer flow. Can you outline quickly? Just so we know if we need special accounts.

[20:40] Anika Desai: Typically you’ll have a partner test project and a test buyer project. You procure your own product as a test buyer. Then you verify that your integration receives the entitlement. If you’re using the Cloud Commerce Partner API, you can query entitlements. If you’re using webhooks, ensure those are wired. Since you’re doing a console-based claim flow, you can also validate by retrieving entitlement status from your backend.

[21:08] Cole Summers: We’re using the partner API and a sync job, plus on-demand verify endpoint. Webhook we considered but didn’t want to rely solely on it.

[21:19] Miguel Alvarez: That’s fine. Webhook can be flaky if not retried. Polling plus retry is okay, just mind quotas.

[21:30] Nadia Rahman: For quotas, do you have ballpark? Like requests per minute? We’re not huge but we want to be safe.

[21:38] Miguel Alvarez: It depends on the project and API. I’ll send the doc. But generally, if you do a sync every 5 minutes and on-demand for onboarding, you’re fine.

[21:53] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[21:55] (pause)

[21:56] Ben Carter: A small UX question: when entitlement is not found, do you recommend we show “wait 10 minutes” or “wait 2 minutes”? We don’t want to over-promise.

[22:06] Anika Desai: I’d say “a few minutes” and allow retry. And show a timestamp “last checked at” to reassure them you’re doing something.

[22:18] Ben Carter: Nice idea.

[22:20] Chris Osei: Another edge case: procurement might buy in a different Google identity than the engineer uses (like billing@company.com). That means auto-detect entitlements won’t work.

[22:31] Anika Desai: Exactly. That’s why inputting entitlement ID is helpful, or a separate “admin invites user” workflow.

[22:41] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll make sure docs call that out.

[22:45] Miguel Alvarez: On billing, one more thing: if you’re doing token usage, define what “token” means. Different models count differently. You should base it on what you count internally, but documentation should say it’s per model tokenizer.

[23:01] Cole Summers: Good point. Our API already reports token usage per request in the response metadata. We can use that as source of truth.

[23:10] Nadia Rahman: And we can expose daily usage summaries in console to match marketplace billing.

[23:15] Miguel Alvarez: That’s helpful for customer trust.

[23:19] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. Let’s talk about dimension naming and plan structure. It sounds like recommended is:
- Hosted plan with usage dimensions (tokens, embeddings)
- Dedicated plan as subscription, possibly with an overage usage dimension
- Private plan as subscription
- Compliance add-on as bundle plans (Hosted+Compliance etc)
Is that fair?

[23:44] Priya Shah: Yes.

[23:46] Miguel Alvarez: Yes, that would be a clean structure.

[23:49] Cole Summers: For Dedicated overage, would we meter tokens or something else? Because customers might still care about tokens, not GPU hours.

[23:59] Miguel Alvarez: If the overage is “extra usage beyond included”, tokens is okay. If it’s “extra capacity”, maybe hours. But tokens is more straightforward given your product.

[24:12] Cole Summers: Great. We’ll think through included vs overage.

[24:16] Chris Osei: I want to make sure we leave with concrete outputs. Cole will send a proposed mapping table and example payloads. Anika and Miguel will send docs and constraints. Ben will share screenshots/wireframes.

[24:31] Stephanie Nguyen: One question: in GCP marketplace, do customers expect to get credits / trial? We offer free credits on our website; does marketplace support that?

[24:41] Priya Shah: Marketplace trials exist in some contexts but not universally. Many partners handle trials outside marketplace or do a low-cost starter plan. If you want a trial, we can discuss, but it may complicate approval.

[24:56] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll keep it simple for now.

[24:59] Ben Carter: Another thing: we have a dedicated onboarding docs page. Is it okay to link external docs from the listing?

[25:07] Priya Shah: Yes, you can link to documentation. Just make sure it’s stable URLs.

[25:12] Chris Osei: We’re finalizing vanity redirects for marketplace. Okay.

[25:16] (minor audio glitch)

[25:18] Nadia Rahman: Can we ask about time window for metering submissions? Like can we send usage events delayed by a day?

[25:26] Miguel Alvarez: There is a window; don’t send extremely late. A few hours delay is okay. A day is sometimes okay but not ideal. Send as close to real time as possible. Again, I’ll send guidance.

[25:43] Nadia Rahman: Got it.

[25:45] Cole Summers: For retry logic, if API errors, we retry with exponential backoff. If it fails for a long time, we queue. We can cap backlog.

[25:54] Miguel Alvarez: That’s fine. But make sure you don’t exceed the allowed backfill window.

[26:02] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay.

[26:04] Priya Shah: Any other questions from Redwood before we wrap?

[26:09] Stephanie Nguyen: I have one more: procurement question. Some buyers will ask “does buying through marketplace change the support terms / SLAs?” We have dedicated support tiers. Do you see any constraints on what we can say?

[26:23] Priya Shah: You can state support terms clearly. Just avoid promising things you can’t deliver. If there’s a premium SLA, you can make it a plan or an add-on, but it should be consistent.

[26:37] Ben Carter: We’ll align with our support team.

[26:40] Chris Osei: Okay. Let’s do a quick recap and next steps.

[26:45] Chris Osei: Recap:
- Dimension strategy: keep Hosted usage-based with a small set of dimensions (tokens, embeddings), use subscription plans for Dedicated/Private, consider bundled plans for compliance add-ons.
- Use stable IDs, don’t key logic off display names.
- Handle entitlement propagation delays with friendly UI + retry.
- Implement idempotency for metering events and alert on 4xx errors.
- Run staging test: subscribe -> entitlement -> org link -> API key -> sample traffic -> verify metering -> cancellation/plan change.

[27:21] Stephanie Nguyen: And action items: Cole will send draft mapping + payload examples, Ben will send UX screens, Anika/Miguel will send docs on quotas/rounding/validation.

[27:33] Anika Desai: Yep.

[27:35] Miguel Alvarez: Yep, I’ll send the metering validation checklist and rounding recommendations.

[27:40] Priya Shah: And once you’ve done the staging test, we can do a short follow-up to review results and any issues.

[27:48] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect. Thanks everyone.

[27:51] (call continues with scheduling chatter)

[28:00] Chris Osei: I’ll send the notes and propose a follow-up next week.

[28:05] Priya Shah: Great.

[28:07] Meeting ended (recording continued briefly)

[53:58] (end of recording)

title: Model Resilience Propensity Index & Field Probe Playbook
author: Ava Nguyen
text:
Define a lightweight, operational index (Model Resilience Propensity Index, MRPI) to quantify risk of service-impacting model supply events for customers and produce a reproducible field-probe playbook that triggers procurement/rollout actions. The MRPI combines telemetry signals (latency/availability drift, quantization regressions, provenance churn), model compatibility fragility, and regional capacity volatility into a single actionable score with thresholds that map to playbook steps (investigate, canary, procurement alert, fallback activation).

1) MRPI score spec documented with contributor formulas and sample calculations for three representative customers; 2) Field probe playbook drafted with step-by-step runbook (investigate -> canary -> procurement trigger -> rollback); 3) Two synthetic probe workloads implemented and runnable in CI; 4) Prototype dashboard mock (console) visualizing MRPI by region/model; 5) Stakeholder sign-off from SRE, Sales Ops, and Solutions Engineering.

MRPI spec doc (Confluence)
Field probe runbook (playbook)
2 synthetic workload harnesses (GitHub)
Console dashboard mock (Figma)
Procurement trigger mapping sheet

Rationale: customers increasingly ask for proactive model-fallback triggers rather than reactive SLAs; MRPI should be lightweight and explainable.
Trade-off: include model-behavioral regressions (quality) vs keeping index operationally simple. Start with telemetry + supply signals, add quality signal v2.
Decision so far: normalize signals to 0-100 and weight by observed incident contribution (initial weights: telemetry 50, capacity volatility 30, compatibility 20). We will recalibrate after 4 weeks of probes.
Link: MRPI skeleton draft: https://redwood.atlassian.net/l/MRPI-draft (confluence)
Link: synthetic probe repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/mrpi-probes (stub)
Potential follow-ups: integrate MRPI into Console alerts and create per-customer tuning profiles for enterprise accounts.

2026-02-11 Ava Nguyen: Kickoff meeting with SRE and Solutions Eng. Agreed on scope: index + playbook + two probes. Assigned Diego as PM lead.
2026-02-18 Diego Morales: Drafted initial signal inventory. SRE recommended adding 'regional provisioning variance' metric. Updated dependencies to include ENG-18422 (batching telemetry infra).
2026-02-24 Priya Shah (SRE): Prototype telemetry feed available for three regions. Noted missing historical capacity churn data—Sales Ops to provide procurement timelines.
2026-03-02 Michael Tan (Sales Ops): Shared anonymized procurement lead times for 12 enterprise customers; will intake into weighting calibration.
2026-03-05 Diego Morales: Updated acceptance criteria to require stakeholder sign-offs and dashboard mock. Next: create two synthetic workloads and PR for probe harness.
