title: Orchestrating Multi-Model Pipelines for Cost-Latency Tradeoffs (PRD)
author: Aisha Kaur
text:
Summary:
This PRD defines a product initiative to add first-class orchestration for multi-model pipelines in Redwood Inference. The goal is to let customers declare multi-step pipelines (e.g., embed -> rerank -> generate) composed of different model variants and to automatically optimize routing and instance selection for cost and latency tradeoffs while preserving per-pipeline SLOs.

Background and motivation:
- Customers commonly chain multiple model calls in a single feature (e.g., cheap encoder for retrieval, higher-cost reranker or generator).
- Current Redwood surface treats calls independently; customers must implement orchestration client-side or in application backends, leading to duplicated logic and missed opportunities for cross-request batching, KV cache reuse, and cost-aware routing.
- Providing a managed pipeline orchestration layer improves unit economics (lower cost per end-to-end request), reduces latency via coordinated batching and cache reuse, and centralizes rollout and variant management for pipeline steps.

Goals (what success looks like):
1) API surface for declaring pipelines composed of named steps, model selectors, and SLO targets.
2) Runtime orchestration that optimizes placement/routing to meet user-specified end-to-end latency SLO while minimizing expected cost.
3) Automatic cross-step batching and KV/prefix cache reuse when steps involve the same serving runtime and model family.
4) Integrated metrics and traces surfaced in Redwood Console per-pipeline: end-to-end latency, per-step latency, cost breakdown, and failure rates.
5) Migration path for existing single-call customers to adopt pipelines with minimal code changes.

Non-goals:
- This initiative does not implement an end-to-end workflow engine with arbitrary conditionals and long-running orchestration (we focus on synchronous pipelines for inference requests).
- We will not initially support third-party execution (external webhooks) as a pipeline step.

User personas and primary use cases:
- Product/ML Engineer integrating a multi-step search+generate feature who wants a single SLO and visibility into bottlenecks.
- Platform team creating cost-windowed routing policies for enterprise tenants to stay within budget while meeting latency SLOs.
- Solutions engineer building a reference template for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that customers can adopt.

High-level design overview:
- Pipeline Descriptor: declarative JSON schema that describes steps (name, model selector, input mapping, resource hints), SLOs (p95 latency target, availability), and cost preference (aggressive-cost | balanced | aggressive-latency).
- Planner: Service that converts a descriptor into a per-request plan: assigns candidate model variants for each step, decides whether to colocate steps on the same instance/pool for cache reuse, and estimates cost/latency distributions.
- Execution Fabric: Extends existing serving runtime to accept multi-step request envelopes, enabling intra-request batching, KV cache rehydration, and shared IO handling.
- Adaptive Runtime Policies: Uses feedback (observed latencies, queueing) to swap in cheaper variants or add burst capacity when SLO violations are observed.

Key product requirements:
1) Pipeline Descriptor API (v1):
 - POST /pipelines (create), GET /pipelines/{id}, PUT /pipelines/{id}, DELETE /pipelines/{id}
 - Minimal example payload (JSON):

 {
 "name": "rag-search-generate",
 "steps": [
 {"id": "encode", "model_selector": "small-embed:dynamic", "timeout_ms": 50},
 {"id": "retrieve", "type": "internal_retrieval", "timeout_ms": 100},
 {"id": "rerank", "model_selector": "medium-ranker:latest", "timeout_ms": 120},
 {"id": "generate", "model_selector": "large-gen:quantized", "timeout_ms": 300}
 ],
 "slo": {"p95_ms": 600, "availability": 0.999},
 "cost_preference": "balanced"
 }

2) Planner constraints and outputs:
 - Inputs: pipeline descriptor, tenant plan (Dedicated/Hosted/Private), runtime capacity snapshot, historical step latencies, and cost models.
 - Outputs: chosen variant per step, placement hint (same-pool | separate-pool), batching window suggestion (ms), and estimated end-to-end latency and cost.

3) Runtime behaviors:
 - When steps are colocated and cache-compatible, share KV caches and avoid repeated tokenization where possible.
 - Allow cross-step continuous batching when customer SLO and step timeouts permit (configurable batch window 1-50ms).
 - Fall back to independent execution paths on incompatibilities (model family mismatch, security restrictions for private deployments).

4) Observability requirements (exposed in Console):
 - End-to-end p50/p95/p99 latency, per-step latency histogram, per-request cost breakdown (tokens + model-hours), batch size distribution, and SLO breach traces.

5) Security and privacy:
 - Respect tenant isolation: pipelines for Private deployments must be executed within tenant-only pools.
 - Audit logs for pipeline creation and plan changes.

SLOs and acceptance thresholds (product-level):
- Default target: p95 end-to-end latency within declared SLO 95% of calls in a week.
- Cost delta: for balanced preference, expected end-to-end replication must reduce or not increase total customer spend compared to naive client orchestration in 75% of customer workloads (measured in alpha).
- Availability: pipeline endpoints inherit tenant availability SLAs (Hosted: 99.9%, Dedicated: 99.95).

Compatibility matrix (important constraints):
- Hosted: full feature set for supported model families (Redwood-verified).
- Dedicated: supports co-located pooling and private capacity policies; customers can opt-out of cross-tenant batching.
- Private (VPC/on-prem): supports orchestration but requires enabling shared KV cache option in config and may not support automated burst region fallback.

Example configuration table (text-table):
- Fields: name, type, required, example
- name: string, required, "rag-search-generate"
- steps: list, required, see example above
- slo.p95_ms: integer, required, 600
- cost_preference: enum, optional, "balanced"

API and CLI examples:
- Create pipeline (curl):
 curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/pipelines -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d @pipeline.json

- Run pipeline synchronously (client call):
 POST /v1/pipelines/{id}/invoke { "input": {"query": "how to reduce token cost"} }

Rollout plan and milestones:
1) Alpha (Q1): API-only pipeline descriptors stored in control plane; planner returns static plans but execution runs as sequential calls (no runtime improvements). Target: 5 internal customers and 2 reference templates.
2) Beta (Q2): Execution fabric accepts envelope requests; add cross-step batching and KV reuse for verified model combinations. Add Console insights.
3) GA (Q3): Add adaptive runtime policies, cost/preference knobs, and enterprise controls for Dedicated/Private. Provide migration tooling.

Success metrics (measurable):
- Adoption: 20+ customers converting at least one feature to a pipeline within 3 months of GA.
- Cost improvement: median end-to-end cost reduction >= 12% on RAG pipelines measured across early adopters.
- SLO stability: fewer than 3% of pipeline calls with p95 > declared SLO in steady state.

Operational considerations and runbook snippets:
- Alerting: Create alert when pipeline SLO error budget burn > 40% in 24h or rolling p95 exceeds target by 20% for 30m.
- Runbook (SLO breach):
 1) Identify offending pipeline and step via Console traces.
 2) Check planner recent decisions; if a cheaper variant was selected recently, roll forward a canary with a higher-latency-but-higher-throughput variant.
 3) If systemic, throttle new pipeline creations and open paging incident.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Planner makes suboptimal choices leading to repeated rollbacks. Mitigation: allow operator override and safe default to "balanced" or tenant-specified pinned variants.
- Risk: Cross-step batching increases tail latency for some workloads. Mitigation: conservative default batch-window and per-pipeline tuning.

Open questions (for product and eng discussion):
- Should pipeline descriptors allow conditional branches (if-else) for v2?
- How to represent non-ML steps (retrieval or DB lookups) formally in the descriptor?
- What is the economic model for charging per-pipeline orchestration? per-step tokens only, or small orchestration surcharge?

Owner and contacts:
- Product lead: Aisha Kaur (product).
- Eng leads: Daniel Meyer (serving runtime), Priya Raman (planner & optimization).
- SRE/Oncall: Jorge Alvarez.

Appendix: example planner output (JSON, simplified):
{
 "pipeline_id": "rag-search-generate",
 "chosen_variants": {"encode": "small-embed-v2-quant", "rerank": "medium-ranker-v3", "generate": "large-gen-q8"},
 "placement_hint": "colocate-steps-0-2",
 "estimated_p95_ms": 520,
 "estimated_cost_usd": 0.0092
}

Notes on measurement approach:
- Run A/B experiments on staged traffic to compare "client orchestration" vs Redwood orchestration using identical inputs and measure cost + latency distributions.
- Use workload classes (short prompt, medium prompt, long prompt) to stratify evaluation.

Next steps:
- Kickoff design review (week of 2026-03-08).
- Implementation spike for planner cost/latency models (2 sprints).
- Internal alpha with two reference templates: RAG and retrieval + summarization.

References:
- See Console observability spec for metrics instrumentation guidance.
- See runtime-architecture docs for current KV cache capabilities.

title: Shiproom runner: personal prep log and sticky notes
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Purpose: quick, scannable personal notes for running the shiproom and weekly readiness sync. Organized as prep items, live-run cues, and follow-up actions. Not a polished playbook — my sticky running list + prompts to escalate.

DAY-BEFORE / 24-48H CHECKS (quick hits)
- Validate Dedicated pool health dashboard (console > Dedicated > Pool-5). Look for 90th pct latency spike > 20% vs baseline. If spike: page SRE and tag 'pool-5'.
- Confirm model pin assignments for weekend rollouts: model = rwx-v2-quant, pinned to image-2026-02-28. Cross-check with model-catalog ticket.
- Ensure canary capacity reserved: 3 instances w/ low-priority burst. If not reserved, open ticket to infra (email infra-runbooks).
- Verify last smoke-run results (smoke/last-run.json) — critical checks: health endpoints, prefix caching, stream stability. Mark any failing check with TODO.

MEETING AGENDA (for my 10–15 min run)
1) Quick status (30s each): Hosted API, Dedicated, Private — 3 bullet lines max.
2) Go/No-Go candidate items (3) — call out owner for decision.
3) High-risk regressions & mitigations (A/B, rollbacks, fallback).
4) Open action items from last week (owners + ETA).
5) Escalations and customer-impacting items.

GO/NO-GO CHECKLIST (my shorthand)
- Safety: latest canary passed golden prompt set? [yes/no] — if no -> NO-GO and block rollout. Owner: Priya.
- Latency: 95th <= SLO (hosted) and Dedicated 90th within committed window? [ok/warn/fail] Owner: Jordan.

LIVE-RUN CUES (during shiproom)

SMOKE-TEST QUICK-LOOK (ordered)
1) /health (all regions) — expect 200 and healthy=true.
2) golden prompt generation (3 variants) — check for coherent output and stable token length.
3) streaming socket smoke (5 simulated clients) — no connection resets.
4) KV cache hit-rate sanity check (> 30% for typical workloads).
5) auth flow: token validation for dev key and prod key.

RISKS I CARE ABOUT (notes to self)
- Quantized model edge cases: hallucinations on long-context prompts unseen in evals. Watch for uptick in hallucination rate on live eval monitors.
- Autoscale cold starts: small percentage of cold starts can push P95 over threshold. Keep warmup policy on for first 2h post-deploy.

NOTES-TO-SELF / RUN-TIME SNIPPETS

- One-sentence status template for quick updates: "Area — short-state (ok/warn/fail) — top-1 mitigation if warn/fail". Use this when I call status.

ESCALATION CONTACTS (quick)

MY PERSONAL CHECKLIST BEFORE HAND-OFF

title: Structured audit export, PII redaction evidence, and intake for privacy-scan SIEM ingest
text:
Issue summary: Customer requests a one-time export of structured audit events (API calls, tokenized user identifiers, key management events) covering the past 12 months plus a rolling 90-day stream mapping for ingestion into their privacy scanning SIEM. They require evidence that PII fields have been redacted consistently and a manifest showing checksums and chain-of-custody for delivered artifacts.

Impact: This is an enterprise compliance milestone tied to a scheduled privacy audit with BrightHealth AI's legal team. Without the export and redaction evidence they cannot complete their external privacy attestation.

Requested artifacts and format:
- Monthly full bulk export (12 months) as NDJSON compressed tarball (gz) with index manifest (sha256 checksums).
- Rolling 90-day streaming export as NDJSON slices (1-day blobs) in S3 with lifecycle policy.
- Mapping file from Redwood audit fields to Elastic Common Schema (ECS) names.
- Redaction report describing which fields were redacted and the algorithm used (deterministic tokenization vs hashing), sample of 10 anonymized records showing before/after.
- Chain-of-custody manifest (timestamped, signed by Redwood service account) and delivery audit log showing who initiated and confirmed export.

Background/Constraints: BrightHealth AI handles PHI and is subject to additional privacy scrutiny; they cannot receive raw PII. They prefer not to have SSNs or email addresses present in any form. They are open to deterministic tokenization that preserves linkage (stable pseudonyms) but need documentation and an explanation of re-identification risk.

Preferred delivery: Pre-signed S3 URLs (expiring link) for each artifact plus a single zipped evidence bundle. Provide an estimated size and ETA for each deliverable.

Acceptance criteria:
- All artifacts delivered to pre-signed S3 with checksums and manifest.
- Redaction report approved by BrightHealth AI security contact.
- SIEM mapping document validated by customer (comments addressed).

Notes: Internal runbook for large exports suggests chunking by week to avoid timeouts; export job may need quota bump for S3 put traffic.

2026-03-10 11:05 - Jordan Patel (Eng): Confirmed we can produce NDJSON tarballs and 90-day slices. Asked SRE to estimate export size and any rate limits for scheduled S3 put operations. Proposed staged export over 48-72 hours to avoid throttling.

Noted that bulk export uses the audit-exporter service (repo: github.com/redwood-inference/audit-exporter) and that we may need a temporary quota increase on S3 egress and PutObject rate. Linked INT-501 for quota request.

2026-03-11 10:20 - BrightHealth AI (customer): Responded in support portal: Deterministic pseudonyms OK if we receive the KMS key provenance and documented risk assessment. Also asked for sample records before bulk delivery (10 records) and confirmation that email and SSN are removed entirely.

title: ValeHealth on-prem implementation capture
author: Priya Nandakumar
text:
Call notes (2024-09-17) — discovery with ValeHealth (CTO: Aaron Li, SecOps: Maya Singh, Arch: Dan Ochoa)

- Context: ValeHealth is a mid-sized digital health provider planning to run conversational triage + discharge-summary generation inside their data center (air-gapped option discussed). They must not send PHI outside their network. Primary asks: private control plane with VPC peering to their corp network, KMS/HSM integration for key material, audit logs for every inference, and 12 month retention for audit records.

- Key constraints called out by customer:
 - PHI: full PHI scope, must meet SOC2 + HIPAA controls.
 - Network: strict egress rules; anything that talks to hosted control plane needs explicit allow list.
 - Hardware: they will provision 2x A100 80GB per zone initially, plan to add 4x after pilot.
 - Throughput target: 12 concurrent triage sessions, average 40 tokens/response, target p95 token latency per token <= 90ms (end-to-end p95 for a 200-token response <= 18s) — customer expects interactive feel.
 - Burst behavior: expect spikes morning 8–10AM and post-op 3–5PM.

- Functional reqs (high level):
 1) On-prem Redwood Private with local model hosting and local KV/prefix caching.
 2) VPC-only control plane connectivity (can run in their VPC or peered) — no public IPs on inference nodes.
 3) KMS or HSM integration: must support AWS CloudHSM or on-prem Thales via KMIP.
 4) Audit logs: immutable tamper-evident logs for each request (user id, route, token counts, prompt hash).
 5) Structured outputs: discharge summary templates + JSON schema enforcement + function-calling hooks.
 6) Streaming WebSocket support for triage chat UI.
 7) Canary deploys and fast rollback; cannot have model drift affecting PHI fidelity.

- Non-functional / ops notes:
 - Warmup: with A100s expect ~20–40s cold start for large Llama-family models to reach peak throughput. Need pre-warm policy for scheduled windows.
 - Batch sizing: small batch sizes to preserve latency SLO; recommend continuous batching with low-latency cutoff (15ms).
 - KV cache: prefix caching will significantly cut token generation for repetitive triage prompts; plan to instrument cache hit rate in pilot.
 - Quantization: they want FP16 or 4-bit quant for cost; warn: 4-bit may slightly degrade token-level probabilities -> risks for hallucination in medical text. We should plan eval prompts + acceptance criteria.
 - Telemetry: customer wants token-level cost/latency breakdown exported to Splunk (on-prem) every 1 minute.

- Gotchas / open technical risks:
 - Network egress policy: Control plane components that check for model updates may require egress. Customer requires whitelisting; need to enumerate IPs and acceptable update cadence. Offline update flow (airgap) must be documented.
 - HSM cert exchange: support for KMIP versions and cert rotation timeline — Ops needs runbook for emergency rotation.
 - Model licensing: some open models require attribution; legal to confirm whether ValeHealth agrees to the model license and distribution in-country.
 - Tokenization mismatch: current front-end uses older tokenizer library; we need to validate prompt/encoding parity to avoid token count surprises and cost overruns.
 - Long output trimming: discharge summaries sometimes exceed 1,000 tokens; need to support streaming + progressive flush to UI and chunked audit records.

- Example acceptance tests ValeHealth suggested (rough):
 1) PHI redaction test: send synthetic PHI and ensure logs do not contain raw PHI in plaintext except authorized fields.
 2) Latency test: 200-token generation p50 < 2s, p95 < 18s under steady load of 12 concurrent sessions.
 3) Regression test: standard eval suite of 150 prompts for hallucination / clinical accuracy; failure rate < 3% vs baseline model.

- Quick numbers back-of-envelope (for sizing discussion):
 - If we run Llama-3-classic-70B FP16 on A100-80: single GPU peak concurrency for low-latency ~6–8 simultaneous single-stream sessions (depends on context length). With 2 GPUs expect ~12–16 sessions — matches their initial 12 target.
 - If they quantize to 4-bit, can increase concurrency ~1.5x but verify regressions.

- Prompts / eval plan notes to self:
 - Set up a small eval harness with their sample chart notes (deidentified) + golden summaries from clinicians. Use rouge/med-sa metrics and human spot checks.
 - Create prompt templates that force structured JSON output with explicit "extractionConfidence" fields so UI can flag low-confidence sections for clinician review.

- Compliance & legal items to loop in:
 - Legal: confirm data residency policies and model license acceptability.
 - Security: run threat model for Private control plane; provide pen-test window.
 - Privacy: document data retention and deletion for audit logs (they asked 12 months but want ability to purge per request).

- Action items / next steps (owners + dates):
 - Priya: Draft on-prem architecture sketch & airgap flow; include IP whitelist and update cadence -> due 2024-09-23.
 - Jordan: Prep rough cost/throughput matrix comparing FP16 vs 4-bit and likely concurrency -> due 2024-09-25.
 - Evan: Prototype tokenizer parity check using ValeHealth frontend sample prompts; report tokenization deltas -> due 2024-09-26.
 - Rita: Open legal thread with licensing & PHI handling questions; sync with Legal -> create ticket VALE-124 by 2024-09-20.
 - Schedule: Book follow-up workshop for pilot scoping (architect deep-dive + security) w/ ValeHealth and infra ops -> target week of 2024-09-30.

- Meeting artifacts to attach to pilot folder (TODO):
 - Synthetic PHI test vectors (anonymized)
 - Clinician gold-summaries (deid) for eval harness
 - Network diagrams and firewall rules template for their infra team

- Notes to self (raw):
 - Keep canary window small, ensure rollback by model tag (do not rely on in-place weights swap without versioned checkpoints).
 - Need a short (1–2 slide) cheat sheet on expected latency/cold-start behavior for sales to set expectations.
 - Consider offering a Managed Updates opt-in where we push vetted model/security updates on a monthly cadence to reduce their ops burden.

- Questions to raise in next call:
 1) Can ValeHealth provide a stable internal registry (S3 or Artifactory) for model artifacts and container images?
 2) Which exact HSM vendors do they have on-prem? (Thales, AWS CloudHSM, Gemalto?)
 3) Do they expect encryption-in-use (SGX/Confidential VMs) beyond KMS-at-rest?

End of raw capture.

-- Priya (notes kept informal, will formalize into pilot scoping doc after internal sync)

title: Pinned model unexpectedly demoted during edge rate-shedding, causing intermittent canary responses
text:
Issue summary: Customer (Novum HealthTech) observed that several user sessions that were pinned to their dedicated model version gpt-large-v1 started receiving responses from the canary variant intermittently during a peak traffic window. Impact: ~8% of requests from pinned sessions returned canary outputs between 2026-03-10T14:02 and 2026-03-10T14:45 UTC, causing subtle semantic differences in model output for live users. Pinned sessions should not be demoted under normal operation.

Environment: prod-us-east (dedicated capacity pool: novum-pool-3).

Steps to reproduce:
1) Create a session with version pin header X-Model-Pin: gpt-large-v1 for a tenant on novum-pool-3.
2) Simulate sustained burst of requests from many tenants to trigger edge rate-shedding (we used a controlled load test matching observed QPS).
3) Observe routing decisions in trace and request logs (trace IDs included below) where session affinity token is present but route resolves to canary variant.

Expected behavior: Requests with an active pin should route to the pinned model variant until pin expires or is explicitly changed.
Observed behavior: During the rate-shedding window our edge layer deprioritized pinned routes and allowed canary routes to be selected to satisfy SLOs; pinned sessions saw intermittent responses from canary variant.

Relevant logs/traces (sample):
- trace: us-east:trace-20260310-14:12:35: t=trace-8af3cf (session token: s-9c2b). Route decision: edge-proxy rate-shed priority=low -> routing-layer selected fallback route canary/gpt-large-v1-canary.
- request id: req-4f7a2f9b: pin header present, backend assigned: canary node id cn-42.

Notes: Customer reported via support channel #support-novum and provided 6 sample request IDs. We reproduced locally using controlled traffic and confirmed similar route inversion under the same rate-shedding config.

1) Pin session to gpt-large-v1 via X-Model-Pin header.
2) Generate a synthetic QPS spike across multiple tenants to trigger edge rate shedding policies.
3) Observe routing decisions in trace logs for pinned sessions.
4) Verify that the backend returned canary variant responses intermittently.

Selected sample traces: trace-8af3cf (see description), trace-8af3d1, trace-8af3e2. Edge proxy logs show 'rate-shed: true' with policy id rs-edge-priority-2. Routing-layer debug shows 'pin-resolve: ok' then 'deprioritize-pin: true' decision event. Serving runtime logs show request handed to canary pool node cn-42 with model tag gpt-large-v1-canary.

2026-03-10 14:20 UTC - Initial reproducible case validated by SRE: controlled load caused edge rate-shed to activate and routing decisions to deprioritize pinned flows.
Hypothesis A: Edge rate-shedding policy incorrectly treats pinned routes as low-priority under global contention due to missing pin-priority override in policy evaluation.
Hypothesis B: A short-circuit in routing-layer evaluation reorders candidate list after pin check when edge-proxy attaches a 'shed' tag, leading to selection of canary nodes with higher free capacity.
Checked config: edge rate-shedding rules (rs-edge-priority-*) did not include explicit 'pin:true' clause prior to 2026-03-10; default behavior was to evaluate available capacity only.
SRE ran a test toggling pin-priority flag in staging which preserved pinned routing under simulated edge load; suggests config deficiency rather than runtime bug.
Related PR 6b9f4d3 updated routing-layer to accept 'shed' tags and reorder candidate list for best-effort SLO compliance; change did not include safeguard for pinned sessions.
Cross-referenced SUP-31147 for earlier pinning anomalies during rollouts; different trigger but similar symptom of pin overshadowing.
We collected additional telemetry: ~92% of pinned requests stayed pinned, ~8% diverted during peak short window; average diversion duration per session was 1-3 minutes.
Engineering determined root cause: policy config omission — rate-shedding prioritized global SLOs without honoring explicit pin flags.

Customer (Novum) initial: 'We started seeing odd responses in prod around 14:05 UTC. Several ongoing user flows returned an older canary output. This is breaking a small fraction of user workflows.'
Support (Maya): 'Thanks — we're investigating. Can you share request IDs and whether pin header was present?' (attached 6 IDs).
SRE (Ethan): 'Reproduced with controlled load. Edge policy rs-edge-priority-2 active. Pin header checked but deprioritized by shed tag. Engaging routing team.'
Routing eng (Sofia Nguyen): 'Found that recent reorder logic added to favor low-latency nodes when 'shed' tag is present. That logic didn't exempt pinned sessions; proposing a config hotfix to treat pinned:true as highest priority.'
Customer acceptance: 'Workaround acceptable if we get a mitigation and root cause. Please advise ETA.'
Support update (Maya): 'We have a hotfix planned to land within the hour to add a pin-exempt clause to the edge evaluation. We'll follow up once change is deployed and confirm telemetry.'
SRE follow-up: 'Hotfix deployed 2026-03-10T15:05 UTC. Post-deploy checks show diversion rate dropped to 0.2% in subsequent 60 minutes; customer confirmed no further user complaints.'

Root cause: Edge rate-shedding policy omitted an explicit 'pin' exemption; combined with routing-layer reordering for shed-tagged nodes, pinned sessions could be demoted. Mitigation: 1) Hotfix (config change) applied to edge policy to set 'pin:exempt' in evaluation clause (deployed 2026-03-10T15:05 UTC). 2) Routing-layer patch (PR#1587) added defensive check to prevent candidate reordering for sessions with active pin tokens. Post-deploy verification: diversion <0.5% and customer confirmed. Follow-ups: schedule a test matrix to cover rate-shedding + pin combinations, add automated regression test to CI for pin-exempt behavior, and update runbook.

Hotfix deployed to prod-us-east at 2026-03-10T15:05 UTC (edge config rs-edge-priority-2 updated).
Routing-layer change merged PR#1587 and rolled out in canary + prod on 2026-03-11.
Customer notification sent 2026-03-12 with incident summary and follow-up plan.

Add CI test that simulates edge rate-shedding while sessions have active pins (owner: routing-team).
Update Runbook: include step to verify pin-exempt flag when modifying rate-shedding rules (owner: SRE).
Audit other rate-shedding policies across regions to ensure pin exemptions exist (owner: platform-ops).
Schedule post-incident review and include findings in the fortnightly reliability forum (owner: Eng Manager).

title: Deprecate legacy capability schema; add runtime hint headers, function-call credits, and streaming degradation policy
author: Maya K. Suresh
text:
Motivation: We have multiple downstream needs that couldn't be satisfied by the legacy model capability schema: (1) lightweight, per-request runtime hints that the routing layer and serving runtime can use without deserializing the full model profile; (2) a transparent metering knob for tool/function calling (customers asked for per-invocation crediting separate from token billing); and (3) richer guidance for streaming fallbacks so clients can degrade more gracefully when a model variant switches to a lower-throughput tier. This PR introduces three related surfaces: capability_headers, function_call_credit, and streaming_degradation_policy, alongside an OpenAI-compatible shim that surfaces structured-output hints in /v1/models list responses.

Summary of changes (high level):
- API: Add optional capability_headers map to /v1/models and /v1/models/:id responses. These are short key/value runtime hints intended for fast routing decisions (examples: "supports_prefix_cache": "true", "max_prefetch_tokens": "256").
- Catalog schema: Deprecate legacy capability_schema.v1 (kept as legacy_capabilities for migration) and introduce capability_schema.v2 that references compact headers + full capability document. Migration docs added.
- Billing: Introduce function_call_credit as a first-class optional numeric field on model profiles and endpoints. This allows the billing system to attribute cost for tool/function call ops independently; SDKs and console will display credits usage.
- Streaming: Add streaming_degradation_policy on model profiles to expose a list of ordered fallbacks and suggested partial-output tokens thresholds (helps clients decide when to switch to a summarized streaming path). Also include preferred_prefetch_hint to suggest prefix caching window.
- OpenAI compat: Update the /v1/models listing returned by the OpenAI-compat shim to include capability_headers and structured_output_hints under the "capabilities" umbrella so downstream OpenAI-compatible clients can discover behavior without touching Redwood-specific endpoints.
- Docs & SDK: Docs page describing migration, examples for reading capability_headers and consuming streaming_degradation_policy; Python and TypeScript SDK surfaces to parse new fields.

Commits (summary):
- commit 1: api: extend model list + get handlers to populate capability_headers and streaming_degradation_policy (handlers and serializers)
- commit 2: catalog: add models_v2 schema, migration script to copy legacy_capabilities into full_profile and generate default headers
- commit 3: billing: record function_call_credit into usage events and expose in billing UI (console changes)
- commit 4: sdk/docs: parse helpers and docs for migration and examples

Files changed (representative):
- src/api/handlers/models_list.go (updated serializer and OpenAI-compat shim)
- src/catalog/schemas/models_v2.json (new compact schema)
- tools/migrations/migrate_capabilities_v1_to_v2.go (migration script)
- services/billing/credits.go (add function_call_credit aggregation)
- console/src/components/model/ModelDetails.tsx (show capability headers and credits)
- sdk/python/redwood/models.py (new fields + helper parser)
- docs/migrations/capability_headers_migration.md (migration and rollback guide)

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests: added for serializer and parser behavior (capability_headers omitted vs present), billing aggregation tests for function_call_credit.
- Integration: end-to-end test in perf-canary that validates streaming_degradation_policy is honored by the router under simulated capacity pressure; canary shows no increase in 95p latency on main model variants.
- Backwards compatibility: /v1/models still returns legacy_capabilities field for consumers that haven't migrated; the OpenAI-compat shim prefers capability_headers but will fall back to legacy_capabilities when capability_headers is absent.

Migration strategy & rollout:
- Stage 1 (canary): populate capability_headers from existing full capabilities via migration script; run canary for 2 days to ensure no regression in routing or billing.
- Stage 2 (gradual): expose new headers to 20% of API responses; monitor routing decisions and SDK parsing errors.
- Stage 3 (opt-in enforcement): allow customers to opt-in to strict schema validation via a console toggle (default off).
- Final: Deprecate legacy schema via announcement; grace period until 2026-06-01, after which legacy_capabilities may be removed for new write operations.

Review conversation (condensed):
- Owen Park: "Large change — please ensure migration script is idempotent and add a safety flag so we can revert on dataset problems." — Author: "Migration is idempotent; added --dry-run and --cutover flags in migrate_capabilities_v1_to_v2.go; documented in migration md."
- Lina Gomez: "Need to ensure function_call_credit can't be negative and that default is 0 where absent; also clarify how it interacts with token billing." — Author: "Validation added; billing pipeline will emit both tokens and function_call_credit events. Release notes updated to clarify pricing semantics."
- Harriet Zhao: "Does the streaming_degradation_policy open us up to oscillation if multiple routers act on hints?" — Author: "Router change includes a small randomized jitter and a dead-time to prevent oscillation; added comment in routing code and unit test."
- QA (Slack): reported one flaky test in console snapshot related to ModelDetails layout — fixed by stabilizing test data ordering in the SDK.

CI summary: initial run had lint warnings (long line in models_list.go) and one flaky integration test; both addressed in follow-up commits. Final status: all checks passed (unit, lint, integration, e2e canary). Performance canary showed stable tail latency; billing integration tests validated function_call_credit emitted for simulated tool calls.

Rollout notes for operators:
- The migration tool writes a migration_log to S3; if any migration errors occur, the --rollback flag will reverse schema updates made to the catalog DB.
- Feature gate: runtime.capability_headers (default: enabled for all API nodes in next release). If issues appear, ops can disable gate per region to return legacy behavior immediately.

Decision rationale and follow-ups:
- We intentionally kept capability_headers compact and stringly-typed to avoid heavyweight schema churn; full capabilities remain available for deep inspection and compatibility with existing tooling.
- Follow-ups: ENG-2639 to add UI visualization for streaming_degradation_policy, ENG-2670 to instrument per-function-call credit telemetry in the billing dashboard, and ENG-2692 to add a half-life cache invalidation for capability_headers to support fast rollbacks.

Merge outcome: Squash merge by Lina Gomez on 2026-02-19 after approvals from all reviewers and green CI. Release note entry drafted and scheduled for the 2026-02 minor release.

Add new capability header fields (capability_headers) and introduce function_call_credit metric for per-call accounting; deprecate legacy capability schema v1 with migration path; add streaming degradation policy and prefetch hint support. Non-breaking for read-only clients; write-migration recommended before 2026-06-01.

text:
maria: Heads-up @eng-runtime — AcmeCorp escalated after the 10:00 canary. They say function calls are either missing or getting arguments interleaved. They gave an example where a single tool call used to come back as {user_id, session_id}, now it's showing {session_id, user_id} or sometimes the tool call is omitted entirely.

kevin: Can you paste the request_id and a minimal repro? :eyes:

maria: request_id=rc-20240227-88a3. Customer sent the original prompt and model reply.
Acme: "prompt": "FetchUser(user_id=\"u-123\", session_id=\"s-456\")"
Acme: model reply (expected tool call): "CALL FetchUser {user_id:\"u-123\", session_id:\"s-456\" }"
Acme: model reply (observed): "CALL FetchUser {session_id:\"s-456\", user_id:\"u-123\" }"
Acme: or sometimes just plain text: "I couldn't find that user" without any CALL.

maria: Customer says it started right after our canary at 10:00 UTC (deploy id deploy-20240227-7).

olga: Noted. We pushed the request-mapper + batching kernel changes at 1709118000 (10:00). Could be related to batching/stream ordering or a mapper transformation. Any logs from their failing runs?

maria: I captured a curl repro for them: 
```
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat/respond \
 -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-ACME' \
 -d '{"model":"redwood-v1-chat","input":"FetchUser(user_id=\"u-123\", session_id=\"s-456\")","tools":[{"name":"FetchUser","params":["user_id","session_id"]}]}'
```
Expected: single tool invocation with params in order. Observed: sometimes params reversed, sometimes no tool call.

kevin: What variant/weight was the canary on? Also any downstream proxies?

maria: Canary: redwood-v1-chat@v1-quant-p3, rollout=10% traffic for canary group. Customer traffic was routed to canary bucket. No proxy on their side — direct API.

olga: Quick check: batching changes touched the streaming chunk boundaries and KV partitioning. If multiple concurrent requests share a batching slot, we may have a race that merges param buffers. Hypothesis: interleaving happening in continuous-batching path for short sequences.

kevin: Can you pull the server logs for rc-20240227-88a3 and grep for FetchUser? I want to see raw toolcall emission before the mapper. Also confirm if this is reproducible locally with same variant.

maria: Logs attached to ZD-98765. Quick repro on our side: 3/10 runs had swapped param order, 2/10 omitted tool call entirely.

dave: I can roll back the request-mapper change on the canary group immediately if we want to stop new incidents. Rollback ETA ~8-10m.

olga: While rollback is in flight, I'll push a guard that serializes param writes in the batching path to prevent buffer interleave. If that mitigates, we can then do a full patch.

kevin: Patch + rollback plan sounds good. Please post the small config change so I can apply to the hotfix branch.

olga: Patch is tiny, add this guard in serving/runtime/batcher.cc: 
```
std::scoped_lock lock(params_write_mutex);
// preserve param append order per-request
```
I'll open a PR now and kick the canary test.

maria: Customer on phone now — they're seeing a reduction but still 1/20 misses. They're ok holding while we monitor.

dave: Rollback completed on canary group at 1709123800. Traffic back to stable variant. Monitoring for 15m.

kevin: Olga's guard merged to hotfix -> deployed to canary edge at 1709123860. Running 1000 quick synthetic calls, will report back.

olga: Synthetic runs show no interleaving after guard. Looks good on p3 quant nodes.

maria: Acme confirms they no longer see missed tool calls after rollback+hotfix. They asked for postmortem and mitigation notes.

kevin: I'll draft a short postmortem and add regression tests for param ordering + end-to-end toolcall checks in CI.

maria: Thanks team — closing this loop with the customer and attaching ZD-98765 updates. :white_check_mark:

title: Accept-queue buildup from ephemeral prewarm handshake triggering sustained 5xx wave
text:
Issue summary:

Starting 2026-03-12 23:12 UTC, Acme Retail (dedicated tenant) reported a sustained elevation in 5xx responses for streaming/chat routes. Error pattern shows a stair-stepped increase in API gateway 502/503 responses lasting several hours with intermittent short recoveries. Customer impact: their storefront assistant fell back to degraded behavior (timeouts and truncated responses) across peak shopping hours.

Impact:
- Elevated 5xx rate (~12% of requests to streaming chat routes at peak).
- Increased tail latency for successful responses (+400ms p95).
- Customer-visible partial message truncation and reconnect loops.

Environment:
- prod:us-east (Dedicated capacity pool assigned to Acme Retail)
- Models: redwood-open-7B for chat, acme-embedder-v2 for on-the-fly embeddings

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) High concurrency burst from Acme's client at ~23:10 UTC with many long-lived streaming connections + a simultaneous bulk embedding upload job.
2) Ephemeral runtime prewarm subsystem begins spawning warmup workers and performing TLS handshakes to the proxy/acceptor.
3) API gateway accept queue depth rises, new connections see delayed accept or early RST.
4) Proxy returns 502/503 where gateway reports upstream unavailable.

Observed logs & traces (examples):
- api-gateway logs: repeated accept() latency spikes, backlog exceeded, upstream reset when handing to ephemeral-proxy.
- ephemeral-proxy logs: repeated TLS renegotiation failures "handshake timeout" for short-lived prewarm connections; many half-open sockets.
- serving-runtime logs: series of evictions/oom warnings shortly after prewarm wave; KV cache writes spiked and NVMe write latency increased (iowait).
- kernel metrics: netstat shows SYN_RECV/SYN_SENT queue growth and increased orphan sockets.
- kernel backlog: somaxconn / net.core.somaxconn counts reached limit on several nodes.

Initial hypotheses tested:
- Hypothesis A: API gateway threadpool starvation from large-sidecar healthchecks. (ruled out after thread pool metrics remained within normal ranges)
- Hypothesis B: Autoscaler activity removed warmed workers mid-prewarm causing handshake storms and connection churn. (partial evidence: scale-in events correlate with start of 5xx staircase)
- Hypothesis C: Local NVMe IO saturation due to ephemeral runtime KV-cache snapshotting created backpressure, causing worker OOMs and upstream restarts. (strong evidence: correlated nvme latency spikes and increase in runtime evictions)

Investigation notes:
- Correlated timeline across systems indicates the initial trigger is a coordinated arrival of long-lived streaming connections + a bulk embedding job from the tenant. The prewarm subsystem responds by launching warmers that perform multiple short TLS handshakes to the proxy layer. When autoscaler concurrently scales in to save costs (based on memory-util thresholds), there is a window where warmers are being torn down while new warmers spin up — increasing handshake churn and SYN backpressure at the acceptor.
- NVMe write amplification was observed at the time of the spike: frequent small writes from the runtime's KV-cache checkpointing increased iowait which in turn delayed worker threads, increasing connection hold time and accept queue growth.
- Kernel backlog tuning (somaxconn) on affected nodes was at default; raising backlog would temporarily reduce accept failures but not address root cause.

Temporary mitigations applied (timeline):
- 2026-03-12 23:40 UTC: Routed Acme tenant traffic to a reserved warm pool (fallback pool) to reduce prewarm pressure; immediate 5xx reduction to ~1.5%.
- 2026-03-12 23:55 UTC: Reduced prewarm concurrency for Acme's tenant from 8 -> 2 per node and disabled aggressive KV-cache snapshotting for the affected runtime group.
- 2026-03-13 01:10 UTC: Increased somaxconn on edge acceptor nodes as short-term relief.

Permanent remediation plan (work items):
1) Autoscaler policy change (ENG-998): modify scale-in thresholds to avoid concurrent scale-in during active prewarm phases for dedicated tenants (canary patch in staging).
2) Prewarm handshake backoff (RUNTIME-1421): implement exponential backoff and connection reuse for prewarm workers to reduce SYN bursts.
3) KV-cache snapshot batching (RUNTIME-1422): reduce small-file NVMe write amplification by batching checkpoints and using async fsync.
4) Kernel/infra tuning (OPS-776): formally increase accept backlog and tune net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog on acceptor tiers for dedicated pools.
5) Observability: add an alert rule that correlates prewarm spawn rate, NVMe iowait and accept queue depth to catch emergent patterns early (MON-312).

Resolution notes / current status:
- Customer traffic was stabilized by routing to reserved warm pool and adjusting prewarm concurrency. No data loss observed.
- Engineering owners assigned for remediation items 1-4. Estimated ETA for full rollout of fixes: 2 weeks after code review and staging validation.

Follow-up actions for CS/Support:
- Schedule a joint postmortem session with Acme on 2026-03-18 to review mitigations and planned changes.
- Offer temporary traffic smoothing guidance and safe concurrency knobs to the customer until permanent fixes land.

References & cross-links:
- Live dashboards: /dashboards/tenant/Acme-Retail/accept-queue-backpressure
- Kernel backlog notes: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPS/accept-queue-backpressure-runbook
- Related internal ticket: INT-3301 (autoscaler scale-in timeline investigation)


2026-03-13 00:05 - Maya Chen: Initial customer report received; triaged as P1 due to impact during peak. Captured timeseries and escalated to on-call infra.
2026-03-13 00:22 - Diego Alvarez: Reproduced accept queue growth on staging with synthetic prewarm pattern. Observed NVMe iowait correlation. Creating mitigation plan to route tenant to warm pool.
2026-03-13 00:45 - SRE Team (via #support): Warm pool routing completed. Monitoring shows 5xx rate dropped from 12% -> 1.8% within 3 minutes. Suggest keeping warm pool active until autoscaler policy patch.
2026-03-13 02:00 - Priya Nair (Runtime Eng): Assigned RUNTIME-1421 and RUNTIME-1422 for backoff and KV snapshot batching. Will open PRs for review this week.
2026-03-13 10:18 - Diego Alvarez: Kernel backlog tuning applied on acceptor nodes; documented changes in OPS-776. Need to validate across more tenants before global roll.
2026-03-14 09:02 - Maya Chen: Customer notified of interim fixes and invited to postmortem. Customer accepted concurrency knobs and will test reduced concurrency during next campaign.

title: Temporary offsite prototyping lab access and cross-border secure device return for contractor
text:
Issue summary: A new contract engineering team will operate a one-week prototyping lab at our London satellite site (eu-west). They require temporary building badge access, one hotdesk with dual-monitor rig, a secure locker for prototype hardware, and instructions for returning two sensitive development devices to the US R&D office after the engagement. Impact: Without temporary access and clarified return logistics, the contractor cannot start scheduled work and sensitive devices are at risk of mishandling during cross-border shipping.

Context and constraints: Contractor is non-employee, needs visitor badge valid 2026-03-15 to 2026-03-21. Devices include 2 hardware dev boards with encryption modules; export control and customs paperwork required. Customer-facing work is not involved; this is an internal R&D engagement under NDA.

1) Contractor arrives onsite on Day 1 and cannot access lab doors with visitor badge due to missing group membership in access list.
2) Facilities attempts to issue temporary badge but shipping paperwork for device return not yet approved by Security/Legal.
3) Contractor leaves at end of engagement without properly logged chain-of-custody for two devices, increasing risk during cross-border courier handoff.

2026-03-10 11:03 - Marcus Lee (Facilities): Noted availability of hotdesk and locker. Need Security signoff for device handling and approved carrier list for export. Assigned to Security for paperwork.
2026-03-10 14:20 - Priya Desai (Security): Can approve chain-of-custody and tamper-evident packaging process. Need device serials and classification (ECCN). Requested Legal review for export documentation.
2026-03-11 08:45 - Legal (via comment): Confirmed devices fall under controlled category; provided template commercial invoice and required end-user declaration. Asked for value and part numbers.
2026-03-11 15:30 - Marcus Lee: Arranged temporary badge creation for 2026-03-15 through 2026-03-21; instructed reception to escalate if badge denied. Coordinated locker key and combination with on-site security.

Workaround implemented: temporary visitor badges provisioned with explicit escort requirements; secure locker and hotdesk allocated. Security and Legal provided export paperwork templates; contractor submitted serials and part numbers and signed chain-of-custody forms. Courier (DHL corporate) booked for 2026-03-22 pickup with required customs documents attached. title: Gateway bifurcation for graceful multi-region takeover with per-connection KV checkpointing
author: Maya Chen
text:
Problem: During regional disruptions we currently perform blunt traffic drains or full cutovers that can truncate long-lived streaming sessions and lose in-flight KV state. This causes visible client disconnects, token replays, and SLO violations for tail latency and availability.

Goal: Implement a gateway bifurcation pattern that enables graceful takeover between two active regions that share a coordinated per-connection KV checkpointing mechanism, short token-grace window, and circuit-decay policy. The mechanism should: preserve active streaming attachments where possible, reduce user-visible interruptions, maintain SLOs for p95/p99 latency, and allow progressive traffic rebalancing with automated load-shedding triggers and circuit breakers for overloaded endpoints.

New gateway bifurcation control plane can execute staged traffic split 100% -> 80/20 -> 50/50 -> 0% with per-connection checkpointing applied during each stage
Active streaming sessions can resume on target region with KV checkpoint replay within token-grace window for >= 95% of test sessions in canary
Circuit-decay policy triggers and drops low-priority background requests while preserving high-priority tokens; measured p99 latency remains within SLO (<= 800ms) during 70% simulated surge
Automated rollback when telemetry shows error-rate delta > 2% or SLA budget burn > 30% in 10m window
End-to-end observability: dashboards for per-connection handoff success rate, checkpoint latency, token-grace expirations, and circuit-breaker activations are available in Console
Runbook updated with step-by-step operator commands and emergency cutover procedure

Bifurcation model: introduce a light-weight control plane API that instructs edge gateways to enter a 'bifurcate' mode where connections are tracked and checkpoints emitted at defined safe boundaries (e.g., sentence boundaries or invocation end for non-streams)
KV checkpointing uses existing prefix cache format but augments with 'handoff-metadata' containing sequence id and minimal opaque resume token
Token-grace window: short TTL (default 45s) during which requests with valid resume token are allowed on destination region before full auth revalidation, configurable per-customer
Circuit-decay: instead of hard reject on threshold breach, reduce priority of non-interactive routes progressively using weighted drop and backoff so that interactive sessions retain headroom
We will avoid synchronous cross-region KV replication; instead use per-connection snapshot + opportunistic async pre-warm on destination to keep overhead low

Edge changes: gateway will emit checkpoint artifacts to S3-backed artifact store (or internal blob cache) keyed by connection-id and region, with signed short-lived pointer visible to target region
Control plane: bifurcate controller service with APIs: /start-bifurcate, /advance-stage, /rollback, /finalize. Controller computes staged percentages and pushes policies to gateways via gRPC config streams
Resume flow: destination gateway receives resume token, fetches checkpoint, rehydrates KV cache and replay last few tokens to restore deterministic decoder state; if checkpoint unavailable or stale, fallback to canonical stateless retry path
Load-shedding triggers: telemetry-driven rules based on queue depth, GPU headroom, and p99 latency; rules feed into controller which adjusts split and activates circuit-decay rules
Safety nets: global circuit-breaker per-customer that can instant-fail new sessions to protect cluster and prevent cascading failures
Backwards compatibility: non-streaming and stateless flows unaffected; default behavior for customers not opted-in remains original cutover path

Phase 0 - Internal Canary: deploy bifurcate controller and edge code to test cluster; run synthetic suite with deterministic streams (2/10 - 2/24)
Phase 1 - Limited Canary: enable feature for internal services only, monitor handoff success and token-grace expirations, iterate on checkpoint size and pre-warm thresholds (3/1 - 3/8)
Phase 2 - Customer Canary: opt-in 3 low-risk customers with long-lived streams; run staged splits with progressive % increases (3/9 - 3/16)
Phase 3 - Ramp: enable auto-split for broad traffic with conservative defaults and telemetry thresholds; maintain human-in-loop for first 48 hours (3/17 - 3/24)
Rollback: emergency commands in runbook to abort and redirect all bifurcate traffic back to original region and invalidate resume tokens

Per-connection metrics: checkpoint_size_bytes, checkpoint_emit_latency_ms, resume_fetch_latency_ms, resume_success_bool
Handoff metrics: handoff_attempts_total, handoff_success_rate, handoff_fallback_rate
SLOs: p95/p99 latency pre/post-handshake, availability per-region, error-rate by route
Circuit metrics: circuit_open_count, average_decay_rate, dropped_requests_by_priority
Alerting: conservative alerts for handoff_success_rate < 90% in 5m and p99 latency regression > 20% vs baseline

Automated unit tests for checkpoint serialization/deserialization and token signing
Integration tests with simulated cross-region resume using local artifact store
Chaos tests: introduce network partitions and verify controller rolling advance/rollback semantics
Load tests: synthetic streams plus background embedding/ingest traffic to evaluate circuit-decay efficacy
Canary dashboards and SLIs tracked during each stage; automatic gates for phase transition

Resume token leakage: mitigated by short TTLs and signature verification; requires security review
Large checkpoints may add storage/IO pressure during mass handoffs; mitigation: cap checkpoint size and prefer incremental diffs
Checkpoint replay may diverge for non-deterministic model serving paths (e.g., sampling); mitigation: restrict replay to deterministic sampling or force deterministic mode during handoff windows
Increased control plane complexity and blast radius if controller miscomputes split — mitigations: rate limits, circuit-breakers, and manual abort
SLO trade-off: during surge the system may favor availability of interactive sessions by dropping background work; this needs clear product communication

2026-02-12 - Maya Chen: Spike complete. Validated checkpoint schema and small prototype emitting artifacts to internal blobstore. Observed average checkpoint size 4.2KB for 99% of streams.
2026-02-18 - Diego Alvarez: Decided on token-grace default 45s after review with Security; submitted initial API contract for controller. PR drafted: runtime#10234
2026-02-25 - Priya Nair (SRE): Load-shedding rules proposed; will instrument queue-depth and GPU headroom as primary signals. Asked for additional dashboards for pre/post split comparisons.
2026-03-02 - Lina Ortega (Design): Console mockups for staged split controls and handoff metrics reviewed and approved. Minor UX changes requested for emergency abort workflow.
2026-03-09 - Diego Alvarez: Began internal canary. Observed handoff_success_rate 94% with median resume_fetch_latency 120ms. Two failure modes: expired token in 6% of attempts and checkpoint chunk missing in 2% due to transient upload failures. Mitigations planned for retry/backoff and pre-warm replication.
2026-03-12 - Omar Haddad (Security): Completed security review for token signing and artifact ACLs. Recommended rotating signing keys every 24h for canary stage.
