title: Marketplace onboarding walkthrough (internal dry run) — subscription → org provisioning → first key
author: Ben Carter
text:
Internal walkthrough of the end-to-end marketplace onboarding flow to validate the UX and docs before submission. Team identified confusion around org linking for existing Redwood orgs, unclear messaging during entitlement propagation delays (AWS especially), and missing docs for the "already subscribed" and "multiple subscriptions" edge cases. Engineering confirmed expected entitlement API error codes and noted where console should map them to actionable retry guidance. Docs team flagged needed screenshots and a clearer separation of AWS vs GCP steps, plus a single canonical "How marketplace billing maps to usage" section to reduce support tickets.

AWS/GCP marketplace subscription confirmation and entitlement propagation
Console entrypoint for marketplace customers (org linking vs create new org)
Entitlement verification API behaviors and error states
First API key creation and first successful request path
Docs gaps: step-by-step, troubleshooting, and where security links live
Metering dimension/SKU mapping visibility and billing expectations
Telemetry: funnel events and what we can measure reliably

Do we want to allow linking a marketplace subscription to an existing org without requiring org owner role, or keep strict owner/admin requirement?
Should the console show the purchased SKU name (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) or only show entitlements/limits (tokens/min, capacity) to avoid mismatch with marketplace labels?
What’s the maximum entitlement propagation delay we should message as ‘normal’ before we recommend opening a support ticket?
Do we need a dedicated troubleshooting page per marketplace (AWS vs GCP), or one shared page with provider-specific callouts?

Chloe Martin — Update console error copy for entitlement propagation delays: include expected wait time, refresh button, and ‘check again later’ guidance (due 2026-02-12)
Alex Martinez — Add a marketplace onboarding doc section: ‘Link subscription to existing org’ + required roles/permissions (due 2026-02-11)
Elliot Price — Add docs troubleshooting for common entitlement error codes (E_ENTITLEMENT_NOT_FOUND, E_SUBSCRIPTION_NOT_ACTIVE, E_ORG_ALREADY_LINKED) with user-facing next steps (due 2026-02-13)
Cole Summers — Confirm final marketplace billing dimensions displayed in internal billing catalog match AWS/GCP submission fields; share mapping table link for Docs (due 2026-02-10)
Nadia Rahman — Verify telemetry events fire for retry/refresh clicks and for successful org link completion; propose dashboard for time-to-entitlement (due 2026-02-14)
Markus Klein — Provide ‘first call’ curl/SDK snippet specifically for marketplace users (includes where to find org slug + API key) to add to docs and example app (due 2026-02-12)

Run the same dry-run in staging with a fresh AWS subscription and measure entitlement sync latency end-to-end
Update docs pages and console copy, then re-run internal dry-run focusing on edge cases (existing org + multi-subscription)
Finalize screenshots/diagram list for marketplace listing assets once the console entrypoint UI is stable
Send updated onboarding narrative to Partnerships for inclusion in AWS/GCP submission materials

Meeting header
Date: 2026-02-07
Start time: 9:03 AM PT
Duration: 46 min
Title: Marketplace onboarding walkthrough (internal dry run) — subscription → org provisioning → first key
Attendees: Ben Carter, Chris Osei, Markus Klein, Chloe Martin, Ethan Park, Cole Summers, Nadia Rahman, Alex Martinez, Elliot Price, Kira Thompson

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Walked through AWS and GCP marketplace subscription flows and the Redwood console onboarding entrypoint.
- Identified gaps in error messaging for entitlement delays and missing docs for org linking edge cases.
- Confirmed expected entitlement verification API responses and discussed telemetry events.

[00:00] Ben Carter: Cool. Okay, we’re recording. This is our internal dry run for marketplace onboarding. Goal is: pretend we’re a buyer coming from AWS or GCP Marketplace, and we go subscription, entitlement, org provision, first key, first request. And we call out every “wait, what?” moment.

[00:19] Chris Osei: Yep, and we’ll capture action items. I’m taking notes. Let’s keep it kind of brutal.

[00:26] Chloe Martin: I can share my screen. I’m in staging console right now.

[00:31] Ben Carter: Great. Chloe, can you start with the “I just subscribed” path?

[00:37] Chloe Martin: Yep. So imagine the marketplace listing sends you to this URL, /onboarding/marketplace. We’ve got the provider selector at the top, AWS or GCP. Right now it defaults to AWS.

[00:49] Elliot Price: Quick flag, we don’t yet have the final vanity URLs. But yeah, conceptually.

[00:54] Chloe Martin: Right. So first step is “Connect your marketplace subscription.” There’s an input for “Account ID” and “Subscription ID.” In AWS it’s the customer identifier, and in GCP it’s the entitlement name.

[01:08] Markus Klein: As a customer, do I know what those are? That’s already, like, a thing.

[01:12] Alex Martinez: That’s my first docs gap. We need screenshots of where to find those in each marketplace portal.

[01:17] Ben Carter: Yeah, plus we need to handle “I don’t have it” and link to “contact procurement admin.”

[01:24] Chloe Martin: Exactly. If I paste in a dummy one, we call the entitlement verification endpoint. Ethan, do you want to confirm what we return when it’s not found?

[01:32] Ethan Park: Sure. In staging right now, the endpoint is returning E_ENTITLEMENT_NOT_FOUND if we can’t match. But… in AWS, for the first like, couple minutes, it might not exist yet because the entitlement sync job hasn’t picked it up.

[01:47] Cole Summers: Or AWS hasn’t actually pushed it yet. That’s the “propagation delay” thing.

[01:51] Ben Carter: So the UX needs to say: “This can take X minutes,” not “you did it wrong.”

[01:57] Chloe Martin: Right now it says, literally, “Not found. Check values.” Which is… not great.

[02:04] Chris Osei: Action item. Chloe, update copy for entitlement delays, with refresh/retry and expected time window.

[02:10] Chloe Martin: Yep.

[02:12] Nadia Rahman: Also, when they hit refresh, can we log an event? Because we want to know how many people get stuck here.

[02:17] Chloe Martin: We added a click event, but I’m not sure if it’s wired on this screen yet.

[02:22] Nadia Rahman: I’ll verify.

[02:25] Ben Carter: Keep going. Let’s assume entitlement is found.

[02:28] Chloe Martin: Okay. When found, we show: “You’re entitled to Redwood Hosted — Marketplace.” And then we ask: “Do you want to create a new Redwood org or link to an existing org?”

[02:40] Markus Klein: That’s good. What happens if they already have an org, but they’re not the owner? Like an engineer set up an org last year.

[02:49] Chloe Martin: Right now we require org admin. If you choose “existing org,” you have to be signed in and have permissions.

[02:56] Alex Martinez: We need to document that, super explicitly. Otherwise support gets “I can’t link.”

[03:01] Elliot Price: And the doc should say “Ask your org owner to link the marketplace subscription.”

[03:05] Ben Carter: Do we want to allow non-admin to request linking? Like a “send request to admin” workflow?

[03:12] Ethan Park: Not in this iteration. That’s product work.

[03:15] Chloe Martin: Yeah, for now we show an error that says, “You don’t have permissions.” But it doesn’t say what to do.

[03:21] Chris Osei: Another action item: improve that error state with guidance.

[03:25] Chloe Martin: Yep.

[03:26] Chloe Martin: Okay, selecting “create new org.” We ask for org name, region preference, and then we show the “data processing region” dropdown.

[03:36] Kira Thompson: Region naming needs to match our residency language. Like “US” vs “us-east-1.” We should use customer-friendly names.

[03:42] Elliot Price: Also, docs need to clarify what region affects. Like model runtime region vs where logs are stored.

[03:48] Ben Carter: We should align with the security packet wording, otherwise we contradict ourselves.

[03:53] Ethan Park: From an implementation standpoint, this sets the control plane region and where inference is served by default. But you can still route per request depending on policy, for Hosted.

[04:03] Markus Klein: That’s too nuanced for onboarding. We should say “Default region for serving and logs” and then “contact us for constraints.”

[04:11] Chloe Martin: When you click “Provision,” it triggers org creation and also ties the entitlement to the org.

[04:18] Cole Summers: And from billing, that’s the moment we start metering under the marketplace account.

[04:22] Ben Carter: Wait, do we meter before linking? Or only after org link?

[04:26] Cole Summers: We meter usage. If there’s no org, there’s no usage. But technically the subscription exists. So yeah, practically after org is created/linked.

[04:33] Nadia Rahman: For telemetry, we should track time from “entitlement verified” to “org linked.” That’s our friction point.

[04:39] Chloe Martin: Here’s the provisioning status screen. It’s a spinner that says “Creating org… syncing entitlements…”

[04:46] Markus Klein: Please add an ETA or at least “usually < 2 minutes.” Otherwise people bounce.

[04:52] Chloe Martin: It currently has no time estimate, just “This may take a few minutes.”

[04:57] Ben Carter: We need the copy to be provider-specific. AWS entitlement delays are longer than GCP, in our experience.

[05:04] Ethan Park: Yep, AWS can be like 5–15 minutes in worst case, if their side is slow. GCP is typically faster.

[05:10] Elliot Price: We should not promise 2 minutes then.

[05:12] Ben Carter: Right, maybe: “Often under 5 minutes, sometimes up to 15.” And then a “If longer than 30, contact support.”

[05:20] Dev Patel: (joins late) Sorry, I’m late—support call ran over.

[05:23] Ben Carter: Hey Dev. Perfect timing. We’re on the “entitlement delay” messaging. What’s your preference for escalation?

[05:29] Dev Patel: If it’s over 30 minutes, open a ticket. But we should also ask them to confirm the subscription is ‘Active’ in the marketplace portal. Half the time it’s ‘Pending acceptance’ or whatever.

[05:39] Chloe Martin: Good point. We can add a link “Check subscription status in AWS/GCP portal.”

[05:44] Alex Martinez: Docs can include that as step zero. “Confirm subscription is active.”

[05:49] Chris Osei: Captured.

[05:52] Chloe Martin: Okay, provisioning completed. Now we land in “Create your first API key.”

[05:58] Markus Klein: This is good. Do we also show the model name to test against?

[06:02] Chloe Martin: We show a suggested model in a dropdown. It’s currently “rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct” in staging.

[06:09] Markus Klein: That might not exist in every region or SKU.

[06:12] Cole Summers: Also, for Dedicated and Private SKUs it’s different, not just a model list.

[06:17] Kira Thompson: Our docs need to branch here: Hosted marketplace SKU gets “call the API.” Dedicated gets “request capacity + provisioning steps.” Private gets “deployment kickoff.”

[06:25] Ben Carter: Yeah. This dry-run is mostly Hosted path, but we should at least note where Dedicated/Private diverge.

[06:32] Chloe Martin: After key creation, we show a code snippet: curl, Python, Node. It’s pulling the org slug and the base URL.

[06:41] Alex Martinez: Can we include a “copy to clipboard” and a “run in browser” button?

[06:45] Chloe Martin: Copy exists. “Run in browser” not yet.

[06:49] Markus Klein: For first success, a simple “Test request” button helps. Especially when their environment variables aren’t set.

[06:55] Ben Carter: Agree. But might be out of scope.

[06:58] Ethan Park: It’s also a security question: we’d be issuing a request from the console environment.

[07:03] Marcus Lin: (briefly) Just make sure it doesn’t leak keys in logs or analytics.

[07:07] Nadia Rahman: Right now we redact the key, but I’ll double-check.

[07:11] Chloe Martin: Okay, now we simulate first request. Markus, you want to drive? You can use the sample curl.

[07:17] Markus Klein: Sure. (typing) Okay, I’m getting a 401.

[07:22] Chloe Martin: Wait—did it include the header as “Authorization: Bearer”?

[07:25] Markus Klein: I pasted it. It says “X-API-Key” but I might’ve… oh I see, it’s “X-Redwood-Key” in this snippet.

[07:33] Alex Martinez: That’s a docs bug or a snippet bug. Our public docs use “Authorization: Bearer” for some endpoints and “X-API-Key” for others.

[07:41] Ethan Park: The gateway accepts both, but the snippet should be consistent.

[07:45] Ben Carter: This is exactly why we’re doing this. Action item to fix the snippet in console and docs.

[07:51] Chloe Martin: I’ll take it. The console snippet template is in the onboarding component.

[07:56] Markus Klein: Once I correct it, it works. I get a streaming response.

[08:01] Ben Carter: Great. Now, edge cases. Let’s do “existing org” link path.

[08:06] Chloe Martin: Switching to “Link existing org.” It lists orgs I have access to.

[08:12] Elliot Price: If you have many orgs, do we have search? Some enterprise folks have like 20.

[08:17] Chloe Martin: No search yet. It’s a dropdown.

[08:20] Ben Carter: Probably okay for now.

[08:22] Chloe Martin: Okay, selecting an existing org. Click “Link.”

[08:26] Chloe Martin: Here’s an error: “E_ORG_ALREADY_LINKED.” It’s literally the raw code.

[08:33] Alex Martinez: Oof. That’s not customer-friendly.

[08:36] Chloe Martin: Yeah, we need to map codes to messages.

[08:39] Ethan Park: That’s from the entitlement service. It means that org already has a different subscription linked.

[08:44] Cole Summers: Or the same subscription was already linked, and we’re idempotent but returning that code.

[08:49] Ben Carter: What should the user do? If it’s already linked, we should say “You’re all set,” and then route them to create key / usage.

[08:56] Chloe Martin: Agreed. Right now it’s blocking.

[08:59] Dev Patel: Support perspective: this is a top ticket. People try again and think it failed.

[09:04] Chris Osei: Action item: code mapping, E_ORG_ALREADY_LINKED should be success path.

[09:08] Chloe Martin: Yep.

[09:10] Nadia Rahman: And track that event. It’s a “repeat attempt” indicator.

[09:13] Ben Carter: Let’s talk multi-subscription. If a company buys Hosted via marketplace and later buys Dedicated via marketplace. How do we represent that?

[09:22] Cole Summers: Billing catalog supports multiple entitlements per org. But the UX doesn’t. It assumes one subscription.

[09:28] Ethan Park: There’s a ticket for multi-subscription edge cases. We’re not fully done.

[09:32] Markus Klein: We’ll hit this in enterprise. They’ll start with Hosted usage and then procurement will want Dedicated with a commit.

[09:39] Kira Thompson: Docs need to say “contact sales/support for upgrades” for now, unless we truly support it self-serve.

[09:44] Ben Carter: Right. We should not pretend self-serve upgrade works if it doesn’t.

[09:49] Chloe Martin: Okay, switching to GCP provider. Here, the input is “Entitlement ID.” Same general flow.

[09:57] Elliot Price: Do we have separate docs pages per cloud? The UI changes slightly.

[10:01] Alex Martinez: I think we should. Otherwise it’s too confusing.

[10:05] Ben Carter: On listing pages, they’ll want cloud-specific instructions anyway.

[10:09] Chloe Martin: For GCP, when entitlement is found, the response returns the “billing account id” and the “plan.” But I’m not showing it right now.

[10:17] Cole Summers: Please don’t show the billing account id in UI; it’s not needed and might freak people out.

[10:22] Chloe Martin: Got it.

[10:24] Ben Carter: Cole, can you confirm we’re aligned on the marketplace SKU naming and internal meters? We had that mismatch last week.

[10:30] Cole Summers: Mostly aligned. The Hosted dimension is tokens. Embeddings is separate. Rerank is separate. The mismatch was around a legacy “requests” dimension. We’ve removed it. But docs should say “billing is token-based,” not “request-based.”

[10:43] Elliot Price: Yep, we’ll update.

[10:45] Ben Carter: Another user story: procurement buys via marketplace, engineer gets notified, goes to console, but they don’t know they need to start at /onboarding/marketplace. How do they discover it?

[10:56] Chloe Martin: We added a banner on the normal onboarding page: “Purchased via marketplace? Start here.” But it’s only visible if you have no API key.

[11:06] Markus Klein: If they already have keys, they might not see it. But they still need to link subscription for billing.

[11:11] Ethan Park: That’s tricky. You can have keys and still be unlinked.

[11:14] Dev Patel: Then we need a console settings page: “Marketplace subscriptions” with link/unlink status.

[11:20] Chloe Martin: Not built yet.

[11:22] Ben Carter: For this launch, at minimum, docs should mention “If you already have an org, go to Settings → Billing → Marketplace” (if it exists) or give a direct URL.

[11:33] Chloe Martin: We can create a hidden route. But we need to decide.

[11:36] Chris Osei: Noting as open product gap. We can decide in go/no-go.

[11:41] Alex Martinez: Another docs gap: “Who can create API keys?” We should clarify roles and recommend creating a service account key.

[11:48] Marcus Lin: And we should mention key rotation best practices, without over-promising. Like “rotate regularly,” “store in secrets manager.”

[11:55] Elliot Price: We can link to the general API key management doc.

[12:00] Ben Carter: Cool. Let’s jump to troubleshooting. What happens if entitlement verification returns “subscription not active?”

[12:07] Ethan Park: E_SUBSCRIPTION_NOT_ACTIVE. That usually means the marketplace purchase is not accepted, or it’s cancelled.

[12:13] Chloe Martin: Right now we show “Not active.” No guidance.

[12:17] Dev Patel: Guidance should be “Check marketplace portal status,” “confirm you used the right account,” and “if you’re using a private offer, confirm it’s accepted.”

[12:28] Ben Carter: And include private offer activation timing. That’s another common question.

[12:34] Markus Klein: I’ve seen customers ask “We accepted the private offer, why are limits still the old tier?” That’s basically entitlement sync delay or wrong subscription link.

[12:43] Nadia Rahman: If we track entitlement changes, we can detect that mismatch and alert.

[12:48] Cole Summers: The meter mapping should update immediately once entitlements update, but the console might cache.

[12:54] Chloe Martin: Console caches org billing status for like 60 seconds. Not huge.

[12:59] Ben Carter: Okay. Let’s do a quick docs review: Elliot/Alex, what pages exist right now, and what’s missing?

[13:07] Elliot Price: We have a draft “AWS Marketplace onboarding” page and “GCP Marketplace onboarding” page. What’s missing is: (1) where to find the subscription identifiers, (2) existing org linking steps, (3) a troubleshooting section with these exact errors, and (4) clarifying billing dimensions: tokens vs embeddings.

[13:27] Alex Martinez: Also, we should have a simple diagram: Marketplace → Redwood entitlement service → Redwood org provisioning → API key → first call. People like a picture.

[13:36] Kira Thompson: And for Dedicated/Private SKUs, we need a “What happens after purchase?” page. Because it’s not immediate.

[13:43] Ben Carter: Right. That’s procurement-led, they expect an onboarding motion.

[13:48] Markus Klein: For Dedicated, it’s “we confirm region, GPU type, throughput, then we provision capacity.” That can be days.

[13:55] Chloe Martin: The console shouldn’t imply immediate usage for Dedicated/Private. We might need a different post-purchase screen.

[14:03] Ethan Park: That’s also gating; Dedicated requires internal provisioning.

[14:07] Ben Carter: Okay. We’ll log that as out-of-scope for Hosted launch but needs a clear message.

[14:13] Chris Osei: Noted.

[14:15] (crosstalk)

[14:16] Ben Carter: Let’s do a “happy path” recap as if we’re writing the listing “How it works” section. Step 1 subscribe, step 2 open Redwood console marketplace onboarding, step 3 verify entitlement, step 4 create or link org, step 5 create key, step 6 run example.

[14:32] Alex Martinez: We also need to mention “entitlement can take a few minutes.” That’s a step.

[14:37] Dev Patel: And “if over 30 minutes, contact support with these IDs.” We should define what IDs: subscription id, org id, timestamp.

[14:45] Chloe Martin: We can show a “Copy diagnostics” button on the error state. That would save support time.

[14:51] Ben Carter: That’s a great idea, but might be too much before launch.

[14:55] Chris Osei: Could be a stretch, but let’s capture it.

[14:58] Nadia Rahman: Even without “copy diagnostics,” we should log correlation ids and tell user “include correlation id.”

[15:05] Ethan Park: We already generate request id in the API response. But the UI needs to display it.

[15:10] Chloe Martin: Currently it doesn’t.

[15:12] Ben Carter: Alright. Another gap: security docs. We should link the marketplace security overview from onboarding.

[15:19] Elliot Price: Where do we want that link? In docs and in the listing. But in the console too, maybe under “Need security info?”

[15:27] Marcus Lin: As long as the wording is approved. Don’t say “HIPAA compliant” or anything.

[15:31] Ben Carter: We’ll stick to “SOC 2 report available under NDA” type language.

[15:36] Alex Martinez: The docs page should also include “shared responsibility” quick bullets. Marketplace reviewers expect it.

[15:43] Ben Carter: Great. Switching gears: instrumentation. Nadia, what funnel events do we have and what’s missing?

[15:51] Nadia Rahman: We have: marketplace_onboarding_viewed, entitlement_verify_clicked, entitlement_verify_success/failure, org_create_started, org_link_started, org_link_success/failure, api_key_created, first_request_doc_clicked (if they click docs). What’s missing is: refresh retries count, time-to-entitlement in backend vs UI, and a “gave up” signal. We can approximate “gave up” by no further events within 30 minutes.

[16:19] Ben Carter: Perfect. That ties to our success metrics.

[16:23] Cole Summers: Also ensure billing dimension mapping is logged at org link time; it helps debugging mismatches.

[16:30] Ethan Park: Careful with PII, but dimension names are fine.

[16:34] Chloe Martin: One more UX thing: on the “verify entitlement” step, we should allow sign-in later. Right now it forces you to sign in before even checking entitlement.

[16:44] Markus Klein: Customers might want to verify without creating an account first.

[16:48] Ben Carter: But if we verify without sign-in, what do we do next? We still need an org.

[16:53] Alex Martinez: We can verify and then say “Sign in to continue.” That’s less friction.

[16:59] Ethan Park: As long as we’re not exposing too much entitlement info without auth.

[17:04] Chloe Martin: We can show just “Verified” without details.

[17:08] Ben Carter: Okay, capture as maybe nice-to-have.

[17:12] Chris Osei: Noted.

[17:14] (brief pause)

[17:16] Ben Carter: Let’s do a quick run-through of the listing FAQ questions we keep hearing: “How long until I can use it?”, “How does billing work?”, “Can I use my existing org?”, “What if I have multiple subscriptions?”, “Who do I contact for support?”, “Where are security docs?”

[17:33] Dev Patel: On support: marketplace customers should still use support portal, but we should also mention “for procurement issues contact your cloud provider.” People get confused.

[17:42] Ben Carter: Right. And we should include the cloud provider’s refund policy is not controlled by us.

[17:47] Cole Summers: Also credits/trials: we probably can’t do free credits through marketplace easily. Need to be careful.

[17:54] Ben Carter: Yeah, no mention of free credits in marketplace listing unless confirmed.

[17:59] Elliot Price: Docs can say “For trials, contact sales.”

[18:03] Markus Klein: That’s fine.

[18:05] Chloe Martin: Quick check: On the API key page, we don’t explain rate limits or quotas for marketplace SKU. Should we?

[18:12] Ben Carter: We should at least link to “Usage limits.” Customers will ask “why am I throttled.”

[18:18] Alex Martinez: We can add a callout “Your quota is set by your plan. View in Settings.”

[18:23] Chloe Martin: Okay.

[18:25] Ben Carter: Alright, we’re at about 20 minutes. Let’s go through action items and confirm owners.

[18:31] Chris Osei: I’ve got: Chloe updating entitlement delay messaging + mapping raw error codes to friendly messages, Alex/Elliot adding docs for identifiers + org linking + troubleshooting, Cole confirming final billing dimensions + sharing mapping table, Nadia verifying telemetry for retries and building dashboard proposal, Markus providing marketplace-first quickstart snippet.

[18:55] Ben Carter: Great. Any other gaps we didn’t capture?

[18:59] Kira Thompson: Dedicated/Private divergence needs a doc page. Even if simple.

[19:04] Elliot Price: Yep, I’ll coordinate with Kira on that. But we should confirm scope.

[19:09] Ben Carter: Put it as a follow-up. We can do a minimal “After purchase” page for each SKU.

[19:14] Ethan Park: Engineering-wise, the biggest risk is entitlement sync reliability. But we’re working on retries and idempotency.

[19:22] Nadia Rahman: If the sync job fails, we need alerting thresholds. Otherwise, customers are stuck.

[19:27] Ben Carter: That’s part of platform work. Ethan, can you sync with Priya/PagerDuty on that?

[19:32] Ethan Park: Yep.

[19:33] Ben Carter: Cool. Let’s wrap with go/no-go criteria: (1) no raw error codes in UI, (2) docs pages published with identifiers + troubleshooting, (3) snippet headers consistent, (4) telemetry confirms we can measure time-to-first-token, and (5) entitlement delay messaging is accurate.

[19:53] Chris Osei: I’ll post notes in the project channel.

[19:55] Ben Carter: Thanks all. Ending recording.

(Recording ends; meeting continued briefly off-record)

domain: 日常协作与非结构化讨论
title: eng-runtime
text:
anna: Heads-up — seeing repeated OOM spikes on paged-attn when KV prefetch is enabled together with batch_trigger=8. Happens on long-context workloads; profiler shows a compaction cost spike and kernel falling back to the generic attention path. Logs + small trace attached below.

mike: Which model / seq_len distribution? Is this on dedicated or hosted?

anna: lightweight repro on dedicated (dev pool). Model: redwood/open-6b, typical seqs: 4096 tokens (50% long, 30% med, 20% short). Config snippet:

```
prefetch_window: 6
batch_trigger: 8
workspace_size_mb: 2048
kv_cache_policy: paged
allocator: default
```

ravi: Hmm. Prefetch window 6 means we pre-allocate blocks for lookahead, combined with batch_trigger=8 we're coalescing many streams that each allocate ephemeral workspace slices. Compaction gets invoked often -> allocator churn. Sample from perf: 

```
[perf] compaction_start t=0.42s
[perf] moved_blocks=312 freed_bytes=24MB
[perf] kernel_select: fallback=naive_attention (no fast kernel available — fragmented)
```

jen: I reproduced locally. When compaction runs it does a bunch of small frees which invalidates kernel workspace placement and ruins the fast-kernel alignment. Also noticed KV prefetch allocs are pinned to hot buckets (hot/cold segregation mismatch).

perf-bot: memory-pressure summary for thread 1919002468: peak_rss=13.6GB peak_gpu=11.9GB compaction_events=14 OOM_events=3 kernel_fallbacks=9

mike: Short-term mitigation: reduce prefetch_window to 2 and lower batch_trigger to 4. Medium-term: consider enabling slab_coalesce and increasing max_reuse_age so freed blocks get repurposed instead of triggering compaction. Example flags: `slab_coalesce=true`, `max_reuse_age=3`

anna: Tried that on a canary run. Results after 200 requests: peak_gpu down ~12%, compaction_events down to 4, OOMs -> 0. Latency p50 +3ms, p95 +18ms (acceptable for this workload).

ravi: Good. I also sketched a change to the batch_trigger heuristic so it accounts for `estimated_kv_cache_pressure`. Pseudocode: 

```
if estimated_kv_cache_pressure > threshold:
 trigger_batch_at = max(1, batch_trigger - 2)
else:
 trigger_batch_at = batch_trigger
```

This reduces the chance of merging many streams that will each cause small KV prefetch allocations.

jen: I'll put up a canary rollout config with an automatic rollback if kernel_fallbacks > 5/min. Canary config:

```
rollout: canary
fraction: 10%
monitor: kernel_fallback_rate, oom_count
rollback: kernel_fallback_rate > 5/min OR oom_count > 0
```

anna: Sounds good — thanks. I'll coordinate with perf to run longer stress runs (10k requests) and post updated flamegraphs.

mike: Long-term we should also evaluate: 1) prefetch as soft reservations (no pinned blocks unless cold misses happen), 2) compact-on-idle instead of immediate compaction, 3) add kernel-aware allocation hints so prefetched blocks align to fast-kernel stride.

anna: Adding those to the follow-up checklist. Posting current flamegraph + trace link in a follow-up message. :thumbsup:

text:

Found a broken anchor in the 'audit event fields' section that the old link points to. Can legal + security skim the query examples for bad phrasing or accidental PII exposure?

ops-rita: small ops nit: the CLI export sample in the PR uses --kms-key placeholder but no example ARN. Please use an example like arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123456789012:key/abcd-ef01 and show how to copy the exported bundle to a customer bucket with aws s3 cp and a presigned URL.

jess-docs: right, the broken-link-checker flagged one internal reference. I pushed a tiny patch to align the anchor text and updated the TOC.

compliance_rob: wording pass from compliance with one change: in the retention table replace "indefinite" with "customer-managed (no default)" for Private deployments. Hosted defaults should still show example value 90 days.

sec_ari: security approves the RBAC snippet. Could you add a one-line note: "Do not run queries that export raw tenant PII without customer consent and proper KMS envelope encryption."

title: MintLance concurrent session stall causing truncated completions and temporary invoice/billing delta during us-east peak
text:
Issue summary:
During a sustained traffic peak on 2026-03-10 09:02-09:46 UTC MintLance experienced high rates of truncated responses (clients reported streaming connections closing mid-completion) and a subsequent unexpected billing delta attributed to duplicate acknowledgement accounting.

Impact:
- ~12% of requests from MintLance in us-east experienced truncated streaming completions (partial transcripts).
- Brief billing spike visible on customer's invoice preview window for the affected timeframe (~$480 extra before automated credit).
- Customer-facing producers reported degraded UX for chat features during morning traffic peak; no data exfiltration identified.

Environment:
- Redwood prod cluster in us-east serving MintLance dedicated pool (dedicated capacity, pool-id dl-mintlance-1).
- Models routed to rw/opt-6.7b-quantized-v2 with streaming enabled.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) High concurrency from MintLance runtime jobs starting at ~09:02 UTC.
2) KV prefix cache miss flood (many new conversation prefixes) increased per-request setup cost.
3) Serving runtime started shedding long-lived streaming connections under backpressure; some connections closed with 499/stream-reset.
4) Client retries combined with router-level partial-ack duplication produced duplicate billing events for a subset of short-lived retries.

Logs / evidence pointers:
- SRE dashboard: links to request-rate, tail latency, and streaming-reset graphs in Grafana (see related_confluence_pages).
- Example streaming trace: request-id 1a7b2f4d showing abrupt grpc stream close at 09:12:18 UTC (attached to internal trace).
- Billing ledger row samples in BigQuery: project redwood-billing.mintlance_tmp.billing_events_20260310 showing duplicate ack events for request-id hash range xxxxx..yyyyy.

Initial hypothesis: concurrent KV cache miss and a rare router backpressure path combined to close streaming connections without completing token accounting.

Timestamps and findings:
- 09:02 UTC: MintLance concurrent job window begins (customer reported a scheduled batch of user sessions).
- 09:07-09:20 UTC: KV cache miss rate spiked to 1400% of baseline for the dedicated pool; eviction churn increased CPU on serving nodes.
- 09:10 UTC: Router ingress observed queue growth; router began responding with RESET_STREAM to long-lived streams when per-node inflight tokens exceeded safety threshold.
- 09:12 UTC: Several clients retried immediately; retry logic created short-lived requests that completed quickly and created duplicate ack entries in billing pipeline due to idempotency gap for streaming-early-terminations.

Hypotheses validated by logs:
- We found router logs showing explicit RESET_STREAM events correlated with the same request-ids as truncated traces.
- Billing pipeline consumer acknowledged events twice when stream token accounting did not include retry-de-dup metadata (race between ack persistence and retry dedup token write).

Temporary mitigations applied during incident:
1) Increased per-router streaming inflight safety threshold for dl-mintlance-1 by 25% to reduce premature resets.
2) Applied a KV cache TTL bump and warmed common prefixes via a preheat job to reduce miss churn.
3) Issued a manual billing credit to MintLance while investigation proceeded.

Open risks noted:
- Similar mis-specified client retry windows could retrigger duplicate ack behavior unless idempotency tokens are enforced end-to-end.

2026-03-10 09:15 - Alex Morgan (SRE): Acknowledged incident; pivoting to router logs and kv-cache metrics. Noted RESET_STREAM spikes from 09:08-09:18 UTC.
2026-03-10 09:28 - Priya Raman (Support): Notified MintLance CS lead (J. Ortega) of degraded experience and that engineering is investigating. Promised ETA for follow-up within 2 hours.
2026-03-10 10:05 - Ethan Cole (Eng): Applied temporary router inflight threshold increase and warmed KV prefixes. Observed drop in streaming resets within 3 minutes. Monitoring for billing duplication events continues.
2026-03-10 11:20 - Finance Ops (M. Deng): Issued $480 credit to MintLance invoice as temporary remediation; will reconcile next billing cycle if necessary.
2026-03-11 14:00 - Priya Raman (Support): Sent post-incident summary and action plan to MintLance; scheduled working session for 2026-03-12 to review retry semantics and SDK guidance.
2026-03-12 16:30 - Ethan Cole (Eng): Deployed idempotency token write fix to billing ingestion (PR merged: github.com/redwoodinference/billing/pull/1421). Monitoring looks stable in us-east and us-west.
2026-03-13 09:00 - Priya Raman (Support): Confirmed with MintLance that client-side UX issues were resolved after server-side fixes; customer accepted the credit and requested follow-up doc on SDK retry guidelines.

Root cause: a combination of KV cache miss storm causing serving node CPU pressure and a router safety path that reset long-lived streams when inflight tokens exceeded threshold. Client retry behavior plus a small idempotency gap in the billing ingestion pipeline produced duplicate ack/billing events.

Fixes implemented:
- Short-term: increased router threshold and warmed KV prefixes during the incident window; issued customer credit.
- Medium-term: patched billing ingestion to validate idempotency tokens on early-terminated streams (PR merged and deployed 2026-03-12).
- Long-term: engineering backlog items added to: (1) improve backpressure flow to allow graceful drain rather than immediate RESET_STREAM; (2) enhance KV warm-up heuristics for dedicated pools during scheduled batch windows; (3) publish SDK retry guidance and recommended backoff windows for customers.

Follow-ups / action items (owners and ETA):
- ENG-OPS: implement graceful stream-drain flow in router (owner: Ethan Cole, ETA: 2026-04-05).
- PLAT-DEV: KV preheat/runbook for scheduled batch windows (owner: S. Navarro, ETA: 2026-03-28).
- DX/Docs: SDK retry guidance and example configs for dedicated customers (owner: Lena Ortiz, ETA: 2026-03-20).
- FINANCE: reconcile credit in next billing run and confirm final adjustment (owner: M. Deng, ETA: 2026-03-20).

Status: Incident resolved; customer satisfied with remediation and credit. Postmortem published at related_confluence_pages.

title: Runway Velocity & Decision Guardrails for SSO/SAML and Audit-Log Compliance Deliveries
author: Ravi Patel
text:
Goal: Define an executable milestone cadence and a small set of deterministic release guardrails that tie evidence velocity to release gates for SOC2/ISO and SSO/SAML + audit-log features. Rationale: Current compliance work drifts between squads because acceptance is qualitative and reviewer load is high. We need quantitative runway signals ("Runway Velocity") and clear pass/fail gates so product releases either ship with provable controls or are scoped down with documented mitigations. Scope: SSO/SAML integration, audit-log capture/retention pipeline, evidence artifacts (docs, tests, dashboards), security sign-off, and automation to reduce reviewer time. Out of scope: full org-level SOC2 readiness plan (this is delivery-level gating for product launches). Stakeholders: Security (lead: Anika Verma), Platform Eng (lead: Daniel Kim), Observability (lead: Jorge Alvarez), Legal (review), Customer Success (for enterprise customers), QA and Release Engineering. Deliverables: 1) Runway Velocity metric definition and Grafana panel, 2) Decision guardrail checklist and automated gate enforcement in release pipeline, 3) Standardized evidence template and checklist, 4) Runbook for rollback/mitigation when gates fail, 5) OKR mapping showing how gate success rolls up to Assurance OKRs.

Runway Velocity metric defined and documented: formula, inputs, and criticality weights
Grafana dashboard showing historical velocity and projection for next 4 weeks is available
Release guardrail implemented as a checklist with binary checks for critical controls (>=90% completion) and soft checks for low-risk items
Automated gating hook added to canary pipeline that blocks canary promotions when any critical guardrail fails
Standard evidence template stored in Drive and linked from PR templates
Security sign-off workflow captured and represented as a single Slack approval step and a ticket flag
At least two pilot releases complete the gate workflow (internal feature + external enterprise trial) and documented learnings

2026-02-02 - Kickoff: Reviewed PRD with Security and Platform. Decision: prioritize SSO end-to-end test and retention validation for audit logs. Action: ENG to prototype velocity metric (owner: Daniel Kim).
2026-02-10 - Trade-off discussion: Automation increases lead time initially but reduces reviewer time by ~30%. Agreed to scope automation to critical controls only for first iteration.
2026-02-18 - Engineering update: Initial Grafana panel ETL complete (PR: github.com/redwood/observability/pulls/482). Panel exposes 'evidence_completed' and 'evidence_total' by week. Need weighting for 'critical' vs 'non-critical' artifacts.
2026-02-24 - Security feedback (Anika): Require full SAML E2E smoke (login, role mapping, session invalidation) before sign-off. Also requested retention proof for 90 days. Added as critical control.
2026-03-03 - Decision: Guardrail thresholds set to 90% for critical controls, 70% for non-critical. Fallback: if critical <90%, release may proceed only with documented mitigation, customer opt-in flag, and additional monitoring for 30 days.
2026-03-05 - PM update: Draft evidence template uploaded to Drive and linked to PR template. Link added below. Need UX for clear checklist display in Console when a customer requests enterprise onboarding.
2026-03-09 - Cross-functional review: Observability to add an alert when projected runway < 3 weeks. Release Engineering to implement gating hook in CI (ENG-82111).
2026-03-10 - Updated acceptance criteria: Added requirement for two pilot releases to validate operational playbook and rollback steps. Next steps: schedule pilot windows in Cycle 2026-W10 and 2026-W12.

title: Introduce defaults-suggester: heuristic profiles for batching, cache TTLs and quantization presets
author: Asha Patel
text:
Context: Teams repeatedly ask for sensible defaults for batching, cache TTLs and quantization when onboarding models to Redwood. Currently defaults live in multiple places and require manual tuning with evals and internal heuristics. Goal: ship a small, auditable suggestion system that observes recent workload signals and proposes conservative default profiles for batching.window_ms, batch_size caps, prefix/KV cache TTLs, and quantization presets. The suggester is opt-in by default and produces human-readable suggestions surfaced in the Console and via a new API endpoint.

What this PR does: 1) Adds a lightweight offline heuristic engine (defaults-suggester) that consumes short-term aggregated telemetry (per-route QPS, median latency, 50/95/99 latency quantiles, token length distribution) and maps to a ranked set of suggested profiles. 2) Introduces a new API: POST /optimize/v1/suggestions which returns JSON suggestions with confidence scores and an explanation string. 3) Wire up Console: a Suggestions panel on per-route settings with an Apply & Preview flow that shows estimated unit-cost delta and latency impact. 4) Add a gated runtime flag so the runtime can accept a profile payload for immediate application (useful for Dedicated/Private workflows). 5) Provide a small set of canonical profiles (conservative, balanced, aggressive) for batching and quantization, plus TTL presets for prefix/KV caches. 6) Add end-to-end test coverage and benchmark harness runs comparing before/after for representative traffic shapes.

Design notes and trade-offs: - The engine intentionally errs conservative: suggestions will never increase batch window beyond a route-level safety cap derived from SLA settings. - Quantization suggestions prefer per-model family presets (e.g., OPT/GPT-like) and include fallbacks; we do not auto-apply quantization in-host, suggestions only. - Telemetry ingestion is opt-in; customers can disable telemetry for suggestions in account settings. For Private installs the suggester can be run locally against their telemetry export. - Suggestions include an estimated unit-cost delta computed from our unit-econ model; we expose the formula in the Console and include the prompt/eval link so teams can validate quality impact.

Files touched: runtime/batching/suggester.go, optimize/suggester/service.go, api/handlers/suggestions.go, console/src/routes/RouteSuggestionsPanel.tsx, console/src/api/suggestionsClient.ts, docs/operations/defaults-suggester.md, config/profiles/default-profiles.yaml, tests/e2e/suggestions_flow.test.ts, bench/harness/suggester_traffic_shapes.yaml, telemetry/migrations/add_suggester_event.sql, scripts/ci/bench-suggester.sh

Testing: - Unit tests for mapping heuristics and profile ranking. - E2E test simulating three traffic shapes (short chat, assistant longform, embeddings micro-bursts). - Benchmarks: microbenchmark harness run on a c6g-xlarge-equivalent cluster with representative models showed median latency change within +3% for conservative profiles and unit-cost reduction up to 24% for balanced profiles on nuclear workloads. Results attached to the CI artifact and linked in the console patch notes.

Rollout plan: feature gated. Step 1: merge behind feature flag and enable suggestions only for internal org and canary customers. Step 2: collect feedback for 2 weeks. Step 3: enable Console UI for self-serve with telemetry opt-in prompt on first usage. Step 4: document caveats and add guided eval for teams that accept aggressive quantization suggestions.

Open questions / TODOs: - Add an explicit opt-out banner in Console per compliance request (tracked in ENG-7922). - Provide an exportable CSV of suggestion history for audit. - Consider a future ML-backed suggestion engine once we have more signal.

References: Linear items ENG-7842, ENG-7901. Internal benchmark dashboards: /dash/bench/suggester/33219.

This description is intentionally high-level; see docs/operations/defaults-suggester.md for the full spec and the API contract.

Marco Ruiz: Nice end-to-end. Two quick questions: 1) telemetry sensitivity — what fields are we exporting? 2) safety cap logic: please clarify how SLA caps are enforced so we don't regress p99 for high-priority routes.
Asha Patel (reply): Telemetry is aggregated and windowed, we only ingest per-route QPS/latency quantiles and token length histograms. No raw prompts or user identifiers. SLA caps are derived from route.metadata.sla_ms if present else global-default-sla; batch window is min(suggested, sla_safe_window). Added comments and unit tests (see runtime/batching/suggester_test.go).
Priya Nair: Benchmarks look promising. Can we add a small canary that surfaces the suggested unit-cost delta in Console before apply? UX should show the estimate and a confidence score.
Asha Patel (reply): Added preview UI and the confidence score from the ranking function. Preview includes a cost/latency estimate computed from the unit-econ model. Updated Console tests accordingly.
Daniel Kim: Please add a feature flag to avoid automatic runtime exposure in Dedicated until security signoff. Also add a telemetry opt-in toggle on account-level configs.
Asha Patel (reply): Added runtime.gated.features.suggester boolean guard and account.suggestions.telemetry_opt_in. Documented both in the runbook.

Introduce a conservative, opt-in defaults suggester that recommends batching and cache TTL profiles plus quantization presets. Suggestions are surfaced in Console with cost/latency estimates and are gated behind account-level telemetry opt-in. Useful for teams who want quick, audited starting points for unit-econ driven tuning.

Enable feature flag runtime.gated.features.suggester=false by default in main cloud. For canary orgs set to true via admin console. Ensure bench artifacts are uploaded to /artifacts/bench/suggester/33219 before enabling wide rollout.

title: Per-request audit sampling proof and SIEM forwarder integrity request for PCI scope
text:
Issue summary:
Customer requests cryptographically verifiable evidence that per-request audit events (for interactive generation API calls) are being forwarded to their SIEM without loss or re-ordering, and that export manifests are HSM-attested.

Impact:
ApexBanking is in PCI scope and needs proof that no records were dropped or omitted during a scheduled export and that per-request identifiers map to the events delivered to their SIEM. This blocks their internal compliance sign-off for a production rollout.

Environment:
prod region eu-west; account tenant_id=apex-4521; SIEM endpoint: s3-transfer->ftps->customer SFTP (fingerprint provided offline).

Observed behavior / request:
- Customer ran an on-demand export in the Console for 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z to 2026-03-03T23:59:59Z and reports ~0.7% fewer events in the delivered NDJSON than expected per their inbound token-metered usage.
- They request: (A) a signed sample bundle (HSM/attested manifest) covering that 72-hour window with preserved per-request request_id and hashed user_id fields; (B) a chainproof mapping from request_id -> delivered object path + per-batch HMAC; (C) verification steps they can run to validate integrity locally.

Steps to reproduce (customer):
1) Console -> Activity -> Exports -> Create export -> select tenant apex-4521, window 2026-03-01 to 2026-03-03 -> Delivery target: SFTP.
2) Wait for transfer complete notification.
3) Compare line count of ndjson with 'Token usage' CSV from Billing API for same time window.

Logs / artifacts provided by customer:
- Export delivery manifest (redacted) uploaded to our secure dropbox (link provided in ticket).
- Billing usage CSV (redacted).
- SFTP server logs showing inbound object receipt timestamps (screenshot).

Request / acceptance criteria:
- Deliver an HSM-signed manifest that includes per-batch HMACs and a resume token for each file in the bundle.
- Provide a short verification script (python/bash) and instructions to validate the HMAC chain and confirm event counts.
- If any events are missing, provide a reconcile report explaining whether events were filtered at source (redaction), dropped by the forwarder, or failed during delivery retries.

2026-03-12 09:18 - Aisha Romero (reporter): Opening ticket with ApexBanking for HSM-signed evidence of export integrity. Customer provided the manifest screenshot and billing CSV via secure link.
2026-03-12 12:04 - Support (Liam Patel): Acknowledged. Requested the exact export UUID and the SFTP server fingerprint. Asked whether customer can share a sample request_id they expect to find in the delivered bundle.
2026-03-12 14:35 - ApexBanking (customer reply): Provided export UUID export-20260301-72-apex4521, SFTP fingerprint sha256:AA:BB:CC (provided off-channel), sample request_id r-20260301-7a4f. Notes they observed line-count delta only for generation events, not audit-only traffic.
2026-03-13 08:22 - SRE (Elena Morales): Initial log sweep: forwarder lambda for tenant apex-4521 had 2 transient 5xx retries on 2026-03-01 03:12Z. Kafka consumer lag peaked at 1.5k messages for ~4 minutes. No hard ack failures recorded. Posting investigation notes into ticket.
2026-03-13 11:10 - Support (Liam Patel): Requested infra to assemble a signed proof bundle and to compute per-batch HMACs using current KEK. Escalating to infra-oncall for manifest attestation.
2026-03-14 10:05 - Infra-oncall (Marco Chen): Confirmed HSM available. Noted recent KEK rotation on 2026-02-28; will include key version metadata in manifest. ETA for signed sample bundle: 2026-03-15 EOD.
2026-03-14 15:30 - ApexBanking: Customer clarified they require masked user identifiers (SHA256 with tenant salt) in the sample bundle and a matching mapping file (hashed_user_id -> pseudonym_id) redacted in delivery.

Checked forwarder telemetry: three delivery attempts for file export-20260301-72-apex4521.part-0001; transfer succeeded on attempt 3, time delta 00:01:12 between upload and SFTP ACK.
Kafka consumer group offsets show spike in lag 2026-03-01T03:10:00Z - 03:15:00Z affecting partition p-7 which carries generation events for tenant apex-4521. Estimated 1.2k messages delayed but later consumed and forwarded in batch-20260301-03:17:xx.
No records indicate payload-level filtering for PCI fields; redaction is performed at export-time if tenant policy requires it. Customer's tenant policy shows 'mask_payment_data: true' which can reduce line count relative to raw token-meter counts if some events are deduplicated or suppressed by policy.
HSM key rotation log: KEK v3 used to sign manifests starting 2026-03-01 00:00:00Z; previous KEK v2 retired 2026-02-28. Need to include key version and cert chain in attested manifest for customer verification.
Preliminary hypothesis: transient consumer lag combined with our batching window may have caused slight re-batching that aligns differently with the customer's expected 'per-request' tokens. The count delta may be explained by deduplication of system-generated telemetry events not considered in their token CSV. Need to produce sample evidence to confirm.

Infra to generate HSM-signed sample bundle for export-20260301-72-apex4521 including per-file HMACs and key version metadata (Marco Chen).
Support to provide customer with verification script and short runbook that validates HMAC chain and counts (Liam).
If discrepancy remains after review of signed bundle, open an internal action to replay consumer partition p-7 for the time window and provide a reconcile report that maps raw events -> delivered files.
Coordinate delivery to customer's compliance mailbox using approved SFTP fingerprint and verify receipt before closing ticket.

title: Attestation-aware Secrets Gateway roadmap and terraform notes
author: Asha Patel
text:
Purpose:

This draft defines the design and staged rollout plan for an "attestation-aware" secrets gateway for private (VPC / on-prem) deployments. The gateway centralizes secret distribution and enforces hardware-backed key operations (HSM/KMS) combined with node attestation. The focus is operational hardening: key management patterns, secrets lifecycle, terraform module recommendations, upgrade and rollback procedures, and audit/logging requirements for compliance.

Goals:
- Provide a single control plane for secrets that can interoperate with customer-managed HSMs (on-prem or cloud) and our KMS adapter.
- Enforce attestation-based release of DEKs to runtime nodes (VMs / containers) to ensure only verified hosts can unwrap keys.
- Minimize blast radius when migrating keys or upgrading modules; provide clear terraform migration steps and rollbacks.
- Produce tamper-evident audit trails and integrate with existing observability pipelines.

Non-goals:
- Implementing full PKI for customer environments (we rely on existing attestation providers: TPM, Nitro Enclaves, or GCP/AWS attestation services).
- Replacing customer HSM vendors; focus on interop and fallback.

High-level architecture (textual):
- Secrets Gateway (SG): stateless control plane deployed in customer VPC; authenticates operator and clusters, stores metadata only.
- KEK Manager: interacts with customer KMS/HSM via configured connectors (cloud KMS, network HSM, HSM appliance over PKCS#11). Holds only KEK references, not plaintext DEKs.
- DEK Store (encrypted): encrypted blob store (object store or vault) in customer environment; encrypted under KEK.
- Attestation Service: verifies node identity and health (TPM quote, cloud attestation token) and issues a short-lived attestation credential used to request DEK unwrapping.
- Secrets Agent (on node): requests DEKs from SG after presenting attestation token and mTLS identity; caches DEKs in memory with TTL + automatic wipe on signals.

Key flows:
1) Provisioning: Operator registers KEK connector in SG with PKCS#11 URI, connector credentials, key ID. Terraform-managed resource: redwood_secrets_kek_connector.
2) Secret write: Operator uploads secret to SG API; SG generates DEK (random), encrypts secret with DEK, calls KEK Manager to wrap DEK -> stores wrapped DEK + ciphertext in DEK store.
3) Node fetch: Node performs attestation -> obtains attestation token -> mTLS to SG -> SG validates attestation / policy -> asks KEK Manager to unwrap DEK (transient) -> returns plaintext DEK to SG just long enough to encrypt transport to node (or uses ECDH established session) -> node receives and decrypts secret locally.
4) Rotation: Operator triggers key rotation; new DEK generation and rewrap. Support rolling rewrap without downtime via dual-KEK acceptance window.

Operational hardening patterns:
- Always prefer HSM for KEK operations; configure offline HSM policies for high-sensitivity KEKs.
- Use split knowledge / dual-operator approval for KEK rotations on production class secrets.
- Enforce short attestation token lifetimes (<= 30s) and single-use tokens where backend supports it.
- Secrets Agent must zero memory on SIGTERM and provide explicit API to purge memory on SIGKILL tolerant platforms.
- Use envelope encryption: SG never persists plaintext DEKs to disk. Logs must redact all DEK plaintext.

Terraform module notes (recommendations):
- Module name: redwood/secrets-gateway/aws (or /gcp /onprem depending on provider). Keep provider-specific pieces behind small wrapper modules.
- Versioning: Semver for modules. Breaking changes only on major bump.
- Resources to expose:
 - variables: keystore_connector (object/string ref), deks_bucket (string), attestation_provider (enum), node_agent_config (map), audit_sink (string), admin_principals (list).
 - outputs: gateway_url, sg_service_account, kek_connector_id, audit_sink_id.
- Example minimal variables block for terraform uses (text snippet):
 variable \"keystore_connector\" { type = string }
 variable \"deks_bucket\" { type = string }
 variable \"attestation_provider\" { type = string }
- Important: implement "import" helpers (terraform import) for existing KEKs and DEK blobs. Provide a migration script that imports existing SecretsGateway state into the module state: scripts/terraform/import_existing_keys.sh (see migration steps below).
- Lock provider versions and add explicit lifecycle rules to prevent accidental destroy: lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } on critical resources when env == "prod".

Upgrade and migration plan (high level):
- Preconditions: backups of wrapped-DEK blobs, KEK connector configuration exported, snapshot of SG configuration, full test suite passing in staging.
- Stage 1 (canary): Deploy new module to staging namespace; run end-to-end test where node attestation -> fetch -> decrypt cycle is exercised with staged HSM connector. Verify audit entries and metrics.
- Stage 2 (pilot): Deploy to one customer tenant (non-critical) or to one AZ within customer VPC. Use traffic shaping to limit live traffic and increase observability.
- Stage 3 (gradual rollout): For each customer region, perform a rolling gateway update with the following steps per region:
 1) terraform plan and review.
 2) terraform apply in canary subnet (1 instance). Verify attestation flow.
 3) Run rewrap test: generate test secret, rotate DEK, verify both old and new DEKs valid within acceptance window.
 4) Increase SG replicas and switch traffic.
 5) Remove old connectors after confirmation window.
- Rollback plan: keep previous module version in a branch that can be applied quickly. If unwrapping starts failing, immediately reverse to previous version and run a reconciliation script that rewraps any DEKs that were rekeyed under new KEK back to previous KEK, using backed-up plaintext OR via HSM facilitate multi-wrap (if available).

Terraform-specific migration steps (detailed):
- Step 0: Export current state: aws s3 cp s3://<deks-bucket>/metadata/backup-YYYYMMDD.json ./backup.json
- Step 1: Map existing KEKs to new terraform resource ids: create a mapping file (keystone-map.csv) with columns: existing_key_id, provider, suggested_tf_id.
- Step 2: Use terraform import for each KEK connector: terraform import module.sg.redwood_kek_connector["<tf_id>"] <existing_key_id>
- Step 3: For DEK blobs: if module maintains list objects, import via terraform import aws_s3_object.dek["<blob_name>"] <bucket>/<path>
- Step 4: Apply plan in dry-run mode: terraform plan -var-file=pilot.tfvars -out=pilot.plan
- Step 5: Apply: terraform apply pilot.plan
- Step 6: Run smoke tests and audit checks.

Secrets lifecycle acceptance tests (smoke checklist):
- Write secret -> read from node agent -> verify plaintext matches.
- Force attestation failure (tamper test) -> ensure secrets not returned.
- Rotate KEK -> ensure old DEKs still decrypt during acceptance window.
- Simulate HSM unavailability -> verify fallback policy: either deny unwrapping or use secondary KEK only if explicitly permitted.
- Verify audit entry emitted for every wrap/unwrap with fields: operation, subject (node id or operator id), timestamp, kek_id, secret_id, attestation_status.

Audit & logging requirements:
- Structured audit events (JSON): include event_id, operation, actor, subject_id, kek_id, attestation_result, outcome, request_id. Do not include plaintext or raw DEKs.
- Tamper-evident ledger: support streaming of audit events to a write-once object store or append-only service (configurable by customer). Provide optional signed checkpoint metadata for periodic snapshots.
- Retention: default 90 days hot, 1 year cold; customer config override supported via module variable.
- Integrations: ELK (Logstash -> ES), Splunk HEC, and syslog. Provide example fluent-bit config blocks in the module docs.
- Alerts: alert if unwrap failure rate > 0.5% in 5m window or if abnormal spike in rotation operations.

HSM/KMS interop considerations and edge cases:
- PKCS#11 vs Cloud KMS APIs: provide adapter layer. PKCS#11 connectors must run in a hardened subnet and use mTLS to SG.
- Network HSM latency: add retry/backoff in KEK manager and avoid blocking attestation path for more than 10s.
- Multi-KMS setups: support multi-wrap (wrap DEK under multiple KEKs) to allow migration with zero-downtime fallback. Document the increased storage and complexity costs.
- Attestation dropout: if attestation provider temporarily fails, do not fallback to unconditional unwrapping. Use configurable emergency procedure requiring operator approval recorded in the audit log.

Observability metrics (suggested):
- secrets_gateway.requests.total, secrets_gateway.unwrap.success, secrets_gateway.wrap.success, secrets_gateway.attestation.failures, secrets_gateway.kms.latency_seconds (p95,p99), secrets_gateway.memory_dek_cache_size.
- Tag metrics by customer_tenant, region, kek_id. Export to Prometheus and set SLOs: unwrap latency p95 < 200ms (local HSM), p95 < 1.5s (network HSM).

Security checklist (pre-deploy):
- [ ] KEK connectors validated with test keys in staging HSM.
- [ ] Terraform module with prevent_destroy in prod-critical resources.
- [ ] Audit sink configured and smoke-tested.
- [ ] Attestation provider integration verified (TPM quotes validated in staging nodes).
- [ ] Secrets Agent signed binaries and reproducible build provenance available.

Open questions / risks:
- Can all customer HSMs support transient unwrap operations without exposing DEK? (some older appliances may require adaptations).
- How to handle air-gapped customers who cannot reach our attestation CA? Proposed: provide local CA distribution and offline attestation mode but requires operator approval and manual audit steps.
- Customer regulatory needs for longer audit retention or different storage location. Module needs retention config per-tenant.

Next actions / owners:
- Prototype adapter for PKCS#11 node -> Diego (due 2024-12-10).
- Create terraform import helper scripts and docs -> Linnea (due 2024-12-05).
- Build staged canary runbook with exact tests -> Marcus (due 2024-12-08).
- Run tabletop for rollback scenarios with SRE -> Asha (due 2024-12-01).

Appendix: quick command snippets
- Example import command for KEK connector:
 terraform import module.sg.redwood_kek_connector["cust-onprem-hsm-01"] pkcs11://token-label/key-id-0

- Example smoke curl (node requesting secret):
 curl -v -k --cert node-agent.crt --key node-agent.key \
 -H "Authorization: Bearer <attestation-token>" \
 https://secrets-gateway.internal/v1/secrets/read?name=service/a/postgres

- Minimal fluent-bit output config for audit sink (example):
 [OUTPUT]
 Name es
 Match secrets-gateway.audits
 Host elk-logging.local
 Port 9200
 Type _doc

End of draft.

Notes: this file is an iterative working doc; treat as draft until owner marks as final.

title: Welcome carousel + progressive disclosure for Dedicated capacity setup
author: Lena Park
text:
Design a compact entry experience for teams starting a Dedicated capacity trial that introduces key decisions (capacity sizing, autoscale policy, SLA tier) using a short welcome carousel and progressive disclosure panels. title: introduce-session-decorator-to-simplify-cross-sdk-streams-and-credential-rotation
author: Noah Rivera
text:
Context: Multiple SDKs exposed slightly different streaming iterator ergonomics and credential refresh hooks which made cross-language examples and platform integrations brittle. This PR introduces a lightweight SessionDecorator abstraction and a small set of shared semantics (ResumeToken v2 + telemetry markers) to harmonize behavior across Python/TypeScript/Go. Goal: make stream consumers simpler to implement, provide a single place for automatic credential rotation and graceful resume, and add telemetry points to measure reauth/backpressure heuristics.

What this changes (high level):
- Add SessionDecorator (py/ts/go) that wraps an existing stream handle/iterator and: automatically refreshes credentials on auth failures, exposes a simple resume_token API, and emits telemetry events for: credential_refresh_attempt, credential_refresh_success, resume_attempt, resume_success, resume_fail.
- Introduce ResumeToken v2 semantics: small stable opaque token returned at stream checkpoints; safe to persist short-term for fast reconnection.
- Unify async iterator ergonomics: all SDKs now offer .stream() returning an async/pullable iterator with a single .resume(resume_token) helper. This removes previously divergent push/pull naming.
- Add backpressure hint optional argument (hint: "latency" | "throughput") to stream factory to allow runtime routing optimizations in Dedicated/Hosted.
- Deprecate older streamResume and token-swap callback signatures; provide compatibility shims for one release cycle.
- Bump SDK versions: python -> 0.42.0, typescript -> 1.12.0, go -> 1.7.3.
- Tests: unit coverage for decorator edge cases, integration tests exercising auth rotation against the dev auth-proxy, and cross-SDK interoperability smoke tests.

Implementation notes:
- Python: session_decorator.py implements an async generator wrapper that catches AuthExpired errors, triggers the provided credential_provider.refresh() and retries from a resume_token. Adds small coordination via an async Lock so concurrent reauth attempts coalesce.
- TypeScript: sessionDecorator.ts implements an async iterable class that mirrors the Python contract, exports a withSessionDecorator factory that preserves stream typing.
- Go: session_decorator.go adds a StreamDecorator type with Resume(ctx, token) and Start(ctx) iterator model; uses channels to translate push->pull where necessary.
- Telemetry: lightweight events emitted to existing "sdk.stream" namespace with fields: event_type, sdk_lang, duration_ms, error_class. These are instrumented behind a toggle so customers can opt into increased telemetry retention.

title: Adaptive sparkline density and column compression mode (prototype)
author: Asha Gupta
text:
Prototype an adaptive table density mode that blends compact row layouts with inline sparkline microcharts and a reversible column compression mode. Goal is to reduce vertical space for high-cardinality datasets while preserving key signals (trend sparklines, sort/filter affordances, and accessible keyboard navigation). This ticket covers design exploration, prototype Figma frames, developer handoff tokens, and a lightweight usability test with 6 internal reviewers.

Prototype frames in Figma demonstrating: default/compact/compact+sparkline states and compressed column state
Interaction spec for entering/exiting compression mode (keyboard + mouse + persisted preference)
Design tokens mapped for spacing, typography, and sparkline mini-chart colors; tokens named to align with core theme tokens
Accessibility checklist passed: tab order preserved, aria-labels for compressed cells, contrast for sparkline strokes
Developer-ready component spec including prop surface for: density, sparkline-on/off, compression-threshold, accessible-label-fn
Lightweight usability feedback notes captured and follow-up tickets created for prioritized engineering work

Trade-offs: we prefer reversible compression that keeps data discoverable over automatic column hiding. Performance mitigation strategy: viewport-gated rendering + server-side precomputed mini-series for heavy datasets. Will propose a telemetry metric to measure sparkline render cost and visibility.

2026-03-01 - Lucas Herrera: Created first Figma frames and shared with PM and Eng. Noted trade-off: sparklines require per-row render budget — recommended sampling strategy for large pages.

title: typed errors + ergonomic iterable reconnect API across SDKs
author: Anya Patel
text:
Motivation: Developers repeatedly hit vague runtime errors when streams failed (auth handshake, transient network) and had to implement ad-hoc parsing logic to decide whether to retry, resume, or surface an error. This PR introduces language-native typed error classes across the three SDKs (Python/TypeScript/Go) and a unified ergonomic iterable reconnect API for stream consumers.

What this change does: 
- Introduces TypedError/StreamError subclasses with machine-friendly error_code, retriable, and suggestion fields across SDKs.
- Adds a new StreamIterable API (python: StreamIterable, ts: createStreamIterable, go: StreamIterator) that yields typed result objects and automatically attempts a single reconnect on retriable failures by default with backoff tuning. Reconnect behavior is configurable by the caller.
- Deprecates low-level sync callback hooks (on_chunk/on_error) in favor of async iterables/promises/iterators to improve ergonomics and parity.
- Adds structured telemetry hooks (opt-in) so apps can key metrics by error_code without brittle string matching.
- Small refactors: move common auth-retry utility into internal/sdk-common, update changelogs and bump SDK package versions.

Backward compatibility and migration: 
- Old callback APIs are still present but marked deprecated; they will emit one deprecation log per process and are scheduled for removal in the next major. Migration notes are added to each SDK CHANGELOG.
- Typed error shapes are additive; existing code catching broad exceptions will continue to work but can opt-in to typed handling for clearer logic.

Testing and rollout: 
- Unit tests added for typed error construction, serialization, and iterable reconnect edge cases. Integration tests simulate transient auth failures with a test double of the runtime.
- Canary rollout to Dedicated region us-west-2 for 72 hours before full merge.

Checklist: 
- [x] Python implementation and tests
- [x] TypeScript implementation and tests
- [x] Go implementation and tests
- [x] Changelogs and version bumps
- [x] Docs snippet in quickstarts repo pointing to new API example

References: Linear ENG-1987, SUP-402 (customer-facing incident), internal design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-1987/stream-reconnect-typed-errors (internal link).

Ethan Park (request changes): The StreamIterable reconnect loop looks like it could retry non-idempotent streams when the model resumed in a different conversation state. Please add a guard for non-resumable streams or require explicit caller opt-in.
Anya Patel (reply): Added an explicit 'resumable' flag to the StreamIterable constructor and documented the caller opt-in behavior. Default remains conservative (single reconnect only for resumable streams).
Lina Gomez (nit): Could you flatten the error_code enum names for TS (avoid nested namespaces) and add a migration mapping in the changelog?
Anya Patel (reply): Flattened the enum, added mapping snippet to TYPESCRIPT changelog. Thanks for catching the nits.
Priya Varma (approve): Verified Python unit tests and manual smoke against canary dedicated cluster; LGTM after CI green.

Adds typed SDK error classes and a new ergonomic iterable reconnect API for streaming across Python/TS/Go SDKs; bump SDK versions: python 1.8.0, typescript 2.3.0, go v0.9.1.

title: Edge switch ARP proxying leads to VPN client IP duplication and intermittent routing to wrong host
text:
Issue summary: Several users reporting intermittent loss of access to internal services while connected to corporate VPN. Symptoms include duplicate IP conflict alerts on endpoints, frequent VPN re-auth events, and traffic appearing to be routed to a different on-prem host (service 10.23.5.12). Impact: ~8% of VPN sessions in us-west over the last 48h experienced short blackholes (30-90s) impacting git pushes, internal CI jobs, and ssh sessions. Scope: affects users on Wi-Fi SSID 'Redwood-Corp' behind specific edge switches in building SF2 rack 7.

1) Connect laptop to 'Redwood-Corp' Wi-Fi in SF2 building (tested on macOS 13 and Ubuntu 22.04)
2) Establish VPN session to redwood-vpn-usw.redwood.net (WireGuard-based corporate VPN)
3) Trigger continuous ping to an internal host (ping -i 0.2 10.23.5.12)
4) Observe intermittent duplicate IP warnings on client and packets forwarded to an unexpected MAC on the L2 domain
5) Reproduce frequency increases when there is a short burst of multicast/mDNS traffic on the same AP's radio

Client syslog excerpt: 'kernel: arp: IP address 10.23.8.45 claimed by 00:11:22:33:44:55 (conflict)'
Switch (edge-sw-7) log: 'proxy-arp conflict detected for 10.23.8.45, source 00:66:77:88:99:AA bridging-port 5'
Packet capture (pcap) snippet: ARP reply for 10.23.8.45 with two different source MACs within 120ms
VPN server metrics: client rekey count spike (client 10.23.8.45) correlated to timestamp 2026-03-12T14:12Z
Internal service (10.23.5.12) reported TCP reset spikes aligning with client blackholes

Hypothesis 1: Edge switch proxy-arp configured for legacy NAT path is responding to ARP for VPN-assigned addresses from an overlapping DHCP pool, causing two active ARP entries on the LAN.
Hypothesis 2: A misconfigured VXLAN/bridge on edge-sw-7 is advertising ARP for the VPN subnet into the campus L2 segment when multicast bursts occur.
What we tried: - Disabled proxy-arp on edge-sw-7 port-channel to AP group temporarily (no immediate reduction). - Isolated a suspect AP by moving a test client to a different AP (blackhole persisted only when client served by AP-7A). - Captured pcap on AP, switch uplink, and VPN server concurrently for correlated timestamps (pcaps saved to /mnt/logs/INT-460811/pcaps/).
Preliminary find: ARP 'gratuitous' replies with VPN client IP are being injected by the switch's 'proxy-arp' feature only when the AP's multicast queue exceeds threshold. The switch returns ARP for the same IP with a different MAC that matches a spare management interface in rack 7 (00:66:77:88:99:AA).

Intermittent connectivity loss for internal developer workflows (git/ssh/CI). Approximately 8% of VPN sessions in the SF2 us-west site affected in the window; potential for data-transfer retries and CI flakiness. No customer-facing outage but notable developer productivity hit.

1) Placed affected edge switch (edge-sw-7) in monitoring schedule and enabled debug logging for proxy-arp events.
2) Temporarily increased DHCP lease affinity for VPN pool for clients in SF2 to reduce the window for IP reuse.
3) Asked campus networking team to disable 'proxy-arp' global feature on a staging switch and observe (ongoing).
4) Notified platform reliability and CI owners of potential re-run needs for impacted jobs (Slack #incidents and #platform-alerts).

2026-03-11 09:18 - Jonah Reed: Assigned to network; will coordinate switch config changes and gather pcaps. Next action: schedule maintenance window if we need to push config rollback.
2026-03-12 15:25 - Priya Shah (campus-net): Reproduced proxy-arp responses on edge-sw-7 when AP multicast queue > 70%. Suspect firmware 1.2.3 on these switches has a known misc bridging bug. Opened ticket with vendor (TAC-889233).
2026-03-13 08:52 - Jonah Reed: Vendor TAC confirmed the switch may respond to ARP for non-local subnets under multicast overload in 1.2.3. Recommended immediate mitigation: set 'proxy-arp disable' on VRF for AP VLANs and upgrade firmware to 1.2.6.
2026-03-14 07:30 - Aisha Malik: Applied 'proxy-arp disable' to edge-sw-7 in staged maintenance window (07:00-07:15). Monitoring: VPN rekey spikes reduced from 47/hr to 2/hr for affected clients in the first 24h.
2026-03-14 10:02 - Jonah Reed: Confirming RFC and rollout plan for global fix. Proposed follow-up: firmware upgrade across SF2 rack 4-9, audit for proxy-arp enabled on other edge switches, and update config baseline to explicitly disable proxy-arp for VPN/DHCP subnets.

Switch firmware (1.2.3) bug caused proxy-arp behavior under high multicast load leading to ARP advertisements for VPN-assigned addresses. This created ephemeral duplicate IP assignments on the L2 domain and caused VPN clients to experience routing blackholes and rekeys.

Mitigation applied: 'proxy-arp disable' set on edge-sw-7 AP VLANs during maintenance window 2026-03-14 07:00-07:15.
Temporary workaround: increased DHCP lease affinity and moved high-multicast APs to separate RF profile to reduce multicast bursts.
Permanent fix: planned firmware upgrade to 1.2.6 across SF2 edge switches (racks 4-9) and config baseline change to disable proxy-arp for VPN/DHCP subnets. Vendor TAC provided patch notes and recommended upgrade path.
Follow-ups: - Create change request CR-2026-0415 for firmware rollout. - Run campus-wide audit script to detect 'proxy-arp' enabled instances and remediate. - Add regression test to onboarding checklist for AP multicast stress.
Status: Partial fix applied and validated; full remediation scheduled (see CR-2026-0415).
