title: Tribe Liaison & Status-Wire Protocol: Incident Playbook
author: Leah Park
text:
Overview:
This playbook defines the Tribe Liaison role and the Status-Wire communication protocol used for coordinated incident response across teams (platform, runtime, SRE, customer success, and engineering tribes). It is intended for incidents with cross-team impact (multi-service degradation, multi-region latency spikes, or model-quality regressions affecting production).

Purpose:
- Reduce cross-team friction and duplicated messaging during incidents.
- Provide a repeatable activation workflow for public and customer-facing communications.
- Offer templates and checklists for rapid, consistent status updates and post-incident evidence collection.

When to activate the Status-Wire:
1) Any P0 or P1 incident declared by SRE / Incident Commander.
2) Sustained SLO deviation > 5 minutes affecting > 1 customer or > 10% of traffic.
3) Model-quality regression that causes repeated error responses or hallucination rates above threshold.

Roles & Responsibilities:
- Incident Commander (IC): overall incident authority; owns triage decisions and escalation to execs.
- Tribe Liaison (TL): single named engineer from each affected tribe. TLs consolidate technical findings and represent their team on the Status Wire. Responsible for:
 - Rapidly validating impact and proposed mitigations for their domain.
 - Contributing one-line status and next steps for each wire update.
 - Collecting evidence artifacts (logs, traces, perf snapshots).
- Bridge Operator: manages the incident bridge, recording timeline and action items.
- Communications Lead (Comms): drafts customer-facing updates, coordinates legal/compliance review if required.
- Customer Success Rep: prepares prioritized customer impact list and coordinates direct outreach where needed.

Activation checklist (first 10 minutes):
1. IC declares incident and sets severity.
2. Pager alert: On-call SRE acknowledges and opens bridge.
3. IC assigns an engineered TL per affected tribe (platform, runtime, model-infra, console).
4. Bridge Operator posts Status-Wire channel link (Slack #status-wire-<incident-id>) and pins initial incident summary.
5. TLs post immediate 1-line: "{team}: impact (yes/no), likely root area, immediate mitigation". Example: "Runtime: partial KV-cache eviction causing 40% increased tail latency; restarting cache nodes as mitigation"
6. Comms drafts and posts first customer notice (see templates).

Escalation matrix (quick reference):
| Role | Primary | Secondary | Escalation threshold | Contact method |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Incident Commander | SRE Lead on-call | Eng Director on-call | >30 minutes to containment | Pager / Phone |
| Tribe Liaison | Team on-call engineer | Team tech lead | No mitigation found in 20 minutes | Slack DM / Pager |
| Comms Lead | Support Ops | Head of CS | Customer SLA breach or regulatory impact | Slack / Email |

Runbook snippets (copy into service runbooks):
- inference-gateway:
 1) Check service health: curl -fsS https://health.redwood.internal/inference-gateway/metrics || true
 2) Query recent traces: otel-cli query --service inference-gateway --last 15m
 3) If error-rate > 2% and tail-latency > 800ms, toggle canary fallback: curl -XPOST https://admin.redwood.internal/route/fallback -d '{"route":"/generate","model":"gptx-small-fallback"}'
- kv-cache:
 1) Inspect eviction log: gcloud logging read "resource.labels.instance_id=\"kv-cache\"" --limit 200
 2) Rehydrate hot-keys from snapshot: /opt/tools/kv-rehydrate --snapshot s3://redwood-cache/snaps/latest --keys hot-keys.txt

Status-Wire messaging cadence:
- Initial (T+10m): Brief impact, services affected, immediate mitigations in progress, expected next update in 30 minutes.
- T+30m: Progress update including measurable signposts (error-rate, latency, traffic diverted) and next steps.
- Every 30—60m afterward: update until containment. Shorten cadence to 15 minutes if customer-impacting or high uncertainty.
- Containment achieved: merge into final incident summary and begin postmortem timeline.

Customer-facing templates (copy/paste-ready):
- Short status page entry (public):
 Title: "Degraded API latency for text generation — investigating"
 Body: "We are investigating increased latency affecting text-generation API requests in US-West. Impact: intermittent delays up to ~4s for a subset of requests. Current actions: rolling restart of KV cache nodes and routing a portion of traffic to fallback model variants. Next update: in 30 minutes. Affected customers will receive direct notices if they meet SLA thresholds."

- Email / CS message (for affected customers):
 Subject: "Service update: transient delays for Redwood text generation — {incident-id}"
 Body: "Hi {customer_name},

We are actively responding to an incident affecting text-generation latency in {region}. Some requests are experiencing elevated latency or transient errors. Our SRE and runtime teams have deployed mitigations (cache restarts and traffic routing) and are monitoring recovery. We will provide another update at {time} or sooner if status changes. We apologize for the disruption and will share a detailed post-incident report within 72 hours.

If you require escalation or mitigation assistance (e.g., pinning model variants or temporary throttling), reply to this message and your Customer Success lead will coordinate.

— Redwood Support"

Game day and simulation plan (quarterly):
- Objective: exercise cross-tribe coordination and Status-Wire to validate SLAs and communications.
- Frequency: quarterly for SRE + product-critical tribes; monthly light drills for new joiners.
- Duration: 90 minutes.
- Roles assigned in advance: IC, Bridge Operator, 3 TLs, Comms, CS.
- Scenario example: synthetic KV eviction at scale causing 30% tail latency increase and 5% error-rate.
- Success criteria: containment within 45 minutes, customer-facing update within 10 minutes, complete evidence capture (traces/logs/metrics) uploaded to incident ticket.

Post-incident evidence & postmortem template:
- Attachments required in postmortem: timeline (with T+ minute markers), logs (last 60 minutes per service), relevant traces (span IDs), Mitigation steps, Root cause analysis, Action items with owners and SLA for completion.
- Postmortem outline (use this header structure):
 *Summary*
 *Impact* (customers, SLOs)
 *Timeline* (bullet list with timestamps)
 *Root Cause*
 *Contributing factors*
 *Immediate remediation*
 *Long-term fixes*
 *Action items (owner + due date)*
 *Verification plan*

On-call rotation fairness & handoff checklist:
- Primary rotation length: 9 days (3-person rotation recommended for fairness).
- Shadowing: new on-call engineers shadow for 2 rotations.
- Handoff checklist (mandatory before shift end):
 1) Confirm no ongoing incidents assigned.
 2) Share any active mitigations, experiments, or rollouts in last 12 hours.
 3) Verify Escalation list and on-call contacts are up-to-date.
 4) If any open action items: add clear owner and ETA.

Bridge & tooling references:
- Incident bridge template: Zoom link pinned in channel; Google Doc timeline template: https://docs.internal.redwood/incident-timeline-template
- Dashboards:
 - SRE Living Dashboard: https://grafana.internal.redwood/d/ll1/sre-living-dashboard
 - Model Quality Monitor: https://grafana.internal.redwood/d/mq/model-quality
 - Token-level cost/latency: Console -> Observability -> Token Insights
- Runbook registry: Confluence runbook index (add link to service runbook pages).

Quick checklist for the Tribe Liaison (TL):
1) Join bridge and post one-line status.
2) Verify logs and traces for your domain and attach evidence to bridge notes.
3) Propose emergency mitigation and estimate time-to-contain.
4) Commit to follow-up artifact (e.g., heap dump, timeline snippet).

Appendix: sample Slack status-wire message (copy-paste)
```
[Status-Wire] Incident: INF-2026-842
IC: @sre-oncall
Services: inference-gateway (P), kv-cache (P)
Runtime: Restarting 2/3 cache replicas; expected partial recovery in ~12m. Error-rate peaked at 4.1%; tail latency 95p=950ms. Next update in 30m.
TLs: @runtime-tl (runtime), @platform-tl (platform), @modelinfra-tl (model)
```

Operational notes & governance:
- All incident owners must file a postmortem for P0/P1 incidents within 72 hours of containment.
- Action items must be tracked in the central incident board and have clear owners and due dates.
- Quarterly reviews: the Incident Review Council will audit a sample of postmortems for completeness and follow-through.

Related pages and references:
- Incident evidence collection standard, SLO definitions, Runbook registry.

Contact & ownership:
- Primary owner: Leah Park (SRE, Incident Ops)
- Secondary owner: Marcus Chen (Runtime)

title: add multipart/form-data handling, strict content-type validation, and payload limit enforcement for API tool/file inputs
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Motivation: users integrating tool/function calling and file uploads via the OpenAI-compatibility endpoints were sending a wide variety of content-types and very large multipart requests which caused inconsistent runtime behavior, high memory pressure, and unexpected acceptance of unsupported payloads. This PR introduces a focused, backwards-compatible implementation for multipart/form-data parsing on the OpenAI-compatibility path, strict Content-Type validation for tool/file inputs, and deterministic payload limits both per-file and per-request. Summary of changes: 1) Add a streaming-safe multipart parser that yields parts rather than buffering entire requests; 2) Validate Content-Type of each part (whitelist: text/*, image/*, application/json, application/octet-stream with explicit size checks); 3) Enforce configurable limits: max_file_size (default 10MiB), max_total_request_size (default 50MiB), max_parts_count (default 20). These defaults are conservative and documented; they can be overridden at tenant or route level via API config. 4) Hook validation into the OpenAI-compat layer so existing client integrations get predictable errors (400/413) with structured error bodies when inputs are rejected. 5) Add detailed unit and integration tests and end-to-end tests for streaming uploads and for the dedicated Dedicated/Private ingress paths. Backwards compatibility notes: this does not change the non-multipart JSON body semantics. Existing users who relied on accepting arbitrary large file uploads should update their tenant config or use Redwood Dedicated with higher quotas. Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind feature.enable_multipart_input (off by default); staged rollout to internal dogfood tenants, then gradual roll to 10%, 50%, 100% via config rollout. Checklist: - [x] Streaming-safe multipart parser implemented - [x] Content-Type whitelist + validation errors - [x] Per-file and per-request size enforcement + configurable defaults - [x] OpenAI-compat error mapping and structured error shapes - [x] Tests: unit, integration, e2e - [x] Docs: compatibility notes and config guide - [x] Telemetry: counters for rejected parts and throttled requests - [x] Migration & rollout plan included Testing notes: the multipart parser uses a small constant memory footprint for each active part and yields part metadata to the handler; large parts trigger a streaming drain with early termination (413 response) to avoid OOM. Integration tests exercise combination of binary and text parts, wrong content-types, and boundary cases around the configured limits. Telemetry: added metrics api.multipart.rejected_content_type, api.multipart.rejected_size, api.multipart.accepted_parts and a hist for part sizes. Implementation details: - parser: runtime/multipart/stream_parser.py - validator: api/validation/multipart_validator.py - compat layer: api/openai_compat/input_adapter.py - config: config/defaults/multipart.yaml - docs: docs/openai-compat/multipart.md - tests: tests/unit/test_multipart_parser.py, tests/integration/test_openai_compat_multipart.py Error shape examples (structured output): when a part is rejected we return 413 with a JSON body {"error":{"type":"request_too_large","message":"part exceeds max_file_size","meta":{"part_name":"file","limit_bytes":10485760}}} and 400 for unsupported content-types with type unsupported_media_type. Observability: trace spans added around parse->validate->route dispatch to help pinpoint latency regressions. Related items: Linear ENG-2728 (multipart uploader stability), PM-146 (OpenAI compat feature parity).

Liam Chen: key question — do we need to special-case application/pdf? many partners send PDFs as application/pdf; current whitelist would block it. Suggest adding application/pdf or making whitelist configurable per-tenant.
Aisha Patel: replied — agreed, added application/pdf to tenant_whitelist in config and made default conservative. Added test case + note in docs explaining why binary blobs should be limited.
Ravi Singh: please ensure the validator surfaces clear errors for multipart boundary parsing failures; I saw a flaky crash in an initial run.
Aisha Patel: replied — parser now catches malformed boundary exceptions and returns a 400 with error.type=malformed_multipart and includes low-signal debug id for tracing; updated tests.
Sofia Alvarez: approved — addressed my comments about metrics naming and added a suggestion to include counter tags for tenant_id and route_id.
CI Bot: integration-tests failed on first run due to test harness timeout; rerun completed successfully.
QA: noted an edge case where client SDK retries might double-submit large files; added a recommendation in docs and an optional idempotency header support in adapter.

Added multipart/form-data support on OpenAI-compat API paths with strict content-type validation and configurable per-file and per-request size limits. Default limits: 10MiB per file, 50MiB per request. Feature is behind a feature flag and can be enabled per-tenant. See docs/openai-compat/multipart.md for migration steps.

title: consolidate-sampled-context-anchors-and-cost-delta-annotations
author: Priya Menon
text:
Motivation: Long-tail requests and multi-turn sessions make it hard to correlate expensive tokens with the actual prompt context. Alert noise for cost spikes often stems from superficially similar traces that differ in a few context tokens. This PR introduces two complementary observability primitives: (1) sampled context anchors — compact, privacy-safe snapshots attached to selected traces that let engineers inspect a representative prefix without storing full payloads; and (2) cost-delta annotations — span-level annotations that capture the incremental token cost relative to a baseline (baseline = first N tokens of the session or pinned model variant), enabling per-span cost-attribution and easy identification of regression candidates.

What this change does (high level):
- Adds a lightweight sampled-context store and recorder in the runtime that writes encrypted, k-anonymized anchors for 1% of long-tail sessions (configurable). Anchors include token fingerprints, anonymized prompt length buckets, and hashed prompt-context tags for grouping (no raw PII/token content stored).
- Adds cost-delta annotations into the tracing pipeline: each model-stage span now carries cost.delta and cost.baseline fields (numeric micro-units). These are added as span attributes and surfaced to OTEL and internal trace indexer.
- Dashboard updates: new dashboard panels on Console -> Observability that show per-route cost-delta distribution, anchor-cluster heatmap (session groups), and annotated trace + anchor join views.
- Alert tuning: new alerting rule that groups alerts by anchor-hash first and surfaces a single grouped alert for clusters of similar high-cost traces (reduces noisy duplicates). Added docs and runbook snippets for triage.

Implementation notes and constraints:
- Context anchors are generated at the runtime layer (redwood/service/runtime) before caching/quantization to avoid skew. Anchors emit a deterministic anchor-hash derived from a salted rolling-hash; the salt is customer-scoped to avoid cross-tenant correlation.
- Cost delta math: cost.delta = observed_token_cost - baseline_token_cost, baseline_token_cost is computed using a rolling median of the first 32 tokens for the route/model combo and periodically recomputed by a background aggregator.
- Privacy compliance: anchors are truncated and tokenized into fingerprint sketches; feature flags and customer-level opt-out is supported.
- Performance: profiling showed a 0.2% median p99 added latency on typical requests in our stage perf lab; batching and non-blocking flush paths mitigate the tail impact.

e7fd3b0: runtime: add sampled-context-anchor generator with opt-out flag
d1c9a6f: tracing: append cost.delta and cost.baseline attributes to model spans
9b88221: indexer: add anchor-hash join key and compact indexer path
4c2f8aa: console: add dashboard panels and saved queries for cost-delta and anchor clusters
ab3e4f5: alerts: introduce grouped anchor-based alert rule and doc runbook
ff12d8b: tests: add unit tests and perf-lab smoke harness
c0b5e2d: docs: observability guide and runbook snippets

Evan Carter: Left a few inline comments about the anchor hashing entropy. Asked for a short doc explaining how the salt is generated and rotated. Approved after changes.
Luca Marin: Requested an explicit opt-out path for enterprise Private deployments and noted a missing unit test for the indexer join. Verified tests after fix and approved.
Jade Huang: Focused on alert UX; asked for grouping threshold to be configurable from Console. Verified dashboard UX and approved.
Author (Priya Menon): Addressed comments; added salt rotation doc, opt-out flag for private installs, and a test for the indexer join. Responded to Jade with screenshots and added a toggle to the dashboard config.

Added sampled context anchors for long-tail session triage and per-span cost-delta annotations. New Console dashboards for cost-delta distributions and anchor clusters. Alert grouping by anchor-hash to reduce duplicate cost alerts. Feature gate and enterprise opt-out available.

title: Dispatch surface playback: edge vs core econ memo
author: Maya Patel
text:
TL;DR:
We ran a small set of controlled playback tests to compare dispatch semantics across edge-forward dispatch (short hops to nearby edge cells with small prefetch), core-tiling multiplexing (centralized GPU tiles with larger batching windows), and a hybrid with KV-prefetch evictions. Results show: edge-dispatch-prefetch gives best p50 and p95 for short responses (<=128 tokens) at a modest cost premium; core-tiling-multiplex achieves far better $/1k tokens for long outputs (>=512 tokens) but suffers p99 regressions under bursty arrival; hybrid-evict trades in slightly higher median latency for better p99 and solid $/1k for mid-length responses.

Why we ran this (context):
- Product asks for a short, shareable comparison to inform routing policy defaults for chat-lite vs doc-embed routes.
- We need simple knobs that map to developer-facing toggles: prefer-edge, prefer-core, hybrid-prefetch.
- This is intentionally lightweight — not exhaustive — but focused on practical, explainable deltas to communicate with PM and Console teams.

Experiment setup (short):
- Date: 2026-05-15 to 2026-05-17.
- Hardware: G-core (A100x2) for core tiles; Edge cells running T4-equivalent virtual nodes (quantized runtime).
- Model: open-llm v2-3B (float16 in core, int8 quantized at edge).
- Workloads: 3 synthetic mixes: 
 * Short-burst: 80% <= 64 tok, 20% 128 tok (chat-lite mimic)
 * Mid-thread: 60% 128-256 tok, 40% 256-512 tok (assistant flows)
 * Long-pour: 100% >=512 tok (document summarization)
- Traffic shape: poisson baseline + injected microbursts (10s, 100req/s spikes) to exercise tail behavior.
- Measurement: p50, p95, p99 latency on response-ready (end-of-stream), tokens/sec observed, and computed $/1k tokens using current infra cost model (GPU-hour amortized + infra egress).

Configs tested (names used below):
- edge-dispatch-prefetch: nearest edge cell, small prefetch window (prefetch 16 tokens, KV cache enabled), quantized runtime.
- core-tiling-multiplex: central core fleet, tiling multiplex scheduling, larger batching window (50ms), float16 kernels.
- hybrid-evict: route initial tokens to edge (prefetch 32), then stitch/resume on core if session length > 256 or predicted tail; KV eviction policy to avoid cache thrash.

Raw (annotated) numbers (mid-thread workload, 10k requests each):

Config | p50 ms | p95 ms | p99 ms | tokens/sec | $/1k tokens
--------------------------|--------|--------|--------|------------|-------------
edge-dispatch-prefetch | 72 | 180 | 420 | 1,350 | $0.145
core-tiling-multiplex | 120 | 350 | 1,150 | 3,800 | $0.062
hybrid-evict | 95 | 240 | 470 | 2,200 | $0.085

Notes on numbers: p99 for core spikes when bursts coincide with long outputs — batching helps throughput but hurts tail. Edge has lower medians due to proximity + quantized runtime but unit cost is higher because T4 nodes have lower utilization and int8 inefficiencies on our current kernels. Hybrid avoids the worst tail by stitching early tokens locally and moving heavy tails to the core when predicted, which balances p99 and $/1k.

Short-burst workload summary (best config per metric):
- p50: edge-dispatch-prefetch (42 ms)
- p95: edge-dispatch-prefetch (112 ms)
- $/1k: core-tiling-multiplex ($0.058) but p95/p99 worse

Long-pour workload summary:
- Core-tiling-multiplex dominates in $/1k and tokens/sec (as expected). p99 improves if burst smoothing is applied (admission control). Edge becomes prohibitively expensive for >512 token outputs.

ASCII latency profile (mid-thread, approximated CDF buckets):
- edge-dispatch-prefetch: [<=100ms: 64%] [<=300ms: 90%] [<=500ms: 98%]
- core-tiling-multiplex: [<=100ms: 28%] [<=300ms: 76%] [<=1000ms: 96%]
- hybrid-evict: [<=100ms: 48%] [<=300ms: 86%] [<=500ms: 97%]

Operational implications and trade-offs:
- Developer UX (chat-lite): prefer-edge gives snappier interactive feel. Cost delta is modest at low scale but compounds at volume. Recommend UI default "prefer-edge" for chat-lite small volumes with an opt-out in Console for cost-conscious teams.
- Enterprise/default: prefer-core or hybrid for high-throughput/long-inference pipelines. Core routing improves unit economics and should be promoted for summarization, batch embeddings, and long-chats.
- SLO design: if customers require p95 < 200ms for chat, edge or hybrid is necessary for short responses; but p99 SLOs need admission control and burst smoothing in core deployment to be viable.

Caveats & open questions (things to follow up):
- Kernel inefficiencies: our quantized int8 kernel on edge shows a per-token penalty for certain attention shapes; rebenchmark after kernel patch (PR #342).
- Network variability: tests used emulated edge latencies; run a small customer-realistic replay to confirm.
- Cost model sensitivity: $/1k uses current amortization assumptions; re-run with alternate GPU pricing (spot vs reserved) for a sensitivity table.
- Stitching overhead: hybrid transition points used a simple heuristic; potential for ML-based tail prediction to reduce unnecessary core handoffs.

Recommended next steps (practical):
1) Share this note with Console + Router owners and ask for A/B of default route for new chat-lite workspaces (2-week experiment).
2) Re-run mid-thread tests after quant kernel patch and with spot pricing assumptions (owner: Evan).
3) Build small visual one-pager for PD and Sales that explains the three knobs (prefer-edge, prefer-core, hybrid-prefetch) with the 3-line summary and a simple cost/latency matrix.
4) Add hybrid handoff telemetry in the onboarding trace (small schema change) to measure handoff rate and end-to-end join latency in real traffic.

Appendix: quick checklist for replicability
- seed traffic generator: scripts/bench/playback_v2 with config: mid-thread.json
- model commit: open-llm/v2-3b@sha:f3a2c4
- runtime flags used: --batch-window-ms=50 (core), --edge-prefetch=16 (edge), --kv-evict=adaptive (hybrid)
- cost calc script: pricing/calc_unit_cost.py --amort=on-demand --include-egress

Notes-to-self (raw):
- push a short slide deck to /product/presentations after Evan's kernel results.
- add a small experiment to try prefetch=64 on edge to see if p99 improves (may hurt p50).
- consider adding 'prefer-core-for-long' automated route: client-side hint + server-side enforcement.

End of memo.

-- Maya
(rough draft; will tidy into one-pager once follow-ups done)

title: M1 MacBook DEP re-enroll fails: third-party kext blocks MDM profile & cert install after depot repair
text:
Issue summary:
After depot repair (logic board replacement) of Apple Silicon MacBooks, several devices fail to complete DEP/MDM re-enrollment during OOBE. The MDM profile push stalls and the SSO cert/profile does not install. A third-party kernel extension (legacy VPN client kext) is present on the image and appears to intercept network stack initialization during first-boot, preventing MDM from completing.

Impact:
- ~6 devices failed re-enroll in the last week after depot repairs; devices remain unmanaged and cannot receive corporate certs/policies.
- Affected users are blocked from corporate VPN and SSO until manual remediation.

Context/Notes:
- All affected units are Apple Silicon (M1/M2) models returned from repair with a replaced system board.
- Image includes a legacy enterprise VPN that installs a kernel extension for older macOS versions; the kext is code-signed but not notarized for Apple Silicon-specific requirements.
- On Intel Macs this did not present at scale; appears tied to kext load order and the new hardware IDs after logic board swap.

1) Use depot repair flow; replace logic board on M1 MacBook and restore company image via DEP image tool.
2) Boot device into OOBE with network available (corporate Wi-Fi or ethernet via dock).
3) Device checks in with DEP, Apple MDM push begins but stalls on profile installation step 'com.redwood.mdm:install-profile'.
4) Observe that sysdiagnose shows kernel extension related logs and the mdm-agent log shows repeated network initialization failures.

DEP check-in completes but MDM profile push stalls. mdm-agent repeatedly logs: 'network stack init failed - interface not ready' and macOS kernel reports 'kext com.company.vpn attempted unsupported operations on Apple Silicon'.

Device should complete DEP/MDM re-enroll automatically during OOBE, install SSO certs and corporate profiles without manual intervention.

mdm-agent: 2024-11-15T09:12:17Z ERROR network: interface not ready

kernel: Nov 15 09:12:16 kextd[54]: com.company.vpn: attempted to register deprecated network filter (not supported on arm64e)
system.log excerpt: DEP: token validated, pushing profiles (profileID=com.redwood.sso) - stalled at 98%

Initial triage by mac-ops: reproduced on staging image with legacy VPN kext present.
Disabling the VPN kext prior to OOBE (via post-image script that removes the kext bundle) allows MDM to complete normally.
Kext is signed by vendor but not notarized for M1-specific requirements; notarization warning appears in kext load messages.
Hypothesis: on new system board hardware IDs, the kext attempts a network-level hook earlier in boot and blocks system network interfaces until degraded, causing mdm-agent timeouts.
Checked DEP portal: device records are correct; no Apple-side MDM flags indicate block.

Priya Nair (mac-ops): 'I can reproduce on MBP18,1 with the vendor kext present. Removing the kext before runbook upload fixes enrollment. Need to confirm scope of devices with this kext.'
Aaron Kim (SecOps): 'Vendor confirmed they have an M1-compatible signed driver but we require notarization and an updated installer that avoids early network hooks. Asking for vendor ETA.'
Jordan Lee (reporter): 'Opened INT ticket after 4 devices returned from repair this week failed. Will pause autopilot-like reassign workflows until remediation.'

Workaround applied: depot imaging pipeline modified to detect and remove legacy VPN kexts on Apple Silicon builds prior to shipping. Mac-ops will reimage affected units and perform manual profile push where needed. Vendor engaged for notarized M1-friendly installer; security requested vendor PR to remove kernel-level hooks and move to NetworkExtension framework.

Follow-up actions:
- Ship a patched image by 2024-11-20 without legacy kexts for Apple Silicon fleet (assigned to mac-ops).
- Vendor action item logged; expect vendor ETA in 5 business days (tracked in related_github_pr).
- Add a post-repair verification step in depot runbook to validate MDM check-in within 10 minutes of OOBE.

2024-11-16: mac-ops rolled a temporary image removal step for kexts; 3/3 reimage attempts succeeded and devices checked into MDM.
2024-11-17: SecOps confirmed vendor engagement; vendor PR submitted to GitHub (see related_github_prs).
Follow-up ticket created to audit all Apple Silicon images for legacy kernel extensions (INT-1000457).

title: Developer Shield: SDK Chaos & Recovery Lab
author: Maya Chen
text:
Summary:
This lab is a hands-on developer-ready guide for intentionally breaking SDK integrations, observing telemetry "golden traces", and validating recovery strategies against Redwood inference endpoints. The goal is to provide a repeatable workshop that SDK authors, platform engineers, and support oncall can run in ~90 minutes to verify resilience SLA behaviors and canonical fixes.

Goals:
- Create deterministic fault patterns targeting SDK -> runtime interactions (timeouts, partial responses, truncated streams).
- Validate observability: traces, spans, logs, and token-level cost telemetry for each failure mode.
- Exercise client-side fallbacks (retry jitter, streaming resume, local cache) and server-side graceful degradation (model variant fallback, rate-aware routing).
- Produce documented artifacts: golden-trace examples, regression tests, and a triage checklist for support.

Prerequisites:
1) Developer machine with Python 3.10+ and Node.js 18+.
2) Access to a Redwood dev tenant (api key with dev-level quota).
3) Local test harness repo cloned: git@github.com:redwood-inference/sdk-chaos-lab.git (or use the starter scaffold below).
4) Docker (for running a local network proxy/fault injector) and curl.

Quickstart scaffold (clone + bootstrap):
1. git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/sdk-chaos-lab.git && cd sdk-chaos-lab
2. cp .env.example .env && edit REDWOOD_API_KEY and REDWOOD_BASE_URL if needed
3. make deps # installs node_modules and pip env
4. ./scripts/start-proxy.sh # starts the fault-injection proxy on localhost:8080

High-level lab exercises (90 minutes):
1) Golden-trace capture (15–20m)
 - Objective: record a baseline successful call for the workload (embed -> retrieve -> generate).
 - Steps: run scripts/capture_trace.py --scenario baseline --output traces/golden_baseline.json
 - Expected output: spans for http.request, sdk.deserialize, runtime.kv_cache_hit metrics.

2) Timeout and retry behavior (20m)
 - Fault: the proxy introduces a 1200ms delay for the first POST to /v1/generate.
 - Client expectations: Sane client-side timeout (default 1s) should trigger retry logic with exponential backoff; the SDK should not double-bill tokens when retrying.
 - Commands: ./scripts/inject_fault.sh --type delay --path /v1/generate --ms 1200 --once
 - Validation: run examples/python/stream_resume_test.py and assert: one logged retry, one successful response, token_cost metric unchanged compared to baseline.

3) Truncated stream and resume semantics (20m)
 - Fault: proxy truncates server-sent event stream mid-response.
 - Client behavior to validate: library should surface a resumable id/token and resume the stream without user-visible duplication.
 - Example (Node):
 const r = await Redwood.generateStreaming({ prompt, resume: true });
 // on 'truncated' event the client should call r.resume()

4) Partial model fallback (15m)
 - Fault: simulated out-of-capacity on preferred model (m-latest) causing 503 on cold start.
 - Desired platform reaction: automatic fallback to m-latest-quantized variant or regional replica within 200ms.
 - Validation: ensure request latency remains below 800ms and output quality regression < 2% on the golden prompt set. Use scripts/quality_check.sh --baseline traces/golden_baseline.json --target traces/fallback_run.json

5) Telemetry and cost guardrails (10m)
 - Validate that trace includes token_count, model_variant, quantization_profile, route_key, and billing_unit fields.
 - Confirm alert firing: a synthetic gauge (sdk.request.latency.p50) exceeding 1s triggers an alert in the sandbox paging channel.

SDK patterns and canonical code snippets
- Python retry wrapper (idempotent generation calls):

 import time
 import requests

 def call_with_retries(payload, max_attempts=3):
 backoff = 0.2
 attempt = 0
 while attempt < max_attempts:
 attempt += 1
 try:
 resp = requests.post(
 "http://localhost:8080/v1/generate", json=payload, timeout=1.0
 )
 resp.raise_for_status()
 return resp.json()
 except requests.exceptions.Timeout:
 time.sleep(backoff)
 backoff *= 2
 continue
 raise RuntimeError("exhausted retries")

- Node streaming-resume pattern:

 const { RedwoodClient } = require('@redwood/sdk');
 const client = new RedwoodClient({ baseURL: process.env.REDWOOD_BASE_URL });

 async function streamingExample() {
 const stream = await client.generateStream({ model: 'm-latest', prompt: 'Hello' });
 stream.on('error', async (err) => {
 if (err.code === 'TRUNCATED') {
 await stream.resume(); // library handles token-prefix dedupe
 } else {
 throw err;
 }
 });
 }

Golden trace format and required fields (table):
- The lab standard for a golden trace is a JSON file with a top-level array of spans. Each span in the array must contain the following string fields:
 - trace_id
 - span_id
 - parent_id (nullable string allowed; include as empty string if none)
 - name (e.g., http.request, sdk.serialize, runtime.infer)
 - start_ts (ISO 8601)
 - end_ts (ISO 8601)
 - attributes (a flattened comma-separated key=value list including model_variant, token_count, route_key, billing_unit)

Example attributes string: "model_variant=m-latest,token_count=42,route_key=us-east-1,billing_unit=gen_token"

Triage checklist (support-friendly):
1) Reproduce the failure with the lab harness using the same API key and region.
2) Capture and attach the golden trace and failing trace.
3) Check telemetry for double-billing: token_cost spikes immediately after retries.
4) If truncated stream: confirm resume id exists in traces (span name runtime.stream.resume).
5) If fallback occurred: compare model_variant attributes between baseline and failing trace.
6) File a regression ticket including: failing_trace.json, command run, SDK version, and proxy logs.

Config matrix (copyable CSV row for quick reference):
"scenario,proxy_fault,client_timeout_ms,expected_behavior,primary_validation"
"baseline,none,1500,success,golden_trace match"
"delay-first-post,delay(1200ms),1000,retry-with-backoff,no double-billing"
"truncate-stream,truncate-after-3-chunks,2000,resume-able stream,resume span present"
"model-oom,503-on-cold-start,800,auto-fallback,latency<800ms"

Operational notes and ownership:
- Lab owner: eng-developer-experience (primary: Maya Chen).
- Oncall escalation: if the lab reproduces a production bug, open an incident in PagerDuty and tag "runtime-serving" and "sdk".
- Persist golden traces under s3://redwood-dev-golden-traces/sdk-chaos-lab/ with role-based ACLs.

Rollout and integration guidance (how teams should use this lab):
- SDK authors: integrate one golden-trace capture into CI for each major release (post-merge job). If a change causes a >5% regression vs the golden baseline, block the release.
- Platform: run the full lab in the dedicated staging cluster before deploying model-serving kernel changes or routing logic changes.
- Support: use the triage checklist when customers report truncated streams or unexpected token billing.

Artifacts to produce after running the lab:
- traces/golden_baseline.json (golden)
- traces/failure_mode_<name>.json (failing traces)
- coverage/regression_<sdk-version>.md (short summary)
- ticket templates/auto-fill for support with fields pre-populated from the harness run

References and related docs:
- eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/sdk-resiliency-orchestrator-and-ops-playbook-2026
- eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-streaming-troubleshooting-2025
- security-and-compliance/incident-response-security/streaming-data-retention-policy

Appendix: common canonical fixes (short list)
- Ensure idempotency tokens are attached to generation requests; server will dedupe within 30s window.
- Surface resume IDs for streaming RPCs and persist a short-lived local buffer to permit dedupe.
- Add token-cost snapshot before and after retries in telemetry to detect billing anomalies.
- If model fallback is frequent, add a cold-start pre-warm task for high-SLA tenants and/or enable burst-capacity for the dedicated pool.

Contact:
- Maya Chen (owner, eng-developer-experience) - maya@redwood.ai
- Support escalation alias: support-oncall@redwood.ai

title: Customer disputes status page accuracy during us-east degradation (status showed Operational while streaming requests failed)
text:
Customer (Lattice Financial) reports that during the 2025-11-07 us-east degradation they experienced elevated errors and streaming disconnects, but our public status page showed "Operational" for the relevant timeframe. Customer is requesting (a) confirmation that Redwood recognizes the outage and (b) clarification on why the status page did not reflect the impact.

Issue summary:
- Customer observed: intermittent 5xx/stream resets on streaming chat completions in us-east; elevated end-user error rates.
- Redwood status page observed by customer: "All Systems Operational" (no component marked degraded/outage until after their peak impact window).
- Customer concern: status page is too coarse (global/hosted API only) and/or incorrectly classified impact (streaming vs non-streaming, per-region impact not reflected).

Impact (customer-reported):
- Duration: ~20–30 minutes (approx 16:05–16:35 UTC per customer); residual retries for another ~10 minutes.
- Symptoms: SSE stream dropped mid-response; some requests returned 502/504; retries succeeded.
- Affected endpoints: /v1/chat/completions (stream=true).

What we need to do:
1) Validate the timeframe and whether our internal incident timeline matches customer evidence.
2) Provide a customer-facing explanation for the status page mismatch without disclosing sensitive capacity/customer-specific details.
3) Capture action items feeding into the status page transparency upgrades project (component taxonomy + signal mapping + comms process).

Customer-provided artifacts (summarized):
- Request IDs: LF-7b2c1e, LF-7b2c33, LF-7b2c8a (sample)
- Error codes: 502/504; stream disconnect without final event.
- Region: us-east only (customer also has low-volume eu-west traffic not impacted).

Internal notes:
- Internal incident opened: INC-2025-1107-USE1-STREAMING (SRE).
- Public status page components at time were too coarse (Hosted API global), and our automated classifier did not mark the correct component/region promptly.
- Known gap tracked by SRE: inability to represent "Streaming (us-east)" separately from "Hosted API"; led to delayed and ambiguous external comms.

Requested outcome for closure:
- Provide written acknowledgement + corrected timeline to customer.
- Share our planned improvements: new component granularity (product surface + region), standard comms templates, and faster time-to-first-update goals.
- Confirm whether any post-incident summary will be published and when.

2025-11-07 16:52 UTC - Dev Patel (Support): Ticket opened from Lattice Financial escalation. Customer says their app error rate spiked, but status page showed Operational. Assigning Rachel Kim (Ent CS) and looping SRE on-call for evidence + timeline. Related internal incident per #incidents: INC-2025-1107-USE1-STREAMING.
2025-11-07 17:06 UTC - Rachel Kim (Enterprise CS): Acknowledged to customer and requested exact timestamps + request IDs. Customer asks specifically: "If Redwood had an outage, why was it not on the status page?"
2025-11-07 17:22 UTC - Rafael Mendes (SRE): Confirmed we had a us-east streaming degradation. Primary symptom: increased streaming disconnects and elevated gateway 5xx for a subset of traffic. Incident declared internally at ~16:09 UTC; mitigated by 16:34 UTC; monitoring through 16:50 UTC. Status page update was delayed due to component ambiguity (only "Hosted API" global component) and incomplete signal mapping for streaming-specific metrics by region.
2025-11-07 17:28 UTC - Allison Grant (Observability): Sharing internal dashboard link for verification (internal): "Status Component Health > us-east > streaming" panel (new panels added recently; not yet wired into status automation). Metrics show disconnect spike coincident with incident timeline. We can export a screenshot if needed, but avoid including internal URLs in customer email.
2025-11-07 17:44 UTC - Dev Patel (Support): Drafted customer response with (1) acknowledgement of impact, (2) internal timeline, (3) explanation that status page component granularity did not allow us to reflect streaming-only + region-only issues accurately, and (4) commitment to improvements. Requested SRE review to ensure we don’t over-promise SLA language.
2025-11-07 18:10 UTC - Sean Gallagher (SRE sponsor): Approved phrasing. Key points to include: we’re improving component granularity (streaming/embeddings/reranking per major region), standardizing incident comms templates, and adding automated checks to reduce time-to-first-update. Do not include root-cause specifics that reference customer-specific capacity or vendors; keep it to a root-cause class (e.g., "regional dependency / infrastructure issue") until postmortem is finalized.
2025-11-08 09:15 UTC - Rachel Kim (Enterprise CS): Sent customer response. Included timeline and stated we’ll publish a short post-incident summary once reviewed for confidentiality. Customer replied asking if they can rely on per-region status going forward; we responded that this is in progress and we’ll notify once live.
2025-11-10 14:03 UTC - Christine Wong (Status transparency implementer): Logging this ticket as a concrete example for status page transparency upgrades. It demonstrates the need for: Hosted API vs Streaming separation; per-region visibility; and clear guidance on when to mark "Degraded Performance" vs "Partial Outage" for latency/disconnect-heavy events.
2025-11-11 10:40 UTC - Dev Patel (Support): Customer confirmed acceptance of explanation and requested we share the post-incident summary link when available. No further action required from customer side.
2025-11-12 16:25 UTC - Rachel Kim (Enterprise CS): Closing the loop: customer satisfied; keeping follow-ups tracked under status page transparency upgrades workstream (component taxonomy + mapping + templates).

Resolved customer dispute by providing verified internal incident timeline and acknowledging a status page mismatch due to overly coarse components and incomplete streaming/region signal mapping. Customer accepted explanation. Follow-ups captured for the status page transparency upgrades initiative: implement per-capability/per-region components (including Streaming us-east), improve signal-to-component mapping to prevent misclassification, and standardize incident update templates + approval flow for faster time-to-first-update.

domain: 日常协作与非结构化讨论
title: eng-runtime
text:
akshay: Quick signal from today's load test: paged-attn with small block_size=64 under high sequence variance is causing lots of micro-evicts and a perf cliff (latency tail and occasional OOM).

maria: Ugh, saw that on a customer trace too. Can you paste the flame/profile?

akshay: Dropped a short perfdump in the thread. Key points: compaction time is dominating when we try to coalesce many tiny free ranges, and the allocator spends cycles scanning buckets. CPU-side kernel selection flips to the fallback kernel mid-request because workspace estimate grows.

ell en: Can you share the KV cache hit distribution? Might be related to eviction churn.
akshay: KV hit rate is fine overall (~82%) but there are hot streams that continuously touch new blocks, causing fragmentation. The paged block reuse allocator tries to salvage partial blocks but our compaction threshold triggers full copy compaction too often.

paul: Ideas: 1) implement a "salvage-first" opportunistic reclaim that extracts contiguous subranges without full compaction; 2) add a lightweight bitmap to each block to speed free-range detection; 3) introduce a watermark to prevent kernel fallback by reserving a tiny extra workspace for worst-case transient growth.
maria: I prototyped (2) a while back — bitmap reduced compaction scan by ~40% in microbench. We didn't hook it to the eviction policy though.
akshay: Sketching a combined approach: salvage-first + soft-evict watermark + adaptive block_sizing on hot streams. Pseudocode for the eviction heuristic I tested:

```
if fragment_pct > 30% and active_streams < 4:
 salvage_contiguous_ranges()
elif fragment_pct > 60%:
 schedule_full_compaction(async=true)
else:
 prefer_block_reuse()
```

runtime-bot: Perf alert: paged-attn kernel fallback triggered 14 times in last 10m for pool:gpu-a1

ellen: Salvage-first needs to be O(1) in the common case. If it's doing memcopies for each tiny subrange we lose the win. Maybe coalesce at remap time (defer physical copies until threshold).

paul: Also saw that batching heuristics exacerbate it — large batches cause longer-lived KV entries so eviction churn overlaps with slow compaction. We should bias batch packing to prefer requests with higher KV hit probability when fragmentation is high.
maria: Agree. We can add a batch_score = hit_prob - frag_penalty and let the scheduler prefer higher score in that pool.
akshay: Logged some numbers from the test run:
- baseline (block_size=64): p95 latency 420ms, p99 1.9s, throughput 320 tok/s
- salvage-first + bitmap: p95 260ms, p99 640ms, throughput 480 tok/s
- salvage-first + watermark(8MB extra): p95 210ms, p99 310ms, throughput 510 tok/s

infra-ci: Run note: test job 1987654300 archived at https://ci.internal/runs/1987654300 (contains perfdump + heapmap).

maria: Nice. Any regression risks? What about memory overhead of bitmap + watermark?
akshay: Bitmap adds ~1-2% memory per block; watermark is configurable per pool and has strict bounded reservation. I also found a corner-case where async compaction + kernel fallback interact — compaction wins a race and frees workspace mid-generation causing a tiny corruption in a stress test. Repro steps in the perfdump.

ell en: We should add a lightweight correctness guard: when async compaction frees memory, signal kernel-selection to re-evaluate and delay applying reclaimed region until the current request's kernel has safely finished. Cheap fence.

title: prepack-int8-weights-and-smoothquant-fuse-with-kernel-lane-allocator
author: Anika Rao
text:
Motivation: INT8 inference for large decoder models showed suboptimal memory layout overhead and extra dequant steps when combined with smoothquant-style per-channel scaling. This PR introduces a weight prepack path and a small kernel-lane allocator that lets the runtime fuse smoothquant dequantization into the kernel dispatch without materializing intermediate dequant tensors. Goals: 1) lower wall-clock latency for first-token and steady-state by removing memory-bound dequant copies, 2) reduce peak GPU memory for multi-tenant workloads by prepacking int8 weights in a compact layout and sharing lane metadata across batches, 3) keep compatibility with existing KV cache and continuous-batching pipelines. What changed (high-level): - New weight prepack module (src/runtime/kernel/int8_weight_prepack.cc/h) that produces a packed INT8 layout with per-channel scale/zero-point metadata optimized for our vectorized GEMM kernels. - Kernel adapter hooks (src/runtime/kernel/kernel_adapter.cc) to accept packed weights and apply smoothquant per-channel scaling on-the-fly inside the GEMM launcher when the model has smoothquant metadata. - Kernel lane allocator (src/runtime/scheduler/lane_allocator.cc/h) that assigns model weight lanes to worker threads/GPU streams so packed weights can be reused across microbatches without copying. - KV cache coordinator updates (src/runtime/scheduler/kv_cache_coordinator.cc) to pin KV cache blocks to the same lane affinity when the request uses pinned weights, avoiding cross-lane synchronization. - A shortfall fallback: when model uses dynamic shape patterns incompatible with lane reuse, runtime falls back to previous dequant-copy path automatically. Performance: microbenchmarks on a 32B decoder model (batch sizes 1..8, seq len 1..1024) show median token latency improvement of 9-16% at steady state and 18-28% for first-token latency on Ampere A100, with peak memory reduction of ~12% at high concurrency. Compatibility/risks: The change touches low-level kernel dispatch. We limited the surface by gating packed-weight paths behind a model feature flag and added runtime checks for per-channel metadata version. Rolling plan: staged canary rollout on Dedicated pools with a 2-hour canary window, monitor latency, token error-rate regressions, and memory counters. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for weight prepack and kernel adapter - [x] Integration test exercising smoothquant models through hosted API - [x] Performance bench scripts added - [x] Migration doc and feature flag gating - [x] Observability: added counters for lane cache hits/misses, packed-weight size. Related: ENG-3421 (quant kernel latency), ENG-3498 (kv cache affinity).

Marcus Li: Overall this looks solid; can you add a short docstring describing the layout produced by the prepack method? I had to trace through the code to confirm alignment guarantees.
Anika Rao: Added header docstrings and a diagram in prepack_smoothquant_notes.md per Marcus' request.
Diego Torres: The lane allocator is clever. Concern: potential starvation if many small requests contend for lanes. Suggest adding a fairness counter or aging policy.
Anika Rao: Added simple LRU aging policy and a unit test to simulate heavy small-request contention; PTAL.
Priya Nair (SRE): We need an observability signal for fallback-to-copy rate; ops will want to alert if it spikes after rollout.
Anika Rao: Added metrics runtime.quant.packed_weight_fallback_count and added to Console dashboards as part of the rollout task.
Marcus Li: CI failure on clang-format fixed in latest commit; approving pending perf numbers in canary.
Diego Torres: Verified no regression on tokenization edge-case tests; merging after canary.

title: introduce-token-stage-cohorting-and-route-matrix-alerting
author: Maya Chen
text:
Context: long-tail token cost and multi-stage latency spikes frequently surface only when a request traverses several model-serving stages (tokenization, encoder, decode, fallback). Existing alerts were per-route and per-quantile but lacked a compact way to group requests by 'stage footprint' and automatically route alerting weight to the stage(s) most likely responsible. Motivation: reduce alert noise and accelerate RCA by grouping invocations into stage-aware cohorts and deriving a route x stage alert matrix that attributes SLO violations to the most likely pipeline stage. What this PR does: 1) Adds a lightweight token_stage_cohort service that computes a deterministic cohort key per invocation based on stage-level metrics (token counts per stage, kv-cache hit pattern, decode-batch size) and stores short-lived cohort aggregates. 2) Introduces an alert route-matrix generator that consumes cohort rollups and emits alert bindings which bias escalation to the top-k stages for that route. 3) Adds a new dashboard focused on cohort drift, stage heatmaps, and per-cohort cost/latency breakdown to help oncall quickly validate root cause hypotheses. 4) Wires the generator into the existing alerting pipeline with a safe canary rollout and automatic quiet-window attenuation to avoid regressing noise. Compatibility and rollout: service defaults to read-only mode until flagged by a feature flag; alert generation starts cross-account in a low-sensitivity mode (only P90/P99) and is then ramped after 72h of monitoring. Testing: unit and integration tests added; ran a 48h synthetic replay against production-like traces (see test run in CI). Checklist: - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Dashboard panels - [x] Docs for oncall and runbook - [x] Feature-flagged rollout Plan for operators: deploy to staging -> enable feature flag -> monitor cohort drift and false-positive rate -> bump sensitivity -> full rollout. Links: Linear ENG-1248 (cohorting design) and PM-432 (dashboard spec).

Diego: Can cohort keys be stable across model version rollouts? Added suggestion to include model-version hash in key derivation. Response: we now namespace cohort keys with model-major-version and include fallback mapping in cohort_store.proto.
Priya: Alert noise risk—please limit initial sensitivity and provide quiet-window behavior. Response: implemented quiet-window attenuation and low-sensitivity defaults; documented in docs/observability/token-cohorting.md.
Liam: test coverage looks good but add an e2e replay with partial KV-cache misses. Response: added synthetic KV miss replay in tests/integration/test_cohorting_flow.py and CI run shows stable results.

title: Production Change Management Standard (v2)
author: Aisha Rahman
text:
h1. Purpose
This policy defines what constitutes a production change at Redwood Inference and the minimum requirements to plan, approve, execute, and validate the change. The goal is to minimize customer impact while maintaining developer velocity.

h1. Scope
Applies to all production environments for the Hosted API and Console, including:
* Hosted API control plane and data plane services
* Console UI and backend
* Shared platform dependencies (routing, auth, billing metering, observability agents)

Out of scope: customer-managed environments for *Private deployments* (see the Private Deployment Change Policy), and vendor-managed changes outside Redwood’s control (cloud provider maintenance).

h1. Definitions
* *Production:* Any environment serving external customer traffic (including canary and regional production).
* *Production change:* Any change that can affect confidentiality, integrity, availability, latency, cost, or correctness for customer-facing workloads.
* *Change owner:* The person accountable for end-to-end execution and follow-through.
* *Approver:* A designated peer/manager/SRE/security reviewer depending on risk tier.
* *Change record:* A durable record (ticket + links) capturing intent, risk, approvals, execution, and validation results.

h1. Change types
|| Change type || When used || Required approvals || Notes ||
| Standard | Low risk, pre-approved pattern (e.g., doc-only, internal dashboard query fixes, non-prod config) | 1 peer approval | Must match an approved standard template |
| Normal | Most code/config deploys to production | 1 peer approval + (1) service owner approval | Requires pre-deploy verification, canary, and comms assessment |
| Emergency | Active incident mitigation or preventing imminent customer impact | On-call incident commander (IC) + service owner approval (as available) | Retrospective change record required within 24 hours |

h1. What counts as a production change (non-exhaustive)
* Any deployment to production clusters (including canary regions)
* Any change to routing policies, fallback policies, or model selection rules
* Any change to auth, RBAC, API keys, rate limits, quotas, or billing meters
* Any schema migration, backfill, or data retention configuration change
* Any infrastructure change that affects capacity, autoscaling, or failover
* Any change to observability pipelines that could reduce visibility (logs, metrics, tracing)

h1. Minimum required artifacts
For every production change, the change owner must create a change record that includes:
* Summary of change and customer impact assessment
* Rollback plan (explicitly stated, even if “re-deploy previous build”)
* Verification plan (how we will know it worked)
* Links to: PR(s), build(s), dashboards, runbook used, and any migration plan
* Approvals (captured in the change record)

h1. Risk assessment checklist
Answer these before requesting approval:
1. Could this change affect auth, data paths, encryption, logging, or retention?
2. Could this change change request routing, batching, caching, or model version selection?
3. Could this change materially change token accounting/billing?
4. Is there any data migration/backfill involved?
5. Is rollback fast and safe (< 10 minutes) and does it revert the customer experience?

If “yes” to any of 1–4, the change is *Normal* at minimum and may require Security Review (see Secure SDLC requirements).

h1. Approvals
* *Peer approval:* A reviewer from the same engineering org who is familiar with the subsystem.
* *Service owner approval:* The tech lead or on-call owner for the service being changed.
* *SRE gate:* Required when the change affects capacity, SLO-sensitive paths, traffic routing, or any failover config.
* *Security gate:* Required when the change touches auth, secrets, encryption, audit logging, PII, or data retention.

h1. Change windows and freezes
* Default window: weekdays 09:00–16:00 local time for the primary owning team.
* Changes are prohibited during declared change freezes.
* Additional restrictions apply when error budgets are low (see “Change Freeze and Risk Assessment”).

h1. Execution requirements
All production changes must:
1. Use the documented runbook for the target system (Hosted API or Console).
2. Perform a canary rollout for traffic-bearing services unless explicitly exempted in the change record.
3. Confirm observability before and after (golden signals and specific dashboards).
4. Have a clearly defined rollback trigger and a “stop the line” principle.

h1. Communications requirements
Change owner must determine if customer communications are required:
* *Planned maintenance:* Status page notice and direct customer comms if any material impact is expected.
* *No expected customer impact:* Internal announcement in #eng-releases and on-call awareness if during core hours.
See “Planned Maintenance and Change Communications” for templates and required lead time.

h1. Post-change validation and closure
Within 60 minutes after completion, the change owner must:
* Validate key SLO metrics and error rates are within normal bounds
* Confirm canary is healthy before full rollout
* Update the change record with results and attach screenshots/links
* File follow-ups for any issues discovered

h1. References
* Prod Deployment Gates (Hosted API + Console)
* Hosted API Deploy Runbook
* Console Deploy Runbook
* Rollback and Post-change Validation
* Change Freeze and Risk Assessment
* Secure SDLC: Security Review Requirements for Prod Changes
* Planned Maintenance and Change Communications

title: span-timeline-playbook-grooming-notes
author: Maya Thompson
text:
Purpose and scope:
This is a portable playbook-style doc for planning the span timeline (waterfall) surface in the Console trace viewer. Focus: practical interaction patterns for exploring long requests, span grouping, quick filters, and debug-friendly annotations. Intended audience: product, frontend, SRE, and UX who will ship the first iteration (MVP) for Q1 roadmap.

High-level goals (why):
- Help engineers quickly pinpoint latency hotspots in multi-model requests (KV cache misses, routing fallbacks, model switch latencies).
- Make it cheap to triage production incidents without switching to raw logs (link out when needed).
- Provide a compact summary view plus progressively revealed detail (progressive disclosure).

Constraints and assumptions:
- Must work for traces up to 10kms (long traces) and 200 spans without freezing the UI.
- First pass will support server-side timestamps + durations; no distributed tracing correlation yet (future).
- Prefers purely client-side rendering with virtualization for rows.

MVP surface (what to build):
1) Compact timeline (collapsed spans by default):
 - Row per span group (service.action) with count and aggregated duration range (p50/p95).
 - Tap/expand to animate open slot into full span rows beneath.
 - Visual cue for long-tail spans: thin red overlay on portion > threshold.

2) Span detail flyout:
 - Header: span name, service, duration, start offset, tags (key/value), request id.
 - Tabs: Metadata (headers/attrs), Logs (linked), Events (KV/cache hits), Raw JSON (copy).
 - Quick actions: "Copy timing", "Open in logs", "Create ticket" (prefill fields).

3) Filters & quick probes bar (persistent top strip):
 - Text search over span names + attributes (syntax: name:token, tag:key=value).
 - Prebuilt quick filters: long > 500ms, error spans, model-fallback, cache-miss.
 - Toggle: group-by-service / group-by-operation / show-only-errors.

4) Time-slice scrubber and zoom controls:
 - Mini-waterfall overview (Sparkline) with a brush to zoom time ranges.
 - Keyboard shortcuts: shift + drag to select, +/- to zoom, space to play animation.

Interaction notes and micro-flows:
- Expand flow: click on row -> row animates open -> fetch per-span details (lazy) -> arrow to first child span -> keyboard focus goes into expanded region.
- Inspect-range: user highlights a time window in the scrubber -> timeline reflows showing only spans intersecting window; counts of hidden spans shown as collapsed badge.
- Multi-select: shift+click selects multiple spans -> aggregate action bar appears with suggested next steps (trace compare, export, make ticket).

Wireframe description (ASCII sketch for devs):
[Header bar: trace id | duration | region | download]
[Quick probes bar: (search) | [long>500ms] [errors] [cache-miss] [group:service]]
[Mini-sparkline scrubber]\\n--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
| Row 1: auth-service.login (grouped) | #####----- 120ms p95 | [v] |
| (expanded) child spans: | [span bars with offsets and red warning] |
| Row 2: routing (service) | --###------- 40ms p95 | [v] |
| Row 3: model-serving (group) | -----####--- 420ms p95 | [!] |
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Footer: selected span details / copy buttons / open link to logs]

Accessibility and performance notes:
- All interactive elements must be keyboard focusable; aria labels for span durations e.g., 'span x duration 220ms start 1.3s'.
- Use row virtualization and canvas-based mini-waterfall rendering to reduce DOM counts.
- Defer heavy JSON formatting until user opens Raw JSON tab.

Open questions / discussion items (to resolve in grooming):
- How do we represent concurrent spans that overlap heavily? (Option A: stacked lanes per service, Option B: layered single lane with translucency). Decision needed by next sync.
- Should group-by default to service or operation? Metric: fewer clicks for common debug path.
- What threshold values for quick filters are product-configurable vs hard-coded?

Backlog & acceptance criteria (scoped for first 2 sprints):
- RW-2241: Timeline base rendering + virtualization
 - AC: Load traces with up to 200 spans, initial render < 300ms, maintaining 60fps scroll.
- RW-2242: Expand/collapse row groups with lazy span fetch
 - AC: Expanding a group fetches child spans and reveals them; keyboard focus lands on first child.
- RW-2243: Span detail flyout with tabs and logs link
 - AC: Flyout opens within 200ms, logs link is present and opens new tab to logs view with query prefilled.
- RW-2244: Quick probes & filters bar
 - AC: Text search supports name: and tag: syntax; presets shown and toggles update timeline live.

Implementation notes for engineers:
- API: propose trace GET /v1/traces/{id}?level=grouped|full&time_window=start,end. Grouped returns aggregation metadata for each group.
- Client: use react-virtualized for rows, canvas for sparkline. Avoid full JSON parse until flyout open.
- Metrics to capture: render_time_ms, expand_latency_ms, filter_apply_ms, avg_spans_loaded_per_trace.

UX validation plan:
- 3 quick guerrilla usability sessions with internal engineers (15 minutes each) to validate expand/collapse mental model.
- One incident-runbook test: have SRE resolve a seeded slow-model-fallback case using only Console trace viewer; record time to resolution.

Notes to self (brain dump):
- Consider a small 'annotation' feature where engineers can pin a comment to a span (private to org) — high value for knowledge transfer.
- Might want to show model version pins in the span bar for model-serving spans.
- If we support RL fallback, mark those spans with a distinct icon so they stand out in grouped view.

Next steps & owners:
- Design: Elena to produce high-fidelity mocks for stacked-vs-layered overlap options by 2025-11-20.
- Frontend: Raj to spike canvas-based sparkline and virtualization; report perf numbers by 2025-11-28.
- Backend: Samir to draft grouped trace API and example payload by 2025-12-02.
- Product: Maya to host grooming session w/ SRE on 2025-11-12 to decide default grouping and quick-filter thresholds.

Revision log:
- 2025-11-04 Maya created initial playbook.
- 2025-11-12 updated with SRE notes from grooming (meeting minutes linked in Confluence).
- 2026-02-20 added acceptance criteria and ticket IDs for sprint planning.

Unresolved: finalize overlapping span visualization; put on agenda for 2026-02-28 design sync.

title: Nano-tiering experiments scratchpad
author: Maya Chen
text:
Goal: quick, intuition-first set of micro-tier experiments for low-touch SMB & hobbyist flows. Keep things cheap/simple for <10k MAU seed projects, but don't incentivize abusive high-throughput workloads. This is a personal scratchpad — lots of heuristics and TODOs.

Assumptions (back-of-envelope):
- GPU cost baseline: use amortized per-token cost from infra team: 1 GPU-hour ~ $3.50 (spot blended) for inference on 8-bit quantized medium model. This maps to ~ 5M tokens/hour in steady streaming workloads (conservative). => infra token-cost = $3.50 / 5e6 = $0.0000007 / token (~0.70 $/M tokens).
- Add infra overhead (orchestration, storage, network, support) x1.6 => unit cost ~ $1.12 /M tokens.
- Payment processor + margins + churn buffer => target gross margin target 65% => suggested price per M tokens = cost / (1 - margin) = 1.12 / 0.35 = ~$3.20 /M tokens. Round to simple numbers.

User behavior estimates (for small tiers):
- Typical hobbyist: 20 API calls/day, avg request 300 tokens in + 200 tokens out = 500 tokens/call => 10k tokens/day ~ 300k tokens/month.
- Small startup dev: 200 calls/day -> 100k tokens/day -> 3M tokens/month.
- Sandbox heavy: spike bursts are important; need burst cap for < 1 hour windows.

Tier sketches (for experiment matrix):
1) Nano (free-ish): 500k tokens/month included, 30 req/min burst to throttle, email-only support. Add-on packs available.
2) Sprout (entry): $5 / month => 1.5M included tokens, soft rate-limit 60 req/min, no SLA, basic analytics. Overage: $5 /M tokens.
3) Builder (most likely convert): $25 / month => 10M included tokens, 250 req/min, basic SLA, webhook retries, monthly usage analytics. Overage: $3 /M tokens.
4) Scale (paid, committed): $250 /mo => 200M included tokens, dedicated burst pool 1k req/min, 99.9% availability target (hosted). Overage: $1.8 /M tokens or discounted add-on reserved capacity.

Rationale behind numbers:
- Nano free cap chosen to cover typical hobbyist exploratory usage (~300k/mo). 500k avoids early-day blocking and increases virality potential.
- Sprout price anchored to $5 because perceived low friction; included tokens priced at ~ $3.33 /M (5$/1.5M) which is slightly above suggested retail $3.2/M but cheap enough. Overage high to nudge to upgrade.
- Builder is the 'trials convert' tier: effective price = $2.5 /M across included 10M at $25 => attractive cost, gets dev teams comfortable.
- Scale is for small teams who want predictable spend and capacity; economically justified vs payg if sustained.

Burst mechanics & abuse control (sketch):
- Each account gets a token refill bucket per minute computed from included tokens * burst factor. For nano/sprout, burst factor lower (x3 of steady qps), for builder x8, for scale negotiable.
- Rate-limit circuit-breaker: sustained QPS > allowed for >10s => throttle to baseline. Spikes <10s allowed.
- Protect free tier via fingerprinting and progressive verification: email -> phone -> card for larger bursts.

Alternate anchoring: session-bundles vs tokens
- Session-bundle: useful for voice/chat where tokens correlate poorly per 'interaction'. A session bundle = 1,000 tokens equiv. Offer small pack pricing (e.g., 50 sessions / month) for UX-focused apps.
- Hybrid: include N sessions + M tokens. Sessions consume tokens once threshold crossed. Complexity tradeoff: easier to think about UX vs harder billing engine.

Experiment matrix to run (short-term):
A) A/B pricing test: Sprout $5 with 1.5M vs SproutPro $8 with 4M included. Measure upgrade rates & retention over 30 days.
B) Free cap change: free 500k vs free 750k (narrow experiment to see activation lift). Watch abuse pattern (ratio of accounts with >1M usage).
C) Overage elasticity: set overage at $5 /M vs $3 /M for Builder and observe churn/upgrade.

Quick sensitivity calcs (for ops):
- Break-even tokens per month per paying account (consider blended margin): if price = $25 and unit cost = 1.12/M tokens => at $25 you can support ~22.3M tokens before cost eats revenue (25 / 1.12 * 1M = 22.3M tokens). But we target usage lower, so 10M included is safe.
- If average Builder payload = 10M tokens/mo and 10k accounts => infra spend = 10M * 10k * 1.12/1e6 = $112k/month. Revenue = 25 * 10k = $250k/month => gross margin ~ 55% (below 65 target) — need to tighten or upsell.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Validate infra token cost with infra team: is 5M tokens/hour realistic across models (mix of short/long seq)? get per-model profiles.
- How to implement session bundles in billing platform? estimate engineering effort.
- Decide whether free tier should persist on account-level or per-project-level (billing vs org).
- Edge-case: chat apps that use large context windows (50k) — how to price? Consider 'context surcharge' or per-context-block pricing.

Notes to self: keep the pricing language simple on the landing page — round numbers, emphasize included tokens and burst capacity. For first experimental launch, keep overage intentionally punitive to push upgrades rather than risk large pay-as-you-go churn.

Slack refs: convo in #pricing from 2025-10-29 — Jonah posted activation benchmarks. See JIRA-PRC-548 for rollout infra work.

End of scratchpad. Will iterate after infra cost check and A/B test results.

title: Smoother autoscaler signal and gateway backpressure for dedicated pools
author: Priya Natarajan
text:
Summary: Introduces a smoothing layer in the Dedicated Autoscaler and a lightweight backpressure signal propagated from the gateway to fleet controllers. This reduces autoscaler thrash on spiky traffic and gives gateways a controlled way to shed load gracefully against per-pool soft capacity and throughput guarantees.

Motivation: Customers on Dedicated have reported oscillations when short bursts cross autoscaler thresholds and then recede; this leads to unnecessary GPU spin-ups and billing variance, as well as transient error spikes. The gateway currently responds with 429s or fallback heuristics; we need a first-class, observable mechanism that cooperates with autoscaling and preserves headroom for SLA-critical requests.

Changes in this PR:
- Autoscaler: add Exponential Moving Average (EMA) smoothing of utilization and request rate with configurable half-life per-pool. New config fields: smoothing_window_ms, smoothing_alpha (derived).
- Soft capacity & grace tokens: each pool now tracks a small ephemeral token bucket (grace_tokens) to allow short bursts without triggering scale-up, decaying over time and replenished by underutilization.
- Gateway backpressure: add a new X-Redwood-Backpressure header and a compact gRPC/backchannel (gateway->controller) event to advertise desired ingress rate reductions per-route when pool smoothed_utilization > threshold.
- Controller/gateway handshake: gateway subscribes to per-pool backpressure_quota updates; controllers include backpressure_rate in scheduling decisions and expose metrics.
- Telemetry: new metrics smoothed_utilization, grace_tokens_available, backpressure_rate, backpressure_rejections. Add Prometheus labels for pool_id, model_id, and region.
- API schema: extend dedicated pool spec with smoothing and backpressure knobs; added validation and defaults.
- Console/docs: admin UI now surfaces smoothing window and current backpressure state with guidance.
- Tests: unit tests for smoothing math, integration e2e that injects burst traffic and asserts reduced scale-up churn and controlled 429 behavior.

Checklist:
- [x] Design review with SRE and Runtime teams (ENG-2147)
- [x] Unit tests for smoothing and token bucket
- [x] Integration e2e simulating bursty traffic
- [x] Telemetry dashboards updated
- [x] Migration notes and rollout plan
- [x] Backwards-compatible API schema changes (defaults safe)

Implementation notes:
- EMA parameters chosen to have ~30s half-life by default; pools serving low-latency workloads can set shorter windows.
- Grace tokens default to 2 tokens per pool; a token represents ~1s worth of headroom at pool's nominal throughput.
- Backpressure is advisory: scheduler will attempt to respect backpressure_rate before rejecting; only when backpressure persists will the gateway return 429s.
- To avoid unsafe throttling loops, backpressure updates include a monotonic seq and TTL.

Breaking changes: none expected; all new fields are optional with safe defaults.

Rollout plan: staged rollout: 1) feature gated off by default; 2) enable on Canary Dedicated clusters for 48h; 3) enable for opt-in customers with console toggle; 4) enable by default after 2 weeks of stable metrics.

Migration: API customers can ignore new fields; operators upgrading on-prem should ensure controllers and gateway are updated together.

Testing:
- Unit and integration tests added under tests/e2e/dedicated_smoothing_test.go
- Load test harness reproduces 1-2 minute burst profiles and asserts scale-up events reduced by >=50% while 95th-p99 latency impact <5% in our baseline.

Commits (high level):
- 0f9a8b2: controller: add smoothing math and metrics
- 1b3d2c4: gateway: backpressure header + backchannel client
- 8a7f6e1: api: add dedicated pool schema changes + validation
- c3e4d5b: telemetry: register new metrics and dashboards
- d4f2a9f: console: show per-pool smoothing/backpressure state
- f5b6c7d: tests: unit + e2e harness for burst scenarios

Files changed (high level):
- controller/autoscaler/smoothing.go: implement EMA and smoothing helpers (approx. 220 LOC)
- pkg/allocator/soft_capacity.go: grace tokens and soft capacity decisions
- gateway/backpressure/handler.go: header parsing and backchannel emitter
- api/config/v1/dedicated_pool.yaml: schema additions and docs
- telemetry/metrics_registry.go: new metric registration
- console/src/pages/pool/BackpressureCard.tsx: UI surface
- tests/e2e/dedicated_smoothing_test.go: load test harness
- helm/charts/redwood/templates/pool-config.yaml: default knobs
- ops/rollout/2026-03-dedicated-smoothing.md: rollout instructions

Small illustrative snippets:
- smoothing.go (EMA core): "smoothed = alpha*instant + (1-alpha)*smoothed"
- handler.go (gateway header): "if hdr := req.Header.Get(\"X-Redwood-Backpressure\"); hdr != \"\" { parseAndApply(hdr) }"

CI and checks:
- CI: go build, unit tests, linters (golangci), frontend unit tests
- e2e pipeline run on canary (k8s)
- Initial CI run: failed flakiness in e2e; reran and passed on second attempt.

Review thread summary:
- Marco Alvarez (SRE): requested clearer backpressure-to-scheduler contract and TTL handling. Response: added monotonic seq + TTL and explicit scheduler fallback behavior (controller will not reduce scheduling below 50% of nominal unless pool explicitly marked best-effort).
- Leah Kim (Runtime): asked for benchmark numbers for default EMA half-life; Response: added results from synthetic bursts showing 60% reduction in scale-ups with 30s half-life.
- Owen Patel (Security): requested audit logging for backpressure events; Response: added structured audit logs under telemetry/backpressure_events.
- Reviewer approvals: Marco Alvarez approved after TTL addition; Leah Kim approved after benchmark numbers; Owen Patel approved after audit logs.

Merge and post-merge actions:
- Merge method: squash and merge
- Post-merge: created a follow-up issue to add gauntlet tests against real customer workloads (ENG-2210)
- Updated canary dashboards and set alert: DedicatedPool.SmoothedUtilization > 95% for 5m -> page oncall

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: misconfigured smoothing window could delay needed scale-ups -> mitigation: default conservative half-life and admin override to disable smoothing per pool.
- Risk: backpressure loops between gateway and controller -> mitigation: monotonic seq + TTL + min-scheduling floor.

Release notes: "Improves autoscaler stability by smoothing utilization signals and introduces an advisory backpressure mechanism from gateway to controllers to reduce churn on short bursts. Operators: feature is opt-in and has safe defaults; see admin docs for tuning guidance."

CI status: pass
