title: Conditional multitenant rate limiter priority skew causing transient under-enforcement
author: Lina Chen
text:
Intermittent cases where per-key priority overrides combined with per-org and per-route policies result in transient under-enforcement (requests allowed when they should be throttled). Observed as short windows of elevated usage for a small set of tenants after shard reassignment and policy hot-reload. This ticket captures investigation, repro, short-term mitigation, and a long-term fix plan.

Transient over-allow for small number of tenants leading to underbilling and potential customer perception issues; visible as short-lived bursts up to ~2x expected throughput for affected keys. Affects hosted and dedicated clusters during rolling updates or instance restarts.

1) Create two tenants T1 and T2 sharing a shard (sticky-shard assignment enabled).
2) Configure per-org policy: default priority = low, per-route quota = 1000/min.
3) Configure per-key override for a service key K1 belonging to T1: priority = high, burst credits = +200.
4) Start a steady stream of requests from T1 at near-quota rate; verify enforcement hitting quota windows.
5) Trigger a shard reassignment for one edge node (simulate instance bounce or maintenance) while simultaneously applying a policy hot-reload that changes route fallback behavior.
6) Observe a ~10-30s window where requests for K1 are allowed beyond quota; metrics show credits attributed to the wrong in-memory bucket and enforcement checks returning allow from fast-path cache.
7) Collect tracer spans and edge logs for the window; reproduce locally using the shard-reassignment harness and time-accelerated policy reloads.

edge: allow decision fastpath: key=K1 shard=sh-23 cache_hit=true priority=high quota_window_id=2026-03-12T10:04:00Z
shard-reassign: lease=renewal failover->sh-27 old_owner=sh-23 new_owner=sh-27
policy-hot-reload: version=v2026-03-12-1 route-fallback=enabled
meter-commit: credits_applied target_bucket=org:T2:key:Kx unexpected=true amount=200

A race between sticky-shard mapping update and policy hot-reload causes fast-path cache entries (priority and credit pointers) to be re-keyed incorrectly. Per-key overrides store a pointer to a tenant-scoped credit bucket; during reassignment we are dereferencing a stale pointer and applying credits to the wrong tenant's bucket. Enforcement uses the fast-path decision if cache present, so the wrong credits cause an allow where a deny should occur.

Replayed the sequence in staging using the shard-reassign harness. With no policy reload the issue did not occur. When timed policy reload coincided with reassignment, we reproduced the over-allow consistently. Enabling stronger pointer validation (temporary patch) eliminated the over-allows in the harness.

Sticky-shard pointer (in-memory bucket reference) is validated only by shard id but not by tenant id during fast-path credit application. Policy hot-reload mutates the route/priority indices while a shard transfer copies pointers; combined these can produce a transient pointer that points at an unrelated tenant's bucket. Enforcement fast-path accepts the cache without full tenant-level validation.

Short-term patch deployed to staging: on fast-path cache hit, perform tenant-id validation on the cached credit pointer before applying credits. Also increased grace period on shard handoff to reduce overlap. Rolled patch to canary edge fleet.

1) Canary for 2 hours on low-traffic region with added telemetry (done). 2) Gradual ramp to 30% of traffic with continued trace sampling for next 24 hours. 3) Full rollout after 48 hours if no regressions. 4) Follow with a database reconciliation backfill job to detect credits misapplied in last 7 days and create accounting fixes if needed.

Refactor in-memory credit pointer representation to be immutable and namespaced by tenant+shard+route. Replace pointer dereference fast-path with a lightweight validation token check (versioned binder). Add unit and property tests for concurrent shard handoff + policy reload scenarios.

Add deterministic concurrency tests to runtime-policy-simulator: combinations of shard reassignment, policy hot-reload, per-key overrides, and burst credit application. Add e2e test in CI harness that exercises rolling updates with randomized interleavings. Add a smoke check after canary verifying no over-allow traces in last 10 minutes.

PM (Aisha Kapoor): prioritize mitigation; billing reconciliation may be needed if misapplied credits persist beyond 24h.
Security (Rajiv Patel): no PII involved in pointers but ensure tracing does not expose tenant ids in public dashboards.
Observation: reproduces more reliably when policy reload contains route fallback toggles rather than pure priority edits.

title: Optimize 1.3 release notes — Performance Profiles & Cost Telemetry
author: Marina Alvarez
text:
Summary
-------
This document summarizes the Redwood Optimize 1.3 release (GA: 2026-02-20). Optimize 1.3 introduces Performance Profiles, Telemetry-based Cost Estimator, latency-tier presets for the Console, and several SDK/CLI usability improvements. The release targets customers using Redwood Optimize to tune Dedicated and Hosted inference for predictable unit economics and simplified rollout of quantization/batching recommendations.

Highlights
----------
- Performance Profiles (feature flag: optimize.performance_profiles): per-model, per-workload profiles that capture measured latency/throughput/cost at multiple sequence-length distributions. Profiles power auto-suggestion rules and the new cost estimator.
- Telemetry-based Cost Estimator: end-to-end estimator that uses historical request shape telemetry (prefix length, tokens-per-request, hit rates) to produce monthly cost projections and sensitivity analyses.
- Latency-tier Presets in Console: new predefined profiles (S0: <50ms p95, S1: <120ms p95, S2: <250ms p95) that automatically tune batching and cache TTL recommendations.
- SDK v0.18.0: new Optimize client with async estimate_cost() and get_performance_profile() helpers; breaking rename of estimate() -> estimate_cost().
- CLI: redwood optimize export-profile <model> -> writes a reproducible YAML profile used for Dedicated scheduling.
- Migration & compatibility: recommended default quantization profiles unchanged; deprecated optimize.legacy_hint removed (see Migration notes).

What’s new (detailed)
---------------------
1) Performance Profiles
 - Description: Profiles record observed stat distributions for: sequence_length, tokens_generated, request_rate (qps), prefix_cache_hit_rate. Each profile stores measured p50/p95 latencies and per-token GPU time across representative buckets (short/medium/long).
 - Storage: profiles are stored in the customer namespace (s3-backed), versioned, and visible via Console and API.
 - API preview: POST /v1/optimize/profiles {"model":"redwood-7b-v1","workload":"chat-short"} -> returns profile id and recommendations.
 - Owner: Optimize team (owner: Deepa Nair).

2) Telemetry-based Cost Estimator
 - Inputs: time window (default 30d), model(s), deployment mode (hosted/dedicated), commitment tier, sequence-length histogram.
 - Output: month-over-month projection (USD), token breakdown (input/system/output), sensitivity table (how cost changes if average tokens/request increases by +10/25/50%).
 - Accuracy caveats: estimator factors in measured batching efficiency and prefix cache hit rate; for cold-start or sparse telemetry customers, the estimator uses conservative defaults (see config below).
 - Console: new "Cost Projection" panel on Optimize pages with download CSV button.

3) Latency-tier Presets
 - Presets: S0 (ultra-low latency), S1 (balanced), S2 (cost-efficient). Each preset maps to batching window targets, max batch size, and prefix_cache_TTL suggestions.
 - Implementation: presets are applied as heuristics on top of Performance Profiles and can be overridden by route-level policy.

4) SDK & CLI changes
 - SDK v0.18.0: function rename estimate() -> estimate_cost(); new async wrapper; returns structured CostEstimate object. See SDK guide for migration snippet.
 - CLI: new export-profile command produces a YAML suitable for Dedicated scheduler. Example: redwood optimize export-profile redwood-13b-v2 --window 7d --out profile.yaml

Migration notes and breaking changes
----------------------------------
- Deprecated field removed: optimize.legacy_hint (previously used for heuristic-only recommendations). Action: remove any usages in saved route configs. Failure to remove will return 400 in API calls that include the field.
- SDK rename: update code references estimate() -> estimate_cost(). Simple search-and-replace sufficient for most codebases.
- Profile format changes: profile v1 -> v2 adds buckets for "prefix_cache_hit_rate". Dedicated scheduler accepts both v1 and v2, but v1 profiles will be automatically converted on import with a best-effort fill (read-only). We recommend re-exporting profiles after conversion.

Configuration snippets and examples
----------------------------------
- Console: Toggle Performance Profiles via Admin -> Optimize feature flags -> optimize.performance_profiles (default: off for existing tenants; on for new tenants).

- Example API request (cost estimate):
 POST /v1/optimize/estimate_cost
 Content-Type: application/json

 {
 "model": "redwood-13b-v2",
 "deployment_mode": "dedicated",
 "window_days": 30,
 "sequence_histogram": {"short": 0.7, "medium": 0.25, "long": 0.05},
 "commitment_tier": "std-monthly-1"
 }

 Response (truncated):
 {
 "monthly_cost_usd": 11500.32,
 "cost_per_1k_output_tokens": 2.87,
 "sensitivity": {"+10%_tokens_per_request": 12650.35}
 }

- SDK migration example (Python):
 # before
 cost = optimize_client.estimate(model="redwood-7b-v1", window_days=30)
 # after
 cost = await optimize_client.estimate_cost(model="redwood-7b-v1", window_days=30)

Rollout plan
------------
- Canary: 2026-02-18 -> enable Performance Profiles for 10 pilot tenants (selection criteria: medium-sized Dedicated customers with diverse request shapes). Monitor p95 latency impact and console correctness.
- Gradual rollout: 2026-02-20 -> enable for new tenants and opt-in for existing tenants via Console.
- Full enforcement: 2026-03-10 -> deprecate legacy_hint on route configs (400 returned if present).

SLOs and observability
----------------------
- Optimize service SLO unaffected: 99.9% availability for API endpoints.
- Cost estimator-specific: 99% of estimates generated within 2s for inputs with cached Performance Profiles; 95% within 5s for uncached inputs.
- Telemetry metrics exposed: optimize.profile_generation.count, optimize.estimate_latency_ms.p95, optimize.estimate_cache_hit_rate. Dashboards: /dashboards/optimize/1-3-release-estimates

How to opt-in / try it today
---------------------------
1) Console: Admin -> Feature flags -> toggle optimize.performance_profiles -> follow "Enable" flow to accept data-sharing for profile generation.
2) API: POST /v1/optimize/profiles?action=generate with model + window_days.
3) CLI: redwood optimize export-profile --generate redwood-7b-v1 --window 7d --out my-profile.yaml

Owner and support
-----------------
- Product owner: Deepa Nair (Optimize)
- Engineering lead: Samir Gupta (Optimize infra)
- Support: support@redwood.ai (use tag: optimize-1.3)
- Runbook: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/optimize-profile-generation-runbook

Known issues and limitations
---------------------------
- Cold telemetry causes conservative cost projections (noted in UI). We plan a future release (1.4) to add synthetic workload injection to reduce conservatism.
- Some legacy Dedicated accounts with strict region restrictions may see profile import failures due to S3 path policies; workaround: use CLI export/import via local file.

Full changelog (selected)
------------------------
- 1.3.0 (2026-02-20): GA release. Added Performance Profiles, Cost Estimator, Console presets, SDK 0.18.0, CLI export-profile.
- 1.3.0-rc1 (2026-02-10): Canary with 10 tenants; fixed profile-merge race leading to duplicate buckets.

Feedback and next steps
-----------------------
- We're actively collecting feedback via the Optimize workspace channel and customer QBRs. Priorities for 1.4: synthetic workload generation, improved estimator calculus for multi-model ensembles, and automated rollback suggestions when recommendations cause SLA regressions.

Appendix: reproducible profile YAML example
-----------------------------------------
name: redwood-13b-v2-chat-short
version: 2
model: redwood-13b-v2
workload: chat-short
buckets:
 - name: short
 pct: 70
 p95_latency_ms: 42
 tokens_per_request: 28
 - name: medium
 pct: 25
 p95_latency_ms: 120
 tokens_per_request: 160
 - name: long
 pct: 5
 p95_latency_ms: 420
 tokens_per_request: 1024
prefix_cache_hit_rate: 0.34
recommendations:
 batching: {max_batch_size: 128, target_window_ms: 8}
 quantization: {profile: qc-2-8bit, expected_cpu_savings_pct: 18}

If you need help migrating or want the Optimize team to run a custom projection for your account, contact Deepa or open a ticket with support (tag: optimize-1.3).

title: Reduce GPU workspace and peak memory via arena tuning, checkpointing, and scratch buffer refactor
author: Asha Kumar
text:
Motivation: production LLM inference at large batch and sequence lengths frequently hits GPU workspace/peak memory limits, forcing use of larger instances or conservative quantization. This PR reduces peak GPU allocations and working set by combining three complementary changes: (1) a conservative activation checkpointing path for transformer blocks that trades minimal CPU recompute for up to 25-40% activation RAM reduction at long sequence lengths; (2) a unified arena allocator tuning for per-stream scratch buffers and temporary kernels, reducing fragmentation and per-request overhead; (3) refactoring scratch buffer lifetimes in the CUDA kernel wrappers so scratch allocations are reused across micro-batches inside the continuous-batching loop. Design: activation checkpointing is opt-in per model variant via a new config flag model.runtime.activation_checkpointing: "auto|off|aggressive". The default "auto" enables checkpointing when offloaded KV/cache is enabled and the estimated peak reaches configured thresholds. Arena allocator changes include: a smaller max-block size for short-lived temporaries, bucketized free-lists for 512B-8MB ranges, and a fallback slow-path that reclaims whole-stream arenas on schedule boundaries. Scratch buffer refactor centralizes buffers on the BatchWorkspace object and pins those allocations to per-GPU streams to avoid cross-stream synchronization. We added microbenchmarks and a realistic ChatML workload to the perf suite to validate both latency and throughput under mixed request sizes. Results: on our A100 40GB testbed with batch=8 and seq=4096, peak GPU memory reduced by ~36%, soft latency increase <=3% p50 and throughput steady or improved in ground-truth workloads due to reduced OOM/backoffs. Backwards compatibility and safety: the changes are gated behind feature flags and require model authors to opt into activation checkpointing for small models; we provide an automated suggestion tool in the optimizer that proposes flags based on profiling sample traces. Rollout plan: staged rollout as default for Dedicated customers after two weeks of Canary (this PR includes canary toggles). Checklist: - [x] bench and microbench added - [x] unit tests for arena invariants - [x] smoke tests for continuous batching with scratch reuse - [x] documentation updates (runtime flags + upgrade notes) - [x] performance dashboard panels for memory/arena churn Additional context: this is part of ENG-1972 which targets inference cost reduction for long-context workloads. See linked performance dashboards and linear ticket for traces and flamegraphs.

Miguel Santos: Nice end-to-end. Please add an explicit integration test that steps through canary toggles and verifies arena reclaim on schedule boundaries (requested).
Asha Kumar (author): Added arena_reclaim_canary_test in tests/unit and extended perf harness to run with canary on/off; pushed follow-up commit.
Eliot Park: Activation checkpointing looks good but we should be careful about CPU recompute spikes on memory-constrained hosts. Can you add a simple memory/proc utilization monitor to the perf harness to detect swap or CPU throttling?
Asha Kumar: Added cpu-memory monitor sampling in perf harness; results show CPU recompute increased user-time by ~12% but stayed within host capacity on our canary fleet.
Soraya Chen: Please document the knob semantics in runtime_flags.md and call out known regressions for seq<512 where checkpointing can slightly increase latency; mark as opt-in for smaller models.
Asha Kumar: Updated docs and added upgrade_notes section with recommendation to keep checkpointing off for small models and priority queues.
CI: initial linux-gcc build failed due to a missing header in cuda_wrapper.cu; author fixed in commit 3 and retriggered. CI: all checks green on re-run.

Reduced GPU peak memory and workspace fragmentation via arena tuning, optional activation checkpointing, and scratch buffer reuse. Expected memory drops up to ~40% on long-sequence workloads; opt-in checkpointing for small models. Includes new runtime flags and perf dashboards.

Enable model.runtime.activation_checkpointing=auto in canary clusters first. Watch memory/arena_churn and cpu_user_time panels. If user_time rises above expected thresholds, disable checkpointing for that model variant. Canary window: 2 weeks before org-wide Dedicated rollout.

title: Regional fallback priorities & logs — post-call inventory
author: rafael_mendes
text:
From: Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwoodinference.com>
To: Elena Ruiz <elena.ruiz@medthink.health>
Cc: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwoodinference.com>, Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie.nguyen@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Fri, 3 May 2028 15:22:00 -0700
Subject: Regional fallback priorities & logs — post-call inventory

Thanks for the call earlier, Elena — good alignment on the high-level constraints. Per our discussion, I wanted to capture a short inventory of the items we need to confirm so we can scope a targeted technical deep-dive next week. I attached a simple diagram and an ops inventory CSV template to speed things up.

Action items / clarifying questions for MedThink (please reply inline if easier):
1) Residency / pinning: which datasets must remain in-region (EU-only / US-only)? You mentioned patient records must stay in the EU for EU patients; confirm whether backups/snapshots are allowed outside the EU if they are encrypted and access-controlled.
2) Failover order and allowed cross-region replication: if a primary EU region is degraded, do you require warm-standby in the same region only, or is cross-region failover to US/APAC acceptable for short windows? Any maximum allowed RPO/RTO?
3) Logs & telemetry: do MedThink logs contain PII/PHI (patient identifiers, SSNs, full names)? If yes, do you expect redaction at ingest, tokenization, or that logs be retained on-region only? What is your default retention window (you mentioned 90 days as a baseline during the call) and do you need longer-term archival (e.g., 1–7 years) for audit?
4) Backups & snapshots: frequency expectations for DB/model snapshotting, and whether incremental backups may be stored cross-region. Are immutable snapshots required?
5) Key management and attestations: will you require customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for on-rest encryption? Any need for HSM-backed key rotation logs delivered monthly?
6) Audit evidence: please indicate the list of artifacts you need from Redwood to satisfy procurement/security (SOC 2, access logs, key rotation logs, model inference logs, redaction proofs).

Proposed next steps (from our side):
- We can run a focused tech session (45–60m) with our infra engineer and a solution architect to walk through pinning flows, failover scenarios, and sample log redaction patterns.
- If you can populate the attached ops inventory CSV and return it, we’ll produce a draft MAM (mutual action map) with dates/cutovers.
- We’ll also prepare a short export of how logs look today (sanitized sample) and a preliminary cost delta for region-locked storage vs cross-region backups.

Attachments: REDWOOD_PINNING_DIAGRAM.pdf (diagram), medthink-ops-inventory-template.csv (CSV).

Thanks again — I’ll coordinate scheduling once we see preferred attendees and availability.

Best,
Rafael Mendes
Senior AE, Redwood Inference
r.mendes@redwoodinference.com
+1 415-555-0184

From: Elena Ruiz <elena.ruiz@medthink.health>
To: Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Tom Baxter <tbaxter@medthink.health>
Date: Sat, 4 May 2028 09:05:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Regional fallback priorities & logs — post-call inventory

Hi Rafael — thanks for the clear list. Below are our answers to help you scope the deep-dive; I pasted the items you asked for and added quick notes.

1) Residency / pinning:
- Patient clinical records (PHI) must remain in-region (EU) for EU patients.
- Operational metadata (service-level telemetry that does not include patient-identifiers) can be replicated to US for analytics if pseudonymized and access controlled.
- Backups of PHI: acceptable to store in US if encrypted with customer-managed keys and access is restricted to named personnel only — otherwise must stay in EU.

2) Failover order and cross-region replication:
- Preferred failover hierarchy: EU primary -> EU warm standby -> US emergency failover.
- Cross-region failover to US is permitted only for declared emergency windows (max 4 hours), must be pre-approved in runbook.
- Target RPO 15 minutes for active datasets; RTO target 30 minutes for critical APIs.

3) Logs & telemetry:
- Logs do contain limited PII (hashed patient IDs and occasional email addresses).
- We expect redaction at ingest for any free-text fields that might include PHI; hashed IDs are acceptable if the hash keys are kept on-region.
- Retention: default operational logs 90 days; audit logs 3 years. Long-term archival to our secure archive is possible after 90 days (encrypted, on-region if PHI).

4) Backups & snapshots:
- Daily incremental snapshots; weekly full snapshots.
- Immutable weekly snapshots for 90 days for critical datasets. Cross-region incremental copies only for analytics (non-PHI) or encrypted/full-access restricted backups with CMK.

5) Key management and attestations:

title: Bursting 5xx errors caused by API gateway backpressure amplifying runtime thread exhaustion on dedicated pool
text:
Issue summary: Starting ~2026-03-13T18:10Z we observed an elevated 5xx rate from the /v1/embeddings route for customers on dedicated pool dsp-6-us-east. Error surface: predominantly 502/503 returning from the API gateway with upstream runtime exits. Impact: multiple batch embedding jobs for NimbleSearch failing, ~12-18% request error rate for the tenant, visible increases in retries and customer timeouts.

Impact: Customer-reported batch uploads failing; customer-facing retry storms exacerbated backend pressure. Several internal alerts fired: apigw_5xx_rate_high, runtime_unexpected_exit, dsp-6_gpu_util_spike.

1) Submit concurrent embedding batches to customer-specific route (tenant id T-NIMBLE-22) with 8 parallel workers and batch size 256.
2) Observe rising 502s at the API gateway within 5-7 minutes.
3) Check runtime pod logs for SIGABRT / 'pthread_create' errors and thread pool exhaustion warnings.

- apigw: 502 rate rose from baseline 0.4% to 15% between 18:10 and 18:25 UTC.
- runtime rtm-04 (dsp-6-us-east) logged repeated: 'error: pthread_create: Resource temporarily unavailable' and 'fatal: cannot spawn thread' at 18:12:34 UTC.
- kernel/messages show 'task: pid XXXX killed by SIGABRT' around same window.
- GPU util for pool spiked to 92% and NVML reported frequent driver resets for a subset of nodes.

Initial hypothesis: aggressive prefetching + apigw hedged retries caused connection and work-queue pileup leading to thread exhaustion in the serving runtime.
What we checked: thread counts, ulimit/nproc, runtime threadpool settings, recent config sweeps. No recent runtime code deploys in us-east at incident start; a config bump to prefetch.window_size was rolled out globally at 17:55 UTC (INT-331002 linked).
Findings: rtm-04 hit process-level thread limit (nproc soft limit reached) while other nodes showed high accept-queue lengths. The apigw retry backoff was not honoring the reduced capacity threshold; hedged retries amplified work.
Possible contributory factors: customer workload with large batches (size 256) producing many short-lived threads per request path; the dedicated autoscaler lagged behind request surge.

2026-03-13T17:55Z - config sweep: prefetch.window_size increased (internal change INT-331002).
2026-03-13T18:08Z - first apigw 5xx alert for dsp-6-us-east.
2026-03-13T18:12Z - runtime rtm-04 logs thread create failures.
2026-03-13T18:20Z - Support engaged SRE, opened temporary rate limit on tenant route.
2026-03-13T18:35Z - Autoscaler scaled up 2 nodes but observed some nodes still in crashloop.
2026-03-13T19:05Z - Hotfix PR merged to add backpressure respect in apigw retry logic (github.com/redwood/infra/pull/3842).

Applied immediate mitigations:
- Scaled dedicated pool dsp-6 by +3 nodes to absorb burst.
- Added tenant-level temporary rate-limit to 60rps for NimbleSearch routine jobs to stop retry spin.
- Rolled back global prefetch.window_size for dsp-6 to previous value to reduce work amplification.
- Enabled apigw soft-backoff so hedged retries won't flood runtimes while autoscaler warms up.

Root cause addressed by a two-part fix: 1) runtime hardening to allocate a bounded worker thread pool (prevents unbounded pthread_create) and better nproc fallback handling, and 2) apigw change to honor backend capacity signals and avoid hedged retry amplification. Hotfix (infra PR #3842) deployed into us-east on 2026-03-13 19:05Z and runtime patch rolled on 2026-03-13 19:40Z. Post-deploy: 5xx rate dropped back to baseline ~0.6% within 20 minutes.
Resolution steps recorded and communicated to NimbleSearch. Incident declared mitigated at 2026-03-13T19:50Z; full resolution pending follow-ups.

- Create a runbook entry for 'thread/worker pool exhaustion' and include detection thresholds.
- Adjust autoscaler warmup policy for dsp-* pools to be more aggressive for batch-heavy tenants.
- Add tenant-level preflight checks for large-batch embedding uploads with recommended batch sizes.
- Audit prefetch config rollout gating so we don't apply global prefetch increases without region-specific safety checks.
- Add metric alert to detect 'pthread_create failure' log pattern and auto-throttle affected tenants.

2026-03-13T18:22Z - Aisha Patel (Support): Customer NimbleSearch reports repeated failures when uploading large batches. They see '502 Bad Gateway' after ~3-5 minutes. Added as P1 and escalated to SRE oncall.
2026-03-13T18:30Z - Marcus Li (SRE): Observed pthread_create failures on rtm-04. Suspect runtime worker explosion. Temporarily rate-limiting tenant and requesting immediate scale-up. Investigating whether nproc/u limits are being hit.
2026-03-13T18:40Z - Eleni Georgiou (Serving Eng): Confirmed runtime spawns >800 threads per process under current settings for this request shape. Preparing a bounded-pool hotfix; will coordinate patch and restart strategy.
2026-03-13T18:50Z - Aisha Patel (Support): Customer accepted temporary rate limit as workaround; reported immediate reduction in failed uploads after limit applied.
2026-03-13T19:10Z - Marcus Li (SRE): Hotfix to apigw to respect backend capacity merged and deployed (PR #3842). Monitoring for downstream improvement.
2026-03-13T19:45Z - Eleni Georgiou (Serving Eng): Runtime patch deployed to 6 nodes in dsp-6 set. Nodes stable; watching for any regressions. Post-patch logs show no further pthread_create failures.
2026-03-13T20:00Z - Aisha Patel (Support): Notified customer NimbleSearch that incident is mitigated. Customer requested postmortem and guidance on safe batch sizes.
2026-03-14T09:00Z - Marcus Li (SRE): Follow-up note - autoscaler warmup policy adjusted for dsp-6; will monitor next 48h for any drift.

title: Migrate interaction tokens to theme variable layer and resolve hover glow regression
author: Maya Torres
text:
Summary: Migrate all interactive state colors and elevation effects (hover, focus, active, disabled, pressed, and loading overlays) from component-local tokens into the new theme variable layer so they resolve consistently across light/dark/high-contrast themes. While doing this migration, fix a visible hover 'glow' regression that appears on icon-only and compact buttons when motion is reduced and when both inner and outer shadows are applied.

Background: During the tokens consolidation in Q4 we introduced per-component state tokens for buttons to support rapid experiments. Those tokens diverged from the theme layer and produced inconsistent hover/active treatments in some combinations: dark theme + high-contrast + reduced-motion. A recent customer bug report surfaced a flicker/glow where stacked shadows briefly show as double outlines on icon-only buttons when moving the pointer or programmatically toggling loading state.

Goal: Ensure all button interactive states are sourced from theme variables (not component-level overrides), eliminate the stacking shadow/glow regression, and add automated visual/interaction tests to catch regressions across themes and motion preferences. Deliverables: token migration PR, Figma token update, updated component docs, automated Cypress+Percy snapshots, accessibility signoff.

Out of scope: Rewriting button anatomy or changing visual language beyond aligning existing tokens to the theme; any JS runtime batching of hover events (handled by runtime team).

All button variants (primary, secondary, ghost, destructive, link, icon-only, compact) read hover/focus/active/disabled/loading colors and shadow values from theme variables
No visual difference in baseline appearance after migration for default theme; intended fixes only resolve the hover/glow regression
Hover glow regression reproduced in a test harness before the fix and verified resolved after changes in light/dark/high-contrast
Reduced-motion preference preserves semantics (no new motion introduced) and no double-shadow artifacts
Figma token set updated and cross-checked with the new theme variables; figma link added to PR
Unit/visual tests added: component-level storyshots and e2e visual snapshots across themes and reduced-motion
Design documentation updated with migration notes, reasoning, and a short troubleshooting section for future regressions

2026-02-16 - Maya Torres: Filed after a customer reported double outline on icon buttons in high-contrast. Attached initial screenshots and minimal repro steps.
2026-02-20 - Evan Gupta: Confirmed repro locally. Root cause appears to be overlapping CSS box-shadows: one from the component hover token and one from an outer focus ring variable. Proposed approach: move both to theme variables and dedupe by expressing focus as outline rather than stacked shadow for compact/icon buttons.
2026-02-25 - PM review (Jordan Lee): OK to proceed with migration; prioritize preserving backwards visual parity. Blocked on Figma token naming convention finalization.

Noted a keyboard focus visibility regression for ghost variant when focus ring switched from shadow to outline; requested a variant fallback to maintain 3px minimum visible focus in high-contrast. Adding follow-up task.
2026-03-09 - Evan Gupta: Addressed a11y note by adding a high-contrast focus color token and ensuring focus outline thickness using border-image technique for extreme scale. Percy snapshots now match baseline except for one dark-theme compact icon case (still investigating).

Compare Percy snapshots across light/dark/high-contrast themes for button stories
Test reduced-motion: set prefers-reduced-motion: reduce in OS and confirm no double-shadow or added motion

title: streaming-session-snapshot-client-ack-add-resume-token-openai-compat
author: Sana Patel
text:
Motivation: Improve streaming resilience for mobile/unreliable clients and make client-initiated cancel behavior idempotent while preserving OpenAI compatibility. This PR introduces a 'streaming session snapshot' model and explicit client ACK semantics so disconnected clients can reconnect and resume without inconsistent tool calls or duplicate function invocations. Includes small API surface additions (resume_token, session_id, seq) exposed in the OpenAI-compatible streaming adapter.

Summary of changes: 1) Protocol: add optional query/header parameters: X-Redwood-Session-Id (UUID), X-Redwood-Resume-Token (opaque token), and X-Redwood-Seq (monotonic integer). Server will emit a resume_token event at checkpoint boundaries (full structured object flush points) to allow resumption. 2) Client ACK semantics: streaming responses now include an ACK event type ("ack") that clients can send to confirm they received the last checkpoint; server holds tool-call/side-effect commits until ACK or until server soft-timeout expires. 3) Idempotent cancel: client-initiated cancel now accepts a cancel-with-reason payload and returns an idempotency token; repeating cancel requests with the same idempotency token is a no-op. 4) Server-side grace window: implement a configurable soft grace period (default 30s) after disconnect where session state and pending tool call fences are retained to allow resume. After grace window expiration the session is garbage collected. 5) Function-calling/structured output: ensure structured JSON blocks are flushed at checkpoint boundaries; add deterministic boundaries to avoid partial structured chunks on reconnect. 6) OpenAI compatibility layer: expose resume_token as a top-level SSE event named "resume_token" and support incoming resume headers for existing SDKs; keep the text/event-stream framing compatible with existing clients.

Why this is different from previous proposals: previous work focused on reconnect/retry-backoff and teardown safety. This PR couples explicit checkpoint metadata and client ACKs to avoid duplicate function calls and to provide a concrete resume point that is safe across network blips. It is optimized for tool calling workloads where side effects must be constrained to once semantics.

Commits (high-level): [1] protocol: add session id and resume token headers and wire through adapter; [2] runtime: checkpoint serializer and resume token generation; [3] runtime: hold-and-commit mechanism gated by client ACK and grace window; [4] api: idempotent cancel endpoint and cancel idempotency token; [5] openai-adapter: SSE event renames and backward-compatible parsing; [6] tests: end-to-end resume and duplicate-cancel tests; [7] docs: streaming lifecycle migration guide and SDK hints.

Files changed (high-level): api/streaming_adapter.py (protocol parsing and headers), runtime/checkpoint_manager.rs (checkpoint persistence and GC), runtime/tool_fence.rs (hold/commit logic), openai_compat/sse_adapter.go (resume_token event), stdlib/net/ack_client.py (SDK helper), tests/integration/test_resume.py, docs/streaming-lifecycle.md.

Small illustrative snippets: - in SSE stream: event: resume_token

 data: {"token":"<opaque>","seq":42,"session_id":"..."}

- cancel endpoint: POST /v1/streams/:id/cancel {"reason":"user_abort","idempotency_token":"abc123"} -> 202 {"cancelled":true,"token":"abc123"}

Testing: added deterministic unit tests for checkpoint boundaries and a flaky-network harness that simulates TCP drops and validates resume semantics across reconnects. End-to-end tests ensure that function-calling side-effects execute exactly once when clients follow ACK/resume contract. Performance: microbenchmark shows ~3% p99 overhead for sessions with frequent checkpoints (configurable), negligible for typical chat flows.

Migration notes: - Backwards compatible: clients that do not send session headers keep existing behavior. Resume support is opt-in (server issues resume_token only when session_id provided). - SDKs: quick helper added in python/ts/go SDKs (std ack helper) and docs updated with example reconnect flow. - Operators: new config runtime.streaming.grace_window_seconds (default 30) and runtime.streaming.max_session_persist (default 10m).

Rollout plan: feature-flag rollout behind 'stream_session_snapshot' flag. Start with internal beta, then enable for hosted customers on request, then GA after 3 weeks of monitoring. Alerts: added SLO-level alert if resumed session failure rate > 1% over 1h.

Known limitations & follow-ups: - Resume requires client to retain resume_token; tokens are opaque and ephemeral. We will later add signed tokens for cross-region resume. - Tool-call fences add memory pressure while session is in grace window; follow-up to add spill-to-disk for very large pending calls (ENG-2210).

Checklist: [x] design doc linked, [x] unit tests, [x] e2e tests, [x] docs updated, [x] SDK helpers, [x] load test run, [x] security review (RBAC/headers sanitized).

Release notes: Introduces optional streaming session resume through session_id/resume_token and client ACK semantics to avoid duplicate tool invocations on reconnects. Backwards compatible by default. See docs/streaming-lifecycle.md for usage and SDK examples.

Leo Zhang: Can we avoid holding tool fences in memory for >grace_window? Suggest spill-to-disk or bounded queue. (addressed in follow-up ENG-2210).
Aisha Gomez: Edge-case: what happens if client ACK is lost and resume_token used? Proposed server-side re-emit on reconnect if session still valid. Implemented and covered by e2e tests.
Tomás Ribeiro: Please document the backward compatibility with existing SSE parsers. Added details to docs and openai adapter contains toggles to keep legacy event shapes.

title: Ops Orchestra: Company-wide Access, Change, Data, Procurement, Vendor, and Travel Procedures
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Overview

Purpose
This document (Ops Orchestra) defines the canonical, company-wide procedures for access and permissions, change management, data classification & handling, procurement and expenses, vendor onboarding & management, travel policy, and a small library of standard templates. It is intended for managers, approvers, and people-ops/finance partners who execute or govern cross-functional operational processes.

Scope
Applies to all Redwood Inference employees, contractors, and vendors that require platform, finance, or HR-related access or services. Exceptions must be approved by the relevant owner_team and logged in the change registry.

Owners and SLAs
- Document owner: finance-legal
- Primary operational leads: Security (access changes), Eng-SRE (infrastructure change runs), Finance (procurement/expenses), People-Ops (travel & benefits)
- Target SLA for routine approvals: 72 business hours
- Emergency/expedited approvals: same-day (see Emergency change section)

1) Access & Permissions
1.1. Access model
- Roles: Employee, Contractor, Service (machine identity), Admin
- Principle of least privilege (PoLP) is required for all roles. Role permissions must be justified in the access request ticket.
- Temporary access: granted using time-bound roles (max 14 days for privileged work).

1.2. Request and approval flow
1. Submit access request via internal access-portal (link: /internal/tools/access-portal). Include: owner, justification, resources, duration, and approver group.
2. Security review: Security reviews high-scope requests (production, key stores, billing).
3. Grant: System auto-provisions where templates exist; otherwise manual provisioning by Cloud Ops within SLA.
4. Verification: Requester confirms access; owner_team marks request closed.

1.3. Access matrix (example)
| Resource class | Typical roles allowed | Approval required | Max duration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Production inference cluster | Platform-engineer, Release-engineer | Security + Team Lead | 7 days (expirable) |
| Billing and invoices | Finance, Accounting | Finance Manager | 30 days |
| Audit logs / SIEM | Security | Security Lead | 14 days |
| Private console (VPC) | Customer Success (with customer consent) | Security + Customer Success Director | 14 days |

1.4. Periodic review
- Quarterly entitlement review for Admin and privileged roles. Teams must certify access within 10 business days of quarterly notification.

2) Change Management
2.1. Classification
- Standard change: low-risk, pre-approved templates, no downtime (automated).
- Normal change: scheduled, requires change ticket and 72-hour review window.
- Emergency change: unplanned, immediate action required to restore availability or reduce security risk. Must be retrospectively reviewed by CAB.

2.2. Change Advisory Board (CAB)
- Membership: Eng-SRE, Platform, Security, Product, and one Finance/Legal representative.
- Weekly meeting cadence for normal changes; emergency convened ad-hoc.
- Approval criteria: risk, roll-back plan, test plan, owner, monitoring & alerting updates.

2.3. Change request template (required fields)
- Title
- Owner & approvers
- Type (standard/normal/emergency)
- Rollout window & maintenance window
- Backout/rollback plan
- Canary/verification steps and SLOs to observe
- Impacted services and customers

2.4. Deployment checklist (example)
1. Create change ticket in change-registry (link: /internal/tools/change-registry).
2. Attach runbook and rollback commands.
3. Confirm tests in staging and smoke tests.
4. Schedule and notify stakeholders 48 hours before the window.
5. Execute canary rollout; monitor latency/error metrics for 30 minutes.
6. Proceed to full rollout if health criteria met, otherwise initiate rollback.

3) Data Classification & Management
3.1. Classification levels
- Public: Safe for external publication.
- Internal: Company-internal operational data; limited sharing outside Redwood prohibited.
- Confidential: Business-sensitive data (contracts, pricing, non-public benchmarks).
- Restricted: Regulated or customer-sensitive data (PII, PHI, encrypted customer payloads).

3.2. Handling rules by class
- Storage: Restricted must be stored in customer-dedicated or encrypted buckets with KMS key rotation; Confidential must use company-managed encryption.
- Access: Restricted requires two-factor and documented business justification.
- Transit: TLS 1.2+; internal tunnels must be encrypted and use mutual authentication where possible.
- Retention: See table below.

3.3. Retention & Disposal (summary)
| Data class | Default retention | Disposal action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public | N/A | No action required |
| Internal | 3 years | Archive to long-term internal store, remove direct access |
| Confidential | 7 years | Secure delete and log shred event |
| Restricted | Customer-specific / regulatory | Follow customer or legal retention schedule; certify deletion with KMS key rotation |

3.4. Data breach playbook (high level)
1. Contain: Isolate affected resources.
2. Notify: Security incident channel and CISO.
3. Assess: Determine scope and classification of exposed data.
4. Remediation: Revoke credentials, rotate keys, patch vulnerability.
5. Notification: Legal decides customer/regulator notifications.
6. Post-incident: Postmortem and remediation tracking.

4) Procurement & Expenses
4.1. Procurement thresholds & approval matrix
- Purchase Request (PR) < $5,000: Manager approval (auto in procurement system).
- $5,000 – $50,000: Finance Manager + Procurement review.
- $50,000 – $250,000: Procurement Director + Legal review.
- > $250,000: VP-level approval and board notification for multiyear commitments.

4.2. Preferred vendors and vendor rationalization
- Teams should use preferred vendors list in procurement portal. If a new vendor is required, request a Vendor Exception with justification and complete the risk questionnaire.
- Vendor Exception approvals target SLA: 5 business days.

4.3. Expense policy highlights
- Travel expenses must include original receipts for amounts > $75.

title: Priority-weight transition lag results in background-flushes consuming burst credits and causing early 429s for interactive routes
text:
Issue summary:
SkylineChat reports repeated early 429s affecting low-latency chat routes after their account was promoted to an enterprise plan with higher burst credits. The tenant experiences normal throughput for bulk/background flush jobs but interactive SSE/chat endpoints begin receiving 429s within minutes of the promotion.

Impact:
- Intermittent 429s on interactive chat routes (SSE & websocket) causing degraded real-time UX for SkylineChat customers.
- Bulk ingestion (background flushers) shows increased token consumption and appears to be draining burst credits during the transition window.
- Customer reports business impact: chat sessions dropping for end-users during peak business hours.

Environment:
- Tenant: SkylineChat (enterprise)
- Region: prod-us-west primary, spillover to eu-west reported
- Models: redwood-2-large for chat, redwood-1-quantized for background encode
- Config: priority-split enabled with separate lanes for interactive (high) and background (low) traffic; recently changed weight thresholds as part of onboarding.

Steps to reproduce / observed sequence:
1) Promote tenant plan to enterprise (increase burst credits + priority weights)
2) System kicks off background flushes to catch up (many short-lived parallel workers)
3) Within ~3-7 minutes interactive connections begin seeing 429 responses
4) Token accounting shows large sink from background workers attributed to the same tenant during the transition window

Observed behavior (logs/metrics):
- Ingress rate-limiter traces show priority_ladder transition event at 2026-03-08T14:02:11Z then a burst of low-priority background-worker calls between 14:02:12Z-14:09:00Z.
- Example token-accounting line (edge logs):
 [2026-03-08T14:04:37Z] tenant=skylinechat route=/v1/generate tokens=23872 worker=flush-coordinator-22 priority=LOW counted=true
 [2026-03-08T14:04:38Z] tenant=skylinechat route=/v1/chat tokens=12 session=abc123 priority=HIGH result=429 reason=quota_exhausted
- Rate-limiter debug shows window refill event delayed by ~45s after promotion due to epoch swap on rate-controller nodes.
- Prometheus metrics: rate_limit_token_pool_available{tenant="skylinechat"} dropped from ~120k to <4k in the transition window; background_worker_token_rate spiked x8.

Expected behavior:
- Priority promotions should not allow background flushers to siphon newly-allocated burst credits before interactive lanes get rebalanced; interactive sessions should be prioritized during and immediately after plan change.

Temporary mitigations attempted by Support/Customer:
- Customer paused background flushers (reduced worker parallelism) which restored interactive success within ~30s.
- Support toggled a temporary soft-isolate flag that pins interactive routes to a protected burst pool; prevented further 429s for the duration.

Investigation notes and hypotheses:
- Hypothesis A: Rate-controller epoch exchange during tier update causes a short window where refill assignments are not synchronized across origin and edge, allowing background workers to claim new credits first.
- Hypothesis B: Priority weight recalculation happens asynchronously; background lane retains older token slice until the weight update completes, resulting in effective over-allocation to background workers.
- Hypothesis C: Orchestrator warms up many parallel short-lived flush workers after promotion; our per-route token attribution (edge-side) misattributes some of those against interactive route token pools when path normalization occurs (signed-url/callbacks).

Next steps / action items:
- Engineering (rate-limiter team) to reproduce epoch-swap refill lag in staging using the plan-promotion script; create a deterministic integration test reproducing the race. (assigned: Diego)
- Add short-term guard: when a tenant plan changes, apply a 120s protected window that favors interactive lanes for refill allocation. (owner: rate-limiter)
- Add logging around refill assignment decisions and add metric: refill_lag_seconds per-tenant. (owner: telemetry)
- Consolidate runbook steps for customers performing plan upgrades to reduce parallelism of background workers during the first 5 minutes. (owner: customer-success)

Workaround provided to customer:
- Recommended action: pause background flush worker pool and resume gradually with concurrency capped at 2 for the first 5 minutes post promotion.
- Support applied a temporary route-protect flag while engineering works on the long-term fix.

Attachments / evidence:
- rate-limiter traces: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/rate-limiter/tenant-skylinechat/trace-2026-03-08
- support convo: https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C0123ABCDE/p1678643200

Resolution notes: (in progress)
- Short-term protective guard implemented as tenant flag (rollout candidate) and tested in staging.
- Root-cause reproduction pending; target for patch and global rollout: 2026-03-20.

2026-03-08 14:15 - Lena Park (Support): Customer opened ticket after noticing dropped chat sessions immediately following enterprise promo. Provided initial logs and authorized Support to pause background workers.
2026-03-08 14:28 - Diego Martinez (SRE): Confirmed refill-lag pattern on edge traces; queued this to rate-limiter team for deeper investigation. Added linked issue SUP-762318 for a similar epoch-swap investigation.
2026-03-09 09:12 - Priya Rao (Rate-limiter eng): Reproduced race locally with plan-promotion script; observed refill assignment lag when controller leader rotates. Drafting fix to ensure refill assignments are transactional with leader election.
2026-03-11 11:43 - Customer Success (Ana Gomez): Sent step-by-step recommended onboarding checklist to SkylineChat to avoid immediate parallel flushes after plan changes; customer applied guidance and reported improvement.
2026-03-12 16:00 - Diego Martinez (SRE): Deployed temporary protected-window flag to a small canary subset; no further 429s observed during canary promotions. Planning broader rollout after PR review: https://github.com/redwood-inference/edge/pull/1892

In Progress - temporary guard enabled for canary tenants; engineering patch and global rollout planned.

title: Normalize OpenAI invocation envelope, clarify tool-selection signals, and add stream-resilient framing
author: Asha Menon
text:
Motivation: Several customers and internal evals showed inconsistent behavior when the OpenAI-compat layer returned tool selection signals (e.g. 'tool_choice' with ambiguous metadata) across streaming and non-streaming modes. This caused duplicate tool invocations, incorrect schema inference, and brittle downstream tool routers in Redwood Dedicated/Private deployments.

This PR introduces a deterministic normalization step for the OpenAI invocation envelope, plus stream-resilient framing for tool/message fragments. The goal is to: 1) make the compatibility layer emit a single canonical selection signal for every invocation, 2) map OpenAI tool schemas into a stable internal schema with minimal changes for existing customers, and 3) make streaming fragments idempotent and re-assemblable at the service edge.

What changed (high level):
- New package: pkg/openai/normalize_invocation.go — normalizer that transforms incoming OpenAI-style responses into Redwood's canonical InvocationEnvelope. It collapses multiple tool signals into one selected_tool hint and preserves tool confidence/metadata in a stable metadata map.
- Tool schema mapper: pkg/tooling/tool_schema_mapper.go — conservative mapping rules for OpenAI 'parameters' -> Redwood typed schema, including type coercion rules and a small whitelist for nested objects.
- Streaming: server/streaming/frame_parser.go updated to add fragment IDs and checksum headers for tool/message fragments. Parser now supports out-of-order fragments and dedup by fragment id+checksum.
- API layer: server/api/openai_adapter.go updated to call the normalizer before routing to tool routing pipeline; updates to response shape sent back to clients to maintain OpenAI wire-compatibility while ensuring a single 'selected_tool' semantic in the internal router.
- Docs: docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md with migration notes and examples.

Compatibility notes:
- Outbound API responses remain OpenAI-compatible: we do not change the visible OpenAI fields returned to customers. Internally, however, the runtime will prefer the normalized 'selected_tool' hint to decide which tool to invoke. In the rare case of conflicting tool signals, the normalizer uses (in order): explicit_invocation field, highest-confidence tool_choice, then deterministic fallback to first available tool that matches schema.
- Customers who implemented custom tool routers based on raw tool_choice fragments should migrate to using the new normalized hint or consult the docs which show a 1-line change to switch to the normalized envelope.

Testing and rollout plan:
- Unit tests for mapping rules and type coercions included.
- Integration tests: simulated streaming sessions with fragmented tool metadata; verified idempotent assembler under network reorders.
- Canary rollout: staged to 10% of traffic for hosted API for 48 hours, then to Dedicated nodes behind a feature flag. Private installer includes an opt-in toggle for the first release cycle.

Migration steps for operators (short):
1) Review docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md for the mapping table.
2) If you have custom routers, update to read the normalized 'selected_tool' header from the invocation payload.
3) Toggle feature flag if running Redwood Private/Dedicated during rollout.

Related work: links to internal Linear tasks ENG-7421 (tool-selection ambiguity), ENG-7553 (stream-fragment dedup).

Rationale for not changing public wire format: minimize breaking client changes while fixing internal flakiness in tool invocation semantics.

Release notes summary: Normalizes OpenAI invocation envelopes to ensure a single canonical tool-selection signal, improves streaming fragment resilience, and provides safe mapping rules for tool parameter schemas. Operators with custom routing should follow the migration guide in docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md.

Leo Carter (request changes): The mapping looks reasonable but I worry about nested parameter coercions. Can we add a strict-mode toggle for operators who want to reject coercions rather than coerce?
Asha Menon (author): Added a 'coercion_mode' config to tool_schema_mapper with 'permissive' and 'strict' options and documented it in the migration guide. Also added unit tests covering both modes.
Maya Singh (comment): CI initially failed on a flaky streaming test — I saw we added a small sleep in the assembler. Can we avoid sleeps and use deterministic signaling?
Asha Menon (author): Reworked assembler to use a fragment arrival map keyed by fragment-id+checksum and removed the sleep. Tests updated accordingly.
Rui Zhang (approved): Verified canary traces and the duplicated-tool incident no longer reproduces under the test harness. Approving for merge.

Normalize OpenAI invocation envelopes: canonical internal selection hint (selected_tool), stream fragment resilience (ids + checksum dedupe), and conservative tool parameter mapping with a strict/permissive toggle. No public wire-format breaking changes. Operators with custom routers should read docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md for migration steps.

title: Longform reading scrapbook: compression, KV heuristics, and RAG probes
author: Hector Alvarez
text:
Purpose and quick orientation:
- Dumping a multi-day scatter of readings and half-formed experiment ideas focused on three related pain points we keep hitting in Redwood inference: (1) long-context token/kv management, (2) quantization + tiny-bit compression tradeoffs, (3) RAG/knowledge-retention failure modes when you combine heavy compression with retrieval.

High-level intuition summary (my current mental model):
- KV cache is the single biggest latency/cost lever for long-context use-cases at serving time. If we can aggressively identify stable prefixes or repeat subsequences and compress their KV representations, we reduce memory bandwidth and GPU DRAM pressure without changing model outputs much.
- But compression is brittle: lossy encodings (PQ, quantized SVD, learned compressive layers) induce distributional drift that looks small on synthetic next-token perplexity but amplifies in RAG-style multi-step generation (the classic small-perturbation -> hallucination cascade).
- Practical rule of thumb: high compression on old turns (>= N tokens back) OK for stateless generation; near-term KV entries (last M tokens) need much higher fidelity.

Papers and threads I skimmed (quick notes and actionable bits):
1) "Adaptive KV compression for long-context transformers" (paper X, arXiv)
 - Key idea: per-key importance score + tiered storage (full, 8-bit, 4-bit, compressed vector) with runtime migration.
 - Interesting eval: they measure generation quality with a 2-step retrieval+generation pipeline; small drop in ROUGE but big drop in factuality once compressed keys are used in attention.
 - Takeaway: implement importance scoring (attention recency, token-level entropic signal, and retrieval hit-rate) and simulate a 3-tier cache in our local infra.

2) "Low-bit matrix sketching for KV layers" (paper Y)
 - Fast hardware-friendly sketcher that keeps dot-product fidelity for sparse attention. Really promising for CPU-hosted caches.
 - Implementation note: integration requires kernel-level support or a staged de/serialization when moving to GPU. Might be good for Dedicated nodes where we control the runtime.

3) RAG instability notes (various conference talks + community threads)
 - When retrieval and compressed KV interact, model often overfits to compressed context artifacts; hallucinations often start at hallucinated citation tokens (weird markers).
 - Practical mitigation: calibrated retrieval scoring (confidence-aware masking), hallucination detectors that watch for sudden entropy drops, and short-term cache reset after retrieval events.

Conference takeaways (NeurIPS workshop-style, paraphrased):
- People are leaning into hybrid solutions: keep a small high-fidelity L2 cache (GPU DRAM) for last 1–2k tokens, move older context to compressed L3 (NVMe compressed blobs) with quick decompress kernels, and reconstruct only top-K relevant old spans on miss.
- Several groups experiment with "context stitching": keep a lightweight signature (8–16B) per span to quickly decide whether to partially reconstruct or skip. This aligns with the paper X importance-score idea.

Open questions / hypotheses to test (priority order):
1) Does a simple recency+attention-weight threshold (computed from a small sample) capture enough signal to put 90% of old KV entries into a high-compression tier with <1% end-user metric regression? (High impact if true.)
2) How does 4-bit vs 6-bit dynamic quantization behave for attention keys vs values? I suspect keys are more tolerant to low-bit quant since they primarily serve dot-product similarity, values carry richer semantics and need higher precision.
3) Can we use a learned small projector (a local lightweight MLP) to compress KV entries such that decompression is cheap and the projection is tuned to preserve the internal attention geometry? (Risk: it adds CPU/GPU op overhead; benefit: learned compression may beat generic PQ.)

Short experiment plan (local rig / cheap first pass):
- Dataset: subset of commons dialogues + some internal customer chat logs (anonymized) — pick long-context sessions > 4k tokens.
- Baseline: current KV store (no compression). Measure token-level perplexity, generation EM on QA sets, and hallucination proxy (facts mismatch count).
- Step A: implement 2-tier simple: last 1024 tokens = full; older = 8-bit rounded quant. Run synthetic replay to measure delta.
- Step B: add recency+attention score filter to promote hot older entries back to full. Track the hit-rate and cost savings.
- Step C: evaluate small learned projection compression vs PQ. Keep metric suite same.
- Measure: GPU DRAM usage, avg request latency (p50/p95), tokens per second, and hallucination proxy.

Engineering considerations and rough runtime implications:
- Serialization format: use an aligned binary blob with per-key signatures to allow quick skip. On Dedicated, we can push a fused kernel to decompress top-K entries inline; for hosted API we'll need a safe per-request CPU decompress path to avoid noisy neighbor problems.
- Migration strategy: run A/B with canary traffic; keep deterministic fallback to original KV (no compression) for mismatch cases. Observability: add a per-request flag describing whether compressed entries used, compression tier distribution, and a per-request reconstruction time.

Unresolved thoughts / brain dumps:
- Could we piggyback LM-based "reconstructor" that given compressed KV tries to regenerate a candidate span and we only keep reconstructor scoring on the side? (sounds expensive but maybe amortizable).
- Idea: for RAG-heavy flows, include a quick "sanity head" that reranks outputs based on a small off-policy verification model (cheap classifier).
- TODO: check INF-3421 notes (Ravi) for the existing RAG regression cases — some overlap likely.

Immediate next steps (this week):
- Prototype two-tier quantization on CPU-backed KV for replay dataset (me).
- Sync with Mika to see if her kernel patch for fast 4-bit dotprod is ready to test (Ravi to loop her in).
- Create a short internal experiment spec and link to JIRA INF-3421.

Notes to self (meta):
- Keep notes messy — this doc will be the canonical messy dump. Move polished experiment plan into shared_drives/engineering/applied-ml when we lock the approach.

Random links I kept hitting:
- Lightweight sketcher repo (local copy): https://github.com/example/kv-compression-experiments
- NeurIPS workshop slides: https://tinyurl.com/context-stitching-2027 (saved copy in drive)
- Related internal tickets: JIRA INF-3421, INF-3560

End of dump.

title: Horizon Quay AI Infrastructure
author: Maya Chen
text:
Account profile and negotiation notes:
- Profile: Horizon Quay is a global maritime logistics SaaS (port ops + scheduling). Heavy real-time chat+assistant for ops centers; embeddings for manifest search; reranking for ETA predictions.
- Capacity ask: Reserved pool sized for 8 sustained A100-equivalent GPUs per primary region (NA + EU). Expected steady-state: ~350–600 RPS for short payload chat (avg token window 256). Burst to ~1k RPS during shift changes.
- Performance targets: P95 text-gen latency <= 80ms, P99 <= 220ms for chat on dedicated pool; throughput guarantees of 500 RPS sustained per region.
- SLA position (customer asks): 99.95% uptime across dedicated pools; 30% credit at 99.9–99.95; 50% credit below 99.9; request for monthly credit cap and cumulative measurement window.
- Redwood counterproposals discussed: baseline 99.95 SLA with quarterly reconciliation; credit schedule tiered: 99.9–99.95 = 10% service credit, 99.5–99.9 = 30%, <99.5 = 60% (proposal to legal). Redwood wants max cap at 6 months' fee.
- Maintenance windows: customer requires predictable maintenance windows not during shift-change windows (06:00–09:00 UTC). Proposed weekly 02:00–04:00 region-local maintenance with 72h advance notice; emergency maintenance with 48h notice and rolling failover.
- Support / escalation: Horizon Quay requires 24/7 hotline for Sev1 with 15-minute acknowledgement, 2-hour remediate SLA target for critical infrastructure, 4-hour for Sev2. Redwood proposes 15min ack, 1h initial response, remediation time objective to be defined per incident severity in SOW.
- Throughput guarantees & reserved GPU planning: plan includes capacity buffer for 1.5x expected steady-state; autoscaling burst into shared pool allowed with pre-authorized fallback; need explicit routing policy for latency-first vs cost-first (customer wants latency-first for ops-critical calls).
- Security/compliance: customer requires SOC2 Type II report, KMS integration for customer-managed keys, audit logs retained 12 months, option for EU-only residency for EU traffic.
- POC summary (3 weeks):
 * Week 0: onboarding, network peering, SSO test (SAML).
 * Week 1: model import + inference validation, baseline latency/throughput profiling.
 * Week 2: load testing to 1.2x forecast, KV/prefix cache tuning, batch tuning.
 * Week 3: SLA stress scenarios, failover drill, cost/perf report and recommended reserved sizing.
- POC status: onboarding complete; peering and SSO in staging done; load tests scheduled 2026-03-15. Initial latency targets met on small-scale tests; sustained throughput test pending.
- Procurement notes: finance wants committed capacity discount tiers and an option to convert to Dedicated Reserved on annual renewal. Legal flagged service credit language and liability cap.
- Quote history: pricing deck sent 2026-02-28 (drive link). Redwood gave two sizing options: 8x reserved (latency-priority) and 12x with burst (cost amortized). Horizon Quay prefers 8x + autoscale to shared.
- Direct quotes from stakeholders: "We cannot accept blackouts during port shift windows — any maintenance must be out of peak or have a clear failover plan." — Head of Ops.
- Next steps (concrete): Redwood to produce SLA redline + SOW by 2026-03-17; schedule legal review call 2026-03-22; run scheduled load test 2026-03-15; finalize forecasted ARR and draft PO template after pricing revision.
- Internal AE reminders: capture agreed uptime measurement buckets, document monthly reporting cadence, confirm escrow/backup plan for on-prem fallbacks.

title: Audit log ingestion: buffering + retry/backpressure semantics + failure-mode tests
author: Marcus Lin
text:
## Context
Audit events are becoming a hard requirement for enterprise (Hosted/Dedicated) and especially Private deployments. As we instrument more sensitive actions, we are seeing that the ingestion path is the limiting factor for reliability: transient sink outages, regional partitions, and backpressure can cause drops, long delays, or (worse) services blocking in unpredictable ways.

This ticket hardens the audit event ingestion pipeline with:
- bounded buffering (in-memory + durable where appropriate)
- explicit retry policy with jitter/backoff and retry classification
- clear backpressure behavior (what happens when buffers fill)
- failure-mode / chaos-style tests so we can prove behavior and avoid regressions

## Current behavior (summary of observed issues)
- Producers often do best-effort HTTP fire-and-forget to the ingestion API. On timeout/5xx we sometimes drop events without a consistent metric.
- Some producers retry aggressively (tight loops) causing thundering herd during outages; others never retry.
- During sink degradation (Kafka/stream backlog, exporter slowdown), ingestion API returns 429/503 but producer behavior is inconsistent.
- Private: installer/upgrade tooling sometimes runs in constrained environments; losing events during upgrades is common because there is no durable buffer.

## Goals / non-goals
### Goals
1) Define and implement the ingestion reliability contract for sensitive-action audit events (practical at-least-once) with bounded buffers.
2) Ensure services behave predictably when the audit sink is down/slow:
 - do not melt down core services
 - do not silently drop sensitive events
 - expose clear metrics so SRE can detect and respond
3) Provide failure-mode tests that simulate:
 - ingestion API down
 - sink backlog / slow downstream
 - network partitions / packet loss
 - producer restarts with buffered events

### Non-goals
- Building a customer-facing audit log UI
- Changing event schema/taxonomy (covered by ENG-4821/4822); we only add transport semantics + tests

## Proposed design (implementation direction)
### Producer-side library (preferred default)
- Add an async audit publisher in the shared audit library:
 - bounded in-memory queue (configurable, default sized by service QPS)
 - background worker(s) to publish batches
 - exponential backoff with jitter on retryable failures
 - classify retryable vs non-retryable (e.g., 400/validation error is non-retryable; 408/429/5xx retryable)
 - emit metrics: enqueue_rate, dequeue_rate, retry_count, drop_count, queue_depth, publish_latency

### Durable buffering (where required)
- For “must-audit” sensitive actions (RBAC changes, credential lifecycle, routing/policy changes, export config, retention/residency changes):
 - persist event to a local WAL (write-ahead log) before acknowledging the admin action where feasible.
 - publish from WAL asynchronously; on restart, replay.
- Hosted/Dedicated services: WAL on local disk (or ephemeral + backed by node disk), size-limited with rotation.
- Private installer/upgrade tooling: spool to a local file buffer (e.g., JSONL with checksums) and flush when ingestion is reachable.

### Backpressure behavior (explicit)
- When in-memory queue is full:
 - default: drop non-sensitive (or non-must-audit) events with a clear metric and log at WARN with rate limiting.
 - must-audit events: attempt WAL write; if WAL cannot be written (disk full / permissions / corruption), fail the admin action with 503 and a deterministic error code (so customers know this is “audit pipeline not healthy”).
- When WAL is full (size cap reached):
 - treat as must-audit failure for must-audit events (return 503 for the admin action)
 - for non-must-audit: drop with metric

### Delivery semantics and duplicates
- We assume at-least-once delivery is acceptable; duplicates must be expected.
- Require event_id presence (ENG-4830) so downstream and SIEM guidance can dedupe.
- Retries must not regenerate event_id.

### Ingestion API behavior (server-side)
- Return explicit status codes:
 - 202 accepted for async ingestion
 - 429 when throttling/backpressure (include Retry-After)
 - 503 when sink unavailable
- Add server-side buffering where appropriate (short-lived queue) to avoid rejecting brief spikes.

## Acceptance criteria
- When the downstream sink is unavailable for 30 minutes, producers with must-audit actions:
 - do not lose events (WAL replay after restart)
 - do not exceed configured disk cap; if cap reached, must-audit admin actions fail with 503 + documented error code
- When downstream is slow (p95 publish latency > 5s), producer queue depth increases but:
 - service CPU/mem remains within +10% of baseline
 - no request handler thread starvation / deadlocks
- Metrics and dashboards show:
 - drop_count = 0 for must-audit event types
 - end-to-end delivery latency p99 < 5 minutes under normal conditions
- Failure-mode tests run in CI (or nightly) and validate:
 - retry behavior conforms to backoff spec
 - WAL replay works after forced restart
 - backpressure returns expected status codes and does not produce unbounded memory growth

## Test plan (failure modes)
- Unit tests (library):
 - retry classification, jitter/backoff, queue overflow behavior
 - WAL append + replay + corruption handling
- Integration tests (local env):
 - run a fake ingestion server that returns sequences: 503 -> 202, 429 with Retry-After, timeouts
 - verify published count == enqueued count for must-audit types
- Chaos / staging:
 - temporarily block egress from a canary service to ingestion endpoint
 - inject sink latency/backlog (rate limit consumer)
 - verify alerts + runbook steps are actionable

## Rollout / migration
- Phase 1: ship producer library changes behind feature flag (audit.publisher.v2)
- Phase 2: enable for Control Plane + Console backend (highest customer impact)
- Phase 3: enable for API Gateway admin endpoints + Private installer
- Phase 4: enforce must-audit semantics for the sensitive action list (ties to coverage gating)

## Open questions
1) Which exact event types are “must-audit” (fail admin action if cannot persist)? Proposed set aligns with PM-938 list; confirm with Naomi/Olga.
2) WAL location/permissions in Kubernetes (Hosted/Dedicated) and disk sizing defaults.
3) Private installer identity: if operator identity is missing, do we still treat events as must-audit? (Proposed: yes; actor.type=system/operator_unknown but must log action.)

## Owners / reviewers
- Owner (SRE): Sean Gallagher
- Security Eng reviewer: Kevin Osei
- Platform reviewer: Ethan Park
- GRC consult: Olga Petrov

## References
- ADR: Audit Event Delivery Guarantees (Confluence)
- Related tickets: ENG-4835 (alerts), ENG-4830 (correlation IDs), ENG-4827 (exporter normalization)
- Customer signals: SUP-18510 (duplicate events on retries), SUP-18421 (Private missing events)

2026-02-03 (Sean Gallagher): Drafted producer retry/backoff spec + queue/WAL semantics. Shared in #eng-sre for feedback; consensus: must-audit should fail closed once WAL cap hit, but only for admin/sensitive actions.
2026-02-10 (Kevin Osei): Confirmed Security preference: at-least-once with documented dedupe guidance; no requirement for exactly-once. Need explicit error code for “audit unavailable” so Support can triage quickly.
2026-02-14 (Rafael Mendes): Added staging game-day outline to validate sink outage behavior; propose running after dashboards/alerts are live (ENG-4835).
2026-02-21 (Ethan Park): Control Plane can persist to node disk for WAL; request: keep library defaults conservative to avoid disk churn on high-volume endpoints.
2026-02-24 (Sean Gallagher): Implementation started in shared audit publisher: bounded queue + retry classification + metrics. WAL implementation in progress; targeting canary in control-plane first.

Naomi Feldman (2026-02-05): Please document customer-facing behavior for: (a) what happens when audit logging is misconfigured in Private, (b) whether admin actions can fail due to audit sink issues. We need aligned wording for security reviews.
Logan Wright (2026-02-12): For coverage dashboards: please emit a metric when must-audit action fails due to audit pipeline (distinct from generic 5xx) so we can separate product outages from audit enforcement.
Aisha Bello (2026-02-19): Once metrics names are finalized, loop me in so we can wire alert thresholds without redoing dashboards.

title: introduce KV freelist defragmenter and selective hot-prefix pinning
author: Samuel Harkness
text:
Motivation: under high-concurrency, the paged KV cache freelist would fragment after repeated allocations/frees of mixed-size blocks, increasing allocation latency and causing more frequent slow-path compaction. This PR adds an opportunistic freelist defragmenter that compacts adjacent free pages on free-paths and a lightweight hot-prefix selective pinning policy so frequently-accessed key prefixes avoid costly eviction. Goals: reduce p99 allocation latency, lower background compaction pressure, and improve tail latency for workloads with hot prefixes (chat sessions, long contexts).

Summary of changes:
- Opportunistic freelist defragmenter run inline on frees when a small threshold of contiguous free segments is observed (configurable).
- Compact-on-free path that coalesces adjacent free pages into larger blocks to improve reuse for larger token sequences.
- Adaptive reuse scoring: tracks short-term reuse frequency per page bucket and prefers reuse of high-score pages.
- Hot-prefix selective pinning: a small resident pin set for top-N hot key prefixes with LRU eviction; pins are persisted across ephemeral reconnects to stabilize performance.
- Scheduler hint: allocator exposes a gentle backpressure hint to the request scheduler when fragmentation crosses configured thresholds so the scheduler can delay batch growth and avoid thrashing.
- Tests and microbenchmarks: new unit tests for defragmenter invariants and a throughput/latency benchmark demonstrating behavior across workload mixes.

Compatibility: fully opt-in via runtime config flags (defaults are conservative).

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc linked in PR
- [x] Unit tests
- [x] Microbenchmark
- [x] CI green after flake fix
- [x] Perf measurements attached

Related tickets: Linear ENG-4823 (KV fragmentation), ENG-4781 (hot-prefix regressions).

2026-02-11 Aisha Patel: Can you explain why defrag on free runs inline? Concerned about tail latency impact during large frees.
2026-02-11 Samuel Harkness: We only run inline when the free forms at most 3 adjacent segments and the page cost estimate is under a low threshold; larger coalesces are scheduled to background worker. Added config knobs and doc comment explaining tradeoffs.
2026-02-12 Marcus Liu: The hot-prefix pin set is good, but can we bound memory? Also request a small unit test to assert pin eviction behavior.
2026-02-12 Samuel Harkness: Added bounded pin set (default 64 entries) with LRU eviction and tests for eviction semantics (tests/kv/pinning_eviction.rs).
2026-02-13 Ellen Park: Benchmarks look promising; p99 alloc latency dropped ~28% on our mixed chat workload. One nit about naming: prefer 'compact_on_free' to 'coalesce_on_free' for clarity.
2026-02-14 Aisha Patel: LGTM after addressing the inline-run comment and adding a short comment in allocator.rs showing the heuristic. Approving.
2026-02-18 Merge Bot: squash merged by Samuel Harkness — merge commit abc123def4567890

title: Stellar Sparrow Games
author: Maya Chen
text:
Inbound via blog post -> signup. CTO (Ravi Patel) demoed chat use case on 2026-03-02 (Fireflies ff:2026-03-02-ssg-call-72). Small studio building a realtime social turn-based mobile game with in-game global chat + match lobbies. Primary ask: hosted, low-friction API (self-serve) they can integrate this week for an internal alpha. 

Key technical constraints: p50 latency target <= 80ms for short chat exchanges (avg 8-12 tokens per message), sustained concurrent players ~300-600 during peak, cost sensitive (economy on tokens for chat), need streaming responses (SSE/Websocket) + message-level moderation/higher precision spam filtering. 

Security/Compliance: prefer public cloud, but need SSO (SAML) for admin console, audit logs for moderator actions, and contract clause around chat content retention. Concerned about data residency for EU players (they're NA-first but EU launch Q3).

Abuse/ops requirements (very important): automated profanity filter + ML-based spam detection, custom blocklist for player IDs, webhook for immediate bans, per-player rate limiting, per-route quotas, detection of bot-like rapid messaging. Asked specifically: "Can we get a realtime moderation hook and an events webhook for autoban decisions?"

POC plan: 2-week self-serve trial using hosted API keys -> measure p50/p95 latency, run load test with 500 simulated clients, evaluate moderation endpoints, compare cost per MAU. If perf and moderation meet bar, move to pilot (paid).

Quotes/voices: "We need something that doesn't add 200ms to every chat message — players notice that immediately." — CTO. 

Communications: Devon (product) pinged via gmail thread: thread:1729-ssg-inbound-03. Shared pricing deck and security Qs (drive links). SE call scheduled 2026-03-16 to walk SDK + streaming example.
