text:
Amanda: Quick Q — we're staring down Q3 reserved GPU commits. Need a region-by-region thumb for 8x A100-equivalent capacity (steady inference workload). Focus: committed price, egress exposure, preempt/spot risk, and procurement lead time. TL;DRs please.
Karthik: OK — did a quick skim of cloud quotes + our usage curves. Short version: us-east has the cheapest committed unit price and lowest egress to our US customers; eu-west is ~10% more, but we have a negotiated enterprise add-on there; ap-southeast is most expensive + higher egress.
Maria: Also call out latency to EU customers (we need <60ms p95 for chat). eu-west helps avoid cross-region tail latency.
Eli: For embedding-heavy traffic we could mix A10G-like SKUs in ap-southeast for cost, but that hurts long-context gen. Worth considering for regional embedding caches.
billing-bot: FYI: current enterprise discount in eu-west1 = 7% on committed usage (applies to sustained commit only). No guaranteed discounts in ap-southeast in current contract.
Karthik: I put a tiny calc together (simplified):
```
# dollars per GPU-hour (illustrative)
us-east: on-demand 24.0 -> committed 17.0 (≈29% savings)
eu-west: on-demand 27.0 -> committed 18.9 (≈30% savings)
ap-southeast: on-demand 31.0 -> committed 22.0 (≈29% savings)
# egress penalty (per TB/month)
us-east -> users: low; eu-west -> moderate; ap-southeast -> high (+20% cost)
# naive break-even (months) for 12mo commit vs on-demand at our forecast
us-east: ~8-9 months
eu-west (with 7% extra): ~6-7 months
ap-southeast: ~12-14 months
```
Amanda: Nice. Two follow-ups: (1) how brittle is capacity in each region (can we get the committed vms/kernels we want on timeline)? (2) if we do multi-region fails over, what's the egress hit for cross-region KV/cache rehydration?
infra-bot: Capacity note: us-east fleet availability = high for A100-like SKUs. eu-west availability = medium; procurement lead ~3-6 weeks for reserved pools. ap-southeast availability = low for large contiguous commitments; expect 8+ weeks or need to accept alternate GPU models.
Julian: Cross-region cache rehydration: if we fail EU->US we estimate ~0.5-1.2TB/day per 100k active sessions depending on prefix/cache hit. That scales egress fast and adds latency.
Maria: That matters for SLOs. If we place majority in us-east and route EU traffic cross-region during outages, p95 likely doubles. Not acceptable.
Eli: Ops suggestion — commit baseline in-region per major market to protect SLO, then keep a small cross-region hot-standby for short-term spikes. Use async KV warmup to reduce rehydration volume.
Karthik: Quick proposal from the numbers + constraints: commit 40% capacity in us-east (cheap + availability), 40% in eu-west (SLO + discounted commit), 20% in ap-southeast (smaller commit, accept mixed SKUs). Keep a 10% global burst pool on low-cost spot-ish capacity for short-lived surges.
Amanda: Can you run the NPV-ish test quickly: with expected utilization 70% steady plus 20% seasonal spikes, does that allocation give cost + SLO wins vs 100% us-east commit + cross-region failover?
Karthik: Rough NPV: 3-year window, discount 6% annual, factoring egress & discount. Short answer: multi-region commit wins on SLO and gives modest cost delta (~+3% spend) vs single-region commit once you add expected cross-region egress and SLA penalties. If SLO breaches cost >5% of revenue (conservative), multi-region is strictly better.
billing-bot: Note: any multi-region commit will need territory-specific contracts; eu-west requires an amendment to apply current negotiated term to the new capacity. Lead legal ~2 weeks.
Maria: Ops risk: ap-southeast mixed SKUs means one code path for quantized models, another for large-precision gen. That's technical debt if we scale.
Eli: We can mitigate by putting embedding-only traffic on cheaper SKUs and keep gen-models centralized in us/eu. That reduces ap egress and lowers commit size.
Amanda: Sounds like we're converging. Actionables: (1) Karthik to prepare a 12-month committed ordering plan by region + NPV spreadsheet (2) infra to confirm procurement timeline for the exact SKUs (3) legal to draft eu-west amendment (4) product/ops to validate SLO routing plan.
Julian: I'll scope the cache warmup plan and estimate egress for worst-case failover. ETA 48h.
Karthik: I'll post the spreadsheet in the thread later today — will include sensitivity to spot availability and 6/12/36 month commit lengths.
Amanda: Thanks — vote: :thumbsup: if you agree with the 40/40/20 split + small global burst. Anyone object?
Maria: :thumbsup:
Eli: :thumbsup:
Julian: :thumbsup: (pending cache numbers)

title: Latency Sculptor — daily notes and triage
author: Sanjay Patel
text:
Morning dump (walkthrough of last 36h):

- Symptom: intermittent p99 spikes on hosted inference for chat route (mistral-variant) during small concurrent bursts (~40-60 rps). p50/p90 stable, p99 jumps from ~230ms to ~1.6s for short windows of ~30-90s.
- Observed correlated signals: KV-cache hit-rate drops from ~95% -> ~60%; batching rate increases (more micro-batches), and one worker instance showed sustained GPU memory fragmentation warnings in logs.
- Alerts: infra-alert INF-4321 triggered twice; paging rotation went to Mina on second page.

Initial hypothesis/notes:
- KV cache eviction storm: suspect an eviction boundary bug where a single large request (long context) causes a cascade that invalidates shards aggressively, causing cache cold starts and extra decoding cost. The p99 aligns with warmup decode cost plus new KV fetch.
- Batching sensitives: when requests are too small but bursty, scheduler creates many tiny batches; continuous batching backlog is low but dispatch overhead is higher. Combined with frequent cache misses, tail latency compounds.
- Memory fragmentation: kernel allocator doing many small allocations (attention KV slices) causing fragmentation -> occasional copy-outs leading to stalls. Might match the worker logs (fragmentation warnings).

Quick repro plan (local / canary):
1) Repro script: replay real traffic snippet that triggered INF-4321 with original headers. Use replay-tool with tokenization-preserving mode. (TODO: extract trace from observability — get recording id from the alert).
2) Inject synthetic long-context request (len ~8k tokens) in a small burst to simulate eviction. Measure cache hit-rate and per-token latency.
3) Try toggles: a) KV-cache conservative eviction policy b) force quantized-kv-path c) disable continuous-batching for that route. Compare p99 across runs.

Commands/notes to run quickly:
- fetch traces: ./scripts/trace-fetch.sh INF-4321 --since 2026-03-08T00:00Z --out tmp/trace-4321.json
- replay: python tools/replay.py --trace tmp/trace-4321.json --mode token-preserve --concurrency 40 --target canary-3
- perf counters: nvprof and simple memstats snapshots on canary-3 during replay.

Immediate tasks (short):
- [ ] Pull the full trace and filter to long-context requests (Sanjay) — due today EOD.
- [ ] Add temporary route throttle (burst cap) for chat:mistral-variant on hosted to reduce burst surface (Priya) — coordinate with ops to avoid customer impact.
- [ ] Roll a canary with KV-cache policy fallback (conservative) and compare p99 (Mina + Sanjay).
- [ ] Reproduce locally with replay and confirm whether fragmentation log lines co-occur with spikes (Sanjay).

Longer-term investigations (notes / brainstorm):
- Eviction policy tuning: we should consider a sliding-window LRU that is sticky for small contexts and more aggressive for large contexts (long-request penalty). Current policy appears size-only and can thrash.
- Batching policy: adaptive micro-batch cutoffs based on recent inter-arrival times per-route. The scheduler currently uses global thresholds; per-route heuristics could reduce tiny-batch overhead.
- Memory allocator: evaluate jemalloc alternatives or tuning (tcache sizes, arena counts) for GPU-side allocator used by our attention kernels. If fragmentation confirmed, try coalesced allocation paths for KV buffers.
- Observability: need a KV-cache evictions metric exposed per-shard + eviction-causes tag (size-evict vs time-evict vs manual). Right now it's opaque.

Triage notes from Slack threads: 
- Priya: "saw a cluster of >1s p99 around 03:14 UTC; queues backed up; one node OOM-killed but restarted quickly"
- Mina: "can reproduce with a 6k token request mixed with many 20-60 token requests; disabling continuous-batching reduces p99 but costs throughput"
- Ops: recommended token-bucket limiter as quick mitigation for hosted tier; want to avoid breaking customer SLAs.

Edge cases found in quick code skim: 
- cache/shard_manager.cc line ~412: eviction loop uses `while (used_bytes > limit) pop_oldest()`; but pop_oldest has an early-return when encountering a 'pinned' item — this can leave used_bytes > limit and trigger another eviction pass that may clear multiple shards unexpectedly. Add a safeguard counter and logging.
- dispatcher/scheduler.py: per-route queue aging is globalized; the micro-batch flush condition uses global timeouts which misclassifies bursts with mixed sizes.

Hypothesis experiments (A/B):
A) ConservativeKV: change eviction threshold + disable large-object fast-path for 24h canary.
B) PerRouteBatching: enable per-route inter-arrival heuristic for chat routes on a small fleet.
C) AllocTune: jemalloc tcache reduce for worker container to see if fragmentation improves.

Metrics to collect (must add to dashboard):
- KV-cache hit-rate (per route, per-shard) 1m/30s granularity
- Eviction rate and eviction-cause histogram
- Batch size distribution and batch-dispatch latency histograms
- p50/p90/p99 per model variant and per-canary instance
- GPU allocator fragmentation metric (RSS vs allocator-reported used)

Meeting action items (short bullet updates for sync):
- Today 11:30am sync: quick demo of repro + expected mitigations. Bring canary logs + nvprof snapshots. (Priya leading)
- Postmortem owner assignment: Sanjay (draft) — due 3 days after incident close.

Random thoughts / heuristics to write down:
- "Favor stability over micro-ops" — in high tail situations, a small throughput hit (throttling, conservative eviction) buys 10x reduction in p99.
- Consider an explicit "long-request" tag at ingress so downstream cache/batching can treat it differently rather than inferring from size.

Open questions:
- Are there recent merges that changed eviction semantics? (check PRs merged in last 7 days affecting cache/shard_manager).
- Does the canary fleet run the exact same jemalloc build as prod? Small allocator build differences can show up only at scale.

Notes to self (todo when calm):
- Add small logging patch to shard_manager to emit eviction-cause and pinned-count every 1000 evictions. Keep it low-overhead.
- Add a lightweight per-route batching metric to the request pipeline; it can be a counter + moving average of inter-arrival times.
- Draft a small customer-facing blurb for CSE explaining temporary burst caps if ops ask to communicate.

End of dump. Will iterate on repro steps after trace fetch.

-- Sanjay

title: Quantization Profiles (Public Docs) — Customer Documentation Plan
author: Elliot Price
text:
## Summary
This page defines the plan for customer-facing documentation for the Quantization Profile Library (opt-in). The goal is to help customers safely enable quantization profiles per route, understand limitations and compatibility, run appropriate evaluations, interpret observability signals, and roll back quickly if needed.

This is an internal planning doc for Redwood Docs + DevEx and will be used as the source of truth for docs IA, required examples, and cross-team review gates.

## Audience and use cases
**Primary audiences**
- Software engineers and ML engineers integrating Redwood routes who want to reduce cost/token.
- Platform teams managing production change control (audit logs, RBAC, rollbacks).

**Customer use cases we need to support in docs**
1. Enable an approved quantization profile for a single route (hosted API).
2. Enable profile for a route with region/tier constraints (Dedicated + multi-region hosted).
3. Validate quality and latency before expanding traffic.
4. Diagnose output changes, elevated fallback rate, or latency regressions.
5. Roll back (route-level disable; global kill-switch is internal-only but mention its existence at a high level).

## Goals (docs)
- Make it clear this is **opt-in** and **route-scoped** (v1), with baseline behavior unchanged when disabled.
- Provide a simple “happy path” enablement flow with copy-pastable examples (Console + API/SDK).
- Set expectations on **compatibility constraints** and **fallback behavior** (deterministic, baseline precision fallback).
- Provide a lightweight but concrete evaluation best-practices section that customers can follow without needing Redwood internal harnesses.
- Provide troubleshooting steps tied to the actual product signals customers will see (Console warnings/errors, request metadata, audit history, and dashboard panels).

## Non-goals (docs)
- Do not position this as automatic tuning/recommendations (out of scope for v1).
- Do not publish internal-only implementation details (artifact signing specifics, internal service names, kill-switch runbooks).
- Do not promise universal profile coverage across all models/GPU SKUs.

## Product language and terminology
We need consistent, customer-friendly wording:
- **Quantization profile**: A versioned, Redwood-validated configuration for running a specific model variant using a specific quantization method/precision combination.
- **Profile library**: The set of published profiles per model variant. Customers choose a profile for a route.
- **Route-level enablement**: Profiles are enabled per route, not globally for all tenant traffic (v1).
- **Fallback**: If a request is incompatible (hardware/sequence length constraints) or profile application fails safe checks, Redwood serves using baseline precision for that request (or route) while emitting an event.

Avoid ambiguous language:
- Avoid saying “Redwood automatically picks the best profile.”
- Avoid “lossless” claims. Use “aims to preserve quality” and emphasize eval/monitoring.

## Information architecture (public docs)
We will publish a small cluster of pages under: **Optimize → Quantization Profiles**.

### Page 1: Overview (concept + safety model)
**Proposed title:** “Quantization Profiles (Preview/Beta)” (or “Quantization Profiles” once GA)

**Outline**
- What quantization profiles are and why they reduce cost.
- Opt-in and route-scoped behavior.
- High-level lifecycle: published profiles, versioning, deprecations.
- Safety model summary:
 - Compatibility checks before enablement.
 - Deterministic selection.
 - Fallback to baseline.
 - Auditability and change history.

**Callouts**
- “Start with a canary route; expand after evals.”
- “Not all models/regions support all profiles.”

### Page 2: Enablement guide (Console + API/SDK)
**Proposed title:** “Enable a quantization profile for a route”

**Required elements**
- Console walkthrough (with screenshots once UX is final):
 1) Navigate to Route → Performance/Optimize → Quantization
 2) Choose model variant + eligible profiles
 3) Read compatibility warnings
 4) Confirm change (modal) and review expected impact
 5) Verify enablement and view change history

- API example (REST) for updating route config
 - Show setting `quantization_profile_ref` to a specific profile ID/version.
 - Show how to reset to `default` / disable.

- SDK examples
 - Python and TypeScript: configure route setting; retrieve route state; handle incompatibility errors.

**Verification steps**
- Confirm in Console that route shows “Enabled” and which profile is selected.
- Show how to verify in request metadata (e.g., response headers or trace attributes) that a profile was applied vs fallback.
- Show where to find fallback/latency/cost deltas in dashboards.

### Page 3: Compatibility + limitations
**Proposed title:** “Compatibility, constraints, and fallback behavior”

**Include**
- What compatibility depends on:
 - Model ID + model variant
 - Deployment mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private as applicable)
 - GPU class/SKU (expressed as customer-friendly names)
 - Max context / sequence length limits
 - Region constraints (if/when supported in route policy)

- Customer-facing compatibility matrix
 - If we can’t maintain a full matrix, we must at least publish:
 - “Supported GPUs by profile type” (e.g., INT8 supported on X, FP8 on Y)
 - “Max supported context per profile” for popular models
 - Decide format: table in docs + downloadable CSV updated weekly (recommended).

- Fallback semantics
 - Define what happens when incompatible:
 - If enablement time: block with clear error and remediation.
 - If request time: safe fallback to baseline; emit a signal; no infinite retry loops.

- Limitations / known caveats
 - Output differences are possible.
 - Some profiles may be labeled “Experimental” with narrower guardrails.
 - If customers pin to a profile version, it won’t change unless they update.
 - If we ever add “recommended” aliases, document that aliases may move and how we prevent silent changes (see Open Questions).

### Page 4: Evaluation best practices
**Proposed title:** “How to evaluate quality and latency before rollout”

**Customer-friendly guidance**
- Suggested evaluation approach:
 - Identify representative prompts (production samples + edge cases).
 - Run baseline vs profile-enabled comparisons.
 - Use A/B sampling (e.g., 1–5% traffic) with a rollback threshold.

- What to measure
 - Quality: task-specific metrics (pass@k, exact match, ranking metrics) + human review where appropriate.
 - Latency: p50/p95 decode latency and time-to-first-token.
 - Cost: cost/token and throughput.

- Rollout strategy
 1) Enable in staging on a non-critical route
 2) Canary in production (small % traffic)
 3) Expand gradually with monitoring

- Provide explicit “stop conditions”
 - Elevated fallback rate
 - Increased error rate
 - Statistically meaningful quality regression on a defined slice

**Note:** We cannot publish Redwood’s internal thresholds verbatim if they are considered sensitive, but we can publish recommended guardrails (e.g., “predefine acceptable deltas and require sign-off”). We will align with Selene Huang (quality guardrails) on what’s safe to disclose.

### Page 5: Troubleshooting + rollback
**Proposed title:** “Troubleshooting quantization profiles”

**Structure: symptom → likely cause → how to confirm → resolution**

Required symptoms:
- Console says profile is incompatible
 - Common causes: wrong model variant, unsupported GPU class, context length exceeds profile limit.
 - Resolution: choose another profile; reduce max tokens/context; use baseline.

- Output quality changed unexpectedly
 - Confirm: compare baseline vs profile, check whether fallback occurred (mixed behavior can look inconsistent).
 - Resolution: disable profile; run eval; contact support with request IDs.

- p95 latency increased
 - Confirm: look at per-route latency panels; check TTFT vs decode; check batching/caching changes.
 - Resolution: disable profile; adjust route concurrency/batching; consult Redwood support.

- Elevated fallback rate
 - Confirm: dashboard panel + route events.
 - Likely causes: requests exceed profile constraints; region/GPU mismatch; deployment drift.
 - Resolution: tighten route constraints; pick compatible profile; disable.

- 5xx errors after enabling
 - Confirm: error class; check if errors correlate with specific profile version.
 - Resolution: disable; provide audit event ID and request IDs to support.

Rollback instructions (customer-actionable)
- Disable at route level (Console + API snippet).
- Verify disablement and that requests are using baseline.

We should also include:
- “What information to include in a support ticket” checklist:
 - Org/tenant ID
 - Route name/ID
 - Model + variant
 - Profile ID/version
 - Region/deployment mode
 - Approx timeframe
 - Request IDs/traces
 - Observed metrics (fallback rate, p95 latency)

## Required code/examples (public docs)
We will maintain a single authoritative set of snippets and import them into the docs site.

**REST (pseudo)**
- GET route settings (show current model + quant state)
- PATCH route settings to set profile ref
- PATCH route settings to disable / reset to default

**Python SDK**
- Update route quantization setting
- Validate compatibility result handling
- Verify applied profile via response metadata

**TypeScript SDK**
- Same as Python, plus typing for errors.

Docs dependencies:
- Final field names and error shapes must match control-plane API.
- Confirm the exact response fields that indicate `applied` vs `fallback` vs `disabled`.

## Console UX copy and warnings (alignment)
We will mirror Console language in docs to minimize confusion.

Warnings to standardize:
- “This change may affect output quality. Evaluate before ramping traffic.”
- “This profile is only compatible with <constraints>. Requests outside constraints will fall back to baseline.”
- “Pinning a profile version ensures deterministic behavior until you change it.”

We will coordinate final wording with Tessa Morgan (UX lead) and Kenji Nakamura (rollout/controls designer).

## Review, launch gating, and update cadence
**Reviewers required before docs merge**
- Applied ML: Arjun Desai (profiles lead) + Selene Huang (guardrails)
- Runtime: Noah Patel (runtime architect)
- Platform/Console: Chloe Martin (Console backend lead)
- SRE/Release: Connor O'Brien (rollout lead)
- Security/RBAC: Naomi Feldman (RBAC/audit requirements)

**Release stages and docs behavior**
- Beta/allowlist:
 - Docs are public but clearly marked “Beta” with known limitations.
 - Include a “Contact Support to enable” note if feature is behind an allowlist.

- GA:
 - Remove Beta banner.
 - Publish compatibility matrix link and clear deprecation policy.

**Update cadence**
- Compatibility matrix and profile coverage: weekly updates (aligned with profile publishing cadence).
- Troubleshooting section: update after each beta incident/support trend.

## Success criteria (docs)
- ≥80% of beta design partner enablements completed without synchronous Redwood help.
- Reduction in support tickets that are purely “how do I enable/disable?” (shift to higher-signal issues).
- Median time-to-rollback for customers (self-serve) < 10 minutes after following docs.
- Docs telemetry: high completion rates on enablement guide; low bounce on troubleshooting due to missing information.

## Open questions
1. **Alias semantics:** Will we expose “recommended/latest” aliases in v1 GA or only pinned profile IDs/versions? If aliases exist, we must document how we prevent silent changes (e.g., aliases only change on customer action vs Redwood updates).
2. **Customer-facing compatibility matrix:** What is the minimum viable matrix we can keep current without excessive operational load? (Proposal: publish for top 10 models + major GPU classes first.)
3. **What can we safely publish about quality thresholds?** We should align with Applied ML on whether to include specific numeric deltas or keep it as qualitative guidance.
4. **Request metadata surface:** What is the final customer-visible mechanism to confirm applied profile (headers, response fields, trace attribute)? This must be stable.

## Action items
- (Docs) Elliot Price: draft public docs pages 1–5 and route through review (target by 2025-03-14).
- (DevEx) Monica Patel: finalize Python + TS snippets and ensure they match SDK releases.
- (Console) Chloe Martin: confirm final Console labels, error strings, and change history UX for screenshot capture.
- (Applied ML) Arjun Desai / Selene Huang: approve public-facing evaluation guidance and guardrail language.
- (SRE) Connor O'Brien: verify rollback instructions align with operational reality and dashboards customers can access.

## Notes
- Keep customer docs consistent with the PRD’s promise: **opt-in**, **auditable**, **deterministic**, and **reversible**.
- Prefer “how to verify” sections over deep internals; customers need confidence that the setting is actually applied and understand when/why fallback happens.

title: Go-Live Protocols: Cross-Org Communications & Escalation
author: Priya Patel
text:
Summary
-------
This document defines the cross-organizational go-live protocol used by Redwood Inference for enterprise tenant cutovers. It focuses on communications, stakeholder coordination, and an escalation ladder tailored for high-risk or high-visibility customers. Use this runbook as the canonical checklist for the 72 hours before, during, and 72 hours after a cutover where multiple teams (Customer Success, SRE, Solutions Engineering, Product, and Sales) must be coordinated.

Scope
-----
- Applies to: Dedicated and Private deployment go-lives and tenant migrations with SLA commitments (any customer with an enterprise contract or > $50k monthly spend).
- Out of scope: self-serve trial accounts, routine model-only updates without routing changes.

Goals and SLOs to Protect
-------------------------
- Availability SLA target to protect during cutover: 99.9% (monthly) for production routes.
- Immediate remediation thresholds (trigger escalation):
 - Error rate spike: sustained >5% errors for 5 minutes across tenant endpoints.
 - Latency spike: P95 latency >2000ms for 10 minutes.
 - Token cost anomaly: >200% of projected token spend in 30 minutes.
 - KV cache miss-rate >30% sustained for 15 minutes (for cache-sensitive workloads).

Pre-Cutover (T-72 to T-1 hours)
-------------------------------
1. Confirm stakeholders and channels
 - Primary CSM (Customer Success Manager): name + mobile number.
 - Tech lead (Customer): contact + escalation path.
 - Solution Engineer (SE): responsible for ingress, API contract verification.
 - Oncall SRE/Platform owner: PagerDuty schedule and runbook owner.
 - Slack channels: #cs-<customer>-go-live (private channel), #oncall-redwood, #se-ops.
2. Telemetry sanity checks — must pass before proceeding:
 - Synthetic journey (happy path) passes end-to-end: <customer> -> Redwood API -> response < 1s.
 - PromQL checks: error_rate/instance < 0.005 for 10m; p95_latency_query < 1500ms.
3. Canary plan and acceptance criteria
 - Canary traffic: route 1% of production for 30 minutes with zero critical errors.
 - Acceptance: no P0/P1 incidents during canary and no regression in model quality metrics (if applicable).
4. Whitelist and firewall confirmations
 - Verify ingress IP ranges, customer egress rules, and TLS client certs.

During Cutover (T0 to +4 hours) — Immediate Checklist
----------------------------------------------------
- Primary communications protocol:
 - All updates posted to #cs-<customer>-go-live every 10 minutes during the first hour, then every 30 minutes until stable.
 - The CSM posts customer-facing status updates; technical details posted to private channel only.
- Live monitoring dashboard (owner: Oncall SRE):
 - Tenant-specific dashboard showing throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, KV cache hits, token consumption.
- Escalation triggers (first responder must escalate within 5 minutes if triggered):
 1) P0: service unavailable for customer routes — immediate page to P1 oncall and notify Engineering Director.
 2) P1: sustained SLO breach (see thresholds above) — page SE and PM, start RCA and mitigation steps.
 3) P2: model quality regression detected — notify Applied ML and SE; consider traffic switch to verified model snapshot.

Escalation Ladder (contact order and responsibilities)
----------------------------------------------------
| Level | Trigger example | Primary contact | Secondary contact | Action required |
|-------|-----------------|-----------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| L1 (CSM) | Customer questions, minor errors | CSM | SE | Acknowledge to customer within 15m, open internal thread |
| L2 (SRE) | Error rate >5% | Oncall SRE | SRE Lead | Execute diagnostics, apply mitigations (rate-limit, route switch) |
| L3 (SE/PM) | Persistent degradation >30m | Solutions Engineer | Product Manager | Coordinate config changes, model fallback, communicate to customer executives |
| L4 (Exec) | SLA breach or major incident | Head of Customer Success | Head of Engineering | Declare incident, engage legal/finance if SLA credits likely |

Note: The table above is intended as a quick reference. The full escalation paging list with phone numbers and PagerDuty IDs is stored in /confluence/people-ops/rosters and in the private channel pinned messages.

Common Mitigations (ordered by lowest customer impact first)
----------------------------------------------------------
- Increase routing to a higher-capacity pool (if Dedicated: burst pool)
- Apply tenant-level throttles to protect shared resources (quota reduce to 30% of projected steady-state)
- Enable model fallback: route to last-known-stable model snapshot
- Temporarily switch customer to hosted API endpoint (if allowed by contract)
- Quiesce long-running batch jobs from the customer side

Rollback and Safe-fail Strategies
--------------------------------
1. Safe rollback to previous routing config (SE executes):
 - Command: curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal.redwood/v1/route/revert -d '{"tenant":"<tenant-id>","to_config":"<previous-config-id>"}' 
 - Confirm routing table via: kubectl get svc ingress-<tenant> -o yaml (requires ops role)
2. Tenant quiesce API (customer-facing graceful shutdown):
 - POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/tenants/<tenant>/quiesce?actor=ops
 - Expected behavior: existing requests drain, new requests return 429 with Retry-After header.
3. Emergency switchback to hosted region: update DNS TTL and apply traffic policy TTL=30s for faster re-routing.

Communication Templates
-----------------------
- Customer-facing 1-line (acknowledge): "We are investigating increased latency for your production routes and will provide an update within 15 minutes. No action required from your side unless we ask."
- Customer-facing status update (10m cadence): include short bullet list: observed metric, action taken, owner, ETA for next update.
- Internal P0 page message sample:
 - "P0: <customer> production routes returning 503s since 08:12 UTC. Oncall SRE investigating. Initial hypothesis: ingress proxy thread exhaustion. Paging SRE Lead and SE. Next update in 5 minutes"

Telemetry checks / Queries (examples)
----------------------------------
- PromQL (errors): sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant="<tenant>",status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant="<tenant>"}[5m])) > 0.05
- Token consumption anomaly (example):
 - Query: increase(token_count_total{tenant="<tenant>"}[30m]) / expected_token_rate > 2.0
- Synthetic validation command (curl):
 - curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" -d '{"input":"synthetic health check"}' | jq '.latency_ms'

Post-Cutover (T+4 to T+72 hours)
--------------------------------
- Stability window monitoring: SRE to keep watch for 72 hours; escalate on any SLO breach.
- Cost and quota reconciliation: Finance Ops and CSM to review token consumption, forecast delta, and apply quota protections if needed.
- Customer QBR prep: collect first-week metrics and any incident notes for the 30-day QBR.

Runbook Ownership and RACI
-------------------------
- CSM: customer comms and executive escalation.
- SE: onboarding technical lead, API contract signoff, whitelist verification.
- Oncall SRE: monitoring, mitigation, and platform config changes in emergencies.
- Product/Applied ML: model quality regressions and rollbacks.
- Finance Ops: post-cutover cost anomalies and quota adjustments.

Appendix A — Playbook Checklist (copyable)
-----------------------------------------
- [ ] Confirm private channel and all stakeholder contacts pinned
- [ ] Telemetry smoke test passed (synthetic happy path)
- [ ] Canary plan scheduled and accepted by SE and SRE
- [ ] Firewall/whitelist config validated by Network team
- [ ] PagerDuty rotations confirmed and escalation contacts available
- [ ] Customer-facing status template approved by CSM
- [ ] Post-cutover QBR slot scheduled with customer (within 30 days)

Appendix B — Links and References
--------------------------------
- Tenant cutover checklist (internal): /confluence/customer-success-and-support/enterprise-onboarding/onboarding-handback-and-first-90-days-ops-guide-2026
- Incident comms templates: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-communication-templates
- PagerDuty runbook: https://pagerduty.com/orgs/redwood-incidents (private)

Appendix C — Escalation Contact Quickview
----------------------------------------
- Oncall SRE: pagerduty (PD ID: PD12345), Slack: @oncall-sre, mobile: +1-555-0102
- SE on duty: Slack: @se-ops, mobile: +1-555-0148
- CSM (Primary): Priya Patel, Slack: @priya.cs, mobile: +1-555-0190

Revision History
----------------
- 2027-02-10: Created by Priya Patel.
- 2027-03-02: Reviewed and clarified rollback steps; added expense reconciliation task (Marisol Gomez).

Notes and governance
--------------------
Keep this page updated after every enterprise go-live. If the customer contract contains additional communication obligations (e.g., weekly executive summaries), add them to the post-cutover tasks and pin them in the customer channel.

title: Kernel Snapshot Observability Contract and Diagnostic Playbook
author: Asha Patel
text:
Summary:
This page defines the Kernel Snapshot Observability Contract used by the serving runtime to capture lightweight, deterministic kernel-level state for fast post-hoc diagnostics, profiling correlation, and benchmark reproducibility. The contract describes snapshot contents, TTL/retention semantics, collection cadence, storage indexing, query semantics, and the recommended operational playbook for using snapshots during incidents and regressions.

Why we need a formal contract:
- Reduce triage time: snapshots provide a small, self-contained view of kernel scheduling state across shards without requiring full traces.
- Reproducible regression hunts: standardized fields make automated delta comparison (hashes/digests) possible across releases and benchmarks.
- Safe production capture: contract enforces size and cost limits to keep collection cheap and non-disruptive.

Scope and goals:
- Scope: GPU-scheduling kernels, kernel selector hints, active batch queue heads, kvcache hot entries metadata, and per-request token-progress markers. Not intended to replace full GPU traces or perf counters.
- Goals: <= 2KB compressed per snapshot per shard typical, capture latency < 5ms end-to-end, snapshot ingestion availability 99.9%.

Contract: snapshot manifest fields (string names and semantic description)
- manifest_type: "kernel-snapshot-v1" (identifies schema version).
- timestamp_utc: RFC3339 string (origin of capture).
- host_id: runtime host identifier (short hash).
- shard_id: logical shard name/id.
- kernel_hint: canonical kernel name in scheduler (e.g. "attn_sharded_kv_v2").
- active_requests: comma-separated list of up to 8 request_ids with short metadata (see Active Request Encoding below).
- batch_head_shape: concurrency/sequence-length tuple (e.g. "concurrency=12;avg_seq=128").
- kv_hot_prefix_digest: 64-bit hex digest of most-frequent KV prefixes (comma-separated up to 4).
- queue_depth: integer (number of queued kernel tasks).
- slot_usage_pct: integer 0-100 (measured GPU slot occupancy estimate).
- mem_watermark_mb: integer (resident MB attributed to shard at capture).
- fallback_flags: short tokenized list of active degradation flags (e.g. "quantized-fallback,eviction-throttle").
- capture_id: uuid string (unique id for this snapshot).
- sample_hash: sha1 hex of the canonicalized manifest (for fast equality checks).

Active Request Encoding (embedded): up to 8 items, each encoded as colon-separated tokens: request_id|model:ver|priority|est_remaining_tokens
Example: "r1234|redwood/7b:2026-03-01|p2|est32"

Size and performance constraints:
- Uncompressed manifest must be <= 8KB. Producers MUST gzip the payload before upload.
- Capture must be non-blocking for request latency: producers should sample at scheduling safe points (e.g. pre-dispatch / post-eviction) and limit synchronous work to timestamping and copying small metadata.
- Max capture cadence per shard: 1 snapshot / 5s by default; bursts up to 1/second allowed during active debugging windows.

Capture lifecycle and TTL semantics:
- Local ephemeral cache: snapshots are kept in-memory for 30s to enable immediate correlation with live traces.
- Short-term storage: snapshots forwarded to an indexed store with 7-day retention for operational triage.
- Long-term archive: on-demand (by capture_id or sample_hash) snapshots older than 7 days may be kept in cold archive for 90 days if pinned by a runbook or regression alert.
- Automatic eviction: snapshots exceeding store quotas are evicted by oldest-first per-host.

Storage & indexing conventions:
- Index keys: sample_hash, capture_id, host_id, shard_id, kernel_hint, timestamp_utc.
- Tags: release_tag (e.g. "canary-2026-03-10"), experiment_id (if collection was triggered by an experiment), incident_id (if captured during an incident).
- Searchable fields must be text-tokenized and exact-match filterable for sample_hash and kernel_hint.

Producer responsibilities and API contract:
1) Capture API (local agent): POST /v1/internal/kernel-snapshot 
 - Headers: X-Host-ID, X-Shard-ID, X-Capture-Src (auto|manual|diag).
 - Body: gzip'd manifest (UTF-8).
 - Response: 202 Accepted with JSON {"capture_id":"...","sample_hash":"...","ingest_ts":"..."}.
2) Backoff: if remote ingestion errors with 5xx more than 3 consecutive times, agent falls back to local retention only and emits metric runtime.snapshot.ingest.failures.
3) Priority: manual-triggered captures (via runbook) should include X-Capture-Priority: high and are exempt from per-shard cadence limits for a 60s window.

Query and diagnosis workflow (runbook):
1) Triage start: on a latency SLO violation or kernel regression alert, runbook owner initiates "snapshot-hunt".
2) Retrieve matching snapshots by filter: sample_hash, kernel_hint, timeframe, release_tag.
3) Run a delta comparison on sample_hash across canary vs baseline to find divergence.
4) If sample_hash matches but incident persists, escalate to full trace capture: enable continuous tracing for affected shards (see profiling-playbook integration below).

Integration with profiling playbooks and benchmarking suite:
- Profiling correlation: snapshots are lightweight keys to join streaming traces and microbenchmarks. Include capture_id in trace span attribute: runtime.kernel_snapshot.capture_id.
- Benchmark gating: nightly benchmarks must capture a deterministic snapshot for each workload and store sample_hash in benchmark results CSV. Regression rule: any benchmark run where the sample_hash distribution differs from baseline for > 20% of shards triggers a quality alert.
- Kernel scheduler experiments: when rolling out kernel changes, collect snapshot cohorts (baseline/canary) and run a pairwise hash-difference analysis as part of the release checklist.

Release gating checklist (minimum):
- Collect cohort snapshots for baseline and canary for 24 hours with at least 1000 snapshots per cohort.
- Run automated sample_hash cluster analysis and ensure no new kernel_hint set appears in >5% of canary shards unless intentionally rolled out.
- Verify average slot_usage_pct and queue_depth remain within +/- 10% of baseline.
- Sign-off required by runtime-scheduling and profiling owners.

Alerting and SLOs:
- Metric: runtime.snapshot.ingest.latency_p50 < 30ms, p95 < 100ms.
- Metric: runtime.snapshot.size_bytes_p95 < 4096 bytes compressed.
- Alert: snapshot-ingest-error-rate > 0.5% sustained for 5m -> paging to infra-oncall.
- Alert: sample_hash-drift-score > 0.2 across canary vs baseline -> notify runtime-release-team.

Known limitations and mitigations:
- Not a full trace: snapshots are intentionally small and do not include per-kernel GPU counters. Use them to triage and then escalate to detailed tracing.
- Digest collisions: sample_hash uses sha1 of a canonicalized manifest; collisions are possible but extremely unlikely. If collision suspected, attach raw manifest comparison.
- Cost: high-frequency snapshots across all shards increase storage costs; default cadence and burst limits are enforced by agents.

Operational playbook: incident example (step-by-step)
1) Pager fires for high tail latency on model X.
2) Oncall: run "snapshot-query --kernel attn_sharded_kv_v2 --since 5m --format table" across implicated shards.
3) If sample_hash variance high between recently-deployed canary and baseline: run pairwise-diff tool and note differing fields.
4) If mem_watermark_mb spike correlates with queue_depth rise -> trigger immediate spillover rollback (see runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook).
5) Capture extended traces for 10 minutes and mark capture_ids of interest.

CLI examples and snippets:
- Query tool (example):
 # list snapshots matching kernel and timeframe
 snapshot-query --kernel "attn_sharded_kv_v2" --since "2026-05-01T12:00:00Z" --limit 200 --output json

- Minimal producer example (bash curl):
 payload=$(printf '{"manifest_type":"kernel-snapshot-v1","timestamp_utc":"%s","host_id":"h-abc123","shard_id":"s1","kernel_hint":"attn_sharded_kv_v2","active_requests":"r1|m:1|p1|est24","batch_head_shape":"concurrency=8;avg_seq=64","kv_hot_prefix_digest":"%s","queue_depth":12,"slot_usage_pct":72,"mem_watermark_mb":12288,"fallback_flags":"none","capture_id":"%s"}' "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" "deadbeefcafebabe" "$(uuidgen)")
 echo "$payload" | gzip -c | curl -s -X POST -H "Content-Encoding: gzip" -H "X-Host-ID: h-abc123" -H "X-Shard-ID: s1" --data-binary @- https://internal-ingest.redwood/v1/internal/kernel-snapshot

Appendix A — Example canonical manifest (pretty-printed):
{
 "manifest_type": "kernel-snapshot-v1",
 "timestamp_utc": "2026-05-03T14:12:02Z",
 "host_id": "h-0a1b2c",
 "shard_id": "s1",
 "kernel_hint": "attn_sharded_kv_v2",
 "active_requests": "r1234|redwood/7b:2026-03-01|p2|est32,r1240|redwood/7b:2026-03-01|p1|est8",
 "batch_head_shape": "concurrency=12;avg_seq=128",
 "kv_hot_prefix_digest": "0x9f8e7d6c",
 "queue_depth": 4,
 "slot_usage_pct": 68,
 "mem_watermark_mb": 11876,
 "fallback_flags": "quantized-fallback",
 "capture_id": "6f8d7b2a-2a5c-4b8e-9bf0-0a1c2d3e4f5a",
 "sample_hash": "a1b2c3d4e5f6..."
}

Ownership and contacts:
- Primary owner: Runtime Observability (oncall: #infra-runtime-observability)
- Reviewers: see metadata above.
- Escalation path: runtime-scheduling -> eng-sre -> infra-ops.

Change history and notes:
- 2026-01-12: initial draft and prototype collector written (A. Patel).
- 2026-03-18: added benchmark integration rules and sample_hash gating (M. Ivanov).
- 2026-05-03: tightened ingest latency SLO and clarified retention windows (D. Kim).

References:
- Profiling playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/continuous-runtime-profiling-strategy-2026
- Kernel telemetry: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/kernel-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025
- Release gating: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/canary-sla-oracle-and-benchmark-gate-spec-2026

title: Introduce stepped batching policy, quant-safety linter, and unit-econ smoke tests
author: Asha Patel
text:
Motivation and summary:

We observed that single-threshold batching (max-batch-size only) can yield large cost variance across mixed workloads: small short requests suffer latency when waiting for large batch thresholds, but lowering thresholds increases per-token cost under high QPS. This PR introduces a small, operationally conservative stepped batching policy that trades off a couple of microseconds of scheduling overhead for much more stable unit economics across variable request size/QPS.

What this PR does (single-string summary):
- Implement 'stepped' batching policy in the serving runtime: the scheduler can be configured with an ordered list of candidate batch sizes (e.g., [1, 4, 16]) and per-step latency bounds. The runtime opportunistically serves smaller batches when latency SLOs are tight and ramps to larger steps when throughput allows.
- Add a `quant-safety` static linter that inspects quantization profiles and model graph ops to catch unsafe combinations (e.g., per-channel quant on ops we don't support in the CUDA/XT kernels, or FP16-only fused ops missing fallback). The linter emits warnings and suggested safe profiles.
- Add 'unit-econ smoke tests' to the CI: lightweight workload simulator that runs short generation workloads across a small matrix of batch sizes, quant profiles, and cache settings, and verifies cost-per-token regressions are within expected bands. Smoke tests run in ~8 minutes and gate regressions for perf/infra changes.

Implementation notes and commits (high-level):
- commit 1: runtime: stepped batcher core + scheduler hooks (api contract unchanged; new config block under route->batching)
- commit 2: runtime: careful backpressure handling and metrics (per-step latency histograms, step_transition_counter)
- commit 3: tooling: quant-safety linter as a CLI subcommand and CI check (bin/quant-linter)
- commit 4: tests: unit-econ smoke test harness + CI job + small golden baselines (ci/smoke/unit-econ/)

Files touched (high level):
- services/serve/scheduler/stepped_batcher.rs (new)
- services/serve/config/batching.yaml (docs + examples updated)
- runtime/metrics/registry.rs (added step-level metrics)
- tools/quant-linter/main.go (new)
- tools/quant-linter/rules/*.go (rules for op compatibility and fallbacks)
- ci/smoke/unit-econ/run_smoke.py (new harness)
- ci/.github/workflows/unit-econ-smoke.yml (CI job)
- sdk/python/examples/bench/stepped_batch_example.py (example config)
- docs/observability/batching.md (explain metrics and when to use stepped batching)
- tests/integration/serve/stepped_batcher_endtoend.test (integration test)

Small config example included in docs (snippet):

 batching:
 strategy: stepped
 steps:
 - size: 1
 max_latency_ms: 20
 - size: 4
 max_latency_ms: 50
 - size: 16
 max_latency_ms: 200

Notes on design choices: we intentionally keep the default step set conservative (1,4,16) to avoid surprising throughput regressions for large sustained QPS. The scheduler uses a tiny state machine to avoid flip-flopping between steps: a step transition requires a short stabilization window (configurable, default 50ms).

Quant-safety linter details:
- Static analysis of exported model graph + quant profile.
- Rules added: unsupported op-quant combos, precision funnel points (places where FP32->INT8 may lose critical dynamic range), and kernel mismatch with our CUDA kernels.
- Linter outputs machine-readable JSON and human-friendly summaries used by CI to annotate PRs. Example output: "WARN: op=matmul, quant=per_channel_int8 -> kernel_fallback_needed"

Unit-econ smoke tests:
- Simulate 1m equivalent tokens split across generated short (avg 12 tokens) and long (avg 160 tokens) requests to mimic chat + summarization mixes.
- Measure median latency, p95, and cost_per_1000_tokens. Failures trigger an artifact dump with token/time traces to help reproduce locally.

Review conversation (high-level transcript):
- Miguel: "Nice approach. Can we make the step list hierarchical per-route? Some customers want different steps for embeddings vs generation."
- Author (Asha): "Yes — config supports per-route batching blocks. Examples added to docs and example config file."
- Jade: "Quant-linter looks solid; add an allowlist for customers with known model exceptions."
- Author: "Added allowlist file support and tests for the allowlist behavior (tools/quant-linter/allowlist_test.go)."
- Evan: "CI time looks okay, but make sure smoke tests don't flake on low-QPS CI runners."
- Author: "Added retry + seeding and reduced variance; smoke runs ~8 minutes on our CI images."
- Miguel (approval): "Approve after green CI and one more perf run on canary infra."

CI summary: initial run had one transient failure in smoke tests on ubuntu-latest runner due to clock skew; rerun succeeded. All checks now green.

Backward compatibility and rollout:
- No breaking API changes. The batching config is additive; if customers omit strategy, existing behavior (legacy max-batch-size) remains.
- Enabled stepped batching only when explicitly configured. We plan to roll out conservative defaults in the Dedicated face as an opt-in for early customers.

Testing and perf numbers (representative):
- Mixed workload (40% short, 60% long) on g4dn.xlarge: median latency improved ~6% vs single-threshold tuned for throughput and cost-per-token reduced ~12% compared to always-on small-batch strategy. p95 latency was within the configured budgets for the step set above.

Follow-ups and todos (post-merge):
- ENG-2101: automatic step-suggestor that profiles live traffic and proposes step tuples per-route.
- Add telemetry to Redwood Console to visualize step transition heatmaps per-route.
- Expand quant-linter rules to cover model conversion tooling and add auto-fix suggestions where safe.

Merge details:
- Merge method: squash and merge.
- Final merge commit: "squash: stepped batching + quant-linter + unit-econ CI (Asha Patel)"

If you want to run locally: see sdk/python/examples/bench/stepped_batch_example.py and tools/quant-linter/README.md for quickstart.


Adds a stepped batching policy with conservative defaults, a static quantization-safety linter to catch incompatible quant profiles, and a new suite of unit-econ smoke tests for CI. No user-facing API changes; operational defaults improved.

This PR bundles runtime, tools, and CI changes to keep the feature integrated end-to-end. Kept scope tight to make reviewable while providing clear follow-ups for automatic tuning and Console UX.

title: resume-download-hang-notes
author: Lucas Nguyen
text:
Context:
- Intermittent model load failures in staging: large checkpoint ( ~210 GB tar) will start downloading fine but stalls during resume/seek and never completes. Affects resume logic in blobstream -> tar stream -> shard reader path.
- Repro rate ~3/20 downloads in staging (k8s). Prod unaffected so far but worried about edge-case on poor networks.

Symptoms observed (from agent + proxy logs):
- Client issues GET with Range header to GCS signed URL. Typically requests range starting at byte N where N is resume offset.
- Server returns: HTTP/1.1 200 OK (not 206) for range request in ~30% of failing cases -> client code treats as fallback but then confusion in Content-Length vs expected remaining bytes.
- When 200 is returned we see Content-Length ~= full object and streaming attempt does chunked transfer; our BlobStream expects Content-Range/206 and does a single ranged read.
- Often the connection hangs after ~50-200MB transferred; stack shows blocked on read() in python requests (urllib3) with an open socket. Kernel stats show TCP retransmits and then connection reset.

Logs (sanitized):
[2026-02-16T03:14:12Z] blobstream: starting range request url="<signed-url>" range="bytes=137438953472-"
[2026-02-16T03:14:12Z] http-client DEBUG: > GET /... HTTP/1.1
[2026-02-16T03:14:12Z] http-client DEBUG: < HTTP/1.1 200 OK
[2026-02-16T03:14:12Z] http-client DEBUG: < Content-Length: 2251799813685248
[2026-02-16T03:16:03Z] blobstream: read stalled after 123MB transferred; last byte=137562383616
[2026-02-16T03:17:44Z] k8s: pod restart backoff due to readiness probe fail

Reproduction steps I used locally (quick):
1) Create signed URL for object (gsutil signurl)
2) curl with Range header to simulate resume: 
 curl -v -H "Range: bytes=137438953472-" "<signed-url>" -o /tmp/chunk.part
Observations: sometimes curl returns 200 + huge content-length and streams; sometimes returns 206 and only the requested range. The failing case tends to be the 200 response.

Quick experiments (commands tried):
- gsutil -D cp gs://redwood-checkpoints/llama-13b/ckpt-2025-11.tar ./ (works or stalls depending on run)
- curl -v -H "Range: bytes=0-1048575" "<signed-url>" -> 206 expected, usually OK
- curl -v -H "Range: bytes=137438953472-" "<signed-url>" -> sometimes 200; when 200: response header Content-Length==object_size (not remaining)
- python requests stream test:
 import requests
 r = requests.get(url, headers={"Range": "bytes=137438953472-"}, stream=True, timeout=(5,120))
 for chunk in r.iter_content(65536):
 process(chunk)
 -> chunk iteration blocks indefinitely after some MB
- tcpdump on node during hang: repeated retransmit (SYN/ACK?) and eventually FIN; remote resets.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Signed URL generation + caching on CDN side: signed URL sometimes routes to a backend that doesn't support range/206 properly (edge case in GCS/Cloud CDN), returning 200 and then inconsistent streaming behaviour.
2) Large resume offset + HTTP/2: interaction between our client (urllib3 over httpx?) and server: http/2 stream flow-control where server advertises large content-length, then stalls if client window not updated.
3) Middleboxes (sidecar/proxy) in k8s (istio/Envoy) rewrites Range headers or mishandles 206 responses for large offsets, causing proxy to buffer and then fail.
4) Tar reader/backpressure bug: our TarStream tries to seek/rewind on a stream that doesn't support random access and we get into a read-then-seek deadlock.

Notes on 206 vs 200 behavior:
- RFC: servers MUST reply 206 for Range if satisfiable. If 200 returned, client must assume server ignored Range. Our code currently treats 200 as 'fallback to full download' but still uses expected remaining bytes to set a read deadline -> mismatch. Need robust handling: if 200, compare Content-Length to expected remaining; if Content-Length > remaining then assume full object and restart with full download or abort.

Data points from telemetry: (last 48h)
- 37 total checkpoints downloaded by staging nodes
- 9 downloads logged partial-range requests (resume)
- 3 downloads stalled for >2 minutes and triggered pod eviction
- Failure cohort: all from nodes in us-central1-c, via node pool with custom sidecar version v1.8.2

Quick patches attempted (on staging):
- Patch blobstream: if response.status_code == 200 and content-length > remaining_bytes: close connection and retry without Range (full download). Reduced hang frequency but increased egress bandwidth (bad).
- Switch http client to requests.adapters.HTTPAdapter(pool_connections=100, pool_maxsize=100) to avoid connection reuse oddities; no measurable change.
- Added retry on socket timeout with exponential backoff (max 3). Brought success on 2/3 prior failing runs.

Stack trace (before retry patch) when hung (python):
 File "/app/blobstream.py", line 212, in _stream_range
 for chunk in resp.iter_content(chunk_size=65536):
 File "/opt/python/lib/python3.10/site-packages/requests/models.py", line 753, in iter_content
 for chunk in self.raw.stream(chunk_size, decode_content=True):
 File "/opt/python/lib/python3.10/site-packages/urllib3/response.py", line 818, in stream
 data = self.read(amt=amt, decode_content=decode_content)
 File "/opt/python/lib/python3.10/site-packages/urllib3/response.py", line 624, in read
 data = self._fp.read(amt)
 File "/usr/lib/python3.10/http/client.py", line 458, in read
 s = self.sock.recv(left)
# blocked here until socket closes

Ideas to probe next (short checklist):
- [ ] Collect server-side GCS logs for signed URL accesses around timestamps: 2026-02-16T03:10-03:20Z (ask infra for logs). Need to check if 206 or 200 was returned upstream.
- [ ] Reproduce with direct GCS XML API (no signed URL) to rule out CDN/signed-url layer.
- [ ] Try curl --http1.1 to force HTTP/1.1 vs default http2 to test flow-control hypothesis.
- [ ] Run test with no sidecar (bypass istio) on a few nodes to check proxy influence.
- [ ] Add more aggressive detection in blobstream: if read stalls for >15s and bytes_transferred < min_rate then abort and retry. Record metrics (bytes/sec) for postmortem.
- [ ] Validate tar reader path: make sure we do not attempt to seek on streaming response; convert to read-and-write-to-tempfile when resume not supported.

Notes-to-self:
- Edge case may be combination of server returning 200 + client expecting partial content and then holding on to socket for long time. Fixing to treat 200 as a hard mismatch and immediately restart full download or abort seems the safest short-term fix.
- Long-term: support resumable downloads via GCS compose / chunked upload pattern or use objectRange RPCs that are guaranteed to return 206.

Open questions:
- Why would GCS signed URL sometimes route to a node that returns 200 for a Range request? Is there a backend version skew?
- Are there load-balancers in front of GCS that rewrite Range?
- Is our signed URL malformed when resume offset > 2^32? (unlikely but check)

Useful links / refs:
- GCS signed URL docs (range requests): https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls
- RFC7233 Range Requests: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7233
- GitHub issue: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/issues/612 (related: tar streaming/backpressure)

Next actions (short term):
1) Push blobstream quick fix: detect 200-on-range -> abort and retry without range (or switch to tempfile), add metric -> rollout to staging canary.
2) Run controlled reproduce forcing http1.1 vs http2 and sidecar on/off.
3) File ENGINF follow-up to collect GCS edge logs and ask Cloud support if signed URL behavior is expected.

-- Lucas

title: Responder rotation synthesis and deferred postmortem protocol
author: Priya Shah
text:
Overview:

This playbook describes Redwood's responder rotation synthesis process and a lightweight Deferred Postmortem (DPM) protocol for incidents that meet defined criteria. It combines on-call scheduling practices, a structured bridge handoff procedure, and customer-facing messaging templates designed for speed and clarity. The goal is to reduce cognitive load during high-impact events and to ensure timely learning when full postmortems are not immediately practical.

Scope:
- Applies to: SRE, Serving Runtime, Platform, and Incident Response stakeholders.
- Excludes: low-priority alerts that resolve without human intervention (see 'Auto-resolved alerts' below).

Definitions:
- Responder rotation synthesis: periodic review and rebalancing of on-call shifts, handoffs, and escalation ladders to maintain equitable load and coverage.
- Deferred Postmortem (DPM): a time-boxed post-incident review that defers non-critical analysis until stakeholders are available, while still capturing root evidence and action items immediately.

Key principles:
1) Fast stabilization first: prioritize containment and customer impact minimization.
2) Minimal friction handoffs: standardized bridge transfer reduces repeated context overhead.
3) Continuous learning: short DPMs for low-severity incidents; full postmortems for Sev1/Sev2.
4) Equity in rotations: no responder assigned >36 hours continuous duty without relief.

On-call rotation design (synthesis process):
1. Quarterly synthesis review (owner: SRE lead):
 - Pull the last quarter's on-call logs and pager counts.
 - Calculate median and 95th percentile pager counts per responder.
 - Identify top-10% busiest windows and common root causes.
2. Rebalance rules:
 - Move noisy services to a dedicated micro-rotation if they account for >25% of pages.
 - Limit night-weekend primary duty to volunteers in the rotation unless emergency staffing required.
3. Local fairness check (monthly):
 - Team leads run a 15-minute review in the first week of each month to confirm schedule fairness and swap if needed.

Rotation constraints (config):
| Constraint | Value | Rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| Max continuous on-call | 36h | Prevent fatigue and degraded decision-making |
| Minimum handoff overlap | 15m | Time to summarize bridge state and outstanding actions |
| Max weekly duty | 56h | Prevent single-responder overload across teams |
| Handoff notes retention | 90d | Auditability and incident reconstruction |

Bridge handoff procedure (step-by-step):
1) Pre-handoff checklist (outgoing):
 - Summarize incident timeline, current hypotheses, mitigation steps in progress, and customer impact.
 - Confirm runbook page(s) in Bridge tab are current and link to traces/log queries.
2) Live handoff (over bridge):
 - 5–15 minute verbal summary; ensure incoming acknowledges critical mitigations.
 - If unresolved customer-impacting work remains, assign an owner and ETA.
3) Post-handoff (incoming):
 - Record a 1-line status in the incident timeline and attach a minimum evidence set (logs, traces, alert IDs).

Incident lifecycle and DPM decision matrix:
- If incident is Sev1 or multi-tenant Sev2 -> full postmortem required within 72 hours of remediation.
- If incident meets ALL of the following, use DPM: single-tenant, <30 minutes customer-visible impact, known cause, effective mitigation applied at resolution.
- Otherwise triage for full postmortem.

Deferred Postmortem (DPM) protocol (when to use and how):
Purpose: capture essential facts and actions quickly when resource constraints or ongoing high operational tempo would make a full postmortem impractical in 72 hours.
DPM steps (owner: incident lead):
1) Within 8 hours of incident resolution: populate DPM template with
 - 1-line summary, impact window (start/end), services affected, severity, and customer impact.
 - Evidence snapshot (link to logs, runbook used, mitigation commands).
2) Create action items with clear owners and SLAs (default: 14-day action SLA).
3) Flag DPM for follow-up in the next synthesis meeting.
4) If DPM reveals systemic risk or unresolved unknowns, escalate to full postmortem.

DPM template (minimum fields):
- Title (1 line)
- Date/time window
- Affected services and teams (comma-separated)
- Immediate mitigations executed
- Evidence links (logs, traces, alert IDs)
- Action items (owner | due date | description)
- Decision to close DPM or escalate (yes/no)

Escalation and timeline expectations:
- Immediate: severity declaration and customer status update within 30 minutes of detection for Sev1/Sev2.
- Short window: initial triage and bridge stand-up within 60 minutes.
- DPM creation: within 8 hours.
- Full postmortem: published within 72 hours for Sev1/Sev2.

Customer communications templates (for bridge operator use):
- Initial status (first 30m):
 "We have identified an issue affecting [feature/service]. Our team has engaged and is investigating. We will provide an update within 30 minutes."

- Follow-up status (post-triage):
 "Update: The issue is caused by [brief cause]. Mitigations underway include [actions]. Current impact: [scope]. Next update scheduled at [time/ETA]."

- Resolution notice:
 "Resolved: The issue affecting [service] has been mitigated at [time]. Root cause and next steps will be published in a follow-up note or postmortem."

- SLA-credit preliminary message (if applicable):
 "We are assessing impact against our SLA commitments. If you are eligible, we will follow up with credit details once our postmortem is complete."

Game day design and schedule (90-minute template):
- Goal: validate handoff, DPM creation, and customer comms speed.
- Attendees: 1 bridge operator, 2 responders, 1 product EM, 1 customer success observer.
- Timeline:
 00:00 — Inject alert and distribute pager
 00:05 — Bridge up and first customer status sent
 00:20 — Handoff simulation between responders
 00:45 — DPM skeleton completed and action items assigned
 01:05 — Demo of status page update flow and mock SLA notice
 01:20 — 15-minute retro and lessons logged

Runbook snippets (examples):
- Quick KV-cache eviction (serving-runtime):
 "# Commands
 kubectl exec -n runtime svc/cache-operator -- cache evict --pattern=*
 # Verify: tail logs for 200 responses to health endpoint for 5m"

- Throttle mitigation (traffic spike):
 "1) Move non-critical traffic to burst_throttle=true route.
 2) Increase instance headroom by policy 'scale-now' for model-serving service.
 3) Notify customers via status page if >5% error rate persists after 5m."

Ownership and metrics (who owns what):
- On-call synthesis owner: SRE manager (quarterly cadence).
- DPM governance: Incident review council (product + SRE rep)
- Bridge operator: maintains status templates and runbook links.
- Metrics to track: mean time to ack (MTTA), mean time to remediate (MTTR), percentage of incidents resolved with DPM, action-item closure rate within 14 days.

Audit and retention:
- DPMs and postmortems retained for 2 years in the incident archive.
- Handoff notes retained for 90 days.

Related pages and references:
- Link: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-evidence-collection-standard (internal)
- Link: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/kv-cache-eviction (internal)

Appendix: triage decision quick chart:
- High latency + multi-tenant -> Sev1 -> full postmortem
- Short outage <30m + single-tenant + known fix -> DPM
- Repeated flapping events -> escalate to hypothesis-driven postmortem

Revision history:
- 2026-01-12 — created by Priya Shah
- 2026-02-02 — added DPM SLA guidance (review: Miguel Alvarez)
- 2026-03-01 — formalized rotation constraints and game day template (review: Sara Kim)

title: Activation safeguards and initiative tide for Private VPC waves
author: Ava Martinez
text:
Objective: Define and sequence the quarterly activation plan for customer-hosted Private/VPC deployments with prescriptive safeguards. This ticket consolidates operator rituals, preflight checks, roll-forward/rollback gates, and OKR-linked success signals so that waves of customers can be activated with minimal incident risk and clear escalation paths. Scope includes: canary cohort definitions, compatibility verifier checklist, upgrade window taxonomy, automated gating logic, runbooks for failed activations, and telemetry signals that feed the Console activation dashboard.

1) A documented activation choreography describing wave cadence, canary criteria, and safety gates is approved by Eng and Security. 2) Preflight compatibility verifier spec and a reference script are merged to the private-infra repo. 3) Console shows an 'activation health' panel with the baseline signals (errors/sec, P95 latency, auth failures). 4) Runbooks for abort/rollback and an automated rollback circuit are drafted and validated in a staging wave. 5) OKR metrics and cohort targets are captured in the project board and linked to rollout milestones.

2026-01-12: Kickoff with Eng, Security, and Solutions. Agreed scope and delivery window. PM to draft activation choreography doc.
2026-01-22: Engineering proposed two-stage canary (internal -> lighthouse customers). Raised dependency on ENG-40122 (installer immutability work).
2026-01-30: Security reviewed high-level guardrails; requested KMS edge-case handling and an audit log retention note. Flagged security_review_required.
2026-02-05: Design review of Console panel mockups. Designer suggested adding time-to-rollback ETA and a 'confidence' indicator. Added to acceptance criteria.
2026-02-14: Draft preflight compatibility verifier prototype uploaded to Drive and requested validation from three lighthouse customers. Added test matrix for kernel/driver combos.
2026-02-22: Cross-team sync. Agreed to ship verifier script and Console activation health panel to staging by 2026-02-28. Planning staging wave tentatively for 2026-03-10.

Installer/driver incompatibilities across customer hardware causing wave delays
KMS/HSM integration edge cases delaying canary sign-offs
Insufficient telemetry coverage for early detection of regressions
Customer onboarding windows conflict with their maintenance cycles

Finalize activation choreography doc and circulate for engineering sign-off by 2026-01-20 (COMPLETE: draft done)
Prioritize ENG-40122 in next sprint and track blocker impact
Instrument the Console activation health panel hooks and ship a staging dashboard
Run a dry-run activation in staging with internal tenants on 2026-03-10
Capture OKR success signals and map to cohort progression metrics

title: dynamic-scratch-reuse-and-fanout-aware-kernel-selection-to-reduce-peak-gpu-workspace
author: Maya Chen
text:
Motivation: observed high peak GPU workspace usage for mixed-sequence inference (short+long requests) and multi-query fanout workloads. Existing arena tuning + static activation checkpointing provided good average memory savings but left headroom in two patterns: (1) transient scratch buffer spikes from kernels that allocate per-op temp buffers, and (2) suboptimal kernel choices when the operator fanout (key/value heads * queries) changes runtime characteristics. This PR implements two complimentary mechanisms to reduce peak workspace: 1) dynamic scratch reuse: a runtime scratch allocator that tracks short-lived temp regions by lifetime buckets and reuses buffers across operators within the same execution frame, avoiding repeated allocations and reducing fragmentation; 2) fanout-aware kernel selection: extend the kernel-selector to consider request fanout and KV cache reshaping costs when choosing between tiled/packed attention kernels and the low-memory fused attention kernels.

Summary of changes: implemented a lightweight scratch manager in runtime/scratch_manager.{cpp,h} with a lock-free free-list per-sizeclass and lifetime-tagging. Hooked the scratch allocation path into the kernel interface and modified critical kernels (attention, rotary, layernorm) to request scratch via the manager. Added a fanout heuristic in runtime/kernel_selector.cpp that uses observed Q*K fanout counters (collected per-model) to pick kernels that trade compute for lower transient memory. Added a compatibility path so that models pinned to older kernel profiles will continue to run the legacy selector. Integrated unit and microbenchmarks under benchmark-lab/ with a new benchmark script fanout_memory_profile.py and an end-to-end e2e memory test that simulates interleaved short/long requests.

Performance results: on A100-40GB with GPT-2 style model (1B params) and mixed workload (50% seq_len=32, 50% seq_len=1024) peak workspace dropped from 16.8GB to 12.1GB (~28% reduction). For high-fanout Q=16 tests the transient peak reduced by ~34% when the fanout-aware kernel was selected. End-to-end latency impact: median latency for long requests increased ~2.3% in a worst-case knob-on scenario where the low-memory kernel is used; this is within the SLA tradeoff and we expose a config flag to prefer latency vs memory at policy-level.

Compatibility and rollout strategy: feature gated behind runtime flag runtime.scratch_reuse.enabled=false by default in this PR; we plan a phased rollout: enable on non-production clusters for 2 weeks, then opt-in for Dedicated clusters with memory pressure, finally flip default after one week of metrics monitoring. Kernel selection heuristic is additive and can be disabled with runtime.kernel_selector.fanout_heuristic=false. Added telemetry metrics: runtime.scratch_reuse.alloc_reuse_ratio, kernel_selector.fanout_decision_count and memory.scratch_peak_by_model.

Testing: added unit tests for scratch manager lifecycle and size-class reuse; added integration tests that assert no OOM on synthetic high-fanout scenarios; ran infra e2e-bench and observed stable results. CI: linux-unit-tests, cuda-smoke, and e2e-bench run green in the final run. Created a small fuzz harness to ensure lifetime tagging prevents use-after-free across frames.

Backward compatibility: no breaking API changes; the kernel interface signature extended with an optional scratch_token but remains backward-compatible with default nullptr behavior. Documentation: runtime/README.md updated with configuration knobs, and redwood-docs/ops/gpu-memory-tuning.md includes recommended settings for Dedicated customers.

Notes: this PR intentionally avoids changing global arena sizing heuristics in this iteration — that will be a follow-up to measure impact of scratch reuse on arena fragmentation (ENG-1919). Also, we identified a secondary opportunity to compress KV cache layout when fanout>8; tracked separately under ENG-1875.

Alex Ortega: Nit - please add a short note on concurrency model for the free-lists. Also, can we expose a knob to limit max per-frame scratch?
Maya Chen (author): Added concurrency notes in scratch_manager.h and exposed runtime.scratch_reuse.max_frame_scratch (default large).
Priya Nair: Verified benchmarks locally on p4d; I saw similar 26-30% peak reduction. One request: add a test ensuring legacy kernel path still used when model pinned.
Maya Chen (author): Added model-pinned test and compatibility checks in kernel_selector.
Samir Patel: Approved after CI green. Left a follow-up to audit arena metrics (ENG-1919).

Reduced peak GPU workspace by ~28% for mixed short/long workloads via dynamic scratch buffer reuse.
Added fanout-aware kernel selection which reduces transient memory for high-query fanout workloads.
Exposed runtime knobs to tune memory vs latency tradeoffs: runtime.scratch_reuse.enabled and runtime.kernel_selector.fanout_heuristic.
