title: Private upgrades technical deep dive (design partner) - upgrade plan, backups, rollback
author: Markus Klein
text:
Northstar walked through current pain points upgrading their on-prem Redwood Private environment: upgrades are high-touch, require manual sequencing between control plane components and data plane, and rollback is mostly 'restore from VM snapshot and hope'. They emphasized air-gapped constraints (no outbound internet), strict change windows, and audit evidence requirements.

Redwood reviewed the planned upgrade workflow (preflight checks -> plan generation -> backup -> staged rollout -> verification) and discussed which prechecks should block vs warn (storage headroom, DB connectivity, OIDC reachability). Backup approach was discussed across CSI snapshots and logical DB dumps, with Northstar noting they do not have consistent snapshot support across clusters.

Key concerns were around schema migrations (lock timeouts, partial upgrades), deterministic rollback hooks, and how artifacts are verified offline (checksums/signatures). The call ended with agreement on beta prerequisites, a rollback drill, and a short list of environment details Northstar will provide.

Current on-prem upgrade workflow and failure modes
Air-gapped artifact delivery and verification (checksums/signing)
Preflight checks: cluster health, storage, RBAC/SSO, networking/DNS/TLS, DB readiness
Backup/restore: CSI snapshots vs logical dumps, encryption/KMS expectations
Rollback semantics: partial upgrade handling, schema migration guardrails
Beta timeline, success criteria, and a rollback drill

Meeting header
Date: 2025-05-28
Time: 4:03pm - 5:00pm PT
Duration: 57 minutes
Call type: Technical deep dive

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Markus Klein, Fatima Noor, Bruno Silva, Irene Choi, Sean Gallagher
Northstar Health Systems: Priya Raman, Evan Wu, Marisol Chen, Jake Miller

---

[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool, I think we’re recording. Um, thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is to go deeper on the upgrade and rollback stuff for Private, especially for on-prem, air-gapped. We’ve got Fatima, Bruno, Irene, Sean here.

[00:15] Priya Raman: Sounds good.

[00:16] Markus Klein: Priya, do you wanna start with what you all do today for upgrades and, like, where it’s painful?

[00:24] Priya Raman: Yeah. So currently our process is basically, we schedule a maintenance window, we… we download the new package from our internal mirror, we do a Helm upgrade, and then it’s like, fingers crossed. The ordering is not obvious. We’ve had one incident where control plane came up but data plane got stuck because of… I think it was a migration? And rollback was manual.

[00:47] Jake Miller: The rollback is basically, we restore etcd snapshots and PV snapshots where we can, but not all clusters have the same storage. Sometimes we revert the whole node pool image. It’s… it’s messy.

[01:01] Evan Wu: Yeah and the charts have hooks but they don’t always run in the order we expect. Like pre-upgrade jobs time out and then Helm rolls back but the DB already got migrated.

[01:16] Sean Gallagher: Yep, that’s the exact class of issue we’re trying to kill. Partial upgrades + schema migration side effects.

[01:23] Markus Klein: Great context. Fatima, do you wanna give the 2-minute overview of the new approach we’re implementing?

[01:30] Fatima Noor: Sure. So the direction is: the installer generates an upgrade plan first, it’s a versioned artifact that lists stages and steps. Before doing anything, we run preflight checks—cluster health, storage headroom, DNS/TLS, RBAC, database connectivity, and also artifact availability. Then we orchestrate backups. After that we execute the plan in phases: control plane first, then data plane, with readiness gates. If something fails, we have deterministic rollback entry points that use stored state from the plan execution.

[02:05] Priya Raman: When you say installer—this is the redwood-private-installer CLI, right? Not Helm itself?

[02:10] Fatima Noor: Correct. Helm still does the actual apply of charts, but we wrap it with an orchestrator so we can be consistent and auditable.

[02:19] Marisol Chen: Auditable meaning we can show, like, exactly what checks ran and what was backed up?

[02:24] Fatima Noor: Exactly. Plan output persisted, precheck results, backup IDs, and upgrade start/stop events.

[02:31] Irene Choi: And timestamps, plus versions: current version, target version, and what artifacts were used.

[02:39] Marisol Chen: Okay.

[02:41] Markus Klein: Evan, can you describe your on-prem constraints? Like how air-gapped are we talking.

[02:47] Evan Wu: Fully. No outbound internet. We have an internal artifact mirror for container images and we can host a chart repo internally, but it’s manual. Also we need checksums for everything. Our security team won’t allow “curl random thing during upgrade.”

[03:06] Marisol Chen: And signatures if possible. Checksums alone are… better than nothing, but ideally there’s a signing chain.

[03:13] Fatima Noor: Yep. So we’re adding bundle verification: manifest, checksums, and optional signatures. The installer will fail early if the bundle doesn’t match.

[03:24] Priya Raman: Can it operate with, like, a USB drop? We sometimes do physical transfer to the restricted enclave.

[03:30] Fatima Noor: That’s a supported model. The bundle is basically a directory or tarball with a manifest file plus all referenced artifacts.

[03:40] Bruno Silva: And on the Terraform side for VPC it’s a bit different, but for on-prem we’ll document “offline registry endpoint” variables too, so the installer knows where to pull from without going to the public registry.

[03:54] Evan Wu: Okay. Biggest pain for us is, if Helm upgrade fails, we don’t know what state we’re in. Like, was the database migrated? Was it halfway? And then we get stuck.

[04:08] Sean Gallagher: Right. So we’re defining “rollback hooks” as part of the plan. The critical part is: schema migrations have to be guarded. We’re implementing idempotency checks and lock timeouts. Also, we’re biasing to backwards-compatible changes when possible so rollback doesn’t require “un-migrating” data.

[04:28] Jake Miller: That’s good in theory but we’ve seen migration jobs hold locks for a long time.

[04:32] Sean Gallagher: Yep. We’ve been tuning defaults—like statement timeouts and lock timeouts—so a bad migration doesn’t freeze the cluster. And the precheck will also test DB connectivity and maybe space.

[04:45] Priya Raman: Can we dig into prechecks? Which ones are blocking? Because we don’t want the system to block over something we accept risk on.

[04:52] Fatima Noor: For beta, we’re proposing a mix. Blocking: unsupported version jump, missing artifacts, DB not reachable, insufficient storage headroom for backups, and cluster not healthy (like nodes NotReady). Warning: OIDC reachability maybe, depending on your setup, and DNS latency, stuff like that.

[05:15] Marisol Chen: OIDC reachability as a warning seems dangerous? If auth breaks, we can’t log in.

[05:21] Irene Choi: The nuance is, some customers have break-glass local admin. If you have that, we can make it warn; if you don’t, it should block.

[05:30] Jake Miller: We do have break-glass but it’s painful and audited.

[05:35] Priya Raman: Our preference is: block if OIDC is required for operator access. If it’s only for end-user, maybe warning.

[05:44] Fatima Noor: That’s fair; we can make it configurable, like policy.

[05:50] Markus Klein: Marisol, what would you need from an audit standpoint for “we ran prechecks”?

[05:56] Marisol Chen: We need a record of what ran, outcome, and ideally configuration and versions. Also backup encryption verification. And who initiated it.

[06:06] Markus Klein: Got it.

[06:08] Sean Gallagher: We’re also planning to emit audit events: upgrade started, prechecks pass/fail, backup complete, rollback invoked. Those events can go to your SIEM if you have an integration.

[06:21] Marisol Chen: Okay, that’s good.

[06:24] Evan Wu: Precheck for storage headroom—how do you calculate that? Because our PVs are not all on the same backend.

[06:31] Irene Choi: Great question. We’re probably going to start with a conservative heuristic. If CSI snapshots are available, we’ll check snapshot capability and ensure there’s enough capacity for snapshot deltas, but that’s hard to estimate. If we do logical backups, we’ll check the backup target volume has X free GB and that DB size is below that.

[06:53] Evan Wu: We have Ceph in one cluster and local PV in another. Snapshots only on Ceph.

[07:00] Irene Choi: Yeah, that’s common. In that case we’d pick the backup strategy per environment: CSI snapshots for Ceph cluster, and logical dumps + config export for the local PV cluster.

[07:13] Jake Miller: Logical dump meaning, like, pg_dump?

[07:16] Irene Choi: Yes, for Postgres. Or whatever backing DB is in your Private deployment—most folks are Postgres. Plus we back up config and the installer state.

[07:26] Priya Raman: What about secrets? We don’t want secrets copied around.

[07:30] Irene Choi: We don’t copy raw secret values if we can avoid it; we store references and rely on your KMS/HSM for actual material. But for on-prem, it depends—if you’re using Kubernetes secrets, we need to be explicit about what’s included.

[07:46] Marisol Chen: Yeah, we use an internal secrets manager, not just K8s secrets. We can’t have the installer dumping secrets in cleartext.

[07:53] Fatima Noor: Understood. We can scope backups to exclude secret values and document prerequisites. We can also encrypt the backup artifacts with customer-provided keys.

[08:04] Bruno Silva: For on-prem, we’re going to support pointing the installer at a KMS endpoint if you have one inside the environment. Otherwise, passphrase-based encryption is a fallback, but less ideal.

[08:18] Jake Miller: Okay.

[08:20] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about upgrade ordering. Evan you said control plane vs data plane got out of order sometimes.

[08:27] Evan Wu: Yeah. Like, the console upgraded, but the “serving” components didn’t, and we saw mismatch.

[08:33] Sean Gallagher: So we’re explicitly splitting phases. Control plane first: API, console, controllers, DB migrations. Wait for ready. Then data plane: runtime/serving deployments, gateways, etc. There are readiness gates between phases.

[08:50] Priya Raman: Is that still Helm? Or separate charts?

[08:53] Fatima Noor: Still Helm charts, but with hooks + ordering, and the installer enforces stage transitions.

[09:02] Evan Wu: Helm hooks have bitten us, honestly.

[09:05] Fatima Noor: Yep. We’re adding explicit timeouts and fail-fast behavior. And more importantly we persist state so if it fails, the rollback command knows what happened.

[09:18] Jake Miller: What does rollback actually do? Like “helm rollback” only?

[09:22] Sean Gallagher: It depends on where you are. If it’s an early failure before migrations, it’s basically revert chart versions. If migrations have run, rollback may involve restoring from backups or switching to a compatible older app version that can still read the newer schema (that’s the backwards-compat work).

[09:41] Priya Raman: And if you can’t go back, you’ll tell us?

[09:44] Sean Gallagher: Exactly. The plan has rollback metadata per step. Some steps are “non-reversible” and then rollback requires restore, not just “undo.”

[09:55] Marisol Chen: That needs to be very clear. We can’t have ambiguity in a change window.

[09:59] Markus Klein: Agree. That’s why the plan is meant to be human-readable too, not just machine.

[10:04] Evan Wu: Also, artifact mismatch is a common problem for us. Someone updates the internal mirror but not the chart version, or vice versa.

[10:12] Fatima Noor: Bundle manifest addresses that. The plan generation step verifies artifact presence and digest. It won’t proceed if the digest doesn’t match what’s expected.

[10:25] Priya Raman: Is the digest pinned in the plan, or in some compatibility file?

[10:29] Fatima Noor: In the bundle manifest and in the plan output. The plan references exact artifact versions.

[10:36] Bruno Silva: And for VPC customers, Terraform can pin versions too; but for on-prem, the bundle is the primary mechanism.

[10:45] Jake Miller: What about model cache? We’ve had upgrades that nuked the cache and caused a performance issue after.

[10:51] Sean Gallagher: Great point. We’re treating model cache as “rebuildable” but operationally it matters. The plan will have steps like “drain traffic / warm cache” and rollback will consider it. We’re not promising cache preservation in v1 but we can avoid deleting it unless necessary.

[11:10] Evan Wu: Please don’t delete it during upgrade. Even if it’s rebuildable, it’s like hours.

[11:14] Sean Gallagher: Understood. Default will be to preserve and only invalidate if version requires it.

[11:21] Irene Choi: Also, storage headroom check will consider cache volumes if they’re on the same PVs.

[11:28] Priya Raman: Another requirement: no downtime if possible, but we can accept some. What’s the expectation?

[11:35] Markus Klein: For in-place upgrades, there might be a small control plane blip depending on DB migrations. We’re trying to make it minimal. For serving, we do rolling, but if you’re at capacity, you might see increased latency.

[11:50] Jake Miller: We can plan a maintenance window. We just need predictability.

[11:54] Markus Klein: Okay.

[11:55] (crosstalk)

[11:56] Marisol Chen: Sorry, one more thing: logging. We need logs retained for at least 90 days for change evidence.

[12:02] Sean Gallagher: Audit events can be shipped. For installer logs, we can include them in a support bundle and you can store them internally. We’ll document what’s in there.

[12:14] Priya Raman: Support bundle includes upgrade plan output too?

[12:17] Fatima Noor: Yes, that’s the intent.

[12:20] Markus Klein: Maybe we walk through a hypothetical upgrade flow. Fatima, can you do that? Like commands.

[12:26] Fatima Noor: Sure. Something like:
1) `redwood-private upgrade plan --target 1.14.0 --bundle /mnt/bundles/1.14.0`
It outputs a JSON plan plus a human summary.
2) `redwood-private upgrade precheck --plan plan.json`
3) `redwood-private upgrade backup --plan plan.json`
4) `redwood-private upgrade apply --plan plan.json`
And if failure: `redwood-private upgrade rollback --plan plan.json --to-stage control-plane` or `--restore backup-id` depending.

[13:02] Evan Wu: That’s helpful.

[13:03] Priya Raman: The plan JSON—can we parse it? We might want to store it in our change system.

[13:09] Fatima Noor: Yes, schema is stable-ish. We’ll share a draft. It’ll include stages, steps, dependencies, rollback info.

[13:19] Marisol Chen: Will it include a risk score?

[13:21] Markus Klein: We have internal change management risk scoring. For customers we can include warnings like “risky jump” if version compatibility matrix says so.

[13:31] Sean Gallagher: And prechecks can output severity: block / warn / info.

[13:36] Jake Miller: Version compatibility matrix—what’s supported? We’re usually behind.

[13:42] Sean Gallagher: Initially we’re optimizing for N-1 to N. Like one minor step. If you’re multiple versions behind, we might require intermediate upgrades, and we’ll flag it.

[13:54] Priya Raman: That’s going to be a challenge. We’re on… I think 1.11? and you’re talking 1.14.

[14:00] Markus Klein: That’s good to know. For beta, we can target one hop to validate the machinery, but longer term we’ll add multi-hop guidance.

[14:10] Evan Wu: If it blocks, can it still produce a plan so we can see what would happen?

[14:14] Fatima Noor: Yes. Plan generation can succeed but precheck will block, and it’ll tell you why.

[14:21] Priya Raman: That’s actually what we want.

[14:24] Irene Choi: On backup: do you have a preferred backup target? NFS? Object store?

[14:29] Evan Wu: We have an internal S3-compatible object store for some clusters. Not in the restricted one.

[14:36] Irene Choi: Okay. For restricted cluster, we can write to a mounted volume, and you can export it after.

[14:43] Marisol Chen: Must be encrypted at rest.

[14:45] Irene Choi: Yup. Either storage-level encryption or installer-level encryption.

[14:50] Jake Miller: Another issue: We need a hard stop if nodes are under disk pressure. We had that once and upgrade made it worse.

[14:58] Fatima Noor: Node disk pressure will be a blocking precheck.

[15:02] Sean Gallagher: And we can check kube events for Evicted pods etc.

[15:08] Priya Raman: Great.

[15:10] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about what “success” looks like post-upgrade. Jake, what do you verify today?

[15:16] Jake Miller: Mostly we check pods are running, API responds, and we do a smoke test—generate a response. But we don’t have good metrics.

[15:26] Sean Gallagher: We’ll provide an upgrade dashboard: error rate, latency, migration duration. For on-prem, you can use our observability pack if you’re running Prometheus/Grafana.

[15:39] Evan Wu: We are.

[15:40] Sean Gallagher: Great. Then we can provide alert thresholds too.

[15:44] Marisol Chen: Does the dashboard help with audit?

[15:47] Sean Gallagher: More operational, but combined with audit events it does.

[15:52] Priya Raman: Okay.

[15:53] Markus Klein: I want to make sure we capture the top pain points to feed into beta requirements. I heard: ordering, partial DB migrations, artifact mismatch, and inconsistent snapshot support.

[16:06] Priya Raman: Also, “who can run upgrades” is important. Needs RBAC.

[16:10] Marisol Chen: Yes, RBAC and break-glass. And SSO integration. During upgrade we sometimes lose SSO.

[16:18] Fatima Noor: Precheck can validate RBAC and that the service account has required permissions. For SSO, we can check reachability to IdP.

[16:28] Evan Wu: One more thing: DNS. In our enclave, DNS can be flaky.

[16:33] Irene Choi: DNS resolution check will be included. And TLS certificate validity. We can catch expired certs before upgrade.

[16:42] Jake Miller: Good.

[16:44] Markus Klein: We’ve got about 40 minutes left; let’s go deeper on rollback semantics because that’s usually the scary one. Sean, can you describe “rollback entry points” with an example.

[16:55] Sean Gallagher: Yeah. Think of the plan as stages: prechecks, backup, control-plane upgrade, data-plane upgrade, verification. If we fail during control-plane upgrade before applying schema changes, rollback is “revert charts and configs.” If we fail after schema changes, rollback might require restore of DB snapshot. So the rollback command reads the stored state: which steps completed, what backup IDs exist, and then executes rollback hooks in reverse order.

[17:25] Evan Wu: Reverse order meaning last step undone first.

[17:28] Sean Gallagher: Exactly.

[17:29] Priya Raman: Can we choose “stop and hold” instead of rollback? Like, for us, sometimes we want to fix forward.

[17:36] Sean Gallagher: Yes. There’ll be a “pause” / “manual intervention required” mode. The plan output should tell you which step failed and suggested remediation.

[17:48] Jake Miller: But the biggest problem is, once you’ve run a migration, “fix forward” may be hard.

[17:53] Sean Gallagher: Agree. That’s why we’re focusing on backwards-compatible migrations and guardrails.

[18:00] Marisol Chen: How do you guarantee backwards-compatible? That’s not always possible.

[18:04] Sean Gallagher: We can’t guarantee for all time. We can say: in supported upgrade paths, we require migrations to be safe for rollback or require snapshot restore as the rollback method. That’s part of compatibility policy.

[18:20] Priya Raman: So we’ll have a doc that says “supported upgrade paths” and what rollback guarantees are.

[18:25] Markus Klein: Yes.

[18:27] Evan Wu: For on-prem, do you test this? Like end-to-end in CI?

[18:32] Fatima Noor: We’re building an integration test matrix: different k8s versions, storage backends, VPC vs on-prem-ish scenarios, and failure injection.

[18:45] Jake Miller: Failure injection meaning you simulate a migration timeout?

[18:48] Fatima Noor: Exactly. Or precheck failures.

[18:51] Sean Gallagher: And we’ll track rollback frequency too.

[18:56] Priya Raman: Great.

[18:58] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about your maintenance window constraints. How long is typical?

[19:03] Priya Raman: Usually 2 hours, but change freeze around end of quarter. We can do a beta window mid-June.

[19:12] Markus Klein: Okay.

[19:13] Evan Wu: But we need a rollback plan before we do it.

[19:16] Markus Klein: Absolutely. We propose a rollback drill planning session.

[19:21] Jake Miller: Like a tabletop.

[19:22] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[19:24] Marisol Chen: We also need to validate bundle verification. We have a policy: all binaries must be signed.

[19:31] Fatima Noor: We support checksums now and optional signatures; we can align with your policy. The signing authority might be ours or yours depending on how you repackage.

[19:44] Marisol Chen: Ideally you sign, and then we validate.

[19:47] Fatima Noor: Makes sense.

[19:49] Evan Wu: Quick question: What about Kubernetes version compatibility? We’re on 1.28.

[19:55] Irene Choi: That should be supported. We’ll confirm with the matrix.

[19:59] Sean Gallagher: The installer will check K8s version as part of prechecks.

[20:05] Priya Raman: Okay.

[20:06] Markus Klein: Any competitor solutions you evaluated for this? Just to understand baseline.

[20:12] Priya Raman: For inference we looked at Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, but we can’t use them. For internal we looked at KServe. But the upgrade story is also hard.

[20:25] Evan Wu: SageMaker too, but not on-prem.

[20:28] Markus Klein: Got it.

[20:31] Irene Choi: On backups, one question: Do you have a DB external to the cluster or in-cluster Postgres?

[20:38] Evan Wu: In-cluster, currently.

[20:40] Irene Choi: That makes snapshot strategy more important.

[20:44] Jake Miller: We could move it external but that’s another project.

[20:48] Irene Choi: Understood.

[20:50] Sean Gallagher: In-cluster DB upgrades also need care. We’ll sequence DB components before app layers.

[20:58] Priya Raman: Another pain: We don’t know what changed between versions. Release notes are sometimes too high level.

[21:05] Markus Klein: We’re adding a customer-facing changelog specifically for Private, including “upgrade notes” and “breaking changes” callouts.

[21:14] Marisol Chen: Needs security impact notes too.

[21:16] Markus Klein: Yep.

[21:18] Evan Wu: Can you make the precheck output actionable? Like “run this kubectl command” to fix.

[21:24] Fatima Noor: That’s a goal. Each check will have remediation pointers.

[21:31] Jake Miller: Please include “what’s blocking” in one line. Not like a wall of text.

[21:36] Fatima Noor: Noted.

[21:39] Markus Klein: Alright. Maybe we get more concrete: for your environment, what prechecks would you want to be hard blockers?

[21:48] Priya Raman: Blockers: unsupported version jump, DB not reachable, nodes not ready, disk pressure, insufficient backup target space, and missing artifact checksums. Also if SSO is down and no break-glass.

[22:06] Marisol Chen: TLS cert expiry too.

[22:08] Evan Wu: And the ability to pull images from our internal registry. We’ve had auth token issues.

[22:14] Bruno Silva: Registry auth check is on the list. We can validate image pull secrets by doing a dry-run pull.

[22:23] Evan Wu: Great.

[22:25] Jake Miller: Warnings: maybe like “your cluster is at 80% CPU” — we can accept that.

[22:31] Sean Gallagher: Yep.

[22:33] Irene Choi: Another one is “PV snapshot capability” - if you selected snapshot backup but snapshots aren’t supported, that should block.

[22:40] Evan Wu: Totally.

[22:42] Markus Klein: Good. On rollback: what would you consider an acceptable rollback guarantee?

[22:49] Priya Raman: For beta: if upgrade fails, we can restore to pre-upgrade state within the maintenance window. That’s the goal.

[22:58] Jake Miller: Like < 60 minutes to restore.

[23:01] Marisol Chen: And evidence of what happened.

[23:04] Sean Gallagher: We can aim for that. Restore time depends on backup type and data size.

[23:11] Irene Choi: We might want to measure your DB size and estimate restore time.

[23:15] Evan Wu: It’s around 180 GB.

[23:18] Irene Choi: Okay, logical restore might be slower. Snapshot restore would be faster if available.

[23:26] Evan Wu: In our Ceph cluster we can do snapshots.

[23:29] Irene Choi: Then we’d strongly recommend snapshots for that one.

[23:34] Priya Raman: But our restricted enclave is the one without snapshots.

[23:38] Irene Choi: Then we’ll tune the logical backup/restore and maybe do a verification step ahead of time.

[23:46] Jake Miller: Verification step meaning test restoring in staging?

[23:49] Irene Choi: Exactly.

[23:52] Markus Klein: That might be part of beta prep.

[23:56] Marisol Chen: Also: do you back up config and “state”? There’s some config in CRDs.

[24:02] Fatima Noor: Yes, config export includes CRDs/CRs relevant to Redwood, plus installer state.

[24:10] Evan Wu: Okay.

[24:12] Sean Gallagher: One subtlety: we need to coordinate control plane and data plane in rollback too. If DP upgraded and CP didn’t, we can get weirdness.

[24:20] Jake Miller: Yeah.

[24:22] Sean Gallagher: That’s why we gate phases and record stage completion.

[24:28] Priya Raman: Are you planning blue/green?

[24:31] Markus Klein: Not initially. We considered it, but it’s expensive and operationally heavy for on-prem. This is in-place with deterministic rollback hooks.

[24:44] Evan Wu: Makes sense.

[24:46] Markus Klein: Any other must-haves before you’ll do beta?

[24:51] Marisol Chen: Documentation. Not just “run this command” but what it does.

[24:56] Jake Miller: And support coverage. If it goes bad, we need someone on the line.

[25:01] Markus Klein: We can coordinate with Support and SRE for the beta window.

[25:06] Priya Raman: Also, we need to know what data leaves the cluster. Ideally none.

[25:11] Markus Klein: For on-prem, none unless you ship logs. The installer can operate fully offline.

[25:18] Marisol Chen: Good.

[25:20] Evan Wu: One more detail: Helm itself wants to call home sometimes? Not really, but chart dependencies maybe.

[25:26] Fatima Noor: We’ll vendor dependencies into the bundle so no network calls.

[25:33] Evan Wu: Perfect.

[25:35] Markus Klein: We’re at about halfway. Let’s pause and do a quick recap of what we’re taking away, then we can open it up for Q&A.

[25:43] Markus Klein: Takeaways: (1) you need a deterministic, auditable plan and clear blockers, (2) air-gapped artifact verification with checksums/signing, (3) backup strategy varies by cluster; snapshots where possible, logical backup otherwise, (4) rollback must be explicit about what’s reversible vs restore-required.

[26:03] Priya Raman: Yep.

[26:04] Markus Klein: Okay, questions.

[26:06] Evan Wu: About the plan JSON. Is it stored in the cluster? Or only local.

[26:10] Fatima Noor: Both options. By default we persist it as a Kubernetes secret or configmap plus local copy, but we can configure storage.

[26:19] Marisol Chen: Kubernetes secret storage might violate our policy if it includes sensitive info.

[26:24] Fatima Noor: The plan itself shouldn’t include secrets. It might include endpoints and versions.

[26:30] Marisol Chen: Okay.

[26:32] Jake Miller: What if the installer host dies mid-upgrade?

[26:36] Fatima Noor: That’s why state is persisted. You can resume from another host using the stored state.

[26:44] Jake Miller: Nice.

[26:46] Sean Gallagher: And we’ll make operations idempotent, so retries won’t make it worse.

[26:53] Evan Wu: Can you “dry run” the upgrade? Like show what would change.

[26:57] Fatima Noor: Plan generation is basically that, plus we can do Helm diff.

[27:03] Priya Raman: That would help with approvals.

[27:06] Bruno Silva: If you’re using Terraform for any parts, we also have a variable for upgrade windows to integrate with your scheduling.

[27:14] Priya Raman: On-prem we don’t use Terraform much.

[27:17] Bruno Silva: Understood.

[27:20] Marisol Chen: Do you have SOC 2 reports that mention change management?

[27:24] Markus Klein: Yes, we can share under NDA. But for on-prem, your controls are primary; our tool helps produce evidence.

[27:34] Marisol Chen: Okay.

[27:36] Jake Miller: Another technical question: If a migration times out, what happens? Does the job retry automatically?

[27:42] Sean Gallagher: We’re careful there. Some migrations can be retried safely, others cannot. The job will fail and the installer will mark that step as failed with a reason. Then you can choose to retry or rollback.

[27:56] Jake Miller: Okay.

[27:57] Evan Wu: And lock timeouts are configured by you?

[28:01] Sean Gallagher: Defaults by us, configurable by you via values/config.

[28:07] Priya Raman: Good.

[28:09] Irene Choi: On the storage check: we should confirm how your PVs are provisioned. If it’s dynamic provisioning, we can check storageclass capacity maybe. If it’s static local PV, we may need node-level checks.

[28:25] Evan Wu: It’s a mix.

[28:27] Irene Choi: Okay, we’ll follow up with a questionnaire.

[28:32] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about timing for beta. You said mid-June.

[28:37] Priya Raman: Yes. But we need at least 2 weeks to do internal change approval.

[28:42] Markus Klein: So we should aim to provide docs and precheck list by end of next week.

[28:48] Fatima Noor: That’s doable.

[28:50] Marisol Chen: Include the data handling and encryption details.

[28:54] Fatima Noor: Yes.

[28:56] Jake Miller: Also, can we test in staging first? We have a staging cluster but it’s not identical.

[29:01] Sean Gallagher: We should. Even if not identical, it helps validate plan and basic hooks.

[29:08] Evan Wu: Staging has snapshots. Prod restricted doesn’t.

[29:12] Irene Choi: Then we should also do a logical backup restore test somewhere.

[29:17] Priya Raman: Okay.

[29:18] Markus Klein: Anything else you want to see in the plan output? Like downtime estimate.

[29:25] Jake Miller: If you can estimate, great, but not required.

[29:28] Priya Raman: Risk warnings are more important.

[29:32] Fatima Noor: We can include “expected impact” fields but might be best-effort.

[29:38] Marisol Chen: I’d rather have honest uncertainty than fake precision.

[29:42] Markus Klein: Yep.

[29:44] Evan Wu: One more: Our operators prefer non-interactive mode. Can the installer run fully unattended?

[29:50] Fatima Noor: Yes. It can run with flags and produce logs. We might have a confirmation prompt for risky actions but you can override with `--yes`.

[30:01] Evan Wu: Great.

[30:02] Markus Klein: We’re getting close to wrap. Let’s do a quick pass on concrete next steps and owners.

[30:08] Markus Klein: Fatima will send bundle format overview + precheck list. Bruno will send version pinning / artifact source override notes. Irene will send backup strategy recommendations. Sean will send verification checklist + dashboard pointers. Priya will confirm OIDC reachability and storage backend details. Then we schedule a rollback drill planning session.

[30:33] Priya Raman: Works.

[30:35] Marisol Chen: Please include signature verification details.

[30:38] Fatima Noor: Yep.

[30:40] Jake Miller: And if possible, share an example plan JSON.

[30:44] Fatima Noor: Will do.

[30:46] Markus Klein: Great. Before we end, any last questions?

[30:50] Evan Wu: None from me.

[30:52] Marisol Chen: Good.

[30:53] Jake Miller: All set.

[30:55] Markus Klein: Awesome. Thanks everyone.

---
Note: Transcript auto-generated; speaker attribution may be imperfect in places.

Redwood to send draft precheck list + which items will be blocking vs warning for beta.
Northstar to confirm storage backend details (Rook/Ceph vs local PV) and whether CSI snapshots are available in prod.
Redwood to share offline/air-gapped upgrade bundle requirements and signing/checksum verification flow.
Schedule a 60-minute rollback drill planning session (tabletop) before beta upgrade window.
Northstar to provide a redacted sample of their current upgrade runbook and maintenance window constraints.

Fatima Noor: Share on-prem/air-gapped bundle format overview + required inputs (registry mirror, chart repo mirror) by 2025-05-30.
Bruno Silva: Follow up with Terraform variables for version pinning + artifact source overrides relevant to on-prem by 2025-06-03.
Irene Choi: Provide recommendation for snapshot approach per storage backend (CSI vs logical dump) and retention defaults by 2025-06-04.
Sean Gallagher: Draft what 'upgrade success' verification checklist looks like (health checks + dashboards) by 2025-06-05.
Priya Raman (Northstar): Confirm whether OIDC/SSO can be reachable from the cluster during maintenance window; note any change-freeze constraints by 2025-06-03.

- ClearSight requirement: minimal retention of PII and PHI in any hosted logging/analytics (you mentioned: prefer no storage at all; audit evidence required).
- Questions for us: can Redwood support a true 0-retention mode for token logs and request traces, or do we need to offer a short retention window?

Subject: Re: Post-call recap & next steps — data handling questions

Thanks Aditya — great notes and thanks for moving quickly. A few clarifications from our side:

- ClearSight handles sensitive patient billing data. Anything that could be tied back to a patient (name, DOB, MRN, invoice numbers, or full addresses) is considered PHI for this engagement.
- Our preference is to avoid retention of request/response text in any analytics or logs — effectively 0 retention for tokenized logs. We understand there are implementation nuances; if 0-retention is impossible we would consider a very short window (<=7 days) with firm deletion and attestations.
- We need to see Redwood's most recent SOC 2 report and a description of keys/where logs are stored. Procurement will require a short MOA for the pilot; legal expects to review any retention carveouts.

Folks — forwarding ClearSight's ask (see thread below). Key asks: 0-retention for token logs if possible, otherwise <=7 days with attestations; SOC2 and encryption details; MOA for pilot.

Laura: can you outline technical options we can offer (hosted toggles, Dedicated, Private deployment tradeoffs)?
Vivek/Marissa: I'd like a short commercial approach (pilot terms + any required credits).

I'm attaching the customer's security doc they shared for context.

Aditya

From: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.com>
To: Aditya Rao <aditya.rao@redwood.com>, Vivek Kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Sat, 23 May 2026 11:15:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Fwd: ClearSight security requirements — need options & legal wording

Aditya / team — technical summary and options we can propose to ClearSight:

Option A — Hosted, strict short-retention
- Configure request/response logging to "no-persist" mode for this account: that prevents writing full transcript logs to long-term analytics stores.
- We still maintain ephemeral KV cache for active sessions (needed for decoding and reduced token cost). That cache is in-memory and rotated; not written to disk by default.
- Provide 7-day retention window for token-level debug traces + automated deletion job. We can produce deletion attestations and an audit log of deletion events.
- Encryption at rest (AES-256) + customer can opt out of platform analytics.
- Pros: fastest time-to-value; cons: we cannot guarantee absolute 0-retention for transient operational traces in hosted mode.

Option B — Redwood Dedicated / Private deployment
- Dedicated pools with customer-managed KMS and configuration to disable all logging pipelines — supports effectively 0 retention for request/response artifacts.
- Requires procurement lead time (2–6 weeks) and network setup; better for regulated PHI workloads.
- We can include stronger SLAs and on-prem audit capabilities.

Recommended commercial packaging for pilot:
- 90-day pilot on Hosted with 7-day short-retention + deletion attestations while customer evaluates Dedicated. If they need 0 retention we move to Private deployment.
- Deliverables: SOC 2 report, data handling playbook, deletion attestations.

Attachments I will share for the customer: redwood-soc2-report-2025.pdf (attestation), and a short tech note on "no-persist" toggles.

Laura Bennett
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
laura.bennett@redwood.com

title: Unexpected egress flip from EU to APAC during high-rate embedding batch causing P99 latency burst
text:
Issue summary: Customer observed a sudden P99 latency spike for small-batch embedding requests. During the window (~2026-03-12 09:15-09:35 UTC) requests that should have egressed in eu-west were routed to ap-southeast, adding ~220ms network RTT and causing downstream timeouts in their ingestion pipeline.

Impact: Production ingestion pipelines for Streamline Analytics degraded (10% request failures, 25% higher token latency). Affects users pinned to eu-west and using batch-embeds endpoint.

Environment: prod | eu-west (tenant: streamline-prod, customer-tier: enterprise)

Steps to reproduce: 
1) Send concurrent small-batch embedding calls (batch size 8, concurrency 40) to /v1/embeddings with tenant API key from EU.
2) Observe egress path in edge logs and p99 latency in Grafana.
3) Repeat during off-peak — issue appears correlated with higher control-plane heartbeat jitter.

Observed behavior: During burst, control-plane reports for tenant showed delayed residency stamp refresh; edge selected nearest healthy edge (ap-southeast) as fallback for some connections. TLS handshakes and auth token validation retried against APAC edges causing auth retries and additional latency.

Expected behavior: Requests from eu-west pinned tenants should egress through EU edges unless strict residency is unset or explicit fallback policy permits cross-region egress.

Logs/metrics referenced: grafana/dashboard/embeddings/tenant-streamline-p99 (snapshot attached in comments), edge-proxy logs (edge-eu-01, edge-eu-03), control-plane healthcheck timeline (2026-03-12T09:14:50 -> 2026-03-12T09:16:20). Slack thread: #support-streamline-212022

Temporary impact mitigation: Workaround applied to pin tenant to eu-central-edge pool to avoid dynamic fallback while we investigate.

2026-03-12 09:27 - Maya Patel (Support): Raised ticket after customer reported spike. Attached sample request IDs and Grafana p99 screenshot.
2026-03-12 09:33 - Alex Kim (SRE): Confirmed mixed egress paths in edge logs for token=tsk_streamline_prod_XXXX. Correlating with control-plane heartbeat lag for tenant stamp refresh.
2026-03-12 09:45 - Jamie Ortiz (Networking): Noticed DNS rebinds on eu-edge NATs around 09:15 that could have contributed to session reestablishment to nearest healthy edge.
2026-03-12 10:02 - Support (to customer): Temporary pin applied and connections restarted. Asking customer to validate. They reported immediate improvement to baseline latency around 10:10 UTC.
2026-03-12 15:20 - Alex Kim (SRE): Added preliminary investigation notes and created follow-up engineering task. See PR link in related_github_prs.
2026-03-13 08:05 - Customer (Streamline Analytics): Confirmed mitigation worked for now; asked for RCA and preventive measures.

Data collected: edge-proxy traces, control-plane residency refresh logs, DNS logs from eu-edge NAT cluster. Pattern: intermittent delay in control-plane TTL refresh for residency stamp (~35-90s) under high concurrent embed churn. During that window, edge token validation path falls back to 'nearest healthy edge' bucket which currently includes APAC edges by proximity metric when EU edges show transient auth timeouts. Hypothesis: a combination of DNS rebinds at NAT + control-plane heartbeat suppression triggers transient stamp expiry and fallback-routing. Reproduced in staging with synthetic churn at ~40 concurrent batch requests. Correlated with increased control-plane GC pauses in the same timeframe (GC activity in control-plane host cp-14).

Mitigation: Reapplied tenant strict pin to a dedicated eu-edge pool and performed graceful connection drain -> immediate latency return to baseline. Root cause: transient control-plane heartbeat lag combined with NAT/DNS rebinds allowed the residency stamp to be treated stale, which triggered fallback routing logic that selected APAC edges. Permanent fixes planned: 1) Increase control-plane heartbeat alerting and reduce stamp expiry threshold; 2) Harden fallback routing policy to prefer region affinity longer when stamp is near-expiry; 3) Network ops to investigate NAT/DNS rebind frequency and patch; 4) Deploy control-plane GC tuning PR (https://github.com/redwood-inference/control-plane/pull/9876). Follow-ups tracked in INT-451900 (engineering task) and SUP-742913 (similar customer case).

ENG: PR#9876 - GC tuning and heartbeat backoff (target release 2026-03-20)
NETOPS: Investigate NAT/DNS rebinds on eu-edge cluster (ticket INT-451901)
PLATFORM: Add residency-stamp-near-expiry metric and alert (runbook update)
CS: Share postmortem with customer and schedule 1:1 RCA call

title: Cobalt Brookline Analytics
author: Ethan Morales
text:
Primary: support virtual agent that answers product docs and tickets using embeddings + reranking. Secondary: internal doc search for product teams. Must support multi-tenant routing, region residency for EU customers, and maintain audit trail of inference requests. Latency SLOs target p95 < 800ms for chat, embeddings throughput ~200 req/s for nightly batch indexing. Will start on hosted API for quick validation then move to Dedicated/VPC for stability and compliance.

Account: mid-market analytics SaaS. Product: customer-facing search + support assistant. Started with hosted API trial (Jan) to validate embeddings quality and cost profile, now moving to Dedicated/VPC for predictable latency and data isolation. AE/Ethan running evaluation; SE Priya leading POC. CSM Liam looped for contract terms if we convert.

Key quote from CTO on 2026-01-12 demo call: "We need guaranteed isolation + audit trail before legal will sign — SOC2 plus SAML is non-negotiable."

POC summary: 2-week hosted POC validated KB embeddings and reranking quality (recall + precision acceptable). Next stage: 4-week Dedicated POC in customer VPC (Redwood Dedicated) to test autoscale, KV cache warm-start, and p95 latency under 50 concurrent chat sessions.

Security ask list (provided to Redwood 2026-01-20): SOC2 Type II report, SSO/SAML metadata exchange, audit log retention policy, KMS integration pattern, data residency confirmation for US-EAST and EU regions, deletion+retention controls for user data. Legal expects redlined contract with standard security addenda.

Procurement note: Budgeting ~ $120k-$180k ARR depending on committed capacity. CPO indicated willingness to sign annual commit if SLA meets p95 < 800ms for chat at target concurrency. Cost sensitivity: moderate; willing to trade slight cost for determinism (dedicated pools).

Internal flags: SE asked for quantized model guidance — which model/quantization profile hits p95 targets vs token cost. Priya requested a recommended config by 2026-02-11.

Stubs: Drive deck (pricing + POC runbook), Fireflies for demo + security walkthrough, Jira tickets for infra questions.

Planned Dedicated POC: 4 weeks. Goals: validate p95 latency under concurrency (50 users), verify KV cache warm-up, test model fallback behavior, run penetration test on VPC endpoints, validate audit log fidelity and retention policy (1 year). Deliverables: perf report, security evidence pack (SOC2 excerpt, SAML logs), cost projection for 12-month commit.

Legal/security requires: SOC2 Type II report (latest), SAML/SSO integration guide, audit log schema and retention controls, KMS integration approach (customer-managed keys preferred), data residency statement for EU region, and proof of physical access controls for Dedicated hardware. Customer requested an attested runbook for incident response and access revocation timeline.

Security sign-off pending (legal requires SOC2 + SAML + audit log retention policy)
Procurement Q3 budget window – needs approval by 2026-05
Clarify KMS/HSM integration and key ownership model
Region residency confirmation for EU customers in roadmap

1) Redwood to supply SOC2 evidence bundle + SAML metadata by 2026-02-11. 2) SE to deliver model/quantization recommendation and target config (Priya) by 2026-02-11. 3) Schedule Dedicated POC kickoff (tentative 2026-02-15) pending security sign-off. 4) Procurement to confirm budget and commit band by 2026-05.

Customer has enterprise customers in EU — data residency and auditability are driving the Dedicated requirement. They prefer minimal vendor lock-in; asked about exportable model snapshots and KV cache persistence. They are evaluating pricing against Anthropic/Vertex for committed capacity. Redwood's differentiation: clearer observability (token-level cost breakdown) and routing/fallback options were called out positively in demo.

2026-01-08: Intro discovery call (AE Ethan) — identified primary use-cases and data sensitivity
2026-01-12: Hosted API demo + Fireflies transcript — validated generation quality for support flows
2026-01-20: Security questionnaire submitted (customer) — SOC2 + SSO emphasized
2026-01-28: Tech deep-dive w/SE (Priya) on Dedicated architecture — discussed KV cache and autoscale
2026-02-02: Pricing refresh email from AE with committed capacity tiers — customer asked for example SLOs
2026-02-05: SAML test scheduling call; Priya to provide ADFS metadata

text:

Mariner wants a pilot scale test on Dedicated, clarity on billing anomalies, and security/compliance next steps. Agreed action items around benchmarks, pricing, and logs. Follow-up demo of Dedicated pool performance and a security packet scheduled.

recent uptime incidents and RCA
cost variance and token billing anomalies
dedicated vs hosted capacity tradeoffs
pilot benchmark plan and timeline
security and audit package for SOC2/SAML/KMS

Can Redwood guarantee latency SLOs for peak 95th pct?
How do quantization/packing recommendations impact cost vs accuracy?
What audit logs are available for on-prem/private deployments?

Mariner to share 3 canonical prompt sets and failure cases by 2026-12-01

Benchmarked 48h initial stress run agreed

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-27
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Luis (Redwood CSM), Priya (Mariner Head of Platform), Noah (Mariner CTO), Maya (Mariner SRE), Evan (Mariner Finance)

Auto-generated summary (may be rough): quick sync on cost spike last week, two short outages, ask for dedicated pilot, security pack request.

[00:00] Samira (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll run through the recent events and then jump to pilots and action items. hope that's ok.
[00:18] Priya (Mariner): yep thanks, appreciate you all squeezing this in. we had a customer incident last thursday, traffic surge plus a bad fallback, so want to make sure we don't see that again.
[00:32] Ethan (Redwood): yeah we saw the logs, we're pretty sure it was an autoscale handoff timing issue plus an index cache cold start. k v cash wasn't primed, essentially.
[00:45] Maya (Mariner): when you say k v cash do you mean the prefix cache? our engineers saw long tail token times.
[00:56] Ethan (Redwood): yeah prefix KV cache, sorry the transcript-ish, sometimes it's written as 'KV cash' in the logs. we had slower than expected warmup for long-context flows.
[01:10] Noah (Mariner): the main user impact was 2x latency and some 504s at peak for about 7 minutes. our SLAs with internal stakeholders hit alarms.
[01:25] Luis (Redwood CSM): we captured the runbook and the alerting timeline, we'll share that in the post-meeting notes.
[01:34] Evan (Mariner): also we saw a cost spike on the bill — line items for streaming tokens look higher than the token counts we expected, can you help explain?
[01:47] Samira (Redwood): yes that's important. we want to reconcile usage vs billing. there are a few levers: batching windows, streaming overhead, and model selection (quantization). possible double-counting on some retries.
[02:03] Priya: do you have any immediate fix? we can't have surprises for finance.
[02:07] Samira: short term, we can adjust client side timeouts and enable prefix caching aggressively; medium term, run a dedicated pool pilot to flatten tail.
[02:18] Maya: our security team also wants to know what logs we'd get if we moved to Private VPC or Dedicated, especially for audit and SSO.
[02:27] Ethan: for Dedicated and Private we offer audit logs, token-level traces, and KMS integration, but we'll share the exact schema. note that on some OOB hosted modes we redact a few fields for privacy.
[02:40] Noah: will that satisfy SOC2?
[02:43] Luis: in our experience yes, we provide the security pack, and customers combine that with their own controls. we have SAML SSO, RBAC, full retention policies. we'll send the SOC2 appendix.
[02:55] Priya: ok good. back to cost: Evan, any specific threshold you need?
[03:00] Evan: we need a projection for Q1 spend assuming two growth scenarios: conservative vs aggressive. we also want to know savings if we commit to reserved capacity.
[03:12] Samira: we'll model both. reserved capacity typically reduces per-token unit cost by 18-28% depending on burst profile and quantization level.
[03:23] Priya: what's the tradeoff for latency if we push heavier quantization? some of our NLP models need fidelity.
[03:31] Ethan: quant 4-bit gives big cost wins but can slightly change output characteristics; we recommend A/B testing on your canonical prompts. Redwood Optimize will run suggestions and we can tie quality regression alerts to your prompt set.
[03:48] Maya: I'd like to see examples of where quant changed outputs. can you share past evals?
[03:52] Ethan: yes, we'll share a small eval suite.
[03:55] Samira: proposed pilot — 2 weeks parallel run on a Dedicated pool sized for your 95th percentile, run streaming and batch workloads, capture latency P95/P99, KV hit rates, and cost per 1k tokens.
[04:10] Priya: timeline?
[04:13] Samira: kick off next week, run two weeks, deliver results the following week. so rough end date: benchmarks in by 2026-12-18.
[04:23] Noah: can we accelerate to 48 hours for a first pass?
[04:25] Ethan: yes we'll do an initial 48h stress run and then the longer soak. we'll share the 48h readout by 2026-12-08.
[04:36] Evan: make sure the cost calc ties to our billing export fields — we cross-check on our side.
[04:42] Luis: we'll include a billing mapping spreadsheet.
[04:46] Priya: on reliability — can Redwood do automatic fallback to smaller models or different region for graceful degradation? we want a soft degrade not full outage.
[04:57] Ethan: yes, routing policies can fallback to compatible model variants or region fallbacks; we also have automatic circuit breaker policies we can tune. note there are latency tradeoffs if you cross regions.
[05:12] Maya: what about cold-start mitigation? our production flows have long prefix tokens.
[05:18] Ethan: autoscale pre-warm and prefix prefetching are the two main levers. for long starters we can keep warmed replicas for known heavy prefixes.
[05:28] Priya: curious about telemetry — how granular are the traces?
[05:32] Luis: token-level timing, per-route histograms, and KV-hit metrics. we'll share a telemetry sample dashboard.
[05:40] [10m mark] Samira: quick recap — we'll run a 48h dedicated bench, Samira sends pricing, Mariner sends prompt set and logs.
[10:50] Priya: can you include a burst buffer option? during campaigns we have short spikes.
[10:54] Samira: yes burst capacity is configurable; we'll show pricing for reserve+burst vs pure on-demand.
[11:07] Evan: on the bill spike — can you identify retries that might have doubled token consumption?
[11:14] Ethan: we saw a spike caused by client retries plus streaming chunk re-encoding; we'll instrument and flag retried requests in the benchmark.
[11:27] Noah: one more item — feature flagging strategy; when we roll new models we want a canary that fails closed to lowest-cost path.
[11:37] Ethan: rollouts support canaries and A/B with automatic fallback; we can map traffic percentages and tie to quality metrics.
[11:48] Maya: please document the rollback windows and where the logs appear in our cloud console.
[11:54] Luis: will do.
[12:00] [20m mark] Samira: let's talk security checklist quickly — SAML, KMS, audit retention. what else do you need?
[12:08] Priya: encryption at rest for customer vectors, HSM for keys is preferred. and a red-team report if possible.
[12:17] Luis: we support KMS/HSM and will provide a compliance pack; red-team we can share high-level results, some details are confidential.
[12:26] Maya: retention windows — can logs be exported to our SIEM?
[12:29] Ethan: yes export to S3 or BigQuery and forward to SIEM, we have templates.
[12:35] Evan: ok finance will want the pricing workbook before we commit.
[12:39] Samira: we'll send two pricing scenarios.
[12:42] [30m mark] Priya: any known limitations in Dedicated for on-prem embedding workloads?
[12:50] Ethan: embeddings on Private can work but large vector stores will need tuning; latency vs cost tradeoff exists if you pin to on-prem. we'll share a design note.
[13:05] Priya: thanks. and for the pilot, who should be our main contact?
[13:08] Samira: Ethan for technical, Samira for commercial, Luis for onboarding.
[13:15] Noah: good. final ask — can Redwood run an emergency drill with our oncall to simulate a failover?
[13:23] Luis: yes we can coordinate a failover runbook exercise.
[13:29] Samira: action items recap in chat now. any other questions?
[13:35] Priya: none from me.
[13:38] Maya: no.
[13:40] Evan: no.
[13:42] Samira: great thanks everyone we'll follow up with the pricing and bench plan. bye.

END TRANSCRIPT

title: KV cache ghost refcount decay detection, snapshot sanitization, and rolling-heal playbook
author: Ava Patel
text:
Summary: During a capacity surge on 2025-11-08 we observed a slow but persistent memory growth on several serving nodes which culminated in degraded tail latency and two short-lived OOMs. Investigation showed a new class of 'ghost' entries in the KV prefix cache: entries whose refcount had decayed below zero (underflow) due to an interaction between async compaction, prefetch migration, and a recent refcount optimization. These ghost entries never surfaced as normal cache misses and therefore were not collected by the existing eviction heuristics, leading to gradual slab exhaustion on hot shards. This ticket captures detection heuristics, an emergency snapshot sanitization runbook, a staged rolling-heal design (scheduled drains + isolated snapshot rewrite), telemetry improvements, and a rollout/verification plan.

Memory growth first seen 2025-11-06, customer latency degradation at p95/p99 experienced across dedicated and hosted clusters on 2025-11-08. Two nodes hit transient OOMs and auto-recovered (restarts). No persistent data loss; customer requests were served with fallbacks but experienced elevated errors and higher per-token latency. Estimated affected capacity 8% of serving fleet during surge window.

Concurrency bug: an optimization in the refcount update path batched decrement operations to reduce atomic ops. Under a race where async compaction rewrites slab bitmaps concurrently with prefetch migrators moving KV records across buckets, the batched decrement could be applied twice for the same logical record. This produced negative refcounts and left entries in an invisible 'ghost' state that bypassed eviction score updates. Compaction also left behind partial tombstone metadata which confused the slab reclaim heuristics.

A1: Emergency snapshot sanitization script - implement and run a conservative scanner to detect negative refcounts and mark entries for reclamation. Owner: Marcus Li. Due: 2025-11-18.
A2: Prefetch/refcount critical section rewrite - ensure decrement operations are idempotent and move batched application under compaction locks. Owner: Priya Nair. Due: 2025-11-22.
A3: Scheduled rolling-heal plan - implement scheduled small drains (10-15min) per shard during off-peak for 2 weeks to allow safe slab rewrite without customer-impacting restarts. Owner: SRE Team (lead: Daniel Kim). Due: 2025-11-26.
A4: Eviction heuristics patch - add ghost-detection heuristic: treat entries with refcount < 0 or missing eviction timestamp as high-priority reclamation candidates. Owner: Elena Garcia. Due: 2025-12-02.
A5: Telemetry expansion - emit refcount histograms, negative-refcount counter, slab-fragmentation gauge, and open traces when a snapshot sanitization runs. Owner: Observability (lead: Omar Hassan). Due: 2025-11-20.
A6: End-to-end test harness - add a fault-injection test that simulates compaction/prefetch races and validates snapshot sanitizer removes ghosts without losing live entries. Owner: QA (lead: Mei Chen). Due: 2025-12-05.
A7: Post-rollout review and automation - automate periodic snapshot sanitization in maintenance windows and add alerting when negative-refcount rate > 0 over 10m. Owner: Marcus Li. Due: 2025-12-12.
A8: Documentation - update runbooks and run the incident playbook with SRE for on-call run-through. Owner: SRE runbooks (lead: Priya Nair). Due: 2025-11-30.

Add metric: kvcache.refcount.negative.count (counter) - increment every time sanitizer detects a negative refcount
Add gauge: kvcache.slab.fragmentation_pct (percent) - updated on compaction completion
Add histogram: kvcache.eviction.latency_ms - measure time from detection -> reclaimed
Trace: attach sanitizer-run-id to traces and correlate with allocation spikes (link to dashboard)
Alert: create kvcache_negative_refcount_rate > 0 for 10m -> P1 alert to oncall

Stage 0 (canary): run snapshot sanitization in read-only mode against one non-production fleet to validate detection (no reclamation). Owner: Marcus Li. Window: 2025-11-18 02:00-04:00 UTC.
Stage 1 (pilot): run sanitizer in reclamation mode on 5% of low-traffic shards with automated validation and crash-safe checkpoints. Monitor memory, latency, errors. Rollback if p99 latency increases > 15% or error rate > 2x baseline. Window: 2025-11-19.
Stage 2 (gradual): start scheduled rolling-heal drains: drain 3% of shards every 30m during off-peak, run sanitization, and bring back. Target fleet complete in 72h. Abort conditions: OOMs, persistent error spikes, or eviction backlog growth. Owner: SRE.
Stage 3 (global): deploy refcount idempotency and eviction heuristic patches with canary traffic gating then full roll. Tie to runtime-1.21 release and monitor for 7 days.

Post-sanitization memory regression test against replayed workload for 48h
No new negative-refcount increments in metrics for 72h after full rollout
p50/p95/p99 latency at or below pre-incident baseline within 2% for 7 days
Run the fault-injection harness in CI and require green before merging patches

Confluence runbook draft: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/KVCache+Sanitization+Playbook (internal)
PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/9187 - sanitizer implementation (draft)
PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/9210 - refcount idempotency and lock rework
Dashboard: https://dashboards.redwood.ai/d/kvcache/ghost-refcount-ops - key charts for verification
Related historical ticket: ENG-527890 for eviction backpressure playbook
Decision: We prioritize in-place sanitization + scheduled draining over full fleet restart to minimize customer impact. Agreed 2025-11-13 in incident follow-up meeting by eng + SRE + PM.
Follow-up meeting scheduled: 2025-11-27 16:00 UTC (post canary review).

title: Dedicated capacity options and phased activation proposal
author: sofia_ivanova
text:
From: Sofia Ivanova <sofia.ivanova@redwood.ai>
To: Elaine Wong <elaine.wong@meridiantx.com>, Dr. Aaron Patel <aaron.patel@meridiantx.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-05-19T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Dedicated capacity options and phased activation proposal

Hi Elaine / Aaron,

Thanks again for the time today — great to hear more about Meridian's inference profile and the 24/7 clinical batch inference windows you expect in Q4. Attached is a short set of dedicated capacity options that map to the throughput and availability targets we discussed. I've summarized three pragmatic paths below so you can pick the shape that best fits procurement and risk appetite.

Attachment: dedicated-offer_v2.pdf (PDF, 2 pages)
Attachment: capacity-lane-diagram.png (PNG, 1 image)

Options (high level)
1) Baseline Guard (cost-focused)
 - Cluster: 16x A100-equivalent GPUs (mixed T4/RTX for warm lanes)
 - Minimum guaranteed GPUs: 8 (business-hours baseline)
 - Ramp: 8 -> 12 (30 days) -> 16 (60 days)
 - Safety buffer: 10% burst pool for scheduled windows
 - Notes: best unit-cost; acceptable for non-latency-critical batch jobs.

2) Anchored SLA (balanced)
 - Cluster: 32x A100-equivalent GPUs (homogeneous fleet)
 - Minimum guaranteed GPUs: 16 (always available)
 - Ramp: 16 -> 24 (30 days) -> 32 (90 days)
 - Safety buffer: geo-fallback lanes (regional failover) + warm cache prefill
 - Notes: predictable tail latency targets, recommended for mixed real-time + batch workloads.

3) Burst-Ready (latency-first)
 - Cluster: 48x A100-equivalent GPUs (reserved + burst capacity)
 - Minimum guaranteed GPUs: 24 (business peak)
 - Ramp: 24 -> 36 (30 days) -> 48 (120 days) with two incremental activation waves
 - Safety buffer: hot standby pods for sub-second failover
 - Notes: higher cost but preserves 99.9th % latency SLOs under unpredictable load.

Operational considerations and tradeoffs
- Warmup: full KV-cache warmup for the 48-GPU configuration takes ~36 hours; incremental waves reduce customer-facing risk.
- Quantization profiles: we can recommend an 8-bit quantized variant for non-critical workloads to reduce effective GPU footprint by ~25% — Karthik has the bench numbers and I'll loop him for a detailed chart.
- Billing: reserved capacity monthly commit with credits for unused burst hours; details in the attached PDF.

Suggested next steps
- You pick preferred path (Baseline / Anchored / Burst-Ready) and target SLA (standard / extended).
- We propose a 30-day canary on the first ramp wave for field validation (small production traffic + dedicated tracing).
- We'll issue an updated DocuSign with the chosen option and a 30-day signature window to lock capacity.

Can you let us know which path you want us to flesh out by end of week? If you prefer, we can hop on a short call to walk through tradeoffs.

Best,
Sofia Ivanova
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
sofia.ivanova@redwood.ai | +1 (415) 555-0182
Redwood Inference

Hi Sofia — thanks for the clear options and the attachments. Helpful. A couple of quick clarifications before we review internally with procurement: 

1) For the Anchored SLA option, does the "geo-fallback lanes" imply cross-region replicas that we pay for as reserved capacity, or are those burst-only (pay-as-you-go) nodes?
2) What do you recommend for the minimum during business hours if our nightly batch spikes to 300k tokens/min for 2 hours — do we size to the spike or rely on burst windows?
3) Procurement is asking that any reserved capacity be cancellable with a 60-day ramp-down clause after quarter renewal; will that be reflected in the contract?

We like the idea of a 30-day canary. Also, our technical lead Dr. Patel asked whether you can document estimated warmup costs (in token-hours) for each wave so we can include them in our run-rate model.

Elaine
Elaine Wong
VP Product Operations, Meridian Therapeutics
elaine.wong@meridiantx.com | +1 (617) 555-0124

On 5/19/26 09:12, Sofia Ivanova wrote:
> [original message attached]

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
To: Elaine Wong <elaine.wong@meridiantx.com>, Sofia Ivanova <sofia.ivanova@redwood.ai>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-05-20T08:47:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity options and phased activation proposal

Hi Elaine, Sofia — quick technical clarification and a concrete proposal for Dr. Patel's warmup question.

Geo-fallback lane model
- We can provide geo-fallback as reserved hot-standby replicas (counted against committed capacity) or as on-demand burst nodes. For predictable failover and SLA-backed RTOs I recommend reserving a small standby fleet (4–6 GPUs) in a secondary region — this keeps failover time <120s. If you prefer not to reserve, on-demand nodes are possible but add variability in failover and cost.

Warmup and token-hour estimate (rough)
- Baseline Guard (16 GPUs): full prefix/KV warmup ~8 GPU-hours (prefill small KV sets) -> estimated 12,000 token-hours of work at an average token-rate of 1.5k tokens/min per GPU during warmup.
- Anchored SLA (32 GPUs): incremental warmup per wave ~18 GPU-hours -> estimated 45,000 token-hours.
- Burst-Ready (48 GPUs): cold-to-hot activation ~36 GPU-hours; if we prefill caches ahead of traffic, we reduce effective warmup to ~12 GPU-hours but that requires reserved burst windows + scheduled prefill calls.

Quantization tradeoff (cost impact)
- Using an 8-bit profile for non-critical batch scoring reduces GPU-dwell by ~20–30% on average. That can drop the effective committed GPU count for Baseline by 2–3 GPUs. Procurement flexibility

title: Cerulean Support Networks
author: Maya Santos
text:
Summary: Cerulean is a B2B contact center operator (outsourced support across retail + fintech customers). They need a Dedicated deployment to guarantee 24/7 capacity for agent-assist and automatic ticket summarization. Primary driver is reliability during spikes (seasonal retail peaks + fintech month-ends) and strict data residency for EU/US customers.

Key requirements / quotes: 
- "We cannot have agent context timeouts when volume jumps — must have reserved throughput and predictable fallbacks." — Head of Support Ops (R. Delgado)
- 2000 concurrent active agents at peak, target p95 latency <120-200ms for streaming suggestions, sustained throughput budgeted ~40k-70k inference requests/minute (mix of short prompts + long wrap-up generations).
- Need isolated capacity (VPC) with explicit burst policy: baseline reserved QPS with ability to burst 2-3x for 30-60 min windows.
- Use cases: real-time agent suggestions (inline in Zendesk), end-of-interaction ticket summarization (concise, 3-line TL;DR + suggested tags), tool-calling to trigger ticket escalations / CRM field updates, automated quick-replies for chat channels.
- Integration: Zendesk + Salesforce connectors required; plan to swap to SFDC-case routing for enterprise customers.
- Metrics for acceptance: p95 latency under 200ms for agent-assist, fallback rate <1%, summarization F1 against human references >0.82, cost per 1k requests within agreed threshold.
- Security/compliance: SSO/SAML (Okta), SOC2 type II, audit logging with 12-month retention, KMS-managed keys, fine-grained retention controls per customer region. Legal insists on subprocessor list and right-to-audit clause.
- Observability needs: token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency dashboards, root-cause traces for spike incidents. Must integrate with their SRE PagerDuty rota.

POC notes and findings: 
- Pilot exposed two issues: 1) short KV cache TTL causing repeated context tokenization; recommended caching config reduced token cost by 22% during pilot. 2) morning shift spike (09:00–10:00 PST) produced throttling on shared pool — motivates Dedicated reserved capacity.
- SE recommendation: Dedicated pool with autoscale disabled for baseline + scheduled burst windows; pre-warm KV caches and enable prefix caching for common templates.

Commercial / timeline: 
- Procurement aiming to sign for Q2 2025 (forecast 2025-03).
- Estimated ARR ask for proposal: $250k–$750k depending on burst SLA and on-prem connector.

Stubs / links: Fireflies ff_20241211_2b7c9d (pilot kickoff), drive deck link above, thread th_1f8a2b3c4d_20241215 (security thread).

title: Runner service account token exfiltration alert: rotate tokens and validate CI access paths
text:
Issue summary:
Security monitoring flagged potential exfiltration of a long-lived service token tied to a fleet of ephemeral CI runners. Alert originated from log anomaly: identical token used from two distinct datacenter IP ranges within a 5 minute window. Impact: potential unauthorized access to private repositories and deployments; immediate mitigation required for release pipelines scheduled tonight.

Impact:
- Nightly release pipelines (release-nightly) and a handful of ad-hoc build jobs are at risk of unauthorized usage.
- No confirmed production changes yet, but token reuse pattern suggests credential may be leaked to an external CI job runner.

Environment:
- prod control plane, primary runner pool in us-east-1, ephemeral runners launched via autoscaler with service-account tokens minted by internal token-service.

Steps to reproduce / observed sequence:
1) 2026-03-13T18:02Z: Security alert (Evidently: auth-anomaly-20260313-17) flagged token XXXXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX used from IP A and B.
2) Investigated runner logs: token XXXXXX appears in runner bootstrap logs for runner-id r-3487 and r-3491.
3) Token issuance log shows token minted by token-service for service-account ci-ephemeral-deployer at 2026-03-13T17:58Z with TTL 24h.
4) Access patterns include git fetch and artifact upload attempts to s3-bucket "ci-artifacts-prod".

Immediate requests:
- Rotate all active tokens for service-account ci-ephemeral-deployer and issue short-lived replacements (1h TTL) for any upcoming scheduled jobs.
- Block any outstanding runner sessions that present the old token.
- Audit artifact uploads and git pushes between 2026-03-13T17:50Z and 2026-03-13T18:20Z.

Timeline and hypotheses:
- 2026-03-13T17:58Z token minted by token-service (log id ts-98231).
- 2026-03-13T18:02Z security alert for token reuse from multiple geo-ip blocks.
- Hypothesis A: token printed into a job log or artifact and then scraped by a scanning service or malicious actor.
- Hypothesis B: compromised runner bootstrap image contained a hardcoded token (unlikely, but check image digest).
- Hypothesis C: token-service issued a duplicate due to race and same token reused on two runners (race condition in token-service code).
Findings so far:
- Runner bootstrap scripts do not print tokens intentionally; however, one community script in customer templates folder was discovered in an older job that echoed env on error (CI job id 77312).
- Image digests for r-3487 and r-3491 match the current official ephemeral-runner image: sha256:fdc9..., no unauthorized modifications.
- Token-service code review shows a retry path that can return the same token if request ID deduplication occurs; engineering hypothesis plausible.
Logs & evidence locations:
- token-service logs: /var/logs/token-service/ts-2026-03-13.log (search ts-98231)
- runner audit: gs://redwood-ci-logs/runner/audit/2026/03/13/
- security alert: SIEM event auth-anomaly-20260313-17 (Slack #sec-alert archived thread)

Ava Martinez (reporter) 2026-03-13: Raised after SOC flagged token reuse; requesting immediate token rotation and kill of affected runners.
Samuel Cheng (assignee) 2026-03-13: Acknowledged. Initiating emergency rotation for ci-ephemeral-deployer; will create short TTL tokens for scheduled jobs. Requesting SRE to isolate runner pool.
Lena Ortiz (SRE) 2026-03-13: Isolating runner subnet and revoking existing tokens at the gateway level. Patching autoscaler to stop spawning new ephemeral runners from that SA until rotation completes.
Morgan Patel (Security) 2026-03-14: Found one suspicious artifact upload attempt; quarantine copy saved to secure bucket for forensic analysis. Suggest scanning artifacts for leaked secrets and checking access logs for third-party IPs.
Samuel Cheng 2026-03-14: Short-lived tokens issued (1h TTL) and deployed to release-nightly job definitions. Documented mitigation in runbook and linked a follow-up engineering ticket to fix token-service dedupe retry path.

Mitigation steps executed 2026-03-14:
1) Revoked all active tokens for service-account ci-ephemeral-deployer in Vault and invalidated tokens at the gateway layer.
2) Issued new short-lived tokens (1h) and patched CI job definitions for release-nightly and related pipelines.
3) Quarantined suspicious artifact and initiated forensic scan.
4) SRE temporarily drained and reprovisioned the affected runner pool with fresh images.
5) Created follow-up engineering ticket INT-738211 to implement token-service fix (prevent duplicate token issuance under retry) and another task INT-738212 to add automated token-leak detection on artifact uploads.
Post-mortem/next steps:
- Engineering to harden token-service by 2026-03-20 and add extra logging for request IDs.
- CI config update to set default TTL for ephemeral tokens to 1h.
- Add a pre-flight check to runner bootstrap to redact env prints and fail if dangerous debug flags are present.
- Security to run backward scan for other service-accounts to ensure no further exposures.
Status: mitigations completed; further engineering work scheduled.
