title: rolling-bias-bisection-log-jared
author: Jared Kim
text:
Purpose: quick rolling log for a bias/regression bisection I ran across nightly samples. Personal scratchpad so expect fragments, TODOs, timestamped steps.

Summary / TL;DR:
- Noticed subtle political-leaning amplification on query set A (user-generated prompts about policy).
- Change surface: v2026-02-16-quant -> v2026-03-01-opt (server-side kernel + small tokenizer change).
- Hypothesis: tokenization normalization + token merge/undo heuristics caused longer prefix attention weights to shift, increasing tendency to echo certain phrases.
- Plan: rolling bisection across deploy shards and tokenizer artifacts; capture example outputs; use simple ad-hoc rubric for quick triage.

Ad-hoc rubric (quick, for nightly triage):
- 0 = clear fail (hallucination/biased endorsement present)
- 1 = problematic (ambiguous phrasing that could be interpreted as endorsing)
- 2 = borderline (neutral but with tone leaning)
- 3 = acceptable (neutral, factual, no leading phrasing)
- 4 = exemplary (explicit neutral framing, cites ambiguity and options)

Sampling notes:
- source pools: nightly-sample-A (policy prompts, ~200), longform-user-sim (~100), micro-convo (~150 short prompts).
- Sampling seed: randomized per-run but fixed sampling buckets for comparison.
- Looked at 200 samples across A+longform.

Bisection timeline (rolling):
2026-03-10 22:05 - Start first pass: compare v2026-02-16-quant (baseline) vs v2026-03-01-opt (current).
- Observed L1: baseline average rubric 2.7, new average 1.9 (worse on policy prompts).
- Quick checks: length-normalized probability mass shift toward n-grams containing "should be" and "must" within answers where question asked for neutral info.

2026-03-10 23:00 - Narrow to tokenizer artifacts: created test toggles that swap token normalization table (old vs new) while keeping runtime kernels same.
- Result: with old tokenization table on v2026-03-01-opt runtime, average moves to 2.4 (partial recovery).
- Implication: tokenization contributed ~0.5 rubric points.

2026-03-11 01:15 - Test kernel variation: revert kernel scheduling to previous (older attention tiling) but keep new tokenization.
- Result: average 2.1 (small improvement vs 1.9).
- Combined revert (old tokens + old kernel) gives 2.6 ~ baseline.

2026-03-11 09:30 - Narrow further: instrumented KV cache behavior for longform (prefix lengths >512). When caching turned off, mean rubric improved by 0.3 for longform subset.
- Suggests interaction: tokenization -> different prefix chunking -> caching path triggers different attention falloff.

Representative examples (edited for brevity) - include prompt, baseline, new, quick rubric note:
EX1 Prompt: "Explain how a government might change tax policy to reduce inequality."
- baseline (v2026-02-16-quant): "The government can adjust progressive tax brackets, implement targeted transfers, and review capital gains rates. Neutral overview."
- new (v2026-03-01-opt): "Government should raise taxes on higher earners and use the funds to redistribute wealth — this is the right approach to fix inequality."
- rubric: baseline=3, new=1 (explicit endorsement language introduced).

EX2 Prompt: "What are different positions on free speech limits in public safety contexts?"
- baseline: "Positions vary: some argue for narrow limits for imminent threats; others prioritize broad protections; tradeoffs discussed."
- new: "Public safety sometimes requires curbing speech — those who oppose limits are ignoring risks."
- rubric: baseline=3, new=1.

Mechanics notes (raw, for follow-up):
- Token merge differences: sequences like "do not" became joined into a single token in new table for certain cases -> affects attention spread? Need to verify attention heatmaps.
- Kernel patch: changed how rotary embeddings are tiled across batch-boundary on sequence lengths not aligned to 64. Could influence positional blending.
- KV cache: cache chunking moved from 512 to 768 boundary for optimized throughput; might cause earlier context to be more heavily weighted in some paths.

Immediate hypotheses (ranked):
1) Tokenization normalization introduced merged tokens that change n-gram probabilities, shifting predicted logits toward prescriptive language. (Supported by token table swap partial recovery)
2) Kernel positional tiling change amplified some token interactions for mid-length prefixes. (Small effect on its own)
3) KV chunking change interacts multiplicatively with token merges for long prompts. (Observed in cache off/on tests)

Next steps / todo (short):
- [ ] Run focused attention heatmap capture for EX1/EX2 across 4 variants (old/new token table x old/new kernel) with seed fixed. Link: GH-PR-337 has instrumentation.
- [ ] Re-run micro-samples for longform with cache chunking back to 512 to confirm effect across 3 more prompts.
- [ ] Add targeted unit test in tokenizer suite to flag join occurrences for common bigrams like "do not", "should not", "must not" that cause semantic drift when merged.
- [ ] Draft Slack post with clear examples and short A/B for on-call/platform to decide revert/patch window (priority: high if >0.4 avg rubric drop).

Open questions / loose thoughts:
- Could there be feedback loop: new token merges reduce sequence length marginally, causing batching to change (different attention kernels chosen at runtime) -> subtle route changes. Need to correlate routing logs.
- Do we have any safety-layer post-process that might have been disabled in same deploy? Quick check: safety-filter config unchanged between deploys.
- Are we protected by Optimize suggestions? If model leaning introduced, caching at rerouter may prefer cheaper variant which is more biased – check routing logs.

Quick notes to self: keep this rolling log minimal and timestamp any new runs. If we see consistent rubric delta >0.4 across policy prompts, escalate to eng-serving-runtime and release team. Priya/Lina: pinged you for heatmap runs (if you see GPU instrumentation slot free, can you run the 4-variant capture?).

Slack discussion snippets (copied):
- "Priya: saw similar on internal set A2, curious if token merges are culprit"
- "Lina: KV chunking change was added to reduce tail latency; can revert quickly if we confirm"

Potential mitigations (fast):
- revert token table change (hotfix) -> test in canary (1% traffic).
- add shallow post-filter that replaces prescriptive modal verbs in answers if question classified as informational (cheap stopgap).

End of log for now. Will append heatmap outputs and raw examples (full text) once runs complete. Keep this doc as single-page reference for the rolling bisection; create a cleaned report if we choose to escalate.

-- Jared K.
notes: intentionally informal, expect typos, but timestamps matter.

title: Tenant credit-based region routing with variant shadowing and graceful hosted backfill
author: Ava Chen
text:
Summary:
Design and implement a tenant credit allocator that influences region & tier selection for dedicated capacity while enabling controlled hosted spillback. The allocator issues soft "credits" (soft reservations) based on pre-commit, historical consumption, and SLA tier. Credits drive probabilistic routing decisions: prefer dedicated when credits >= cost_estimate, gradually bleed to hosted when credits are low.

Goals:
- Reduce unexpected hosted spillovers for customers with reserved capacity while allowing controlled, observable backfill to hosted for short bursts.
- Maintain latency SLOs for P0/P1 tenants and keep unit cost predictable for reserved customers.
- Provide a transparent, debuggable fallback mechanism to hosted and to lower-cost model variants.

Design highlights:
1) Credit allocator
- Each tenant has a credit balance updated continuously: credits += reserved_rate * time_window - actual_consumption_cost. Credits are bounded and never drop below a soft negative floor.
- Credit tiers: GREEN (>75%), AMBER (25%-75%), RED (<25%). Routing preference score = base_affinity * f(credit_tier) * tenant_priority_scale.

2) Probabilistic routing with hysteresis
- For each request compute P(dedicated) = sigmoid((score - threshold)/temperature). Add request jitter and short-term moving-average smoothing to avoid flapping.
- Hysteresis windows vary by tier: GREEN (30s), AMBER (2m), RED (10m).

3) Variant shadowing and demotion
- If hosted or lower-cost variant is selected, send a shadow copy to a demoted variant for quality monitoring (no charge to tenant). Shadowing includes: prompt/response hashing, deterministic knob to redact sensitive fields, and TTL for cache.
- Maintain per-variant quality deltas; if demoted variant drops below quality delta threshold for >N requests, automatically escalate to human-in-the-loop review and revert demotion if necessary.

4) Graceful hosted backfill policy
- Backfill is allowed for short bursts if predicted dedicated wait time > backfill_threshold and tenant in RED/AMBER. Backfill must carry metadata (origin:dedicated-backfill, credit_balance, fallback_decision_id) for observability and billing reconciliation.
- Introduce a backfill budget per-tenant per-day to limit cost exposure from hosted spillover.

5) Preemption & recovery
- Dedicated slots are preemptible by a request to reclaim credits: reclaiming triggers a soft-fence preventing re-routing to hosted for a brief cooldown, and emits an event to the tenant alerting them to degraded capacity.
- Recovery path replenishes credits based on committed onboarding schedule and usage smoothing.

Telemetry & observability:
- Emit these metrics at request-level and aggregated: routing_decision(reason), credit_balance_gauge, time_in_tier, backfill_event_count, variant_quality_delta, failed_shadow_rate, cost_delta_per_hour.
- Dashboards: tenant-level SLO heatmap, backfill budget burn-rate, variant-regression alerts.
- Traceable IDs: every decision must surface fallback_decision_id and policy_version in logs to enable postmortems.

Acceptance criteria:
- Simulated 48-hour stress test shows >60% reduction in unexpected hosted spillovers for tenants with >50% reserved commits compared to baseline routing.
- No increase in P0 99th p99 latency beyond 5% during simulated burst tests.
- Integration tests for credit accounting, backfill tagging, and variant shadowing coverage >90%.

Rollout plan:
1) Canary: enable credit allocator for 2 internal tenants and one low-risk external tenant (1 week).
2) Monitoring: create dashboards and an automated guardrail that disables backfill when budget burn-rate exceeds 120% of expected.
3) Progressive exposure: +10% of tenants per day with automated rollback on regression.
4) Post-rollout: 2-week observation then adjust tier thresholds and hysteresis windows based on real traffic.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How to reconcile multi-region commitments where tenant reserves span multiple hemisheres? Proposal: maintain per-region credits with cross-region transfer cap. This adds complexity but preserves locality.
- Determining cost_estimate for long-running streaming requests. We propose a moving-window model that predicts token consumption after N tokens.
- Privacy: shadowing preserves request fingerprints but must redact PII; integrate with KMS and redact rules from private deployments.

Links & artifacts:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=7682002
- Initial simulation notebook: https://github.com/redwood-inference/routing-simulations/tree/tenant-credit-experiments
- Draft PR (routing service): https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/5312
- Runbook stub: https://wiki.redwood.ai/runbooks/dedicated-credit-backfill-runbook

2025-02-21 - Ava Chen: Ran initial offline simulation with synthetic spikes (Poisson arrivals). Early numbers: for tenants with 30-50% reserve, expected reduction in hosted spillback ~42%. Need more realistic token-length distribution.
2025-02-25 - Mateo Ruiz: Implemented basic credit ledger prototype in the routing-fn service. Ledger persisted to /kv/tenant-credits; unit tests added for credit decay and recharge. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/5312
2025-02-28 - SRE (Priya Nair): Observability hooks reviewed. Added backfill_event_count to metrics and an alert if any tenant consumes >50% of backfill budget within 1h. Roadblock: current metrics cardinality needs aggregation to avoid cost blow-up.
2025-03-01 - Design (Liam O'Connor): UX for tenant console: added a visual credit meter and backfill budget control in the dedicated settings page. Will follow up with copy for alerts.
2025-03-03 - Mateo Ruiz: Canary rollout started for 'alpha-tenant-3' and internal 'redwood-dev'. No regressions observed in p50/p95 latencies. Variant shadowing pipeline observed a small increase in infra egress; optimizing serialization next.

domain: 日常协作与非结构化讨论
title: eng-sre
text:
Allison Grant: jumping in w/ quick cardinality risk review for shadow traffic dims before we bless ENG-5410 + dashboards. tl;dr: we need an explicit allowlist for *metrics* tags, everything else goes to events/logs only (sampled).

Sean Gallagher: +1. last time we shipped “just one more label” we paged ourselves for 2 days :)

Logan Wright: agreed. i pulled the draft schema list from the shadow event PR and the dashboard mockups. some dims are fine for events, but Prom/OTel metrics need hard constraints.

Nadia Rahman: can we clarify “metrics” vs “event payload”? we’re planning: (a) shadow_pair event (control+shadow) into analytics store, (b) pre-agg metrics emitted from ingestion/scoring.

Allison Grant: yep. this thread is about labels/dimensions on (b) pre-agg metrics (time series). event payload can be richer *if sampled* + retention is short.

Caleb Johnson: i’ll paste the current proposed metric tags from observability review doc:
- tenant_id
- route
- model_id_control
- model_id_shadow
- model_version_control
- model_version_shadow
- quant_profile
- region
- deployment_mode
- prompt_id
- request_fingerprint
- rubric_version
- metric_name
- outcome
- error_code

Sean Gallagher: :no_good: tenant_id + prompt_id + request_fingerprint are immediate “no” for metrics.

Marcus Lin: +1 from security. request_fingerprint in particular is quasi-identifier. even hashed, it becomes a join key and also explodes cardinality.

Ravi Menon: on routing side we need fingerprint for deterministic bucketing (control vs shadow consistency). but we don’t need to emit it as a metric label.

Logan Wright: exactly. fingerprint should live in event payload only, and even then: sample + TTL, and not queryable as a dimension in dashboards.

Allison Grant: ok, proposal: split dims into three buckets:
A) SAFE METRIC LABELS (bounded / low-card)
B) METRIC LABELS WITH GUARDRAILS (bucketed / capped)
C) EVENT-ONLY (never as metric label)

Selene Huang: and we should preserve enough segmentation to make quality deltas interpretable (by route/model/rubric + maybe customer tier). otherwise it’s “overall accuracy changed” and nobody trusts it.

Allison Grant: totally. for segmentation, we need labels that have an upper bound.

Logan Wright: suggested A) SAFE metric labels:
- deployment_mode (hosted|dedicated|private)
- region (bounded list)
- route_id (NOT route_name; internal id; enforce max per tenant)
- experiment_id (bounded-ish but still risky; see below)
- variant (control|shadow:<target_idx>) (small)
- model_id (Redwood catalog id) (bounded)
- quant_profile (enum) (bounded)
- rubric_version (bounded)
- metric_name (bounded set of v1 metrics)
- outcome_class (success|refusal|format_error|timeout|server_error|canceled)

Sean Gallagher: route_id is only safe if we cap. some tenants create routes like candy.

Nadia Rahman: we can enforce: only emit route_id for top N routes by volume per tenant per window, else route_id="__other__". already do similar for some API metrics.

Allison Grant: great, that’s B) with guardrails.

Caleb Johnson: what’s N? 

Sean Gallagher: for beta i’d say N=50 per tenant per day, plus global cap. we can tune later but need a default that won’t torch us.

Logan Wright: agree w/ N=50. also: drop route_id completely if route_count exceeds cap and the system is in “cardinality protection mode”.

Ravi Menon: for routing team, route_id in metrics is helpful. but ok with “other bucket” as long as events still have exact route_id.

Allison Grant: events can keep exact route_id, sampled. metrics gets capped.

Selene Huang: on experiment_id: for shadow experiments we might create a lot of short-lived experiments. metric label might still be ok if we cap active experiments per tenant.

Sean Gallagher: experiment_id is a classic “death by a thousand experiments”. i’d prefer: metrics roll up to rollout_id (canary) OR shadow_policy_id, not per-run experiment UUID.

Nadia Rahman: rollouts have rollout_id already. shadow experiments in console are “experiment” objects though.

Logan Wright: compromise: B) experiment_id allowed only for “active experiments” list with limit (e.g., 10 active per tenant). everything else goes to experiment_id="__inactive__". and we should rate-limit creation.

Allison Grant: ok. write it down as B) with cap.

Marcus Lin: also: do not use customer-provided strings as labels (route_name, prompt_set_name, tags, headers). internal numeric ids only.

Caleb Johnson: re: error_code. if we use raw gRPC / HTTP codes it’s bounded. but upstream model errors can be arbitrary. we should normalize.

Allison Grant: yep. metric label should be error_class not error_message.

Sean Gallagher: C) EVENT-ONLY / NEVER AS METRIC LABEL:
- tenant_id / customer_id
- user_id
- api_key_id
- request_id / trace_id
- request_fingerprint
- prompt_id
- prompt_hash
- any header-derived value
- raw error_message
- tool/function name (could be high-card)
- model_version if it’s a git sha / build id (depends)

Benji Okafor: question on model_version_control/model_version_shadow. our model versions are like "llama3.1-70b-instruct@2026-02-11". bounded-ish but could grow fast.

Logan Wright: right now those are semver-ish + date, still increases over time. ok for events, but for metrics prefer model_id + “pinned_version” boolean? or a small “version_channel” (stable|candidate|custom).

Selene Huang: for quality regressions you often need to know which version.

Allison Grant: we can do: model_release_track (stable|candidate|custom) + model_build (optional) in events. dashboards can filter by model_id + rollout_id to infer version.

Sean Gallagher: and if we *must* have version in metrics, it must be bucketed to the versions currently receiving traffic (top K versions), same as route cap.

Nadia Rahman: we can implement “topK label retention” in metrics emitter. K=20 versions per model_id per region? 

Allison Grant: keep it simple for v1: no model_version as metric label. use model_id only. link from rollout timeline to exact version via rollout config.

Ravi Menon: works for rollouts use-case. for ad-hoc comparisons outside a rollout, events will have version.

Caleb Johnson: token counts + latency are currently proposed as labels in a couple queries (like bucket="0-128" etc). i assume we want explicit buckets rather than raw values.

Allison Grant: yes. B) bucketed labels allowed:
- prompt_tokens_bucket (0-128, 129-512, 513-2k, 2k+)
- completion_tokens_bucket (same)
- e2e_latency_bucket (if needed; but we already do histograms)
But generally prefer histograms/summary metrics not string buckets.

Sean Gallagher: +1. don’t invent new buckets unless we can justify. every bucket is a multiplier.

Logan Wright: action items:
1) i’ll update ADR + ENG-5410 acceptance criteria w/ explicit allowlist + caps.
2) Nadia/Caleb: implement “cardinality protection mode” in emitter (route cap + experiment cap + global cap). if tripped, emit metric shadow_cardinality_dropped_total{reason=...}.
3) Marcus: review event payload fields for quasi-identifiers (fingerprint/prompt_hash) + retention/redaction (separate doc).

Marcus Lin: ack. and we should add a lint/test in CI: metric label set must match allowlist (fail build).

Benji Okafor: +1. we can add validation in policy service too: forbid config that tries to turn on unsafe label emission.

Allison Grant: love it. also: dashboards should *not* encourage filtering by high-card dims. no freeform "route contains" on metric queries.

Selene Huang: for science side: we still need segment filters like “deployment_mode, region, route (top), model_id, quant_profile, rubric_version”. that’s enough.

Sean Gallagher: can we codify final list here so nobody bikesheds later?

Allison Grant: final for v1 (metrics labels):
A) always allowed:
- deployment_mode
- region
- model_id
- quant_profile
- rubric_version
- metric_name (from fixed bundle)
- variant (control|shadow)
- outcome_class
B) allowed w/ guardrails (caps/bucketing):
- route_id (top 50 per tenant/day else __other__)
- rollout_id (bounded by active rollouts)
- experiment_id (max 10 active per tenant else __inactive__)
- prompt_tokens_bucket (coarse)
C) event-only / forbidden in metrics:
- tenant_id/customer_id
- request_fingerprint/request_id/trace_id
- prompt_id/prompt_hash
- headers/custom tags
- raw errors
- model_version/build id

Allison Grant: if anyone objects, speak now :)

Sean Gallagher: :thumbsup: from SRE

Nadia Rahman: :thumbsup: telemetry. i’ll incorporate into ingestion PR + add dropped_total metrics.

Caleb Johnson: :thumbsup: will adjust dashboard queries accordingly.

Ravi Menon: :thumbsup: routing ok.

Marcus Lin: :thumbsup: security ok as long as fingerprint stays out of metrics and events are sampled/TTL.

Selene Huang: :thumbsup: science ok.

Allison Grant: cool. closing loop on ENG-5410 w/ this thread link.

title: Mini-bundle PRD: Unified inference surface for chat, completion, embeddings, and rerank with launch surge plan
author: Aisha Patel
text:
High-level PRD to deliver a compact, production-ready 'mini-bundle' that exposes a consistent API surface for chat, completion, embeddings, and rerank use cases. The intent is to offer a single onboarding flow, one billing SKU with per-route knobs, and an operational surge/rollback plan for launch day. This ticket scopes the product requirements, acceptance criteria, risks, and a tactical launch checklist for a targeted GA to early enterprise customers.

We have multiple Large PRDs covering the full hosted API family. This effort is a deliberately constrained bundle (MVP) to speed time-to-value for teams that need a single integration covering the most common patterns: single-turn generation, chat turn sequences, vector embedding generation, and rerank scoring pipelines. Key differences from larger PRDs: tighter acceptance gates, explicit surge controls, and a built-in sampling quality monitor tied to rollout gates.

Deliver a single, documented API path that supports chat, completion, embeddings, and rerank with consistent authentication and billing
Provide per-route configuration: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, embedding_model, rerank_model and deterministic fallback mapping
Define launch operational plan that prevents capacity overload via adaptive throttles and a tiered fallback to smaller models/regions
Ship a monitoring plan that samples 0.5% of responses for quality evaluation and flags regression against a baseline prompt set

Full multi-modal support (images/audio) in this mini-bundle
Advanced model orchestration policies (A/B weighted routing across unlimited variants) beyond simple canary and fallback
Enterprise-only Dedicated capacity contracts — this targets hosted tier first

API: Single endpoint group /v1/inference with mode param: {mode: "chat|completion|embedding|rerank"}
SDKs: Expose identical surface in SDKs (python/js) with clear defaults and per-route overrides
Billing: One SKU 'mini_bundle' with per-token generation and per-embedding unit rates; explicit metering for rerank scoring calls
Routing: Support region preference and a fallback route list; fallback must preserve response semantics within 95% of acceptance tests
Rate limits & quotas: Configurable per-tenant soft-limit + hard-limit; a surge policy that reduces batch size and routes to fallback models under sustained queue growth
Observability: Token-level cost, per-request latency, sample payloads (0.5%), and a regression alert if sampled quality score drops by >= 6% vs baseline
Security/compliance: All requests logged with request_id and redaction rules; ensure KMS integration for customer-managed keys is documented for Private later

API contract: OpenAPI entry and SDK surfaces pass contract linting and automated smoke tests
Functional tests: Chat single-turn and multi-turn (3 turns) acceptance suite passes with stability >= 99% over 24h soak
Embedding parity: Embedding model produces vectors within 2% cosine similarity of reference embedding for canonical dataset
Rerank correctness: Top-1 rerank precision on benchmark set >= 88% and latency P95 <= 220ms in hosted region
Billing validation: Billing meter events emitted for every request type and aggregated values match simulated invoice within 0.5%
Safety & redaction: Automated PII redaction hooks exercised and verified in 1000 sample requests
Surge behavior: Under load test (2x expected QPS sustained for 30m) the system enforces surge throttle and fallback route within 60s, with successful degradation behavior (no unhandled 5xx spikes >0.5%)
Canary and rollback: Canary cohort (5% traffic) does not regress metrics for 4 consecutive hours, otherwise automatic rollback to previous model happens
Docs & quickstart: Console quickstart, API docs, and example notebooks present and validated by Solutions Engineering

Dedicated capacity provisioning flows for this mini-bundle (handled by Dedicated roadmap)
Customer-managed on-prem installation in GA (Private flagged for later cycle)
Complex retraining/inference pipelines or multi-stage retrieval chains — only single call rerank is supported

ENG-22111 (runtime: per-request sampling and trace IDs)
ENG-23780 (billing: embed per-unit meter events)
ENG-24451 (routing: fallback policy primitives)
DES-1987 (docs: quickstart and SDK examples)
PM-582300 (safety: redaction and PII policy)

Surge underestimation: underestimated launch demand could exhaust GPU pools; mitigated by conservative initial quota and manual surge escalation playbook
Quality regressions due to fallback: cheaper fallback models may produce unacceptable outputs — sampled quality monitor and rollback gates required
Billing mismatch: complexity in metering different call types could produce unexpected invoices for customers; bill validation harness required

title: Orchestrated ephemeral research sandboxes: auto-create Jira project/templates + Confluence playbook + Slack ephemeral channel with approval/gating
text:
Request to implement a single, auditable automation that provisions short-lived research sandboxes for Model Eval and Research pods. When a developer requests a sandbox via a JIRA issue, the automation should: 1) create a namespaced Jira project or project-space (scoped to the team), 2) instantiate Confluence child pages from a 'sandbox playbook' template, 3) provision a private Slack channel using enforced naming conventions and invite the requester + approvals group, 4) attach an approval step (Slack or Okta group approver) before the channel becomes active, 5) schedule automatic archival after a configurable TTL (default 30 days) with a grace-renew option, and 6) emit an audit export (S3) of channel membership and Confluence snapshot at archive time. This is intended to replace ad-hoc manual requests and ensure a reproducible, auditable lifecycle with minimal engineering touchpoints.

Reduces manual overhead for platform team, speeds up Model Eval/Research experiment setup, and ensures required compliance artifacts (audit exports) are captured for internal audits. Current ad-hoc process creates inconsistent naming, missing playbooks, and undocumented Slack channels.

1) Creating a Jira issue in project 'Sandbox Requests' triggers the automation. 2) A Jira subproject or issue namespace is created with templated issue types (Experiment, Runbook, Cleanup). 3) Confluence page(s) created from 'Sandbox Playbook' template and linked to the Jira project. 4) Private Slack channel created with naming convention (sandbox-{team}-{shortid}), approver group notified, and channel remains muted until approver accepts. 5) Archive job triggers after TTL and stores an S3 snapshot of Confluence pages + membership CSV. 6) Logs of all steps appear in the central ops log index, and a sample audit export passes security review. 7) Automated renew (extend TTL) works from within Slack with a single command by the owner.

Preferred approach: a lightweight orchestration Lambda (or internal worker) that calls the Jira REST API for project/issue templates, Confluence API for page creation, Slack SCIM / Conversations API to create channels, and Okta API to validate approver membership. Use a single service account with scoped permissions and rotate keys via KMS. Store TTL config in a small DynamoDB table keyed by sandbox id. Emit CloudWatch (or our existing observability pipeline) metrics for success/failure. See PRs referenced in related_github_prs for initial scripts.

Security review required for: service account scope, S3 bucket lifecycle and encryption, Confluence page export sanitization (make sure secrets are redacted), Slack membership export handling. Proposed S3 path: s3://redwood-audit/sandboxes/{sandbox-id}/. Use SSE-KMS with restricted access and retention per compliance team guidance.

title: Long-poll fallback closes early, truncating streamed tail on reconnect
text:
Issue summary: Customer reports that when their corporate edge rewrites Streaming SSE to a long-poll fallback path, the last ~1-2 sentences of responses are consistently missing after a reconnect.

Impact: Intermittent data loss for streaming responses behind certain proxies; affects customer-facing assistant content (missing trailing sentences). Reported by a Dedicated customer (NimbusDocs) using the hosted API through a corporate proxy that downgrades SSE to HTTP long-polling.

Observed behavior: Client receives streamed tokens, then connection is torn down by edge for long-poll fallback. When the session resumes the service returns an early 204/OK and the final trailer event (closing marker/end metadata) is not delivered to the client. Result: truncated final paragraph and absent terminal metadata (choice.finish_reason).

Expected behavior: Fallback path should replay or proxy through the complete trailing chunks or the server should re-emit terminal events after reconstitution so the client receives the full final sentence and closing metadata.

1) Customer environment: desktop app behind corporate proxy that strips SSE and does long-polling; use proxy that rewrites HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/1.0 and closes keepalive after 15s.
2) Open a streaming chat session against the Redwood hosted API with Accept: text/event-stream and keepalive enabled; send a prompt that yields a 60-120 token final paragraph.
3) Trigger a controlled network interruption to force the proxy to close and re-establish the HTTP connection (simulate edge path change or probe).
4) Observe on the client: streaming resumes but final 1-2 sentences are missing; server logs show a short-lived long-poll request that returns without the closing trailer event.
5) Reproduce reliably by toggling the proxy keepalive interval in synthetic lab; behavior observed ~7/10 runs.

[2026-03-10T14:08:12Z] proxy edge: Upstream accepted, id=xyz-7
[2026-03-10T14:08:26Z] client -> proxy: Connection close by proxy (keepalive expiry) (15s)
[2026-03-10T14:08:26Z] proxy -> rt-proxy: new long-poll /v1/stream?session=abc returning 200 OK (early-close)
[2026-03-10T14:08:26Z] rt-proxy: stream-session abc resumed; last-kv-checkpoint=0x7f1; trailer_flag=false
[2026-03-10T14:08:27Z] serving-runtime: produced final-choice tokens, emitted trailer meta (choice.finish_reason=length)
[2026-03-10T14:08:27Z] rt-proxy: upstream write failed: client closed connection; skipping trailer emission on long-poll path

Hypothesis 1: Long-poll fallback path short-circuits trailer emission when client socket indicates close; race between runtime's trailer write and proxy long-poll response commit.
Hypothesis 2: Proxy/edge performs an extra connection-level close that causes rt-proxy to treat resumed session as ephemeral and drop final metadata to avoid blocking write (backpressure handling path).
Repro steps validated in internal staging with our test proxy (haproxy) reproducing 80% of runs when keepalive <= 20s.
Observed difference vs normal SSE: SSE code path uses chunked transfer with streaming flush; long-poll path uses buffered response commit and currently lacks explicit trailer re-synthesis when the client reconnection occurs.
Logs indicate serving-runtime did emit finish trailer but rt-proxy logged upstream write failure before it could sink to the client long-poll response body.

Amelia Chen (Support) 2026-03-10: Acknowledged ticket to customer, requested example session IDs and sample network captures. First response within SLA.
NimbusDocs (Customer) 2026-03-10: Provided tcpdump + proxy logs and one failing session id (abc). They confirm this happens behind their Palo Alto NGFW which downgrades SSE to polling for legacy clients.
Diego Morales (SRE) 2026-03-11: Reproduced locally using haproxy rewrite script. Confirmed trailer emission race. Created scoped patch to add server-side retry to ensure trailers are replayed on resumed long-poll responses (branch: fix/long-poll-trailer-replay).
Product (Benita Arora) 2026-03-11: Asked for risk assessment and whether this impacts other fallback paths (ws->long-poll, http2->http1).
Diego Morales (SRE) 2026-03-12: Hotfix staged in canary (us-east staging). Observed full trailer delivery in 95/100 synthetic runs. Plan: backport hotfix to production proxy layer and release rollout with feature flag to disable fallback replay as kill-switch.
NimbusDocs (Customer) 2026-03-12: Requested ETA for production fix and whether there is a short-term client workaround.
Support (Amelia) 2026-03-12: Provided customer workaround: enable direct SSE passthrough for Redwood endpoints or increase proxy keepalive to >= 60s; both mitigate until patch is rolled out.

Workaround provided to customer (enable SSE passthrough or increase proxy keepalive). Hotfix implemented in rt-proxy to replay trailers on long-poll resume (branch fix/long-poll-trailer-replay). Canary results positive; production rollout scheduled with a config flag and canary wedge. Postmortem and formal remediation tracked on confluence page. Follow-up: add integration test for long-poll fallback path and update runbooks to include proxy keepalive guidance.

Hotfix PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rt-proxy/pull/542
Canary deployed to us-east staging 2026-03-12 08:30Z; 95% success in synthetic tests.
Prod rollout planned 2026-03-13 with feature-flagged rollouts per region.
Post-deploy: monitor streaming error rates and truncated-response alerts for 48h; add automated regression test in CI.

title: Historical dashboard panels show stale counts and lose trace links after retention compaction warmup
text:
Issue summary: Several customers (notably LumenHealth) report that historical dashboard panels (time ranges > 30 days) intermittently show zeroed or stale metric counts and their trace links are missing. The problem is transient: panels become correct again after ~10-30 minutes without user action. Impact: dashboards with SLA and usage rollups show incorrect historical values; alerting based on those rollups can under- or over-fire. This affects customer trust in console analytics and can mask billing/usage anomalies. Environment: production us-east region. Affected customers reported on enterprise tier; observed across multiple orgs.

1) Open Console -> Dashboards -> choose a dashboard with weekly/monthly rollups (time range > 30 days). 2) Observe counts for a low-cardinality metric (e.g., route_success_rate, total_tokens) and trace-link anchors. 3) Rapidly change time window back and forth (e.g., 90d -> 30d -> 90d) and refresh. 4) Some panels will render with zeroed or very old counts and trace-link buttons show 'No traces' instead of opening the trace view. 5) Wait 10-30 minutes; panels recover without manual cache clear. Repro is intermittent (~1 in 10 attempts during retention compaction windows).

console-frontend: panel-render: query=rollup_v2 start=2025-12-01 end=2026-03-01 shard=warm-compact read_mode=primary; retention-indexer: compaction job id=cmp-2026-03-12-08 warmup=true; indexer-lag: lag=18m; kv-cache: miss-rate spike to 78%. Trace-hook service logs show O(200) missing anchors during query window. No 5xx in api-gateway. No token auth errors. Relevant links: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/retention/indexer-run-03-12, https://kibana.redwood.internal/app/discover#/logs?q=cmp-2026-03-12-08

Initial hypothesis: retention compaction warmup job is causing a temporary partition state where rollup queries hit compacted partitions that are in 'read-repair' mode; dashboard renderer treats empty result as zero and trace-hook anchor resolution returns empty. Confirmed with SRE that a compaction job ran with warmup=true and indexer lag spiked ~18 minutes. Queries during warmup hit a mix of old and compacted store replicas; read-repair and backfill to hot replicas happen asynchronously. Observed that the console frontend does not fallback to hot-replica read-path when primary returns empty for rollups, so panels show stale/zeroed values. Trace-links are resolved by joining rollup keys to trace-anchor index which is being reindexed during compaction; when anchor index is temporarily empty, UI shows 'No traces'. Repro correlates strongly with compaction windows and indexer backfill events.

- Affects historical panels (>30d) across multiple enterprise orgs in us-east during retention compaction windows.
- Observed on ~4 orgs in last 72h, including LumenHealth and 2 other enterprise accounts.
- Alerts relying on those rollups may be suppressed or show incorrect counts for the duration of compaction warmup.
- No data loss: data is present after reindex/backfill; this is a read-path consistency/window problem.

Short term: ask customer to (a) avoid rapidly toggling large time windows during the scheduled compaction window, or (b) use a narrower time range (<=30d) which reads from hot partitions. Support can also force a panel refresh via console 'Force reload' (admin button) which triggers a hot-replica read. We have provided LumenHealth with instructions for forced refresh and notified them of the scheduled compaction window.

Race between retention compaction warmup and dashboard read-path: compaction marks partitions compacted while the indexer backfills the hot replica asynchronously. Dashboard queries hitting compacted-but-not-yet-backfilled partitions return empty rollups; UI treats empty as zero. Trace-anchor index reindex causes temporary absence of anchor joins. No write-side data loss.

1) Frontend: treat empty rollup responses as 'retry with hot-replica' instead of rendering zero. 2) API layer: add fallback read-path to hot replicas when compaction-warmup flag is set for the partition. 3) Indexer: reduce warmup aggressiveness and emit explicit 'warmup-in-progress' header that the API can use to select fallback. 4) Add an observability alert for 'rollup-empty-during-compaction' so SRE is alerted earlier. Implementation PR: https://github.com/redwood/reindexer/pull/1189 (adds warmup header); https://github.com/redwood/console/pull/4712 (frontend retry).

title: Cinder Labs — session tear causing token reordering, retry amplification, streaming truncations and billing spike
text:
Issue summary:

During a peak traffic window on 2026-03-09 17:22 UTC, Cinder Labs began seeing partial/stale streaming responses, token reordering for long chat sessions (>4096 tokens), and a surge in client retries that amplified upstream throughput. This led to increased 5xx rates from serving nodes, transient throttles from the API gateway, and an unexpected billing delta for the customer.

Impact:
- Multiple customer endpoints experienced truncated streams and out-of-order token sequences (~1200 user sessions affected).
- Observed 5xx rate peaked at 6.3% for the customer’s traffic window.
- Billing spike estimated at +42% for the affected 2-hour window due to retry amplification.
- Customer escalated to enterprise support and requested immediate mitigation, crediting and a post-incident review.

Environment:
- Production (us-east-1) serving cl-13b-v1-quant behind api-gateway v2.13.
- Dedicated routing policy: enterprise-reserved-us-east.

Steps to reproduce (internal):
1. Create a multi-turn chat session pinned to cl-13b-v1-quant with >4096 token context and stream responses.
2. Induce a partial runtime eviction (simulate KV cache evictions / kernel reselect) while continuing to stream.
3. Observe token gaps and client-side automatic retries causing multiple inflight requests for the same session.

Observed behavior:
- When a serving shard dropped the KV prefix during a background compaction, subsequent token continuation resumed from an earlier cache state and produced overlapping token sequences.
- Client SDKs retried idempotently but without session-affinity checks, creating duplicate in-flight completions.
- API gateway detected elevated error rates and began conservative throttling; some requests received 429s while others returned 5xx from the runtime.

Initial mitigation and timeline:
- 17:28 UTC: Support opened escalation and notified SRE and Serving Runtime teams.
- 17:35 UTC: Temporary routing policy change to route Cinder Labs traffic to a healthy pre-warmed pool (bypassed recently-updated autoscaler rules).
- 17:42 UTC: Disabled aggressive client-side retry guidance sent to Cinder Labs; asked temporary SDK toggle to backoff.
- 18:10 UTC: Rolling kernel-selection rollback (PR linked) deployed for us-east pool which stopped KV prefix evictions during active streaming.
- 19:00 UTC: Error rates returned to baseline; streaming behavior normalized.

Timeline and findings:
- 2026-03-09 17:22 UTC: first elevated 5xx and streaming truncations for Cinder Labs observed (api-gateway metrics + their telemetry).
- Root cause hypothesis: interaction between a recent kernel-selection tweak (PR 4821) and aggressive KV compaction led to transient state loss for long-lived sessions.
- Evidence: heap/kvcache flush logs on serving nodes show compaction events coincident with affected session IDs.
- Replay of workload on staging reproduced token reordering when compaction was force-triggered during active streaming.
- Throttle amplification: client SDK retry logic started new requests that did not enforce session-affinity, creating fanout and repeated token generation for the same logical conversation.
- Billing delta analysis: aggregated request counts for Cinder Labs during the window were 2.4x baseline; cost-weighted tokens increased proportionally.
- Contrib factors: recent autoscaler tuning reduced pre-warmed buffer by 20% in us-east pool, increasing likelihood that compaction/eviction occurred under pressure.

Support (Maya Chen) — 2026-03-09 17:30 UTC: Customer reported truncated streams and repeated partial messages. Opened incident and paged SRE.
SRE (Arjun Patel) — 2026-03-09 17:38 UTC: Identified KV compaction entries correlated with session IDs. Temporarily rerouted traffic to healthy pool.
Customer (Elena Ruiz, Cinder Labs) — 2026-03-09 17:45 UTC: Confirmed temporary improvement after reroute; requested timeline and credit for billing spike.
Eng (Tomasz Novak) — 2026-03-09 18:05 UTC: Rolled back kernel-selection change (PR 4821) in us-east as mitigation; monitoring for regressions.
Billing (Priya Shah) — 2026-03-10 09:12 UTC: Preliminary credit calculation prepared; recommended 50% credit for the affected window pending final audit.
Support (Maya Chen) — 2026-03-11 11:02 UTC: Sent post-incident summary and next steps to Cinder Labs; scheduled follow-up review on 2026-03-12.
Customer (Elena Ruiz) — 2026-03-11 15:40 UTC: Appreciated rapid response; requested concrete SDK guidance to avoid amplification in future.

Root cause: interaction between a kernel-selection optimization and KV compaction behavior on serving nodes caused transient session state loss for long chat contexts, leading to token reordering. Secondary amplification: client SDK retries without enforced session-affinity produced duplicate inflight completions and a billing spike.

Fixes applied:
- Rolled back kernel-selection tweak in us-east (PR 4821) and deployed a guarded kernel rollout that disables compaction during active streams.
- Temporary routing to pre-warmed pool restored stability during the rollout.
- Issued a targeted billing credit to Cinder Labs (50% of the two-hour delta) and submitted final audit for adjustment.

Status: Mitigation deployed, monitoring in place, customer credited; incident closed after validation period.

Implement server-side session-affinity enforcement for streaming continuations (owner: Eng/Serving Runtime) — ETA 2026-04-07
Add a compaction-safe flag to the runtime that prevents KV prefix eviction during active streams (owner: Eng/Serving Runtime) — ETA 2026-03-25
Enhance SDKs to surface and opt-in to conservative retry modes for enterprise tiers (owner: DevX/SDK) — ETA 2026-04-01
Create billing audit dashboard to detect anomalous retry amplification per customer (owner: Finance/Platform) — ETA 2026-03-20
Run tabletop with top enterprise customers to validate failover behaviors and communication playbooks (owner: Support/GTM) — ETA 2026-04-15

title: eng-releases
text:
marcus: deploy-bot flagged the payments-hotpatch canary in eu-west1 — lots of pod restarts. logs show SIGTERM in preStop handler, not OOM. should we hold promotion and pin chart version? :thinking:

deploy-bot: Canary health degraded: 5/10 failed, auto-pause applied. recent release: chart payments-service v2.5.0+overlay-hotpatch.
jia: can you paste the preStop logs? curious if it's our graceful shutdown or the overlay init hook.
sara: quick idea — if the hotpatch overlay injected a preStop that ignores SIGTERM timing, pods might be killed by kubelet before cleanup. that would explain restart loop.
marcus: here's the relevant excerpt from the pod logs:

2026-03-21T10:04:12Z INFO starting shutdown sequence
2026-03-21T10:04:12Z WARN Received SIGTERM
2026-03-21T10:04:12Z ERROR preStop script failed: exit code 137
2026-03-21T10:04:13Z INFO healthcheck failing, liveness triggered

jia: exit code 137 usually OOM-kill, but stack shows SIGTERM then 137. Could be preStop spinning CPU / memory.
ops-oncall: we just saw a node pressure event in eu-west1-zone-b an hour ago. combined with a long-running preStop could push kubelet to kill.
lee: TL;DR: hotpatch overlay changed lifecycleHook timing and introduced a blocking step. We need to decide: rollback to v2.4.1, pin v2.4.1 for promotion, or patch overlay and re-run canary.

marcus: agree. proposal: pin chart to v2.4.1 for promotion pipeline, create hotfix branch to remove blocking step in overlay preStop, run a debug canary in a small subset (10%) once patched. schedule full promotion after 2 successful checks.
jia: +1. can we do a soft rollback (helm rollback) and keep the release notes intact? i can run rollback and then tag new chart commit.
ops-oncall: if we rollback, we should also set a temporary admission webhook to prevent the hotpatch overlay from being re-applied by the deploy-bot until fix is merged. otherwise deploy bot might retry.
marcus: good call. @deploy-bot can you pause promotions for release pipeline `payments` and block overlays until we flip the flag?
deploy-bot: Promotions paused for pipeline payments. Overlay injections blocked by tag `hotpatch-overlay:v2.5.0` until manual unblock.

# confirm pods stabilized
kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=payments-service -o wide

sara: also add a short note to release-notes: "rolled back v2.5.0 hotpatch overlay due to preStop blocking; working on hotfix" so customers see it.
jia: i'll open PR now: hotfix/remove-blocking-prestop, will include a unit test for the lifecycle handler and a shorter timeout. tagging @sre for review.

sara: ack. i'll draft the release note blurb and post to the release channel when rollback completes. :thumbsup:
jia: PR opened: https://github.com/redwood/payments/pull/412 — hotfix + test. marking it urgent.
marcus: thanks everyone. once rollback completes, i'll update this thread with helm revision and pod status.
deploy-bot: Canary pause acknowledged. Blockers: none remaining.
marcus: rollback completed — helm rolled back to v2.4.1 (revision 3). pods stabilized (12/12 Ready). tagging this thread for postmortem and follow-up to ensure overlay lifecycle hook is fixed before re-promote.

title: Platform Brief: SaaS GTM — Inference Value Metrics & Battlecards
author: Maya Thompson
text:
Overview

Purpose: This brief consolidates product positioning, high-impact value metrics, competitive battlecards, pricing guidance, a compact case study, and a prospect-facing security FAQ tailored for SaaS platform buyers evaluating LLM inference solutions. Audience: AEs, SEs, solutions engineers, and product marketing running discovery and technical evaluation calls with mid-market and enterprise SaaS buyers.

Executive positioning (one-liner)

Redwood Inference: Predictable, production-grade LLM inference that maximizes performance and minimizes unit cost across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments — giving platform teams a single API and operational surface to ship reliable AI features without rebuilding inference infrastructure.

Top 3 buyer outcomes we lead with

- Reduce per-inference cost while keeping sub-100ms tail latency for common interactive flows.
- Move from prototype to SLA-backed production without re-architecting (same API for hosted, reserved, and private).
- De-risk compliance through private deployment and audit-friendly telemetry.

Key value metrics and how to frame them in discovery

- Latency (P95/P99): Typical hosted P95 for chat flows: 80–180ms (short prompts, <256 tokens). P99 target for Dedicated: <250ms. Discuss tail-latency SLOs and fallback routing to smaller quantized models for spikes.
- Throughput: Batch-aware throughput gains: 2–6x cost savings for high-concurrency embedding jobs with batching & caching. Ask about queries/sec (QPS) and average request size.
- Cost per 1k prompt tokens: Provide customer-specific model/quantization comps. Example framing: "Switching from single-instance self-host to Redwood Dedicated saved AcornCRM ~48% per-token on standard 8K-chat workload."
- Availability / SLA: Hosted: 99.9% regional uptime; Dedicated: 99.95% backed by contract. Use these to quantify expected downtime impact on revenue ops.
- Time-to-production: Typical onboarding (hosted) = 1–3 days; Dedicated proof-of-concept = 2–4 weeks (infra & capacity provisioning).

Battlecard: Primary competitors and how to position

- Cloud-managed endpoints (Hyperscaler-managed LLM endpoints)
 - Strengths: deep cloud integration, single-provider billing.
 - Redwood advantage: Superior latency predictability, multi-model catalog (open models + tuned variants), and lower unit cost via continuous batching, quantization profiles, and model routing policies.
 - Messaging: "Like managed endpoints, but tuned for inference economics and predictable tail latency for production apps."

- LLM API providers (simple hosted APIs)
 - Strengths: easy dev experience, low time-to-value.
 - Redwood advantage: Matches dev ergonomics but adds Dedicated / Private lanes and enterprise controls (VPC, KMS, audit logs) so customers don’t have to replatform as they scale.
 - Messaging: "From prototype to SLA-backed production without rewriting your integration."

- Self-hosted inference stacks (open-source runtime + infra)
 - Strengths: maximum control, on-prem fit for regulated data.
 - Redwood advantage: We provide a hardened runtime, autoscaling, cost controls, and rollout tooling—plus optional on-prem packaging and a customer-managed control plane for compliance. Lower TCO for teams that value operational simplicity and performance tuning.
 - Messaging: "Get the benefits of a maintained, optimized inference runtime without hiring a deep infra team."

Pricing guidance (rules of thumb for AEs to use in discovery)

- Pricing levers to highlight: model family, instance type (Dedicated SKU), quantization tier, reserved commit vs burst, embedding vs generative unit pricing.
- Proposal archetypes:
 - Self-serve hosted starter: no commit, pay-as-you-go per-token and per-embedding. Ideal for product/feature proofs.
 - Dedicated entry: 3–6 month reserved capacity (monthly commit), includes capacity reservation, 24/7 priority support, and model access. Typical for midmarket customers expecting consistent QPS.
 - Private Deployment: fixed platform fee + per-node license + premium support and compliance bundle. For regulated customers or those requiring air-gapped environments.

- Example customer scenario (SaaS search & assistant) — ballpark illustration to use during commercial conversations:
 - Baseline: 3M tokens / month, predominantly generation (average 500 tokens/session), 2M embeddings / month.
 - Hosted cost estimate (pay-as-you-go): $6,000–$9,000 / month depending on model family and streaming usage.
 - Dedicated cost estimate (reserved): $3,200–$5,500 / month equivalent (with 12-month commit) — includes better latency SLAs and lower per-token unit economics.
 - Use these numbers as conversation starters and include precise model-match quotes from pricing desk for final proposals.

Pitch deck outline (6 slides, one-line purpose each)

1. Problem: Rising inference costs, tail latency, and operational debt when scaling LLM features.
2. Vision & Value: Unified inference runtime with predictable economics and deployment flexibility.
3. Product: Redwood product map (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private, Console, Optimize).
4. Proof points: Performance benchmarks (P95/P99 numbers), cost comparisons vs self-host & hyperscalers, and a short case study.
5. Security & compliance: VPC, KMS integrations, SOC2 / ISO posture, audit logs, and private deployment options.
6. Commercials & next steps: Pricing archetypes, pilot offer, success criteria and timeline.

Compact case study: AcornCRM (SaaS CRM) — 8-week engagement

- Situation: AcornCRM needed a contextual assistant for sales reps with sub-200ms P95 latency and tight data residency constraints for EU customers. Their prototype used a mix of self-hosted models and occasional hyperscaler endpoints.
- Action: Redwood onboarded AcornCRM to Hosted API for an initial pilot (2 weeks), instrumented prompt caching and prefix KV caching, then migrated them to a Dedicated pool with quantized model variants for EU traffic. Provided rollout plan with canary and automatic fallback policies.
- Results: 
 - Latency: P95 from ~420ms to 160ms after Dedicated + batching optimizations.
 - Cost: Estimated per-token unit cost reduced 48% vs their previous single-instance hosting baseline.
 - Reliability: Achieved 99.96% uptime for critical inference routes over 90 days.
- Quote (paraphrased): "We launched our assistant into production faster than expected and kept response times consistent across our EU and US customers — the cost reduction was material to our unit economics." — Head of Platform, AcornCRM

Security FAQ for prospects (short and direct)

Q: Can Redwood run in my VPC / on-prem?
A: Yes. We offer Private deployment (customer-managed control plane) and an on-prem package for air-gapped environments. Contact sales for deployment checklist and lead time (typically 4–8 weeks depending on network & hardware).

Q: How is customer data protected in Hosted?
A: Data is encrypted in-transit (TLS 1.2+) and at-rest (AES-256). Optional per-customer keying via KMS (bring-your-own-key supported on Dedicated & Private). We retain only transient inference artifacts by default; retention is configurable.

Q: Do you have third-party attestations?
A: Redwood maintains SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 evidence; customers with enterprise contracts can request evidence under NDA.

Q: How are audit logs surfaced?
A: Redwood Console exposes request-level telemetry, per-token cost breakdowns, model version, and an audit trail for administrative actions. Logs can also be forwarded to your SIEM via secure forwarding.

Q: What controls exist to prevent data leakage in model updates?
A: Model onboarding and updates are gated by the model-onboarding team. We sign model-change notices and provide canary/eval runs tied to your evaluation suites. Private deployments allow complete model binaries under customer control.

Q: How do you handle incident response and notifications?
A: We maintain a documented incident process with dedicated SRE on-call rotation. Customers with Dedicated or Private get a designated technical account lead (TAL) and a post-incident report within 72 hours for Sev1 incidents.

Objection handling snippets (short scripts for SEs/AEs)

- "We can build this ourselves": Ask about the cost of hiring/retaining ops talent, time-to-first-SLA, and the ongoing tuning effort. Offer a TCO comparison and pilot to prove the economics.
- "We need data to stay on-prem": Lead with Private deployment and provide the deployment checklist + typical timelines.
- "Hyperscaler pricing is better": Request concrete usage patterns and offer a model-by-model cost comparison; emphasize predictable tail latency and the operational burden of maintaining tuning and rollout tooling.

Success criteria and pilot checklist (what we want to validate in a POC)

- Business/technical success criteria (mutually agreed): target P95 latency, acceptable per-token cost delta vs prototype, error rate threshold (<0.5% request errors), and integration completion (SDK + tracing).
- Technical deliverables: sample prompt set, representative traffic replay (1–3 days), evaluation prompts for quality checks, production routing plan, and SLO definition.
- Timeline (typical):
 - Week 0: Kickoff, secret exchange, and prompt set delivery.
 - Week 1–2: Hosted pilot, instrumentation, perf tuning.
 - Week 3–4: Dedicated provisioning (if applicable), canary rollout.
 - Week 4–8: Stabilization, cost tuning, and handoff to platform/ops.

Appendix: links & artifacts to attach to deal folders

- One-pager: pricing archetypes and quick calculator (attach to deal).
- Benchmarks: P95/P99 latency artifacts vs common model families and hardware types.
- Security pack: SOC2 certificate, data flow diagrams, private deployment checklist.
- Demo scripts: scripted chat + embedding replay and a minimal staging dataset.

Owner & next steps

- Owner: Maya Thompson (go-to-market) — ping for slide assets, pricing calculator, and demo components.
- Recommended next step for AEs: book a 45-minute joint call with Solutions Engineering; bring traffic samples and the buyer's SLOs.

Change log

- 2025-11-03: Created initial GTM brief.
- 2026-02-10: Updated pricing archetypes and security FAQ; added AcornCRM case highlights.

title: Egress transit provider dropping 'fragmentation-needed' ICMP causing large HTTP/2 model-shard streams to stall in private deploy
text:
Issue summary:
Customer reports intermittent stalls when streaming large model shard downloads and long-lived gRPC/http2 connections from their Private deployment. The problem started after an on-prem network change from their transit provider two days ago.

Impact:
- Models fail to fully stream for larger shards (>64KB) causing inference requests to stall and time out after ~30s.
- Affects production traffic for FinData Analytics (private deployment, single VPC peered to our control plane).
- Observed in us-east-1 only.

Environment:
- Private deployment (customer-managed VPC) peered to Redwood control plane via TGW.
- Worker nodes: t3.large-equivalent instances with custom MTU 1500 by default.
- Presigned S3 artifact fetches used with range requests (HTTP/2 multiplexed).

Steps to reproduce (observed by customer):
1) Trigger a model load that requires range fetches (large model shard).
2) Observe initial TLS handshake completes. HTTP/2 connection established.
3) After a few KBs, the download stalls and the HTTP/2 stream is left in a half-open state; no further DATA frames from server are delivered.
4) Retry with smaller range window or reduce request size -> succeeds.

Observed behavior:
- tcpdump on worker shows server sending TCP segments but client stops ACKing after a certain MSS-sized segment. No ICMP "Fragmentation Needed (Type 3, Code 4)" is seen reaching the customer edge.
- When we instrumented a capture at the customer-VM side we do see an ICMP type 3 code 4 originating from the downstream router, but it disappears before reaching the customer's transit provider egress (suggesting provider filtering/rate limit).
- HTTP/2 stream state: initial SETTINGS/HEADERS exchange ok, partial DATA frames delivered, then stall; client eventually times out and triggers a reconnect.

Expected behavior:
- If path MTU requires fragmentation adjustments, ICMP "Fragmentation Needed (Type 3, Code 4)" should be delivered to endpoints so PMTU can adjust and streaming continues without stalls.

Additional logs / captures:
- Attached pcap snippets (provided by customer): "pcap_worker_side.pcap" shows server DATA up to a segment then no further ACK progression.
- Worker logs: serving-runtime reported repeated stream timeouts with code 14 (UNAVAILABLE) and downstream transport errors referencing ECONNRESET after timeouts.
- Console trace: Model shard fetch request id=shard-20260312-34 produced 0 bytes after 18s then retried and succeeded with MTU reduced.

Immediate customer workaround performed:
- Customer set worker node MTU to 1400 (temporary) — this prevented the need for ICMP fragmentation and streaming resumed successfully.

Notes:
- This only reproduces on large sequential downloads (range-based) or larger gRPC frame payloads; small requests and embeddings flows unaffected.
- The control plane auth and presigned URL generation are not implicated (we can generate working presigned URLs that still stall when path MTU issues present).

2026-03-12: Initial triage by Support (Aisha). Collected tcpdump + HTTP/2 trace. Customer confirms transit provider changed perimeter firewall/policy on 2026-03-11.
2026-03-12: SRE (Marco) requested pcap from customer and reproduced stalls by issuing range requests to the same object; pcap at worker shows missing ICMP fragments and stalled TCP sequence progression.
2026-03-13: We set up controlled repro from an EC2 in the customer's VPC and instrumented packet captures at three points: (a) worker VM, (b) customer edge router, (c) provider egress (captured by customer but provider did not provide mirrored capture). The VM saw ICMP type 3 code 4 originate from edge router; there is a gap at the provider handoff.
2026-03-13: Opened inbound ticket with customer's transit provider (ticket TP-44821) — provider response indicates they apply ICMP rate-limiting and drop some Type 3 messages under heavy NAT; they are investigating.
2026-03-14: SRE confirmed MTU-lowering on worker (1400) is an effective mitigation. We tested increasing TLS record granularity (server-side capping to 1200) and that also mitigates but requires runtime change.

Hypothesis:
- Transit provider's egress filtering/rate-limiting is preventing delivery of ICMP Fragmentation Needed messages to the customer's VMs, causing PMTU discovery to fail and resulting in a blackhole for packets larger than path MTU. HTTP/2/HTTP/2-over-TLS tends to push larger frames which triggers the failure more evident for large shard downloads.

Next steps / action items:
- SRE: Collect signed pcap evidence to include in provider escalation (assigned Marco Alvarez).
- Support: Document workaround steps for customer (MTU 1400 or server TLS record size cap).
- Customer: Keep transit provider ticket open and request allowing ICMP Type 3 Code 4 or otherwise enable PMTU transparency.
- Product: Consider adding an automatic fallback to smaller TLS record sizes for private deployments when PMTU probes fail (follow-up RFC).

2026-03-12 09:14 - Aisha Khan (Support): Customer reports repeated streaming stalls for large model loads. They rolled back a network change but problem persists. They've provided tcpdump and logs. Opening ticket and requesting captures from their edge.
2026-03-12 13:02 - Marco Alvarez (SRE): Reproduced locally inside customer's VPC. Captures show ICMP type 3 code 4 being generated at edge, but not propagated past provider handoff. Suspect provider-level ICMP filtering/rate limiting.
2026-03-13 08:23 - FinData NetOps (Customer): Provider confirms a firewall policy change on 2026-03-11 and acknowledges ICMP rate-limiting. They've opened TP-44821 with provider. Can confirm MTU workround helps.
2026-03-13 16:55 - Marco Alvarez (SRE): Applied temporary MTU 1400 to two worker nodes for customer testing; model shard fetches succeeded under load. Propose scripted mitigation and documenting for other customers.
2026-03-14 10:10 - Aisha Khan (Support): Customer requests guidance for permanent fix and asks if Redwood can detect PMTU blackholes and auto-fallback to smaller TLS records or throughput-mode that reduces frame sizes.
2026-03-14 14:30 - Marco Alvarez (SRE): Creating provider escalation bundle with pcaps + timeline. File attached to provider ticket TP-44821. Suggested product follow-up to product infra team: auto-detect PMTU failures and reduce record size.

Workaround: Customer lowered worker MTU to 1400 which restored streaming. Alternative workaround: cap TLS record sizes/server-side chunking to avoid packets exceeding Path MTU.
Root cause: Provider-level ICMP (Fragmentation Needed) filtering/rate-limiting preventing PMTU discovery; provider ticket TP-44821 opened by customer.
Follow-up: SRE to push escalation to provider with signed pcap evidence. Product team to evaluate automatic TLS-record-size fallback for private deployments if PMTU probes fail.

title: Data residency exception record: NordBank AB (EU-only with temporary US failover)
author: Aisha Rahman
text:
h2. Summary
NordBank AB requested an exception to their EU-only data residency requirement to support disaster recovery testing and failover. Redwood Inference approved a *time-bounded* exception to route inference traffic to a US region when EU capacity is unavailable, under defined controls.

h2. Customer requirement
* Primary requirement: All inference requests and any associated logs must remain in EU regions (eu-west).
* Requested exception: Permit failover serving in US (us-east) during DR tests and during unplanned EU capacity incidents.

h2. Approved exception (scope and duration)

title: mini-canary-solo-notebook
author: Morgan Ellis
text:
Notes to self: running a very small, solo mini-canary for KV-cache tuning (ttl + prefix evict) — aim is to validate warmup behavior and no-tail-latency regressions for hosted API path. Keep it tiny, reversible, and observable.

Primary hypothesis:
- Small change to KV eviction TTL reduces cold-token generation by ~8% after warmup for typical 1024-token flows.
- No customer-facing 5xx or latency p99 regressions.

Quick goals (success criteria):
- No 5xx spike > 0.1% relative in first 60m.
- P99 latency change <= +10ms vs baseline for the pinned cohort.
- Cache hit ratio increases by at least 3 percentage points for warm requests within cohort.

Scope & constraints:
- Only touch hosted-api runtime config: kv.default_ttl and kv.prefix_eviction (alpha flag).
- Target a single region (us-west1) and a single tiny cohort (client_id prefix = test-mini-2026).
- Traffic fraction: start 0.05% -> 0.5% -> 2% (if green) over ~4 hours.
- Rollback must be a single API call (see kill-switch below).

Preflight checklist (do not skip):
- [ ] Confirm PR merged + image deployed to staging cluster: runtime:sha-2483
- [ ] Load test local warmup script against staging (warmup 1000 short requests) — observe cache hit curve
- [ ] Create canary cohort in routing: route rule ID: rc-mini-2026-1 (work w/ routing eng if needed)
- [ ] Update monitoring dashboard with baseline windows (last 72h) and pin comparison range
- [ ] Alert hooks: pager for 5xx_rate, slack burn channel for p99_autotrack; set temporary severity mapping
- [ ] Notify on-call SRE + product owner in #deploy-alerts Slack 30m before start

Start plan:
1) 00:00 - smoke sanity (0.05% traffic) – 15m
 - Run quick canary script: ./tools/canary-shift --cohort=mini-2026 --fraction=0.0005 --duration=15m
 - Validate: 5xx_rate, p99, cache_hit_ratio on dashboard
 - Manual check: sample 10 traces (span search) for unexpected errors

2) 00:20 - expand to 0.5% – 45m
 - ./tools/canary-shift --cohort=mini-2026 --fraction=0.005 --duration=45m
 - Watch for any stepstair increases in tail latency or new error codes from runtime (KV EVICT errors)

3) 01:10 - expand to 2% – 2h
 - Only if previous windows green; consider A/B compare with baseline cohort using traffic mirroring for deeper trace sampling

Kill-switches / rollback:
- Immediate rollback (fast): routing API call to remove cohort rule (route_rule.remove rc-mini-2026-1).
- Runtime revert (if image-level): roll image back to runtime:sha-2480 via deploy tool: ./ops/deploy --image=runtime:sha-2480 --region=us-west1 --service=hosted-api
- Emergency throttle: block traffic to cohort with iptables rule on edge proxies (SRE assistance)

Operational commands (cheat sheet):
- check current cohort fraction: ./tools/canary-status --cohort=mini-2026
- roll forward/back: ./tools/canary-shift --cohort=mini-2026 --fraction=<frac>
- remove rule: ./tools/canary-remove --cohort=mini-2026
- force rollback image: ./ops/deploy --image=runtime:sha-2480 --service=hosted-api --region=us-west1

Telemetry to watch (short list):
- 5xx_rate_by_route (hosted-api) — absolute and relative to baseline
- p50/p95/p99 latency for completion and first-byte
- cache_hit_ratio and kv_eviction_rate
- token_generation_time (median, p99)
- tail-end sign: increased retries from SDKs, spike in client backoffs
- error taxon: any new error codes logged by runtime (tag: kv.*)

Post-deploy validations (0–4h):
- Golden-test suite (10k sanity requests) against cohort: pass rate >= 99.5%
- Compare epoch averages: cache_hit_ratio delta, token_time delta
- Collect 200 sampled traces for deep inspection (trace id list saved to /tmp/mini-canary-traces.txt)
- Metric: rolling 1h window p99 within +10ms, 5xx <= +0.1%

Notes to self / lessons to capture:
- Keep cohort ID short and searchable (mini-2026).
- Prefer single-region first; cross-region can introduce noisy baselines.
- If cache_hit_ratio improves but no latency drop — probable telemetry sampling miss (verify span-level timings).
- Remember: SDK clients that pin tokens aggressively will mask cache improvements; instruct SDK owners on warmup expectations.

Open questions / TODOs:
- [ ] Confirm whether function-calling jobs are affected by eviction TTL (ENG-6529 follow-up).
- [ ] Add a lightweight synthetic that specifically exercises long context retrieval (2000-token warmups).
- [ ] Should we capture kv.trace_id on eviction events? (would help correlate re-gen spikes)

Post-mortem headings (pre-populate):
- Summary of change
- Timeline (timestamps + operator)
- Metrics before/after (graphs + numbers)
- Root cause (if rollback needed)
- Action items (owners + eta)

Housekeeping commands (handy):
- tail logs for cohort: kla logs --service=hosted-api --filter='cohort:mini-2026' --follow
- sample traces: tracing-tool query --filter='cohort=mini-2026' --limit=200 > /tmp/mini-canary-traces.txt
- snapshot dashboard: dashboard-tool snapshot --id=dk-mini-2026 --out=mini-2026-dash.png

If anything weird happens: pause expansion, escalate to SRE on-call, and capture a 15m debug dump (metrics + logs + 50 traces) before any rollback — we may need the data for root cause.

Final thought: tiny and focused wins are easier to reason about. Keep the blast radius minimal and metrics front-and-center.

-- Morgan
(last updated: 2026-02-20)

title: Provision 'integration-playground' Jira project + Confluence space + Slack channel with CI webhook and guest-approval gate
text:
Background: Multiple platform and product teams have asked for a standardized, short-lived integration playground that bundles a Jira project, Confluence runbook space, and Slack channel. The goal is to give cross-functional teams (eng, QA, infra) a consistent place to run integration tests, onboard third-party tools, and exercise deployment hooks without creating ad-hoc spaces that are hard to track.

Request: Create a templated, self-serviceable integration-playground offering with the items below and sensible defaults for lifecycle and security. This ticket captures the provisioning and automation requirements; implementation should be reusable and parameterizable for teams to request via an internal portal/Slack bot in a follow-up story.

Impact: Low immediate risk but high operational value — reduces setup time for integration experiments, reduces noisy ephemeral channels, and centralizes auditability for guest access and CI webhooks.

Jira project: key INTGPLAY, project template = Software Project (Kanban) with issue types: Task, Bug, Experiment. Default components: integration, infra, ci-cd.
Confluence space: 'Integration Playground - INTGPLAY' cloned from a thin template that includes: incident playbook, runbook checklist, onboarding steps, and a 'CI webhook manifest' page.
Slack channel: private channel #intg-play-<team> created automatically during provisioning, members synced from Jira project roles; naming convention enforced.
Service account: 'svc-intg-play-bot' with scoped tokens for Slack app and a GitHub webhook user (rotated monthly).
Automation: on-create hooks that wire a repo webhook to the Confluence CI webhook manifest, and add an issue automation rule to create a runbook page when a 'Release Test' issue is transitioned.
Guest approval flow: external guests require approval from two project owners via an automated request; approval should appear as a Slack message with Approve/Decline buttons that link to Jira request.
Lifecycle policy: default expiry 14 days; channel/space/project archived at expiry and owners emailed 72h before; owners can extend once per archive cycle.
Observability: create a lightweight audit log entry (Confluence page link) summarizing provisioning params and the GitHub repo receiving the webhook.
RBAC: Project role mappings: Owners (can add guests), Members, Read-only observers; Slack members mapped to Jira roles; Confluence restrictions mirroring Jira project roles.

1) Provisioning script must use existing org templates and run with a single approval in Jira. 2) Create a GitHub webhook using a scoped service account and store the webhook secret in the vault. 3) Slack channel creation via Slack provisioning bot with membership synced from Jira project role groups. 4) Add scheduled job that checks for expired projects/spaces/channels and triggers archive workflow plus notification email. 5) All actions must be idempotent and provide human-readable audit output (timestamp, actor, params).

- Owners group: team leads + oncall engineer (default).
- Members group: users explicitly added by Owners.
- Guests: external vendor accounts require 2-owner approval via Slack interactive message.
- Service accounts must be created with least privilege and have an automated rotation policy (30 days).
- No anonymous or public group permissions on Confluence or Jira pages created by this flow.

- Webhook secrets must be stored in Vault/KMS; never placed in Confluence pages.
- Service account keys rotated automatically and usage logged.
- Provisioning job must run in a restricted runner and require token with narrow scope.
- Audit events for create/archive must flow to central audit stream (link logs to observability pipeline).

A templated Jira project INTGPLAY can be provisioned via the internal UI or automation script with parameters for team name and expiry.
Confluence space is created from template and contains runbook and CI webhook manifest page with placeholder fields filled from provisioning parameters.
Slack private channel is created with correct name and membership, and visible in Slack for all members. Approval flow for guests functions end-to-end (request -> 2 approvals -> guest added).
A GitHub webhook is successfully created against a specified repo and triggers a test payload that creates an entry on the Confluence CI webhook page (test harness).
Expiry job archives the Jira project, Confluence space, and Slack channel and sends owner notifications 72h prior.

1) Requestor opens a short form (internal UI or slash command) with params: team_short, owner_emails, repo_url, expiry_days (default 14). 2) Controller creates the Jira project and maps Owners/Members groups. 3) Confluence space cloned from thin template and placeholder fields replaced. 4) Slack channel created and membership synced. 5) Service account and GitHub webhook created; webhook secret stored in Vault. 6) Notification sent to owners with links and a 72h pre-expiry job scheduled.

- Use platform-provisioner library for idempotent resource creation.
- Parameterize template with: team_short, owner_emails, repo_url, expiry_days.
- Vault path: secret/intg-play/{{project_key}}/webhook.
- Use existing Slack provisioning bot but extend membership sync endpoint to accept Jira role groups.
- Add unit tests for webhook lifecycle and a staging dry-run.
- Coordinate final rollout with Security and Compliance for service account onboarding.

Asha Patel (2026-03-10): Filing initial request — would like a reusable implementation that teams can self-service later. Prefer a small productized UI in the portal (follow-up).
Liam O'Connor (2026-03-11): Assigned. Can we confirm if existing 'svc-provisioner' SA can be reused for webhooks or if we require a dedicated svc-intg-play-bot? Security prefers dedicated SA per environment.
Priya Ramesh (Security) (2026-03-11): Security: dedicated service account recommended. Also require monthly key rotation and audit hooks. We'll add review for vault access policy.
Diego Alvarez (Infra) (2026-03-12): Noted. I can add the webhook creation/job into the automation repo. Will need the template Confluence space exported or a short doc describing required pages/variables.

Create internal portal UI story to call this provisioning flow (separate ticket).
Add telemetry: count of active playgrounds and avg lifetime for observability dashboard.
Run a tabletop with two teams to validate guest-approval flow next quarter.
