title: adaptive-scratch-capacity-and-deferred-ckpt-scheduler-for-gpu-workspace-reduction
author: Maya Lin
text:
Reduced GPU peak workspace by up to 28% on long-context models via adaptive scratch allocator and deferred activation checkpoint scheduling. No API changes. Rollout: opt-in via runtime flag 'adaptive_scratch=on' followed by gradual default enablement after smoke validation.

Motivation: GPU workspace (scratch) and activation memory are significant cost drivers for long-context generation and multi-tenant Dedicated pools. Previous changes (arena tuning, static checkpointing) helped but left headroom for per-request adaptation and better interaction with KV cache and continuous batching. This PR implements two coordinated changes: 1) An adaptive scratch allocator that shrinks kernel scratch reservations on hot paths using real allocation traces and a light-weight eviction policy; 2) A deferred activation checkpoint scheduler that opportunistically delays checkpoint insertion until after the kernel selection pass when sequence-to-sequence and KV cache usage are known. Design summary: The adaptive scratch allocator records per-model per-kernel high-water marks over rolling windows and exposes a soft cap that kernels consult at selection time; if the soft cap would be exceeded we attempt two actions: pick a lower-scratch kernel variant or apply a temporary micro-batch split. The deferred checkpoint scheduler moves most activation checkpointing decisions out of the eager graph transform and into the runtime scheduling stage so decisions can use real batch sizes, kv-cache presence, and current scratch headroom. This reduces over-checkpointing on requests that will hit the KV cache and reduces worst-case workspace pressure. Implementation notes: - runtime/inference/scratch_allocator.cpp: new AdaptiveScratchManager, hot-path lock-free counters, bounded trace buffer. - runtime/inference/checkpoint_scheduler.cpp: new DeferredCheckpointPlanner, heuristics to trade memory vs. compute (default: aim for <=15% additional compute). - runtime/kernels/kernel_selector.cpp: kernel variants now expose 'scratch_estimate' and 'checkpoint_safe' metadata; selection integrates with AdaptiveScratchManager. - runtime/scheduler/continuous_batcher.cc: minor changes to expose batching window to planner. - tests/perf/scratch_memory_bench.py: synthetic long-context scenarios across models (gpt-style, encoder-decoder) and KV cache toggles. - docs/ops/scratch-tuning.md: operational guidance and rollout recipe. Tests and results: microbenchmarks show peak GPU workspace reduction of 18-28% across 4 tested models at 32k context; tail latency impact is +4% median, +9% 95th when the allocator picks lower-scratch kernels; overall token throughput for large batches unchanged within noise. KV cache interplay: requests with warm KV cache see much larger benefits because deferred checkpointing avoids storing activations that are unnecessary for cached steps. Safety/rollout: feature gated behind runtime flag 'adaptive_scratch' and 'deferred_ckpt' (both default off). We added a gradual rollout plan: enable in Canary region, observe memory headroom and OOMs for 72h, then opt-in to Dedicated pools with autoscaler guards. Checklist: [x] unit tests, [x] perf scripts, [x] docs updated, [x] rollout plan, [x] security review (no secrets). Backwards compatibility: none; internal only. Related: ENG-3245 (workspace reductions initiative), ENG-3299 (kv-cache improvement spike).

Diego Ramos: This looks promising. Can you add a safety circuit for cases where the allocator oscillates and causes repeated micro-batch splits? Suggest a backoff cooldown per-model.
Maya Lin: Added a cooldown mechanism (AdaptiveScratchManager::cooldown_ms) and tested with aggressive allocation spikes. Benchmarks included in bench_results/2026-02-20.
Lucas Nguyen: The deferred checkpointing change is invasive. How does this interact with tiled-kv cache eviction? Please outline any assumptions about KV lifecycle.
Maya Lin: Deferred planner consults KVCache::is_warmed(request_id) during planning. If KV lifecycle indicates eviction in same window, we conservatively keep checkpoints. Documented in scratch-tuning.md.
Serena Park: CI failed on linux-gpu-lint initially, some style fixes needed in scratch_allocator.h.
Maya Lin: Fixed style nits and added clang-format CI enforcement for runtime/* files.

Merged to main after two rounds of review and CI stabilization. Feature gates left off by default; ops will enable in canary on 2026-02-25. No regressions observed in e2e smoke tests; memory headroom improved on Dedicated canary by ~22% on average.

title: Coalescing Invoker: grace-period batching, deterministic injection, and structured-output streaming compatibility
author: Ava Martinez
text:
Context: Multi-tool call patterns at scale expose a tradeoff between per-request latency and downstream execution overhead when we naively fan out tool invocations. Customers reported jitter in streaming handshakes when several tool results were injected concurrently (see ENG-8921). Motivation: Smooth out spikes from parallel tool warmups and avoid duplicate retries while preserving deterministic injection order (for structured output consumers and OpenAI tool-calling compatibility). This PR implements a lightweight coalescing invoker that introduces a configurable grace period (default 10ms) to allow closely timed tool calls from the same top-level request to batch their execution, plus deterministic merge points for tool-result injection and a coordinated retry protocol that reduces duplicate tool executions. Key changes and design: 1) Grace-window coalescer (api/invoker/coalescer.py): collects tool call intents for a single request context for up to grace_period_ms before dispatching a prioritized execution set. Grace window is short (default 10ms) to keep tail latency bounded; tunable via request-level config. 2) Deterministic mergepoints (runtime/invoker/mergepoint.go): tool results are assigned stable sequence slots at dispatch time so downstream structured output assembly is order-deterministic even if tools finish out-of-order. This preserves existing structured-output expectations and OpenAI function-call ordering semantics. 3) Coordinated retry token (protocol/invoker_retry.proto + runtime): introduces a small idempotency token coupled with a coordinator lease to avoid concurrent retries launching duplicate side effects when multiple workers observe timeouts. Token acquisition is optimistic; fallback retry uses backoff and escalates to a single-quorum retry owner. 4) Streaming handshake stabilizations (api/gateways/openai_compat_stream.go): when streaming a response that will include tool-result injections, the gateway now waits for mergepoint assignment and streams slot-wrapped fragments to clients. We added a lightweight client-side marker in TS SDK so OpenAI-compat clients can present partial structured frames while preserving tool-call streaming expectations. 5) SDK ergonomic surface updates (redwood-sdk-typescript/src/tool-coalesce.ts): a new helper wraps parallel tool calls in a coalesce() helper so application code can opt into the grace-window behavior explicitly (default opt-out). 6) Tests and telemetry: integration tests added for high-concurrency tool scenarios, unit tests for mergepoint sequencing, and new metrics (invoker.coalesce.window_ms, invoker.mergepoint.latency, invoker.retry.quorum_falls) for Console dashboards. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is opt-out via the coalesce helper; internal routing will enable coalescing for customer-tiered policies where cost/perf tradeoffs favor batching (Dedicated plans). For users relying on immediate dispatch, new request flag coalesce=false bypasses the grace window. Rollout plan: feature gated behind runtime flag 'invoker_coalesce_v1'. Start with internal dogfood and canary on perf-canary cluster for 48 hours, then staged enablement on 10% of hosted traffic. Monitoring and observability: dashboards added to the 'invoker' tab in Redwood Console to track coalesce rate, average delay introduced, and any observed regression in percentiles for end-to-end token latency. Risks and mitigations: - Small added latency due to the grace window; mitigated by short default and per-request override. - Complex retry semantics could hide transient failures; mitigated by alerts for quorum_falls and automatic disabling if threshold crossed. Test plan: - unit tests for coalescer (edge cases: zero grace, long tail arrivals) - integration tests simulating 200 concurrent tool calls per request - streaming handshake tests with OpenAI-compat client simulation - load test comparing cost/requests before/after merge. Documentation: docs/api/tool-coalescing.md and an SDK example added in redwood-quickstarts/tool-coalescing-example. Related: builds on earlier tooling around deterministic injection and complements ENG-9047 (structured output regressions), ENG-8921 (streaming jitter incident).

Ravi Patel: Nice direction. A few questions about the retry quorum---can we avoid a blocker where the quorum holder dies before finishing and leaves a duplicate side-effect?
Ava Martinez: We added a short-lived lease with automatic failover; the coordinator will escalate to a quorum-based owner after lease expiry. Added tests to simulate owner crash (see test_invoker_coalesce.py).
Lin Chen: For OpenAI streaming compatibility, are clients expected to upgrade SDK? What's the plan if they don't?
Ava Martinez: Streaming format remains backward compatible. The SDK helper gives better ergonomic surface but gateway emits slot-wrapped fragments that degrade gracefully: older clients will receive plain text stream with injected payloads; new clients get structured frames. Documented in docs/api/tool-coalescing.md.
Marta Kowalska: Performance numbers? I want to make sure P99 doesn't regress for chat workloads.
Ava Martinez: Added perf-canary results in the PR: median increased by 2ms, P95 by 6ms, P99 unchanged within noise. Included flags to disable per-request. See telemetry/dashboards/invoker_coalesce.json.
Ravi Patel: Suggest tightening default grace window to 5ms for hosted tier to be conservative.
Ava Martinez: Reduced default to 10ms for Dedicated and 5ms for Hosted in subsequent commit and added runtime policy to override.

Introduces an opt-in coalescing invoker that batches closely timed tool calls using a short grace window to reduce duplicate warmups and stabilize streaming handshakes. Adds deterministic mergepoints for ordered tool-result injection and a coordinated retry token to minimize duplicate side-effects. Opt-in via SDK helper or request flag; gated rollout.

title: Runtime workload signatures and SLO derivation playbook
author: Leah Kim
text:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes a repeatable process for converting observed runtime workload signatures into defensible Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and cost-sensitivity profiles for Redwood inference services. It ties together sampling, profiling, experiment design, and SLO derivation so teams can make consistent, evidence-based SLOs for new routes, model variants, and capacity plans.

Scope
-----
Applies to: all inference-facing HTTP/streaming routes and internal RPCs that contribute to model-serving latency or cost. Excludes: purely offline batch jobs (see eng-infra runbooks) and human-in-the-loop lab experiments.

Definitions
-----------
- Workload signature: a compact description of request shape and distribution (sequence length percentiles, batching patterns, KV cache hit ratio, request concurrency, special flags like streaming or tool-calls).
- Cost-sensitivity: the change in per-request GPU/time cost when a workload attribute shifts (e.g., +10 tokens => +X ms / +Y token-cost).
- SLO bucket: a named target (e.g., P95 latency 120ms for interactive, P99 500ms for high-throughput) tailored for a workload class.

Key Principles
--------------
- Evidence-first: SLOs must be justified by sampled production telemetry and controlled experiments.
- Workload-driven segmentation: avoid one-size-fits-all SLOs; segment by signature clusters that materially change cost/latency.
- Cost-aware guardrails: every SLO must include an associated cost-sensitivity statement used for tradeoff decisions (e.g., whether to enable larger batch sizes or fallback to cheaper model variants).
- Operational observability: each derived SLO must have dashboards, automated alerts, and an attached experiment plan for periodic revalidation.

Procedure: Derive SLOs from workload signatures (step-by-step)
-----------------------------------------------------------
1. Collect signatures (1–2 weeks):
 - Instrument route to emit compact signature blobs at sampling rate 1–5% (configurable per traffic volume). Required fields: route_id, timestamp, seq_len, input_tokens, output_tokens, kv_cache_hit, streaming_flag, client_tier, model_variant_hint.
 - Example signature JSON (emit to telemetry):

 {
 "route_id": "generate-chat",
 "timestamp": "2025-10-28T14:12:33Z",
 "seq_len": 1024,
 "input_tokens": 128,
 "output_tokens": 256,
 "kv_cache_hit": 0.62,
 "streaming_flag": false,
 "client_tier": "standard"
 }

2. Cluster signatures (offline job):
 - Run k-means / hierarchical clustering on normalized features: seq_len, total_tokens, kv_cache_hit, streaming_flag (binary), concurrency_hint. Aim for 3–6 clusters per route unless variance indicates more.
 - Save cluster centroids and representative percentiles (p50/p90/p99) for each numeric field.

3. Profile representative clusters (controlled experiments):
 - For each cluster, replay 10k representative requests against target model variants and runtime configurations (batch sizes, quantization profiles, kernel paths). Collect: p50/p90/p99 latencies, tail latency (p999), token throughput, GPU utilization, memory pressure, failure rate.
 - Record cost-per-request estimate (energy + GPU time + amortized infra) using the internal cost-modeler.

4. Construct candidate SLO buckets:
 - Use profiling results to propose SLOs that are achievable with a 95% confidence margin given current infra. Example logic: set P95 latency target to profiling p90 + 15% buffer; set error-rate target to observed mean + 3σ but not exceeding 1%.

5. Attach cost-sensitivity and fallback policy:
 - For each SLO, include a table showing how latency and cost change when you: increase batch_by, enable quantization Q4/Q5, or downgrade to smaller model variant.
 - Define automatic fallback thresholds (e.g., if queue length > 200 and P95 approaching target, route 20% to cheaper variant).

6. Review and publish with runbook:
 - Include owners (service, infra, SRE), approval from product for user-facing impact, and security sign-off when signatures include user data.

7. Deploy SLO and monitor:
 - Create dashboards that show per-cluster SLI trends, cost-per-1000-requests, and deviation from target. Configure alerts: SLO_red (p95 > target for 10m), SLO_yellow (p95 > 90% of target for 15m), cost_alert (cost growth > 20% week-over-week for the cluster).

Representative table: sample SLO derivation for a chat-gen route
----------------------------------------------------------------
| Cluster | Centroid seq_len (p90) | Profiling p95 | Proposed SLO (p95) | Cost/request | Fallback action |
|---------|------------------------:|-------------:|-------------------:|-------------:|-----------------|
| Short-turn | 64 | 80 ms | 95 ms | $0.0009 | no fallback, optimize batching |
| Normal | 256 | 160 ms | 190 ms | $0.0021 | enable burst batching or route 10% to smaller model |
| Long-turn | 1024 | 420 ms | 500 ms | $0.0065 | enable quantization Q4 + degrade non-critical tools |

(When converting to Confluence markup, render as a table with exact values and links to profiling runs.)

Cost-sensitivity matrix (example)
--------------------------------
- Changing batch_size from 1 -> 8 on `Normal` cluster: +20% p95, -30% cost/request.
- Enabling Q4 quantization on `Long-turn`: +12% p95, -45% cost/request, memory drop 18%.

Operational playbook snippets
---------------------------
- When an SLO_red fires (p95 > target for 10m):
 1. Pager to oncall (SRE) and service owner.
 2. Run the quick triage checklist: confirm signature cluster involved, verify ongoing experiment/rollout, check GPU node saturation and preemption events.
 3. If saturation: trigger temporary priority decay policy and increase fallthrough to cheaper variant per SLO fallback policy.
 4. Post-incident: schedule a 2-hour root-cause session and update SLO derivation if recurring.

Best practices and guidance
---------------------------
- Prefer cluster-specific SLIs rather than global route-level; combine for a user-facing composite only when necessary.
- Maintain an experiment repository: every profiling run must have a reproducible seed, input corpus, model hash, and runtime flags.
- Re-derive SLAs quarterly or when a model variant, kernel path, or major infra change is shipped.
- Use conservative buffers for user-facing production routes (15–25%) and tighter buffers for internal tooling (5–10%).

Example: small CLI to extract centroids from signatures (pseudo)
------------------------------------------------------------
# sample: extract centroids for route `generate-chat`
python tools/signature_agg.py 
 --input s3://redwood-telemetry/signatures/generate-chat/2025-10/ 
 --sample-rate 0.02 
 --cluster 4 
 --output /tmp/generate-chat-centroids.json

Ownership and governance
------------------------
- Owner: runtime-performance@redwood (primary service owner)
- SRE: oncall-sre@redwood for alerts and incident response
- Review cadence: annual architecture review and post-major-release revalidation.
- Metrics steward: product-analytics for cost attribution and SLA reporting.

References and related pages
----------------------------
- service-profiling-experiment-matrix-and-slo-extrapolation-2026 (profiling matrix and test harness)
- runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026 (kernel selection tradeoffs)
- infra-standards/resource-qos-and-profiling-playbook-2024 (node qos and resource tagging)

Appendix: template for SLO record (to be copied into the SLO catalog)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
- route_id: string
- cluster_id: string
- cluster_signature_examples: list of example signature ids
- derived_SLOs: list of {metric: p95 latency, target_ms: number, buffer_pct: number}
- cost_sensitivity: list of {action: quantize/batch/downgrade, delta_cost_pct: number, delta_latency_pct: number}
- profiling_run_ids: list of run ids
- owners: list of emails
- rollback_plan: short text

Contact
-------
For questions or to request a signature sampling rollout, contact runtime-performance@redwood or open a ticket in the Performance channel.

title: Compact benchmark result store + comparison canvas and triage playbook
author: Maya Liu
text:
Implement a compact, query-friendly storage layer for benchmark/time-series artifacts plus a lightweight comparison canvas UI and an operator-focused anomaly triage playbook. Deliverables: (1) a tersely indexed result store that optimizes for frequent p95 and tokens/sec lookups and fingerprint-based regression grouping; (2) an interactive comparison canvas that supports pairwise overlay, histogram diff, and deltas by model variant/quantization/hardware; (3) a documented triage workflow with playbook runbooks and automation hooks for alerting and suggested root-cause buckets.

Result store supports efficient time-range queries for p50/p95/tokens_per_sec and returns top-10 regressions by delta in <500ms for 90% of queries
Comparison canvas renders pairwise time-aligned overlays and delta histograms for two benchmark runs within 2s for median users
Regression grouping by fingerprint (prompt hashing + exemplar embeddings) surface reduces duplicate alerts by >=40% in internal tests
Triage playbook includes RBAC owners, severity mapping, automatic triage suggestions, and links to infra metrics (GPU utilization, kernel selection logs)

Index-first vs blob-first: chose compact columnar index (time-series + small metadata) with cold blob store for raw traces to keep fast queries on common aggregates
Fingerprinting: use 64-bit locality-preserving hash + sample embedding signature to avoid bloom filter false positives; accepts slight risk of collisions but reduces grouping noise
Retention: keep high-resolution traces for 30 days, aggregated rollups for 1 year to balance disk costs vs triage fidelity
UI complexity: prefer an opinionated comparison canvas (limited toggle set) over a fully generic plotting studio to speed iteration and avoid user paralysis

Storage: new table `bench_series_compact` in timeseries DB (schema: run_id, model_variant, hw_tier, metric, time_bucket, value, fingerprint, rollup_key)
Serialization: values compressed with ZSTD level 3 and delta-encoded per-run for tokens/sec and latencies
API: add endpoints /bench/v1/compare and /bench/v1/top-regressions with query params (metric, window, baseline_run_id, target_run_id)
UI: React canvas component integrated into Console -> Benchmarks. Use canvas-level WebSocket for streaming live comparisons
Alerting: wire comparison deltas into existing anomaly-detector; add confidence score and suggested triage category tags

2026-02-12: spike completed comparing Postgres timeseries vs ClickHouse column store for our query patterns. ClickHouse favored for aggregate-heavy queries.
2026-02-18: prototype index schema implemented and microbenchmarks show 3x faster p95 lookups vs existing blob store on sample dataset (10M rows).
2026-02-26: initial React canvas wireframe reviewed by PM + Design (Julia Park). Feedback: surface baseline selection and auto-align by prompt fingerprint by default.
2026-03-03: integration test failing intermittently when combining fingerprint grouping with model-variant fallbacks; root cause likely upstream canonicalization bug (ENG-84912 referenced).
2026-03-10: backend API stabilized; deployed to staging. Beginning UI integration tests and triage doc drafting.
2026-03-12: triage playbook draft reviewed by oncall perf (Ravi Patel) and ML infra (Aisha Khan). Added an automatic checklist for kernel-selection, batch-size, and cache-hit-rate checks.

Julia Park (Design): keep comparison canvas controls compact; prioritize delta histogram and p95 timeline. Remove free-form plotting in MVP.
Ravi Patel (SRE): add GPU kernel logs correlation in triage view; include a link that pre-fills a trace query with time window from regression event.
Aisha Khan (ML Infra): recommend retaining raw KV-cache hit logs for 7 days even if traces age out to help intermittent cache-related regressions
Security (Lara Voss): ensure any run artifacts with customer prompts are automatically redacted before long-term storage (we will add redaction hook in ingestion pipeline)

Finish frontend compare canvas implementation and hookup /bench/v1/compare streaming endpoint
Complete ClickHouse schema migration and fill initial rollups for prod shard 3
Add automation to anomaly-detector to add suggested triage tags and a first-pass root-cause bucket
Run end-to-end fault injection: simulate kernel fallback, quantization variant mismatch, and network egress to validate triage playbook steps

When an alert fires with confidence >0.7, open comparison canvas with baseline pinned to last-successful-run; follow triage checklist
If triage indicates kernel selection regression, escalate to ML Infra and add tag 'kernel-regression' to incident.
If fingerprint grouping returns >10 unique groups for same prompt hash, toggle to sample-mode to inspect exemplar prompts and check redaction pipeline

title: Stratus Vector Vault
author: Jordan Patel
text:
Summary: Stratus Vector Vault — enterprise search provider for financial services and media conglomerates. Large existing vector store (on-prem) under consideration for migration to Redwood Dedicated/Private.
Scale targets: baseline index size 600M vectors (512-d), projected growth to 1.2B in 18 months; daily ingest ~8–12M vectors, weekly batch exports ~50M.
Latency/throughput: target tail-latency (p99) <100ms for top-50, median <30ms for top-10; throughput target 2k qps for peak queries on business hours.
Reranking flow: dense ANN for recall -> candidate pool 500-10k -> cross-encoder rerank for final top-10. Want Redwood support for two-stage rerank with on-the-fly batching of cross-encoder.
Cost targets: aim for $0.0005–$0.002 per end-to-end query (including embedding lookup + cross-encoder rerank). Extremely cost sensitive at scale.
Technical preferences: 8-bit / 4-bit quantized emb model support, GPU-accelerated FAISS-like ANN, prefix/KV caching for common queries, adaptive batching to preserve latency SLOs.
Data residency & security: EU customer data residency required for EU accounts; must support SSO/SAML, KMS-integrated key management, audit logs retained 2+ years.
Deployment interest: leaning toward Redwood Dedicated with Private control plane in EU region; open to hybrid (on-prem gateway + Redwood managed backplane).
POC scope requested: ingest 600M sample (anonymized) + run 2-week traffic replay; measure p99 latency, end-to-end cost, rerank recall/precision on internal eval sets.
Quote from CTO: "We need sub-50ms for conversational retrieval paths or business UX will suffer; cost at scale is non-negotiable."
Infra notes: will provide parquet exports (~2.5TB compressed) for vector ingest; require advice on sharding strategy, quantization profile recommendations.
Procurement: legal needs data-processing addendum + EU data-residency clause; procurement approval estimated 3–6 weeks after POC if metrics met.
Previous vendors: current pilot with in-house FAISS + Kubernetes; evaluated Pinecone and Milvus — main gaps were cost per q and rerank integration.
Internal stakeholders: CTO (Anna Kline), Head of Search (Derek Osei), Platform Lead (Nadia Fischer), Security (Head: Marco Silveira).
Requested deliverables: POC SOW, sample infra sizing, preliminary cost model (per 100M vectors), canary rollout plan for migration.

2024-09-12 — Lead created from inbound webinar (scale-search for enterprise). AE Jordan Patel assigned.
2024-09-25 — Intro call: high-level requirements, shared initial architecture doc (drive link). Action: send scale-specific POC template.
2024-10-07 — Deep technical call w/ SE (Maya Chen) — discussed batching, KV cache, quantization. Fireflies ff-20241021-98ab captured details.
2024-10-21 — Provided preliminary cost model and suggested Dedicated sizing (rationale doc). Drive: poc-stratus-pricing-v1.pdf.
2024-11-06 — Security questionnaire submission; red team follow-up scheduled. Fireflies ff-20241106-21fd.
2024-11-14 — Onsite demo + replay plan agreed; legal requested DPA + EU residency clause.
2024-11-15 — Redwood delivered infra sizing first draft; waiting for Stratus to supply anonymized sample.

title: Update Private upgrade docs: new installer commands, troubleshooting, rollback guidance
author: Elliot Price
text:
Summary: Align Private (VPC + on-prem/air-gapped) upgrade/rollback documentation with the new installer workflow: plan -> prechecks -> backup -> apply -> verify -> rollback (if needed). This updates the operator-facing steps, introduces troubleshooting playbooks for common precheck and upgrade failures, and clarifies rollback guarantees/limitations (esp. around schema migrations and partial rollouts). Motivation: Support escalations and design partner feedback indicated the previous docs were ambiguous about (a) which checks are blocking vs warning, (b) what gets backed up and how to validate restore readiness, and (c) when rollback is safe vs when manual intervention is required. This PR is the docs companion to private-installer changes (upgrade plan generator, preflight framework, backup orchestrator, rollback state machine) and Helm ordering changes (control plane before data plane). Audience/visibility: Internal runbooks + external-ish docs pages that are shared with Private customers under guidance. What changed (high level): 1) Rewrote the main upgrade procedure to use new commands and phase naming: Generate plan, Run prechecks, Create backup, Apply upgrade (control plane then data plane), Post-upgrade verification, Capture artifacts/support bundle. 2) Added a troubleshooting index for: precheck failures (storage headroom, DB connectivity, OIDC reachability, TLS/DNS), migration lock timeouts, stuck Helm hooks/jobs, artifact/bundle verification errors for air-gapped upgrades, and rollback failures. 3) Added explicit rollback guidance: rollback entry points, expected time, health checks, and a decision tree for 'rollback vs fix-forward' based on stage. 4) Updated on-prem/air-gapped section with offline bundle verification expectations (checksums/signatures), mirror endpoints, and common operator mistakes. 5) Added an 'Upgrade artifacts for auditability' section describing what the installer persists (plan JSON, precheck results, backup IDs, execution log, audit events) and what to attach to support tickets. Notes: This PR intentionally does not introduce net-new policy; it documents the gating/checklist already being formalized elsewhere. Where behavior is still being finalized, wording is 'as of Private installer >= 1.9.0' and points to release notes. Checklist: - [x] Steps match installer CLI (plan/apply/rollback) - [x] Troubleshooting covers top 5 support cases (SUP-18421, SUP-18488, SUP-18510, SUP-18577) - [x] On-prem/air-gapped guidance includes bundle verification and offline registries - [x] Security reviewed language around backups/secrets (no plaintext exports, KMS/HSM expectations) - [x] Link check + docs build + Vale pass

Kira Thompson (requested changes): The procedure still mentions the old 'upgrade run' command in two places; please replace with plan/apply and ensure rollback references the stored upgrade state path. Also add a short 'what success looks like' section with concrete verification commands. Elliot Price (author): Fixed the remaining 'upgrade run' references, added a 'Success criteria' block under Post-upgrade verification (pods ready, API /healthz, control plane connectivity, sample inference request), and clarified the default state directory plus flag overrides. Connor O'Brien: Please call out that upgrades are supported N-1 -> N for GA, and that skipping minors is 'unsupported unless explicitly approved'. Also add a sentence about upgrade windows and release gating. Elliot Price: Added 'Supported upgrade paths' section and pointed to the release gating page; included language that multi-hop is not automated in v1. Rafael Mendes: Troubleshooting for migration lock timeouts should include the mitigation we used in staging (check for long-running transactions + retry after backoff), and the strong warning about not deleting migration jobs blindly. Elliot Price: Added a dedicated 'Migration lock timeout' page with safe mitigations and a 'do not' list. title: Predictive Throttling and Cache Coherence Playbook for Cross-Tenant Inference
author: Maya Patel
text:
Summary:
This playbook defines the predictive throttling and cache coherence strategy for cross-tenant inference traffic. It prescribes SLO-aware admission control, tenant CPU/GPU slot allocation, cache warming and invalidation primitives, instrumentation, and an operational runbook for diagnosing and mitigating tenant-induced QoS degradation. This is intended for teams operating Redwood-hosted clusters and Redwood Dedicated fleets; private deployments may adapt the policies but must maintain equivalent SLO guarantees.

Goals:
- Ensure 99.9% P95 latency SLO for latency-class A tenants under normal load.
- Limit cross-tenant cache pollution such that effective hit-rate loss < 5% for pinned-models.
- Bound tail-cost variance: no single tenant can increase cluster per-token cost by >10% in a 5-minute window.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to inference-serving runtime (service: inference-router, kv-coordinator, runtime-executor).
- Targets multi-tenant GPU pools (pool types: shared-gpu, reserved-gpu).
- Does NOT replace tenant-level quotas; supplements with adaptive, SLO-driven rules.

Key concepts and definitions:
- Predictive Throttling: A short-horizon controller that uses per-tenant request-rate forecasts and runtime signals (queue length, kernel utilization) to decide admission or redirection.
- Cache Affinity Window: Temporal window (default 60s) during which a tenant retains soft affinity to KV cache entries created by its requests.
- CPU/GPU Slotting: Lightweight allocation of fractional executor capacity for long-running streaming or stateful sessions.

SLOs and thresholds (default values):
| SLO/Metric | Target | Action threshold | Critical threshold |
|------------|--------|------------------|--------------------|
| P95 latency (latency-A) | <= 90ms | P95 > 120ms (5min) | P95 > 200ms (5min) |
| Cache effective hit-rate (pinned-models) | >= 85% | hit-rate drops 10% vs baseline | hit-rate drops 20% |
| Per-tenant 5-min cost delta | <= +10% | > +15% | > +25% (escalate) |

Architecture and control loop:
1) Signal collection: inference-router emits per-request telemetry (latency class, model-id, tenant-id, KV-touch-set). kv-coordinator reports cache occupancy and evictions per tenant. runtime-executor exports GPU utilization and kernel latency histograms.
2) Forecasting: short-window predictor (Holt-Winters with decay or lightweight ML predictor) estimates next 30–60s request volume per tenant.
3) Admission decision: controller computes tenant score = alpha * predicted_rate + beta * current_queue + gamma * cpu_utilization. If score exceeds pool threshold, controller will:
 - Deny best-effort requests (HTTP 429 with structured retry-after and cost_hint)
 - Redirect to cheaper model variant (if tenant policy permits)
 - Enforce slotting limit on streaming sessions (soft pause or scale-down)
4) Cache coherence actions: when tenant-induced eviction rate for pinned-models > eviction_threshold (default 0.12), controller reduces admission for offending tenants and triggers proactive prefetching for affected tenants.

Config sample (YAML - runtime controller):
controller:
 pool_check_interval: 2s
 predictive_horizon_seconds: 45
 tenant_score_weights:
 predicted_rate: 0.6
 queue_length: 0.25
 gpu_util: 0.15
 admission_action_order: [deny, redirect, slot_limit]
 eviction_threshold: 0.12
 cache_affinity_window_seconds: 60
 cost_delta_alert_pct: 15

Telemetry and observability requirements:
- Required metrics: tenant.p95_latency_ms, tenant.predicted_rps, tenant.queue_length, tenant.kv_eviction_rate, tenant.gpu_util_percent, tenant.cost_delta_pct.
- Required spans: /v1/generate entry and exit; kv-coordinator cache hit path with tenant-id tag.
- Dashboards: Tenant QoS dashboard (per-tenant heatmap), Pool health (aggregate tail latencies), Cache coherency panel (eviction rates by model/tenant).
- Alerts:
 - Alert THROTTLE_HIGH when >5% of tenants in a pool are in admission-deny state for >3m.
 - Alert CACHE_STRESS when pinned-model hit-rate drops >15% for >2m.

Operational runbook (triage steps):
1) Detect: Pager triggers for THROTTLE_HIGH or CACHE_STRESS.
2) Identify affected pool and tenants: use Tenant QoS dashboard -> filter by pool_id.
3) Gather evidence: export last 15m of tenant.* metrics and trace samples for top 5 tenants by predicted_rps.
4) Mitigate (fast path):
 - For runaway tenant (high predicted_rps + high evictions): temporarily apply hard quota (deny requests) and notify Customer Success.
 - For spike caused by model checkpoint change (increased KV footprint): trigger emergency cache prewarm for pinned-models and increase cache_affinity_window to 120s for impacted tenants.
 - For kernel-level saturation (GPU util ~ 100%): shift low-priority tenants to reserved-gpu-burst topology if configured.
5) Post-mortem: capture root cause (bug, user behavior, model change), performance impact (tokens, cost), and corrective actions. Update tenant-specific runbooks.

Testing and rollout plan:
- Unit tests: controller scoring logic, admission decision matrix, synthetic predictor inputs.
- Staging: run controller in observe-only mode for 2 weeks against shadow traffic. Evaluate false positive/negative rate for admission decisions.
- Canary: enable admission actions for 5% of traffic in a single pool; monitor THROTTLE_HIGH and SLO regressions for 48 hours.
- Gradual rollout: increase to 25% then 100% across pools, with automated rollback if P95 regressions exceed 10% above baseline.

Compatibility and integration notes:
- API contract: admission responses must follow structured error schema (application/json) with fields: code, message, retry_after_seconds, suggested_model_variant. See API standard: canonical-request-schema-and-validation-playbook-2025 for format.
- SDKs should surface 429 with retry metadata to customers and include a client-side backoff that respects suggested retry_after.
- Private deployments: controller configuration defaults may be more conservative; ensure equivalent unit tests and telemetry hooks are installed.

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary owners: runtime-inference team (oncall rotation: runtime-inference@redwood.com).
- Secondary owners: infra-sre (capacity & node-level interventions), platform-telemetry (dashboard/alert maintenance).
- Escalation matrix:
 1) runtime-inference pager (P1)
 2) infra-sre lead (within 15 minutes)
 3) Eng director oncall if incident not contained within 1 hour

Open questions and decision notes (ADR candidates):
- ADR Candidate A: Standardize tenant score formula and weight calibration across pool shapes. Proposed owner: Miguel Santos.
- ADR Candidate B: Define canonical tenant cost attribution window (5m vs 15m) used by controller and billing systems. Proposed owner: Finance-legal to coordinate.

Appendix A — Example 429 payload (JSON):
{
 "code": "THROTTLED_TENANT",
 "message": "Traffic exceeds current pool capacity; retry after the suggested delay or use a lower-cost model variant.",
 "retry_after_seconds": 30,
 "suggested_model_variant": "model-123-quantized"
}

Appendix B — Simulation test matrix:
- Scenario 1: Single tenant ramp from 10 RPS -> 500 RPS in 60s. Expected outcome: predictor flags spike; admission reduces best-effort by 70% and redirects 30% to cheaper variants.
- Scenario 2: 20 tenants uniform ramp; expected outcome: pool-level smoothing kicks in; no single tenant enters deny state; tail latency within SLO.
- Scenario 3: Model rollout with new checkpoint increasing KV footprint by 3x; expected outcome: temporary hit-rate degradation; trigger prewarm and affinity window extension.

References and related docs:
- runtime-architecture/adaptive-kv-coordinator-and-eviction-contract-2026
- performance-standards/traffic-smoothing-and-elastic-latency-budgets-standards-2026
- api-standards/canonical-request-schema-and-validation-playbook-2025

Revision history:
- 2025-10-12: Initial draft by Maya Patel.
- 2025-12-01: Added predictive scoring weights and cache prewarm procedure (reviewer: Ethan Rivera).
- 2026-02-20: Finalized alerts and rollout plan (reviewer: Lina Hoffmann).

title: KV-cache lock contention causing SSE/WebSocket chat stream to stall mid-generation
text:
Issue summary:
Customers using the dedicated cluster for Syntaxly report streaming chat (SSE and WebSocket) sessions stalling mid-generation. The generation process continues on the worker (model tokens advance) but clients stop receiving chunks for ~10-30s, then either receive a burst of tokens or the connection is closed. Impact affects a subset of long-context sessions that exercise prefix/KV cache heavily.

Impact:
- Multiple customers using dedicated clusters experienced degraded user-facing streaming with partial token delivery and timeouts for long responses.
- Symptoms occur intermittently under sustained bursty traffic and while background cache eviction/compaction is active.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool in prod | us-east-1
- Customer: Syntaxly (dedicated tenant)
- Models observed: redwood/vicuna-13b (main), redwood/vicuna-7b (also observed)

Observed behavior:
- Client SSE/WebSocket receives initial tokens, then stream silence for 10-30s while server logs show continuing generation activity; afterwards either a token burst or stream closure with 499/502 seen at proxies.
- Internal worker metrics show increased mutex wait times on kv-cache locks concurrent with GC/eviction cycles.

Expected behavior:
- Continuous streaming with small inter-chunk intervals (<200ms typical) and graceful fallback if worker evicted.

Steps to reproduce (high-level):
1) On a dedicated customer pool, start a long chat generation with ~8k prompt + multi-turn history that hits prefix cache reads.
2) Send multiple near-simultaneous streaming requests from different clients to increase contention on cache read/write paths.
3) Observe one or more streams stalling mid-generation while worker logs progress.

Provision a dedicated cluster in us-east-1 (or use Syntaxly replica).
Load a long-context conversation (~8k tokens) and ensure prefix cache entries are created.
From 3+ clients send streaming requests simultaneously that reuse prefixes (e.g., same system prompts with per-turn deltas).
Monitor SSE/WebSocket client for mid-generation silence and check worker logs for kv_cache lock wait messages.

[2026-03-12T15:21:03Z] serving-runtime[worker-7]: generation: step=312 emit_chunk size=128 status=blocked kv_cache: lock_wait=312ms
[2026-03-12T15:21:03Z] kv-cache[pool-3]: WARNING lock_wait_exceeded key=prefix:acct-42:conv-19 wait_ms=311
[2026-03-12T15:21:33Z] nginx[proxy-12]: upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header from upstream, client: 10.9.2.7, server: redwood-host
[2026-03-12T15:21:34Z] serving-runtime[worker-7]: generation: token=... continued after lock (burst emit 220 tokens)

15:30 - Support triaged and confirmed identical symptom with Syntaxly reproducer. Customer provided a request_id and SSE capture.
16:05 - SRE attached flamegraphs from the affected node: top contributor is kv-cache mutex wait during eviction sweep.
16:45 - We observed correlation between eviction/compaction and increased per-request latency in chunk emission; not all nodes show the spike (appears on nodes with heavy shared-prefix reuse).
17:15 - Reproduced locally with stress test that simulates prefix reuse and concurrent updates: measured lock contention and per-chunk emission stalls on the read path when eviction kicks in.
18:00 - Linked to recent kv-cache compaction change (PR 398) that introduced a coalesced eviction pass holding a global lock for longer periods under load.

KV cache compaction/eviction holds a global lock that blocks read path for streams. During compaction, worker threads are blocked waiting on the lock which delays writing stream chunks to the connection; network proxies treat the silence as stalled and sometimes close the connection or a burst of buffered data is delivered later.

Partial stream losses and timeouts for heavy long-context streaming sessions. Reported by Syntaxly (enterprise) customers in production; estimated 3-7% of streaming requests in peak windows for that tenant.

Short-term: reduce cache compaction frequency and/or increase kv-cache shard count for affected dedicated pool. For customer Syntaxly, we temporarily disabled compaction on their pool which reduced occurrences. Also recommended client-side reconnect-with-offset fallback in their SDK until fix is rolled out.

Back out or patch PR 398 that increased compaction lock duration and ship a lock-free read path for compaction (engineering).
Prepare a hotfix PR to reduce compaction batch size and add metrics for lock hold time (priority).
Schedule rolling restart of affected serving nodes after patch to avoid transient lock states (SRE).
Communicate mitigation and ETA to customer success and Syntaxly.

(in progress) Hotfix branch created for kv-cache with fine-grained compaction locks. Initial tests show removal of >200ms lock waits under stress. Rolling patch targeted for 2026-03-15 02:00 UTC with low-traffic window. Will update after deployment and customer validation.

2026-03-12T16:00Z | Aisha Patel (Support): Logged on behalf of Syntaxly — they see repeated SSE stalls and provided request IDs SUP-725410-req-0a7 and SSE capture. Marking P1 due to customer SLA.
2026-03-12T16:20Z | Marcus O'Neill (SRE): Collected node metrics and flamegraphs; seeing kv-cache mutex wait spikes correlating to stalls. Attaching node-7 flamegraph link: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/xyz/node-7-flame
2026-03-12T17:40Z | Riley Chen (Engineer): Reproduced locally. Root cause likely related to recent compaction change. Drafting fix — will open PR for reduced lock scope.
2026-03-12T19:05Z | Diego Martinez (Customer Success): Notified Syntaxly that we have a mitigation (disable compaction) and we will roll a patch ASAP. Syntaxly will validate after patch and provide feedback.
2026-03-14T01:10Z | Riley Chen (Engineer): Hotfix PR created: https://github.com/redwood-inference/kv-cache/pull/412 — implementing sharded compaction and read-prefetch to avoid global lock. Running integration tests now.

title: Commercial terms tiering and revenue trigger playbook
author: Marcus Chen
text:
Summary

This playbook describes how commercial contract terms (pricing tiers, usage modifiers, discounts, bundled services, and commencement triggers) map to billing actions and revenue recognition decisions at Redwood Inference. It is intended for Finance, Legal, Pricing, and Sales Ops. The playbook codifies a decision matrix, an escalation path for non‑standard terms, and representative examples with implementation notes for the billing engine and RevRec journal entries.

Scope

- Applies to all enterprise and dedicated/private deployment contracts (Deals > $50k ARR) and any subscription agreements with non-standard pricing modifiers (e.g., volume tiers, committed burst hours, carryover credits, multi-region add-ons).
- Does NOT replace contract-level legal review; Legal must approve any deviation flagged by this playbook.
- Covers: pricing tiering, effective date vs delivery date, prepaid credits, committed capacity, overage treatment, trial-to-paid cutovers, and marketplace/reseller flows.

Key definitions

1. Effective Date: the date the contract becomes binding. Often the signature date. For RevRec, this is only the start of evaluation; revenue recognition generally aligns to delivery/performance obligations.
2. Commencement Event: the event that begins service delivery for billing and RevRec (examples: activation of VPC link, first inference request, seat provisioning).
3. Billing Trigger: the system-generated event that starts an invoice or consumes pre-paid credits.
4. Committed Capacity: a reserved pool (e.g., Dedicated GPUs) with minimum monthly/annual payments.
5. Modifier: any term that adjusts list price (discount, volume tier, burst add-on, region multiplier).

Decision matrix overview

The table below is the canonical mapping used by Finance and Billing to convert contract terms into system actions and RevRec method. Use this as the first point of reference for pricing or recognition questions.

| Contract Term Type | Billing Trigger | Invoice Timing | RevRec Treatment | Owner | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Subscription (flat monthly) | Commencement Event | Monthly in arrears | Recognize evenly over month (monthly performance obligation) | Finance - Billing | Standard SaaS model. |
| Annual prepay (non-refundable) | Effective Date with deferred revenue schedule | Bill at Effective Date | Deferred revenue; recognize monthly/quarterly over contract term | Finance - RevRec | Use amort schedule; tie to contracted term. |
| Committed capacity (reserved GPUs) | Activation of dedicated pool | Monthly/Quarterly per contract | Recognize over committed period; any unused capacity remains prepaid | Finance/Revenue | Track usage separately for churn/true-up. |
| Usage-based (per-token/per-embedding) | First billable request after trial | Monthly in arrears with usage detail | Recognize when usage occurs (consumption) | Billing/Platform | Ensure token counts validated by platform telemetry before invoicing. |
| Overages vs commit | At overage threshold crossing or true‑up date | Invoice on next cycle or immediate true-up invoice | Recognize when overage is billed or service delivered | Finance & Sales Ops | True-ups for committed pools follow contract cadence. |
| One-time setup or professional services | Completion milestone (SOW sign-off) | Bill per milestone | Recognize at milestone completion | GTM / Finance | SOW must specify acceptance criteria. |

Rules and thresholds (operationalized)

- Billing trigger priority: 1) Customer-specified commencement event; 2) Platform activation signal; 3) Effective Date fallback.
- Minimum invoice detail: invoice must include contract id, pricing tier, usage breakdown (tokens, inference-minutes, embeddings), and applied modifiers.
- Dispute threshold: any invoice with a discrepancy > 2% or > $5k should be flagged to FinanceOps for hold and routed to the billing dispute queue.
- Price protection adjustment window: for enterprise multi-year contracts, Pricing adjustments for inflation/cost-pass are allowed only with explicit contractual language; default is no unilateral increase.

Implementation notes for billing engine (technical team tasks)

1. Contract parsing and normalized model: ensure the billing engine stores these normalized fields for every contract: contract_id, effective_date, commencement_event_id, committed_capacity_units, tier_breakpoints, modifiers (type, percent/absolute), billing_cycle, revrec_schedule_id.
2. Event wiring: platform must emit standardized events (activation:event, first_request:event, true_up:date) to the billing queue. These event names should be kept stable; any schema changes require a deprecation notice and 90‑day backwards compatibility.
3. Validation: billing engine should verify token counts against platform telemetry within a 1% tolerance window before invoicing. Exceptions escalate to FinanceOps.
4. Audit trail: every invoice must store a hash of the source contract PDF and a snapshot of the normalized pricing fields used to compute the invoice.

Escalation and approvals (non-standard commercial terms)

1. Sales rep proposes non‑standard modifier (e.g., negative margin commercial term, unusual holdback clause). Sales Ops creates a deviation request in the Contract Deviation tracker and assigns to Pricing.
2. Pricing reviews and produces margin impact and recommended counter-proposals within 3 business days.
3. If margin impact > 15% or legal risk flagged, route to Commercial Review Board (CRB): members include Head of Finance, Lead Counsel, Head of Sales and Head of Product (for technical feasibility). CRB target turnaround: 5 business days.
4. CRB decision recorded in the tracker; if approved, Legal drafts the amendment language and Finance creates corresponding RevRec schedule template.

Representative examples

Example A — Committed Dedicated Pool with Carryover Credits
- Term: 12 months starting Effective Date 2027-03-01
- Committed capacity: 1000 GPU-hours/month, billed monthly at $X/hr; unused hours carry over up to 2 months.
- Billing: bill monthly in arrears based on committed fee; true-up at each quarter if usage > committed + carryover.
- RevRec: Deferred recognition of committed fee over 12 months. Carryover does not change RevRec schedule; usage recognized when consumed.

Example B — Marketplace Reseller Flow (3rd party billing)
- Term: reseller contract; Redwood receives a wholesale payment and transfers service via connector.
- Billing: Redwood invoices reseller per wholesale schedule; reseller invoices the end customer.
- RevRec: Redwood recognizes revenue on delivery to reseller when performance obligation to reseller is satisfied (typically at activation). Ensure reseller agreement includes KPMG-style reseller clauses to determine gross vs net treatment.

Journal entry examples (simplified)

- Annual prepay $120k on 2027-07-01 for 12 months:
 DR Cash $120,000
 CR Deferred revenue $120,000
 Monthly recognition (each month): DR Deferred revenue $10,000; CR Revenue $10,000

- Usage invoice $4,500 for March (tokens verified):
 DR Accounts receivable $4,500
 CR Revenue $4,500

Operational checklists

Onboarding a new enterprise contract (FinanceOps checklist):
1. Receive signed contract; attach PDF to contract record and compute normalized fields.
2. Confirm commencement event and set automated event wiring in platform (owner: Platform Integrations).
3. Create RevRec schedule in accounting system and link schedule id to contract record.
4. Configure rates/tiers in billing engine; create test invoice and route to Sales Ops for validation.
5. Release to Live: confirm first event emissions and invoice generation on next cycle.

Quarterly controls (Finance / RevRec):
- Reconcile deferred revenue schedules to signed contracts and billing records; material variances (>1% or $10k) require a variance memo.
- Review committed capacity utilization across customers; highlight high unused rates (>30%) for Sales to consider commercial remediation.
- Audit 10 random invoices for accuracy of token/usage counts and pricing application.

Change management and documentation

- Any change to billing trigger names or contract normalization schema must be submitted via the Change Request process and include: migration plan, test cases, communication plan, and rollback steps.
- Store canonical pricing modifiers and templates in the Pricing Library (Confluence page) with versioning.

Appendix: sample billing trigger YAML (for platform integrators)

```yaml
contract_id: REDW-2027-0345
effective_date: 2027-03-01
commencement_event: platform.activation.vpc_link
billing_cycle: monthly
pricing:
 base_subscription: { amount: 20000, currency: USD }
 committed_capacity: { units: 1000, unit_type: gpu_hour, price_per_unit: 1.25 }
 modifiers: [ { type: volume_tier, breakpoints: [10000,50000], discounts: [0.03,0.07] } ]
revrec_schedule_id: RS-2027-334
```
Contact and ownership

- Primary owner: Marcus Chen (Finance — Billing) — for operational questions and playbook updates.
- Legal intake and escalation: Priya Nair (Lead Counsel).
- Platform integration owner: Diego Alvarez (Head, Platform Integrations).

Revision history

- 2026-10-15: Initial draft (Marcus Chen).
- 2026-11-02: Added marketplace reseller flow and journal examples (reviewers: Priya Nair).
- 2027-01-11: Published; clarified event wiring and dispute thresholds (approved by CRB).

Related documents

- See contract clauses guidance for KMS/escrow/residency: /confluence/finance-and-legal/contracts-and-legal-process/contract-clauses-escrow-kms-data-residency-2026
- RevRec timing reference: /confluence/finance-and-legal/revrec-and-billing/subscription-billing-cutover-and-revenue-timing-2027

Questions or required updates

Open questions should be routed to the Finance Ops Slack channel #finance-billing and tagged with the contract id and short summary. Urgent legal escalations should be emailed to legal-escalations@redwood.com with the contract id in the subject.

title: Hardware tuning profiles pack - weekly sync
author: Talia Benson
text:
Meeting: Hardware tuning profiles pack - weekly sync
Date: 2025-12-03
Start time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees (Redwood): Talia Benson, Hiro Tanaka, Sofia Ivanova, Irene Choi, Rina Kobayashi, Claire Dubois, Ethan Park, Benji Okafor, Omar El-Sayed, Kira Volkov, Sean Gallagher, Vanessa Ortiz

Auto-summary (generated)
- H100 preset looks net-positive on throughput with a tail-latency caveat that improved after the fairness patch; need one more matrix run to confirm.
- L40S remains the main stability risk due to long-context OOM; KV-cache budgeting guardrails are close but need validation.
- B200 stays behind experimental flag; limited fleet access + driver/CUDA constraints; need stricter gating and region-level disable.
- Perf-canary gates are noisy; plan to adjust thresholds and use multi-run aggregation.

Topics
1) Milestone check: profile pack v0.3.0 content
2) H100 benchmark deltas (balanced vs throughput-first)
3) L40S OOMs + KV cache guardrails
4) B200 experimental profile status and fleet constraints
5) Override order / loader edge cases (SKU strings, MIG)
6) Perf-canary + rollout guardrails

[00:00] Talia Benson: Alright, we’ll get started. This is the hardware tuning profiles weekly. Goal today: quick status from Kernels, Scheduling, Infra, Bench. Then blockers and next steps. We’re aiming for v0.3 pack content freeze end of week-ish, depending on the last matrix run.

[00:22] Talia Benson: Hiro, can you start with H100 kernel side? What changed since last week.

[00:28] Hiro Tanaka: Yeah. So kernel autoselect heuristics by sequence length buckets are in good shape. We adjusted the cutoffs. Previously we were switching too early and it hurt prefill on the mid bucket—like 2k to 4k tokens. Now it’s more stable.

[00:45] Hiro Tanaka: Also, the “balanced” preset is basically stable, but we still have a couple knobs I’m not sure we should freeze in the profile. Specifically the block size toggle—um the one that picks the fused attention variant. It’s safe on H100 SXM, less sure on PCIe.

[01:03] Irene Choi: And we do have both in fleet. The hosted pools are mostly SXM, dedicated varies.

[01:08] Hiro Tanaka: Exactly. So I want to guard on memory bandwidth / device name.

[01:13] Ethan Park: Just to clarify, guardrails here means the profile includes “applies_if” rules, right? Like “sku_family=h100” plus “form_factor=sxm” or “hbm>=80GB”?

[01:25] Hiro Tanaka: Yeah, that’s the idea.

[01:27] Talia Benson: Okay, so for v0.3 we keep it simple: H100 with explicit differentiation if needed. Ethan, that’s compatible with the schema we landed?

[01:35] Ethan Park: Mostly. We can do it without nesting complex expressions. But we need to keep it readable. Also we have to be careful with string variants. Like “NVIDIA H100 PCIe” vs “H100-80GB” and sometimes the cloud provider adds junk.

[01:49] Irene Choi: Yeah. We’ve got a list. I’ll send the updated list after this.

[01:54] Talia Benson: Great. Sofia, scheduling side?

[01:58] Sofia Ivanova: On scheduler: the big change is we picked up Marcus’s fix for prefill/decode fairness. That was the tail regression we saw when continuous batching was set more aggressively. The patch basically prevents decode starvation when we have a few long prefills.

[02:17] Sofia Ivanova: On the benchmark runs from yesterday, p95 improved. It’s not totally gone in the worst-case streaming scenario, but it’s within the guardrail bands we discussed with SRE.

[02:28] Sean Gallagher: Which band? Like, what are we talking.

[02:31] Sofia Ivanova: For the streaming chat workload at concurrency 64, p95 went from +18% to +6% versus baseline, while tokens/sec stayed +11%. So still a trade, but it’s less scary.

[02:45] Sean Gallagher: Okay. +6% might be acceptable if we’re honest about expected behavior and we can rollback quickly.

[02:52] Talia Benson: Rina/Claire, can you anchor this with the matrix summary? Are those numbers representative or cherry picked.

[02:59] Rina Kobayashi: Um, it’s representative for the “streaming mix” bucket. We have three main mixes right now: non-streaming summarization, streaming chat, and long-context Q&A. The streaming one is the noisy one.

[03:12] Claire Dubois: Also, we still don’t have the “tool calling” pattern in the matrix. Applied ML asked for that because the stop-token and structured output changes the decode pacing. I can add it but we won’t have perfect realism for v0.3.

[03:25] Talia Benson: Understood. Let’s add a lightweight version, not derail.

[03:30] Omar El-Sayed: Can I jump in on “long-context Q&A” because that’s where L40S is exploding.

[03:35] Talia Benson: Yep, go ahead.

[03:38] Omar El-Sayed: So L40S OOMs aren’t just “too big KV”. It’s fragmentation plus some caching behavior. When we do long prompts with moderate concurrency, the KV cache budget expands and we don’t reclaim fast enough. I’ve got a guardrail patch that caps KV per request and shifts to a more conservative eviction.

[03:59] Rina Kobayashi: Is that the thing that was called “KV cash” in the logs? Sorry, I keep reading it like money.

[04:04] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah, the logs are… not great.

[04:08] Benji Okafor: Also the config key name is “kv_cache_budget_mb” and someone’s typo’d it in one of the YAML examples. We should fix docs before it becomes a support issue.

[04:17] Talia Benson: Please capture that as an action item; we can fold into docs PR.

[04:22] Omar El-Sayed: For L40S: with the cap, OOMs went away in my local repro, but p50 got slightly worse on short prompts due to more frequent evictions.

[04:33] Sofia Ivanova: That’s expected. The question is: does it hurt p95 a lot.

[04:38] Rina Kobayashi: We didn’t finish the full L40S matrix because the perf-canary runner died mid run. It’s flaky.

[04:45] Kira Volkov: That’s the same flake I’ve been tracking. The job sometimes pins CPU and the driver resets. It’s not strictly a runtime regression.

[04:54] Vanessa Ortiz: That might be the runner node type. Those L40S boxes have weird CPU steal. We can allocate a different host class.

[05:02] Talia Benson: Okay, but for the pack release we need stable validation. Can we prioritize making L40S runner stable this week.

[05:10] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes, I’ll sync with infra CI folks. We can reserve a pool.

[05:15] Talia Benson: Great.

[05:17] Talia Benson: B200 status. Irene?

[05:20] Irene Choi: Limited access. We have, like, two nodes in us-east and one in eu-west. Driver is the big constraint. Some nodes are on a different branch; CUDA minor version mismatch. So we can’t run the same build everywhere.

[05:36] Hiro Tanaka: Also kernel differences. Some of the H100 heuristics don’t port cleanly. We have to keep the B200 profile experimental and strict-check the driver/CUDA. If check fails, fallback to generic.

[05:50] Ethan Park: The loader supports “requires” with min runtime version and min driver. But we need to decide what we log and what we do when it doesn’t match.

[05:59] Benji Okafor: Current behavior is: if incompatible, log warning, select default profile. But in Private deployments, warnings get ignored. We added startup log matrix in the runtime to show runtime version vs profile version. People will still ignore it.

[06:14] Sean Gallagher: From oncall perspective: I want a big obvious metric: selected_profile, source, and whether we fell back due to compatibility.

[06:22] Kira Volkov: That’s in the metrics PR. It emits “profile_selected{profile=..., source=..., reason=...}” basically.

[06:31] Talia Benson: Okay. For B200, we stick to “off by default” and enable in one pool only. We also need a clear rollback toggle.

[06:41] Irene Choi: Already planning to disable by pool config. But we need override precedence: fleet default vs per-pool vs per-customer.

[06:49] Ethan Park: That’s the ADR. In short: default is in runtime, pack overlays, then fleet/pool overrides, then customer overrides, then per-route overrides. Env var remains highest priority for emergency.

[07:03] Sean Gallagher: Env var at highest priority makes me nervous, but I get why. For emergency we want it.

[07:08] Talia Benson: Let’s park ADR debate; we have to ship.

[07:12] Claire Dubois: Can I ask about “expected behavior” language. Last week we had a docs thread: we need to avoid sounding like we guarantee p95 improves.

[07:20] Talia Benson: Correct. We say “expected behavior under this workload envelope”. We explicitly call out tradeoffs and failure modes.

[07:28] Sofia Ivanova: I’ll add a line: throughput-first can increase tail latency, especially streaming and long-prefill mixes. Balanced mode is default for Hosted. Throughput-first maybe for Dedicated batchy workloads.

[07:42] Hiro Tanaka: +1. Also some kernels are better at long seq but worse at short seq. That’s why the bucketization exists.

[07:51] Rina Kobayashi: On H100 matrix: overall tokens/sec improved 8–15% depending on model family. p50 latency improved slightly on non-streaming. p95 on streaming is variable but less bad after fairness fix.

[08:04] Claire Dubois: Which models are in the matrix again? For notes.

[08:08] Rina Kobayashi: Three families: Llama-style 70B-ish, a smaller 8B-ish, and an embedding model. I’m not saying names because we keep swapping the exact ones, but it’s consistent.

[08:20] Talia Benson: Good. Put the exact model pins in the benchmark artifact, not in this call.

[08:25] Kira Volkov: Perf-canary gates: right now thresholds are too tight for p95 on streaming. We’re failing builds due to noise. I propose we run each scenario three times and gate on median. Also widen band for the known noisy buckets.

[08:41] Sean Gallagher: Please run that by SRE. We can’t widen too much and miss regressions.

[08:47] Kira Volkov: Yeah. We can keep strict bands on error rate, OOM, and queue depth. p95 can be median-of-3 with narrower band.

[08:57] Benji Okafor: On queue depth: the new backpressure settings can change queue behavior. It might look “worse” but it’s actually protecting latency. We need to define the metric expectation.

[09:08] Sofia Ivanova: Exactly. A slightly higher queue depth might be fine if tail latency is stable. But if queue grows without bound, that’s bad.

[09:17] Talia Benson: We need a consistent oncall triage list: which dashboards, which metric thresholds mean rollback.

[09:23] Sean Gallagher: For rollback criteria, I want: p95 latency +10% sustained 15 minutes on top routes OR error rate above X OR OOM events > 0 in that pool post-deploy. Plus a “customer ticket spike” clause.

[09:40] Talia Benson: Great. Capture in runbook.

[09:43] (crosstalk)

[09:44] Vanessa Ortiz: Also autoscaling. If we change batching, throughput changes, autoscaling may react weirdly. We should watch utilization and scale oscillations.

[09:54] Irene Choi: Yep. Some pools have different scaling policies. We’ll do staged rollout: one canary pool per region, then 10%, then 50%, then 100.

[10:06] Talia Benson: Okay, let’s get more detailed on H100: balanced vs throughput-first. Sofia, what knobs differ.

[10:13] Sofia Ivanova: Balanced: lower max batch tokens, more strict prefill/decode fairness, smaller queue limits. Throughput-first: higher max batch tokens, more aggressive continuous batching window, less strict fairness.

[10:28] Hiro Tanaka: And kernel side: throughput-first allows selecting kernels that are slightly worse for short sequences but better for long, to maximize aggregate tokens/sec.

[10:40] Claire Dubois: That aligns with workloads: summarization batch jobs vs chat.

[10:45] Talia Benson: So default: Balanced for Hosted. For Dedicated, we can let customers pick. For Private, default Balanced but document override.

[10:56] Benji Okafor: On Private override: Helm values wire in the profile pack and also allow overriding per deployment. We should include safe “known good” examples.

[11:07] Ethan Park: And validation: if someone sets nonsense values, config validation should fail fast.

[11:13] Sean Gallagher: Fail fast is good, but in production it might brick a rollout.

[11:18] Ethan Park: Right. We only fail fast for invalid types/out-of-range. For optional keys, we ignore unknown keys with a warning. That was the compromise.

[11:30] Talia Benson: Okay.

[11:32] Talia Benson: Let’s check blockers. Rina: what’s blocking the next benchmark report.

[11:37] Rina Kobayashi: Two things: L40S runner flake and missing one H100 rerun after the fairness fix merged. The H100 rerun should finish today if the queue cooperates.

[11:49] Kira Volkov: The H100 queue is fine. L40S is the one with, like, random driver resets.

[11:55] Vanessa Ortiz: I’ll get you a reserved node class by tomorrow.

[12:00] Rina Kobayashi: Great.

[12:02] Talia Benson: Irene: any infra blockers.

[12:05] Irene Choi: Only B200 access. We can’t do a full matrix. I can get NVIDIA to lend us more for a week, but not guaranteed.

[12:14] Hiro Tanaka: For v0.3, maybe it’s fine if B200 remains “experimental preview” with limited validation.

[12:22] Talia Benson: That’s consistent with leadership: experimental, gated, clear fallback. No broad enablement.

[12:30] Claire Dubois: Can we ensure docs say “B200 profile requires driver X / CUDA Y” and “not supported in all regions”.

[12:38] Ethan Park: Yes, and runtime logs show compatibility matrix.

[12:42] Benji Okafor: Plus a debug endpoint to dump effective runtime config. Oncall can ask a customer to run it in Private.

[12:50] Sean Gallagher: That’s huge. As long as it’s gated/secured.

[12:54] Benji Okafor: It’s internal-only by default; for Private we require an explicit enable flag and auth.

[13:01] Talia Benson: Cool.

[13:03] (brief pause)

[13:05] Talia Benson: Let’s talk about override precedence edge cases: MIG and multi-GPU nodes. Irene, did we decide per-device vs per-node.

[13:14] Irene Choi: Most of our serving nodes are single GPU, but some Dedicated has multi. MIG is rare but exists.

[13:22] Ethan Park: The current loader selects a profile per process based on detected GPU 0. If you have mixed GPUs, that’s a problem. But we don’t support mixed in one node anyway.

[13:33] Sean Gallagher: What about MIG slices. The device name can include “MIG 1g.10gb” etc.

[13:40] Irene Choi: Yep, that breaks naive string matching. I’ll include the variants we saw.

[13:46] Hiro Tanaka: Kernel presets on MIG are risky. We should treat MIG as “unknown” and choose conservative defaults.

[13:54] Sofia Ivanova: Scheduling also changes; smaller memory means smaller KV budgets. So yes, conservative.

[14:00] Talia Benson: Okay, we’ll add guardrail: if MIG detected, don’t apply tuned profile unless explicitly allowed.

[14:08] Ethan Park: That’s easy.

[14:10] Talia Benson: Now canary rollout plan. Sean, what do you need.

[14:15] Sean Gallagher: I need the runbook to be explicit: which toggle disables profiles for a pool, and where to look. Dashboard should have panels segmented by selected profile. And alert thresholds should be enumerated.

[14:30] Kira Volkov: Observability pack has the new panels. We can link them.

[14:34] Sean Gallagher: Also: who’s on point during rollout windows. I don’t want a Friday night surprise.

[14:40] Talia Benson: We’ll coordinate with release train owner but for now: staged in business hours. Irene, can we commit to that.

[14:47] Irene Choi: Yes.

[14:49] Talia Benson: Great.

[14:51] (transcription note: multiple speakers)

[14:52] Sofia Ivanova: One more thing: the throughput-first preset can cause token latency spikes if the request mix has lots of short prompts. We should keep it opt-in.

[15:02] Hiro Tanaka: Yep.

[15:04] Claire Dubois: That’s also about workload envelope. We should put a table: recommended for “batchy summarization, non-streaming”, not recommended for “interactive streaming chat with tight p95”.

[15:15] Talia Benson: Good, docs will include.

[15:18] Talia Benson: Anything else from Bench.

[15:21] Rina Kobayashi: I want to mention one thing: embedding workloads. The tuned profiles didn’t help much; maybe 1–2% variance. But they didn’t hurt. So we can say “no meaningful change expected.”

[15:33] Talia Benson: Great.

[15:35] Omar El-Sayed: On L40S: we should define safe-by-default memory behavior. Like KV budget is a function of free memory. But we can cap at X. Right now I used 65% of available memory, leaving headroom.

[15:48] Sean Gallagher: Headroom is good. OOMs are the worst.

[15:52] Sofia Ivanova: But if headroom is too big, throughput suffers.

[15:56] Omar El-Sayed: Yep. That’s the trade.

[15:59] Talia Benson: For v0.3: stability > max throughput on L40S.

[16:05] Hiro Tanaka: Agree.

[16:07] Talia Benson: Okay, quick pass on timeline. Today: H100 rerun finishing. Tomorrow: Irene sends SKU variants + reserved L40S runner plan. End of week: v0.3 content freeze pending L40S validation.

[16:23] Benji Okafor: And integration tests for override precedence are in review. I’ll push to merge by Friday.

[16:30] Ethan Park: Schema validation is already merged.

[16:33] Talia Benson: Great.

[16:35] (The transcript continues; mid-section includes detailed Q&A on perf-canary thresholds, startup logging, and B200 gating checks.)

[24:10] Kira Volkov: One thing: gating on p95 as an absolute number is hard because different runs are noisy. That’s why I’m pushing relative change vs baseline on the same runner.

[24:22] Sean Gallagher: Relative change is fine as long as baseline is recent. Otherwise it drifts.

[24:28] Claire Dubois: We can pin baseline artifacts per runtime release. The matrix runner can store last green baseline.

[24:36] Rina Kobayashi: Yeah, the runner emits a summary JSON artifact. We can compare.

[24:44] Talia Benson: Okay.

[31:05] Irene Choi: For the EU-west B200 node: we already saw weird regressions last time. I’d prefer we disable by default there until we know the driver is consistent.

[31:15] Hiro Tanaka: Agreed.

[31:17] Benji Okafor: That can be a pool override that forces profile “generic-safe”.

[31:24] Sean Gallagher: Perfect.

[38:02] Claire Dubois: Quick doc note: please stop saying “guarantee”. Say “expected”. Also we should include “known failure modes”: long prompt distributions, fragmentation, MIG.

[38:16] Talia Benson: Yes.

[42:40] Talia Benson: Recap time. H100: we’re close, one rerun after fairness fix, likely lock balanced preset. L40S: must fix runner flake and validate KV budget guardrail across long-context bucket. B200: experimental flag, strict version checks, disable in EU-west by default. Perf canary: adjust to median-of-3, tighten non-latency metrics. Runbook: concrete rollback thresholds and toggles.

[43:10] Talia Benson: Did I miss anything.

[43:12] (crosstalk)

[43:13] Sofia Ivanova: No, that’s it.

[43:15] Hiro Tanaka: I’ll share the final bucket mapping options in Slack.

[43:18] Rina Kobayashi: I’ll publish the artifact once H100 rerun finishes.

[43:21] Irene Choi: I’ll send SKU strings and MIG variants.

[43:25] Sean Gallagher: Please add rollback criteria draft in the runbook doc by Friday.

[43:32] Talia Benson: Done. Thanks everyone.

End of transcript

H100: lock Balanced preset knobs for v0.3.0 pack and rerun workload matrix with updated prefill/decode fairness fix
L40S: land KV-cache budgeting guardrails and rerun long-context buckets; confirm no OOMs and watch p95 impact
B200: keep experimental flag; add stricter version checks and disable-by-default in EU pools; request more fleet access for a full matrix run
Infra: update GPU SKU string normalization list (PCIe vs SXM variants, provider strings) and feed into detection logic
Perf/Canary: tighten gates to reduce noise; move from single-run thresholds to 3-run median for p95 where possible
Docs/Runbook: draft ‘expected behavior’ curves + explicit non-guarantees; add oncall playbook for quick disable per pool

Hiro Tanaka - Confirm final H100 kernel autoselect seq-len bucket mapping for profile v0.3.0; share diff + rationale in #eng-runtime - Due 2025-12-05
Sofia Ivanova - Re-run streaming-heavy scenarios after fairness fix and report p95 deltas (H100 balanced vs throughput-first) - Due 2025-12-06
Rina Kobayashi - Publish the standardized benchmark artifact for the latest H100 + L40S runs (matrix runner output + notes) - Due 2025-12-05
Claire Dubois - Update workload matrix doc to include tool-calling / stop-token patterns requested by Applied ML (lightweight version for v0.3.0) - Due 2025-12-09
Irene Choi - Provide updated list of GPU SKU strings seen in fleet (incl. MIG suffixes) and confirm detection fallback when ambiguous - Due 2025-12-04
Benji Okafor - Verify override precedence integration test coverage for per-pool disable toggle and per-route override - Due 2025-12-06
Kira Volkov - Propose revised perf-canary gates to reduce flake (median-of-3, widen band on low-QPS buckets) and route for SRE sign-off - Due 2025-12-09
Sean Gallagher - Draft rollback criteria text for runbook (p95, error rate, OOM, queue depth) and confirm alert routing - Due 2025-12-05
