title: Approval: time-boxed aggregated session dump (redacted) for security investigation
text:
Request from Security to produce an aggregated, redacted snapshot of user session metadata and non-sensitive model telemetry to support an ongoing phishing investigation. This is not a full raw export — the goal is a minimized, inspectable artifact that preserves sequence-level timing and routing characteristics but strips or tokenizes any potential PII and model outputs. Requestor: Security (Ben Carter). Context: post-alert triage for suspicious account activity impacting three enterprise customers.

Investigative need only; dataset will be used by Security and Legal to determine scope of suspected account compromise. Low risk if redaction is performed correctly; high compliance risk if raw customer outputs or unredacted PII are exposed.

aggregated session timeline (session ids + event timestamps)
route-level latency histogram for selected buckets
tokenized prompt/response fingerprints (hashes) only — no cleartext outputs
config snapshot (model version, kernel hints) for the affected time window

1) Exclude full-text model outputs. 2) Replace user identifiers and email-like tokens with deterministic pseudonyms (UID-<hash>). 3) Hash prompts/responses with SHA256 and include only the first 8 chars of the hex as a fingerprint. 4) Strip any detected PII using the PII detection rule set v3.2. 5) Manual spot-check by Compliance on a 1% sample prior to sharing. All steps recorded in the artifact manifest.

Read-only access to the generated artifact for Security + Legal for 48 hours after delivery; artifact must be deleted from temporary storage at expiry and deletion confirmed in ticket.

1. Narrow time window: 2026-03-04T14:00:00Z to 2026-03-04T18:00:00Z.
2. Run serving-runtime aggregated query job with --include-metadata --exclude-fulloutputs flags.
3. Pipe raw output through redaction pipeline (pii-scrub v3.2 + token hashing).
4. Store artifact in temporary S3 bucket with restricted ACL and server-side encryption.
5. Notify Compliance for 1% manual sample review.
6. Upon approval, grant read-only signed URL to approvers and attach manifest to ticket.

Initial alert triggered by anomaly detector: unusual ratio of streaming disconnects to token counts for three customer orgs.
Affected model variants: rwd-1-large and rwd-1-quantized (snapshot at 2026-03-04).
Preliminary metric: 3x increase in prefix retransmissions; likely caused by network retries affecting streaming join logic.
No evidence yet of exfiltration of customer outputs; need fingerprints to correlate with customer-reported samples.

Pending approval. Compliance requested minor change to redaction plan (include salt for pseudonym hashes). Action: SRE to add salt and rerun a fresh sample for Compliance sign-off.

2026-03-10 | Aisha Kapoor: Opening ticket per Security request. Attached alert digest and sample metric graphs. Requesting Legal and Compliance sign-off prior to data generation.
2026-03-10 | Priya Nair (Legal): Please ensure the pseudonymization salt is stored separately from the artifact and that deletion actions are auditable.
2026-03-11 | Nina Cho (SRE): Can produce the aggregated dump but need an approved temp bucket name and retention TTL. Recommend s3://redwood-temp/si-17422/ with 48h lifecycle.
2026-03-11 | Ben Carter (Security): Confirmed scope and provided a list of three tenant IDs to include. Also requested hashes of the top 10 suspicious prompt fingerprints once artifact is ready.
2026-03-12 | Aisha Kapoor: Updated redaction plan to include per-ticket salt and audit entry requirements. Asking SRE to produce a 1% sample and tag it "sample-for-compliance" for manual review.

title: WardenCode SafetyWorks
author: Ava Martinez
text:
Customer profile: small platform company building a safety and linting layer for developer IDEs. Primary product is an on-prem deployable copilot that runs code analysis, executes limited test suites, and surfaces build logs to devs without exposing internal secrets.

Key requirements and asks (verbatim / paraphrase):
- "We need function-calling in the copilot to run unit tests in a sandbox and return test summaries + failing stack traces."
- Ephemeral runner: process isolation, FS restrictions, network egress blocked by default.
- Low-latency streaming crucial for in-line completions and test-run feedback (target: <50ms token latency for local plugin).
- Model/version pinning: deterministic behavior across releases; rollback capability.
- Audit trail: every tool call and returned artifact must be logged for compliance.
- Data residency: some customers require EU-only storage for logs.

POC scope notes:
- Build a Proof-of-Concept that wires Redwood Private in a VPC to the WardenCode staging environment. POC features: tool/function call handler that spins ephemeral containers, captures build logs, streams token-by-token results to IDE plugin, and enforces sandbox policies.
- SE to provide recommended quantization/model family for the code agent (suggested: Llama-variant 7B quantized + pinned weights for POC).

Commercial/ops notes:
- Interested in Dedicated for predictable throughput for their internal developer teams; Private for regulated enterprise customers.
- Cost sensitivity around per-container compute overhead; asked for Optimize recommendations to lower unit cost via caching and batching for background lint jobs.

Quotes from calls:
- "If a test runner can execute in a locked sandbox and return a structured result, we can replace our brittle webhook approach."
- "We need proof that running linters/tests with tool-calls won't leak secrets — can you show an architecture with HSM/KMS and limited mount points?"

Open questions (to resolve in POC):
- How will KV cache and prefix caching interact with ephemeral containerized tool executions?
- SLA expectations for streaming token delivery from Private deployments.

Recommended next actions (AE/SE):
- Deliver sandbox architecture diagram and sample security checklist by 2026-03-01.
- Stand up POC environment week of 2026-03-08.
- Schedule partner legal + security working session (w/ Redwood security) and capture required artifacts (SOC2, network ACL template).

2025-11-02: Lead created via developer community signup (plugin alpha).
2025-11-18: Intro call (AE + SE) — discussed IDE copilot integration and streaming requirements; customer emphasized sub-50ms token latency for completions.
2025-12-09: Demo of hosted API throughput; WardenCode requested model pinning and predictable token costs for squad-level deploys.
2026-01-15: Security sync — legal asked about retention controls and audit logs; asked for KMS options and SOC2 evidence.
2026-02-10: POC kickoff call (Fireflies ff-20260210-wardencode-demo) — scope: IDE plugin + test-runner tool-calling; need sandboxed ephemeral containers for executing unit tests and linters.
2026-02-18: Deep dive with infra team (ff-20260218-security-sync) — network topology, egress restrictions, and air-gap feasibility discussed.
2026-02-20: Provided first draft of POC plan + pricing deck; awaiting security feedback and legal on data residency clauses.

need ephemeral sandbox for test runner
legal review on data retention policy
clarify dedicated pool pricing model

Complete sandbox POC; finalize network topology doc; security review sign-off scheduled for 2026-03-05.

text:
Incident Bot: :rotating_light: Pager: GPU runtime OOM spike on cluster-psi-4 in us-west-2. 80% of requests failing. paging oncall
Maria Chen: ack, taking it
Jonah Patel: I have the pager, pulling logs now
Priyanka Rao: quick look shows abrupt growth in GPU resident on replica r-42 — KV cache + big batch tail visible in traces
Asa Green: which customers are seeing failures?
Customer Success Bot: Impacted: acme-inc (prod), luma-ai (prod). 5xxs up ~5-6x, CS notified.
Samir Iqbal: doing a quick nvidia-smi/dmesg dump, will paste shortly
Jonah Patel: logs dump ->
```sh
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,memory.used,memory.total --format=csv
index, name, memory.used [MiB], memory.total [MiB]
0, A100-40GB, 39400 MiB, 40536 MiB
1, A100-40GB, 39510 MiB, 40536 MiB
```
Maria Chen: runtime metrics: KV cache size ~38GB on r-42, allocator shows high external fragmentation in recent GC logs
Priyanka Rao: hypothesis list: 1) KV-cache growth + fragmentation, 2) long-tail large-batches coalescing, 3) GPU allocator fragmentation -> inability to satisfy new large allocations -> OOM
Asa Green: mitigation options — (A) cap max batch to 2048 tokens, (B) force KV eviction/compaction on the node, (C) restart the heavy replica, (D) fall back routed traffic to smaller model variant
Jonah Patel: applying option (A) now — updating hosted-routing policy to cap per-request batch to 2048 for model redwood/gpt-medium-v1
Ops Bot: Runbook link: https://redwood.runbooks/oom-gpu — Recommended live steps: cap-batch, evict-kv, controlled restart, escalate to infra if kernel pagefaults persist
Maria Chen: initiating eviction sweep on r-42 (evict threshold 0.6 -> 0.4)
Samir Iqbal: scheduling a graceful restart of r-42 if eviction doesn't bring resident memory down in 5m
Priyanka Rao: collecting perf/NVTX traces -> uploading s3://redwood-ops/incident/2370001234/trace.zip
Jonah Patel: add any logs to that S3 path. common commands we used:
```bash
# collect runtime logs for last 10m
sudo journalctl -u redwood-runtime --since '10 minutes ago' > /tmp/runtime.log
# nvml memory snapshot
python -c "import pynvml; pynvml.nvmlInit(); print(pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetMemoryInfo(pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetHandleByIndex(0)))"
```
Ops Bot: Customer impact note: 5xx rate rose from 0.2% -> 6.1% between 15:32-15:48 UTC. Mitigation window started 15:50 UTC.
Maria Chen: eviction reduced resident memory by ~4GB on r-42; 5xx rate dropping to ~1.5% now
Asa Green: hold monitoring — if 5xx >2% for 10m we perform restart
Priyanka Rao: uploaded hypothesis matrix to S3: [KV-cache fragmentation, batch tail causing large contiguous allocations, kernel allocator fragmentation, possible mem leak in quantized path]
Jonah Patel: owners: Maria (eviction & timeline), Priyanka (trace analysis), Samir (restart & infra ops), Asa (customer comms)
Maria Chen: timeline CSV uploaded -> s3://redwood-ops/incident/2370001234/timeline.csv. Will consolidate minute-by-minute and append logs
Samir Iqbal: performing graceful drain and restart of r-42 now — ETA ~2m
Maria Chen: post-eviction and restart snapshot: GPU0 used ~12GB, system looks stable on that replica
Priyanka Rao: capturing a sample offending request for repro:
```json
{"req_id":"rq_8a3f","batch_size":5120,"model":"gpt-medium-v1","tokens":9200}
```

title: p0-hostedapi-coalescer-tcp-slowstart-congestion-retro-2026-06-30
author: Ava Martinez
text:
Summary:

On 2026-06-30 at ~03:42 UTC we observed a large-scale degradation impacting streaming sessions on the Hosted API for ~18 minutes, with elevated TTFB and tail latency and a ~12% increase in 5xx for streaming endpoints. Root cause analysis points to an interaction between the recently deployed edge coalescer optimization, TCP slow-start behavior on certain kernel versions, and an emergent autoscaling gap for edge workers handling high fanout. The coalescer change intended to reduce small-packet overhead by buffering outbound chunks for short windows; under sustained high-concurrency bursts this resulted in synchronized flushes that amplified TCP slow-start congestion across a subset of backend connections, causing persistent queueing and connection stall symptoms.

Severity and Impact:

- Severity: P0 (customer-facing outage affecting latency SLOs and increasing 5xx)
- Impacted surfaces: streaming generate endpoints (HTTP/2 and websockets) across eu-west-1 and us-west-2 regions, affecting ~6% of traffic by token volume during window
- Customer-visible effects: slow initial bytes (TTFB increases from p50 20ms to p50 180ms, p99 > 2s), intermittent stream stalls requiring reconnects, increased timeout-triggered 5xx from gateway timeouts
- Duration: ~03:42 UTC to ~04:00 UTC (root cause mitigations rolled at 03:58 UTC, full recovery and normalization by 04:00 UTC).

Detection and Triage:

- Alerting: the on-call SRE received a P0 streaming-latency alert triggered by p99 streaming latency crossing the threshold and a correlated surge in internal streaming timeouts.
- Initial hypothesis: downstream model inference slowdown or backplane congestion.
- Quick triage findings: model-serving fleet metrics (GPU utilization, request latency within model hosts) were normal. Edge proxy egress queues showed bursts and synchronized flush patterns.
- SRE team pulled packet and connection-level metrics from edge hosts, and traced several sample sessions which showed repeated small-chunk flushes clustering into larger bursts.

Timeline (high level):

- 03:32 UTC: minor increase in streaming session creation rate noted (pilot release from internal app that added fanout).
- 03:42 UTC: automated p99-latency alert fired for streaming endpoints. SRE paged.
- 03:44 UTC: triage ruled out model host issues; edge egress queues and kernel socket retransmit counters elevated.
- 03:48 UTC: hypothesis formed — interaction of coalescer flush window + TCP slow-start causing congestion amplification.
- 03:50 UTC: mitigation plan executed: rollback of the coalescer heuristic (edge-proxy rollback PR merged and rolled to 10% canary -> 50%).
- 03:56 UTC: observed reduction in synchronized flushes on canary hosts, p99 latency decreased.
- 03:58 UTC: full rollback completed across affected edge pools.
- 04:00 UTC: metrics normalized, SLOs restored, page resolved.

Root Cause Analysis:

Primary root cause: The edge coalescer optimization (deployed 2026-06-29) introduced a small buffering window (configurable 4-8ms) that aggregated small application writes into fewer larger packets to reduce syscalls and per-chunk overhead. Under normal loads this improved CPU efficiency and reduced egress packet rate. However, when a sudden high-concurrency fanout event occurred, many connections entered flush cycles aligned to the coalescer window, causing multiple buffered flushes to hit the kernel transmit queue at near-simultaneous moments.

On hosts running Linux kernel 5.19.x with autotuning tcp_autosize engaged, these simultaneous bursts triggered TCP slow-start and congestion avoidance across corresponding peer connections. Because many connections shared constrained NIC ring resources and experienced similar RTTs, the effect amplified: packets were delayed, retransmits increased, and application-level egress queues filled. The coalescer's flush alignment meant the bursts were not spread out, so the usual smoothing that prevents per-packet congestion did not occur.

Contributing factors:

- Autoscaling lag: the edge worker pool scaling policy relies on p95 egress latency and queue depth. The surge was short (minutes) but high-concurrency; autoscaler did not respond fast enough, leaving some hosts with elevated queueing.
- Canary rollout gap: the coalescer change was rolled 100% in production with a single-step deployment across edge pools; no staggered regional canary exposed the problem at lower blast radius.
- Kernel interaction: specific kernel versions with aggressive autotuning made slow-start behavior worse for synchronized bursts. We lacked targeted kernel regression tests in our CI.
- Observability blindspot: we lacked an easy-to-query view correlating application flush timing with socket-level retransmit spikes (we had metrics for both separately, but not aligned traces).

Why prior mitigations didn't prevent outage:
- Circuit breakers and per-connection rate limits are designed for long-lived misbehaving clients; they did not trigger because connections were healthy but flush-synchronized.
- Existing autoscaling thresholds prioritized sustained increases over short instantaneous fanout spikes.

Mitigations and Rollforward Actions Taken:

1) Immediate (during incident):
- Rolled back coalescer heuristic across affected edge pools. Rollback proved effective (observed smoothing of flushes and drop in retransmits within 2–6 minutes).
- Temporarily relaxed gateway timeouts and increased worker queue limits to avoid timeout-triggered 5xx while rollback propagated.

2) Short-term (next 72 hours):
- Reintroduce the coalescer behind a regional canary with 1% traffic for 24h, 5% for next 24h, monitoring socket-level metrics and flush alignment.
- Add a fast-path in edge-proxy: if per-host socket retransmit rate > threshold, disable coalescer locally to avoid creating synchronized bursts.
- Tune autoscaler to consider short-lived burst signals (add a burst-detection metric: sudden delta in concurrent streams over 30s) and scale-out more aggressively for edge worker pools.

3) Long-term (quarter roadmap):
- Add CI tests exercising coalescer under synthetic bursty fanout workloads and multiple kernel versions (5.15–6.1 matrix).
- Invest in socket-level tracing: a new tracing pipeline to correlate app-level write timestamps and kernel TCP events (retransmits, cwnd changes) per-flow for sampled sessions.
- Rework coalescer algorithm to jitter flush windows per-connection to avoid global alignment, and make flush jitter configurable by region and kernel codepath.
- Add canary deployment gating that checks both application and kernel-level metrics before full rollout.

Action Items (owners and ETA):

- SRE/Triage: Create an alert for synchronized flush patterns (metric: fraction of egress writes clusters within 5ms windows) — owner: Ravi Patel — ETA: 2026-07-07
- Edge: Implement local coalescer disable on high-retransmit — owner: Diego Alvarez — ETA: 2026-07-12
- Platform: Autoscaler policy update to add burst-detection signal — owner: Hannah Kim — ETA: 2026-07-09
- Applied ML: Add model-serving smoke checks to rule out model-host contribution for streaming regressions (doc) — owner: Sofia Nguyen — ETA: 2026-07-15
- Observability: Add sampled socket-level trace pipeline and dashboard — owner: Observability Team (linked) — ETA: 2026-08-01
- Delivery: Update rollout guardrails to require regional canaries for edge-proxy heuristics — owner: Release Engineering — ETA: 2026-07-05

Runbook / Playbook Updates:

- Immediate update: Add a section in Hosted API Streaming runbook for "coalescer-induced flush bursts" with quick mitigations (rollback, increase gateway timeouts, temporarily disable coalescer via feature flag).
- New diagnostic steps: how to pull egress write histograms, kernel tcp_retransmits per-socket, and map to application writes (scripts: tools/trace-coalescer).

Lessons Learned:

- Small micro-optimizations at the edge can have macro-level systemic impacts when they interact with kernel networking behavior. Always test across kernel/version matrix and under synthetic bursty fanout workloads.
- Canarying needs to include both application-level and low-level platform signals (kernel, NIC) — surface these signals into deployment gating.
- Autoscalers should consider short, high-amplitude bursts (seconds–minutes) when they cause SLO violations even if not sustained.

Metrics and Evidence Collected:

- Timeline-aligned graphs (attached to Linear ticket LIN-4123): p99 streaming latency, egress write rate, kernel tcp_retransmits, NIC tx_ring_busy, worker queue depth, worker CPU.
- Packet captures from three affected hosts showing clustered write timestamps and corresponding increased retransmit counts.

Open Questions / Follow-ups:

- Should the coalescer be reworked to operate per-stream rather than per-host? (tradeoffs: CPU overhead vs smoothing benefits)
- Are there NIC offload settings (TSO/GSO) interactions we need to consider with coalescer behavior? Plan: schedule hardware-level validation with infra.
- Evaluate whether other recent micro-optimizations could produce similar alignment effects (search PRs since 2026-06-01).

Appendix (short technical notes):

- Edge-proxy PR: github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/981 (coalescer change)
- Rollback PR: github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/984 (rollback/disable flag)
- Incident ticket: LIN-4123
- Kernel versions observed: 5.19.14 (eu-west-1 pool), 5.19.12 (us-west-2 pool), 5.15.x hosts showed milder effect in canary testing.

Post-incident retrospective meeting scheduled: 2026-07-08 15:00 UTC (SRE + Edge + Observability + Release Eng).

Notes to on-call and readers:
- If you encounter a future streaming latency spike, check coalescer flag state first (fastest mitigation), then kernel retransmit metrics, then worker queue depths.
- Keep the rollback play handy and prefer staged canaries for edge heuristics until new jittered algorithm is validated.

Document history:
- Drafted by Ava Martinez (SRE) during incident triage
- Reviewed by Ravi Patel, Diego Alvarez, Sofia Nguyen
- Last updated with action items and dates on 2026-07-06 by Ava Martinez

title: Ashbourne retail edge pilot jot
author: Maya Chen
text:
Context / quick summary:
- Ashbourne Retail: 12 pilot kiosks across 3 flagship stores. Goal: realtime conversational product search + receipt-parsing at point-of-sale (no cloud roundtrip ideally).
- Pilot mode: private deployment (VPC), single rack per store (edge appliance), model pinned to a smaller, quantized LLM variant. Need <150ms median token latency for short prompts (recommendations/FAQ).

Call notes (2025-01-12 kickoff):
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood), Samir (Redwood SE), Leo (Ashbourne infra lead), Priya (Ashbourne product), Hannah (store ops).
- Business ask: reduce returns friction and speed up in-store assistance. Primary UX is typed or voice-short prompts at kiosk.
- Non-functional: strict PII rules (no customer phone/email leaving VPC), 3s max end-to-end for a full multi-turn session.
- Ops: stores have 1x edge appliance (server) with 2x A10G GPUs on premise behind NAT. Bandwidth intermittent; prefer local inference.

Technical capture (requirements + constraints):
- Model selection: want open-ish model to avoid licensing costs. We proposed Redwood-compact-v2-8q (8-bit quant, recommended) or a distilled 3B as fallback.
- Memory: A10G + 24GB GPU RAM. With KV cache and 8k context, 8q model likely fits but need runtime mem plan. Prioritize lower kv-cache retention to keep mem headroom.
- Tokenization: receipts and product SKUs require consistent tokenizer; add pre-token normalization step (remove store-specific SKU prefixes via rule).
- Caching: enable prefix caching for static prompts (store inventory corpus + policy snippets). We'll test cache hit rates; recommend TTL 48h for inventory snapshots.
- Privacy/KMS: Ashbourne uses vendor-managed KMS; they asked if Redwood can integrate customer KMS inside VPC control plane. Follow-up with security team.
- Routing/fallback: if GPU saturated or network partitions, fallback to hosted API (but Must not send PII). Need automatic scrub before fallback and clear audit logs when fallback used.

Gotchas & unknowns (red flags to resolve):
- GPU swap/perf: A10G isn't as predictable under bursty traffic (multiple kiosks hitting simultaneously). Need a throttling policy per-store to preserve SLO for all kiosks.
- Cold start: first request after idle has ~500ms extra setup (disk -> GPU). Consider pre-warm cron or a heartbeat ping from kiosk manager.
- Audio path: kiosks will send short audio clips; transcription options: do local whisper-small on CPU or send to hosted ASR? Local CPU transcribe will increase latency and CPU usage; we should test whisper-small on the edge appliance before deciding.
- Inventory freshness: they want near-real-time inventory (minutes). Can't re-download full snapshot frequently; propose delta sync + inventory index pushed to cache. Need data schema from Ashbourne.
- PCI/Network: network egress allowed only to specific Redwood IPs in dedicated breakout; confirm with their network team. Also firewall rules for control plane -> edge appliance (for rollouts) need to be ironed out.

Short experiments to run (MVP):
1) On-prem inference footprint test (Samir): deploy quantized model on A10G emulator, run 1/2/4 kiosk concurrency to measure median token latency, peak GPU mem, and KV cache impact. Collect perf traces.
2) Pre-tokenization rules (Maya + Priya): build small rule engine to normalize SKUs and masked PII patterns; create 200 synthetic receipts to test tokenization token counts.
3) ASR microbenchmark (Leo): run whisper-small on CPU vs hosted ASR for 2s audio median; measure total time and CPU contention.
4) Fallback scrub demo (Maya): create a demo flow where PII fields are detected and redacted before fallback to hosted API; include audit log entry.

Immediate action items (who/when):
- Samir: run model footprint tests and upload CSV perf results to linked PR (due 2025-01-19).
- Leo: confirm firewall & egress constraints and share network diagram (due 2025-01-16).
- Priya: provide inventory schema and example snapshots (due 2025-01-15).
- Maya: prototype pre-tokenization + redaction script and push to github, include sample receipts (due 2025-01-18).
- Security sync: set 30min meeting to discuss KMS integration + audit requirements (Maya to schedule with Ashbourne security + Redwood security) (target 2025-01-14).

Notes-to-self / quick reminders:
- Keep fallback 🔒: fallback must never transmit raw customer PII. If cannot redact confidently, route to 'error' state and return safe fallback message.
- Consider quantization fallback policy: if model generation quality drops below threshold on small prompts (we'll check BLEU/EM-like heuristics on retrieval), automatically route critical flows to a slightly larger model.
- Pre-warm strategy: use a lightweight ping every 30s for active store hours (store hours 9am-9pm local). Might add cost but reduces tail latency.

Potential follow-ups for pilot next week:
- Demo checklist: 1) simple kiosk convo (search -> product card), 2) receipt parse -> autofill return form, 3) offline degraded flow (no network) -> show fallback to cached results.
- Success metrics: median token latency <150ms, end-to-end <1.5s for typical query, accuracy of receipt extraction >95 on our sample set, no PII leaks in fallback tests.

Raw snippets / quick commands (for Samir):
- Start local perf run: python infra/bench/run_inference.py --model redwood-compact-v2-8q --gpus 2 --concurrency 4 --prompt-file tests/ashbourne/prompts-short.json --trace out/ashbourne-run.csv
- Token-normalizer quick regex (POSIX): s/STORE_[A-Z]{3}-(\d{6})/\1/g # strip store prefix from SKUs

Open questions to chase in security meeting:
- Can we get KMS HSM-backed key provisioning in their VPC? Or will they allow Redwood-managed CMKs scoped to that account?
- Audit log retention requirement (Ashbourne asked for 12 months vs Redwood default 90d). If 12 months we need storage + RBAC plan.

End of jot. Will tidy into formal pilot-runbook once the perf numbers come in. For now this is working scratchpad: lots of TODOs, ephemeral notes, and a capture of the kickoff call.

-- Maya

title: At-Risk Account Intervention Checklist & Tactical Save Plays
author: Sofia Ramirez
text:
Purpose:
This working doc is a tactical checklist and set of short-form playbooks for intervening on at-risk accounts in the 90-day window before renewal. It is intended for CSMs, AMs, and CS leadership to run structured 30/60/90 day intervention sprints, escalate effectively to execs, and execute tested save plays while preserving revenue and relationships.

Context & assumptions:
- Scope: mid-market to enterprise customers on Redwood Hosted and Dedicated tiers.
- Use when a customer meets >=2 high-risk signals (see Signals section) or when renewal likelihood < 50% in the CRM.
- This doc is intentionally lean — copy templates into PS notes, Jira tickets, or customer-facing decks as needed.

Key signals (trigger set):
- Usage drop: 30%+ decline in average monthly tokens or API calls vs prior quarter.
- Feature regression: critical features (streaming, dedicated routes, private VPC) failing or high error rates (>3% 7-day).
- Financial flag: overdue invoices >30 days or procurement stalls past PO deadline.
- Sentiment: NPS follow-up negative + no response to outreach in 14 days.
- Product fit: repeated quality regressions (inference latency up 2x or cost per 1k tokens up >25%).

Triage (first 72 hours) — rapid diagnostic probe:
1) Owner: Assigned CSM (or AM) creates a triage ticket in JIRA (link template) and tags solutions-engineering and SRE.
2) Quick health snapshot (CSM):
 - Top 3 usage metrics (tokens/day, response latency p95, error rate).
 - Support ticket count and severity in last 30 days.
 - Billing status and contract renewal date.
3) Outreach: Send templated "We see activity change" email (template below) and schedule a 30-minute discovery call within 3 business days.
4) Diagnostic asks to customer: consent for brief logs/KV cache diagnostics, permission to run traffic replay (if Dedicated/Private).

30-day recovery sprint — prioritized plays (ordered):
- Play A: Engagement Reset (low friction) — owner: CSM
 Actions: deep discovery call, bring in Solutions AE for ROI refresh, share tailored usage dashboard, set 2-week checkpoints.
 Success metric: scheduled renewal conversation + concrete commitment on next actions.

- Play B: Technical Rescue (medium friction) — owner: Solutions Engineering + SRE
 Actions: hotfix or config change (batching tweaks, quantization profile update), temporary routing to a stable model variant, priority support escalation SLA, run smoke tests and provide metrics within 48 hours.
 Budget/Approval: may need PS hours; pre-approve small contingency credit (see offers below).

- Play C: Commercial Bridge (higher friction) — owner: AM + RevOps
 Actions: propose temporary credit/discount tied to performance SLAs, restructure billing cadence, or pilot Dedicated capacity for a fixed period.
 Approval process: small offers (<= $10k) approved by AM lead; >$10k requires RevOps sign-off.

60-day escalation matrix (if 30-day plays inadequate):
- Condition: No booking commitment and risk remains high.
- Steps:
 1) Prepare Exec Brief (one-pager) — include health metrics, timeline of actions, customer exec contact, concrete ask (e.g., PO by date or trial extension + credit).
 2) Trigger: CSM requests Exec Sync with CS Director and Customer Exec Sponsor.
 3) Offer: introduce "Recovery Runway" package — 90-day focused support, weekly ops reviews, up to 40 hours of Solutions Eng dedicated time, and a conditional discount if SLAs not met.

Exec escalation template (email subject + body):
- Subject: "[Action requested] Exec-sync request: <Customer> renewal at risk (Renewal: YYYY-MM-DD)"
- Body (short):
 Hi <LeaderName>,

 Quick brief: <Customer> (ARR $X, Tier) is at elevated renewal risk. Key signals: 35% usage drop, p95 latency 3.2s, billing dispute open.
 Actions taken: discovery call (MM/DD), technical hotfix deployed (MM/DD), offered short-term credits.
 Ask: Exec intro to <Customer Exec> this week to align on procurement timeline and approve Recovery Runway.

 Attach: one-page PDF (health snapshot + timeline).

 Thanks,
 <CSM Name>

Save plays & acceptable concession ladder (ordered lowest to highest cost):
1) Free concierge onboarding hours (up to 8 hours) + priority triage.
2) Short-term credit (1–2 weeks) applied to next invoice for platform instability.
3) Performance SLA addendum (trial) — guarantee latency/cost targets for 60 days or credit.
4) Discount on renewal / usage rebate (sliding scale tied to adoption recovery).
5) Contract restructure (term change, capacity swap) — escalation to RevOps/Legal.

Customer-facing templates (short versions to paste into email thread):
- Engagement Reset invite: "Hi <Name>, we noticed platform usage dip and want to make sure everything is working for you. Can we schedule a 30m call this week to align on immediate needs and a recovery plan? — <CSM>"
- Technical Rescue note: "We deployed a config change to your route and temporarily routed traffic to variant X. Please validate and share logs; we'll follow up in 48h with metrics."
- Recovery Runway offer: "We can provide a 90-day Recovery Runway: weekly ops calls, dedicated engineering hours, and a conditional credit if we miss agreed SLAs. Would you be open to a 2-week pilot?"

Internal checklist for the save sprint (CSM to tick off):
- [ ] Create triage JIRA ticket and add linked artifacts
- [ ] Pull last 90 days usage + trend chart into shared deck
- [ ] Schedule discovery call + invite Solutions Eng if needed
- [ ] Post-call: update CRM with risk score and next steps
- [ ] If technical: open support priority case and request SRE attention
- [ ] If commercial: build offer + get approval from RevOps
- [ ] Draft exec brief if no progress by day 30
- [ ] Run weekly stakeholder syncs and log meeting notes in drive

Measuring success (KPIs for the intervention):
- Renewal outcome: renewed vs churned (primary)
- Time to commit: days from triage to signed commitment
- Health delta: % improvement in key metrics (tokens/day, p95 latency) at 30/60/90 days
- Customer satisfaction: follow-up CSAT or NPS change

Knowledge nuggets & playbook notes (lessons from saves):
- Fast technical wins often stem from routing to an older stable model variant and rolling config changes (less risky than immediate quantization swaps).
- Commercial concessions tied to measurable recovery milestones preserve ARR better than unconditional discounts.
- Exec-to-exec conversations are most effective when coupled with a concrete narrow ask (approve X hours / PO by date).

title: Air-gapped deployment intake - Oceanic Regulatory Labs
author: Maya Chen
text:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-10-07 09:30 PT (recorded)
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Nair (CTO, Oceanic Regulatory Labs), Lucas Reed (Head of IT), Marta Silva (Compliance), Tom Becker (Infra Manager)

Summary:
Quick intake to understand Oceanic's requirements for an air-gapped / on-prem Redwood Private deployment: hardware constraints, approval process for offline updates, network isolation, and compliance/audit expectations. Initial alignment on next steps and deliverables.

Topics covered:
- Air-gap packaging and offline update cadence
- Hardware compatibility (GPU SKUs, NICs, storage topology)
- HSM/KMS and key provisioning in offline environments
- Audit logs, retention, and SOC2/ISO expectations
- Canary/update rollback processes without inbound internet

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, and Diego our solutions engineer is here — we'll run through a few questions about your air-gapped needs.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Thanks, Maya. We appreciate it. Quick intro: Oceanic is a regulated lab doing marine biometrics research, lots of PII-ish metadata and internal patient-study artifacts, so we need a fully isolated environment. We're evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private but leaning heavy to private / on-prem.
[00:36] Lucas Reed: Yeah, and from infra perspective we can't have outbound ports open from the inference nodes, approvals for an internet egress are months.
[00:44] Diego Alvarez: Totally understood, Lucas. We see that often. Couple quick clarifying q's before we dive deep — what's your expected peak throughput (rps or tokens/sec) and what's the model family you expect to run? Do you have a preferred GPU vendor?
[01:05] Tom Becker: Model-wise we'll be running a mix — large re-ranker and a T5-like for internal summarization, and some proprietary fine-tuned Llama-variant. We are currently standardizing on NVIDIA A40s and a few older V100s for cost reasons, but we're open to adding Ampere or newer if validated.
[01:28] Diego Alvarez: OK that helps. For A40s we typically recommend specific CUDA/driver combinations and a set of tuned kernels — in air-gapped setups we provide a packaged runtime that includes the validated drivers + runtime layers. We'll need to map exact driver versions to your NVMe layout.
[01:49] Priya Nair: One key question: how do offline updates work? We can't allow pull from the internet for model patches.
[01:57] Maya Chen: Great question. In our private/offline flow we ship signed artifacts — think tarball with a signature that your security team validates via a detached sig and our public cert. There's an operator tool that performs local install. For policy, updates can be staged on a jump box that has controlled transfer via USB or airlock procedure.
[02:21] Marta Silva: Sorry, can you repeat the signature flow? Our compliance team wants KMS-backed signatures.
[02:25] Diego Alvarez: Yeah, so the artifact is signed by Redwood's build infra. In more advanced deployments we integrate with the customer's HSM where we persist the verification key; you can do an on-site key ceremony and we can support verifying signatures against your HSM-managed keys. Note: in some transcripts the tool name appears as kay vee cache, but we mean KV cache — key/value.
[02:47] Lucas Reed: Couple of red flags: storage. We're mostly NVMe local with a 2-node storage head for redundancy, not a big SAN. How does Redwood handle model sharding and disk requirements?
[03:01] Diego Alvarez: Good note. We support model sharding across nodes and can stream weights from NVMe with mmap-friendly loaders. For low-latency, we recommend keeping the KV cache on local RAM or NVMe depending on model size. For multi-node setups we use a metastore to coordinate cache placements. We should run a capacity planning workshop to map model sizes to NVMe requirements.
[03:28] Tom Becker: Will the metastore need separate network connectivity?
[03:31] Diego Alvarez: It's typically over the private cluster network — no internet. We can operate over the cluster VLAN. But we'll want to confirm MTU sizes and NIC offload capabilities (RDMA optional) because that affects latency for multi-node.
[03:51] Priya Nair: On the compliance side, we need immutable audit logs for inference events, including token counts, input hashes, who requested, and which model version was served. Retention is 7 years for some data.
[04:07] Marta Silva: Right. And we need tamper-evident logs. Can you integrate with our Splunk/ELK?
[04:12] Maya Chen: Yes — our Private offering streams logs to local collectors (filebeat/td-agent). We can deliver cryptographic log chaining if needed and integrate with your SIEM. We'll share the log schema.
[04:24] Lucas Reed: Also curious about SSO and user management — SAML? OAuth?
[04:28] Diego Alvarez: We support SAML 2.0 for admin console SSO and can integrate Redwood Console access through your IdP. For service-level auth between internal services we use mTLS and token-based service accounts.
[04:40] Tom Becker: Any special network port requirements during install? We can't open many ports to the internet, but intra-cluster is fine.
[04:47] Maya Chen: For the installer itself, if you truly can't allow egress, the installer is fully offline. The typical install needs a jumpbox to transfer artifacts and container images. If you allow short-lived egress for initial validation, that reduces manual steps, but we can do full offline.
[05:03] Priya Nair: What about models — can we bring our own model artifacts? We have a fine-tuned Llama model with a custom tokenizer and proprietary vocab.
[05:12] Diego Alvarez: Yes, BYOM is supported. We will need the model format and tokenization routine. For quantized artifacts we recommend 4-bit or 8-bit profiles we have validated; your tokenizer/custom vocab will be bundled and verified. In air-gapped setups, we validate the artifact externally and provide a signed bundle that you import.
[05:32] Lucas Reed: Do you do any on-site support for installation?
[05:35] Maya Chen: For enterprise/private customers we offer a professional services engagement: on-site assistance, remote runbooks, and a handshake for the first deployment. That is usually contracted separately.
[05:47] Priya Nair: Another operational question: how are rollbacks handled if a model release causes regressions and we can't fetch a fallback from internet?
[05:55] Diego Alvarez: We strongly recommend keeping a local artifact repository with multiple pinned versions. Our rollout tooling in private mode can do canary/beacon deploys internally and automatically route to previous pinned versions if health checks fail. Since everything is local, rollback is just switching symlinks and restarting a small subset of nodes — but network and storage must be resilient.
[06:18] Marta Silva: On the audit front, who has access to logs? We need RBAC controls by role and also inclusion of approval workflows.
[06:25] Maya Chen: Redwood Console supports RBAC with granular roles plus SAML group sync. Approval workflows can be integrated via webhooks to your ticketing system, or you can have a manual signoff.
[06:38] Lucas Reed: For hardware, Diego mentioned drivers — can you supply validated driver bundles? Our policy prohibits arbitrary downloads onto nodes, so having vetted driver tarballs will help.
[06:50] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we provide validated driver + runtime bundles. In some prior installs we've provided signed OS packages and driver images that your infra team whitelists. We'll include checksums for validation.
[07:02] Tom Becker: Network isolation still worries me — what happens for downstream telemetry/metrics? We can't push telemetry externally, but need the observability data locally.
[07:11] Diego Alvarez: Our private deploy has a local metrics stack (Prometheus + Grafana) plus optional push gateways. You can choose to keep all telemetry onsite. For remote support, we can do a periodic masked snapshot that you export to us via secure transfer for debugging.
[07:28] Priya Nair: Any constraints on inference latency vs batching? Our workflows are sub-second for some queries, but others are batched overnight.
[07:37] Diego Alvarez: We recommend using dynamic batching with latency SLOs for interactive endpoints and heavy batching for offline jobs. In offline/on-prem environments you control the batching windows. For latency-critical flows, we tune kernel selection and avoid disk-based KV lookups. Also quantization choices affect CPU/GPU inference time.
[08:02] Maya Chen: Quick check — does your procurement need an initial budget number to route approvals?
[08:06] Priya Nair: Yes. A ballpark number that separates Dedicated-hosted pricing from Private on-prem capital + support is helpful.
[08:13] Maya Chen: We'll send a rough TCO showing monthly usage vs capex amortization for on-prem — Diego, can you surface the hardware SKU recommendations?
[08:20] Diego Alvarez: Yep, I'll include A40 and A100 options and an estimate for number of cards per expected QPS.
[08:26] Lucas Reed: One more: air-gapped vulnerability management — how do security patches get applied for the runtime?
[08:33] Diego Alvarez: We publish signed OS and runtime patch bundles on our release cadence. For critical CVEs, we can fast-track an emergency bundle. The bundle is applied via your change control process; we can do validation runs in a staging cluster first.
[08:49] Priya Nair: Can Redwood's runtime run on non-NVIDIA hardware? We have a couple of AMD MI250 boxes on prem intended for HPC workloads.
[08:58] Diego Alvarez: We have workstreams for AMD and other vendors but the validated path today is NVIDIA; AMD support is possible but requires additional validation and kernel work. We should capture that as a compatibility ask.
[09:12] Tom Becker: Any particular OS distros you recommend? We're predominantly on RHEL 8.5 and some Ubuntu 22.04 nodes.
[09:19] Diego Alvarez: RHEL and Ubuntu are both supported. For RHEL we supply RPMs; for Ubuntu we do debs. We'll list tested kernel versions in the compatibility matrix.
[09:28] Maya Chen: Let's talk about governance: who signs off on updates internally?
[09:31] Marta Silva: For compliance, updates to models or runtime require dual approvals: Security + Compliance signoff. We also require a rollback plan and regression tests.
[09:42] Maya Chen: Got it. We can include a recommended change-control runbook in the package.
[09:46] Lucas Reed: From a networking side, what ports are needed for cluster management vs model serving?
[09:50] Diego Alvarez: We'll provide a table. Typically HTTPS for console (configurable), mTLS ports for intra-service comms, and ephemeral ports for streaming. We'll try to minimize the surface area.
[10:02] Priya Nair: Anything about data residency? We will keep all model and input data on prem, but logs may need to be redacted before any export.
[10:10] Diego Alvarez: We support configurable redaction hooks and can apply deterministic hashing of PII fields before logs leave the cluster.
[10:18] Tom Becker: For the install timeline, what's realistic?
[10:21] Maya Chen: From contract to first deployment typically 8-12 weeks for new private installs including PS engagement, longer if custom kernel work is required.
[10:30] Priya Nair: Our internal legal wants to see indemnities for model behavior and data processing — is there an enterprise contract template?
[10:37] Maya Chen: Yes — our legal team has an enterprise template and we can share redlines.
[10:41] Marta Silva: Also need info on data deletion guarantees and revocation of keys.
[10:45] Diego Alvarez: We can provide a key revocation process. For complete model deletion we provide wipe scripts that remove cached weights and zero-out NVMe regions if required by policy.
[10:58] Lucas Reed: Perf question — can you run benchmarks on prem with our hardware?
[11:03] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we can. We'll package a lightweight benchmark harness that runs in your cluster and reports latency/throughput numbers. The harness can be run offline and the results exported.
[11:13] Tom Becker: Do you support multi-tenant on the same cluster? We might want separate namespaces for different research groups.
[11:19] Diego Alvarez: Yes, multi-tenant with resource quotas and RBAC per namespace is supported.
[11:25] Priya Nair: One last operational — retention and long-term archive of models: can Redwood integrate with our offline tape/archive strategy?
[11:31] Maya Chen: We can integrate with object storage connectors; for tape/archive we typically rely on your archival process importing the signed model bundles into tape. We'll document the archive workflow.
[11:41] (brief cross talk)
[11:50] Maya Chen: Alright, thinking about next steps — Diego will produce a hardware compatibility matrix; I'll share packaging spec and examples of our signed artifact flow. We'll also put together a TCO sketch.
[12:03] Priya Nair: That sounds good. Please include the compliance team on all docs.
[12:08] Marta Silva: Yes, cc me please.
[12:12] Maya Chen: Will do. Anything else from Oceanic?
[12:15] Lucas Reed: Not from infra, thanks.
[12:17] Tom Becker: No, that covers it.
[12:19] Diego Alvarez: We'll send the artifacts and schedule the capacity workshop — suggest week of Oct 20?
[12:24] Priya Nair: Week of Oct 20 works.
[12:27] Maya Chen: Great, we will follow up with calendar invites and share the docs. Thanks everyone.

Wrap / Links referenced:
- Packaging spec (will share link): [redwood-internal]/private/airgap-packaging-spec (placeholder)
- Example signed-artifact flow doc: https://redwood.example.com/docs/airgap-signed-artifacts (placeholder)
- Benchmark harness repo (zip): delivered as artifact in follow-up

Call ended at ~00:52:10

Recap (verbatim-like):
Maya: Next steps — Diego to deliver HW matrix; Maya to share packaging spec and TCO; Oceanic to share inventories and compliance requirements. We'll target week of Oct 20 for capacity workshop.

Notes on transcription quality: Some product names were transcribed oddly (kay vee cache -> KV cache), and there are small speaker attribution errors near the end.

End of transcript.

Share air-gap deployment checklist and packaging spec
Schedule on-prem capacity planning workshop (deep dive w/ infra)
Provide initial cost estimate for Dedicated vs Private (including HW amortization)
Send SOC 2/ISO and KMS/HSM integration whitepaper

Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE): Produce hardware compatibility matrix (GPU SKUs, NVMe, NICs) for Oceanic - due 2025-10-14
Maya Chen (Redwood AE): Share packaging spec + airgap install steps and offline update cadence doc - due 2025-10-10
Lucas Reed (Oceanic): Provide current cluster inventory and maintenance blackout windows - due 2025-10-13
Marta Silva (Oceanic Compliance): List required audit logs and retention periods (sys + app) - due 2025-10-15

elena: TL;DR first: we can provide SOC2 evidence bundles, ISO mappings, export audit logs, and support BYOK. details below and owners named.

priya: SOC2/ISO evidence: we produce a packaged bundle (control mappings, logs, config snapshots, and test artifacts). request via the compliance form: https://bit.ly/rwd-compliance. include `org`, `project`, `control_scope` and `evidence_owner`. expect 3 business days for full manual packs. :hourglass_flowing_sand:

dan: audit-log exports: hosted tenants get exports to our managed bucket `s3://redwood-logs/audit/<region>/` by default. private & VPC deployments export into customer buckets via an IAM role we create. default retention = 90 days; to request 180/365 days set `retention_days` in your compliance request. example export pattern: `s3://<customer-bucket>/redwood/audit/<cluster-id>/YYYY/MM/DD/`

liz: perms question — does product need to create buckets or do you handle role setup?

d an: recommended: Interface Endpoints (AWS PrivateLink backed) for control-plane & API traffic. PrivateLink is the path we use for hosted-managed integrations. VPC peering is allowed only for eval/test but not recommended for prod due to routing limits & security surface. ping eng-platform for a short arch review.

priya: KMS/BYOK: we support AWS CMKs + BYOK with imported key material. rotation: automatic AWS rotation is supported for CMKs; for imported keys we require a rotation schedule in the onboarding doc. we generally advise rotation every 90 days for high-sensitivity customers. HSM-backed flows are available — contact security for the onboarding checklist.

text:
Kate L: Quick sync — after yesterday's vuln triage we should revisit SIEM export retention and who can request exports. Sandbox tenants leaked a stack trace that contained user identifiers.
Jason H: Oof. What retention window was that export using?
Kate L: The subscription was set to 90 days. SOC wants 365 for security signals, but legal flagged the PII exposure.
Priya S: Two threads: 1) tighten retention for non-prod to 30d unless explicitly approved; 2) gate exports with stricter RBAC + KMS wrapping for any full-raw export.
Dan R: Agreed. We can reuse the ephemeral key-unwrap flow we discussed for forensic snapshots. For exports we add a new role export/unwrap-role that requires an approval ticket and SSO step.
Priya S: +1. Also recommend we inject a redaction transform in the export pipeline for fields marked as pii in the schema registry. That way partial exports are safe by default.
Maria V: Legal needs to sign off on the exact fields to mask. I'll loop them in but we should design the default to err on the safe side.
Jason H: Cost concern — larger retention -> higher SIEM storage costs. For security signals we can compact older raw events into tokenized summaries after 60d. Keep full detail only for approved cases.
Kate L: For incident response, oncall needs a fast path to request full data. Proposal: a timeboxed elevation (max 2 hours) that creates a scoped CMK unwrap permission and logs the approver and reason.
Dan R: Implementation sketch:
```json
{
 "Statement": [
 {"Effect":"Allow","Action":"kms:Decrypt","Resource":"arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/EXPORT-UNWRAP","Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:PrincipalTag/approval_ticket":"SEC-4321"},"DateLessThan":{"aws:CurrentTime":"2024-06-01T14:00:00Z"}}}
 ]
}
```
This would be minted by the approval service and auto-revoke.
security-bot: Created SEC-4321 (RBAC + export gating) and attached a checklist: https://rwd.internal/SEC-4321/checklist :lock: 
Priya S: We should add an audit hook that records: requester, approver, reason, ticket id, KMS key id, and export hash. Tie that to the long-term audit store (immutable).
Kate L: Agreed. Also add an alert if >1 export per tenant per 24h that includes pii fields.
Maria V: One more: ensure dev tools (devbox, local debug exports) cannot export raw logs by default. Make an explicit dev-export role that strips pii and reduces retention.
Jason H: I'll scope the RBAC changes and open a PR with the policy diffs. Expect a draft by EOD.
Dan R: I'll prototype the approval service changes + token minting. Putting a short runbook here: https://rwd.internal/runbooks/export-approval-v2
Kate L: Thanks — once PRs are up, let's schedule a 15m review with Legal and SOC. Want to move fast on this one. :thumbsup:

title: Northstar Customer Support AI
author: Monica Patel
text:
Primary driver is safe model upgrades for their support agent product. They want quality gating without user impact: mirror sampled prod traffic to candidate variants (new model version + quant profile + prompt changes), score asynchronously, and make go/no-go decisions during canaries. Must integrate with rollout policies and support fast disable (kill switch). Prefer Dedicated (predictable throughput + isolation) with VPC deployment; open to starting on Hosted API for initial prototyping if data handling is acceptable.

High-volume chat completions for support-agent flows (tool/function calling + structured JSON outputs). Also uses embeddings + reranking for retrieval. Mix of short and medium contexts; peak traffic during business hours. They care about multilingual (EN/ES/FR) and channel-specific prompts (email vs chat).

User path: p95 < 900ms for typical turns (excluding tool latency), p99 < 2.0s; streaming preferred for long answers. Throughput target discussed: ~250-400 RPS peak across tenants; wants predictable capacity for major launches. Shadow path must be isolated and fail-open with strict timeouts.

Must-have v1 metrics (customer language): (1) JSON/format adherence for tool outputs, (2) refusal/safety rate (avoid over-refusals), (3) instruction-following proxy (answers the question / uses provided context), (4) regression alerts with confidence intervals. Asked specifically for: 'show me a red/green gate on the canary when format drift happens' and 'don’t ship a model that starts adding extra keys to our schema'.

They have been burned by "silent" regressions during model upgrades: same latency/cost, worse resolution rate and more escalations. They want shadow testing as a default part of every rollout: sample 0.1%–1% of traffic, run shadow variants (2 candidates max), and compute deltas by segment (language, workflow type). Explicit requirement: no impact to user response; if shadow target or scoring is down, the user path must remain healthy (fail open).

Support conversations can include PII (names, emails, order numbers). They will not allow long prompt/response retention by default. Asked for: redaction/allowlist controls, truncation, hashed identifiers, and short retention (they suggested 7 days for scored artifacts; less if possible). Need auditability: who created/edited experiments, when sampling changed, who exported examples.

Medium-high sensitivity to incremental scoring/storage cost. They want to understand how sampling rate maps to scoring compute. Will likely accept add-on pricing if it replaces their current manual evaluation workflow and reduces incident risk during upgrades.

Northstar is using an existing vendor for primary LLM calls but lacks a reliable quality gating story. Their VP Eng emphasized: 'We can’t afford a bad rollout that tanks CSAT for two weeks.' They see Redwood’s differentiation as production serving + rollouts + quality metrics in one console (vs stitching together vendors).

Need written defaults for shadow traffic retention/redaction (prompt/response) and ability to enforce per-tenant overrides
Wants clear guardrails that shadowing cannot affect user-path latency/quotas (fail-open + circuit breaker)
Data residency requirement: keep all artifacts in US (phase 1); EU later

Schedule security + architecture review (shadow traffic data handling + SLOs); propose 2-week Dedicated POC with shadow experiments enabled on 1 production route at 0.5% sampling.

2026-01-22: Technical deep dive (Dedicated + rollouts) focused on shadow evals/quality gates; discussed sampling + statistical power and where scoring runs. (Fireflies: 2026-01-22-technical-deep-dive-shadow-evals-and-rollouts)
2026-01-28: Follow-up email thread: asked whether quality signals can trigger auto-rollback vs advisory only, and how confidence intervals are shown in Console. (Gmail thread: 20260110-shadow-traffic-prd-review-and-launch-plan)
2026-02-05: Beta-style check-in: reviewed early dashboard mockups and asked for per-segment filters (language, channel, tenant) but warned about cardinality. (Fireflies: 2026-02-05-beta-checkin-shadow-traffic-quality-metrics)
2026-02-12: SE shared draft API surface for shadow experiments + RBAC expectations; customer requested audit log entries for experiment changes and export of aggregates. (Internal doc link shared)

Account context
- Northstar Customer Support AI = multi-tenant support-agent platform (B2B) used by ecommerce + SaaS support orgs.
- Current pain: canary model changes are hard to validate for quality; they only detect issues via downstream support metrics (CSAT drop, escalations) days later.

What they want from Redwood
- Dedicated capacity (VPC) is the end state; will consider starting with Hosted API for a limited-scope POC if we can demonstrate data controls.
- Shadow traffic: mirror production requests to candidate variants while returning control response; score async; surface quality deltas next to latency/cost.
- Quality gates attached to rollouts: show pass/fail + CI bands; support alerting and (eventually) auto-rollback.

Key quotes / call snippets
- 'We’ve had upgrades where everything looked fine on latency and cost, and then our agents started failing tool calls because JSON drifted.'
- 'We need a way to validate quality without putting customers in the blast radius.'
- 'If shadow traffic can ever slow down the user path, it’s a non-starter.'

Requirements (detailed)
- Workload types: chat completions w/ function/tool calling (structured outputs), embeddings + reranking for retrieval.
- Segmentation: need breakdown by language, workflow (refund, shipment, troubleshooting), and customer tenant; OK with bucketing/limited cardinality.
- Sampling: start 0.1%–0.5%, ramp to 1%+ once stable; wants guidance on statistical power and auto-stop conditions.
- Data retention: prefer <= 7 days for raw prompts/responses; scored aggregates can be retained longer. Must have redaction/truncation options and clear defaults.
- Compliance: SSO/SAML, audit logs, KMS; wants an explicit statement about where scoring runs and how artifacts are stored.

Open questions / risks
- Auto-rollback: they asked for it, but are OK if v1 is advisory with alerts as long as it’s in the roadmap.
- Cardinality: they want tenant-level drilldowns; we need to set expectations (bucketing/filters, example sampling, limits).
- Residency: US-only initially; EU expansion later (they have EU customers but can route evaluation traffic to US for now if contract allows).

Next steps
- SE (Dylan) to propose POC plan: 1 route, 1 candidate variant, 0.5% sampling, v1 metric bundle (format adherence + refusal + instruction-following rubric).
- Share written guardrails: fail-open semantics, timeouts, circuit breaker, scoring lag behavior.
- Schedule security review with Marcus Lin / Kevin Osei focused on retention/redaction and auditability.

title: Dedicated + Private: Enclave zoning, control-plane handshake, and emergency failover narrative (SIG/SOC2 ask)
author: dylan_brooks
text:
From: Rosa Chen <rosa.chen@regulusbank.com>
To: dylan_brooks@redwood.ai
Cc: security@regulusbank.com
Date: Tue, 12 May 2026 08:14:00 -0700
Subject: Enclave zoning + control-plane handshake details for SIG pack

Dylan,

Thanks for the quick intro last week. Regulus' compliance team is going through SIG and needs a short narrative and supporting artifacts that show how Redwood isolates customer workloads for Dedicated and Private deployments. Specifically we need:

- A short (1-2 page) narrative describing enclave zoning (service planes, tenant compute vs shared infra), the control-plane handshake and authentication flow for Dedicated vs Private, and the emergency failover behavior when a Dedicated pool fails over to a compatible host.
- A network diagram that clearly labels trust boundaries, KMS/HSM control-plane connections, and egress choke points. Redactions are fine for IPs.
- A control-handshake sequence diagram (message flow) for initial bootstrapping, certificate rotation, and session teardown.
- A short note on key egress controls (what outbound ports are allowed, where monitoring/agent telemetry flows) and an evidence artifact for SOC2 (log retention pointers or sample alert).

Can you get a draft of the narrative + artifacts by end of day May 20? If helpful, we can do a 30-minute sync with your security/infra folks early next week.

Rosa Chen
Director, Security Assurance

Attached (zipped): enclave-zoning_v1.pdf, control-handshake_sequence.png, kms-boundary_matrix.csv, egress-playbook.md

Executive narrative (summary):
Redwood deploys Dedicated and Private workloads into logically separated enclave layers. Each deployment separates three primary planes: control plane (orchestration & identity), data/compute plane (model inference), and telemetry/observability. Tenant compute runs in isolated host pools (Dedicated) or tenant VPCs (Private) with network-level ACLs and microsegmentation applied at the service edge. Shared services (e.g., centralized monitoring, update orchestration) run in a separate management enclave with tightly scoped peering.

Control-plane handshake (high-level):
- Bootstrap: Host authenticates to Redwood control services using an X.509 certificate provisioned at image creation; initial attestation includes image hash + signed CSR.
- Session: Post-bootstrap, mTLS is established between host agent and control endpoints. Short-lived session tokens (rotated by the control plane) authorize config pulls and model pull requests.
- Rotation / revocation: Certificate rotation is automated on a scheduled window or on explicit revocation events. If rotation fails, the host is quarantined and marked for remediation; failover traffic is routed to standby hosts.

Emergency failover:
- Trigger: host health degradation, kernel-level faults, or degraded I/O to attached model cache triggers automated evacuation.
- State sync: lightweight checkpoints for KV cache and model metadata are streamed to nearby standby nodes; full model artifacts are pulled from the model registry on failover.
- Blast radius mitigation: routing policies isolate failing hosts at the service edge; tenant affinity is maintained where possible and traffic is throttled to maintain upstream SLOs.

KMS/HSM note: The kms-boundary_matrix.csv attached lists which components invoke external KMS, whether keys are customer-managed (BYOK), and typical call flows. In Dedicated we support customer-managed keys for encrypting model artifacts at rest; in Private we support both customer-managed and hardware security modules in-customer-network.

Egress controls:
- Only outbound egress to model registry (HTTPS), telemetry endpoints, and KMS endpoints is allowed from compute hosts.
- Agents use TLS 1.2+ with certificate pinning to known endpoints.

title: Runtime Experiment Scorecard and Telemetry SLA
author: Asha Mehta
text:
Summary
-------
This document defines a unified experiment scorecard and a minimal telemetry SLA for runtime experiments, kernel-level canaries, and benchmark-driven rollouts. It bridges architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling, benchmarking, release gating, and on-call runbooks so that engineers and SREs can run reproducible experiments with clear pass/fail criteria.

Scope
-----
- Applies to: runtime feature experiments, kernel variant canaries, quantization rollouts, and model-variant A/B tests run in hosted and dedicated deployments.
- Excludes: user-facing product A/B tests unrelated to inference runtime behavior.

Why this exists
----------------
We observed variability between bench microbenchmarks and live traffic (tail latency regressions, subtle token-cost changes, KV-cache warmup differences). That undermines rollouts. The scorecard + telemetry SLA ensures experiments have signal fidelity, observability, and clear remediation steps.

Scorecard: pass/fail axes
------------------------
Each experiment run must record a scorecard. Minimum axes (all numeric, reported at 99th, 95th, and mean as indicated):

1) Latency (ms)
 - p99 latency vs baseline (target: <= +5% delta)
 - p95 latency vs baseline (target: <= +3% delta)
 - mean latency (target: <= +2% delta)
2) Throughput (req/s)
 - Sustained throughput under canonical load (target: >= 98% of baseline)
3) Token unit cost (USD/token or internal cost units)
 - Per-token cost change (target: <= +4% delta)
4) Failure rate (5xx/timeout)
 - Error rate (target: < 0.1% absolute increase)
5) Kernel preemption count / backpressure events
 - Absolute counts and rate per 10k requests (target: no increase beyond historical 95th percentile)
6) KV-cache hit rate and cold-start warmup curve
 - Hit-rate curve and time-to-90%-steady-state (target: within baseline envelope)
7) Quality-relevant regressions (output-level metrics, tying to evaluation harness)
 - BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-sim delta or application-specific eval set pass rate (target: no regression beyond alert threshold)

Each axis is graded as: pass / warn / fail with a short rationale field. The final decision is: fail if any axis is fail OR more than two axes are warn.

Telemetry SLA (minimal contract)
--------------------------------
The experiment telemetry must be available in the canonical observability stack within the following windows:
- Metrics (timeseries): within 1 minute of generation.
- Traces (sampled detailed traces): available in trace storage within 5 minutes.
- Kernel-level events (preempt, handoff, slot-abort): ingested and queryable within 30 minutes.
- Bench artifacts (microbench outputs, raw traces, sample payloads): uploaded to experiment object store within 1 hour.

Required telemetry labels/tags (schema)
- experiment_id: string
- run_id: string
- kernel_variant: string
- model_variant: string
- node_pool: {dedicated, hosted, private} (string)
- kvcache_epoch: integer (stringified)
- sequence_length_bucket: {short, medium, long} (string)
- traffic_cohort: string

Example metric naming conventions (timeseries)
- runtime.latency.p99.{kernel_variant}.{model_variant}
- runtime.kvcache.hit_rate.{node_pool}.{sequence_length_bucket}
- runtime.kernel.preempt.count.{kernel_variant}
- runtime.cost.per_token.{model_variant}

Experiment orchestration (procedural checklist)
------------------------------------------------
1) Define hypothesis and scorecard (owner: experiment author).
2) Register experiment in experiment ledger with experiment_id and target cohorts.
3) Provision canary capacity (node_pool and kernel_variant pinned) and record kernel_variant metadata.
4) Run synthetic benchmark (bench harness) for at least N=3 sustained loops; collect microbench metrics.
5) Shadow traffic or low-percentage real traffic for 24 hours (or N requests if traffic low).
6) Collect telemetry and compute scorecard axes.
7) If pass, promote to wider canary (30% traffic) and repeat step 6 for 48 hours.
8) If pass again, initiate rollout with staged increments and continuous monitoring.
9) If any stage fails, follow rollback runbook immediately.

Benchmarking harness: minimum requirements
----------------------------------------
Table: harness config (as a simple ASCII table)

| key | expected value / example | rationale |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|-----------|
| workload_profile | conversational-chat, short-completion, reranking | cover common shapes |
| request_rate | synthetic: 100–200 RPS per node; canary: mirror live | stress check |
| sequence_length_dist | short: 1–32, medium: 33–256, long: 257+ | bucket coverage |
| replication_factor | 3 | reduce sample noise |
| telemetry_sampling_rate | 100% metrics, 10% traces, 1% full kernel traces | cost tradeoff |
| run_duration | microbench: 15m; full: 24h | warmup capture |

Benchmark outputs (artifacts)
- summary.json (scorecard axes, percentiles)
- traces.tar.gz (sampled traces mapped to requests)
- microbench.csv (per-run detailed timings)
- kernel_events.log (preempt/handoff records)

Kernel scheduling considerations for experiments
------------------------------------------------
- Avoid mixing kernel variants with very different preemption semantics in the same node pool during an experiment. This creates hard-to-interpret backpressure signals.
- When testing preemptive kernel variants, include a control cohort pinned to a non-preemptive kernel to differentiate scheduler-side artifacts from upstream workload variability.
- Record kernel credit accounting deltas and slot occupancy histograms. These must be included in the scorecard telemetry.

Profiling playbook (quick-action steps)
--------------------------------------
1) Detect: anomaly triage starts when p99 latency delta > +8% or error rate delta > +0.2%.
2) Collect: increase trace sampling for experiment_id to 100% for 10 minutes and trigger immediate kernel_events collection.
3) Snapshot: create a bench snapshot (replay corpus of 10k requests captured from canary).
4) Isolate: replicate offending workload in sandbox with a 1:1 traffic replay. Capture GPU occupancy, kernel latencies, preempt counts.
5) Hypothesize: use heap map and NVLink counters to check for interconnect or memory-copy hotspots.
6) Mitigate: throttle offending traffic cohort or fallback to baseline kernel_variant.
7) Remediate: iterate on kernel parameter, or revert rollout; document in the experiment ledger.

Sample CLI snippets
-------------------
- Run bench harness:
 
 ./bench-runner --experiment-id exp-2025-0423 --profile conversational-chat --rps 150 --duration 15m --output ./artifacts/exp-2025-0423/

- Increase trace sampling for experiment:
 
 rb-control telemetry set-sampling --experiment exp-2025-0423 --traces 100 --duration 10m

- Pull kernel events for run:
 
 rb-control events fetch --run exp-2025-0423 --type kernel_events --out kernel_events.log

Release gating and rollbacks
-----------------------------
Release gates are evaluated against the scorecard and telemetry SLA. Gate rules:
- Canary -> 30% -> wide rollout. Each gate requires: telemetry SLA met, scorecard pass, no outstanding high-severity known issues.
- Automatic rollback triggers:
 - p99 latency regression > 12% sustained for 10 minutes
 - error-rate increase > 0.5% absolute sustained for 5 minutes
 - kernel preemption rate spike beyond 5x baseline with correlated tail-latency increase

Known issues to monitor during experiments
-----------------------------------------
- KV-cache cold-start nonlinearity: some large-context workloads exhibit long tail warmup spikes. Mitigation: pre-warm cache with shadow traffic and set warmup threshold in deployment config.
- Slot-abort cascade under microburst: certain scheduler configurations can trigger cascading slot aborts, visible as short-lived error bursts. Mitigation: admission-controller smoothing and burst token bucket.
- NVLink blips impacting cross-GPU attention kernels: monitor nvlink_retransmit_rate metric and correlate with kernel latency. Mitigation: fall back to single-GPU execution for affected kernels.

Runbooks (links to actionable pages)
-----------------------------------
- Immediate rollback runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026.json
- Kernel preemption investigation: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/priority-inversion-detection-and-mitigation-playbook-2026.json

Owner and escalation
--------------------
- Experiment owner: author listed in experiment registration (primary contact).
- Runtime oncall: first escalation for perf regressions.
- Kernel scheduler engineering: secondary escalation for kernel-level anomalies.

Appendix: artifact examples
--------------------------
Example summary.json (minimal):

{
 "experiment_id": "exp-2025-0423",
 "run_id": "r1",
 "latency": {"p99": 152.3, "p95": 83.1, "mean": 31.4},
 "kvcache": {"hit_rate": 0.86, "time_to_90": 420},
 "kernel_preempt_count": 23
}

Contact and ownership
---------------------
For questions or to propose changes to the scorecard or telemetry SLA, open a PR against this doc and notify reviewers. For operational exceptions, request a documented exception with a proposed compensating control from runtime SRE.

Revision history
----------------
- 2024-04-15: initial draft (Asha Mehta)
- 2024-09-02: added kernel-event ingestion SLA and sample naming conventions (Ethan Park)
- 2025-11-02: tightened canary gating thresholds and added CLI snippets (Sofia Ruiz)
