title: AtlasHealth — Contract stretch + region onramp review
author: Maya Patel
text:
Quarterly renewal/expansion check-in focused on adding EU region, testing private VPC path, and bumping Dedicated capacity by 30%. Customer raised latency budget vs cost concerns and requested a short benchmarking pilot and updated pricing. Action items surfaced around security docs, billing amendment, and an on-prem checklist.

Meeting header:
Date: 2028-11-09 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Connor (CSM), Rachel Morgan (AtlasHealth), Samir Khan (Atlas CTO), Olivia Park (Platform), Evan Blake (Procurement)

Auto summary (auto): Customer is evaluating a 12-month extension with a 30% capacity uplift and wants to enable an EU region immediately; exploring private VPC pilot in Q1 2029. Security docs (SOC2, SAML, KMS/HSM) requested. Benchmark pilot to validate latency/cost tradeoffs.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining. quick check, i think we have the usual suspects — rachel, samir, olivia, evan — can you hear me okay?
[00:06] Rachel: yes, loud and clear. morning for some of us — afternoon — yeah all good.
[00:12] Maya: awesome. objective today is to align on the renewal timeline, the proposed 30% dedicated bump, and the EU onramp, plus any blockers for a private/VPC pilot.
[00:20] Samir: perfect. we got your note, and procurement's looped in — evan will be the sign-off owner. main thing from our side is latency — our clinicians demand snappy responses — but budget is tight so want to see the numbers.
[00:32] Diego: totally, so high level — Dedicated can give you predictable throughput; the p99 will depend on model shape and prompt length — from what we saw in the eval you sent, most requests average ~900 tokens with spikes to 2k. our routing + prefix KV cash (sic) helps, but we should run a short pilot to quantify.
[00:50] Olivia: small note — we prefer to start in hosted EU and then flip to VPC if we like it. migrating shouldn't be a huge deal but need to understand egress/billing and keys.
[01:03] Connor: i'll drop the VPC checklist after the call — it's the usual: network ranges, peering, KMS info, audit log endpoints.
[01:10] Rachel: on security — SOC two is fine; can you share the SOC 2 plus ISO pack? also want SSO via SAML and RBAC mapping.
[01:21] Maya: yes we'll share our security one-pager and the full SOC2 report. we also have the KMS integration guide — diego will paste that link.

[01:35] Speaker 6: sorry just joined, quick question — what's the fallback if your eu region is saturated?
[01:40] Diego: good one — we have smart routing policies. default is to failover to nearby region (eu-west -> us-west fallback only if policy allows) or to a cheaper/compatible model variant; we can set strict latency-first routing for production so requests don't go cross-continent.
[01:56] Samir: ok, cost. how does dedicated pricing vs hosted differ for committed blocks?
[02:02] Maya: dedicated is a reservation-style commit — predictable monthly fee with a token-based add-on if you burst. hosted is pay-as-you-go. with a 12-month commit we can structure a tiered discount and capacity burst buffer. we'll propose specifics in the amendment.

[02:20] Rachel: timeline — we want EU region live by end of November if possible, or early December latest. is that realistic?
[02:28] Diego: for hosted EU yes, it's almost a flipping of a flag if capacity is available; for VPC/private onboarding that'll be a Q1 2029 activity — involves network provisioning and audit window.
[02:38] Olivia: can we do quick sanity benchmarks in eu-west this week? even 48 hours would help.
[02:44] Diego: yes, we can run a 2-week bench pilot with your traffic sample. initial smoke runs possible within 48 hours — need a test API key and the prompt set.
[02:53] Olivia: we'll prepare the set.

[03:00] Evan: proc question — if we extend the contract and then want to reduce capacity after 6 months, is that allowed?
[03:06] Maya: depends on the term. typically commits are fixed for the period but we can include a quarterly re-eval clause or a staged uplift with a partial break clause — i'll propose language.
[03:15] Samir: any hidden egress charges when moving data between regions or into our VPC?
[03:21] Diego: egress is cloud provider cost; for hosted EU to your VPC there is data transfer — we'll surface estimates and options to minimize egress (edge caching, prefix caching).

[03:35] Rachel: security — how do you do key rotation in Private? our compliance team insists on HSM-backed rotation quarterly.
[03:43] Diego: private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM; rotations are supported, and we record key metadata in audit logs. small caveat — rotations require a short rekey window for any long-lived KV cache tokens. we'll put that in the runbook.
[03:58] Speaker 6: there's some noise on the transcript — transcripts sometime say KV "cash".
[04:03] Maya: yeah fireflies loves that one.

[04:10] Maya: let's walk the proposed pilot plan: 1) Redwood provisions a hosted EU sandbox with a Dedicated-like profile, 2) Atlas pushes representative traffic for 2 weeks, 3) Redwood runs latency/cost breakdown and knob tuning (batching, quant profiles), 4) decide on VPC pilot. agreed?
[04:26] Rachel: agreed. what telemetry do you need? traces, per-token breakdown?
[04:30] Diego: traces + per-token cost, token-level latency histograms, and trace ids so we can map to your backend. also sequence length distribution.

[04:40] Olivia: regarding model variants — if we quantize a variant to reduce cost, what's the risk to hallucination/quality?
[04:47] Diego: depends on the model and quant format; for many of the Llama-family variants the difference is minor for classification but can impact generation in edge cases. Redwood Optimize will run a quality regression against your eval set and flag regressions.

[04:58] Evan: procurement — can you provide a redlineable amendment asap?
[05:03] Maya: yes, we'll do a draft SOW + amendment with the 30% uplift and a staged payout; target to get that by next tues (2028-11-13).

[05:12] Samir: on costs — can we get a blended unit price if we commit 12 months + an EU region?
[05:18] Maya: yes, that's standard — blended pricing across regions with a small premium for private. i'll include two options: hosted-eu-first and dedicated-reserved-first.

[05:28] Diego: operational note — if you want strict p99 < 90ms we may need to increase instance density and reduce batching; that increases per-token cost. we can show the tradeoff in the bench.

[05:40] Rachel: ok, decision points then: 1) do the 2-week bench in EU (yes), 2) sign 12-month with 30% uplift (tentative until bench results), 3) plan VPC pilot for Q1.
[05:52] Maya: great. i'll recap after the call.

[05:58] Connor: action — i'll send runbook and onboarding link now; diego will follow up with pilot questions.
[06:05] Diego: quick note, please include sample worst-case prompts so we can hit tail latency scenarios.
[06:10] Olivia: will do.

[06:15] Maya: any final blockers?
[06:18] Samir: none for now, just need the amendment and bench results.
[06:22] Rachel: same. also could you include the SLA response windows and escalation contacts?
[06:27] Maya: yes, that goes in the SOW.

[06:35] Maya: thanks everyone — we'll send the docs and schedule follow-ups.
[06:40] Evan: thanks.
[06:42] Rachel: thanks all.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: medium — occasional word swaps (e.g., KV cash), speaker attribution minor errors. Links mentioned: docs.redwood.io/vpc-onboard (runbook), internal bench sheet (link to be shared by diego).

title: Pin governor: controlled fallback windows and variant throttling for pinned model versions
author: Aisha Khan
text:
Problem: Customers who pin model versions require guarantees that pinned traffic will not be silently rerouted to incompatible variants during regional capacity events or enforced deprecations. Current fallback behavior is coarse: it either allows a global automatic substitution (risking API surface regressions) or rejects traffic (customer-visible errors).

Goal: Implement a 'pin governor' policy that enables controlled, observable fallback windows with variant throttling and staged deprecation escalation. The governor should: (1) prefer same-version variants in other regions when compatible, (2) apply per-variant throttles (traffic shaping) during capacity shortfalls, (3) expose a grace/deprecation timeline with telemetry and auto-notifications, and (4) publish performance profiles so substitution decisions respect latency/cost SLO tradeoffs.

Scope: design + runtime implementation + console UX for policy configuration + telemetry dashboards + rollout plan. Not in scope: new quantization formats or model conversion tooling (those are separate onboarding tasks).

Pinned endpoint will not return 5xx due to immediate global substitution for 95% of simulated regional outages; instead traffic will be throttled or routed with a visible fallback reason.
Operators can configure a per-pin 'fallback window' (0-72 hours) and an optional 'variant throttle' (0-100%) via API and Console.
Performance profile publishing: for any candidate variant, runtime picks substitution only if published profile meets the pinned version's latency/quality thresholds or is explicitly allowed by policy.
Telemetry dashboard shows per-pin fallback events, % traffic diverted, average token latency delta, and estimated cost delta within 5% of actual charges for test load.
Security review signoff completed (KMS/metadata handling for pin reasons and audit logs).
Integration tests that simulate: regional AZ failure, variant mismatch, and deprecation TTL expire, all passing in CI with deterministic assertions.

Design doc for pin governor and policy schema (Confluence)
Runtime: implement policy evaluator and per-variant token-level throttler
Routing: update smart router to prefer compatible same-version variants and respect throttle hints
Console: add pin policy UI and validation
Telemetry: dashboard + alert rules + structured fallback events to logging stream
E2E tests and chaos sims (regional isolation, warmup behavior)
Security review and audit-log schema
Gradual rollout plan and canary with 5 internal customers

2026-03-10 - Aisha Khan: Kickoff meeting notes posted to Confluence. Initial spike goals: measure warmup delta between same-version variant in other region vs. local fallback and quantify cold-start latency at 512 token context. Link: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Pin+Governor+Spike
2026-03-11 - Marco Diaz: Spike complete. Observations: warmup penalty when routing to a warm peer in 'us-west-2' is ~12ms median for 128-token responses but 160ms 95th for cold model variant in different quantization. Action: require published performance profiles to include cold/warm percentiles and quantization flags. Data uploaded: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/abcd123/pin-spike-compare
2026-03-12 - Priya Nair (PM): Reviewed design draft. Requested explicit revert behavior when substitution increases hallucination signals beyond policy threshold and a notification SLA for impacted customers. Added to acceptance criteria.
2026-03-12 - Security (Liam O'Connor): Flagged that pin metadata (reason, customer-contact, fallback-window) must be encrypted at rest and included in audit records for Private deployments. Marked security_review_required = true.
2026-03-13 - Marco Diaz: RFC posted for internal review (runtime PR referenced). Runtime PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1789. Console mockups in Drive: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1XyPinGovernorMocks
2026-03-13 - Aisha Khan: Telemetry query skeleton added to repo (telemetry/queries/pin_fallbacks.sql). Dashboard draft: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/abcd123/pin-fallback-telemetry. Note: need to add unit tests to ensure fallback_reason enum stays stable.

title: SLO observability pipeline design and validation
author: Maya Patel
text:
Summary:
This document defines a canonical design and validation workflow for the SLO observability pipeline used by Redwood Inference SRE. It covers metric selection, collection guarantees, aggregation/rollups, validation and backfill procedures, automated error-budget actions, and runbook primitives for SLO burn incidents. The goal is to ensure SLOs are measurable, auditable, and actionable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Provide an end-to-end pattern for converting raw telemetry into trusted SLO state and automated operational responses.
- Scope: All production services that expose external-facing customer APIs (text generation, embeddings, chat) and internal platform surfaces that carry user-visible traffic (control plane routes). Does not cover purely experimental or internal feature branches.

Key terms:
- SLI: Service Level Indicator, the raw metric (ex: successful_response_ratio).
- SLO: Service Level Objective, target on an SLI (ex: 99.95% availability over 30d).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO.
- Burn: sustained error-budget consumption above policy threshold.
- Rollup window: the aggregation interval used for SLO reporting (default 1m -> 5m rollup).

Design principles (non‑negotiable):
1) Deterministic aggregation: every request must map to at most one SLI event with an immutable timestamp and context tags (service, cluster, region, model_variant, route_id, customer_tier).
2) Single source of truth: SLI ingestion must originate from the service emitter and flow through a validated pipeline into the metrics system (Prometheus/Thanos) and the SLO store (Cortex-backed SLO service).
3) Observability parity: SLO-relevant metrics must be present in both real-time alerting (Prometheus) and long-term retrospective stores (Parquet on object storage).
4) Testability & replayability: all ingested raw events are checkpointed for 72 hours to enable replays for validation/backfill.
5) Ownership & audit trail: each SLO has a single owner team and an audit log of changes (who, when, why).

Required telemetry and labels (table):
- name | type | required labels | retention
- request_count | counter | service, route_id, model_variant, region, outcome, status_code | 13 months
- request_latency_ms | histogram | service, route_id, model_variant, region, quantile_tag | 13 months
- kv_cache_hit | counter | service, model_variant, region | 6 months
- upstream_fallback | counter | service, route_id, fallback_reason | 1 year

SLI definitions (examples with PromQL):
1) Availability SLI (success ratio):
- definition: ratio of successful responses to total requests with customer-visible status codes
- PromQL example:
 sum(rate(request_count{service="api-public", outcome=~"success|partial_success"}[5m])) / sum(rate(request_count{service="api-public"}[5m]))
2) Latency SLI (p95 tail):
- definition: fraction of requests with latency <= 500ms on production tier routes
- PromQL (using histogram_quantile):
 histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_ms_bucket{service="api-public", route_id=~"/v1/.*"}[5m])) by (le)) <= 500
3) Correctness SLI (rerank/semantic scoring):
- definition: automated evaluation success rate for structured outputs on daily sample sets (see "daily-evals" job)

SLO targets and windows (examples):
- api-public availability: target 99.95% over 30d, 99.9% over 7d (secondary)
- embeddings-latency: 95% of requests <= 200ms over 14d
- control-plane-ops: 99.99% availability over 30d
Note: Each SLO must include a rationale paragraph in the SLO metadata explaining customer impact and cost tradeoffs.

Error budget policy and automated actions:
- Soft thresholds (informational): 10% of monthly error budget consumed -> notify owner via Slack SLO channel, generate weekly burn report.
- Hard thresholds (automated mitigation): 25% of monthly error budget consumed -> reduce non-essential background jobs (auto-pause batch refresh), scale down low-priority replication, and enable degraded-mode routing to warm standby models.
- Emergency threshold: 50% of monthly error budget consumed in 24h -> trigger runbook SRV-BURN-01 and open an incident/P1.
- Reconciliation: all automated mitigations must be logged in the SLO audit trail with an auto-generated runbook decision entry.

Validation & backfill workflow (step-by-step):
1) Pre-deploy checks (CI): unit tests for emitters, schema validation for metric labels, and a synthetic traffic job that asserts metric emission at canary load.
2) Canary validation (first 48h): compare canary and baseline SLI rates (delta < 0.05%). If deviation > 0.2% open a preflight review.
3) Backfill/replay steps when gaps detected:
 a) Identify gap window from checkpointed raw events.
 b) Replay events into a validation namespace and compute SLI.
 c) If replay SLI differs from production SLO by > 0.1% for availability or > 2% for latency quantiles, escalate to SRE and platform-observability.
 d) Once fixed, record a backfill job and annotate the SLO with the correction.
4) Post-deploy audit (30d): scheduled SLO-quality report comparing metric drift, cardinality growth, and rollup accuracy.

Runbook primitives (short snippets):
- SLO-BURN-ALERT (P2)
 1) Pager fires when 25% monthly budget consumed AND 14d budget slope > 0.5%/day.
 2) Triage: confirm signal (run PromQL queries, check for client-side retry storms).
 3) Immediate mitigations: route to lower-cost model_variant, enable prefix KV cache bypass, disable non-critical telemetry.
 4) If mitigations reduce burn rate to <10%/day, move to monitoring state; otherwise escalate to on-call P1.

- SLO-BACKFILL (Runbook)
 1) Owner tags the SLO and requests replay from the checkpoint store.
 2) Validation lead runs replay in staging namespace, generating a JSON report (schema below).
 3) If consistent, merge backfill and update SLO notes.

Alert rule YAML example (PrometheusAlertmanager-style):
- alert: SLO_MonthlyBudgetBurnHigh
 expr: (1 - (sum(rate(request_count{service="api-public", outcome=~"success|partial_success"}[30d])) / sum(rate(request_count{service="api-public"}[30d])))) > 0.0025
 for: 30m
 labels:
 severity: warning
 runbook: SRV-BURN-01
 annotations:
 summary: "SLO monthly burn > 25% for api-public"

Metric quality gates (automated checks executed nightly):
- cardinality growth < 15% week-over-week per service
- required labels present on 99.9% of samples
- histogram bucket completeness (no missing buckets for last 7 days)
- replay parity: replayed SLI within 0.1% of live SLI for availability metrics

Operational tooling integrations (recommended):
- Checkpoint store: S3 bucket with lifecycle 90d for raw events, archived Parquet for 13 months.
- Replay engine: containerized job (replayctl) that accepts window and SLO id and writes to validation Prometheus namespace.
- SLO dashboard: Cortex-based SLO store surfaced in Redwood Console with token-level filters.
- Automation: a lightweight runner (runbook-exec) to apply the automated mitigation actions via infra API.

Ownership, audits and change control:
- Every SLO must live in the SLO registry and include: owner, escalation channel, rationale, and approval history.
- Changes to SLO thresholds require: owner sign-off + SRE peer review + a 72h monitoring window post-change.
- Audit record sample: "2025-01-21 | Maya Patel | raised availability target for api-public from 99.9->99.95 | reason: enterprise SLA increase"

On-call playbook excerpt (when called from PagerDuty):
1) Acknowledge and capture initial facts: affected routes, burn rate, recent deploys, and capacity signals.
2) Run the triage notebook (link in SLO dashboard) that executes canonical PromQL queries and summarizes upstream errors, client retry patterns, and capacity headroom.
3) If evidence points to capacity saturation, coordinate with capacity on-call to run quick scale (see capacity rapid scale checklist).
4) Notify product & customer success if an incident is declared (include estimated customer impact and mitigation timeline).

Rollout checklist for the observability pipeline (preflight):
- emitter library updated and released
- CI metric schema checks pass
- checkpointing to S3 enabled for the service
- canary traffic tests green for 48h
- SLO created in registry with owner and rationale
- automated mitigations reviewed and simulated in staging

Appendix: example JSON report schema for replay validation (single-line fields):
- replay_id, slo_id, start_ts, end_ts, baseline_availability, replay_availability, diff_pct, action_taken

Related references:
- SLO escalation and capacity triggers (internal page)
- Error budget orchestration playbook (internal page)

Document maintenance:
- Owner: engineering (SRE); review cadence: quarterly or after any major SLO incident.
- Last review: 2025-02-03 (Maya Patel).

title: Add signal suppression + false-positive guardrails (internal org filtering, min-volume gates)
author: Mei Lin
text:
Context: During the NA pilot we’re seeing a non-trivial number of “vanity” intent triggers and a couple of true false positives (notably Quartz Commerce) resulting in unwanted outreach (see SUP-3392). This PR adds a set of guardrails to reduce noise while keeping recall for genuinely sales-worthy signals. Summary of changes: (1) Suppression windows: prevent re-routing the same signal type for the same account within a configurable cooldown (default 14d for intent, 7d for reliability/usage) unless severity increases. We store last_routed_at by (workspace_id, signal_type) and compare against current signal_score + severity. (2) Internal/test org filtering: blocklist/allowlist logic for Redwood-owned workspaces and known test tenants; also filters “example.com” style seeded domains and sandbox workspaces tagged by billing. This is applied before scoring so we avoid polluting analytics tables and HubSpot with internal activities. (3) Minimum-volume gates: require minimum sustained volume for threshold signals (tokens/spend/429s) to reduce one-off spikes; add a separate gate for “docs intent only” that requires either (a) 2+ distinct sessions across 48h or (b) docs intent + at least one supporting product event (workspace invite spike, API key rotation, or repeated rate-limit). (4) Confidence floor: enforce a minimum confidence threshold for routing (default 0.65) with per-signal overrides, and write suppressed candidates to a side table for tuning. (5) Auditability: whenever we suppress we emit a structured log and a metric with reason codes (cooldown, internal_org, min_volume, confidence_floor). Tradeoff notes: This will reduce total routed tasks (expected 25–40% drop based on pilot cohort replay), but should materially reduce spam/false positives. We explicitly bias toward fewer tasks while we tune thresholds; suppressed events remain queryable for later adjustment. Testing: Added unit tests for suppression keying + cooldown behavior, internal org matching, and min-volume gating; added a replay test against a sanitized subset of the pilot cohort to validate volume impact. Follow-ups: (a) Add UI surfacing of “suppressed signals” for triage (see DES-412), (b) Re-evaluate doc intent heuristics once we have docs instrumentation improvements from Elliot (docs session identifiers), and (c) Consider account-level suppression when Marketing nurture is active (separate workstream with Tyler/Camila).

Key changes: services/plg_signal_router/suppression/guardrails.ts (new guardrail evaluation pipeline and reason codes); services/plg_signal_router/config/signal_guardrails.yaml (defaults for cooldown, min-volume gates, confidence floor); analytics/jobs/daily_signal_aggregator/min_volume.sql (add sustained-volume windows + distinct-day checks); services/plg_signal_router/internal_org/filter.ts (new internal org matching + explicit deny/allow lists); services/plg_signal_router/hubspot/route.ts (skip routing on suppressed results; still write suppressed to analytics); services/plg_signal_router/metrics.ts (new counters: suppressed_total{reason}, routed_total{signal_type}, candidate_total); tests/plg_signal_router/guardrails.test.ts (unit tests for cooldown/severity escalation, min-volume gates, internal matching); tools/replay/pilot_cohort_replay.ts (sanitized replay runner used for before/after counts). Illustrative snippet (guardrail evaluation): if (isInternalOrg(account) && !isExplicitlyAllowed(account)) return suppress('internal_org'); if (!passesMinVolume(signal)) return suppress('min_volume'); if (!passesCooldown(lastRoutedAt, signal)) return suppress('cooldown'); if (signal.confidence < confidenceFloor(signal.type)) return suppress('confidence_floor'); return allow();

Logan Wright (requested changes): Cooldown keying looks right, but can we ensure severity escalation bypasses cooldown only when we have a material delta? Right now it’s >0.01 score, which is too sensitive and will re-spam on minor fluctuations. Also please make sure suppressed candidates are still written with enough context (signal_type, score, reason, window_start/end) so we can tune. Mei Lin (reply): Good call. Updated severity bypass to require either (a) score delta >= 0.15 or (b) severity enum increases (e.g., MED->HIGH). Also added window_start/window_end and score/confidence into suppressed_candidates table + logs. Priya Natarajan: For internal org filtering, I like the deny-by-default for Redwood domains, but please confirm we’re not accidentally suppressing legitimate customers with shared email domains (contractor scenarios). Can we rely primarily on workspace flags rather than email domain? Mei Lin: Agreed; updated to prioritize workspace.billing_account_type==INTERNAL or workspace.tags includes 'redwood-internal'. Domain-based suppression is now a fallback heuristic only when billing metadata is missing, and it requires both domain match AND org_created_by seed script flag. Isabelle Laurent: From an ops standpoint, can we tune cooldowns per region/tier without code changes? (Pilot EMEA wants longer cooldown on intent-only docs views.) Mei Lin: Yes—cooldowns are now config-driven in YAML and read at runtime. Added keys for intent_docs_only_cooldown_days and per-tier overrides (self_serve vs enterprise_trial). David Kim: HubSpot side effects: please ensure we aren’t creating tasks and then immediately suppressing in retries (idempotency). We’ve had issues where the candidate is evaluated twice in the same run. Mei Lin: Added an idempotency guard: suppression decision happens before HubSpot calls; also ensured we persist last_routed_at only after successful HubSpot task creation. Added a test for double-evaluation. Dr. Aisha Rahman: Privacy review: internal org filtering is fine, but ensure the suppressed_candidates table doesn’t include raw URLs or page titles from docs views—keep it to enums/counts. Mei Lin: Updated schema: docs intent stored as doc_category enum + count + distinct_sessions, no raw URLs/titles. Approvals: Logan approved after severity change; Priya approved after internal filter adjustment; Isabelle + David approved with config/idempotency; Aisha approved with docs intent sanitization.

Internal: Reduce PLG signal noise by adding cooldown suppression, internal org filtering, and min-volume gating; emit suppression reason metrics for tuning; mitigates false-positive outreach risk noted in SUP-3392.

title: Elevated 5xx series errors traced to backend proxy degradation causing runtime failovers
text:
Issue summary: Starting 2026-03-10 02:12 UTC we observed an elevated rate of 5xx responses from the hosted endpoint used by ParcelAI. Symptoms appeared as 502/503/504 spikes from the API gateway and an increased cadence of serving-runtime process restarts tied to failover logic. Impact affected a single dedicated tenant (ParcelAI) running on Dedicated capacity in us-east-1.

Initial hypothesis: A combination of degraded proxy performance (increased socket churn and TLS renegotiation fallbacks) plus aggressive autoscaler cooldowns caused upstream runtimes to experience connection pressure and trigger failover/restart orchestrations, amplifying 5xx rates.

Customer-visible errors: sustained 5xx rate ~12% of requests to prediction endpoint over a 45-minute window, increased p95 latency from 120ms to 1.8s, streaming sessions dropped mid-response for ~18% of long-polling requests. ParcelAI reported production traffic errors and some user-facing timeouts affecting order processing features.

1) Send sustained concurrent streaming requests (~200 concurrent sessions) to tenant ParcelAI's /v1/chat/stream endpoint in us-east-1.
2) Observe gateway returning elevated 502/503s after roughly 5-10 minutes as connection churn increases.
3) Check serving-runtime logs for repeated 'upstream connection closed' and 'failover triggered' messages correlating with gateway 5xx timestamps.

API Gateway metrics: 2026-03-10 02:15-03:00 UTC -> 5xx spike from baseline 0.4% to 12.3% (mauve-prod-apigw-us-east).
Proxy logs: repeated TLS handshake fallback to lower cipher family and SYN retries on connection pool (proxy-03-us-east). See /var/log/proxy/proxy-03-2026-03-10.log lines 3421-3450.
Serving runtime: repeated 'evicting-kv-cache' entries prior to restart and 'failover: takeover by replica' at 02:27:14 UTC (runtime-tenant-378).
Tracing: distributed trace id trace-0b3f2a shows connection reset at apigw -> proxy boundary and subsequent request retries that hit downstream capacity limits.

02:30 UTC - Support (Maya) confirmed customer impact and escalated to SRE (Diego).
02:38 UTC - Correlated gateway 5xx increase with a simultaneous rise in proxy TCP retransmits and TLS renegotiation fallback events on proxy hosts. Packet drops and increased RTOs observed on instance proxy-03.
02:50 UTC - Observed autoscaler activity: several serving-runtime replicas were terminated as part of a scale-down that coincided with the spike, suggesting autoscaler cooldowns and scale-down thresholds contributed to capacity insufficiency during connection churn.
03:05 UTC - Reproduced partial failure in staging by artificially inducing connection churn on proxy to validate hypothesis (test run id repro-2026-03-10-proxy-churn).

02:12 UTC - First alerts from SRE dashboards (5xx rate).
02:20 UTC - Pager and Slack alert to #support and #sre-incidents.
02:38 UTC - Initial mitigation: reduced connection keepalive timeout on apigw to 30s to relieve stale sockets.
02:55 UTC - Emergency autoscaler override: increased min replicas for ParcelAI serving pool by +2 to provide breathing room.
03:12 UTC - Temporary proxy config adjustment rolled out to disable aggressive TLS renegotiation fallback on proxy-02/03/04.
03:40 UTC - 5xx rate gradually declined to <1.5% as runtime restarts decreased and connection queue lengths stabilized.

Maya Chen (Support) 2026-03-10 02:22 UTC: Customer reported spike in production errors. Collecting request IDs and duration metrics.
Diego Alvarez (SRE) 2026-03-10 02:36 UTC: Seeing proxy retransmit and TLS fallback rates spike. Hypothesis: proxy is dropping sessions which leads to upstream retries and runtime failovers.
ParcelAI (Customer) 2026-03-10 02:47 UTC: Confirmed reduction in user errors after you pushed the change. Thank you, still seeing occasional drops but much improved.
Diego Alvarez (SRE) 2026-03-10 04:10 UTC: Applied follow-up fix to autoscaler policy and created INT follow-up for deeper root-cause analysis: INT-2299.
Maya Chen (Support) 2026-03-11 09:15 UTC: Scheduled a post-incident call with ParcelAI for 2026-03-12 to review SLA credits and mitigation timeline.

Mitigation applied: temporarily increased ParcelAI serving pool min replicas, tuned autoscaler cooldown to avoid scale-down during high connection churn, and disabled aggressive TLS fallback on proxy hosts. Result: 5xx rate returned to baseline (<1%) by 03:40 UTC.

Permanent follow-ups: INT-2299 (deep dive into proxy socket backlog and TLS negotiation behavior), PR #943 to add autoscaler hysteresis for dedicated tenants with streaming-heavy workloads, and a runbook update (linked above) that documents emergency knobs. Customer offered SLA credit; CS to confirm.

Create INT-2299 for root cause RCA and capacity test plan (assigned to Diego).
Hardening: implement autoscaler hysteresis and streaming-aware scale-up policy (PR #943 referenced).
Observability: add specific alert for proxy TLS-fallback rate and connection queue depth to detect early degradation.
Schedule post-incident review with ParcelAI and internal stakeholders (2026-03-12).

title: Edge retry queueing causes intermittent model pin bypass during staggered rollout
text:
Issue summary:
During a controlled staggered promote of model redwood/open-compact-v1 for customer MuseAI, a subset of requests that were expected to remain pinned to the customer's previous stable version were routed to the new canary variant. The divergence only appeared under moderate edge retries and when the edge async queue exceeded ~120ms.

Impact:
- Intermittent mismatched outputs for ~0.6% of MuseAI requests for a 14 minute window on 2026-03-10.
- User-facing churn: some sessions suddenly received responses from canary with differing tokenization behavior.
- Customer reported degraded inference quality and asked to rollback.

Observed behavior patterns:
- Requests that initially hit the pinned route sometimes triggered an async retry (edge-proxy retry path) due to transient 504 from a regional gateway.
- The retried request re-entered the routing decision path after the pin TTL had been refreshed but the routing cache had been invalidated, causing route recalculation to prefer the canary in the current weight window.
- The original routing context (pin token) was not preserved across the async retry hop, so the retry was evaluated as a fresh request and could lose affinity.

Timeline (abridged):
- 2026-03-10 14:08 UTC: MuseAI starts a staged promote (10% traffic to canary).
- 14:24 UTC: Edge observed small spike of 504s to backplane during a transient network blip.
- 14:24–14:38 UTC: Higher-than-normal async retry queueing; discrepancy window.
- 14:36 UTC: MuseAI reports inconsistent outputs via support channel.
- 14:50 UTC: Support triaged and engaged SRE, disabled async retry path for the customer path as immediate mitigation.

Why this is unique/different from related tickets:
- Not a pure pin TTL drift or canary weight bug; root cause is loss of routing context at retries combined with edge queueing and routing cache invalidation. This produces intermittent bypasses tied to retry timing rather than deployment ordering.

Temporary mitigation in place:
- Disabled the async-retry code path for requests touching MuseAI tenant routes in us-east.
- Reverted a recent edge-proxy change to retry windowing (PR #1847) for canary-path optimizations.

Next steps (short):
- Implement context-preserving retry semantics so retries carry version-affinity tokens.
- Add guard to routing recalculation to respect active session pins for in-flight retries.
- Add synthetic canary tests that exercise retries and routing cache invalidations in CI.

Deploy a staggered promote with weight 10% canary and 90% stable for a model with session pinning enabled.
Introduce a short-lived gateway error (e.g., return 504 from regional gateway) to force edge async retry path and ensure retry queueing exceeds ~100ms.
Observe routing logs: initial request shows pin token X, retried request lacks token or gets recalculated and routes to canary.
Confirm by capturing request_id and route decisions in the edge-proxy traces (trace-id header).

[2026-03-10T14:24:12.927Z] edge-proxy: req=abc123 tenant=museai route=pin(stable@v12) upstream=regional-gw us-east status=504 -> queued-retry
[2026-03-10T14:24:13.052Z] edge-proxy: retry req=abc123 retry_id=abc123-1 re-evaluate-route cache_hit=false route_decision=canary@v13
[2026-03-10T14:24:13.053Z] serving-runtime: allocated slot on canary pool, model=redwood/open-compact-v1@v13 session_pin=null
[2026-03-10T14:25:02.110Z] tracer: pin-token expired? ttl_remaining=0 route_cache_invalidate=true

Edge-proxy change PR #1847 introduced an optimization that allowed retries to re-run routing to prefer lower-latency pools; this inadvertently dropped session pin tokens when retrying via async queue.
Routing cache invalidation windows coincided with canary weight adjustments from rollout controller, increasing likelihood of diverging decision during retries.
We reproduced locally by instrumenting the edge-proxy to drop the X-Session-Pin header on retry; when preserved, the issue did not reproduce.
Metric traces show retry->canary correlation: requests with >80ms retry latency had a 5x higher probability of losing pin affinity.
No evidence of serving-runtime misbehavior; issue surface is at edge-routing layer.
Related historical tickets for pin TTL and rollout weighting are linked to cross-reference design constraints (see SUP-81234 for rollout weight smoothing notes).

Mitigated: disabled async-retry path for affected tenant routes and reverted the retry windowing optimization. A code fix to preserve session pin on retries is scheduled and prioritized in the edge-proxy backlog.

2026-03-10 14:40 - Support (Maya): Customer reports that some sessions suddenly produced older tokenization than baseline; asked for immediate rollback if needed.
2026-03-10 14:52 - SRE (Jonas): Disabled async-retry path for MuseAI routes in us-east. Noted drop in mismatched responses after action.
2026-03-10 15:12 - Eng (Priya Kumar): We reproduced locally by simulating 504 and observed header loss on retry. Preparing PR to carry session-pin header through retry path.
2026-03-11 09:05 - PM (Liam Chen): Please add regression test to ensure retries preserve routing context across cache invalidations. Assigned to edge-proxy team.
2026-03-13 11:27 - SRE (Jonas): Patch merged to edge-proxy but behind feature flag: edge-proxy PR #1859. Will schedule a canary rollout with telemetry to verify.
2026-03-13 11:40 - Support (Maya): Notified customer of mitigation and timeline for permanent fix. Customer accepted the temporary mitigation and asked for postmortem once complete.

Edge-proxy: Implement context-preserving retry flow and enable by default (owner: edge team, ETA: 2026-03-20).
Routing: Add a safeguard to respect in-flight pin tokens during cache invalidation windows (owner: routing team, ETA: 2026-03-22).
CI: Add a synthetic suite to simulate retries under rollout weight change scenarios (owner: dxe, ETA: 2026-03-19).
Postmortem: Produce incident postmortem and update runbooks to include retry+pin interaction notes (owner: SRE, ETA: 2026-03-25).

title: Oncall rotation deconflict and duty-concierge procedures
author: Sofia Tran
text:
Summary
-------
This doc defines the deconfliction process for overlapping on-call assignments, the Duty Concierge role (a short-lived coordination persona), and standardized procedures for quiet windows, after-hours escalation, and runbook handoffs. It is intended for SRE/Platform/Serving teams who operate Redwood inference endpoints and for engineering managers who approve rotations.

Why this exists
----------------
As Redwood scales with more services (serve-runtime, request-router, kv-cache, console-api), we see two recurring failures: (1) duplicate pagers causing fractured ownership during handoffs, and (2) poorly coordinated quiet windows that delay mitigation. The Duty Concierge pattern reduces cognitive load on responders and keeps customer communication and exec escalation consistent.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all 24/7 responder rotations for production inference endpoints and critical control plane services.
- Does NOT replace escalation matrices for business continuity events (legal/compliance-led incidents).
- Includes guidance for game-day simulations and postmortem evidence collection.

Key roles and responsibilities
-------------------------------
- Primary Oncall (Responder): owns initial triage, containment, and assigning remediation tasks.
- Secondary Oncall (Backup): takes over if Primary is unavailable or incident escalates beyond scope.
- Duty Concierge (Coord): 2–6 hour coordination role during busy handoffs and major incidents. Responsibilities:
 - Deconflict overlapping pages across services.
 - Orchestrate status page and customer comm updates.
 - Temporarily own cross-service ticketing (create single incident ticket and tag owners).
 - Escalate to Incident Commander if impact > P1 threshold.
- Incident Commander (IC): formal incident lead for P1s; not every Duty Concierge is an IC.

Rotation deconflict policy
--------------------------
1. Single active pager rule: only one person should actively page per incident type for a given tenant/region. If multiple pages fire, the first acknowledged responder becomes Primary. Secondary responders should acknowledge with status only ("standing by").
2. Overlap window: when a new rotation starts, outgoing and incoming oncall overlap for 30 minutes (standard) unless manager approves shorter window. During overlap the Duty Concierge should be appointed for at least the first handoff.
3. Emergency takeover: if two primaries claim ownership simultaneously, the Duty Concierge (if present) will mediate. If no Duty Concierge, the first ACK timestamp wins; create an incident ticket and designate an IC within 15 minutes.

Duty Concierge procedure (step-by-step)
---------------------------------------
1. During a planned handoff or after a major event, create a single incident ticket in Jira: project INF-INC; include all paged services and initial evidence (grafana links, paging logs, error traces).
2. Post a short note to #ops-bridge Slack channel: include ticket link, list of affected services, current severity, and suggested owner. Use the template: "[DutyConcierge] Incident INF-INC-<num>: <short summary> — Primary: @username — Status: triage".
3. If customer-facing, prepare a status page draft (see templates below) and hold for Primary ACK. Duty Concierge publishes only after Primary confirms content.
4. Maintain a one-line running log in the Jira ticket with timestamps for each major action (containment, rollback, scale event) until IC declared.
5. At end of coordination window (default 4 hours), hand over the ticket to Primary for ongoing remediation or to the IC for full incident management. Include a short handoff checklist.

Quiet window (after-hours) rules
--------------------------------
- Definition: a quiet window is a pre-declared minimal-notification period during which only high-severity incidents (P1) will generate external customer notices. Quiet windows are used for maintenance and holiday shifts.
- Quiet window thresholds: only alerts that meet P1 criteria (impacting >5% of tenants OR error rates causing >25% p99 latency regression) generate immediate external comms. Everything else is acknowledged in-team and elevated after 30 min if unresolved.
- Process:
 1. Before entering a quiet window, Duty Concierge (or oncall lead) must tag scheduled maintenance in Status Page with planned start/end and risk level.
 2. Configure alert routing: non-P1 alerts route to a low-noise channel and an email digest to rotation lead.
 3. During quiet window, oncall must confirm receipt for any paging event within 5 minutes; if no ACK, escalate to Secondary.

Runbook: KV cache eviction storm (example)
----------------------------------------
Purpose: common cause of sudden p95 latency spikes on serve-runtime when upstream clients trigger mass key invalidations.
Symptoms:
- Rapid increase in cache eviction rate (>1000 evictions/min per pool)
- p95 token latency > 2x baseline and increase in serve-runtime 5xx errors
- "OOM eviction" or "KV checksum mismatch" in serve-runtime logs
First responders:
1. Acknowledge page and set incident severity: if client-facing impact >3 tenants, set P1; otherwise P2.
2. Capture evidence:
 - Grafana dashboard: Runtime -> kv-cache -> eviction-rate (time range last 30m)
 - Logs: kubectl logs --selector app=serve-runtime -n prod --tail=200 | grep "evict"
 - PagerDuty: copy alert payload to Jira ticket.
3. Containment steps (ordered):
 a. Use console-api to temporarily raise per-tenant cache TTLs: POST /api/admin/cache-config {"tenant":"<id>", "ttl_s": 7200} (requires admin role).
 b. If TTL change not possible, scale serve-runtime pool by +20% using autoscaler override: kubectl patch hpa/serve-runtime-hpa -p '{"spec":{"minReplicas":<new>}}'.
 c. If errors persist, rollback latest config change to serve-runtime (git tag release) and restart pod set.
4. Long-term remediation: enable detailed tracing for affected tenant, run workload replay in staging, file a change request to add rate-limits on client invalidation API.
5. Post-incident: collect heap profiles, eviction histograms, and store in S3 under s3://incidents/<ticket>/evidence.

Postmortem and evidence checklist
----------------------------------
- Postmortem owner assigned within 72 hours.
- Evidence required in ticket before postmortem draft:
 - Time-series graphs (p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, eviction rate).
 - Relevant logs with ORCID (at least 2 correlated traces).
 - Config changes list (git commits) in 48 hours window.
 - PagerDuty activity log (ACKs, escalations).
 - Customer impact summary (tenants affected, estimated % requests lost).
- Postmortem template (use as headings in Confluence):
 - Summary and impact
 - Timeline (minute-level for first 2 hours)
 - Root cause analysis
 - Contributing factors
 - Remediation and owner(s)
 - Detection and mitigation improvements
 - Follow-up action items with due dates and owners

Game day and simulation checklist (30–90 minute drill)
------------------------------------------------------
- Objective: validate Duty Concierge handoff, status page publishing, and triage within SLO.
- Pre-reqs (2 days before): select scenario (e.g., multi-region capacity failover), nominate ICs, create a synthetic ticket.
- During drill:
 1. Trigger simulated alert (use chaos-monkey lab).
 2. Duty Concierge creates the incident ticket and posts to #ops-bridge.
 3. Primary must ACK in <5 minutes; if not, Secondary takes over.
 4. Duty Concierge drafts and publishes status page update within 20 minutes of the incident start.
 5. Runbook steps exercised and evidence uploaded.
- After drill: 1-hour retro with action items captured in the ticket.

Status page and customer comm templates
--------------------------------------
- Internal short status (Ops Bridge):
 [INF-INC-<num>] <short summary> — Impact: <service(s)> — Status: TRIAGE — Owner: @<user> — ETA: <hh:mm UTC>

- External status template (public):
 Title: Service disruption affecting <service> in <region>
 Body: We are investigating an issue impacting <description of functional impact>. Our engineers are actively triaging; we'll update this page every 30 minutes or as new info becomes available. Affected customers: <list/tenants>. Next update: <hh:mm UTC>.

- Executive briefing (email/Slack to execs):
 Subject: [Action Required] P1: <short summary> — INF-INC-<num>
 Body: One-line impact, estimated customer count, mitigation in progress, immediate customer-facing message, and expected ETA. Include link to Jira ticket and status page.

Escalation thresholds (summary table)
-------------------------------------
| Severity | Customer impact threshold | SLA action | Notify |
| P1 | Any production endpoint down for >5% tenants OR full-region outage | Exec briefing within 30m, legal + sales notified | Pager to IC + execs |
| P2 | Significant degradation (p95 latency >x2 baseline or >25% error spike) | Status page update within 60m | Pager to Primary + Secondary |
| P3 | Minor degradation or single-tenant issue | Internal ticket only, periodic email digest | Ticket assignment |

Appendix: quick commands and dashboard queries
------------------------------------------------
- Grafana: runtime.kv-cache.eviction_rate > 1000 for last 5m
- kubectl: kubectl rollout undo deploy/serve-runtime -n prod --to-revision=<rev>
- cURL status update draft: curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $STATUS_API_TOKEN" -d '{"title":"...","body":"..."}' https://status.redwood.ai/api/v1/incidents

Document governance
--------------------
- Owners: Eng-SRE oncall program (primary), Serve Runtime team (secondary).
- Review cadence: annually or after any P1 with customer impact.
- Training: incorporate Duty Concierge role into new-joiner oncall bootcamp and include a simulated rotation handoff in the first 30 days.

Related pages and references
---------------------------
- Incident operator handbook (link internal)
- PagerDuty integration spec (link internal)
- Postmortem template (link internal)

Contact
-------
For questions about this procedure or to request a rotation exception, contact oncall-program@redwood.ai or @sofia.tran on Slack.

title: pluggable-reauth-hooks-and-typed-stream-adapters
author: Ishaan Patel
text:
Introduce a pluggable reauthentication hook and a small, strongly typed streaming adapter for the Go SDK to improve cross-SDK parity with Python/TS, reduce auth edge-case retries, and make streaming ergonomics easier for consumers. This PR implements a lightweight ReauthProvider interface that callers can implement to provide proactive token refresh, an optional background lease-renewal goroutine for long-lived streams, and a typed StreamAdapter that emits rich events (Chunk/Heartbeat/Resume) instead of raw io chunks. Motivation: teams saw intermittent 401 surface during long-running chat sessions and awkward retry semantics when token rotation happened mid-stream; the goal is to give Go integrators the same control surface already available in other SDKs while keeping the default UX simple (no-op provider). This change is opt-in: existing consumers keep current behavior unless they pass a non-nil ReauthProvider when creating a client or stream. The PR includes a cross-repo contract test harness snapshot (tests/contract/stream-reauth.json) used locally in CI and a bump to go-sdk v1.6.0. Note: parts of the implementation intentionally decouple reauth triggers from the backoff scheduler to allow site-specific token refresh strategies (KMS, delegated tokens, STS).

Maya Thompson: Nice separation of concerns. Question: can we expose a context cancellation signal to the ReauthProvider so it can abort long-running refresh calls?
Ishaan Patel: Good call. Added ctx parameter to ReauthProvider.Refresh(ctx) in second commit and updated callers to propagate stream contexts.
Luca Romano: I saw a flaky test on CI for the heartbeat timer, added a suggestion to use a deterministic clock in tests.
Ishaan Patel: Updated adapter_test.go to inject a fake clock; helps stabilize CI and local runs.
Priya Desai: Documented migration notes and called out that default behavior is unchanged unless ReauthProvider is provided. Approving after docs update.

Added opt-in ReauthProvider for proactive token rotation, typed StreamAdapter that surfaces heartbeat/resume events, improved stream ergonomics, fixed double-refresh race, bumped go-sdk to v1.6.0.

title: FinBank x Redwood — Private DR + backup/restore technical deep dive
author: Markus Klein
text:
FinBank walked through DR requirements for a Redwood Private VPC deployment (plus a smaller, restricted environment with limited egress). Key asks: enterprise RPO/RTO targets, deterministic restore into a clean cluster, encryption with customer-managed keys, and evidence/validation of restores. Redwood described the Day-2 toolkit direction: control-plane backups (manifest + encrypted artifact), optional scheduled backups via Helm CronJob, least-privilege S3+KMS patterns, and post-restore validation/smoke tests. Discussion covered whether Kubernetes resources are included (Redwood will back up Redwood control-plane/state + critical Helm values; Kubernetes/etcd snapshots are separate and only for cluster-level recovery), handling of secrets (references vs secret material), KMS/HSM constraints, and offline/air-gapped-ish restore workflows (signed bundles, no outbound calls, local checksum verification).

FinBank target RPO/RTO and DR scenarios (cluster loss vs region outage)
Backup scope: control plane state, config DB, object store references, routing/tenant config
Kubernetes backup tools (Velero) vs Redwood snapshots; etcd snapshot caveats
Encryption: envelope encryption, KMS key ownership, rotation, and KMS outage behavior
Air-gapped / restricted egress operations: signed artifacts, offline docs, deterministic bundles
Restore validation: smoke tests, health checks, audit log continuity, and evidence artifacts

FinBank (Tom Reyes) - Send current target RPO/RTO and DR runbook constraints (including maintenance windows) - due 2025-02-03
FinBank (Nina Shah) - Confirm KMS/HSM requirements (AWS KMS vs CloudHSM, key policies, allowed cryptographic operations) - due 2025-02-03
Redwood (Colin O'Donnell) - Share reference architecture for S3+KMS backup bucket + least privilege IAM and staging-restore workflow - due 2025-02-05
Redwood (Hanae Suzuki) - Share Redwood encryption approach summary (envelope encryption, key rotation expectations, what happens if KMS is unavailable) - due 2025-02-05
Redwood (Sean Gallagher) - Provide a sample restore validation checklist + what logs/metrics are produced for evidence - due 2025-02-07
Redwood (Markus Klein) - Schedule follow-up: 60-min working session to map FinBank components to backup scope and pick supported storage backend - due 2025-02-04

Redwood to send draft backup/restore + DR overview/runbook links and validation checklist.
FinBank to confirm desired DR archetype (single-region restore-in-place vs multi-region failover) and the acceptable RTO window for control plane vs audit logs.
Schedule a follow-up workshop with FinBank SRE/SecArch to finalize encryption/key handling and air-gapped-ish packaging needs.

Meeting header
Date: 2025-01-29
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 min
Title: FinBank x Redwood — Private DR + backup/restore technical deep dive
Attendees (Redwood): Markus Klein, Colin O'Donnell, Hanae Suzuki, Sean Gallagher
Attendees (FinBank): Aisha Patel, Tom Reyes, Nina Shah, Leo Grant

Auto-generated notes (Fireflies)
Summary: Discussed DR expectations and backup/restore approach for Redwood Private, including encryption and restricted-egress operations. Confirmed scope boundaries between app-level backups and Kubernetes/etcd recovery.
Questions: What’s included in the Redwood backup artifact? How do keys work? Can restores be validated automatically? What about limited outbound egress / "air gap" constraints?

Transcript
[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is to go a bit deeper than the usual “yes we support DR” and actually talk through what we back up, how restore works, and what we can do in restricted environments. Aisha, do you want to set context from your side?

[00:18] Aisha Patel: Yeah. Thanks Markus. So we’re evaluating Redwood Private for, basically, an internal gen-AI platform. The big blocker is Day-2 ops. We have to show DR readiness to our risk team. And we have two environments: one normal AWS VPC, and another more constrained enclave where outbound egress is… not zero but very controlled.

[00:39] Tom Reyes: And from SRE side, we need clear RPO/RTO per component. Like, control plane config can be maybe 15 minutes RPO, but audit logs are… we have different retention and export requirements.

[00:53] Nina Shah: Plus encryption. Customer-managed keys, and we want to understand if you ever store secret material in the backup, or if it’s just references. And how you handle KMS outages.

[01:05] Markus Klein: Yep, makes sense. Colin and Sean are here to go into the runbook-y pieces, and Hanae for keys/secrets.

[01:13] Colin O'Donnell: I can start with scope. When we say “backup/restore for Redwood Private,” we’re talking primarily about the Redwood control plane state and critical configuration state required to deterministically recreate the deployment: tenant config, routing policies, model pins, auth config, and the internal config database that tracks those. We’re not trying to replace cluster-level disaster recovery.

[01:34] Tom Reyes: So not like Velero everything in the cluster.

[01:37] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly. We see people reach for Velero as a blunt instrument, and it can work, but it’s also a foot-gun if you restore secrets or CRDs in the wrong order. Our approach is: Redwood produces a versioned backup artifact for Redwood-owned state. If you also want to use Velero, we’ll provide guidance for what to include/exclude, but we don’t rely on it.

[02:00] Sean Gallagher: And from an operational standpoint, our runbooks are basically split into: (1) consistent control-plane backup, (2) restore to a fresh cluster or existing cluster, and (3) DR plans by archetype, like single-region restore-in-place.

[02:15] Aisha Patel: What’s “consistent” mean here? Do you stop the world?

[02:19] Sean Gallagher: Not fully stop-the-world, but we do a quiesce step for writes in the control plane. Think “pause mutations” briefly so we get a coherent snapshot of the config DB plus the related manifests/values we need. It’s on the order of seconds to, worst case, a minute depending on environment.

[02:40] Tom Reyes: That quiesce impacts inference?

[02:42] Colin O'Donnell: Inference data plane stays serving. You might temporarily block admin operations like creating a new tenant or changing routing policy. Existing traffic continues. We’re careful about that separation.

[02:55] Leo Grant: Where does the backup get stored? We’d prefer S3 in-region with KMS.

[03:01] Colin O'Donnell: S3+KMS is the default reference. We also have customers who require NFS. For GCS it’s possible but usually only if the deployment is in GCP. For AWS VPC, we’d recommend S3 with bucket policies that only allow access from the backup service account role, and SSE-KMS with your CMK.

[03:24] Nina Shah: Can you clarify the encryption model? Is it just SSE-KMS or do you do application-level encryption before upload?

[03:32] Hanae Suzuki: Great question. We’re moving toward envelope encryption at the artifact level. So the installer/backup tool generates a data key, encrypts the archive locally (AES-GCM), and then encrypts the data key with KMS (or a KMS provider interface, potentially HSM-backed). That way if someone misconfigures the bucket encryption, the artifact is still encrypted.

[03:57] Nina Shah: And the plaintext data key never leaves memory?

[04:00] Hanae Suzuki: Correct. It’s generated and used in-process, and only the encrypted DEK is stored alongside the artifact metadata.

[04:08] Tom Reyes: What exactly is in the archive? Like do you dump Postgres?

[04:13] Colin O'Donnell: It depends on the backing store, but conceptually yes: a consistent snapshot of the config DB plus a manifest file that describes versions, checksums, and component inventory. In some installs it’s Postgres, in others we’ve seen managed equivalents. The runbook calls out the supported snapshot method per datastore. We also capture critical “installer inputs” like Helm release values so you can redeploy deterministically.

[04:40] Aisha Patel: Do you back up Kubernetes objects? Like CRDs, deployments, secrets?

[04:45] Colin O'Donnell: We do not back up the whole cluster. We’ll capture the Helm values and Redwood-specific config objects that are necessary to reconstruct. For CRDs, the safe path is: reinstall the correct Redwood version (which includes CRDs) then restore state. We’ve had issues when folks restore CRDs from old versions and then controllers behave weird.

[05:09] Sean Gallagher: If the cluster itself is corrupted, then you’re in “cluster DR” territory. That’s where etcd snapshots, managed control plane restore, or IaC rebuild come in. We can provide guidance, but it’s separate from app-level restore.

[05:26] Tom Reyes: Okay, but in a real incident we might need both.

[05:29] Sean Gallagher: Totally. Our DR plan docs basically say: choose the failure mode. If it’s “oops we deleted a namespace” or “config DB is bad,” app restore. If it’s “etcd is toast,” then cluster restore first, then app validation.

[05:45] Leo Grant: In the region loss scenario, do you support cross-region restore?

[05:51] Colin O'Donnell: Today the baseline is single-region restore into a clean cluster in the same region. Cross-region is doable if your dependencies are replicated: S3 CRR or copying artifacts, database snapshots to the other region, and you pre-provision the cluster. We can document the pattern but we won’t magically replicate your infra.

[06:14] Aisha Patel: For our risk review, we need to say something like: “RPO 15 minutes, RTO 2 hours” for control plane. Is that realistic?

[06:22] Sean Gallagher: It can be, depending on the size and your automation. For RPO, if you run scheduled backups every 15 minutes and they complete consistently, yes. For RTO, restore time depends on: provisioning a cluster, pulling images, running the restore job, then validation. Two hours is reasonable if you have infra ready.

[06:49] Tom Reyes: Do you have an automated restore drill? Like we can run weekly in staging.

[06:54] Sean Gallagher: That’s part of what we’re building. The idea is: a scheduled restore drill in a non-prod environment that pulls the latest backup, restores to a staging cluster, runs smoke tests, and emits metrics like restore_duration_seconds and last_restore_success_ts.

[07:14] Nina Shah: Evidence is big for us. We need artifacts. Logs, timestamps, checksums.

[07:19] Hanae Suzuki: The backup tool produces a manifest with: backup format version, platform version, list of components, SHA256 checksums, and the encrypted key blob. That manifest can be stored alongside the archive. You can hand it to auditors. We also plan to emit audit events around backup/restore actions.

[07:43] Tom Reyes: That manifest is signed?

[07:46] Hanae Suzuki: We’re planning two layers. Checksums for integrity, plus bundle signing for offline distribution of the tooling itself. For the backup artifact, we can optionally sign manifests. The core must-have is that the artifact is encrypted and integrity-checked.

[08:08] Leo Grant: On the restricted environment: no outbound calls. How does the restore tool behave if it tries to reach your hosted endpoints?

[08:16] Colin O'Donnell: It should not need to. For Private, the backup/restore operations are local to the cluster. The only external dependency is your storage backend (like S3). In air-gapped or restricted egress, you’d use an internal S3 endpoint or NFS. The tooling and docs would be shipped as an offline bundle.

[08:38] Aisha Patel: We’re not fully air-gapped, but basically NAT is blocked except allow-listed domains. Can you support a mode that never tries to “phone home”?

[08:48] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. We have a “no external calls” posture for on-prem style installs, and we can apply that to restricted VPCs too. For example, image pulls would come from your internal registry mirror.

[09:03] Tom Reyes: Let’s talk about secrets. Are secrets in the backup? Like DB passwords, OAuth client secrets.

[09:10] Hanae Suzuki: By default, no. We don’t want secret material in the backup artifact. We back up references: secret names, where to find them, maybe the ARN of a secret in Secrets Manager, that sort of thing. On restore, you’re expected to have those secrets provisioned in the target environment.

[09:31] Nina Shah: Good. But then restore is not fully self-contained.

[09:34] Sean Gallagher: Right, but it’s deterministic if you treat secrets as inputs. Our restore runbook has a pre-flight checklist: “Confirm secrets exist,” “Confirm KMS key access,” “Confirm bucket access,” etc. In regulated environments, secret exfiltration via backup is usually a bigger problem than requiring re-provisioning.

[09:59] Tom Reyes: What about rotating keys? If we rotate the KMS key, can we still restore old backups?

[10:06] Hanae Suzuki: If you rotate by rewrapping within KMS (keeping old key versions available), you’re fine. If you disable or schedule deletion of old key material, you could lose ability to decrypt. We recommend a key lifecycle policy that preserves decrypt for the retention window.

[10:25] Nina Shah: And if KMS is down during backup?

[10:29] Hanae Suzuki: For backup creation, if we can’t encrypt the DEK with KMS, we fail closed. We don’t want a backup artifact produced that’s not properly encrypted. For restore, if KMS is down, you can’t decrypt the data key, so restore can’t proceed. That’s part of your dependency chain for DR.

[10:52] Leo Grant: So KMS availability impacts RTO.

[10:55] Sean Gallagher: Exactly. Most customers treat KMS as a tier-0 dependency. If you’re in AWS, KMS is pretty reliable, but you can also consider multi-region keys depending on your DR design.

[11:10] Aisha Patel: How do you validate restore? Like, what’s the “smoke test” specifically?

[11:16] Sean Gallagher: Minimum: control plane health endpoints are green, background controllers are running, config DB migrations are at expected version, and the Redwood API responds. Then we run a few synthetic requests: create a test tenant (or check an existing tenant in staging), validate routing policy loads, and run a tiny inference request against a known model with expected output shape.

[11:45] Colin O'Donnell: We also validate that model pins and fallbacks are restored. People forget that routing policies are part of “state.”

[11:53] Tom Reyes: Do you validate audit logs?

[11:56] Sean Gallagher: We can validate that audit logging is enabled and that export jobs are configured. Whether you can “replay” logs depends on your retention pipeline. Separate doc from security covers audit log backup/retention.

[12:14] Nina Shah: In our world, audit logs need 1 year retention, immutable storage. That’s usually separate from app DR.

[12:20] Markus Klein: Yeah, we typically treat audit log export as its own pipeline—like to your SIEM or to WORM storage. We can connect the dots but it’s not in the core control-plane backup.

[12:33] Tom Reyes: I want to pressure-test the “no Velero” thing. In practice, we already use Velero for our clusters.

[12:40] Colin O'Donnell: Totally valid. The reason we’re cautious is ordering and version mismatch. If you use Velero to back up namespaces, you might restore a state where CRDs exist but controllers are a different version, or vice versa. If you do Velero, we recommend: exclude Secrets (or at least be explicit), exclude CRDs, and treat Velero as “cluster resource convenience,” while Redwood backup is the source of truth for control-plane state.

[13:13] Tom Reyes: So two-layer approach.

[13:15] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly.

[13:19] Aisha Patel: Can you walk through a restore into a fresh cluster? Like the order.

[13:25] Sean Gallagher: Sure. High-level order:
1) Provision the target cluster and baseline dependencies (ingress, storage class, cert-manager if used).
2) Install Redwood Private at the target version (same or compatible) via Helm/installer.
3) Ensure required secrets and KMS/bucket access exist.
4) Run restore job: download artifact, verify checksums, decrypt, apply DB restore, apply config objects.
5) Run post-restore validation hook (smoke tests) and produce a validation report.
6) Switch traffic: DNS/TLS, or update internal load balancer targets.

[14:08] Leo Grant: DNS/TLS is a pain. We’d prefer to keep the same endpoint.

[14:12] Sean Gallagher: For same-region restore, you can keep the same DNS name. If you’re restoring to a new cluster, you can reuse the certificate if you manage it centrally, or re-issue with the same SAN. The runbook includes the “don’t forget to update certs” checklist.

[14:31] Nina Shah: For encryption, do you support customer-provided keys in an HSM? We sometimes use CloudHSM.

[14:39] Hanae Suzuki: We’re designing a KMS provider interface. Our first-class is AWS KMS. CloudHSM tends to come in via KMS Custom Key Store or your own service. We’ll need to confirm specifics: do you require all crypto ops in HSM, or just key storage? If it’s KMS Custom Key Store, it can work. If it’s a bespoke API, we’d likely need a provider plugin.

[15:10] Tom Reyes: And in the constrained enclave, we can’t call AWS public endpoints. We use VPC endpoints.

[15:16] Leo Grant: Yeah, PrivateLink endpoints for S3 and KMS.

[15:20] Colin O'Donnell: That’s compatible. We’ll document it: S3 Gateway Endpoint, KMS Interface Endpoint, and then restrict bucket policy by VPC endpoint.

[15:31] Nina Shah: Least privilege on IAM is another risk item. We need to show it doesn’t require broad S3 permissions.

[15:38] Colin O'Donnell: We can share a minimal policy: GetObject/PutObject/ListBucket on the backup prefix, and kms:Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey on the CMK, plus maybe DescribeKey. No wildcard admin.

[15:56] Markus Klein: We have Terraform modules we can share as a starting point.

[16:02] Tom Reyes: How do you do retention? Do you delete old backups?

[16:08] Sean Gallagher: We don’t automatically delete unless you configure it. On S3, we recommend lifecycle policies for retention. On NFS, you’d do rotation via cron or the backup job. But we’ll emit metrics like “bytes_written” so you can see growth.

[16:30] Aisha Patel: RPO wise, is 15 minutes the minimum?

[16:34] Sean Gallagher: Technically you can do more frequent, but it’s a tradeoff with load and operator comfort. 15 minutes is a common starting point. Some do hourly, some do 5 minutes for very critical configs.

[16:48] Tom Reyes: What’s the failure mode if a backup partially uploads?

[16:53] Colin O'Donnell: The manifest includes expected size and checksums. Restore verifies checksums. If it’s partial/corrupt, restore fails fast. For backup creation, we upload to a temp key then atomically “promote” (rename/copy) so the “latest” pointer only moves when complete.

[17:18] Nina Shah: That’s good.

[17:20] Markus Klein: Let’s check if we’ve hit the key questions: scope, encryption, restricted egress, validation.

[17:27] Aisha Patel: I have another one: version compatibility. If we upgrade Redwood, can we restore an old backup?

[17:35] Colin O'Donnell: We’re adding backup format versioning. Restore checks compatibility: same major, maybe N-1 minor, depending on migrations. If incompatible, it tells you and points to migration steps. We’re trying to avoid “it restores but subtly breaks.”

[17:57] Tom Reyes: We’ve seen that with other vendors. Like “it worked” but half the config is missing.

[18:02] Sean Gallagher: Yeah, we want deterministic outcomes. Also the validation step is meant to catch missing routing policies or tenant config.

[18:12] Nina Shah: Can you produce a report we can attach to a ticket? Like “restore completed, here’s the checks.”

[18:19] Sean Gallagher: Yes. The restore job can output a JSON-ish report and also human-readable. It will include timestamps, artifact ID, checksums verified, and smoke test results.

[18:36] Leo Grant: On the cluster side, you mentioned etcd snapshots. Do you have a runbook?

[18:42] Sean Gallagher: We do, but it’s more of a Kubernetes ops runbook. For managed EKS, etcd snapshots are not directly accessible. For self-managed, you can restore etcd, but it’s risky. We’d rather you rebuild the cluster from IaC.

[19:02] Tom Reyes: That’s aligned with our current practice.

[19:06] Aisha Patel: One concern: our risk team wants “DR game day” evidence. Do you support that?

[19:12] Markus Klein: We can absolutely support a game day. Rafael on our side usually owns the template, but Sean can share the checklist. Typically we do a staging drill: simulate cluster loss, restore, measure time.

[19:30] Tom Reyes: We’d do it in staging first, then maybe a controlled prod drill.

[19:34] Sean Gallagher: That’s what most do.

[19:37] Nina Shah: I want to circle back on air-gap. You said offline bundle. What does that include?

[19:45] Colin O'Donnell: A deterministic bundle layout: the backup/restore CLI, any required container images (or a way to load them into your registry), checksum manifest, signature file, and offline docs. The idea is you can verify it without network.

[20:06] Nina Shah: Signed with what? GPG?

[20:09] Colin O'Donnell: Likely GPG or Sigstore-like approach depending on your environment. For fully offline, GPG is common. We’ll provide the public key and you verify signature.

[20:23] Tom Reyes: And the backup artifact itself is separate, signed or not.

[20:27] Hanae Suzuki: Correct. Bundle signing is for the tooling so you trust what you’re running. Artifact integrity is via checksums and optional signature.

[20:38] Aisha Patel: Okay. I think we have enough to write the initial risk memo, but we need concrete docs.

[20:44] Markus Klein: Yep. We’ll send what we have in draft plus a short “how to think about DR” guide.

[20:50] Tom Reyes: Before we wrap, can we list the things that are explicitly out of scope so we don’t get surprised later?

[20:57] Colin O'Donnell: Sure. Out of scope for Redwood backup: model weights themselves (unless you store them in your own artifact repo), GPU node images, underlying Kubernetes cluster state, and any external systems like your IdP or SIEM. We back up Redwood control plane config and state needed for deterministic redeploy and routing.

[21:22] Nina Shah: And secrets are references, not payload.

[21:25] Hanae Suzuki: Correct.

[21:27] Leo Grant: And storage backends supported are S3 and NFS primarily.

[21:31] Colin O'Donnell: Yes.

[21:33] Markus Klein: Great. Let’s do next steps. Tom, Nina—can you send us your target RPO/RTO and KMS/HSM constraints? We’ll send over the S3+KMS pattern, plus validation checklist.

[21:48] Tom Reyes: Yep. I’ll send what we have. RPO probably 15, RTO 2 hours for control plane, maybe 24 hours for some logs, but I’ll confirm.

[21:59] Nina Shah: I’ll confirm HSM. We might be okay with KMS multi-region keys. But I need to check.

[22:05] Markus Klein: Perfect. We’ll schedule a follow-up working session early next week.

[22:11] Aisha Patel: Sounds good.

[22:13] Sean Gallagher: Thanks everyone.

[22:15] (crosstalk)
[22:16] Markus Klein: Thanks.

Note: Fireflies transcription ended early due to participant drop; remaining discussion (approx. 35 min) continued on the same themes with deeper Q&A on VPC endpoints, bucket policy examples, and restore drill cadence. Key takeaways and action items above reflect the full call per Redwood notes.
