title: KMS Evidence Serialization and RBACv2 Claims Spec
author: Asha Patel
text:
Purpose:
This spec standardizes how Redwood serializes cryptographic evidence derived from KMS/HSM operations for downstream RBACv2 attestation, SIEM ingestion, and long-term archival. It focuses on: (1) canonical event shape for audit events, (2) RBACv2 claim mappings needed for key custody checks, (3) evidence collection automation recipes, and (4) HSM fallback/verification sequences for rotation windows and BYOK onboarding.

Scope:
Applies to: hosted API key material, dedicated and private deployments using Customer-Managed Keys (CMKs/BYOK), HSM-bound master keys, and transient/ephemeral keys used by serving runtime. Excludes application-level data encryption patterns that do not touch KMS/HSM.

Background and goals:
- Provide a minimal, verifiable JSON shape that SIEM and Evidence Store can index efficiently.
- Ensure RBACv2 claims are emitted with each evidence bundle so policy engines can validate whether a key action was authorized.
- Enable automated testable checks after rotation or failover (integrated into CI and ops runbooks).

Key concepts and identifiers:
- key_id: stable UUID v4, not human-friendly. Format: key://{region}/{tenant_id}/{key_uuid} e.g. key://us-west-2/t-1234/7f3b9e2a-...
- key_version: semantic string, e.g. v1, v1-2024-11-21
- material_origin: one of [redwood-kms, customer-byok, hsm-ns0]
- custodian_principal: RBACv2 principal id (format: user|service|role:{id})

RBACv2 claims mapping (fields emitted with evidence):
- rbac_claims.principal_id -> custodian_principal (string)
- rbac_claims.action -> enum [key:generate, key:rotate, key:revoke, key:export, key:assign-policy]
- rbac_claims.policy_version -> policy hash or id (string)
- rbac_claims.mfa -> boolean or method string (e.g., 'webauthn')
- rbac_claims.scope -> list of strings (e.g., [tenant, project, environment])
Note: Emit full principal chain for cross-team operations: principal_chain -> ["role:sec-admin:alice","service:rotation-agent"]

Canonical audit event JSON (stringified in SIEM body):
{
 "event_type": "kms.key.operation",
 "timestamp": "2024-11-21T14:32:10Z",
 "key_id": "key://us-west-2/t-1234/7f3b9e2a-...",
 "key_version": "v1-2024-11-21",
 "operation": "key:rotate",
 "status": "success",
 "material_origin": "hsm-ns0",
 "initiator": "service:rotation-agent",
 "rbac_claims": {
 "principal_id": "role:sec-admin:alice",
 "action": "key:rotate",
 "policy_version": "policy-9c4f",
 "mfa": "webauthn",
 "scope": ["t-1234","project-inference"]
 },
 "evidence_links": ["s3://evidence-prod/keys/t-1234/7f3b9e.../bundle-20241121.tar.gz"],
 "hashes": {"manifest_sha256": "...", "key_thumbprint": "..."},
 "notes": "rotation triggered by scheduled policy; automatic canary verify queued"
}

SIEM ingestion mapping guide:
- Index fields: event_type, timestamp, key_id (tokenize on /), operation, status, initiator, material_origin, rbac_claims.principal_id, rbac_claims.action, manifest_sha256.
- Alert rules: (1) key:export by non-admin principal -> immediate P1; (2) rotate failure > 3 attempts -> P1; (3) BYOK upload with missing HSM-attestation -> P2.
- Recommended ingestion: bulk compress bundles for evidence storage, push event metadata to SIEM (no raw key material). Evidence store should be treated as separate S3 bucket with restricted access and WORM-like retention.

Evidence bundle composition (archive stored off-SIEM):
- manifest.json (includes list of files, offsets, hashes, key_id, key_version, material_origin)
- acsk_attestation.txt (HSM attestation statements, where applicable)
- rotation_trace.log (detailed command/response trace with timestamps)
- rbacsnap.json (snapshot of RBACv2 claim resolution at moment of operation)
- canary_verification.json (results of sample decryption/signature test)

Automation recipes (ops runbook snippets):
1) Rotation automation should produce: manifest.json, rbacsnap.json, hashes, then atomically upload bundle to evidence S3 and emit SIEM event with evidence_links.
2) Verification pipeline: after rotation, run canary using temporary ephemeral key_version; record canary results to canary_verification.json and push metric to datadog: kms.rotation.canary.{success|failure}.
3) Evidence retention policy: default 2 years for tenant keys; HIPAA/PDF regulated tenants up to 7 years (config per tenant metadata).

HSM fallback choreography for failed rotations:
- Detect failure (rotation agent sees non-idempotent state) -> mark key as 'rotation-in-progress' and notify SRE + custodian via PagerDuty.
- Snapshot RBAC resolution and export rbacsnap.json immediately.
- If HSM node unresponsive, attempt fallback to secondary HSM pool with approved cross-signing; if fallback fails, enter 'degraded' state and publish SIEM event event_type: kms.key.failover.requested with reason.
- Post-incident forensics: run the evidence collector with flags --include-volatility --collect-processes and attach results to incident ticket.

BYOK onboarding checklist (brief):
- Tenant provides key material in wrapped form and KMS metadata.
- Validate attestation: if HSM-backed, require vendor attestation blob and parse into acsk_attestation.txt.
- Run rbacsnap resolution: ensure at least one custodian_principal has role:byok-approver.
- Emit SIEM event key:byok.upload with masked key identifier and evidence_links.

Verification and offline attestations:
- All manifests must include a manifest_sha256. Evidence store computes archive-level sha256 and publishes difference if any.
- For critical rotations, require dual-operator approval: both principals' rbacsnap chains must be present and signed.

Operational queries and dashboards (plausible list):
- Rotation success rate by region/tenant (90d window)
- Average time between rotation start and canary success
- Number of key:export events by principal (alert when > 0 for non-admins)
- Evidence ingestion lag (time between operation timestamp and evidence bundle available)

Developer notes and integration points:
- SDK: evidence bundle uploader lives in github.com/redwood-inference/kms-evidence-automation. Use client.upload_bundle(manifest, files) which returns evidence_links array to include in emitted event.
- RBACv2: ensure policy engine can produce policy_version hashes; include GUID mapping for legacy policies.
- SIEM: ingest must validate manifest_sha256 and reject events pointing to missing evidence.

Open questions and TODOs (work-in-progress):
- Should we include partial encrypted material for faster offline verification? (privacy vs. verification tradeoff)
- Standardize tenant-specific retention overrides in tenant metadata API (currently ad-hoc).
- Define archival format for multi-year WORM compliance across regions.

Appendix: sample rbacsnap.json (abbreviated):
{
 "resolved_at": "2024-11-21T14:31:50Z",
 "key_id": "key://us-west-2/t-1234/7f3b9e2a-...",
 "principal_chain": ["role:sec-admin:alice","service:rotation-agent"],
 "policies": [{"id":"policy-9c4f","hash":"9c4f...","perms":["rotate","assign-policy"]}]
}

This document is purposely prescriptive about emitted claims and evidence composition to make downstream verification deterministic. Feedback requested from platform-engineering (integration tests for uploader), SRE (failover scenarios), and compliance (retention and WORM requirements).

raw_metadata.title: KMS Evidence Serialization and RBACv2 Claims Spec

title: Python SDK sends 'Bearer Bearer' in Authorization header for some configs
text:
Issue summary: Customer upgraded to redwood-sdk-python v0.9.4 and began receiving 401 Unauthorized. Their proxy logs show Authorization header is 'Bearer Bearer <key>' (double prefix). They previously passed api_key='Bearer <key>' (historical pattern from other vendors). Impact: auth failures in one service until rollback. Steps: (1) Initialize client with api_key that already includes 'Bearer ' (2) SDK adds Bearer prefix again (3) API rejects. Expected: SDK should accept raw key only OR detect and avoid double prefix and warn.

Ava Chen (Support): Customer insists they have always stored the value with the prefix; they missed this requirement in docs.
Ethan Park (DevEx): This is technically misconfiguration, but we should add a guardrail: if api_key starts with 'Bearer ' then strip the prefix and log a warning.
Ava Chen: Provided workaround: store raw key only (no prefix).
Ethan Park: Marking as closed with docs + validation improvement tracked separately (INT-771).

text:
maria: heads up — several customer streams dropped after ~60s only when traffic goes through the edge proxy. client sees a clean connection close, server logs show no application error. anyone seen this pattern?

devon: can you paste a repro? env, curl, logs?

maria: minimal repro: `curl -v -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" "https://api.redwood.example/v1/stream/long?user=test"`
server emits a comment heartbeat every 30s like `:

` (SSE comment) and occasional `data:` events. dump shows TCP RST from 10.0.3.12 (edge) at 60.02s.

aj: 60s smells like an idle timeout somewhere (envoy/nginx/ cloud LB). our default envoy route config in prod had `idle_timeout: 60s` a while back. but I thought we had keepalive pings.

liam: confirmed — envoy's connection manager will terminate if it thinks the upstream is idle. It only considers application-level bytes; SSE comments are a single-line starting with `:` which should still be bytes though. Are those heartbeats being buffered/encoded by the runtime?

maria: good question — runtime does `write(":

")` as an uncompressed chunk. but looking at the proxy tcpdump the last upstream packet we see from the server is 0 bytes before 60s (maybe due to chunked encoding headers only at start). Means our heartbeat never made it out, or proxy ate it.

aj: can we reproduce with `openssl s_client` or `nc` so we see raw TLS frames pre-proxy? if heartbeat leaves the server but proxy drops it, config change required.

maria: I repeated with `curl --no-buffer` and also saw the server's `: heartbeat` in app logs but not in pcap at the proxy.

sre-oncall: tagging this as P1 for prod impact — several customers hit session drops on streaming routes. Adding `sse-edge-termination` alert.

devon: theory: our edge has `proxy_buffering` or an HTTP/1.1 keepalive check that expects non-comment data to consider stream active. Some middleboxes consider lines starting with `:` as comments and ignore for idle timers. If true, options are: (1) change runtime to emit `data: 

` heartbeats instead of comments, (2) bump idle timeout in envoy/edge, or (3) send periodic tiny `data: ping` events.

liam: ops concerns with (2) — increasing idle timeout global could tie up worker connections under high concurrency. (1)/(3) preferred. We also need a metric to detect this class of termination: currently we only have `stream_close_total` with generic reasons. Missing `edge_terminated_idle` dimension.

maria: agree. quick mitigation: runtime patch to emit `data:  

` (non-empty data payload) every 25s. That should be safe for clients and satisfy proxy idle detectors. I'll prototype.

aj: we should add a console rollout toggle per-route to flip heartbeat style (comment vs data) and a canary rollout to 10% customers for 24h. UX note: console should show `sse.heartbeat.last_seen` and `sse.edge_termination_rate` on the per-route dashboard.

devon: telemetry gap: ingestion pipeline currently drops `connection_close` with reason codes from the edge. Need to enrich traces with `edge_reason` tag and route id. Without that we can't correlate customer reports to config.

sre-oncall: creating incident stub and linking this thread. Also adding a dashboard tile under `Redwood Console -> Streaming -> Connection Health` for now so support can triage.

liam: small nit — ensure we don't regress bandwidth/cost with data heartbeats. If heartbeats are 8 bytes per 25s per connection, math looks fine for our scale but call it out in PR.

maria: quick test on staging: patched runtime to send `data: ping

` every 25s. spinning up 500 concurrent streams via k6 and no edge terminations after 5m. pushing a PR now.

devon: thanks — also let's add an envoy route config experiment behind feature flag `edge.sse_heartbeat_style` so infra can try longer term solutions without deploy churn.

aj: created GH issue in eng-infra to add `edge_reason` to telemetry and a console card for `sse.connection_lost_by_edge`. assigning to @liam.

maria: PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/432 — patch + test + canary plan.

proxy-bot: deploy job queued for patch `runtime/sse-heartbeat` -> canary (10%) -> monitor `sse.edge_termination_rate`.

devon: once canary looks good, schedule a config change in envoy to keep `idle_timeout` at 60s but document why heartbeats use `data:` for streaming routes.

sre-oncall: follow-up: let's also add a synthetic check that connects to a streaming route and verifies heartbeat persistence for 3 consecutive minutes; alert if fails.

liam: acked — will add to infra playbook.

maria: thanks everyone — filing retrospective notes in the incident doc with root cause: edge idle detector ignores SSE comment-only heartbeats. remediation: runtime change + telemetry + console rollout toggle.

title: Apportion token billing for streamed multi-tenant requests with intermittent KV hits
author: Priya Nair
text:
Background: Streaming request flows sometimes interleave model token generation with KV/prefix cache hits. In multi-tenant batches we observe cases where some stream frames are satisfied entirely from cache (zero model tokens) and others require model execution, and the current accounting attributes cost to the whole batch or to the first requester, causing unfair quota burns and surprising billing reports.

Problem: Two main incorrect behaviors have been reported: (1) quota/rate-limit windows charging based on aggregated batch size rather than per-tenant chargeable tokens, leading to early throttles for tenants who mostly hit cache; (2) billing that charges token units for frames satisfied by prefix/KV cache in some batch fusion paths. Both cause customer confusion and incorrect quota enforcement.

Goal: Implement an attribution algorithm that: (A) charges only the model-executed token units to tenants; (B) apportion batch-level GPU cost (when we bill per-batch or per-slot) across tenants by a defensible heuristic when requests are fused; (C) ensures rate limits and quota counters reflect chargeable tokens (not attempted tokens that were short-circuited by cache). This should preserve latency SLOs and be implementable without blocking streaming optimization paths.

Proposed approach:
1) Instrument per-request token accounting at the runtime boundary that distinguishes: attempted_tokens, cache_served_tokens, model_generated_tokens.
2) Charge tokens toward customer quota and rate-limit counters using model_generated_tokens only.
3) For GPU/billing attribution when batch fusion happens across tenants, compute a proportional apportionment: allocate the batch GPU time and per-batch overhead cost in proportion to model_generated_tokens per tenant in that fused batch. If model_generated_tokens == 0 for all tenants (unlikely but possible for cache-only batch), fall back to equal-split or attribute to tenant that initiated the RPC (configurable).
4) Handle streaming frames: maintain a lightweight per-stream accumulator that updates as cache hits or model gen occur; billing and quota updates are committed periodically (end-of-stream or on configured checkpoint), with ability to push interim deltas to reduce tail risk.
5) Backfill and reconciliation: for historical batches where we overcharged, provide a reconciliation pipeline that replays runtime accounting logs and emits adjustments to billing/quotas.

Engineering notes:
- This requires runtime hooks in the batching layer to tag per-subrequest token counts prior to coalescing into physical batches and to propagate attribution metadata to the metering pipeline.
- The metering pipeline must accept per-request delta updates (incremental counters) rather than only batch-level totals.
- To avoid perf regressions, tag propagation should be compact (8-16 bytes per subrequest) and optional behind an opt-in config for early rollout.

Trade-offs and alternatives:
- Simpler option: treat any fused batch as charged to the initiator (fast to implement, but unfair). Rejected.
- Conservative option: continue charging on attempted_tokens for quota enforcement and issue credits later. This avoids under-enforcing quotas in real time but perpetuates early throttles.
- Chosen approach favors correctness for customers while keeping an emergency fallback to conservative enforcement if telemetries show evasion or abuse.

Runtime exposes per-subrequest counters: attempted_tokens, cache_served_tokens, model_generated_tokens
Quota and rate-limit counters increment only by model_generated_tokens in both single-tenant and fused-batch paths
Billing records (per-invoice line) reflect model_generated_tokens and proportional batch-cost apportionment for fused batches
Integration tests simulating mixed cache-hit ratios validate that tenant A with 90% cache hits is not throttled earlier than tenant B with 10% cache hits under same request rate
Reconciliation job can locate and emit adjustments for misattributed charges for a given two-week window
Rollout gated by telemetry thresholds: no >1% request latency regression and <0.1% increase in metering pipeline CPU/memory cost in first 48h

Phase 1 (canary): enable tag propagation and per-request delta reporting for 5% of hosted accounts in us-west1 for 72h. Verify telemetry thresholds. Phase 2 (expand): 25% rollout and enable proportional apportionment for fused batches with reconciliation dry-run enabled (no live refunds). Phase 3 (full): 100% rollout, enable reconciliation actions and billing adjustments, and update SDK/Docs. Each phase has rollback toggles and a kill-switch to revert to attempted_tokens enforcement.

Update SDK docs to explain that quotas are charged on model-generated tokens and add guidance on expected behavior for streaming + caching. Add server-side feature flagging API. Update billing FAQ with example scenarios and reconciliation procedure.

1) Short-term: opt-in config for early adopters. 2) Mid-term: default-on for hosted customers; notify Dedicated customers 4 weeks in advance with migration notes for on-prem runtime patches. 3) Long-term: include attribution metadata in exportable billing CSVs and update customer billing UI to show cache-saved tokens per invoice.

2026-03-02: Spike implemented to measure tagging overhead; observed 9 bytes avg tag payload when compressed.
2026-03-05: Design review with PM and Runtime. Rafael suggested proportional by model_generated_tokens; PM requested a conservative fallback for edgecases.
2026-03-09: Security: no PII in tags; verified with security team.
2026-03-11: Telemetry thresholds and test plan added after integration test failures that exposed race when a stream checkpoint occurred mid-batch.
Next: implement reconciliation pipeline and begin canary rollout

Priya Nair 2026-03-01: Added initial proposal after customer incident CTO-453 where a tenant saw early throttles due to cache-heavy coalesced batches.
Rafael Ortiz 2026-03-04: Implementing runtime tagging spike; will submit PR for tag propagation next week.
Maya Li (PM) 2026-03-06: Please ensure UI billing breakdown is ready before full rollout so customers can see cache-saved tokens.
Security Team 2026-03-09: Reviewed tags; OK with encryption-in-transit and no PII storage. Recommended retention limits for tag traces.
DevOps 2026-03-10: Need a migration window for Dedicated customers to apply runtime patch; propose 4-week notice and automation scripts.
Rafael Ortiz 2026-03-12: Landed runtime PR in canary branch; scheduling canary for 2026-03-18.

title: Quantization Deployment Safeguard Framework for Hopper (E4M3/E5M2)
author: Ava Chen
text:
Goal: Ship a repeatable, safety-first deployment framework for enabling FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) profiles on Hopper GPUs with automated calibration, staged rollouts, and deterministic rollback guarantees. Scope covers: an automated calibration runner (golden seeds + dataset sampling), per-layer scaling verification, latency and jitter telemetry baselines, canary gating heuristics, and a fail-safe that reverts requests to stable INT8 variants when accuracy or tail latency thresholds are breached. This ticket focuses on the orchestration and guardrails so model teams can opt into FP8 with low operational risk.

Key pieces: 
- Calibration harness: orchestrates offline and online calibration passes, records per-op scales, and stores canonical quant metadata. Supports seeding, repeatable RNG, and a "shadow" inference mode that computes FP8 outputs in parallel for statistical validation.
- Golden evaluation: curated prompt set (500 examples across short/long tail, safety-sensitive cases) with automated accuracy metrics (perplexity delta, top-k token differences, structured-output schema checks).
- Canary orchestration: progressive traffic ramp (0.1% -> 1% -> 10% -> 50%) with automatic hold/rollback on metric violations. Metrics: average token-level divergence, accuracy regression (>0.5% flag), 99.9th latency delta (>15% flag), error-rate spike (>2x baseline).
- Telemetry & alerts: new telemetry keys (quant.deploy.latency_tail, quant.deploy.token_divergence, quant.deploy.shadow_mismatch_rate). Dashboards and SLOs added to Console.
- Rollback primitives: instant routing rule flip to INT8 model variant, with stateful KPIs persisted for postmortem. Hysteresis and cool-down windows to prevent flapping.

Out-of-scope: core kernel optimizations and per-chip micro-tuning (handled by runtime/infra tickets). This ticket coordinates integration points and the safety automation so that enabling FP8 becomes a low-friction product feature for both Hosted and Dedicated customers.

Automated calibration runner commits artifacts to canonical S3 path and produces a metadata JSON with per-layer scales and activation stats.
Canary orchestration fully automated: progressive traffic increase with metric checks and automatic rollback to INT8 on breach.
Console shows FP8 badge and a deployment page with latency/accuracy charts and quick rollback button.
Shadow mode available to all Dedicated clusters and one Hosted region for initial trials.
Regression on golden set < 0.5% for token-level metric and no >1 critical structured-output failures in baseline models.

Finalize telemetry keys and implement metric ingestion pipeline (owner: telemetry team, due 2025-03-10).
Runtime: expose circuit-breaker API and fast routing rule flip (owner: runtime, due 2025-03-10).
QA: implement chaos test for canary (owner: SRE/QA, due 2025-03-12).
PM/Design: Console badge and deployment page mockups (owner: UX, due 2025-03-06).
Eng: add per-layer date-token calibration fixes (subtask ENG-831556).

2025-02-12: Kickoff meeting notes uploaded. Decided to use a reproducible seed set and store calibration artifacts in S3 path: s3://redwood-quant/calibration/eng-831555/. Action: infra to grant read/write to calibration service (PR#6421).
2025-02-18: Early prototype of shadow runner completed. Shadow mode runs +2-5% CPU overhead and records per-token logits diff. Observed a median token divergence of 0.12 on small model baseline; flagged long-tail prompts for review.
2025-02-22: PM feedback from Priya Kapoor: require explicit "opt-in" switch per project and a visible badge in Console indicating FP8 is active. Added to scope as UI acceptance criteria.
2025-02-25: Telemetry schema proposal posted: quant.deploy.{latency_p50,latency_p99,latency_p999,token_divergence,shadow_mismatch_rate,error_rate}. Dashboard wireframes linked (Confluence: /display/INF/FP8+Deploy+Dashboards).
2025-02-28: Validation run against golden set (N=500) on hopper-e5m2: 99.7% of examples within 0.5% accuracy threshold. Two structured-output regressions identified (invoice-date extraction). Created follow-up ENG subtask to add targeted calibration for date tokens (ENG-831556).
2025-03-01: Review with runtime team (lead: Sanjay Rao). Decision: use hysteresis window of 10 minutes for rollback to avoid flapping; require 3 consecutive evaluation windows to trigger automatic rollback. Runtime will expose a circuit-breaker API by 2025-03-10.
2025-03-03: Canary plan approved by SRE. Canary percentages and hold conditions codified in canary-config.yaml in repo: github.com/redwood-inference/quant-deploy/PR-6492. QA to run chaos experiment that kills 1/3 of quant nodes during 10% ramp to validate graceful fallback.
2025-03-04: Blocker: need dataset approval from privacy/compliance for one customer-specific golden set. Engaging Privacy team; until approval, that customer will be excluded from auto-canary.

title: Serving Identity and Customer Asks - Brief
author: Asha Menon
text:
One-pager purpose:
Quick reference for core serving identity and the concrete asks we should be making of buyers during product-led and sales-assisted motions. Target audience: GTM leads, field reps, product marketers, and solution architects who need a short, consistent narrative and a set of practical hooks.

Context:
- Market signal: buyers increasingly treat model choice as table-stakes; their procurement decision is dominated by how inference is run in production (latency, cost, reliability, SLAs).
- Gap: Many vendors sell models or model-hosting, but few provide a practical playbook to make inference predictable and economical across environments.

Core idea (one sentence):
Redwood turns inference from a fragile, bespoke engineering project into a predictable, measurable service that teams can operate like any other critical API.

Why this resonates (thesis):
- Engineering leaders care about operational risk and developer velocity; inference should not be an exotic special-case that drags down product cadence.
- Platform teams need consistent primitives they can standardize across product lines (routing policies, rollouts, observability).
- Finance/Procurement care about unit economics and predictable spend; usage-only billing and reserved capacity options map to real budget controls.

Primary buyer personas and moment-to-moment asks:
1) Product/ML Engineer (early adopter, PLG motion)
 - Pain: experiments hit inconsistent latency and costs, prototypes fail to scale.
 - Ask: "Give me an easy API I can prototype against and a clear upgrade path to predictable capacity."
 - Hook: Free tier + dev-focused SDKs + transparent perf profiles.

2) Platform/Infra Lead (enterprise, sales-assisted)
 - Pain: multiple teams implementing inference differently; SLOs are missed; audits and data isolation concerns.
 - Ask: "Help us standardize serving across teams and give us controls for SLAs, routing, and private deployment."
 - Hook: Dedicated pools, VPC/private control plane, KMS/HSM integrations.

3) Finance/Head of Ops (procurement stage)
 - Pain: token-level spend surprises; burst costs during peaks.
 - Ask: "Can you make costs predictable and show me hard unit economics?"
 - Hook: Reserved capacity pricing, per-token transparency, cost-optimization tooling.

Key messages (short lines for decks/emails):
- "Predictable inference: the same API from prototype to SLA-backed production."
- "Control costs without sacrificing latency — intelligent batching, caching, and routing do the heavy lifting."
- "Deploy on your terms: hosted, dedicated, or private control plane for regulated workloads."
- "Operational primitives first: rollouts, tracing, cost attribution, and automated fallbacks."

Differentiated proof points to surface quickly:
- Benchmark: median 95th-percentile latency numbers for common open models on our hosted tier (link to perf profiles).
- Case study snippet: customer X reduced per-inference cost by 37% after adopting Redwood Optimize + reserved capacity.
- Feature proof: built-in canary rollouts and automatic model fallbacks preserved SLAs during a regional outage (internal postmortem reference).

Competitive framing (how we want reps to position vs different vendor types):
- Against model-centric APIs: "Models are table stakes. Redwood sells the predictable service that makes models usable at scale."
- Against raw cloud endpoints: "Cloud VMs give you flexibility but not the opinionated runtime, batching, and routing needed to keep costs and latency in check."
- Against self-hosted runtimes: "If you care about speed-to-production and ongoing ops burden, Redwood removes the heavy lifting while giving you the controls you need."

Common objections and succinct rebuttals:
- "We can host it ourselves to save money." → "Many teams can for a narrow window; Ongoing ops, regional failover, and consistent SLAs are hidden costs that quickly erode that savings. We help you quantify and avoid those surprises."
- "We’re tied to cloud X and can’t move." → "Redwood supports routing and placements by region and hardware, and we offer private deployments that meet strict networking requirements."
- "Your latency sounds optimistic for large models." → "Share a simple request pattern (seq length, concurrency). We’ll run a targeted perf profile and show expected P95/P99 numbers on your workload."

Tone and narrative style guidance for collateral:
- Be pragmatic and engineering-friendly: use measurable outcomes, not hype.
- Emphasize 'control' and 'operational predictability' over model performance claims.
- Use concrete metrics and short customer vignettes rather than abstract buzzwords.

Success metrics for the narrative (what to measure post-rollout):
- Conversion uplift in PLG funnel from dev sign-up to reserved capacity purchase (+ lift target: 12% q/q).
- Reduction in pre-sales security/RFP cycles for Private deployments (reduce average days-to-contract by 20%).
- Demo-to-pilot flow: time from first demo to production pilot < 45 days for targeted accounts.

Next tactical steps (immediate):
- Sync with field marketing to create a 1-page 'serving checklist' for demos and discovery calls (owner: Priya).
- Create a short perf-profile template sales can request from engineering to generate on-demand P95/P99 numbers (owner: Diego).
- Draft two one-paragraph customer vignettes (startup and regulated enterprise) for homepage and sales deck (owner: Ellen).

Open questions we should resolve quickly:
- Standardized perf-profile inputs: what minimal telemetry do we need from customers to produce an accurate P95/P99 estimate?
- Pricing thresholds for cross-sell from hosted to dedicated that trigger an automated outreach.

Notes to self / rough ideas: (brainstorm fragments)
- Consider a small 'inference health score' badge we can show in the console and in the sales deck (latency/cost/SLO readiness).
- Short script for SDRs: 3 lines to get to buyer pain ('Are you struggling with inconsistent latency? What does your per-token bill look like last month? Would you accept a quick perf snapshot we run on your pattern?')

Document history: initial draft Nov 2025 (Asha), field inputs Dec 2025 (Diego), marketing edits Jan 2026 (Priya), engineering perf template added Feb 2026 (Ellen).

End of brief.

title: Compatibility safety net strategies for private control plane upgrades
author: Priya Kapoor
text:
Purpose
This is a working runbook that collects strategies, lightweight tooling patterns, and Terraform notes intended to provide a compatibility safety net during control-plane upgrades for Private deployments (VPC / on-prem). The focus here is minimizing customer-visible API changes, preserving in-flight state, and keeping quick rollback paths. This is intentionally operational and engineer-facing — not a marketing doc.

Scope and constraints
- Applies to Private control plane upgrades (components: control-plane API, placement/orchestration, runtime agent handshake).
- Excludes heavy data-model migrations that require DB downtime (those should be handled via dedicated migration jobs).
- Assumes customer VPCs may have restricted egress and that artifact distribution might be via signed bundles (airgap).

Goals
- No more than 10s of added tail-latency during normal traffic after cutover.
- No customer API contract-breaking without an opt-in migration window.
- Clear automated rollback triggers based on SLO regressions and error budgets.
- Maintain ability to serve older runtime versions by introducing compatibility adapters rather than hard-cutting clients.

High-level approach (safety-net tiers)
1) API negotiation / header-based versioning shim (non-invasive):
 - Deploy a small gateway-side adapter that inspects X-Redwood-Client-Version (or similar) and rewrites/augments requests for older agents.
 - Adapter resides in control-plane edge; cheap and reversible.
 - Use for small contract changes: renamed fields, swapped enum values, optional params.

2) Runtime feature flags + dual-protocol acceptance: 
 - Introduce feature-gated endpoints on control plane that accept both V1 and V2 payload shapes; gate with tenant-level flags.
 - Default to V1 behavior unless tenant explicitly opts in.

3) Proxy-level KV cache mirroring / warmup: 
 - Before cutting over, run background jobs that pre-populate runtime KV caches with expected model prefixes to avoid cold-start regression spikes.
 - For private deployments, provide an offline warmup bundle (tar.gz) customers can load into local cache priming job.

4) Canary-by-tenant + traffic shaping: 
 - Ship control-plane new release to small tenant slices first (use tenant labels).
 - Gradually ramp producers of high-throughput traffic later.

Preflight checklist (quick)
- [ ] Verify Terraform plan against known state (capture plan output to artifact).
- [ ] Confirm artifact signing and offline delivery path for airgapped customers.
- [ ] Run compatibility tests: api-contract smoke, runtime handshake, kv-warmup simulation.
- [ ] Backup control-plane DB snapshot and export critical config keys.
- [ ] Validate observability (traces, metrics, logs) ingestion for new binaries.

Operational probes (what to watch)
- Error increase: 5xx rate > baseline + 2x in any 5m window => immediate throttle/rollback evaluation.
- Latency: p95 > baseline + 30% for 10m => investigate batching/queueing regressions.
- Cache-miss surge: sustained cache miss delta > 5x baseline for 15m => trigger KV warmup and consider rollback.
- Authentication failures: any uptick in auth/token errors for control-plane agent registrations -> block progressive rollout.

Rollback triggers and automated rollback plan
- Triggers (any 2 of the following within 20m):
 * p95 latency spike above threshold,
 * 5xx error-rate doubling,
 * >10% reduction in throughput for top-10 tenants,
 * Breakage of agent handshake (registration failure rate >1%).
- Automated actions:
 1) Route new-tier traffic back to previous control-plane instances (routing flag flip).
 2) Scale down new control-plane replicas gracefully (drain connections with 30s grace).
 3) Re-apply previous Terraform state via saved plan (see notes below).
 4) If DB migrations executed, run explicit backout scripts (these must be vetted preflight).

Terraform module notes (practical)
- Module version pinning: always pin control-plane module versions in tenant manifests. Keep module changelog entry for every exported var that affects public API.
- Immutable artifacts: store signed artifact id and checksum as a variable; do not rely on 'latest' image tags.
- State locks: require manual approval step to unlock state in airgapped or high-risk tenants.
- Plan capture: store terraform plan output in S3/MinIO and tag with upgrade run id. This becomes the canonical rollback plan.
- Minimal diff approach: expose 'feature_toggle' variables per tenant to apply compatibility flags without code deploys.

API compatibility design patterns (concrete)
- Additive-only approach for fields: prefer adding optional fields with defaults parsed by both old and new agents.
- Deprecation window: advertise deprecations for at least 90 days; allow opt-in to new behavior during that time.
- Version negotiation header example: X-RW-API-Version: "1.3". Gate breaking transforms behind adapter that checks this header.
- Operational escape hatch: X-RW-Compatibility=legacy to force legacy handling for specific requests.

KV/state migration strategy (non-disruptive technique)
- Shadow-migrate: write dual-writers for new branch but keep reads from legacy until canary shows parity.
- Reconciliation job: compare digest counts and top-k keys between old and new stores; fail cutover if >0.1% divergence on hot keyset.
- Cold-start mitigation: provide a bulk-snapshot restore operation that can hydrate runtime caches from control-plane export.

Telemetry preservation and trace continuity
- Maintain trace-id pass-through between runtime and control-plane. If header name changes, introduce adapter that maps old->new ids.
- Preserve search tags and tenant ids to keep historical dashboards functional.
- Backfill strategy: if a short telemetry gap occurs, run a focused backfill using retained logs and export to observability tenant workspace.

Airgapped / offline customer considerations
- Deliver signed bundle with both old and new control-plane binaries + migration scripts.
- Provide 'upgrade lab' script that can be executed by customer SRE with automatic preflight checks and dry-run.
- Ensure KMS/HSM key rotation plan is included; avoid automatic rotation during cutover window.

Runbook: step-by-step (0 -> full cutover)
0) PREP: gather plan id, backup ids, owner pager, and Slack channel.
1) DRY-RUN: apply module with feature_toggle only (no binary update). Run smoke tests.
2) CANARY-1: deploy control-plane nodes with new binary to canary pool (tenant labels small). Monitor 30m.
3) CANARY-2: widen to medium pool; enable KV warmup jobs for medium tenants. Monitor 1h.
4) ROLL: ramp to 50% by request-weighted routing. Keep legacy adapter enabled.
5) OBSERVE: collect metrics/traces and run automated parity checks.
6) COMPLETION: flip feature_toggle to default=true for a second, then deprecate adapter after 90 days.

Quick incident notes (what to do if things go wrong)
- If agent registrations fail: flip routing to legacy control-plane and contact infra team to pause rollout.
- If DB schema mismatch detected: stop new control-plane writes immediately and run reconciliation; notify platform DB team.
- For irreversible migration steps discovered in-flight: escalate to the upgrade owner and run postmortem to avoid repeat.

Open TODOs / follow-ups
- Build a lightweight adapter prototype (node/Go) that can run in the edge and hold shims for at least five typical field transforms. Owner: Daniel.
- Add terraform plan capture hook into our CI pipeline and store per-run artifacts for 180 days. Owner: Aisha.
- Define exact SLO thresholds per tenant size class for automated rollback logic. Owner: Priya.

References and example commands
- Capture terraform plan: terraform plan -out=plan.binary && terraform show -json plan.binary > plan.json && upload-to-artifact-store plan.json
- KV warmup job (example): python tools/kv_warmup.py --bundle kv-snapshot.tgz --target runtime://10.0.5.3:9000 --concurrency 8
- Rollback apply (safe): terraform apply -input=false -auto-approve saved/plan-id-1234.tfplan

Post-cutover checklist (24h)
- [ ] Confirm per-tenant error rate within historical baseline.
- [ ] Validate that 100% of canary tenants have no handshake regressions.
- [ ] Sweep audit logs for any auth/key anomalies.
- [ ] Schedule adapter sunsetting and communication plan if no issues after 90 days.

Appendix: quick compatibility shim examples
- Field rename shim pseudocode: if missing(request.new_field) and request.old_field: request.new_field = transform(request.old_field)
- Header rewrite: if header X-RW-API-Version absent -> set to 1.0 (legacy)

This is a draft — please add observations from dry-runs, canary metrics, and any edge-case failures encountered. Keep notes below as plaintext samples of incident timelines for the postmortem.

title: Discrete Stabilization Catalog and Escape-Hatch Playbook
author: Maya Chen
text:
Overview

This document is a compact, operator-friendly catalog of stabilization patterns and 'escape-hatch' procedures for on-call engineers and bridge operators responding to service instability (latency oscillation, transient SLO regressions, noisy-neighbor stalls, KV cache avalanches, and multi-tenant degradation). It is intentionally concise so teams can act quickly without flipping through multiple runbooks. Use this as a decision surface: identify the pattern, follow the associated rapid steps, and escalate to deeper runbooks as needed.

When to use this catalog

- Fast-moving incidents where the priority is to restore customer-facing behavior within the first 30 minutes.
- Multi-service degradations where automated routing or fallback toggles can limit blast radius.
- Game day scenarios and tabletop rehearsals as a quick reference for action owners.

Guiding principles

1) Minimize blast radius: prefer targeted mitigations (route, limit, degrade) over global shutdowns.
2) Observe then act: gather a minimal evidence set (traces, P99, token rates, eviction metrics) before irreversible actions.
3) Keep customers informed: if an incident impacts tenants for >10 minutes, publish a short status page note and add periodic updates.

Stabilization patterns (catalog)

Pattern: Latency oscillation (periodic P99 spikes)
- Symptoms: P99 jumps to 300–800ms in bursts for 3+ cycles; throughput sustained.
- Likely causes: asynchronous background batches, intermittent GC on model workers, autoscaler thrash.
- Rapid mitigations (escape-hatch):
 1. Attach live profile: run the tracing hook (obs/trace-link) for the last 10 minutes.
 2. Toggle conservative batcher mode: /api/admin/batcher?mode=conservative -> reduces batch size and prioritizes latency (no config restart).
 3. Pin to lower-seq-length model variant for affected route (route config -> set model_variant=fast-latency).
 4. If oscillation continues, enable per-route rate-limiter at 80% of normal QPS for 15 minutes.

Pattern: Noisy neighbor GPU saturation
- Symptoms: single-host GPU util spikes to 98% while others at 60%; specific tenant latency increases.
- Likely causes: oversized burst jobs, driver-level memory leak, misbehaving private deploy.
- Rapid mitigations:
 1. Identify host via metrics (gpu-alloc / host-id).
 2. Migrate affected reservations: run CLI migrate-reservation --host HOSTID --target pool-safe.
 3. If migration fails, drain the host (drain-host HOSTID) and enable fallback to prewarmed dedicated pool.
 4. Notify infra-sre and open a follow-up ticket with host logs.

Pattern: KV cache avalanche / mass eviction
- Symptoms: sudden spike in cold-start token latency; cache-miss rate > 60%; downstream P95 token latency increases.
- Likely causes: model rollout that changed prefix patterns, cache TTL misconfig change, or eviction due to memory pressure.
- Rapid mitigations:
 1. Re-enable prefix-KV sticky policy (config: cache.prefix_policy=sticky).
 2. Roll back model rollout to previous version for the offending route.
 3. Gradually ramp requests back with canary traffic (10% -> 25% -> 50%).

Escape-hatch inventory (actions you can invoke immediately)

Table: quick inventory of escape-hatches
| Action | Owner | Trigger | Immediate rollback criteria | CLI / Console path |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Route-level rate limit (soft) | runtime | P99 > 300ms for 5m | P99 < 250ms for 10m | Console -> Routes -> Rate limits |
| Switch to fast-latency model variant | runtime | SLO regression + regression test pass | Traffic restored and qualitative checks pass | /api/route/update -> model_variant |
| Batcher conservative mode | serving-runtime | P95 token latency > threshold | P95 < baseline for 10m | /api/admin/batcher |
| Drain host and migrate | infra-sre | GPU saturation on host | Host rebalanced and utilization < 70% | infractl drain-host HOSTID |
| Re-enable KV sticky policy | platform | sudden cache-miss spike | cache-miss < 15% for 20m | Console -> Caching -> Prefix policy |

Step-by-step runbooks (short forms)

Runbook: Rapid route-level throttling (ten-minute stabilization)
1. Trigger: Alert: route.<service>.p99.latency > 400ms for 3 minutes.
2. Evidence to collect (first 5 minutes):
 - P95/P99 traces (jaeger link), top 5 trace spans, and token counts.
 - Queue depth and drop rates from queue-metrics dashboard.
 - Identify recent config changes (deploys in last 60m).
3. Action: apply a soft rate limit at 80% of normal QPS for the affected route.
 - Console -> Routes -> Edit -> Add soft_limit=80% with 15m TTL.
4. Observe for 5–10 minutes. If P99 falls below target, start a slow ramp back (90% -> 100% over 20 minutes).
5. If P99 does not improve, switch model variant to fast-latency and notify product.

Runbook: Noisy-host containment
1. Trigger: single-host GPU util >95% and tenant errors rising.
2. Evidence: host metrics, active reservations, and running job list.
3. Action: mark host as draining, migrate non-critical reservations, re-route latency-sensitive jobs to prewarmed pool.
4. Communication: post on #ops-bridge channel and update status page if >10 minutes.

Customer status templates (short, copy-paste)

Status update — initial (within 10m):
"We are investigating elevated latencies impacting model inference for some customers. Engineers are actively identifying the source and applying mitigations. We will post an update within 15 minutes. Impact: partial for some API routes."

Status update — action (after mitigation applied):
"We have applied a temporary mitigation (rate limiting / model variant switch) which has reduced error rates and latency for affected requests. We are continuing to monitor and will follow with a detailed post-incident note."

Status update — recovery (when stable):
"Service performance has returned to normal. We are running a set of post-incident checks and will publish a short summary and follow-up actions within 48 hours."

Template: customer-facing root cause summary (48h)
- Impact: summary of who was affected and approximate timeframe.
- Root cause: short one-line cause.
- Resolution: actions taken and why they work.
- Follow-ups: planned infra/config changes, rollback/rollforward schedule, and timeline for completion.

Game day and drill guidance

Purpose: validate the escape-hatch catalog under stress, exercise communication cadence, and confirm rollback criteria are understood.

Suggested exercises (1–2 hours each)
- Latency oscillation drill: simulate GC spike on a model worker and practice toggling batcher conservative mode and model-variant pinning.
- Cache-eviction drill: deploy a synthetic traffic pattern to cause cache churn; practice re-enabling sticky policy and ramping canary traffic.
- Noisy neighbor drill: mark a host as saturated and exercise drain/migrate and failover into prewarmed pool.

Exercise checklist
- Pre-run: assign Bridge lead, Evidence owner, and Customer comms owner.
- During run: collect prescribed evidence, make one mitigation, and document timestamps.
- Post-run: 30-minute retro capturing time-to-first-action and time-to-recovery, plus a 1-page remediation plan.

Ownership and escalation matrix

- Bridge lead: first 30 minutes orchestration and status page publication.
- Evidence owner (runtime/op-observability): collects traces, SLO dashboards, and relevant logs.
- Infra escalation: infra-sre on-call for host-level actions (drain, migrate).
- Product/Model PM: notified when model variant or behavior change is required.

Escalation thresholds (examples)
- If incident expected to exceed 60 minutes OR customer-impacting errors > 5% of tenant traffic, escalate to SRE manager and Customer Success lead.
- If more than 3 tenants report degraded service directly, open a Sev2 and engage GTM lead.

Post-incident guidance

1. Evidence capture: attach SLO timelines, sample traces, and commands executed to the incident timeline.
2. Blameless postmortem: follow the postmortem template (timeline, root cause, contributing factors, corrective actions, owners, and ETA).
3. Runbook updates: if an escape-hatch was used, update this catalog with notes on effectiveness and add a section on 'when not to use'.

Appendix: CLI snippets and config quick-reference

- Apply soft route rate limit (example):
 curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://admin.redwood/api/routes/route-id/rate-limit" -d '{"soft_limit":0.8, "ttl_minutes":15 }'

- Switch model variant (example):
 curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://admin.redwood/api/routes/route-id/model-variant" -d '{"variant":"fast-latency" }'

- Drain host (example):
 infractl drain-host --host HOSTID --reason "noisy GPU saturation"

Configuration table (example thresholds)
| Metric | Alert threshold | First action | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| route.p99.latency | >300ms for 5m | soft rate limit 80% | runtime |
| host.gpu.util | >95% for 2m | drain host | infra-sre |
| cache.miss.rate | >50% | re-enable sticky policy | platform |

Related pages and links

- Include links to the full runbooks: runtime emergency runbook, infra host recovery runbook, and postmortem template.

Revision history

- 2025-11-02: created by Maya Chen.
- 2026-06-18: added noisy neighbor containment steps (reviewer: Arjun Patel).
- 2027-03-14: expanded escape-hatch inventory and added game day exercise checklist (reviewer: Lina Gomez).

title: Rollout Orchestrator: Signal Aggregation & Trace Bridge for Variant Health
author: Priya Kapoor
text:
Goal: Build a console-first Rollout Orchestrator feature set that aggregates signal streams (latency, error rate, token cost, semantic drift) across variants and ties them to traces and per-route telemetry. Deliver a single-pane Variant Health view with a Trace Bridge that can surface sampled traces linked to rollout deltas and allow operators to pivot between A/B, canary, and shadow traffic comparisons.

Background: Customers currently use separate dashboards and traces to investigate rollout regressions. This creates a slow feedback loop during canary and A/B experiments. The Orchestrator will combine time-aligned aggregated metrics, divergence summaries, and trace snippets so operators can make faster rollout decisions and optionally trigger auto-rollback.

Scope: Console UI components and backend telemetry aggregation pipeline only. Not in scope: changes to serving runtime scheduling or new model variants. Scope details:
- Aggregation: rollup token-level cost, p95/p50 latency, top-3 error fingerprints, and semantic divergence score per-variant and per-route.
- Trace Bridge: follow a request from aggregate metric spike to N sampled traces (client request -> route -> model variant) and show KV-cache hit/miss annotations and batch size.
- Diff Views: side-by-side delta visualization for any two variants or time windows; supports A/B splits and shadow vs live.
- Auto-rollback integration: pluggable policy rules (thresholds, evaluation windows, cooldown). When enabled, Orchestrator emits a decision event to the deployment service.

Acceptance criteria:
1) Console shows Variant Health for a selected route within 5s of selection and renders diff overlays for two variants.
2) Trace Bridge returns 3 sample traces correlated with the metric spike and annotates per-step metadata.
3) Aggregated metrics align with existing per-route dashboards within a 3% margin on p95 and error rate.
4) Auto-rollback rules can be created in the UI and successfully fire a dry-run decision against staging deployment without mutating production.

Key trade-offs and decisions we debated:
- Sampling vs full tracing: initial launch will use adaptive sampling to bound storage and latency; plan to tune sampling weight for rollout traffic.
- Aggregation window: 1m buckets provide fast feedback but increase noise; default to 1m with 5m smoothing option.
- Diff visualization: lightweight statistical summary vs full distribution plotting; we will ship summary + small sparkline and add full distributions in follow-ups.

Telemetry and metrics to track post-launch:
- Time-to-insight: median time from alert to a trace being surfaced.
- Precision of rollback triggers: percent of dry-run rollbacks that would have prevented a degraded SLO.
- Console latency: 95th percentile time to render Variant Health UI.

Notes for engineering: backend requires a rolling-join between metric aggregates and sampled trace index keyed by route+variant+time. Keep join window configurable. Provide an API for the console to request aligned metrics and traces.

1) Variant Health UI renders for selected route with two-variant diff in <5s; 2) Trace Bridge returns 3 representative traces annotated with KV/cache/batch info; 3) Aggregated metrics match per-route dashboards within 3%; 4) Auto-rollback dry-run can be executed from UI without changing production deployments.

2026-02-22 - Priya K.: Kickoff meeting with Eng and Design. Agreed to MVP scope: aggregation, trace bridge, simple diffs, auto-rollback dry-run only.
2026-02-26 - Ethan M.: Spike complete. Prototype shows adaptive sampling plus a small index for sampled traces. Backend needs a high-cardinality join strategy; proposing pre-aggregated keys at route+variant+bucket.
2026-03-02 - Lina Torres (Design): Initial mockups uploaded to Figma. Emphasis on quick signal triage: heatbar for error spikes, and a stacked cost/latency view.
2026-03-05 - Security review request filed (ENG-9102). Security flagged data retention of traces; recommend 30d retention for rollout traces by default and 90d for enterprise plan.
2026-03-08 - Infra note from Marcus O.: We should cap trace fetch to 250KB payloads for console requests to keep UI fast. Backend will return a short summary if traces exceed budget with a link to raw trace archive.
2026-03-10 - Priya K.: Scope locked for Cycle 2026-W09. Moving to implementation. Design and backend tasks split into tickets and assigned to ENG-8841, ENG-8842, ENG-8849.

title: eng-sre
text:
Maya: Heads-up: seeing gaps when linking traces to Loki logs for GPU preempt events in eu-west1. Kibana shows traces with span_id 0xabc123 but Loki returns nothing for the same trace_id. Anyone else?

Jon: saw something similar during last surge, might be index rotation or relabel mismatch. what's the trace id? paste sample?

Maya: trace_id=af3e9b7c4d12, root span id 7f4d. Kibana query I ran: trace.id: "af3e9b7c4d12" -> shows spans. In Loki I ran: {job="gpu-runtime"} |= "trace_id=af3e9b7c4d12" and got nothing.

Terry: can you try a looser LogQL: {app="node-gpu"} |~ "trace_id.*af3e9b7c" | line_format "{{.message}}" ? sometimes the field gets mangled by promtail pipeline.

Maya: ran that, still no hits. Prometheus shows gpu_preempt_total{region="eu-west1"} spiked at the same time though. Could be agent-side formatting or an ingest drop.

Ivan: check loki_ingester_protos_dropped_total and any pushgateway errors in the same timeframe. Was there a grafana alert?

Jon: Grafana recorded loki_ingester_protos_dropped_total +320 at 2026-03-15T14:02Z. Also noticed s3 backend had a handful of 5xx around then. Coldstore writes were delayed.

Maya: FWIW Kibana returns spans with source: "agent-collector-eu-west1" and the raw span messages include trace=0xaf3e9b7c4d12 (note the 0x prefix) whereas our Loki searches used trace_id=af3e9b7c4d12 (no 0x). Might be a normalization mismatch.

Terry: good find — promtail/ingest pipelines historically had a relabel step that preserves 0x prefix. If some agents send 0x and others don't, we end up with split indexes. Check the promtail pipeline regex.

Jon: found the promtail config in repo:
```
- action: replace
 source_labels: [__line]
 target_label: trace_id
 regex: '.*trace=(0x[0-9a-fA-F]+).*'
 replacement: '$1'
```
That keeps the 0x, so searches without it miss lines.

Maya: pushed a quick canary promtail patch to strip optional 0x: regex '0x?(?P<tid>[0-9a-fA-F]+)' and replacement '$tid'. Deployed to eu-west1 canary hosts.

sre-bot: deploy-bot: rollout started for promtail config update to eu-west1 (canary).

Ivan: after deploy, try re-running Loki queries with both IDs: {job="gpu-runtime"} |= "af3e9b7c4d12" OR |= "0xaf3e9b7c4d12". Also check loki_client_ingest_errors for the earlier drop window.

Maya: re-run after canary — Loki now returns the agent flush and preempt stack lines. Correlation works: trace spans in Kibana map to logs in Loki. Looks like a combination of ingest drops + trace-id normalization caused the gap.

Jon: nice. Follow-ups: (1) propagate promtail regex change to all regions, (2) add unit/integration test for trace-id normalization in the log pipeline, (3) tweak loki_ingester_protos_dropped_total alert to fire earlier (warn at lower threshold) and add runbook. I'll open PRs for 1 and 2 and a Grafana dashboard tweak for 3.

Terry: filing postmortem doc: https://app.docs/redwood/postmortems/pm-gpu-trace-correlation-eu-west1

Maya: thanks team :raised_hands:

title: operator-session-jwt-escrow-and-audit-nonce-anchoring
author: Maya Patel
text:
Motivation: reduce risk of operator-session replay and accidental cross-tenant key usage by introducing an ephemeral operator JWT escrow flow tied to KMS-wrapped operator session keys, and anchor audit events with a nonce signed using the same escrow key. This PR implements session-scoped RBAC tokens for operators, a KMS escrow/unescrow handshake to wrap ephemeral session keys with customer CMKs (when available), and an audit nonce anchoring mechanism so every mutating operator action can be tied cryptographically to the operator session.

What changed (high level):
- Add session-scoped RBAC support: operator sessions can be created with ephemeral claims that expire and are revocable via the new session manager. Sessions are represented by a short-lived JWT plus a session-id that must be presented for operator API calls.
- KMS escrow: when a tenant provides a CMK, the session manager will request an escrow-wrapped session key (EncryptUsingKey) and store only the wrapped blob. Service-side operations that need to act on behalf of the tenant will unescrow (Decrypt) via a tight audit path that logs the key-id used. For hosted tenants without CMKs, the platform fallback uses a platform-wrapped ephemeral key with additional operator-scoped constraints.
- Audit nonce anchoring: every operator mutation now requires a per-session monotonic nonce signed with the session key. The audit writer records nonce, session-id, operator-id, and wrapped-key-id; a validation layer rejects out-of-order or replayed nonces for the session.
- Observation and metrics: added session lifecycle metrics (sessions_created, sessions_revoked, unescrow_calls_total), audit_nonce_rejections, and a per-tenant KMS-wrap proportion gauge.
- Docs and migration: docs/rbac/session-scoped-roles.md and upgrade notes describing optional tenant CMK onboarding, rollback plan, and canary rollout strategy.

Compatibility and rollout:
- Backwards compatible: existing operator tokens remain valid; new sessions opt-in via the feature flag "session_escrow_enabled" at operator-account level.
- Canary: rollout plan included: start in staging, enable for internal tenant 42, monitor audit_nonce_rejections and unescrow latencies, then enable for 10% of production operator traffic before full rollout.
- Fallbacks: if KMS unescrow fails, request is rejected by default for tenants with CMKs; for non-CMK tenants we fall back to platform-wrapped key path and emit a security audit event.

Security considerations:
- Limits and quotas: throttled KMS unescrow calls to avoid accidental key-exhaustion; per-operator session rate limits enforced.
- Key exposure: the service never stores unwrapped session keys; unwrapped keys live only in an in-memory enclave for the duration of the operation and are zeroized afterwards.
- Audit retention: audit records include wrapped-key-id but not raw key material. Migration to longer retention for tenant keys is opt-in and controlled by retention_policy features.

Migration checklist (in-PR):
- [x] feature flag and operator API gate
- [x] session manager with revoke endpoint and server-side tests
- [x] KMS escrow glue and integration tests (mocked KMS + small e2e)
- [x] audit writer changes and nonce validator
- [x] docs and upgrade guide + Linear ticket references
- [x] metrics + dashboard draft

Related: Linear ENG-1987 (operator-session-escrow design), ENG-2041 (audit-pipeline-consistency). SUP-4219 captures a customer request to bind operator actions to tenant CMKs for audits.

Diego Martinez: Nice design. Please add a unit test for the nonce monotonicity on session reconnect — I saw an edge case where sequence resets could be abused.
Maya Patel (author): Added tests for reconnect cases and clarified behaviour in session_manager.go comments. Also added a reconciliation job note in docs.
Ava Chen: We should surface KMS latency as a tag on audit events so we can correlate slow unescrow with tenant errors. Add a metric and propagate it in the audit payload.
Maya Patel (author): Added unescrow_latency_ms metric and included it in the audit envelope and dashboard draft.
Ethan Zhao: CI failed on flakey TestSessionRevocation; looks related to timing. Please add a retry-aware assertion and increase the test timeout.
Maya Patel (author): PTAL — increased timeout and refactored the test to be less timing-sensitive. Re-ran CI, all checks passed.

Review outcome: Approved by Diego Martinez and Ava Chen. Ethan gave final thumb after CI green. Merge method: squash and merge.

Threat model updated: operator replay attacks mitigated by signed nonces + monotonic session counters. KMS usage is audited with wrapped_key_id and rate-limited. New in-memory enclave ensures unwrapped keys do not persist. No plaintext keys written to storage. Recommended follow-ups: HSM attestation for enclave and short-lived CMK aliases for high-risk tenants.

Operator session escrow + audit nonce anchoring: Introduces ephemeral session-scoped operator tokens with optional tenant CMK escrow, KMS-wrapped session keys, and nonce-based replay protection for operator mutations. Feature is behind the 'session_escrow_enabled' feature flag and is opt-in per-tenant. See docs/rbac/session-scoped-roles.md for migration steps.

Rollout steps: enable flag in staging -> enable for internal tenant 42 -> monitor metrics (audit_nonce_rejections, unescrow_latency_ms, sessions_revoked) -> 10% production canary -> full rollout. Emergency rollback: disable feature flag which returns system to legacy operator token behaviour. If KMS unescrow errors spike, set tenant to fallback-mode via admin console.

title: Spectra dedicated footprint & memory trade-offs (KV cache + quantization)
author: diego_fernandez
text:
From: Diego Fernandez <diego.fernandez@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@spectra.ai>
Date: Mon, 15 Nov 2027 09:12:00 -0800
Subject: Spectra dedicated footprint & memory trade-offs (KV cache + quantization)

Alex — great talking last week. As promised, I wanted to capture next steps for a dedicated capacity proposal focused on model-specific memory sizing. High level: you mentioned Llama-3-70B as the primary production model with occasional Mistral-30B usage for lighter loads. Key things we need from you today so engineering can size a Dedicated pool:

- realistic peak RPS and p50/p95 latency targets
- typical and max context lengths (and % of calls hitting large contexts)
- expected caching behavior (how often prefixes repeat)
- any constraints on deployment (single region, private VPC)

If you can send a 48–72h sample of traffic (CSV is fine) and the procurement doc, I’ll route to infra and we’ll produce a two-option sizing: conservative (no quantization / FP16) and aggressive (4-bit weight quant + KV offload).

I attached a small template for traffic (spectra_traffic_sample.csv) — fill cols and send back. I’ll loop in Ben (SE) and Marissa (Capacity) for the engineering breakdown.

From: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@spectra.ai>
To: Diego Fernandez <diego.fernandez@redwood.ai>
Cc: Procurement Team <procurement@spectra.ai>
Date: Mon, 15 Nov 2027 10:03:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Spectra dedicated footprint & memory trade-offs (KV cache + quantization)

Thanks Diego — attaching the sample and the procurement summary (spectra_pricing_request.pdf). Quick answers inline:

- Peak traffic: ~120 requests/sec sustained during business hours; bursts up to ~200rps for short periods.
- Latency goal: p50 < 250ms, p95 < 600ms for completion (we can relax for very long contexts).
- Models: primary = Llama-3-70B (90% of traffic); secondary = Mistral-30B (10%).
- Context: typical prompt ~1k tokens; 20% of calls use long context (16k–32k), ~2% hit full 64k in testing.
- Cache: we expect ~55–65% prefix reuse for user sessions (high reuse on conversational flows).
- Compliance: must run in a US region; vendor SOC2 required — procurement included the checklist.

Let us know if you need more granularity (per-endpoint token distribution).

From: Diego Fernandez <diego.fernandez@redwood.ai>
To: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Evelyn Hart <evelyn.hart@redwood.ai>
Cc: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@spectra.ai>
Date: Mon, 15 Nov 2027 14:20:00 -0800
Subject: Fwd: Spectra dedicated footprint & memory trade-offs (KV cache + quantization)

Ben / Marissa / Evelyn — forwarding Spectra's traffic sample and procurement summary. Highlights: 120rps sustained (~200rps bursts), Llama-3-70B primary, ~20% long-context (16–32k), 2% 64k test calls, ~60% cache reuse. They want two posture options:

1) Conservative: FP16 weights, minimal offload, maximize latency SLAs
2) Cost-optimized: aggressive weight quant (4-bit variant), KV offload to NVMe for cold tails, targeted batching/caching to hit cost targets

Specific asks for the response: per-model GPU mapping, per-request KV memory estimate (and formula), guidance on quant impact on model residency and inference latency, and rough Dedicated pool size for their latency target. Can you sketch an estimate and attach a quick sim (kv sim + per-gpu headroom)? Spectra asked for a pricing ballpark for both options.

— Diego

From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>
To: Diego Fernandez <diego.fernandez@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Evelyn Hart <evelyn.hart@redwood.ai>
Cc: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@spectra.ai>
Date: Tue, 16 Nov 2027 09:35:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Spectra dedicated footprint & memory trade-offs (KV cache + quantization)

Team / Alex — ran a quick sizing pass against their sample and sketched two candidate pools. Summary first, details below and attached "spectra_kv_sim.xlsx" with per-token KV curves.

Summary (approx):
- Model residency: Llama-3-70B (baseline FP16 weights + activations) typically needs ~160–180 GB of GPU RAM to host model state with operational headroom. At FP16 that implies multi-GPU model-parallel (2x H100-80GB with sharded weights) or a single 80GB with weight offload — not ideal for latency.
- Quantized option: 4-bit weight quant (Q4 variants) reduces on-device weight size ~3.5x vs FP16. That lets Llama-3-70B weights fit into a single H100-80GB instance (weights ~45–55 GB) leaving room for KV and activations. Latency penalty for decode is small (~5–12% depending on kernel maturity).
- KV cache sizing: from our empirical sims, FP16 KV uses ~0.9 GB per 1k tokens for L3-70B. Thus: 16k ~=14.4GB, 32k ~=28.8GB, 64k ~=57.6GB (per concurrent session). With ~60% cache reuse, effective steady-state KV memory demand drops by similar factor for conversational hotspots.
- Offload strategy: use NVMe-backed KV offload for cold tails (cheap storage, higher tail latency). Keep hot prefixes in-GPU and tune eviction to target p95. Offload reduces required GPU RAM but increases variance in p95 latency for long-context rare calls.

Recommended Dedicated pool sizes (to hit p50 <250ms, p95 <600ms at 120rps sustained):
- Conservative (FP16, minimal quant): 18 H100-80GB GPUs configured across model-parallel sets for L3-70B (effectively ~9 model instances with autoscale headroom). This prioritizes latency and avoids offload for 32k contexts.
- Cost-optimized (Q4 weights + KV offload): 10 H100-80GB GPUs with aggressive packing and a small NVMe cluster for KV offload; apply per-route caching to keep most sessions in GPU memory. Expected cost delta: ~45–55% lower infra cost vs conservative but p95 of 64k cold calls may exceed their p95 target unless we increase hot-memory retention.

Operational notes / tradeoffs:
- Canary plan: start with 2% of traffic on quantized instances for 2 weeks, monitor hallucination/regression via eval prompts and quality telemetry.
- Latency vs quant: Q4 introduces slight decode overhead; but our optimized kernels shrink the throughput delta. If Spectra demands strict p95 across all 64k calls, we must keep a small pool of FP16 instances for fallback (recommended: 2–3 model-parallel FP16 nodes).
- Sizing formula (high level): GPU_resident_memory = Quantized_weight_size + KV_hot + Activation_headroom + OS/runtime overhead. KV_hot ~= tokens_hot * kv_bytes_per_token (we measured ~0.9GB per 1k tokens in FP16 for L3-70B).

I attached the sim; Marissa, can you convert these into a pricing ballpark for their procurement doc? If Alex is comfortable, we’ll propose a pilot: 6 Dedicated GPUs (quantized) for 30 days with telemetry and a canary mix, then expand to full pool.

title: On‑Prem Control Plane: deploy checklist + Terraform module roadmap
author: Priya Patel
text:
Purpose and scope:
This document is a tactical checklist and implementation notes for initial setup, capacity growth, and rotation/upgrade activities for the private control plane (on‑prem / VPC customer deployments). It focuses on practical Terraform module layout, state/secret handling, deterministic rollout steps, and verification checks — aimed at solutions engineers and SREs running customer installs or our internal test clusters.

Why this exists:
- We have multiple variants of private control plane installs (cloud VPC + customer onprem). The same core components must be reproducible and auditable.
- This file captures a minimal, repeatable sequence and a proposed Terraform module roadmap to reduce friction and outages during upgrades/rotations.

High‑level deployment topology (reference):
- Management plane (control plane) services: api-gateway, auth, config-store, rollout-controller, metrics-collector.
- Data plane: model-serving workers (separate repository/infra).
- Shared infra: ingress LB / load balancer (NAT where required), internal DNS, cert management, central logging/metrics, KMS/HSM for keys.

Prerequisites (customer & operator checks):
- Network: customer provides VPC/CIDR ranges, reserved subnets for control plane, NAT/gateway details. Confirm route tables and allowed egress to update endpoints.
- DNS: internal DNS zone created, and a wildcard entry or loadbalancer A record available.
- Certificates: ACME or customer-supplied certs; if ACME is used, ensure ACME challenges can reach the cluster.
- KMS/HSM: KMS key ARN or HSM connection details (for secrets at rest) — test encrypt/decrypt before provisioning.
- Storage: object store endpoint for remote Terraform state (S3-compatible / GCS) with a lifecycle and versioning.
- Access: Operator SSH + kubeconfig bootstrap access to initial nodes. IAM or equivalent RBAC bindings for operators.

Terraform module layout (recommended roadmap):
1) infra-network (module): VPC/subnets, route tables, NAT, internal NLB (if required). Variables: cidr_base, public_subnets, private_subnets, nat_gateway_count. Outputs: internal_lb_dns, cidr_allocations.
2) infra-security (module): security groups/firewall rules, network policies, bastion host config. Variables: operator_cidrs, allowed_ports.
3) controlplane-core (module): control plane services (deployed as k8s manifests or Nomad jobs), config-store (etcd or managed db), api-gateway. Variables: cp_version, node_counts, replica_subnet_map. Outputs: api_endpoint, metrics_endpoint.
4) secrets-kms (module): KMS integration, secret encryption envelopes, key rotation schedule helper. Variables: kms_key_id, rotation_window_days.
5) state (module): remote state backend setup (s3/gcs buckets, locking dynamo/lock table). Variables: backend_bucket, lock_table, encryption.
6) observability (module): logging sinks, metrics exporter, prometheus/grafana bootstrap.
7) upgrade-pipeline (module): helper resources for canary releases and blue/green URL records.

Notes on module design principles:
- Keep modules idempotent and small — one responsibility per module.
- Avoid embedding sensitive values in tfvars; prefer remote secret injection via KMS/secret manager.
- Make outputs explicit and minimal, use locals internally.

State & locking guidance:
- Always use remote state with encryption and locking (S3 + Dynamo for AWS, GCS + CloudSQL advisory locks for GCP).
- Use separate state per logical environment (customer-production, customer-staging) and per module group for risky components (controlplane-core separate from infra-network).
- Snapshot state before planned upgrades and tag snapshots with ticket id + timestamp.

Initial deployment sequence (conservative):
1) infra-network: apply network module and verify subnets & routing.
2) infra-security: deploy firewall/security groups and confirm operator access.
3) state: provision remote state buckets/locks and migrate local state if any.
4) secrets-kms: create KMS keys, test encrypt/decrypt using the operator credentials.
5) controlplane-core (bootstrap mode): apply a minimal control plane (1 replica per component) to initialize etcd/config-store and operator endpoints.
6) observability: wire up metrics/logging; sanity-check metrics ingestion.
7) controlplane-core (scale to target): increase replicas, validate HA and leader election.
8) upgrade-pipeline: create canary records and configure rollout controller.

Scaling guidance and capacity planning:
- Seed sizing: start with 3 control plane nodes for HA if using etcd; if resource constrained use 1 for initial but upgrade to 3 within the same maintenance window.
- CPU/Memory: baseline for control plane components: 2 vCPU / 8GB per control node; increase based on request QPS and number of managed workers.
- Autoscaling: only enable autoscaling for stateless components (api-gateway, controllers). Keep storage databases sized manually.
- Batching & KV cache: recommend configuring KV caches with fixed memory caps and TTLs; monitor hit-rate as load increases.

Upgrades and rotations (principled approach):
- Semantic versioning: tag controlplane images with semver. Build upgrade paths and block unsupported jumps (e.g., disallow 1.x to 3.x without intermediate).
- Canary first: deploy new version to 10% of control nodes (or separate canary set) with traffic steering for non-critical routes.
- Rolling upgrade: drain one node, run upgrade, validate, then move to next. For databases, follow database-specific upgrade notes first.
- KMS key rotation: schedule key rotation during a low-traffic window. Steps: create new key, rewrap sensitive secrets in a staging bucket, test decrypt under new key, then promote. Keep old key enabled until final verification.
- Certificate rotation: use short maintenance windows, update ACME or cert bundles, restart only ingress or gateway components when possible.

Rollback playbook (fast failure response):
- If post-upgrade tests fail: revert traffic to previous canary/blue environment.
- For Terraform changes that caused drift: restore last known working state snapshot to remote state and run a targeted apply with --replace on impacted resources.
- Database schema changes: always include backward-compatible migrations. If an incompatible migration is detected, restore DB from pre-upgrade snapshot.

Verification checklist (post‑deploy/scale/upgrade):
- API health endpoints return 200 and expected schema.
- Leader election stable for config store/etcd.
- Metrics: request latencies within SLA; error rate below threshold.
- Logs: no crashing pods in last 15 minutes.
- KMS: test secret read/write using operator credentials.
- DNS: internal records resolve and TLS completes handshake with expected cert.
- Rollout logs: no unrecoverable errors in controller logs.

Common gotchas and troubleshooting notes:
- Network MTU mismatches causing gRPC timeouts — standardize MTU across hosts.
- Clock skew breaks cert validation and leader heartbeats — ensure NTP/chrony configured.
- Implicitly open egress for ACME can cause failures in air‑gapped installs; require customer to provide certs in that case.
- Terraform drift from manual kubectl changes: keep everything in code and document temporary manual operations with a Jira ticket.

Operational run examples (commands and hints):
- terraform init -backend-config="bucket=redwood-cp-state" -reconfigure
- terraform plan -var-file=customer.tfvars -out=plan.tfplan
- terraform apply "plan.tfplan" --auto-approve (only from CI with approved PR and tag)
- To rotate a control node: cordon <node>; drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data; terraform taint module.controlplane.aws_instance.node[0]; terraform apply

Air‑gapped and restricted environments notes:
- Replace remote state bucket endpoints with customer S3-compatible endpoints and ensure network peering.
- Provide an image registry mirror and update image_pull_secrets.
- Ship a cluster-bootstrap bundle (charts + manifests + certs) and a guided operator script.

Open action items / roadmap (proposal):
- Split controlplane-core into smaller modules per subcomponent (auth, gateway, config-store) for more targeted upgrades.
- Add a terraform-provider-backed canary-record resource for automated traffic steering.
- Create a standard upgrade test harness that runs smoke tests against canaries and produces an approval artifact for CI.

Appendix: quick preflight template (copy for customer):
- network_cidr: ___________
- internal_dns_zone: ___________
- kms_key_id: ___________
- operator_cidr_ranges: [___________]
- object_store_endpoint: ___________
- cert_strategy: [acme | customer]

Contact and escalation:
- Owner: Priya Patel (eng-private-deployments)
- Oncall SRE rotation: see internal roster (linked_artifacts)
- Slack channel: #private-cp-ops

Notes and provenance:
- Drafted during customer POC 2024‑11; incorporates learnings from two air‑gapped installs and an AWS VPC deployment.
- Intended as a living document; please file PRs against infra repo or create a drive copy for customer‑specific modifications.
