title: Stripe-affinity allocator and compact-safepoint playbook for KV cache fragmentation mitigation
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Problem statement: our KV cache continues to exhibit long-lived fragmentation on high-concurrency workloads (many short chats + mixed sequence lengths). Fragmentation increases per-token costs and occasionally causes suboptimal eviction storms that spike tail latency or trigger failover to slower model variants. Goal: implement a low-risk, incremental allocator + background compaction choreography that reduces long tail fragmentation without materially affecting generation latency or batch throughput. Approach summary: 1) introduce a stripe-affinity allocation layer that slices per-GPU KV pools into many micro-stripes and pins entries to stripes based on request fingerprint and temporal locality heuristics; 2) maintain per-stripe soft/hard watermarks and fast local eviction policies to avoid global compaction for small churn; 3) implement compact-safepoints (coordinated low-impact windows) where we perform relocation/compaction of hot holes using hop-buffered moves and cooperative throttling with the continuous-batcher; 4) expose fragmentation telemetry and relocation cost metrics to Console for rollouts and alerts.

End-to-end e2e benchmark showing at least 30% reduction in fragmentation ratio (free-holes bytes / total KV bytes) on mixed short-and-long sequence workload compared to baseline
No >5ms increase in median generation latency for steady-state serving during background compaction at default throttling settings
Relocation/compaction aborts safely rollback without data loss and do not cause OOMs under 99th percentile load
Console dashboard includes new fragmentation metric, hole-age histogram, and relocation cost-per-token; alerts for fragmentation_ratio > 0.18 for >10m

Design: finalize stripe-sizing heuristics and mapping from request fingerprint to stripe (Aisha)
Proto: implement stripe-affinity allocator (Marco) - internal API + unit tests
Coord: implement compaction coordinator with leader election per-GPU (Marco)
Batch integration: add cooperative backpressure hooks into continuous-batcher (Ruth)
Telemetry: add fragmentation_ratio, hole_runlength_histogram, relocation_latency_p50/p95 to Console (SRE)
Perf: run mixed workload perf sweep and cost-sim on dedicated test rig (perf eng)
PR: prepare RFC and Confluence doc and gather design review from Runtime/Infra (Aisha)
Rollout: staged canary: 5% -> 25% -> 100% with automated rollback on latency regressions

Stripe sizing heuristics: target stripe capacity so that expected in-flight entries per stripe is small (10-100) to keep local compaction cheap; compute from median working set per model and tokens/sec distribution.
Per-stripe watermarks: soft_watermark triggers local eviction; hard_watermark prevents new pins and surfaces backpressure to request router/batcher.
Compaction safepoints: scheduled during observed micro-idle windows (low request rate for a GPU) or opportunistically inside low-priority batch slack; safepoint window is bounded to 200ms max per invocation to cap latency jitter.
Relocation protocol: hop-buffered move with pin-swap: allocate small temporary buffer in pinned host/GPU memory, copy source->temp->target, update metadata atomically; abort path restores pointers.
Cooperative throttling: credit-based system where batcher grants relocation credits proportional to current SLO slack. Credits consumed per byte moved; credits replenish with observed lower latency.
Size-aware lanes: large KV entries (top 5% by size) are isolated into dedicated stripes to avoid blocking many small relocations.
Failure modes and mitigation: if relocation fails mid-way, mark target slot quarantined and schedule async healing; ensure quarantined slots do not count against free capacity until healed.
Upgrade/rollback strategy: feature-flagged rollout with runtime flag to disable relocation on a per-GPU basis. Configurable thresholds in Console for aggressive/ conservative mode.
Telemetry plan: hole_age_histogram (buckets in seconds/minutes), fragmentation_ratio, relocation_bytes_per_minute, relocation_ops_per_minute, relocation_error_rate, allocator_meta_size_bytes.
Risk: small increase in 99.9th latency during heavy compaction spikes. Mitigation: aggressive throttling to zero and canary rollout; add automatic regression detection via perf guardrails.

2026-03-10 - Aisha Patel: Initial writeup. Prototype idea inspired by 'stripe' allocation used in storage systems; intention is to bias by temporal locality and minimize large global compactions.
2026-03-10 - Marco Chen: Spike notes: stripe-affinity dramatically reduces cross-tenant relocation in simulation if stripe count > 128. However, too many stripes increase allocator metadata (RAM) on each GPU. Trade-off: choose stripe count by KV pool size and observed concurrency. See spike results attached.
2026-03-11 - Ruth Gomez: Continuous-batcher impact: we need a soft-contract where compaction uses credits and only consumes credits from a shared budget tied to current tail-latency budget. Proposed implementation: batcher exposes remaining_latency_budget_ms() and compaction withdraws credits before relocation.
2026-03-11 - Design review (Sana): prefer hop-buffered memmove vs pausing kernels during relocation to avoid stalling token generation. Make sure relocation copies are pinned and double-buffered to avoid fragmentation amplification.
2026-03-12 - Marco Chen: Implemented prototype branch (github.com/redwood/rt/PR-1489). Early unit tests pass; running perf harness now. Noted a pathological case where very-large KV items (long contexts) cause stripe hot-spotting; plan to add size-aware stripe assignment (large entries get hashed into size-aware lanes).
2026-03-12 - Aisha Patel: Reviewed telemetry plan. Add alert for relocation_error_rate > 0.5% in a 5m window to trigger automatic throttle to zero and alert on-call.
2026-03-12 - Marco Chen: Re: rollout. Will add opt-in feature flag per-customer and per-GPU label to allow safe testing on Dedicated clusters before global rollout.
2026-03-12 - Perf-eng: scheduled long-running mixed workload (100k requests) to measure hole-age decay and compaction overhead. Results expected 2026-03-16.

title: prefill-playbook-compiler-and-quant-profile-registry
author: Priya Menon
text:
Motivation: We need a deterministic, auditable way to convert high-level prefill/batch playbooks (tenant-facing YAML) into concrete defaults, quantization profile bindings, and simulated unit-econ estimates. This PR adds a Playbook Compiler service + CLI and a light-weight Quant Profile Registry to centralize presets used by Redwood Optimize and the Dedicated autoscaler.

Summary of changes: adds a compile-time validation pipeline for playbooks, a rules engine that materializes per-tenant candidate defaults, a simulation step that produces unit-econ deltas (cost/latency/quality), and a small HTTP registry for quant presets. Also includes a CLI (rwctl playbook compile/export) for SREs and solutions engineers to produce deterministic artifacts for rollouts.

What this solves: previously defaults were scattered across heuristics in runtime and the Console; teams had to run ad-hoc sims. The new compiler gives repeatable outputs, migration paths, and a discoverable registry of quant profiles that can be referenced by name from policies. This reduces onboarding friction and makes canarying safer.

Scope: server-side Go service (pkg/playbook-compiler), a CLI shim in tools/rwctl, small Express-compatible admin API (server/admin/quant-registry) for CRUD on quant presets, unit and integration tests, docs (docs/playbooks/compile.md), and e2e simulation harness (tests/e2e/prefill-sim).

Design notes: playbooks are validated against a JSON Schema; compiler runs three phases: 1) normalize (resolve tenant overrides and feature flags), 2) synthesize defaults (batch sizes, cache TTLs, prefill thresholds, quant profile binding), 3) simulate (synthetic request stream to estimate per-token unit-econ and 95th latency). Output is a signed artifact (v1) that can be consumed by Dedicated/Private agents or uploaded to Console as a rollout candidate.

Backward compatibility and migration: the compiler emits 'legacy_mappings' for fields still consumed by older runtime versions. The quant registry supports both named profiles and raw profile blobs; runtime will fall back to inline profile if registry lookup fails. Migration docs included.

Testing: added 78 unit tests, 6 integration tests that run a small simulated workload, and a smoke test for the CLI. CI initially failed due to a time-sensitive e2e flake; added deterministic seed and improved test isolation.

Security: registry API requires admin token; payloads are validated and size-limited. No secrets stored.

Checklist: - [x] Compiler service implemented - [x] CLI for compile/export - [x] Quant registry API and DB migration - [x] Tests and simulation harness - [x] Docs and migration guide - [x] Telemetry (metrics: compiler_runs, compile_errors, sim_estimates_emitted)

Commits: see commits list field for per-commit descriptions.

Merge notes: squash-merged after CI green and approvals from Ethan and Marta. The new service is feature-flagged (prefill.compiler_v1) and will be enabled for internal sandbox tenants first.

Follow-ups: - wire Console UI to present compiled candidates (follow-up ENG-1933) - add a periodic garbage-collector for stale quant presets (ENG-1998)

Ethan Cole: Overall looks good. A few nit comments on rule ordering and an edge-case where tenant overrides might wipe prefill thresholds. Please add a test for that case.
Priya Menon (author): Added test 'TenantOverridePreservePrefill' and updated normalization to preserve explicit low-level overrides. Pushed fix in c7d8f11.
Marta Alvarez: The simulation estimates look reasonable, but we should be careful exposing raw latency outputs in logs. Suggest we only ship aggregated percentiles (p50/p95) to telemetry.
Priya Menon: Switched telemetry to emit p50/p95 and a 'sim_bucket' histogram. Updated metrics and docs.
Jun Park: Small nit: prefer semantic version in artifact name (playbook-artifact:v1) to make future upgrades explicit.
Priya Menon: Done - artifacts now include semantic version and compiler git SHA.

Introduce Playbook Compiler (v1) and Quant Profile Registry: deterministic compilation of tenant playbooks into rollout artifacts, simulation-based unit-econ estimates, and a discoverable registry for quant presets. Feature-flagged rollout; see docs/playbooks/compile.md for migration steps and RWCTL usage.

title: Demo tenant hitting 429 throttling during live customer demo (Northstar Payments)
text:
Issue summary
- During a live SE-led demo for Northstar Payments, the Redwood demo tenant began returning HTTP 429 responses mid-flow (streaming chat + tool call step). This caused the demo to stall and required switching to backup screenshots for the Console section.

Customer impact
- Live demo interruption (~6–8 minutes). Customer saw repeated 429s and intermittent retries.
- Risk: undermines reliability story and raises concern about quota predictability/noisy-neighbor.

When / where
- Date/time: 2025-11-12 ~19:10–19:25 UTC
- Environment: prod / us-east
- Tenant: Redwood internal demo org ("demo tenant")

Observed behavior
- Chat/completions requests started returning:
 - 429 Too Many Requests
 - Response headers included rate-limit remaining=0 (per-minute)
- Retries from demo app increased request volume, exacerbating throttling.

Expected behavior
- Demo tenant should be sized for at least 2 parallel demos, with headroom for retries/streaming and synthetic traffic seeding.

Steps to reproduce (as seen during call)
1) Start demo app scenario runner (streaming chat)
2) Execute tool-calling step (adds 1–2 additional calls)
3) Open Console in parallel (refreshes usage/cost panels)
4) Within ~2 minutes, observe 429s

Initial hypotheses
- Demo API key configured with self-serve default RPM/TPM limits.
- Synthetic traffic generator + live demo sharing same project/key.
- Parallel demos earlier in the hour consumed burst capacity; rate-limit window not reset.

Investigation notes
- Checked gateway logs for the demo org/project: throttles triggered on request-rate limit (RPM), not GPU capacity.
- No elevated 5xx in serving runtime; this was an API gateway quota/rate-limit enforcement event.
- Console page refreshes were not the root cause but contributed to request count and distracted during recovery.

Mitigation applied (during incident)
- Temporary quota uplift applied to demo org/project in us-east:
 - Increased RPM cap + burst allowance
 - Increased TPM cap to reduce retry amplification for streaming
- Confirmed new limits took effect within ~60 seconds; 429s stopped.

Root cause
- Demo tenant was provisioned with quota defaults intended for standard self-serve tenants, and our automation did not reliably apply the higher demo profile. Additionally, synthetic traffic seeding was configured to use the same project/key as live demos, consuming part of the minute-based request budget.

Resolution
- Short-term: raise demo tenant quotas and move synthetic traffic generator to a dedicated "seed" project/key to isolate from live demo activity.
- Long-term: update demo tenant provisioning automation defaults to always apply demo quota profile + create separate scoped keys (live-demo vs seed-traffic), and add a demo healthcheck gate that verifies quota/rate-limit settings before SEs start a call.

Customer-facing notes (what SE said)
- Framed as: "We hit our safety rate limit in the demo environment; production customers set limits appropriate to their workloads, and Dedicated capacity has separate controls. We’ll adjust the demo tenant so it never happens again."

Follow-ups / action items
- [DONE] Document immediate workaround in demo runbook: if 429s occur, switch to backup mode and run healthcheck.
- [DONE] Add healthcheck validation for quota/rate limits and surface clear pass/fail output (linked PR).
- [DONE] Provisioning automation: ensure demo profile quotas applied idempotently; prevent seed job from sharing live-demo key.
- [TODO] Add alerting on demo-tenant approaching RPM/TPM caps (warning threshold) routed to demo on-call alias.

Workarounds (SE playbook)
- Run demo tenant healthcheck endpoint; if quotas not applied, page #support and switch to backup screenshots.
- If throttling persists, pause synthetic traffic generator for the live window and retry after 60s rate-limit window reset.

Notes on data/security
- All traffic is synthetic/demo; no customer data involved.

References
- Slack: #support and #sales thread (internal) around live demo throttling
- Confluence: Demo capacity/quotas runbook + demo tenant reset runbook
- Related: SUP-4189 (Console dashboards empty; seed traffic generator separation work overlaps)

title: HelixWave Console — usage paths & per-route cost breakdown demo
author: Jordan Park
text:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-09-17
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Samantha Ruiz (HelixWave), Ethan Cole (HelixWave), Rhea Kapoor (HelixWave)

Summary:
High-level console walkthrough focused on per-route usage analytics, cost decomposition, and options for pilot (hosted vs dedicated). Customer concerned about unit economics, data residency and KMS.

Topics:
- Console: usage paths and per-route dashboards
- Cost breakdown: per-route, per-token, embedding vs generation
- Routing policies: latency vs cost
- Security: SOC2, KMS, VPC/private
- Pilot scope and next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick off, um, quick intro — I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood, and with me is Liam, our solutions engineer.
[00:07] Samantha Ruiz: Hi, Samantha here — Head of Platform at HelixWave. Thanks for squeezing us in, we wanted to focus on how you break down costs per feature path, like Chat -> Summarize -> Search endpoints.
[00:15] Liam Ortiz: Yep, great. We'll jump into the console, show per-route lenses, the cost decomposition, and then the Optimize suggestions for batching and quantization.
[00:24] Ethan Cole: Quick note — FinOps needs to see expected monthly burn for 5 million tokens, and we need to map those to our product teams.
[00:32] Jordan Park: Understood. Rhea, are you owning the sample traffic export? That will help the cost modeling.
[00:37] Rhea Kapoor: I can pull weekly logs, yeah. We use a mix of embeddings for search and text generation for summaries, roughly 70/30.
[00:45] Liam Ortiz: Cool. Ok, sharing my screen — this is the Routes dashboard, you'll see top-left the global usage heatmap, then per-route tiles. Each tile breaks down tokens, latency P95, and cost per 1k tokens.
[01:02] [screen noise] Liam Ortiz: One thing, the transcription might say 'KA cache' sometimes — it's KV cache, sorry.
[01:10] Samantha Ruiz: That's fine. Walk us through how you attribute cost to routes — is it based on route tags or service name?
[01:18] Liam Ortiz: We allow both. You can tag incoming requests at the SDK level or via header routing, and the console aggregates by tag. For attribution we use the route ID plus model variant — so if you run a cheaper quantized variant behind the same route, it shows as a separate cost line.
[01:35] Ethan Cole: So we can see 'Search-prod-embed' vs 'Search-prod-llm' separately?
[01:39] Liam Ortiz: Exactly. And the cost breakdown shows raw GPU time estimate, token billing estimate, and an infra amortization line — that's our reserved capacity allocation when you're on Dedicated.
[01:51] Samantha Ruiz: How accurate are those infra amort numbers? We have reserved instances elsewhere and need predictable mapping.
[01:58] Jordan Park: The console uses your committed capacity profile and training/compute hours to apportion fixed infra costs across routes. For hosted customers it's an estimate, for Dedicated customers we can pull actual usage from your reserved pool which makes it within ~5% accuracy.
[02:13] Rhea Kapoor: How do you handle cache hit savings — say we have prefix caching for summarization, will the console show token savings?
[02:20] Liam Ortiz: Yes, we show cache hit rate and the estimated 'avoided tokens' metric — it's a separate column in the per-route table. Also our Optimize engine will recommend prefix caching policies for high-duplicate prompts.
[02:33] Ethan Cole: On the Optimize suggestions — does it automatically recommend quantization levels? We're sensitive about output quality.
[02:39] Liam Ortiz: It suggests quantization profiles per-model and per-route based on your eval set and latency/cost targets. You can preview recommended profiles and run a quality check A/B — the console ties diffed eval results back to the route.
[02:52] Samantha Ruiz: If we accept a recommendation, is there a rollback? We need safety nets for production.
[02:57] Jordan Park: Yes — rollouts are canary-based, you can split traffic percentages, and automatic fallback to previous model variant if quality drops or latency SLO violated.
[03:08] [crosstalk] Rhea Kapoor: So for pilot we could start with 10% traffic to a quantized model and watch evals?
[03:12] Liam Ortiz: That's the standard approach. Also we have per-route SLO alerts — you'll get an alert if latency or quality regresses.
[03:20] Ethan Cole: Data residency — we need logs and KV cache to remain in our VPC. Is that possible in Private deployment?
[03:28] Jordan Park: Absolutely. Private gives you customer-managed VPC and optional on-prem. Our control plane remains separate unless you opt for the full Private control plane where nothing leaves your network.
[03:40] Samantha Ruiz: KMS integration — we use AWS KMS and an HSM for certain keys. How do you handle key management?
[03:47] Liam Ortiz: We support KMS and bring-your-own-HSM in Private. For hosted customers we integrate with customer-managed keys via cross-account access, and we log key usage. We'll send the KMS integration notes after the call.
[03:58] [00:03:59] Jordan Park: Competitors question — anyone comparing to Anthropic or hosted endpoints?
[04:05] Ethan Cole: We looked at Anthropic and Vertex but they don't have the same per-route economics tooling, that was our main pain.
[04:12] Liam Ortiz: Right. Another difference is our runtime-level batching and KV cache metrics which directly tie to cost savings you can measure in the console.
[04:22] Samantha Ruiz: How do you charge for embeddings vs generation? We run embeddings at scale.
[04:27] Jordan Park: Embeddings are shown as separate routes and token units are normalized; pricing tiers can be set per-route. For the POC we can set a separate quota and alerts so finance can see embeddings burn isolated.
[04:39] Rhea Kapoor: Can we get a sample pricing sheet mapped to our projected 5M tokens? Like a line-item for each major route?
[04:45] Jordan Park: Yes — Jordan will send a per-route cost matrix. We'll plug your sample traffic and run a model selection + routing policy to give a monthly estimate and a sensitivity analysis.
[04:58] Ethan Cole: About SLA — what's included for Dedicated?
[05:03] Liam Ortiz: Dedicated includes an SLA for queueing latency and uptime, with credits for missed SLOs. We also have optional premium support blocks.
[05:11] Samantha Ruiz: Any gotchas — cold start, kv cache warmup?
[05:15] Liam Ortiz: Cache warmup can cause early higher latency; our recommendations include pre-warming sequences and a small warm traffic guard. Also cold-start variance is minimized by our preallocated pools in Dedicated.
[05:26] [05:26] Rhea Kapoor: Are there recommended practices for route naming? We have messy service names.
[05:31] Liam Ortiz: Route naming matters for attribution. We recommend a canonical naming scheme product-env-feature, e.g., search-prod-embed. The console supports mappings if you need to alias tags.
[05:42] Samantha Ruiz: Ok, recap — we want a) pricing mapped to our 5M tokens, b) SOC2 + security docs, c) a 3-week pilot scope, d) sample traffic analysis. Anything else?
[05:53] Jordan Park: We'll also include recommended quantization profiles and a proposed canary rollout plan for the pilot.
[06:00] Ethan Cole: Timelines — can we start pilot early October? We need purchase approval by end of September.
[06:07] Jordan Park: We can aim for 2025-10-01 pilot kickoff pending approvals. I'll follow up with pricing and a proposed pilot runbook.
[06:15] Samantha Ruiz: Great. Thanks, everyone.
[06:17] Jordan Park: Thanks — we'll close here. Liam and I will send the docs.

[12:00] Liam Ortiz: Jumping back in — now on the Cost Explorer. This view lets you slice by day, by route tag, by model family. You can also export hourly cost CSV to S3 for downstream FinOps tools.
[12:20] Ethan Cole: Export to S3 is important. We want hourly granularity and mapping to our internal cost center. Can you add a custom label?
[12:27] Liam Ortiz: Yep, you can define custom cost center tags and the export includes them.
[14:40] Rhea Kapoor: On instrumentation — do you capture user_id or PII in logs? We want to ensure we can mask or tokenize.
[14:47] Jordan Park: Logs can be configured to drop or hash PII at ingestion. For Private deployments we can also enable on-prem log sinks so nothing leaves the VPC.
[18:00] Liam Ortiz: Quick demo of SDK header tagging: here's a 2-line snippet, set header 'x-rd-route: search-prod-embed' — that flows through and shows up in the console attribution.
[20:10] Samantha Ruiz: Nice. For the sample traffic Rhea will upload, what's the expected format?
[20:17] Liam Ortiz: JSONL of requests with route header and timestamps works best. We'll provide a template.
[24:00] Jordan Park: Walkthrough of the Optimize tab — you'll see suggestions ranked by potential monthly savings. Each suggestion has estimated impact and a risk score.
[27:30] Ethan Cole: How do you calculate risk score?
[27:33] Liam Ortiz: It's heuristic: eval-quality delta, historical variance, and a model-specific quality baseline. You can tune sensitivity in the Optimize settings.
[30:00] Liam Ortiz: Autoscaling and burst — Dedicated supports guaranteed baseline and burst buckets. Burst draws from a shared pool, we meter burst separately so you can see actual burst spend in the console.
[33:20] Rhea Kapoor: Is there a hard cap to prevent runaway spend during a traffic spike?
[33:25] Jordan Park: Yes — per-route quotas and global caps exist. You can configure hard stop thresholds and soft alerts.
[36:40] Liam Ortiz: Observability — we emit per-request traces you can hook into Jaeger or our tracing UI. We also expose a per-route cost/time breakdown in traces to help perf debugging.
[38:10] Samantha Ruiz: For audit — how long do you retain audit logs? We need 12 months for compliance.
[38:17] Liam Ortiz: By default hosted retains 90 days; Dedicated and Private can extend retention to 12+ months with add-on retention blocks.
[41:00] Ethan Cole: Procurement questions — PO process and invoicing cadence?
[41:07] Jordan Park: We invoice monthly for hosted usage. For Dedicated we can do monthly or quarterly invoices against committed spend, and we accept PO/Net30 for enterprise contracts.
[44:12] Samantha Ruiz: Legal — any standard terms that are blockers for us? Data processing agreements?
[44:19] Jordan Park: We have a DPA and standard enterprise addenda; we'll share the legal pack. For Private deployments we can customize language around data residency.
[47:50] Liam Ortiz: Returning to the console — here's an anomaly detection alert feed. You can tune sensitivity and route-level channels (pager, slack, email).
[50:00] Rhea Kapoor: For the POC can we get a sandbox with synthetic traffic so we can validate rollouts without touching prod?
[50:07] Liam Ortiz: Yes, sandbox workspaces are standard. We'll provision a sandbox workspace and seed it with mock traffic so you can test A/B and canary safely.
[52:10] Ethan Cole: Okay finance will need a line-item estimate and a total cost of ownership doc; that plus the security pack will get us through approval.
[52:20] Jordan Park: We'll include a TCO slide that shows three scenarios: hosted, dedicated, private — with sensitivity to token volume and cache hit improvements.
[55:30] Samantha Ruiz: Any final questions from your side?
[55:34] Rhea Kapoor: One small one — is there a programmatic way to pull the per-route cost via API for our internal dashboards?
[55:40] Liam Ortiz: Yes, we have a Usage API that returns per-route breakdowns hourly. We'll send API keys for the trial environment.
[55:50] Jordan Park: Great — recap of next steps: pricing matrix, SOC2/security docs, KMS notes, sample traffic template, sandbox workspace, and proposed pilot runbook.
[56:05] Ethan Cole: Sounds good. We'll confirm internal go/no-go by Friday 2025-09-19.
[56:12] Jordan Park: Perfect. Thanks again.
[56:18] Samantha Ruiz: Thanks team.
[56:22] Jordan Park: End call.

References shared:
- Link: /decks/helixwave-pilot-proposal.pdf (shared)
- Link: /docs/security/soc2-pack.pdf (to be sent)
- Link: /sheets/helixwave-traffic-sample.xlsx (customer to upload)

title: Decision-level routing observability: decision logs, per-hop metrics & trace linking
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Add end-to-end observability for smart routing decisions so engineers and SREs can answer: why was a request routed to region X or tier Y, when did fallback to a model variant occur, and what was the per-hop latency breakdown? Deliverables include a decision-log schema, trace/span linking for routing hops, per-hop metrics instrumentation, Console dashboards, and queryable storage with retention policy. Must exclude prompt contents and PII, support sampling policies, and be safe for high-throughput production traffic.

Decision log schema documented and reviewed in Confluence with fields: decision_id, request_id, timestamp, client_region, chosen_region, routing_tier, fallback_variant, reason_code, variant_latency_ms, total_routing_latency_ms, trace_id, span_id, sampling_rate, model_id, token_count; no prompt text or user PII stored.
Runtime emits decision log events to the routing Kafka topic (routing.decisions) for 100% of error/fallback cases and 5% of successful fast-path cases; sampling is configurable via feature flag.
Each routing hop creates a span linked to the overall request trace; traces visible in existing tracing backend and correlated to decision logs by trace_id.
Per-hop metrics (enqueue_ms, dispatch_ms, model_infer_ms, network_ms) emitted to metric system with tags: region, tier, model_variant, customer_tier, decision_reason.
Console surfaces a new Routing Decisions dashboard: aggregated fallback rates by region/tier, per-hop latency percentiles, and a trace+decision lookup UI; queries return results under 5s for 30d retention.
Privacy check completed: audit confirms no prompt content, only model_id and token_count are stored; security signoff recorded in ticket comments.
Canary rollout plan executed: instrumentation behind feature flag and enabled for internal orgs before wider enablement.

Schema proposal posted: https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/routing-decision-schema (draft). Use snake_case field names to match existing logging conventions.
Event pipeline: runtime -> routing.kafka.producer -> streams -> clickhouse(routing_decisions) and a low-latency materialized view for Console queries. Consider parquet export to s3 for long-term retention.
Sampling: implement deterministic sampling by client_id hash for non-error traffic; always sample all fallback/error decisions and requests tagged with customer_impact=high.
Trace linking: add trace_id/span_id to decision log, create a short-lived routing span for each policy evaluation hop; instrument with opentracing-compatible headers used by our observability stack.
Per-hop metrics: emit timers per hop with tags for hop_index, policy_type (region_select|tier_route|fallback), chosen_node, and model_variant. Use histogram buckets aligned with existing latency SLOs.
Privacy: do not capture prompt text or embeddings. Add a scrubber that strips any user-provided metadata fields that look like emails/SSNs before writing to logs.
Storage & retention: routing_decisions table TTL 90 days; materialized view for Console 30 days. Cost estimate attached in comments.
Feature flag: runtime.flag.routing_observability with per-org whitelist for rollout. Default off for public tenants until privacy & cost signoffs complete.
Backfill: small backfill utility to populate clickhouse for last 7 days from Kafka if needed for dashboards; limited to internal orgs only.

Instrumentation: add decision logging and per-hop spans to runtime policy engine (ENG runtime team)
Pipeline: add topic routing.decisions and streams job to populate clickhouse (ENG infra)
Console: new dashboard and trace+decision lookup UI (ENG console)
Privacy review: security team to audit log schema and scrubber (Security)
QA: load test sampling and storage to validate cost and query latency (SRE/QA)
Rollout: enable feature flag for internal orgs, run 2-week canary, then widen (PM + Eng)
Docs: update runbooks and docs for incident triage using decision logs (DX)
Cost analysis: estimate ClickHouse storage and Kafka throughput, include in ticket comments (FinOps)
Small backfill utility and migration plan (ENG infra)
Add e2e tests that assert trace_id propagation and presence of decision_id in logs.

title: POC traffic thermography + SLA definition - GraniteBank
author: Jared Kim
text:
Discovery and POC scoping focused on workload characterization for a 4-week pilot. Key metrics: baseline QPS ~12, expected peak bursts to 180-230 QPS, concurrency target 40-70, average input tokens ~35-60 and average model output tokens ~220-380. Success criteria: P99 generation latency under 350ms for interactive flows, 99.9% availability during pilot, cost envelope within provided budget. Bench plan: replay production traces in week 2, run controlled burst tests and tail latency characterization, deliver report and sizing recommendations by end of week 3.

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-21 15:00 PST
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jared Kim, Priya Natarajan, Lena Ortiz (Redwood) - Marta Ruiz, Elliot Cheng, Samir Patel, Olivia Hart (Granite Bank)

Optional auto-generated: Summary present, action items listed

[00:00] Jared: Hey everyone thanks for joining, looks like we have a full house. Quick intro, I'm Jared on the AE side, Priya is our solutions engineer, Lena is your CSM. Marta, do you want to kick with a quick recap of your goals?

[00:15] Marta: Sure, thanks Jared. We're trying to scope a POC to validate serving a conversational assistant inside our mobile banking app. Main concerns are latency during the peak morning window, cost predictability, and of course data residency and audit logs. We gave you a high level of traffic but want Redwood to help translate that into capacity and SLA ask.

[00:35] Jared: Great. Priya, want to take us through what we'll need for workload thermography?

[00:40] Priya: Yeah so the first thing is request trace — timestamps, request size, response length distribution. Ideally a week of traffic, sanitized. From your note we saw baseline QPS around 10-15, but you mentioned some bursts up to two to three hundred? Wanted to confirm.

[01:05] Elliot: Right so current prod graph shows baseline 12 QPS, typical concurrency around 18, but our peak events — like morning auth and promos — spike to 180 to 230 QPS for short windows, around 90 to 120 seconds. That causes retries and longer tails.

[01:25] Priya: That helps. For modeling we separate steady-state QPS from burst topology. For steady-state we'd size for 12 QPS with concurrency 20ish; for burst we look at 200 QPS transient with concurrency approaching 60 to 80 depending on token lengths.

[01:45] Marta: Token lengths: most of our prompts are short — 20 to 60 input tokens — but model completions average 220 to 320 tokens because the assistant gives contextual steps. We saw in a sample that the output often gets long if user asks for step-by-step.

[02:05] Jared: So to confirm, concurrency metric we want to use is in-flight requests (open streams) not just QPS, because of long outputs. Priya, can you remind them about KV cache and prefix caching effect on throughput?

[02:25] Priya: Absolutely. If you can cache user context (prefix caching) and warm KV cache for common templates, effective tokens per request drop and latency improves. For the POC we'll run both cold and warmed cache scenarios. Note: our autotuner will recommend batching thresholds but for interactive flows we keep batching small to preserve latency.

[02:50] Olivia: Quick Sec question — Samir, do you want to ask about KMS and logs?

[02:55] Samir: Yeah, we need to know what keys are customer-managed, how audit logs are retained, and whether we can require TLS mTLS to Dedicated nodes. Also SOC two evidence and ISO are must-haves.

[03:15] Lena: We'll send the security pack — SOC 2 attestation, network diagrams, KMS options (bring-your-own and Redwood-managed), and our retention policies. Priya will attach notes on on-prem-ish VPC peering options.

[03:30] Marta: Good. Back to metrics — what should our success criteria look like at the end of the POC?

[03:35] Priya: From our experience, make them be measurable: 1) P99 gen latency under X (we suggested 350ms for your interactive target), 2) SLO for availability 99.9% during test windows, 3) throughput support for peak bursts without >1% error rate, 4) cost per 1k tokens within your budget envelope. If you want stricter latency we can try Dedicated with more aggressive batching and quantization.

[04:05] Elliot: If we go Dedicated, what are the quantization tradeoffs? We care about output quality for financial guidance.

[04:12] Priya: Quantization (8-bit/4-bit) can reduce memory and increase throughput but sometimes introduces subtle quality regression. For finance intents we recommend running evals on your prompt set; Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profile per model. We'll include a quality regression test in the bench plan.

[04:35] Jared: Let's put tentative numbers on the board. Baseline: 12 QPS, concurrency 20, avg input tokens 40, avg output tokens 260. Burst: target synthetic test at 200 QPS sustained for 90s, concurrency spike to 70, tail latency P99 target 350ms. Is that acceptable as a starting point?

[04:58] Marta: That matches our internal calculations, yes. We'll aim to produce sanitized traces that show those bursts.

[05:10] Priya: Benchmark plan — four-week pilot suggested: Week 0 (prep) data ingestion and replay tooling; Week 1 (baseline runs) run steady-state replay and confirm config; Week 2 (burst tests) run controlled bursts and tail profiling; Week 3 (retrospective) compile results, model/quantization recommendations and cost estimate; Week 4 decision and optional roll-forward. We can compress to three weeks if Granite is ready with traces.

[05:40] Elliot: For the replay tooling, what do you need format-wise?

[05:44] Priya: CSV or newline json with timestamp, request_id, prompt_len_tokens, expected_response_len_tokens, metadata (anonymized user cohort). We'll provide a template. Also we prefer to get typical success/failure rates to reproduce error handling.

[06:05] Samir: About networking — will we need a VPC peering for the Dedicated pilot or is a private endpoint enough?

[06:10] Priya: We support both. For strict isolation and mTLS we recommend VPC peering for the Dedicated capacity trial. For hosted pilot we can do private endpoints + strict egress rules. We'll note tradeoffs in the security doc.

[06:30] Jared: Budget question — Marta, Olivia, you mentioned a target monthly spend for POC?

[06:35] Olivia: We have a provisional budget for the pilot, roughly equivalent to two mid-size GPU months. We want an estimate though — per-token cost and Dedicated seat monthly.

[06:45] Priya: We'll produce a cost projection alongside the bench report, showing per-1000-token costs across steady and burst scenarios and a blended monthly projection. Also show sensitivity to quantization and batching.

[07:00] Marta: On success criteria, also include quality gates: mean BLEU-ish for template match, and no unsupported hallucinations for regulatory Q&A. We'll share a small test set for that.

[07:10] Priya: Good call — include a small labeled prompt set to run regression tests post-quantization. We'll run automatic checks and flag any deltas.

[07:25] Jared: Logistics and timeline recap — can we commit to the following: you (Granite) provide traces by 2026-11-25; we run baseline and burst in the week starting 2026-11-30; Redwood delivers report by 2026-12-10; decision meeting week of 2026-12-14. Sound right?

[07:50] Marta: Yes that works, assuming we can hit the trace scrub deadline.

[08:00] Samir: We'll start security review in parallel, but expect follow-ups about data-in-transit and KMS separation.

[08:08] Priya: Noted. Also small note — if you plan to enable tool-calling or function-style responses, that changes token patterns a bit; include that in the tracer if possible.

[08:25] Elliot: We'll add a marker for function calls in the trace.

[08:30] Olivia: Are there any competitors we should be aware of that Redwood sees in the enterprise banking space?

[08:35] Jared: Some customers evaluate SageCloud and a few infra vendors like Infera. For banks, the differentiators are VPC/on-prem options and auditable log streams. We'll compare in the follow-up deck.

[08:50] Marta: Last question — what's the risk that during the burst tests we see model OOM or kv cache thrash?

[08:58] Priya: If tokens-per-request are large and concurrency spikes, OOM risk increases without proper quantization and kernel selection. That's why we plan kernel/compilation profiles and will advise on model shard size. We'll also run memory-pressure scenarios to identify thresholds.

[09:20] Jared: Great. I'm going to summarize next steps and owners.

[09:25] Jared: Action items: Jared send bench template and replay tool; Marta provide traces; Priya schedule bench kickoff; Samir review security pack. We'll attach a checklist in follow-up email.

[09:40] Marta: Thanks all. Looking forward to the test.

[09:46] Jared: Thanks, meeting adjourned.

(End of transcript)

Notes on transcript quality: auto transcription had several mis-hearings around product names ("Redwood Dedicate" vs "Redwood Dedicated"), some numeric tokens mis-transcribed in the first pass; we validated numbers during the call.

title: Operator cognitive mapping session notes (dec 2026)
author: Maya Chen
text:
Objective:
Run a small lab (6 participants) to surface where console task flows impose cognitive load on operators managing model rollouts and incidents. Capture wireframe reactions, unexpected mental models, and candidate backlog items for quick UX fixes and higher-effort investments.

Participants: (internal + customer mix)
- P1: Platform engineer (mid-market fintech)
- P2: ML infra lead (AI-native startup)
- P3: SRE (enterprise)
- P4: Developer (internal Redwood sandbox)
- P5: Solutions engineer (customer-facing)
- P6: DevEx engineer (Redwood)

Method:
- 60 minute moderated remote session per participant
- Tasks given as goal statements (not step-by-step) to reveal assumptions
- Eye-tracking heatmaps for 3 sessions (lab), screen recordings for all
- Post-task 5‑point cognitive load rating (1 easy — 5 very heavy)
- Quick SUS-lite score at end + open feedback

Wireframes tested:
- A: Rollout overview (single-page, canary + fallback lanes)
- B: Incident triage modal (one-click rollback vs staged rollback)
- C: Cost/latency per-model route comparison table with inline suggestions

High-level findings (ranked by frequency + impact):
1) Information density on Rollout Overview -> confuses mental model of "active" vs "candidate" versions. 5/6 participants hesitated ~12–20s when asked "which model is serving production?"
 - Root cause: terminology mismatch (we use "active" and "candidate"); customers think "current" and "previous"
 - Suggestion: copy change to "Current / Candidate" + subtle chip color semantics documented in tooltip (quick win).

2) Triage modal forces too many decisions at once -> high cognitive load (avg rating 4.2).
 - Observed behavior: participants defaulted to "rollback to last stable" even when staged deploy would be better.
 - Friction point: rollback is presented as primary action but lacks quick context (how much traffic would be rerouted? which routes?).
 - Suggestion: reduce options to primary + "more details" collapse, surface estimated impact numbers inline. (mid-sized effort, owner: product + eng)

3) Cost/latency table helpful but noisy. Participants scanned for 8–10s then asked "where do I click to reduce cost?"
 - Need: clear recommended action per-row (e.g., "Suggest: lower batch size / use 8-bit quantized variant").
 - Suggestion: add a small action menu per model row with recommended affinity (quick wins: show top 1 recommendation).

4) Keyboard-first interactions were expected by power users but largely missing. 3/6 explicitly asked for quick keyboard shortcuts (toggle canary, acknowledge alert).
 - Suggestion: add a command palette (Cmd-K) to the backlog. (JIRA:CONSOLE-4521)

5) Accessibility: color contrast on canary/caution chips failed WCAG contrast for one palette variant; screen-reader labels for dynamic alerts were inconsistent.
 - Suggestion: accessibility story in backlog (audit + fixes). Minimum compliance before GA for customer tier X.

Microcopy and affordance notes (concrete edits):
- Replace "candidate" with "staged" in UI strings where it refers to a non-serving version.
- Tooltip for "Promote" should include: "Promote to 100% traffic over 10 minutes (configurable)" instead of current terse line.
- Change modal header from "Rollback options" -> "Resolve degraded performance" to reduce alarm framing.

Observed mental models and consequences:
- Participants expected rollout to mean "traffic percentage shifts" not just version flags. Several clicked on version badges expecting a percentage slider. We do present percentages but buried in an inspect panel.
- Many participants treat "alerts" as transient and expect a sticky timeline of related events. They wanted a compact timeline view adjacent to incident modal.

Quotes (verbatim where possible):
- "I don't know which version is live — the color looks like 'active' but the label says 'candidate' so I'm not sure." — P2
- "Why are you making me pick rollback type before I know what the impact is? I need impact numbers first." — P3
- "This is useful but I don't know how to act on it. It should say 'Recommended: enable caching' or similar." — P5

Quantitative markers captured:
- Average task time (critical tasks): 2.8x longer than expected from prototype benchmark
- Avg cognitive load rating: 3.7 overall, 4.2 for triage modal
- SUS-lite median: 62 (indicative of bordering on usability concerns)

Backlog grooming (prioritized):
- P0 (quick wins, 1–3 sprint work):
 - CONSOLE-4521: Add command palette (Cmd-K) and bind to top 5 actions (toggle canary, promote, rollback, open incident timeline, search models) — owner: devex — estimate: 5d
 - CONSOLE-4522: Copy changes: "candidate" -> "staged"; header text edits for rollback modal — owner: content + UX — estimate: 1d
 - CONSOLE-4523: Per-row recommended action pill in cost/latency table (show top recommendation) — owner: product-engineering — estimate: 3d

- P1 (mid-term, remediation and instrumentation):
 - CONSOLE-4530: Incident triage: show estimated traffic impact & quick preview before surfacing rollback options (design + backend data contract) — owner: serving-runtime + product — estimate: 3 sprints
 - CONSOLE-4531: Accessibility audit and fixes (contrast, aria labels) — owner: sre + ux — estimate: 2 sprints

- P2 (bigger bets):
 - CONSOLE-4548: Integrated timeline pane next to incident modal plus correlation of recent rollouts, logs, and alerts — owner: observability + product — estimate: 4–6 sprints
 - CONSOLE-4552: Traffic-percentage slider on rollout overview with inline simulation of cost/latency impact — owner: dedicated + product — estimate: 6 sprints

Acceptance criteria (examples):
- CONSOLE-4521 (Command palette): accessible via Cmd-K/Ctrl-K, searchable, executes top actions in <=1s, keyboard focus states pass a11y tests.
- CONSOLE-4523 (Recommendations): each row shows exactly one clear recommendation with rationale text and a direct action button that opens quick-config modal.

Open questions / risks:
- Data availability: can serving-runtime return live estimated traffic impact quickly enough for the triage preview? (engineering to validate)
- Copy connotations: does switching "candidate" -> "staged" break any existing user education or API docs? Need sweep across docs and SDK guides.
- Regulatory customers: timeline + logs adjacent to incident modal may surface PII; need consult security/compliance.

Next steps (1–2 week runway):
- Sync with serving-runtime on feasibility for estimated-impact API (owner: Maya + Arjun) — target: 2026-12-10
- Implement copy quick fixes and ship as patch (CONSOLE-4522) — owner: content — target: 2026-12-14
- Start command-palette spike (CONSOLE-4521) — owner: devex — demo in next sprint planning
- Schedule accessibility trio session with SRE, design, and PM to scope CONSOLE-4531

Appendix: session-level raw notes (selected)
- P1: struggled to find "promote" after scanning top header; expected it in version row. Time to task: 2m05s. Comment: "I want one-click promote if I know tests passed."
- P4: suggested a favorite/shortcuts list for teams that manage >30 models.
- P6: flagged an existing bug where the rollback modal shows stale latency numbers for 30–60s after state change (filed separate bug).

Minimal wires attached: (see linked_confluence) — wires include annotated microcopy and 2 variants of triage modal (condensed vs progressive disclosure).

Notes-to-self: preserve participants' quotes almost verbatim in design review deck; prioritize triage modal changes for Q1 roadmap if engineering can supply impact numbers via a light-weight contract.

Status: In review by product + eng; awaiting feasibility feedback on impact API and accessibility estimate.

title: Optimize walkthrough: Prefetch vs sessionization KV economics — SablePoint Capital
author: Maya Chen
text:
Redwood AE/SE ran a focused Optimize console demo to compare prefetch (lookahead) vs sessionized KV caching for SablePoint's high-concurrency quant trading assistant. Discussed latency budget, expected cache hit rates, and a proposed sandbox pilot with targeted workload replay and cost model spreadsheet.

Pilot plan: 3-day replay into sandbox with model variants and traffic spikes
Start with session KV caching; enable lookahead selectively
Provision Dedicated pool if guaranteed p95 is required during market open
Redwood to provide cost workbook, KMS/SOC2 docs, and sandbox template

Maya Chen: Send detailed cost workbook and Optimize console export (due 2027-01-04)
Diego Ruiz: Stand up sandbox cluster and preload model variants for A/B (due 2027-01-07)
Anita Rao: Provide 48 hours of anonymized request traces and latency SLOs (due 2027-01-05)
Priya Desai: Confirm KMS/HSM requirements and acceptable data residency (due 2027-01-06)

Maya to share cost model spreadsheet and sample workload template by 2027-01-04
Diego to provision a sandbox with 3-day workload replay and send access instructions by 2027-01-07
Priya to share security questionnaire items and required KMS integration doc by 2027-01-06
Schedule pilot kickoff (1 hour) w/ infra + ML on 2027-01-11

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-28 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~68 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Anita Rao (SablePoint Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Platform), Priya Desai (Security), Noah Patel (Product), Mike Harris (Guest)

Auto-generated summary: Redwood Optimize demo focused on prefetch (lookahead) vs session KV caching. Walked through cost model scenarios in the console and discussed pilot bench.

Topics: Prefetch vs sessionization, batch sizing, KV TTL and eviction, Sandbox pilot, security/KMS

---- Transcript (timestamps approximate, ASR imperfect) ----
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, happy holidays, we'll try to keep this tight. I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Diego, our SE. Today we'll run an Optimize playbook: prefetch (lookahead) versus session KV cache for your workload, walk through the cost model in the console, and propose a small pilot.

[00:25] Anita Rao: Nice to meet you all. We're especially interested in saving on tokens for our assistant — it's latency sensitive, spikes around market open, high concurrency.

[00:37] Diego Ruiz: Totally. Quick clarifying question — is your current production routing go to a single model type or multi-tiered (like 7B cheap + 70B for fallback)?

[00:46] Liam O'Connor: We do a hybrid: mostly a distilled 8B variant for day-to-day, but for complex reasoning we send to a larger 32B. Fallbacks are manual right now.

[00:58] Diego Ruiz: Got it. That's helpful because prefetch tends to pay off differently depending on model fan-out. We'll show a few scenarios: pure-prefetch, session-only, and a hybrid where prefix hits prime a larger model's KV cache.

[01:12] Anita Rao: Quick note — our latency SLO is 180ms p95 for front-office queries, but some back-office analytics can be relaxed.

[01:20] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll keep that in the tradeoff matrix. Okay, I'll share my screen and open the Optimize console. (screen share noise)

[01:46] Diego Ruiz: Opening the cost model tab. The Console has a scenario builder — you can set request distribution, concurrency, average prompt length, and then toggle caching policies. For SablePoint, we put a sample: 20% long-form (200–400 tokens), 60% short (20–80), 20% follow-ups.

[02:10] Noah Patel: That distribution sounds right. Our follow-ups often reuse the same instrument context, so prefix caching could be high value.

[02:22] Diego Ruiz: Exactly — follow-ups are the low-hanging fruit. First scenario: session KV cache with per-session TTL of 30 minutes and a moderate hit rate assumption of 40%. On the right you can see predicted token savings and cost per 1000 requests.

[02:40] Anita Rao: Is that 40% conservative? In early tests we saw 55% but that included client-side dedup.

[02:48] Diego Ruiz: We intentionally used conservative hit rates; Optimize also lets you import historical traces to estimate hit curves. We'll demo that shortly. The console predicts ~23% token cost reduction for this session strategy at your baseline concurrency.

[03:05] Maya Chen: Second scenario: prefetch / lookahead of the next-turn prefixes. This pushes more prefixes into the KV cache proactively so subsequent calls are shorter. Prefetch increases write bandwidth and slightly increases initial latency on the triggering call, but dramatically reduces downstream token cost if hit rates are high.

[03:28] Liam O'Connor: Our concern there is write IOPS during open — market open is a spike. Would prefetch amplify tail latency?

[03:36] Diego Ruiz: Good question. In our runtime, prefetch is implemented as asynchronous lookahead and can be configured to run on a lower priority queue or offloaded to a dedicated cache priming pool. That means the caller doesn't always wait synchronously for the write. The tradeoff is more burst capacity for prefetching.

[03:56] Priya Desai: From security side, any prefetching that persists user PII into cache needs controls — TTL, encryption, and audit logs. We use customer-managed KMS so we need details on KMS integration.

[04:07] Maya Chen: We'll share our KMS/HSM integration doc. The cache is encrypted at rest and keys can be integrated with your KMS. Also we show audit trails in the Console export.

[04:18] Diego Ruiz: Back to economics — for the same request distribution, prefetch showed a 32–38% token reduction in our sim when hit rate of prefetched prefixes was 60–70%. But if hit rate drops below ~30% prefetch can cost more because of extra priming tokens.

[04:40] Anita Rao: So looks like hybrid might be safest: session caching for all sessions, and selective prefetch for workflows we can predict.

[04:49] Diego Ruiz: Right — we usually recommend an operational plan: start with session KV caching (easy wins), measure effective hit rate post-deploy, and then enable lookahead selectively on high-confidence flows (e.g., instrument lookup + follow-ups).

[05:05] Maya Chen: I'll flip to the scenario matrix — here's a heatmap of latency vs cost for three strategies across concurrency curves. Note the cost slope flattens with batching.

[05:20] Noah Patel: Can you explain how batching interacts with session cache? Our app often aggregates 6-8 short requests into micro-batches on the client.

[05:29] Diego Ruiz: Sure. Continuous batching at the runtime level groups in-flight requests; session cache helps reduce token count per request so the net effect is multiplicative: fewer tokens per request and better packing efficiency. But beware: very large batches can increase individual tail latency — we model p95/p99 separately.

[05:50] Liam O'Connor: What about model variants — if we warm a KV cache for the 8B, but then route to 32B for a fallback, do you keep caches in sync?

[05:58] Diego Ruiz: We support cache routing policies. You can either maintain separate caches per model or set up cache compatibility mapping. For heavy fallbacks you might prime the larger model's cache with prefixes from the smaller model when semantics line up. That increases priming cost but reduces cold-start hits on fallback.

[06:20] Anita Rao: Could that double-count tokens in the cost model? We want to avoid underestimating costs if we prime multiple models.

[06:28] Diego Ruiz: Great point. In the Console we allow you to model multi-model priming overhead explicitly — there's a checkbox to include cross-model priming tokens. We also surfaced a line item in the breakdown: priming writes, read hits, net tokens served, and expected latency delta.

[06:50] Maya Chen: Switching to the trace import — Diego, do the import. We asked Anita earlier for a 48-hour anonymized request trace. If you upload it, Optimize fits an empirical hit curve.

[07:05] Diego Ruiz: (upload sound) Uploaded. The parser found session IDs, average prompt length 68 tokens, median concurrency 120 during spikes. The inferred likely prefix reuse shows a potential 47% hit ceiling for session caching, and 62% for targeted lookahead with top-3 candidate prefixes.

[07:31] Anita Rao: That aligns with our internal estimate. Nice that it infers sessionization. How deterministic is the inference?

[07:38] Diego Ruiz: It's heuristic — uses repeat n-gram overlap and session IDs. We always recommend validating with a quick pilot to measure real-world hit rates.

[07:46] Maya Chen: Now the cost spreadsheet export — you'll see per-strategy sheets: baseline, session-only, prefetch, and hybrid, with per-token cost, priming overhead, and burst capacity needs. I'll scroll to the hybrid sheet.

[08:02] (paper rustle)

[08:08] Diego Ruiz: Hybrid shows a projected 29% cost reduction vs baseline with p95 latency within 150ms under normal load; during spikes with limited burst config it edges to 205ms p95 unless you provision burst capacity or enable automatic fallbacks to a cheaper model for tail traffic.

[08:28] Liam O'Connor: For SLAs we need a guaranteed p95 under heavy open-market loads. Is that a Dedicated capacity conversation?

[08:36] Maya Chen: Yes — Dedicated gives you predictable throughput and burst headroom. You can also mix: run hosted for normal ops and a Dedicated pool for peak windows to hit your SLA without huge overprovisioning.

[08:50] Priya Desai: On compliance, we need to ensure logs are retained for 13 months and that KMS key rotation won't break cache decrypts. Is that supported?

[08:59] Diego Ruiz: Rotation is supported with a grace period; we can outline procedures in the SOC2/ISO docs we share. Logs are exportable to your SIEM and retention windows are configurable on Private deployments — for Hosted there are retention limits you can extend under an enterprise agreement.

[09:20] Noah Patel: About the sandbox pilot — what's the data flow? We prefer to replay traces rather than real production traffic.

[09:28] Diego Ruiz: Absolutely. The recommended pilot is: 3-day replay of anonymized traces into a sandbox cluster provisioned with your model variants, simulate peak concurrency, collect hit rates, tail latencies, and a cost delta. We'll send a template for trace formatting.

[09:45] Anita Rao: Sounds reasonable. How long until we see results?

[09:49] Maya Chen: Once we get the trace, Diego can run the replay and return a 1–2 day summary with console exports.

[09:55] (short pause, background)

[10:10] Diego Ruiz: A practical note on TTL and eviction: for session caches we typically start with 30–60 minutes TTL and LRU eviction; for markets with very high uniqueness (lots of ad-hoc prompts) you could go shorter. TTL interacts strongly with cost — longer TTL increases hit rate but increases memory. The Console shows memory footprint estimates given TTL and expected cardinality.

[10:36] Liam O'Connor: Do you provide cardinality estimators or bloom filters to help keep memory low?

[10:42] Diego Ruiz: We expose approximate counting sketches and an estimated unique session projection in the Optimize export. Also support approximate dedup and fingerprinting strategies to reduce cache pressure.

[10:55] Priya Desai: For encryption, is cache content tokenized or raw prompt stored? We want personal data stripped before caching.

[11:05] Maya Chen: You should definitely strip PII — best practice is to run a pre-caching sanitizer. Redwood supports a plugin hook to do that before caching; we can add rules in the sandbox run.

[11:18] Anita Rao: Could you show the priority queue options for prefetch?

[11:22] Diego Ruiz: Sure — under runtime config you can choose synchronous prefetch, async low-priority, or async offloaded pool. In the demo the offloaded pool shows negligible p95 impact on the initiating call but requires capacity headroom during spikes.

[11:40] Maya Chen: Jumping quickly to failure modes: if cache storage is exhausted we fall back to live generation; we also have graceful fallbacks to a cheaper model variant to preserve latency SLOs.

[11:52] Noah Patel: Any guidance on cost thresholds to trigger automatic fallback?

[11:57] Diego Ruiz: We recommend rule-based thresholds: e.g., if write IOPS or memory usage > 80% of provisioned, start probabilistic prefetch throttling; or route new sessions to a cheaper model for a rolling window. The Console can simulate those policies.

[12:15] Anita Rao: Can we run a 50/50 A/B comparing hybrid strategy vs session-only in our traffic?

[12:21] Diego Ruiz: Yes — we support canary rollouts and traffic splitting. For pilot maturity, we usually do a canary to 20% of traffic for a day, measure hit rate and latency, then ramp. We'll add that as a pilot step.

[12:34] Maya Chen: Recap: import traces, run 3-day sandbox replay, get console export, then do small canary in prod or a mirrored stream. We'll capture security requirements and agreement for KMS.

[12:46] Priya Desai: We'll need contract language around data retention and key management. Please send sample amendment.

[12:52] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll include a sample SLA amendment and SOC2 package in the packet.

[13:01] (longer pause — mid-call Q&A continues, summarizing a few smaller clarifications)

[42:12] Diego Ruiz: (mid-call) Quick deep dive on the modeling math — the Console's hit model is basically H = 1 - exp(-alpha * reuse_rate * ttl), where alpha is observed stickiness, reuse_rate is estimated from your trace. It's approximate, but it's transparent so you can tune parameters.

[42:35] Anita Rao: Interesting, we like transparent equations. Could we get the model parameters exported?

[42:40] Diego Ruiz: Yes — the export includes the inferred alpha and TTL curve samples.

[43:05] Noah Patel: One thing — we use strict audit logging to an internal SIEM. Will sandbox logs be isolated?

[43:12] Diego Ruiz: Sandbox logs can be pulled via S3 or a secure endpoint; we'll give you access tokens. We recommend not shipping raw prompts — use anonymized replays.

[44:00] Maya Chen: Alright, we're approaching the last 10 minutes. Final objections/concerns?

[44:12] Priya Desai: KMS integration, retention windows, and auditability are our immediate blockers. Also a legal on cross-model priming token accounting.

[44:22] Maya Chen: We'll put those in the packet. Any other technical asks?

[44:30] Liam O'Connor: Could we get an estimate of Dedicated sizing if we wanted guaranteed p95 at market open?

[44:36] Diego Ruiz: Yes — for your peak concurrency numbers from the trace, the Console's capacity planner suggests starting with a 4-GPU Dedicated pool with autoscale headroom; we'll include the sizing worksheet in the workbook.

[44:50] Anita Rao: Great.

[44:54] Maya Chen: Next steps recap — I'll send the cost workbook and SOC2/KMS docs; Diego will provision the sandbox; Anita will share traces; Priya will enumerate security constraints. We aim to have the pilot kickoff around Jan 11th.

[45:10] Noah Patel: That timeline works for us.

[45:18] Maya Chen: Any final quick Qs?

[45:24] (brief chatter)

[45:40] Maya Chen: Okay thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with the packet and calendar invite. Happy holidays.

[46:00] (meeting wrap noise)

End of transcript.

-- Quick export notes: The Optimize console generated 4 sheets (baseline/session/prefetch/hybrid), a hit-curve plot, and a JSON export of inferred parameters. We referenced a sandbox template at: https://redwood.ai/sandbox-template (note: placeholder link)

Final recap (auto):

title: Tidal Elm Solutions
author: Maya Patel
text:
SMB POC: integrate Hosted API streaming + function-calling into web chat widget. Priority: streaming UX (low latency) + reliable structured output. Targets: median token latency <50ms, end-to-end response time <600ms for short replies, error rate <1%. Cost sensitivity high. Must use public cloud, prefer SOC2 friendly provider and SSO later.

Inbound SMB trial sign-up (self-serve). Wants Hosted API for in-app chat + agent tool-calls. Running POC on Node (redwood-js 0.9.2) in public cloud. Main pain: structured JSON mode + function-calling breaks on streaming responses.

Symptoms observed: 
- When using 'response_format: JSON' + function schema, the streamed tokens sometimes produce invalid JSON chunks (truncated arrays/object), downstream parser throws 'Unexpected end of input'.
- Function calls occasionally arrive with missing required fields (e.g. 'tool_args' null) when streamed and reconstructed client-side.
- Intermittent: server returns function_name match but schema validation fails on final assembled payload.

Customer quote: "Streaming is great for UX but half our calls fail because the JSON parser chokes on the stream — we only see the error once the UI tries to parse."

Repro attempts so far (from customer): 
- Reproduced locally with sample convo: call model with streaming=true, response_format JSON schema (nested arrays), client reconstructs chunks into buffer and JSON.parse on 'end'. Failure rate ~15% in their environment.
- Tried switching to non-streamed mode: function-calling works reliably (slower UX).
- Tried increasing chunk timeout and reassembly logic; mitigates but does not eliminate.

Redwood logs / artifacts: 
- Customer provided streaming trace (linked INF-2487) showing sequence ids and token offsets.
- We saw instances where 'stream: done' arrives but last token repeated partial escape sequences.

Technical hypotheses: 
- Client-side reassembly logic sensitive to escape sequences / multibyte tokens; partial tokens split across frames.
- Schema validator on client assumes whole-object boundaries that don't map to token frames.
- We might need server-side framing helper (structured-chunk boundaries) or guidance on robust reassembly.

Requested by customer: 
- Engineering session to walk through streaming trace and share recommended client reassembly snippet for Node + browser.
- Example code that uses incremental JSON parser (sax-like) or our recommended safe pattern (buffer until top-level JSON complete).
- Clarify behavior of function-calling when streaming: are function payloads guaranteed to be emitted as contiguous tokens? (Customer says no).

Internal notes / suggested immediate actions: 
- SE (Carlos) to prepare minimal repro repo (node) that uses streaming + function schema and logs chunk boundaries. Share by 2026-03-12.
- AE (Maya) to schedule 60m debug w/ infra (Ali) + SDK engineer (Priya). Target 2026-03-16.
- Create support ticket INF-2487 and attach streaming trace, sample prompts, and customer's reconstruction code.

Next steps (short): 
- Collect sample request IDs from customer for last 10 failures.
- Provide recommended reassembly approach and small JS utility (stream-safe-parse) to customer.
- If reproable, propose small server-side change: optional 'structured_frames' flag that emits top-level JSON frame separators to simplify client parsing (discuss feasibility).

Key risk: SMB wants quick fix; low ARR but high chance to convert to paying within 60 days if streaming UX fixed.


Schedule 60m joint debug session w/ infra engineer and customer. Customer to provide sample streaming trace + function schemas. Share quick repro script for node/redwood-js.

2026-02-20: inbound self-serve signup, free trial started (hosted_api).
2026-02-25: AE outreach (Maya) — initial qual questions answered via email.
2026-03-01: short demo recorded (30m) focusing on chat + tool-calling UX. Fireflies id ff_20260302_27345.
2026-03-02: Customer reported first streaming JSON parse failures; provided example trace and sample code.
2026-03-05: SE (Carlos) looked at logs, asked for more request IDs; opened support ticket INF-2487.

title: ConvoScale Dynamics
author: Ethan Cole
text:
- Mid-size SaaS contact center platform, heavy ecommerce customer base.
- Primary objective: reduce live agent volume via automated chat deflection and quick ticket triage.
- Extremely cost-sensitive: measures success by cost per deflected chat (target <$0.06/chat at scale).
- Want to avoid full on-prem; preference for VPC + dedicated pools for peak windows.
- On call: support spikes during US holiday sales windows (Black Friday/Cyber Mon) — must handle 10-15x baseline for short windows.
- Interested in Redwood Optimize recommendations (batching, KV prefix caching, model quant profiles).
- Quote from CTO: "We can accept slightly higher p90 latency if unit cost drops 3x — primary KPI is deflection cost and NPS impact."
- SE feedback: lean toward 4-bit quantized LLMs for bulk deflection + full-precision for escalation and agent assist.
- Want routing policy: small-quantized model for initial deflection, fallback to larger model for ambiguous cases, and dedicated pool for peak commitments.
- Mentioned previous vendor tests: canned responses too generic; need structured tool-calling (order lookup, refund flow) and safe grounding.
- Legal asked about retention controls and audit logs; security wants SOC2 attestation and SSO/SAML integration with Okta.
- POC currently running: deflection funnel + cost dashboard; initial numbers promising but need stress test up to 5k concurrent sessions.
- Pricing ask: committed burst windows & hybrid pricing model for unpredictable ecommerce spikes.
