title: Security review: Transatlantic processing, subprocessors & supply-chain controls - AsterTech
author: Samira Patel
text:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-10-28 14:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Marquez (Redwood SE), Julia Hammond (AsterTech Head of Security), Marcela Ruiz (AsterTech Legal), Ben Cho (AsterTech Platform)

Auto-generated Summary (brief, may be incomplete):
Redwood walked through their data residency controls, region-affinity routing, KMS options including BYOK and escrow, subprocessor notification practices, and audit artifacts (SOC 2 / ISO). Customer asked for stronger contractual guarantees around EU-only processing for certain PII, clarified subprocessors list and change-management, and asked about audit logs, RBAC, SSO/SCIM provisioning. Agreed next steps: share SOC2/ISO docs, subprocessor inventory, draft contract clause, and schedule technical POC for EU-pinning.

Topics: Data residency and region pinning, cross-border processing, KMS/BYOK options, subprocessors & supply-chain, SOC2/ISO artifacts, RBAC/SSO, audit log retention

Action items (auto): see action_items field above

Transcript body:
[00:00] Speaker 1 (Samira): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samira from Redwood, AE on the account. With me is Diego, our solutions engineer. How's the audio?
[00:06] Speaker 2 (Diego): can you hear me okay? mic's a bit low.
[00:09] Speaker 3 (Julia): yes, loud and clear. thanks.
[00:11] Speaker 1 (Samira): Great. quick agenda — high-level security posture, region pinning mechanics, KMS/BYOK options, subprocessors lifecycle, and then Q&A. we'll try to leave 15 minutes at end for legal specifics.
[00:24] Speaker 4 (Marcela): that works. from legal side we'll want any contractual text for the EU-only processing guarantee. not just an implementation note.
[00:30] Speaker 2 (Diego): totally understood. I can walk through how our routing policy works and what we can enforce at the control plane versus what needs to be expressed in the contract.
[00:37] Speaker 5 (Ben): quick context from platform — we run in aws eu-west and us-east; we need assurance that model inference and logs with EU-personal data never leave EU without explicit authorization. also curious about KMS separation.
[00:48] Speaker 1 (Samira): got it. Julia, could you outline the scope of "EU-only" for you — is it strictly inference compute plus logs, or also backups, metrics, and metadata?
[00:57] Speaker 3 (Julia): primarily inference and logs that include PII; backups we can discuss but prefer keep backups in region too. metrics are ok to be aggregated outside EU if pseudonymized.
[01:07] Speaker 2 (Diego): OK. so our platform supports region affinity and region pinning at route and workspace level. practically that means requests from your EU routes can be routed to EU-hosted inference nodes only. For the things that can leak, we have three control layers — routing policy, data plane enforcement, and contractual subprocessor restrictions.
[01:23] Speaker 4 (Marcela): can you confirm whether telemetry and audit logs contain raw prompt text? that's a risk for us.
[01:30] Speaker 2 (Diego): by default, logs capture request IDs, latency metrics, model versions, and token counts. We do have optional request body logging for debugging but it's disabled for EU pinned tenants unless you opt in. there may be edgecases in third-party monitoring agents — we can disable those.
[01:43] Speaker 3 (Julia): that's good but we need proof — SOC 2 artifact that shows log sampling and redaction policies.
[01:49] Speaker 1 (Samira): yes we can share SOC 2 Type II report and our ISO 27001 certificate. we'll put the redaction and logging controls in the security pack.
[01:56] Speaker 5 (Ben): about KMS — we want customer-managed keys for EU data and ideally HSM-backed. does Redwood support BYOK or customer KMS integration?
[02:04] Speaker 2 (Diego): we support two main KMS models: Redwood-managed keys (standard) and BYOK via customer-managed KMS (we integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault). For BYOK you upload a key or configure a key policy and we reference it from the EU region. For HSM-only escrow, we have an enterprise option that plugs into dedicated HSM endpoints — that's usually part of Private deployments.
[02:21] Speaker 4 (Marcela): when you say "reference it from the EU region" — can you guarantee the key material never leaves the EU?
[02:27] Speaker 2 (Diego): yes — if you configure an EU KMS key and restrict key policy to EU principals and endpoints, the key material lives in the EU region. our service calls KMS endpoints in-region for envelope encryption. the unencrypted data never leaves the region when the route is pinned.
[02:41] Speaker 3 (Julia): what's your fallback behavior if EU capacity is saturated? we can't have cross-border failover without legal approval.
[02:48] Speaker 2 (Diego): good question. our default is to fail closed (reject requests) if region pinned capacity is exhausted, but we can configure a controlled fallback with explicit allow-listing to specific regions — this is only available with Dedicated or Private deployments and must be contractually approved.
[03:04] Speaker 5 (Ben): Is there a way to have policy-level audit that shows every time fallback was considered? we need an immutable trace.
[03:11] Speaker 2 (Diego): yes, audit logs capture routing decision events, including reason codes (capacity, health, policy). those are included in the customer-facing audit stream and can be forwarded to your SIEM in EU via webhook or syslog.
[03:23] Speaker 4 (Marcela): subprocessors — please send the current list and your policy for notifications and objections. we need at least 30 days notice before adding a processor that could access EU data.
[03:34] Speaker 1 (Samira): our standard subprocessor notification window is 30 days; customers can object within that period and we either remove or proceed with approved contractual mitigations. we'll attach our subprocessor inventory and the DPA language that covers notification and right to object.
[03:45] Speaker 3 (Julia): do you use any third-party observability agents that might ship data to the US? we had an incident with another vendor where traces were forwarded.
[03:53] Speaker 2 (Diego): we use a combination of first-party telemetry and vetted third-party services. For EU-pinned tenants, we can disable third-party forwarders and route observability to an EU-only endpoint; we also support forwarding to your own collector. we'll include the list in the pack.
[04:08] Speaker 5 (Ben): how about supply-chain — small question: who builds/compiles the runtime and where is it stored?
[04:15] Speaker 2 (Diego): the runtime is built in our CI in EU and US build farms; artifacts are signed. for customers requiring EU-only supply chain, we can arrange dedicated build pipelines as part of private/on-prem packages. signing keys are rotated and stored in KMS.
[04:30] Speaker 3 (Julia): would you provide SBOMs and build attestations?
[04:33] Speaker 2 (Diego): yes — we provide SBOMs and can provide signed build attestations on request.
[04:38] Speaker 4 (Marcela): any third-party subprocessors in the US that could see EU data?
[04:42] Speaker 1 (Samira): standard list includes CDN provider, metrics aggregator, and a managed storage provider; for EU-pinned customers, we route to EU instances of the same providers where possible. we'll send the full inventory.
[04:53] Speaker 3 (Julia): on RBAC and SSO — how do you manage admin access across environments?
[04:58] Speaker 2 (Diego): we integrate with SAML/SSO and SCIM for provisioning. RBAC supports workspace roles (admin, engineer, auditor) and token scoping. for enterprise, we support time-bound elevation and session MFA enforcement.
[05:11] Speaker 5 (Ben): do you support session recording or long-lived API keys for automation? we prefer short lived tokens.
[05:17] Speaker 2 (Diego): short-lived tokens via our OAuth flow and support for rotating service principals is the default. long-lived keys are discouraged and can be restricted.
[05:24] Speaker 3 (Julia): how long do audit logs retain? we need 12 months of immutable audit for compliance.
[05:29] Speaker 2 (Diego): default retention is 90 days; we have configurable retention tiers up to 7 years as an add-on. immutable retention snapshots and export to your archive are supported under enterprise contracts.
[05:40] Speaker 1 (Samira): marking a note — add retention options to the security pack.
[05:44] Speaker 4 (Marcela): can you include the exact fields you keep in audit trails? we need user id, action, timestamp, request URL, decision reason, and routing decision.
[05:53] Speaker 2 (Diego): yes that's all captured — we'll extract schema and send.
[05:57] Speaker 3 (Julia): about data deletion — if we delete a user or dataset, is that propagated to backups and K/V caches? we need proof of logical delete and a timeline for physical deletion.
[06:06] Speaker 2 (Diego): deletes trigger asynchronous workflows; logical delete is immediate, physical purge from live stores occurs within a configurable window (default 30 days), and backups follow a separate retention purge schedule unless you opt-in for immediate purge which we offer under private agreements. we'll document timelines.
[06:22] Speaker 3 (Julia): what's the process for emergency legal requests from other jurisdictions — how do you notify customers?
[06:29] Speaker 1 (Samira): we have a legal process for government requests and a transparency report. we push notifications to the customer's security contact and log the request in the audit stream. for EU-pinned customers we also apply an additional review before any export.
[06:41] Speaker 4 (Marcela): competitor question — how do you compare to MegaModelCloud's regional guarantees?
[06:45] Speaker 2 (Diego): MegaModelCloud offers region affinity but often has implicit fallback; our differentiator is fail-closed defaults for region pins, and contractual guardrails to force Dedicated/Private for sanctioned cross-border fallbacks.
[06:59] Speaker 5 (Ben): ok. Marcela — any legal blocking points for us today?
[07:03] Speaker 4 (Marcela): we'll need to review the exact DPA language and the subprocessor addendum. Also the BYOK clause and key escrow terms — if there's an escrow mechanism it needs to be auditable.
[07:14] Speaker 1 (Samira): absolutely. we'll provide a draft with specific language.
[07:18] Speaker 3 (Julia): on the technical POC — what would Diego need from us to stand up an EU-pinned test?
[07:24] Speaker 2 (Diego): ideally a small test workspace, sample inputs (pseudonymized), and a KMS key (or we'll demo with Redwood-managed EU key). we'll also need the specific routes you want pinned and any RBAC constraints.
[07:36] Speaker 5 (Ben): timing wise we can provision a workspace early next week.
[07:40] Speaker 1 (Samira): great. we'll note that as a next step.
[07:44] Speaker 2 (Diego): quick note on encryption-in-transit — our control plane uses mTLS between control and data planes; data plane communications are TLS1.3 with forward secrecy.
[07:53] Speaker 3 (Julia): do you support hardware-backed attestation for the data plane nodes?
[07:57] Speaker 2 (Diego): we support optional AMD SEV and Intel TDX for dedicated/private nodes and can provide attestation artifacts. for hosted, we use cloud VM attestations — we can include evidence.
[08:10] Speaker 4 (Marcela): can we require that any subprocessor in the US who processes EU-pseudonymized data cannot export raw text off-region?
[08:18] Speaker 1 (Samira): contractual restriction possible. operationally, we route such processing to EU instances of those subprocessors; where not possible we use alternatives or remove the subprocessor for that customer.
[08:29] Speaker 3 (Julia): what's your SLA if we choose Dedicated? important for us is latency and guaranteed region availability.
[08:36] Speaker 2 (Diego): Dedicated comes with committed capacity and region SLAs; we can commit to multizone EU deployments and reserved GPU pools. we'll provide the SLA doc.
[08:46] Speaker 5 (Ben): backlog question — how are model updates handled for pinned workloads? do you get automatic model pushes?
[08:52] Speaker 2 (Diego): customers can pin model versions; we support canary rollouts and manual approval. auto-updates are off by default for pinned workspaces.
[09:00] Speaker 3 (Julia): great, that covers model drift concerns.
[09:03] Speaker 1 (Samira): quick pause — any other high-level things?
[09:06] Speaker 4 (Marcela): we've flagged one redline in procurement: a clause preventing any third-party transfer of EU personal data unless consented. can you provide a DPA language that maps to that?
[09:15] Speaker 1 (Samira): yes. we'll propose language that aligns with standard EU DPA with right to object to subprocessors and a 30 day notice window.
[09:23] Speaker 2 (Diego): technical note — for routing we attach geo-coordinates and region tags at ingress; those tags are used by the scheduler to place work on region-compliant nodes. that tag is immutable for a request once ingress validation passes.
[09:37] Speaker 3 (Julia): important. and the tag is recorded in audit logs?
[09:40] Speaker 2 (Diego): yes, request tag and decision published in audit event.
[09:44] Speaker 5 (Ben): do you support custom retention timelines per dataset?
[09:48] Speaker 2 (Diego): yes — dataset-level retention controls are available in Private/Dedicated; hosted customers can request custom retention tiers as part of enterprise plan.
[09:57] Speaker 4 (Marcela): can you promise data residency in the contract only for on-prem or also for hosted?
[10:03] Speaker 1 (Samira): we offer contractual residency guarantees for hosted with region pinning, but for the strongest assurance we typically recommend Dedicated or Private packages — hosted gets standard guarantees plus technical controls; Dedicated/Private can get explicit escrow, no-fallback clauses, and stronger attestations.
[10:20] Speaker 3 (Julia): do you have any customers with similar constraints you can reference? even anonymized would help.
[10:25] Speaker 1 (Samira): yes — a European fintech client uses Dedicated with BYOK and has a no-fallback clause; we can provide a sanitized case study.
[10:34] Speaker 2 (Diego): moving toward Q&A from technical side — any requests for the POC specifics?
[10:39] Speaker 5 (Ben): we'd like an EU-only POC hitting a small model endpoint, plus the routing audit stream forwarded into our SIEM. also test a simulated capacity saturation to see fail-closed behavior.
[10:50] Speaker 2 (Diego): noted. we'll prepare a test plan for the POC.
[10:54] Speaker 3 (Julia): on-subprocessor consequence — if you add a subprocessor in the US, what's the approval flow?
[10:59] Speaker 1 (Samira): we notify customers 30 days in advance. if you object, we either remove the subprocessor for you or proceed with supplemental safeguards.
[11:09] Speaker 4 (Marcela): is there any recording of requests that happen in the control plane that might carry personal data?
[11:14] Speaker 2 (Diego): control plane logs include user IDs and resource ids but not full request payloads. data plane handles payloads; we have separation of duties to minimize exposure.
[11:24] Speaker 3 (Julia): can we get a diagram of separation?
[11:28] Speaker 2 (Diego): yes, we'll include architecture diagrams highlighting separation boundaries.
[11:31] Speaker 1 (Samira): wrapping up — agreed next steps and action items as in the notes. I'll summarize and follow up in email with attachments.
[11:40] Speaker 5 (Ben): one last thing — do you offer an indemnity for data breaches caused by subprocessors?
[11:46] Speaker 1 (Samira): typical indemnity language is limited; we do have breach notifications and incident response commitments, plus cyber insurance. we'll share the legal team contact and typical indemnity language as a draft.
[11:58] Speaker 3 (Julia): alright thanks, we look forward to the security pack.
[12:01] Speaker 1 (Samira): thanks everyone, talk soon.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker overlap and small transcription errors; some proper nouns might be misspelled (e.g., subprocessors names).

title: docs: document tool-calling compatibility differences (payload + streaming)
author: Ibrahim Khan
text:
## Summary
Adds explicit compatibility notes for tool calling when using Redwood via the OpenAI-compatible surface area. This is primarily a docs change, but it closes the gap that caused a few recent “copy/paste” examples (in Redwood docs + community snippets) to imply behaviors that the compat layer either doesn’t support or intentionally normalizes.

## Motivation
We saw repeated confusion around:
- Payload shape differences (e.g., `function_call` vs `tool_calls`, presence/absence of `id`, what’s required in tool result messages)
- Streaming behavior during tool calls (partial arguments, ordering, when `finish_reason` arrives)
- Expectations around “parallel tool calls” and mixing assistant text + tool calls in the same streamed turn

These misunderstandings showed up in support tickets (SUP-18421, SUP-18452) and in the DevEx parity audit work (ENG-4821). This PR documents the reality so that Redwood examples/docs can safely link to a canonical compat note and avoid overpromising.

## What’s included
- New page: `docs/compat/tool-calling.md`
 - Side-by-side examples of request/response payloads
 - Streaming transcripts showing partial tool args and final assembly expectations
 - Explicit “Not supported / differs from OpenAI” callouts
- Updates to `README.md` and `docs/compat/streaming.md` to link to the new tool-calling page
- Adds a small “Known pitfalls” section tailored to compat users (partial args, JSON parse, tool result role)

## Key compatibility notes captured
- **Tool call representation:** The compat layer accepts OpenAI-style `tools` and returns `tool_calls` on assistant messages; legacy `function_call` is not documented and should not be used in new examples.
- **Tool call IDs:** `tool_call_id` is required for tool result messages; some models omit/rename fields in intermediate streaming chunks, so examples must assemble the final `tool_call_id` and `arguments` from deltas before invoking tools.
- **Streaming partial args:** `arguments` may be streamed as partial JSON fragments; clients must not `json.loads()`/`JSON.parse()` until the tool call is complete.
- **Parallel tool calls:** Multiple tool calls can appear in one assistant turn, but ordering/streaming interleaving is model-dependent. Examples should treat tool calls as an array and iterate deterministically after finalization.
- **Mixing content + tool calls:** Do not assume assistant `content` will be present alongside `tool_calls` in the same message. Some backends emit empty content when tool calls are present.
- **Finish reasons:** `finish_reason` may arrive only on the final chunk; streaming consumers should not rely on early `finish_reason` to decide that tool args are complete.

## Why this lives in redwood-openai-compat
We want a single source of truth for compat-specific constraints, so the main docs/SDK repos can link out instead of duplicating nuanced edge cases (which then diverge). This also makes it easier to keep up with changes in the compat adapter.

## Testing
- `pnpm lint` (docs)
- `pnpm test` (link checker)
- Manual verification of code blocks against the current compat adapter behavior using the internal “golden transcript” fixture referenced in ENG-4822

## Follow-ups
- Update redwood-docs tool-calling guide to include a short compat callout + link to this page (tracked in ENG-4826)
- Ensure SDK examples that mention OpenAI compat default to the “assemble deltas, then parse” pattern

Checklist:
- [x] Docs have explicit “differs from OpenAI” callouts
- [x] Streaming example avoids parsing partial JSON
- [x] Links validated (no redirects introduced)
- [x] PM terminology matches PM-412 signoff (uses “structured output” vs “JSON mode” consistently where referenced)

Brian Murphy (review): The callout about `function_call` is good, but be explicit that we don’t guarantee accepting legacy `function_call` requests through compat. People will copy/paste. Also, in the tool result example, please show the `tool` role message with `tool_call_id` (not a made-up `tool_result` role).

Ibrahim Khan (author): Good catch. Updated language to “not supported / not documented” and changed the tool result snippet to use `role: "tool"` + `tool_call_id`.

Wei Chen (review): Can we add one line that warns against assuming content+tool_calls co-exist? This is a frequent docs comment.

Ibrahim Khan (author): Added a dedicated bullet + updated the streaming transcript to show empty `content` while tool calls are being emitted.

Dana Lo (review): In the TypeScript ecosystem, folks parse `arguments` per chunk. Please add a short snippet that shows buffering/assembling. Doesn’t need to be language-specific, but a pseudocode block helps.

Ibrahim Khan (author): Added “assembly pseudocode” section and linked the canonical event nomenclature doc (internal) for future alignment.

Brian Murphy (final): Approving. This should reduce the number of ‘tool args truncated mid-stream’ tickets we’ve been seeing.

title: Streaming throughput metric mismatch (customer dashboard vs Redwood export) — suspected token accounting double-count in streaming
text:
Customer (Vidorama) reports inconsistent throughput numbers for their Dedicated deployment when using streaming responses.

Issue summary
- Vidorama is comparing:
 1) Redwood Console throughput panel (tokens/sec) for their Dedicated deployment, and
 2) Their internal measurement based on streamed tokens (client-side) + Redwood usage export.
- They see Redwood Console tokens/sec ~1.8–2.1x higher than their client-side computed throughput for the same time windows.
- Discrepancy appears only for streaming (non-streaming requests match within ~5–10%).

Impact
- Customer confusion + concern about Dedicated throughput SLO reporting accuracy.
- Potential false positives/negatives in SLO compliance if the canonical throughput metric is inflated for streaming.

Customer-provided details
- Workload: chat completions, streaming enabled (server-sent events).
- Typical request: prompt 1–2k tokens, completion 150–400 tokens, 20–60 concurrent streams.
- Sampling window: 5-min rolling, comparing against their Prometheus counters.

Redwood initial checks (Support)
- Confirmed customer is hitting the correct deployment_id and region (us-east).
- Confirmed they are not mixing model variants in the comparison window (pinned to llama-3.1-70b-instruct; occasional mixtral bursts were excluded by customer).
- Confirmed they are not counting input tokens in their client throughput metric (they only count generated tokens).

Steps to reproduce (internal)
1) Run load test against a Dedicated deployment with streaming enabled.
2) Compare:
 - streaming token counter used by throughput dashboard (server-side), vs
 - sum(completion_tokens) from request final usage events (server-side) and/or reconstructed deltas.
3) Observe that for streaming requests, the dashboard-aligned metric increases faster than final usage totals.

Investigation notes (SRE/Obs)
- Hypothesis A: double-counting streamed completion tokens (both per-chunk deltas and final usage event contribute to the same counter).
- Hypothesis B: retries/resumes on stream reconnects cause duplicated deltas.
- Hypothesis C: mixed attribution labels (route vs deployment) cause aggregation overlap.

Findings
- We can reproduce consistent ~2x inflation when streaming is enabled and client consumes the full stream.
- Root cause identified in telemetry emission path:
 - For streaming responses, we emit per-chunk token deltas (used for near-real-time throughput).
 - At stream termination, a final usage event is emitted.
 - In the current pipeline, the dashboard throughput counter was incremented by BOTH the per-chunk deltas and the final usage event for the same request.
- This does NOT affect billing totals (billing uses finalized usage only). It affects the real-time throughput metric used in dashboards and SLO evaluation.

Workaround (until fix rollout)
- For customer reporting, use finalized completion token metrics (request end) for streaming workloads:
 - completion_tokens_total (finalized) / wall time
- Avoid using real-time streaming throughput panel for contractual/SLO comparisons until patched.

Next actions
- Engineering to patch streaming accounting to ensure final usage does not also increment the streaming delta counter (or to separate metrics cleanly).
- Backfill: no backfill planned; we will annotate the dashboard for the affected time range and document the known issue.
- Customer comms: provide written explanation that billing is unaffected; commit to patch timeline and a short validation report post-deploy.

2025-02-21 10:14 PT — Owen Phillips (Support): Customer ticket opened after Vidorama noticed Redwood Console tokens/sec ~2x their internal measurement on streaming. Non-streaming looks normal. Requesting SRE/Obs help; tagging Aisha Bello.
2025-02-21 12:02 PT — Aisha Bello (SRE): Acknowledged. Pulling metrics for deployment_id provided by customer. Initial glance: tokens/sec is unusually spiky and high during periods dominated by streaming traffic.
2025-02-22 09:37 PT — Sergio Costa (Observability): I can reproduce in staging with a scripted SSE client. Suspect dashboard is aggregating both stream deltas and final usage. Need confirm on emitter path in serving-runtime.
2025-02-23 14:18 PT — Logan Wright (Telemetry): Found candidate: token counter increments on chunk delta AND again on finalize handler. This would produce ~2x under full consumption. Filing fix with serving-runtime owners.
2025-02-24 11:26 PT — Aisha Bello (SRE): Confirmed billing exports are correct (final usage only). The problematic series is the near-real-time throughput metric used in the dashboard and SLO evaluator. Recommending we temporarily treat streaming throughput dashboard values as best-effort until patch.
2025-02-25 16:40 PT — Owen Phillips (Support): Sent customer interim update: billing unaffected; mismatch is in streaming throughput visualization/metric; offered workaround using finalized usage tokens. Customer asked whether this impacts Dedicated SLO credits—told them we will validate SLO evaluator inputs and share fix ETA.
2025-02-27 13:05 PT — Aisha Bello (SRE): Fix PR is up: sources/github/redwood/pr-19422-fix-throughput-metric-double-counting-streaming.json. Plan: canary in us-east Dedicated pools first, then global rollout if stable.
2025-03-01 09:22 PT — Aisha Bello (SRE): Patch deployed to prod/us-east. Verified in internal load test: streaming tokens/sec now matches finalized usage within ~3–6% over 5m windows. Monitoring for 24h; no regressions so far.
2025-03-02 10:11 PT — Owen Phillips (Support): Customer confirmed their numbers now align with Redwood Console within expected variance. Closing ticket. Follow-up: add dashboard annotation for 2025-02-10 through 2025-03-01 and link to known issue in Dedicated throughput SLO FAQ.

Resolved by patching streaming token accounting to prevent double-counting (per-chunk deltas + final usage). Deployed to prod/us-east on 2025-03-01 and validated against load tests and customer confirmation. Billing was not impacted. Ticket closed after customer confirmed metrics alignment.

title: Embeddings index consistency and rollback workarounds
author: Elena Morales
text:
Overview
--------
This page documents common failure modes we see for customer-managed or Redwood-managed embeddings indexes, recommended short-term workarounds to restore service, and longer-term fixes to prevent recurrence. It is intended for Customer Success, Support Engineers, and the Embeddings SRE/Infra teams.

Scope
-----
- Applies to vector indexes used with Redwood's embeddings API, including: local index servers (faiss/hnsw), managed index service, and third-party vector DB connectors (Milvus, Pinecone, Weaviate).
- Addresses consistency problems (missing vectors, partial queries, index drift), indexing failures during bulk ingest, and rollback/restore guidance.

Impact and priority guidance
---------------------------
- P0: Index returns wrong vectors for >20% of queries, or customer-facing search/generation failures. Immediate page + incident.
- P1: Partial degradation (increased latency, missing results <20%). Open escalation ticket and apply quick fix within 4 business hours.
- P2: Non-critical background failures (reindex jobs failing but fallbacks exist). Track in backlog.

Owners and escalation contacts
----------------------------
- Customer Success (first responder): #cust-success, oncall cs lead (cs-lead@example.com).
- Embeddings Infra / SRE: #infra-embeddings, oncall (infra-emb-oncall@example.com).
- Integrations / Connectors: #platform-connectors.

Detection checklist (signals to watch)
------------------------------------
1) Telemetry / Alerts
- Index error rate > 0.5% for 5m (alert).
- Query hit-rate drop > 30% vs baseline (30d rolling).
- Unexpected reindex job failures with non-zero exit code.

2) Customer-reported symptoms
- Identical queries return different top results across time windows.
- Recently-ingested documents do not appear in search results.
- High latency on embedding-lookup calls.

Symptoms -> Likely causes -> Immediate action (table)
---------------------------------------------------
| Symptom | Likely cause | Immediate action |
|---|---|---|
| Missing recent documents | Partial ingest failure (batch abort) | Re-run incremental ingest for affected batches; verify via sample queries |
| Query returns stale vectors | KV cache serving old embeddings | Invalidate prefix cache for impacted keyspace; force cold read |
| Higher-than-expected false positives | Wrong vector dimension / model mismatch | Validate embedding model version; temporarily route queries to compatible model variant |
| Index returning 500 errors | Index process crash / OOM | Restart index pod; inspect OOM logs; scale up memory if reproduces |
| Inconsistent shard responses | Corrupt shard or split-brain | Quiesce writes, trigger shard re-sync, or restore last known-good snapshot |

Quick fixes (playbook)
----------------------
These are ordered from least intrusive to most. Prefer non-destructive options first.

1) Verification and scoped rollback
- Step 1: Ask customer for a minimal failing query set (3–10 examples) and time window.
- Step 2: Re-run queries against the same index with a strict timestamp filter to reproduce.
- Step 3: If problem is limited to a single ingest batch, re-run the ingest for that batch. Use the ingest job ID and the incremental ingest API: 

 curl -X POST "https://api.redwood.com/v1/ingest/retry" \
 -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
 -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
 -d '{"ingest_job_id":"INGEST_JOB_ID"}'

- Step 4: Verify results by running the customer's example queries and checking top-5 similarity scores differ from baseline by > 0.

2) Cache invalidation
- When stale vectors are suspected, invalidate prefix/KV cache for the index keyspace: 

 curl -X POST "https://internal-admin.redwood.local/v1/cache/invalidate" \
 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
 -d '{"namespace":"indexes","key_prefix":"index-<INDEX_ID>-kv"}'

- Confirm by comparing timestamps on vectors returned and re-running queries.

3) Snapshot rollback (managed indexes only)
- Preconditions: We have a validated automatic snapshot policy and a snapshot taken prior to the incident.
- Steps: 
 1. Put index into read-only mode (no writes).
 2. Create an incident branch and notify customer of potential write loss after snapshot rollback.
 3. Restore snapshot to a new index instance using the internal restore tool: 

 redwood index restore --snapshot-id SNAPSHOT_ID --target-index restored-index-<INCIDENT_ID> --region us-west-2

 4. Run a smoke test using customer query set. If restored index meets quality checks, perform cutover routing.

- Cutover rollback considerations: keep original index for 72 hours to allow delta reconciliation.

4) Rebuild strategy (when snapshot not available or corrupt)
- Run parallel rebuild to a new index instance. Use staged rollback: 
 - Start incremental rebuild with throttling: redwood index rebuild --source-batch-list BATCH_IDs --throttle 250/s
 - Monitor build success rate and sample top-n results.
 - Once parity reached on verification queries, switch traffic.

Operational validation criteria (minimum before cutover)
-----------------------------------------------------
- Sample accuracy: For customer-provided verification set, top-5 recall >= 95% of baseline or pre-incident run.
- Latency: P95 lookup latency <= 1.5x baseline and absolute P95 < 300ms for managed indexes in production tiers.
- Error rate: < 0.1% 5m rolling.

Permanent mitigations and engineering requests
-------------------------------------------
1) Preflight schema validation in ingest pipeline (reject mismatched dimension vectors).
2) Improve snapshot frequency for high-change customers (default 4h -> 1h for enterprise).
3) Add a lightweight background parity checker that compares recent ingest batches against the index every 30 minutes and alerts on divergence > 5%.
4) Improve connector backpressure behavior to avoid partially applied batches when downstream errors occur.

Monitoring and alerting recommendations for CS/SRE
-------------------------------------------------
- Metrics to surface to customer and internal dashboards: ingest_success_rate, index_build_progress, top_k_recall_on_verification_set, prefix_cache_hit_rate.
- Recommended alert thresholds:
 - ingest_success_rate < 98% for 30m -> P1
 - top_k_recall_on_verification_set < 90% -> P0
 - index_build_progress stalls for > 15m without progress -> P1

Customer communication template (short)
-------------------------------------
Subject: Incident update — embeddings index for <customer-name>

We detected inconsistent search results impacting a subset of queries. We have isolated the affected index and are running an incremental rebuild. Expected recovery window: 2–6 hours. There is no evidence of data exfiltration. We will notify you after verification tests complete or sooner if the window changes.

Next steps we will take:
- Re-run failed ingest batches and validate results
- Restore from snapshot if incremental rebuild fails
- Provide post-incident summary and plan to prevent recurrence

How CS should engage engineering
--------------------------------
1) Open a Priority ticket with embedding-infra and include: customer name, index ID, ingest job IDs, sample failing queries, and timestamps.
2) Ask Infra to create a temporary read-only replica for forensic analysis before any destructive operation.
3) Coordinate customer-facing communications; avoid promising specific cutover times until validation criteria are met.

Post-incident checklist (RCA & follow-up)
----------------------------------------
- Collect: ingest logs, index build logs, snapshot logs, telemetry around cache invalidation, and thread dumps if crashes occurred.
- Determine root cause classification (ingest, cache, index binary, connector).
- Create engineering ticket for permanent fix with owner and target milestone.
- Offer customer a mitigation plan (snapshot frequency change, managed rebuild voucher) depending on severity.

Appendix: Useful CLI snippets and queries
----------------------------------------
- List recent snapshots for index:
 redwood index snapshots --index-id <INDEX_ID> --limit 10 --format json

- Trigger a controlled rebuild for specific batches:
 redwood index rebuild --index-id <INDEX_ID> --batches "batch1,batch2" --concurrency 16

- Sample verification query (embedding + similarity):
 curl -X POST "https://api.redwood.com/v1/embeddings/query" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"index_id":"<INDEX_ID>","query_embedding": [0.123, ...], "top_k": 5 }'

References
----------
- SDK Embedding Integration Playbook: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/integration-guides/sdk-embedding-integration-and-operational-playbook-2026
- Index snapshot and restore internal runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/index-snapshot-restore-2025

Revision history
----------------
- 2026-02-10: Created by Elena Morales (published)
- 2026-03-01: Added snapshot rollback procedure and updated validation criteria (reviewed by James Li, Nora Patel)

title: POC Weekly Sync - Crestline Model Serving Pilot
author: Maya Patel
text:
Weekly POC check-in focused on performance tuning and business-case closeout. SE presented intermediate throughput/latency numbers; customer raised QA around long-tail latency and data residency. Agreement on running a 12-hour mixed-sequence benchmark, sending updated pricing, and locking success criteria for an exec closeout next week.

Meeting Header: 2025-04-10 16:00 PDT | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Maya, Ethan, Lena, Samuel, Priya

[00:00] Maya: ok, hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, this is our weekly crestline pilot sync. I'm Maya with Redwood, Ethan's with me from SE. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Lena: hey it's Lena, I have Priya and Sam on from our side.
[00:12] Samuel: Sam here, platform eng.
[00:15] Priya: Priya, product.
[00:17] Ethan: Hi all, Ethan, I'll run through the perf slides and the new micro-benchmarks we pushed this week.

[00:28] Maya: super. Agenda — quick results review, tuning notes, make sure success criteria map to what you need, and then agree on next steps for exec closeout.

[00:40] Ethan: ok so high level, we ran three test profiles: short chat prompts (avg 40 tokens), medium support cases (avg 180 tokens), and long-document summarization tails (avg 1,200 tokens). We exercised our dedicated 2xA100 pilot and the hosted fallback path for overflow.

[01:05] Ethan: numbers — p50 latencies for short were ~85ms, p95 ~170ms, p99 ~290ms on the dedicated pool with batching enabled. For medium, p50 ~210ms, p95 ~420ms, p99 ~780ms. Long tail is where variance goes up — average token throughput held but the p99 hit around 1.8s in a couple of runs.

[01:36] Lena: ok that's useful. The thing we care about is p99 for our SLA for end-user interactive flows — anything above 500ms starts to degrade UX. So the 1.8s spikes are concerning.

[01:50] Ethan: sure, we dug into this. A few contributing factors: 1) sequence length variance causes cache eviction pressure on the KV cache; 2) batching policy — some of the batches were growing to 64 tokens which helps throughput but adds latency for small requests; 3) we didn't have quantization enabled for the long-form model variant in some runs — enabling 4-bit quant reduced memory and lowered stall events in the runtime.

[02:20] Samuel: can you explain the KV cache bit? We heard "K V cash" in an earlier test note and that confused our infra team.

[02:26] Ethan: ha yeah transcription artifact — it's KV cache, key-value cache for past tokens. When you have many long sessions the cache grows and occasionally triggers internal GC-like flows in the runtime, which can spike latencies. Our optimization is to persist prefix cache to memory-mapped files and slide small-session traffic onto a lightweight path.

[02:52] Priya: is that change risky? We need to understand fail-open behavior — if the cache becomes unavailable does latency spike or do requests fallback gracefully?

[03:02] Ethan: good question. The runtime has graceful degradation — if prefix cache misses, we fall back to recomputing contexts which adds cost but keeps latency bounded. We also have an automated fallback to a lower-latency quantized model variant if latency breaches the SLO.

[03:20] Maya: and we showed the tension earlier — you can tune for cost or latency. For Crestline interactive use-case you said latency is more important, right Lena?

[03:28] Lena: yes, interactive flows first. Batch processing we can cost-optimize later.

[03:32] Ethan: so action plan for perf: 1) enable 4-bit quant on the long model in the dedicated cluster, 2) reduce max batch size for interactive route to 8, 3) enable prefix persistence to reduce evictions, and 4) schedule an extended multi-hour run to capture long-tail behavior.

[03:55] Samuel: what's the expected impact? numbers?

[03:58] Ethan: we expect p99 for interactive to drop from ~1.8s to sub-500ms in most runs; for medium flows p99 should move into ~600-700ms range. Throughput per-GPU may fall ~10–15% with smaller batches but net latency SLOs will be satisfied.

[04:20] Priya: ok. On the business side we need the cost model — if throughput drops, what does that do to our unit economics?

[04:27] Maya: we'll update the spreadsheet — I can run two scenarios: latency-first (smaller batches + quant) and cost-first (higher batches, more aggressive caching). We'll show expected cost per 1k requests and monthly spend for your projected volume.

[04:42] Lena: good. Also on compliance: we need SOC 2 artifacts, encryption at rest, and KMS integration details. Who's our contact for that?

[04:50] Maya: that's me — I'll drop the security pack after this call. Ethan has the tech specifics for KMS/HSM integration.

[04:58] Ethan: we support customer-managed keys via KMS, HSM options for on-prem, and audit logs that include token-level routing if you enable extended retention. Note: we redact prompt text in logs unless you opt in for debug.

[05:18] Samuel: retention and residency — the pilot is in our VPC, but we want to ensure data never leaves the region for EU customers. Can Redwood pin instances to region?

[05:28] Ethan: yes — Dedicated pools can be region-pinned. For Private deployments we can do air-gapped on-prem installs if needed. For this pilot we'll ensure nodes are in the same region and we'll enable strict routing.

[05:40] Lena: one practical ask — we saw a few misattributed tokens in the logger where user ids were truncated, could be a parsing bug, can the SE look?

[05:48] Ethan: noted — I'll triage the logging pipeline. That might be downstream of our anonymization layer where we truncate metadata; we'll check the parser.

[05:58] Maya: ok good. Now on closeout — our goal this week is to produce a short exec packet showing that performance meets your success criteria and a pricing ask so your procurement can sign off. Priya, can you share the final success criteria list?

[06:10] Priya: yes. We're aligning internally but top line: interactive p99 < 500ms 95% of the time on production-like load, throughput to sustain 120 QPS with 5 concurrent long sessions, and SOC2 plus KMS proof. Also a commercial cap so monthly cost stays under $X for the pilot — I'll share exact dollar cap after internal sync.

[06:34] Lena: and one more — ability to route degraded sessions to a fallback model with slightly lower accuracy but guaranteed sub-400ms latency.

[06:42] Ethan: we can set a policy-based routing rule for that — e.g., if latency prediction > 350ms, route to low-latency variant.

[06:50] Maya: perfect. Next steps recap — Ethan runs the 12-hour mixed benchmark, Maya sends pricing and security pack, Samuel finalizes VPC access, Priya sends signed success criteria. We'll tentatively schedule an exec wrap for week of Apr 21.

[07:08] Samuel: one more ops question — during benchmark are you going to push with the exact client surface we use (same prompt mix and tokenization)? We want apples-to-apples.

[07:16] Ethan: yes, please upload your canonical prompt seed file to the shared folder; we'll run it unchanged. We'll also seed synthetic long sessions to stress the cache.

[07:24] Priya: do you have a template for the exec packet?

[07:28] Maya: yes — one pager with key metrics, risk items, cost delta, and recommended commercial path. I'll attach it to the action items and mock one up by EOD Friday.

[07:36] Lena: ok thanks. Any blockers?

[07:39] Maya: only the VPC access and Priya's signoff on success criteria.

[07:44] Priya: I can do internal sync tomorrow, will try to get signoff by Tuesday.

[07:48] Ethan: I'll kick off the benchmark tomorrow afternoon after I get the prompt seed and VPC credentials.

[07:52] Maya: great. Quick note on competitors — you asked about Anthropic and SageMaker earlier. Anthropic's managed offering has consistent latency but less tuning surface; SageMaker can be cheaper at scale but requires more ops. We position Redwood as middle ground: high performance with ops-light experience.

[08:10] Lena: understood. We're balancing speed of integration with eventual cost.

[08:14] Maya: ok last thing, I'll capture these as formal action items and I'll share minutes. Thanks everyone, we'll reconvene same time next week unless you prefer exec slot earlier.

[08:25] Priya: same time next week is fine.

[08:28] Maya: thanks all, talk soon.

End of transcript.

Notes: transcript includes occasional minor mishears; timestamps approximate. Shared artifacts referenced: shared benchmarks spreadsheet (link: /drive/crestline/pilot/benchmarks), security pack (link: /drive/crestline/security-pack.pdf), exec packet template (link: /drive/templates/exec-packet.pdf).

Ethan: run end-to-end throughput + 99th percentile latency test with KV-cache enabled; due 2025-04-14
Maya: send pilot pricing table + cost model; due 2025-04-17
Priya: gather success-criteria sign-off list from product + legal; due 2025-04-15
Samuel: provision access to test VPC subnet and add Redwood IP allowlist; due 2025-04-13

Ethan to run 12-hour mixed-sequence throughput benchmark (short + long tails) and upload results to shared benchmarks spreadsheet by 2025-04-14
Maya to send updated dedicated pricing for 4xA100 pool and a 1-month pilot discount proposal by 2025-04-17
Crestline to confirm security contact for SOC2/ISO artifacts (who will sign NDA) by 2025-04-15
Schedule executive wrap-up with Crestline stakeholders and Redwood leadership for week of 2025-04-21 (AE to propose 2 slots)

title: docs
text:
maria: Pushed a small PR to normalize code example identifiers per-language and add a docs-snippet linter. It updates quickstarts, SDK snippets, and the migration guide. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/docs/pull/4928

alex: Nice. What's the linter doing exactly?

maria: It checks three things: 1) language fence label (python/js/ts), 2) identifier casing matches language convention (snake_case for python, camelCase for js/ts), 3) no cross-language canonicalization of variable names. I added the linter to docs CI as an optional job for now.

jamal: Optional job is fine to start. Do you have examples of failures?

maria: Yep, included in the PR description. Example failure from a migrated snippet:

```
// js
const resp = await client.generate({ model_name: "redwood-alpha", prompt: "hi" })
```

The linter flags `model_name` in the js block and suggests `modelName`.

tara: Love that. Can the linter also suggest idiomatic replacements rather than just flagging? That'll speed up reviews.

maria: It currently suggests replacements using a small ruleset: snake_case <-> camelCase mappings for common identifiers (model_name <-> modelName, api_key <-> apiKey, dataset_id <-> datasetId). We can expand.

alex: Any impact on existing docs anchors/links? We had a few anchors that changed variable names inside headings.

maria: Ran the link-checker too. Fixed 4 internal anchor mismatches. One external link to security policy is blocked pending product signoff; left a TODO in the PR.

jamal: Good catch. Also, we should avoid changing identifiers inside code blocks that are API contract examples (like request/response JSON) if the backend actually expects camelCase. How are we detecting that?

maria: The linter rules include an allowlist comment marker. If an example is intentionally canonicalized to API payload naming (e.g., // api-payload) reviewers can add `<!-- docs-lint: allow-case -->` above the block. The CI will skip flagged blocks with that marker.

tara: Solid. On the glossary front, did you change anything? There's the ongoing serving/inference alias debate.

maria: Tagged lexicon-bot to create a suggestion to map search terms to both.

lexicon-bot: Created glossary suggestion #239: "serving (alias) -> inference" and added search synonyms so both terms surface.

alex: Can we add a short CONTRIBUTING blurb? One paragraph that says: "Prefer idiomatic identifiers per language in code examples; if the example demonstrates an API payload use the api-payload marker."

tara: I'll draft the paragraph after the PR merges and add it to docs/contributing.md.

maria: One more thing — I added a small test matrix in the PR showing sample snippets across Python/JS/TS and how they should look. After merge I'll open a follow-up to apply the script across other repos (examples repo, tutorials).

jamal: Reviewing now. Left three inline comments: two wording tweaks and one around the allowlist marker syntax.

ci-bot: docs-snippet-lint job started for PR #4928. Report will post as a comment when complete.

maria: Thanks all. Please review; if +1s by EOD I'll flip the linter to required in CI and run the bulk migration in a separate PR.

title: Priority fanout thrashing causing periodic 5xx spikes and connection oscillation for Composify Labs
text:
Issue summary:
Customer (Composify Labs - Dedicated) reported a pattern of elevated 5xx responses beginning 2026-03-13 18:10 UTC and recurring in ~10-15 minute clusters. Errors correlate with small-payload, very high QPS traffic routed with high-priority flags (priority-fanout). Impact: intermittent failures on production chat endpoint, elevated tail latency and stream disconnects.

Impact:
- Multiple customer calls failing with 5xx (502/503) for ~30% of requests during each wave.
- User-facing timeouts and aborted streaming sessions; Composify reported retries that compounded load.
- Business impact: degraded SLA for dedicated tenant, customer engineering actively blocked.

Environment:
- Dedicated tenant pool in prod us-east (reserved GPU pool).
- API Gateway -> Ingress prioritizer -> routing layer -> serving-runtime pool (pinned model redwood/gpt-7b-ctx16k).
- Recent autoscaler/priority tweak deployed 2026-03-12 (optimize prefetch warmup).

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Send many small, parallel chat requests with high-priority header (X-Rdwd-Priority: high) that fan out to multiple shards.
2) Observe short-lived bursts where API returns 502/503 for a subset of concurrent streams and non-streaming requests.
3) In the same period, runtime shows rapid connection churn and several worker restarts.
4) When traffic drops, system recovers; issue reappears on next burst.

Observed behavior:
- API Gateway logs show upstream reset/502s and 503s clustered to same routing buckets.
- Serving runtime logs report "KV cache contention" and "eviction thrash" followed by worker soft-restart (watchdog).
- Scheduler shows rapid prefetch invalidations and immediate refills for priority lanes.
- Autoscaler did not scale quickly enough due to short window and rapid oscillation.

Expected behavior:
- High-priority fanout should be handled without elevated 5xx floor; prefetch and KV cache should smooth warmups without causing thrash or worker restarts.

Logs & metrics (excerpts):
- apigw/us-east access: 2026-03-13T18:12:07Z 502 upstream-reset tenant=comp_lab shard=13
- runtime/shard-13: 2026-03-13T18:12:09Z "kvcache: lock_wait>150ms" "prefetch: invalidation=312"
- runtime/shard-13: 2026-03-13T18:12:10Z "watchdog: soft-restart triggered by memory-eviction-spike"
- autoscaler/events: 2026-03-13T18:12:15Z scale_up_attempt shard=13 reason=queue_growth but aborted due to cooldown

Additional context:
- Customer uses aggressive retry logic in their client (2 immediate retries) which amplified the waves.
- No platform-wide deploys during incident window except the autoscaler tweak on 03-12.
- Related historical tickets show similar patterns during priority reshuffles (linked issues).

Timeline:
- 2026-03-13 18:15 UTC: Initial report from CS after customer call.
- 18:20 UTC: SRE reproduced burst locally with small-payload high-priority load.
- 18:30 UTC: Observed KV cache lock contention and immediate worker soft-restarts.
- 18:45 UTC: Applied temporary workaround (route high-priority fanout to a fallback route with larger prefetched KV cache).

Hypotheses considered:
1) Prefetch/kv cache invalidation loop for high-priority lanes is causing lock contention and eviction thrash, leading to runtime watchdog soft-restarts -> 5xx.
2) Autoscaler cooldown and rapid oscillation prevents timely scale-up for short bursts, causing queueing and upstream resets.
3) API gateway request fanout combined with client retry amplification is creating ephemeral connection storms that exhaust accept-queues.

Evidence:
- kvcache lock_wait metrics spike in exact time windows of 5xx.
- Worker restart logs reference high eviction churn.
- Autoscaler logs show aborted scale attempts during the wave.

Next steps (in progress):
- Engineering to instrument per-tenant kvcache lock histograms and add throttling on invalidation rate (assigned runtime-team).
- Temporarily route Composify high-priority traffic to fallback route with pre-warmed shards (mitigation applied at 18:45 UTC).
- Triage autoscaler cooldown policy for short-burst responsiveness; consider faster warmup for dedicated tenants.
- Ask Composify to reduce client-side immediate retries to prevent amplification during our mitigation window.
- Create a canary test to simulate small-payload high-priority fanout to validate fix.

2026-03-13 18:21 - CS (Morgan L.): Customer reported 502/503 spikes starting ~18:10 UTC. They noted retries made things worse. Requested urgent assistance.
2026-03-13 18:25 - SRE (Jayden K. Patel): Reproduced with a synthetic client. Observed kvcache lock wait >150ms and runtime soft-restart. Routing to runtime shard 13 shows repeated invalidations.
2026-03-13 18:30 - Eng (Priya S.): Hypothesis: prefetch invalidation loop for priority lanes. Will add tracing to prefetch path and rate-limit invalidations. ETA 4 hours for first patch.
2026-03-13 18:45 - Ops (Jayden K. Patel): Temporary mitigation applied: rerouted Composify high-priority traffic to pre-warmed fallback route. Customer still seeing reduced errors; monitoring closely.
2026-03-13 19:05 - CS (Morgan L.): Composify confirms error rate dropped from ~30% to ~4% during last wave after mitigation. They ask for permanent mitigation plan and timeline.
2026-03-14 09:10 - Runtime Team Lead (Priya S.): Added instrumentation PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/5042 to rate-limit invalidation bursts and expose per-tenant lock metrics. Requesting review.
2026-03-14 12:00 - SRE (Jayden K. Patel): Autoscaler cooldown removed for dedicated pre-warm policy in us-east; monitoring for oscillation. Will coordinate rollout with infra.

Workaround applied: high-priority traffic for Composify routed to pre-warmed fallback pool at 2026-03-13 18:45 UTC reducing error rate. Full fix in progress: runtime PR to add invalidation rate-limiter and per-tenant kvcache tracing (PR opened). Autoscaler prewarm policy adjustment proposed and partially rolled out for dedicated tenants in us-east. Postmortem and permanent remediation plan scheduled after verification.

title: PRD: Integrated Fallback Analytics & Cost Reconciliation (IFACR)
author: Asha Patel
text:
Summary:
This PRD defines the Integrated Fallback Analytics & Cost Reconciliation (IFACR) product: a set of telemetry, reconciliation logic, and tooling to (1) measure and attribute cost impact from automatic fallback and variant routing, (2) surface customer-facing fallback events and economics in the Console, and (3) produce auditable billing adjustments and credit recommendations for customers and billing systems.

Background and motivation:
Redwood’s runtime performs automated fallback to lower-cost or lower-fidelity model variants during capacity, latency, or error events. Current gaps:
- Telemetry and billing systems cannot attribute end-to-end token/compute cost changes to individual fallback incidents.
- Customer Console shows fallback occurrences but lacks per-event economic impact estimates or consolidated reconciliations.
- Finance and CS teams spend manual effort reconciling credits and explaining cost anomalies after major incidents.

Goals (what success looks like):
1) Accurate attribution: For >95% of fallback events, compute the delta in token/compute cost attributed to the fallback within the earnings window.
2) Customer visibility: Expose per-tenant fallback economics in Console with drilldowns and downloadable reconciliation reports.
3) Automated reconciliation: Produce suggested credit lines or invoice adjustments that Finance can accept/reject; reduce manual reconciliation time by 80%.
4) Low overhead: Telemetry and offline reconciliation jobs add <5% additional cost to aggregated telemetry pipeline.

Non-goals:
- This PRD does not change fallback routing policies or SLA guarantees.
- This PRD does not implement automated customer refunds without Finance approval.

Key stakeholders and owners:
- Product (owner): Asha Patel
- Eng (implementation): Runtime telemetry & billing infra teams (owners: Jian Li, runtime; Miguel Torres, billing infra)
- Finance: Sara Goldberg
- CS/Support: Priya Menon

Scope and major components:
1) Event-level recording: Augment runtime events with a standardized FallbackEvent envelope containing: request_id, tenant_id, original_variant, fallback_variant, timestamp, reason_code, token_counts (input/added), kv_cache_state, sequence_length, latency_metrics.
2) Simulation cost model: Deterministic cost-simulator that replays request traces against variant performance/cost profiles to compute "expected_cost" vs "actual_cost" per event.
3) Aggregation and reconciliation pipeline: Batch jobs that compute per-tenant delta, group by timeframe, and generate reconciliation artifacts (CSV + JSON).
4) Console surfaces: UI card per-tenant showing total fallback delta for selected window, top reasons, top endpoints affected, and download link to reconciliation report.
5) Finance workflow: Admin console flow to review suggested credits with audit trail.

Functional requirements (MUST):
- FR-1: Runtime must emit FallbackEvent for every fallback action within 1s of decision.
- FR-2: FallbackEvent schema must include fields: request_id, tenant_id, route_id, original_variant, fallback_variant, reason_code, prefetch_hit, tokens_consumed_estimate, kv_cache_eviction_flag, timestamp.
- FR-3: The cost-simulator must accept a trace file (newline-delimited JSON) and output per-event {expected_cost_usd, actual_cost_usd, delta_usd}.
- FR-4: Reconciliation pipeline must produce per-tenant reconciliation reports in CSV and signed JSON, partitioned by billing cycle (UTC).
- FR-5: Console must display fallback delta aggregated by day/week/month and support downloading last 90-day reconciliation reports.
- FR-6: Finance UI must provide a review action that records approver name, decision, credit_amount_usd, and reason; an immutable audit entry must be stored.

Non-functional requirements (MUST):
- NFR-1: End-to-end latency for the reconciliation batch (<24 hours) for 99% of tenants.
- NFR-2: Reconciliation results must be reproducible: running the same inputs through the simulator produces identical outputs (seeded randomness disabled).
- NFR-3: Storage of reconciliation artifacts must be encrypted-at-rest and available for 2 years for audit.
- NFR-4: The telemetry augmentation must not increase per-request p99 latency by >25ms.

API / Schema examples:
- FallbackEvent (newline-delimited JSON; required fields):
{
 "event_type": "fallback",
 "request_id": "req_01G23AB4",
 "tenant_id": "tnt_5678",
 "route_id": "chat-v1",
 "original_variant": "rwd-gpt-medium-v1",
 "fallback_variant": "rwd-gpt-small-q8",
 "reason_code": "capacity_constrained",
 "tokens_input": 34,
 "tokens_generated": 112,
 "timestamp": "2026-03-20T14:12:22Z",
 "latency_ms": 320
}

- Cost-simulator CLI example:
$ redwood-simulate-cost --trace-file traces/2026-03-20.ndjson --variant-profiles profiles/2026-03-01.json --out reconciliations/2026-03-20.json

Aggregation / Reconciliation output (CSV columns):
billing_cycle_start_utc, tenant_id, total_expected_usd, total_actual_usd, total_delta_usd, num_fallback_events, top_reason
2026-03-01, tnt_5678, 123.44, 98.12, -25.32, 42, capacity_constrained

Console UX requirements (high level):
- UX-1: A new "Fallback Economics" panel on the Tenant Billing page showing: total delta (USD), % of bill impacted, top 3 routes, top 3 reasons, link to download reconciliation CSV.
- UX-2: Drilldown for each route showing time-series of fallback delta and example events (redacted request ids).
- UX-3: Export must include signed JSON that Finance can ingest.

Rollout plan and milestones:
1) Phase A (pilot, 6 weeks): enable telemetry for 10 pilot tenants (low-volume), implement cost-simulator, and run reconciliation jobs daily to validate deltas. Deliverable: pilot reconciliation reports and a short QBR with Finance.
2) Phase B (internal launch, 8 weeks): expand to all dedicated tenants and internal Redwood accounts; build Console panel and Finance review UI (admin only). Deliverable: internal launch and updated runbook.
3) Phase C (public beta, 12 weeks): open to hosted tenants with opt-in; add quota to limit simulator runs per tenant; refine UI and SLA for reconciliation windows.
4) Phase D (GA, 4 weeks): global rollout, Billing integration for suggested-credit ingestion, and enable downloadable signed reports for 2-year retention.

Acceptance criteria (must pass to ship):
- All FRs and NFRs implemented and verified via automated tests and 2-week trial with at least 20 tenants.
- Console displays accurate aggregated delta (within 3% of simulator batch) for at least 95% of checked time windows.
- Finance has an accept/reject flow wired to billing pipeline; at least one test credit applied in sandbox billing and reconciled.

Telemetry, observability and monitoring:
- New metrics: fallback_event_count, fallback_delta_usd_sum, fallback_simulator_latency_ms, reconciliation_job_success_rate.
- Alerts: reconciliation_job_success_rate < 99% over 1h; fallback_simulator_latency_ms.p95 > 5s; backlog of unprocessed fallback events > 24h.
- Dashboards: per-tenant fallbacks, global daily delta heatmap, and reconciliation job backlog.

Billing and pricing implications:
- Product decision: suggested credits are advisory; Finance applies final credit. IFACR will provide a small admin fee line item when Finance performs manual reconciliations during GA (proposal: $50/incident or 1% of credit amount, whichever is higher) — requires legal/finance approval.
- Packaging: Console access to Fallback Economics included for Dedicated customers; Hosted customers must opt-in during beta; additional Analytics Add-on planned for 2027 that includes historical trend reports.

Security and privacy considerations:
- All exported reports must redact PII and any customer content.
- Access control: Console reconciliation reports are accessible only to Admins with billing_read or billing_admin role.
- Audit logging: All Finance actions (approve/reject credit) must be immutably logged with operator identity and timestamp.

Open questions and decisions needed:
- Q1: Should suggested credits be displayed as line-items on the invoice automatically or only as Finance-suggested actions?
- Q2: Threshold for auto-accept credits for small amounts (proposed: < $5).
- Q3: Storage retention beyond 2 years for enterprise/regulatory customers — create opt-in archival path?

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Simulator model drift leads to disputed credits. Mitigation: Versioned variant-profiles and deterministic simulation; include model version and profile hash in reconciliation artifact.
- Risk: Console shows sensitive usage patterns. Mitigation: Redact request text, only surface aggregated counts and redacted example ids.

Operational runbook (high level steps for incident during reconciliation failures):
1) Identify failing reconciliation job in "Reconciliation Jobs" dashboard.
2) Run diagnostic: redwood-simulate-cost --trace-file sample --variant-profiles current --verbose
3) If job backlog >24h, trigger manual replay for impacted billing cycles and notify Finance/CS list.
4) For data integrity concerns, freeze Finance approval and escalate to runtime/billing infra oncall.

Appendices:
A) Fallback reason_code taxonomy (initial): capacity_constrained, latency_spike, gradient_failure, kernel_oom, ratelimit_fallback.
B) Example reconciliation JSON schema (signed):
