title: Stratos AgentFlow
author: Marcus Li
text:
Summary: Mid-market B2B SaaS (product analytics) building outbound SDR chat assistants that operate in realtime (low-latency streaming) and must perform CRM/email/calendar actions via tool-calling. Evaluating hosted first to validate UX and latency SLOs, then likely move to Dedicated for predictable throughput and reserved concurrency.

Key quotes / snippets: "We need streaming replies that start under 150ms p50 and 250ms p95 for short replies when agent is live."
"Tool calling must be deterministic — createLead, sendEmail, scheduleMeeting hooks need robust failure/fallback modes."

Technical priorities: streaming token-level partials, tool calling (webhook signing + idempotency), deterministic function outputs for CRM actions, low cold-start latency for model variants, prefix caching for repeated prompts, multi-region routing with US-only data residency.

POC ask: 2-week hosted POC focusing on a simulated SDR workload (50 concurrent agents, bursts to 200), demo runtime streaming + function calling, tooling to exercise CRM/email/calendar actions against sandbox Salesforce + Gmail/Exchange. POC success criteria: p50 streaming < 150ms, p95 < 400ms, function-call success > 99% in sandbox, token-cost estimate within projected budget.

Commercial: Interested in usage-based pricing for hosted; will request Dedicated quotes for committed capacity if POC validates. Top concern: streaming costs at scale and predictable billing for large concurrent sessions. Asking for sample billing model: per-session baseline + per-token during active streaming.

Security & compliance: SOC2 mandatory, SSO/SAML for console, KMS integration for customer keys, audit logs export to SIEM, 90-day retention by default with options. Legal team flagged data residency (US only) and wants evidence of VPC/private deployment for Dedicated.

Integrations: Salesforce (create/update lead/contact, add activity), Gmail + O365 send-email + calendar invites, internal CRM API webhook. SE notes: we should demo function-calling wiring to the Salesforce sandbox and show signed webhook callback with idempotency token (important ask).

Risks: if hosted API streaming < SLA they will push for private on-prem evaluation. Concerned about model drift: wants automated evals on prompt sets tied to quality alerts.

Next steps: schedule 45m tech scoping with SE (Lina) to lock success metrics and test scenarios, set up sandbox credentials, provide pricing model template, and sign standard NDA for sandbox logs.

Begin 2-week hosted POC (streaming + tool-calls) week of 2026-03-22

title: Northbridge Payments x Redwood — Benchmark report walkthrough (latency/$) + methodology Q&A
author: Stephanie Nguyen
text:
MEETING HEADER
Title: Northbridge Payments x Redwood — Benchmark report walkthrough (latency/$) + methodology Q&A
Date: Jul 2, 2025
Start time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 47 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood) — AE
- Markus Klein (Redwood) — Solutions Engineer
- Priya Desai (Northbridge Payments) — Director, Platform Engineering
- Michael Tran (Northbridge Payments) — ML Engineer
- Anna Becker (Northbridge Payments) — Security & Procurement

Auto Summary (draft)
- Redwood walked through the public benchmark landing page and explained the latency-per-dollar metric and supporting metrics (p50/p95 latency, throughput, $/1M tokens).
- Northbridge raised concerns about workload fit (their traffic is bursty, streaming chat + long context) and whether Redwood’s published numbers can be replicated.
- Redwood clarified methodology: prompt set v3 production mix, fixed concurrency bands, warmups, caching/batching policy as documented, and stability gates/variance reruns.
- Discussion on deployment options for EU: Hosted EU region vs Dedicated capacity for predictable p95 and data isolation; Private/VPC mentioned as future option.

Topics
- Interpreting latency/$ vs tokens/sec
- Fairness + “apples-to-apples” model comparisons
- Replication: manifests, Docker runner, and what a customer can reproduce
- Region variability (eu-west vs us-east) and p95 stability
- Security posture and data residency constraints

Action items (verbatim)
- Stephanie: email Northbridge the benchmark methodology link + FAQs + a 1-pager on “how to replicate” (by EOD Fri)
- Markus: share sample run manifest + CLI flags used for region sweep runner and explain stability gates (by Fri)
- Priya/Michael: provide token distribution targets and 2–3 sanitized prompts for PoC (next week)
- Anna: send Northbridge’s baseline security questionnaire + data retention requirements (next week)

Questions captured
- “Is caching on in your public numbers? If yes, what kind?”
- “If we run the same harness, will we see the same latency/$ within some confidence interval?”
- “How do you prevent cherry-picking regions, times, or prompt mixes?”
- “What happens to p95 when there’s noisy neighbors on Hosted?”

TRANSCRIPT

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. Hi everyone, thanks for making the time. I’m Stephanie, account exec here at Redwood. Markus is with me, solutions engineering. The goal today is pretty straightforward: we’ll walk through the benchmark report live, how to read the numbers, and then we can spend the rest on methodology and whether it maps to your workload. Sound okay?

[00:16] Priya Desai: Yep, that’s what we want. We got forwarded the report internally and… there’s enthusiasm, but also skepticism.

[00:23] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s healthy.

[00:24] Markus Klein: Totally.

[00:25] Michael Tran: Yeah I’m the skeptic, I guess. Mostly around like, can we reproduce it and does it match our traffic.

[00:31] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. And Anna, anything specific you want to make sure we cover?

[00:35] Anna Becker: Data residency and basically if this becomes a procurement thing, what we’re buying. Hosted vs dedicated, and what logs you keep.

[00:42] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect. We’ll touch that.

[00:44] Markus Klein: I’m gonna share my screen.

[00:49] Markus Klein: Okay, so this is the public landing page. You’ll see the interactive table—models down the left, regions across the top. The default view is “latency per dollar” which is basically milliseconds of end-to-end latency you get per dollar spent. Lower is better. There’s also a toggle for p50 and p95 latency, throughput, and cost per 1M tokens.

[01:12] Michael Tran: Wait “latency per dollar” is lower better? That’s a little unintuitive.

[01:17] Markus Klein: Yeah, fair. It’s one of those units where we debated the label. Think of it as: if you spend one dollar, how much waiting time do you buy. Less waiting per dollar is better. If you flip to “tokens per dollar,” higher would be better. We chose this because it maps to p95 latency + spend, but we keep the underlying metrics visible.

[01:35] Priya Desai: Do you expose tokens per second too?

[01:38] Markus Klein: We do, but we push people to look at p95 and cost, because raw tokens/sec can hide queueing, and it doesn’t capture user experience when concurrency goes up.

[01:48] Stephanie Nguyen: And, just to state the obvious: this is not a “fastest model ever” claim. It’s about production economics in specific workloads and regions with our runtime.

[01:57] Michael Tran: Okay. What’s the workload though. That’s the first thing.

[02:02] Markus Klein: Great question. If you click “Methodology,” there’s a summary, and then a full methodology doc. The short version: we use prompt set v3 “production mix,” which includes both prefill-heavy and decode-heavy requests. We run across a few context length buckets. We also run at defined concurrency levels, with warmups, and we do repeated runs with stability gates.

[02:27] Michael Tran: When you say “production mix,” is that your production? Or like some made-up mixture.

[02:33] Markus Klein: It’s a curated mix built by our Applied ML team based on aggregated patterns we see across customers, plus public eval prompts that are safe to share. It’s not one customer’s traffic. And we publish the exact distributions we used—token counts, prefill/decode ratios—so you can judge fit.

[02:52] Priya Desai: Our workload is mostly chat, streaming, and long context. Like, 8k to 16k input sometimes, then short outputs.

[03:01] Markus Klein: Yep. That’s prefill-heavy. The report includes a context-length filter. Let me flip to the 16k bucket.

[03:11] Markus Klein: (scrolling) Okay, now you see numbers change. You’ll also see that some models degrade more than others on long prefill. That’s why we include that filter.

[03:22] Michael Tran: Are these all on the same GPU type?

[03:25] Markus Klein: Within a region, we run on a standardized fleet configuration for that run series. We don’t mix instance types within the sweep. Across regions, GPU type can differ—so we call it out in the methodology, and we normalize cost based on our actual metered infrastructure costs.

[03:41] Michael Tran: So it’s “Redwood cost” not like AWS list price.

[03:45] Markus Klein: Correct. The metric is based on what you pay Redwood for tokens in Hosted, and for Dedicated we can translate to effective $/1M tokens based on the commit size. The public report is primarily Hosted pricing. We’re careful there.

[03:57] Stephanie Nguyen: For your side, we’d likely talk Dedicated if p95 and predictability is the priority. But the report is still useful to pick a model and region.

[04:08] Anna Becker: Dedicated meaning isolated hardware?

[04:11] Stephanie Nguyen: Dedicated capacity pool, yes—data isolation, predictable throughput, and we can align on an SLA.

[04:18] Priya Desai: Okay, keep going.

[04:21] Markus Klein: So here’s a specific example. If you pick, say, Model A vs Model B—(pause) sorry, the model names are showing. The key is: in eu-west, you’ll see p95 is stable within a band. We publish p95, not just p50.

[04:38] Michael Tran: But p95 can be gamed too. Like if you run it at low concurrency.

[04:42] Markus Klein: 100%. That’s why concurrency is explicit. We run at multiple concurrency bands—think 1, 8, 32, etc. And we show where the knee is.

[04:52] Priya Desai: Do you show all of those in the public table?

[04:55] Markus Klein: The table defaults to a “representative” concurrency, but you can expand to see the other bands, and the PDF has charts that show the curve. Also, we provide CSV/JSON export for the full dataset.

[05:08] Michael Tran: Export is huge, actually. Because I want to compare it to our internal harness.

[05:14] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[05:16] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s a common ask. We’ve got customers using the dataset to shortlist models, then they run their own prompts on a smaller pilot.

[05:25] Michael Tran: Okay, I’m going to be blunt: is caching enabled in these numbers?

[05:29] Markus Klein: Good blunt question. We have a documented caching policy. In the main benchmark runs we do not rely on cross-request semantic caching, but we do allow runtime-level optimizations like KV cache reuse *within* a request and continuous batching. Prefix caching is controlled; we call out exactly whether it’s on and under what conditions.

[05:49] Michael Tran: That’s kind of the whole thing, right. If you have prefix cache and your prompt set repeats, you win.

[05:55] Markus Klein: Agree. That’s why we avoid repeated prompts in the public prompt set and we randomize certain parts. And the dataset includes cache hit rate metrics; if you see suspiciously high hit rates, that’s a red flag. We also have reviewers on the Applied ML side who check for that.

[06:14] Priya Desai: So the point is it’s not “we turned on magic caching.”

[06:18] Markus Klein: Correct.

[06:19] Stephanie Nguyen: And legally we can’t, and don’t, claim that your workload will match ours 1:1. We try to be transparent so you can map it.

[06:29] Anna Becker: When you say “prompt set,” is that public?

[06:32] Markus Klein: Parts are public, parts are internal. The methodology describes the composition. The reason some prompts aren’t fully public is licensing / safety, but the distributions and tokenization stats are published.

[06:45] Michael Tran: That’s… okay. But for replication, it matters.

[06:50] Markus Klein: For replication, what we provide is: the harness code path, the runner container (Docker image), the run manifest schema, and the config knobs. You can run it with your own prompts and see relative differences.

[07:04] Michael Tran: I want to replicate *your* numbers.

[07:07] Markus Klein: You can get close, but I want to set expectations: you won’t reproduce the exact same p95 down to the millisecond because regions, fleet load, and internet conditions vary. What we aim for is reproducibility within a confidence interval, and we publish variance and stability checks.

[07:25] Priya Desai: What’s the interval?

[07:27] Markus Klein: For most runs, p95 variance across repeats needs to be under a threshold—think single-digit percent—otherwise it auto-reruns. If it stays noisy, we flag it as unstable and exclude it from headline charts.

[07:41] Michael Tran: That sounds like cherry-picking again: you exclude bad runs.

[07:45] Markus Klein: Fair concern. The exclusion rules are published. It’s not “bad results,” it’s “unstable measurements.” If the measurement is unstable, it’s misleading to present a single number. And we keep the raw logs internally for audit.

[07:59] Stephanie Nguyen: Also, we can show you in a PoC what the stability looks like for your workload. That’s honestly the point.

[08:07] Michael Tran: Okay. Another: are competitor baselines in here? I saw some mention in the blog.

[08:13] Stephanie Nguyen: In the public report we’re very careful. We sometimes provide contextual baselines where we can do apples-to-apples, but we avoid “Vendor X is slower” claims without full substantiation. On this page it’s mostly Redwood results.

[08:27] Markus Klein: Internally we look at other providers—like Bedrock endpoints, OpenAI, Fireworks, Together—just to sanity check. But latency paths differ, and pricing differs, so we do caveats.

[08:40] Priya Desai: Our leadership is comparing you to Bedrock because they already have AWS enterprise agreements.

[08:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep, very common. What we see is: Bedrock is a good default for procurement, but when teams need tighter p95, or better unit cost at higher concurrency, or more control over model versions and rollouts, they come to us. Dedicated is often the deciding factor.

[09:04] Anna Becker: And if we needed VPC?

[09:06] Stephanie Nguyen: We have Private deployments too—VPC, and on-prem for regulated. For this use case, you’re asking EU residency and predictable performance; we can start with EU Hosted or Dedicated in EU. Private is an option if network isolation becomes mandatory.

[09:22] Michael Tran: So for this benchmark, did you run in EU? Which region?

[09:26] Markus Klein: Yes—eu-west. Also us-east and some APAC, depending on availability. The table shows which regions are included.

[09:36] Priya Desai: Our customers are in Germany and France mostly, so eu-west is relevant.

[09:42] Markus Klein: Good.

[09:44] Michael Tran: Here’s another fit question: our traffic is spiky. Like lunchtime spikes. Does this benchmark include burst behavior or just steady-state?

[09:52] Markus Klein: The benchmark is steady-state at fixed concurrency for measurement. Burst behavior is more about autoscaling and queueing. On Hosted, we have rate limits and scaling policies; on Dedicated, you control burst headroom. But it’s not a “burst test” per se.

[10:10] Priya Desai: Okay, but in production, p95 goes to hell during bursts.

[10:15] Markus Klein: Totally. What we usually do in PoC is run two scenarios: steady-state at target concurrency, and then a burst ramp test to observe queueing and tail behavior. That’s outside the public report but we can run it with you.

[10:28] Stephanie Nguyen: And to tie it back to purchase decision: if burst p95 is key, that’s an argument for Dedicated so you’re not sharing capacity.

[10:36] Anna Becker: Dedicated means you can guarantee the capacity in EU? Like, contractually.

[10:42] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes, with a commit and SLA language. We’d size it based on tokens/sec, context length, and concurrency, and build in headroom.

[10:52] Michael Tran: I want to go back to how you compute latency/$ because that’s the headline. Is it like p95 latency divided by cost?

[10:59] Markus Klein: Close. It’s a normalized metric combining end-to-end latency components and effective cost per token. The exact formula is in the methodology. We also show the raw components so you can compute your own. We don’t hide it behind a black box.

[11:15] Michael Tran: Do you include network latency? Like from where.

[11:19] Markus Klein: The measurement is from the runner in-region, to avoid “my office Wi-Fi” variability. End-to-end includes request overhead but within a controlled network environment.

[11:31] Priya Desai: That’s good for isolating compute, but our clients are global.

[11:35] Markus Klein: Yes. For client latency, you care about distance + CDN/edge routing. That’s separate. We can provide region selection guidance and multi-region failover.

[11:48] Stephanie Nguyen: In your case it sounds like EU primary, and maybe US for some internal tools?

[11:53] Priya Desai: Possibly.

[11:55] Markus Klein: Also streaming. Michael, you mentioned streaming chat. The benchmark includes a non-streaming measurement by default, because streaming definitions vary—time-to-first-token vs time-to-last-token. We do have TTFT metrics in some internal charts.

[12:12] Michael Tran: That’s a big deal for us. TTFT is the KPI.

[12:16] Markus Klein: Understood. In PoC we can measure TTFT and steady decode rate. Publicly, we’re cautious because it’s easy to mislead. But it’s measurable.

[12:28] Priya Desai: Is your API OpenAI-compatible? Like can we drop in.

[12:32] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes, we have compatible endpoints and SDKs. We can cover that separately.

[12:37] Anna Becker: I want to understand logs. Are prompts stored?

[12:41] Stephanie Nguyen: By default, we don’t use your prompts for training. Logging is configurable; we have redaction options. For Dedicated/Private, we can align on retention and audit logs. There’s also enterprise controls like SSO/SAML, RBAC.

[12:55] Anna Becker: We’ll need that in writing.

[12:58] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep. We’ll send our security packet.

[13:02] Markus Klein: Going back to the table—let me click into the “download dataset” action. This gives CSV and JSON. The JSON includes schema versioning and a changelog field.

[13:12] Michael Tran: Nice.

[13:14] Markus Klein: Each row includes: model ID, region, context bucket, concurrency, p50/p95, throughput, and computed latency/$ plus confidence notes.

[13:27] Michael Tran: Confidence notes?

[13:29] Markus Klein: Like “rerun_count=2” or “variance_flag=false.” Again, transparency.

[13:37] Priya Desai: Okay but how do I know you didn’t run it at 3am when nobody’s using the cluster.

[13:44] Markus Klein: Good callout. We reserve capacity for benchmark sweeps specifically to avoid noisy neighbors, and we run repeated sweeps at different times. We publish the run window. And internally we keep raw run manifests with timestamps.

[13:59] Michael Tran: So it’s not “on the same shared Hosted cluster as customers.”

[14:03] Markus Klein: The benchmark environment is controlled. Otherwise it’d be chaos. The point is to measure the runtime and region performance, not incidental traffic.

[14:13] Priya Desai: But then it doesn’t represent real Hosted.

[14:16] Markus Klein: It represents what Hosted can do under normal conditions, but yes, any shared system has variance. That’s why for strict SLOs we suggest Dedicated.

[14:27] Stephanie Nguyen: I’ll just underline: the benchmark is a starting point. The sales motion is: shortlist from benchmark, validate with your prompts, then decide Hosted vs Dedicated.

[14:38] Michael Tran: Okay. If we wanted to replicate, what do we need? Like literally.

[14:43] Markus Klein: We can give you a Docker image—pinned deps—plus a CLI command. You choose region, model, concurrency, and prompt set. It outputs a manifest JSON and result JSON. If you want to run against our public prompt set, we can provide the parts that are shareable and you can substitute your own for restricted pieces.

[15:05] Michael Tran: And we can run it from our VPC?

[15:08] Markus Klein: You can run the runner from wherever, but for clean comparison you’d run it in the same cloud region. We can help you spin a small runner instance in eu-west.

[15:18] Priya Desai: Would that violate anything? Like sending prompts out.

[15:21] Anna Becker: Depends on the prompts.

[15:23] Stephanie Nguyen: For PoC, we recommend sanitized prompts, or synthetic but representative token structure. We can also sign appropriate agreements depending on data sensitivity.

[15:34] Michael Tran: Another issue: Our prompts have a lot of repeated boilerplate, like policy text. Prefix caching could help, but it’s not in your benchmark. So your benchmark might understate your advantage.

[15:46] Markus Klein: That’s true. And it’s actually a good point: in your workload, enabling prefix caching could improve both latency and cost. We avoid that in the benchmark to keep it fair, but in production we absolutely want to use it where safe.

[16:00] Priya Desai: Okay so the benchmark is conservative in that sense.

[16:03] Markus Klein: In that particular dimension, yes.

[16:06] Michael Tran: Unless someone else is doing it and you’re not.

[16:08] Markus Klein: Sure, but then it’s workload-specific. We can test it.

[16:13] Stephanie Nguyen: This is why we talk about “economics controls.” We’ll help you pick the right levers.

[16:20] Priya Desai: I’m looking at the p95 numbers here and they’re… lower than what I see with Bedrock for similar models. Why.

[16:30] Markus Klein: Several reasons could explain it: kernel selection, continuous batching, queueing policies, and the fact we’re measuring in-region without internet variability. Also, model versions and quantization profiles can differ. It’s hard to do apples-to-apples with managed endpoints.

[16:49] Michael Tran: Do you quantize in this benchmark?

[16:52] Markus Klein: We use published/standard serving profiles for each model. If quantization is used, it’s documented. We avoid non-standard “lab-only” configs. Again: publishable, defensible.

[17:06] Priya Desai: Who signs off on this? Like is it marketing or engineering.

[17:10] Stephanie Nguyen: Engineering owns the methodology and data. Marketing owns presentation. There’s a review chain including legal.

[17:18] Anna Becker: Good.

[17:20] Michael Tran: If we do a PoC, can we get Dedicated immediately? Or do we start on Hosted.

[17:27] Stephanie Nguyen: Depends on timeline and capacity. Often we start with Hosted in the right region to iterate quickly, then we size Dedicated once we know concurrency and context distribution.

[17:39] Priya Desai: We have a deadline. We need to show something in four weeks.

[17:43] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s doable. We can do a 2-week technical PoC and then a 2-week procurement/security parallel path.

[17:51] Anna Becker: Security path is never 2 weeks.

[17:54] Stephanie Nguyen: Fair. But we can start now.

[17:57] Markus Klein: For PoC success criteria, can I ask: what are your SLOs? p95, TTFT, cost target.

[18:05] Priya Desai: For interactive chat, TTFT under 500ms would be ideal. For batch jobs, we care about throughput and cost.

[18:14] Michael Tran: And for p95 end-to-end, under 2 seconds for typical prompts, but long context will be bigger.

[18:22] Markus Klein: Great. And concurrency?

[18:24] Priya Desai: Steady maybe 50 concurrent, burst to 200.

[18:29] Markus Klein: Perfect. That’s the kind of input that matters more than the benchmark headline.

[18:36] Michael Tran: I still want to know: can we reproduce your eu-west numbers within, say, 10%.

[18:42] Markus Klein: Likely yes if you run the same harness in the same region with the same model version and parameters, during similar conditions. But I don’t want to promise 10% for p95 without seeing it. We can treat it as an experiment: we’ll run a joint reproduction run and compare.

[18:59] Stephanie Nguyen: And if we’re outside 10%, we’ll diagnose: queueing, rate limits, runner placement, etc.

[19:07] Priya Desai: Okay.

[19:09] Anna Becker: On procurement: who is subprocessor, where is data stored.

[19:14] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll share the DPA and subprocessors list. For EU, data residency options exist; for Dedicated we can constrain where data is processed. Logs retention is configurable. We’ll follow up.

[19:27] Michael Tran: Another fairness question: prompt set. If it’s not fully public, then it’s not fully reproducible.

[19:35] Markus Klein: Totally fair. What we do is: we publish the measurable properties of the prompt set—token distributions, mix categories—so you can create a similar synthetic set. And we publish enough of the set to validate the harness. Plus the code and configs. It’s not perfect, but it’s transparent.

[19:54] Priya Desai: Okay. What about model list? Are these the models you support in production.

[20:01] Markus Klein: The report distinguishes “supported” and “experimental” models. Supported means we have validated profiles and SLO expectations. Experimental means available but not recommended for strict production without extra testing.

[20:15] Michael Tran: That’s good. We’ve been burned by “preview” endpoints before.

[20:20] Stephanie Nguyen: Same.

[20:21] Markus Klein: Can I ask what models you’re using today?

[20:25] Michael Tran: Mix. Some OpenAI for English support, and Bedrock for EU constraints. We’re trying to move more to open models for cost.

[20:34] Priya Desai: And we need consistency across regions.

Markus will set up a runner and we’ll pick two or three models from the benchmark that look good in eu-west for long context. Then we run both steady-state and a burst ramp.

title: Prompt heuristics: templates and failure cases (2026)
author: Maya Patel
text:
h1. Overview
This page consolidates Redwood Inference prompt heuristics, copy/paste templates, and known failure cases for common short instruction tasks:
* binary/multiclass classification
* extractive structured output (JSON)
* rewrites with a constrained style

It is derived from applied experiments and is intended to be broadly reusable (not a personal scratchpad). The focus is pragmatic: maximize reliability under latency and parsing constraints, especially for streaming responses.

h2. Scope and non-goals
* In scope: prompt patterns for 0–3 shot tasks; output formatting constraints; example ordering; streaming-safe delimiters; canonicalization rules.
* Out of scope: full benchmark harness design, model-specific finetuning, or long-form agent prompting.

h2. Current recommendations (TL;DR)
1. Prefer short, explicit role + constraints over long rationale priming for latency-sensitive tasks.
2. For structured extraction, enforce a strict JSON-only contract and include canonicalization rules (e.g., strip currency symbols).
3. Use explicit block delimiters (XML-ish tags) to reduce boundary confusion in streaming.
4. Avoid chain-of-thought prompting. If you need justification, request a one-line "reason" field explicitly (and only when downstream accepts it).

h1. Tested heuristics (what worked, what didn’t)
h2. H1: Explicit role + short constraints beat long rationale priming
* Finding (2026-03): Consistently true for classification + extraction at low shot counts.
* Rationale: Long explanations increase variance and can bleed into the response format.

h2. H2: Example ordering effects (positive-first vs negative-first)
* Prior observation: negative-first examples caused borderline positives to flip negative in 3-shot classification.
* Updated finding (2026-03): ordering effects shrink substantially if:
 * labels are defined once and constrained to an explicit set
 * the final answer is requested under a fixed key (e.g., "Label:" on its own line)
 * examples are symmetric in length and style
* Practical recommendation: still default to positive-first for binary sentiment-like tasks, but treat ordering as a tunable parameter rather than a rule.

h2. H3: Delimiter tokens matter for streaming
* Finding: using explicit tags (e.g., <EXAMPLE>…</EXAMPLE>) reduced malformed structured outputs in streaming compared to freeform separators (e.g., "### EXAMPLE").
* Recommendation: standardize on tag-based delimiters for any prompt that must be parsed.

h2. H4: JSON constraints reduce verbosity and improve parse success
* Finding: "Return EXACT JSON" with an explicit schema reliably reduces paraphrasing.
* Caveat: Without canonicalization instructions, models will often preserve currency symbols or units.

h1. Standard templates (copy/paste)
All templates below are designed to be streaming-friendly and parser-friendly.

h2. Template A — extraction to strict JSON (1-shot)
Use for invoices, receipts, order summaries, and any simple entity/field extraction.

{code}
You are a concise extractor.
Return EXACTLY one JSON object and nothing else.
Schema (all values are strings):
{"product":"...","price":"...","quantity":"..."}

Canonicalization rules:
- price: digits and decimal point only (e.g., "7.25"); strip currency symbols and commas
- quantity: digits only when present; otherwise "unknown"

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Bought 3 packs of AA batteries (Model X) for $9.99 each"
Output: {"product":"AA batteries (Model X)","price":"9.99","quantity":"3"}
</EXAMPLE>

Now extract from the input below.
Text: "<INPUT_TEXT>"
Output:
{code}

Notes:
* The canonicalization block is required if downstream expects normalized numerics.
* If you need multiple items, define an array schema explicitly (and update parsers accordingly).

h2. Template B — classification with tag separators (up to 3-shot)
Use for sentiment/triage/moderation-style labeling.

{code}
You are a brief classifier.
Valid labels: POSITIVE, NEGATIVE.
Return the label only.

<EXAMPLE>
Input: "Loved the service, will come back!"
Label: POSITIVE
</EXAMPLE>
<EXAMPLE>
Input: "Item arrived broken and no reply from support."
Label: NEGATIVE
</EXAMPLE>
<EXAMPLE>
Input: "Average experience, shipping slow but product ok."
Label: NEGATIVE
</EXAMPLE>

Input: "<INPUT>"
Label:
{code}

Optional hardening line (use when the model keeps adding explanations):
* "Do not output any other words, punctuation, or JSON. Output only POSITIVE or NEGATIVE."

h2. Template C — rewrite to tone (zero-shot)
Use for customer comms rewrite, concise summaries, or tone adjustments.

{code}
You are a rewrite assistant.
Rewrite the following customer message to be formal and concise (one sentence).
Do not add new facts.

Message: "<MSG>"
Rewritten:
{code}

h1. Known failure cases and mitigations
h2. F1: Currency symbol leakage in extraction
* Symptom: price values include "$" (or other currency symbols), breaking numeric parsers.
* Example input: "Total: $12.00"
* Bad output: {"price":"$12.00"}
* Mitigation: include canonicalization rule "digits and decimal point only" and provide a 1-shot example that demonstrates stripping symbols.

h2. F2: Example-order bias in borderline classification
* Symptom: borderline positives label as NEGATIVE more often when first example is negative.
* Updated mitigation: enforce "Return the label only" plus symmetric examples; consider adding a neutral/borderline example if task allows (but beware label leakage if the dataset distribution is skewed).

h2. F3: Streaming truncation causing malformed JSON
* Symptom: missing closing brace or partial object when network interrupts or token boundaries cut awkwardly.
* Mitigations:
 1. Keep examples short (< 50 tokens per example for extraction).
 2. Put schema and constraints immediately before the answer.
 3. Prefer one JSON object (not pretty-printed) to reduce token count.
 4. If the client supports it, validate braces and retry once with a "repair" prompt.

h2. F4: Rationale/chain-of-thought contamination
* Symptom: model outputs reasoning text even when asked for JSON/labels.
* Mitigation: remove chain-of-thought priming; explicitly forbid additional text.
* Policy note: Do not request chain-of-thought in production prompts. If justification is needed for UX, request a separate field like "reason" and treat it as non-authoritative.

h2. F5: Extra keys added to JSON output
* Symptom: model adds fields like "currency":"USD" or "confidence":0.82.
* Mitigations:
 * "Return EXACTLY the keys in the schema; do not add any other keys."
 * Provide an example where an extra key would be tempting but is omitted.
 * In downstream parsing, reject unknown keys (preferred) or ignore them (only if product tolerates it).

h1. Mini-results summary (internal quick evals)
These are small-sample directional results intended to guide defaults; they are not full benchmarks.

h2. Setup
* Tasks: binary sentiment classification; receipt-like extraction
* Temperatures: 0.0, 0.2, 0.7
* Few-shot: 0, 1, 3
* Runs per cell: N=50 (updated from earlier N=20 scratch runs)

h2. Highlights
* Extraction:
 * Temp=0.0 + strict JSON + canonicalization rules: price normalization correctness ~96% (previously ~89% without canonicalization).
 * Temp=0.2 increases symbol leakage and key drift; only use if you accept retry/repair logic.
* Classification:
 * Role-only + "label only" constraint: stable across 0–3 shot.
 * Adding short explanations after examples increased variance and increased non-compliant outputs (extra text).

h1. Operational checklist (before shipping a prompt)
1. Define the output contract unambiguously (label-only or strict JSON schema).
2. Add canonicalization rules for any field with units/symbols (currency, dates, counts).
3. Keep examples short and stylistically symmetric.
4. Add hard-stop constraints: "Return only X" / "Return EXACT JSON".
5. Test with streaming on/off and validate parse success.
6. Log representative failures (input, prompt, raw output, model/version, temperature) to the evals tracker.

h1. Open questions / follow-ups
* How much do these behaviors shift across quantization variants (int8 vs int4) in hosted environments?
* For multi-label classification, what is the best delimiter strategy for preventing label drift (comma-separated vs one-per-line)?
* For extraction involving multiple currencies, what is the policy: preserve currency code as separate field vs normalize to a base currency?

h1. Change log
* 2026-03-12: Standardized on <EXAMPLE> tag delimiters; added canonicalization rules section; updated mini-results to N=50 per cell; clarified policy to avoid chain-of-thought prompting.
* 2026-02-25: Initial consolidation from applied-ml experiments and failure logs.

title: Arboretum Labs — Integration Discovery: Developer Onramp & Proxy
author: Claire Mendoza
text:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-04
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Claire Mendoza (Redwood AE), Devon Park (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Arboretum Head of Platform), Luis Ortega (Arboretum Lead ML), Priya Rao (Arboretum Security), Tom Bolton (CTO)

Summary:
Arboretum is evaluating Redwood for a mixed deployment: hosted for low-latency consumer-facing features, Dedicated for steady throughput, and a Private/VPC option for regulated pipelines. Primary engineering questions focused on SDK integration (JS/Python), adapters for LangChain and LlamaIndex, gateway/proxy patterns for on-prem, how rate limiting and quotas surface to clients, and what observability hooks (OpenTelemetry/Jaeger/trace ids) Redwood exposes. Security touched on KMS integration, audit logs, and SOC2 artifacts. Next steps: bench, security packet, and follow-up pilot kickoff.

Topics discussed:
- SDK quickstart, LangChain + LlamaIndex adapters
- Gateway / proxy vs sidecar vs direct SDK calls
- Rate-limits: per-token, per-route, global quota semantics
- Observability: traces, per-request token/cost metrics, logs/retention
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs

Transcript:
[00:00] Claire Mendoza: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, great to meet you all. We're Claire at Redwood, AE. Uh, quick round of intros?
[00:10] Maya Chen: Hi I'm Maya, Head of Platform at Arboretum. We run a mixed fleet — some cloud microservices, a few on-prem data pipelines.
[00:18] Tom Bolton: Tom, CTO, focused on architecture and compliance.
[00:22] Luis Ortega: Luis, lead ML eng, I'll be hands-on for the pilot.
[00:25] Priya Rao: Priya, security, I'll be the compliance reviewer.
[00:29] Devon Park: Devon here, Redwood SE, I usually do the integration and bench stuff.
[00:33] Claire Mendoza: Cool, thanks. High level Arboretum goal: embed a set of LLM features in our search and docs product — some low latency chat, embeddings for semantic search, and a nightly batch reranker. We saw your doc on Dedicated pools and Private VPC so wanted to align on integration model and operations.
[00:50] Maya Chen: Right, and our primary constraints are: one, data residency for PII pipelines; two, predictable unit economics for high-traffic flows; three, instrumentability — we need fine grained metrics.
[01:02] Devon Park: Makes sense. For SDKs we support Python and Node — we have sample quickstarts. Are you using LangChain or LlamaIndex in your stack?
[01:10] Luis Ortega: We're mostly LangChain for orchestration, but some teams use LlamaIndex on the search path. We need both adapters to be easy to drop in.
[01:18] Devon Park: Great — Redwood's SDK has first-class LangChain connectors, and the community LlamaIndex adapter is maintained in the repo. Small caveat: the adapter naming in the docs sometimes spells LlamaIndex as llama-index or Llama Index, so our quickstart has exact import snippets.
[01:32] Luis Ortega: Ha yeah, we've hit that typo before. For LlamaIndex, do you preserve chunk-level metadata so we can do selective retrieval?
[01:40] Devon Park: Yes, retrieval is passthrough; the embedding pipeline tags vectors with original chunk IDs. We also surface the vector-id in response metadata so downstream services can re-hydrate.
[01:52] Priya Rao: From security perspective, how does the gateway/proxy option look? We can't push certain data out directly to hosted endpoints without encrypting keys in KMS.
[02:00] Claire Mendoza: Two patterns: 1) direct SDK calls from services into Redwood-hosted endpoints with VPC peering and private networking for Private deployments, or 2) a gateway/proxy sidecar you run — that can be used with Dedicated or Private. The sidecar handles local auth, credential injection, and rate-limit enforcement locally.
[02:18] Tom Bolton: If we run a sidecar on-prem, how do we handle model upgrades or rollbacks? We don't want to patch a fleet manually.
[02:26] Devon Park: Good question. For Dedicated/Private we push runtime configs from the Redwood control plane. Sidecars pull a signed manifest and support canary rollouts per cluster. You can pin model versions per route so rollouts are controlled.
[02:40] Maya Chen: What about observability — we need trace IDs through the whole pipeline. Can Redwood propagate trace context so we can stitch together traces in our Jaeger?
[02:49] Devon Park: Yes, we support OpenTelemetry headers. Outgoing responses include trace-id and we can export spans to your OTLP collector (self-hosted or vendor). We also provide per-request token and cost metrics as tags.
[03:03] Maya Chen: Per-request token costs as tags? So I can see cost per API call in our traces?
[03:07] Devon Park: Correct — token_count, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, and cost_usd are available as attributes. That helps for SLO and cost allocations.
[03:16] Luis Ortega: That's useful. For rate-limits: do you expose headers like X-RateLimit-Remaining or do clients need to call a separate quota API?
[03:24] Devon Park: We expose standard headers (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset) for the hosted API. For Dedicated we support both headers and a telemetry endpoint that returns quota usage per key. For Private, you can surface those locally via the sidecar.
[03:41] Priya Rao: And quotas can be defined per-customer, per-route, and per-model?
[03:45] Claire Mendoza: Yes, policies are flexible: per-api-key, per-route, per-model, and global account caps. We can also configure burst windows separately from steady-state RPM.
[03:55] Tom Bolton: We're also worried about cold-start latencies for occasional large requests. Do you have KV cache warmup or prefix caching?
[04:04] Devon Park: Our runtime supports KV-cache warmup and prefix caching; for large batched workloads we recommend Dedicated with pre-warmed workers. The control plane can prefetch common prompts into cache on rollout.
[04:17] Luis Ortega: On the topic of cost: what's the unit economics for a dedicated pool vs hosted? Ballpark figures to budget.
[04:24] Claire Mendoza: I'll send the exact pricing sheet but rough: hosted pay-as-you-go is higher per-token but no infra commitments. Dedicated has a monthly commit and lowers per-token inference costs significantly. Private has a base platform fee plus infra. We'll attach a spreadsheet.
[04:38] Maya Chen: For the pilot we want to test three flows: 1) low-latency chat on hosted, 2) batch reranker on Dedicated, and 3) PII-handling pipeline on Private/VPC. Can Redwood support running those in parallel?
[04:51] Devon Park: Absolutely — routing policy can route requests by tag: 'latency' -> hosted, 'batch' -> dedicated, 'sensitive' -> private. We can demo routing rules in the pilot.
[05:02] Priya Rao: On KMS: Can Redwood integrate with our AWS KMS or an HSM? We need keys never visible to Redwood control plane for certain data.
[05:10] Devon Park: We have KMS integrations for hosted customers using a Customer-Managed Key (CMK) via AWS IAM roles. For the strictest requirements we offer a private deployment with HSM-backed key material, where the key operations are performed in customer-managed VPC.
[05:24] Priya Rao: Audit logs: retention and export options?
[05:28] Claire Mendoza: Audit logs are available for Dedicated and Private. Hosted has audit events but retention is shorter unless you add the compliance pack. We can stream logs to your S3/GCS or to a SIEM via secure forwarder.
[05:40] Luis Ortega: On the SDK experience — latency on small chat messages is important. Is there a websocket streaming option?
[05:45] Devon Park: Yes, streaming via websockets or SSE for both hosted and dedicated. Private supports streaming too but depends on your proxy configuration. The JS SDK auto-reconnects and resumes token streaming where supported.
[05:58] Maya Chen: A few gotchas we've seen: LangChain chain-of-thought prompts can leak context if KV cache isn't invalidated properly. Is cache eviction deterministic?
[06:08] Devon Park: Eviction policies are tunable: time-based TTLs, LRU, and manual invalidation via API. For sensitive workloads we recommend not caching full prompts and instead caching only embeddings or non-PII artifacts.
[06:22] Tom Bolton: We run internal traffic shaping — is there a way to have Redwood signal backpressure so our gateway can shed load?
[06:29] Devon Park: We have per-route congestion backoff headers and a 'queue-length' metric in the response for Dedicated, so your gateway can implement circuit-breaking.
[06:38] Luis Ortega: For LlamaIndex adapter, can we store retrieved node ids and pass them back to the model for streaming re-rank?
[06:45] Devon Park: Yes, retrieval metadata is preserved and passed as structured tool-calls in streaming responses. There can be small differences between LangChain and LlamaIndex payload formats; our adapter normalizes them.
[06:58] Maya Chen: Onboarding time — how long to get pilot up and running? We're aiming for pilot week of Aug 16th.
[07:04] Claire Mendoza: That timeline is doable. Typical flow: 1 week to get creds and network setup, 1 week for SDK/adapter integration and smoke tests, then bench and 1-week pilot. So kickoff the week of Aug 16 fits.
[07:16] Priya Rao: A question on encryption in transit: do you support mTLS between sidecar and Redwood control plane?
[07:22] Devon Park: Yes, mTLS is supported for Private deployments and optional for Dedicated. Hosted supports TLS with client certs for certain enterprise plans.
[07:33] Luis Ortega: For our perf bench, what tooling do you recommend? We can give sample payloads — do you have a recommended harness?
[07:40] Devon Park: We usually run k6 for concurrency and a small python harness for token-level metrics. I'll run a bench from our side against your sample and share raw logs plus a CSV of latency/cost breakdown.
[07:52] Tom Bolton: Regarding fallback policies: if hosted is saturated, can we failover to a smaller, cheaper model automatically?
[07:58] Devon Park: Yes — routing policies can map to fallback chains. For example: preferred=high-quality-llm, fallback=quantized-lowcost-variant. We also support gradual degrade by switching to summary-only responses.
[08:11] Maya Chen: Are there any known limits on embedding dimensionality or vector store compatibility we should be aware of?
[08:17] Devon Park: We support standard vector dims up to 4096; for very large dims we recommend dedicated pools. We have connectors for FAISS, Pinecone, and you can stream embeddings into your own vector service.
[08:30] Claire Mendoza: Okay quick pause — I want to confirm action items and next steps. Devon will run the bench; I'll send pricing and topology docs; Priya will send compliance Qs; Arboretum will provide sample payloads and a list of routes to test.
[08:43] Priya Rao: I'll also send the specific data categories that can't leave our VPC.
[08:47] Luis Ortega: We'll aim to get sample payloads by Aug 6.
[08:50] Claire Mendoza: Great. Any final questions before we wrap?
[08:54] Tom Bolton: One small detail: can we get an export of per-token cost logic so finance can model spend?
[08:59] Claire Mendoza: Yes we'll include the cost model CSV — tokens, encoder/decoder split, and expected per-token microcost for both hosted and dedicated.
[09:09] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. Sounds good — excited to try the pilot.
[09:12] Claire Mendoza: Thanks — we'll follow up with the packet shortly.

title: Consolidate overlay tokens and micro-elevation steps for dense component surfaces
author: Ava Martinez
text:
Current token set has grown organically and contains overlapping overlay colors and coarse elevation steps that cause noisy visuals in dense UIs (tables, compact cards, action lists). This ticket consolidates semantic overlay tokens and introduces a 4-step micro-elevation scale optimized for high-density surfaces. Goal: reduce visual clutter, improve contrast consistency, and provide clear migration paths for components that render many stacked surfaces.

We observed inconsistent overlay usage across components: some teams used opaque semantic overlays (fog-1/2) while others applied shadow-only elevations. Dense surfaces like table rows, compact controls, and small cards amplify these inconsistencies, creating perceived noise and accessibility regressions at smaller sizes. Current elevation steps (none, low, medium, high) are too coarse for micro-interactions and stacked overlays (e.g., popovers on dense tables).

Introduce a consolidated set of semantic overlay tokens (surface-overlay-*/surface-muted-*) and a micro-elevation ramp (elev-micro-0..3) with corresponding shadow and alpha blends. Update token naming to be explicit about intent (overlay vs. elevation) and provide guidance and migration helpers for components: buttons, rows, tables, tooltips, popovers, and charts with overlays.

Use semantic tokens (overlay/muted/foreground) rather than surface-level color names to reduce misuse across themes.
Provide a separate micro-elevation ramp instead of reusing existing elevation steps to avoid breaking larger-card visuals.
Alpha overlays are preferred for subtle emphasis to keep chroma constant across themes; however, we will keep one solid overlay token for high-contrast modal backdrops.
Opted for 4 micro-steps to balance perceptible depth with minimal v. fine-grained complexity; adding more steps increases developer burden and choice friction.
Tradeoff: tighter visual system may require small visual tweaks on dashboards and charts — we will provide tooling and automated diff previews to accelerate review.

surface-overlay-01..04: alpha-blend overlays with increasing opacity for localized emphasis (usable on any base surface)
surface-muted-01..02: low-contrast tints for disabled/placeholder surfaces
elev-micro-0..3: shadow + subtle lift; designed for compact stacks (row popovers, tooltips, dropdowns)
elev-standard-0..4: alias to existing system for backward compatibility
type-scale-adjustment: small-step typography tokens (type-sm/compact) for dense tables and labels
radius-compact: new radius tokens (r-compact-0..2) to unify small controls

All overlay and elevation combinations must pass WCAG AA contrast for interactive controls; examples and automated checks will be included in the token test harness.
Provide light/dark previews and a11y delta report for each component migration PR.
Avoid relying on shadow alone to convey interactive state; pair with focus outlines or color shifts for keyboard users.

Add new tokens to tokens.json and CSS variables: --surface-overlay-01..04, --elev-micro-0..3, --radius-compact-0..2, --type-compact-*.
Create mapping layer in token compiler so components can opt-in to :compact mode via component props or token context.
Provide a migration CLI that lists files using deprecated tokens (e.g., overlay-legacy, elev-low) and suggests replacements.
Update React component API defaults: Table.Row, Card.Compact, Button.Small should switch to compact tokens behind a feature flag.
Add visual diff snapshots to CI for affected components and a token diff page in Console for designers to review.

New tokens merged and available in tokens package and compiled CSS variables.
At least: Button (small/primary/secondary), Table.Row (compact), Chart.Legend overlay, Tooltip, and Popover components updated to use new tokens with visual tests passing.
Automated contrast reports show no regressions on high-impact views (dashboard, analytics table).
Migration CLI can detect >=90% of in-repo usages of legacy overlay/elevation tokens and propose mappings.
Design sign-off on Figma spec and Console token diff preview.

Phase 1 (token release): add tokens to tokens package, publish beta package, update Console token diff page. (2 weeks)
Phase 2 (component opt-in): update components behind feature flag; enable for internal staging and run visual diffs. (2 weeks)
Phase 3 (broad migration): flip opt-in for low-risk components and provide migration PRs for larger surfaced components (tables, charts). (3 weeks)
Phase 4 (cleanup): deprecate legacy tokens and remove after one release cycle, provide detailed changelog. (2 weeks)
Rollback: feature flags per component and token aliases to map to previous visuals if quick rollback needed.

Risk: Small contrast regressions on legacy pages — Mitigation: run tokenized contrast reports before flip and keep per-page fallbacks.
Risk: Developers misapply overlay tokens — Mitigation: document clear usage examples and add linter rules for token domains (overlay vs elevation).
Risk: Unintended performance impacts from extra CSS variables — Mitigation: compile variant bundles for compact mode and lazy-load token CSS where applicable.

Figma: Compact Density Token spec - https://www.figma.com/file/abcd1234/compact-density-tokens
Confluence: Design doc - Consolidated Overlay Tokens - https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/DS/Overlay+Consolidation
GitHub draft PR (tokens): https://github.com/redwood-inference/design-tokens/pull/783
CI visual diff job: https://ci.redwood.ai/job/visual-diff/compact-density
Token diff preview in Console: /console/tokens/diff/compact-density

Please review naming conventions closely — we prefer intent-first names (surface-overlay-*) over color-based names.
Check the micro-elevation visual scale at 8px, 12px, and 16px row heights to ensure perceived depth is subtle but noticeable.
Designers: confirm Figma components use updated token references (do not hardcode RGBA values).

title: Auto-allocation failing: vendor payee name variation triggers manual review and split-payment hold
text:
Issue summary:
Accounts Payable auto-allocation is failing for a batch of supplier invoices where the payee name in the invoice (free-text) does not match the canonical vendor record. The payments pipeline flags these invoices for manual review and, for some, splits the payment across multiple ledger entities, causing a hold on the scheduled payout run.

Impact:
- 18 invoices (total $45,920 USD) stuck in 'manual review' state preventing the weekly payrun (next run scheduled 2026-03-13 02:00 UTC).
- Affected suppliers include two recurring vendors: Nimbus Data Services and Hightide Consulting.
- Finance ops cannot release payments until manual reconciliation is completed; this may cause late fees with one supplier.

Environment:
- Production AP pipeline (payments-engine v3.6.1)
- Reconciliation microservice (recon-svc v2.1.0)
- Vendor master reference: vendor_master-prod (region: us-west)

Observed behavior:
- Invoices with payee names like 'Nimbus Data, LLC' and 'Nimbus Data Services Inc.' did not match vendor_master entry 'Nimbus Data Services'. The auto-match routine returns status NOT_MATCHED and _split_allocation: true_ for some invoices where the system attempted to allocate across two subsidiary entities (US / EU) based on ambiguous tax id missing.
- Logs show payee_normalizer returning two candidate matches and the matching scorer falling below the threshold (score 0.62, threshold 0.75).
- The payments scheduler flagged these invoices and excluded them from the commit file for the ACH run.

Expected behavior:
- Minor variations in legal suffix (LLC/Inc./Ltd) and punctuation should be normalized and match the vendor_master entry when tax ID or bank account matches are present. If ambiguous, the system should surface a single tentative match instead of triggering split allocations.

Steps to reproduce (observed on prod ingestion flow):
1) Upload invoice PDF with payee header 'Nimbus Data, LLC' and tax id empty via AP UI.
2) Ingested by OCR/ingest pipeline (ingest-svc v1.8.0) which emits payee_name = 'Nimbus Data, LLC'.
3) Auto-match executed by payments-engine; normalizer emits candidates ["Nimbus Data Services","Nimbus Data"], scorer returns top score 0.62.
4) Matching logic treats score < 0.75 and missing tax id as ambiguous -> sets split_allocation=true and routes to manual-review queue.

Attachments / logs (snippets):
- payments-engine.log (2026-03-10T14:04:22Z): MATCH_ATTEMPT invoice=INV-2026-0034 payee_raw='Nimbus Data, LLC' candidates=['Nimbus Data Services','Nimbus Data'] scores=[0.62,0.58] result=NOT_MATCHED
- recon-svc.log (2026-03-10T14:04:25Z): ALLOCATION_DECISION invoice=INV-2026-0034 split_allocation=true reason='ambiguous_tax_id'
- scheduler.log (2026-03-11T01:50:00Z): PAYRUN_EXCLUDE invoice=INV-2026-0034 status='manual_review' payrun=2026-03-13

Relevant links:
- Slack thread: #finance-ops (thread t12345)
- Confluence: /display/FIN/Payee+Normalization+Runbook

Notes:
- This problem started spiking on 2026-03-08 after deploy of payments-engine v3.6.1 (PR #5462). We should consider whether the new fuzzy-matcher thresholds or the recent change to split allocation behavior (INT-329012) are related.

Upload invoice PDF with payee 'Nimbus Data, LLC' via AP UI
Confirm OCR sets payee_name = 'Nimbus Data, LLC'
Observe payments-engine matching run and candidate scores
See invoice routed to manual-review with split_allocation=true and excluded from next payrun

2026-03-10T14:04:22Z payments-engine MATCH_ATTEMPT invoice=INV-2026-0034 payee_raw='Nimbus Data, LLC' candidates=['Nimbus Data Services','Nimbus Data'] scores=[0.62,0.58] result=NOT_MATCHED
2026-03-10T14:04:25Z recon-svc ALLOCATION_DECISION invoice=INV-2026-0034 split_allocation=true reason='ambiguous_tax_id'
2026-03-11T01:50:00Z scheduler PAYRUN_EXCLUDE invoice=INV-2026-0034 status='manual_review' payrun=2026-03-13

2026-03-10 15:12 - Priya Kapoor (Finance Ops): Flagged batch in #finance-ops — 18 invoices pending manual review. Requested engineering assist to avoid weekly payrun miss.
2026-03-10 16:30 - Mateo Ruiz (Platform Eng): Reproduced locally against prod snapshot. Fuzzy matcher top score frequently 0.58-0.66 for these payee variations. Investigating threshold change in v3.6.1 PR #5462.
2026-03-11 09:04 - Priya Kapoor (Finance Ops): One supplier (Hightide Consulting) emailed about possible late fee. Holding payments is high-impact. Prioritize please.
2026-03-11 11:20 - Mateo Ruiz (Platform Eng): Temporary workaround proposed: lower matching threshold from 0.75 to 0.65 for known-repeating vendors when bank account or tax id partially matches. Will run canary for today's manual review queue.
2026-03-12 08:45 - Alyssa Chen (Finance Ops Manager): Approved canary change for vendor whitelist. Asked engineering to prepare rollback plan and to add a more explicit audit flag in the UI so CS can triage faster.
2026-03-12 10:10 - Mateo Ruiz (Platform Eng): Deployed canary to 10% of payruns and ran reconciliation script to re-evaluate 18 invoices; 12 moved to AUTO_MATCH and included in staging payrun commit. Monitoring for false positives.

Change introduced in payments-engine v3.6.1 tightened fuzzy-matcher threshold from 0.7 -> 0.75 (PR #5462).
Normalizer treats legal suffixes (LLC/Inc) differently now; normalization rule set v1.4 removed some aliasing entries for 'Nimbus' cluster.
Short-term fix: apply vendor-whitelist override to reduce threshold for repeated vendors with prior matching history.
Long-term: expand canonical alias table, add deterministic matching fallback using bank_account and tax_id precedence, and add clearer triage UI metadata (candidate scores visible to ops).

Temporary mitigation: Deployed threshold override for vendor-whitelist (applied to Nimbus & Hightide) and reprocessed the 18 invoices; 12 auto-matched and scheduled for inclusion in next payrun. Remaining 6 require manual tax-id confirmation. Follow-up action items created: 1) Reintroduce alias mappings for 'Nimbus' cluster (PR draft created), 2) Add bank-account-first deterministic matching path, 3) Add audit view for match-candidates in AP UI. Planned permanent fix timeline: deploy alias mapping and deterministic path by 2026-03-20.

title: incidents
text:
IncidentBot: :rotating_light: Heads up: possible incident-adjacent issue reported via Support — some customers seeing 4xx when using quickstart templates. Suspected cause: new template telemetry header. Thread for triage + mitigation.

Christine Wong: I’m on. What’s the current symptom + blast radius?

Priya Shah: From SUP intake: “works in Postman / local, fails in corp network.” Getting 400/403 from their proxy before request reaches us. Started after they updated to the newest template. I’ll paste the snippet they shared:
```
> POST https://api.redwoodinference.com/v1/chat/completions
< 403 Forbidden
< Server: CorporateProxy
< X-Proxy-Error: disallowed_header

Blocked header: X-Redwood-Template
```

Monica Patel: That matches what we just added in quickstarts PR-115 (template-origin tagging). Header name in code: `X-Redwood-Template: rag-agent` and `X-Redwood-Template-Version: 0.4.0`.

Logan Wright: Ugh. Some enterprises run “allowlist headers only” proxies. Even if our gateway accepts it, their proxy can hard-fail.

Brian Murphy: Confirming: we allowlist those headers at our edge (PR-18421). But that only helps once traffic reaches us. If their proxy rejects unknown `X-*`, we can’t fix server-side.

Christine Wong: Do we have a quick repro? Anyone able to simulate with a strict proxy locally?

Ibrahim Khan: I can spin up a quick nginx in “underscores_in_headers off” mode but that’s different. The customer error is explicit “disallowed_header”. Some Zscaler configs do this.

Allison Grant: Also note: if we try to move it to baggage/trace headers, some networks block those too. `traceparent` is usually allowed but not guaranteed.

Monica Patel: Immediate mitigation: make telemetry headers opt-in in templates (default off). CLI can ask during init or a config flag/env.

Dev Patel: +1. Support needs a simple workaround we can hand to users today.

Priya Shah: What should we tell them right now? “Remove the header”? In templates it’s automatic.

Monica Patel: For current users: set env var to disable tagging and redeploy. We already have a config module; we can add something like:
`REDWOOD_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY=0`
and skip adding `X-Redwood-Template*` headers.

Brian Murphy: Alternative: move identifier to `User-Agent` (most proxies permit). Example: `User-Agent: redwood-quickstart/rag-agent-python/0.4.0` appended to whatever the HTTP library sets.

Logan Wright: For KPI measurement, `User-Agent` is acceptable for a first pass (lower risk). We’d need the gateway to pass it through unchanged (it does). Analytics can parse it.

Christine Wong: Any downside? Some SDKs set UA; we’d be concatenating. But that’s fine.

Kaitlyn Nguyen: Security/privacy note: whatever we send must not include user identifiers, org names, repo names, etc. Template name + version only.

Monica Patel: Agree. We’ll keep it to fixed strings.

Owen Phillips: FYI I’m seeing the same pattern in a Solutions Eng Slack DM from a prospect. They said “proxy strips all non-standard headers; returns 4xx”. So likely not isolated.

Christine Wong: Let’s make this a mitigation plan:
1) Hotfix templates to disable custom telemetry headers by default.
2) Provide workaround: disable flag/env var; upgrade templates.
3) Follow-up: move template tagging to `User-Agent` (opt-in) + update docs.

Logan Wright: I’ll update telemetry requirements: treat custom headers as “best effort” and not required for success metrics. We can still track “template install/init” events separately.

Priya Shah: I’ll draft a troubleshooting blurb for docs + support macro:
- Symptom: 403/400 from corporate proxy
- Fix: disable template telemetry headers (`REDWOOD_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY=0`) or upgrade to next patch
- Explanation: some proxies block unknown headers

Dev Patel: Please include a copy/paste snippet in the macro.

Monica Patel: Here’s what it’ll look like in Python template client init:
```py
if config.template_telemetry_enabled:
 headers["X-Redwood-Template"] = TEMPLATE_NAME
 headers["X-Redwood-Template-Version"] = TEMPLATE_VERSION
```
Default `template_telemetry_enabled = False`.

Brian Murphy: From platform side: nothing urgent to deploy. But we should add a note in the gateway docs that template telemetry headers are optional and may break behind strict proxies.

Allison Grant: If we do `User-Agent` tagging, please don’t put it into span attributes as-is (cardinality). Use normalized values only.

Christine Wong: Assigning owners:
- Monica: patch templates + CLI docs, PR today
- Priya: support macro + docs troubleshooting update
- Logan: adjust KPI spec / analytics expectations
- Brian: sanity-check UA pass-through + confirm no downstream sanitization

Alex Martinez: Jumping in — let’s prioritize the “default off” change. We can’t have templates fail in enterprise networks.

Monica Patel: Acknowledged. I’ll cut a patch release (0.4.1) for both Python + TS templates. We’ll add a release note: “Telemetry headers now opt-in due to proxy compatibility.”

Priya Shah: For the existing customer ticket, I’ll reply now with the workaround and note a patch is coming.

Brian Murphy: Quick test result: our edge forwards `User-Agent` as received; no rewriting. So UA tagging is viable.

Christine Wong: Great. Any indication of impact to users not behind proxies? None — only those strict networks.

IncidentBot: :memo: Status update requested. Current state: mitigation in progress (template change). No service degradation observed.

Monica Patel: PR up internally; should merge within the hour. I’ll ping Dana for TS template parity.

Christine Wong: Once merged, please post the exact env var and the release version so Support can point to it.

Monica Patel: Final names:
- Env: `REDWOOD_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false` (more explicit)
- Default: false
- Docs: “If you’re behind a corporate proxy, keep this disabled.”

Dev Patel: Works for Support.

Priya Shah: +1, clearer than `=0`.

Logan Wright: I’ll align dashboards to use UA tag if present, otherwise rely on init events + repo/CLI download telemetry.

Christine Wong: Cool. Marking as contained once patch is out + workaround communicated.

IncidentBot: :white_check_mark: Triage complete. Next check-in after template patch release is published + Support macro updated.

title: Hosted canary rollout: traffic split in us-east not matching Console config (canary receiving ~25% when set to 10%)
text:
Issue summary
Customer reports that the canary cohort is receiving substantially more traffic than configured for a Hosted route rollout. Console shows canary set to 10% (after being reduced from 25%), but observed canary traffic remains ~22–27% in us-east.

Impact
- Customer sees increased cost/latency regression exposure compared to intended 10% canary.

title: Capacity conversation cafe - ops notes (informal)
author: Maya Chen
text:
Context: informal midweek 'conversation cafe' after standup. Goal: surface small ideas and low-cost experiments we can try this sprint to improve regional tail latency and reduce wasted warm tokens. Not a formal runbook update — raw notes and hypotheses.

Date: 2026-08-19
Facilitator: Maya Chen
Attendees: Ethan, Rashmi, Jonas, Priya (+ a few drop-ins from SRE shift)

High level summary:
- Short experiments proposed: lightweight cross-region slot borrowing prototype, model-family-specific prewarm windows, and an adaptive cheap-priming layer for cold long-context requests.
- Observed problem: 95th/99th latency spikes correlate with bursty long-context chat sessions (>=1024 tokens) in EU-west and APAC during peak minutes.
- Quick metric snapshot (from last 24h dashboards):
 - Global GPU slot fill: 78% avg, regional variance EU-west 91%, US-west 66%, APAC 72%
 - Queue wait median: 120 ms, 95th: 1.8 s, 99th: 3.6 s
 - Warm-token waste (estimate): 11.3% of tokens billed are from prewarm prefixes not used due to session truncation

Notes / raw observations:
- Jonas: EU-west burst pattern looks like a handful of customers running long chat threads during their morning. These sessions are sticky and take multiple GPU windows. The routing policy currently pins by customer which causes local saturation.
- Rashmi: We could allow ephemeral cross-region handoff for read-only inference (low-sensitivity customers) to smooth hits. Need to evaluate networking latency vs. priming cost.
- Ethan: Proposed prototype: 'borrowed slot' RSVP flow — if local queue > threshold and remote region has available slots and RTT < 80ms, move request with metadata (mark as borrowed). Fall back to pinned region if model-variant mismatch.
- Priya: We should be cautious with billing attribution and SLA messaging; borrowed slots change customer region visibility. Add a header to responses so customers can opt-in in beta.

Ideas & experiments (lightweight, rank-ordered):
1) Cheap-priming shim (2–4 tokens tokenized primer) for very long requests that typically cold-start KV caches. Hypothesis: small cheap primer reduces KV miss amplification and reduces downstream warm-token spend. Implementation: insert a zero-effect primer token pair (e.g., "​") at dispatch for sequences longer than 1024 tokens. Test on sample of 5 heavy customers. (Owner: Ethan)

2) Region-borrow MVP: allow non-sensitive routes to accept cross-region forwarding with RTT cutoff 80ms and cost threshold X (config flag). Add flags: allow_borrow, borrow_max_tps. Start with Canary customers only. (Owner: Jonas)

3) Model-family batch-sched shim: detect llama-family vs opt-family vs mix and use different max_batch_size and latency SLOs per family. Quick config toggle in balancer to test one family for 48h. (Owner: Rashmi)

4) Prewarm window heuristics: when a customer opens a session and sends short messages (<50 tokens) but later sends long messages, our current prewarming window is too short. Idea: keep a soft prefix cache per session for 2x previous max length or 30s whichever is larger. (Owner: Priya)

Risk notes / questions to escalate:
- Cross-region borrow introduces data residency/regulatory risks for enterprise customers. Need product gating and an allowlist. (Raised: Priya)
- Billing/usage attribution complexity for borrowed slots — finance needs to sign off on how to report inter-region cost. Add to JIRA-OPS-1987.
- Potential negative UX: slightly higher RTT for borrowed requests (if network unpredictable). Need to measure error/fallthrough rate.

Quick experiment design details (cheap-priming):
- Population: 5 identified heavy chat customers in EU-west (consent from customer support).
- Metric targets: reduce 99th token latency by >=10% and warm-token waste by >=5% within 7 days. Secondary: no regression on per-request generation quality (basic sampling-based sanity checks).
- Instrumentation: tag requests with header X-CP-PRIMER and emit per-session primer_used boolean to metrics.
- Rollout: 5% -> 25% -> 100% for those customers after success checks.

Operational runbook snippets (temporary):
- If borrower fails RTT check or model mismatch: fallback to original region with logging event BORROW_FAIL_{reason}. Alert at BORROW_FAIL rate > 1% per minute for canary set.
- If priming causing hallucination or tokenization breaks (edge cases with non-printable primers), auto-kill primer flow and revert config. Add guard: primer tokens must be in UTF-8 safe set.

Action items (owner, by-date):
- Ethan: implement cheap-priming shim prototype + instrumentation (due 2026-08-25)
- Jonas: prototype borrow flow in balancer (read-only alpha) + test harness for RTT gating (due 2026-08-27)
- Rashmi: prepare model-family batching toggle and run 48h experiment on opt-family traffic (due 2026-08-24)
- Priya: write product note and permission gating for borrowed slots; draft opt-in header semantics (due 2026-08-23)
- Maya: coordinate with customer-support to reach out to the 5 heavy customers for consent to test cheap primer (due 2026-08-20)

Open questions to discuss next standup:
- How do we measure 'warm-token waste' precisely across multi-tenant caches? Is there an existing metric we can repurpose?
- Should borrowed slot be a first-class routing policy or an emergency backstop only?
- How to communicate trial features to enterprise customers while keeping SLA promises?

Notes to self / scribbles:
- Consider adding an 'economics leash' to borrowed slots: only borrow if estimated net cost per token lower than local prewarm cost + expected latency penalty.
- Small thought: if we add cheap-priming globally, agree on token content that is Unicode invisible and robust in different tokenizers. Might need tokenizer tests across top-6 models.

Relevant links & references:
- Jira: JIRA-OPS-1987 (billing attribution for cross-region flow)
- Confluence: priming strategies (internal draft) https://confluence.redwood.team/pages/priming-strategies-2026
- Slack channel: #gpu-ops for immediate followups

Closing: informal session was productive — we have 3 small low-risk experiments to try this sprint. We'll reconvene in async thread with early telemetry and decide whether to continue or revert.

---
Raw appendices (telemetry snippets grabbed in meeting):
1) EU-west heavy session sample (timestamps omitted for PII):
 - 4 sessions > 1200 tokens in 20-min window -> local queue 2.1x baseline, 99p latency 3.9s
2) Sample log line for BORROW_FAIL: {event: BORROW_FAIL, reason: MODEL_MISMATCH, origin_region: eu-west, target_region: us-east, rtt_ms: 102} (we'll add structured schema later)

End of notes.

title: eng-runtime
text:
devon: Heads up — canary running NCCL 3.5.2 on A100 pools is showing intermittent p2p queue-depth stalls. tail latency spikes ~3x on 99th for multi-GPU inference.

maria: ugh, saw that in the dashboard. any quick repro or logs?

devon: attaching excerpt from the canary job logs, truncated: 
```
[nccl] socket send failed: Resource temporarily unavailable
[nccl] enqueue timeout after 200ms, queue_depth=64
TRACE: collective allreduce timed out, retries=3
```

ashok: queue_depth=64 is our default for the runtime. 3.5.2 seems to hit backpressure more often vs 3.4.x. could be handshake pacing changes.

lina: can we try lowering queue depth + enable adaptive backoff? there are two knobs: `p2p.queue_depth` and `collective.backoff_ms`. small change first (queue_depth -> 48) to measure throughput/latency tradeoff.

devon: quick experiment: lowered to 48 in a canary, tail latency dropped ~30% but throughput lost ~8% on that microbench. still saw occasional enqueue timeout.

maria: 8% throughput loss is acceptable temporarily if it stabilizes latency for customer SLAs. what about increasing backoff jitter?

ashok: propose patch to runtime config: 
```yaml
p2p:
 queue_depth: 48
 adaptive_backoff: true
 backoff_ms: 50
 max_backoff_ms: 1000
collective:
 retry_limit: 5
 handshake_timeout_ms: 5000
```
This enables exponential backoff with jitter. should reduce hot socket retries.

devon: sounds good. need to test memory/KV cache impact too. also observed some kernel-level EAGAINs in dmesg on one node. may be driver/CUDA interplay.

lina: we should gate this behind canary + perf regression harness. add canary rule: fail if 99th latency increases >10% or throughput drop >12% vs baseline.

infra-bot: canary created: runtime-nccl-adaptive-backoff-2399994321. 50 pods in us-west1-a.

maria: if canary passes, we need rollout plan for Dedicated pools. suggest staged rollout by region with a 1-hour ramp and automatic rollback on error budget breach.

ashok: note on cost: lowering queue_depth and adding backoff increases CPU/latency overhead; will raise per-token marginal cost slightly for hosted. include cost note in release.

devon: one more experiment: on a smaller mixed-arch pool (A100 + H100) the stalls are worse. likely p2p parity issues. recommend we avoid mixed-arch for now while we evaluate NCCL 3.5.x.

lina: ack — add policy to smart-routing: prefer homogeneous pools for multi-GPU inference until we validate.

maria: action items:
- ashok: land config change behind feature flag + perf tests (ETA 4h)
- devon: run mixed-arch canary and collect kernel logs (ETA 2h)
- lina: update rollout playbook and smart-routing policy (ETA 6h)

devon: starting kernel log collection now. will paste compressed dmesg snippets if I see EAGAIN from nvlink. :mag:

infra-bot: canary update: 10/50 pods reporting enqueue timeouts, 40/50 stable. collecting traces.

maria: thanks. if the canary keeps these numbers we'll sign off on the adaptive backoff config and schedule a region-by-region rollout with a rollback on error budget triggers. :thumbsup:

devon: one last note — keep NCCL rollback path validated (3.4.x pinned image); raising a small runbook to avoid surprises during TTL windows.

ashok: added runbook PR: `docs/rollouts/nccl-3.5-backoff.md` with rollback commands and commands to force pinned image: 
```bash
kubectl set image ds/inference-runtime inference=redwood/runtime:nccl-3.4.9-pinned -n inference
kubectl rollout restart ds/inference-runtime -n inference
```

lina: cool. will schedule post-mortem if we need rollback.

maria: fine-grained testing next 8h. keep updates in this thread.

devon: will update with kernel log snippets and perf dashboards.

(ends)
