title: Crucible Health: inference latency spike + transient 5xx on /v1/generate (INC-9821)
text:
Customer escalation relayed by Stephanie Nguyen. Crucible Health reported sudden latency spike and burst of 5xx on inference endpoint /v1/generate beginning ~2026-08-28 07:55 PDT. Reported impact: median latency increased from ~120ms to ~900ms; throughput dropped from ~250 req/s to ~150 req/s for Crucible production key; initial customer-observed 5xx rate ~8% during the window; multiple batches timed out and downstream throttles triggered. Customer had a critical demo at 10:00 PDT.

Immediate hypotheses (serving): autoscaler oscillation under burst + degraded single shard causing head-of-line blocking.

Immediate mitigations executed: emergency scale-up of dedicated pool (target +20% capacity) + temporary concurrency limit increase + drain suspected bad instance(s) + enable routing of new requests to compatible fallback model variant (lower context) to reduce per-token work.

Outcome (updated after investigation): improvements observed within ~9–12 minutes; throughput returned to baseline and tail latency normalized after draining the degraded node(s) and reverting autoscaler policy.

Updated root cause (post-incident): the triggering event was an autoscaler policy update that reduced stabilization/cooldown and interacted poorly with a burst in queue depth, causing scale oscillation. One GPU instance concurrently entered a degraded driver state (intermittent kernel launch stalls rather than a hard OOM), amplifying tail latency and increasing request timeouts which surfaced as 5xx at the gateway. The instance replacement lag plus oscillation extended the incident duration.

Impact (finalized): peak 5xx rate revised to ~6–8% (varied by minute) with ~10–12 minute period of elevated errors; throughput dipped to ~60% of baseline at trough. No evidence of data integrity or security issues.

2026-08-28 (Stephanie Nguyen): Forwarded urgent report from Crucible. Asks: infra/serving triage immediately; CS to own comms + schedule exec sync 09:00 PDT; finance to pre-approve priority burst capacity if needed. Customer attachments: request_logs_20260828.zip, detailed_kpi_snapshot.csv.
2026-08-28 (Marcus Lin): Initial hypotheses: autoscaler oscillation under sudden burst + failing shard causing head-of-line blocking. Immediate actions: emergency scale dedicated pool (+20%), temporarily increase max concurrency, route new requests to secondary model variant (lower context), isolate/drain problematic instance(s). ETA for measurable improvement: ~8–12 minutes after scale. Will update INC-9821.
2026-08-28 (Hannah Schmitt): On comms. Proposed external update: mitigation in flight; expect improvement within ~10 minutes; reconvene 09:00 PDT. Requested temporary SLA exception window + demo support. Asked finance to greenlight burst billing pending postmortem.
2026-08-28 (Stephanie Nguyen -> customer): Sent external update: emergency scaling, drain suspected degraded instance, fallback routing enabled. Set expectation of measurable improvement in 8–12 minutes and 09:00 PDT exec sync.
2026-08-29 (Marcus Lin): Investigation summary shared internally/with customer on thread: reverted autoscaler policy update; added cooldown to prevent oscillation; drained/reprovisioned affected instance; hotfix to prevent recurrence. Impact noted as ~8% peak 5xx and ~10 minute window. Action items: customer postmortem by EOD; harden autoscaler testing + canary for autoscaler changes; product routing knob for rapid cross-model fallback; finance confirm priority-burst billing terms.
2026-09-01 (Marcus Lin): Correction after deeper node telemetry review: primary node issue was intermittent driver/kernel launch stalls (no sustained OOM). Updated remediation: rolled new base image + added driver health-check gate to remove degraded nodes faster; autoscaler change now includes 30m canary + enforced cooldown floor. Linked PRs: serving-runtime#18422 (health gate + faster eviction), infra-autoscaler#771 (cooldown floor + canary checklist).
2026-09-03 (Stephanie Nguyen): Closed internal ticket after customer postmortem delivered and follow-up technical review scheduled for next week. Finance confirmed no additional burst-capacity charges for incident window; goodwill credit handled via CS.

title: Migrate chart theme tokens to CSS variables and accessibility hydration
author: Maya Chen
text:
We need to standardize chart visual tokens by migrating the current JS-based token surface to CSS custom properties (CSS vars) and introduce a lightweight runtime hydration toggle for accessibility testing. Current problems: (1) theme tokens for charts live in multiple places (component-level JS, hard-coded chart renderer values, and legacy CSS fallbacks) which makes small visual updates error-prone; (2) runtime theme switches cause full re-mounts of chart canvases increasing perceived latency; (3) accessibility QA requires toggling high-contrast and reduced-motion variants without large perf regressions. This ticket covers design decisions, token naming conventions, migration strategy, and a controlled rollout for charts (time-series, sparkline, bandline) to use CSS variables exposed by the design system, plus a minimal JS hydration layer that maps tokens into renderer configuration only when necessary (e.g., high-contrast mode or user-selected palette). Goals: reduce DOM/JS churn during theme changes, make tokens consumable by non-React surfaces (raw canvas renderers), improve the team's ability to ship color updates with minimal risk, and provide a11y toggle with predictable performance.

Chart color, spacing, and typography tokens are defined as CSS custom properties and documented in the design system tokens page
Renderer can read fallback values from CSS vars without requiring a full component remount
High-contrast and reduced-motion modes can be toggled at runtime with <100ms median impact on first-paint for charts under representative load
Unit and visual regression tests updated to reference token names instead of hard-coded hex values
Design token migration PR merged and release notes added to design-system-1.12

Audit current chart token locations (component JS, renderer defaults, legacy CSS) and produce mapping table
Propose canonical token namespace and names (chart-*) and publish in tokens spec
Create CSS var shim that maps existing theme tokens to new CSS vars for backwards compatibility
Implement renderer read-path: prefer CSS var lookup, fallback to current JS token if var not present
Add a11y runtime hydration toggle to only reconfigure renderer when an a11y preference changes
Measure perf: baseline current mount/hydration, measure after CSS var approach, record p95/p50 latency
Update Figma tokens and export snippets for engineers
Ship a canary build behind feature flag and coordinate with front-end infra for rollout

title: Soft-cancel signal and timed reconnect window for OpenAI-compat streaming
author: Priya Menon
text:
Context and motivation:
Clients and downstream SDKs have been filing incidents where a transient network disconnect or accidental client-side cancel caused a hard termination of a server-side generation mid-critical-tool invocation. This leads to duplicated side-effects when clients retry and poor UX for long-running tool calls. ENG-1842 asked for a safer, backward-compatible streaming lifecycle control that: (1) gives the client a soft-cancel option to request an early but safe end-of-stream, (2) provides a short, server-backed reconnect/resume window so clients can reconnect and resume without restarting the model state, and (3) tightens server-side eviction policy to avoid resource leakage.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a client-visible soft-cancel signal that the OpenAI-compat adapter accepts as "soft_cancel": true in the stream preamble; server treats this as a hint to stop producing new tool invocations, flush structured outputs, and close streams at a safe cutpoint rather than an immediate hard abort.
- Implements a timed resume window (resume_window_ms, default 30_000ms) with short-lived resume tokens returned in the stream termination envelope. A reconnect within the window with the resume token allows the connection manager to rehydrate KV cache and continue where possible.
- Updates server eviction to maintain ephemeral session metadata for the resume window; sessions are aggressively garbage-collected after window expiry.
- Preserves structured output and function-calling semantics across soft-cancel+resume boundaries. If a function call was in-flight, we mark it as 'incomplete' in the termination envelope and allow SDKs to decide whether to re-run.
- Adds observability: new metrics (stream_soft_cancel_total, stream_resume_attempts, stream_resume_success) and alert tweaks to avoid noisy paging for expected reconnects.

Checklist (PR-level):
- [x] Implementation in runtime adapter and connection manager
- [x] Typescript SDK support for resume token handshake and soft-cancel preamble
- [x] Unit tests for session lifecycle and resume window
- [x] Integration test in stream_simulator that reproduces race between disconnect and function-call completion
- [x] Docs and migration notes for OpenAI-compat clients
- [x] Instrumentation and dashboard updates

Commits (summary):
- ae3f2b9 add: resume token envelope and resume_window_ms handling in openai_compat adapter
- 4b7d0c1 feat: connection manager: keep ephemeral session metadata for resume window
- d98a79e fix: ensure KV cache rehydration only for compatible model variants
- 0c2a5f4 feat(sdk/ts): streaming client handshake for soft_cancel + resume token
- b5c3a11 test: stream_simulator integration test for disconnect+resume race
- f7a1d2e docs: openai_compat streaming docs + migration section

Files changed (high level):
- pkg/stream/connection_manager.go: new session store layer (ephemeral TTL), resume token validation, metrics hooks. Small new helper ~180 LOC.
- pkg/stream/protocol/openai_compat.go: parsing of soft_cancel in preamble, termination envelope with resume token/resume_window_ms, compatibility handling for older clients.
- pkg/stream/heartbeat.go: improved heartbeat to update last-seen for resume window and to emit resume candidate metrics.
- sdk/typescript/src/streaming.ts: handshake additions, client option softCancel(), automatic small-retry for reconnect-with-resume.
- docs/openai_compat/streaming.md: new section describing soft-cancel semantics and examples for SDKs.
- internal/testing/stream_simulator.go: adds simulate-flaky-network and reconnect-with-resume scenario for CI.
- console/alerts/stream-timeouts.json: tuned thresholds and one-shot suppression window to avoid paging on expected transient reconnects.
- charts/streaming/values.yaml: minimal default for resume_window_ms and metric configs.

Compatibility notes:
- The soft-cancel field is optional; older clients will ignore it. Servers that do not opt-in to resume_window_ms behave as before (hard termination). The OpenAI-compat adapter will only emit resume tokens when resume_window_ms > 0. No breaking API changes.

Testing and CI:
- Unit test matrix added for 3 model variants and various sequence lengths.
- Stream_simulator integration test initially exposed a flake where KV cache rehydration raced with model warmup (failing test in CI run #1). Fix applied (d98a79e) and CI stabilized.
- CI checks: go-unit, go-integration, ts-unit, lint, e2e-stream-sim. Final run: all passing.

Review thread (selected):
- Yara: "Can we add a metric that tags resume failures by failure reason (token-expired/model-mismatch)? Also please ensure the termination envelope doesn't leak internal IDs."
- Author (Priya): "Added resume_failure_reason tag and redacted internal IDs in the termination envelope (see ae3f2b9). Also updated docs to call out best practices for retries."
- Carlos: "Nits: rename resume_window_ms -> resume_window_ms to be explicit on units (ms). Add a small comment on expected cost model for holding ephemeral sessions."
- Eliot: "Integration test looks comprehensive; recommend small timeout increase on sim to reduce flakiness in CI."
- Carlos: "Approved after nit fixes."

CI timeline and actions:
- 2026-02-12 08:11 UTC: CI run #1 (go unit/integration) - e2e-stream-sim failed due to KV rehydration race.
- 2026-02-12 10:02 UTC: Patch (d98a79e) landed to gate rehydration on warmup signal.
- 2026-02-13 02:18 UTC: Full CI re-run - all checks passed.

Merge outcome:
- Squash-merged into main on 2026-02-15 by main-bot. Changelog entry added under release-candidate. No rollout guard required; feature behind opt-in config flag resume_window_ms > 0.

Migration guidance for SDKs and clients:
- SDKs should surface an opt-in softCancel() option and expose resume token storage for short-lived reconnections. The TS SDK change included here demonstrates the minimal handshake; server will ignore unknown preamble keys for older clients.

Follow-ups captured in ENG-1917:
- Dashboard for resume success rate and per-customer resume latency.
- SRE runbook for investigating resume failures and recommended escalation thresholds.

If revert is needed: the opt-in flag means a quick config rollback (resume_window_ms -> 0) will restore previous behavior without any state migration.

References: ENG-1842 (design doc link: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-1842/soft-cancel-and-resume-window-design), internal perf notes and console dashboard PR linked in the design doc.

Introduces a soft-cancel client signal and a bounded reconnect/resume window for OpenAI-compatible streaming sessions. Improves graceful disconnect handling and reduces inadvertent cold restarts. No public API breaking changes; opt-in fields for compat layer.

alex: Noticed the autoscaler thrashing on GPU nodepools after a couple short AZ network blips this morning. Nodes get marked NotReady -> pods reschedule -> we spawn new GPUs, then scale down again. Cost and pod disruption spike.

mona: Ugh. Which flags are we shipping on CA right now?

alex: We accidentally left a super-aggressive test config: --scale-down-unneeded-time=45s and --scale-down-delay-after-add=0. Also saw --expander=random.

ryan: That's the root cause. For GPU pools I recommend a conservative baseline to add hysteresis:
- --scale-down-unneeded-time=12m
- --scale-down-delay-after-add=20m
- --scale-down-delay-after-failure=8m
- --scale-down-unready-time=25m
- --expander=least-waste
- --max-empty-bulk-delete=1

alex: Agree. Additional operational controls: annotate nodes running long-running GPU workloads with `cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict=false` and configure a tiny warm-pool (min=1) for GPU nodepools so short blips don't force a cold spin-up.

sasha: Cost note: keeping min=1 in eu-west adds roughly ~0.05 GPU-hours per hour to baseline. I'll add to cost dashboard.

title: MagnetWell - Serving mode evaluation: latency & throughput
author: Alex Kim
text:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-29 08:00 PT / 15:00 UTC
Duration: 49 min
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Daniel (Redwood CSM), Jared (CTO - MagnetWell), Mina (Lead ML Eng), Samir (SRE), Lena (PM)

Summary:
MagnetWell is evaluating hosting modes (hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private) with an emphasis on p95 latency targets for low-latency interactive features and high-throughput token/sec batch scoring. Primary constraints: sub-300ms p95 for 512-token streaming responses, peak concurrency ~1.2k concurrent open streams, periodic token storms of 150k tokens/sec for 3-5 minutes in burst scenarios. Discussed tradeoffs, KV cache strategies, quantization and routing/fallbacks. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run a short token/sec benchmark plan on Dedicated, share security docs and pricing.

Topics (auto): Hosting modes; p95 targets; Streaming vs non-streaming; Concurrency modeling; Token/sec benchmarking; Security and compliance

--- Transcript ---
00:00 Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, quick round of intros?
00:05 Jared: Jared Cole, CTO, MagnetWell. We're trying to understand whether to go hosted, reserved/dedicated, or private e.g. VPC-hosted behind our network.
00:10 Mina: Mina, ML lead. I'm mostly worried about the p95 when we do streaming multi-turn assistant stuff.
00:15 Samir: Samir, SRE, I'll own the oper side and hard SLOs.
00:18 Alex: Great. Priya, do you want to run the agenda?
00:20 Priya: Sure. We'll cover current workload profile, p95 targets, concurrency and streaming profile, then tradeoffs and suggested benchmark plan. We'll also cover security asks.
00:28 Lena: Quick note — we have a product launch in mid-September and need a decision by Aug 15 if possible. Tight timeline.
00:34 Priya: Got it, that helps. Can you share current numbers — qps, tokens per request, and what p95 you target today?
00:40 Mina: Right now in-house we see average request size 220 tokens, but longer flows hit 500-600 tokens. For the assistant use-case we need p95 under 300 milliseconds for streaming-first experience for approx 512 token responses. Today we get like 800–1,200ms p95 which is too slow.
00:58 Alex: Ok that's useful. And concurrency?
01:02 Mina: At steady-state we expect 250 concurrent conversations, but peak spikes up to 1,200 concurrent open streaming sessions during promos. Also occasionally the scoring pipeline will flood with token bursts, say 100–150k tokens/sec for short 3–5min bursts during events.
01:20 Priya: Nice detail. So two distinct workloads: low-latency streaming with many concurrent connections, and short high-throughput token storms. Both are solvable but we pick different levers — dedicated pools for predictable tail latency, plus KV prefix caching and transient autoscaling for bursts.
01:38 Samir: Two immediate asks: 1) we need predictable p95 to keep frontend SLAs; 2) we need audit logs and KMS integration for keying.
01:47 Alex: On the KMS side we support customer-managed keys for Private and Dedicated via KMS integration — real note: we'll share the KMS doc. For hosted there's envelope encryption and SOC2 but not CMK.
01:58 Mina: That's important. Also what's the realistic p95 we can expect with Hosted? We have a concern that hosted might have variable tails because of multi-tenant cold starts.
02:10 Priya: For streaming short responses on our hosted tier we've seen p95 in the 180–320ms range for 256–512 token responses depending on model and region; dedicated pools consistently hit lower tails — think 120–220ms p95 — because you control the GPU pool and we can pin model variants/quantization. But hosted gives the fastest time to value.
02:33 Jared: So dedicated seems attractive. What about cost delta roughly? We want to know opex delta vs hosted.
02:41 Alex: We'll send a detailed pricing sheet but rough rule — dedicated moves you from pure usage to a committed pool model. Per-token cost can drop significantly especially with batching and cache. But you pay baseline reserved capacity. For token storms, dedicated + autoscale/burst works well.
02:58 Mina: Can you explain how KV cache prefixing would help streaming p95? I know the theory but not the operational details.
03:06 Priya: Sure. If many requests share initial prefixes or system prompts we can cache KV states so future requests avoid recomputing earlier layers. That reduces per-token compute. In streaming cases it cuts steady-state token generation work. Also continuous batching for non-streaming scoring requests increases throughput without hurting tails much.
03:28 Samir: Any caveats re: state eviction or memory pressure on KV caches in multi-tenant hosted?
03:32 Priya: In hosted we limit per-tenant KV retention and use weighted eviction; in dedicated private you control retention policy and memory sizes. For MagnetWell's burst profile, dedicated gives much more flexibility.
03:44 Lena: On Private / VPC option — we'd need on-prem or VPC peering because of HIPAA concerns for some workflows. Does Redwood Private support HSM/KMS?
03:53 Alex: Yes, Private can integrate with your KMS/HSM and on-prem package is available for air-gapped needs. We'll attach the compliance matrix.
04:03 Mina: Ok good. Let's pivot to benchmarking — can Redwood run a small benchmark to validate p95 and token/sec for us?
04:12 Priya: Yes. Our usual plan: we run a 48-hour token/sec run on a dedicated pool with your representative prompts and one hosted quick run for baseline. We'll instrument p50/p95/p99, end-to-end streaming latency including first-byte, and tokens/sec sustained for 5-minute windows and 1-minute windows. We'll also test fallback behavior and cold start degradation.
04:35 Jared: What inputs do you need from us?
04:37 Priya: Samples of prompts, typical payload sizes, expected concurrency curve (minute-by-minute or hour-by-hour), and target SLOs. We'll want a small test harness or can run our generator if you share templates.
04:47 Mina: I'll put together 10 prompt templates and token distribution.
04:50 Samir: How do you simulate network jitter? Our users are global and we see variable region latency.
04:56 Priya: We can run regionally in us-west, eu-west and apply synthetic network latencies. Also we test with different model variants and quantization paths — quantized 4-bit vs fp16 — to show cost/latency tradeoffs.
05:12 Alex: Quick question from Jared earlier — are there any auto-fallbacks if dedicated pool saturates?
05:18 Priya: Yes, policy-based routing can fallback to compatible variants or hosted instances. You can configure hard fail vs degrade modes. We'll show a canary and fallback config in the benchmark.
05:28 Jared: Ok I want to dig into numbers — what's a good baseline for 512 token streaming p95 on A100 class hardware vs H100, and how does batching affect that?
05:39 Priya: Ballpark: on H100 with optimized kernels and fq4 quant we often see ~100–160ms p95 for 512 tokens in dedicated streaming optimized runtime; on A100 it's typically +20–40% tail depending on kernel support. Continuous batching helps non-streaming. For streaming, batching only applies to initial prefix or mixed-request scenarios; too much batching can hurt streaming first-byte.
06:05 Mina: And tokens/sec? If we need to sustain 150k tokens/sec for bursts, what pool size would you recommend?
06:12 Priya: It depends on model size and quant. For a 7B-class model quantized 4-bit, you'd likely need 6–8 H100-equivalent GPUs to sustain 150k tokens/sec with margin. For 13B-class it could be double. We'll propose a specific config in the benchmark plan.
06:28 Samir: That helps. Another SRE question: do you support per-route rate limits and graceful throttling with headers so our frontend can degrade gracefully?
06:36 Alex: Yes, per-route quotas, token-level cost headers, and explicit retry-after semantics. We'll send the docs.
06:42 Lena: On security, we need SOC2, ISO, SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit trails — are these in the enterprise bundle?
06:50 Alex: Yes, SOC2/ISO are standard for enterprise; SAML SSO and RBAC and retention controls are in enterprise. We'll attach the security pack. For Private we can map to your internal audit stack.
06:59 Mina: There's often a gap between theoretical p95 numbers and real app -- e.g., frontend assembling tokens and network overhead. Can we run an E2E synthetic from our staging with your dedicated pool?
07:09 Priya: Absolutely — we can set up a VPC peered dedicated test and run an E2E harness from your staging infra. That will capture network and client-side assembly overheads.
07:19 Jared: Good. One concern: if we use hosted initially and later migrate to dedicated/private, how disruptive is that?
07:25 Alex: We built the API to be consistent — same client calls, model naming. Migration is mostly config-level: pin model versions, update routing to the dedicated endpoint, and a short validation. We can help with a migration runbook.
07:36 Mina: Ok, let's talk about metrics we'll want from the benchmark report — p50/p95/p99 per region, tokens/sec sustained and burst, cost per 1k tokens for each mode, and KV cache hit rates.
07:47 Priya: We'll include all that, plus the per-route latency breakdown and token-level cost header samples. We'll also include whether quantization caused any measurable regen quality regressions for your prompts.
07:58 Samir: On the quality front: we need to be careful with aggressive quantization if it changes hallucination or answer fidelity. Do you run evals tied to prompt sets?
08:06 Priya: Yes, Redwood Optimize will run evals and quality regressions on prompt sets — we can run your ground-truth checks as part of the plan.
08:13 Lena: Timeline recap — we're aiming for decision by Aug 15. Can Redwood commit to pushing benchmark results by Aug 6 so we can review?
08:20 Alex: Yes, if we get assets by July 31 we can run the 48-hour benchmark and aim to deliver results by Aug 6.
08:27 Jared: Great. Minor nit — do you log prompt content in hosted? We have sensitive PII in some prompts.
08:34 Alex: Hosted by default redacts PII in storage and has configurable retention; for full control you want Private or Dedicated with customer-managed retention. We'll put that in the security doc.
08:42 Mina: For test harness we have some long context + tool calls, so we also want to simulate function/tool calling overheads.
08:49 Priya: We'll include function-call payloads and multi-turn flows. We'll simulate tool latencies and measure end-to-end.
08:55 Jared: Any other gotchas we should be aware of?
09:00 Priya: Cold-starts and model variant compatibility are typical; we'll show warmup policies, checkpoint preloads, and hot cache strategies. Also routing for multi-region failover if a region gets saturated.
09:12 Samir: For autoscale during bursts, how fast can you spin up extra nodes?
09:16 Priya: With pre-warmed images and burst pools we can scale in 30–90 seconds depending on the backend. For strict SLOs we recommend a small reserved buffer plus a burst pool to avoid hitting cold-start tails.
09:29 Mina: That probably fits. Anything else on pricing?
09:32 Alex: Pricing note: we'll show committed pool examples and a hybrid — keep base steady on dedicated and route overflow to hosted for cost efficiency.
09:41 Daniel (CSM): From a customer success angle we'll schedule a check-in after the benchmark to walk the report.
09:46 Alex: Great. Quick recap and ownerships: Priya -> benchmark plan and run; Alex -> security docs + pricing; Mina -> prompt templates + token projections; Samir -> network constraints and SLOs; Daniel -> schedule follow-up. Everyone ok?
09:59 Jared: Yep.
10:00 Lena: Yes.
10:02 Alex: We'll target the Aug 6 delivery. Thanks all.
10:06 (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mishears - 'KV cash' in autosave, 'S S O' spelled out, and product names sometimes truncated. Shared artifacts references: benchmarking spreadsheet (drive link: https://drive.redwood.example/magnetwell-benchmarks), security pack (link: https://redwood.example/security-pack), pricing spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.example/pricing/magnetwell).

title: Arcstone Secure Networks
author: Maya Singh
text:
Background: Arcstone runs telemetry and NOC operations for multiple regional power utilities. Evaluating a private/on-prem LLM to accelerate incident triage, SOP retrieval, and runbook summarization.

Key constraints: air-gapped data center footprint in two regions, no persistent outbound connectivity from inference nodes, must present KMS/HSM flow for key material locally, strict retention controls and audit trails for all prompts and responses. Customer repeatedly: "no model weights leaving our network; must be verifiable".

POC ask: ship a self-hosted bundle for an isolated rack (4x A100 equiv), validate model variants (fp16, int8), demonstrate prefix caching and deterministic audit logs for 30-day window. They want a small canary first (30 concurrent chat sessions, 50 req/s embedding backfill), then scale to 500 concurrent sessions.

Commercial: procurement expects a 3-year reserved commit for Dedicated/Private; initial ARR target $500k-$1.5M. Legal/security want SAML SSO, SOC2 evidence and an on-site penetration report before signature.

Quote from CISO (2026-02-08 call): "We will not accept any outbound telemetry that includes user queries or weights — metadata-only health pings only, and we must be able to flip off telemetry at boot."

Stubs and next artifacts: POC plan uploaded to Drive; requested demo logs and sample audit-export format. SE to produce KMS/HSM integration diagram and HSM test harness.

air-gapped deployment acceptance criteria not yet formalized
HSM/KMS integration proof required
final POC budget approval from procurement

Finalize SOW and schedule on-site security audit window; legal to sign DSA/BAA

on-prem air-gapped bundle: inference runtime, audit exporter, KMS/HSM connector, no egress telemetry

Milestone 1: Deliver offline install bundle and docs
Milestone 2: On-site install + smoke tests (week 4)
Milestone 3: Audit log validation + performance tuning (week 6)
Milestone 4: Scale test and handoff to ops (week 10)

2026-02-08 — POC kickoff webinar (SE on-site for architecture review)
2026-02-22 — Security deep-dive with CISO + infra (requested HSM diagram)
2026-03-03 — Live review of security FAQ; legal asked for DSA template
2026-03-09 — Capacity planning call; Arcstone provided rack spec and trial hardware dates

AE/Maya: intro + pricing; SE/Liam: architecture and install plan; CISO: compliance gating; Procurement: budget timeline Q3; quote being updated to include on-prem audit addendum.

High strategic value — reference case for utilities vertical. Prioritize SE time for HSM integration. If POC succeeds, open channel for Dedicated reserved capacity conversion.

Procurement timeline long; legal needs multiple redlines on telemetry and export controls; air-gap acceptance tests may extend POC by 2-4 weeks.

title: runtime-fingerprint-onboarding-and-shadow-compatibility-checklist-2026
author: Maya Chen
text:
Overview:

This document defines the runtime fingerprinting and shadow-compatibility checklist used by Model Onboarding and the Eval team to verify that a model artifact is compatible with Redwood serving runtimes (hosted, dedicated, private) and safe to promote into production shadowing. The goal is to capture deterministic and non-deterministic runtime signals so teams can anticipate quality regressions introduced by kernels, quantization, KV cache differences, tokenizers, and batching behavior.

Motivation:

- Models with identical weights can behave materially differently under different runtime stacks (quant kernels, mixed precision, sequence-length optimizations).
- Late-stage surprises (coherence drops, hallucination shifts, functioncall decoding errors) are expensive in production.
- A standardized fingerprint and gating checklist reduces promotion risk and speeds onboarding.

Definitions:

- Runtime fingerprint: A compact set of telemetry artifacts (microbench responses, slice-anchor outputs, determinism seeds, tokenization examples, KV-cache delta signatures) that characterize how a model behaves under a given serving runtime and configuration.
- Shadow compatibility: A boolean decision to allow traffic mirroring to a candidate model in shadow mode (non-traffic-affecting) based on fingerprint proximity to the baseline and passing quality & stability gates.

Scope and applicability:

- Applies to all models entering Redwood hosted, dedicated, or private deployments.
- Required for: major model upgrades (architecture, tokenizer, quant profile), quant-shadow cohorts, and migrations between runtime families (e.g., cuBLAS->kernel-optimizer).

High-level process (1-line):

1) Generate fingerprint artifacts -> 2) Run deterministic microbench & slice probes -> 3) Compare against baseline fingerprint -> 4) Run shadow cohort with telemetry gating -> 5) Promote or rollback.

Runtime fingerprint components (required):

- Tokenization signature: token ids & byte offsets for 150 canonical prompts (see tokenization sample list below).
- Microbench harness: per-kernel per-sequence-length stepwise log-prob arrays for 12 synthetic prompts (3 seeds each).
- KV-cache delta signature: hashed set of KV-cache root-diffs captured at step 8 and step 64 for long-context models.
- Determinism seeds: deterministic log-probability vectors for 20 seed values and a variance summary.
- Functioncall trace baseline: canonical functioncall examples (3 variants per function) with expected JSON schema shapes.
- Embedding drift snapshot: average cosine to production embedding centroid for 50 anchors.

Fingerprint generation checklist (detailed steps):

1. Prepare artifact bundle:
 - Create model artifact with pinned weights + tokenizer + quant profile (if applicable).
 - Tag artifact: service_name:model_name:artifact_hash (e.g., redwood-search:reranker:v2:sha256:abcd).

2. Run tokenization signature job:
 - Command: ./tools/tokenize-signer --model-artifact <artifact_tar> --seed-corpus samples/token-sample-150.json --out token-signature.json
 - Confirm: no unknown token warnings, consistent header fields.

3. Execute microbench harness:
 - Run: redwood-eval --harness microbench --artifact <artifact> --sequence-lengths 32,128,512 --seeds 42,101,202 --output microbench.json
 - Verify: p95 step latency per token and stepwise log-probs exist for each kernel path.

4. Capture KV-cache deltas (for models with > 128 context):
 - Run an 80-step generation, sample cache dumps at step 8 & 64 using the runtime hook (see runtime-ops docs).
 - Produce hashed delta signature: sha256(kv_step8 || kv_step64).

5. Determinism sweep:
 - Run 20 fixed-seed generations and compute variance per token position. Save as determinism.json.

6. Functioncall baseline validation:
 - Execute 9 functioncall prompts. Confirm JSON schema compliance and consistent argument ordering for positional APIs.

7. Embedding centroids:
 - Compute 50-anchor embeddings, compare cosine distribution vs baseline. Save embedding-snapshot.json.

Shadow compatibility checklist (gating thresholds):

- Tokenization: 0 unknown-token warnings; average tokenization length delta <= 2 tokens for same prompt set.
- Determinism: per-token variance median <= 1e-6; max per-token variance threshold = 1e-4.
- Microbench log-prob drift: KL divergence (candidate || baseline) across microbench seeds <= 0.015.
- Embedding drift: median cosine similarity >= 0.985 to production centroid.
- Latency p95: <= 120 ms (hosted dev tier), <= 80 ms (dedicated SLO class A) for seq=128 tests.
- KV-cache delta entropy: hashed-diff Hamming distance <= 0.02 (normalized) from baseline.
- Functioncall schema match: 100% pass. Partial schema drift must have documented migration plan.

Gating policy (pass/fail rules):

1) HardReject: any Functioncall schema mismatch or unknown-token warnings -> block shadowing.
2) SoftReject: microbench KL > 0.03 or embedding median cosine < 0.97 -> require remediation and re-run.
3) ConditionalPass: minor token-length delta or marginal latency increase (<= 10% over baseline) -> allow limited shadow cohort with shortened TTL and tighter telemetry.

Shadow cohort orchestration (operational steps):

1. Create shadow cohort config (example YAML below).
2. Start redwood-shadow-runner in mirror mode for 1% of traffic, forward responses to observability sink only (no user exposure).
3. Enable additional probes: priming-cohort, cornercase-sampler, and latency-tail-capture for the candidate artifact.
4. Monitor rolling windows: 5m/30m/24h for SLI deltas and the fingerprint re-check every 30 minutes.
5. If any HardReject triggers, immediately stop mirroring and cut a rollback ticket.

Example shadow cohort config (shadow-cohort.yaml):

service: redwood-chat
model_artifact: redwood-chat:assistant-xl:sha256:ef12ab34
cohort:
 mirror_ratio: 0.01
 ttl_hours: 24
 extra_probes:
 - priming-cohort
 - latency-tail-capture
 - functioncall-monitor
 telemetry_sinks:
 - redwood-observability:eval-ingest
 - s3://prod-eval-archives/sha256/ef12ab34
gating:
 tokenization_delta_max: 2
 microbench_kl_threshold: 0.015
 embedding_cosine_min: 0.985
 p95_latency_max_ms: 120

Operational monitoring (metrics and dashboards):

- Core SLIs to visualize in the shadow dashboard:
 - eval.fingerprint.tokenization.delta (per-hour)
 - eval.fingerprint.kl_microbench (per-probe)
 - eval.embedding.cosine.median (hourly)
 - runtime.latency.p95.seq128 (5m/30m)
 - eval.functioncall.schema_fail_rate (rolling 1h)
 - eval.kvcache.hamming_norm (delta signature score)

- Alerting rules (default):
 - Severity P1: any HardReject -> Pager to ModelOnboard-1 oncall.
 - Severity P2: microbench KL > 0.03 sustained for 30m -> Slack alert to #model-onboarding and ticket auto-created.
 - Severity P3: latency p95 > SLO + 20% sustained for 1h -> email to owners.

Rollout and rollback criteria (decision table):

| Outcome | Action | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| All gates pass | Promote to 10% live traffic after 24h | ModelOnboard Team Lead |
| ConditionalPass | Extend shadow to 48h with 0.5% mirror and run compensating probes | Eval Lead |
| SoftReject | Block promotion, open remediation ticket, require re-fingerprint after fix | Model Owner |
| HardReject | Stop mirror immediately, revert to baseline artifact, run incident review in 48h | SRE + Model Onboard |

Example CLI commands (common operations):

- Generate fingerprint: ./ci/fingerprint-run --artifact sha256:ef12ab34 --out /tmp/fingerprint_bundle.zip
- Start mirror: ./tools/redwood-shadow-runner --config shadow-cohort.yaml --start
- Run local microbench: redwood-eval --harness microbench --artifact ef12ab34 --out microbench.json
- Re-run deterministic sweep: python ./scripts/determinism_sweep.py --artifact ef12ab34 --seeds 0..19 --out det.json

Telemetry artifacts and storage policy:

- Fingerprint bundle (token_sign, microbench, kv_delta, determinism, embedding-snapshot) is stored in S3 under prod-evals/<artifact_hash>/fingerprint-YYYYMMDD.zip for 1 year.
- Short-term telemetry (5m/30m windows) retained in Prometheus for 90d; aggregated monthly rollups in BigQuery for 3 years.

Checklist to sign off onboarding (pre-shadow):

- [ ] Artifact uploaded with pinned tokenizer + quant profile hash.
- [ ] Tokenization signature generated and validated.
- [ ] Microbench harness executed for required sequence lengths and seeds.
- [ ] KV-cache deltas captured for long context models.
- [ ] Determinism sweep variance within threshold.
- [ ] Embedding snapshot compared; median cosine >= threshold.
- [ ] Functioncall baseline passed 100%.
- [ ] Shadow cohort YAML reviewed by SRE and Eval teams.
- [ ] Dashboards & alerts configured and tested in staging.
- [ ] Ownership recorded in the model registry with contact info.

Ownership and contacts:

- Model Onboarding Lead: Maya Chen (author) — @mchen
- Eval Lead: Arjun Patel — @apatel
- Runtime SRE: Lina Gomez — @lgomez
- Observability Owner: Sofia Martinez — @smartinez

Appendix: tokenization sample list (first 8 of 150):

1) "Translate to Spanish: The server returned an unexpected error code 503."
2) "Summarize the following legal clause: The purchaser warrants..."
3) "Compose a subject line for a password reset email for a fintech app."
4) "Extract dates and amounts from: Invoice #4312 dated 2025-03-01 for $4,200."
5) "Convert this markdown into JSON: - name: 'Redwood' - role: 'inference'"
6) "Functioncall test: create_event(title="Team sync", time="2026-01-15T10:00Z")"
7) "Long-context priming: [repeat a 800-token primer about prior conversation state]"
8) "Edge-case prompt: <script>alert(1)</script> What is the safe sanitized output?"

Notes and future work:

- Track a compact fingerprint vector embedding to allow fast nearest-neighbor comparisons across artifacts (outstanding infra ticket INF-2026-114).
- Add automated suggestion engine that maps fingerprint deltas to likely causes (quant kernels, tokenizer change, or decoding differences).

Related artifacts and references:

- Service: redwood-eval (internal) - eval harness repository: git+ssh://git.redwood/internal/eval-harness
- Runtime ops: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/release-notes
- Model registry: https://registry.redwood.internal/models

Revision history:

- 2025-11-12: Created (Maya Chen).
- 2026-01-04: Thresholds tightened for embedding cosine after cross-team review (Arjun Patel).
- 2026-02-15: Added KV-cache delta hashing procedure and sample YAML (Sofia Martinez).

title: Customer VPC Lite Log Bundle - PRD Kickoff
author: Priya Raman
text:
Purpose:
This doc is an early PRD kickoff for a lightweight, customer-facing VPC log bundle that provides the minimum audit surface customers and Redwood need for onboarding, change review, and low-cost forensics. Goal is to offer a compact, signed log package (the 'lite bundle') customers can opt into during Private deployment onboarding.

Context and problem statement:
- Customers running private deployments often require an auditable trail of networking changes, operator actions, and handshake events between Redwood control-plane and customer-managed network (peers, NATs, firewall rules).
- Full fidelity packet-level telemetry and long retention are expensive and often unnecessary for routine validation. Customers ask for: simple, verifiable logs for compliance review, rapid triage, and occasional investigations.
- We need a small, easily parsed artifact that balances cost, privacy, and investigative value while fitting into existing Private onboarding flows.

Non-goals:
- Not a replacement for (or direct transport of) SIEM/flow records at full fidelity (e.g., NetFlow/PCAP).
- Not real-time streaming analytics platform. Lite bundle will be produced on demand/periodic basis.

Success metrics (initial):
- Time-to-first-bundle for onboarding customers: <= 48h after enabling opt-in.
- Size: typical bundle <= 5 MB/day for small-to-medium VPCs (customer must opt in to higher fidelity).
- Query/forensic turnaround: 95th percentile retrieval < 10 mins for last-30-day bundles (SLA defined for support).
- Customer satisfaction: NPS question for onboarding artifacts >= 4/5 in pilot cohort.

High-level design:
1) Bundle contents and format (compact JSONL + manifest):
 - A per-day compressed JSONL file (gzip) named bundle-YYYYMMDD.jsonl.gz.
 - Each line = single JSON object with minimal schema (see below).
 - Accompanying manifest.json with: bundle_version, generated_at (ISO8601), bundle_sha256, signature (control-plane KMS), and indexing pointers (offsets per event-type).

2) Core event schema (one-liners: fields kept intentionally small):
 - ts: ISO8601 timestamp (string)
 - ev: short event type ("handshake", "route-change", "egress-rule", "keystore-rotate", "operator-action")
 - src: origin id ("control-plane", "cust-agent", "edge-operator")
 - target: resource id (VPC id / gateway id / route-table id)
 - actor: short username or service id (optional, hashed for PII minimization)
 - change_hash: SHA256 of diff payload (opaque)
 - ticket: customer ticket id / runbook ref (optional)
 - meta: small CSV-like tag string (e.g., "prod,canary")
 - ctx: short context code (optional) - used to link to longer diagnostics in secure export
 Notes: We intentionally avoid embedding raw configs; change_hash provides a pointer for retrieval under tighter controls.

3) Signing & tamper-evidence:
 - Each manifest signed with Redwood control-plane KMS key (RSA/ECDSA).
 - Additionally compute per-file sha256 checksums.
 - Quick verification script provided to customers (python / bash) to validate signature and checksums.

4) Export and retention semantics:
 - Default retention: 30d in Redwood-managed S3-like object store behind customer ACL (customer-controlled export).
 - Export-on-demand: support immediate export to customer S3 or preconfigured SIEM sink (see security section).
 - Long-tail retention: customers can request archival (90/365/ever) under enterprise contract (billing impact).

5) Access controls and privacy limits:
 - Bundles are generated by Redwood on a per-customer basis using job runner with least privilege.
 - Sensitive fields (actor) are hashed by default; customers can opt-in to include raw identifiers via signed request from their security contact.
 - Bundles stored encrypted with per-customer CMKs; keys never exported.

6) Approval gate / handoff UX (customer-managed networking onboarding flow):
 - Step 1: Customer enables "Lite Audit Bundle" during onboarding UI with checkbox and purpose selection (for compliance / incident response / auditing).
 - Step 2: Redwood schedules a preflight handshake: control-plane performs connectivity check and emits a 'handshake' event to the bundle.
 - Step 3: Customer reviews manifest in UI (human-readable summary) and clicks Approve to proceed with operator actions that require pre-approval (e.g., route injection).
 - Approvals are auditable: approval event recorded into the next bundle with actor and decision (approve/reject) + ticket link.
 - Rollback: if customer rejects, control-plane auto-rolls back based on last-known-good (-LK) snapshot; rollback event recorded.

7) Forensics retrieval model:
 - High-level logs in bundle point to 'change_hash' — resolving a hash triggers a secure retrieval process that returns the full change blob after an automated policy check (ACL + timebox).
 - Retrieval is rate-limited and logged in a separate retrieval-audit channel (not included in lightweight bundles to avoid circular bloat).

8) API contract (initial):
 - GET /customers/{id}/bundles?from=YYYY-MM-DD&to=YYYY-MM-DD -> list of bundles + manifest URLs
 - GET /customers/{id}/bundles/{bundle_id}/manifest -> signed manifest.json
 - GET /customers/{id}/bundles/{bundle_id}/download -> presigned URL (HTTPS, time-limited)
 - POST /customers/{id}/bundles/{bundle_id}/resolve -> body: {"change_hash": ".."} -> returns presigned artifact for full blob if policy allows (audit note returned).
 (Auth: mTLS or token tied to customer's onprem SAML/SCIM config)

9) Operational runbook (support & SRE):
 - Generation job runs nightly; retry policy: exponential backoff x3.
 - On generation failure: create a support ticket automatically PD-logs-auto-{customer}-{date}.
 - SRE must provide a 4-hour business-hours SLA for bundle generation issues during onboarding pilot; escalate path described.

10) Cost estimate (rough):
 - Assumptions: 200 customers in pilot, avg 3MB/day per customer -> storage ~18GB/month + egress spikes when exporting.
 - Estimated monthly infra cost (storage + compute bundling + signing) in pilot: $2,200 – $4,000.
 - Billing model: included for first 30d onboarding; then tiered per-GB outbound for exports + optional retention fee.

11) Rollout plan (phased):
 - Phase 0 (pilot): 10 customers, manual opt-in, support-assisted validation, one-week cadence for bundle generation, feedback loop.
 - Phase 1 (self-serve): UI checkbox + basic manifest preview, API for download, default 30d retention.
 - Phase 2 (enterprise): per-customer CMK, extended retention options, SIEM connectors, signed retrieval SLA.

12) Implementation notes and technical risks:
 - Risk: Customers will want more fidelity (packets/flow) than the lite bundle supports -> need clear guardrails and escape-hatch playbook.
 - Risk: Signature and key management complexity for private deployments with customer CMKs. Plan: reuse existing KMS integrations and generic key-wrapping approach.
 - Risk: Cost blow-ups from large VPCs -> add rate-limiting and default sampling policy.

Unresolved questions / TODOs:
- Define exact hashing scheme for change_hash and where full blobs are stored (encrypted or customer-keyed).
- UX: what does the manifest preview show in the onboarding flow? (paper mockups required).
- Compliance: confirm whether hashed actor values meet SOC2 / ISO requirements for evidence.
- SRE: finalize generation schedule (nightly vs 4-hour window for high-risk customers).
- Legal: retention terms language for customer contracts.

Action items (owners):
- Priya: coordinate pilot signups and create one-page customer-facing FAQ (due 2025-03-14).
- Marcus: proto generator script + verification tool (initial PR by 2025-03-07).
- Ellen: wireframes for manifest preview and approval CTA (in product board by 2025-03-10).
- Samir: cost model refinement and billing contract language (draft 2025-03-17).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally lightweight and conservative on data included. The design aims to minimize PII leakage and storage egress while still enabling meaningful audits. Expect follow-up PRDs for a higher-fidelity / SIEM-focused offering.
- Please comment inline on whether change_hash should be reversible conditioned on legal hold or if we should require customer-provided keys for full blob retrieval.

Attachments / examples (quick):
- Example JSONL event (one line): {"ts":"2025-02-10T14:12:03Z","ev":"handshake","src":"control-plane","target":"vpc-1234","actor":"hash:0f3a..","change_hash":"sha256:abcd..","ticket":"TKT-3456","meta":"prod,initial"}
- Example manifest (human-readable preview): bundle_date: 2025-02-10, events: 13, size_bytes: 3142, signed_by: redwood-kms-v1

End of draft.

Version history:
- 2025-02-12: initial draft (Priya)
- 2025-03-03: added API contract and rollout phases (Marcus)
- 2025-03-07: updated cost estimates and action items (Priya)

title: Rollback state machine + idempotency rules for Private upgrades (handle partial steps safely)
author: Rafael Mendes
text:
Context
Private upgrades are moving to a staged, auditable workflow with prechecks + backups + deterministic rollback. This ticket defines the rollback state machine and idempotency rules across installer + Helm phases, including how we represent partially-applied steps and how rollback should behave when we’re mid-upgrade.

Problem statement
In-place upgrades frequently fail in the middle (DB migration lock timeout, chart rollout stuck, artifact mismatch, node disruption). Our old guidance was either “try again” or “restore from backup manually,” which caused inconsistent outcomes and longer MTTR. We need:
- a single source of truth for upgrade/rollback progress
- deterministic behavior under retries
- explicit handling of partial upgrade states (some steps applied, others not)
- clear operator UX + logs suitable for support bundles

Goals
1) Define a rollback state machine that can resume safely after interruption.
2) Ensure every step is idempotent or has a compensating action (and we record when compensating actions are unsafe).
3) Provide clear rules for when rollback is allowed vs blocked (e.g., irreversible migrations).
4) Make behavior consistent across VPC and on-prem/air-gapped.

Non-goals
- Multi-hop rollback across multiple major versions. Rollback here means “return to the last known-good version from immediately before this upgrade attempt.”
- Attempting to automatically recover from all schema edge cases; some cases require explicit manual intervention.

Proposed state model (installer-owned)
We persist an UpgradeRun record in the installer state store (local + optionally ConfigMap/Secret in cluster depending on mode):
- upgrade_id (UUID)
- started_at / completed_at
- from_version / to_version
- environment (vpc|onprem), cluster_id
- plan_hash (hash of generated upgrade plan)
- backup_id + backup verification result
- stage state: NOT_STARTED | RUNNING | SUCCEEDED | FAILED | ROLLED_BACK
- step state per stage with attempt counters + last_error

Primary invariant: the installer is the authority on “what we think happened,” but it must reconcile with cluster reality on resume (see Reconciliation rules).

Stages + steps
We align stages to the plan artifact and chart ordering work:
Stage A: Prechecks
- A1 run preflight checks
- A2 confirm operator acknowledgement (if warnings present / risk score threshold)

Stage B: Backup
- B1 create backups (snapshots and/or logical dump based on backend)
- B2 verify backup (basic restore validation checks per strategy doc)

Stage C: Control plane upgrade
- C1 fetch/verify artifacts (including offline bundle signatures)
- C2 helm upgrade control-plane chart
- C3 wait for CP readiness gate

Stage D: Data plane upgrade
- D1 helm upgrade data-plane chart(s)
- D2 wait for DP readiness gate

Stage E: Post-upgrade verification
- E1 smoke checks (API health, control-plane connectivity, critical jobs)
- E2 mark upgrade complete + emit audit events

Rollback entry points (what “rollback” means)
Rollback can be invoked when:
- any stage after B1 has started (i.e., we have a backup OR we explicitly confirm we’re rolling back without backup)
- operator passes “are you sure” acknowledgement if backup missing or verification failed

Rollback should attempt, in order:
1) Roll back helm releases to previous revision (control plane then data plane), respecting ordering rules.
2) Restore persisted config/state if changed by installer (only if we have an explicit previous snapshot; otherwise no-op).
3) Restore DB only if:
 - backup exists AND
 - schema migrations are not flagged as “backwards-incompatible without restore” OR operator explicitly chooses full restore.

We must support two rollback modes:
- “Rollback charts only” (fast, no DB restore) for failures in chart rollout where DB is untouched.
- “Rollback + restore” (charts + DB restore) for failures after DB migrations started/applied.

Idempotency rules
Each step must be one of:
- Idempotent: safe to rerun without changing outcome (preferred).
- Idempotent-with-check: safe if we check for a marker/condition first.
- Compensatable: not idempotent, but has a defined compensating action.
- Non-compensatable: requires manual intervention; installer must stop and explain.

Rules we are enforcing:
- Every step writes a durable completion marker (in UpgradeRun + where applicable a cluster-side marker).
- Steps must tolerate being restarted after process crash and after partial completion.
- No step may assume previous steps completed unless the state machine indicates SUCCEEDED AND reconciliation confirms.

Reconciliation rules (resume behavior)
When resuming an upgrade/rollback run, installer reconciles “what we think happened” with cluster reality:
- Helm reconciliation: read release history to determine current revision and pending operations.
- Migration reconciliation: query migration table to detect last applied migration and whether a migration is “in progress” (guardrails around locks/timeouts).
- Backup reconciliation: verify backup artifacts exist and are readable; if missing, rollback+restore is blocked.

If reconciliation contradicts stored state, we:
- log a “state divergence” event
- prefer cluster reality for safety
- require operator confirmation if proceeding could cause data loss (e.g., installer thought no migration ran, but migration table shows new version)

Handling partially-applied steps (examples)
1) Failure during CP helm upgrade (C2)
- Cluster may be in pending-upgrade state.
- Behavior: attempt helm rollback CP to previous revision. If rollback succeeds and CP readiness passes, proceed to mark stage C as ROLLED_BACK. DP is left untouched unless it was already upgraded.

2) Failure during DB migration job triggered by CP upgrade
- Migration might have applied some changes.
- Behavior: block “charts-only rollback” unless we can prove migration set is backwards compatible (via migration guardrail metadata). Offer two options:
 - Full restore (preferred) using backup_id.
 - Stop with manual intervention steps if restore not possible.

3) Failure after DP upgrade started (D1), CP healthy
- Behavior: rollback DP chart first. If DP rollback fails or resources stuck terminating, require operator to resolve (force delete, etc.) before proceeding.

4) Upgrade retried after crash during backup creation (B1)
- Behavior: check if snapshot exists with matching backup_id; if yes, continue B2 verification; if no, restart B1 and record prior attempt as superseded.

Operator UX requirements
- `redwood-private upgrade` stores UpgradeRun + prints upgrade_id.
- `redwood-private rollback --upgrade-id <id>` is the primary path.
- Default behavior: safe-by-default (will not attempt destructive actions without confirmation).
- Output should include: current stage, last successful step, reason for failure, what rollback will do, what it will NOT do.
- Support bundle must include UpgradeRun JSON + step logs + helm status outputs.

Auditability
Emit audit log events:
- upgrade.started, upgrade.prechecks.passed/failed, upgrade.backup.completed/failed, upgrade.stage.completed, rollback.invoked, rollback.completed/failed
Include: upgrade_id, from/to version, environment, operator identity (where available), plan_hash, backup_id.

Open questions / decisions
- Where to persist UpgradeRun for on-prem installs that do not allow cluster writes? Decision: store locally by default; if kube access is present, also mirror a sanitized record to a ConfigMap for supportability.
- Migration “backwards compatibility” signal: Decision: add metadata to migrations (in main redwood repo) to indicate rollback safety; default is unsafe unless explicitly marked safe.

Acceptance criteria
- Installer maintains a persistent state machine for upgrade + rollback and can resume after interruption.
- Rollback command can handle:
 - partial CP upgrade
 - partial DP upgrade
 - migration failures (blocked unless restore available)
- Steps are idempotent or have compensating actions documented in the plan output.
- Operator messaging makes it unambiguous when data restore will occur.
- Support bundle includes last UpgradeRun, plan summary, and rollback attempt logs.

Implementation notes / links
- Related PR (rollback command + state machine): sources/github/redwood-private-installer/pr-4862-rollback-command-and-state-machine.json
- Migration guardrails work: sources/github/redwood/pr-29210-migration-guardrails-and-backward-compatible-schema.json
- Rollback semantics spec: sources/confluence/eng-private-deployments/upgrade-and-rollback/rollback-semantics-and-hooks.json
- ADR: sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-private-upgrade-plan-and-rollback-contract.json

Testing
- Add e2e scenario: induce failure mid-CP rollout and verify rollback returns system to pre-upgrade health.
- Add e2e scenario: migration lock timeout -> rollback blocks charts-only and prompts for restore.
- Add retry/resume scenario: kill installer mid-run; resume completes deterministically.

Rollout plan
- Beta behind feature flag for design partners (one VPC, one on-prem).
- Default to “charts-only rollback” when DB migration not started (detected via reconciliation).
- Require explicit confirmation for restore actions and for proceeding in divergent state cases.

2025-04-17 — Rafael Mendes: P0 after SUP-18421. We need deterministic behavior when upgrades fail mid-migration; support can’t keep doing bespoke recovery instructions.
2025-04-22 — Benji Okafor: Drafted state machine + reconciliation rules. Key call: treat migration rollback as unsafe unless migration metadata says otherwise. Will sync with Michael on migration markers.
2025-05-01 — Michael Nguyen: +1 on “unsafe by default” for migrations. We should gate charts-only rollback if any migration in the target set has run (migration table check). Also recommend explicit lock timeout + idempotency markers (see PR-29210).
2025-05-06 — Sean Gallagher: Make sure rollback never auto-restores DB unless operator opts in (data loss risk). Also require audit event on rollback invoked + completed.
2025-05-13 — Connor O'Brien: Please align stage naming with the plan generator output; release notes and support docs depend on consistent terms (Prechecks/Backup/CP/DP/Verify).
2025-05-28 — Benji Okafor: Implemented UpgradeRun persistence + step retry counters. Added state divergence detection (helm revision vs stored state). Pending review from SRE + Security.
2025-06-03 — Marcus Lin: Security review: ensure support bundle redacts secrets; UpgradeRun can include backup_id but must not include KMS material or credentials. OK to mirror sanitized state to ConfigMap.
2025-06-11 — Rafael Mendes: Ran rollback drill in staging. Found DP rollback can hang if workloads have PDBs too strict; filed follow-up to adjust readiness gates/timeouts in charts (ENG-4860 dependency).
2025-06-18 — Benji Okafor: Landed via installer PR-4862. Docs follow-up tracked in ENG-4899 to ensure runbook includes the two rollback modes + restore prompts.

title: Borealis Banking — Inference governance, escape hatch & migration constraints
author: Samira Patel
text:
Initial discovery with Borealis Banking focused on governance constraints (data residency, KMS), evaluating migration from OpenAI and Anthropic, and confirming escape-hatch options (private/VPC, dedicated pools). Customer is sensitive to latency for customer-facing chat and to per-call PII retention; they want a short micro-benchmark and security docs before a pilot decision.

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-25
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Recording link: https://redwood-recordings.internal/ff/ff-2026-09-25-7843 (placeholder)
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Jae Kim (Redwood SE), Marco Alvarez (Redwood SE), Ryan Cho (Borealis Head of ML), Amira Singh (Borealis VP Platform), Derek Lu (Borealis Infra), Priya Menon (Borealis Data Privacy), Tommy Rhee (Borealis SRE)

Summary (auto):
- Borealis is evaluating exit/port from OpenAI/Anthropic for customer support and fraud detection features. Primary concerns: data residency, KMS integration, SOC2/ISO artifacts, and predictable latency for customer chat.
- They run 250k token-equivalent requests/day with 95th p99 latency target of 300ms for short-turn chat (prompt+response). Currently using OpenAI + a vLLM cache layer for internal tooling.
- Redwood options discussed: Hosted API for initial pilot, Dedicated capacity for predictable throughput and SLA, Private (VPC/on-prem) for high-regulated flows.
- Agreed next steps: micro-benchmark, security docs, pricing spreadsheet, follow-up on private deployment feasibility.

Topics: governance, KMS/HSM, escape hatch/private deploy, vLLM/TGI compatibility, benchmark plan, timeline (POC in Oct/Nov)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samira: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm Samira, i'm the AE on the account from Redwood Inference. we've got Jae and Marco here from our engineering team. how's everyone?
[00:16] Ryan: hi, thanks. i'm Ryan, head of ML at Borealis. quick intros on our side: Amira runs platform, Derek infra, Priya is our privacy lead, tommy on sre.
[00:27] Samira: awesome. want to do a quick agenda? i'll cover product options and pricing outlines, Jae will do a short compatibility/latency Q, then we can dig into compliance.
[00:37] Amira: yep sounds good.
[00:41] Jae: cool, i'll start with what we typically see in these port-outs — okay so the usual mix is OpenAI on customer chat, anthropic for safety functions, and then sometimes folks run vLLM or TGI locally to get lower latency for internal tools. is that similar to you?
[00:56] Ryan: yep that's basically us. we also have a vLLM caching tier in front of OpenAI for frequently asked questions — it's reduced cost but we've been hitting memory pressure and ops churn.
[01:11] Jae: makes sense. two big things to check: model compatibility (do your prompts and evals run with Redwood-hosted models) and runtime escape-hatch — i.e., if you need to move to private or dedicated with same API and rollbacks.
[01:26] Derek: important for us: we can't send PII outside certain regions. we need to evaluate a private deployment or dedicated pools in region, and key management has to be customer-controlled for some workloads.
[01:39] Samira: absolutely. Redwood Private supports a VPC control plane and on-prem options, and we integrate with KMS — we have customers using customer-managed KMS/HSM. we'll share the KMS integration guide after the call.
[01:52] Priya: can you confirm retention for prompts and logs in hosted mode? our compliance team wants explicit TTLs and audit logs, plus SOC2 artifacts.
[02:03] Marco: yes, hosted has configurable retention and we emit audit logs per request. for high-security flows you'd typically go to Dedicated or Private where logs can be routed to your syslog or cloud storage under your control.
[02:17] Ryan: short question on eval parity — we run a taxonomy of prompts (about 1200 evals) and need to make sure output quality matches baseline from OpenAI and Anthropic. how disruptive are model diffs?
[02:30] Jae: good one. we usually do side-by-side evals with the customer's prompt set. sometimes there are style differences, but we support model-weight pinning and can route to fallback variants to maintain parity. the plan would be: run micro-benchmark with your eval set and report regressions.
[02:48] Amira: and how fast can that happen? we want results before the procurement window in early Oct.
[02:55] Samira: we can run a first pass in 72 hours if you provide the prompt pack and a small sample workload. Jae — is that right?
[03:03] Jae: yeah 48–72 hours for the initial run, then another week for deeper analysis if we find diffs. we'll provide a spreadsheet with token costs, latencies, and a regression summary.
[03:16] Tommy: latency — you mentioned p99 latency targets, what's realistic on Hosted vs Dedicated? our customer-facing chat needs p99 < 300ms for short responses.
[03:28] Marco: okay so there's two parts: model inference latency and network overhead. for short-turn chat (< 256 tokens) Hosted in region typically yields 150–300ms p99 for optimized models; Dedicated can get you lower variance and SLA-backed numbers because of reserved GPU pools; Private (on-prem) is best for sub-100ms if you colocate near your frontends and run a reduced model.
[03:50] Derek: are you supporting vLLM or TGI-based runtimes for private deploy? we currently use vLLM with some custom kernels.
[03:58] Jae: we support compatibility with vLLM/TGI artifacts — model formats and kv cache patterns — but there are nuances in kernel selection and quantization. we can ingest your checkpoint and run a compatibility test. sometimes we find differences in past-key-values handling that affect long-context tasks.
[04:18] Ryan: ok noted. what about fallback routing — like if hosted capacity is saturated, can requests failover to a cheaper model or different region without user-visible regressions?
[04:31] Marco: yes, smart routing is a Redwood feature — routing by policy (latency, cost, region). we can configure automated fallback to compatible model variants. there will always be some output variance, so we recommend canary and A/B rollouts tied to your eval checks.
[04:46] Priya: on the security side, do you have SOC2 and ISO artifacts we can review? plus encryption at rest and in transit?
[04:55] Samira: yes, SOC2 Type II, ISO 27001 cert, and we encrypt data in transit with TLS and at rest with customer keys where needed. we'll attach the compliance pack.
[05:07] Amira: for the pilot, what's the recommended start: Hosted or Dedicated? we want a quick POC but also to limit data leaving our control.
[05:16] Jae: suggested path: start with Hosted for speed-of-onboarding for lower-risk prompts (non-PII). run eval parity and micro-benchmarks. for regulated flows, spin up Dedicated capacity in your region and then move to Private for the highest assurance.
[05:30] Ryan: what about cost modeling — how do we evaluate token cost vs dedicated monthly commit?
[05:36] Samira: we'll send a pricing spreadsheet showing per-token hosted costs, and example reserved capacity pricing for Dedicated with commit tiers; that will include burst and autoscale policy cost examples.
[05:48] Tommy: one operational question — do you provide per-token tracing or trace id so we can correlate SRE traces with downstream logs?
[05:56] Marco: yes, we include request-level tracing hooks and token-level cost breakdowns in the Console. you can export traces to your tracing system.
[06:06] Derek: for Private, how invasive is the control plane? we have air-gapped lanes for payments processing, prefer minimal footprint.
[06:14] Jae: we have two private models: VPC-hosted control plane where control plane talks over secure peering and you host inference nodes, and a fully on-prem package. the on-prem is heavier but supports air-gapped installs; the VPC option is often a good compromise.
[06:29] Priya: regarding KMS/HSM — can we bring our HSM for key wrapping?
[06:34] Marco: yes, customers have used BYOK via cloud KMS plus HSM integration. we'll include the KMS/HSM integration doc.
[06:41] Ryan: procurement will want an escape-hatch clause — if Redwood hosted changes TOS or model behavior we need a plan to pivot to private within X weeks. is there a standard playbook?
[06:52] Samira: we maintain an escape hatch playbook for enterprise — includes model export guidance, sample infra provisioning scripts, and recommended rollback timelines. we'll share a redacted playbook. timeline for full pivot depends on model sizes and infra readiness but we aim for a staged porting plan of 4–8 weeks for most customers.
[07:10] Amira: 4–8 weeks — that aligns with our risk tolerance. for the POC we'd want a pilot with scoped traffic and an SLA.
[07:18] Samira: yes, we can do a timeboxed POC with a dedicated pool and success criteria around latency, cost, and eval parity.
[07:25] Ryan: speaking of parity, are there guardrails or eval alerts if model quality regresses after a rollout?
[07:32] Jae: Redwood Optimize ties model metrics to your eval sets and raises regression alerts. you can auto-fallback to the previous model or route to a fallback family.
[07:44] Priya: quick question — data residency — if we choose Hosted, can you guarantee EU-only residency for certain requests?
[07:52] Marco: yes, region routing policies exist. you can pin requests by region or tenant to EU-only infrastructure. for stricter needs, Dedicated in-region or Private is preferred.
[08:02] Derek: jotted notes — we have to provide sample traffic (30k req/day) and top 50 prompts, plus our compliance Q list. we'll put that into a Google Drive.
[08:12] Samira: perfect, send that over and we'll get started.
[08:16] Jae: one more nuance — if you're using vLLM locally, the KV cache semantics can differ on offload. if you rely heavily on prefix caching, we should benchmark that path specifically.
[08:27] Ryan: noted. we'll include the vLLM configs.
[08:31] Amira: timeline question — procurement window is mid-october; we'd like a recommendation by Oct 6.
[08:38] Samira: we'll target sharing the initial benchmark and docs by Sept 29, and then a recommendation package by Oct 6.
[08:44] Tommy: any blockers on our side? none beyond providing artifacts.
[08:48] Priya: would like to review the SOC2 and the escape-hatch playbook before any PII is sent.
[08:55] Samira: understood, we'll gate PII until the legal/compliance review.
[09:00] Ryan: ok sounds good. last thing — do you have any customers in financial services who have done a similar migration? references?
[09:08] Samira: yes, we have a regulated fintech that did staged migration last quarter; i'll provide a redacted case study and a reference contact with permission.
[09:16] Amira: great.
[09:18] Samira: recap of next steps: I'll share pricing and compliance pack, Jae will run micro-benchmarks with your eval set, Marco will attach KMS and private deploy docs, and we'll reconvene week of Oct 5 to discuss pilot constructs. any other items?
[09:33] Derek: no. thanks.
[09:35] Ryan: thanks everyone.
[09:38] Samira: thanks all — we'll follow up via email with artifacts.

End of transcript.

References and links mentioned:
- Hosted vs Dedicated pricing spreadsheet (sent after call)
- KMS/HSM integration guide (link placeholder)
- SOC2 / ISO compliance pack (link placeholder)
- Escape hatch playbook (redacted link placeholder)
- Benchmark template and eval spreadsheet (link placeholder)

Keywords: migration, escape-hatch, private-deploy, dedicated-capacity, vLLM compatibility, TGI, SOC2, KMS, audit-logs, p99 latency, eval parity

title: Starter credit & micro-tier pricing notes
author: Maya R. Chen
text:
Purpose: rough, single-person scratchpad for a low-friction starter package + onboarding credits aimed at small businesses and early PLG signups. Not a proposal; just numbers + ideas to test with product/growth.

Context / goals:
- convert self-serve signups to paid within 14–30 days
- keep first-dollar friction low (easy to experiment w/ product)
- avoid heavy discounting of committed capacity while still giving tangible value
- keep unit economics breakeven target: >50% gross margin after infra and caching improvements

High-level ideas to explore:
1) Tiny free credit for new accounts (e.g., $7 equivalent) that maps to token credit rather than time-limited credits.
2) Starter monthly plan for "small apps" (1–3 developers) — low commitment, built-in burst credits, modest included tokens.
3) Pay-as-you-go (default) with optional auto-convert to starter plan after hitting a usage threshold.
4) Usage package bundles: tokens + request concurrency / faster tier as add-ons.

Assumptions (very rough, to iterate):
- infra (hosted) cost to serve: $0.0025 per 1k tokens (after batching, KV cache savings for typical chat/workload).
- marginal storage & infra ops amortized: ~$0.0003 per 1k tokens.
- total unit cost baseline: $0.0028 per 1k tokens.
- retail target price (bench): $0.02 per 1k tokens for lowest non-committed plan (~85% gross margin target initially).
- average session = 750 tokens (150 prompt + 600 response) for a small app chat flow.

Token math examples:
- Cost to serve one typical session: 0.75 * ($0.0028 per 1k) = 0.75 * 0.0028 = $0.0021 per session.
- Retail price if charged at $0.02 per 1k tokens: 0.75 * 0.02 = $0.015 per session.
- Gross margin per session: (0.015 - 0.0021) / 0.015 = ~86% (good headroom to subsidize starter credits).

Starter plan (sketch): "Starter" – $29 / month
- Included: 1,500,000 tokens (~2k sessions at 750 tokens)
- Equivalent token price: $29 / 1.5M = $0.0193 per 1k tokens (~aligns w/ $0.02 retail).
- Overage: $0.025 per 1k tokens.
- Burst credits: +100k tokens as monthly "burst" pool for spiky usage
- Limits: 2 concurrent streams, 90-day rollback for trial conversions

Economics for Starter plan (back-of-envelope):
- Monthly infra cost for included tokens: 1,500 * 0.0028 = $4.20 (since 1,500k tokens * $0.0028 per 1k) -> wait math: compute precisely: (1,500,000 / 1,000) * 0.0028 = 1500 * 0.0028 = $4.20.
- Gross margin on included tokens: $29 - $4.20 = $24.80 -> ~85.5% margin on included usage (high).
- If average Starter customer uses 500k tokens -> revenue recognized portion: (500/1500) * $29 = $9.67 realized; infra cost = (500 * 0.0028) = (500k/1k*0.0028)=500*0.0028 = $1.40 -> margin on realized usage still strong.

Free credit offer idea:
- New signups get $7 of token credit (non-stackable) mapped to ~350k tokens at $0.02 per 1k.
- Cost to us: infra for 350k tokens = (350 * 0.0028) = $0.98.
- If 3% of free-credit users convert to Starter within 30d, CAC subsidy can be small and pay back quickly.

Alternative micro-tier: pay-monthly micro plan ($9/mo)
- Included 300k tokens, overage $0.03 per 1k, 1 concurrent stream.
- Infra cost for included tokens: 300 * 0.0028 = $0.84 -> margin ok if average churn < 60% month1

Trigger-based auto-upgrade flow (product idea):
- If a PAYG user spends >$12 in 14 days, prompt: "Switch to Starter for $29/mo and save X%" showing break-even token counts.
- Provide one-click conversion and transfer remaining credits pro-rated.

Key levers & experiments to run:
- Experiment A: $7 credit vs $12 credit. Track conversion -> Starter and conversion -> paid overall. Measure net CAC.
- Experiment B: Starter price $29 vs $39 with different included tokens (1.5M vs 2.5M). Measure ARPU and churn.
- Experiment C: Overage price elasticities (0.02 vs 0.03) — measure revenue when users exceed included tokens.
- Experiment D: Make caching-enabled models default for Starter to reduce unit cost on typical patterns.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Validate infra cost assumptions with infra team and real traces (batch factor, cache hit rates).
- How do embeddings usage and long-context models change the averages? Need separate tiering for embedding-heavy apps.
- Policy for unused included tokens on cancellation/upgrade? (prorate?)
- Billing cadence for burst credits: monthly reset vs rolling window?
- How to present effective per-1k pricing clearly in the UI (avoid confusion around tokens vs messages).

Notes to self:
- Keep starter price psychologically anchored at $29 (common SaaS anchor).
- Keep free-credit small but meaningful — aim to let devs build a quick sample app or call the chat flow ~20–30x.
- Track 14-day retention and 30-day paid conversion as primary success metrics for these offers.

Quick sensitivity table (manual mental calc):
- If infra cost double (0.0056 per 1k) -> Starter margin on included tokens drops to ~70% but still acceptable initially.
- If average session grows to 1250 tokens (bigger responses) -> sessions per 1.5M tokens drop from 2k -> 1200 sessions. Evaluate UX tradeoffs and sample prompts in onboarding to keep sizes small.

Action items:
- Ask infra for a cost dump: real per-1k at 1k/10k/100k/1M token volume with caching on/off (due 2026-03-10).
- Wire up simple product modal copy and A/B test flow.
- Add micro-plan to pricing page as experiment (feature flag).

End of scratchpad.

(FYI: this is a single-user scratchpad; share selectively.)
