title: Ironcrest weekly pulse: bench debrief & routing decisions
author: Maya Chen
text:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-01
Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood, AE); Liam O'Connor (Redwood, SE); Dr. Ana Valdez (Ironcrest, CTO); Samir Patel (Ironcrest, Lead ML Eng); Jordan Reyes (Ironcrest, Platform Eng)

Summary: Quick sync on week-two POC bench results vs incumbent (NimbusAI). We reviewed latency deltas, throughput headroom, cache behavior, and options for routing + dedicated slots. Agreed next steps for a focused head-to-head and to exchange raw CSVs and configs.

Topics: bench numbers, kv cache effects, quantization profile, routing fallback, dedicated slot request, SOC2/KMS Qs, scheduling of deep-dive.

Action items (recap) at end.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — we want to run through the numbers from last nights runs, talk about what changed since the midweek tune, and agree next steps. hi Ana, Samir, Jordan.
[00:23] Ana: Hey Maya, thanks. yes we're tight on time today, got a leadership sync after this but wanted to get the numbers and anything that blocks our gating decisions.
[00:37] Samir: hey all. We're primarily interested in the p95 delta vs Nimbus, and also the end-to-end throughput at peak traffic.
[00:50] Liam: perfect. quick note — the runs we did were with Redwood hosted config: batching=auto, batch_size cap 64, kv cache on, quantize=8-bit dynamic, and routing rules set to prefer low-latency nodes in us-west. baseline run from Ironcrest used Nimbus default with their autoscaler and no kv caching.
[01:13] Jordan: okay good to know, that difference might explain the throughput gap we saw. can you just run numbers?
[01:20] Maya: yes. headline: median token latency improved, p95 for short-chat workload was 82ms on Redwood vs 128ms on Nimbus under the same concurrency profile. throughput — we measured sustained 720 requests/sec on Redwood nodes at 1024-token max with 8 workers, Nimbus sustained about 470 rps before they started shedding.
[01:48] Ana: those are promising numbers. can you confirm tokenization/parsing was identical? we had a prior case where tokenization discrepancies made apples-to-oranges.
[02:01] Liam: good call. we ran the exact same prompt corpus and tokenizer binary; small variance came from their pre-processing microservice which adds a 5-8ms overhead, so we stripped that out for the head-to-head numbers reported.
[02:18] Samir: hmm, the p95 improvement looks great but the tail — did you capture p99? we care about the worst-case for user journeys.
[02:27] Maya: p99 was 310ms on Redwood vs 660ms on Nimbus for that short-chat set under the 700rps sustained test. we think the difference is KV cache hit patterns and our routing — Redwood's warm KV cache avoided repeated KV loads on many sessions.
[02:46] Jordan: what about larger context lengths? our internal tests use up to 2048 tokens for some flows.
[02:53] Liam: we ran a 2k token pass too — throughput dropped (expected) but the relative latency delta shrank: p95 about 320ms Redwood vs 410ms Nimbus at 250rps. So Redwood still ahead but margin reduces as context grows.
[03:15] Ana: were these runs on shared hosted capacity? we've been debating dedicated slots for stable tail SLOs.
[03:23] Maya: yes these were hosted. we can provision dedicated slots — that gives you pinned GPU capacity, predictable throughput, and you'll likely see the p99 tighten up. we can estimate the committed capacity needed based on your peak qps.
[03:36] Samir: any data on cost delta? throughput is great but we can't double our inference bill.
[03:42] Maya: initial cost estimate: with batching and kv caching enabled Redwood lowered token-unit cost by ~28% vs Nimbus for this workload. exact numbers in the CSV I'll share. Dedicated price has commit options to reduce unit cost further.
[03:56] Jordan: how much of the improvement is from quantization? we've observed accuracy regressions at 8-bit on our CCD model.
[04:03] Liam: good catch — quantization contributed about 8-12% of the token cost savings and 5-10% latency improvement for the decoder-heavy pieces. but we tested eval prompts and didn't see accuracy drift beyond your tolerance on the sampled set; however we'll run more evals with your production samples.
[04:22] Ana: please run the evals; accuracy is a hard requirement. also we need SOC2 evidence and KMS integration info for audit.
[04:30] Maya: we'll share the security pack — SOC2 Type II attestation, SSO/SAML docs, and KMS/HSM options.
[04:36] Samir: routing — you mentioned fallback policies. in a cross-region outage we need deterministic fallback to an equivalent model; can Redwood do model variant fallback automatically?
[04:46] Liam: yes — our smart routing can define policy: prefer region A, fallback to quantized variant in region B, fallback to lower-latency smaller model, etc. we can make it per-route and tie it to SLA thresholds.
[04:58] Jordan: curious — when fallback to smaller model happens, what's observability surface? we want to track per-request which variant served it.
[05:06] Liam: tracing header on requests, route-level metrics, and token-level cost breakdown in the console. you can set alerts on regressions in quality or latency.
[05:18] Maya: small aside — we also captured error rates. Redwood error rate during the sustained 720rps test was 0.14% vs Nimbus 0.9% (timed out and 5xx).
[05:30] Samir: that's a meaningful operational delta. ok so next up for us is to run the disabled-KV cache head-to-head because our flow can't rely on cache for privacy reasons.
[05:41] Liam: yep, that's on our side to execute. we'll run the 2-hour head-to-head with kv disabled and identical autoscale behavior.
[05:48] Ana: can you also test with single-model pinned (no model variant fallback) to emulate our compliance constraints?
[05:56] Maya: yes — we'll run one pass pinned to the same model family and same weights, then another pass with fallback enabled so you can compare.
[06:05] Jordan: on the dedicated slot ask — what's the lead time if we want to trial a dedicated GPU pool? we might want to spin a small reserved pool for two weeks.
[06:14] Maya: we can provision a short reserved pool (burstable) in about 48 hours for dev/demo. For enterprise private deployment (VPC) it's longer, typically 2-3 weeks for network setup and KMS integration.
[06:26] Samir: network question — if we go dedicated in hosted but within our VPC peering, can we use our own KMS keys?
[06:33] Liam: yes, we support customer-managed keys via supported KMS providers for dedicated and private deployments. audit logs support and HSM options available.
[06:41] Ana: good. any red flags you saw in the runs?
[06:45] Liam: nothing major, but one anomaly: around minute 37 of the long run we saw a spike in queuing time. digging in, small GC pause in the model worker and a routing rebalance during a node rotation. We have mitigations: pre-warm and stagger node rotations, and improved GC settings for the runtime.
[07:07] Maya: we can also pin a small buffer of spare workers during your peak window to avoid rotations then.
[07:13] Samir: about the dev test dataset we'll upload — should we anonymize or can Redwood handle PII?
[07:20] Maya: Redwood will handle PII per enterprise terms, but for bench sharing it's simpler if you anonymize payloads. we'll sign the NDA addendum for raw traffic if needed.
[07:31] Jordan: ok we'll prepare an anonymized slice first.
[07:35] Ana: on the security pack — send it to our security inbox and I'll route.
[07:40] Maya: will do.
[07:43] [08:00] Liam: quick note about the CSV — columns included: timestamp, endpoint, model_variant, tokens_in, tokens_out, p50, p95, p99, node_id, cache_hit, error_code. we'll attach it.
[08:13] Samir: perfect. can you also include the raw histograms for tail latency, not just percentiles?
[08:18] Liam: yes, histograms and raw samples.
[08:22] Maya: ok wrapping up, recap and owners: Maya share CSV & security pack; Liam run KV-disabled head-to-head; Samir/Jordan provide sample traffic and open VPC peering request; schedule deep-dive for routing.
[08:38] Ana: sounds good. one last question — competitor mentions: Nimbus claimed they could hit 800rps at 512 tokens in their latest private config; why did they plateau at 470rps in your run?
[08:51] Liam: likely because Nimbus runs heavier pre/post-processing and their default batch scheduler has a different latency-first policy which reduces throughput. Also their autoscaler cadence caused small hiccups under step-load. We did a small test enabling their throughput-optimized profile and they reached ~560rps but with increased tail latency.
[09:12] Samir: that's helpful. ok we'll review and sync again after the head-to-head. thanks everyone.

Recap & next steps (verbatim):
- Redwood to share raw CSV and runbook (Maya) by 2026-10-02.
- Redwood SE to run a 2-hour head-to-head with KV disabled (Liam) and report p50/p95/p99 + histograms by 2026-10-04.
- Ironcrest to provide anonymized production traffic sample and SSO test user (Samir/Jordan) by 2026-10-05.

title: Event-sieve + continuation-token middleware for Python SDK streaming chat
author: Nina Alvarez
text:
Problem: Customers integrating long-lived streaming chat sessions report difficulty reconciling partial state after transient network failures, duplicate fragments, and client-side filters (eg. profanity or signal-based trimming). Existing SDK patterns focus on general checkpointing or replay but lack a lightweight, composable middleware that simultaneously: 1) filters irrelevant events early in the pipeline (reducing client work and telemetry noise), 2) emits compact continuation tokens that capture just the minimal resume point and necessary sideband metadata, and 3) provides deterministic idempotent application semantics so resumed sessions do not double-apply fragments.

Goal: Implement an "event-sieve + continuation-token" middleware for the Python SDK that offers an ergonomic hook for user filters, produces small continuation tokens for network-resume, and integrates with our telemetry and retry policies. The middleware should be easy to opt into, compatible with sync/async streaming surfaces, and include examples showing common patterns (signal filtering, incremental metrics, and safe partial-output commits).

Middleware implemented and exported as python_sdk.streaming.middleware.EventSieveContinuation
Supports both sync generator and async iterator streaming APIs without API surface divergence
Continuation token format is compact (<= 1KB typical), forward-compatible, and documented
Resuming a stream with a continuation token results in deterministic output: no duplicate final messages or double-applied side effects for configured idempotent sinks
Configurable filtering DSL exposed to customers (predicate function or declarative match rules)
End-to-end integration test coverage: network disconnect + resume, event filter change and stable resume behavior, telemetry counters emitted
Performance overhead measured: median added latency per-event < 250us on p3-like hardware for default sieve
Docs + example notebook and two sample recipes merged to docs site and python sdk examples repo
Design reviewed and security_review_required flagged if continuation token contains PII

Continuation token model: opaque base64 JSON with fields: last_event_id, ordered_watermark, small sideband checksums for prefix hash, optional filter-version tag
Event sieve: chainable pipeline stage executed before user callbacks; accepts predicate(fn(event) -> bool) and transformer(fn(event) -> event) hooks
Idempotency: recommend sink contract where each sink implements apply(event_id, event_payload) -> commit_token; middleware will track commit_token in continuation token to avoid reapply
Sync/async compatibility: implement core logic in sync functions, provide async wrappers using to_thread or async generators to avoid duplicating complex logic
Backpressure: sieve must be non-blocking by default; heavy predicates should run on executor and exposed to users in examples
Telemetry: emit counters 'sieve.dropped', 'sieve.passed', 'continuation.issued', 'continuation.resumed', plus histograms for token_size_bytes and resume_latency_ms
Security: continuation token will be signed with HMAC using SDK key store; if PII allowed by user config, require explicit opt-in and mark token as sensitive in logs
Backward compatibility: token parser will accept previous format versions; include migration tests
Fallback: when continuation not accepted by server, SDK should attempt full-replay path with a bounded retry and consult user-provided conflict handler

2026-03-02 Nina Alvarez: Initial write-up and prototype with two predicate styles (callable and simple DSL). Prototype uses naive JSON continuation token with last_event_index and prefix_hash.
2026-03-04 Samir Patel: Benchmarked prototype; baseline per-event overhead ~180us when predicate is simple attribute check. Noted that heavy regex predicates add 1-2ms unless executed in threadpool.
2026-03-06 Security review: flagged continuation token signing and opt-in for PII. Decided to sign tokens with SDK HMAC and mark opt-in path. Samir to add KMS integration ticket if customer requests server-verified tokens.
2026-03-08 Design review notes: prefer minimal state in token (last_event_id + sink_commit_hint) over full prefix. Add 'filter_version' tag so changing customer predicate invalidates resume by default.
2026-03-09 QA: Wrote resume integration test harness simulating interleaved partial-fragment and network drop. Found edge case where server replay injects finalization event; added conflict handler hook to allow client to decide merge or replace.
2026-03-10 Samir Patel: Draft PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/python-sdk/pull/1289 (WIP). Planning docs and cookbook next.

title: SDK mini-workshop playset + content backlog
author: Maya Chen
text:
Goal: a repeatable 30–45 minute mini-workshop that gets engineers from zero -> instrumented SDK call with basic telemetry and a smoke test. This doc is a playset (agenda + assets list + quick snippets) + a content backlog for short-form collateral. Status: working draft; intended for hands-on sessions run by DE reps and for inclusion in self-serve labs later.

1) Core constraints / design principles
- Keep idempotent: all exercises should be runnable in <30 minutes on laptop with free account keys.
- Minimal deps: Node (latest LTS) and Python examples only; no Docker required.
- Observable by default: instrument 5 telemetry events + one latency histogram.
- Failure-safe: provide sample network/cold-start mitigation guidance.

2) 30m running agenda (fast path)
- 0–3m: intro + expected outputs (demo of chat/embeds)
- 3–8m: set up CLI creds + scaffold (git clone, npm/pip install)
- 8–18m: Make first call (hello world generation) + streaming quickcheck
- 18–26m: Add telemetry hook (event names below) and run smoke assertion (tokens < threshold, status 200)
- 26–30m: Failover toggle demo: swap to local stub to show graceful degradation
- Stretch: 30–45m: add one prompt evaluation test and compare outputs across two model presets

3) Assets to ship (MVP):
- repo: workshop-stub (template code + README + smoke tests)
- one-pager: "30m SDK micro-workshop" (slides + speaker notes)
- short gifs: creds setup, streaming response, telemetry dashboard snapshot
- lab checklist: pre-reqs, firewall notes, known flaky networks

4) Code snippets (kept tiny for doc)
- Node quickstart (pseudo):
 const Redwood = require('@redwood/sdk');
 const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY });
 const res = await client.chat.create({ model: 'redwood-1-small', messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Summarize X in 20 words' }] });
 console.log(res.text);

- Python quickstart (pseudo):
 from redwood import RedwoodClient
 c = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_KEY'))
 out = c.generate('Explain mutexes simply')
 print(out.text)

5) Telemetry & smoke assertions (consistent names)
- events: ["sdk.start", "sdk.request.sent", "sdk.token.received", "sdk.request.error", "sdk.test.assertion"]
- tags: model, region, sample_app, cadence
- minimal histogram: request.latency_ms (buckets at 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000)
- smoke assertions: HTTP 200, tokens_consumed < 300 (configurable), response not empty, latency < 1000ms for demo model

6) Failure modes & recovery steps (teaching moments)
- 401/invalid key: repro steps + quick copy of how to rotate key in console
- High latency: toggle to 'fast-latency' model variant and re-run smoke
- Partial streams: instruct to fall back to non-streaming call and capture full output
- Networking (company VPNs): add note to disable corporate proxy for labs or use personal hotspot

7) Content backlog (prioritized)
- 1: workshop repo + one-pager guide + speaker notes (MVP)
- 2: 3x short gifs for marketing/devexp pages
- 3: quick video (5m) demonstrating failover + telemetry dashboard walkthrough
- 4: multi-language snippet pack (Go + Java + Ruby) – stretch goal
- 5: canonical smoke test suite to run in CI for SDKs

8) Measurement & success criteria
- adoption metrics: workshops run, repos forked, CI runs of smoke tests
- qualitative: participant self-report (post-lab survey: 3 questions)
- technical: % of sessions where students complete full fast path in <30m

9) Operational checklist for running a session
- pre-run: verify workshop repo token seeded, slide deck open, telemetry dashboard template ready
- during-run: record participant issues (channel + short GitHub issue template)
- post-run: collect feedback, convert top 3 pain points into tickets, schedule follow-up docs work

10) Open questions / TODOs
- Can we include an offline stub that simulates prefix caching behavior? (Priya to prototype)
- What's the minimal user-space telemetry SDK we can ship to avoid DIY instrumentation? (SRE consult)
- Decide canonical demo model set (cost vs latency tradeoffs) – propose: redwood-1-small (demo), redwood-1-medium (compare)

Notes for follow-ups: create small GH issues for each backlog item, run two internal pilot workshops (DE + Solutions Eng) and capture timestamps for friction points. Keep this doc lean — intended to be copy/pasted into a more formal Confluence page once MVP assets exist."

title: Tenant latency regression detection and circuit-breaker runbook
author: Priya Menon
text:
Summary
-------
This runbook describes the detection, automated mitigation, and operator playbook for tenant-facing latency regressions in private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It codifies SLO thresholds, Prometheus alert rules, automated circuit-breaker actions, customer-impact scope checks, communication templates, and post-incident validation. The goal is to reduce user-visible latency degradations and provide predictable, reversible mitigations that preserve correctness and compliance.

Scope and audience
------------------
- Scope: Redwood private deployments (VPC-connected control plane and on-prem runtime). Covers model serving request latency for tenant routes (generation/chat/embeddings) and the orchestration of fallback/circuit-breaker actions.
- Audience: Field operators, SRE on-call, Private Deployments support engineers, Customer Success for escalations.

Why this matters
-----------------
- Latency regressions are the most visible SLA breach to product teams; they can be caused by cache eviction, kernel changes, autoscaling anomalies, noisy neighbors, or model swap regressions.
- Automated detection + conservative circuit breaking prevents noisy tenants from degrading cluster-wide SLAs and provides a safe tripping mechanism while preserving customer data isolation guarantees.

Key definitions and SLOs
------------------------
- Tenant P99 request latency (100–4096 token requests): target <= 150ms (soft), alerting threshold >= 250ms sustained over 5m (actionable), critical >= 500ms sustained over 3m (escalation).
- Request error rate (5xx) should remain < 0.5% per tenant per 10m window.
- Circuit-breaker: an automated traffic-steering policy that routes affected tenant traffic to a compatible fallback model variant (quantized, smaller model) or to a degraded QoS path (strict token-rate limit + shorter max length) to preserve availability.

Detection signals and alert rules (examples)
-------------------------------------------
- Primary PromQL alert examples (adapt and localize to customer metric names):
 - Latency surge (actionable):
 ALERT TenantLatencySurge
 IF histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"runtime\",tenant=~\"$tenant\"}[5m])) by (le)) > 0.25
 FOR 5m
 LABELS {severity=\"page\"}
 ANNOTATIONS {summary=\"Tenant {{ $labels.tenant }} p99 latency >250ms for 5m\"}

 - Critical latency regression:
 ALERT TenantLatencyCritical
 IF histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"runtime\",tenant=~\"$tenant\"}[3m])) by (le)) > 0.5
 FOR 3m
 LABELS {severity=\"page\"}

 - KV cache miss storm:
 ALERT KVCacheMissStorm
 IF sum(rate(kv_cache_miss_total{tenant=~\"$tenant\"}[2m])) by (tenant) / sum(rate(kv_cache_requests_total{tenant=~\"$tenant\"}[2m])) by (tenant) > 0.2
 FOR 2m

- Secondary signals: pod restarts, GPU throttle metrics, enqueue Q length, model swap events, storage I/O saturation. Use these to reduce mean time to root cause.

Escalation and ownership
-------------------------
- First responder: current SRE on-call for private deployments.
- If ticket requires customer communication, assign Customer Success engineer and the private-deploy field lead.
- Security or data concerns: immediately notify Security on-call (see incident communication templates).

Automated mitigation (circuit-breaker) design
--------------------------------------------
The circuit-breaker is implemented as an orchestrated policy with three selectable mitigations. It must be enabled by default with conservative triggers and always log signed evidence for compliance.
- Mitigation A (transparent): reduce tenant concurrency (token/inference rate) by 30% and enable strict prefix KV cache favoring hot keys. Fastest, reversible.
- Mitigation B (fallback model): route traffic to a verified smaller/quantized model variant with compatible API. Preserves functionality at lower throughput cost. Use when cache-based mitigations fail for 3m.
- Mitigation C (degraded QoS): enable per-request truncation to 512 tokens and enforce 1s hard timeout before returning partial results. Use for customer-accepted emergencies only.

Automated action sequencing (recommended)
1. On TenantLatencySurge alert (5m): trigger Mitigation A automatically. Create incident ticket with auto-populated diagnostics.
2. If latency remains above actionable threshold after 3m post-MitigA: execute Mitigation B and notify CS with pre-filled customer impact template.
3. If Mitigation B fails to restore latency within 3m or errors increase >0.5%: notify lead SRE and on-call; consider Mitigation C after manual approval.

Sample circuit-breaker API calls (pseudo-CLI)
---------------------------------------------
- Apply concurrency throttle:
 curl -X POST https://controlplane.internal/api/v1/tenants/$TENANT/circuit-breaker \n -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' \n -d '{\"action\":\"throttle\",\"concurrency_pct\":70,\"reason\":\"auto-latency-surge\"}'

- Swap to fallback model variant (safe swap):
 redwoodctl swap-model --tenant $TENANT --from model-id:1.2.0 --to model-id:1.1.0-quant --grace-period 30s --kv-preserve true

Operational triage checklist (operator steps)
-------------------------------------------
1. Validate alert -> confirm tenant p99 abnormality in telemetry and check correlated signals (KV miss, pod CPU, GPU mem, restarts).
2. Review recent control-plane events (model swap, canary rollout, config change) in the last 60 minutes.
3. If Mitigation A not yet applied, allow automation to run; if already applied, escalate to Mitigation B.
4. Run quick k8s health checks on serving pods:
 - kubectl -n runtime get pods -l tenant=$TENANT
 - kubectl -n runtime logs <pod> | tail -n 200
5. If fallback model active, validate output quality against a small prompt-set (run local eval harness):
 - echo 'Quality check prompt' | redwoodctl eval --tenant $TENANT --model fallback-model-id
6. If restored, follow post-incident remediation steps (below). If not restored, open high-priority incident channel and assign action owners.

Customer communication templates (short forms)
--------------------------------------------
- Initial acknowledgement (within 15m):
 Subject: [Redwood] We are investigating increased latency for your deployment
 Body: We are seeing elevated request latency for your tenant (p99). Our automated mitigations may be active temporarily. This may result in slower responses or shorter outputs. We will post updates every 30 minutes until resolved.

- Status update (after mitigation applied):
 We have applied a temporary traffic shaping and, if needed, a fallback model to preserve availability. We will share detailed diagnostics and next steps in the follow-up report.

Post-incident remediation and follow-up
--------------------------------------
- Root cause analysis (3–7 days): collect traces, KPIs, model artifacts, and control-plane logs. Document RCA in the internal incident tracker with corrective actions and owners.
- Remediation examples: kernel rollback to previous runtime build, KV cache size increase, model quantization tuning, tenant-specific QoS policy adjustments.
- Regression guard: add the triggering prompt set to the model-onboarding/regression suite and schedule a canary for future model swaps.

Testing and game-day validation
------------------------------
- Quarterly drills: simulate a 2x KV miss storm across a synthetic tenant to validate automated mitigation sequencing and customer comms.
- Add automated unit tests for circuit-breaker policy enforcement and audit trail generation in the CI pipeline.

Telemetry and evidence retention
-------------------------------
- Retain 1Hz request traces + 1s histograms for the tenant for 14 days for post-mortem. Store signed mitigation decision logs for compliance (30 days default, configurable per customer contract).

Ownership and runbook maintenance
--------------------------------
- Runbook owner: Private Deployments SRE (on-call rotation).
- Review cadence: Every 6 months or after any major change to runtime, model catalog, or control plane.

Appendix A — Quick PromQL snippets
----------------------------------
- Tenant p99 over 5m: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{tenant=\"$T\"}[5m])) by (le))
- KV miss ratio: sum(rate(kv_cache_miss_total{tenant=\"$T\"}[2m])) / sum(rate(kv_cache_requests_total{tenant=\"$T\"}[2m]))

Appendix B — Related runbooks and references
--------------------------------------------
- steady-state-ops-and-cost-optimization-playbook-2026.json (steady-state guidance)
- model-hot-swap-and-quantization-fallbacks-playbook-2026.json (fallback model variants and compatibility)
- tenant-observability-mapping-and-dataflow-contract-2026.json (metric and trace contracts)

title: align-reauth-to-heartbeat-add-typed-stream-decorators-and-bump-sdks
author: Maya Chen
text:
Context and motivation: Several customer incidents showed token refreshs firing independently of the streaming heartbeat, which caused unnecessary reauth churn on long-lived streaming sessions. At the same time, language SDKs lacked a small set of ergonomically-consistent stream helpers that made consumer code resilient to brief reauth windows and restartable on transient transport errors. This PR introduces a small session shim that aligns reauth scheduling to the connection heartbeat (reduces mid-stream churn), plus typed stream decorators for Python/TypeScript and a StreamHandler pattern for Go.

What this PR does (single-string body): - Introduces heartbeat-aligned reauth scheduler: schedules refresh attempts in a jittered window relative to the latest successful heartbeat, and stalls aggressive refresh attempts if a stream heartbeat indicates the session is active. This reduces unnecessary credential swaps during healthy streams. - Adds Python async decorator @resilient_stream to wrap AsyncIterator/AsyncGenerator consumers with transparent reattach+resume semantics and exponential backoff profiles. - Adds TypeScript typed async generator decorators (resilientGenerator) with streaming-friendly retry presets and a small examples folder. - Adds Go StreamHandler interface + resilient reconnect helper that encapsulates credential refresh hooks and backoff wiring. - Bumps SDK versions: python -> 2.5.0 (minor), typescript -> 1.13.0, go -> v1.9.2. - Tests: unit and integration tests covering scheduling windows and stream decorator resume semantics. - Docs: migration guide and small examples demonstrating patterns.

Checklist: - [x] Design review (ENG-5123) - [x] Unit tests for scheduler and decorators - [x] Integration tests against ephemeral testbed - [x] Docs + migration guide - [x] SDK version bumps and release notes - [x] CI green (some flaky tests retried)

Commit summary (high level): feat: add scheduler/sessions shim; feat: language-specific stream helpers; chore: sdk bumps; test/docs. See commits array for messages.

Files changed (high level): See changed_files array; main functional changes are under sdk/* and docs/examples. The session shim is in sdk/*/cred/scheduler and the language helpers are under their respective streaming/ directories.

Review conversation summary: - Anders flagged a potential race between heartbeat updates and background refresh; I added a compare-and-update guard and extended unit tests to cover concurrent heartbeat pings. - Priya asked to normalize retry presets across languages; added a shared presets table and documented differences in the migration guide. - Diego requested stronger logs at INFO level for refresh attempts; added structured logs to Python and TS helpers and a traced span in Go.

CI: Full matrix run (py/ts/go) initially had two flaky integration tests on the TS generator; reran and they passed. All checks green at merge time.

Migration notes: Consumers using long-lived streams should prefer the new decorators/handler. For Python: decorate your async generator with @resilient_stream(backoff_profile='conservative') and remove manual reauth scheduling. For TS: wrap your async generator via resilientGenerator(...) helper. For Go: implement the StreamHandler interface and use stream.ReconnectWrap to get automatic reconnect and credential refresh coordination.

Why this change is safe: Scheduler defaults preserve previous refresh frequency for non-streaming sessions; stream-aligned behavior is opt-in via the new SessionConfig.wait_for_heartbeat flag (default true for streaming helpers). SDK bumps are minor and do not change runtime APIs except for the addition of these helpers and a small credential scheduler option.

Merge outcome: squash and merge.

Anders Holt: Can heartbeat updates and the refresh ticker race? If the heartbeat arrives while a refresh is in flight we could be renewing unnecessarily.
Maya Chen (author): Added a compare-and-set on the session.last_heartbeat timestamp and short-circuiting if last_heartbeat > refresh_start_time. Added unit test test_concurrent_heartbeat_refresh.
Priya Kapoor: Please make retry presets consistent across languages and document any language-specific tradeoffs.
Maya Chen: Introduced presets.json and documented differences in docs/sdk/streaming-decorators.md. Presets are implemented as first-class objects in TS/Python and as config structs in Go.
Diego Ruiz: Add an INFO log for refresh attempts so we can correlate in prod.
Maya Chen: Added structured logs and an optional trace/span name configuration (session.trace_name).

Introduced heartbeat-aligned reauth scheduler to reduce mid-stream credential churn; added resilient stream decorators for Python and TypeScript and a StreamHandler pattern for Go; bumped SDK versions (py 2.5.0, ts 1.13.0, go v1.9.2). See docs/sdk/upgrade-2.5.0.md for migration steps.

Python: use @resilient_stream on long-lived async generators; TypeScript: wrap generators with resilientGenerator; Go: implement StreamHandler and call stream.ReconnectWrap. Update session config to opt into heartbeat-aligned refresh behavior if you rely on manual refresh scheduling.

title: Enterprise customer unable to update routing policies (control plane config write failures, 500s)
text:
Issue summary
- Zenlytics (enterprise) cannot create/update routing policies in the Redwood control plane. UI and API requests fail with 500 errors.

Customer impact
- Customer is blocked from: (a) updating routing policy weights, (b) pinning model version for a new rollout, (c) adding a new fallback region.
- Live inference traffic continues to serve, but customer cannot make policy changes and is stuck on last-known-good policy config.
- Customer indicates an urgent business need to shift traffic due to performance issues on a model variant; inability to change policy is time-sensitive.

Timeline (UTC)
- 2026-01-29 16:05: Customer reports in shared Slack + opens support ticket.
- 16:12: Support reproduces via API; escalated to SRE + Platform Control Plane.
- 16:25: Incident channel created; initial mitigation/workaround attempted.
- 17:10: Root cause narrowed to control plane config write path (DB transaction + audit log write) under specific payload size/shape.
- 18:05: Hotfix deployed to us-east control plane API.
- 18:18: Customer confirms ability to update policy via API; Console still intermittently fails due to retry logic.
- 19:10: Console retry/backoff change rolled out; errors resolved.

How to reproduce
1) PUT /v1/routing/policies/{policy_id} with policy payload >= ~200KB (customer has many routes + per-route conditions).
2) Observe HTTP 500 and no policy update.

Observed errors
- API response:
 - HTTP 500
 - body: {"error":"internal_error","message":"failed to persist policy config"}
 - response headers include x-request-id (examples below)

Customer-provided request IDs (x-request-id)
- 01JH2K6Q7S2W9N7D2K6D9M0FQK
- 01JH2K7A2F0S8Y3K1C1C5WQ8TX

Support reproduction notes
- Repro confirmed from Redwood side using customer-scoped token (impersonation) in us-east.
- Console (ops + customer) surfaced generic error toast; Network tab shows 500 from /console-api/routing/policy.

Initial triage / hypotheses
- Auth/RBAC rejected writes? (ruled out: requests pass authz and fail in persistence step)
- Control plane DB contention / transaction timeout? (partially true)
- Audit log write path failure causing overall transaction rollback? (confirmed)

Investigation notes (engineering)
- Primary oncall: Platform Control Plane (Ethan Park) with SRE support (Rafael Mendes).
- Findings:
 - A recent change increased audit log payload size by including full pre/post config diffs for routing policies.
 - For large policy payloads, the audit log row exceeded a DB row/TOAST threshold and triggered a slow write; combined with a strict transaction timeout caused rollback.
 - Control plane API returned a generic 500 without a structured error code, which slowed down triage.

Mitigation / workaround provided to customer
- Temporary workaround offered at 16:40 UTC: split policy update into smaller incremental PATCH operations (per-route) to reduce payload size.
- Customer attempted; reduced but did not eliminate failures (still hit the audit log path for some operations).

Fix implemented
- Hotfix (18:05 UTC):
 - Changed audit logging to store a summarized diff (hash + top-level fields) for routing policy writes; full payload stored in object store asynchronously when needed.
 - Increased transaction timeout specifically for the policy write path with bounded retry on serialization failures.
- Console (19:10 UTC): adjusted retry/backoff and surfaced a more actionable error message including request-id.

Customer confirmation
- 18:18 UTC: Customer confirms policy updates succeed via API.
- 19:22 UTC: Customer confirms Console UI updates succeed; no further 500s observed.

Incident taxonomy + ownership mapping (for Reliability Program)
- Proposed classification (v1 taxonomy): Control plane outage > Config write/CRUD failures.
- Primary owner: Platform Control Plane.
- Secondary/consulted: SRE (incident process + comms), Smart Routing (validation layer), Observability (dashboards/alerts for error rate).
- Note: This ticket is being used as a concrete example in the ownership mapping table to keep "control plane config writes" distinct from "routing/fallback misbehavior" and "auth/RBAC failures".

Requested follow-ups
- Add structured error code for config write failures (e.g., CONTROL_PLANE_CONFIG_WRITE_FAILED vs INTERNAL_ERROR) and emit as metric label (low-cardinality).
- Add an alert for elevated 5xx on control-plane write endpoints, segmented by endpoint group (read vs write).
- Document known limit guidance: recommend policy size limits + how to structure complex routing policies.

Customer communications
- Rachel Kim provided customer-facing update cadence (every 30 min) in shared Slack; avoided attributing specific DB internals, focused on mitigation and restoration timeline.

Attachments / links
- Incident channel: #incidents (internal) referencing INC-2026-01-29-CP-CONFIG-WRITES
- Shared customer channel: #zenlytics-redwood (internal reference)
- Grafana (internal): Control plane API 5xx + latency spikes in us-east during incident window

Next update
- Close ticket after 48h monitoring window and confirm no recurring write failures; keep one-week watch alert for elevated write failures on policy endpoints.

2026-01-29 16:12 UTC — Dev Patel (Support): Acknowledged. We can reproduce 500s on routing policy update in prod us-east. Pulling in SRE + Platform Control Plane. Request IDs: 01JH2K6Q7S2W9N7D2K6D9M0FQK, 01JH2K7A2F0S8Y3K1C1C5WQ8TX.
2026-01-29 16:20 UTC — Rafael Mendes (SRE): Treating as Sev1 (customer blocked from config changes). Creating internal incident INC-2026-01-29-CP-CONFIG-WRITES. Please keep request-id in all updates; we’ll correlate in logs.
2026-01-29 16:33 UTC — Ethan Park (Platform Control Plane): Confirmed failing in policy persistence step after authz passes. Seeing transaction timeouts correlated with large payload sizes. Investigating audit-log write path; will propose hotfix.
2026-01-29 16:42 UTC — Rachel Kim (CS): Customer tried splitting updates (PATCH smaller changes) but still sees intermittent failures. They need to shift traffic today due to latency issues on current model variant.
2026-01-29 17:12 UTC — Ethan Park (Platform Control Plane): Root cause likely audit log payload size + strict transaction timeout. Implementing hotfix to summarize audit diffs and async full payload storage; aiming to deploy to us-east first.
2026-01-29 18:07 UTC — Rafael Mendes (SRE): Hotfix deployed to control plane API (us-east). Monitoring 5xx rate on write endpoints; initial drop observed. Please ask customer to retry policy update and report request-id if any failures persist.
2026-01-29 18:18 UTC — Dev Patel (Support): Customer confirms API policy update now succeeds. Console still failed once; likely needs UI retry/backoff improvements. Logging follow-up with Console team separately if it persists.
2026-01-29 19:12 UTC — Ethan Park (Platform Control Plane): Console retry/backoff patch rolled out. Also added request-id propagation to UI error toast so Support can triage faster next time.
2026-01-30 16:05 UTC — Dev Patel (Support): 24h check: no further write failures reported; control plane write 5xx back to baseline. Proposing we resolve and keep monitoring for 48h.
2026-02-01 09:40 UTC — Rachel Kim (CS): Customer confirms stability and successful policy changes through weekend. OK to close on our side.
2026-02-01 10:10 UTC — Rafael Mendes (SRE): For taxonomy/ownership mapping: logging this as Control plane outage > Config write/CRUD failures (primary owner Platform Control Plane). This incident will be referenced in the owner mapping table to avoid misclassifying as Routing fallback misbehavior.

Resolved via control plane hotfix to reduce audit-log write payload and add bounded retries; Console retry/backoff improved and request-id surfaced. Customer confirmed ability to update routing policies via API and Console; no recurrence observed during 48h monitoring.

title: Aukwood Searchworks
author: Jordan Malik
text:
Inbound lead via document search blog post -> clicked 'compare embeddings'. Company: Aukwood Searchworks (SMB knowledge-management SaaS). Primary ask: make doc search reliable + affordable. Wants hosted API self-serve first, may move to Dedicated later if traffic grows. POC scope: embed ~50k docs, support real-time upserts, run semantic re-ranking on top-k = 50 runs, target end-to-end p95 latency <200ms for query paths (embedding lookup + rerank). Cost sensitive - looking to keep hosted monthly spend < $2k during POC. Prefer open/verified models; asked about Redwood model catalogue and recommended embedding models. Tech questions from CTO (Ana R.): "Can we do incremental upserts + deletes with Pinecone? Will embeddings be stable across model upgrades?" SE notes: explained semantic-rerank pattern (sparse BM25 fallback, vector retrieve -> model rerank) and suggested caching top-k rerank results for hot queries. They asked about connectors: Pinecone, Supabase (pgvector), Weaviate. Also asked about sample code for 'Pinecone + Redwood hosted API reranker' and 'serverless ingestion pipeline' — SE to provide sample repo. Security: SOC2 required, SSO planned in Q1, retention/audit logs asked. Legal: DPA required before production ingest. Competitive context: they trialled OpenAI (too costly) and a DIY LLM + Faiss setup (maintenance overhead). Next steps: AE to send pricing + starter repo (drive links), SE to schedule technical demo (code walkthrough), POC kickoff targeted week of 2024-11-12. Blockers: internal budget approval and final vector DB choice. Short notes/snippets from calls: "We need predictable costs — not burst surprises", "If reranking reduces false positives by 30% that's a win". CRM tags: inbound, doc-search, embeddings, pinecone, hosted-api.

2024-10-12 - Website signup from doc-search landing page; trial credits requested
2024-10-13 - Automated API key issued (trial)
2024-10-25 - Discovery call (Jordan + Elliot + CTO - 45m)
2024-10-30 - Technical follow-up: ingestion demo with Pinecone, request for reranking sample
2024-11-01 - Fireflies transcript uploaded (ff_20241101_aukwood_intro)
2024-11-05 - Confirmed POC scope and metric targets

AE to send pricing deck + starter repo; SE to demo Pinecone connector; POC kickoff week of 2024-11-12

title: SLA metric definitions, measurement method & escalation path
author: nikhil_sharma
text:
From: Steve Morales <steve@acme.com>
To: nikhil_sharma@redwood.com
Cc: legal@acme.com
Date: Mon, 21 Jun 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Re: SLA metric definitions, measurement method & escalation path

Nikhil — thanks for the draft. Our legal team has circulated a few targeted asks around how uptime is measured and how credits are calculated. Summary of their points (see attached PDF for clause markup):

- Measurement window: Acme requests a rolling 30-day availability calculation rather than calendar-month to reflect usage spikes.
- Exclusions: maintenance windows should be limited to a monthly 4-hour maintenance window per region; any additional planned downtime needs 7 days' notice and cannot be used to accrue credits.
- Credit formula: propose credits tied to minutes of unavailability during the measurement window (simple linear schedule). Current draft uses percentage-based buckets — legal prefers explicit minute bands and a cap per month.
- Proof/evidence: Acme requires exportable audit logs (request IDs + timestamps) and a monthly availability report delivered to Acme SREs.
- Escalation path: when availability falls below the threshold for two consecutive days, they want an on-call bridge including Redwood engineering, Acme SRE, and the AE.

Can you confirm which of these we can accept as written versus which require RL/ops internal sign-off? We want to avoid open-ended maintenance carve-outs.

Thanks — Steve

Attachments: OrderForm_ACME_v3_redline.pdf

From: nikhil_sharma <nikhil_sharma@redwood.com>
To: kimberly_park@redwood.com, lauren_bishop@redwood.com
Date: Mon, 21 Jun 2027 10:05:00 -07:00
Subject: Fwd: SLA metric definitions, measurement method & escalation path

Looping legal and contracts — forwarding Steve's note and Acme's marked-up Order Form. Key asks summarized below. Please weigh in with concrete alternate language if there's any risk. We need an internal take before I get back to Steve (ideally EOD tomorrow).

Quick internal asks: 
- Ops: can we support rolling 30-day availability? What additional telemetry/export work would be required to generate those monthly reports on Acme's cadence?
- Legal (Kim): are minute-based credit bands workable vs the percent-bucket approach currently in the draft? Any liability or precedent concerns?
- Sales (Lauren): any commercial flexibility on cap levels or notice windows that you want us to preserve?

Context: this is a mid-market account; they've signaled volume but not committed to Dedicated yet. We should be pragmatic but avoid open-ended audit obligations.

Attachments referenced: OrderForm_ACME_v3_redline.pdf, SLA_Metrics_Appendix_draft.docx

Thanks — Nikhil

>
> - Measurement window: Acme requests a rolling 30-day availability calculation rather than calendar-month to reflect usage spikes.
> - Exclusions: maintenance windows should be limited to a monthly 4-hour maintenance window per region; any additional planned downtime needs 7 days' notice and cannot be used to accrue credits.
> - Credit formula: propose credits tied to minutes of unavailability during the measurement window (simple linear schedule). Current draft uses percentage-based buckets — legal prefers explicit minute bands and a cap per month.
> - Proof/evidence: Acme requires exportable audit logs (request IDs + timestamps) and a monthly availability report delivered to Acme SREs.
> - Escalation path: when availability falls below the threshold for two consecutive days, they want an on-call bridge including Redwood engineering, Acme SRE, and the AE.
>
> Can you confirm which of these we can accept as written versus which require RL/ops internal sign-off? We want to avoid open-ended maintenance carve-outs.
>
> Thanks — Steve
>
> Attachments: OrderForm_ACME_v3_redline.pdf
From: kimberly_park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
To: nikhil_sharma@redwood.com, lauren_bishop@redwood.com
Date: Tue, 22 Jun 2027 11:38:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Fwd: SLA metric definitions, measurement method & escalation path

Nikhil — reviewed Steve's asks and the attached redline. My read and suggested positions below. I have annotated the draft Order Form (see SLA_Metrics_Appendix_draft.docx) with strike/add comments. High level: we can accept most items with guarded language and operational limits.

1) Rolling 30-day measurement: acceptable if we keep a clause that final availability is calculated from Redwood's monitoring system and that Redwood's time-series is the single source of truth. Proposed sentence: "Availability shall be calculated on a rolling 30-day basis as measured by Redwood's monitoring tooling; Customer may request a report as set forth in Section X." This prevents parallel claims from Acme using their own tooling.

2) Maintenance windows: propose to counter with a monthly 6-hour maintenance window per region (not 4), but add a clause requiring Redwood to provide at least 48 hours' notice for any scheduled maintenance that may impact availability. We should not agree to a 7-day minimum for non-critical maintenance; that would cause operational friction.

3) Credit formula: we will not agree to uncapped per-minute liability. Counter-proposal: minute-band credits capped at X% of monthly fees (we should keep the cap as a negotiable figure but recommend 25% for mid-market). Suggest explicit band table in appendix; I'll draft the wording.

4) Evidence and logs: we can provide exportable event logs and a monthly availability report. Add data retention and redaction language: logs provided for SLA evidence will be redacted for other customers' data and provided in CSV format with request IDs and timestamps. Also include a clause that forensic-level log exports (full request traces) are subject to a data access request and may incur a nominal fee.

5) Escalation bridge: acceptable with scope. Recommend: automated alert + escalation to AE and SRE up to 48 hours after threshold breach; after 48 hours require an engineering bridge. We should not commit to on-call intervention for transient anomalies.

Next steps: I will produce a marked counterparty appendix by EOD tomorrow and flag the Order Form for commercial cap numbers. Lauren, can you advise on cap guidance (25% vs 15%)? Ops (will need ops to confirm rolling 30-day exports are feasible) — I will cc Ops once we have a draft.

Regards,
Kim

title: eng-platform
text:
lina: heads up — exported audit bundle for tenant=acme had actor set to `service:orchestrator` for ~2000 rows. i think actor resolution v1 collapsed the chained service hops, but we need user-level attribution for legal.

sam: ugh, saw that too when running the adjudication job. quick sample:
```
{"ts":1670000000,"tenant":"acme","actor":{"id":"service:orchestrator","hint":"user:uid:1234"},"change":...}
```

jordan: are the hints reliable everywhere? we used them as a fallback because not all requests carry full actor enrichment.

lina: not totally. some older routing flows (pre-rollout) only stamped the immediate service identity. the hint field exists but isn't consistently populated across the ingest path.

olivia: proposal: for exports we should include both `actor_resolved` (best effort user id/display) and `actor_raw` (what the service stamped). keeps the snapshot reproducible and forensics-friendly.

sam: SGTM. add telemetry events so we can measure how often resolved != raw. e.g. `export.actor_resolution.status = {resolved, fallback, unknown}`.

jordan: also need to consider export size/quota: re-resolving thousands of actors during export spikes will hit k8s API + identity cache. we should queue/resume and respect export throughput quotas.

lina: good catch. maybe run resolution offline during export bundle creation with a retry/backoff and emit a small summary for UI. won't block the NDJSON rows — just attach a manifest.json with resolution map.

olivia: UI/console note: console needs a badge when export contains ambiguous actors, with a link to the manifest. minimal UX copy: "Some actors are service-stamped; see export manifest for resolution hints."

sam: can we avoid a full re-run for existing exports? i'd rather not rehydrate all historical bundles. for new exports we can enable v2. for old ones, we can attach a lightweight index in-place by running resolution lazily on demand.

lina: yep — rollout plan: add API flag `actor_resolution=opt-in|v1|v2` on export creation. default for now remains v1. flip to v2 via canary (tenant flag) and monitor telemetry.

jordan: pseudocode for flag handling: 
```
POST /exports { tenant:..., actor_resolution: 'v2' }
worker: stream events -> emit row(actor_raw) -> enqueue resolution job -> write manifest.json when done
```

olivia: telemetry events we want: `export.requested`, `export.actor_resolution.start`, `export.actor_resolution.complete`, `export.manifest_attached`, plus histograms for extra API calls per export.

sam: ops: create a quota exception path so large historical backfills don't count against live export quotas. add silent rate-limit headers so UI can warn.

lina: security: ensure the resolved user id fields respect PII redaction settings. if a tenant hides user IDs, manifest should contain hashed pseudonym only. add `x-export-pii-mode` header to enforce.

jordan: leaving note about signing: presigned export links must include signature of final manifest to avoid tampered actor mapping. deploy-bot: can we wire a small rollout token for this?

deploy-bot: @lina created canary release export-actor-resolve:v2 -> env=staging -> rollout=10% tenants; automated smoke tests queued.

lina: thanks. next steps:
- olivia: update console badge + download modal copy (small PR)
- sam: add telemetry counters + histograms (prom + traces)
- jordan: implement manifest writer + offline resolution job (worker)
- me: API flag + quota exception flow + doc stub

olivia: i'll add a mockup to the export modal and put it in product backlog.

sam: i'll start a quick bench to estimate extra calls per 100k rows and post numbers here.

lina: if anyone objects to the plan pls speak now otherwise i'll mark this as ready and open the tracking RFC. :thumbsup:

jordan: no objections from infra side. sounds safe. :+1:

olivia: good to go.

audit-bot: note: created issue REDWOOD-EXPORTS-541 for actor-resolution-manifest (assigned: jordan).

lina: closing thread — i'll file the RFC and attach the telemetry schema. cheers.

title: docs
text:
emma: FYI mkdocs deploy failed on prod: a bunch of anchors 404ing after the mdx include refactor. https://ci.redwood/infer-build/17665/logs

jia: ugh ok. is this the same include reorder we landed yesterday?

emma: yeah, PR #4219 — I see local build passes but CI linkcheck flags fragments. deploy-bot posted the diff in the logs.

sam: small checklist: 1) did the include change headings (h2->h3) 2) slugify differences between docusaurus vs mkdocs 3) relative path canonicalization

marta: @sam re: slugify — mkdocs ascii-folding strips emoji and some punctuation, mdx inline HTML leaves raw ids. could produce different anchors for the same heading.

emma: here's a repro: in the page we include a snippet file that has a heading `## Usage (beta) :sparkles:`. mkdocs slug becomes `usage-beta` but the reference in another page uses `usage-(beta)` so the fragment breaks.

jia: ahhh emoji in heading. recommended fix: remove emoji in the generated heading or add explicit header id e.g. `## Usage {#usage-beta}` in the snippet.

sam: or normalize the cross-page link to the slug produced by mkdocs. but that requires us to know renderer slug rules. better to add explicit ids in the snippet to be stable across toolchains.

marta: quick patch: add explicit id to the snippet and add a tiny test in the docs CI that runs mkdocs linkcheck + a slug normalize step. I'll open a followup PR.

emma: cool. can someone push the snippet fix to #4219 so the failing deploy can be unblocked?

jia: pushing quick commit now. patch is just: in examples/quickstart.md snippet -> change `## Usage (beta) :sparkles:` to `## Usage {#usage-beta}` and remove emoji.

deploy-bot: build triggered for branch docs/fix-snippet-usage -> running linkcheck + mkdocs build

sam: also add a one-line note in the migration guide about heading id stability when migrating from docusaurus -> mkdocs. had a couple surprises when we changed slugify libs.

emma: agreed — add to docs/migration/docusaurus-to-mkdocs.md under "Headings & Anchors" with the explicit id recommendation and a short command to find problematic headings: `rg "[:emoji:]|\(|\)" docs/ | sed -n '1,200p'` (very rough).

marta: PR opened: #4221 — includes snippet id + migration note + tiny CI linkcheck tweak (retry flaky network). tagging @emma @sam for review.

emma: quick review done, left one nit about the sed example. otherwise thumbs up. :thumbsup:

jia: CI is green on the patch branch, deploy requeued.

deploy-bot: deploy succeeded: prod docs site updated (yay).

sam: nice. follow-up: create a lint rule in docs pre-commit to warn on emoji in headings and suggest `{#id}`. low pri but will save future headaches.

marta: will add to the backlog and maybe do a small precommit hook.

emma: thanks all. saved the morning. :coffee:

marta: note for posterity: tag in the release notes that we changed include handling; some older external links might 404 until authors add explicit ids.

sam: filed internal FYI ticket for that.

emma: closing thread once the deploy bot confirms prod.

deploy-bot: final status: success, linkcheck warnings only (no broken fragments).

text:
maya: FYI a new user hit a 402 on first quickstart call. They followed README exactly and got `Error: Request failed with status code 402`.

devon: That's usually a billing gate. Is the workspace marked billing_required?

maya: Yes server log: {status:402, error:"billing_required", request_id:"req_zz12"}. The client only retried once and showed a generic axios error.

samir: Two small fixes: 1) JS SDK should treat 402 as a non-retriable onboarding error with a help_url to the org billing page; 2) sample Next server should warn when `x-workspace-id` header is missing (common with dev proxies like Vercel).

onboard-bot: Suggested DM: "It looks like your workspace needs billing setup. See https://docs.redwood.ai/onboarding/billing"

devon: Assigning: SDK PR (samir, 2d), sample warning & README note (maya, 1d).

title: workload-sculptor-cli-mini-batcher-and-quant-tiering
author: Maya Chen
text:
Motivation: provide a lightweight, engineering-facing analysis and suggester (CLI + runtime hints) that produces per-route batching and quantization tier recommendations using sampled traffic, token distributions, and a simple unit-econ model. This reduces manual tuning for common workloads and enables safe, observable defaults for inference cost controls.

What this PR introduces: single-string CLI 'redwood sculptor analyze' that ingests a small traffic sample or evaluation prompts, produces a ranked list of candidate batch sizes, a compact quant-tier map (A/B/C tiers), and an annotated risk score for each suggestion. Adds a runtime "mini-batcher" hint that prefers many small microbatches for latency-sensitive routes (configurable) and a safe fallback path to previous scheduler behavior. Includes config schema extensions for "quantTiers" and "miniBatchHint" with sensible defaults.

Checklist: - [x] CLI and analysis engine implementation - [x] Runtime scheduler hook and unit tests - [x] Integration tests against smoke model and small synthetic traffic - [x] Docs and quickstart example - [x] Telemetry events for suggested change adoption and regression guardrails - [x] Linting and CI fixed after initial run

Usage summary (single-line examples are included in docs): run 'redwood sculptor analyze --sample ./traffic.json --model gpt-small --route /generate' to get recommendations. Output includes estimated tokens/cost saved, suggested batch size, quant-tier mapping (tier_A,tier_B,tier_C), and a conservative accuracy delta estimate based on eval prompts if provided.

Safety and rollout: suggestions are advisory only; the runtime requires an explicit apply step (or a rollout via Console) to change serving config. The runtime scheduling accepts a boolean guard 'enforceMiniBatchForRoutes' and an on-degradation fallback to model-size-preserving variants (e.g., fallback to float16) for routes that see output-quality regressions.

Implementation notes: the econ model is intentionally simple (token-rate x latency SLO x per-GPU cost) so teams can reason about numbers and extend it. We added telemetry hooks to measure pre/post token cost and accuracy on provided eval prompts so that the Optimize team can later build RL-style policy tuning on top.

Backwards compatibility: schema additions are opt-in; defaults keep current behavior. No DB migrations required; workload profiles are optional local artifacts or stored as an appendix in existing profile store (new key 'sculptor-profiles' but not required at runtime).

Related: ENG-5781 (econ cli kickoff), ENG-5799 (mini-batcher scheduling spec), SUP-2147 (customer asked for safer quant recommendations).

Ibrahim Patel: Nice focused tool — helps bridge the gap between profiling and ops. A few asks: add a telemetry field for "suggestion_confidence", unit-tests for the scheduler when many small concurrent routes exist, and ensure the CLI returns non-zero exit codes on parse errors.
Maya Chen (author): Thanks — added suggestion_confidence to telemetry and a new scheduler test 'TestMiniBatcherHighConcurrency'. CLI now returns structured codes; updated tests.
Sofia Martinez: Please ensure the default quant-tier mapping is conservative (tier_A should not recommend int8 unless model flagged as 'quant-verified'). Also, docs should show the safe-fallback lifecycle.
Maya Chen: Adjusted default mapping: tier_A -> q4_0 by default; introduced 'quantVerified' boolean in suggestions. Docs updated with fallback flow.
Ethan Brooks: CI flagged a lint error in pkg/config/schema_v2.json; once fixed, approve. Also request a smoke e2e in perf-canary that runs the suggester on 10k synthetic requests.
Maya Chen: Fixed linting, added a lightweight canary job in ci/perf-scripts (kept it gated to nightly).
Ibrahim Patel: Approving — tested suggested batch sizes against synthetic traffic and saw 18-26% token cost reduction for tail-insensitive routes with no quality regression in our eval set. Recommend monitor alerts on adoption.

Introduce 'workload-sculptor' CLI to generate per-route batching and quantization suggestions; add 'mini-batcher' runtime hint to improve tail latency for latency-sensitive routes; safe defaults are applied only when explicitly accepted. See docs/econ/workload-sculptor.md for usage and migration guidance.

This is a non-breaking, opt-in feature. Recommend staging rollout: enable CLI and telemetry in staging, run nightly canary, then enable 'enforceMiniBatchForRoutes' flag via Remote Config for a small set of routes. No DB schema changes required.

Expected unit-econ improvements for workloads with skewed token distributions and mix of latency/cost constraints. Early testing shows 15-30% cost improvements on batch-friendly routes; microbatched latency-sensitive routes see stable tail latency with small throughput tradeoffs. Telemetry added to monitor suggestion adoption and quality regressions.

Unit tests covering scheduler behavior, integration smoke test with sample traffic, docs example verified, CI lint fixes applied, telemetry events validated in staging namespace

ENG-5860: build a web UI in Console to preview and apply sculptor suggestions
ENG-5871: extend analysis to consider dedicated capacity pricing for Reserved GPU pools
ENG-5899: automated A/B rollout recipe for applied suggestions

title: Runbook: Upgrade-related alerts and mitigation (Redwood Private)
author: Rafael Mendes
text:
## Purpose
This runbook covers alerts and common failure modes that occur during **Redwood Private** upgrades (VPC and on-prem/air-gapped). It provides:
- Fast triage steps to distinguish expected upgrade noise vs. actionable incidents.
- Mitigation playbooks for the most common alert categories (error rate spikes, DB migration issues, control-plane connectivity, capacity/resource pressure, and certificate/identity problems).
- Clear escalation and rollback decision points.

This runbook is intended for **SRE on-call** and release captain support during planned upgrade windows.

---

## Scope
**In scope**
- Alerts triggered during an upgrade window for a single Private environment.
- Installer-driven upgrades (redwood-private-installer), Helm upgrades, control-plane/data-plane rollouts.
- Post-upgrade verification and “upgrade stuck” scenarios.

**Out of scope**
- Initial install failures (use Private install runbook).
- Long-term performance tuning (use serving-runtime performance playbooks).

---

## Definitions
- **Upgrade window**: Time interval approved via Private change-management policy; should be annotated in dashboards.
- **Control plane (CP)**: Redwood Private control-plane services (API, auth, orchestration, audit events).
- **Data plane (DP)**: Model-serving/worker components and runtime pods serving inference.
- **Prechecks**: Installer preflight checks that must pass (or be explicitly waived) before upgrade proceeds.
- **Rollback**: Installer-driven rollback using stored upgrade state and rollback hooks.

---

## Preconditions / what you need before acting
1) Confirm the upgrade is planned and within an approved window:
- Check #eng-releases for the release captain post.
- Check change ticket / calendar entry (per policy).

2) Identify environment details:
- Customer/environment name
- Deployment type: VPC vs on-prem/air-gapped
- Target version and current version
- Cluster context name (kubectl)

3) Ensure you have access:
- Cluster admin (or delegated) for the customer environment
- Read access to CP logs/metrics (or customer-provided export for on-prem)

---

## Fast triage checklist (do this first)
1) Is this during an active upgrade?
- Installer: `redwood-private status` or `redwood-private upgrade status` (exact command depends on installer version).
- Kubernetes: check for Helm hooks / jobs running.

2) Determine blast radius:
- Are customer inference requests failing?
- Is CP unreachable (Console/API) or only DP affected?
- One namespace or cluster-wide?

3) Confirm whether the alert is expected transient noise:
- During CP restart, brief spikes in 5xx can occur if readiness gates are misconfigured.
- During DP rollout, short-lived error spikes can occur if load is not drained.

4) If the alert is severe, stabilize first:
- If traffic is impacted: rate limit at edge / reduce load / pause rollout.
- If DB is unhealthy: stop further rollout steps and protect the DB.

---

## Dashboards and signals to pull up
- **Upgrade health dashboard** (Grafana): precheck failures, migration duration, error rates during upgrade windows, rollback frequency.
- **API/Ingress**: 5xx rate, latency p95/p99, saturation.
- **Kubernetes**: pod readiness, restart counts, job status, node pressure.
- **Database**: connection saturation, locks, migration progress.
- **Audit events**: upgrade start/stop, prechecks pass/fail, backup complete, rollback invoked.

On-prem note: if Grafana is not reachable, request screenshots/exports from the customer operator or use the support bundle (if enabled) that includes upgrade traces.

---

## Alert taxonomy (what it usually means)
Use this as a routing table for first response.

| Alert category | Examples | Usually indicates | Primary owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Customer request failures | 5xx spike, error budget burn | bad rollout, readiness/route issue, CP down | SRE + Platform |
| DB migration issues | migration duration > threshold, lock timeout, schema mismatch | unsafe migration, DB resource limits, stuck job | Platform (migrations) + SRE |
| Control-plane connectivity | CP healthcheck failing, OIDC/JWKS fetch fail | network/DNS/TLS, outbound egress, cert rotation | Platform + Infra + SRE |
| Kubernetes health | pods crashloop, nodes NotReady, image pull backoff | resource pressure, registry access, bad image | Infra + SRE |
| Storage/backup | snapshot failed, PV insufficient | CSI/EBS issues, retention misconfig | Infra + SRE |

---

## Common thresholds / when to treat as incident
Treat as an incident (page SRE on-call) if any of the following occur during an upgrade:
- API 5xx rate > 2% sustained for 5 minutes (or customer-reported outage).
- CP health endpoint down > 2 minutes.
- DB migration job running > 20 minutes with no progress indicators, OR lock timeout errors repeating.
- Kubernetes: > 20% of DP pods NotReady for > 10 minutes (with active traffic).
- Rollback invoked or required (always page release captain + SRE lead).

If you are unsure, err on the side of escalating early during upgrades.

---

## Playbook A: Error rate spike during upgrade (5xx / elevated errors)
### Symptoms
- Ingress/API 5xx rate spike.
- DP errors (timeouts, upstream unavailable).
- Latency p99 increase.

### Likely causes
- CP upgrade restarted services before readiness gates were effective.
- DP rollout drained capacity too aggressively.
- Misconfigured routing/fallback policy during rollout.
- Incompatible version pair (unsupported path).

### Checks
1) Confirm phase:
- Is Helm applying CP phase, DP phase, or post-upgrade jobs?

2) Identify failing component quickly:
- Ingress logs: upstream errors vs application 5xx.
- `kubectl get pods -A | grep -E 'CrashLoopBackOff|Error|ImagePullBackOff'`
- `kubectl -n <ns> describe pod <pod>` for readiness probe failures.

3) Validate readiness + routing:
- Are readiness probes failing due to dependency (DB, OIDC)?
- Are services receiving traffic before warm-up completes?

### Mitigation (stabilize first)
- Pause/stop rollout steps if supported by installer:
 - If installer supports pause: `redwood-private upgrade pause` (or equivalent).
 - If Helm is mid-run: stop automation and avoid re-running Helm until state is understood.
- Reduce load:
 - Temporarily lower DP concurrency or scale DP up if capacity allows.
 - Apply conservative rate limiting at ingress if available.
- If only DP is failing and CP is healthy:
 - Roll back DP chart phase first (preferred) if rollback hooks support partial rollback.

### If mitigation fails
- Trigger rollback using installer rollback command:
 - `redwood-private rollback --to <previous_version>` (exact flags vary).
- Ensure rollback includes:
 - Helm release rollback (CP then DP per ordering).
 - Config/state reversion.
 - Post-rollback health verification.

### Escalation
- Page **Release captain (Connor O'Brien)** if error spike persists > 10 minutes or rollback is being considered.
- Pull in **Ethan Park** if CP services are failing startup.

---

## Playbook B: DB migration issues (timeouts, locks, schema mismatch)
### Symptoms
- Alert: migration duration exceeded.
- Logs: lock timeout, deadlock detected, “relation does not exist”, “cannot cast type”, or repeated retry loops.
- CP pods crashloop due to failed schema validation.

### Likely causes
- Migration not fully backward-compatible (CP/DP mismatch during staged rollout).
- DB underprovisioned (CPU/IOPS) causing long-running locks.
- Connection pool saturation during migration.

### Checks
1) Identify migration job/pod:
- `kubectl -n <cp-namespace> get jobs,pods | grep -i migr`
- Inspect logs:
 - `kubectl -n <cp-namespace> logs job/<migration-job> --all-containers=true`

2) Confirm DB health:
- Check active connections and saturation (customer-managed DB may require their DBA).
- Look for long-running transactions and lock waits.

3) Confirm expected migration behavior:
- If migrations are designed to be idempotent, repeated attempts should not corrupt state.

### Mitigation
- Stop further rollout progression until DB is stable.
- If lock timeout errors are present:
 - Reduce app load if the CP is still serving traffic.
 - If safe and approved, temporarily increase DB resources (IOPS/CPU) during the window.
- If schema mismatch indicates a partial upgrade:
 - Prefer **rollback** if migration is not backward-compatible (do not “force” forward without platform owner approval).

### Rollback decision rule (DB-specific)
Rollback if any of the following are true:
- Migration is declared non-reversible/non-backward-compatible in release notes.
- CP cannot start because it expects new schema and migration cannot complete.
- Lock contention is causing customer impact and cannot be stabilized quickly.

### Escalation
- Page **Michael Nguyen (Config persistence & migrations)** for any migration lock/deadlock or schema mismatch.
- If customer-managed DB needs intervention, involve **Support escalation SME (Owen Phillips)** to coordinate with customer DBA.

---

## Playbook C: Control-plane connectivity failures (healthcheck down, auth/OIDC issues)
### Symptoms
- CP health endpoint failing.
- Console/API login failures.
- Logs show OIDC discovery/JWKS fetch failures, TLS handshake errors, DNS resolution failures.

### Likely causes
- Egress restrictions (on-prem/proxy) blocking identity provider.
- DNS/TLS misconfiguration during upgrade.
- Network policies tightened or reset by chart upgrade.

### Checks
1) Health endpoints and service readiness:
- `kubectl -n <cp-namespace> get pods` and check readiness.

2) DNS and egress from CP pods:
- Exec into a CP pod and test DNS:
 - `nslookup <idp-host>`
 - `curl -vk https://<idp-host>/.well-known/openid-configuration`

3) Certificates:
- Confirm cert secrets exist and were not rotated unexpectedly.

### Mitigation
- If egress blocked: coordinate with customer network team to temporarily allow required endpoints.
- If DNS misconfigured: revert known-good CoreDNS config or network policy; validate quickly.
- If chart introduced stricter network policy unexpectedly: roll back chart revision.

### Escalation
- Involve **Victor Alvarez (Networking reviewer)** for network policy/egress/DNS issues.
- Involve **Marcus Lin (Security engineering)** if TLS/cert chain changes are suspected to be policy-related.

---

## Playbook D: Kubernetes rollout failures (CrashLoop, ImagePull, NotReady nodes)
### Symptoms
- Pods in CrashLoopBackOff.
- ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull.
- Nodes NotReady, DiskPressure, MemoryPressure.

### Likely causes
- Offline registry/mirror misconfigured (common for on-prem/air-gapped).
- Resource requests/limits changed with new version.
- Node pressure due to parallel upgrades + backups.

### Checks
- `kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -n 50`
- `kubectl -n <ns> describe pod <pod>` for image pull and resource errors.
- Verify registry endpoints from nodes/pods.

### Mitigation
- If ImagePull errors:
 - Validate artifact mirror endpoints and credentials.
 - For air-gapped: confirm bundle verification passed and images exist in offline registry.
- If node pressure:
 - Scale up cluster if possible.
 - Reduce concurrent rollout (one component at a time).
 - Pause backups/snapshots if they are saturating IO.

### Escalation
- Pull in **Irene Choi / Vanessa Ortiz** for cluster capacity/node lifecycle issues.

---

## Playbook E: Backup/snapshot failures during upgrade
### Symptoms
- Installer reports backup step failed.
- Snapshot job fails; CSI/EBS snapshot errors; insufficient space.

### Mitigation
- Do not proceed with destructive upgrade steps if backup is required by policy.
- If storage headroom is insufficient:
 - Expand volumes where supported or free space.
 - Re-run prechecks/backup step only after remediation.

### Escalation
- Infra on-call + storage SME (Irene Choi).
- If customer insists on proceeding without backup: follow change-management exception process and obtain explicit approval (SRE lead + Release Eng).

---

## Rollback guidance (when and how)
### When to rollback
Rollback is recommended when:
- Customer impact persists and mitigation cannot restore service quickly.
- Migration issues indicate unsafe forward progression.
- Control-plane cannot reliably authenticate/serve.
- Version compatibility policy flags the path as unsupported.

### How to rollback safely (high-level)
1) Confirm backups exist (and are valid) if rollback requires restore.
2) Use installer rollback so that rollback hooks run in the correct order.
3) Verify post-rollback health:
- CP healthy and authenticated.
- DP serving and error rate normal.
- DB accessible and stable.

### Post-rollback expectations
- Capture upgrade plan + execution logs in support bundle.
- Emit/verify audit events for rollback invoked/completed.

---

## Escalation rules and ownership
### Paging / engagement order
- **SRE on-call (primary)**: triage, stabilize, comms, coordinate.
- **Release captain (Connor O'Brien)**: any upgrade pause/abort/rollback, any release-wide pattern.
- **Platform CP lead (Ethan Park)**: CP startup/readiness, compatibility gating failures.
- **Migrations owner (Michael Nguyen)**: DB migration failures, schema mismatch.
- **Infra lead (Irene Choi)**: cluster health, storage, registry connectivity.
- **Networking (Victor Alvarez)**: DNS/egress/network policy.
- **Observability (Allison Grant)**: missing signals, dashboard gaps, audit/event validation.

### When to declare incident vs. continue as planned work
Declare an incident if:
- Customer workload is down or materially impaired.
- Upgrade is stuck with unclear recovery.
- Rollback is required.

Otherwise, treat as “upgrade task with elevated attention,” but keep comms in #eng-releases and document decisions.

---

## Communication templates (internal)
### Update in #eng-releases
Include:
- Env/customer, current phase (CP/DP/migrations/backups), time started
- Symptoms and key metrics (5xx %, CP health status, migration progress)
- Action taken (pause/scale/rollback)
- ETA for next update

Example:
"[Private Upgrade] <env> upgrading <N-1 -> N>. Observed 5xx spike (3.4%/5m) during DP rollout; paused upgrade, scaling DP +2 replicas, investigating readiness probe failures. Next update in 15m."

### Update to Support (if customer impacted)
- Confirm whether this is within maintenance window.
- Provide current status, whether rollback is being evaluated, and the next update time.

---

## Evidence and auditability (do not skip for enterprise environments)
During upgrades/rollbacks, ensure the following artifacts are captured:
- Upgrade plan output (stages/steps, versions, artifact digests)
- Precheck results (pass/warn/block)
- Backup status and identifiers (snapshot IDs or logical backup markers)
- Upgrade/rollback start/stop timestamps
- Operator actions (pause/resume/rollback)

If audit events are missing, note it explicitly and open a follow-up ticket to Observability.

---

## Post-event checklist
After stabilization (upgrade completes or rolls back):
1) Add incident-bot annotation/tag linking the upgrade window and release artifacts.
2) File follow-ups:
- Missing precheck → add/adjust precheck severity.
- Migration issues → add guardrails/timeouts; consider safer multi-phase migrations.
- Readiness/routing issues → tighten Helm hook ordering and readiness gates.
3) Update this runbook if new failure mode occurred.

---

## Appendix: quick commands
### Kubernetes
- Pods/events:
 - `kubectl get pods -A`
 - `kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -n 100`
- Logs:
 - `kubectl -n <ns> logs <pod> -c <container> --since=30m`
- Rollout status:
 - `kubectl -n <ns> rollout status deploy/<name> --timeout=5m`

### Helm
- `helm -n <ns> history <release>`
- `helm -n <ns> status <release>`
- `helm -n <ns> rollback <release> <revision>` (use only when aligned with installer rollback semantics)

### Installer (examples; exact commands vary by version)
- `redwood-private upgrade plan --from <v1> --to <v2>`
- `redwood-private upgrade run --plan <path>`
- `redwood-private upgrade status`
- `redwood-private rollback --to <previous_version>`

---

## Owner / maintenance
- Owner: SRE (Rafael Mendes)
- Review cadence: every Private release train (quarterly) or after any rollback event
- Last verified in staging: 2025-06-17 (Q2 Private release train)
