title: Internal IT/admin users receiving 403 in Console (missing permissions) during RBAC v2 dogfood
text:
Issue summary:
Internal IT/admin users (Okta group: "IT-Admins" and "Corp-Helpdesk") are getting blocked in the Redwood Console during RBAC v2 dogfood with "You don’t have permission" / 403 errors. They cannot access org settings pages needed for provisioning and support.

Impact:
- IT cannot perform basic admin workflows (user provisioning checks, role assignments, org-level settings) during dogfood.
- Support/IT escalations increasing because admins cannot self-serve.
- Risk: perceived instability of RBAC v2 rollout; potential to slow down internal dogfood readiness.

Environment:
- Console: prod (internal dogfood)
- Authz: RBAC v2 feature flag enabled for Redwood internal org
- Identity: Okta SSO with group->role mapping

Who is impacted:
- David Kim (IT)
- Fiona McCarthy (SecOps)
- On-call internal admins attempting to triage permission-denied reports

Symptoms / error:
- Console shows toast/banner: "Permission denied" and fails to load Org Settings -> Users/Roles
- Network calls fail with HTTP 403
- Denial debug header (for admin requests) indicates missing permission for console endpoints

Steps to reproduce:
1) Login to Console with Okta user in "IT-Admins" group
2) Select Redwood internal dogfood org
3) Navigate to Settings -> Users
4) Observe 403 from console backend

Expected:
IT-Admins should have at least read/write access for org user/role management and ability to view audit logs for support purposes.

Actual:
Existing group mapping grants a legacy v1 role which does not map cleanly in v2. Under deny-by-default enforcement, Console endpoints now require explicit permissions and the IT-Admins role binding does not include the Console permission set.

Notes:
- This appears after enabling RBAC v2 dogfood flag and after adopting deny-by-default middleware for Console backend routes.
- Similar denial pattern reported in #help, but this ticket focuses on internal admin access for IT/SecOps.

2025-01-28 09:12 PT - David Kim (Reporter): Noticed since yesterday afternoon: IT-Admins can log in but cannot open Settings -> Users / Roles. Console shows permission denied and page is blank. This blocks provisioning troubleshooting for new hires. Please advise on correct role binding under RBAC v2 dogfood.
2025-01-28 09:34 PT - Kaitlyn Nguyen (Assignee): Acknowledged. Please paste a request ID from the failed call (from DevTools) and confirm which Okta groups the user is in. Also confirm whether you’re in the Redwood internal org or a test org.
2025-01-28 10:02 PT - David Kim: Request ID: req_7d3b1c1f1a. User in Okta groups: IT-Admins, Corp-Helpdesk. Org: Redwood Internal (dogfood).
2025-01-28 10:25 PT - Felix Schneider (Console): Pulled logs for req_7d3b1c1f1a. Denied on action permission: "console.org.users.list" (exact string in log) at scope org=redwood-internal. Denial reason code in log: MISSING_PERMISSION. User had bindings only for legacy role "admin" (v1) which in v2 mapping does not include Console permissions (only a subset for API key mgmt).
2025-01-28 10:41 PT - Kaitlyn Nguyen: Confirmed: This is a migration gap in our default mapping for internal admin groups. In v2, Console backend endpoints require explicit console.* permissions; the legacy mapping grants control-plane.* but not console.*. Proposing immediate workaround: bind IT-Admins to built-in template "Org Admin" in Redwood Internal org until we finalize an "Internal Admin" template.
2025-01-28 11:05 PT - David Kim: Workaround sounds ok. We need IT to be able to manage users/roles + view audit logs. We do not want IT to have billing admin by default if avoidable, but can accept temporarily for dogfood.
2025-01-28 11:22 PT - Jordan Lee (Policy engine): +1 on short-term fix. Longer-term: add a first-party role template "IT Support Admin" (org-scoped) with users/roles read-write, audit log read/export, no billing, no secret rotation. We should generate it in the policy bundle and document recommended internal group mapping.
2025-01-28 12:10 PT - Kaitlyn Nguyen: Implemented immediate fix in Redwood Internal org: created role binding: Okta group "IT-Admins" -> role template "Org Admin" at org scope. Also added "Corp-Helpdesk" -> "Read-only Auditor" temporarily so Helpdesk can at least view user lists and audit logs. Please re-login and confirm.
2025-01-28 12:37 PT - David Kim: Confirmed after logout/login: Settings -> Users loads, can invite/remove users and edit role assignments. Audit log page loads as well. Thanks. Requesting follow-up to reduce scope (remove billing permissions) before broad dogfood.
2025-01-29 09:18 PT - Naomi Feldman (PM): Tracking follow-up action: define internal-facing role template (IT Support Admin) and update internal Okta mapping guidance. Please link any proposed permission set to the Role Templates & Matrix page.
2025-01-30 14:05 PT - Chloe Martin (Console backend): Adding note: we should ensure Console pages have clearer “why denied” UX for internal dogfood. Current experience is blank page + toast. We should at least show required permission + escalation path for admins (ties to denial reason codes + debug header).
2025-02-03 10:28 PT - Kaitlyn Nguyen: Follow-ups captured below. Closing this internal support ticket since access is restored via role binding change; remaining work will be tracked in engineering/product tickets.

Resolution:
- Added org-scoped role bindings for Okta groups IT-Admins and Corp-Helpdesk in Redwood Internal org.
- Verified IT-Admins can access Console org admin workflows.

Root cause:
- Legacy/v1 role mapping did not include newly required console.* permissions under deny-by-default middleware.

Follow-up actions:
1) Create/ship "IT Support Admin" role template (no billing) in policy bundle; update internal mapping docs (Owner: Jordan Lee / Naomi Feldman).
2) Add guardrail: internal dogfood checklist must validate IT/SecOps access before enabling flags broadly (Owner: Connor O'Brien).
3) Improve Console denied state to display required permission + link to request access (Owner: Tessa Morgan / Felix Schneider).
4) Add an automated check/test ensuring built-in admin templates include required console.* permissions for Settings pages (Owner: Leila Farouk).

Role binding fix applied in Redwood Internal org: mapped Okta groups IT-Admins -> Org Admin (org scope) and Corp-Helpdesk -> Read-only Auditor (org scope). Access verified by reporter. Follow-up work created to introduce a narrower IT Support Admin role template and improve denied-state UX.

title: AuroraTech partnership: proposed MSA/DPA template revision
author: aditya_rao
text:
From: Liam O'Neill <liam.oneill@auroratech.com>
To: aditya_rao@redwood.ai, vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai
Cc: Sara Patel <sara.patel@auroratech.com>, legal@auroratech.com
Date: Sun, 29 Nov 2026 09:12:00 -0500
Subject: AuroraTech partnership: initial MSA/DPA edits and SOW questions
Attachments: Aurora_MSA_redlines_v1.docx (docx), Aurora_DPA_comments.pdf (pdf)

Hi Aditya & Vanessa,

Thanks again for the demo last week — excited about the potential fit between Redwood's private deployment and our regulated edge use case. We've run our legal and security review against Redwood's draft MSA, DPA, and the SOW template. Please find two attachments: a redlined MSA and a short PDF with DPA comments.

title: PRD: RBAC v2 (Enterprise Controls)
author: Naomi Feldman
text:
## Summary
RBAC v2 is Redwood Inference’s next-generation authorization layer designed for regulated enterprise workloads across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. RBAC v2 provides least-privilege access control with deny-by-default enforcement, consistent permissions across product surfaces, scoped role bindings (org/project/environment/cluster), and auditability of authorization decisions for SOC2 evidence and enterprise security questionnaires.

This PRD defines: (1) the customer problem and target personas, (2) functional requirements for the platform, API Gateway, control plane, and Console, (3) success metrics and guardrails, and (4) a phased release plan with migration and compatibility constraints.

## Problem statement
Redwood’s existing authorization model (RBAC v1 and/or mixed service-local checks) is insufficient for enterprise buyers who require:
- Least-privilege access control (separation of duties, minimal default permissions).
- Provable enforcement (consistent permission checks across Gateway, control plane services, and Console).
- Clear auditability (who attempted what, on which scoped resources, what policy was evaluated, and why it was allowed/denied).
- Operational usability (role templates, permission search/viewer, and actionable denial guidance).

In practice, current gaps show up as:
- Inconsistent enforcement across endpoints (Gateway vs service checks; unannotated endpoints).
- Coarse roles that over-grant and fail separation of duties.
- Limited ability to scope permissions (e.g., operator needs access to a specific environment/cluster, not the whole org).
- Permission-denied errors that are hard to troubleshoot (no clear reason, no "why denied" guidance, incomplete audit context).

## Goals
1) Canonical permission model
- Define a consistent, versioned permission catalog covering sensitive actions across Hosted API, Console, control plane, Dedicated, and Private operations.
- Establish a stable naming convention and deprecation/versioning policy.

2) Deny-by-default enforcement
- Ensure all security-relevant requests are evaluated against RBAC v2 policies.
- Prevent bypasses due to missing annotations/middleware.

3) Enterprise-grade scoping
- Support role bindings scoped to org, project, environment, and (for Private) cluster.
- Provide clear semantics for how scopes apply to resources and actions.

4) Auditability and evidence
- Log authorization decisions with context (subject/action/resource/scope/policy version/decision/denial reason).
- Produce evidence-friendly artifacts: permission inventory, role matrix, coverage reports, and audit samples.

5) Operator and admin UX
- Provide role templates and a role/permission viewer.
- Provide "why was I denied?" guidance, with safe exposure controls.

## Non-goals (v2)
- A general-purpose customer-configurable ABAC/policy language (custom rule scripting).
- Re-architecting authentication/identity beyond integration points (SSO remains; RBAC is authorization).
- Perfectly eliminating all legacy roles immediately (migration requires compatibility and staged rollout).

## Target customers and deployment modes
- Enterprise customers in regulated industries (financial services, healthcare, insurance) requiring strict access controls and audit log export to SIEM.
- Deployment modes:
 - Hosted API + Console
 - Dedicated capacity
 - Private deployments (VPC and on-prem), including installer/admin bootstrap flows

## Personas
### Persona A: Security Admin (customer)
Responsibilities:
- Define least-privilege roles and separation of duties.
- Manage users, groups, and role assignments.
- Validate audit logs and support internal audits.
- Respond to incidents and coordinate emergency access.

Pain points today:
- Hard to grant read-only/auditor access without over-granting.
- Limited transparency into what a role actually allows.
- Insufficient audit context to prove authorization decisions.

What success looks like:
- Can assign standard templates (Security Admin, Auditor, Deployment Operator) with minimal changes.
- Can scope access to specific projects/environments.
- Can export audit logs to SIEM with allow/deny decision context.

### Persona B: Platform Operator (customer)
Responsibilities:
- Operate model serving and routing policies safely.
- Manage deployments, capacity, and environment-specific configurations.
- Troubleshoot production issues quickly.

Pain points today:
- Either lacks access to needed operational actions or is granted broad admin.
- Permission errors lack actionable detail.
- Unclear which actions are allowed in which environments.

What success looks like:
- Can do day-to-day operations (routing, rollouts, capacity changes) scoped to an environment/cluster.
- Denied actions include a clear next step (request role / contact admin), and admins can debug quickly.

### Persona C: Redwood Internal Support / Solutions Engineer (internal)
Responsibilities:
- Help enterprise customers configure roles, troubleshoot 403s, and validate controls during security reviews.

What success looks like:
- Clear documentation, stable templates, and an internal playbook.
- Quick triage of denial spikes during migration (feature flags, dashboards, logs).

## Key user journeys
1) Onboarding (enterprise)
- Customer enables SSO and provisions initial org admins.
- Customer applies role templates (Security Admin, Auditor, Operator) and binds them to IdP groups.

2) Scoped operations
- Operator updates a routing policy in Environment: “prod-us-east” within Project: “payments”.
- Authorization must evaluate with environment scope and record the decision.

3) Audit readiness
- Auditor exports audit logs for last 30 days with decision context and filters by project/environment.
- Logs are SIEM-compatible and include policy version identifiers.

4) Migration safety
- Existing customers upgrade without breaking existing workflows.
- Dual-read mode detects and flags discrepancies between v1 and v2 decisions.

5) Emergency access (break-glass)
- Time-bound elevation with approval, high-visibility logging, and post-use review.

## Functional requirements
### 1) RBAC v2 primitives and semantics
REQ-1.1 Permissions
- The system MUST have a canonical, versioned permission catalog.
- Permissions MUST be granular enough to support separation of duties across:
 - Org/user/role management
 - API key creation/rotation/revocation
 - Secret management and integrations (KMS/HSM references, credential rotation)
 - Routing policy changes (including fallbacks and region routing)
 - Model pinning/version rollouts/canaries
 - Data retention/residency configuration
 - Private deployment administrative operations (installer bootstrap, cluster config changes)
 - Audit log export and configuration

REQ-1.2 Roles
- The system MUST support named roles as collections of permissions.
- The system SHOULD support both:
 - Built-in role templates (managed by Redwood policy bundle)
 - Custom roles (customer-defined) with explicit permission selection

REQ-1.3 Role bindings and scopes
- The system MUST support binding principals (users, service accounts, IdP groups) to roles at the following scopes:
 - Org
 - Project
 - Environment
 - Cluster (Private deployments)
- Scope inheritance MUST be defined and documented (e.g., org-level binding applies to all projects/environments unless overridden by deny rules).
- Scopes MUST be representable in audit logs and denial reasons.

REQ-1.4 Deny-by-default
- Any request requiring authorization MUST be denied unless an allow decision is computed.
- The evaluation MUST be deterministic for a given policy version and subject context.

### 2) Enforcement and API behavior
REQ-2.1 Standard enforcement points
- The platform MUST enforce authorization consistently across:
 - API Gateway (first-line check)
 - Control plane services (defense-in-depth; must not trust gateway alone)
 - Console backend endpoints
- Endpoint metadata MUST include required permission(s) and resource/scope mapping.

REQ-2.2 Coverage guardrails
- The build/release process SHOULD fail if security-relevant endpoints are missing permission annotations.
- The team MUST maintain a coverage report for endpoints/jobs mapped to permissions.

REQ-2.3 Error semantics
- Denied requests MUST return a standardized error response.
- The response MUST be safe by default (no sensitive policy details to non-admins).
- The response SHOULD include:
 - A stable denial reason code
 - A human-readable message
 - A request id / trace id
- For authorized admins (or in explicitly enabled debug mode), the response MAY include:
 - Missing permission(s)
 - Evaluated scope
 - Policy version id

### 3) Console UX requirements (admin tooling)
REQ-3.1 Role templates
- Console MUST provide a set of built-in role templates appropriate for enterprise use.
- Console MUST explain intended usage and scope for each template.

REQ-3.2 Role and permission viewer
- Console MUST allow searching and viewing permissions by name, description, and product area.
- Console MUST show which permissions are included in a role and where that role is bound.

REQ-3.3 Role assignment flows
- Console MUST allow binding roles to users/groups at org/project/environment scope.
- Console SHOULD support bulk assignment and import/mapping patterns for IdP groups.

REQ-3.4 "Why denied" guidance
- Console MUST display a user-friendly permission-denied state with next steps.
- Console SHOULD provide an admin-only view explaining the denial reason code, missing permission, and evaluated scope.

### 4) Audit logging and SIEM export
REQ-4.1 AuthZ decision logging
- The audit log pipeline MUST include authorization decision context for relevant events and explicit authorization checks:
 - Subject identity (user/service account), org id, and authn method (SSO/API key)
 - Action/permission
 - Resource identifiers and scope
 - Policy version id (and policy bundle version if applicable)
 - Decision: allow/deny
 - Denial reason code (if deny)
 - Request id / trace id

REQ-4.2 Export and retention
- Audit log export MUST include the above fields and map cleanly to common SIEM schemas.
- The system SHOULD support filtering by scope (project/environment) for enterprise use cases.

### 5) Migration and backwards compatibility
REQ-5.1 Compatibility
- During migration, the system MUST avoid breaking existing customers’ access.
- The system MUST support a staged rollout using feature flags.

REQ-5.2 Dual-read / discrepancy detection
- The platform SHOULD support dual-read mode (evaluate v1 and v2) to detect mismatches.
- Mismatches MUST be observable (metrics + logs) and triageable.

REQ-5.3 Default mappings
- The system MUST provide default role mappings from legacy roles to RBAC v2 templates.
- The system SHOULD provide a safe path for customers to customize roles post-migration.

### 6) Break-glass controls (enterprise + internal)
REQ-6.1 Time-bound elevation
- Break-glass elevation MUST be time-bound and require explicit approval.
- Break-glass actions MUST be highly visible in audit logs.

REQ-6.2 Monitoring and alerting
- Break-glass usage MUST trigger alerts to SecOps.
- The system SHOULD require post-use review and documentation.

### 7) Performance, reliability, and safety
REQ-7.1 Latency budget
- Authorization evaluation MUST add minimal overhead and avoid cross-region dependencies where possible.
- The system SHOULD use safe caching scoped to subject/policy version and invalidated on role/policy changes.

REQ-7.2 Availability
- Authorization failures MUST fail closed by default.
- Any break-glass exemption path MUST be explicitly controlled and auditable.

REQ-7.3 Regression prevention
- The platform MUST maintain integration tests covering critical sensitive actions (e.g., key rotation, role changes, routing edits).

## Out-of-scope / future considerations
- Customer-defined deny rules and policy conditions beyond RBAC (ABAC-like conditions).
- Fine-grained data-plane authorization for prompt/content access (separate initiative).
- Delegated administration patterns beyond role bindings (e.g., approval workflows for specific actions).

## Requirements prioritization (MVP vs follow-on)
### MVP (must ship for enterprise pilots)
- Canonical permission registry + inventory coverage baseline
- Gateway middleware deny-by-default with standardized errors
- Control plane endpoint annotations + enforcement
- Built-in role templates + minimal Console role assignment flows
- Audit logging schema extension + SIEM export support for authz fields
- Feature flags + dual-read mode + rollback plan

### Follow-on (post-pilot)
- Full custom role editor UX with advanced permission search and diffs
- Expanded scope UI (cluster-level workflows for Private)
- Admin debug tooling improvements (policy evaluation traces)
- Coverage gates broadened to additional services/jobs

## Success metrics
Product outcomes
- Enterprise security reviews: reduce time-to-approve for RBAC/audit sections (measured via Sales/SE feedback) by 30%.
- Supportability: reduce RBAC-related support tickets per pilot account after week 2 by 50%.

Technical metrics
- Authorization coverage: 100% of designated “sensitive endpoints” annotated and enforced in gateway + service.
- Deny rate monitoring: baseline deny rate established; alert on sudden spikes (e.g., >2x week-over-week) during rollout.
- Latency impact: P95 incremental authz evaluation overhead <= 5 ms for Hosted control plane requests (measured at gateway), and <= 10 ms for Private deployments with local control plane.
- Audit completeness: >= 99.9% of authz decisions for covered actions have decision context fields populated.

Security/compliance metrics
- Evidence readiness: permission catalog, role matrix, enforcement standard, and audit log samples packaged for SOC2 and customer questionnaires.
- Break-glass: 100% of break-glass events include approval record + post-use review within 5 business days.

## Analytics, logging, and dashboards
- Dashboard: authz allow/deny counts by permission, scope, deployment mode, and customer tier.
- Dashboard: discrepancy rate (dual-read mismatches) by endpoint/permission.
- Dashboard: authz evaluation latency (gateway + service), cache hit rate, and error rate.
- Logs: structured denial reason codes and request ids to support rapid triage.

## Dependencies
- Permission registry/policy bundle repo (role templates generated from YAML; versioned artifacts).
- API Gateway middleware + endpoint annotation framework.
- Control plane service adoption (org/users/roles, routing, model pinning/rollout, audit export).
- Audit log pipeline + exporter (SIEM mappings).
- Console UX and backend endpoints for role management.
- Private installer bootstrap for initial admin bindings and IdP group mapping guidance.

## Risks and mitigations
Risk: Migration causes denial spikes for existing admins/operators.
- Mitigation: feature-flag rollout, dual-read comparison, explicit default mappings, and a rollback plan.

Risk: Missing annotations lead to bypasses or inconsistent enforcement.
- Mitigation: coverage gating in CI, centralized permission registry, and defense-in-depth checks in services.

Risk: Debug information leaks sensitive policy details.
- Mitigation: admin-only debug headers, strict gating, safe error defaults, and audit logging of debug usage.

Risk: Cache staleness leads to incorrect allow decisions.
- Mitigation: cache keying by policy version, short TTLs, invalidation on role changes, and metrics/alerts for anomalies.

## Phased release plan
Phase 0 — Discovery & inventory (Weeks 0–4)
- Produce permission inventory and sensitivity tiers.
- Identify endpoints/jobs lacking consistent checks.
- Align naming conventions and scope semantics.

Phase 1 — Design finalization (Weeks 3–8)
- Finalize RBAC v2 primitives, scope model, and evaluation flow.
- Finalize audit log decision fields and denial reason codes.
- Publish enforcement standards and endpoint annotation requirements.

Phase 2 — Implementation (Weeks 6–16)
- Land gateway middleware deny-by-default.
- Annotate + enforce control plane endpoints; add coverage tests.
- Implement policy evaluator client with safe caching.
- Implement audit log schema changes + SIEM export mapping.
- Console MVP: role templates, assignments, permission viewer/search.

Phase 3 — Pilot rollout & validation (Weeks 12–24)
- Internal dogfood with IT/admin workflows.
- Enterprise pilots (Private + Dedicated) behind feature flags.
- Monitor deny rates, latency, mismatch rates; iterate on role templates.
- Publish customer-facing guidance and support playbooks.

Phase 4 — GA and deprecation (Post-pilot)
- Default-enable RBAC v2 for new enterprise orgs.
- Expand GA to all customers after stability and documentation thresholds.
- Begin deprecating legacy RBAC v1 roles/paths with a published timeline.

## Open questions
- Scope inheritance and precedence: how do we resolve org-level grants vs narrower-scoped bindings (and future deny rules)?
- Project vs environment boundaries for key actions (routing policy edits, model rollouts) across Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.
- Minimum viable custom roles for MVP: do we require custom roles at pilot, or templates-only plus API support?
- Which denial reason codes are safe to expose to end users vs admins, and how do we gate that exposure?

## Acceptance criteria (for MVP pilot readiness)
- Permission inventory published and referenced by engineering; at least the “enterprise-sensitive” set mapped to permissions.
- Gateway and service checks are active for the sensitive set with deny-by-default.
- Audit logs include authz decision context fields for covered actions and are exported to SIEM correctly.
- Console provides role templates and role bindings at org/project/environment scopes.
- Feature flags, dashboards, and rollback plan are in place and tested.
- Documentation: customer guidance + internal runbooks + support triage steps are published.

title: Context boundary exploration — notes & small experiments
author: Fenna Lee
text:
Quick orientation
-- why I care: production apps keep hitting weird behaviour when prompt length crosses certain thresholds (abrupt drop in slot-filling accuracy, hallucination spikes). Need better intuition for: where is the model "boundary" vs our infra (KV cache, batching, truncation)?

Reading highlights (short + my takeaways)
1) "Chunked Retrieval + Re-rank for Long Context" (internal reading notes)
 - idea: treat retrieval hits as soft prefixes, re-rank short chunks rather than stitching huge context.
 - takeaway: re-ranking reduces noise but adds latency; tradeoff sweet spot is 2-4 chunks at 512 tokens each for our typical docs.
 - infra implication: can send 2 parallel retrieval requests and 1 re-ranker call; need per-request latency budget < 80ms for search + 120ms for re-rank to keep overall < 250ms.

2) "KV warmup dynamics" (paper X; lecture notes)
 - observation: initial tokens are expensive and influence subsequent attention distribution; models show higher perplexity until KV buffer fills with topical tokens.
 - my experiment idea: measure downstream QA accuracy vs warmup length (0, 8, 32 tokens) while fixing total token budget. Expected: small warmup (8) reduces hallucination on first answer generation.

3) "Prefix-caching vs Full-KV caching" (various docs + Slack threads)
 - prefix cache (store final layer activations for common instruction prefixes) helps latency but can mismatch when retrieval returns slightly changed phrasing.
 - heuristics: use fuzzy-match threshold on prefix hash; store multiple prefix variants with LRU; serve fallback to full KV when mismatch probability high.

Handy quotes / paraphrases
- "Metrics don't lie, but they don't tell the whole story" — meaning accuracy vs user-perceived quality diverge when latency constraints force truncation.
- "There is often an infra-induced cliff, not a model one" — i.e., our batching/pinning policies sometimes cause large effective context drops when queueing behavior changes.

Notes-to-self: quick experiments to run (priority order)
A) Controlled QA degrade curve (high value)
 - dataset: 500 short QA pairs + 100 multi-document synthesis tasks
 - experiment axes: total_context_budget (512..8192), retrieval_chunks (0,1,3), warmup_tokens (0,8,32), quantized vs fp16 model variant
 - metrics: exact match / F1, rouge-L for synth, hallucination score (binary heuristic), tail latency p95, cost/tokens
 - infra: use dedicated dev pool (dev-dedicated-2) pinned to A100-40GB; disable autoscaling; single client concurrency 8
 - success criterion: identify contiguous region where quality drops >8% but latency improves <50ms — that's where we can apply adaptive fallback.

B) KV-cache divergence test (low effort)
 - create 200 synthetic prompts where retrieval returns paraphrases of same doc. Compare: prefix-cache hit rate vs full-kv match, and check accuracy difference.
 - log: prefix_hash, fuzzy_score, answer_variance.

C) Batch shape stress test (ops)
 - vary batch sizes with same avg sequence length; monitor model kernel selection (int8 path vs fp16), GPU utilization, and per-token latency. Hypothesis: at certain batch shapes our kernel selector swaps to a slower matmul routine. Confirm.

Quick implementation notes / commands (for me)
- use bench harness: scripts/bench/context-boundary-run.py --dataset data/qas-small.json --model redwood/open-7b-v2 --budget 2048 --retrieval-chunks 3 --warmup 8 --concurrency 8 --out results/ctx-boundary/ (add --dry-run to validate)
- log format should include prefix_hash, kv_hits, kv_size_bytes, kernel_version, gpu_sm_util, p50/p95_latency_ms, cost_per_1k_tokens

Open questions + hypotheses (to log in experiments)
- Q1: Is the apparent cliff in accuracy correlated more strongly with token budget or with kernel selection change? (need to capture kernel_version at inference time)
- Q2: Do paraphrase-heavy retrievals cause more prefix-cache misses than literal-match returns? (likely yes; quantify fuzzy threshold)
- Q3: Can we design a cheap re-ranker model that runs on CPU to avoid re-rank latency? Rough idea: compressed lightweight bi-encoder + small cross-encoder fallback.

Small design sketch: adaptive context controller
- Inputs: client SLA (p95 latency target), query complexity signal (estimated from prompt length + retrieval score), recent model quality signal (rolling eval on held-out prompts)
- Outputs: routing decision: {use-full-context, chunk+rerank, reduce_retrieval, use-quantized-variant}
- Policy heuristics: if p95 latency budget tight and retrieval precision high -> chunk+re-rank; if warmup token cost high and chain-of-thought needed -> use-full-context on dedicated pool
- Implementation notes: stateless policy server (lambda) reads recent metrics from metrics-store, outputs policy; minimal state in request path to keep latency small.

Logging / instrumentation changes asked for
- add kernel_version to token-level traces
- export prefix_hash and fuzzy_score for every retrieval hit
- push per-request 'quality_score' from eval harness if available

Useful links I keep returning to
- internal: confluence/context-boundary-playbook (linked above)
- notes: https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07198 (example paper on memory caching patterns)
- discussion: https://redwood.slack.com/archives/C0INFER/p1670001110000

Todo (next week)
- get Owen's help to wire kernel_version into traces (JIRA-1129 assigned)
- run small KV divergence test (target: Monday morning run)
- prototype tiny re-ranker on CPU (Mika volunteered to pair)

Random brain-dump / fragments (will sort later)
- consider hybrid caching: prefix cache for first N tokens + streaming KV for remainder. Possibly a cheaper prefix fingerprint + small Bloom filter to avoid heavy false positives.
- think about UX: if app notices hallucination spike, surface "context limit encountered" to users? risky.

End notes: this doc is intentionally messy. Goal is an executable set of small experiments and an emergent design for adaptive routing. Will move proven bits to confluence + add a one-pager once we have a crisp curve.

title: Lightweight SLO governance, lift plan & QA checklist
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight, cross-functional companion for shipping SLOs and simple governance that small product squads can follow without heavy process overhead. It combines a short lift plan, QA checklist for canaries, and a practical governance pattern for SRE and product partners.

Why this exists (problem statement):
- We repeatedly see small services either: (a) ship SLOs that are too strict and trigger noisy paging, or (b) avoid SLOs entirely because the process looks heavy.
- Need a minimal, repeatable pattern to get predictable availability guarantees, clear owner signals, and safe rollout without blocking feature velocity.

Scope and constraints:
- Focus: model-serving endpoints, feature request proxies (API gateway), and latency-sensitive middleware used by hosted API and dedicated deployments.
- Not in scope: long-running batch jobs, infra-only daemons (those follow platform SRE runbooks).

Principles (keep it light):
- 1-page SLO per feature/service. If it fits on a Confluence blurb + a dashboard, it’s good.
- Use 2–3 signals max (latency p50/p95 and request error rate or client-side error rate).
- Start loose, tighten with evidence. Use error budget experiments to validate.
- Prefer automated alerts that escalate to Slack + ticket before paging unless error budget burning is severe.

Quick lift plan (8 working days; intended for small squad + SRE partner):
Day 0: Kickoff: 30m sync, pick SLO owner (product/feature lead) and SRE reviewer. Create ticket (JIRA-XXXX).
Day 1: Draft SLO statement + success criteria. Example: "99.7% of API calls return 200 or 2xx within 200ms p95 per 1h window".
Day 2: Identify telemetry events and dashboard team (Observability). Instrument missing metrics (basic timers/counters).
Day 3: Create dashboard skeleton in Console (latency, count, errors, error-budget burn).
Day 4: Define alerting thresholds (warning at 30% burn/day, page at 60% burn in 1h).
Day 5: Canary rollout plan & QA checklist; rehearse failure injection locally or staging.
Day 6: Canary deploy 10% traffic for 2h. Monitor dashboard and runbook checklist.
Day 7: Canary review, adjust thresholds, update runbook with specific remediation steps.
Day 8: Full rollout and short retrospective (what we learned, owners).

RACI (compressed, as bullets):
- Responsible: Feature owner (sets SLO, signs off instrumentation), SRE reviewer (validates correctness).
- Accountable: Product engineering manager owns final decision to ship SLO.
- Consulted: Observability team (metric names, dashboard), QA (test scenarios).
- Informed: Oncall rotation, support (CS) for customer comms.

Minimal SLO template (one-liner + context):
- Title: short service + signal (e.g., "embed-service latency p95 200ms")
- SLO statement: "Over a rolling 30d window, 99.5% of requests should have p95 latency <= 200ms."
- Signals: metric_name_latency_p95, metric_name_2xx_ratio, request_volume
- Data window: 30d rolling (we use 30d default for product-facing features; infra can use 7d)
- Error budget policy: 1) If burn hits 30%/day -> create ops-ticket and paired pager-lite (Slack + ticket escalation). 2) If burn hits 60% in 1h -> page primary oncall.
- Owner: name + backup oncall alias

Canary & QA checklist (practical, bite-sized):
- Preconditions: CI green, infra capacity checks, smoke tests pass.
- Metric sanity: Ensure latency and error metrics are populated for staging traffic for 24h.
- Synthetic test: run 3 synthetic scenarios (normal, burst, error-rate spike) and capture dashboard.
- Failure injection: simulate an upstream 500 + increased latency for 5m, verify SLO metrics reflect it and runbook steps trigger correctly.
- Backfill checks: confirm there are no gaps in metric ingestion for the last 48h.
- Canary duration & traffic: 2–6h at 5–15% traffic depending on feature blast radius.
- Rollback criteria: if p95 increases > 2x baseline AND error-rate > 1% absolute for 10m -> rollback or throttle.

Lightweight governance pattern (for teams that resist heavy comms):
- Monthly SLO health email (auto-generated) to the squad + stakeholders; keep it 3 bullets: trend, current burn, action needed.
- Quarterly SLO review: 20m demo at squad retro + 10m SRE feedback.
- Exception flow: to change an SLO (tighten/loosen) submit a one-paragraph justification and link to data. SRE reviewer has 3 business days to respond.

Runbook starter (fill-in fields):
- Trigger: exact alert name / condition (e.g., slo-latency-p95-warning)
- Immediate steps: check recent deploys -> check infra capacity -> check upstream errors -> switch to lower-cost variant / degrade non-essential features
- Escalation: create ticket JIRA-XXXX, notify #sre-ops and ping oncall-primary
- Recovery validation: synthetic check passes for 30m, error budget stop burning for 60m
- Postmortem cadence: if page fired, 72h postmortem; if just warning, retro note.

Telemetry and dashboards (obs team notes):
- Required series: request_count, success_count, error_count (4xx/5xx), latency_p50/p95/p99, downstream_latency, queue_length
- Cardinality: prefer aggregated series by route + environment; avoid high-cardinality labels by default. If you need per-customer, open a request with Observability.
- Dashboard templates: use the "SLO-mini" template in Console (deck link above).

Decision heuristics for fallback & graceful degradation:
- If upstream dependency hits 2xx ratio < 95% and retrying increases p95 by > 25%, switch to cached / degraded mode.
- Use feature flags for graceful degradation; default to safe-fail closed behavior for user-facing flows.

Operational play examples (short):
- Example 1: Model-serving memory leak -> symptom: p95 latency rising and error budget burn; immediate action: route new requests to a healthy pool, scale out nonstateful workers, open bug ticket.
- Example 2: Region outage -> detect via region-specific error spike; action: route to fallback region with lower-cost model variant and notify customers on status page.

Open questions & follow-ups (we should discuss at next SLO office hours):
- Should we standardize default canary durations per product line? (proposal: 4h for user-facing, 2h for internal infra)
- What’s the minimal synthetic coverage we require per feature? (proposal: 3 scenarios)
- Define a shared glossary: "page vs ticket vs warning" thresholds across teams.

Next steps (action list):
- Aisha: create JIRA-XXXX and link SLO template (today).
- Mateo: add SLO-mini dashboard template to Console and document metric names (2 days).
- Mei: draft runbook fill-in and put a runbook stub in the repo (3 days).
- Daniel: schedule canary experiment for the next feature launch and invite SRE (this week).

Notes to self / scratch fragments:
- Keep thresholds soft for first 30 days.
- Avoid per-customer paging; prefer aggregated alerting + targeted customer comms from CS.

References:
- Confluence SLO template (link above), Observability dashboard primer, example PR for instrumentation (PR:1812).

-- end --

title: Audit Log Event Taxonomy — Optimization Config (Safe apply + rollback) [working sheet]
author: Kevin Osei
text:
Context / why this exists
- Feature: Safe apply + rollback mechanism for Optimization Configs (batching, caching, quantization profiles).
- Enterprise ask: complete, queryable, exportable audit trail of all config lifecycle actions with strong actor attribution + before/after context.
- This sheet is the proposed event taxonomy + required fields. It’s intended to unblock:
 - product/security review (Naomi / Marcus)
 - engineering implementation (ENG-4826)
 - SIEM export mapping (Splunk/Datadog/Chronicle)

Non-goals (for v1)
- Not designing the entire audit pipeline; focusing on event names + payload schema.
- Not defining every metric/tag used for rollout gating; only what needs to appear in audit.

Principles
1) Every operator action that can change runtime behavior must generate an audit event.
2) Events must be: immutable, append-only, time-ordered (within reasonable clock skew bounds), and exportable.
3) Include enough fields to answer: who did what, to what scope, when, from where, what changed, what was the result, and how to correlate across systems.
4) Avoid leaking sensitive content (no prompts, no raw config blobs if they contain secrets/keys).

Terminology (aligning across teams)
- Optimization Config: top-level object (per tenant/model/region scope) controlling batching/caching/quant settings.
- Version: immutable snapshot; version_id is stable. “Active version” is a pointer per scope.
- Rollout: staged apply (canary %, shard-based, etc.) resulting in active version change over time.
- Scope: tuple of tenant_id + (model_id | model_family) + region + deployment_mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private).

Event naming conventions (proposal)
- Namespace: "optimization_config".
- Format: optimization_config.<noun>.<verb>
 - Example: optimization_config.version.created
- All events include: event_name, occurred_at, outcome, and stable correlation identifiers.

Event taxonomy (v1)

A) Version lifecycle
1. optimization_config.version.created
 - When a new immutable version is created.
 - Trigger: API/Console/automation.

2. optimization_config.version.validation_requested
 - Operator requested validation (schema + semantic). Separate from apply.

3. optimization_config.version.validation_succeeded
4. optimization_config.version.validation_failed
 - Include failure_class + validation_errors summary.

5. optimization_config.version.deleted (NOTE: do we allow this?)
 - Strong default: NO deletion; only “retracted” or “superseded”.
 - If deletion exists for non-prod/test tenants, must be logged.

B) Rollout / apply workflow
6. optimization_config.rollout.started
 - A rollout job created to move a given scope from current active version to target version.

7. optimization_config.rollout.progressed
 - Rollout moved to next stage (e.g., 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%).
 - We may throttle emission (stage boundaries only) to avoid noisy logs.

8. optimization_config.rollout.paused
9. optimization_config.rollout.resumed
10. optimization_config.rollout.canceled
 - Canceled != rollback. Rollout may stop mid-way; active version could be mixed by shard until repaired.

11. optimization_config.rollout.completed
 - Completed successfully; active pointer set for scope.

12. optimization_config.rollout.failed
 - Include failure_reason + failed_stage + whether automatic rollback was executed.

C) Promotion semantics (if we support environments)
13. optimization_config.version.promoted
 - Promotion from "staging" -> "prod" OR from "candidate" -> "blessed".
 - Needs explicit source_env, target_env.

D) Rollback workflow
14. optimization_config.rollback.requested
 - User initiated rollback action (Console button/API call).

15. optimization_config.rollback.completed
16. optimization_config.rollback.failed
 - Must include from_version_id, to_version_id, rollback_scope.

E) Access control / authorization relevant to audit
17. optimization_config.authorization.denied
 - When a principal attempts an apply/rollback action without permissions.
 - Useful for incident investigations and customer security review.

F) Integrations / external signals (optional for v1, but requested by SRE)
18. optimization_config.gate.evaluation_started
19. optimization_config.gate.evaluation_failed
20. optimization_config.gate.evaluation_succeeded
 - NOTE: These are *not* human actions, but have compliance value (prove gates existed).
 - If we decide to log them, keep payload minimal and avoid metric spam.

Payload schema: required fields (applies to all events)

Core envelope
- event_name: string (see taxonomy)
- event_version: string (e.g., "1") — allows schema changes without breaking exports
- occurred_at: RFC3339 timestamp (UTC)
- emitted_at: RFC3339 timestamp (UTC) (when written to audit store) — helps identify pipeline delays
- environment: string (prod | staging | dev | private) — private = customer control plane
- outcome: string (success | failure | denied | partial)
- severity: string (info | warning | critical)

Actor attribution
- actor_type: string (user | service | system)
- actor_id: string (redwood_user_id OR service principal id)
- actor_email: string (if user and available; ok to omit for service)
- actor_role: string (RBAC role at time of action; important even if role later changes)
- authn_method: string (sso | api_key | oauth | session)
- authz_policy: string (policy bundle version/hash used for decision)

Request context
- request_id: string (edge request id)
- trace_id: string (distributed trace id) (optional but strongly recommended)
- console_session_id: string (if initiated via Console)
- source: string (console | public_api | internal_api | automation | private_operator)
- client_ip: string (or best-effort; for private deployments may be "customer_network")
- user_agent: string (if available)

Target identifiers
- tenant_id: string
- org_id: string (if tenant maps to org; optional but requested by enterprise)
- deployment_mode: string (hosted | dedicated | private)
- region: string (e.g., us-east-1)
- model_id: string (e.g., "rw-llama-3-70b") or "*" for wildcard scope

Config identifiers
- optimization_config_id: string (stable id for config object)
- target_version_id: string (immutable)
- previous_version_id: string (if applicable)
- rollout_id: string (for rollout events)
- change_id: string (stable id that ties create/validate/apply/rollback events for one "change")

Human intent / justification (required for apply + rollback)
- reason: string (free text; enforced non-empty for production scopes)
- ticket_ref: string (Jira/Linear/Incident id; enforced for prod)
- approver_id: string (optional for v1; likely required by some customers)
- approver_email: string (optional)

Diff / what changed (summary only)
- diff_summary: string
 - Example: "batching.max_batch_tokens: 8192 -> 12288; caching.prefix_cache: false -> true"
- risk_level: string (low | medium | high)
- risk_factors: string (comma-separated) (e.g., "quant_profile_change,cache_toggle")

Failure details (only for outcome != success)
- error_class: string (validation_error | gate_failed | apply_failed | timeout | conflict | unknown)
- error_message: string (short; no secrets)
- error_details_ref: string (pointer to internal logs or run id; not exported to customers)

Field notes / constraints
- PII/Sensitive: do not include prompt text, request body that contains user data, or full config blobs if they contain secret material.
- For quantization profile changes: include quant_profile_id + quant_profile_version_id as identifiers, but do not embed eval datasets.

Event-specific fields (additions)

For optimization_config.version.created
- created_from_version_id: string (optional) (if cloned)
- config_source_ref: string (e.g., "console_editor", "terraform")

For validation_* events
- validation_suite: string (schema | semantic | compatibility)
- validation_errors: string (one-line, redacted) (e.g., "max_batch_tokens exceeds GPU memory estimate")

For rollout.started / completed / failed
- canary_strategy: string (percent | shard | tenant_subset)
- canary_percent_initial: string (e.g., "1")
- canary_percent_final: string (e.g., "100")
- gate_set: string (e.g., "default_prod_gates_v2")

For rollback.*
- rollback_type: string (one_click | api | private_operator)
- rollback_reason_code: string (latency_regression | elevated_5xx | quality_regression | mis_scoped_apply | other)

For authorization.denied
- denied_action: string (apply | rollback | promote | validate)
- requested_scope: string (serialized scope tuple)

SIEM export expectations
- Retention (Redwood-managed / Hosted + Dedicated):
 - Default: 365 days searchable in Console; 7 years in cold storage for enterprise add-on (TBD).
 - Export: near-real-time stream to customer SIEM for enterprise (Splunk HEC / S3 / webhook).
- Private: customer retains logs in their own control plane; we must document fields + how to forward.

Mapping to common schemas (rough)
- Splunk CIM: map actor_email->user, client_ip->src, event_name->action, tenant_id->app/tenant.
- OCSF (if we adopt): event_name as activity_name; actor_* into actor; target identifiers into resource.

Open questions / decisions needed
1) Do we log gate evaluation events as audit events, or keep them in metrics only?
 - SRE wants traceability; Security cautious about volume/noise.
 - Proposal: log only gate boundary results (succeeded/failed) per stage, not continuous samples.

2) Deletion semantics
 - Strong recommendation: no delete in prod; support "retracted" state instead.

3) Approvals
 - Do we require explicit approver for high-risk changes (quant profile, cache toggle at large scope)?
 - If yes, we need additional events: optimization_config.change.approved / rejected.

4) Customer visibility
 - Customers should see *their* events only; internal-only fields (error_details_ref, internal user ids) must be filtered.

5) Event ordering + race conditions
 - We need a consistent definition: "rollback.completed" means control-plane pointer updated AND runtime applier acknowledged at least N% of workers? (Engineering to confirm.)

Notes from review (2026-01-10 thread w/ Aisha Rahman + Marcus)
- Aisha: require request_id + authz_policy version for compliance sign-off.
- Marcus: add actor_role snapshot at time of action; roles can change later.
- Naomi: enforce ticket_ref + reason on production rollouts; allow exemption for incident rollback with incident id.

Action items
- [Kevin] Align field names with implementation PR-19941 schema (avoid drift). Owner: Kevin Osei. Due: 2026-01-15.
- [Jordan] Confirm which actions are permissioned under new "optimization change operator" role and ensure denied events are emitted. Due: 2026-01-20.
- [Benji] Confirm meaning of rollout.completed vs partial apply and what runtime acknowledgement fields we can safely log. Due: 2026-01-20.
- [Sean] Provide minimal gate_set names + stage boundary definitions to avoid over-logging. Due: 2026-01-22.

Appendix: proposed canonical event list (copy/paste for engineers)
- optimization_config.version.created
- optimization_config.version.validation_requested
- optimization_config.version.validation_succeeded
- optimization_config.version.validation_failed
- optimization_config.rollout.started
- optimization_config.rollout.progressed
- optimization_config.rollout.paused
- optimization_config.rollout.resumed
- optimization_config.rollout.canceled
- optimization_config.rollout.completed
- optimization_config.rollout.failed
- optimization_config.version.promoted
- optimization_config.rollback.requested
- optimization_config.rollback.completed
- optimization_config.rollback.failed
- optimization_config.authorization.denied
- optimization_config.gate.evaluation_started (optional)
- optimization_config.gate.evaluation_succeeded (optional)
- optimization_config.gate.evaluation_failed (optional)

title: Unusual spike in IdP-signed JWT usage across multiple internal accounts
text:
Issue summary:
We observed an anomalous spike in authentication events where IdP-issued JWTs (SAML->OIDC pipeline) were used to exchange for short-lived service tokens. These exchanges originated from a small set of IPs that are not common for our workforce and targeted multiple internal service and user accounts.

Impact:
- Potential credential or token re-use affecting 3 internal accounts and multiple service tokens issued to CI/CD runners.
- No evidence yet of data exfiltration, but some high-privilege service tokens were minted and used to call internal admin APIs.
- Could affect deployment pipelines and onboarding workflows if tokens are revoked without a coordinated mitigation.

Environment:
- Production SSO (IdP: corporate Okta) federated to Redwood SSO proxy in us-east-1.
- Time window: 2026-03-12 03:12:00 UTC -> 2026-03-12 03:45:00 UTC.

Observed indicators / logs:
- Auth audit logs show ~180 token exchanges with IdP-signed JWTs in the 33-minute window.
- Source IPs: 34.120.12.87, 34.120.13.192 (ASN / cloud provider observed).
- User agents: headless-bot/1.2, python-requests/2.31.0 (some variance).
- Several exchanges returned service tokens with admin-scoped claims for infra-ops account.
- No immediate 5xx or runtime errors observed on admin APIs; however, token usage patterns were unusual (burst requests to /v1/admin/keys).

Steps to reproduce (for validation):
1) Query auth audit index: query by event_type:token_exchange AND source_ip in [34.120.12.87,34.120.13.192] AND timestamp between 2026-03-12T03:00:00Z and 2026-03-12T04:00:00Z.
2) Correlate returned token IDs with internal token-usage logs in service-audit index.
3) Verify Okta org logs for suspicious OAuth/OIDC grant activity for the same time window.

Initial mitigation actions taken:
- Rotated affected service keys for svc-data-ingest and infra-ops.
- Forced SSO session revocations for implicated human accounts (alice@redwood.com).
- Throttled token exchange endpoint for non-corp IP ranges and added temporary WAF rule to block the two IPs.
- Opened an incident bridge and notified Legal and Product Security.
- Created this internal-support ticket to capture investigation and follow-up remediation tasks.

03/12 03:20 UTC - Alert from auth-monitoring: token_exchange_rate > 25/min for SSO proxy; triggered oncall.
03/12 03:25 UTC - Confirmed 180 exchanges from two external IPs; fetched raw auth logs and correlated to service-audit.
03/12 03:28 UTC - Hypothesis A: credentials/token capture from phishing or compromised CI/CD runner. Hypothesis B: misconfigured third-party integration replaying JWTs.
03/12 03:34 UTC - Checked Okta sign-in logs: no interactive human sign-in from these IPs, but several token-grant events via service app client. Opened ticket with Okta support for additional metadata.
03/12 03:40 UTC - Identified a CI runner artifact that had environment variable containing long-lived client assertion; rotated that credential and invalidated prior tokens.
03/13 09:00 UTC - SRE ran forensics on the two IPs: both map to ephemeral cloud VMs; abuse reports filed with provider.
03/14 10:30 UTC - Security team requested expanded audit retention for token_exchange logs and started payload-level parsing to extract JWT ids for replay detection.

Aisha Patel (Reporter) 2026-03-12: Initial detection and mitigation steps listed. On-call will coordinate rotations.
Diego Morales (Assignee) 2026-03-12: Applied WAF block for observed IPs and forced session revocations for implicated users. Continuing log correlation.
Priya Shah (Product Security) 2026-03-12: Requesting Okta export of app-level grant logs and list of affected app client IDs; also advise rotating any CI client assertions.
Samir Gupta (SRE) 2026-03-13: Found a Jenkins runner in project 'release-automation' with a stale service assertion. Rotated and removed hard-coded token from job config. Investigating whether token was exfiltrated via job artifacts.
Legal 2026-03-13: Please collect timeline for any external communications; we'll prepare a notice template if customer-facing impact is discovered.
Diego Morales 2026-03-14: Filing for a post-incident review once we confirm no further exchange spikes. Recommend making token-exchange rate limit permanent for non-corp ranges.

Complete full token lineage mapping for all exchanged tokens during window and mark any sessions/tokens for permanent revocation where appropriate.
Coordinate with Identity team and Okta support to determine the exact grant flow used and whether the client application was configured with overly-broad scopes.
Implement a permanent rule in API gateway to restrict token_exchange endpoint to corp IP ranges and known CI egress ranges, with an allowlist for validated third-party integrators.
Schedule a postmortem (blameless) with SRE, Product Security, and Build/CI owners. Link: https://confluence.redwood.com/display/SEC/INT-130001-Postmortem
Assess whether additional EDR/forensics on implicated developer workstations is warranted based on CI findings.

Partial mitigation complete: affected credentials rotated, WAF blocks applied, Okta support engaged. Full root cause pending confirmation of whether token values were exfiltrated from a CI artifact or replayed by a third-party integration. Postmortem scheduled. No customer data confirmed accessed at time of last update.

Revisit rate-limiting thresholds for token_exchange endpoint as a platform configuration item for Q2 roadmap.
Add automated alert for abnormal ratio of token_exchange events to interactive sign-ins for any given account.
Ensure CI templates do not accept raw client assertions and add linting check in internal-tools repo.

title: Northlake Customer Support AI
author: Ava Chen
text:
Account summary (Northlake Customer Support AI)

Firmographics / context
- Mid-market support platform building AI agent add-on for live chat + email. They sell to SaaS + fintech; have a few customers that demand tighter audit + retention controls.
- Stack today: mix of vendor LLM APIs + some self-hosted experimentation. They want to standardize on one inference platform and stop hand-tuning batching.
- Deployment: prefers VPC for production (customer expectations + data isolation). Open to starting hosted API for POC.

Primary use case
- Support-agent chat (streaming) with tool calling.
 - High sensitivity to time-to-first-token (TTFT) and streaming smoothness (chunk cadence).
 - They explicitly said: "If the agent pauses for 2–3 seconds mid-stream, our users think it broke." 
- Secondary: summarization of long tickets, embeddings + reranking for internal KB retrieval.

Requirements (captured across discovery + demo)
- Latency
 - Streaming endpoints are the critical path. They asked for a clear 'FAST' tier that they can set-and-forget.
 - Targets they mentioned (not formally committed yet): TTFT < ~350–500ms p95 (region-dependent), and p99 "no multi-second stalls" during decode.
 - Concern: under bursts, they see tail latency spikes with other providers (queue depth grows; token streaming becomes bursty).
- Traffic shape
 - Concurrency: normal 50–120 concurrent chats; peak events 300–600 concurrent (product launches / incident storms).
 - Prompt lengths: mix of short chat turns + occasional long context (ticket history + KB snippets). They admitted their worst-case prompts are "ugly" (copy/paste logs).
 - Mix: streaming chat dominates daytime; summarization batch jobs off-hours.
- Cost
 - Cost sensitive but not at the expense of perceived responsiveness. They like the idea of cost-efficient tier for async summarization, but want guardrails.
 - Asked whether tier defaults can be applied per-route (streaming chat fast; summarization cost-efficient).
- Model preferences
 - They’re model-agnostic but asked about strong 8B/70B class options for agent chat; they want fallback behavior if a model family is constrained.
 - They care about output stability during rollouts; asked how Redwood detects regressions when changing batching defaults.
- Controls / ergonomics
 - Key request: "Fast as the default for streaming." They do not want to tune max_batch_tokens / wait_ms knobs directly.
 - Wants visibility into the effective profile + why it was chosen (override vs default vs overload mode). Reason codes resonated.
 - Wants an easy override mechanism for enterprise: route-level policy in Console, plus a header/SDK param for experiments.

Security / compliance notes
- Asked for: SSO/SAML for Console, audit logs (who changed policies/tiers), retention controls, and KMS integration for any stored config/telemetry.
- Confirmed that tier selection should not change data handling/logging; they were sensitive to "does fast tier log more?" Answer: no; runtime behavior only.

Buying / stakeholders
- Champion: Head of Product (agent experience) + platform lead (infra). Procurement will care about VPC + SLA.
- They want a concrete rollout story: start hosted, then Dedicated VPC once metrics prove out.

Open questions / follow-ups
- Need their real workload stats: prompt-length distribution (prefill tokens), response length distribution (decode tokens), and streaming on/off split per route.
- Need to align on which SLO tier maps to which endpoints (fast for streaming agent chat; standard for internal tools; cost-efficient for async summarization).
- They asked for guidance on overload behavior per tier (shed load vs increase batching). We should propose a default overload policy for their agent route and show what happens at peak.

Risks
- Mixed workloads on same capacity: they may run streaming chat and summarization concurrently; if they do, we need clear route separation or policy precedence to avoid chat p99 getting dragged.
- Tail latency expectations are aggressive; we should set expectations with published tier definitions and highlight that fast-tier protects tail via tighter wait budgets + admission control.

Next steps (agreed)
1) Northlake sends: 7-day traffic shape snapshot (tokens in/out, prompt buckets, concurrency over time, streaming ratio).
2) Redwood (Ethan Park) provides: POC plan + how to force FAST tier for streaming endpoints (include SDK/header example) and how to monitor TTFT + p99.
3) Redwood to propose Dedicated VPC sizing + override/precedence approach for peak-hour protection.
4) Schedule security checklist review (SSO/SAML, audit log export, retention controls) once POC metrics are positive.

2026-01-29: Inbound via website demo request. Notes: 'agent streaming latency is our #1 KPI; customers feel it immediately.'
2026-02-03: Demo w/ Ava Chen + Ethan Park. Walked through tiered batching (fast/standard/cost-efficient) and how it affects queueing + batching. Customer asked for 'fast tier default for all streaming routes'.
2026-02-12: POC check-in (Fireflies). Shared early canary learnings on fast-tier p99 protection and reason codes ('why this profile'). They agreed to provide real prompt-length histogram + concurrency profile.
2026-02-18: Dedicated discussion. Asked about per-tenant overrides + precedence (customer override > route policy > tier default).
2026-02-26: Technical follow-up: clarified that tier selection changes runtime behavior only (batching/admission/backpressure), not logging/retention of prompt data.

Needs clearer guarantees around streaming tail latency (p99) and time-to-first-token under burst
Security review: asks for retention controls + audit log export details (they have regulated customers)
Wants a single 'fast default' that is safe without tuning (concerned about batching foot-guns)

Run a 7-day hosted API POC with streaming chat on FAST tier + capture TTFT/p95/p99 and cost deltas vs current provider; in parallel, Redwood to propose Dedicated VPC sizing + override/precedence plan for their peak hours.

title: Axiom Payments - duplicate streaming replies and sudden throttling causing transaction failures
text:
Issue summary: Between 2026-03-10T02:05 and 2026-03-10T03:30 UTC Axiom Payments reported duplicated streaming responses and a surge of 5xx errors plus client-observed throttling that caused ~18% of payment API calls to fail or be delayed beyond customer SLOs.
Impact: Transaction creation requests experienced duplicate model outputs (duplicate intents leading to double-charges in downstream processing) and elevated latency/timeouts across the us-east region. Customer reported immediate business impact (failed settlements).
Environment: Production (us-east) serving via Hosted API for enterprise tenant using model redwood-ggml-13B pinned version v2026-02-25. Customer on enterprise plan with dedicated routing policy.
Steps to reproduce: 1) Send a stream-based chat request with small initial prompt and repeated 'confirm' function call; 2) Observe two or more streamed final responses within 1s window for same request id; 3) Repeat under sustained concurrent load (~120 rps) and observe API gateway returning 429s or 502s.
Observed behavior: Streaming connection returned duplicate final chunks for ~12% of streams; API gateway returned 429s with message 'rate-limited' while backend showed no corresponding throttling in dedicated pool metrics.
Initial notes: Customer escalated to CS at 02:20 UTC. Triage opened and declared Sev1 due to financial impact. Temporary mitigation requested and SLA credit asked for.

2026-03-10 - Maya Chen (Customer): We saw duplicate confirmations and some failed settlements. This is critical for today’s batch. Please advise workaround ASAP.
2026-03-10 - Carlos Ruiz (Support): Acknowledged. Eng oncall paged. Can you provide sample request IDs?
2026-03-10 - Maya Chen (Customer): Provided request ids: req_8f3a2b, req_8f3a2c, req_8f3a2d and a slack thread #support-axiom with screenshots.
2026-03-10 - Priya Nair (Oncall SRE): Investigating. Initial traces show multiple ACKs for the same stream ID; duplications originate at api-gateway -> stream-multiplexer handoff. Metrics: stream_ack_rate spiked ~2x at 02:04 UTC.
2026-03-10 - David Lee (Serving): Rolling back recent routing rule changes in us-east. Noted a recent config push 2026-03-10T01:58 by infra/terraform PR 1045.
2026-03-10 - Carlos Ruiz (Support): Customer notified of temporary rollback and traffic reroute to us-west cluster. They confirm partial recovery at 03:10 UTC.
2026-03-11 - Customer Success (Elena Park): Follow-up scheduled for postmortem and SLA credit discussion. Customer requested detailed root cause and timeline.
2026-03-13 - Carlos Ruiz (Support): Final resolution recorded and postmortem link shared. Customer accepted remediation steps and SLA credit plan.

Timeline and evidence: At 01:58 UTC an infra routing config (PR 1045) introduced a new streaming multiplexer path intended to reduce cold-starts. At 02:03 UTC stream_ack_rate doubled and stream session state reconciliation lagged. Traces (trace ids: 7a1b3c, 7a1b4d) show api-gateway re-sending stream init frames when backend did not immediately ACK due to a lock contention in the multiplexer: this resulted in duplicate final chunks being emitted when the delayed original ACK arrived. Concurrently, a defensive token-bucket rate limiter in api-gateway had a regression that treated these duplicate frames as new requests and incremented counters, causing the gateway to return 429s even though dedicated pool metrics were below thresholds. Key logs: /logs/stream-multiplexer/2026-03-10.log lines 1124-1168; apigw metrics spike at 02:04. Root cause: a combination of (1) a non-idempotent stream init handshake in the multiplexer introduced by config change, and (2) a rate-limiter edge-case that double-counted retries. Evidence: reproducible with provided request ids when replayed in a staging environment with the problematic multiplexer enabled.

Immediate fixes applied: 1) Rolled back the multiplexer path (infra PR revert) at 02:45 UTC which stopped new duplicates; 2) Disabled the new token-bucket defensive code path causing double-counts at 03:00 UTC; 3) Temporarily routed Axiom Payments traffic to us-west cluster for the remainder of the window; 4) Increased dedicated pool headroom by +20% for Axiom until full fix is deployed. Permanent remediation: 1) Code fix PR #2387 removed the non-idempotent handshake and adds idempotency tokens for stream inits; 2) Rate limiter fix added de-duplication check for retry frames and a test harness; 3) Add a canary rollout guard for infra routing changes and telemetry alerts for stream_ack anomalies. Follow-ups and customer remediation: Postmortem meeting scheduled 2026-03-15; agreed SLA credit of one week of enterprise plan; instrumentation dashboard created (link below) and alerts added.

title: Runtime failure inoculation and experimentation manual
author: Evelyn Cho
text:
Overview

This document defines Redwood's recommended practice for failure inoculation experiments against the serving runtime. The goal is to run controlled, measurable experiments that surface weak points in: kernel scheduling, KV-cache consistency, model swap safety, preemption and eviction, cross-tenant interference, and network/service mesh degradations — while preserving customer SLAs and ensuring fast rollback.

Scope and motivation

- Scope: hosted, dedicated, and private runtime topologies. Focus area for this manual: experiments that exercise the inference serving stack layers (dispatcher, scheduler, kernel, kvcache, model loader, and network fabric).
- Motivation: proactively discover degradations and channel findings into kernel/scheduler hardening, autoscaling rules, runtime admission policies, and fidelity fallback contracts.

Definitions

- Failure inoculation: deliberate, controlled introduction of adverse conditions to observe system resilience and recovery behavior.
- Experiment runbook: documented steps for preflight, execution, measurement, and rollback.
- Safety envelope: pre-declared constraints that must not be violated (SLO breach thresholds, impacted tenants, time windows).

Safety policy and gating

Before any experiment is scheduled the following gates must be satisfied:

1) Business and customer gate
- No running experiments against paid enterprise Dedicated clusters without explicit customer approval.
- Hosted experiments must restrict to synthetic tenants and test API keys; production traffic must not be targeted.

2) SLO safety envelope (hard thresholds)
- Global p95 API latency must not exceed baseline p95 + 30% for more than 5 minutes.
- Error rate (5xx) must remain below 0.5% of baseline traffic during the experiment window.
- Token-generation fairness: no single synthetic tenant may consume > 10% of cluster dispatch capacity unless previously authorized.

3) Operational staffing
- At least two on-call engineers from eng-serving-runtime must be present during the experiment (primary + observer).
- SRE must be notified and on standby if the experiment could affect cross-tenant routing.

Experiment types and intent

A. Scheduler perturbation
- Intent: validate scheduler credit accounting, priority inversion detection and graceful backpressure.
- Action examples: artificially throttle kernel dispatch for a priority tier; inject slot starvations to simulate device contention.
- Key metrics: kernel queue length, per-priority p99 latency, kernel rejection rate, scheduler admission counters.

B. KV-cache warm/cold transition
- Intent: exercise cache warmup paths and eviction ripple effects during model swap.
- Action examples: evict selected tenant shards, simulate cold model swap (flush local cache + remote fetch delays).
- Key metrics: kvcache miss rate, model load time, tail latency during first 100 tokens after swap.

C. Model swap and fallback orchestration
- Intent: verify canary/rollout safety, fallback to lower-fidelity model variants, and KV consistency post-swap.
- Action examples: trigger a staged model push to a small cohort, then force a full-swap while artificially raising checksum mismatch errors in the loader.
- Key metrics: successful fallback count, consistency reconciliation time, error surface for model artifact validation.

D. Network fabric degradation
- Intent: validate RPC timeouts, gRPC retry behavior, and graceful degradation when inter-node latency increases.
- Action examples: introduce 50-250ms RTT between dispatcher and GPUs inside the test topology, or inject packet loss of 0.5-2%.
- Key metrics: request retry rate, end-to-end token latency, CPU scheduling spikes attributable to increased RPC stalls.

E. Thermal and power throttling simulation
- Intent: emulate GPU thermal throttling and observe kernel preemption/backoff reactions.
- Action examples: reduce available compute quota to a worker to simulate thermal step-down.
- Key metrics: kernel reschedule rate, preemption counts, impact on concurrent tenants.

Experiment design template (always populate)

- Experiment ID: runbook-{YYYYMMDD}-{short-name}
- Owner(s): (name, pager)
- Objective: one-sentence hypothesis
- Target topology: (hosted/dedicated/private) and cluster IDs or labels
- Safety envelope: list of SLO thresholds and excluded tenants
- Steps: numbered preflight -> inject -> observe -> withdraw -> analysis
- Measurement sheet: queries and dashboards to collect (see example observability queries)
- Rollback criteria: explicit conditions that trigger an immediate abort and remediation steps
- Postmortem required: Y/N (postmortem required for any experiment that triggers a safety-envelope violation)

Preflight checklist (must be completed and signed off)

1) Create Experiment ticket in the experiments board and link the runbook.
2) Confirm synthetic tenants and test api-keys are configured; validate routing isolation.
3) Ensure TTL and billing freezes for synthetic tenants to avoid unexpected charges.
4) Record baseline metrics for at least 15 minutes pre-injection: p50/p95/p99, 5xx rate, kernel queue depth, kvcache hitrate.
5) Notify SRE and product ops with time window and pager contacts.

Execution procedure (sample)

1) Start live observability snapshot: run the collection job to capture high-resolution traces for the next 30 minutes. Command: curl -X POST https://observability.internal/api/snapshots -d '{"scope":"experiment-run"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $OBS_TOKEN'

2) Apply failure injection via the chaos service:
- Scheduler throttle example:
 curl -X POST https://chaos.internal/v1/inject \
 -H "Authorization: Bearer $CHAOS_TOKEN" \
 -d '{"type":"scheduler-throttle","target":"priority=low","duration_s":300,"params":{"drop_rate":0.15}}'

3) Monitor critical dashboards: kernel queue depth, scheduler admission logs, per-priority tail latency.

4) Observe for the pre-declared timebox (suggested 5 minutes for initial smoke). If any rollback criteria met, execute rollback (step 6).

5) Withdraw injection: call the chaos service to remove the perturbation.

6) If rollback criteria met, escalate following the runtime incident process:
- Immediate action: cancel injection and run remedial script to re-stabilize dispatchers:
 kubectl -n runtime-system rollout restart deployment/dispatcher --selector=cluster=test-cluster
- Notify affected owners in #runtime-incidents and switch on emergency traces (increase sampling to 100% for 5 minutes).

Rollback criteria (examples)

- latency.p99.global > baseline.p99 * 1.5 for more than 3 minutes
- 5xx rate spike to > 1% sustained for 2 minutes
- model loader error rate > 0.2% for any active model group

Observability and measurement examples

- Required dashboards: "Experiment control plane" (admission counters, chaos events), "Kernel surface" (queue depth, execution latency), "KV-cache" (hit/miss, eviction churn).
- Example queries (Prometheus-like):
 - kernel_queue_depth{cluster=\"test-cluster\",priority!="system"}
 - histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(kernel_exec_duration_seconds_bucket[2m])) by (priority)
 - sum(rate(kvcache_miss_total[1m])) by (shard)

- Trace collection: enable distributed traces with tags: experiment_id, injector, owner. Use trace span enrichers to attach kernel hint and scheduler decisions.

Analysis and acceptance criteria

- Post-experiment analysis must include: timeline graph aligned to injection start, delta vs baseline for p50/p95/p99, error annotation, and any kernel-level anomalies (excess preemptions, stalls, failed kernel launches).
- Acceptance: if all metrics return within the safety envelope within 10 minutes of withdrawal and no undetected data corruption is observed, mark experiment as "non-disruptive". Otherwise, mark for follow-up remediation and potential code fixes.

Channeling findings into engineering workflow

- Findings are filed as "Experiment Findings" tickets with tags: experiment_id, severity (S1-S4), component (scheduler/kernel/kvcache). Include reproducible script and minimal repro trace link.
- Remediation priority: P0/P1 (blocker/regression) mapped to oncall and relevant code owners.

Experiment catalog (example entries)

| Experiment ID | Focus area | Short description | Blast radius | Last run | Owner |
|---------------|------------|-------------------|-------------:|---------:|-------|
| runbook-20260115-sched-throttle | scheduler | throttle low-priority kernel dispatch to validate admission | small (test cluster) | 2026-01-15 | Marcus Liu |
| runbook-20260201-kv-evict | kvcache | evict tenant shard to observe warmup penalty | small | 2026-02-01 | Priya Natarajan |
| runbook-20260122-model-swap-fuzz | loader | staged model swap while injecting checksum mismatches | medium | 2026-01-22 | Evelyn Cho |

Practical tips and anti-patterns

- Tip: prefer short, repeated pulses over a single long blast. Short pulses reveal transient cascading effects with lower blast radius.
- Tip: pair every experiment with a synthetic probe that asserts correctness (e.g., deterministic prompt set with golden responses for fidelity checks).
- Anti-pattern: running wide blast experiments during major releases or when kernel-rollout is in progress.

Integration with release and canary process

- Canary experiments should include at least one failure inoculation scenario (scheduler perturbation or kvcache cold start) in the pre-release gate when enabling new kernel variants.
- Release checklist item: confirm the canary cluster has passed the designated inoculation scenarios within the last 72 hours.

Templates and artifacts to attach to experiment tickets

- experiment-runbook.yaml (example below)

 id: "runbook-{{date}}-{{short}}"
 owner: "team/person"
 topology: "test-cluster"
 safety_envelope:
 p99_latency_multiplier: 1.5
 max_5xx_rate: 0.01
 inject_steps:
 - name: "scheduler-throttle"
 - name: "wait-5m"

- observation-query-list.txt containing the PromQL queries and trace sampling instructions.
- representative trace and kernel log bundle upload link.

Frequently asked questions

Q: Can I run these on Dedicated customer clusters?
A: Only with written customer consent and a scoped, agreed blast radius. For Dedicated clusters we recommend using a cloned environment or staging VPC.

Q: What if my experiment causes a regression that only manifests after 24 hours?
A: If a delayed regression is suspected, mark for extended monitoring and create a long-running regression ticket. Increase retention of relevant traces and logs for at least 72 hours.

Ownership and contacts

- Experiments steward: eng-serving-runtime-experiments@redwood.ai
- On-call escalation: see /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/eng-sre/runbooks for the oncall roster and escalation matrix.

Versioning and audit trail

- Every experiment ticket must attach the exact chaostool manifest and experiment-runbook.yaml. The experiment control plane persists start/stop events and injector logs to S3://experiments-buckets/{experiment-id}/. Maintain a short audit summary in the ticket including who approved and who executed.

Appendix: quick checklist (one-line)

- Create ticket -> Confirm synthetic tenancy -> Baseline metrics -> Notify SRE -> Run with observer -> Withdraw -> Validate metrics -> File findings.

Contact and feedback

Send questions or proposed additions to the manual to Evelyn Cho (evelyn@redwood.ai) or open a PR on the team wiki page.
