title: Compact scratch allocator and activation snapshotting to reduce GPU workspace
author: Marina Kline
text:
Motivation: production multitenant inference workloads showed sporadic OOMs on medium-sized GPU instances when prefix caching and long-context runs were combined with background continuous-batching. This PR introduces two orthogonal memory-reduction techniques: 1) activation snapshotting — a lightweight, eviction-friendly checkpoint that stores compact metadata for activations to allow later partial recomputation instead of holding full activation slabs, and 2) a scratch compactor for per-request temporary buffers that reduces fragmentation and enables coalescing of short-lived scratch allocations across micro-batches. The changes also include scheduler tuning to align KV-cache shard residency with compacted scratch windows so that hot shards are kept contiguous and do not force extra workspace growth. Impact: in our microbench harness (multi-stream, 8 concurrent streams, auto-batching) peak workspace on an A100-40GB fleet dropped ~18% and average per-request GPU memory dropped ~12%, with tail latency unchanged (+0.4ms median). The PR is conservative by default: both features are opt-in via runtime flags (enable_activation_snapshot, scratch_compaction_level) and fall back to current checkpointing when models request strict deterministic execution. Includes unit and perf tests, canary rollout plan in release notes.

Init: add snapshot data structures and compacted slab allocator interface
Implement: scratch_compactor with greedy-pass and occupancy map
Scheduler: align KV-shard placement to compacted scratch windows
Runtime: expose flags and plumbing for activation snapshots and compactor
Tests: add microbench harness and regression tests; fix memory leak in allocator destructor
Docs: perf notes and rollout steps

Diego Ramos: Nice improvement; can we get numbers for large-sequence (8k) generation? Also add a safety check to avoid snapshotting when deterministic seeds are required.
Marina Kline: Added 8k-generation numbers to docs/perf report and added a runtime guard (preserve_det_state) that skips snapshotting when true.
Anika Shah: There was a flaky test on CI (allocator_dtor on ppc64). I suspect a missing fence in free path.
Marina Kline: Reworked free path with explicit device synchronization fence on platforms that require it, reran CI; test stabilized.
Priya Menon: Approving pending a short changelog blurb and a canary rollout plan for Dedicated customers.
Marina Kline: Added release notes & canary rollout to docs/perf/reports and updated CHANGELOG entry.

Add opt-in activation snapshotting and scratch compaction to reduce GPU workspace and fragmentation. Default behavior unchanged; opt-in flags: enable_activation_snapshot, scratch_compaction_level (off|conservative|aggressive). Reduces peak workspace (~18%) and avg per-request GPU memory (~12%) for multi-stream workloads in internal microbench. See docs/perf/reports/2026-02-snapshot-compactor.md for details and canary rollout plan.

title: Sundew Systems
author: Marina Cortez
text:
SMB inbound exploring hosted API. Wants model selection guidance (Llama vs Mistral vs Qwen), strict cost targets, SOC2 required. POC planned; next = technical Q&A + perf/cost table.

Inbound SMB lead — founder-led engineering team. Evaluating Redwood hosted API as primary self-serve path. Key themes from discovery:
- Workloads: customer support bot + internal doc search + short-form summarization for chat replies.
- Traffic: early stage, baseline ~2-3 QPS, expected peak ~8-12 QPS during business hours.
- Latency targets: P95 <= 350ms for live chat; willing to accept 500-600ms for longer summarization jobs.
- Cost sensitivity: high. Target cost per 1k input+output tokens ~<$0.50 in production. Wants guidance on quality vs cost tradeoffs.
- Model shortlist: exploring Llama 2 (13B), Mistral-Instruct (7B/8B), and Qwen family (7B/14B). Asks: which variant gives best f1 for our support prompts vs tokens billed? Also interested in quantized / distilled variants for cost.
- Routing/fallback: prefer single hosted endpoint; open to automatic fallback to a cheaper model for non-critical queries. Wants to understand impact on output consistency.
- Features required: streaming, function/tool-calls for ticket creation, structured output (JSON) support.
- Security: SOC2 required for contract, SSO/SAML later, audit logs mandatory. Public cloud acceptable; no VPC right now.
- POC plan proposed: 1) Redwood hosted API keys for 2-week POC using 3 model variants (Llama2-13B, Mistral-Instruct-7B, Qwen-14B), 2) run prompt set (35 canonical queries) and measure accuracy, latency P95, and cost/1k tokens, 3) review results and pick a production variant + fallback policy.
- Quotes/feedback from founder on call: "We want a clear tradeoff table — show us where quality drops and how much we save."
- Internal constraints: procurement needs one-page pricing + SOC2 attestation. Finance will review ARR band for commit thresholds.
- AE/SE notes: provide sample request/response size estimates, example streaming curl, tokenization guidance, and suggested batch sizes. Recommend Redwood Optimize report for quick batching/caching suggestions.
Next steps (short): schedule 30m technical Q&A with SE, provide POC checklist + quickstart link, share SOC2 report and sample perf logs. SE to prepare preliminary cost comparison (approx cost per 1k tokens) for the three model families using our sample prompt set.

title: Selective Telemetry Ejection & PII Suppression Demo - Ember Finance
author: Maya Chen
text:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-28 15:42 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Maya, Liam (Redwood); Priya, Daniel, Aisha (Ember Finance)
Links shared: https://redwood.example.com/security/ember-finance (security pack), https://redwood.example.com/console-demo (console GIF)

Summary:
Quick demo of request-storage controls in Console + API examples for selective telemetry ejection, PII suppression rules, and ephemeral request storage. Covered KMS/HSM integration options and enterprise retention defaults. Agreed to spin up pilot org with ephemeral request storage and run latency benchmarks.

Topics covered:
- Console toggles: request storage on/off/ephemeral, retention windows, manual ejection
- Redaction profiles: regex, ML PII detectors (heuristic), and token-level masking
- API flags: store_request=false, pii_policy=standard, telemetry_eject_rule=prefix-match
- KMS integration and audit logs
- Pilot next steps and benchmarks

Action items (recap): see metadata action_items above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you squeezing us in, uh Priya, Daniel, Aisha, glad to meet you. Liam and I will run through the console toggles and then swing to the API examples.
[00:18] Priya Singh: Thanks Maya, excited to see how we can limit logs — compliance is the big ask, we need to make sure nothing sensitive leaves our environment.
[00:24] Liam O'Connor: Totally, we'll show two patterns: ephemeral request storage which never lands on disk after inference completes, and selective telemetry ejection where we proactively strip fields before persisting.
[00:36] Daniel Kwan: Quick Q up front — is the request_storage flag per-tenant or per-route? We have mixed workloads; some routes can log for debugging.
[00:45] Liam O'Connor: Good question — you can set at three levels: org-default, route-level override, or on individual API calls with header overrides (x-redwood-store: false). So you can keep debug routes logging while customer-facing ones are ephemeral.
[00:58] Aisha Roberts: When you say "ephemeral" what's the retention window, like zero or 24 hours? Our legal wants zero persistent copy.
[01:07] Liam O'Connor: Ephemeral is zero-persistent by default — the payload is held in memory and KV cache but not written to request storage. We do have an "ephemeral+buffer" mode for short replay debugging (configurable to 1 hour). That mode still encrypts in transit and in-mem.
[01:23] Priya Singh: Ok, good. Also need to hear about redaction — we have PHI tokens and account numbers, want deterministic masking.
[01:30] Maya Chen: We'll demo the console redaction profiles — regex-based rules you can upload, plus our ML PII detector which tags tokens and can either mask or eject the whole field.
[01:38] [00:01:40] Speaker 4: (low audio) - can you show an example?
[01:45] Liam O'Connor: Sure — switching to screen. (brief pause) So here is the Console > Data Controls tab, you can see the default profile called "Redwood Standard". You can create a custom profile and add rules. For Ember I'd suggest: regex for account numbers, ML detector for names/dates, and a tokenization ejection pattern for anything that looks like SSN.
[02:12] Daniel Kwan: When you say "tokenization ejection" do you mean we drop tokens pre-inference or after inference? We need to preserve prompt context sometimes.
[02:22] Liam O'Connor: We have two modes: pre-token ejection — remove tokens before they hit the model (safer for PII but loses context), and KV-level mask — keep a masked placeholder in the prompt so model still sees structure, e.g., replace with [PII_REDACTED]. You choose per-rule.
[02:39] Priya Singh: Can the mask be reversible for our SREs (like hashed + lookup) — or is it one-way?
[02:46] Liam O'Connor: It's configurable: you can choose irreversible redaction, reversible hashed token stored in a KMS-protected store, or ephemeral reversible only within a bounded TTL. Reversible requires explicit KMS permissions and audit logging.
[02:59] Aisha Roberts: Audit logging is critical — we need proof we redacted. Does your audit show the original or only the action?
[03:06] Maya Chen: Audit logs show metadata and the rule that triggered the redaction, but the original plaintext can be redacted from logs depending on your compliance profile — if you enable reversible storage, the original is gated behind KMS access and recorded in the audit.
[03:20] Priya Singh: Okay that's helpful. Walk us through an API example — we want to implement minimal changes client-side.
[03:26] Liam O'Connor: On the API side you have request flags. Example cURL: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" -H "x-redwood-store: false" -d '{"input": "..."}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate. Also you can pass "pii_policy": "strict" in the JSON to apply server-side ejection.
[03:46] Daniel Kwan: Is there a latency cost for server-side PII detection? We care about 95th percentile latency.
[03:52] Liam O'Connor: There is some modest overhead — the ML PII detector runs in a streaming pass; we optimize with batching. For most short requests it's ~10-30ms extra; for larger body text it may be higher. We'll include perf numbers in the benchmark but you can pre-tag on client if latency is critical.
[04:09] Priya Singh: Does the detector run on Dedicated or Private in the same way?
[04:13] Liam O'Connor: Yes — runtime parity across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. On Private you can deploy the detector in your VPC and route calls locally; the console still controls the ruleset via your private control plane.
[04:25] Aisha Roberts: Our legal asked about encryption at rest for the temporary buffer. You mentioned KMS earlier. Is that customer-managed?
[04:32] Maya Chen: For Dedicated and Private you can use customer-managed KMS/HSM. Hosted supports Redwood-managed KMS with options to bring your own key in enterprise plans.
[04:41] [00:04:41] Priya Singh: Any SOC 2 or ISO docs for this?
[04:44] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll send the SOC2 package. It's the first action item. Also our compliance pack includes a sample configuration showing how to disable request storage and still get metrics.
[04:55] Daniel Kwan: Metrics? If we turn off storage, can we still get per-model latency and cost metrics?
[05:01] Liam O'Connor: Yes — telemetry metrics are aggregated and de-identified. We provide token-level cost, latency percentiles, and error counts without storing full request payloads. You can enable metrics-only mode — we store headers and timing but not request body.
[05:14] Priya Singh: That sounds promising. How do you handle third-party integrations — we use Datadog and SIEM tools.
[05:20] Maya Chen: We emit structured telemetry events and you can choose to route them to your monitoring. The events are schema-controlled so no PII fields by default; any custom links back to original request require explicit consent and storage toggles.
[05:34] Aisha Roberts: Talk to me about deletion requests — if a user asks to delete their data, can you guarantee removal from all logs?
[05:41] Liam O'Connor: Yes, Redwood has an ejection API: POST /orgs/{id}/eject with selectors. It runs a targeted purge across request storage and backups (subject to retention windows). For ephemeral mode there's nothing to delete, but for stored mode we will run the purge and return an audit ticket.
[05:58] [00:05:58] Speaker 2: (overlap) — do you support regex across nested JSON payloads?
[06:03] Liam O'Connor: Yep — rules support JSONPath selectors and regex, plus ML detectors for free text fields.
[06:10] Priya Singh: Demo time — show the console toggle for request-storage off.
[06:14] Liam O'Connor: (screen share) In Console > Routes > /payments we open the route config, toggle Request storage = Off, and hit Save. From there, new calls have header x-redwood-store: false by default. For existing routes you can run a migration to drop stored payloads.
[06:32] Daniel Kwan: When you flip that toggle, does it immediately block writes or does it wait for an in-flight grace period?
[06:38] Liam O'Connor: It's immediate for new requests. For in-flight requests, we complete the operation but mark them for deferred ejection if they're in the buffer. We also expose a "flush" action to clear the buffer on demand.
[06:49] Priya Singh: Can we demo a redaction rule?
[06:52] Liam O'Connor: Creating one now: name = Ember-Account-Regex, selector = $.payment.account_number, regex = (\d{4}-\d{4}-\d{4}), action = mask (last 4). Save. Now run a sample request.
[07:09] [00:07:10] (API POST sample shown)
[07:15] System: Request received (masked in logs) — redaction rule matched, masked value = ****-****-1234.
[07:22] Aisha Roberts: Nice — can we make it remove entirely instead of mask?
[07:26] Liam O'Connor: Yes, change action to "eject_field" and it will remove the JSON key before persisting. Note that changes how the model sees the prompt — if you need model context, use mask instead.
[07:38] Daniel Kwan: Any way to test redaction rules safely in prod without affecting users?
[07:42] Liam O'Connor: Console has a "dry run" mode that simulates rules and shows counts/hits but doesn't persist changes. You can also run in a QA org.
[07:52] Priya Singh: Suppose we want token-level suppression that removes just names but keeps grammar — will that break model quality?
[07:59] Liam O'Connor: Masking names with placeholders preserves grammar and usually keeps quality intact. Fully removing tokens can reduce context and sometimes increase hallucinations — that's part of the tradeoff we'll measure in the pilot.
[08:12] Maya Chen: Quick interjection — on Optimize, we can suggest redaction configs that minimize quality loss while hitting compliance targets. It looks at your prompt patterns and suggests which fields to mask vs eject.
[08:23] Priya Singh: Is that the "Optimize" product? We haven't seen that.
[08:26] Liam O'Connor: Yes — Redwood Optimize. Example: it analyzed your typical payment flows and suggested only mask last 4 digits while ejecting full SSN patterns. It also provides estimated token-cost delta.
[08:36] Daniel Kwan: Can Optimize run offline against a sample dataset so we don't send live customer data?
[08:41] Maya Chen: Totally. You can upload a scrubbed prompt corpus or run a local Optimize job in Private that never leaves your VPC.
[08:51] Priya Singh: Let's talk about incident response — if there's a leakage, how do we rotate keys and ensure data isn't recoverable?
[08:58] Liam O'Connor: For customer-managed KMS we recommend rotating keys and then invoking a rekey-and-eject process. Re-encryption or key destruction can make stored backups unrecoverable; we pair that with audit tickets.
[09:10] Aisha Roberts: One compliance nuance — some regulators require ability to produce original content for audits, so we may need reversible storage for a brief period. Is that supported?
[09:18] Liam O'Connor: Yes configurable TTL for reversible mode and auditor access can be implemented with cross-org SSO + time-limited KMS grant. Everything's audited.
[09:29] [00:09:29] Priya Singh: Can we see the audit logs UI?
[09:33] Liam O'Connor: (navigates) Here, Console > Audit logs — filter by event type (redaction, ejection, key-access). Each event shows timestamp, rule id, actor, and an audit ticket link. If original was removed, the payload column shows 'REDACTED'.
[09:47] Daniel Kwan: Do logs ship to our SIEM in a way that retains the mapping to rule IDs so we can correlate?
[09:53] Liam O'Connor: Yes we emit rule IDs and hash of request ID; you can correlate without exposing payload.
[10:01] Priya Singh: A few risk items from our side: 1) We need reproducible deletion; 2) We need no PII in third-party metrics; 3) We need an SLA on the ejection job. Are those manageable?
[10:11] Maya Chen: We can commit to ejection SLAs in enterprise contracts, and all three items are supported — we'll surface them in the compliance pack.
[10:19] Aisha Roberts: About retention windows — do you support custom retention per-route?
[10:23] Liam O'Connor: Yes per-route retention windows (e.g., 0, 24h, 30d) and global org defaults.
[10:29] [00:10:29] (brief silence)
[10:33] Daniel Kwan: Performance question again — if we route PII-heavy traffic to a dedicated pool that runs redaction as a pre-step, does that reduce latency overhead?
[10:42] Liam O'Connor: It can. Dedicated pools co-locate detectors and model instances, reducing network hops. Also you can pre-process client-side to further cut latencies.
[10:50] Priya Singh: Cost considerations — does redaction add to token billing?
[10:54] Liam O'Connor: We bill tokens consumed by the model. Pre-inference ejection reduces tokens billed because fewer tokens are sent to the model. Masking doesn't typically change token count much. Optimize will estimate cost delta.
[11:06] Maya Chen: We're at the halfway mark — any other blockers?
[11:09] Priya Singh: Two more: 1) Data residency — we need EU data to stay in EU. 2) SSO and RBAC integration.
[11:16] Liam O'Connor: Data residency supported by region selection; on Private, you control the physical location. For SSO we support SAML and OIDC and fine-grained RBAC in Console.
[11:26] Aisha Roberts: Vault & HSM specifics — can we get a diagram showing where keys live?
[11:31] Maya Chen: We'll attach an architecture diagram in the follow-up email.
[11:35] Daniel Kwan: On the API flags, is there a way to default to not storing and opt-in per-request? We prefer default-off.
[11:42] Liam O'Connor: Yes set org-default to store:false and allow route-level opt-in. The default is controllable.
[11:47] Priya Singh: Let's run a quick end-to-end test: toggle route to ephemeral and send a sample payment request.
[11:51] (demo request fired)
[11:55] System: Received request, storage mode = ephemeral, no payload persisted. Telemetry event emitted: {event: "request_processed", route: "/payments", latency_ms: 87} (payload omitted)
[12:07] Priya Singh: I see the telemetry, but not the body. Exactly what we want.
[12:11] Maya Chen: Great — one note: if you need post-mortem debug, we recommend ephemeral+buffer for a short TTL with strict access controls.
[12:21] Daniel Kwan: Any limitations on file uploads or attachments? We send PDFs sometimes.
[12:26] Liam O'Connor: Attachments can be piped through the same pipeline and redaction rules can apply to text extracted by OCR; large binary objects are stored separately and subject to the same retention toggles.
[12:40] Aisha Roberts: Our audit team will want a demo of the ejection API; can Liam provide a scripted example?
[12:45] Liam O'Connor: Yep I'll include ejection API examples and sample curl in the follow-up.
[12:49] Priya Singh: What about false positives in ML detectors? We can't silence customers because of aggressive redaction.
[12:55] Liam O'Connor: You can tune sensitivity and add allow-list patterns. Also Optimize can suggest a threshold that balances recall vs precision for your corpus.
[13:07] [00:13:07] Maya Chen: Quick commercial question — any timeline constraints for pilot?
[13:12] Priya Singh: We'd like to start a pilot in early October and run 4 weeks.
[13:16] Maya Chen: Sounds good — we'll aim for provisioning the pilot tenant by 2026-10-05.
[13:22] Daniel Kwan: Billing — will trial be free or metered?
[13:25] Maya Chen: Standard trials are usage-metered with a credit; enterprise pilots can be structured. We'll propose options in the next email.
[13:33] Aisha Roberts: A quick security question — if we do reversible storage, what prevents a rogue engineer from decrypting data?
[13:40] Liam O'Connor: Access is gated by RBAC and KMS grants; key access is audited and requires time-limited elevated privileges. We can also enforce approval workflows for key operations.
[13:52] Priya Singh: Could we get an SLA for ejection job times? We may need 24-hour max on large ejections.
[13:58] Maya Chen: We'll propose SLA terms for the pilot and for enterprise contracts.
[14:05] Daniel Kwan: Any sample config for Datadog mapping?
[14:08] Liam O'Connor: Yes, I'll include a sample mapping.
[14:11] Priya Singh: Last thing — are there pre-built compliance templates for banking/finance?
[14:16] Maya Chen: We have templates for finance, healthcare, and retail. We'll include the banking template in the follow-up.
[14:22] (wrap-up)
[14:24] Maya Chen: Ok recap — we will: 1) Send SOC2 + KMS docs (Maya), 2) Provision pilot org with ephemeral default and Ember redaction profile (Liam), 3) Provide ejection API examples and Datadog mapping (Liam), 4) Ember will confirm pilot metrics and legal owner (Priya).
[14:41] Priya Singh: Thanks everyone, this was really useful. We'll follow-up internally and aim to confirm by next week.
[14:48] Maya Chen: Appreciate your time — we'll get the email out today and schedule the benchmarking slot.
[14:55] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional audio drop at 00:01:40 and 00:07:10, small mis-recognitions of product name ("Redwood Optimize" sometimes transcribed as "Redwood Optimizer"). Some filler words preserved.

title: StreamFrame fidelity harness and model shim for function-call/backcompat testing
author: Asha Patel
text:
Build a repeatable regression harness that validates streaming frame-level fidelity, function-call boundary preservation, and structured-output JSON schema compatibility across model variants and runtime changes. This ticket implements a new lightweight model shim to emulate older function-call contracts and exercises it with a set of golden prompts and negative cases so the CI can detect accidental contract regressions before deploy.

A harness exists that can replay 1k golden prompts and assert frame-level diffs (token boundaries, event types, error frames) in under 30 minutes on CI runners.
Function-call scenarios: shimmed older contract and current contract are exercised; differences are surfaced as structured diffs with root-cause suggestions.
Structured-output validator: JSON Schema + JSONPath checks run as part of tests; failures produce example failing output and minimal repro prompt.
CI gate: PRs that touch streaming, serializer, or func-call runtime code must run the harness and block on new failures (flaky-test backstop ticket created if flakiness > 5%).
Dashboard: an aggregated compatibility score on Console + a weekly digest to #runtime-alerts in Slack is available for the last 30 days of CI runs.

2025-02-20: Spike completed comparing current stream event model to legacy function-call wire contract; identified three mismatches in 'tool.end' framing.
2025-02-24: Implemented prototype shim that rewrites function-call events to legacy envelope for the harness; initial smoke tests passing locally (50/50 golden set).
2025-02-27: Design review with PM and DRI (Diego) — agreed to add explicit token-boundary assertions and to include deliberate timing jitter cases to catch race conditions.
2025-03-02: CI worker image updated (python-3.11 + rust-toolchain) and harness containerized; running nightly job against headless model snapshots for baseline collection.
2025-03-04: Discovered a flaky case around partial toolcall truncation on a long-prefix prompt; added deterministic seeding and a new failing golden prompt to the corpus.

Harness must be easy to extend for future contract variants (e.g., multiplexed streams). Include metadata on each golden prompt describing expected model, tokenization assumptions, and chaos-injection knobs. Coordinate on rollout with Release Engineering to add CI quota for longer nightly baselines.

title: ADR: Example-Level Payload Shape for Streaming Tool Calls
author: Brian Murphy
text:
## Status
Published (applies to examples in docs, quickstarts, and SDK READMEs).

## Decision summary
For **developer-facing examples** that demonstrate *streaming tool calls*, Redwood will standardize on a **minimal, stable event envelope** and a **canonical tool-call object shape**:

- Streaming events shown in examples MUST include:
 - `event` (string)
 - `data` (object)
- Tool call identity MUST be represented as `tool_call_id` everywhere (stream deltas, final tool call, and tool-result messages).
- Tool call arguments MUST be treated as **an opaque string during streaming**:
 - partial updates: `arguments_delta` (string)
 - final: `arguments` (string)
 - parsing happens **only after** the tool call is complete.

This ADR intentionally defines the **example-level** payload shape (what we show and teach), not the full internal wire format.

## Context / problem
Across Python/TypeScript/Go and the docs site, streaming tool-calling examples diverged in:

- Field naming (`id` vs `tool_call_id`, `function.name` vs `name`).
- Whether arguments were shown as JSON objects vs strings.
- How partial arguments were represented during streaming.
- How parallel tool calls were assembled when deltas interleave.

These inconsistencies contributed to:

- Copy/paste failures and type mismatches (e.g., TS example failures).
- Confusion about “truncated” arguments mid-stream (SUP-18421): users attempted to parse JSON before the stream completed.
- Support load due to unclear guidance on delta assembly and tool-result linkage.

The refresh project requires a single mental model that is consistent across SDKs and documentation.

## Goals
1. Provide a simple, consistent model for assembling tool calls from streaming deltas.
2. Avoid encouraging fragile behavior (incremental JSON parsing, relying on internal fields).
3. Make examples resilient to model variability (argument emission timing, interleaving).
4. Keep parity with common industry patterns (OpenAI-style semantics) without claiming strict wire compatibility.

## Non-goals
- Redesigning Redwood’s underlying streaming protocol.
- Defining every field available in the raw streaming payload.

## Decision details
### 1) Canonical event names used in examples
Examples will use the following `event` names. SDKs may expose richer objects; examples should map to these concepts.

| Event | When it fires | Required fields in `data` | Notes |
|------|---------------|---------------------------|-------|
| `message.delta` | Assistant message text arrives incrementally | `message_id`, `content_delta` | `content_delta` is appended to a per-message buffer. |
| `message.done` | Assistant message is complete | `message_id`, `content` | Examples may omit if the SDK returns final content elsewhere; if present, it is authoritative. |
| `tool_call.delta` | Tool call arguments arrive incrementally | `tool_call_id`, `name` (optional), `arguments_delta` | Deltas may interleave across multiple tool calls. Do not parse JSON here. |
| `tool_call.done` | Tool call arguments are complete | `tool_call_id`, `name`, `arguments` | `arguments` is a complete JSON string (still validate before use). |
| `response.done` | No more events for the response | `response_id` (optional) | Marks end-of-stream for the example loop. |
| `error` | Stream fails or server returns an error | `code`, `message` | Examples should demonstrate a single retry policy or a clear abort. |

Rationale: dot-separated names are readable in logs, consistent across languages, and avoid leaking internal event taxonomies.

### 2) Canonical tool call object shape
Examples will represent a tool call as:

- `tool_call_id` (string): stable identifier for the call
- `name` (string): tool/function name
- `arguments_delta` (string): partial JSON text during streaming
- `arguments` (string): complete JSON text when done

**Arguments are always strings** in streaming examples.

Rationale: during streaming, the JSON is frequently incomplete and not parseable. Representing deltas as strings prevents users from writing broken “parse on every chunk” logic.

### 3) Tool-result messages MUST reference `tool_call_id`
When returning tool output back to the model, examples must send a tool-result message that includes the `tool_call_id`:

```json
{
 "role": "tool",
 "tool_call_id": "call_01HZZ...",
 "content": "{\"temperature_f\": 71, \"conditions\": \"clear\"}"
}
```

Rationale: a stable link is required for parallel tool calls and avoids ambiguity when multiple tools share the same name.

### 4) What examples should *not* show
To keep examples stable and avoid implying unsupported semantics, examples should not depend on:

- Internal IDs unrelated to tool execution (e.g., per-token counters, shard IDs).
- Incremental JSON parsing of arguments.
- Assuming tool call `name` arrives before `arguments_delta` (models differ).
- Assuming tool calls cannot interleave.

If the SDK exposes a richer native event type, examples may log it behind a debug flag, but the canonical logic should operate on the minimal fields above.

## Example transcript (canonical)
Below is the reference shape used in docs/quickstarts for streaming tool calls.

### Tool definitions (request)
```json
{
 "model": "redwood/sonoma-3",
 "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in Seattle right now?"}],
 "tools": [
 {
 "type": "function",
 "function": {
 "name": "get_weather",
 "description": "Fetch current weather for a city.",
 "parameters": {
 "type": "object",
 "properties": {
 "city": {"type": "string"},
 "units": {"type": "string", "enum": ["metric", "imperial"]}
 },
 "required": ["city"]
 }
 }
 }
 ]
}
```

### Streaming events (response)
```json
{"event":"message.delta","data":{"message_id":"msg_1","content_delta":"Let me check that for you."}}
{"event":"tool_call.delta","data":{"tool_call_id":"call_1","name":"get_weather","arguments_delta":"{\"city\":\"Sea"}}
{"event":"tool_call.delta","data":{"tool_call_id":"call_1","arguments_delta":"ttle\",\"units\":\"imperial\""}}
{"event":"tool_call.delta","data":{"tool_call_id":"call_1","arguments_delta":"}"}}
{"event":"tool_call.done","data":{"tool_call_id":"call_1","name":"get_weather","arguments":"{\"city\":\"Seattle\",\"units\":\"imperial\"}"}}
{"event":"response.done","data":{"response_id":"resp_1"}}
```

Notes:
- `name` may be omitted on subsequent `tool_call.delta` events; examples must cache it if needed.
- The arguments are intentionally shown as JSON text, not a JSON object.

## Assembly rules (normative for examples)
Examples (across languages) must implement the following assembly rules:

1. Maintain a map keyed by `tool_call_id` with:
 - `name` (string, optional until first seen)
 - `arguments_buffer` (string)
2. On `tool_call.delta`:
 - Append `arguments_delta` to `arguments_buffer` for that `tool_call_id`.
 - Do not parse.
3. On `tool_call.done`:
 - Prefer `arguments` from the done event if provided.
 - Parse once (`JSON.parse` / `json.loads`) and validate against the tool schema.
4. If the stream ends without `tool_call.done`:
 - Treat as incomplete.
 - Either retry the request (if safe and idempotency is configured) or surface a clear error.

This directly addresses the “arguments truncated” support issue: arguments are expected to look incomplete mid-stream.

## Parallel tool calls
Examples must assume:

- Multiple tool calls may be active.
- Deltas may interleave across tool calls.

Canonical behavior:
- Use `tool_call_id` as the sole key.
- Never assume “the latest tool call” is the target of a delta.

## Compatibility guidance (docs copy)
Docs should include a short callout:

- “Streaming tool-call arguments are emitted as text deltas and may not be valid JSON until the tool call is complete. Always assemble and parse after `tool_call.done`.”

If a page discusses OpenAI-compatibility, it must clarify that:

- The Redwood examples use OpenAI-like semantics (tool definitions + tool result messages), but the raw streaming payload may contain additional fields and may not be byte-for-byte identical.

## Alternatives considered
1. **Expose the full raw streaming payload in examples**
 - Pros: transparent.
 - Cons: noisy, unstable, encourages reliance on non-contractual fields.

2. **Represent arguments as JSON objects in deltas**
 - Pros: “feels typed.”
 - Cons: not feasible when JSON is incomplete; encourages incremental parsing and fragile merge logic.

3. **Standardize on OpenAI’s exact streaming schema**
 - Pros: familiarity.
 - Cons: limits Redwood’s ability to evolve payloads; risks implying strict compatibility where edge cases differ.

We chose a minimal envelope that is stable, teachable, and implementation-agnostic.

## Consequences
### Positive
- Cross-language parity improves (shared mental model and fixtures).
- Examples become more robust to model variability and interleaving.
- Reduced support burden from premature JSON parsing and ID confusion.

### Negative / tradeoffs
- The example-level shape is a simplification; docs must avoid implying it is the full wire contract.
- SDKs may need small adapter helpers to map native stream types to the canonical fields used in examples.

## Rollout plan
- Apply this ADR to:
 - Docs code tabs (Python/TS/Go)
 - Quickstarts “agentic workflow” template
 - `redwood-examples` runnable samples
- Add golden transcript tests that validate:
 - `tool_call_id` stability
 - interleaving correctness
 - presence of `tool_call.done` before parsing

## Open questions
- Whether `message.done` should be mandatory in the example envelope for all SDKs (some SDKs provide final message out-of-band). For now it is optional, but `response.done` is required in transcript-style examples.

## Owner
API Standards / DevEx parity: Ibrahim Khan (tech lead) with review by Brian Murphy (API/SDK semantics).

title: Conjoint Scan for Quantization Recommendation - proposal
author: Aria Chen
text:
Purpose:

This is a proposal for a lightweight, workload-driven 'conjoint scan' approach to produce per-workload quantization recommendations (INT8, FP8, 4-bit mixed) that explicitly trade off cost, latency, and quality. The goal is a reproducible scoring pipeline and a small recommendation service that can suggest a) single-model quantization profiles and b) per-route hybrid strategies (e.g., FP8 for short responses, 4-bit for high-volume background jobs).

Background / motivation:

- We already have many qualitative heuristics and pointwise sensitivity scans, but teams struggle to pick a single knob when multiple axes move simultaneously (batching, sequence length, KV cache hits, per-layer quantization).
- Conjoint analysis is a natural fit: treat quantization decisions as a set of factors with levels and learn a utility model from sparse, structured experiments rather than exhaustive per-layer sweeps. The output is interpretable utilities (weight multipliers) that we can combine with a customer's cost/latency/quality preferences to produce a ranked shortlist.

Approach overview (high-level):

1) Define factors and levels. Each candidate experiment is a configuration vector. Candidate factors: bitwidth strategy, quant method, policy for input caching, batch size, kernel selection (fast path vs precise path), and a sequence-length bucket. Example levels:
 - bitwidth strategy: [FP16 baseline, FP8, INT8, 4-bit mixed]
 - quant method: [symmetric per-tensor, per-channel, GPTQ-lite]
 - cache policy: [no-prefix-cache, prefix-cache, KV-snapshotting]
 - batch size: [1, 4, 16]
 - kernel: [faster-attn, exact-attn]
 - seq bucket: [<=128, 129-512, >512]

2) Fractional design + adaptivity. Use a fractional factorial starting plan (~48 configurations) chosen to cover main effects and pairwise interactions for the most important axes (bitwidth x seq bucket, bitwidth x batch). Then run an adaptive stage driven by a lightweight surrogate model (XGBoost or GP) to explore regions near Pareto-optimality.

3) Measurement suite. For each configuration, collect: per-token cost (profiled GPU time converted to $ using our costing table), p95 latency measured end-to-end, quality delta vs FP16 baseline (LL logprob change, and a small set of automated evals per workload such as F1/ROUGE/EM where appropriate). Also collect failure modes (nan, token divergence heuristics) and memory headroom.

4) Utility modeling. Fit a simple linear-conjoint (or hierarchical Bayesian) model where utility = w_cost * normalized_cost + w_latency * normalized_p95 + w_quality * normalized_quality_drop + error. Provide per-workload priors and allow users to express tradeoff weights or select presets (latency-first, cost-first, quality-first). The trained model outputs expected utilities and uncertainty for unseen configs.

Decision surface and recommendation output:

- For a given workload (profiled seq distribution, typical batch, and business weights), the system ranks configs and returns: top-3 recommended quant profiles, expected delta to baseline (cost %, p95 ms, quality drift), and a confidence score. It also produces a compact explanation: which factors drove the gain (e.g., "4-bit yields 60% cost reduction for seq<=128 but has noticeable quality drift on code completion prompts").

Toy cost example (illustrative numbers only):

Baseline FP16 single-token cost: 0.10ms/token -> per-token compute $0.000012.
- FP8: 0.065ms/token -> $0.0000078 (35% cost reduction)
- INT8: 0.054ms/token -> $0.0000065 (46% cost reduction)
- 4-bit mixed: 0.040ms/token -> $0.0000048 (60% cost reduction)
However, quality metric (LL loss increase / relative): FP8: +0.8%, INT8: +1.6%, 4-bit: +4.2% for sensitive reasoning prompts. Latency p95 improvements vary with batching: 4-bit helps most at batch sizes >=4 where kernel throughput dominates.

Experiment logistics and infra needs:

- Runner: reuse the existing microbenchmark harness in github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks with small additions to capture eval sets and sequence distribution sampling.
- Storage: each run uploads a compact JSON summary to S3 and to the recommendation DB.
- Cost accounting: convert profiled GPU-ms to dollars using the internal cost table (linked in CONFLUENCE-OPT/7842).
- Safety net: automatically mark configs that trigger stability signals (OOB memory, token repeats) and exclude them from recommendations unless user explicit opt-in.

Rollout plan and outputs:

Phase 0 (2 weeks): prototype fractional design and measurement harness for 2 models (Llama-variant and a small opt-in customer model). Produce reproducible run of 48 configs for one workload.
Phase 1 (4 weeks): adaptive stage, utility model fit, produce per-workload recommendations and a small web UI for manual inspection.
Phase 2 (2 weeks): integrate with Optimize suggestions (console) as a "suggest quant profile" button and run a small internal A/B on low-risk routes.

Metrics to track:

- Accuracy of predicted cost deltas (MSE vs measured).
- Quality regressions observed in production (number of alerts per 1M tokens after applying recommendation).
- Adoption rate (routes that accept recommendation change and stay changed for >7 days).
- Percent of recommended configs that are Pareto-dominated when measured fully (we want low false-positive rate).

Open questions and design choices:

- Granularity: per-model vs per-route vs per-prompt-set recommendations. Tradeoff: per-prompt-set is most accurate but operationally heavy. Start per-route with optional per-prompt-set sampling.
- How to represent quality for generative vs discriminative tasks? Proposed: use LL-delta + task-specific metric pool and expose both.
- Interaction with rollout policies: recommended profile should have a recommended rollout policy (canary samples & automatic rollback threshold).

Next steps (owner and short tasks):

- Aria: implement fractional experiment chooser in bench harness (1 week).
- Ravi: add cost conversion and upload hook (3 days).
- Lena: assemble 3 representative workloads and small eval suites (1 week).
- Noah: prototype the utility model sketch and show demo ranking (2 weeks).

Appendix: quick checklist for experiment run

- pick workload and upload small eval set (200 prompts stratified by length)
- choose fractional design seed (48 configs) and run on 3 repeats
- collect: raw GPU-ms per-token, p50/p95 latency, LL per-prompt, eval metrics, memory usage
- compute normalized features and fit conjoint utility model
- generate top-3 recommendations and sanity-check via targeted human eval on top candidate

Notes / rationale extras:

- Conjoint framing reduces combinatorial explosion by focusing on marginal utilities rather than full combinational coverage.
- It produces interpretable weights we can display to customers ("you care twice as much about latency than quality").
- The approach is complementary to the more exhaustive per-layer GPTQ flows; we can use the conjoint tool to pick candidate bitwidth/methods and then hand off to the GPTQ path for per-layer tuning if needed.

If this approach sounds reasonable, I propose starting the Phase 0 prototype this sprint and circling back with run artifacts for review.

title: Helio SprintLabs Copilot
author: Ethan Park
text:
Summary: Helio SprintLabs is building an IDE copilot integrated into their enterprise IDE that emphasizes near-instant streaming completions for developer UX. Primary ask: consistently fast Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) for completion streaming + predictable token budget behavior so editor doesn't 'blink' or overload the language model.

Recent customer feedback / paraphrased quotes:
- "TTFT must feel instant — target <80ms for first token on warm paths; jitter must be minimized (<10ms ideally)" — Head of Platform
- "We need backpressure in the editor: if generation stalls or token budget near-exhausted, return a graceful partial completion and a stable fallback" — Lead UX Engineer

Technical requirements (from calls):
- Primary workload: low-latency code completion streaming (single-line and multi-line completions), small-context code chat for quick lookups.
- Latency targets: TTFT <80ms warm, <150ms cold-first (acceptable if KV-cache warmup unavoidable).
- Jitter: p95 jitter <12ms; p99 <30ms.
- Throughput: per-customer peak 120 concurrent live sessions, average completion length 40–120 tokens.
- Token budget model: per-session soft budget 1500 tokens/day with priority decay; need hooks to signal client when 75% and 90% thresholds reached.
- Backpressure behavior: prefer server-driven pacing (stream chunk sizes) + an immediate ability to send "partial final" tokens if connectivity drops.
- Model/version pinning: must pin to a verified low-latency variant (requested: "mosaic-lite-latopt-v2" as primary) with automated fallback to smaller quantized variant for overflow.
- Caching: warm KV cache strategies, prefetch top-N token prefixes for hot repo contexts.
- Autoscale policy: hybrid burst to hosted for spikes but prefer Dedicated for steady throughput.

Security/Compliance notes:
- SSO (SAML) and org-level audit logging required. KMS integration for secret handling. Data retention controls by customer.

POC plan and metrics to validate:
- Run dedicated perf matrix across three configs: Hosted baseline, Dedicated (2xA100 equivalent), Dedicated + quantized kernel.
- Measure: TTFT median/p95/p99, jitter p95/p99, bytes-per-token, server CPU/GPU utilization, partial-completion rate under backpressure.
- Acceptance criteria: median TTFT <70ms on warm for typical repo stimuli; p95 TTFT <120ms; jitter targets above. Session token budget signaling must hit client hooks in >=95% of tests.

Open items / asks for Redwood:
- Provide recommended streaming chunk config (chunk size vs frequency) and sample client backpressure API.
- Template for model pinning config and guidance on safe fallback chains.
- Cost estimate for Dedicated POC (2 nodes + burst to hosted) — see Drive pricing doc.

Next steps (short):
- 2026-03-10 — POC perf run (Ethan/Riley present) — evaluate Dedicated nodes.
- 2026-03-17 — Post-POC review and security checklist signoff.

Steno / CRM shorthand: TTFT SLOs/ jitter = gating; token-budget hooks = must-have; model pinning + graceful fallback = blocker until POC proven.

2026-01-15 — Lead created after inbound trial sign-up (IDE copilot plugin).
2026-02-05 — Intro call (Ethan/Riley): demo of streaming and pinning; Helio engineers emphasized low jitter.
2026-02-18 — Questionnaire + security checklist returned (SAML + KMS noted).
2026-02-22 — Tech deep-dive with infra: discussed KV-cache warmup, prefix caching, batching windows.
2026-03-02 — POC kickoff: Helio provided sample repo + latency SLOs; scheduled perf run on 2026-03-10.
2026-03-09 — Pre-run sync; agreed to test two model variants and backpressure configs.

title: Unified Inference Consumption Paradigm — Product Overview and Roadmap
author: Asha Patel
text:
Summary

Purpose: This document defines the "Unified Inference Consumption Paradigm" (UICP) — a product-level model that unifies usage patterns, billing primitives, and operational controls across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. UICP is intended to reduce customer confusion, improve predictability of unit economics, and create a clear migration path between short-term experimentation and long-term committed capacity.

Audience
- Product managers and pricing owners
- Engineering teams (billing, runtime, routing)
- Customer success and sales (for contract conversations)
- Finance (forecasts and revenue recognition)

Key goals
1) Simplify: present a small set of clearly documented consumption primitives that map to typical customer journeys (prototype -> scale -> enterprise).
2) Align: ensure meter semantics are identical across hosting modes whenever feasible so product analytics and customer invoices match expectations.
3) Optimize: enable feature-level levers (routes, batching, caching) to be surfaced as cost controls customers can apply per-application.
4) Grow: create packaging that reduces friction for upgrades (e.g., credits applied toward reserved capacity).

Core concepts and definitions
- Unit primitives: token-generation-unit (TGU) and embedding-unit (EU). A TGU represents 1k generated tokens of model output (billed at model-profile rates). An EU represents 1 embedding vector invocation.
- Route: a logical endpoint customers configure that maps to a model, routing policy, and cost-slo profile (e.g., route: chat-low-latency).
- Bundle: a purchasable allocation of TGUs/EUs with attributes {term, refundable_credits, route_scoped}. Bundles may be on-demand (monthly) or committed (annual).
- Route-aware bundles: bundles tagged to one or more routes so customers can buy reservations for high-value endpoints without committing for all consumption.
- Effective price: dynamic per-call price calculated from model profile, route-level optimizations (batching, cache-hit-rate adjustment), and bundle discounts.

Illustrative billing example
- Model: open-llama-70B-qk8, baseline rate: $0.020 / TGU.
- Customer purchases a 12-month bundle: 1,000,000 TGUs for $12,500 (effective $0.0125 / TGU).
- Route optimization credit: their chat route has expected 15% KV cache hit; effective per-call cost adjusts to $0.0106 / TGU for that route.

Requirements (summary table)
| Requirement ID | Description | Priority | Owner | Acceptance criteria |
| RQ-001 | Unified meter semantics for TGUs/EUs across Hosted/Dedicated/Private | Must | Billing | All three modes report identical token counts for identical requests within +/-1% observed variance over 7d test window |
| RQ-002 | Route-aware bundle support in billing pipeline and UI | Must | Product & Billing | Bundles can be created that are route-scoped, show remaining usage, and apply discounts on invoice lines |
| RQ-003 | Effective-price telemetry exported to Console & cost API | High | Eng Runtime | Console shows modeled vs actual spend breakdown per-request and per-route for last 30d |
| RQ-004 | Migration flow: credits conversion for upgrades from Hosted to Dedicated | High | Sales Ops | Tooling converts remaining prepaid credits into usable reservation discounts with clear audit trail |

Product capabilities (feature list)
- Consumption catalog: standardized descriptions and example invoices for each bundle type.
- Route tagging and per-route controls in Console (risk controls: max QPS, latency tier, fallback variant).
- Billing API enhancements: purchase, query balance, allocate to routes, and programmatic refunds.
- Effective price estimator: SDK endpoint that returns an estimated per-call cost given model, sequence length distribution, and route config.
- Metering reconciler: daily job to compare runtime counters with billing counters and surface anomalies >1%.

Architecture overview (high level)
- Metering pipeline: runtime -> normalized event stream (token events, embed events) -> aggregator -> reconciler -> billing ledger.
- Route-aware middleware: runtime attaches route metadata to every request that is persisted through the event stream so bundle application is deterministic.
- Price engine: standalone service that calculates effective price and exposes the estimator API to Console and SDKs.

Roadmap and milestones (timeline)
- Q1 2026: design sign-off for UICP; implement token nomenclature and small-scale test harness (owner: Eng Billing).
- Q2 2026: implement route metadata propagation in runtime and telemetry (owner: Eng Runtime).
- Q3 2026: billing pipeline changes: bundles, route-scoped discounts, and UI prototypes (owner: Eng Billing + Console).
- Q4 2026: pilot with 3 customers across SMB and mid-market for route-aware bundles; iterate on legal contract templates (owner: Sales + Customer Success).
- Q1 2027: GA with full billing export compatibility and SDK estimator (owner: Product + Eng).

Rollout plan (canary -> pilot -> GA)
1) Internal canary: enable UICP in staging and a subset of internal customers; run reconciler for two business cycles, verify variance <1.5%.
2) Customer pilot: invite 3 customers representing different personas (startup, platform team, regulated enterprise). Pilot window: 30–60 days with dedicated success engagement.
3) GA: enable self-serve purchase in Console, add documentation and migration guide, publish examples and pricing matrix.

Customer migration and support notes
- Migration path for Hosted to Dedicated: offer automated credit conversion, route export/import tooling, and a migration checklist.
- For Private deployments: offer a local price-engine release that can be run in air-gapped mode and a final reconciliation report to be uploaded to the Redwood billing service.
- Support SLAs: Sales Ops and Customer Success to own conversion disputes for the first 90 days after pilot signoff.

Success metrics and KPIs
- Reduction in pricing-related support tickets by 30% after GA.
- Average time to convert a paid Hosted customer to Dedicated reduces from 45 days to 20 days.
- Billing variance between runtime and billing ledger <1% in production for 95% of customers.
- Net revenue retention uplift via route-aware bundles for mid-market customers by 12% YoY.

Operational considerations and guardrails
- Default fallback: if route metadata is missing, fall back to tenant-level bundle application; log and alert owner team.
- Fraud detection: anomalies in token usage (spikes >10x baseline) trigger an automated hold and a billing review workflow.
- Backcompat: historical invoices continue to reference legacy unit names until archive cutoff (12 months).

Open questions and decisions to make
- Pricing alignment: should effective-price estimator consider GPU-hour equivalent to inform enterprise procurement discounts? (Decision owner: Finance).
- Refund policies: what portion of committed bundles are refundable in the first 90 days? (Decision owner: Legal + Finance).
- Private deployment reconciliation cadence: daily vs weekly for air-gapped customers? (Decision owner: Eng Private Deployments).

Next steps (action items)
- Product: finalize acceptance criteria for RQ-001..RQ-004 by 2026-11-30 (owner: Asha Patel).
- Engineering: create trackable tickets for route metadata propagation and price-engine API by 2026-12-07 (owner: Diego Marquez).
- Sales: select pilot customers and draft pilot contract template by 2027-01-15 (owner: Rina Sato).

Appendix: example CLI flows
1) Create route-aware bundle (example):
 redwood billing create-bundle --name "chat-reserve-100k" --tgus 100000 --term 12m --routes chat-low-latency --price 1250
2) Query effective price (example):
 curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" \n https://api.redwood.ai/v1/cost-estimator?model=open-llama-70B-qk8&seq=512&route=chat-low-latency

References
- See pricing catalog and token definitions in: /confluence/product-docs/pricing-and-packaging/token-bundle-flex-enterprise-metering-2026-08-20.json
- Related requirements: /confluence/product-docs/requirements/tenant-aware-cost-and-slo-management-prd-2026-11-01.json

Document history
- 2026-01-08: Drafted initial problem statement (Asha Patel)
- 2026-04-14: Added architecture and billing examples (Diego Marquez)
- 2026-11-15: Finalized roadmap and pilot plan; published (Asha Patel)

title: Evaluator CLI and Sidecar Plugin Spec
author: Ava Martinez
text:
Summary

This document defines the specification for the Evaluator CLI (evalctl) and the Sidecar Plugin Contract used by Redwood's eval harness. It formalizes command semantics, plugin manifest fields, telemetry expectations, failure modes, and rollout guidance for both hosted and private (dedicated/VPC) evaluator deployments. The goal is to enable consistent, auditable, and pluggable evaluators across teams and tenants while minimizing operational surprises during onboarding and mixed-precision/quant shadowing.

Goals
- Provide a single, stable CLI for running local, CI, and on-host evaluations.
- Define a minimal sidecar plugin API so third-party or customer-supplied evaluators can integrate with our shadow mesh.
- Surface required telemetry and artifact outputs for traceability, reproducibility, and automatic triage.
- Specify failure semantics and a safe rollback/stop mechanism for high-risk eval sweeps.

Scope and non-goals
- Scope: token-level and prompt-level evaluators, synthetic probe runners, function-call validators, and compact shadow probes.
- Non-goals: UI/Console integrations (visualization details live in product docs) and heavy-weight dataset catalog formats (these remain in prompt-sets-and-benchmarks).

Terminology
- evalctl: the evaluator command-line tool consumed by CI, local dev, and on-host runners.
- sidecar plugin: an executable or HTTP service that implements the plugin contract to run evaluator workloads in a given environment.
- probe: a single test case or input used by an evaluator.

Contract overview
- Protocols supported: stdin/stdout JSON lines; HTTP/JSON REST (v1); and gRPC proto v1.
- Manifests: plugins must provide a plugin manifest file (YAML) describing capabilities, resource hints, and artifact outputs.
- Outputs: all evaluators must emit a standardized results envelope and an artifacts index.

Evaluator CLI (evalctl)
- Primary commands and semantics:
 1. evalctl init --manifest <path>: validates a plugin manifest and performs a dry-run capability test. Exit codes: 0=ok, 2=validation error, 3=permission/fatal.
 2. evalctl run --manifest <path> --workdir <dir> [--slice <slice-id>] [--mode local|ci|shadow] [--concurrency N] [--telemetry-level minimal|standard|verbose]
 3. evalctl collect --workdir <dir> --artifact-index out/index.json --output <s3://...|gs://...|local>
 4. evalctl stop --run-id <id> --graceful/--force

- Example usage:
 $ evalctl run --manifest ./plugin.yaml --workdir /tmp/eval-123 --mode shadow --concurrency 4
 $ evalctl collect --workdir /tmp/eval-123 --artifact-index out/index.json --output s3://eval-artifacts/tenant-a/2026-06-01

Plugin manifest (YAML) - minimal example
---
name: functional-reranker-evaluator
version: 0.3.1
protocols: ["stdin-jsonl", "http-json-v1"]
capabilities:
 - functioncall-validation
 - multiseed
resource_hints:
 cpu: "2"
 mem_mb: "4096"
 gpu: "0"
outputs:
 results_envelope: "results.jsonl"
 artifacts_index: "index.json"
telemetry_endpoint: "https://telemetry.redwood.internal/ingest"
health_check: "/healthz"
---

Fields explained
- name, version: semver used for promotion gating. New minor versions require in_review and a rollout plan.
- protocols: enumerates supported IPC forms. Plugins must support at least one protocol.
- capabilities: free-form tags that the eval mesh uses for routing (e.g., functioncall-validation, kv-cache-sensitive, quant-aware).
- resource_hints: best-effort hints used by the orchestrator for capacity decisions.
- outputs: relative file paths in the workdir that the plugin must produce. See "Outputs and artifact index" below.

Sidecar plugin API (HTTP JSON v1)
- Endpoints and expected payloads:
 GET /healthz -> 200 {"status":"ok","version":"0.3.1"}
 POST /run -> 202 Accepts a RunSpec JSON, returns {"run_id":"uuid-v4","eta_seconds": int}
 POST /stop -> 200 Accepts {"run_id": ... , "signal": "graceful|force"}
 GET /status?run_id=<id> -> 200 {"run_id":..., "state":"running|completed|failed|stopped","progress":0.0}
 GET /artifact-index?run_id=<id> -> 200 returns the artifacts index JSON file

RunSpec JSON (stringified example)
{
 "run_id": "string (optional, auto-generated)",
 "slice_id": "string",
 "probe_manifest": "s3://.../slice-manifest.json",
 "seeds": [42, 7, 2026],
 "mode": "shadow|ci|local",
 "telemetry_level": "minimal|standard|verbose",
 "max_examples": 10000
}

Outputs and artifact index
- Required artifact outputs (placed in workdir/out/<run_id>/):
 - results.jsonl (newline-delimited JSON with standardized ResultEnvelope)
 - index.json (artifact index described below)
 - optional: html-report.zip, debug-traces.tar.gz

Artifact index JSON (index.json) - required fields (stringified example)
{
 "run_id": "uuid",
 "started_at": "ISO8601",
 "completed_at": "ISO8601",
 "results_file": "results.jsonl",
 "summary": "out/summary.json",
 "checksums": {"results.jsonl":"sha256:..."},
 "telemetry_digest": "sha256:..."
}

ResultEnvelope (one per line in results.jsonl)
- Minimal fields: probe_id, input_hash, output_text, score (optional), metadata (map).
- Example line:
{"probe_id":"anchor-003","input_hash":"sha256:...","output_text":"...","score":0.87,"metadata":{"seed":42,"latency_ms":123}}

Telemetry and observability
- Required telemetry events:
 - eval.run.start (run_id, plugin_name, slice_id, mode)
 - eval.run.progress (run_id, percent, sampled_latency_ms)
 - eval.run.complete (run_id, result_counts, summary_metrics)
- Telemetry must include stable identifiers: run_id, plugin_name, tenant_id (when applicable), and slice_id.
- Minimum metrics reported at 1-minute granularity: examples_processed, avg_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, failures_count.

Failure modes and remediation
- Validation errors (exit code 2): manifest or probe format is invalid. Remediation: fail-fast in CI; do not promote manifest.
- Runtime OOMs: plugin should write a tombstone file out/error_tombstone.json with reason and last N lines of stderr. Orchestrator will mark the run as failed and trigger an automated host-side capture.
- Silent drift (evaluation produces zero-length results): considered severity P1 for shadow runs. Automated triage will escalate to eval-oncall when the results rate < 1% of expected for two minutes.

Security and privacy constraints
- Sidecars operating on private deployments must honor tenant privacy: no telemetry outbound to hosted telemetry endpoints unless explicitly configured in the manifest and approved by privacy team.
- Artifacts containing PII must be encrypted at rest; index.json must include an encryption flag.

SLOs and gating for promotion
- Plugin correctness SLO for promoted validators: >= 99.5% successful runs on representative slices during a 72-hour shadow window.
- Performance SLO: median per-probe latency should be within 3x of the canonical evaluator for the same slice at promotion time.
- Safety gate: any run producing >0.5% hallucination-class failures on audited probes must block auto-promotion.

Onboarding checklist (required steps)
1. Create plugin manifest and commit to eval repo.
2. Run `evalctl init` locally and fix validation warnings.
3. Execute `evalctl run --mode local` on a representative slice and collect artifacts.
4. Submit a promotion request with telemetry links and artifacts.
5. Complete a 72-hour shadow run in the shadow mesh with `telemetry_level=standard` and provide the artifact index.
6. Product/ML reviewer and security reviewer sign-off.

Rollout and rollback procedure
- Canary rollout: 0.5% traffic -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with at least 1 hour steady-state per step for high-cost/nightly jobs.
- Rollback: `evalctl stop --run-id <id> --force` for active runs; remove manifest from routing tables and revert promotion tag.

Operational runbook (fast path)
1. Alert: "eval.run.rate-drop" triggers paging to eval-oncall.
2. Run `evalctl status` for top recent run_ids.
3. Pull artifacts: `evalctl collect --workdir /srv/eval/<run_id> --output /tmp/collect` and inspect out/error_tombstone.json.
4. If manifests were recently promoted, mark them as suspect in the promotion registry and roll back to previous version.

Ownership and contacts
- Spec owner: Ava Martinez (Applied ML Infra).
- Runtime integration: Runtime Serving team (eng-serving-runtime).
- Observability contract: Eng Platform (dashboards-and-alerts).

Related pages and artifacts
- Evaluator certification curriculum (link above) contains the reviewer checklist referenced in the onboarding steps.
- Example plugin implementations live in repo: git://internal/redwood/eval-plugins (see README/plugin-examples).

Appendix A: Example CI job snippet
```yaml
jobs:
 eval-run:
 steps:
 - checkout
 - run: evalctl init --manifest plugin.yaml
 - run: evalctl run --manifest plugin.yaml --workdir ./work --mode ci --concurrency 2
 - run: evalctl collect --workdir ./work --artifact-index ./work/out/index.json --output s3://eval-ci-artifacts/${GITHUB_RUN_ID}
 - run: curl -X POST $PROMOTION_ENDPOINT -d '{"artifact_index": "s3://..."}'
```

Appendix B: Example ergonomic debug workflow
- Developer: `evalctl run --mode local --concurrency 1 --telemetry-level verbose`
- If the plugin crashes, inspect workdir/out/error_tombstone.json, tail workdir/logs/plugin.stderr and open a ticket with copied artifacts and run_id.

Document history
- 2026-02-10: Draft created (Ava Martinez).
- 2026-04-01: Added telemetry digest requirement (Daniel Cho).
- 2026-06-12: Clarified artifact index and gated fields; moved security constraints to dedicated section (Priya Nair).

If you are implementing a new evaluator or integrating a third-party plugin, start with the manifest example and run `evalctl init`. For policy exceptions (exposing telemetry outbound from private deployments) contact security@redwood.internal with the exception request attached to the promotion ticket.

title: Saffron Stacksmith
author: Maya Chen
text:
Account overview: Saffron Stacksmith builds a VS Code extension for multi-language teams; focus on low-latency inline completions, stream-first UX, and per-developer rate limiting.

Recent activity / timeline:
- 2024-09-02: Intro call (Maya) — brief product demo, initial interest in streaming completions + model pinning.
- 2024-09-18: Follow-up: sent architecture doc + draft SLA (drive link).
- 2024-10-08: Prod demo with SE (Daniel) — validated end-to-end latency ~60ms median with hosted model; asked about 30-40ms targets. (FF-20241008-873)
- 2024-10-29: Security sync — SSO requirements, audit logging scope, retention windows discussed (FF-20241029-121).
- 2024-11-05: Email thread re: pricing commitment levels and burst capacity for peak coding sessions.

Use-case / requirements summary (from product + eng):
- Primary workload: VS Code extension providing inline suggestions & streaming completions for JS/TS, Python, Go.
- UX: streaming token-by-token updates to editor; ability to cancel/rewind suggestions quickly.
- Latency SLO: target 30-50ms per token for single-user requests; P95 < 150ms across team.
- Throughput: average 2-4 concurrent editors per seat during team coding sprints; spike handling for 150 concurrent devs across org.
- Model needs: prefer open models + ability to pin model versions per release (model versioning + rollbacks).
- Cost sensitivity: medium — willing to trade cost for latency for core product users; needs optimizer suggestions.
- Routing/fallback: automatic fallback to smaller quantized models on Dedicated or local cache if hosted capacity constrained.
- Auth / limits: org SSO (SAML), per-developer token limits, API keys for extension instances, clear rate-limit headers.
- Security: strong audit logs, configurable retention, EU data residency for subset of customers, KMS integration for secret material.

POC scope and acceptance criteria:
- 2-week POC (extension branch) that demonstrates: streaming completion with <70ms median token time, model pinning UI working, and basic per-user throttling.
- Security: SSO smoke test + audit log entry verification for sample sessions.
- Metrics: token-cost report and latency breakdown visible in console.

Quotes / call notes (shorthand):
- "If we can get token-level latency to ~40ms it's a product win" — Saffron CTO.
- "Need to ensure offline/poor-network behavior is graceful — fallback to local cached suggestions" — lead eng.

Open questions for Redwood:
- Exact semantics of per-user rate limits (burst vs sustained).
- Whether model pinning supports staged rollouts (canary) across extension versions.
- Data residency mapping for EU customers (which data is persisted).

Next steps (short):
- SE to deliver POC build by 2024-11-20.
- Security to provision SSO test account (pending).
- Pricing follow-up scheduled 2024-11-22.

CRM notes style: fragments, action items, links to drive + FF + jira. Keep concise for AE weekly sync.

Good technical alignment on streaming and model pinning. POC scope agreed; security gating SSO + residency. Pricing to confirm depending on Dedicated vs hosted mix.

Medium risk: heavy reliance on low-latency SLAs and EU residency. Potential competitor pressure from GitHub Copilot on price. Engineering lift for per-user throttles and local fallback could delay close.

Looking at mid-market commit (~$40k-$150k ARR) if POC hits latency + security gates. Dedicated capacity considered for predictable latency; Optimize add-on requested for cost suggestions.

title: Orchestrator session TTL and probabilistic splitter for model-version pin + rollout interactions
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Background: As teams run model-version rollouts (canary and A/B), interactions between session-level pinning, region/tier routing, and fallback model variants produce surprising behaviors: sessions bounce between variants when autoscaling triggers node reassignments, probabilistic canaries get skewed by sticky session caches, and tracing tools show mismatched version attribution for multi-request flows.

Problem statement: We need a routing coordinator that preserves developer intent for: 1) session-level pinning (a user/session should see the same model variant across related requests for a TTL); 2) gradual rollouts via probabilistic split or traffic percentages; and 3) deterministic fallback when capacity/region constraints force degrade paths. The coordinator must be low-latency, consistent across multi-replica serving pools, observable, and reversible (safe rollbacks).

Proposal overview: Implement an "Orchestrator Session Coordinator" (OSC) that sits in the routing layer and is responsible for: (A) assigning and persisting lightweight per-session assignment tokens (not full DB writes) with a configurable TTL; (B) applying a stable probabilistic split function for new sessions tied to a rollout id + salt; (C) honoring region/tier routing constraints and only choosing variants compatible with target SLOs; (D) exposing deterministic fallback ordering when preferred variant isn't available; (E) providing debug tracing and metrics (assignment entropy, per-variant request rates, reassignment events).

Key constraints: 1) Latency overhead must be <= 1ms p50 to not break low-latency SLOs; 2) The OSC cannot rely on synchronous coordination with a centralized DB for every request; 3) It must interoperate with existing session-cookie, API-key, and client-provided session-id inputs; 4) Support for VPC/private deployments where cross-region state sync may be limited.

High-level design: use a hybrid approach: a deterministic split function for first-touch assignment (hash(session-id, rollout-id, salt) -> bucket) combined with an optional short-lived assignment cache (local LRU + distributed sticky cache backed by Dynamo/Redis for hosted where available). The orchestrator will attach a signed assignment token (base64 + HMAC) to the response or include it in an update header, enabling stateless verification and avoiding DB hits for read-mostly flows. If the token is absent, the deterministic split is used. Reassignment occurs only after token TTL expiry or explicit invalidation by rollout controller.

Why different from prior work: Existing tickets mostly focus on affinity or sticky routing. This ticket coordinates three things: short-lived signed tokens (stateless verification), deterministic-first-touch bucket assignment for rollouts, and a graceful fallback policy that prefers in-region, same-tier variants but falls back by scoring compatible variants rather than naive priority lists.

Architecture components: 
- Router plugin (OSC) integrated into the Request Router service. 
- Assignment token format: version|rollout_id|variant|expires_at|salt|signature (base64).
- Deterministic split: 64-bit FNV hash over concatenated inputs, mapped into [0,1) then compared with rollout percentages. 
- Local cache: bounded LRU (configurable size per instance). 
- Distributed sticky cache: optional Redis cluster for hosted (TTL aligned with token TTL). Private deployments can opt-out and rely on tokens + deterministic split. 
- Fallback scoring: score = region_match*R + tier_match*T + model_compatibility*C + recent_error_penalty*E - latency_penalty*L. Tunable weights configured via console. 

Trade-offs considered: 
- Token approach reduces DB lookups but adds header size and slightly increases response payload. Acceptable for text API responses. 
- Full central store gives stronger guarantees for cross-instance stickiness but harms p50 latency. 
- Deterministic split ensures reproducible assignment without state but can't be updated retroactively; token invalidation enables forced reassignment. 
- For session privacy, tokens are signed and contain no PII.

Observability plan: Emit assignment events (assignment.created, assignment.reused, assignment.invalidated, assignment.expired) with labels: rollout_id, variant, region, tier, assignment_ttl_remaining. Add dashboards: per-rollout skew vs target, token hit/miss rate, reassignments timeline, fallback invocations.

OSC assigns initial variant deterministically when no assignment token exists
Assignment token verification succeeds and is used by router to maintain variant across short-lived sessions
Probabilistic split percentages observed in production match configured rollout percentages within 1% after 10k sessions
Fallback scoring chooses in-region compatible variant and falls back gracefully when preferred capacity is unavailable
End-to-end p50 routing added latency <= 1ms, p95 <= 3ms in canary environment
Metrics exist for assignment entropy, token hit rate, and reassignment counts
Migration path documented for Dedicated and Private customers (opt-out to tokenless deterministic only mode)

Design router plugin API and token schema (PR: core/router#xxxx)
Implement deterministic split module (unit-tested with edge cases)
Add local LRU cache and optional Redis sticky cache layer (feature-flagged)
Wire fallback scorer into route selection path and expose weights in config service
Add metrics/trace points and dashboards (console-team coordination)
Integration tests across multi-region simulator and latency-sensitive harness
Canary rollout to small set of tenants with rollback hooks

Phase 1: Feature-flagged internal canary in staging for 2 weeks with synthetic traffic and 3 real tenants. Phase 2: Gradual enable 1% of production traffic with automated rollback if reassignment rate > 0.5% or p50 latency regression > 1ms. Phase 3: Open to all tenants, configure token TTL default 30 minutes, console exposes toggle to switch to tokenless deterministic mode for Private deployments. Provide runbook for support to force-invalidate tokens per-rollout.

Unit tests for hash-split boundary conditions and salt rotations
Property tests to ensure deterministic stability across language/platforms
Integration test with simulated node failures to validate fallback scorer
Load test to verify p50/p95 router latency with LRU cache enabled/disabled
Canary e2e test that checks percentage distribution vs configured target

- For hosted customers, enable Redis sticky cache by default but allow per-tenant opt-out.
- For Private customers, default to token-only + deterministic split.
- Document API header 'X-Redwood-Assignment' and SDK helpers for reading/writing tokens.
- Provide admin API to invalidate tokens for a rollout id so we can force reassignment during emergency rollbacks.

2026-02-21 - Aisha Patel: Initial writeup posted. Requested input from console and infra on observability/cost tradeoffs.
2026-02-25 - Diego Martinez: Prototype for token schema implemented; discovered header size issues when prompts include large context — switched token to response header only.
2026-03-03 - SRE (Liu Wei): Suggested safety guard to avoid token issuance when instance load > 85% to prevent hotspotting.
2026-03-10 - Product (Marta Rossi): Confirmed rollout console UX requirement to display per-variant effective traffic and live reassignment events.
2026-03-14 - Diego Martinez: Integration tests passing in canary cluster; preparing PR for review.
