title: Replay hypothesis & breakpoint trace lab - Peregrine Commerce
author: Jordan Lee
text:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-03-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Daniel Wu (Redwood SE), Markus Feld (Peregrine Infra Lead), Sana Iqbal (Peregrine SRE), Liam O'Connor (Product), Aisha Romero (Security)

Summary (auto): quick hands-on lab to validate request replay, hypothesis-driven debugging using Console traces and breakpoints, discuss data handling and dedicated capacity tradeoffs.

Topics: replay workflow, trace breakpoints, KV cache mis-hits, error-rate triage, SOC2/KMS questions, dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs.

----- Transcript -----
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining. quick intro? I'm Jordan with Redwood, AE. Priya and Daniel from our observability team are on. 
[00:06] Markus: Hey all, Markus here, infra. We're focused on an intermittent 5-10% latency spike that coincides with some upstream timeouts.
[00:12] Sana: yeah hi, Sana SRE. we've got replay logs and a sample trace set.
[00:15] Jordan: perfect. goal for today is to run a replay hypothesis lab in the Console so we can exercise the exact request paths and show how breakpoints and trace playbacks help isolate the error clause. also cover data protection and dedicated options. sound good?
[00:24] Liam: yes that sounds great. curious about the dedicated pool sizing too.
[00:27] Priya: ok, i'll drive the console demo, show the trace map, then we’ll drop in breakpoints and replay a subset. fair warning transcription may spell some product names funny — e.g., the runtime shows up as Redwood Opti-mize in some logs, you'll see variants.
[00:38] [00:38] Priya: hopping into the Console now, i've loaded the request inspector view. you can see the request timeline on the left, each token timing, prefix cache hits — sometimes transcribed as K V cash — you'll see those hits/misses.
[00:52] [00:52] Priya: here's a sample trace where the downstream call to our recommendation microservice times out at ~280ms and then the runtime falls back to a smaller model variant which increases token generation time.
[01:05] Sana: is that automatic fallback? we thought fallback was only configured for canary routes.
[01:09] Priya: by default we have a policy that allows model variant fallback to keep tail latency bounded; can be disabled per route. you can see the policy in the trace metadata — it's tagged as "fallback_policy: smart_route_v2" but speech-to-text sometimes shows it as fall back police.
[01:22] Daniel: i'll point out the trace correlation id at top is the same as in your replay batch.csv — that's how we stitch logs across services.
[01:29] Markus: curious: when you replay, does it reconstruct KV cache state? we found cache warmup matters.
[01:34] Priya: good question. the replay tool replays requests but doesn't automatically reconstruct remote KV cache unless you enable prefix/KV recording and restore. we have a 'cache-priming' mode in the Console that will run a quick warmup before the replay.
[01:46] [01:46] Priya: ok dropping in a breakpoint at the downstream call boundary — look at the callout. breakpoint allows you to pause and inject a synthetic response so you can confirm whether the downstream timeout is the root cause.
[01:58] Liam: can you show the step where we drop in a synthetic 200 vs a slow 500 to see how the Redwood runtime reacts?
[02:03] Priya: yep. running first with a synthetic slow response — watch how the overall token generation stalls and then the runtime triggers the fallback. note the trace shows kv cache miss, and there's a small spike in token compute time.
[02:18] [02:18] Priya: now inject a positive synthetic response — that path completes under target SLO and no fallback. so hypothesis: intermittent downstream slow responses -> fallback -> longer gen time -> visible latency spikes.
[02:30] Markus: ok makes sense. is there telemetry to measure how often fallback happens and cost impact?
[02:35] Daniel: yes, in Console you get per-route metrics: fallback rate, average token cost, model-switch count. our Optimize tab will suggest quantization or batching tweaks to reduce cost when fallback increases token churn.
[02:46] Aisha: from a security POV we need to know if replayed traffic leaves our VPC or touches Redwood logs in a way that could include PII.
[02:53] Jordan: great point. short answer: hosted replay uses Redwood's secure path by default and you can enable customer-managed VPC for Private deployments. we keep replay payloads encrypted at rest and in transit; SOC2 docs give the specifics. i'll send the SOC2 + KMS brief after the call. transcription might show "KMS" as K M S or K M S key, just FYI.
[03:10] Aisha: and retention? we need to avoid storing traces with PII.
[03:13] Priya: Console has redaction hooks and we support on-the-fly PII scrubbing via regex rules before storing traces. you can also set retention windows per namespace; we recommend short retention for sensitive flows.
[03:23] Sana: for the replay, we can redact at source and provide sanitized traffic capture. we'll share that.
[03:27] [03:27] Priya: ok next, i'll run a 1k-request replay from your uploaded capture (name shows up as peregine_capture.csv in the UI, sometimes STT mangles it to peregrine). starting now, enabling cache-priming.
[03:40] [03:40] Priya: replay progress bar at 25%. you'll notice the Console logs list request-level timings; there is also a flamegraph view showing where time is spent: token decode, model forward, network wait for downstream svc.
[03:55] Priya: here at 42% we see a cluster of slow tails — grouping by correlation id shows it's the same downstream endpoint. i'll mark those as suspect and create a hypothesis filter.
[04:08] Liam: can the filter be exported to our SRE toolchain? we use PagerX.
[04:12] Daniel: yes you can export a list of correlation ids and timestamps as CSV. integration with PagerX via webhook is supported for alert enrichment.
[04:21] [04:21] Priya: small hiccup in demo video feed — sorry, my console had a lag.
[04:26] Jordan: no worries. while priya recovers, quick qualification question — what's your preferred deployment path? are you leaning hosted first or do you want Private/VPC from day one?
[04:35] Markus: we prefer hosted for initial eval but need VPC path by pilot. security needs SSO/SAML and HSM/KMS support.
[04:41] Aisha: yes SSO + audit logs are critical; also need to know where logs live.
[04:44] Jordan: we support SAML SSO, RBAC roles, and detailed audit logs in both Hosted and Private. for on-prem or air-gapped we provide a packaging option with customer-managed keywrapping. i'll attach the deployment checklist.
[04:55] Priya: back — replay finished. overall fallback rate was 8.2% in this run, average p95 increased by ~210ms on affected requests. i'm uploading the replay results and heatmap.
[05:07] Priya: drill into a slow sample, you can see token-by-token timing: token 1-50 are fine, at token ~73 there's a 180ms pause waiting for upstream. speech to text sometimes shows 'token pause' as 'taken pause'.
[05:20] Sana: is there a way to tune fallback thresholds so we don't flip to a smaller variant on transient blips?
[05:25] Priya: yes you can configure route-level thresholds: e.g., require consecutive failures N within T seconds before fallback. you can also set a latency budget to prefer timeouts over fallback.
[05:36] Markus: what about cost? switching variants increases tokens and cost, right?
[05:40] Daniel: correct, fallback can increase token consumption because sometimes the smaller model performs more decoding steps for the same output, and if you re-request you double-count tokens. Console's Optimize module will estimate cost delta and suggest batching/quant profiles to mitigate.
[05:55] [05:55] Priya: showing the Optimize suggestion panel now — for your workload it recommends enabling prefix cache for routes X and Y, and a 4x request batching window during off-peak. it also suggests switching one route from fp16 to int8 quant which reduces latency on T4-like infra.
[06:11] Liam: model quantization concerns the accuracy of outputs. have you seen regressions?
[06:15] Priya: we run A/B eval sets — Optimize shows expected quality delta. for many instruction-style prompts the int8 delta is negligible; we include a quality sandbox to validate.
[06:24] Aisha: will those evals or logs include our sample text? we need to ensure eval data is private.
[06:29] Jordan: evals run in a customer-scoped environment and data remains in your namespace — but we'll share the exact data flow diagram in the security brief.
[06:38] [06:38] Priya: ok switching to request-forensics flow: when you click a trace and choose 'replay with breakpoint', we capture a forked execution trace and you can compare before/after timelines side-by-side. it's handy for root-cause once you hypothesize a downstream fault.
[06:51] Sana: nice. can we automate alerts when a new spike pattern appears?
[06:55] Daniel: yes, there's anomaly detectors you can train on token-level latency signatures. they can trigger external webhooks or create incidents in PagerX.
[07:04] Markus: about dedicated pools — if we go dedicated, do we get pinned GPUs and guaranteed KV cache?
[07:09] Priya: Dedicated gives reserved GPU capacity and can pin model variants to instances for warm cache. you still retain the same Console and control plane; the difference is isolated capacity and predictable throughput.
[07:20] Markus: what's the SLA?
[07:23] Jordan: Dedicated SLAs started at 99.9% and we offer escalation paths for enterprise. SLA details will be in the dedicated contract appendix I'll share.
[07:33] [07:33] Priya: small demo tangent — i'm toggling a request to show 'trace playbook' where we attach a remediation script that can be triggered automatically if a breakpoint identifies a recurring timeout. it can, for example, re-route a route to a different region.
[07:47] Liam: interesting — does re-routing preserve session context? we need to ensure in-flight user conversations don't lose state.
[07:52] Priya: we preserve KV keys and session metadata; re-route is at the model-routing layer so the session tokens are forwarded. there are caveats for region-bound data, but that's surfaced in the playbook config.
[08:05] Aisha: about audit logs and evidence for compliance — do you keep immutable copies or can customers export them?
[08:11] Daniel: you can get an export; in Private/VPC mode logs can be shipped to your S3 or SIEM via secure connectors. we also support write-once retention for audit evidence.
[08:23] Jordan: quick pause for questions. anything else red team-wise?
[08:26] Aisha: just to confirm HSM integration for key wrapping?
[08:29] Jordan: yes, we integrate with major cloud HSMs and can support BYOK (bring your own key) for Private deployments. note in hosted we can offer envelope encryption with Redwood-managed KEK if that's approved.
[08:42] Priya: demo note: some terms in the transcript may appear as 'break point' or 'break point trace' merged, or 'KV' as 'K V'. apologies for STT artifacts.
[08:49] [08:49] Priya: showing final replay summary: 1k requests, 82 fallback events, p95 delta +210ms, estimated incremental monthly cost if unaddressed ~$4.8k. Optimize suggests prefix caching and raising the fallback threshold to bring fallback to <1%.
[09:03] Markus: can you reduce fallback while keeping latency SLO?
[09:06] Priya: yes: combine a slightly higher fallback threshold with preemptive cache priming and a short client-side retry window. that keeps SLO while avoiding model switches for single blips.
[09:17] Daniel: for the pilot we'd recommend a 2-week replay + live canary where we measure fallbacks and cost delta.
[09:23] Jordan: next steps recap: we'll run an extended 1k/5k replay with your redacted capture, share the replay heatmap, security brief, and pricing sketches. we'll plan a dedicated sizing deep dive if pilot metrics warrant.
[09:36] Liam: sounds good. Markus/Sana will assemble the sanitized capture and policy.
[09:41] Markus: yes we'll have that to you by Friday.
[09:44] Aisha: expecting SOC2, KMS, retention diagram from Jordan.
[09:47] Jordan: yep will send during EOD Thursday.
[09:51] Priya: final note: Console has a 'playback audit' view that shows who ran replays and which keys were used — useful for compliance reviews.
[09:59] Sana: great, appreciate the walkthrough.
[10:02] Jordan: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the artifacts.

End of transcription.

Artifacts referenced (links shown as placeholders):
- Replay heatmap: https://console.redwood.ai/replays/preview/ff-998234 (placeholder)
- SOC2 + KMS brief: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2-kms-brief (placeholder)
- Pricing sketch (dedicated vs hosted): https://redwood.ai/sales/quotes/CRM-998234 (placeholder)

title: Mixed-priority cgroup and soft-quota playbook for multi-tenant inference
author: Maya Chen
text:
Summary

This playbook defines a pragmatic, deployable policy and reference implementation pattern for enforcing mixed-priority resource controls on Redwood inference nodes. It combines OS-level cgroups, a soft-quota crediting algorithm, and scheduler-level hints to guarantee tenant fairness for bursty traffic while protecting latency-sensitive SLAs. The goal is predictable SLOs with controlled cost and graceful degradation under contention.

Scope

- Applies to dedicated GPU hosts and shared GPU slice deployments used for multi-tenant inference.
- Covers CPU, GPU memory residency, NVLink and PCIe bandwidth gating, and host-level network egress shaping where supported.
- Does NOT replace cloud provider-side hard quotas or hypervisor limits; this is an infra-layer policy implemented inside Redwood-managed nodes.

Definitions and terminology

- Soft-quota: a rate-style allocation enforced by token/credit accounting rather than hard kernel-level denial. Gives tenants temporary burst capacity until credits are exhausted.
- Cgroup profile: named resource envelope mapped to a tenant route or model variant (e.g., low-priority-batch, standard-realtime, realtime-guaranteed).
- Preemptible slot: runtime slot eligible for preemption when higher-priority work arrives. Clients may receive a retryable 429 with retry-after hints.
- Credit refill window: interval on which soft-quota credit balances are replenished.

Principles

1) Prioritize latency SLOs for realtime-guaranteed tenants; starvation-avoidance for all others.
2) Make policies observable and auditable: every decision must emit events and metrics.
3) Prefer non-destructive throttling before eviction.
4) Provide transparent billing signals: exhausted credits should generate usage traces and billing-affecting tags.

Service model and mapping

- Map inbound request classes to cgroup profiles at the edge ingress (edge-proxy or inference gateway) based on API token, route, or customer contract.
- Example profile names: realtime-guaranteed, standard, burstable, spot-preemptible.

Resource profile table (reference)

Profile | GPU share | CPU share | Burst credits per minute | Preemptible
---|---:|---:|---:|---:
realtime-guaranteed | 60% | 4 CPUs | 0 | false
standard | 25% | 2 CPUs | 100 credits | true
burstable | 10% | 1 CPU | 1000 credits | true
spot-preemptible | 5% | 0.5 CPU | 5000 credits | true

Operational invariants

- P95 latency for realtime-guaranteed must remain under 80 ms for 2kB prompt workloads under nominal load.
- P99 latency degradation must be limited to 3x baseline under accepted degraded mode.
- No tenant should consume >2x its configured long-term average without exhausting burst credits.

Soft-quota algorithm (summary)

1) Each profile has a token bucket: capacity (burst cap) and rate (sustained).
2) Requests consume tokens proportional to an estimate of per-request GPU time (token_cost = base_cost + size_factor).
3) When tokens are available, allow request and deduct tokens. When depleted, attempt polite throttling: apply queueing/backoff first (retry-after 150–500 ms depending on queue depth), then reject with 429 when queue > max_queue_len.
4) Credits are replenished on a 1s tick with leaky-bucket refill semantics; windows can be tuned per workload.

Cgroup & kernel-level controls (implementation notes)

- Use systemd.slice + unified cgroup v2 where available. For GPU residency/visibility we use Nvidia MIG or runtime-controlled CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES mapping. For non-MIG GPUs, rely on process-level CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES combined with per-process niceness and CPU bandwidth controls.
- Example cgroup layout (text description): root/rdw/guaranteed.slice, root/rdw/standard.slice, root/rdw/burstable.slice, root/rdw/spot.slice.
- CPU bandwidth values set with systemd CPUQuota= and MemoryMax= where applicable.

Example cgroup profile YAML (to be consumed by node agent)

profile_name: standard
labels: ["multi-tenant", "standard"]
cpu_quota_percent: "25%"
gpu_share_percent: "25%"
burst_capacity_tokens: "1000"
refill_rate_tokens_per_s: "16"

(node-agent will translate to systemd + token-bucket state on startup)

Preemption and eviction policy

- Soft preemption: first step is to stop accepting new requests for preemptible profiles and burn down queues. Provide clients with a Retry-After header. Emit PreemptionWarning event to tracing.
- Hard eviction: only when soft preemption fails for longer than 30s AND SLOs for realtime-guaranteed are violated by >10% over a rolling 1m window. Evicted sessions are checkpointed if runtime supports incremental KV-cache persistence; otherwise return structured error with model-invocation-id for audit.

Telemetry and SLI set (required metrics to emit)

- profile.request_rate (per-profile, r/s)
- profile.token_balance (gauge)
- profile.rejects_429 (counter)
- node.gpu_utilization (gauge)
- node.preemption_events (counter with reason label)
- request.latency_p50/p95/p99 (per-profile)

Alerting thresholds (recommended)

- SLO breach alert: realtime-guaranteed.p99 > 120 ms for 2 consecutive 1m windows -> page SRE oncall.
- Exhaustion alert: profile.token_balance < 1% of capacity for 5m -> create sustained-throttling ticket.
- Preemption storm: node.preemption_events > 10 in 1m -> create incident and auto-scale farm capacity.

Testing and validation

- Synthetic load: use the perf-harness tool with a mixed-profile manifest. Example CLI:
 rdw-perf start --manifest tests/manifests/mixed-bursty-50-30-20.yaml --duration 10m --trace=on
- Chaos test: inject CPU throttling (stress-ng) and GPU memory pressure (cuda-memtest) during a 30m soak; verify token balances and preemption events are emitted and SLOs respected.
- Contract tests: run end-to-end convergence tests in staging where billing tags, traces, and token accounting are validated.

Rollout plan (canary -> gradual -> global)

1) Implement node-agent feature flag behind runtime.flag.soft_quota_v2. Deploy to 2 canary nodes in staging.
2) Run mixed synthetic load for 24h and validate metrics/alerts.
3) Canary in production: enable on 5 nodes serving non-critical tenants for 48h with increased sampling.
4) Gradual rollout: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% of nodes, with 6h observation between steps.
4a) If preemption storm or SLO regressions are observed, auto-rollback to previous flag state.

Operational runbook (summary)

- Detect: Alert for realtime-guaranteed.p99 and node.preemption_events.
- Mitigate: Increase node pool capacity (scale up dedicated nodes) or temporarily reduce burst refill rates via platform API: POST /admin/quota/adjust {"profile":"burstable","refill_rate":4}.
- Recover: If hard eviction triggered, restart affected runtime with persisted KV-cache, and run postmortem with request ids (attach trace ids to incident).

Ownership and change control

- Primary owner: infra-scheduling@redwood.com (team: eng-infra).
- Secondary owner: serving-runtime@redwood.com for runtime integration.
- Any config changes to default profiles must go through CHANGE-FEATURE ticket and be approved by owners; large profile changes require a 1-week staged rollout and telemetry gating.

Security and privacy considerations

- Token accounting and audit logs must not include PII. Traces related to billing or chargebacks should be stored in restricted retention with RBAC.
- Ensure GPU-side libraries are up-to-date to avoid kernel CVEs that could allow cross-tenant leakage.

Appendix: Example node-agent CLI and YAML patch

# Apply a new profile
rdw-agent apply-profile --file profiles/burstable.yaml

# Query balances
rdw-agent profile-status --profile burstable --format json

YAML (profiles/burstable.yaml)
profile_name: burstable
cpu_quota_percent: "10%"
gpu_share_percent: "10%"
burst_capacity_tokens: 5000
refill_rate_tokens_per_s: 80
queue_max_len: 64
preemptible: true

Related docs and references

- See GPU fleet soft-quota eviction policy (eng-infra) for cross-reference.
- See ADR: adaptive-priority-fairness for bursting for background rationale.

Change log

- 2025-10-12: Draft created by Maya Chen.
- 2025-11-03: Added refill tuning guidance after staging tests.
- 2026-03-01: Published after canary verification and reviewer sign-off.

Contact

For questions or rollout coordination, contact infra-scheduling@redwood.com or open a ticket in #infra-scheduling on Slack.

title: Ephemeral CI-scoped API key provisioned to internal service after suspected credential-harvest form submission
text:
Issue summary: Security team detected an ephemeral API key issued by our CI system that was used to access internal billing metadata and a staging-only service. The key creation timestamp correlates with a high-volume external form submission to a third-party survey provider. Impact: Potential short-lived access to internal endpoints and metadata. No confirmed data exfiltration yet. Action required: containment, audit, and improved detection.

1) External form submission observed to service 'example-survey-provider.com' at 2026-03-12T09:12:30Z
2) CI webhook triggered a pipeline 'deploy-from-external-pr' which spins a runner and requests ephemeral credentials from internal token-service
3) Token-service issued a time-limited API key (scopes: ci:read, billing:metadata:read) to CI runner ID 'runner-17fc',
4) That API key was used to call /internal/billing/metadata and /staging/feature-toggle endpoints between 2026-03-12T09:13:05Z and 09:18:40Z

token-service audit: 2026-03-12T09:13:01Z issued key id=ephemeral-3c9a scope=ci:read,billing:metadata:read issued_to=runner-17fc origin=ci-webhook
api-gateway: 2026-03-12T09:13:05Z GET /internal/billing/metadata 200 key=ephemeral-3c9a src_ip=35.212.44.9 geo=LV
api-gateway: 2026-03-12T09:14:12Z GET /staging/feature-toggle 200 key=ephemeral-3c9a src_ip=35.212.44.9 geo=LV
ci-logs: 2026-03-12T09:11:58Z webhook-received payload_id=extform-98ab pipeline=deploy-from-external-pr referer=https://example-survey-provider.com/form/abc
vault-audit: 2026-03-12T09:12:58Z token_request path=token-service/issue method=POST authenticated_service=ci-controller caller=runner-17fc

2026-03-12T09:25:00Z - Aisha Khan: Initial detection from platform-telemetry alert 'ephemeral-key-unusual-geo' fired. Observed single ephemeral key issued then used against internal endpoints. Escalating to Security and SRE.
2026-03-12T09:33:12Z - SRE - Daniel Wu: Confirmed api-gateway logs show LV (Latvia) geolocation which is unexpected for this CI runner. Runner mapping shows runner-17fc is usually eu-west; investigating runner assignment service.
2026-03-12T09:47:40Z - Security - Maya Patel: Blocking the source IP 35.212.44.9 at edge and revoking ephemeral-3c9a. Recommend rotating any long-lived tokens associated with pipeline service account 'ci-controller'.
2026-03-12T10:05:30Z - Platform Eng - Ravi Menon: Revoked ephemeral key id=ephemeral-3c9a via token-service revoke endpoint. Confirmed subsequent requests with that key return 401. Adding temporary rule to deny k=/internal/billing/* for ephemeral keys until scope review.
2026-03-12T11:20:05Z - Security - Maya Patel: Noted correlation between high-volume external form POSTs (extform-98ab) and webhook payloads to our CI webhook URL. Investigating whether the external form contains malicious JS or if credentials were captured by a customer-facing form and replayed by attacker. Open request to vendor to pull raw payloads.
2026-03-12T13:02:00Z - SRE - Daniel Wu: We've quarantined runner-17fc images and disabled auto-provisioning temporarily for pipelines triggered by external webhooks. Creating detection: if token-service issues keys with unexpected geolocation in <5min window, create Sev1 alert.

Hypothesis 1: User-submitted form contained JS that captured a webhook secret or user token and replayed it to trigger CI pipeline. Evidence: multiple recent external form submissions with referer header pointing to survey provider and similar payload shape.
Hypothesis 2: Malicious actor automated submissions to the external form, causing CI to provision runners that request ephemeral keys; runner images may have been compromised or misconfigured to use different egress IPs.
Query run: gcloud logging read 'resource.type="api_gateway" AND jsonPayload.keyId="ephemeral-3c9a"' --limit 50 returned 4 hits between 09:13 and 09:18 UTC
Vault audit review: token-service logged request from authenticated_service=ci-controller; need to validate whether pipeline used correct OIDC claims. OIDC token issuance timestamps align with pipeline trigger times.
SAML/SSO check: No suspicious interactive logins observed for ci-controller service account. No long-lived access keys appear in Vault for ci-controller except for standard read-only tokens.
Risk assessment: Scoped ephemeral key limited to read-only billing metadata and CI read; nonetheless access to billing metadata could expose customer billing identifiers and usage patterns. Treat as potential data exposure until cleared.
Telemetry gap: No existing rule to flag ephemeral key issuance with geo mismatch vs expected runner assignment. Added detection backlog item.
Potential false positive indicators: Some third-party CI runners legitimately egress from varied IPs; need to cross-check runner allocation logs.

Containment: revoked ephemeral key id=ephemeral-3c9a, blocked src IP 35.212.44.9, temporarily disabled external webhook-triggered pipelines, quarantined runner image. Remediation: rotated ci-controller long-lived tokens, added a policy to token-service to reject key issuance for requests with geolocation mismatch, created detection rule 'ephemeral-key-unexpected-geo', and updated CI webhook runbook with validation steps (verify HMAC secret and payload schema). Follow-up: Security to request payloads from external survey vendor, SRE to implement runner provenance checks, and Product to evaluate whether external webhook feature needs additional user-facing warnings. Ticket status: In Progress — follow-up work tracked in INT-947613 (runbook update) and SEC-1245 (detection engineering).

1) Security - request raw payloads from example-survey-provider and correlate IPs and headers (owner: Maya Patel, due: 2026-03-14)
2) SRE - implement runner provenance check and block if mismatch (owner: Daniel Wu, due: 2026-03-18)
3) Platform - add HMAC verification and stricter validation to external webhook endpoint (owner: Ravi Menon, due: 2026-03-17)
4) Detection - implement rule in platform-telemetry to alert on ephemeral key issuance with geo mismatch and automated revocation policy (owner: Security Detect Eng, due: 2026-03-16)
5) Post-incident: schedule tabletop to review webhook exposure model and update external integrations guidance (owner: Maya Patel, due: 2026-03-24)

title: Automated stale-macro-retirement runner unexpectedly deleting active routing macros during low-traffic windows
text:
Issue summary:
The automated 'stale-macro-retirement' background runner removed a subset of routing macros that were erroneously flagged as stale during a maintenance window with reduced telemetry. These macros were still referenced by active autoroute bindings and resulted in routing failures for internal support flows and several internal agent jobs.

Impact:
- Multiple internal support routes returned 404-style routing errors (no matching macro) between 2026-03-05 02:10 and 2026-03-05 03:00 UTC.
- ~42 internal tickets were autoreassigned to fallback queues; some SLA calculations were delayed.
- No customer-facing outages, but internal escalation tooling and SLA reporting showed gaps.

Environment:
- Support tooling cluster: prod-support-1 (us-east)
- Template indexer version: v3.7.2
- Retirement runner service: stale-macro-retirement v1.4.0 (k8s cronjob)

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Simulate reduced telemetry by truncating last-modified timestamps for a subset of macros (test harness used in lower env).
2) Run the retirement runner against indexer snapshot with low activity window flag set.
3) Observe that macros with sparse recent-hit counters but with active bindings were marked stale and retired.

Expected behavior:
- Retirement runner must consult autoroute binding index and running queue references before deleting any macro; macros that are referenced by active bindings should be skipped.

Actual behavior:
- Retirement runner only consulted last-access timestamps and TTL thresholds; it did not consult cross-reference index because of a timing race where the indexer snapshot had not yet finished a partial sync. The runner then issued retire calls which triggered downstream unbind operations.

Immediate workaround applied:
- Disabled the cron trigger for stale-macro-retirement at 2026-03-05 03:05 UTC.
- Ran a reconciliation job to restore retired macros from the template index backup snapshot (index-backup-2026-03-05-01). Restored 38 of 40 macros; two macros required manual recreation due to concurrent edit conflicts.

Notes on urgency:
- P1/Sev1 because internal routing instability affects SLAs and automated escalations used for priority customer cases even though customer-facing generation remained unaffected.

2026-03-05 03:20 - Diego: initial triage shows retirement runner logs contain 'marked stale' events with no cross-ref check entries.
2026-03-05 04:00 - SRE (Maya Chen): observed indexer partial-sync spike at 02:55 UTC that coincides with runner start; likely race between index snapshot and runner. Indexer reported GC activity and truncated hit counter payloads during rolling compaction.
2026-03-05 06:10 - Eng (Ravi Singh): reviewed runner code path v1.4.0: early-exit branch when indexer health API returns 503 leads runner to assume stale state rather than pausing. Newer design doc required runner to backoff; config drift found in deployment manifest (backoff disabled).
Hypothesis: retirement runner triggers on TTL + last-access with no authoritative containment check if indexer snapshot is incomplete. Under low-traffic windows, temporary absence of binding references can look like staleness.
Telemetry gap: missing event that should record 'binding-check-pass' due to binary compatibility issue introduced by indexer v3.7.2 and the runner's client lib pinned to v3.6.x.

2026-03-05T02:11:04Z stale-macro-retirement INFO retiring macro macro-usrnotif-221 (last_access=2025-12-12T14:21:00Z, ttl_days=60)
2026-03-05T02:11:05Z template-indexer WARN binding-lookup failed for macro-usrnotif-221: 503 Service Unavailable
2026-03-05T02:11:05Z stale-macro-retirement ERROR binding-check-unavailable, proceeding with retire due to config.allow_retire_on_index_fail=true
2026-03-05T02:12:10Z autoroute-service ERROR route-eval failed: missing-macro macro-usrnotif-221
2026-03-05T02:55:31Z template-indexer INFO completed partial-sync (duration=00:03:24), reclaimed references=0

2026-03-05 - Asha Patel (Support): Filed after on-call flagged mass fallback routing. Noted that indexer logs show partial-sync and runner logs show retire without binding checks.
2026-03-05 - Diego Morales (Assignee): Reproduced in staging by forcing indexer partial-sync; confirmed that runner lacks safe-guard when indexer returns 5xx. Disabling cron and starting restore now.
2026-03-05 - Maya Chen (SRE): Restored macros from snapshot; two macros had concurrent edits and require manual verification. Will patch indexer to avoid GC during nightly windows.
2026-03-06 - Ravi Singh (Eng): Root cause narrowed to config drift in deployment: allow_retire_on_index_fail set true in prod manifest. Preparing hotfix to change default to 'pause_on_index_unavailable' and add binding-check retry/backoff. Draft PR created: support-tooling#842.
2026-03-07 - Diego Morales (Assignee): Hotfix merged to main and staged to canary (support-tooling v1.4.1). Canary passed 24h smoke; scheduling full rollout after runbook updates. Still monitoring metrics for unintended retire events.
2026-03-09 - Asha Patel (Support): Requesting runbook updates to add steps for 'disable cron + restore from index backup' and communication checklist for internal teams when retire events occur.

Change default behavior of retirement runner to 'pause_on_index_unavailable' and implement exponential backoff before proceeding with retire operations.
Add authoritative binding-check phase that consults autoroute binding index (with retries) prior to retire call.
Upgrade runner's client lib to be compatible with template indexer v3.7.x and add integration tests for partial-sync cases.
Update deployment manifests to avoid config drift: require explicit opt-in for allow_retire_on_index_fail and add CI gate.
Publish and attach a runbook: disable cron -> restore from snapshot -> manual reconciliation steps -> notify #support and #ops channels.
Run a one-off audit of retire events in the last 90 days to detect similar silent deletions (query: retire_events where binding_check_skipped=true).

1) Complete PR for hotfix and roll out to prod (owner: Ravi)
2) Update runbook and coordinate tabletop with Support & SRE (owner: Diego)
3) Perform audit query and report findings by 2026-03-16 (owner: Asha)
4) Close ticket after 72h of stable metrics post-rollout

Pending - mitigation implemented by disabling cron and restoring most macros from backup. Hotfix merged and canary passed; full rollout pending runbook updates and audit.

title: rerank-seedset-and-slice-strategy-briefing-2026
author: Priya Shah
text:
Notes and concrete proposal for generating a compact but representative seedset for reranker onboarding. Focus: pragmatic pairwise labeling protocol, stratified sampling quotas, ndcg baselines, and lightweight slicing to catch regressions early.

Current onboarding runs use large random samples which are expensive and miss rare failure modes. We need a small high-signal seedset (5k-15k examples) that: controls for intent distribution, surface-level difficulty, click-depth differences, and domain novelty. This doc proposes sampling rules + annotation schema + initial pilot observations.

Principles: 1) stratify on intent (informational, navigational, transactional, conversational), 2) enforce length buckets for queries and candidates, 3) force a 20% slice of cold domains (low training density), 4) include synthetic paraphrase clusters for robustness, 5) prioritize queries with divergent baseline ranks across models. Implementation: sample 10k queries -> for each, sample top-10 candidates from baseline model A and top-10 from candidate model B -> dedupe -> collapse to rerank tasks of 6 candidates average. Target final: ~12k pairwise judgments (approx 70k pair comparisons).

Quota draft (target=12k pairs):
- intent: informational 40%, transactional 25%, navigational 20%, conversational 15%
- query-length: short (<3 tokens) 30%, medium (3-7) 50%, long (>7) 20%
- domain novelty: warm 80%, cold 20%
- click-depth: first-page hits 70%, deep-clicks 30%
Notes: quotas are soft; sampling is two-stage (query stratification then candidate diversification).

Pairwise preference task: show annotator a query + two candidate results (title+snippet). Ask: 'Which result would you click or find more relevant to the query?' Options: A, B, No Preference, Both Bad. Guidelines: prefer direct answer to informational, and conversion relevance for transactional. Spotlight shallow heuristics (spam, duplicate, wrong entity). Include examples for ambiguity and edge cases. Time per label target: 12-18s. Gold set: 500 seed pairs with consensus >=3/3.

Labels allowed: A (prefers A), B (prefers B), Tie/NoPreference, BothBad, Flag: Unsafe. Metadata per pair (collected offline): candidate lengths, model-origin tags, baseline-rank-diff. For evaluation we collapse Tie into 0.5 split for ndcg ranking simulations and BothBad treated as lowest relevance.

UI: two-column A/B, highlight query tokens present in snippet, show source model tag, optional 'why' text box for conflict cases. Quality controls: hidden golds (from gold set), attention checks, and time floor. Compensation baseline aligned with previous pilots (target labeling throughput 180-300 pairs/hr per annotator).

We compute ndcg@k on inferred relevance scores from pairwise labels by converting pairwise wins into cardinal scores using Bradley-Terry scaling (fast approx) and also simple aggregation buckets: Relevant (1), Partially (0.5), Not (0). Report ndcg@1, @3, @5, and mean reciprocal rank (MRR) for intact comparability. Use bootstrap CI at 1000 resamples. Regression detection threshold: delta ndcg@3 < -0.003 flagged for immediate look. Reference: internal stat notebook (repo link in linked_artifacts).

Slicing dims (priority order): 1) intent 2) domain novelty 3) query ambiguity (annotator disagreement > 20%) 4) candidate-length mismatch (long snippet vs short) 5) presence of numbers/entities. For each slice we compute per-slice ndcg and pairwise win rates. Alerting: any slice with >1% absolute drop in ndcg@3 vs baseline triggers auto-issue creation (ticket template noted in linked_artifacts).

Pilot (1.2k pairs) run summary: average annotator agreement 0.78 (Krippendorff alpha ~0.62). Synthetic paraphrase cluster examples increased disagreement but uncovered 2 recurrent failure modes: 1) model over-preferences for copy-and-paste snippets (high lexical overlap but lower answer density) 2) entity hallucination in long snippets. Quick wins: add 'answer density' derived feature to slice monitor and expand cold-domain sampling to 30% for next round.

1) finalize gold set (Priya + Ethan) by 2026-03-05. 2) Implement parity UI changes in eval tool (Omar) - ETA 2 weeks. 3) Run full seedset generation job (12k pairs) once gold set done. 4) Add automatic slice alerting hook to evaluation pipeline (JIRA:RINF-1287). 5) Draft short doc for solutions-eng about what slices mean for customers.

Representative query examples used in pilot: 
- 'how to reset my router' (transactional, short)
- 'best running shoes for marathon training' (informational, long)
- 'github redwood inference api' (navigational)
- synthetic paraphrase cluster: 'reset wifi modem' / 'factory reset router' / 'restore router default settings'
Annotation edge case notes: when both candidates present partially complementary info prefer the one that answers the core intent.

Follow-on: explore active learning seed selection (uncertainty + diversity), consider pairwise-to-list conversion experiments, measure correlation between pairwise-derived ndcg and click-simulated offline metrics.

Internal refs: confluence:rinf/rerank-eval-playbook, prior pilot results at github:repo/re-ranking/pilot-2025, eval dashboard: https://console.redwood.ai/evals/rerank/seedset-2026

Forwarding MerchantCo alert. Customer reports 18% error rate + high tail latency impacting orders. They asked explicitly about cross-region failover.

Redwood Inference
From: hannah_schmitt@redwood.com

Triage notes (initial):
- Observed region: us-west-2 (AZ a/b) starting 08:47 PST; cluster p95 token latency jumped from ~210ms to 1.8s.
- Error class: transient 502/504 tied to KV cache thrashing and accelerated retry amplification; autoscaler shows worker churn and repeated model reloads.
- Cause hypothesis: a sudden shift in long-sequence requests from MerchantCo (their new batch job) with higher-than-normal sequence lengths + high concurrency caused KV cache eviction pressure; combined with a small regression in kernel path for our quantized runtime on a subset of instances.

Immediate recommended mitigations (actionable):
1) Route 20-30% of MerchantCo traffic to us-east-1 (canary) for 15 minutes. Monitor p95 and error-rate delta.
2) Increase KV caching window for MerchantCo on west-2 (config change) to reduce evictions; this requires a minor runtime flag flip (non-disruptive).
3) If canary shows improvement, gradually shift to 100% in 30m.
4) If errors persist, apply emergency fallback: pin MerchantCo to the latest stable model variant on dedicated pool (requires exec permission for priority pin).

Attachments: I pulled recent traces and a 10-minute p95 extract (p95_latency_log.txt) — contains timestamps and kernel-level errors.

Risks: cross-region steer may hit higher tail latency for other customers if their routing is dependent on west-2; network ACLs and VPC peering for MerchantCo are validated but we should notify their infra. Also a priority pin/eviction of other customers is a heavy hammer and requires leadership sign-off.

I'll start canary routing once Tessa confirms and Ops gets sign-off from account/leadership for the pin if needed.

-Hannah

Redwood Inference

title: Embeddings pricing heads-up and benchmark talking points (scratch)
author: Zoe Park
text:
Purpose:
- Scratchpad for an internal heads-up note + quick all-hands talking points about an embeddings pricing adjustment and a set of benchmark highlights we want teams to know before external comms.
- Keep this informal: notes to self, Qs, suggested phrasing for comms, and who to ping.

Context (short):
- Optimize shipped the new batching + cache profile for popular embedding workloads (dense-sim use cases). Perf tests show ~35% lower avg cost per 1k vectors and 20% p50 latency improvement in our hosted cluster.
- Finance/product want to adjust list pricing tiers for embeddings (tier thresholds + unit price) to better reflect lower unit costs and capture value.
- We need an internal alignment note for GTM, Sales Ops, Solutions Eng, Support, and SRE before any external announcement.

Draft internal subject line (options):
- "Heads-up: Embeddings unit price & benchmark highlights (internal)"
- "Internal: Upcoming embeddings pricing & perf summary — FYI + Qs"

Draft short email (internal) — option A (concise):
Hi all,

Quick heads-up: we’re planning to adjust embeddings pricing and want you to have the benchmark highlights up front. Early summary: new Optimize profile reduces avg unit cost by ~35% on common workloads and improves p50 latency ~20%. We’re proposing modest list price changes to reflect lower costs while preserving gross margin.

Why you should care: Sales + SE should expect updated quoting guidance; Support should read the benchmark notes in case customers ask about perf differences; Infra/SRE should expect a small config rollout window next week.

See details below + linked artifacts. Please flag any immediate concerns by EOD Thu.

—Zoe

Longer draft email (for product + sales ops inbox):
Hi product/gtm/sales-ops,

Working draft: we recommend moving embeddings unit price from X -> Y for volumes > 100k vectors/month, and adjusting the mid tier thresholds. Rationale: Optimize cost improvements (benchmarks attached) allow us to reduce price slightly while keeping projected margin.

Attached: benchmark notes (short), cost model (CONF link), internal quote examples for top 10 customers.

Open Qs:
- Final margin target from Finance (asked @Priya, awaiting reply).
- Should we grandfather existing customers for n months or do immediate migration? (Sales ops preference?)
- External comms timeline — do we align with the Optimize minor release next week?

Action items:
- Marcus: finalize cost model and recommended price points (due Thu).
- Priya: confirm margin floor and approval process (due Fri).
- Omar: prepare SE FAQ with two example customer messages (due Fri).

All-hands / Leadership talking points (30–60s):
- Quick opener: "We’ve made targeted infrastructure and runtime improvements to our embeddings stack. Early results show material cost and latency improvements for common retrieval and similarity workloads."
- Why it matters: "Lower per-vector costs mean customers can embed more content for the same spend, and we can offer more competitive pricing while protecting margins."
- Reassurance: "No customer data changes, no model quality change — purely runtime and batching/cache improvements. We’ll provide guidance for any pricing transitions."
- Call to action: "If you work with customers on pricing / procurement, review the GTM note and flag anything we should raise in leadership syncs."

Anticipated internal Q&A (quick answers):
Q: Are we changing model or model quality?
A: No — model checkpoints and embedding vectors unchanged. This is serving/runtime acceleration and smarter batching + cache.

Q: Will customers see different vector outputs?
A: No. Outputs are identical. Only throughput/latency and cost per token/vector are improved.

Q: Will this break existing billings / accounting?
A: We’ll do price migration logic in billing platform (Sales ops leading). We expect a small number of edge cases — Finance will run retroactive checks.

Q: Who should Sales direct customers to?
A: SE + Solutions Eng first, then product if there are product-level questions. Pub contact: solutions-eng@redwood.ai (placeholder).

Notes to self / rough bench bullet points (for inclusion in a one-pager):
- Test harness: retrieval-sim synthetic + two real customer workloads (legal-search, support-search).
- Metrics: avg cost per 1k vectors: baseline $0.011 -> new $0.007 (approx -35%). p50 latency: baseline 42ms -> new 33ms. p95 roughly unchanged for long tails; we should call that out.
- Workload profile: benefits concentrated on small-to-medium vector sizes with steady request rates (bursty workloads see less improvement unless cached).
- Risk: caching introduces potential cold-start artifacts; SRE to monitor cache hit distributions and eviction patterns.

Unresolved / open questions (TO DECIDE):

title: Lightweight session stabilizer with replayable shadow safeguard
author: Ayesha Malik
text:
Adds a lightweight session-stabilizer and replayable-shadow safeguard to the rollout controller to improve canary/A-B promotions for sessionful workloads. Motivation: our current staged-promote flow can prematurely promote model variants that break user sessions under slow KV-cache warming and transient routing skew; this PR introduces a non-blocking session quiesce probe, compact session checkpoints (snapshots), and a replayable shadow rehearsal mode that runs a sampled, synthetic replay of live traffic against the candidate model before commit. Key behaviors: (1) stabilizer enforces a minimum session-cohort consistency window during ramp-up to avoid split-affinity anomalies; (2) snapshots are compact (delta encoded) and stored in the rollout ledger so staged rollback can rewind to a known good session mapping; (3) replayable shadow runs on a fraction of traffic with deterministic seeding and preserves ordering to exercise session paths; (4) telemetry gates (latency, user-facing error rate, session-drop metric) are evaluated by the rollout engine and can trigger automatic backout with rewindable snapshots; (5) dry-run mode allows ops to preview snapshot generation and replay without altering routing. Implementation notes: added a new stabilizer plugin (stabilizers/session_stabilizer.go) and a compact snapshot serializer (snapshot/delta_serializer.go); extended the rollout ledger schema with snapshot metadata and retention hints; added a controlled shadow-replay worker pool with deterministic sampling and kv-cache warmup stalls to better surface regressions. Tests and validation: unit tests for snapshot compacting and stabilizer heuristics; integration harness that spins up a mini_shadow_rehearsal job and asserts deterministic replay traces against golden prompts; load-smoke e2e in perf-canary demonstrates no >1% additional p95 token latency overhead when shadow replay is enabled at 5% traffic. Backwards compatibility and rollout safety: the feature is off by default and gated behind rollout policy flags; snapshots use a new namespaced ledger bucket to avoid collisions; we included migration code that will be no-op for customers who do not enable the policy. Checklist: [x] design doc linked ENG-4021; [x] unit + integration tests added; [x] docs page and quickstart updated; [x] feature-flag gating; [x] added rollback playbook snippet. Related: ENG-4127 (telemetry gate tuning), SUP-221 (customer incident that motivated session regressions).

Jonah Park: Nice approach; can you clarify the cost tradeoff for retained snapshots? Suggest retention defaults and a TTL policy.
Ayesha Malik: Reply: snapshots are delta-encoded and capped; default retention is 3 revisions per rollout with 7d TTL; added config and doc note.
Diego Ramos: Request changes: ensure deterministic sampler uses global seed derived from rollout id to avoid cross-run variance.
Ayesha Malik: Reply: addressed, sampler seed now rollout-scoped; added unit and integration tests to assert determinism.
Priya Singhal: Approve after minor docs nits fixed.
CI Bot: All green after rerun of flaky e2e; merging when ready.

Introduce session-stabilizer plugin to reduce session affinity regressions during staged rollouts.
Add replayable shadow rehearsal mode to run deterministic, sampled replays before promotion.
Snapshots (delta-encoded) enable rewindable rollbacks for sessionful workloads.

title: Noise triage layers, synthetic canaries, and autoresolve playbook
author: Aisha Khan
text:
Background: We continue to receive noisy paging for transient region-level SLO blips caused by downstream cache thrashing and bursty KV-cache misses during heavy prefix patterns. On-call teams are burning cycles on alerts that resolve before human intervention, which lengthens meantime-to-ack and reduces trust in pager signals. Goal: Implement a multi-layer triage and mitigation system that (1) reduces human pages for high-noise signals, (2) surfaces high-confidence incidents requiring immediate action, and (3) automates safe short-term remediation (autoscale, circuit-breaker triggered load-shed, and synthetic canary reruns) with an autoresolve path when automated fixes succeed. This ticket covers the design and delivery of the alerting rules, synthetic canaries, runbook updates, and playbook automation for the primary production region and the multi-region failover path.

Pager volume for transient SLO Blip alerts reduces by >=50% during non-incident traffic spikes (measured over 14-day window)
Critical incidents still page immediately and have clear high-confidence predicates that bypass suppression
Automated mitigation (circuit breaker to load-shed + controlled model fallback) executes without human approval for targeted low-impact classes and successfully remediates >=70% of matched events
Synthetic canary suite reruns within 30s of an alert and flags regressions to a separate critical channel
Updated on-call runbooks documented with step-by-step playflows, and a napkin runbook for SRE-on-call
Post-rollout measurement dashboard (tokens-per-request, tail latency P99, page counts) published and linked in ticket

Step 1: Introduce two-tier alerting predicates: (A) noisy-suppression layer for low-confidence bursts using temporal hysteresis and correlated signal gating, (B) high-confidence layer that bypasses suppression and pages immediately
Step 2: Add short-lived auto-remediation actions: enable internal circuit-breaker to shed best-effort traffic class, scale a reserved node pool by +20% via autoscale API, and route a subset of traffic to model-variant fallback (quantized variant)
Step 3: Implement synthetic canaries: lightweight probe requests that mirror common prefix patterns; execute in region and cross-region; compare response latency and perplexity delta against baseline
Step 4: Implement autoresolve: remediation runs validation via synthetic canaries; if canaries pass for 2 consecutive runs (30s apart) then system auto-resolves alert and records evidence
Step 5: Update runbooks: add decision-tree for when to escalate to on-call, how to manually trigger circuit-breaker off/on, and post-incident remediation steps
Step 6: Safe rollout: start in staging, then 10% of traffic in canary region, then regional gradual rollout with rollback gates based on canary metrics
Notes: Must avoid mask-and-forget: every suppressed alert must create a hidden ticket/record with metadata to enable later analysis and SLG audits

Week 1: Design review with PM/Design/SRE, finalize alert predicates and canary payloads (design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SRE/ENG-84671+Noise+Triage+Design)
Week 2: Implement alert rule changes and synthetic canaries in staging; instrument new metrics (suppressed_count, auto_remediation_count, canary_pass_rate)
Week 3: Run 2-week dark launch in prod (suppression active but pages only to #alerts-suppressed channel), collect baseline
Week 4: Enable autoresolve for low-impact classes in a single region (us-west-1) behind feature flag; monitor for 72 hours
Week 5: Expand autoscale/autorem remediation cross-region and enable low-volume traffic routing to fallback models; follow with incident simulation
Final: Full rollout with dashboard and runbook training for on-call teams

title: RiverMoss SaaS Platform
author: Aisha Grant
text:
Mid-market product org building an in-product AI assistant + knowledge search. Trialed Redwood Hosted API for two weeks; primary objective was to validate latency and cost under realistic user traffic. Good integration velocity (SDK + streaming). Key metrics from trial: 2-week trial ~120M tokens, average daily QPS ~6, peak 35 QPS during business hours spike, median latency 95ms (us-east-1) for 1k-token responses. Token mix observed: chat flows ~30% of calls (avg 640 tokens total), embeddings/search calls ~50% (avg 600 tokens per request due to multi-chunking), reranking/short prompts ~20% (avg 120 tokens). Preliminary Redwood proposal suggests a 4-GPU Dedicated pool with autoscale for bursts; customer requested cost delta between reserved vs monthly flex. Pricing conversation notes: prefer 12-month reserved commit if unit economics are within 15% of Hosted API blended cost; want clear billing for KV cache/embedding storage. Security: SOC2 required, SSO/SAML integration mandatory, KMS for key management, and a soft requirement for EU data residency for EU customers. Open questions: exact traffic distribution by route (chat vs search) at GA, expected token growth per monthly active user, and retention/retire policy for embeddings. title: Lift-off SDK checklist + telemetry manifest (draft)
author: Aisha Kapoor
text:
Purpose:
This is a compact, pragmatic draft for a "lift-off" developer path for new SDK adopters. The goal is a 5-step lightweight flow that gets an engineer from signup -> sample app -> instrumented telemetry and to a first successful call in under 20 minutes.

Audience:
- Product engineers integrating Redwood APIs for the first time
- SEs running quick pilots with customers
- Internal bootcamp instructors who need a minimal reproducible demo

Constraints / design principles:
- Keep cognitive load low: one path that works end-to-end (happy path) before branching into advanced options
- Telemetry-first: every quickstart should include a minimal telemetry manifest so customers see usage and cost signals from minute one
- Language-agnostic samples (JS + Python, but single-file examples)
- No infra required: use hosted API and a tiny local server for callbacks if needed

Lift-off flow (five steps, concise):
1) Account + API key: short checklist (verify billing, region selection, basic quota)
2) Clone sample repo: `git clone github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-starter && cd sdk-starter`
3) Install & run minimal example (JS): `npm i && NODE_ENV=dev node examples/lift-off.js` — default prints generation stream and token cost estimate
4) Wire telemetry: copy `telemetry-manifest.json` into repo, run `node tools/telemetry-smoke.js` to emit events to the sandbox collector
5) Inspect console/console.redwood: see per-token latency, cost, and sample trace; validate output quality against the example prompts

Minimal SDK example (JS, single file):
(placed in examples/lift-off.js in repo)
- imports: `import Redwood from '@redwood/sdk'`
- call: `await redwood.chat.create({model: 'rwd-std-1', messages: [...]})`
- prints token counts + time-to-first-byte + inference-id for trace linking

Telemetry manifest (minimal required fields):
- event: sdk.init (api_key_hash, sdk_version, lang)
- event: request.sent (timestamp, model, route, prompt_hash, estimated_tokens)
- event: response.received (timestamp, inference_id, latency_ms, actual_tokens, status)
- event: cost.estimate (request_id, estimated_usd)
Notes: manifest should be a file users can drop into the sample repo. Collector is sandbox-only in the quickstart; production wiring covered in separate doc.

Preflight checklist for DX team (internal):
- [ ] Example repo builds in CI for Node 18 and Python 3.11
- [ ] Telemetry smoke harness added to PRs
- [ ] Quickstart page includes single animated gif showing 20-min path
- [ ] Error messages include clear remediation steps (auth, region, rate limit)

Acceptance criteria for a successful lift-off:
- user runs example and sees a generated message + token/cost lines in <20 minutes
- telemetry events appear in the sandbox console and are linkable to the inference trace
- README has one troubleshooting section with three top failures and commands to fix them

Edge / extras (optional sections to add later):
- Canary branch that swaps model to quantized variant when latency > X ms
- Local-mode runner for devs wanting no network dependency (uses small LLM shim)
- Mini-check to show batching benefits: run 10 parallel prompts and compare per-token cost

Open questions / TODOs:
- Which exact telemetry fields are PII-safe (we should avoid storing prompt text in telemetry by default)? Owner: Claire Z.
- Do we prefer `sdk.init` to be auto-emitted inside the constructor or explicit in examples? Trade-off: simplicity vs. surprise in production events. Owner: Miguel S.
- Do we include an integration example that uses Dedicated routing policy? Might be confusing in quickstart. Owner: Aisha K.

Notes to self (drafty):
- Keep wording conversational: "Run one command" > "Follow the instructions below"
- GIF should show dev running example, opening console, clicking a trace, seeing cost breakdown

Next steps / small backlog (first 6 weeks):
- Week 1: polish example code and telemetry manifest; add CI smoke tests (owner: Benji)
- Week 2: craft one-pager landing doc for onboarding flow (owner: Aisha)
- Week 3: record 60s walkthrough GIF + slate for docs site (owner: Claire)
- Week 4: publish sample repo, link from quickstart site, set up feedback collector (owner: Miguel)

Links / references:
- GH starter: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-starter (internal)
- Related Confluence draft: CONFLUENCE-UI/SDK-ONRAMP-1234
- Telemetry spec (WIP): GH: redwood-inference/telemetry-spec#12

If you use this doc: please leave comments inline in the sample repo PR and ping me in #devexp.

-- end of draft --

title: Link congestion profiles + tensor-slicing experiments
author: Diego Morales
text:
Purpose:
This note collects a set of microbenchmarks and end-to-end experiment logs investigating link congestion patterns when using tensor-slicing (model parallelism) and short-pipeline configurations. Goal: identify where throughput loss and latency spikes come from (NVLink saturation vs NIC/PCIe vs host CPU feeding), and produce a concise set of NCCL/env tuning knobs we can try in the runtime.

High-level hypothesis (prior to testing):
- Large tensor shards that require frequent all-reduce on gradients/kv-cache metadata will produce bursty NVLink traffic intra-node and stress the IB/NIC interconnect cross-node.
- Small micro-batches with pipeline stages increase the number of synchronization points and exacerbate link contention, leading to higher p99 latency even if average throughput looks OK.
- Properly sized slice/chunk + overlap of compute + transfer should reduce observed peaks and increase effective token throughput.

Hardware and software baseline:
- Nodes: 2x DGX-style nodes, each with 8x A100 80GB (NVLink mesh).
- Interconnect: Mellanox HDR200 (200Gb/s) InfiniBand between nodes.
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04 kernel 5.15 + OFED 6.x stack.
- CUDA: 12.1, NCCL: 2.18.x (build from source with MXM/UCX disabled and UCX enabled in some runs), PyTorch 2.2 nightly.
- Runtime: internal serving-runtime branch feature/parallel-shard-streaming (PR 412).
- Microbenchmark tool: nccl-tests (custom build), custom torchrun scripts to exercise tensor-slicing and pipeline stages. Profilers: nsys, nvprof for short kernels, and nvidia-smi dmon + nvlink stats via nvidia-smi nvlink -g 0

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Vary shard count (tensor-parallel groups): 1, 2, 4, 8 (intra-node hotpath).
- Vary pipeline stages: 1 (none), 2, 4.
- Batch sizes / micro-batch tokens: 1, 4, 16.
- NCCL config sets: default, NCCL_ALGO=tree, NCCL_ALGO=ring, NCCL_BUFFSIZE=1048576, NCCL_TOPO_FILE set (manual), NCCL_P2P_LEVEL=SYS.

Representative commands used:
- nccl-tests all_reduce: "./build/all_reduce -b 8 -e 512M -f 2" (ran with mpirun across GPUs to sanity check peak allreduce throughput)
- Launch model shards: "torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 --nnodes=2 --node_rank=0 run_shard.py --tp 4 --pp 2 --micro-batch 4"
- Profiling: "nsys profile -o run_tp4_pp2 -t cuda,nvtx,osrt torchrun ..." and short kernel captures with "nvprof --profile-child-processes --print-gpu-trace ..."
- NVLink counters: "nvidia-smi nvlink -g 0" polled every 100ms via a small loop to capture transient spikes.

Key measured observations (summary):
1) Intra-node NVLink saturation is not constant: we observed short peaks (100-400ms) where a particular GPU link pair hit 80-95% of measured max, then fell back. These peaks coincide with synchronous all-reduce boundaries from tensor-sharded ops.
2) Cross-node IB utilization grows with shard count and smaller micro-batches. With tp=8 and micro-batch 1, end-to-end throughput (tokens/sec) drops ~28% compared to tp=4 for same total batch because synchronization frequency increased.
3) Switching NCCL_ALGO to tree for large power-of-two group sizes reduced p99 latency spikes by ~18% on some runs (likely fewer hops and less oscillation in buffer scheduling). However tree sometimes lost peak aggregate bandwidth versus ring for steady-state large messages.
4) Enabling NCCL_P2P_LEVEL=SYS (force using PCIe+NVLink topology hints) helped intra-node performance when we set NCCL_BUFFSIZE to 1MB; without buffsize tuning we saw frequent re-chunking and transient stalls.
5) Pipeline stages: PP=4 with micro-batch=1 produced much higher latency variance. Increasing micro-batch to 4 reduced p99 but increased per-sample latency. There is a trade-off — for serving, micro-batch=2 or overlapping pipelined compute with async transfers appears promising.

Representative numbers (throughput and latency p50/p99):
- Config A (tp=4, pp=2, micro=4, NCCL default): 22.8k tokens/sec, p50=45ms, p99=210ms
- Config B (tp=8, pp=2, micro=1, NCCL default): 16.5k tokens/sec, p50=62ms, p99=430ms
- Config C (tp=8, pp=2, micro=1, NCCL_ALGO=tree, NCCL_BUFFSIZE=1048576): 18.9k tokens/sec, p50=55ms, p99=350ms
(These are end-to-end serving numbers from the runtime with simulated request arrival pattern, not raw nccl-tests numbers.)

Profile artifacts and what they reveal:
- nsys flamegraphs: clear vertical bands where many GPUs stall on communication syscall or NCCL ops. These align with all-reduce boundaries after an attention block.
- nvlink counter dumps: bursty TX/RX (per-link) with near-saturation windows during gradient/kv-sync points. Average link utilization was moderate, but variance large.
- nvidia-smi dmon: minimal sustained GPU SM idle during steady compute, indicating compute/comm overlap is roughly OK except around sync points.

Tuning checklist (what reduced issues in experiments):
- Increase NCCL_BUFFSIZE to ~1MB for our workloads to reduce re-chunking overheads.
- Try NCCL_ALGO=tree for group sizes >= 8 where p99 spikes dominate.
- Set NCCL_P2P_LEVEL=SYS and provide an explicit NCCL_TOPO_FILE to encourage NVLink-first paths intra-node.
- Where cross-node traffic is high, try UCX-based transport (NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0 with UCX enabled) and set UCX_NET_DEVICES to the IB interface.
- Tune model shard sizing: avoid too many tiny shards (tp>8) when micro-batch is small. Prefer increasing micro-batch for higher tp or introduce request batching at runtime.
- Pipeline overlap: implement non-blocking send/recv + compute/transfer overlap in our streaming runtime to hide NVLink bursts. We have a prototype in PR 412.

Failure cases and oddities observed:
- On one node we saw a persistent 10-15% throughput delta versus identical node (same firmware) caused by a single GPU reporting link errors; a warm reboot and firmware reflash resolved it. Keep this in our troubleshooting checklist.
- With NCCL built without UCX we saw worse cross-node behavior for small messages; UCX + tuned NCCL_BUFFSIZE improved small-message latency significantly.

Next immediate experiments (short list):
- Run a controlled IB-only stress test (ib_send_bw with the same message sizes observed in nccl captures) to validate whether IB fabric can sustain the observed burst patterns.
- Sweep NCCL_BUFFSIZE across 128KB..4MB for tp=4 & tp=8 to find sweet spot for our attention + kv-cache patterns.
- Implement a lightweight tracepoint in runtime around shard-sync to collect exact timestamps of send/recv completion (will allow correlating NVLink bursts to model operator boundaries).
- Try 'chunked' tensor-slice strategy where we group multiple small tensors into a single larger NCCL op to reduce message count.

Decisions and proposal for runtime changes:
- Short-term: enable per-deployment default of NCCL_BUFFSIZE=1MB and explicit NCCL_P2P_LEVEL=SYS for our NVLink clusters. Expose toggle in runtime config with rationale.
- Mid-term: implement async transfer + aggregation of small comms in the shard layer (reduce number of sync points).
- Long-term: add a topology-aware router that picks placement of shards to minimize high-contention links for hot paths (costed feature).

Notes to reviewers:
- These runs are reproducible on the lab cluster (rack-2). See linked_artifacts for PR and JIRA. The scripts used are under the PR; reach out to Priya for run ids and raw nsys captures.
- This is intentionally informal; the goal is to capture findings and next steps quickly. If we decide to standardize tuning knobs, we'll create a cleaner runbook for operations.

Unresolved questions:
- What is the safe universal NCCL_BUFFSIZE across all cluster types (PCIe-only, NVLink, mixed)?
- Can we detect at runtime when bursty syncs are about to happen and adaptively increase overlap?

End of file.

title: Tenant affinity hash compression collision routes production traffic to wrong region
author: Aisha Kapoor
text:
Production customer reported a surge window where a portion of their requests were routed to the EU region instead of their pinned US-dedicated pool. Root cause appears to be an affinity-key compression change that introduced hash collisions for high-throughput tenants. Collision made the routing comparator prefer a geo-neighbor region variant for a subset of requests, bypassing the tenant's dedicated capacity and causing errors and increased latency.

Between 2026-03-11T22:14Z and 2026-03-11T22:48Z, 1.7% of Customer A's requests hit EU-hosted variants. Errors spiked (502/timeout) and latency P95 increased from 80ms to 420ms for those requests. Alerting channels showed Dedicated pool saturation but routing chose region-fallback instead of queued back to dedicated or throttled.

Routing should preserve tenant-scoped affinity and respect explicit dedicated pool pinning. In capacity-saturated windows, failover should demote to compatible variant within same tier/region or apply configured fallback policy, not choose an incompatible region that lacks dedicated capacity.

Deploy the routing change that enabled affinity-key compression (commit 8f3b1a2)
Simulate 10k rps tenant traffic with repeating affinity hints to force hash collision probability
Observe route decisions in policy-evaluator logs (debug routing.trace=true) and compare chosen region/model for colliding keys
Verify that compressed-keys with identical 64-bit hash sometimes resolve to the same routing bucket across unrelated tenants

High — customer-visible errors and latency regressions for a production tenant with dedicated capacity. Potential revenue and SLA exposure. Affected both Hosted and Dedicated paths when the compression codepath is enabled.

A change introduced to reduce affinity-key storage (affinity-key compression) replaced full tenant+hint strings with a 64-bit truncated hash. Under high-throughput repetitive hints, hash collisions occurred and the policy-merge code used the compressed key as the primary lookup for affinity, causing cross-tenant bucket pollution and incorrect region selection in the presence of tie-breakers.

Revert the affinity-key compression rollout at service edge (hotfix revert of commit 8f3b1a2)
Scoped config: disable compression for tenants with dedicated pools via runtime flag routing.compress_affinity=false
Emergency scaling: temporarily increase dedicated pool autoscaling threshold for affected tenant to reduce visible errors

Rollback compression until a collision-resistant encoding is implemented (e.g., 128-bit hash or HMAC with tenant salt)
Update policy-evaluator to never use compressed key as sole affinity discriminator; fall back to explicit tenant-id when present
Add deterministic tests and fuzzing in CI to exercise high-throughput repeated hints and measure collision rates
Add telemetry: collision_count metric, per-tenant collision alerts, and synthetic-checks during canary rollouts

Merge hotfix that disables compression globally (hotfix/revert-affinity-compress) — roll out to staging then canary 10% hosts — monitor collision_count and routing correctness
After validation, roll to production in waves by region with pre- and post-deployment QA
Once new encoding is implemented and tested, enable for non-dedicated tenants behind a feature flag and increase coverage incrementally

Unit tests for policy-evaluator to ensure tenant-id supersedes compressed key
Load test with 50k RPS synthetic tenant using repeating hints to confirm collision rate is ~0
End-to-end test: create a scoped dedicated pool and verify routing never selects other regions during saturation
Integration test: validate collision_count increments only when intentional hash collisions are fed

2026-03-12 — Aisha Kapoor: Initial triage. Suspect compression collision. Customer A oncall reported sustained errors. Escalating to SRE + routing owners.
2026-03-12 — Liam Chen: Rolled hotfix to disable compression in canary; telemetry shows collision_count dropping to 0 for canary hosts.
2026-03-13 — Priya Desai (SRE): Dedicated pool autoscaler bumped for Customer A as temporary relief. Recommended revert for full fleet tomorrow.
2026-03-14 — Design review: routing UX should display affinity compression flag in tenant settings; product to prioritize in next cycle.

title: Kernel graffiti: morning quick-capture
author: Elliot Chen
text:
morning graffiti - quick capture (not polished)

Top-of-mind items to triage and experiment on today:

1) intermittent kv-cache poisoning on prod-dedicated-2
- symptoms: requests for long-prefix workloads sometimes fall back to cpu-path after 2-10s; observed TTL spike and cache miss storm.
- quick repro attempt: replay trace RW-20260311-1442 (from RW-2987). local dev repro with --seq-len=1024 + synthetic prefix hits 40% miss for key shards 3..5.
- hypothesis: race between async cache writeback and eviction thread when batch flush > threshold (16MB). eviction logic uses LRU but metadata updates not multi-thread safe under high append.
- immediate mitigation: lower async_batch_flush_ms to 20ms on dedicated-2 pool (canary) + throttle concurrent writes.
- TODO: add stricter atomic update path in cache metadata (Rajiv) — small patch to use per-shard mutexes (see PR #542). follow up perf cost.

2) micro-batching oddness on short-lived routes (chat-streaming)
- observed: batching window sometimes collapses to 1 when concurrent_senders spikes briefly even though target batch_size=8.
- notes: suspect poor window warmup with rapid open/close patterns (mobile clients).
- experiment plan: implement exponential backoff for window shrinkage instead of immediate collapse (Aisha to pair). write quick flag feature gate 'microbatch-soft-shrink'.
- measurement: add histogram for effective batch sizes over 24h and compare route /v1/chat-stream vs /v1/generate.

3) tail latency debugging checklist
- gather traces (x-ray) for top-5 tail traces last 2 hours: ids RW-TL-3409, RW-TL-3412, RW-TL-3417.
- check kernel preemption logs: kernel-sched* events around timestamps. look for CPU steal or GPU context switch thrash.
- check model-compile fallsbacks (quantized->fp16) that increase kernel launch time. add a label in traces if fallback occurred.

4) adhoc perf microbench notes
- run ./bench/micro_batch --model small-llama --batch 1..16 --seq 256 repeat 10, collect p50/p95/p99. attach csv to RW-2987.
- add a toggled path to disable 'prefetch_kv' and compare throughput — hypothesis: prefetch helps for long sequences but harms very short seq due to extra memcpy.

5) small triage items (one-liners)
- investigate noisy gc logs on worker-45 (likely python wrapper leak). quick grep: last restart 2026-03-11T03:12Z.
- add alert: 'kv-cache-miss-rate > 5% for 5m' to console (temp).
- clarify SLA fallback policy doc: which model variants are allowed to serve when dedicated exhausted? follow up with product console team.

6) experiments I want to try this week (note to self)
- adaptive batch sizing: dynamic target batch based on route latency SLO and current queue depth. simulate using loadgen.
- compact metadata encoding for kv-cache (8->6 bytes) to reduce memory churn. prototype in a branch and measure gc.
- try a tiny per-request path that avoids scheduler for ultra-low-latency routes (bypass pool) — measure cost of lost packing.

7) meeting talking points for 10:30 sync with SRE and infra
- rolling canary for async_batch_flush_ms change: plan, rollback, metrics to watch.
- potential impact on memory pressure if we reduce flush interval (more frequent smaller writes) — need to track wall-clock memory usage.
- request: allocate 2 extra p3 nodes for a controlled soak of microbatch-soft-shrink.

8) random thoughts / unresolved questions
- if we make cache metadata updates lock-free using CAS, will we still hit ABA with recycled entries? need safe epoch-based reclamation.
- would prefix-aware batching (grouping requests by shared first k tokens) improve hit rate significantly? how much overhead to compute signatures at ingress?

CLI commands I ran this morning (paste for reproducibility):
- ./scripts/trace-fetch rw-20260311-1442 --out traces/20260311-1442.json
- jq '.events[] | select(.type=="kv")' traces/20260311-1442.json | head -n 100
- docker exec -it runtime-worker-45 /bin/bash -c 'grep -i oom /var/log/runtime/*.log || true'

Next immediate actions (today):
- ping Rajiv about PR #542 and schedule 30m pair to review mutex approach (Elliot)
- flip microbatch-soft-shrink feature gate in staging and gather 2h histograms (Aisha)
- open small doc for 'cache-atomicity-proposal' and link to RW-2987 (Elliot)
- add transient alert to console for kv miss rate (SRE)

Notes to self: keep these scratchy, move actionable items to tickets asap. this file is my rapid capture; might prune and push to confluence later.

-- E.C.

Helio Health, Inc.
Addendum to Master Services Agreement Inference Request Log Retention

Effective Date: 2025-06-05
Parties: Redwood Inference, Inc. (Provider) and Helio Health, Inc. (Customer)

1. Definitions
Inference Request Logs means logs that may include prompt and completion text (payload) and associated request metadata (timestamps, model id, token counts, latency, status code).

Notwithstanding any default retention settings, Provider agrees to the following for Customers Hosted API usage in the EU region (eu-west):

- Payload (prompt + completion) retention: Seven (7) days
- Metadata-only retention: Ninety (90) days

3. Deletion
Provider will delete payload logs on a rolling basis such that payload logs older than seven (7) days are no longer available in Providers log storage systems for Customer.

All other terms of the Agreement remain in effect.

Helio Health, Inc.: /s/ Dana Lowell
