domain: 日常协作与非结构化讨论
title: eng-platform
text:
Maya: quick heads-up, observability noticed a recurring cost delta for traces that hit late-enrich. graph shows cohorts A/B diverging after enrichment windows :eyes:
Kevin: can you paste the query/agg window?
Maya: yeah — simplified: 
```
select cohort_id, sum(cost) from traces
where ingested_at >= now() - interval '7 days'
group by cohort_id
```
but the delta appears only when we call external tenant-lookup during enrichment (late join).
Sam: this sounds like the classic "billing key appears late" problem. when we enrich late we either retro-fix rows (expensive) or we attribute to a fallback bucket. which are we doing now?
Maya: currently fallback -> "unknown" bucket, then a reconciliation job tries to patch once billing lookup succeeds. patch success rate ~70% and the rest stays unknown.
Irene: unknown bucket is causing product chargeback mismatch for a handful of large tenants. finance flagged it.
Kevin: what's the root cause? race in edge vs enrich? or missing id to match later?
Maya: mostly missing stable join keys — edge proxies don't always forward customer_id; sometimes we only have ephemeral session_id. late-lookup uses session->account mapping and that lookup fails for older sessions.
Sam: proposal: add a provisional_billing_key to envelope as soon as edge sees any hint, with a TTL and a provenance tag. then reconcile with authoritative key later if available. that way queries can optionally prefer provisional keys for near-real-time cost routing but opt-out for final billing. tradeoffs: more cardinality and a potential small delta due to provisional misassigns.
Irene: cardinality concern is real. can we compress by emitting a cohort fingerprint instead of full tenant id? finance needs real tenant ids for chargeback, though.
Kevin: we could do a two-tier approach: provisional_cohort (low-card) + final_billing_id (nullable). realtime dashboards use cohort, billing uses patched final id post-reconcile. reduces O(1) blowup in real-time indexing.
Sam: sounds reasonable. adds complexity: query layer needs to join provisional->final mapping during historical queries. we'd also need a stable reconciliation log so backfills are deterministic.
Maya: here's a minimal envelope change I sketched:
```
"envelope": {
 "trace_id": "...",
 "provisional_billing_key": "acct:123||cohort:v2",
 "provisional_ttl": 86400,
 "final_billing_key": null,
 "billing_provenance": "edge-probe-v1"
}
```
we'd only add ~12-40 bytes per envelope typical.
Irene: can we avoid adding fields on every envelope by sending a separate lightweight "provisional-key" event for the trace_id? that lessens schema churn for storage engines that pay per-field.
Sam: separate event helps storage but complicates ingest ordering — we need to guarantee the provisional event arrives before any aggregation consumes the trace. that adds backpressure requirements.
Kevin: ordering can be solved by weak-consistency: if aggregation doesn't see key, it marks as soft-missing and defers finalization for X seconds. But we already do deferred finalization for other reasons.
Maya: ops and ingestion folks: ingest-bot shows recent enrollments — we could canary this by rolling provisional_key only for traffic tagged "experiment/prov-billing". low-risk. @ingest-bot what does rollout look like?
ingest-bot: canary path available. we can route 2% of edge traffic with injection flag. backfill workers can be throttled.
Sam: testing plan: 1) RFC with schema + reconciliation contract 2) infra canary for 2% 3) reconcile job run daily for canary cohort 4) validate finance reports against gold source.
Kevin: perf/cost estimate? more fields => index size up ~1.5% for canary. reconciliation job cost negligible relative to impact.
Irene: finance acceptance criteria: discrepancy <0.1% and no tenant sees undercharge window > 24h.
Maya: action items: Sam to write RFC, Kevin to prototype query join helper, Maya to run small canary once infra flags are ready. timeline: RFC by next Wed, canary in ~2 weeks.
Sam: noted — I'll open the RFC and link it here when ready.
Kevin: +1. also let's add a small explainer for SRE on failure modes.
Irene: :thumbsup:
Maya: thanks all — tagging product ops to keep finance in the loop. linking doc when RFC lands.

title: POC workload throughput patterns & autoscale playbook - Orchid Labs
author: Eleanor Park
text:
[Header]
Date: 2026-06-12 16:00 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Eleanor Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Liu (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Orchid Head of ML), Lina Gomez (Orchid SRE), Tom Reed (Orchid CTO), Cindy Zhao (Orchid Product)

Summary:
Quick POC scoping focused on sizing reserved GPU pool, defining burst strategy to Redwood hosted for peaks, and fallback policies to smaller/quantized variants. Agreed on concrete success criteria (latency SLOs, throughput targets, and cost envelope) and next steps to run a benchmark in staging.

Topics:
- Current LLM workload profile and sequence length distributions
- Concurrency targets and p95 latency SLOs
- Reserved capacity sizing and autoscale rules with burst to hosted
- Fallback model variants and canary policy for degraded capacity
- Security and data residency concerns for POC
- Timeline and deliverables for load test

Transcript body:
00:00:05 Eleanor: all right everyone thanks for joining — we got about an hour — Um quick roll call?
00:00:11 Samir: hi Samir here, Lina here, Tom and Cindy are on. audio a little spotty for Tom.
00:00:18 Eleanor: great, Marcus and Priya from my side, Marcus will run the technical bits. Goal today is to size the reserved GPU commit for your two-week POC and define autoscale/burst fallback rules.
00:00:32 Marcus: hi hi, quick agenda: workload profile, bench metrics, sizing, fallback/modes, and final checklist.
00:00:41 Cindy: perfect — we're very focused on minimizing latency for end users and keeping costs under our existing internal target — so tradeoffs matter.
00:00:48 Marcus: sure — maybe start with current traffic. Samir can you share typical qps, avg tokens, and peak windows?
00:00:55 Samir: yeah so our production calls are... uh two main features: short prompts (search rerank + snippet gen) avg 18 tokens, and long summarization up to 1,200 tokens but that only ~5% of calls. baseline traffic today is ~120 rps, peak around 420 rps during batch jobs or marketing pushes. concurrency per user thread is low, but aggregate concurrency is high during spikes.
00:01:25 Priya: when you say 420 rps is that across all endpoints?
00:01:29 Samir: yes across endpoints; rerank is most frequent — we also have scheduled bulk jobs at 3am causing sustained bursts.
00:01:36 Lina: to add, our 95th percentile latency target is 350 ms for short prompts, and 2s for long ones. Cost goal is to not increase inference ops spend more than 15% during the POC.
00:01:48 Marcus: ok good. For sizing we map to tokens/sec and model perf. Which model family are you testing?
00:01:55 Samir: we were planning to try the open-1.4 variants you recommended last week, plus a quantized 8-bit fallback. some references called it 'open-1.4-q8' or RW-1-4 in notes, so apologies if names are off.
00:02:08 Marcus: no worries, names often get munged by calendar notes. We'll benchmark a baseline FP16 variant and a q8 variant. For throughput numbers we need average sequence length histogram and request groups — can you share a sample day CSV?
00:02:20 Samir: yes, we'll attach that.
00:02:23 Marcus: mechanistically, for reserved capacity we recommend sizing for sustained baseline plus buffer: i.e., baseline sustained 120 rps -> token/s calc: 120 rps * 18 tokens = 2160 tokens/sec for short path; long path adds occasional load. A single A100-equivalent GPU in our tests handled ~9k tokens/sec for this model in FP16 under steady state with concurrency tuned. So a conservative reserved pool of 1-2 GPUs covers baseline with headroom.
00:02:50 Tom: does that account for KV cache memory and prefix caching? we do a lot of chat-like interactions with long context windows.
00:02:58 Marcus: good call — yes the throughput numbers assume KV cache hits for incremental tokens; very long sequences increase memory pressure and lower effective throughput. If your usage skews long, we factor that with per-session state sizing which could move you to 2-3 GPUs reserved.
00:03:14 Lina: for the POC we only need to cover 80% of expected peaks with reserved, and rely on burst to hosted for the extreme ~20%. we prefer that to buying extra reserved capacity.
00:03:23 Eleanor: that's a common pattern — reserved for predictable load, burst to hosted Redwood pools for spikes, with automatic fallback to quantized variants when hosted is saturated. we need to define the autoscale triggers and fallback order.
00:03:35 Marcus: rule proposal: keep reserved pool sized to baseline + 30% buffer. Autoscale policy: if queued requests > 60s or CPU/GPU util > 85% for >30s, allow burst to hosted up to X instances; then if hosted pool also saturated, fallback to q8 model variant with same routing.
00:03:51 Cindy: how do you estimate cost during burst? our finance team will ask.
00:03:55 Eleanor: we'll send a burst worksheet that models per-token cost across reserved vs hosted vs q8 fallback; you can plug in your traffic histogram. We'll also show cost delta if you choose to reserve 2 GPUs vs 1.
00:04:06 Marcus: one nuance: bursts to hosted preserve request ordering but may increase tail latency. for very latency-sensitive short prompts, we can configure a policy to prefer local reserved first and only burst non-critical endpoints.
00:04:19 Samir: can we do per-route policies? e.g., rerank stays local, summarization can burst.
00:04:23 Marcus: absolutely — Redwood routing supports per-route weight and per-model fallback lists. We'll propose a mapping: rerank -> local-only until util>90% then host fallback; summary -> allow immediate burst.
00:04:36 Tom: what about canary/failback if model version has quality regression on q8? we can't expose users to broken outputs.
00:04:42 Priya: we recommend a canary pass: route 5% traffic to q8 variants for short window and run quick evals comparing embed/semantic drift with a small prompt set. If metrics exceed threshold, auto-failback to FP16 or route to hosted FP16. Redwood Optimize can run these regressions during the POC.
00:04:59 Samir: how long to set the canary window?
00:05:02 Priya: for POC, 10-30 minutes is typical to get statistically useful signals for short prompts. we'll pick a small eval set you provide.
00:05:11 Lina: network/cloud egress for burst — data residency? Our data classification says customer PII cannot leave VPC without DPA. That might block bursting to hosted.
00:05:21 Eleanor: noted — if PII or regulated traffic can't leave your VPC, we can still support burst if you allow redaction or client-side de-ident; otherwise we'll need to run burst to a dedicated private pool (Redwood Dedicated) which is pricier. For POC we can scope a subset of traffic that is non-PII for burst tests.
00:05:39 Cindy: ok we'll identify a non-PII slice.
00:05:42 Marcus: another fallback is to run a smaller quantized model inside your private deployment; that keeps data in VPC but requires we provision extra reserve GPUs. Tradeoff between security and incremental cost.
00:05:53 Tom: what about pre-warming and cold-starts during sudden peaks?
00:05:58 Marcus: we do continuous batching and pre-warm policies. cold-starts are mostly a problem with auto-scaler bringing new nodes up; Redwood's burst uses a warm pool in hosted infra to reduce cold-start time to ~200-400ms for small models; larger models might be 600-1,200ms. For strict p95 350ms short prompt SLO we should ensure warm pool or route to reserved.
00:06:18 Samir: ok that means for rerank route we must keep warm pool local or require strict reserved.
00:06:22 Eleanor: yes. We'll enumerate per-route settings in the workbook.
00:06:26 Marcus: on metrics we will capture p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and cost per 1M tokens. We'll also track model output quality deltas for canary.
00:06:36 Priya: for the benchmark runner we'll use a replay of your sample traffic with synthetic timing and interleaving. Marcus will send a script; we recommend run lengths of 30-90 minutes to capture variance.
00:06:47 Samir: what about session affinity? our application pins session state to a user, so if routed across different nodes we need sticky KV cache or it increases token costs.
00:06:56 Marcus: good point. We can enable session affinity on the routing layer for duration of a session, and Redwood's KV cache can be sharded. That reduces duplicated context transmission. sticky routing adds slight load imbalance but usually worth it.
00:07:08 Lina: okay, timeline — we'd like to run the POC load test week of 6/22 and have results the following week. Is that feasible?
00:07:15 Eleanor: yes, if we get the sample traffic and staging access by 6/16 we can run tests 6/22 and share results by 6/24. That fits a two-week POC cycle.
00:07:23 Marcus: action items: Marcus send bench runner, Eleanor send pricing/burst worksheet, Samir provide traffic CSV.
00:07:29 Samir: noted.
00:07:31 Tom: security docs — please send SOC2 summary and network diagram for private option.
00:07:36 Eleanor: we'll attach the SOC2 summary and our private deployment checklist.
00:07:40 Priya: small technical aside on fallback ordering: recommended order is reserved FP16 -> hosted FP16 -> hosted q8 -> local q8 (if private allowed) -> degrade to cached responses or partial result if all else fails.
00:07:53 Cindy: partial results would be acceptable only for batch jobs, not live user interactions.
00:07:57 Marcus: noted — we'll include an explicit degrade policy per route.
00:08:02 Samir: any recommended monitoring thresholds to avoid thrashing?
00:08:06 Marcus: yes — hysteresis is important: require nat > threshold for 30s and cool-down of 60s before reversing. Also use rolling 1-minute averages for utilization.
00:08:15 Lina: can Redwood show token-level cost in the console during POC?
00:08:18 Eleanor: yes, the Console shows token and per-model cost breakdown. We'll enable a 1-minute granularity dashboard for the load run.
00:08:26 Tom: latency vs cost question — our product folks will likely push for lower cost even if p95 slightly increases; how to surface tradeoffs quickly?
00:08:34 Eleanor: Redwood Optimize provides tradeoff sims: you can toggle quantization level and batching and see simulated cost and expected latency. For POC we'll run 2 axis experiments: FP16 vs q8 and batch size 1 vs 4. We'll share results in a spreadsheet.
00:08:47 Samir: what's the recommended reserved commit number again?
00:08:49 Marcus: baseline 1 GPU if your workload is short sequence heavy; 2 GPUs if long context sessions >200 tokens are frequent. Given your current histogram (18 tokens mostly, 5% long) I'd recommend 1 reserved GPU + hosted burst and local q8 fallback. That's the lowest cost path for a POC.
00:09:05 Cindy: what about autoscaling upper bound to prevent runaway cloud spend?

00:09:17 Lina: good. We'll want that.
00:09:19 Samir: one more operational question — how do you test correctness/regression when falling back to q8? sometimes rerank order changes subtly and we can't accept that.
00:09:28 Priya: we'll configure automatic A/B eval on a small golden set of prompts and compare rerank NDCG or other metric you choose; exceed threshold --> auto-failback. We'll also log examples for manual review.
00:09:40 Samir: great.
00:09:43 Marcus: any blockers on our side?
00:09:46 Tom: only the data residency constraint for PII. We'll provide a non-PII traffic slice. Also we need finance to sign off on short-term burst budget — I'll loop them in.
00:09:56 Eleanor: excellent. To recap quick: reserved 1 GPU baseline, autoscale to hosted for spikes with cap, fallback order defined, canary plan for q8, bench runner and traffic CSV to be shared, schedule load-run week of 6/22.
00:10:12 Samir: yep.
00:10:14 Eleanor: ok we'll follow up with workbook and scripts. Marcus do you want to add any config specifics?
00:10:19 Marcus: I'll add a sample autoscale YAML and the routing table example showing per-route policies. I'll drop links in the email.
00:10:26 Marcus (later): Also note — if you want to test dedicated private burst (no data leaving VPC) we can scope a short Dedicated eval but that usually adds 2-3 days for provisioning.
00:10:36 Cindy: not for this POC. maybe later.
00:10:39 Tom: timeline on security docs?
00:10:41 Eleanor: we'll send within 24 hours.
00:10:44 Samir: okay thanks all.
00:10:46 [Crosstalk]
00:12:50 Eleanor: (summary) action items restated: pricing worksheet, bench runner, sample traffic, schedule test. Any other questions?
00:13:00 Lina: none.
00:13:02 Cindy: thanks.
00:13:05 Tom: thanks.
00:13:10 Eleanor: great meeting, we'll email notes + next steps.

[End of recording — remainder of the hour used for side technical clarifications between Marcus and Lina about per-node memory configs which are in Marcus' follow-up doc. audio faint for Tom around 00:22:00-00:25:00]

title: Status Page and Incident Comms: Guidance for Rollout-Related Issues
author: David Kim
text:
h1. Purpose
This page explains when a rollout issue should be communicated via the status page and how to coordinate communications during a rollback or prolonged fallback.

h1. Definitions
* Rollout issue: any degradation caused by a planned model version change, routing change, or runtime configuration update.
* Incident: a customer-impacting event that meets the incident declaration criteria.

h1. When to post a status page update
Post a status page update if any of the following occur:
* Any widespread Hosted API impact lasting > 15 minutes (elevated 5xx, timeouts, or severe latency)
* Any Dedicated customer experiences SLA-impacting degradation and requests formal comms
* Any Private customer experiences impact outside the approved change window
* A rollback is initiated after > 25% traffic ramp OR after any customer notification has been sent

h1. Required content of a rollout-related status update
Include:
* What users are experiencing (symptoms)
* Impacted surfaces (Hosted/Dedicated/Private, regions, request types)
* Current mitigation (automatic fallback active, manual rollback in progress, traffic capped)
* Next update time (commit to a timestamp)
* Where customers can get support

h1. Coordination model
* Incident Commander (IC): owns the status page message content and cadence.
* Customer Success: owns account-specific communications for Dedicated/Private.
* Engineering owner: provides technical updates and ETA for rollback.

h1. Rollback comms
If rollback is initiated:
1. Notify #incidents and #support with a short summary and mitigation step.
2. Update the rollout plan with the rollback trigger and time.
3. If the status page is used, explicitly state that we reverted to the prior model version (avoid internal ids unless customers pin versions).

h1. After-action requirements
If a rollout issue required status page comms, the associated postmortem MUST link to:
* the rollout plan
* router policy ids (old/new)
* the thresholds that triggered rollback
* customer communications artifacts (tickets/emails)

title: Introduce Idempotency-Scope header and Retry-After-Range for OpenAI compat and tool-stream stability
author: Lina Chen
text:
Motivation: Clients and platform routing need a clearer, machine-readable separation between per-request idempotency and longer-lived conversation/session idempotency, and operators need a deterministic retry guidance window rather than a single Retry-After hint. This PR introduces two compatible surface changes to the OpenAI bridge and streaming runtime: 1) a new Idempotency-Scope request header (Idempotency-Scope: request|session|conversation) that disambiguates how idempotency keys are interpreted and persisted by the adapter and routing layer, and 2) a Retry-After-Range response header (Retry-After-Range: <min-seconds>,<max-seconds>) which gives callers a recommended retry window to support smarter backoff strategies and smoother autoscaling. In addition, this PR standardizes the structured error envelope returned by the OpenAI-compat shim to include {"code","message","retryable","retry_after_hint_seconds","idempotency_hint"} where applicable and adds a single-line streaming error frame format for tool/function-call streams (frame_type:error payload:<json-string>). Design summary: - Idempotency-Scope is advisory but authoritative for the OpenAI shim: when Idempotency-Scope=request the idempotency-key is treated as a single atomic request key; when session or conversation the adapter will attempt to correlate incoming keys across the session identifier (customer-provided) and preserve a scoped result lease for the configured lease TTL. The default behavior remains request-scoped for existing clients if the header is absent. - Retry-After-Range is emitted by rate-limiters and the serving runtime when we can estimate a best-case and worst-case window (e.g., 30,120). Consumers may choose any retry policy within that range; our SDKs will include an opt-in helper to adhere to the window semantics. For legacy single-value Retry-After we continue to set the header for compatibility. - Streaming errors: tool/function-call streams now emit a dedicated error frame as a single-line event to avoid protocol framing ambiguity. The frame contains the standardized envelope and, when a retry is applicable, includes retry_after_hint_seconds and idempotency_hint (e.g. "retry_after_hint_seconds":45, "idempotency_hint":"session:abcd1234" ). - OpenAI mapping: 429/503 map to code="rate_limit", 409 map to code="conflict" with retryable=false unless accompanied by a Retry-After-Range; validation errors map to code="invalid_request". Implementation notes: - OpenAI adapter: header parsing and mapping implemented under openai/adapter/headers.go, with unit tests and a small compatibility shim so missing headers fall back to prior logic. - Runtime: rate limiter updates in runtime/ratelimit/heuristic.go to compute a conservative min/max window and surface it via HTTP and internal gRPC for Dedicated/Private. - Streaming: new frame serializer in stream/frame.go and new parser in stream/parse_test.go to validate single-line JSON error frames. - SDKs: brief helpers added in redwood-sdk-python/ and redwood-sdk-typescript/ to surface Idempotency-Scope and parse Retry-After-Range; helpers are opt-in and behind a feature flag. Compatibility and rollout: - No breaking change: existing clients that do not send Idempotency-Scope continue to behave as before (request-scoped). Retry-After-Range is additive; we still emit Retry-After for single-value clients. - Feature gated: the adapter toggles for private/dedicated customers are behind feature flags; hosted rollout will start as opt-in for beta customers for two weeks then auto-toggle based on SDK opt-ins. Testing and verification: - Unit tests covering header parsing and mapping (openai adapter unit tests). - Integration tests with simulated throttling to assert Retry-After-Range values are well-formed and that SDK helpers respect the window. - Streaming e2e harness updated to assert single-line error frames are emitted and to validate idempotency_hint propagation during tool-call retries. Docs and migration guidance: - Added a concise spec doc to docs/openai-compat/idempotency-retry.md that describes header semantics, sample flows, and recommended SDK usage. - Migration notes advise clients to start adding Idempotency-Scope when they want session-level deduplication and to rely on Retry-After-Range for smarter backoff rather than tight fixed retries. Rollout checklist: - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] SDK helpers behind flag - [x] Docs update - [x] Beta rollout to 5 hosted customers - [x] Monitor telemetry for increased duplicate suppressions Risk and alternatives considered: We considered an opaque lease token approach (analogous to previous "lease" work) but chose an explicit Idempotency-Scope header to make behavior observable and debuggable across the OpenAI mapping layer and user agents. The Retry-After-Range intentionally provides a bounded window to allow servers to communicate uncertainty rather than forcing a single fixed backoff value. Summary of impact: improves client/platform behavior under rate pressure, reduces accidental duplicate tool invocations for session-level workflows, and yields better automated retry policies across SDKs and integrators.

Adds Idempotency-Scope and Retry-After-Range headers for clearer retry semantics; normalizes OpenAI-compatible error envelope; introduces a single-line streaming error frame with structured fields; opt-in header-driven behavior, no forced breaking changes.

Ava Patel: This addresses the ambiguity we saw in the payments team's incident where session-level replays caused duplicate charges. The header naming looks good but please add explicit TTL docs for session scope.
Lina Chen (author reply): Added TTL guidance in docs and clarified that TTL is policy-driven per deployment in the adapter README.
Diego Morales: Can we guarantee Retry-After-Range won't leak internal timing? Suggest rounding to seconds and capping max to a configured threshold. Also add a metrics tag for whether range was provided vs single Retry-After.
Lina Chen (author reply): We round to seconds and cap by runtime config; added metric runtime.rate_retry_range.present in metric exports. PTAL.
Marcus Nguyen: Approve after small nits on test coverage and ensuring SDK flag defaults to false. Tests look thorough.
Lina Chen: Addressed tests and defaulted flags to false; added integration scenario with simulated 429 bursts.
QA (automated): Verified stream error frames are one-line JSON events and SDK helper parses Retry-After-Range correctly.

title: Quickstart Templates: KPI + telemetry requirements (events, tags, dashboards)
author: Nikhil Sharma
text:
Goal
Define a minimal, privacy-safe telemetry spec for Quickstart Templates (RAG + agents) so we can measure adoption + activation ("time-to-first-success"), and so Console/Analytics can segment template-originated traffic.

This ticket produces:
1) Event + tag definitions (what we capture, where it’s emitted, cardinality rules)
2) Source-of-truth definitions for KPIs (especially TTFS)
3) Implementation guidance for SDK/templates + gateway allow-listing
4) Dashboard requirements for Console/Analytics

Context
DevEx is shipping language templates + a small CLI (init/doctor) and wants to measure:
- template adoption (created projects, active installs)
- activation (successful first run)
- retention (active installs after N days)
- support deflection (docs/troubleshooting effectiveness)

Constraints
- Must not leak prompts, user content, PII, or customer identifiers.
- Must avoid high-cardinality dimensions in metrics.
- Tagging must work behind restrictive corporate proxies; telemetry should be opt-in and degrade gracefully.

Non-goals
- Full product analytics instrumentation for all SDK usage.
- Any per-user tracking requiring customer consent flows.
- Capturing document contents, embeddings payloads, or tool outputs.

Proposed measurement model (high level)
We measure template success primarily via:
A) CLI/template-local events (init, doctor, deploy) -> sent to analytics via a lightweight endpoint (opt-in)
B) API request tagging (template tags on inference calls) -> server-side derived KPIs (first successful completion)
C) OTel spans/metrics (for operational visibility) -> not used as the primary source for product KPIs

KPI definitions (v1)
1) Activation rate: % of installs that reach a first successful completion within 60 minutes of init
- numerator: installs with a "first_success" within window
- denominator: installs with init

2) Time-to-first-success (TTFS)
TTFS is computed per install_id as:
- start: template_init timestamp (CLI) OR first tagged API request timestamp (fallback if CLI telemetry disabled)
- end: first API response that meets "success" criteria
- report median / p75 / p90 by template_name + language

Success criteria (for the API-derived end event):
- HTTP 2xx from inference endpoint
- streamed responses must complete normally (no client disconnect before final chunk) OR non-streaming returns a complete response
- response has > 0 output tokens
- not classified as a retry-exhausted/network failure

3) Template retention (D7)
% of installs that have >= 1 tagged successful completion on day 7 (UTC) after init

4) Support deflection proxy metric
Reduction in template-related tickets per 100 active installs (requires Support tagging alignment; tracked separately)

Telemetry: required tags (used for segmentation)
These are the only tags we intend to use for KPI dashboards.

Tag keys (stable):
- rw.template.name: e.g. "rag-agent"
- rw.template.lang: "python" | "typescript"
- rw.template.version: semantic version from template release (e.g. "0.3.1")
- rw.template.install_id: UUID v4 generated on init (stored locally in .redwood/template.json)
- rw.template.channel: "cli" | "github" (set by scaffolder; github = user cloned/copied)

Optional tags (allowed but not required for v1 KPIs):
- rw.template.deployment: "local" | "docker" | "kubernetes" | "fly" | "render" (bounded set)
- rw.template.vectorstore: "local" | "hosted" | "none" (bounded set)

Rules
- install_id must be random (UUID v4) and never derived from user/device identifiers.
- Do not include repo name, file paths, hostname, email, org name, customer_id, IP address, prompt text, retrieved chunks, or tool output.
- Values must be from bounded enumerations where possible. template.version is the only semi-unbounded field; OK for event analytics, NOT for metrics cardinality.

Where tags are emitted
1) API request tagging (primary)
Templates must attach the tags to inference requests via a Redwood-supported mechanism.
Implementation guidance (v1):
- Prefer a single allow-listed header carrying encoded key/value pairs (validated at gateway)
 - Header name: "x-redwood-template-tags"
 - Format: semicolon-separated "k=v" pairs; keys restricted to the list above; values length-limited (<= 64 chars per value)
- If header is blocked by a corporate proxy, templates must allow users to disable it via env var:
 - REDWOOD_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY=off
- For users who disable headers, we still compute partial TTFS using first tagged API request if available; otherwise only CLI funnel metrics (if enabled)

2) CLI events (secondary)
CLI emits minimal events to Redwood analytics endpoint (opt-in). These events are useful for funnel drop-off analysis that the gateway can’t see.

CLI event schema (all fields optional except event_name + timestamp):
- event_name
- timestamp
- rw.template.name/lang/version/install_id/channel
- outcome: "success" | "failure" (for doctor/deploy)
- error_class (bounded; see below)

Event list (v1)
A) CLI events
1. template_init
- emitted when CLI scaffolds a project successfully
- includes: name/lang/version/install_id/channel

2. template_doctor_run
- emitted at start and end (two events or one with outcome)
- includes outcome and error_class if failure

3. template_deploy_attempt
- emitted when user runs deploy command (if we ship it in v1) OR runs guided deploy script

4. template_deploy_success

B) API-derived “activation” events (server-side)
These are derived by Analytics from tagged traffic; templates do not emit explicit “success” events.
5. template_first_tagged_request
- first time we see install_id on an API request

6. template_first_success
- first time we see a successful completion per install_id

Error taxonomy (bounded values)
Used ONLY for CLI outcomes + (optionally) template-local error reporting; not required for API-derived KPIs.
- auth_invalid_key
- auth_missing_key
- quota_rate_limited (429)
- quota_insufficient_balance
- network_timeout
- network_dns
- network_tls
- streaming_disconnect
- tool_schema_validation
- retrieval_empty
- retrieval_backend_error
- config_invalid
- otel_exporter_misconfigured
- unknown

Dashboard requirements (Console/Analytics)
1) Templates overview
- Active installs (7d)
- Activation rate (60m)
- Median TTFS (by template + lang)
- Top failure classes from CLI doctor (last 7d)

2) Funnel dashboard
init -> first_tagged_request -> first_success -> deploy_success (if available)
- drop-off at each step
- breakdown by lang and channel (cli vs github)

3) Operational correlation (link-out)
From a segment (template_name/lang) provide links to:
- template-tagged traffic filters in Console usage analytics
- SLO dashboard from observability-pack (latency, error rate, streaming disconnect rate)

Open questions / decisions
- Decision: make header-based tagging opt-in and documented due to known proxy header restrictions. Default remains ON for CLI-created projects, but README must include “turn off telemetry tags” option.
- Decision: do not use OTel as KPI source-of-truth (sampling + customer-controlled collectors make it unreliable for adoption metrics).

Acceptance criteria
- Written spec (this ticket) reviewed by DevEx + Observability + Privacy/Security.
- Analytics can compute TTFS and activation rate using:
 - CLI init events when available
 - API-derived first_success from tagged requests
- Cardinality guidelines documented and agreed (no freeform tags).
- Console/Analytics owners confirm dashboard fields and filtering requirements.

Links / related work
- PR: redwood-quickstarts #115 (template telemetry tags)
- PR: redwood monorepo #18421 (gateway allowlist for telemetry header)
- PR: redwood monorepo #18439 (Console filter for template-tagged traffic)
- Thread: #devex "template-telemetry-tagging-and-privacy" (opt-in + redaction)

Notes for implementers
- SDKs should expose a safe, explicit hook for passing template tags without requiring userland header mutation.
- Ensure request-id propagation: log fields must include Redwood request_id and install_id (install_id only if telemetry is enabled).
- Any telemetry endpoint for CLI must accept anonymous, unauthenticated events OR use API key with strict rate limits; do not require user identity.

2025-02-06 (Nikhil Sharma): Creating as P0 so we don’t ship templates without measurable activation. Need TTFS definition + tagging mechanism that won’t explode metric cardinality.
2025-02-10 (Logan Wright): Drafted initial event list. Strong recommendation: derive "first_success" server-side from tagged requests rather than trusting client-side events.
2025-02-12 (Allison Grant): +1 on bounded attributes. Please avoid template.version on metrics; OK for event analytics. Also do not attach install_id to OTel metrics (traces/logs OK).
2025-02-18 (Marcus Lin): Privacy review notes: install_id must be random; forbid repo name / hostname. Provide explicit opt-out env var and ensure redaction processors cover headers in logs.
2025-02-25 (Henry Cho): Ensure success criteria accounts for streaming completion; don’t count partial streams as success. Also want dashboard breakdown by language + channel.
2025-03-02 (Brian Murphy): Gateway can allowlist a single header with strict validation + max length; prefer one header over many to reduce proxy issues and simplify support.
2025-03-05 (Sergio Costa): Dashboards: funnel + TTFS + activation are straightforward once tags are in warehouse. Need stable tag keys and a clear mapping doc for Console filters.
2025-03-10 (Nikhil Sharma): Incorporating incident learnings: some corp proxies block unknown headers. Mark tagging as opt-in with documented disable flag; CLI still usable without it.
2025-03-13 (Logan Wright): Final spec agreed. Action items moved to ENG tickets for SDK hooks + request-id propagation; Console team confirmed filter requirements.

title: Reserve slicing & preemptable mix — sketch
author: Aisha Rahman
text:
Purpose:
This is a working spreadsheet sketch and short rationale for a reserve-slicing offering: allow customers to break a large reserved GPU commit into smaller independently sized and timed 'slices', and optionally mix in a tranche of preemptable / spot-backed capacity to materially reduce blended unit costs while protecting a baseline of reserved throughput.

Context and motivation:
- Problem we keep seeing: customers commit to large monthly reserved pools to get predictable unit economics but then underutilize or have lumpy seasonal demand. This creates either wasted spend or conservative over-commit.
- Traditional approaches (single monolithic annual/monthly commit) force customers to pick one point on the utilization curve. We want a configurable middle ground: smaller slices + optional preemptable mix + phased activation windows.
- Goal: improve average utilization, reduce customer sticker price for the same effective sustained throughput, and keep our utilization high.

Key concepts (quick definitions):
- Slice: a sub-commit of N GPUs for a defined window (example: 10 GPUs for 90 days). Customers can hold multiple slices with overlapping windows.
- Baseline reserved capacity: the minimum guaranteed non-preemptable GPUs covered by reserve pricing.
- Preemptable tranche: separate pricing for preemptable GPUs (lower $/hr) with no SLA; customers can choose a % mix.
- Blended effective unit price: weighted average $/GPU-hour across baseline + preemptable + any overage pay-as-you-go.

Assumptions for modeling (cells referenced in the attached sheet tabs):
- Hourly costs to Redwood (infra amortized): non-preemptable GPU = $2.80 / GPU-hour; preemptable = $1.20 / GPU-hour.
- Market payg price we charge today baseline: $4.00 / GPU-hour non-preemptable payg.
- Target reserved discount: 35% vs payg (variable by term and commitment).
- Slice min size: 4 GPUs; max: matched to customer's peak.
- Typical customer profile simulated: steady baseline 20 GPUs 24/7 plus weekly burst to 50 GPUs for 4 hours per day.

Model structure (spreadsheet tabs and columns):
- tab: scenario_inputs (cells: baseline_demand_gpus, burst_gpus, burst_hours_per_day, calendar_days, preemptable_mix_pct, reserved_term_days, slice_size_gpus, slice_activation_schedule)
- tab: slice_costing (rows: slice_1..slice_n; cols: slice_size, term_days, price_per_gpu_hour_reserved, effective_discount, amortized_monthly_fee)
- tab: utilization_sim (minute/hour granularity; simulates demand and maps to baseline reserved, preemptable tranche, and payg overflow)
- tab: breakeven (simple analytic formulas for: threshold_utilization_pct where reserved becomes cheaper vs payg; breakeven_days for each slice)

Sample formulas (put these into the sheet):
- reserved_hourly_price = payg_hourly_price * (1 - target_discount)
- slice_total_hours = slice_size * term_days * 24
- slice_cost = slice_total_hours * reserved_hourly_price
- customer_effective_price_blended = (reserved_hours*reserved_price + preemptable_hours*preemptable_price + payg_overflow_hours*payg_price) / total_consumed_hours
- breakeven_util_pct = (reserved_price - preemptable_price) / (payg_price - preemptable_price) (approx for 2-tranche mix)

Numerical example (concrete scenario):
- Customer wants ~20 sustained GPUs. They agree to 16 GPUs reserved baseline in two slices of 8 GPUs for 90 days each (phased start), and choose 25% preemptable mix for burst coverage.
- Numbers: payg_price=4.00, reserved_discount=35% -> reserved_price=2.60, preemptable_price=1.20
- If utilization of reserved slice is 75% (i.e., 12/16 GPUs effectively used on average), blended unit price (rough calc):
 reserved_component = (12*2.60) / 12 = 2.60 (for those reserved hours)
 preemptable_component assume 4 GPUs * 24h * 30d * 1.20 -> lowers blended price when bursts use preemptable instead of payg
 blended roughly = ~2.20 / GPU-hour vs payg 4.00 (customer savings ~45%)
- For Redwood, blended margin remains positive because our internal costs baseline assumed $2.80 non-preemptable and $1.20 preemptable. Show amortized profitability in 'slice_costing' tab.

Tradeoffs & policies we need to define (policy cells / product rules):
- Slice cancellation: allow early cancellation with sliding credit schedule (e.g., credits proportional to unused days but apply 10% admin fee).
- Slice re-assignment: allow customers to shift activation windows between slices with 30 days notice; last-minute shifts allowed only if capacity available.
- Preemptable floor: ensure at least X% baseline non-preemptable is purchased for larger customers to protect SLA-sensitive workloads.
- Auto-fallback: when preemptable capacity not available, automatic fallback to payg at a negotiated capped rate to avoid customer outages (helps adoption).

Sensitivity testing to add (recommended sheet views):
- Vary reserved discount 25%/35%/45% and show delta to customer monthly bill for given utilization curves.
- Vary preemptable mix (0%/15%/30%/50%) and show Redwood blended margin and utilization.
- Vary slice granularity: 4/8/16 GPU slices and see administrative overhead vs utilization improvement.
- Probe churn scenarios: customers that underutilize in month 1 but ramp in month 2 – show 3-month rolling utilization and effective price.

Open questions & risks to validate with SRE/Infra finance: 
- Availability SLO for preemptable tranche and realistic preemptable uplift factor in real fleet (is our preemptable supply reliably available for 6 months windows?).
- Accounting treatment: how to amortize committed revenue for slices spanning multiple fiscal periods. Finance needs the amortization schedule template (sheet: acct_amort).
- Edge-case pricing: how to price for extremely bursty but infrequent usage (e.g., 2 hours/day bursts but 10x magnitude). Does a slice still make sense vs pure payg?
- Operational complexity: inventorying many small slices increases orchestration and billing complexity; need an SLO for ops cost per slice.

Proposed next steps (owners + timeline rough):
- Engineering (Marco): add hourly simulation harness to 'utilization_sim' tab and wire to our historical telemetry to validate model (2 weeks).

Maya: Heads-up — EU cloud partner reports increased tail latency after we updated marketplace node image from ROCm 5.4 -> 5.6 last night. They see p99 spikes and some request queuing.

Maya: Image: `redwood/llm-runtime:rocm-5.6-2026-03-21-eu`, kernel 5.15.90-rt, amdgpu 6.1.1. Repro: `make bench RUN=serve_bench BATCH=4 SEQ=1024` — no OOMs, just p99 spikes to ~900ms.
Diego: Quick checklist: (1) check amdgpu module parameters (prefetch, large-paged), (2) verify ROCm hipBLAS is not falling back, (3) confirm udev firmware blobs loaded.
infra-bot: Telemetry alert: node eu-3 showed KV cache eviction bursts at 02:13UTC. Metric: kv_evictions/sec = 12 -> 48 for 2 minutes.

Ethan: Might be a kernel tunable interacting badly with ROCm 5.6 memory allocator. Diego, can you run `sysctl -a | grep vm` and post relevant ones?
Diego: Posted snippet: `vm.swappiness=10`, `vm.dirty_ratio=20`, `vm.max_map_count=262144`. Nothing crazy. Also `cat /sys/module/amdgpu/parameters/prefetch` -> `1`.
Zoe: From product: partner asks for recommended action — rollback listing or keep and patch? They want a 6-12 hour ETA.
Diego: Short mitigation we can try: build a `rocm-5.6-compat` image that forces `amdgpu.prefetch=0` and enables hugepages. That avoids changing customer app while altering kernel module params. We can do image-level modprobe.d + sysctl on boot.
Maya: Good plan. Partner prefers non-invasive image change. If that doesn't resolve, fallback to marketplace listing rollback.
Ethan: I'll run a canary with `rocm-5.6-compat` on our EU staging nodes. Command: `k run bench --image redwood/llm-runtime:rocm-5.6-compat --replicas 3 --bench serve_bench --args "--batch 4 --seq 1024"`.
infra-bot: CI job `marketplace-smoke (rocm-5.6-compat)` queued.

Bench results (staging): p50=38ms p95=150ms p99=220ms (improved vs partner repro)
```
Diego: Flamegraph show spike in `memcpy_async` during p99; switching prefetch=0 reduced copy stalls. Also verified hipBLAS still on device.
vendor-bot: FYI vendor kernel team confirmed a change in 6.x kernels that affects amdgpu prefetch heuristics; they suggested a driver-side fix but estimate 2-3 weeks for stable rollout.
Maya: So immediate path: (A) publish `rocm-5.6-compat` image to marketplace and update listing with “temporary module param to mitigate latency” + run 24h canary; (B) if partner still sees spikes, rollback to `rocm-5.4-stable`.

title: Multi-dimensional cost & latency scoring service for per-route/model/customer insights
author: Devin Park
text:
Goal: Build a service that produces a consistent, explainable breakdown of per-request cost and latency attributed to route, model variant, and customer. The output feeds Console dashboards, routing policies, and chargeback reports. The service must be real-time to near-real-time (<= 60s materialization) for the majority of common queries, and support historical rollups for billing windows.

Scope and non-goals:
- In scope: attribution of token-level compute cost (inference GPU/time), amortized infra (node-hours, memory), and network egress; latency decomposition by stage (ingress, queuing, kernel compute, KV/cache hit/miss, egress); canonical keys: route_id, model_id, model_variant, customer_id, region, timestamp.
- Out of scope for initial roll-out: per-call prompt content classification or third-party credit allocation.

Design summary:
1) Ingest layer: consume request and trace events from existing Kafka topics (request-metadata, runtime-span-events, billing-meter). Enrich events with model profiles (chip, quantization, perf-profile) from the model catalog cache.
2) Online scoring pipeline: Flink job (scoring-service-v1) performs streaming joins, maintains per-key state in RocksDB, computes rolling-window aggregates (1m, 5m, 1h), and emits scored records to a materialized store. Scoring function combines token counts, measured GPU milliseconds, kernel efficiency multipliers, and region price table to compute an "apportioned_cost_v1" and latency percentiles/histograms.
3) Storage and OLAP: write aggregates to ClickHouse for long-term analytical queries and to a low-latency materialized store (Redis+TTL or Materialize) for Console queries with 1 minute SLAs.
4) API: expose /api/v1/insights/cost-breakdown and /api/v1/insights/latency-breakdown supporting filters by route/model/customer, time-window, and percentile. Responses include both raw aggregates and an explain vector tying cost/latency components to inputs (e.g., tokens * model_cost_rate, cache_hit_adjustment).

Key constraints and trade-offs discussed:
- Accuracy vs latency: Exact per-token GPU accounting requires more detailed tracing that increases pipeline throughput pressure. We adopt a hybrid approach: use measured GPU-ms when available; otherwise fallback to model-profile-based estimates. This keeps tail latency low while maintaining bounded error.
- Storage cost: Storing full per-request traces is cost prohibitive. Aggregates preserved at 1m/5m/1h reduce footprint while keeping sufficient fidelity for Console usage.
- Complexity: Chose Flink streaming with RocksDB for stateful joins to enable windowed scoring and fast recovery. Alternatives evaluated: Materialize (simpler queries, but heavier operational constraints for cardinality) and Spark Structured Streaming (higher latency for windowing).

Acceptance criteria:
- End-to-end pipeline processes synthetic test traffic and produces per-route/model/customer cost and latency breakdowns within 60s of event time for 95% of records in staging.
- API returns correct totals that reconcile within 0.5% against the billing rollup (sampled test).
- Dashboard panels in Console render top-100 routes by cost and show componentized latency histograms.
- Canary rollout plan with feature flag and auto-rollback on mismatch >2% compared to golden baseline.

Rollout plan:
- Week 1: Wire up ingestion and model-profile enrichment in staging. Smoke tests and load tests at 2x typical staging traffic.
- Week 2: Launch Flink job in canary mode writing to a shadow ClickHouse table and materialized store. Run reconciliation jobs comparing shadow vs current production rollups for 24h.
- Week 3: Enable read API for internal Console users behind feature flag. Validate query latencies and correctness.
- Week 4: Gradual ramp to 25%, 50%, 100% production traffic with monitoring thresholds for token accounting divergence, pipeline lag, and ClickHouse write errors.

Operational concerns and monitoring:
- Alerts: pipeline-lag > 300s, sink-errors > 1%/m, reconciliation-delta > 2%, consumer-rebalance rate spikes.
- Observability: per-job throughput, RocksDB state size, checkpoint durations, Kafka consumer lag, ClickHouse insert tail-latency, API p95/p99.
- Runbook: documented actions for state corruption, checkpoint loss, or regional price-table drift.

Follow-ups and future enhancements:
- Add per-model-quantization multipliers for better cost granularity.
- Extend attribution to include auxiliary services (replicas, caching lane overhead).
- Investigate approximate sketching (DDSketch) to reduce histogram storage while preserving percentile accuracy.

Links:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INFR/Multi-dim+Scoring+Design
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/1429
- Staging dashboard: https://dashboard.redwood.ai/d/console-analytics/cost-latency-insights

2026-02-20 10:12 - Devin Park: Initial ticket created after QBR call. Need to prioritize near-real-time use cases for Console and routing fallback decisions.
2026-02-24 16:05 - Architecture review: Recommend Flink + RocksDB for stateful scoring. Materialize considered but rejected for now due to cardinality concerns.
2026-03-02 09:33 - Asha Patel: Prototype ingestion working in staging. Observed 12% additional CPU on ingestion fleet under 3x staging load; created ENG-35710 to investigate backpressure handling.
2026-03-05 14:48 - PM review (Sofia Marin): Ensure billing team is included in reconciliation acceptance criteria. Added dependency on ENG-31245 for cost attribution primitives.
2026-03-10 11:01 - Security (Liam O'Connor): Confirmed no new sensitive PII fields stored. Will require KMS check for materialized store if retention extends beyond 90 days.

title: GPU Warm-Pool Cross-Account Handoff Runbook (2025)
author: Marisol Ortega
text:
Summary

This document describes the step-by-step oncall protocol for performing a cross-account GPU warm-pool handoff when the primary tenant capacity is exhausted and a burst to a secondary AWS account is required. It covers preflight checks, the handshake sequence between warm-pool-manager instances, IAM role-chain assumptions, emergency (time-boxed) IaC changes, verification, rollback, and observability.

This runbook is intended for oncall engineers (Infra SRE and GPU Fleet) who manage multi-account GPU bursting and warm-pool orchestration.

What changed in 2025 (read first)

- Triggering thresholds were tightened to reduce customer-facing tail latency.
- Handshake tokens now default to TTL 120 seconds (was 180s) due to replay-risk hardening.
- warmctl was renamed to gpuctl in the oncall bastion images (warmctl remains as a compatibility alias on some older regions).
- The cross-account role name changed to "redwood/gpu-warm-pool-handoff" (old name "redwood/warm-pool-handoff" still exists in a few legacy accounts; see IAM notes below).
- Router overrides are applied via router-admin (not direct /router/configs/apply) in most regions.

When to run this

- Automatic trigger: capacity-sentry signals BOTH:
 - sustained 90th-percentile queue time > 2.0s for 3 minutes (was 2.5s)
 - warm-pool saturation > 95% for 3 minutes
- Manual trigger: customer-facing latency incidents, region impairment, or when the allocation controller requests cross-account burst.

Preflight (5 minutes)

1) Confirm incident context and scope: affected tenant(s), region(s), and SLO impact.
2) Check SLO dashboard (tenant-specific):
 - 99th-pct latency target: 450ms token-serving (was 500ms)
 - Queue-time SLO: 95th-pct < 1.0s (was 1.2s)
3) Verify warm-pool health in both accounts: check warm-pool-manager metrics for:
 - active leases
 - available GPUs
 - preheat success rate
4) Confirm this is not a control-plane issue:
 - allocation-controller error rate
 - router-admin config push latency

Quick commands (run from the oncall bastion with appropriate MFA)

- Check capacity-sentry alerts:
 curl -s https://prometheus.internal/api/v1/query?query=capacity_sentry_alert

- List warm pool instances (k8s):
 kubectl -n infra get pods -l app=warm-pool-manager -o wide

- Inspect lease table:
 psql -h leases-db.internal -U infra_user -c "select * from leases where state in ('handshake','read_only') order by created_at desc limit 20;"

- Confirm gpuctl is available:
 which gpuctl || which warmctl

Roles and architecture notes

- warm-pool-manager: service running in every account responsible for preheating GPUs, tagging instances, and performing handshake.
- burst-orchestrator: global controller that decides the target account for overflow.
- capacity-sentry: SLO monitor and alerting signal source.
- xnet-egress: per-account egress proxy for cross-account traffic with bandwidth-aware shaping and compression (replaces egress-shim in most regions).
- lease-daemon: lightweight agent on compute nodes that accepts ephemeral leases and streams KV-cache seeds.
- router-admin: service that manages router sidecar route overrides and propagates configs.

Handshake protocol overview (high level)

1) burst-orchestrator determines target account and issues an ephemeral handshake token (default valid for 120 seconds; configurable).
2) warm-pool-manager in target account validates the token via IAM role chain and creates a placeholder Lease record in read-only state.
3) Source warm-pool-manager begins KV-cache seed transfer using the lease token and an mTLS-authenticated channel to the target account's lease-daemon.
4) After successful seed receipt, the target upgrades the Lease to Active and router-admin applies a route override so tenant requests flow to the new pool.

Detailed emergency handoff procedure (approx. 15–30 minutes)

Step 0 — Notify stakeholders (2 minutes)

- Announce on #infra-oncall and page the GPU Fleet oncall (PagerDuty) with priority P2.
- Include region, tenant(s), current queue time, warm-pool saturation, and whether this is multi-region.

Step 1 — Confirm IAM and trust boundary (3 minutes)

- Validate the target account has the cross-account role configured.
 - Preferred role name: "redwood/gpu-warm-pool-handoff"
 - Legacy role name (some accounts only): "redwood/warm-pool-handoff"

- Quick check (from source account):
 aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::TARGET_ACCOUNT_ID:role/redwood/gpu-warm-pool-handoff --role-session-name handoff-check

- If assume-role fails:
 1) retry with legacy role name
 2) if still failing, escalate to cloud-accounts team (Slack: #cloud-accounts, oncall: @cloud-accounts). Do not proceed.

Step 2 — Issue ephemeral handshake token (1 minute)

- From burst-orchestrator console:
 POST /api/v1/handshake {"source_account":"A","target_account":"B","ttl_s":120}

- Record token id and TTL in the incident timeline.

Step 3 — Reserve capacity in target pool (3 minutes)

- In target account run one of the following (prefer gpuctl):
 kubectl -n infra exec deploy/warm-pool-manager -- /bin/gpuctl reserve --token <TOKEN_ID> --count <n_gpus>

- Sizing guidance:
 - Reserve predicted peak + 15% (was 10–20% above predicted peak); avoid over-reserving during partial incidents.

- If reserve fails due to account quotas, run the Quota quick path (below).

Step 4 — Seed transfer and KV-cache sync (6–12 minutes)

- Initiate transfer from source warm-pool-manager:
 /usr/local/bin/gpuctl transfer-seed --token <TOKEN_ID> --target-endpoint https://lease-daemon.target.internal:8443 --profile fast

- Watch transfer metrics in Prometheus:
 - warm_seed_transfer_duration_seconds
 - warm_seed_transfer_error_count
 - xnet_egress_bandwidth_utilization

- Expected durations:
 - 90% < 75s for a 4GB seed over inter-region link (with compression enabled)

- If transfer stalls > 150s (was 180s):
 1) reduce concurrent shards (--shards 4)
 2) retry once
 3) if repeated failures, abort and fall back to DNS-level routing (see Fallback options).

Step 5 — Activate lease and switch routing (2–4 minutes)

- On target:
 kubectl -n infra exec deploy/warm-pool-manager -- /bin/gpuctl activate --token <TOKEN_ID>

- Apply router override via router-admin (preferred):
 router-admin override set --tenant TENANT_ID --pool target-account-pool --ttl 30m

- Legacy (only if router-admin is unavailable in the region):
 POST /router/configs/apply with route override: route { tenant: "TENANT_ID", pool: "target-account-pool" }

- Wait for propagation:
 - typical: 60–90 seconds
 - if propagation exceeds 3 minutes, check router-admin backlog and config push error rate.

Verification (5 minutes)

- Confirm incoming requests are served from target pool:
 - sample last 100 requests and confirm trace header x-redwood-pool indicates target pool
- Confirm token billing tags and cost attribution are set:
 - check cost-annotator logs for token_id tag
- SLO check:
 - observe latency and queue-time dashboards for the affected tenant for a 10-minute window
 - expect queue-time to drop by >= 40% after routing changes stabilize

Rollback and fallback options

- If KV-cache transfer fails irrecoverably:
 - run fallback DNS-level routing to a best-effort cached model in a regional pool:
 /usr/local/bin/gpuctl fallback-dns --tenant TENANT_ID --region REGION_CODE

- To fully rollback (deactivate target pool):
 kubectl -n infra exec deploy/warm-pool-manager -- /bin/gpuctl deactivate --token <TOKEN_ID> --force

- Post-rollback:
 - ensure lease state in leases-db is set to "aborted"
 - add trace ids and token id to the incident record

Quota quick path (when target reservation fails)

1) Check current quota:
 aws service-quotas get-service-quota --service-code ec2 --quota-code L-ABCDEFGH --region <REGION>

2) If instantaneous quota bump is configured (emergency-bump role):
 aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::TARGET_ACCOUNT_ID:role/redwood/instant-quota-bump --role-session-name qb

3) Execute the emergency bump:
 - Preferred path (2025): run the quota-bumper workflow:
 quota-bumper run --account TARGET_ACCOUNT_ID --region REGION --delta-gpu +X --reason "GPU warm-pool handoff"
 - Legacy path (only if workflow unavailable): Terraform apply against iac/quotas/emergency-bump.tf with variables:
 --var 'account=TARGET_ACCOUNT_ID' --var 'delta_gpu=+X' and set -auto-approve.

Only the cloud-accounts engineer should execute quota bumps; page them if necessary.

Observability and dashboards (ongoing)

- Prometheus metrics to watch:
 - warm_pool_active_leases{account,region} (target should increase)
 - warm_seed_transfer_rate_bytes
 - capacity_sentry_queue_time_seconds
 - xnet_egress_bandwidth_utilization
 - router_admin_apply_duration_seconds

- Logs:
 - lease-daemon logs (stdout) aggregated in kibana index leases-logs-*/_search
 - look for "seed-received" and "seed-commit" events

- Traces:
 - sampling key x-redwood-trace-token in Jaeger should show cross-account hops

Post-incident tasks (owner: GPU Fleet)

1) Create a postmortem within 48 hours if the handoff was non-trivial or if SLOs were missed. Include timeline and seed-transfer traces.
2) If quota bumps were used, reconcile cost center tags and submit billing adjustment within 5 business days.
3) If transfer retries occurred >2x, open a backlog ticket for transfer optimization and include transfer artifacts (logs, histogram).

Security considerations

- Handshake tokens are single-use and TTL-limited (default 120s). Never paste tokens into external channels.
- All cross-account transfers must happen over mTLS endpoints; confirm certificate fingerprint before starting (see cert-check below).
- Do not run routing overrides without an incident ticket id in the override description/annotation.

Cert check (one-liner)

- openssl s_client -connect lease-daemon.target.internal:8443 -servername lease-daemon.target.internal | openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256
- Confirm fingerprint matches entry in keyring:
 kubectl -n infra get configmap handoff-keyring -o yaml | grep <fingerprint>

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: GPU Fleet (PagerDuty alias: #gpu-fleet-oncall)
- Secondary: cloud-accounts (Slack: #cloud-accounts)
- Networking: #infra-networking
- Escalation path:
 - after 10 minutes of blocked handoff, escalate to SRE manager
 - start a P1 bridge if customer impact is P1 or if >1 enterprise tenant is impacted

Change control and IaC notes

- Any permanent changes to the handoff role, token TTL defaults, or the transfer protocol must be implemented in Terraform and go through infra GitHub repo CI/CD gates.
- PR requirements:
 - unit test for token TTL enforcement
 - integration test that mocks assume-role
 - canary rollout policy for gpuctl binary

- Emergency IaC patch (only cloud-accounts):
 - update terraform/modules/iam/roles.tf
 - run: terraform plan -var 'account=TARGET_ACCOUNT_ID' && terraform apply -auto-approve
 - run terraform fmt and policy-as-code checks before apply unless explicitly waived by cloud-accounts oncall during an active incident

Appendix: common failure modes and remediation

| Symptom | Probable cause | Remediation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Seed transfer stalls at 0% | xnet-egress throttling or misrouted endpoint | Reduce shards; ensure correct lease-daemon endpoint; contact networking if sustained >5min |
| Assume-role fails | Missing trust policy or SCP denial | Validate role ARN; check org SCP; escalate to cloud-accounts |
| Router override not applied | router-admin backlog or propagation error | Reapply override; check router-admin queue depth; restart router sidecar only as last resort |

Change history

- 2024-11-12: Initial draft (Marisol Ortega)
- 2025-02-08: Clarified quota quick path and added cert-check (Ethan Kwan reviewer)
- 2025-11-03: 2025 refresh: gpuctl rename, token TTL default 120s, tighter triggers, router-admin override path, xnet-egress naming (Sofia Almeida reviewer)

Related reading

- GPU capacity runway and warm-pool sizing whitepaper for sizing heuristics.
- xnet-egress operational runbook for bandwidth shaping and compression settings.
- IAM role naming and session policy standard.

Contact matrix

- gpu-fleet-oncall: pagerduty/@gpu-fleet-oncall
- cloud-accounts: slack/#cloud-accounts
- networking: slack/#infra-networking

End of runbook

title: Avelon - QBR: Stability, Burn, Roadmap Orientation
author: Jordan Park
text:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-11
Time: 09:00 PT / 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood CSM); Dana Lowe, Ravi Menon, Priya Shah, Leah Kim (Avelon)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be fuzzy):
- Focus: quarterly health check on usage, cost burn, and upcoming roadmap alignment for Avelon inference workloads.
- Key blockers: VPC routing limits, unexpected tail latency on long-context workflows, cost surge in experimentation buckets.
- Agreed next steps: Redwood to provide trimmed pricing scenario for a 3-month pilot and run a focused tail-latency benchmark on the Dedicated pool with the customer's trace. Security deep-dive to follow.

Topics:
- usage trends and burn profile
- latency SLOs and tail behavior
- Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs for compliance windows
- roadmap features: prefix caching, autoscale/burst, quantization suggestions

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Park: Okay uh good morning good afternoon everyone thanks for joining the Avelon quarterly sync. I think we have an hour so we'll try to cover usage, burn, and then walk through roadmap alignment stuff. Maya's going to jump into the perf numbers.

[00:22] Maya Singh: Hi all, thanks. quick caveat my slides are in the deck link in the chat. I ran the end-to-end 95 and 99 latencies last night, used their sample traffic from last month, and also tried a long-context path (about 2K tokens). Results — the Dedicated pool with burst enabled hit 95th at ~180ms and 99th at ~420ms for the short context. Long context tails were noisy, 99th up to 1.6s. These numbers are roughly consistent with what we saw in June but there's been an uptick in the experimentation namespace which increases prefix cache churn.

[01:10] Dana Lowe: 1.6 seconds on the 99th for the long contexts, is that with KV cache on? we thought we had prefix caching configured.

[01:20] Maya Singh: Yes, it was with prefix caching enabled but the workload has a lot of varied prefixes and the KV cash — cash in transcript — yep, kv cash churn is high, so cache hit rate is low for those calls. We can tune the cache TTL and also suggest smarter batching windows.

[01:45] Ravi Menon: Quick question on the Dedicated vs hosted math — our security team is clear they'd prefer private for PHI experiments, but finance is worried about the committed spend. How do you recommend we balance the latency guarantees vs the cost hit?

[02:05] Jordan Park: Good question. Short answer, Dedicated gives you predictable headroom and better tail control because you control the GPU pool sizing and kernel choices. Hosted is cheaper on trials and for spiky workloads if you accept a broader latency distribution. For PHI we usually steer customers to Private or Dedicated plus VPC peering for auditability and KMS integration.

[02:38] Leah Kim: on the finance side we saw last month a 48% increase in non-prod inference spend; that's largely from the model-sandbox project. Is there a way to throttle or cap that so we don't blow the pilot budget?

[02:55] Carlos Ruiz: We can add per-namespace quotas and rate-limits, and also suggest a cost-saving plan: quantized model variants for sandbox and batching to reduce token unit cost. Also there's an optimize report we can run to give exact tail savings per config. I'll put that in the follow-up.

[03:18] Priya Shah: Also on network, we hit some V-P-C route limits when we attempted cross-region calls; that caused request retry storms and spiked our token usage. Is that something Redwood's side can help debug or is that strictly on our infra?

[03:36] Maya Singh: We can help instrument the retries — we have tracing hooks you can turn on that show request routing and fallback policy. Often it's a combination: the customer's LB retries plus our routing fallback to other regions. We'll need packet-level traces from your infra to fully diagnose but we can isolate which path is triggering reroutes.

[04:02] Dana Lowe: Security question: we need SOC two evidence and SAML SSO integration, K-M-S key wrapping, and audit logs for every token request. Do you have those artifacts or is that separate engagement?

[04:20] Jordan Park: We have SOC 2 Type II cert and a security pack; Maya will schedule a security deep dive. For SAML we support SAML 2.0 with SCIM provisioning; KMS integration supports customer-managed keys for Private and Dedicated via our KMS bridge. Audit logs are available with optional extended retention add-on. We'll share the security doc link after the call.

[04:55] Ravi Menon: If we do dedicated with KMS and VPC, what's the timeline to get it running in production? We're aiming for mid-November for full rollout.

[05:10] Maya Singh: Typical lead for Dedicated w/ VPC + customer KMS is 6–8 weeks once we have access for network setup and your infra team completes the peering checklist. If you want mid-November we should start the provision/runbook in late-September.

[05:35] Dana Lowe: ok that fits. Another item: we had a quality regression on the latest quantized model — 2% BLEU drop on one eval set. Are you able to advise? We can't accept that in prod.

[05:50] Maya Singh: Yep, we saw similar in some workloads — quantization often shifts distributions. We recommend mixed precision for critical paths or using a calibration subset to tune the quant profile. Our Optimize team can run a quick eval/rollback plan.

[06:12] Leah Kim: back to cost — Jordan, can you present a trimmed pilot pricing that includes an option: dedicated small commit + burst credits vs hosted unlimited but throttled? We want a clear cost floor and an overage behavior.

[06:28] Jordan Park: Absolutely, I'll share a three-scenario model: hosted scaling, small Dedicated commit with burst credits, and a Private pilot option. I'll include predicted monthly spend and a worst-case tail assumption.

[06:44] Priya Shah: For the benchmark you ran, can you re-run with our production trace for 9/02? that will help show expected 99th and cost per token.

[06:55] Maya Singh: yes please send the trace, ideally scrubbed for PHI; we can run the 9/02 trace with both hosted and dedicated configs and capture p95/p99 plus cost delta.

[07:10] Ravi Menon: Competitor check — we did a POC with Anthropic briefly; their tail seemed better in small batch tests but cost was higher. Any notes on when Redwood would prefer one kernel path vs another?

[07:25] Maya Singh: We pick kernels based on sequence length distribution and model arch; for long contexts we use attention kernels optimized for streaming. title: Fidelity Experiments Sandbox: Developer Kit & Metrics Playbook
author: Maya Ortega
text:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook describes the Fidelity Experiments Sandbox — a self-service kit for product and engineering teams to run controlled fidelity/latency/cost experiments against Redwood inference surfaces (hosted, dedicated, private). The goal is to make reproducible, auditable experiments that measure end-to-end economics and user-facing fidelity changes before any commercial rollout.

Scope
- Audience: product managers, ML engineers, platform engineers, solutions engineers.
- Environments: staging (primary), canary-hosted (secondary), local-dev (developer preview).
- Not in scope: production billing migrations and any changes to live pricing without separate legal/finance sign-off.

Key concepts
- Fidelity profile: a named set of model/runtime knobs (quantization, sequence budget, prompt-truncation policy, sampling temp) used for experiment runs.
- Fidelity score: a synthetic metric combining quality regressions on prompt sets, hallucination rate, and token-generation divergence (0-100, higher=closer to baseline).
- Economics trace: per-request cost, per-1000-token cost, and aggregate cost for the experiment window.
- Sandbox runner: a reproducible job that replays traffic or synthetic sessions against a fidelity profile and collects telemetry.

Sandbox components and interfaces
1) Sandbox Runner (service: sandbox-runner)
 - Accepts: fidelity_profile id, scenario manifest, input corpus, concurrency, duration.
 - Outputs: fidelity_scorecard.json, telemetry.tar.gz, billing_trace.csv.
2) Developer SDK (package: redwood-experiments-sdk)
 - Python and Go client examples included.
 - CLI: redwood-experiments run --profile <id> --scenario <file> --duration 30m
3) Local Prefetch Proxy (optional)
 - Purpose: enable offline replay with cached embeddings and k-v prefixes so local developers can run realistic end-to-end experiments without touching live model endpoints.
4) Fidelity Decision Service (FDS) (service: fidelity-decision)
 - Simulates production decision logic (route by latency/cost tier, fallback policy) so experiments match runtime routing behavior.

SLOs, metrics and thresholds to collect
- Primary metrics (per-experiment):
 - fidelity_score (target >= 90 for parity experiments)
 - p50/p95 generation latency (ms)
 - per-1k-token cost (USD)
 - regression_count (number of prompts with unacceptable output change)
- Secondary metrics:
 - hallucination_rate
 - average_response_length (tokens)
 - KV cache hit ratio
- Thresholds (example):
 - If fidelity_score < 85 => FAIL
 - If p95 latency increases > 30% over baseline => FLAG for engineering review
 - If per-1k-token cost increases > 20% without fidelity improvement => REVIEW with economics team

Experiment templates (copy-and-run)
1) Baseline parity test (validation)
 Steps:
 1. Create fidelity_profile: baseline (default model + current quantization).
 2. Run sandbox-runner with recorded production sample: 30m, concurrency=10.
 3. Collect fidelity_scorecard and billing_trace.
 4. Confirm baseline fidelity_score >= 95 and store as canonical baseline.
2) Low-cost quantization trial
 Steps:
 1. Define fidelity_profile: quant-4bit-aggressive + prompt-preserve=short.
 2. Run against same input corpus as baseline with sandbox-runner for 60m.
 3. Evaluate fidelity delta, hallucination_rate, and cost delta.
 4. If fidelity_score >= 90 and cost delta >= 18% -> mark candidate for canary.
3) Latency-first routing simulation
 Steps:
 1. Attach FDS with route policy prioritizing p50 < 75ms.
 2. Run mixed traffic scenario (50% short chat, 50% long generation).
 3. Validate routing fallback behavior and per-route economics.

Example experiment manifest (YAML)
---
scenario_name: semantic-search-fidelity-test
fidelity_profile: quant-8bit-conservative
input_corpus: s3://experiments/2026-06/semantic-search-sample.json
concurrency: 25
duration: 45m
metrics: [fidelity_score, p95_latency_ms, cost_per_1k_token, hallucination_rate]
---

Billing & crediting rules (summary table)
| Scenario type | Credit policy | Notes |
|---------------|---------------|-------|
| Development replay | no billing | local proxy; developer credits not consumed |
| Staging sandbox (team) | consumption tracked; credits nominal | uses staging meter; credited to experiment budget |
| Canary public traffic | billed at reduced rate; credits apply | must have finance-approved ticket |

Ownership and roles
- Product owner: Maya Ortega — defines experimental goals, approves pass/fail criteria.
- Platform owner: Liam Chen — maintains sandbox-runner, SDKs, and proxy images.
- ML owner: Priya Kapoor — defines fidelity profiles, evaluation prompt-sets, and gold-answers.
- Finance reviewer: Noah Alvarez — validates crediting and billing outcomes.

Pass/fail and release gating rules
1) Experimental pass if:
 - fidelity_score >= 90 AND
 - p95 latency <= baseline_p95 * 1.15 AND
 - cost change <= +20% unless sponsor approves higher delta.
2) Candidate must pass one canary window (24h with minimum 10k requests) before product rollout.
3) Any safety regression (hallucination uptick > 5% absolute) fails the experiment immediately.

Data capture, privacy and retention
- Telemetry captured: request_id, route, profile_id, latency_ms, token_count, model_variant, fidelity_flags.
- PII policy: experiments may only use anonymized user prompts; recorded corpora must be scrubbed by Solutions or Data Privacy before storage.
- Retention: fidelity_scorecards and telemetry retained for 180 days in experiments S3; longer retention requires compliance approval.

SDK & CLI quickstart
- Install: pip install redwood-experiments-sdk==0.4.0
- Run baseline: redwood-experiments run --profile baseline --scenario ./scenarios/baseline.json --duration 30m --out ./results/
- Generate report: redwood-experiments report ./results/2026-06-10 --format html

Operational runbook (common issues)
- Runner fails to start: check staging IAM role and S3 path access (owner: Platform).
- Divergent baseline: confirm canonical baseline corpus and rerun with identical seed.
- Cost telemetry gaps: ensure billing_trace exporter is enabled in sandbox-runner config (config key: exporters.billing=true).

Rollout checklist for a successful candidate
1. Verify experiment pass and sign-off from ML, Platform, and Product.
2. Run 24h canary in hosted region with production routing (use minimal user-visible cohort).
3. Monitor fidelity_scorecard live; have rollback policy ready in FDS.
4. Open finance ticket for billing migration and credit adjustments.
5. Schedule release notes and customer comms with GTM.

Appendix A — fidelity_score calculation (example)
- fidelity_score = 100 - (10 * normalized_regression_rate) - (5 * normalized_hallucination_rate) - (3 * normalized_divergence)
- Normalization: each sub-metric scaled to 0-1 relative to baseline sample set.

Appendix B — sample JSON result snippet
{
 "experiment_id": "exp-2026-06-10-01",
 "fidelity_score": 92.4,
 "p95_latency_ms": 312,
 "cost_per_1k_token_usd": 0.87
}

Related pages and references
- See: /confluence/product-docs/requirements/prd-fidelity-decision-service-and-sdk-2026-06-02 for the FDS contract.
- See: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity for staging capacity quotas and reservations.

Contact and support
- For platform issues: eng-platform oncall (pager duty).
- For billing questions: Noah Alvarez (finance).
- For fidelity evaluation questions: Priya Kapoor (ML).

Change log
- 2026-06-10: Initial creation.
- 2026-07-22: Added cost gating thresholds and canary window guidance.
- 2026-09-02: Clarified retention policy and sample manifest format.

title: Aperture Realtime Conductor
author: Evelyn Park
text:
Summary: Aperture builds a personalization/reranking layer for high-traffic e-commerce sites. Very latency- and cost-sensitive — business metric: page conversion uplift while keeping per-request cost below internal target.

Key requirements: p95 latency under 40ms end-to-end for ranking and personalization calls; sustain 8k-12k req/s typical with spikes to 20k; graceful degradation to smaller models during peak; audit logs + KMS for keys; VPC peering for private traffic.

From CTO (Paraphrase): "We need predictable latency — spikes kill conversion. If p95 slips above ~40ms we see measurable drop in add-to-cart. Cost target is tight; quantization + batching must actually reduce unit cost without hurting quality."

Optimization interest: explicit ask for Redwood Optimize playbook — batching strategy per route, prefix/KV caching for repeat session tokens, recommended quantization profiles (int8 / awq) for Llama-family 13B and fallback 7B, and automated benchmarking harness we can run against our traffic shape. Also want token-level cost breakdown and per-route SLO reporting in Console.

POC notes: Sent synthetic workload script (github link in drive). SE request: compare 13B int8 vs 7B int4 fallback on latency/cost/quality for same prompts. Order of testing: baseline (no batching), continuous batching (1–4 request windows), aggressive batching for non-latency-critical routes, KV prefix cache warm vs cold.

Stated risks/blockers: internal security wants SOC2 report and encryption at rest checks; network needs VPC peering and static egress IPs for allow-listing; procurement needs estimated ARR band for sign-off.

Short action items (from AE/SE): 1) Run Redwood perf benchmark (3-day) with our S3 traffic; 2) deliver quantization recommendations + quality delta matrix; 3) provide VPC peering checklist and sample IAM/KMS config; 4) price model for Dedicated vs Hosted with burst policy.

Interested in automated benchmark artifacts (latency histograms, token-cost heatmaps), can provide sample traffic + golden prompts. Want canary rollout support for model updates and quick rollback on regressions.
