title: API gateway backpressure causing elevated 5xx rate and upstream runtime crashloops for tenant
text:
Customer VectorRetail reports a sharp increase in 5xx responses from the Redwood API beginning 2026-03-14 09:12 UTC. Errors correlate with elevated connection queue length at API gateway and rapid restarts of runtime pods serving the tenant's dedicated pool. Impacting production traffic for multiple storefront features; some requests see repeated 502/503 chains and streaming sessions drop mid-response.

Issue summary:
- Elevated 5xx rate observed for tenant VectorRetail starting 2026-03-14 09:12 UTC, concentrated in us-east region.
- Symptoms: API gateway returning 502/503/504; long latencies followed by upstream connection resets; serving-runtime pods for the dedicated pool entering crashloop back-to-back.
Impact:
- Several VectorRetail storefront endpoints are erroring for end users and internal health checks. Estimated 25% error rate for requests routed to dedicated pool at peak.
Environment:
- prod-us-east (dedicated pool for VectorRetail).
- Model traffic: mix of redwood/open-8b-v1 and redwood/compat-4x-slim, mostly short chat completions and streaming.
Timeline (high level):
- 09:12 UTC: customer reports first errors.
- 09:15 UTC: Platform metrics show queue growth at API gateway and increased upstream 5xx.
- 09:18 UTC: Several runtime pods restarted; some pods repeatedly OOM or exit 137 within 30s of start.
- 09:30 UTC: SRE throttled incoming requests to the pool and engaged temporary rate-limiter to stabilize.
- 10:05 UTC: Partial stabilization after reducing concurrency and applying memory limit rollback on runtime image.
- 11:00 UTC: Customer still observes intermittent 502s during streaming sessions.

1) Send a burst of concurrent streaming chat completion requests (50-100 parallel connections) to the VectorRetail tenant endpoint in prod-us-east.
2) Use payloads that request streaming with moderately long response (max_tokens ~1024) and frequent small chunks to encourage KV cache usage.
3) Observe API gateway queue length metric and per-route 5xx rate within 1-3 minutes.
4) Monitor serving-runtime pod logs for OOMs, kernel-fallback lines, and crashloop exit codes.

2026-03-14T09:16:22Z apigw: queue_length=348 backlog_ms=4123 route=vector-retail/streaming 5xx_count=42
2026-03-14T09:17:03Z runtime-pod-7fdc OOMKilled: memory usage 14.8GB of 16GB allocated (exit_code=137)
2026-03-14T09:17:05Z runtime-pod-7fdc kernel: rtx memcpy fallback invoked for attention kernels

2026-03-14T09:29:58Z autoscaler: warmup_attempts=3 scale_up_blocked_reason=api_rate_throttle

We started seeing spikes of 502/503 around 09:10 UTC and a lot of our streaming sessions drop. This affects checkout preview and chat assistants. Please advise; we are on a marketing push today.

2026-03-14T09:20Z Support (Aisha Park): Acknowledged — opening incident and escalating to SRE. Collecting logs and metrics. Please share tenant request IDs if available.
2026-03-14T09:25Z SRE (Marco Liu): Noted high apigw queue_length and several runtime pod restarts; hypothesis: backpressure at gateway plus memory pressure on dedicated runtime leading to OOM crashloops. Pausing automated scale actions to prevent flapping.
2026-03-14T09:40Z Support (Aisha Park): Customer provided sample request IDs: r-vec-000124, r-vec-000130, r-vec-000145. Forwarded to SRE for trace lookup.
2026-03-14T10:00Z SRE (Marco Liu): Applied temporary mitigation: lowered per-tenant concurrency limit from 80->30, increased max_cached_prefix to reduce KV thrash, rolled back a recent runtime memory-change config. Seeing 5xx rate drop from 25%->8%.
2026-03-15T08:30Z Product (Priya Sharma): Noted this tenant was on a recent model variant rollout (compat-4x-slim) yesterday; we should verify kernel selection and quantization profile interactions.
2026-03-15T09:10Z SRE (Marco Liu): Running controlled soak with synthetic traffic; observing stable behavior with concurrency cap and reverted runtime mem config. Continuing monitoring for 24h.
2026-03-15T11:00Z Customer (VectorRetail - ops@vectorretail.com): Confirming improved behavior after throttling; still occasionally see a dropped streaming chunk ~1/min.
2026-03-15T11:30Z Support (Aisha Park): Scheduling follow-up call with VectorRetail to review traffic patterns and recommend batching/streaming knob adjustments.

Initial hypothesis: Apigw queue pressure due to tenant burst + upstream slow kernel path causing long-lived connections and connection accumulation.
Observed frequent kernel-fallback messages in runtime logs indicating fallback from optimized attention kernel to slower memcpy-based path which increases CPU/memory pressure.
OOMs correspond to model variant memory allocation spikes; deduced that the recent runtime config lowered headroom for ephemeral tensors during streaming.
Autoscaler warmup was blocked by API-side rate limiting which prevented gradual scale-up and resulted in concentrated load on few pods, leading to thrashing.
No evidence of underlying hardware failure; GPU metrics per-node are within expected ranges but per-pod memory usage spikes correlate with long streaming sessions and KV cache misses.

Combination of API gateway backpressure during a tenant burst, a recent runtime memory config change that reduced headroom for streaming workloads, and blocked autoscaler warmup due to rate-limiter interactions. These factors concentrated load on a small set of pods, causing OOMs and crashloops that amplified 5xx responses.

A) Revert the memory headroom change that reduced runtime ephemeral allocation (done 2026-03-14 09:50 UTC).
B) Adjust apigw per-tenant concurrency controls to smoother degradation policy and add circuit-breaker soft-queue limits (scheduled).
C) Add autoscaler rule to ignore short-term API rate-limit throttles during warmup or surface a warmup override for dedicated pools (investigating).
D) Run model-variant kernel-selection validation for compat-4x-slim under streaming workloads to identify quantization/kernel fallback triggers (P2 engineering task).
E) Follow-up with VectorRetail on recommended client-side rate limiting/backoff and batching best practices (scheduled call).

Temporary mitigation: lowered tenant concurrency cap and rolled back recent runtime mem config which reduced OOMs and runtime restarts. Applied increased KV cache size to reduce prefix thrashing.
Result: 5xx rate dropped from ~25% peak to sustained ~5-8% with most streaming sessions successful. Customer reported improved experience but occasional single-chunk drops persist (~1/min).
Permanent work items: implement apigw soft-queue circuit-breaker, autoscaler warmup override, and kernel-selection validation for the model variant. Assigned to SRE/Runtime/Platform teams.
Customer communication: committed to 48h monitoring window and follow-up meeting to review changes and traffic shaping recommendations.
Status: Incident partially mitigated — monitoring in progress until control changes are implemented and validated.

Complete engineering action items B-D, validate with synthetic and customer traffic, and review post-incident in 72 hours. Owner: Marco Liu.

title: Streaming race after auth token refresh causes interleaved paragraphs and missing closing punctuation
text:
Issue summary: Customer reports that long-running SSE streams intermittently return interleaved paragraph fragments and sometimes omit final punctuation after a short auth token rotation. Impact: QuantaDocs observed 3-7% of streaming responses missing closing punctuation or containing sentences where paragraphs are mixed (two paragraphs merged with parts out of order). This leads to downstream parsing failures for their document ingestion pipeline. Environment: Production, us-east-1, Dedicated tenancy with token rotation frequency: 5 minutes for short-lived session tokens. Steps to reproduce (observed by customer): 1) Start an SSE chat session to /v1/streams with a standard system+user prompt that elicits a multi-paragraph long-form answer (~300-500 tokens). 2) Allow the session to be open for >3 minutes. 3) Trigger an auth refresh (customer-side or via normal rotate) or wait for automatic token refresh to happen. 4) Client reconnects/resumes using the session id/last-event-id; sometimes receives interleaved fragments from two worker backends. Expected: Resume should stitch fragments in order and preserve terminal punctuation. Actual: On ~3-7% of attempts, the resumed stream contains chunks that interleave paragraph fragments (e.g., the end of paragraph 1 followed by the beginning of paragraph 3, then the remainder of paragraph 2), and in ~1% the closing punctuation for the final paragraph is missing. Additional notes: Customer uses an HTTP reverse proxy before the client which preserves Last-Event-ID header. They rely on the server-provided resume token in SSE body. They experimented with longer token TTL and saw reduced frequency.

Open SSE stream to /v1/streams with a prompt returning multi-paragraph output (~400 tokens)
Keep the connection idle for >3 minutes so token rotation will occur on client or server side
Allow auth-flow to issue a new short-lived token, then perform reconnect/resume using Last-Event-ID or resume token
Observe assembled stream for out-of-order paragraph fragments and missing final punctuation

Initial support triage: reproduced at low rate on staging when forcing short token TTL to 10s and performing reconnect during mid-generation.
Hypothesis 1: resume routing race — resume request can be routed to a different worker which begins producing the next sequence before the previous worker finishes sending its tail; mismatch in sequence ordering in assembly logic causes interleaving.
Hypothesis 2: token rotation causes a transient double-connection window where both workers consider themselves authoritative for the session; last-event-id hints diverge between workers.
Observed evidence: logs show overlapping seq numbers and two workers (worker-08 and worker-12) with partial_choice_ids pc_43 and pc_44 both sending segments within milliseconds of each other. Assembly reported "mismatch" and sequence array indicates out-of-order arrival: [202,203,201].
Edge-proxy behavior: proxy preserves Last-Event-ID header, but when cookie/token rotates, client may open a new TCP connection that LB routes to a different backend; LB sticky session TTL observed to be 30s so not always sticky across rotates.
Reproducer: integration test created that simulates rotation mid-stream and triggers reconnect; failing rate ~5/1000 on local agent with two simulated workers; increasing inter-worker arbitration (locking) reduced failure rate to zero in the test harness.
Potential regressions: recent change in resume orchestration (PR #2387) touched worker handoff and reduce-lock path for resume speed — may have opened a microwindow where two workers can both believe they should serve the resumed stream.

2026-03-10 15:10 - Aisha Gomez (Support): Initial report from QuantaDocs included example outputs and two sample transcripts. Customer attached last-event-id values and observed that parser failed when final punctuation missing. Asked for session logs and requested customer to reproduce with debug header X-Debug-Resume: true.
2026-03-10 18:04 - Ravi Patel (SRE): Reproduced locally with forced token TTL=12s. Captured worker logs showing overlapping seq numbers. Filed INT-4312 for cross-team handoff to serving-runtime to investigate resume arbitration.
2026-03-11 09:25 - Lina Becker (Serving Runtime Eng): Noted PR 2387 altered optimistic resume fast-path; adding forced lease check eliminated interleaving in repro. Testing patch to add a short global resume lease (50ms) to ensure previous worker drains before new worker emits tail chunks.
2026-03-12 11:47 - QuantaDocs (Customer): Confirmed regression visible after small traffic spike. They validated that increasing token TTL to 10 minutes reduced incidence but is not acceptable for their security posture. Asked for ETA on fix and whether there is a recommended workaround beyond TTL increase.
2026-03-13 08:30 - Ravi Patel (SRE): Scoped workaround: set reverse-proxy to preserve connection affinity for 30s across auth refresh, or use long-poll fallback (non-streaming) for critical documents. Patch candidate under review by Serving Runtime team.
2026-03-13 14:02 - Lina Becker (Serving Runtime Eng): Patch #2399 created to add resume lease and a stricter sequence handshake between workers. Running canary in dedicated infra for QuantaDocs starting 2026-03-14.

Workaround: customer set reverse-proxy affinity for 30s and temporarily increased token TTL to 10 minutes (reduced failures to <0.1%). Permanent fix: serving-runtime patch #2399 (adds short resume lease + stricter sequence handshake) merged and scheduled for staged rollout. Follow-ups: 1) QA regression for resume fast-path to add synthetic test forcing mid-generation rotate; 2) Monitor canary metrics for interleaving events in us-east-1; 3) Update runbook with guidance for customers using short-lived auth tokens during long-lived SSE streams. Ticket remains open until canary completes and customer confirms resolution.

author: Noura El-Khoury
text:
Redwood and SkyForge aligned on a co-marketing plan for Redwood’s public benchmark report launch. SkyForge will place a newsletter blurb in the July issue and optionally amplify via marketplace/social, contingent on receiving final copy + a compliant “how we measured” snippet and approved visuals under embargo. Redwood will provide a partner-ready copy block with conservative claims (no “fastest overall” language), a co-branded image, UTM-tagged links, and an embargoed briefing doc. Both teams agreed to a 24–48 hour approval buffer and a single source-of-truth for the headline metrics and disclaimers.

Embargo date/time alignment and pre-brief logistics
Shared messaging: latency/$ framing, disclaimers, and what not to claim
Newsletter placement details (slot, word count, CTA, UTM)
Asset list: co-branded image, landing page URL, PDF link, webinar mention
Approval workflow (brand + legal) and timeline

Can SkyForge reference specific regions (e.g., EU) in the newsletter, or should it stay generic?
Do we include the webinar CTA in the same newsletter slot, or keep it to the landing page?
What’s the latest time SkyForge can receive “final-final” assets and still hit send?
Should we avoid any competitor mention entirely in partner channels?

Redwood to send embargo details + partner briefing one-pager (incl. approved claim language + disclaimers) by 2025-06-27 EOD PT.
SkyForge to confirm newsletter placement (date, audience segment, character limits) and provide UTM requirements by 2025-06-28.
Redwood to deliver two copy variants (short/long) + one co-branded image + link bundle by 2025-07-01.
SkyForge to run internal brand/legal review and return edits by 2025-07-03.
Both teams to schedule a 15-min final go/no-go the day before launch.

Noura El-Khoury — Send SkyForge embargo + launch timeline + review checkpoints — due 2025-06-27
Soojin Lee — Provide partner-safe messaging block (what we can/can’t say) and approved headline metric phrasing — due 2025-06-27
Ben Carter — Generate UTM-tagged links for newsletter + marketplace listing + social — due 2025-07-01
Wei Chen — Package “methodology in 5 bullets” snippet + disclaimer text for partner use — due 2025-07-01
Priya Desai — Confirm newsletter issue date, placement, and word-count/format constraints — due 2025-06-28
Evan Brooks — Confirm whether marketplace banner/module is available during launch week — due 2025-06-28

Meeting Header
Date: Jun 26, 2025
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 46 min
Attendees: Noura El-Khoury, Soojin Lee, Ben Carter, Wei Chen (Redwood Inference); Priya Desai, Evan Brooks, Marta Kowalczyk (SkyForge Cloud)

[00:00] Noura El-Khoury: Cool, recording just started. Thanks everybody for making time. This is our partner co-marketing sync for the benchmark report launch. Goal today is embargo timing, messaging alignment, and the newsletter placement details. Priya, Evan, Marta — thanks for joining.

[00:18] Priya Desai: Yeah, of course. We’ve been looking forward to this. We just want to make sure we’re, you know, not stepping on any legal landmines with benchmarks.

[00:27] Soojin Lee: Same. We are very, very allergic to “fastest” claims unless they’re narrowly scoped with methodology. So we’ll keep it clean.

[00:36] Ben Carter: And also make sure the links are measurable. We’ll do UTMs so both sides can attribute.

[00:43] Evan Brooks: Great. I can cover the newsletter mechanics and what our marketplace team can do.

[00:50] Noura El-Khoury: Perfect. Quick agenda: one, embargo and dates. Two, the copy block and what we want SkyForge to say. Three, where it lands — newsletter, maybe marketplace, maybe social. Four, review process.

[01:06] Noura El-Khoury: On embargo: we’re targeting launch week in early July. We’re still finalizing the exact day internally because legal review is… doing legal review.

[01:17] Marta Kowalczyk: (laughs) Always.

[01:19] Noura El-Khoury: Yeah. The current plan is a public landing page plus interactive table plus PDF report. We’d like to pre-brief you under embargo so your comms can go out same day.

[01:35] Priya Desai: What does “under embargo” mean for you? Like we can have it in our scheduling tool but not send? Or we can’t even share internally?

[01:44] Soojin Lee: You can share internally with folks who need to approve — marketing leadership, brand, legal — but we’ll ask you to keep it on a need-to-know list and not forward broadly.

[01:55] Wei Chen: We can also provide a short “partner briefing” PDF so it’s not like the full 30-page report flying around.

[02:03] Evan Brooks: That helps. Our standard is we can accept embargoed assets 5 business days before send. If it’s shorter than that, it’s still possible but risk.

[02:14] Noura El-Khoury: Understood. We can commit to a partner pack by July 1 at the latest. Does that still work for your July newsletter issue?

[02:24] Priya Desai: The July issue has two waves. One is July 9, the other is July 16. If you’re launching week of the 8th, we can try to align with the 9th.

[02:36] Ben Carter: That’s great. If our launch is the 9th, we’d want you to send the same day, ideally within a few hours.

[02:44] Evan Brooks: Usually our send is 8am Pacific.

[02:48] Soojin Lee: That’s fine as long as the landing page is live. We’ll coordinate exact hour.

[02:55] Noura El-Khoury: Ok. Let’s assume: Redwood launch day July 9, SkyForge newsletter July 9 at 8am PT, pending our final confirmation.

[03:08] Priya Desai: Works as a placeholder. We’ll need final assets no later than July 3 for approvals, realistically.

[03:14] Noura El-Khoury: Yep, we can do that.

[03:17] Noura El-Khoury: Messaging. So the headline we’re using publicly is around “latency per dollar” — basically production inference economics. It’s not just tokens per second. It normalizes cost and latency.

[03:31] Marta Kowalczyk: Is it literally written as latency slash dollar? Like “latency/$”? That can look a little… crypto.

[03:38] Soojin Lee: (laughs) We’ve had that debate internally too. In partner channels we can write it as “latency-per-dollar (latency/$)” once, then just “latency-per-dollar.”

[03:51] Priya Desai: Ok. And are you comparing against other providers? Or is it just Redwood across regions.

[03:57] Soojin Lee: The public report is Redwood-first. We may include limited contextual baselines with strong caveats, but partner copy should not mention competitors. That’s the safest path.

[04:09] Wei Chen: We will include a methodology snippet: models tested, regions, concurrency, prefill/decode mix, caching policy. But in the newsletter we keep it to a couple bullets.

[04:21] Evan Brooks: Can you give us a single sentence we can reuse that’s legally blessed?

[04:26] Soojin Lee: Yes. Something like: “Redwood published a reproducible benchmark on production inference economics across multiple regions, including p50/p95 latency and cost-per-1M tokens, with full methodology and configs.”

[04:41] Priya Desai: Nice. And then what’s the CTA? Is it “read report” or “try Redwood” or something.

[04:48] Ben Carter: Ideally “Explore the interactive benchmark” as primary, and secondary “Get started with hosted API” for developers. But we can tailor if your audience is more enterprise.

[05:01] Evan Brooks: Our newsletter audience is mixed: cloud architects, some devs. But the highest click-through is usually “interactive” tools, not PDFs.

[05:10] Ben Carter: Perfect. We’ll set the main link to the interactive page and include a small “Download PDF” secondary link if there’s room.

[05:20] Noura El-Khoury: The other thing is we want to include a SkyForge angle. Not “we ran it on SkyForge GPUs” — because we didn’t — but more like: Redwood supports deployments across hosted/dedicated/private and runs in cloud environments like SkyForge.

[05:36] Evan Brooks: Careful: we should not imply it runs on SkyForge unless there’s a marketplace listing or validated integration.

[05:42] Noura El-Khoury: Right. Good call. We can position it as “available via SkyForge Marketplace” if that’s accurate.

[05:48] Evan Brooks: It is accurate; your listing is live, but it’s currently a “contact us” style listing, not click-to-deploy. We can still feature it.

[05:58] Priya Desai: If you want to mention marketplace, we need the exact listing name and URL.

[06:04] Ben Carter: I’ll generate UTMs for that too.

[06:07] Wei Chen: Also: disclaimers. We’ll give you a short disclaimer text that says results vary by workload, measured on specific configs, and so on.

[06:18] Marta Kowalczyk: In the newsletter, do you want us to include disclaimers? We usually have limited space.

[06:23] Soojin Lee: Ideally a short one-liner like “See methodology for details; results vary by workload and configuration.” And we can link “methodology” to the section on the landing page.

[06:35] Priya Desai: That’s doable.

[06:37] Noura El-Khoury: Next: placement. Priya, can you talk us through the constraints? Like word count, image, etc.

[06:45] Priya Desai: Sure. The newsletter module is typically 70–120 words with one image. If you want two links, that’s fine, but we prefer a single primary link. We can do a headline, short body, then a CTA button.

[07:01] Ben Carter: Great. We’ll give you a headline + 2 variants: 80 words and 120 words.

[07:06] Evan Brooks: We can also add a marketplace tile same week, but that’s separate. That requires creative in 1200x628 and a short blurb.

[07:15] Noura El-Khoury: That’s interesting. Is that guaranteed inventory or “best effort”?

[07:20] Evan Brooks: More like best effort unless we reserve it this week. I can check.

[07:26] Marta Kowalczyk: If you do marketplace tile, please keep the copy more product-y than “benchmark-y.” Like “Optimize inference economics” not “we beat X.”

[07:36] Soojin Lee: 100%.

[07:38] Noura El-Khoury: Ok, so far. Let’s talk approvals and what’s sensitive. Soojin, can you outline what phrases we want to avoid.

[07:46] Soojin Lee: Yes. Avoid: “fastest,” “best,” “industry-leading,” “number one,” anything absolute. Avoid implying SkyForge endorses the benchmark results. Avoid competitor call-outs. And don’t say “guaranteed savings.” Instead: “measured,” “observed,” “in our tests,” “see methodology.”

[08:06] Priya Desai: That’s consistent with our policy too.

[08:09] Wei Chen: We’ll include an approved “safe language” block so your team can copy/paste.

[08:16] Evan Brooks: Quick question: are you guys using time-to-first-token? Our audience asks for that.

[08:22] Soojin Lee: We have TTFT for streaming, but we’re debating how much to highlight it in v1. The main metric is latency-per-dollar with p50/p95 latency and cost per million tokens as supporting.

[08:36] Marta Kowalczyk: If you don’t have TTFT public, don’t mention it in our channel.

[08:41] Soojin Lee: Agree.

[08:43] Noura El-Khoury: Ok. Now, timeline check. Redwood will send partner pack by July 1. SkyForge needs final by July 3. Can we do a two-step: “draft assets” by July 1, “final assets” by July 3?

[08:57] Priya Desai: That’s fine as long as the draft is 90% there. Our legal hates last-minute changes.

[09:04] Soojin Lee: Understood. The only changes between draft and final should be numbers or date/time, not core claims.

[09:11] Ben Carter: And from tracking perspective, if the URL changes, we’ll redirect. But ideally it won’t.

[09:18] Noura El-Khoury: Let’s talk about the “shared messaging” angle. We want to position Redwood as developer-first inference platform, and SkyForge as a cloud partner enabling workloads. We don’t want it to feel like a random benchmark drop.

[09:33] Priya Desai: For our newsletter, we typically frame it as “Partner Spotlight” or “New Research.” What’s your preference?

[09:40] Soojin Lee: “New research” works, but I’d avoid “research” if it implies academic. Maybe “New benchmark report.”

[09:49] Marta Kowalczyk: “Benchmark report” is fine.

[09:52] Evan Brooks: Also, we can add a line: “Now available via SkyForge Marketplace.” That ties it back.

[09:59] Noura El-Khoury: Great.

[10:02] (small crosstalk)

[10:03] Ben Carter: On UTMs: we’ll provide one link for newsletter and one for marketplace tile. Then you’ll see performance in your own analytics, and we’ll see it in ours.

[10:12] Priya Desai: We can’t always guarantee UTMs stay intact because of our link wrapper, but we can try.

[10:17] Ben Carter: Totally. If you have your own link wrapper parameters, send them and we’ll integrate.

[10:24] Noura El-Khoury: Ok. Let’s pause and see if there are any concerns.

[10:28] Priya Desai: Biggest concern is we don’t want our brand associated with “Redwood is cheaper than AWS” or something like that.

[10:34] Soojin Lee: Same. We will not put that in partner assets.

[10:38] Priya Desai: Second is timing. If Redwood slips by a week, does your team still want the July 9 slot?

[10:45] Noura El-Khoury: If we slip, we may move you to July 16. We’ll give you a firm go/no-go 48 hours ahead.

[10:53] Evan Brooks: Ok, just let us know. If you’re not live, we can’t run the module.

[11:00] Wei Chen: Also: asset sizes. We’ll deliver a 1200x628, plus an SVG logo lockup if needed.

[11:08] Marta Kowalczyk: Please no SVG in email. PNG is safer.

[11:12] Wei Chen: Got it.

[11:14] Noura El-Khoury: I want to spend a few minutes on the “embargo brief.” It’ll have: what’s launching, what’s new, approved copy, FAQ responses if people ask “how did you measure.”

[11:28] Priya Desai: Can you add a short “if asked about competitor baselines” line? Even if we don’t mention, people might reply.

[11:35] Soojin Lee: Yes. Something like: “The report focuses on Redwood performance; any comparisons are contextual and methodology-bound. For details, refer to the methodology section.”

[11:46] Priya Desai: Perfect.

[11:48] Evan Brooks: If we do marketplace tile, we’ll need a short headline like 45 characters. And a subhead maybe 90.

[11:56] Noura El-Khoury: We can provide that. Something like “Explore latency-per-dollar benchmarks” and “Interactive results by region and model.”

[12:06] Marta Kowalczyk: I’d avoid “by model” if model names are sensitive. But I think it’s okay.

[12:11] Soojin Lee: The landing page will have a curated model set; it’s fine to say “by model.”

[12:16] Ben Carter: Also, we’re doing a webinar the following week. Optional: include “Join the webinar” as a secondary CTA, but only if there’s room.

[12:26] Priya Desai: I would not include that in the main module. Too many CTAs reduces clicks.

[12:30] Noura El-Khoury: Fair. We can keep webinar on landing page.

[12:34] Wei Chen: We’ll add a small callout on the landing page “Live walkthrough on X date.”

[12:40] Evan Brooks: Ok.

[12:42] Noura El-Khoury: Jumping ahead — review workflow. We’ll send copy + image + link bundle to Priya and Evan. You route to your legal/brand. We’ll have Soojin + our legal review any edits. Turnaround target 24 hours.

[12:57] Priya Desai: Great. Please put everything in one doc. If it’s scattered across email threads, it gets messy.

[13:04] Ben Carter: We can do a single Google doc plus a zip for images.

[13:08] Priya Desai: Perfect.

[13:10] (brief pause)

[13:12] Marta Kowalczyk: Can I ask a dumb question? What exactly is “latency per dollar.” Like the denominator is GPU cost? Token cost? People will ask.

[13:20] Soojin Lee: Not dumb. In the report, we define it as end-to-end request latency normalized by the effective cost of generating the output under the same config. It’s computed from measured throughput and our published price-per-token for hosted, plus infrastructure costs for dedicated contexts where applicable. But again, partner copy should just say “latency-per-dollar metric; see methodology.”

[13:44] Wei Chen: We’ll give you a one-sentence explanation that is not math-heavy.

[13:49] Marta Kowalczyk: Great.

[13:51] Evan Brooks: Another question: are you going to say “regions: North America, Europe, APAC”? We like that global angle.

[13:58] Noura El-Khoury: Yes, we can say “multiple regions” and list them generically. If we list specific region codes, we have to make sure they’re supported and stable. Lukas from EMEA is pretty sensitive about that.

[14:12] Priya Desai: For us, “EU and US coverage” is good enough.

[14:16] Soojin Lee: Great.

[14:18] Ben Carter: From a performance standpoint, we’ll also have an on-page disclaimer about variance and reruns. That’s good to point to.

[14:25] Priya Desai: Good.

[14:27] Noura El-Khoury: Ok, Evan, can you confirm next steps on your side: newsletter slot and marketplace tile check.

[14:34] Evan Brooks: Yes. I’ll confirm by tomorrow whether we can reserve a marketplace module for that week. Newsletter slot is available for July 9, but we need final by July 3.

[14:45] Noura El-Khoury: Great.

[14:46] Priya Desai: And I’ll confirm the word count and the exact template — headline limit, CTA button text.

[14:53] Noura El-Khoury: Perfect.

[14:55] (The conversation continues with minor clarifications on formatting and tracking)

[15:02] Ben Carter: Button text — would “Explore benchmark” fit? Or do you prefer “Learn more.”

[15:06] Priya Desai: “Explore benchmark” is fine. “Learn more” is too generic.

[15:10] Wei Chen: Great.

[15:12] Soojin Lee: And for the headline, something like “New: Benchmarking production inference economics.”

[15:18] Marta Kowalczyk: That’s good. Just don’t make it sound like a “survey.”

[15:22] Soojin Lee: Yep.

[15:25] Noura El-Khoury: Ok, we’re at time. Let me recap and then we’ll drop.

[15:30] Noura El-Khoury: Recap: Target send date July 9 8am PT, pending Redwood final launch confirmation. Redwood delivers draft partner pack July 1: copy variants, one image, link bundle with UTMs, and a short methodology/disclaimer snippet. SkyForge confirms constraints and optional marketplace tile by June 28, and provides edits back by July 3. We do a quick go/no-go the day before.

[15:56] Priya Desai: Sounds right.

[15:58] Evan Brooks: Yep.

[16:00] Marta Kowalczyk: Thanks everyone.

[16:02] Noura El-Khoury: Thank you. We’ll follow up by email today with the action items.

(Transcript ends — Fireflies note: some sections were not captured due to crosstalk and brief audio drop around 10:02.)

alex: Hey folks — PR #2401 is up and ready for review: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-inference/pull/2401

alex: Summary: tweak KV cache eviction threshold + add a cold-prefix short-circuit that routes cheap models for cold prefixes. Goal: reduce token cost for low-hit workloads while keeping tail latency acceptable.

alex: Key changes:
- Eviction threshold: `EVICT_THRESHOLD = 0.5` (was 0.6)
- New config `cold_prefix_timeout_ms = 800`
- Routing fallback to `gptx-small-int8` for prefixes with low reuse

priya: taking a look. does this increase cache churn for high-concurrency workloads?

sam: quick read — looks reasonable. can we export `cache_evictions_per_min` and `fallback_route_count` metrics before merging?

kevin: cc @maria @ops-sre — need perf/rollout signoff. Also pls add a feature flag so we can canary it.

maria: I can run a staging smoke tomorrow AM. pls add a canary flag + a short perf job (1k reqs, seq=128) and post results.

alex: pushed changes: added `kv_routing_canary=true`, metric exports, and a small perf harness. bench results:

`````
baseline: p50=18ms p95=72ms cost/token=$0.00072
canary: p50=19ms p95=75ms cost/token=$0.00068 (-5.6% cost)
`````

alex: Notes: p95 up ~4% in synthetic run, cost down ~5-6% — probably ok for most customers but want ops signoff for Dedicated traffic.

ops-sre: Recommend canary rollout 5% for 24h, watch `fallback_route_count` and `p95_latency` alerts. :thumbsup:

priya: LGTM from perf side, small nit: rename `cold_prefix_timeout_ms` to `cold_prefix_ttl_ms`.

alex: updated PR with rename. ci-bot: build passed, all tests green. Can anyone add an approval so I can merge in tomorrow's window?

sam: Approved. :+1:

kevin: Approved. merging after staging canary if no regressions.

title: Rollback semantics and hooks (Redwood Private upgrades)
author: Michael Nguyen
text:
## Purpose
This page defines **rollback semantics** for Redwood Private upgrades and the **hook contracts** used by the installer and Helm charts to rollback safely and deterministically.

Goals:
- Provide clear **entry points** for rollback across phases (precheck → backup → control plane → data plane).
- Define a **hook interface** for components (control plane services, data plane workloads, storage/migrations) to participate in rollback.
- Make rollback **safe by default**, **idempotent**, and **auditable**.
- Document how to handle **partial upgrades**, **schema migrations**, and **model cache/state**.

Non-goals:
- Full blue/green cutover for every Private environment (see ADR).
- Guarantee rollback after every possible irreversible data migration (we require explicit “rollback supported” signaling per release).

---

## Definitions
- **Upgrade attempt**: one execution of an upgrade plan by the private installer.
- **Upgrade state**: persisted record of plan version, steps executed, artifacts, and checkpoint outputs.
- **Rollback**: coordinated process to restore the deployment to the **previous known-good version (N-1)** using stored state + backups + component hooks.
- **Control plane (CP)**: Redwood Private control plane services (API, auth, scheduler/orchestrator, console backend, upgrade controller).
- **Data plane (DP)**: model serving runtime, routers, worker pools, ingress sidecars, and per-model caches.
- **Rollback supported**: release declares that rollback from N to N-1 is supported given the documented constraints.

Version convention:
- Default supported upgrade path is **N-1 → N**. Rollback is **N → N-1**.

---

## Rollback invariants (must always hold)
1. **No automatic rollback without operator confirmation**, except when explicitly configured (`--auto-rollback-on-failure`) and only before “Point of No Return” (see below).
2. Rollback must be **deterministic**: given the same stored upgrade state and artifacts, rollback performs the same actions in the same order.
3. Rollback must be **idempotent**: re-running `rollback` after a failure must either continue safely or no-op completed steps.
4. Rollback must preserve **auditability**:
 - Emit audit log events for rollback start/stop and per-stage outcomes.
 - Store the rollback run log and final outcome in the support bundle.
5. Rollback must favor **availability over performance**: safe/known-good configuration first; optimization re-tuning later.

---

## Rollback entry points
Rollback can be invoked from three primary entry points:

### 1) Pre-deploy / “no changes applied”
**When:** prechecks or artifact validation fails before any Kubernetes resources or databases are modified.

**Semantics:** No rollback is needed. Installer prints a failure summary and remediation steps.

**Required behavior:**
- Persist a failed upgrade attempt record (for audit/support).
- Do not modify the stored “current version” pointer.

### 2) In-place changes applied, but before the Point of No Return
**When:** some CP/DP resources have been updated, but we have not performed any irreversible schema changes.

**Semantics:** Rollback is supported via:
- Reverting Helm releases to previous chart/app versions.
- Restoring config/state from saved checkpoints.
- Clearing/reconciling caches.

**Default behavior:** Offer rollback interactively; allow `--auto-rollback-on-failure`.

### 3) After the Point of No Return (PoNR)
**When:** a step marks PoNR reached (typically schema/data migration that is not guaranteed reversible).

**Semantics:** Rollback may still be possible, but only with **explicitly supported** restore paths:
- Full database restore from backup snapshot taken at the start of the upgrade attempt.
- “Down migrations” only if the release provides them and they are declared safe.

**Required behavior:**
- Installer must require explicit confirmation with a typed acknowledgement:
 - `--confirm-rollback-after-ponr "I UNDERSTAND THIS MAY CAUSE DATA LOSS"`
- Installer must print a prominent warning describing potential data loss and downtime.

---

## Rollback triggers
Rollback may be initiated by:
- Operator: `redwood-private rollback` (recommended).
- Operator: `redwood-private upgrade --rollback` (roll back the most recent attempt).
- Automation: `--auto-rollback-on-failure` (only pre-PoNR).
- SRE/Support guided recovery (manual steps may be required for PoNR scenarios).

Rollback should be recommended (but not auto-triggered) when:
- CP health checks fail for > 10 minutes after upgrade.
- DB migration step exceeds configured timeout AND cannot be safely resumed.
- DP error rates exceed rollback thresholds during the upgrade window (see SRE runbook).

---

## Persisted upgrade state (required for rollback)
The installer persists an **upgrade state record** (stored in the private installer state store; mirrored in the support bundle) containing:
- Upgrade attempt ID
- Previous version (N-1) + target version (N)
- Artifact digests (charts/images/bundles) for both N-1 and N
- Completed steps and timestamps
- Checkpoint outputs (e.g., Helm revision numbers, migration IDs applied, config snapshots)
- PoNR flag + the step that set it

Minimum required checkpoint outputs:
- Helm release name + namespace + revision for CP and DP releases
- DB migration baseline (last applied migration ID at start)
- Backup snapshot IDs and verification status

---

## Hook model
Rollback is driven by a set of hooks executed by the installer and/or Helm. Hooks are used to:
- Quiesce traffic
- Prevent concurrent writes
- Restore prior configuration
- Roll back schema changes (when supported)
- Reconcile runtime caches

### Hook phases
Hooks are executed in phases:
1. `rollback.pre` (quiesce & safety gates)
2. `rollback.restore` (revert versions and restore state)
3. `rollback.post` (health checks, cleanup, unlock)

### Hook contract (all hooks)
Each hook must:
- Be **idempotent**.
- Have a **bounded runtime** and a clear timeout.
- Produce structured output for logs (stdout/stderr) and an explicit exit code.
- Avoid printing sensitive values (secrets, tokens). Print resource names/IDs only.

Hook input context (conceptual; passed via env vars/args depending on implementation):
- `UPGRADE_ATTEMPT_ID`
- `FROM_VERSION` (N)
- `TO_VERSION` (N-1)
- `PONR_REACHED=true|false`
- `BACKUP_SNAPSHOT_IDS` (if applicable)
- `DRY_RUN=true|false`

Hook result semantics:
- **Success**: installer continues.
- **Retryable failure**: installer may retry (default: 3 retries with exponential backoff) if hook is marked retryable.
- **Fatal failure**: installer stops and instructs operator to run manual recovery.

### Hook registration
Components participate in rollback via:
- **Helm hooks** for Kubernetes resources and Jobs.
- **Installer-managed hooks** for environment-level tasks (artifact switching, bundle validation, backup restore orchestration).

We standardize on these labels/annotations for Kubernetes Jobs used as rollback hooks:
- `redwood.ai/hook-type: rollback`
- `redwood.ai/hook-phase: pre|restore|post`
- `redwood.ai/hook-component: control-plane|data-plane|db|cache|network`
- `redwood.ai/hook-timeout-seconds: "600"` (string because annotations)

---

## Ordering rules (deterministic rollback)
Rollback ordering must prevent partial incompatibilities. Ordering is:

### Phase A — Safety gates (`rollback.pre`)
1. **Acquire upgrade lock** (prevent parallel upgrades/rollbacks).
2. **Freeze external automation** (e.g., disable GitOps reconciliation if configured; print operator instructions).
3. **Quiesce traffic**:
 - Option A (preferred): set DP routers to “drain mode” (stop accepting new requests; allow in-flight completion).
 - Option B: apply ingress maintenance policy (return 503 with retry-after) when drain mode is unavailable.
4. **Pause background jobs**:
 - Scheduled evals
 - Model warmers/prefetchers
 - Token accounting batch jobs

### Phase B — Restore (`rollback.restore`)
5. **Control plane rollback first** (CP must be compatible with DP rollback actions and migration tooling):
 - Roll back CP Helm release(s) to prior revision OR apply pinned N-1 artifacts.
 - Wait for CP readiness gates.
6. **Database/schema handling** (see “Schema migrations” section):
 - If PoNR not reached: ensure no further migrations run; restore baseline-compatible settings.
 - If PoNR reached: restore from snapshot and verify.
7. **Data plane rollback**:
 - Roll back DP chart revisions to N-1.
 - Disable any N-only features in DP config.
8. **Model cache/state reconciliation**:
 - Clear or invalidate caches that may contain N-only formats.
 - Rebuild indices lazily post-rollback.

### Phase C — Post checks (`rollback.post`)
9. **Health checks**:
 - CP API readiness + auth readiness
 - DB connectivity
 - DP readiness + basic inference smoke test (if enabled)
10. **Unquiesce traffic** (drain off / ingress restored).
11. **Unlock + finalize**:
 - Persist rollback outcome
 - Emit audit events
 - Print operator summary and next steps

If any step fails:
- Stop and print the **exact failing step**, last successful checkpoint, and a one-command retry.
- If failure occurs after traffic is quiesced, keep traffic quiesced unless operator opts out.

---

## Partial upgrades: how rollback behaves
A “partial upgrade” is any attempt where at least one of these occurred:
- CP Helm revision changed
- DP Helm revision changed
- DB migration executed
- Config/state schema changed

Rollback uses the persisted step list to determine what to revert.

Rules:
- If only **DP** steps ran (CP untouched), rollback may still roll back DP first, but must confirm CP compatibility (the compatibility policy gate must pass for N-1 DP with N CP).
- If **DB migrations** executed, rollback must consult PoNR and migration metadata (see below).
- If **artifact mismatch** is detected (e.g., chart digest differs from recorded), rollback stops and requires operator to provide correct artifacts or bundle.

---

## Schema migrations (DB) and rollback
Schema migration behavior is the most common PoNR driver.

### Migration categories
Each release must classify migrations as one of:
- **Reversible**: safe down-migration supported and tested.
- **Forward-only but compatible**: old application version can run against the new schema (backward compatible).
- **Irreversible**: cannot guarantee old version correctness; PoNR is reached.

### Default policy
- We default to **forward-only but backward compatible** migrations.
- PoNR is set only when a migration is marked **irreversible**.

### Rollback behavior by category
1. **Reversible**
 - Run down migrations as part of `rollback.restore`.
 - Must be idempotent and guarded by migration IDs.

2. **Forward-only but compatible**
 - Do not run down migrations.
 - Ensure CP/DP config is set to N-1 values.
 - Keep schema as-is; N-1 services must be confirmed compatible.

3. **Irreversible (PoNR)**
 - Restore DB from backup snapshot taken at upgrade start.
 - Warn operator about data loss since snapshot time.

### Required guardrails
- Migration runner must enforce lock timeouts and bounded blocking.
- Migrations must have explicit per-step timeouts and emit progress.
- Installer must capture:
 - starting migration ID
 - ending migration ID
 - whether PoNR was reached

---

## Model cache/state during rollback
Model cache issues are a frequent rollback footgun because cache formats, quantization metadata, or routing tables can change between versions.

### Cache types
- **KV/prefix caches** (in-memory, per-pod): safe to drop.
- **Disk caches** (PVC-based): may contain versioned formats.
- **Global model registry metadata** (DB/object store): must remain consistent with CP version.

### Rollback policy
- In-memory caches are always dropped by restarting DP pods during rollback.
- Disk caches are handled based on declared compatibility:
 - If cache format is **backward compatible**: preserve PVCs.
 - If cache format is **not guaranteed compatible**: invalidate by bumping cache namespace key or deleting cache directories (preferred) rather than deleting PVCs.

### Required versioning mechanism
DP cache keys must include:
- `model_id`
- `model_version`
- `runtime_cache_schema_version`

On rollback, the runtime must:
- Set `runtime_cache_schema_version` to the N-1 value.
- Avoid reading N-formatted cache entries.

### Operator-facing note
Rollback may temporarily increase cold-start latency due to cache invalidation. This is expected.

---

## Helm hook specifics (Kubernetes)
Charts must implement rollback-safe behavior.

### Requirements
- Any hook Job must:
 - specify `activeDeadlineSeconds`
 - be restartable or safe to re-run
 - have clear logs and exit status
- Pre-delete hooks must not delete shared state unless explicitly intended.
- Chart changes must avoid schema assumptions that prevent N-1 resources from applying.

### Recommended Helm patterns
- Use a separate “rollback coordinator” Job triggered by the installer that:
 - sets a ConfigMap flag `redwood.ai/upgrade-mode: rollback`
 - runs component hooks in order (or triggers component jobs)
- Use readiness gates that can be satisfied on N-1.

---

## Installer CLI behavior
### Commands
- `redwood-private rollback` rolls back the latest upgrade attempt by default.
- `redwood-private rollback --attempt <id>` targets a specific attempt.
- `redwood-private rollback --dry-run` prints planned actions and validations.

### Output requirements
Rollback output must include:
- Attempt ID
- From/to versions
- Whether PoNR was reached
- Backups involved
- Step-by-step progress with explicit component names

Example (abbreviated):

1) Validate rollback artifacts (N-1 bundle) ... OK
2) Acquire upgrade lock ... OK
3) Drain ingress ... OK
4) Rollback control-plane (helm revision 42 -> 41) ... OK
5) DB restore required (PoNR reached) ... restoring snapshot snap-0f12ab... OK
6) Rollback data-plane (helm revision 108 -> 107) ... OK
7) Invalidate model disk cache namespace ... OK
8) Health checks ... OK
9) Restore ingress ... OK

Result: ROLLBACK_SUCCEEDED (duration 18m32s)

---

## Failure handling and retry semantics
- Hooks marked retryable may be retried up to 3 times.
- If a retryable hook still fails:
 - installer stops
 - prints the next safe manual action
 - leaves the system in the safest known mode (typically traffic quiesced)

Manual intervention examples:
- GitOps controller continuously re-applies N resources.
- DB snapshot restore fails due to storage constraints.
- Artifact mirror lacks N-1 images/charts.

---

## Auditing and supportability
Rollback must emit audit events (minimum):
- `private.upgrade.rollback.started`
- `private.upgrade.rollback.step.completed`
- `private.upgrade.rollback.failed`
- `private.upgrade.rollback.completed`

Required event fields (high level):
- `attempt_id`, `from_version`, `to_version`, `ponr_reached`, `environment_id`, `operator_identity`, `artifact_digests`

Support bundle must include:
- upgrade/rollback plan artifacts
- installer logs
- per-hook job logs
- the final state record

---

## Release requirements to claim “rollback supported”
A Private release may claim “rollback supported” only if:
- Compatibility policy includes N ↔ N-1 checks for CP/DP components.
- Migrations are classified and documented (reversible / compatible / irreversible).
- Backup snapshot strategy is validated for supported storage backends.
- CI includes at least one N-1 → N → N-1 cycle in an ephemeral environment.

---

## Appendix A — Hook interface example (Job template)
Below is a representative Kubernetes Job hook template used by charts. (Exact fields may vary by chart; follow current chart conventions.)

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
 name: redwood-rollback-db-check
 namespace: redwood-system
 labels:
 redwood.ai/hook-type: rollback
 redwood.ai/hook-phase: restore
 redwood.ai/hook-component: db
 annotations:
 redwood.ai/hook-timeout-seconds: "900"
spec:
 backoffLimit: 0
 activeDeadlineSeconds: 900
 template:
 spec:
 restartPolicy: Never
 containers:
 - name: rollback-db
 image: registry.redwood.ai/private/db-tools:${IMAGE_TAG}
 args: ["rollback", "--attempt", "$(UPGRADE_ATTEMPT_ID)"]
 env:
 - name: UPGRADE_ATTEMPT_ID
 valueFrom:
 configMapKeyRef:
 name: redwood-upgrade-state
 key: attempt_id

---

## Appendix B — Operator decision checklist (when to rollback)
Roll back when:
- CP cannot become ready within the documented timeout and logs indicate config/schema mismatch.
- DP error rate stays above the upgrade alert threshold after the stabilization window.
- Migration is stuck and cannot safely resume.

Do NOT roll back immediately when:
- Only one DP pool is failing readiness (try pool-level remediation first).
- A precheck warning is triggered post-upgrade (address warning; do not rollback).

For detailed alert thresholds and escalation rules, see the SRE runbook: “upgrade-related alerts and mitigation.”

title: Heterogeneous-bandwidth-aware allreduce fanout with KV-shard coalescing and comm/compute overlap
author: Maya Chen
text:
Motivation: on mixed-cluster deployments we observed long tail latency and suboptimal throughput for tensor-parallel allreduce when nodes have heterogeneous NVLink/intra-node bandwidths or asymmetric cross-node links. Smaller microbatches and low-latency applications (streaming chat) disproportionately hit these tails.

This PR introduces a bandwidth-aware fanout planner and a KV-shard coalescing pass that together reduce cross-node stalls and improve overlap between communication and compute. It also adds a narrow-copy optimized kernel for strided small-chunk merges and a runtime hook that maps comm streams to physical links based on a link-rate profile discovered at startup.

What changed (high level):
- Fanout planner: builds a minimal spanning fanout for allreduce that avoids slow links and increases per-hop concurrency when it detects bandwidth heterogeneity. The planner prefers intra-node NVLink-RDMA pairs, then high-rate cross-node links, and uses low-rate links only as fallback.
- KV-shard coalescer: groups adjacent KV cache shards into aligned coalesced writes to reduce the number of small allgathers. This reduces per-step launch overhead and amortizes DMA for common prefix cache hits.
- Stride-optimized memcpy kernel: a small, vectorized kernel for <4KB strided copies used by the coalescer; reduces memcpy time by up to 3x in microbenchmarks.
- Stream mapper: startup probe collects link bandwidths (via existing topo_probe) and creates stream->link mappings to route collective streams away from congested links.
- Scheduler tweak: a light-weight scheduling hint that encourages launching compute kernels on the stream that finished the local reduce, improving KV reuse and overlap.

Benchmarks: (multi-node, 8xA100-80GB, TP-4)
- Throughput: +18% median for 512-token workloads with batch size 8; +11% median for batch size 2.
- P99 latency: reduced by 24% for streaming microbatch workloads (<=2 microbatches).
- Small allgather count: reduced by 38% for a realistic prefix-caching trace.
- Overhead: startup probe adds ~45ms to init time on first run; negligible once cached.

Compatibility and safety:
- The fanout planner is opt-in via config flag "runtime.bandwidth_fanout.enabled" (default: true for Dedicated and Private, false for Hosted until canary completes).
- Fallbacks: if topology probe fails or detects homogeneous links, planner falls back to existing balanced tree.
- Unit and integration tests added; new runtime flag is gated behind a feature flag at rollout.

Checklist: 
- [x] Perf microbenchmarks
- [x] Unit tests for planner and coalescer
- [x] E2E smoke on CI
- [x] Docs: added runtime flags and rollout notes
- [x] Bench dashboard entry (Linear ENG-4281)

Related: ENG-4219 (heterogeneous link investigation), ENG-4281 (bench dashboard and canary plan).

Notes: this is intentionally conservative in memory use for the coalescer (max 1.5x temporary buffer). We plan a follow-up to expose a memory/perf knob and to extend the stream mapper to NVSwitch-aware topologies.

Diego Alvarez: Nice work — planner looks solid. Two concerns: (1) how do we ensure the planner doesn't create hotspots on high-bandwidth links? (2) can the coalescer accidentally increase mem usage in pathological KV layouts?
Maya Chen (author): For (1) planner bounds per-link concurrent fanout degree and we prefer fanout breadth over depth when bandwidth headroom is available — added comments and a unit test that simulates a single high-capacity link. For (2) coalescer enforces a 1.5x temporary buffer cap; I added a regression test that mirrors EXTREME_KV layout and it passes. See tests/unit/test_kv_coalescer.cc
Priya Natarajan: CI showed a flaky on the e2e smoke (timeout). I reran and it's green. Please add a brief note in the canary doc about rollback steps if p99 increases in the first 24h.
Lucas Meyer: approved
(bench numbers look believable; we should run on a heterogeneous NVSwitch+NVLink cluster before broad rollout).

Improves TP allreduce performance on clusters with heterogeneous link bandwidth by introducing a bandwidth-aware fanout planner and KV-shard coalescing. Adds a small stride-optimized memcpy kernel and stream mapping to reduce comm/computation stalls. Opt-in flag and canary plan included.

title: Deterministic Playback Manifest format (draft)
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Purpose:
This is a working sketch of a lightweight, self-contained manifest format intended to capture everything needed to deterministically replay an inference session (or a set of requests) across model rollouts, runtime variants, and quantization changes. The goal is to make postmortems, regression triage, and model A/B comparisons reproducible without requiring full environment cloning.

Non-goals (for v1):
- Not attempting to capture private customer data; manifests should be able to reference redacted payloads or point to secure storage locations.
- Not a full provenance ledger; this is focused on deterministic playback for debugging/regression.

Design principles:
- Minimal: small manifest that references artifacts rather than embedding bulk blobs.
- Deterministic intent: include all inputs that can affect output (tokenizer, seed, model artifact id, runtime config, injected policies).
- Portable: JSON-compatible, human-readable, and easy to attach to support tickets or GitHub issues.
- Privacy-aware: fields that may contain PII must be flagged and optionally replaced with redaction pointers.

Top-level fields (v1):
- manifest_id: short id (UUID recommended)
- created_by: name/email of the authoring agent (person, system)
- created_at: ISO date
- source_context: freeform string describing the scenario (UI flow, API route)
- requests: ordered list of request descriptors (see below)
- environment: runtime/environment snapshot (hardware/host tags, region, container image)
- model_artifact: model id + exact artifact checksum (sha256) + quantization profile id
- tokenizer: tokenizer version id + checksum + tokenizer config (if nonstandard)
- runtime_flags: map-like list of runtime knobs that influence execution (e.g., use_kv_cache=false)
- deterministic_seeds: list of PRNG seeds used for sampling or other non-deterministic logic
- telemetry_refs: pointers to associated logs, traces, and metric snapshots
- privacy_policy: small token describing redaction level (none, partial, strict)
- signature: optional signed blob for integrity verification (OIDC/JWKS compatible)

Request descriptor (ordered list element):
- request_id: short id (monotonic in manifest)
- timestamp: ISO timestamp of original request
- api_route: e.g., \"/v1/generate\" or \"/v1/chat/completions\"
- client_sdk: client library and version (if applicable)
- raw_payload_ref: pointer to stored payload (S3/GCS/secure-store) OR inline (redacted) string
- input_checksums: list of checksum objects (tokenization checksum, raw text checksum)
- sampling_config: temperature/top_k/top_p/typical_p/seed (if used)
- pre_hooks: list of transformations (name@version + diff/checksum) applied by client or proxy
- post_hooks: list of response transformations (e.g., de-identification, markup)
- expected_response_signature: optional small fingerprint of the original response to enable quick divergence checks
- fallback_policy_trace: if fallback occurred during original call (e.g., switched to smaller model), record decisions and timestamps

Environment (examples):
- host_os: ubuntu-22.04
- runtime_image: redwood/runtime-infer:2025-10-21
- gpu: a100-80gb (or cpu)
- region: us-west-2
- concurrency_profile: \"single-req\" | \"batched\"

Telemetry references:
These are URIs (or internal artifact ids) pointing to:
- structured trace (jaeger/span id)
- token-level metrics (latency per token)
- server logs (filtered range)
- resource utilization snapshot (GPU memory thread dump)

Privacy notes:
- raw_payload_ref should be used in combination with privacy_policy. For strict privacy, manifest contains only a redaction pointer that trusted ops can use to fetch the unredacted artifact.
- tokenizer checksums avoid including raw text; a small mapping table may be included for debugging if permitted.

Example (toy manifest snippet as text):
{
 \"manifest_id\": \"m-3c9f2d4b\",
 \"created_by\": \"aisha@redwood.ai\",
 \"created_at\": \"2025-11-02T15:04:12Z\",
 \"source_context\": \"support-ticket #12345 - user reported hallucination on invoice extraction\",
 \"model_artifact\": \"gptx-4-quant-v2:sha256=abcd1234...\",
 \"tokenizer\": \"tokenizer-v3:sha256=ef56...\",
 \"requests\": [
 {
 \"request_id\": \"r1\",
 \"timestamp\": \"2025-11-01T22:10:03Z\",
 \"api_route\": \"/v1/chat/completions\",
 \"raw_payload_ref\": \"s3://redwood-playback/12345/payload-r1.json.redacted\",
 \"input_checksums\": [\"tok:sha256:fff...\", \"raw:sha256:aaa...\"],
 \"sampling_config\": \"temp=0.0;seed=42\"
 }
 ],
 \"runtime_flags\": [\"use_kv_cache=true\", \"kv_prefetch=on\"],
 \"deterministic_seeds\": [\"global_seed=42\"],
 \"telemetry_refs\": [\"jaeger://spanid/abc123\", \"s3://redwood-playback/12345/token_metrics.json\"]
}

Repro playback flow (implementation notes):
1) Validate: check manifest signature (if present), model artifact checksum, tokenizer checksum. Bail if missing required artifacts.
2) Acquire artifacts: pull model variant + tokenizer. If quantization profile mismatch with available runtime, follow policy: either simulate (not ideal) or fail fast and record mismatch in report.
3) Materialize inputs: fetch raw_payload_ref (honoring privacy) and apply pre_hooks in order. Recompute tokenization checksum and assert equal to manifest's checksum.
4) Configure runtime: apply runtime_flags and sampling_config. Seed RNGs.
5) Execute: run request(s) single-threaded in deterministic mode (disable nondeterministic kernels where possible) and capture token logs + timings.
6) Compare: compute response fingerprint and compare with expected_response_signature. Record diffs at token, sentence, and semantic (embedding distance) levels.
7) Report: output an artifacts bundle (resulting tokens, metrics, delta report) and attach back to the manifest.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is the exact fingerprint algorithm for responses? (sha256 on normalized tokens vs embedding similarity)
- How to best represent batched vs multiplexed traces in a compact way?
- Policy for model mismatches: fallback simulation? automatic shim?
- Integration with onboarding flow: ergonomic UI in Console to upload manifest and run playback with controlled cost limits.

Notes to self (implementation cadence):
- v1: implement minimal server tool that accepts manifest, validates artifacts, runs single-request deterministic playback, emits delta report (Q1 2026).
- v2: support multi-request sessions, integrated debugger UI, signed manifests for customer upload (Q2 2026).

Short checklist for next sync with SRE/Serving Runtime:
- confirm which runtime knobs are accessible via API and which require image rebuilds
- verify deterministic kernel availability across GPU types
- prototype small corpus of manifests from recent incidents for validation

End of sketch.

(Loose, rough — meant as a personal draft for discussion. Will refine schema into a JSON Schema and example artifact layout after feedback.)

title: Offload handoff choreography — scratchpad
author: Elena Park
text:
Context and goal:
- This is a working sketch for how an LLM session (active KV/cache + in-flight tokens) can be offloaded from a hot GPU instance into colder storage or another node with minimal latency penalty and safe resume semantics.
- Motivations: preemption, autoscaling (drain), cross-tier migration (dedicated -> private), edge-snapshotting for client handoff.

Non-goals (for this draft):
- Full encryption key lifecycle (we assume envelope encryption and a KMS exists)
- Billing semantics or quota accounting details (separately tracked)

Key constraints and invariants:
- Resume must be idempotent for replay up to an at-most-once effect model on side effects (functions/calls).
- Handoff should not require global synchronous locks across the fleet; prefer lease + compare-and-commit patterns localized to session owner region.
- Keep hot-path latency impact under 2ms for the typical handoff flow (best-effort; bulk transfer happens async).
- Allow partial resume when only subset of context is available; provide graceful degradation.

Actors and concepts:
- Session owner (hot process): current GPU worker holding KV and token buffers.
- Offload coordinator: lightweight control plane component that orchestrates transfer. Could be colocated with node-agent.
- Target store: object store / S3-like + optional warm worker pre-warming endpoint.
- Resume agent: process on target that claims the session and reconstructs runtime state.
- Lease token: short-lived cryptographic token granting exclusive write/commit rights during handoff.
- Merkle manifest: compact digest of snapshot fragments to validate integrity and support partial fetch/resume.

High-level choreography (happy path):
1) Hot worker notices drain or preemption -> prepare snapshot. Snapshot has two layers:
 - Manifest: small JSON with metadata, fragment list, merkle root hashes, sequence numbers, pinned model version, KV schema version.
 - Fragments: chunked binary blobs (context blocks, tokenizer state, ephemeral caches).
2) Hot worker writes fragments to target store with temporary prefix (e.g., tmp/session-1234/{frag}). Each write returns an upload id.
3) Hot worker computes manifest, including per-fragment upload ids and merkle hashes, and POSTs manifest to Offload coordinator with a request to "commit-offload".
4) Coordinator issues a Lease token (short TTL) and records pre-commit metadata in control-plane KV (idempotent entry: session-1234 -> pending, owner: node-X).
5) Hot worker finalizes manifest commit by calling Coordinator.commit(manifest, lease). Coordinator validates merkle root vs fragment uploads and atomically flips state to "offloaded" and returns resume_endpoint + resume_token.
6) Coordinator makes the object keys immutable (e.g., move from tmp/ to live/ or set ACLs) and notifies target warmers.
7) On resume, resume agent presents resume_token to Coordinator, which validates and issues a short session-level lease for exclusive restoration.
8) Resume agent lazily fetches manifest, verifies merkle root, streams fragments, reconstructs KV/slot state.
9) Once reconstructed, resume agent performs compare-and-swap with Coordinator to claim live session ownership.
10) If success, Coordinator marks session "active" and revokes original owner's lease.

Failure modes and mitigation (notes):
- Partial upload: manifest verification fails -> coordinator rejects commit, hot worker retries with missing fragments.
- Double-commit attempts: Commit flow is idempotent against identical manifest hashes. Use manifest-hash CAS.
- Resume during fragment eviction: include fallback route to request delta pull from originating node if fragments not yet tightened in object store.
- Stale resume token replay: tokens are single-use; store small replay cache keyed by token/hmac.
- Coordinator loss: use control-plane replicated KV (raft/consensus) or less strongly: allow stateless coordinator backed by durable store.

API sketches (very rough) - control plane endpoints and shapes (text sketch):
- POST /offload/request
 body: {"session_id":"s-1234","node_id":"node-x","expected_seq": 987, "snapshot_hint":{"seq_range":"980-987","size_bytes":...}}
 returns: {"upload_prefix":"tmp/s-1234/","upload_urls":[...]}

- POST /offload/commit
 body: {"session_id":"s-1234","manifest_hash":"sha256:...","manifest":"{...}","lease_proof":"sig..."}
 returns: {"status":"accepted","resume_token":"rt-...","live_prefix":"live/s-1234/","resume_endpoint":"worker-claim.example:443"}

- POST /resume/claim
 body: {"session_id":"s-1234","resume_token":"rt-...","requesting_node":"node-y"}
 returns: {"status":"ok","session_lease":"lease-...","restore_plan":"..."}

Lease properties and TTL tuning:
- Keep commit lease TTL small (10-30s), enough for commit handshake but to fail fast on dead workers.
- Resume lease TTL slightly longer (30-120s) to allow reconstruction and small anti-entropy.
- Coordinators should support lease extension RPC guarded by monotonic counters from node to avoid theft.

Merkle/fragment design rationale:
- Merkle allows partial verification (so resume agent can stream only needed fragments and check integrity).
- Fragments should be aligned to semantic boundaries (e.g., tokenizer-chunks, latest prompt delta, recent KV subset) to support partial rehydrate and cost-effective transfer.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Do we want server-side encryption key rotation per fragment? Impacts resume flow.
- How to instrument and surface per-offload cost (bytes, egress) to billing?
- Backup plan for long-tail restores when object-store evicts fragments (pinning vs ephemeral tiering).
- Should we integrate with cache hints from Optimize (e.g., mark fragment hot-score)?
- Interaction with function/tool-calls: if a function was invoked mid-session, we must record idempotency tokens and ensure replays don't double-run side effects.

Quick ASCII diagram (happy path):
 [hot node] --upload--> [object store(tmp)]
 | |
 | commit(manifest) |
 v v
 [coord svc] <---record--- [object store(live)]
 | |
 | resume_token |
 v v
 [resume node] --fetch--> [object store(live)] --verify--> [resume node runtime]

Notes to self and next steps:
- Prototype small PoC that: captures runtime snapshot (KV + last N tokens) -> writes 4 fragments -> manifest -> coordinator commit -> resume on another local worker. Measure wall-time and latency of resume under different snapshot granularities.
- Add test harness that injects partial uploads, coordinator fail, and resume token replay to validate invariants.
- Document a lightweight client-side library for workers to produce manifest and fragment semantics (python + go prototypes).

Sign-off: rough, needs iteration. Keep this file as the canonical scratchpad until we stabilize API names and move to a proper spec doc.

title: Thread Weave: customer compact brief and request synthesis (May 2026)
author: Priya Nair
text:
Executive snapshot:

This is a compact synthesis ("Thread Weave") of recent field conversations with five mid-market and two enterprise customers (pods A–E). Goal: surface the highest-confidence asks + quick probes we can run with engineering and solutions to (1) unblock short-term adoption friction, (2) validate where product work yields largest MRR/retention lift, and (3) capture easy ops patches for CS enablement.

Topline themes (high-level):
- Predictable unit cost & billing visibility: heavy signal across customers that token-attribution for mixed workloads (chat + embeddings + reranking) is opaque and causes finance friction.
- Failure-mode tolerance & graceful fallback: customers with hybrid Dedicated + Hosted strategies need transparent fallback rules and clear SLA trade-offs when Dedicated is at capacity.
- Fine-grained observability: requests want token-level traces correlated to routes, model versions, and customer request IDs — not just aggregate per-route stats.
- Private deployment friction: KMS rotation, auditability (HSM logs), and deterministic startup times for on-prem/air-gapped installs.
- Embeddings scale/UX: bulk upsert semantics, conflict resolution, and more explicit cost heuristics for large batch indexing.

Representative customer quotes (verbatim fragments):
- "We saw a 30% cost delta between our dev and prod traffic but couldn't explain why — the console charts are fuzzy." (Pod C - fintech)
- "When dedicated falls over, we want a policy that says 'serve degraded but local-first' rather than opaque timeouts." (Pod A - consumer search)
- "We need to rotate keys offline and provide a signed attestation for auditors; vendor-managed rotation doesn't cut it." (Pod E - healthcare)

Priority lanes (hypothesis + quick metric to validate):
1) Billing transparency lane
 - Hypothesis: Adding per-route per-model token attribution and a cost-explain report will reduce billing disputes by 60% for customers surveyed.
 - Validation metric: #support-billing tickets per customer month (baseline) and time-to-resolve.
 - Low-effort probe: Add a downloadable CSV in Console with token breakdown for last 7 days (route, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, estimated_cost).

2) Graceful fallback / capacity policy lane
 - Hypothesis: Explicit fallback policies in the deployment config (serve-variant: degrade | queue | error) will reduce client-incurred downtime and improve perceived reliability.
 - Validation metric: number of failed requests vs successful fallbacks during simulated capacity loss in Dedicated test cluster.
 - Probe: Ship a canary UI in Console (experimental) to define per-route fallback policies and expose current active policy in traces.

3) Observability and trace correlation lane
 - Hypothesis: Token-level tracing for top 5 routes will decrease time-to-debug by 40% for SREs and solutions engineers.
 - Validation metric: mean time to root cause (MTTR) on recent incidents involving incorrect prompts or KV cache misses.
 - Probe: Pilot token-level trace export (compressed) for two customers — instrument SDK to attach request_id and client_trace_id.

Concrete feature asks (compiled and normalized):
- Cost explain export (console): downloadable CSV + per-request attribution (route, model, temp, tokens). Owner: Product-hosted-api.
- Fallback policy flags (api + console): per-route policy, canary rollout, auto-failover order. Owner: Product-console + Serving-runtime.
- Token-level trace correlation: request_id propagation, token timing, KV cache hit/miss markers. Owner: Observability + Serving-runtime.
- Dedicated burst autoscaling guardrails: short-term burst capacity with guaranteed best-effort vs reserved. Owner: Dedicated product + Infra.
- Private deployment KMS key rotation workflow (offline support + rotation report PDF). Owner: Private-deployments + Security.
- Embeddings bulk-upsert API and conflict resolution strategies (upsert-only, merge-policy, dedupe-by-hash). Owner: Hosted-api + Optimize.

Impact vs Effort quick mapping (subjective):
- High impact / low effort: cost explain CSV export; fallback policy UI toggles; improved support doc templates for billing.
- High impact / medium effort: token-level traces (pilot); embeddings bulk-upsert.
- Medium impact / high effort: Private KMS offline attestation flow; Dedicated burst autoscaling policy engine.

Unresolved signals and open questions to triage (for Eng/Product):
- Which existing tracing data points are safe to surface without PII leakage for customers on Shared-hosted? (security/privacy gating).
- What is the cost/throughput penalty for enabling token-level traces on production serving runtime across p99 latency SLAs?
- How to map token attribution to mixed-model pipelines where a single user request fans out to multiple model calls?

Suggested immediate next steps (30 / 60 day):
- 7 days: CS to run a focused poll across top-20 paying customers to confirm priority of Billing vs Observability asks; synthesize results into Confluence page. Owner: Priya.
- 14 days: Engineering to scope a minimal CSV export implementation (APIs and Console link) and estimate dev days. Owner: Evan + Eng infra lead.
- 30 days: Launch billing CSV pilot with Pods B/C and collect support ticket delta. Owner: CS + Product-hosted-api.
- 60 days: If pilot shows >25% reduction in query tickets/time-to-resolve, prioritize richer per-request explain in the roadmap.

Patchwork / quick CS playbook (scripts & templates):
- Support template: "How to explain token billing" (one-pager with examples for chat + embeddings mixed flows).
- Troubleshooting checklist: Dedicated fallback — how to validate fallback policy is active, reading Console liveness.
- Pre-sales FAQ: private deployment audits — list of current attestations and gaps.

Notes to self (scratch):
- Mentioned Slack threads: #cs-billing, #dedicated-failovers — link later in Confluence.
- Possible cross-team sync: Product + Serving-runtime + Observability next Wed. Suggest 30m cross-functional stand.

Appendix: quick raw signal snippets (unedited):
- "We're losing faith in the numbers — the token counts jump when we switch to long-context prompts." (Pod B)
- "A fallback that serves a smaller model automatically with a human-readable reason would be ideal." (Pod D)

End of brief.

Action owners & sign-off:
- Priya Nair (owner, CS synth) — priya@redwood.ai
- Evan Clarke (engineering liaison) — evan@redwood.ai

Please add comments inline in this doc (highlighted) or flag urgent asks in #cs-billing on Slack.
