title: HaloQuest hosted embeddings + rerank orientation
author: Maya Chen
text:
Intro demo of Redwood hosted embeddings + reranking endpoints focused on search relevance for HaloQuest's product catalog. Discussed index options, rerank model mix-in, latency-vs-cost tradeoffs, security requirements (SOC2, KMS, SSO), and proposed pilot plan with benchmarks and a short POC using their subset of catalog data.

Hosted embeddings API
Reranking endpoint (two-step retrieval + rank)
Indexing and chunking strategy
Latency vs cost and batching
Caching and prefix/KV caching
Security: KMS, SOC2, audit logs, SSO/SAML
Pilot scope and success metrics

[00:00] Maya Chen (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood Inference, with Ravi our solutions engineer. Good to meet you all.
[00:08] Laura Kim (HaloQuest): Hi Maya, hi Ravi. Thanks for doing this, our search relevance is kinda the top priority this quarter.
[00:15] Maya Chen (AE): Awesome—today we'll walk through the hosted embeddings and reranker flow, show the console, and outline a low-effort pilot you can run. We'll keep it practical.
[00:24] Ravi Patel (SE): Quick agenda: one, how we generate and serve embeddings; two, retrieval + rerank architecture; three, latency and cost levers (batching, quantization); four, security/compliance stuff; five, next steps.
[00:38] Diego Martinez (HaloQuest): Sounds good. For context, we have ~30M SKUs and a product feed that updates hourly. We use an in-house store with a vectordb (FAISS right now) and a microservice stack. Our P95 query latency target is under 200ms from ingress to result, but we've been seeing 400–800ms with our current reranker.
[00:55] Ravi Patel (SE): Got it. A couple clarifying Qs: is your current reranker an on-device smaller model or are you routing to a hosted LLM? And what's your current embeddings dim and vector index config?
[01:06] Diego Martinez (HaloQuest): We're using a 768-d embedding from the open-source encoder and FAISS flat index, CPU-only. Reranker is a transformer in a separate service, tuned but hungry on latency.
[01:18] Maya Chen (AE): Helpful. With Redwood hosted inference you can do two patterns: single-call where you call a generation model for ranking, or the more common retrieval + embeddings + lightweight neural rerank step. For most e-commerce customers we recommend the two-step: dense retrieval with embeddings then a specialized reranker on a smaller ranker model to preserve latency cost balance.
[01:36] Anita Roy (HaloQuest/Infosec): From a security standpoint we need SOC2, SSO through our IdP, KMS for keys, and audit logs surfaced to Splunk. Can you cover those?
[01:47] Ravi Patel (SE): Absolutely. Redwood Hosted supports SOC2, SAML SSO, and KMS integrations (AWS KMS/HSM options). We also emit request-level audit logs that can be routed to your SIEM; we'll show the console audit view.
[01:59] Samir Alami (HaloQuest/CTO): Also interested in data residency — some of our merchants require EU-only storage for PII.
[02:07] Maya Chen (AE): We can pin datasets and model routing by region. For the hosted offering we have EU regions; for strict residency we'd discuss Dedicated or Private later. But for the pilot we can demonstrate EU routing.
[02:19] Ravi Patel (SE): Jumping into the demo—I'll share my screen. Here is the Redwood Console: model catalog, embeddings endpoints, rerank endpoint.
[02:28] [screen share noise]
[02:33] Ravi Patel (SE): Embeddings API is straightforward: POST /v1/embeddings with model param, batch encoding supported up to X items per batch. You can configure dimension and quantized variants. For large catalogs we suggest offline batch encode and store vectors in your DB; then use our vectors-compare endpoint or bring your own FAISS / Milvus.
[02:49] Priya Singh (HaloQuest/Product): When you say "quantized variants"—does that change the embedding quality much? We need relevance preserved for synonyms and typo handling.
[02:57] Ravi Patel (SE): Good Q. Int8 or 4-bit quantization reduces memory and can slightly change distances; in practice for rerank pipelines we often keep full float embeddings for candidate retrieval and apply quantized vectors for cheap similarity lookups in a cache tier. We can A/B compare quality on your prompts during the pilot.
[03:14] Diego Martinez (HaloQuest): What about refreshes? Catalog updates hourly — reindexing 30M SKUs each hour is heavy.
[03:20] Maya Chen (AE): Our Optimize toolkit recommends incremental reencode strategies: chunk updates, upsert only changed SKUs, and use prefix caching to reduce QPS for unchanged items. You can schedule background batching jobs and use delta indexes.
[03:31] Ravi Patel (SE): Also, for rerank we support hybrid retrieval (embedding + lexical) so you can fall back on BM25 for cold starts, that often reduces the rerank candidate set and protects latency.
[03:44] Laura Kim (HaloQuest): Could you show a typical request/response for a rerank call? We want to see payload sizes and latency numbers.
[03:50] Ravi Patel (SE): Sure. Here's an example: POST /v1/rerank with original query + top-K candidate passages (id, text, embedding). The rerank model scores and returns ordered ids with scores and optional explanation tokens. Latency for a 10-candidate rerank on our standard rank-small model is ~60ms p95 in hosted for US-west region; if you use a larger cross-attention model it goes up to 180–250ms.
[04:14] Diego Martinez (HaloQuest): 60ms p95 sounds good, but end-to-end is what matters. If retrieval is 70ms and network 20ms, adding rerank 60ms hits 150ms which is acceptable. But our current stack right now doesn't batch well and we have spikes.
[04:26] Ravi Patel (SE): You can tune batching and concurrency at the client side. Redwood's SDK supports continuous batching on the runtime, which can merge similar incoming requests to improve throughput while honoring latency SLOs. We can set a max batch latency, or min batch size, whichever you prefer.
[04:40] Priya Singh (HaloQuest): Can the SDK plug into our Java microservices easily?
[04:44] Maya Chen (AE): Yes — we have official SDKs for Python, Node, and a lightweight HTTP guide for Java. The Java guide includes examples for async batching and streaming responses.
[04:53] Anita Roy (HaloQuest/Infosec): On the compliance side: do you keep raw queries and responses? What's the retention and how do we control purge?
[05:00] Ravi Patel (SE): You can configure retention per-tenant—default is 90 days for hosted; enterprise customers can set custom retention windows. For PII-sensitive flows we recommend tokenization before sending, or a Private deployment. We also support an option to disable retention entirely for a given API key.
[05:14] Laura Kim (HaloQuest): Good to know. We'd want an option to redact user-provided PII before hitting the API.
[05:19] Rav i Patel (SE): Yep, we have pre-request hooks and a content filter pipeline you can enable in the console.
[05:26] Samir Alami (HaloQuest/CTO): Back to economics — what's typical per-query cost for the two-step flow?
[05:33] Maya Chen (AE): It depends on model choices and candidate counts. Rough ballpark: embeddings encode (amortized offline) cost is low; retrieval is dominated by your index infra cost; hosted rerank cost for a rank-small model might be $0.0006–$0.002 per call depending on tokenized input size and tokenization. For a 10-candidate rerank across a product description of 100 tokens each, estimate around $0.0012 per query. We'll send a tailored pricing sheet.
[05:57] Diego Martinez (HaloQuest): Could we run an experiment with a cheap quantized ranker to validate signals before moving to full model?
[06:03] Ravi Patel (SE): Absolutely—that's the Optimize play: run split tests across quantized vs float rerank models and measure NDCG on your labeled holdout. We'll show the eval harness integration.
[06:13] [10 minutes of screen demo showing console, sample dashboard, audit logs — paraphrased]
[16:20] Ravi Patel (SE): Here's the Console's per-route dashboard. You can see tokens, latency P50/P95/P99, cost by model, and trace links to a request. Notice the fallback policy we configured for high latency windows: it automatically switches to a cheaper ranker or reduces top-K.
[16:39] Priya Singh (HaloQuest): That automatic fallback could be huge for peak shopping hours.
[16:44] Maya Chen (AE): Yep—you can set thresholds and fallback models per route.
[16:49] Diego Martinez (HaloQuest): For the pilot, we'd like to use our 500k most active SKUs and run a weekday A/B split — can Redwood handle the ingestion and benchmarking?
[16:57] Ravi Patel (SE): Yes. Typical pilot: ingest subset, run encode job, point your retrieval to either hosted compare endpoint or your existing FAISS index, run live A/B, measure CTR/NDCG and latency. We provide a benchmark spreadsheet template.
[17:12] Laura Kim (HaloQuest): What's the setup time? Our engineers are tight on cycles.
[17:17] Maya Chen (AE): For a lightweight pilot we estimate 2–3 weeks to get meaningful metrics: week one ingestion & encode, week two live A/B and tuning, week three analyze and recommend production rollout. If you want Redwood to do more of the heavy lifting we can assign an onboarding SE.
[17:32] Samir Alami (HaloQuest/CTO): Will dedicated capacity be necessary for us at scale?
[17:37] Ravi Patel (SE): Depends on throughput and SLA needs. Hosted often suffices for initial production tiers; for predictable high-throughput with tighter latency SLOs, a Dedicated pool gives reserved GPUs and network locality. We can model your QPS and recommend.
[17:51] Priya Singh (HaloQuest/Product): Any gotchas with our FAISS setup?
[17:55] Ravi Patel (SE): A few: flat indexes are fast for recall but memory heavy; IVF+PQ reduces memory but affects recall unless you tune nprobe. Also make sure chunking strategy for long product docs is aligned with rerank input expected size. We can provide recommended chunk sizes per model.
[18:09] Diego Martinez (HaloQuest): We're worried about billing surprises past the pilot. Does Redwood provide cost alerts?
[18:15] Maya Chen (AE): Yes — Console supports quota enforcement, per-key hard limits, and anomaly alerts on spend. We can also set daily budget caps.
[18:25] Anita Roy (HaloQuest/Infosec): Can you show how audit logs appear? We need to map fields to our SIEM events.
[18:31] Ravi Patel (SE): On the audit view here, each request has time, API key, route, model, token usage, and a hashed user id; you can add correlation ids. We can demo a sample Splunk ingestion via S3 or direct syslog.
[18:46] [minor crosstalk, connection blip at 18:53–19:05]
[19:06] Laura Kim (HaloQuest): OK can we talk success metrics — what should we measure in the pilot?
[19:11] Maya Chen (AE): Suggested: NDCG uplift on labeled queries, CTR change on search results, and tail latency (P95). Set thresholds like +5–7% NDCG or 10% CTR lift as success criteria.
[19:26] Priya Singh (HaloQuest/Product): We have a small labeled dataset of 2k queries; is that enough for a pilot?
[19:31] Ravi Patel (SE): It's enough to get a signal. For robust statistical confidence we'd prefer 5–10k but 2k can reveal directional improvement. We'll integrate with your eval harness.
[19:42] Diego Martinez (HaloQuest): Any immediate integration steps we should prep?
[19:46] Maya Chen (AE): Prepare a sample of 500k SKU JSONL, mapping doc_id, title, description, and metadata fields. Also share a small labeled query set, and create an API key for the pilot environment (we can provision).
[19:58] Samir Alami (HaloQuest/CTO): From procurement — what's the pilot cost? Do you discount pilots?
[20:04] Maya Chen (AE): We usually offer a pilot credit and flexible short-term pricing to start. We'll include numbers in the follow-up.
[20:12] Anita Roy (HaloQuest/Infosec): One more security question — what about data in flight? TLS and mutual TLS?
[20:18] Ravi Patel (SE): We support TLS 1.2/1.3 and mTLS for Dedicated/private. Hosted supports standard TLS with client cert options if needed.
[20:28] Laura Kim (HaloQuest): Great. Let's talk timeline — we want to kick off in early May if possible.
[20:33] Maya Chen (AE): That aligns well. We'll propose a kickoff doc.
[20:37] [demo wrap-up and Qs for 5 more minutes — paraphrased]
[26:00] Maya Chen (AE): Quick recap: run a 3-week pilot on 500k SKUs, use hosted embeddings + small reranker, measure NDCG/CTR and P95 latency, compare quantized vs float model. Redwood provides console, audit logs, and an onboarding SE option.
[26:20] Diego Martinez (HaloQuest): Sounds good. Two quick technical follow-ups: 1) we need example code for incremental upserts to FAISS and 2) sample pipeline for offline embedding encode.
[26:32] Ravi Patel (SE): I'll put both in a shared repo — incremental upsert script, and an async encoder job example.
[26:40] Maya Chen (AE): Ok, any other questions?
[26:44] Priya Singh (HaloQuest/Product): None right now.
[26:46] Anita Roy (HaloQuest/Infosec): Not from security.
[26:48] Samir Alami (HaloQuest/CTO): No, thanks.
[26:50] Maya Chen (AE): Great. We'll follow up with the pilot doc, pricing, security packet, and the benchmark spreadsheet.
[26:58] Laura Kim (HaloQuest): Thanks team, excited to try this.
[27:02] Maya Chen (AE): Thanks everyone — we'll send assets within 48 hours.

title: Operator runbook: Quiet cutovers and automated fallback orchestration for private deployments
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Summary:
This runbook describes the operator-facing procedures for performing quiet cutovers (low-noise, low-risk upgrades), controlled canary rollouts, and automated fallback orchestration for Redwood private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It combines preflight checks, phased traffic steering, automated health gates, and forensic-safe rollback so field engineers can perform upgrades with minimal impact to customer SLAs.

Scope:
- Applies to: Private control plane and tenant-serving runtime upgrades, model swaps, and runtime configuration changes in VPC and air-gapped on-prem installs.
- Not covered: full datacenter evacuations and vendor hardware recall processes (see field-handoff docs).

Owner & escalation:
- Runbook owner: Platform Delivery (eng-private-deployments)
- Primary oncall: Private Deploy SRE rotation
- Escalation path: Private Deploy SRE -> Runtime Team Lead -> Head of Platform -> Customer Success (for customer comms)

Key definitions:
- Quiet cutover: A staged upgrade that minimizes telemetry noise and user-visible errors by using small traffic steps, proactive cache warming, and KV-prefix preservation techniques.
- Fallback orchestration: Automated change that routes traffic back to the last-known-good model/version/pool when health gates fail.
- Health gate: A programmatic condition (latency, error rate, token loss, output regression) that must be met before advancing rollout.

Preflight checklist (complete before any cutover):
1) Stakeholder notifications: notify Customer Success and account owner if cutover affects customer SLA boundaries.
2) Snapshot state: take KV/cache snapshot and model version manifest:
 - CLI: `redwoodctl snapshot kv --tenant <TENANT_ID> --out /tmp/kv-snap-<TIMESTAMP>.tar.gz`
3) Capacity & cadence: ensure at least 20% spare serving slots across the target pool or pre-provision burst nodes.
4) Telemetry baseline: capture 30m baselined metrics for the target route(s):
 - LAT_p50/p95, tokens/sec, errors/min, model_quality_score (if enabled)
5) Run quick regression eval set locally for new model variant (if model swap): `eval-harness run --suite smoke-small --model new-model:tag`
6) Confirm artifact signatures for on-prem images (airgapped): verify SHA256 and sigstore attestations.

Health gate thresholds (recommended defaults; tune per-customer):
| Metric | Gate type | Threshold to advance | Threshold to abort and rollback |
|--------|-----------|----------------------|----------------------------------|
| p95 latency | safety | <= baseline * 1.25 | > baseline * 1.5 for 5m |
| errors/min | safety | <= baseline + 3 | >= baseline + 10 for 3m |
| requests with degraded output | quality | <= 1% | >= 3% for 10m or failing smoke evals |
| token amplification | cost | <= 1.2x baseline | >= 1.5x sustained 10m |

Note: Baseline values must be computed from preflight telemetry (last 30m steady-state).

title: Polish cross-SDK auth safety, streaming ergonomics, and e2e interop
author: Sofia Chen
text:
Motivation: Over the last two quarters customers reported subtle auth race conditions during stream reconnects and inconsistent ergonomics across the Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs. This PR consolidates the auth lifecycle surface, tightens retry defaults for streaming contexts, and harmonizes ergonomics (pause/resume, cancel semantics, typed async iterators) so client code can migrate with minimal friction.

What this changes (high-level): Introduces an AuthProfile abstraction shared conceptually across SDKs (not a new centralized package in this PR) to standardize token refresh windows, preflight checks, and telemetry tags emitted during refresh/fallback events; tightens streaming retry presets when a token refresh is in-flight to avoid double-inflight requests; adds pause()/resume() and graceful_cancel() helpers to stream handles with deterministic semantics; unifies method names and parameter order across SDKs for parity; adds end-to-end interop tests that exercise credential handoffs and stream resume across language bindings; bumps SDK minor versions to reflect ergonomic changes.

Commit summary: 1) Introduce auth lifecycle tests and fixtures (e2e harness) 2) Add stream ergonomics API to TS/Go/Python SDKs (pause/resume/graceful_cancel) 3) Implement latency-aware retry preset for streaming and guard against concurrent reauth races 4) Add telemetry tags (auth.stage, auth.reason) and instrumentation hooks for rollout analysis 5) Docs: migration guide and examples for common patterns 6) TS lint fixes and smaller follow-up commits to address CI failures.

Files of note changed: redwood-sdk-python/redwood/session.py (stream handle helpers + auth shim), redwood-sdk-typescript/src/stream/handle.ts (typed async iterator and pause/resume), redwood-sdk-go/auth/refresh.go (concurrency guard and backoff profile), docs/migration/sdk-auth-2.0.md (migration notes and examples), tests/e2e/sdk_interop/test_auth_stream.py (interop harness + docker compose config), examples/streaming-auth-examples/* (small samples).

Compatibility and migration: The surface-level renames are additive or aliased to previous names when possible. We provide a short migration guide (docs/migration/sdk-auth-2.0.md) and deprecation warnings at runtime for any renamed entry points. No breaking behavior introduced for synchronous API flows; streaming clients should follow the migration steps to adopt the new pause/resume helpers for deterministic reconnect behavior.

Testing and CI: Added ~12 new unit tests across the SDKs and 3 cross-language e2e tests that run in the CI matrix. Initial CI run failed TypeScript linting and a flaky go race in refresh.go; both were fixed in follow-up commits. All CI checks are green on merge. Local perf smoke tests show ~3–6% tail-latency reduction for reconnect-after-refresh scenarios due to reduced duplicate inflight token refreshes.

Risks and mitigation: The main risk is client-side misuse of pause/resume leading to blocked request loops; mitigations include: clear docs, runtime validation that resume cannot be called before pause, and telemetry to detect misused patterns. Another risk is telemetry / metric churn; added tags are opt-in behind a flag for hosted customers while we evaluate noise.

Related work: ENG-2034 (auth rollouts and telemetry), ENG-2110 (stream ergonomics research).

Release notes: Add SDK helpers for pause/resume and graceful stream cancel; unify auth refresh windows and add latency-aware streaming retry presets; e2e interop tests added; minor version bumps: python -> 2.1.0, typescript -> 1.6.3, go -> 1.8.0.

Merge: Squash-merged to main after approvals and green CI.

Ethan Park (requested_changes): Please add a metric for 'reauth_attempts' and make the concurrency guard opt-out for older servers. Also adjust the TS linter rule. — Sofia: added reauth_attempts metric and an env var REDWOOD_OLD_AUTH_COMPAT to relax the guard, updated CI config.
Marta Lopez (approved): Tests look good; small nit about error wording in session.py; resolved.
Julian Wu (comment): Curious about the runtime cost of telemetry tags. — Sofia: telemetry is behind a runtime flag and the tag emission path is low-overhead (fast path no-op when disabled).

Add pause/resume/graceful_cancel helpers for stream handles; unify auth refresh semantics across SDKs; introduce latency-aware streaming retry presets; add e2e interop tests and migration guide; bump SDK minor versions for py/ts/go.

Coordinate SDK releases: publish Python 2.1.0, TypeScript 1.6.3, Go 1.8.0. Alert integrators about optional telemetry flag REDWOOD_SDK_AUTH_TELEMETRY (off by default) and REDWOOD_OLD_AUTH_COMPAT for legacy servers.

title: Console debug and ops walkthrough - EduTech platform
author: Ben Harper
text:
Redwood team walked EduNext through the Console's debugging and observability surface: request logs, distributed traces, error analysis, and the Optimize suggestions for reducing token costs. Customer is evaluating Dedicated vs Hosted, needs SOC2/compliance notes and a pilot to benchmark latency with their prompt-heavy workflows.

[00:00:00] Ben (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call — alex, priya, dana from edunext, and from our side maya and carlos. we'll do a run through of the console tracing, some request logs and an example debug flow. the demo will be about 35 minutes then Q&A.

[00:00:18] Alex (EduNext): Yep sounds good. trying to figure out where we can catch perf issues in prod; our main worry is tail latency and also some weird 500 spikes last week.

[00:00:30] Maya (Redwood SE): great, i'll share my screen — sorry if the cursor is laggy — i'm in the Redwood Console, opening the Observability tab. first, request logs, you can see the per-request rows: request id, model, route, tokens in/out, latency, status.

[00:00:48] Priya (EduNext SRE): are the logs raw payloads available? we need to keep PII out but want to see prompt lengths and tokenization stats.

[00:00:55] Maya: yes, raw request logs are exportable. by default we redact PII fields if you opt in to the data protect mode; otherwise the logs show the full prompt and response body. you can also pull the logs via our API or S3 export. (slight stutter) i think i have the export pane open now.

[00:01:12] Ben: quick question on retention — what's the default retention on hosted vs dedicated?

[00:01:18] Carlos (Redwood CSM): hosted is 30 days by default, dedicated customers can configure longer retention up to 365 days if they opt into the observability add-on. for private deployments retention is customer-managed.

[00:01:30] Dana (Product PM): nice. show us the trace view you mentioned where you can see the per-token breakdown.

[00:01:36] Maya: absolutely. switching to Traces. so each trace corresponds to a request flow; if you have an orchestrated call with a few steps or tool calls you'll see subspans. here is one we pulled from the demo route — you can see the queue time, kernel execution time, kv cache hit/miss, and network egress. note the trace timestamps and the service hops — sometimes the UI will show 'model fallback' when we auto-route to a cheaper model to avoid overloading.

[00:02:10] Alex: hm when you say kv cache, is that the prefix cache? we had an issue where repeated prefixes weren't caching.

[00:02:16] Maya: yes, our 'KV cache' label is shorthand for the in-memory prefix cache and the persistent prefix store. in the trace you can click into the kv cache span and see the keys checked and the hit ratio. i can filter trace spans by 'kv_miss' to find problematic runs.

[00:02:33] Speaker 5: (unlabeled) — sorry—

[00:02:34] Priya: what about sampling? we don't want to export full traces for every request due to cost.

[00:02:37] Maya: good point — sampling policy is configurable. default is 1% for high volume routes, but you can set rule-based sampling (e.g., sample all 5xx or token>2000). we also have an on-demand trace capture — a toggle that, when enabled for a route, will capture full traces for the next N requests.

[00:02:56] Alex: that's useful. could you show an example where an error is correlated to a model fallback?

[00:03:00] Maya: sure. opening an error trace record — note the timeline: request arrives, queue latency spikes, model route returns a 429, the router automatically falls back to a smaller model, then we see a regressed quality score and the fallback span includes the 'reason: capacity' meta. the Error Analysis pane aggregates error types by route and model version.

[00:03:25] Ben: can you search by correlation id? like if our app logs include the request id, how do we jump straight to that trace?

[00:03:31] Maya: you can paste a request-id or session-id in the top search bar; we support OR queries across request id, user id, and custom tags. we also surface the link-back-to-source that you can drop into Jira or your bug tracker.

[00:03:45] Priya: on security — audit logs, RBAC. we need to know who pulled raw requests and when.

[00:03:52] Carlos: audit logs are part of the Dedicated and Private packages; they include who accessed the logs, what exports were requested, and admin actions. we also integrate with SSO/SAML for user identities and map roles to console permissions.

[00:04:05] Alex: do you support SAML attributes to map to RBAC groups? we want devs vs infra to have different permissions.

[00:04:10] Maya: yes, you can map SAML attributes to roles. we'll share our SSO config doc — i'll include the metadata file in the follow-up.

[00:04:18] Dana: okay, show the request replay or debug-run capability you mentioned earlier.

[00:04:22] Maya: right, Request Replay — pick a historical request, click 'replay', it replays against a sandbox variant of the model or against an instrumented route. you can change the model version or quantization profile and see the token-level diff and latency change. i'll demo a short replay now — switching model from rdx-3-large to rdx-3-small-quant. see latency drops by 120ms but the 'semantic drift' score increases.

[00:04:50] Alex: semantic drift score? how is that computed?

[00:04:53] Maya: it's an internal metric that compares embeddings of the original response vs replayed response and scores the divergence; we also tie to your eval prompt sets when available. it's not perfect but helps flag regressions during rollouts.

[00:05:05] Priya: what about rate limiting and throttling visibility? sometimes our app hits a burst and we see truncated responses.

[00:05:10] Maya: the console shows rate limit events per route. there's a throttle pane that breaks down requests rejected due to burst limit or concurrency cap. for Dedicated we can increase concurrency or enable burst capacity for predictable windows.

[00:05:24] Ben: (interject) for your prompt-heavy workloads, Maya, we recommended batching and prefix caching; did the Optimize suggestions section show suggestions for this account?

[00:05:31] Maya: yes, Optimize -- it scanned route telemetry and suggested a caching window for common prefixes, recommended quantized model families for certain low-stakes routes, and showed an estimated cost delta. i've got an example — here's a route with 42% repeated prefix; enabling prefix cache for 30s should reduce tokens by about 27% per our estimate.

[00:05:52] Alex: how confident are those numbers? we need real numbers against our workload.

[00:05:56] Maya: the estimates come from token-level histograms and observed hit rates; for final validation we suggest a canary rollout and A/B metrics. we can run a 1-week pilot and capture delta on tokens and latency — that's what most customers do.

[00:06:08] Priya: SLOs — can we alert on tail latency > 500ms p99?

[00:06:12] Maya: yes, alerts are configurable — p50, p90, p95, p99, error rate. alerts can be routed to PagerDuty, Slack, or email. we also support custom Webhook integrations.

[00:06:22] Alex: earlier you mentioned the ability to export traces — what format and how big are they? we worry about storage cost.

[00:06:28] Maya: you can export in JSON or OTLP (OpenTelemetry) and push to S3 or your OTel backend. size depends on sampling and whether you include raw payloads; per-trace JSONs for typical chat sessions are around 5-30 KB.

[00:06:41] Priya: can you programmatically link our internal correlation ids into Redwood traces?

[00:06:45] Maya: yes we accept custom tags on requests — x-correlation-id — and those appear as searchable fields. we recommend instrumenting the SDK to always pass your trace id.

[00:06:52] Dana: there's been mention of 'model fallback' — if that happens during peak, do you surface that as an event?

[00:06:57] Maya: we log fallback events and they show up in the Events timeline; you can alert on fallback rate so you know when routing decisions dip into lower-tier models. fallback reason metadata is included: e.g., capacity, error, or explicit policy.

[00:07:12] Alex: any demo of a real debug session where you root-caused a 500?

[00:07:15] Maya: yes i'll walk through a case. (narration) here's a spike where the service experienced a downstream BPE tokenizer error — in the trace a subspan shows tokenizer failing with exception 'bpe_invalid_byte' which caused the runtime to throw 500. i clicked the stack trace in the span and saw the model sig mismatch — customer had uploaded a slightly different tokenizer config in their private model bundle. once we corrected the tokenizer config, the errors went away.

[00:07:44] Priya: interesting — how do you surface stack traces without exposing secrets?

[00:07:48] Maya: stack traces are sanitized; we remove environment variables and file paths. in Private deployments we can provide richer debug hooks since the environment is controlled by the customer.

[00:07:58] Alex: what's the overhead of tracing — do we add 50ms to requests?

[00:08:02] Maya: minimal. sampling and the show-time trace capture has a small serialization cost (usually <5ms) and kernel timing is recorded natively on the host. heavy debug mode adds more overhead so we don't enable it by default.

[00:08:12] Ben: ok switching to some procurement notes — high-level pricing will be in the deck i'll send, but for Dedicated we have monthly reserved capacity plus an observability add-on. any compliance docs you need?

[00:08:23] Dana: SOC2 is a must. and we need to review KMS integration for key management.

[00:08:27] Carlos: we'll attach our SOC 2 and ISO docs in the follow up. KMS integration is supported for Dedicated and Private; we have an HSM option for enterprise.

[00:08:36] Alex: for the pilot, we want a config where logs are retained for 90 days and traces sampled at 5% with 100% capture for errors and 5xx. is that doable?

[00:08:44] Carlos: absolutely — that's a typical pilot profile. i'll note that in action items.

[00:08:50] Priya: one more on observability — do you provide a single pane for cross-route cost attribution? we need to show product owners cost per route.

[00:08:58] Maya: yes, the Cost Explorer breaks down token spend by route, model, and user. you can also export per-token billing level data into BigQuery.

[00:09:06] Ben: wrapping up — any open questions?

[00:09:10] Alex: timeline: if we run a 1-week pilot starting 4/21, when could we expect results and a follow-up?

[00:09:15] Carlos: results within the week of pilot, then a review session following. we'll set a follow-up the week of 4/28.

[00:09:20] Dana: please send the console recording and the trace export example.

[00:09:24] Ben: will do. thanks everyone.

[00:09:28] (end of recording)

Auto-generated sections (may be imperfect):

Topics covered: console observability / traces / request replay / error analysis / Optimize suggestions / RBAC and audit logs / pilot next steps.

Action items (auto): Ben - pricing; Maya - trace export + recording; Priya - SSO metadata.

Questions asked: retention windows, sampling policy, request replay overhead, audit logs availability.

Notes on transcription: occasional overlap, speaker labels sometimes auto-populated as "Speaker 5" for a short bit. There are minor mis-hearings (e.g., 'rdx-3' sometimes transcribed as 'rocks three').

References mentioned: Redwood Dedicated pricing sheet (will be attached), SSO config doc (link to be shared), trace OTLP export sample (to be sent).

Recap / next steps: see action items; target pilot kickoff week of 2025-04-21; follow-up review week of 2025-04-28.

title: High tail latency after enabling aggressive KV prefetch + eviction policy with 4-bit quant profile; request safe unwind and preflight checks
text:
Issue summary: After tenant applied an aggressive optimization bundle (enabled KV prefetch=true, eviction_policy=aggressive_ttl, quant_profile=4-bit-fast) around 2026-03-12T09:10Z, they reported persistent tail latencies (95-99p) on text-generation endpoints. This appears to be correlated with cache churn and increased GPU kernel stall time when the quantized path hits cold prefixes.

Impact: Customer-facing latency spikes up to 2.5s tail; sustained error-free throughput decreased ~18% for this tenant. Affects production traffic for a healthcare scheduling product (SLA-sensitive).

Background: NimbusHealth runs on a dedicated pool with pinned capacity. They recently accepted a recommended optimization bundle from the console which combined aggressive KV prefetch (to warm caches), a TTL-driven eviction policy to free memory, and a 4-bit quantization profile to lower token cost. The combination was not validated against this tenant's long-prefix distribution.

Request: Customer is asking for immediate safe unwind steps and preflight checks we can run before reapplying any optimization. They want a staged rollback with low disruption and a checklist to avoid recurrence.

Desired outcome: Restore tail latency to baseline (<300ms p95) and provide a validated preflight that would catch prefetch+eviction+quant incompatibility for similar tenants.

1) On a dedicated tenant with long prefix workloads, enable KV prefetch=true and set eviction_policy=aggressive_ttl via console for a target model (redwood/gptx-13b-4bit)
2) Apply quant_profile=4-bit-fast and start traffic at baseline TPS for tenant for 30-60 minutes.
3) Observe p95/p99 latency increase and higher GPU stall metrics (kernel_wait_time) and cache miss rate in console traces.
4) Reproduce across two separate client prefixes to confirm distribution-sensitive failure mode.

Support triage 2026-03-12: confirmed config change triggered ~09:10Z. No infra node failures recorded.
SRE hypothesis: aggressive TTL eviction + prefetch is causing repeated large KV loads while quantized kernels incur longer cold-start kernel setup for wide prefixes, creating contention on GPU streams.
Observed that fallback 8-bit model has lower tail but higher average cost; suggests quant path amplifies cold prefix cost.
Cache-layer traces show bursts of full KV shard reads coincident with eviction sweeps (eviction windows align with tenant traffic patterns).

Advised customer to immediately set kv_prefetch=false for the tenant and reduce eviction aggressiveness (eviction_policy=standard_ttl). Applied changes via support console at 2026-03-12T10:05Z. Initial watch showed p95 drop from ~900ms to ~320ms within 5 minutes.

Workaround applied: kv_prefetch disabled and eviction_policy reverted to standard_ttl. Customer confirmed perceived latency improvement and agreed to a staged re-test. Next steps: produce and run a preflight script that simulates tenant prefix-length distribution against candidate optimization bundles; engineering will add a conservative gating rule to the console to warn when prefetch+aggressive_eviction+<5bit quant is selected together. Engineering follow-up ticket created.

2) SRE: Build a preflight validation script and add to support runbooks - due 2026-03-19
3) DOCS: Update optimization docs with best-practice for long-prefix workloads - due 2026-03-22
4) Customer success: schedule a post-change verification call with NimbusHealth for 2026-03-14

domain: 日常协作与非结构化讨论
title: eng-ml
text:
anika: Observed weird residual drift after reverting to nearest-anchor in prime-compress. Symptoms: attention mass recovers but generated answers still lose grounding for specific long-prefix patterns (~32k+). Short repro and minimal logs.

anika: Repro: RUNTIME=dev ./onboard.sh --model marlin-48k-int3 --ctx 48k --priming prime-compress --quant int3 --seed 99 > /tmp/marlin-prime.log 2>&1

mario: Interesting. So nearest fixed the head-level collapse but not end-to-end fidelity? Any quant-path differences between runs?

jess: I ran a differential with and without compress (nearest anchor) and A/B compared sample fidelity. Attention topk looked OK but token-level KL/CE still up by ~1.2 nats on a diagnostics set.

li: could be a subtle phase bias introduced by quantized packing combined with stride shrinking. If we compress blocks, we also rescale effective positional frequency (we implicitly downsample positions into anchors). Quantization noise can cause a small systematic phase rotation when you reconstruct keys.

anika: I pulled the low-level complex dot product diagnostics: per-kv-phase-angle delta clusters around +0.0017 radians for anchors near 31.5k-32.5k. It's small but across many heads it accumulates.

mario: small angle * number_of_heads -> noticeable destructive interference. Did you try applying a tiny compensating rotation when reconstructing KV entries?

jess: quick hack: multiply reconstructed key vectors by a complex phase correction exp(-1j * delta(theta)) where delta is computed from (orig_pos - anchor)/stride * beta. I tested beta=0.48 and saw sample fidelity recover ~0.8 of the gap.

anika: snippet I used (python-ish, sanitized):```
# reconstruct_kv.py (sanitized)
def apply_phase_correction(kv_keys, orig_pos, anchor, stride, beta=0.48):
 rel = (orig_pos - anchor) / float(stride)
 delta = rel * beta * BASE_PHASE_SCALE # BASE_PHASE_SCALE from rotary config
 # apply complex rotation to key vectors (split real/imag in packed format)
 cosd = np.cos(-delta); sind = np.sin(-delta)
 k_re, k_im = kv_keys[...,0], kv_keys[...,1]
 k_rot_re = k_re * cosd - k_im * sind
 k_rot_im = k_re * sind + k_im * cosd
 kv_keys[...,0], kv_keys[...,1] = k_rot_re, k_rot_im
 return kv_keys
```

li: neat. That directly undoes a linear-in-rel offset. How did it behave across quant modes?

jess: Ran int3 and int4 variants. With beta tuned per-quant-mode (int3: 0.48, int4: 0.35) we recovered CE to within 0.1 of baseline for our eval shard. Also ran --quant-skip-reshape to verify effect is not from reshape ordering.

mario: Where's BASE_PHASE_SCALE coming from? If rotary uses ctx-scaled base freq, this must be computed per-model from rotary config. Danger: hardcoding could mis-calibrate across models.

anika: agreed — we compute BASE_PHASE_SCALE = mean(layer_rotary_scale * freq_factor) from the model config at load-time. The beta is then a small heuristic learned via a quick grid on a tiny validation set.

li: We should avoid heuristics in production unless we have a clear theoretical derivation. Is there a closed-form for expected phase drift given quant error and anchor rounding bias? If so we can set beta deterministically.

jess: Short derivation: rounding/packing produces an expected per-dimension quantization bias q_bias ~ E[quant_error], which induces an effective rotation angle proportional to q_bias / |k| times the local frequency. Anchor re-anchoring multiplies that by relative offset rel. Beta approximates the proportionality constant. I'll add math to the ticket.

mario: Ok pragmatic plan: (1) land a guarded phase-correction fallback behind a flag --prime-phase-corr that defaults off; (2) add an autotune job during onboarding that runs a tiny grid for beta per-quant-mode and records recommended beta into model metadata; (3) add unit tests that simulate quant noise + anchors and assert reconstruction dot(k_query, k_recon) delta < epsilon.

anika: I created a CI job for autotune and quick regen: https://ci.redwood/org/jobs/3323456789-autotune and pushed minimal logs.

ci-bot: Job 2026-03-23T15:12:01Z started: 3323456789-autotune (owner: jess). Logs: https://ci.redwood/org/jobs/3323456789-autotune/logs

jess: quick results: int3 beta=0.49, int4 beta=0.36, float16 beta~0.0 (no correction needed). CE gap closed ~90% on our small shard. Artifacts: https://ci.redwood/org/artifacts/3323456789/autotune.json

li: followups: (a) add unit test under tests/kv/phase_corr_test.py that injects synthetic quant noise and anchors to validate bound, (b) add model-catalog metadata field `priming_phase_corr` with per-quant recommended beta, (c) run full 64k sweep with the flag enabled to ensure no regressions.

mario: also flag to ops: we need to record the autotune artifact in onboarding so Dedicated/Private deployments can opt-in (and not silently change outputs). Add note to onboarding checklist.

anika: I'll file the onboarding ticket and attach autotune artifacts + a short explainer. Jess/mario/LI please include your PRs for the flag and unit tests.

jess: will open PR with the guarded flag + autotune integration and include the simple python implementation above. I'll also add an integration test that runs the small eval shard with and without correction to show delta.

ci-bot: Job finished: 3323456789-autotune (status: success). Artifacts: https://ci.redwood/org/artifacts/3323456789/autotune

mario: sounds good. One policy note: default-on heuristics are dangerous; keep default off and record recommended beta in onboarding metadata. Ops/SE can enable per-customer after validation.

anika: agreed. tagging @product later for catalog note. Closing loop on this thread once PRs land. :white_check_mark:

title: multitenant-gpu-consolidation-exercise-notes
author: Sofia Martinez
text:
Context:
Customer: Customer Sigma (finance vertical), wants to consolidate 3 internal ML teams onto a single Dedicated pool to reduce spend and simplify ops. Current state: each team runs independent single-model endpoints on A100-like instances, overprovisioned for peaks. Goal for POC: demonstrate safe consolidation with predictable latency SLO (p95 < 350ms), cost reduction target >= 30% vs current committed spend, and an autoscale policy that prevents noisy-neighbor regressions.

High-level approach:
- Build a small multi-tenant pool (initially 2 x A100-80GB equiv) with per-tenant QoS controls and predictable routing rules.
- Implement workload-aware autoscaler that considers active KV cache hit-rate, current token/sec, and per-route latency headroom.
- Run a 48h stress experiment with synthetic and recorded traffic from each team; measure p50/p95, throughput, and token cost.

Assumptions and inputs we used for quick math (POC assumptions, make explicit to customer):
- Model mix: 70% chat/complete requests (avg 220 tokens/request), 30% embeddings (avg 512-d vectors, 1.6k tokens/request equivalent compute).
- Median concurrent sessions pre-POC: team A: 120, team B: 45, team C: 30 -> aggregate median concurrency ~195. Peak concurrency: +2.5x burst factor -> ~490.
- Per-GPU sustained throughput: A100-80GB baseline approx 2000 tokens/sec for chat model (quantized int8 path), embedding model throughput higher due to shorter context; we conservatively treat embedding CPU+GPU pipeline as equivalent to 1500 tokens/sec.
- KV cache expected hit-rate: 12% (workload has some repetition), prefix caching reduces token generation by approx 10% effective.
- Cost estimates used: A100-80GB equivalent purchased on Dedicated pool: $2.80/hr (effective blended cost after reserved discount). H100-like: $5.90/hr (note: numbers are illustrative for customer discussion).

Quick consolidation cost simulation (6-month window):
- Baseline (current): each team separate; effective committed hours: 3 x 24/7 x 1 GPU = 3 * 24 * 30 * 6 = 12,960 GPU-hours. At $2.80/hr -> $36,288.
- Consolidated pool initial commit: 2 GPUs baseline, with autoscale up to 5 for burst windows. Steady-state expected commit to hit SLA: 2 GPUs * 24*30*6 = 8640 GPU-hours -> $24,192.
- Estimated autoscale burst delta (additional hours for month-long simulation): approx 700 extra GPU-hours -> $1,960.
- Total expected 6-month spend (consolidated) ~ $26,152 -> ~28% reduction vs baseline.
- Sensitivity: If median concurrency shifts +20%, autoscale adds 1 permanent GPU and costs rise ~12% (clear knob to monitor).

Autoscale policy proposal (POC config idea):
- Metrics: primary = aggregate_inflight_requests (per-second smoothed), secondary = observed_p95_latency (sliding window 5m), tertiary = KV_cache_hit_rate.
- Scale-up rules: +1 GPU when inflight > 180 per GPU_capacity_threshold OR observed_p95_latency > target_latency * 1.15 for 3 consecutive 30s windows.
- Scale-down rules: -1 GPU when inflight < 90 per GPU for 10m and p95_latency < target_latency * 0.9 and cache_hit_rate stable (>8%).
- Cooldown: 5m on scale-up, 15m on scale-down for stability.
- Max concurrency per GPU target: 220 concurrent generation sessions (~safe headroom for tail-latency bursts).
- Canary rule: if p95 > 450ms for two minutes after a scale event, trigger automated rollback to last-known-good routing (route heavy teams to reserved lane or hosted fallback).

QoS / tenant isolation controls (recommended):
- Per-tenant route weight: reserve guaranteed slots (e.g., team A=55% baseline concurrency reservation, B=25%, C=20%) enforced by request admission at the routing layer.
- Token rate limits per-tenant to protect throughput during storms.
- Soft-priority queues: promote latency-sensitive short requests, batchable embedding requests placed in lower priority queue to increase batching efficiency.
- Fallbacks: define per-tenant fallback to smaller quantized model or hosted API in case of sustained quota exceed.

Experiment plan (POC runbook):
1) Week 0 - prep: ingest real recent traffic traces (anonymized), synthetic generator scripts, baseline SLO dashboard. Baseline CPU/GPU perf runs with sample payloads.
2) Week 1 - small closed traffic run: 2 GPUs, 24h, low burst. Validate latency and cost telemetry, tune admission control.
3) Week 2 - scaled stress: introduce peak bursts (2.5x) and KV-cache warm/cold dynamics, measure autoscale reaction and tail latency.
4) Week 3 - tenant shuffle + failure injection: kill one GPU, simulate network hiccups, ensure graceful degradation (route to hosted or fall back to smaller model).
5) Week 4 - report and handoff: run extended 48h replicant, produce final TCO and recommendations.

Runbook checklist for engineers (play-by-play during run):
- verify admin keys and tenant bindings are correct
- enable token-level billing and per-route tracing for first 24h
- run eviction/GC probe to confirm KV cache sizes and eviction rate under load
- continuous perf dashboard (p50/p95/p99, queue depth, batch sizes, GPU util%)
- after each major test, snapshot model KV-state, config, and load generator seed for reproducibility

Preliminary observations from lab experiments (notes):
- Multi-tenant batching gained ~14% throughput due to cross-tenant batch packing for embeddings (unexpected but repeatable in lab).
- Noisy-tenant effect visible when Team A runs long-chat sessions with >2k tokens — this drove p99 spikes; admission control prevented spillover.
- Quantized int8 performance for chat model reduced per-token compute by ~1.6x but increased variance on long sequences; choose hybrid: int8 for short/medium sequences, fp16 for long chat flows.

Open questions for customer workshop:
- Are there hard regulatory constraints that force per-tenant hardware isolation? If yes, consolidation will be limited to logical isolation only.
- Acceptable fallback mix: hosted fallback acceptable for non-PII traffic? (we need explicit approval).
- Upcoming model changes: customer expecting to onboard a 70B dense model in next quarter — should influence longer-term capacity commit.

Suggested deliverables for POC proposal doc to customer:
- 2-page SLA and autoscale behavior summary (visual diagrams)
- 1-page cost sensitivity chart (+/- concurrency and GPU price)
- 1-runbook appendix with step-by-step escalation and rollback actions
- 48h lab report with perf traces and config snapshots

Action items (owners):
- Sofia: assemble the 48h traffic synth (deadline 2024-08-19)
- Raj: implement autoscale prototype (PR link above) and add canary rollback hook (deadline 2024-08-23)
- Lina: build dashboard (alerts for p95 > 350ms, queue depth > 500, cache_hit_rate drop > 5pp) and initial runbook text (2024-08-20)
- Marcus: prepare sample cost sheet for customer including H100 vs A100 scenarios (2024-08-21)

Notes-to-self: keep the POC conservative on scale-down to avoid oscillation; emphasize observability (traces + per-token cost attribution) in proposal. Also, include example curl snippets for tenant routing and the hosted fallback test in the final appendix.

End of notes.

title: JWT refresh mid-session causes orphaned function executions and duplicated external webhook calls behind private API gateway
text:
Issue summary:
Customer reports duplicate external webhook invocations and orphaned function call side-effects when their client SDK performs an automatic JWT refresh mid-stream while connected to a Private deployment behind an internal API gateway. Duplicates show up as repeated outbound POSTs to the same webhook with slightly different idempotency metadata.

Impact:
- Customer observed repeated charges in downstream system (payment webhook) for ~12 orders over a 3-hour window.
- Affects single customer cluster in their Private deployment (FinVault production cluster).
- Risk: financial reconciliation and potential regulatory exposure.

Environment:
- Redwood Private deployment (v2025-12-03) on customer-managed VPC
- Customer SDK: python-sdk v0.9.8 (auto-refresh enabled)
- Ingress: internal API gateway (company-managed) performs header cleaning and routing to Redwood private control plane
- Network: mTLS with short-lived JWTs (60s TTL) rotated by auth service

Steps to reproduce (as reported):
1) Start Python streaming session using function-calling (sdk.generate_stream with tools enabled) to orchestrate a checkout flow.
2) Mid-stream (~35s in) customer auth service returns a refreshed JWT via a background refresh and client replaces Authorization header on the socket without reconnecting.
3) SDK continues the stream; outgoing function call triggers an external webhook.
4) Customer sees the webhook endpoint receive 2–3 POSTs for the same logical action within seconds.

Observed behavior:
- Outbound webhook requests include an idempotency header that appears truncated or normalized differently by gateway (e.g., idempotency-token: "ord-9f8c..." vs "ORD-9F8C...").
- Server logs show the same request being retried in the runtime with overlapping request IDs after the JWT swap.
- Webhook server reports duplicate processing for 11/12 of the events.

Expected behavior:
- Mid-session JWT refresh should be transparent to the runtime and SDK without causing duplicate function invocations or replays.
- Idempotency tokens must be preserved verbatim across proxied requests so downstream systems can deduplicate.

Logs / snippets provided by customer:
- client debug logs (python): "Refreshed JWT, swapping Authorization header mid-stream, resuming socket"
- runtime snippet: "received_request id=3a7b... parent_stream=st-99a; kvcache_hit=false; resume_token=tok-44"
- gateway access logs show header-normalization rule: lowercase-all-headers=true

Additional context:
- Customer is on a Private deployment with custom gateway header sanitation rules.
- They intentionally rotate JWTs aggressively for compliance.
- They use our function-calling pattern where each \"tool\" maps to an external webhook with downstream non-idempotent side-effects (billing).

2026-03-01 09:12 - Support (Aisha Malik): Acknowledged. Escalating to SRE and Eng. Added P1 and requested logs + replay instructions. Asked customer to pause webhook processing as a mitigant if possible.
2026-03-01 10:03 - SRE (Priya Shah): Noted gateway header-normalization. Hypothesis: header canonicalization is modifying idempotency token case/format causing runtime to treat calls as different or SDK to retransmit. Also possible: mid-stream auth header swap triggers a transport-level reconnect and SDK retry logic replays function call without de-dupe metadata. Collecting tcpdump and runtime request traces.
2026-03-01 14:36 - Customer (FinVault - ops@finvault.com): Provided tcpdump, gateway config snippet, and example webhook POSTs. Confirmed gateway lowercases header names and strips unknown header characters. Asked for recommended immediate mitigation.
2026-03-02 08:21 - Engineering (Diego Alvarez): Reproduced locally with private-like proxy that lowercases headers and short JWT TTL. Observed that when Authorization header is swapped in-band, the SDK's internal stream library flips to 'soft-reconnect' mode which resends the last tool invocation after re-establishing the control frame. Instrumentation shows runtime receives duplicate tool invocation frames with different request_meta.idempotency_value (case-normalized). Opened PR to make SDK preserve idempotency metadata at the application layer and add stronger dedupe on runtime if idempotency token exists header-agnostically.
2026-03-02 15:00 - Support (Aisha Malik): Shared temporary mitigation: configure gateway to passthrough our idempotency header (x-redwood-idempotency) and disable header normalization; or increase JWT TTL to avoid mid-stream rotation. Customer applied passthrough rule and reported immediate reduction in duplicates.

Findings:
- Reproduction succeeded when proxy lowercases header names and removes non-alphanumeric characters, which modified the idempotency token case and occasionally truncated hyphens.
- SDK behavior: during an in-band Authorization swap the underlying websocket/stream client transitions modes, and because function-call acknowledgement had not yet been observed by the client, it retried the tool call. The SDK retry used the in-memory idempotency token which had been normalized by the gateway (case changed), so downstream webhook saw a different token.
- Runtime mitigation gap: runtime deduplication currently checks idempotency tokens using case-sensitive equality on headers; when headers are mutated by proxies, the runtime cannot dedupe.
Hypothesis validated by: reproducing with a local envoy config that lowercases headers and forces a header rewrite mid-stream.
Next steps proposed:
1) Short-term: recommend customers set gateway passthrough for x-redwood-idempotency and/or increase JWT TTL. Support to provide config snippets ASAP.
2) Medium-term (ENG): SDK patch to include idempotency token inside the streaming control frame payload (application-level) so proxies cannot mutate it; PR opened: serving-runtime/pull/2124 and python-sdk/pull/486.
3) Long-term (ENG): runtime to implement case-insensitive idempotency header normalization and token canonicalization (strip non-alphanum preserved characters) and stronger single-source dedupe keyed by request-id + canonical token.

Workaround implemented and validated:
- Customer updated their gateway to passthrough x-redwood-idempotency and disabled header lowercasing for requests to the private control plane.
- Customer temporarily increased JWT TTL to 5 minutes to avoid mid-stream refreshes during active sessions.
Permanent fix plan:
- Merged python-sdk change to embed idempotency token in control frames (python-sdk v0.9.9).
- Serving runtime PR (idempotency canonicalization + case-insensitive compare) merged to main; will ship in v2026-03-15 scheduled private deployment patch.
Follow-ups:
- Post-deploy validation runbook created and linked: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/JWT+Rolling+Keys+Runbook (added a checklist item about idempotency passthrough).
- Customer will run a canary for 48h after patch; Support to monitor billing webhook traffic and confirm no duplicates.
Status: In Progress (workaround applied; permanent fixes merged and scheduled).

Duplicates caused 11 duplicate webhook-side charges affecting 12 orders. Mitigated by gateway passthrough and TTL increase; awaiting runtime + SDK rollout for full remediation.

raw_metadata.resolution: Workaround applied; permanent fixes merged and scheduled for deployment

title: Capacity Orchestration Experiments & Q2 Playbook — Dedicated Pools + Predictive Autoscale
author: Anika Patel
text:
Goal: Produce a runnable Q2 playbook that proves two predictive autoscale strategies for dedicated GPU pools (time-series demand predictor + fast-warm reservoir) and a set of measurable rollout criteria. Scope includes experiment design, metric instrumentation, dashboarding, two canary rollouts, and a decision gate for GA readiness. This ticket consolidates PM-level milestones, success metrics, and cross-functional asks for Eng, SRE, Console, and Billing.

Design doc with experiment matrix and traffic slices approved by Eng and SRE
Two independent autoscale strategies implemented in staging and smoke-tested under synthetic traffic
Dashboards show warm-pool utilization, prewarm latency, cost delta per token, and failure/retry rates
Canary rollout plan with rollback triggers and runbook validated in one customer-simulated scenario
Decision: one strategy recommended for Q3 soft-launch or clear reasons to iterate further

2025-02-21: Instrumentation landed and dashboard prototype published
2025-03-07: Staging canary run #1 (time-series predictor)
2025-03-21: Staging canary run #2 (fast-warm reservoir)
2025-03-28: PM decision gate and playbook published

Use two independent strategies in parallel rather than iterative A/B to collect orthogonal signals
Scope excludes changes to tenancy or pricing contract language for this quarter — billing implications will be a follow-up
All canary runs must include one real customer traffic mirror where the customer has opted in

Predictive model cold-starts lead to spike in prewarm cost without latency gains
KV cache warming behavior in long-tail workloads may invalidate synthetic test results
Insufficient visibility into per-route cost makes tradeoffs hard to quantify
Customer-facing degradation if rollback automation is incomplete

title: Larkline AssistCo
author: Jordan Kim
text:
SMB helpdesk automation provider wants hosted API for ticket summarization + agent-assist. Needs structured JSON outputs and tool-calling to tag/update Zendesk tickets. Early discovery; self-serve signup -> 2-week POC on public cloud. Key goals: low-latency summaries, predictable cost per ticket, audit logs and retention controls.

Inbound via Intercom trial signup 2026-02-09 → filled 'interest: ticket summarization + automation'
Customer: SMB support automation vendor building hosted SaaS (ticketing + agent assist); self-serve signup first, likely expand to dedicated in future
First contact (2026-02-10): Jordan Kim intro call — AE noted product-market fit around small-mid enterprises, strong PLG motion
Primary workflow: ingest incoming emails/tickets, auto-generate concise summaries, propose structured 'next_steps' and 'escalation_flag', optionally call external tooling to tag tickets or add internal notes

Technical note from SE (Maya): will want sample streaming behaviour and function-calling examples; asked for quickstart + small test key

title: Fast tier tail-latency protection (wait budget + admission control + anti-starvation)
author: Sofia Ivanova
text:
Implement tail-latency protections for the FAST SLO tier.

Problem:
With more aggressive continuous batching + mixed workloads, FAST tier p99 is sensitive to (a) queueing delay from wait-to-batch and (b) head-of-line blocking when long-prefill requests accumulate. We need explicit FAST-tier protections so “fast” is predictable under concurrency, while still avoiding starvation of long prompts.

Scope:
- Tighter wait budget for FAST tier (time-based cap on queueing before admission/scheduling).
- Admission control for FAST tier under overload (prevent queue blow-ups, preserve p99).
- Starvation prevention so long-prefill requests eventually run even when short requests dominate.

Non-goals:
- Global routing changes (handled by existing smart routing policies).
- Per-tenant auto-tuning of knobs (this is tier-default behavior + safe heuristics).

Owner notes:
This ticket is runtime-side; policy/config surfaces are in ENG-18422/ENG-18430. We should expose enough metrics/reason codes so SRE can validate behavior during canary (ENG-18429/ENG-18426).

1) FAST tier meets tier SLO gates in benchmark-lab + perf-canary for top model families on target hardware classes (per SLO doc referenced in ENG-18421).
2) Under overload, FAST tier does not exhibit unbounded queue growth: queue depth plateaus via admission control and/or shedding, with explicit reason codes emitted.
3) Anti-starvation: long-prefill requests are not indefinitely deferred by a stream of short requests (validated via mixed prompt-length scenario in perf suite).
4) Streaming: time-to-first-token (TTFT) for FAST tier does not regress beyond the agreed gate (tracked in perf suite and dashboards).
5) Changes are guarded behind tiered-batching feature flag and can be disabled via kill switch (ENG-18431 / PR-28480 dependency satisfied).

Implemented FAST-tier protections in scheduler:

A) FAST-tier wait budget
- Add tier-specific max_queue_wait_ms_fast (tighter than standard), applied before joining a batch.
- If wait budget is exceeded, request is forced into next eligible batch (or handled by overload mode if admission cannot occur safely).

B) Admission control / overload mode hooks
- Add per-tier queue depth and in-flight token budget guards.
- When FAST tier is over guardrail, transition to overload behavior:
 - stop increasing batch size for FAST tier (prefer smaller, more frequent batches)
 - optionally shed new FAST-tier requests based on policy (HTTP 429/503 depending on upstream) with clear telemetry
 - emit reason code: overload_admission_block / overload_shed

C) Anti-starvation
- Introduce age-based priority boost: requests accrue “age credits” while queued.
- Add max_defer_count: requests that have been skipped N times are forced eligible.
- Maintain a small reserved prefill slice for long-prefill bucket to guarantee progress (bounded impact to FAST p99 by capping slice).

D) Observability
- FAST-tier metrics tagged by tier with cardinality controls (coordinate with PR-28492 / hotfix PR-28544 if needed).
- Emit tracing span + structured reason code when:
 - wait budget triggered
 - admission blocked/shed
 - starvation prevention forced eligibility

Primary code path: scheduler admission + batch formation loop (prefill/decode balancing).

Perf / correctness validation:
- Unit tests for wait budget + max_defer_count behavior (deterministic queue simulations).
- Integration test with mixed prompt-length buckets (short chat + long summarization) at concurrency ramps.
- Streaming scenario: validate TTFT distribution and chunk cadence at steady-state QPS.
- Overload scenario: verify queue depth plateaus + reason codes emitted; verify system remains responsive (no deadlock/starvation).

Pass/fail:
- Must pass perf suite gates for FAST p99 and TTFT per ENG-18421 thresholds.
- Must show bounded queue depth under synthetic overload (guardrail thresholds documented in rollout checklist).

1) Land behind tiered-batching feature flag (ENG-18431).
2) Internal canary in one region + top 1-2 model families.
3) Expand to hosted API subset (small % of FAST-tier traffic) with SRE watching:
 - FAST p99 latency, TTFT
 - queue depth, admission block rate
 - shed rate and customer-visible error rate
4) If stable for 48h and perf-canary remains green, expand to broader hosted.
5) Dedicated remains opt-in pending Dedicated override precedence checks (ENG-18430).

Rollback:
- Flip kill switch to disable FAST-tier protections (revert to standard-tier behavior) OR disable tiered batching entirely depending on symptom.
- If telemetry cost spikes due to tier labels, deploy cardinality hotfix (PR-28544) and temporarily reduce sampling.

2026-01-16 — Sofia Ivanova: Marking P0. We need explicit FAST-tier protections before we default any batching profiles. Please coordinate with Sean/Aisha on which metrics they need to page on (FAST p99 vs TTFT).
2026-01-22 — Omar El-Sayed: Initial plan: implement max_queue_wait_ms_fast + per-tier admission guardrail based on queue depth and in-flight token budget. For anti-starvation, proposing age-based priority + max defer count rather than hard partitioning queues (keeps utilization decent). Will share graphs after first benchmark run.
2026-02-02 — Marcus Reed: Mixed workload scenario added locally shows head-of-line when long prefill dominates. Suggest we add a cap on “prefill share” for FAST tier to keep decode moving; otherwise TTFT jumps even when p50 looks fine.
2026-02-07 — Omar El-Sayed: Implemented prefill share cap + wait budget. Early results: FAST p99 improved ~12–18% on chat-heavy mix, but saw starvation risk for long-prefill bucket at high QPS. Working on max_defer_count + age credits.
2026-02-13 — Allison Grant: Please ensure reason codes are low-cardinality. We’ve been burned by putting raw thresholds or queue IDs into tags. Prefer enum reason_code + tier label only.
2026-02-18 — Omar El-Sayed: Added starvation prevention (age credits + max_defer_count=3). Verified with synthetic queue test: long-prefill requests complete within bounded time even under continuous short traffic. Next: hook into tracing and expose counters for wait_budget_triggered and forced_eligible_due_to_starvation.
2026-03-03 — Rafael Mendes: For canary, we need explicit abort thresholds (FAST p99 regression, shed rate, error budget). Please add suggested thresholds to the rollout checklist doc once we have baseline numbers.
2026-03-08 — Omar El-Sayed: Opened PR-28458 with wait budget + admission guardrails + anti-starvation. Perf suite: FAST p99 gate passes on A100; borderline on H100 for one model family due to increased context-switching. Adjusted cap values and rerunning.
2026-03-12 — Sofia Ivanova: Reviewed PR. Main ask: clarify overload behavior contract (what errors bubble up) and ensure kill switch disables the whole behavior cleanly. Also confirm streaming TTFT doesn’t regress with max_defer_count logic.
2026-03-15 — Omar El-Sayed: Addressed review. Overload mode now emits reason_code=overload_admission_block and returns standardized upstream signal; kill switch verified. Streaming TTFT stable in benchmarks (no measurable regression within noise).
2026-03-18 — Connor O'Brien: Confirmed included in runtime-1.22 cut. Please coordinate with SRE on canary schedule; release notes will reference “FAST tier tail latency protections” and point to dashboards.

title: Degradation controlplane patterns
author: Marin Alvarez
text:
Working notes for a compact, operator-friendly control-plane approach that enforces deterministic graceful degradation across model variants, tenant slices, and regions. Focus on auditable decisioning and measurable user impact

We operate heterogeneous fleets (hosted + dedicated + private). When pressure or failures happen we tend to have ad-hoc fallbacks. Need a small set of patterns that control-plane teams can reuse, with clear telemetry requirements and safe rollout steps.

Create a small vocabulary for degradation levels (L0..L3) and map model builds to them
Specify capacity-slicing semantics for multi-tenant pools and how admission control interacts with downgrade
Define control-plane policy primitives and examples operators can apply
List concrete testing/rollout steps and telemetry to validate user impact
Document operational runbook actions tied to each degradation trigger

Pattern: treat each request as (tenant, route, region, cost_estimate). Control plane evaluates policy predicates and yields an ordered candidate list of (variant, capacity_slice, region_target). Runtime enforces deterministic step-down and reports chosen_variant and reason. Cross-region spillover is conditional on route-level latency budget and region health signals.

Named slices: premium, standard, best-effort; slices carry soft token/sec and concurrency targets
Steady-state reservation for premium slice; standard can burst into reserved free capacity; best-effort is lowest priority
Admission procedure: pre-check token-budget -> if exceed then attempt bounded queue -> if queue full then degrade model -> if degrade impossible then reject
Slice quotas are per-tenant per-region. Cross-region pooling only used for spillover after local downgrade fails within latency budget

L0 - Full fidelity: float/FP16 or high-precision quantized model, full KV caching, full context window
L1 - Performance-optimized: aggressive quantization (e.g., 8-bit), fewer decoding passes, warmed caches where possible
L2 - Distilled/medium: smaller architecture with similar API but reduced reasoning fidelity and shorter context support
L3 - Best-effort tiny: minimal model for syntactic/completion tasks; last-resort fallback or short-answer-only mode

match(T): boolean predicate on request metadata (tenant, route, prompt_length)
prefer: ordered list of variants annotated with degradation level and latency/cost guards
latency_budget_ms: numeric guard used for cross-region decisions
spillover: allow|deny with ordered region preference
queue_policy: drop-oldest|drop-new|bounded-wait and queue_timeout_ms
Example policy (stringified): "policy finance-payments { match: tenant ==\"enterprise\" && route == \"document-summarize\"; prefer: [\"llm-xl-v3@L0\", \"llm-xl-v3-8bit@L1\"]; fallback: [\"llm-m-distilled@L2\"]; latency_budget_ms: 320; spillover: allow(region_order=[\"us-west-2\",\"us-east-1\"]); }"

Deterministic step-down: runtime must try variants in declared order; never randomly sample competing variants during pressure
Guarded spillover: do cross-region routing only if estimated RTT + processing <= latency_budget_ms
Quota-first: when slice quota exceeded, prefer bounded queueing before model downgrade for short spikes
Context-aware selection: for long prompts prefer variants that support larger context even if higher cost; policy can declare route_hint=long_context

Per-policy metrics: chosen_variant, fallback_count, queue_drops, reject_count
Quality hooks: golden-prompt scoring for L0 vs L1/L2 cohorts and drift alerts if score delta > threshold
Operational alerts: sustained fallback_rate > 5% over 10m -> ops; cross-region-spillover > 15% traffic -> paging
Cost telemetry: token_cost_estimate per-request and rolling tenant spend delta when policies change

Shadow mode: evaluate policy decisions and log differences without altering live routing for 24-72h
Canary: route subset (1-5%) through new policy with automated quality comparison on golden prompts
Chaos test: simulated region blackhole + load spike to validate deterministic step-down and runbook triggers
Preflight checks: policy vetter rejects policies that raise expected avg token cost for premium tenants without approval

Variant unhealthy: control plane flags variant -> runtime steps to next ladder level; operator investigates GPU errors, kernel logs, infra metrics
Unplanned cross-region spillover: confirm latency budgets, check region health, redeploy compatible model builds to target region or enable burst pools
High fallback rate alert: investigate root cause (scaling misconfig, model regression, traffic pattern change); rollback policy pointer if needed
Emergency rollback: immediate policy pointer swap to last stable version triggers deterministic mapping and restores previous behavior

Expose degradation info to customers (response header) vs keep internal-only? Tradeoffs include transparency vs surface area for abuse
How to maintain tokenizer and behavior compatibility across quantized/distilled builds? Need automated semantic regression tests
Should we support fractional degradation (e.g., A/B across variants) or stick to deterministic ladders for predictability?
What SLA commitments can we promise for Dedicated vs Hosted when degradation occurs? Need legal/product alignment

title: Field friction: quant standup notes and quick triage
author: Maya Chen
text:
Context:
Quick capture from Friday standup + immediate triage (short, rough). Focus: weird regressions in 4-bit KV-onboarding for hawthorn-7b variants and a persistent p50 latency bump when prefetch is enabled on GPU pools. Not a formal postmortem yet — this is the working log for next steps and owners.

Summary (top-line):
- Observed a relative TER (token error / mismatch rate on edge eval) increase from ~2.1% -> 3.8% after model was onboarded with our default 4-bit quant profile and KV-prefetch enabled. (Evals: convo-robustness-small, summarization-standard)
- P50 latency for short-chat workloads increased by ~12% on dedicated-n1 GPU pool when prefetch + microbatching enabled; p95 stable.
- Failure mode: occasional KV-cache mismatch leading to drifting generations on continuation tasks (repro on smaller subset). Likely interaction between our token-aligned caching and new integer remapping in the quant path.
- Immediate customer impact: none reported in prod yet — this is staged/dedicated onboarding traffic. Still priority-high for onboarding pipeline.

Observed signals & quick evidence:
- Eval diffs (Ethan ran): convo-robustness-small: baseline FP16 perplexity 14.2; 4bit-quant w/ default profile perplexity 14.8; but mismatch cases concentrate on multi-turn pronoun resolution examples.
- Short-chat latency: baseline p50 42ms -> 47ms with prefetch; p95 unchanged ~120ms. Microbatch config used: batch_size=8, batch_delay=5ms.
- Log signature: KV checksum mismatches flagged in debug trace (kv-checksum != expected) ~0.4% of requests; higher on runs with heavy short prefixes and lots of cache hits.
- Repro note: running the same model with prefetch disabled reduces mismatch rate to ~0.05% (orders of magnitude).

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Integer remap collision: new 4-bit packing layers remap some outlier activations; when we write/read cached KV blocks we apply a different packed ordering that creates bit-level discrepancies for rare tokens. Prefetch exacerbates because it writes precomputed packed blocks before runtime path completes remap checks.
2) Race between prefetch writer and runtime resharder (less likely): prefetch writes blocks earlier; if runtime applies final remap/transpose later the stored layout mismatches read layout.
3) Microbatch reordering: batching reorder policy with short latency windows may be replaying token ids in an unexpected order for 4-bit, exposing a latent indexing bug.

Immediate actions (owners + ETA):
- Disable prefetch for hawthorn-7b default profile in dedicated-n1 pools until a patch (temporary safety). Owner: Priya (actioned 2029-06-18).
- Add checksum-on-write + read-verify for KV cache in quant path (cheap guard) to detect and auto-invalidate suspect blocks. Owner: Lukas; prototype by 2029-06-21.
- Run focused ablation: 4-bit packing v1 vs v2, prefetch on/off, microbatch on/off across the failing testset (10k requests). Owner: Ethan; results by 2029-06-20.
- Add deterministic repro harness: 25-seed replay for multi-turn pronoun resolution examples (to capture drift). Owner: Maya; due 2029-06-20.
- Postmortem kickoff if checksum still triggered after above.

Short experiment plan (Ethan notes):
- Matrix: packing-profile {v1, v2, v2-remap-fix}, prefetch {on, off}, microbatch {on(8,5ms), off}. 2k requests per cell across convo-robustness-small. Measure TER, perplexity, p50/p95 latency, kv-checksum-fail.
- Quick perf expectation: packing-profile v2-remap-fix should match baseline TER if hypothesis 1 is correct.

Triage logs / quick debug artifacts:
- Example failure (abbreviated):
 - prompt: "User: Where did Maya leave the keys?\n Assistant: She left them on the kitchen table.\n User: What color were they?"
 - baseline: "They were silver."
 - 4bit-prefetch: "They were red." (inconsistent pronoun resolution)
 - debug: kv-checksum mismatch for block id 0x7a9c; write-timestamp 13:24:02.314

Notes from Lukas (implementation quick notes):
- Packing v2 uses chunked nibble layout with remap map R; current cache serializer assumes contiguous nibble ordering (legacy). Prefetch path uses serializer V1 by mistake for some code paths. Looks like a simple codepath mismatch (serializer versioning missing).
- Will add metadata header in cache blob with serializer version and simple CRC. If mismatch, invalidation and regen.

Blocking / questions:
- Do we want to auto-roll back existing dedicated slots that used default profile? (Risk: small unless workload hit) -> Decision: for now do not auto-rollback; disable prefetch only.
- How to instrument user-facing metrics to detect this type of drift early in hosted run? We should add a lightweight "context-stable" probe in eval harness that runs on a tiny sample of sessions and compares last-turn logits with baseline for divergence. Owner: Product/Optimize sync to discuss.

Follow-ups and timeline:
- 2029-06-18: prefetch disabled for hawthorn-7b default profile (Priya) - DONE
- 2029-06-20: deterministic repro harness + Ethan's ablation results - IN PROGRESS
- 2029-06-21: checksum guard prototype in quant cache (Lukas) - WIP
- 2029-06-22: decision meeting with runtime & infra to evaluate rollout of serializer header + auto-invalidate (scheduled 11:00 PT). Attendees: Maya, Lukas, Priya, Ethan, Noor, runtime eng lead.

Loose ideas (brainstorm):
- Make prefetch writer more conservative for quantized blobs: write only when sequence length > threshold or when auto-verified by runtime step.
- Maintain a tiny (8-byte) fingerprint per cached block computed from raw fp32 before quantization so we can cheaply detect structural divergence later without full CRC overhead.
- Add an on-deploy integration test that replays 100 multi-turn examples through new serializer/packing to catch this class of mismatch.

Notes to self (Maya):
- This is a good reminder: serialization versioning is cheap insurance. Add to onboarding checklist.
- Tie a small eval probe (10 sessions) to onboarding flow for any quant profile changes — if divergence > threshold, fail the rollout.

Open action list (short):
- [Priya] Disable prefetch for default profiles (done).
- [Ethan] Run full ablation matrix; collect metrics (due 6/20).
- [Lukas] Add serializer header + CRC and quick invalidation path (prototype 6/21).
- [Maya] Create onboarding checklist PR and add eval probe hook (6/20).
- [Noor] Prep runtime meeting notes and capacity impact estimate for disabling prefetch (6/21).

Quick decisions made in-standup:
- No customer rollback yet; prefer targeted config change (prefetch off) + quick guard.
- Prioritize checksum guard over full serializer refactor for immediate mitigation.

Misc capture (random):
- Found a related TODO in GH PR 4132: "align serializer versions in prefetch module" — flagged PR to patch.
- Minor: we should update docs in Confluence to explicitly call out serializer version in cache design doc.

If there are blockers or you want a deep-dive, ping in #applied-ml-quant and add "FRICTION" to the thread title.

-- end of quick standup capture --
