title: KV cache warmup stall causing increased latency for rapid repeated prompts
text:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that when they replay short conversational prompts in quick succession (5–10s intervals), observed tail latency for repeat requests increases ~2x after the first two requests. This appears specific to repeat prompts that should hit the prefix/KV cache.

Impact:
- PromptlyAI production customers are experiencing slower-than-expected responses on multi-turn quick-replay flows (chat previews and autosave previews).
- Error rate is not elevated (no 5xx at API layer) but p95/p99 latency degrade from ~180ms to ~380ms on affected replicas.

Environment:
- Redwood hosted (dedicated pool) in us-east-1, tenant PromptlyAI (dedicated).
- Model: gptx-14b-instruct pinned to v2026-02-28.

Steps to reproduce (customer supplied):
1) Send short prompt sequence (seed prompt + 2 repeat prompts) with streaming enabled and short inter-request gap (6s).
2) Observe normal latency for first two requests.
3) On subsequent rapid repeats, latency increases and streaming buffers appear to flush slower, sometimes triggering client-side timeout at 10s.

Observed logs/metrics (customer and support):
- Replica-level trace shows cache miss/partial-hit patterns on prefix lookup followed by synchronous KV fetch (~50–120ms additional).
- Serving-runtime metrics show an increase in kv_cache_prefetch_stalls and kv_lookup_sync_reads on the affected nodes.
- No corresponding CPU/GPU pressure spikes; memory utilization normal.

Workaround provided so far:
- Temporarily routed PromptlyAI traffic to warm pool (warmed replicas) which reduced latency back to baseline.
- Customer can also increase inter-request gap to >20s to avoid stall triggering.

Initial hypothesis: a race in the prefix-KV prefetching path causes subsequent requests to wait for a background warmup task that previously was fast. Evidence: kv_cache_prefetch_stalls metric correlates tightly with p99 latency spikes.

What we checked:
- Dashboard (Grafana) panels for kv cache hit ratio, prefetch latency, and request routing (link: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/kv/kv-prefetch?orgId=1).
- Replica logs for the timeframe: search for 'kv_prefetch_block' and 'cache_index_mismatch'. Found intermittent 'cache_index_mismatch' warnings on 3 replicas.
- Compared two model variants: v2026-02-28 (affected) and v2026-02-14 (older). Older variant did not show same prefetch_stalls.

Hypotheses under validation:
1) Index regeneration TTL mismatch causes prefetch to fall back to synchronous disk/KV store reads for entries that looked cached but require rehydration.
2) A scheduler change last week (scheduler PR 8001) adjusted background prefetch concurrency, exposing a contention window under rapid repeated short contexts.
3) Eviction policy change caused high-churn prefixes (short repeated prompts) to thrash across KV shards leading to extra network hop latency.

Next steps planned:
- Reproduce internally with PromptlyAI sample trace using a dedicated replay harness (SRE assigned).
- Add extra logging around kv index lifetime and prefetch task handoff.
- Roll back scheduler concurrency tweak on a small canary pool if reproduction succeeds.

Support (Maya Chen) 2026-03-10: Customer reported p95/p99 increase from 180ms -> ~380ms on replay flows. They provided request IDs and a small replay script. Asked for full trace and tenant routing info.
Customer (PromptlyAI - Rajiv Sinha) 2026-03-10: Provided request IDs and mentioned issue started after model pin v2026-02-28 rollout. Notified they cannot increase inter-request gap in their UX flow.
SRE (Liam O'Connor) 2026-03-11: Correlated kv_cache_prefetch_stalls with the timestamps. Observed 'cache_index_mismatch' warnings on 3 nodes. Spun up a warmed replica set and routed traffic -> latency normalized.
Engineering (Sofia Martinez) 2026-03-11: Noted scheduler PR 8001 changed prefetch worker pool size from 8 -> 4 to reduce background load. Suggest reverting on canary. Opened PR to add more robust index TTL checks.
Support (Maya Chen) 2026-03-12: Informed customer of temporary routing workaround and asked to approve canary rollback test during low traffic window. Customer approved.
SRE (Liam O'Connor) 2026-03-12: Canary rollback scheduled for 2026-03-13 02:00 UTC. Will monitor kv_prefetch_stalls, p99 latency, and error budgets.

Workaround applied: traffic routed to warmed replica pool which restored baseline latency. Root cause under validation; likely regression in prefetch concurrency + index TTL handling. Canary rollback of scheduler concurrency change planned. Permanent fix will include TTL consistency checks and fallback cold-read batching to avoid synchronous stalls.

title: Log redaction, KMS & tenant ops intake - Borealis Trust
author: Maya Patel
text:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-30
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Liu (Redwood SE), Isabel Chen (Borealis Head Cloud Ops), Marcus Doyle (Borealis CISO), Priya Singh (Borealis Compliance)

Summary:
Quick intake to understand Borealis Trust constraints around KMS residency, log retention and redaction, tenant isolation for multi-tenant workloads, and whether Redwood Hosted or Dedicated or Private fit their compliance posture. High-level ask: can Redwood guarantee no plaintext prompt storage outside EU region, support BYOK via HSM/KMS, and provide log redaction before long-term storage for audit?

Topics covered:
- KMS/BYOK & HSM requirements
- Log capture, redaction, retention windows
- Tenant isolation and evidence for auditors
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs for financial services
- Next steps: SOC2/HIPAA artifacts, runbook, pilot pricing

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Alright, good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. Quick sound check?
[00:05] Isabel Chen: Hi, sound good. Isabel here.
[00:07] Marcus Doyle: Marcus, loud and clear.
[00:09] Priya Singh: Priya, on my side too.
[00:12] Ethan Liu: Ethan from Redwood, hey all.
[00:15] Maya Patel: Cool. So the goal today is to map Borealis' security and ops constraints. We'll take notes and then propose a path — hosted, dedicated or private. Marcus, can you kick us off with the compliance must-haves?
[00:28] Marcus Doyle: Sure. So primary — we are regulated trust services, need strong data residency in EU, GDPR compliance, plus some UK-specific controls. HIPAA isn't a primary requirement but we do have PHI-like fields in some docs and may need BAA for specific pilots.
[00:42] Marcus Doyle: The big ask is keys: we cannot have provider-managed keys outside our control. BYOK, ideally HSM backed, with key residency in our cloud tenant. We also need audit evidence of key usage.
[00:55] Priya Singh: And on logs: we need the ability to redact PII before logs go into long-term object storage. Short-term transient logs for debugging ok, but they should be automatically purged, and only redacted/aggregated records kept for more than 30 days.
[01:12] Isabel Chen: Also, we run a shared tenant model internally — any Redwood deployment must give us strong logical tenant isolation and the ability to carve off dedicated pools for higher-risk workloads. So multi-tenant defaults are fine if cryptographic isolation and network boundaries are present.
[01:28] Ethan Liu: Thanks — that helps. Quick clarifying question: when you say "audit evidence of key usage" — do you need HSM-level attestation (e.g., Cloud HSM logs) or is KMS API access logs sufficient?
[01:40] Marcus Doyle: KMS API logs are baseline. For high-risk workloads we'd like attestation. If Redwood supports connecting to our KMS or HSM as the key store (BYOK), that's preferable.
[01:52] Maya Patel: Good — so BYOK + KMS integration is a priority. On hosted mode, we do support BYOK via customer-managed KMS keys in certain regions, and an HSM-backed flow for Dedicated/Private. Ethan, can you speak to the key flow?
[02:05] Ethan Liu: Yeah. For Redwood Hosted we have an option where customers bring keys in Cloud KMS (we call it BYOK path) — Redwood requests short-lived envelopes and does not persist plaintext key material. For Dedicated and Private, we can either integrate into the customer's VPC KMS endpoint or run in their on-prem HSM. However, the hosted path has caveats around full audit attestation — some attestation materials are available but not HSM attestation in some regions.
[02:32] Priya Singh: That caveat matters. If we can't get attestation for Hosted, we might need Dedicated. How about logs? Hosted by default stores transcripts for 90 days for debugging — can that be shortened and redaction applied?
[02:45] Ethan Liu: We can configure retention in Dedicated and Private. Hosted has configurable retention but there are platform constraints. We also support on-the-fly redaction hooks — you can supply a set of redaction rules or use an agent that strips PII before logs are persisted. Note: these redaction hooks run before long-term storage but may appear in short-term ephemeral logging for 24-72 hours depending on system traces.
[03:10] Isabel Chen: What's "on-the-fly redaction hooks" exactly? Is that something in the customer's side or Redwood's runtime?
[03:15] Ethan Liu: It's a pipeline we offer where a redaction plugin executes in the request path — essentially a configured filter step that normalizes and masks tokens matching rules before the request gets stored in object storage or observability backends. For Dedicated/Private we can put that filter inside the VPC so raw prompts never leave the customer boundary.
[03:30] Marcus Doyle: Do you have controls to prevent kernel memory or kv cache dumps from leaking sensitive tokens into logs? We saw issues with some runtimes where kv cache contents were recorded in traces.
[03:41] Ethan Liu: Good point. Our runtime has modes that limit kv cache dumping for traces and we can disable verbose tracing in production. For audits we can provide sanitized traces and justify that debugging traces do not contain full prompt content. I'll note that as a required deliverable.
[03:56] Maya Patel: For regulatory evidence — Marcus/ Priya — would a SOC2 Type II report plus architecture diagrams and a runbook showing key flows be sufficient to sign off on a POC?
[04:07] Priya Singh: That would cover most. We also need to review the BAA language if we have PHI in any flow. And we will want to see RBAC controls, SSO/SAML integration, and just-in-time access logs for operations.
[04:21] Maya Patel: Redwood supports SSO via SAML/Okta and RBAC with granularity for token-level ops. For audit logs we emit admin actions, token creates, and model rollout events. Ethan, any notes on admin/audit log retention?
[04:33] Ethan Liu: Admin audit logs are configurable. Hosted: 90 days default, extendable as an add-on. Dedicated/Private: you control retention and can ship logs to your SIEM via secure forwarders. We can also support region-locked log sinks to keep logs within EU.
[04:50] Isabel Chen: Important: our auditors will ask for chain of custody for logs. So we need signed hashes or an evidence trail. Do you do log signing?
[04:59] Ethan Liu: We don't do signed hashes out-of-the-box currently, but we can provide immutable object storage configuration guidance and integrate with customer-side signing in the pipeline. That's a rare ask but doable in Dedicated/Private.
[05:12] Marcus Doyle: Pricing/tradeoffs question — sounds like Private gives us the strongest guarantees. What are the main differences in cost and ops between Dedicated and Private from your view?
[05:22] Maya Patel: Short answer: Dedicated is Redwood-managed hardware reserved for you inside our regions — we handle patching and some ops, you get predictable capacity and better isolation. Private is fully customer-managed control plane or on-prem — more engineering on your side but maximum control. Pricing: Dedicated is mid-tier, Private is premium due to support and deployment complexity. We'll send a pricing sketch.
[05:41] Priya Singh: We also require the ability to run periodic vulnerability scans and to receive scan reports. Is that compatible?
[05:47] Ethan Liu: Yes, for Dedicated and Private we can allow scheduled scans on the customer-owned network boundary; on Hosted we provide our own vulnerability attestations and scanner reports but don't expose internal hosts.
[05:58] Isabel Chen: One more: can Redwood guarantee that raw prompts won't be replicated to third-party analytics vendors? We use a set of analytics tools and want assurance that PII is never forwarded.
[06:08] Ethan Liu: We don't sell customer data. Integrations that forward telemetry (e.g., metrics exporters) are opt-in; we can configure filters to strip PII. For Hosted, integrations are optional and documented. We'll call this out in the security pack.
[06:24] Maya Patel: Good. Technical deep dive requests — Marcus, do you want a timeline for an SE-led feasibility that includes a network diagram review?
[06:31] Marcus Doyle: Yes please, an SE-led session where we walk through our VPC, KMS endpoints, and sample data flows. Also Marcus: we may want a short bench where you run synthetic loads to validate latencies under our expected token mix.
[06:42] Ethan Liu: We can do both. For benchmarking we'll need sample prompt shapes and token counts. We can run a small in-region bench on Dedicated or a Private pre-prod to model costs.
[06:53] Priya Singh: On the redaction side, can you do pattern-based and ML-based redaction? Some of our records are semi-structured and patterns won't catch everything.
[07:03] Ethan Liu: We support both pattern-based (regex rules) and a configured ML redact step — the ML step runs inside the VPC for Private/Dedicated; for Hosted the ML step can run either in-region or via a managed plugin with stronger safeguards. There is a small false positive/negative tradeoff that we can quantify on sample data.
[07:24] Isabel Chen: Any limitations we should know about for realtime redaction latency? We have a latency SLO of <300ms 95 for certain flows.
[07:32] Ethan Liu: Redaction adds overhead. Pattern-based is negligible (<10-20ms typically). ML-based redaction could add 30-80ms depending on model. We can tune via async post-processing in lower SLO flows or smart sampling for logs.
[07:49] Maya Patel: OK, sounds like action items forming. Before we recap, any other security or procurement items?
[07:55] Marcus Doyle: Contract: we require breach notification windows and specific SLA clauses around key compromise. Also want to see indemnity language aligned with our counsel — we'll send redlines later.
[08:06] Maya Patel: Understood. We'll share standard legal templates and can iterate.
[08:10] Priya Singh: Also, please include a short checklist of required artifacts for auditor review — e.g., SOC2, BAA, KMS integration diagram, runbooks, RBAC screenshots.
[08:20] Maya Patel: We'll include that. Recap and next steps:
[08:24] Maya Patel: 1) Redwood to share SOC2 Type II, security pack including KMS integration notes and redaction docs by 2026-07-02.
[08:33] Maya Patel: 2) Ethan to schedule a 60–90 minute SE-led feasibility with Marcus to review VPC/KMS and run a shallow bench — target week of 2026-07-06.
[08:45] Maya Patel: 3) AE to prepare pilot estimate and pricing for Dedicated and Private options by 2026-07-05.
[08:52] Isabel Chen: We'll also share our log retention policy and sample data shapes for the redaction tests by 2026-07-03.
[08:59] Marcus Doyle: Good. One ask: when you send docs, flag any items that are caveats for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private so our security team doesn't miss them.
[09:09] Ethan Liu: Will do. We'll label hosted caveats clearly.
[09:12] Maya Patel: Great. Anything else?
[09:14] Priya Singh: No, that covers it. Thanks.
[09:17] Maya Patel: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with notes and links.
[09:21] End of recording.

References mentioned (links/names to include in follow-up):
- Redwood security pack (SOC2, HIPAA/BAA), Redwood KMS integration notes (will be attached)
- SE runbook template and private deployment diagram sample
- Benchmarking plan template and sample workload shapes

Notes on transcript quality: occasional stutters, couple of terms transcribed imperfectly ("kv cache" as "kv cash" in one place), some speaker overlap near 06:40.

title: devex
text:
maria: heads up — a customer running the onboarding sampleapp hit a cascade: 429s during token rotation, client retried and created duplicate sessions, they saw double charges. logs attached (redacted). @jon @sahil can you eyeball?
jon: can you paste the minimal repro + which SDK version they used? did the sample app set an Idempotency-Key header?
maria: repro: user signs up -> sampleapp exchanges token -> a 429 from inference endpoint -> client retries automatically. sampleapp is using python SDK v0.9.2 (the quickstart). it doesn't expose idempotency in the example. log excerpt: 
```
WARN create-session failed 429 {"retry_after":0.8}
INFO retrying request id=null
INFO create-session success id=sk_xxx
```
jon: ok that pattern screams unsafe replay on 429 + token refresh. without an idempotency key the backend treats retries as distinct.
sahil: two quick notes: 1) backoff should be exponential with full jitter (avoid synchronized retries), 2) sample apps should demonstrate setting an Idempotency-Key for any mutation. also FYI node+go SDKs already have helper that auto-generates idempotency keys for non-streaming mutates; python is behind here.
claire: do we want the sampleapp to opt-in or make idempotency a default for create-session flows? making it default in SDK could change semantics for some customers.
kevin: recommendation: default SDK behavior = exponential backoff with full jitter + NOT auto-idempotify unless endpoint annotated as safe-for-auto-idempotency. config knobs: `safe_replay_window` (default 10s), `retry.base_ms=100`, `retry.cap_ms=2000`, `retry.attempts=6`. example pseudo: 
```
# backoff (full jitter)
backoff = min(cap_ms, base_ms * 2**attempt)
sleep = random.uniform(0, backoff)
```
and python snippet to add idempotency header in sampleapp: 
```python
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}", "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4())}
resp = requests.post(url, json=body, headers=headers)
```
maria: thanks — i can open a tiny PR to the sampleapp showing header injection + recommend SDK upgrade in the quickstart. i'll also file a ticket to add parity for python SDK helpers. should we also add a short note in onboarding that token refresh can cause spurious retries?
sahil: yes add a short explainer in onboarding docs and link to the retry/backoff playbook. also add a test-case in sampleapp e2e simulating 429 during refresh.
claire: assign the python parity ticket to @sahil? or @kevin? whoever owns python SDK.
kevin: i'll take the parity ticket and coordinate a small API to opt into auto-idempotency with explicit annotation on mutation calls.
maria: great — i'll open the sampleapp PR now and include changelog + small why-note. tagging this thread for follow-up: will post PR link and ticket id here. :thumbsup:
deploy-bot: CI passed for maria/sampleapp#42, staging deploy queued.
maria: awesome, thanks all — i'll follow up with PR/ticket links and a tiny onboarding blurb.

title: Pinned session reverts during tiered canary: sidecar snapshot desync triggers fallback routing
text:
Issue summary: During a staged (tiered) canary rollout for redwood-open-gpt-3.5-v1, a subset of tenant sessions that were previously pinned to the promoted variant unexpectedly reverted to the default fallback variant. Impact: customer-visible mixed-model responses for ~3% of requests from Meridian Analytics' production traffic in us-east; increased latency for affected requests due to additional routing and KV cache misses. Timeline: 2026-03-10 09:10 UTC - deploy start for tiered canary; 09:22 UTC - first customer report; 09:30-10:00 UTC - increased 5xxs and quality complaints; 10:15 UTC - Support triage. Observed behavior: some sessions lost model affinity and were routed to a fallback variant; this coincided with sidecar snapshot refresh events on a subset of edge pods. Expected behavior: pin affinity should persist across sidecar snapshot refreshes and control-plane rollouts until explicit unpin or pin TTL expiry. Steps to reproduce: 1) Create tiered canary rollout with staged weights and pin variant for a test tenant; 2) Trigger sidecar config refresh (simulated by restarting sidecar or pushing a SIGHUP); 3) Send session traffic with pinned token and observe routing; 4) Reproduce by toggling edge header rewrite feature flag. Logs & artifacts: edge-proxy logs show header rewrite events at same timestamps as routing flips; sidecar snapshot logs show a full snapshot replace (snapshot_id changed) and an applied config hash mismatch with control-plane; KV cache miss logs for pinned sessions; sample request IDs: rq-0a1f23, rq-0a1f98, rq-0b2c11. Attachments: packet captures and a short trace are in the ticket attachments (internal).

Initial hypothesis: sidecar snapshot replace caused pin metadata to be dropped locally on edge pods that applied new snapshot before pin reconciliation completed.
Correlated timing between snapshot replace and a partial control-plane propagation delay (10-14s window) in us-east region.
Found header rewrite rule that migrates legacy session-cookie to new token format; during rewrite the pin-token field was being stripped by an older sidecar build on ~7% of pods.
Reproduced in the staging cluster by applying an older sidecar image plus the header rewrite: pinned token removed on snapshot apply and route fallback triggered.
Checked rollout orchestration logs: canary weight adjust and snapshot distribution overlapped; reconciliation controller did not retry pin sync fast enough when snapshot applied mid-window.
No evidence of model-serving node eviction or GPU preemption; serving runtime healthy for promoted variant.

Priya Desai (2026-03-10 09:35): Customer reported 'we're seeing different answers mid-session, some requests go to older model' - provided request IDs and sample outputs.
Jordan Ellis (2026-03-10 10:05): Handoff to SRE to check edge snapshot behavior and sidecar versions across us-east; escalated to infra team.
Marcus Liu (SRE) (2026-03-10 11:20): Confirmed sidecar binary mismatch on ~6 out of 90 edge pods in us-east; those pods show snapshot replace events exactly at 09:18-09:24 UTC.
Elena Park (Control Plane) (2026-03-11 08:50): Found a timing edge in the pin-reconciliation backoff; filing PR to add a forced sync when snapshot ID increments during an active pin window.
Jordan Ellis (2026-03-12 07:10): Temporary mitigation applied: disabled header rewrite during ongoing tiered canary for Meridian and kicked a targeted pin-resync job against affected edge pods.
Priya Desai (2026-03-12 08:00): Customer confirmed reduced incidence and reported no further mixed-model responses after mitigation for last 12 hours.
Marcus Liu (2026-03-12 09:05): Pending follow-up: patch sidecar to preserve pin-token on rewrite and add telemetry to detect snapshot-induced pin drops.

A race between sidecar snapshot replacement and control-plane pin-reconciliation caused pin metadata to be stripped on edge pods running an older sidecar build that applied an incompatible header rewrite. The strip led to routing logic treating the session as unpinned, invoking fallback routing to a default variant.

Disabled the header rewrite flag for affected tenant during the canary window and ran a targeted pin-resync job against edge pods in us-east. This restored session affinity for affected tenants within ~30 minutes.

Short term: keep header rewrite disabled for Meridian until sidecar patch is deployed. Medium term: merge sidecar PR to preserve pin-token across rewrite and add a forced pin-sync when snapshot ID changes; add critical telemetry and an alert on pin-drop rates. Long term: adjust rollout orchestration to avoid snapshot distributions that can overlap with active pin windows or make reconciliation immediate on snapshot increment.

Customer is on a Dedicated contract; follow-up retrospective scheduled with product and infra teams to update the canary runbook and add explicit guidance about header rewrites during pin-sensitive rollouts.

title: cost-garden-batchlet-prefetcher-and-quant-bucketizer
author: Maya Chen
text:
Add tenant-aware micro-batcher (batchlet) and quantization bucketizer; introduce CLI dry-run for cost suggestions; telemetry and docs added.

Context: Customers with bursty micro-traffic and long-tail sequence lengths are seeing unpredictable unit economics because a single global batching + quantization default can't cover both low-latency interactive routes and high-throughput batchy routes. This PR introduces two coordinated pieces: (1) Batchlet prefetcher/controller: a lightweight tenant-aware micro-batcher that selects a small set of candidate batch shapes per-tenant and applies conservative prefix-caching heuristics to reduce per-token cost without violating latency SLOs; (2) Quant Bucketizer: a compact mapping from (model, sequence-length-range, batch-shape) -> quant-profile that lets us pick quantization presets tuned for unit-econ. Motivation: give engineering teams safe, observable defaults that reduce tail cost while enabling rapid rollback and dry-run simulation. High-level changes: - New runtime component batchlet_controller (Go) with policy hooks and telemetry events. - New quant bucketizer service (Python) and a small deterministic registry file (yaml) with candidate profiles (int8/q4/awq-lite). - CLI tool (cost-garden) dry-run mode to simulate tenant traces against chosen batchlet+quant combos and emit estimated unit-econ deltas. - Telemetry: new metrics (batchlet.batch_shapes, quant.bucket_choice, econ.estimated_token_cost_delta) and an e2e smoke test in CI. - Docs: cost-guides/cost-garden.md with rollouts and safety notes. Safety: The controller defaults to conservative batch sizes, always respects tenant latency SLOs, and contains a fast fail-over to previous global defaults if observed retry/error rate increases by >3x in 5m. Rollout plan: feature flag gated; starts as opt-in on Dedicated and Private tenants; CLI dry-run recommended before enabling. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for batchlet controller and quant bucketizer - [x] e2e smoke test against synthetic burst traces - [x] Telemetry events emitted and wired to ingestion - [x] Docs and rollout guide - [x] Performance microbench on p3 and a100. Related: ENG-3345 (tenant microburst stabilization), SUP-1123 (customer incident investigating cost spikes).

Arjun Patel: Nice approach — can you call out which quant presets we consider safe for LLMs with output logits (no fp16-rewrite)? Also include a short SLO-preserving invariants section in the README.
Maya Chen (author): Added invariants section to docs and restricted candidate_registry.yaml to q4_0 and awq-lite profiles for safety; noted fallback behavior.
Lena O'Connor: Please ensure telemetry emits low-cardinality tags for tenant tier and batch_shape. Also add a CI job to fail on missing metrics definitions.
Maya Chen: Added metrics_definitions.yaml entry and CI job e2e-batchlet; addressed low-cardinality tagging for tenant_tier in batchlet_publisher.go.
Diego Ramos: Unit tests look good, but add a small benchmark showing expected latency impact at p95 for a 50ms SLO before merge.
Maya Chen: Added microbench results to the PR description and a short performance doc; benchmarks run on p3 and a100 show p95 latency increase <6ms for conservative shapes and >18% unit cost reduction on synthetic traces.

Experimental: Feature flag default off for Hosted; on by opt-in for Dedicated/Private. Use `cost-garden --dry-run` to preview tenant impact. See docs/cost-guides/cost-garden.md for operator checklist and rollback steps.

title: POC scoping — Multilang invoice extraction (Lacuna Solutions)
author: Jordan Meyers
text:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-27
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Meyers (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Carlos Vega (Redwood Solutions Eng), Ethan Park (Lacuna Head of ML), Sofia Martinez (PM), Liam O'Connor (SRE), Nadia Li (Localization)

Summary:
Quick scoping call to align on scope for a POC focused on multilingual invoice extraction (10 languages, EU+NA), define success criteria (precision/recall targets by field), understand workload size (avg tokens per doc, concurrency), and plan a small benchmark run on open models via Redwood hosted and dedicated routing options. Discussed tradeoffs (latency vs cost, quantized weights vs FP16), data residency and audit logs for EU region.

Topics covered:
- POC goals and timeline
- Data set and language coverage
- Workload sizing and throughput expectations
- Model shortlist ideas and quality tradeoffs
- Benchmark plan and metrics (QA sets, latency p50/p95, cost per doc)
- Deployment modes (hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC)
- Security requirements (SSO, KMS, retention)

(00:00) Jordan Meyers: hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me all right?
(00:04) Ethan Park: yes, loud and clear, thx Jordan.
(00:07) Priya Singh: good afternoon, im Priya from the SE team, i'll focus on perf and bench details.
(00:12) Sofia Martinez: hi, Sofia, PM on invoices, excited to scope this out.
(00:16) Liam O'Connor: Liam here, i look after infra and SRE concerns.
(00:20) Jordan Meyers: quick agenda — align success criteria, confirm dataset and languages, sizing, and agree next steps. maybe 45 minutes then we iterate. sound ok?
(00:28) Nadia Li: also want to highlight localization edge cases — cursive fonts, mixed-language fields in invoices.

(01:05) Ethan Park: to ground the convo, our main requirement: field extraction for invoice number, vendor name, total_amount, tax_breakdown. We're also evaluating vendor matching confidence score. Target is high precision on totals (>=98%) and recall on line items >=92% but we can be pragmatic.
(01:30) Priya Singh: got it. for the POC scope it's helpful to pick 2 tiers of truth: strict for totals/tax and relaxed for vendor-name matching, since names vary. For measurement we'll use token-level and entity-level F1.

(02:10) Jordan Meyers: workload sizing — Ethan, what's your volume? concurrency? expected peak?
(02:16) Ethan Park: right now in prod we process ~180k invoices/month, peak batch days up to 12k/day. For the POC initial slice we'd like to run 5k docs over 2 weeks, but also simulate spike concurrency of ~30 qps for extraction microservice.
(02:35) Carlos Vega: 30 qps for NLP extraction ok, that's modest. need to know average seq length after OCR — tokens per invoice?
(02:42) Liam O'Connor: our OCR pipeline yields roughly 1.2k tokens per invoice on average, but some large invoices hit 6k tokens. we can sample and give distribution.
(02:50) Priya Singh: good, that distribution matters for batching and KV cache sizing. we normally test p50/p95 seq lengths to choose batch windows and kernel selection.

(03:30) Sofia Martinez: languages -- we need English, Spanish, French, German, Dutch, Polish, Portuguese, Italian, Swedish, and occasional Japanese. Localization team will provide language breakdown.
(03:45) Nadia Li: note Japanese has different tokenization and OCR noise, will need special prompts and possibly model with better CJK handling.

(04:20) Jordan Meyers: model shortlist — initial thinking from Redwood: a mix of 1) a strong 70B open encoder-decoder quantized model tuned for extraction, 2) a compact 13B variant with instruction tuning, 3) a multilingual 30B that historically handles EU languages well, and 4) a baseline small 7B for throughput comparison. we can provide names and performance profiles in the follow-up.
(04:45) Ethan Park: any thoughts on accuracy differences between the 30B and 70B for vendor matching? costs will matter.
(04:53) Priya Singh: empirically the 70B gives better zero-shot layout/occr robustness — usually 3-7% absolute on F1 for messy docs vs 30B. but latency and unit cost go up severalx. with Redwood Optimize we can show batching/quant tradeoffs that reduce cost while preserving most quality.

(05:30) Liam O'Connor: on infra mode: we prefer hosted for speed, but EU data residency + audit logs are required for regulated clients. is Redwood Private an option?
(05:40) Jordan Meyers: yes, Private (VPC) is available; we can run the control plane in Redwood but data and inference in an EU region or on a dedicated pool. we support KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs. for the POC we can demo hosted EU region and if it meets needs, propose a dedicated pool for production.

(06:20) Sofia Martinez: how fast can we get benchmarks? we want a quick run to decide on model choice within two weeks.
(06:28) Priya Singh: we can run an initial sweep within 3-4 days after you send sample data. that would be lightweight (10-20% of docs) to get initial p50/p95 latencies and token costs. full run across all languages maybe 7-10 business days.

(07:05) Ethan Park: success criteria — let's be explicit: accuracy: total_amount precision >=98%, total_amount recall >=95%, invoice_number F1 >=96%, vendor name recall >=90% (with human review for borderline cases). Latency: per-doc extraction p95 < 750ms in production for single-invoice requests, or for batch processing throughput of 30 qps sustained. Cost: target cost per invoice < $0.02 (we know this is tight).
(07:40) Priya Singh: that cost target depends heavily on model choice and batching — with a quantized 13B we can be closer to that cost but might underperform on messy docs. we should include a human-in-loop fallback for vendor-name verification to keep cost bounded.

(08:20) Carlos Vega: regarding benchmarking metrics, we'll capture: field-level precision/recall, end-to-end extraction latency (cold/warm), tokens/kg (cost proxy), and percent of docs flagged for human review. We'll also run stress tests for concurrency to validate autoscaling.

(09:05) Liam O'Connor: SSO and RBAC — we'll need SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning for users, and role-based access for the audit logs. encryption at rest with customer KMS is mandatory. can Redwood support HSM-backed KMS?
(09:20) Jordan Meyers: yes — Redwood Private supports customer KMS and HSM integration. hosted can also integrate with cloud KMS in EU region. we'll include security docs.

(10:00) Sofia Martinez: one risk is OCR noise; do you recommend cleaning at OCR stage or rely on model prompts to normalize?
(10:08) Priya Singh: both. best results come from a light OCR normalization (remove headers, unify date formats) plus robust prompt engineering. for multilingual cases, custom tokenization and language-specific prompts help. we often run small prompt sweeps as part of the bench.

(11:00) Ethan Park: any required artifacts from Redwood for procurement? SOC2 type II, data processing agreement, and EU data residency attestation.
(11:10) Jordan Meyers: we'll attach our compliance pack (SOC2, ISO summary), sample DPA, and private deployment whitepaper in the follow-up.

(12:00) Priya Singh: back to model tradeoffs: we propose these concrete candidates — not model vendor names but size/trait descriptors:
- Model A: 70B multilingual, high-quality, FP16 or int8 quantizable, best for messy OCR
- Model B: 30B multilingual balanced, strong EU languages, lower latency than A
- Model C: 13B quantized cost-optimized, decent for clean OCR and high throughput
- Model D: 7B baseline for throughput baseline and fallback routing

(12:40) Sofia Martinez: ok — to prioritize, we want to see empirical F1 on our sample set and the cost/latency matrix. also include a recommendation for which model to use in canary vs production.

(13:10) Jordan Meyers: for the POC plan timeline i suggest:
- By 2026-03-31: Lacuna shares samples + language breakdown
- 2026-04-01: Redwood delivers model shortlist + bench plan + cost estimates
- 2026-04-06 to 2026-04-10: lightweight bench sweep (10-20% samples)
- 2026-04-13 to 2026-04-20: full benchmark and SLA tuning, iterate on prompts
- 2026-04-27: POC review + recommended production plan

(14:10) Ethan Park: that timeline works for us as long as cost estimates are clear.

(14:40) Carlos Vega: small note on metrics collection — we'll provide a benchmark sheet template (CSV) you can fill with ground truth; we'll compute per-field metrics and visualize.

(15:05) Nadia Li: one nuance: Japanese invoices sometimes embed English amounts in different formats; expect increased false negatives. can we have a plan to isolate CJK in the bench?
(15:15) Priya Singh: yes we'll tag language-specific subset and run CJK-specific runs with tailored prompts and tokenizers.

(16:00) Sofia Martinez: procurement wise, what does a short-term POC contract look like if we need dedicated pool for benchmarking?
(16:08) Jordan Meyers: we can do a short POC engagement (30 days) with a reserved pool + bench credits. cost depends on chosen capacity; we'll include options in the follow-up.

(16:45) Ethan Park: are there recommended fallback policies if model latency spikes?
(16:50) Priya Singh: yes — Redwood supports smart routing: fallback to smaller model for non-critical fields, or route to canary region. we can demo automatic degrade policies in the POC.

(17:20) Jordan Meyers: ok let's capture next steps again — i'll send the model shortlist + cost spreadsheet. Priya will run bench harness and propose SLO/cost tradeoff matrix. Ethan/Sofia will send samples and confirm acceptance criteria.

(17:45) Sofia Martinez: thanks everyone, this was helpful. we'll sync on the samples today.
(17:50) Jordan Meyers: great, thanks all, talk soon.

Recap / Action items (repeat):
- Redwood: model shortlist + bench plan + compliance pack (SOC2, DPA, EU residency note) by 2026-04-01.
- Customer: Provide anonymized invoice samples (PDF + OCR text) and language distribution by 2026-03-31.
- Redwood SE: prepare benchmark harness and latency/cost SLO matrix by 2026-04-03.

References mentioned: "benchmark sheet" (will be shared as CSV), POC engagement template, Redwood Private whitepaper, compliance pack.

End of transcript.

title: Tool-call atomicity: streaming handshake and deterministic result-injection API
author: Marisol Vega
text:
Motivation: We continue to see flakiness and subtle ordering bugs when user prompts trigger multiple parallel tool/function calls while streaming responses. The core problem is a mismatch between streaming chunk boundaries and when tool results are injected into the generated token stream. This PR introduces a negotiated streaming handshake plus a deterministic result-injection contract (idempotent tokens + sequence markers) to make multi-tool streaming robust across the OpenAI-compat layer and SDKs.

Summary of changes: added a light-weight streaming-handshake protocol that runs as part of the connection init (client -> server -> ack) to advertise support for deterministic injection and per-call idempotency tokens; implemented a ResultInjector component in the serving runtime that accepts tool outputs annotated with an idempotency token and a sequence offset; modified the OpenAI-compat streaming adapter to honor handshake negotiation and emit compatible event frames ("tool_start", "tool_result", "tool_end", plus existing "data" frames); extended python/typescript SDKs with ergonomic helpers to 1) create idempotency tokens for tool invocations, 2) register callbacks that receive deterministic tool frames even when responses are replayed from cache or resumed after transient disconnects.

API/Protocol sketch (example): client sends: {"type":"handshake_capabilities","capabilities":["deterministic_injection","idempotency_token"]} server responds: {"type":"handshake_ack","session_id":"s_xxx","supported":["deterministic_injection"]} During stream the server emits: {"event":"tool_start","tool":"weather","call_id":"call_123"} then: {"event":"tool_result","call_id":"call_123","idempotency":"tok_abc","seq":1,"payload":{...}} Finally: {"event":"tool_end","call_id":"call_123"}. The SDK helpers rehydrate these frames into single tool-result objects and guarantee deduplication by idempotency token.

Design notes: - Atomicity: tool-result frames are applied at a single logical insertion point in the generated token stream (we record the insertion offset and apply deterministic replays). - Resume behavior: client reconnects present their last-observed seq/idempotency tokens; server can resume or replay exact frames without risk of double-injection. - Backwards compatibility: handshake is optional; if not negotiated the server falls back to pre-existing best-effort injection. The OpenAI-compat adapter exposes the new frames as extension events while preserving standard text/event-stream fallback.

Testing: added unit + integration coverage: - deterministic replay tests for the injector (including out-of-order arrival and duplicate delivery) - streaming handshake E2E tests between python SDK and local runtime - load test verifying latency regression less than 3% under multi-tool stress compared to baseline. CI initially flagged an intermittent test in streaming_adapter.rs; I fixed a race in the test harness and re-ran pipelines.

Docs and examples: console/docs/tooling/streaming-handshake.md contains a migration guide and code snippets for python/ts. Added 'tooling:experimental' note in console to avoid surprising GA customers.

Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind runtime config (tools.deterministic_injection = off by default). We'll enable for a small percent of traffic for 48 hours and monitor: token duplication alerts, stream-error increase, and tool-latency percentiles. If stable we will flip the flag and remove the experimental note in 2 weeks.

Arjun: Left suggestions around the handshake payload size and whether we need feature-discovery vs boolean cap flags. Suggested switching to an extensible key/value list. Author reply: switched to capabilities list and trimmed payload to ~128 bytes.
Samantha: Asked about cost/latency impact on hot paths and whether we can avoid copying tool payloads. Author reply: injector uses zero-copy when possible; benchmark shows 2.1% median latency increase under stress (within target).
Diego: Requested explicit tests for cache-replay + handshake mismatch (server older runtime). Author reply: added integration test that simulates older runtime behavior and verifies fallback to best-effort injection.
Arjun: Approved after small nits fixed
Samantha: Approved
CI: All checks passed on rerun (unit/integration/lint/perf)

title: Rapid endpoint creator: collapse patterns and copy experiments
author: Maya Chen
text:
Purpose and TL;DR:

This note collects experiments for a compact, rapid endpoint creation flow that defaults to safe choices for new users while exposing advanced controls to power users. It also contains multiple microcopy variants for the model version pinning affordance (modal and inline) and sketches for error/fallback messaging. Goal is to settle on a single compact interaction pattern for the MVP and a longer list of backlog experiments (A/B test candidates).

Context and constraints:
- Problem: current create-endpoint flow is long and forces many decisions up-front. Teams want a 30–60s happy-path so devs can test models quickly.
- Requirements: must integrate with model catalog, respect pinned model versions, allow quick rollback to latest compatible variant, and preserve audit metadata for Private/Dedicated customers.
- Safety: default should be: latest verified model variant for the selected model family, autoscale off (single replica), no local overrides to sampling/temperature unless user expands advanced.

Wireframe notes (compact flow):
1) Single-column modal (Rapid Create) – default collapsed advanced panel
 - Top row: Model selector (search + small inline tag showing model family + version chip)
 - Below: Endpoint name (auto-generated placeholder: "my-model-endpoint-1") and small toggle: Public API key enabled (on/off) with short hint text
 - Primary CTA: "Create endpoint" (blue) — creates endpoint with defaults and returns to list with success toast and inline link to console route
 - Secondary: "Create and open" (outline) — creates and opens endpoint details page (for immediate testing)
 - Collapsible accordion: "Advanced settings" (chevron) — reveals target replicas, concurrency, GPU tier, model quantization suggestion, and model pinning toggle
 - Footer: small text: "Need a dedicated pool? See Dedicated plans" which links to product docs

2) Advanced panel (collapsed by default) – progressive disclosure principles
 - Quick suggestions row (one-line) with small CTAs: "Use cost-optimal config" | "Use low-latency config" (both apply a preset inline; user can still fine-tune)
 - Model pinning control: radio buttons "Auto use latest compatible" (default) and "Pin to version" with dropdown of recent versions and a small icon explaining rollback behavior
 - Rollback policy selector: (dropdown) Manual | Canary (10%) | Auto-fallback (to lighter variant on failure)
 - Save as template checkbox (small)

Microcopy experiments: model pinning (inline and modal)
- Variant A (explicit-action first):
 - Inline label: Pin model version
 - Helper: "Pin this endpoint to a specific model version so predictions are stable. Choose 'Auto' to always use the latest verified build."
 - CTA when pinned: "Pinned to v2025-01-15 • Change"

- Variant B (risk-focused):
 - Inline label: Stable outputs (pin version)
 - Helper: "Pinning prevents unexpected output regressions after model updates. Good for critical pipelines."
 - Tooltip copy on hover: "Pins increase reproducibility, but may miss bugfixes — use canary for gradual rollouts."

- Variant C (business-focused):
 - Inline label: SLA-backed version pin
 - Helper: "Enterprise only: lock version and enable SLA monitoring."
 - Small badge if private/dedicated customer: "SLA available"

Confirmation modal copy (when user pins during create):
- Title options: "Lock endpoint to model version?" | "Confirm pin to v2025-01-15"
- Body candidate 1: "Pinning ensures this endpoint will always use version v2025-01-15 of Model-X. You can unpin later or create a canary roll-out to test newer versions."
- Body candidate 2 (short): "This will lock the endpoint to the selected model version. Production traffic will remain unchanged after future model upgrades unless you change this setting."
- Primary CTA: "Confirm and create" (danger/solid)
- Secondary: "Create without pinning"

Error and fallback messaging (examples for inline toast and endpoint details):
- When pinned version is missing in a region: "Pinned version not available in selected region. Endpoint created in fallback mode using latest compatible variant. See details."
- When pin conflicts with hardware: "Selected version requires GPU type A; your plan only supports GPU type B. Choose a different version or upgrade capacity."
- Rollback toast after failed deploy: "Traffic automatically failed over to fallback model (v2024-12-07). We rolled back to keep latency/SLOs. Check audit logs for details."

Accessibility notes:
- All radio/button groups must have aria-labels and short accessible descriptions for screen readers explaining what pinning changes do
- Keyboard flow: collapse/expand should be reachable via Enter and Space; focus should move to the first control inside expanded panel

Backlog grooming (prioritized list)
P0 (MVP):
 - Implement single-column rapid-create modal with collapsed advanced panel (deliverable: prototype + usability test)
 - Default model selection heuristics: latest verified variant; show version chip
 - Pin to version toggle with confirmation modal text variant B (short)

P1:
 - Add quick presets (cost-optimal, low-latency) and wire their telemetry events
 - Add canary rollout option and telemetry to record canary success/failure
 - Audit log entry template for pinned/unpinned actions (for Private customers)

P2:
 - A/B test microcopy variants A and B for pinning helper text across new user cohorts
 - Add per-route per-model token cost estimate in advanced panel
 - Add inline suggestions for quantization (e.g., 4-bit) with expected cost delta

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Should "Pin to version" be default for enterprise customers? (Pros: reproducibility; Cons: more support tickets when customers expect automatic fixes)
- Languages: microcopy needs quick localization pass — which strings should be prioritized? (Confirmation modal, inline helper, and toast failures)
- Should rollback/fallback messaging be opt-in for private deployments to avoid automatic fail-overs?

Prototype test plan (quick usability check):
- Recruit 6 internal engineers (3 infra/platform, 3 app devs)
- Tasks: create an endpoint for a test app in < 90s; pin version; open advanced panel and set canary; simulate pinned-version unavailable and observe toast messaging
- Success metrics: median task time < 90s, task completion 90%+, 0 critical accessibility failures

Notes from last sync (Feb 6):
- SRE requested explicit checkbox for auto-fallback to ensure operators opt in
- Solutions Eng: prefer explicit confirmation copy that references rollback behavior and linking to support runbook
- Engineering: backend needs a deterministic API to report "isPinned" and fallback chain for UI to show in details page

Next steps (this doc owner):
- Build hi-fi modal in Figma and link new copy variants to components (action: Maya) — due Feb 24
- Create a short demo flow in staging to validate API for isPinned and fallback chain (action: Diego) — due Feb 21
- Create JIRA tasks for audit logs and telemetry events (action: Product Ops)

Raw ideas for future experiments (put into backlog):
- "Pin drift detection": email/report when pinned endpoints fall behind latest verified version by >3 releases
- "Auto-regen sample": when model updated, run a small eval on pinned endpoints and surface quality delta metrics to owner
- "Pin-by-snapshot": allow pinning to an evaluation snapshot (prompt set + model hash) rather than version string

Notes-to-self (quick):
- Keep copy concise in primary flow; users want minimal friction
- Save long explanations for documentation and tooltips, not the modal body
- Record every user action as telemetry event (create_endpoint, open_advanced, pin_version, confirm_pin)

End of draft.

Design artifacts and links will be attached in the Figma prototype once hi-fi is ready. For now, use the rough wireframe description above when building the initial prototype.

title: Release plan: runtime-1.19 TP stability (Dedicated-first canary + rollback criteria)
author: Connor O'Brien
text:
Owner: Connor O'Brien (Releases)
Tech leads: Noah Patel (runtime), Hiro Tanaka (kernels), Sofia Ivanova (scheduling)
SRE DRI: Rafael Mendes
Support/CS: Owen Phillips / Rachel Kim

Context
We’ve had repeated Dedicated and high-throughput Hosted timeouts attributable to TP stalls (incl. Feb 17 Sev1). runtime-1.19 includes stability hardening (scheduler fairness/collective ordering, NCCL stream sync, watchdog + safe abort/drain, KV cache safety, improved surfacing + observability). This ticket defines the release gates, canary schedule, Dedicated-first sequencing, rollback criteria, and comms checklist.

Scope of release (runtime-1.19 TP stability changes)
- Scheduler guardrails to prevent collective starvation (ENG-4824, PR-21841)
- NCCL stream/event synchronization hardening (ENG-4825, PR-21853)
- TP watchdog timeout + safe abort/drain path (ENG-4826, PR-21860)
- TP heartbeat + stall reason codes + tracing enrichment (ENG-4823, PR-21834 + PR-21872)
- KV cache compaction safety in TP (ENG-4827, PR-21866)
- Load-shedding on TP stall signals (PR-21875)
- API-layer error surfacing for NCCL/abort semantics (PR-21912)
- Alert/dashboards updates (observability-pack PR-412)
- Perf-canary TP stress scenarios (perf-canary PR-188) + benchmark-lab repro harness (benchmark-lab PR-97)

Release goals (what “good” looks like)
1) Reduce TP-induced request hang/timeout rate on Dedicated A100/H100 clusters by >=80% vs runtime-1.18 baseline under peak load.
2) No Sev1/Sov2 incidents attributable to TP stalls during canary window.
3) Improve time-to-triage: on-call can classify stall as compute vs comms vs scheduler within 10 minutes using dashboard + structured logs.
4) Ensure watchdog/abort does not cause cascading failures (no restart storms, no elevated 5xx due to false positives).

Gating checks (must pass before first Dedicated canary)
A) Code / build gates
- All TP stability PRs merged behind intended flags and included in runtime-1.19 release branch.
- CI: GPU integration tests green (including fault injection tests from PR-21905 when landed).
- Config defaults reviewed (no silent behavior changes in Hosted unless explicitly intended).

B) Functional + reliability gates (pre-canary)
- Repro harness (benchmark-lab PR-97) can deterministically trigger prior hang signature on runtime-1.18 and no longer hangs on runtime-1.19 for >=10 consecutive runs.
- Perf-canary TP stress suite (ENG-4828 / perf-canary PR-188):
 - Long context + bursty concurrency scenario: no hard hangs; watchdog triggers (if enabled) produce controlled abort + drain and do not wedge nodes.
 - p99 latency regression <= 5% vs baseline for “steady-state decode” scenario with stream sync hardening enabled.
 - Throughput regression <= 3% for median traffic mix (prefill/decode mixed) OR documented justification + mitigation (toggle/conditional sync).

C) Observability / on-call readiness gates
- Dashboard panels merged + deployed (observability-pack PR-412) and reviewed with SRE (Aisha Bello / Sergio Costa).
- Alerts configured but set to “ticket only” for first 24h of canary (no paging) unless we see real stalls.
- Runbook updated and linked in alert annotations (Confluence: runtime-tp-hang-mitigation + tp-stall-triage-playbook).
- Support-facing workaround doc updated with new version/flag guidance (Confluence CS/Support known issues page).

Feature flags / rollout knobs (must be explicitly tracked)
- tp_watchdog_enabled (default OFF in Hosted; ON for Dedicated canary only)
- tp_watchdog_timeout_ms (model-size tiered defaults; start conservative to avoid false positives)
- tp_nccl_sync_hardening_enabled (start ON in canary; ability to disable if perf regression)
- tp_scheduler_collective_fairness_enabled (ON; should be safe/correctness improvement)
- tp_stall_load_shed_enabled (ON in canary after first 24h if signals are stable)

Canary schedule (Dedicated-first)
Phase 0: Internal validation (T-3 to T-1 days)
- Run benchmark-lab repro + perf-canary TP scenarios on A100-80GB and H100 test clusters.
- Confirm dashboards/alerts show expected signals (heartbeat, in-flight collective counters, stall reason tags).
- Create a “canary war-room” Slack thread in #eng-releases and add DRIs.

Phase 1: Dedicated canary (Day 0–2)
- Select 1–2 Dedicated accounts with known TP timeout history + willingness to canary (target: Acme AI if aligned via PM-911 / CS).
- Roll 10% of replicas in the selected Dedicated clusters to runtime-1.19.
- Enable watchdog + extra NCCL logging for a bounded 4–6 hour window if approved (coordinate with INT-2219; ensure log sampling + redaction policy).
- Monitor: request timeouts, TP heartbeat gaps, drain events, NCCL errors, p99 latency, GPU utilization anomalies.

Phase 2: Dedicated expansion (Day 2–4)
- Increase to 50% replicas for canary accounts if no rollback triggers.
- Extend to 2–3 additional Dedicated clusters (mix of A100 and H100) with moderate traffic.
- Turn on tp_stall_load_shed_enabled after 24h if false positive rate is acceptable.

Phase 3: Dedicated full rollout (Day 4–7)
- Roll 100% replicas for Dedicated clusters (staged by region).
- Keep alerts “paging” enabled for SRE once confidence is high (after 48h at >=50% rollout with no major issues).

Phase 4: Hosted rollout (post-Dedicated success)
- Roll to Hosted canary clusters (lowest-risk region first).
- Watch for changes in streaming timeout rates and cancellation-path behavior (PR-21890).
- Gradually expand to all Hosted regions.

Rollback criteria (hard stop)
Immediate rollback to runtime-1.18 or disable flags if any occur during canary:
- Any repeatable hang where replicas wedge and do not recover via drain within 10 minutes.
- Increase in customer-visible 5xx or timeout rate by >0.5% absolute for canary accounts over 60 minutes, attributable to runtime behavior.
- Watchdog false positives: drain/restart events >3 per hour per cluster without corresponding request timeout reduction.
- p99 latency regression >10% sustained for >2 hours vs baseline, not explained by traffic mix changes.
- NCCL error rate spikes correlated with sync hardening changes (and not present in baseline).

Rollback actions (order of operations)
1) Disable tp_watchdog_enabled (fast mitigation if false positives/drain storms).
2) Disable tp_nccl_sync_hardening_enabled if perf regression / unexpected NCCL behavior.
3) Reduce TP concurrency caps (temporary mitigation; see known issues/workarounds doc).
4) Roll back runtime image to runtime-1.18 for impacted cluster(s).
5) If node-level wedging occurs: drain node pool, recycle GPUs; engage SRE incident process.

Comms checklist
Before Dedicated canary (T-24h)
- Notify SRE on-call + SRE leadership (Sean Gallagher / Rafael Mendes) with:
 - rollout window
 - flags to be enabled
 - dashboards + runbook links
 - rollback triggers

title: Runbook: Rollback and Post-change Validation (Hosted API + Console)
author: Connor Obrien
text:
h1. Purpose
This runbook defines the required steps to rollback a production change and the required post-change validation steps (including after a rollback). It applies to Hosted API and Console.

h1. Guiding principles
* Prefer fast rollback over extended debugging when customer impact is ongoing.
* Rollback should return the system to a known-good state with minimal risk.
* Always leave a trace: update the change record and incident timeline.

h1. Preconditions
* Identify the last known-good build (image digest or build number).
* Identify what changed: code deploy, config/policy bundle, schema migration, feature flags.

h1. Rollback decision criteria
Rollback immediately if:
* Canary or post-deploy gates fail (error/latency regression beyond thresholds)
* New Sev2+ customer impact appears plausibly correlated
* Data correctness, billing, auth, or routing correctness is in question

h1. Rollback steps (generic)
1. Stop further rollout
 * Pause deployments and disable automated promotions.
2. Revert highest-leverage toggles first
 * Disable or revert feature flags / routing policy bundles associated with the change.
3. Redeploy prior build
 * Redeploy the previous image digest to the impacted region(s).
 * For Hosted API, roll back region-by-region starting with the canary/most impacted region.
4. Validate health
 * Confirm service readiness and key smoke tests pass.
5. Document
 * Update change record with: trigger, rollback start/end time, and final state.

h1. Special cases
* Schema migrations:
 - If a forward-only migration was applied, rollback may require a compensating forward fix rather than reverting binaries.
 - Always involve the service owner and SRE on-call.
* Auth/RBAC changes:
 - Validate both positive and negative authorization outcomes after rollback.

h1. Post-change monitoring window (required)
For any production change (successful or rolled back):
* Enhanced monitoring for at least 60 minutes after the system is stable.
* Confirm: error rate, p95 latency, saturation metrics, and a representative customer workflow.

h1. Closure requirements
A change record is not closed until it includes:
* Final deployed build identifiers (or confirmation of rollback)
* Links to dashboards used and observed outcomes
* Follow-up tickets for any discovered issues

h1. Related pages
* Production Change Management Standard (v2)
* Hosted API Deploy Runbook
* Console Deploy Runbook
* Prod Deployment Gates: Hosted API and Console

title: Aurora ML Pilot — Weekly Cost & Tuning
author: Emma Clarke
text:
Weekly POC sync to review token economics and tuning experiments. Reviewed tokens/sec/$ baselines, caching hit improvements, and batching tradeoffs. Agreed on next tuning steps: increase KV/prefix cache retention, try hybrid batching (dynamic batch up to 8), and run a focused latency-sensitive benchmark for p95 SLA. Follow-ups: updated cost model sheet, revised pilot config, schedule throughput window.

Emma Clarke: Send revised pilot config (cache + batching) by 2025-07-11
Ravi Patel: Prepare 15-min p95 latency benchmark run and script by 2025-07-13
Diego Ramos: Provide real-world prompt distribution sample (1k prompts) by 2025-07-12

Redwood to push updated pilot YAML with cacheTTL=600s and dynamic_batch_max=8
Customer to approve a 2-hour throughput window next week (prefer Tues 07/15) for p95 tests
Redwood to update cost projection spreadsheet with new cache-hit assumptions and share annotated version

Shared cost model spreadsheet: https://redwood.app/sheets/aurora-pilot-costs (view-only)
SE notebook: https://redwood.app/notebooks/aurora-benchmarks (contains raw tokens/sec logs)
Security/infra doc referenced: /docs/private-deployments/kms-audit.pdf

Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-09 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Emma Clarke (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CTO - Aurora ML), Diego Ramos (ML Engineer), Priya Nair (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto): quick economic deep dive + tuning list.

[00:00] Emma Clarke: All right, good afternoon everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick check in — is this still the weekly pilot sync for Aurora?
[00:12] Lena Ortiz: yes, yep this is good, thanks. Diego and I are here. Priya might jump in a bit later.
[00:20] Ravi Patel: Cool. Agenda today, tokens per dollar baseline, cache numbers from last run, and then batching experiments and impact on p95. Any additional items?
[00:28] Lena Ortiz: maybe a quick note on the on-prem infra ergonomics, but keep it short.

[02:05] Ravi Patel: Ok starting with the baseline: last week we ran model variant A (we'll call it l2-13b-q4) on Redwood Dedicated pool. Measured raw throughput at steady state: ~14,800 tokens/sec per GPU node at batch size 1, cost math gave us
[02:22] Diego Ramos: wait, 14.8k tokens/sec per node? that seemed high compared to our earlier runs (we were seeing 9k).
[02:32] Ravi Patel: right so note the difference — your earlier runs used sequence length 512 and this was using shorter median sequences ~120 tokens; the distribution matters a lot. The tokens/sec/$ in our cost sheet right now is 12,000 tokens per dollar for the baseline mix (batch1, no cache).
[02:52] Lena Ortiz: where does that 12k come from? I thought our previous calc said 8k tokens/$ after infra overheads.
[03:02] Emma Clarke: Good callout — the spreadsheet (linked in notes) had two tabs: raw inference cost and infra overheads. The 12k is inference-only; our recommended customer-facing metric includes the infra overhead + dedicated reservation amortization which brings it down to ~8.6k tokens/$, so table uses both.

[05:15] Priya Nair: (joins) Sorry, quick context: our finance needs the tokens per dollar that include network / cloud egress. So please keep that higher-level number.
[05:25] Emma Clarke: noted. We'll propagate the full-cost number in the next sheet.

[06:10] Ravi Patel: Cache results — we enabled prefix caching and KV caching last Thursday for the session that ran with a warm-up period. Hit rate observed: 42% prefix hits and 18% KV hits which combined to approx 46% total token-level savings on average for that workload. That maps to a cost reduction of ~36% in tokens/$ when you apply hit-rate scaling.
[06:37] Diego Ramos: how consistent was that hit-rate? Our production prompt set is pretty bursty, I was worried warm-up would be poor except for a few flows.
[06:45] Ravi Patel: Good question. The hit-rate varied — for the FAQ/generation flows hits were 60-65% but for open-ended assistant prompts it was <10%. The overall 46% is a weighted average using the sample prompt distribution you gave us. If you change distribution (more long-form) the benefit drops.
[07:10] Lena Ortiz: so if we could bias more traffic toward canned responses we get the 36% cost saving, but that's product-level. For the POC we need a conservative number.

[08:05] Emma Clarke: Right — we suggested showing both optimistic (46% hit) and conservative (25% hit) projections. The conservative projection still yields about 18% cost reduction.

[09:30] Ravi Patel: Batching — we tested batch sizes of 1, 4, 8, and dynamic up-to-32. Cost per token decreased with batch size: ~12k tokens/$ at batch=1 -> ~31k tokens/$ at batch=8 (inference-only), but tail latency increases. p95 latencies: batch1 p95 ~120ms, batch8 p95 ~420ms, dynamic-8 p95 ~230ms in our run due to batching window heuristics.
[10:05] Diego Ramos: That p95 jump to 420ms is too big for our UI. We need <=300ms p95 for interactive prompts.
[10:12] Ravi Patel: understood. That's why we proposed hybrid: dynamic batching with max 8 but with latency guard for requests tagged 'interactive' to bypass batching (route to priority lane).
[10:25] Emma Clarke: we can set route tags in the call (metadata) so priority traffic is served with batch=1; background tasks can be batched aggressively. That keeps perceived latency low but still captures batching savings on non-critical traffic.

[12:45] Priya Nair: Any ops complexity to do that on Redwood Dedicated? We run in VPC and our security team prefers minimal routing complexity.
[12:55] Ravi Patel: No extra infra — routing policies live in the control plane. We just need consistent request metadata keys. We'll provide SDK snippet.

[14:02] Lena Ortiz: Let's talk numbers for the hybrid approach — if 30% of traffic is interactive and bypasses batching, and 70% is batched at effective batch 6, what's net tokens/$?
[14:15] Ravi Patel: quick ballpark — using our bench numbers: interactive (batch1) yields 12k tokens/$, batched portion (batch6 approximate) yields 28k tokens/$. Weighted: 0.3*12k + 0.7*28k = 24.8k tokens/$. That's ~2.8x improvement over all-batch1. After infra overhead your customer-facing number will be lower, maybe 1.9x improvement.
[14:45] Diego Ramos: Good. Can we validate that with a run that mimics 30/70 split?
[14:52] Ravi Patel: Yes — that's the focused throughput window we want to run. We'll instrument tags for interactive vs batchable.

[17:30] Emma Clarke: On cache retention — we set TTL 60s in the pilot. Increasing to 600s increased hits in our long-run test, but risk of stale responses for very dynamic prompts. For Aurora's taxonomy, 600s looked safe for FAQ and system prompts.
[17:50] Diego Ramos: I'm concerned about privacy/regulation — cached content might include PII. Are cached tokens encrypted and audit-logged?
[18:00] Ravi Patel: yes — KV/prefix cache entries are encrypted at rest with customer KMS and audit logs tied to the control plane. We'll attach the security note. (slight pause) sometimes the transcript tool says KMS as K-M-S or K-M-Z, apologies.
[18:20] Priya Nair: Good, please send the exact KMS steps to on-board.

[20:10] Ravi Patel: Ok moving to fallback model variants: we tested quantized variant (q4->q8?) sorry q4_0 quant on variant B, which is slightly cheaper per token but quality drop on long-coherence prompts. We recommend canary routing: try cheaper variant for batchable background tasks, keep high-fidelity model for interactive.
[20:45] Lena Ortiz: makes sense. Customer success question — how do we measure quality regressions? We have a set of 200 eval prompts we can run.
[20:55] Emma Clarke: perfect, we'll plug those into Redwood Optimize eval harness and surface quality delta and token delta side-by-side.

[23:05] Diego Ramos: About the cost projection sheet — I noticed numbers in the infra tab didn't include reserved capacity discounts we expect from our procurement (15%).
[23:15] Emma Clarke: we built the sheet flexible — there's a 'discount' cell. If you give us the expected discount we can recalc. For now we used conservative 0% in the public sheet.

[25:12] Ravi Patel: Proposed experiment run list: 1) 2-hour mixed workload with 30/70 interactive/batched tags (throughput + p95) 2) 24-hour cache TTL sweep (60s, 300s, 600s) to measure stability 3) Model-variant canary for background tasks. Which should we prioritize?
[25:35] Lena Ortiz: prioritize 1 and 2. We want the quick win on cost.

[27:40] Priya Nair: Ops note — we can give a reserved maintenance window Tues 07/15 02:00-04:00 UTC. That should be low-traffic for us.
[27:50] Emma Clarke: Great, we'll aim for that.

[30:05] Ravi Patel: Quick nit: we saw some transcription noise in the initial test logs (some token dropping) — that's probably a metrics export bug, not inference bug. We'll fix the logger and reshare raw logs.

[33:20] Diego Ramos: Minor UX ask — can we get a dashboard tile that shows cache hit-rate and effective tokens/$ in near real-time?
[33:28] Emma Clarke: yes that's doable — Redwood Console has a per-route KPI tile; we'll add a pre-configured Aurora route tile and share link.

[38:10] Lena Ortiz: Pricing ask — if we run dedicated nodes with autoscale burst, is there a simple estimate for peak vs steady cost?
[38:22] Emma Clarke: In the cost sheet we added a 'peak factor' slider. Example: steady 4 nodes, peak 8 nodes for 10% of time -> blended cost increases by ~18% for that usage profile. We'll annotate the sheet with that sample.

[41:05] Ravi Patel: Quick check on security review items — Priya, anything outstanding that blocks the TTL/cache change?
[41:12] Priya Nair: Just need the KMS integration doc and confirmation that audit logs are retained 90 days.
[41:20] Emma Clarke: We'll attach SOC2+KMS docs in the follow-up.

[46:00] Emma Clarke: Recap — agreed experiments: 2-hour mixed throughput (target Tues 07/15 02:00-04:00 UTC), TTL sweep for 24h after that, and model-variant canary for background tasks. Action owners in the sheet. We'll update cost projection with a conservative and optimistic scenario and push the new pilot YAML (cacheTTL=600, dynamic_batch_max=8) by Friday 07/11.
[46:35] Lena Ortiz: Sounds good. Also please make sure the p95 targets are clearly shown for interactive route.
[46:45] Diego Ramos: I'll upload the 1k prompt sample and the 200-eval set by Friday.

[49:00] Emma Clarke: Anything else?
[49:05] Priya Nair: No, that covers infra concerns.
[49:10] Lena Ortiz: No, thanks everyone.
[49:20] Emma Clarke: Thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invite and the config change diff.

End transcript.

Shared artifacts referenced: cost sheet, bench notebook, security KMS doc.

Call end.

title: Postmortem: SEV-2 Dedicated autoscaler stuck at min capacity (2026-02-09)
author: David Kim
text:
The Dedicated autoscaler stopped scaling above min due to a metrics query change that returned empty series for a subset of clusters.

Two Dedicated customers in us-west experienced sustained queueing and timeouts. p99 latency exceeded 6s for ~70 minutes; timeout rate peaked at 3.2%.

13:22 UTC: Support escalated customer reports of timeouts on Dedicated pools (us-west).
13:28 UTC: SRE on-call confirmed queue depth rising and no scale-out events.
13:40 UTC: Identified autoscalermetrics query change deployed earlier that day.
14:05 UTC: Hotfix applied to autoscaler query; scale-out resumed.
14:20 UTC: Queue depth normalized; timeouts subsided.
14:47 UTC: Incident resolved.

A refactor in the autoscalerPromQL query switched label matching from cluster_id to cluster. Some clusters emitted cluster_id only, causing the query to return no data and preventing scale decisions.

Primary detection was via customer escalation; internal alerting on scale-out suppression was missing.

Rolled forward a hotfix restoring label compatibility and added a fallback query when no series are returned.

Once identified, the fix was small and low risk. Capacity was available to scale immediately.

Insufficient alerting on autoscaler making no decisions; canary did not include clusters with legacy labels.

Add alert: autoscaler decision loop sees empty metrics for >5 minutes (SRE; due 2026-02-25).
Add integration test covering both cluster and cluster_id labels (Infrastructure; due 2026-03-05).
Update Dedicated release checklist to require canary across at least one legacy-labeled cluster (Infrastructure; due 2026-02-22).
