title: Staged runtime version gate and probe plan (draft)
author: Maya Chen
text:
Purpose:
- Lightweight, repeatable plan for safe staged upgrades of the on-prem/runtime control plane and serving runtime for private deployments (VPC/appliance).
- Focus: avoid behavioral regressions, preserve API compatibility, and ensure fast, low-risk rollback path.
- This is a living draft: expect follow-ups after the first two rehearsals.

Scope and assumptions:
- Targets: private-deployments running runtime v1.x -> v2.0 (major ABI and kernel selector changes; quantization path changes).
- Control plane API is the managed shim (no breaking changes expected), but runtime wire/protobuf versions change.
- Customers may have heterogeneous hardware (A100 + T4 + older cards).
- Terraform is the canonical infra config. We must not require manual tfstate surgery except for emergency rollback.

Exit criteria (per-stage):
- Unit-level: all smoke and model-load tests green on upgraded nodes for 1h.
- Integration-level: canary traffic passes latency, error-rate, and QPS thresholds over 4 hours (see gating metrics below).
- Observability: no new 5xx error classes, output-similarity delta within accepted bounds (see regression gating).
- Rollout conditional: if any critical gating metric breached, stop and run rollback checklist.

Gating metrics (primary):
- p95 latency (tokens/sec) does not regress > 20% vs baseline for the canary fleet.
- 5xx rate remains < 0.1% absolute increase.
- Output similarity score (BLEU/embedding-cosine) for golden prompt set >= 0.98 baseline.
- Resource OOMs or GPU driver resets: zero tolerated.
- Cost-per-token bump detection: tracked but not gating for first two rehearsals.

Staging and traffic plan:
1) Canary pool creation (TF): carve out a dedicated canary node pool (label: upgrade-canary-<id>) with isolation from customer traffic.
 - TF snippet (concept):

 resource "runtime_node_pool" "canary" {
 name = "upgrade-canary-2025-02"
 count = 2
 node_type = var.node_type_canary
 labels = { role = "upgrade-canary" stage = var.upgrade_stage }
 taints = ["upgrade=exclusive:NoSchedule"]
 }

 - Note: Use taints/labels to ensure only synthetic and test traffic lands on these nodes. Do not change customer-facing pools until step 4.

2) Shadow rehearse (no traffic): deploy new runtime on canary pool, start with shadow mode (duplicate requests, no responses returned to caller).
 - Validate model loads, kv-cache handshake, and sequence length paths.
 - Collect: kernel selection logs, quantization runtime warnings, and remaining fallback branches exercised.

3) Synthetic probe traffic (low QPS): ramp from 1 QPS -> 10 QPS over 30 minutes.
 - Blackbox tests: API contract checks, malformed-input fuzz, streaming/resume tokens, function-calling flow.
 - Golden prompt suite: 120 prompts covering short/long context, caching-advantaged prefixes, and edge tokenizer cases.
 - Automated regression scoring: run nightly comparison job that computes embedding cosine between baseline outputs and canary outputs.

4) Canary + constrained production shadowing (traffic to canary at 1% of production):
 - Use weighted routing in the gateway. Routing config must be expressible in TF (route_weight field).
 - Observe: latency p50/p95, error class distribution, and model-answer divergence.

5) Canary push (gradual): if step 4 green for 4 hours, move to 5% for 1h, then 20% for 2h, then 50% for a rolling 6h window before full cut.

6) Full cutover: update TF to replace node pool references and scale new fleet to target size with autoscaling policies copied from baseline.

Terraform considerations and notes:
- All canary node pools and route weights must be expressible via module inputs; avoid ad-hoc manual console edits.
- Add feature flag in the runtime-module: "accepts_v2_kernel" boolean and "binary_version_tag" string. Default false for stable branches.
- Example variable additions (tf module):

variable "upgrade_phase" {
 type = string
 description = "one of: shadow, canary, partial, full"
 default = "shadow"
}

variable "force_kernel_selector" {
 type = string
 description = "optional override for kernel selection to force legacy path on mixed HW"
 default = ""
}

- Keep old node pool definitions live for at least 24h after full cut (rapid rollback window).
- Record the current tfstate snapshot id and module versions in the upgrade runbook metadata.

Compatibility checklist (pre-upgrade):
- API surface: run automated API contract verifier (protobuf hash compare) for all customer-facing endpoints. Any minor schema changes must have shims.
- KV cache layout: ensure new runtime reads legacy KV prefixes and can fallback to prefix-transparency mode.
- Model artifacts: verify model-quantized variants are available for the new runtime; if not, block upgrade.
- Hardware compatibility: verify kernel selector maps each node type to a supported kernel; fallback to CPU path if not possible.
- Plugin hooks: ensure function-calling and tooling integrations still honor prior call semantics.

Rollback strategy (fast and safe):
- Preferred: scale old node pool back up and shift route weights away from new runtime (zero-downtime rollback). Steps:
 1) Pause new-runtime autoscaler.
 2) Scale legacy node pool to previous size (TF apply new count).
 3) Update route weights to 0% -> new runtime, 100% -> legacy (via TF).
 4) Drain new runtime nodes (graceful) and monitor for any in-flight request errors.
 5) After stable 1h, destroy new-runtime pool if necessary.
- Emergency (if TF manipulation delayed): use gateway emergency override (admin endpoint) to flip routing immediately, then reconcile TF state.
- State reconciliation: after rollback, run state audit: compare runtime binary versions, model cache versions, and KV prefix counters.

Telemetry gating and alerting:
- Create a temporary dashboard for the upgrade run with following panels: p50/p95 latency by route, 4xx/5xx heatmap, kernel fallback rates, GPU memory pressure, model load errors, output-similarity score.
- Alerts (severity):
 - Sev1: sudden jump in 5xx > 0.5% absolute, or GPU driver resets detected -> immediate rollback.
 - Sev2: output-similarity < 0.95 on golden set for 30m -> investigate, consider pause.
 - Sev3: cost-per-token +30% sustained for 2h -> post-mortem.

Operational playbook (step-by-step checklist):
- Pre-window (24–72h):
 - Run contract verifier and model artifact inventory.
 - Coordinate with SRE, support, solutions-eng for runway (on-call coverage).
 - Snapshot TF state and tag release artifacts.
 - Prepare runbook binder (links to TF runs, playbook, and rollback checklist).
- Upgrade window:
 1) Create canary pool (TF apply).
 2) Deploy runtime binary to canary in shadow mode.
 3) Run smoke tests and synthetic probes.
 4) Ramp to constrained production traffic per schedule.
 5) If green, follow ramp schedule to full cut.
- Post-cut (0–72h):
 - Keep increased observability retention (48h).
 - Keep legacy pool live for 24h.
 - Run canary harvest job: collect examples of any output divergence > threshold.
 - Post-mortem if any gating metric tripped.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Finalize exact regression metric (BLEU vs embedding-cosine vs task-specific eval).
- Decide default canary pool size for small vs large customers (should be autosize policy driven).
- Verify if KMS/HSM migrations impact model-key access during the switch.

Appendix: quick TF emergency commands (ops team):
- snapshot tfstate: terraform state pull > state-YYYYMMDD.json
- scale legacy pool quickly: terraform apply -var="legacy_count=5" -target=module.runtime_node_pool.legacy
- override route weights via gateway API: curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" "$GATEWAY/api/v1/routes/weights" -d "{"route":"default", "weights": {"new": 0, "legacy": 100}}"

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep first two rehearsals internal; invite a single trusted customer for the third rehearsal.
- Expect micro regressions around streaming/resume; add extra test cases for that.
- When in doubt, stop the ramp and run controlled rollback.

End of draft.

title: Guardrails: cooldown windows + fairness enforcement for shared burst pools (anti-starvation)
author: Talia Benson
text:
Implement burst guardrails in the admission controller to prevent noisy-neighbor and starvation behaviors when multiple Dedicated tenants borrow from shared Redwood-managed burst pools.

Scope:
- Cooldown windows to dampen burst oscillation and prevent “thrash” (rapid admit/deny cycles) that amplifies tail latency.
- Fairness enforcement across tenants borrowing from the same pool, aligned with ADR selection (token-bucket / WFQ hybrid).
- Anti-starvation protections so small tenants are not permanently throttled by a few large tenants.

Non-goals (this ticket):
- Global fleet safety cap / circuit breaker logic (tracked in ENG-4902).
- Customer-facing console UX for burst usage (tracked in ENG-4855).

Primary owners: Keiko (implementation/guardrail tuning), Jordan Lee (policy semantics/determinism), Mina/Ravi (routing behavior expectations), Sean (SLO guardrails).

Key references:
- Confluence design spec: sources/confluence/product-docs/design-specs/burst-pool-architecture-and-guardrails.json
- ADR admission semantics: sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-burst-pool-admission-control-semantics.json
- ADR fairness model: sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-fairness-model-for-shared-burst-pools.json

1) Cooldown enforcement
- Admission controller enforces a per-tenant cooldown window after a tenant exceeds configured burst ratio / cap (or after sustained burst activity), to prevent rapid re-entry into burst.
- Cooldown parameters are policy-configurable (default duration, and what events trigger cooldown).
- Denial reason is deterministic and stable during cooldown (e.g., BURST_DENIED_COOLDOWN_ACTIVE).

2) Fairness enforcement
- Tenants competing for a pool are throttled/admitted according to configured fairness weights (tier/priority) while respecting hard caps.
- Implementation prevents “unbounded” consumption by a single tenant when pool demand is high.
- No unexpected priority inversion (higher tier should not be starved by lower tier), while also avoiding starvation of lower tiers.

3) Anti-starvation protections
- Provide a minimum progress guarantee under sustained contention (e.g., periodic tokens / minimum refill rate or starvation detector that temporarily boosts).
- Explicit test coverage for 3+ tenant scenarios with mixed sizes and tiers.

4) Determinism and telemetry lag
- Admission decision must be deterministic for a given request and the same view of telemetry/policy (avoid oscillation from laggy signals).
- Provide guard conditions/smoothing to reduce unfair denials under telemetry delay.

5) Observability + operator clarity
- Metrics emitted for cooldown-triggered denials and fairness-throttle denials.
- Debug output includes which guardrail fired and the evaluated limits/weights (safe for internal use; redaction rules handled elsewhere).

6) Rollout
- All behavior guarded behind feature flag / per-region allow-list (rollout gates implemented in ENG-4848 / feature flags PRs), with safe defaults (fairness enabled, conservative cooldown).

Proposed approach (matches ADR direction):

A) Token bucket per tenant, backed by pool-level capacity
- Each tenant has a bucket with:
 - refill_rate: derived from tenant baseline reservation and configured burst limits
 - capacity (burst): max tokens accrued (limits burst spike length)
 - weight: tier-based multiplier (e.g., gold > silver), applied to refill
- A request is admitted as “burst” only if:
 - tenant is burst-enabled and below per-tenant caps
 - pool has remaining headroom
 - tenant has sufficient tokens (or passes anti-starvation condition)

B) Cooldown window
- Trigger events:
 - Tenant exceeds max_burst_ratio over a sliding window
 - Tenant hits per-tenant max burst concurrency threshold (optional; dependent on available signals)
 - “Guardrail breach” events when neighbor impact indicators exceed threshold (SLO gate is separate, but cooldown can be triggered locally too)
- Cooldown state stored with:
 - cooldown_until timestamp
 - last_trigger_reason (for debugging and metrics)

C) Anti-starvation
- Starvation detector tracks time since last admitted burst request under contention.
- If starved beyond threshold, allow a limited “minimum progress” admit per interval (bounded, cannot exceed hard caps).

D) Determinism
- Use discretized time slices for refill calculations (e.g., 1s buckets) and clamp telemetry inputs.
- Smooth pool utilization inputs to prevent per-request toggling when signals jitter.

E) Denial reason codes
- Extend denial codes (or reuse existing ones from ENG-4881/PR-23795):
 - BURST_DENIED_COOLDOWN_ACTIVE
 - BURST_DENIED_FAIRNESS_THROTTLE
 - BURST_DENIED_POOL_SATURATED
 - BURST_DENIED_TENANT_CAP

Notes:
- We should be careful not to conflate “tenant cap reached” vs “fairness throttle” because Support needs to explain behavior (see SUP-28503 patterns).

- [x] Confirm fairness algorithm parameters + defaults with Jordan (weights, refill derivation)
- [x] Implement per-tenant token bucket state machine in admission controller
- [x] Implement cooldown state + config policy fields
- [x] Add anti-starvation logic + bounds
- [x] Add unit tests (single-tenant cooldown, multi-tenant fairness, starvation scenario)
- [x] Add simulation test / integration test scenario (3 tenants; 1 aggressive; verify others get progress)
- [x] Export metrics for cooldown/fairness denials
- [x] Coordinate routing behavior for fairness/cooldown denials (retry vs fallback guidance)
- [x] Document tuning guidance + oncall knobs (caps, weights, cooldown duration)
- [x] Rollout behind feature flag and default conservative thresholds

2025-03-12 (Keiko): Drafted token bucket params proposal. Default weights: gold=1.3, silver=1.0, bronze=0.8. Cooldown default: 120s after sustained burst_ratio>1.8 for 60s. Flagging determinism risk if we compute refill using high-resolution timestamps per request.

2025-03-18 (Jordan): +1 to discretized refill windows (1s). Also want explicit invariant: given same policy snapshot + same telemetry snapshot, decision must be stable. Telemetry lag mitigation should be inside admission controller (don’t rely on routing retries).

2025-03-24 (Keiko): Implemented cooldown state + reason codes locally. Found that cooldown-trigger condition based on instantaneous utilization is too noisy; switching to rolling window counters in controller.

2025-04-02 (Keiko): Multi-tenant fairness tests added. Observed starvation when one tenant continuously submits large requests and tokens refill slowly for smaller tenants; adding minimum-progress admit every N seconds when contention is sustained.

2025-04-11 (Mina/Ravi): Routing behavior: for BURST_DENIED_FAIRNESS_THROTTLE, gateway should backpressure/queue briefly (bounded) vs immediately falling back to non-dedicated. For BURST_DENIED_COOLDOWN_ACTIVE and BURST_DENIED_TENANT_CAP, return 429 with retry-after guidance (documented in docs PR).

2025-04-22 (Sean): Reviewed guardrail thresholds; asked for clear metrics panel “fairness_throttle_denials” and a derived SLI: non-burst p95 latency delta during burst windows. Not blocking this ticket but must be wired into dashboards (ENG-4833).

2025-04-29 (Keiko): Merged PRs and validated in staging with synthetic load. Cooldown reduces admit/deny oscillation. Starvation detector ensures at least one admit per 10s per tenant under contention (bounded by hard cap).

2025-03-10 (Talia Benson): Creating as a separate guardrails ticket so we can track cooldown/fairness/anti-starvation independently of the admission controller skeleton. Please keep any parameter changes (defaults) visible here; PM + SRE want to review before beta enablement.
2025-03-12 (Keiko Yamamoto): Will implement as token bucket per tenant with tier weights + cooldown. Question: do we want cooldown to block *all* burst admits or only additional burst above some “soft cap”? My preference: hard block during cooldown to make behavior explainable and reduce thrash.
2025-03-13 (Jordan Lee): Agree on explainability. Also: cooldown should be policy-expressible (rules engine), not hardcoded. Let’s make trigger conditions explicit in config, with safe defaults. Determinism: compute refill using discretized time slices (e.g., 1s) and clamp telemetry inputs.
2025-03-19 (Mina Haddad): From routing POV, we need clear separation between “pool saturated” vs “fairness throttle” vs “cooldown”. We’ll treat fairness throttle as transient and can retry/queue briefly; cooldown/cap should be surfaced to client with retry-after so they can shape traffic.
2025-04-03 (Sean Gallagher): Please add a metric that differentiates cooldown-trigger denials from fairness denials. Oncall needs to know if we’re denying because we’re protecting neighbors (cooldown) vs expected contention behavior (fairness).
2025-04-12 (Keiko Yamamoto): Hit an edge case in simulation: telemetry lag causes controller to think tenant is over ratio and enter cooldown too aggressively, leading to “unfair” denials. Adding smoothing/guard conditions; will land as follow-up hotfix PR if needed.
2025-04-29 (Keiko Yamamoto): Marking Done. Cooldown + fairness + anti-starvation are in, tested, and behind flags. Remaining follow-ups are mostly tuning + dashboards (tracked elsewhere).

Risks:
- Overly aggressive cooldown defaults could cause customer surprise (spikes denied) even when pool has capacity.
- Anti-starvation mechanism can become a loophole if bounds are not strict (must remain capped and auditable).
- Telemetry lag can still cause misclassification of burst ratio; smoothing must not mask real overload.

Follow-ups (not blocking Done):
- Ensure dashboards include fairness vs cooldown denial breakdown (ENG-4833).
- Validate behavior during game day scenarios with induced telemetry delay (ENG-4862).
- Confirm Support playbook includes these denial codes and recommended customer retry patterns (ENG-4881).
- Revisit default cooldown duration after beta retro (target: shorter cooldown + better smoothing if safe).

Subject: Initial compute profile and throughput targets

Priya,

Thanks for the intro call yesterday. We pulled together the traffic profile and an initial set of goals (attached). High level:
- Primary LLM workload: clinical summarization + long-context retrieval-augmented generation. Average prompt ~250 tokens, expected generation ~750 tokens (so ~1k tokens per call).
- Peak ingestion bursts from batch jobs arrive as sporadic spikes (~10–15 min windows) that can double call rate.
- Target SLO: p95 end-to-end inference <= 1200 ms for the user-facing path.
- Expected initial pilot traffic: 800–1,500 calls/min peak (13–25 calls/sec).
- Prefer a dedicated pool (for data separation) and we want 2–3x headroom for marketing and forecast variability.

Can you share a recommended deployment profile (GPU types/skus, approximate tokens/sec capacity, suggested headroom, and an estimated monthly committed footprint we should budget for)? Attached is our profile workbook: nebula_compute_profile.xlsx

Also, quick question: do you recommend KV-prefix caching for our retrieval patterns? We have a fair amount of repeated contexts.

Appreciate any modeling you can share prior to the follow-up with our infra team next Wednesday.

Aaron — thanks for the workbook and the clear targets. We've looped in Ben and Karthik to run a short model-of-record so we can present a concrete capacity proposal ahead of next Wednesday.

Two quick clarifications that will change the numbers:
1) When you say "batch bursts" — are these arriving as many concurrent short requests (many clients simultaneously) or as fewer, long-running single requests? That changes batching efficiency assumptions.
2) Do we have a rough distribution of cacheable prefixes (any % of calls that are exact repeats)? If you can add a column in the workbook for "expected prefix-repeat %" that will help our KV hit modeling.

From: Priya Natarajan <priya.natarajan@redwood.ai>

Date: 2027-03-30T09:20:00-07:00
Subject: Fwd: Initial compute profile and throughput targets

(Forwarding Aaron's profile — internal thread to capture model assumptions and recommendation.)

Ben / Karthik — see Aaron's traffic sketch. I ran an initial set of assumptions below; please sanity-check and add your numbers. We'll fold into the external proposal.

Assumptions (baseline)
- Model family: Llama-3-13B, distilled/config tuned for clinical summarization. We will propose two runtime variants: FP16 on H100 (latency-first) and 4-bit quantized on A100-class for cost-optimized.
- Average tokens per call: 1,000 (250 prompt + 750 gen).
- Peak calls/sec (pilot): 25 cps (1,500 calls/min).
- Effective batching efficiency: 55% for user-facing requests (mix of interactive + batching), 80% for scheduled batch windows.
- Prefix/KV cache hit: base case 25% (reduces generation tokens by ~35% for cached calls).

Modeling results (back-of-envelope):
- H100 (FP16) single-VM slab (4x H100 effective concurrency topology): ~9,000 tokens/sec sustained for interactive workloads at p95 target ~450–600 ms (with warm KV cache).
- A100 (4-bit quantized) single-VM slab (8x A100 fractional share): ~5,500 tokens/sec sustained, p95 700–900 ms.

Capacity math (targeting pilot peak 25 cps -> 25,000 tokens/sec nominal):
- With 25% KV hit and 55% batching efficiency, net tokens/sec demand drops to ~13,500 tps equivalent of heavy compute.
- H100 option: need ~2 slabs (2 x 9,000 = 18,000 tps) to cover demand + comfortable headroom. Add 25% headroom => 3 slabs.
- A100 quantized option: need ~3 slabs (3 x 5,500 = 16,500 tps) + 25% headroom => 4 slabs.

Recommendation (pilot):
- Latency-first: 3 H100 slabs (dedicated) configured with KV prefix caching enabled for clinical templates, target p95 <= 600 ms, pilot committed footprint: 3 slabs.
- Cost-first: 4 quantized-A100 slabs with higher batching thresholds and aggressive prefix caching, target p95 <= 900 ms, pilot committed footprint: 4 slabs.

Operational notes (important for SLO fit):
- Warmup lanes: pre-warm 1 slab during the daily morning ramp and keep 1 slab on standby to absorb spike windows. We expect cache warming to reduce observed tail latency by ~20% after 15–30 minutes.
- Burst policy: auto-burst to host pool with overflow to lower-cost quantized variants if saturated; recommend a fallback policy in the canary to avoid 5xx spikes.
- Monitoring: token-level tracing + p95/p99 by route and by model variant. We should instrument a 2-week regression suite to watch output quality after quantization.

Costs rough estimate (monthly committed):
- 3 H100 slabs pilot: ballpark $XXk/month committed (we'll produce real $ numbers in the external doc).
- 4 A100 slabs pilot: ~40–55% lower committed compute cost but higher latency tail risk.

Ben/Karthik: fill gaps (precise tokens/sec per slab, realistic p95 under mixed traffic, and solid monthly figures). I'll fold into the pilot proposal and send to Aaron.

—Priya

title: Planned Change: SLO / Error Budget Impact Review Requirements
author: Grace O'Connor
text:
## Purpose
This document defines the minimum SRE review steps for planned changes that may impact availability, latency, or throughput SLOs for any production environment (Hosted, Dedicated, Private).

## When this review is required
SRE review is required for any change that is classified Medium/High/Critical risk under the Production Change Management Policy, or any change that:
- Requires disabling alerts
- Requires a maintenance window
- Has a credible risk of increased 5xx, latency regression, or capacity shortfall

## Required checks (attach evidence/links)
### 1) Current SLO state
- Confirm current 30-day error budget remaining for impacted services/tenants.
- If error budget remaining is below 25%, attach an explicit risk acceptance from Engineering + SRE lead.

### 2) Capacity + saturation
- Confirm GPU and request capacity headroom for the expected window.
- Confirm no overlapping capacity events (region maintenance, fleet migrations, known shortages).

### 3) Monitoring coverage
- Identify the “watch list” metrics for the change window (at minimum: 5xx rate, P95 latency, saturation/queue depth, restarts/OOM, and synthetic checks).
- Confirm alerts are enabled and routed to an active on-call.

### 4) Rollback feasibility
- Validate that rollback can be executed within the defined “time-to-restore” target for the customer (or platform).
- Identify the decision point for rollback (e.g., after control-plane or after data-plane).

### 5) Change overlap
- Confirm no concurrent high-risk changes affecting the same customer/region.
- If overlap exists, record mitigation or reschedule.

## Go/No-Go criteria from an SRE perspective
SRE will recommend GO only if:
- Error budget is healthy or risk acceptance is documented
- Monitoring is ready and on-call coverage confirmed
- Rollback plan is concrete and feasible
- Customer comms plan exists when customer-visible

## Minimum evidence checklist (copy/paste into change record)
- [ ] Error budget screenshot/link
- [ ] Capacity headroom note (GPU + queue)
- [ ] Alert routing confirmation
- [ ] Rollback time estimate + decision point
- [ ] List of services/routes impacted

title: Praxis Health — options for private connectivity (VPC peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN)
author: jasmine_liu
text:
From: Evan Brooks <evan.brooks@praxishealth.com>
To: Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwood.com>
Cc: Priya Singh <priya.singh@praxishealth.com>
Date: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 09:32:10 -0800
Subject: Connecting Redwood Private — recommended path for Praxis

Hi Jasmine,

Thanks again for the demo last week. Praxis is moving toward a private deployment for our PHI workloads and the infra team asked me for a recommendation between three options: VPC peering (account-to-account), AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints / NLB), or a site-to-site VPN into our on-prem data center. Their priorities are:

- End-to-end encryption and no internet egress for inference traffic
- Low single-digit ms latency from our app tier (us-west-2) to the model endpoints
- Simpler operational model (fewer cross-account networking objects)
- Auditability / minimal blast radius for compromised creds

We host most of our services in an on-prem colo but are running a big portion in us-west-2 in the Praxis AWS account. Can you outline the tradeoffs briefly and any constraints we should be aware of? Also: any preferences from Redwood on which pattern makes upgrades/rollouts easiest?

Appreciate it — Evan

--
Evan Brooks
VP, Platform Engineering | Praxis Health

From: Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwood.com>
To: Evan Brooks <evan.brooks@praxishealth.com>
Cc: Priya Singh <priya.singh@praxishealth.com>
Date: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 11:05:33 -0800
Subject: Re: Connecting Redwood Private — recommended path for Praxis

Evan — thanks for the clear list of priorities. Short answer up front: we generally recommend a hybrid approach for customers with both on-prem and cloud footprints. Below is a short matrix, followed by a recommendation tailored to your requirements. I attached a one‑pager and an initial diagram.

Quick matrix (latency / security / ops / cross-account):
- VPC peering: lowest latency for same-region VPCs, simple L3 routing; no transitive peering (per‑account setup required); cross-account peering is supported but each peering is an object to manage. Good for high-throughput low-latency within AWS.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): strong security (private endpoints per service), no route-table peering changes, supports cross-account without exposing VPC routes; slightly higher per‑request cost and additional NLB overhead. Great for minimizing blast radius and removing broad network access.
- Site-to-site VPN: flexible for on‑prem -> cloud; depends on customer gateway throughput and encryption settings; can add latency and jitter vs native cloud paths.

Tailored recommendation for Praxis:
1) Use PrivateLink for Redwood control & inference control-plane traffic (API calls, auth, model selection). PrivateLink minimizes wide VPC exposure and fits your audit/no-egress requirement.
2) For heavy bulk payloads (if you need to stream large batches of requests or upload datasets from on‑prem), colocate an ingress VPC in your Praxis AWS account and use VPC peering to avoid extra hop costs and provide lower latency between app tier and the ingress VPC.
3) Keep a redundant S2S VPN from your colo to the Praxis AWS account for fallback and maintenance windows (also useful for initial bootstrap if you don't want to open BGP immediately).

Operational notes:
- We'll recommend PrivateLink endpoints per AZ and an NLB in our service account; Praxis will need to create interface endpoints in your VPCs.
- DNS: use private hosted zones and conditional forwarding so service names resolve to iface endpoints.
- For model rollouts, PrivateLink helps with safe fallbacks since traffic is scoped to the endpoint — we can rotate backends without broad route changes.

Next step: I want Ben from Solutions to add specifics on throughput and MTU considerations; Kim will confirm security/KMS checklist. Can we schedule a 30-min call? I included two attachments: praxis-reqs-summary.pdf and praxis-initial-options-diagram.png.

Thanks,
Jasmine Liu
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
To: Evan Brooks <evan.brooks@praxishealth.com>, Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwood.com>
Cc: Priya Singh <priya.singh@praxishealth.com>
Date: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 08:14:02 -0800
Subject: Re: Connecting Redwood Private — recommended path for Praxis

On Wed, Nov 18, 2026 at 11:05 AM Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwood.com> wrote:
> Evan — thanks for the clear list of priorities. Short answer up front: we generally recommend a hybrid approach...

Adding some technical trade-offs and practical numbers from an infra perspective:

PrivateLink (recommended control plane):
- Throughput: Interface endpoints accept traffic to NLBs — expect per‑AZ throughput constraints based on the NLB sizing; for steady high-TPS workloads we size a couple of NLB targets and tune connection reuse.
- Latency: adds ~1–3ms vs in‑VPC when using iface endpoints in the same AZ. Typically fine for sub‑10ms targets.
- Security: traffic never traverses the public internet; IAM + endpoint policies can lock down callers.

VPC peering (intra-AWS, low latency):
- Pros: L3 routing, no NAT for egress, bidirectional connectivity once peered.
- Cons: No transitive peering (if you want many AWS accounts to reach the Redwood endpoint you need multiple peerings OR an aggregated transit VPC). Peering also requires route table management and care with IP CIDR overlaps.

Site-to-site VPN (on-prem):
- Throughput depends on your customer gateway and AWS VGW/transit throughput. Expect higher jitter; for low-latency interactive inference this is often slightly worse than cross‑AZ AWS paths.
- Recommendation: use S2S for management/fallback and for bulk sync if you have large dataset uploads from colo.

Hybrid pattern we recommend for Praxis:
- PrivateLink for API/control + short inference bursts (keeps blast radius small).
- A peered ingress VPC in Praxis account for sustained/high-throughput local traffic (apps talk to that VPC; peering gives minimal latency).
- S2S VPN to colo as backup and for cost-effective archive uploads.

Operational checklist (short):
- Verify non-overlapping CIDRs for peering; if overlap exists, use PrivateLink or a transit model.
- Set MTU to 9001 only if the whole path supports jumbo frames; otherwise 1500.
- Use BFD for rapid route failover on S2S if you run BGP.
- Monitor TCP connection reuse and tune keepalive on client SDKs to reduce NLB connection churn.

I attached a short notes file (ben-private-deploy-notes.md) with rough throughput numbers and an example NLB target group sizing formula. Happy to walk through on the call.

—Ben
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Quick security items to add to the design:
- KMS / key separation: Praxis should use a customer-managed CMK (AWS KMS) and optionally an HSM for any key material that must never leave your control. We support envelope encryption so customer keys remain primary for access control.
- Audit logs: ensure VPC flow logs and PrivateLink Flow logs are enabled and forwarded to your SIEM (we recommend a dedicated ingest S3 + Glue partitioning to keep retention manageable).

title: sse-anchored-offset-fence-and-deferred-tool-ack-recovery
author: Maya Chen
text:
Background: We observed a rare class of failures where interleaved SSE fragments combined with delayed function/tool-call sentinel events produced malformed partial JSON or reordered tool call deliveries to downstream adapters. This typically manifests when: (1) a large model response is fragmented across TCP frames with non-deterministic chunk boundaries, (2) a function-call sentinel (fn_call start/stop) arrives split across fragments, and (3) upstream retries/resends produce a late-arriving chunk that should have been anchored to an earlier sequence. Problem: the existing reassembly logic relied on a simple linear byte window and last-seen sentinel heuristics which allowed two problems: a) "offset drift" where a late fragment would be stitched without verifying an anchored epoch causing JSON seam corruption, and b) tool-call ordering regressions when an fn_call stop token was observed after the reassembly finished and the adapter had already dispatched a synthetic call. What this PR does: introduces an "anchored offset fence" that ties fragment assembly to an epoch anchor (per-stream checkpoint) and requires a fence-ack for out-of-window late fragments before they can mutate a previously emitted JSON span. Adds a deferred-tool-ack handshake between the SSE reassembler and the OpenAI compatibility adapter so that fn_call boundaries are not acknowledged to adapters until the reassembler proves post-facto continuity of the sentinel span. This reduces duplicate or out-of-order function/tool deliveries while preserving low-latency emission in the common case. Key changes: - Reassembler: anchored offset fence with epoch checkpoints and a lightweight sequence checksum used to validate late fragment grafting. - Adapter: deferred-tool-ack API: adapters can opt into a short-duration lease (configurable, default 30ms) where tool-call dispatch is held until the reassembler clears the fence or times out. - Metrics/tracing: new metrics sse.anchored_fence.* and tracing spans for fence_acquire/release, plus a debug-only reassembly digest for post-incident capture. - Backwards compatibility: default behavior is opt-in via compatibility flag openai.legacy_deferred_ack=false; enterprise customers can enable by default in their Private/Dedicated configs. - Tests: add deterministic fuzz harness and integration tests simulating split-sentinel, late-graft, and reordered-fragment scenarios. Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked in Linear ENG-4801 - [x] Unit tests for reassembler fences and checksums - [x] Integration tests for adapter handshake and timeout fallback - [x] Perf validation to confirm median latency impact < +3ms on streaming emits - [x] Metric and dashboard updates

Luis Ortega (2025-01-14): Can you clarify the conditions under which the fence drops fragments instead of grafting? We need deterministic behavior for audits.
Maya Chen (2025-01-15): Answered: the policy is 'verify checksum -> graft if ok; otherwise mark tombstone and emit a debug seam marker' — added unit tests to ensure tombstones are registered and prom metric increments.
Rupali Shah (2025-01-16): Suggests lowering default lease to 20ms for hosted to reduce impact on low-latency customers.
Maya Chen (2025-01-17): Updated default to 30ms and made hosted override via runtime config. Added perf microbench showing 30ms has <3ms P50 penalty; 20ms regresses P50 by ~6ms in our test workload.
Ben Greer (2025-01-19): Approves after nit on logging verbosity removed and added a debug-only trace flag.

Design notes: The anchored fence trades a small window where emission can be deferred for correctness in rare split/sync cases. We avoid global stalls by scoping fences per-stream and per-epoch. The checksum is intentionally weak (rolling xor+len) to be cheap; if incidents require stronger validation we can upgrade to a lightweight CRC. Backoff/fallback: if the fence does not clear within lease timeout, the adapter will emit the best-effort event and mark it with sse.reassembly.fallback=true to allow downstream causal reconciliation.

Added 12 unit tests and 5 deterministic integration tests covering: split sentinel across three fragments, late graft within epoch, late graft beyond epoch (tombstone), function-call stop after reassembly, and adapter timeout fallback. Fuzz harness found two edge cases which are fixed: missing final newline causing sentinel ambiguity (fixed by newline-normalization prepass) and double-escaped delimiters (fixed by normalizing escape runs).

New metrics: sse.anchored_fence.acquire_total, sse.anchored_fence.release_total, sse.anchored_fence.tombstone_total, sse.deferred_tool_ack.acquired, sse.deferred_tool_ack.timed_out. Dashboard included at metrics/dashboards/sse_anchored_fence.json for oncall. Alert: fire if tombstone_total / reassembly_attempts > 0.01 over 5m.

Feature gated under openai.legacy_deferred_ack flag. Gradual rollout plan: enable for internal staging first (2 days), then for all hosted-rc customers with monitoring enabled (3 days), then default on Dedicated/Private after customer opt-in window. Migration note: older adapters that do not implement the deferred ack will continue to receive events as before; the reassembler will default to backward-compatible immediate ack mode if adapter does not register the lease.

Fixes reassembly-induced partial JSON/structured-output corruption and prevents duplicate/out-of-order function/tool call deliveries by adding an anchored offset fence and a deferred-tool-ack handshake. Opt-in under openai.legacy_deferred_ack; recommended for customers experiencing split-sentinel errors.

- Deploy reassembler + adapter change to staging cluster and enable openai.legacy_deferred_ack=true for 48h. - Add temporary e2e smoke in canary pipeline to exercise split-sentinel flows. - Monitor sse.anchored_fence.tombstone_total and sse.deferred_tool_ack.timed_out closely for first 72h.

If customers report stalled streaming emits, check sse.deferred_tool_ack.acquired vs timed_out. If timed_out spikes, consider lowering lease in hosted runtime or enabling immediate-emit fallback for the affected tenant. Use debug trace to inspect reassembly digest for incident triage.

title: Slice-wise latency/quality signal mapping for hybrid batching and KV-cache configs
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Background: Recent config rollouts (larger batching windows + more aggressive KV cache TTLs) demonstrate measurable token-cost and median-latency wins but sporadic quality regressions on some prompt slices (multi-turn dialogs and long-instruction completions). This ticket implements a repeatable, slice-aware evaluation pipeline that correlates latency quantiles with a set of quality metrics for each slice and surfaces actionable regression signals when config/model changes move us along the latency↔quality frontier.

Goals:
- Produce nightly slice-level tradeoff matrices (per config variant) mapping latency quantiles (p50/p95/p99) to quality metrics (semantic-similarity AUC, exact-match on QA pairs, BLEU/ROUGE-L for seq2seq slices, hallucination rate for knowledge prompts).
- Define automated alert rules that consider both direction and magnitude (e.g., quality drop >3% on a high-traffic slice, while overall median latency improves >10%).
- Integrate results into the Console (per-route dashboard) and CI gating for config rollouts so we can prevent harmful config pushes.

Approach:
1) Slice definition: start with existing slice taxonomy (length bins, conversational-turns, instruction-vs-fewshot, code-generation) and add traffic-weight metadata. Store canonical slice set in Drive (see attachments).
2) Eval harness: extend the nightly harness to produce per-request latency traces (client+server) and map each request to a slice. Compute p50/p95/p99 latencies and lossless quality metrics.
3) Statistical testing: use paired bootstrap and Cohen's d for effect size; flag statistically significant regressions with minimum absolute thresholds to avoid noise.
4) Dashboarding & alerts: push slice-level CSVs to the Console backend and create templated Grafana panels & Alert rules. Also emit CI artifact JSON for PR gating.

Trade-offs considered: aggressive TTLs reduce cost but can hurt multi-turn coherency; larger microbatch windows improve throughput but add tail latency risk for small requests; decided to track request-size-distribution so we can attribute changes to traffic mix vs config change.

Deliverables: nightly CSVs, Console dashboard panels, PR-level artifact, alerting rules, and a short runbook for on-call triage.

Nightly job produces a per-config, per-slice CSV with p50/p95/p99 latency and the selected quality metrics
Console has a new per-route "Slice Latency vs Quality" panel displaying heatmap and trend lines
Alerting rule created: any slice with traffic_weight > 0.01 and quality_drop >= 3% AND median_latency_improvement >= 10% triggers a P1 investigation ticket
PR gating artifact JSON is generated for every config-change PR and CI fails gated rollouts that cross configured regression thresholds
Runbook created and linked in attachments explaining triage steps and rollback policy

2026-02-20 Aisha Patel: Created ticket after post-rollout incident where a TTL bump reduced token cost by 12% but caused a 4% QA-exact-match drop on long-instruction slice.
2026-02-25 Design review with PM: agreed slice taxonomy should include 'code', 'conversational', 'single-turn-instruction', and 'long-instruction'. PM (Sofia Nguyen) asked for traffic-weighted alerts.
2026-02-28 Perf feedback (Liam O'Connor): Suggested capturing server-side queuing latency separately from model compute to isolate batching effects.
2026-03-03 Engineering sync: implemented latency capture in the harness (client+server), added per-request metadata mapping to slices. Baseline run against runtime-1.20 completed — attached baseline CSV.
2026-03-05 Miguel Torres: Opened PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/2183 to add slice exporter and bootstrap test harness; left comments for more deterministic random seeds in eval generation.
2026-03-07 QA: Observed an interesting pattern — p99 spikes correlate with a small bucket of requests that trigger long KV-cache miss paths. Decided to add a 'kv-miss' binary tag for instrumentation.
2026-03-10 Aisha: Merged PR for CSV exporter into staging. Next: add Grafana panels and CI gating artifact. Blocking: infra job quota for nightly runs (ticketed with infra@).

title: Sable Tech - Hosted Embeddings + Rerank API Walkthrough
author: Maya Chen
text:
Redwood AE+SE demoed the hosted embeddings and reranking endpoints, showed Console Optimize suggestions for batching and caching, discussed tradeoffs between hosted vs dedicated for latency and cost, and agreed next steps for a 2-week pilot + perf benchmark.

Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-09
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 44 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Sable Tech Head of Search), Lina Gomez (ML Engineer), Markus He (Platform Lead)
---
Auto-summary: show hosted embeddings endpoint, demo rerank API, Console walkthrough (Optimize recommendations), discuss security/VPC and pilot next steps

00:00:03 Maya: alright good afternoon everyone, um thanks for joining, i think we've got about 45 minutes, i'll be quick on intros — i'm Maya, AE at Redwood, with Diego our solutions engineer.
00:00:12 Ravi: hey thanks, ravi here, we'll jump in, we've been evaluating vector stores and thinking about reranking to improve our ecom search relevance
00:00:18 Diego: awesome. quick agenda, we'll demo the hosted embeddings endpoint, then the reranker flow (candidate retrieval -> embeddings -> rerank), show the Console for observability and Optimize suggestions, then Q&A and next steps. sound good?
00:00:30 Lina: yup, sounds great. we care most about latency for product page search and cost per query.
00:00:36 Markus: and security, we need encryption at rest with KMS, SSO and audit logs.

00:03:05 Diego: jumping into the API — first the embeddings call. i'll paste a curl: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/embeddings -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -d '{"input":"red wool sweater, size m","model":"rwd-embed-compact-512"}'. the response gives a 512-d float vector, normalized by default.
00:03:35 Lina: small question — do you always normalize? we use cosine sims primarily
00:03:40 Diego: yes we normalize on the client side in our SDK if you want, but the hosted embeddings are L2-normalized by default so cosine is equivalent to dot for ranking. that helps with consistent scoring across dims.
00:04:02 Ravi: what about dimensionality options? 512 vs 768 tradeoffs?
00:04:08 Diego: good callout. 512 reduces storage and per-query compute; 768 sometimes gives slightly better recall. Optimize can recommend model/quantization based on your recall SLO from sample evals.
00:05:10 Maya: switching to rerank. our typical flow we recommend: Retriever (approx nearest neighbor, e.g., Pinecone or your own ANN) to fetch top 100, then we do a small cross-encoder rerank using the Redwood rerank endpoint which calls a lightweight cross-attention model — it's a hosted API you call with the candidate texts and query.
00:05:30 Lina: do you have a demo sample?
00:05:32 Diego: yep i'll show an end-to-end. i'll simulate retrieval by returning 12 candidates from our sample index, then post to /v1/rerank with payload: {"query":"best wool sweater for winter","candidates":[...],"model":"rwd-ranker-small"}. Response is ranked_ids + scores.
00:06:00 (screen share noise)
00:06:04 Markus: small nit — how expensive is that per candidate? we can't rerank thousands per q; we typically rerank top 10-50.
00:06:13 Diego: exactly, we recommend reranking top K where K is typically 10-50. cost scales linearly with candidates for cross-encoder style models. Optimize can recommend split approach: a cheap fast-scorer to get to 100 then a higher-quality cross-encoder for top 10.
00:07:00 Ravi: and latency? our SLO is 150ms p95 on product search queries.
00:07:06 Diego: hosted can deliver ~70-150ms p95 depending on model size and sequence length. for tighter SLOs we propose Dedicated reserved capacity or edge routing. we showed in benchmarks that rwd-ranker-small on hosted at 512 tokens median was ~45ms for the rerank call alone, but end-to-end retrieval + rerank pushes p95; caching prefixes and KV cache reduces repeated prompt cost.
00:08:00 Lina: you mentioned caching — how does that plug in?
00:08:05 Diego: Redwood runtime has prefix/KV caching; for rerank we cache encoded candidate KV entries so repeated candidates don't re-encode. Console Optimize will show cache hit rates and suggests TTLs.
00:08:30 Maya: jumping to Console — Diego, can you show the route-level latency breakdown?
00:08:36 Diego: sure. (console nav) here you see per-route token counts, p50/p95 latency, and cost per 1k tokens. under Optimize tab we surface batching suggestions and quantization toggles. for example, it suggests dynamic batching for low qps with a 20ms batching window to save ~18%/token.
00:09:20 Ravi: interesting, we saw similar gains with batching in our experiments. but concern: batching increases tail latency sometimes.
00:09:27 Diego: yep tradeoff — Optimize gives simulations: if you set batch window to 20ms expected latency goes up 10ms but tokens per second improves and cost drops. you can set per-route SLOs and the platform enforces fallback to single-request mode when tail approaches SLO.
00:10:10 Markus: security questions: VPC/private deployment — we need to know whether hosted keeps logs, and how KMS integration works.
00:10:18 Maya: good Q. hosted stores minimal audit logs for debugging; by default payloads are processed in-host but you can opt into Private deployment or Dedicated with VPC peering for strict isolation. we support customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest and bring-your-own-key for Private. we'll share SOC2 and ISO artifacts.
00:10:45 Markus: what about retention windows for logs?
00:10:48 Maya: default 30 days for logs with configurable retention for enterprise. retention and access are controlled via RBAC and SSO/SAML.
00:11:20 Lina: curious about integration effort — we run on k8s and use OpenSearch for candidate retrieval. does Redwood require a specific vector store?
00:11:27 Diego: no — Redwood's hosted embeddings and reranker are agnostic. you can use any ANN store (Pinecone, Milvus, OpenSearch) or your own. we provide SDK helpers and a reference pipeline (retriever -> rerank) in our examples repo.
00:12:00 Ravi: can reranker operate with a single API call that returns final ranked docs (i.e., retrieval + rerank in one)?
00:12:08 Diego: not currently as a single managed call when using external ANN stores; we keep retrieval decoupled so customers can use their store. for customers who want a fully managed pipeline we offer Redwood Dedicated + integrated vector store in roadmap (we mentioned that last quarter).
00:13:10 Maya: quick note on cost: embeddings are charged per 1k input tokens/vectors; rerank calls charged per candidate-token ops. We'll include estimated cost for your traffic in the pilot proposal.
00:14:00 (demo sample searches)
00:15:05 Diego: showing a failure mode — when candidate set has near-duplicates, cross-encoder helps push the more relevant doc up. see here example: query "waterproof hiking boot" top retrieval returns 3 that are generic; rerank surfaces product with "Gore-Tex" mention higher.
00:16:22 Lina: do you support custom reranker fine-tuning or soft prompts?
00:16:27 Diego: at the moment we support instruction tuning via prompt templates and scoring weight adjustments. fine-tuning of cross-encoders is an enterprise add-on — we can discuss offline.
00:17:05 Ravi: ok good. for our holiday catalog we had a big spike — how does Redwood handle bursty traffic?
00:17:12 Maya: Dedicated has reserved pools and burst capacity; hosted has autoscaling but bursts can increase cost. Optimize will estimate burst cost and recommend reserved capacity breakpoints.
00:18:00 Markus: we need SLOs and SLA language — can you provide that?
00:18:05 Maya: yes we'll include SLA matrix in the pilot addendum (99.9% uptime on Dedicated, hosted varies by tier).
00:20:00 (brief digression on embedding quantization)
00:20:10 Diego: quantization options: 8-bit/4-bit post-training quantization for embeddings storage reduces footprint ~2-4x with minor recall impact; Optimize suggests quantization levels from sample eval metrics.
00:21:15 Lina: show us an example of Optimize suggestion?
00:21:20 Diego: (Console) here's an Optimize suggestion: for route /search, it recommends: "Enable dynamic batching window 20ms; enable prefix KV cache for product descriptions; use rwd-embed-compact-512 and 8-bit quantization" with expected 22% cost savings and <2% recall drop on sample set.
00:22:00 Ravi: that sounds promising. we'd want to run our own eval suite — can we upload sample prompts/labels?
00:22:07 Diego: yes, Console supports uploading eval sets. we can run regression checks per rollout and fire alerts when MRR drops.
00:23:50 Markus: any compliance folks on your side?
00:23:55 Maya: security & compliance will participate in the next call; we'll include the security pack and a contact for SOC2 queries.
00:24:30 Lina: what's the timeline to get a pilot running? we want ~2 weeks to validate quality and perf.
00:24:36 Maya: realistic — 1-2 weeks to stand up a hosted pilot (token keys + sample data + small traffic), 2-3 weeks for detailed perf results.
00:25:10 Diego: i'll outline the micro-benchmark we'll run: 10k docs, simulate 100 qps bursts and 5 qps steady, measure p50/p95 end-to-end for hosted and a dedicated config.
00:26:00 (customer clarifying dataset)
00:27:10 Ravi: our dataset has many near-duplicates and long product descriptions (avg 250 tokens), will that change latency?
00:27:18 Diego: yes sequence length impacts token processing — reranker tokenization and cross-attention scale with sequence length. Optimize will recommend truncation strategy and candidate snippet extraction to keep effective token count reasonable.
00:28:30 Lina: about metrics — we'll want MRR, NDCG and p95 latency tracked.
00:28:36 Diego: absolutely Console exposes custom metrics dashboards for that.
00:30:00 (15-minute live benchmark teaser)
00:35:00 Maya: ok wrapping up, let's recap next steps and owners.
00:35:10 Maya: Diego, you'll run the perf micro-benchmark and share numbers; Maya will send pilot proposal and security docs; Markus will send compliance checklist.
00:35:30 Markus: agreed. also please include a sample contract with data residency options.
00:36:00 Ravi: thanks — we'll review and aim to have internal sign-off by end of Feb.
00:36:12 Lina: any follow up call cadence?
00:36:16 Maya: propose a 30-min POC kick-off the week of 2027-02-22 and weekly 30-min check-ins during the pilot.
00:37:05 Diego: quick note — link to sample demo notebook: https://github.com/redwood-inference/examples/tree/main/embeddings-rerank and security pack: https://redwood.ai/security-pack.pdf
00:38:10 (brief chitchat)
00:42:00 Maya: thanks everyone, we'll send notes and action items.
00:42:20 Ravi: great, thanks Maya, Diego.
00:42:28 Meeting end.

Post-call recap block:
- Pilot scope: Hosted embeddings + rerank for product search on a 10k sample dataset. 2-week pilot with perf benchmarks comparing hosted vs dedicated.
- Links shared: demo notebook, security pack, pricing sheet (to be sent).

text:
maria: Hey all — planning a short cross-team push to add a standard set of GPU pool metrics for Hosted + Dedicated. Need alignment on names, labels, sampling, and dashboard UX. Proposed core metrics: SM_occupancy, sm_memory_bytes, queue_depth, req_latency_p50_p95_p99. Who wants to own ingestion + schema?
aj: Quick q — how do we want to treat Dedicated vs Hosted? Same metric names with a label `pool_type` or separate metrics? :thinking_face:
devon: I'd vote same metric with `pool_type` label. But watch label cardinality: avoid tenant_id on high-cardinality time series. Keep per-pool_id and pool_type. Sampling: 10s emit, 1m rollup for dashboards.
lucas: +1 on labels but we should call the occupancy metric `gpu_sm_occupancy_ratio` (0..1) to avoid confusion vs absolute SM counts. Also add `gpu_memory_used_bytes` and `gpu_memory_total_bytes` so we can compute fragmentation.
sre-bot: ALERT RULE SUGGESTION: queue_depth > 100 for 5m in Dedicated pools => paging. Posting to #eng-oncall.
ops-jen: For quotas: we need queue_depth + per-tenant token consumption to enforce soft quota. Are we okay with emitting tenant_id as a metric label? security asked no PII in high-cardinality metrics.
maria: ops-jen: agree — don't emit tenant_id in metrics. Use tenant hash in traces only. For quotas, the API will call the quota service which will join metrics via pool_id and request metadata.
devon: Implementation note — runtime can emit these via the existing metrics client. Quick proto: ```
message GpuPoolSample {
 string pool_id = 1;
 string pool_type = 2; // "hosted" | "dedicated"
 double gpu_sm_occupancy = 3; // 0..1
 uint64 gpu_memory_used_bytes = 4;
 uint64 gpu_memory_total_bytes = 5;
 uint32 queue_depth = 6;
 map<string, double> latency_pxx = 7; // keys: p50,p95,p99
}
``` Please review naming.
aj: small nit — map in proto can be messy for our exporter. Maybe explicit `p50_ms`, `p95_ms`, `p99_ms` fields.
lucas: Also add `instance_type` label (e.g., a100-40g, 3090) for cost dashboards.
maria: Rollout plan: 1) emit v0 metrics with `gpu_..._v0` prefix for 2 weeks, dashboards in Console team pick v0. 2) After feedback, flip to stable names and deprecate v0. We'll canary by deploying to a subset of Hosted pools and one Dedicated tenant. 3) Provide runbook + alerts. Can we get owners: ingestion: devex-infra (devon), dashboard: console (aj), alerts/runbook: eng-sre (lucas), quota integration: ops (ops-jen).
ops-jen: ack, will carve out work to wire quota service to read the new metrics. We'll avoid tenant_id in metrics; will correlate at request time.
devon: I'll open the metrics PR and include both proto and exporter changes. Also will emit a short-lived wire format `gpu_metrics_v0` topic in telemetry for two weeks.
aj: I'll start a Console PR to add panels: occupancy heatmap, memory headroom, queue depth timeseries, and a per-pool table with p95 latency. UX note: show Hosted/Dedicated toggle and allow filtering by instance_type.
maria: Great. Can we sync tomorrow 10am? If so I'll post an RFC with the exact field names and example Grafana queries. :thumbsup: \nlucas: :eyes: please add suggested alert thresholds to the RFC (queue_depth, memory headroom %) and include cost per-instance_type calc.

maria: thanks — assigned action items in the RFC. Meeting scheduled. :white_check_mark:

title: Mistral Systems - POC quality/eval scoping & benchmark plan
author: Maya Chen
text:
Kickoff scoping for a 4-week POC focused on quality evaluation and benchmarks. Agreed on success criteria (precision/recall targets, hallucination thresholds, latency SLOs), agreed to collect 5k user queries for golden/regression sets, plan for weekly checkpoints and an end-to-end benchmark run. Action items: share golden prompt template, Redwood to propose batch/latency configs, customer to send sample traffic and security requirements.

success criteria definition (quality & latency)
workload sizing and traffic sampling
golden prompts and regression test construction
hallucination and format checks
scoring approach and acceptance thresholds
timelines and weekly checkpoints
security/compliance constraints (VPC, KMS, SOC2)

Redwood: send golden prompt template + eval rubric by 2026-10-23
Customer: provide 5k anonymized query samples and top-20 intents by 2026-10-27
Redwood SE: run initial perf bench on sample traffic and share config by 2026-10-29
Schedule weekly syncs: Tuesdays 10am PT starting 2026-10-26

Maya Chen - Share pricing + pilot SOW draft - due 2026-10-24
Liam O'Neill - Create benchmark harness and initial run on open model variants - due 2026-10-29
Alice Park - Export and anonymize 5k sample queries + intent mapping - due 2026-10-27
Nina Gomez - Send security questionnaire and KMS requirements - due 2026-10-25

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-21 16:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Alice Park (Head of ML, Mistral), Raj Patel (Engineering Manager), Nina Gomez (CISO)

Summary (auto): kickoff POC quality eval scoping. discuss golden prompts, regression sets, hallucination checks, scoring and run cadence.

[00:00] Maya: okay hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. this is Maya from Redwood Inference, i'll hand it off to Liam in a bit to go deeper into the benchmark approach. quick intros?
[00:18] Alice: hi i'm Alice, head of ml at Mistral, we own the customer-facing query pipeline, looking to improve response accuracy and reduce hallucinations for our helpdesk assistant.
[00:27] Raj: Raj here, lead eng, i'll be responsible for data plumbing and running the POC infra.
[00:32] Nina: Nina, security and compliance, i'll be validating KMS and audit log needs.
[00:38] Maya: great. high level objective: 4 week pilot to validate model quality and cost/latency tradeoffs before we decide between hosted or dedicated infra. success criteria we typically see are both quality thresholds and performance SLOs, does that align?
[00:52] Alice: yes, we want to see measurable uplift versus baseline — precision on entity extraction, and a hallucination rate below ~2% on critical intents. latency should stay under 400ms p50 end-to-end but we can be flexible.
[01:11] Liam: quick clarifying Q: when you say hallucination, do you mean factual hallucination on policy/regulatory questions, or extraneous inventing of contact info? that changes the checks we run.
[01:22] Alice: both, but priority is policy/regulatory hallucinations. extraneous info is secondary.
[01:28] Raj: on traffic, we can pull last 30 days, about 120k queries, but we'll need to sample. what size do you need for stable stats?
[01:38] Liam: usually for quality eval we recommend a golden set of 500-1000 canonical cases per intent for scoring, plus a 5k holdout sample to drive regression and load profiling. 5k gives reasonable confidence intervals for aggregate hallucination metrics.
[01:52] Maya: and timing wise we can ingest the samples, run initial model sweeps in week 1, tune configs week 2, larger stress/throughput and final acceptance in week 3-4. propose weekly checkpoints.
[02:06] Alice: sounds good. could you outline what the golden prompts look like? we've had trouble keeping prompt variants consistent across teams.
[02:14] Liam: sure — golden prompts are short canonical prompts plus expected structured outputs. for your use case we'll capture: user message, system persona, few-shot examples when relevant, and expected json schema for the assistant response. we also include negative cases to test hallucination.
[02:31] Raj: about format checks — our downstream parsers are brittle. if the model occasionally drops fields, that's a showstopper. can we enforce schema conformance in the eval?
[02:40] Liam: absolutely — we'll run automated format validation: schema presence, field types, required keys. we'll flag partial-outputs and score them separately. pattern: pass/fail for schema, then quality score for content.
[02:52] Nina: on data security — we need VPC peering or private link for the pilot and KMS for any material we persist. do you support bring-your-own-kms?
[03:02] Maya: yes, for Redwood Private we support customer KMS/HSM integrations and VPC connectivity. for hosted pilots we can provision a private peering and encrypted-at-rest options; persistent logs can be configured to use your KMS in the Private plane. we'll send the security spec.
[03:18] Nina: also SOC2 + audit log retention requirements — we'll share the questionnaire.
[03:22] Maya: perfect. Liam — can you talk through the scoring approach and thresholds?
[03:26] Liam: sure. our typical scoring approach has multiple signals: 1) exact match / schema pass rate (binary), 2) semantic similarity / rubric scores for free text fields (0-5), 3) hallucination binary flags, 4) latency percentiles. we compute weighted composite score per intent with weights customer-specified. For acceptance, we'd propose: schema pass >= 98%, hallucination <= 2% on critical intents, mean rubric >= 4.0, and p50 latency < 400ms. those are starting points.
[04:02] Alice: weights make sense, can we set higher weight on hallucination for regulatory intents?
[04:07] Liam: yes, per-intent weight table. we'll template that and you can edit.
[04:12] Raj: for benchmarks, do you run on open models only by default or do you include quantized variants? cost is a big driver for us.
[04:19] Liam: we run both. initial quality sweep includes a selection of open models and quantized variants where available. for perf/cost we run dedicated-optimized builds and simulate your traffic pattern — burstiness, average seq len. we'll include token-level cost estimates.
[04:36] Alice: curious — how do you simulate prefix caching and KV cache effects? those change latency/cost a lot.
[04:41] Liam: we replay sessions preserving conversation prefixes where possible; our harness supports KV cache warmup scenarios and we can run with/without caching to show delta. we'll note assumptions.
[04:52] Raj: timeline question: if we provide samples by next Tuesday, when would you have a first benchmark?
[04:57] Liam: assuming samples by 2026-10-27, we can produce an initial quality sweep and perf report by 2026-10-29/30; that fits the 4-week cadence with iterative tuning.
[05:08] Nina: what about logging and PII — we need partial redaction. do you offer automated redaction or do we need to preprocess?
[05:15] Maya: you can preprocess or we can help. for pilots customers usually provide anonymized sets; Redwood can also run in a redaction mode but we'd discuss retention windows. we'll include guidance in the security docs.
[05:28] Alice: what does regression testing look like? we want to make sure future model swaps don't regress on golden cases.
[05:34] Liam: regression harness stores golden prompts + expected outputs and runs nightly or on deploy. we compute delta metrics and highlight statistically significant regressions. for the POC we'll run regression on each candidate model and keep a leaderboard.
[05:45] Raj: fine. sample size for statistical significance — is 5k enough to detect a 1% change in hallucination?
[05:51] Liam: 5k gives decent power for several percent changes; detecting 1% at high confidence may need larger sample or stratified sampling of critical intents. We'll propose a small power analysis with your sample distribution.
[06:05] Alice: can you show an example of a golden prompt and the scoring rubric?
[06:09] Liam: yes i'll attach a template after the call. example: Prompt: "User: My refund was charged twice, order 12345, what do i do?" System: persona + schema. Expected fields: intent: "refund_request", entity.order_id: "12345", resolution_steps: list. Scoring: schema pass/fail, entity match exact, resolution adequacy rubric 0-5.
[06:30] Maya: note on deployment choice — if you need predictable SLOs and isolation, Dedicated is recommended; hosted is fastest to start. Both are supported for the POC. any constraints on procurement or timelines?
[06:44] Alice: procurement window is narrow — decision ideally by early December. pilot must demonstrate both quality and cost viability.
[06:52] Raj: also we will need canary style rollout guidance if we switch to production.
[06:57] Liam: we'll include rollout playbook: canary > A/B > full flip with automatic fallback to baseline if regression detected.
[07:07] Nina: last sec — please include retention and deletion controls in the SOW.
[07:12] Maya: noted. recap: Redwood to send golden prompt template, eval rubric, security spec, and initial timeline. Mistral to send sample queries + intent mapping. Weekly syncs and Liam to run the initial bench.
[07:28] Alice: thanks all. we're aligned.
[07:31] Maya: great, will follow up via email.

Auto-generated action items: see metadata.

Notes about transcript quality: some names transcribed inconsistently (e.g., KV cache sometimes as "K V cache"), occasional filler 'uh' and cut words, speaker labels are accurate.

title: Dedicated pool service-level amendment & queueing playbook
author: sean_gallagher
text:
From: Nina Park <nina.park@starlit.ai>
To: sean_gallagher@redwood.com
Date: 2026-12-18T09:14:00-08:00
Subject: Dedicated pool — request for SLA amendment around queueing/tail latency

Hi Sean,

Hope you’re well. I’m leading infrastructure at Starlit AI (we use Redwood Dedicated for our production LLM endpoints). Over the last two quarters we’ve seen recurring tail-latency events during our nightly retraining and batch traffic windows that are impacting SLAs for downstream customers.

Our ask: can Redwood provide an amendment to our Dedicated pool SLA that includes two items:

- Guaranteed reserved headroom (burst reservation) for our pool during scheduled windows (we’re proposing a 10% headroom carved out of our committed GPUs).
- Queueing priority for a specific model variant (starlit-prod-v2) so critical inference traffic is admitted ahead of low-priority batch jobs during contention.

We’re trying to avoid running more redundant infrastructure and would prefer a contract amendment rather than immediate capacity increases. Please let me know what information you need (current committed GPU count: 60 gpus; typical sustained steady-state RPS: ~1,100 requests/min; peak windows: daily 02:00–05:00 UTC with short spikes up to 5x).

If useful I can pull our tail-latency SLO violations and a short diagram of our traffic profile. We’d like an initial feasibility and cost estimate in the next 7–10 business days.

procurement@starlit.ai

Hi Nina — thanks for the clear note and the numbers, this is helpful.

Looping in Marissa (account lead) and Karthik (SRE/Product) to scope feasibility and a commercial approach. A few clarifying Qs we’ll need to size an amendment:

- When you say 10% headroom, do you mean 10% of committed GPUs reserved (e.g., 6 GPUs out of 60) or 10% of expected CPU/GPU utilisation headroom?
- Can you share an anonymized sample of a 24-hour RPS timeline (UTC) and the hourly token distribution? That helps with batching and KV-cache sizing.
- Are the peak spikes at predictable cadence (e.g., aligned to ETL/retrain jobs) or bursty and random?

Marissa/Karthik — can you review internal constraints we need to account for: queue preemption behavior, priority token admission, and whether we can map a model-variant-level priority without impacting overall pool fairness? If there are obvious cost levers (burst reservation pricing, guaranteed concurrency slabs), flag them and we’ll include in the response.

I’ll coordinate a 30–60 minute call next week after we have a first-pass feasibility note.

—Sean
Sean Gallagher
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
sean_gallagher@redwood.com


From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: sean_gallagher@redwood.com, karthik_iyer@redwood.com
Date: 2026-12-22T10:30:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated pool — request for SLA amendment around queueing/tail latency

On Dec 19, 2026, Sean Gallagher wrote:
> Marissa/Karthik — can you review internal constraints we need to account for: queue preemption behavior, priority token admission, and whether we can map a model-variant-level priority without impacting overall pool fairness?

Quick internal runbook / proposed amendment summary below (first pass):

- Reserved headroom: add a "burst reservation" equal to 6 GPUs (10% of committed 60 GPU capacity). Reservation is billed as an additive monthly fee and guarantees capacity during contention windows.
- Priority admission: create a model-variant priority token for "starlit-prod-v2". Priority will operate as soft-preemption: high-priority requests are admitted ahead of best-effort batches but will not evict in-progress high-priority inference. This avoids cold model reload churn.
- Queueing SLOs (proposed): 95th percentile latency target for standard gen (<= 120ms for requests <= 512 tokens), 99th percentile <= 400ms. Tail exceptions tied to documented scheduled maintenance windows.
- Maintenance carveouts: allow up to two scheduled maintenance windows/month where we can perform rolling maintenance with reduced headroom guarantees (must be pre-notified 72 hours).
- Telemetry & regression alarms: include a shared dashboard link and a weekly digest of SLO violations for 90 days post-amendment.
- Pricing: propose a fixed monthly burden for burst reservation + incremental per-token surcharge for prioritized admission above a threshold. Exact numbers to be provided after Karthik's capacity model.

Attachments I will send with the external reply: SLA-amendment-diff.pdf (redline) and queueing-playbook-v1.docx (technical playbook with admission and KV/cache hints).

Karthik — can you confirm the operational feasibility and whether the soft-preemption model works with our current continuous-batching runtime? Also flag any performance regressions we should call out in the redline.

- Region: us-east
- Routes: /v1/chat/completions, /v1/embeddings
- Auth: enterprise API key (account: PROXIMA-ENT-014)

## What customer is seeing
- 429 response body includes Redwood reason codes (examples pasted by customer):
 - "reason": "overload_protection_admission"
 - "reason": "quota_exceeded" (less frequent)
- Response headers observed:
 - Retry-After: 1 (sometimes 2)
 - X-Redwood-Request-Id present
 - X-Redwood-Throttle-Reason: overload_protection_admission (most common)

## Customer notes
- They run bursty workloads: 10–30s spikes during market-open events.
- Client currently retries immediately with fixed 100ms delay and no jitter.

## Steps to reproduce (customer)
1) Send ~800–1200 RPS bursts to /v1/chat/completions with streaming disabled.
2) Concurrently send embedding bursts (~2k RPS) during the same window.
3) Observe 429 rates rising from <0.2% to 6–12% during bursts.

## Expected behavior
- Enterprise priority should protect them during fleet pressure; customer expects either stable acceptance or clearly defined, predictable throttling limits.

## Actual behavior
- Customer sees throttling during burst windows and requests clarification on:
 1) Why enterprise traffic is being rejected
 2) Whether the 429s are overload shedding vs quota
 3) Whether Redwood can grant a temporary burst exception / larger budget

## Initial support response (guidance provided)
- Confirmed that the new system returns distinct reason codes and customers should key their retry/backoff behavior on:
 - "quota_exceeded" (respect quota windows; reduce steady-state rate)
 - "overload_protection_admission" (transient overload; respect Retry-After; use exponential backoff + jitter)
- Recommended changes:
 - Use exponential backoff with full jitter; cap concurrency; do not retry immediately.
 - Honor Retry-After; treat 429 as a signal to shed load client-side.

## Investigation notes (internal)
Hypothesis: us-east protected-route capacity protection enabled for Proxima allowlisted accounts; per-route/per-tier admission control is active and may be gating bursts more aggressively than intended for this customer’s contractual traffic shape.

Checks performed:
- Correlated spike with protection annotations in hot-route dashboard (SRE): overload protection activated for route-group "chat" + "embeddings" during a concurrent regional pressure event.
- Confirmed most 429s for this account carry reason=overload_protection_admission (not quota).
- Verified no corresponding 5xx spike; p99 latency for enterprise class remained within SLO during event, indicating protections are working for fleet health but customer’s burst profile is being clipped.

Open questions
- What is Proxima’s contracted peak/burst behavior (RPS and token/s) for these routes?
- Is Proxima being routed to a stricter per-route budget due to route-group defaults?

## Requested outcome
- Explain semantics and provide an actionable plan.
- If eligible, grant a temporary burst exception with guardrails (time-boxed, monitored), or propose a dedicated capacity option.

Provided immediate guidance: honor Retry-After, implement exponential backoff + jitter, and send us 10 sample X-Redwood-Request-Id values from 429s and 200s around the same time window.
