title: Short-lived SSE disconnects during long-running telemetry streams cause truncated final block and duplicate heartbeat frames on resume
text:
Issue summary: Customer (Nimbus Health) observed intermittent short TCP/TLS handoff events during long-lived SSE telemetry sessions. When those handoffs occurred the stream would resume but the final application-level 'end' chunk was missing and the client received one or more duplicated heartbeat frames. Impact: Several production streams for real-time device telemetry saw truncated final paragraphs and missing end-of-stream metadata. This caused Nimbus Health's post-processing job to treat sessions as incomplete and triggered follow-up alerts and duplicate downstream summaries. Observed frequency: ~3-4 occurrences/hour for a subset of sessions lasting >6 minutes. Reported first via support channel on 2026-03-10 04:12 UTC.

1) Start a long-running telemetry SSE session to /v1/streams/telemetry with keepalive enabled and session_id header set
2) Simulate an upstream idle probe from an edge load balancer (tcp RST after 30s idle) or trigger a client network change (cellular->wifi) during the stream
3) Allow client to reconnect using our resume protocol (last_seq parameter) and observe the final blocks emitted
4) Note occurrences where the terminal 'end' event does not arrive but heartbeat frames are duplicated and prefixed to resumed payload

2026-03-10T03:59:47.123Z INFO sse-gateway conn_id=ck1tx.. keepalive_sent seq=987
2026-03-10T04:00:17.456Z WARN edge-proxy conn_id=ck1tx.. upstream_idle_probe RST
2026-03-10T04:00:17.460Z INFO sse-gateway conn_id=ck1tx.. resume_request session_id=therm-42 last_seq=987
2026-03-10T04:00:17.472Z INFO serving-runtime request_id=rv-9182 emitted_chunk seq=988 payload_part=...
2026-03-10T04:00:17.473Z INFO sse-gateway conn_id=ck1tx.. heartbeat seq=988 duplicate=1
2026-03-10T04:00:17.474Z ERROR sse-gateway conn_id=ck1tx.. end_event_not_emitted session_id=therm-42

2026-03-10 04:20 UTC - Priya Shah: Investigating — asked Nimbus for an example session_id and approximate timestamps. Requesting packet captures and client SDK version.
2026-03-10 05:15 UTC - Nimbus Health (support): Provided session_id=therm-42 and pcap from affected device. Noting duplicate heartbeat observed in client logs.
2026-03-10 09:02 UTC - SRE (Marco Li): Correlated conn_id ck1tx.. to edge-proxy instance apg-12. Edge logs show idle probe around the time of the gap. Opening INT-420 to track edge config change impact.
2026-03-11 11:30 UTC - Priya Shah: Deployed a canary of PR 2147 to sse-gateway to force atomic emission of terminal 'end' event and stronger ordering of keepalive/heartbeat frames.
2026-03-12 02:45 UTC - Nimbus Health: Confirmed no further truncated sessions for previously affected session IDs after 12 hours. Closing as resolved from customer perspective.

Initial hypothesis: edge-proxy idle RST during a brief network hiccup left sse-gateway in a partially closed state, causing a race between keepalive emission and terminal chunk flush
Trace analysis: sequence gaps and duplicate heartbeat flag indicate gateway retransmitted heartbeat while serving-runtime was simultaneously finalizing the stream; ordering not guaranteed when upstream socket closed mid-flush
Reproducer: forcing a 30s idle RST from our internal apg-style probe reproduced missing end_event in canary under specific timing (client resume within 100-200ms of RST)
Client-side contribution: Nimbus client SDK retried immediately and attempted resume with last_seq causing gateway to interleave replayed heartbeat and resumed payload

Race condition in sse-gateway where in-flight terminal chunk flush and scheduled keepalive/heartbeat could be interleaved after a mid-flight upstream TCP RST, leading to the terminal 'end' event being dropped under tight resume timing

Rolled out inference-runtime PR 2147 which ensures atomic terminal event emission and orders heartbeat frames behind terminal flush. Applied a short backoff on client resume acceptance to tolerate in-flight socket tear-downs. Deployed to canary on 2026-03-11 and global rollout completed 2026-03-12.

PR 2147 modifies sse-gateway flush path to wait for terminal payload write to complete before accepting resume from the same session_id
Added a small server-side resume-grace-window (250ms) to allow upstream socket close to be observed and avoid interleaving
Updated SSE runbook with new troubleshooting steps and added a dashboard for heartbeat-duplication rate
Notified Nimbus Health of the fix and kept monitoring for 24 hours of impacted session IDs

OPS-1: Add a synthetic long-lived SSE test that injects upstream idle probes and validates terminal end emission (owner: SRE)
ENG-2: Instrument sse-gateway metrics to expose heartbeat_dup_count and end_event_drop_count per instance (owner: Serving Runtime)
DOC-3: Update client SDK resume guidance to include exponential backoff recommendations (owner: Developer Experience)
SEC-4: Review edge-proxy idle probe configuration for other customers with long-lived streams (owner: Network)

title: Pilot onboarding ops and staging clearance review
author: Samir Patel
text:
Weekly POC sync focused on onboarding progress, staging gateway clearance, initial latency/throughput bench notes, and next actions around SSO/KMS and KV cache fallback. Agreement to run 48h stress with mixed traffic after creds handed off.

Onboarding progress and outstanding infra tasks
Gateway / staging credentials and DNS routing
Initial latency and qps bench results
KV cache priming and fallback policies
SSO/KMS integration timeline and audit logging

Samir Patel - share updated perf spreadsheet and cost assumptions - due 2027-02-19
Marta Lopez - confirm staging VPC peering and upload gateway cert - due 2027-02-18
Lena Ortiz - prepare short runbook for KV cache priming and failure mode - due 2027-02-20
Anika Bose - provide KMS key ARN and security checklist feedback - due 2027-02-22

Redwood to provision staging gateway once creds confirmed
Customer to run 48h mixed-traffic stress window and share logs
Schedule security deep-dive with Veridian security team next week (Samir to coordinate)
Agree SLO targets and success criteria before production cutover

Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-17
Start time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Lena (Redwood SE), Priya (CSM), Raj (Veridian Eng Lead), Marta (Veridian DevOps), Tom (PM), Anika (Security)

Summary (auto): quick run through of access gating, bench numbers from last 24h trial, checklist for staging gateway, and clarifying security/KMS handoff. Plan to run a longer stress window once staging creds are in place.

[00:00] Samir (AE): okay, hi everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call, uh we have Samir, Lena, Priya from Redwood, and Raj, Marta, Tom and Anika from Veridian. does that look right?
[00:10] Raj: yep, that's us, thanks.
[00:12] Marta: yep, hi all.
[00:14] Samir: great. agenda is lightweight today: onboarding status, gateway cred handoff, brief perf notes from the last 24 hour smoke, and security/KMS check.
[00:22] Tom (PM): sounds good. main thing for us is making sure the staging environment mimics production enough to validate the fallback behavior and cost numbers.
[00:32] Lena (SE): yeah, and just to set expectations, our small smoke yesterday used the rdl-moon-7b variant and we saw tail latency spikes at around 1% of requests when sequence lengths hit ~1,200 tokens. so that's probably attributable to batching behavior and the default token cutoff.
[00:48] Raj: sorry, rdl-moon-7b? I thought you were running the 13B that we discussed.
[00:52] Lena: ah, yes, for the initial smoke we used the 7B because it's faster to iterate, we have results for the 13B too but it's still uploading. the 13B (rawmond-13B? sorry that name got mangled in the notes) showed slightly higher median latency but similar p95 once batching was tuned.
[01:12] Marta: for staging we really need the same quant/profile as prod. can you confirm the quantized artifacts will match?
[01:20] Lena: good question. the build we've pushed is INT8 quant for that model family; there may be a small difference vs your on-prem quant profile. we can produce a matching artifact if you want — that would require a short recompile step and we'll coordinate.
[01:36] Anika (Security): on the security side, we need to validate KMS integration and ensure audit logs flow to our SIEM; also SSO via SAML, not OIDC. is SAML supported in the staging control plane?
[01:48] Priya (CSM): we have SAML for Dedicated and Private deployments; for the hosted plane there's limited SAML support. for your pilot, since you prefer VPC/private control plane, SAML will be available.
[02:02] Anika: okay, please send the exact SAML metadata fields we need.
[02:06] Samir: action — we will drop the SAML metadata and a quick KMS checklist in the thread after the call.
[02:12] [02:15] Raj: quick question on gateway creds — Marta mentioned earlier some trouble with DNS mapping to the staging gateway. any blockers?
[02:20] Marta: yeah so we tried to swap in the gateway cert but our internal CA chain looked different and the handshake failed. i can share the openssl debug output but we need the cert in PEM bundle with the intermediate.
[02:34] Samir: understood. lena, can you confirm the format we expect?
[02:38] Lena: yep, PEM bundle with full chain, and we also support PKCS12 if your infra prefers it. i'll post an example.
[02:46] Marta: when you post, can you also include the expected SANs? we had an issue where the hostnames didn't line up with our internal routing.
[02:54] Samir: yes, we'll provide exact SAN list and a curl example.
[03:01] Tom: on the benching side, can you summarise the throughput/latency numbers from the last run? i saw a spreadsheet but it's a little dense.
[03:08] Lena: sure i can do a short summary: 24 hour smoke with bursty traffic (2-3 qps average, peaks to 12 qps) - median latency for the 7B was ~150ms token generation (this is token gen time not end-to-end), p95 around 520ms, p99 in the 1.2s range on the heavier sequences. inference cost per 1k tokens on that instance profile is about $X. for the 13B the median shifted to ~220ms and p95 to ~650ms but again that's with default batching; we can lower p99 by tightening max batch window but that increases median slightly.
[03:50] Raj: what about KV cache and prefix caching? we expect longer conversations and don't want to hit full recompute each time.
[03:58] Lena: good, we enabled prefix/KV caching in staging — although we noticed cache warmup takes some requests; priming strategy helps. if a node gets evicted there's a fallback to rehydrate from the full context or to a smaller model variant. this is the preconfigured fallback policy we mentioned: try same model, if unavailable fall back to an unquantized variant, then to a smaller size.
[04:20] Marta: fallback is fine as long as it's logged and we can correlate on the request id. the audit trail is key.
[04:27] Priya: logs include request id and model variant; we'll ensure log retention meets your compliance needs.
[04:33] Anika: retention window? we need at least 90 days of request-level metadata for audits.
[04:38] Samir: we can offer 90 days as an add-on, default is 30. we'll document that in the security pack.
[04:44] [05:00] Tom: timeline question — when will staging be gated green for us to run a 48 hour stress?
[05:05] Samir: if Marta can confirm VPC peering and upload the gateway cert today or tomorrow, we can provision the staging gateway in 24 hours. then we recommend a short smoke and then the 48h stress in 48-72 hours. so earliest is around Friday if creds land tomorrow.
[05:22] Marta: i can aim for tomorrow morning, but i also have to get the infra team to open two firewall ports; that's on me.
[05:28] Raj: i'll help coordinate with infra.
[05:30] Anika: on KMS, our key admin needs the exact IAM permissions list to create the key policy. can you share that?
[05:37] Lena: yes, we'll share the minimal IAM statements and a sample key policy. also note we support HSM-backed keys if you require.
[05:44] Anika: HSM would be preferred but we need to weigh cost. for pilot we'll go with KMS-backed and evaluate HSM for long term.
[05:55] [06:10] Samir: quick note on SLOs — i know product wants p95 under 700ms for typical queries. we'll put together a proposal for batch windows, token caps, and fallback thresholds to meet that.
[06:22] Tom: important to include cost delta if we tighten batch windows; we need to present that to the finance sponsor.
[06:29] Samir: understood, we'll include a small delta table.
[06:33] [06:40] Raj: any concerns about data residency? our EU patients data can't leave region.
[06:45] Priya: for private we can pin region; we also support per-tenant routing to keep traffic in EU region. we'll note that in the infra checklist.
[06:54] Anika: and encryption in transit and at rest?
[06:57] Lena: TLS in transit, and at rest with KMS-managed keys. some metadata logs we can encrypt with your key if needed.
[07:06] Marta: small gotcha — when we turned up the initial proxy, internal requests took an extra 80ms due to SNAT, can you recommend a routing approach to avoid hairpinning?
[07:16] Lena: yes, we recommend using policy-based routing and advertising the staging subnet in the peering so traffic doesn't hairpin through the NAT gateway — we'll provide a diagram.
[07:28] [07:45] Tom: ok, to close — who is owning the run of the 48h stress and the pass/fail criteria?
[07:52] Samir: Redwood will provision and monitor, but Veridian will execute the workload and share telemetry. pass/fail criteria: no more than 1% error rate, p95 below 700ms for the sample set we agree on, and no secret leakage or audit failures.
[08:08] Raj: sounds fair. we'll add the exact traffic mix to the shared sheet.
[08:14] Priya: i'll set up a follow-up security deep-dive invite for next Wednesday and add tasks to the playbook.
[08:22] Anika: please add our security lead in the invite (i'll DM the address).
[08:26] Samir: action recap: i'll post SAML/KMS checklist, Lena will post PEM cert example and SANs, Marta will confirm peering and certs, Raj will coordinate infra, and we'll schedule the 48h stress window once staging gateway is up.
[08:44] Tom: one last thing — can you add a note about model-variant fallbacks in the runbook? we want explicit mapping e.g., 13B -> 7B -> 3B if under memory pressure.
[08:52] Lena: will do, and i'll include explicit model names and the expected quality delta.
[08:56] Samir: perfect. thanks everyone, see you at the security deep dive next week.
[09:00] Meeting ended.

title: eng-runtime
text:
kayla: Heads-up — since 03:10 UTC I'm seeing sustained P99 latency regressions on eu-west GPU fleet. Correlates with a steady stream of 'max_batch_full' events and a growing prefill queue. Screenshot of dashboard in thread (link).

tom: yep noticed it too. p50 ~85ms, p95 ~160ms, p99 jumping from ~220ms -> ~470ms in bursts. admission metrics show repeated 'max_batch_reached' spikes every ~30s.

cheng: digging in packer logs now. Pack window still 6ms, max_batch_size configured to 128 on that pool, but admission is capping at 96 because of headroom_policy. When many mid-length seqs land we see pack fragmentation + long head-of-line wait for the batch to fill. That's the tail.

lina: interesting — are these mostly short-chat requests or long-completions? sequence_length histogram?

tom: mostly mixed. 60% short (<64 tokens), 30% medium (64-512), 10% long. But traffic shape shifted — more short concurrent requests from a demo customer. That increases pressure to fill big batches, so short requests end up waiting for large ones to complete.

kayla: recorded a snippet from runtime logs showing admission decisions: 
```
[2025-07-13T03:12:14Z] admission: slot=pool-eu-1 max_batch=128 used=96 waiting=22 reason=max_batch_full
[2025-07-13T03:12:14Z] vmalloc: headroom enforced -> cap=96
[2025-07-13T03:12:15Z] batch_execute: seqLens=[32,512,48,16,256,...] KV-prefill=true prefill_ms=140
```

dmitri: that prefill_ms=140 is the killer. We're hitting prefill on lots of batches because of long seq items in the mix; then smaller requests stuck behind the prefill KV load.

cheng: theory: static max_batch + static headroom isn't matching the new mixed workload. We should try either reducing max_batch for that pool or enabling dynamic_max_batch based on recent seq_len quantiles. Also consider per-request priority for short requests so they don't block.

sre-bot: ALERT: fleet.admission.max_batch_full rate x5 over baseline (1m avg) — alert muted by kayla at 03:15 UTC

lina: can we quick experiment with lowering max_batch to 64 in eu-west-canary? That should reduce pack wait time and lower prefill contention, at the cost of throughput.

tom: +1 for canary. Also suggest enabling fast-path for small seqs: packer rule to prefer filling small buckets first and carve out mini-batches for them.

kayla: spun up a canary change: 
```yaml
pool: eu-west-1a
max_batch_size: 64
headroom_policy: dynamic
pack_window_ms: 4
prefill_limit_ms: 80
```
Applied at 03:20 UTC to 5 nodes (canary).

cheng: observing canary metrics now — initial p99 dropped from ~480ms -> ~200ms for canary nodes within 2 minutes. Non-canary still elevated. Rolling canary to 20 nodes.

dmitri: cost note — reducing max_batch increases per-token cost ~4-7% in our sims. We should balance SLO compliance vs unit cost for eu customers. Logged in infra-cost board.

lina: action items: 1) roll canary to 30% if p99 stays <250ms (lina), 2) enable packer small-request fast-path in next deploy (cheng), 3) evaluate dynamic_max_batch prototype in staging (tom), 4) add short-request priority header for demo customer (kayla).

tom: also flagging network jitter — I see occasional 50-80ms RTT spikes between control-plane and nodes at same AZ coincident with some batch slowness. Could amplify head-of-line. SRE to correlate.

kayla: good catch. @dmitri can you pull the control-plane RTTS for the last 30m?

dmitri: pulling now, will paste a small chart shortly.

sre-bot: INCIDENT-TRACK: 2025-07-13 | eu-west batch head-of-line SLO misses | severity=P2 | linked alerts: fleet.admission.max_batch_full, runtime.prefill.latency

cheng: TL;DR: root causes likely (1) static max_batch/headroom mismatch for mixed short+long workload, (2) KV prefill contention, (3) occasional control-plane RTT jitter. Short term: reduce max_batch and enable small-request fast-path. Medium term: dynamic max_batch + admission weighting + per-request priority.

lina: I'll follow up with a short postmortem template once we stabilize. For now we keep the canary roll and monitor. :thumbsup:

kayla: thanks all — I'll update the incident ticket and close the loop once canary hits 30% and p99 holds.

title: Overload protection dashboards and alerting spec (Hosted API)
author: Aisha Bello
text:
## Purpose
This page specifies the dashboards and alert thresholds used to operate **Hosted overload protection** (circuit breakers + load shedding) across the request path (gateway → routing → runtime).

Goals:
- Detect overload early (before tail latency and timeouts spike).
- Make breaker/shed behavior observable, explainable, and safe to tune.
- Provide a single “what’s happening?” view during incidents (with links to runbooks and toggles).
- Keep **metric cardinality bounded** and alerts actionable (avoid paging for expected, controlled shedding).

Non-goals:
- Detailed policy design (see policy engine integration doc).
- Full per-tenant dashboards (only surfaced for targeted investigations; default views are tier/region/model).

## Audience
- SRE oncall, Platform oncall (gateway/policy), Smart Routing oncall, Serving Runtime oncall
- Support/CS (read-only): interpreting new overload errors and correlation IDs

## Dashboard stack + conventions
- Platform: Grafana + Prometheus (via Telemetry Platform)
- Data sources: gateway metrics, routing metrics, runtime saturation metrics, and SLO-toolkit classification
- Time zones: all dashboards default to UTC
- Standard variables (must exist on each dashboard):
 - `region` (e.g., `us-east`, `us-west`, `eu-central`)
 - `tier` (e.g., `hosted_self_serve`, `hosted_enterprise`, `dedicated`)
 - `route` (e.g., `chat.completions`, `embeddings`, `rerank`)
 - `model` (canonical model ID, e.g., `rw-mistral-7b-instruct`, `rw-llama-3-70b`)

Cardinality rules:
- **Do not** label metrics with raw `tenant_id` or `api_key` by default.
- Tenant-level drilldown must be behind a separate “debug” dashboard and only for short retention.
- Use **bucketed** prompt length and token counts (e.g., `prompt_tokens_bucket`, `max_tokens_bucket`) rather than raw values.

## Dashboard set (required)
### 1) Executive overview: “Overload protection — Control plane & serving health”
Primary use: incident triage; 5-minute read.

Panels (top → bottom):
1. **Availability + latency context (SLO-aligned)**
 - p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency by route
 - error rate split by class: `2xx`, `4xx`, `5xx`, and `overload` (per ADR-014)
 - timeouts (client cancel + server timeout)

2. **Breaker and shedding summary**
 - breaker open rate (events/min) by layer: gateway / routing / runtime
 - shed rate (% of requests rejected/degraded) by reason
 - Retry-After presence rate (% overload responses with Retry-After)

3. **Capacity/saturation indicators**
 - runtime queue depth (prefill/decode), utilization proxy
 - token/sec saturation ratio (actual / target)
 - memory/KV cache pressure proxies (exported gauges)

4. **Top contributors**
 - top regions by shed rate
 - top models by breaker opens
 - top routes by overload errors

Links:
- Oncall runbook: Hosted overload circuit breaker runbook
- Status page language + customer guidance: overload errors and retry guidance

### 2) Breakers deep dive: “Circuit breakers — state, reasons, and policy outcomes”
Primary use: determine *why* a breaker opened and whether it is behaving correctly.

Panels:
- Breaker state timeline (Closed → Open → Half-open) by `breaker_name` and `region`
- Breaker open reasons (stacked) by `reason`:
 - `gpu_queue_depth_high`
 - `scheduler_backlog_high`
 - `token_saturation_high`
 - `memory_pressure_high`
 - `dependency_unhealthy`
 - `regional_capacity_low`
 - `policy_manual_override`
- Evaluation outcomes:
 - % of requests matching each policy rule (tier defaults vs overrides)
 - policy evaluation latency (p50/p95)
 - policy engine errors (should be ~0; never cause fail-open without explicit policy)

Required annotations:
- Policy changes (config deploys)
- Rollout toggles/canary start/end
- Regional incidents (from incident-bot)

### 3) Load shedding outcomes: “Admission control — shed/degrade/fallback breakdown”
Primary use: understand customer impact and whether the system is degrading safely.

Panels:
- Request outcomes (stacked): `admitted`, `shed`, `degraded`, `fallback_routed`
- Shed by HTTP status (`429`, `503`) and stable overload error code
- Fallback attempt rate and success rate (routing)
- Bounded retries / loop prevention counters (routing)
- Streaming-specific controls:
 - stream concurrency cap hit rate
 - stream session early termination rate (should be near 0; investigate spikes)

### 4) Runtime saturation: “Serving runtime — queues, throughput, and memory pressure”
Primary use: identify genuine GPU saturation vs upstream misconfiguration.

Panels:
- Prefill queue depth and decode queue depth (gauge + p95 across pods)
- Admission wait time (time spent queued)
- Token/sec throughput by model family
- Saturation ratio (actual/target) and throttle signals
- KV cache occupancy and eviction rate
- Memory fragmentation proxy (if exported) and OOM/alloc failure rate

Notes:
- Runtime signals should be aggregated at `model + region` granularity with bounded pod labels.

### 5) Customer experience: “Overload errors — semantics, headers, and correlation”
Primary use: verify we are returning consistent, supportable error responses.

Panels:
- Overload responses by error code (stable taxonomy)
- Retry-After distribution (p50/p95; seconds)
- Correlation ID presence rate
- Client retry storm indicators:
 - request rate amplification (inbound vs admitted)
 - repeated identical idempotency keys (if available) without success

## Standard metric definitions (canonical)
The exact metric names may vary per service namespace; the following fields are required in some form.

### Gateway / control plane
- `gateway_requests_total{route,region,tier,code}`
- `gateway_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route,region,tier}`
- `gateway_overload_actions_total{action,reason,route,region,tier}`
 - `action ∈ {shed,degrade,admit}`
- `gateway_breaker_state{breaker_name,region}` (0=closed,1=open,2=half_open)
- `gateway_breaker_open_total{breaker_name,reason,region}`
- `gateway_retry_after_set_total{route,region,tier}`

### Routing
- `routing_fallback_attempts_total{from_model,to_model,region,tier}` (aggregate; do not include tenant)
- `routing_fallback_success_total{from_model,to_model,region,tier}`
- `routing_loop_prevention_total{reason,region}`
- `routing_policy_eval_errors_total{region}`

### Runtime
- `runtime_queue_depth{queue,model,region}` where `queue ∈ {prefill,decode}`
- `runtime_admission_wait_seconds_bucket{model,region}`
- `runtime_tokens_per_second{model,region,phase}` where `phase ∈ {prefill,decode}`
- `runtime_saturation_ratio{model,region}`
- `runtime_kv_cache_pressure{model,region}` (gauge, normalized)
- `runtime_oom_total{model,region}`

### SLO classification (slo-toolkit)
- `api_errors_total{class,route,region,tier}` where `class ∈ {success,customer_error,server_error,overload}`

## Recommended alerting philosophy
1. **Page on unexpected failure, not controlled shedding.**
 - Controlled shedding (overload errors with correct semantics) is a *degradation mode*.
 - We page when shedding is high/sustained, misclassified, or caused by bugs (e.g., missing Retry-After, policy engine failing, breaker flapping).

2. **Use multi-window burn rates for customer-visible SLOs** and pair with “root signal” alerts.

3. **Prefer symptom + cause pairing.** Example: page on sustained overload + runtime saturation, not just one.

4. **Avoid per-tenant paging by default.** Escalate tenant-specific issues via Support/Jira unless it indicates systemic regression.

## Alert thresholds (initial defaults)
These are initial thresholds used for canary/GA. They should be tuned per region/model after baseline collection.

Table: paging alerts (P1/P2)
| Alert | Severity | Condition (per region, unless noted) | Duration | Rationale / Notes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| High end-to-end error budget burn (Hosted API) | P1 | SLO burn rate > 14x (5m) AND > 2x (1h) | immediate | Standard SRE multi-window burn. Uses SLO-toolkit classification. |
| Sustained overload shed rate high | P1 | `shed / (admitted + shed) > 8%` (hosted_self_serve) OR `> 3%` (hosted_enterprise) | 10m | Self-serve can shed more than enterprise; enterprise threshold tighter. |
| Breaker flapping | P2 | breaker transitions > 6 opens per 10m for any `breaker_name` | 10m | Indicates threshold instability or bad signal. |
| Missing Retry-After on overload responses | P2 | `retry_after_present_rate < 98%` for overload responses | 15m | Prevents retry storms and aligns with client contract. |
| Policy engine errors | P1 | `policy_eval_errors_total` > 0.5% of requests OR any sustained 5xx from policy service | 5m | Policy engine must be highly reliable; errors can amplify outages. |
| Routing fallback success collapse | P2 | fallback success rate < 70% while fallback attempts > baseline + 3σ | 15m | Suggests misconfig, capacity depletion, or loop-prevention over-triggering. |
| Runtime queue depth critical | P1 | `runtime_queue_depth{queue=decode} > critical_threshold` (per model family) | 10m | Indicates decode backlog; triggers tail latency/timeouts. Use tuned thresholds. |
| Runtime OOM spike | P1 | `runtime_oom_total` increases > 3 in 10m for a model/region | 10m | OOM often causes cascading failures; page quickly. |

Table: ticket alerts (non-paging)
| Alert | Action | Condition | Duration | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| Overload errors trending up | Ticket | overload class errors > baseline + 2σ | 30m | Used during early rollout to tune thresholds. |
| Increased stream cap hits | Ticket | stream cap hit rate > 1% | 30m | May be expected during bursts; investigate if persistent. |
| Correlation ID missing | Ticket | correlation ID present rate < 99.5% | 30m | Debuggability regression. |

## Per-tier guidance (what “good” looks like)
- hosted_enterprise:
 - Prefer: graceful degradation (fallback routing, feature reduction) over raw shedding.
 - Expect: low sustained shed rate; short Retry-After; minimal breaker flapping.

- hosted_self_serve:
 - Prefer: predictable shedding with clear errors over timeouts.
 - Expect: shed during bursts; must remain consistent and retry-safe.

- dedicated:
 - Overload protections should primarily enforce tenant isolation and protect control plane; runtime saturation should be addressed by capacity scaling.

## Required annotations and runbook links
Dashboards must include:
- A pinned link panel:
 - “Hosted overload circuit breaker runbook”
 - “Runtime overload mitigation runbook”
 - “Overload error taxonomy (ADR-014)”
 - “Admission control layering (ADR-015)”
- An annotations query for:
 - config deploys affecting overload policies
 - incident-bot breaker state announcements
 - rollout toggles / canary flags

## Example PromQL snippets (reference)
Note: metric prefixes may differ by service. Treat these as patterns.

Shed rate (per region, tier):
- sum(rate(gateway_overload_actions_total{action="shed",region=~"$region",tier=~"$tier"}[5m]))
 / sum(rate(gateway_overload_actions_total{action=~"admit|shed",region=~"$region",tier=~"$tier"}[5m]))

Breaker open rate (per breaker):
- sum(rate(gateway_breaker_open_total{region=~"$region"}[5m])) by (breaker_name, reason)

Retry-After presence rate:
- sum(rate(gateway_retry_after_set_total{region=~"$region"}[5m]))
 / sum(rate(api_errors_total{class="overload",region=~"$region"}[5m]))

Runtime decode queue depth (p95 across pods aggregated to model/region):
- quantile_over_time(0.95, runtime_queue_depth{queue="decode",region=~"$region"}[5m])

## Operational checklist (for GA readiness)
- [ ] Executive overview dashboard is live for each production region
- [ ] Breaker deep dive dashboard includes policy-change annotations
- [ ] Alerts are wired to #eng-oncall with correct paging routes
- [ ] Runbook links are correct and accessible to Support (read-only)
- [ ] Cardinality review completed (no tenant_id in default dashboards)
- [ ] Thresholds validated against perf-canary burst scenario and at least one production canary region

## Owners and escalation
Primary owner (dashboards/alerts): **Aisha Bello (Eng SRE)**

Escalation during incidents:
- Breaker/policy issues: Ethan Park / Jordan Lee
- Routing fallback issues: Mina Haddad / Elena Popov
- Runtime saturation signals/behavior: Sofia Ivanova / Omar El-Sayed
- Telemetry platform issues: Logan Wright

## Change management
- Any changes to paging thresholds require:
 - PR to observability-pack alert rules (or equivalent)
 - review from Eng SRE + relevant subsystem owner
 - post-change note in #eng-oncall with rationale and expected behavior

## Changelog
- 2025-12-06: Updated tier-specific sustained shed thresholds; added Retry-After presence alert after enterprise report.
- 2025-11-19: Added breaker flapping alert and routing fallback success collapse alert; standardized annotation sources.
- 2025-10-28: Initial spec for canary rollout (executive overview + breaker deep dive).

title: Expressive mobile-first palette and compact scale overhaul
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Update Redwood's design tokens with a mobile-first intent: introduce an expressive but accessible color palette, compress the typography scale for small screens, rationalize spacing/radius steps, and simplify elevation layers for cross-platform parity. This ticket covers token definitions, Figma token file updates, engineering migration notes, and accessibility checks.

New color palette exported as semantic tokens (surface, text, interactive, positive, caution, negative) with WCAG AA contrast for body text at small sizes
Typography scale reduced to an 8-step compact scale with clear mapping from legacy sizes and migration table
Spacing/radius defined as a 6-step modular system with explicit use-cases (stack/gutter/card/padding)
Elevation simplified to four semantic levels with token names usable in CSS/Android/iOS runtimes
Figma file updated and linked; Engineering PR includes automated token migration scripts; design review approved
No visual regressions on core product routes (Console dashboard, API keys page, Model catalog) beyond acceptable thresholds

Adopt semantic token naming rather than low-level color tokens (e.g., text-primary instead of gray-700) to enable swapping palettes per theme/region
Compact typography: move from 12-step to 8-step scale; map legacy tokens using a migration table in the PR
Spacing: use a 6-step scale (s0..s5) with scale factors of 4px, 8px, 12px, 16px, 20px, 28px to better fit mobile density
Elevation: reduce to surface-0..surface-3 with simplified shadow recipes tuned for mobile compositing performance
Introduce explicit fallback/alias tokens for backward compatibility for at least 2 release cycles

Reducing the typography steps and spacing granularity simplifies component layouts and reduces token surface area, but may require per-component tweaks to maintain pixel-perfect parity on desktop. Providing aliases increases initial complexity in the token build pipeline but reduces churn for downstream components.

Eng review requested: ensure token names follow existing naming conventions or provide a compatibility layer (alias tokens) for 2 releases. Plan for a Node-based migration script to rewrite CSS custom properties and update mobile JSON bundles. Benchmark visual diffs on staging via Percy/Galaxy. Backend config flags available to gate rollout by customer tier.

PM - Jordan Kim: Please ensure the new palette supports high contrast accessibility mode; highlight colors for charts need to maintain separability at small sizes.
Engineering - Priya Desai: Migration script should include a dry-run mode and a changelog of updated files. Also flag components that use computed tokens (JS-in-CSS) for manual audit.
Design - Lena Sørensen: Reduced radius set looks cohesive on mobile but needs visual QA for data tables on desktop where compactness could harm legibility.
Accessibility - Omar Greene: Confirm contrast ratios at 14px and 12px body sizes with both normal and bold weights; provide test cases in storybook

Incorporate engineering feedback into token build flow (due 2026-03-16)
Publish updated Figma token file and notify component owners (due 2026-03-18)
Open PR with token JSON + migration script and request staged rollout (target 2026-03-22)
Run accessibility contrast sweeps and include results in PR description

DES-27847 - Create migration script and alias mapping for legacy tokens
ENG-4542 - Integrate token build into CI and add dry-run output artifact
PM-119 - Coordinate release notes and migration guide for partners
DES-27848 - QA pass: visual diffs on key product surfaces and cross-device screenshots

domain: 日常协作与非结构化讨论
title: people-ops
text:
Olivia K: hey team — quick question about timing. my partner's due date is flexible and we may need to travel internationally at short notice. what's the recommended cadence for filing paperwork, and how do we avoid payroll/top-up gaps if dates move?
Maya (People Ops): congrats! best practice: submit a parental_leave_request as soon as you have a window (even if tentative). that reserves your spot for benefits and lets payroll flag the account. you can update dates later.
Olivia K: if we get a 48h change, will payroll still apply the top-up without a retro?
Ben (Payroll): short answer: usually yes if change falls before our payroll cutoff (Fri 3pm PT). for <48h changes we can still handle it but might run a small retro adjustment. email payroll@redwood.com right after any change and cc your manager to speed things up.
Rhea (Benefits): add: mark the form field "flex_start: true" for uncertain windows. benefits will pre-authorize the top-up period. we'll still need final supporting docs (birth certificate, placement docs, passport pages) within 30 days of the start date.
Chris (Manager): ops side: please create a 1-page "critical tasks" doc and nominate two coverage owners. I'll cover weekly demos and oncall for the first 2 weeks. schedule a 20m handoff before departure.
Olivia K: is there guidance for travel reimbursements and whether they're taxable? we'll likely have flights + legal fees.
Rhea (Benefits): travel for adoptive/parental placement: eligible for reimbursement under the family travel policy. cap: $2,500 for domestic, $4,000 for international (per event). tax treatment depends on jurisdiction; we'll flag the claim for tax review. submit via expenses with code FAMILY_TRAVEL.
Maya (People Ops): timeline checklist link: https://intranet.redwood/hr/parental-checklist (upload portal + sample runbook). quick checklist snippet:
```
parental_leave_request
- name:
- leave_type: adoption/birth/surrogacy
- tentative_start_date:
- flex_start: yes/no
- estimated_duration:
- coverage_contacts (2):
- travel_reimbursement_needed: yes/no
- supporting_docs_pending: yes/no
```
Ben (Payroll): also note payroll code: PARENT_TOPUP. if you request partial remote work during leave, indicate % schedule in the form so payroll calculates top-up pro-rata.
Olivia K: for international cases, do we need notarized docs up front?
Rhea (Benefits): sometimes. embassy or consulate copies and notarized parentage documents speed up downstream processes. benefits will tell you exactly what's needed after you submit the request.
hr-bot: Ticket created: PARENT-1789901234. A People Ops specialist will reach out within 1 business day to set up a benefits + payroll call.
Olivia K: thanks everyone — i'll file the tentative form now and share the runbook draft for coverage. will ping here after I hear from the rep. :pray:

author: ava_chen
text:
From: Nina Shah <nina.shah@acme-example.com>
To: Ava Chen <ava.chen@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Thu, Feb 12, 2026 at 9:43 AM
Subject: Urgent: Redwood Private upgrade keeps rolling back

Hi Ava,

We attempted the 2.8.0 -> 2.9.0 upgrade last night. Its been "rolling back" for hours and never completes. The UI now says "Rollback in progress" indefinitely.

Can you advise? We can share logs.

Nina

---

From: Ava Chen <ava.chen@redwoodinference.com>
To: Nina Shah <nina.shah@acme-example.com>
Cc: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwoodinference.com>, Ethan Park <ethan.park@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Thu, Feb 12, 2026 at 10:01 AM
Subject: Re: Urgent: Redwood Private upgrade keeps rolling back

Thanks Nina were looking. Can you attach the installer controller logs around the rollback start?

In the meantime: are you seeing any mention of a "rollback lock" or repeated rollback retries?

Ava

---

From: Nina Shah <nina.shah@acme-example.com>
To: Ava Chen <ava.chen@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Thu, Feb 12, 2026 at 10:22 AM
Subject: Re: Urgent: Redwood Private upgrade keeps rolling back

Attached installer-controller-logs.txt. There are repeated lines like: "scheduling rollback retry" and it never clears.

---

From: Ethan Park <ethan.park@redwoodinference.com>
To: Ava Chen <ava.chen@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Thu, Feb 12, 2026 at 10:48 AM
Subject: Re: Urgent: Redwood Private upgrade keeps rolling back

This matches the stuck rollback / rollback loop we saw (likely RRB-17). Workaround: delete CM `installer-rollback-lock` in the redwood-private namespace, then restart installer-controller. Id recommend we share steps with guardrails + ask them to confirm name/namespace before deleting.

---

From: Ava Chen <ava.chen@redwoodinference.com>
To: Nina Shah <nina.shah@acme-example.com>
Date: Thu, Feb 12, 2026 at 11:08 AM
Subject: Re: Urgent: Redwood Private upgrade keeps rolling back

Nina we have a workaround that has unblocked this in our lab. If youre comfortable running a couple k8s commands, please do the following (and confirm youre in the *redwood-private* namespace):

1) `kubectl -n redwood-private delete cm installer-rollback-lock`
2) `kubectl -n redwood-private rollout restart deploy/installer-controller`

This should allow the rollback to complete. Please reply with the outcome + any remaining errors.

We are also tracking a patch to prevent the rollback loop from happening again.

title: Contributor Toolflow and Privileges Playbook
author: Asha Patel
text:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook documents the standard tool access lifecycle for contributors at Redwood — from first-day provisioning through promotions, cross-team rotations, and final deprovisioning. The emphasis is on fast enablement, least-privilege by default, auditable changes, and clear manager/engineer responsibilities.

Audience: people-ops, hiring managers, engineering managers, IT, security reviewers, and new contributors.

Summary of goals:
- Ensure 95% of new hires have usable accounts and core tool access within 8 business hours of start.
- Enforce least-privilege role assignments for 90% of contributors by role templates.
- Complete deprovisioning within 24 hours for offboarded contributors (per security SLA).

Key principles
- Least privilege: grant only the roles required for the contributor’s current responsibilities.
- Role templates: use standardized permission packages (see Role → Tool mapping).
- Manager-driven exceptions: any deviation requires manager justification and a 90-day review.
- Auditability: every access change must be recorded in Okta and the access-request ticket.

Role → Tool mapping (canonical templates)
| Role | GitHub | GCP (project) | Datadog | Jira | Slack | Console/Secrets | Notes |
|------|--------|----------------|---------|------|-------|----------------|-------|
| IC-Engineer-Level-1 | repo:read | viewer | dash:read | dev-project | full | vault:read | Standard new-hire dev access (no prod) |
| IC-Engineer-Level-2 | repo:write | dev-editor | dash:read | dev-squad | full | vault:read | Can merge to non-protected branches; needs sprint leads approval for protected branches |
| IC-Engineer-Level-3 | repo:admin* | staging-editor | dash:write | squad-admin | full | vault:deploy | Elevated staging access; production access by exception and 90-day review |
| Platform-Engineer | repo:admin | multi-project | dash:write | infra | full | vault:admin | Broad access required for ops teams; requires security onboarding checklist |

*repo:admin for Level-3 is scoped to staging and infra-adjacent repos only.

Provisioning process (first-day onboarding)
1) Hiring manager creates a People Ops onboarding request in Workday/HRIS and links the candidate start date.
2) Manager files an Access Request ticket in Jira using template: "Access Request: New Hire - <NAME> - <TEAM> - <ROLE TEMPLATE>". Include start date and required projects.
3) people-ops triages: validates manager, picks correct role template, and initiates Okta provisioning flows.
4) Core accounts to create: Okta account, GitHub account (SAML link), Slack, GCP IAM invite, Datadog, Confluence.
5) Owner (people-ops) confirms repo and project invites; manager completes the New Hire Checklist and schedules Security Onboarding session.

Expected times:
- Okta and Slack: within 2 hours of ticket acknowledgement.
- GitHub & GCP invites: within 4 hours.
- All core tooling active and verified: target within 8 business hours.

Manager checklist for first 3 days
- Verify that the contributor can clone the repo and run the local dev script (tools/dev-setup.sh).
- Confirm access to Jira board and Datadog dashboards used by the team.
- Run through the security checklist: 2FA enforced, passwordless keys setup, vault read only.
- Submit permission escalation requests for protected branches if needed (see Escalation flow).

Permission escalation flow (protected or prod access)
1) Engineer or manager opens a "Privilege Escalation" Jira ticket with justification, duration, and list of specific resources.
2) Security reviews and responds within 2 business days. If approved, a scoped temporary role is created (max 90 days).
3) Audit log entry created; approver is added as owner.
4) 7 days before expiry, system sends reminders to the owner and manager to extend or revert access.

Cross-team rotations and role transitions
- When a contributor changes teams, the new manager must:
 - Open a change request ticket to add new role template and remove prior team templates.
 - Schedule a knowledge transfer and update on-call and pager duty rosters if applicable.
 - Verify completed de-escalation of previous team secrets and remove access to prior projects.
- people-ops will run an automated script (rotation-reconcile) that compares current Okta groups to team rosters and flags mismatches weekly.

Promotion-specific tool changes
- Promotion to IC-3 or above triggers a permissions review: expected changes include elevated staging permissions and write access to internal infra repos.
- Manager must document the promotion in the "Promotion Access" ticket and indicate any necessary temporary exceptions.

Deprovisioning (offboarding)
1) Offboard event triggers: manager submits Offboard ticket in Jira or HRIS marks termination/leave.
2) Immediate actions (within 2 hours): suspend Okta session, remove Slack privileges, revoke long-lived GitHub tokens.
3) Secondary actions (within 24 hours): remove GCP and Datadog access, rotate any secrets where the contributor was a maintainer.
4) Final reconciliation (within 72 hours): people-ops confirms all access removed and produces an audit report attached to the Offboard ticket.

Escalation playbook for stuck provisioning
- If new hire lacks access after 8 business hours: manager escalates to people-ops-ops channel and pings the people-ops oncall.
- If an access change is refused by security for unclear reasons: open a security-appeal with evidence and invite the security reviewer to a 30-minute working session.

Audit and quarterly clean-up
- Quarterly automated audit runs across Okta, GitHub org, GCP IAM, and Datadog.
- Flags generated: stale groups (>90 days), inactive users with elevated roles, long-lived tokens.
- people-ops and security jointly triage and close flags within 30 days.

Tooling snippets and examples
- Access request JSON example (paste into Jira ticket):
 {"candidate": "First Last", "team": "Platform", "role_template": "IC-Engineer-Level-2", "projects": ["project-dev-a", "project-infra-test"], "start_date": "2026-11-01", "justification": "Standard onboarding for backend engineer"}

- CLI to verify GitHub team membership (example):
 gh api repos/org/repo/teams --jq '.[] | select(.name=="platform") | .members_count'

Ownership and SLAs
- people-ops: primary owner for provisioning and deprovisioning SLAs.
- Security: owner for privilege escalations and audits.
- Team manager: owner for role correctness and business justifications.
- SLA targets: provisioning complete within 8 business hours (95%), deprovisioning within 24 hours (100% for suspension).

Templates & attachments
- New Hire Access Request (Jira template): create issue type ONBOARD-ACCESS with fields: name, start_date, role_template, projects, repo_list, manager_approver.
- Offboard checklist (attached to offboard ticket): suspend Okta session, revoke tokens, rotate secrets, remove from oncall, archive workspace.

Common FAQs
- Q: What if the new hire needs production access on day 1?
 A: Production access requires an explicit Privilege Escalation ticket plus security approval. Expect 48–72 hour lead time.
- Q: Who can request temporary elevated roles?
 A: Only the hire’s manager or a Director-level approver; all requests create audit trail entries.

Change history
- 2026-03-15 — initial draft (Asha Patel).
- 2026-07-07 — added rotation-reconcile automation notes (reviewers: Evan Liu).
- 2026-10-02 — tightened escalation SLA and clarified deprovisioning target windows (Priya Kapoor).

Related resources
- Security onboarding checklist: /confluence/security-and-compliance/incident-response-security/security-onboarding-checklist-2025
- Onboarding toolchain mapping: /confluence/company-handbook/05_internal-tools/onboarding-toolchain-access-and-career-checkpoints-2025.json

Contact
- people-ops oncall: #people-ops-urgent (Slack).
- Security escalation: security-escalations@redwood.ai

End of playbook

title: Evaluation & Quality Workshop: prompt sets, regression alerts, A/B splits - XyloTech
author: Samira Patel
text:
Walkthrough of Redwood's Eval/Quality monitoring: building prompt-sets, configuring regression alerts, running A/B traffic splits and interpreting AB compare results. Customer interested in pilot for support docs summarization product; concerns: latency impact, cost of continuous eval, and SSO/KMS requirements.

Customer is piloting a support doc summarization feature; primary metrics: F1 on extraction, hallucination rate, latency. Strong interest in private deployment for residency and KMS. Preferred pilot: 4-week with nightly sentinel + weekly full eval and AB split for candidate model.

[00:00] Samira: hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you all hear me?
[00:02] Maya: yep loud and clear, thanks for doing this.
[00:05] Jon: hi all, i'll be demoing the eval console and AB compare flows, i might jump into the console in a bit.
[00:10] Tom: quick agenda from our side, we want to see how prompt sets map to alerts, how the regression signal is computed, and what it looks like to do traffic splits across model variants.
[00:22] Samira: perfect, we'll start high level then do a live prompt-set import. also happy to cover security questions at the end.
[00:30] Jon: (screen) ok opening the EvalOps console, top-left is Prompt Sets, you can upload CSVs or create programmatically via API. a prompt-set is just a labeled set of inputs + expected outputs or metrics.
[00:47] Ana: when you say expected outputs, is that strict matching or can it be scorer-based?
[00:52] Jon: good question. we support both exact match labels and scorer functions — you can use a rubric, or a reranker, or an automated metric like BERTScore. you can chain metrics.
[01:05] Luca: is the scorer executed in Redwood or do we call our own evaluation endpoint?
[01:10] Jon: by default Redwood will compute builtin metrics on the server side; for custom scoring you can attach a webhook to forward outputs to your scoring service and we ingest the result, so either works.
[01:22] Maya: lets say we have 500 prompts from our support transcripts, we want to run nightly regressions and alert if doc-summa F1 drops by more than 3 points — easy?
[01:30] Jon: totally. in the Alerts tab you create a regression alert, pick the metric (F1), set the baseline (last 30 days median), and threshold — we compute significance with bootstrap so you won't get noisy ticks.
[01:45] Tom: is the baseline configurable per prompt subset? we have high-priority prompt categories vs low priority.
[01:50] Jon: yes you can tag prompts and create alerts scoped to tags or a prompt-set. tags also let you create tiered paging rules.
[01:58] Maya: ok nice. Priya: on the product side, how is the AB compare surfaced?
[02:02] Priya: we show side-by-side metric deltas and per-prompt diffs, plus a waterfall to see which prompts drive the regression. you can filter by label or by model variant.
[02:15] Jon: launching AB compare demo — starting traffic-split wizard. you can route percentage to a stable vs candidate model, or route by user cohort.
[02:28] Luca: we need traffic-split that honors region and data residency, can we restrict candidate only to EU region instances?
[02:36] Samira: yes, in Private/Dedicated you can pin model variants to regions, routing policies can include region constraints. if you're on hosted we'd recommend model variants with region affinity; for strict residency we'd look at Private.
[02:50] Maya: how about costs — continuous nightly evals for 500 prompts across multiple models, is that going to be expensive?
[02:58] Jon: cost depends on token counts and whether you run full inference or use cached outputs. Redwood supports prefix/KV caching so for many support prompts with similar prefixes, cost reduces. also Optimize suggests batching and quant profiles to drop per-token cost.
[03:15] Tom: can we do lightweight sentinel checks daily and full eval weekly?
[03:18] Jon: yes, you can schedule multiple eval jobs with different coverage; alerts can be tied to either. common pattern we see: cheap sentinel alerts (10–20 prompts) daily + full smoke test (500 prompts) weekly.
[03:33] Maya: show us an example where an A/B compare highlighted a regression and we rolled back automatically.
[03:38] Jon: flipping to a case study — here's an ecom customer: candidate model introduced hallucination on price answers, AB compare showed a 7% precision drop on price-extraction prompts, we had an automatic fallback policy that rolled traffic back to stable and created a ticket.
[03:55] Ana: what triggered the rollback, the alert or manual?
[03:58] Jon: both possible — you can configure an automatic action on critical alerts; most teams prefer manual review with auto-flagging.
[04:07] Maya: about integrations — we use SSO with Okta and KMS via AWS, any blockers?
[04:12] Samira: we support SAML/Okta SSO and KMS integration for Private; in Hosted we offer managed encryption at rest and KMS-handoff options for enterprise.
[04:24] Luca: audit logs required for our compliance team — can we store full evaluation logs for 365 days?
[04:30] Samira: yes with the enterprise observability add-on you can retain logs and we provide per-token breakdowns, user-level access controls and exportable audit trails.
[04:40] Tom: question on latency impact — running evals shouldn't slow production, right?
[04:44] Jon: evals run asynchronously on separate pools by default; A/B traffic splits are real-time but you can route evaluation-only traffic to dedicated inference workers. important design: don't route control-plane evals through your production path.
[04:58] Maya: ok demo to import a prompt-set — (typing noise) uploading CSV now — mapping columns: id, prompt, expected_label, tags.
[05:10] Jon: we detect columns and let you preview. note: try to avoid long context fields in CSV; heavy tokens blow up cost.
[05:20] Ana: oops one of our expected labels had markdown, it got sanitized — is that normal?
[05:25] Jon: the parser will escape common markup; you can set a raw_text flag if you want literal processing.
[05:33] Samira: quick interjection, if you want we'll share the sample prompt-set format and a tiny ingestion lambda that our customers use.
[05:38] Maya: please do.
[05:40] Jon: running an on-demand eval job — selecting models: stable-v1 (quantized) vs candidate-ptx (float). submitting job... job queued.
[05:55] (pause, typing)
[06:10] Jon: results streaming — per-prompt diffs show candidate worse on 12 prompts, combined metric delta -2.9 F1.
[06:20] Tom: can the console show the original model output next to candidate output?
[06:23] Jon: yes side-by-side with diff highlights and token-level alignment when available.
[06:30] Maya: the per-prompt view is great. can we add comments for the team?
[06:33] Jon: yep annotate and assign to reviewers; annotations get surfaced in the eval timeline.
[06:40] Priya: want to call out the regression alert config UI — here you can tweak sensitivity, minimum sample size and who gets paged.
[06:50] Ana: paging — we use PagerDuty.
[06:52] Samira: Redwood integrates with PD, Slack, e-mail and Jira. you can route alerts to different PD services per prompt tag.
[07:00] Maya: what about model rollouts — can we do gradual canary and auto-promote if metrics look good?
[07:05] Jon: yes rollout policies include canary stages, metric gates and auto-promote after X hours with stable deltas. you can tie gates to eval metrics in real-time.
[07:15] Luca: curious about private deployment — if we want to keep everything in our VPC and run evals there, is that supported?
[07:20] Samira: yes Private installs include EvalOps console; metrics and dashboards can be run on-prem and we provide a private control plane option. you can also bring-your-own-KMS and SSO.
[07:32] Maya: any prebuilt connectors for Salesforce/Intercom to pull prompts?
[07:36] Jon: we have connectors for Zendesk, Intercom, and a REST ingestion endpoint. many customers use small ETL jobs to export recent conversations into prompt-sets.
[07:48] Tom: ok pricing ask: rough estimate for 100k eval tokens/week across two model variants and nightly sentinel checks?
[07:56] Samira: i'll need to run numbers but rough ballpark on hosted with caching and batching we usually see X per 1k tokens — (Samira clarifies) i'll send a modeled estimate in the follow up.
[08:10] Maya: any hard limits on prompt-set size?
[08:13] Jon: not really; console pages results and we recommend slicing into sets > 10k for runs, but you can store millions with enterprise retention.
[08:22] Ana: transcription note: the automated speaker tags sometimes flip for us, just FYI.
[08:26] Samira: yep that's expected, we'll correct in notes.
[08:30] (wrap)
[08:31] Samira: ok quick recap of next steps, we'll send the security snippet, sample prompt-set, cost estimate and propose a pilot date.
[08:40] Maya: thanks — we'll reconvene once we pick pilot cohort.
[08:44] Jon: thanks all, follow up will include exported screenshots of the AB compare and the webhook example.
[08:50] (call ends)

title: Bulk audit log delivery and security assertions for upcoming vendor audit (SIEM ingestion + AUP attestation)
text:
Issue summary:
Customer BrightLedger is undergoing a third-party vendor security audit in two weeks and requested: (1) a full export of account-level audit events for calendar year 2025, (2) SIEM-compatible delivery (Splunk CEF or NDJSON with timestamp + sig fields), and (3) signed evidence for control assertions (AUP acceptance confirmation, KMS usage for log encryption, and log retention/immutability statements). Impact: audit deadline is 2026-03-24. Customer requires chain-of-custody metadata and statement of retention policy.

Environment / scope:
- Customer account: brightledger-prod-001
- Region: us-east-1
- Time range: 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-31 UTC
- Record types requested: API request/response events, token usage metadata (anonymized IDs), auth events (login, token create/revoke), model-inference start/stop events, audit config changes, and SIEM-relevant metadata (user_agent, src_ip when available).

Requested output/format options (customer preference):
1) NDJSON, one event per line, ISO8601 timestamp in top-level field "@timestamp", fields: event_type, user_id (hashed), resource, region, request_id, outcome, signature_hash.
2) Splunk CEF mapping (field mappings provided by customer).

Customer also attached a security questionnaire section (they highlighted need for: KMS key usage logs, rotation cadence, HSM-backed key statements, and evidence of immutable object storage for audit logs).

Initial triage: Support verified the customer's account, confirmed they have Enterprise contract and allowed export rights. Checked audit-export service health dashboard — no service incidents in us-east in the requested window. Located a recent export job template PR in infra repo that added NDJSON output and checksum manifest (PR#8421).

Technical tasks performed so far:
- Generated a 1-week sample export for 2025-07-06..2025-07-13 and placed it in an internal staging S3 path: s3://redwood-support-exports/SUP-71902/sample/ (access-controlled).
- Validated NDJSON schema against customer's mapping; small field mismatch found (we use "region" while customer expected "aws_region"). Noted mapping change required for final export.
- Verified KMS key id used for log-at-rest in prod: arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:111222333:alias/redwood-logs. Confirmed rotation cadence: 90 days (per key metadata).
- Confirmed that export pipeline supports generating per-file sha256 checksums and signed manifest.

Open blockers:
- Need explicit signed AUP attestation from Redwood Security lead (CS to route).
- Customer requested logs with src_ip; our PII policy redacts full IPs by default — need legal/CS approval to provide truncated/partial IPs or hashed IPs. Linked INT-4120 for policy approval.

[2026-03-10] Maya Patel (Support): Logged request and opened SUP-71902. Customer provided security questionnaire PDF and Splunk CEF field mapping. Requested timeline: complete export and deliver signed evidence by 2026-03-17 to allow auditor prep.
[2026-03-10] Customer (BrightLedger - Audit Team): Attachments: BL_audit_q1_2026.pdf. Customer confirms they need both NDJSON and CEF, but NDJSON is the minimum acceptable format.
[2026-03-11] Carlos Vega (SRE): Created sample export for one-week range and uploaded to staging S3. Noted region field mismatch. Assigned to infra for mapping change; referenced PR#8421.

title: Support Automation: Unified Admin Catalog & Task Runner
author: Rohit Patel
text:
Goal: Provide a single searchable catalog of admin utilities and runbooks where each runbook is represented as a first-class task (runnable via Console, API, or CLI) and backed by safe execution policies. This work unifies a grab-bag of scripts, interactive shells, and ad-hoc runbooks into a typed, permissioned task surface that support engineers and oncall can invoke quickly.

Scope:
- Build a metadata registry for runbooks (tags, inputs, outputs, estimated duration, RBAC requirements, audit annotations).
- Implement a lightweight task runner (runworklet) that accepts typed params, performs dry-run checks, and emits structured telemetry.
- Add Console UI hooks: quick-run, parameter presets, historical runs, and one-click rollback where applicable.
- Integrate with existing telemetry (Datadog dashboard + traces) and the incident timeline so runs are correlated with incidents.
- Safety: input validation, credential scoping (credentialed steps must use ephemeral privileged session), preflight canary and circuit-breaker policies.

Trade-offs discussed:
- We favor typed inputs + strict validation over freeform scripts to reduce blast radius, which increases upfront engineering work for wrapping legacy scripts.
- Live-preview/dry-run adds latency to the first execution but dramatically reduces error rate; decided to make dry-run optional but recommended for high-risk steps.
- We will not attempt to fully auto-convert all legacy runbooks in first iteration; prioritization will be by run frequency and incident impact.

Success metrics:
- 40% reduction in time-to-remediate for the 10 most common incident classes within 8 weeks of rollout.
- 80% of runbook executions include structured telemetry and outcome tags.
- No high-severity security findings during initial security review.

Deliverables:
- Metadata registry service + small schema and migration for existing runbooks.
- Runworklet runner service with API + CLI.
- Console quick-run surface and history panel.
- Migrations/wrappers for top 15 runbooks.

Notes: Link to design sketch and API contract in Confluence and the spike PR in GitHub (see links).

Catalog entries can be created/edited with tags, RBAC fields, and typed inputs
Runworklet can execute a dry-run and a real run; both produce consistent telemetry events
Console shows run history and allows re-run with parameter presets
Audit records capture invoker identity, inputs, and outcome for every run

Phase 1: scaffold registry and typed schema; provide migration script for 5 high-priority runbooks
Phase 2: implement runner with ephemeral credential proxy + dry-run; integrate Datadog spans and metric tags
Phase 3: Console wiring, RBAC enforcement, rollout to oncall group via feature flag

title: Feature-slice sprint notes: rapid gated experiments
author: Omar Khan
text:
Quickbrain: goal is a tiny, repeatable flow for carving out a narrow feature slice, shipping it to a tiny percentage of traffic, and learning fast (K=3 experiments per sprint).

Why: long features take forever; teams need a way to validate interaction assumptions and perf/cost impact before full rollout. This is a personal scratchpad + lightweight proto for 2-week sprint experiments.

Core idea (one-liner): define a minimal surface (API + UX endpoint + metrics) that can be toggled and observed independently, with automatic rollback if latency/cost/quality triggers fire.

Principles / constraints:
- Keep model/runtime changes minimal: prefer routing + micro-policy over model edits.
- Must be reversible in < 10m (feature off / traffic drained).
- Instrumentation first: every slice includes golden prompt set and automatic micro-eval.
- Cost SLO guardrails by default (per-request estimated token cost).
- Default to 0.5–2% traffic for initial slices.

Proposed pieces (minimal MVP):
1) Slice definition format (YAMLish):
 - id: stable id
 - route: API route or front-end flag
 - matchers: simple traffic selectors (user cohorts / tenant / header / cookie)
 - model_variant: optional override
 - budget: per-minute token cap or $ cap
 - metrics: list of metric ids to stream
 - rollback_triggers: latency > X ms, error rate > Y, quality drop > Z

2) Quick toggle UI (Console microview):
 - small card: name, traffic % slider, start/stop, last 24h metrics sparkline
 - quick notes field, owner, expected duration

3) Runtime routing hooks:
 - evaluate matchers at proxy edge, short-circuit to slice if matched
 - ensure KV cache compatibility across slices (avoid sticky state mismatch)

4) Safety net / auto-rollbacks:
 - streaming alerting rule that marks slice as degraded and flips to fallback variant
 - background drain job: stop assigning new requests to slice and wait 30s for in-flight to finish

5) Micro-eval harness:
 - run a small prompt set on every candidate model variant; store pass/fail and average score
 - tie to alert trigger: if eval score drops > 5% relative to baseline, mark for rollback

Success metrics (for the experiment itself):
- Time from slice creation -> first telemetry visible < 10m
- Canary failure rate <= baseline + 1.5x in first 24h
- Observed decision: ship (expand), iterate (tweak), or kill within 7 days

Example user stories (short):
- As a product PM, I can create a feature slice that targets 1% of traffic and attach an eval set so I can validate output quality without risking all users.
- As an SRE, I can set an automatic per-slice token budget so an experiment can never exceed $X/day.
- As an engineer, I can add a route matcher that targets only enterprise tenants in eu-west and see a small dashboard for requests routed.

Implementation sketch (phased):
Phase 0: manual wires + router flag prototype (1 sprint)
- engineer sets header+flag at proxy; small dashboard reading logs via query
Phase 1: slice config + console toggle + light automation (2 sprints)
- schema, console card, simple routing policy, per-slice metrics in Console
Phase 2: auto-rollbacks + micro-eval integration + cost budgeting (2 sprints)
Phase 3: templated slices + experiment library + infra for stateful slices (4 sprints)

Open questions / parking lot:
- How to handle slices that must modify model prompts (prompt plumbing + provenance)?
- Sticky sessions and cached KV: do we enforce sticky hash or forbid stateful slices?
- Metrics signal design: how do we avoid false positives in quality evals for small sample sizes?
- Ownership model: should slices be namespaced per-team with quota?
- Billing/chargeback: how to show per-slice cost to owning team?

Immediate next actions (for next 48h):
- Draft minimal slice schema (YAML) and post to #product-experiments for feedback (me)
- Spike a console toy: card + slider (Drew)
- Wire up a Prometheus query for per-slice QPS / p95 / estimated tokens (Maya)

Notes to self:
- Keep scope small; shipping a toggle + visible metrics is > 80% of value.
- Reuse existing rollout code where possible (canary infra?).
- Think through user privacy for per-tenant evals.

References / potential hubs:
- look at: GH PR#412 (feature-slice proto)
- convo: #product-experiments, #sre-rollouts
- similar idea: "mini canaries" notes in infra/sre drive (find later)

End-of-scratchpad.

(rough, fragmented — will polish into a 1-pager once spikes land)

title: Catamaran Inference Ops
author: Sofia Patel
text:
Summary: Financial trading platform evaluating Redwood Dedicated / Private for low-latency inference (decisioning + chat ops). Priority = deterministic p95/p99 under peak load; streaming behavior must be aligned with product UX.
Workload profile: mixture of streaming chat (ticketing and human-in-the-loop alerts) and synchronous scoring for trading signals. ~35% streaming, 65% non-streaming. Average request size: 800 tokens for scoring, 1.5k tokens for some analyst chat flows.
Targets proposed by customer (initial): non-streaming: p50 <= 30ms, p95 <= 120ms, p99 <= 300ms; streaming first-byte (server-to-client) p50 <= 15ms, p95 <= 80ms, p99 <= 250ms. Wants p95 guarantee for tail latency credits in SLA.
Measurement ambiguity: customer currently measures end-to-end from client (mobile/web) including client processing and WAN. Redwood measures at gateway + runtime. Need alignment: agree to publish both server-side and RUM-style client metrics and a mapping for peering/last-mile delta.
Routing & fallback: must support deterministic fallback to a smaller quantized model (90% feature parity) if latency SLOs are violated. Must preserve order for streaming partial responses when falling back.
Capacity ask: design to sustain 1k sustained RPS at 1k tokens avg with 3x burst headroom to 3k RPS. Customer prefers H100-class nodes but open to A100 with multi-instance and quantized variants. Wants guidance on reserved fleet sizing and expected utilization targets.
SLA asks: specific credit schedule for p95 breaches, regional residency (EU/NA) for accounting/regulatory streams, mandatory audit logging per request (token-level audit) for compliance audits.
Instrumentation goals: agree on the following measurable events for SLOs: client-invoke (client timestamp), edge-arrival (load balancer), request-dispatch (runtime), first-token-emitted, last-token-emitted, response-delivered (edge). Correlate IDs across traces and expose sample traces in Console.
Success criteria for POC: 1) measured p95 under synthetic mixed workload <= target for two 4-hour runs, 2) pass security checklist and peering tests, 3) validated model fallback preserves stream semantics, 4) runbook for operational escalations.
Quote from CTO on call: 'We need guarantees that the tail won't blow up during market open — and we need to be able to explain the delta between what users see and what you measure.'
