title: local-data-sovereignty-fallback-orchestration-runbook-2026
author: Ava Kim
text:
Summary:
This runbook documents the local data sovereignty and fallback orchestration pattern used for Redwood Private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It defines when and how tenant traffic should be routed to local model variants, what safeguards to use to preserve data residency guarantees, operator procedures to trigger and recover from fallbacks, and telemetry & SLO thresholds that drive automation.

Goals:
- Maintain data residency: ensure PII and regulated data never leaves customer-controlled networks during fallback.
- Preserve availability: keep inference capacity online with best-effort local models when control-plane or cross-region links are impaired.
- Ensure safe rollbacks: provide clear operator steps to revert automated actions with minimal config drift.

Scope:
- Applies to Private deployments that run a hybrid control plane (customer control plane + Redwood managed components) or fully air-gapped on-prem stacks.
- Covers network partition/failure, control-plane outage, upstream model catalog unavailability, and degraded cross-region links.
- Does NOT cover hardware-level GPU failures or kernel-level runtime bugs (see hardware failover docs).

Assumptions and prerequisites:
- Private deployment runs these services: redwood-control-agent, private-operator, edge-proxy (service-lb), rt-inference, kvcache-service.
- Customer has configured a local model cache (min 1 warm model per critical route) and an allowlist of model IDs that are permitted to be used in-scope for local processing.
- KMS/HSM keys for local encryption are available and reachable from the compute tier.

Ownership:
- Incident owner: oncall-private-ops (primary).
- Fallback orchestration: infra-platform-team (automation).
- Security & data residency validation: security-compliance (review and approval).

Key SLOs and thresholds that drive fallback:
- Control-plane API error rate > 2% sustained for 5 minutes -> begin staged local fallback (step 1).
- Cross-region bandwidth degradation > 60% of baseline for 10 minutes -> prepare local routing but do NOT fail traffic until control-plane errors observed.
- Local model cold-start time > 10s at 95th percentile after priming -> raise playbook alert to operator.
- Local inference latency p99 must remain < 600ms post-fallback for critical routes; if exceeded, trigger degradation policy to reduce response size or invoke cached responses.

High-level orchestration patterns:
1) Passive priming: maintain a warm local model cache for critical tenant routes. Regularly refresh KV-caches and checkpoint files during low-traffic windows.
2) Staged activation: fallback occurs in stages: traffic shadowing -> partial routing (10-30%) -> full cutover. Each stage waits for health gates.
3) Policy guardrails: use the allowlist and residency rules to prevent models that require external telemetry or third-party calls from being used during offline mode.

Configuration snippets (example automation policy YAML):

automation_policy: |
 name: "local-fallback-policy-tenant-critical"
 triggers:
 - type: control_plane_error_rate
 threshold_percent: 2
 window_sec: 300
 - type: bandwidth_degradation
 region: "primary->secondary"
 threshold_percent: 60
 window_sec: 600
 stages:
 - name: shadow
 traffic_percent: 0
 verify_health: true
 wait_sec: 120
 - name: partial
 traffic_percent: 20
 verify_health: true
 wait_sec: 300
 - name: full
 traffic_percent: 100
 verify_health: true
 wait_sec: 180
 residency_enforcement: "strict"
 allowed_models: ["local/gptx-small-v1", "local/embedding-sparse-1"]

Operator runbook: step-by-step for automated fallback:
1) Alert triage (0-5 min): confirm control-plane error alerts (redwood-control-plane) and cross-region telemetry. Check grafana dashboard: "Private / Control Plane / Errors" and "Network / Inter-region Throughput".
2) Verify residency policy: ensure allowed_models list is intact in /etc/redwood/private-config.yaml and that KMS is reachable.
3) Kick off shadowing stage if automation did not start: run CLI on private-operator box:
 - sudo /opt/redwood/bin/operator ctl begin-shadow --tenant $TENANT_ID --policy local-fallback-policy-tenant-critical
4) Monitor shadowing: verify shadow profiles in the "shadow-traffic" table on the operator UI and confirm no data egress events in the telemetry stream.
5) If shadowing healthy for 2 minutes (no model exceptions, p95 latency stable), progress to partial routing:
 - sudo /opt/redwood/bin/operator ctl set-traffic-split --tenant $TENANT_ID --percent 20
6) Health gates at each stage:
 - error-rate (local inference) < 1%
 - KV cache hit rate > 70%
 - p99 latency < configured limit (default 600ms)
7) If any gate fails, rollback one stage and re-prime model caches (see Cache re-priming below). Notify security-compliance if data residency policy was close to violation.
8) When full routing completes, mark incident: annotate runbook in incident tracker and set recovery actions.

Manual fallback: when automation is disabled or unsafe
- If automation is off, follow the CLI steps above; for emergency full cutover run:
 - sudo /opt/redwood/bin/operator ctl emergency-cutover --tenant $TENANT_ID --force --reason "$INCIDENT_ID"
- Emergency cutover requires two approvers from infra-platform-team and security-compliance.

Cache re-priming procedure:
1) Stop inference endpoints for the tenant on a single node: systemctl stop redwood-rt-inference@$TENANT_ID
2) Remove stale KV entries: /opt/redwood/bin/kvtool prune --tenant $TENANT_ID --older-than 72h
3) Start priming job (background): /opt/redwood/bin/priming-job --tenant $TENANT_ID --model local/gptx-small-v1 --concurrency 4 --duration 10m
4) Verify KV hit rate > 70% and memory usage within expected bounds.

Rollback & upgrade coordination (day-2 guidance):
- Rollback policy: prefer configuration rollback over model rollback. Revert operator policy first, then restore traffic split to last known good value.
- If rollback involves a model swap (hot-swap), use staged rollbacks: partial -> shadow -> off. Do NOT revert to hosted-only mode in restricted residency customers without explicit approval.
- Upgrade windows: schedule control-plane upgrades during low-traffic windows and ensure warm models are available in at least two zones. Communicate planned maintenance at least 72 hours in advance to the customer.

Telemetry, alerts and dashboards (key metrics):
- control_plane_api.error_rate (by tenant)
- network.region_throughput (primary->secondary)
- local_inference.latency.p95/p99
- kvcache.hit_rate
- data_egress.events (counts of external egress attempts)
- operator.automation.stage (current fallback stage)
Alert routing:
- PAGER: private-ops@pagerduty (severity P1 for control_plane_api.error_rate > 5% for 2 minutes)
- EMAIL: infra-platform-team for warnings

Security and compliance considerations:
- Enforce strict residency_enforcement during fallback: all outbound connectors disabled by policy; no telemetry with PII forwarded outside the VPC.
- KMS rotations: local key rotations MUST be applied before any model priming job if rotation occurred in the previous 24h.
- Audit: record the full operator CLI transcript and store in secure evidence bucket with retention 7 years for regulated customers.

Testing and validation matrix (recommended):
1) Simulation: emulate control-plane errors by returning 5xx for 6 minutes; verify runbook triggers and staged cutover completes.
2) Network: throttle inter-region link to 40% bandwidth for 15 minutes and validate that fallback does not trigger until control-plane errors occur.
3) Residency: run a synthetic PII query and confirm no egress logs recorded during fallback.
4) Load: run 1k QPS synthetic load during partial routing and verify p99 latency stays within SLA.

Post-incident checklist and evidence capture:
- Timestamped incident timeline (UTC).
- Snapshots of dashboards and operator logs (redwood-control-agent, private-operator).
- Copy of automation policy used and final allowed_models list.
- Post-incident review: assign owners, list root causes, and planned mitigations.

Appendix A: quick CLI commands
- Check policy status: sudo /opt/redwood/bin/operator ctl policy-status --tenant $TENANT_ID
- Start priming job: sudo /opt/redwood/bin/priming-job --tenant $TENANT_ID --model $MODEL --duration 10m
- Emergency rollback: sudo /opt/redwood/bin/operator ctl rollback --tenant $TENANT_ID --to-tag $TAG

Appendix B: common failure modes and mitigations
- Problem: local model OOM after cutover -> Mitigation: reduce concurrency, enable quantized model profile, evict non-critical tenants.
- Problem: KMS unreachable during priming -> Mitigation: fall back to cached DEKs for 15 minutes and run health-checks that require KMS unavailable flag.

References and links:
- Private deployment control plane topology (reference architecture)
- Operator CLI reference: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-deploy-operator-cheat-sheet-for-field-installations-2027
- Security policy: private-deploy-telemetry-data-classification-policy-2026

Change log:
- 2026-01-15: Initial draft (Ava Kim).
- 2026-02-10: Added automation policy examples and security gating (Priya Nambiar).
- 2026-03-02: Reviewed and published; updated SLO thresholds and CLI paths (Diego Ramos).

title: SRE decision lattice for degradation and postmortem evidence
author: Priya Malhotra
text:
Overview:

This page defines a compact but actionable decision lattice that SREs will use when facing capacity pressure, SLO breaches, or service degradation. It pairs decision thresholds (error-budget burn rates, capacity utilizations, latency tails) with prescriptive mitigations and evidence standards required for incident reviews and postmortems. The intent is to shorten time-to-decision, standardize escalation, and ensure we collect the right telemetry for causal analysis.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to all public-facing inference and orchestration services in the Redwood runtime (gateway-api, model-router, kv-cache, batch-scheduler).
- Intended audience: oncall SREs, service owners, platform engineers, support escalation leads.
- Not a replacement for service-specific runbooks; this lattice is a cross-cutting policy for multi-service incidents.

Quick summary (decision lattice):
1) Observe: Alert triggers and initial triage (5m window).
2) Classify: SLO type impacted (availability | latency | freshness | correctness), tenant scope (single-tenant | multi-tenant), and severity (S1|S2|S3).
3) Quantify: Error budget burn rate, p99 latency delta, capacity headroom percentage.
4) Act: Choose mitigation from the mapped action set (traffic shaping, degrade features, scale pool, failover to variant model).
5) Evidence: Collect required telemetry artifacts and tag the incident with evidence IDs for the postmortem.
6) Review: Run standardized postmortem with a causal map and action owners.

SLOs and thresholds (examples for runtime services):
| Service component | SLO metric | Target | Measurement window | Burn-rate thresholds (30m) | Immediate action |
| gateway-api | successful-response-rate | 99.95% | 30d rolling | > 2x burn -> P1 | throttle non-critical endpoints; apply tenant fairshare |
| model-router | p99 inference latency (small inputs) | < 450ms | 14d rolling | > 3x burn -> P1 | fallback to quantized variant; enable prefix-KV cache |
| batch-scheduler | job success rate | 99.9% | 7d rolling | > 1.5x burn -> P2 | pause low-priority queues; surface queue metrics to ops |
| embeddings | embedding-throughput | 95th percentile throughput | 14d rolling | > 2x burn -> P1 | route to dedicated pool; reduce batch size |

Error budget policy and mapped mitigations:
- Burn rate calculation: rolling 30-minute window burn = (expected_errors / allowed_errors) normalized to period.
- Burn rate bands and actions (automated where possible):
 - Normal (<1x): monitor.
 - Elevated (1–2x): owner notified; increase sampling and metric fidelity.
 - Critical (2–3x): oncall begins mitigation workflow; limited traffic shaping and capacity ramp.
 - Emergency (>3x): declare P1; invoke cross-region failover, rollback recent model/version, throttle all non-essential endpoints.

Capacity planning and synthesis model:
- Capacity unit: RDPU (Redwood Deployment Processing Unit) — represents a measured token-CPU/GPU capability for our runtime.
- Planning inputs: historical token QPS (90/95/99th), model memory/KV pressure, quantization factor, expected growth for next 90 days, SLA commitments (dedicated vs hosted).
- Buffer targets by criticality (percent of 99th demand):
 - Gold (Dedicated SLA): 40% buffer headroom
 - Silver (Enterprise hosted): 25% buffer headroom
 - Bronze (Self-serve): 10% buffer headroom
- Capacity run cadence: monthly forecast refresh + weekly emergency capacity check post-deploy.

Capacity onboarding checklist (must be completed before tenant goes live):
1) Run the synthetic-canary (10k tokens across targets) and verify SLOs on test pool.
2) Provision RDPU with requested buffer headroom.
3) Configure tenant quota and fairshare weights.
4) Attach telemetry labels: tenant_id, model_family, quant_profile.
5) Pre-register rollback model variants and ensure latency fallbacks are available.

Reliability initiatives and experiments (example roadmap items):
- Q2: Capacity-surge drills — simulate 3x burst on embeddings and run failover + synthetic remediation.
- Q3: Prefix cache warmup optimization — shorten cold-start tail by 35% in targeted model families.
- Q4: Auto-conversion safety net — automated rollback test harness for model variant rollouts.

Incident evidence and postmortem standards (required artifacts):
- Timeline: 5-minute aggregation covering 30 minutes before alert -> 2 hours after resolution. Must include event markers for deploys, config changes, traffic shifts.
- Telemetry snapshot (must be attached):
 - raw request logs (sampled by request_id) covering affected tenants (min 1% sample if high volume)
 - metrics: p50/p90/p99 latency, success_rate, cpu/gpu_util, kv_cache_hit_rate, queue_depth
 - tracing spans for any service in call path (gateway-api -> model-router -> runtime-exec)
 - capacity allocations by pool (RDPU per region), autoscale events, and scale decisions
- Evidence id: create a single S3 artifact prefix using the incident number (e.g. s3://redwood-incident/INC-2024-1234/evidence/). Attach to postmortem.

Postmortem template (minimum sections):
1) Summary (1–2 sentences)
2) Impact (users, tenants, revenue risk)
3) Timeline with evidence IDs
4) Root cause analysis (with causal map)
5) Mitigations applied during incident
6) Remediation and follow-up actions (owners + due dates)
7) Learning and experiments to validate

Operational tooling and useful commands:
- Dashboards: SLO-overview (team), Capacity-allocations (infra), Degradation-lattice (oncall).
- Key alert rules (examples):
 - gateway-api: p99 latency > 500ms for 10m -> SEV2
 - model-router: error-rate > 0.2% for 5m and > 2x baseline -> SEV1
 - kv-cache: hit_rate drop > 10% vs baseline for 5m -> SEV2
- Help commands (kubectl + infra):
 - List capacity pools: rgctl capacity list --region us-west-2 --format table
 - Inspect model-router health: infractl service status model-router --region eu-central-1
 - Re-route traffic to fallback pool: rrouter promote --tenant $TENANT --fallback-pool quantized-v2 --force

Automated evidence collection snippet (example):
- CLI to collect evidence bundle for incident:
 REDWOOD_INC=INC-2024-1234 ./bin/collect-incident-evidence --services gateway-api,model-router,runtime-exec --window "2024-05-10T09:20:00Z/2024-05-10T11:00:00Z" --out s3://redwood-incident/INC-2024-1234/evidence/

Runbook: sustained SLO breach (P1 decision path)
1) Confirm alert and quantify (burn rate >3x in 30m).
2) Run immediate mitigations in parallel (3 operators recommended):
 a) Operator A: apply traffic shaping and tenant-level fairshare. Command: rrouter throttle --tenant $TENANT --percent 50
 b) Operator B: route critical traffic to dedicated pool: rrouter promote --tenant $TENANT --pool dedicated-hot-1
 c) Operator C: inspect recent deploys: infractl deploy history --service model-router --since 2h
3) If mitigations insufficient after 10m, escalate to SRE lead and enable cross-region failover: rrouter failover --service model-router --region us-east-1
4) Collect evidence bundle (see CLI snippet) and tag incident.
5) Post-incident: create postmortem within 5 business days and schedule a follow-up QA test that replays the synthetic canary.

Runbook: capacity surge (unexpected demand)
1) Detect: autoscale events > 2x baseline or sustained GPU utilization > 85% for 10m.
2) Rapid response: increase pool autoscale max by 30% if allowed by quota: rgctl capacity adjust --pool model-pool-a --scale 1.3
3) If quota exhausted, apply degradation: reduce non-essential embeddings precision and increase batching for bulk jobs.
4) Notify sales and CS for affected tenants if enterprise SLA may be compromised.
5) After stabilization: run capacity postmortem and include a forecasting action item.

Validation and exercises:
- Monthly: evidence-collection drill — oncall must produce a valid evidence bundle within 45 minutes for a seeded SLO breach.
- Quarterly: cross-team capacity rehearsal — model teams, platform, and SRE run a 3-hour drill with a scripted traffic spike.

Appendix A — sample autoscaler YAML (illustrative):
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: AutoScalePolicy
metadata:
 name: model-pool-autoscale
spec:
 metric: token_qps
 target: 12000
 minRDPU: 4
 maxRDPU: 120
 cooldownSeconds: 180
 scaleStepPercent: 20
---

Appendix B — severity taxonomy (short):
- SEV1 (P1): SLO breach with multi-region user impact or >10% of premium tenants impacted. Immediate cross-team response required.
- SEV2 (P2): Elevated latency or partial degradation affecting limited tenant groups. Rapid oncall response.
- SEV3 (P3): Minor intermittent errors with workarounds and negligible customer impact.

Ownership and escalation matrix:
- First responder: oncall SRE for service (gateway-api or model-router).
- Escalation: SRE lead -> Platform engineering -> Product on-call for customer-facing coordination.
- Executive notification: triggered for SEV1s that exceed 60 minutes or have >5% revenue impact.

Related references:
- link: /confluence/eng-sre/operational-tooling/slo-observability-pipeline-design-and-validation-2025
- link: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/predictive-error-budget-pulse-and-capacity-hedging-playbook-2026

Contact and ownership:
- Document owner: Priya Malhotra (SRE)
- Maintenance cadence: review quarterly or after any SEV1 postmortem that implicates the lattice.

Last updated: 2025-11-02

title: Audit & Access Logs — retention windows, exports, and deletion process
author: rishi_malhotra
text:
From: Jane Doe <jane.doe@acme.com>
To: rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai
Cc: Acme Corp Security <security@acme.com>
Date: Tue, 5 May 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Quick Q on audit/access log retention & exports

Hi Rishi,

We're working through our compliance checklist for a pilot and need a crisp summary of Redwood's current behavior for audit and access logs. Specifically:

- What are the default retention windows for (1) access logs (authn/authorization/connection events) and (2) audit logs (configuration changes, admin actions)?
- Can we export raw logs (including timestamps, actor, action, resource, and request IDs) on demand? Formats? Delivery targets (S3/GCS/CSV/JSON)?
- Is there an automated deletion workflow we can trigger for specific tenants (e.g., we need 90-day deletion for one environment)?
- Do logs ever contain customer input (payload) or only metadata/IDs?

We need this to complete our internal risk review. If you can point me at a short spec or attach a sample export, that would help a lot.

Thanks,
Jane
Jane Doe
Security Engineer, Acme Corp

From: rishi_malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>
To: Jane Doe <jane.doe@acme.com>
Cc: monica_patel@redwood.ai, neha_kapoor@redwood.ai
Date: Tue, 5 May 2026 11:03:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Quick Q on audit/access log retention & exports

Hi Jane — thanks for the clear list. Short answers up front, then a couple of notes plus attachments.

Summary:
- Access logs (connection/auth events): default retention 90 days for Hosted.
- Audit logs (admin/config changes): default retention 365 days for Hosted; Dedicated/Private customers can configure longer/shorter retention via policy.
- Exports: yes — ad hoc and scheduled exports supported. Formats: JSON (structured), CSV (flattened). Delivery: S3, GCS, Azure Blob, or console download; we also provide a streaming API for near-real-time delivery.
- Deletion: tenant-scoped deletion APIs and scheduled retention policies exist for Dedicated/Private. For Hosted, we support scheduled retention (e.g., set 90d) and manual deletion requests via support ticket for special cases.
- Payloads: logs do not store plain customer inputs. We log metadata and identifiers (request_id, user_id hashed/pseudonymized).

Attached: audit_log_spec_sheet.pdf (high-level fields exported) and export_instructions_v1.md (console/API steps).

A couple of caveats:
- For Hosted customers, very short retention (<30 days) or deletion-for-DSR requests require Legal/Security review — we typically validate scope and retention timeline before executing a manual purge.
- For Dedicated/Private, customers can pin retention and we provide tools to run on-demand exports to your cloud bucket without Redwood staging the data.

If you'd like, Monica can run a quick demo of the export flow into your S3 sandbox and Neha can confirm the data minimization guarantees.

Next steps: do you want a 30-minute walkthrough tomorrow?

Best,
Rishi
Rishi Malhotra
Senior Account Executive, Redwood Inference

From: Monica Patel <monica_patel@redwood.ai>
To: Jane Doe <jane.doe@acme.com>, rishi_malhotra@redwood.ai
Date: Wed, 6 May 2026 08:22:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Quick Q on audit/access log retention & exports

Thanks Rishi — happy to help. A couple practical notes that might be useful for Acme: 

- If you want to try an export yourself: Console -> Observability -> Audit Logs -> Export -> Choose format (JSON recommended) -> Destination (S3/GCS/Azure). We also support specifying a time window and filtering by actor or resource.
- For scheduled delivery, set up an export job (cron-like) and provide an IAM role for S3/GCS; we do the writes directly into your bucket.
- For Hosted accounts where we need to perform a manual deletion, please open the support ticket with the tenant ID + exact UTC window and we will coordinate with Security.

I've dropped a short playbook in the shared drive here: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1aBcD_example_export_playbook — it includes example curl commands for the streaming API.

If you want, I can start an export to the sandbox bucket Acme gave us (if you confirm the bucket name and role).

Cheers,
Monica
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Jane Doe <jane.doe@acme.com>
To: monica_patel@redwood.ai, rishi_malhotra@redwood.ai
Cc: Acme Corp Security <security@acme.com>
Date: Wed, 6 May 2026 10:01:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Quick Q on audit/access log retention & exports

Monica — that playbook link is exactly what we needed. Thank you.

We can provide an S3 bucket (acme-logs-pilot) and an IAM role. I'll confirm bucket details in a separate secure note.

Two follow-ups for Neha/Redwood Security: 
- For compliance, we need written confirmation that exported audit logs never contain raw customer prompts/inputs.
- For the deletion workflow: if we request a tenant-scoped purge (90-day window), what is the typical SLA and what evidence do you provide once deletion is complete?

If it's easier, we can hop on a short call tomorrow.

Best,
Jane

From: Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.ai>
To: Jane Doe <jane.doe@acme.com>, rishi_malhotra@redwood.ai, monica_patel@redwood.ai
Date: Fri, 7 May 2026 15:40:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Quick Q on audit/access log retention & exports

Hi Jane — Neha from Security here. Quick confirmations and suggested artifacts: 

1) Data minimization: Redwood audit and access logs contain metadata (timestamps, request_id, status codes, actor identifiers). We do not log full customer prompt/response payloads as part of audit/access logs. If a customer enables additional request logging for debugging (opt-in), that is gated and documented; otherwise, payloads are not included.

2) Exported log contents: Exports include the fields listed in the attached spec; PII is not included by default. Identifiers are pseudonymized (SHA-256 truncated) where necessary. If Acme has specific PII concerns, we can work through a mapping/filters before export.

3) Deletion workflow and evidence: For Hosted tenants, we provide the following process for a tenant-scoped purge: 
 - Customer opens a support request with tenant_id and UTC time range.
 - Security performs scope validation and schedules the purge (typically within 3–5 business days for standard requests).
 - After purge, we provide a signed deletion report (timestamped audit showing objects removed and storage paths), plus an export of the deletion job logs for your records.

For Dedicated/Private, customers can run the purge themselves against their buckets; we supply CLI/answers and review if requested.

4) SOC2: We are SOC2 Type II compliant (report available under NDA); additional compliance artifacts can be shared through our security portal.

Happy to provide the signed statement above on company letterhead if that helps Acme's risk team. Let me know and we will route it through Legal.

Regards,
Neha Kapoor
Head of Security & Compliance, Redwood Inference

title: Hosted API SLOs: Enterprise Route Tiers (Hot-route capacity protection)
author: Aisha Bello
text:
## Purpose
This document defines **per-route SLOs and error budget policy** for Redwood Inference’s **Hosted API** as it relates to **hot-route capacity protection** (tier-aware quotas, priority routing, and controlled shedding).

The intent is to:
- Explicitly define **enterprise vs best-effort** expectations for the highest-traffic routes.
- Make overload behavior **measurable and supportable** (clear SLIs + dashboards + alerts).
- Align alerting to overload protection so we page on **enterprise degradation**, not expected best-effort shedding.

## Scope
**In scope**
- Hosted API routes: `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings`, `/v1/rerank`, `/v1/completions`.
- Tiered behavior: **Enterprise (Protected)** vs **Best-effort (Standard/Self-serve)**.
- SLOs for **availability**, **latency**, and **overload responses (429)**.
- Alert thresholds and error budget burn policy.

**Out of scope**
- Dedicated and Private SLOs (tracked separately).
- Model-quality or semantic correctness SLIs.

## Definitions
### Route tiers
We classify requests into one of the following tiers at the gateway/policy engine:
- **Enterprise (Protected):** SLA-bearing tenants and allowlisted enterprise accounts for protected routes. These requests receive priority admission and are protected during fleet pressure.
- **Best-effort:** all other traffic. Best-effort may be throttled earlier and more aggressively to preserve fleet health and enterprise budgets.

### Protected routes
Protected routes are selected based on:
- Fleet-wide traffic concentration (hot routes)
- High enterprise SLO/SLA coupling
- Known overload blast radius

Current protected route set:
- `/v1/chat/completions` (includes streaming)
- `/v1/embeddings`
- `/v1/rerank`
- `/v1/completions` (legacy; still used by some enterprise SDKs)

### Overload / throttling semantics
Requests may be rejected with HTTP **429** for:
- **Quota/rate limit enforcement** (tenant policy)
- **Overload shedding/admission control** (fleet protection)

We distinguish causes via standardized reason code headers/payloads (see Support doc for exact fields). For SLO accounting, we treat quota-throttled and overload-shed requests differently by tier (see SLI rules below).

## SLIs (what we measure)
All SLIs are computed per **route x region x tier** using the standard metrics set.

### 1) Availability SLI (server success)
**Definition:** percentage of requests that return an eligible success response.

- Success codes: `2xx` (and `3xx` if any internal redirects apply; typically none)
- Failures: `5xx`, `408`, `499` (client disconnect) are counted as failures unless explicitly excluded by route-specific rules below.

**Tier handling of 429:**
- **Enterprise:** `429` due to *overload shedding/admission control* counts as **unavailable** (because enterprise is protected; overload shed should be rare and indicates under-provisioning or misconfiguration).
- **Best-effort:** `429` due to overload shedding/admission control does **not** count as unavailable (it is expected behavior under pressure). Quota/rate-limit 429s are not counted as availability failures for either tier.

**Note:** 429 classification must be based on the reason code emitted by gateway/policy engine, not inferred from rate.

### 2) Latency SLI
Latency is measured at the gateway edge (request receive to first byte / completion) and reported as:
- **TTFB (time-to-first-byte)** for streaming endpoints.
- **E2E response time** for non-streaming.

We maintain distinct latency SLO targets per tier and route (see tables below).

### 3) Overload activation SLI (operational)
Not a customer-facing SLO, but required for on-call safety.

We track:
- **shed_rate** (fraction of requests rejected due to overload by tier)
- **admission_control_active** (boolean/ratio time in state)
- **queue_depth / scheduler_lag** for the backing pools

These drive alerts and annotations on the enterprise SLO dashboards.

## SLOs (targets)
### General notes
- SLOs are evaluated over a **rolling 28-day window**.
- Unless specified, targets apply per region (e.g., us-east, eu-west).
- We define both **p95 and p99** latency objectives for enterprise; best-effort uses p95 as primary.

### Availability SLOs by route and tier
| Route | Tier | Availability SLO | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `/v1/chat/completions` | Enterprise (Protected) | 99.95% | 429 overload-shed counts as failure. Quota 429 excluded. |
| `/v1/chat/completions` | Best-effort | 99.5% | 429 overload-shed excluded from availability; still tracked separately. |
| `/v1/embeddings` | Enterprise (Protected) | 99.95% | Batch requests included. |
| `/v1/embeddings` | Best-effort | 99.5% | 429 overload-shed excluded. |
| `/v1/rerank` | Enterprise (Protected) | 99.9% | Lower traffic; still protected. |
| `/v1/rerank` | Best-effort | 99.5% | 429 overload-shed excluded. |
| `/v1/completions` | Enterprise (Protected) | 99.9% | Legacy route; fewer dependencies but included for enterprise compatibility. |
| `/v1/completions` | Best-effort | 99.0% | Best-effort only; deprecation path in progress. |

### Latency SLOs by route and tier
Latency objectives are defined in terms of:
- **Chat streaming:** TTFB p95/p99
- **Non-streaming:** E2E p95/p99

| Route | Tier | Latency SLO (primary) | Latency SLO (secondary) | Measurement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming) | Enterprise (Protected) | TTFB p95 ≤ 450ms | TTFB p99 ≤ 900ms | Gateway TTFB |
| `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming) | Best-effort | TTFB p95 ≤ 900ms | (informational) p99 ≤ 1800ms | Gateway TTFB |
| `/v1/chat/completions` (non-streaming) | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 1.8s | E2E p99 ≤ 3.5s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/embeddings` | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 350ms | E2E p99 ≤ 800ms | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/embeddings` | Best-effort | E2E p95 ≤ 700ms | (informational) p99 ≤ 1.5s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/rerank` | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 550ms | E2E p99 ≤ 1.2s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/rerank` | Best-effort | E2E p95 ≤ 1.2s | (informational) p99 ≤ 2.5s | Gateway E2E |

**Notes / caveats**
- Latency SLOs assume nominal prompt and response sizes. Excessive prompt length or extreme max_tokens increases may be subject to policy limits; those requests are still included in latency metrics unless explicitly rejected by policy.
- Where fallback is permitted (route/model policy), latency SLI measures the actual served path; dashboards must annotate fallback activations.

## Error budgets
### Error budget calculation
For an SLO target **T** over a 28-day window:
- Error budget = **1 − T**

Examples:
- 99.95% availability ⇒ 0.05% error budget (≈ 21.6 minutes of downtime equivalent over 28 days)
- 99.5% availability ⇒ 0.5% error budget

We track budgets separately per:
- route
- region
- tier

### Error budget policy (what we do when we burn)
**Enterprise (Protected) routes**
- If burn is elevated, the default stance is **protect SLOs over throughput**.
- Allowed mitigations (in priority order):
 1) Tighten best-effort admission control thresholds (shed earlier)
 2) Temporarily reduce best-effort burst allowances
 3) Increase enterprise reserved capacity / pool weights (if available)
 4) Enable guarded fallback policies where contractually allowed
 5) As last resort: temporary enterprise throttling with exec/on-call approval and proactive comms

**Best-effort routes**
- Best-effort can be shed under pressure; we do not page purely on best-effort 429 shedding.
- If best-effort availability drops due to 5xx (not 429 overload-shed), we investigate as a normal reliability regression.

### Budget stop-the-line triggers
For enterprise protected routes, any of the following triggers a “stop the line” review in the weekly reliability sync (or async in #eng-sre if urgent):
- Availability error budget burn ≥ **50%** in 7 days
- p99 latency SLO violated for ≥ **2 hours** in a day (sustained)
- Overload shedding observed for enterprise traffic (non-zero sustained) outside planned game day / load test windows

## Alerting (paging + ticketing)
### Alert principles
- Page on **enterprise** impact (availability/latency) and on conditions that predict imminent enterprise impact.
- Do not page on expected best-effort shedding unless it indicates misconfiguration or runaway protection (e.g., shedding at low utilization).
- Use multi-window burn rate to avoid flapping.

### Enterprise availability burn alerts (recommended)
For each protected route x region:
- **Page (Sev2):** 28d SLO burn rate with multi-window thresholds
 - Fast burn: 5m and 1h windows > **14x** budget burn
 - Slow burn: 30m and 6h windows > **6x** budget burn
- **Ticket:** 2h and 1d windows > **2x** burn

### Enterprise latency alerts
For each protected route x region:
- **Page (Sev2):** p99 latency SLO violated for **15 minutes** AND admission control active (or queue depth high)
- **Ticket:** p95 latency SLO violated for **60 minutes**

### Overload protection operational alerts
These are predictive/guardrail alerts. Configure as:
- **Page (Sev2):** enterprise overload shedding sustained
 - enterprise `shed_rate` > **0.1%** for **10 minutes** (any protected route)
- **Ticket:** best-effort shedding unexpectedly high at low utilization
 - best-effort `shed_rate` > **20%** for **15 minutes** AND GPU utilization < **65%** (indicates policy mis-tuning or signal errors)
- **Ticket:** queue depth / scheduler lag sustained without corresponding shedding
 - queue depth > threshold for **10 minutes** with `admission_control_active=false` (indicates missing trigger wiring)

### Paging routing
- Primary: **#eng-oncall** and SRE pager rotation
- Secondary: **#eng-platform** for policy/gateway issues, **#eng-runtime** for scheduler lag/queue depth anomalies

## Dashboard requirements (minimum)
Every protected route must have:
- Availability by tier (enterprise vs best-effort)
- Latency p95/p99 by tier (and TTFB for streaming)
- 429 rate split by reason code (quota vs overload)
- shed_rate and admission_control_active
- queue depth and scheduler lag for backing pools
- Annotations for config changes, feature flag toggles, fallback activation

See the dashboard spec for panel/query naming conventions.

## Operational guidance
### How to interpret 429s for SLOs
- **Enterprise 429 overload-shed:** treat as incident-worthy and investigate capacity signals, admission thresholds, route budgets, and pool weights.
- **Best-effort 429 overload-shed:** expected under pressure; use this to validate the protection is working (enterprise should remain stable).
- **Quota 429 (any tier):** not an SLO failure; route to Support/Solutions for policy adjustment if needed.

### Change management
Changes that affect enterprise SLOs require:
- Feature flag + region canary
- Dashboard annotation
- Rollback plan
- Confirmed alert routing and runbook link in incident-bot message

## Ownership
- SLO definitions and alert policy: **SRE (Rafael Mendes / Aisha Bello)**
- Metric correctness and tagging: **Telemetry (Logan Wright)**
- Enforcement behavior (429 reason codes, gateway semantics): **API Gateway (Amara Diallo)**
- Priority routing/admission control behavior: **Smart Routing (Mina Haddad)**

## Revision history

BitTrade Scorer: scenario planner for INT8 / FP8 / 4-bit
author: Maya Patel
text:
Overview:

This working doc introduces the 'BitTrade' scorer — a compact, spreadsheet-friendly scoring heuristic to compare quantization choices (INT8, FP8, 4-bit) across cost, latency, and quality for production inference workloads. The goal is to provide product and infra owners a small decision surface they can use to quickly choose quantization families and safe rollouts based on measured evals and latency traces.

Audience and scope:
- Primary: product-optimize, serving-runtime, infra, and solutions engineering teams doing model serving cost optimizations.
- Scope: model variants targeted for serving (7B, 13B, 70B), online LLM workloads with SLOs (p99 latency targets, token budget), and offline batch embed workloads.
- Not in scope: model architecture search, training-time quantization-aware training experiments.

Design principles:
1) Simplicity: 1 numeric score that combines cost, latency, and quality differences so non-ML teams can rank choices.
2) Transparency: each component of the score is interpretable (savings or loss).
3) Tunable: weights can be adjusted per product line (e.g., chat vs bulk embedding).

Scoring formula (BitTrade v0.9):
- Inputs for each (model, quant) variant:
 - baseline_cost_per_1k_tokens (USD) — float
 - quant_cost_per_1k_tokens (USD) — float
 - baseline_p99_latency_ms (ms)
 - quant_p99_latency_ms (ms)
 - baseline_quality_score (higher is better, e.g., normalized QA accuracy, or 1 - relative PPL)
 - quant_quality_score

- Derived metrics (spreadsheet formula style):
 - cost_savings_pct = (baseline_cost_per_1k_tokens - quant_cost_per_1k_tokens) / baseline_cost_per_1k_tokens
 - latency_savings_pct = (baseline_p99_latency_ms - quant_p99_latency_ms) / baseline_p99_latency_ms
 - quality_loss_pct = (baseline_quality_score - quant_quality_score) / baseline_quality_score

- Score (higher is better):
 - score = w_cost * cost_savings_pct + w_latency * latency_savings_pct - w_quality * quality_loss_pct
 - default weights for general-purpose workloads: w_cost=0.4, w_latency=0.3, w_quality=0.5 (note quality penalized more; can be tuned per product)
 - normalize score to range roughly [-1, 1] in the spreadsheet by dividing by (w_cost + w_latency + w_quality) if desired.

Interpreting scores:
- score > 0.25: strong candidate for production rollout (subject to A/B eval).
- 0 <= score <= 0.25: marginal candidate; consider canary with strict rollback and hard quality checks.
- score < 0: do not roll out (quality degradation outweighs savings).

Example scenario table (CSV-friendly rows you can paste into a sheet):

scenario_name,model_name,baseline_cost_per_1k_tokens,quant,cost_per_1k_tokens,baseline_p99_ms,quant_p99_ms,baseline_quality,quant_quality,cost_savings_pct,latency_savings_pct,quality_loss_pct,score
chat-s1,redwood-open-7b,0.018,INT8,0.011,120,95,0.87,0.865,0.3889,0.2083,0.0138,0.4*0.3889+0.3*0.2083-0.5*0.0138
chat-s1,redwood-open-7b,0.018,FP8,0.013,120,100,0.87,0.868,0.2778,0.1667,0.0230,0.4*0.2778+0.3*0.1667-0.5*0.0230
embed-bulk,redwood-open-13b,0.045,4bit,0.028,220,190,0.94,0.90,0.3778,0.1364,0.0426,0.4*0.3778+0.3*0.1364-0.5*0.0426
qa-small,gptx-70b,0.12,INT8,0.08,340,260,0.92,0.91,0.3333,0.2353,0.0109,0.4*0.3333+0.3*0.2353-0.5*0.0109

Note: the last column is a formula placeholder; in your sheet replace with explicit numeric evaluation.

Guidance for metric selection:
- Quality metric: pick a product-aligned metric (e.g., Exact Match / F1 for QA, embedding cosine drop on benchmark, human-rated helpfulness). Convert all quality metrics to a normalized [0,1] scale prior to the score.
- Latency: use p99 end-to-end token throughput or cold-start-sensitive percentile depending on SLOs. For chat, p99 response tail matters more; for embeddings, median may be sufficient.
- Cost: include all infra cost per token (GPU amort + memory footprints + infra overhead). If you have reserved capacity discounts, use effective marginal cost.

Safety margins and rollout rules (recommended):
1) Safety thresholds: require quality_loss_pct <= 1.5% absolute (or <= X relative depending on metric) for any canary.
2) Latency SLO: quant_p99_ms must be <= baseline_p99_ms * 1.15 for chat SLOs (configurable).
3) Progressive rollout: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with quality and infra checks at each step.
4) Auto-fallback: if quality regression alert triggers or p99 latency exceeds threshold, automatically route traffic back to baseline model.

Use cases and quick heuristics:
- Cost-first background batch (embeddings): prioritize 4-bit or aggressive INT8 if score positive; relax quality requirements (w_quality = 0.2).
- Latency-critical chat: bump w_latency to 0.4, w_quality to 0.6, and prefer FP8/INT8 combos that preserve quality.
- Mixed workloads on Dedicated pools: compute per-model score, then solve knapsack-style allocation for GPU slots (separate spreadsheet that uses score as utility).

How to integrate into existing Optimize tooling:
- Provide a CSV upload endpoint for eval results (model, quant, cost, p99, quality) that returns computed score and recommended action.
- Add a 'BitTrade' preset to Optimize UI with adjustable weights and safety thresholds.
- Hook scoring into rollout automation (console): recommended canary percent and automatic guardrails.

Open questions / assumptions:
- Does cost_per_1k_tokens account for accounting-level reserved capacity amortization? Need infra finance input.
- Which quality normalization should be canonical across products (we have different units for QA vs embedding similarity)? Propose building product-level converters maintained in Optimize.
- How to reflect user-perceived quality thresholds (human eval) into an automated score? Consider a penalty multiplier for any metric that shows non-linear human sensitivity.

Next steps / action items:
- (Owner: Maya) Create canonical CSV template and example sheet (due 2024-10-12).
- (Owner: Liam) Wire up cost-per-token calculator that pulls reserved vs on-demand accounting (due 2024-11-01).
- (Owner: Sofia) Add data ingest for p99 traces and normalize pipeline (due 2024-11-15).
- (Owner: Ravi) Prototype UI slider controls for weights and rollout safety in Optimize console (due 2024-12-01).

Appendix A: small worked example (numeric evaluation)
- Baseline: redwood-open-7b, cost 0.018 /1k, p99 120ms, quality 0.87
- INT8: cost 0.011 /1k, p99 95ms, quality 0.865
 - cost_savings = (0.018-0.011)/0.018 = 0.3889
 - latency_savings = (120-95)/120 = 0.2083
 - quality_loss = (0.87-0.865)/0.87 = 0.0057 (~0.57%)
 - score = 0.4*0.3889 + 0.3*0.2083 - 0.5*0.0057 = 0.1556 + 0.0625 - 0.0029 = 0.2152
 - Interpretation: marginally good – could proceed to a small canary with strong quality checks.

Appendix B: quick checklist for SRE before rollout
- Validate KV cache behavior with quantized kernels (cold vs warm cache token profiles).
- Spike test at target throughput; verify tail latency under realistic batch mixes.
- Check memory growth and OOM rate on quantized builds.

Document history and notes:
- v0.1 initial concept (2024-09-18)
- v0.5 added normalization and example table (2024-10-05)
- v0.9 tuned weights and added rollout guidance (2024-12-02)

Comments and feedback welcome in-thread or addable as inline notes in the sheet.

title: Enforce response_contract with strict-mode and streaming safety for structured outputs
author: Maya Chen
text:
Motivation: Customers consuming structured outputs (response_format / response_contract) reported subtle inconsistencies when streaming partial tokens or when tool/function-calling pipes through the OpenAI compatibility layer. This PR introduces a first-class 'response_contract' concept with a strict validation mode, plus streaming-safety fallbacks and clearer error semantics. Goals are: 1) ensure schema-validated outputs are enforced for non-streaming and streaming flows, 2) provide graceful fallback to deterministic non-strict outputs when partial streams cannot be reconciled, 3) keep OpenAI compatibility behavior stable for existing integrations. Summary of changes: - Add ResponseContract type and parser in server/response_contract/ (Go) that canonicalizes response_format definitions and compiles a lightweight validator used at both runtime and in the streaming layer. - Implement strict_mode flag on response_format: default off for backward compatibility; when on, server rejects final output that fails validation with structured error codes. - Streaming safety: streaming layer now buffers and validates schema-consistent JSON tokens as they arrive. If a stream contains irreversible partial output (ambiguous trailing token) the stream triggers an automatic graceful fallback: continue streaming with an explanatory structured warning event and final validation performed server-side; on strict_mode the request is marked failed and client receives structured error with validation details. - Tool/function-calling: function call responses are validated against function-defined output_contracts and tool results are re-validated when embedded into the main response. Added integration points so tool plugins can opt out for legacy tools. - OpenAI compatibility layer: maintain previous behavior by default. For API calls that set response_contract but also use the openai_compat flag, the compatibility layer forwards the response_contract and returns OpenAI-shaped error payloads when compatibility mode is requested. - Error model: introduce structured error codes: RESPONSE_CONTRACT_VIOLATION, STREAMING_AMBIGUOUS_STATE, TOOL_OUTPUT_MISMATCH. Each error includes a machine-friendly code and a human message. - Telemetry & observability: new metrics (response_contract.validation_failures, response_contract.stream_fallbacks) and traces tagged with contract_id and strict_mode. - Tests: added unit and integration tests for strict/non-strict, streaming fallback, tool-calling permutations, and openai_compat scenarios. Rollout plan: 1) Feature gated behind a config flag response_contract.strict_mode in runtime config (default false). 2) Canary rollout to 5% traffic for 48h with alerting on validation_failures > 0.5% of requests; automatic rollback script included. 3) Enable for customers who opt-in via Console or API. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is unchanged; schema enforcement requires explicit response_contract in the request or customer opt-in. Known limitations: - Extremely large schemas (thousands of properties) have validation CPU cost; we include a budgeted short-circuit path that treats validation as async for very large schemas (results reported via post-check webhook) — documented in release notes. - Streaming buffer trades small extra latency for correctness; we tuned default buffer window to 150ms which we found acceptable in benchmarks. Related work items: Linear ENG-1428 (contract validation core), ENG-1499 (streaming safety), SUP-3312 (customer-reported tool mismatch). Checklist: - [x] Add runtime types and validator - [x] Streaming buffer + fallback path - [x] Tool/function calling validation hooks - [x] OpenAI compatibility mapping + error translation - [x] Metrics and tracing - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Docs and console flag entry Observability and alerts: added Grafana panel reference (redwood/response-contract) and an alert rule for response_contract.validation_failures. Documentation: see docs/response-contract.md and SDK notes for Python/TS on shape of errors and opt-in flows.

Leo Martinez: please add a short-circuit path for very large schemas to avoid blocking the worker thread — otherwise LGTM.
Maya Chen: added async short-circuit + webhook option (see last commit).
Aisha Kapoor: can we expose an API-level explain() helper that returns the schema path that failed? Suggest adding minimal support in the SDKs.
Maya Chen: added explain() shim in SDKs and a non-blocking explain endpoint; it's safe-guarded behind the opt-in flag.
Ben Howard: integration tests flaked on first CI run due to flaky streaming e2e; re-ran and all green.
QA (SRE): confirm the defaults are off and telemetry emits when enabled; verified on canary.
Product: confirm messaging and console UX for opt-in — accepted.

- Introduces response_contract with optional strict_mode for schema-validated structured outputs.
- Streaming safety: automatic fallback and explicit STREAMING_AMBIGUOUS_STATE error when streaming cannot maintain schema guarantees.
- Tool/function outputs are validated against declared output_contracts; new TOOL_OUTPUT_MISMATCH error code.
- OpenAI compatibility remains the default; setting openai_compat returns OpenAI-shaped validation errors.
- New telemetry: response_contract.validation_failures, response_contract.stream_fallbacks.

This PR aims to be conservative: strict_mode is opt-in. We will monitor validation_failures and tool mismatch rates during the canary window before recommending wide enablement.

title: Introduce priority token lanes and invocation trellis dashboard for fine-grained cost/latency attribution
author: Ananya Rao
text:
Motivation: We currently attribute token cost and latency at the invocation level, but important operational signal is lost when tokens with different runtime priorities are aggregated (e.g., user-interactive vs background prefetch vs system prompts). This PR introduces a lightweight runtime tag — priority token lanes — plus an invocation trellis visualization to expose per-lane token counts, cost, and latency timelines. Summary of changes: (1) Runtime: add token_priority enum and propagate as a per-token metadata bit in the invocation envelope; metrics emitter tags token counters and histogram labels with priority_lane; tracing: add lane-aware spans and a compact lane ID to trace attributes; (2) Metrics: instrument lane-scoped counters, p99/p50 token-latency histograms per lane, lane-tagged CPU/GPU kernel time estimates; (3) Dashboards: new "Invocation Trellis" dashboard that lays out lane timelines across an invocation, plus a cost breakdown panel that slices spend by lane and model stage; (4) Alerts: add SLO-oriented alert rule templates that optionally ignore low-priority lanes (configurable) and a lane-based suppression gate for noisy background workloads; (5) Telemetry rollout and compatibility: metrics use new tag priority_lane with a fallback value "unspecified" to preserve compatibility; all changes are guarded behind a feature flag telemetry.priority_lanes with gradual rollout. Implementation notes and decisions: - We chose an enumerated lane set (interactive, background_prefetch, system, analytic) to limit cardinality and make aggregation simple. - Token-level tagging is emitted only for the first token of each contiguous lane segment by default (sampling path) to avoid high cardinality in high-throughput paths; full token tagging can be enabled for debug traces. - Tracing adds a short lane_id to spans (1 byte) to keep overhead low; OpenTelemetry attributes are used so downstream collectors can use the tag. Rollout plan: start feature-flagged in staging for 48h (telemetry.priority_lanes=partial), run synthetic generation at 100inv/s and evaluate cost deltas; open to 10% of production traffic after gating on no perf regressions and <0.5% increase in metric cardinality. Migration notes for users: dashboards are opt-in for accounts; customers who use tenant-level billing reports will see lane slices only after the platform enables the flag for their tenant. Checklist: - [x] Runtime token tag + propagation - [x] Lane-aware metrics and histograms - [x] Invocation Trellis Grafana dashboard JSON - [x] Alert templates and runbook additions - [x] Unit + integration tests for tag propagation - [x] Perf microbenchmarks and budget evaluation - [x] Feature flag gating and staged rollout Testing performed: unit tests for envelope propagation, integration tests against a local collectd and jaeger stack, performance microbench comparing main runtime with and without lane tagging (median latency diff +0.3%). Known limitations: high-cardinality workloads that enable full per-token tagging may increase cardinality — we provide a limiter configuration. Future work: auto-classify lanes based on request metadata and a per-tenant sampling policy for lane tagging.

Miguel Torres: Can we bound cardinality more aggressively? Suggested enum-only approach — agree to keep enums and add limiter (response: added limiter config and default sampling path)
Kai Nguyen: Small nit on PromQL labels; prefer 'lane' over 'priority_lane' for consistency (response: kept priority_lane to be explicit but added alias rule in metrics exporter)
Lena Schmidt: Please add a runbook entry describing expected cost delta (response: added runbook note and release notes)
QA (reply): Integration fixtures show stable latency; requested a follow-up to add end-to-end telemetry check in canary pipeline (response: created ENG-5499)

title: On‑Prem Kubernetes: Proactive Upgrade Playbook + Terraform module notes
author: Nadia Chen
text:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for planning and executing proactive, low-downtime upgrades of on‑prem Kubernetes clusters (bare metal & vSphere). It also captures notes for Terraform modules used in provisioning control/worker planes and BMC/vSphere resources. This doc is intentionally pragmatic: checklists, commands, failure modes, and module-level guidance for the infra repo.

Scope and goals:
- Supported environments: bare-metal with IPMI/BMC provisioning and vSphere VMs managed by Terraform.
- Goals: 
 - Zero-to-minimal customer-facing downtime for control plane and worker upgrades.
 - Reproducible Terraform workflow for bootstrapping/repairing clusters.
 - Clear rollback and node-replacement playbooks.
- Not in scope: application-level migration strategies (assume apps have PodDisruptionBudgets or can tolerate rolling restarts).

Assumptions and preconditions:
- Cluster created with kubeadm (or upstream kubeadm-like flow) and containerd as CRI.
- All nodes are reachable by the control plane and have working NTP (chrony) and DNS entries.
- External load balancer in front of control plane (HAProxy or NSX) with health checks.
- Persistent storage: Rook (Ceph) or external NFS; operations differ — see Storage section.
- Terraform state is locked (remote backend like S3-compatible or HashiCorp Cloud).

Inventory checklist before upgrade:
- kubectl cluster-info and node list 
 - `kubectl get nodes -o wide`
- Control plane node health: `kubectl get componentstatuses` and `kubectl -n kube-system get pods -o wide`
- API server latency check: sample `curl` to LB VIP and to each control-plane ip:443
- Backup: etcd snapshot + upload to object storage
 - `ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /tmp/etcd-snap.db --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=... --cert=... --key=...`
- Kubeconfig export: store a copy off-cluster
- Prometheus/alerts: ensure no unresolved critical alerts (or acknowledge them before starting)

Pre-upgrade quick wins (reduce blast radius):
- Ensure PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs) exist for critical apps
- Ensure fewest number of daemonsets that will be restarted (eg node-exporter fine)
- Confirm nodeAutoUpgrade not enabled in Terraform (we want manual control)

Terraform module notes (infra repo):
- Module topology: split modules for (1) provisioning primitives (bmc/ipmi or vsphere), (2) base OS image + cloud-init, (3) network/dns, (4) k8s-cluster (kubeadm configs, bootstrap tokens, kubeconfigs), (5) load-balancer and monitoring hooks.
- Recommended variable patterns: minimal required in root module, everything else defaulted in child modules. Keep secrets out of repo: use vault/TF_VARs or KMS-encrypted file.
- Important module variables: `bmc_username`, `bmc_password_secret_id`, `image_url`, `ssh_pub_keys`, `cluster_name`, `kubeadm_config_map`, `control_plane_count`, `worker_count`, `vsphere_datacenter`, `vsphere_datastore`, `lb_vip`.
- Outputs to expose: `kubeconfig`, `control_plane_ips`, `lb_vip`, `bmc_inventory_ids`, `terraform_provider_versions` (for audits).
- Apply order: 1) provisioning (BMC/vSphere) 2) base OS + cloud-init 3) network/dns 4) LB 5) bootstrap control plane 6) join workers. Use `-target` sparingly for repair.
- Tainted resource policy: prefer recreating worker VMs via `terraform taint module.worker.vm[...]` over in-place upgrades for kernel/OS drift. Record tainted indexes in PR description.
- Recommended provider pinning: `hashicorp/vsphere ~> 2.4` and `projektfarm/ipmi ~> 0.3` (adjust to current repo).

Provisioning & bootstrapping notes (bare-metal):
- PXE/iPXE steps: keep a versioned iPXE script in infra repo. Example snippet to inject the image URL and cloud-init metadata: `kernel http://images.internal/vmlinuz initrd=initramfs.img ip=dhcp url=$IMAGE_URL console=ttyS1`
- Cloud-init: include `runcmd` steps to register SSH key, write kubeadm join token placeholder, and call `systemd` unit to wait for the provisioning service.
- BMC: ensure BMC users have limited privileges; use out-of-band network. For IPMI flashing and power cycle tests run a dry-run before maintenance window.

Control plane upgrade strategy (kubeadm flow):
1) Backup etcd snapshot + verify integrity.
2) Upgrade kubeadm binary on first control plane node.
3) Run `kubeadm upgrade plan` to list supported versions.
4) Upgrade control plane one node at a time: 
 - `kubectl cordon <node>`
 - `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --pod-selector='!critical'` (adjust pod-selector for infra pods)
 - `kubeadm upgrade apply v1.X.Y` on that node (control-plane upgrade path per kubeadm docs)
 - Restart kubelet if needed and verify `kubectl get cs` and `kubectl -n kube-system get pods -o wide`
 - Uncordon once healthy: `kubectl uncordon <node>`
5) Repeat for remaining control-plane nodes.
6) Upgrade kubelets and kubectl on workers (rolling, drain each worker, upgrade kubelet, restart, uncordon).

Notes for low-downtime control-plane upgrades:
- Keep the LB in front of control plane with health checks that tolerate short API restarts.
- Do not upgrade two control plane nodes at the same time unless you have quorum considerations and etcd cluster resilience tested.
- Validate webhook admission controllers and CRD conversion webhooks; if they block, pause their pods before control-plane upgrades.

Worker upgrade strategy (rolling):
- For each worker: 
 1) `kubectl cordon <worker>`
 2) `kubectl drain <worker> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data` 
 3) Recreate or upgrade OS/kernel/container runtime (use orchestration: SSH+Ansible or terraform replace)
 4) Upgrade kubelet & kube-proxy binary to target version 
 5) `systemctl restart kubelet` and verify `kubectl get nodes` shows Ready
 6) `kubectl uncordon <worker>`
- If large stateful workloads present, ensure successful failover of PVs (Rook) or increase PDBs accordingly.

Stateful storage (Rook/Ceph) specific guidance:
- Never drain more than one Ceph OSD per node at a time. Prefer OSD graceful eviction using `ceph osd crush reweight` and `ceph osd out` if replacing nodes.
- Upgrade Rook operator first, verify health, then upgrade Ceph cluster. Follow upstream Rook docs for the operator lifecycle.
- For external NFS, ensure the server can handle reconnects; plan a maintenance window if you need to move NFS pods.

Rollback and recovery patterns:
- Etcd rollback: restore snapshot to a restored cluster or a single-control-plane node (documented step-by-step with etcdctl restore flags).
- Node failure mid-upgrade: if a control-plane node fails during upgrade, remove it from LB, complete the upgrade on remaining nodes, then reprovision the failed node from terraform (taint + apply) and rejoin.
- Recreate worker: `terraform taint module.workers.vm[index]` -> `terraform apply` will recreate and join via cloud-init join token or SSM hook.
- If control plane becomes unhealthy and quorum is lost, follow emergency steps: 
 - Isolate offending control plane nodes, attempt to restore etcd from last known good snapshot to one node, then scale control plane up.

Pre-flight checklist (run immediately before window):
- All backups taken & verified (etcd snapshot, config backups)
- Slack channel + paging on-call + runbook owner present
- Block automated CI/CD deploys to cluster during upgrade
- Firewall and NAT rules checked so LB health checks will succeed
- A copy of terraform state and working directory available on jump host

Quick commands and cheatsheet:
- List versions: `kubectl version --short`
- Run etcd snapshot (on control plane): see earlier etcdctl example
- Kubeadm upgrade plan: `kubeadm upgrade plan`
- Drain worker: `kubectl drain node-05 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data`
- Recreate VM (terraform): `terraform taint module.workers.vm[3] && terraform apply -target=module.workers.module.vm[3]`

vSphere-specific notes:
- Use the vsphere module to create templates; keep templates immutable and version-tagged.
- Use vCenter alarms to detect VM-level issues during the window.
- Prefer vSphere Tools upgrades outside the kernel/CRI upgrade window.
- If performing storage vMotion or datastore maintenance, ensure CSI driver is updated first and PVs have `WaitForFirstConsumer` or proper topology.

Common failure modes and mitigations:
- API server flapping: temporarily increase LB health-check threshold and give control plane more time to become healthy; pause upgrade and investigate controller-manager logs.
- Node stuck in NotReady after upgrade: check CRI socket, containerd logs, and certificate expiry. If kubelet fails for kernel reasons, revert to known-good kernel or reprovision VM.
- Etcd quorum loss: restore snapshot to new control plane; follow emergency restore playbook.

Post-upgrade validation checklist:
- All nodes Ready and schedulable
- Critical system pods in kube-system are Running and Ready
- Smoke tests for key APIs (list namespaces, create job, create CRD, delete)
- Load testing for control plane if possible (small synthetic load)
- Metrics and dashboards show stable latency and no large increases in API error rates
- Create a short postmortem if anything non-trivial happened

Open TODOs & follow-ups (repo tasks):
- [ ] Add automated preflight check script to infra repo that validates NTP, DNS, LB health, and etcd snapshot.
- [ ] Move BMC secrets into Vault with Kubernetes auth and rotate weekly.
- [ ] Add terraform `plan` -> `apply` gating with a Jenkins/GitHub Actions job that annotates PRs with target nodes.
- [ ] Build a small `drain-and-upgrade` operator that can perform safe rolling upgrades for non-critical apps (RFC in CONFLUENCE-8492).

Notes to the reader: this is a working draft. If you are executing an upgrade, copy this doc into a temporary maintenance doc and stamp your commands into a runbook. If any step is unclear, call the on‑call infra engineer in Slack channel #infra-ops immediately.

Revision history:
- 2025-11-12: initial draft (Nadia Chen)
- 2026-01-05: added Terraform module recommendations and taint policy (Ethan Park)
- 2026-02-08: added Rook/Ceph notes and vSphere hints (Sofia Martinez)

Contact: Nadia Chen (nchen@redwood-inference.com)

title: Interim onboarding equipment acceptance form and temporary VPN token escrow process
text:
Background: HR is piloting a faster new-hire onboarding flow for international hires that splits device shipment and role activation. We need a short-term process to accept custody of devices and to escrow VPN tokens/service-accounts while legal and shipping paperwork complete. This ticket captures the proposed interim acceptance form, controls, and asks IT/Security for sign-off and implementation guidance.

Without a clear interim acceptance and escrow process teams are either delaying hires (slower ramp) or shipping devices to personal addresses and sharing VPN tokens informally (security and audit risk). This affects ~5 hires/month in the pilot cohort and any future international bulk shipping windows.

1) Provide a one-page interim acceptance form (digital) that HR collects and stores in a secured S3 bucket with access logged.
2) Issue time-limited VPN token placed in company-managed escrow vault (KMS-backed secret with 7-day TTL) and mark the hire's account as 'onboarding-limited' until ID verification and desk review complete.
3) Require device serials recorded; device activation blocked in fleet MDM until 'verified' flag toggled by IT.

- Is placing a short-lived VPN token in a KMS-backed secret vault acceptable for audit purposes?
- What minimum TTL is recommended to avoid repeated manual rotations while limiting exposure?
- Any objections to storing scanned acceptance form in secured S3 path: s3://redwood-onboarding/pilot-2026-03?
- Should we create a dedicated onboarding service account or reuse existing loaner pool accounts?

Security: initial check with Security shows KMS-backed secrets with TTL are supported by our vault provider; audit log retention must be set to 90 days for pilot. IT: Fleet MDM can enforce 'non-active' until verification but requires a manual API call to flip 'verified' flag for now. HR: digital signature via DocuSign prototype works but needs a legal clause re: personal shipping addresses.

1) Create s3 path and apply bucket policy for grp-hr-onboarding and grp-it-ops.
2) Provision vault secret template and test TTL rotation workflow in staging.
3) Add a 'onboarding-limited' role in IAM and a small automation to attach it to new hires until verification.
4) Document manual steps for toggling MDM 'verified' flag and assign rota for first 30 days.

2026-03-10 09:12 - Maya Chen (HR): Opening ticket after pilot retro; attaching initial form draft to Confluence. Requesting IT/Security review before launching second cohort.
2026-03-10 10:05 - Alex Rivera (Security): TL;DR - KMS secrets with 7-day TTL is reasonable for pilot if audit retention is 90 days. Need legal to sign off on address clause.
2026-03-10 15:41 - Priya Patel (IT Ops): We can gate MDM activation. I'll add a small endpoint to flip verification but it will be manual for the first two weeks; automation can follow.
2026-03-11 08:22 - Devon Alvarez (Assignee): Created staging vault secret and tested TTL rotation. PR for IAM role drafted: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/1827
2026-03-12 11:05 - Legal (via comment): Suggest adding explicit liability language for shipments to non-company addresses; will provide redline by EOD 2026-03-13.

(Pending) Awaiting Legal redline and Security final sign-off. Once approved IT will deploy the onboarding-limited role and the vault secret template to prod. HR will pilot with 5 hires and report back after 30 days.

title: Copperfield Nimbus Solutions — Dedicated sizing + security notes (GTM working doc)
author: Diego Alvarez
text:
Company: Copperfield Nimbus Solutions (copperfieldnimbus.com)
Segment: mid-market collaboration SaaS (in-app assistant + enterprise doc search)
Current sales posture (as of 2026-03-18): moving from Evaluation → Procurement/Legal (Dedicated). Forecast is still tentatively May but risk if procurement cycles.
Primary contacts: Maya Chen (buyer/champion), Tom (infra lead).
Redwood team: Diego (SE), Priya (CSM/Security).

Hosted API trial validated UX/quality. Next phase is Dedicated primarily for (a) predictable tail latency under chat concurrency, (b) data isolation, (c) VPC connectivity. Customer is also asking for clearer unit economics for a mixed chat + embeddings workload.

Updates vs earlier assumptions:
- Their nightly embedding/index job is larger than first stated; they want a narrower window (finish before 06:00 local).
- They walked back the strictest latency ask slightly for p50, but are more focused on consistent p95 during peak chat concurrency.
- Security team confirmed SOC 2 + audit logs are required; data residency is now "US only" (not multi-region).

Use cases: support-agent, doc-search, embeddings, reranking, summarization, chat.
Traffic shape (latest projection from 2026-03-12 sizing follow-up):
- Baseline: 60 QPS
- Expected growth (6 months): 140 QPS
- Peak: 260 QPS (daytime sync + product launches)
Concurrency:
- Planning for ~150 concurrent chat sessions at peak (KV cache active)
Token mix (from Hosted trial + updated estimate):
- ~55% short (<=64 tokens)
- ~35% medium (64–512 tokens)
- ~10% long (>512 tokens)
Average tokens/request now modeled as:
- avg request tokens ~200
- avg response tokens ~160
- combined per-request tokens ~360
Monthly token forecast:
- Base case: ~1.5B tokens/month
- Burst/headroom planning: up to ~3.0B tokens/month during launch months
Latency targets (customer-stated):
- Chat: p50 < 180ms, p95 < 450ms under peak concurrency (measured from their app server)
- Embeddings: throughput prioritized over single-request latency; must clear nightly batch within ~4 hours

NOTE: This is a GTM working plan; final sizing pending last-mile model choice + safety/quality gate.

Proposed tiers (3 environments):
1) Dev/Staging
- Goal: functional testing + smaller-scale load tests
- Suggested: 1 small compute slice; allow queueing; minimal reserved

2) Prod Baseline
- Goal: cover ~60–140 QPS steady-state with stable p95 for chat
- Suggested: reserve for baseline concurrency; allow burst scaling for periodic spikes

3) Prod Peak
- Goal: handle 260 QPS peaks + higher concurrent sessions during sync events
- Suggested: additional reserved capacity OR pre-warmed burst window during known events

Open model preference:
- Customer prefers "medium/large" class models with fallback.
- Updated preference: default medium model for most chat; fallback to smaller model for low-criticality requests and to protect p95 under burst.

Autoscaling expectation:
- They want a clear story for steady QPS + flash bursts (their sync jobs can ramp quickly). We should demo the scale-up behavior and the expected time-to-serve at peak.

Customer requirements (confirmed on 2026-03-14 security follow-up):
- SSO via SAML for admin portal (required)
- SOC 2 report (required)
- Audit logging (required) with retention: 13 months (same as earlier)
- KMS integration (required); prefer customer-managed keys pattern
- Data residency: US only (updated; previously discussed generically as "data residency")
- VPC deployment + VPC peering (required)

Additional asks that emerged:
- They asked about SCIM provisioning (nice-to-have; not a hard blocker for initial launch).
- They asked for a standard DPA + subprocessors list early in legal review.

Network/VPC notes:
- Blocker was "network peering details"; Tom confirmed they can do standard VPC peering with a fixed CIDR reservation on their side. Need to schedule a peering window and confirm any MTU constraints + routing rules.

Audit log scope clarification (action item):
- They want admin actions + model invocation metadata (request id, timestamps, org/project id), but do NOT want raw prompt/response in logs by default. (We should confirm our defaults and configuration knobs.)

Earlier blocker: "clarify token pricing for mixed chat + embedding workload".
Current direction discussed internally:
- Present separate line items for chat/completions tokens vs embeddings tokens to keep the mental model simple.
- Include committed throughput tier(s) plus burst pricing.
- Provide a worksheet that maps their QPS/concurrency/token-mix assumptions into monthly cost ranges (base vs burst month).

Customer sensitivity:
- They are comparing vs OpenAI + Anthropic and an internal inference stack. Primary value props they cite: predictable latency + data isolation + simpler ops than in-house.

As of 2026-03-18:
- Finance approval: still pending (internal budget approval on their side)
- Procurement/legal timeline risk: they requested DPA + subprocessors list before redlines
- Technical: final confirmation of token mix under production UI launch (we only have trial data)
- Success criteria: need explicit definition of "acceptable" p95 at peak + measurement methodology (their app server vs our gateway metrics)

2) Priya: share SOC 2 package + audit logging overview + KMS integration pattern; include data residency (US-only) statement. Due 2026-03-19.
3) Schedule VPC peering window with Tom + Redwood SRE (include CIDR/routing checklist). Target week of 2026-03-24.
4) Pricing: deliver mixed workload worksheet with separate chat vs embeddings estimates + committed vs burst. Due 2026-03-22.

title: Audit retention: role-aware filtered data dump
author: Aisha Rahman
text:
Provide a secure, role-aware bulk dump capability for audit logs from the Console that supports CSV, JSON, and NDJSON outputs while respecting RBAC v2 filters, retention policies, and SSO-backed admin permissions. The goal is to let enterprise admins and compliance teams extract query-scoped audit slices (time-window, actor, resource, action, outcome) for offline analysis and e-discovery without exposing redacted fields to users who lack privileges. Must handle multi-GB exports via cursored incremental downloads, enforce rate and size limits, and produce manifest metadata (query, applied filters, snapshot_time, schema_version).

Admins with export permission can request a filtered dump from Console and receive a download link when ready
RBAC v2 filters are enforced server-side; results never include fields flagged as 'sensitive' unless requester has explicit allow-list role
Supports CSV, JSON, NDJSON formats; manifest with schema and applied filters included in export bundle
Large exports (>500MB) are produced as multipart blobs with cursored pagination and resumable downloads
All export requests are logged to an immutable audit stream (separate from the exported data) with requester identity from SSO/SAML
Exports respect tenant-level retention and cannot retrieve records older than retention cutoff unless super-admin override is used (and is itself audited)

Server-side query engine will apply RBAC v2 masking rules before serialization
Use cursor-based incremental listing (time+id cursor) to avoid deep OFFSET scans on BigTable/ClickHouse
Export worker will stream directly to pre-signed object storage to minimize memory; manifest JSON recorded in metadata store
Encryption-in-transit and at-rest required; generated download links expire after configurable TTL
Rate limit export initiation per org and throttle per concurrent worker to preserve runtime throughput

Decided against synchronous on-the-fly CSV generation for >100k rows to avoid blocking request threads; background worker + presigned link chosen
Chose cursor (time+id) approach over purely time-windowed pagination to ensure deterministic ordering during concurrent writes
Opted to implement NDJSON as default for JSON exports to simplify incremental parsing for downstream tooling
Will gate inclusion of 'request_payload' and 'response_content' fields behind a separate sensitive-data allow-list to reduce blast radius

Test with synthetic 50M-row dataset to validate cursor stability and worker memory bounds
Verify RBAC masking across combinations: org-admin, security-reader, billing-admin, auditor_role
Test resumable multipart downloads and resume after simulated network failure
Pen test for indirect disclosure via manifest metadata (avoid including raw user identifiers unless necessary)
