title: Adaptive SLO Shepherding & Capacity Fencing Playbook
author: Aria Chen
text:
Overview

This playbook codifies an adaptive approach we call "SLO shepherding" for day-to-day SRE operations: proactively protecting critical SLOs by applying capacity fencing, tenant reservations, and temporary degradation policies while preserving error-budget fairness across tenants. It combines measurement, automated tooling, and human guardrails to avoid surprise outages and prevent long reconciliations after incidents.

Scope & applicability

- Applies to multi-tenant inference services: inference-gateway, model-host-pool, and routing-proxy.
- Intended for services with latency or availability SLOs and where capacity is a constrained resource (GPU pools, KV cache memory, or token throughput).
- Not intended for non-production dev environments or single-tenant dedicated customers (those use dedicated capacity contracts).

Goals

1. Keep critical customer-facing SLOs within target (example target: 99.95% availability monthly; p99 latency < 350ms for small text-gen).
2. Avoid global emergency scaling that undermines fairness: use fenced capacity to protect tiered SLAs.
3. Provide clear, repeatable runbooks for Capacity Fencing events and Post-Incident Review evidence.

Key service SLOs (examples)

| Service | SLO (primary) | Window | Alert threshold |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| inference-gateway | p99 latency < 350ms | 30d rolling | p99 > 350ms for 30m |
| model-host-pool | request success rate >= 99.95% | 30d rolling | 1h error rate > 0.5% |
| routing-proxy | availability >= 99.9% | 30d rolling | 15m availability < 99% |

Error budget policy summary

- Error budget = 1 - SLO. Consumption is measured at the service-level per 30-day window.
- Progressive response tiers based on burn rate (30m burn-rate windows):
 1. Mild burn (burn rate < 2x): notify owner, enable additional tracing.
 2. Elevated burn (2x–5x): restrict non-critical background workloads; throttle batch ingestion by 30%.
 3. Severe burn (>5x or >50% of remaining budget): apply Capacity Fencing (see below) and escalate to SRE lead.

Capacity fencing model (high level)

Capacity fencing = temporarily reserving a percentage of pool resources for critical tenants or SLO classes, enforcing soft quotas for lower tiers, and enabling rapid rollback steps.

Rules of thumb for fence sizing:
- Critical SLO pool reservation = max(10% of pool, 2x typical peak tokens/sec of top-3 tenants).
- Hedge for warmup = +15% additional reservation for model-host-pool to cover KV cache pressure.
- Minimum fence time = 5 minutes; maximum auto-fence time = 2 hours before manual review.

Reservation tiers (example configuration)

| Tier | Guarantee | Typical enforcement |
|---|---|---|
| Tier-1 (platinum) | Hard reservation (capacity locked) | Dedicated slots on model-host-pool; preempt lower tiers if needed |
| Tier-2 (gold) | Soft reservation (priority) | Priority queuing + token-priority shaping |
| Tier-3 (standard) | Best-effort | Subject to throttles and batch shedding |

Runbook: Emergency Capacity Fence (quick steps)

1. Trigger conditions (one or more):
 - SLO alert enters "Severe burn" state.
 - Sustained autoscaler failure causing accelerated eviction.
 - Cross-region saturation (>90% regional GPU pool for >10m).
2. Initial triage (first 10 minutes):
 - Confirm telemetry: run `curl -s https://telemetry-intake/api/v1/query -d 'service=inference-gateway&metric=p99_latency'`.
 - Notify on-call SRE in #oncall-sre and update incident channel.
 - Snapshot current capacity: `kubectl get pods -l app=model-host-pool -o wide` and `redis-cli INFO memory` for KV cache standing.
3. Apply a temporary fence:
 - Invoke capacity controller API: `POST /ops/reservations` with payload (example below).
 - Start with a conservative fence (reserve 10% of pool) and monitor p99 for 5m.
 - If no improvement, escalate to reserve 25% and optionally reduce batch ingestion.
4. Throttles and graceful degradation:
 - Enable token-priority shaping for background tenants.
 - Reduce max_context_length to 1024 for standard tier: toggle via feature-flag `feature.max_context_reduction`.
5. Communication and timeline:
 - Update incident channel every 10 minutes with CPU/GPU util, p99 latency, and error budget remaining.
 - If fence stands >30 minutes, convene SRE lead + product owner decision.

Example reservation payload (YAML)

```
# POST /ops/reservations
service: model-host-pool
scope: region-us-west-2
reservation_id: fence-20280305-aria
duration_minutes: 60
reservations:
 - tenant_group: tier-1
 reserved_gpu_shares: 12
 - tenant_group: tier-2
 reserved_gpu_shares: 6
policy: preempt-lower-tiers
auto_expire: true
```

Automated tooling hooks

- Capacity Controller: `ops-capacity-controller` (internal service) exposes `/ops/reservations` and `/ops/preview-reservation` for dry runs.
- SLO Watcher: `slo-watcher` computes burn rates and notifies `oncall-sre` via PagerDuty when thresholds met.
- Telemetry dashboards: `slo-ops/inference-gateway` (Grafana); ensure p99, p50, error-rate, GPU-util, and KV-cache-hitrate are visible on one pane.

Incident review & evidence standards

Every event where Capacity Fencing was applied must include the following artifacts in the post-incident package:
- Timeline: minute-level timeline of actions (who, when, what).
- Telemetry exports: p99 series, error-rate, GPU util, queue depth for the incident window and 24h prior.
- Reservation decision rationale: why fence size and duration chosen.
- Rollback artifacts: commands used to revert fences and toggles.
- RCA summary (5–10 sentences) and remediation owner with expected completion date.

Incident review checklist (required fields)

1. Was the fence auto-triggered or manual?
2. Source of overload (traffic surge, model regression, autoscaler bug, external region issue).
3. Evidence that fence improved SLOs (graphs or quant stats).
4. Any customer-facing degradation or API-level contract changes.
5. Follow-up actions (who and ETA).

SRE operational playbook: day-to-day shepherding tasks

- Daily: Review SLO Watcher digest between 09:00–10:00 PT. Note tenants with persistent high burn.
- Weekly: Run fairness audit script to verify reserved vs actual consumption: `python tools/fairness_audit.py --window 7d`.
- Monthly: Recompute reservation baselines based on 95th percentile token/sec per tenant and schedule capacity rebalancing if trend >15% growth.

On-call procedures and escalations

- First responder: apply temporary soft throttles and open incident.
- Second responder (SRE lead): evaluate fence sizing, approve hard reservations.
- Product/security escalations: required if degradation affects compliance-sensitive tenants or if data-plane failures expose PII concerns.

Rollout & verification for changes to fencing logic

1. Feature-flag behind `ops.fencing.v2`.
2. Canary in staging with synthetic traffic profile that simulates: spike, slow-burning sustained increase, and cache-heavy workload.
3. Metrics to validate: p99 latency reduction, fairness index (see appendix), and false-positive fence rate.

Ownership and governance

- Primary owner: eng-sre (team: runtime-capacity), oncall rota: eng-sre/runtime-capacity.
- Product alignment: product-inference owns SLA tiers definitions.
- Quarterly review: SRE lead to present fencing efficacy in reliability-initiatives retro.

Appendix: fairness index and sample queries

- Fairness index (simple): FI = reserved_share / observed_consumption. Target FI ∈ [0.8, 1.2] over a 7d window.

Sample PromQL (pseudocode)
```
sum(rate(tokens_served[5m])) by (tenant_group) / sum(rate(gpu_seconds[5m])) by (tenant_group)
```

SQL-like query to compute error budget spend per tenant (example):
```
SELECT tenant_id, SUM(1 - success_rate) AS budget_used
FROM slo_events
WHERE service = 'inference-gateway' AND ts >= '2028-02-01'
GROUP BY tenant_id;
```

Related pages & references

- See /eng-sre/runbooks/slo-provisioning-and-backfill-orchestration-runbook-2026 for reservation lifecycle.
- See /eng-sre/operational-tooling/slo-observability-pipeline-design-and-validation-2025 for telemetry instrumentation standards.

Change log

- 2028-01-10 (Aria Chen) — Drafted initial playbook.
- 2028-02-20 (reviewers) — Incorporated fairness audit steps and sample payloads.
- 2028-03-05 (published) — Clarified alert tiers and fence auto-expiry behavior.

Contact

Primary owner: eng-sre/runtime-capacity (alias: #eng-sre-runtime-capacity). For immediate help, ping oncall-sre or escalate via PagerDuty rule `slo-shepherding-pager`.

title: RFC: Export Redwood Private audit logs to customer-owned object storage
author: Connor OBrien
text:
Context: multiple Redwood Private design partners are blocked on exporting audit logs into their own storage accounts for retention + SIEM ingestion. This PR adds an RFC doc and a prototype sink interface (no production deployment changes yet).

Proposal
- Add a pluggable Sink interface (S3Sink, GCSSink) with shared batching/compression behavior
- Standardize event format as JSONL and object naming scheme `redwood-audit/v1/tenant_id=.../cluster_id=.../date=.../part-xxxxx.jsonl.gz`
- Auth: AWS AssumeRole via IRSA + ExternalId required; GCP Workload Identity Federation (no static keys)
- Delivery: at-least-once, with local disk buffering and backpressure

Out of scope
- Azure Blob
- Hosted API / Dedicated usage

Notes
- Security requirements draft referenced in Confluence (to be finalized by Security)
- Support-driven intake tracked via INT-883

Checklist
- [x] RFC text reviewed by Private Deployments
- [x] Security review on auth model
- [ ] Product sign-off on supported sinks list

Commits
- add sink interface + noop sink
- add rfc doc w/ partitioning + schema

Changed areas
- pkg/sink/sink.go
- pkg/sink/s3.go (prototype)
- pkg/sink/gcs.go (prototype)
- docs/rfc/private-audit-log-export.md

Review conversation
Diego Fernandez: Please align the object naming with the installer values schema we already use in Private. Also call out NATS JetStream as the source in Private.
Connor OBrien: Updated RFC to reference JetStream and kept the naming scheme stable.

Aisha Rahman: ExternalId MUST be required for AssumeRole. Also we should say encryption at rest is required (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS).
Connor OBrien: Added ExternalId requirement and an encryption section.

Dev Patel: Prototype GCS auth in this PR is vague; can we link to the WIF docs we plan to use?
Connor OBrien: Added links in the RFC doc and a TODO for implementation details.

Outcome
Closed (RFC accepted; implementation will happen in follow-up PRs). Closed in favor of implementation PR #157.

domain: 日常协作与非结构化讨论
text:
Incident Bot: Postmortem thread created for INC-2025-02-16 (Dedicated burst beta) — elevated tail latency + burst circuit breaker oscillation. Please add findings + action items here.

Rafael Mendes: Dropping quick summary from today’s review so we can converge on action items for GA hardening. This is focused on circuit breaker behavior + guardrails (not general capacity sizing).

Rafael Mendes: Impact recap:
- Window: ~11:18–11:33 PT
- Scope: us-east / H100 shared burst pool (beta)
- Symptom: non-burst tenants saw p95 and p99 latency jump (mostly tail amplification), plus increased 429s from gateway for a subset of burst traffic.
- We also saw the global circuit breaker flapping (open/close cycles) which made the behavior hard to reason about.

Sean Gallagher: +1. From oncall perspective, the breaker “helped” but was noisy and late. Primary SLO we’re protecting is non-burst Dedicated latency; we need the breaker to be earlier + monotonic (once open, stay open for a minimum).

Peter Holtz: Root behavior as seen from routing:
- Admission controller started denying w/ `FLEET_SAFETY_CAP` and `POOL_SATURATED` intermittently.
- Routing fell back to baseline capacity but got a mix of “retry soon” vs “hard deny” semantics depending on which path the request hit.
- Resulted in burst clients doing retries that amplified load right as the breaker toggled.

Keiko Yamamoto: From guardrails side, the flapping looks tied to two signals we used in the breaker:
1) pool saturation computed from allocator telemetry (laggy)
2) p95 delta for neighbor impact (fast-ish but noisy)
When telemetry lag spikes, saturation appears to drop -> breaker closes -> load surges -> breaker opens again.

Allison Grant: Confirming telemetry lag. We had a 45–90s lag on the “in-use GPUs” metric due to a scrape backlog + label explosion from a misconfigured job (separate issue but it means we need breaker logic resilient to lag).

Sergio Costa: I pulled the graphs. The “telemetry_lag_seconds” panel hits 80s right before the first breaker close. After that, every close aligns with lag spikes. Also note the neighbor p99 delta is spiky because low-volume tenants swing a lot.

Vanessa Ortiz: Fleet note: the pool wasn’t actually “free” when the breaker thought it was. Allocator had outstanding placements but telemetry said capacity recovered. That’s why we saw queue depth rising even when breaker closed.

Jordan Lee: Design-level finding: breaker state machine is currently too eager to close. It treats “below threshold for N samples” as recovery, but samples aren’t independent when the inputs are stale.
Proposal: incorporate a “staleness budget” into the policy evaluation. If either saturation input OR neighbor-impact input is stale beyond X, we should bias toward safety (stay open / reduce burst caps) rather than closing.

Ethan Park: +1 and we can enforce determinism. Right now, two requests that land on different admission controller instances can see different breaker states during transitions (because state propagation is eventual). For GA we probably need:
- a single source of truth for breaker state per pool (or strongly consistent cached value w/ TTL)
- explicit “decision_epoch” so routing can reason about changes.

Mina Haddad: From Smart Routing view: we need denial semantics to be consistent across breaker states. Today we do:
- some denials return retryable 429 w/ `Retry-After`
- some return non-retryable `burst_denied` w/ reason
Customers will implement different retry loops and that changes load. For GA, breaker-open should return a predictable response shape and recommended backoff.

Lauren Bishop: Product ask: whatever we do, we need something CS can explain in one sentence. “Burst temporarily unavailable due to fleet safety; baseline unaffected.” The flapping undermines trust.

Talia Benson: Can we capture action items with owners + target dates? Goal is to have these landed before the GA staged rollout gate.

Rafael Mendes: Findings (proposed):
1) Circuit breaker close criteria doesn’t account for telemetry staleness; closes too early.
2) No minimum-open time / cooldown, leading to flapping and retry amplification.
3) Denial semantics aren’t uniform (retryable vs non-retryable), increasing client-driven load during breaker transitions.
4) Neighbor-impact signal is noisy for low-volume tenants; needs smoothing and “minimum sample” gating.
5) Breaker state propagation can be inconsistent across admission controller replicas.

Sean Gallagher: Agree with those 5.

Peter Holtz: + add “routing fallback behavior during breaker open must be deterministic.” I saw cases where fallback landed on a different model variant due to capacity heuristics. That’s probably okay, but it should be explicit when breaker is open.

Rafael Mendes: Action items draft (please edit):
A) Add telemetry staleness guard: if `telemetry_lag_seconds > X` OR allocator heartbeat stale, breaker cannot close; optionally force open. Owner: Allison + Jordan. Target: end of week.
B) Minimum-open window + exponential recovery: once open, stay open >= 5 min; on recovery, ramp burst caps up gradually (not immediate close). Owner: Keiko + Peter. Target: next sprint.
C) Uniform denial contract for breaker-open state: single reason code (`FLEET_SAFETY_OPEN`), always include `Retry-After` with jitter guidance. Owner: Mina + Ethan. Target: next sprint.
D) Neighbor-impact smoothing + sample threshold: require min request volume per tenant before considering tail deltas; use EWMA and clamp spikes. Owner: Sergio + Allison. Target: next sprint.
E) Stronger breaker state consistency: publish breaker state in control plane/policy engine w/ versioned epoch; replicas read via same cache key w/ TTL, no local recompute. Owner: Ethan + Jordan. Target: design by mid-next-week, implement following.
F) Oncall runbook update: add “breaker flapping” section and immediate mitigation (force-open + cap reduction) w/ commands. Owner: Rafael + Sean. Target: this week.

Allison Grant: For (A)/(D): we already added smoothing in the hotfix branch for telemetry lag denial starvation (related). We can extend that pattern to breaker close logic. I’ll open a small PR with:
- `telemetry_lag_seconds` label reduced cardinality (pool-level only)
- a policy rule: `if lag > 30s => breaker_state = OPEN` (or `HOLD_OPEN`)
We should be careful about false positives though.

Jordan Lee: I’m ok with “HOLD_OPEN” vs “force open” to avoid triggering every time scrapes hiccup. But in this incident, we needed “stay open longer” not “open immediately.” Maybe:
- if OPEN, do not transition to CLOSED unless lag < 15s for 3 consecutive minutes
- if CLOSED, allow OPEN on either (saturation high) OR (neighbor-impact high), regardless of lag.

Keiko Yamamoto: For (B): we can implement a simple hysteresis + cooldown:
- thresholds: open at 0.92 saturation, close at 0.75 (plus lag gate)
- min open 5m
- close requires both saturation low + neighbor-impact normal
Also, “ramp up” can be token-bucket refill rate adjustments rather than binary breaker.

Peter Holtz: Works for routing too. If breaker is OPEN but admission controller still returns some admits due to “ramp,” routing needs to be told the effective cap is reduced, otherwise it’ll keep pushing.

Ethan Park: For (E): we can store breaker state in the same KV we use for pool config snapshots (already versioned). Admission controller reads snapshot at start of request evaluation (single read). That gives determinism within a request.
We still need a writer. Who owns the writer loop? admission controller itself, or separate “breaker manager”?

Vanessa Ortiz: Please not a separate service right now. If admission controller writes breaker state per pool based on inputs, that’s fine, but make sure it’s rate-limited and won’t DDoS the KV store.

Sean Gallagher: + if admission controller is the writer, we need to ensure it still works during partial outage (KV degraded). Default should be “safer”: open / reduce caps.

Mina Haddad: For (C): strongly prefer “always retryable with backoff” for breaker open? But we also need to prevent retry storms.
Maybe:
- return 429 with `Retry-After: 2` (or computed)
- include body field `retryable=true` and reason code
- for some reasons (tenant cap reached) return 429 but with longer retry after

Rafael Mendes: For GA readiness, Support asked for stable reason codes. So +1 on a single code for breaker-open, and keep other codes for tenant cap / cooldown / pool saturated.

Sergio Costa: For (D): we should compute neighbor impact at pool-level (aggregate) rather than tenant-by-tenant deltas. Tenant deltas are useful for forensics, but breaker shouldn’t trip on a tiny tenant’s p99 spike.

Allison Grant: Agree. Breaker signal should be something like: “non-burst p95 > baseline_p95 * 1.25 for 3 min” computed over all non-burst tenants in the pool.

Peter Holtz: That matches how routing thinks about it too.

Talia Benson: Can we lock owners?
- (A) Allison/Jordan
- (B) Keiko/Peter
- (C) Mina/Ethan
- (D) Sergio/Allison
- (E) Ethan/Jordan
- (F) Rafael/Sean

Lauren Bishop: Please add “customer comms snippet” to the runbook or enablement doc. CS will need exact language on flapping mitigation / expectations.

Rafael Mendes: Good call. Adding:
G) Customer-facing comms template for breaker-open periods (beta + GA). Owner: Lauren + Rachel (cc). Target: next week.

Sean Gallagher: Also add gating:
H) Rollout gate: if non-burst p95 regresses > 10% for 10m in any region, automatically hold burst at 0% and page. (I think this is already in-flight but we should track it.) Owner: Sean + Peter. Target: before GA.

Rafael Mendes: Captured.

Harish Reddy: Fleet ops note: for testing, we should replay a synthetic burst with induced telemetry lag (scrape backpressure) to validate “no flapping.” Put that into game day runbook.

Rafael Mendes: Nice. Adding:
I) Game day scenario: induced telemetry lag + burst spike; validate breaker stays open and denial contract stable; ensure baseline SLO holds. Owner: Rafael + Keiko + Allison. Target: before next game day.

Jordan Lee: I’ll start a design doc comment for “breaker state machine v2” with the HOLD_OPEN + hysteresis rules and staleness gates. Will link here.

Ethan Park: I’ll open an ENG ticket for the state consistency (epoch + snapshot read). We should tie it to the existing fleet safety cap work so it doesn’t drift.

Sergio Costa: I’ll update the dashboard panels to show breaker state transitions as annotations + include telemetry lag overlay by default. Would’ve made this 5x faster.

Rafael Mendes: Great. Please paste links to tickets/PRs in-thread as they go up so we can close the loop.

Sean Gallagher: One more: we should explicitly document “breaker-open does not affect baseline Dedicated capacity” and ensure that’s true in routing. During incident, a few baseline requests got 429 due to shared gateway overload policy. Might be separate but worth tracking.

Peter Holtz: I saw that too. It’s gateway-level overload protection, not the burst breaker. But we should align so baseline has higher priority when breaker opens.

Rafael Mendes: Adding:
J) Ensure baseline traffic priority is preserved when breaker opens (gateway + routing). Owner: Peter + Mina. Target: next sprint.

Rafael Mendes: Current action list: A–J above. I’ll summarize into the formal postmortem doc after folks add ticket links. :memo:

title: Isolate egress label leak that causes intermittent cross-tenant DNS cache hits
author: Maya Chen
text:
Summary:
A small subset of Dedicated clusters has seen intermittent cross-tenant DNS cache hits after control-plane rebalances and router path changes. The result is transient DNS responses that resolve private service names from a different tenant under high churn. Multiple enterprise customers escalated (notably Acme Health and FinSight) after observing private hostnames returned in client-facing logs.

Observed behavior and telemetry:
- Spike in resolver error reports and privacy alerts starting 2026-03-03; correlated with node rebalances and peering route churn events.
- Affected requests show egress proxy label reuse: ephemeral proxy label (constructed from host+path) was being reassigned to a different tenant before existing per-label DNS cache entries expired.
- KV cache + DNS TTL mismatch: cached A/AAAA responses lingered under the reused label namespace, causing requests from the new tenant to hit stale DNS entries.
- Failure windows are short (30s-3min) but reproducible in staging with controlled peering flaps.

Reproduction steps (staging):
1. Provision a dedicated pool with two tenant namespaces and enable VPC peering to the same external resolver.
2. Seed DNS cache by making resolver calls from tenant A to private.hostname.internal.
3. Trigger router reassign/rebalance to move egress path from node X to node Y (simulate network flap).
4. Immediately make identical resolver calls from tenant B; observe that responses occasionally match tenant A's cached results.

Root cause hypothesis (confirmed by debugging):
- Egress label assignment currently encodes ephemeral properties but is not strictly namespaced by tenant when recycled quickly during path failover.
- When a label is reused, we do not atomically invalidate or namespace-share DNS cache entries per-tenant; the DNS cache is keyed by label and resolver tuple, so reuse allows cross-tenant hits.
- Under heavy rebalancing, connection tracking entries (conntrack) and proxy label lifecycles become out of sync, leaving a window where label -> cached DNS mapping is valid but now associated with the wrong tenant.

Immediate mitigation (hotfix):
- Toggle A: Force single-path egress (disable multipath) for affected Dedicated pools via control-plane flag to stop label churn (rollback safe). Applied to two impacted fleets on 2026-03-06; reduced customer reports by ~90%.
- Toggle B: Short-term DNS cache TTL clamp per-ephemeral-label to 5s for newly-assigned labels to reduce exposure window.

Proposed permanent fix (implementation plan):
1) Label scoping change (server-side): modify label allocator to include tenant ID as a mandatory prefix in the ephemeral label namespace. This prevents label reuse across tenants unless explicitly shared. (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4821)
2) Atomic cache invalidation: on label reassignment, emit a label-deprecation event that triggers immediate DNS cache invalidation for the old label-->resolver keys.
3) Conntrack cleanup: ensure conntrack entries are flushed for the old label on failover and make cleanup idempotent across controllers.
4) Add invariants and unit tests to the egress label allocator and DNS cache to assert tenant affinity.

Rollout plan and monitoring:
- Canary (2026-03-13): Deploy label scoping and cache invalidation to 5% of Dedicated capacity in a low-risk region. Monitor metrics: cross-tenant-dns-alerts, resolver-5xx-rate, tenant-isolation-violations (custom metric).
- Ramp to 25% after 6h if no regression, full rollout in 48h.
- Post-deploy verification: run repro harness (automated peering-flap) in canary and validate no cross-tenant DNS hits.
- Rollback: Flip scoping flag off and re-enable single-path egress if any privacy regressions observed.

QA and validation:
- Test harness updated in infra-tests repo to simulate peering flaps and assert no DNS cross-tenant leakage. (Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/Dedicated+Egress+Labeling+Postmortem)
- Staging run completed 2026-03-09 with synthetic load; observed elimination of reproducer in 35/36 runs.

Follow-ups and outstanding items:
- Postmortem write-up and customer communication draft (owner: Maya Chen).
- Add an SLO and alert for label-reuse anomalies.
- Audit other cache layers (prefix/KV cache) for similar label-key assumptions.
- Backfill changelog and mention under runtime-2.4.1 release notes.

Artifacts and links:
- Hotfix PR (TTL clamp): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4789
- Permanent fix PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4821
- Staging repro harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra-tests/compare/egress-label-harness
- Confluence incident doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=1558423

2026-03-05 - Maya Chen: Customer Acme Health escalated after private hostnames appeared in logs. Triage started, assigned to Liam.
2026-03-06 - Liam O'Connor: Enabled single-path egress on two affected fleets as immediate mitigation; customer reports dropped significantly. Created hotfix PR to clamp TTL.
2026-03-08 - Infrastructure: Reproducer added to infra-tests; able to consistently replicate in staging with peering flap script.
2026-03-10 - Code review: Runtime PR #4821 opened for label scoping change. Requested additional unit tests around conntrack cleanup.
2026-03-12 - QA: Staging runs (36) after patch show 1 intermittent failure; investigating race condition around cache invalidation ordering.
2026-03-12 - Product (Elena Rodriguez): Notified CSMs and started drafting customer-facing RCA template to share once fix is in canary.

title: Quarantine Telemetry and Escalation Lattice: Dashboard & Operator Spec
author: Ellen Chen
text:
Summary:
This document defines the telemetry dashboard and escalation lattice used during service quarantine events and staged reintegration. It standardizes signals, alert thresholds, operator flows, and dashboard panels so that platform operators and oncall engineers have a single, consistent surface for identifying quarantine candidates, executing soft-quarantine actions, and tracking SLO impact during reintegration.

Goals:
- Provide a single-pane dashboard for quarantine decisions and real-time impact analysis.
- Reduce noisy alerts by grouping telemetry into an escalation lattice (prioritized signals + tolerances).
- Define deterministic operator procedures for soft quarantine, partial eviction, and staged reintegration.
- Produce clear SLO/usage delta estimates to inform customer- and product-level comms.

Scope:
- Applies to multi-tenant LLM inference services and platform-side components that affect global throughput (routing, batching, cache).
- Focused on operational detection (Grafana + Prometheus), Alertmanager rules, and the operator checklist invoked by the oncall.
- Not a replacement for legal/regulatory containment steps for customer data compromise (see security-and-compliance).

Dashboard overview:
- Dashboard name: Quarantine Lattice — Live Incident View
- Primary consumers: Platform operators, oncall SREs, Runtime Owners
- Location: Grafana folder: /platform/operator/quarantine-lattice

Panels (high-level):
1) Candidate scoring heatmap (left) — aggregated per-service quarantine_score (0..100).
2) Signal rollup table (center) — per-service rows with metric columns: error_rate, tail_latency_p95, token_burn_delta, kv_cache_misses, eviction_rate, tenant_priority_score.
3) SLO impact simulator (right) — slider inputs for percent_traffic_moved showing projected SLO burn over next 1h/6h/24h.
4) Active quarantine contexts (bottom) — list of currently-quarantined services with start_time, operator, mode (soft/partial/hard), and recent actions.

Key metrics and PromQL suggestions:
- quarantine_score (computed service label): composite derived in recording rules. PromQL example (as recording rule expression):
 - name: quarantine_score
 expr: >-
 clamp_max(
 (increase(service_errors_total[5m]) / max(1, increase(service_requests_total[5m]))) * 50 +
 (histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(service_latency_bucket[5m])) / 0.5) * 20 +
 (increase(kv_cache_misses_total[10m]) / max(1, increase(kv_cache_hits_total[10m]) + 1)) * 15 +
 (token_burn_delta[5m] > 1000) * 15
 , 100)
- error_rate: increase(service_errors_total[5m]) / max(1, increase(service_requests_total[5m]))
- tail_latency_p95: histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(service_latency_bucket[5m]))
- token_burn_delta: increase(service_token_consumption_total[5m]) - baseline_token_rate (baseline per-tenant config)
- kv_cache_misses: increase(kv_cache_misses_total[5m])

Escalation lattice (concept):
- Purpose: reduce cognitive load by ordering signals and mapping them to discrete operator actions. Each level has: signal set -> threshold -> suggested operator action(s) -> automatic safeties.

Levels (examples):
- Level 0 — Informational (score 0-29):
 - Signals: small error upticks (<0.5%), low cache miss changes.
 - Action: monitor, add annotation.
- Level 1 — Operator attention (score 30-54):
 - Signals: error_rate > 1% sustained 10m OR p95 increase > 2x baseline.
 - Action: open incident context, run quick health checks, consider soft-quarantine for noisy endpoints.
- Level 2 — Soft quarantine (score 55-74):
 - Signals: persistent elevated token_burn_delta > 2x baseline OR sustained cache eviction spike.
 - Action: enable soft-quarantine (traffic reduction via weight 0.7 -> 0.3), attach mitigation notes, start SLO impact sim.
- Level 3 — Partial eviction (score 75-89):
 - Signals: severe error_rate (>5%) OR p95 > 4x baseline OR token_burn_anomaly leading to capacity saturation.
 - Action: partial eviction of tenant (route 50% traffic away), suspend background batch jobs, enable emergency autoscale if available.
- Level 4 — Hard quarantine (score >=90):
 - Signals: sustained service-wide failures or data integrity concerns.
 - Action: hard quarantine (route 100% traffic away), notify product and customer-success, escalate to pager rotations.

Alerting rules and thresholds (examples for Alertmanager):
- alert: QuarantineCandidateHigh
 expr: quarantine_score > 55 and absent(up{job="runtime"}) == 0
 for: 5m
 labels: severity=page
 annotations: summary: "High quarantine score for {{ $labels.service }}"
- alert: QuarantineScoreSpiking
 expr: increase(quarantine_score[10m]) > 30
 for: 2m
 labels: severity=high

Routing & notification:
- Alerts at Level 1 -> Slack #platform-ops (no page), add ticket in incident-tracker with tag quarantine:investigate.
- Level 2 -> Platform SRE rotation notified (page), start 30m timer and follow operator checklist.
- Level 3 -> Platform SRE + Runtime Owner paged, primary engineer added.
- Level 4 -> All-hands page to #platform-incident and direct SMS pager, notify CSM for impacted customers.

Operator checklist: (invoked when score >= 55)
1) Confirm context: check active deploys, recent config changes, and ongoing experiments.
2) Validate telemetry: verify Prometheus query ranges and Grafana panel alignment.
3) Annotate incident: add start_time, operator, rationale to dashboard Active Quarantine Contexts panel.
4) Soft-quarantine step (if chosen):
 a) In the routing control UI execute: set-service-weight {{service}} 0.3 --reason "soft_quarantine" --expires 30m
 b) Run smoke test against canonical prompt set: ./scripts/smoke-test --service {{service}} --promptset quarantine-smoke-2026.json
 c) Observe SLO simulator for 10m; if SLO burn < 0.5% projected, keep reduced weight and schedule deeper investigation.
5) Partial eviction (if escalated):
 a) Scale down tenant routing: set-service-weight {{service}} 0.0 for public traffic, enable isolated test route.
 b) If capacity freed, validate throughput recovery and check cross-tenant degradation metrics.
6) Hard quarantine: route to fallback model variants; notify product & CSM; prepare rollback plan.
7) Document all actions and attach links to runbook in incident ticket.

Safety controls and automatic safeties:
- Auto-revert timers: every soft-quarantine has an expiry default 30m; operator can extend.
- Quarantine throttle: platform will only allow 3 concurrent soft-quarantines per region unless overridden by SRE lead.
- Auto-failback: if quarantine action causes >2x SLO burn for other tenants, platform automatically rebalances traffic back and paged.

Runbook CLI snippets (examples):
- Soft quarantine: rwlctl set-weight --service svc-foo --weight 0.3 --duration 30m --tag "soft_quarantine"
- Partial eviction: rwlctl set-weight --service svc-foo --weight 0.0 --duration 12h --tag "partial_eviction"
- Snapshot metrics: promtool query --expr 'increase(service_errors_total[5m])' --label service=svc-foo > /tmp/snapshot-svc-foo.log

Table: Suggested thresholds (service-level defaults)
| metric | level-1 | level-2 | level-3 | level-4 |
| error_rate | >1% sustained 10m | >2% sustained 10m | >5% sustained 5m | >10% sustained 1m |
| p95 latency (x baseline) | 1.5x | 2.0x | 4.0x | 8.0x |
| quarantine_score | 30 | 55 | 75 | 90 |
| token_burn_delta (tokens/5m) | 200 | 1000 | 5000 | 20000 |

Post-incident and retrospective hooks:
- Automated artifact capture: when a quarantine action is taken the system will attach a runbook bundle (logs, prom snapshot, and routing diffs) to the incident ticket.
- Retrospective template: use the Quarantine Retrospective template that captures timeline, root cause hypotheses, mitigation effectiveness (did soft quarantine reduce system pressure?), and follow-ups (technical debt, dashboard gaps).
- Mandatory blameless postmortem if hard quarantine lasted >1h or impacted >5% of total tokens served for >6h.

Run metrics to review after a quarantine event (first 24h):
- Time-to-detection (TTD): from first abnormal metric to quarantine action. Target <= 10m.
- Time-to-stabilize (TTS): from action to error_rate returning to baseline. Target <= 60m for soft quarantines.
- Regression rate on other tenants: % of tenants whose p95 increased >20% during action. Target < 5%.

Implementation roadmap (next 6 months):
1) Q2 2026 — implement quarantine_score recording rule and dashboard panels; add SLO simulator widget. Owner: Observability team.
2) Q3 2026 — integrate routing-control CLI with Grafana buttons (one-click soft quarantine). Owner: Eng Platform.
3) Q4 2026 — build simulation harness to run quarantine impact scenarios against historical traffic (capacity lab). Owner: Runtime + Platform.
4) Q1 2027 — policy engine: automatically suggest quarantine actions with confidence intervals and enforce concurrency limits. Owner: Platform Ops.

Ownership and contact points:
- Dashboard owner: Observability (owner: Aisha Patel, aisha@redwood.ai)
- Escalation policy owner: Platform SRE (owner: Luis Moreno, luis@redwood.ai)
- Routing-control service: runtime-router (team: Eng Serving Runtime)

Appendix A — Example Grafana panel JSON (abridged):
{"title": "Candidate heatmap", "type": "heatmap", "targets": [{"expr": "quarantine_score", "refId": "A"}]}

Appendix B — Quick verification checklist for automation engineers adding a new quarantine rule:
- Ensure recording rule has a clear description and test vectors.
- Add unit tests validating scoring function with synthetic telemetry.
- Add a dashboard-only feature flag so panels can be toggled during rollout.
- Confirm Alertmanager routing groups for severity=page and severity=high follow the lattice mapping.

Notes and rationale:
- The lattice approach reduces operator guesswork: by mapping composite scores to explicit actions we reduce escalations and speed decisions.
- Soft-quarantine prefers controlled traffic reduction instead of immediate hard routing changes to limit collateral damage.

Related resources:
- Platform routing-control API docs: /confluence/eng-platform/how-tos/routing-control-api-2025
- Incident ticket template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process/standard-incident-template
- Quarantine smoke test prompts: /confluence/eng-platform/quickstarts-and-templates/quarantine-smoke-sets

Revision history:
- 2026-02-15: Initial draft by Ellen Chen.
- 2026-03-01: Published after review with Observability and Platform SRE (reviewers: Luis Moreno, Aisha Patel, Tomás Rivera).

End of document.

title: Hybrid IdP SAML NameQualifier change causes tenant-scoped service-account bindings to be rejected (403) in private deployment
text:
After the customer's IdP changed SAML NameQualifier values during a maintenance rollout, CloudLedger's service account assertions no longer map to the expected tenant identity in our private deployment, resulting in consistent 403s for admin/service operations.

Issue summary:
Customer reports 403 responses for admin API calls and service account flows shortly after their IdP (on-prem ADFS + cloud proxy) pushed a configuration change that normalizes NameID/NameQualifier values. Impact:
- Admin console access is blocked for service workflows (automated backups, key rotations).
- Several scheduled jobs fail and trigger downstream errors in the customer's product.
Environment:
- Private deployment (VPC) with tenant-scoped RBAC and ingress path rewrite enabled.
- Requests flow through customer-managed IdP proxy -> Edge ingress -> private control plane.
Expected behavior:
- SAML assertions from the IdP map to tenant-scoped service-account identities and are accepted.
Actual behavior:
- SAML assertion subject contains NameID and a NameQualifier that does not match the tenant prefix in our tenant resolution logic; our auth layer rejects the assertion as unmapped, returning 403.
Notes: this started immediately after the IdP maintenance window and affects all service accounts that rely on SAML subject mapping.

1) Customer triggers a service account token exchange via SAML assertion (SAML response generated by IdP with new NameQualifier).
2) Request traverses customer IdP proxy -> edge ingress; ingress rewrites path and forwards assertion to private control plane auth endpoint.
3) Auth layer attempts tenant resolution by concatenating tenant prefix + NameQualifier -> fails mapping lookup -> returns 403.
4) Reverting IdP to previous NameQualifier restores normal mapping and clears 403s (reported by customer).

Excerpt from private control plane auth logs (sanitized):
[2026-03-11T09:12:04Z] auth.evaluated_assertion tenant_lookup="tenant-prefix:acme-corp" expected_namequal="https://idp.acme.com/tn1" actual_namequal="https://idp.acme.com/tn1-v2" result=NOT_FOUND status=403 request_id=req_0a7f

<Subject>
 <NameID NameQualifier="https://idp.acme.com/tn1-v2">service-account-automation@acme</NameID>
</Subject>

03/11 10:00 - Support triage: reproduced 403 in staging by rewriting NameQualifier on test SAML response; tenant resolution routine does strict equality match (prefix + NameQualifier) and fails.
03/11 13:35 - Confirmed customer IdP maintenance changed NameQualifier semantics; they applied a namespacing update to multi-tenant proxy (adds -v2 suffix for proxy routing).
03/12 08:20 - Ingress team validated that path rewrite is not stripping NameQualifier but does perform header normalization; nothing dropped in transit.
03/12 14:50 - Hypothesis: tenant resolution should tolerate NameQualifier suffix changes (semantic namespace variations) or consult IdP metadata alias list.

Dana Koh (Support): Customer reports immediate failure after IdP maintenance; provided SAML response and timestamps. Asked customer to share IdP metadata and recent change logs.
Customer (CloudLedger): Confirmed change history: added namespacing to NameQualifier to support routed IdP proxies. They can rollback but prefer a platform-side tolerant mapping to avoid future disruptions.
Marcus Chen (Auth Eng): Reproduced locally; strict matching in tenant resolver is intentional for safety. Propose short-term workaround and long-term fix. Assigned to auth team for patching.
SRE (Ingress): Verified request body unchanged, base64 SAML response reaches auth endpoint. No TLS or proxy errors observed.

Tenant resolver currently performs strict concatenation of tenant prefix and NameQualifier. IdP introduced a variant NameQualifier (suffix -v2) for proxy routing. Resolver should consult IdP metadata aliases or perform normalized prefix match when mapping service-account NameID to tenant; otherwise legitimate assertions are rejected.

1) Ask customer to rollback NameQualifier change in IdP while we prepare patch (fastest immediate mitigation).
2) Temporary allowlist: add explicit mapping for NameQualifier variants in tenant metadata (requires customer-provided list).
3) Implement tolerant matching in tenant resolver (see long-term fix).

Workaround applied: customer rolled back NameQualifier change during support window which restored service workflows (confirmed 2026-03-12 02:17 UTC). Auth engineering implemented a short-lived configuration option to map the new NameQualifier variant to the existing tenant mapping (deployed to private customer control plane 2026-03-13).
Long-term: auth team will implement alias-aware tenant resolution (RFC created, PR link below) that reads IdP metadata aliases and supports controlled suffix normalization. Follow-up action: schedule patch for private deployments and add automated test coverage for NameQualifier variants.

Auth RFC: https://confluence.redwood.company/display/AUTH/NameQualifier-Alias-Resolution-2026
Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/auth/pull/843

title: Approval request: timeboxed obfuscated session handoff to Privacy triage for customer incident
text:
Issue summary: Request for short-lived, obfuscated session handoff from Support to Privacy Triage to investigate a suspected customer PII exposure during a streaming session in prod.

Impact: Low-volume event affecting 2 customer sessions across us-west; customer has reported redacted snippet that may include a token-like string. No confirmed exfiltration; request is precautionary to validate redaction patterns and confirm no downstream storage.

Justification: Privacy team needs targeted session context (only first 200 tokens of each session plus metadata) to validate redaction rules and confirm whether post-processing stored any sensitive fragments. Support already attempted local redaction and sampling but requires Privacy engineers to run pattern checks and replay in a sandbox.

Access requested: Two obfuscated session snapshots (session IDs provided), each reduced to first 200 tokens, all user-provided free-text replaced with salted hash except token-like strings left for pattern analysis. No API keys, no full raw traces. Access window: 6 hours.

Duration and scope: 2026-03-14 09:00 UTC to 2026-03-14 15:00 UTC (6 hours). Data will be accessed only from Privacy VPC sandbox. No extracts allowed outside approved VPC.

Data minimization and audit controls: Only fields requested (session_id, timestamp, truncated_obfuscated_payload, model, region, route) will be provisioned. All access will be logged; KMS audit enabled; access recorded to internal audit log and linked to this ticket.

Approvals required: Security approval for obfuscation method and ephemeral KMS unwrap, Privacy lead sign-off for triage, and SRE notice for any sandbox replay.

Requester: Maya Chen (Support)

Notes: This is NOT a general log access request; it is scoped and timeboxed to reduce compliance surface area. If Privacy requests deeper slices, a new approval with legal signoff will be required.

2026-03-11 15:22 - Maya Chen: Created request after customer reported suspicious snippet. Provided session IDs and initial redaction attempt. Requested Privacy-led review for pattern confirmation.
2026-03-11 17:05 - Elena Torres (Privacy): Acknowledged. Need confirmation on obfuscation algorithm (salted SHA256) and whether the hashed values are reversible. Also request assurance that no key material is included. Pending Security review.
2026-03-12 09:30 - Ravi Kapoor (Infra): Confirmed we can provision ephemeral snapshot with enforced KMS policy and timebound IAM role. Will prepare a sandbox pod and an audit stream to the security log. Need explicit list of fields to include.
2026-03-13 11:12 - Security (Omar Ruiz): Reviewed obfuscation method. Salted SHA256 ok if salt is ephemeral and not stored. Approve conditional on ephemeral salt rotation and no write-access to persistent stores from sandbox. Security will generate the IAM role and KMSEncrypt/Decrypt policy.
2026-03-14 07:58 - Maya Chen: Updated ticket with final obfuscation spec and confirmed sessions: session-20260310-8a7f and session-20260312-3c2b. Requested provisioning window 09:00-15:00 UTC.

Support reproduced redacted snippet locally; pattern looks like a 40+ char token interleaved with punctuation. Initial log crawl shows two sessions with similar structures. No evidence of persistent write to customer blob store (billing pipeline and long-term archive show no new objects at the timestamps). Network egress audit for the host shows normal traffic; no unusual external IPs. Privacy requested an obfuscated view to validate regexes against token-like fragments without exposing raw user text.

Approved by Security (Omar Ruiz) and Privacy lead (Elena Torres). Infra (Ravi) provisioned ephemeral sandbox and IAM role at 2026-03-14 08:50 UTC. Snapshot exported to sandbox as truncated_obfuscated_payload and made available to Privacy triage. Access window enforced and all accesses logged. No sensitive content found by Privacy; follow-up: update regex-based redaction rule and deploy to streaming preprocessors (Follow-up task created: INT-629305). Ticket resolved after post-triage verification and audit log review.

Resolved - timeboxed obfuscated snapshots provided and privacy triage completed; recommended redaction rule update and no evidence of persistent exposure.

title: Kestrel Labs: hosted API timeouts when using structured output (JSON schema)
text:
Issue summary:
Kestrel Labs is seeing intermittent request timeouts (client-side 60s) when enabling structured output with a JSON Schema. Same prompts complete successfully when structured output is disabled.

Impact:
- Kestrel’s production workflow for contract analysis is failing intermittently.
- Reported failure rate ~8–15% depending on schema size.

Environment:
- Hosted API (OpenAI-compatible endpoint)
- Region: us-east
- Models: atlas-7b-instruct and atlas-13b-instruct

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Send chat completion request with structured output enabled and a JSON Schema with ~40 properties and nested arrays.
2) Stream disabled.
3) Observe timeout on ~1/10 requests; retries often succeed.

Notes:
Customer says this started after they switched from tool-calling output to JSON Schema structured output (mid-July).

Aisha Rahman (Support): Customer provided request IDs: req_7c2f..., req_9b11..., req_2a0d... All show long tail latency then gateway timeout.
Diego Fernandez (Runtime): Pulled traces. The slow requests correlate with schema validation + constrained decoding path. The model is spending a long time in token sampling with low temperature + many constraints.
Ethan Park (SRE): Confirmed p99 latency spike for route /v1/chat/completions when structured_output=true. Only visible on a subset of pods after autoscale. Suspect cache fragmentation.
Diego Fernandez (Runtime): Workaround: set max_output_tokens lower and simplify schema (avoid large anyOf/oneOf), or switch to tool-calling for now. We also rolled a config change: increased internal structured-output step timeout from 45s -> 75s for enterprise tier in us-east.
Aisha Rahman (Support): Customer confirmed improvement after config change; still sees occasional long responses on very large schemas but no longer hitting gateway timeout.
Resolution: Marking Resolved. Follow-up action: add a known-issue entry and instrument a separate metric for schema size vs constrained decoding wall time.

title: Crescent Analytics — Contract intake & security sprint
author: Priya Sharma
text:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-15
Start: 18:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Priya Sharma (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Alex Kim (Redwood CSM); Jenna Lee (Crescent Procurement), Omar Rahman (Crescent Legal), Lila Tran (Eng Lead), Tom Brooks (CTO), Erin Park (Security)

Summary: Quick procurement intake focused on MSA/DPA redlines, SLA expectations, KMS/invoice and PO pathing. Lots of security clarifications; engineering requested a short perf spike to validate token throughput. Goal: get contract redlines, security artifacts, and a timeline for PO/desktop pilot.

Topics: MSA redlines; DPA data residency and deletion; SOC2/ISO attestations; SSO/SAML + SCIM provisioning; KMS/HSM and customer key options (bring-your-own-key); SLA uptime and latency SLOs; pricing approvals and invoicing cadence; on-prem vs VPC options for regulated workloads.

Transcript: 
[00:00] Priya Sharma: Okay everyone, thanks for making time. Uh, super appreciate it. I'll do a super brief agenda — go over the contract pathway, what we need from procurement/legal, and then Marco will jump into the security/arch questions.

[00:18] Jenna Lee: Sounds good. We have about an hour. Main thing for us is to understand the DPA and MSA exceptions, and also what SLAs we can expect for latency, because we have some customer-facing SLAs we need to map.

[00:30] Marco Diaz: Hi all. Quick intro — Marco, solutions engineer at Redwood — I'll cover the VPC/private options and what BYOK looks like, and run through a small perf spike plan.

[00:40] Omar Rahman: From legal, hi. I saw a couple of redlines in the doc you sent, Priya. We flagged indemnity and data processor clauses. Also, need clarity on breach notification timelines.

[00:50] Priya Sharma: Totally. We expected some of that. We have a standard MSA that we can annotate — the key items we've seen in enterprise are indemnity caps aligned to fees, faster breach notification thresholds (we typically do 72 hours), and more explicit subprocessor lists in the DPA.

[01:10] Lila Tran: On the engineering side, we mostly want to know whether the inference endpoints will ever return customer data in logs, how long KV cache persists if we use dedicated pools, and whether we can pin a model version for a rollout.

[01:25] Marco Diaz: Short answers — we offer a masked-logs mode where payloads are not persisted for debugging; default retention is 30 days but dedicated can be changed, and yes you can pin model version and do canary rollouts. 

[01:40] Erin Park: Can you clarify the BYOK flow? We're on AWS KMS and have strict key control — we cannot have keys exported.

[01:50] Marco Diaz: For BYOK we integrate with customer KMS via a wrapped key approach. Redwood never has your raw key material — it's wrapped/unwrapped inside an HSM in our private control plane. We can also provide an HSM attestation report; it's similar to what other vendors provide.

[02:10] Tom Brooks: Is that the same for on-prem deploys? We might look at the on-prem package for one of our regulated products.

[02:18] Priya Sharma: On-prem is a separate offering — data never leaves your network there. The contract and support terms differ; usually that's an enterprise license with a platform fee and support SLA. We'll put that option in the MSA appendix.

[02:35] Omar Rahman: Back to breach notification: 72 hours is acceptable but we need to see the flowchart — who notifies whom, and will you provide us with incident logs? Also, do you maintain an audit trail accessible to customers?

[02:48] Marco Diaz: We maintain audit logs and can provide a time-limited customer portal view and export for audit parties. For incidents we'll provide initial notification within 72 hours, then a follow-up with root-cause timeline and any affected customer data details.

[03:05] Jenna Lee: On procurement timing — our cycle is three weeks if legal and security sign off quickly, but it usually goes longer. We need to know if Redwood accepts standard PO terms and if invoicing can be monthly or net-30.

[03:20] Priya Sharma: Yes we accept POs for Dedicated and Private deals. Hosted usage billing is typically monthly, net-30 for enterprise, but we can discuss different billing cycles for annual reserved commits. We'll flag that in the commercial redlines.

[03:40] Lila Tran: For the performance spike — we want to push 20 concurrent sessions, about 5k tokens per minute each, to simulate some long-context behavior. Is that feasible?

[03:50] Marco Diaz: Yep, feasible on Dedicated. For hosted we'll run a limited spike, but to get a clean signal we prefer a short Dedicated sandbox. We'll run a 1-hour spike and capture latency p95/p99 and token/sec metrics.

[04:10] Erin Park: Can we get the list of subprocessors? We need names and locations for our DPA.

[04:16] Priya Sharma: Absolutely. We'll provide the current subprocessor list and include geographic regions. Note subprocessors change; the DPA includes a notification clause and we can pre-agree high-risk subprocessors.

[04:30] Omar Rahman: On indemnity — we propose a carve-out for third-party IP claims and a mutual limitation to direct damages capped at 12 months' fees. Your MSA had something like 6 months; can we negotiate to 12?

[04:45] Priya Sharma: We usually benchmark to 6–12 months depending on tier; for Private deployments and large commitments we can agree to 12 months. I'll mark that for redline.

[04:58] Tom Brooks: A practical question — what is your SLA for latency? Our SLAs with customers require 500ms p95 for simple prompts.

[05:06] Marco Diaz: For shorter prompts we can meet low-latency p95 in hosted at typical network conditions, but heavy long-context workloads increase latencies. For Dedicated we can target fixed latency SLOs — we can surface token/sec and p95/p99 numbers from the perf spike and propose a contractual SLO with credits for breaches.

[05:30] Jenna Lee: Do you provide SOC 2 type II and ISO attestation? We need to collect those for vendor intake.

[05:36] Priya Sharma: Yes we have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 — we'll share the certs and the summary of control mappings.

[05:45] Erin Park: And pen tests? Any shared summary of recent pentest findings?

[05:52] Marco Diaz: We do periodic pen tests. We can share a sanitized executive summary and remediation timelines.

[06:00] Omar Rahman: A few nitty-gritty items: DPA needs a deletion clause that guarantees deletion of customer data on termination within X days, and proof of deletion for any caches or backups. Also we request a list of jurisdictions you transfer data to for processing.

[06:14] Priya Sharma: Standard is 30 days for deletion from live stores, backups have a longer retention window but we can provide certification that primary copies are destroyed. We'll provide the jurisdiction list and annotate where subprocessors operate.

[06:30] Lila Tran: On the engineering side, can we get a sandbox environment with logs disabled or scrubbed? We don't want our PII test strings captured.

[06:40] Marco Diaz: Yes, we can provision a scrubbed logging sandbox. We'll also enable a redaction filter for obvious PII patterns. For deeper PII we recommend tokenization on your side prior to callout.

[06:58] Priya Sharma: Okay, circling back to the procurement path — Jenna, you mentioned three weeks optimistic. What's the list of documents you need from Redwood to start vendor gating?

[07:06] Jenna Lee: We'll need the executed MSA draft, DPA, SOC 2/ISO certs, subprocessors, a sample invoice and PO template, and an initial SOW or appendix for the Dedicated pool if applicable. Also cost breakdown for committed vs burst pricing.

[07:20] Priya Sharma: Great — we'll package: annotated MSA/DPA redlines, subprocessor list, SOC2/ISO, sample invoice, and the Dedicated appendix with pricing tiers. Marco will add perf spike outputs.

[07:32] Tom Brooks: About pricing — if we commit to a quarterly reserved capacity for Dedicated, do we get lower token rates and guaranteed capacity? What's the spillover policy?

[07:42] Priya Sharma: Reserved capacity gives you predictable throughput at a discounted unit price. We offer burst policies that allow a percentage of extra capacity at a higher overage rate. We'll include exact numbers in the pricing appendix; typical discounts are 20–40% depending on term and size.

[07:58] Omar Rahman: On termination, we need to ensure continuity — a clause that allows export of model state and KV caches within a defined window. Is that feasible?

[08:08] Marco Diaz: We can export KV cache snapshots and model config; for large models the artifacts can be sizeable but we will provide an export and transfer mechanism. We'll add technical details in the appendix.

[08:22] Erin Park: Clarify network connectivity for VPC — do you support private peering, Transit Gateway, or only public endpoints with VPC controls?

[08:30] Marco Diaz: We support AWS VPC peering and PrivateLink equivalents in other clouds. For Private deployments, we have an air-gapped option. We'll run through the peering diagram in the architecture workshop.

[08:45] Jenna Lee: Is Redwood willing to sign a mutual NDA supplement to the MSA for pre-contract PoC data?

[08:52] Priya Sharma: Yes, we can sign an addendum NDA. We'll include a short PoC addendum in the materials.

[09:05] Lila Tran: Quick question — do you provide SCIM for user provisioning? We want automated user lifecycle for our devs.

[09:12] Marco Diaz: SCIM + SAML SSO are supported for enterprise accounts. We'll include a schematic for SCIM endpoints and attribute mappings.

[09:25] Tom Brooks: Any surprises on export controls or restricted countries? We operate in EU and US; data residency matters for some customers.

[09:32] Priya Sharma: We support EU region deployments and can restrict processing to certain regions per contract. Export controls will follow our legal/compliance policy; we'll flag any constraints up front.

[09:45] Omar Rahman: For the DPA, we may need a few custom clauses: subprocessor notification windows shortened to 10 days, option to audit subprocessors for high-risk processing and a data deletion certification. Are those likely to be accepted?

[09:56] Priya Sharma: Subprocessor notification of 10 days is aggressive but we can offer a compromise: 15 days for high-risk subprocessors and a right to review — auditing subprocessors is typical for larger commitments; we'll capture that in the DPA appendix.

[10:12] Jenna Lee: Let's talk timeline again: If you share the annotated docs by Wednesday (11/18) and we can get legal digest in a week, is there an internal Redwood sign-off pattern we should expect?

[10:22] Priya Sharma: Yes — after we exchange redlines there's an internal legal and commercial review which usually takes 3–5 business days, then procurement engages finance for PO terms. We'll try to keep the cycle tight.

[10:36] Marco Diaz: For the perf spike I propose: Redwood provisions a sandbox cluster, Crescent provides sample payloads and a single API key, we run a 1-hour spike at a pre-agreed concurrency, then share metrics and logs.

[10:48] Lila Tran: OK we'll prepare the sample payloads and remove actual PII.

[10:55] Priya Sharma: Great — final quick recap and owners. Priya will post annotated MSA/DPA, SOC2/ISO, subprocessor list. Marco will run perf spike and attach results. Erin will review the secure-architecture doc with Marco in the workshop. Jenna will confirm PO template and timeline. Omar to send high-priority legal redlines within 48 hours if possible.

[11:15] Omar Rahman: I'll try for 48 hours but likely 72. Some items need internal counsel review.

[11:22] Priya Sharma: That's fine — we account for that. Any other blockers?

[11:30] Tom Brooks: No blockers. Thanks everybody.

[11:34] Jenna Lee: Thanks — talk soon.

[11:36] Priya Sharma: Thanks, we'll follow up with the packet by Wednesday.

title: Weekly pilot — seqlen prioritization & first-token latency huddle
author: James Miller
text:
Mid-poc sync focused on reducing time-to-first-token and stabilizing streaming handshake for varied sequence lengths. Agreed to run kernel gating experiments and to exchange traces and prompt sets. Discussed viable tradeoffs between dedicated and hosted routes for their compliance needs.

Meeting header: 2026-02-27 10:30 PT — 48 minutes. Attendees: James Miller (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Logan Reyes (Redwood SRE), Sara Collins (Aurelia Head of ML), Miguel Ortega (Platform Eng), Tina Zhao (Infra Lead).

[00:00] James Miller: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um let's do a quick agenda — TTFT numbers, streaming handshakes, sequence-length kernel gating, and then action items. Sara, Miguel, anything to add?

[00:22] Sara Collins: No, that's perfect. We're mainly worried about first-token regressions we saw after the quantization change last week. p95 jumped and, um, we've seen some handshake timeouts on stream.

[00:38] Priya Shah: Right, thanks Sara. Quick call out: we pushed a conservative quantized kernel last Tuesday which improved throughput but we saw a p95 bump in TTFT for short prompts. We suspect the kernel selection path adds a tiny decision overhead that compounds in microburst patterns.

[01:05] Miguel Ortega: Just to give context — our workload is a lot of short clinical note completions, avg seqlen ~ 28 tokens, but there are spikes where a long patient history comes in and sequences hit 1.2k. The mixed profile seems to confuse the runtime.

[01:28] Logan Reyes: That matches what our profiler showed: the runtime was switching paths at inference time when it detected longer tail sequences which caused KV reallocation and small GC-ish pauses. Probably not GC but memory reshuffle.

[01:45] Tina Zhao: Also we run inside a VPC with strict egress rules, so fallback to hosted variants is trickier. We have to keep everything within the private deployment; that's why dedicated/dedicated-like predictable latency is important to us.

[02:04] James Miller: Understood. Two immediate levers: 1) Sequence-length gated kernel selection — pick kernel variant at request admission based on expected effective seqlen and stick to it for the request, avoid mid-request switching. 2) Streaming handshake tuning — make the handshake lighter and overlap more with model warmup.

[02:32] Priya Shah: We ran a quick offline test: when we pin the kernel at admission for seqlen bucket <64 we reduced TTFT p95 by ~18% on our dev rig. But in production microburst arrivals that interleave short and long requests cause queuing oddities.

[02:52] Sara Collins: I want to understand the tradeoffs — does pinning at admission risk suboptimal kernel for long tail sequences? Like if a request is mis-categorized initially.

[03:08] Priya Shah: Good question. Mitigation: admission uses a cheap seqlen estimate from the prompt prefix (we already compute prompt tokenization upstream). For borderline cases we set a short guard-band and use a hybrid KV layout that supports both without full reallocation. It's slightly more memory but much cheaper than a mid-request swap.

[03:37] Miguel Ortega: Any numbers on memory overhead? We have tight limits on GPU memory for our Dedicated node pools.

[03:46] Priya Shah: Roughly +4–6% VRAM on average for hybrid path on our 32GB-ish templates. We can run a targeted test against your instance sizes to confirm.

[04:00] James Miller: Actionable: Priya will run kernel gating tests with quantized vs float variants using Aurelia's sample prompts. We'll include a mem profile.

[04:10] Miguel Ortega: On streaming: our infra team saw ~15% of streams fail the initial handshake under bursts; the client then retries which doubles latency. Is there a way to make the handshake idempotent or faster?

[04:27] Logan Reyes: We have two ideas — reduce the handshake RTT by moving part of the negotiation to a pre-warm path (staged handshake) and accept optimistic streaming frames with a soft-accept fallback. Both require some client change but minimal.

[04:48] Tina Zhao: Client changes are ok as long as they don't require broad SDK churn. We use a custom wrapper around the SDK currently.

[04:58] Priya Shah: For the optimistic frames approach we can gate it behind a 'pilot' flag; Redwood's hosted SDK can opt-in and your wrapper can follow. That would reduce time-to-first-byte for streaming by letting the model start sending tokens while finalizing some non-critical headers.

[05:20] Sara Collins: That sounds promising — what's the failure mode? If the handshake fails after we've started sending token frames do we lose correctness?

[05:30] Logan Reyes: We build in an idempotent token ACK. If the handshake ultimately fails the client drops frames and retries the request; worst case you have one extra roundtrip but we avoid the initial full timeout. In practice it's cut down p99 from 1.8s to 1.2s in our internal tests.

[05:52] Miguel Ortega: Can you replicate that in our environment where we have the VPC NAT throttle? Those NAT transients seem to exacerbate handshake timeouts.

[06:03] James Miller: Yes — we'll include the VPC egress conditions in the bench. Miguel — please share a short window of your NAT metrics and we'll replay similar conditions in the pilot.

[06:13] Miguel Ortega: Sure, will do.

[06:18] Sara Collins: One other thing: we noticed TTFT regressions correlate with KV cache misses when the system switches to longer sequences; our long prompts flush prefix cache more often. Is there a recommended caching policy?

[06:34] Priya Shah: For doc-heavy prompts we recommend an LRU prefix cache with size tuned by observed prefix reuse. Also adaptive prefix caching where repeated patient IDs or templates are pinned for a short TTL — that reduced cache churn in a healthcare pilot we did last quarter.

[06:55] Tina Zhao: That sounds good, but pinned TTLs sound like extra state — how do you surface that for our infra team?

[07:03] Priya Shah: We can expose a small telemetry endpoint and a config flag in the control plane. We'll provide a suggested starting config and the Redwood Console will show pin hit rates.

[07:18] James Miller: Let's walk through today's benchmark results quickly — Priya?

[07:23] Priya Shah: I shared a short perf doc earlier. TL;DR: baseline hosted config — p50 TTFT 120ms, p95 430ms, p99 980ms; after quantized kernel swap we saw p50 drop to 95ms but p95 rose to 520ms and p99 to 1.05s. When we pinned small seqlen kernel at admission we saw p95 340ms and p99 900ms, so improved tail.

[08:00] Miguel Ortega: So quantization improved median but hurt tail. Any visibility into why p99 increased slightly?

[08:10] Priya Shah: The heavier kernel selection logic plus occasional path switches caused transient queueing. Also memory defragmentation during path swap — small but visible in tails. Pinning solves the path switch.

[08:28] Sara Collins: Are these numbers from Redwood's hosted infra or a dedicated sim?

[08:34] Priya Shah: These are run on hosted dev cluster with similar GPU types but without your VPC constraints. We need to run the dedicated/pilot bench against your Dedicated node to be accurate.

[08:47] Tina Zhao: We also need to compare idle vs cold-start behavior; some of our requests coincide with cold cache after nightly batch jobs which creates longer tails.

[08:58] Logan Reyes: We can simulate cold-start by clearing KV caches between runs in the bench. We'll add that axis.

[09:08] Sara Collins: Anything we should be cautious about from the security side? You mentioned a small telemetry endpoint — must be within our VPC and audit logged.

[09:17] James Miller: Absolutely. We'll deliver a minimal network diagram and specify that telemetry is optional and can be routed to your KMS-backed secure endpoint. We'll include SOC2 attestations and audit log options.

[09:30] Miguel Ortega: Could you also include the per-token cost delta for the hybrid gating? We need to present cost vs latency tradeoff to procurement.

[09:40] Priya Shah: We'll include a unit economics table — expected tokens/sec delta, resource utilization, and estimated $/1M tokens for each path.

[09:50] Tina Zhao: On timeline — what's realistic for the kernel gating experiment and the streaming optimistic frames trial?

[09:58] James Miller: Proposal: kernel gating experiments by 2026-03-03 with results shared; streaming optimistic frames prototype for SDK by 2026-03-08, then a short pilot run in your staging environment.

[10:12] Sara Collins: Works for us.

[10:16] James Miller: Great. Recap of action items: Priya runs kernel gating tests and includes memory profile; Miguel shares traces and NAT metrics; James sends security + pricing; Logan adds cold-start axis to benches. We'll reconvene next Friday same time.

[10:32] Miguel Ortega: Quick question — did we decide on hosted vs dedicated for the pilot?

[10:37] James Miller: We left that open — short term we'll run dual runs: hosted baseline and dedicated pilot run to compare. Given your VPC needs likely dedicated will win, but the bench will confirm.

[10:49] Sara Collins: Also please include a simple A/B prompt set where we instrument prompt prefixes so we can see where prefix pins help.

[10:58] Priya Shah: Will do.

[11:02] James Miller: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with notes and scheduling stuff. End.

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts: 'KV cache' transcribed as 'K-V cash' in some utterances. Speaker overlap at 04:50 and 09:50 produced minor attribution errors.

Redwood to run 2 new microburst experiments using sequence-length gated kernels by 2026-03-03
Customer to share 48-hour tail-latency traces and representative prompt set by 2026-03-01
Schedule side-by-side hosted vs dedicated 1k requests benchmark with streaming enabled (AE/SE owns scheduling)

Priya Shah — set up kernel gating experiment (quantized path vs float) and share perf sheet — due 2026-03-03
Miguel Ortega — export p50/p95/p99 TTFT and stream handshake traces for last 2 days — due 2026-03-01
James Miller — send security snapshot (SOC2 + minimal network diagram) and pilot pricing options — due 2026-02-28

title: Ephemeral tenant shelf and circuit epoch guard
author: Priya Kapoor
text:
Motivation: During a production incident last week we observed tenant recovery flapping when nodes with partially-drained KV caches rejoined. That flapping caused rapid circuit reopen/close cycles and triggered SLO alerts for the affected region. This PR introduces two coordinated features: 1) an ephemeral tenant-shelf that temporarily places low-priority tenant requests into a short-lived queue while the system heals, and 2) a circuit-epoch guard which binds circuit state transitions to epoch windows to prevent rapid reopen oscillations. The design aims to reduce cascade reopens, smooth SLO enforcement during regional rejoin events, and provide clear telemetry for postmortem analysis. Summary of changes: - New TenantShelf component in serving/runtime to accept and hold low-priority requests with configurable shelf TTL and max depth. - EpochGuard added to circuit-breaker state machine: transitions require an epoch stamp and minimum quiesce interval; stale epochs are rejected with clear metrics. - A new policy config (shelf.policy) to tie tenant weight, priority, and eligibility for shelving. - Graceful rollout: default disabled; enabled via runtime flag and guarded feature gate for canary. - Backward compatibility: shelf is permissive and falls back to existing behaviour if disabled. Checklist: - [x] Design doc (link: Linear ENG-4821) - [x] Unit tests for TenantShelf and EpochGuard state transitions - [x] Integration test with regional rejoin simulation - [x] Load test at 2x typical tenant burst - [x] Observability added (metrics and traces) Related work: references ENG-4803 (kv-drain coordination), ENG-4785 (tenant prioritizer). Rollout plan: merge to main behind feature gate, enable on canary region for 24h, monitor slo.delta and circuit.flip_rate for 6h, expand to other regions if stable. If regression observed, feature gate can be toggled off and a fast rollback will be performed. Notes: This PR intentionally keeps the TenantShelf in-memory for this iteration to simplify rollback; a follow-up will persist shelf metadata to avoid lost-in-flight telemetry during long drains.

Diego Morales (2026-02-10): Design looks sound. Two asks: make shelf TTL configurable per-tenant and ensure we don't deadlock on shelf drain paths.
Priya Kapoor (2026-02-10): Addressed both items; added per-tenant override and reworked drain path to use non-blocking TTL timers.
