title: incidents
text:
Incident Bot: :rotating_light: *INCIDENT* (beta) - "rollout split mismatch" reported by Northstar in us-east. Expected canary=10%, observed ~35-45% over last 10m. Route: `hosted/chat/northstar-support-prod`. Rollout: `rlt_7f2c`.

Sean Gallagher: seeing the same in our cohort dashboard. us-west looks ~10% +/- noise, eu-central ~9-11%. us-east is way off.

Aisha Bello: pulling quick numbers from metrics.
`sum(rate(rw_infer_requests_total{route="hosted/chat/northstar-support-prod",region="us-east",cohort="canary"}[5m])) / sum(rate(rw_infer_requests_total{route="hosted/chat/northstar-support-prod",region="us-east"}[5m]))`
= 0.39 right now.

Rafael Mendes: ack. is this impacting latency/error? customer-facing impact?

Sean Gallagher: error rate stable, but this is a safety issue if the new model is bad. We should treat as sev2-ish for beta. Let's contain.

Mina Haddad: on it. This is traffic-splitting enforcement in data plane. If it’s only us-east, could be hash input mismatch on that cluster or a config propagation issue.

Ravi Menon: +1. First check: are we using the same `cohort_key` in us-east? It’s supposed to be `tenant_id + route_id + stable_user_key` with fallback to request_id if missing.

Emily Zhao: I can check the us-east router build / config digest. Might be running slightly different commit?

Vikram Singh: grabbing router logs for rlt_7f2c in us-east. any recent deploy?

Aisha Bello: latency p95 is slightly up on canary vs baseline (not huge): baseline 820ms, canary 910ms in us-east over 15m. errors flat.

Rafael Mendes: mitigation: can we pause rollout / force canary=0 in us-east only?

Hannah Rivera: orchestrator supports pause globally; region-scoped override is behind flag but I think Smart Routing has region weights per rollout? Mina confirm.

Mina Haddad: yes, routing primitive has per-region enforcement weights. Quickest is set canary weight to 0 in us-east (keep 10% elsewhere). Alternatively pause the rollout which sets all regions to baseline.

Sean Gallagher: do region 0% if safe, to minimize disruption. But only if we’re confident it won’t wedge state.

Elena Popov: I can push a config patch to set `regions.us-east.canary_pct=0` for rlt_7f2c. Will take ~2-3 mins to propagate.

Dylan Brooks: FYI Console shows rollout at step 10% with soak timer running. If we do region override, Console won’t reflect it yet (known gap). Marissa: heads up.

Marissa Cole: yep, understood. For beta customer safety > UI accuracy. We’ll message Northstar through support channel.

Rafael Mendes: +1. Let’s do it.

Elena Popov: applying patch now.

Incident Bot: Change requested by @Elena Popov: "Set rlt_7f2c canary_pct=0 in us-east" (config pipeline: `routing-prod`).

Vikram Singh: while that propagates, here’s log sample from us-east router:
```
rollout_id=rlt_7f2c route=hosted/chat/northstar-support-prod region=us-east
cohort_key_source=header:x-rw-user-key
cohort_key_present=false
fallback_source=ip
hash_seed=route_id_only
assigned=canary
```
That looks suspicious: `hash_seed=route_id_only`??? should include tenant_id at least.

Ravi Menon: whoa. That `hash_seed` field indicates the "v0" cohorting code path. That would skew based on NAT IP distribution too.

Emily Zhao: checking build stamp in us-east: it’s on `router@1.38.2` but others are `1.38.3`. us-east missed the rollout during last deploy window.

Mina Haddad: ok so we have version skew. 1.38.2 uses legacy cohorting fallback behavior (route-only seed when user key missing). That can absolutely produce mismatch.

Sean Gallagher: root cause candidate: us-east routers running old version, using IP fallback and route-only seed => canary assignment biased.

Aisha Bello: config patch has landed. Observed canary pct in us-east is dropping: 0.22 -> 0.11 over last 2m.

Elena Popov: confirming propagation complete on all us-east POPs. should converge to ~0 within a few mins.

Rafael Mendes: good containment. Next action: get us-east routers to 1.38.3 ASAP.

Emily Zhao: I can kick a redeploy for us-east only. Need release channel sign-off since we’re mid-beta.

Sean Gallagher: do it. This is safety-related.

Incident Bot: :information_source: Deployment requested: `router` to `us-east` version `1.38.3` (requested by @Emily Zhao).

Hannah Rivera: meanwhile I’ll pause the orchestrator step timer? If Console is still counting soak at 10% but us-east is effectively 0, it may confuse auto-stop logic.

Aisha Bello: auto-stop checks are per-region AND global? Right now stop-condition evaluator is using global aggregates with region tag optional. For this rollout we set `regions=["us-east","us-west","eu-central"]` but evaluator is looking at all regions combined.

Sean Gallagher: so with us-east at 0 canary, global canary traffic decreases, which could extend time to significance. That’s ok short-term.

Mina Haddad: agreed; don’t pause orchestrator unless necessary. Just note in activity log / internal timeline.

Marissa Cole: I’ll DM support to tell Northstar “we temporarily disabled canary in us-east while we fix routing layer, no action needed.”

Dylan Brooks: can we add a banner in Console? probably not in time, but I’ll log a follow-up issue.

Vikram Singh: more logs from us-east show `cohort_key_present=false` a lot. Northstar doesn’t send x-rw-user-key consistently; they rely on our default. Our default should use `x-request-id` but it looks like 1.38.2 uses IP first. That’s the skew.

Ravi Menon: yep 1.38.3 changed fallback precedence: `x-rw-user-key` > `x-rw-session-id` > `request_id` (stable for retries) > last resort IP. Also fixes hash seed to include tenant+route.

Emily Zhao: redeploy started. ETA 8-10 mins.

Incident Bot: DeployBot: `router us-east` rolling update in progress (10% -> 50% -> 100%).

Aisha Bello: metrics update: us-east canary pct now 0.01 (effectively off). us-west and eu-central remain ~0.10.

Rafael Mendes: ok. once redeploy done, we can remove region override and go back to intended 10% globally.

Sean Gallagher: careful: remove override after confirming cohorting logs show expected hash inputs and observed split matches.

Mina Haddad: +1. Let’s verify on one POP first.

Incident Bot: DeployBot: `router us-east` update complete. version=1.38.3

Emily Zhao: us-east now on 1.38.3 across the fleet.

Vikram Singh: checking new logs:
```
rollout_id=rlt_7f2c region=us-east
cohort_key_source=header:x-rw-user-key
cohort_key_present=false
fallback_source=request_id
hash_seed=tenant+route
assigned=baseline
```
Looks good.

Aisha Bello: if we keep us-east override at 0, split stays 0 there. If we revert override, should stabilize at ~10%.

Elena Popov: I can revert the override now.

Sean Gallagher: do it, but watch for a few minutes. also note we might still see variance if they don’t send stable user key and request_ids are random per request (not per user). That’s ok though; expected distribution still correct.

Elena Popov: reverting us-east override back to configured canary_pct=10.

Incident Bot: Change requested by @Elena Popov: "Revert rlt_7f2c us-east canary_pct to 10".

Aisha Bello: watching.

Rafael Mendes: for follow-up: we need an alert for region version skew on router + a guard in control plane to block rollouts if region not on min version.

Mina Haddad: yes. Also add a metric: expected_pct vs observed_pct with threshold alert, per region.

Dylan Brooks: and Console should display a warning when region override / kill switch applied, even if internal-only.

Marissa Cole: +1. also for beta, we should recommend customers send `x-rw-user-key` or `x-rw-session-id` for more stable cohorting. Docs note?

Sean Gallagher: Aisha, what’s split now?

Aisha Bello: us-east canary pct is climbing to ~0.08 over 5m, trending to 0.10. Looks within noise now.

Sean Gallagher: cool. marking contained / resolved. keeping thread open for action items.

Rafael Mendes: Action items:
1) Prevent region version skew (release process / deploy guard) - @Emily Zhao
2) Control plane check: require router_min_version for rollouts + fail closed if region stale - @Mina Haddad @Ravi Menon
3) Add observed vs expected split alert per route/region/rollout - @Aisha Bello
4) Update runbook "bad split" with version-skew diagnostic and emergency region override steps - @Rafael Mendes
5) Docs: recommend stable cohort keys headers - @Marissa Cole @Wei Chen

Mina Haddad: ack on #2. Will file ENG issue and link to the routing PRs.

Ravi Menon: ack. also we should backport the fallback precedence fix into a patch release and enforce it as minimum.

Emily Zhao: ack #1. I’ll work with releases to ensure us-east can’t drift (and add a monitor on deploy parity).

Aisha Bello: ack #3. I can start with a dashboard panel + simple alert: |observed-expected| > 0.15 for 10m.

Sean Gallagher: closing as resolved once Northstar confirms. :thumbsup:

Marissa Cole: support says Northstar sees expected behavior again and is unblocked.

Incident Bot: Status updated: *RESOLVED* (root cause: router version skew in us-east using legacy cohorting fallback; mitigation: region canary disabled + router redeploy).

title: Service Nexus: VPC stenciling and controlled egress — POC notes
author: Asha Nair
text:
Context and goal:

This doc captures the design thinking, trade-offs, and a short runbook for a customer POC we ran to validate a ‘Service Nexus’ pattern: a small, hardened shared-services VPC + minimal footprint control plane in customer VPCs, with tightly controlled egress and DNS "stenciling" to enforce allowed destinations and reduce data exfil risk for private inference. The customer requirement: run Redwood Private inference inside their account with the ability to reach only a narrow set of vendor endpoints (metrics, S3 artifact pulls, KMS) and to ensure DNS resolution is auditable and can be pointed to either customer resolvers or Redwood-managed resolvers depending on tenancy model.

High-level topology options considered (quick):

1) Direct VPC Peering + private DNS delegation
 - Pros: lowest latency, straightforward route tables, simple for single-region.
 - Cons: scaling across many customer accounts/regions becomes O(n^2) peering, no transitive routing, limited control plane for central egress.

2) Transit Gateway + central egress appliance
 - Pros: scales to many VPCs, central route controls, we can deploy egress proxies/NATs in a central hub.
 - Cons: cost on TGW, slight added hop/latency, additional inter-account roles and attachments.

3) PrivateLink (Interface VPC Endpoints) + DNS forwarding (recommended for narrow-surface POC)
 - Pros: least peripheral attack surface (no route propagation), supports cross-account, caller stays in customer VPC, simpler security model for private endpoints.
 - Cons: per-endpoint ENIs/cost, not suitable for full general internet egress, needs DNS records and conditional forwarding.

Design pattern we validated in POC (Service Nexus, hybrid of 2 + 3):

- Customer VPCs attach to a lightweight shared-services VPC via Transit Gateway for scale. For customers with a single account/regional footprint we validated peering as a fast path option.
- Centralized egress cluster in the shared-services VPC: egress proxy fleet (envoy/mTLS) behind autoscaling and ALB/NLB, and a small NAT pool for non-proxied traffic (artifact S3 pulls).
- DNS stenciling: customer resolver (Route 53 Resolver endpoints) or /etc/resolv.conf stub to forward certain domains to the shared-services resolver. Non-allowed domains resolve to NXDOMAIN locally.
- PrivateLink endpoints exported to the customer account for Redwood-specific control-plane APIs (metrics ingestion, auth/token exchange). These endpoints are only reachable over VPC endpoints and require mTLS and token-based attestation.

DNS control and stenciling details:

- For private inference we need exact behavior for two domain classes:
 * internal vendor domains (metrics.redwood-inference.internal, artifacts.redwood-s3.internal) -> resolved by shared-services Route53 private hosted zone
 * public domains that must be blocked or forwarded (e.g., outbound to general internet) -> blocked via forced NXDOMAIN or resolved to internal blackhole IPs when necessary.

- Implementation alternatives tested:
 A) Route 53 Resolver inbound/outbound endpoints + resolver rules: forward *.redwood-inference.internal to shared-services resolver; block other zones via resolver rule pointing to a blackhole IP.
 B) Customer-side DNS stub resolver (dnsmasq in transit VPC) with allowlist config; simpler to audit and run as container.
 C) Kubernetes cluster-level CoreDNS with policy plugin when workload is in k8s; allows per-namespace whitelists.

- POC decision: use Route 53 Resolver rules for the initial POC and use a small fleet of dnsdist as secondary enforcement (faster iteration for customers that want to host their own).

Egress control (policy and enforcement):

- Two enforcement layers: network (route/NAT/proxy) and application (egress proxy + allowlist).
- Route-level: only advertise routes to shared-services TGW attachment for allowed prefixes. Unadvertised ranges implicitly unreachable.
- Proxy-level: Envoy-based egress mesh that enforces SNI/DNS/HTTP Host allowlist and performs TLS origination where we need to authenticate to downstream services (e.g., signed mTLS).
- Artifact retrieval (S3, model blobs): use VPC Gateway endpoints and a small NAT pool only for cross-account S3 if customer requires. Prefer presigned URLs over general outbound HTTP for better access control.

Service endpoints and access control: concrete items we implemented in the POC

- PrivateLink for auth/ingest: create an NLB in shared-services, create an Interface Endpoint Service, allowlist customer account id via endpoint policy.
- Route53 private hosted zone in shared-services (redwood-internal.local) with NS delegation of subzones to customer VPCs when we need split-horizon semantics.
- IAM/SG: endpoint SGs are locked down to customer subnets/ENI CIDRs and only accept mTLS or short-lived bearer tokens.

Operational runbook (short) - smoke tests we ran during the POC:

1) DNS resolution
 - dig @<resolver> metrics.redwood-inference.internal +short -> must return private IP
 - dig @<resolver> google.com -> NXDOMAIN or blackhole IP (as per policy)

2) Endpoint connectivity
 - curl --resolve metrics.redwood-inference.internal:<port>:<private-ip> https://metrics.redwood-inference.internal/health -v
 - tcpdump -i eth0 host <shared-services-egress-ip> and curl to validate SNI and mTLS handshake

3) Artifact retrieval
 - aws s3 presign get-object --bucket redwood-artifacts --key model-v1.bin | xargs curl -I

Sample AWS CLI snippets used in the lab (POC):

- create interface endpoint (PE):
 aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id vpc-012345 --service-name com.amazonaws.vpce.us-west-2.vpce-svc-12345678 --vpc-endpoint-type Interface --subnet-ids subnet-aaa,subnet-bbb --security-group-ids sg-xxxxx

- resolver rule to forward a zone to central resolver:
 aws route53resolver create-resolver-rule --creator-request-id rule1 --domain-name redwood-internal.local --rule-type FORWARD --target-ips Ip=10.2.5.10,Port=53 --resolver-endpoint-id rslvr-out-abc

Performance and cost notes from the POC:

- Transit Gateway adds ~1-3ms median hop compared to direct peering in the same AZ; throughput is dominated by ENI limits on interface endpoints for high-throughput telemetry ingestion.
- PrivateLink costs scale per-ENI; for scale customers evaluate using a small set of regional endpoints + a high-throughput NLB rather than many per-AZ endpoints.
- DNS forwarding adds negligible CPU but adds a small resolution latency (~1–4ms) depending on the resolver chain.

Security and compliance considerations:

- Audit: Route 53 Resolver query logging to S3 + CloudWatch for a 30 day retention (customer requirement varied).
- Egress L4/L7 telemetry: Envoy access logs to central observability, token exchange audit logs retained per customer SLA.
- Key management: allow only customer KMS for any customer-provided secrets; Redwood holds tokens for managed model store only under contractual data handling terms.

POC open questions and next steps:

- How does the customer want split-horizon for third-party CDNs (fast external model pulls) vs blocked external DNS? Need specific domain list.
- Should we provide an optional lightweight customer-side DNS appliance image (AMIs/container) for customers that cannot use R53 Resolver?
- Capacity test: validate PrivateLink ENI scaling under sustained 5000 req/s ingestion for telemetry (next sprint).

Action items (owners):

- Asha: publish Terraform module skeleton for shared-services TGW + Endpoint service (draft by 2025-03-09).
- Liam: capture allowed domain list template and example resolver rules (by 2025-03-05).
- Sofia: run throughput test for Interface Endpoint scaling and report CPU/ENI saturation points (by 2025-03-16).
- Ben: produce a one-page customer-facing diagram and short security spec for the SRE/security review (by 2025-03-12).

Appendix: short checklist for customer POC kickoff

- [ ] Confirm customer account IDs and region list
- [ ] Agree on allowed outbound domains and artifact buckets
- [ ] Confirm KMS key usage and cross-account grants
- [ ] Decide TGW vs peering (based on number of VPCs and cross-account requirements)
- [ ] Set up resolver logs and short retention for initial testing

Notes-to-self style fragments from the workshop (raw):

- "If customer insists on zero TGW cost, peering + PrivateLink can be ok for <3 accounts, otherwise TGW win"
- "Consider offering a managed DNS policy package where we keep a curated allowlist and rotate blackhole responses"
- "Edge-case: customer uses non-AWS DNS that blocks forwarding; fallback is to ship a dnsmasq container in customer kube infra"

End of notes.

title: Resilient streaming schema: fallback stubs and idempotent tool-relay semantics
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Problem statement: Clients consuming streamed structured output must be able to make progress even when downstream tool invocations fail or when the network cuts the stream. Current behavior either aborts the emit entirely or leaves consumers with partial, non-actionable payloads. We need a pragmatic contract that ensures predictable consumer behavior, clear retry semantics for function/tool calls, and measurable observability for debugging and economics.\n\nGoals:\n- Define a minimal, deterministic start-of-stream stub that gives downstream services enough schema and provenance to act (routing, caching, UI placeholders).\n- Specify idempotent tool-relay semantics and tokens so tool calls can be retried safely across disconnects and platform failovers.\n- Describe a bounded fallback policy (graceful degradation) that prefers useful partial outputs over silent failures.\n- Provide clear acceptance tests, observability signals, and a canary rollout plan.\n\nNon-goals:\n- Not addressing large-scale protocol negotiation across different client SDK versions (handled in follow-up).\n- Not providing exact cost-optimization heuristics for batching — that remains in Optimize workstream.\n\nDesign summary:\n1) Start stub: for every streamed request the platform must emit a single well-formed stub JSON as the first record (if streaming is used). The stub contains: request_id, schema_version, model_variant, short_status ("in-progress"), required_output_keys (list), and optional resume_token (opaque string). Consumers can use this stub to allocate UI slots or pre-warm caches.\n2) Progressive objects: subsequent items are full or partial records with a 'progress_id' that maps to required_output_keys. Every partial record includes an 'is_final' boolean.\n3) Tool-relay semantics: tool invocation requests from the model are emitted as "tool_call" frames with: tool_name, args_hash, idempotency_key (generated by platform if model doesn't supply), submit_timestamp. The platform will accept tool_call frames and return a tool_call_ack (tool_call_id, status: queued). The platform guarantees at-least-once delivery to third-party tool adapters but provides idempotency semantics keyed by idempotency_key to allow exactly-once logical behavior where tools support it.\n4) Timeouts & fallbacks: each tool_call has a configurable soft_timeout (recommended default 4s) and hard_deadline (default 30s). On soft_timeout the platform emits a "tool_stub" containing minimal expected response shape (per schema) and a recommendation to retry. On hard_deadline the platform emits a tool_error frame with standardized error_code and optionally a replacement stub depending on fallback policy.\n5) Resume & reconciliation: resume_token in stub enables clients to reconnect and request missing progress_ids. Tokens are single-use; platform will accept resume requests up to 24 hours depending on retention policy. Reconciliation includes a delta list describing which progress_ids were completed so client can request only missing parts.\n6) Security & audit: every tool_call frame is logged with request_id, tool_name, op_hash and stored in audit logs. Tool payloads marked sensitive must be redacted in standard logs and only appear in encrypted audit stores accessible to compliance roles.\n\nTrade-offs considered:\n- Emitting stubs increases token count and latency for tiny requests, but greatly reduces error handling complexity for integrators.\n- Idempotency tokens shift some responsibility to model authors; platform can synthesize tokens when absent but will prefer model-generated keys for cross-request deduplication.\n\nSuccess metrics:\n- consumer-visible error rate for streamed structured requests drops by 50% in first month after rollout.\n- resume success rate >= 98% for reconnects within 24 hours.\n- tool_call duplicate execution rate <= 0.5% for tools that support idempotency; platform-initiated duplicates recorded separately.\n

A1: First-record stub is emitted for 100% of streaming structured responses within 50ms of connection establishment in canary region.
A2: Each tool_call frame must produce either a tool_call_ack or a tool_error within soft_timeout; soft_timeout behavior must be observable via metric 'tool_call_soft_timeout_rate'.
A3: Resume flow: given a valid resume_token clients can reconnect and obtain a delta list; automated e2e test must validate reassembly of a previously interrupted 12-part stream.
A4: Idempotency: when model supplies the same idempotency_key for repeated tool_calls, the downstream tool adapter must receive the operation at most once logically; integration tests simulate at-least-once delivery and dedup is validated by comparing op_hashes in audit logs.
A5: Fallback stubs: when a tool hard_deadline elapses, the platform emits a validated replacement stub conforming to the recorded schema; schema conformance tests assert shape and required keys.
A6: Observability: traces include request_id and any tool_call_id, and logs surface 'resume_token' issuance and use; dashboards show tool_call_latency_p50/p95, resume_success_rate, stub_emitted_rate.
A7: Security: sensitive tool args are redacted by default in runtime logs; security review sign-off required before rollout to production.

Unit: parser/generator tests for stub and tool_call frames ensuring valid JSON and required keys.
Integration: platform <-> tool-adapter harness that injects fail/slow behaviors and validates ack/replay paths.
E2E: client SDK replay test that opens stream, forces disconnect at N=3, reconnects with resume_token and verifies complete reconstruction.
Chaos: simulate platform pod restart during active tool_call and ensure idempotency and resume behavior meet acceptance criteria.
Load: synthetic workload of 10k streaming sessions/hour to verify stub emission rate and latency in canary region.

2025-02-05: Kickoff meeting — agreed on stub-first contract and default timeouts (soft 4s / hard 30s). Action: ENG to prototype tool_call_ack shape.
2025-02-10: Design review — security requested redaction scheme; added audit store requirement. Action: Security to provide redaction spec by 2025-02-14.
2025-02-16: Opted for platform-synthesized idempotency_key when model does not provide one (decision to reduce integration friction).
2025-02-18: PRD in review; PM requested explicit rollback criteria in case of increased tool duplicate rate post-rollout.

Q1: Retention window for resume tokens — default 24h ok for enterprise customers with long-running clients?
Q2: Should platform synthesize idempotency_keys using deterministic hashing across model revision upgrades?
Q3: What is required behavior for clients that don't consume the stub first (legacy SDKs) — do we need compatibility mode?

Canary: 1% of streaming traffic in us-west-2 for 3 days, monitor resume_success_rate and tool_call_duplicate_executions.
Ramp: 10% for 48 hours if canary metrics within thresholds, then 50% for 72 hours.
Full: 100% after 7 days with weekly check-ins for first month.
Rollback: if tool_call_duplicate_executions > 1% or resume_success_rate < 95% for 4 hours, rollback to previous streaming contract and open incident review.

title: Postmortem: EU-West capacity shortage and region fallback (2025-03-03)
author: Hiro Tanaka
text:
h2. Summary
On 2025-03-03, a GPU capacity shortfall in eu-west-1 impacted a subset of Hosted and Dedicated traffic pinned to that region. Mitigation required activating *automatic region fallback* (eu-west-1 -> us-east-1) for eligible routes until additional capacity was brought online.

h2. Impact
* Elevated p95 latency and increased 429/503 responses for region-pinned routes in eu-west-1.
* Customers: 7 Hosted orgs and 1 Dedicated tenant with optional cross-region allowance enabled.
* Duration: ~41 minutes of degraded performance; ~18 minutes of hard errors for the most constrained pool.

h2. Timeline (UTC)
* 09:42: Capacity alert: available_gpu_count < 5 in eu-west-1 pool rw-a100-eu-01.
* 09:48: Saturation exceeded 95% and queue wait climbed > 400ms.
* 09:51: Mitigation: enabled *region fallback* for "chat-default" and "embeddings-default" where customer policy allows cross-region.
* 09:54: Router began directing overflow to us-east-1 for eligible traffic.
* 10:03: Error rate dropped; latency partially recovered.
* 10:23: Added 8 GPUs to eu-west-1 pool; disabled region fallback after stabilization.

h2. Mitigation details
We toggled a router policy flag:
* Primary region: eu-west-1
* Fallback region: us-east-1
* Triggers: saturation > 90% OR 503 rate > 0.5%
* Eligibility: routes not marked "data_residency_strict"

h2. Root cause
A delayed GPU delivery + slow provisioning left the eu-west-1 pool below the forecasted headroom for a scheduled customer load test.

h2. What went well
* Region fallback prevented a full outage for eligible traffic.
* On-call followed the capacity runbook and coordinated with Infra quickly.

h2. What went poorly
* We lacked a clear customer-facing flag indicating whether cross-region fallback was enabled for a tenant.

h2. Action items
1) Add tenant-level UI indicator and API field for cross-region fallback eligibility. Owner: Eng Platform.
2) Improve capacity forecasting for scheduled load tests and Dedicated bursts. Owner: Eng SRE.
3) Add automated comms template for region fallback events. Owner: Incident Response.

h2. References
* Incident ID: INC-2025-0303

title: Deployment path clarification: isolation expectations and next steps
author: sergio_alvarez
text:
From: Sergio Alvarez <sergio_alvarez@redwood.com>
To: Katie Winters <katie.winters@finxbank.com>
Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-08-02T10:15:00-07:00
Subject: Deployment path clarification: isolation expectations and next steps

Hi Katie —

Thanks again for taking time this morning. Quick recap and a set of clarifying questions so we can prepare the right technical deep-dive: 

Recap of what I heard
- Primary concern: strict data isolation for regulated customer data (transactional PII and logs).
- Goal is to ensure data and audit logs remain within FinX control and to understand whether model weights or inference execution in vendor-managed infra is acceptable.

High-level deployment options (summary):
- Hosted API: fastest to go-live but runs in Redwood-hosted multi-tenant environment — not a fit if you require vendor-zero persistence or customer-only key control.
- Dedicated capacity: customer-dedicated GPU pool managed by Redwood. Can be configured with VPC peering or private network connectivity and customer-managed KMS for at-rest encryption. Model runtime still occurs on Redwood-managed hardware.
- Private (VPC/on-prem): full customer-controlled deployment (VPC or on-prem package) — model weights and runtime live in your environment; recommended when regulators disallow any vendor-managed persistence or access.

Questions for you before the technical call
1) Is the non-negotiable requirement that model weights and any cached inference artifacts must never be stored in Redwood-managed hardware?
2) Do you require logs and telemetry to be pushed into an AWS account owned by FinX (S3/CloudWatch) as a hard requirement?
3) Any particular compliance references (e.g., specific regulator guidance or audit language) we should map to?

Next steps
- If you confirm (1) or (2) above, we’ll prep two tracks for the deep-dive: Dedicated with VPC-connect design and Private on-prem/VPC deployment design.
- I’ve attached a short security one-pager and a deployment requirements template to collect the network/security details we’ll need.
- Proposed time for the technical meet: Thurs 2026-08-05 09:00 PT — please confirm.

Thanks,
Sergio Alvarez
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
sergio_alvarez@redwood.com | +1 (415) 555-0123

Attachments: redwood_security_one-pager.pdf, deployment_requirements_template.xlsx

From: Katie Winters <katie.winters@finxbank.com>
To: Sergio Alvarez <sergio_alvarez@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-08-02T15:42:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Deployment path clarification: isolation expectations and next steps

Sergio —

Thanks for the summary. A few clarifications: 
- Our compliance and internal audit teams require that customer data (including PII and transactional logs) never persist in a vendor-managed bucket or storage for more than transient memory (i.e., must be exported to our S3/GCS and then purged on our schedule).
- We also have a strong preference for customer-managed encryption keys. If Redwood can support a model where logs/metrics are streamed into an FinX AWS account and keys are customer-managed, that helps a lot.
- On model weights: our initial posture is that model weights used for inference may remain on vendor-managed hardware only if we have legal and technical assurances (audit logs, key separation, and contractual controls). If those cannot be met, we'll need Private deployment.

I think your proposed approach (two-track prep) makes sense. Please include any examples of customers who used Dedicated with VPC-connect + customer KMS, and any differences we should expect versus a Private on-prem install. Also include an estimate range for committed monthly cost for Dedicated (ballpark GPUs/month) — procurement will need that for early review. Our procurement contact is Samuel Jones (samuel.jones@finxbank.com).

-Katie
Katie Winters
Head of Cloud Risk & Compliance
FinX Bank

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>
To: Katie Winters <katie.winters@finxbank.com>, Sergio Alvarez <sergio_alvarez@redwood.com>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-08-03T09:10:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Deployment path clarification: isolation expectations and next steps

Hi Katie —

Thanks for the clear constraints; I wanted to add technical color so you can see where Dedicated vs Private typically diverge in practice: 

Dedicated capacity (what we call Redwood Dedicated)
- Hardware: dedicated GPU nodes logically isolated to your tenant. The infrastructure (hosts, device drivers, hypervisor/containers) is still managed by Redwood.
- Networking: supports VPC peering or private peering (transit), and we can arrange private endpoints so control plane traffic is limited.
- Key management: supports customer-managed KMS (bring-your-own-key) for at-rest encryption of persisted artifacts we control; logs and telemetry can be exported to your AWS account via secure sinks.
- Model weights: typically loaded onto Redwood-managed GPUs at runtime; ephemeral caches can be configured to minimize persistence. We can document cache lifetimes and purge behavior and provide audit hooks.
- Tradeoffs: much faster provisioning and lower ops burden for FinX; still requires contractual and technical controls if your policy forbids vendor-hosted weights.

Private deployment (VPC-hosted or on-prem package)
- Hardware and runtime live in your environment (either in your VPC where you control instances or fully on-prem air-gapped appliances).
- You retain full control of keys, storage, and model artifacts. Redwood provides a private control plane or an appliance package depending on the engagement.
- Tradeoffs: highest isolation and easiest to satisfy conservative auditors, but longer lead times and additional SW/HW integration work.

Options and asks from FinX for next step prep
1) Confirm whether model weights absolutely cannot be present on vendor-managed hardware even transiently (yes/no).
2) Provide a sample network CIDR and whether you prefer VPC peering or an S3-forwarding-only model for logs.
3) Compliance pack request: we’ll send our SOC2 summary and prior deployment diagrams. Can you share the specific control numbers your auditors will validate?

I’ve attached our SOC2_summary.pdf and a VPC connect reference diagram (vpc_connect_arch.png). If it helps, we can share anonymized case notes of customers who adopted Dedicated with customer KMS and VPC export for logs.

Happy to join the technical deep-dive and walk through a proposed architecture.

Best,
Rishi Malhotra
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

title: Access Provisioning and Spend Journeys (Company Playbook)
author: Asha Patel
text:
Overview

Purpose
This playbook centralizes company-wide routines for: access and permissions, change control, data handling, procurement and expense requests, vendor onboarding, and travel approvals. It is intended for requestors, approvers, finance, security, and operations teams.

Scope
Applies to all Redwood employees, contractors, and vendors that require systems access, make purchases on behalf of Redwood, or manage configuration changes to production or corporate systems. Exceptions must be approved by Finance + Security.

Principles (short)
- Least privilege: grant the minimum permissions required.
- Clear ownership: every access/expense/change has a named owner.
- Auditability: decisions and artifacts are retained for 3 years (longer for regulated customers).
- Separation of duties: requester ≠ approver for material spend and production changes.
- Risk-based controls: higher-risk assets require additional validation.

Roles & Responsibilities
- Requestor: submits request with business justification and expiry.
- Approver: validates business need and policy compliance.
- Provisioner: implements the access, change or purchase. For infra changes, this is the engineering owner.
- Finance: validates budget and PO requirement for purchases > $5,000.
- Security: performs risk review for access to sensitive assets (PCI/PHI/Customer PII).
- Vendor Ops: manages supplier onboarding and contract records.

1) Access & Permissions: request-to-provision workflow
A. Access categories
- Standard internal apps: Google Workspace, Slack, Okta-managed SSO apps.
- Sensitive systems: production clusters, customer data stores, KMS/HSM, audit logs.
- Service accounts and API keys

B. Request flow (numbered steps)
1. Requestor fills the Access Request form in the internal portal. Required fields: owner, justification, asset identifier (service name), role, required duration, and risk notes.
2. Automated validation: system checks manager alignment, existing approvals, and if request touches sensitive assets.
3. Approver(s) notified: manager for standard access; manager + security for sensitive. Approvals are timeboxed to 48 hours.
4. Provisioner executes via IaC or identity provider. Provisioning must include an audit tag: "provisioned_by=<engineer>" and expiry metadata.
5. Post-provision review: owner confirms least-privilege within 7 days.
6. Revocation: requests with duration automatically expire; ad-hoc revocations are processed within 4 business hours for sensitive assets.

C. Example Access Request JSON (for integration):
{
 "request_id": "REQ-2026-0123",
 "requestor": "alice@example.com",
 "asset": "redwood-prod-cluster-3",
 "role": "read-only",
 "justification": "Support ticket #45121 - debug customer issue",
 "expiry": "2026-03-31"
}

D. Minimum approval matrix (table as text)
- Manager approval: any standard internal app.
- Manager + Security: access to customer data, KMS, or production write access.
- Manager + Security + Infra Eng lead: service accounts, long-lived keys (>90 days), or configuration write for core infra.

E. Access reviews
- Quarterly automated recertification for all roles.
- Monthly manual review for owners of assets classified high or critical.

2) Change Management (applies to infra and critical apps)
A. Change types
- Routine (low risk): config changes with no customer impact.
- Standard (planned): scheduled deploys within existing CI/CD gates.
- Emergency: rollbacks or fixes for live incidents.

B. Change lifecycle (numbered)
1. Submit a Change Request (CR) in the change tracker. Include: impact statement, rollback plan, test plan, scheduled window, and approver list.
2. Risk assessment: automated scoring based on affected services, blast radius, and user counts. Score > 7 requires Security + SRE signoff.
3. Approval: standard changes require SRE or owning eng manager; high-risk changes require cross-team approval and a canary plan.
4. Execution: operator runs the change following the runbook (include CLI snippets or playbook links).
5. Post-deploy verification: health checks and metric baselines for 60 minutes; if deviations exceed thresholds (5% traffic error rate increase or 30% latency tail degradation), initiate rollback.
6. Post-change review: update CR with lessons learned within 3 business days.

C. Emergency changes
- Emergency changes may bypass normal lead times but must be documented in the tracker within 24 hours and reviewed by the incident review board within 72 hours.

3) Data Management (classification & retention)
A. Classification levels
- Public: safe to publish externally.
- Internal: company-only, low sensitivity.
- Confidential: product roadmaps, non-public contracts.
- Restricted: customer PII/PHI, payment data — requires encryption at rest, access controls, audit logs.

B. Retention & deletion
- Default retention: documents and logs - 3 years.
- Customer PII/PHI: retention per contract or legal requirement; ensure secure deletion procedures and certs of destruction.

C. Data handling rules
- No customer data in personal devices or uncontrolled cloud storage.
- Use approved S3 buckets with encryption-and-logging policy for backups.

4) Procurement & Expenses
A. Purchase thresholds and approvals (table as text)
- <= $500: Manager approval.
- $501–$5,000: Manager + Finance cost center approval.
- > $5,000: Manager + Finance + Procurement (PO required).
- > $50,000: Procurement lead + Legal + Finance (contract & SLAs required).

B. Request-to-purchase flow (numbered)
1. Submit Purchase Request (PR) in the procurement portal with business justification, vendor, estimated cost, and budget code.
2. Finance validates budget availability within 2 business days.
3. Procurement reviews vendor terms and recommends PO or contract.
4. Once approved, Procurement issues a PO and Finance arranges payment terms.

C. Expense reporting and travel
- All expenses recorded within 10 business days of transaction. Receipts required for any expense > $25.
- Corporate card use: allowed for approved subscriptions and travel only. Disputes to be raised within 30 days.

5) Vendor Management
A. Onboarding checklist (numbered)
1. Vendor risk classification (low/medium/high) based on access and data processing.
2. Security questionnaire and evidence collection (SOC2, ISO, penetration test reports as relevant).
3. Contract template with data handling and breach notification clauses; Legal review required for high-risk vendors.
4. Technical integration: restrict network access to least-privilege IP ranges, short-lived credentials, and dedicated service accounts where possible.
5. SLA & monitoring: define uptime, support channels, escalation points, and regular review cadence.

B. Offboarding
- Revoke all credentials, confirm return or destruction of data, and archive contract artifacts. Vendor Ops must complete offboarding checklist within 5 business days.

6) Travel Policy (brief)
- Approvals: Manager pre-approval required for any travel. Trips with reimbursement > $2,000 require Finance pre-approval.
- Per-diem & limits: domestic hotel limit $250/night; international evaluated per region (Finance provides country caps).
- Booking: use corporate travel vendor where available; exceptions require manager justification.

7) Templates & Forms (links and examples)
- Access Request Form: internal portal link (use template ID: ARF-2025).
- Purchase Request Template: include vendor, justification, budget code, and anticipated SOW.
- Change Request Template: include test plan, rollback, and impact matrix.
- Vendor Security Questionnaire: checklist with required evidence fields.

8) Escalation & Audit
- Escalate unresolved approval delays > 72 hours to the team director.
- Security incidents involving vendor or data must follow the Incident Response policy and be reported to Security Pager within 1 hour.
- Audit cadence: internal audit team runs an annual review; targeted audits occur after significant incidents.

9) Metrics & KPIs to monitor
- Time-to-provision (median target: 24 hours for standard apps).
- Time-to-approve purchases (median target: 3 business days).
- Quarterly access recertification completion rate (target: 95%).
- Number of emergency changes and post-change rollback rate (target rollback < 5%).

Appendices
A. Example CLI snippet to revoke an API key (for infra owners)
$ redwoodctl keys revoke --key-id=svc-abc-123 --reason="project-complete"

B. Sample approval language (copy-paste for approvers)
"I approve this request as the owner/manager. I confirm budget and business justification, and I understand the access will expire on the date specified."

C. Frequently Asked Questions (short)
Q: Who to contact for fast-track access?
A: Managers may request an expedited path; security must approve for sensitive assets. Fast-track is intended only for critical customer-impact scenarios.

D. Change history
- 2025-03-02: Playbook created (Asha Patel).
- 2025-10-15: Added vendor onboarding checklist (Priya Desai).
- 2026-02-14: Updated thresholds and revocation SLAs (Liam Torres).

References
- Incident Response (security-and-compliance/incident-response-security)
- Authorization Lifecycle (policies-and-process/authorization-lifecycle-and-procurement-patterns-2029)
- Procurement templates (policies-and-process/templates)

Contact
For questions or proposed updates, email policy-ops@redwood.ai or open a PR against the central playbook repository.

title: Cleanup stale test instances and grant access for infra-eco team
text:
Overview:
We have identified a set of long-running/stale test instances (mostly ephemeral GPU VMs and a few reserved volumes) that were created during several internal spike projects in Q4 2025 and have not been claimed. They are incurring small but persistent costs and cluttering the resource inventory.

Impact:
- Monthly spend ~ $1.2k (estimated) for these instances/volumes.
- Inventory noise for infra capacity planning and autoscaler reports.
- Potential security surface (old SSH keys / stale service accounts) if left indefinitely.

Requested actions:
1) Confirm the attached CSV list and terminate instances flagged as STALE-ORPHAN after 72h grace window.
2) Snapshot and retain any volumes that appear to contain non-temporary data (owner label present) and add to archived-volumes S3 bucket.
3) Create an infra-eco service account and grant Miguel Reyes (infra) and Priya Desai (cost-ops) read/write access to the archived bucket and tagging permissions for the affected project.
4) Add a short runbook entry to /confluence/runbooks/instance-cleanup (or link in ticket) describing the verification steps and approval flow.

Steps to locate instances:
- Console path: Cloud Console > Compute > Instances. Filter by label: "spike=true OR temp=true OR created_by=automation-test" and running > 30 days.
- See attached CSV (stale-instances-list-2026-03-01.csv) for pre-filtered candidate list.

Suggested runbook summary (for runbook doc):
- Notify owners via tag-owner email (attempt 48h).
- If no reply, snapshot volumes (if non-empty) to archived-volumes, tag snapshot with INT-7832 and timestamp.
- Terminate instances and record instance IDs in ticket comments.
- Update billing tag on project to "archived" for this set to ensure cost tracking.

Rollback/backout:
- Restore from snapshot if unintended data loss occurs; snapshots retained for 30 days.

Notes and links:
- Related support thread: INT-7720 (previous cleanup run Feb 2026).
- Cost dashboard: https://internal-dashboard.redwood/costs/q4-2025 (internal link).
- Please check ACLs before granting access; follow least-privilege principles.

title: Excess 429s during nightly billing-sweep capacity refresh (mid-window refill anomaly)
text:
Issue summary:
Customer reports a recurring spike of 429 responses between 00:10–00:25 UTC during their nightly billing/usage sweep. The spike correlates to a platform-side token refill event that runs as part of billing finalization. Impact: several dozen production clients (on the customer's dedicated pool) saw transient failures for short-lived streaming sessions and concurrent API calls.

Impact:
- ~18% increased error rate (429) for the customer's API keys during the 15-minute window.
- Client-side retries cause additional amplified traffic leading to cascading backpressure.
- Customer has scheduled bulk warmups at 00:05 UTC which may be interacting with the refill.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (DocuSift dedicated tenant) in us-east
- Production traffic pattern: many short-lived streaming sessions + periodic bulk warmup tasks nightly

Desired outcome:
- Understand why global refill (billing sweep) causes mid-window token accounting to temporarily over-throttle the tenant despite available quota afterward.
- Provide a mitigation path or config guidance to avoid production impact during midnight maintenance windows.

1) Have a dedicated tenant with scheduled warmups at 00:05 UTC (many short streaming sessions).
2) Ensure tenant has a per-tenant quota with a refill aligned to daily billing sweep at 00:15 UTC.
3) Run concurrent short streaming sessions and several bulk generation calls between 00:05–00:20 UTC.
4) Observe 429s concentrated around 00:10–00:25 UTC window.

Note: Customer provided an automated replay trace of the pattern for March 8–10 which reproduces the spike every night.

Selected sample from edge-gateway logs (us-east) aggregated for SUP-801999 window:
[2026-03-09T00:09:58Z] key=ds-prod-01 conn=start session_id=abc123 route=/v1/chat tokens=0
[2026-03-09T00:10:12Z] key=ds-prod-01 response=429 reason=token_quota_exhausted window_id=2026-03-09T00:00
[2026-03-09T00:10:13Z] key=ds-prod-01 response=429 reason=token_quota_exhausted window_id=2026-03-09T00:00
[2026-03-09T00:11:45Z] billing-agent EVENT=refill_start tenant=docusize window=2026-03-09T00:00
[2026-03-09T00:12:02Z] billing-agent EVENT=refill_complete tenant=docusize added_tokens=250000
[2026-03-09T00:12:15Z] key=ds-prod-01 response=200 tokens_consumed=102

Observations: 429s begin before refill_start in most traces; many are clustered during the refill. Edge logs show short period where token accounting rejects requests even though refill occurs a few seconds later.

Hypotheses considered:
- Refill race: refill occurs but accounting layer sees a transient negative window balance due to ordering between health checks and refill ledger updates.
- Burst accounting: scheduled warmups at 00:05 create burst buckets that deplete the short window immediately before refill, and our token-smoothing logic applies a protective throttle until refill finished.
- Billing sweep lock: billing agent takes a lock on tenant ledger during finalization which temporarily prevents token allocations leading to short-term 'hard' 429s.

What we've checked so far:
- Confirmed rebuild of refill ledger entries for the tenant shows refill batch writes completed within 40–120ms.
- Edge telemetry shows many short-lived streaming sessions re-establishing connections in the window causing concurrency churn.
- Replica lag on the quota read path was minimal (avg < 50ms) but spikes up to 400ms during the sweep on one replica.

Next steps planned:
- SRE to run a targeted canary of billing sweep with increased logging around ledger lock acquisition (owner: Tomás Rivera).
- Experiment: shift customer warmup schedule to 00:30 UTC for 48 hours to validate warmup/refill interaction.
- Add a temporary rule to exclude the refill maintenance window from aggressive per-route protective throttles for this tenant.

- For immediate mitigation, ask customer to shift scheduled warmups to 00:30–01:00 UTC as a stop-gap.
- We can temporarily bump the tenant burst window (route weight) for the midnight period via a per-tenant override while we complete investigation.
- Client-side: advise exponential backoff with jitter and cap concurrent short-lived streams during maintenance windows.

2026-03-10 Priya Shah: Opened ticket after customer reported automated alarms at 00:12 UTC showing spike in 429s. Attached replay traces.
2026-03-10 Aisha Malik: Acknowledged. Assigning to SRE for ledger/replica checks and to Billing for sweep behavior review.
2026-03-11 Tomás Rivera (SRE): Replica lag spike noted on quota-read replica 3 between 00:09–00:13 UTC. Will instrument lock timing on next sweep run.
2026-03-11 Billing-Team-Bot: Billing sweep job v2.7 (rolled 2026-02-28) adds per-tenant reconciliation step which may briefly lock the ledger. Filing infra PR to make reconciliation non-blocking: github.com/redwood/billing/pull/72
2026-03-12 Aisha Malik: Temporarily applied tenant route-weight override for DocuSift for 00:00–01:00 UTC window to reduce 429s — monitoring metrics for two nights.
2026-03-12 Customer (DocuSift SRE): Confirmed error rate dropped after override on 2026-03-12 night. Seeking root cause patch timeline and permanent config guidance.

Workarounds applied: per-tenant midnight route-weight override and customer shifted warmups for testing.
Longer-term fix: Billing team opened PR to remove blocking ledger lock during sweep and implement asynchronous reconciliation (PR #72). SRE to add guard in rate-limiter to allow transient requests to pass if a refill is in progress and refill write timestamp is within 500ms.
Follow-ups:
- Track PR rollout and post-deploy monitor for three midnight cycles.
- Create runbook entry: 'handle-refill-contact-points' describing how to triage similar midnight refills and recommended customer warmup scheduling.
- Customer success to coordinate timeline with DocuSift; SRE to confirm when non-blocking billing sweep is live.

- Billing PR: github.com/redwood/billing/pull/72
- Instrumentation ticket: INT-42021 (quota-replica-lock-timing)
- Runbook draft: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/OPS/pages/Refill+Window+Runbook

title: SLO-aware Batchline Debug Scratchbook
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Overview:
This is a working scratchbook for the "batchline" experiments — an SLO-aware variant of the continuous batching scheduler. The idea: give each request a small "tailbudget" allocation (ms) derived from its SLO, age, and priority. The batchline then forms batches while respecting a global tailbudget budget and per-tenant slot-credit limits. Purpose is to reduce p99/p999 spikes for mixed-length workloads without severely harming throughput.

Why this is different (quick):
- Moves beyond fixed timeouts by accounting for per-request tail budget
- Uses soft credits (slot-credit) to avoid starving low-priority tenants during microbursts
- Tries to shape flush decisions with a tiny ML-calibrated estimator for remaining model time (rough estimate) rather than constant thresholds

Goals / success metrics:
- Primary: reduce p99 by >= 20% on mixed chat+summarization workload under 60% GPU utilization
- Secondary: keep throughput drop <= 10% and median latency degradation <= 5%
- Tertiary: reduce frequency of 5x p99 spikes (events where p99 exceeds 5x baseline p99)

Hypotheses:
H1: Tailbudget-aware flush will convert a portion of p99 spikes into p95 improvements because we avoid flushing big batches early for tiny requests.
H2: Slot-credit backpressure will keep tail starvation low compared to fixed-priority demotion.
H3: Estimator noise matters — if the remaining-token estimator has >30% error, batchline decisions degrade and we see throughput loss.

Workload and test harness:
- Workload: synthetic mix reflecting production inter-arrival and length distribution (60% short chat ~ 20–80 tokens, 30% medium completion ~ 200 tokens, 10% long summaries ~ 1000 tokens). Burstiness profile taken from production replay (sample window: 2025-08-07 12:00–14:00).
- Harness: local cluster of 4x A100-equivalent nodes (dev infra), using trace-replay harness (replay tool v0.9.2).
- Measurement windows: 30m warmup, 1h experiment, 30m cooldown. Aggregations by 5m windows.

Configs tried (labelled):
- BL-BASELINE: current continuous-batcher (fixed timeout 8ms, max-batch 64)
- BL-TB: batchline with tailbudget per request, same max-batch and default slot-credit 4
- BL-TB-EST: BL-TB + estimator enabled (lightweight token-time predictor)
- BL-TB-SC8: BL-TB with slot-credit=8 (more aggressive accumulation)
- BL-TB-FLUSHHYST: BL-TB + hysteresis on flush (minimum hold 2ms after first non-full batch formed)

Quick run notes (commands used):
- ./harness replay --trace ./traces/aug7_mixed.json --config conf/bl-tb.yaml --duration 1h --out results/bl-tb
- profiling: cpuprofiler + nvprof runs attached via staging probe container; profiler flags: --samples-per-sec 500

Results (summary numbers aggregated across 1h window, relative to BL-BASELINE):
- BL-BASELINE: p50 12ms, p95 180ms, p99 420ms, throughput 100k tokens/s (baseline)
- BL-TB: p50 13ms (+8%), p95 140ms (-22%), p99 330ms (-21%), throughput 96k tokens/s (-4%)
- BL-TB-EST: p50 14ms (+16%), p95 130ms (-28%), p99 290ms (-31%), throughput 92k tokens/s (-8%)
- BL-TB-SC8: p50 12.5ms (+4%), p95 150ms (-17%), p99 310ms (-26%), throughput 94k tokens/s (-6%)
- BL-TB-FLUSHHYST: p50 13ms (+8%), p95 135ms (-25%), p99 305ms (-27%), throughput 95k tokens/s (-5%)

Interpretation / notes:
- Tailbudget gating yielded consistent p95/p99 wins across configs while only modestly impacting median/throughput.
- Estimator (BL-TB-EST) gave best tail numbers but increased median/throughput hit; plausible that estimator made more conservative flushes (overestimation of remaining time).
- Slot-credit tuning matters: raising credits to 8 reduces p50 impact but slightly worsens p95 vs estimator configuration. There's a sweet spot around 4–6 for our workload.

Profiling & bottleneck notes:
- Kernel hotspots: attention kernel still dominates per-token GPU time; batch coalescing slightly increases per-kernel occupancy but overall GPU utilization climbed ~8% which explains some throughput drop.
- CPU-side: scheduler lock contention visible during microbursts (stack traces show contention in batch_allocator::allocate_slot). Under BL-TB a new atomic slot-credit operation increased contention at spikes — need to micro-optimize (see below).
- NVTX traces: flush events align with short-request floods; BL-TB shifted flush timing reducing wasted model computation due to early flush of long requests.

Failure / anomaly cases spotted:
- Edgecase: long-running summary requests occasionally exhausted tailbudget and got preempted mid-batch leading to rare 2x p999 spikes (investigate preemption path).
- Under synthetic pathological input (all long, then all short) BL-TB-EST caused oscillation in batch sizes — estimator being reactive to sudden length-phase change. Simple smoothing of estimator predictions fixed oscillation in a follow-up run.

Actionable follow-ups (short):
1) Fix atomic hotpath: replace atomic slot-credit decrement with per-thread batch-local accrual + periodic reconcile (reduce contention). Owner: Diego. ETA: 1 sprint.
2) Add lightweight exponential smoothing to estimator (alpha=0.2) and re-run BL-TB-EST to measure throughput recovery. Owner: Mei. ETA: 1 week.
3) Add a guard in preemption path to avoid midway preemptions of long requests when their remaining tailbudget < 2ms; instead mark for immediate fallback to lower-cost variant. Owner: Omar. ETA: 2 weeks.
4) Run larger cluster/region replay (staging) to validate scalability (8–16 nodes). Owner: Aisha. ETA: next month.

Longer-term / research ideas:
- Integrate small learned cost model per-model-version that predicts expected tail contribution conditioned on prefix tokens and model temperature. Could push estimator error below 20%.
- Global tailbudget marketplace across tenants: trade SLO budget for optional cost bump (premium path).
- Combine with KV cache awareness: if a request is heavily cached, we can be more aggressive grouping it even if long.

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- Push PR skeleton for slot-credit micro-optim to git (PR link above).
- Add unit tests for preemption guard and estimator smoothing.
- Collect additional traces for 'pathological-phase-change' workload.

Open questions / discussion prompts for next sync:
- Is 10% throughput hit acceptable for 25–30% p99 reduction? Product might accept if p50 degraded <10% and no SLA regressions for paid customers.
- Can we pursue a hybrid mode that toggles estimator on only for high tail-risk tenants?

Appendix: sample config snippet (conf/bl-tb.yaml):

# (note: YAML here as a literal string example)
scheduler:
 mode: batchline
 tailbudget_ms_default: 50
 slot_credit_default: 4
 flush_hysteresis_ms: 2
 estimator:
 enabled: true
 smoothing_alpha: 0.2

Experiment raw logs: results/ (attached in drive folder).

End of scratchbook.

title: Fidelity-Latency-Cost Probe (mixed-length workload)
author: Ravi Patel
text:
Status: exploratory probe for rmx-7b-ql8 onboarding.
Owner: Ravi Patel (eng-applied-ml).
Summary:
This doc captures a focused probe into latency/cost/quality tradeoffs for a mixed-length production-like prompt set. The goal is to surface practical operating points for initial onboarding and an early rollout plan. Unlike previous sweeps that used synthetic uniform prompt lengths, this test intentionally skews the workload to reflect customer telemetry: many short prompts plus a long-tail of long requests.

Motivation and scope:
- Candidate model: rmx-7b-ql8 (quantized 8-bit variant shipped for evaluation).
- Workload shape: 60% short (<50 tokens), 30% medium (50-200 tokens), 10% long (200-1024 tokens). We observed this distribution in telemetry for three pilot customers.
- Controls tested: batching target (1,4,8,16,32), cache mode (off, prefix-cache, per-client-KV with TTL 30s), and max_tokens cap (64, 128, 256, 512).
- Hardware: Dedicated A100-sim nodes (4xA100 per pool), inference runtime with dynamic-kernel selection.
- Quality metric: promptset-specific F1/EM hybrid (normalized) computed against labeled completion target. Primary quality target: <= 2% degradation vs baseline policy.

Experimental setup:
- Promptset: 4200 labelled prompts (mix of short/medium/long). We partitioned into: 3k short/medium samples for throughput/latency, 1.2k long for stability and cost.
- Warmup: 15 minutes steady traffic per run to populate prefix caches.
- Measurement window: 10 minutes steady-state after warmup.
- Cost proxy: token-cost calculated from observed tokens/sec and inferred per-GPU cost: $0.28/hour per GPU (internal reserved cost). Converted to $/1M output tokens for parity.
- Baseline: batch=1, cache=off, max_tokens=512. Baseline quality=100% (reference).

Key results (representative slices):
Note: numbers are median across 3 repeats. Throughput in tokens/sec, latency in ms, cost in $/1M output tokens, quality as % of baseline.

-- Short-heavy workload slice (60% short):
Batch | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | tokens/sec | $/1M tokens | quality
1 | 34 | 78 | 13,200 | 22.1 | 100%
8 | 58 | 190 | 38,400 | 8.1 | 99.8%
16 | 92 | 420 | 44,900 | 6.9 | 99.5%
32 | 160 | 980 | 48,200 | 6.4 | 98.9%

Observations: increasing batch reduces per-token cost significantly for short prompts but p95 climbs rapidly beyond batch=8. Quality impact minimal up to 16, then small regressions at 32 likely due to KV cache eviction timing and tokenization edge effects.

-- Mixed workload (overall distribution):
Batch | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | tokens/sec | $/1M tokens | quality
1 | 86 | 230 | 10,900 | 26.8 | 100%
4 | 120 | 310 | 23,700 | 12.4 | 99.9%
8 | 160 | 520 | 35,500 | 8.3 | 99.6%
16 | 230 | 920 | 40,100 | 7.4 | 99.1%

Observations: mixed workloads expose long-request tail that increases p95 across the board. Batch=8 gives a sweet spot for cost without blowing p95 for many customers; p95 ~520ms is borderline for interactive apps.

-- Long-request slice (10% long):
Batch | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | tokens/sec | $/1M tokens | quality
1 | 420 | 980 | 1,800 | 160.7 | 100%
4 | 700 | 1,800 | 4,900 | 59.3 | 99.7%
8 | 1,100 | 3,200 | 8,600 | 33.7 | 99.3%

Observations: long requests dominate cost. Max_tokens cap has direct cost impact here (see below).

Max_tokens cap sweep (mixed workload, batch=8, cache=prefix enabled):
Cap | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | tokens/sec | $/1M tokens | quality
64 | 120 | 310 | 22,000 | 13.4 | 96.2% (drops: truncation hurts quality on long prompts)
128 | 140 | 420 | 28,600 | 10.4 | 98.5%
256 | 160 | 520 | 35,500 | 8.3 | 99.6%
512 | 180 | 600 | 37,700 | 7.8 | 100%

Observations: cap <=128 reduces cost but can induce meaningful quality regressions on tasks that require longer completions. 256 looks like a pragmatic compromise for most customers; 64 is only acceptable for very latency-sensitive but low-fidelity use cases.

Cache modes (batch=8, max_tokens=256):
Mode | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | tokens/sec | $/1M tokens | quality
cache=off | 180 | 620 | 30,200 | 9.8 | 99.7%
prefix-cache | 160 | 520 | 35,500 | 8.3 | 99.6%
per-client-KV-30s| 145 | 460 | 38,000 | 7.8 | 99.6%

Observations: enabling prefix caching yields ~15-25% cost reduction and improves p50 slightly. Per-client KV with short TTL gives best p95 improvements for conversational scenarios where same-user prefixes repeat shortly. Be mindful of memory footprint.

Stability/regression notes:
- We saw a rare p95 spike correlated with GC pause events on runtime host during batch=32 runs; need SRE follow-up to rule out host-level resource saturation.
- Quality regressions at batch >=32 appear non-random: mismatch in beam search termination for certain tokenization boundaries. Filed JIRA-RINF-1251 to track.
- One outlier customer with 25% long requests will see cost >2x vs median; recommend per-customer capacity sizing or model pinning.

Recommendations (initial onboarding defaults):
1) Canary config (recommended): batch_target=8, adaptive_window enabled, prefix-cache enabled, max_tokens=256, per-client-KV disabled for initial canary (enable selectively). Start at 5% traffic for 48h with strict monitors on p95 latency and quality regression (new promptsets).
2) If canary stable, ramp to 25% over one week. For high-interactivity customers, offer an alternative profile: batch_target=4, max_tokens=128, prefix-cache on.
3) For customers with heavy long-tail (>15% long requests), recommend model pinning to a higher-capacity variant (rmx-13b-ql8) or a dedicated pool with lower batch targets.
4) Operational guardrails: auto-fallback policy to smaller model variant on p95 breach >2x baseline; cost/latency alert when $/1M tokens for a customer exceeds 3x expected.

Open questions / next steps:
- Run same sweep on rmx-13b-ql8 and compare quality gains vs cost uplift (JIRA item created).
- Instrument per-token breakdown across kernel choices to understand where p95 climb originates at high batch sizes.
- Validate results on Dedicated vs Dedicated+NVLink topology (we tested on A100-sim only).
- Add stress test to reproduce GC-related p95 spikes (eng-sre action).

Quick checklist for replication:
- PR to runtime with kernel flags: --adaptive-batch-window, --prefix-cache=true
- Experiment script: tools/eval/run_probe.sh --model rmx-7b-ql8 --batches "1,4,8,16,32" --caps "64,128,256,512" --cache-modes "off,prefix,per-client-30s" --duration 00:10:00
- Data: s3://redwood-evals/probe/mixed-length-4200-v1.jsonl

Notes to reviewers:
- This is an applied probe intended to guide a conservative onboarding default. It's intentionally pragmatic: we prioritize small quality regressions for cost wins, but do not accept regressions >2% on the labeled promptset without explicit product sign-off.
- Please comment on the canary ramping cadence and any additional telemetry you'd want in the rollout dashboard (token-level cost breakdowns, per-prompt quality heatmap, batch composition histogram).

-- Ravi

title: Latency SLO tiers definition (fast / standard / cost-efficient)
author: Aisha Bello
text:
## Purpose
This document defines Redwood Inference’s customer-facing latency SLO tiers—**fast**, **standard**, and **cost-efficient**—and the numeric targets associated with each. These tiers are used by runtime defaults (workload-aware batching), routing/policy evaluation, and SRE error-budget governance.

This is the normative reference for:
- Published (or publishable) tier semantics
- Numeric latency targets (p50/p95/p99) for key measures
- Streaming-specific considerations (TTFT vs per-token cadence)
- How tier choice maps to runtime profiles, routing, and overload behavior

## Scope
Applies to:
- **Hosted API** (default tier behavior and per-route policy)
- **Dedicated** (default tier behavior plus explicit customer overrides)
- **Private** (tier semantics supported; exact targets may be hardware-dependent and governed by contract)

Endpoints in scope:
- Chat/text generation (streaming and non-streaming)
- Structured output / tool calling (measured as generation)

Out of scope (tracked separately):
- Embeddings and reranking latency SLOs
- Console latency
- Cross-region routing policy changes beyond existing smart routing

## Definitions (what we measure)
We track multiple latency measures because “fast” for streaming is different from “fast” for non-streaming.

### Generation modes
- **Streaming**: server sends incremental tokens (SSE / chunked transfer). The user experience is dominated by time-to-first-token and steady output cadence.
- **Non-streaming**: server returns the full completion in one response. The user experience is dominated by end-to-end latency.

### Core measures
1) **TTFT (Time to First Token)**
- Definition: time from request acceptance at the inference gateway to first token emitted.
- Applies: streaming only.
- Primary drivers: prefill time, queue wait, admission control.

2) **Token cadence / inter-token latency (ITL)**
- Definition: time between emitted tokens (steady-state decode cadence).
- Applies: streaming only.
- Primary drivers: decode batching, contention, KV cache locality.

3) **E2E latency**
- Definition: time from request acceptance to final byte of response.
- Applies: non-streaming (and can be reported for streaming, but is not the primary SLO).
- Primary drivers: queueing + prefill + decode throughput.

### Measurement boundaries
- Start: request accepted by **Inference Gateway** (post-auth, post-quota).
- End:
 - TTFT: first token emitted to client
 - E2E: final response byte written

### Normalization and reporting
- Latency is reported as p50/p95/p99.
- Targets are defined per tier under a **reference workload envelope** (see “Workload envelope & fairness”).

## Tier semantics (customer-facing meaning)
### Fast
Optimized for interactive experiences and streaming endpoints where tail latency matters. Uses tighter queue wait budgets and stricter admission control to protect p99.

Typical use cases:
- Support agent assist (streaming)
- Real-time copilots
- UX where users wait on the first token

### Standard
Balanced default for most workloads. Designed to provide predictable latency with good cost/performance.

Typical use cases:
- Mixed streaming + non-streaming
- Product features with moderate concurrency
- General API usage

### Cost-efficient
Optimized for throughput and $/token with looser tail-latency protection. Intended for batch-like workloads that can tolerate higher tail latency.

Typical use cases:
- Summarization jobs
- Offline content generation
- Analytics pipelines

## Numeric SLO targets
Targets below apply to **generation** requests within the reference workload envelope.

### Reference workload envelope (used for SLO evaluation)
These SLOs assume:
- Prompt length: p95 prompt tokens ≤ 2,048
- Completion length: p95 completion tokens ≤ 1,024
- Mixed prompt distribution allowed (short + long), but not adversarial (see “Exclusions”)
- Concurrency: within documented per-model capacity guidance or contracted Dedicated capacity
- Models: Redwood-supported model families with published performance profiles on a given hardware class

If a customer workload deviates materially (e.g., very long prompts, extreme bursts, unusually high tool-call overhead), SRE and Runtime treat the tier as a *best-effort* objective unless explicitly contracted.

---

### Streaming targets (primary)
**Metric A: TTFT (ms)**

| Tier | p50 | p95 | p99 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| fast | 180 ms | 450 ms | 900 ms |
| standard | 250 ms | 650 ms | 1,200 ms |
| cost-efficient | 400 ms | 1,100 ms | 2,000 ms |

**Metric B: Inter-token latency (ms/token)**

| Tier | p50 | p95 | p99 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| fast | 18 | 35 | 60 |
| standard | 22 | 45 | 80 |
| cost-efficient | 30 | 70 | 140 |

Notes:
- ITL is computed over the decode phase excluding the first token.
- “fast” tier prioritizes TTFT and p99 ITL stability over absolute throughput.

---

### Non-streaming targets (primary)
**Metric C: E2E latency (seconds)**
Targets are defined for a standard “interactive-sized” request. For evaluation we use a normalized reference: prompt=512 tokens, completion=256 tokens.

| Tier | p50 | p95 | p99 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| fast | 0.85 s | 1.60 s | 2.80 s |
| standard | 1.10 s | 2.20 s | 3.80 s |
| cost-efficient | 1.80 s | 4.00 s | 7.00 s |

Notes:
- For non-streaming, E2E includes full decode time; cost-efficient tier may batch more aggressively, increasing tail latency.

## Streaming-specific considerations
### What “good” looks like
For streaming endpoints, users perceive:
1) **TTFT** (did anything happen quickly?)
2) **Cadence** (is it producing steadily?)
3) **Stalls** (did it freeze mid-stream?)

Therefore:
- Fast tier is SLO’d primarily on TTFT and ITL, not total E2E.
- Standard tier should be “good enough” for most streaming UI.
- Cost-efficient tier is allowed to trade occasional cadence stalls for throughput.

### Stall detection (secondary indicator)
We also track a secondary metric:
- **Decode stall rate**: % of streams with any inter-token gap > 500 ms.

Guideline (not a hard SLO gate for initial rollout):
- fast: < 0.5%
- standard: < 1.0%
- cost-efficient: < 3.0%

## How tiers map to runtime profiles and policies
### High-level mapping
Tier selection determines the runtime scheduler/batching profile:
- Queue wait budget (max_wait_ms)
- Maximum batch size (tokens and/or requests)
- Prefill/decode balancing heuristics
- Admission control thresholds
- Overload behavior (backpressure vs shedding)

The exact knob values are defined in the runtime design doc and may vary by model family/hardware class.

### Policy evaluation order (effective tier)
When multiple sources specify a tier, the effective tier is resolved in this order:
1) **Customer override** (Dedicated tenant/cluster override; or Private deployment config)
2) **Route policy** (per-route tier pinned in control plane)
3) **Request-level hint** (only if allowed by route policy; otherwise ignored)
4) **System default** (currently: standard unless otherwise stated)

If a model/hardware combination cannot satisfy a tier’s constraints, the system may apply a compatible profile and emit a reason code (see “Telemetry & reason codes”).

### Routing interaction
Tiers integrate with smart routing as follows:
- Tier is part of the routing policy input (along with region, model pinning, and customer tier).
- Routing should not silently change a customer’s pinned model version, but may fail over to a compatible deployment of the same model version in another region/cluster when permitted.
- During capacity constraints, fast tier requests are prioritized for tail latency protection; cost-efficient tier may see earlier backpressure.

### Overload behavior by tier (expected)
- fast: earlier admission control; protect p99; prefer shedding to uncontrolled queue growth.
- standard: balanced admission control; moderate backpressure.
- cost-efficient: tolerate larger queues and batches; protect fleet efficiency; shed only when queue growth becomes unsafe.

## Error budget treatment and SRE governance
### What qualifies as SLO compliance
A tier is considered “green” for a scope (model family + region + deployment mode) when:
- p95 and p99 targets are met over the rolling evaluation window (see below)
- No sustained regressions beyond allowed burn rates

### Evaluation window
- Primary: rolling **28-day** window for SLO reporting.
- Operational: rolling **6-hour** and **24-hour** windows for burn-rate alerting.

### Burn-rate alerting (initial thresholds)
We alert on fast tier regressions more aggressively due to UX sensitivity.

Recommended paging policy (subject to on-call tuning):
- fast tier p99 TTFT or p99 ITL: page if 6-hour burn rate ≥ 2x and 24-hour burn rate ≥ 1x.
- standard tier p95 TTFT/E2E: ticket if 6-hour burn rate ≥ 2x; page only if customer-impacting incident.
- cost-efficient: ticket by default; page if accompanied by elevated errors/timeouts or broad fleet impact.

(Exact alert rules live in the observability pack; this document defines intent.)

### SLO vs availability/error rate
Latency SLOs are evaluated independently of availability SLOs. However, overload mitigation (shedding) can shift failure modes from latency to errors; SRE treats that as an incident if error rates breach availability SLOs.

## Exclusions and caveats
The following are excluded from tier SLO evaluation unless explicitly contracted:
- Client-side latency (network between client and Redwood edge)
- Retries performed by client SDKs
- Requests exceeding maximum supported token limits or violating documented payload constraints
- Adversarial or pathological prompt patterns that intentionally trigger worst-case compute (e.g., extremely long single requests that monopolize decode, repeated large tool payloads)
- Customer-induced throttling delays (rate limit backoff)

Dedicated/Private note:
- Dedicated and Private deployments may have custom hardware, isolation, or routing constraints; targets may be adjusted in contracts. The tier definitions still apply, but numeric targets become “contractual SLOs” where specified.

## Telemetry and reason codes (required for tiered defaults)
To make tiers explainable and debuggable, services must emit:
- `tier_effective` label (fast|standard|cost_efficient)
- `tier_source` (default|route_policy|request_hint|customer_override|compatibility_fallback)
- `profile_id` (stable identifier for runtime knob set)
- `selection_reason_code` (see runtime spec; examples: `TIER_DEFAULT`, `OVERRIDE_DEDICATED`, `MODEL_CONSTRAINT`, `OVERLOAD_MODE`, `STREAMING_FASTPATH`)

Required dashboards:
- Latency histograms by tier/model/region
- TTFT and ITL for streaming routes
- Queue depth and admission rejects by tier
- Batch size distribution by tier

Cardinality guidance:
- Do not tag by tenant by default in fleet-wide metrics.
- High-cardinality breakdowns (tenant, route) must use sampled or on-demand tracing.

## Operational playbook (when targets are missed)
1) Confirm scope: which tier, model family, region, and mode (Hosted vs Dedicated) is affected.
2) Identify regression class:
 - Increased queue wait (queue depth up, admission rejects up)
 - Prefill slowdowns (TTFT up, GPU utilization pattern shift)
 - Decode contention (ITL p99 up, batch sizes up)
3) Check policy:
 - Did effective tier change? (tier_source, reason codes)
 - Was there a compatibility fallback?
4) Mitigate:
 - Reduce rollout percentage / disable feature flag for tiered defaults
 - Pin affected routes to standard or fast (as appropriate)
 - Adjust overload thresholds (temporary) if safe
5) Escalate:
 - Runtime Scheduling (Sofia Ivanova / on-call)
 - SRE (Sean Gallagher / on-call)

## Change management
Any changes to:
- Numeric tier targets
- Measurement boundaries (TTFT/E2E definition)
- Policy precedence rules

…require:
- Review by Eng SRE owner (Sean Gallagher or delegate)
- Runtime Scheduling lead sign-off (Sofia Ivanova or delegate)
- Product sign-off for customer-facing semantics (Hosted API + Dedicated PM)
- Update to perf suite gates and dashboards

## Appendix: Recommended customer messaging (internal)
- fast: “Best for interactive and streaming experiences; prioritizes tail latency stability.”
- standard: “Balanced default; good latency with strong cost/performance.”
- cost-efficient: “Optimized for throughput and cost; higher tail latency is expected.”

Do not promise exact numbers to customers unless in an SLA/contract. Public docs should describe relative behavior and provide guidance on choosing tiers.
