title: Queued holdback preemptor with KV segmentation and soft-fairness
author: Maya Chen
text:
Background: Continuous batching improves GPU utilization by aggregating tokens across concurrent requests, but long-running or very large requests and aggressive KV cache residency can starve latency-sensitive traffic. Existing preemption strategies are either too heavy-handed (hard interrupts causing cache churn) or too timid (latency SLO violations for small queries).

Proposal summary: Implement a queued holdback preemptor that combines: 1) a per-queue holdback quota to reserve GPU memory and KV cache slabs for low-latency traffic; 2) KV segmentation (hot, warm, cold slabs) with soft eviction signals to reduce cold-churn; and 3) a soft-fairness scheduler that uses time-slice yields and graceful preemption windows to satisfy SLOs while maximizing throughput.

Key ideas/novelty:
- Holdback quotas: instead of instantaneous global preemption, each latency-sensitive queue gets a small reserved token budget (holdback) that guarantees admission during brief bursts without evicting large KV state.
- KV segmentation: split KV cache into hot/warm/cold segments per model-version and maintain per-queue allocation counters. Cold segment evictions are aggressive; hot segment evictions require soft-preempt coordination to avoid k-v warmup storms.
- Soft preemption semantics: preemption happens in two phases — a yield request (runtime yields CPU/GPU slice and marks request as preemptible) and a hard interrupt after a grace window. Yielding allows the serving runtime to flush interim tokens from batches and avoid orphaned KV pointers.
- Fairness algorithm: weighted deficit round robin (W-DRR) across tenant groups with a fairness weight derived from SLA tier + recent SLO breach profile. Short requests (<100ms expected) get preferential deficit adjustment to keep tails low.
- Memory-aware admission: admission controller consults a compact GPU memory estimator (includes KV slab reservations) and rejects or defers large requests if they would push expected peak beyond configurable headroom.

Acceptance criteria / success metrics:
- p99 latency for latency-sensitive queues decreases by >=15% under mixed load compared to baseline preemptor.
- End-to-end throughput remains within -5% of baseline for steady-state workloads.
- KV cache hit rate for hot segment remains within 3% of baseline; cold churn reduced by >30%.
- Preemption hard-interrupt rate below 5% of all preemption events; majority should be yield-based.
- No increase in GPU OOM incidents in canary cluster.

Implementation plan (high level):
1) Prototype holdback quota and simple admission gate in runtime (feature flag).
2) Add KV segmentation metadata and soft-eviction API (separate flag).
3) Implement W-DRR scheduler with yield-first semantic and grace window (configurable 100-500ms).
4) Integrate memory estimator into admission and add metrics/exposed traces.
5) Run canary A/B: baseline vs holdback+segmentation on two identical dedicated pools for 72h.
6) Iterate on parameters and roll out to more clusters with gradual traffic ramp.

Testing & validation:
- Synthetic mix: 70% short chat (<=150 tokens), 20% medium (<=800 tokens), 10% long (>2k tokens).
- Run 24/72h perf jobs capturing p50/p95/p99, throughput, KV hit rates, preemptions (yield vs hard), GPU memory headroom, and fragmentation.
- Chaos tests: inject sudden large-request surge and observe eviction patterns and SLO impacts.

Rollout plan:
- Feature-flagged canary in runtime-1.20 image on a single dedicated pool (canary group).
- If canary passes acceptance (metrics above) for 72h, enable on 10% of traffic across regions with monitoring alarms.
- Full rollout gated by post-rollout SLO metrics and sign-off from platform reliability.

Open risks & mitigation: 
- Risk: KV warmup storms when cold slabs promoted rapidly after preemption. Mitigation: throttle promotions with token-bucket and prefer warm-prefetch on predicted short request patterns.
- Risk: underestimated GPU memory footprint leads to OOMs. Mitigation: conservative headroom defaults and immediate auto-fallback to baseline preemptor on OOM detection.
- Risk: Complexity of W-DRR tuning across tenants. Mitigation: start with simple per-tier weight mapping and expose admin tuning in Console.

Documentation & observability:
- New metrics: kv_segment_hit_rate_{hot,warm,cold}, preemption_events_{yield,hard}, holdback_utilization, admission_deferrals, gpu_memory_estimate, fairness_deficit_queue_length.
- Traces: preemption_decision_trace with decision path and memory snapshot.
- Runbook: add "holdback preemptor" section with fallback steps and how to revert feature flag.

Notes: This ticket focuses on the control-plane/algorithmic changes and light runtime hooks. Deeper KV storage compaction optimizations will be a follow-up (separate ticket).

2026-03-11 - Maya Chen: Initial draft spec posted. Main open question: default holdback size. Proposing 2% GPU mem or up to 128MB per queue (whichever is smaller) as conservative start.
2026-03-11 - Alex Rivera (review): Love the soft-preempt idea. Need clarity on how yield interacts with existing continuous-batcher windowing; suggest adding a marker so batcher can prefer non-yielding work first.
2026-03-12 - Liam O'Connor: Implemented feature-flagged holdback admission stub. Added metric hooks for holdback_utilization. Pushed branch runtime/holdback-preemptor (WIP).
2026-03-12 - SRE (review): Please ensure auto-fallback path includes K8s pod eviction metrics and alerting. Also request a conservative default for grace window (200ms).
2026-03-12 - Maya Chen: Updated spec to set default grace window to 200ms and holdback limit to min(2% GPU, 128MB). Added required metrics and runbook entry.
2026-03-12 - PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4127 - WIP: holdback admission + metrics
2026-03-12 - Perf note: local microbenchmarks (n=3) show p99 improvement of ~12% on synthetic mixed load with holdback only. Need full KV segmentation to reach target.

title: Companion Warm-Pool Proxy & Tenant Stowage — PRD sketch
author: Leah Chen
text:
Context:
This is a sketch for a complementary mechanism to existing Dedicated autoscaling and burst strategies: a lightweight "companion" warm-pool proxy that mediates short-lived tenant bursts and a tenant "stowage" concept to temporally relocate low-priority work into cheap, pre-warmed slots. The goal is to reduce cold-start latencies for bursty tenants while preserving strong tenant isolation and predictable SLOs for reserved capacity customers.

Motivation / Problem statement:
- Many customers purchase reserved capacity but still have microburst patterns (e.g., >10s of high QPS for <60s). We need to avoid frequent cold starts while keeping isolation and billing clarity.
- Hard prewarmed pools (hot pools) are expensive to keep active for every tenant.
- Existing burst lanes either degrade latency or risk cross-tenant interference when oversubscription occurs.

High level concept:
1) Companion Warm-Pool Proxy (CWP): a lightweight proxy service that sits between tenant routing and the Dedicated serving pool. It maintains short-lived, soft-warmed model worker slots that are "paired" with a customer's reserved capacity but live in a separate runtime plane.
 - Soft-warmed: model weights loaded with quantization-ready kernels but without persistent KV cache for ongoing sessions.
 - Time-to-serve target: <150ms additional overhead for the first token for microbursts <90s.
 - CWP enforces per-tenant burst budgets and observable headroom signals to the autoscaler.

2) Tenant Stowage: when Dedicated pools are at risk of contention, we offer a graceful stowage lane for background/low-priority requests. These requests are routed to ephemeral, cheaper warm slots that accept best-effort quality and can be throttled or answered with shorter contexts.
 - Use cases: backfill reranking, non-interactive embeddings, batched fine-tuning preprocessing jobs, low-priority analytics transforms.

Core behaviors and controls:
- Admission policy: each tenant gets a companion config: {companion-size, burst-window, stowage-eligibility}. Admins can opt-in per SKU.
- Budgeting: companions consume a burst-credit ledger (time-decay credits). Credits refill with reserved capacity usage and monthly top-ups for committed customers.
- Degradation ladder: primary serving (reserved pools) -> CWP fast-warm path -> stowage -> fallback to hosted variants (if configured).
- Isolation guarantees: CWP instances are single-tenant processes where feasible; where multi-tenant is used, strict cgroups and network shaping apply. Memory and GPU memory caps enforce per-instance isolation.

Autoscaling integration:
- Observability hooks: CWP exposes headroom, warm-slot utilization, recent first-token latencies as metrics. The dedicated autoscaler consumes these to decide on prewarm actions in the main pool.
- Predictive prewarm: use short-term windows (5–30m) derived from CWP burst traces to request additional reserved capacity from the capacity broker (soft warm) rather than on-demand cold starts.
- Soft failover: if autoscaler cannot supply more reserved slots, CWP scales up internal warm pool (within budget) and signals degraded latency band to customers.

Cost & billing model proposals:
- Companion surcharge: small % fee on top of reserved capacity for each tenant using companion warm pool (tiered by companion-size).
- Stowage discount band: stowage requests billed at a discounted per-token rate but with weaker SLOs (documented).
- Burst credits visible in console and line-itemed on invoices.

Operational considerations / runbook notes:
- On sustained high utilization (>5m over threshold), CWP should automatically promote warm slots to persistent reserved workers via the capacity broker to avoid repeated conversions.
- Eviction policy: least-recently-used companions trimmed first; stowage requests throttled according to bucket token refill.
- Incident signals: abnormal first-token latencies or repeated promotion failures should trigger an ops page and create a high-severity ticket assigned to dedicated-capacity-oncall.

Security & compliance:
- Companion processes must respect same KMS/HSM flows and audit logging as reserved pools.
- Stowage lanes should be opt-in for customers with regulated data; by default, tenant-stowage disallowed for data-classified workloads unless explicitly approved.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How much of the CWP must be single-tenant to maintain acceptable isolation vs cost? (estimate: small tenants -> multi-tenant; enterprise -> single-tenant).
- Granularity of credit refill: per-hour vs per-minute. Faster refill gives better UX but makes billing more complex.
- Interaction with preemption: when capacity is tight, should companions be preemptible if higher-tier tenants need it? Likely yes, but need explicit SLA contracts.

Technical notes / prototype plan:
- Phase 0: implement a proxy shim that fronts an existing warm pool implementation; collect burst telemetry for 30 customers. Instrument first-token time, cold-start count, and stowage acceptance rate.
- Phase 1: add companion ledger and simple prewarm strategy (threshold-based) in autoscaler. Expose UI in console to configure companion-size and stowage flags.
- Phase 2: upgrade to predictive prewarm using 1-hour sequence models; integrate cross-tenant headroom broker.

Metrics to validate success (initial):
- Reduction in 1st-token latency p95 for microburst windows by >=40% compared to baseline without CWP.
- Reduction in cold-start rate per tenant by >=70% during measured burst events.
- Cost delta: companions should not increase unit cost by more than 8% for committed customers (goal).

UI / Console controls (sketch):
- Companion config panel: enable/disable, companion-size slider, burst window selector, stowage toggle.
- Burst ledger viewer: live credits, burn rate, refill projections.
- Observability tab: headroom timeline, warm-slot utilization, promoted-slot events.

Risks & mitigation:
- Risk: companions encourage customers to rely on microbursts instead of right-sizing commitments -> Mitigation: tiered pricing + visible cost projection that discourages abuse.
- Risk: cross-tenant leakage in multi-tenant companion mode -> Mitigation: strong OS-level isolation, strict quotas, telemetry-backed anomaly detection.

Action items / next steps:
- [Leah] prototype proxy shim and gather burst telemetry (2 weeks).
- [Marco] design companion-ledger schema and proposed billing entries (1 week).
- [Aisha] security review for stowage lane (1 week).
- [Omar] run small pilot with 3 committed customers and report early metrics (4 weeks).

Notes to reviewers:
This is intentionally a rough sketch — looking for feedback on: 1) whether companion warm pool is a product distinction (vs just more prewarming), 2) acceptable budget/credit models, and 3) whether stowage introduces unacceptable compliance surface area.

---
Revision history:
- 2026-02-15 Leah Chen: initial sketch and outline
- 2026-02-22 Marco Ruiz: added ledger/billing ideas
- 2026-03-02 Aisha Patel: security constraints and opt-in rules
- 2026-03-10 Omar Williams: operational runbook and pilot checklist

title: Low-bit compression profiles for ranking model with slice-aware NDCG/MRR audit
author: Asha Patel
text:
Define, calibrate, and validate low-bit (FP8/INT8) compression profiles for the production reranker model with an emphasis on slice-consistent ranking metrics. Deliver a calibration workflow that produces per-profile artifacts and an automated audit that reports NDCG@1/3/10 and MRR breakdowns across traffic slices (query difficulty, user cohort, document length). This ticket covers profiling design, calibration harness changes, and runway for a shadow rollout gating rule.

Produce at least three distinct compression profiles: fp8-layerwise, int8-global, and hybrid-perblock, each with calibration artifacts (scale/zero-point or FP8 exponent tables) stored in model-registry.
Calibration workflow runs end-to-end in CI for a representative 50k query sample and outputs slice-level metrics (NDCG@10, NDCG@3, NDCG@1, MRR) and per-layer activation distribution deltas.
Define pass/fail gating: no slice should regress more than 0.5% absolute NDCG@10 or 1.0% relative MRR compared to baseline float32; documented rollback thresholds exist.
Create a lightweight 'slice-regression' dashboard panel in Console dev workspace that displays daily drift for the three profiles across top 6 slices.
Provide an operator runbook: how to run calibration locally, interpret artifacts, and perform a shadow deploy with automatic fallback to float32 when slice regressions exceed thresholds.
Deliver a short comparison report (PDF) with Monte Carlo stability results (10 seeds) and recommended default profile for Dedicated vs Hosted tiers.

Design per-layer scaling strategy and hybrid rounding rules (quant scheme doc).
Extend calibration harness to accept stratified sampling by slice key and emit per-slice metrics CSVs.
Implement FP8 exponent table generation and INT8 histogram-based symmetric/asymmetric calibration modes.
Integrate artifacts upload to model-registry with metadata: profile-name, seed, sample-size, commit-hash.
Add unit+integration tests for serialization/deserialization of calibration artifacts.
Implement Console dashboard telemetry wire-up and slice label mapping.
Run 10x Monte Carlo calibration runs on staging and collect stability statistics.
Draft shadow-rollout policy and rollback automation playbook for Canary and Dedicated deployments.

Use per-layer dynamic scaling for FP8 to reduce mantissa saturation on attention layers; agreed to use exponent biasing described in design doc.
Use asymmetric INT8 for embedding projections and symmetric INT8 for attention matmuls after microbenching latency vs accuracy trade-offs.
Calibration sample will be stratified by query difficulty decile and user_cohort to expose worst-case slices rather than global averages.
Gating thresholds set conservatively initially (0.5% absolute NDCG@10) and will be relaxed after two weeks of production shadow telemetry with manual review.

Unit tests: quant math utilities, FP8 table compute, INT8 histogram binning.
Integration: run calibration harness against 50k sample and validate artifacts uploaded to model-registry.
Regression: compute NDCG@1/3/10 and MRR on golden validation set and compare to float32 baseline across slices.
Stability: Monte Carlo 10 seeds, report mean/std of slice-wise NDCG and MRR.
Performance: measure 99th percentile token latency and end-to-end latency change when using hybrid profile on a Dedicated GPU pool.

Avoid reusing previous 'calib' binary; new harness uses modular io that matches model-registry URIs.
We should prioritize the hybrid-perblock profile for Dedicated customers because it offers better latency/accuracy tradeoff in microbenchmarks.
Edge case: very long documents (>=2048 tokens) show asymmetric degradation in NDCG@1; add a guard in serving to force float32 for these requests until further investigation.
Follow-up ticket recommended to automate threshold tuning using production shadow telemetry and Bayesian optimization.

title: RRB-17: Private installer rollback loop / stuck rollback during upgrade
text:
Issue summary:
Customers upgrading Redwood Private 2.8.0 -> 2.9.0 can enter an infinite rollback retry loop. UI shows "Rollback in progress" and never completes.

Impact:
- Upgrade/rollback does not converge; customer cluster remains in degraded state.
- Support load + customer trust risk.

Environment:
- Private installer 2.9.0
- Kubernetes (various), observed in us-east + eu-west

Suspected root cause:
Rollback cleanup hook exits before clearing rollback lock (ConfigMap `installer-rollback-lock`), causing controller to retry indefinitely.

Workaround (customer-safe):
1) Confirm namespace `redwood-private`
2) `kubectl -n redwood-private delete cm installer-rollback-lock`
3) `kubectl -n redwood-private rollout restart deploy/installer-controller`

Acceptance criteria / fix:
- Always best-effort clear lock
- Add TTL + loop detection to stop retries and surface actionable status
- Add metric + alert when rollback retries >3 in 10m

Comments:
- 2026-02-12 Jordan Blake: Related to incident INC-2147. See Slack #incidents thread_ts=1770937323.
- 2026-02-13 Priya Natarajan: Patch in progress; will land in 2.9.1. PR: redwood-private-installer#842.
- 2026-02-14 Dev Patel: Added metric `installer.rollback.loop_detected` and proposed alert threshold.

domain: 日常协作与非结构化讨论
title: support
text:
maria_support: FYI — customer ACME hit a burst of 429s and then observed duplicate order creation when their client retried. They think our SDK defaults might be too aggressive. Escalating for engineering help.

maria_support: attaching the snippet they sent:
```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 3
x-rate-limit-remaining: 0
x-rate-limit-reset: 24
{"error":"rate_limit"}
```

raj_engineering: thanks — do we know which SDK version they're on and whether they're sending an idempotency key for order creation? also did the client respect Retry-After or ignore it?

maria_support: they're on sdk-js v1.4.2, no idempotency key. here's the snippet of their client config they pasted:
```js
const client = new RedwoodClient({
 retry: { strategy: 'linear', attempts: 6, baseDelayMs: 200 },
});
client.createOrder(payload);
```
They say requests were concurrent from many users (50+ concurrent requests per sec), then many 429s, then retries that resulted in duplicate orders.

oliver_sdk: that config explains it — linear backoff + no jitter + 6 attempts is a recipe for synchronized retry spikes once quota resets. older SDK defaults we inherited were conservative for availability but bad for client-side herd.

oliver_sdk: immediate mitigations: 1) require customers to set an idempotency key for mutating endpoints (orders/payments). 2) have clients honor Retry-After header strictly. 3) switch to exponential backoff with full jitter for SDK defaults (e.g., expo base 100ms, max 5s, attempts 4).

raj_engineering: can you paste a minimal repro we can run locally to see the failure pattern? would like to replicate the quota-reset spike.

maria_support: customer repro (they used bash + curl):
```bash
# run 60 parallel create requests over 2s
for i in $(seq 1 60); do 
 curl -s -X POST "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/orders" "-H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' " "-H 'Content-Type: application/json' " "-d '{"item":"widget","qty":1}' &
done
wait
```
They reported many 429s then client retried and some requests succeeded twice (no idempotency token).

raj_engineering: perfect — I'll run that against a staging quota with our throttling. I want to capture the timings and whether Retry-After appears on all throttled responses. also checking whether our rate-limit headers are consistent across frontends.

oliver_sdk: temporary SDK patch customers can apply until we ship a default change:
```js
const client = new RedwoodClient({
 retry: {
 strategy: 'expo_jitter',
 attempts: 4,
 minDelayMs: 100,
 maxDelayMs: 5000
 },
 defaultIdempotency: true // injects idempotency-key header for create APIs
});
```
This reduces synchronized retries and prevents duplicates for most create flows. Also set the client to respect 429 Retry-After header and stop retrying beyond that window.

raj_engineering: server-side notes: we should ensure x-rate-limit-reset is precise (seconds till reset) and include Retry-After in 429 always. if frontends sometimes omit headers under overload that could break client heuristics. I'll add a check in the throttle middleware.

maria_support: I'm going to share the temporary patch and idempotency guidance with ACME now. they asked if duplicates imply billing issues — will escalate to billing if they confirm doubled charges.

incident-bot: Ticket #INC-2024-386 created: support->engineering escalation for 429 + duplicate-create repro. Link: https://tickets.redwood.ai/INC-2024-386

oliver_sdk: I'll open a PR to change sdk-js default retry strategy to expo_jitter + lower attempts and add a runtime warning when making mutating calls without an idempotency key. PR will reference this ticket.

raj_engineering: thanks — follow-ups for action items: (1) me: add server-side header consistency tests, (2) oliver: PR + changelog, (3) maria: send workaround + ask customer to confirm duplicates.

sara_cs: thanks all — sound plan. please ping me once ACME confirms billing impact so we can coordinate refunds if needed. :thumbsup:

title: Memory graft quarantine + KV journal reconcile for cross-env fragmentation leading to GPU OOMs
author: Priya Nair
text:
Summary:
Several customers across Hosted, Dedicated and Private tiers reported spikes in latency followed by GPU OOMs during large-chat bursts. Root cause analysis indicates a correlated sequence: an allocator 'graft' event (cross-shard memory refactor) exposed a small window where KV journal writes could drift from the in-memory KV index. Over time the drift produces ghost entries and tombstone miscounts that increase fragmentation and reduce available contiguous GPU page allocations. When large-session prefix/KV caches were loaded concurrently, the allocator could not satisfy large contiguous allocations and triggered OOMs.

What we observed:
- Incidents concentrated on multi-tenant hosts and some Dedicated nodes with long-lived sessions and prefix caching enabled.
- Symptoms: small, contiguous allocation failures, rapid slab fragmentation, rising tombstone counts on the KV journal, slow KV lookups, increased page allocation retries.
- Customer impact: intermittent 5–30m windows of high error rates (500s + rejected requests) and GPU OOM crashes; affected several enterprise customers (support escalations open).

Immediate mitigations applied (done 2026-03-02 to 2026-03-04):
1) Emergency runtime config change: reduce max contiguous allocation request size on Hosted to force more conservative batching (rolled by Marco, ~20% traffic).
2) Canary emergency rollback: disabled aggressive prefix warmup on 3 Dedicated pools to stop re-triggering large contiguous allocations.
3) Added an ephemeral watchdog to surface tombstone count > threshold to Ops and auto-quarantine sessions creating >10K journal writes/min.

Workplan / technical solution (this ticket):
A) Implement a "memory graft quarantine" mode: when journal/index delta is detected at reconciliation time, automatically place affected session arenas into a soft-quarantine ring. Quarantined arenas are prevented from making large contiguous allocations; they are drained and compacted asynchronously. This is a short-term runtime feature to prevent immediate OOM cascades.
B) KV journal reconciliation: add a lightweight, background reconciler that replays recent KV journal entries with idempotent checksums and rehydrates the in-memory index. The reconciler uses monotonic watermarks so it never reorders committed entries.
C) Index integrity checks: introduce periodic checksum snapshots (per-shard) and a fast verify that runs during compaction. On mismatch, trigger a local reconcile and metric alert.
D) Allocator improvement: a small allocator policy change to prefer hybrid-slab allocations for large prefix caches to avoid starving contiguous page pools. Also add preflight checks to fail gracefully before OOM.

Design decisions and tradeoffs:
- We chose soft-quarantine rather than immediate eviction to avoid data loss and preserve prompt KV coherence for live sessions. This increases background compaction load but minimizes customer-visible failures.
- The reconciler is intentionally conservative (idempotent replays + checksums) to avoid introducing ordering regressions. It will run with a low-priority IO budget to limit impact on latency-critical paths.
- We do not introduce global stop-the-world compaction; all fixes are per-shard and opportunistic to preserve SLA requirements.

Implementation notes / PRs:
- Runtime patch: allocator/graft-quarantine + reconciler implementation (WIP) — PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/12874 (draft)

title: Developer Canvas: stream boarding and partial commit playbook
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Purpose
This is a working PRD draft that outlines a developer-centric streaming onboarding surface (the "Developer Canvas") and a playbook for partial-commit semantics when tool-calls and structured output interleave. The goal is to reduce time-to-first-success for engineers integrating Hosted API streaming + tool calling while keeping failure modes observable and deterministic for rollouts.

Problem statement
- Developers integrating incremental streaming with tool-calls frequently get tripped up by three failure classes: (1) opaque partial outputs when a tool call fails mid-stream, (2) divergent client/server expectations for when an incremental result is "committed", and (3) limited visibility during first-run onboarding (hard to reproduce flaky behavior).
- Current SDK surfaces provide low-level stream frames but not a developer narrative that maps to onboarding steps (sketch -> preview -> commit). Customers build bespoke wrappers and still hit edge cases around resumption and idempotency.

Primary goals
- Provide a Developer Canvas: a recommended onboarding flow and SDK helpers that walk engineers through sketch -> preview -> commit phases.
- Define a partial-commit protocol for streaming frames that includes explicit staging, tentatively-committed, and final-committed markers with clear failure semantics for tool calls.
- Add lightweight telemetry and invariants to make first-run failures diagnosable with minimal backend changes.

Non-goals
- This doc does not propose replacing the low-level streaming frame format. It layers ergonomics and semantics on top of existing frames.
- Not addressing full offline-first resumability or heavy-weight transactional guarantees (those are separate proposals).

Developer Canvas: onboarding flow (high level)
1) Sketch (exploratory)
 - Client opens a session and requests streaming generation with "sketch=true" flag.
 - Server streams early partial text and typed suggestions for tools (e.g., detected action candidates).
 - No side effects invoked in this phase; tool-call proposals are only annotated as "suggested_tool".
2) Preview (confirmable)
 - Client may request a "preview" snapshot (stable partial result) that is idempotent and addressable by snapshot_id.
 - If client triggers a tool-call from preview, server marks those tool-calls as "tentative"; runtime will route to tool execution but records a provisional commit token.
3) Commit (finalize)
 - Client issues a commit request referencing snapshot_id and any chosen tool-call tokens.
 - Server treats commit as the authoritative switch: tentative tool results become durable, and the session advances to final-committed output.
 - If commit never arrives, tentative work is garbage-collected after TTL; client may retry using snapshot replay.

Partial-commit semantics (playbook)
- Frame taxonomy (developer-facing):
 - FRAME_SKETCH: free-form incremental tokens, not addressable for side effects.
 - FRAME_SNAPSHOT: stable snapshot frame, contains snapshot_id, schema version, lightweight diff from last snapshot.
 - FRAME_TENTATIVE_TOOL: a tool-call result emitted during preview; tagged with tentative_token and provenance.
 - FRAME_COMMIT: commit acknowledgement referencing snapshot_id and tentative_token(s).
- Failure modes and recommended SDK handling:
 - Tool execution fails before commit: emit FRAME_TENTATIVE_TOOL with error metadata; SDK surfaces an onTentativeError callback and shows the preview with a clear "tool failed (retry)" affordance.
 - Commit races (two clients try to commit same snapshot): server returns COMMIT_CONFLICT error; SDK should expose optimistic retry with merge callback.
 - Missing commit (client disconnects): server retains tentative artifacts for configurable TTL (default 2 minutes) and emits a session tombstone for observability.

Tool calling constraints and guidelines
- Idempotency: all tentatively-invoked tool calls must accept a tentative_token and be idempotent or return a deterministic error that maps to retry semantics.
- Side effect deferral: tool providers should support a "finalize(token)" path used by the server only after a commit. This keeps expensive side effects from being visible until the user confirms.
- Observability contract: every tentative tool invocation writes a minimal event to the platform trace (token, tool_name, latency_ms, result_hash or error_code). This enables debugging without exposing full PII.

Structured output and schema evolution
- Snapshots carry a schema_version string (semver-like) and an optional canonicalizer_hint. SDKs should:
 - Validate structured frames against declared schema_version and expose a validationErrors list on the snapshot.
 - Support lightweight downgrade path: when a newer server schema appears, SDK exposes a compatibility shim that maps fields to the client model or shows a suggested migration.
- Partial frames may include typed attachments (JSON pieces). The Canvas surface shows a preview JSON tree with fields marked "tentative" vs "committed".

SDK ergonomics (recommendations)
- High-level primitives to ship in official SDKs:
 1) CanvasSession: open({model, sketch:true|false}) -> returns session handle + helper methods.
 2) onSketchUpdate(callback(frame_text, approx_tokens))
 3) requestSnapshot() -> Promise(snapshot_id, stable_frame)
 4) invokeTentativeTool(snapshot_id, tool_spec) -> returns tentative_token, observable promise for tentative result
 5) commit(snapshot_id, tentative_tokens[]) -> returns final result or conflict error
 6) resume(snapshot_id) -> replay and rehydrate local state
- UX-first defaults:
 - Safe defaults: sketch streaming should not auto-invoke tools unless the developer explicitly enables auto-tool.
 - Prefetching: SDK can prefetch model warm pools when requestSnapshot is called to shorten preview latency.
 - Backpressure: SDK provides a backpressure API (pause/resume) to allow clients to throttle rendering when partial frames are emitted faster than UI can apply.
- Example integration snippet (pseudo):
 // open canvas in exploratory mode
 const s = CanvasSession.open({model: 'redwood-2-stream', sketch:true});
 s.onSketchUpdate(text => renderDraft(text));
 const {snapshot_id} = await s.requestSnapshot();
 const tentative = await s.invokeTentativeTool(snapshot_id, {name:'search', query:'customer invoice 173'});
 // show preview UI with tentative result and "Confirm and commit" button
 await s.commit(snapshot_id, [tentative.token]);

Telemetry and observability
- Minimal telemetry points to emit for each Canvas lifecycle: session_open, sketch_update (sampled), snapshot_created, tentative_tool_invoked, tentative_tool_completed, commit_attempt, commit_result.
- Attach low cardinality labels: model_family, region_hint, snapshot_size_bucket, commit_latency_bucket.
- Provide a dev-mode trace exporter (opt-in) that includes snapshot diffs and tentative tool call payload hashes to help debugging during integration.

Operational considerations and rollout plan
- Phase 0 (experiment): ship SDK helpers (CanvasSession, snapshot API) behind a feature-flag; support only text-only sketches (no tool invocations). Limited to internal dogfood teams.
- Phase 1 (preview): add tentative tool invocation plumbing with TTL semantics and lifecycle telemetry; expose to a small set of beta customers.
- Phase 2 (general availability): finalize API ergonomics, SLA docs for commit durability, and add admin controls for tentative artifact TTL and GC.

Backward compatibility and migration
- Existing streaming customers continue to function unchanged; Canvas flags are opt-in.
- For clients that adopt snapshots, we provide a replay endpoint (resume(snapshot_id)) to replay to either server-side or client-side.

Open questions and risks
- Do tool vendors accept the finalize(token) contract? Need vendor-signoff and possibly a shim layer for legacy tools.
- Cost: tentative tool execution may double early compute in preview scenarios. Need analytics to understand incremental spend.
- Security: snapshot payloads may contain sensitive user data; ensure platform-level redaction rules and snapshot encryption-at-rest.

Next steps (short term)
- Engineering spike: implement snapshot metadata and tentative_token plumbing in runtime (2w).
- SDK spike: implement CanvasSession in JS + Python (1w each) and internal demo app.
- UX: design preview UI patterns (confirm/undo affordances) and error states (1w).
- Product: recruit 3 beta customers for Phase 1 by EOY and define SLA language for commit durability.

Appendix: short checklist for integration reviewers
- Does the client opt into sketch mode explicitly?
- Are tentative tool calls tagged with tokens and trace events?
- Is there an observable TTL for tentative artifacts and a clear GC story?
- Does SDK expose validation errors for structured snapshots?
- Are conflicts surfaced to clients as retriable errors with merge hints?

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally pragmatic: focus on incremental adoption without breaking current streaming integrations. Feedback welcome on token TTL defaults and whether to surface finalize() directly to third-party tool adapters.

title: rbac policy 'not_in' operator fallthrough grants unexpected access when claim missing in private deployment
text:
Issue summary: Atlas Retail observed that several service accounts and a subset of human users were granted admin-level routes in their private VPC deployment despite RBAC policies that should exclude them via a 'not_in' expression. Impact: Incorrectly permissive access to admin/config APIs for a small number of identities, risk of configuration changes. Environment: Private deployment (customer-managed control plane), prod-us-east region, customer using SSO via their IdP with claims delivered as JWT to the identity-proxy. Observation window: 2026-03-12 22:30 - 2026-03-13 03:00 UTC. Steps to reproduce: 1) Customer provided a minimal policy that allows action if user.entitlements not_in ["admin", "superuser"] 2) Send request with JWT that omits the 'entitlements' claim altogether 3) Call to /admin/config returns 200 and allowed instead of denied. Expected behavior: Missing claim should be treated as empty set and 'not_in' should evaluate to true for empty set only if semantics intended; policy author expected deny when admin exclusion is required. Observed behavior: Policy evaluator treats missing claim in 'not_in' as a non-match that bypasses exclusion, resulting in grant. Customer impact: Two internal teams escalated (SRE and Platform) and temporarily halted config pushes. No data exfiltration detected.

1) Customer defines policy: allow if user.entitlements not_in ["admin", "superuser"]
2) Acquire JWT from IdP that omits entitlements claim (token valid for authN)
3) Call admin API route through identity-proxy and observe 200 OK
4) Inspect policy-evaluator logs and request trace (trace_id: trace-20260313-34b9)

2026-03-13T00:11:45Z authz-eval INFO allow user=svc-ordering token_kid=abcd1234 trace=trace-20260313-34b9 expr='user.entitlements not_in [\"admin\",\"superuser\"]' claim=ABSENT
2026-03-13T00:11:45Z proxy INFO request forwarded route=/admin/config status=200 trace=trace-20260313-34b9
JWT payload (redacted): {"sub":"svc-ordering@atlas", "email":"svc-ordering@atlas.example", /* entitlements claim not present */ }

Leah Park (Support): Initial report received from Atlas Retail. They included traces and a minimal policy example. Blocking their ability to push config; asked for escalation.
Diego Morales (SRE): Reproduced locally with a mock token. Policy evaluator returned ALLOW when entitlements absent. Created local debug build with extra logging. Tagging eng-authz.
Priya Nair (AuthZ Eng): Looking into boolean ops and value coercion in the policy evaluator. Hypothesis: not_in implementation does a string-contains check and treats absent as empty string which short-circuits differently than spec.
Atlas Retail (Customer): Confirmed workaround of explicitly setting entitlements claim to [] for service accounts mitigates. Requested timeline for patch and whether rollback/mitigation will be supported in their private control plane.
Diego Morales (SRE): Opened INT-4456 to track rollout/patch automation for private deployments. Requested canary rollout to dedicated infra before pushing to private updater.

Summary: AuthZ engine's expression runtime performs 'not_in' by iterating subject values and checking membership against target list; when claim is absent the evaluator treats subject as a single empty string value leading to membership checks that return false and overall expression evaluating to true. Repro steps run in a dev harness mirrored customer config. Reproduced with token missing 'entitlements'. Additional tests: - token with entitlements: ['readonly'] -> correctly allowed - token with entitlements: ['admin'] -> correctly denied - token with absent entitlements -> incorrectly allowed. Root cause hypothesis: backward-compatible change in the policy-eval library (v2.14.0) introduced value coercion for absent claims. Related PR suspected: https://github.com/redwood-inference/authorization/commit/5f7e2b3. Impact surface: Private deployments that rely on omission semantics for exclusion policies. Risk: Moderate-high for private customers using exclusion-based RBAC.

Workaround: Advise Atlas Retail to set entitlements claim to empty array for service accounts and short-lived tokens; this required a small IdP mapping change. Temporary policy recommendation provided: add explicit exists(user.entitlements) and deny if not exists. Fix: AuthZ team prepared fix to treat absent claims as empty set in 'not_in' semantics and to avoid coercing absent -> empty string. Patch PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/authorization/pull/869. Deployment plan: canary merge to staging on 2026-03-15, rolling release to hosted and a patch bundle for private control plane customers on 2026-03-18. Follow-ups: document 'missing-claim' semantics in policy language reference; add unit tests for absent-claim cases. Customer communication: emailed timeline and temporary mitigation steps; customer accepted workaround and asked for confirmation post-rollout.

AuthZ eng to add regression tests for all membership operators: in, not_in, any_of, all_of
Add monitoring alert for unusual increases in admin-route allows per tenant
Prepare KB article for private customers about claim absence semantics and policy patterns

title: Add cohort-aware changelog enricher and perf baseline seeder
author: Priya Natarajan
text:
Introduce a cohort-aware changelog enrichment pipeline and a perf baseline seeder to improve release notes quality and initial performance expectations for newly onboarded model variants. The change adds an enrichment worker that consumes sampled telemetry and onboarding probe results, computes sample-weighted deltas per cohort, and emits human-readable summary assertions and suggested baseline numbers for the release composer. A lightweight SQLite indexer records cohort sample weights and fast lookup keys to avoid recomputing on every run. The PR also adds a small CLI entrypoint (rmr changelog enrich) and a seed script that writes initial baseline entries into the model registry so downstream automation and dashboards have an initial reference. Motivation: reduce manual work for release authors, provide reproducible baseline numbers for canary rollouts, and improve changelog context for customers. No breaking API changes to existing onboard manifests; the enrichment is opt-in via registry config and feature flag.

Improves release note clarity and provides reproducible perf baselines for newly onboarded variants. Expected to reduce time spent by release authors and reduce canary regressions. Small runtime cost if run inline; default is background worker to avoid onboarding latency.

To enable enrichment for a registry: 1) set registry.config.enricher.enabled=true, 2) run scripts/seed_baselines.py --registry <url> --since 30d, 3) ensure background worker service is deployed (deploy/enricher.yml).

Added unit tests for indexer boundary conditions and a small end-to-end CI job that runs seed_baselines against a dev registry snapshot. Integration test that hit sampling flakiness now retries up to 2 times and records flake metadata for triage.

- Cohort-aware changelog enrichment: auto-generated human-readable deltas with sample-weighted numbers.
- Perf baseline seeder: populates initial baseline entries for new variants to help rollouts.

Adds cohort-aware changelog enrichment and initial perf baseline seeding. The enrichment computes sample-weighted deltas to produce concise release notes and seeds initial baseline numbers for variants to aid canary rollouts and dashboards. Opt-in via registry config and feature flag. No breaking changes.

Marta Kovac: Overall LGTM. Two requests: 1) ensure the indexer uses a streaming cursor to avoid high memory use for large sample dumps, 2) add a short note about privacy implications when sampling user prompts.
Priya Natarajan: Addressed both. Indexer now streams rows and an opt-out sampling flag was added. Updated docs to call out collection window and anonymization in changelog_enricher.md.
Diego Alvarez: Can the seed script be idempotent? If we run seed_baselines twice we should not duplicate entries.
Priya Natarajan: Seed script now uses upsert semantics keyed by model_id+variant+cohort_hash. Added test that runs seed twice to ensure idempotency.
Samir Patel: Integration test shows a 2s median extra latency when enrichment runs inline during onboarding; recommend running as background job for heavy models.
Priya Natarajan: Switched default to background worker with a flag to run inline for quick local dev. Noted tradeoff in docs.
Marta Kovac: Approved after changes.
Diego Alvarez: Approved.

title: Differential SLO hedging and failover staging for private control planes
author: Maya Chen
text:
Problem: Private and dedicated control planes host multiple customers with divergent latency and throughput SLOs. During cross-region failover or platform upgrades we currently apply coarse-grained throttles which either over-isolate healthy customers or under-protect the control plane, causing cascading latency spikes. We need a safer, more granular approach that: 1) applies region-aware hedging/circuit-breaker hysteresis, 2) stages failover with observable safety checkpoints, and 3) introduces per-customer differential admission controls for private deployments without requiring tenant-wide quiesce.

Goals: 
- Prevent noisy-customer failures from causing global control plane instability during upgrades or region failovers.
- Maintain differentiated SLO targets (e.g., gold/silver/bronze customers) with clear degradation windows.
- Provide deterministic rollback/holdpoints during rolling upgrades to avoid unbounded error amplification.

Success criteria (measurable):
- Control-plane error budget burn rate reduced by >= 60% during staged failovers (compare historical incidents).
- No more than 5% of gold-tier requests see latency > 3x SLO during upgrade windows.
- Automated circuit-breaker triggers are actionable and have < 2 false-positive activations per quarter in staging fleet.

Proposed design: 
1) Differential admission controller: per-customer token buckets with priority weights (gold/silver/bronze) that operate at the front of private control plane proxies. These buckets are backfilled from a region-level grace pool during transient saturation. Implementation: admission logic in ingress proxy (fastpath in C++/Rust) with config served from control plane config service.

2) Hysteresis-aware circuit breakers: circuit breakers evaluate both short (30s) and medium (5m) windows and require a sustained threshold crossing plus a recovery cooldown before re-enabling. This prevents flip-flop during network flaps. Breaker decisions annotated with reason codes and correlation IDs (for tracing).

3) Failover staging with checkpoint gates: introduce explicit holdpoints in rollout orchestrator: pre-check (Synthetics pass, queue depth < threshold), mid-roll (traffic split 10/90 with automated KPIs check for 10 minutes), post-roll (observability window 30m). Each gate exposes a pass/fail metric and can trigger automated rollback and reduced concurrency for subsequent stages.

4) Localized shedding tiers: if region capacity is constrained, automatically shed lower-priority traffic first and route higher-priority requests to warm standby regions based on affinity and latency budget. Plan includes per-request metadata to enable predictable routing decisions without exposing tenant identifiers in control-plane logs.

Observability and alerts: 
- New SLO dashboards per customer priority class and per-region error budget.
- Synthetic traffic profiles that exercise KV cache and long-context workloads to detect regressions early.
- Alert rules: SLO burn rate > 4x for 5 minutes (critical), circuit-breaker open fraction > 10% for 3m (warning).

Safety and rollout plan: 
- Stage 0 (staging): unit + integration tests, fuzz admission controller with synthetic high-churn customers.
- Stage 1 (canary small): enable differential admission for 2 internal customers in a single private control plane. Observe 48h.
- Stage 2 (regional): enable hysteresis breakers + failover gates in a non-critical region across a subset of private planes. Run end-to-end chaos (netem) during off-peak.
- Stage 3 (global): full rollout with automated rollback triggers and manual holdpoints for first 24h.

Runbook excerpt (incident playbook): 
- Trigger: automated gate fails or SLO burn > threshold.
- Immediate: reduce new allocations to region by 30%, expand admission bucket conservatively to gold only, evict low-priority long-running workflows.
- If instability persists > 10m: execute partial rollback to previous runtime build and hold rollout at next gate. Notify affected customers via private control plane status channel.

Open questions / trade-offs: 
- Complexity vs latency: per-request priority checks add ~0.7–1.5ms on fastpath; need microbenchmarks to confirm acceptable overhead.
- Config surface: how much per-customer tuning should be exposed to account teams vs managed by platform defaults?
- Consistency: deciding how to sync admission counters across replicas without adding high QPS control traffic. Options: probabilistic proxies with eventual reconciliation (favored) vs strong central allocator (simpler reasoning but more coordination).

Testing and verification: 
- Load tests with mixed priority classes and malformed request spikes.
- Chaos exercise: region-link partition with progressive rollback validation.
- Backfill simulation using historical traffic traces to estimate heatmaps of bucket starvation.

Deliverables: 
- PR: ingress-admission + breaker-state machine (links to draft PRs below).
- Dashboard: priority-class SLO dashboard and automated gates.
- Runbook: incident actions for private control planes.

Artifacts (draft links):
- Design doc: https://docs.redwood.ai/private-controlplane-differential-slo (draft)
- Draft PR (ingress): https://github.com/redwood-inference/ingress/pull/789
- Draft PR (orchestrator gates): https://github.com/redwood-inference/orchestrator/pull/402
- SLO simulation dataset: gs://redwood-slo-sim/2026/mar/differential-sim.csv

Next steps (short term):
- Finish microbenchmarks for admission fastpath (owner: Arjun) by 2026-03-11.
- Implement hysteresis timeline and start unit tests (owner: Maya) by 2026-03-15.
- Schedule chaos window with infra for Stage 2 (owner: SRE lead Priya Rao) by 2026-03-18.

2026-03-02 Maya Chen: Initial scoping done with SRE and Product. SRE concerns about cross-replica syncing noted; prefer probabilistic shedding approach. Added success criteria and basic gating plan.
2026-03-04 Priya Rao: Agreed to run canary experiments in r-us-central-2. Need capacity reservations for warm standby regions; SRE will create reservations ticket. Also requested synthetic profiles for long-context tests.
2026-03-06 Arjun Patel: Microbench harness prototype shows ~1.1ms p50 overhead on admission check in Rust fastpath with zero allocation. Will optimize and re-run. Beginning work on breaker-state machine tests.
2026-03-08 Product (Lara Gómez): Asked for clarity on customer-visible guarantees during Stage 3. Proposed we publish an opt-in degradation SLA for customers who want strict isolation. Adding to design doc.
2026-03-09 Maya Chen: Updated rollout plan to include explicit mid-roll KPIs and extended holdpoint times after offline review. Marking security_review_required=true; security to review logging hygiene for customer metadata redaction.

title: Retry quarantine causing delayed/duplicate tool calls when ack window overlaps with backoff (Python/TS/Go clients)
text:
Issue summary:
Customer ClarityApps reports unexpected duplicate external tool (webhook) invocations and long delays before tool confirmations are persisted when their orchestrator uses SDK retries across multiple worker processes. Behavior appears only under load and after a transient 503 from the serving runtime.

Impact:
- Duplicate webhook posts observed (3-4 duplicates) for about 1% of requests during a 15-minute window.
- Some tool confirmations arrive >30s after initial invocation which causes the customer orchestrator to mark tasks as timed out and re-enqueue, resulting in duplicates and extra billing.
- Affects production traffic in us-east region for their dedicated fleet.

Environment:
- Customer using Redwood Dedicated (reserved gpu pool) in us-east-1
- Orchestrator: homegrown Python service with mixed TS and Go worker processes that use Redwood SDKs (py v1.8.2, ts v2.3.0, go v0.9.1)
- Model pinned to redwood-chat-medium-1

Steps to reproduce (as provided):
1) Start the orchestrator with 30 concurrent workers (mix of Python and Go).
2) Issue streaming requests that include a tool/function call (webhook) with idempotency-key header generated per-task.
3) Simulate a transient backend error by throttling a single serving node (describe: short 503 spike).
4) Observe the webhook endpoint from customer side and the SDK client logs.

Observed logs (customer snippets):
- client (py) after 503: "retrying request after backoff: attempt=2 backoff_ms=1200 quarantine_id=qc-73a2"
- serving-runtime: "WARN Quarantine: queued retry 8342 for session s-4f3, ack_window_end=2026-03-10T14:02:17Z"
- customer webhook: duplicate POST at 14:02:18.119, 14:02:18.703, 14:02:20.112

Notes on idempotency header usage (customer):
- Per-task idempotency key: sha256(task_id + worker_pid) (this differs per worker process and thus per re-enqueue)
- SDKs are setting x-redwood-idempotency and x-redwood-quarantine-bucket headers

Desired outcome:
- Prevent duplicates or provide clear guidance and a recommended pattern for orchestration that avoids this duplication under transient failures.
- Provide mitigation/workaround for ClarityApps' immediate window and an engineering runbook item if this is runtime behavior.

2026-03-10 15:12 - Support (Aisha): Opened ticket after initial triage with CS. Customer attached logs and described orchestrator pattern. Notified on-call SRE.
2026-03-10 15:27 - SRE (Marco): Confirmed customer saw duplicate webhook posts in ngrok capture. Asked customer to provide SDK client debug logs for all worker types and the idempotency key value used per attempt.
2026-03-10 16:02 - Customer (ClarityApps - Dev): Provided logs and sample idempotency key generation code. Noted different worker PIDs generate unique keys on re-enqueue which they think may be the cause.
2026-03-10 18:45 - Support (Aisha): Suggested temporary workaround: make idempotency key stable across re-enqueues (use global task_id) and increase ack timeout in orchestrator to 45s. Customer to test and report.
2026-03-11 09:10 - Customer: Tested with stable idempotency key (task_id only). Duplicate webhook count dropped to 0.3% during a smaller induced 503 test. Still seeing delayed confirmations in a subset of cases.
2026-03-11 11:30 - Eng (Marco): Reproduced locally with a dedicated mini-cluster using py/ts/go workers. Observed 'Quarantine' state where retries were held in a per-session queue and released after ack window expiration causing clustered replays (duplicates) when worker identity changed. Filed reproduction PR for runtime instrumentation. Reference PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/5041
2026-03-12 08:22 - Eng (Marco): Added note that quarantined retry batching is by-design to prevent thundering herd, but current idempotency key semantics (per-worker) prevent dedupe across re-enqueues. Need guidance and a potential runtime improvement to log per-quarantine dedupe events.
2026-03-12 13:00 - Support (Aisha): Customer accepted temporary mitigation. Requested ETA for runtime change and whether we can backport to their Dedicated fleet.

Summary of findings:
- Root cause is interaction between: (1) runtime 'retry quarantine' behavior that batches/delays retries for a session; (2) customer-generated idempotency keys that vary per worker process (pid included); (3) release of quarantined retries after ack window triggers clustered replays leading to multiple webhook invocations.
- Runtime quarantine groups retries per-session and releases them based on ack_window_end to avoid immediate thundering-herd retries. This is intended.
- Because idempotency keys were not stable across re-enqueues, deduplication at caller side and some server-side matching could not suppress duplicates.
- Python/TS/Go SDKs already set x-redwood-idempotency header when provided; however, we do not normalize or override customer-provided keys.

Repro steps performed by Eng:
- Created synthetic orchestrator that re-enqueues to different worker PIDs (simulate container restart) and induced 503 on a single serving node. Observed 2-4 duplicate webhook posts in the cluster release window.

Telemetry notes:
- Instrumentation added in PR #5041 to emit quarantine release counts and per-session dedupe metrics. Early telemetry shows 0.9% of quarantined releases under load cause >1 webhooks where idempotency_key varied.

Hypotheses for mitigation:
1) Customer-side: make idempotency key stable for the logical task (task_id only) — already effective per customer test.
2) Runtime-side: accept and honor an additional header (x-redwood-idempotency-scope) that indicates dedupe across re-enqueues and worker migrations; requires spec and SDK changes.
3) Runtime: on quarantine release, optionally de-duplicate by computing canonicalized hash of payload+task_id when idempotency header is missing or different — risk: accidental suppression when payload legitimately differs.

Next steps:
- Short term: document recommended idempotency pattern for orchestration (use global task_id, do not include pid or ephemeral salt). Share advisory with customer.
- Medium term: design API/SDK additions for cross-worker stable idempotency header (x-redwood-idempotency-scope) and a runtime config flag for quarantine release dedupe. Draft RFC.

Pending - temporary mitigation provided and accepted by customer.

Workarounds applied:
- Customer changed idempotency key generation to use stable task_id only. Observed significant reduction in duplicates during induced tests.
- Customer increased ack timeout on orchestrator to 45s to reduce re-enqueue race window.

Planned engineering actions:
- RFC for 'cross-worker idempotency scope' header and SDK guidance (owner: SDK team).
- Instrumentation changes merged in PR #5041 to better surface quarantine release dedupe events. Will monitor telemetry for two weeks before scheduling runtime behavior change.
- If telemetry shows >0.5% duplicate rate in production for dedicated customers after advisory, schedule runtime de-duplication change (low-risk rollout).

Follow-ups:
- Assign action item for Developer Docs to publish 'Orchestrator idempotency patterns' by 2026-03-20.
- CS to follow up with ClarityApps on 2026-03-13 to confirm production behavior and close ticket when satisfied.

title: Three-Tier Commitment Map — personal OKR scratchpad
author: Devon Clarke
text:
PURPOSE
A compact personal framework to align day-to-day work with a single north-star for the quarter. Treat this as a working scratchpad — experiments, quick metrics, and candid retros.

OVERVIEW (Why this format)
- Problem: my weekly focus drifts between deep product work and reactive meetings.
- Solution: a three-tier commitment map that ties a quarterly Objective to monthly levers and daily rituals.
- Outcome: clearer signal for prioritization and a small set of measurable progress indicators.

NORTH-STAR OBJECTIVE (Q1 2025)
- Objective: Reduce customer-reported latency regressions in hosted-api flows and cut median tail token-cost by 18%.
- Rationale: latency and unit-cost are the two levers that unlock higher adoption for latency-sensitive PLG demos.

MONTHLY LEVERS (what I will push)
1) Feb — Model routing experiments: set up two fallback policies and measure SLO hit-rate in Canary (goal: 95% SLO for 99th percentile latency).
2) Mar — Cache surface optimizations: prefix cache for 3 high-traffic prompts, measure token reduction (goal: 12% token reduction for these flows).
3) Apr — Batching & quantization tuning for Dedicated dev cluster to reduce per-token latency variance.

DAILY RITUALS (small habits to sustain progress)
- 45min uninterrupted deep block (M/W/F) for code/bench experiments.
- End-of-day 10-min note: one finding, one blocker, one micro-action.
- Weekly Friday 30-min review: update this doc, log metrics, pick next week's lever.

KEY METRICS (baseline -> target -> current)
- 99th percentile latency (hosted-api): 520ms -> 420ms -> 495ms (2025-03-02)
- Median token-cost for top-5 flows: $0.0045/token -> $0.0037/token -> $0.0042/token
- Canary SLO hit-rate (99th): 88% -> 95% -> 91%
- Monthly active experiments running: 0 -> 3 -> 1 (cache rollout in progress)

HYPOTHESES & SMALL EXPERIMENTS
- H1: Adding a lightweight routing rule (prefer lower-latency variant for <200 token requests) will reduce median latency without significant cost increase. (Experiment: A/B on 10% traffic for two weeks)
- H2: Prefix cache on the three top intents will reduce token-cost by >=10% for those flows. (Experiment: instrument cache-hit rates + cost per session)

EXPERIMENT LOG (short)
- 2025-02-18: Canary policy v1 deployed to eu-west-1 (10% traffic). Observed 3% improvement median, no change at 99th. Logged to L-3421.
- 2025-02-27: Cache stubbed for support-ticket prompt A. Hit rate 28% in first week; token reduction ~6%.

WEEKLY CHECK-INS (selected entries)
- 2025-02-14: Kickoff. Set up Linear issue L-3421. Slack thread started (#perf-playground). Prioritized model routing and cache.
- 2025-02-21: Spent deep-block on routing rules. Discovered mismatch in sequence-length estimates from toolbar. Need small telemetry fix.
- 2025-02-28: Cache experiment shows signal but not enough. Plan: expand to second prompt and add TTL tuning.
- 2025-03-02: Quick retro below; decide to shift one deep-block from Friday -> Thursday to sync better with SRE pairing session.

RETROSPECTIVE (what worked / what didn't)
- Worked:
 * Focused deep blocks produced measurable prototype changes (routing policy + cache stub).
 * Weekly Friday review keeps momentum and forces a decision boundary.
- Didn’t work:
 * Too many ad-hoc meetings ate a deep-block last week. Need stricter calendar hygiene.
 * Instrumentation gaps (sequence-length estimation) slowed the routing experiment.

DECISIONS & TRADEOFFS
- Tradeoff: prefer small routing rules that change decision surface but not model variants to avoid output-quality regressions.
- Decision: hold off on aggressive quantization changes until canary shows stable latency reductions from routing + caching.

BLOCKERS (ask for help)
- Need one SRE pairing slot to add the telemetry patch (seq-length estimate). Requested in #perf-playground with slack ping to @Ava.
- Request permissions to spin a small Dedicated dev pool for batching experiments (estimate: 1xA10x4 for 2 weeks).

NEXT ACTIONS (priority-ordered)
- [ ] Merge telemetry patch for sequence-length estimates (owner: me; target: 2025-03-06).
- [ ] Expand cache experiment to second prompt and set TTL to 60s (owner: me; target: 2025-03-09).
- [ ] Schedule 2x2h pairing session with SRE to validate canary routing configuration (owner: Ava; target: 2025-03-07).
- [ ] Open infra request for Dedicated dev pool (owner: me; linked: L-3429).

NOTES TO SELF
- If experiment noise > 7%, add longer-run bootstrap and rely less on single-week readouts.
- Be conservative with rollout percentages for any change that touches model selection. Keep a rollback plan.

ENDPOINTS/QUICK LINKS
- Linear: L-3421 (routing), L-3429 (infra request).
- Slack: #perf-playground thread (pinned messages summary).
- Confluence draft: perf-deep-dive (private draft)

Signed — Devon
(Use as canonical weekly scratchpad. Archive to personal-notes if status -> final)

title: sales
text:
Maria: ScarletBank wants to kick off a POC — they require SSO (SAML), SCIM provisioning (delta + bulk), RBAC with AD group sync, domain controls (TXT verification), and a completed security questionnaire. They also asked for Dedicated pricing and committed throughput numbers by Friday. Can eng/security chime in?
Alex: Ack. We'll need their IdP metadata and which NameID format they expect. Also confirm ACS URL and whether they want SP-initiated or IdP-initiated flows.
Sam: Please drop the security questionnaire PDF here; we'll answer SOC2 status, encryption (KMS/HSM), key rotation, and data residency. Quick Q: do we log SCIM events with user-attributed audit IDs? We should confirm retention.
Jordan: For SCIM, we support PATCH ops and incremental (delta) syncs. Default group mapping is `members -> roles`. If they need claim-based RBAC we'll map groups to roles on ingest. Example SCIM PATCH body we usually share:
```
PATCH /scim/v2/Users/2819c223-7f76-453a-919d-413861904646
Content-Type: application/json
{
 "schemas": ["urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:PatchOp"],
 "Operations": [{"op":"replace","path":"name.givenName","value":"Jane"}]
}
```
Maria: ScarletBank also asked about domain verification for tenant isolation — do we require DNS TXT or can they upload a verification file?
Alex: We support TXT or HTTP file verification. DNS example to send them:
`_redwood-verification.scarletbank.com TXT "rbw-tenant-abc123"`
Sam: Also capture these controls they flagged: SAML signing cert rotation policy, SCIM provisioning least-privilege model, admin actions audit trail retention (they want 1 year). For Private/Dedicated we can commit to 1-year audit retention; hosted defaults to 90 days unless enterprise add-on.
Maria: Pricing ask — they want Dedicated monthly commit vs hosted pay-as-you-go. Ops/finance, can you give a ballpark?
Jordan: Ballpark: Dedicated reserved GPU pod ~ $18k/month per pod (depends on shape), plus throughput tiers (per-10k token/req) and enterprise private flat license ~$10k/month for support/compliance. I'll loop in finance for an official quote.
Alex: Next steps: schedule a 45m technical call tomorrow; I'll collate IdP metadata + SCIM attribute-mapping doc and drop answers to the questionnaire in this thread.
Maria: Great — I'll DM ScarletBank to grab IdP metadata and the completed questionnaire; assigning @Jordan to tenant provisioning once we have SAML metadata. :raised_hands:
oncall-bot: Reminder: create trial tenant request ticket #TB-4321 for ScarletBank POC
Maria: Thanks — keeping Friday deadline in mind. I'll update the thread with the completed questionnaire and attach the docs.
