title: incidents
text:
incident-bot: P1 alert — high rate of tool/function-call parser errors for tenant 'Saffron Health' on dedicated pool ded-eu-3. Error rate spiked to 48% for tool_call responses in the last 5m. Paging oncall. link: https://grafana.redwood/alerts/1965432100 :rotating_light:

Diego (Eng Oncall): Acked. I'm on it. Which stack — runtime or gateway? Any obvious recent deploys?

incident-bot: Recent model variant rollout to 'rwd-open-llama-v2-7b-q' on ded-eu-3 ~ 25m ago. Gateway routing unchanged. Errors are JSON parse failures from tool outputs (invalid schema). Top error sample: `parse_error: Unexpected token` (see logs).

Maya (SRE): @Diego thanks. @Harini can you confirm if Saffron reported customer-facing failures?

Harini (Customer Success): We just got a page from their oncall. Several of their customers saw tool actions fail (orders, scheduling). Saffron-SRE says ~120 failed tool calls in last 10m, intermittent 502/parse errors. They flagged that tool payload keys changed (camelCase -> snake_case). They're on a dedicated pool so tenant isolation is preserved but impact to their workflows is high.

Saffron-SRE: Confirming — our production users saw a stream of failures after ~10:37 UTC. Example failing response from Redwood: 
```json
{"tool_name":"create_appointment","arguments":"{\"patient_id\":123, \"appointment_time\": \"2026-03-15T10:40:00Z\"}"}
```
We expect structured JSON in `arguments` (not a string) and field `patientId` (camelCase). Parser is choking when arguments is a stringified JSON. We didn't change anything on our side.

Diego (Eng Oncall): That payload makes sense — looks like model produced stringified JSON instead of object and changed key casing. This smells like a model function-schema regression introduced in the new variant.

Maya (SRE): Impact assessment: Saffron only on ded-eu-3, so blast radius limited to them. Risk: can't just rollback the dedicated infra quickly if it's a single tenant-managed variant. We can either: 1) rollback model in that pool; 2) apply parser shim at gateway to coerce into expected shape; 3) enable conservative fallback (disable toolcalls for Saffron temporarily). Thoughts?

Simon (Platform): If we rollback model variant for ded-eu-3, we need a redeploy across that pool — doable but has 5-10m time to converge and potential brief disruption. Gateway shim is faster (edge transform) and reversible. We have a small shim we used previously for schema-drift: repo: infra/toolcall-shims.

Eva (SRE): Can we try the shim as first mitigation to buy time? Add transformation: if arguments is a string, attempt JSON.parse; map snake_case -> camelCase for keys listed in Saffron's schema. Quick patch can be applied to the routing lambda in front of the parser.

Diego (Eng Oncall): I can roll that out. Plan: 1) enable ephemeral shim for tenant_id:saffron on gateway; 2) monitor errors/latency; 3) if mitigation fails, rollback model. Applying shim now.

Diego (Eng Oncall): Applying shim — running helper: 
```bash
# apply tenant-level transform
curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $OP' \
 https://api.redwood/internal/adm/shim -d '{"tenant":"saffron","shim":"parse-arguments-and-case-map-v1"}'
```

incident-bot: Deploy started by Diego (request id: ci-1965432100-apply-shim). Canary will route 5% of saffron traffic through shim for 2m then 25% then 100%.

Maya (SRE): Runbook link: https://redwood/runbooks/toolcall-schema-drift — note recommended safe mode is to disable toolcalls if parsing cannot be recovered.

Saffron-SRE: Thanks — we see a drop in failed tool calls immediately. Error rate down from 48% -> 6% in the last 3m after the shim. Please keep us posted, we will keep CS updated.

Harini (Customer Success): Noted, Saffron is confirming business impact reduced. They're ok with shim for now but want permanent fix.

Diego (Eng Oncall): Canary success — promoting to 25% then 100%. Monitoring token-level latency — small +20ms increase for shim path. No new errors.

Eva (SRE): Observability notes: captured example transformed payload post-shim: 
```json
{"tool_name":"create_appointment","arguments":{"patientId":123,"appointmentTime":"2026-03-15T10:40:00Z"}}
```
Shim also added a safe parse guard to avoid throwing on malformed strings.

Simon (Platform): I'll open infra PR to harden shims and add tenant-scoped toggles + audit logs. Also scheduling model rollback verification in case this recurs.

Maya (SRE): Quick RCA hypothesis: new model variant changed function-calling behavior (stringified arguments + snake_case). Root cause likely model tokenizer/adapter patch or function schema blanking. We need to sync with model-onboarding team.

Diego (Eng Oncall): Filing ticket now: INF-8672 — model variant rwd-open-llama-v2-7b-q introduced function-call schema change; create regression test with Saffron prompt set.

Saffron-SRE: Verified 0% new production errors after full shim rollout. We'll accept shim short-term. We need timeline for permanent fix (rollback or model patch) — prefer rollback if it doesn't cause downtime.

Harini (Customer Success): I'll coordinate SL and postmortem with Saffron. They want a writeup and ETA.

Maya (SRE): Action items: Diego — keep shim enabled and produce rollback playbook if needed (due 1h). Simon — infra PR for shims + tenant toggles (due EOD). Eva — add regression alert for function-call schema delta (alerts+dashboards). Harini — CS comms with Saffron. I'll take the incident to postmortem.

Diego (Eng Oncall): Adding note: if we ever need to rollback model variant for a dedicated pool, we should use staged deployment to avoid flapping. I'll prepare playbook lines.

incident-bot: Incident mitigated for now (P1 -> P2). Monitoring will auto-close if error rate stays <2% for 30m. Incident channel will be kept open for handoff.

Maya (SRE): Handoff to Eva for the overnight watch. Eva, can you own the next 4h and coordinate with the model-onboarding folks tomorrow?

Eva (SRE): Taking watch. I'll ping model team and schedule triage with them in their timezone.

Diego (Eng Oncall): Thanks all. Harini, please send the brief to Saffron. We'll follow up with postmortem and long-term remediation plan. :white_check_mark:

Saffron-SRE: Appreciate the fast response, team. We'll be available for any follow-up testing.

Maya (SRE): Closing note: postmortem scheduled for 2026-03-16 09:00 UTC. Attach logs/trace ids to INF-8672.

Diego (Eng Oncall): End of thread.

title: Prompt heuristics experiments scratchpad
author: Maya Patel
text:
Goal: quick notes & experiment ledger for prompt heuristics — build a small library of templates + failure cases to iterate with the hosted API. Mostly personal, messy, includes raw outputs, TODOs.

Context / motivation:
- Want robust few-shot templates for short instruction tasks (classification, extractive QA, rewrite).
- Observed instability across temperature and ordering; need heuristics that generalize across models and quantization variants.
- Start from pragmatic rules rather than huge eval harness.

High-level heuristics I want to test (hypotheses):
1) Explicit role + short constraint outperform long rationale priming for 1–3 shot tasks under latency budgets.
2) Putting the positive example(s) first then the negative(s) reduces hallucination in binary classification.
3) Using tag tokens (### EXAMPLE) helps when using streaming responses because model learns block boundaries.
4) For extraction tasks, prefer “Return as JSON: {key:value}” templates to avoid verbose paraphrases.

Experiment matrix (fast runs):
- Model: small/medium/large (toy runs on gpt-small / gpt-medium / gpt-large-like) — use hosted dev creds.
- Temp: 0.0, 0.2, 0.7
- Few-shot count: 0, 1, 3
- Example ordering: positive-first, negative-first, mixed
- Priming style: role-only vs role + example explanation vs role + chain-of-thought
- Output constraint: plain text vs JSON vs YAML-like

Quick templates to copy/paste (placeholders in <>):
Template A — role + JSON extraction (1-shot):
"""
You are a concise extractor. Given text, return JSON with keys: product, price, quantity.
Example:
Text: "Bought 3 packs of AA batteries (Model X) for $9.99 each
"
Output: {"product":"AA batteries (Model X)", "price":"9.99", "quantity":"3"}

Now extract from the input below:
Text: "<INPUT_TEXT>"
"""

Template B — classification with tag separators (3-shot):
"""
You are a brief classifier. Use labels: {POSITIVE, NEGATIVE}.
### EXAMPLE
Input: "Loved the service, will come back!"
Label: POSITIVE
### EXAMPLE
Input: "Item arrived broken and no reply from support."
Label: NEGATIVE
### EXAMPLE
Input: "Average experience, shipping slow but product ok."
Label: NEGATIVE

Now classify:
Input: "<INPUT>"
Label:
"""

Template C — rewrite to tone (zero-shot with instructions):
"""
You are a rewrite assistant. Rewrite the following customer message to be formal and concise (one sentence).
Message: "<MSG>"
Rewritten:
"""

Few-shot set examples used in the notebook (raw):
- EX1 classification positive: "Service was amazing, staff helpful." -> POSITIVE
- EX2 classification negative: "Order missing items, support unhelpful." -> NEGATIVE
- EX3 extraction (invoice-like): "Invoice 552: 5 widgets @ $2.50 each" -> {product: widgets, price: 2.50, quantity: 5}

Observed failure cases (logs, raw snippets):
1) Extraction fails on currency symbols -> model returns "$2.50" instead of normalized number when temp>0.
 - Example input: "Total: $12.00"
 - Output: {price: "$12.00"} (bad) vs expected {price: "12.00"}.
2) Classification flip when first example is negative (3-shot):
 - Ordering negative-first -> model labels borderline positive text as NEGATIVE 45% of trials at temp=0.2.
3) Streaming truncation glue: when examples use long explanations, streaming token boundary cutting can produce malformed JSON (missing closing brace).
4) Chain-of-thought contamination: if we include a short explanation after examples, sometimes model replicates the internal reasoning in the final output (not desirable for downstream parsers).

Mini-results notes (quick manual runs, counts are small N=20 per cell):
- Temp=0.0 + JSON constraint -> extraction normalized numbers 89% correct
- Temp=0.2 + role-only -> classification accuracy 82% (pos/neg); adding short example explanations drops to 75% (more variance)
- 3-shot vs 1-shot: marginal lift (~3 points) but increased hallucination in extractive tasks when examples are too verbose.

Debug examples (copied outputs):
Input: "Bought 3x AA battery pack (Model B), $7.25 each"
Template A (temp 0.2) -> {"product":"3x AA battery pack (Model B)", "price":"$7.25", "quantity":"3"}
Notes: price contains $; want normalized. Hack: post-process strip non-digits. But better: prompt explicitly: "Return price as digits only (e.g. 7.25)".

Ordering experiment quick log:
- positive-first, temp=0.0, accuracy=86%
- negative-first, temp=0.0, accuracy=78%
- mixed, temp=0.2, accuracy=80%
Takeaway: positive-first seems slightly more stable for balanced tasks.

Ideas to try next (short list):
- Force format tokens: wrap JSON in <OUTPUT>...</OUTPUT> tags to reduce streaming truncation parsing issues.
- Minimal examples: keep examples to <50 tokens each for extraction tasks.
- Prepend a one-line canonicalization instruction: "When extracting prices, strip currency symbols and return decimals only." Test whether model obeys more than post-processing.
- Try injected parsing hint: "Return EXACT JSON, no extra keys or explanation." See effect on refusals/hallucination.

Edge cases to capture in eval set (small):
- multiple currencies in one text
- shorthand numbers (1k, 2M) -> normalize? decide policy
- ambiguous quantity words (a dozen, several) -> map to unknown or approximate?

Open questions / unresolved:
- Is there a general rule for example ordering across task families or is it task-specific? Need more systematic N.
- How much does tokenization/quantization (int8 vs int4) affect these behaviors? Evan suggested running one sweep on ded-quantized nodes.
- Are tag tokens worthwhile for large-scale streaming workloads? Small overhead but possibly reduces hallucination—cost tradeoff unknown.

Quick TODOs (prioritized):
- [ ] Automate N=50 runs for ordering x temp for one classification dataset (Priya to help) — LINK ticket REDW-4821.
- [ ] Add canonicalization line to Template A and test N=100 on hosted dev region (low cost).
- [ ] Prototype <OUTPUT> tag wrapper and test streaming truncation failures (Evan).
- [ ] Capture examples where model returns extra keys (e.g., adds "currency":"USD") and decide whether to reject or accept.

Notes-to-self: keep prompts short, explicit, and machine-friendly for parsing. Avoid chain-of-thought inside examples unless the task benefits (creative tasks). Log everything — small manual runs are noisy but surfaced a lot of concrete failure modes.

Misc references / bookmarks:
- internal convo: #prompt-heuristics on Slack (see pinned messages)
- quick eval notebook: github.com/redwood-inference/quick-promptexps (branch: heuristics-scratch)

End of scratchpad (still messy).

text:
Maya: quick one on the compact card error that shows under small widgets — it gets truncated and users miss retry. want a very short microcopy + a11y checklist. Jared: what about 'Save failed. Retry.' super short and actionable. Evelyn: Love brevity. also need an aria-live announcement so screen readers pick it up. set aria-live="assertive" and test with VoiceOver. Maya: proposing three variants we can A/B in canary: 1) 'Save failed. Retry.' 2) 'Couldn't save. Retry.' 3) 'Save failed. Connection?' Which one fits two tight lines and reads crisply? Tom: 1 feels clean. prefer button label 'Retry' to keep verb short. Jared: UI constraint: smallest breakpoint allows ~30 chars before clipping; 1 and 2 are equal lengthish. We'll cap to two lines and ellipsize rest. Evelyn: accessibility notes to include in the PR: - aria-live example: ```html
Save failed. Retry.
``` - ensure the Retry button receives focus only when user navigates, not auto-focus. - color: current orange token ("warning") fails contrast on small text. suggest #D9534F or #E11D2B for >4.5:1 against white. Maya: about a secondary tiny link for 'Report' or 'Help' — thoughts? worried it'll crowd the compact layout. Tom: skip visible secondary link in compact view. We can surface help in expanded state or under ellipsis. copybot: microcopy suggestion for expanded tooltip: 'If this keeps happening, contact support.' keep that out of compact variant. Jared: impl notes: add a stable data-testid to the error element and inject without animation so SRs get consistent announcements. Add a test asserting the aria-live text equals the visible copy. Evelyn: also verify error icon + text meet contrast and that text size doesn't drop below 12px on mobile. avoid moving focus unexpectedly. Maya: plan: land variant 1 ('Save failed. Retry.') with button 'Retry', update color token to #D9534F, no visible help link in compact. I'll push PR to style-tokens branch and drop link. Tom: let's canary it for a week and monitor support tickets. Maya: PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/ui/pull/2468 — includes copy tokens, aria-live example, contrast token change. copybot: :white_check_mark: automated checks queued. title: Asteria Health pilot weekly - privacy, retention & SSO handoff
author: Samir Patel
text:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-20
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Elena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Noah Kim (Redwood CSM), Maya Chen (Asteria Head of Security), Liam O'Connor (Asteria Platform), Dr. Noor Rahman (Asteria Compliance), Priya Singh (Asteria DevOps)

Summary:
Short weekly touch for POC: focus on SSO handoff, audit log format and retention controls, SOC2 artifacts and one small bench to confirm audit ingestion. Confirmed open items and owners.

Topics:
- SAML/SCIM SSO integration status
- Audit logs: schema, retention, ingestion cadence
- Data retention options for sensitive PHI fields and scrub rules
- SOC2 evidence deliverables and KMS/HSM questions
- Next steps: bench test and handoff timeline

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: okay hey everyone thanks for making time, this is the weekly pilot touch for Asteria, hopefully a short focused one, audio's okay?
[00:10] Maya: yeah hi, audio's good, thanks.
[00:15] Elena: Cool, I'll kick off with current status on SSO since Priya and Liam raised a few items last week.
[00:22] Elena: We pushed the staging SP metadata to the link you sent, we saw the assertion fail on first try because the NameID format was urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:nameid-format:transient which your IdP isn't issuing, so we switched to email address and that landed; there may be a mapping mismatch for groups/roles.
[00:45] Priya: yeah we saw that, our IdP is Okta, and our groups map is a bit custom. We can push a SCIM patch but need the attribute map from you.
[00:55] Elena: absolutely, I'll send a SCIM attribute mapping table. Note though, SCIM patch endpoints in our staging may return 409 for unknown attributes, so be ready to filter on your side.
[01:20] Liam: quick Q — is Redwood doing user provisioning via SCIM or just group sync? We want full deprovisioning for security.
[01:28] Samir: we support both; typical pilot uses SCIM provisioning + SAML for SSO. For deprovisioning we have soft-delete TTL and immediate token revocation hooks, but we'll need to align retention policy.
[01:40] Maya: On retention — we have PHI in some of the payloads (very small subset). We need a retention config to drop PII after 90 days and keep aggregate logs for 365. Can you map what we can redact vs what Redwood needs for model quality?
[01:58] Elena: yes, we can configure field-level retention. The runtime supports prefix/KV cache, and we can redact or pseudonymize before it's persisted to audit logs. Small caveat: if you redact model inputs earlier, it may affect evals but we can maintain hashed identifiers for rollout correlation.
[02:20] Dr. Noor: hashed identifiers are acceptable for our auditors as long as salt management is documented and irreversible.
[02:30] Elena: we'll provide the salt rotation and KMS usage docs — currently we recommend using a customer-managed KMS for Private deployments; for hosted we can integrate with your cloud KMS with envelope encryption.
[02:45] Priya: does Redwood support HSM-backed keys? Our compliance requires HSM for key custody for certain datasets.
[02:52] Samir: yes, we have HSM integrations, you can present an HSM-backed KMS or we can integrate via partner HSM — will add that to artifacts.
[03:05] Noah: quick note — I uploaded the SOC2 crosswalk last week into the shared drive, Samir will follow up with the cert binder.
[03:15] Samir: correct, I'll send the full SOC2 Type II binder and the control mapping doc to Asteria.
[03:22] Maya: thanks, auditors will want evidence for key rotation and access logs.
[03:28] Samir: understood. We'll include KMS rotation policy and sample audit log snippets.
[03:35] Liam: on audit logs — what schema are you emitting? Our SIEM team depends on consistent fields: timestamp, user_id, action, model_id, request_id, token_count, latency_ms.
[03:48] Elena: Great question — our current audit payload includes: ts, uid, req_id, model, route, tokens_in, tokens_out, lat_ms, error_code, retention_tag. But sometimes the transcript text field is full text and may contain PHI, we usually send a pointer to the stored blob if you have stricter retention.
[04:10] Liam: can we ingest via HTTPS push or do you support streaming to Kinesis/SQS?
[04:15] Elena: both, staging supports HTTPS push webhook, and for production we support Kinesis, Pub/Sub, Event Hubs — we'll provide example connectors. For the POC we recommend HTTPS webhook to your SIEM ingestion endpoint.
[04:30] Priya: okay we'll stand up a webhook receiver and try ingesting a few sample events.
[04:36] Elena: I'll drop an example payload (note: sometimes 'KV cache' was transcribed in older notes as 'kiv cache' so ignore that typos), but payload fields are as I said.
[04:50] Maya: also I want to confirm retention UI — can we set per-field retention windows per model?
[04:58] Elena: yes per-model and per-field. We expose retention policies as JSON config — sample: {"model": "redwood-1", "fields": {"transcript": "90d", "meta": "365d"}} — in staging you can set via console or API.
[05:20] Liam: will that be audited in the change logs? We need traceability of policy changes.
[05:26] Samir: yes all retention config changes are tracked in audit logs and tied to the admin user; we can include a sample change record.
[05:35] Dr. Noor: excellent. On SOC2 and the control set, we need mapping for logical access, change mgmt, encryption at rest, incident response.
[05:46] Samir: we'll add the mapping doc — and include the incident response playbook summary.
[05:52] Elena: small technical note on SSO: Okta default group claims size can cause truncated assertions if you push many groups; we suggest SCIM for group membership. Also for role-based RBAC in Redwood Console we map Okta groups to Redwood roles.
[06:10] Priya: good to know. We'll limit to primary groups for now.
[06:14] Liam: about logs retention, how easy is it to purge records if we need to for legal requests?
[06:20] Elena: we have on-demand redaction APIs — you can call the purge endpoint with request_id or user_id and choose immediate deletion from the active store and flag for archive purge; there's also freezer retention for cold backups which we can coordinate with legal hold.
[06:36] Maya: are backups encrypted separately? If backups are in AWS S3 do you use SSE-KMS?
[06:42] Samir: yes we use SSE-KMS for backups and support customer-managed CMKs for the private mode. For hosted we hold the wrapped key but you can bring your own key for the Private deployment.
[06:55] Dr. Noor: there's sometimes confusion between 'hosted' and 'private' modes in terms of who manages keys — can you summarize?
[07:02] Samir: Hosted: Redwood manages key envelope but can integrate with customer KMS for envelope keys; Private/VPC: customer manages keys end-to-end and we only store references. We'll put this in the crosswalk.
[07:18] Elena: moving to audit ingestion bench — for next week we'd like to run a 30 minute test where we pump ~5k events to your SIEM and measure latency; Noah will coordinate the timeslot.
[07:30] Noah: I'll set up a calendar invite for 2027-11-30 14:00 UTC and include required endpoints.
[07:36] Priya: that works. Also small perf ask — will redwood metrics include token-level breakdown per request for our billing reconciliation?
[07:44] Elena: yes we emit token counts and cost metadata; you can map that to your internal billing. Note cost metadata in staging may be mocked.
[07:55] Liam: competitor question — DeepServe flagged a faster ingest pipeline; how is Redwood's audit throughput?
[08:01] Samir: we've seen sustained 10k events/sec in dedicated mode with batching; for hosted POC you'll be in the 500-2k/sec range depending on payload size and concurrency. We default to batching to reduce overhead.
[08:17] Maya: acceptable for POC. Another ask from audits: show us proof of separation of environments (staging vs prod) and data flow diagrams.
[08:27] Samir: yes, we'll share network diagrams and environment separation docs.
[08:32] Dr. Noor: one more — auditors want to see least privilege on API keys, do you support token scoping?
[08:39] Elena: yes API keys can be scoped by model, by route, and by retention policy; we can generate scoped service accounts.
[08:48] Liam: on the SSO handoff, what's the expected effort from our team to finalize the integration?
[08:53] Samir: For full SAML + SCIM + audit flows, estimate 2-3 full days of engineering on your side: provisioning SP, mapping attributes, firewall rules for webhooks. We'll try to minimize by providing templates.
[09:06] Priya: okay that's doable. We'll plan for a 2 day effort next week.
[09:12] Maya: small question on retention artifacts — can you provide example redaction logs that show what was redacted and by whom?
[09:19] Elena: yes redaction logs include admin_id, request_id, fields_removed, reason_code, timestamp. We'll provide sanitized examples.
[09:28] Liam: are there any GDPR considerations we should surface now? We have EU users and need data locality.
[09:33] Samir: for EU data residency we can pin to region and keep control plane in Private mode; for hosted we'd require data region selection and we maintain region-scoped storage. We'll share the region residency matrix.
[09:48] Dr. Noor: can you also show us retention TTL enforcement tests? Auditors like test evidence.
[09:53] Elena: yes we'll include test scripts and example results.
[10:00] Noah: quick sync on timeline — are we still targeting pilot completion by mid-December?
[10:05] Samir: yes target hasn't changed: pilot wrap and go/no-go by 2027-12-15, with final review week of 2027-12-20.
[10:14] Priya: that gives us enough time.
[10:18] Maya: anything blocking from Redwood side to run the bench?
[10:22] Elena: only the webhook endpoint from Asteria and the test SP provisioning. Once those are up we're golden.
[10:30] Liam: final question — OIDC support? Some internal apps use OIDC instead of SAML.
[10:36] Elena: we support OIDC for service accounts but SAML is first-class for SSO; we can provide OIDC client details if you prefer.
[10:42] Maya: thanks.
[10:44] Samir: okay to recap quickly — action items as we discussed: I'll send SOC2 artifacts and control mapping; Elena will send SAML metadata/SCIM map and example audit payloads; Noah will schedule the 11/30 bench; Asteria to provision SP and webhook. Any additions?
[10:58] Dr. Noor: please include the salt rotation schedule for hashed identifiers.
[11:03] Elena: will do.
[11:08] Samir: great. We'll confirm next meeting time — same time next week?
[11:12] Maya: yes midday UTC works.
[11:15] Samir: perfect, thanks everyone.
[11:20] [closing chatter and confirmation of artifacts]

End of transcript.

title: Per-prompt risk budgets and gradual fallback policies for staged model flips
author: Priya Kapoor
text:
Problem: Current canary and A/B workflows evaluate regressions at aggregate route and session levels which can miss prompt-level quality degradations that disproportionately affect specific customers or intents. This ticket designs and prototypes a per-prompt risk budgeting system that ties eval scorecards to routing weight and an automated fallback policy. The goal is to reduce likelihood of broad rollbacks while containing regressions quickly by throttling traffic for risky prompt fingerprints and escalating high-severity failures to human reviewers.

Overview of approach: implement a prompt-level attribution pipeline that tags requests with prompt-fingerprint IDs, computes rolling scorecard metrics per-fingerprint and cohort, and maintains a short-lived risk budget for each fingerprint that is consumed on quality hits. The rollout controller will consume these budgets to progressively reduce exposure for variants (A/B or canary) before triggering a global rollback. Integrations: routing controller, golden-set evaluator, console alerts, and audit logs.

Key innovations: 1) risk budgets per prompt fingerprint with decay and refill; 2) causal attribution (which variant produced the regression) using shadowed dual-write and probabilistic tracing; 3) progressive fallback that first steers only affected fingerprints to stable variants, then scales back overall traffic if budgets exceed thresholds; 4) human-in-loop gating for high-impact fingerprints with one-click quarantine from Console.

Prompt fingerprinting pipeline produces stable fingerprint IDs for >95% of long prompts in production traffic
Per-fingerprint scorecards (accuracy, toxicity proxy, perplexity) published to metrics backend with 1m granularity
Risk budget engine reduces variant weight for offending fingerprints without changing routing for unrelated traffic
Console surface shows per-fingerprint risk state and one-click quarantine that creates audit-loggable policy changes
End-to-end test: simulated regression on 5 synthetic golden prompts causes localized throttling and not a global rollback
Runbook updated and postmortem checklist added to oncall rotation

Design fingerprint key schema and collision handling (Priya)
Implement lightweight fingerprinting library in runtime (ENG runtime team)
Metric exporters and per-fingerprint scorecard pipeline (Marco)
Risk budget service with decay/refill and policy API (backend)
Routing controller hooks to consult risk budgets during traffic weighting (routing)
Console UI for quarantines and risk visualization (Product/Design)
Integrate with golden/gated prompt sets and existing eval harness
Create simulation job to validate behaviour on historical traffic

2026-02-05 - Marco: Prototype exporter instrumented in canary runtime build. Observed 3% of requests missing fingerprint due to streaming chunking; adding reassembly step in client-side SDK.

2026-02-27 - Marco: Simulation on last 7 days of traffic with injected regressions. Results: localized throttles reduced exposure by 82% within 4 minutes for top-10 fingerprints. Edge case: highly similar prompts map to same fingerprint; adding secondary session-signature as tie-breaker.

title: TypeScript SDK retries on HTTP 400 responses, causing duplicate request + billing concern
text:
Issue summary:
Northwind AI reports that the Redwood TypeScript SDK is retrying requests that return HTTP 400 (Bad Request). They observed multiple request IDs for what they believe is a single client call, and raised concern about duplicate billing and/or duplicated side effects in their application.

Impact:
- Customer observed 2–3 identical requests sent for a single application action when the API responds with 400.
- Customer concerned this could lead to duplicate charges and/or duplicated downstream actions (they log each attempt and tie it to billing / user-visible behavior).
- Support + on-call had difficulty triaging because TS error surface did not clearly indicate whether the error was retryable and what triggered the retry.

Customer report (from email + support portal):
- SDK: @redwood-ai/sdk (TypeScript) v2.8.0 (customer-reported)
- Runtime: Node 18
- Pattern: calling chat.completions.create() with a request that sometimes returns 400 (validation failure). SDK appears to retry anyway.
- Evidence: logs show 3 request_id values within ~2 seconds, all 400, same payload.

Environment:
- Region: us-east-1
- Endpoint: api.redwoodinference.com

Steps to reproduce (internal):
1) Use TS SDK v2.8.0.
2) Send an invalid request that triggers a gateway/service 400 (e.g., missing required field or invalid parameter type).
3) Observe SDK retry loop (backoff) and multiple requests emitted.

Expected behavior:
- 400s should not be retried by default.
- The SDK should return a non-retryable, typed error and include request_id if present.

Actual behavior:
- In certain 400 responses, the retry middleware treats the failure as retryable and retries up to the default max attempts.
- Customer sees multiple request IDs (one per attempt).

Notes / hypotheses:
- The retry middleware appears to misclassify some 400 responses as “network errors” due to an exception during error body parsing (e.g., non-JSON error body or unexpected content-type). When parse fails, status is not propagated to the retry classifier.
- This is aligned with other parity findings: different SDKs handle “error parsing failure” differently; TS path can drop status_code and request_id.

Billing clarification (preliminary):
- Platform billing is token-based for successful generations/embeddings. 400 responses should not bill tokens; however, the customer may still see request counts and/or gateway logs that look like “multiple attempts”, and they may have internal metering tied to request volume.
- Independently of billing, duplicate attempts can create duplicate application side effects if the customer couples the API call to a non-idempotent operation.

Request IDs provided by customer (example set):
- rw_req_01HNTW9VZ9J2R3… (400)
- rw_req_01HNTW9W1P8K5A… (400)
- rw_req_01HNTW9W3F0M2C… (400)
(These were within one client action window; exact IDs stored in the private Zendesk attachment, not reproduced here.)

Ask:
- Confirm whether TS SDK is retrying 400s and under what conditions.
- Provide workaround to customer ASAP.
- Align with SDK parity initiative: retryable codes + typed error taxonomy + conformance tests to prevent regressions.

2026-01-29 09:18 PT — Dev Patel (Support)
Acknowledged customer escalation. Asked for: TS SDK version, snippet showing retry config (if any), and 3 request_ids + approximate timestamps. Noted that SDK retries are expected on 429/5xx, but not on 400. Opened as P1 due to billing concern.

Shared immediate workaround: set maxRetries: 0 in client config until we confirm behavior.
2026-01-29 10:02 PT — Customer (Northwind AI) via support portal
Confirmed @redwood-ai/sdk 2.8.0, Node 18, running behind a corporate proxy. They see 3 attempts on a single call when the error is 400. They associate retries with possible double-charging because their internal cost dashboard counts requests. They asked whether Redwood bills for failed requests.

They provided logs showing three request IDs and identical payload hash.
2026-01-29 10:30 PT — Owen Phillips (Support Escalation Eng)
Pulled gateway logs for the provided request_id set. Confirmed: all three requests returned HTTP 400 with ~5–20 ms service time. No streaming involved. Response size small. Error body for at least one attempt was not JSON (content-type text/plain) due to an upstream validation error path.

Conclusion: the client truly sent 3 requests. Not a duplicate server-side processing artifact.
2026-01-29 11:15 PT — Ibrahim Khan (SDK TL) (internal note)
This matches a known parity issue: TS retry middleware can treat “failed to parse error response” as retryable because it throws before constructing the HttpError with status_code. If the retry classifier sees a generic error without status, it goes down the network-retry path. Need to ensure status is captured even if body parsing fails, and never retry 400.

Flagging Dana Lo to investigate in TS repo; also aligns with ENG-5126 error taxonomy work.
2026-01-29 13:05 PT — Dana Lo (TS SDK Owner)
Reproduced locally with v2.8.0:
- When error response is JSON, status=400 is preserved and shouldRetry=false.
- When error response is text/plain (or JSON parse throws), the SDK throws a generic error prior to wrapping it, so our retry middleware sees “unknown error” and retries.

Plan:
1) Refactor error parsing so we always preserve HTTP status + headers and build a typed error even when body parsing fails.
2) Tighten shouldRetry to require an explicit retryable classification (429/5xx/408/504 + network timeouts) rather than defaulting unknown errors to retry.
3) Add conformance coverage: 400 with non-JSON body must not retry.

ETA: patch release within a week; will link PR.
2026-01-29 14:10 PT — Dev Patel (Support)
Responded to customer with billing clarification:
- Redwood does not bill tokens for requests that fail with 4xx before generation.
- They may see multiple request records because the client retried.

Provided mitigation until fix is released:
- Configure client retries off (maxRetries: 0) or restrict retryableStatusCodes to [408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504].
- Log request_id + retry_count for correlation.

Asked whether they rely on any side-effectful behavior tied to request submission; recommended idempotency keys where applicable (even though chat/embeddings are typically safe, their surrounding workflow might not be).
2026-01-31 16:42 PT — Dana Lo
Opened fix PR and requested review: sources/github/redwood-sdk-typescript/pr-1298-unify-retry-middleware-and-error-shapes.json
Key changes:
- Ensure HttpError is constructed even when response body parse fails.
- Attach status_code, request_id (if present), and retryable flag.
- Update retry classifier: do not retry when status_code is 400–499 (except 408/429), regardless of parse failures.

Also added tests for non-JSON 400 response body.
2026-02-02 09:05 PT — Allison Grant (SRE/Standards)
Reviewed retry classification against standard. Confirmed retryable defaults should include 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504 + network errors/timeouts, and must not include 400. Requested one additional guard: if Retry-After is present on a 4xx that is not 429, ignore it for retries.

Suggested adding telemetry fields (retry_count, status_code, request_id) to align with the parity logging plan.
2026-02-03 11:20 PT — Dana Lo
Merged fix + follow-up for Retry-After parsing/jitter alignment: sources/github/redwood-sdk-typescript/pr-1307-retry-after-parsing-and-backoff-jitter.json
Cut release v2.8.2.
Release notes include: “Fix: do not retry HTTP 400 when error body parsing fails; improved typed errors with request_id + retryable flag.”
2026-02-03 12:00 PT — Dev Patel (Support)
Informed customer of v2.8.2 and provided upgrade guidance + confirmation steps:
- Upgrade @redwood-ai/sdk to 2.8.2.
- Run a controlled invalid request; verify only one request_id appears and retry_count remains 0.
- Keep maxRetries: 0 in prod until upgrade completes.

Re-answered billing question: token billing not incurred for these 400s; if they need an invoice-level confirmation, we can route to finance but logs indicate no successful generations on those request_ids.
2026-02-06 15:37 PT — Customer (Northwind AI)
Upgraded to 2.8.2 in staging. Confirmed no retries on 400 anymore. Their internal request counter is now consistent. Asked for a short written statement they can share internally that 4xx validation failures do not incur token charges.

No further issues.
2026-02-10 10:12 PT — Dev Patel (Support)
Provided final billing statement and closed ticket. Customer confirmed resolved in production after rollout.

Follow-ups:
- Ensure conformance suite covers “400 + non-JSON body” across SDKs.
- Ensure docs/migration notes mention the retry classifier change and how to tune maxRetries.
2026-02-10 10:20 PT — Ibrahim Khan (internal)
Logged as an input to SDK parity effort: this bug is a concrete example of why error taxonomy must preserve status_code/request_id even on parse failures. Will reference in parity matrix and conformance fixtures.

Resolved in TypeScript SDK v2.8.2 by ensuring HTTP status/request_id are preserved even when error-body parsing fails, and by tightening retry classification so 400 is never retried by default. Customer mitigated by disabling retries until upgrade. Billing concern addressed: 4xx validation failures did not incur token charges.

Customer upgraded to TS SDK v2.8.2; confirmed 400 responses are not retried and internal metering no longer shows duplicate attempts. Provided written clarification that 4xx validation errors do not incur token billing.

title: Interactive Pathway Cards and Rollback Explorer for Tenant Connectivity
author: Avery Chen
text:
Design an interactive, scan-first surface in the Private Console that helps operators quickly understand tenant cluster connectivity and perform safe rollback actions for recent upgrade rollouts. The core idea is a compact set of 'Pathway Cards' that summarize connectivity, recent latency/egress trends, and a contextual rollback explorer that shows what will change if a rollback is initiated.

Private clusters have complex inter-region networking and upgrade workflows. Operators told us they want a single-pane way to: (1) see which tenant requests flow through which hop, (2) understand cost/latency exposure per path, and (3) trigger safe rollbacks with clear impact previews. Existing designs are scattershot across the cluster and rollout pages.

(1) Reduce mean time to awareness for path-level failures; (2) Surface cost/latency trade-offs inline with connectivity; (3) Provide a friction-minimized rollback flow that shows simulated outcomes before commit.

1) Tenant Pathway List: compact cards per logical path (eg. tenant-gateway -> edge-proxy -> cluster-nodes -> external-egress). Each card shows status chip, 1-hr latency sparkline, 24h egress cost estimate, and an Expand action.
2) Expanded Card Modal: shows step-by-step hop visualizer with packet-loss %, median latency, last successful health check, and overlay toggles (Latency / Cost / Bandwidth).
3) Rollback Explorer: timeline scrubber of recent rollouts for the selected path, delta preview of routing and capacity changes, flagged dependent tenants, and a one-click safe-rollback with preflight checklist.
4) Simulation Mode: 'What-if' toggle that runs a dry-run against the routing policy engine and displays potential failover routes and cost delta.

Figma frames include compact list, expanded details modal, rollback timeline, and simulation overlay. See frames: Pathway_List_v3, Pathway_Expanded_v2, Rollback_Explorer_v1.

https://www.figma.com/file/ABCDEFG/tenant-pathway-cards-2025
https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1example-design-artifacts

Pathway List renders correctly for tenants with 1-10 routing hops
Expanded Card shows hop-level metrics and health check history
Rollback Explorer simulates the chosen rollback and surfaces at-risk tenants
Design tokens and spacing align with console style guide
Edge cases: offline clusters and missing metrics show graceful placeholders and clear next steps

Security review: ensure rollback dry-run does not leak internal topology to non-admin roles. Ops requested an 'undo' snackbar after rollback with a 5-minute reversal window. Accessibility: keyboard focus order for expanded cards must be tested.

1) Use card-first approach (list -> expand modal) instead of inline expansion to keep the list scannable. 2) Simulation Mode will be bounded to role=operator and requires audit-log entry. 3) Cost overlay will show estimated 24h delta, not real-time billing data (privacy and API limits).

Overloading the card UI with too many metrics could reduce scanability. Telemetry APIs may not provide consistent per-hop egress breakdown for all clusters — fallback will show aggregated regional costs. Rollback automation must be conservative; push confirmation and dependency warnings.

Backend contract: GET /internal/paths?tenant_id=... -> returns ordered hops, health, latency_samples, cost_estimate_24h. ENG-1842 tracks batching and caching for these calls. Rollback flow requires POST /rollouts/rollback-preview and POST /rollouts/rollback (with dry_run flag). Engineers have requested simulated payload examples in the spec folder.

PRD: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INFER/Pathway+Cards+PRD
Design Figma: https://www.figma.com/file/ABCDEFG/tenant-pathway-cards-2025
Telemetry contract (proto): https://github.com/redwood-inference/telemetry/pull/412

2025-02-14 - PM Morgan Patel: Suggest adding an explicit 'impact surface' line for cost-sensitive tenants.
2025-02-16 - Eng Samir Gupta: Backend needs an aggregated path-cost API; created ENG-1842 to track telemetry contract.
2025-02-20 - Design critique (Cross-team): Consider moving the simulation mode to a secondary action to reduce accidental use — Riley to prototype confirmation flow.

1) Iterate prototype to address feedback about simulation placement (due 2025-02-25). 2) Hand off annotated Figma frames and redlines to ENG. 3) Schedule cross-team review with SRE to validate failure-mode messaging. 4) Prepare A/B test plan for rollout visibility and rollback usage metrics.

QA should validate: card list pagination, expanded modal accessibility, rollback preview accuracy for both single-tenant and shared-tenant rollouts, audit log entries on simulation and real rollbacks.

title: Scheduled digest emails: tracehook query param sanitized to trace_hook, causing 404s and missing trace context
text: Issue summary: Customers receive scheduled digest emails for dashboard alerts, but the deep links back to the console lose trace context. The tracehook query parameter is being changed from 'tracehook' to 'trace_hook' by the email templating pipeline, and the console rejects the modified parameter, returning a 404 and therefore dropping trace linkage for all triggered alerts in the digest. Impact: - ClarityHealth reports missed trace links on scheduled alert digests for 18 dashboards across two orgs. - Customers cannot jump from an alert email to the associated console view, slowing investigation (support/CS escalation). - Loss of trace context causes SLO/alert correlation gaps for affected routes. Environment: - Prod (us-east) scheduled digest worker: alert-formatter v2.11.4, emailer v1.6.0, console v3.2.1 - Affected orgs: clarity-prod and clarity-staging (org merge history exists) Steps to reproduce: 1) Create a dashboard with an alert that includes a tracehook link (console -> scheduled alert config). 2) Add a high-cardinality route filter (route param in query string) to the scheduled alert. 3) Wait for scheduled digest run (or trigger via POST /api/v1/scheduled-runs). 4) Inspect email HTML body and the alert deep-link URL. Observed behavior: - Link in email HTML: https://console.redwood.dev/org/clarity-prod/dash/123?trace_hook=eyJ... (note underscore) - Clicking link returns console 404 and no tracehook context is attached to the session. Expected behavior: - Link should be: https://console.redwood.dev/org/clarity-prod/dash/123?tracehook=eyJ... and open console with trace context resolved. Preliminary investigation notes: - The email HTML is generated by alert-formatter service which calls the templating helper in emailer. The helper runs a sanitize pass to prevent XSS explosions in customer-supplied strings. - Trace: alert-formatter:v2.11.4 -> emailer:v1.6.0 -> sanitizer:mustache-sanitize@0.9.3 (internal fork). The sanitizer has a normalization rule that converts consecutive alphanumeric segments separated by non-alphanumeric chars into snake_case. In the sanitization step the parameter key 'tracehook' is seen in an interpolated fragment and the sanitizer rewrites it to 'trace_hook'. - Nginx edge and console validate the exact 'tracehook' parameter name; trace_hook is treated as unknown and rejected by the dashboard link handler (403 -> 404 surface). - The behavior was introduced after the sanitizer bump on 2026-02-28 during a templating dependency update. No change to console input validation was done concurrently. Next steps planned: - Short term mitigation: add an edge rewrite rule to map trace_hook -> tracehook for scheduled-digest endpoints in prod/us-east. (Workaround applied 2026-03-11 21:10 UTC for clarity-prod, verified links restored). - Medium term fix: remove the aggressive key-normalization from the sanitizer pipeline for alert URLs and add a whitelist exception for known tracehook keys. Create internal PR to revert or patch sanitizer behavior. - Long term: add automated unit test to alert-formatter/emailer that asserts no query-key rewrite for tracehook and add integration test covering scheduled digest email deep-linking. Related artifacts: - Sample broken email HTML (snippet): View dashboard - Sample expected URL: https://console.redwood.dev/org/clarity-prod/dash/123?tracehook=eyJhbGci... 2026-03-10 09:22 - Hannah Park (Support): Customer reported scheduled digest links 404ing; provided sample email HTML and dashboard IDs. 2026-03-10 11:05 - Ethan Rivera (SRE): Reproduced in prod/us-east by triggering scheduled run. Confirmed parameter name rewrite in email body. Collected emailer and alert-formatter logs (attached to ticket). 2026-03-11 02:40 - Maya Chen (Platform Eng): Verified sanitizer upgrade on 2026-02-28. Locally reproduced sanitizer rule that normalizes 'tracehook' -> 'trace_hook' when parameter is generated via template interpolation. 2026-03-11 20:55 - Ethan Rivera (SRE): Rolled out temporary CDN rewrite mapping trace_hook -> tracehook for scheduled-digest domain on prod/us-east. Customer confirmed links now land on console and trace context restores. 2026-03-12 08:15 - Product (Aisha Patel): Logged follow-up INT ticket to remove normalization rule and add tests. Prioritizing for next minor release. Sanitizer normalizes interpolated keys. Reproducible on local branch of sanitizer. No evidence of console-side change; console correctly enforces expected param name. CDN rewrite is a safe short-term mitigation but brittle for other keys. Need whitelist and tests. Temporary CDN/edge rewrite mapping trace_hook -> tracehook applied in prod/us-east for scheduled-digest host. Customer notified. For customers in other regions, open support ticket to apply region-specific rule if impacted. Mitigation applied (CDN rewrite) and verified on 2026-03-11. Code fix in progress: PR created to patch sanitizer (github.com/redwood/alert-service/pull/7342). INT-9012 tracks removal of aggressive key-normalization and test additions. Change will ship in alert-formatter v2.11.5. - Ensure migration plan in INT-9012 includes a canary and monitoring for scheduled-digest link failures. - Add post-deploy synthetic that triggers a scheduled digest and validates returned email link contains 'tracehook' param exactly. - Communicate to CS and customer once v2.11.5 is released with remediation steps.

title: Microbatching, KV Sharding, and MoE Cost Tradeoffs — Arch Tuning for Llama/Mistral/Qwen
author: Avery Lopez
text:
Detailed technical session focused on reducing tail latency and unit cost for high-throughput LLM inference in Peregrine's private VPC. Covered microbatch sizing, KV cache sharding strategies, rope decay/scale implications for Llama/Mistral/Qwen, MoE router throttling and cost modeling, and quantization impacts on accuracy and memory. Agreed on a next-step benchmark matrix and on-prem POC in Peregrine's lab cluster.

Avery: Share perf spreadsheet with baseline numbers and recommended config (due 2026-05-18)
Samir: Draft KV-sharding test plan and microbatch scripts (due 2026-05-21)
Marco: Provision VPC test subnet and credentials for POC (due 2026-05-20)

Redwood to run 1k/2k seq length benchmarks with hybrid quantization profiles and 4 batching window sizes
Customer to provide representative prompt set + sample traffic shape
Schedule on-prem POC week of 2026-05-25; Redwood SE to join

Meeting header
Date: 2026-05-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Avery Lopez (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jules Martin (Redwood SE), Elaine Chen (Peregrine CTO), Marco Reyes (Infra), Nirav Shah (ML Lead), Priya Kapoor (SRE)

Auto-summary: technical deep-dive covering batching, kv cache, rope scaling, MoE costs, quantization and VPC considerations. Action items captured at end.

[00:00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick run of show — Samir will walk the runtime perf considerations, we'll dig into KV sharding and microbatching, then talk MoE routing costs and rope scaling specifics for your Llama / Mistral / Qwen mix, and finish with on-prem/VPC requirements.
[00:00:18] Elaine: Sounds good. We're mostly worried about tail latency and overall token cost — our product is conversational with very spiky traffic.
[00:00:25] Samir: Right, and that's actually going to drive a lot of the config choices. Two quick clarifiers: what are your typical sequence lengths and the percent of long-turn conversations?
[00:00:32] Nirav: Median seq is about 120 tokens, 90th percentile around 900, but we have a long-tail to 2k+ for context windows on some users.
[00:00:40] Priya: Also important: everything needs to live inside our VPC, we have to integrate with our KMS and audit logs — SOC2 is on the roadmap.
[00:00:48] Jules: Great, thanks. I'll call out design patterns as we go — microbatching windows, prefix caching, KV sharding topology, and then MoE-specific things like router overload and expert capacity.

--- Microbatching and latency tradeoffs ---
[00:01:12] Samir: Microbatching increases throughput but adds queueing latency. Our runtime defaults to a ~4–8ms window at X requests per worker, but for your tail we should consider an adaptive window that collapses when queue depth is low. For example, at median seq 120, microbatch size 8 with continuous batching gives good GPU utilization. But at 900–2k, the per-token compute dominates and you want smaller microbatches to avoid multiplying tail latency.
[00:02:05] Marco: Can you quantify the tradeoff? We need ballpark dollars per million tokens with different batchings.
[00:02:12] Samir: Sure — rough numbers off our baseline runtime: with a Mistral-like 34B quantized to int8 and microbatch 8 you can get ~2.3M tokens/hour per A100-equivalent. Shrink microbatch to 2 you drop throughput ~30–40% but tail P99 improves by 25–40ms depending on seq. Cost per million tokens moves accordingly — we'll put precise rates into the spreadsheet.
[00:03:01] Elaine: How about streaming & partial responses? Our front-end shows token streaming and we can't have big front-end stalls.
[00:03:08] Samir: Streaming interacts with batching — smaller microbatches mean earlier first token latency. Redwood supports head-of-line priority for streaming requests so they can bypass batching windows in latency-sensitive modes.

--- KV cache sharding/topology ---
[00:04:05] Samir: KV cache is the big lever for long context. Options: per-GPU local KV (fastest but replication heavy), sharded KV across GPUs with a router (good memory efficiency but network overhead), or hybrid where recent prefixes are local and long-tail caches live on a remote fast KV store. For your 2k contexts, per-GPU local KV becomes memory taxing quickly — with Llama-2 style attention keys and 2k seq, one shard can burn through GPU memory.
[00:05:00] Nirav: What about KV sharding for Qwen — any gotchas?
[00:05:05] Jules: Qwen uses slightly denser KV due to its rotary encodings; rope scaling can interact here. We recommend a 16-way sharded KV for 2k seq on 80GB GPUs to keep per-device memory under control. That does introduce a cross-GPU allgather every token for certain operations unless you use pipeline parallelism tuned for KV locality.
[00:06:02] Marco: Network overhead concerns — we're on a 100Gb fabric in our lab, but if we go on-prem with smaller racks we may be 25Gb.
[00:06:11] Samir: 100Gb is fine for sharded KV at moderate QPS. At 25Gb you need to either increase local KV fraction or accept higher tail latency. Another option is to co-locate experts/routers with KV shards to reduce cross-host traffic — essentially affinity scheduling.

--- ROPe scaling and positional encodings ---
[00:08:00] Samir: Rope scaling is subtle: scaling RoPE/rotary values when you up the context window can give you longer extrapolation but you can also destabilize probability mass for older tokens if you scale too aggressively. For Llama, we tend to use linear rope decay with a small alpha to maintain stability; Mistral has been more robust to mild rescaling. Qwen is model-dependent — we'll check the vendor notes but expect you may need to retune the decay factor when moving to 2k/4k windows.
[00:09:02] Nirav: Any impact on KV cache invalidation?
[00:09:06] Jules: If you change rope parameters you must recompute KV encodings or you get mismatch. That means model variant pinned per deployment — rolling the model with new rope scaling is a heavy op. Prefer runtime-level techniques first (cache eviction policies) until you commit to retraining or fine-tuning with different rope.

--- MoE routing costs & throttling ---
[00:11:20] Samir: For MoE models the router is the cost control point. Two big things: expert fanout (k) and expert capacity. Higher k increases quality slightly but multiplies dispatch overhead. Also token copying to multiple experts increases memory and compute at routing time. Our recommendation for cost-sensitive workloads is k=1–2 with capacity-fold of 1.25–1.5. For bursty traffic you may see router overload where queued tokens wait for expert slots; we implement overflow queues and graceful degrade to dense model variants.
[00:12:02] Marco: So what's the price delta vs dense models?
[00:12:08] Samir: It depends — with a 64-expert MoE and well-packed traffic you can save 2–3x in FLOPs for the expert layers vs a dense 70B, but routing and memory overhead plus peak expert loss can reduce those gains. Our cost model in the sheet simulates realistic burst patterns and shows effective savings of 1.4–2x in most enterprise scenarios, less if your traffic is highly spiky or you need k=4.
[00:12:55] Elaine: Is it safe to mix MoE and dense in different routes?
[00:13:01] Jules: Absolutely — Redwood supports route-based model selection. For short context, low-latency routes use dense quantized models; for long-context batch jobs you can route to MoE variants. Also automatic fallback if router is overloaded.

--- Quantization: int8 / int4 / hybrid ---
[00:14:30] Samir: Quantization is a spectrum: int8 usually gives near-native quality for most models with big memory wins, int4 needs careful per-layer calibration and can drop accuracy on instruction-heavy tasks. Hybrid quantization (int8 for attention/FFN critical kernels, int4 elsewhere) is a strong sweet spot. For Mistral we've seen ~6–8% memory drop with int8 and ~12–18% with mixed int4 but quality hits vary by prompt. We recommend running your eval prompts through quantized candidates before rolling.
[00:15:20] Priya: Does Redwood do GPU kernel selection automatically? We use some NVIDIA optims and also some open kernels in our stack.
[00:15:28] Samir: Yes — runtime picks kernels by model, sequence length and hw. For int8 we default to optimized cuBLAS/cuDNN paths where available, fall back to custom kernels for int4. There's a perf delta; we'll list per-model kernel recommendations.

--- VPC / on-prem specifics ---
[00:16:40] Avery: Quick ops note — Peregrine needs Private deployment with customer-managed control plane and KMS/HSM for keying. Also audit logs for inference events (token-level logs optional). What restrictions do you have on telemetry?
[00:16:55] Elaine: We can share anonymized telemetry; raw prompts must not leave the VPC.
[00:17:02] Jules: That's compatible — Redwood Private can run the serving plane inside your VPC and route metrics to a separate observability endpoint that you control, or ship only aggregated stats. For SOC2 readiness we support SAML SSO, RBAC, and KMS integrations with Azure/AWS/GCP KMS or customer-managed HSMs.

--- Deep dive: example perf configs ---
[00:18:50] Samir: Example config A (low-latency): dense Mistral-34B int8, microbatch 2, priority for streaming, local KV fraction 0.6, no MoE. Expected P50 first-token ~40ms on A100-type, P99 ~220ms depending on network.
[00:19:20] Samir: Example config B (cost-efficient long-context): MoE-64 expert variant, k=1, microbatch 8, sharded KV (16-way), hybrid quantization int8+int4, affinity scheduling, expected throughput gains 1.6–1.9x but P99 higher under spikes.
[00:19:45] Nirav: How do we measure QoE when we try quantized MoE? Any recommended evals?
[00:19:52] Jules: Use held-out prompt sets across your top 50 failure cases, measure semantic similarity, hallucination rate, and a small human rating panel for edge cases. Redwood Optimize can automate some of this and generate regression alerts.

--- Adversarial and edge cases ---
[00:21:30] Samir: A few pitfalls we've seen: 1) Changing rope without KV recompute, 2) mixing quantized and non-quantized keys accidentally, 3) router spill to main thread causing GC with python runtimes. Avoid mixed encodings in a single route and pin model versions for long tests.
[00:22:05] Marco: You mentioned affinity scheduling — does Redwood surface that in the control plane?
[00:22:10] Jules: Yes, in the Console you can annotate workloads with placement hints and set autoscaler policies by route. Those are enforced by the orchestrator.

--- Live Q&A and clarifications ---
[00:24:00] Elaine: If we want to try a small on-prem pilot, what are the minimum rack requirements?
[00:24:07] Samir: For a representative pilot with 2k seq and sharded KV you want at least 4x80GB GPUs on 100Gb with a head-node for routing and one fast NVMe for remote prefix store. If you only have 25Gb, scale down sharding and accept higher tail.
[00:24:35] Nirav: For the POC, can we start with 2x A100 80GB and scale?
[00:24:40] Jules: Yes for a tiny POC but expect limited sharding and you'll be CPU-bound on routing if QPS hits. We recommend starting with 4 GPUs for realistic MoE routing tests.

[00:26:00] Marco: On the security side, how do we audit token access? We need to show who requested what in a way that doesn't expose content.
[00:26:10] Avery: We support hashed token-level audit trails where we log metadata and a hash of the prompt. Full content can be stored only inside your KMS-protected store if you choose.

--- Benchmarks & metrics to capture ---
[00:27:00] Samir: For benchmarking capture: per-token throughput, first-token latency, tail percentiles (P90/95/99), memory footprint per device, KV hit rate, router queue length, expert utilization, and algorithmic ops for MoE layers. Also run synthetic burst tests to emulate your peak zones and a real traffic replay.

--- Example exchange about unexpected transcription artifacts (meta) ---
[00:30:10] Speaker 2: (inaudible)
[00:30:14] Samir: Sorry, could you repeat?
[00:30:16] Marco: I said we'll share the traffic shape — 95th percentile burst is 120 requests/sec for a 30s window, then cooldown.

--- Wrap-up and next steps ---
[00:58:00] Avery: Recap: Redwood will share the perf spreadsheet, microbatch scripts and initial benchmark plan. Peregrine will provision VPC test access and share prompt/traffic samples. Plan for on-prem POC week of 2026-05-25.
[00:58:30] Elaine: That's great — appreciate the thoroughness.
[00:58:40] Nirav: One more ask — can you include an example of the fallback policy when a router gets overloaded? We need docs for our SRE playbook.
[00:58:52] Samir: Yep — we'll include the fallback flow: degrade to dense route, increase retry backoff, and throttle non-priority requests.
[00:59:10] Jules: I'll put links to the console screens and the affinity policy docs in the follow-up email.
[01:00:00] Avery: Thanks all — end call.

---
APPROVED WORDING (Hosted API – EU Region)

Q: Where is customer content processed?
A: When a customer selects an EU region for Redwood Hosted, customer content (e.g., prompts/inputs and model outputs) is processed within the selected EU region for the purpose of serving the request.

Q: Is customer content stored at rest by default? If yes, for how long and where?
A: By default, Redwood does not use customer prompts/inputs or model outputs to train foundation models. Storage and retention of customer content depend on the specific product configuration and customer agreement. Where storage is enabled for operational reasons (e.g., troubleshooting with customer approval), data is retained for a limited period and handled in accordance with Redwood’s data retention policy. Customers may request deletion as described in Redwood’s customer-facing retention/deletion overview.

Q: Where are logs stored?
A: Redwood generates service logs and audit/security-relevant logs to operate the service (e.g., authentication events, administrative actions, and system health telemetry). Log storage and retention depend on deployment mode and customer configuration. Redwood can support EU-region deployments where logs and related operational data are stored and processed in the selected EU region.

Q: Is any data replicated cross-region for DR/backups?
A: Redwood does not replicate customer content cross-region by default for EU-region deployments. Business continuity and disaster recovery controls are implemented at the service level; cross-region replication, if required, is handled only by explicit customer request/contracted configuration.

Q: Can support staff outside the EU access our data?
A: Redwood restricts internal access to customer data on a least-privilege basis. Where access is required for support or incident response, it is authorized, time-bound, and logged. APPROVED WORDING (Dedicated – EU Region)

APPROVED WORDING (Private – VPC / On‑Prem)

A: For Redwood Private, the customer controls where the system runs (e.g., customer VPC or on-prem). Customer content is processed within the customer-controlled environment. Operational telemetry and support access can be configured to meet customer requirements; any access is governed by customer-approved controls and auditing.

title: Intermittent TTFB regressions for streaming completions when API gateway connection reuse interacts with proxy buffering
text:
Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent increases in time-to-first-byte (TTFB) for streaming completions. The symptom is that some streaming requests return initial tokens after a 2-6s delay even though request enters the serving runtime quickly. Impact: customers see perceived latency spikes for interactive flows and partial timeouts when clients have strict idle time windows. Observed at scale across multiple backends in us-west and reproduceable in limited cases from internal synthetic tests.

Observed behavior:
- Requests accepted by API gateway and routed to serving cluster immediately (backend request logs show sub-200ms queuing).
- First chunk from serving runtime often delayed by multiple seconds before being flushed to client. Subsequent chunks stream normally after first flush.
- When we disable proxy buffering on edge (apigw/nginx) the TTFB returns to expected ~120-300ms range.

Why this is likely: preliminary triage indicates a protocol/conn-reuse mismatch between API gateway (proxy) keepalive behaviour and the serving runtime's chunking strategy. When proxy buffering is enabled and the proxy reuses a keepalive connection that previously saw a large header/tracing payload, it sometimes buffers until either (a) a buffer threshold is reached, or (b) the backend explicitly flushes by closing or hitting a chunk boundary we do not trigger. This causes the first-chunk delay but not subsequent tokens once the stream is warmed.

1) Use customer streaming API with small prompt (~80 tokens) against redwood/bison-2-7b in us-west.
2) Ensure client keeps a short idle timeout (2-5s) between request start and consuming first token.
3) Send 100 concurrent streaming requests over a reused keepalive connection from same client IP.
4) Observe distribution of TTFB; ~15-30% of requests exhibit 2-6s TTFB while others respond fast.
5) Toggle proxy_buffering off on the APIGW/nginx side and re-run; issue disappears in synthetic test.
6) Re-enable buffering and run with a clean TCP connection per request; TTFB regressions reduce substantially.

api-gateway access: 2026-03-09T18:52:12Z GET /v1/streams 200 upstream_latency=0.18s downstream_latency=2.64s conn_reuse=true
serving-runtime: 2026-03-09T18:52:12Z request_id=abc123 stage=generate first_token_emitted=2.3s kv_warmup=0.05s
load-balancer tcp: 2026-03-09T18:52:12Z conn_id=97 last_used=2026-03-09T18:50:12Z keepalive_ms=90000
edge-proxy (nginx) error: 2026-03-09T18:52:12Z buffered 1 bytes waiting for flush: proxy_buffering=on

2026-03-10 - Aisha Khan (Support): Customer NimbleDocs reported frequent user-facing stalls starting 2026-03-08 after a traffic spike. Provided initial logs and sample request/response headers.
2026-03-10 - Diego Martinez (SRE): Reproduced with internal loadtest. Noticed correlation with connection reuse and presence of large trace headers. Opening investigation with edge team.
2026-03-11 - Priya Rao (Edge Eng): Found nginx proxy_buffering and proxy_http_version differences when connection reused after large header set. Suggested testing disabling proxy_buffering as quick mitigation.
2026-03-11 - Customer (NimbleDocs): Verified turning off 'proxy_buffering' in their test environment eliminated stalls in 200/200 samples.
2026-03-12 - Diego Martinez (SRE): Rolled a config change to disable proxy_buffering for streaming routes in canary; monitoring telemetry for regressions.
2026-03-12 - Aisha Khan (Support): Notified customer about temporary mitigation and ETA for permanent fix.

Hypothesis 1: proxy_buffering combined with keepalive reuse causes proxy to wait for enough data or connection-close to flush first chunk. Evidence: disabling buffering returns normal TTFB.
Hypothesis 2: large tracing headers from upstream clients sometimes change buffer allocation path and push proxy into a different flush policy. Evidence: requests with >8KB combined headers show higher probability of stalls.
Telemetry: 95th percentile TTFB for streaming endpoints jumped from ~480ms to ~2.8s for a subset of connections with conn_reuse=true between 2026-03-08 and 2026-03-09.
Reproduced locally using nginx with proxy_buffering=on and proxy_http_version=1.1 vs off; behaviour matches customer reports.
Risk: disabling proxy_buffering increases upstream load and may expose backend to small write amplification; need to tune keepalive and buffer thresholds.
Follow-ups: add a low-risk canary for proxy_buffering=false on streaming routes, add metric for 'first_chunk_delay' to per-route dashboards, and audit header size distribution for customers.

Mitigation applied: disabled proxy_buffering for streaming routes in APIGW canary (rolled to 10% of edge hosts). Also aligned keepalive timeouts between APIGW (now 120s) and load balancer to avoid reuse windows that previously exposed the bug. Permanently: engineering will add an explicit backend flush hook for first-chunk emission and add a feature flag to prefer flush-on-first-chunk for streaming models. Customer notified and accepted workaround. Postmortem planned; estimated full rollout after performance validation.

1) Instrument first_chunk_delay metric and add alert at 1.5s for streaming endpoints
2) Implement explicit flush-on-first-chunk in serving-runtime (PR opened)
3) Run load test with proxy_buffering disabled at 50% edge capacity to measure upstream load impact
4) Communicate permanent fix ETA to NimbleDocs and update docs on streaming tuning
