title: Runtime Fallback & Graceful Degradation Playbook
author: Lena Hart
text:
Operational runbook and engineering guidance for automatic fallback and graceful degradation behaviors in the Redwood serving runtime. Covers triggers, architecture interactions, scheduler implications, profiling and benchmarking guidance, and step-by-step incident remediation.

Overview:

This playbook describes the intended behavior and operational steps for runtime-level fallback and graceful degradation across Redwood Inference deployments. It targets on-call SREs, runtime engineers, and platform product owners who must ensure applications meet latency and availability SLOs under degraded conditions (e.g., spot evictions, model OOMs, regional capacity constraints, extreme tail-latency events).

Goals and SLO impact:

- Primary goals:
 - Keep requests successful and bounded in latency by applying controlled degradation rather than failing hard.
 - Maintain transparency to customers (logs, metrics, traces) when fallbacks occur.
 - Provide deterministic, testable fallback policies that interact cleanly with kernel scheduler decision-making.
- SLO considerations:
 - Availability SLO: keep request success rate >= 99.9% across primary+fallback flows.
 - Latency SLO: p95 <= 250ms and p99 <= 600ms for standard small-response routes; fallback flows may relax latency SLO but must be documented in per-route dashboards.
 - Error budget accounting: fallback-induced higher latency counts against the latency error budget but not necessarily the availability budget if response semantics are preserved (200 OK with degraded payload).

When to engage fallback layer:

Fallback layer should be applied when one or more of the following triggers fire (automated):
1) Serving node failure modes: GPU OOMs, VMM crashes, container restarts above threshold (>=3 in 5m).
2) Resource saturation: queue length > config.queue_threshold or CPU/GPU utilization sustained > 92% for 60s.
3) Tail-latency surge: p99 request latency for a model > configured model.p99_threshold for 60s.
4) Regional capacity shortage: target region has < 10% of baseline free capacity and cross-region failover policy exists.
5) Model regression detection: quality monitoring signals output regression (eval set drop > 3% absolute) and defined auto-fallback rule is enabled.

Architecture integration (how fallback fits in the runtime):

- Placement: Fallback logic lives in the routing and execution orchestration layer (service: runtime-router). The runtime-worker accepts policy decisions (serve, downgrade, cache-hit, reject) returned by router.
- Policy store: Policies (per-route) are defined in the control plane config-store and propagated as immutable rollout keys. Each policy key maps to a fallback strategy bundle.
- Execution paths:
 - Normal path: route -> schedule -> worker -> model -> response.
 - Fallback path examples:
 - Model-variant downgrade: route -> schedule -> worker -> quantized-or-smaller-model -> response.
 - Cached-prefix reply: route -> cache-check -> cached-response -> response.
 - Short-circuit: route -> runtime-synthesizer -> short-summary response (used for long-running synth).
 - Regional fallback: route -> alt-region-router -> remote-worker -> response.
- Observability: All fallback decisions emit a fallback.reason tag and fallback.variant tag on traces and metrics. Billing and cost analytics receive a fallback.flag to attribute cost differences.

Fallback strategies and recommended order (policy template):

1) Prefetch & Cache (least-visibility change)
 - Serve cached completion or prefix when TTL not expired.
 - Use for high-QPS, low-variance routes (embeddings, re-ranking).
2) Quantized / Smaller model variant
 - Serve from a model variant with smaller memory footprint or int8 quantization.
 - Keep model-variant performance profile available in model catalog.
3) Partial-response / Synthesis
 - Return partial tokens up to configured token limit + summary flag.
 - Mark response with metadata: degraded: true, reason: partial-response.
4) Cross-region routing
 - Use only when network latency increase is acceptable vs local unavailability.
5) Hard reject / 503 fallback
 - Final resort when no compatibility policy exists; provide diagnostics link in body.

Kernel-scheduler considerations:

- Prioritization policy: The kernel scheduler should expose preemption hints for fallback flows. For example, models used in fallback (smaller quantized variants) receive lower CPU/GPU priority class so that primary models reclaim resources first.
- Eviction thresholds: Scheduler must support two eviction windows: graceful and immediate. Graceful eviction attempts to flush in-flight KV caches and migrate small models; immediate eviction kills the process when node health is compromised.
- Continuous batching interaction: When switching to smaller model variant, kernel should recompute batching windows (batch_size, batch_timeout) because per-token latency and throughput profiles change. The runtime must trigger a batching reconfigure hook on model-switch.

Profiling & benchmarking guidance during fallback mode:

- Benchmark plan: Run a paired A/B microbenchmark comparing normal variant vs fallback variant across the following axes: cold-start latency, steady-state latency, p99, throughput at target concurrency, memory footprint, and token throughput.
- Profiling checklist (oncall):
 1) Capture perf traces (nvprof / nsight) and runtime traces (OpenTelemetry) for both normal and fallback variants.
 2) Compare KV-cache hit rate and batching efficiency before/after fallback.
 3) Measure syscall and GPU kernel latencies; look for stall patterns indicating memory pressure.
- Metrics to surface on dashboards: fallback.count, fallback.latency.delta, fallback.impact_pct_of_requests, fallback.model_variant, fallback.trigger_reason.

Operational runbook (step-by-step):

Detection:
1) Alert fires: FALLBACK_POLICY_TRIGGERED OR model.p99_exceeded.
2) Oncall acknowledges and posts to incident channel (ops/runtime-fallback).

Immediate triage (first 10 minutes):
1) Confirm scope: run queries:
 - curl -sS "https://runtime-metrics.internal/api/v1/route_status?route=<route>"
 - rtfctl route inspect <route> --fields=queue_len,model_variant,uptime
2) Check node and scheduler health:
 - kubectl get pods -n runtime -l app=runtime-worker -o wide 
 - k8s node metrics: kubectl top nodes | sort -nr -k3
3) Determine fallback type currently in use via logs/traces (search for fallback.reason tag).
4) If fallback variant is active and correctness is acceptable, follow stabilization steps below.

Stabilization steps (10–60 minutes):
1) If queue backpressure is root cause, temporarily increase per-route max_workers or enable short-burst scaling (config: autoscale.burst=true) for up to 30 minutes. Document change and set timer.
2) If model OOMs triggered fallback, scale up node group (add nodes) or enable model eviction order: evict large non-critical models first.
3) If degradation due to bad model quality (detected by eval alerts), toggle model.quality_block to stop rollout and enable previously-validated variant.
4) Apply temporary route-level policy: set fallback.strategy=cache-first, max_tokens=128, respond_with_degradation_flag=true.

Rollback and permanent fix (1–24 hours):
1) If configuration/rollout caused the issue, revert the rollout using the control-plane rollback CLI: cpctl rollout revert <rollout_id>.
2) If capacity is root cause, schedule a capacity bump and update scaling policy: infra-iac PR to increase gpu_pool.capacity by recommended amount.
3) If kernel scheduler misbehavior suspected, collect scheduler dump and escalate to runtime-scheduler team: runtime-scheduler@redwood.ai. Include scheduler dump path and most recent kernel-profile tarball.

CLI and debug commands (common):
- rtfctl policy get <route>
- rtfctl model variants <model_id>
- curl -sS https://runtime-router.internal/healthz
- kubectl logs -n runtime <pod> -c worker --since=15m | grep fallback
- oc promql 'sum(rate(fallback_total[5m])) by (route)'

Config snippet (example policy - YAML):

---
route: /v1/generate/summarize
policy_key: minor-degrade-v1
fallback_policy:
 order: [cache, quantized_variant, short_response, cross_region]
 cache_ttl_s: 30
 quantized_variant: model-xy-q8
 short_response_max_tokens: 64
 cross_region: us-west-2
 circuit_breaker:
 consecutive_errors: 5
 reset_after_s: 300
---

Post-incident checklist:
- Create incident summary and link telemetry artifacts (traces, perf tarballs, scheduler dump).
- Run regression tests for the route(s) impacted.
- Schedule a postmortem within 3 business days.
- Add unit/e2e tests for new fallback behavior to prevent regressions.
- Review related model onboarding checks (ensure quantized/variant profiles exist).

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary oncall: runtime-sre team (alias: oncall-runtime@redwood.ai).
- Scheduler and kernel issues: runtime-scheduler@redwood.ai.
- Model quality regressions: applied-ml-and-evals@redwood.ai.
- Product and customer notifications: customer-success@redwood.ai.

Release notes and change history: 
- 2025-11-10 (Lena Hart): Initial draft of playbook.
- 2026-01-08 (Marisol Vega): Added kernel-scheduler preemption guidance and batching reconfigure hook.
- 2026-02-14 (Priya Nair): Expanded operational runbook and added config examples and CLI debug commands.

Appendix A — Known edge cases and mitigation: 
- Cached prefix staleness: Ensure cache invalidation hooks run on model rollout. Add checks: cache_version == model_variant_version.
- Quantized variant mismatch: Validate outputs with a lightweight semantic-similarity check before enabling in routed traffic.
- Cross-region data residency: Cross-region fallback must be disabled for routes marked with confidentiality: restricted.

Appendix B — Test plan for changes to fallback policies:
1) Unit tests for policy evaluation logic.
2) Integration tests simulating node failures and verifying fallback paths (run in staging with chaos tests).
3) Performance benchmark: 48-hour soak with periodic simulated OOMs to verify no latent memory leak in fallback variants.

Related artifacts: 
- Telemetry dashboards: runtime/fallbacks-overview, runtime/fallback-latency-impact.
- Perf artifacts stored at: s3://redwood-test-artifacts/runtime/profiles/fallback-tests/
- Playbook canonical ID: RBWF-2026-04

Contact & feedback:
If you find gaps or incorrect thresholds, please file a PR against this page or email the document owner (Lena.Hart@redwood.ai). For urgent escalations contact oncall-runtime@redwood.ai.

title: Autocapacity signal mismatch causing regional GPU thin-spot and elevated p99s for NimbleRetail dedicated pool
text:
Issue summary:
NimbleRetail reports sustained p99 latency elevation (2.8s -> 8.1s) and intermittent request timeouts from their dedicated GPU pool in us-west-2 during mid-day traffic. The symptoms coincide with a regional autoscaler event where capacity did not materialize despite node-level capacity being available elsewhere in the region.

Impact:
- Customer-facing model endpoints experienced p99 latency regressions and ~3% increases in 5xx error rate for ~90 minutes.
- Affected routes include short-chat streaming and embeddings.
- Revenue-impacting SLA risk; customer flagged to Enterprise CS.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: nimble-dedicated-usw2 (customer-reserved cluster)
- Region: us-west-2 (prod)

1) Route sustained short-stream load (~600 qps short inference requests, avg tokens 60) to nimble-dedicated-usw2.
2) Simulate background long-context validation sweep (internal service) generating periodic KV-prefetch bursts.
3) Observe autoscaler decision and GPU attach logs when burst occurs.

Observed behavior: autoscaler observed a decrease in attach success rate and deferred new slot handout for ~12 minutes despite overall free GPU inventory reported in regional allocator.
Expected behavior: autoscaler should re-balance and attach available GPUs within policy SLO (<=60s) or trigger fallback routing to compatible variants.

Selected logs and metrics attached inline:
- autoscaler/events: 2026-03-10T14:12:03Z scale-eval: score=0.12 -> decision: hold (reason: ephemeral-prefetch-loss)
- allocator/attach: 2026-03-10T14:12:05Z attach-failed code=ATTACH_BACKOFF reason=prefetch_lock
- serving/runtime: 2026-03-10T14:13:10Z batcher-delay p99=7200ms

Hypothesis: prefetch-induced I/O pressure increases allocator latency and triggers hold heuristic in autoscaler. Opened GH PR to relax hold threshold temporarily.

Checked allocator health metrics: attach latency histogram shows a 2-3x spike correlated with kv-cache growth windows.
Observed a class of background jobs (internal validation sweep) that fire periodic long-context validations every 5 minutes; these overlap with customer short-stream windows.
Autoscaler decision path: hold heuristic combines local attach success rate and tail attach latency; observed stale telemetry leading to conservative hold decisions despite free inventory in other racks.

title: Prorated free-tier redistribution during segmented batch run led to unexpected provisional credit movement
text:
Issue summary: Customer reports that a scheduled multi-segment batch embedding job on 2026-03-09 consumed their free-tier buffer in an unexpected way. The billing console shows a provisional credit transfer from their free-tier bucket to a different cost center, leaving Mapflow with a negative provisional balance on the interim invoice (INV-2026-03-09-778).

Impact: Customer's provisional balance briefly went negative (~$312.45) and autopay was paused by their finance guardrails; features relying on reserved capacity are at risk if not resolved. This is urgent for their month-end close.

Environment: production (us-east). Multi-segment batch job launched from Mapflow's orchestration at 2026-03-09T02:18:22Z. Job touched two subaccounts via a routed microbatch strategy (primary cost_center: mapflow-core, secondary: mapflow-analytics-ml).

Steps to reproduce (observed): 1) Customer runs segmented batch across two subaccounts and the job uses the same API key with subaccount prefixing enabled. 2) Our postback pipeline receives interleaved postbacks for the two segments. 3) Provisional free-tier buffer appears to be applied to a later subaccount's window, then redistributed during hourly smoothing, causing a transient negative provisional line on invoice INV-2026-03-09-778.

Relevant identifiers and timestamps: Mapflow job id: mf-job-20260309-77; postback fingerprints: pb-0a7f1c, pb-0a7f1d, pb-0a7f2a; provisional invoice id: INV-2026-03-09-778; account id: org-mapflow-77.

Expected behavior: Free-tier buffer should be applied at the org level and not temporarily reallocated across unrelated cost centers during postback reorder/reconciliation.

Customer asks: 1) immediate corrective credit, 2) explanation of root cause and steps to prevent recurrence, 3) confirmation that future segmented batch runs will not re-trigger autopay holds.

1) Launch a multi-segment batch using a single API key with subaccount prefixes enabled (recreate with small test batch). 2) Force a slight out-of-order postback delivery by delaying the second segment's postbacks (simulate with network delay). 3) Observe provisional credit application in console and provisional invoice line movement within the same hourly window.

2026-03-10 | Support (Diego Moreno): Acknowledged receipt. Reached out to Mapflow for clarification on the segments and requested the job id and any orchestration logs. Q: Did you recently change subaccount tagging?
2026-03-10 | Customer (Elena Park, Mapflow): Confirmed no change to tagging. Provided mf-job-20260309-77 and orchestration logs (attached). Asked for expedited fix because finance autopay is blocked.
2026-03-11 | Billing Eng (Aisha Patel): Noted irregularity in hourly aggregation: postbacks for two cost centers were interleaved; provisional free-tier buffer appears to have been consumed by a later aggregation window due to out-of-order postback handling. Opening investigation with SRE to confirm reconcile semantics.
2026-03-11 | SRE (Marcus Liu): Correlated postback fingerprints; we observed a delayed SQS batch delivery (visibility timeout reset) causing pb-0a7f2a to be processed before pb-0a7f1d. This triggered a short-lived redistribution in the hourly accumulator. Continuing to triage with reconciler owners.
2026-03-12 | Support (Diego Moreno): Informed customer we will issue a provisional credit memo immediately and provide timeline for permanent fix. Asked for confirmation to apply provisional credit now.
2026-03-12 | Customer (Elena Park): Approved provisional credit application and requested a postmortem once resolved.

Initial hypothesis: postback reordering + hourly smoothing algorithm applies free-tier delta on a first-seen basis, so out-of-order postbacks can temporarily reduce the org-level free-tier buffer for the later-aggregated cost center.
SRE findings: delayed SQS delivery for a subset of postbacks (pb-0a7f2a) due to transient broker throttling at 2026-03-09T02:21Z. Delivery sequence changed compared to origin timestamps. Aggregator treats arrival order for provisional allocation, leading to redistribution within the same hourly window.
Reconciler owner notes: hourly_postback_aggregates is eventually consistent and runs smoothing that can reassign provisional credits when late-arriving postbacks are merged. No permanent double-charge observed; issue is transient provisional movement that impacted autopay guardrail checks.
Scope: We see similar small occurrences in trailing windows when interleaved batches from the same key touch multiple cost centers, but frequency is low (<0.01% of hours across all orgs last 30d).

2026-03-12: Created provisional credit memo CM-2026-03-12-901 for $312.45 and applied immediately to Mapflow's account to unblock autopay. Finance notified; customer confirmed autopay resumed.
Short-term mitigation: Tweaked postback-processor visibility timeout and added a sanity window in hourly aggregator to only reassign free-tier buffers after an out-of-order threshold is exceeded (config change rolled to prod 2026-03-12 11:30 UTC).
Permanent fix: Merged reconciler PR #3456 to make the hourly aggregator ordering-resilient (changeset deployed to canary on 2026-03-13; full rollout scheduled 2026-03-17 pending canary results).
Follow-up: Create monitoring alert for cross-cost-center free-tier delta spikes (owner: billing team). Drafting postmortem to link here when complete.
Customer follow-up: Postmortem and apology note to be sent to Elena Park by 2026-03-18.

title: Data sovereignty & logging discovery - Constellation Bank
author: Ethan Park
text:
Meeting header: 2025-06-18 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~48m | Recording: auto
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Leah Gomez (Redwood SE), Marco Reyes (Constellation - Head Cloud & Data), Aisha Khan (Constellation - InfoSec), Tom Elliot (Constellation - Compliance)

Auto summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- Constellation is evaluating options for running Redwood LLM workloads with strict EU/US data residency and FINRA-like audit retention requirements.
- Primary concerns: storing raw transcripts, long-term audit logs, cross-border backups, SOC2 evidence, HIPAA/GLBA overlap for certain products.
- Redwood AE/SE explained Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs, logging controls, KMS/HSM options, and potential mitigations.
- Next steps: share compliance pack, pricing, network scoping, run benchmark under NDA.

Topics: data residency, log retention, encryption at rest, KMS, private deployment, SOC2/ISO, GLBA/FFIEC, PCI-DSS mention, redaction hooks, audit logs, export restrictions.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Ethan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, quick mic check—can you hear me okay?
[00:05] Marco (Constellation): Yep, loud and clear.
[00:07] Aisha (Constellation): All good here.
[00:09] Ethan: Awesome. I'll do a 5 minute intro, Leah will cover the technical controls and then we'll get into your questions. The goal is to understand your residency and logging constraints so we can map to Hosted, Dedicated, or Private.
[00:22] Marco: Cool. High level, Constellation has two product buckets. One is customer-facing chat assistants (EU customers) where we cannot move transcripts outside EU; the other is back-office analytics which can run in US but with stricter audit logs for 7 years. We also have to satisfy GLBA and internal FFIEC guidance.
[00:42] Ethan: Understood. When you say cannot move transcripts out of EU, do you mean raw request/response payloads, or any derived embeddings/metadata as well?
[00:50] Marco: Primarily raw transcripts and anything that can be used to reconstruct PII. Metadata like latencies or token counts are fine but no raw content outside region.
[01:01] Leah (Redwood SE): Got it. Practically that maps to per-region tenancy. On Hosted, we can pin to an EU region for data at rest and we have policy controls to disable cross-region replication, however backups might be a sticking point depending on retention policy.
[01:15] Tom (Compliance): Can you give us specifics on backups? If everything is EU-only, we need to ensure no offsite restore in US.
[01:22] Leah: Yes, so we have two patterns: Hosted EU-only mode and Private (VPC) where the control plane is customer-managed. In Hosted EU-only, backups are stored in the same region and we can disable global replication for your org. Note: our standard Hosted contracts have shared control plane for multi-region failover unless you request Dedicated or Private.
[01:38] Aisha: What's the evidence for that? We need an attestation or docs for our auditors.
[01:42] Ethan: We'll send the SOC 2 + ISO pack and a short note describing regional backup controls. We'll also include a diagram showing encryption and KMS boundaries.
[01:49] Marco: Good.
[01:50] Leah: Quick note on keys — we support customer-managed KMS for Dedicated and Private. Hosted supports Redwood-managed KMS by default but you can elect a bring-your-own-key flow for enterprise tiers and we integrate with common cloud KMS and H S M providers.
[02:03] Marco: B-Y-O-K is important. Our policy says customer keys for production PII must be used.
[02:07] Leah: Then Dedicated or Private is the recommended path. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and single-tenant GPU pools, but the control plane still talks to Redwood services unless you go Private where the control plane is self-hosted or VPC-hosted.
[02:20] Ethan: To be transparent, Private solves the cross-border control plane issue entirely—you're running the control plane in your environment, we provide the package and support. It is heavier ops work but gives max isolation.
[02:31] [crosstalk] Marco: And network egress? We need to ensure logs don't leak egress to a third country.
[02:36] Leah: Yes, you can restrict egress with VPC-only endpoints and private peering. We can provide a peering checklist and subnet/security group templates. We'll include that in the follow-up.

[02:50] Marco: On logging: we are required to retain audit logs for seven years for certain transactions — traceability of who called the model, what prompt template was used, and a hash of the response. But we cannot retain raw transcripts longer than 30 days without explicit consent. How does Redwood separate audit logs from raw request storage?
[03:12] Leah: We separate three layers: 1) Access/audit logs (who, when, model version, route) which are metadata and can be retained long-term; 2) Request/response payloads (raw transcripts) which we store by default for 30 days for debugging and can disable or shorten retention; 3) Derived artifacts like embeddings — those are treated as customer data and follow region policies. We can implement field-level redaction so payloads are masked before storage.
[03:34] Tom: Field-level redaction—who does it? Is it at your edge or do we need to pre-process?
[03:38] Leah: We offer client-side redaction libraries, and also server-side pre-ingest hooks where you can specify regex or JSON paths to redact. There is some latency tradeoff if you do synchronous server-side redaction.
[03:47] Marco: Are redactions reversible? We need to ensure redaction isn't reversible by Redwood or anyone.
[03:52] Leah: Redaction is irreversible; we hash redacted segments with a salted hash if you'd like to keep a reference pointer. The salt can be customer-provided via KMS so Redwood can't reconstruct.

[04:05] Aisha: For HIPAA — we also have a small set of internally facing clinical workflows. Would Redwood sign a BAA?
[04:12] Ethan: We have customers under HIPAA. We can discuss BAA in parallel; initial step is to review your use case and data flows. BAAs are supported on Private and Dedicated plans generally. Hosted can be evaluated but requires specific contractual addenda.
[04:26] Aisha: Okay. What about logging of full prompts for eDiscovery? Our legal team asks for legal hold capabilities.
[04:33] Leah: We can export audit logs to customer S3 buckets or SIEM. For legal hold, we can toggle retention flags and put data under retention hold, but again that implies raw content retention — which contradicts your earlier 30 day rule — so we'd need a policy definition per data class.
[04:49] Marco: Right, so some datasets need 7yr audit metadata, some raw transcripts 30 days.
[04:54] Leah: Exactly — we can implement a tagging policy so certain routes are auto-classified. Tagged routes can be routed to Dedicated or to a private tenant where you permit longer raw retention.

[05:05] Tom: About regulators — if they request data, what is the process? Cross-border requests are our pain point.
[05:11] Ethan: Process is: Redwood supports export requests via documented process; for Private deployments, you control the data and handle legal requests. For Hosted/Dedicated, we assist but we may need legal coordination. We can provide an export log with hash references and explain the chain of custody.
[05:26] Marco: Can you guarantee no debug logs with PII ever leave the host region — like transient logs?
[05:31] Leah: We have a debug-mode that can capture extra traces but it's opt-in per request and flagged. For production we recommend not enabling full debug capturing. We can ensure transient logs aren't persisted to cross-region buckets.

[05:45] Ethan: Quick question—are you leaning to Hosted with strict configs, Dedicated, or Private? Which is your risk posture?
[05:53] Marco: Risk posture is cautious. For customer-facing EU chat: needs strong residency and customer keys — likely Dedicated or Private. For back-office analytics: might use Hosted EU but we need longer audit retention exported to our SIEM.
[06:06] Aisha: Also we have to feed logs into our SOC tooling — Splunk. Do you have connectors?
[06:11] Leah: Yes, we have S3 exports + direct Splunk HEC ingestion in Dedicated and Private. For Hosted we support periodic S3 exports.

[06:23] Marco: One concern: we use tokenization for payment tokens. Do you have PCI implications?
[06:28] Ethan: Redwood doesn't store raw card numbers by default. If your workflow sends raw card data, you should tokenize before calling the model. We can support pre-ingest tokenization or a sidecar that strips out PANs. For PCI-sensitive flows you probably want Private deployment or a certified PCI environment.
[06:45] Tom: For the seven year audit logs — who is responsible for retention costs?
[06:49] Ethan: If logs are exported to your bucket, retention costs are yours. If stored on Redwood's retention tier, it's part of an add-on (we'll include pricing).

[06:58] Marco: On SSO and role-based access—SSO via SAML is required, and we need fine-grained RBAC for model rollout controls.
[07:05] Leah: We support SAML and OIDC. RBAC is available on Dedicated/Private with per-route permissions; Hosted enterprise also has RBAC but with some limits on custom roles.

[07:16] Aisha: Audit trail for admin actions—who changed keys, who deployed new model versions—this is critical.
[07:21] Leah: That's part of the admin audit logs. It's retained separately and can be exported. We can include the specific schema in the compliance pack.

[07:30] Ethan: I'll pause and ask if there are any immediate blockers for you to move to a pilot?
[07:35] Marco: NDA and assurance on key management. We'll want a short pilot where keys are customer-managed and model endpoints are EU-only. Also we need a benchmark that shows latency under your batching for 512 token sequences.
[07:49] Leah: We can run that. For the latency benchmark we'll need a small sample traffic profile and we'll supply a test harness. Note: Dedicated gives more predictable p99 latencies. Hosted has best time-to-value.

[08:02] Tom: Another question — who has access to the KV cache? Can the cache contain PII?
[08:07] Leah: KV cache is ephemeral and local to the GPU node. By default it's not persisted across restarts, but for safety we recommend not caching PII or using tokenization. We also offer an option to disable caching for sensitive routes.
[08:19] Marco: Does disabling cache impact cost heavily?
[08:22] Leah: It can increase CPU/GPU compute and latency; cost delta depends on token volume. We'll model that in the pricing matrix.

[08:31] Aisha: For encryption at rest, we want AES-256 and customer key control. You mentioned KMS — which vendors?
[08:36] Leah: We integrate with AWS KMS, Google KMS, Azure Key Vault and HSM partners like Thales and AWS CloudHSM. For Private we can wire into on-prem HSMs.
[08:48] Marco: Do you do key rotation?
[08:50] Leah: Yes, key rotation policies are supported; rotations can be scheduled and we maintain a key history for decryptable artifacts. For anything you want to be irreversibly redacted we use hashing as discussed.

[09:01] Ethan: I'm going to share a couple of quick links in the follow-up: SOC2 pack, Private deployment whitepaper, network peering checklist and the bench harness.
[09:09] Marco: Great.

[09:12] Aisha: One more operational note — our internal auditors will ask for an incident response SLA and proof of forensically sound logs in case of compromise. Do you have playbooks?
[09:22] Leah: We have an IR playbook and incident reporting timelines for enterprise customers. For Dedicated we have a 24h initial response SLA; for Private we coordinate IR with your team since you're hosting. We'll include a redacted playbook in the pack.

[09:36] Ethan: Ok, quick recap and then we'll do Q/A. Recap: 1) You'll likely pilot EU-only customer-facing chat on Dedicated or Private with customer-managed KMS; 2) Back-office analytics could be Hosted with exported audit logs to your SIEM; 3) We'll send compliance artifacts, peering checklist, pricing, and benchmark harness.
[09:55] Marco: Yep, that sounds right.

[10:00] Tom: Are there any known limitations around encrypted backups — like metadata that still leaks region info?
[10:06] Leah: Metadata like object size and timestamps exist; we can minimize metadata exposure but not eliminate it entirely. If absolute metadata minimization is required, Private is the path.

[10:15] Marco: Final question—do you support country-level data residency controls for EU member states separately, or only region-level (eu-west-1 etc)?
[10:23] Leah: Currently region-level (cloud region) controls are the primary mechanism. Country-level would need Private or specialized hosting in that country — we can consult on options and partners for country-specific hosting.

[10:36] Ethan: Thanks — let's open the floor for any detailed questions?
[10:40] Marco: Not at the moment — just looking forward to the docs.
[10:42] Aisha: We'll review the SOC2 and get back with specific control mappings.
[10:46] Ethan: Great.
[10:47] Leah: One more note: if you choose Dedicated we can run a short security assessment with your team and map control gaps. For Private we have an install guide and an air-gapped checklist.
[10:58] Marco: Perfect.

[11:00] Ethan: Okay, next steps quick list: Ethan to send SOC2/ISO and pricing; Leah to send peering checklist and bench harness; Marco to share residency spec; schedule technical scoping for next week.
[11:14] Tom: We'll target the scoping for June 25th.
[11:17] Ethan: Works for us. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email.
[11:21] Marco: Thanks.

[11:25] (call ends)

Notes on transcription quality: There are a few minor mis-hearings, e.g., HSM sometimes transcribed as "H S M", KV as "K V", and some punctuation missing.

References/links mentioned (will be included in follow-up): https://redwood.example.com/compliance/soc2.pdf, https://redwood.example.com/docs/private-deployments, https://redwood.example.com/network/peering-checklist

Explicit next steps (from transcript):
- Ethan: Share SOC2/ISO pack and pricing matrix (Ethan Park)
- Leah: Draft VPC peering checklist and bench harness + network diag (Leah Gomez)
- Marco: Provide Constellation's residency + regulator list (Marco Reyes)

End of transcript.

title: SLO vs Burn decision session - Mirador Labs
author: Ethan Brooks
text:
Discovery focused on per-token economics vs latency SLOs. Mirador is evaluating hosted -> dedicated -> private path; main constraints are a $25k/month budget for inference, 150ms 95th pct latency target for user-facing prompts, and strict SOC2 compliance. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot scoped to 1k qps burst with sample prompts, Redwood to send cost model spreadsheet and SSO/security pack.

current inference stack and telemetry
per-token pricing and model choices
impact of batching and KV (prefix) caching
deployment options: hosted vs dedicated vs private
security: SOC2, SSO, KMS
pilot scope, timeline, and success criteria

Ethan Brooks | Send detailed hosted vs dedicated cost model spreadsheet with sample workload rows and batching assumptions | 2027-04-25
Sara Kim | Prepare short benchmark guide for KV-cache effects and recommended batching parameters for Mirador prompts | 2027-04-26
Ana Ruiz | Share 3 representative prompt sets and average token lengths for user-facing and background tasks | 2027-04-23
Kevin O'Leary | Confirm regulatory contact and SSO/KMS constraints (do we need HSM?) | 2027-04-27

Redwood to model cost scenarios (hosted/dedicated/private) using customer's prompt samples
Customer to provide prompt samples and current telemetry for token lengths
Schedule 30m pilot kickoff once samples received (target week of 2027-05-03)
Exchange security questionnaire and SOC2 artifacts via shared drive link

Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-04-22
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Ethan (AE, Redwood), Sara (SE, Redwood), Ana (Head of ML, Mirador), Kevin (CTO, Mirador), Jules (SRE, Mirador)

[00:00] Ethan: ok hi everybody thanks for joining on a Thursday afternoon, appreciate it. quick introductions?
[00:09] Ana: hi yeah I'm Ana, head of ML at Mirador. we run most of our user facing NLP features inhouse; right now it's on prem with some cloud bursts.
[00:18] Kevin: Kevin here, CTO. budget is a hard ceiling — we're looking at roughly $25k / month for inference initially.
[00:25] Jules: Jules, platform, I'll be owning the deployment and network pieces.
[00:29] Ethan: great. Sara is our solutions engineer — she'll go through some of the tradeoffs and numbers.
[00:35] Sara: hi all. quick agenda — understand your stack and constraints, talk per-token economics, describe batching and prefix/KV cache levers, and go over deployment options and security. any changes?
[00:46] Ana: sounds good. I want to make sure we can hit a 95th pct latency of ~150ms for user prompts; background jobs can be slower.
[00:54] Ethan: noted — so low latency for interactive pieces is a primary SLO. also confirm: SOC2 is required?
[00:59] Kevin: yes SOC2 and need SSO via SAML, plus customer-managed KMS ideally. we can consider HSM later.
[01:08] Sara: good to know. on the cost side, per-token pricing will vary by model — open heavy models cost more compute per token. we compare hosted per-token list prices vs dedicated committed capacity which changes unit economics.
[01:23] Ana: when you say dedicated committed capacity, is that like reserved GPUs with a predictable rate and lower per-token?
[01:29] Sara: exactly — Dedicated is effectively reserved capacity; you pay for the pool monthly but get much lower per-token run time since scheduling overhead and multi-tenant tax are reduced. caching and batching also amplify that.
[01:39] Ethan: quick aside — sometimes transcripts will say "Redwood Dedicate" — sorry, that was a tongue twister — the product is Redwood Dedicated.
[01:46] Jules: ha. ok. can you walk through an example? our median prompt token length is ~60 tokens, user-facing. background inference is 240 tokens.
[01:55] Sara: sure. example scenario: hosted using a mid-size open model — let's assume 0.6ms/token GPU time (this is illustrative). at small qps, per-token cost includes overheads; with batching of ~8 we'll amortize overheads and get ~0.45ms/token effective. with KV-cache for our user prompts (we saw many shared prefixes) you can cut generation time by maybe 30% because of prefix reuse.
[02:17] Ana: so caching helps a lot for our chat-like flows. how often would you need cache hits to be worth it?
[02:22] Sara: if you see 15-20% prefix reuse that's already meaningful; at 40% reuse it's a game-changer. note that cache efficacy depends on prompt formatting and whether you send full context each time.
[02:33] Kevin: latency concerns — if we batch too much to reduce cost, does that push us over the 150ms 95th?
[02:40] Sara: yes that's the tradeoff — batching improves throughput and lowers per-token cost, but per-request tail latency can increase. Redwood supports adaptive batching with latency SLOs: you set a max acceptable latency and we batch under that constraint.
[02:52] Ethan: we also have routing policies — critical calls can be routed to a low-latency pool (dedicated) and cheaper calls to a burst or lower tier. that lets you keep important SLOs while optimizing cost.
[03:03] Ana: the budget is tight — can you sketch a pilot we can run to validate numbers?
[03:09] Sara: yes — typical pilot: you give us three representative prompt sets + qps/traffic windows. we run a 2-week pilot in hosted or dedicated (your choice) with controlled load, measure token counts, latency percentiles, cache hit rates. Redwood will return a CSV with modeled per-token numbers for hosted, dedicated w/commit, and a private deployment estimate.
[03:28] Jules: for private/on-prem what changes? do we still get your console for metrics?
[03:33] Ethan: private includes a control plane that can be customer-managed; the console can be run in an air-gapped mode or via a private connectivity link depending on the package. there are more integration steps (network, KMS) and licensing fees. unit costs are typically higher for small scale but you gain data residency and control.
[03:49] Kevin: any red flags on compliance? we need KMS and SSO and an audit log stream we can pull into our SIEM.
[03:56] Sara: we integrate with major KMS providers and support SAML for SSO. audit logs are available; we can set up a push to your Splunk/Datadog using a secure forwarder. we'll include SOC2 docs in the security pack.
[04:09] Ana: about model choice — we're debating between an open LLaMA-ish variant vs a distilled model; how does that affect per-token cost?
[04:16] Sara: model size matters — bigger models use more GPU cycles per token. Distilled or quantized variants can be up to 3-4x cheaper per token but might lose quality. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles by workload; for retrieval-augmented prompts you often don't need the largest model.
[04:33] Kevin: does Redwood have a way to automatically fallback if capacity is constrained?
[04:37] Ethan: yes — automatic fallback policies can route to a compatible smaller model or to a different region/instance tier. we can define per-route policies and prioritize by SLA.
[04:47] Jules: operationally, we need to know how autoscaling and burst capacity are billed for dedicated. is burst billed separately?
[04:53] Sara: burst capacity is optional; for dedicated you reserve a baseline pool and can configure burst tiers that spin up extra capacity billed at a higher short-term rate. in the spreadsheet we'll show both amortized and on-demand burst numbers.
[05:05] Ana: what's the typical unit from your hosted price list? tokens? per-token per-1k tokens?
[05:10] Ethan: typically we publish per-1k-token units for completions plus an embedding unit where relevant. in the model-level sheet we'll show per-1k tokens and translate to per-request numbers using your average token length.
[05:21] Kevin: timeline — we want a pilot in May. can you support a quick kickoff?
[05:25] Sara: yes if you send prompt samples and expected qps by next Tues we can provision and start the pilot week of 2027-05-03. pilot run will be 14 days with mid-pilot check-in.
[05:36] Ana: ok I'll get the prompt sets over. one more thing — logging and PII handling. we do not want raw user messages stored off-site. is there an option for ephemeral logs?
[05:46] Ethan: for hosted we can configure no-persist or limited retention. dedicated/private gives you stronger controls. we'll note that in the security pack.
[05:55] Jules: network — do you support VPC peering or private link?
[06:00] Sara: yes both options depending on region; for private we do customer-managed networking.
[06:05] Kevin: any immediate upsides to starting hosted pilot vs deploying dedicated from day one? I'm weighing speed vs cost.
[06:12] Sara: hosted is fastest to start and gives you real metrics to model cost. Dedicated reduces per-token cost with the commitment but requires more ops lead time. many teams do hosted pilot then convert to dedicated once they have stable traffic and SLOs.
[06:26] Ethan: to summarize — Redwood will: send pricing/cost-model spreadsheet, send SOC2/security pack + SSO/KMS integration notes, and S E will prepare KV-cache and batching benchmark notes. Mirador will: send prompt samples and confirm internal security contact.
[06:40] Ana: good recap. can we also get an illustrative example line item for 50k user prompts/day?
[06:45] Sara: yes we'll include a sample row showing token math, batching assumptions, cache hit rate scenarios.
[06:52] Kevin: thanks all. any blockers?
[06:55] Jules: none from infra besides getting the CIDR ranges for peering but that's after pilot scope.
[07:01] Ethan: great — we'll follow up with emails and attach the docs. thanks for your time.

End of transcript.

Shared artifacts referenced during call:
- Cost model template (link): https://redwood.example/sheets/mirador-cost-model (note: placeholder)
- Security pack (link): https://redwood.example/docs/security-pack.pdf
- Benchmark guide (will be provided by Sara)

Transcript has natural ASR artifacts: some proper nouns and product names may be slightly off in the capture. The customer emphasized a hard budget, tight latency SLO, and SOC2/SSO/KMS needs. Pilot timing target: week of 2027-05-03.

title: HubSpot Workflows + Properties Spec (PLG-to-Sales Signal Routing) — v1
author: David Kim
text:
Doc purpose
This spec defines the HubSpot CRM configuration required to support the PLG-to-sales signal routing pipeline (telemetry → aggregation/scoring → HubSpot). It covers:
- Custom properties (Company + optional Custom Object)
- Lists/views for triage
- Workflows and task templates
- Required HubSpot API scopes + implementation guardrails
- Ops implementation checklist + validation steps

Audience
- HubSpot Admin / Biz Systems (David Kim)
- Sales Ops (Isabelle Laurent)
- Marketing Ops (Tyler Benson)
- Growth/PLG (Ben Carter)
- Stakeholder reviewers: Sales leadership (Stephanie Nguyen), CS (Jasmine Liu), SE (Markus Klein), Security/Privacy (Dr. Aisha Rahman / Marcus Lin)

Status / current decisions
- We will ship MVP using Company properties + timeline notes + tasks.
- We will not rely on HubSpot sequences for the initial pilot (tasks/templates only).
- We will keep customer-level telemetry out of HubSpot. HubSpot will only store aggregated signals, classifications, and minimal metadata needed for follow-up.
- Ownership must preserve existing owners (esp. CSM-owned accounts / active opportunities). If no owner, use region mapping; if no region mapping, round-robin pool per pilot rules.

Definitions
- PLG signal: A qualified (or near-qualified) “sales-worthy” event derived from self-serve usage and/or intent (docs/pricing/security).
- Signal types (non-exhaustive): scale (sustained volume/spend velocity), reliability (repeated 429s, latency errors), compliance (security docs views, VPC/Private docs intent), expansion (multi-workspace/team growth).
- Signal windowing: daily aggregation; qualification uses last-7d / last-30d windows depending on signal type.

HubSpot data model (MVP)
Option A (MVP): Company-only
- Store a compact, human-readable last signal summary + key numeric rollups directly on the Company record.
- Add timeline events (notes) per routed signal (one per deduped signal key per suppression window).
- Create a follow-up task assigned to the owner (AE/SDR) with due date and template based on signal type.

Option B (Post-MVP): Custom Object “PLG Signal”
- Track each signal as a record with properties; associate to Company + primary Contact.
- Use for reporting attribution and suppression logic inside HubSpot.

We will implement Option A for pilot and keep schema compatible with Option B.

1) Company properties (create in HubSpot)
Property group: “PLG Signals (Redwood)”

Core routing + summary properties
1. ri_plg_signal_last_seen_at
- Type: datetime
- Description: Timestamp of the most recent routed signal (as written by router service).
- Example: 2025-05-27T18:42:11Z

2. ri_plg_signal_last_type
- Type: enumeration (single-select)
- Allowed values:
 - scale_usage
 - scale_spend_velocity
 - reliability_429s
 - reliability_latency
 - intent_dedicated_docs
 - intent_private_vpc_docs
 - intent_security_faq
 - intent_pricing
 - expansion_workspaces
 - expansion_org_invites
 - other
- Notes: keep values stable for reporting. Add new types via change request (see “Change control”).

3. ri_plg_signal_last_summary
- Type: multi-line text
- Description: Human-friendly summary for AEs. Keep < 500 chars where possible.
- Example: “Sustained token growth (7d avg +38% WoW), 12× 429s in last 48h. Dedicated docs viewed 3×. Recommend Dedicated eval + batching guidance.”

4. ri_plg_signal_score
- Type: number
- Description: 0–100 score from scoring service. Used for sorting/triage; not a hard gate in HubSpot.

5. ri_plg_signal_confidence
- Type: enumeration (single-select)
- Values: low | medium | high
- Description: Router-provided confidence (ties to suppression rules; low should not auto-create tasks in pilot unless whitelisted).

6. ri_plg_signal_qualified
- Type: boolean
- Description: True when signal met routing threshold and task was created.

7. ri_plg_signal_suppressed_until
- Type: datetime
- Description: If suppression active, do not create tasks; still allow property updates and timeline note if needed (pilot decision: no note for suppressed; only metrics).

8. ri_plg_signal_suppression_reason
- Type: enumeration (single-select)
- Values:
 - recently_contacted
 - active_open_opp
 - existing_csm_owner
 - marketing_nurture_conflict
 - internal_test_org
 - low_confidence
 - customer_opt_out
 - hubspot_rate_limit_backoff
 - other

9. ri_plg_signal_next_step
- Type: enumeration (single-select)
- Values:
 - create_task
 - notify_csm
 - monitor_only
 - no_action
- Description: Router recommendation; actual action still controlled by workflows.

10. ri_plg_signal_owner_rule
- Type: multi-line text
- Description: Debug string written by router (“preserve_owner: true”, “region: NA”, “rr_pool: NA_PILOT_AE”). Helps triage routing disputes.

Usage and intent rollup properties (MVP rollups only; keep minimal)
11. ri_usage_tokens_30d
- Type: number
- Description: Total tokens (30d) for the workspace/org mapped to the company.

12. ri_usage_tokens_7d
- Type: number

13. ri_usage_spend_usd_30d
- Type: number (currency)

14. ri_usage_spend_velocity_7d_usd
- Type: number
- Description: 7d spend velocity ($/day) as computed by analytics.

15. ri_reliability_429_count_7d
- Type: number

16. ri_reliability_error_rate_7d
- Type: number
- Description: % error rate (rounded to 2 decimals). Define denominator in scoring service; in HubSpot treat as informational.

17. ri_intent_docs_last_14d
- Type: multi-line text
- Description: Comma-separated intent events with counts.
- Example: “/docs/dedicated (3), /docs/private/vpc (1), /security/faq (2), /pricing (1)”

18. ri_account_region
- Type: enumeration (single-select)
- Values: NA | EMEA | APAC | LATAM | unknown
- Description: Used only as a fallback for routing; prefer data from billing country / self-serve signup.

19. ri_account_tier
- Type: enumeration (single-select)
- Values: self_serve | growth | enterprise | unknown
- Description: Derived; used for prioritization.

20. ri_plg_signal_outreach_status
- Type: enumeration (single-select)
- Values:
 - not_contacted
 - attempted
 - connected
 - meeting_booked
 - evaluation_started
 - opp_created
 - disqualified
 - do_not_contact
- Description: Sales-owned outcome tracking for attribution.

21. ri_plg_signal_outreach_status_last_updated
- Type: datetime

Opt-out / customer sensitivity
22. ri_plg_signal_customer_opt_out
- Type: boolean
- Description: If true, router must never create tasks/notes; only internal dashboards. This is set manually by Support/CS/Sales Ops.
- Notes: Required due to SUP-3392 class issues.

Property group: “PLG Admin (Redwood)” (restricted permissions)
23. ri_plg_signal_last_router_run_id
- Type: single-line text
- Description: Idempotency/audit reference for the last upsert.

24. ri_plg_signal_last_hubspot_task_id
- Type: single-line text

25. ri_plg_signal_last_hubspot_note_id
- Type: single-line text

Permissions guidance
- “PLG Admin (Redwood)” should be editable by HubSpot Admin + Sales Ops only.
- “PLG Signals (Redwood)” readable by Sales/CS/SE; editable by Sales for outreach status + DNC, and by router integration user for all router-managed fields.

2) (Optional / post-MVP) Custom object: PLG Signal
Not required for pilot, but define now to avoid rework.
Object name: PLG Signal (ri_plg_signal)
Associations: Company (required), Contact (optional), Deal (optional)
Recommended properties:
- ri_signal_id (string; primary key from router)
- ri_signal_type (enum; same as company last_type)
- ri_signal_score (number)
- ri_signal_confidence (enum)
- ri_signal_detected_at (datetime)
- ri_signal_window (enum: 1d | 7d | 30d)
- ri_signal_dedupe_key (string)
- ri_signal_summary (text)
- ri_signal_payload_redacted (text; optional; MUST NOT include PII; only high-level counts)
- ri_signal_status (enum: routed | suppressed | dismissed | converted)

3) Lists and views
Goal: give AEs/SDRs a “signal review queue” without building a separate UI.

Active Signal Queue (Company saved view)
Filters:
- ri_plg_signal_qualified = true
- ri_plg_signal_last_seen_at is within last 14 days
- ri_plg_signal_outreach_status is any of (not_contacted, attempted)
Sort:
- ri_plg_signal_score desc
Columns:
- Company name
- Owner
- ri_plg_signal_last_type
- ri_plg_signal_score
- ri_plg_signal_last_seen_at
- ri_usage_spend_usd_30d
- ri_reliability_429_count_7d
- ri_intent_docs_last_14d
- ri_plg_signal_last_summary

Suppressed / Monitor-only view
Filters:
- ri_plg_signal_suppressed_until is known AND is after today
OR
- ri_plg_signal_next_step = monitor_only
Columns:
- Company name
- ri_plg_signal_suppression_reason
- ri_plg_signal_suppressed_until
- ri_plg_signal_last_type

CS Expansion Candidates view
Filters:
- ri_plg_signal_last_type in (expansion_workspaces, expansion_org_invites)
- existing customer flag = true (use existing property if present; if not, define “ri_is_paid_customer” boolean from billing integration)
- ri_plg_signal_next_step = notify_csm OR owner is CSM

Marketing conflict audit list
Filters:
- ri_plg_signal_suppression_reason = marketing_nurture_conflict

4) Workflows (HubSpot automation)
Principles
- The router service is the source of truth for routing decisions; HubSpot workflows should be thin (mostly notifications, task templates, and guardrails).
- Avoid loops: changes made by workflows should not retrigger the router.
- Use a dedicated integration user for router API updates and lock down permissions.

Workflow A: “PLG Signal → Create Follow-up Task (Pilot)”
Trigger enrollment:
- ri_plg_signal_qualified becomes true
AND
- ri_plg_signal_customer_opt_out is not true
AND
- ri_plg_signal_outreach_status is empty OR = not_contacted

Actions:
1) If Company owner is unknown → assign owner based on ri_account_region (if present) else put into round-robin list (Sales Ops to define assignment rules).
2) Create Task (see task templates section) based on ri_plg_signal_last_type.
3) Set ri_plg_signal_outreach_status = not_contacted (only if empty).
4) Send internal notification (Slack/email) to owner (optional; pilot decision: email only to reduce noise).

Notes:
- Ensure re-enrollment is OFF; we do not want multiple tasks per day for the same company.
- Suppression is handled by router; HubSpot workflow should still check ri_plg_signal_suppressed_until (if set and > now, do not create task).

Workflow B: “PLG Signal → Notify CSM (Expansion / Existing Customer)”
Trigger:
- ri_plg_signal_next_step = notify_csm
OR
- ri_plg_signal_last_type in (expansion_workspaces, expansion_org_invites)
AND
- paid customer = true

Actions:
- Create internal task for CSM OR send notification to CSM team inbox (CS preference).
- Add note: “Signal suggests expansion; coordinate outreach to avoid duplicate touches.”

Workflow C: “Outcome logging reminders (Anti-stale)”
Trigger:
- Task created by Workflow A is overdue by 7 days
AND
- ri_plg_signal_outreach_status in (not_contacted, attempted)

Actions:
- Create reminder task: “Update PLG outreach status + disposition.”

Workflow D: “Do Not Contact enforcement”
Trigger:
- ri_plg_signal_outreach_status = do_not_contact OR ri_plg_signal_customer_opt_out = true
Actions:
- Close any open PLG signal tasks
- Set ri_plg_signal_suppressed_until = now + 180 days (manual override permitted)

5) Task templates
Task naming convention
- Prefix all tasks with: [PLG Signal]
- Include signal type + recommended motion (Dedicated vs Private vs monitor)

Template 1: [PLG Signal] Scale / Spend Velocity → Dedicated eval
- Applies to: scale_usage, scale_spend_velocity
- Due: 1 business day
- Notes (task body):
 - Confirm current workload (model, tokens/day, peak TPS, regions)
 - Ask about: cost sensitivity, latency SLOs, burst patterns
 - CTA: offer Dedicated capacity + benchmark plan
 - Link: Playbook section “Scale signals” (Confluence)

Template 2: [PLG Signal] Reliability (429s/latency) → Stabilize + Dedicated
- Applies to: reliability_429s, reliability_latency
- Due: same day
- Notes:
 - Acknowledge impact; ask about user-facing symptoms
 - Offer quick mitigation (rate limits, retries, batching, caching)
 - Position Dedicated for predictable throughput + isolation

Template 3: [PLG Signal] Compliance intent → Private/VPC discovery + security handoff
- Applies to: intent_private_vpc_docs, intent_security_faq
- Due: 1 business day
- Notes:
 - Discovery: data residency, retention, audit logs, SSO/SAML, KMS requirements
 - If healthcare/fintech/regulatory flags: loop SE + Security early
 - Link: Security FAQ (internal) + call scheduling guidance

Template 4: [PLG Signal] Dedicated intent (docs/pricing) → fast follow-up
- Applies to: intent_dedicated_docs, intent_pricing
- Due: 2 business days
- Notes:
 - Ask what triggered research (cost, reliability, procurement)
 - Offer sizing + rough commit ranges (stay within pricing guardrails)

Template 5: [PLG Signal] Expansion (workspaces/invites) → multi-team rollout
- Applies to: expansion_workspaces, expansion_org_invites
- Due: 2 business days
- Notes:
 - Confirm teams/use cases; propose org-wide plan
 - Coordinate with CSM if existing customer

6) Required HubSpot API scopes + integration user
Integration user
- Create a dedicated HubSpot private app (or OAuth app) for the signal router service.
- Name: “redwood-plg-signal-router”
- Store secrets in approved secret manager; rotate quarterly (or on incident).

Scopes (minimum viable)
- CRM objects: companies (read/write)
 - To search by domain / external ID and update properties
- CRM objects: contacts (read; optional write)
 - Read to locate primary contact if needed; avoid writing PII from product telemetry
- CRM objects: tasks (write)
 - Create tasks for owners
- CRM objects: notes (write)
 - Append timeline note with summary (no raw events)
- Owners (read)
 - Resolve owner IDs; route deterministically
- Pipelines / deals (read)
 - Check for open opportunities to suppress new tasks (if this logic is in HubSpot; preferred to be in router)

Rate limit considerations
- HubSpot APIs are rate limited; router must batch where possible and implement exponential backoff (see INT-1843).
- HubSpot workflows should not create cascading API calls.

7) Timeline note format (standard)
Title line:
“PLG Signal: {type} (score={score}, confidence={confidence})”
Body:
- Detected: {timestamp}
- Summary: {ri_plg_signal_last_summary}
- Rollups: tokens_7d={...}, spend_30d=${...}, 429s_7d={...}
- Recommended motion: Dedicated | Private/VPC | Monitor
- Router run_id: {ri_plg_signal_last_router_run_id}

Redaction rules
- Do NOT include: prompt text, user identifiers, IP addresses, exact endpoint paths tied to a user, or per-request logs.
- OK to include: aggregated counts, high-level docs categories, and numeric rollups.

8) Change control
- Any change to enumerations for ri_plg_signal_last_type or outreach status values must be approved by Sales Ops + Product owner (Nikhil Sharma) and documented in ADR addendum.
- Any new property that could be construed as personal data must be reviewed by Security/Privacy (Dr. Aisha Rahman / Marcus Lin) before creation.

9) Ops implementation checklist (HubSpot Admin)
Setup
[ ] Create property groups: “PLG Signals (Redwood)”, “PLG Admin (Redwood)”
[ ] Create company properties 1–25 as specified (validate types and enum values)
[ ] Set permissions: restrict “PLG Admin (Redwood)” edits
[ ] Create saved views (Active Signal Queue, Suppressed, CS Expansion Candidates)
[ ] Create task templates (5 templates) with naming convention
[ ] Create workflows A–D with enrollment criteria and re-enrollment OFF
[ ] Confirm owner routing rules (region mapping + round-robin pools) with Sales Ops
[ ] Create integration user/app “redwood-plg-signal-router”; grant minimum scopes
[ ] Confirm audit log retention and access controls for integration user

Validation (pre-pilot)
[ ] Test company lookup by domain and by external ID field (if used)
[ ] Dry run in sandbox: property upsert + note + task creation
[ ] Verify: creating/updating properties does not trigger unintended workflows
[ ] Verify: suppression fields prevent task creation
[ ] Verify: DNC/opt-out closes tasks and prevents new ones
[ ] Verify: CSM notification workflow triggers only for paid customers
[ ] Verify: timeline note format renders cleanly; no raw telemetry

Pilot launch (NA cohort)
[ ] Create a pilot list (NA self-serve cohort) and share view with pilot AEs
[ ] Confirm SDR/AEs have a place to leave disposition (ri_plg_signal_outreach_status)
[ ] Schedule weekly review of false positives + threshold tuning with Growth (Ben Carter) and Eng (Logan Wright)

Ongoing ops
[ ] Monitor HubSpot API errors/429s (via router dashboards; see ENG-7824)
[ ] Monthly audit: properties used, workflow errors, task volumes by signal type
[ ] Quarterly: rotate app secret + confirm scopes unchanged

Appendix A: Ownership + suppression alignment (summary)
- Preserve existing owner if: active deal owner exists OR company already has assigned AE/CSM owner (per routing ADR).
- Suppress task creation if:
 - ri_plg_signal_customer_opt_out = true
 - ri_plg_signal_suppressed_until in the future
 - open deal in pipeline stage beyond qualification (router preferred)
 - contacted within last X days (router preferred; X=14 pilot default)
- Marketing nurture conflict: router sets suppression reason; HubSpot should not override.

Appendix B: Reporting fields (minimum)
- Meeting booked rate by signal type: filter companies with outreach_status=meeting_booked and last_type
- Opp created rate: outreach_status=opp_created
- Time-to-first-touch: ri_plg_signal_last_seen_at → first task completion time (task timestamps)

Open questions
1) Do we need a dedicated field for “primary workspace/org id” on company for debugging? If so, place it in “PLG Admin (Redwood)” and restrict.
2) Should we store “last 3 signals” summary fields on company (vs only last)? Might be helpful but adds property sprawl. For pilot: no.
3) Marketing suppression: do we enforce suppression in HubSpot using Marketing email enrollment? Current plan: router sets suppression_reason=marketing_nurture_conflict based on shared calendar/list from Marketing Ops.

Revision notes
- 2025-06-12: Added customer opt-out field + DNC workflow following SUP-3392 learnings; clarified suppression precedence; updated rate limit guidance after INT-1843.

title: Axion Sprout
author: Ethan Park
text:
Founders building a conversational fintech assistant for SMB accounting customers. Primary motivators: low-latency chat for agents (<150ms p95 ideal), high-quality embeddings for invoice/search, and deterministic reranking for suspicious tx alerts. Starting with hosted API to iterate; 'VPC-curious' once usage grows. Early security asks: SOC2 snapshot, SSO/SAML, audit logs, KMS integration. Cost-sensitive but willing to commit if latency and reliability stable. Quote from CEO: "We need predictable latency — not just average, p95 matters for UX." Trial shows sporadic p95 spikes during bursts; customer logged sample trace ids. They submitted Fireflies transcript for intro call. Wants a short eval matrix to compare Redwood hosted vs competitors on latency/cost. AE recommended Redwood Optimize suggestions for batching and cache.

title: TritonWorks - Burst SLA discovery
author: Samira Khan
text:
Discovery call to align on TritonWorks' latency (p95) SLAs, concurrency and burst behavior, streaming vs non-streaming paths, and whether Hosted/Dedicated/Private best fits their compliance profile. Customer requested a benchmark run with representative prompts and wants cost/throughput estimates for a Dedicated pilot and a Private (VPC) option for regulated customers. title: Crypto Ops on-call & BYO-HSM playbook review with Veridian Bio
author: Hannah Kim
text:
Meeting header: 2026-12-28 15:00 UTC · duration ~49m · attendees listed above

Summary: Quick sanity check and operational runthrough of Redwood's BYO-HSM integration and proposed crypto-ops on-call playbook. Veridian is evaluating a private deployment path with customer-managed HSM for key custody, needs clarity on guardrails: emergency rotation, key escrow, audit trail, SSO/RBAC controls, and network egress.

Topics: BYO-HSM connector, TLS in-transit guarantees, envelope encryption, KMS key lifecycle, HSM failover, escrow, SOC 2 audit evidence, RBAC and SSO mapping, playbook for on-call rotations and emergency key compromise response.

Action items (discussed verbally; see action_items list above).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Hannah Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we got like 50 minutes, so we'll try to walk through the playbook and then leave time for questions. I'm Hannah from Redwood, AE. Diego and Lena are our SEs.
[00:12] Dr. Priya Rao: great, thanks, Hannah. quick context: Veridian is moving sensitive assay metadata into a model-backed service. Compliance wants customer-controlled keys — they asked for BYO-HSM evaluation.
[00:22] Hannah Kim: understood. the goal today is to show how Redwood supports BYOK via HSM connectors, what the failover story looks like, and how the on-call crypto ops playbook would operate.
[00:30] Diego Martinez: quick callout — there are two common modes we see: full key custody via your HSM (we call it external KMS), or Redwood-managed keys with bring-your-own-wrapping keys. both have tradeoffs.
[00:44] Samir Patel: when you say external KMS, what's the exact connection pattern? do we do an mTLS tunnel to an HSM appliance in our DC or a cloud-HSM endpoint?
[00:54] Diego Martinez: both supported. our connector can perform mutual TLS to cloud-HSM APIs (e.g., AWS CloudHSM, Azure KeyVault HSM endpoints) or to an on-prem gateway that proxies to an HSM appliance. typical flow: model inference service requests envelope key from Redwood runtime, runtime issues KMIP/PCKS or cloud API call to your HSM, gets wrapped DEK back.
[01:12] Elena Gomez: mm-hmm. and we want to avoid any plaintext key material leaving our vault. so the question is: does Redwood ever see keys in the clear in any path?
[01:20] Diego Martinez: no. design is envelope encryption: the DEK (data encryption key) is generated in the runtime but immediately wrapped by your KMS/HSM and Redwood stores only wrapped keys. if you choose full external key generation, your HSM can generate the DEK and return a wrapped DEK — Redwood never has the unwrapped key. caveat: some legacy connectors require a short-lived session key, but we have mitigations.
[01:36] Dr. Priya Rao: about audit logs — our auditors expect immutable evidence of key usage: who requested the key, timestamp, operation type. can Redwood forward or correlate HSM usage logs with request traces?
[01:48] Lena Park: yes, we can correlate. runtime emits request-level trace IDs and stores token-level audit entries in our audit log. for BYOK, we ingest the HSM operation events (push/pull) via a secure webhook or aggregated syslog depending on your environment and then correlate on trace id. note: the HSM's native logs remain authoritative for crypto ops.
[02:05] Thomas Reed: network question — we run an egress proxy and private endpoints only. what's the required egress pattern for cloud HSMs? we can't open everything.
[02:13] Diego Martinez: we'll provide a minimal IP/FQDN allowlist and mTLS fingerprint. for on-prem gateway, we just talk to an internal address, so no internet egress is required. we'll need a small set of ports for health checks and for the runtime <-> gateway comms.
[02:25] Elena Gomez: emergency key rotation: say a key is suspected compromised at 0100 on a Sunday — what's the playbook? does Redwood support immediate revocation and rewrap of all DEKs?
[02:34] Marcus O'Neil: short answer: yes, but caveats. Redwood supports instant revocation flags and a forced fallback model — traffic can be routed to a fallback key or a lower-tier model that uses a different key while we perform rewrap. we provide tools to bulk rewrap DEKs using a new master key. must coordinate with your HSM for policy.
[02:52] Dr. Priya Rao: we need a documented runbook for on-call rotation steps: who contacts which HSM administrator, how the orchestration runs (automated vs manual), verification checks, and rollback.
[03:02] Hannah Kim: that's exactly what the playbook draft covers — we'll share the link. it includes escalation paths, CLI commands and API calls, recommended smoke tests (sample inference request patterns), and an auditor-friendly checklist.
[03:15] Samir Patel: about key escrow — auditors sometimes expect a dual-control escrow to recover keys if the HSM is destroyed. do you support storing an encrypted escrow copy in a separate region or with a third-party escrow provider?
[03:26] Diego Martinez: yes, options include: (1) customer-managed escrow within their HSM cluster; (2) encrypted backup to customer-controlled object storage with envelope encryption using a secondary HSM key; or (3) third-party escrow partners. each option has different SLA implications.
[03:37] Elena Gomez: is there a way to test failover without touching production keys? we want a rehearsal flow.
[03:43] Lena Park: absolutely — POC harness can provision a test key and run a dry-run rotation against a staging dataset. Diego will set that up in the POC.
[03:50] Dr. Priya Rao: SSO/RBAC mapping: we require granular role separation — crypto ops cannot see application tokens, and engineers cannot perform key deletion. how do you model RBAC for KMS actions?
[04:01] Diego Martinez: Redwood's control plane provides role-based policies. you can map your SAML groups to roles (e.g., crypto-ops-admin, key-operator, auditor). we support just-in-time admin elevation for emergency ops and audit trails for any elevation. we also integrate with SCIM for group sync.
[04:15] Samir Patel: our internal policy also mandates hardware attestation for any HSM nodes. we use TPM-backed attestation. can you validate attestation attestations? (laughs)
[04:26] Hannah Kim: yes — for private deployments we can verify attestation proofs and include attestation reports in the onboarding checklist. note: cloud-HSM services vary. we documented supported attestation flows in the playbook.
[04:36] Elena Gomez: one subtlety — tokenization path for PII: we want deterministic tokens for lookup but random for downstream model calls. is that supported with your envelope model?
[04:47] Diego Martinez: you can configure the DEK usage so that deterministic derivation uses a KDF with per-tenant salt inside your HSM. Redwood can orchestrate the KDF call under the HSM policy so plaintext never leaves. for downstream model calls we use ephemeral DEKs.
[04:58] Thomas Reed: audit retention and export — auditors want signed exportable logs for 7 years. what can Redwood provide?
[05:06] Lena Park: we support long-term export to customer-controlled S3 with object-level signing (optional), and we can stream logs to your SIEM via secure forwarders. retention policies are configurable.
[05:16] Dr. Priya Rao: SOC 2 evidence — can you provide an itemized mapping of Redwood's controls vs our SOC2 policy statements? we need to show logging, separation of duties, incident response.
[05:26] Marcus O'Neil: yes, we'll share our SOC 2 Type II report and a controls mapping template. we also attach audit trails for any BYOK flows used during the POC.
[05:35] Hannah Kim: quick demo segment? Diego, do you want to screen-share the playbook and a sample key rotation? (note: screen-share referred to but not recorded in transcript).
[05:44] Diego Martinez: i'll narrate — step 1 generate test key in HSM; step 2 provision key binding in Redwood; step 3 run smoke inference; step 4 flip key alias; step 5 bulk rewrap job. i should call out timing — bulk rewrap depends on dataset size and batch window; for large token volumes we recommend a staged roll.
[06:05] Elena Gomez: are there throttles or rate limits from Redwood during rewrap? we can't have tokenization blocked for hours.
[06:12] Diego Martinez: rewrap is a background job; we throttle to respect latency SLOs. you can opt for a priority rewrap which runs faster but may impact per-request latency briefly. we'll surface cost and latency impact in the console.
[06:24] Samir Patel: any regulatory issues with cross-border key backup? we have EU data residency constraints.
[06:29] Lena Park: escrow backups can be region-locked to EU regions; we support multiple geographic vaults. if keys must never leave the EU, you can keep HSMs and backup storage in-region and configure runtime to only use EU endpoints.
[06:40] Dr. Priya Rao: encryption-in-transit question: we need to prove TLS 1.3 with mutual auth end-to-end from client to HSM gateway — can Redwood attest to that in logs?
[06:50] Diego Martinez: yes, we record TLS version and mTLS fingerprint in connection metadata, and that can be included in the correlated audit record.
[06:58] Elena Gomez: what about key rotation frequency — auditors like scheduled rotation plus emergency rotations. can Redwood automate scheduled rotation policies?
[07:07] Marcus O'Neil: scheduled rotation policies are supported — specify frequency, rotation window, and rollout policy (immediate vs staged). rotation itself is orchestrated with your HSM according to your policy.
[07:18] Thomas Reed: curious about HSM firmware upgrades — can we enforce maintenance windows?
[07:22] Hannah Kim: yes, maintenance windows and planned outage scheduling is supported for private deployments; we also provide a maintenance mode to drain traffic and failover.
[07:31] Samir Patel: are there known limitations with particular HSM vendors? we use a mix — one on-prem Thales, one cloud vendor in EU.
[07:39] Diego Martinez: we have tested flows for major vendors (Thales, Utimaco, AWS CloudHSM, Azure KeyVault HSM). edge cases exist for older KMIP versions; we'll document required firmware/API minimums in the onboarding checklist.
[07:52] Elena Gomez: for the POC, can we do a tabletop of an incident and simulate an on-call response?
[07:58] Lena Park: yes, we'll include a tabletop script in the playbook and run a dry tabletop during the POC week.
[08:05] Dr. Priya Rao: last thing — we need assurance about crypto key escrow access controls. if an escrow backup is stored in S3, who can unseal it? we want dual control and M-of-N unseal flows.
[08:16] Diego Martinez: supported pattern: backup wrapped with a recovery key that is split using Shamir (m-of-n) and stored with separate custodians. Redwood can integrate that pattern into the backup automation; the unseal requires multiple custodians to provide their shares.
[08:29] Samir Patel: good. that's about it for high-level questions.
[08:33] Hannah Kim: great. quick recap of next steps — we'll share SOC2 report, the HSM/BYOK runbook, and set up the POC calendar. Diego will own the POC prep. Elena will own on-call verification and Samir provides the network diagram.
[08:47] Dr. Priya Rao: thanks all. we'll review the docs and come back with any additional control-specific asks.
[08:53] Hannah Kim: thanks, everyone. wrapping up now.

Notes about transcript quality: there are a few mis-heard words and occasional speaker attribution mistakes (e.g., Marcus and Diego overlapping at 02:52). The document refers to a playbook link and internal deck: https://redwood.example.com/docs/byo-hsm-playbook (placeholder link).

End of transcript.

title: TypeScript SDK missing Authorization header in edge runtime during streaming
text:
Issue summary: Customer sees 403 Forbidden when calling streaming chat completions from a Next.js Edge Runtime using redwood-sdk-typescript v1.4.0. Non-streaming calls sometimes work; curl works consistently. Impact: partial outage for end-user feature behind streaming endpoint. Steps: (1) Next.js Edge route handler (2) create client with apiKey (3) call chat.completions.stream() (4) request fails with 403; headers in their proxy logs show Authorization missing. Notes: likely a fetch/Headers serialization issue in edge runtime.

Chloe Martin (Support): Customer provided HAR + proxy logs showing no Authorization header on failed requests.
Dev Patel (DevEx): We use undici in node; Edge uses global fetch. There is a code path that builds Headers from a plain object and may drop 'authorization' when value is undefined (race with async key load).
Customer (Hearthside): apiKey is set; we confirmed it logs correctly. Only streaming path fails.
Dev Patel: Found bug: streaming helper constructs request init twice and overwrites headers; the second init loses Authorization in edge environment due to Headers merge semantics.
Chloe Martin: Workaround: pass explicit headers in request options; confirmed by customer.
Dev Patel: Fix shipped in v1.4.1; customer confirmed 200 OK and streaming stable.
