Transcript
[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, I think we’re at time. Thanks everyone for joining. This is Liam, I’m the TAM on the Acme account. The goal today is security and compliance review specifically for the SIEM-ready audit export beta. Priya, Mark, Elaine, Tom — thanks for making time.
[00:15] Priya Shah: Yep, thanks Liam. We’re mainly trying to close out the open questions from our vendor intake. We saw the beta note and we want to understand what’s real today versus roadmap.
[00:25] Liam O'Rourke: Totally. And just setting expectation up front: beta is hosted and dedicated deployments first. Private / on-prem patterns we can discuss at a high level but we’re not committing to support that in beta.
[00:37] Elaine Wu: That’s fine. We are currently hosted with you, but we do have regulated workloads that might go dedicated, so I’ll want to understand that boundary.
[00:45] Liam O'Rourke: Great. Quick intros on Redwood side: Simran is solutions architect, Colin is our solutions engineer who’s been deep in the Splunk integration, and Kevin is security engineering — audit semantics and policy.
[00:57] Kevin Osei: Hey all.
[01:00] Colin O'Donnell: Hi everyone.
[01:02] Simran Kaur: Hey.

[01:07] Liam O'Rourke: Priya, do you want to kick off with top questions?
[01:11] Priya Shah: Sure. Biggest ones: 1) what audit events are actually included, 2) do you have delivery guarantees for SIEM export, 3) retention and backfill — like if Splunk is down for a day, what happens, and 4) RBAC — who can configure exports and who can see delivery status.
[01:29] Mark Denson: And from SOC: we need to know if this is at-least-once and how we dedupe. Also what the “event id” looks like, because Splunk dedupe is always… fun.
[01:41] Tom Alvarez: I’m also looking for network patterns. Is this outbound from your side to our HEC endpoint, and do you support allowlists, and TLS validation, that kind of stuff.

[01:53] Liam O'Rourke: Perfect. Kevin, can you start with audit event schema and what’s in/out from a privacy lens?
[02:00] Kevin Osei: Yep. So we have what we call audit event schema v2. The key differences: every event has a stable event_id, timestamp fields, a category taxonomy, and consistent actor/action/resource. The intent is that it maps cleanly into SIEMs.
[02:16] Kevin Osei: Required fields — generally: event_id, emitted_at (timestamp), observed_at depending on the producer, tenant_id/workspace_id, actor.type (user, service account, api key), actor.id, action, resource.type, resource.id, and outcome (success/failure) plus a reason code if there’s a failure.
[02:37] Elaine Wu: When you say actor.id, is that like email address?
[02:40] Kevin Osei: Good question. For human users, it’s a stable internal user identifier. We avoid raw email in the canonical fields. We may include a display string in some cases but it’s subject to our PII minimization rules. The idea is: you can correlate with your IdP via your own mapping, but the audit event itself shouldn’t leak more than necessary.
[03:02] Priya Shah: Does it include IP and user agent? That can be sensitive but we also need it.
[03:07] Kevin Osei: It’s “where applicable.” For interactive console actions and certain API calls, we capture source_ip and user_agent. For internal service-to-service actions, it’s often absent. Also, there’s policy that we do not log full request payloads, prompts, or model outputs in audit events.
[03:27] Mark Denson: Ok, so no prompts, no completions. That’s good.
[03:31] Kevin Osei: Right. We’ll log the fact that an API key created a model deployment change, or changed an export config, but not the content of what you ran.

[03:43] Colin O'Donnell: Just to add, in the SIEM export, we send those same audit events. We don’t create a separate “SIEM event” with extra fields, because that can drift.
[03:51] Tom Alvarez: So the export is basically a stream of the audit log.
[03:54] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly.

[03:58] Priya Shah: Categories — can you give examples?
[04:02] Kevin Osei: Sure. Examples: auth.*, access.*, org.*, billing.*, model.*, deployment.*, key_management.*, audit_export.*. The exact list we’ll send as part of the beta pack.
[04:16] Priya Shah: We’ll need that list.
[04:18] Kevin Osei: Yep, we can provide it. And you can filter on categories and actions.

[04:24] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s talk delivery semantics — Mark’s question on dedupe. Colin?
[04:30] Colin O'Donnell: So the exporter is at-least-once delivery. Meaning: we may deliver the same event more than once under retry conditions, but we aim to never drop events within the retention/backfill window. The primary key for dedup is event_id.
[04:48] Mark Denson: So not exactly-once.
[04:50] Colin O'Donnell: Correct, not exactly-once. Exactly-once across Splunk HEC, network failures, retries — it’s not realistic. Instead we do: checkpointing + retries with backoff. And we strongly recommend dedup in Splunk by event_id.
[05:08] Mark Denson: What’s the format of event_id? UUID?
[05:11] Colin O'Donnell: It’s UUID-ish, yeah. It’s globally unique. We can share examples.
[05:15] Kevin Osei: It’s stable per event and deterministic from the event emission path, not like “random per export.” So retries keep the same event_id.

[05:26] Priya Shah: What about ordering? Like if someone disables an API key and then tries to use it, order matters.
[05:33] Colin O'Donnell: We don’t guarantee strict global ordering across all categories. In practice, within a tenant and within a short window, it’s close, but because we’re batching and exporting asynchronously, you should treat it as near-real-time with some reordering possible. Timestamps are authoritative.
[05:52] Priya Shah: Okay.

[05:55] Tom Alvarez: On HEC, Splunk can 429 you. How do you handle that?
[05:59] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. We handle 429 with exponential backoff and a circuit breaker per destination token. We also cap batch sizes and compress payloads. If Splunk is throttling, export lag increases; we surface that in status.
[06:18] Mark Denson: And does it drop after some time?
[06:20] Colin O'Donnell: It shouldn’t drop inside the backfill window. If it exceeds max lag, we can auto-pause the export to protect the system, and you can resume after issues are cleared.
[06:32] Priya Shah: Auto-pause sounds… scary. That means we stop getting events.
[06:37] Colin O'Donnell: It’s a safety mechanism. The idea is: if downstream is down for long enough, we don’t want unbounded queue growth or repeated hammering. When paused, we keep checkpoint state and you can resume, and we’ll replay from last checkpoint.

[06:57] Elaine Wu: Let’s define “backfill window.” What’s the actual number?
[07:01] Liam O'Rourke: In beta, the default backfill that you can request on config is up to 7 days. Kevin, correct me if that’s changed.
[07:08] Kevin Osei: That’s right for beta. There’s also Redwood internal retention of the underlying audit stream, which is longer than 7 days, but the “customer-configurable backfill” is 7 days in beta.
[07:20] Elaine Wu: What’s your retention for audit logs?
[07:24] Kevin Osei: For hosted, we retain audit events for 90 days in our control plane logging system today. Export is considered the customer’s long-term retention mechanism.
[07:35] Elaine Wu: Can you put that in writing for SOC2 questionnaires?
[07:38] Kevin Osei: Yes, we have standard evidence language: Redwood retains audit logs for a defined period and customers are responsible for downstream retention once exported. We’ll send you the language.

[07:52] Priya Shah: So scenario: Splunk is down for 36 hours. We come back. Do we lose anything?
[07:59] Colin O'Donnell: If Splunk is down, exporter retries. Lag grows. If it crosses max lag threshold, it pauses. When you resume, we replay from checkpoint, subject to the backfill window and retention. If it’s within 7 days, you should be able to recover.
[08:18] Priya Shah: And if it’s 10 days?
[08:20] Colin O'Donnell: In beta, that’s where we’re limited. We’d need to handle it case-by-case. GA roadmap includes longer backfill and tooling.
[08:30] Elaine Wu: Ok, so we need that clearly stated as a limitation.
[08:33] Liam O'Rourke: Agreed.

[08:36] Mark Denson: For dedupe in Splunk: do you recommend using event_id as _key or in a lookup?
[08:43] Colin O'Donnell: Typically you ingest event_id as a field. Then you can use Splunk’s dedup command or a summary index approach. We can share recommended SPL. Most customers do dedup in correlation searches rather than at index-time, because index-time dedup can be tricky.
[08:59] Mark Denson: Right.

[09:02] Tom Alvarez: Network: does Redwood call our Splunk? Or do we pull?
[09:06] Colin O'Donnell: For Splunk HEC, it’s outbound push from Redwood to your HEC endpoint. You provide the endpoint URL and token. We validate destination hostnames against an allowlist pattern on our side to reduce SSRF and misconfig.
[09:22] Tom Alvarez: Can you support IP allowlisting from your egress?
[09:26] Colin O'Donnell: We can provide our egress IP ranges by region for hosted. For dedicated, it depends on how your dedicated cluster is configured, but yes we can support stable egress addresses.
[09:39] Tom Alvarez: We’ll need those ranges.
[09:41] Liam O'Rourke: We’ll include that in the follow-up.

[09:46] Priya Shah: Encryption: TLS, token storage, at rest.
[09:50] Kevin Osei: In transit: TLS 1.2+ for all destinations. For Splunk HEC specifically, we require HTTPS; we validate certs — no plain HTTP.
[10:02] Kevin Osei: At rest: the exporter uses encrypted storage for checkpoints and queues. Secrets like HEC tokens are stored encrypted using our KMS-backed secrets store. Access is restricted to the exporter service identity.
[10:18] Priya Shah: Are tokens ever logged?
[10:20] Kevin Osei: No. We treat them as secrets. They are redacted from logs and not included in audit events. Also, support staff do not have direct access to raw tokens.
[10:31] Elaine Wu: “Not have direct access” — do you have break glass?
[10:35] Kevin Osei: There is controlled break-glass for production incidents, with approvals and audit trails, but it is not used to view customer secrets. The access path is designed to avoid exposing secrets; operational actions are things like rotating references, disabling an export, etc.

[10:54] Mark Denson: Do you log admin actions like “export config changed”?
[10:58] Kevin Osei: Yes. Changes to export configuration are themselves audit events under audit_export.* category, including who changed it and what was changed at a high level (not the secret value).
[11:13] Priya Shah: That’s good.

[11:16] Liam O'Rourke: On RBAC, I’ll let Kevin and Colin tag-team. Who can configure exports.
[11:22] Kevin Osei: The model is least privilege. There are specific permissions: view audit exports, manage audit exports, rotate credentials reference, and view delivery status.
[11:34] Kevin Osei: Default roles: Org Admin typically can manage exports; Security Auditor role can view configuration and status but not modify destinations. You can customize roles if you have custom RBAC.
[11:49] Elaine Wu: Can you separate “view events” vs “view status”? Sometimes GRC wants evidence of controls but not necessarily operational details.
[11:56] Kevin Osei: Yes. “View delivery status” is separate from “view audit logs.” And the export feature is also gated behind a feature flag per tenant during beta.

[12:09] Priya Shah: And does the act of exporting create additional data exposure? Like can a rogue admin point it to their own Splunk?
[12:16] Kevin Osei: That’s a core threat model point. Mitigations include: RBAC boundaries, destination validation, and we recommend customers restrict who has manage privileges. Also, we can restrict allowed destination domains per tenant in some cases. In beta, it’s more manual, but it’s on the roadmap.
[12:34] Tom Alvarez: Is there an egress allowlist enforcement?
[12:37] Colin O'Donnell: We have hooks to validate destinations. For Splunk, we validate hostname and scheme. For S3, we validate bucket ownership patterns if using cross-account role. For Datadog it’s fixed endpoints.

[12:54] Priya Shah: Wait, so you support Datadog too?
[12:57] Liam O'Rourke: In beta, initial destinations are Splunk HEC, Datadog Logs intake, and generic S3 delivery. For Acme, we understand you’re Splunk-first.
[13:07] Mark Denson: Yes, Splunk.

[13:10] Elaine Wu: On data residency: we operate US only for this pilot. Any cross-region movement?
[13:16] Kevin Osei: Export runs within the region your Redwood control plane and tenant are in. We don’t intentionally ship audit events across regions for export. If you choose a Splunk endpoint in a different geography, then that’s your routing choice.
[13:31] Tom Alvarez: That’s fine.

[13:34] Mark Denson: Operational visibility: how do we know if exports are failing? Are there alerts? Or is it just a dashboard.
[13:41] Colin O'Donnell: There’s a status endpoint that the Redwood Console surfaces: export lag, last successful delivery timestamp, and last error message (sanitized). Internally we have dashboards and alerts. For customers, during beta we can set up notifications via support, but customer-configurable alert webhooks is likely GA.
[14:02] Mark Denson: So we can’t get an immediate alert today.
[14:05] Liam O'Rourke: Not self-serve in beta. What we can do is agree on an SLO and we’ll proactively monitor. Also we can provide guidance on querying “last seen event” in Splunk.
[14:18] Priya Shah: We’ll probably want both: query-based detection and vendor monitoring.

[14:25] Elaine Wu: Can you clarify again retention and deletion semantics? Like if we delete a user, do audit logs delete?
[14:31] Kevin Osei: Audit logs are immutable records for security. We don’t delete historical audit events when an identity is deleted. We may pseudonymize or reference by stable ID. That’s standard for compliance.
[14:44] Elaine Wu: Ok.

[14:47] Priya Shah: What fields are considered “sensitive” and redacted?
[14:51] Kevin Osei: Anything like raw tokens, passwords, private keys, prompt content, model outputs, request bodies — prohibited. For IP/user agent, we include where justified; we don’t include precise geo enrichment. For emails, generally avoided.
[15:09] Priya Shah: Good.

[15:12] Tom Alvarez: For Splunk HEC, do you support mTLS?
[15:16] Colin O'Donnell: Not in beta. We do TLS with server cert validation. If mTLS is required, we should capture that as a follow-on requirement.
[15:25] Tom Alvarez: Ok, not a blocker for dev.

[15:29] Mark Denson: Event volume: do you have ballparks? We need to size indexes.
[15:35] Liam O'Rourke: We can provide rough estimates based on your usage. For most teams it’s not massive, but if you do high-volume API activity, it can add up.
[15:44] Colin O'Donnell: Also, the exporter batches — you’ll see bursts rather than one event per HTTP request.
[15:52] Mark Denson: Right.

[15:55] Priya Shah: Do you have an allow/deny filter? We might not want billing events in Splunk.
[16:00] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. Filters support allowlist and denylist by category and action. You can also filter by actor type or resource type. We recommend default: allow security-relevant categories and block noisy ones.
[16:16] Priya Shah: Is filtering evaluated at export time or at ingestion time?
[16:20] Colin O'Donnell: In the exporter. Config is validated in the control plane API; evaluation occurs in exporter on the stream.
[16:29] Priya Shah: Okay.

[16:32] Elaine Wu: For compliance evidence, we need: description of audit log content, retention period, export guarantees, encryption, and RBAC. Can Redwood provide an FAQ doc?
[16:42] Liam O'Rourke: Yes, we have a security FAQ specifically for the beta. We’ll send it, and we can tailor wording for your questionnaire.
[16:50] Kevin Osei: We’ll also include the “beta limitation” statement: at-least-once delivery; 7-day backfill; no private/on-prem in beta.

[17:02] Mark Denson: About dedupe: If I get duplicates, are the timestamps identical?
[17:07] Colin O'Donnell: emitted_at stays the same. In Splunk you might see different _indextime, obviously. But the payload’s timestamps should be stable.
[17:17] Mark Denson: Great.

[17:20] Priya Shah: How do you prevent partial batch loss? Like if you send 500 events and network drops.
[17:27] Colin O'Donnell: We batch, but checkpointing is based on “acknowledged” deliveries. If a batch fails, it will retry. That’s where duplicates can occur if Splunk accepted some events but failed the request. So again: dedupe by event_id.
[17:45] Priya Shah: Makes sense.

[17:48] Tom Alvarez: For outbound, do you support proxy settings? We have an outbound proxy in some environments.
[17:54] Colin O'Donnell: In hosted, we don’t support customer-specific proxies for exporter egress in beta. In dedicated, we have more flexibility. But for now, easiest is: expose HEC endpoint to our egress IPs.
[18:10] Tom Alvarez: Okay.

[18:12] Elaine Wu: Are audit export config changes logged as well? You said yes, but do you log “test connection” actions?
[18:19] Kevin Osei: Yes, test connection triggers an audit event too, indicating it was executed and whether it succeeded, without exposing secrets.
[18:28] Elaine Wu: Great.

[18:31] Liam O'Rourke: Maybe we can walk through a concrete flow. Colin, how does Acme set it up?
[18:37] Colin O'Donnell: In Console, under Settings → Audit Exports (beta), an Org Admin creates a destination: Splunk HEC URL, token reference, optional index/source/sourcetype, and filters. Then you run Test Connection, then enable. Status page shows lag and last error.
[18:57] Priya Shah: Token reference — meaning we paste the token in console?
[19:02] Colin O'Donnell: In beta, yes, you paste it in a secure field and it gets stored encrypted. Longer term there’s roadmap for secret manager integrations.
[19:13] Priya Shah: Ok.

[19:15] Mark Denson: Can you send to multiple destinations? Like Splunk + S3 archive.
[19:20] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, multiple exports per tenant are supported. Each has its own filters and checkpoints.
[19:27] Elaine Wu: But RBAC needs to control that. We don’t want proliferation.
[19:31] Kevin Osei: Right, it’s governed by “manage audit exports” permission.

[19:37] Priya Shah: On PII: user agent can contain weird things. Do you sanitize?
[19:43] Kevin Osei: We store it as-is when present, but we cap length and we do not include request headers beyond user agent. If your policy requires not collecting it, we should discuss — today it’s not a tenant-level toggle, but we can mark as a requirement.
[20:02] Priya Shah: Understood.

[20:05] Tom Alvarez: Any support for customer-managed keys, like bring-your-own KMS?
[20:10] Kevin Osei: For hosted, secrets are stored under Redwood-managed KMS keys. For dedicated/private we can discuss customer-managed keys; again, not in scope for beta, but it’s on the enterprise roadmap.
[20:25] Elaine Wu: Okay.

[20:27] Mark Denson: I want to confirm what fields we can use in Splunk for correlation. actor.id, action, resource.id, outcome, source_ip sometimes, and event_id. Correct?
[20:37] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. And category helps a lot for use cases.
[20:41] Mark Denson: Perfect.

[20:44] Priya Shah: Can you give examples of events? Like API key created, role changed, export paused.
[20:50] Kevin Osei: Yep. We’ll send sample JSON events. For example: “rbac.role.updated”, “api_key.created”, “audit_export.destination.updated”, “audit_export.delivery.paused”.
[21:06] Priya Shah: Great.

[21:09] Liam O'Rourke: Anything else on compliance / evidence?
[21:12] Elaine Wu: We’ll need a statement about SOC2 mapping: like this supports logging/monitoring controls, but it’s not a substitute for our own monitoring. Also what you said about customer responsibility for downstream retention.
[21:26] Kevin Osei: Yes, we can provide that phrasing.

[21:30] Priya Shah: One more: Can you guarantee “no loss” within retention? Or do you hedge.
[21:36] Colin O'Donnell: For beta, we don’t offer contractual guarantee. We do engineering target: deliver with at-least-once semantics, retries, and checkpointing. We track exporter lag and delivery success rate internally. For GA, we expect to attach SLOs.
[21:54] Priya Shah: Ok, that’s an important nuance.

[21:57] Mark Denson: If the exporter pauses, do we get notified?
[22:01] Liam O'Rourke: During beta, we’ll monitor and notify via support channel / email. Not automatic webhook yet.
[22:08] Mark Denson: Fine.

[22:10] Tom Alvarez: Splunk HEC endpoints: ours are behind a load balancer, TLS cert from our internal CA. Will that work?
[22:18] Colin O'Donnell: If it’s an internal CA not publicly trusted, our exporter likely won’t trust it. We need publicly trusted cert chain, or we need to discuss dedicated with custom trust store. For hosted beta, it’s public trust only.
[22:34] Tom Alvarez: Good catch. Our dev HEC does have a public cert. Prod might be internal.
[22:40] Priya Shah: We can start with dev.

[22:43] Liam O'Rourke: Great — thanks for flagging early.

[22:47] Elaine Wu: How about support access: can Redwood view our audit events?
[22:52] Kevin Osei: Support can access limited operational logs and metrics. Access to raw audit event payloads is restricted and audited. For troubleshooting, we generally ask customers to provide sample event_id and timestamps rather than us browsing payloads.
[23:08] Priya Shah: Ok.

[23:10] Mark Denson: Are there any known gaps? Like event coverage.
[23:14] Kevin Osei: Coverage is good for admin/security actions: auth, RBAC, key changes, export changes, model deployment config changes. There are always gaps — we’re expanding categories. We also have a process for adding new event types with security review.
[23:30] Mark Denson: Alright.

[23:32] Liam O'Rourke: I think we’ve hit the big topics. I want to do a quick recap and then action items.
[23:38] Liam O'Rourke: Recap: audit schema v2 with stable event_id, categories, actor/action/resource. Export to Splunk HEC is push, TLS-only, at-least-once with retries, duplicates possible, dedupe by event_id. Beta has 7-day backfill window; Redwood retains audit logs 90 days; customer retains in Splunk. RBAC: manage vs view permissions; config changes are audited. Encryption: tokens stored encrypted via KMS-backed secrets store; redaction in logs.
[24:10] Priya Shah: That matches my notes.

[24:13] Liam O'Rourke: Action items: Redwood will send the beta Security FAQ and evidence language, sample events, and Splunk setup guidance. Acme will confirm Splunk endpoint details, egress allowlist needs, and conventions for index/sourcetype.
[24:28] Tom Alvarez: And we’ll confirm the cert situation for prod.
[24:32] Liam O'Rourke: Yes, thank you.

[24:35] Elaine Wu: Can you also include the limitation statement explicitly: no mTLS, no private support.
[24:41] Liam O'Rourke: Yep.

[24:44] Mark Denson: And if you can, include a suggested Splunk search to verify ingestion.
[24:49] Colin O'Donnell: Will do.

[24:52] Liam O'Rourke: Great. We’ll follow up via email. Thanks everyone.
[24:57] Priya Shah: Thanks.
[24:58] Mark Denson: Thank you.
[25:00] Elaine Wu: Thanks.
[25:01] Tom Alvarez: Bye.

(Recording ended early; remaining scheduled time unused.)

- Minimal evidence: system description, control-owner roster, sample log snippets, retention policy, and a short control-matrix mapping (see attached checklist)

Ben Carter

ben.carter@redwood.com | (415) 555-0197

title: Python SDK: streaming requests appear to ignore configured timeouts (hangs indefinitely on slow/stalled stream)
text:
Issue summary:
Customer reports Python SDK streaming calls do not respect configured timeouts. Non-streaming requests time out as expected, but streaming can hang indefinitely when the connection stalls mid-stream (no bytes received) or when the proxy buffers.

Customer impact:
- Production worker processes hang, consuming concurrency slots.
- Customer sees elevated end-to-end latency and occasional request pileups.
- They are hesitant to enable streaming broadly until timeouts are reliable.

Customer context:
- Company: Northwind AI (enterprise)
- Networking: behind corporate egress proxy (TLS intercept) + occasionally slow upstream
- Observed: most frequently when stream starts but then stops emitting chunks for >60s

SDK / environment:
- redwood-sdk-python version: 0.17.2 (per customer)
- Python: 3.11
- HTTP client: httpx (via SDK)
- Deployment: k8s, us-east

Expected behavior:
When user configures a timeout (e.g., 10s overall), streaming generator should raise a timeout exception and abort underlying connection when no data is received within the configured window (or when overall timeout elapses).

Actual behavior:
Streaming generator continues waiting for bytes (appears to block indefinitely) even though `timeout` was passed to the client.

Steps to reproduce (customer repro, adapted):
1) Configure the SDK with a short timeout.
2) Initiate a streaming chat completion.
3) Simulate a stalled stream (customer sees this behind proxy; we reproduced with a local proxy that accepts upstream, sends initial headers + a partial chunk, then stops sending bytes).
4) Observe Python iterator blocks without raising a timeout.

Repro snippet (customer-provided, sanitized):
```python
from redwood import Redwood

client = Redwood(api_key="<redacted>", timeout=10) # seconds

with client.chat.completions.stream(
 model="rw.chat.v1",
 messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a long answer about caching."}],
) as stream:
 for event in stream:
 print(event)
```

What customer sees:
- In certain cases, iteration blocks on `for event in stream:` and never returns.
- No exception is raised.
- Killing the process is the only way to reclaim capacity.

Logs / evidence:
- Customer supplied request IDs where available (they often cannot get request_id when stuck because no terminal event):
 - request_id: rwreq_01HRQJ9Z2W6J6M7KEXAMPLE
- When it does fail, they occasionally see `httpx.ReadTimeout` on non-streaming endpoints, but not on streaming.

Initial hypothesis:
Timeout is being applied to initial connect / request send, but streaming read loop is not enforcing read/overall timeouts consistently. Potentially an httpx streaming iterator path where read timeouts aren’t triggered if the socket is kept open but yields no bytes, or the SDK isn’t passing the timeout config into the streaming context / iter loop.

Requested outcome:
- Confirm whether this is a known issue/regression.
- Provide a workaround (customer needs something they can deploy this week).
- Provide an ETA for a fix release and link to the PR(s) for tracking.

2026-01-17 09:12 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Thanks for the detailed repro. A couple of quick questions so we can reproduce precisely:
1) Can you confirm whether you set `timeout` on the Redwood client vs per-request?
2) Do you see the hang after *any* tokens are streamed, or can it also hang before the first event?
3) If you can share, do you have a proxy vendor/name (Zscaler, Netskope, etc.)?

In the meantime, as a mitigation, can you wrap the streaming loop in your own overall timeout (thread/alarm/async cancellation depending on your setup) so you can abort the worker if it stalls? We’ll look for an SDK-level fix so you don’t need to maintain that long-term.
2026-01-17 10:03 PT — Customer (Northwind AI)
1) We set `timeout=10` on the client (constructor). Not per-request.
2) Mostly after some tokens. It starts streaming, then stalls and never resumes.
3) Zscaler (TLS inspection enabled). We can’t change this.

We already have a crude watchdog that kills the pod if a request exceeds 120s, but that’s disruptive (drops in-flight jobs). We need the SDK to throw a timeout so we can retry or fail gracefully.
2026-01-17 11:28 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Got it. Looping in the Python SDK owner (Sabrina) + SDK parity TL (Ibrahim). We’ve seen a few proxy-related streaming stalls; we’ll confirm whether our configured timeout is enforced during the streaming read.

Next update by EOD Monday with either workaround guidance or an identified fix path.
2026-01-20 09:41 PT — Sabrina James (Python SDK)
Confirmed repro internally using a local “stalling proxy” (accepts connection, sends headers + first SSE event, then stops sending bytes).

Findings (0.17.x):
- The client-level `timeout` is mapped to httpx request timeout for request setup.
- In the streaming path, we were not consistently applying an overall timeout guard around the event iterator.
- With certain proxy/socket behaviors, httpx doesn’t raise `ReadTimeout` in our loop because we’re effectively waiting on the streaming response iterator without a bounded read window in a way that triggers the configured timeout.

Plan:
- Implement the standardized timeout model for Python (connect/read/overall) and enforce overall timeout for streaming iteration.
- Ensure cancellation closes the underlying response and surfaces a typed SDK timeout error that includes `request_id` when available.

Tracking PRs:
- PR-850 (timeout model plumbing)
- PR-854 (streaming disconnect handling + error typing)

Workaround (immediate):
Until the fix ships, wrap the stream consumption in an application-level overall timeout and explicitly close the stream on timeout. If you’re using sync code, you can do this with a watchdog thread that calls `stream.close()` and aborts the request; for async, use `anyio.fail_after` / `asyncio.wait_for` around the stream consumption.

We’ll provide a concrete snippet once we confirm the best pattern with minimal side effects.
2026-01-20 14:12 PT — Ibrahim Khan (SDK parity TL)
Adding: this is in-scope for the cross-language timeout standard. The new default model is:
- connect timeout
- read timeout (max time between bytes/events)
- overall timeout

Streaming will primarily enforce read + overall. We’ll also add a conformance fixture so TS/Go/Python all fail fast on stalled streams the same way (and with consistent error fields).
2026-01-21 08:37 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Customer-facing workaround snippet (sync) proposal — please confirm, Sabrina:

```python
import time
import threading

MAX_SECONDS = 30

with client.chat.completions.stream(...) as stream:
 deadline = time.time() + MAX_SECONDS

 def watchdog():
 while time.time() < deadline and not stream.closed:
 time.sleep(0.25)
 if not stream.closed:
 stream.close()

 t = threading.Thread(target=watchdog, daemon=True)
 t.start()

 for event in stream:
 # handle event
 pass
```

This is not perfect but better than killing the pod.
2026-01-21 10:05 PT — Sabrina James (Python SDK)
Confirmed the snippet is directionally OK. Two notes:
1) Encourage customers to set MAX_SECONDS > their expected generation time, and treat this as “overall timeout”.
2) After `stream.close()`, the iterator should exit; some environments may raise an exception depending on where the underlying socket is. They should catch and treat as timeout.

Fix status:
- PR-850 updated to support an explicit overall timeout wrapper for streaming consumption.
- We’ll surface a `RedwoodTimeoutError` (typed) with fields: `request_id` (if known), `timeout_ms`, and `phase` (connect/read/overall).

ETA:
Targeting python sdk 0.18.0 early next week pending CI + review.
2026-01-27 16:22 PT — Sabrina James (Python SDK)
Fix merged and released in redwood-sdk-python 0.18.0.

Release notes (high level):
- Streaming now enforces overall timeout consistently.
- Read timeout is applied to stalled streams (no bytes) where possible.
- Streaming timeout errors are typed and include request_id when available.

PRs:
- pr-850-timeout-model-connect-read-overall
- pr-854-streaming-disconnect-handling-and-errors

Also added conformance fixtures coverage in pr-857 (includes a stalled-stream test).

Docs:
Migration notes updated to clarify the timeout behavior and config names.
2026-01-28 09:02 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Sent customer upgrade guidance:
- Upgrade to redwood-sdk-python >= 0.18.0
- Set explicit overall timeout (example: `timeout={"overall": 30, "read": 10, "connect": 5}` depending on their config format)
- Log `request_id` from errors/events for Support triage

Asked them to confirm behavior in their Zscaler environment.
2026-02-03 15:18 PT — Customer (Northwind AI)
We upgraded to 0.18.0 and deployed to a subset.

Results:
- Previously hanging streams now terminate with a timeout exception around ~30s as expected.
- We can catch and retry safely in our job runner.

One note: when it stalls after tokens, the exception doesn’t always include request_id (makes sense because it’s mid-stream and we don’t always have it). But this is still a big improvement.

You can close this ticket.
2026-02-04 09:11 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Closing as resolved. Follow-up: we should ensure request_id is emitted in the initial streaming response headers/events consistently to maximize chance of capturing it before a stall (linking to INT-1182 request_id visibility work).

Resolved by shipping redwood-sdk-python v0.18.0 with standardized timeout model and explicit enforcement of overall/read timeouts for streaming consumption. Provided workaround (application-level watchdog + stream.close()) for pre-upgrade mitigation. Customer confirmed fix in production subset and requested closure.

title: Possible credential-spray triggered account lockouts across multiple internal users
text:
Multiple internal accounts experienced high volumes of failed SSO logins followed by several successful logins and eventual account lockouts. Initial detection came from our identity provider (Okta) anomalous sign-on alert rule. This ticket tracks triage, containment, and investigation steps for suspected credential-spray or harvested-credential reuse potentially originating from an external phishing campaign.

2026-03-10 03:42 UTC - Okta anomalous sign-on alert triggered: > 150 failed attempts across 12 unique usernames in 30 minutes
2026-03-10 03:45 UTC - Automated account lockouts applied for 9 accounts per policy
2026-03-10 04:00 UTC - Two accounts showed successful sign-ins from unfamiliar IPs and new device fingerprints
2026-03-10 04:12 UTC - SRE/On-call notified via #security-alerts Slack; session revocation and emergency MFA challenges initiated
2026-03-10 05:08 UTC - Customers: none (internal-only incident). Legal and Security leadership paged; incident declared internal-security-investigation

Okta syslog snippet: event=failed_signon count=18 username=ajenkins ip=45.132.19.8 user_agent=Mozilla/5.0
Okta syslog snippet: event=successful_signon username=mkhan ip=203.0.113.49 device=Windows-Edge-105.0
AWS CloudTrail: ConsoleLogin Failed for 3 attempts from 45.132.19.8 against role/redwood-internal
VPN logs: no correlated access from those IPs within same window
Auth service (internal): refresh_token use from revoked session id=... blocked by revocation check

Geo-IP for attacker IPs show distributed proxies: RU/UA/CDN/Tor exit nodes; multiple IPs clustered to two ASN ranges
User agent strings are generic and change across attempts; no single exploited SSO integration detected
SAML assertions inspected; no forged assertions seen — attacker appears to be using valid credentials rather than SAML replay
Cross-check with phishing reports: #sec-phish channel contains a user-reported suspicious email to several employees received 2026-03-09 21:10 UTC with a credential prompt link
Okta risk score was elevated for the successful sign-ins; MFA prompt was validated but users completed MFA — possible MFA fatigue or coercion, or legitimate MFA prompts following credential reuse
Preliminary hypothesis: large-scale credential stuffing using harvested credentials from external breaches or targeted phishing; not an Okta configuration compromise
No evidence yet of lateral access to production clusters or secrets exfiltration; IAM keys rotation not triggered automatically

Marcus Liu (2026-03-10 04:05 UTC): Initial alert forwarded to Security Ops. Blocking rules in WAF are not expected to help SSO endpoint. Starting session revocation for affected users.
Samira Khan (2026-03-10 04:18 UTC): Forcing password reset and revoking active sessions for 9 locked accounts. Requesting SRE to list recent token grants and check token-cache TTLs for anomalies.
Evan Brooks - SRE (2026-03-10 05:22 UTC): Confirmed no anomalous API spikes in serving-runtime; IAM console attempts limited to service accounts flagged. Will run a quick audit of AWS CloudTrail for cross-account access.
Priya Shah - Legal (2026-03-10 05:45 UTC): No customer data involved per initial review. Keep Legal looped if any evidence of exfiltration or regulatory scope changes.

Containment in progress: affected accounts forced password reset, all active sessions revoked, suspicious IPs blocked at edge where feasible, password policy and MFA prompts reinforced via mandatory reset. Incident remains open pending root cause confirmation and full audit of privileged access.

Complete forensics on CloudTrail and Okta logs for the full 72-hour window
Review phishing email artifacts and obtain hosted page captures for IOC extraction
Deploy additional rate-limiting on SSO endpoints and temporary stricter lockout thresholds
Rotate any service account keys that may have been used during the window and audit IAM role assumption logs
Draft internal notice summarizing recommended user actions (password reset, check device, report suspicious emails)
Schedule post-incident review and update runbooks with lessons learned

title: Allocator bump and soft-OOM simulation report
author: Aria Chen
text:
Summary:

This document describes a reproducible simulation and postmortem of a class of incidents we call "allocator bump" leading to soft-OOM symptoms in mixed tenant GPU nodes. The goal is to provide:
- A concise defect description and root-cause hypothesis.
- A repeatable test harness and config used for simulations.
- Observable signatures (metrics, traces, kernel logs) for fast detection.
- Mitigations, short-term runbook steps, and long-term remediation options.

Background and impact:

We observed intermittent increases in per-request allocator reservation (an "allocator bump") during mixed workloads involving long-context chat and short-shot embed requests. The bump causes cross-tenant eviction churn and transient soft-OOM: allocation failures that do not immediately kill processes but trigger repeated kernel preemption and degraded latency for 3–10 minutes. Impacted customers experienced increased tokenization latency, higher error rates (502/504) on heavy tails, and elevated cost due to repeated KV-cache warmups.

Key symptoms observed in production:
- Sudden rise in node-level "reserved_bytes" (>20% above baseline) without corresponding increase in active sessions.
- Rapid eviction events across shards: eviction_rate increase by 5–15x.
- GPU CUDA OOM-type warnings followed by scheduler preemption events (see kernel logs).
- Traces show repeated cold-kv cache hits and model swap churn.

Root-cause hypothesis (short):

A combination of a kernel-level allocator regression and an uncommon sequence pattern (many concurrent short-lived requests interleaved with a few long-context generations) causes the allocator to allocate larger contiguous blocks for attention state than expected. The allocator fragmentation / rounding policy then prevents efficient compaction, bumping the effective reserved footprint and triggering eviction cascades. Regression window: kernel runtime change v2.14.1 -> v2.15.0.

Repro harness and test plan (exact steps):

Prerequisites:
- Test cluster with 4 heterogeneous GPU nodes (A100x4 and A10x4 mixed pool).
- Load generator: runtime-loadgen v0.9.0 (local binary).
- Model bundles: long-context chat (context 8192, model: redwood-7b-fast-ql) and short embed endpoint (seq_len 32, redwood-embed-small).
- Node config: kvcache_enabled=true, allocator_compaction_threshold=0.65, prefetch=on

1) Baseline run (validate steady state):
 - Start 100 concurrent short requests (qps 200) for 10m.
 - Start background 2 long-context sessions (persistent approach) each producing 2–3 generations per minute.
 - Collect metrics: node/reserved_bytes, eviction_rate, kernel_logs, tracer spans.

2) Stress run (trigger bump):
 - Increase short request concurrency to 600 (qps 1200) maintaining the 2 long-context sessions.
 - Run for 20m.
 - Observe reserved_bytes and eviction spikes.

Commands used (examples):

# start short-run generator
./runtime-loadgen --mode embed --qps 200 --concurrency 100 --model redwood-embed-small --duration 600

# start long-context sessions (simplified)
./runtime-loadgen --mode chat --persist-sessions 2 --model redwood-7b-fast-ql --context 8192 --rate 3/m --duration 1800

Collecting traces and kernel logs:
- Enable kernel debug level 3 on test nodes: sudo sysctl -w runtime.kernel.debug=3
- Start continuous trace sampling for allocation events: tracerctl start --events allocator:alloc,allocator:free,kernel:preempt --out alloc-trace.json

Repro results (observed):
- Baseline: reserved_bytes stable at ~12GB per node; eviction_rate low.
- Stress: reserved_bytes climbed to 18–22GB on A100 nodes over 2–5 minutes; eviction_rate spiked 8x.
- Traces show a recurring pattern: a long-generation allocation grabs a contiguous block, short jobs request many small allocations; allocator rounds small allocations into larger blocks when a fragmentation threshold is hit, then compaction does not free those blocks immediately (compaction gated by idle window), producing the bump.

Detection signatures (for alerting):
- Metric alert: node.reserved_bytes > node.reserved_bytes_p99 * 1.25 for 2m AND node.eviction_rate > 3x baseline.
- Trace signature: repeated allocator:alloc followed by kernel:preempt within 2s for the same process id, >50 occurrences in 5 minutes.
- Log grep pattern: "Allocator: compact skipped (idle_window)" repeated for multiple shard ids.

Short-term mitigations (runbook steps):
1) On detection, immediately increase compaction aggressiveness on affected nodes:
 - sudo runtimectl set allocator.compaction_policy aggressive
2) Temporarily drain new long-context sessions from the node: mark node cordon for long-context routes by updating routing policy:
 - runtime-router update-pool --node node-12 --route-pattern "/generate-long" --weight 0
3) If eviction churn is high, enable conservative admission for short requests: limit concurrency to 300 per node.
4) Collect full alloc-trace and kernel logs, attach to incident ticket.

Long-term remediation options (prioritized):
- P1: Fix kernel allocator rounding (release patch v2.15.1) to avoid rounding small allocations into large contiguous chunks under mixed load.
- P2: Add proactive compaction triggers tied to eviction_rate rather than only idle windows.
- P3: Improve routing heuristics to co-locate long-context and long-lived KV cache sessions on denser nodes and avoid mixing with high-churn short embedding lanes.
- P4: Metric-level SLOs for reserved_bytes and proactive autoscaling triggers for mixed pools.

Design notes and tradeoffs considered:
- Aggressive compaction has CPU/latency cost; we recommend gating it to nodes exhibiting sustained eviction > 3x baseline.
- Preventing allocator rounding will improve fragmentation but requires careful testing across kernels/accelerators (NV and AMD).

Telemetry and dashboards to add:
- New panel: Allocator footprint heatmap (reserved_bytes by shard, 1m resolution).
- Alert: "Allocator bump in mixed pool" with runbook link.
- Trace quicklink to the "allocator-alloc" event stream in the incident view.

Appendix A — Compact reproduction config (YAML):

cluster:
 pools:
 - name: mixed-gpu-pool
 nodes: 4
 types: [A100, A10]
runtime:
 allocator:
 compaction_threshold: 0.65
 rounding_granularity: 256KB
 compaction_policy: conservative
 kvcache: true
loadgen:
 short_embed:
 qps: 1200
 concurrency: 600
 seq_len: 32
 long_chat:
 sessions: 2
 context_len: 8192
 rps_per_session: 0.05

Appendix B — Example kernel log excerpt (sanitized):

[2025-03-12T14:05:03Z] allocator:alloc shard=shard-7 pid=2103 size=24MB rounded=32MB
[2025-03-12T14:05:03Z] allocator:alloc shard=shard-9 pid=4157 size=4KB rounded=256KB
[2025-03-12T14:05:04Z] kernel:preempt victim=pid=4157 reason=eviction
[2025-03-12T14:05:04Z] allocator:compact skipped shard=shard-7 reason=idle_window

Appendix C — Ownership and follow-ups:
- Incident owner: Aria Chen (serving-runtime)
- Kernel patch owner: Mei Tanaka (kernel-and-scheduling)
- Runbook update: SRE (oncall) to add detection signature and immediate compaction command.
- Timeline: aim to ship allocator rounding fix in 2 weeks (v2.15.1) with canary in non-production pools, 1–2 week observability validation window.

Contact and escalation:
For questions or to run the reproduction locally, ping #serving-runtime on Slack and add the tag "allocator-bump". For urgent customer impact, follow the oncall escalation in the oncall roster and attach the alloc-trace.json artifact.

Document history:
- 2024-11-12: created by Aria Chen (initial simulation notes).
- 2024-12-05: added production traces and mitigation commands after incident INC-2024-714.
- 2025-03-18: expanded runbook steps and shipped detection rule draft.

title: Adaptive throttle and SLO first-response runbook (draft)
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Purpose:
This is an on-call friendly, bite-sized runbook for common API failure profiles we keep seeing in production: client-facing timeouts, HTTP 429s (rate limits), degraded streaming responses (partial chunks / stalls), and sudden elevated error rates (5xx). The focus here is first-response actions, short mitigations to restore SLOs, and next-step owners for follow-up.

Scope / assumptions:
- Applies to public Redwood API (edge fleet) and Dedicated routing layer.
- We assume responder has runbook access, PagerDuty, and cluster-read permissions.
- Quick mitigation is preferred over deep debug during high-severity incidents.

High-level incident classification (quick):
- Timeouts: median latency spikes above SLO (p50/p95 crossing) and many client-side socket timeouts.
- 429s: elevated rate-limit responses from gateway or model backend, often correlated with token burst or cascading retries.
- Degraded streaming: partial or zero streaming chunks for >10% of requests, client-side stalls >5s between chunks.
- Elevated error rate: 5xx spike sustained for >5m or error budget burn >50% in 1h.

First-response checklist (0-15 minutes):
1) Acknowledge pager + set Slack channel (#sre-incident) + create short incident thread with title + severity.
2) Capture quick telemetry:
 - Check API gateway dashboards: request rate, 429 rate, backend error rate, p50/p95 latency.
 - Query time-series: graphite/Prometheus panels: api.requests.* api.errors.* api.latency.*.
 - Run these quick commands (kubectl/ops CLI):
 - ops infra tail logs-ingress --filter gateway=api-gateway -n prod 15m
 - ops telemetry query "sum(rate(api_requests_total[5m])) by (route)"
 - Identify if single route/model or broad cross-route.
3) If client-visible SLO is failing, flip to mitigation mode (do shortest effective action).

Mitigation playbook by symptom:
A) Timeouts (end-to-end request timeouts):
- Signs: socket timeout events, p95 latency >> baseline, CPU/GPU not saturated but queuing high.
- Quick actions (ordered):
 1) Check upstream model pool health (ops infra pool-status) and queue depth for KV caches. If a specific model variant is slow, route traffic to a compatible replica/model variant via routing override.\ 2) Increase short-term concurrency limit for affected pool (if autoscaling stuck) and trigger immediate scale-up: ops infra scale pool <pool-id> --scale 2x --ttl 10m.
 3) Enable degrade-mode: reduce max tokens or force shorter generation defaults for public gateway (temporary policy) to drop average latency.
 4) If backend timeouts persist, enable fallback policy to a lower-capacity but stable model (configured in routing policies as fallback: model-small-v2).
- Communications: mention affected routes and ETA for mitigation in Slack.
- Follow-up owners: infra -> investigate autoscaler logs, serving-runtime -> examine kernel stalls.

B) 429s (rate limit rejections):
- Signs: rapid increase in 429 count, often accompanied by client retry storms.
- Quick actions: 
 1) Confirm source of 429: edge rate limiter vs upstream model quota. Dashboards: limiter.hit_rate, limiter.queue_length.
 2) Short-circuit global throttles if safe: temporarily increase global rate limit for tier=prod by +20% using admin-console or ops CLI: ops throttle set global --multiplier 1.2 --reason "incident emergency".
 3) If 429s from a single tenant, isolate that tenant by applying stricter burst limits and add a short-term blocking rule to protect platform.
 4) If client retry patterns detected, engage SE/CS to contact customer (if external) and ask to back off. Post-incident: roll out more sensible retry guidance and jittering in docs.
- Safety: avoid unlimited increases; monitor CPU/GPU and error rates after change.

C) Degraded streaming (stalls / truncated chunks):
- Signs: client logs show long pauses between stream chunks, partial outputs with no final token.
- Quick actions:
 1) Identify if degradation is at proxy (ingress) or model runtime: compare ingress-to-kernel latency correlation panels.
 2) If ingress-side, restart a small subset of proxy pods behind LB (rolling restart of 10%): kubectl rollout restart deploy/api-proxy -n prod --max-unavailable=1.
 3) If runtime-side stalls, disable streaming for affected routes and serve full-response (non-stream) fallback temporarily to preserve correctness. Update headers: X-Serve-Mode: non-stream (config change).
 4) If KV-cache eviction is causing stalls, increase cache size or pin hot keys for a short period (serving-runtime team action).
- Note: streaming fallbacks will increase tail latency; communicate to product/ops.

D) Elevated error rates (5xx spikes):
- Signs: sustained error % above SLO, stack traces show consistent failure class (OOM, assertion, grpc errors).
- Quick actions:
 1) Narrow scope: are errors concentrated to single cluster/region/model? Use telemetry by region/model.
 2) If OOM/eviction-related: reduce batch sizes and force smaller batch windows in serving layer. Example command: ops serving update-config --batch-window-ms 10 --max-batch 8 --selector pool=pool-x.
 3) If widespread and unknown cause: open universal fallback route to 'safe' model (models-fallback) and enable automitigate flag.
 4) If API gateway shows malformed requests causing crashes, enable strict request validation and drop suspect payloads while logging.
- After mitigation, set incident owner for deep postmortem.

Escalation & communications:
- PagerDuty severity mapping (work in progress): Sev3 = partial degradation, Sev2 = customer-visible SLO broken for >10% customers, Sev1 = platform-wide outage.
- Notify product and CS for customer-impacting mitigations. Keep Slack channel updated every 15 minutes until stable.
- Use incident template in Confluence for timeline and decisions.

Short commands cheat-sheet (sane defaults):
- Check rate/latency: ops metrics get api.request_rate --window 5m; ops metrics get api.p95_latency --window 5m
- Restart small set of proxies: kubectl rollout restart deploy/api-proxy -n prod --max-unavailable=1
- Scale pool quickly: ops infra scale pool <pool-id> --scale 2x --ttl 10m
- Enable fallback route: ops routing set-fallback --route /v1/generate --target model:small-stable --ttl 20m
- Update throttle multiplier: ops throttle set global --multiplier 1.2 --reason "incident emergency"

Post-incident (owner actions):
- Owner: create incident ticket with timeline, root-cause hypothesis, and list of mitigations tried.
- Metrics to capture for postmortem: request_rate, error_rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, 429_rate, streaming_chunk_interval distribution, model-kernel queue depth, autoscaler decisions.
- Suggested fixes: refine retry guidance, add circuit-breaker at client-proxy boundary, implement adaptive per-tenant backpressure, improve observability for streaming chunk intervals.

Operational notes / open questions:
- We need a safe default throttle multiplier and a playbook for when increasing global throttle causes backend errors (what to do if error rates rise after increasing throughput?). TODO: formalize thresholds.
- Investigate adding a streaming heartbeat metric (chunk-heartbeat) to detect stalls earlier.
- Confirm whether ops CLI has permission guard for "ops throttle set global" in PROD — add audit log step.

Appendix: quick links and references:
- SLO dashboard: https://telemetry.redwood.example/dashboards/api-slos
- Incident template: https://confluence.redwood.example/display/ENG/Incident+Template
- Retry guidance doc: https://confluence.redwood.example/display/DEV/Retries+and+Backoff

Notes to self (rough):
- Keep this doc short and actionable; move deeper analysis to postmortem.
- Share with serving-runtime and infra leads for validation.
- Once validated, convert key plays into automated runbook actions (playbook runner).

End of draft runbook.

title: Sev-1 Communication Requirements (Status Page + Customer Notifications)
author: Evelyn Hart
text:
h2. Goal
Ensure consistent, timely communication during Sev-1 incidents across Hosted and Dedicated customers. This page defines *what must be communicated*, *who does it*, and *when*.

h2. Scope
Applies when incident severity is Sev-1 (customer-visible outage or severe degradation) or when IC declares 'comms mode'.

h2. Roles and responsibilities
* Incident Commander (IC): owns message accuracy and cadence; delegates drafting if needed.
* Customer Success Escalation Manager (CSEM): owns direct enterprise outreach and coordination for Dedicated customers.
* Support On-call: monitors inbound tickets, ensures macros match the current incident status.
* SRE On-call: provides technical status, mitigation progress, and ETA confidence level.

h2. Required channels
* Status page: public (when impact is broad or uncertain).
* Email: targeted to affected enterprise contacts when impact is Dedicated-only or customer-specific.
* Slack internal: #incidents plus the incident channel created by incident-bot.

h2. Cadence
* Initial acknowledgement: within 10 minutes of Sev-1 declaration.
* Updates: every 30 minutes while customer impact is ongoing.
* Resolution message: within 15 minutes of mitigation being confirmed.
* Post-incident summary: within 1 business day (public-facing is optional; customer-facing for enterprise is required).

h2. Content requirements (status page + email)
Each update must include:
* What customers are seeing (symptoms)
* Affected surfaces (Hosted API regions, Dedicated clusters, specific model families)
* Current mitigation steps
* ETA statement with confidence level (high/medium/low)
* Workarounds (if any)

Avoid:
* Overly specific internal details (hostnames, precise exploit details)
* Blaming language

h2. Dedicated-specific communication
If impact is isolated to one or more Dedicated clusters:
* CSEM must notify impacted customers directly (email + optional call).
* Include: whether a maintenance action is required (e.g., rolling runtime restart), expected duration, and whether customer traffic will fail over.
* If a hotfix rollout is planned, provide the rollout window and the rollback criteria in customer-friendly terms.

h2. Templates (copy/paste)
*Initial status page message*

We are investigating reports of elevated errors and latency affecting Redwood Inference. We will provide updates every 30 minutes until resolved.

*Update message*

We have identified the issue and are applying mitigation steps. Some requests may continue to see errors or increased latency. Next update in 30 minutes.

*Resolution message*

The issue has been mitigated and service is returning to normal. We are continuing to monitor closely.

h2. Related pages
* /policies-and-process/change-management/emergency-change-policy-v3
* /status-page-and-comms/status-page-update-runbook

title: Inter-region bootstrap synchronization, bandwidth-constrained upgrades, and deterministic rollback criteria
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Problem statement: customers operating Private/VPC deployments across multiple regions (or multi-site corporate datacenters) need a predictable, auditable upgrade and bootstrap process that works under constrained cross-site bandwidth and in air-gapped environments. Current upgrade flows assume ample inter-region bandwidth and simple mirroring, which causes long upgrade windows, missed SLAs, and opaque rollback behavior when syncs fail. This ticket defines requirements and acceptance criteria for: 1) deterministic inter-region bootstrap synchronization under bandwidth caps; 2) staged upgrade orchestration that can shed non-critical traffic and prioritize control-plane/critical data; and 3) explicit, deterministic rollback triggers and automated operator playbooks suitable for air-gapped and bandwidth-constrained customers.

AC-1: A documented inter-region bootstrap plan exists that lists required artifacts, priorities (control-plane, runtime images, operator manifests, signature files), and maximum per-site bandwidth ceilings configurable by customer.
AC-2: Upgrade orchestration supports a 'bandwidth-shed' mode that automatically sequences artifact transfer in priority order and enforces a configurable bytes-per-minute cap per peering link without human intervention.
AC-3: Deterministic rollback conditions are defined and implemented: artifact checksum mismatch, KMS key rotation failure, >15% node loss in a single site for >5 minutes, or failed canary health checks for 3 consecutive probe windows trigger an automated rollback or operator alert depending on policy.
AC-4: Air-gapped customer acceptance: the bootstrap plan includes an offline artifact bundle format and validation steps; a dry-run local validation command verifies artifact integrity and operator actions without egress and returns a pass/fail exit code.
AC-5: Upgrade window SLOs: for N-site deployment where inter-site link is <100 Mbps, the orchestration can complete control-plane upgrade within defined time budget (configurable; default 45 minutes) while leaving data-plane serving degraded no more than 10% CPU latency increase for majority of workloads.
AC-6: Telemetry and audit: every artifact transfer, signature verification, and rollback decision is emitted to the customer's audit log and to the Redwood Console (or local collector) with minimal schema that includes timestamps, checksums, bytes transferred, and decision reason.
AC-7: Operator runbook exists with play-by-play steps for manual intervention, and it has been validated in at least two internal QA runs with simulated bandwidth constraints and one air-gapped dry run.
AC-8: Backwards compatibility: existing private deploy customers who do not opt into bandwidth-shed mode see no change in default behavior unless explicit configuration is applied.
AC-9: Automated tests: e2e upgrade test harness includes a throttled-network scenario and an air-gapped file-install path; these tests are green in CI on the release branch.
AC-10: Customer-facing docs and checklist published in Confluence and linked from Console within release notes.

Phase 0 (spec+design): final review with Security and Migrations — 2 weeks
Phase 1 (control-plane only canary): enable bandwidth-shed for control-plane artifacts between two non-production sites with telemetry collection enabled — 1 week
Phase 2 (canary runtime): run staged runtime upgrade with 10% of customer capacity in downgraded bandwidth link and validate rollback triggers — 2 weeks
Phase 3 (pilot customers): onboard 2-3 pilot customers with varying network characteristics (air-gapped, low-bandwidth inter-site, normal) — 3 weeks
Phase 4 (GA): enable feature as opt-in and publish docs, run post-deploy audit for first 24h for pilot customers — 1 week

Step 0: Preflight checks — connectivity matrix, available disk, k8s operator version, KMS key accessibility (or offline key presence).
Step 1: Generate signed artifact bundle with manifest and prioritized object list for targeted sites.
Step 2: Initiate control-plane update on leader site and enable bandwidth-shed limits for peer replication links.
Step 3: Perform canary health checks (liveness, readiness, KV cache warmup) for 15m; if any check fails 3x mark canary failed and trigger rollback.
Step 4: Stage runtime images to remaining sites in priority order (control plane, operator, runtime-critical libs, optional assets).
Step 5: Validate signatures and checksums on arrival; if mismatch, mark artifact invalid and abort staged propagation, notify operator with remediation steps.
Step 6: Promote staged site once health checks pass and aggregate latency/cost metrics are within thresholds.
Step 7: Post-upgrade scrub: validate model-serving correctness with smoke evals and run token-rate performance test for 10m.
Step 8: If rollback decision is made, perform deterministic reverse-order rollback using signed rollback manifests and log every action to audit stream.

Network-throttle e2e: simulate 50 Mbps and 10 Mbps inter-site links; measure completion time and correctness of artifact application.
Air-gap dry-run: produce offline artifact bundle, transfer via simulated physical media, perform local validation without egress.
Chaos: induce node drain and simultaneous artifact mismatch to validate rollback policy and observability.
Performance-safety: measure tail latency for inference while upgrade runs in bandwidth-shed mode; must remain within 10% of baseline 95th percentile latency.
Audit validation: check that every upgrade step produces audit events with required fields and that events can be ingested by customer SIEM.

artifact.transfer.bytes
artifact.transfer.duration_ms
artifact.verify.status
site.node.failure_rate
canary.health_pass_rate
upgrade.rollback.invocations
site.p95_inference_latency
inter_region.link_utilization

Trade-off: aggressive parallel replication reduces total upgrade time but increases risk of cascading failures if checksums diverge; bandwidth-shed mode chooses safety by default.
Open question: should rollback be automatic for checksum mismatch in air-gapped sites where operator cannot fetch replacement artifact? Proposal: abort and require operator manual approval for irreversible actions.
Operational consideration: include a 'simulated' dry-run option in Console that shows transfer plan and estimated time under current caps without performing writes.
UX: provide clear customer-facing UI to set per-link caps and artifact priorities; defaults should be conservative for non-expert operators.

title: Burst Fabric Simulation Lab Operator & IaC Conformance
author: Maya Patel
text:
Summary

This doc describes the design and operational runbook for the GPU Burst Fabric Simulation Lab (BurstLab) operator and the accompanying Terraform/IaC conformance checklist. BurstLab is a self-service sandbox for validating multi-region/burst workloads, preemption-fallback logic, and IaC safety gates before changes are promoted to production GPU pools. The goal is to reduce rollout risk for autoscalers, burst-orchestrators, and tenant-facing network egress policies.

Key outcomes
- Automated simulation of burst scenarios (sudden large allocations, spot preemption waves, egress saturation).
- IaC conformance checks that validate topology, routing, and egress-burst constraints.
- CI gating: safe promotion only when simulations and telemetry assertions pass.
- Clear incident playbook for common failure modes discovered by lab runs.

Scope and boundaries
- Scope: GPU allocation, warm-pool handoff, egress routing under burst, cross-region replica fallbacks, and Terraform module compatibility.
- Out of scope: customer-facing billing reconciliation (handled elsewhere), model-level token accounting instrumentation.

Owners and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-infra: capacity-team (oncall: @capacity-oncall)
- Secondary owner: eng-infra: cloud-networking
- CI/CD owner: eng-infra: ci-team
- Emergency contact: Pager duty for infra SRE (page policy: Severity 1)

Architecture overview (text diagram)

BurstLab operator sits in a staging AWS/GCP account and orchestrates ephemeral multi-region test clusters. Text diagram:

[BurstLab controller] -> creates -> [test GPU pool A (us-west1)] -> attaches -> [burst-orchestrator]
 \-> creates -> [test GPU pool B (europe-west1)] -> attaches -> [warm-pool replicator]

A traffic generator submits synthetic inference traffic via a tenant-proxy that exercises: batching, KV cache hit/miss patterns, long-tail sequence lengths. The operator can inject failures: simulated spot preemption, egress NAT exhaustion, and TC/iptables route blackhole.

Prerequisites
- Burstable staging accounts with isolated VPCs and ephemeral IAM roles (see Terraform module: burstlab/account-module).
- Access to test image registry: gcr/redwood-infra-burstlab and a signed image promotion flow.

Terraform/IaC conformance checklist (table-style bullets)
- Module version pinning: terraform >= 1.4, modules pinned to a release tag.
- Network CIDR safety: test-subnets must be /22 or larger and annotated with purpose=burstlab.
- Egress guardrail: nat-gateway count >= expected-burst-egress/64MBps.
- IAM least privilege: ephemeral role sasl/burstlab-runner limited to create:test-* prefixed resources.
- KMS & secrets: all test artifacts must use customer-managed test KMS key with key policy: allow principals from burstlab account.
- CI token scoping: GHA runner tokens expire in < 1h and are restricted to project:test only.

Terraform snippet (example)

```hcl
module "burstlab_account" {
 source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-infra/terraform-modules.git//burstlab-account?ref=v0.12.0"

 account_name = "burstlab-staging-usw1"
 region = "us-west1"
 vpc_cidr = "10.40.0.0/16"
 tags = {
 purpose = "burstlab"
 }
}
```

CI/CD gating and pipeline example (GitHub Actions snippet)

- Pipeline phases: plan -> apply-test -> simulate -> assert -> destroy
- Gate rule: PR cannot be merged unless simulation assertions pass in the last successful workflow run.

GHA snippet:

```yaml
name: BurstLab Conformance
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
 plan:
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest
 steps:
 - uses: actions/checkout@v4
 - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
 - run: terraform init
 - run: terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan

 apply-test:
 needs: plan
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest
 steps:
 - run: terraform apply -auto-approve plan.tfplan
 - run: ./scripts/launch-burstlab.sh --profile ${{ secrets.BURSTLAB_ROLE }}

 simulate:
 needs: apply-test
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest
 timeout-minutes: 120
 steps:
 - run: ./scripts/run-burst-scenarios.sh --scenarios all

 assert:
 needs: simulate
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest
 steps:
 - run: ./scripts/check-telemetry-assertions.sh --ci

 destroy:
 if: always()
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest
 steps:
 - run: terraform destroy -auto-approve
```

Simulation scenarios (examples)
1) Rapid tenant spike: 10k concurrent small inference requests over 30s to test autoscaler reaction and KV cache miss storm.
2) Spot wave: terminate 40% of nodes in us-west1 in a coordinated window to validate warm-pool seeding and cross-region fallback.
3) Egress saturation: flood NAT gateway to exceed allocated throughput to test egress-sharding logic and tenant backpressure.
4) Kernel update ripple: deploy quantized kernel change and assert latency regression < 5% p95.

Telemetry assertions (pass/fail criteria)
- Allocation success rate: >= 99.5% across the 5m window post-spike.
- Eviction cascade depth: <= 2 (no more than 2 handoff hops).
- Tenant request p95 latency regression: < 10% vs baseline.
- Token billing hook verified: synthetic tokens recorded in staging billing sink.

SLOs used by this lab (for gating)
- Simulation pass rate required: 100% of defined assertions for critical PRs.
- Allowed transient flakiness: no more than 1 non-critical assertion failure per week for the ci:burstlab job.

Runbook: failure modes & remediation

Mode A: Plan/apply fails due to module pin mismatch
- Symptom: terraform plan errors with provider version mismatch.
- Triage steps:
 1. Check workflow logs for exact provider requirement.
 2. Confirm tfenv/terraform setup in GHA matches pipeline version.
 3. If module requires provider bump, open a follow-up PR to update module references and add a changelog entry.

Mode B: Allocation success < SLO after spike
- Symptom: allocation success 93% in 5m window.
- Immediate steps:
 1. Page capacity-oncall.
 2. Run `./scripts/collect-cluster-state.sh --since 10m` and attach to the page.
 3. Check warm-pool sizes: `kubectl -n burstlab get hpa,warmpool` and confirm desired replicas.
 4. If warm-pool not seeding, manually increase warm-pool to target and re-run scenario.

Mode C: Egress NAT saturation causing cross-account fallout
- Symptom: persistent SNAT exhaustion, TCP resets for external storage replication.
- Immediate steps:
 1. Switch burstlab test VPC to backup egress (egress-fabric-fallback) via console toggle.
 2. Throttle synthetic traffic generator: `kill -SIGTERM $(cat /tmp/burstlab-gen.pid)` and backoff.
 3. Patch Terraform nat-gateway count and reapply with a canary target.

Investigation checklist
- Gather: terraform state, kube events, node-level dmesg, cloud provider event feed (preemptions), and NAT gateway metrics.
- Telemetry queries: preemption_count_by_zone, kv_cache_miss_rate, nat_snat_errors, allocation_failure_reasons.

Safety & cost controls
- Each run is limited by default budget tags and an automatic destroy step. Runs exceeding $2000 estimated cost abort and notify finance.
- Test accounts are flagged so billing export streams are separated from prod.

Promote-to-prod criteria
1. Module and network changes must pass BurstLab simulation with zero critical assertions failing in 3 consecutive runs.
2. A performance benchmark (p95 latency delta) must be within the accepted regression window (< 5% for non-quant kernel changes; < 10% for large kernel experiments).
3. Runbook steps documented and reviewed by at least two reviewers.

Operational play: how to run a manual ad-hoc simulation
1. Checkout repo: `git clone git@github.com:redwood-infra/burstlab-operator.git`
2. Create ephemeral workspace: `make workspace && export TF_WORKSPACE=pr-<id>`
3. Apply with test role: `terraform apply -var-file=tests/pr-<id>.tfvars -auto-approve`
4. Launch scenario: `./scripts/launch-scenario.sh spike --concurrency 10000 --duration 30s`
5. Record run id and attach logs to PR.

Postmortem requirements for failed gates
- If a PR fails the gate, author must: attach failing run id, telemetry dashboards, and a short failure summary in PR description.
- If failure causes production impact, open a full incident with Sev classification and link to burstlab run ids that reproduce the issue.

Appendix: diagnostic commands
- Collect node telemetry: `for n in $(kubectl get nodes -o name); do kubectl logs -n kube-system $n || true; done`
- Check NAT metrics (GCP example): `gcloud compute routers get-status <router> --region=us-west1`
- Retrieve preemption feed: `aws ec2 describe-spot-instance-requests --filters Name=state,Values=active,closed`

References
- See Terraform module catalog: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/module-stability-testing-and-rollback-catalog.json
- Burst orchestrator design notes: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-burst-fairshare-lattice-allocator-playbook.json

Notes and future work

title: Introduce invocation affinity matrix and proactive alert resolver
author: Maya Chen
text:
Motivation: We observe recurring noisy SLO alerts created by correlated bursts that cross tenant thresholds without reflecting distinct root causes. Current per-invocation alerts fire independently and cause paging fatigue. This PR adds a first-class invocation affinity metric and a proactive alert resolver that groups related invocations into cohorts and suppresses/attenuates alerts when an upstream affinity signal indicates a single shared cause.

What this PR does: Adds a streaming affinity index computed at aggregation time (invocation_affinity{route, model, tenant, window}) derived from co-occurrence of invocation fingerprints, kernel contention signals, and token-phase overlap. Adds a Grafana panel to visualize the affinity matrix and an alert resolver that consumes the affinity index to decide alert coalescing and attenuation thresholds. The resolver is opt-in and governed by per-route policies (console + config).

Design notes: The affinity index is an approximate, bounded sketch (count-min + LRU eviction) to limit cardinality. Affinity score = weighted sum( fingerprint_cooccurrence, kernel_backpressure_correlation, kv_cache_overlap, token_phase_alignment ). We expose both raw and normalized scores to aid dashboarding and tuning. The proactive resolver applies a configurable hysteresis window and supports three actions: suppress, attenuate (raise threshold), and group (single alert with multi-invocation details).

Telemetry/metrics added: - invocation_affinity_score (histogram) - invocation_affinity_cohort_size (gauge) - resolver_action_count (counter) - resolver_decision_latency_ms (summary) - cohort_correlation_errors (counter)

Dashboards: New panel under Observability / Invocation cohorts: affinity matrix heatmap, cohort size timeseries, resolver action rate sparkline, example invocation bundle drilldown. Panel includes quick-links to related traces and log samples with pre-populated filters.

Alerting: Introduces an experimental alert rule template that leverages the resolver to reduce duplicate alerts across highly-affined invocations. Default behavior is off; rollout is gated behind a feature flag and gradual per-tenant opt-in.

Rollout and safety: - Feature gated by feature_flag:observability.invocation_affinity - Default config: resolver off for free-tier tenants; gradual enable for enterprise tenants with 2-week canary. - Fallback: resolver is stateless; if it fails, rules fall back to existing per-invocation alerts. All resolver decisions are logged to an audit metric for post-rollout analysis.

Testing: Unit tests for affinity sketch behavior, e2e tests that simulate correlated bursts, integration tests for dashboard links. Added a synthetic replay job that replays historical bursts to validate resolver attenuation without impacting production.

Performance: The affinity sketch uses sharded in-memory buckets with a soft size cap; measured median extra CPU per serving shard ~0.8%, 95p ~3.1% under heavy burst workloads. Token latency overhead measured <0.5ms tail in internal bench runs.

Security and privacy: Affinity calculations are performed on hashed invocation fingerprints; no raw prompt content is persisted. Access to cohort drilldown requires the existing tracing/dashboard RBAC scope.

Migration: No DB migrations. Config schema adds optional resolver policies in existing observability config.

Next steps: - Monitor resolver_action_count and cohort_correlation_errors for the first canary tenants - Iterate on dashboard UX based on SE feedback - Add an operator CLI to bulk-opt-in tenants once safe.

Introduces an invocation affinity matrix metric, a visualization panel for cohort affinity, and an opt-in proactive alert resolver to reduce noisy SLO alerts by correlating related invocations before alerting. No public API breaking changes.

Liam: Requested clarifications on eviction policy and choice of sketch; suggested a unit test for collision behavior.
Author (Maya): Added design notes and unit tests for collision cases; reduced default sketch size to limit memory.
Priya: Asked for more conservative default resolver behavior for free-tier tenants; requested dashboard drilldown link to redact PII.
Author: Updated rollout section and added hashed-first filter to drilldown links.
Ethan: Perf concerns — asked for benchmark artifacts.
Author: Attached bench run CSV and added note in PR about measured CPU and tail latency impact.
Approval: Liam and Priya approved after changes; Ethan approved after perf data update.

1) add affinity sketch + ingestion path; 2) add resolver engine and config; 3) grafana dashboard + dashboard links; 4) tests and synthetic replay; 5) docs + console hooks
