alex_sales: Quick question — Acme's renewal is due in 30 days. CS wants to propose a blended retainer + usage commit instead of the standard uplift. Can pricing weigh in on whether we can offer a smaller annual retainer + variable usage discount, and what that does to ARR math? Also, can Deal Desk accept POC credits as part of the package to cover their in-flight evaluation?

lexi_pricing: Short answer: yes, we can structure a retainer+usage blend. Typical constructs: 1) Base retainer (covers some steady-state calls) + overage at discounted rate, or 2) Minimum committed tokens/month with roll-up credit. Need to know expected monthly usage distribution to quantify.

alex_sales: They reported avg 120M tokens/month in last 6 months, spike pattern M-F. POC currently using ~15M tokens and will finish in 3 weeks. They want POC credits to be applied to first-quarter usage.

jamal_se: From SE side — POC still blocked on one security Q: key rotation + BYOK. Sara, can we sign off to let POC continue under a limited scope while legal finalizes the addendum? Customer also asked for guaranteed 1000 RPS during peak testing window.

sara_security: We need the security questionnaire answers back from them (question #22 on KMS usage). We can provision a temporary sandbox with Redwood-managed keys to unblock the POC, but BYOK requires a separate MSA addendum and KMS attestation. If CS wants to run POC with our keys, we should capture it in an Acknowledgement email.

maria_csm: Customer is sensitive to long-term lock-in. They prefer a 12-month term but with quarterly usage reconciliation and an opt-out at month 9 with a small termination fee. Also asked about price protection if model prices drop.

lexi_pricing: Pricing options I see: A) 12mo retainer $X/month (covers 40% baseline) + usage at 70% of list; B) Commit-based: annual commit = 1.1x current run-rate with 10% uplift discount; C) Hybrid: refundable retainer credited into first two quarters, then usage rate steps down. For POC credits: Deal Desk usually accepts a capped credit applied to Q1 invoice if it's less than 5% of ARR and documented in SOW.

deal-desk-bot: New deal desk request created: DD-7421. Please attach proposed SOW, POC credit amount, and approval justification.

alex_sales: Thanks — Lexi can you sketch the numbers for option C (refundable retainer credited Q1+Q2) and how that maps to ARR and committed throughput? I want to present a clean option to the customer. Also need a short blurb we can show legal for the BYOK timeline.

lexi_pricing: I'll drop a simple example: assume current annualized run-rate = $1.8M. Option C: refundable retainer = $120k (credited $60k Q1, $60k Q2). Annual usage commit = $1.5M at 15% discount vs list. Net effective ARR year1 = $1.5M + ($120k - $120k credited) = $1.5M. Effectively reduces upfront cash risk for customer; helps us lock a commit. I'll add the math and a one-liner for legal re: BYOK timeline ("POC can run on Redwood-managed keys; BYOK onboarding targeted within 45 days post-signature; full BYOK in MSA addendum").

jamal_se: For the RPS request, we can offer a tested performance window: 1 hour load test at 1000 RPS on dedicated pool for the POC. Need to schedule and book capacity with eng-infra — will require a ticket.

maria_csm: I'll confirm with the customer they accept refundable retainer credited over Q1+Q2 and the opt-out clause. Also will push for signing the limited sandbox Acknowledgement so POC can continue.

alex_sales: Great. Next steps: Lexi to upload a one-page pricing summary + line items into DD-7421, Maria to secure sandbox acknowledgement email, Jamal to open infra ticket for the 1-hour load window, Sara to prepare the BYOK / temporary-keys blurb for legal. I'll loop in Sales Ops if we hit non-standard termination fees. :thumbsup:

title: Orchestrate clearance lanes for PRD handshakes across Eng/Design/Legal
author: Maya Patel
text:
Coordinate a lightweight, auditable sign-off flow for PRDs that have conditional rollout or scope-change risk. This ticket defines the clearance lanes (engineering impact, design acceptability, legal/regulatory sign-off), required artifacts, timeline for responses, and fallback triggers for the first 3 pilot PRDs (Private VPC upgrade, Dedicated autoscale policy change, Structured output typed responses). Goal: reduce review cycles and avoid late scope rework by establishing clear owners, SLAs, and acceptance criteria.

A single PRD review checklist template exists and is linked in the PRD; fields include: security considerations, infra impacts, UI changes, migration plan, rollout gating conditions, and test prompts
Each pilot PRD has named reviewers from Eng, Design, and Legal with explicit SLA to respond in 5 business days or mark a blocking issue
A documented fallback/rollback condition for launch (e.g., disable feature flag, pin model version, revert routing policy) is agreed and included in PRD
Sign-off events are recorded in the PRD with timestamp and reviewer comment; at least one PRD has completed full cross-team sign-off in pilot
Metrics dashboard (link in PRD) is created/updated to show latency, error rate, and cost delta for the feature following rollout

title: eng-ml
text:
Priya Rao: Heads-up — our eval runner is flaky on the quantized-v2 onboarding suite. CI reported a 0.04 drop in BLEU on one run, then back to baseline on rerun. stack: `evals/runner.py::run_all`
Mike Chen: Ugh. Did the job show differing lengths or just metric jitter?
Priya Rao: Metric jitter mostly. Same prompts, same seeds (we thought). Logs show `seed=42` passed but outputs diff across runs.
Alyssa Gomez: Common culprits: sampling params (temp/top_p), nondeterministic CUDA kernels, or RNG not propagated to all libs. Are we doing do_sample=True anywhere?
Jordan Li: We default to sampling with `temperature=0.8, top_p=0.9` for some evals. That will be nondet even with same seed if decode uses sampling across threads.
Priya Rao: The eval config for quantize tests uses the canonical config from onboarding.yaml — it sets `do_sample: true`. The weird bit is we see differences even when we change to `do_sample: false` for some runs.
Mike Chen: If `do_sample=false` but we still see nondet, then it's likely from floating point / kernel order or dropout/amp. Which runtime? cudnn, torch 2.x?
Priya Rao: Runner is on a K80 prod node for CI debug and on A100 infra for nightly. Torch 2.1 in both. Quantized model uses int8 kernels on A100 (faster) and fallback ops on K80.
Alyssa Gomez: A100 int8 kernels sometimes reorder operations; also make sure `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` and `torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True` are set during eval setup. But note that quantized kernels may not be covered by those flags.
Jordan Li: Another angle — are we resetting RNGs per example? We seed at process start, but token sampling can be parallel across batch dim so RNG streams differ per batch ordering. I usually do `generator = torch.Generator(device).manual_seed(seed + shard_id)` and pass explicit generator to sampling operations.
Priya Rao: Good point. Our runner calls `model.generate(...)` without explicit `generator=`.
Mike Chen: Patch suggestion: always pass an explicit generator built from root seed + example index. Also add a small harness for reproducibility: run the same eval N times (N=5) and compute median metric and std. Fail CI if std > threshold.
Alyssa Gomez: Agreed. Also: add a deterministic decode mode for evaluations where we want bit-for-bit repeatability. It would enforce `do_sample=False`, `temperature=0`, `top_k=1`, and `generator` usage. Name it `deterministic=True` in eval config.
Priya Rao: I can add `deterministic` flag to eval schema. What about GPU-level nondet from quant kernels?
Jordan Li: For that, record a golden artifact (reference outputs) from a chosen baseline environment (A100 with Intel RT kernels) and treat other runs as comparators. We can compute a stable similarity metric (e.g., chrF/BLEU diff tolerance) and allow small differences due to quantization. For CI gating of regressions, gate on median across 3 seeds run on the same hardware.
Mike Chen: For CI wiring: 1) run per-commit quick eval in cheap env with deterministic mode, 2) nightly multi-seed non-deterministic checks on target infra (A100) comparing to golden baseline, 3) on-failure, auto-run debug job with expanded logging.
Priya Rao: What expanded logging do we need? I propose: seed, generator states (torch.get_rng_state hex), torch.cuda.get_rng_state_all for GPUs, model version, quantization config, and full decode tokens.
Alyssa Gomez: Yes. Also log sampling params: temperature, top_p, top_k, do_sample, and beam params. And artifacts: outputs.jsonl per run.
Jordan Li: Small pragmatic items: 1) Add `--repeat N` CLI to runner that runs the same eval N times and writes `outputs_run_{i}.jsonl`. 2) Add a simple `compare_runs.py` that computes metric mean/std and hashes outputs.
Priya Rao: I'll open a PR with the deterministic flag + generator plumbing and a CI job change to run `--repeat 3` for onboarding suites.
Mike Chen: Can you also include an integration test that runs the same prompt through quantized model and FP model on the same seed and asserts that difference is within expected envelope? Store envelopes per-model in a small `golden_metrics` json.
Alyssa Gomez: We should also include a note in the onboarding checklist: "Run quantized bring-up with 3 seeds, record median metric, add noise tolerance label if quantization expected to shift baseline."
infra-bot: @Priya Rao created debug job `evals/repro-debug/1751234567` on ci-redwood (queued).
evals-ci: CI note: running `evals/onboarding --suite quantized-v2 --repeat 3 --deterministic false` on a100-1. Artifacts will be stored under s3://redwood-evals/tmp/1751234567/
Priya Rao: I'll monitor the job and attach outputs. If we still see nondet under deterministic mode, we'll escalate to runtime/eng-runtime for kernel-level investigation.
Mike Chen: Thanks — this should reduce random flakes and make regression alerts actionable. :thumbsup:

title: Skeletal SDK handshake & tool telemetry PRD (draft)
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Purpose:
This doc collects a lightweight/low-friction PRD sketch for a minimal (skeletal) SDK handshake and tool-proxy lifecycle, with a focus on streaming ergonomics, structured-output fallbacks, and compact telemetry that helps us reason about latency vs. cost tradeoffs in-hosted.

Context and problem statement:
- Teams want fast/low-footprint host integrations (mobile, edge). Full-featured SDKs are heavy and create tight coupling: large state, complex session persistence, and lots of telemetry noise.
- Hosted API streaming + tool-calls surface is growing complex: partial responses, tool-lease semantics, resumable sessions, and client-side prefetching. We need a small baseline API shape that SDKs and third-party clients can adopt without heavy dependency.
- Current drafts in product bin are rich and prescriptive. This doc is intentionally minimal: define the absolute minimum handshake surface, a compact telemetry schema, and a small set of progressive (staged) behaviors for clients to opt into.

Goals (MVP):
1) Define a skeletal handshake that supports: resumable session token, optional compact prefetch hint, tool-proxy lease id.
2) Define a small telemetry payload (<= 12 fields) that is stable across SDKs and cheap to emit (sampled at 1% by default).
3) Provide explicit structured-output fallback guidelines when partial/invalid JSON arrives mid-stream.
4) SDK ergonomics: tiny runtime footprint, single-file import, explicit opt-in advanced features (prefetch, full session persistence).

Non-goals:
- Full-blown streaming grammar or complex client-side snapshotting.
- Heavy SDK features (local tool execution shims, full offline-first).

High-level API sketches (sketchy, for discussion):
- POST /v1/streams (start) -> 201, returns {session_token, resume_cursor, tool_lease_ids[]}
- PATCH /v1/streams/{session_token}?resume_cursor={cursor} (resume) -> resumes partial output
- POST /v1/tool-proxy/lease -> returns {lease_id, ttl_seconds, budget_units} (leases are lightweight, renewed or auto-expire)

Handshake payload (client -> hosted):
{
 "client_id": "sdk_x.y.z",
 "resume_token": "opt-string",
 "prefetch_hint": "small|medium|none",
 "fidelity_hint": "skeleton|concise|full"
}
Notes: fidelity_hint is a concise annotation clients can send to indicate acceptable verbosity/structured depth. Not a strict contract, but a routing preference for the serving layer.

Tool-proxy lifecycle (intent):
- Tool proxies are ephemeral objects hosted by Redwood to isolate third-party tool invocations.
- Leases control parallelism and billing isolation: basic lease includes TTL, budget_units (count), and light provenance tag.
- SDKs should hold at most one active lease per host-session to keep footprint small.

Structured-output fallback rules (consumer-facing guidance):
1) If stream emits well-formed JSON chunk -> accept.
2) If we see a truncated/invalid JSON at close or interruption, attempt a single automatic recovery: append closing tokens based on expected schema (e.g., close bracket) and validate.
3) If recovery fails, deliver partial JSON plus a small metadata envelope: {"_partial": true, "_approx_schema": "choices[0].message.content"}.
4) SDK should expose a simple helper: parse_partial_stream(payload_stream) -> (items[], warnings[]).

Telemetry (compact schema):
- token_count (int)
- first_byte_ms (int) latency to first token
- end_to_end_ms (int)
- tool_proxy_hits (int) number of tool calls during session
- tool_proxy_latency_ms (int) aggregated
- prefetch_bytes (int) bytes served from prefetch cache
- batch_size_hint (string) e.g. small/medium/large
- fidelity_hint_used (string) echoed from client
- resume_used (bool)
- error_code (string|null) if terminal error
- sample_rate (float) the sampling fraction for this payload
- sdk_id (string) lightweight id (no PII)

Emission policy: sample 1% by default (configurable at account tier). Use structured logs/JSON for ingestion. Keep payloads under 1KB.

SDK ergonomics proposals (skeletal):
- Single file, ~5–10KB minified runtime. Expose two entry points: startStream(opts) and resumeStream(opts).
- Minimal memory: no persistent disk rows unless user opts-in.
- Event-first model: on('partial'), on('toolcall'), on('complete'), on('fallback') — simple callbacks rather than complex state machines.
- Helper utilities: parse_partial_stream, renew_tool_lease(lease_id), compact_telemetry().
- Defaults: backoff jitter, 2 retries for tool-lease acquisition, 0.1s heartbeat when idle (opt-out).

Security / compliance notes:
- Tool-lease creation should require tenant-scoped authorization and must be auditable.
- Prefetch hints must not cause prefetch of PII-enabled inputs; enforce server-side guardrails.
- Resume tokens are short-lived JWT-like signed tokens; minimal claims to avoid leakage of user content.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Fidelity hint semantics: advisory vs enforced? (Recommend advisory; enforcement requires server-side rewrite rules and increases complexity.)
- Lease billing model: units vs time? (Units preferred for predictable cost across short-lived bursts.)
- How aggressive should automatic JSON repair be? (Start conservative: single close-token attempt; more aggressive repair requires evals.)

- Consider an opt-in developer flag to snapshot entire session to object-store for debugging (off by default).
- Edge case: clients that hold many parallel sessions (mobile pushing many small requests). Limit: default max 4 leases per SDK install.

title: Tenant FinOps Cutover & Governance Playbook
author: Maya Lopez
text:
Summary

This playbook defines the operational and governance steps Customer Success, SRE, and FinOps must follow when performing a tenant-level cutover that changes billing or capacity controls (examples: moving a customer from trial to committed Dedicated, enabling quota-protector webhooks, or toggling per-tenant burst limits). The goal is to ensure cost predictability, tenant safety, and clear rollback paths while minimizing customer-visible disruption.

Scope and When to Use this Playbook

- Applies to any tenant cutover that will alter: billing plan, reserved capacity assignment, per-tenant rate/quotas, or cost-protecting automations.
- Not for routine model version upgrades or small config tweaks that are covered by our standard canary rollout playbooks.

Definitions

- Cutover: The event during which a tenant transitions from one financial/operational state to another (e.g., trial -> paid committed, hosted -> dedicated, or quota cap changes).
- FinOps Gate: A pre-approved financial control threshold that requires Finance + CS sign-off before enabling.
- Safety Net: Automated quota/fallback rules that prevent unbounded spend or dangerous latency regressions.

Stakeholders and Responsibilities

- Customer Success (CS): primary contact for customer comms, scheduling, and acceptance.
- FinOps: validate contract terms, commit levels, and billing triggers; approve FinOps Gates.
- Eng SRE / Platform: implement routing changes, capacity reservations, and alerting.
- Oncall (runtime): 72-hour monitoring and first-responder for incidents.
- Account Executive (AE): commercial ownership, billing follow-up.

Prerequisites (pre-cutover checklist)

1) Contract & Billing
 - Verified signed MSA and SOW in Salesforce with committed throughput and billing start date.
 - Billing metadata (billing_contact_email, billing_entity_id, billing_region) present in tenant metadata.
 - FinOps has generated the pro-forma invoice and validated charge schedule.

2) Technical Readiness
 - Tenant tags: "tier=dedicated|hosted", "finops_commit_id=<id>", and "slo_profile=<profile>" set in tenant record.
 - Capacity reserved: GPU pool assignment and reservation confirmed in capacity inventory.
 - Quotas: quota config (requests/min, tokens/day, embedding-ops/day) created in quota service. Example JSON stored in deployment ticket.

3) Observability and Alerts
 - Dashboards prepared: Tenant Overview, Cost Burn Rate, Token Distribution by Route, Cache Hit Rate, p99 Latency.
 - Alerts provisioned (see Alert matrix section).
 - Billing report configured to deliver daily usage CSV to FinOps and CS (S3 or internal bucket).

4) Communication
 - Cutover schedule agreed with customer and internal teams (UTC timezone).
 - Customer-facing FAQ and rollback expectations drafted.

Cutover Phases

Phase A — Pre-cutover (T-minus 72 to 2 hours)
1. Confirm tickets and approvals: ticket in triage board links to contract and capacity reservation.
2. Run validation script locally or via CI to verify tenant config:

 $ ./tools/validate-tenant-config --tenant-id T-12345 --assert-quotas --assert-tags

 Expected output: PASS for quotas, tags, billing metadata.

3. Snapshot current state: export tenant routing, quota, and billing metadata to the ticket.

4. Create safety net override set: temporary conservative quotas one tier below target for first 24 hours unless FinOps approves full limits.

Phase B — Cutover execution (T0)
1. Put a short maintenance marker on the tenant dashboard (visible to customer): "Planned change in progress — effective <time>".
2. Apply billing plan change via Billing API (example):

 curl -X POST https://billing.internal.redwood/v1/tenants/T-12345/plan
 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"
 -H "Content-Type: application/json"
 -d '{"plan":"dedicated-committed-v2","commit_units":1000000,"effective_date":"2026-02-01"}'

3. Assign capacity and update routing tags via Platform API:

 curl -X PATCH https://platform.internal.redwood/v1/tenants/T-12345/config
 -H "Authorization: Bearer $PLATFORM_TOKEN"
 -H "Content-Type: application/json"
 -d '{"tags":{"tier":"dedicated","gpu_pool":"pool-west-3"}}'

4. Apply quota and safety-net policies: post the final quota JSON to Quota Service. Example snippet: 

 {
 "tenant_id": "T-12345",
 "quotas": {
 "requests_per_minute": 1200,
 "tokens_per_day": 2000000,
 "embedding_ops_per_day": 50000
 },
 "safety_net_mode": "soft-guard",
 "soft_guard_thresholds": {"spend_usd":1000, "tokens":500000}
 }

5. Confirm route propagation and capacity allocation in the platform. Watch for immediate alert triggers.

Phase C — Immediate validation (T0 + 0–2 hours)
1. Smoke tests from multiple regions: generation, streaming, embeddings. Use the customer test harness or synthetic runner.
2. Compare baseline metrics (pre-snapshot) to current within tolerance: token rate ±30%, p99 latency <= baseline*1.5, cache hit rate not falling >10%.
3. If safety-net thresholds hit, implement automatic throttle sequence: reduce requests_per_minute by 50% and notify CS & FinOps.

Phase D — Stabilization (T0 + 2–72 hours)
1. 24h: FinOps reconciles daily usage CSV and confirms expected burn rate.
2. 48h: CS calls customer for acceptance check and to confirm no functional regressions.
3. 72h: If metrics stable and FinOps approves, remove safety-net overrides and promote quotas to final values. Otherwise, escalate per rollback decision tree.

Alert Matrix (recommended thresholds)

| Alert name | Trigger | Primary owner | Escalation window |
|-----------|---------:|---------------|-----------------:|
| Tenant: Cost burn spike | spend_rate > projected_rate * 1.4 for 30m | FinOps | 30m -> Pager -> Eng SRE |
| Tenant: P99 latency high | p99 > SLO * 1.5 for 10m | Runtime oncall | 10m -> Pager -> Eng Platform |
| Tenant: Token quota breach | tokens_today > quota * 1.05 | CS/FinOps | 5m -> Auto-throttle -> Pager |
| Tenant: Cache hit drop | cache_hit_rate drop >= 15% | Runtime oncall | 30m -> Investigate |

Rollback Decision Tree (high level)

- If latency or error rate spikes and cannot be mitigated within 20 minutes with route/fallback changes -> rollback to previous routing tag and billing plan.
- If cost spike is due to customer activity but within agreed commit -> engage AE + FinOps to absorb; if outside commit and rapidly increasing -> enable hard-guard quotas and notify customer.

Rollback Procedure (commands)

1. Revert routing tag:

 curl -X PATCH https://platform.internal.redwood/v1/tenants/T-12345/config
 -H "Authorization: Bearer $PLATFORM_TOKEN"
 -H "Content-Type: application/json"
 -d '{"tags":{"tier":"hosted","gpu_pool":"shared-default"}}'

2. Revert billing plan: call Billing API to set plan back to previous value (store previous in snapshot).

3. Re-apply previous quota JSON from snapshot.

Communication Templates

- Customer notification (pre-cutover):

 Subject: Planned account update on <DATE> — brief downtime unlikely

 Hi <Customer Contact>,

 We will apply your requested plan changes on <DATE> at <TIME UTC>. Services will remain available; we will monitor performance closely for 72 hours and follow up with an acceptance call. If you have a specific traffic window to avoid, please let us know.

- Customer notification (if safety-net throttle applied):

 Subject: Temporary throttle applied to protect account from unexpected spend

 Hi <Customer Contact>,

 We detected a rapid increase in usage and have temporarily limited request throughput to protect against unanticipated charges. This throttle is reversible and will be reviewed immediately by your CS and our FinOps team. Expect an update within 30 minutes.

Post-cutover Tasks and Reconciliation

- FinOps: reconcile daily usage vs projected commit; flag discrepancies >10% for AE follow-up.
- CS: customer acceptance form filled and added to account record.
- SRE: close monitoring dashboard and add any new alerts discovered to the alert library.
- Billing: confirm invoice generation scheduled correctly.

Quarterly Review and Handover

- CS + FinOps will include the tenant in the next QBR if commit >= $50k/mo or if any cutover required manual FinOps interventions. QBR items should include: usage trend, cost-per-1k tokens, cache optimisation opportunities, and recommendations for model/quantization adjustments.

Runbook Annexes

- Example Grafana alert rule (pseudo):

 alert: TenantCostSpike
 expr: increase(tenant_spend_usd_total{tenant_id="T-12345"}[30m]) / (expected_rate) > 1.4
 for: 30m

- Quota API example (JSON) — see "quotas.json" attached to ticket.

Operational Notes and Best Practices

- Always snapshot before any cutover and keep the snapshot in the ticket; it is the single source for rollback.
- Prefer "soft-guard" for first 24–72 hours unless customer explicitly requests full limits at T0.
- Automate daily usage exports to reduce manual reconciliation errors.
- Ensure AE is copied on FinOps anomalies that may affect contract renegotiation.

Appendix: Acceptance Checklist (to be signed by CS & Customer)

1) Billing plan activated and verified in Billing UI (screenshot attached).
2) Quotas applied and smoke tests passing from three regions.
3) Daily usage delivery to FinOps confirmed.
4) Temporary safety-net policy in place for T0+72h.
4) Acceptance call scheduled for T0+48h.

If any item is not complete, mark cutover as paused and follow the pause checklist in the ticket.

Contact and Escalation Roster

- CS Lead: Maya Lopez (pager: #cs-lead)
- FinOps: Jordan Kim (pager: #finops)
- Runtime oncall: Oncall rotation (see internal roster)
- Platform engineer responsible for tenant routing: Sofia Patel

Document History

- Created: 2026-01-10 by Maya Lopez
- Reviewed: 2026-01-25 by Jordan Kim, Sofia Patel, Liam Chen
- Published: 2026-02-02

title: Implement telemetry-driven surge-smoothing and guided customer communications for hosted-5xx waves
author: Aisha Kapoor
text:
Several high-severity customer escalations during recent production windows traced to multi-tenant hosted API 5xx waves. Root pattern: short bursts of connection/fanout pressure at the edge cause increased backend tail latency, which combined with client SDK retries and per-request fanout into multiple runtime shards leads to amplified request storms and transient KV cache churn. This ticket implements a telemetry-driven surge-smoothing layer plus a guided communications playbook so we can (a) blunt amplification quickly, (b) preserve SLOs for high-priority tenants, and (c) standardize customer messaging during incidents.

Per-tenant surge score exposed in Console and Datadog within 60s of onset
Edge admission controller enforces a smoothing window that reduces immediate backend fanout by >=40% under test load
Default SDK retry policy doc updated and a temporary client advisory shipped to affected customers
Canary rollout of smoothing logic to 10% of traffic with no customer-visible increase in error rate
Reusable customer messaging templates live in Confluence and accessible from the incident runbook

Feb 12: Initial triage — correlated 5xx spikes with edge connection pool saturation and amplified retries; assembled cross-functional triage (SRE, runtime, SDK)
Feb 13: Short-term mitigation deployed: edge-side aggressive keepalive reclaim and a proxy-level slow-start admission gate (hotfix) — reduced immediate error rate by ~28% for observed tenants
Feb 14: Added detailed tagging on request context (tenant_id, route, sdk_version, retry_count) and shipped expanded telemetry to Datadog dashboards
Feb 17: Implemented a first-pass tenant leaky-bucket admission algorithm and performed load tests simulating mixed-tenancy surges
Feb 18: Created customer comm templates and incident checklist in Confluence; notified three affected customers with mitigation plan and ETA

Finalize adaptive smoothing algorithm (moving-average + priority boost for SLA tiers) and loop in product for policy defaults
Roll out smoothing to 25% canary traffic and collect telemetry for 48 hours
Coordinate with SDK team to publish a recommended temporary retry configuration and an explanatory changelog entry
Implement automatic route-level fallback to Dedicated fastpath for customers with matching contracts and high surge score
Run tabletop with Solutions and Support to validate customer comm flow and SLAs

2025-02-12 Diego Morales: Found a correlation between edge connection queue growth and increased backend retries. Spike happened after a third-party client started a bulk job. Repro script saved in /playbooks/repro-edge-surge.md.
2025-02-13 Priya Shah (SRE): Hotfix reduced immediate 5xxs but deferred some load to long-tail latency — we need the smoothing window to preserve P95.
2025-02-15 Marcos Rivera (Runtime): KV cache churn observed in long sequences; adding pre-eviction cooldown to batch compaction helped in staging.
2025-02-18 Jenna Liu (Product): Will review policy defaults tomorrow. Need clear opt-in for Dedicated fastpath to avoid unexpected billing impacts for customers.
2025-02-19 Support Handoff: Templates reviewed; added a short FAQ and guidance on when customers should switch SDK retry toggles.

Primary cause: simultaneous client retries + proxy fanout under short-lived upstream congestion
Secondary cause: default SDK retry settings lacking built-in jitter and tenant-awareness
Operational gap: no easy way in Console to surface tenants approaching surge thresholds — added task to address UX

Notify affected customers with tailored advisory within 2 business hours of incident detection
Provide temporary recommended SDK settings and step-by-step rollback guidance
Offer Dedicated fastpath evaluation for customers with contractual needs; include cost/latency tradeoffs
Post-incident summary and action items to be posted to Customer Success and attached to customer ticket

title: Autoscaler: add predictive scaling signal provider interface + staleness checks
author: Mei Lin
text:
Summary: This PR introduces a pluggable forecast provider interface for Dedicated autoscaling and wires it into the autoscaler signal pipeline with strict staleness validation and safe fallback to reactive scaling when forecasts are unavailable/invalid. This is intentionally scoped to plumbing + safety; it does not change the default scaling policy behavior unless predictive mode is explicitly enabled via feature flag and config. Motivation: Enterprise Dedicated customers have predictable traffic ramps (time-of-day, scheduled jobs) and want scaling to happen ahead of demand. Before we can blend predictive and reactive signals, we need a stable interface boundary, observability for availability/staleness, and deterministic fallback behavior. Design overview: - New interface `ForecastProvider` (control-plane friendly but implemented in fleet autoscaler for now) that returns a time series forecast for a deployment/region for a configured horizon. - Staleness checks: forecasts are rejected if `generated_at` is older than `max_forecast_age` (default 10m) or if the newest forecast point is older than `max_point_age` (default 5m). - Fallback behavior: if the provider errors, times out, returns empty, or fails validation, we mark prediction as unavailable and continue using reactive signals only. We also emit a structured reason code for auditability and metrics. - Feature gating: predictive reads are behind `dedicated_predictive_autoscaling` (account/deployment-scoped flag handled in later PR); this PR includes only a local kill-switch in autoscaler config and a safety default to disabled. - Determinism: the autoscaler loop records both `requested_prediction` and `prediction_status` (available/unavailable + reason) in the decision context so downstream PRs can clamp/bound/choose signals without ambiguity. API / types: - `ForecastRequest { deployment_id, region, model_id?, horizon_seconds, step_seconds, now }` - `ForecastResponse { generated_at, points: [{ ts, rps, tokens_per_sec? }], confidence?: 0..1, source }` - Reason codes for invalidation: `provider_timeout`, `provider_error`, `stale_generated_at`, `stale_points`, `empty_forecast`, `invalid_shape`. Observability included: - `dedicated_autoscaler_prediction_available{deployment_id,region}` (0/1) (NOTE: deployment_id label will be replaced with hashed id in metrics PR; left as TODO but gated behind debug metric sink in prod). - `dedicated_autoscaler_prediction_rejected_total{reason,region}` counter. - Decision log field `prediction.status` and `prediction.reason` added to the autoscaler structured log event (not the compliance audit log; that’s in ENG-22146). Testing: - Unit tests for staleness validation, shape validation, and timeout fallback. - Integration test with a fake provider simulating partial outages and slow responses; ensures autoscaler loop continues and does not block scaling decisions. Rollout / safety: - No behavior change by default. Predictive mode remains disabled. - On provider failure, we always fall back to reactive. No scale-to-zero risk from missing predictions (explicitly handled: null/empty forecast is treated as unavailable, not as zero demand). Follow-ups (not in this PR): - Policy-level blending and arbitration between reactive saturation/queue depth and prediction (ENG-22140/ENG-22142). - Metrics naming/cardinality alignment to observability standards (ENG-22143). - Account/deployment scoped feature flag plumbing (ENG-22148).

Vanessa Ortiz (review): Can we guarantee the autoscaler loop never blocks on the provider call? If forecast service is slow, I don’t want it to extend decision latency or cause missed ticks.
Mei Lin (author): Yes — provider call is wrapped with a 250ms timeout (configurable). On timeout we mark prediction unavailable with reason `provider_timeout` and proceed. Added an integration test asserting the loop tick completes under slow provider.
Sana Farid (review): Staleness semantics: generated_at vs point timestamps. We’ve seen cases where generated_at is fresh but the forecast points lag due to backfill. Please validate both, and add explicit reason codes so we can measure which failure mode we hit.
Mei Lin (author): Updated validation to check both `generatedAt` and `lastPoint.ts`. Added reason codes `stale_generated_at` and `stale_points`, plus a counter `prediction_rejected_total{reason}`.
Jordan Lee (review): Minor: please avoid using deployment_id as a metric label in prod. This will explode cardinality. Can you gate it or leave TODO wired for later?
Mei Lin (author): Good call. I gated the per-deployment gauge behind the existing debug metrics sink (only enabled in staging/canary). In prod we emit only region-level counters until ENG-22143 lands with hashed IDs / approved label set.
Rafael Mendes (review): Please confirm the fallback cannot be interpreted as zero demand. We had prior incidents where null got cast to 0 and scaled down aggressively.
Mei Lin (author): Confirmed. `null` / empty forecasts are treated as unavailable; we never convert them into a numeric target. Added a regression unit test `empty_forecast_does_not_change_desired`.
Vanessa Ortiz (approval): Looks good. The timeout + reason codes are the right safety baseline. Approved once CI is green.
Samantha Roy (approval): Approved. Telemetry fields are consistent with our structured logging conventions.

autoscaler/predictive: introduce ForecastProvider interface + request/response types
autoscaler/predictive: implement staleness + shape validation (generated_at + point freshness)
autoscaler/predictive: add timeout wrapper + fallback to reactive on errors
autoscaler/logging: include prediction status + rejection reason in decision context logs
tests: unit tests for validation + integration test with fake provider

Interface sketch (TypeScript-ish):

export interface ForecastProvider {
 getForecast(ctx: Context, req: ForecastRequest): Promise<ForecastResponse>;
}

export type ForecastResponse = {
 generatedAt: number; // unix ms
 source: 'forecast-service' | 'static-schedule' | 'none';
 confidence?: number;
 points: Array<{ ts: number; rps: number }>;
};

Validation behavior:
- reject if Date.now() - generatedAt > maxForecastAgeMs
- reject if points.length == 0
- reject if last(points).ts < now - maxPointAgeMs
- on reject => prediction unavailable => reactive-only path

Internal: Dedicated autoscaler now supports a forecast provider interface with staleness validation and safe fallback to reactive scaling when predictions are unavailable.

title: eng-infra
text:
alex: Quick heads-up — I opened a PR to tweak the frontend Deployment rollout and default replica settings for session-manager. Trying to reduce burst CPU during deploys and avoid flapping liveness checks. PR: https://git.internal/r/redwood/session-manager/pull/412

maria: Seen it. TL;DR of changes?

alex: Changing Deployment.strategy to RollingUpdate with maxSurge: 20% and maxUnavailable: 25%, minReadySeconds: 10. Also lowering default replicas from 6 -> 4 and adding podDisruptionBudget adjustment.

jin: Can you paste the Deployment snippet? want to eyeball probe config quickly.

alex: Sure — excerpt from the manifest:```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
 name: session-manager
spec:
 replicas: 4
 strategy:
 type: RollingUpdate
 rollingUpdate:
 maxSurge: 20%
 maxUnavailable: 25%
 minReadySeconds: 10
 template:
 spec:
 containers:
 - name: session-manager
 resources:
 requests:
 cpu: "250m"
 memory: "512Mi"
 limits:
 cpu: "1"
 memory: "1Gi"
 livenessProbe:
 httpGet:
 path: /healthz
 port: 8080
 initialDelaySeconds: 15
 periodSeconds: 10
 readinessProbe:
 httpGet:
 path: /ready
 port: 8080
 initialDelaySeconds: 5
 periodSeconds: 5
```

maria: initialDelaySeconds 15 for liveness looks tight if app cold-starts >15s. We saw similar flaps in Canary last week. Suggest bumping to 30 and make readiness stricter.

sam: Also note: HPA is enabled for this service. If HPA is present, TF-managed replicas get overwritten at runtime. Check autoscaler target metrics before lowering replicas in TF.

alex: Good catch — HPA exists. I left replicas in k8s manifest as 4 but plan to put TF replicas change in a follow-up only if we decide to remove HPA. For now thinking to set pod minReplicas in HPA to 3 and target CPU 60%.

jin: If HPA minReplica is 3 and you set Deployment replicas 4, controller will reconcile to HPA values anyway. So either set Deployment replicas to HPA.min or let k8s default.

lee: On secrets wiring: the new config mounts a credentials secret for token rotation. If this is deployed in Dedicated, make sure the secret annotation points to the KMS key:```hcl
resource "kubernetes_secret" "session_token" {
 metadata {
 name = "session-token"
 annotations = {"kms.redwood.com/key" = var.kms_key_id}
 }
 data = { token = filebase64("./secrets/token.txt") }
}
```

alex: Thanks — I'll add the KMS annotation. Also added minReadySeconds because we observed ~8s warmup. Aim is reduce 429s on rollout.

maria: Regarding rollout strategy numbers: 20% surge + 25% unavailable seems odd because they can overlap and spike capacity. I'd prefer maxSurge: 1 (or 25%) and maxUnavailable: 0 for safer in-prod. What's the traffic pattern during deploys?

alex: Traffic is bursty but typically low for this service (internal sessions). We want to avoid big concurrency jumps leading to OOMs. Maybe set maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 25%?

sam: For safer path: maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 plus increase readiness initialDelay. That avoids deleting old pods until new is ready.

jin: Also consider lowering container probe timeouts instead of initialDelay if checks are noisy. And set terminationGracePeriod to 60s so connections drain.

alex: Updated PR with suggested changes: maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0, liveness initialDelay 30, readiness initialDelay 10, terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60. PTAL @maria @jin @sam.

deploy-bot: canary started — deploying session-manager to canary pool (2 pods). Monitor: https://observability.internal/d/redwood/session-manager/canary

lee: I'll check KMS annotation flow and secrets rotation after canary finish.

maria: Quick code-review: left 2 small comments on PR (probe paths + PDB minAvailable). Should be quick.

alex: Thanks all. If no objections I plan full rollout tomorrow 03:00 UTC. cc @oncall

sam: +1 from infra side.

jin: +1, but watch memory usage during canary.

lee: Ready to approve once KMS annotation is in PR.

alex: will update now, thx :thumbsup:

title: Baseline Compliance Reporting Pack (Customer + Internal Audit)
author: Olga Petrov
text:
## Purpose
The Baseline Compliance Reporting Pack (“Compliance Pack”) is a standardized, on-demand evidence bundle for security reviews and audits. It is designed to reduce ad-hoc evidence gathering by providing consistent, repeatable exports covering:
- Retention controls (configuration + change history)
- Audit logging coverage + time-window exports
- Data residency and processing regions summary
- Access control / RBAC configuration summary
- Evidence collection checklist aligned to SOC 2 / ISO-style expectations

This page defines the minimum content (“baseline”), data sources, output formats, and intended audiences. The baseline is deliberately conservative: it includes what most enterprise customers request during procurement/security review while minimizing sensitive internal-only details.

---

## Audience and distribution
### Primary audiences
1) **Customer Security/Compliance reviewers** (external)
- Goal: answer common questionnaire prompts and provide verifiable evidence artifacts.
- Delivery: customer-ready package with redactions applied (see “Customer-facing vs internal variants”).

2) **Internal audit / GRC** (internal)
- Goal: support internal audits, SOC 2 evidence collection, and control testing.
- Delivery: internal package with additional operational fields and references.

3) **Security Engineering / SRE** (internal)
- Goal: validate coverage, detect gaps, and provide supporting telemetry context.

### Customer-facing vs internal variants
The Compliance Pack is generated in one of two variants:
- **Customer-facing** (default for external sharing):
 - Excludes internal hostnames, cluster IDs, ticket links, and sensitive operational annotations.
 - Aggregates or hashes identifiers where feasible.
 - Includes only the requested time window.
- **Internal**:
 - Includes internal service identifiers and deeper operational metadata.
 - May include links to dashboards/runbooks and internal control mappings.

**Note:** All customer-facing packs must be reviewed for confidentiality classification before sharing if generated from a Private deployment environment with customer-specific infrastructure identifiers.

---

## Baseline contents (what is included)
A baseline Compliance Pack includes the following reports and attachments.

### 1) Executive summary (cover page)
**Purpose:** Provide context, scope, and definitions.
**Includes:**
- Customer/tenant identifier (as configured)
- Environment type: Hosted / Dedicated / Private
- Regions in scope
- Report time window (start/end, timezone)
- Pack version + generator version
- Data classes covered + exclusions
- Contact for questions (Security & Compliance alias)

### 2) Audit log coverage summary
**Purpose:** Demonstrate that audit logging is enabled, what is captured, and where it is stored.
**Includes:**
- Covered audit event categories (e.g., AuthN/AuthZ, API key lifecycle, user/admin actions, policy changes, console actions)
- Event source systems included (control plane, console, IAM)
- Integrity expectations (append-only semantics at store level; export signed checksums where supported)
- Known limitations / gaps (explicitly listed)

**Output:**
- `audit_log_coverage_summary.pdf` (customer-ready narrative)
- `audit_log_coverage_summary.json` (machine-readable)

### 3) Audit log export (time-windowed)
**Purpose:** Provide a verifiable export of audit events for a requested time window.
**Includes:**
- Time-windowed event export with filters applied (see templates)
- Export manifest with record counts and checksum
- Field dictionary

**Output:**
- `audit_logs.csv` (default for customer readability)
- `audit_logs.jsonl` (newline-delimited JSON for analysis)
- `audit_logs_manifest.json` (counts, filters, checksum)

**Notes:**
- For large windows, exports may be sharded (e.g., `audit_logs_part_0001.csv`).
- Filters/templates are documented in the audit exporter templates page.

### 4) Retention configuration export
**Purpose:** Provide customer-configured retention settings by data class, including defaults and overrides.
**Includes:**
- Effective retention policy (resolved) per data class
- Policy inheritance/precedence (tenant default vs override vs region-specific override where supported)
- Exceptions (e.g., disabled logging modes, legal hold status summary)
- Change history summary (who changed what, when)

**Output:**
- `retention_policy_effective.json`
- `retention_policy_change_history.csv`
- `retention_policy_readme.pdf` (definitions + interpretation guidance)

### 5) Data residency / region processing summary
**Purpose:** Answer “where is data processed/stored?” questions for regulated customers.
**Includes:**
- Control plane region(s) in use
- Data plane region(s) receiving inference traffic
- Telemetry storage regions for included data classes
- Residency commitments/constraints configured for the tenant (where applicable)
- Explicit statement of out-of-scope items (e.g., third-party incident tooling) with rationale

**Output:**
- `data_residency_summary.pdf`
- `data_residency_summary.json`

### 6) Access control and RBAC summary
**Purpose:** Provide evidence of access governance for the tenant/environment.
**Includes:**
- RBAC roles and permissions (effective)
- Users, service accounts, and group memberships (customer-facing may omit user emails; internal includes more identifiers)
- SSO status (SAML/OIDC enabled, enforcement settings if applicable)
- API keys inventory summary (counts; key material never exported)
- Admin actions related to access control from the audit log window (cross-reference)

**Output:**
- `rbac_summary.pdf`
- `rbac_roles_permissions.json`
- `rbac_principals.csv`

### 7) Evidence collection checklist (baseline)
**Purpose:** Provide a repeatable checklist aligned to common control expectations.
**Includes:**
- What was collected (artifacts list)
- Where it came from (source systems)
- Who generated it (actor) and when
- Review/sign-off fields

**Output:**
- `evidence_checklist.xlsx` (internal) and/or `evidence_checklist.csv` (customer-friendly)
- `evidence_manifest.json`

---

## Out of scope for baseline (explicit exclusions)
The baseline Compliance Pack does NOT include:
- Full “bring your own GRC” integrations (beyond standard exports)
- Arbitrary per-field redaction policies (handled under separate logging standards)
- Full incident response records, on-call notes, or internal incident tickets
- Customer request/response payload content beyond what is already captured per configured logging/retention settings
- Continuous compliance monitoring dashboards (links may be provided internally, not exported as evidence)

If an enterprise customer requests items outside baseline, open a Security & Compliance intake and track as an exception.

---

## Data sources (systems of record)
The generator assembles the pack from these sources:

1) **Audit logs store + exporter**
- Source: Audit log storage (control plane)
- Interface: audit-log-exporter (time-windowed export + templates)
- Outputs: CSV/JSONL + manifest

2) **Retention policy service (control plane)**
- Source: Retention policy configuration + change history
- Interface: retention policy export endpoint
- Outputs: effective policy JSON + change history CSV

3) **Identity and access management (IAM) / RBAC service**
- Source: roles, bindings, principals
- Interface: RBAC reporting endpoint
- Outputs: RBAC JSON + principal CSV

4) **Deployment metadata + region configuration**
- Source: tenant/deployment metadata service
- Interface: region summary endpoint
- Outputs: data residency JSON/PDF narrative

5) **Pack generator service**
- Source: orchestration + manifests + rendering
- Interface: internal job API + console download
- Outputs: packaged ZIP + signed checksum (where supported)

---

## Output format and packaging standards
### Package structure
All packs are delivered as a single ZIP archive:
- Naming: `redwood-compliance-pack_<tenant>_<env>_<YYYYMMDD>_<windowStart>-<windowEnd>_v<packVersion>.zip`
- Root includes:
 - `/README.pdf` (how to interpret artifacts)
 - `/manifest.json` (artifact list + hashes + generation metadata)
 - `/reports/` (PDF narratives)
 - `/exports/` (CSV/JSON/JSONL exports)

### Supported formats (baseline)
- **PDF**: customer-readable narratives and summaries
- **CSV**: tabular exports for audit and RBAC
- **JSON / JSONL**: machine-readable exports and manifests

### Versioning
- **Pack version**: semantic version (e.g., `1.0`) indicating included sections and contract to customers.
- **Artifact schema versions**: each JSON export includes a schema version field in its top-level metadata (or in manifest for JSONL).
- Backwards compatibility: baseline changes must be additive within a major version. Any breaking field removals/renames require a major version bump.

---

## Generation and delivery expectations
### Generation modes
- **On-demand** (primary): requested by Security/CS/SE during security review.
- **Scheduled** (internal): optional monthly/quarterly for internal audit readiness.

### SLO targets (baseline)
- Packs for ≤ 7-day audit log windows should complete generation within **60 minutes** in Hosted/Dedicated.
- Private deployments may vary based on customer-managed storage performance; provide a best-effort estimate and document constraints.

### Access controls
- Only authorized roles may generate/download packs:
 - `security_admin` (Security & Compliance)
 - `tenant_admin` (customer-side, where enabled)
 - Approved break-glass roles (internal only; audited)
- All pack generations are themselves audit-logged.

---

## Minimum fields (artifact schemas)
This section defines baseline expectations; see ADR-018 for detailed schema rules.

### Audit log export: required columns/fields
- `timestamp`
- `event_type`
- `actor_type` (user/service)
- `actor_id` (customer-facing may be pseudonymized)
- `target_type`
- `target_id` (as applicable)
- `action` (create/update/delete/rotate/login/etc.)
- `result` (success/failure)
- `source_ip` (customer-facing: include if contractually allowed; otherwise omit)
- `request_id` / `correlation_id` (internal required; customer-facing optional)

### Retention policy: required fields
- `policy_version`
- `effective_at`
- `data_classes` (request logs, audit logs, traces/metrics, artifacts where applicable)
- `ttl_days` (or equivalent duration)
- `purge_semantics` (scheduled deletion; idempotent retries)
- `legal_hold` (enabled/disabled + scope summary)

### RBAC summary: required fields
- `roles`
- `permissions`
- `bindings`
- `principals` (with least-privilege indicators where supported)
- `sso_enforcement` (enabled/disabled)

---

## Review, approvals, and change control
- Owner: **GRC (Olga Petrov)** owns baseline definition and customer-facing narrative templates.
- Security engineering (Marcus Lin) approves changes impacting confidentiality/redaction.
- Product (Naomi Feldman) approves customer-facing scope commitments.
- Changes to baseline contents require a changelog entry and (if customer-facing) an update to the Security FAQ.

---

## Known limitations (as of baseline v1.0)
- Data residency summary is a best-effort mapping based on configured regions and known storage locations; it does not replace contractual commitments.
- Some Private deployments may not support all exports until required backing services (audit log store/exporter) are installed and configured.
- Verification of deletion (purge success) is not exported as a baseline artifact; it is available via internal dashboards/runbooks and may be provided on request.

---

## Changelog
- 2025-03-12: Clarified customer-facing redaction rules for identifiers; added explicit artifact naming standard and manifest requirements.
- 2025-02-24: Added RBAC principal export and SSO enforcement status to baseline.
- 2025-02-10: Initial baseline definition (v1.0 draft).

text:
maria: Hey team — spotted a latency regression on the quantized path for rwd-base when running batch=8, seq=1024 (about +15% p99). Can someone run a quick smoke nsys + torch.profiler capture on a dedicated RTX node? Need small, redacted artifacts for analysis and a flamegraph export.

jake: I can take this. Which node and exact command? want kineto or legacy traces?

maria: thanks! use a single-GPU rtx60 node (dedicated-dev-rtx60-03). Kineto preferred. Run a short warmup then 3 measured iters. capture should include nvtx and osrt. target artifact <200MB if possible. sample command:```bash
# warmup + 3 iters capture
nsys profile --output=/tmp/prof-3032109876 --trace=nvtx,osrt -t cuda,osrt -f true -- python3 run_infer.py --model rwd-base-qlora --batch 8 --seq 1024 --warmup 20 --iters 3
```

with torch.profiler.profile(
 schedule=torch.profiler.schedule(wait=1, warmup=1, active=3),
 activities=[torch.profiler.ProfilerActivity.CPU, torch.profiler.ProfilerActivity.CUDA],
 with_stack=True,
 profile_memory=True,
) as prof:
 run_step()

```

li: if you can, please set env `RW_PERF_REDACT=1` before running so we strip session ids. also stick to public sample input (no customer data).

domain: 日常协作与非结构化讨论
title: eng-platform
text:
anya: Quick thread — sketching a Console UX and runtime semantics for per-route redaction PRESETS + how they should affect sampling and quota math. Pasting a minimal config and a few questions. feedback pls.

sam: nice. do you mean presets like 'max-redact' vs 'allow-debug' that ops can toggle per-route?

anya: yeah — presets are named bundles of redaction + sampling defaults. idea is to let customers pick a preset on a route instead of configuring ten toggles. e.g. admin endpoints use 'max-redact', public SDKs use 'dev-debug'.

kevin: curious about implications for usage billing and quota enforcement. if we strip PII from payloads, do we still count tokens the same? customers will ask.

anya: proposal: tokens are counted against request/response after redaction for billing and quota. reason: reduces surprises (if we drop large attachments they shouldn't count). but we need to be transparent in Console so folks don't think traffic magically vanished.

sam: agreed on transparency. console should show pre/post token estimate and a small histogram of redaction savings. also need to show sample-rate applied when route is 'ephemeral-debug'.

anya: example minimal preset draft: 
```yaml
presets:
 max-redact:
 remove_pii: true
 mask_fields: [email, ssn, phone]
 inline_truncate: 256
 preserve_kv_cache: false

 dev-debug:
 remove_pii: false
 sample_rate: 0.02
 preserve_kv_cache: true

routes:
 /v1/generate:
 preset: max-redact
 quota: {monthly_tokens: 5000000}

 /v1/debug/interactive:
 preset: dev-debug
 quota: {monthly_tokens: 200000}
```

kevin: small nit: preserve_kv_cache false on max-redact could increase latency for repeated prompts — ok tradeoff, but should be explicit in Console tooltip. also we need to decide whether sampled captures (1 in N) are stored in audit logs unredacted for legal teams.

anya: on sampled captures: suggest sampled audit copies are still redacted if the route's preset is max-redact. for requests with legal hold they can opt-in to an "exempt-audit" route that requires DSR & auditing approvals.

devon: ops-bot: can we run an experiment pipeline mapping preset -> observable signals? need metrics: token_savings_pct, avg_latency_ms, sample_capture_ratio, quota_burn_rate.

ops-bot: @devon queued metric job: preset-observability-2024-06. will report to #telemetry-daily.

sam: UX questions: 
- How do we represent mixed-mode routes (preset + per-tenant overrides)?
- Should preset changes be versioned with rollout (canary) and diff preview in Console?

anya: answers: 
- allow tenants to opt into stricter preset or inherit. display inheritance chain in Console.
- yep — every preset change becomes a rollout artifact; Console shows a preview diff (pre/post token estimate + sample capture change). Canary rollout for 1%/10%/100%.

kevin: implementation question: do we evaluate redaction before routing and sampling decisions or after? e.g., routing by tenant tier might depend on unredacted metadata (email domain) — need ordering.

anya: ordering proposal: 1) minimal routing headers (tenant id, route id) decide routing 2) redaction applied to body/attachments 3) sampling decision (for audit capture) uses redaction-masked payload unless sampling policy explicitly opts into raw-inspect (requires legal approval).

sam: that ordering maps to privacy-first principle. just flagging that it will break some legacy heuristics that relied on raw content for dynamic routing. we should provide a migration guide.

kevin: last point — quota math: if sample_rate < 1, do we bill tokens for sampled copies? i.e., if we capture an extra redacted copy for auditing, double-count?

anya: billing rule: charge for tokens in the authoritative request/response path only. audit/store copies are metered separately under 'audit storage units' (not customer tokens) so billing is transparent. We'll add a billing FAQ in Console.

sam: action items:
- anya: draft Console mockups (preset list, inheritance UI, diff preview) by EOD Fri
- kevin: spec telemetry metrics and quota/billing FAQ by Mon
- devon: experiment job config to compute token_savings_pct for three routes by Thu

anya: thanks. cc @ops-bot for rollout playbook — we should include a 'revert preset' quick action. :thumbsup:

ops-bot: noted: rollout playbook checklist will include canary, quota gate, revert action, legal review link.

kevin: one more: include a tiny line in Console that says "redaction may affect downstream model behavior" — for customer expectations.

anya: good call, will add.

sam: ok let's sync Wed 10am to review mocks + metrics.

kevin: 👍

devon: have a quick draft on the experiment infra, will post results as soon as job completes.

anya: closing thread — thanks all.

title: Postmortem: Hosted API latency spike and model fallback activation (2025-02-11)
author: Ava Chen
text:
h2. Summary
On 2025-02-11, the Hosted API experienced elevated p95 latency on /v1/chat/completions for ~23 minutes. Mitigation included activating an automatic model fallback policy to keep requests flowing while we reduced load on the primary model pool.

h2. Impact
* Customer-facing: increased latency, intermittent timeouts, elevated 5xx for some bursts.
* Affected product: Redwood API (Hosted).
* Affected tiers: primarily Free and Growth tiers on the default route.

h2. Timeline (UTC)
* 17:06: Alert fired: Chat latency p95 > 4.0s (threshold 2.0s) for 5 min.
* 17:11: On-call confirmed queueing on primary model pool (rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct).
* 17:14: Mitigation: enabled *automatic model fallback* on the router policy for the default route.
* 17:16: Router began automatically rerouting overflow traffic to rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct (fallback target) when saturation exceeded 85%.
* 17:22: Latency recovered; errors returned to baseline.
* 17:29: Fallback policy left on for 30 additional minutes to protect SLO.

h2. What we changed (Mitigation)
We activated a policy-based *auto-fallback* on the router:
* Primary: rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct
* Fallback: rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct
* Trigger: saturation > 85% OR queue wait > 250ms
* Scope: /v1/chat/completions, tier in {free, growth}

h2. Root cause
A mis-sized continuous batching configuration on the primary pool caused queueing to grow quickly under a bursty prompt distribution (longer-than-expected context lengths).

h2. Detection
Automated latency and queue-wait alerts fired correctly, but we lacked a dedicated alert for “fallback activated” to help confirm mitigation status.

h2. Action items
1) Add a first-class router metric + alert: fallback_activated_count by route/model. Owner: Eng Platform.
2) Update the on-call runbook to include the fallback policy toggle and rollback conditions. Owner: Eng SRE.
3) Re-tune batching defaults for rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct on A100 pool. Owner: Serving Runtime.

h2. References
* Related page: Router policies and safe-mode toggles (internal)
* Incident ID: INC-2025-0211

title: POC Hypercare Onboarding Checklist and Labs Schedule
author: Aisha Park
text:
Working doc for managing the immediate hypercare phase after POC kickoff. Focus: shorten time-to-first-success, structured lab sessions for customer engineers, and clear ownership for rollback/fallbacks.

Purpose:
- Capture an actionable onboarding checklist and day-by-day lab schedule to get customer dev + infra teams to a deterministic demo/validation state within 10 working days.
- This is intentionally pragmatic: a mix of synchronous labs and asynchronous setup tasks, with explicit fallbacks and 'fast fail' gates.

Context and constraints:
- Customer: fintech startup, regulated data; on-prem private deployment evaluated.
- Goal: prove inference latency < 80ms P95 for 256-token prompts under 5 RPS and embedding throughput of 200 qps for batch embed jobs.
- Timebox: 2-week POC window, first week focused on integration + smoke, second week on accuracy/regression checks and performance tuning.
- Resources: 1 solutions engineer (Aisha), 1 infra lead (Miguel), 2 customer engineers (CE-Lead + CE-Dev).

Prework (before Day 0):
- Customer to provide network connectivity diagram and IP allowlist.
- Customer to create a service account and share KMS test key (or provide details for HSM integration notes).
- SE to prepare a compact model bundle (quantized) and a reference prompt set (50 queries).
- Setup a shared Slack channel and one PagerDuty escalation for the POC window.

Day-by-day labs schedule (high level):
- Day 0 (Kickoff call): align success criteria, confirm roles, run through emergency rollback plan. Quick demo of the sample app.
- Day 1 (Network + Access lab): validate IPs, test certificate handshake, confirm KMS integration; SE does live walkthrough of container startup logs and CLI.
- Day 2 (Model ingestion + routing lab): push model bundle, verify model catalog entry, exercise routing policy to fallback model variant.
- Day 3 (Inference smoke + latency baseline): run 100 sample requests, capture P50/P95, check KV-cache behavior for repeated prefixes.
- Day 4 (Batch embedding run): run embedding job on 10k rows; inspect throughput, memory footprint; iterate on batch size settings.
- Day 5 (Canary & trace day): execute canary rollout with 5% traffic, collect traces and token-level cost breakdown.
- Day 6 (Offline tuning day): SE tunes batching and quantization profile; infra lead validates GPU metrics under load.
- Day 7 (Customer self-run lab): customer engineers perform scripted integration and produce runbook notes.
- Day 8 (Regression checks): run prompt set, run quality checks vs baseline; collect failure cases for follow-up.
- Day 9 (Final demo prep): consolidate dashboards, prepare slides and short recording of flows.
- Day 10 (Final demo & handoff): demo to stakeholders, capture decision (go/no-go), list next steps for Dedicated or Private procurement.

Task tracker (as checklist, mark status during daily standups):
- [ ] Kickoff scheduled and calendar invites sent
- [ ] Network allowlist verified
- [ ] Service account + KMS access validated
- [ ] Model bundle uploaded and sanity-tested
- [ ] Latency smoke run completed (baseline metrics saved)
- [ ] Embedding full-run completed and logs archived
- [ ] Canary rollout executed and traces saved
- [ ] Runbook draft created by customer engineers
- [ ] Final demo recording created
- [ ] Post-POC evaluation meeting scheduled

Fast failures & fallbacks (explicit):
- If model upload fails repeatedly: fall back to 'hosted-sample' model and validate the orchestration behavior.
- If KMS/HSM not available within 48 hours: pivot to test KMS tokens (ephemeral) and mark as compliance risk in the final report.
- If latency targets not met on private infra: propose a Dedicated pilot with same config and compare perf numbers (automate side-by-side run).

Acceptance criteria (short list):
- Measurable: P95 latency < 80ms for target sample under the stated RPS OR clearly documented perf delta with proposed mitigations.
- Functional: customer app can make authenticated requests and receive streaming responses in expected format.
- Operational: runbook with steps to restart services, rotate keys, and roll back model versions exists and is validated by the customer engineers.
- Security: minimal audit logs enabled and an acceptance note from security reviewer (could be an email).

Metrics to capture (for wrap-up doc):
- Latency P50/P95/P99, token throughput, GPU utilization, memory headroom, embedding qps, average token cost estimate.
- Number of retries / 5xx errors during each lab.
- Time-to-first-success (TFS): time from kickoff to first successful authenticated inference returned to the customer app.

Known risks & mitigations:
- Network complexity (multi-VPC peering): schedule pre-lab with customer network team; reserve extra day for troubleshooting.
- Nonstandard KMS/HSM: have a fallback config with ephemeral test keys and highlight as compliance discussion item.
- Customer-side CI gating: ask customer to allocate one engineer full-time during Days 1-3.

Notes to self and TODOs (informal):
- Bring a small script to scrape token-level cost from the trace export (Miguel will help finalize).
- Prepare two short troubleshooting playbooks: `restart-agent` and `reindex-model-cache`. Keep them < 10 steps.
- Remind CE-Lead to export sample errors and share the top 5 failure traces before Day 8.
- Consider a short 20-min office-hours on Day 6 for informal Q&A. Put placeholder in calendar.

Post-POC handoff checklist:
- Final metrics snapshot uploaded to Confluence
- Runbook accepted and signed off by CE-Lead
- Decision recorded (next: Dedicated trial / Private deployment / Stop)
- If go: create procurement ticket and initial Dedicated capacity estimate.

Unresolved questions (to capture in final report):
- Does customer need SIEM integration for audit logs or is S3 export sufficient?
- Are there any regulatory constraints on model weights leaving the premises? Need legal sign-off.

Appendix: quick command snippets (for labs)
- Model push: `rwdctl model push --bundle model.tar.gz --name poc-test-v1`
- Start agent: `rwdctl agent start --config poc-minimal.yaml`
- Simple latency probe: `ab -n 100 -c 2 http://localhost:8080/v1/infer`

This doc is a working artifact — update checklist statuses daily and paste short standup notes under the top section. Keep final version tidy before sending to customer as a readout.

2025-02-12 Kickoff and security alignment (owner: Aisha)
2025-02-13 Network verification + KMS test (owner: Miguel)
2025-02-14 Model push and routing validation (owner: Aisha)
2025-02-15 Latency smoke tests and tracing (owner: Riley)
2025-02-16 Embedding batch run (owner: Priya)
2025-02-17 Canary rollout and traces (owner: Aisha)
2025-02-18 Offline tuning and office hours (owner: Miguel)
2025-02-19 Customer self-run lab and runbook review (owner: CE-Lead)
2025-02-20 Final regression and demo prep (owner: Aisha)
2025-02-21 Final demo and decision capture (owner: Stakeholder Group)

P95 latency < 80ms for 256-token samples under 5 RPS OR documented mitigation plan
Authenticated API calls succeed and streaming responses validated
Customer engineers can follow runbook to restart services and rotate keys
Security reviewer provides sign-off note or a formal exception

title: OpenAI Chat Completions wire symmetrizer and response fidelity guard
author: Ava Chen
text:
Purpose: Implement a compatibility layer that converts between Redwood's internal chat event model and the OpenAI Chat Completions (v1) request/response wire format while preserving streaming fidelity, function/tool-call semantics, structured output envelopes, and message provenance.

Scope:
- Request-side: map Redwood chat/message model -> OpenAI request payloads (messages, system/user/assistant roles, function schemas) with a pluggable sanitizer and idempotency token.
- Response-side: ingest OpenAI streaming chunk/event sequences and reconstruct Redwood streaming frames, ensuring structured JSON objects are validated and tool/function calls are emitted as first-class events.
- Maintain backwards-compatibility for legacy clients relying on OpenAI-styled SSE framing.
- Emit telemetry and per-token latency/cost signals for Console traceability.

Out of scope: model-side behavioral adjustments (prompt engineering), Dedicated autoscaling changes, private deployment-only networking plumbing.

Requests generated by the symmetrizer from Redwood chat objects produce semantically equivalent OpenAI ChatCompletions payloads in unit tests (>= 95% coverage for mapped fields)
Streaming responses from OpenAI-like providers are reconstituted into Redwood stream frames with preserved chunk ordering, function call start/finish boundaries, and incremental content deltas
Function/tool call events are emitted exactly once with complete arguments parsed into Redwood ToolCall schema and an idempotency token attached
Structured-output objects embedded in assistant messages are validated against provided JSON schemas; invalid payloads produce a structured error event without dropping the entire stream
Telemetry includes: first-byte latency, per-chunk token counts, tool invocation counts, and a compact provenance header that traces original request id -> provider request id -> response id
Compatibility mode can be toggled (strict-openai | permissive-redwood) without server restart and is exercised by integration tests
No regression in existing Redwood streaming tests (compare baseline traces) and load tests show <5% tail latency increase for 95th percentile compared to current proxy

Draft request and response mapping tables (fields, transforms, default fallbacks)
Implement OpenAI wire marshaller for requests with sanitizer hooks for user metadata and function schema injection
Build stream reassembler that consumes provider SSE/chunk stream and emits Redwood streaming frames including tool-call boundaries
Add JSON schema validator for structured-output blocks and error-envelope emitter
Instrument telemetry hooks in marshaller and reassembler (tracing ids, token counters)
Create unit and integration tests including recorded golden streams and a local fake provider for edge cases
Prepare migration notes and console dashboard tiles for new provenance fields

2026-02-26 - Ava Chen: Initial ticket created after design sync with PM. Captured high-level mapping goals. Linked design note in Drive (see links).
2026-03-02 - Diego Martinez: Spike completed to replay a set of recorded OpenAI SSE streams. Found two failure modes: partial chunk JSON split inside a delta and function call argument chunks arriving interleaved with regular text deltas.
2026-03-04 - Priya Singh (PM): Clarified product requirement that function calls must surface to customers as a single atomic event in the Console; partial tool args should be reassembled, not surfaced mid-call.
2026-03-05 - Diego Martinez: Implementation note - added buffer boundary detection using RFC-4180-like chunk reassembly + heuristic for 'role' switches. Trade-off: adds small memory buffer per-stream (configurable).
2026-03-07 - Liam O'Neil (Design): Reviewed the structured-output error UX. Recommended emitting a WARNING event with a compact example and a link to the raw payload in infra logs instead of truncating content.
2026-03-09 - Diego Martinez: PR opened for marshaller and reassembler: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-inference/pull/4728. Contains unit tests and fake provider harness. Requesting review from runtime and telemetry leads.
2026-03-11 - Rajesh Kulkarni (Runtime): Code review feedback: ensure backpressure signals from Redwood runtime are propagated to provider stream consumer to avoid unbounded buffering. Added to tasks.
2026-03-12 - Diego Martinez: Adjusted implementation to attach idempotency token header (X-RW-Req-Id) and emit 'prov' field in trace events. Running perf regression suite now.
2026-03-12 - QA: Found flaky test where tool-call finalization event was lost when provider sends termination without explicit finish token. Added test and mitigation strategy: finalize on stream close if open tool-call present.

Design trade-offs: we prefer preserving provider chunk boundaries where possible to give clients identical streaming shape, but for safety we coalesce small JSON fragments to ensure valid structured blocks.
Performance consideration: per-stream reassembly buffer is configurable; default 64KB with fallback to fallthrough mode that emits raw chunks plus a warning when exceeded.
Rollout plan: feature flag behind 'oa-wire-symmetrizer'; start with 5% of hosted traffic, monitor tool-call correctness metric and 95th latency for 48h, then ramp.
Fallback behavior: on provider schema parsing error, emit structured ERROR event with raw payload link and continue streaming if possible.
