title: Private upgrade failed during DB migration (lock timeout) — control plane unavailable after Helm upgrade
text:
Issue summary
- Customer attempted in-place upgrade of Redwood Private in their VPC environment.
- Upgrade failed during database migration step; control plane pods entered CrashLoopBackOff due to migrations not completing.

Impact
- Control plane API unavailable (customer reported 503s from internal console + deployment controller).
- Data plane inference endpoints continued serving existing workloads but config changes/rollouts were blocked.
- Estimated customer impact window: ~35 minutes degraded management plane.

Environment
- Customer: Cascade Financial Group (Private/VPC)
- Region: us-east (customer VPC)
- Upgrade path: Private 1.14.3 -> 1.15.0
- Storage: EBS-backed PVCs
- DB: Postgres (in-cluster StatefulSet)

What happened (operator timeline)
1) Customer ran installer upgrade, which applied updated Helm charts.
2) Pre-upgrade job launched DB migration ("redwood-control-plane-migrate").
3) Migration job repeatedly failed with lock timeout waiting on relation locks; subsequent control plane deployments remained blocked.

Symptoms
- Installer output ended on: "Running schema migrations" then reported failure.
- Kubernetes:
 - Job redwood-control-plane-migrate failed, backoff limit reached.
 - Deployments redwood-control-plane-api / redwood-console showed readiness failures.
- Postgres showed long-running transactions (suspected background worker + stale connection from old version).

Customer request
- Immediate recovery steps and guidance on whether they can safely rollback to 1.14.3.
- Confirmation this is a known migration issue and whether a patch is available.

Attachments / logs (sanitized)
- kubectl logs job/redwood-control-plane-migrate:
 - "ERROR: canceling statement due to lock timeout"
 - "DETAIL: Process 1876 waits for ShareLock on transaction 903184; blocked by process 1762"
 - "STATEMENT: ALTER TABLE prompts ADD COLUMN prompt_hash text NOT NULL DEFAULT ''"
 - "migration failed: timed out acquiring advisory lock"

- Postgres log excerpt:
 - "LOG: process 1762 still waiting for ShareLock on transaction 903184 after 30000.000 ms"

Notes
- This appears consistent with prior staging behavior where migrations held locks longer than expected, especially when long-lived connections exist.
- Customer performed upgrade during a maintenance window but did not restart DB / drain old control plane pods prior to migration.

Immediate goals
- Restore control plane availability.
- Provide safe fallback plan (pause/rollback) and prevent recurrence.

Internal triage checklist
- Verify if this migration exists in 1.15.0 only and whether it is safe/idempotent.
- Determine if lock_timeout defaults are too aggressive in private environments.
- Confirm recommended recovery path and document in runbook / precheck guidance.

2025-04-18 09:12 PT — Dev Patel (Support): Customer reports upgrade failed during DB migration and console is down (503). Asked for kubectl logs + installer output. Started incident bridge and tagged #incidents + #eng-sre.
2025-04-18 09:26 PT — Owen Phillips (Support, assignee): Confirmed symptoms match migration job backoff. Requested: `kubectl get jobs -n redwood`, `kubectl logs job/redwood-control-plane-migrate -n redwood --tail=200`, and Postgres logs around failure timestamp.
2025-04-18 09:40 PT — Sean Gallagher (SRE): Looked at shared logs. This is lock_timeout + stale txn behavior. Recommend: scale down control plane deployments to 0 to release old connections, then re-run migration job. If still blocked, restart Postgres pod. (Minimize blast radius: DP should keep serving.)
2025-04-18 10:02 PT — Customer (Cascade): Scaled down `redwood-control-plane-api` and `redwood-console` to 0; migration job still fails with lock timeout. Postgres shows one long-running transaction from "redwood-worker".

2025-04-18 10:15 PT — Michael Nguyen (Eng - Config persistence & migrations): Migration uses advisory lock + ALTER TABLE. If another session holds lock, job retries but fails quickly due to aggressive lock timeout. Workaround: terminate blocking backend + rerun migration. Longer term fix: make migration idempotent + increase lock timeout with progress logging. Mentioned upcoming guardrails PR.
2025-04-18 10:24 PT — Owen Phillips (Support): Guided customer to identify and terminate blocker:
- `kubectl exec -n redwood sts/postgres-0 -- psql -c "select pid, state, now()-xact_start as xact_age, query from pg_stat_activity where xact_start is not null order by xact_age desc;"`
- `select pg_terminate_backend(<pid>);`
Then re-run the migration job by deleting the failed job pod and re-applying the hook (or `helm upgrade --reuse-values` if needed).
2025-04-18 10:41 PT — Customer (Cascade): Terminated blocker PID and re-ran migration job; completed successfully. Scaled control plane deployments back up; console is reachable again.
2025-04-18 11:05 PT — Rafael Mendes (SRE): Suggested customer verify post-upgrade health:
- `kubectl rollout status deploy/redwood-control-plane-api -n redwood`
- `kubectl get pods -n redwood | egrep 'CrashLoop|Error'`
- Confirm version endpoints show 1.15.0
Also recommended adding an upgrade precheck to catch long-running DB transactions and confirm lock_timeout settings.
2025-04-19 08:20 PT — Owen Phillips (Support): Follow-up: asked customer for total downtime and whether any inference traffic was affected. Shared internal runbook snippet and suggested scheduling rollback drill once rollback command ships.
2025-04-21 09:10 PT — Connor O'Brien (Release Eng): Linking fixes in flight:
- DB migration guardrails + safer defaults: sources/github/redwood/pr-29210-migration-guardrails-and-backward-compatible-schema.json
- Chart ordering separation CP/DP to reduce partial outages: sources/github/redwood-helm-charts/pr-2204-split-control-plane-and-data-plane-rollout-phases.json
- Rollback command/state machine for Private installer (future): sources/github/redwood-private-installer/pr-4862-rollback-command-and-state-machine.json

Resolved via operational workaround.

Root cause (most likely)
- Migration job failed due to lock contention + aggressive lock_timeout while a long-running transaction from a stale control plane worker held locks.

Customer recovery steps used
1) Identified and terminated blocking Postgres backend (pg_stat_activity + pg_terminate_backend).
2) Re-ran migration job; migrations completed.
3) Brought control plane deployments back up and verified readiness.

Preventative actions / follow-ups
- Engineering fix: DB migration guardrails and safer defaults (idempotency checks, lock timeouts, clearer logging): sources/github/redwood/pr-29210-migration-guardrails-and-backward-compatible-schema.json
- Packaging fix: separate control plane and data plane rollout phases with readiness gates to reduce partial upgrade blast radius: sources/github/redwood-helm-charts/pr-2204-split-control-plane-and-data-plane-rollout-phases.json
- Docs/runbook update: add explicit "check for long-running transactions" and termination guidance; link in Private upgrade runbook: sources/confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/private-upgrade-runbook.json

Customer-facing notes
- No data loss observed.
- Data plane inference remained available; management plane was unavailable for ~35 minutes.
- Customer requested stronger rollback guarantees; tracked under SUP-18488 (separate ticket).

title: Offline Test Harness and Observability Quickstart
author: Priya Kapoor
text:
Overview

This quickstart documents the recommended offline test harness for SDK and API integrations plus the paired observability checks you should run before a canary or public rollout. The goal is to provide a repeatable, low-friction way to: replay representative traffic, validate client-side and runtime telemetry, exercise streaming/fallback behavior, and generate deterministic golden outputs for regression tests.

When to use this quickstart

- Preparing a canary release for an SDK or client adapter.
- Validating model/quantization/serialization changes against a curated prompt set.
- Reproducing support issues reported from production traces without hitting live endpoints.
- Running nightly regression runs as part of the docs-site CI.

Goals and success criteria

- Replays run locally or in CI using recorded inputs and expected golden outputs.
- Key telemetry emitted (latency, token counts, kv-cache hits, batching stats, error codes) and ingested by the observability pipeline.
- Streaming fallbacks and chunk reassembly exercised with no data loss in >95% of test cases.
- Actionable alerts and triage playbook entries generated when regressions are detected.

Prerequisites

1. A copy of the sample harness repo (private): git@github.com:redwood-inference/devx/offline-harness.git
2. Access to the local SDK proxy (redwood-local-proxy) or a mocked endpoint.
3. A set of recorded traffic files in JSONL format (see "Recorded traffic format" below).
4. Basic familiarity with our telemetry schema (link in related_pages).

Recorded traffic format

Each line is a single JSON record representing a single request and expected metadata. Minimal example: 

```json
{
 "id": "req-20250217-0001",
 "route": "/v1/generate",
 "model": "redwood-llm-3b-v1",
 "input": "Summarize the following text: ...",
 "streaming": true,
 "expected_output_file": "goldens/req-20250217-0001.txt",
 "metadata": {"customer_tier": "self-serve", "region": "us-west-2"}
}
```

(For the purposes of the harness the metadata key/value pairs are treated as opaque labels that can be used to vary routing/overrides in tests.)

Quickstart: Run a single replay locally

1. Clone the harness repo and install deps: 

```bash
git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/devx/offline-harness.git
cd offline-harness
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

2. Start the local SDK proxy in capture mode (captures outgoing requests to `logs/offline-capture.jsonl`):

```bash
redwood-local-proxy --mode capture --out logs/offline-capture.jsonl 
# or use the docker image for stability in CI: docker run -v $PWD/logs:/workspace/logs redwood/local-proxy:stable capture --out /workspace/logs/offline-capture.jsonl
```

3. Replay a specific file against a mock server: 

```bash
python replay.py --input test-records/req-batch-001.jsonl --proxy http://localhost:8080 --mode compare --goldens-dir goldens/ --telemetry-out telemetry/out.jsonl
```

4. Inspect results: the harness produces a `results/` folder with per-request diffs and `telemetry/out.jsonl` with emitted telemetry.

Batch mode and CI integration

- Use the `--concurrency` flag to simulate multiple parallel clients. Recommended default for CI is 8.
- Use `--seed` to ensure deterministic ordering for golden comparisons.
- The harness exits non-zero if a configured percentage of requests fail the golden comparison (default 1%).
- For nightly regression jobs, run on a pinned model commit SHA in an isolated CI job and store artifacts in S3 (/ci-regressions/YYYY-MM-DD/).

Observability checklist (what to assert)

- Telemetry fields emitted per request: 
 - request_id, start_ts, end_ts, total_tokens_in, total_tokens_out, latency_ms_p50/p95/p99, kv_cache_hits, batch_size, model_variant, error_code
- Alerts and thresholds to add temporarily during rollout: 
 - p95 latency increase > 20% from baseline (auto-create incident ticket)
 - token inflation (tokens_out/tokens_in) > 1.5 for generation models
 - streaming chunk reorder or missing chunk rate > 3%
- Dashboards to check before/after: 
 - SDK: request rate by route, latency percentiles, error codes;
 - Runtime: GPU utilization, batch sizes, KV cache hit ratio;
 - Cost: tokens per minute, average cost per request (estimated).

Sample config matrix (YAML)

Name | Purpose | Key flags | CI cardinality
-----|---------|-----------|----------------
basic-local | single-request smoke | streaming: false, concurrency: 1 | PR job (fast)
adjusted-batching | check batching paths | concurrency: 8, batch_max_tokens: 512 | Nightly
streaming-edge | exercise chunking/fallback | streaming: true, chunk_size: 512, reorder_seed: 42 | Regression

Example YAML for a CI job: 

```yaml
job_name: offline-harness-regression
records: test-records/critical-path-2026.jsonl
concurrency: 8
seed: 42
golden_threshold_pct: 0.5
telemetry_sink: s3://redwood-ci-artifacts/telemetry/offline-harness/2026-02-10/
compare_mode: fuzzy # options: exact, fuzzy
```

Golden file comparison modes

- exact: byte-for-byte match (use only for fully deterministic outputs such as embeddings or reranked ids).
- fuzzy: token-level similarity thresholds and whitespace-insensitive diffs. Configurable via `fuzzy_score_threshold` (default 0.87).

Example: validate streaming reassembly

1. Use the `streaming-edge` scenario YAML.
2. The harness replays requests with deliberate network jitter and reorder seeds.
3. It reconstructs the received chunks into complete responses and runs comparison against goldens using the configured compare_mode.

Command to run in CI: 

```bash
python replay.py --ci --config ci/jobs/offline-harness-regression.yaml --upload-artifacts s3://redwood-ci-artifacts/
```

Telemetry ingestion and debug workflow

1. The harness emits line-delimited JSON telemetry to `telemetry/out.jsonl`. Each record contains both SDK-observed metrics and runtime-supplied fields (model_variant, kv_cache_hits).
2. CI job uploads telemetry to S3 and triggers an ingestion lambda that writes to our observability dataset.
3. For quick triage, run `scripts/telemetry-aggregate.py telemetry/out.jsonl` to generate a local HTML report with p50/p95 and histogram PNGs.

Sample troubleshooting checklist

- If diffs are noisy: switch compare_mode to fuzzy and increase `fuzzy_score_threshold`.
- If streaming chunks fail reassembly: verify proxy is not truncating chunk boundaries and check `chunk_size` agreement between client and mock server.
- If telemetry is missing runtime fields: ensure the mock runtime honors the `X-Runtime-Metadata` header used by SDKs to surface model_variant and kv metrics.

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: eng-developer-experience (Priya Kapoor).
- Secondary: eng-serving-runtime (Diego Alvarez) for runtime telemetry fields.
- For CI infra issues: eng-platform oncall.
- Escalation path: create a ticket in JIRA under project DEVX with label `offline-harness` and ping #devx-oncall.

Appendix: commonly-used commands and examples

- Capture mode via SDK proxy (local): `redwood-local-proxy --mode capture --out logs/capture.jsonl`
- Replay a single request and write diffs: `python replay.py --input test-records/one.jsonl --mode compare --goldens-dir goldens/`
- Aggregate telemetry: `python scripts/telemetry-aggregate.py telemetry/out.jsonl --html report.html`

Related considerations and next steps

- Consider adding a lightweight Web UI for per-request diffs if diff volume is high.
- Integrate with the docs-site CI so failing golden comparisons block merges on critical-path PRs.
- Expand the sample record set to include longer-context (>4k token) scenarios, multi-tool function calls, and embedding bulk jobs.

If you have questions or want the private harness repo added to your team, open a request with eng-developer-experience and include the GitHub team.

title: Establish upgrade compatibility matrix and pinning strategy for Terraform modules/providers for Private VPC
author: Maya Chen
text:
Problem: Private (VPC) customers run their infra with a combination of Redwood Terraform modules (redwood/private-vpc, redwood/db, redwood/networking) and cloud providers (hashicorp/aws, hashicorp/azurerm, hashicorp/google). We currently lack a single canonical compatibility matrix mapping Redwood Private releases to tested Terraform module versions and provider constraints, which leads to upgrade surprises (provider API changes, module inputs renamed, drift).

Goal: Produce an upgrade compatibility matrix and a clear version pinning policy for Terraform modules and providers that we will publish in the private-deployments repo and Confluence, enforce via CI, and use as the source-of-truth for upgrades and customer runbooks. The matrix must cover: Redwood Private control-plane release, recommended module versions, provider versions/constraints, known breaking changes, and required tfengine/terraform version.

Scope: Only affects Private (VPC) deployment IaC maintained by Redwood. Includes testing and CI changes (plan-only gating), documentation, and an upgrade runbook. Does NOT include customer-managed forks except where we publish recommended pins for customers to consume.

Outcomes: 1) Compatibility matrix artifact in the repo; 2) Pinning policy committed to modules (module versions and provider constraints); 3) CI checks that fail if module/provider pins fall outside matrix; 4) Runbook for in-place upgrades with health-check checklist.

Matrix published as markdown at docs/terraform-compatibility.md in private-deployments repo and linked from Confluence
All active redwood/private-* modules have explicit module versions and provider constraints updated in main branch according to the matrix
CI pipeline includes a terraform plan job against the latest sandbox that validates provider/module versions and fails on drift
Upgrade runbook with step-by-step canary process, rollback commands, and health-check thresholds exists and is reviewed
At least one end-to-end upgrade test (control-plane 2026.02 -> 2026.03) executed in staging and results attached to ticket

Audit current module and provider versions across infra repos (private-deployments, onboarding-templates) - ENG owners: Liam/Carlos
Define pinning policy doc: allowed constraint formats, vacuuming cadence, and deprecation policy
Create compatibility matrix template (CSV/Markdown) and populate for previous three releases
Implement CI gating: plan-only job that checks providers.lock and module versions against matrix
Write upgrade runbook and health-check scripts (k8s readiness, service-level pings, database connectivity, IAM validation)
Stakeholder review with PM and Security, incorporate feedback
Publish final matrix and announce to Support/SE teams, update onboarding templates

2026-03-01 Maya Chen: Triage note - multiple customers reported breakages after provider upgrades last quarter. Created ticket to centralize compatibility info and enforce gates.

title: Private (On‑Prem) Backup/Restore + Audit Log Retention Guide (Day‑2 Ops)
author: Aisha Rahman
text:
h1. Purpose
This page defines the supported backup/restore workflow and audit log retention/export patterns for *Redwood Private (on‑prem / restricted egress / air‑gapped)* deployments.

It consolidates commonly-audited requirements raised by regulated customers (e.g., healthcare) including:
- Encrypted backups with customer‑managed keys (CMK)
- Clear separation of *cluster recovery (Kubernetes/etcd)* vs *application-level restore (Redwood control plane)*
- Long-term audit log retention (7–10 years) with immutability/WORM patterns
- Evidence artifacts for auditors (manifests, checksums/signatures, restore validation reports, exporter gap detection)

h1. Scope and ownership model
h2. What Redwood backs up (application-level)
Redwood Private backups focus on *control-plane state and critical configuration* required for a deterministic redeploy:
- Redwood control-plane configuration database
- Redwood control-plane metadata/state required for tenant configuration and routing policy restoration
- Redwood-managed Helm release versions + values (for Redwood components)
- Redwood CRDs and Redwood-specific resources *as inputs to restore* (see pre-flight requirements)

h2. What Redwood does NOT back up
- *Kubernetes cluster recovery artifacts* (e.g., cluster-wide etcd snapshots) are owned by the customer’s Kubernetes operations practice.
- Request payloads, prompt bodies, and inference content are not included in standard control-plane backups.
- Raw secret material is *excluded by default* (see “Secrets handling”).

h2. Boundaries: etcd restore vs Redwood restore
Use two distinct runbooks:
1) *Cluster recovery (customer-owned)*: recover Kubernetes control plane (including etcd) when the cluster is corrupted.
2) *Redwood application restore (Redwood-supported)*: restore Redwood control-plane state into a *clean/rebuilt* Kubernetes cluster.

Important: Restoring etcd snapshots that include stale Redwood resources can create conflicts (e.g., stale finalizers, CRD/version mismatches). For DR validation, prefer a clean cluster + Redwood restore.

h1. Backup artifact format and integrity
h2. Backup artifact components
Backups are produced as an encrypted bundle with:
- A *manifest* containing: backup ID, timestamp, software version(s), format version, component list, checksums, and restore prerequisites.
- Encrypted payload(s) containing the backed-up control-plane data.

h2. Integrity and tamper evidence
- Each component is hashed; the manifest records checksums.
- As of Private Toolkit v1.8+, manifests can be signed using *Sigstore/cosign (offline key mode)*. (Older deployments may still use GPG signatures; both are supported during migration.)
- Optional policy: store backup artifacts in immutable/WORM storage for stronger tamper resistance.

h1. Encryption model (CMK, air-gap, KMS/HSM)
h2. Envelope encryption (DEK/KEK)
Backups use *envelope encryption*:
- Backup data is encrypted with a *Data Encryption Key (DEK)*.
- The DEK is wrapped by a *Key Encryption Key (KEK)* controlled by the customer’s KMS/HSM.
- Only wrapped DEKs are persisted; DEKs are intended to be ephemeral in memory.

h2. Supported key providers (on-prem)
The Private key provider interface supports:
- On-prem KMS services with an HTTP API via the provider layer
- HSM integration via *PKCS#11* (commonly used for Thales/Entrust setups) where operationally permitted

Notes:
- Exact compatibility depends on HSM policy (wrap/unwrap allowed, key types, network segmentation). Validate permitted operations early.
- Restore requires unwrap access; if the HSM disallows unwrap in the restore environment, restore will fail by design.

h2. KMS/HSM availability behavior
Default posture is secure-by-default:
- If KMS/HSM is unavailable at *backup time*: backup *fails* (default) to avoid producing artifacts that cannot be attested as encrypted under the customer KEK.
- If KMS/HSM is unavailable at *restore time*: restore fails because the DEK cannot be unwrapped.

A “break-glass local key” mode exists for specific non-production use cases, but it is *disabled by default* and requires an explicit configuration flag + logged approval.

h2. Key rotation expectations
Many regulated customers require annual rotation.
- Backups created under an older KEK remain decryptable as long as the ability to decrypt old wrapped DEKs remains available (e.g., KMS key versioning).
- If KEK versions are retired before the retention window, customers must rewrap or re-encrypt retained backups.

Operational guidance:
- Either retain KEK versions for the entire retention period, or schedule periodic rewrap to the active KEK.

h1. Secrets handling (secure-by-default)
h2. Policy
The design intent is: *backup references, not secrets*.
- The backup tooling excludes Kubernetes Secret values by default.
- Backups may include references (secret names, external secret paths, KMS key IDs) needed to rehydrate secrets from the system-of-record.

h2. If secrets exist only as Kubernetes Secrets
If a customer keeps secret material only in-cluster, they must implement a separate secrets DR strategy (customer-owned). Redwood will not silently include secret plaintext in control-plane backups.

h2. “Forbidden resource” validation
As of Private Toolkit v1.8+, the backup verification step checks manifests for forbidden resource types (e.g., Kubernetes Secret payload inclusion). Misconfiguration should fail closed.

h1. Storage targets and retention
h2. Where backups can be written
Backups can be written to:
- NFS (common on-prem default)
- S3-compatible object storage (recommended when immutability/object lock is required)

h2. Retention enforcement
Two layers exist:
- *Tool-level retention* (e.g., keep N days) is available for convenience.
- For regulated environments, prefer *storage-backend lifecycle policies* (harder to tamper with; supports dual-control workflows).

h2. Immutability/WORM patterns
Recommended patterns:
1) Backups: checksums + signed manifest + restrictive write permissions; optionally replicate to immutable storage.
2) Audit logs: export to object storage with immutability/object lock, or export to NFS then replicate to a compliance archive system.

Ownership: Redwood produces the backup/export artifacts and provides supported runbooks; customers own the archival platform and retention configuration.

h1. Restore workflow and validation (auditor-ready)
h2. Restore pre-flight checklist
Before restore, ensure:
- Target cluster is healthy and time-synchronized (NTP). If drift exceeds policy threshold, restore should warn or fail.
- Required CRDs exist at expected versions.
- KMS/HSM connectivity and unwrap permission is validated.

Default drift threshold guidance:
- Warn at >200 ms drift
- Fail at >1 s drift (customer may tune)

h2. Restore validation report
The restore workflow generates a report suitable for audit evidence. Typical fields include:
- Backup ID, backup timestamp, restore timestamp
- Backup format version, Redwood version
- KMS provider identifier (not keys), unwrap success/failure
- Checksums verified (yes/no) + counts
- Components restored + ordering
- Post-restore health checks executed and results

Post-restore validations commonly include:
- Control plane API readiness
- Ability to list tenants and read routing policy configuration
- Auth configuration loads successfully
- Dependency connectivity checks
- Optional smoke inference call (if a data plane is present and policy permits)

h2. Restore drill cadence (recommended)
For regulated environments:
- Quarterly full technical restore drill into a clean cluster (preferred)
- Monthly tabletop review of DR runbooks and access prerequisites
- Staging environment monthly technical drill is common when feasible

h1. Audit logs: export, schema, retention, and gap detection
h2. Audit event scope
Redwood Private emits audit events for control plane actions, including:
- Configuration changes
- Auth changes
- Administrative actions
- System events relevant to control-plane governance

Audit logs do *not* include prompt bodies by default. For PHI-heavy environments, prompt/request logging is typically disabled by policy.

h2. Export modes
Two common patterns:
1) *Near real-time* forwarding to SIEM for short RPO (minutes)
2) *Batch export* to durable storage for long-term retention and immutability

Supported batch export formats:
- JSON Lines (JSONL) with stable fields (timestamp, actor, action, resource, result, correlation IDs)
- Parquet (optional) for long-term cost/performance (where customers standardize on it)

h2. Export reliability and evidence
Exporter includes safeguards and evidence outputs:
- Cursor/checkpointing to avoid pagination gaps
- Metrics (Prometheus-style) including last-exported timestamp, event counts, failure counts
- Optional “gap detection” checks to flag missing windows

h2. Audit log RPO (cluster-loss window)
If audit logs are stored locally before export, cluster loss can create a loss window.
Best practice:
- Stream to SIEM with an RPO measured in minutes
- Run batch exports frequently enough to meet archival requirements

h1. Evidence pack: what Redwood can provide
Redwood-supported artifacts that customers commonly use for audits:
- Supported runbooks for backup/restore and audit export
- Backup job logs including backup IDs, timestamps, and outcome
- Backup manifest per backup (format version, component list, checksums)
- Signed manifest verification procedure (offline)
- Restore validation report outputs
- Exporter metrics and dashboards/alerts (or exported metrics snapshots)

Customer-owned complementary evidence typically includes:
- Tickets/change records showing scheduled execution and approval
- Storage lifecycle/immutability configuration screenshots or policy exports
- Access control/RBAC and HSM policy documentation (separation of duties)

h1. Least privilege and separation of duties
Recommended controls:
- Backup writer service account: minimum required read access + write-only (append-only where possible) to the backup target.
- Restore operator: can run restore workflows but should not directly access KEK unwrap permissions unless policy requires.
- HSM/KMS policy enforces separation: operators can initiate workflows; key custodians authorize unwrap.

h1. Air-gapped/offline bundle considerations
- Offline bundles are delivered as signed artifacts with checksums.
- No external network calls are required during install/upgrade in air-gapped mode.
- Telemetry is optional and should be disabled in air-gapped deployments.

h1. Operational FAQ (common customer questions)
- *Does the backup contain PHI?* Standard control-plane backups should not contain request payloads or prompt bodies. Audit logs can contain identifiers depending on configuration; treat audit archives according to your compliance classification.
- *Do you back up Kubernetes/etcd?* Not as part of Redwood control-plane backup. That is cluster recovery and remains customer-owned.
- *Can we prove backups/audit logs weren’t tampered with?* Use checksums + signed manifests; prefer immutable/WORM storage for audit logs.
- *What happens if KMS/HSM is down?* Backups fail by default; restores fail until unwrap capability is available.

h1. Change log
- 2026-03-10: Updated signatures guidance to cosign (offline) as primary; documented PKCS#11 HSM support; added JSONL+Parquet export options; clarified secure-by-default break-glass behavior.
- 2025-06-18: Added exporter gap detection and Prometheus metrics evidence recommendations.
- 2025-02-25: Initial publication based on regulated customer security reviews (on-prem backup/restore + audit retention requirements).

title: Dedicated Throughput SLO (Formal Definition)
author: Sean Gallagher
text:
## Purpose
This page defines the canonical Service Level Objective (SLO) for **Dedicated throughput** at Redwood Inference, including:
- SLI and metric semantics (tokens/sec as canonical; when requests/sec is used)
- Measurement windows and aggregation
- Exclusions and “not counted” conditions
- Burn-rate alerting and error budget policy
- Reporting requirements and ownership

This is the formal reference used by SRE, Observability, Infra/Fleet, and Product when implementing dashboards, alerts, incident classification, and customer-facing reporting.

## Scope
### Applies to
- **Dedicated deployments** (hosted in Redwood-managed infrastructure) with a **committed throughput floor** recorded in control plane configuration.
- Deployments where a customer has:
 - A pinned **model family + major version** (e.g., `llama-3.x`, `mistral-large.x`) and
 - A configured **max context length** within the supported range for the purchased hardware shape.

### Does not apply to
- Shared/Hosted API (non-dedicated) traffic
- Private (VPC/on-prem) deployments (separate SLOs)
- “Best-effort” Dedicated trials without a committed throughput floor

## Definitions
- **Deployment**: A Dedicated inference endpoint identified by `deployment_id` and bound to a region and hardware pool.
- **Route**: A logical API capability within a deployment (e.g., `chat.completions`, `completions`, `embeddings`). For this SLO, throughput is evaluated at the **deployment level**, with route breakdowns used for diagnostics.
- **Committed Throughput Floor (CTF)**: The minimum throughput Redwood commits to sustain for a deployment under defined conditions. Expressed as **tokens/sec** (canonical) or **requests/sec** (only for non-tokenized routes; see below).
- **Observed Throughput**: Throughput computed from Redwood-side metering and timing, scoped to eligible requests.
- **SLO Window**: The evaluation interval used to determine compliance for a point in time (5 minutes).
- **Error Budget**: The allowed fraction of SLO windows that can be below the committed floor over the compliance period.

## Canonical SLI and SLO
### Canonical throughput metric (SLI)
**SLI name:** Dedicated Throughput Floor Attainment

**SLI definition (per deployment):**
For each `deployment_id`, compute the fraction of eligible 5-minute windows in which the **observed output token rate** meets or exceeds the committed floor.

A 5-minute window is considered **good** if:
- `observed_tps(deployment_id, window) >= committed_tps(deployment_id) * 1.00`

A window is **bad** if:
- `observed_tps(deployment_id, window) < committed_tps(deployment_id) * 1.00`

**Why tokens/sec:** Token throughput is the most stable cross-model, cross-request indicator for generation routes and aligns with customer-perceived capacity for streaming/chat.

### SLO target
**SLO (per deployment):**
- **99.5%** of eligible 5-minute windows over a rolling **30-day** period must be good.

This implies an error budget of **0.5%** of windows per 30 days.

### Requests/sec as a secondary metric
Requests/sec may be used for:
- Non-generative routes where token accounting is not meaningful (rare in Dedicated scope), or
- As an internal diagnostic view (e.g., “QPS at steady state”) alongside tokens/sec.

If requests/sec is used, it is explicitly labeled as a **non-canonical** SLI and must not be substituted for compliance without SRE sign-off.

## Measurement semantics
### Windowing and aggregation
- **Evaluation window:** 5 minutes (tumbling windows)
- **Compliance period:** 30 days (rolling)
- **Aggregation level:** `deployment_id` (primary); `deployment_id + route + model` (debug)

### Observed throughput calculation (tokens/sec)
For each deployment and 5-minute window:
- `observed_tps = eligible_output_tokens / eligible_generation_wall_time_seconds`

Where:
- **eligible_output_tokens** counts output tokens generated for eligible requests whose generation occurs within the window.
- **eligible_generation_wall_time_seconds** is the sum of per-request generation durations for eligible requests, measured at Redwood’s gateway/runtime boundary.

Notes:
- We use **wall time spent generating** rather than total window duration to avoid penalizing low-utilization periods.
- This SLO measures our ability to serve when the customer is asking for capacity, not whether the customer sends enough traffic to saturate the deployment.

### Eligibility rules (what counts as “eligible” load)
A request is eligible if all of the following are true:
1) The request is accepted for processing (HTTP 2xx; not rejected by admission control).
2) The request targets a model and context configuration within the deployment’s contracted support bounds.
3) The request is not customer-throttled (see exclusions).
4) The request is not in a cold/warm-up exclusion window after provisioning or scale events (see exclusions).

### Streaming token accounting
For streaming responses:
- Output tokens are counted when emitted by the runtime, attributed to the originating request.
- We de-duplicate token counters to avoid double counting caused by stream chunk retries.

Operational note: streaming accounting semantics were corrected in **PR-19422** (“Fix throughput metric double counting streaming”). Any backfills or comparisons across that boundary must annotate the change.

### Batching and caching
- Continuous batching and prefix/KV caching are treated as implementation details and are inherently included in observed throughput.
- Customers may see throughput increases due to caching; this does not change the committed floor.
- SLO compliance is evaluated on Redwood-side metered tokens/time, not customer-side client timers.

## Exclusions (non-counted windows/requests)
Exclusions exist to avoid situations where the throughput floor is not meaningful, is externally constrained, or is not under Redwood’s control.

### Request-level exclusions
The following requests are excluded from both numerator and denominator:
- **Customer-side throttling or pacing** that prevents the deployment from being demand-saturated while measuring throughput (e.g., the customer sends traffic well below the committed floor and attempts to interpret low throughput as non-compliance).
- **Client disconnects / cancellations** before generation completes (where Redwood terminates work early).
- **Invalid requests** or requests that violate documented limits (e.g., context > supported max for the purchased shape, unsupported model version).
- **Customer-enforced caps** that materially reduce achievable throughput, including:
 - Very low `max_tokens` combined with high request overhead patterns (evaluated case-by-case; see “edge-case review” below)
 - Customer-set concurrency limits below recommended saturation settings

### Window-level exclusions
The following 5-minute windows may be excluded (removed from total window count) if conditions are met and are annotated in reporting:
- **Provisioning warm-up:** First **15 minutes** after a deployment becomes active.
- **Scale event warm-up:** First **10 minutes** after an approved scale-up/scale-down event that changes active capacity.
- **Planned maintenance:** Approved maintenance windows with customer notice, tracked via change calendar and incident tooling.

### Edge-case review (must be documented)
If a customer workload has atypical characteristics (e.g., extremely long contexts, highly skewed token distributions, tool-calling patterns with minimal output), the account team must request an SRE review to confirm:
- The correct committed floor unit (tokens/sec vs alternative) and
- The correct eligibility and saturation guidance.

## Saturation requirement (practical interpretation)
This SLO is designed to answer: “When the customer is **trying** to use their Dedicated capacity, do we deliver the committed throughput?”

Therefore, compliance reporting only considers periods where the deployment is **meaningfully loaded**.

We define “meaningfully loaded” for a window as:
- `eligible_generation_wall_time_seconds >= 120` seconds within the 5-minute window

If a window does not meet the load threshold, it is treated as **insufficient demand** and excluded from compliance (removed from total). This prevents underutilized deployments from producing misleading ‘low throughput’ windows.

## Metrics (source of truth)
### Required metric labels
All metrics used for SLO evaluation must include:
- `deployment_id`
- `region`
- `tier` (Standard/Plus/Premium)
- `model` (resolved model id)
- `route`

### Canonical metrics (Prometheus-style names)
The evaluator uses the following canonical signals (names reflect our current convention; see the metric registry for exact schemas):
- `ri_dedicated_output_tokens_total{deployment_id,...}`
- `ri_dedicated_generation_seconds_total{deployment_id,...}`
- `ri_dedicated_requests_accepted_total{deployment_id,...}`
- `ri_dedicated_requests_rejected_total{deployment_id,reason,...}`
- `ri_dedicated_streaming_chunks_total{deployment_id,...}` (diagnostic)

Control plane configuration source:
- `ri_dedicated_committed_tps{deployment_id}` (exported from deployment config service)

## SLO evaluation logic (reference)
For each deployment_id and 5-minute window:
1) Compute eligible tokens and eligible generation seconds.
2) If `eligible_generation_seconds < 120`, mark window as **excluded_insufficient_demand**.
3) Else compute `observed_tps = tokens / seconds`.
4) Window is good if `observed_tps >= committed_tps`.

The rolling SLO is:
- `good_windows / eligible_windows >= 0.995` over 30 days.

## Burn-rate alerting
We alert on rapid consumption of the 30-day error budget using burn-rate alerting.

### Parameters
- SLO target: 99.5% (error budget = 0.5%)
- Window size for good/bad decisions: 5 minutes
- Alerts evaluated per `deployment_id` (not fleet-wide)

### Paging vs ticketing
**Paging alerts (customer-impacting / requires oncall response):**
- **Fast burn:** burn rate >= **14x** over **1h** AND burn rate >= **6x** over **6h**
 - Interpretation: likely to exhaust error budget within ~2.1 days if sustained.

**Ticket alerts (investigate during business hours):**
- **Slow burn:** burn rate >= **3x** over **24h**
 - Interpretation: will exhaust error budget within ~10 days if sustained.

### Burn-rate computation
For a given lookback window `T`:
- `error_rate_T = bad_windows_T / eligible_windows_T`
- `burn_rate_T = error_rate_T / 0.005`

Notes:
- Excluded windows (maintenance, warm-up, insufficient demand) are removed from `eligible_windows_T`.
- If `eligible_windows_T` is below a minimum sample threshold (default: >= 6 eligible windows), burn-rate alerts are suppressed to reduce noise.

### Alert routing
- Page: `#eng-oncall` and oncall rotation “SRE - Inference Platform”
- Auto-attach runbook link: “Dedicated Throughput SLO Escalation”
- Auto-include fields: `deployment_id`, `customer_name` (if available), `tier`, `region`, current `observed_tps`, `committed_tps`, top rejection reasons, saturation signals

## Error budget policy (operational gates)
Error budget policy is evaluated per deployment_id.

### Policy thresholds (rolling 30-day)
- **Healthy:** >= 70% error budget remaining
 - Normal change velocity.
- **Watch:** 30–70% error budget remaining
 - Requires SRE review for changes that can impact serving performance (runtime upgrades, kernel toggles, routing policy changes).
- **At risk:** < 30% error budget remaining
 - Freeze performance-risky changes for affected tier/pool unless explicitly approved by SRE lead (Rafael Mendes) and Infra lead (Irene Choi).
- **Exhausted:** SLO below target
 - Treat as an incident for Dedicated customers; engage CS per escalation playbook; credits/remedies handled per commercial terms.

### What counts as “performance-risky” change
Examples:
- Runtime version upgrade, quantization profile change, kernel selection changes
- Routing/admission control changes affecting Dedicated pools
- Fleet capacity rebalancing that changes effective headroom

## Reporting
### Internal reporting (required)
- Daily SLO summary per deployment for SRE and Dedicated Product
- Weekly rollup by tier and region for capacity planning
- Incident linkage: SLO violations must link to incident tickets and postmortems where applicable

### Customer-facing reporting (when applicable)
- Provide a monthly compliance summary upon request for Plus/Premium tiers.
- Reports must:
 - State the committed throughput floor
 - State the achieved compliance (% good windows)
 - List excluded windows with category and timestamps (maintenance, warm-up)
 - Include a short explanation of the “insufficient demand” exclusion

## Ownership and responsibilities
- **SLO semantics + policy:** Sean Gallagher (SRE) (primary), Rafael Mendes (SRE lead)
- **Metric implementation:** Logan Wright (Telemetry), Aisha Bello (SRE implementation)
- **Dashboards:** Sergio Costa (Observability)
- **Committed floor configuration source:** Ethan Park (Control Plane)
- **Fleet capacity to support commitments:** Irene Choi (Infra), Vanessa Ortiz (Fleet)

title: Spotlight warmup lattice and tenant floor — PRD draft
author: Priya Iyer
text:
Summary:

This draft proposes the "Spotlight Warmup Lattice" (SWL) and Tenant Floor constructs to improve Dedicated capacity behavior for short-duration microbursts, long-running sustained ramps, and noisy neighbors. SWL is a layered warmup system that gives priority windows ("spotlights") to tenants who signal imminent load, while Tenant Floor guarantees a minimum compute baseline per committed customer. Combined with a soft-fidelity-swap and a bounded handoff-margin, this design aims to: reduce cold-start latency for bursty traffic, avoid wholesale eviction during demand spikes, and preserve predictable latency SLOs for committed tenants.

Problem statement and context:

Current Dedicated pool behavior suffers across three axes:
- Microburst cold-starts: customers with bursty traffic experience 200–800ms additional tail latency during container/gpu warmup.
- Noisy neighbors: sudden throughput surges from opportunistic tenants can starve SLO-sensitive customers.
- Coarse burst accounting: our existing credit/reservation model is binary (reserve vs burst) and forces blunt eviction or admission decisions, leading to customer surprise and operational toil.

We need a mechanism that is operationally simple for customers to reason about, low friction to adopt, and that gracefully degrades workload fidelity rather than forcing hard evictions.

Goals (measurable):
- Reduce median cold-start token latency for 95th-percentile burst events by 40% within 90 days of rollout.
- Keep committed-tenant 99th-percentile latency within SLA during 95% of detected burst windows.
- Reduce number of manual dedicated-pool escalations from capacity spikes by 60% (quarterly).
- Maintain <=5% monthly additional infra cost due to warm pools across high-utilization clusters.

Non-goals:
- Replace existing dedicated-credit economy completely (this is an additive capability).
- Solve arbitrary multi-region disaster scenarios in first iteration.

Design overview (high level):

1) Spotlight Warmup Lattice (SWL)
- Concept: SWL defines short-lived, small-capacity warm pockets (spotlights) that can be dynamically provisioned for tenants who provide a lightweight pre-warm signal (see API below). Spotlights are layered in a lattice of priority: Top spotlights (for high-SLA tenants) have faster pre-warm paths and lower admission latency; lower spotlights are opportunistic.
- Mechanics: when a tenant signals an upcoming burst (n seconds), the orchestrator attempts to allocate a spotlight slot from a local warm pool. If available, the spotlight binds a fraction of a GPU (vCPU/GPU-slice) and populates KV cache and model weights. The spotlight is timeboxed (default 120s) and will convert to sustained allocation only if burst continues and Tenant Floor economics permit.
- Size & placement: spotlight slots are small (e.g., 2–8 concurrent concurrency units, configurable per tenant class) and should preferentially reuse warm instances on the same host to preserve cache locality.

2) Tenant Floor
- Concept: a soft-minimum compute guarantee for committed customers (monthly reserved capacity). Tenant Floor is expressed as a percentile throughput floor (e.g., 50 rps or X tokens/s) and is enforced by priority admission and protected spotlights.
- Enforcement: when contention occurs, scheduler reduces spotlight/opportunistic lanes first, then preemptible slots, preserving Tenant Floor. Floors are negotiated at reservation time and appear in the customer console as a numeric baseline plus a latency target.

3) Hand-off Margin and Reconciliation
- Concept: to avoid hard failovers when a spotlight is borrowed or converted to sustained capacity, we introduce a "handoff-margin": a bounded borrowing allowance (e.g., up to 20% of a tenant's committed floor for short windows) with an accounting ledger that reconciles usage at billing/settlement.
- Safety: handoff-margin borrowing is rate-limited and time-limited (max continuous 10 minutes), and requires downstream signals to avoid cascading depletion (backpressure + telemetry validation).

4) Soft-fidelity-swap
- Concept: instead of evicting traffic outright under severe pressure, we provide configurable fidelity degrade paths per tenant: lighter model quantization, shorter gen lengths, or fallback to cached completions. Degrades are annotated in response metadata and reversible.

APIs and tenant UX (sketch):
- Pre-warm signal (lightweight): POST /v1/dedicated/prewarm { "tenant_id": "T-123", "window_s": 30, "priority": "spotlight" }
- Floor negotiation appears on console when creating/renewing reservations: "floor_tokens_per_sec" and "floor_latency_ms_p99"
- Visibility: new console tab "Warmup & Floors" showing active spotlights, time remaining, and handoff ledger. Alerts for reconciliation anomalies (e.g., unaccounted handoff > threshold).

Scheduler behavior (pseudo flow):
1. Receive prewarm signal; check local warm pool for free spotlight slots.
2. If free, allocate spotlight (populate caches), mark as reserved for Xs.
3. If no free local slots, attempt cross-host spotlight pin (lower priority).
4. If still none, consider ephemeral spin-up (if cold-start cost < penalty) or respond with estimated warm latency to caller.
5. On sustained high load, convert spotlight to sustained allocation if Tenant Floor and handoff-margin allow; else trigger fidelity-swap and queue advisory to tenant.

Operational runbook (ops-ready summary):
- Detection: SWL emits events when warm pools drop below threshold or when handoff debt crosses 60%.
- Auto-remediation: automated reprovisioning of warm pools across nodes based on heatmaps; temporary widening of spotlights to absorb bursts under low cluster utilization.
- Paging: on handoff ledger anomalies (e.g., >2 tenants borrowing >50% their floor concurrently), page SRE with playbook "swl-handback": revert spotlight conversions and activate fidelity-swap lane.

Cost model & billing reconciliation:
- Spotlights are cheaper per-minute than full dedicated reservation but have a small premium over pure burst usage because of warm pool residency cost.
- Handoff-margin borrowing is tracked as ledger entries; event-level reconciliation occurs daily and is surfaced as usage delta on invoice. Finance/Revenue teams will map handoff usage to soft credits or billable units depending on contract.

Observability and telemetry:
- New metrics: spotlight_alloc_rate, spotlight_success_rate, handoff_debt, tenant_floor_breaches, fidelity_swap_count.
- Dashboards: per-pool heatmap, tenant-level warm success, and a reconciliation report for billed vs ledgerled handoff.

Safety and edge cases:
- Misuse: noisy tenants issuing repeated prewarm signals could bloat warm pools. Mitigation: tokenized prewarm budget per tenant, backoff windows, and cost-based throttling enforced in the control plane.
- Multi-tenant cache thrash: prefer spotlight reuse and host affinity; fall back to disk cache or compressed KV if thrash observed.
- Cross-region signals: prewarm is local only; for cross-region warmup we surface a warning and provide estimate times.

Implementation roadmap (quarterly slices):
- Q1 (prototype): lightweight prewarm API, local spotlight scheduler, warm-pool microservice, basic console surface. Experiment on two dev clusters.
- Q2 (pilot): Tenant Floor proposal on 5 pilot customers, handoff-margin ledger, billing reconciliation prototype, basic fidelity-swap hooks.
- Q3 (scale): broader rollout to 25% Dedicated fleets with autoscale signals driving warm pool sizing, SLO alarms.
- Q4 (polish): regional warm balancing, configurable fidelity-swap policies per tenant, formal SLA updates and pricing artifacts.

Metrics to evaluate success (examples):
- Reduction in cold-start latency for pre-warmed requests (p50/p95/p99).
- Fraction of bursts fully absorbed by spotlight without fidelity-swap.
- Handback debt outstanding and reconciliation latency.
- Customer reported incidents related to evictions.

Open questions & tradeoffs:
1. How large should default spotlight slots be? (2–8 concurrency units is initial guess). Need perf experiments across model families.
2. Billing semantics: should handoff-margin be billable immediately or reconciled monthly? Finance preference required.
3. Security: does cross-tenant warm pool reuse introduce data leakage risk? (We believe not if process isolation + salt per-tenant caches maintained; security review required.)
4. UX clarity: how do we present probabilistic warm guarantees without confusing customers? Need controlled language and examples in console.

Appendix: short experiment plan
- Run A/B: on dev cluster A enable SWL prewarm for selected tenants; cluster B baseline. Simulate 10k microbursts/day, measure cold-start delta, spotlight hit rate, and fidelity-swap triggers.
- Perf matrix: run across gtx-family models, Llama2/Redwood-medium and quantized variants to measure warm residency memory overhead and average spin-up time.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally opinionated: SWL combines operational shortcuts (small warm pools) with conservative economics (handoff ledger) to avoid changing our whole credit model. If reviewers prefer a pure-market model (auctioning spotlights), note that adds complexity for initial launch and likely increases latency for buyers.
- Please review linked eng ticket ENG-4321 for scheduler proto and the infra PR that adds warm-pool service.

Action items for next week:
- Marco: perf microbench for 3 model families (due 2025-01-20).
- Aisha: draft UI copy for "Warmup & Floors" console (due 2025-01-24).
- Kenji: security checklist and isolation threat model (due 2025-01-27).
- Priya: finalize pilot customer list and update pilot SOW draft (due 2025-01-30).

---
Informal notes (brainstorm fragments):
- Consider "credit escrow" where marketplace-like lending ensures spotlights are fungible across tenants with opt-in pooling.
- Long-tail thought: use model-splitting (serve heads on tiny CPU containers while GPU warms) to reduce perceived latency; requires frontend changes.
- Keep console simple: show 3 numbers: active spotlights, floor utilization, and handoff debt.

End of draft.

title: Calibration Lab Notebook: Crosswalk for Multi-Workload Evaluations
author: Nadia Cortez
text:
Overview

This lab notebook describes a practical crosswalk for calibrating evaluation fidelity across heterogeneous workloads. It documents provenance mapping, sampling budgets, annotation/labeler contracts, quantization interaction checks, and regression-triage thresholds so that model onboarding, shadow validations, and periodic audits share a single source of truth. The target audience is applied-ML engineers, evaluators, and platform owners who operate the eval harness and manage model promotion.

Why this document exists

- Multiple teams run separate evaluations (shadow, canary, offline suites) that produce conflicting signals.
- Differences in prompt selection, batch sizes, tokenization, and quant profiles create non-trivial delta in measured metrics.
- When regressions occur we need a reproducible path from a failing customer slice back to a minimal repro evaluation.

Scope

This notebook covers:
1) A canonical calibration matrix that maps workload characteristics to evaluation settings.
2) Sampling and budget rules for each evaluation class (smoke, fidelity, longtail, stress).
3) Annotator/labeler contract templates for behavioral and safety checks.
4) Quantization interaction checklist to detect artifacts introduced by lower-precision inference.
5) Regression triage triggers and triage playbook cross-reference.

Calibration matrix (canonical)

The matrix below captures recommended eval harness config per workload fingerprint. Use these values as defaults; deviation requires a documented justification.

- Workload fingerprint: short-chat-interactive (median prompt tokens < 40)
 - Eval class: smoke + micro-fidelity
 - Batch size: 1–4 (preserve latency SLOs)
 - KV cache: warm and cold runs (50/50 split)
 - Quant profile: FP16 baseline + int8 sanity
 - Sampling: stratified across top-10 intents, 200 samples per intent

- Workload fingerprint: long-context-recall (median prompt tokens 1024–4096)
 - Eval class: longtail + stability
 - Batch size: 2–8 (prefer small to avoid OOM)
 - KV cache: forced cold starts only
 - Quant profile: FP16 + mixed-precision candidate
 - Sampling: focused slices by context-length bins, 500 total samples

- Workload fingerprint: high-throughput-embeddings
 - Eval class: throughput-fidelity
 - Batch size: 256–1024 (in harness simulated batched producer)
 - Quant profile: int8 quantized embedding kernels
 - Sampling: synthetic and real mix, 10k vectors for perf, 1k for embedding drift

- Workload fingerprint: instruction-following-open-domain
 - Eval class: fidelity + safety-sentinel
 - Batch size: 8–32 for cost-fidelity tradeoffs
 - Quant profile: FP16 baseline, int8 must pass acceptance checks
 - Sampling: balanced across instruction templates, 1k–2k samples for release candidates

Sampling and budget rules

- Smoke evaluations: max 1k tokens / model-run, nightly. Purpose: surface obvious regressions.
- Fidelity evaluations: 1–5k labeled examples depending on release risk (higher for public-facing models).
- Longtail/stress: heavy but targeted — only run when promoting to Dedicated or Private or when telemetry indicates increased failure rate for a slice. Budget: 10–50k calls per month per model family.
- Canary/shadow: mirror production traffic for 24–72 hours with a 1:1000 sample ratio for high-volume customers; increase to 1:100 for critical enterprise tenants during initial onboarding.

Annotator / labeler contract (template)

The annotator contract ensures consistency across teams and time. Key fields:
- Objective: the metric(s) being labeled (e.g., helpfulness, instruction-follow correctness, hallucination_present boolean).
- Annotation schema version: semantic version string (e.g., v1.4.0).
- Inter-annotator agreement target: Cohen's kappa >= 0.75 for binary judgments, Krippendorff alpha >= 0.7 for multi-class.
- Minimum context: full prompt + previous 2 turns for multi-turn judgments.
- Labeler qualification: pass gold set at >= 85% before labeling.
- Escalation: ambiguous or safety-tagged items -> safety review queue within 24 hours.

Checklist: quantization interaction tests

Quantization often changes distributional behavior. The following automated checks must be part of the promotion pipeline whenever a quantized runtime is evaluated:
- Deterministic delta check: compare token-level logprobs across FP16 and candidate quantized run on 1k anchor prompts. Threshold: median KL divergence per-token < 0.02.
- Output-stability check: run 3 seeds with same prompts through quantized runtime; token-level edit distance variance threshold < 6% relative to FP16.
- Behavioral regression test: critical intent set (100 seeds) must not drop intent accuracy by > 2 percentage points.
- Safety-sentinel pass rate: must meet the same guardrail thresholds used in production (see quality-guardrails page).
- KV cache integrity: ensure cached state is consistent between FP16 and quantized runtimes on a 200-case sequence replay test.

Operational procedures: from failing telemetry to minimal repro

1) Triage trigger
 - When production telemetry shows a slice breach (response_stability_index delta > 0.12 OR latency P95 regression > 1.5x baseline) an incident ticket is opened by telemetry-scan.
2) Snapshot collection (owner: eval-harness-oncall)
 - Export 500 example sessions from the offending slice (preserve request metadata, model_version, routing_policy).
 - Record runtime config: batch_size, quant_profile, GPU kernel selection, model weights hash.
3) Prioritized repro path (owner: applied-ml-evals)
 - Re-run samples across three environments: FP16 baseline, candidate quantized runtime, and production runtime at same model_version.
 - Use deterministic seeds and tokenization flags identical to production.
4) Root cause checks
 - Diff outputs using semantic similarity metrics (ROUGE-L, BERTScore, normalized edit distance) and token-prob divergence.
 - If differences map to quantization-induced divergence, escalate to quant-profiles team.
 - If differences map to prompt drift or new user-intent patterns, create a prompt augmentation backlog item.
5) Remediation and promotion
 - If regression is confirmed and impacts SLOs, revert rollout or apply fallback routing policy (route to FP16 variant).
 - Author a regression triage summary with minimal repro steps and attach to the incident.

CLI and YAML examples (canonical configs)

# Example eval harness run (shell)
# Run fidelity suite with int8 candidate profile

- command: |
 eval-harness run \
 --suite fidelity \
 --model redwood-xl-2 \
 --quant-profile int8-candidate-v2 \
 --batch-size 8 \
 --seed 42 \
 --out results/redwood-xl-2-int8-v2.json

# Example minimal promotion YAML (eval job)
---
name: promotion-eval
model: redwood-xl-2
variant: int8-candidate-v2
suite: fidelity
samples: 2000
checks:
 - name: token-kl-threshold
 metric: median_token_kl
 threshold: 0.02
 - name: intent-accuracy-drop
 metric: intent_accuracy_delta
 threshold: -0.02
rollout_actions:
 on_fail: fallback-to: fp16-baseline
 on_pass: proceed-to-canary

Ownership, SLAs and metrics to monitor

- Owners: applied-ml-evals (primary), runtime-quant (secondary), platform-oncall (escalation).
- SLOs for evaluation platform: job_success_rate >= 99% (daily), median_run_time for fidelity suite < 90 minutes.
- Key telemetry: response_stability_index, intent_accuracy_delta, median_token_kl, safety_sentinel_fail_rate.

Notes on reproducibility and provenance

- Every eval job must attach an immutable provenance blob: model_weights_hash, tokenizer_version, runtime_kernels, and hardware SKU. Store in S3 under eval-provenance/YYYY/MM/DD/{job_id}.json.
- Use the eval-harness --provenance flag to auto-capture environment metadata.

Appendix: quick checklists

Pre-promotion checklist (applied-ml-evals):
- [ ] Smoke pass on nightly harness
- [ ] Fidelity suite within thresholds
- [ ] Quantization interaction tests green
- [ ] Annotator gold-set agreement verified
- [ ] Provenance blob stored and linked

On regression detection (first 24 hours):
- [ ] Snapshot exported
- [ ] Repro across FP16, quant candidate, production run
- [ ] Triage summary created and linked to incident
- [ ] Rollback or routing policy applied if SLO breached

References and related reading

- See eval-mesh-and-workload-fingerprinting for workload fingerprints.
- See quant-profile-synthesis-and-safety-playbook for quant candidate lifecycle.
- See regression-triage playbooks for detailed incident runbooks.

Contact and feedback

For questions or to propose changes to this calibration notebook open a PR against the confluence source doc or ping the applied-ml-evals slack channel (#applied-evals).
