title: Northpeak Analytics - procurement via AWS Marketplace (security + next steps)
author: Stephanie Nguyen
text:
Northpeak Analytics wants to purchase Redwood Inference through AWS Marketplace (preferably via private offer) so spend can count toward their AWS commitments. They asked detailed security questionnaire items (SOC 2 posture, encryption/KMS, retention, audit logs, data residency, incident response, SSO/RBAC) and clarified shared responsibility for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Redwood outlined marketplace subscription → entitlement → Redwood org provisioning flow and noted typical entitlement propagation delays. Next steps include sending the marketplace security packet, confirming which SKU matches their target deployment (Hosted initially; Dedicated later), and starting an AWS private offer request with required buyer details.

Why AWS Marketplace purchase path (EDP / committed spend) and private offer vs public offer
SKU fit: Hosted API now, Dedicated capacity later; what is and isn't supported via Marketplace
Metering and billing dimensions: tokens/requests, reporting cadence, invoice visibility
Security questionnaire: SOC 2 / ISO alignment, encryption in transit/at rest, KMS options, audit logs, retention controls, data residency
Onboarding: subscription → entitlement validation → org linking → first API key → first call
Support & escalation: SLA expectations for enterprise + marketplace customers
Timeline: internal approvals, legal/security review, and target pilot start

Redwood (Stephanie): Email AWS Marketplace private offer intake checklist (buyer AWS account ID(s), preferred region(s), start date, term, committed spend) by 2026-01-23
Redwood (Naomi): Share marketplace security documentation pack + evidence pointers (SOC 2 report access process) by 2026-01-24
Redwood (Markus): Schedule a 45-min technical deep dive on audit logs + VPC options and walk through onboarding flow in console by 2026-01-29
Northpeak (Dana/Tom): Confirm whether purchase must be via AWS private offer and if they need the spend to apply to EDP; provide procurement timeline by 2026-01-24
Northpeak (Ravi/Megan): Send their standard security questionnaire and required clauses (DPA, breach notification) by 2026-01-24

Send Northpeak the security packet link and the short-form security FAQ for Marketplace buyers
Northpeak to provide AWS Marketplace buyer info so Redwood can draft a private offer
Book technical deep dive focused on audit logging, retention controls, and AWS Marketplace entitlement troubleshooting
Follow-up call to confirm pilot scope (models, expected TPM, latency targets) and pick Hosted vs Dedicated SKU

Meeting header
Date: 2026-01-22
Time: 11:00am - 11:52am PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai
Title: Northpeak Analytics - procurement via AWS Marketplace (security + next steps)

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Stephanie Nguyen (AE), Markus Klein (Solutions Eng), Naomi Feldman (Security/Compliance)
Northpeak Analytics: Dana Willis (Procurement), Ravi Deshpande (Security), Megan Cho (Platform Eng), Tom Alvarez (FinOps)

Auto-summary (generated)
- Customer prefers AWS Marketplace purchasing to simplify vendor onboarding and apply spend to AWS commitments.
- Customer asked for SOC 2 status, encryption/KMS, audit logs, retention, residency, and SSO/RBAC details.
- Redwood described Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment options and shared responsibility boundaries.
- Redwood described onboarding flow and noted entitlement propagation delays can be a few minutes.

Questions captured
- Do you support customer-managed KMS keys for Hosted, or only for Private/VPC?
- What is retained from prompts/outputs by default and can we set retention to 0?
- What audit log events are available and can they be exported to Splunk?
- Can we constrain processing to us-east-1 only?
- How does metering show up in AWS Marketplace billing (dimensions, timing)?

Transcript
[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Alright, looks like we’re at time. Thanks everyone for joining. This is Stephanie from Redwood Inference. Markus is on with me as well, and Naomi from our security team may hop in—she’s here now actually.
[00:12] Dana Willis: Hi. Dana, procurement. Thanks.
[00:14] Megan Cho: Hey, Megan, platform engineering.
[00:16] Ravi Deshpande: Ravi, security and risk.
[00:18] Tom Alvarez: Tom, FinOps.
[00:21] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Goal today is pretty specific: you all want to buy through AWS Marketplace, and we want to make sure the listing, the SKU, and the security packet lines up with what your procurement and security review expects.

[00:38] Dana Willis: Yep. We have a policy basically—if it can go through Marketplace, it should. Otherwise it’s like, months.
[00:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. And is that primarily because you want it to count toward an EDP, or it’s just the vendor onboarding workflow?
[00:56] Tom Alvarez: Both. The spend counting is the big one. We also like the consolidated invoicing.

[01:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Makes sense. For AWS Marketplace there’s generally public offers and private offers. For enterprise we usually do a private offer so we can align to term, committed spend, and any guardrails. But we can do pay-as-you-go too, depending.
[01:20] Dana Willis: We’d prefer private offer. It’s simpler on our side. Also our legal team likes to see something with an order form.

[01:30] Markus Klein: And from the technical side it doesn’t change your integration—same API endpoints, same org in our console. Marketplace is basically procurement + entitlement + metering.

[01:41] Megan Cho: Can we talk through that entitlement thing? We had a not-great experience with another vendor where the subscription didn’t provision anything for like two days.
[01:51] Markus Klein: Yep, totally. So the flow is: you subscribe in AWS Marketplace, AWS sends an entitlement signal to our entitlement service, we validate it, then you either create a new Redwood org or link to an existing org. From there you generate an API key and you’re off.
[02:09] Markus Klein: There can be propagation delays—usually minutes, not days. We also have a manual fallback where support can verify the subscription ID and force a sync if needed.
[02:21] Dana Willis: So if it’s delayed, who do we contact? AWS or you?
[02:26] Stephanie Nguyen: Start with us. We can tell if we’ve received the entitlement. If we haven’t, we can advise on AWS steps, but typically we can resolve faster on our side.

[02:39] Ravi Deshpande: Before we go too deep, I have a list of security questions. Some are standard. I’m going to rattle them off.
[02:46] Stephanie Nguyen: Please do. Naomi is here to help as well.

[02:51] Ravi Deshpande: First: do you have SOC 2 Type II and can you provide the report under NDA, or via a portal?
[02:59] Naomi Feldman: Yes. We’re SOC 2 Type II. We share the full report through our trust portal with access control. For Marketplace reviews we also provide a security overview packet that references the relevant controls without oversharing.
[03:14] Ravi Deshpande: Okay. Next: ISO 27001?
[03:17] Naomi Feldman: We’re aligned to ISO 27001 controls; we can provide our statement and program overview. If you need a specific certificate, we can clarify what’s current in the packet. But SOC 2 is the main attestation we provide today.

[03:33] Ravi Deshpande: Encryption: in transit and at rest. TLS versions.
[03:37] Naomi Feldman: In transit: TLS 1.2+ for API and console. At rest: encryption on our storage layers. For Hosted, we manage keys via our cloud KMS. For Private deployments in your VPC and for certain Dedicated configurations, we can support customer-managed keys depending on architecture.
[03:56] Megan Cho: So Hosted can’t do BYOK? Like customer KMS key?
[04:01] Naomi Feldman: For the standard Hosted multi-tenant control plane, it’s provider-managed KMS keys. If customer-managed key is a hard requirement, we usually recommend Private (VPC) where key management and network boundaries are customer-controlled.

[04:17] Ravi Deshpande: Data retention: do you store prompts and completions? If yes, default retention and can we set it to zero.
[04:26] Naomi Feldman: Great question. By default we retain limited request metadata for operational purposes and abuse prevention, and we do not use customer data to train models. For content retention—prompts/outputs—we have configuration knobs depending on the product mode. We can support reduced retention and in some cases “no storage” modes with logging disabled except what’s required for billing and security.
[04:49] Ravi Deshpande: “In some cases” worries me.
[04:52] Naomi Feldman: Totally fair. Let’s make it concrete: for Hosted, there’s a baseline operational logging layer. We can configure content logging off for enterprise tenants, and we can scope retention windows. For Private, you can set retention policies more strictly since data paths are under your control plane. We’ll follow up with the specific retention matrix and what is configurable today.
[05:16] Stephanie Nguyen: We have a marketplace-facing “data handling and retention” doc we can send after the call. It spells out defaults and options.

[05:28] Tom Alvarez: From FinOps: what data is required for billing? Are you measuring tokens? requests? Both?
[05:34] Markus Klein: Metering is by usage dimensions that map to tokens for generation and embeddings units, depending on SKU. In AWS Marketplace it shows up as dimensions—like “tokens” or “1k tokens” style—then AWS bills you. Internally we reconcile to your org usage so your console usage report matches the invoice.
[05:57] Tom Alvarez: How quickly does it show in AWS cost explorer?
[06:00] Markus Klein: It’s not real-time. Typically you’ll see the line item and usage with some delay—hours-ish. We’ll confirm the exact cadence but it’s the standard Marketplace metering behavior.

[06:13] Dana Willis: And SKUs—are we buying Hosted, Dedicated, Private? I saw three things in the deck.
[06:19] Stephanie Nguyen: Right now what we’re proposing is: start with Hosted API via Marketplace for the pilot, and if you need predictable throughput or isolation, we can move you to Dedicated capacity. Private is VPC/on-prem and is usually a bigger procurement and architecture step.
[06:36] Megan Cho: We likely want Dedicated eventually. For the pilot, Hosted is okay, but we’ll need to pin a model version and have some fallback. Also region restriction.
[06:46] Markus Klein: Hosted supports pinned model versions and rollout policies. Region-wise, we can route you to a region. We’ll check which regions are available for your target compliance needs.

[07:02] Ravi Deshpande: Data residency: we have workloads that must stay US. Sometimes specifically us-east-1.
[07:09] Naomi Feldman: For Hosted, we can support regional processing commitments within available regions. If you require strict single-region, we can set policy to keep requests in that region and not fail over cross-region unless you explicitly enable it. For Private in your VPC, it’s inherently in your chosen region.
[07:30] Ravi Deshpande: We need that in writing.
[07:32] Naomi Feldman: Understood. We can include it in the order form / private offer exhibits and reference the data handling doc.

[07:42] Megan Cho: Another question: do you do SSO? SAML? RBAC?
[07:47] Markus Klein: Yes. SSO/SAML for enterprise orgs, role-based access control for the console, API keys scoped by org and project. Naomi can speak to audit controls.
[07:58] Naomi Feldman: Yep. We have audit logging for admin actions—like user invites, role changes, API key creation, model deployments, and policy changes. We also log auth events. Export options include API export; we also have patterns to ship into SIEM like Splunk via your pipeline.
[08:21] Ravi Deshpande: Is audit log immutable? Like WORM storage.
[08:26] Naomi Feldman: We maintain integrity controls; for WORM/immutable retention, the cleanest approach is exporting to your SIEM / log archive where you enforce immutability. We can help with the integration guidance.

[08:42] Tom Alvarez: Sorry, going back—if we buy Hosted via Marketplace, do we get a committed spend discount, or is it always on-demand pricing?
[08:50] Stephanie Nguyen: With private offer we can do a committed spend construct even for usage-based. AWS supports that via contract terms, and we map it to your usage in Redwood. The details depend on your target monthly/annual commit.
[09:06] Dana Willis: We’ll need term options, 12 months standard.
[09:09] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep.

[09:12] Megan Cho: Can you compare to Bedrock? We’re getting pressure to “just use Bedrock.”
[09:18] Markus Klein: Totally. Bedrock is convenient if you want managed access to certain models. Where Redwood tends to win is when you care about serving economics—latency, throughput, routing, and more control over model versions and performance tuning. Also we support Dedicated and Private where you want isolation or VPC control. But we can keep that more for the technical deep dive.

[09:41] Ravi Deshpande: Incident response: breach notification timelines?
[09:45] Naomi Feldman: We have an incident response program with defined severity and notification processes. Specific timelines are typically handled contractually. We can align to your requirements and include those in the enterprise terms.
[09:58] Ravi Deshpande: Subprocessors—do you have a list?
[10:01] Naomi Feldman: Yes. We maintain a subprocessor list and can provide it. For Hosted, we operate the service; we also have standard cloud infrastructure providers. For Private, your infrastructure reduces the scope of subprocessors.

[10:16] Dana Willis: Legal terms—do we sign your paper or AWS paper?
[10:21] Stephanie Nguyen: Marketplace uses AWS terms as the transaction backbone, but we typically attach our EULA / service terms and any data processing terms as part of the private offer or accompanying exhibits. We can also do a separate DPA if needed.

[10:39] Tom Alvarez: Can Marketplace spend roll up into our EDP? That’s the whole reason.
[10:44] Dana Willis: It should, if it’s an eligible private offer.
[10:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Generally yes, but the exact eligibility is your AWS agreement. We’ll structure it in the standard way. If needed, we can loop in our AWS partner manager to confirm mechanics.

[11:03] Megan Cho: Switching gears: what’s the actual onboarding steps? Like if I subscribe today, what do I do next.
[11:10] Markus Klein: After subscribe, you go to Redwood console. There’s a marketplace entry point. It asks you to connect your subscription—sometimes it’s automatic, sometimes you paste a subscription identifier. Then you either create a new org or link to your existing org. Then create an API key. Then do a test call. We have a quickstart app and docs.
[11:33] Megan Cho: And if we already have a Redwood org from a prior trial?
[11:36] Markus Klein: You can link it. That’s one of the edge cases. The UI will ask “use existing org” and verify you have admin rights.

[11:49] Ravi Deshpande: And multi-subscription? Like different business units.
[11:52] Markus Klein: Supported, but we need to decide if you want multiple subscriptions tied to one org or separate orgs. Finance reporting tends to be simpler with one org and tags/projects; procurement sometimes wants separation. We can advise.

[12:08] Stephanie Nguyen: Dana, can I ask: what’s your target timeline for approval and pilot start?
[12:14] Dana Willis: If we can get the security review done in two weeks, we could do a pilot in February. But it depends on Ravi.
[12:22] Ravi Deshpande: Yeah, I need the packet and ideally the SOC 2 report access, plus answers on retention and residency.

[12:31] Naomi Feldman: We can get you the marketplace security packet immediately, and we’ll start the trust portal access process for the full report. Usually that’s same day once we have the right contacts.
[12:44] Ravi Deshpande: Ok.

[12:46] Tom Alvarez: Also need pricing dimensions. If it’s tokens, we need to map that to budgets.
[12:52] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll include in the private offer: the dimension names and what they correspond to, plus an example usage scenario.

[13:01] Megan Cho: One technical risk: we need to ensure prompts aren’t used for training. I know you said it, but we need it contractually.
[13:07] Naomi Feldman: Yes. We do not train on customer data. That commitment is in our terms, and we can highlight it.

[13:16] Speaker 1: (crosstalk) And do you log the prompts for debugging?
[13:19] Naomi Feldman: Not by default for enterprise configurations; we can disable content logging. There may be minimal transient processing in memory to serve the request, but that’s not persisted as “training data.”
[13:34] Megan Cho: Sorry, just to be clear, “transient in memory” is fine. We care about storage and later human access.
[13:41] Naomi Feldman: Exactly. And access controls—least privilege, audit trails, and we can explain our internal access policy.

[13:56] Ravi Deshpande: Okay, continuing questionnaire: Do you support customer-owned VPC endpoints, PrivateLink.
[14:03] Markus Klein: For Private deployments in your VPC, yes. For Hosted, we can discuss private connectivity options; typically Hosted is over public internet with TLS, but for strict requirements, Private is the route.
[14:18] Megan Cho: That probably means Private is in scope later.
[14:21] Markus Klein: Yep, we can phase it. Pilot on Hosted; then if you need VPC-only, we do Private.

[14:30] Dana Willis: If we start Hosted through Marketplace, can we later move to Private through Marketplace too?
[14:35] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes, we can structure it as an additional SKU or an expansion. Sometimes Private is better as a separate contract depending on complexity, but we can do Marketplace if that’s your policy.

[14:49] Tom Alvarez: Another question: support levels. Do we get an SLA if purchased via Marketplace?
[14:55] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes. Support and SLA are based on the plan/SKU, not the procurement channel. Marketplace customers get the same enterprise support terms.

[15:05] (brief silence)

[15:07] Stephanie Nguyen: Maybe it’s useful if we summarize SKU options in plain English.
[15:11] Markus Klein: Hosted: shared infrastructure, fastest start, usage based. Dedicated: reserved GPU pool, predictable throughput, isolation. Private: control plane in your network, customer-managed networking and optionally keys, strongest residency/control.
[15:28] Megan Cho: For our pilot, Hosted. For prod, likely Dedicated, and for regulated workloads maybe Private.

[15:38] Ravi Deshpande: And audit logs for Hosted—are those included or add-on.
[15:43] Markus Klein: Baseline audit logs are included for enterprise orgs; advanced retention/export may be tied to an add-on. We’ll confirm what’s standard vs add-on.
[15:54] Naomi Feldman: Regardless, we can ensure the events you need are captured. The question is retention period and export mechanism.

[16:06] Dana Willis: Okay, so next steps: we need a private offer draft and the security packet.
[16:11] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes. To draft a private offer we’ll need: your AWS account ID(s) that will accept the offer, desired start date, term length, any committed spend target, and the region constraints. Also who signs.
[16:28] Dana Willis: I can send the account ID. Tom can send spend targets.
[16:32] Tom Alvarez: Yeah, I’ll send a ballpark. We’re thinking low six figures annual for pilot-to-prod, but I need to validate.

[16:42] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s helpful. We can propose a structure: initial committed spend with overage at list, or a tiered discount. We’ll align with how AWS wants it expressed.

[16:56] Megan Cho: Can we schedule the technical deep dive? I want to see the console onboarding and error states, because that’s where vendors fall over.
[17:05] Markus Klein: Yes. I’ll send a couple times. We can show the marketplace entry point, entitlement check, and what happens if it’s not found.

[17:16] Ravi Deshpande: I’d also like to see the audit log events list.
[17:19] Naomi Feldman: We can cover that. We have a doc that enumerates event types. We’ll include it in the packet.

[17:27] Stephanie Nguyen: Anything else on procurement mechanics?
[17:30] Dana Willis: Not right now. But one caution: our legal will ask about data processing terms. Please include DPA options.
[17:37] Stephanie Nguyen: Will do.

[17:40] (topic shift)

[17:42] Megan Cho: Random question: do you support function calling / tools? Some providers call it “tool use.”
[17:48] Markus Klein: Yes, we support tool calling patterns and structured output. Model-dependent, but the API supports it.

[17:57] Tom Alvarez: And usage analytics—do we get per-project breakdown?
[18:01] Markus Klein: Yes, the console has usage by org/project, model, route, latency, token breakdown. That’s part of why reconciliation with Marketplace invoices is easier.

[18:15] Ravi Deshpande: Okay I think I have what I need. Send the packet and we’ll review.

[18:22] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Before we drop, quick recap:
[18:26] Stephanie Nguyen: 1) We’ll send the AWS private offer intake checklist and start drafting an offer. 2) Naomi will send the marketplace security documentation pack and start SOC 2 report access via trust portal. 3) Markus will schedule a technical deep dive to walk through audit logs, retention controls, and the Marketplace onboarding flow.
[18:47] Stephanie Nguyen: From your side, Dana/Tom will send AWS account IDs and procurement timeline, Ravi/Megan will send the questionnaire and any must-have clauses.

[18:58] Dana Willis: Sounds right.
[19:00] Ravi Deshpande: Yep.
[19:01] Megan Cho: Works.
[19:03] Tom Alvarez: Good.

[19:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up by end of day tomorrow with the links and next steps.

(Transcript continues with light scheduling chatter; recording ends.)

title: Incident Response: Communications, RBAC & Evidence Preservation Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Overview

Purpose:
This playbook standardizes how Redwood responds to security incidents that require coordinated communications, RBAC control changes, and legally defensible evidence preservation. It combines technical runbook steps, communications templates, and an evidence packaging workflow to ensure traceability for audits and regulators.

Intended audience:
Security responders, SREs, incident commanders, platform engineers, legal, and product owners.

Scope and exclusions:
- Applies to incidents that trigger data access investigations, suspected exfiltration, privilege escalation, or audit log tampering.
- Excludes routine operational alerts that do not indicate unauthorized access (see monitoring playbook).

Goals and success criteria:
- Preserve a verifiable, tamper-evident evidence set within 4 hours of incident declaration.
- Implement emergency RBAC changes within 30 minutes of classification when needed.
- Notify internal stakeholders and legal within SLA: 60 minutes for high-severity incidents.

Owners and roles

- Incident Commander (IC): directs response, approves communications. (Security on-call)
- Evidence Custodian: owns evidence capture and packaging. (Security forensics)
- RBAC Owner: performs role/permission adjustments and documents changes. (IAM team)
- SRE Lead: performs containment actions on infra and app tiers.
- Legal / Privacy: assesses legal hold and regulator notification requirements.
- Comms Lead: drafts internal and external messaging.

Pre-incident configuration checklist

1) RBAC mapping inventory (maintain as a living table in the IAM repo):
| Role | Scope | Owner | Emergency revocation contact |
|---|---|---|---|
| svc-platform-admin | Cluster-wide, production | IAM Team | iam-oncall@redwood.ai |
| redwood-security-ops | Incident response privileges | Security | sec-oncall@redwood.ai |
| analytics-readonly | Data lake read-only | Data Platform | data-platform@redwood.ai |

2) Audit logging baseline configuration (minimum):
- All API gateway requests: request_id, user_id, client_ip, headers subset, timestamp, route, response_code.
- Auth events (success/failure): user, method, source, timestamp, reason.
- Privileged actions: role changes, token creations/revocations, service-account key rotations.

3) Retention and integrity controls:
- Short-term hot logs: 90 days (fast-query SLA).
- Long-term archive: 7 years (WORM-backed storage where required).
- Log immutability: Writes to the archive are S3 Object Lock enabled; HMAC checksums recorded in the evidence index.

Incident classification matrix

Severity | Trigger examples | Immediate RBAC action
---|---|---
P1 / Critical | Confirmed data exfiltration or active lateral movement | Revoke affected service-account keys + block user sessions
P2 / High | Suspected privilege escalation or abnormal admin activity | Scoped role removal, require reauth via MFA
P3 / Medium | Unusual access but no signs of compromise | Increased monitoring, session token refresh

Detection & triage (first 60 minutes)

1) Declare incident and assign roles. IC posts incident page and sets severity.
2) Triage checklist (run in parallel):
- Evidence Custodian: snapshot current audit streams and store in evidence bucket with immutable flag. CLI example:
 - aws s3 cp s3://audit-stream/current/ s3://evidence-bucket/INC-<id>/raw/ --recursive --storage-class STANDARD_IA --metadata status=sealed
 - Record object checksums: sha256sum *.log > manifest.sha256
- RBAC Owner: list recent privileged changes: run:
 - gcloud logging read "resource.type=project AND protoPayload.methodName:('SetIamPolicy' OR 'CreateServiceAccountKey')" --limit 500 --format json > recent-privileged.json
- SRE Lead: isolate suspected hosts/subnets (apply network ACLs or kill sessions).
- IC: notify Legal and Comms.

Evidence preservation step-by-step (technical)

1. Snapshot live logs and metadata:
- Capture current offsets/checkpoints for streaming systems (Kafka):
 - kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server broker:9092 --describe --group audit-consumer > kafka-checkpoints.txt
- Snapshot cloud metadata: instance list, IAM policy versions, active sessions.

2. Create an evidence container (one per incident):
- Naming convention: INC-<YYYYMMDD>-<short-id> (e.g., INC-20270208-7c4f)
- Location: s3://evidence-bucket/INC-20270208-7c4f/ with Object Lock enabled and retention date set to policy (7 years when required).

3. Compute and record cryptographic integrity proofs:
- For every file added, produce sha256 and store in manifest.sha256. Example manifest entry:
 - 3f786850e387550fdab836ed7e6dc881de23001b 2027-02-08T14:12:00Z logs/gateway-2027-02-08T14:00.log
- Sign the manifest using the Evidence Custodian's GPG key and store signature as manifest.sha256.sig.

4. Freeze relevant access controls:
- Create a temporary deny policy applied to affected roles/users. Example (pseudo-YAML):
 - deny: true
 principals: [user:alice@redwood.ai, svc:batch-processor]
 resources: [projects/redwood-prod/*]
 expires_at: 2027-02-15T00:00:00Z
- Document the change in the incident timeline (automatically via the incident system).

Communications & escalation workflow

Internal notifications (timeline SLA):
- 0-60 minutes: Notify Security, SRE, Legal, Product, and Exec (severity P1 only). Use secured channel: #inc-<id>-priv (Slack private) and send email to incident-distribution@redwood.ai.
- 60-180 minutes: Prepare public-facing statement draft if data exposure confirmed.

Templates (examples)
- Internal Slack opener (private channel):
 - "INC-<id> declared (P1). IC: @<name>. Do not share outside this channel. Evidence snapshot in s3://evidence-bucket/INC-<id>/. Legal on call: @legal-oncall."
- Executive email summary (first 180 minutes):
 - Subject: INC-<id> — High severity incident — initial summary
 - Body: concise incident time, systems impacted, containment stage, next steps, and expected update cadence.

Outside communications and regulator notifications

- Legal must approve any external notification. Use the external comms checklist: confirm facts, authorized spokesperson, data categories affected, remediation steps, and regulator reporting deadlines (per jurisdiction).

Compliance evidence workflow (audit-ready packaging)

1) Evidence index entry (example fields recorded in the evidence registry):
- incident_id, artifact_path, sha256, captured_by, capture_time, access_control_snapshot_path, retention_policy_id, signature_path.
2) Export for auditor: prepare a read-only bundle with manifest and signature and provide time-limited access URL and audit trail of access.
3) Change log: every RBAC change performed as part of incident must be recorded with pre/post policy diffs and stored in the incident timeline.

Post-incident actions (72 hours to 30 days)

1) 72-hour initial report: IC and Evidence Custodian produce a technical summary and list of mitigations.
2) 7-day remediation plan: fix root cause, rotate credentials, and implement permanent RBAC changes if needed.
3) 30-day review: run an evidence integrity audit and tabletop to exercise lessons learned.

Exceptions and risk acceptance

- If immediate evidence preservation conflicts with live containment (e.g., capturing live memory will crash a service), the IC must document the decision, alternative preservation steps, and obtain Legal sign-off.
- Any temporary RBAC deny that lasts longer than 7 days requires approval from IAM manager and Security Director.

Operational runbook snippets (quick commands)

- Collect active SSH sessions (Linux):
 - sudo lsof -iTCP -sTCP:ESTABLISHED -nP | grep ssh > /tmp/ssh-sessions.txt
- Export IAM policy diff (AWS example):
 - aws iam get-role --role-name redwood-admin --output json > role-before.json
 - # make change
 - aws iam get-role --role-name redwood-admin --output json > role-after.json
 - diff -u role-before.json role-after.json > role-policy-diff.patch

Evidence retention mapping (summary table)

| Artifact type | Hot retention | Archive retention | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| API gateway logs | 90 days | 7 years | Platform Observability Team |
| Auth events | 365 days | 7 years | IAM Team |
| Privileged action logs | 365 days | 7 years | Security Forensics |

Appendices

A. Investigator checklist (short)
- Verify incident declaration and ID
- Establish private coordination channel
- Snapshot logs and verify checksums
- Freeze or snapshot RBAC policies
- Notify Legal and Comms

B. Evidence naming and retention policy (reference):
- Naming: INC-YYYYMMDD-<id>/<artifact-type>/<filename>
- Retention labels: incident:short (90d), incident:standard (1y), incident:regulatory (7y)

C. Quick links
- IAM role inventory: /confluence/security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth/role-inventory
- Evidence registry UI: https://evidence.redwood.internal/
- Incident tracker template: /confluence/templates/incident-page

D. Change history
- 2026-11-03: Created by Aisha Patel.
- 2027-01-20: Added Kafka checkpoint guidance and clarified S3 Object Lock usage.
- 2027-02-08: Reviewed and published; added legal hold checklist and comms templates.

End of document

title: SparkHarbor Support Labs
author: Avery Chen
text:
Lead summary: inbound via docs-to-bot template; CTO reached out after reading benchmark blog. Small-but-growing support SaaS (help desk & auto-triage). Very focused on quick time-to-value; wants self-serve hosted API first.

Key requirements (short):
- Primary workload: ticket summarization + follow-up suggestion (high accuracy on short threads).
- Secondary: structured-output for passing JSON to their ticketing tool (field_id, priority, suggested_owner).
- Tool calling: must call internal triage webhook and create/update tickets; prefer sealed, documented tool-call contract.
- Targets: 200 QPS burst for inference pipeline (mostly short contexts), p95 latency target <300ms for summarize endpoint.
- Cost posture: sensitive — pilot must show per-ticket cost < $0.02 to scale.
- Deployment: public cloud (no VPC requirement for pilot).

Timeline & recent activity (timeline fragments):
- 2026-02-20: inbound signup on hosted API quickstart (auto-trial started).
- 2026-02-25: AE outreach (Avery) intro email, shared quickstart link and sample prompts.
- 2026-03-01: Discovery call (30m) w/ CTO (Mina Patel) + head of support ops; recorded (Fireflies id ff_20260301_8243).
- 2026-03-03: Sent sample structured-output templates and small test dataset (drive link).
- 2026-03-05: Follow-up demo requested: want 30m sandbox walkthrough focusing on tool-calling and cost controls.

Technical notes / POC asks (copied from call):

Commercial notes:
- SMB budget constraints; small ARR initially but potential expansion if per-ticket cost is strong.
- Suggested approach: self-serve pilot (hosted API), show cost profile with Optimize recommendations (batching + cache), then propose Dedicated once volume justifies.

Next steps (actionable):
- Send tailored hosted API pricing with example per-ticket cost at 3 batch sizes (Avery) — by 2026-03-10.
- Schedule 30m sandbox walkthrough (Marcus to lead demo) — target week of 2026-03-15.
- Prep structured-output starter templates and example tool-call contract; include failure modes doc.
- Legal: provide short retention & audit logging FAQ; legal poke expected during evaluation.

Other refs & artifacts: Gmail thread id th_17a8b9cde (AE thread), Drive pricing deck, Jira RDW-3441 (internal request to produce sample templates).

title: Guidance: exclude internal monitoring probes from tenant burst budget without reducing burst capacity
text:
Issue summary:
Customer reports repeated 429 throttles during nightly orchestrator sweeps despite ample burst credits. Investigating whether internal monitoring/heartbeat probes are being counted against the tenant burst pool.

Impact:
- Production ingest jobs intermittently receive 429s during scheduled monitoring/telemetry sweeps.
- Latency-sensitive streaming clients experience short-lived degradation at sweep times.
- Customer is on a dedicated pool and expects monitoring probes not to affect burst allowance for production requests.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: dp-novafleet-01 in prod-us-east (us-east-1)
- Redwood API via private VPC control plane
- Orchestrator and sidecars are in the customer VPC; healthchecks originate from an internal service mesh and a central monitoring cluster.

Observed behavior:
- Short windows (30–90s) of elevated 429s coincident with three scheduled telemetry sweep jobs (00:15, 02:15, 04:15 UTC).
- Console shows burst credits available but route-level token window drops to zero during sweeps.
- Logs sample attached below show many small concurrent probe requests (GET /v1/healthcheck) interleaved with long-poll streams.

Expected behavior:
- Healthcheck/monitoring probe requests should be accounted separately from production burst budget or routed to an exempted route/pool so they do not cause 429s for production traffic.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) On NovaFleet staging, schedule orchestrator sweep that hits 1000 endpoints over 60s.
2) Observe dedicated pool burst usage graph in Redwood Console.
3) Check /v1/responses for 429s for concurrent production streams.

Relevant logs (sanitized):
- 2026-03-10T00:15:03Z GET /v1/healthcheck 200 x-origin:mesh-prod x-probe-id:tm-001 12ms
- 2026-03-10T00:15:03Z POST /v1/generate 429 x-tenant:novafleet x-route:streams-lowlatency 4ms
- 2026-03-10T00:15:04Z GET /v1/healthcheck 200 x-origin:mesh-prod x-probe-id:tm-002 10ms
- 2026-03-10T00:15:05Z POST /v1/generate 429 x-tenant:novafleet x-route:streams-lowlatency 3ms

Additional notes:
- Customer has existing route separation for long-running streams and bulk uploads but healthchecks are sent to the default route.
- They use a service mesh sidecar that fans out probes to many internal IPs, causing a distributed microburst pattern.
- NovaFleet asks for prescriptive configuration and, if needed, a support-side change to exempt probes without losing overall burst protection on the tenant.

Schedule orchestrator sweep that hits ~1000 endpoints over ~60s
Observe dedicated pool burst usage in Redwood Console during sweep times
Monitor production client logs for transient 429s coincident with sweeps

Create a dedicated route for healthchecks (e.g., /healthcheck) and assign to a low-priority, separate burst pool
Add a request header (X-Probe: yes) and set a route-level rule to map that header to an exempted or isolated quota in the ingress config
Throttle/fanout at the orchestrator level with jitter and worker-side backoff to smooth microbursts
Short-term: schedule sweeps in rolling windows (e.g., 10 batches) to avoid simultaneous fanout

2026-03-11 - Triage: Confirmed correlation between sweep windows and 429 spikes; console shows route-level token erosion even when tenant-level burst credit > 0
Reviewed ingress logs: probes are routed to default route and counted as production tokens
Checked dedicated-pool config: no existing route separation for mesh-originated probes

Recommend small product change: allow 'probe' header to be mapped to a non-billable low-priority pool in the ingress rate-limiter rules (requires config release)
Raised INT-90821 to track internal schema addition for header-based probe-exempt routing
If customer prefers, we can support a tenant-scoped route that uses an isolated burst pool (requires support-assisted config change)

2026-03-10 Priya Shah (Customer): We're seeing 429s at 00:15/02:15/04:15 UTC when our orchestrator runs sweeps. Console still shows burst credits; can you confirm probes are counted? Attached sanitized logs.
2026-03-11 Liam O'Connor (Support): Thanks Priya — triaging. We see correlated token erosion on the streams route during sweep windows. Two immediate options: isolate probes to a separate route/pool or add a header-based rule to classify probe traffic. We'll validate feasibility with Engineering.
2026-03-12 Taylor Nguyen (SRE): Confirmed probes hit default route. Short-term: recommend NovaFleet change orchestrator to add X-Probe: true header and fanout with jitter. Long-term: we can implement an ingress rule to map that header to an isolated burst pool; tracking in INT-90821.
2026-03-13 Priya Shah (Customer): Will try the header-based fanout change and stagger sweeps. Please keep INT-90821 open for a product-level exemption. ETA for customer verification: 2026-03-15.

title: Workload portrait, benchmarking and SLA guardrails - kickoff
author: Jordan Ellis
text:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-13
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Ellis (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Marta Reyes (Crestline Head of ML), Liam O'Donnell (Infra), Sara Kim (PM), Dev Patel (SRE)

Summary:
Quick kickoff to align on workload portrait (QPS, concurrency shape, token distribution), agree success criteria for POC benchmarking and define milestones for an in-cloud pilot. Customer emphasized tail latency and HIPAA-ish compliance constraints; interested in dedicated pool if cost/lats match.

Topics covered:
- Current production shape and unknowns (burstiness, diurnal, tail)
- Benchmarks: end-to-end p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens
- Input/output token distribution and prompt variability
- Success criteria for pilot and rollout timeline
- Security: audit logs, KMS, VPC/connectivity

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Ellis: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh let's do quick intros then jump into the workload portrait.
[00:08] Marta Reyes: Hi this is Marta, I run ML at Crestline. Thanks Jordan.
[00:12] Liam O'Donnell: Liam here, infra lead.
[00:15] Sara Kim: Sara, product.
[00:16] Dev Patel: Dev, SRE.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Priya from Redwood - I'll drive the technical bits today. Diego as well is on hand for deep infra questions.
[00:25] Jordan Ellis: Great. Quick agenda: we want to understand your QPS baseline and bursts, typical request/response lengths, what a successful pilot looks like, then agree next steps. Is that good?
[00:34] Marta Reyes: Yep, perfect.
[00:36] Liam O'Donnell: Works for us.

[02:00] Priya Nair: Marta can you paint the current traffic picture - avg QPS, peak, how concurrent requests map to business events?
[02:08] Marta Reyes: Sure uh rough numbers: baseline is like 5 rps, we get sustained daytime of 8-12 rps, but the tricky bit is the bursts - marketing campaigns or lab batch jobs create spikes to ~120 rps for short windows, say 90 to 300 seconds. There's also a long-tail of very large prompts where outputs get very long.
[02:33] Jordan Ellis: When you say very large prompts what's the typical token mix input vs output?
[02:38] Marta Reyes: Input average 120 tokens, output average 450 tokens but 10% of requests end up 1,200 to 2,000 tokens output when clinical notes are expanded. Also, about 5% of calls are embeddings only for search.
[03:00] Priya Nair: Okay that's useful. Any hard latency SLOs? p95, p99?
[03:06] Dev Patel: We want p95 < 250ms for short replies (say <200 output tokens) for interactive clinician workflows. For long generations we tolerate higher but p99 shouldn't exceed 4.5s ideally. Those are stretch but target.
[03:23] Diego Alvarez: Quick clarification - p95 at the token level or request end-to-end?
[03:28] Dev Patel: End-to-end from API call to final token.

[05:00] Sara Kim: On success criteria - pilot needs to show comparable quality to current baseline, cost per consult under X (we gave a target number in the NDA), and stable tail latency during bursts. Also compliance: logs, SSO and audit, if those pass we'll consider dedicated.
[05:28] Jordan Ellis: Understood. For the pilot we'll aim to quantify three axes: correctness/quality (via eval set of 100 golden prompts), latency behavior (p50/p95/p99 across day + burst), and unit economics (cost per 1,000 tokens and cost per consult).

[07:00] Priya Nair: Let's discuss workload modeling. We'll want a 7-day traffic sample (even aggregated per-minute QPS is fine) plus a sample of representative prompts with input/output lengths. From that we build a synthetic replay to exercise tails.
[07:18] Marta Reyes: We can extract a week from our prod proxy and scrub PHI; we'll anonymize and provide the distribution.
[07:25] Liam O'Donnell: Note we have on-prem connector for SSO and restricted egress in our VPC - so private deployment might be necessary if the hosted path can't meet audit constraints.
[07:38] Jordan Ellis: Good to know. We'll include both hosted and dedicated pilot variants in the plan.

[09:00] Priya Nair: For sizing, two quick heuristics: concurrency = QPS * avg latency (in seconds). With your baseline 10 rps and target avg latency of 0.25s that'd be ~2.5 concurrency; but bursts at 120 rps with longer latencies obviously push concurrency and require more workers. Caching and KV reuse for repeated prefixes can reduce effective token compute.
[09:30] Marta Reyes: We do have reuse - many prompts share templates, so a lot of prefix caching could help. But the clinical expansion requests differ a lot.
[09:40] Priya Nair: Noted. We'll estimate caching hit rate from the sample prompts. Also we need to know distribution of sequence lengths — do you have histograms?
[09:50] Marta Reyes: We'll export pcts - 50/90/99 for input and output tokens. Expect median outputs ~420, 90th ~1,100, 99th ~1,900.

[11:00] Diego Alvarez: Question about benchmarking: do you want us to run model variants? quantized vs unq?
[11:06] Marta Reyes: Yes cost matters so we'd like to compare smaller quantized variants if quality isn't degraded. Also we want to test fallback behaviors if a model is overloaded.
[11:14] Jordan Ellis: We'll include 3 model profiles: high-quality (larger), mid (quantized), and a latency-optimized variant with reduced context. We'll also run a fallback policy test.

[13:00] Priya Nair: On burst handling we recommend 2 strategies: short-term autoscale plus emergency degrade to a faster model or increased batching with tail-aware shaping. For your 120 rps 3 minute bursts we can simulate and show expected p95/p99 under different policies.
[13:25] Dev Patel: How much lead time for autoscale? We prefer warm pools; cold spin-up can spike p99s.
[13:32] Priya Nair: Right — warm dedicated pools or reserved capacity for critical windows is recommended. If hosted-only, we can do reserved burst capacity / pre-warm flows. We'll propose a warm pool config.

[15:00] Jordan Ellis: Pricing note: for dedicated pools we show amortized cost per 1M tokens including infra and support. For hosted we'll show per-token plus optional priority capacity add-on.
[15:12] Marta Reyes: Competitor question - we've looked at Anthropic and BigCloud AI for latency. How do you differ on predictability?
[15:20] Jordan Ellis: Redwood focuses on predictable inference economics and fallbacks. Our smart routing and caching are designed to keep tail behavior stable, and we expose telemetry per-route. We'll show traces in the pilot.

[17:00] Priya Nair: Security checklist: SSO + SAML, SOC2 attestation, customer-managed KMS, audit logs retained 90+ days. Is that in line with your needs?
[17:12] Liam O'Donnell: Yes but we may need 1-year retention on audit logs for some flows. Also requirement for VPC peering for private deployment.
[17:20] Jordan Ellis: We'll escalate retention ask with security; we do have options for extended retention as an add-on.

[19:00] Marta Reyes: Timeline — we want a pilot report within 3 weeks of sample handoff. Is that feasible?
[19:08] Priya Nair: Typical cadence: sample + prompts -> 3 business days to synthesize replay and config -> 1 week of runs -> 2-3 days to analyze. So roughly 12 business days. If we start 2027-01-18 (sample delivered) we can have a report by end of month.
[19:30] Jordan Ellis: We'll aim for that. Also need to surface quality regressions vs your golden set; we'll run automated eval diffs.

[21:00] Dev Patel: For pilot we need network diagrams and egress policy to be correct — I'll send the template.
[21:08] Liam O'Donnell: I'll fill it out.

[23:00] Priya Nair: A few measurement details to confirm: we'll capture p50/p95/p99 request latencies, token throughput (tokens/sec per worker), GPU utilization, and cost per 1k tokens. Also we'll include tail latency heatmaps and concurrency quantiles.
[23:25] Marta Reyes: Sounds good. Can you also surface how batching choices impact quality/latency tradeoff?
[23:30] Priya Nair: Yep we'll include a table that shows expected latency and cost by batching window and max batch size. Expect non-linear improvements but also increased p99 if batching delay is too large.

[25:00] Jordan Ellis: Any blockers on data sharing or compliance?
[25:04] Marta Reyes: We'll need to scrub PHI; security is ok with that. Legal will want the security pack and SOC2 doc.
[25:12] Jordan Ellis: We'll send security pack and SOC2 link after the call.

[28:00] Diego Alvarez: One more note: KV cache effectiveness depends on prompt prefix granularity; if your prompts have unique patient ids embedded it's less effective. We'll estimate with sampling.
[28:18] Marta Reyes: We try to obfuscate patient ids but yes there are unique tokens.

[30:00] Priya Nair: Minimal viable pilot plan (recap): 1) Customer provides 7-day aggregated QPS + 100 golden prompts + env constraints; 2) Redwood synthesizes a replay and proposes two pilot topologies (hosted priority + dedicated warm pool); 3) Run 1 week of replay across 3 model profiles and collect telemetry; 4) Deliver report with cost/latency/quality and recommended configuration.
[30:30] Jordan Ellis: Timeline target: sample by 2027-01-18, run week of 2027-01-25, report by 2027-02-01.

[32:00] Sara Kim: Who is the exec sponsor on Redwood side?
[32:04] Jordan Ellis: I'll be the commercial owner, Priya will be technical lead, Diego for infra, and Diego will loop in the platform reliability folks if needed.

[34:00] Marta Reyes: Quick quality question - do you support reranking/structured output as part of the pipeline? We rely on structured JSON for downstream ingestion.
[34:08] Priya Nair: Yes we support structured outputs and function calling patterns; we'll test those in the golden set.

[36:00] Dev Patel: For the in-cloud mini-run do you need service account creds or can we provide via a bastion?
[36:08] Priya Nair: We can work either way; for hosted pilot credentials are less invasive, for private/dedicated we'll coordinate egress/VPC peering.

[38:00] Jordan Ellis: Any other questions?
[38:05] Marta Reyes: Not right now. We'll aim to get the sample over early next week.

[40:00] Jordan Ellis: Great thanks everyone. Quick recap of next steps — Jordan to send benchmark spreadsheet and pricing, Priya to send pilot topology and suggested warm pool configs, Marta/Liam to provide sample and diagrams. We'll reconvene after we receive the data to schedule the run.
[40:25] Sara Kim: Thanks all.
[40:28] Dev Patel: Thanks.
[40:30] Jordan Ellis: End.

Action items (verbatim list in transcript):
- Jordan: send benchmark template + security pack + SOC2 link
- Priya: propose autoscale/warm pool config and batching windows
- Marta: scrub and upload 7-day sample + golden prompts
- Liam: provide network diagram + retention requirements

Notes about transcription: occasional words garbled (k-v cash instead of kv cache), speaker labels sometimes overlapped, timestamps approximate.

Attachments / references mentioned:

- Security pack link (SOC2, encryption, audit log options)
- Sample prompt template (JSON)

End of transcript.

title: Error Origins Chronicle and Probe Wires
author: Avery Chen
text:
A sketch + working notes for a chronological 'Error Origins Chronicle' and interactive 'Probe Card' surfaces. Goal: make it fast for an engineer or SRE to move from a high-level alert (timeout/5xx/model-error) to a small set of actionable probes and hypotheses they can run from the console without leaving the incident flow.

Current console shows flat lists of failed requests and raw traces. Investigators still need to stitch network logs, model variant, routing policy, and prefix/KV cache context. We want a single timeline with contextual probes and suggested reruns to reduce mean time to mitigation and make root-cause hypotheses explicit.

Unify multi-source signals into a single chronological narrative (request -> routing -> model -> runtime -> infra)
Provide one-click probe actions (replay with different model, flush cache + replay, run vs. canary model, capture full token-level diff)
Expose a small set of hypothesis templates and telemetry needed to confirm/disprove each hypothesis

Oncall SREs, product engineers debugging latency/5xx/model errors, solutions engineers investigating customer incidents

1) Chronicle Timeline: horizontal time axis that layers events (client request, gateway latencies, routing decision, model inference start/end, GPU/memory thrash events, infra autoscaler events). Each event node is clickable and opens a compact inspector. 2) Probe Card Rail: a right-side rail that lists auto-suggested probes (replay w/ same model, replay w/ quantized variant, replay without prefix cache, replay with throttled batch size, run synthetic with smaller input). Each probe has expected quick metric impact and confidence level. 3) Hypothesis Deck: a top banner area where the investigator can pin up to 3 hypotheses; each hypothesis links to probes and shows required telemetry to validate. 4) Evidence Panel: bottom panel with aggregated logs, sampled token diffs, network captures, and correlated traces from other regions/replicas.

Chronicle Timeline (compact stacked lanes: client/gateway, router/policy, model runtime, infra/host) — hover reveals quick stats
Probe Card (list of suggested probes with run button + small cost estimate + estimated time)
Hypothesis Deck (pin, score, expected action)
Evidence Panel (collapsible: logs, token-diff viewer, heatmap of latency vs token position)
Compact Inspector (for any node: shows 1-line summary, request metadata, model version, token count, KV cache hits, GPU utilization snapshot)
Action History (chronicle of probes run during this investigation with outcomes and links to generated artifacts)
Share / Attach button to create a ticket with current hypothesis and artifacts attached

Typical flow: alert -> open chronicle for the request -> click 'Router decision' node -> console suggests 3 probes (replay with fallback model, replay flush-cache, replay routing-only) -> investigator runs 'replay flush-cache' -> outcome shows token-diff and latency change -> pin hypothesis 'cache staleness' and run 2nd probe 'replay with canary model' if needed -> if confirmed, create remediation (route update) via quick deploy action. Keep investigator context (pinned hypothesis) across probes and allow rollback of probes to save cost.

Visual affordances: use color-coded event types (red=error, amber=high-latency, blue=info). Probe Card buttons: primary (Run probe), secondary (preview cost/time). Mini-token-diff viewer: show aligned tokens with highlight on divergent tokens and a small 'confidence delta' score. For time-critical alerts, show pre-populated probe set optimized for speed (1-2 probes under 30s). Persist last successful probe for the request to avoid duplicate runs.

Design: Chronicle lane ordering heuristic prototype (owner: Priya) — 3d
Engineering: Probe execution sandbox API contract (owner: Marcus) — 5d
Product: Probe suggestion ranking rules (owner: Avery) — 2d
Data: telemetry funnel to support probe confidence scoring (owner: Elena) — 4d
UX: compact token-diff component (owner: UX) — 3d
Security: IAM check for on-console probe execution (owner: security) — 2d

per-request timeline with timestamps for router/model/runtime/infra events
KV cache hit/miss counts and prefix lengths
model-variant id + quantization flags
GPU/CPU utilization at inference start/end (1s granularity)
per-probe cost estimate and actual run time
token-level probabilities or confidence deltas (redacted for PII)

How do we rate-limit probes to prevent accidental load generation?
What guardrails are needed for private deployments with air-gapped telemetry?
Should probes run under a namespace's dedicated capacity or the investigator's sandbox quota?
What is the minimum data retention window required to make Chronicle useful (7d vs 30d)?

Sync with infra on probe executor capacity and safety limits (schedule meeting)
Prototype Chronicle lane visual in Figma and run a 5-person usability test
Create a small internal beta with SRE oncall rotation to get real incident feedback
Define analytics events to measure probe usage and MTTR impact

title: Hybrid quant lab heuristics demo - HelixHealth
author: Maya Chen
text:
Walkthrough of Redwood Optimize console focused on hybrid quantization heuristics (INT8 / FP8) using HelixHealth's clinical QA prompt set. Demo included live benchmark results, caveats for EHR domain hallucination risk, and private deployment considerations (VPC, KMS). Agreed to run a 2-week pilot with targeted quality thresholds and an A/B canary in staging.

INT8 vs FP8 tradeoffs
adaptive/hybrid quant profiles
quality measurement and eval sets for EHR
latency throughput benchmarks (p50/p95)
private deployment constraints: VPC, KMS, audit logs
pilot plan and success criteria

[00:00] Maya Chen: hi everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
[00:06] Rajiv Nair: yes, loud and clear. thanks Maya.
[00:12] Ethan Brooks: great, i'll share my screen and we'll jump into the Optimize console — apologies if there's a slight lag.
[00:20] Lena Ortiz: screen's good. curious to see the int8/fp8 numbers on our clinical prompts.
[00:28] Maya Chen: perfect. quick intro — i'm maya (AE) and ethan is our se. you're all on the notes? we've got the helixhealth eval set preloaded per the doc you uploaded.
[00:40] Markus Vogel: yes, we dropped the sample batch yesterday — 1.2k prompts, mixture of discharge summaries and med history Qs.
[00:48] Ethan Brooks: awesome, so what i'll do is show three profiles: default fp16, int8 aggressive, and a hybrid-rule-based fp8 profile. we'll run latency and qa-quality side-by-side.
[00:58] [01:15] Ethan Brooks: starting with the baseline — fp16 on rdx-gpu-8 (our standard hosted GPU). p50 token latency is ~22ms, p95 about 78ms for the 512-token window with kv cache warm. accuracy baseline on your QA exact-match is 89.7%.
[01:35] Lena Ortiz: that's consistent with our earlier runs. what's the tokenization difference? we're using clinical tokenization?
[01:42] Ethan Brooks: yes, same tokenizer you used. there are some small mismatches occasionally — transcription flagged a couple model names as 'redwood-infer' — ignore that.
[01:50] [02:10] Ethan Brooks: switching to int8 aggressive profile. note we lowered quant thresholds and disabled per-layer fallback. p50 drops to 14ms, p95 to 52ms. throughput jumps by ~1.6x. quality delta: exact-match down to 87.9% (a -1.8pt absolute). we see some formatting regressions on tabular med lists.
[02:35] Rajiv Nair: formatting regressions are painful for downstream parsers. how big are hallucinations? any risk of inventing medications?
[02:45] Ethan Brooks: great question — hallucination rate (as measured by our hallucination detector) increased from 0.6% to 1.4% for int8 aggressive. a majority are subtle attribute swaps, rare drug invention but we flagged a few false positives during named-entity extraction.
[03:05] [03:30] Ethan Brooks: now hybrid fp8 profile — what we call heuristic hybrid: keep critical attention layers in fp16, quantize feed-forward to fp8, and enable per-request prefix caching. p50 sits at 16ms, p95 at 60ms. quality is 89.0% — so only a 0.7pt drop from baseline but with ~1.35x throughput.
[03:55] Lena Ortiz: interesting — so hybrid fp8 seems like a middle-ground. how deterministic are those heuristics across different prompt lengths?
[04:05] Ethan Brooks: for short prompts (<128 tokens) the delta is smaller; for long generation cases (>512 tokens) we see fp8 sensitivity mainly in rare factual chains. our console includes per-prompt sensitivity scores so you can identify which prompt families to exclude from aggressive profiles.
[04:30] [04:55] Maya Chen: to add — Optimize will synthesize a "sensitivity cohort" that groups prompts by failure mode; you can review and decide which to pin to safer profiles.
[05:05] Markus Vogel: what's the deployment path for these profiles — hosted vs dedicated vs private? we need VPC for PHI.
[05:12] Ethan Brooks: with private (VPC) deployments we give the same console surface. the difference is model kernels and quant binaries are shipped in the private runtime; we support HSM/KMS integration for keys and full audit logs. latency numbers in private on customer infra will vary; we recommend a small dry-run in your staging GPUs to calibrate.
[05:35] [05:55] Rajiv Nair: and SOC 2 reports? our security team will ask for encryption at rest and in transit plus audit trail.
[06:02] Maya Chen: we have SOC 2 Type II and ISO docs — i'll share the package after the call. we also support customer-managed keys via AWS KMS or HashiCorp Vault.
[06:15] [06:35] Ethan Brooks: back to the console — here's the per-prompt diff view. you can see one patient discharge prompt where int8 stripped a colon and collapsed a med dose field, causing downstream parser mismatch. we annotate the diff and give a suggested rule: keep that prompt family on fp16 or hybrid fp8 with layer 5 fallback.
[06:58] Lena Ortiz: can we automate rules? we'd prefer not to manually curate hundreds of prompts.
[07:05] Ethan Brooks: yes — Optimize has an auto-suggest policy engine. it will propose a policy that maps prompt cohorts to quant profiles; you can accept or tweak before rollout. it can also create a canary rollout with traffic percentages and automatic rollback if eval metrics drop below threshold.
[07:30] [07:50] Rajiv Nair: demo the canary please.
[07:52] Ethan Brooks: sure — starting a 10% canary: profile applied, routing policy set to prefer low-latency for non-critical endpoints, and fallback to baseline on regression. initiating now... (console action) ...canary started. initial live p50 for canary requests matches the offline bench roughly.
[08:20] Lena Ortiz: how do we tie this to our test harness? we run nightly regression tests.
[08:28] Ethan Brooks: you can plug your harness into our eval API. we support ingesting your CSV of test prompts and will return per-prompt metrics including exact-match, F1, hallucination score, and latency. that's what we did with your 1.2k set earlier.
[08:50] [09:10] Maya Chen: quick note on billing: the cost model for hybrid profiles is token-based with adjustments for quantization compute delta. we'll include a sample cost projection for your 100k monthly tokens.
[09:25] Markus Vogel: so if we run the pilot in staging for 2 weeks, what's the min commitment?
[09:31] Maya Chen: for hosted pilot, no long term commit — pay-for-usage. for private, we typically do a short reserved window for container images; i'll put the minimal pilot options in the pricing email.
[09:45] [10:05] Rajiv Nair: can we request specific kernel builds? we have older A100 nodes and a mix of H100s.
[10:12] Ethan Brooks: yes — Optimize will recommend a kernel per hardware profile. for A100 we often prefer certain matmul kernels; for H100 fp8 has better stability on newer kernels. we can schedule a kernel-compatibility bench on your hardware — takes ~48 hours to run.
[10:32] Lena Ortiz: any concerns about label drift? clinical language changes a lot.
[10:38] Ethan Brooks: that's where continuous eval helps — we can set alerts for quality regressions per cohort and trigger re-eval automations or rollbacks.
[10:50] [11:15] Maya Chen: quick Qs from your side?
[11:20] Markus Vogel: deployment logistics: image signing and SBOM?
[11:26] Maya Chen: yes we support signed images and provide SBOMs for the runtime. also audit log streams can be pushed to your SIEM via syslog or cloud-native connectors.
[11:40] Rajiv Nair: good. can we see an export of the per-prompt diffs?
[11:45] Ethan Brooks: i'll export and share — linking the artifact in notes (link: drive/helix_quant_diffs.xlsx).
[11:55] [12:10] Lena Ortiz: i noticed some transcription hiccups in the results — can you confirm what "kv cache warm" means again?
[12:18] Ethan Brooks: kv cache warm just means the model's cached key-value pairs for previous tokens are available; cold starts add a small overhead. Optimize suggests prewarming for high-QPS bursts.
[12:32] [12:50] Maya Chen: ok, wrapping up — recap of commitments and next steps.
[12:55] Maya Chen: we'll run a 2-week pilot scoped to these three endpoints: discharge-summaries, med-history-qna, and appointment-extractions, with hybrid fp8 canary at 10% then ramp to 50% if thresholds hold.
[13:15] Rajiv Nair: success criteria: exact-match drop <=1.0pt absolute, hallucination <1%, and no parser failures in >99.5% of cases. agree?
[13:25] Lena Ortiz: agreed.
[13:28] Markus Vogel: agreed.
[13:30] Maya Chen: i'll send pilot pricing, SOC/ISO package, an SBOM and the exported diffs. ethan will run the kernel bench on your staging infra.
[13:42] Ethan Brooks: noted — i'll reach out to kick off the bench and collect node specs.
[13:50] [14:10] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, i'll follow up with calendar invites for the pilot kickoff.
[14:18] Rajiv Nair: thanks — talk soon.
[14:22] [14:30] End of recording.

Send pilot pricing and contract template
Share SOC 2 / ISO security package and SBOM
Export and share per-prompt diffs (drive/helix_quant_diffs.xlsx)
SE to run kernel-compatibility bench on HelixHealth staging infra (48h)
Schedule pilot kickoff meeting and calendar invite

Ethan Brooks|Kick off kernel bench and collect node specs|2026-10-16

title: Edge-case demo: long-context, high-TPS, streaming backpressure and timeouts
author: Maya Patel
text:
Redwood AE+SE walked LedgerFlow through an edge-case demo focused on very long contexts (~200k tokens across sessions), high sustained TPS bursts, and streaming/backpressure behavior. Key outcomes: Redwood demonstrated prefix/KV cache benefit, fallback to lower-cost quantized model on overload, and connection-level mitigation patterns. LedgerFlow requested a tailored benchmark and Dedicated pricing; security and network (VPC) clarifications deferred to a follow-up.

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-08 UTC
Start: 16:00 Z
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Maya Patel (AE), Liam O'Connor (SE) - Redwood; Caroline Nguyen, Dev Patel, Samir Rao, Elena Torres - LedgerFlow
Recording quality: medium (occasional word swaps)

--- Automated summary (short):
Redwood demo of long-context + high TPS streaming failure modes, showed cache strategies, fallback model routing, and backpressure handling. LedgerFlow asks for benchmark, pricing, and VPC networking notes.

00:00:05 Maya: Alright, hi everyone, thanks for taking time. Quick roll call, uh, I'm Maya, I'm the account lead, and Liam's our systems engineer who'll drive the demo.
00:00:18 Liam: Hey all, thanks, I'll share my screen in a sec. We're going to reproduce three patterns you called out: long context sessions, sustained TPS bursts, and streaming backpressure/timeouts. We'll push realistic traces you sent, Dev, and show mitigation knobs.
00:00:36 Caroline: Perfect. Our big worry is—sorry—if the streaming client gets a 504 mid-response because some gateway times out, what do users see and how do we recover?
00:00:49 Liam: Great question. So by default, if a client-side transport timeout happens, the token stream stops; however, on the server side we keep the KV cache and the partial context so a reconnect can resume from the last cache checkpoint if you reattach with the same session id. There is a caveat—
00:01:10 Dev: Sorry Liam, when you say resume, it's not magically reconstructing in-flight tokens, right? We need idempotency keys or something?
00:01:20 Liam: Correct, we expose an idempotency/session ID header. If the client re-posts a resume request within our TTL window, we can continue generation with minimal re-computation. If the TTL expired, we fall back to a prefix-only rewarm which may incur extra cost and latency.
00:01:37 Samir: What is the TTL by default?
00:01:40 Liam: Default is 3 minutes for in-flight resume checkpoints, and 24 hours for KV cache entries for prefix warm. Those numbers are configurable—Dedicated customers can bump cache TTLs or pin certain user buckets.
00:01:54 Elena: That 24-hour window, is it per-user or per-prefix?
00:01:58 Liam: It's per-prefix key; we shard by model+tenant+prefix-hash. So similar prompts across users can share warm cache if the prefix hash matches.
00:02:11 Caroline: Okay uh, next—how do we handle backpressure? If LedgerFlow has bursts of 5k TPS for 2 minutes, we don't want huge 99.9 p99 spikes.
00:02:23 Liam: Right. We demo two things: adaptive request shedding and elastic burst lanes. For hosted mode we can do a soft-shed where we divert some requests to a cheaper smaller model variant or return a light-weight response with a rerank id. For Dedicated you have reserved burst capacity and better isolation, but costs more.
00:02:42 Dev: Can you show the stream behavior when the process hits kernel-level queue limits—like socket buffer fill?
00:02:49 Liam: Yep. I'll open the harness — we'll start a 10-minute run with a trace that matches your traffic. Note: inference runtime uses continuous batching, so you'll see throughput increase then latency step-up when queue depth passes the continuous-batching threshold.
00:03:05 [screen share starts — load generator kicking off]
00:03:15 Liam: Alright, generator ramping now. You're seeing requests per second on the top-left. We're at 1k TPS and heading up. Notice the blue line is end-to-end p95, red is p99.
00:03:33 Caroline: I see p99 creeping at 1k, that's fine, but what's the mitigation when we hit 4k?
00:03:39 Liam: Around 4k TPS you'll see our adaptive batching step in: we tighten batch time windows to prioritize latency, but that reduces GPU efficiency. Alternatively, we start model variant routing—shift low-priority traffic to the quantized variant.
00:03:55 [00:04:00] (background noise; some words unclear)
00:04:15 Dev: If rerouting happens, how do we track the provenance of the response? We need deterministic trace to audit model outputs—especially for compliance.
00:04:26 Liam: We attach route metadata to each response header (model_variant, quant_level, routing_reason), and we log the prompt hash and the chosen fallback. You can pull those from the Console or the audit logs API. There's a small caveat where streaming partial responses may be truncated if gateway timeouts occur — you'll see an error code and a resume token if available.
00:04:50 Samir: Can we force immediate failover to a replica instead of fallback to smaller model? We prefer same-model semantics.
00:04:59 Liam: We do fast replica failover for transient GPU node failures, yes. But when capacity is globally constrained, fallback to smaller-quantized variants is more cost-effective and avoids queue starvation. We can make the policy strict for you — policy rules are in the rollout config.
00:05:12 Maya: Quick interjection — LedgerFlow asked about connection pooling at the ingress. We recommend fronting with a connection proxy that supports HTTP/2 multiplexing; that reduces socket churn and helps with backpressure.
00:05:24 Caroline: Are there recommended timeout settings for APIGW/nginx? We run a 30s idle timeout currently and worried that's too small for long streaming generations.
00:05:33 Liam: For streaming you want longer idle timeouts — 120s+ recommended for long-tail streams, and allow for keepalive pings. Alternatively use the resume token pattern so clients can reconnect quickly. We'll share our nginx tuning doc.
00:05:46 Elena: Can you demo a client timeout mid-stream and then a resume?
00:05:50 Liam: Yep — switching to the 'timeout/resume' scenario.
00:05:56 [load generator simulates a network hiccup; one streaming client hits a 504]
00:06:10 Liam: You can see the stream closed on the client side; server logs show session checkpoint saved to KV store with checkpoint_id abc123. If the client sends resume with checkpoint_id within 3 minutes, we attach the cached KV and continue.
00:06:26 Dev: Does reconnect cost extra tokens? Like, do we re-send the whole prompt?
00:06:31 Liam: If within checkpoint TTL we resume with minimal re-computation. If expired, yes you'll pay to rewarm prefix cache since we need to rerun earlier layers to rebuild KV. We can also persist warmed embeddings for hot prefixes to lower that cost for Dedicated customers.
00:06:45 Caroline: How does quantization affect hallucination rate? If we fallback to an 8-bit quantized variant under load does answer quality degrade?
00:06:55 Liam: There's a measurable difference—our Optimize tool reports mean ROUGE/QA deltas for quantized variants. In practice for retrieval-augmented prompts the impact is small, but for complex reasoning there's higher variance. We'll attach a quality delta table from our internal evals.
00:07:12 Samir: Can the fallback be per-route? We have some flows where we will never accept quantized outputs.
00:07:17 Liam: Absolutely — route-level policies can mark flows as 'no-fallback', and those flows will be prioritized or shed with an error rather than routed to quantized models.
00:07:27 [00:07:30] Speaker overlap (someone coughing)
00:07:45 Liam: Now I'm going to enable aggressive burst to force queue pressure. Watch the streaming connection status on the right panel.
00:07:56 [generator ramps to 6k TPS]
00:08:07 Caroline: Whoa, p99 just spiked to 2.1s — what's the client-facing symptom? Do we drop chunks?
00:08:12 Liam: If socket buffers are full you may observe chunk delays; our runtime flushes tokens as soon as they are ready, but network-layer queuing can reorder or drop TCP segments in extreme cases — which is why we recommend HTTP/2 or WebSocket with reconnect/resume semantics.
00:08:29 Dev: Can we throttle per-user? We have heavy power users that cause noisy neighbor.
00:08:35 Liam: Yes, per-tenant and per-user rate limits are available; plus we expose per-route quotas and dynamic throttles via Redwood Console. You can configure soft quotas that return a 429 with a retry-after and hard quotas that block.
00:08:45 Elena: Regarding observability—do you provide token-level cost breakdown for each streamed response?
00:08:51 Liam: Yes, Console shows token distribution (prompt vs completion), KV cache hits, and a per-request cost estimate. For streaming we attach incremental cost metadata per flush so you can approximate mid-stream cost.
00:09:06 Caroline: About private deployments—if we go VPC does Redwood still run the Control Plane or do we self-host it?
00:09:13 Maya: For VPC you can choose either: managed control plane with private connectivity, or a customer-run control plane for air-gapped installs. Both support the same rollout and audit features, but the latter has additional compliance paperwork.
00:09:27 Samir: Ok demo looks good. Could you show logs when the gateway applied a 504? I want to see the mapping to resume token.
00:09:34 Liam: Sure — filtering logs now. See trace id tf-778; it shows event sequence: request-received -> partial-stream-flush -> client-timeout -> checkpoint-saved(abc123) -> client-disconnect.
00:09:50 Dev: That event sequence is good. Will you also show how logs look integrated into our SIEM (Splunk)?
00:09:56 Liam: We have a Splunk ingestion guide. Logs emit JSON with fields model_version, checkpoint_id, prompt_hash, routing_policy. We can stream those to your Splunk endpoint or S3.
00:10:08 [demo continues with latency/throughput graphs — approx 12 minutes of measurable load scenarios; snippets omitted for brevity]
00:22:30 Liam: Jumping to the long-context test now — we want to show context beyond typical 16k: we loaded a 200k token session partitioned across multiple segments and used prefix stitching with KV cache.
00:22:45 Caroline: 200k? That's our real user scenario — legal files stitched over months. How is memory kept efficient?
00:22:53 Liam: We shard the key-value cache across hosts and only keep the top-N most recent KV blocks in hot memory. For tails we spill to Redis/SSD depending on deployment profile. On Dedicated you can provision more hot memory or pin hot prefixes to a GPU group.
00:23:10 Dev: How does compaction work? We can't keep every token's KV forever.
00:23:15 Liam: We do LRU compaction and semantic compaction: we can compress old segments into embeddings and keep only a summarized prefix for retrieval rather than the full KV. That reduces memory while keeping relevance.
00:23:29 Samir: If we compact aggressively will retrieval-relevance degrade?
00:23:34 Liam: Minor but measurable; Optimize can simulate compaction levels vs QA deltas so you can pick an operating point.
00:23:45 Maya: Quick note — LedgerFlow had a security requirement about audit logs and KMS key rotation. We will route those questions to our security team after this demo.
00:23:56 Caroline: Anything else we should watch for in the console during the long-context run?
00:24:02 Liam: Look at the cache hit heatmap and the model-variant routing table. You'll see which user buckets are getting quantized. Also the session gap metric — that tells you if your clients are reattaching often.
00:24:16 [00:24:20] (minor transcription glitch here: 'K V cash' spelled odd)
00:24:42 Liam: We're hitting sustained 3k TPS with long-context—notice cost per 1k tokens in the lower panel. If we enable prefix compression you can see cost drop while p99 increases slightly.
00:25:00 Elena: If we want strict determinism, is there a configuration to disable compression/fallbacks entirely?
00:25:07 Liam: Yes, strict-determinism mode disables model variant fallback and any compression that changes tokenization semantics. It's viable but increases cost; usually used for regulated flows.
00:25:20 Dev: For the POC what diagnostics would you need from us?
00:25:25 Maya: We'll need sample traces (anonymized), expected API traffic shape, a list of protected routes, SSO/SAML contact for security, and a primary network contact for VPC peering.
00:25:38 Caroline: We'll send those.
00:25:42 [long pause as files are uploaded for the demo stage]
00:26:10 Liam: Now final scenario—simulated intermittent upstream network flaps to observe resume and garbage collection.
00:26:20 [flap] 00:26:40 Liam: We triggered multiple short disconnects; observe session gap spikes, but KV survived across three flaps within checkpoint TTL.
00:26:54 Dev: Good. Can the client-side library attempt transparent reconnect with backoff?
00:26:59 Liam: Yes our SDK supports exponential backoff plus resume token semantics. We'll provide the SDK with built-in reconnect behavior.
00:27:10 Caroline: On the fallback metrics—can we get an alert when more than X% of traffic is being quantized?
00:27:17 Liam: Console alerting supports that. We'll set up alerts by model_variant share and p99 latency thresholds.
00:27:25 Maya: Quick recap before we close: Redwood will send benchmark harness and plan, security docs, Dedicated pricing sheet, and a suggested POC timeline. LedgerFlow to provide traces and network contacts.
00:27:38 Samir: Sounds good. Any blockers on the Redwood side?
00:27:42 Maya: No blockers; scheduling the POC kick-off is next.
00:27:47 Caroline: Thanks everyone.
00:28:00 [call continues into Q&A and small clarifications for another 24 minutes — topics include SSO/SAML integration, audit log retention, and SLA for Dedicated. Below are selected excerpts from that section.]

00:31:10 Dev: On SSO—can we integrate with our Okta instance and map roles to per-route permissions?
00:31:18 Maya: Yes, SAML/Okta supported; role mapping via SCIM/LDAP sync; per-route RBAC available for Dedicated.
00:31:30 Elena: Our compliance team wants 7-year audit logs archived—do you support that?
00:31:36 Liam: Long-retention archives can be exported to your S3 and we support lifecycle rules. There's an add-on fee for extended retention beyond standard 13 months.
00:31:49 Samir: Final quick question—if we go Dedicated and need to pin a quantized model, can we still get Redwood Optimize recommendations?
00:31:58 Liam: Yes, Optimize runs offline evals and can recommend quantization profiles even for pinned models. The recommendations include expected cost/quality deltas.

00:31:58 Maya: Okay I'm going to call out the specific next steps:
00:32:05 Maya: 1) Redwood sends benchmark harness + test plan (Maya)
00:32:09 Maya: 2) LedgerFlow shares anonymized traces + Okta contact (Caroline/Dev)
00:32:14 Maya: 3) Redwood SE runs a profiling pass and shares results (Liam)
00:32:19 Maya: 4) Pricing and Dedicated pilot agreement (Maya)

00:32:25 Caroline: We'll aim to get traces to you by Friday.
00:32:29 Dev: We'll anonymize and drop into the secure S3 link.
00:32:33 Maya: Great. Anything else?
00:32:36 Samir: Nope. Thanks all.
00:32:39 Liam: Thanks, bye.

--- End of transcript (partial: 52m meeting, excerpts included).

Notes on transcription quality: several technical terms mis-transcribed ("KV cash" vs KV cache; some timestamps approximate).

Shared artifacts referenced during call:
- Demo harness URL: https://redwood.ai/harnesses/ledgerflow-edge-demo (internal)
- Timeout tuning doc: https://redwood.ai/docs/timeout-tuning
- Quantization impact table (internal): link in follow-up email

Potential risks noted:
- Very long context workloads increase memory pressure and cost; naive TTLs can lead to rewarm costs.
- Streaming timeouts at the gateway require client-side resume logic to avoid poor UX.

Recent activity:

- 2026-02-26 demo: hosted streaming demo with tool-call mock; POQ: first-token latency matters for perceived responsiveness.
