Requirements / constraints (customer language):
- Latency SLO: interactive agent p50 < 150ms for first token in US regions, p95 < 600ms for non-degraded flows; streaming chunk latency < 100ms preferred.
- Throughput: avg 30 requests/second with burst to 200 rps during peaks.
- Tool calling: need deterministic structured outputs (JSON schema enforcement) and function/tool invocation reliability for order-routing to downstream systems.
- Quality gating: must have prompt/eval regression checks before rollouts. Must support A/B tests and canary rollouts with automatic rollback if eval metrics degrade >1.5% CSAT-equivalent.
- Cost sensitivity: mid-market — will trade some latency for cost but want clear per-token economics and recommendations (quantization, batching) from Redwood Optimize.
- Security: SSO (SAML), SOC2, audit logs, KMS integration, option for VPC peering for Dedicated. Data residency required in US and EU for different product segments.

POC scope (agreed):
- 2-week hosted POC: realistic traffic replay (prod-sampled traces) to measure p50/p95 streaming latency, tool-call success rate, and token cost.
- Integrate eval harness: baseline prompts + adversarial tests; run A/B variant to simulate prompt changes and compute regression deltas.
- Produce recommendation: if hosted can't meet p95 targets under burst, produce Dedicated sizing + pricing sketch.

Quotes / call notes:
- Product lead: "we need to ship an agent that feels instant — even small delays kill conversion".
- CTO: "we can't have regressions after each prompt tweak; need eval gates and automatic rollback hooks".

title: Introduce RBAC anomaly detector, KMS usage ledger, and jurisdictional pin gate
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Motivation: customers operating in regulated jurisdictions require stronger evidence about access decisions and KMS usage, plus automated detection of unusual privilege changes. This PR adds three coordinated pieces: 1) an RBAC Anomaly Detector that samples policy decisions and surfaces statistical deviations (new service + control plane telemetry), 2) a KMS Usage Ledger that records per-tenant, per-key KMS call metadata for non-repudiable audit and residency verification, and 3) a Jurisdictional Pin Gate that enforces region-pin policies at the KMS allocation layer and emits canonical audit events for downstream compliance pipelines. The goals are: reduce investigation time for policy breaches, provide provable KMS usage trails for compliance audits, and enforce region pin constraints at the decision point to avoid accidental cross-region key use. Changes in this PR touch: policy evaluation path, audit forwarder, KMS allocation middleware, migrations for the ledger schema, the console telemetry surface, and operator-facing rollout flags. Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked (ENG-9485) - [x] Unit + integration tests for policy sampler - [x] Ledger write path is idempotent and signed - [x] Backwards-compatible migration and feature flag - [x] Console telemetry panels added - [x] e2e scenario for region-pin enforcement (simulated cross-region request) Backwards compatibility: the anomaly detector is opt-in and behind "rbac_anomaly_enabled" feature flag. KMS ledger writes are opt-in per-tenant until a migration window closes. Rollout plan: gradual enablement by tenant cohort, tie ledger writes to audit retention throttles, monitor error rates and key write latency. See commits for incremental scope and the review thread for design clarifications.

Liam Nguyen (2025-02-13): Nice direction. Two asks: (1) how do we bound false positives for the anomaly detector so SRE doesn't get paged? (2) ledger writes need to be resilient to transient DB errors. Can you add backoff and non-blocking fallback?
Aisha Patel (2025-02-13): Replied: added exponential backoff + circuit breaker for ledger writes, detector uses an adjustable baseline window and an anomaly-confidence threshold; default is conservative (only P>0.999 alerts). Added config to route low-confidence alerts to a noiseless 'review' stream instead of pages.
Sofia Alvarez (2025-02-14): We need a clear privacy/legal review for storing KMS call metadata. Please ensure tenant opt-in and a data-retention TTL per-tenant. Also: mandate KMS key-id hashing before storing any identifier in non-secure stores.
Aisha Patel (2025-02-15): Replied: implemented per-tenant opt-in flag, retention TTL, and HMAC-prefix hashing of key IDs before writing to ledger. Sensitive raw IDs are only stored in the sealed PostgreSQL column encrypted with CMK; non-sensitive indexes use hashed prefixes.
Marcus Reed (2025-02-16): Test comment: e2e simulated tenant with region pin should reject cross-region KMS allocation and emit a signed audit event; test flaked once in CI (timing).
Aisha Patel (2025-02-16): Flakiness debug: extended the test timeout and added an eventual consistency assertion for the fanout queue. Reran locally and CI.
Liam Nguyen (2025-02-18): Approve after nit fixes.
Sofia Alvarez (2025-02-19): Approve. Note: legal signoff attached to the Linear ticket SEC-223.

Added opt-in RBAC anomaly detection service, per-tenant KMS usage ledger for verifiable audit trails, and a jurisdictional pin gate preventing KMS allocations across pinned regions. Feature is behind flags; see docs/compliance/kms_ledger_guide.md for tenant opt-in, retention controls, and migration steps.

title: Private deployments: optimization config version pinning and rollback (Helm + installer)
author: Kira Thompson
text:
## Overview
This guide describes how **Private** (VPC/on-prem) operators manage **Optimization Config** versions (batching, caching, quantization profile selection) and execute a safe **rollback** when a change causes latency, error-rate, or quality regressions.

The Private deployment supports the same core semantics as Hosted/Dedicated:
- Immutable **Optimization Config versions** stored in the **private control plane**.
- A single **active version pointer** (per scope) consumed by runtime workers.
- Rollout state tracking + audit events.

This page focuses on operator workflows that do not rely on Redwood-managed infrastructure: **Helm** and the **Private installer (redwood-private-installer / redwoodctl)**.

> Safety note: Rollback is designed to be low-risk and idempotent, but it is not “free.” Some changes (notably cache strategy or quantization profile changes) can cause brief performance transients during worker convergence.

---

## When to rollback
Rollback is recommended when any of the following are observed after an optimization config apply/promote:
- Elevated **5xx** or request timeouts attributable to runtime behavior (not upstream/downstream dependencies).
- Sustained p95/p99 **latency regression** beyond your SLO budget.
- GPU saturation or queueing anomalies after a batching heuristic change.
- Quantization rollout triggers a **quality gate failure** (eval harness) or customer-reported output regression.

### What rollback does (Private)
Rollback sets the active optimization config pointer back to a known-good version and triggers workers to converge.
- The control plane records a **ROLLBACK** event in the audit stream.
- Runtime workers fetch the active version and apply it using an **idempotent applier**.
- The rollout controller (if enabled) tracks progress and final state.

### What rollback does NOT do
- It does not revert unrelated runtime releases, model versions, or infrastructure changes.
- It does not automatically “undo” side effects outside the runtime (e.g., customer app-level caches).
- It does not guarantee immediate token-by-token equivalence for quantization changes; expect a brief convergence window.

---

## Prerequisites / access
### Required access
- Kubernetes cluster admin for the Redwood Private namespaces (typical: `redwood-system`, `redwood-runtime`).
- Control-plane operator credentials (RBAC: `optimization_change_operator` or equivalent).

### Required tooling
- Helm-based installs:
 - `helm`, `kubectl`
- Installer-based installs:
 - `redwoodctl` (shipped with redwood-private-installer)

### Required observability (strongly recommended)
To safely decide rollback success, ensure metrics/logs include tags for:
- `tenant` (or `tenant_id`)
- `model`
- `region` (if multi-region)
- `config_version`

See: *Optimization rollout health dashboard* (internal): `eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/optimization-rollout-health-dashboard`

---

## Key concepts (Private)
### Scopes and “active version”
Optimization config versions can be activated at different scopes depending on your Private topology.

Common patterns in Private:
- **Single-tenant** cluster: global active version applies to all traffic.
- **Multi-tenant** Private (rare, but supported): per-tenant pointer.
- **Per-model overrides**: used when only one model pool needs a different quant profile or caching mode.

### Sources of truth
- **Control plane** is the source of truth for config version objects and the active pointer.
- **Helm/installer values** are used to:
 - Provide initial bootstrap settings, and/or
 - Explicitly pin an active version in “break glass” scenarios.

Operator guidance:
- Prefer control plane version selection when the control plane is healthy.
- Use Helm/installer pinning only when you need to recover from a broken control-plane rollout controller or to force a deterministic version during investigation.

---

## Rollback options (decision table)
| Option | Use when | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| A) Console/API rollback (control plane) | Control plane is healthy; you want auditability and normal semantics | Full audit trail; no cluster-level changes; lowest operational risk | Requires operator access to Console/API and working control plane |
| B) `redwoodctl` rollback (installer workflow) | You operate Private via installer and want a single supported operator command | Standardized; supports air-gapped workflows | Still depends on control plane connectivity inside the cluster |
| C) Helm “pin active version” | Break-glass; need to force a version even if rollout controller is misbehaving | Deterministic; can be applied with standard Kubernetes tooling | Higher risk of drift; requires careful cleanup after incident |

---

## A) Rollback via Console (recommended when available)
### Step 1 — Identify the current active version
In **Console → Optimize → Optimization Configs** (wording may differ by Private branding):
- Select the environment (e.g., `prod`).
- Filter to your scope (global / tenant / model).
- Note:
 - Active version ID (e.g., `ocv_2026_02_14_0017`)
 - Previous known-good version ID (e.g., `ocv_2026_02_10_0009`)

### Step 2 — Review blast radius
Before clicking rollback, confirm:
- Scope (global vs model-specific)
- Expected traffic impact window (usually 2–10 minutes)
- Whether the change included quantization profile updates (expect more noticeable convergence)

### Step 3 — Execute rollback
- Click **Rollback** on the chosen previous version.
- Confirm in the modal (type-to-confirm may be required).

### Step 4 — Verify convergence
Check the rollout status view:
- Status moves: `ROLLBACK_REQUESTED` → `APPLYING` → `COMPLETED`
- Worker convergence should reach your target threshold (default: 95% of workers within 5 minutes; cluster-specific)

### Step 5 — Verify SLO recovery
In dashboards/logs, confirm:
- 5xx rate back to baseline
- p95 latency back within acceptable regression threshold
- GPU utilization and queueing normalize
- For quantization: spot-check eval/quality signals and/or customer-reported symptoms

---

## B) Rollback via installer (`redwoodctl`)
> The exact subcommands can vary by installer version. If your `redwoodctl` output differs, follow the on-screen help and keep the intent (identify active version → rollback to prior version → verify).

### Step 1 — List versions and current active pointer
Run from a machine with access to the cluster (or inside the admin tooling pod):

1) Show active version:
- `redwoodctl optimize-config active --env prod --scope global`

2) List recent versions:
- `redwoodctl optimize-config versions list --env prod --limit 20`

### Step 2 — Roll back to a known-good version
- `redwoodctl optimize-config rollback --env prod --scope global --to-version ocv_2026_02_10_0009 --reason "latency regression after batching update"`

Expected behavior:
- Command returns a rollback request ID.
- Audit event emitted: `optimization_config.rollback.requested`.

### Step 3 — Monitor rollout status
- `redwoodctl optimize-config rollout status --env prod --scope global --watch`

### Step 4 — Post-rollback verification
Minimum checklist:
- Confirm request paths are serving normally (synthetic checks).
- Confirm metric tags include the reverted `config_version`.
- Confirm no workers are stuck on the bad version.

---

## C) Break-glass rollback by pinning via Helm
Use this only when you cannot reliably change the active version via the control plane (e.g., rollout controller stuck, API degraded, or you must force a deterministic version for incident mitigation).

### How pinning works
Pinning forces runtime workers (and/or the config-applier sidecar, depending on your chart) to use a specific optimization config version.

**Important:** After the incident, unpin and return control to the control plane to avoid long-lived drift.

### Step 0 — Gather information
You need:
- Namespace(s) for runtime workers
- The version ID you want to pin (e.g., `ocv_2026_02_10_0009`)

Also capture:
- Current Helm release name(s)
- Current values file(s)

### Step 1 — Update Helm values
In your Private values file (example keys; match your chart’s actual values):

- `optimizationConfig.versionPin: "ocv_2026_02_10_0009"`
- `optimizationConfig.pinMode: "break_glass"`

If your deployment separates control plane and runtime charts, apply the pin in the **runtime** chart.

### Step 2 — Apply the Helm upgrade
- `helm upgrade <release> redwood/runtime -n redwood-runtime -f values-prod.yaml`

### Step 3 — Force worker convergence (if needed)
If workers do not converge promptly (stale cache / missed watch event), perform a controlled rollout restart:
- `kubectl rollout restart deploy/<runtime-deployment> -n redwood-runtime`

### Step 4 — Verify
- Confirm responses include the expected `config_version` (if you enabled the response header option in your gateway/OpenAI-compat layer).
- Confirm error/latency SLOs recover.

### Step 5 — Cleanup (return to normal control-plane ownership)
After mitigation:
- Remove `optimizationConfig.versionPin` and re-apply Helm.
- Ensure the control plane active pointer matches the desired version.

---

## Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
### 1) “Rollback succeeded” but metrics don’t change
**Symptoms:** Console/CLI shows rollback completed, but dashboards still show the bad behavior.

**Causes:**
- You are looking at aggregated metrics without `config_version` segmentation.
- Traffic is still routed to a subset of workers on the old version.
- A separate change (runtime release, model update) is the real cause.

**Fix:**
- Filter by `config_version` and by pool.
- Check rollout status for stragglers.
- Confirm runtime release/version did not change at the same time.

### 2) Mixed worker state after concurrent apply and rollback
**Symptoms:** Some workers report `config_version=A`, others `config_version=B` for longer than expected.

**Causes:**
- A concurrent apply/rollback raced; worker caches or checkpoints lagged.

**Fix:**
- Ensure no other rollout is running; pause rollout controller if supported.
- Trigger a controlled worker restart for the affected pool.
- If persistent, collect logs from config-applier and file a support bundle.

### 3) Quantization rollback causes a transient latency spike
**Symptoms:** Immediately after rollback, latency briefly increases.

**Explanation:**
- Switching quant profiles can invalidate or re-warm runtime caches and change kernel selection.

**Mitigations:**
- Prefer rollback during a low-traffic window when feasible.
- If your topology supports it, roll back per-model pool and ramp traffic back.

### 4) Helm upgrade uses stale values (`--reuse-values`)
**Symptoms:** Pin/unpin doesn’t take effect.

**Fix:**
- Avoid `--reuse-values` during incident operations unless you fully understand the current release state.
- Explicitly provide the values file containing the pin.

### 5) RBAC blocks rollback in Private
**Symptoms:** Operator cannot see rollback action or receives permission denied.

**Fix:**
- Confirm the role binding includes permissions for `optimization_config.rollback`.
- Ensure the operator identity used by Console/API matches your expected SSO mapping.
- Reference: `PM-902-rbac-permissions-for-optimization-changes` (internal tracking).

---

## Audit logging expectations (Private)
Private deployments should emit audit events for config lifecycle actions.

Minimum events to verify are present (names may be versioned):
- `optimization_config.version.created`
- `optimization_config.apply.requested`
- `optimization_config.promote.completed`
- `optimization_config.rollback.requested`
- `optimization_config.rollback.completed`

Recommended required fields:
- actor identity (user/service)
- scope (tenant/model/region)
- from_version / to_version (rollback)
- request_id / correlation_id
- timestamp

If an enterprise customer reports missing rollback events, validate your audit pipeline export (SIEM connector / log forwarder) before assuming the control plane failed to emit the event.

---

## Operator verification checklist (copy/paste)
1) Identify active version before rollback: ________
2) Identify rollback target version: ________
3) Record scope (global/tenant/model): ________
4) Execute rollback (Console/API/redwoodctl/Helm)
5) Confirm rollout status: COMPLETED
6) Confirm majority worker convergence threshold met (target: ____%)
7) Confirm metrics:
 - 5xx back to baseline
 - p95 latency within threshold
 - GPU saturation normal
8) Confirm audit events exported for rollback
9) If break-glass pinning used: unpin and return to control-plane ownership
10) Post-incident: attach timeline + versions to the incident ticket

---

## Getting help / escalation
If rollback does not converge within your expected window (default guidance: 10–15 minutes for typical pools):
- Gather:
 - rollout status output
 - control-plane logs for Optimization Config Service
 - runtime worker logs including config-applier
 - dashboard screenshots filtered by `config_version`
- Escalate to:
 - Private Deployments: Vivek Kulkarni / Bruno Silva
 - SRE guidance (runbook alignment): Sean Gallagher

For internal Redwood ops, also reference: `eng-platform/runbooks/rollback-optimization-config`.

title: Geofence scope & operational failover windows — confirmation and next steps
author: vivek_kulkarni
text:
From: Sara Miller <sara.miller@cloudhealth.com>
To: vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai
Cc: procurement@cloudhealth.com
Date: Mon, 10 May 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Geofence scope and failover windows - initial questions

Hi Vivek,

Thanks for the quick onboarding session last week — we ran it by our security team and have a couple of clarifying asks before we move to signatures. High level we need to confirm:

1) For EU customers: can you confirm all inference processing (tokenization, KV cache, model execution) will be pinned to EU region resources under the hosted plan? We need to be sure no transient hops to US or APAC occur except under an explicit failover scenario.

2) Failover window: our policy allows transient cross-border processing for incident-driven failover, but we require a defined maximum window (our initial baseline is 48 hours) and an operational notification SLA (who to notify, evidence logs). Is Redwood able to commit to a max transient failover window and provide audit evidence when it happens?

3) KMS/keys: what options do you support for regional KMS? Can we bring our own key (BYOK) for EU? If not, what encryption-at-rest boundaries exist?

4) Subprocessors: please share the most recent roster and indicate which subprocessor endpoints may be involved in transient routing (CDN, analytics, telemetry).

We attached our DPA checklist and the subprocessor template — please respond with a short note we can send to Legal to track acceptance, and any DPA addendum you think is required.

Appreciate a reply with suggested language we can include in the DPA. If easier, we can hop on a 30-minute call tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sara
Sara Miller
Head of Security Programs
CloudHealth Inc.

--- Attachment: requested_subprocessor_list_2027-05.csv (fields: name, role, region, endpoint)
From: vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai>
To: Sara Miller <sara.miller@cloudhealth.com>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai, karthik_iyer@redwood.ai, laura_bennett@redwood.ai
Date: Mon, 10 May 2027 11:06:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Geofence scope and failover windows - initial questions

Sara — thanks for the clear list. Looping in Marissa (Legal), Karthik (Ops), and Laura (Product) to make sure we cover both contractual and operational pieces. Below is a concise response and a proposed DPA addendum outline we can share with you.

Short answers up front:
- Region pinning: Yes — Redwood Hosted can be configured with EU-region pinning for inference. That configuration ensures inference compute, KV caching, and transient storage used by the runtime remain in the EU region by default.
- Transient failover: We support a defined transient failover policy. Our standard transient window historically used in large customers has been 72 hours, but we can discuss tightening to 48 hours with appropriate operational constraints. Any cross-region processing is done only when capacity or regional outage dictates.
- Notification & evidence: We provide an operational incident notification within 24 hours of an automated cross-region failover and include time-stamped routing logs (CSV) + request traces for the window. We can add a contractual clause to that effect.
- KMS/BYOK: For Hosted we offer customer-managed keys in select regions — EU BYOK is available via our KMS partner integrations (customer must provision key in their cloud account). For Dedicated/Private deployments BYOK is standard.
- Subprocessors: Attached is our up-to-date roster. We flag components that may be involved during transient routing.

Proposed DPA addendum (high level) — please review, this is what we would include in the contract and DPA:
- Definition: "Transient cross-border processing" = temporary routing of inference requests outside of the pinned region to maintain availability during outages, limited to a maximum cumulative window per incident.
- Max window: 72 hours standard; optional 48-hour negotiated cap for accounts with stricter locality requirements.
- Notification SLA: Redwood to notify primary CloudHealth security contact within 24 hours of an event and provide routing logs within 48 hours.
- Evidence: Time‑stamped routing traces, list of endpoints involved (IPs/domains), and a post-incident summary.
- KMS: BYOK support where available; if not available, encryption keys managed by Redwood KMS with region-bound key material and access logs.
- Escrow/mitigation: Option to require temporary rate limiting or failback policy executed by Redwood on request.

Next steps: Marissa — can your team propose language that maps the bullet points above into DPA clauses (coverage of notifications, windows, and evidence)? Karthik — please confirm operational feasibility of 48-hour vs 72-hour SLAs and what telemetry/logs we can commit to within 48 hours vs 72 hours. Laura — we should document BYOK availability in EU for this account.

Sara — happy to get on a 30 min call tomorrow. Proposed times: Tue 10:00-11:30am UTC or Tue 15:00-16:00 UTC. Which works for you?

Best,
Vivek
SVP, Sales & Partnerships
Redwood Inference

--- Attachments sent: Redwood_DPA_v3_addendum-draft.pdf (working draft)
--- Attachments sent: requested_subprocessor_list_2027-05.csv (Redwood annotated)

Cc: karthik_iyer@redwood.ai, laura_bennett@redwood.ai
Date: Mon, 10 May 2027 14:32:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Geofence scope and failover windows - initial questions

Thanks Vivek — quick legal note to start. We can map the proposed language into DPA text. A couple of suggested changes / asks from Legal:

- Max window: recommend we default to 72 hours in the DPA but include a customer-selectable checkbox for 48 hours during negotiation. That gives Ops breathing room during major outages.
- Notification & evidence: we can commit to notifying within 24 hours and delivering routing logs + trace samples within 48 hours; full packet-level traces may not be available for privacy reasons, but request/response traces and routing headers are available.
- SLA carveouts: we should add carveouts for third-party subprocessor outages and force majeure.

Operational ask for Karthik: please confirm whether we can produce a CSV of routing logs (timestamp, original region, routed-to region, request-id, node-id) and whether logs will include hashes only (no PII) — CloudHealth will need assurance that payloads are not output in logs.

Sara — Laura/Marissa are happy to work with your legal team to draft the final addendum. Vivek — I recommend a short joint call with CloudHealth legal + Security and Redwood Legal + Ops to sign off.

Marissa Cole

Redwood Inference

Vivek / Marissa / team — thanks for the quick and thorough response. CloudHealth Legal and Security reviewed and we can accept the 72-hour default provided we get the following:

- A confirmable notification within 24 hours with routing logs (CSV) — these must include timestamp, request-id, original region, routed region, and the node-id. Hashes only for any user identifiers — no PII in logs.

title: GPU power capping from mixed-precision fallbacks caused autoscaler to shrink capacity and transient tenant starvation
text:
Issue summary:
Customer reported sporadic P99 latency spikes and temporary 5xxs from their dedicated pool during lunchtime traffic on 2026-03-12. Symptoms included: increased attach time to GPUs, evictions from the pool, and sudden autoscaler shrink events followed by tenant request timeouts.

Impact:
- Customer (Acme AI) saw ~20% of their requests return 502/504 during a 14:20–14:35 UTC window.
- Throughput dropped for their pinned routes; internal dashboards showed brief reduction in live GPU attachments for the dedicated pool.
- Affected production flows: low-latency chatlets and short streaming sessions.

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity pool: pool-dedicated-us-east-3 (pinned to HW-family: gdx-48gb-mix)
- Models served: redwood/gpt-x-13b-fp16 (primary), fallback to fp32 when kernel hit frag or mem alignment issues
- Region: us-east-1, prod

Steps to reproduce (approx):
1) Run a short-stream workload with many concurrent, 2–6 token requests interleaved with occasional long requests (1:20 ratio short:long).
2) Force mixed-precision fallback on some requests by sending slightly misaligned sequence lengths and forcing attention patterns that trigger a legacy kernel path.
3) Observe GPU driver logs and autoscaler telemetry over a 15–30 minute window.

Observed behavior:
- GPUs reported repeated power capping events in driver logs (power_limit_changed / pwr cap applied) leading to clock down events and reduced TFLOPS per card.
- Serving runtime noted higher per-request latency due to lower clocks and more kernel retries; metric: kernel_retry_rate spiked 3x.
- Autoscaler observed sustained reduced utilization and fired a shrink (scale-down) decision; scale-down removed a small number of GPUs which led to request failures while attachments were rebalanced.
- Customer's short streams experienced serialized queueing and a rise in 502/504 until the autoscaler stabilized.

Expected behavior:
- Autoscaler should not react to short-lived driver-level power events that transiently reduce clock speed; should consider thermal/power signals as unreliable for capacity shrink decisions.
- Serving runtime should prefer FP16 execution paths for pinned models without downgrading to fallback on short misaligned requests when avoidable.

Logs / telemetry snippets:
- GPU driver: "pwr_cap applied: 160W -> 120W; clocks throttled" (multiple cards, repeated ~every 30s for ~10min)
- Runtime metric: kernel_retry_rate: baseline 0.2 -> 0.65; attach_latency p95: 180ms -> 560ms
- Autoscaler decision trace: shrink triggered at 14:25:12 UTC with decision_reason: "sustained_utilization_below_threshold (5m)"

Attachments / Links:
- customer-provided logs: s3://acme-uploads/sup-250999/log-batch-14-20.tar.gz
- internal dashboard links: https://console.redwood.com/dashboards/dedicated/pool-dedicated-us-east-3?span=15m

Immediate customer-facing summary (first response):
- Acknowledge impact, set customer status to "We are investigating", provide workaround to pin model to FP16 variant and reduce concurrent short-streams while we investigate.

2026-03-12 14:28 UTC | Aisha Patel (Support): Customer (Acme AI) reports 502/504 on pinned dedicated pool. Asking for logs, sample request ids, and timeframe. SLA first response due 2026-03-13.
2026-03-12 15:05 UTC | Diego Martinez (SRE): Got logs. Observed repeated GPU power cap events correlated with latency spikes. Triage to autoscaler and runtime. Escalating to runtime team; allocating on-call CPU/GPU help.
2026-03-12 16:10 UTC | Priya Singh (Runtime Eng): Initial hypothesis: mixed-precision fallback kernels cause hotter power draw due to less efficient memory layout leading to driver power capping on these cards under short-burst patterns. Suggest immediate mitigation: force FP16 path and suppress autoscaler shrink decisions for 10m if shrink is correlated with power cap signals.
2026-03-13 09:22 UTC | Diego Martinez (SRE): Applied mitigation in prod: updated pool autoscaler policy to ignore utilization dips that coincide with driver power_cap events and increased min-replicas by 1 for pool-dedicated-us-east-3. Also enabled 'prefer_fp16' flag for redwood/gpt-x-13b-fp16 for this pool.
2026-03-13 12:40 UTC | Aisha Patel (Support): Informed customer of applied mitigations and requested confirmation that errors have subsided. Customer confirmed reduced 5xxs and improved p95 within 2 hours.
2026-03-14 10:00 UTC | Priya Singh (Runtime Eng): Root cause analysis complete. Filed long-term fix PR to improve kernel selection and to add driver-signals-safe heuristics in autoscaler: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4821. Scheduling rollout window in maintenance next week.
2026-03-14 11:15 UTC | Aisha Patel (Support): Closing customer ticket after customer confirms stable behavior and acceptance of planned rollout. Provided post-incident notes and contact for follow-up.

Hypothesis 1: Mixed-precision fallback kernels cause inefficient memory access patterns increasing instantaneous power draw -> driver power cap applied -> lower GPU clock -> throughput drop.
Hypothesis 2: Short-stream heavy fanout causes workload bursts that push card to peak power frequently; combined with fallback kernels, this breaches power envelope on older card revisions in pool.
Telemetry findings: Correlation found between driver power_cap events and autoscaler shrink timestamps. Power cap events preceded autoscaler shrinks by ~45-90s in most samples.
Kernel-level traces: Certain attention kernel variants used under fallback showed 18% higher GPU compute time on identical batch size compared to preferred FP16 kernel.
Autoscaler policy evaluation: current policy treats sustained_utilization_below_threshold over sliding 5m as reliable; however it does not cross-check driver telemetry (power/thermal) which made it act on transient hardware-level events.
Risk assessment: Without mitigation, repeated events could lead to unnecessary capacity churn and customer-visible errors for pinned dedicated pools under bursty short-stream workloads.
Related past incidents: see SUP-41258 (thermal throttle) for similar clock-down observations; however that incident was caused by ambient thermal conditions not kernel power draw patterns.

Mitigation applied 2026-03-13 09:22 UTC: (1) Set autoscaler to ignore utilization dips coincident with driver power_cap signals for pool-dedicated-us-east-3, (2) increased pool min-replicas by +1 as temporary buffer, (3) enabled prefer_fp16 execution path for redwood/gpt-x-13b-fp16 in that pool.
Customer impact after mitigation: 5xxs dropped from ~20% to <1% during comparable load windows. P95 latency returned to expected range within ~2 hours.
Long-term fixes: PR #4821 updates kernel selection logic to avoid costly fallbacks for short-stream patterns and adds autoscaler cross-check to filter shrink decisions when driver-level power/thermal events are present. Scheduled rollout: progressive canary starting 2026-03-21 with post-rollout validation dashboards.
Follow-ups assigned: Runtime team to complete kernel selection improvements (owner: Priya Singh), Autoscaler team to add driver-telemetry gating (owner: Diego Martinez). Notify capacity-planning for potential hardware refresh for pool-dedicated-us-east-3 in next quarter.
Customer communication: Sent post-incident summary and planned timeline for fixes. Customer accepted workarounds and will monitor during next week. Ticket closed with customer sign-off on 2026-03-14.

title: office-art-and-plants-guidelines-2024
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Title: Office Art & Plant Guidelines

Summary:
This page documents lightweight guidelines for installing office art, plants, and temporary desk decorations at Redwood Inference offices. It is intended to balance aesthetic expression with safety, accessibility, and shared workspace norms. These notes are informal and maintained by People Ops.

Scope:
- Applies to common areas (kitchen, lounges, corridors) and individual desks in open offices.
- Does not replace formal safety or building management policies for structural changes or electrical work.

Guiding Principles:
1. Safety first: no obstructing egress, fire alarms, or emergency equipment. Avoid tripping hazards.
2. Respect shared spaces: avoid strong scents, noisy installations, or items that monopolize common areas.
3. Accessibility: ensure signage/art is hung at a height that does not impede mobility or visibility.
4. Temporary & reversible: most installations should be removable without tools or wall damage.

Approval & Ownership:
- Small desk plants and framed prints: no formal approval required.
- Larger items (floor-standing planters, freestanding sculptures, wall-hung installations > 30" in any dimension): submit a short request to people-ops@redwood.com with location, dimensions, weight, and installation method.
- People Ops is the owner for approvals and coordination with building management.

Installation Guidelines:
- Mounting: prefer adhesive strips rated for drywall where appropriate; for heavier fixtures require building-approved anchors and sign-off.
- Electrical: any installation requiring power must be scheduled with facilities and IT; do not run extension cords across walkways.
- Plants: prefer low-allergen, low-light tolerant species for shared spaces (e.g., snake plant, pothos). Avoid high-fragrance plants in kitchens and meeting rooms.
- ID tags: label any communal plant with owner name and watering cadence if not centrally maintained.

Maintenance & Removal:
- Owners are responsible for upkeep. Facilities may remove items that create hazards or persistent nuisances after one week's notice.
- For space reconfigurations, owners will be asked to relocate or remove personal/communal items within two weeks.

Temporary Exhibitions & Events:
- If a team wants to host a temporary exhibit (art show, maker fair, holiday display), submit a proposal at least 10 business days prior including insurance/waiver details if items are valuable.

Quick Checklist (for submitters):
- [ ] Location & footprint
- [ ] Estimated weight
- [ ] Mounting method
- [ ] Owner & contact
- [ ] Maintenance plan
- [ ] Needed approvals (building/facilities)

Contacts & Related Pages:
- People Ops: people-ops@redwood.com
- Facilities manager: facilities@redwood.com
- Related Confluence: [Company Handbook - Office Policies](/confluence/company-handbook/office-policies)
- Related Confluence: [Space Allocation Guide](/confluence/people-ops/space-allocation)

Change Log:
- 2024-11-12: Initial draft (Aisha Patel)
- 2025-02-10: Updated approval thresholds and plant guidance (Aisha Patel)

Notes:
- This guidance is intentionally lightweight to encourage a pleasant workplace while keeping operations simple. For complex installations or anything involving building infrastructure, coordinate with Facilities and People Ops.

title: Robot identity bootstrap workflow: gated creation, attestation, and audit hooks
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Summary:
Introduce a gated, auditable machine/robot identity bootstrap workflow for service accounts that enforces least-privilege templates, ownership assignment, and periodic attestation. This ticket covers the end-to-end flow: request surface (GitHub PR or Console), automated template selection, approval gating, ephemeral credential issuance, audit-log hooks, and SSO/SAML group mapping for RBAC v2 compatibility. The goal is to reduce manual onboarding, eliminate over-permissive defaults, and make ownership traceable for compliance audits.

Background & motivation:
Current creation flows allow engineers and some admins to call internal APIs to create service accounts. Over time we see many long-lived accounts with broad scopes and unclear owners. Incidents and internal audits highlight two recurring issues: (1) accounts drift to excess privileges and (2) ownership is stale or unknown. RBAC v2 introduces role bindings and SSO group mappings — we need a creation workflow that pushes best-practice templates and ties each account to an owner and an audit trail.

Scope / non-goals:
- In-scope: request UI (Console + GitHub PR template), server-side gating service ("svc-bootstrap"), least-privilege template registry, approval workflow (can be automated), ephemeral credential issuance (short-lived keys or OIDC exchange), periodic ownership attestation webhook, audit-log integration with SIEM, SSO/SAML group mapping push for RBAC v2.
- Out-of-scope: wholesale migration of existing service accounts (separate migration program), key rotation automation for third-party integrations (follow-up).

Acceptance criteria:
- Engineers can create a service account via (A) a standardized GitHub PR template or (B) Console guided flow that selects an appropriate least-privilege template.
- Creation requests are evaluated by svc-bootstrap which returns either: auto-approved (meets template & requester policy), requires 1 approver (for elevated scopes), or blocked (violates policy).
- On approval, the system issues ephemeral credentials (OIDC token exchange + optional short-lived key) and writes a structured audit event to central logging (index: redwood-svc-accounts) with owner, template, justification, and request_id.
- The account is assigned a canonical owner (user or team) with a TTL-driven attestation schedule (default 90 days). If an attestation window lapses without confirmation, the account is locked and listed for cleanup.
- RBAC v2 role bindings are created as minimal as possible; SSO/SAML group mapping is written to the mapping table for downstream enforcement.
- Console surface shows creation request history, owner, last attestation date, and a one-click revoke/rotate action.

Design decisions & trade-offs:
1) Templates vs free-form scopes: Templates reduce variance and are required for self-serve. Allow a "custom" path but require explicit approver and justification to avoid sprawl.
2) Ephemeral creds: Prefer OIDC short-lived tokens where the consumer supports it. Fallback to short-lived keys (24h) for legacy integrations. This reduces blast radius but adds complexity to consumers — we will publish migration docs.
3) Auto-approve heuristics: For low-risk templates and requesters in an allowed group (e.g., platform-engineering), auto-approve to keep throughput. For risky templates, require manual approval to balance security and developer velocity.
4) Audit volume: Every lifecycle event emits structured JSON to the SIEM. We will sample debug-level events but keep critical lifecycle events (create/approve/attest/revoke) always logged.

Implementation plan (high-level):
- Week 1: Build svc-bootstrap microservice skeleton, template registry schema, and GitHub PR template. (ENG-76421-A)
- Week 2: Implement approval rules engine, Console request UI wireframe, and initial SSO mapping API. (ENG-76421-B)
- Week 3: Integrate ephemeral credential issuer (OIDC flow) and key fallback, produce audit event to dev SIEM index. (ENG-76421-C)
- Week 4: Attestation scheduler, lock/cleanup path, Console owner UI, tests, and docs. (ENG-76421-D)
- Week 5: Internal dogfood + security review, telemetry, and rollout plan. (ENG-76421-E)

Telemetry & observability:
- Metrics: creation_requests_total, auto_approvals_total, manual_approvals_total, failed_creations_total, attestation_missed_total, ephemeral_issuances_total.
- Logging: structured audit events include: request_id, template_id, requester_id, owner_id, approver_ids, justification, decision, and timestamp.
- Dashboards: create a Console dashboard for pending attestations and accounts locked-by-policy. Link: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/sa-lifecycle

Security & compliance notes:
- All creation actions require an authenticated identity; Console flows use SSO SAML assertions and GitHub flows require verified commit authorship.
- Audit events are immutable and forwarded to long-term retention for compliance.
- Security review required before roll-out (subtask created).

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Developer friction from mandatory templates -> Mitigation: create low-friction templates and an escape hatch for emergency service accounts with short TTLs and mandatory post-hoc review.
- Risk: Legacy consumers fail with ephemeral creds -> Mitigation: provide a 60-day migration window and short-lived key fallback with monitored usage.
- Risk: Approval bottleneck -> Mitigation: automating approvals for low-risk cases and provide a Slack/Console notification for pending approvals to reduce latency.

Open questions (to decide in kickoff):
- What is the canonical owner model: single user vs team alias? (preference: team alias with optional primary user).
- Default attestation cadence: 90 vs 180 days? (default 90, configurable per template).
- Approved approver scopes: should platform-admins be able to sign off on any template? (likely yes, but track approvals).

References & artifacts:
- Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SEC/Service+Account+Lifecycle+Project (draft spec)
- GitHub PR prototype: https://github.com/redwood-internal/svc-bootstrap/pull/12 (prototype endpoint + schema)
- Compliance ticket: ENG-74211 (audit retention & SIEM mapping)

Next steps (this sprint):
- Kickoff meeting with Security, Platform, and Console: schedule week of 2025-01-20.
- Create svc-bootstrap repo, push PR with API contract and schema.
- Draft Console mockups and GitHub PR template and run quick user interview with 3 engineers.


2025-01-19 - Marco Li: Completed initial API schema draft and pushed to GH prototype (link in references). Need decision on owner model before Week 2 work.
2025-01-22 - Elena Torres (Security): Security review scheduled for 2025-02-02; requested explicit threat model for ephemeral vs long-lived keys.
2025-01-28 - Aisha Patel: Ran 1:1 with Platform Eng leads; consensus to default to team alias owners. Added automated attestation webhook design.
2025-02-03 - Marco Li: Implemented event schema for audit logs; logs forwarded to redwood-svc-accounts index in dev. Test harness added.

title: Operational Psychological Safety and Debrief Protocols
author: Asha Patel
text:
Summary:
This document defines the operational psychological safety (ops-psych) principles and a standardized debrief protocol for incidents, game days, and on-call rotations. The goal is to protect responder wellbeing, improve learning throughput from incidents, and reduce blame-based behaviors that slow down remediation. This is intended to supplement existing incident triage and postmortem processes and applies to all responder roles (first-responder, bridge operator, service steward, and on-call engineers).

Scope:
- Applies to incidents, near-misses, game days, and sustained SLO restoration efforts.
- Covers pre-incident preparation, in-incident communication hygiene, immediate debrief (T+0–24h), and in-depth postmortem synthesis.

Principles (short):
1) People over logs: protect human responders before preserving artifacts.
2) Curious, not accusatory: ask what, how, and why — avoid who-first language.
3) Timely, lightweight learning: capture actionable fixes within 24–48 hours.
4) Iterative improvement: validate fixes via follow-up game days or synthetic checks.

Roles & Ownership:
- Incident Lead (IL): coordinates response and ensures an immediate debrief is scheduled.
- Bridge Operator: runs incident bridge, documents decisions and action owners.
- Steward / Service Owner: owns follow-up remediation and postmortem delivery.
- People-Ops Liaison: supports psychological-safety interventions for high-impact incidents and organizes peer support.

Before an Incident (preparation):
- Mandatory: each responder completes the Ops-Psych micro-course (20 min) and acknowledges the debrief playbook.
- Runbooks must include an explicit ‘people check’ step (owner contact, rotation backup).
- Rotation managers maintain a visible on-call load index per engineer (weekly snapshot). Target max weekly load index = 1.0 (see below).

During an Incident (communication hygiene):
- Use neutral language templates in bridge chat (examples below).
- Pause non-essential escalations during high-cognitive-load phases.
- Assign a single communications lead for external messages.

Immediate Debrief (T+0 to T+24h) — Template and Steps:
1. Schedule: IL schedules 30–45 minute debrief within 6 hours of mitigation or bridge close.
2. Attendees: responders on-shift, bridge operator, service owner, one People-Ops or SRE mentor. Keep attendance voluntary beyond core responders.
3. Agenda (structured):
 - 00–05m: Safety check-in (How is everyone? Any immediate support needed?)
 - 05–10m: Brief factual timeline (no finger-pointing)
 - 10–25m: What surprised us? What worked?
 - 25–35m: Immediate action owners & near-term mitigations (within 72h)
 - 35–45m: Communication plan for customers and leadership, and schedule for postmortem
4. Outputs (must be captured in incident ticket):
 - One-sentence incident summary
 - 3 short observations (factual)
 - 2 proposed actions with owners and target dates
 - People check (who needs follow-up support)

Postmortem Quality Gate (T+24–72h):
- Draft postmortem should be created within 72 hours and include the Immediate Debrief outputs.
- Postmortems must pass the following quality checklist before publication:
 * Clear timeline with source links to traces/alerts (yes/no)
 * Action owners assigned with due dates (yes/no)
 * Root cause analysis focused on systems and processes (not individuals) (yes/no)
 * Proposed verification plan for fixes (smoke tests/game-day) (yes/no)
 * Short executive summary (≤3 sentences) (yes/no)

Runbook Validation Checklist:
- Each runbook entry must include: triggers, quick mitigations (2–3 bullets), escalations, owner contact, and a ‘people-safe’ note (how to pause and request backup).
- Quarterly: sample each high-severity runbook via one simulated run by a cross-team pair.
- Validation Result Table (example):
| Runbook | Last Tested | Tester | Pass/Fail | Notes |
| Serving-GPU-OOM | 2026-05-10 | infra-sim | Pass | Added KV-cache eviction step |

Game Day Debrief Agenda (60–90m):
- Pre-game warmup (15m): technical goals and safety norms
- Simulation window (varies, recorded)
- After-action review (50m): start with feelings check, then timeline, then improvements
- Decide owner and date for follow-up verification

Customer Status and Leadership Communication Templates (examples):
- Short customer status (for live incidents, 2–3 lines):
 "We are investigating increased latency for Redwood text-generation in us-west-2. Our engineers have mitigated the immediate impact and are working on a full restoration. We will provide a next update within 60 minutes. If you need priority support, reply to this message or contact your CSM."

- Leadership incident brief (email/exec summary):
 Subject: [INC] us-west-2 latency — mitigated, investigation ongoing
 Body: 1) What happened (1 line) 2) Impact (tokens/sec, % customers affected) 3) Current status (mitigated/partially degraded) 4) Next steps (owner + ETA)

Neutral Language Examples for Bridge/Chat:
- Instead of: "Who broke the KV cache?" use: "What sequence of events led to the KV cache eviction?"
- Instead of: "You missed the alert" use: "Which alert thresholds did we see and how did they behave?"

Escalation and People-Support Paths:
- For high-stress incidents (severity ≥ 1 hour outage impacting >10% customers) People-Ops will offer a short 1:1 check-in with each on-call participant within 48 hours.
- For traumatic incidents (data loss or customer breach) the company will fund a confidential external counseling session on request.

Action Tracking and Follow-up:
- Use the incident tracker (Jira ticket pattern: INC-YYYY-NNNN). All actions must be entered as subtasks with due dates.
- SRE steward reviews open actions weekly; overdue items escalate to the service owner and responsibility forum.

Measurement and Success Criteria:
- Target: 90% of Immediate Debriefs completed within 24 hours for severity P1/P2 incidents.
- Target: 100% of postmortem quality gates passed for Sev1s within 30 days.
- People metric: reduce oncall burnout index (anonymous pulse) by 20% year-over-year via rotation adjustments and psych-safety interventions.

Appendix A — Short checklists (copyable):
Immediate Debrief Checklist:
- [ ] Schedule 30–45m session within 6 hours
- [ ] Include People-Ops or SRE mentor
- [ ] Capture outputs (1-line summary, 3 observations, 2 actions with owners)

Postmortem Quality Gate Checklist:
- [ ] Timeline with links
- [ ] Actions with owners and dates
- [ ] Root cause analysis (systems/processes)
- [ ] Verification plan
- [ ] Exec summary

Customer Status Template (longer for public status page):
- Title: Degraded performance for Redwood text generation — us-west-2
- Status: Investigating / Identified / Partial restoration / Restored
- Impact: Users may experience 2–10x latency on text-generation routes; embeddings unaffected
- Next update: Timestamp + ETA
- Workaround: Retry with model-redwood-lite or fall back to regional routing (eu-central-1)

Guidance for Rotation Managers (operational):
- Rebalance rotation if a single engineer’s 4-week load index > 1.2.
- Encourage scheduled recovery days after two P1 incidents in a 30-day window.
- Maintain a confidential incident-impact log for each on-call participant (for People-Ops review only).

Change log and next steps:
- 2026-01-15: Initial draft (Asha Patel)
- 2026-03-05: Added runbook validation table and customer templates (Marcus Li)
- 2026-06-10: Incorporated People-Ops escalation flow and counseling guidance (Sofia Moreno)

Related resources / links:
- Incident communication templates
- Postmortem rubric and publishing checklist
- Runbook authoring guide

For questions or to propose edits, contact the People-Ops oncall at people-ops-oncall@redwood.ai or ping @asha on Slack.

title: sales
text:
Hannah Schmitt: Need quick help on EU data residency objection. Prospect (EU bank) wants “EU-only processing + EU-only storage + no US access” for Hosted. What’s the approved phrasing + what do we *not* promise? @Olga Petrov @Daniel Carter @Marcus Lin

Lukas Meyer: +1, similar objection came up in EMEA last week. They’re asking if *anything* touches US systems (logs, support tooling, etc). Want to keep this clean.

Avery Johnson: Same here on another deal. Can we get a pasteable paragraph + a “don’t say this” list?

Priyom Das: They also asked if model routing could ever fail over to a non-EU region under load. Need to confirm.

Marcus Lin: jumping in. First: do NOT promise “EU-only” unless we’re talking Private deployment w/ customer-controlled infra, or we have a written contract amendment that explicitly defines what’s in/out.

Marcus Lin: For Hosted: we can support region selection (incl EU) for request processing, but we should be precise that some operational metadata may be processed/stored outside the selected region depending on the system (billing, abuse prevention, support). We need to use the approved language.

Naomi Feldman: +1. Also: don’t imply “no failover ever.” Our default is to keep traffic in-region if you’ve selected EU, but we can’t blanket guarantee “never leaves EU under any condition” unless it’s explicitly in the commercial terms / Private. Say “region-pinned” and “no cross-region routing by default for customer content” (but avoid absolute words like “never”).

Hannah Schmitt: got it. What’s the exact approved snippet? They’re literally asking for “contractual commitment that all data incl logs stays in EU and only EU staff can access.”

Olga Petrov: Here’s what we can say (approved style). Use “Customer Content” vs “data” to avoid ambiguity. Also do not commit on “EU-only personnel” access.

Olga Petrov: Pasteable response (Hosted + EU region):
“Redwood Inference supports regional processing for Hosted API workloads. When a customer selects an EU region, Customer Content (request prompts and model outputs) is processed in that region. Access to Customer Content is restricted to authorized personnel on a need-to-know basis and is logged. Certain limited operational metadata (e.g., account and billing information, service health telemetry) may be processed or stored outside the selected region as part of operating and securing the service. For stricter residency requirements (including customer-managed networking and data boundary controls), Redwood offers Dedicated capacity in-region and Private (VPC/on‑prem) deployments.”

Daniel Carter: + a compliance note: we should add “Details available under NDA / via the evidence request process.” Do not attach internal diagrams in email.

Daniel Carter: Also, for “contractual commitment” requests: route to Legal + GRC. We can say “We can evaluate specific contractual residency requirements; please share the questionnaire language.”

Lukas Meyer: Can we explicitly address the “failover” question? They’re worried about cross-region fallback.

Marcus Lin: approved approach: “We route based on the region selected; cross-region routing of customer content is not the standard behavior for region-pinned setups.” Don’t use “never.” If they require a hard guarantee, push to Dedicated/Private + contract language.

Naomi Feldman: Also don’t conflate “data residency” with “data retention.” They’ll ask “how long do you store prompts/logs in EU.” That’s a separate set of knobs depending on deployment.

Avery Johnson: Can you list the top “DON’T SAY” bullets? Helps AEs avoid stepping on landmines.

Olga Petrov: DON’T SAY / avoid:
- “We guarantee EU-only storage for all data, including logs/metadata” (too broad; depends on category + contract)
- “We never route outside the EU under any circumstances” (absolute)
- “We have ISO 27001 certification” (unless explicitly true; use “alignment” language only if approved)
- “Only EU employees can access your data” (personnel location commitments aren’t part of standard controls)
- “We can meet GDPR/Schrems II by default” (legal conclusion; we can describe controls + DPA)

Olga Petrov: DO SAY:
- “EU region selection / region-pinning for Customer Content processing”
- “Access is least-privilege, audited, and requires authorization”
- “Dedicated/Private options for stricter residency boundaries”
- “We can review specific contractual requirements with Legal/GRC”

Priyom Das: They asked if prompts are used to train models. Can we include that line or keep scoped?

Marcus Lin: You can include the standard line if it comes up, but keep it separate from residency so it doesn’t read like a new promise. Approved phrasing is “We do not use Customer Content to train Redwood-provided models unless the customer explicitly opts in under a separate written agreement.” (Don’t improvise.)

Stephanie Nguyen: For live deal: recommend we send the snippet + link the canonical residency/retention overview in Confluence, and offer a quick security call w/ GRC. @Hannah Schmitt I can help coordinate.

Hannah Schmitt: super helpful. Can someone drop the Confluence link name so I don’t grab the wrong doc?

Daniel Carter: Use the customer-facing page in the Security & Compliance space: “Data retention and deletion overview” (has residency notes). If they want SOC 2 report / evidence, follow the “SOC 2 customer evidence request playbook” and ensure NDA is in place.

Lukas Meyer: :thumbsup: I’ll reuse the snippet for my EMEA deal too.

Hannah Schmitt: Thanks all. I’ll reply to the prospect with the approved paragraph + “we can evaluate stricter residency / contractual needs via Dedicated/Private” and pull Legal/GRC if they push on absolute EU-only + EU-only personnel. :white_check_mark:

Jordan Blake: +1 on escalation. If this is a gating item, loop me in early so we don’t burn cycles. Use the approved wording only—no custom commitments in email.

Hannah Schmitt: ack. looping you + @Stephanie Nguyen on the thread w/ the account notes.

title: Regal Wealth Management
author: Avery Johnson
text:
Account context (ABM regulated pilot):
- Wealth management platform + broker-dealer arm; governance is heavy (InfoSec + IAM + Risk + Data Governance all have sign-off).
- They are exploring an internal GenAI platform for advisor copilots and client comms; key constraint is auditability + access controls, not just model quality.

What we heard / priorities:
- “We need tamper-evident audit logs we can export to our SIEM. If we can’t show who accessed what, it’s dead.”
- SSO is mandatory. SAML for workforce + SCIM provisioning preferred. They have strict IdP metadata validation and want to see supported patterns.
- Data boundaries: they’re sensitive to client PII; prefer a Private (VPC) deployment. Dedicated was mentioned as a fallback if Private timeline slips, but their first preference is VPC/private control plane.
- Retention/residency: asked about configurable retention and whether logs and inference payloads can be constrained to US-only.
- KMS/HSM: requested clarity on customer-managed keys and key rotation process, esp. for Private.

Current solution / stack notes:
- Today: mixed vendor setup (some workloads on Azure, some AWS). Existing logging pipeline into Splunk; likely wants audit log delivery into S3 + forwarding.
- They have internal platform engineering; do not want to run/patch a full open-source serving stack themselves.

Meetings / activity timeline:
- 2025-05-22: Initial ABM connect (Avery + Fatima). High-level discovery; confirmed VPC/private preference; introduced evidence pack process.
- 2025-05-29: Follow-up with Security + IAM (pre-read: Regulated Security FAQ). Main asks: audit log schema, export options, SAML/SCIM support details, SOC2 scope.
- 2025-06-03: Technical deep dive: audit logs + KMS (Fireflies: 2025-06-03-technical-deep-dive-audit-logs-and-kms-regal-wealth). Focused on required audit fields, export patterns, and operational separation of duties.
- 2025-06-05: Internal Redwood alignment: do NOT over-claim “HIPAA-ready”/compliance language; keep to verified controls; send evidence pack index + NDA process.

Requirements summary (for qualification):
- Workloads: advisor copilot chat (interactive), summarization (async), embeddings for internal knowledge search.
- Latency/SLO: interactive target mentioned informally as ~<1.5s time-to-first-token for chat; throughput expectations TBD (they want a sizing session).
- Reliability: wants multi-AZ story in VPC context and fallback behavior (regional isolation preferred; will not accept cross-region failover without explicit approval).
- Logging: needs request-level audit logs with actor identity (from SSO), model/version, policy decisions (route/fallback), timestamps, and export mechanism.
- Access control: RBAC in console + SSO. Separation between admin and auditor roles.

Evidence pack request (status):
- Requested items (to be shared under NDA): SOC 2 Type II report, encryption-at-rest/in-transit overview, audit log field list + sample payload, retention statement, incident response overview.
- Sent: evidence pack index link (Confluence) + summary of how to request restricted artifacts. Waiting for their vendor risk team to provide NDA template.

Commercial / procurement notes:
- They asked early about procurement path: security review first, then platform engineering sign-off, then vendor risk + legal. Expect a 6–10 week cycle once pilot is approved.
- Budget exists for a platform contract if security gates are cleared. They want a short technical validation rather than a long open-ended POC.

Open questions:
- Do they require on-prem or will VPC satisfy? (Current answer: VPC satisfies; on-prem not requested.)
- Exact SIEM ingest path for audit logs (Splunk HEC vs S3 forwarder). Need to confirm.
- Whether they need per-tenant data segregation (multiple business lines) within a single Private deployment.

Internal guidance:
- Keep claims tight: we can say ‘supports SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logging, customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM integrations)’ but avoid promising specific certifications beyond what’s in the security FAQ/evidence pack.
- Positioning that resonated: ‘Production economics + regulated controls’ and ‘same runtime across hosted/dedicated/private’ so they can start Dedicated if needed and still move to Private later.

Proposed plan (draft):
1) Security questionnaire walkthrough (Olga + Naomi as needed) + evidence pack under NDA.
2) 60-min architecture working session: VPC topology, logging export path, KMS, SSO integration.
3) 2-week validation in VPC: run synthetic prompts + limited sanitized dataset; success criteria = SSO integration complete, audit logs exported, latency/throughput baseline, and rollback/fallback behavior documented.

Risk flags:
- If we can’t provide a clear audit log schema and export story quickly, they will default to incumbent cloud-managed model endpoints.
- IAM metadata validation edge cases could stall; need to preempt with explicit docs/examples and SE support.

Schedule security questionnaire walkthrough + confirm audit log export format/transport (S3/SIEM) and SSO (SAML + SCIM) details; then propose 2-week architecture validation in customer VPC.

Security team requires evidence pack (SOC 2 report under NDA) before any pilot data flows
Internal IAM team has strict SAML metadata validation rules; wants documented constraints + examples
Need confirmation on audit log retention defaults vs customer-configurable policy in Private

title: End-to-End Fidelity Validation Lab Manual — Runtime Benchmarking & Observability
author: Maya K. Ortega
text:
Summary
-------
This lab manual defines a repeatable, end-to-end validation workflow for runtime fidelity, cost and observability when making changes to serving kernel scheduling, quantization profiles, routing/fallback policies, and telemetry enrichment. The manual is intended for SREs, runtime engineers, and performance QA engineers who need deterministic validation before rollouts to Dedicated/Hosted fleets.

Scope
-----
- Controlled lab and CI testbed exercises covering: kernel scheduler changes, model-variant swaps, quantization profile updates, eviction and warmstart behavior, routing fallback correctness, and telemetry/enrichment validation.
- Focus on observable fidelity (semantic quality), SLO preservation (P99 latency, error rate), and telemetry completeness (span coverage, attribute set).
- Excludes upstream model training or dataset curation; assumes validated model weights.

Goals and Acceptance Criteria
----------------------------
- No observable regression in defined prompt suite: prompt-set pass-rate >= 98% (see Acceptance Checklist).
- Latency SLOs preserved: P50 < 60ms, P95 < 120ms, P99 < 300ms for the configured test shape.
- Telemetry signal completeness: 100% of major request traces contain kernel-orchestrator span + kv-cache span + dispatch-daemon span.
- Automated detection of fidelity regressions via diff-based eval and embedding-similarity thresholds.

Testbed Topology (text diagram)
-------------------------------
Lab cluster (isolated VPC) topology:
- traffic-generator -> runtime-gw (ingress proxy) -> router -> dispatch-daemon -> kernel-orchestrator -> GPU-pool / CPU-fallback nodes
- auxiliary services: kv-cache-service, eviction-controller, telemetry-bridge, metrics-exporter, trace-collector

Required services and minimum versions
-------------------------------------
| Service | Min version | Purpose | Owner |
|------------------------|-------------|----------------------------------------|-------|
| runtime-gw | 2.4.0 | Ingress routing, rate shaping | eng-platform |
| kernel-orchestrator | 1.8.2 | Kernel selection & scheduling | serving-runtime |
| dispatch-daemon | 3.1.0 | Request fanout & concurrency shaping | serving-runtime |
| kv-cache-service | 0.9.5 | Prefix/KV caching & warmstart hints | eng-platform |
| eviction-controller | 1.2.0 | Cross-tenant eviction coordination | eng-sre |
| telemetry-bridge | 2.2.0 | Enrich and forward traces/metrics | eng-platform |
| trace-collector (jaeger)| 1.31.0 | Trace capture for E2E correlation | eng-sre |

Baseline artifacts
------------------
- Golden prompt-suite: /data/lab/golden-prompt-suite-2026.json (1000 prompts across short/medium/long sequences).
- Golden embeddings snapshot: /artifacts/golden-embeddings-2026.tar.gz (used for semantic diff checks).
- Baseline kernel metric snapshot: s3://redwood-perf/baseline/kernel-metrics-2026-02-01.json

Benchmarks and Metrics to Capture
--------------------------------
- Latencies: P50, P90, P95, P99, tail-99.9 (end-to-end and kernel-only).
- Throughput: tokens/sec and requests/sec under shaped arrival processes.
- Resource signals: GPU utilization, GPU-memory fragmentation, CPU steal, NIC TX/RX.
- Fidelity: embedding cosine similarity, BLEU-like sequence similarity for deterministic prompts, classification/QA exact match for labeled prompts.
- Observability coverage: % traces with required spans, % requests with sampling_id, % logs with request_id.

Testing Workflows (high-level)
------------------------------
1) Preflight: environment sanity
 - Verify service versions and config (see config-check CLI below).
 - Start trace-collector and telemetry-bridge in debug mode.
2) Baseline capture
 - Run golden prompt-suite against the baseline runtime configuration, store traces/metrics/artifacts.
3) Change under test
 - Apply kernel scheduling change / quantization profile / routing update in isolated test namespace.
4) Controlled replay
 - Replay captured traffic shapes (steady-state, microburst, heavy-tail) and run golden prompt-suite concurrently.
5) Automated fidelity checks
 - Run embedding-similarity diff and per-prompt regression detector.
6) Observability validation
 - Check trace/span coverage and metric cardinality including enriched attributes.
7) Acceptance gating
 - Apply acceptance checklist and sign-off for canary.

Detailed Procedures
-------------------
A. Kernel scheduler change validation (engineer-run)
1. Coordinate with owner and schedule lab window; tag change PR with {lab-validation-needed}.
2. Snapshot baseline artifacts (metrics, traces, outputs).
3. Deploy planner branch to kernel-orchestrator in test namespace: kubectl set image ... --record.
4. Warmstart KV cache hinting: pre-warm top 20 prefixes from golden prompt-suite.
5. Run three workload shapes: steady (r=500 rps), burst (3x for 30s every 5min), tail-heavy (Pareto shape).
6. Capture traces (100% sampling) and metrics at 1s resolution.
7. Run regression detector: python tools/regression_detector.py --baseline s3://... --candidate ./artifacts/candidate-output.json
8. If embedding similarity drop > 0.07 average or > 10 prompts below threshold, abort and file incident.
9. If performance SLOs violated (P99 > 1.5x baseline), revert change and open ticket.

B. Quantization profile update validation (automated pipeline)
1. Pipeline triggers from quantization-profile PR.
2. Build candidate artifacts and deploy to canary pool of 10 GPUs.
3. Run golden prompt-suite with deterministic seeds; capture outputs.
4. Run automatic semantic check: cosine similarity on embeddings (thresholds in acceptance checklist).
5. If any prompt in labeled set loses exact match or similarity below threshold, mark profile as failing.

C. Eviction and warmstart behavior (chaos-style)
1. Start a long-run session workload for warm KV cache builds.
2. Trigger eviction-controller to evict a tenant shard and observe eviction propagation.
3. Verify warmstart hints cause cache warm-up within 60s and P95 latency returns to baseline within 120s.
4. Validate no request leaks or auth errors during handoff.

CLI and Example Commands
------------------------
- Config check: ./tools/lab_config_check.sh --env lab --services runtime-gw,kernel-orchestrator,dispatch-daemon
- Start traffic generator: ./tools/traffic_gen --shape steady --rps 500 --duration 20m --out ./runs/steady-2026-03-01
- Run regression detector: python tools/regression_detector.py --baseline s3://redwood-perf/baseline --candidate ./runs/steady-2026-03-01/outputs.json --report ./runs/report.json

Example config snippet (YAML)
---------------------------
run_id: e2e-lab-2026-03-05
workload_shapes:
 - name: steady
 rps: 500
 duration: 20m
 - name: burst
 rps_profile: "spike:3x:30s:period:5m"
sampling:
 traces: 100%
 metrics_resolution: 1s
fidelity_checks:
 embedding_similarity_threshold: 0.85
 labeled_prompt_exact_match: 0.98

Acceptance checklist (must pass all)
-----------------------------------
- [ ] Regression detector: overall pass (no more than 2% prompts flagged).
- [ ] Latency SLOs: P50/P95/P99 within defined thresholds.
- [ ] Observability: required spans present in >= 99.5% of traces.
- [ ] Resource safety: no GPU memory OOMs; fragmentation delta < 5% vs baseline.
- [ ] No functional errors (auth, 5xx, malformed outputs) above 0.1%.

Signal artifacts and retention
----------------------------
- Traces and metrics for each run stored under s3://redwood-lab-runs/{run_id}/ with retention 90 days.
- Output diffs and reports under artifacts/ in the CI workspace; retain for 30 days.

Failure modes and escalation
---------------------------
- Fidelity regression detected: open a regression ticket (label: perf+fidelity) and notify author + eng-sre.
- SLO breach during lab run: pause test, capture extended traces, and create an incident with severity P2 if breach persists > 15m.
- Observability gap: escalate to eng-platform to verify telemetry-bridge configuration and collector health.

Runbook links and ownership
--------------------------
- Kernel scheduler owner: serving-runtime (oncall alias: #srv-runtime-oncall).
- Eviction-controller owner: eng-sre (alias: #eng-sre).
- Telemetry ingestion owner: eng-platform (alias: #observability).
- Related runbooks: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026

Automation and CI integration
----------------------------
- Recommended: run quantization-profile and small-sample fidelity checks as part of PR gating (fast-path). Full golden-suite runs scheduled nightly or on-demand via the lab pipeline.
- CI artifacts MUST include run_id, git-commit, kernel-orchestrator-image, and quantization-profile-id for traceability.

Appendix: Quick cheat-sheet
--------------------------
- Quick start: tools/lab_bootstrap.sh --run e2e-lab --env lab
- Baseline artifacts: s3://redwood-perf/baseline/
- Who to call: serving-runtime owners (Maya Ortega), eng-sre lead (Leah Thompson), telemetry (Arjun Patel).

Notes and future work
---------------------
- Add synthetic adversarial prompt generator for corner-case fidelity checks (Q3 2026).
- Integrate a lightweight human-in-the-loop review for ambiguous prompt diffs.
- Expand telemetry enrichment assertions to include token-level attributions.

Document history
----------------
- 2026-02-14: Created by Maya K. Ortega.
- 2026-03-05: Updated with quantization pipeline steps and CLI snippets.

title: Verdant Atlas AI
author: Ethan Park
text:
Summary: Stalled after discovery — went dark following delivery of requirements + security pack. Primary interest: personalization & reranking pipeline to improve conversion and AOV. They wanted embeddings for candidate retrieval and a low-latency reranker for top-k scoring; also internal merchant support bot as phase 2.

Timeline / activity (bullets, shorthand):
- 2024-09-12: inbound MQL from growth; AE assigned (Ethan).
- 2024-09-25: discovery call — stakeholders: Carlos Mendes (Head of ML), Priya Rao (Eng Mgr), Liam O'Neill (Infra lead). High-level goals outlined: lift recommendation relevance, reduce manual curation.
- 2024-10-10: ARCH workshop w/ SE Maya — perf targets captured: p99 latency <120ms for chat/responses, steady-state throughput ~150 embeddings/sec, burst to 500; expectation: KV cache + batching. Prefers VPC; US data residency.
- 2024-10-22: sent tailored architecture note + initial sizing (CPU vs GPU options).
- 2024-11-05: delivered formal requirements doc + pricing deck (link). Requested quote for Dedicated pool + hybrid hosted fallback.
- 2024-11-12: security ops call (Fireflies FF-2024-11-12-VA-call1). They requested SOC2 report, KMS/HSM details, retention controls. AE uploaded security pack and suggested Dedicated for isolation.
- 2024-11-15: procurement touchpoint — customer said they needed one more internal budget check; since then no replies to 3 follow-ups (email + 2 LinkedIn InMails).

Use-case / reqs summary (short):
- Primary: embeddings-based personalization + neural reranking of candidate recommendations.

title: Introduce probabilistic capacity-budgeter and soft-preempt adapter for smoother decommits
author: Maya Chen
text:
Motivation: Dedicated fleets see hard decommits during transient demand drops which causes bursty downstream latency and wasted warmup. This PR implements a probabilistic capacity budgeting component and a complementary soft-preempt adapter that together reduce hard preemptions while preserving long-run throughput guarantees.

Design summary: Introduces `capacity_budgeter` (service-level controller) which maintains a probabilistic budget for each pool using configurable percentile forecasts over recent usage windows and a small stochastic safety margin. Budgets are expressed as a fractional allocation of pool slots (0-1) and exposed as metrics for observability. The `soft_preempt_adapter` is a lightweight runtime-side shim that listens to budget revocations and converts immediate hard slot preempts into staged soft-preempt signals: runtime drains new allocations, migrates evictable requests, and issues a soft-fallback window before reclaiming.

Key behaviors: 1) Budgeter uses exponential-percentile smoothing: 95th/75th/50th windows fed into a weighted sampler to produce a target budget and a volatility score. 2) When budget deficit is signaled, soft_preempt_adapter attempts up to N grace cycles (configurable) before issuing a hard preempt; during grace gets a best-effort fallback routing. 3) Telemetry: new metrics `redwood.capacity_budget.pct`, `redwood.capacity_budget.volatility`, `redwood.soft_preempt.events`, and histograms for soft_grace_latency and fallback_routed_ratio. 4) Backpressure contract: controllers downstream may return CHOOSER_PREEMPT_SAFE to indicate they can accept soft preempt fallback. 5) Config: per-pool policy with min-reserve floor and a global conservative cap for safety.

Files touched (high-level): capacity_budgeter/ (controller, policy), runtime/soft_preempt_adapter/ (adapter + small API shim), telemetry/metrics_registry.go (new metric defs), e2e-tests/fleet_soft_preempt.integration (golden tests and simulated traffic), docs/ops/soft_preempt.md (operator guide), config/samples/pool_budget_policy.yaml.

Testing and QA: Unit tests cover budget calculations and volatility scoring; integration harness simulates spike→drop patterns and asserts soft_preempt events reduce hard preempt rate by >= 70% under test traffic. Added a cluster-level canary in staging for 48h before rollout. Load tests measured median tail latency improvement for cold reassigns (-18%) and a 22% reduction in overall evictions in the canary cluster.

Rollout plan: 1) Deploy budgeter service in passive mode (metrics only) for 24h. 2) Enable advisory mode where soft_preempt_adapter only logs decisions. 3) Gradually enable soft_preempt with low concurrency pools (10% of fleet) for 72h. 4) Full rollout if evictions drop and SLOs stable. Feature gate: `prob_capacity_budgeter_v1` and `soft_preempt_v1`.

Backward compatibility: Existing controllers and pool configs remain unchanged; adapters default to conservative behavior. Operators can opt-out by setting min-reserve=1.

Open items and follow-ups: - Add per-tenant weighting into budgeter (ENG-2048). - Improve forecasting with short-term AR model (future PR). - Add dashboards and alerts for volatility spikes.

References: Linear ENG-1987, incident SUP-718, design doc link: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-1987/probabilistic-capacity-budgeter (internal).

Liam O'Connor (2026-02-19): Can we clarify the safety cap math? If the global cap is hit we should prefer hard degrade over unpredictable fallback routing. -- Response: agreed, updated policy.go with global_cap enforcement and unit tests.
Priya Singh (2026-02-20): Telemetry looks good but add a tag for pool_id and tenant to the histograms. -- Response: added labels and small change to metrics_registry.go
Diego Rivera (2026-02-22): Integration harness passed locally but flaked in CI once (timeout). Suggest increasing test timeouts for the staged drains. -- Response: extended timeouts and adjusted the simulated workload seed; CI rerun passed.
Liam O'Connor (2026-02-24): Approving after minor nit on config naming. Looks safe to squash merge.
