title: Cookie-domain rotation during canary causes pinned session eviction for long-poll streaming clients
text:
Issue summary: After a targeted canary that adjusted cookie domain and SameSite attributes for cross-subdomain routing, a subset of long-poll streaming sessions from BrightChat saw their model version pin removed and traffic routed to the fallback model. Impact: ~6% of BrightChat tenant requests in us-east (long-poll streaming) returned responses from fallback variant (rwi-7b-compat) for durations up to 18 minutes. Customer impact: degraded generation quality and intermittent streaming disconnects for live agents.

Environment: production (us-east), Dedicated cluster for BrightChat (tenant id bc-091). Canary change: edge-proxy cookie domain normalization in PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/4872 rolled to 10% (cohort) starting 2026-03-12 03:10 UTC.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Start a long-poll streaming chat session using BrightChat tenant credentials (session cookie set to api.brightchat.com).
2) Observe router affinity header (x-tenant-session) and cookie domain in request/response.
3) Trigger a model request that is pinned to rwi-13b-v1 via tenant pin.
4) Monitor routing decisions in router logs and session-manager for pin refresh events.

Observed behavior: When the canary cohort hit an upstream edge with cookie-domain rewrite set to ".redwood.ai" (intended for drain handling across subdomains), the session cookie returned to the client with a different domain scope. For long-poll clients that reuse the original host-bound cookie, the session-manager validated the cookie as mismatched and treated the session as unauthenticated for pin reconciliation, causing the pinned routing key to be dropped and the request to be evaluated for fallback path. This only affected streams where the client reused the old host-scoped cookie and did not immediately refresh session metadata.

Logs / Traces: Relevant samples in trace-id list: trace: us-east-20260312-8a9b, us-east-20260312-8a9c; edge-proxy logs show Set-Cookie: session=...; Domain=.redwood.ai at 03:17:02 UTC. Router logs show pin_eviction_reason=COOKIE_DOMAIN_MISMATCH and decision=FALLBACK at same timestamps.

Workaround: For affected tenants, toggle canary off for edge cookie rewrite or instruct client to force a session refresh (POST /v1/sessions/refresh). Both steps reduced impact immediately.

Customer comment: BrightChat reported visible quality regression on agent UI and requested immediate mitigation and postmortem.

03/12 03:22 UTC: SRE observed correlation between canary cohort and spike in routing->fallback events for tenant bc-091 (BrightChat).
03/12 03:30 UTC: Confirmed edge-proxy change (cookie domain rewrite) rolled as 10% canary; rollback flag not yet triggered.
03/12 04:05 UTC: Hypothesis A - cookie domain normalization changed cookie scope causing session-manager to treat session as orphaned and drop pin. Evidence: router logs show 'pin_eviction_reason=COOKIE_DOMAIN_MISMATCH'.
03/12 04:30 UTC: Hypothesis B - autoscaler prewarm caused new warm instances without updated session DB mapping and triggered fallback; low evidence, metrics for warm instance churn not significant.
03/12 05:10 UTC: Reproduced locally using BrightChat dev tenant: emulate host-scoped cookie then inject Set-Cookie Domain=.redwood.ai and assert session-manager invalidates pin. Reproducible in staging with long-poll client that does not refresh session metadata.
03/12 06:00 UTC: Temporary mitigation applied: disabled cookie domain rewrite for canary cohort and instructed BrightChat to refresh sessions. Observed pinned routing restored after ~2 minutes for refreshed sessions.
03/13 09:00 UTC: Added extra logging in session-manager for cookie-origin and pin-check path (PR link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/4879).
03/14 01:15 UTC: Confirmed regression window affected ~6% of tenant traffic and lasted up to 18 minutes per affected session before client refresh or session TTL expiry caused natural recovery.

Asha Kapoor (Support) 2026-03-12 03:45 UTC: Acknowledged customer report and opened investigation. Notified SRE and eng-ops channels (#support and #incidents).
Jonah Reed (SRE) 2026-03-12 04:12 UTC: Initial triage - correlates with PR 4872 canary. Pin eviction logs found. Will attempt controlled rollback for the cohort and add session-manager guard.
BrightChat - Samantha Lee (Customer) 2026-03-12 04:35 UTC: Seeing degraded responses for some live agents. We'll apply client-side session refresh but need platform mitigation ASAP.
Jonah Reed (SRE) 2026-03-12 05:05 UTC: Rolled back cookie-domain rewrite for the canary cohort. Monitoring for pin restoration.

Mitigation performed: canary cookie-domain rewrite rolled back for us-east cohort; advised customer to refresh sessions. Added defensive guard in session-manager to accept equivalent cookie scopes for pinned sessions when domain normalization occurs and added tighter logging. Patch PR 4879 merged to staging. Postmortem scheduled and follow-up action items assigned: update canary checklist to include pin invariants, add automated pin-eviction alert, and add e2e test for long-poll session cookie changes.

Complete postmortem and publish to customer (BrightChat) by 2026-03-18.
Backfill e2e test for cookie domain rotation and pinned session behavior (owner: platform/qe).
Add automated alert rule on pin_eviction_reason=COOKIE_DOMAIN_MISMATCH in prod router metrics (owner: sre).

title: Harmonized quarterly roadmap: hosted API & model catalog governance
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Quarterly planning initiative to unify Hosted API roadmap items with the model catalog lifecycle. Goals: 1) Define a single source of truth for model availability, deprecation, and compatibility; 2) Establish canary & rollout guardrails tied to performance and cost OKRs; 3) Create a cross-team cadence (PM/Eng/Design/Research) for release gating and post-deploy evaluation. This ticket captures scope, success metrics, dependencies, and an initial timeline for Q3 planning and operational handoffs.

Canonical model catalog schema and status states (stable, experimental, deprecated) documented and approved
Rollout playbook with canary thresholds (latency P50/P95, regression tolerance, cost per token) reviewed by Eng and SRE
Cross-functional calendar with quarterly gating reviews and owners assigned
Automation tasks for catalog propagation to Hosted API and Dedicated routing completed as PRs or RFCs
Two pilot model rollouts coordinated with telemetry dashboards and alert rules

Trade-offs considered: aggressive model pruning reduces catalog surface area (cost benefit) but increases risk of customer regressions; proposed mitigation: expanded preview window and curated fallback variants.
Canary policy draft: 1% traffic for 48h, monitor P95 latency (+/- 10% threshold), quality regression < 2% on sentinel prompts, cost per token delta <= 15% compared to baseline.
Telemetry: add a per-model dashboard tile showing cost/latency/quality trends; link to dashboard template: https://dash.redwood.com/d/hostedapi/model-overview
Rollout phases: plan -> preview (internal) -> preview (select customers) -> full launch. Each phase requires sign-off from PM, Eng lead, and SRE on metrics.
Governance: quarterly catalog audit led by PM and Research to identify models for promotion/retirement; retention of audit notes in Confluence.

2026-03-02 - PM kickoff: synced with Eng (Nadia), Research (Ravi), Design (Maya). Agreed on canonical lifecycle states and need for deprecation lead time (default 90 days).
2026-03-04 - Eng feedback: runtime team prefers deprecation hooks emitted from catalog to trigger KV cache invalidation; added as dependency ENG-4128.
2026-03-05 - Design feedback: UX needs a model-status badge and a timeline view in Console; created DES-441 for mockups.
2026-03-07 - Decision: Use stable/preview/experimental/deprecated states. Preview models require a canary policy and opt-in route. Action: draft canary thresholds and automation steps.
2026-03-09 - Research note: Evaluation harness will include latency, generation quality (ROUGE/BERTEval), and hallucination regression checks for top-20 prompts. Link: https://confluence.redwood.com/display/ML/Model+Eval+Harness
2026-03-10 - Security: KMS rotation impact considered; private deployments need mirror propagation plan. Security review required for private catalog sync (security_review_required=true).
2026-03-12 - Next steps: draft rollout playbook, schedule cross-team gating meeting for 2026-03-18, and open RFC for catalog schema (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/catalog/pull/187).

title: Stochastic GPU Demand Sampler & Cost Allocation Workbook
author: Maya Thompson
text:
Purpose:
This workbook generates probabilistic hourly demand scenarios (Monte Carlo) for inference workloads and converts those scenarios into recommended GPU provisioning mixes and per-tenant cost allocations. Designed to feed Redwood Optimize scoring and to inform Dedicated/reserved sizing conversations.

High-level approach:
- Inputs tab accepts historical traffic summary (qps by hour, median tokens/request, batchability distribution, cold-start rates, KV cache hit rate) plus business parameters (SLO, penalty cost per missed request, reserved pricing vs preemptible/on-demand).
- Sampler tab runs N Monte Carlo trials for the planning window (typically 28 days but configurable). Each trial samples per-hour demand from fitted distributions and applies workload-level variability (burst probability, diurnal multiplier, weekday/weekend patterns).
- Pool-sim tab maps sampled demand into GPU-hour consumption via model throughput curves and batching efficiency functions. It also models warm vs cold sequence warmup cost and KV cache hit variance.
- Allocation tab performs per-tenant attribution using token-weighted share and a fairness adjustment for tenants with low batchability.
- Output tab summarizes percentile capacity requirements (P50/P75/P90/P95/P99), recommended reserved capacity commit to meet target percentile, and expected blended cost/unit.

Sheet descriptions and key cells (use these names to link downstream tooling):
- Inputs (sheet)
 - Inputs!B2: Planning window days (default 28)
 - Inputs!B3: Trials (Monte Carlo) (default 5,000)
 - Inputs!B5:B12: Historical hourly QPS summary (24 cells, mean)
 - Inputs!B14: Mean tokens per request
 - Inputs!B15: Tokens per request SD
 - Inputs!B17: Batchability distribution (0..1)
 - Inputs!B19: KV cache hit rate mean and sd
 - Inputs!B21: SLO latency ms and per-missed-request penalty $
 - Inputs!B23: Pricing: reserved $/GPU-hour, preemptible $/GPU-hour, on-demand $/GPU-hour

- Sampler (sheet)
 - Uses formula examples for Excel/Sheets: =NORM.INV(RAND(), mean, sd) for per-hour QPS sampling when distribution is approximately normal; fallback Poisson sampling for low counts: =POISSON.INV(RAND(), lambda)
 - Burst toggles: sample Bernoulli with p = burst_probability; when true multiply that hour's demand by burst_multiplier
 - Tokens sampled per request: =MAX(1, ROUND(NORM.INV(RAND(), Inputs!B14, Inputs!B15),0))

- Pool-sim (sheet)
 - Throughput curves (table): rows = model variant (e.g., 13B_fp16, 33B_q4_0), columns = seq_len/beam/batch_size -> tokens/sec per GPU.
 - Effective throughput per trial hour = LOOKUP(model_variant, seq_len)*batching_gain(batchability_sample)
 - GPU-hours required = (sampled_tokens_for_hour / tokens_per_gpu_hour) + warm_start_overhead_hours
 - Preemptible failure modeling: sample outage events with p per hour; if outage occurs, route load to fallback capacity and add penalty hours

- Allocation (sheet)
 - Per-tenant cost share = (tenant_tokens * tenant_batch_penalty_adj) / sum(all_tokens_adjusted) * total_cost_for_hour
 - Low-batchability uplift factor applied to tenants with batchability < 0.3 to account for higher per-token cost
 - Example formula: =IF(Batchability<0.3, TenantTokens * 1.25, TenantTokens)

- Outputs (sheet)
 - Aggregated percentiles across trials for GPU-hours/day and for peak-hour GPU count
 - Recommended reserved commit = P_target_percentile_peak * safety_factor (recommended safety_factor 1.05 - 1.15 depending on business tolerance)
 - Expected blended unit cost = (reserved_hours*reserved_rate + preempt_hours*preempt_rate + ondemand_hours*ondemand_rate) / total_tokens
 - Cost of missed-SLO events = Expected_missed_count * penalty

Key design choices and rationale (explicit so reviewers can tune knobs):
- Use Monte Carlo (5k+) to capture tail risk from correlated bursts across tenants rather than relying on simple peak multipliers. Correlated bursts drive the difference between P90 and P99 provisioning.
- Model batching explicitly as a distribution (batchability) instead of a single multiplier because tenant composition changes (small requests vs long-context). This makes per-tenant allocation more defensible.
- Mix reserved + preemptible + on-demand: reserved covers baseline steady-state at target percentile, preemptible picks up stochastic spikes at ~50-70% cheaper price but with outage modeling, on-demand for immediate failover.
- Include warm-start penalty: models with large KV/state have first-token overhead that reduces effective tokens/sec for first N seconds; important for conversational workloads with many short sessions.

How to use in practice:
1) Paste 28 days of hourly aggregate QPS into Inputs!B5:B676 (or link to a table).
2) Update pricing and model throughput table with the current benchmark numbers from Serving Runtime team.
3) Run sampling with trials >= 2,000 for quick sanity checks, >= 5,000 for final recommendations.
4) Review Outputs P95/P99. Use Allocation tab to produce per-customer cost estimates and to inform chargeback or SKU pricing adjustments.

Diagnostic plots and checks (suggested charts):
- Histogram of peak GPU-hours per trial (showing long tail)
- Time-series heatmap of P95 demand across the planning window (identify persistent daily peaks)
- Per-tenant cost breakout and contribution to tail events (who drives P99)

Limitations and follow-ups:
- Synthetic burst generation is heuristic; validate against historical incident windows and tune burst_probability and multiplier.
- Throughput curves must be refreshed whenever a new kernel/quantization option is introduced. Link to Serving Runtime benchmarks in linked_artifacts.
- Does not model multi-model packing optimization (packing across model families). Consider a follow-up sheet that includes a bin-packing approximation for mixed-model placement.

Notes (work-in-progress):
- TODO: add an "auto-fit" routine that guesses distribution families (log-normal vs normal vs Poisson) for each hour-of-day and selects sampling method automatically.
- TODO: wire outputs into Optimize API scoring endpoint: /optimize/v1/capacity-suggestion with JSON payload described in Confluence linked above.

Example quick sanity-check numbers (base run):
- Planning window 28d, trials 5k => P95 peak GPUs = 112, P99 peak GPUs = 165
- Recommended reserved commit (P95, safety 1.1) => 123 GPUs
- Blended unit cost (tokens per $1k) = 1.2M tokens per $1k (illustrative; update with real prices)

Revision history and authorship log:
- 2025-11-03 Maya T: initial draft workbook and sampling framework
- 2025-12-12 Luis R: added tenant allocation heuristic and low-batch uplift
- 2026-02-10 Anika B: tuned preemptible outage model and added warm-start penalty

If accepted, this workbook will be the canonical feeder for the Optimize "reserve suggestion" endpoint and for Dedicated sizing recommendations. Reviewers: please pay attention to the allocation fairness rule and to the choice of sampling distributions for low-traffic hours.

title: Weekly Pilot Sync - reuse patterns & cache routing
author: Maya Chen
text:
MEETING HEADER
Date: 2025-12-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Sam (Redwood CSM), Jordan (Aureus Lead ML Eng), Leah (Backend), Tomás (Product), Rina (SRE)
Shared artifacts: Pilot dashboard link (redwood.com/s/au-pilot-453), canonicalization doc (shared google drive link), hit-rate csv (shared)

AUTO SUMMARY (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
- Reviewed current KV/prefix cache hit rates (global 18% baseline, week-over-week up from 12%).
- Discussed prompt reuse patterns: session affinity, canonicalization, templated prompts causing low reuse.
- Proposed experiments: prefix canonicalization, prefetch heavy-list queries, TTL bump for stable sessions, 24h production replay.
- Action items: Redwood to send config snippets; Aureus to share logs; schedule dedicated benchmark if improvements not observed.

TOPICS:
- Metrics recap and anomalies
- Prompt normalization / canonicalization rules
- Prefetch strategy and TTL tuning
- Routing/orchestration impacts (region + dedicated fallback)
- Next steps and ownership

TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00] Maya Chen: okay everyone, thanks for jumping on for the weekly sync, um let's do a quick run through of numbers and then go into the tuning ideas. Jordan, do you want to start with any updates on your side?
[00:12] Jordan Meyers: yeah thanks Maya, quick update — we ran the prefix-only patch last night on staging, saw a small bump, like 15 to 18 percent hit, so moving in right direction but not — not where we'd hoped. there's also some noisy traffic from our search ingestion pipeline that skewed some of the numbers.
[00:32] Diego Ramos: cool, thanks. can you clarify whether the 18% is global across all endpoints or just the chat endpoints?
[00:40] Jordan Meyers: that's global, if you isolate the QA microservice it's more like 24, but the conversational channel is lower.
[00:48] Priya Nambiar: one quick note — the staging run didn't include canonicalization rules we discussed (i.e. strip timestamps, normalize user metadata), so I think your reuse ceiling is artificially low.
[00:58] Leah Ito: ah right that was on our backlog, we didn't want to touch production prompt shaping yet.
[01:05] Maya Chen: that's a big one — canonicalization tends to be high leverage. Diego, do you mind walking through a concrete normalization ruleset you recommend?
[01:13] Diego Ramos: sure, high level: 1) remove ephemeral tokens (timestamps, session ids), 2) map synonyms in the product domain (e.g., "order" vs "purchase"), 3) canonicalize date formats, and 4) collapse minor punctuation differences. we'll provide a small regex + deterministic replacer snippet. not perfect but will collapse a lot of variance.
[01:38] Tomás Alvarez: quick Q — will canonicalization risk changing intent? we worry about false merges where prompts that look similar but need different responses get routed to cached results.
[01:47] Priya Nambiar: we handle that by tiered caching: prefix-level for high-confidence canonical matches and a separate fallback path for low-confidence; we can tune threshold. so it's an engineering knob.
[02:00] Rina Kapoor: also want to call out session affinity — a lot of our users have long sessions with minor edits; if we increase TTL for those sessions we can get big win. current TTL 60s, maybe bump to 5 minutes for affinity scenarios.
[02:13] Maya Chen: good point. Diego, suggested prefetching approaches?
[02:16] Diego Ramos: two ideas — proactive prefetch for top-n likely next prompts based on N-gram analysis, and opportunistic prefetch on session start for templates. Prefetch is cheap if hit-rate increases justify the extra tokens; we'll show cost math.
[02:31] Jordan Meyers: we worried about token costs — prefetching could double request volume if misconfigured. need conservative prefetch policy.
[02:40] Diego Ramos: agreed, start with top-1 prefetch and conservative blacklists. and instrument cost.
[02:46] [03:00] Sam Park: quick interjection — on the console we can surface token delta per prefetch experiment so your finance folks can see projected spend. we'll attach that to the experiment.
[03:12] Jordan Meyers: perfect.
[03:15] [03:30] Leah Ito: a messy thing we saw — prompts from mobile have extra boilerplate (OS version, device id) that massively reduces reuse; would canonicalization remove that safely?
[03:42] Priya Nambiar: yes we have pattern examples to strip device metadata; Diego's snippet will include those.
[03:47] [04:00] Diego Ramos: also want to call out KV cache naming — currently some keys include dynamic session tokens; we recommend replacing with stable user or conversation id only when privacy allows. if not allowed, use hashed stable buckets.
[04:14] Jordan Meyers: privacy is strict for us, so we'll need hashing + salt with customer-managed KMS. are those integrations tested?
[04:22] Maya Chen: yes, Private and Dedicated modes support KMS integrations; we can provide a sample HSM/KMS flow. Diego will include the snippet in the doc.
[04:30] [04:45] Tomás Alvarez: curious about routing/orchestration — if cache hit-rate remains low on hosted, we might want a Dedicated fallback for predictable latency. how do we decide threshold?
[04:57] Maya Chen: typical rule is if prefix/KV uplift under canonicalization < 20% and latency variability remains high, we propose a Dedicated run for a week to validate throughput and latency SLOs. we'll do cost/benefit in the note.
[05:10] Diego Ramos: also remember that batching and KV cache interplay — larger batch windows can erode hit-rate if keys are ephemeral; we recommend workload-aware batching.
[05:20] Rina Kapoor: can you give a concrete experiment plan we can run in staging to prove improvements?
[05:26] Diego Ramos: yes: 1) baseline 48h replay with current config (we have that), 2) apply canonicalization rules + hashed key change + TTL bump to 5 minutes for affinity sessions and run 24h, 3) run prefetch top-1 on a small fraction (5%) of traffic for 24h, 4) compare hit-rate, p50/p95 latency, token spend delta. we'll provide scripts and dashboard.
[05:52] Jordan Meyers: timeline for that — we can get logs ready by Friday. we want to run the replay early next week.
[05:59] Maya Chen: great, Diego and Priya will assemble the config today and post into the shared folder.
[06:05] [06:20] Leah Ito: about eviction — what's best practice for prompt eviction heuristics? we saw some prompts get evicted too aggressively causing churn.
[06:30] Priya Nambiar: we usually recommend LRU with weighted recency for templates, and a small protected set for frequently used templates. TTL bump for protected items helps. also smarter eviction that considers token cost of regeneration.
[06:45] Tomás Alvarez: can Redwood's console expose eviction stats?
[06:49] Sam Park: yes we can add an eviction heatmap to the pilot dashboard; we'll turn that on.
[06:55] [07:10] Jordan Meyers: one odd metric — there's a spike of low reuse queries right around 03:00 UTC daily, looks like a batch process. we'll scrub and maybe exclude those from baseline.
[07:20] Diego Ramos: good call, filter those when calculating user-facing hit-rate.
[07:23] [07:40] Rina Kapoor: two quick non-technical asks: SOC2 artifacts and SSO integration docs — legal wants them by next week.
[07:50] Maya Chen: noted, we'll push the SOC2 pack and SAML implementation guide to the shared drive.
[07:56] [08:10] Tomás Alvarez: can we get a quick cost model that shows break-even hit-rate for prefetch at different token sizes?
[08:18] Maya Chen: yes, Diego will include the spreadsheet; we'll also include p50/p95 latency offsets.
[08:24] [08:40] Diego Ramos: one more thought — canonicalization introduces potential false-positives; we'll add a safety threshold and audit logs for cache hits that used canonicalized keys. you can inspect and roll back rules.
[08:54] Jordan Meyers: appreciate that.
[09:00] [09:20] Maya Chen: ok pulling together the wrap: Diego will send the config snippet and prefetch policy, Jordan will deliver logs, Rina will run staging replay, Maya will send pricing and Dedicated fallback plan. any objections?
[09:36] Leah Ito: none.
[09:38] Tomás Alvarez: sounds good.
[09:40] [09:50] Priya Nambiar: I'll also add examples of canonicalization rules (regex) and a short runbook for rolling them back.
[09:57] Maya Chen: great. we'll reconvene next Tuesday same time for results.

CLOSING SUMMARY / RECAP:
- Current hit-rate: baseline ~18% global, 24% on QA service.
- High-leverage experiments: canonicalization (regex-based), TTL bump for affinity, prefetch top-1 on 5% traffic, hashed stable keys for privacy.
- Short-term plan: customer to scrub and upload 48h logs; Redwood to supply config and cost model; run replays and small live prefetch experiment; then reassess for Dedicated.

title: Cafeteria Beanbag and Ambient Noise Guidelines
author: Aisha Khan
text:
Summary

This page documents a lightweight, experimental set of guidelines for beanbag seating and ambient noise considerations in Redwood Inference shared spaces (cafeteria, lounge, and overflow areas). The goal is pragmatic: improve employee comfort and informal collaboration while keeping operational burden low.

Scope

- Applies to: cafeteria, adjacent lounge, satellite huddle areas on main campus and leased offices.
- Does NOT apply to: focus rooms, phone booths, secure rooms, or private customer meeting rooms.

Guiding principles

1. Respect for teammates: conserve shared spaces for implicit consent — assume people nearby prefer moderate noise levels.
2. Minimal ops: prefer low-maintenance furniture and sensors; avoid complex approvals for small purchases.
3. Data-informed: measure and iterate; use a simple decibel sampling process before large rollouts.

Furniture guidelines (beanbags and soft seating)

- Quantity: limit beanbag count per room to 6 units or 25% of casual seating, whichever is smaller.
- Placement: require at least 1.5m clear circulation path; do not block egress or access to kitchen equipment.
- Materials: choose wipeable, flame-retardant covers rated for commercial use.
- Procurement checklist (sample):
 1. Model spec and SKU
 2. Flame retardant certificate (pdf)
 3. Supplier lead time and return policy
 4. Estimated cost per unit
 5. Maintenance plan (wipe schedule)

Ambient noise guidance

- Target levels: daylight cafeteria 45-55 dB typical; lunchtime peaks allowed up to 65 dB for short periods.
- Quiet windows: designate 11:30-12:30 on Tuesdays as a quiet-lunch pilot in one lounge for two quarters and evaluate.

Quick decibel sampling procedure

1. Tools: smartphone with a basic dB meter app (note: consumer apps vary).
2. Sampling: take 6 samples across a 30-minute window during a target time (e.g., Wednesday 12:00-12:30).
3. Record: document median and max values. Store sample note on the facilities ticket with a short comment.

Example CLI-style sample (for reference in case teams use a measurement device):

# pseudo-command for a USB mic logger (example only)
# record 30s segments and write a simple CSV of RMS dB values
# recorder --device /dev/audio1 --interval 30 --out cafeteria-sample.csv

Operational checklist for pilot rollout (one-month pilot)

1. Facilities ops to order up to 4 beanbags for Pilot Location A.
2. People Ops to publish the pilot notice and expectations (quiet windows, cleanup).
3. Facilities to execute sampling on week 1 and week 4 and upload notes.
4. Survey: send a 3-question pulse survey after week 4 (comfort, noise impact, cleanup).

Safety, maintenance, and waste

- Cleaning: wipeable covers weekly; deep-clean monthly.
- Disposal: follow office recycling guidelines; avoid foam landfill where programs exist.

Decision and escalation

- If complaints > 10% of local headcount in pilot area, pause and review.
- Escalation owner: Facilities Lead (email: facilities@example.com).

Ownership and review cadence

- Document owner: People Ops (Aisha Khan).
- Review cadence: pilot review at month 1, full review at month 3.

Related artifacts and references

- See: Office space guidelines (Confluence) for building rules and safety.
- See: Facilities procurement template (Drive) for ordering checklist.

Attachments and sample forms

- Procurement sample checklist (attach to ticket)
- Decibel sampling notes (CSV)

Notes and known limitations

- This is intentionally lightweight and experimental. It is not a binding policy for client-facing meeting rooms or regulated spaces. If a space is used for interviews or customer meetings, revert to formal meeting-room standards.

Revision history

- 2024-11-07 initial draft by Aisha Khan
- 2025-01-15 pilot parameters updated after facilities review

title: LucentWorks security & hosting intake
author: Maya Chen
text:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-30 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (Redwood CSM); Raj Patel (Head Infra), Elena Morales (Sec Eng), Tom Brooks (CTO) - LucentWorks

Summary:
Short intake to validate LucentWorks' security gating for production inference. Key topics: SOC 2/ISO evidence, SSO/SAML & SCIM, RBAC and org separation, audit log export and retention, KMS/BYOK options, data residency and retention windows, private control plane vs hosted trade-offs.

Topics Covered:
- Compliance evidence & timing (SOC 2 + ISO 27001)
- SSO/SAML + SCIM provisioning and RBAC mapping
- KMS options: Redwood-managed vs BYOK with HSM/KMS key rotation
- Audit logs: retention, tamper-evidence, SIEM export (Splunk/Datadog)
- Data retention / deletion guarantees and egress of logs
- Private deployment: VPC peering, private control plane, on-prem options

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and this is Daniel on the technical side. Could each of you quick intros?
[00:08] Raj: Raj here, Head of Infrastructure at LucentWorks. We manage cloud infra and the inference stack decisions land with me and Tom.
[00:13] Elena: Elena, security engineer, I own compliance and app security.
[00:17] Tom: Tom, CTO, mostly listening but will chime on requirements and timeline.
[00:22] Daniel: Great. Quick agenda — we want to confirm your controls baseline and any must-haves for production. We'll try to map to Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.
[00:30] Raj: Our initial preference is hosted or dedicated depending on controls. For PHARMA devs we need strict encryption in motion and at rest, key separation ideally BYOK because of vendor policy.
[00:40] Elena: Also SOC 2 is required, ISO would be nice to see. We need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM with at least 1 year retention, and the ability to retain longer for specific customers.
[00:52] Maya: Totally. We can share SOC 2 and ISO paperwork. For KMS we support Redwood-managed keys and BYOK with customer AWS KMS or external HSM — Daniel can go deeper.
[01:00] Daniel: Quick callout: our BYOK flow supports AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and Bring-Your-Own-HSM using PKCS#11 or cloud HSM endpoints. Rotation policies can be customer-controlled. There are sample terraform and helm snippets we can provide.
[01:15] Elena: How does Redwood prevent key exfiltration in hosted mode? We need assurance keys never leave our control.
[01:24] Daniel: In BYOK for hosted, the master key remains in your KMS. Redwood stores only short-lived wrapping keys, and we integrate using envelope encryption. For HSM-backed keys we do one-way wrapping — the private material never lands in Redwood vaults. We'll send architecture diagrams.
[01:40] Raj: And audit logs? We need immutability or at least tamper-evident logs.
[01:46] Priya: We push all request/response metadata to an append-only service; for enterprise customers we provide log export endpoints. You can ship logs to your Splunk/Datadog/S3 bucket. We can also integrate with your SIEM via syslog or forwarders.
[02:02] Elena: What's retained in logs — full prompt/response or just metadata?
[02:07] Daniel: Default is token-level metadata and request headers. We can configure to capture full payloads for audit, but that's often opted-in due to PII concerns. You can set policy per-route to mask or redact inputs.
[02:20] Tom: We have regulated customer data; by default we can't send full prompts outside our control.
[02:25] Maya: That's expected. For Dedicated or Private you can keep full logs in your environment. Hosted we can do redaction and also route full logs into your S3/KMS so they never persist in Redwood long-term.
[02:38] Raj: SSO — we use SAML 2.0 with SCIM for provisioning. Need RBAC mapping, ability to scope teams to tenants, and separate billing.
[02:47] Priya: We support SAML, OIDC, and SCIM for provisioning. RBAC can be mapped to SCIM groups; we can restrict model access per-org and enforce token scopes. For Private deployments we also support LDAP and on-prem identity proxies.
[03:02] Elena: Can we enforce MFA via our IdP?
[03:05] Maya: Yes, MFA is enforced at the IdP level. We also support conditional access via IdP claims.
[03:11] Raj: Data residency — we need EU region for EU customers, and US-eastern for domestic. How does Redwood handle tenancy and data residency in hosted?
[03:21] Daniel: We provision regional clusters. For Hosted, you can pin your tenant to a region and we provide region-specific storage and keys. For Dedicated you get a reserved pool in your region and Private gives you full control over region and network.
[03:33] Elena: On retention — legally we need to be able to purge customer data within 30 days of request and produce a proof of deletion. Is that supported?
[03:41] Maya: We have data deletion APIs and can provide deletion certificates for Private/Dedicated. For Hosted, deletion is supported and we can produce logs showing deletion events; for additional legal guarantees we recommend Dedicated or Private where you control storage.
[03:54] Tom: Our preference is private control plane if costs and ops are reasonable. What are the gating items?
[04:00] Daniel: Primary gating: network connectivity (VPC peering, PrivateLink), KMS integration (BYOK/HSM), and SCIM/SAML flows for user onboarding. Also audit log export and retention SLA. We can prototype a private control plane in a demo environment.
[04:14] Elena: SOC 2 evidence — we need the most recent report and the list of in-scope controls. Also, do you have ISO 27001 cert? Need scope document.
[04:22] Maya: We'll attach SOC 2 Type II report and ISO 27001 certificate with scope. We'll redact vendor-specific things but provide the control matrix.
[04:30] Raj: What's the typical time to stand up Dedicated vs Private?
[04:33] Daniel: Dedicated we can provision in 2-4 weeks depending on capacity and network; Private (customer-managed control plane) is typically 6-12 weeks due to networking, security review, and testing. On-prem will be longer.
[04:45] Elena: For audit logs, can we retain for 7 years if required? Our legal wants 7y for some studies.
[04:52] Priya: Yes, retention is configurable. For Hosted we can forward to your long-term S3 archive with encryption under your key so Redwood doesn't host the archive. For Dedicated/Private you control retention directly.
[05:05] Raj: Model access controls — can we pin models per-tenant and prevent cross-tenant cache leaks?
[05:12] Daniel: Yes, model pinning and per-tenant compute isolation exists. KV cache is namespaced by tenant and by deployment; we have guardrails to prevent cross-tenant cache leakage. We'll include the technical note about cache isolation and the sequence-length behavior.
[05:27] Elena: Any FedRAMP or health-care specific certifications?
[05:30] Maya: Not FedRAMP currently; for healthcare we support BAA conversations and can provide additional controls in Private deployments. We'll flag compliance gaps and mitigations in the security pack.
[05:40] Tom: What about pen test reports or VAPT?
[05:43] Maya: We can share summary VAPT results and remediation tracker; for detailed reports we require an NDA.
[05:49] Raj: Encryption at rest — is data encrypted with customer keys or Redwood keys?
[05:53] Daniel: By default Redwood-managed keys are used. For Dedicated and Hosted with BYOK, data at rest is encrypted under customer KMS. For Private you can bring your own KMS and control everything.
[06:03] Elena: How are secrets handled for model artifacts and container images?
[06:07] Priya: Images are pulled from registries over mTLS and secrets are injected at runtime with vault-backed ephemeral secrets. Artifacts are stored in encrypted object stores with access policies.
[06:19] Tom: Ok, rough timeline — we want pilot within Q2, production by Q3 if gating is ok. Is that feasible?
[06:27] Daniel: Feasible. Next step is to run through a lightweight pilot: private control plane demo, KMS integration test, and log export validation. We'll need your infra folks to enable VPC peering and provide test keys.
[06:40] Elena: We will also run an internal legal review; please send all certs/docs.
[06:44] Maya: Absolutely. We'll send a package with SOC2, ISO cert, VAPT summary, and the BYOK integration guide. Also will include sample terraform and helm snippets for Private deploy.
[06:55] Raj: Can you provide an estimated cost delta between Hosted with BYOK and Dedicated?
[06:59] Samir: We'll provide a high-level delta sheet; Hosted with BYOK is generally lower monthly cost but less isolation; Dedicated adds reserved GPU capacity and higher cost but gives stronger isolation and control. We'll send numbers.
[07:12] Tom: One last question — audit log tamper evidence, do you support append-only WORM buckets or signed log chains?
[07:18] Daniel: We support forwarding to WORM-enabled S3 and can provide signed log digests (merkle-tree style summaries) on request for high-assurance customers.
[07:29] Elena: That would satisfy legal in many cases.
[07:32] Maya: Great. Quick recap of next steps then.
[07:35] Maya (recap): Action items: Maya to send compliance pack + network diagram; Daniel to prepare BYOK/HSM options and sample config; Elena to send retention policy and legal contact; schedule SE workshop for private control plane next week.
[07:50] Raj: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[07:53] Tom: Thanks.
[07:55] Maya: We'll follow up by email with links to docs and propose times for the workshop.

Notes & references mentioned:
- SOC 2 Type II report (to be sent)
- ISO 27001 cert and scope (to be sent)
- BYOK/HSM integration guide (samples: AWS KMS, GCP KMS, PKCS#11)
- Sample terraform/helm snippets for Private control plane
- VAPT summary (NDA for full report)
- Log export options: Splunk/Datadog/S3 + WORM buckets and signed digests

End of transcript.

title: AcmeCorp: high p99 after enabling speculative-batching + aggressive quant profile — request for safe escape-hatch
text:
Issue summary: Customer enabled two optimizer changes in production for /v1/generate: speculative-batching (enabled at 1s wait threshold) and a new aggressive mixed-precision quant profile (quant-profile: aggressive-e2e). Immediately after the change AcmeCorp observed spiking p99 latency and several timed-out streams.

Impact: Intermittent client timeouts and elevated p99 (~4-6x baseline) for a high-volume tenant lane. Customer reports user-facing errors in a throttled portion of traffic and requests an assisted, low-risk pathway to revert or safe-drain the optimizer changes without extended downtime.

Environment: prod us-east, Dedicated tenant lane for AcmeCorp (enterprise reserved pool), model variants rw-open-3b and rw-compat-1.0, traffic mix: chat streaming + small non-streaming inference.

Desired outcome: step-by-step escape-hatch that minimizes traffic disruption and provides a controlled rollback of speculative-batching and quant-profile with validation gates, plus recommended telemetry to monitor during unwind.

1) Tenant config: speculative-batching: enabled (1s); prefix_cache: enabled (default); quant_profile: aggressive-e2e applied to both variants.
2) Send steady-state streaming chat traffic at ~240 rps for 60 minutes.
3) Observe 95p/99p latency and increased stream disconnects.
4) Check serving-runtime logs for eviction and kernel fallback warnings.

Customer supplied timeline logs and spans: s3://acmecorp-prod-artifacts/2026-03-10/trace-tenant-76142.tar.gz; sample request ids: req-20260310-7a3f, req-20260310-7b1e. Relevant console graphs: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/tenant/AcmeCorp/latency?p=24h. Error snippets include: 
- 'kv_cache_eviction: true, eviction_reason=kv_capacity'
- 'kernel_fallback: float32-path triggered for layer 4 due to quant mismatch'

Initial SRE triage: correlated p99 spikes with high speculative-batching coalescing windows that increased sequence length variance and triggered unexpected KV cache churn. Aggressive quant profile produced intermittent kernel incompatibility for rw-compat-1.0, falling back to slower float32 kernels.
Hypotheses: 1) Speculative batching increased inter-request packing causing larger effective sequences and cache pressure; 2) Aggressive quant interacts with certain kernels, causing rare slow-path execution; 3) Combined effect pushes some RPCs past streaming timeouts.
Telemetry consulted: request-level latency heatmaps, per-shard kernel version logs, KV cache hit/evict counters, and batching histogram via tracing endpoint.
Next steps proposed: capture per-tenant kernel-fallback rate (metric: runtime.kernel_fallback.count by tenant), enable per-tenant batching cap, and stage quant-profile downgrade on a small traffic slice.

Applied per-tenant batching cap: max_batch_size=64 and speculative-batching: wait_threshold lowered to 250ms for AcmeCorp lane (toggled via tenant optimizer overrides). Early metrics show p99 reduction from 1.8s to ~1.1s in the first 45 minutes. Still monitoring.

1) Start with non-disruptive throttles: set speculative-batching wait_threshold=250ms and max_batch_size=64 for AcmeCorp lane (apply via tenant override).
2) Monitor kernel_fallback.count and kv_cache_eviction.rate for 20 minutes.
3) If metrics improve, stage quant-profile downgrade to conservative-e2e for rw-compat-1.0 on 5% traffic (traffic-split via routing config).
4) Validate end-to-end: latency dashboard, streaming success rate, and customer sampling.
5) If step 3 passes at 5% for 30 minutes, ramp to 25% then 100% in 15-minute steps.
6) If any step regresses, perform immediate rollback to previous step and open an incident for deeper kernel/quant interaction analysis.
7) Post-mortem: collect flamegraphs and kernel-call traces, and schedule optimizer regression test for this workload pattern.

In Progress - temporary batching cap applied which reduced p99 by ~40% in initial window. Quant-profile downgrade staged at 5% traffic during maintenance window; awaiting 30-minute validation. No full revert performed yet. Final resolution pending validation; will document final steps and follow-up actions once complete.

- SRE to collect detailed kernel fallback traces and attach to ticket. - PM to triage aggressive-e2e quant profile for rw-compat-1.0 and add regression tests. - CS to confirm client-level retry/backoff guidance with AcmeCorp engineering.

2026-03-10 09:12 - Lena Ortiz: Thanks for flagging this, Marcus is looping in runtime SRE and optimizer PM. We will propose a low-risk unwind plan by EOD.

title: Marketplace Feature Composition Playbook
author: Leah Nakamura
text:
Overview

This playbook defines the product strategy, implementation requirements, rollout plan, pricing guidance, and release checklist for the "Feature Composition" capability in Redwood's Marketplace. Feature Composition allows customers to assemble multiple serving features (e.g., reranking, embeddings, caching, quantization profiles, and A/B fidelity routes) into composable bundles that behave as single consumable units in the Redwood Console and API. The goal is to accelerate customer time-to-value for common consumption patterns while preserving unit economics and observability.

Goals and success metrics

- Primary goal: Deliver a composable marketplace unit that reduces integration time for customers by 40% and increases bundle adoption rate to 20% of active tenants within 6 months.
- Business metrics: bundle revenue share (% of hosting revenue), avg tokens/sec per bundle, churn delta for customers using bundles, and incremental ARPU.
- Product metrics: time-to-first-bundle (console + API), failure rate for composite executions (<0.5%), average per-token latency delta vs baseline (<10ms).

Key concepts and scope

1) Composition unit: a named, versioned artifact that references one or more Redwood services and configuration profiles (model variant, quantization profile, cache TTLs, routing policy).
2) Execution graph: ordered stages (e.g., preprocessor -> model-A -> reranker -> cache-write) with per-stage SLOs and fallbacks.
3) Consumption contract: public interface (API surface + Console UX) plus pricing model that maps internal resource usage to billable units.
4) Compatibility guarantees: each bundle must include a compatibility matrix that lists supported runtime variants (hosted, dedicated, private) and minimal hardware footprint.

Non-goals

- Not intended to replace low-level SDK primitives. Developers will still be able to call individual services directly.
- No cross-tenant data mixing. Composed bundles adhere to tenant isolation rules and existing KMS/HSM integrations.

High-level product requirements (PRD style)

- PR-1: Bundle lifecycle: create / version / deprecate bundles. Bundles must be immutable once published; patch releases allowed (minor metadata only).
- PR-2: Declarative definition: support YAML/JSON bundle manifest with fields: id, name, description, stages (with service, model_ref, variant, resources), pricing_hint, telemetry_tags. Provide schema and sample manifests.
- PR-3: Execution guarantees: transactions across stages must support partial rollback semantics for idempotent stages; non-idempotent side effects must surface compensating actions in logs and alerts.
- PR-4: Observability: dashboards per-bundle with token-level cost breakdown, per-stage latency heatmaps, and error-trace waterfall.
- PR-5: Console UX: bundle composer with drag/drop stages, validation rules, preflight simulation using synthetic workload.
- PR-6: API: stable REST + SDK endpoints for listing, instantiating, and invoking bundles. Invocation should support streaming responses and function-calling where applicable.
- PR-7: Pricing: define a credit model (see Pricing Guidance section). Price preview in the composer and per-invocation estimate in the API.

Design constraints and decisions

- Decision D-1: Bundles will be first-class entities in the metadata service (service: catalog-api). Bundle manifests are stored versioned in the Config Store (service: cfg-store).
- Decision D-2: Execution will reuse existing runtime components; each stage resolves to an internal route token (route-svc) and executes with tenant-scoped quotas.
- Decision D-3: Bundles must declare a deterministic fallback policy: local-model fallback, variant fallback, regional failover, or degrade-to-sampled-response. The runtime will enforce the first compatible fallback.
- Decision D-4: For Private deployments, customers can opt-in to allow vendor-managed composition or run the composer locally via a CLI that emits a validated manifest.

Compatibility matrix (table-like summary)

- Supported modes: hosted (yes), dedicated (yes), private (opt-in, feature parity v1.1).
- Minimal footprints per composition complexity: small (1 model, no rerank) = 4 vCPU / 16GB GPU memory equivalent; medium (2–3 stages incl reranker) = 8 vCPU / 32GB GPU mem; large (multi-model + embeddings + cache) = 16+ vCPU / multi-GPU.

Runtime orchestration and telemetry

1. Resolution: catalog-api resolves manifest -> stage route tokens -> runtime graph.
2. Execution: running under an execution context that tracks request id, tenant id, trace id, and billing tags.
3. Telemetry: span per-stage with attributes: model_ref, variant, tokens_in/tokens_out, cost_estimate, compute_ms, fallback_triggered.
4. Sampling: include 100% sampling for bundle errors; 1% sampling for success traces (configurable per-tenant).

Pricing guidance and credit model

- Pricing primitive: charge per composite token-equivalent. Each stage contributes a token-weight multiplier based on model size and quantization profile (e.g., small model x1, reranker x0.6 per token, large model x2).
- Bundle-level surcharge: marketplace bundles carry a configurable partner surcharge (0–20%) and optional markup for managed bundles.
- Preview tool: composer shows a 30-day estimate (tokens, compute-hours, estimated credits) based on customer observed traffic patterns or synthetic defaults.

Operational runbook (high-level)

1) On-call flow: bundle execution failures that exceed 0.5% error rate for 10 minutes raise P1 to Runtime and Catalog owners.
2) Quick mitigation steps: toggle bundle to degraded mode (console action: disable external side-effects), route all traffic to variant with highest fidelity fallback.
3) Incident playbook: capture request ids, simulate failing manifest with known-good inputs via the preflight runner, and escalate if rollback not effective within 30 minutes.

Rollout timeline and milestones (quarterly phased)

- Phase 0 (Q4 2028): Internal alpha. Deliver catalog-api schema, composer wireframes, runtime graph prototype, and simple charging calculator.
- Phase 1 (Q1 2029): Private beta with 5 customers; console composer, execution telemetry, pricing-preview.
- Phase 2 (Q2 2029): General availability for hosted and dedicated; partner marketplace onboarding flow.
- Phase 3 (Q3 2029): Marketplace partner launch, revenue tracking, and A/B pricing experiments.

Owner and stakeholders

- Product lead: Leah Nakamura (this doc).
- Engineering owners: Runtime (Riley Chen), Catalog & Config (Marco Reyes), Console/UX (Priya Singh).
- Go-to-market owner: Anya Patel.
- Security/compliance reviewer: Edmund Briggs.

APIs and sample manifests

Sample bundle manifest (YAML) — composer will generate and validate this schema:

```
# bundle-manifest.yaml
id: com.redwood.marketplace.compose.simple-summary-v1
name: "Summary-and-Rerank Bundle"
description: "Generates long-form summary then reranks candidate paragraphs for final selection"
stages:
 - name: summarize
 service: model-svc
 model_ref: open-llama-13b-v2
 variant: quantized-8bit
 resources:
 max_seq: 1024
 batch: auto
 - name: rerank
 service: rerank-svc
 model_ref: reranker-bert-large
 variant: standard
 resources:
 max_candidates: 8
pricing_hint:
 token_multiplier: 1.6
 partner_markup_pct: 10
telemetry_tags:
 - marketplace:feature-composition
 - vertical:knowledge
```

Release checklist (pre-GA)

- [ ] Schema stable and documented in cfg-store.
- [ ] Composer UX: synthetic-preflight and cost-preview integrated.
- [ ] Runtime: per-stage SLO instrumentation and fallback enforcement implemented.
- [ ] Billing: credit calculation validated against 3 traffic profiles.
- [ ] Security: threat model review and data residency checks for Private.
- [ ] Docs: developer guide, sample manifests, SDK examples, and migration notes.

Open questions and risks

- Q1: How to price cross-stage cache benefits (cache reduces compute downstream) without double-counting?
- Q2: Partner revenue share models—should we support revenue splits at invocation time or settlement time?
- Risk: Complexity of composed debugging for customers; mitigation: strong preflight simulator and 1-click trace collection.

Appendix: validation tests and KPIs for GA

- Functional tests: manifest validation, end-to-end execution for 8 canonical manifests, preflight fidelity simulation.
- Performance tests: 95th percentile per-bundle latency under 500 RPS with mixed short/long inputs.
- Billing tests: synthetic load that exercises token multipliers; reconciliation within 0.5% vs expected.
- Customer pilots: onboard 5 customers across e-commerce, knowledge, and support verticals; measure integration time and adoption rates.

If you are reviewing this document: please review the manifest schema section and the pricing_hint model. Flag any backward-incompatible metadata changes before the next sprint cut (2028-11-15).

title: Contextual Probe Orchestrator and Hypothesis-Driven Canary Fences
author: Maya Chen
text:
Purpose: Implement a Contextual Probe Orchestrator (CPO) to improve regression detection during staged model flips. The CPO combines stratified live sampling, synthetic perturbation injection, and hypothesis-driven fences to reduce false positives/negatives in automatic rollback decisions. Scope: - Probe bucketization by customer cohort, request size, prompt template family, and recency bucket. - Synthetic perturbation matrix to exercise edge behaviors deterministically (format noise, length extremes, tiled stop sequences). - Per-cohort baseline scorecards computed from rolling windows and bootstrapped confidence intervals. - Hypothesis-driven canary fences: gating rules expressed as statistical hypotheses (e.g., delta > X and bootstrap p < Y) with hysteresis windows to avoid flapping. Acceptance criteria: 1) Offline simulation shows reduction in false rollback triggers vs current heuristic by >= 30% on historical rollouts. 2) Live shadow sweep runs for 48h with <1% false positive rollback alerts when using CPO signals. 3) Automated gating config UI in the Console exposes per-cohort thresholds and an opt-in toggle. Out of scope: major changes to KV cache or kernel scheduling.

scorecard_mean_delta
scorecard_std_change
cohort_regression_rate
bootstrap_p_value
service_latency_p50/p95/p99
token_cost_delta
human-reviewes_per_hour

Primary gate: (scorecard_mean_delta >= 1.8) AND (bootstrap_p_value <= 0.01) measured over a 30-minute sliding window
Secondary gate: cohort_regression_rate >= 0.015 for two consecutive 10-minute windows triggers alert but requires human confirm for rollback
Hysteresis: require 3 successive failing windows OR persistent delta for 60 minutes before initiating automatic rollback
Fallback: if latency p99 increases > 2x OR error rate > 0.5% across global traffic, immediate scaledown to previous model variant

Offline: run historical-sim harness (conftest: rollout-sim-v2) comparing baseline heuristic vs CPO on 12 months of canary data
Shadow sweep: route 100% shadow traffic for 48h with CPO generating alerts but no automated rollback
Staged canary: 5% -> 25% -> 50% ramps with CPO gates enforced and automatic rollback enabled only after opt-in; first run will use human-in-loop for final rollback decision
A/B experiment: run paired A/B for 7 days to validate user-facing metric impact and false positive rate

Introduce probe bucketing service in inference-router to tag requests with cohort metadata
Lightweight synthetic probe engine lives in eval-harness; probes are stored as signed fixtures to ensure reproducibility
Use existing metric pipeline (Prometheus + Mimir) and add a bootstrapping worker for p-value estimation that writes per-cohort summaries to metrics-store
Keep rollout decision workflow in rollout-orchestrator; add new decision hook that consumes CPO signals as input to existing canary state machine

Risk: overfitting probe sets to historical regressions -> Mitigation: rotate and expand synthetic perturbations monthly via auto-generation job
Risk: increased metric compute cost (bootstrap) -> Mitigation: sample cohorts adaptively and fall back to less-expensive t-test when sample size large
Risk: noisy per-customer baselines causing spurious human alerts -> Mitigation: require cohort-level min traffic threshold and blend global baseline when traffic low

Feature flag gating for CPO and per-team opt-in in Console
Canary the orchestrator itself on internal clusters (dev->staging->prod) with synthetic-only traffic first
Enable live shadowing for 7 internal customers and monitor false positive rates before broader rollout

False rollback trigger rate <= 0.5% during shadow runs
Detection lead time: median time to detect real regression <= 12 minutes
Precision of automatic rollback decisions >= 95% on validated regressions
Additional metric cost budget: < 10% increase in metrics compute month-over-month for rollout telemetry

2026-03-02 - Maya Chen: Initial write-up completed. Shared design doc in Confluence (link below). Need alignment on statistical thresholds with Product and ML Research.
2026-03-04 - Arjun Patel: POC for probe bucketing implemented. Found that 20% of traffic lacks stable cohort tags; added plan to backfill model to tager service.
2026-03-06 - Emilie Torres (PM): Reviewed gating logic. Suggested conservative p-value 0.01 and hysteresis to reduce churn. Also requested that console expose a preview simulation for each config change.
2026-03-08 - Nathan R. (ML Research): Ran offline sim on 6 months of data. CPO reduced false triggers by ~37% vs baseline. Attached simulation CSVs and charts.
2026-03-10 - Security review: flagged synthetic probes containing customer PII risks; added rule: probes must be sanitized and reviewed before upload to fixtures store.
2026-03-11 - Arjun Patel: Added lightweight bootstrapping worker and a fallback t-test path. Started integration tests for metric emissions. Draft PR opened.
2026-03-12 - Maya Chen: Schedule gating review with SRE and Console UX for 2026-03-16. Plan to enable shadow sweep 2026-03-18 if approvals are green.

title: Captive-portal / TLS interception by corporate NGFW returns HTML login page for presigned S3 URLs, causing model artifact fetch failures in private deploy
text:
Issue summary:
Customer reports intermittent failures pulling model shard objects from S3 when running a Private deployment behind their corporate NGFW. Instead of binary object, the HTTP range request returns an HTML captive‑portal/login page (200 OK, text/html). This causes model shard validation to fail and the serving node to mark shards corrupted, producing 5xx errors for in-flight inference requests.

Impact:
- Production latency spikes and increased 5xx on a subset (~12%) of artifact range requests.
- Several serving nodes marked unhealthy and restarted model pulls, amplifying load.
- Customer experienced production degradation of one internal ML feature for ~2 hours during business peak.

Environment:
- Private deployment in customer VPC with VPCE to S3 disabled (customer downloads via egress NAT through corporate perimeter).
- Serving runtime version: rwd-infer-1.18.2
- Artifact store: s3://redwood-models-prod/fin/bert-large-serve-v2/

1) Deploy private package into customer VPC with default egress to corporate internet via NGFW
2) Trigger a model load (e.g., scale up serving nodes) to force range GETs for shard files
3) Observe repeated HTTP 200 responses with content-type text/html instead of application/octet-stream
4) Serving runtime logs show checksum mismatch and shard validation failure followed by retry loop

Sample HTTP transaction: GET /bert-large-serve-v2/weights/shard-3?X-Amz-Signature=... -> 200 OK, Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8, body starts with '<!DOCTYPE html>'
S3 request-id: 9D4F12A3ZZZZYYY
Serving node logs: runtime/artifact_fetch.cpp:line 214 checksum mismatch for shard-3, expected 0x1f4b2a got 0x000000
PCAP (customer-provided): tcpdump shows corporate NGFW injecting 302 -> captive.login.local:8080 for the GET request before TLS unwrap

2026-03-10 09:12 - Maya Patel: Customer first reported degradation in #support with screenshot of HTML body returned for shard range requests.
2026-03-10 10:02 - Diego Ramos (Support): Confirmed serving node logs show non-binary responses for range GETs; escalated to SRE for network evidence collection.
2026-03-10 13:40 - SRE (Anya Chen): Packet capture shows TLS is being intercepted/terminated by corporate NGFW which returns captive portal content for outbound HTTPS to S3 hosts that are not allowlisted. Customer policy notes show forced TLS inspection for unknown external hosts.
2026-03-11 08:22 - Customer (Network Ops, Aaron Li): Confirmed corporate NGFW performs HTTPS intercept and redirects unauthenticated devices to captive portal unless destination on exception list. They initially blocked allowlist changes for security review.
2026-03-12 11:05 - Diego Ramos: Proposed mitigations (1) configure VPCE to S3 or (2) request permanent allowlist for redwood-models-prod S3 hostnames and S3 IP ranges; asked customer to trial VPCE first.
2026-03-13 15:30 - Customer (Aaron Li): Started VPCE pilot and reported artifact pulls succeeded during test window; agreed to open change request with infosec to allowlist in long term.

Observed pattern: only requests that traverse corporate perimeter are affected. When the same nodes egress via a jump server with no TLS inspection, pulls succeed consistently.
NGFW replaces original TLS handshake on port 443 with its own certificate (MITM), then forwards request upstream. Presigned S3 URLs are tied to signature + host and expect unmodified TLS; MITM causes intermediate HTML captive portal to be injected when NGFW decides host not authorized.
Range GETs are sensitive because serving runtime expects byte ranges and binary responses; HTML bodies cause checksum mismatch rather than a simple HTTP error code, which triggers retries and node-level corruption detection.
SRE validated that when VPCE to S3 was used (no perimeter egress), artifacts are fetched with correct content-type and checksum matches.
Related internal test: reproduced with curl using presigned URL from a machine behind NGFW -> HTML login response. Reproduced failure window aligns with corporate policy enforcement logs.

Corporate perimeter security appliance is performing transparent TLS interception and captive-portal redirect for non-allowlisted external hosts. This returns HTML login pages for presigned S3 GET requests, which the serving runtime treats as corrupted shards (checksum mismatch).

Short-term workaround: Customer enabled a VPCE for S3 (private endpoint) to ensure artifact fetches do not traverse the NGFW; artifact fetch success confirmed in test. Long-term remediation: Customer infosec will add redwood model storage hostnames/IP ranges to NGFW allowlist and exempt those flows from captive-portal/TLS inspection. Documentation updated with recommended network controls for private deployments and a checklist to avoid TLS interception. Follow-up action: create KB for customers explaining detection indicators and mitigations.

2026-03-13 - Diego Ramos: VPCE deployment validated. Serving nodes fetched all shards successfully; no further checksum errors observed during 24h post-cutover.
2026-03-13 - Support: Sent template allowlist request and recommended CIDR list + S3 hostnames to customer security team.
2026-03-14 - Product Docs: Added 'Avoiding TLS interception' section to Private Deploy networking checklist (https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/DEV/pages/Private+Deploy+Networking)
Follow-up: INT-1142 created to instrument runtime to detect non-binary artifact responses earlier and fail fast with clearer error to aid debugging.

title: Console cached query results and trace links resolve to previous API key after customer rotated API key
text:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that after rotating their API key, Console dashboards and ad-hoc usage queries continue to show results and trace links tied to the previous API key. Clicking trace links from the Console leads to 404s or traces attributed to the old key. This appears to be a cache/staleness problem on the Console/usage-analytics side where cache entries are not invalidated correctly after API key rotation.

Impact:
- Customer cannot reliably link dashboard query rows to live trace anchors (404s)
- Usage numbers in Console may temporarily reflect activity attributed to the old key instead of the new one
- High business impact for this enterprise customer due to audit/compliance reporting needs

Environment:
- Prod environment for BrightHealth AI (org: brighthealth-ai) in us-east-1
- Console version: web-2026.02.14
- Cache-service: redis-cluster-prod-3 (managed), cache-key-prefix v2

Steps to reproduce (as reported by customer):
1) Rotate API key via the Console > API keys > Rotate for org brighthealth-ai
2) Open Usage -> Ad-hoc Query with filter api_key: <new-key> and time range last 24h
3) Observe that panel rows still show request_ids and trace links for requests made with old key
4) Click a trace link -> Console opens trace URL and shows 404 or a trace page with request_id that predates rotation

Observed logs / snippets provided by customer:
- Example request_id seen in Console: req_20260309_7c9f3a8b
- Trace anchor from Console: trace-span-0a1b2c3d (resolves to old-key-owner)
- Customer-side API audit shows calls credited to new key from 2026-03-09T16:12:24Z

Attachments: customer-provided screenshots, session recording, and API audit CSV (uploaded to ticket).

03/10 - Triage by Support (Aisha): Verified customer repro steps in a staging replica. Confirmed Console is serving cached rows that include request_id/trace links linked to old API key after rotation.
03/10 - SRE (Diego): Examined cache key format in cache-service. cache-key included api_key_id in v1 but v2 rollout switched to org_id. Observation: rotation job updates api_key table but does not trigger cache invalidation for entries keyed by api_key_id in legacy caches. Some panels still reading from legacy cache prefix (v2 migration not complete across all pods).
03/11 - Eng (Sana, backend): Looked at request routing and link generation. Trace links are generated using stored request metadata pulled from the usage-analytics index. Indexing pipeline attaches original api_key_id as metadata; on rotation, a downstream migration job expected to remap historical entries but task hasn't completed and migration flag is off.
03/11 - Hypothesis: Two independent issues: (1) Console frontend sometimes reads from legacy cache prefix v1 which is keyed by api_key_id and remains stale post-rotation, (2) indexing migration that would remap historical requests to the org-level view hasn't been run for this customer's partition, so trace anchors reference old api_key values and the live trace lookup uses new key leading to 404s.
Relevant traces/logs: /logs/console/cache-debug/2026-03-10.log, /logs/indexer/migration-partition-42.log (partial failures)

03/10 19:14 UTC - Support instructed customer to open an incognito session and re-run the query to rule out browser-level caching. Incognito showed same results.
03/11 02:32 UTC - SRE manually flushed legacy cache prefix for brighthealth-ai on redis-cluster-prod-3 (keys matching 'v1:org:brighthealth-ai:*'). This momentarily allowed new queries to surface correct request_ids for new key.
03/11 04:00 UTC - Engineering kicked off the per-org indexing migration job for partition 42 (affected customer). Job progress looked healthy but some records failed mapping due to legacy malformed api_key entries.
03/11 09:22 UTC - Added temporary console guard: panels will prefer live index read when an API key rotation event is detected in the last 24h, bypassing cache for affected orgs. Deployed as emergency feature flag rollout (ff/console/rotation-cache-bypass).
03/11 18:11 UTC - Notified customer of workaround and requested confirmation that trace links now resolve.
Customer confirmation 03/11 19:05 UTC: Reported that trace links are resolving for most rows but a small subset (approx 0.8%) remain 404ing.

Aisha Patel (Support) 2026-03-10T18:40Z: Created ticket after phone call with BrightHealth AI. Customer needs audit-aligned usage numbers by EOD 2026-03-12.
Diego Morales (SRE) 2026-03-10T20:05Z: I confirmed cache key mismatch; preparing safe flush plan for redis (will do per-org prefixes during off-peak windows).
Sana Reddy (Backend Eng) 2026-03-11T01:10Z: Index migration job has partial failures - some legacy API key records don't have a valid org_id. Writing a small remediation script to repair mappings for those records.
Support (Aisha) 2026-03-11T09:30Z: Enabled emergency feature flag to bypass console cache for orgs with rotation events. Not ideal long-term but reduces surface for 404s.
BrightHealth AI (Customer) 2026-03-11T19:05Z: Verified after guidance; majority of links correct now. Remaining few traces still 404; will attach examples.

Temporary: Admin/Support flushed legacy cache prefixes for the customer's redis shard and enabled ff/console/rotation-cache-bypass which forces live index reads for orgs with an API key rotation in the last 24h. Customer can also add a dummy query parameter to bust console cache (e.g., ?bust=1) for ad-hoc queries until fix is rolled out.

During the api_key rotation rollout we migrated cache keying to org-level (v2) but not all console pods and the legacy indexing pipeline were fully migrated. Rotation does not trigger invalidation of v1 cache keys nor robustly remap historical usage entries that reference old api_key_id, leaving stale cache and index entries that generate trace links pointing to old key-scoped traces.

Short term: Complete per-org cache flush and finish the indexing remap and remediation script (Sana). Medium term: Update rotation workflow to emit cache-invalidation events and add automated migration verification (Diego/Sana). Add unit/integration tests to prevent future regressions. Deploy fix: patch indexing job to tolerate malformed legacy records and run migration across affected partitions (target: 2026-03-15).

03/12 - Partial remediation completed: cache flush and migration resumed; residual malformed records detected and repaired by remediation script. Feature flag left on for 48h monitoring. Engineering to run full verification across all enterprise orgs.

ENG-7123: Add cache-invalidation hook to api-key rotation service (assigned: Sana Reddy)
SRE-4409: Create safe per-org cache flush runbook and automate (assigned: Diego Morales)
OPS-2311: Run full indexing remap across partitions for enterprise orgs and validate trace link resolution (owner: Platform Eng)
DOC-1294: Update Console admin docs to document cache-busting and rotation impact (owner: DevEx)
SEC-502: Evaluate audit implications and notify compliance team if historical usage attribution changed post-migration

title: Release pipeline failing: GPG verification errors after team signing-key rotation blocking runners
text:
Issue summary:
Since the org signing key (team-release@gpg) rotation on 2026-03-09, the nightly release pipeline run by self-hosted release-runners is failing during artifact verification. The GPG step reports 'BAD_SIGNATURE' on multiple signed artifacts and aborts the pipeline, blocking all release promotion jobs that require signed artifacts.

Impact:
- All release promotion pipelines from the staging branch are failing in prod-us-east.
- No releases can be created or promoted; estimated user-facing impact: none immediate, but blocker for planned hotfix release.
- A subset of release-runners (hosts tagged release-runner-prod-*) are the first to hit the failures.

Environment:
- CI: GitLab self-hosted (runner group: release-runners-prod)
- Artifact registry: internal OCI registry + GPG-signed tarballs in S3 (us-east)
- Key management: internal key-rotation process (ops-runbook), public key published to internal keyserver at keys.redwood.internal

Steps to reproduce:
1) Trigger release pipeline for release-candidate commit SHA XYZ.
2) Pipeline downloads signed tarball from S3.
3) run `gpg --verify artefact.tar.gz.sig artefact.tar.gz` inside runner container.
4) gpg exits with status 2 and prints 'BAD_SIGNATURE' and 'no valid openpgp data found'.

Observed logs/snippets:
- Runner logs (release-runner-prod-07): "gpg: Signature made ... gpg: BAD_SIGNATURE gpg: invalid packet (ctb=0x0)"
- Pipeline job trace shows immediate failure at 'verify-signature' step.

Hypothesis / initial findings:
- The rotated GPG key was pushed to the internal keyserver with a new key ID and fingerprint. Some runners have an outdated keyring cached and still trust the old key fingerprint, while the artifacts are signed by the new key.
- Some signing tooling may have re-encoded signatures with a different packet format (we saw 'invalid packet' in gpg output) — possible gpg version mismatch between signing host and runner containers.
- The keyserver index propagation may be delayed; runners that used a cached lookup received a malformed response.

Immediate mitigation attempted:
- Ops pulled the previous GPG public key from backup and added it to a temporary allowlist on three runners (release-runner-prod-03/04/07) — pipelines for those runners succeeded for a single build (hotfix candidate).
- Bumped the runner container gpg package from 2.2.20 -> 2.3.8 on a canary runner; that canary now fails with 'invalid packet' while older gpg accepted signature, suggesting a compatibility issue.

Next steps planned / asked from infra team:
- Confirm the exact key fingerprint used by the signing process (artifact-signer job) and compare with keys published to keys.redwood.internal. (Assigned to Release Engineering)
- Force-refresh keyring on all release runners via staged job that pulls explicit public key file from S3 and imports to gpg keyring. (Assigned to CI infra)
- Validate gpg binary versions across signing host and runners; if mismatch, plan either to downgrade signing host gpg or upgrade runner containers. (Assigned to Security/Infra)
- Temporarily allow fallback verification to previous key for releases created in the next 24 hours while we fully roll the new key. (Requires Risk approval).

Cross-references:
- Slack: #release-engineering thread: https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C02RELEASES/p1640
- Runbook: Confluence GPG Key Rotation Runbook (link above)
- Related incidents: INT-23011 (previous key rotation fail), INT-23350 (runner keyring drift)

- Pulled signing host logs: artifact-signer@build-01 shows sign command using gpg 2.2.20 and key-id ABCD1234.

title: Horizon Lumina Insights
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Stalled procurement due to technical fit (p95 latency) + security/on-prem requirements and budget freeze. Competitive threat active.

Current status: Stalled — technical evaluation flagged major latency risk. Customer ran a day-long POC on our dedicated stack last month; observed persistent p95 spikes on real traffic (10s of seconds during peak). Streaming responses often arrive in fragmented packets, front-end reassembly causes additional 200-500ms overhead per chunk.

Customer quotes: "We can’t ship a generative assistant if p95 is unpredictable — it breaks UX and SLA with partners."

Key signals: engineering team engaged early (SEs built a custom test harness), but after two weeks the internal sponsor (VP Eng) paused decision citing a company-wide hiring/budget freeze. Meanwhile procurement has held on vendor selection pending security sign-off for on-prem deployment. Security wants full audit log retention + KMS integration + air-gapped options for EU data.

Competitive pressure: During freeze, them evaluating BeamScale AI — claims a streaming SDK with lower latency and an EU on-prem appliance. Sales heard customer mention price advantage (~20%) and a faster timeline.

Why stalled: 1) p95 latency not meeting their SLO (target 300-500ms p95 for chat; POC showed 1.2-3s p95 under realistic workload). 2) Streaming chunk fragmentation + front-end work required. 3) Security insists on on-prem/VPC & auditing; we offered Private but timeline uncertain. 4) Internal champion deprioritized due to budget freeze.

Current risk: High. Without a short perf remediation plan or an on-prem pilot that replicates their traffic pattern, likely to go closed-lost.

Suggested playbook (internal): run isolated on-prem micro-benchmark with HLI packet traces (Marcus/SE to schedule), engage infra partner to propose kernel/config tweaks, propose interim UX mitigation (client-side optimistic typing + lower chunk size), and a one-month credit for further testing. If security block persists, offer expanded audit log demo + KMS integration roadmap.

Contact cadence: Tried re-engage via email 2026-03-02 (no reply), left voicemail 2026-03-05. Last substantive call 2026-02-18 (see ff_2026-02-18_0940).

title: PagerDuty suppression window with correlated trace snippets and automated handoff summaries
author: Avery Kumar
text:
Problem: During high-throughput incidents we see PD alert storms for the same underlying root cause (e.g. kernel OOM, KV cache pressure) resulting in alert fatigue and expensive oncall churn. Current PD alerts create separate incidents even when traces and metric patterns are correlated; oncall handoffs lack concise context (top traces, correlated errors, recent deploys) so follow-ups are slow.

Proposal: Implement a Pd-suppression-and-handoff service that:
- opens a short suppression window (configurable by rule) when we detect a burst of related alerts from the same logical service/component, so we avoid duplicate PD escalations for the same root cause while still creating a single canonical incident.
- runs a correlation pass that groups alerts by fingerprint (service, route, error class, metric signature) and attaches compressed trace snapshots (top spans, KV cache hit/miss indicators) to the canonical incident.
- auto-generates a Slack-thread handoff summary message with key traces, ingestion-safe excerpts (PII redacted), recent deploy hash, and recommended runbook steps. The Slack message includes buttons: Add runbook excerpt, Mark investigated, Create follow-up ticket.
- emits a compact postmortem skeleton to speed post-incident docs: initial timeline, top traces, affected endpoints and estimated error volume.

Design notes and constraints:
- Correlation engine will reuse the existing trace-hash algorithm from tracing-hooks service but include a fingerprint layer that normalizes request path parameters and maps error taxonomy to standardized codes.
- Trace snapshot must be limited to 3 spans max + a 4-line summary; any stderr/log excerpt included must be sanitized via existing log-redaction pipeline.
- Suppression windows are per-customer-tier and per-service; default 2 minutes for P0 bursts, 30s for P1, configurable in console.
- PD incident lifecycle: canonical incident opened immediately for the first alert that meets criteria; subsequent alerts are attached (not new incidents) unless a cooldown expires. We will follow PD best practices for incident urgency and responder escalation.

Success criteria / metrics:
- Reduce duplicated PD incidents by >=40% for correlated burst classes within 3 months of rollout.
- Mean time to first actionable context (time between PD page and Slack handoff summary) < 90 seconds.
- Oncall satisfaction survey improvement in the two teams piloting the feature.

Rollout plan:
1) Implement correlation + suppression in staging. 2) Pilot with infra-sre and runtime-serving teams for low-volume service groups for 2 weeks. 3) Expand to all runtime services with opt-out per-service toggle in Console. 4) GA and include in runbook library.

Backward compatibility & safety:
- Default behavior is off for all services; feature flag gate in Console and ff-rollout via config.
- If correlation service fails, system falls back to current PD behavior (no suppression). Fail-open semantics ensure alerts are not lost.

Open questions:
- Exact fingerprint hashing tolerances (how much path normalization) — need input from product on user-visible trace context.
- UI controls in Console for configuring suppression windows and per-service policies.

Expected deliverables:
- Pd-suppression-and-handoff microservice (k8s service), correlation ruleset, trace snapshot exporter, Slack message templates, Console toggles, unit & e2e tests, runbook templates, documentation and postmortem skeleton generator.
