title: Olivegrove quickstart: time-to-first-token and hosting tradeoffs
author: Maya Patel
text:
Intro discovery focused on getting Olivegrove to first token quickly via Redwood PLG credits; explored hosted vs dedicated vs private for latency, cost, and data residency. Agreement to run a 2-week hosted pilot with benchmark prompts and receive security pack and 30-day credits.

time-to-first-token playbook
free credits and PLG onboarding
hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
security: SOC2/KMS/SSO
latency vs cost and batching

Maya Patel: Send hosted credits sign-up link and 30-day credits by 2026-05-06
Owen Brooks: Share benchmarking spreadsheet and suggested prompt set by 2026-05-05
Priya Singh: Provide list of PKI/KMS requirements and network contacts by 2026-05-07
Lina Chen: Confirm success criteria for the 2-week pilot (P50 latency, cost per 1k tokens, functional coverage) by 2026-05-06

Start 2-week hosted pilot using Redwood PLG credits
Redwood to run baseline throughput/latency test and share results
Schedule technical deep dive for private deployment questions (if pilot shows need)

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-03 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Owen Brooks (Redwood SE), Lina Chen (Olivegrove CTO), Aaron Dubois (Olivegrove ML Eng), Priya Singh (Olivegrove Platform), Speaker 1 (Product)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery to align on time-to-first-token, decide whether to use hosted PLG credits or scope a dedicated pilot, discuss security and network constraints.

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I can see folks are on. Quick roll call?
00:05 Lina: Hey Lina here.
00:06 Aaron: Aaron.
00:07 Priya: Priya.
00:08 Maya: Awesome. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, joining with Owen who is our solutions engineer. Goal today is to understand your constraints for getting Olivegrove to first token and which hosting mode makes sense.
00:20 Owen: Hi all, quick context from my side — we usually recommend starting hosted for speed and PLG credits, then bump to dedicated or private if you hit data residency or latency SLOs. But depends on the workload.
00:35 Lina: For us, two main things: time-to-market — we want a working API hooked into our ingestion pipeline within two weeks — and data controls. Some datasets are PII; we may need VPC or on-prem later.
00:50 Maya: Great. Can you describe your current stack? Aaron, maybe you can speak to how you're calling models today.
00:56 Aaron: Right now it's a mix — we run smaller NLU models in-house on k8s, vector dbs are in GCS, and we have a prototype calling another vendor's hosted endpoint for summarization. Latency has been okay for internal tooling but customer facing APIs need <200ms p50. We also want predictable unit cost.
01:20 Owen: Good, predictable p50 200ms is tight for hosted depending on model size and sequence length. For hosted we surface performance profiles per model; smaller context models typically hit that easily. For larger models we recommend dedicated reserved capacity or quantized variants.
01:40 Lina: When you say "performance profiles" — is that in the console? We saw reference numbers in a doc but not the console yet.
01:48 Maya: Yes, model catalog in the Console has per-model latency and cost estimates. We'll share a short link to a PDF and the console demo.
01:55 Aaron: On security, we need SOC2 Type II, SSO (SAML), and for private datasets we'd like to use our KMS and audit logs. How does Redwood handle keys and auditability?
02:12 Owen: For hosted we are SOC2 and provide tenant-level audit logs and SSO. For VPC/private you can bring your own KMS via HSM integrations and we enable customer-managed keys for model logs. Note: some telemetry is still required for service health but we can scope retention.
02:32 Priya: Do you have a short checklist for what network ports or IP allowlists we'll need? Our security team will want to onboard them.
02:40 Maya: Absolutely — we'll send the network runbook. For quickstarts, most customers start with API keys and no special networking. If you move to VPC we'll provide CIDR ranges and peering steps.
02:52 Aaron: Regarding credits: what's the typical PLG credit package? We want 30 days to try real traffic.
02:59 Maya: We can issue a 30-day credits bundle sized to roughly 500k tokens of high-usage testing, or pick a custom amount. That'll let you prototype and run baseline tests without billing friction.
03:12 Lina: That sounds good. We want to run a synthetic scenario that mimics our peak bursts — can you help with load testing?
03:19 Owen: Yes, we can run a baseline throughput test with your prompt set, measure p50/p90, and recommend batching/caching and model choices. We'll need your representative prompt set — ideally 50-100 samples covering short and long contexts.
03:32 Aaron: I'll put together prompts — we have both retrieval-augmented generation flows and short Q/A.
03:38 Maya: Perfect. For the hosted quickstart path the usual playbook is: sign up with PLG credits, integrate with API key and SDK (we'll share examples), run simple calls to confirm tokenization and costs, then a Redwood SE-run baseline test, then a two-week pilot.
03:56 Priya: How fast can we get to first token — I mean from sign-up to an authenticated api call? In practice.
04:03 Owen: Most teams hit first token in under an hour if they're using a Postman or curl example and have their app ready. From zero to integrated in 1–2 business days for a minimal prototype. If you need VPC or SSO that adds time — usually a week to provision and test SSO, and 2–4 weeks for Private on-prem engagements.
04:25 Lina: If we do a hosted pilot and see latency >200ms, what's the escalation? Do you do model fallbacks automatically?
04:33 Owen: We have routing policies — you can configure fallbacks to a smaller/quantized model or to a dedicated pool. For customers on Dedicated we can reserve GPUs to meet latency. For hosted we'll propose model variants and batching tweaks first — often cheaper than jumping to dedicated.
04:49 Aaron: Any good rules of thumb for cost vs latency tradeoffs? We want to avoid overpaying for low-latency when we don't need it.
04:56 Owen: Sure — short: if p50 under SLO possible with batching and prefix KV caching, stay hosted. If you need strict <100ms p50 at peak, Dedicated is usually better since you get reserved capacity. Also quantization (8-bit) can reduce cost by 30–60% depending on model with modest quality tradeoffs. We'll provide quality regression results tied to your eval prompts.
05:20 Maya: One more practical: onboarding SDKs — do you prefer Python or Node?
05:24 Aaron: Python first, Node later.
05:26 Owen: We'll share our quickstart repo and a Python snippet that plugs into your stack. It has key rotation examples and streaming.
05:35 Speaker 1: Quick question — what about rate limits for PLG credits? We might spike during tests.
05:40 Maya: PLG accounts have default rate limits but we can temporarily raise them for benchmark windows. We'll coordinate with you.
05:47 Lina: Great. Any legal or procurement blockers we should be aware of before pilot?
05:52 Maya: For hosted pilots, standard terms apply. If you need DPA or data residency clauses, we can pre-share our legal pack. For Private deployments, procurement talks are typically 4–8 weeks.
06:05 Aaron: Sounds fine. Can we get a demo of the Console? Even a quick tour of model catalog, billing, and observability?
06:12 Maya: Sure, Owen can screen share after this but we'll also send a short recorded tour.
06:18 Owen: Quick note — observability exposes per-route token counts, latency histograms, and cost breakdown by prompt. That helps tune batching and model selection.
06:28 Priya: If we move to Dedicated, how does autoscaling work? We have variable traffic and don't want to pay for idle GPUs.
06:36 Owen: Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling and burst capacity. You reserve a baseline and configure burst to handle spikes; billing reflects reserved vs burst usage. We also have recommended autoscale policies to hit your SLOs while minimizing idle spend.
06:50 Lina: Okay, let's recap next steps then.
06:53 Maya: Recap: Redwood to send PLG credit link and onboard instructions, Owen to share benchmark spreadsheet and quickstart repo, Olivegrove to provide 50–100 prompt samples and acceptance criteria. Start a 2-week hosted pilot once credits applied.
07:08 Aaron: We'll aim to share prompts by Tuesday and Lina will confirm success metrics.
07:12 Priya: I'll pull network folks in if we need allowlist details.
07:15 Maya: Perfect. Any final questions?
07:18 Lina: No, this is helpful. Thanks.
07:20 Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials and a calendar invite for the baseline test.
07:25 (call ends)

Notes about transcript quality: automated transcript had a few mislabels and some dropped punctuation — verified to "medium" quality.

Attachments referenced: console-demo-recording-link, hosted-credits-signup-link, security-runbook-pdf, benchmarking-spreadsheet-link

End of transcript.

title: Guidance: per-call idempotency token strategy across Python/TS/Go SDKs to avoid orphaned function executions during multi-region failover
text:
Issue summary:\nCustomer reports duplicate external webhook invocations and orphaned downstream jobs when their orchestrator retries streaming function calls during a regional failover. They are using a mix of SDKs (Python backend, TS edge lambda, Go worker) with a serverless orchestrator that reconnects streams and issues retries. The customer is asking for recommended best-practices and a concrete implementation pattern for idempotency tokens that works across SDKs and survives reconnects, routing failover, and retry/backoff policies.\n\nImpact:\n- Observed duplicate side-effects in production (charged by external partner and causing duplicated analytics records).\n- Intermittent during regional failover and reconnection (approx 1-2% of requests during failover windows).\n- Blocks full confidence in enabling auto-retry on orchestrator.\n\nWhat the customer has implemented so far:\n- SDK versions: python-sdk@0.12.1, typescript-sdk@0.9.3, go-sdk@0.7.0.\n- Orchestrator holds ephemeral session IDs for streaming connections and issues retries on disconnect.\n- Function calls include an \"idempotency_key\" header on the client side; the orchestrator sometimes re-writes or re-encodes headers when proxying between regions.\n- External webhook consumer requires a global dedupe key that they persist for 24h.\n\nCustomer asks:\n1) What exact scope should the idempotency token have (session-scoped vs per-call)?\n2) Where should the canonical dedupe key be generated and stored to guarantee at-most-once external side-effects across SDKs and regions?\n3) Any SDK-level helpers or recommended header normalization rules to avoid token corruption during routing?

1) Customer runs a streaming chat completion that uses a function/tool call to post to an external webhook.
2) During streaming, orchestrator triggers a reconnect (simulate network blip or force region failover).
3) Orchestrator retries the last chunk/frame and resends the function invocation without preserving the original canonical dedupe token in a predictable header slot.
4) External webhook receives two distinct dedupe keys (or a missing token) and treats both as separate invocations.
5) Observe duplicate downstream job creation in partner system.

Hypothesis 1: Orchestrator session-scoped IDs are insufficient because reconnect can produce a new session and the temp id placed in a non-canonical header gets lost or rewritten.
Hypothesis 2: Proxy/header normalization during multi-region routing strips or renames the canonical header; SDKs use different header names across language implementations (X-Idempotency vs X-Idempotency-Canonical vs Idempotency-Key).
Observed: python-sdk currently sets 'X-Idempotency-Canonical' when caller supplies canonical_key, but TS SDK sets 'X-Idempotency' and Go SDK sets 'Id-Key' in older versions. This mismatch explains many duplicate paths.
Partial reproduction: engineer simulated a proxy rule that dropped custom headers and reproduced duplicate webhook firing in a test harness.

Priya Patel (Customer): 'We want a pattern that we can implement quickly without changing external webhook API. Can Redwood suggest a canonical header and a fallback header normalization strategy?'
Ethan Zhao (Support): 'Thanks — we'll propose a per-call canonical dedupe token that is generated at the caller (or orchestrator entry) and persisted in the orchestrator's retry-state. We need to validate SDK header names across languages.'
Maya Johnson (SRE): 'Quick mitigation: add a routing policy to preserve X-Idempotency-Canonical and set proxy rules to copy old headers to new canonical header name. Also instrument the proxy to log header drops.'
Luis Martinez (Engineer): 'Action: add cross-SDK unit test that asserts the canonical header name is present during reconnects and build helper to canonicalize incoming tokens to X-Idempotency-Canonical.'

1) Adopt a per-request (per-function-invocation) canonical idempotency token that is generated at the service entry point (edge/orchestrator) and stored in the orchestrator retry-state rather than session ID.
2) Standardize canonical header name: 'X-Idempotency-Canonical'. Update SDKs to set this header in addition to any SDK-local header names for backward compatibility.
3) Orchestrator must persist the canonical key in durable retry metadata so that reconnects/retries reuse the exact token when re-sending function calls across regions.
4) Introduce proxy rules to copy known legacy header names into X-Idempotency-Canonical before forwarding to downstreams (copy X-Idempotency -> X-Idempotency-Canonical, Id-Key -> X-Idempotency-Canonical).
5) Add SDK helpers: generate_dedupe_key(), attach_canonical_header(req), and a middleware that normalizes header names on incoming retransmitted frames.
6) Instrument and add logs to detect header drops (alert if any request in failover window lacks X-Idempotency-Canonical).

Support provided prescriptive pattern: per-request canonical dedupe token generated on orchestrator entry (durably stored in retry-state) and standardized header X-Idempotency-Canonical. Created follow-ups: SDK changes in python/ts/go to set canonical header (github PRs referenced), proxy rule updates, and a runbook for customers enabling safe auto-retry during region failover. Customer accepted mitigation to add proxy copy rules; they will roll out SDK patch next week.

1) ENG: open PRs to add header normalization helpers in all SDKs (linked PR placeholders provided).
2) OPS: add temporary proxy rule to copy legacy idemp headers -> X-Idempotency-Canonical in eu-west and us-east reverse proxies.
3) CS: schedule a 45min call with Acme Analytics to walk through implementation and validate in their staging environment.
4) Close ticket after customer confirms no duplicates in next failover window.

title: Sequential commitment allocator with throttle-frontier and windowed backfill delegator
author: Marina Lopez
text:
Motivation: customers running long-lived Dedicated fleets observed intermittent SLA blips during correlated tenant surges where competing reservation reconciliations and backfills interleaved, causing transient queue amplification and unfair burst consumption. This PR introduces a sequential commitment allocator coupled with a throttle-frontier mechanism and a windowed backfill delegator to provide deterministic per-tenant sequencing, bounded inter-tenant preemption, and safer opportunistic backfill. Summary of changes: 1) allocation/sequencer: introduce a lightweight sequencer that assigns monotonic commitment tokens per tenant request batch to preserve FIFO across reservation reconciliation cycles; tokens are compact 64-bit ids and allow fast in-memory range checks. 2) throttle-frontier: a frontier tracker per pool that exposes an upper commit watermark and a soft throttle signal; when frontier pressure breaches a tunable threshold we apply graded token-holdbacks instead of blunt rejection to preserve throughput while protecting tight SLA tenants. 3) windowed backfill delegator: replaces the previous eager backfill with short time-windowed delegations that prefer local warm pools and decay based on recent eviction churn; this reduces noisy preemption across pools. 4) telemetry & reporting: new per-tenant sequence-lag histogram, frontier-pressure gauge, and backfill-delegation counters; TTLs and tags added for export to observability. 5) rollout: feature gated under runtime flag "sequential-commitments-v1" and default-disabled for Dedicated customers; rollout plan includes canary on 2 dev clusters then staged ramp. Checklist: [x] unit tests for sequencer and frontier logic [x] e2e replay test against synthetic surge traces [x] perf benchmark (steady-state) shows <3% median latency overhead, 15% reduction in tail SLA breaches during burst tests [x] telemetry wired to Console dashboards [x] regression windows and rollback plan documented Design notes: sequencer is intentionally single-writer per-pool to avoid cross-pool coordination; we rely on epoched persistence for graceful restarts. Throttle-frontier uses leaky-bucket style smoothing with two configurable thresholds (warning/critical) and exposes a fast path that avoids allocation stalls for tenants below their committed watermark. Backfill delegator maintains a per-tenant backfill score that decays exponentially and factors in eviction rate to avoid oscillation. Rollback plan: gate off feature flag and revert a single reconciler switch; state is ephemeral so rollback is low-risk. Testing: synthetic surge harness, integration with autoscaler suite, and a dedicated dedicated-fleet-canary in perf-lab. Related: references ENG-2147 for the original incident and ENG-2301 for backlog prioritization. This description intentionally condensed design rationale and the PR includes inline comments for more detail.

Ethan Cole: This overall direction looks solid. Two concerns: sequencer single-writer per-pool could be a hot-spot under extreme control-plane churn; can we prove there's no contention hotspot?
Marina Lopez: We added a sequencer sharding knob and a benchmark that shows <1% CPU increase in worst-case per-pool hot path. Added comment in sequencer.go explaining our single-writer choice and how shard count can be increased at runtime.
Priya Natarajan: Telemetry looks good; please ensure tags include tenant_id, pool_id and commit_epoch for indexing. Also suggest an alert when frontier_pressure>0.9 for 2m.
Marina Lopez: Added tags and an alert proposal in docs/operational/deploy-ramp.md. Adjusted metric cardinality by sampling low-cardinality tenants in high-volume pools.
Samir Patel: Windowed backfill seems safer but I'd like to see how it interacts with the autoscaler reclaim loop; could backfill starvation cause wasted GPU time?
Marina Lopez: The delegator now exposes a backfill-priority floor that autoscaler consults; default floor is 10% which we tuned in perf runs. Documented interaction and added unit test for prioritizer coupling.

Adds a sequential commitment sequencer, throttle-frontier to reduce inter-tenant interference during surges, and a windowed backfill delegator which reduces eviction churn across warm pools. Opt-in via feature flag. Improves burst fairness and reduces tail SLA breaches in surge tests.

Perf lab results: synthetic 10x surge trace reduced 99th percentile token latency by ~18% for reserved tenants while opportunistic backfill throughput retained ~92% of previous levels. Canary rollout completed on 2 clusters without incidents. Flag default remains off for GA.

title: SLO Entropy Scan and Capacity Annealing Playbook (2026)
author: Evelyn Chen
text:
Summary:

This playbook defines the SLO Entropy Scan and Capacity Annealing processes used by SRE to detect latent SLO fragility, proactively rebalance capacity, and reduce unexpected error-budget burn. It combines a periodic 'entropy' analysis of SLO signal instability with an automated annealing workflow that simulates controlled load, validates fallbacks, and adjusts capacity / throttles.

Scope:

- Applies to Redwood public inference endpoints and multi-tenant Dedicated clusters.
- Intended for services with hard latency SLOs (p99 latency, request success rate) and token-based billing impact.
- Not a replacement for incident runbooks; this playbook is a proactive reliability initiative with an associated drill cadence.

Why an entropy-driven approach?

SLOs can be stable on average while hiding discontinuous failure modes caused by workload shifts, model rollouts, or quantization changes. Entropy = an operational metric of SLO signal volatility across dimensions (latency, error-rate, tail token count). High entropy predicts future SLO regression and enables targeted capacity annealing before significant error-budget consumption.

Definitions:

- Entropy Scan: a periodic analytics job that measures day-over-day and week-over-week volatility in SLO telemetry across tenants and routes.
- Capacity Annealing: a controlled procedure to rehearse degraded states and then 'cool' the system via capacity reconfiguration or traffic shaping to return to steady-state with validated mitigations.
- SLO shard: a logical subset of traffic (route/model/tenant) that is tracked as a distinct SLO.

Roles & Responsibility:

- SRE (owner): run scans, approve annealing windows, execute automated anneal jobs, and verify post-runbook KPIs. Owner: eng-sre/team-alpha.
- Runtime Team: implement and validate fallbacks, KV/prefix cache warming, and model variant routing.
- Product/Model Onboarding: provide expected token distributions and rollout plans for new models.
- Oncall: respond to high-severity alerts triggered during annealing drills.

SLO Design Matrix (example):

| SLO Dimension | Metric | Target | Window | Entropy Threshold (alert) | Owner |
|--------------|--------|--------|--------|---------------------------|-------|
| Latency (P99) | request_latency_ms | 250ms | 30d rolling | 3x baseline MAD across 7d | runtime-team |
| Success Rate | success_rate | 99.5% | 30d rolling | >0.5% step-change week-over-week | eng-sre |
| Embedding Freshness | embedding_recompute_ratio | 95% | 14d | >6% variance | infra |
(NOTE: replace example values per-service in the SLO registry.)

Error Budget Policy (condensed):

1) Error budget windows are 30 days by default unless contractual SLAs require otherwise.
2) If a 7-day projected burn-rate > 5x baseline, schedule a mandatory annealing window within 72 hours.
3) If an emergency incident consumes >50% of the remaining budget in <24 hours, raise a P1 and engage product + runtime for rollback.

Entropy Scan Procedure (weekly automated job):

1) Data sources: SLO metrics from metrics-store (prometheus-aggregation), token-level traces from token-evidence pipeline, and model-serving traces (kv-hit/miss rates).
2) Compute per-route entropy: for each shard compute coefficient-of-variation and median absolute deviation (MAD) over 7d and 30d windows and aggregate into an entropy score.

CLI / example queries:

- PromQL (latency volatility):
 - quantile_over_time(0.99, request_latency_ms[7d])
 - stddev_over_time( request_latency_ms[7d] ) / avg_over_time(request_latency_ms[7d])

- Token evidence sampling (SQL):
 - SELECT model, route, COUNT(*) AS tokens, PERCENTILE_CONT(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) FROM token_evidence WHERE ts >= now() - interval '7 days' GROUP BY model, route;

3) Output: CSV with columns {shard, entropy_score, recent_burn_rate, kv_miss_rate, top-ten error messages}. Upload to reliability-dashboard and notify #sre-ops when any shard crosses entropy threshold.

Capacity Annealing Workflow (high level):

Purpose: validate graceful degradation and tune capacity allocation before an incident.

Preconditions:
- Anneal windows are scheduled during low traffic (per-customer blackout windows respected).
- At least one oncall and one runtime engineer are present and reachable.
- Backout plan defined in the runbook (rollback commands / config flags).

Steps (sequence):
1) Authorization: SRE lead approves the anneal job in the reliability dashboard.
2) Canary baseline: capture live baseline traces (10 minutes) and snapshot per-shard SLO metrics.
3) Controlled perturbation: incrementally increase synthetic load or selectively disable cache layers per the anneal plan. Perturbation steps are staged (10%, 25%, 50%, 75% of the targeted stress) with a 5–10 minute observation window between steps.
4) Fallback validation: at each stage verify fallbacks trigger as designed (model-variant routing, quantized fallback, prefix cache warm). Record exact artifact ids and KV-cache heatmaps.
5) Anneal decision gate: if p99 latency rises above 2x SLO or success_rate drops below 90% for >3 minutes, pause and execute immediate cooldown (traffic cutback + template rollback).
6) Cooldown & reconfiguration: apply capacity increases, re-route low-priority tenants, or enable rate-limiting profiles.
7) Post-anneal validation: run smoke canaries and synthetic queries for 15 minutes, then publish anneal report.

Automated commands (examples):

- Start anneal job: curl -X POST https://reliability.redwood.internal/api/v1/anneal -d '{"shard":"nlp-gen-prod", "Plan":"cache-disable-stage"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer ${SRE_TOKEN}'
- Emergency rollback: rctl apply -f rollback-template.yaml --target shards=nlp-gen-prod

Incident Decomposition & Evidence Packaging Standard:

When entropy scan or anneal uncovers a regression requiring incident review, follow these standards for evidence packaging:

Required artifacts (packaged as a single .tar.gz):
- timeline.json (ordered events with UTC timestamps)
- metrics-snapshot.csv (30d baseline + 72h surrounding window)
- token-evidence-sample.json (50 representative tokens with redacted customer ids)
- anneal-runbook-log.txt (if anneal executed)
- tracer-level traces (.zip) for affected services
- configuration snapshot: routing.yaml, autoscaler-state.json

Evidence labeling rules:
- Timestamps must be ISO8601 UTC.
- Customer-identifying fields must be hashed or removed.
- Each artifact must include an "ingested_by" header with SRE run-id.

Operational Tooling & Integrations:

- Reliability Dashboard: reliability.redwood.internal (SRE-owned) displays entropy heatmap, anneal schedule, and per-shard SLOs.
- Alerts:
 - ALERT_SLO_ENTROPY_HIGH (pagerduty) — severity P2, threshold: entropy_score > 0.8 AND projected burn > 3x.
 - ALERT_ANNEAL_FAILURE (slack + p1 pagerduty) — fired when automated anneal step fails to validate fallback.
- ChatOps: /run anneal <shard> starts a preflight check; approved runs post updates to #sre-anneals.
- Telemetry: token_evidence pipeline stores samples in evidence-store (S3), indexed by run-id.

Drill Cadence & Governance:

- Weekly entropy scans run automatically.
- Monthly annealing drills: rotate through top-10 high-risk shards (based on entropy + business criticality).
- Quarterly tabletop with product, model-onboarding, and runtime to review anneal reports and update SLOs.

KPIs & Success Criteria:

- Reduction in 30-day unplanned error-budget burns by 30% within 3 months of adopting annealing.
- Mean-time-to-detect for SLO regressions improved to <30 minutes for shards with entropy alerts.
- 90% of annealing drills complete without triggering emergency rollback.

Runbook Template (text):

- Title:
- Shard name:
- Owner(s):
- Precondition checklist: (1) schedule, (2) oncall notified, (3) rollback ready
- Perturbation plan: (staging steps, durations)
- Metrics to capture: (p99, p90, success_rate, kv_miss_rate)
- Stop criteria: (explicit thresholds)
- Rollback steps: (ordered commands)
- Post-run validation: (smoke queries, traces)

Threshold table (recommended defaults):

| Signal | Warn threshold | Stop threshold | Action |
|--------|----------------|----------------|--------|
| Entropy score | 0.6 | 0.8 | schedule anneal / immediate alert |
| p99 latency uplift | 1.5x baseline | 2.0x baseline | pause anneal, rollback |
| success_rate drop | 0.5% absolute | 2% absolute | traffic cutback, emergency rollback |
Post-Run Report (deliverable):

- executive summary (1 paragraph)
- timeline of events (minute resolution)
- artifacts attached (list of packaged files)
- conclusions and recommended next steps (config changes, SLO tuning, model rollback)
- owners and follow-ups with target dates

Playbook Examples (short):

Example A — High entropy on route /v1/generate:
1) Entropy scan flags /v1/generate with entropy_score=0.72 and projected burn-rate=4x.
2) SRE schedules anneal in 48 hours, notifies product and customer success.
3) Anneal executes with cache-disable stage; fallback to quantized flow validated at 25% perturbation; at 50% perturbation p99 crosses stop threshold, anneal paused and cooldown applied.
4) Post-run: increase cache warmup, add 5% reserved capacity to shard, update SLO runbook.

Example B — Rapid burst causing token-level errors:
1) Token evidence shows top error 'kv-miss-timeout' correlated with a model rollout.
2) Immediate short-term mitigation: enable per-token throttling profile and route new model traffic to dedicated pool.
3) Longer-term: update onboarding checklist to include pre-warm KV caches and an anneal rehearsal before rollout.

Checklist before closing an anneal-related incident review:
- [ ] Evidence package uploaded and validated
- [ ] Post-anneal smoke tests passed 15m after cooldown
- [ ] Action items assigned with owners and due dates
- [ ] SLO registry updated if target changes required

References & related pages:

- SLO registry (internal): /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/slo-attribute-matrix-and-capacity-mapping-manual-2025
- Anneal scheduler API docs: reliability.redwood.internal/api/docs/anneal
- Token evidence pipeline: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/token-evidence-sampling-and-slo-assertion-runbook-2026

Revision history:
- 2026-01-20: created by Evelyn Chen
- 2026-02-12: added CLI examples and evidence packaging rules (review: Amir Khatri)
- 2026-03-01: clarified anneal stop criteria and KPI targets (review: Maya Alvarez)

title: Policy presets and sampling rules for prompts, responses, request logs, and metrics
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Problem: Customers need simple, auditable controls to set how long prompts, model responses, request logs, and aggregated metrics are retained across hosted, dedicated and private deployments. Current retention UX is too coarse (per-tenant or all-or-nothing), and engineering teams rely on ad-hoc scripts for sampled exports and evidence bundling.

Goals: Provide a product-first solution with: 1) a small set of policy presets (Default, Short-lived, PII-minimal, Audit-grade) that teams can apply per-route or per-model; 2) fine-grained sampling rules (percentage, deterministic hashing by user_id/session_id, stratified sampling by route or model) for large-volume traces and metrics; 3) region-aware residency pinning for retention and export; 4) automated evidence bundle generation for audits (signed manifest + hash-chained files) triggered by policy or manual request; 5) API and Console UI for authoring and previewing effective retention for routes and sample sets.

Scope: Console UI (policy presets editor, route selector, preview simulator), public API for retention profiles, sampling engine in the request pipeline, evidence bundler service, migration helpers (preview tool to estimate storage change), integration points with RBAC and KMS for export signing.

Out of scope: Per-prompt semantic classification (PII detection model), long-term archival formats beyond the initial signed bundle, legal counsel sign-off for policy language (we produce artifacts for compliance teams).

Deliverables: UI mockups + interactive preview, API spec, backend sampling implementation with deterministic hashing, evidence bundler lambda/service, migration script and a Canary rollout plan with telemetry and SLO guardrails.

Policy presets available in Console and via API and can be attached per-route or per-model
Sampling engine supports at least three modes: deterministic (hash key), percentage random, and route-stratified sampling
Preview simulator shows estimated retention volume and sample composition before applying a profile
Evidence bundle exports are produced as a signed zip with manifest, checksums, and an audit log entry
Regional residency setting enforces export and storage location decisions and surfaces conflicts in the UI
Migration preview provides estimate of storage delta and recommended sample rates to stay within budget

2026-03-10 Aisha Patel: Drafted ticket after tenant compliance calls; observed 3 customers asking for per-route retention presets.
2026-03-11 Luca Morgan: Added sampling modes and evidence bundle requirement based on ENG feedback; requested a technical spike to validate deterministic hashing cost impact.
2026-03-12 Priya Desai (Eng): Spike results attached — deterministic hashing adds negligible latency (p50 +2ms) but increases KV-index storage; we recommend an indexed keyspace and optional batching for high-throughput routes.
2026-03-13 Elena Rodriguez (Design): Uploaded initial wireframes: policy preset picker + route-level preview. Feedback: make conflict resolution explicit when tenancy-level retention is stricter.
2026-03-14 Product review: prioritized P1; schedule for Cycle 2026-W11. Next: 2-week implementation sprint with eng and design alignment meeting on 2026-03-16. Links to artifacts below.

Trade-offs: Default presets reduce cognitive load but may not cover edge regulatory regimes; allow advanced JSON policy authoring for enterprise tenants.
Storage budgeting: recommend providing customers an estimated monthly cost delta in the preview simulator and an automated sample-rate suggestion to hit their target S3/GCS spend.
Security: evidence bundles must be signed with tenant KMS when available; fall back to platform signing with audit flagging when KMS not present.

title: Runbook: Deploying Hosted API Services to Production
author: Evelyn Hart
text:
h1. Overview
This runbook describes how to deploy Hosted API services (router, inference-gateway, streaming-gateway, embeddings) to production. Follow this in conjunction with the Production Change Management Standard and Prod Deployment Gates.

h1. Ownership
* Primary owner: Eng Platform
* On-call escalation: #eng-oncall and #eng-platform

h1. Preconditions
Before you begin, confirm the following are true:
1. A change record exists and includes summary, risk assessment, verification plan, and rollback plan.
2. Approvals are captured (peer + service owner; add SRE/security as required).
3. CI is green; image digests are pinned (no "latest" tags).
4. You have access to the deployment toolchain and production kube contexts.

h1. Identify the target
* Service(s): router / inference-gateway / streaming-gateway / embeddings
* Region(s): us-east-1, us-west-2, eu-central-1 (deploy canary first)
* Deployment mode: canary then full

h1. Step-by-step procedure
1. Announce intent (internal)
 * Post in #eng-releases with: change record link, services, canary region, start time, rollback trigger.

2. Pre-deploy checks
 * Check current error rates and p95 latency dashboards for the target services.
 * Confirm no active incidents affecting the same services.
 * Confirm error budget posture allows change (see Change Freeze and Risk Assessment).

3. Canary deploy
 * Deploy to canary region (default us-west-2) or 1% traffic slice if supported.
 * Commands (example):
 - "deployctl promote --service inference-gateway --env prod --region us-west-2 --image-digest sha256:..."
 - "deployctl status --service inference-gateway --env prod --region us-west-2"
 * Wait until rollout completes and pods are ready.

4. Canary validation (15 minutes minimum)
 * Run smoke tests:
 - /v1/chat/completions (streaming + non-streaming)
 - /v1/embeddings
 * Validate: error rate, p95 latency, saturation signals, and request timeouts.
 * If metering changed, validate token counts on test account in canary region.

5. Full rollout
 * If canary passes criteria, deploy remaining regions in order: us-east-1 -> eu-central-1.
 * Deploy one region at a time; do not run concurrent region rollouts for router + gateway changes unless explicitly approved.

6. Post-deploy validation (60 minutes)
 * Confirm global dashboards are stable.
 * Confirm no new alerts firing (or document expected alerts and resolution).
 * Confirm logs/traces are visible for the new build.

7. Closeout
 * Update the change record with: canary results, rollout times, dashboard links, and final build identifiers.

h1. Rollback triggers
Rollback immediately if any occur during canary or full rollout:
* Error rate increases by \u003e 0.2% absolute sustained for 5 minutes
* p95 latency increases by \u003e 10% sustained for 10 minutes
* Elevated timeouts or queue depth indicates saturation
* Customer-reported incident plausibly tied to the change

h1. Rollback (quick path)
* Use the previous known-good image digest and redeploy to the impacted region(s).
* If the router policy config changed, revert the config bundle first.
* Follow the dedicated Rollback and Post-change Validation runbook for full steps and post-rollback monitoring.

h1. Notes and tips
* Prefer deploying router changes separately from inference-gateway changes to reduce blast radius.
* If deploying a schema migration, verify backward-compatibility by running mixed-version canary for at least 30 minutes.

h1. References
* Prod Deployment Gates: Hosted API and Console
* Rollback and Post-change Validation
* Planned Maintenance and Change Communications
* Production Change Management Standard (v2)

title: Penumbra adoption, SLA & cost alignment sync
author: Alex Chen
text:
Weekly health/check-in focused on adoption pacing, options to reduce per-token cost via Dedicated and caching, SLA questions for production cutover, and pilot next steps. SE provided configuration-level suggestions and agreed to run a short latency/cost benchmark. Procurement asked about invoicing, SOC2 and KMS options.

Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-02
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Sharma (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood CSM), Maya Lopez (Penumbra Head of ML), Tom Richardson (Platform Engineer), Aisha Khan (Procurement), Luis Ortega (SRE)

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for carving out time today, um we'll run through where adoption is, cost mechanics and SLA questions, and Priya will do a quick tech read. Maya, do you want to kick off with a quick status?

[00:18] Maya (Penumbra): Sure yeah. So, we've rolled out the recommendation feature to 10% of web traffic, that's been for two weeks, we saw a small bump in conversion which is good. The tricky part is latency on the longer context sessions — some requests hit 800ms to 1.2s and that is, uh, above our target. We're also seeing cost in line with our projection but spikes on peak hours.

[00:40] Tom (Penumbra): To add, our infra team saw that KV cache hit rates vary a lot per user session, we have very bursty tails during promos. We're trying to understand whether batching or locking to Dedicated capacity helps more vs improving cache dimensions.

[01:05] Priya (Redwood SE): Yeah, okay. So quick context — Redwood Dedicated (sometimes folks shorthand as Redwood Dedictated in notes) gives you reserved GPU pools which can flatten p99 and give consistent throughput. There's also config knobs on the KV cache and batching window we can tune; for many e-comms workloads increasing prefix caching and smaller batching windows during bursts keeps tail latency down without blowing up token cost.

[01:38] Luis (SRE): Quick question on private network: we can't expose traffic over public internet for PII-enriched requests. VPC peering is a must, and we're also evaluating an on-prem package for the most sensitive flows. What are the options?

[01:52] Alex (Redwood AE): Right. We offer Redwood Private with VPC peering and on-prem options. For the VPC route we provide a customer-controlled control plane and support KMS integrations. Jordan will follow up on the HLD templates.

[02:10] Jordan (Redwood CSM): Yep I'll share the baseline architecture diagram and a checklist.

[02:25] Aisha (Procurement): From billing perspective we need monthly invoicing and clarity on committed spend vs overage billing. Also SOC 2 Type II evidence and, um, do we have ISO stuff?

[02:40] Alex (Redwood AE): We do provide SOC2 docs; ISO is in process, I think we can share current attestations and the compliance pack. On billing, we have reserved capacity contracts that can be monthly or annual — I'll send options.

[03:02] Priya (Redwood SE): Back to latency — a few concrete things: 1) For your 20–30 token latency-critical responses use a pinned, smaller model variant with quantization; 2) Use prefix KV caching aggressively for user-session prompts; 3) set autoscaling buffer on Dedicated to handle promo bursts. We'll provide example config.

[03:35] Maya (Penumbra): We tried a quantized variant yesterday, results were OK but quality dip on named-entity disambiguation. How much risk is there with quantization?

[03:50] Priya (Redwood SE): There is some quality delta; our Optimize tooling suggests per-workload quant profiles and we can A/B test with canary rollouts. You should hold back critical NER flows for full-precision until we have pass rates on your eval set.

[04:17] Tom (Penumbra): On the economics, our finance team flagged that switching to Dedicated will lower per-token unit cost for steady traffic, but there's an up-front commit. Can you walk numbers vs hosted?

[04:31] Alex (Redwood AE): Sure — topline: hosted is pure variable (pay for tokens), Dedicated is committed with predictable monthly cost and lower per-token CPU/GPU amortized. We'll model a 90-day pilot -- show delta for 6/12 month commit. I'll include a simple spreadsheet.

[04:56] Aisha (Procurement): Are there minimums? Also what about termination terms?

[05:05] Alex (Redwood AE): Minimums depend on the Reserved tier; I'll include the standard MSAs and early-termination language. We can be flexible for pilots.

[05:20] [05:20] Priya (Redwood SE): Quick sidebar — for your API patterns, we noticed a lot of repeated context across calls; prefix caching could recover 20–35% token cost on some endpoints. But it's workload dependent; we need token-level traces.

[05:40] Luis (SRE): We can share traces, but some are redacted for PII. We'll produce synthetic traces that mimic the distribution.

[05:55] Maya (Penumbra): Regarding SLA — what's the realistic uptime guarantee? We need 99.9 for the feature to be considered production critical.

[06:10] Alex (Redwood AE): For Dedicated and Private we offer SLA backstops aligned with 99.9 and above depending on tier. For hosted the SLA is lower. We will share the exact SLA table and the error credits policy.

[06:30] Tom (Penumbra): How do we monitor latency across our routes? Can we integrate with our Datadog?

[06:40] Priya (Redwood SE): Yes Redwood Console (sometimes transcribed as Redwood Consol) exposes per-route token cost and latency metrics and we have tracing hooks that forward spans to existing APMs — Datadog, NewRelic. We'll share the integration docs.

[07:05] Maya (Penumbra): On rollout strategies, we want automatic fallback to a smaller model on degraded infra rather than failing requests. Does Redwood support that?

[07:18] Priya (Redwood SE): Yes — smart routing supports policy-based fallback; you can say route to cheaper/compatible variant on overload. There's also canary and A/B rollouts in the Console.

[07:35] Aisha (Procurement): For contract signoff we need contact at Redwood legal — who's assigned?

[07:45] Alex (Redwood AE): I'll loop in our legal lead and your procurement. I'll cc them in the follow-up.

[08:00] [08:00] Priya (Redwood SE): I want to propose a short technical pilot: 2-week benchmark where we run your most common traffic pattern against Hosted, then against Dedicated with KV cache tuned and a quantized model variant. We'll measure TP95, average cost per request, and quality regressions on your eval prompts.

[08:28] Maya (Penumbra): That sounds reasonable. What's the time/cost to run the benchmark?

[08:35] Priya (Redwood SE): For the benchmark itself Redwood can run it; cost will be minimal and we can absorb as part of onboarding for customers heading toward Dedicated. If we need large GPU burn for synthetic load we might ask for a short allowance but normally it's covered.

[09:00] Tom (Penumbra): Two more technical constraints: 1) We have strict egress limits for tokens that go outside our VPC, 2) We need audit logs with per-token metadata for compliance. Can Redwood provide that?

[09:14] Alex (Redwood AE): Audit logs are part of Private deployments and we can surface per-request meta for compliance; we can discuss retention windows. For egress we'll need to scope which flows remain in VPC vs hosted.

[09:30] Maya (Penumbra): On quantization A/B tests, can you run NER-specific tests? That's the main quality gate for us.

[09:42] Priya (Redwood SE): Yes, please send a small eval set focusing on entity disambiguation; we'll run the test and share quality metrics. Keep in mind model variant differences — sometimes smaller quantized variants can be tuned with temperature/penalty to minimize failures.

[10:05] Luis (SRE): A note on networking — if we go VPC peering, how do you handle route failover across regions? Our users are global and we want regional fallbacks.

[10:20] Jordan (Redwood CSM): We can set routing policies by region, and for Dedicated we can provision capacity in multiple regions and have automatic fallback rules. We'll map out options in the HLD.

[10:40] Alex (Redwood AE): Ok let's go through initial timeline and responsibilities. Pilot: scope by next week, run 2-week benchmarking the week after, and then review results and decide commit level.

[11:00] Maya (Penumbra): That timeline works for us, pending procurement review of terms.

[11:15] Aisha (Procurement): We'll need sample invoices and the early termination examples. Also, are there pass-through cloud costs?

[11:27] Alex (Redwood AE): There can be cloud pass-through for certain Private on-prem deployments; for hosted and Dedicated it's baked into the price. I'll itemize those in the pricing sheet.

[11:45] [11:45] Priya (Redwood SE): I'll summarize the recommended config: 1) Dedicated pool with autoscale buffer for promo times, 2) aggressive KV prefix caching and 50–100ms batching window during spikes, 3) quantized smaller variant for non-NER flows; keep high-precision for entity flows with canary tests.

[12:10] Tom (Penumbra): For the KV cache hints, do you support per-customer TTLs? We have sessions that need shorter TTLs for privacy reasons.

[12:22] Priya (Redwood SE): Yes TTLs are configurable per-route; we can set session-based TTL and also redact PII before caching. We'll show sample policies.

[12:40] Maya (Penumbra): Any limitations we should watch for if we move to Dedicated? For example, model upgrades or forced rollouts?

[12:52] Alex (Redwood AE): Model version pinning is supported — you can pin a version to a rollout; upgrades can be scheduled and canaryed. There's no forced model swap without notice; we coordinate major infra upgrades with customers.

[13:12] Luis (SRE): Backup question on KMS — do you support customer-managed keys or only Redwood-managed?

[13:20] Alex (Redwood AE): We support KMS integrations and customer-managed keys for Private deployments and Dedicated depending on contract. We'll clarify in the security pack.

[13:32] Jordan (Redwood CSM): Okay capturing action items. We'll follow up with the architecture HLD, the benchmark plan, the pricing sheet and the compliance pack (SOC2, encryption, ISO notes).

[13:45] Maya (Penumbra): Great. For acceptance criteria — we'll look at TP95 under promo load < 700ms, quality pass rate > 98% on NER eval, and cost per thousand requests reduced by at least 15% versus baseline.

[14:02] Alex (Redwood AE): Noted. We'll aim to deliver the benchmark metrics to match those targets and we'll flag any tradeoffs.

[14:20] Aisha (Procurement): Can we get a draft MSA to review in parallel with the pilot?

[14:30] Alex (Redwood AE): Yes I'll loop legal and share a redline-friendly MSA.

[14:40] Tom (Penumbra): One last thing — competitor question: we've been evaluating ModelServeCo; how do you differentiate on SLO/ops?

[14:50] Priya (Redwood SE): Typical diff is production-first tooling: token-level observability, built-in KV cache, and more flexible deployment modes with predictable economics. We'll put together a short comparison doc.

[15:05] Maya (Penumbra): Ok sounds good. Anything else?

[15:10] Alex (Redwood AE): Quick recap of next steps — I'll send pricing and MSA contacts, Priya will share benchmarks and config notes, Jordan will send the HLD and kickoff calendar. Maya/Tom will supply traces + eval and procurement will review terms.

[15:30] Maya (Penumbra): Thanks everyone.

[15:35] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-transcriptions (e.g., Redwood Dedictated, KV cash) and speaker overlaps.

References shared during call: "Penumbra_pilot_requirements_v1.docx" (attendee link), "redwood-benchmarks-2025-06.csv" (to be shared by Priya), pricing sheet template (to be sent by Alex).

End of transcript.

title: invocation-burst-lens-and-phase-aware-alert-throttler
author: Asha Menon
text:
Motivation: production token/latency tails are often driven by short invocation bursts (fanout or client retry storms) that do not warrant full SRE paging but do distort SLA and cost dashboards. This PR introduces two complementary pieces: 1) Invocation Burst Lens - new metrics + dashboard panels to surface short-lived burst events and their token/latency composition; 2) Phase-Aware Alert Throttler - an alert smoothing layer that debounces alerts based on invocation phase signatures and burst fingerprints. Summary of changes: added lightweight burst detection at the edge (invocation proxy) that emits invocation.burst_start and invocation.burst_member_count, added histogram and slabbed buckets for burst_duration_seconds and burst_token_count, instrumented runtime to tag spans with invocation_phase (init/prefix/stream/complete) and exposed phase-aware latency quantiles (token_phase_latency_p50/p95/p99), added a Grafana dashboard JSON with burst lens panels and an interactive scatter of burst_token_count vs median token_phase_latency, added an alerting rule that delegates to the new throttler which consults recent burst fingerprints and phase distribution before escalating, added unit and integration tests plus a small e2e perf-canary test to exercise controlled burst generation. Checklist: - [x] Add edge emission of burst markers and phase tags - [x] Runtime: phase annotation on spans and metrics emission - [x] Metrics: histograms, gauges, and exemplar wiring - [x] Dashboard: Grafana JSON + README panel descriptions - [x] Alerting: phase-aware throttler service + alert rule examples - [x] Tests: unit, integration, perf-canary - [x] Docs: observability/notes and migration guide Usage notes: burst markers are low-cardinality and sampled; default sampling = 1/1000 invocations, can be increased per-tenant in the console. The throttler runs as a separate small service in the observability stack and uses a fixed-size in-memory LRU of recent burst fingerprints (configurable TTL) to avoid routing transient spikes to on-call. This is a conservative default — teams can opt-out by turning off the throttler in cluster/overrides. Backwards compatibility: all new metrics follow existing naming conventions and are emitted under the telemetry namespace; consumers that don't understand invocation_phase will fall back to aggregate latency metrics. Impact on cost: modest metric cardinality increase under heavy bursty workloads; recommended retention for burst_* metrics is 14 days by default. Rollout plan: staged on canary region -> staging -> global; feature gated behind OBS_BURST_LENS flag and throttler behind OBS_THROTTLER flag. Related: ENG-1987 (burst detection design), ENG-2043 (alerting ergonomics).

Introduces Invocation Burst Lens metrics and a phase-aware alert throttler. New metrics: invocation.burst_count, invocation.burst_member_count, burst_duration_seconds, burst_token_count, token_phase_latency_{p50,p95,p99}. Adds Grafana dashboard 'Invocation Burst Lens' and an optional throttler service to reduce noisy pages during short-lived spikes. Backward-compatible metric names; feature behind OBS_BURST_LENS and OBS_THROTTLER flags.

canary -> staging -> prod over 3 weeks; default flags off in prod until metrics retention and throttler health checks are validated.

Unit tests cover burst detection heuristics and fingerprint LRU eviction; integration tests validate exemplar propagation and histogram buckets; perf-canary runs simulated micro-bursts and asserts that throttler holds on-call for <80% of synthetic bursts while escalating persistent high p99s.

If paging is unexpectedly suppressed after rollout, check throttler logs (/var/log/observability/throttler.log) and circuit-breaker metric observability.throttler.healthy. To force immediate escalation, set OBS_THROTTLER=false in the cluster override and re-evaluate alert rule.

Liam Scott (reviewer): Can we keep burst_id cardinality low? Suggest limiting exemplars to 1/10k for high-volume tenants.
Asha Menon (author): Agreed — default sampling is 1/1000 and exemplars are gated by tenant volume; added config knobs and docs note.
Marina Petrova (reviewer): The throttler introduces additional decision hops in alert path — how do we avoid increased alert latency?
Asha Menon (author): Throttler is intended as a pre-filter for paging decisions and runs synchronously with a 50ms budget; we added a circuit-breaker to fall back to ESCALATE when throttler is unhealthy.
Noah Chen (reviewer): Add a test that produces overlapping bursts and verifies dedup behavior.
Asha Menon (author): Added perf-canary scenario 'overlap-burst.yml' and unit tests for fingerprint LRU behavior.

title: APDEX-Driven Eval Prioritization and Annotation Lifecycle Playbook
author: Derek Huang
text:
Overview

Purpose: Provide a concrete operational playbook that uses an APDEX-inspired scoring signal to prioritize evaluation probes, schedule annotation work, and enforce annotation SLAs aligned to product-level SLOs (latency/quality/cost). This doc defines the metric mapping, prioritization buckets, scheduling architecture, annotation lifecycle, monitoring expectations, and a regression-runbook for APDEX degradations.

Scope: Applies to evaluator pipelines, probe generators, annotation vendors/queues, and the eval-scheduler service used by the Eval Harness. This is intended for mixed workloads (shadow, synthetic, production probes) across Hosted/Dedicated/Private deployments.

Why APDEX for eval ops

- APDEX (Application Performance Index) adapted here gives a single summary score for probe-level utility: combining fidelity, timeliness, and failure rate into a unit we can schedule by.
- Advantages: straightforward thresholds, monotonic prioritization, easy-to-instrument SLAs, and interpretable cost/benefit tradeoffs for annotation spend.

Definitions and signals

- probe_apdex: a normalized score in [0.0, 1.0] representing the evaluator utility of a probe. Higher is better. Computed per-probe and aggregated per-slice.
- fidelity_component: measures semantic alignment with golden answers (0–1). Methods: BLEU/ROUGE where applicable, embedding similarity thresholding for open outputs, and human QA pass rate when available.
- timeliness_component: age and expected relevance score (0–1). Newer user-origin probes get higher score; stale model-output or synthetic probes get lower.
- reliability_component: success rate of deterministic replay + tokenization/format normalization pass (0–1).

probe_apdex = 0.5 * fidelity_component + 0.3 * timeliness_component + 0.2 * reliability_component

(APDEX weights above are default; teams may adjust per workload with approval from Evaluation Infrastructure)

APDEX thresholds and scheduling policy

- Priority buckets (APDEX ranges):
 - P0 (critical): 0.0–0.25 — immediate human review, auto-escalate to regression triage.
 - P1 (high): 0.25–0.5 — fast-path annotation (high-quality crowd or L2 SRE review within 24 hours).
 - P2 (standard): 0.5–0.75 — batched annotation during regular cycles (48–72 hours).
 - P3 (low): 0.75–1.0 — low-cost automated labeling or deferred human review (weekly).

Mapping to evaluator actions:
| APDEX range | Scheduler action | Annotation SLA | Annotation mode | Cost control |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| 0.0–0.25 | immediate queueing to "fast-path" | 4 hours | expert annotator + reviewer | emergency budget flag |
| 0.25–0.5 | priority queue | 24 hours | high-quality crowd | flexible burst credits |
| 0.5–0.75 | standard queue | 48–72 hours | pooled crowd | batched economics |
| 0.75–1.0 | deferred/auto | weekly | automated heuristics / synthetic | minimal spend |

Scheduling architecture and implementation notes

- Eval-scheduler service responsibilities:
 1) Ingest probe metadata and computed probe_apdex.
 2) Assign priority bucket and target SLA window.
 3) Create annotation tasks with required label schema and expected TTL.
 4) Respect tenant and model-level quotas and cost budgets.
 5) Emit metrics to telemetry: eval_scheduler.assigned, eval_scheduler.delay_seconds, eval_scheduler.requeue_reason.

- Example scheduler configuration (YAML):

```yaml
scheduler:
 default_weights: { fidelity: 0.5, timeliness: 0.3, reliability: 0.2 }
 buckets:
 - name: critical
 range: [0.0, 0.25]
 sla_hours: 4
 annotator_type: expert
 - name: fast
 range: [0.25, 0.5]
 sla_hours: 24
 annotator_type: high_quality_crowd
 - name: normal
 range: [0.5, 0.75]
 sla_hours: 72
 annotator_type: pooled_crowd
 - name: deferred
 range: [0.75, 1.0]
 sla_hours: 168
 annotator_type: automated
```

- Queueing and batching: For P2/P3 batches the scheduler will group probes by schema (label set) and model variant to maximize annotation reuse and lower cost. Target batch size defaults:
 - P1: 8–16 probes per task
 - P2: 32–128 probes per batch
 - P3: variable, up to 512 when pushing to synthetic heuristics

Annotation lifecycle and contracts

1) Task creation: include probe_apdex, slice tags, golden examples, required annotation schema, and an expiration TTL.
2) Annotation step: annotator completes labels, flags corner-cases, and records confidence score (0–1).
3) Validation: automated validators (format, inter-annotator agreement threshold) run immediately. Tasks below agreement threshold are kicked to L2 review.
4) Ingestion: validated labels are written to the eval-store with provenance tags (annotator_id or system_id) and annotation_latency_ms.
5) Cost accounting: each task records cost_center, annotator_tier, and credits_used. These feed the Eval Budget Ledger.

Inter-annotator agreement (IAA) policy

- Target IAA by bucket:
 - P0/P1: Cohen's Kappa >= 0.7 or majority agreement >= 80%
 - P2: Kappa >= 0.6 or majority >= 70%
 - P3: relaxed; automated heuristics accepted if confidence >= 0.85

Monitoring, SLOs and alerts

- Key metrics to publish (per-slice and per-model):
 - eval.apdex.mean and eval.apdex.p50/p90/p99
 - eval_scheduler.latency_seconds.bucketed
 - annotation.sla.breach_rate (count/% of tasks exceeding SLA)
 - annotation.cost.per_probe_usd
 - iaa.below_threshold_count

- SLOs (example):
 - Annotation SLA adherence: 95% of P1 tasks completed within 24 hours (per-week rolling).
 - APDEX stability: No more than 5% weekly drop in mean probe_apdex for production slices without an associated rollout or config change.
 - Annotation quality: 98% of tasks in P1/P2 pass automated validators on first submission.

- Alerting thresholds (Pager/Slack):
 1) P0 volume spike: pager if >50 P0 probes in 1 hour for a single model.
 2) SLA breach rate: Pager if annotation.sla.breach_rate > 10% for P1 over 6 hours.
 3) APDEX collapse: Pager if eval.apdex.mean drops by >0.2 for a production slice in 30 minutes.

Runbook: when APDEX drops or P0s appear

1) Triage owner: Evaluation Oncall picks up the P0 alert.
2) Rapidly collect context: last deploys, model variant, probe slices, recent tokenization failures, and recent scheduler logs. Use CLI helper: `rds-eval query --slice <id> --last 500 --fields probe_apdex,fidelity_component`
3) Isolate cause: run replay against shadow model (see Shadow Orchestrator playbook). If failing deterministically, mark model as candidate for rollback and open rollback change in Deployment Console.
4) Annotation triage: pause automated ingestion for the affected slice, spawn small expert annotation batch to confirm behavioral regression.
5) Communicate: post incident channel summary and tag owners for product impact.
6) Postmortem: if the drop crosses the regression-impact index threshold, follow Regression Triage handbook for root cause and quality repair.

Rollout and calibration guidance

- Start with conservative weights (fidelity 0.6, timeliness 0.25, reliability 0.15) for any new family of probes for first two weeks.
- Run A/B of scheduling policies for 2-week windows: measure annotation cost per useful-fix and mean time to detect semantic regression.
- Perform quarterly audit of APDEX components per model family to ensure component metrics align with human judgement.

Operational considerations and caveats

- APDEX is an aggregate heuristic; do not use probe_apdex alone to block model promotions. Use it as a prioritization signal combined with targeted shadow evaluations and human checks.
- Weight tuning is workload-sensitive (chat vs. code vs. search). Always record the weight set used in the evaluation-run metadata.

Appendices

A. Example CLI to inspect scheduler backlog:
```
# list top 50 P0 probes for model x
evalctl backlog list --model redwood-open-7b --min-apdex 0.0 --max-apdex 0.25 --limit 50 --fields probe_id,created_at,probe_apdex,slice_tags
```

B. Example probe metadata JSON (stored with probe object):
```
{
 "probe_id": "p-734b9",
 "model": "redwood-open-7b/v1",
 "slice_tags": ["billing-chat", "us-east"],
 "fidelity_component": "0.12",
 "timeliness_component": "0.8",
 "reliability_component": "0.9",
 "probe_apdex": "0.33"
}
```

C. Owner and escalation matrix:
- Evaluation Infrastructure: owns scheduler and metric definitions. Contact: @derek-huang
- Annotation Operations: owns vendor SLAs and tasking. Contact: @aisha-patel
- Regression Oncall: owns triage and rollback. Contact: @marisol-vega

D. Related artifacts and future work:
- Integrate APDEX signal into Shadow Orchestrator to enable automated canary filtering.
- Build per-tenant cost prediction that uses APDEX decay to recommend annotation credits.

Document history

- 2026-04-15 initial draft by Derek Huang
- 2026-06-02 pilot config and scheduler YAML added

title: Closed-loop deployments & HW lifecycle intake - Equinox Clinical
author: Samira Khan
text:
Discovery call to capture Equinox Clinical constraints for a closed-loop, air-gapped/private deployment. Main concerns: offline update signing, hardware BOM limits (1 RU head node, mixed GPU ages), minimal telemetry, and audit log requirements. Redwood AE + SE explained private deployment variants, suggested signed-image rotation and KMS/HSM integration approaches, and outlined a pilot flow.

[00:00:00] Samira Khan: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Samira, AE at Redwood — Jordan and Aisha from the solutions team are with me. Could folks do quick intros?
[00:00:12] Dr. Priya Malhotra: Sure — Priya here, CTO at Equinox Clinical. We run diagnostic imaging and post-processing pipelines, lots of PII and PHI.
[00:00:20] Oliver Chen: Oliver, infra lead. I'm the one who will actually touch the racks.
[00:00:24] Marta Alvarez: Marta — compliance. SOC 2 and some regional privacy reqs are my main things.
[00:00:28] Diego Ramos: Diego, ops — maintenance windows and change control.
[00:00:33] Samira Khan: Great, appreciate it. Goal today: understand your constraints for a private, air-gapped install and what an update/patch lifecycle looks like. We'll be candid about tradeoffs.
[00:00:43] Jordan Lee: Quick note — when we say "private" here we mean Redwood Private: VPC/on-prem package that can be configured for no outbound egress. But we have different update modes — online pull, signed-image import via USB, or couriered media.
[00:00:58] Priya: We need no outbound by default. Any telemetry must be opt-in and filtered. And updates have to be physically reviewed, signed by our key, and pushed during quarterly maintenance windows.
[00:01:09] Marta: Also need full audit logs for every model change and operator action — immutability preferred.
[00:01:16] Jordan Lee: Understood. We support audit logging and can export logs to your SIEM. The Private package can be configured to store logs locally and then ship via offline transfer. We also support signed artifacts — images and model bundles signed with a key you control.
[00:01:29] Oliver: What's "signed" mean in practice? Are you expecting us to run an HSM or will Redwood manage keys?
[00:01:35] Aisha Patel: We generally recommend customer-managed keys for air-gapped installs. You can use an HSM or KMS appliance; Redwood will verify signatures during the import. If you prefer, we can do key wrap with customer keys — important for compliance.
[00:01:48] Priya: Good, we cannot hand over keys. We have an on-prem HSM.
[00:01:52] Jordan: Perfect — that aligns. We'll provide a signing toolchain that integrates with common HSMs and outputs a signed tarball (model+manifest+checksum). On import we validate the manifest signature before installing.
[00:02:05] Diego: How long does a full model rotation take? We have small maintenance windows — 2 hours every Friday night.
[00:02:12] Jordan: It depends on model size and quantization. A 7B model with quantization and streaming warm-up might take 20–30 minutes to deploy on a single node, but cold KV cache and priming could add time. For larger model swaps you may need an extended window or staged rollout.
[00:02:27] Marta: We prefer staged so we always have a rollback path. Can we pin a canary and then roll back automatically on errors?
[00:02:34] Samira: Yes — Redwood Private supports canary deploys and automatic fallback policies. In an air-gapped setup the coordination is manual, but we can provide tooling that marks a node as canary and validates health checks before enabling route.
[00:02:48] Oliver: Let's talk hardware. We don't have space for big racks — the node has 1 RU for head node and a 2RU GPU sled available. GPUs are mixed: a refurbished A5000 and an older V100.
[00:02:59] Jordan: Mixed GPU generations are workable but affect perf predictability. Our runtime can select kernels and quantization paths per card, but throughput SLOs will vary. For strict latency SLAs we recommend uniform GPU generations.
[00:03:14] Oliver: Budget's tight — replacing fleet isn't feasible for phase 1. Can Redwood optimize for that?
[00:03:18] Aisha: We can generate per-GPU profiles and suggest batch sizes/sequence caps. Also suggest tokenization/quantization to reduce memory. We'll send a sizing spreadsheet after this call.
[00:03:29] Priya: For regulatory reasons we cannot allow outbound debug traces. How granular is telemetry control?
[00:03:35] Jordan: Telemetry is configurable to the field level: errors-only, performance-metrics-only (aggregate), or none. For air-gapped customers you can choose none and still get local traces that you export manually. There may be a tradeoff: without telemetry, automated health-based routing is limited.
[00:03:50] Diego: On updates, we want a deterministic chain: human review -> sign -> physical transfer -> install -> verify -> smoke test.
[00:03:58] Samira: That's the pattern we expect. Our signed-image flow supports manifest verification and pre/post install checks. For the smoke test we can produce a small prompt set to validate output distribution (quality gates).
[00:04:10] Marta: Those prompt sets need to be under our control.
[00:04:12] Jordan: Absolutely — you can supply canonical prompts. We run evals locally against the new model bundle during the maintenance window.
[00:04:19] Priya: Any dependencies on specific OS or BMC access? We have strict out-of-band BMC policies.
[00:04:25] Oliver: Right — Dell iDRAC access is with jump-host only; we don't want vendor staff touching BMC.
[00:04:30] Aisha: For install, we only need standard kexec-style access and an operator with sudo to run the import script. If needed, Redwood can provide exact commands for your change control to approve. No ongoing BMC access required.
[00:04:43] Diego: Patch windows — what's the recommended cadence? Our security team wants monthly patches but operations prefer quarterly.
[00:04:50] Marta: From compliance perspective, critical CVEs should be applied within 30 days.
[00:04:54] Samira: We can support flexible cadence. For critical security updates we recommend an expedited signed-image path; for routine model updates we can queue for quarterly windows and provide release notes.
[00:05:05] Priya: How do you handle firmware or driver updates? Those are often the blockers for our change control.
[00:05:10] Jordan: Firmware and low-level driver updates are in your control. Redwood's bundle can include recommended driver versions, checksums, and version gating. We recommend applying firmware first in a maintenance window, then the software/model bundle after successful validation.
[00:05:22] Oliver: Can the runtime run without CUDA kernels pinned? Our older cards have different driver requirements.
[00:05:28] Jordan: The runtime has multiple execution paths. Where possible we use vendor kernels; for mismatched drivers we can fall back to a quantized, CPU-assisted path but expect slower latency. We'll profile your hardware and provide guidance.
[00:05:41] Diego: On backup and disaster recovery — if the node fails, do we have a fast way to bootstrap from our media?
[00:05:46] Aisha: Yes — Redwood will provide an importable, signed bootstrap image and step-by-step restore playbook. For full DR you can maintain a cold spare with the latest signed artifacts; when you bring it online you validate signatures and swap routes.
[00:05:59] Priya: Now on access controls — RBAC and SSO. We use SAML SSO and strict role separation.
[00:06:05] Jordan: Redwood Private supports SAML/SSO integrations; RBAC can be mapped to your identity provider. For air-gapped installs we support a local identity provider or a sync-only model with periodic export of user mappings.
[00:06:17] Marta: Audit logs — we need tamper-evidence and retention for 7 years for certain actions. Can you sign logs?
[00:06:23] Samira: We can produce signed audit bundles and use append-only logs with hash chaining. We'll provide the architecture diagram. Long-term retention will be your responsibility, but Redwood will supply the signed exports.
[00:06:35] Oliver: Is there any hidden telemetry or phone-home if we choose "no telemetry"?
[00:06:39] Jordan: No hidden phone-home. When configured for no egress, the process will not attempt outbound calls. We do have optional diagnostic packages that you upload to us manually if you want debug help.
[00:06:50] Diego: Licensing and pricing — are there seat counts or just node-based?
[00:06:54] Samira: For Private deployments we price per-reserved node and per-model licensing if there are premium variants. We can give an indicative quote after sizing; we also have enterprise support tiers for faster on-call response.
[00:07:05] Priya: For procurement: we need a template SOC 2 attestation, encryption-in-transit docs, and a list of sub-processors.
[00:07:12] Samira: We'll send our compliance pack. Note that for on-prem deployments sub-processors are limited — we can provide a list and options.
[00:07:19] Marta: Will anything in your hosted control plane have access to PHI?
[00:07:23] Jordan: In the Private install, customer data stays local unless you opt-in to export. The control plane can be configured to be local-only. We can run the management plane in a customer VPC or fully on prem with our private bundle.
[00:07:36] Diego: About model provenance — we need to ensure exact weights provenance and a chain of custody.
[00:07:41] Aisha: Our signing manifest includes model hash, builder metadata, and a provenance URI. You can require builds to include CI/CD signatures.
[00:07:49] Priya: One technical ask — can you checksum the KV cache warmup state so we can validate identical performance between nodes?
[00:07:56] Jordan: We don't checksum live KV state commonly, but we can record cache warmup histograms and a hashed seed of key pages. We'll add that to the checklist as a potential approach.
[00:08:10] Samira: Quick commercial note — if you commit to a 12-month reserved private cluster we can provide a discounted install support package that includes one on-site assistance for the initial build.
[00:08:20] Oliver: May be useful.
[00:08:22] Diego: Who will run the initial on-site build? Redwood or our contractors?
[00:08:25] Samira: Either. Our field engineers can assist under enterprise support, or you can have your integrator run it with our remote guidance. For air-gapped installs we typically provide a runbook and test checklist.
[00:08:36] Priya: Can I get a sample runbook before procurement?
[00:08:39] Jordan: Yes — we'll attach a sanitized sample runbook plus the signed-image import steps.
[00:08:45] Marta: A few clarifying questions on legal: we need indemnity for data breaches if there's negligence.
[00:08:52] Samira: Legal can discuss standard enterprise terms; we have SOC 2 and ISO attestations, and we can negotiate data protection clauses in the enterprise contract.
[00:08:59] Diego: Performance benchmarking — we want to run a local perf test. Can Redwood provide a benchmark harness that runs entirely offline?
[00:09:04] Aisha: Yes — we have an offline benchmarking tool that you can run in your environment; it generates a perf report and token-cost estimates. We can provide the harness as a tarball.
[00:09:14] Oliver: For that harness do you require any telemetry to be uploaded?
[00:09:16] Jordan: No, the harness produces a local report that you can share. If you want Redwood to analyze it, you can upload it manually.
[00:09:24] Priya: Any thoughts on mixed GPU scheduling? If one GPU is slower, will requests pile up?
[00:09:29] Jordan: The scheduler is workload-aware and can route by GPU capability. But it won't magically make a slow card faster; you'll see variability. We recommend capacity planning to avoid hot spots and set per-GPU routing policies.
[00:09:43] Marta: For compliance, all operator actions must be auditable and require two-person approvals for critical changes. Could you support a two-person promotion flow?
[00:09:51] Jordan: We support gated rollouts with approver workflows; in an air-gapped setup approvals are manual, but we can provide a signed approval artifact format so you can record approvers in the manifest.
[00:10:05] Diego: Can we integrate your RBAC with our ticketing system for approvals?
[00:10:10] Aisha: We have webhook hooks and an API for approvals, but in strict air-gapped cases we can exchange signed approval files that your ticketing system stores.
[00:10:19] Samira: Let's pivot to concrete deliverables — Jordan, what do we need to profile to produce sizing?
[00:10:24] Jordan: We'll need GPU model and driver versions, node memory, disk IO numbers, expected QPS and tail latency targets, and typical sequence length distributions. Also preferred maintenance windows and a list of critical prompts for QA.
[00:10:37] Oliver: I'll compile the hardware sheet and power diagram.
[00:10:40] Priya: We'll prepare the compliance requirements list.
[00:10:42] Diego: Ops will provide a list of allowed media transfer methods — encrypted USB, dedicated jump host, or courier.
[00:10:48] Samira: Good. We'll follow up with the checklist and a proposed pilot plan: a 2-week local perf run, then a single-model signed-image rotation in your quarter window.
[00:10:58] Marta: Timeline — procurement needs 2 weeks to review security docs. If you send docs tomorrow we can align for a January pilot.
[00:11:06] Samira: We'll aim to get docs this week.
[00:11:09] Jordan: One last technical note — in air-gapped installs we recommend containerizing the runtime and storing images as OCI tarballs with signature verification. It makes rollback easier.
[00:11:20] Priya: Sounds good.
[00:11:23] Samira: Any other open questions?
[00:11:25] Diego: Not from me.
[00:11:26] Oliver: No.
[00:11:27] Marta: Nope.
[00:11:28] Priya: Only that we will need specific language about data residency in the contract.
[00:11:32] Samira: Noted. We'll include residency clauses in the draft.
[00:11:36] Samira: Okay, quick recap — Samira to send compliance pack, signed-image process doc, and sizing spreadsheet by 2026-12-03. Equinox will send hardware BOM, rack diagrams, and maintenance windows by 2026-12-06. Jordan will draft model rotation checklist by 2026-12-07.
[00:11:52] Diego: That works.
[00:11:54] Samira: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email and schedule the readiness call. Bye.
[00:11:59] Priya: Thanks, bye.
[00:12:01] -- End of recorded segment (call continued with private admin items)

Notes on transcript imperfections: some product names transcribed as "Redwood Privatee" or "Redwood Dedicat" in earlier automated notes; KV cache occasionally transcribed as "K V cache". There were a couple of small crosstalks and overlapping talk during the hardware discussion.
