title: Ops scrumlet: routing backlog & quota observations (2026-06-21)
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Summary:
Quick mid-month scrumlet (15 min) focused on a few noisy signals from last week's routing experiments and quota throttling during overnight windows. Goal: sync on who owns follow-ups and capture a lightweight action list.

Attendees:
- Aisha (owner)
- Miguel
- Liu
- Hannah
- (joined late) Priya (SRE)

Pulse / What changed since last check:
- Routing experiment "prefer-local-az" (A/B) rolled for 3 days: saw small latency wins for bursty short requests but unexpected imbalance in KV-cache hitrates causing extra GPU warmups.
- Quota enforcement spike: several customers experienced transient 429s between 02:00-03:30 UTC on 2026-06-19; root cause appears to be a regeneration race in quota tokens service when autoscaler bumped pods.
- Auth ping latency: p99 auth round-trip increased from 22ms -> 40ms for a 1-hour window during the same autoscaler event (possible cross-calls between auth and quota).

Details / Evidence:
- Miguel: routing logs show 18% higher cache miss rate for short sequences (<32 tokens) on replica group B. PR #987 contains traces and histogram exports.
- Liu: quota service horizon shows token-regeneration bursts correlated with Kubernetes HPA scale-up events at ~02:10 UTC. Pod startup caused a short-lived TTL miscalculation leading to double-issuance checks and then temporary drop-in capacity reported to gateway.
- Hannah: traced increased auth RTT to a sync call auth -> quota -> auth when quota endpoint returned 503; retries added ~18ms per request.

Hypothesis (quick):
1) The routing policy that biases local AZs results in uneven distribution of prefix-cached KV pairs; when traffic shifts, some GPUs warm-up more often (cold token overhead).
2) Quota service race during pod scale-up leads to transient state mismatch; Gateway interprets as exhausted quota resulting in 429s.
3) Auth-service retry path amplifies the surface area.

Immediate mitigations tried (during call):
- Rollback prefer-local-az to baseline routing on Canary cluster B (Miguel) — rolled back 02:45 UTC; observed stabilization within 20m.
- Hotfix to quota registry added temporary in-memory guard to prevent double-issue logic; staged to canary (Liu).

Action items (owners + due):
- Miguel: run a focused load test that simulates short-sequence burstiness against prefer-local-az variant, capture KV cache heatmaps. Due: 2026-06-25.
- Liu: open a postmortem draft for 429 event, include timeline, k8s HPA events, pod logs, and quota-regeneration traces. JIRA-PLTFM-1423 assigned. Due: 2026-06-24.
- Hannah: propose an auth retry budget change to fail-fast on quota 5xxs to avoid long tail latency amplification (PR & proposal). Due: 2026-06-28.
- Aisha: coordinate with SRE (Priya) to add a short-term guard in the autoscaler (cooldown increase for quota-backed services) and record in runbook. Due: 2026-06-23 (in progress).

Decisions made:
- Do not proceed with prefer-local-az rollout beyond canary until cache warming strategies (prepopulate / soft-affinity) are in place.
- Temporary throttling suppression for long tail retries: auth will fail-fast on quota 5xx for 30s after detection.

Open questions / Risks:
- Could the quota double-issue be exacerbated by multi-region control-plane replication lag? (Liu to test config matrix).
- Risk of user impact if we increase autoscaler cooldown: may delay capacity for real spikes; need to tune with synthetic storm tests.
- We do not yet know if some customers saw correlated errors across models; need to check per-customer routing affinity.

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Sketch: pre-warm KV cache by proxying small synthetic prefix requests when routing decision flips. Could be a low-cost background lambda.
- Consider a lightweight leader-election inside quota pods to serialize token-regeneration during scale events (cheap guard).

Follow-up meeting / handoff:
- We'll revisit the status in next weekly platform sync (2026-06-28). If postmortem shows customer-visible impact, schedule an incident review with CS.

Attachments / quick links: 
- Load traces: s3://redwood-platform-debug/runs/2026-06-19-prefer-local-az-traces
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/pltfm/pull/987
- JIRA: JIRA-PLTFM-1423
- Slack thread: #pltfm-routing (pinned: June 19 autoscale spikes)

Misc (informal):
- Miguel: "noticed weird cold start behavior only for requests <32 tokens — feels like an LRU churn issue"
- Hannah: "auth retries noisier than I'd expect; short-circuiting might be the cheapest win"
- Liu: "postmortem will probably recommend a tiny quota registry guard and clearer scale-up checklist"

End of notes.

-- quick signoff: Aisha

title: Long-context burst throughput: INT8/AWQ/FP8 field notes (Feb 2028)
author: Maya Thompson
text:
Summary:

Quick field notes from a small benching pass that looked at how quantized kernels (INT8-GPTQ style, AWQ-derived int8, and FP8 paths) behave when we drive long-context workloads under bursty arrival patterns. Found surprising non-monotonic throughput regressions at large sequence lengths (8k+) for the FP8 path and a batch-shape sensitivity in the AWQ kernel that amplifies p99 latency under short bursts. This doc records what we ran, raw-ish numbers, profiling traces, hypotheses, and next steps.

Motivation / why this felt urgent:
- We are seeing customer reports where long-context agents (>=8k) degrade throughput when traffic spikes; they expect linear token amortization gains but observe bursts of high p99 latency.
- We need to know whether quant variant/kernels or runtime batching/KV handling is the main cause so we can recommend sensible routing/fallbacks.

Testbed (short):
- HW: 1x A100-80GB (DGX-like node), CUDA 12.1, cuBLAS/cuDNN latest on our bench image
- Runtime: serving-runtime @ commit 5b7c9a2 (branch: experimental/quant-burst-probes)
- Models: 13B dense baseline (FP16), GPTQ-int8 variant (gptq-true), AWQ-int8 variant (awq-opt), FP8-compiled variant (fp8-optim)
- Sequence lengths tested: 128, 1024, 8192, 16384 (generation 512 tokens after prefix)
- Arrival shapes: steady small (10 rps, concurrency 1), moderate sustained (50 rps), short burst (200 concurrent arriving within 2s, lasting 10s), sustained burst (50 concurrent for 60s)
- Clients: local bench harness + synthetic KV-cache enabled (key/value cache warm for repeated prompts in same conversation)

Metrics captured:
- tokens_per_sec (aggregate), mean latency (ms), p95, p99 latencies, GPU kernel breakdown (top3 kernels by time), memcpy host<->device times, KV copy times, allocator stalls (ms)

Representative results (raw) — generation of 512 tokens after prefix:
- seq=128:
 - FP16 baseline: 12.8k tokens/s, p95=42ms, p99=78ms
 - GPTQ-int8: 18.3k tokens/s, p95=34ms, p99=62ms
 - AWQ-int8: 17.9k tokens/s, p95=36ms, p99=64ms
 - FP8 path: 19.1k tokens/s, p95=33ms, p99=61ms
- seq=1024:
 - FP16: 8.6k t/s, p95=78ms, p99=140ms
 - GPTQ-int8: 11.9k t/s, p95=66ms, p99=120ms
 - AWQ-int8: 11.6k t/s, p95=69ms, p99=125ms
 - FP8: 12.3k t/s, p95=64ms, p99=118ms
- seq=8192 (key observations start to diverge):
 - FP16: 2.1k t/s, p95=320ms, p99=610ms
 - GPTQ-int8: 2.9k t/s, p95=290ms, p99=540ms
 - AWQ-int8: 2.8k t/s, p95=305ms, p99=620ms (spikey p99 under burst)
 - FP8: 2.1k t/s, p95=410ms, p99=920ms (FP8 lost its earlier advantage; p99 much worse)
- seq=16384:
 - FP16: 1.2k t/s, p95=760ms, p99=1480ms
 - GPTQ-int8: 1.6k t/s, p95=680ms, p99=1300ms
 - AWQ-int8: 1.55k t/s, p95=730ms, p99=1420ms
 - FP8: 0.95k t/s, p95=1010ms, p99=2200ms

Notes on arrival shapes (burst vs steady):
- Under steady traffic the FP8 path roughly tracked expectation (slightly faster than INT8 variants at small seq).
- Short bursts (200 concurrent) exposed oscillations in the FP8 runs: initial token throughput good, then after 3–6s p99 spikes dramatically and throughput drops to ~50% for the remainder of the burst window.
- AWQ-int8 shows batch-shape sensitivity: when many concurrent small requests arrive, the kernel chooses a different vectorization path that increases tail latency by ~25% compared to consolidated batching; this shows up most at seq>=1024.

Profiling extracts (topline, aggregated across run segments):
- FP8 path (seq=8192, during spike):
 - matmul_kernel_fp8_pack (kernel): 44% of GPU time
 - kv_cache_copy (memcpy/host<->device): 18%
 - aten_attention_fp8 (kernel): 16%
 - allocator stalls: aggregated 120ms per request (observed in runtime timeline)
- GPTQ-int8 (same segment):
 - matmul_int8_kernel: 36%
 - kv_cache_copy: 12%
 - aten_attention_int8: 14%
 - allocator stalls: ~45ms/request
- Memory profile: FP8 path had higher transient device memory usage (due to per-layer FP8 scaling tensors kept live) which triggered more frequent small allocations and frees; we see memcpy churn and occasional GC-like stalls in allocator.

Qualitative observations / surprises:
1) FP8's throughput advantage at short sequences does not translate to long-context steady bursts because of two interacting effects: (a) extra metadata + per-layer scaling buffers for FP8 increase device memory footprint and allocation churn; (b) FP8 kernels in our build trigger a different GEMM codepath that is less tolerant of large KV cache strides (cache footprint grows with seq) — combined they induce throttling and p99 blowups.
2) AWQ-int8 sensitivity seems tied to batch-shape detection heuristics. When the runtime forms many small micro-batches vs fewer consolidated batches, the AWQ kernel selects a narrower vector width to avoid register pressure, which is suboptimal for long vectors and amplifies latency.
3) GPTQ-int8 was the most robust across shapes; fewer transient allocations and a mature kernel path help (tradeoff: slightly lower peak tokens/s at tiny seqs vs FP8).

Hypotheses to validate (ranked):
- H1: Allocator churn + transient per-layer buffers in FP8 path cause host/device memcpy thrash when KV cache is large. Validate by forcing a pre-allocated buffer pool and re-running burst.
- H2: Kernel selection heuristics flip at thresholds of sequence length and batch shape; AWQ path heuristics are too eager to change vectorization for micro-batches. Validate by instrumenting kernel selection decisions and forcing single kernel choice.
- H3: Memory bandwidth thrash from KV copies becomes the bottleneck as sequence length grows; mitigating with on-GPU persistent KV or compressed KV reduces p99. Validate by enabling on-GPU KV and measuring delta.

Experiment notes (what I tried quickly):
- Prewarming: warming KV cache reduced cold-start jitter but did not prevent FP8 p99 spike during bursts.
- Force single-kernel flag: forcing FP8 to use the fast GEMM decreased p95 but did not eliminate the p99 spike — allocator stalls still present.
- Pre-alloc pool simulation: mocked a simple arena allocator reduced allocator stalls by ~40% and improved FP8 p99 by ~20% at seq=8192 under burst (promising).

Immediate action items (short list):
- Short-term (this week):
 1) Add instrumentation to record per-request allocator events + kernel selection decision in logs (INF-3297). Owner: Ethan.
 2) Run a focused pre-alloc arena test across FP8/GPTQ/AWQ variants with higher concurrency shapes (owner: Maya).
 3) Add an experimental config that forces GPTQ-int8 fallback for seq>8k for the hosted tier; monitor impact (owner: Jonas).
- Medium-term:
 4) Explore persistent on-GPU KV option for long-context workloads (bench and infra impact).
 5) Work with kernel authors to add a cost model for kernel selection that accounts for KV stride / device allocation pressure.

Open questions / things to log in follow-ups:
- Exact allocation patterns per-layer for FP8 (which tensors are kept live and why).
- Whether the FP8 GEMM codepath can be patched to be more tolerant of wide KV caches (likely low-level work).
- Is AWQ micro-batch heuristic configurable without sacrificing small-seq perf?

Notes to self / rough TODOs in order:
- instrument -> re-run arena -> collect traces -> open a small PR to expose a force-kernel flag to the service -> share a micro-bench run with solutions-engineering to check regressions for a customer use-case.

Appendix (fragile raw trace pointers):
- sample gfx trace: s3://bench-artifacts/quant/long-context/trace-2028-02-12-13-42.gz
- perf summary CSV: s3://bench-artifacts/quant/long-context/summary-2028-02-12.csv

If anyone else on call wants to pick next steps, flag here. My leaning: try the arena prealloc + kernel selection logging first; they are fast and high signal.

-- Maya

title: Runtime Runbook: KV Cache Compaction + Tier-Aware Eviction
author: Rafael Mendes
text:
## Purpose
This runbook describes how to operate **KV cache compaction** and **tier-aware eviction** in the serving runtime. It is intended for **runtime on-call** and **SRE** during canaries and broad rollouts.

Compaction reduces KV allocator fragmentation under mixed sequence lengths + churn. Eviction provides a controlled pressure release to prevent opportunistic, worst-time evictions (or OOM/shedding) during bursts.

This runbook covers:
- Verifying compaction/eviction is enabled (and at what settings)
- Reading core metrics and dashboards
- Common failure modes and triage
- Adjusting budgets/thresholds safely
- Emergency kill-switch and rollback steps

## Scope / systems
**Applies to:**
- Runtime version: **runtime-1.22+** (feature-flagged)
- Deployments: Hosted API pools, Dedicated GPU pools, and Private (where enabled)

**Core components involved:**
- KV arena allocator (pages/blocks + free lists)
- Compaction worker (incremental relocation)
- Scheduler hook (budgeting at prefill/decode boundaries)
- Tier-aware eviction selector (LRU + tier constraints + pinned sessions)

## Safety / correctness notes (read first)
1) **Compaction must be budgeted.** Unbounded relocation can create decode stalls and tail latency spikes.
2) **Never disable correctness checks** (invariants, relocation fences) to “fix perf.” If checks fire, treat as correctness incident.
3) **Eviction is not lossless** for impacted sequences (it can force recompute / slower decode for those requests). Prefer budget tuning before eviction broadening.
4) **Pinned sessions must not be evicted.** If pinned sessions are being evicted, treat as a bug.

## Ownership / escalation
**Primary escalation path (runtime):**
- KV cache / compaction: **Omar El-Sayed**, **Samir Qureshi**
- Scheduler budgeting: **Sofia Ivanova**
- SLO/alerts/rollback policy: **Sean Gallagher**

If there is evidence of correctness risk (allocator invariant violations, relocation fence failures, memory corruption symptoms):
- Page **Noah Patel** (architecture/correctness) and initiate SEV triage.

## Quick start (5-minute checklist)
Use this when you get paged for tail latency / OOM risk and suspect KV fragmentation.

1) Check current runtime config (feature flags + budgets) for the affected pool.
2) Check dashboards:
 - Fragmentation ratio trend
 - Compaction bytes moved / time spent
 - Eviction rate
 - p95/p99 latency correlation
3) If p99 spike correlates with compaction overhead:
 - Reduce compaction budget (time/bytes) OR raise trigger threshold
4) If OOM / allocator pressure correlates with high fragmentation and low free contiguous space:
 - Enable/raise eviction (tier-aware) OR temporarily disable compaction if it is thrashing
5) If symptoms persist >10 minutes or correctness signals fire:
 - Flip kill-switch for the affected pool and rollback canary cohort per rollout policy

---

## How to verify compaction is enabled
### A) Confirm runtime version
From the pool detail page or runtime fleet view:
- Verify runtime image tag includes **runtime-1.22** or later.

### B) Check feature flags (control plane)
Use the runtime config CLI (or equivalent internal tooling). Examples below use `redwoodctl`.

**Get effective config for a pool:**
- `redwoodctl runtime-config get --pool <POOL_NAME> --effective`

Expected keys (names may appear with `kv.*` prefix depending on config layer):
- `kv.compaction.enabled` (boolean)
- `kv.compaction.mode` (scheduler_hook | background_worker | hybrid)
- `kv.compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio` (float, 0.0–1.0)
- `kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step` (int)
- `kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step` (int)
- `kv.compaction.max_bytes_in_flight` (int)
- `kv.eviction.enabled` (boolean)
- `kv.eviction.policy` (tier_aware_lru)
- `kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target` (int)
- `kv.eviction.protect_pinned_sessions` (boolean, must be true)

**Verify at runtime (node-level logs):**
Search for the startup line:
- `KVCompaction: enabled=true mode=<...> budget_ms=<...> budget_bytes=<...> trigger_frag=<...>`
- `KVEviction: enabled=true policy=tier_aware_lru min_free_bytes_target=<...>`

### C) Confirm compaction actually runs
Compaction enabled is not sufficient—ensure it is active under the trigger condition.

In dashboards, look for:
- Non-zero `kv_compaction_steps_total`
- Non-zero `kv_compaction_bytes_moved_total`
- Fragmentation ratio declining after trigger threshold is exceeded

---

## Dashboards and key metrics
Reference dashboard: **Runtime → KV Cache → Compaction/Eviction**

### Metric definitions (high-signal)
Use the standardized names from the metrics standard page; common panels include:

**Allocator health**
- `kv_fragmentation_ratio` (gauge, 0.0–1.0)
 - Interpretation: 0.0–0.15 healthy; 0.15–0.30 watch; >0.30 high fragmentation (model/workload dependent)
- `kv_arena_free_bytes` (gauge)
- `kv_arena_largest_free_block_bytes` (gauge) — strong indicator of practical fragmentation
- `kv_alloc_failures_total` (counter)

**Compaction activity**
- `kv_compaction_steps_total` (counter)
- `kv_compaction_bytes_moved_total` (counter)
- `kv_compaction_time_ms_total` (counter)
- `kv_compaction_budget_exhausted_total` (counter) — indicates budgeting is constraining work
- `kv_compaction_stalls_total` (counter) — should be near-zero; investigate if rising

**Eviction activity**
- `kv_evictions_total{reason=pressure|oom_prevent|policy}` (counter)
- `kv_evicted_bytes_total` (counter)
- `kv_evictions_blocked_total{reason=pinned|tier_protected}` (counter) — validates protections

**Latency correlation (golden signals)**
- `runtime_decode_token_latency_ms_p95/p99` (by model, by pool)
- `request_latency_ms_p95/p99` (by route/model)
- Traces: spans `kv.compaction.step` and `kv.eviction.select` (exemplars)

### Typical healthy patterns
- Fragmentation ratio oscillates but returns to baseline after bursts.
- Compaction bytes moved increases during bursts; **compaction time** remains bounded.
- Eviction rate is low/near-zero except under sustained pressure events.

### Red flags
- Fragmentation ratio trending upward with **flat** compaction activity (trigger not met, disabled, or worker stuck).
- High `kv_compaction_time_ms_total` growth accompanied by p99 latency spikes (budget too high or running at bad scheduler phase).
- Sudden increase in `kv_alloc_failures_total` or OOM events while fragmentation is high (eviction not engaging / min-free target too low).
- Non-zero `kv_evictions_blocked_total{reason=pinned}` followed by evictions from pinned sessions (bug / configuration regression).

---

## Common incidents and how to respond

### 1) Tail latency spike (p95/p99) correlated with compaction
**Symptoms**
- `request_latency_ms_p99` increases within 5–15 minutes of enabling compaction on a canary cohort.
- `kv_compaction_time_ms_total` slope increases sharply.
- Traces show long `kv.compaction.step` spans near decode.

**Immediate actions (least risky first)**
1) Reduce compaction budget:
 - Lower `kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step` by 25–50% OR
 - Lower `kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step` by 25–50%
2) Ensure compaction runs at safe scheduler boundaries:
 - Prefer `mode=scheduler_hook` or `hybrid` with strict decode gating in Hosted pools.
3) Raise the trigger threshold slightly if compaction is engaging too early:
 - Increase `kv.compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio` by +0.03 to +0.05

**If p99 remains elevated for >10 minutes**
- Disable compaction for the canary cohort (keep eviction enabled if safe):
 - Set `kv.compaction.enabled=false` (pool-scoped)
- Follow the rollout rollback criteria (see SRE guardrails page).

**Notes**
- Do not over-correct budgets to zero; you can worsen fragmentation and trigger allocator pressure later in the day.

### 2) GPU OOM / allocator pressure during burst traffic
**Symptoms**
- Rising `kv_alloc_failures_total`
- `kv_arena_largest_free_block_bytes` collapses while `kv_arena_free_bytes` still appears non-trivial
- OOMs in runtime logs, request shedding, or admission control triggers

**Immediate actions**
1) Confirm compaction is enabled and actually doing work.
2) If fragmentation is high (>0.30) and compaction is not keeping up:
 - Increase compaction budget moderately (10–25%) *only if p99 is stable*
3) If free contiguous space is low and OOM risk is immediate:
 - Enable eviction (if not already): `kv.eviction.enabled=true`
 - Increase `kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target` for the affected pool

**If OOM continues**
- Temporarily disable compaction if it is thrashing (high bytes moved + no improvement) and rely on eviction + backpressure:
 - `kv.compaction.enabled=false`
- Escalate to runtime (Omar/Samir) with allocator snapshot + time window.

### 3) Compaction thrashing (high bytes moved, fragmentation not improving)
**Symptoms**
- `kv_compaction_bytes_moved_total` increases continuously
- `kv_fragmentation_ratio` stays flat or increases
- p99 may be flat or elevated

**Actions**
1) Validate trigger/stop conditions:
 - Check whether workload churn prevents stable consolidation.
2) Reduce budget and/or enforce `kv.compaction.max_bytes_in_flight` tighter.
3) Consider shifting mode to `scheduler_hook` (Hosted) to reduce background interference.
4) Capture allocator snapshot and escalate (likely requires allocator heuristics change).

### 4) Requests slow down due to eviction (quality OK, latency worse)
**Symptoms**
- `kv_evictions_total{reason=pressure}` elevated
- Latency increases for affected tier(s) after eviction events

**Actions**
1) Ensure eviction is tier-scoped correctly:
 - Confirm lower-priority tiers are evicted first.
2) Increase `kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target` carefully (can cause more evictions; only do if OOM risk exists).
3) Prefer compaction tuning to reduce need for eviction.

### 5) Correctness / allocator invariant failures
**Symptoms**
- Log lines containing: `KV_INVARIANT_FAILED`, `relocation fence timeout`, `double free`, `page refcount mismatch`

**Actions (treat as SEV)**
1) Immediately flip kill-switch for compaction and eviction in the affected pool:
 - `kv.compaction.enabled=false`
 - `kv.eviction.enabled=false` (unless required to prevent OOM; decide with runtime lead)
2) Halt rollout / rollback cohort.
3) Page Noah Patel and runtime TL.
4) Preserve evidence:
 - Node logs, allocator snapshot (if supported), traces for the incident window.

---

## Feature flags and safe tuning
All changes should be **pool-scoped** and applied to the minimal blast radius (canary cohort first).

### Recommended knobs (in order)
1) `kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step`
2) `kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step`
3) `kv.compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio`
4) `kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target`

### Example: reduce compaction impact during canary
- `redwoodctl runtime-config set --pool <POOL_NAME> kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step=2`
- `redwoodctl runtime-config set --pool <POOL_NAME> kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step=33554432`
- `redwoodctl runtime-config apply --pool <POOL_NAME>`

### Example: enable eviction as an OOM guardrail
- `redwoodctl runtime-config set --pool <POOL_NAME> kv.eviction.enabled=true`
- `redwoodctl runtime-config set --pool <POOL_NAME> kv.eviction.policy=tier_aware_lru`
- `redwoodctl runtime-config set --pool <POOL_NAME> kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target=2147483648`
- `redwoodctl runtime-config apply --pool <POOL_NAME>`

### Validation after a change (required)
Within 10 minutes of apply:
- Confirm config propagation completed (fleet shows new effective config)
- Confirm metrics show expected directional change (e.g., lower compaction time)
- Confirm p99 has stabilized or improved

---

## Kill-switch and rollback procedure
Use this when:
- Canary breaches rollback criteria (tail latency, error rate, or allocator health)
- Correctness signals fire
- You cannot stabilize within the incident SLA window

### A) Kill-switch (pool-scoped)
1) Disable compaction:
 - `redwoodctl runtime-config set --pool <POOL_NAME> kv.compaction.enabled=false`
2) Decide on eviction:
 - If OOM risk is low: `kv.eviction.enabled=false`
 - If OOM risk is high: keep eviction enabled but reduce aggressiveness (lower min-free target) and monitor
3) Apply:
 - `redwoodctl runtime-config apply --pool <POOL_NAME>`

### B) Rollback the canary cohort
Follow release train policy for runtime-1.22:
1) Remove pool from canary cohort (rollout system) OR shift traffic weight to previous runtime version.
2) Confirm traffic drains.
3) Confirm p99 and allocator signals return to baseline.

### C) Post-rollback evidence checklist
Attach to incident ticket / slack thread:
- Affected pool(s), region(s), model(s)
- Before/after config diff
- 30–60 minute metric snapshots (fragmentation, compaction time, evictions, p99)
- Any trace exemplars with long compaction spans

---

## Routine operational checks (weekly during rollout)
1) Audit effective configs for Hosted/Dedicated pools to ensure defaults match policy.
2) Confirm dashboards include required panels (per metrics standard).
3) Review top pools by:
 - `kv_fragmentation_ratio` (p95 over 24h)
 - `kv_compaction_time_ms_total` slope during peak
 - `kv_evictions_total` (rate)
4) Verify alerts are actionable (low noise) and rollback automation is wired.

---

## Appendix: What to collect for runtime team
When escalating, provide:
- Pool name, region, model, runtime version
- Workload description (bursty? long-lived sessions? mixed lengths?)
- Time window (UTC)
- Metrics: fragmentation ratio, largest free block bytes, compaction time/bytes, eviction counts
- Logs around allocator warnings/errors
- Trace IDs with compaction/eviction spans

## Appendix: Terminology
- **Fragmentation ratio:** proportion of free memory unusable for large contiguous KV allocations due to free space being split.
- **Largest free block:** more predictive for OOM than total free bytes.
- **Budgeted compaction:** relocation work capped by time/bytes per scheduler step to avoid impacting decode latency.
- **Tier-aware eviction:** policy that preferentially evicts lower priority tiers and never evicts pinned sessions.

Response includes revocation_time and audit_event_id which we can export.

kevin (Sales-Eng): If they want Private (VPC) there is a ~2 week lead time for entitlements + networking. Dedicated pools can be provisioned faster (as devops-bot indicated). Pricing guidance: Hosted with export = lowest friction; Dedicated gives isolation but adds lead time/cost.

Once we have that we flip the switch and send evidence artifacts.

maria (Security): Yep — I'll upload a sanitized sample (JSONL) to a shared folder and include field descriptions. Expect that in ~2 hours.

olivia (AE): Great — I'll book a 20-min sync with your security lead for tomorrow 10am PT to walk through the artifacts. @julia please confirm. :thumbsup:

julia (AcmeSec): Confirmed. Thanks everyone.

kevin (Sales-Eng): Sending a quick POC quote to your email after this thread.

sam (Solutions): I'll follow up once provision job completes and when exports are wired.

maria (Security): Uploaded sample export: https://files.redwood.ai/shared/acme-sample-audit.jsonl (sanitized). Also attached a short revocation proof doc.

julia (AcmeSec): Received — looks good. Thanks, team.

title: Commit Waste Triage & Fractional Pool Reuse Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Purpose:
This is a practical playbook and accompanying spreadsheet layout for triaging committed (reserved) GPU capacity that is at risk of being underutilized across dedicated pools. The document focuses on a pragmatic, operational approach: how to detect wasted commit, classify it by reuse risk, and apply a fractional pool reuse policy plus chargeback adjustments to recover value while preserving SLAs for contract holders.

Context / problem statement:
- We sell reserved GPU pools (commits) to customers and also operate internal product workloads backed by other pools. Commit mismatches happen frequently when usage trajectories diverge from forecasts (seasonality, model rollouts, customer churn).
- Left unaddressed, committed GPU hours become sunk cost; teams either absorb the cost or we extend refunds/credits. Both have material margin impact.
- Existing approaches (full reallocation, manual negotiation) are high-friction or risky. We need a repeatable spreadsheet-driven triage + automated assignment heuristic to 1) quantify recoverable value, 2) propose safe reuse bands, and 3) recommend chargeback / credit adjustments.

Definitions (for spreadsheet):
- Committed_GH: committed GPU-hours by pool per billing period (e.g., month)
- Observed_Usage_GH: observed GPU-hours (moving window, e.g., last 30 days)
- Forecasted_GH: conservative forward forecast for next 30 days (model + customer signals)
- Idle_GH = max(0, Committed_GH - Forecasted_GH)
- Idle_pct = Idle_GH / Committed_GH
- ReuseTier: classification of idle capacity for reuse: Tier A (low risk, replaceable short-term), Tier B (burst/backfill), Tier C (spot-like / cross-tenant experimental)

High-level approach (three parts):
1) Detection and prioritization (sheet: inputs + signals)
 - Pull committed vs actual usage per-pool (daily granularity) into Sheet1.
 - Compute 7/14/30-day moving averages and short-tail forecast (exponential smoothing).
 - Flag pools where Idle_pct > 12% and Idle_GH > 200 GH (configurable).

2) Triage matrix (sheet: triage)
 - For each flagged pool, score on: forecast confidence (0-1), SLA sensitivity (0=best-effort to 1=hard SLO), financial leverage (committed $/GH), and contractual constraints (billing windows, migration penalties).
 - Example scoring heuristic (spreadsheet formulas):
 Score = 0.4*(1 - Forecast_confidence) + 0.3*(1 - SLA_sensitivity) + 0.3*(Normalized_financial_leverage)
 - Map Score to ReuseTier: Score > 0.7 -> Tier A, 0.4-0.7 -> Tier B, <0.4 -> Tier C.

3) Fractional pool reuse scheduler (sheet: reuse-schedule)
 - For Tier A: allow short-term reallocation windows (2–7 days) with automatic restoration and 30% discount applied to internal/third-party using team for the window.
 - For Tier B: designate for burst/backfill where requests are queued into a burst bucket; chargeback at 50% discount but with preemption guard (10-minute drain notice).
 - For Tier C: expose to cross-tenant spot marketplace; full preemption, steeply discounted credits, explicit data isolation review required.

Spreadsheet layout (recommended tabs and key columns):
- Sheet: pool-inputs (cols: pool_id, owner, region, committed_GH_month, observed_GH_30d, forecasted_GH_30d, idle_GH, idle_pct, contract_end, note)
- Sheet: triage (cols: pool_id, forecast_conf, sla_sensitivity, fin_leverage_usd_per_GH, contract_constraints, score, reuse_tier, recommended_action)
- Sheet: reuse-schedule (cols: pool_id, reuse_tier, available_GH, window_start, window_end, assignee, price_modifier_pct, preempt_window_min, oncall_escalation)
- Sheet: sim-results (scenario, total_recovered_GH, effective_recovery_rate_pct, revenue_recov_usd, risk_estimated_cost_usd)

Key formulas (spreadsheet pseudocode):
- idle_GH = max(0, committed_GH_month - forecasted_GH_30d * (30/period_days))
- idle_pct = idle_GH / committed_GH_month
- normalized_financial_leverage = min(1, (fin_leverage_usd_per_GH / 120)) /* cap to avoid skew */
- score = ROUND(0.4*(1 - forecast_conf) + 0.3*(1 - sla_sensitivity) + 0.3*normalized_financial_leverage, 2)

Example scenario (sample numbers):
- Pool P-420: committed_GH_month=14,400 (6 x A100-80 per day equivalent), observed_GH_30d=8,100, forecasted_GH_30d=7,200 -> idle_GH = 14,400 - 7,200*1 = 7,200 (50%) -> flagged
- Forecast_conf=0.4 (low), SLA_sensitivity=0.2 (batch workloads), fin_leverage_usd_per_GH=0.75 -> normalized_fin=0.006 -> score ~ 0.4*(0.6) + 0.3*(0.8) + 0.3*(0.006) = 0.24 + 0.24 + 0.0018 ~ 0.482 -> Tier B
- Action: place 4,800 GH into burst pool with price_modifier_pct = -50% and preempt_window_min = 10

Chargeback / credits heuristics:
- Goal: preserve customer relationship while recovering marginal cost. Implement a credit-forward policy with these primitives:
 - Short-window reuse (Tier A): internal/partner assignee pays 30% of normal per-GH price as credit returned to commit owner. The owner keeps full contract billing but receives monthly credit for reuse hours (credits cannot exceed a % of bill; default cap = 20%).
 - Burst (Tier B): 50% credit back to pool owner for backfilled hours; receiver pays 50% of tokenized consumption cost; automatic notification + 72-hour reconciliation.
 - Spot (Tier C): 75% discount to receiver, 10% credit to owner (motivated to accept aggressive reuse).
- Implement caps and guardrails (monthly cap per-owner, minimum notice, forced restore on SLA breach).

Operational playbook (how to run weekly):
1) Run detection job (daily) and write to sheet "pool-inputs".
2) Sort triage by Score; raise top 12 items to a short review board (capacity-ops rotation).
3) For items approved for Tier A/B/C reuse, populate reuse-schedule and notify owners + assignees via slack + automated ticket (JIRA).
4) Monitor for restoration events; if observed_usage increases back above 90% of committed, auto-revoke reuse within defined grace window.
5) Reconcile credits monthly and publish a short chargeback summary in billing/ops.

Risk matrix / mitigations:
- False positives on idle detection -> use conservative forecast and require two consecutive windows before Tier A assignment.
- SLA regressions after reuse -> retain 25% of pool as warm spare for restoration and enforce preemption windows.
- Contract/legal constraints -> triage must include contract flag; if contractual prohibition exists, mark as "no-reuse".

A/B rollout recommendation:
- Phase 0 (pilot): 3 pools, internal teams only, manual approvals, 4-week pilot window.
- Phase 1 (scale): 10% of flagged pools, automated notifications, monthly reconciliation, product ops oversight.
- Phase 2 (wide): enable Tier C marketplace with clear ToS and billing integration.

Next steps (practical checklist):
- Build the three-tab spreadsheet and a sandbox run using last 6 months of pool metrics.
- Implement the scoring formulas as visible cells for auditable reasoning.
- Wire a lightweight JIRA flow and slack template for owner notifications.
- Run pilot with product-internal pools and capture metrics: recovered_GH, net_revenue_recov, SLA_incidents (target=0).
- After pilot, iterate credit percentages and cap thresholds based on recovered economics and owner satisfaction.

Notes / open questions:
- What is the acceptable monthly cap per owner for credits (default 20%) vs legal constraints?
- How do we integrate Dedicated billing primitives (monthly commit amortized vs hourly backfill) into existing invoicing?
- Should we surface reuse exposure on the Redwood Console for commit owners (transparency vs operational noise)?

References and links:
- JIRA-DED-482 (triage automation epic)
- Confluence: capacity/pool-ops (operational runbooks)
- GitHub: commit-simulator/pull/87 (sim harness used in analysis)

Appendix: suggested spreadsheet cell examples and sample formulas (to copy/paste)
- idle_GH (cell F2) formula: =MAX(0, C2 - D2) /* where C2=committed_GH_month, D2=forecasted_GH_30d */
- idle_pct (cell G2): =IF(C2=0,0,F2/C2)
- normalized_fin (cell H2): =MIN(1, E2/120) /* E2 = fin_leverage_usd_per_GH */
- score (cell I2): =ROUND(0.4*(1 - B2) + 0.3*(1 - Z2) + 0.3*H2,2) /* B2=forecast_conf, Z2=sla_sensitivity */

title: Response-size Bucketing and Adaptive Rate Protocol for Throughput Runs
author: Eleanor Chen
text:
Summary:

This note documents a complementary methodology for throughput benchmarking focused on response-size stratification and adaptive request-rate bucketing. The approach is intended to improve run repeatability across variable-length generation workloads and to make throughput comparisons between model variants and quantization paths more robust to noise introduced by tail latencies, thermal effects, and platform scheduling.

Motivation and problem statement:

Many production workloads have a broad distribution of generation lengths (short replies, medium completions, long-form). A single aggregate QPS target or a single arrival pattern can hide path-dependent performance characteristics: e.g., long-tail token generation can amplify GPU memory pressure, increase KV cache churn, and push different kernel dispatch paths. Existing staircase/warmup playbooks are useful, but runs still vary when the response length mix changes between experiments.

Goals:

- Produce repeatable throughput estimates that are stable across reruns and small platform drift.
- Surface sensitivity to response-size mix (short/medium/long) as a first-class dimension.
- Provide a light-weight adaptive bucketing layer so load generators can maintain target occupancy without saturating the system abruptly.
- Reduce run-to-run noise with anchor requests and percentile anchoring rather than mean-only signals.

High-level approach:

1) Profile the workload offline to produce a response-length fingerprint: a small sample of representative prompts that produce short (<32 tokens), medium (32–256 tokens), and long (>256 tokens) completions.

2) Create buckets for each response-size class. Each bucket has its own rate schedule and warmup curve. Buckets are mixed at the client according to a `mix` vector matching the target workload, but each bucket is driven independently so we can measure per-bucket throughput and latency.

3) Within each bucket use an adaptive rate controller that targets a desired occupancy metric (e.g., GPU active tokens/s or model concurrency) instead of raw QPS. This controller slowly increases offered rate until a knee is detected. Knee detection uses percentile latency growth (p90 and p99 slope) and GPU scheduling backpressure signals.

4) Anchor the run with periodic deterministic probe requests (a small set of synthetic prompts that are highly repeatable). These anchors run at low frequency throughout the experiment to detect drift and permit cross-run alignment.

Load generator design details:

- Bucketing: 3 buckets = short, medium, long. Each bucket has:
 - id: "short|med|long"
 - sample_prompts: 20 seeded prompts that map to the length class (store in fixtures/response-buckets/)
 - stride: how many parallel clients to assign initially
 - per-bucket pacing: initial qps and max qps cap

- Adaptive rate controller (per-bucket):
 - Warmup stage: exponential growth from 1 RPS to 20% of target over 90s to allow kernel caching and allocator stabilization.
 - Ramp stage: linear increase from 20% -> 100% over configurable window (default 10 minutes).
 - Control rule: if p90 latency increases by >15% between two sampling windows OR GPU queue depth / pending requests grows by >20% then decrease rate by 12% and hold for one stability window. If p90 stable and GPU util < target, increase by 6%.
 - Safety caps: if any GPU memory usage crosses 92% or CUDA OOM occurs, abort the run and flag for investigation.

- Percentile anchoring and trimming: compute p50/p90/p99 per-bucket and global. For reporting use trimmed-mean throughput (drop top and bottom 5% of sliding windows) and report both median and trimmed-mean. Avoid using simple mean token/sec as the only signal.

Anchors and checkpoints:

- Deterministic anchors: inject one anchor request every 30s per host (low volume). Anchors are static seeded prompts that traverse the same codepath and should be deterministic across model versions where semantics unchanged. Use anchor latency to align timelines between runs and detect thermal drift.

- Checkpoints: capture a checkpoint every 3 minutes: snapshot of GPU metrics (util, mem, temp), host CPU load, number of outstanding requests, and per-bucket p90. Store these to object storage with run id for post-run analysis.

Thermal and driver noise mitigation:

- Avoid back-to-back benchmark runs on the same hardware when possible. If unavoidable, insert a 15–30 minute cooldown or a synthetic idling period with small anchor traffic to let temperatures normalize.

- Record thermal sensors and driver version; include process-level cgroups/affinity so we can correlate OS scheduling noise.

Reproducibility checklist (pre-run):

- [ ] Confirm model binary and quantization flags.
- [ ] Confirm kernel selection pins (if any) and runtime environment variables.
- [ ] Reserve GPUs exclusively for the run or use dedicated capacity mode.
- [ ] Upload bucket fixtures (seeded prompts) to the harness artifact store and reference them by checksum.
- [ ] Schedule run start aligned to NTP-synced clock and note run-id.
- [ ] Warm-up the model with micro-primer (see warmup recipe below).

Warmup recipe (micro-primer + steady primer):

1) Micro-primer (3–5 minutes): single-threaded sequence of anchor prompts across all buckets to populate caches and kernel JIT caches. No concurrency, low QPS.
2) Concurrency primer (10 minutes): bring up per-bucket clients to 10% of target concurrency; ensure steady allocation of KV cache and confirm memory plateau.
3) Staircase ramp (5–10 minutes): increase to 50% and then to 80% with short holds at each step (60s). After this stage start adaptive rate controller.

Run duration and analysis windows:

- Minimum steady-state window: 20 minutes after reaching stable-adaptive state. This ensures capture of thermal and scheduling cycles.
- For final throughput numbers, compute metrics over the last 15 minutes of the steady-state window. Use the anchored trimmed-mean throughput and report per-bucket p50/p90/p99.

Failure modes and diagnostics:

- OOMs: capture model allocator logs, increase logging verbosity for that run, rerun with reduced concurrency and compare per-bucket memory footprints.
- Run-to-run drift: compare anchor latencies; if median anchor latency differs by >7% across runs, mark runs as non-comparable and investigate thermal or driver changes.
- High variance but stable median: inspect contention on host network, GC pauses, context switches; correlate host-level vmstat / iostat and perf counters.

Example run manifest (human readable):

run_id: resp-bucket-20241107-01
model: gptx-13b-quant-v2
buckets:
 - id: short, mix: 0.5, target_tokens_per_sec: 10k
 - id: med, mix: 0.35, target_tokens_per_sec: 18k
 - id: long, mix: 0.15, target_tokens_per_sec: 36k
anchor_probe_interval: 30s
checkpoint_interval: 180s
warmup: micro-primer(5m)->concurrency-primer(10m)->staircase(5m)
adaptive_controller: enabled
metrics_to_capture: [gpu_util, gpu_mem, p50/p90/p99, tokens/sec_by_bucket, anchors, host_cpu]

Post-run artifacts and analysis checklist:

- Raw loadgen traces (per-request latencies and sizes) saved to object storage.
- GPU telemetry and checkpoints.
- Anchor time series and checksum of anchor fixture used.
- Run summary CSV with per-bucket trimmed-mean throughput and percentiles.
- Comparison diff against baseline run-id and flagging of significant regressions (>5% throughput or >10% p90).

Open questions and TODOs:

- Determine best canonical bucket cutpoints for our most common customer workloads (produce a catalog).
- Explore automated mix resynthesis: given a customer RPS trace, synthesize an optimal bucket mix rather than sampling.
- Evaluate whether anchors can be made semantic-stable across model-family changes (fall-back anchors for incompatible models).

Notes and references:

- See related experiments: bench-harness/response-fingerprint-experiments (internal repo).
- This method is intentionally conservative: we prioritize signal clarity over micro-optimistic max throughput claims. Use it for engineering comparisons and SLA forecasting, not marketing headline numbers.

Contact: Eleanor Chen (eng-serving-runtime) for run templates, fixtures, and harness scripts.

title: Hotfix: disable INT8 profile on model variant x1 after quality regression
author: Priya Natarajan
text:
Context: During the Quantization Profile Library beta, Applied ML flagged a statistically significant regression on the Redwood internal prompt set ("support_summaries_v2") when enabling profile `qp_int8_calib_v3` on model variant `x1` (model id `rw-lm/atlas-7b`, variant `x1`). This aligns with a design partner report of output drift after enablement (see SUP-27411). We performed an immediate operational rollback by disabling the profile at the affected route(s) and verified recovery, but we also need a hard guardrail to prevent re-enable while we recalibrate/re-evaluate.

Incident references: Slack #incidents thread 1741684000 (quality regression alert during beta) and #eng-ml thread 1740068833 (bench + regression notes). This PR implements a targeted hotfix in the control-plane/policy layer so the profile cannot be applied for `atlas-7b:x1` even if referenced in route config. Runtime remains unchanged; behavior is deterministic: resolution returns baseline precision with an explicit blocked reason.

What changed: (1) Add a known-bad block entry for `model_id=rw-lm/atlas-7b`, `variant=x1`, `quant_profile_id=qp_int8_calib_v3` in the quantization profile constraints/allowlist used by the policy engine. (2) Update compatibility evaluation to treat "blocked" as a distinct outcome from "incompatible" so we can alert/observe separately (metrics tag + audit trail). (3) Add an operator note in the returned compatibility error message surfaced to Console/API (human-readable remediation: "Profile blocked due to quality regression; use default precision or select qp_int8_calib_v2").

Why this approach: Route-level disable is necessary but not sufficient (humans/automation can re-enable). A global kill-switch is too blunt; this is a surgical block with clear observability. This follows the fallback standard: baseline precision is always the safe default.

Risk/rollout notes: This is intended for the release train `release/2025.03` and should be cherry-picked to main after merge. No schema changes. Default behavior unchanged for all other models/variants/profiles. Existing routes that reference `qp_int8_calib_v3` on `atlas-7b:x1` will deterministically fall back to baseline on next config cache refresh.

Rollback notes: If we need to revert this hotfix, revert commit `b3f7c4a` ("block qp_int8_calib_v3 for atlas-7b:x1") and redeploy control-plane. Operationally, the fastest mitigation remains (a) disable profile at route level, and (b) if multiple routes are impacted unexpectedly, use the global kill-switch (ENG-5819 runbook).

Testing: Added unit tests for policy resolution outcomes: applied vs fallback(incompatible) vs fallback(blocked). Verified Console error copy via API snapshot tests. Ran staging smoke: create route config referencing blocked profile -> resolved profile outcome is baseline, metrics emit `quant_profile_resolution=blocked`.

Checklist: [x] Linked incident/support context. [x] Added tests. [x] Release manager sign-off for release/2025.03. [x] Post-merge: notify #eng-ml and #eng-sre; update beta design partner comms (PM-643).

Commits: 1) policy: add known-bad profile blocklist and resolution outcome 2) api: improve compatibility response message for blocked profile 3) tests: coverage for blocked vs incompatible outcome 4) ops: add dashboard tag note + runbook snippet update.

Changed areas (high-level): control-plane policy engine (quant profile constraints), route resolution response shaping, metrics tags, unit tests.

Review conversation (highlights): Arjun requested we scope the block to (model_id, variant, profile_id, profile_version) to avoid future unintended blocks; updated to include explicit `profile_version=3` match. Selene asked for explicit mention of the eval signal that triggered the block and to keep messaging consistent with regression thresholds doc; added note and standardized remediation text. Mina requested we ensure routing doesn't loop on fallback; confirmed we return baseline directly and included regression test from pr-18531 coverage. Connor requested a release note and a clear cherry-pick instruction; added to description and release_notes.

CI: Initially failed on `policy-engine-tests` due to a missing fixture update; fixed in follow-up commit. Final checks: build (pass), unit (pass), integration (pass), lint (pass).

Merge: Squash merged into `release/2025.03` by Connor O'Brien on 2025-03-15.

Prevents enabling quantization profile qp_int8_calib_v3 on model variant x1 via route settings (compatibility guardrail).
Improves operator-facing log/event when a profile is blocked due to known regression (includes remediation text).

author: Jordan Patel
text:
Purpose:
This is a pragmatic kickoff + simplification playbook for onboarding enterprise customers into Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem). The doc focuses on two parallel tracks: the customer network onboarding kickoff checklist and an internal refactor of our TF modules/state layout to reduce drift and speed upgrades. Draft notes, TODOs, and quick commands are mixed in — this is intentionally rough.

Scope and assumptions:
- Target: mid-size to large enterprise with dedicated VPC (single-region) and optional on-prem edge.
- We assume customer will provide: BGP peering parameters OR VPN termination config, CIDR ranges, KMS endpoint information, and an inventory of internal IP allowlists.
- This playbook is NOT a final runbook for airgapped installations (separate doc).

Kickoff checklist (customer-facing, run during first 1–2 calls):
1) Pre-kickoff packet sent (48h prior): short questionnaire for CIDRs, preferred regions, compliance controls, and contact list. Template: <= 1 page.
2) Network diagram sketch: customer internet edge -> transit VPC -> Redwood ingress VPC -> customer-private-subnets (examples below). Get initial CIDR acceptance.
3) SSH/IP allowlist: collect jump/proxy IPs and define access windows.
4) Certificate/KMS: confirm if customer wants to use their KMS (HSM) or Redwood-managed keys. If customer KMS, get IAM policies.
5) TF state preferences: customer-managed state (remote backend) vs Redwood-managed state. NOTE: prefer remote state for private installs to avoid large state migrations later.
6) SLA/Escalation: share SRE on-call rotation and expected RTO for onboarding incidents.

Minimal acceptance diagram (text):
- Transit (customer) --[VPN/BGP]--> Redwood Transit VPC (shared infra) --[VPC peering/PrivateLink]--> Customer tenant VPC hosting Redwood runtime.
- For on-prem, transit represented by SD-WAN appliance -> customer-edge-router -> peering to Redwood transit.

Terraform refactor notes (internal):
Goal: make TF modules more composable across customer topologies and reduce duplication during upgrades. Key points and migration path.
- Module split suggestion:
 - network/core: creates transit VPC, shared route tables, and baseline IAM
 - network/tenant: per-customer VPC, subnets, security groups, endpoint interfaces
 - infra/peering: peering + route propagation resources isolated so replacing peering logic has minimal blast radius
 - secrets/kms: wrapper module around KMS keys and policies (supports BYOK)
- Naming strategy: use stable logical names: redwood-<customer>-tenant-vpc, redwood-<customer>-transit, redwood-<customer>-efs etc. Avoid embedding numeric suffixes where avoidable.
- Variables: prefer structured flat variables (strings & lists) over maps-of-maps to keep plan/apply diffs readable. Example: var subnets = ["10.10.0.0/24", "10.10.1.0/24"] rather than complex map.
- State migration plan (high level):
 1) Create new backend for new module layout (s3/remote with locking).
 2) Import existing real resources into new module state using terraform import per resource id. Keep a running mapping sheet (spreadsheet linked in CON-4821).
 3) Run plan with -target to reconcile the new modules only.
 4) Small batch migration: 1–3 customers per week for the first month.
- Backwards compatibility: modules must accept legacy inputs for 2 release cycles; add validations to warn on deprecated params.

Upgrade and rolling deploy plan (customer tenant VPC changes and runtime upgrades):
- Objectives: zero-or-minimal downtime, predictable routing during kernel/instance upgrades, reversible steps.
- High-level pattern: blue/green-like networking: create new ASGs/instances in same VPC but different subnets/targets, warm caches, switch traffic via load-balancer DNS or route table modification.
- Steps for control-plane upgrade with minimal disruption:
 1) Validate health checks and readiness probes on staging images.
 2) Start 20% of new capacity in tenant VPC (warm).
 3) Gradually shift traffic using LB weight or route priorities (5–10% increments).
 4) Monitor token latency, KPIs, and error rates. Roll back if error rate > 1% over 5 minutes.
- Network-specific upgrades (route changes, peering updates): perform during low-traffic windows, preflight with traceroutes and BGP route dumps. Have rollback plan to restore previous route tables.

Preflight tests (minimum):
- From customer bastion: curl health endpoints for each service and run a 30-second generation load (sample prompt).
- Tracepath to model-serving endpoints, ensure expected path hits Redwood transit (confirm via next-hop).
- Verify KV/cache warming by issuing sequential requests that should hit cache (observe lower latencies).

Common pitfalls & notes to self:
- Customers often reuse small CIDR pools; insist on unique tenant CIDRs early.
- Buried dependency: some customer egress proxies terminate TLS and block mutual TLS to model-backend; confirm certificate passthrough requirements.
- TF gotcha: changing a subnet's availability zone can recreate resources. Prefer AZ-agnostic module designs where possible.

Runbook excerpts (quick commands):
- Verify peering: aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections --filters Name=requester-vpc-info.vpc-id,Values=<vpc-id>
- Check route tables: aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=<vpc-id>
- Terraform import example: terraform import module.network.module.tenant.aws_vpc.customer_vpc vpc-0abcd1234

Open questions (to decide on kickoff):
- Do we require customers to accept provider-side Flow Logs for initial onboarding? (privacy/legal may object)
- Default MTU settings for SD-WAN customers — use 1500 or 9001? Note: jumbo MTU can break path MTU discovery on legacy appliances.

Acceptance criteria for onboarding completion:
- Control plane: all Redwood services report healthy from customer bastion and from Redwood SRE probes.
- Performance: median token latency <= agreed SLO during baseline synthetic test.
- Security: customer KMS access validated and audit logs flowing for initial 7 days.
- Terraform: all resources managed in target backend with no drift alerts for 48 hours.

Next actions / TODOs:
- [ ] Draft short customer packet and send to sales/solutions for review (owner: Maya).
- [ ] Create GH PR to split terraform-modules (owner: Ethan) — start with network/core and network/tenant. See PR 142 for prototype.
- [ ] Schedule dry-run migration with internal staging tenant (owner: Priya) week of 2025-03-03.

Appendix: quick-example TF snippet (intent only)
```hcl
module "tenant" {
 source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//network/tenant?ref=modular-2025-alpha"
 name = "redwood-acme-tenant"
 cidrs = ["10.20.0.0/22"]
 public_subnets = ["10.20.0.0/24"]
 private_subnets = ["10.20.1.0/24"]
}
```
(End of draft)

title: Orbitline Technologies
author: Maya Chen
text:
Summary and background:
- Company: Orbitline Technologies — multi-tenant conversational agent product for SMB and mid-market customers (chat + app actions).
- GTM: sells to product teams; charges per-seat + usage-based API for heavy automation customers.
- Current stage: started with Hosted API evaluation; want clear upgrade path to Dedicated when 95th-percentile qps/concurrency grows.

Recent activity (bullets / shorthand):
- 2026-02-18: Intro call (Maya) — high-level product fit, gave quickstart + sample requests. Wants streaming + tool-calling for agent orchestration.
- 2026-02-25: Fireflies call (ff_9f7a2c0d) — demoed hosted streaming; they ran 2-hour soak with small tenant set. Observed intermittent chunk drops at ~200 concurrent ws connections.
- 2026-03-01: Demo (ff_2b4e1a7c) — SE (Elliot) showed function-calling reliability and fallback to non-streaming; customer asked about automatic fallback policies.
- 2026-03-04: Sent hosted pricing + estimated ARR slide deck (drive link). Awaiting internal budgeting.

Requirements & priorities (customer-stated):
- Latency SLOs: first-streamed-token <300ms for interactive agents; end-to-end response with tool calls <900ms (target).
- Streaming stability is top priority — need stable websocket or server-sent events for 100–500 concurrent streaming connections per tenant.
- Per-tenant quotas: per-tenant rate limits, burst windows, quota carryover and overridable burst allowances for higher-tier tenants. Need per-api-key metering and per-route quotas.
- Tool calling: reliable function-calling and deterministic retries; clear semantics for idempotency and long-running tool responses.
- Metrics & observability: token-level cost breakdown per tenant, per-route latency histograms, streaming error traces.
- Data controls: option to restrict EU customers to EU region (data residency), retention controls and audit logs. SSO/SAML mandatory for admin UI.

POC notes / results so far:
- POC conducted on Hosted API for rapid time-to-value. Used streaming + function calls with a small tenant replication sim (10 tenants).
- Observed: median first-byte latency ~120–180ms, 95th ~420ms under steady-state. Under burst test (200 concurrent streams) saw ~12% of streams drop or experience chunking issues — customer flagged streaming reliability.
- Function-calling worked for single-step actions; multi-step orchestration sometimes hit rate limits quickly with default quota settings.

Customer quotes & paraphrases:
- "We need streaming that doesn't drop mid-session — customers notice and churn."
- "Hosted is great to start; we need predictable unit costs and a migration plan to reserved capacity as we scale."

Next-step & commercial asks:
- Orbitline requests: Dedicated POC scoped to 500 concurrent streaming connections, per-tenant rate limiting demo, and a pricing band for committed capacity (monthly).
- Legal wants a copy of Redwood DPA + SOC2/ISO artifacts; security has follow-ups around KMS integration.

Blockers (short):
- Legal/DPA approval; Budget hold while VP Product confirms ARR; technical proof that streaming at 500 concurrent per-tenant is stable.

Action items (owner):
- Maya: schedule Dedicated POC kickoff week of 2026-03-15.
- Elliot (SE): prepare synthetic traffic profile (qps, concurrency, typical token length) and run internal stability test; demo per-tenant quota config.
- Product: share migration playbook (hosted -> dedicated) and per-tenant billing options doc.

References / links (stubs):
- Fireflies: ff_9f7a2c0d-orbitline-20260225, ff_2b4e1a7c-orbitline-demo-20260301
- Drive: drive://redwood/poc/orbitline-streaming-poc-deck
- Jira: RDW-2124 (streaming stability investigation)
- Gmail thread: gmail_thread_29d8b6-pricing-questions

raw_metadata.next_step: Schedule Dedicated POC (2 weeks) and capture qps/concurrency + sample traffic; provide dedicated pricing band; legal to review DPA.

title: Stillwater Dialogue
author: Maya Chen
text:
Lead source: inbound signup + demo request from in-app widget. CTO (Evan Marquez) + Eng lead (Priya Nambiar) on call 2026-02-18.

- Cost sensitivity: startup budget, expects pay-as-you-go; interested in cost per 1k tokens and potential token batching suggestions.
- Model preference: prefer smaller low-latency variants (eg Llama 2-Chat family or similar) with good safety defaults.
- Routing: want single-region routing (us-west) initially; may add eu later.

title: Data Sovereignty Routing Mosaic: tenant-scoped EU residency + tier fallback
author: Asha Patel
text:
Problem: Customers with EU-only data residency and regulatory constraints require every inference request to stay within EU jurisdictions and forbid cross-border model execution. Current routing can accidentally route to non-EU capacity during degraded states or bursting, and some tenant-level allow/deny controls are not expressive enough for mixed-tier fallbacks.

Goal: Implement a 'Routing Mosaic' policy layer that deterministically enforces tenant-scoped residency constraints while supporting tier-aware fallbacks to compatible model variants (EU-hosted, quantized/local replicas) without violating egress constraints. Provide a clear config schema, runtime enforcement hooks, observability, and a safe rollout path.

Scope: design and implement the policy evaluator and runtime gating (policy + enforcement) for Redwood's request router. This includes: 1) tenant-level residency policy evaluation, 2) per-tenant allowlist/denylist for regions and edge-fallbacks, 3) tier routing rules (hosted/dedicated/private) with precedence, 4) automatic variant mapping to EU-compatible model alternatives when primary is not available, and 5) audit logging and alerts for policy violations.

Out of scope: billing model changes, long-term UI for editing granular policies (console tweaks will be follow-up PM work).

Routing Mosaic policy accepts tenant config and computes a deterministic routing decision that never routes EU-residency traffic outside EU zones.
When primary capacity is unavailable, router selects a model variant that is EU-hosted or runs in-customer VPC; if none exist, request is rejected with specific HTTP 451-like error and audit log entry.
Config supports tenant allowlists and denylists for regions and tiers with clear precedence rules; tests validate precedence matrix.
End-to-end integration tests covering normal, degraded, and burst scenarios; no cross-region egress observed in test harness.
Observability: per-tenant routing decisions logged, metric exposed for 'policy-enforced-fallback' and dashboard created in console-2025.02 release.
Performance: policy evaluation adds <1ms median latency at router injection point under 95th percentile load (validated in benchmark harness).

Policy model: decorators combined into a small expression language: residency == EU AND tenant.blocked_regions NOT CONTAINS eu-west-1 => allow EU-only routing; default deny-exit.
Precedence: tenant-level denylist > tenant-level allowlist > default org policy > global emergency-exit flag.
Fallback mapping: primary model -> candidate variants list ordered by (region affinity, model-compatibility, cost-tier). The runtime will only pick variants that satisfy 'residency' predicate.
Enforcement points: router decision service (fast path), and enforcement middleware at gateway to reject any accidental non-compliant handoffs between internal services.
Audit: immutable audit record with decision reason, policy version, selected variant id (or rejection code), and trace id. Records stored in append-only EU region bucket for customers with residency=EU.
Config schema chosen to be human-editable YAML via console later; for now accept JSON via control-plane API and via tenant bootstrap files for Private deployments.

example config:
{
 "tenant_id": "acct_123",
 "residency": "EU_ONLY",
 "allow_regions": ["eu-west-1", "eu-central-1"],
 "deny_regions": [],
 "tier_routing": {
 "preferred": ["private", "dedicated", "hosted"],
 "allow_burst_to_lower_tier": false
 },
 "fallback_variants": [
 {"id": "model-x-eu-quant", "region": "eu-central-1", "compatible_with": ["model-x"]},
 {"id": "model-x-eu-fp16", "region": "eu-west-1", "compatible_with": ["model-x"]}
 ],
 "emergency_passthrough_allowed": false
}

Notes: router will reject any decision that would cause egress from EU when residency==EU_ONLY. 

1) Feature-flag the policy evaluator behind 'routing_mosaic' gate (control-plane flag).
2) Deploy policy evaluator to staging and run synthetic traffic harness with residency-indexed probes across burst scenarios.
3) Onboard 1 internal tenant (non-customer) with EU_ONLY to validate logs and dashboards (2-week canary).
4) Gradually enable for small customers that opt-in with rollback window; monitor 'policy-violation' metrics and latency regressions.
5) After 4 weeks of stability, flip global default to enforce for all tenants that declare residency=EU_ONLY and document migration steps for Dedicated and Private customers.

Unit: policy expression evaluator matrix tests for residency/allow/deny/tier precedence (coverage >= 95%).
Integration: router + serving runtime harness where we simulate primary capacity OOS and ensure fallback to EU variant occurs or request is denied with 451-like error with decision code 'RESIDENCY_NOCOMPAT'.
Load: policy evaluator stress test at QPS similar to router peak with latency SLAs measured (95th percentile < 3ms per evaluation).
Audit replay: ability to replay audit logs to assert no cross-region egress in test traces.

If fallback variants are not pre-provisioned in EU, requests will be rejected causing customer-facing errors. Mitigation: preflight validator to ensure tenant has at least one compatible EU variant before enabling policy.
Performance overhead if policy evaluator becomes a blocking call on the hot path. Mitigation: cache decisions by (tenant, route, model, token_prefix_hash) and ensure TTLs are conservative.
Operational complexity for Dedicated/Private customers with mixed-region resources. Mitigation: provide validators and a mapping CLI to register local variants.

Metric: redwood.routing.policy.enforced_count (tags: tenant_id, region, reason)
Metric: redwood.routing.policy.violation_count (alerts if > 0 for a tenant with residency=EU_ONLY)
Dashboard: per-tenant routing decisions, recent audit events table, 95th latency of policy eval, and fallback selection histogram.
Alert: pager if any tenant with residency=EU_ONLY observes >5 policy_rejections in 5m window or any 'egress_detected' audit flag.

2025-02-12 Asha Patel: initial draft of goal and acceptance criteria. Added config schema example for discussion.
2025-02-20 Liam O'Connor: added enforcement middleware note and audit storage requirement for EU-only tenants. Asked infra for append-only bucket construction (ticket INF-709).
2025-02-27 Marta Becker (Security): requested threat model and SSO key rotation notes; flagged security_review_required.
2025-03-04 Liam O'Connor: adjusted rollout to include internal canary and added metric names for observability team.

title: Design Spec: Model Version Rollouts (Canonical Plan Template)
author: Monica Patel
text:
h1. Overview
This page defines the canonical rollout plan template for introducing a new LLM model version behind an existing model name (alias) or introducing a new model endpoint that will receive production traffic. It is intended to be copied into a new rollout plan page per change.

h1. When this template is required
Use this template for any of the following:
* Changing the default version behind a model alias
* Introducing a new version that will receive >0% external customer traffic
* Changing routing policy or fallback behavior in a way that affects customer requests

h1. Rollout plan template (copy/paste)

h2. 1) Summary
* What is changing?
* Why now?
* Expected customer impact (best-case and worst-case)
* Who is on point during rollout (name + Slack channel)

h2. 2) Scope
* Environments: Hosted / Dedicated / Private
* Regions impacted
* Customer tiers or allowlists (if any)
* Request types: chat, completions, embeddings, rerank (as applicable)

h2. 3) Versioning and compatibility
* Model alias (if any)
* New version identifier (e.g., rw-llama-3-70b@2025-10-01)
* Backward compatibility notes (tool calling schema, output formatting, tokenization differences)
* Max context and max output token limits

h2. 4) Success criteria (must be explicit thresholds)
Define pass/fail thresholds for each category and the evaluation window. Minimum required categories:
* Reliability: 5xx rate, timeouts, admission rejects
* Latency: p50/p95 end-to-end and time-to-first-token for streaming
* Cost/efficiency: tokens/sec/GPU, cache hit rate, batch efficiency
* Quality: regression guardrail (eval set delta) and customer-reported issues

Include a table with thresholds (example):
||Metric||Window||Pass threshold||Fail threshold||Owner||
|p95 latency|30 min|<= +5% vs baseline|> +10% vs baseline|SRE oncall|
|5xx rate|30 min|<= +0.05% absolute|> +0.2% absolute|Platform oncall|
|Quality score (internal eval)|per run|>= baseline - 0.3|< baseline - 0.7|Applied ML|

h2. 5) Monitoring and dashboards
* Links to dashboards (by service/model/region)
* Alerts to enable (list)
* Trace/log queries for fast triage
* Who watches what at each ramp step

h2. 6) Rollout strategy
* Canary design: what % first, for how long, and what signals decide next step
* Ramp schedule (with timestamps)
* Controls: per-customer allowlist, per-region traffic caps, concurrency caps
* A/B test plan (if used): experiment id, assignment, evaluation criteria

h2. 7) Rollback and fallback
* Rollback trigger conditions (must map to thresholds)
* Rollback procedure reference (runbook link)
* Fallback policy (automatic): target version(s), ordering, and constraints
* What happens for in-flight requests and streaming responses

h2. 8) Customer communications
* Which customers must be notified (Dedicated/Private, contractually sensitive)
* Channel: email, support ticket, status page, in-product banner
* Timeline: before/at/after rollout
* Message content requirements: change summary, risk, opt-out/pinning path, support contact

h2. 9) Approvals
* Change class (per policy)
* Approvers and timestamps
* Approved change window

h2. 10) Post-rollout validation
* Final KPIs after full ramp
* Customer feedback summary
* Follow-up tasks and owners

h1. Notes
* The plan should be treated as the source of truth during an incident.
* If any section is not applicable, write N/A with a brief justification.

title: Bluecrest production latency & error surge — immediate RCA and owners
author: irene_choi
text:
From: Tom Hargreaves <tom.h@bluecrest.com>
To: irene.choi@redwood.com
Cc: elena@bluecrest.com, sre@bluecrest.com
Date: Tue, 22 Jun 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Production: checkout latency spike + errors (us-west)

Irene —

We started seeing a severe degradation in checkout experience at ~08:45 PDT: p50/generation latency jumped from ~120ms to ~900ms, p95 above 3.2s, and our 5m error rate climbed to ~8%. Throughput for the feature dropped ~40% relative to baseline which is causing visible failures in our checkout flow.

title: Calibration run ephemeral snapshots & delegated access handover for FP8/INT8 validation
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Define and implement a first-class lifecycle for calibration job runs and their artifacts in Redwood Console that supports ephemeral snapshots (TTL-driven), controlled handover of artifacts for external review, and accuracy-gated promotion for FP8 and INT8 quantization profiles. The goal is to reduce storage cost, improve auditability for regulated customers, and enable safe delegated access during model validation without creating long-lived, ungoverned artifacts.

Calibration campaigns for multi-tenant customers generate many intermediate artifacts: traces, calibration histograms, per-layer calibration tables, and quant profiles (FP8/INT8). Currently artifacts are stored indefinitely or require manual cleanup. Customers and internal teams have asked for: 1) TTL policies per run, 2) a secure way to share ephemeral artifacts with auditors or model owners, 3) explicit accuracy gating to prevent regressions when promoting quant profiles to production variants. There have been multiple cost spikes and at least one compliance audit finding related to long-lived developmental artifacts.

- Controlled lifecycle for calibration runs and their artifacts (snapshots, logs, quant profiles).
- UI controls in Console to configure per-run TTL and retention tiers (ephemeral, short-term, permanent).
- Delegated access tokens and one-click signed export links for temporary reviewer access.
- Accuracy gating: configurable metric thresholds (e.g., perplexity delta, token-level error rates) and an automated promotion path when thresholds are met.
- Audit logging of all access, exports, promotions, and GC events.
- RBAC surface for who can extend TTLs, promote artifacts, and request exports.

- Re-architecting the calibration executor itself (compute optimizations).
- Cross-tenant artifact sharing beyond delegated read-only exports.
- Long-term cold storage tiering costs (billing will be handled by a separate initiative).

1) Run snapshot model: when a calibration run completes, create a signed, immutable snapshot object with metadata (run_id, model_version, profile_type FP8/INT8, metrics).
2) Allow per-run TTL (default 30d ephemeral) with auto-GC; UI and API to extend or pin snapshots.
3) Delegated access: create time-limited, signed access tokens (link-based) with scope read-only and optional download bundle. Tokens appear in the run timeline and can be revoked; creation requires permission.
4) Accuracy gating: add a promotion workflow that evaluates run metrics against a configurable threshold set attached to the target model alias. Promotion writes promotion events to audit and creates a signed promoted-artifact tag.
5) Audit & retention: every snapshot action (create, export, extend, revoke, promote, GC) produces an audit record (user, ip, action, timestamp) surfaced in Console and exported to customer audit logs (when enabled).

Console: per-run TTL selector visible on run summary and configurable via API
Default TTL set to 30 days for ephemeral snapshots; system GC reclaims artifacts after TTL without manual intervention
Delegated access links are single-use or time-limited and revocable; creation requires 'can_create_exports' RBAC permission
Promotion workflow enforces accuracy gates: attempt to promote a quant profile that fails threshold must be blocked and logged
Audit trail contains action, actor, run_id, artifact_id, and IP; logs exportable to customer S3/KMS integration
E2E tests cover run snapshot creation, TTL expiry, link issuance, link revocation, and promotion success/failure paths
Security review completed and any cryptographic signing using customer KMS keys verified in Private deployments

Unit tests for snapshot metadata creation and TTL enforcement
Integration tests: simulate calibration runs (FP8/INT8), assert artifact bundle created and accessible via link
Security tests: link forgery/resilience, revocation behavior, signed export verification
Load test: create 10k ephemeral snapshots and run GC cycle to validate throughput and S3/listing performance
User acceptance: PM + Design review of Console flows with sample customer (ACME Health)

Phase 1 (internal beta): feature behind feature-flag for Redwood internal teams and early adopter customers
Phase 2 (selected customers): opt-in for customers with calibration volume > X/month; gather feedback and telemetry
Phase 3 (general availability): enable default TTL, RBAC enforced; announce in release notes and migration guide
Migration: provide a one-time bulk 'pin' tool for customers to mark existing artifacts as permanent before GA

Record: action, actor, artifact_id, run_id, model_version, metrics snapshot at time of action
Retention of audit logs configurable per-customer (default 365 days)
Forward audit entries to customer-preferred sink (S3, Splunk, Datadog) when configured
Tamper-evident signing of promotion and export events in Private deployments using customer KMS

Existing artifacts older than new default TTL should not be auto-deleted until a migration window; provide 'pin' CLI and Console flow
Create backend job to backfill snapshot metadata for historical runs to enable TTL application
Communicate with customers 30 days prior to any cleanup GC run that will remove artifacts older than new TTL
