title: Adaptive Authority Runtime and Audit Proxy for RBAC v2
author: Ava Martinez
text:
Build a compact, high-throughput policy evaluation runtime and a sidecar-like audit proxy to enforce RBAC v2 across API, runtime, and console surfaces. Goals: 1) deterministic, low-latency authorization checks for per-request policy decisions; 2) rich, tamper-evident audit events emitted for every decision; 3) easy integration points for SSO/SAML identity assertions and admin controls; 4) seamless rollouts with canarying and automatic fallback to safe defaults. This ticket covers the runtime evaluator, a lightweight authorization middleware (gRPC/HTTP) used by runtime and API, the audit enrichment service, and console integration hooks for admin-level controls.

Scope:
- Implement a compact policy evaluator that supports the RBAC v2 rule model, attribute-based conditions, and versioned policy bundles.
- Provide a pluggable adapter layer so console/API/runtime can call the same evaluation surface (HTTP/gRPC).
- Implement evaluation caching (per-request token KV + short-lived result cache) with invalidation tied to policy bundle updates.
- Build Audit Proxy that records decision context (actor, principal attributes, request path, model, route, cache_hit, decision_reason) and streams events to our audit pipeline (Kafka). Events must be signed/hmaced for integrity before leaving the host.
- Add SSO/SAML hooks: normalize identity claims from IdP into a canonical principal structure consumed by evaluator.
- Admin controls: expose runtime flags (allowlist overrides, emergency breakglass) that can be toggled from Console and surface in audit logs.
- Observability: per-eval latency histograms, cache hit ratio, bundle load times, and error traces.

Out of scope for this ticket: long-term policy authoring UI, migration of existing RBAC policies (will be a follow-up), and cross-region audit archival retention policy (ops work).

Authorization middleware implements gRPC + HTTP endpoints and responds with allow/deny/conditional decisions in <5ms median under synthetic load
Policy bundles can be uploaded and versioned; evaluation uses the pinned bundle version for a tenancy
Audit Proxy emits signed JSON events to Kafka topic 'audit.decisions' and events include canonical principal, request metadata, cache_hit, and policy_version
SAML/SSO adapter normalizes at least two IdP claim formats (Okta, OneLogin) in staging and produces a canonical principal for evaluation
Admin breakglass toggle is callable from Console REST and is evaluated with higher precedence than normal rules
Canary rollout path: 10% of requests routed to new evaluator for 48 hours with auto-rollback on error rate >0.5% or p99 eval latency increase >2x
Unit and integration tests cover evaluator logic, cache invalidation, audit signing, and SSO normalization paths
Documentation: design doc and runbook published, and a migration checklist for existing policies added to docs link

Policy language: choose a simplified JSON-based rule format (fast parse) with an optional Rego translation layer for complex policies; keep evaluator implementation native to reduce overhead
Evaluation architecture: single-file in-memory index per tenant loaded by versioned bundle, deterministic rule ordering to avoid flakiness
Cache strategy: LRU per-process cache keyed by (principal_hash, resource, action, policy_version), TTL 30s, explicit invalidation on bundle update
Audit integrity: events HMAC-signed using node-local key rotated weekly and published hash to audit-metadata topic for verification
SSO normalization: implement an adapter interface with schema mapping rules; perform attribute mapping in middleware before calling evaluator
Admin controls: persisted in config service with change events broadcast over the same bundle bus to ensure consistent enforcement
Failure modes: on evaluator crash or timeout, default to deny for console admin APIs and fail-open for non-admin read-only inference requests with an auditable 'fail_open' flag
Performance target: median eval latency <5ms, p99 <15ms under 5000 RPS per-node synthetic workload
Security review: include threat model for audit tampering, bundle poisoning, and SSO claim spoofing

2026-03-04 Design feedback (E. Patel): proposed admin breakglass precedence needs explicit ordering semantics, added to acceptance criteria
2026-03-06 Security review kickoff: scheduled with Security Team. Initial concerns on HMAC key rotation and cross-host verification; plan to publish signature metadata to Kafka
2026-03-09 QA: integration test harness added; discovered cache invalidation race when bundle updates coincide with high load. Marcus to implement bundle epoch check in evaluator

title: Weekly release train: cut process, RC tagging, and release-notes automation
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Goal: Define and implement a repeatable weekly release train and automated RC-cut workflow for Redwood runtime releases, including RC tagging conventions, release-notes generation, and gating policies for canary rollouts and LTS promotions. Background: we currently make ad-hoc cuts which creates churn for support, inconsistent release notes, and manual gating for canaries. This ticket consolidates the cut checklist, implements CI jobs to create RC tags and draft release notes, wires a Slack notification and release dashboard, and defines rollforward/rollback playbooks. Out of scope: full UI for release creation in Console (follow-up ticket planned).

A weekly CI job creates a candidate RC tag automatically from the main branch on the scheduled cadence
Release notes are generated automatically from merged PR metadata and a curated changelog template and published as a draft to the releases page
Cut process includes automated pre-cut checks: passing smoke e2e, no failing canary alerts, and <0.5% increase in error budget burn during testing window
Canary rollout automation accepts gating signals (SLO, errors, latency) and can pause/rollback without manual intervention
LTS promotion flow requires explicit manual approval and is gated by a stability window and regression metrics

Draft formal weekly cadence doc: cut window, freeze rules, owner rotation (on-call + release lead)
Implement CI pipeline (github actions) to tag RCs using pattern runtime-{major}.{minor}.{patch}-rc{n}
Build release-notes generator that aggregates PR titles, changelog labels, and manual highlights; output markdown and Confluence entry
Add pre-cut automated checks: e2e-smoke, integration-tests, canary-metrics sanity check
Create canary rollout job in Argo Rollouts / our orchestration layer with metric-based gates
Add manual LTS promotion job with approval step and checklist
Document rollback and emergency cut process in runbook and link to incident playbooks

Tagging strategy: semantic-major.minor.patch with separate -rc counter to allow multiple candidates per patch; this minimizes user-facing ambiguity while preserving history
Release notes source: PR metadata + changelog labels (chore/bug/feat/regression) with manual highlights section for PM/Eng lead review
Canary gating: rely on platform SLOs (p95 latency, error-rate) emitted to metrics pipeline instead of ad-hoc smoke scripts to keep automation consistent
LTS policy: promote to LTS only after 4 weekly stable releases and explicit SRE signoff to avoid premature promotions

title: Private VPC upgrade preflight runbook and limited-egress compatibility matrix
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Background: Customers running Redwood Private in sealed or limited-egress VPCs need a deterministic, operator-friendly preflight that validates networking, time/auth dependencies, artifact access modes, and operatorless/offline upgrade constraints before a scheduled upgrade window. Goal: Deliver a prescriptive preflight runbook + machine-readable compatibility matrix that both SRE/ops and customers can run to determine whether an upgrade can proceed or requires a mirrored artifact/rollback plan. Out of scope: full operator rework, image signing implementation (covered elsewhere), and multi-region bandwidth provisioning. Success criteria: >95% of staged upgrades in our lab produce a deterministic PASS/FAIL with remediation hints; customers using the runbook report a measurable reduction in upgrade rollbacks during the first 90 days after rollout.

A1: A human-readable preflight runbook exists with step-by-step checks for: DNS resolution, NTP synchronization, limited-egress mirror verification, TLS cert chain validation, KMS access test (or documented offline KMS rotation procedure), and operator health probe checks.
A2: A machine-readable compatibility matrix (CSV/JSON) enumerates allowed egress hosts, ports, protocols, minimal bandwidth and latency tolerances, and artifact distribution modes (mirror, airgap bundle, bastion fetch).
A3: An automated preflight tool (CLI) executes the runbook checks and emits a PASS/FAIL plus structured remediation hints and a non-zero exit code for gating CI/CD. The tool must be able to run in airgapped mode with a pre-seeded artifact manifest.
A4: Canary validation performed in the lab across three network profiles: Full-egress (control), Limited-egress (mirror allowed to specific hosts), and No-egress (airgapped). Each profile must have documented test outcomes and rollback signal criteria.
A5: The runbook documents operatorless upgrade steps for customers who run the operator in passive mode: how to stage images, verify checksums/signatures, and trigger the local upgrade with deterministic rollback markers.
A6: Telemetry and minimum logs required for post-upgrade triage are specified and can be toggled on in restricted telemetry mode (PII redaction noted).
A7: Runbook and matrix reviewed and signed off by: Network Reliability (ENG), Security (compliance), and Solutions Engineering. Sign-offs are recorded in the ticket comments and linked artifacts.
A8: Integration tests validating preflight tool behavior are added to the private-deploy CI harness and pass in the three network profiles without flakes for 5 consecutive runs.
A9: Customer-facing runbook artifact (Confluence) and downloadable airgap bundle checklist are published in docs.redwood.ai with versioned release notes.
A10: Measurable guardrail: if preflight returns FAIL for any critical check, the upgrade automation must not progress without a manual override and documented exception approval recorded in the operator logs.

Decision: We will ship the runbook and matrix first, followed by the CLI preflight tool in a patch release. Rationale: writing the checks clarifies edge cases and lets customers manually validate earlier.
Trade-off: Complete offline operatorless upgrade automation would delay delivery by 6+ weeks. We opt for documented deterministic steps plus an automated checker for common failure modes.
Risk: Bandwidth shaping and simulated partitions in lab may not capture every customer topology; mitigation includes providing a clear escalation playbook and a list of recommended mirror SaaS/VM appliances.
Implementation note: The compatibility matrix will be versioned and include a "recommended mitigation" column (e.g., local mirror, AST artifact bundle, physical media) to keep guidance prescriptive.
Owner: PM to maintain runbook; ENG to provide CLI; Solutions Eng to author customer checklist variants.

2026-02-20: Draft created after design sync; initial scope includes runbook + compatibility matrix + CLI preflight tool specification.
2026-02-25: Engineering feasibility review — confirmed feasible to emit structured preflight output; estimate revised to 5 points for PM/ENG scope split.
2026-03-01: Security provided requirement list for KMS/manifest verification and telemetry redaction constraints; added airgapped manifest mode to acceptance criteria.
2026-03-04: DevOps completed a first-pass lab canary plan (3 profiles) and documented required test harness changes; flagged bandwidth simulation as risk.
2026-03-08: Solutions Engineering trialed a customer mirror setup and provided two example mirror host patterns; updated compatibility matrix with mirror host allowlist examples.
2026-03-10: Ticket entered In Review; preparing sign-offs from Network Reliability and Security.

QA Lead - Jin Park (2026-03-07): Planned CI jobs for three profiles; flagged flaky DNS tests — recommended adding deterministic resolver stubs in lab harness.

title: Evidence Collection Procedure: Retention Controls + Audit Logs (Baseline Compliance Pack)
author: Olga Petrov
text:
## Purpose
This page defines the repeatable, customer-safe procedure to generate and validate evidence for:
- Retention policy configuration (current state + change history)
- Audit log exports for defined windows and templates
- Verification that retention enforcement (TTL/purge jobs) is operating as expected

This procedure is used for:
- Baseline compliance reporting pack generation (customer-facing)
- Internal audits (SOC 2 / ISO-style evidence requests)
- Security questionnaire follow-ups where standardized artifacts reduce back-and-forth

## Scope
In-scope evidence sources:
- Retention Policy Service (control plane) export: tenant retention settings across supported data classes
- Audit log storage + audit-log-exporter: time-windowed exports (filtered per template)
- Retention enforcement verification metrics + dashboards (SRE-owned)

Out of scope (handled via other procedures):
- Full data inventory / RoPA updates
- Per-field redaction verification (covered by Logging Standards + SDLC controls)
- “Bring your own GRC” integrations beyond export formats

## Ownership + frequency
**Primary owner (GRC):** Olga Petrov
**Technical owners:** Kevin Osei (retention exports + audit-log-exporter), Marcus Lin (SecEng sign-off)
**Operational owner:** Sean Gallagher (SRE for purge/TTL verification)
**Evidence assembler:** Daniel Carter

**Recommended cadence:**
- **Quarterly:** Generate full baseline pack for internal control testing (or when requested by audit).
- **Per customer request:** Generate pack within **5 business days** unless otherwise committed in contract.
- **After material change:** Re-generate pack when retention defaults, supported data classes, audit log schemas, or exporter templates change.

## Access requirements (RBAC)
To execute all steps, you need:
- Access to Redwood Console (Security & Compliance → Retention, Audit Logs, Compliance Pack)
- API credentials for the Retention Policy Service export endpoint (read-only)
- Permission to run audit-log-exporter jobs and fetch output artifacts
- Read access to retention verification dashboards

Approvals:
- If using break-glass access: follow the Security break-glass procedure and ensure audit trail is recorded.
- If evidence includes customer identifiers, store outputs in restricted locations only (see “Storage and handling”).

## Storage and handling (customer-safe)
All generated artifacts must be stored in a restricted evidence location and shared using customer-approved channels.

**Internal storage:**
- Google Drive → Shared drives → Security & Compliance → Evidence → <CustomerName> → <YYYY-MM-DD>
- Access: GRC + SecEng + named requesters only

**Customer delivery:**
- Only deliver the “Customer Package” bundle (see Output format). Do not include raw internal dashboards or internal incident notes.

**Retention of evidence packages:**
- Internal evidence packages are retained per the Security/GRC evidence retention standard (typically 7 years unless otherwise specified). This is separate from product retention controls.

## Output format (what you should end up with)
Deliverables for a standard request should include:
1) **Retention configuration export** (JSON + human-readable summary)
2) **Audit log export** (CSV or JSONL depending on template) for the requested time window
3) **Verification evidence** (screenshots or exported metrics) demonstrating purge health + TTL lag within thresholds
4) **Evidence checklist** completed (who/when/what)

Naming convention:
- `redwood-compliance-pack_<customer>_<env>_<region>_<YYYY-MM-DD>_v<packVersion>.zip`
- Examples:
 - `redwood-compliance-pack_northbridge-bank_dedicated_us-east-1_2025-03-02_v1.0.zip`

## Pre-flight checklist (before collecting anything)
1. Confirm request scope:
 - Customer name + tenant/org ID
 - Deployment mode: Hosted / Dedicated / Private
 - Regions in scope (data residency)
 - Time window for audit logs (start/end timestamps, timezone)
 - Templates required (e.g., Admin Actions, API Key Events, Policy Changes)

2. Confirm there is no active **legal hold** affecting deletion evidence interpretation.
 - If legal hold exists, include hold metadata in the package and note that deletes may be paused for held objects.

3. Confirm retention policy is stable for the window:
 - If customer is actively editing retention settings, take an export immediately after changes and note timestamp.

## Step 1 — Export retention configuration (control plane)
### Option A (preferred): Console export
1) Open **Redwood Console → Security & Compliance → Retention**
2) Select tenant/org
3) Click **Export retention configuration**
4) Choose:
 - Format: `JSON`
 - Include: `effective policy`, `validation constraints`, `change history (last 90 days)`
5) Download and save as:
 - `retention-config_<tenant>_<YYYY-MM-DD>.json`

### Option B: API export (for automation / Private)
Use the Retention Policy Service export endpoint.

Example (illustrative):
- Endpoint: `GET /v1/orgs/{org_id}/retention:export`
- Query params:
 - `include_change_history=true`
 - `change_history_window_days=90`

cURL example:
- `curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
 "https://control-plane.redwood.example/v1/orgs/$ORG_ID/retention:export?include_change_history=true&change_history_window_days=90" \
 -o retention-config_${ORG_ID}_$(date +%F).json`

### Validate the export
Confirm the export includes:
- Export timestamp
- Deployment mode + regions
- Supported data classes and their TTL settings (e.g., request/response logs, audit logs, traces/metrics)
- Any exceptions (e.g., disabled logging, legal hold markers, immutable audit log minimums)
- Change history entries (who/what/when) for the requested window

If anything is missing, stop and file an issue with the owner:
- Retention export issues → Kevin Osei
- Policy schema/validation issues → Jordan Lee / Ethan Park

## Step 2 — Export audit logs for the requested window
### Choose the correct report template
Use the standardized templates defined in **Audit Log Exporter Report Templates** (linked above).

Common templates:
- **Admin & RBAC changes** (role changes, permission grants)
- **Credential events** (API keys created/rotated/revoked)
- **Retention policy changes** (create/update/delete policy, legal hold toggles)
- **Console access events** (interactive admin actions)

### Run audit-log-exporter (Hosted/Dedicated)
1) Determine the source:
 - Audit log store: production audit log cluster for the tenant’s region
2) Run exporter with:
 - Time window: `start_at`, `end_at` (UTC preferred)
 - Filters: `org_id`, `actor_type`, `event_types` per template
 - Output format: CSV for customer readability unless JSONL is explicitly requested

Example (illustrative CLI):
- `audit-log-exporter run \
 --org $ORG_ID \
 --template rbac_admin_changes \
 --start "2025-02-01T00:00:00Z" \
 --end "2025-03-01T00:00:00Z" \
 --format csv \
 --out audit-logs_${ORG_ID}_rbac_admin_changes_2025-02-01_2025-03-01.csv`

3) Verify export integrity:
 - File is non-empty (unless customer expects none; document that)
 - Columns include: `timestamp`, `event_type`, `actor`, `target`, `result`, `ip/region` (as applicable)
 - No internal-only fields are included (exporter should enforce template schema)

### Run audit-log-exporter (Private)
For Private deployments, the exporter may run in the customer’s environment.
1) Provide the customer with:
 - Template name(s)
 - Expected command and required parameters
 - Expected output schema
2) Request that customer returns the exported artifact OR (preferred) have Solutions Engineering run it inside their environment per agreed access.
3) Record who executed the export and where it ran.

## Step 3 — Attach retention config to audit log evidence package
To support security questionnaires, the baseline pack bundles the retention configuration export alongside audit log exports.

1) Ensure both artifacts are in the same folder:
 - `retention-config_<org>_<YYYY-MM-DD>.json`
 - `audit-logs_<org>_<template>_<start>_<end>.<csv|jsonl>`
2) Confirm timestamps:
 - Export timestamps should be recorded in the package manifest (see Step 6)

## Step 4 — Verify retention enforcement health (TTL + purge jobs)
This step provides evidence that retention settings are not “paper controls” and that enforcement is operating.

### Dashboards to use
Use the Retention Controls Verification dashboards (linked above). At minimum capture the following panels for the tenant’s region(s):
- TTL lag (how far past TTL data remains before deletion)
- Purge job success rate
- Purge backlog size
- Purge error rate (by store)

### Metrics to capture (minimum set)
Capture screenshots or exports showing:
- `ttl_lag_seconds` (p95 and max)
- `purge_rows_deleted` (daily trend)
- `purge_failures` (count + rate)
- Backlog indicator (queue depth / rows pending)

### Acceptance thresholds (baseline)
If customer-specific SLOs exist, use those. Otherwise use baseline expectations:
- **Purge failures:** sustained error rate < 1% over 24h
- **TTL lag:** p95 < 24h for core stores (request logs, audit logs) unless a maintenance event occurred (note exception)
- **Backlog:** not monotonically increasing over 48h

### Procedure
1) Select region and store type (request logs, audit logs, traces/metrics where applicable)
2) Set time window:
 - For customer pack: last 7 days (unless requested otherwise)
 - For incident follow-up: last 30 days
3) Capture evidence:
 - Export dashboard panel image(s) OR CSV export of the metrics query
4) Document anomalies:
 - If thresholds are not met, include a short explanation and link to any resolved incident or maintenance note (customer-safe).
 - If there is a known backlog event (e.g., post-maintenance), include the remediation summary and current status.

## Step 5 — Cross-check: retention policy vs enforcement signals
This step ties configuration to enforcement.

1) From retention-config export, record effective TTLs for:
 - Audit logs
 - Request/response logs (if enabled)
 - Traces/metrics (if in scope for the tenant)
2) Confirm the verification dashboard shows:
 - Purge jobs enabled for those stores
 - No “policy drift” alerts (effective policy != evaluated policy)
3) If drift is detected:
 - Stop and notify: Logan Wright (Telemetry) + Sean Gallagher (SRE) + Kevin Osei
 - Do not ship customer package until drift is explained and documented

## Step 6 — Assemble the evidence package + manifest
Create a simple manifest file (human-readable) and bundle all artifacts.

Manifest template (copy/paste and fill):
- **Customer / Org ID:** <...>
- **Deployment mode:** Hosted | Dedicated | Private
- **Regions included:** <...>
- **Requested by:** <Name, email/role>
- **Prepared by:** <Name>
- **Reviewed by:** <Name>
- **Prepared on:** <YYYY-MM-DD>
- **Audit log window:** <start/end, timezone>
- **Audit templates included:** <list>
- **Retention config export timestamp:** <...>
- **Dashboard evidence window:** <...>
- **Notes / exceptions:** <legal hold, maintenance windows, known issues>

Recommended folder structure:
- `/01_retention/retention-config_<org>_<date>.json`
- `/02_audit_logs/audit-logs_<org>_<template>_<start>_<end>.csv`
- `/03_verification/retention-verification_<org>_<region>_<date>.pdf` (or images)
- `/04_manifest/manifest_<org>_<date>.txt`

## Step 7 — Review and sign-off
Minimum review steps:
1) **Security review (Marcus Lin or delegate):**
 - Confirms exports do not include internal-only fields
 - Confirms time windows and templates match request
2) **GRC review (Olga Petrov):**
 - Confirms completeness against the baseline checklist
 - Confirms storage and sharing controls were followed

For high-stakes enterprise deals, include Product sign-off (Naomi Feldman) if the request implies new commitments.

## Troubleshooting guide
### Export is missing expected event types
- Check if template filter is too narrow.
- Confirm audit-log-exporter version supports requested event types.
- Escalate to Kevin Osei with:
 - Org ID, region, template, time window, and a sample of expected events.

### TTL lag is elevated
- Check for recent maintenance windows or backpressure in purge jobs.
- Review purge job logs and backlog panel.
- If sustained beyond baseline, escalate to SRE (Sean Gallagher) and Telemetry (Logan Wright).

### Retention policy export doesn’t match Console view
- Possible caching or policy evaluation propagation delay.
- Re-export after 10 minutes; confirm policy change history.
- Escalate to Control Plane owners (Ethan Park / Jordan Lee) with export timestamps.

## Audit trail requirements
Every evidence collection run must be traceable.
Record (in the manifest and in the GRC tracker):
- Who initiated request
- Who generated exports (and from where)
- The exact time window and templates
- Hashes of artifacts (optional but recommended for internal audits)

## Revision history
- 2025-02-12: Initial published procedure (baseline pack MVP)
- 2025-03-08: Added enforcement thresholds + drift check; clarified Private execution model

title: add-dependency-health-gate-and-slim-builder-for-ci-images
author: Priya Narayanan
text:
Introduce a pre-merge dependency-health gate to fail PRs with high-severity unresolved vulnerabilities and add a slim multi-stage builder image to reduce CI image size and speed up workflows. No user-facing runtime changes.

Motivation: CI has been brittle due to three root causes: transient dependency vulnerabilities that slip through until release, long docker build times and cache churn from large base images, and duplicated build steps across workflows. This PR introduces a lightweight pre-merge 'dependency-health' gate and a slim multi-stage CI builder image that other workflows can reuse. The dependency gate runs fast checks (lockfile integrity, top-level license issues, and a vulnerability scan that flags critical/urgent CVEs). The slim builder reduces image size by removing dev-only packages and consolidating language runtimes into a single, cache-friendly layer. The goal is to reduce CI flakiness, cut median CI image build time by ~40%, and prevent high-severity vulnerabilities from reaching main. Summary of changes: - Add .github/workflows/dependency-health.yml: pre-merge job that runs lockfile-check, dep-tree-lint, oss-vuln-scan and posts a clear status and remediation hints. - Add docker/ci/Dockerfile.slim: multi-stage builder that uses the current official base but extracts only runtime artifacts and installs tooling in a separate layer to maximize cache reuse. - Update .github/workflows/ci-lint.yml and ci-test.yml to use the slim builder image from the registry for build/test steps; fall back to local build when registry image is not available. - Add scripts/dep-health.sh and scripts/fix-lockfile.sh for consistent checks across CI and local dev. - Update ci/README.md with instructions to run the dependency gate locally and how to regenerate the slim image. - Small helper: .github/actions/cache-keying: tweak to include slim image tag so cache hits are more reliable. Checklist: - [x] Add dependency-health workflow and scripts - [x] Add multi-stage slim Dockerfile and publish step in ci-builder workflow - [x] Wire existing CI jobs to use slim image when available - [x] Add helpful failure messages and remediation links - [x] Update docs and READMEs - [x] Add tests for lockfile-check script Commits (high-level): 1) add dependency-health workflow and basic scripts (dep-health.sh, fix-lockfile.sh) 2) introduce docker/ci/Dockerfile.slim and builder workflow 3) hook workflows (ci-lint, ci-test) to try pulling the slim image and fallback to local build 4) CI cache-keying tweaks + docs Updates to files (high-level): - .github/workflows/dependency-health.yml (new) - .github/workflows/ci-builder.yml (new step to publish slim image) - .github/workflows/ci-lint.yml (modified to pull slim image) - .github/workflows/ci-test.yml (modified to pull slim image) - docker/ci/Dockerfile.slim (new) - scripts/dep-health.sh (new) - scripts/fix-lockfile.sh (new) - ci/README.md (updated) - .github/actions/cache-keying/action.yml (tweaked) Review conversation (abridged): - Ethan Cole (review): "Nice approach. A couple of questions: can the vuln scan be rate-limited? also we should avoid failing PRs on moderate severities until we have a triage path." - Author (Priya): "Good points. The oss-vuln-scan is configured to only fail on CRITICAL/URGENT by default; I've added a flag to optionally escalate MODERATE for high-risk repos, but the default is conservative. Added docs that explain how to change the threshold via repo settings." - Marta Rossi (review): "Slim image looks good. I hit a missing build-tool in the slim image when running tests locally (node-gyp)." - Author: "Thanks — added a small build-tools layer for optional dev-only dependencies that is present in the CI image but not in runtime images. The ci-builder publishes two tags: :slim and :slim-dev; workflows pick :slim first and fall back to :slim-dev if a dev-step needs compilation." - Jinsoo Park (review): "Lockfile checksum check is great. We should make the output machine-readable for automation (JSON)." - Author: "Updated dep-health.sh to emit a compact JSON summary when CI sets REPORT_JSON=1, and the workflow uploads it as an artifact for easier triage." CI run history (selected): - First run (on creation): dependency-health job passed, builder publish failed due to registry creds (CI failed) - Push fix (add secret lookup): second run passed dependency-health and successfully published :slim-dev but failed a lint step because cache key missed (cache-miss increased time) - Final run (after cache-key tweak): all CI jobs passed; ci-lint and ci-test used pulled :slim image and median build time on the PR pipeline dropped ~43% measured across 10 runs. Edge cases and notes: - For forks: dependency-health is run in a reduced-mode that only runs local checks (no secret access for publishing); this was documented and the workflow early-returns with a clear message. - Renovate: I added a note in ci/README to recommend enabling renovate's "pr-body" policy so dependency gate output is easier to find on automated updates. - Rollout plan: enable the gate as required for all non-trivial repos (redwood/*) in a staged fashion; initially opt-in for 'redwood-examples' and 'redwood-sdk-*' to monitor false positives. - Security: oss-vuln-scan is a thin wrapper around our internal vulnerability provider; no secrets were added to the scripts; scanning is done via public CVE feeds and the results are solely used to set a PR status. - Backwards compatibility: workflows fall back to the prior local build path when the slim image pull fails. Testing performed: - Local run of dep-health.sh against a purposely modified lockfile to ensure failure path returns non-zero and produces a JSON report. - End-to-end run on the PR with builder publish to staging registry. - Manual smoke test of ci-lint and ci-test pulling the slim image. Next steps (post-merge): - Roll the dependency-health gate to more repositories and add a dashboard showing gate failures by repo. - Add automated annotations that link failing CVEs to remediation tips in the PR UI. - Consider auto-PR creation for safe upgrades (majority non-breaking) once we have triage rules. Overall this PR is primarily CI/ops-level change: no application code changes. It consolidates a few CI patterns and introduces a safety gate to reduce risk from dependency churn.

Ethan: Can the vuln scan be rate-limited? Avoid failing on moderate until triage in place.
Priya: Configured to fail only on CRITICAL/URGENT by default and added docs for threshold.
Marta: Missing node-gyp in slim image when running tests locally.
Priya: Added optional dev layer and published :slim-dev tag; workflows prefer :slim then fall back to :slim-dev.
Jinsoo: Make lockfile checksum output machine-readable (JSON).
Priya: dep-health.sh now supports REPORT_JSON=1 and uploads artifact.

initial run: dependency-health passed; builder publish failed (registry creds)
second run: published :slim-dev; lint job failed due to cache key miss
final run: all checks passed; ci-lint and ci-test used pulled :slim image; median image build time down ~43%

title: support
text:
jordan_customer: Hey — noticed a weird billing/credits mismatch for org_acme_123. Dashboard (Usage > Promo credits) shows 2,400 promo credits remaining, but invoice inv_00AXY finalized yesterday consumed promo credits and left a post-invoice promo_remaining: 0. No subscription change on our side. Can someone take a look?

elaine_support: Thanks Jordan — can you paste the org id + invoice id and a sample request id from the window? Also were those mostly completions or embeddings?

jordan_customer: org_id: org_acme_123, invoice: inv_00AXY, invoice_ts: 2064827000. Mostly completions, a couple small embeddings. Sample request id: req_abc123. Dashboard snapshot time (top-right) showed promo snapshot 2064825000 reporting 2400.

kevin_billing: pulling ledger now. Quick note: our invoice finalizer applies credit buckets in a specific order (reserved -> expiring promos -> non-expiring promos). We recently changed ordering for backfills. Are you expecting FIFO? @mira_engineer can you check token-metering vs invoice aggregator for req_abc123?

mira_engineer: Looking at req_abc123. Token-meter shows total_tokens: 25000, promo_deduct: 25000, free_pool_used: 0, post_invoice_balance: 0. Dashboard cache snapshot and ledger state may have diverged due to a backfill job. Can you run the usage API for that time window and paste the raw? Example:

```
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/usage?org=org_acme_123&start=2064824000&end=2064828000"
```

jordan_customer: ran the call, got: `{\n "org": "org_acme_123",\n "total_tokens": 25120,\n "promo_applied": 25000,\n "promo_remaining": 0,\n "last_snapshot_ts": 2064825000\n}`. But UI still shows 2400. Promo metadata in dashboard shows promoA (id promo_A_77) expiring 2065000000.

kevin_billing: OK I can see an invoice finalizer job at 2064827200 that consumed credits. There's also a backfill ledger mutation (rollback/reapply) for a previous promo (promo_B_02) at 2064827100 that reallocated 2400 credits between internal buckets. Looks like the backfill and finalizer ran concurrently and finalizer consumed the credits after the reallocation, leaving the UI cache stale. This is a race between backfill + invoice finalization.

elaine_support: TL;DR repro: 1) Customer had two promos (promoB older, promoA newer). 2) Ops ran a backfill/rollback on promoB to fix an earlier misallocation (this created a backdated ledger mutation). 3) Invoice finalizer ran and, because the ledger snapshot occurred after the backfill, it applied credits from the adjusted bucket and zeroed out the promoA balance in the finalized invoice. Dashboard cache still had the old snapshot until UI cache refresh.

mira_engineer: Proposed immediate mitigation: restore the original ledger state for those 2400 credits and issue an invoice adjustment credit (adj_INV_204) to reverse the unexpected consumption. Longer term: change invoice finalizer to take an atomic snapshot before applying backfills, and/or reorder backfill jobs to avoid running during invoice finalization windows. Filing a bug.

kevin_billing: Filed BL-789 to track. I'm issuing a manual credit of 2,400 promo tokens to org_acme_123 now and generating an invoice adjustment adj_INV_204. Jordan — will that be OK while we root-cause?

jordan_customer: That would help, thanks. Also can we get a note or banner in the UI about possible 5-10 minute lag after invoice finalization/backfills? We rely on live promo counts for throttling customer flows.

ops-bot: Incident BL-789 created by kevin_billing. Priority: high. Assigned: mira_engineer, elaine_support.

mira_engineer: Temporary fix applied: created ledger credit tx_restore_7745 and invoice adj_INV_204. Verified usage API now returns `promo_remaining: 2400` and ledger shows tx_restore_7745. Waiting for billing-cache TTL to expire (<10m) for UI to reflect change.

jordan_customer: Confirmed UI updated — promo shows 2,400 again. Thanks for the quick turnaround :heart: :raised_hands:

elaine_support: Closing once billing confirms final reconciliation on next run. Follow-up items: add audit-log link for promo ledger mutations in dashboard, and push a patch to invoice finalizer to snapshot prior to backfills.

kevin_billing: Notes for internal triage: BL-789 -> root cause: concurrent backfill + invoice finalizer ordering. Impact: visible promo mismatch for small number of orgs, possible transient negative post-invoice promo_remaining in API. Fix: atomic snapshot + backfill scheduling.

mira_engineer: I'll pair with infra on a small change: invoice-finalizer will now create a read-only snapshot key `invoice_snapshot_ts` before accepting any ledger mutations for the same invoice window. Rolling this to prod tomorrow off-hours.

jordan_customer: Appreciate the detail & fix. Will open a support ticket if anything pops up during our next billing cycle.

elaine_support: Marking thread resolved for now. If anything else appears please reopen. :thumbsup:

title: Back-of-Envelope fidelity pad — quick checks and oddities
author: Amir Haddad
text:
Purpose: quick, scribbly notebook for fast fidelity checks and capturing weirds. Not polished — mostly brain-on-paper.

Top-level hypothesis:
- Recent rollout of kq8 quant profile seems to increase terse hallucinations on short-context prompts (~<80 tokens) when the prompt includes enumerated lists.
- Observable signal: sudden drop in precision for fact recall (dates/names) accompanied by an increase in confidence tokens (e.g., 'definitely') in the same output.

Quick ad-hoc rubric (0–3) — use for small batches (20–50 samples):
- Correctness (facts preserved) 0/1/2/3
- Conservatism (avoids hallucination) 0/1/2/3
- Fluency (grammatical + coherent) 0/1/2/3
- Brevity alignment (matches expected length) 0/1/2/3
- Safety/TOX (no policy violations) 0/1/2/3

Scoring notes: 0 = unacceptable, 3 = production-quality. For quick runs, average across samples; flag any sample with Correctness <= 1.

Recent micro-run (2025-11-29): 40 samples, seed sampling, avg temperature=0.2, model variant=kq8-fast (deployed canary)
- Avg Correctness: 1.7
- Avg Conservatism: 2.5
- Avg Fluency: 2.9
- Brevity: 2.2
- Safety: 3.0

Notable failure modes (examples):
1) Prompt: "List the first three presidents of Xland and the year each took office."
 - Expected: names + years from canonical doc.
 - Output (kq8-fast): "A. Harkin (1991), B. Marlow (1995), C. Trel (1999)." — invented names, confident tone.
 - Rubric: Correctness=0, Conservatism=0, Fluency=3
 - Quick thought: prefix cache or quant rounding might be biasing towards short, name-like tokens. Check vocab merges around proper nouns.

2) Prompt: "Short pros/cons bullets for switching to dedicated instances for inference"
 - Output: reasonable bullets but occasionally repeats the same bullet with slightly changed wording (duplication).
 - Rubric: Correctness=2, Conservatism=2, Fluency=2
 - Note: duplication frequency has risen post-kernel-update-3. Could be decoding artifact with narrower beam? Need to compare decoding knobs.

3) Prompt: "What's the weather like today in Oslo?" (short chat)
 - Output: specific temperature and precipitation details (hallucinated).
 - Rubric: Correctness=0 (should say to check live API), Conservatism=0
 - Note: model is overconfident on ephemeral facts; perhaps calibration regressed. Flag for quality monitor.

Micro-bisect log (quick):
- 2025-11-30 09:12 — reran 20-sample batch on kq8-stable (older kernel): avg Correctness 2.6 — big delta vs kq8-fast.
- 2025-11-30 09:45 — swapped tokenizer from v2 -> v2b (minor merges) on kq8-fast: no obvious improvement.
- 2025-11-30 10:20 — lowered chunking window (KV flush policy) for short contexts: slight improvement in duplication but not in invented facts.

Hypotheses to test (next quick experiments):
- Run head-to-head with fp16 baseline on identical hardware for 100 short factual prompts (setup: temp=0.0, greedy). Measure precision of named entities.
- Check tokenization boundaries for common surname prefixes — are certain merges causing tokenization to favor rare-name token completions?
- Run calibration probe: ask for verifiable facts followed by "I might be wrong" and measure decline in confident assertions.

Actionable short-term checklist: 
- [ ] Create a JIRA ticket with 5 failing prompt examples and link to this doc (JIRA-ML-987 placeholder).
- [ ] Schedule 30-min sync with serving-runtime to reproduce on dedicated staging (include kq8-fast and fp16).
- [ ] Push 2 samples from each failure mode to eval dashboard (tag: "kq8-fast-regression").
- [ ] Add a quick guard in rollout: for canary > 5% of short-fact failures, auto-fallback to stable.

Notes-to-self / loose ideas:
- Might be worth adding an explicit heuristic to avoid single-token proper-noun completions when prompt contains a list indicator ("1.", "-", etc.).
- For the duplication issue: try a brief run with repetition_penalty=1.5 + top_p 0.95 and observe.

Unresolved questions:
- Is the hallucination spike correlated with particular hardware (A100 vs H100)? Need telemetry join.
- Could a small change in past-kv-serialization quant noise cause rare proper-noun drift? (ask infra about kernel rounding).

If I had a spare hour: run 200 prompts in parallel across the 3 variants and produce a quick chart of correctness vs latency to show product folks. For now — this is the scribble.

Footer: short-term memory: remind to move top 3 reproducible fails into confluence page CONFLUENCE-1234 and ping Enzo.

title: Lingua Nimbus CX
author: Riley Chen
text:
Background: leading European SaaS provider for omnichannel contact centers; growth in Nordics + France.
Top priorities: accurate locale-aware translation (not just literal), tone adaptation for regions (FR polite vs. UK informal), and reliable tool-calling from agent UI (ticket updates, macro application).
POC scope: evaluate translation fidelity, latency under surge (Black Friday sim), and integration with existing CRM macros.
Security: MUST meet GDPR residency for FR customers; SSO (SAML) + audit trail + KMS for keys. Prefer private control plane for EU customers.
Quote from Elena: "We need translations that preserve customer sentiment and escalate tone when appropriate — not flattened machine output."
Current stack: homegrown message bus, Salesforce for CRM, in-house macro service, Postgres for ticket store. Want Redwood runtime to call macros and write back ticket summaries.
Decision drivers: 1) can Redwood maintain p95 latency under 200ms at 300 concurrent agents? 2) clear routing/fallback to smaller / cheaper models without losing escalation quality. 3) support for on-prem/EU nodes + KMS integration.
Procurement notes: Legal requested sample DPA and SOC2 evidence; Security wants an infra runbook for on-prem deployment.
Voice from SE on last demo: response quality good on en/fr/es; two failure modes observed on es-xx locale idioms (needs prompt tuning).

Run 2-week POC with EU on-prem nodes; SRE deep-dive + security checklist sign-off

title: Intermittent serving degradation from tenant burst exposing autoscale sizing gap
text:
Issue summary:
Customer CloudPaper AI reports repeated timeouts (client 504) and elevated p95/p99 token latency for requests pinned to their dedicated GPU reservation between 2026-03-09 22:00 UTC and ongoing. Impact is intermittent but recurring during tenant-driven bursts.

Impact:
- Multiple production requests timing out (504) and streaming disconnects reported by the customer.
- Elevated p95 (2.3s -> 7s) and p99 tail spikes up to 18s for short text generation endpoints.
- Customer facing UX regressions and increased error rate; they asked for urgent mitigation.

Environment:
- Dedicated reservation: redwood-dedicated-cc-prod-09 (4x A100s), us-east cluster
- Customer traffic pattern: frequent long-sequence streaming jobs and a handful of concurrent long-stream sessions from a single tenant process.
- Autoscale policy: target based on pod GPU utilization (avg), min_replicas=1, max_replicas=6, cooldown=300s.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Tenant issues a sudden burst of 30 concurrent long-seq streaming requests (seq_len ~ 2048).
2) Pods serving the tenant show near-saturation on SM% and kernel queuing increases.
3) Autoscaler does not scale quickly because average GPU util stays under threshold (due to a mix of idle short requests and a few saturated pods).
4) Scheduler queues requests, micro-batches overlap, KV cache thrash observed, leading to p95/p99 spikes and 504s.

Observed behavior:
- GPU SM% per-saturated pod >95% for sustained periods.
- Cluster-level GPU utilization averaged ~62% (below autoscale trigger).
- Request queue depth on the per-tenant routing queue climbed >200 for short windows.
- Streaming sessions aborted after client-side 30s timeout (customer SDK default).

Expected behavior:
- Autoscaler should react to per-pod saturation or queue length and bring up capacity fast enough to maintain p95 below 2s for this workload pattern.

Artifacts attached / logs referenced:
- Grafana dashboards: serving/runtime/p95, node/gpu-sm, autoscale/activity (links provided to customer and infra).
- Sample traces: trace IDs provided to SRE channel.
- Kernel logs: show repeated SM stalls and occasional nvlink retries.

Initial triage summary:
- Hypothesis: Autoscaler policy relying solely on average GPU utilization masks localized saturation caused by uneven traffic distribution (noisy tenant).
- Secondary contributor: Long-sequence streaming jobs hold GPU context and induce KV cache churn that increases effective per-request cost.
- Immediate mitigation options: temporary tenant isolation (soft reservation), add per-tenant queue-based scaling metric, or increase min_replicas for this reservation.

2026-03-10 Elena Park (Support): Received report from CloudPaper AI. They included example request IDs and SDK logs showing client 504s. Marking P1 and escalating to SRE because customer is on dedicated reservation.
2026-03-10 Marcus Li (SRE): Acknowledged. Pulling relevant dashboards and queue metrics. Asked customer for exact request IDs and timestamps (provided). Assigned to Marcus Li (SRE) and Triage team.
2026-03-10 Marcus Li (SRE): Observed sustained SM% spikes on two pods pinned to cloudpaper-tenant shard. Cluster-level util is moderate; per-pod distribution is skewed. Uploading screenshots to ticket and #support-us-east channel.
2026-03-11 Support: Notified customer we are investigating and proposed a short-term mitigation: increase min_replicas to 2 for the reservation and enable tenant soft-reservation. Customer approved temporary change.
2026-03-11 Ops (Automation): Applied temporary override: redwood-dedicated-cc-prod-09 min_replicas=2 for CloudPaper AI reservation. Observed immediate reduction in p95 from ~7s to ~2.4s during a smaller repeat burst. Metrics attached.
2026-03-11 Marcus Li (SRE): Performed deeper trace analysis. Found queue depth spikes correlate with long-seq streaming sessions from a small set of client IPs. Autoscaler cooldown of 300s prevented fast scaling during short spikes. Filed follow-up action to change scaling signal to include per-pod 95th percentile GPU latency / request queue length.
2026-03-12 Product (Platform): Proposed autoscaler enhancement RFC to consider per-pod latency and queue backlog as scaling signals. Referenced PR #4802 that adds a queue-based metric collector (staging validation in progress).
2026-03-12 CloudPaper AI (Customer): Confirmed temporary improvement but requested a durable fix. Asked for timeline for autoscale change or a recommended long-term reservation sizing guideline.
2026-03-12 Marcus Li (SRE): Committed to two-track plan: 1) short-term policy change + reservation sizing recommendation within 48 hours, 2) medium-term autoscaler change in ~2-3 sprints with a canary rollout. Added related_confluence link for runbook updates.

Checked serving-runtime logs for noisy-tenant markers: tenant_id=cloudpaper-42 shows high long-seq session counts at 2026-03-09 22:03-22:18 UTC.
Kernel telemetry: increased SM stalls and higher memory copy times on affected pods; nvlink errors transient but not primary root cause.
Autoscaler analysis: current metric is cluster_avg_gpu_utilization. This allowed saturated pods to be masked by idle or low-util pods in the same reservation.
KV cache observations: repeated cache misses when requests hit newly scaled pods, causing additional token latency for affected sessions.
Reproduction in staging: simulated 25 concurrent long-seq streams; observed same pattern when autoscale uses average util with long cooldowns. Changing scale signal to per-pod 90th percentile GPU latency reduced tail significantly.
Related historical tickets: see SUP-9271 (sustained throughput drop), SUP-48210 (pipeline saturation). Patterns overlap but root cause here is autoscale signal masking localized saturation.

Temporary mitigation applied: min_replicas increased to 2 for the customer's reservation and soft-reservation applied to reduce noisy-tenant spillover. Customer reports immediate improvement; p95 back to ~2s in observed windows.

Planned permanent fixes:
- Short term: provide CloudPaper AI sizing guidance (recommend increasing reserved GPUs for sustained long-seq workloads or using smaller per-stream batching) and update runbook. ETA: 48 hours.
- Medium term: implement autoscaler to include per-pod queue-length / p95 latency as a scaling signal and reduce cooldown for surge handling. PR #4802 implementing queue-based metric collector is in review; canary rollout scheduled for next sprint.

Follow-ups:
- Update Dedicated Autoscale Runbook to include noisy-tenant isolation steps.
- Consider per-tenant soft reservations for heavy long-seq workflows.
- Track action item ENG-OPS-1753 to validate autoscaler changes across 2 clusters.

2026-03-11: Temporary min_replicas=2 override rolled for customer reservation by ops-automation; watch metrics for 24h.
2026-03-12: Customer confirmed reduction in error rate; remaining action is product change to autoscaler and runbook update.
ENG-OPS-1753 created to track autoscaler enhancement and runbook updates.

title: ADR-013: Incident Bot v2 diagnostics data sources, permissions, and audit requirements
author: Kaitlyn Nguyen
text:
## Status
Published.

## Date
2025-02-14 (last updated 2025-04-08)

## Owners
- Primary: Security Eng / Authn & Authz (Kaitlyn Nguyen)
- Co-owners: SRE Incident Automation (Miles Thornton), Platform Control Plane (Ethan Park)

## Problem statement
Incident Bot v2 will automatically attach deploy context, tenant-safe config diffs, and saturation/telemetry signals to incident threads (#incidents and #eng-oncall). To do this safely and reliably, we need to decide:
1) Which internal systems are the sources of truth for each data type.
2) How the bot authenticates and is authorized to access these sources (least privilege, tenant isolation).
3) What audit events must be emitted for compliance and incident review.
4) What alternatives we are explicitly not choosing (and why).

This ADR governs production access for Incident Bot v2 diagnostics only. It does not change who can declare incidents, page, or manage incident metadata.

## Decision summary
Incident Bot v2 will retrieve diagnostics data only through well-defined service APIs (no direct DB queries) using a dedicated service identity with narrowly-scoped permissions. Privileged reads (tenant-aware config diffs and tenant-scoped telemetry) must emit structured audit events to the central audit log pipeline.

Data sources are:
- Deploy context: Deploy Metadata Export API (Release Engineering) + Service Registry lookup
- Config diffs: Config Service Diff API (Platform Control Plane) with server-side redaction
- Telemetry/saturation signals: Telemetry Query Service (Telemetry Platform) with query budgets + tenant-safe primitives
- Error budget burn / SLO links: SLO Toolkit Link Generator (SRE)

Access is:
- Default: least-privilege bot scopes, tenant-safe fields only, redacted diffs, bounded telemetry queries
- Elevated (break-glass): time-bound on-call escalation for Sev0/Sev1 incidents to access expanded config diff context (still redacted for secrets/PII) with additional audit requirements

## Context and requirements
### Functional requirements
- The bot must attach a consistent “first 5 minutes” context payload for common incident classes:
 - Deploy regressions (recent deploys, canary status, commit SHA, related PRs)
 - Misconfiguration (feature flags, routing policy, quotas/rate limits, model pins) via diffs
 - Saturation (GPU utilization, KV cache pressure, queue depth, scheduler/backpressure) + dashboard links

### Security/compliance requirements
- Strict tenant isolation: bot must not be able to enumerate other tenants or leak customer-specific details into Slack.
- Slack is considered an internal tool but not a system of record for sensitive configuration. Therefore:
 - Config diffs must be redacted server-side.
 - Bot output must be “customer/tenant-safe by default”.
- All privileged access must be auditable:
 - Who/what accessed which tenant/service, from which Slack thread/incident context, at what time.
 - The reason and severity level when break-glass is used.

### Reliability requirements
- Bot must remain usable during partial outages and elevated error rates:
 - timeouts/retries/backoff
 - caching and request coalescing
 - graceful degradation: link to dashboards instead of live queries when upstream is unhealthy
- Telemetry query cardinality and cost must be bounded.

## Chosen data sources
### Source-of-truth mapping
| Data needed | Source | Access method | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Recent deploys (service, image SHA, rollout phase, canary state) | Deploy Metadata Export (Release Eng) | Internal HTTP API: `deploy-metadata-export` | Primary source for “what changed”. No tenant data.
| Service ownership + canonical service identifiers | Service Registry | Internal HTTP API: `service-registry` | Avoids joining deploy events by ad hoc tags.
| Tenant-safe config diffs (flags, routing policy, quotas, model pins) | Config Service | Internal HTTP API: `config-service/diff` | Server-side redaction + allowlist.
| GPU saturation + queue depth + KV cache pressure + scheduler backpressure | Telemetry Query Service | Internal HTTP API: `telemetry-query-service` | Enforces query templates, budgets, and label constraints.
| SLO/error budget burn links | SLO Toolkit | Internal HTTP API: `slo-toolkit/link` | Produces parameterized URLs; no direct TSDB queries.

### Rationale for each source
1) **Deploy Metadata Export** was chosen over scraping CI/CD logs or GitHub because it directly encodes rollout phase/canary status and is already normalized for service/region.
2) **Config Service Diff API** was chosen over reading from the config store directly because redaction and authorization must be enforced centrally and consistently.
3) **Telemetry Query Service** was chosen over allowing the bot to query Prometheus/Clickhouse/Datadog directly because we need query budget enforcement, template constraints, caching, and a stable interface across deployment modes.
4) **SLO Toolkit** was chosen over embedding complex dashboard URL logic in the bot because it centralizes link formats and ensures consistent region/route/time-window parameters.

## Permission model
### Identity
Incident Bot v2 runs as a non-human service identity:
- Name: `svc-incident-bot`
- Environment: prod/staging identities are separate
- Auth mechanism: mTLS + short-lived service tokens (issued via internal identity provider)
- Slack: bot uses Slack app credentials for message rendering, but all internal data fetches must use the service identity above.

### Authorization: scopes and policies
Access is granted using service-to-service scopes. The bot will not have broad read access; it will have only the minimal diagnostics scopes.

#### Baseline scopes (always enabled)
- `deploy.read:metadata` (read-only deploy context)
- `service-registry.read` (service lookup)
- `config.read:diff_redacted` (tenant-safe diffs only; enforced allowlist)
- `telemetry.read:diagnostics_templates` (only pre-approved query templates; bounded)
- `slo.read:link_generator` (URL generation only)

#### Restricted scopes (break-glass)
- `config.read:diff_expanded_redacted` (expanded diff context; still secrets/PII redacted)
- `telemetry.read:tenant_scoped` (tenant-scoped telemetry templates with stricter budgets)

Break-glass is allowed only for:
- Incident severity: Sev0 or Sev1
- Time window: max 60 minutes per activation
- Approved actors: on-call SRE and delegated incident commander roles
- Mandatory justification: incident ID + short free-text reason

### Where authorization is enforced
- **Config Service** enforces tenant boundaries and redaction. Bot is never allowed to request raw config values for sensitive keys.
- **Telemetry Query Service** enforces template selection, label constraints (no unbounded labels), and query budgets.
- **Deploy Metadata Export** is read-only and contains no tenant-specific customer data; still requires service authentication.

### Tenant isolation rules
- The bot may request tenant context only when it can bind the request to a specific incident thread payload (service + region + tenant ID as provided by incident command metadata or explicit user input).
- The bot may not:
 - list tenants
 - search tenants by name/email/domain
 - query across all tenants for “top offenders”

### Redaction rules (config diffs)
Config diffs returned to the bot must be safe for Slack by default.

Server-side redaction requirements:
- Always redact:
 - secrets/keys/tokens/certs
 - any value matching known secret patterns (high-entropy strings, JWT-like forms)
 - customer identifiers beyond Redwood tenant ID (e.g., email domains, org names) unless explicitly allowlisted
- Allowlist categories (examples):
 - feature flag boolean state and rollout percentage
 - routing policy target model/version pins (as internal model IDs)
 - quota/rate-limit numeric thresholds (no customer PII)

Diff output constraints:
- Truncate large diffs (default: first 50 changed fields) and provide “expand” action which still returns redacted results.

## Audit logging requirements
### Audit event triggers
An audit event must be emitted when Incident Bot v2 performs any of the following:
- Reads a tenant-scoped config diff (baseline or break-glass)
- Uses break-glass to access expanded config diff context
- Executes tenant-scoped telemetry templates (break-glass)

Deploy metadata reads and SLO link generation do not require audit events by default because they are not tenant-sensitive; however, service-level access logs must still exist for operational debugging.

### Required audit event fields
Each audit event must include (minimum):
- `event_name` (e.g., `incident_bot.config_diff.read`)
- `timestamp`
- `actor_type` = `service`
- `actor_id` = `svc-incident-bot`
- `requesting_user` (if initiated by an interactive Slack action): Redwood user ID and Slack user ID
- `incident_id` and `slack_thread_ts` (or message permalink)
- `severity` (Sev0–Sev3) when available
- `tenant_id` (Redwood tenant ID)
- `service` / `route` / `region` (as applicable)
- `scope_used` (baseline vs break-glass scope)
- `result` (success/denied/error/timeout)
- `redaction_applied` (true/false) and `redaction_profile_version`

### Retention and review
- Retention: align with Security audit log retention policy (see “Incident Bot access audit”).
- Review:
 - Security Engineering performs monthly sampling for break-glass usage.
 - SRE leadership reviews any spike in denied requests or unusual tenant access patterns.

## Considered alternatives (and why we rejected them)
### A) Direct database reads from config store or deploy tables
Rejected.
- Violates least-privilege and makes redaction/authorization harder to centralize.
- Creates tight coupling between bot and storage schemas.
- Increases blast radius if bot is compromised.

### B) Allow the bot to query the primary metrics backend directly
Rejected.
- High risk of expensive queries and cardinality blowups during incidents.
- Hard to constrain queries without a dedicated query gateway.
- Query templates and caching are necessary to keep bot reliable under load.

### C) Have responders run manual slash commands with personal credentials
Rejected as the primary path (still allowed as fallback).
- Inconsistent output and high cognitive load.
- Adds friction during the first 5 minutes.
- Personal credential usage complicates auditing and increases the chance of accidental leakage into Slack.

### D) Render diagnostics only in Console (not in Slack)
Rejected.
- Slack is the operational control plane during incidents. Requiring context switching delays triage.
- Console deep links are still required, but Slack needs the summarized “card” view.

## Consequences
### Positive
- Strong security posture with tenant-safe defaults and centrally enforced redaction.
- Clear operational boundaries and query cost controls via Telemetry Query Service.
- Auditability for sensitive reads supports compliance and post-incident investigations.
- Data source interfaces are stable and versionable (APIs, not storage).

### Negative / tradeoffs
- Additional engineering work to maintain query templates, budgets, and redaction profiles.
- Some investigations may require break-glass flows, which adds process overhead.
- If a source API is down, bot cards may degrade to links/cached results.

## Implementation notes
- Bot requests must include an idempotency key derived from (incident_id, thread_ts, card_type, time_window) to support retries.
- Telemetry Query Service should support:
 - per-template maximum time range (default 30 min)
 - per-request cost budget
 - response caching (e.g., 60–120 seconds) and request coalescing
- Config Service Diff API should support:
 - diff against last known good config version
 - partial propagation awareness (return propagation status where available)
 - redaction profile versioning and test coverage to prevent regressions

## Open questions
- Do we need audit events for non-tenant telemetry reads if the request includes customer-impact hints (e.g., “top tenant by error rate”)? Current decision disallows those queries; revisit if requirements change.
- Should break-glass activation require explicit incident commander acknowledgement in Slack (two-person rule) for Sev0? Proposed for future iteration if misuse becomes a concern.

## Appendix: event names (recommended)
- `incident_bot.config_diff.read`
- `incident_bot.config_diff.read_break_glass`
- `incident_bot.telemetry.query_tenant_scoped`
- `incident_bot.break_glass.activate`
- `incident_bot.break_glass.expire`

## Appendix: glossary
- **Tenant-safe**: Data that does not contain secrets, PII, or customer-identifying information beyond Redwood tenant ID, and is safe to display in internal Slack channels.
- **Break-glass**: Time-limited elevated access used during high-severity incidents, with mandatory audit and justification.
- **Query template**: Pre-approved telemetry query shape with bounded labels and cost controls.

title: SDK transactional batching and failure modes playbook
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Summary:
This playbook documents recommended patterns for transactional batching inside Redwood SDKs and client integrations, the expected failure modes, signal collection, and an operational runbook for diagnosing and mitigating issues in production. It is intended for SDK engineers, integration authors, and services that implement request orchestration (e.g., gateway proxies, sidecars, or edge adaptors).

Goal and scope:
- Goal: make batching predictable, debuggable, and safe for workloads that require transactional semantics (per-request ordering, single-attempt semantics, and partial-failure policies).
- Scope: SDK-side batching logic and client-facing orchestration. Does not cover server-side runtime kernel optimizations (see eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture).

When to use transactional batching:
1) High-throughput, low-latency workloads where amortizing model invocation cost is required, and
2) When callers require per-request ordering or consistent KV-cache behavior across a multi-request transaction.
Avoid transactional batching when request idempotency cannot be guaranteed or when partial success must be exposed immediately to callers.

Core patterns (summary):
- Aggregated Batch Boundary: group requests by identical model, prompt-schema, and quantization profile. Use a deterministic hash of (model, route, input-shape, quant-profile) to select bucket.
- Transactional Envelope: each logical request includes a per-request envelope (request_id, client_trace_id, intent_flags: {abort_on_partial, allow_partial, require_all_or_none}). The envelope tags the tokens in the batch and is used for demultiplexing responses and rollback decisions.
- Two-phase commit (soft): for operations that have visible side effects (e.g., external DB writes triggered by model output), prefer a soft 2PC at the orchestration layer: prepare (get model outputs), validate locally, then apply side-effect. SDKs should provide a "prepareOnly" flag when applicable.
- Time/Size triggers: batching must flush on either max_batch_size or max_batch_latency_ms. Default values: max_batch_size=8, max_batch_latency_ms=25 for interactive flows; configurable per-route.
- Fallback route: always define a single-request fallback path when the batcher detects an error pattern that could indicate model incompatibility or transient resource exhaustion.

Implementation checklist for SDK authors:
- Envelope fields present on every request: request_id (UUID v4), client_trace_id (optional), route_name, priority_hint.
- Deterministic bucketing function (documented and unit-tested).
- Per-batch manifest: list of request_ids, per-request prompt offsets, per-request expected token limits. Persist manifest in-memory until response demux completes.
- Timeout semantics: per-request deadline must be enforced independently of batch deadlines. Respect caller-provided context timeouts.
- Cancellation and Abort: callers must be able to cancel a request; SDK should mark request as canceled and drop its slot from the response mapping (server may still produce tokens; SDK discards them).

Common failure modes and detection signals:
1) Partial demux (some requests in batch have no mapped response): signals: missing request_id in server response, mismatch in token counts per manifest. Telemetry: batch.complete=false, demux_missing_count>0.
2) Out-of-order tokens for a single request: signals: server-side token reorder logs, client sees tokens with decreasing seq numbers. Telemetry: token_seq_reorder_count per request.
3) KV-cache divergence across batched requests: signals: repeated prefix completions for the same request_id across subsequent requests; increased latency for cache warmups.
4) Latency SLO slip caused by large batch build-up: signals: queue_depth high, avg_batch_latency_ms > target, increased p95/p99 latencies.
5) Resource exhaustion and backpressure (GPU OOMs, CPU stalls): signals: runtime OOM metrics, rejection rates, grpc errors 13 / 14.

Telemetry, dashboards and alerting (required signals):
- Per-route: batch_rate, avg_batch_size, avg_batch_latency_ms, p95_batch_latency_ms, demux_missing_rate, token_seq_reorder_rate.
- Per-host/runtime: batch_concurrency, batch_queue_depth, runtime_inflight_batches, gpu_oom_rate.
- Traces: include request_id and batch_id as top-level trace tags. Ensure sampling keeps 1% of batches for full trace capture and 100% of errors.
- Dashboards: "Batching health" panel (avg_batch_size, demux_missing_rate, p99_response_time) and "Batching incidents" list showing last 50 failures with request_ids.
- Alerts: trigger when demux_missing_rate > 0.5% over 5m AND avg_batch_latency_ms > target + 50ms. Also alert on batch_queue_depth > 2x configured threshold.

Diagnostics and triage steps (runbook):
1) Start with the Batching health dashboard and find offending route(s). Note time window and impacted request_ids.
2) Check per-host runtime logs for OOM or kernel errors. If OOM, escalate to eng-serving-runtime on-call.
3) Inspect recent traces (sampled) for batch_id: verify manifest vs response mapping. If response lacks request_id tags, note server-side protocol regression.
4) Reproduce locally with the SDK debug harness: sample config used in production (max_batch_size, latency, route) and inject failures with the local replayer.
5) If demux_missing: toggle the SDK batcher to single-request fallback for the route using the runtime feature-flag (FF: batcher.force_single_request.<route>). Verify error rate falls to zero, then open a corrective issue.
6) If out-of-order tokens: enable token-seq-verify in SDK debug build and collect traces; consider adding a token_seq checksum in envelope to detect corruptions earlier.
7) After fix: run a staged canary (10% traffic) for 30 minutes, verify demux_missing_rate < 0.05% and latency back to baseline.

Config reference table (suggested defaults):
- max_batch_size: 8 (interactive) | 64 (throughput)
- max_batch_latency_ms: 25 (interactive) | 150 (throughput)
- max_concurrent_batches: 16 per host
- per_request_deadline_ms: must be <= caller_deadline_ms; SDK should enforce.
- fallback_policy: "single_request_on_error" | "retry_split"
- abort_policy: "fail_batch" | "drop_request" | "soft_commit"

Sample SDK snippet (pseudocode):
```
// Create an envelope and submit to batcher
envelope = {"request_id": uuid4(), "route":"chat-completion-v2", "intent_flags": {"abort_on_partial": true}}
batcher.submit(envelope, input_payload, deadline_ms=1200)

// Batcher configuration (json)
{"max_batch_size":8, "max_batch_latency_ms":25, "fallback_policy":"single_request_on_error"}
```

Rollout guidance and feature flags:
- Default to non-transactional batching for new SDK releases. Gate transactional batching behind an explicit opt-in flag per-route.
- Use progressive rollout: 0% -> 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%. At each step, monitor demux_missing_rate and tail latencies.
- Provide a kill-switch (runtime override) to disable batching per-route across a cluster for immediate mitigation.

Ownership and SLAs:
- SDK batching library ownership: eng-developer-experience (primary), eng-serving-runtime (consult).
- On-call: SDK library maintainers rotate primary pager for SDK regressions. For runtime kernel issues, engage eng-serving-runtime on-call.
- Targets: demux_missing_rate < 0.05% at p99 traffic; batch_latency SLO: p95 <= configured max_batch_latency_ms + 30ms.

Appendix: 
- Known incompatibilities: models that rewrite prompts or that do aggressive context truncation may be unsuitable for batching with transactional semantics.
- Example incident summary template (to file in postmortems): include route, batch_id, sample request_ids, root cause, mitigation steps, and long-term fix.

Related pages and references:
- eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture (batching kernel notes)
- eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/sdk-profiling-cost-debugging-quickstart-2026 (profiling harness)

Contact and questions:
- For SDK changes and reviews: @Aisha Patel (author) and eng-developer-experience on-call.
- For runtime failures: page eng-serving-runtime on-call Slack channel.

Change log:
- 2025-03-12: created initial draft.
- 2025-06-02: added telemetry thresholds and alert rules.
- 2025-10-08: clarified rollback/abort policies and default config values.

title: Postmortem and action plan: reservoir misallocation, KV-cache thrash and burst token-bucket rewrite
author: Maya Patel
text:
Follow-up to the dedicated-cluster capacity event on 2026-02-10 that caused elevated tail latency and tenant evictions across a subset of GPU pools. Root causes included reservoir misallocation (cold-start reservations placed on fragmented hosts), KV-cache thrash from a heavy short-lived workload, and an overly permissive burst policy that allowed sustained bursts to starve neighbours. This ticket captures the incident summary, technical findings, and an actionable plan to harden tenant isolation and burst behaviour.

On 2026-02-10 we observed a multi-tenant capacity degradation in three dedicated clusters in us-west1. Symptoms: rising 99th percentile token latency, spike in container evictions, and increased OOM/kvcache miss churn. Investigation revealed a combination of (1) a reservoir allocation algorithm that favored minimal host count during cold-start placement, resulting in uneven reservation fragmentation; (2) a client workload that generated repeated short sessions and invalidated KV cache entries, dramatically increasing memory pressure; and (3) the soft-burst token-bucket permit which allowed tenants to consume sustained additional slots for multiple minutes, leading to eviction cascades. Remediation: immediate manual rebalancing and temporary lowering of soft-burst multiplier. Long-term: implement per-tenant weighted reservoirs, KV cache TTL smoothing, and a deterministic token-bucket rewrite with decay and preemption rules.

Reservoir misallocation: the placement algorithm attempted to minimize host count for new reservations which concentrated small reservations on a few hosts and prevented future consolidation. This created fragmentation and limited room for bursts.
KV-cache thrash: high churn workload (many short-lived sessions) caused frequent cache invalidation and inefficient prefix reuse, increasing memory and GPU page faults.
Burst policy gap: current soft-burst policy allowed sustained bursts up to 2.5x baseline for up to 10 minutes without global fairness checks; no global token accounting across tenants on the same host.
Eviction cascade mechanism: the eviction controller used host-level thresholds without tenant-weighted priority, so heavy tenants triggered evictions impacting best-effort tenants.
Telemetry blind spots: missing per-tenant burst credits and lack of early-warning on growing reservation fragmentation hampered fast automated mitigation.

2026-02-10 02:17 UTC - First customer report: elevated tail latency in us-west1 dedicated cluster
2026-02-10 02:28 UTC - Pager duty: SRE engaged and began triage using cluster-level dashboards
2026-02-10 02:55 UTC - Temporary mitigation: reduced soft-burst multiplier from 2.5x to 1.2x and paused non-critical scheduling
2026-02-10 04:10 UTC - Manual rebalance: moved six fragmented reservations to free hosts, decreasing eviction rate
2026-02-10 06:00 UTC - Incident declared resolved for customer-facing errors; internal follow-up opened

title: optimize-rotary-qkv-interleave-and-flashv4-block-fusion
author: Asha Patel
text:
Improved attention throughput for long-context serving: new FlashAttention-v4 block fusion and rotary QKV interleaving reduce p99 token latency on GPU instances and lower token cost by up to 18% for chat workloads.

Motivation: reduce per-token overhead for long-sequence serving workloads and simplify fallback compatibility across attention variants. Summary: introduces an experimental FlashAttention-v4 block-fusion kernel plus a runtime transform that interleaves rotary-multiplied Q/K/V memory layout to reduce memory touches and improve vectorized loads; adds scheduler hints for continuous-batching to prefer low-latency batches for short requests and high-throughput packing for long requests. Changes include CUDA kernels, C++ runtime wiring, Python integration test updates, and perf harness additions. Design notes: the block-fusion kernel fuses QK compute, rotary application, and softmax scaling into a single fused path for blocks up to 128 tokens, falling back to the existing vectorized path for larger blocks; the QKV interleave transform reorders per-layer KV cache layout to an interleaved Q-K-V contiguous format which improves coalesced global loads on Ampere and Hopper architectures. Backwards compatibility: runtime supports a feature flag (attn.flashv4.enabled) and falls back to previous FlashAttention implementation when models are pinned or the kernel fails safety checks. Rollout plan: gate behind 10% canary on Dedicated, validate with the perf canary job, expand to 50% after 48h if error budget holds, then gradually enable by default. Checklist: [x] unit tests for kernel shaders; [x] integration tests for KV restore across warm restarts; [x] perf harness and baseline numbers added; [x] feature flag and metrics; [x] docs note in perf-tuning.md. Benchmarks (internal, p95/p99 token latency on g4dn equivalent): baseline FlashA-v3: p95=12.8ms, p99=25.3ms; this PR FlashA-v4 w/ interleave: p95=10.4ms (18.7% improvement), p99=20.9ms (17.4% improvement). Cost impact: synthetic request mix shows ~12-18% reduction in token GPU time. Risks and mitigations: fused kernel increases complexity and may surface numerical differences; added deterministic numeric tolerance checks and golden-output evals on a set of regression prompts. Related work: follows up on ENG-2972 (batching scheduler tweaks) and ENG-2150 (kv cache layout experiments).

Marco Li: Nice work — can we add a micro-benchmark that isolates the interleaved load improvement? Suggested adding a small kernel-level benchmark.
Asha Patel: Added perf/bench/long_context_suite.py and a microbench driver for interleave in commit b2c4d55. Results included in PR description.
Evelyn Torres (request changes): Please add a safety check that falls back if NVCC computes divergent numerics on older drivers. Also noted missing CI coverage for restore on warm restart. 
Asha Patel: Implemented driver-version guard and golden-output warm-restore test in c3d8f11; CI now runs warm-restore on the smallest GPU target.
Samir Khanna: Approved after re-run of perf CI showed stable numbers and kernel memory usage within budget.
