title: lane-aware contextual eval focalizer: CI adapter for intent-segmented prompt checks
author: Asha Patel
text:
Motivation: some regressions only surface for particular user-intent cohorts or usage lanes (short queries vs long-form, transactional vs exploratory). This PR adds a CI adapter that selects and weights prompt-set slices (lanes) by contextual metadata, runs lane-specific evals in parallel, and synthesizes a lane-aware regression signal that gates merges only when meaningful lanes degrade.

What this change implements: contextual_focalizer CI adapter + lane aggregator + lightweight lane-profile config. The adapter: 1) reads lane definitions from eval-config/lane-profiles.yaml (static but overridable by CI env), 2) samples prompts by lane using feature selectors (intent tag, avg_tokens, user_tier), 3) runs eval shards in parallel (respects existing eval runner), 4) aggregates lane-level metrics (accuracy, semantic-similarity, token-efficiency) into a weighted lane-score and exposes a compact JSON report for the CI pipeline.

Why this approach: avoids single-number masking of regressions across heterogeneous usage; enables targeted rollbacks or canaries for affected lanes; integrates with existing smoke/eval gates and is designed to be low-cost (sample budgets per lane).

Checklist: 
- [x] Add adapter implementation and unit tests
- [x] Add integration test pipeline config (ci/workflows/lane-eval.yml)
- [x] Add lane-profiles.yaml with examples and docs
- [x] Ensure deterministic seeding for sampling to avoid flakiness
- [x] Add metrics exporter hook for Redwood Console ingest

Compatibility notes: The adapter is opt-in via CI env VAR EVAL_LANE_FOCALIZER=1. Default lane profiles are conservative; existing eval runners unchanged unless flagged.

Related Linear tasks: ENG-2471 (lane-aware eval prototype), ENG-2505 (CI gating UX follow-up).

Miguel Rivera: Nice direction — can we avoid sampling bias when lane sizes are imbalanced? Suggest adding per-lane min-sample floor and exposing effective sample count in the report.
Asha Patel: Added per-lane min_sample in lane-profiles.yaml and included effective_sample_count in the JSON report (see tests).
Claire Zhou: Please confirm the seeding guarantees across parallel runners; tests flaked locally for me. Also ask to make the default thresholds configurable (not hard-coded).
Asha Patel: Deterministic seed fixture added. Thresholds moved into eval-config/thresholds and CI reads them from EVAL_THRESHOLDS path; updated docs.
Samir Gupta: Quick nit — exporter hook should tag metrics with lane name and sample_count. Also we should rate-limit export to reduce cardinality. Could you add a small counter?
Asha Patel: Exporter now emits lane tags and a summary metric (lane_sample_count) and rate-limits to one export per minute per lane when run in parallel; implementation uses an in-memory debounce during a run (CI lifespan).

title: Introduce token-group-index and downsampled rollups to reduce cardinality noise in token-level metrics
author: Priya Nair
text:
Motivation: Token-level metrics are extremely useful for attributing cost and latency, but high-cardinality token values and long-tail prefixes generate noisy dashboards and extremely large rollup tables. This PR introduces a token-group index (compact semantic bucketing) plus a downsampled rollup path to reduce storage and alert noise while preserving signal for anomalies and SLO regressions.

Summary of changes: compact token-group index service that maps raw token prefixes to an opaque group id using a hash+semantic-similarity tier; new downsampled-rollup aggregation pipeline that keeps full-resolution samples for heavy hitters and retains statistically representative sampled aggregates for long-tail groups; new instrumentation hooks to annotate spans with token_group_id and sampling_reason; dashboards and alert tuning to use token_group_id by default to reduce cardinality-driven alert fatigue.

Design highlights: (1) Token grouping happens at service edge before ingestion. We use a two-tier policy: deterministic prefix hashing for very short prefixes and a lightweight semantic fingerprint (BERT-lite) for longer prefixes, combined via a stable mapping stored in a compact LRU-backed index. (2) Rollups: heavy-hitter detection keeps exact per-token counters for top-N groups per minute; for remaining groups we emit reservoir-sampled summaries and merge them into downsampled histograms stored as compact protobufs. (3) Backwards compatibility: raw_token remains available behind a flag; all new queries can join on token_group_index when requested. (4) Alerts: token-level SLOs were noisy; updated alerting rules aggregate on token_group_id with adaptive thresholds and a noise-suppression cooldown.

Why this is different from earlier work: prior PRs added rollups and microtrace-synthesis; this PR focuses on upstream grouping and an explicit downsampled aggregation pipeline to reduce cardinality at the ingestion boundary rather than post-hoc aggregation, which reduces ingestion costs and tracing cardinality across both hosted and private deployments.

Checklist:
- [x] Implement token_group_index service and in-process client
- [x] Add span annotation and SDK toggle for token_group_id
- [x] Implement downsampled rollup aggregator and compact storage format
- [x] Update Prometheus/metrics exporter to include token_group labels and sampling_reason
- [x] New Grafana dashboards for group-level cost/latency distribution
- [x] Alert tuning: replace noisy per-token alerts with group-based thresholds
- [x] Unit & integration tests for index, aggregator, and query paths
- [x] Migration plan and feature flag for gradual rollout

Testing and validation: unit tests cover index mapping invariants and sampling correctness (reservoir downsampling tests); integration test validates that for synthetic heavy-hitter traffic we retain exact counters and downstream queries match expected aggregates; load test ran on benchmark-lab with representative traffic for 24h and showed a 4.3x reduction in ingested distinct token labels and a 2.1x reduction in storage for rollup tables at 99th percentile load. CI run included full rt-tests and nightly benchmarks.

Rollout plan: behind feature flag defaulted off. Step 1: enable in hosted staging for 10% of routes and monitor group-level SLOs. Step 2: expand to 50% and enable sampling_reason metrics to validate anomaly detectability. Step 3: flip default for non-sensitive tenants; remaining customers can opt in. Private installer includes opt-in toggle in the helm chart with safe rollback path.

Backward compatibility and privacy: raw token values remain optional; default behavior strips raw_token for retention policies that require minimization. Token grouping intentionally returns opaque group ids (g-xxxxx) to avoid leaking full tokens in dashboards.

Known limitations: edge grouping uses a lightweight semantic fingerprint that is intentionally lossy; some false merges may occur for semantically similar short tokens. We mitigate by keeping heavy-hitter exact counters and providing a manual nomination flow for groups that need to be split.

Followups: (1) Add ML-backed dynamic re-clustering for groups that exhibit drift (ENG-3184), (2) explore an alternative HLL-backed uniqueness sketch for low-memory cardinality detection (ENG-3190).

Related: Linear ENG-3109, ENG-3121. Internal doc: https://redwood.internal/obs/token-group-index (private).

Evan Brooks: Can you quantify the false-merge rate from the semantic fingerprint? We need that to understand alert suppression risk.
Priya Nair: Added a short experiment in the PR description and included synthetic load results — false-merge rate measured ~0.4% on our synthetic corpus for tokens longer than 6 chars. Also added heavy-hitter exact-counters to eliminate impact on top-N items.
Miguel Alvarez: Please ensure the prometheus cardinality doesn’t regress in multi-tenant envs — can we add a per-tenant cap for label explosion?
Priya Nair: Added per-tenant token_group cap in exporter and a guard that drops token_group labels when cap exceeded (configurable), documented in installer values.
Sofia Jensen: Are the group ids stable across restarts? We rely on stability for long-term SLO reporting.
Priya Nair: Yes — mapping is persisted in the compact index with stable hashing and checkpointing. Documented in service README and covered by integration test that simulates restarts.

title: Postmortem: Elevated KV cache evictions increased costs and latency (2026-03-02)
author: Maya Srinivasan
text:
## Summary
On 2026-03-02 we observed a rise in KV cache evictions across the hosted fleet, leading to higher prefill compute, increased per-request latency, and higher unit cost.

## Customer impact
- Duration: 2 hours 12 minutes
- Symptoms: p95 latency +18% on long-context workloads; cost per 1k tokens +9%
- Scope: Hosted API, primarily long-context chat routes

## Detection
- Alert: cache eviction rate exceeded 5% on multiple clusters
- Cost dashboard: sudden increase in prefill FLOPs per token

## Timeline (UTC)
- 13:06: Eviction alert triggers
- 13:20: Runtime on-call confirms elevated evictions on A100 clusters
- 13:38: Mitigation: reduce max batch size for affected models; increase cache reservation
- 15:18: Evictions return to baseline

## Root cause
A batching policy change increased concurrent sequence lengths beyond the KV cache reservation assumptions for long-context workloads. The policy improved throughput on short prompts but caused memory pressure on mixed workloads.

## Contributing factors
- Mixed workload distribution not represented in canary
- Insufficient observability for "cache headroom" at the model instance level

## Follow-up action items
1. Add model-instance metric for KV cache headroom (reserved vs used) and alert on sustained <10% headroom. Owner team: Observability. Priority: P0.
2. Update batching policy to be workload-aware (cap concurrency when long-context requests dominate). Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P0.
3. Add perf-canary scenario for mixed short/long workloads and verify eviction rate <1%. Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P1.
4. Add cost guardrail: alert when prefill FLOPs/token increases >7% week-over-week for a model route. Owner team: SRE. Priority: P1.
5. Document safe batching configuration defaults by model family and GPU type in the serving runtime standards. Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P2.

## Lessons learned
Throughput optimizations must be evaluated against mixed production distributions, not single-mode benchmarks. Cache headroom should be a first-class SLO for long-context serving.

title: POC Accelerator — 90min Workshop Cheatsheet
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Purpose:
This is a compact facilitator cheat sheet to run a focused 90-minute customer POC accelerator session. Intended for Solutions Engineering leads running short, outcome-driven workshops where the goal is to validate integration assumptions, prove a small surface area of value, and define the next-phase delivery plan.

Audience:
- 1–2 customer product/engineering reps (technical decision maker + implementation owner)
- 1 customer PM or business stakeholder (optional)
- Redwood: 1 SE lead (facilitator), 1 SE engineer (sandbox support)

Pre-work (send 3 days before):
- Lightweight form: architecture snapshot, primary API consumer flows, success metric(s) for POC (quantitative/qualitative)
- Access: temporary API key for Redwood hosted sandbox OR SSH access to customer staging (if Private), sample dataset (CSV JSON) subset (<= 1000 rows)
- Runbook link and brief checklist for the customer contact: confirm network egress, IP allowlist, and sample credentials

Tech prerequisites (verify before day-of):
- Sandbox verified: demo model loaded, 1 test endpoint responding within 30s
- Seed data validated and sanitized (PII removed)
- Test prompts and expected outputs available in a single document
- Jupyter / Colab link or Postman collection ready for interactive testing

Success criteria for the session (choose 2–3 measurable goals):
- End-to-end request/response validated on customer sample data in session
- Latency and cost estimate for baseline throughput (e.g., 200 qps estimates) discussed and a realistic next-step config proposed
- Customer agrees to a scoped follow-up: e.g., 2-week pilot with quantifiable metrics and an owner assigned

90-Minute Agenda (timeboxed):
0–10 min: Introductions & framing
- Quick intros, roles, and one-sentence goals from each attendee
- Facilitator states scope: what we will and won’t do in 90min; align success criteria

10–25 min: Current state & constraints (customer walkthrough)
- Ask for a 5–7 minute architecture walkthrough: data sources, producers/consumers, security constraints
- Clarifying q's (keep to max 5): authentication, throughput targets, audit/compliance needs

25–50 min: Live integration + smoke test
- SE engineer runs through the integration plan: endpoint, payload example, token/keys
- Execute 3 smoke tests on customer sample data (happy path, edge case, failure mode)
- Capture outputs in shared doc and timestamp results

50–70 min: Results review + performance quick-check
- Discuss observed outputs: correctness, hallucination cases, failure modes
- Quick latency and cost sanity check using Redwood Optimize heuristics (example calc)
- If mismatch, capture root causes and immediate mitigations

70–85 min: Roadmap & next-phase proposal
- Present 3 recommended next steps (pilot scope, tech tasks, evaluation plan)
- Agree on owners, timeline, acceptance criteria
- Risk register: top 3 risks and mitigations

85–90 min: Wrap-up & immediate action items
- Confirm owners for follow-up, 3 deliverables and dates, and whether additional access is needed
- Ask for verbal buy-in (yes/no/maybe) and next meeting cadence

Facilitator cues and script highlights:
- Opening line: "We have 90 minutes to validate one concrete integration and outline a short pilot. By the end you should have a test that runs on your data and a clear next-step."
- When customer drifts: "To keep this useful for everyone, can we park that and capture it as a follow-up?"
- When tech stalls: "We’ll switch to a recorded run and post the logs for deeper debugging—let’s still capture the symptom and any error output now."

Slide skeleton (10–12 slides, quick speaker notes):
1) Title + Goals (note: list the 2–3 success criteria for the session)
2) Agenda + timeboxes (remind people of the 90-minute boundary)
3) Customer context slide (single architecture diagram)
4) POC scope and constraints (what we’ll validate)
5) Integration diagram (endpoints, auth, data flow)
6) Live test plan (cases: happy, edge, fail)
7) Live results (blank before session; fill during)
8) Observations (quality, errors, latency, cost)
9) Recommended pilot options (3 levels: quick win, medium, deep)
10) Acceptance criteria & success metrics
11) Risks & mitigations
12) Next steps, owners, dates

Speaker note examples:
- Slide 4: "We will validate: (A) an end-to-end request using your sample data, (B) one edge case, and (C) an integration resilience scenario (e.g., transient 503)"
- Slide 9: "Tier 1: 2-week smoke pilot, objective: verify E2E correctness over 1k messages. Tier 2: 6-week pilot with throughput tests and model variant comparison."

Live-run checklist (for SE engineer):
- Confirm correct API key and endpoint in environment variables
- Sanity call: curl /health or minimal SDK call -> expect 200 in < 5s
- Run 3 test payloads, capture raw responses, strip timestamps if needed
- Save logs and link to meeting notes (timestamped)

Breakout / hands-on prompts (if you split into two groups):
- Group A: Focus on prompt engineering — try 3 prompt templates on sample and capture output differences
- Group B: Focus on integration resilience — simulate slow upstream, network timeouts, and measure behavior
- Deliverable from each group: 3 bullet findings and one recommended tweak

Evaluation checklist (end of session):
- E2E test executed: yes/no
- Key owner assigned for pilot: name/email
- Pilot scope document agreed: yes/no
- Timeline set (dates): yes/no

Common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Pitfall: Customer expects full production quality results in 90min. Mitigation: Reiterate scope; show minimal acceptance criteria for demo vs pilot.
- Pitfall: Missing credentials or blocked egress. Mitigation: Have a backup demo dataset and pre-baked video recording of a run.
- Pitfall: Too many stakeholders, signals get fuzzy. Mitigation: Keep decision-maker focused on acceptance criteria and ask for a single owner.

Post-session follow-up template (send within 24h):
- Subject: "Recap + agreed next steps — POC Accelerator (date)"
- Body bullets: summary of what we proved, three observations, agreed pilot scope, owners, dates, and links to logs/artifacts.
- Attachments: filled slide deck (with live results), raw response logs, short how-to for the pilot env setup

Handoff checklist for handover to delivery team:
- Customer contact and primary owner
- Confirmed dataset and access credentials
- Baseline acceptance criteria and success metrics
- Any temporary configuration used in demo (API keys, mock services)

Appendix: quick prompt examples to include in shared doc:
- Classification prompt (binary): "Label the user message as 'support' or 'billing' only. Return single word."
- Summarization prompt: "Summarize the following conversation in <= 25 words, highlight any action items."
- Reranking prompt: "Given a list of candidates, score from 0-1 by relevance to query, return top 3 ids and scores."

Notes to facilitator (final):
- Keep energy high: this format is short—move deliberately and capture everything.
- Use the shared doc as the single source of truth for results and action items.
- If you hit a blocker, convert it into an actionable ticket with owner and due date before the session ends.

End of cheatsheet.

title: AegisCode Regulatory Copilot
author: Jordan Park
text:
Account summary: enterprise trading platform (market risk + clearing) exploring an on-prem/VPC code copilot for engineering orgs. Primary drivers: reduce dev time when pairing against proprietary trading libraries, enforce code policies, full audit trail for regulatory exams.

SSO via SAML (Okta) + SCIM provisioning. Need per-team model pinning and rollback policies; immutable model versioning required for audit.

title: Legal onboarding accelerator: MSA & DPA escalation + pricing pathway
author: Maya Chen
text:
Header:
Date: 2025-03-11
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Devon Park (Redwood SE), Sophie Alvarez (Brightline Procurement), Markus Ibsen (Brightline Legal), Ravi Patel (Brightline Security)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be partial):
Quick escalation of MSA/DPA points, clarify SLA requirements and pricing exceptions pathway. Discussed private deployment vs hosted data residency, KMS integration, and procurement approval flow. Agreed to exchange redlines and schedule a finance+proc meeting.

Topics: MSA redlines, DPA exceptions, SLA targets (p95 latency, monthly uptime), pricing exceptions & approvals, VPC/private deployment options, KMS/HSM, pilot scope and timeline.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: All right hi everyone thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, i have Devon with me from engineering, how are you folks?
[00:10] Sophie: Hey thanks Maya, doing well, appreciate you setting this up. We wanted to move the MSA along and also get clarity on the DPA — our counsel's got a few notes.
[00:18] Markus: Yes, hi — Markus here. We sent high-level redlines yesterday but wanted to walk through a couple of specific items, like data retention, and liability caps.
[00:26] Devon: Hi Markus, hi Sophie, quick note: I'll try to keep the tech bits brief but want to call out where hosting affects legal concerns — e.g., private deployment changes the scope of our obligations.
[00:34] Sophie: Great. If it's ok we'll start with procurement timeline, then jump to the technical constraints and legal items.
[00:41] Maya: Sounds good. Sophie, what's your needed timeline for onboarding?
[00:45] Sophie: We're aiming for a go/no-go to vendor selection by end of month. Procurement needs pricing approvals and MSA signoff; finance wants clarity on overage billing and price floors. We may need a pricing exception if the committed capacity is under X GPUs.
[00:58] Maya: Understood. We can map pricing pathways — there's the standard hosted pricing and then reserved/ Dedicated pricing and private deployment licensing. We can put together a clear path for exceptions.
[01:10] Markus: On the MSA, the main asks: more explicit audit rights, data residency guarantees, stronger indemnity language for PHI. We're in healthcare so PHI concerns are front and center.
[01:22] Devon: Right, technically we support VPC-only private instances and on-prem packages. For PHI we'll recommend Private with customer-managed KMS/HSM, audit logs, and put controls in place — though some of those require enterprise licensing.
[01:35] Sophie: Can you say more about KMS integration? Our security team wants proof we can do a customer-managed key.
[01:40] Devon: Sure. Redwood supports bring-your-own-key patterns — we can integrate with most cloud KMS providers, and we offer an HSM-backed option for Private deployments. There's some work for key rotation and ledgering to align with your audit policies. I'll follow up with a short tech memo.
[01:57] Markus: Do you have SOC2/ISO attestations? Our legal wants those attachments with the DPA.
[02:02] Maya: Yes we have SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001 certs; I'll share the cert bundle and the security whitepaper link after the call.
[02:10] Sophie: Excellent. On the DPA, Markus flagged a 3rd party subprocessors list — we need visibility and the ability to object to certain sub processors.
[02:19] Devon: We can provide a current subprocessor list; policy is to notify customers about changes and there's a process for high-risk objections, though typically that ties into the Private/ Dedicated options.
[02:29] [02:30] Sophie: Okay. For SLA specifics, our SRE wants p95 inference latency under 500ms for short prompt workloads and 99.9% monthly availability. Is that feasible?
[02:40] Maya: For hosted, we have published performance profiles; 500ms p95 is achievable with certain model classes and batching configs, but at scale you hit tradeoffs. With Dedicated we can give tighter SLOs and carve a commitment for that 99.9% availability.
[02:55] Devon: One nuance: latency SLOs depend on model choice, sequence length, and KV cache hit rates. We can reserve capacity to meet the SLOs but if you want PHI controls and private routing that increases cost.
[03:10] Markus: Cost is ok if it's justified. The procurement question is how to document pricing exceptions and approvals — do we need a separate MSA exhibit or a PO workflow?
[03:20] Maya: We typically handle pricing commitments via an order form / exhibit tied to the MSA. For exceptions, we can add an Appendix that outlines the approved exception and approval matrix. We'll supply template language.
[03:30] Sophie: Good. Also finance asked: how do overage rates work with usage spikes from seasonal surges?
[03:36] Maya: Overage is at the committed-tier rate or an established surge rate; for Dedicated we can do burst capacity at a negotiated multiplier. We'll include example calculations in the pricing sheet.
[03:47] [03:50] Ravi: Quick security note — we need clarity on logs retention and redaction for PHI. Can Redwood redact logs or do we need to route logs to our SIEM?
[03:58] Devon: The platform can redact at ingestion for certain fields but for full auditability we recommend forwarding logs to your SIEM via secure forwarding; for Private deployments we can also configure log sinks into your VPC.
[04:14] Sophie: That's helpful. Markus, any legal non-starters?
[04:18] Markus: The liability cap currently tied to fees is concerning for PHI; we want higher cap or carveouts for data breach. Also need stronger breach notifications and SLA credits spelled out.
[04:28] Maya: We can propose language for carveouts and an escalation playbook. We usually see compromise with a higher cap for specific PHI incidents and clear notification timelines (e.g., 72 hours).
[04:40] Markus: 72 hours is workable if we have a remediation plan and cooperation obligations.
[04:46] [04:50] Sophie: On subprocessors we will send a list of vendors we cannot allow and ask you to confirm compatibility.
[04:56] Devon: OK we'll do a subprocessors matrix and flag any that are a concern.
[05:02] Maya: I'll upload an annotated MSA with our baseline redlines and call out the high-priority items.
[05:07] Sophie: Great. I also want a clear list of stakeholders for approvals; procurement typically needs CPO and finance signoff.
[05:14] Maya: Good, we'll include a one-pager that maps approvals to names/roles.
[05:18] [05:20] Markus: One more legal point — IP indemnity around model outputs. We need assurance on third-party content and how Redwood handles claims.
[05:27] Devon: Model output IP is tricky. We provide indemnity for code/exact model artifacts in specified cases, but we recommend a usage policy and a training data disclosure in the DPA/appendix. We'll write conservative language to limit exposure.
[05:42] Sophie: Ok. For procurement gating, what's your normal internal time for MSA negotiation once redlines are exchanged?
[05:48] Maya: For straightforward redlines, 1-2 weeks. For deeper legal and security escalations that involve our enterprise team, 3-6 weeks typically.
[05:57] Sophie: Noted.
[06:00] [06:05] Maya: Pricing pathway — Devon, do you want to explain Dedicated vs Private cost drivers?
[06:09] Devon: Sure. Hosted (pay-as-you-go) has lowest startup friction but variable costs. Dedicated is reserved GPU capacity with a monthly commit — better unit economics and predictable latency. Private includes licensing and network integration costs; usually higher fixed fee but required for strict residency/PHI controls. Quantization and batching can reduce per-token cost.
[06:30] Sophie: If we commit to a pilot (3 months) with a small dedicated pool, can we get a temp price lock?
[06:36] Maya: Yes we can provision a pilot PO with locked pricing for the pilot duration and then renegotiate at scale.
[06:41] [06:45] Markus: For SLAs during pilot, can you offer a reduced commitment but with reporting that meets our compliance needs?
[06:52] Devon: We can provide monitoring access and weekly reports; SLA credits usually require a baseline commit, but we can put in a tailored reporting annex for pilot.
[07:02] Sophie: Good. Next up — procurement needs the DPA specifics. Do you accept our standard DPA or want to use Redwood's?
[07:10] Maya: We prefer Redwood's DPA for speed, but we will map your changes. If you send your redline we'll do a side-by-side and call out any hard stops.
[07:20] Markus: We'll send redlines; expectation is to have an initial response within 3 business days. Is that ok?
[07:25] Maya: Yes that aligns with our SLA.
[07:28] [07:30] Sophie: On the data residency front, we need EU-only processing for a subset of workloads. Can you route requests to a region and guarantee no egress?
[07:38] Devon: Yes for Hosted we can enforce region routing; for full guarantee we recommend Private or Dedicated located in EU region with contractual egress restrictions. There are network egress audits we can provide.
[07:50] Sophie: Excellent.
[07:53] Maya: Quick note — I'll also attach our KMS/HSM spec and an architecture diagram to the shared folder. The link will be in the follow-up email.
[07:59] [08:00] Ravi: A practical ask: can you share a short checklist of the security controls we can evaluate quickly? We have a 1-week window for the initial security review.
[08:07] Devon: Yes I'll produce a 1-2 page checklist: KMS support, encryption-at-rest/in-transit, logging, RBAC/SSO, network isolation, and audit trails.
[08:16] Sophie: Please include expected artifact delivery dates in that checklist.
[08:19] Devon: Will do.
[08:21] [08:30] Maya: Let's talk about procurement approvals — Sophie, who signs off on pricing exceptions?
[08:34] Sophie: Typically CPO for vendor selection and CFO/finance for commercial exceptions. I'll confirm exact names and share.
[08:40] Maya: Great. We want to avoid surprises in pricing committee; we'll prepare a one-page economics summary and an example invoice.
[08:48] Markus: Back to liability — if we accept higher cap for PHI incidents, we need a defined mitigation plan and obligations.
[08:56] Maya: Understood. We can attach an incident response appendix to commit to cooperation, timely notifications, and specific remediation steps.
[09:04] [09:10] Sophie: Two quick procedural things: 1) where do you want us to upload redlines? 2) Do you require NDA before sharing architecture?
[09:18] Maya: Upload redlines to the shared drive link that I'll send; NDA — we can share the general architecture now, but for deeper docs we can sign a mutual NDA; I think you already raised one earlier?
[09:28] Sophie: We have a standing NDA but I'll double-check and confirm.
[09:32] Devon: Also small detail — if you want logs routed to your SIEM we'll need a network peering window and some firewall rules; we can draft that out.
[09:41] [09:45] Maya: Any other blockers?
[09:47] Markus: Not blockers, just wanting timelines. If we get your memos and the annotated MSA this week, legal can turn around initial review within 5 business days.
[09:58] Maya: Perfect. We'll aim for that.
[10:01] [10:05] Sophie: On pricing exceptions: if we put a pilot PO for 3 months with a small committed GPU count, we will need a clause that allows us to convert to enterprise commit or terminate with 30 days.
[10:15] Maya: That's reasonable, we can include pilot termination terms and conversion steps.
[10:20] Devon: From operations side, we'll need a kickoff call with your platform team to map network and monitoring. Recommend a 1-hour technical onboarding session after paperwork.
[10:31] Sophie: Ok plan that.
[10:34] [10:40] Maya: Quick recap before we close — action items and owners: I'll upload the annotated MSA and certs; Devon will produce the security checklist and Private deployment memo; Sophie will circulate procurement approvers and vendor restrictions; Markus will send DPA redlines.
[10:54] Sophie: Yep. Also ask that you include examples of SLA credit calculations in the appendix.
[11:00] Maya: Will do.
[11:03] [11:10] Markus: Thanks everyone, this was productive.
[11:12] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with the shared link and a proposed timeline.
[11:16] Sophie: Thanks, bye.
[11:18] Devon: Bye.

End of transcript.

References and shared artifacts mentioned during call:
- "Annotated MSA (to be uploaded)" — placeholder link: https://drive.redwood.example/msa-annotated (will be shared)
- Security whitepaper and SOC2/ISO bundle (Maya to attach)

title: Opportunistic emitter: model admission, metrics, and rollback playbook
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for onboarding and running "opportunistic emitter" model variants in the serving runtime. The emitter is the component that produces speculative tokens ahead of confirmed tokens (opportunistic decode that may later be accepted or discarded). The doc focuses on safe model admission, observable acceptance criteria, automated rollback triggers, and the KV cache invariants that must hold across speculative handoffs.

Context and motivation:
- We have several models that leverage lookahead/emitter behavior to reduce perceived latency and increase throughput for short-turn workloads.
- Prior experiments revealed subtle KV cache staleness bugs and rare token divergence that only show up at scale.
- This playbook codifies a gated rollout path so we can safely surface the latency benefits without regressing output quality or violating customer SLAs.

Goals:
- Define automated and manual acceptance gates for a new opportunistic emitter variant.
- Specify the minimal metrics, smoke tests, and invariants required before promotion to higher rings.
- Describe deterministic rollback actions and quick mitigation steps for incidents.

Non-goals:
- This doc is not a kernel implementation guide (see kernel routing RFC). It focuses on integration, monitoring and ops for model admission.

Terminology:
- emitter: speculative token generator overlaying the primary decode path.
- accept path: the canonical forward decode path that confirms tokens into the KV cache.
- speculative token: token produced by emitter that may be discarded.
- model variant: a signed model build + kernel/quantization profile.

Acceptance criteria (must all be met for promotion):
1) Correctness:
 - Token-level divergence vs baseline <= 0.05% for top-1 across the canary traffic (see QoE harness).
 - End-to-end semantic regression tests: no regression in the top-10 eval prompts used for rollout.
2) Latency:
 - Median tail (p95) token latency improvement >= 8ms over baseline for targeted workload.
 - No upstream: increased latency introduced by the emitter coordination step must be < 2ms on median.
3) Cost/Throughput:
 - Throughput (tokens/s) delta measured under synthetic load within +-5% of expected.
4) Stability / Errors:
 - Error rate (5xx + decode-falls-back-to-safe) < 0.1% over 48h canary.
 - No observed KV cache inconsistency alerts (see KV invariants below).
5) Observability:
 - Full traces with emitter span and kernel selection attributes present in traces.
 - Sampled QoE recordings for at least 10k sessions with diff tool output attached.

KV cache invariants (must be asserted in runtime and by integration tests):
- Invariant A: Any accepted token sequence must overwrite speculative KV entries for the same session and prefix; speculative entries must be tombstoned upon acceptance.
- Invariant B: Speculative entries must carry version tags that are monotonic; the accept path must validate version <= current to avoid regressions.
- Invariant C: Speculative entries must be garbage-collected within configurable TTL (default 10s) if not accepted; a GC trace must be emitted.
- Invariant D: On handoff between kernels (e.g., quantized -> fp16), KV format downgrade/upgrade must be lossless or trigger an immediate safe-fallback.

Admission flow (high-level):
1) Local validation: PR build runs unit tests + KV invariant checks + quick decode smoke.
2) Integration canary (internal traffic): route 0.5% of internal traffic to emitter variant for 48h. Capture full traces, QoE diffs, and KV invariants.
3) External canary (subset of customers): route 1–5% of external production traffic for 72h with heavy sampling and alerting on regressions.
4) Ramp: progressively increase to 25%, 50% with a weekly checkpoint.
5) Promote to global if all metrics are green and product/solutions sign-off is recorded.

Kernel compatibility matrix (summary, updated per model):
- Kernel A (optimized attention v3): supported -- requires emitter to use kernel prefetch hooks.
- Kernel B (quant-llm-4bit): supported with a conservative preference (no early prefix rewrite).
- Kernel C (fp32 fallback): supported but will run on accept path only (no speculative fastpath).
Notes: always include the exact kernel commit hash in the model bundle metadata.

Rollout gating and rollback triggers (automated):
- AUTO-ROLLBACK triggers immediately (0% routing) if any of:
 * QoE divergence rate > 0.3% in 30m sliding window (QoE divergence = semantic eval failures + hallucination score).
 * Error rate spike: decode failures or KV validation failures > 0.5% in 15m.
 * Latency p95 regression > 30% sustained for 10m.
 * Missing critical spans in traces (>1% of sampled requests).
- SOFT-ROLLBACK (throttle to 0.1%): if non-critical anomalies occur (e.g., increased tail, small cost deltas) while ops investigate.
- Manual rollback: runbook for on-call to follow (see "Incident: rollback steps" below).

Automated rollback actions (what the control plane will do):
1) Immediately set routing weight to 0 for the variant.
2) Invalidate speculative KV entries for in-flight sessions belonging to the variant (emit tombstones).
3) Switch affected sessions to accept path kernel with extra tracing enabled.
4) Create incident stub on PagerDuty and attach last 200 affected traces to the incident.

Incident: rollback steps for on-call (short checklist):
- Confirm trigger condition from dashboards and raw logs.
- Execute cloud-control rollback command: rwctl rollout cancel --variant <id> --force
- Run KV audit: scripts/kv-audit --session-sample=500 --since=1h and attach results.
- Notify Solutions/CS for noisy customers (include list of affected session ids).
- Run postmortem triage: tag PRs/commits and schedule deep-dive within 48h.

Required telemetry and dashboards (minimum):
- metric.emitter.token.accept_rate (per model variant, per region)
- metric.emitter.speculative_reuse_ratio (fraction of speculative tokens accepted)
- metric.kv.validation.failures (per session)
- trace.span:emitter.* (include kernel.commit, model.variant, session.id)
- qoe.diff.rate (daily, 1h, 5m rollups)
- alert:emitter.auto_rollback (hooks into routing control plane)
Quality harness / tests to run pre-admission:
- Deterministic replay of 10k golden prompts with top-k sampling parity check.
- Stochastic harness: 100k prompts sampled with production-like temperature and prompt length distribution; compute divergence histograms.
- KV consistency fuzzing across multi-kernel handoffs (inject simulated kernel failovers).
- Long tail soak: 72h soak under 1.5x normal traffic volume.

Open smoke test commands (dev-friendly):
- python infra/smoke/emitter_smoke.py --model <variant> --count 200 --trace
- rwctl trace dump --filter model.variant=<id> --last 1h > /tmp/emitter-traces.json
- scripts/kv-checker.sh --sessions 200 --assert-invariants

Playbook checklist for PR / release notes (must be present in PR description):
- Model bundle hash and kernel commit
- Expected perf gain and measurement harness description
- Canary plan (time windows, traffic %s, rollback thresholds)
- Contact list for triage and escalation
- QoE sample prompts used in acceptance (attach as CSV)

Unresolved questions / TODOs:
- How to standardize the speculative token TTL across regions with different latency characteristics? (ops input required)
- Should we bake a delta-CRF that compares emitter output to accept path in real time and reduce routing based on model drift? Tradeoffs: added cost vs detection speed.
- Investigate microsecond-level jitter in kernel prefetch hooks observed on AmpereA100 pods; potential HW scheduling implications.

References and related docs:
- See also: kernel-routing-rfc, kv-cache-lease-proposal, speculative-decode-integration-playbook (older).
- GH PR: redwood/realtime#4217 contains the initial emitter prototype and unit harness.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally prescriptive — the runtime needs clear gates for any speculative/emitter feature. Expect to iterate thresholds after the first 3 internal canaries.
- If you have suggestions for telemetry names or specific alert thresholds, add comments inline or attach linked artifacts.

Author notes (quick):
- Aisha: added KV invariants and rollback CLI steps.
- Jonah: will add canary traffic generation job and update the GH PR.

title: HTTP vs gRPC streaming / chunking: field notes and microbenchmarks
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Summary:

Quick notes from a focused run comparing HTTP streaming (chunked responses + HTTP/2) to gRPC server-side streaming for small-to-medium token bursts. Goal was to isolate networking/transport overheads and backpressure behavior when the runtime emits tokens in small increments (1-64 tokens per flush). We also measured the delta when Envoy proxy sits between clients and the runtime.

Why this matters:
- Our runtime uses fine-grained token emission to support low-latency streaming for chat features. Small writes can cause non-obvious overhead at the kernel and proxy layers.
- Quantifying the tradeoffs helps Decide defaults for flush frequency / chunk size and whether customers should prefer gRPC or HTTP/2 for their integration.

Experiment goals:
- Measure P50/P95/P99 latency per token and end-to-end response completion time for identical service logic across transports.
- Measure CPU overhead on server for different flush sizes.
- Observe backpressure behavior: does the runtime stall when client consumes slowly? Do proxies introduce queueing that affects tail latency?
- Quick sanity check of HTTP/1.1 chunked (with TCP_NODELAY vs default), HTTP/2 (h2), and gRPC (http2-based) with and without Envoy.

Testbed and config:
- Server: 8 vCPU, 1xA10G-like GPU (mocked inference service that emits tokens per configured flush), Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 6.x, tuned tcp_mem default.
- Client: colocated in same AZ for baseline; remote (cross-AZ) for one run.
- Proxy: Envoy v1.30 with default HTTP/2 settings; one run with http/1.1 to test translation cost.
- Workload generator: custom bench harness (bench/network_streaming_runner.py) - uses grpcio and httpx for HTTP/2 tests; configurable flush sizes, concurrency, and delay between client reads.
- Token sizes: 10B token payload (simple JSON per token), simulated CPU cost per token kept constant to isolate networking.
- Flush sizes: 1 token, 4 tokens, 16 tokens, 64 tokens. Also a batched non-streaming baseline that returns entire response at once.

Commands used (examples):
- HTTP/2: httpx.AsyncClient(http2=True); curl --http2-prior-knowledge --no-buffer 
- gRPC: grpc-stub with server streaming; client reads stream.as_completed()
- Envoy: simple listener to upstream mapping with http2 on both sides; logs at debug for flow control windows.

Metrics collected:
- client-per-token-latency-ms (time from send request to receive token chunk)
- end-to-end completion time (first byte to last byte)
- server CPU% & system CPU (collected via top/collectl)
- socket-level retransmits and send/recv queue depths (ss, netstat, proc/net/dev)
- connection-level flow-control events from Envoy logs (when available)

Key results (summary):
- gRPC (server-streaming) gave the lowest 50/95 tail for 1-token flushes: P50 ~ 2.3ms, P95 ~ 9.1ms, P99 ~ 24ms (local AZ).
- HTTP/2 streaming (httpx/curl prior-knowledge) had slightly higher tails: P50 ~ 3.8ms, P95 ~ 12.7ms, P99 ~ 36ms for 1-token flushes.
- HTTP/1.1 chunked with TCP_NODELAY enabled was comparable to HTTP/2 for P50 but worse at P95/P99 due to head-of-line blocking in some cases.
- Envoy in the middle added 0.8-2.4ms median overhead and amplified tail: with Envoy P99 moved from ~24ms to ~47ms for gRPC 1-token flush runs in our environment.
- Increasing flush size reduces networking overhead but increases first-token latency (application-level): moving from 1->16 tokens reduced CPU overhead by ~18% and reduced P95 by ~35% but increased time-to-first-token by ~10-30ms depending on base token emission rate.
- Server CPU: small flush sizes increase syscalls and user->kernel transitions. Measured sys CPU increase of ~12% for 1-token flush vs batched, and 6% for 4-token flush.

Representative numbers (local AZ, single client, single connection):
- gRPC, flush=1 -> P50 2.3 ms, P95 9.1 ms, P99 24.0 ms, total completion 420 ms (for 100 tokens), server CPU 41%
- HTTP/2, flush=1 -> P50 3.8 ms, P95 12.7 ms, P99 36.0 ms, total completion 438 ms, server CPU 44%
- HTTP/1.1 chunked, flush=1 -> P50 3.6 ms, P95 17.8 ms, P99 65.2 ms, total 460 ms, server CPU 48%
- gRPC, flush=16 -> P50 6.8 ms (first token), P95 11.2 ms (subsequent tokens), P99 20.8 ms, total completion 360 ms, server CPU 34%
- Batched (no streaming) -> first byte 120 ms, P95 of delivery 120-130 ms, server CPU 29%

Observations and likely causes:
- Flow control interaction: gRPC's framing and client libraries appear to be more efficient at incremental reads; the runtime saw fewer pending bytes on socket with gRPC vs raw chunked HTTP/1.1, reducing kernel copy overhead.
- Envoy behavior: Envoy introduces an internal buffer between upstream and downstream; small writes from upstream get coalesced but also buffered if downstream hasn't consumed. Envoy's connection pool/idle timeout and HTTP/2 window sizing caused bursts to be delayed while watermarks adjust.
- TCP_NODELAY: enabling TCP_NODELAY reduced latency for 1-token flushes in HTTP/1.1 but increased packet-per-token overhead leading to higher CPU. The tradeoff looks unfavorable for high-concurrency cases.
- Kernel-level batching: when multiple small writes are coalesced into single TCP segments, P50 improves but P99 can still suffer due to delayed ACKs or Nagle interactions if not explicitly disabled.

Backpressure experiments (slow client read):
- Setup: client intentionally sleeps 10ms between reads to simulate slow consumer.
- gRPC: server-side send calls started to block only after ~64KB of unacked data; client-side observed smooth slowdown but no spike in tail beyond expected.
- HTTP/1.1 chunked: server send calls returned EAGAIN earlier with default socket buffer sizes; runtime saw send loop stalls and increased context switches.
- Envoy in the middle: made backpressure effects worse because it buffers a few KBs and then exerts backpressure on upstream only once its internal watermarks hit. This created a delayed, larger stall event on the server side (i.e., not gradual).

Actionable takeaways:
1) For streaming-first experiences where token-at-a-time latency matters (chat UX), recommend gRPC server-streaming as the default SDK transport for enterprise customers when using the dedicated/private offering. It provides lower tail and cleaner backpressure behavior in our tests.
2) For hosted HTTP clients (web browsers) where gRPC-web isn't an option, prefer HTTP/2 streaming and configure runtime defaults to emit in small batches (e.g., 4 tokens) instead of 1 token. This balances latency and CPU.
3) If customers must use HTTP/1.1 chunked, provide clear guidance: enable TCP_NODELAY only when low concurrency and accept higher CPU; otherwise instruct to use slightly larger flush sizes (16 tokens) to avoid syscall storms.
4) Add default Envoy tuning in our reference proxy config to reduce tail amplification: increase per-connection HTTP/2 initial window and lower upstream buffer watermarks, and add explicit small_write_coalescing when possible. Document tradeoffs.
5) In the runtime, expose a simple knob: flush_token_count with sensible defaults per deployment type (hosted/dedicated/private).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Multi-client scenarios at higher QPS: these tests are single-connection. Need to scale to 50-200 concurrent streams and observe connection-level behavior (window updates, cross-talk).
- Evaluate gRPC-web (Envoy proxy path) for browser clients: does translating gRPC-web->gRPC amplify overhead similarly to Envoy h2->h2 path?
- Investigate a lib-level optimization to coalesce small writes into a single writev call per event loop tick to reduce syscalls while preserving low time-to-first-token.
- Test with realistic token sizes (varying from 5 bytes -> 200 bytes) and random jitter in emission to reflect model KV cache behavior.

Notes-to-self / TODOs:
- Re-run with 200 concurrent streams across 4 client VMs and attach pcap for a tail case where Envoy caused 200ms stall.
- Open a follow-up PR to our reference-envoy-config repo with suggested watermarks (PR draft created: see linked_artifacts).
- Add support in bench harness to record socket-level cwnd/rcv_space snapshots periodically.
- Share this note with Console team (Lena) for flags UI so customers can set flush_token_count in the console.

Experimental artifacts & pointers:
- bench harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/tree/main/networking
- small write coalescing PoC: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/879
- related JIRA: JIRA-ISSUE-1421 (envoy tail investigation)

Conclusions (short):
- gRPC wins in tail and backpressure stability for token-at-a-time streaming.
- HTTP/2 is acceptable and simpler for browser/backward compat but requires tuning and slightly larger flush batches.
- Envoy is convenient but amplifies tail behavior unless tuned; default configs currently hurt streaming latency.

If we want to be conservative in product defaults: choose gRPC for SDKs, HTTP/2 for browser flows with flush=4 default, and update docs/console with guidance and proxy tuning.

End of notes.

title: reserve-vs-payg-mix-simulations
author: Evan Brooks
text:
Quick sim notes: payg vs reserve mix (personal scratchpad)

Context / goal:
- Need a simple model to decide what % of revenue should be captured as reserved contracts vs PAYG for H1 2025 growth plan.
- Focus on unit economics at token-level for gen calls (chat) + small embeddings traffic.
- Keep it intentionally rough — want order-of-magnitude sensitivity and a few candidate bundles.

Assumptions (baseline)
- avg gen token length per call (response only): 100 tokens
- tokens per prompt (user+system): 40 tokens
- total tokens per request = 140 tokens
- avg requests per MAU (monthly active user doing LLM ops) = 120 requests/month (≈4/day)
- tokens per MAU/month = 140 * 120 = 16,800 tokens ≈ 17k

Costs (infra)
- marginal inference cost per 1k tokens (hosted) = $0.006 per 1k tokens (baseline) -> $0.000006 per token (this is purely infra GPU amortized + infra ops)
- embedding cost per 1k dims call = $0.012 per 1k tokens equivalent (if mixing embeddings, treat separately)
- overhead (storage, tracing, billing, SRE) add ~25% on top of infra marginal -> blended marginal = 1.25 * infra
- blended marginal per token = $0.0000075 (rounded)

Revenue and price points
- PAYG list price (example candidate) = $0.00003 per token (5x blended marginal) -> gross margin per token = 0.0000225 (~75%)
- Reserved (committed monthly) blended discount candidate = 40% off PAYG -> reserved price per token = $0.000018 per token (margin ≈ 58%)
- Enterprise reserved + SLA premium: $0.000022 per token (lower discount but SLA/guarantee revenue)

Simple unit-econ per MAU (monthly)
- PAYG revenue per MAU = 17k tokens * $0.00003 = $0.51/mo
- PAYG cost per MAU = 17k * $0.0000075 = $0.1275 -> contribution = $0.3825
- Reserved revenue per MAU (if they commit same usage) = 17k * $0.000018 = $0.306 -> cost = same 0.1275 -> contribution = $0.1785

Observation: PAYG contribution per MAU > reserved contribution per MAU because reserved has discount but provides predictability. But reserved gives committed ARR and lower churn. Need to model churn sensitivity.

Scenario: convert 25% of PAYG usage to reserved contracts (mix)
- Suppose 10k MAUs total
- Baseline all PAYG revenue = 10k * $0.51 = $5,100/mo -> $61.2k/yr
- If 25% (2.5k MAU) convert to reserved -> reserved rev = 2.5k * $0.306 = $765/mo, PAYG rev from remaining 7.5k = 7.5k * $0.51 = $3,825/mo -> combined = $4,590/mo -> down from $5,100 -> delta -$510/mo but predictability increases and gross margin mix shifts slightly
- Contribution: PAYG contribution 7.5k * 0.3825 = $2,869, reserved contribution 2.5k * 0.1785 = $446.25 -> total contribution = $3,315.25 vs all PAYG contribution = $3,825 -> drop in contribution of ~$510 -> same as revenue drop above

Why still a win? (qualitative)
- Reserved contracts enable capacity planning, allow us to schedule cheaper long-lived instances -> actual infra cost for reserved might be lower than blended marginal used above if we change instance mix (e.g., dedicated GPUs at higher utilization). There's optional delta: reserved infra cost multiplier 0.85 (15% lower per-token cost). If we apply that: reserved cost per token = 0.000006375 * 1.25? (need consistent calc) -> effectively reserved contribution improves by ~10-15%.
- Reduces churn and acquisition costs (we avoid CAC for those seats monthly) -> if CAC payback time improves by X months this offsets margin drop.

Quick sensitivity tests (notes):
- If PAYG price is 3x marginal instead of 5x, PAYG becomes barely profitable; reserved becomes comparatively worse. Need to pick PAYG markup to both capture value and leave room for discounted reserved deals.
- If avg tokens per MAU is actually 50k (power users), reserved deals become proportionally more attractive to customers (capex predictability) and to us (volume discounts, smoother load).

Candidate small bundles / packaging ideas (rough)
1) Starter PAYG (free tier for up to 10k tokens/mo), then PAYG block pricing (first 1M tokens at $0.000035, next at $0.000025) -> gives price anchoring and volume incentive
2) Micro-reserved monthly packs: buy X tokens/month at 40% off PAYG; X tiers {50M, 200M, 1B} with rollover of unused tokens for 1 month. Simpler than seat+rate.
3) Session-bundle: small upfront for 30-day session credits (targeting RAG apps with stable usage). Unclear how to meter across short vs long LLM sessions.
4) Enterprise reserved with SLA + dedicated pools + long-term commit (12/24 mo) priced with blended model (flat platform fee + per-token discounted rate).

Open questions / TODOs
- Need to run traffic histogram across customers to understand percentiles of tokens/MAU (top 5% drives what %) -> affects where to anchor tiers.
- How much lower can infra marginal actually be if we shift reserved to Dedicated pools? Talk to infra (Carlos) to get per-token cost at 70% utilization on reserved sku.
- Model churn impact: estimate CAC and churn improvement for reserved (conservative: churn drop from 7% -> 4% monthly). Run NPV for 12/24 mo horizon.
- Consider non-linear discounts: larger reserved should have steeper discounts but also require minimum commit ARR. Need to simulate elastic demand.

Quick mental experiments (numbers to sanity check)
- If we set PAYG = $0.00004/token (6.7x blended marginal) and reserved = 45% off -> reserved = $0.000022 -> reserve contribution per MAU = 17k*(.000022 - .0000075) = ~$0.246 -> now reserve starts to look more OK vs PAYG contribution of $0.51 - $0.1275 = $0.3825

Notes to self:
- Present this as a 1-slide summary: 3 bullets (tradeoff: margin vs predictability), 1 chart (revenue vs % reserved), 1 ask (infra per-token at 70% util).
- Run a quick cohort sim in sheet: columns = MAU, avg tokens/month, % convert reserved, reserved discount, infra delta, CAC impact -> compute ARR, contribution, NPV.

References / links in my head:
- similar playbook from back-infrastructure at other startups: prefer smaller monthly reserved packs for SMBs, larger multi-year for enterprise.
- Slack convo thread #pricing-rev from May had notes on anchor pricing (Maya) -> follow-up: ask Maya for her raw usage histograms.

End.

(very rough; capture before meeting with product + infra next Wed)

title: Vendor gate criteria, data escrow & SLA synthesis - Azura Health
author: Maya Patel
text:
Procurement and legal alignment call to validate vendor gate criteria for Azura Health: MSA/DPA redlines, required SLA minima, data escrow expectations, KMS/SSO/KPI items, and timing for pricing/PO sign-off. High-level agreement on pilot + escrow + next legal redline exchange; technical runbook and pilot SLOs to follow.

MSA redlines and acceptable liability cap
DPA and data residency / data classification requirements
Data escrow and escrow agent/triggering events
SLA targets (p99 latency, uptime) and remedies/credits
KMS / BYOK / HSM options and key rotation
SSO/SAML and RBAC integrations
Pricing approvals, PO timing, and pilot economics
Technical runbook and pilot (canary) scope

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 50 minutes, so we'll run through a quick vendor gate checklist then open for legal/tech questions.
[00:12] Jenna: Great, thanks. We just want to be clear on what exactly triggers the gate - is it PO + signed MSA or do you need SOC 2 report first?
[00:20] Maya: Good question. Our normal flow is PO + signed MSA, we put SOC 2 in as an attachment / attestation, and we can provide the report under NDA. For Azura, we can also do a conditional pilot before full-go as long as the DPA is in place.
[00:35] Ravi: Conditionals... okay. From security we need crypto controls around keys and explicit egress map. If you offer BYOK, what's the KMS model?
[00:44] Oliver: We support customer-managed keys via standard KMS providers and HSM workflows. There's a few implementation paths: Redwood-hosted KMS with envelope encryption, or customer keys in their cloud KMS with an integration we call BYOK. There's some perf tradeoffs in crypto path but it's supported.
[01:05] Tom: Sorry to jump in, is there an option where we keep the KV cache on-prem? We have latency sensitive flows for clinical triage.
[01:12] Sam: Speaker note - Kv-cache phrasing sometimes shows up, we can do dedicated capacity (Redwood Dedicated) which pins GPUs in region and reduces latency and keeps data isolated. That would be the recommended route for low-latency clinical inference.
[01:28] Laura: On the legal side, my team will need to see indemnity and liability caps. Standardly we ask for 1x to 3x of fees as cap or $10M, which is what our procurement playbook uses. Where do you typically land?
[01:40] Maya: For enterprise we usually land at a liability cap tied to fees for hosted API — often 1x annual fees; for Dedicated or Private we look at a higher cap and limited carveouts. But we can discuss specific numbers.
[01:52] Laura: Also data escrow -- we want an escrow that covers model weights and customer data at termination. Triggering events: insolvency or failure to deliver SLA for 30 days.
[02:03] Maya: Understood. We can include escrow language. Important clarifier: model weights vs customer prompts/derived data - we typically escrow customer owned artifacts and agreed artifacts, not proprietary open-source models. We'll propose language.
[02:18] Ravi: I want to call out audit logs and WORM storage, do you provide immutable logs for access?
[02:25] Oliver: Yes we have audit logging per tenant; retention is configurable. For Private deployments we can ship logs to your Splunk/Datadog. For hosted we'll retain logs for the agreed period and can export on request.
[02:38] Jenna: Pricing question: procurement needs to know if there's any egress fee or storage fee hidden after pilot.
[02:44] Maya: We put egress on in cases where customers pull large volumes out of our network; typically most customers don't hit egress charges for API usage, but for dedicated S3 syncs or raw model artifacts you might see transfer costs. We will call these out explicitly in the pricing sheet we send.
[02:58] Evan: Is there an escrow cost? Do vendors charge for escrow deposits or monthly fees?
[03:03] Maya: There's usually an annual escrow fee — varies by escrow agent and the artifacts being held. We can get you an estimate.
[03:10] Laura: On DPA, our compliance requires data classification: PHI cannot leave region and needs to be encrypted at rest with keys under our control. Is Redwood able to do region-restricted hosting?
[03:21] Oliver: Yes, we support region pinning with dedicated or private deployment and can integrate with your KMS for key control. For hosted API there are region-specific endpoints and data residency options but the strongest guarantee is Dedicated/Private.
[03:36] Ravi: About SLA metrics: we need p99 latency under 300ms for inference on the primary route and 99.95% uptime. What are your standard SLOs?
[03:46] Sam: Our public SLA for hosted is 99.9% with SLOs tuned per-model and per-route. For Dedicated we can negotiate 99.95% with capacity commitments and fallback policies. P99 latency depends on model/size; we can profile with a short benchmark.
[04:00] Tom: If we move to Dedicated, what happens if you can't meet throughput during spike? Auto-burst? Fallback to smaller model? We need predictable degrade behavior.
[04:09] Oliver: We configure automated fallback policies — routing to a quantized variant or a regional fallback. For guaranteed throughput you set reserved capacity and burst buffer. Those are usually captured in the SLA and runbook.
[04:22] Jenna: For procurement checklist, we need: signed MSA, DPA with Azura redlines, SOC2 report, price schedule, PO. Anything else?
[04:31] Maya: Also we add a security questionnaire (we'll send our standard sec pack), and the technical runbook for onboarding.
[04:37] Laura: On IP: we need a carveout that derivative outputs are Azura's, not Redwood's, and any models trained on Azura data are under Azura's control.
[04:46] Maya: We can accept a use-case-limited IP assignment for customer data derivatives; full model retraining on customer data has separate commercial terms. We'll flag that in the MSA proposal.
[04:58] Ravi: Escrow agent: do you have a preferred agent? We prefer one with healthcare experience.
[05:04] Maya: We typically work with Ironclad escrow partners and can propose two options that are used in enterprise deals; we'll include the agent and sample clause.
[05:12] Evan: Timelines — procurement needs top-level dates. What's reasonable between initial MSA and production?
[05:18] Maya: Typical is 4-8 weeks depending on redlines and SOC2/attestation availability. Pilot can begin earlier under DPA only, but we ask for a PO for pilot expenses.
[05:28] Jenna: For internal sign-off we will need price certainty. Can you commit to not increasing rates during the first 12 months of the agreement?
[05:36] Maya: Yes we can include price protection for the first year in the SOW.
[05:41] Laura: On remedies, we need a well-defined credit formula tied to downtime.
[05:46] Sam: We'll propose a tiered credit schedule aligned with SLA misses in the MSA appendix.
[05:51] Tom: Technical ask — can you show us an example runbook for a production cutover? That will help infra sign-off.
[05:58] Oliver: We'll prepare a runbook with sequence: cert exchange, VPC peering, routing, run-of requests, KV warm-up and traffic cutover steps.
[06:10] Jenna: ok let's confirm next steps and due dates.
[06:13] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send MSA + DPA with proposed escrow clause by 11/24. Laura to return mandatory redlines by 11/28. Tom/OIiver runbook session week of 11/29. Jenna to confirm procurement timing by 12/01. Any other items?
[06:28] Laura: Please include a clear list of what will be escrowed and the trigger events.
[06:31] Maya: Will do.
[06:33] Evan: One more question — are there any competitor items we should know that change terms?
[06:37] Maya: We've seen customers push for broader IP rights with some providers, and some competitors bundling model licensing. Redwood focuses on predictable serving + observability rather than model ownership; we'll call that out in the SOW.
[06:49] Ravi: Alright thanks all.
[06:51] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email and upload the docs to the shared folder.
[06:56] (end)

Redwood to circulate MSA + proposed escrow clause by 2027-11-24
Azura legal (Laura) to send must-have redlines and IP carveouts by 2027-11-28
Schedule technical runbook deep-dive with Tom + Oliver (week of 2027-11-29)
Procurement (Jenna) to confirm budget window and PO timeline by 2027-12-01

Maya Patel: Send initial MSA/DPA with escrow language included - due 2027-11-24
Laura Kim: Provide list of mandatory legal redlines and any non-negotiable clauses - due 2027-11-28
Tom Baker: Share network egress map and VPC peering constraints - due 2027-11-26
Oliver Reed: Prepare pilot SLO and runbook doc for canary test - due 2027-11-30

title: Contract Oracle and Synthetic Harness Specification
author: Priya Ramanathan
text:
Summary
-------
This document specifies the Contract Oracle and Synthetic Harness (COSH) used to validate API and runtime behavior across model rollouts, runtime kernel changes, and client SDK updates. COSH is a lightweight, opinionated test harness that generates deterministic synthetic traffic, exercises contract boundaries, and evaluates observable side effects (metrics, traces, logs) against a versioned oracle.

Scope
-----
- Applies to public API surface area used by customer-facing SDKs (text-generation, chat, embeddings, streaming).
- Includes REST and streaming endpoints, request/response schemas, error and retry semantics, and runtime degradation/fallback behavior.
- Excludes internal infra-only endpoints (admin, billing).

Motivation
----------
We run frequent changes to model variants, quantized kernels, and routing policies. Traditional schema-only contract tests miss behavioral regressions introduced by runtime fallback, early-exit streaming, and probabilistic model outputs. COSH provides:
- An executable oracle that encodes expected behaviour for a set of representative prompts and request patterns.
- Synthetic traffic with controlled randomness and determinism seeds so results are reproducible across CI runs.
- Observability assertions that verify telemetry emission and stability during rollouts.

Definitions
-----------
- Oracle: A versioned artifact (JSON) that contains canonical expectations for a request set: normalized tokens, expected status classes, allowed ranges for numeric scores, and required telemetry labels.
- Harness: The executable runner that replays synthetic workloads against a target environment and evaluates results against an oracle.
- Deterministic seed: A PRNG seed stored with the oracle to reproduce the same tokenization/beam-selection traces for non-deterministic model outputs.

Design Principles
-----------------
- Determinism where possible: use seeds, fixed model weights (when benchmarking), and deterministic tokenizers for oracle generation.
- Lightweight and hermetic: COSH should run in CI as a job that completes in < 20 minutes for core suites and < 90 minutes for extended suites.
- Observability-first: tests assert telemetry (metrics/traces) in addition to payload correctness.
- Progressive coverage: core, extended, and stress tiers to balance CI time and signal quality.

Specification
-------------
1. Oracle format (JSON)
 - metadata: id (sha256), created_at, author, target_api_version, oracle_version
 - tests: list of test cases; each test case is a flat-record with fields: id, description, endpoint, method, request_payload (string), expected_status (one of: success, client_error, server_error, degraded), allowed_response_schema_hashes (list of hashes), numeric_assertions (list of `{metric_name, min, max}`), telemetry_expectations (list of `{span_name, min_count}`), seed (integer)

 Example (excerpt):
 {
 "id": "core-001",
 "description": "short-chat-completion-stable",
 "endpoint": "/v1/chat/completions",
 "method": "POST",
 "request_payload": "{\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Summarize the policy in one sentence.\"}], \"max_tokens\":60}",
 "expected_status": "success",
 "allowed_response_schema_hashes": ["sha256:..."],
 "numeric_assertions": [{"metric_name":"token_count","min":"10","max":"70"}],
 "telemetry_expectations": [{"span_name":"runtime.infer","min_count":"1"}],
 "seed": "42"
 }

2. Harness modes
 - dry-run: validate oracle JSON syntax and schema only.
 - local: run harness against a developer-local environment with mocking options.
 - ci-core: run core test set in CI for each PR touching API surface or runtime.
 - ci-extended: nightly job against canary and staging clusters to catch low-frequency regressions.

3. Test tiers and budget
 - Core tier: 120–200 test cases, CI runtime target < 20m. Failure blocks PR if related files change.
 - Extended tier: 800–2,000 cases, nightly only. Used for regression detection.
 - Stress tier: 10k+ synthetic events, used in dedicated performance pipelines.

4. Assertions and tolerances
 - Exact match assertions allowed for deterministic fields (status codes, JSON schema hashes, top-k token IDs when seeded).
 - Range assertions for numeric metrics (latency_ms, token_count) with annotated SLAs.
 - Telemetry assertions: require presence of critical spans (runtime.dispatch, runtime.infer, api.auth) and dimension labels (model_variant, shard_id, request_class). Missing critical spans marks the test as failed.

Observability contract
----------------------
- Each test run must emit a test-run trace with tag: test.run_id and test.oracle_id. Traces should link to per-request runtime traces via parent/child relationships.
- Metrics to assert in core suite:
 - cosh.test.success_rate (goal >= 99% for core suite in staging)
 - cosh.runtime.infer.latency.p50/p95/p99 (values depend on test profile; see appendix)
 - cosh.telemetry.span_presence (boolean per required span)

CI integration
--------------
1. PR validation:
 - If a change touches any of: api schema, client SDKs, runtime kernel, routing, or model manifests, run ci-core.
 - ci-core failures for changed areas block merge; failures unrelated to changed files produce non-blocking warnings and create a ticket.

2. Nightly pipeline:
 - Run ci-extended against staging and canary. If core success_rate drops by > 2 percentage points vs. previous successful run, auto-open an incident for investigation.

3. Artifact storage:
 - Oracles are stored in the contract-oracle S3 bucket with key pattern: oracles/{target_api_version}/{oracle_id}.json and signed by the author using repo GPG.

Rollout and Canary guidance
---------------------------
1. Canary policy: when rolling a model or runtime change, run the core harness against the canary cluster before traffic ramp. If any core test fails with expected_status != success or missing telemetry spans, abort rollout and trigger rollback.
2. Progressive enablement: if canary passes, run a 2-hour extended run with sampling at 10% traffic in production (metric-driven ramp). Monitor cosh.test.success_rate and cosh.runtime.infer.latency.p95.

Runbook: failed core suite
-------------------------
1. Triage owner: oncall-runtime (pager duty).
2. Immediate steps:
 a. Retrieve last successful oracle id and recent run artifacts from S3.
 b. Compare failed test IDs and diffs in response schema hashes.
 c. If telemetry spans are missing, check tracer agent versions and environment variable injection in deployment.
 d. If numeric assertions violated (latency/token_count), check recent infra events (GPU preemption, autoscale) and routing logs.
3. Escalation:
 - If > 20% core tests failing or success_rate < 90%, page oncall-sre and oncall-infra; treat as Sev2.

Ownership and governance
------------------------
- COSH steward: Priya Ramanathan (eng-infrastructure).
- Owners: eng-serving-runtime (primary), eng-infra (support for CI and artifacts), eng-dx (SDK integrations).
- Review cadence: core suite and oracle format reviewed quarterly; oracle artifact rotation annually.

Appendix A — Example CLI usage
-----------------------------
# validate oracle
redwood-cosh validate --oracle s3://oracles/v1/core-2026-01-20.json

# run core suite against staging
redwood-cosh run --oracle s3://oracles/v1/core-2026-01-20.json --target staging --mode ci-core --output results/core-staging-2026-03-08.json

Appendix B — Core test matrix (excerpt)
--------------------------------------
| test_id | endpoint | intent | key_assertions | latency_budget_ms |
|---------|--------------------------|-------------------------|---------------------------------|-------------------|
| core-001| /v1/chat/completions | short summarization | status=success, span=infer | 250 |
| core-012| /v1/completions | streaming long-form | partial_chunk_count>=3, span=stream.write | 1200 |
| core-024| /v1/embeddings | vector stability | vector_dim=1536, cosine_stable >0.95 | 100 |

Notes and limitations
---------------------
- COSH does not attempt to prove semantic equivalence for open-ended generation — we use token-level or schema-level checks with human-in-the-loop for extended validation.
- Oracle maintenance is an operational cost: owners must keep gold samples up-to-date when intentional behavioral changes are introduced.

Change history
--------------
- 2026-01-20: Initial draft by Priya Ramanathan.
- 2026-03-08: Published after review; added CI integration details and failure runbook.
