title: Offline-forensics SIEM mapping request: sample redaction policy, resume-token consistency checks, and evidence bundle checklist
text:
Issue summary:
Customer (Peregrine Financial) requests an ad-hoc offline-forensics evidence bundle for a suspected data-exfiltration investigation. They want: a sample SIEM mapping for Elasticsearch/Carrier (ELK) showing field-level redaction examples; a reproducible resume-token/offset validation procedure so they can resume a historical ingest consistently; and a checklist for the evidence bundle we will hand off (checksums, RCF/TAR manifest, timezone normalization notes).

Impact:
- Investigator needs immediate delivery of a minimal, verifiable evidence package covering 2026-03-01 to 2026-03-03 tenant activity.
- Without consistent resume tokens and replayable offsets, their SIEM ingest may miss or duplicate events during playback.

Environment:
- Production tenant: peregrine-prod-42 (enterprise account).
- Region: us-east-1.
- Primary delivery target requested: SFTP to customer-owned endpoint, fallback: presigned S3 object.

Requested deliverables (customer asked for examples + runbook):
1) A sample ELK field mapping that demonstrates redaction of PII and reversible pseudonymization patterns (sample payloads and mapping).
2) An automated resume-token validation script/harness (shell + curl examples) that proves idempotent replays for a given time window.
3) Evidence bundle checklist: file manifest with SHA256 hashes, RFC3161 timestamps for snapshot start/end, and an index tying exported events to original audit stream offsets.
4) A short runbook for our Support/SRE to produce the bundle on-demand and certificate steps for signing the manifest.

Steps to reproduce (for Support to produce sample artifact):
1. Identify tenant activity query for peregrine-prod-42 covering 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z to 2026-03-03T23:59:59Z.
2. Use internal playback tool (playback-v2) with --emit-resume-token to create an export and capture tokens at hourly boundaries.
3. Produce two sample ingest files: raw-events.jsonl (no redaction) and redacted-events.jsonl (PII redaction applied).
4. Generate manifest.json with per-file SHA256 and RFC3161-signed timestamp.
5. Transfer to staging SFTP and run resume-token re-ingest using our SIEM connector to verify no duplicates/holes.

Logs / snippets:
- Example resume token (hour boundary): rt_20260301_12Z::offset=342193::crc=7b1f4a9c
- Example mapping snippet (ELK): source.user.email -> PII_REDACT(email_hash)
- Manifest example line: {"file":"redacted-events-2026-03-01T12Z.jsonl","sha256":"c4a1e3...","rfc3161_ts":"2026-03-12T14:02:13Z"}

Investigation notes so far:
- Initial export run by Support (2026-03-10 09:12Z) succeeded for a 2-hour slice; resume tokens were captured.
- We observed one boundary token mismatch during re-ingest caused by UTC-to-local normalization applied in internal transform pipeline. Hypothesis: legacy transformer applied customerTZ (America/New_York) normalization to event timestamps before manifesting offsets.
- Action taken: reverted transformer in staging and re-ran hourly replay for 2026-03-01T12:00Z-14:00Z; offsets matched and no duplicates on replay.

Customer-supplied context (from initial email):
- They received duplicated session-start events when replaying our feed into their ELK cluster; duplicates correspond to hour-boundary files.
- They asked for demonstrable steps we followed plus a signed manifest for chain-of-custody.

Acceptance criteria (customer):
- Deliverable package includes: redacted sample, raw sample, signed manifest, resume-token verification log, and runbook steps they can re-run.
- Demonstrated re-ingest with zero-duplicate outcome for the requested window.

Priority and follow-up:
- Customer asked for expedited turnaround; treating as P1/Sev1 for evidence production.
- If we cannot deliver full package within SLA window, provide incremental artifacts (first: redaction mapping + partial manifest) and notify customer.

2026-03-10 09:20Z - Zoe Patel: Opened ticket after email from Peregrine SOC. Customer attached sample duplicate events and asked for signed manifest + runbook.
2026-03-10 10:05Z - Ethan Rivera (assignee): Acknowledged. Will produce a 6-hour sample export and investigate token boundary behavior. Tentative ETA: 2026-03-11 end-of-day.
2026-03-10 15:40Z - SRE (Maya Chen): Observed TZ normalization in transformer-legacy pipeline. Performed test replay in staging; boundary tokens aligned after disabling transformer. Uploading test logs to /artifacts/sup-750321/initial-run.log.
2026-03-11 08:12Z - Customer (Peregrine SOC): Confirmed duplicates reduced after last ingest run but asked for full signed manifest and instructions to resume ingest without reintroducing duplicates.
2026-03-12 11:33Z - Ethan Rivera: Preparing evidence bundle. Included preliminary manifest and runbook draft in the artifact bucket. Will schedule SFTP transfer once customer confirms endpoint details.
2026-03-12 14:00Z - Zoe Patel: Notified customer about change in transformer behavior and recommended a short coordination call to verify SFTP credentials and acceptance tests.

Root-cause hypothesis: timestamp normalization applied pre-manifest caused resume-token offsets to be recorded in localized epoch, while our replay tool expects canonical UTC offsets. Repro steps validated by disabling legacy transformer in staging. Next: create deterministic export path that emits canonical UTC timestamps and add an ingest-side de-duplication idempotency check (event-hash + offset) in runbook.

1) Produce full evidence bundle for 2026-03-01..2026-03-03 (raw + redacted + manifest + token-verification logs). 2) Share SFTP instructions and request fingerprint for SFTP key. 3) Run replay verification with customer in a joint test window and capture final signed manifest. 4) If requested, open INT ticket to harden transformer to emit canonical UTC consistently.

raw_metadata.summary: Offline-forensics SIEM mapping request: sample redaction policy, resume-token consistency checks, and evidence bundle checklist

title: Demo tenant Console dashboards not populating metrics (empty graphs) in demo project
text:
Issue Summary:
Console dashboards for the demo tenant are showing empty graphs (no cost/latency/error data) for the primary demo project during dry runs and at least one live customer call. This breaks the Observability portion of the standard demo (Console tour).

Impact:
- SEs cannot reliably show token-level cost, latency percentiles, error rates, or rollout dashboards.
- Creates "product looks empty" perception even though the API is working.
- Requires last-minute manual workarounds (running synthetic traffic generator, changing time ranges, switching projects).

Customer / Context:
- Demo tenant used for sales demos (internal), but used in customer-facing calls.
- Reported after a demo runthrough where the API steps succeeded but the Console remained empty.

Environment:
- Demo org + projects in prod control plane (us-east)
- Console: prod
- Telemetry ingestion: prod

Expected Behavior:
- Demo project dashboards show recent traffic (last 15m / last 1h) with realistic distributions.
- Default landing state should not be empty if synthetic traffic is running.

Actual Behavior:
- Console dashboards show empty charts (no data) even after several demo API calls.
- Some views show an "empty state" that does not guide the user to select the correct project/time range.

Steps to Reproduce:
1) Login to Console and switch to Demo Org.
2) Select project "demo-observability" (or the default demo project).
3) Navigate to Dashboards > Latency and Dashboards > Cost.
4) Set time range to "Last 15 minutes".
5) Observe empty graphs.
6) Meanwhile, run a few chat completion requests against the demo route and confirm 200 responses.

Notes / Observations:
- In some cases, switching time range to "Last 24 hours" shows data, suggesting freshness/time-range defaults are a factor.
- When synthetic traffic generator is manually started, data appears after ~5–10 minutes, but this is too brittle for live demos.

Initial Links:
- Slack thread: sources/slack/sales/1741446203.json ("live-demo panic—dashboards are empty")
- Runbook: demo tenant reset + verification checklist (see related confluence pages)

Request:
- Identify whether this is (a) ingestion not receiving events, (b) Console querying wrong project/time range, (c) synthetic traffic job not running, or (d) demo seed config missing required routes/events.
- Provide a fast, reliable pre-demo check + remediation path.

2025-11-12 - Markus Klein (Reporter): We had the demo API steps working but the Console was empty (cost/latency). This blocks the observability module. We need a deterministic fix; the workaround of "change to last 24h" is not acceptable in a customer call.
2025-11-12 - Allison Grant (Assignee): Taking triage. First hypothesis: synthetic traffic generator job not running (or stuck) so dashboards depend on sparse manual calls. Second hypothesis: Console default filters (project selection/time range) are landing on a project with no telemetry. Pulling telemetry ingestion logs for demo org + checking the demo-traffic job status.
2025-11-12 - Logan Wright: Quick check: ingestion shows *some* events for demo org but mostly in bursts. For the time window 16:00–16:20 PT, demo-observability had <10 requests. That’s not enough to populate certain aggregated views. We should ensure the synthetic generator runs continuously and emits the specific event types Console dashboards expect (request.completed, token.usage, error.*).
2025-11-12 - Chloe Martin: Confirmed Console empty state is confusing: if no project is explicitly selected, some dashboard views render empty without prompting. Also, the default time range is "Last 15m" which can be empty if the synthetic traffic job is paused. I can patch the empty-state to (1) default to the seeded demo project and (2) show a CTA to start synthetic traffic / link runbook.
2025-11-13 - Allison Grant: Found that the demo synthetic traffic generator was not enabled in one of the demo namespaces after a reset. The reset script re-seeded org/projects/routes but did not restart the generator job. Manual remediation: start demo-traffic-generator preset "observability" and wait ~7 minutes; dashboards populate. We need this automated in reset/healthcheck.
2025-11-13 - Sean Gallagher: Adding this as a demo SLO concern (dashboard freshness). Suggest demo healthcheck includes: (a) last_ingested_event_age < 5m for demo-observability project, (b) synthetic generator running, (c) Console can query metrics endpoint successfully. If any fail, return a clear PASS/FAIL with suggested commands.
2025-11-14 - Allison Grant: Implemented immediate workaround in the runbook: after reset, run the synthetic traffic job and verify by checking "Requests" count > 100 in last 15m. Also advising SEs to switch to "Last 1h" if needed while we ship a better default/empty-state.
2025-11-15 - Allison Grant: Resolved by (1) ensuring synthetic traffic generator is started by default for demo tenant and (2) Console empty-state improvements merged. After deploying, dashboards show data in last 15m consistently within 2–3 minutes of reset completion.

Telemetry: Ingestion pipeline healthy; events present but insufficient volume during certain windows.
Root cause appears to be a reset/seed gap: demo tenant could be reset to a state where traffic generator is stopped/disabled, leaving dashboards reliant on sparse manual demo calls.
Contributing factor: Console empty-state + default time range does not guide users when no data in last 15m and/or when the wrong project is selected.
Verified by starting the generator manually and observing metrics appear within ~5–10 minutes.

Resolution:
- Enabled/verified demo synthetic traffic generator preset for the demo-observability project as part of standard reset.
- Updated Console empty-state / default selection behavior so the seeded demo project is easier to land on and empty graphs provide actionable guidance.

Workaround (for field, before full rollout):
1) Run demo-traffic-generator preset "observability".
2) Wait 5–10 minutes.
3) In Console, set time range to Last 1h and confirm request volume > 100.

Validation:
- After reset + generator start, latency/cost/error dashboards populate consistently.
- Manual demo calls alone are no longer required to avoid empty graphs.

Add a demo healthcheck that asserts "dashboard freshness" (last_ingested_event_age) and generator job status; surface as a single PASS/FAIL for SEs.
Update demo tenant reset automation to be fully idempotent for generator job enablement (no manual post-reset steps).
Add alerting on demo dashboards data freshness (e.g., no events for >10m during business hours) routed to demo on-call alias.
Document expected time-to-populate after reset (target: <= 3 minutes) and include in SE checklist.

raw_metadata.summary: Demo tenant Console dashboards not populating metrics (empty graphs) in demo project

title: Fallback model not triggering during overload (customer receives 503 OVERLOADED instead of routed fallback)
text:
Issue summary
Banyan Search reports that their configured fallback model is not being used during overload events. Instead, requests fail with 503 and Redwood overload error codes.

Customer expectation
When primary model (rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct) is overloaded, Redwood should route to configured fallback (rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct) per their tenant policy.

Impact
- Customer sees elevated failed requests during traffic spikes rather than degraded (lower quality) responses.
- Affects production search assistant experience and increases client retry pressure.

Environment
- Hosted API
- Region: us-east
- Route: /v1/chat/completions
- Streaming: mostly enabled

Customer configuration (as described by customer)
- Primary: rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct
- Fallback: rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct
- Trigger condition: overload (customer referenced 'circuit breaker open')

What the customer is seeing (excerpt)
- HTTP 503
- Error payload (representative):
 code: OVERLOADED
 message: "Service temporarily overloaded. Please retry."
 correlation_id: rwcorr_01JEMNQZJ5J9P2G6E3R9K8V6M2
 retry_after: (present for some responses; missing for some per SUP-2860)

Steps to reproduce (internal)
1) Identify Banyan tenant_id and active routing policy.
2) Induce overload condition (or replay from perf-canary) where gateway admission control sheds requests.
3) Confirm whether routing attempts fallback model when overload is detected.

Initial hypothesis
Fallback routing is only attempted when overload is detected at routing/runtime stages. When overload occurs at the gateway admission layer (breaker open / shed), the request is rejected before routing executes, so no fallback can occur. Additional suspicion: loop-prevention logic may be suppressing fallback when the request already contains an attempted-model chain header.

Requested outcome
- Confirm whether fallback is expected to work under gateway-level shedding.
- If not currently supported, provide clear customer guidance and (if safe) enable fallback-on-gateway-overload for this tenant as an exception/feature flag.
- Ensure Retry-After is consistently present on overload errors.

2025-12-09 09:12 PT — Owen Phillips (Support): Customer (Banyan Search) reports fallback not triggering. They configured fallback from 70B -> 8B for overload, but still getting 503 OVERLOADED during peak. Provided correlation IDs and noted they are using streaming on /v1/chat/completions in us-east. Creating ticket and pulling in routing/SRE.
2025-12-09 09:28 PT — Dev Patel (Support readiness): Confirmed this aligns with multiple questions we’re getting since overload protection canary. Linking SUP-2860 as customer also mentioned missing Retry-After on a subset of responses.
2025-12-09 10:05 PT — Peter Holtz (Routing reliability): Looking at traces for rwcorr_01JEMNQZJ5J9P2G6E3R9K8V6M2 — request is being rejected at gateway admission (breaker open) with shed_reason=gateway_concurrency_cap before smart-routing service is called. So fallback cannot occur because routing is not invoked in this path. This matches ADR-015 layering behavior.
2025-12-09 10:19 PT — Peter Holtz (Routing reliability): Confirmed tenant policy has fallback configured, but current behavior: fallback is only evaluated on downstream overload signals (routing/runtime) and certain error codes. Gateway-level shedding is treated as terminal to stop retry storms and protect downstream. We need to align with Product whether we want optional 'fallback_when_breaker_open' semantics.
2025-12-09 10:42 PT — Nikhil Sharma (Product owner, Hosted API): For now, we should be explicit: fallback is best-effort and may not apply when admission control rejects early. However, for enterprise customers we can consider allowing fallback on gateway overload with strict guardrails (bounded retries, no loops, only within compatibility group). Please propose a safe tenant-scoped override if feasible.
2025-12-09 11:10 PT — Rafael Mendes (SRE lead): +1. If we allow fallback on gateway overload, need to ensure we’re not just shifting load to the fallback pool and causing broader instability. Suggest: only allow if fallback targets a different capacity pool/priority class and enforce additional max_tokens cap under duress.
2025-12-10 08:55 PT — Elena Popov (Routing signals integration): Found second issue: in cases where routing is invoked (runtime returns overload), fallback was suppressed for Banyan because loop-prevention saw attempted_models already populated from a previous internal retry. There’s a bug: we’re persisting attempted_models across an internal redirect even when the first attempt never reached the model backend due to a fast-fail overload. That makes the router think it already tried the fallback and stops.
2025-12-10 09:30 PT — Ravi Menon (Fallback routing architect): Root cause seems twofold:
(1) Most failures happen pre-routing (gateway admission sheds) => fallback not possible.
(2) In the subset that reaches routing, a header bookkeeping issue causes loop-prevention to incorrectly block fallback.
Proposed fix: clear attempted_models when the failure is classified as 'admission_shed' vs 'model_attempted'. We can hotfix routing to only append attempted_models after a backend attempt is made.
2025-12-10 10:15 PT — Amara Diallo (Gateway middleware): Confirmed gateway emits overload classification as 'gateway_admission_shed' with reason codes concurrency_cap / token_bucket. It does not call routing service in this path. If we want fallback here, it needs a design change (admission would have to consult routing policy, or we let some fraction through to routing for fallback evaluation).
2025-12-10 11:05 PT — Peter Holtz (Routing reliability): Action items:
- Ship routing hotfix for attempted_models bookkeeping so loop-prevention doesn’t suppress valid fallback (owner: routing team).
- For Banyan: offer immediate mitigation via tenant policy update: prefer us-west secondary region for fallback (if acceptable) or temporarily raise dedicated priority class for fallback model pool during their peak window.
- Provide customer-facing clarification: fallback is best-effort; early admission shedding returns explicit OVERLOADED with Retry-After and correlation_id.
- Ensure Retry-After consistency is tracked via SUP-2860/PR-18472 rollout.
2025-12-11 14:22 PT — Peter Holtz (Routing reliability): Hotfix deployed to us-east routing service: only append attempted_models after a backend dispatch; do not treat gateway admission shed as a model attempt. Verified in staging replay: when runtime overload occurs (not gateway shed), fallback triggers to rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct and returns 200. When gateway shed occurs, still returns 503 (as designed).
2025-12-12 09:00 PT — Owen Phillips (Support): Responded to customer with findings and mitigation:
- Confirmed most errors were gateway admission shedding, which currently does not route to fallback.
- We fixed a bug that could suppress fallback when routing was reached.
- Recommended client respect Retry-After + exponential backoff with jitter.
- Offered optional tenant-scoped enablement for 'fallback on breaker open' once available; for now, we can explore a scheduled capacity adjustment / alternate region policy if they want.
Customer acknowledged and asked us to monitor next peak window.
2025-12-13 08:40 PT — Peter Holtz (Routing reliability): Monitored Banyan during peak: fallback activation observed for runtime overload cases; overall 503 rate decreased, but gateway sheds still occur at extreme spikes. No evidence of fallback loops after hotfix. Marking resolved; tracking follow-up enhancement separately to support safe fallback on gateway breaker-open if Product approves.

Resolved with routing hotfix: loop-prevention/attempted_models bookkeeping bug prevented fallback from triggering in some overload scenarios. After deployment, fallback works when overload is detected at routing/runtime stages. Gateway admission shedding remains a terminal response by design (no fallback attempted) to prevent overload cascades; customer was informed and given mitigation guidance (Retry-After/backoff, optional policy/capacity adjustments).

raw_metadata.summary: Fallback model not triggering during overload (customer receives 503 OVERLOADED instead of routed fallback)

domain: 日常协作与非结构化讨论
title: eng-sre
text:
Sam: FYI support ticket #78921 — customer reports p99 API latency from eu-central jumped from ~120ms to ~900ms around 10:03 UTC. They saw requests egressing to us-east IPs. attaching their probe output.

Maria: thanks, linking the ticket. do we have any infra changes around that time? autoscaling events? :mag_right:

ops-bot: Alert: edge-pop-eu-central latency spike detected (p99 +650ms) at 2026-03-17T10:02:58Z. Related traces: t=grp-394.

Jon: I skimmed infra logs — no recent deploys. Quick check of our edge-dns logs shows increased NXTTL responses from the regional resolver pool at 10:01-10:04. possible resolver churn.

Lee: Customer sent traceroutes, here's the first hop they captured:
```
traceroute to api.redwood.ai (52.14.23.10), 30 hops max, 60 byte packets
 1 10.0.0.1 0.8 ms
 2 203.0.113.45 1.2 ms
 3 * * *
 4 54.210.11.5 (us-east-1) 320.4 ms
 5 52.14.23.10 322.1 ms
```

Sam: that looks like a geo-detour to us-east. customer is in Frankfurt. they also attached DNS query history showing intermittent answers pointing to us-east A records.

Jon: can you paste the DNS query sample? also which resolver are they hitting (ISP)?

Lee: ISP resolver is isp-frankfurt.net (203.0.113.45). DNS snippet: 
```
; 10:01:12.123 QUERY example.api.redwood.ai A from 203.0.113.45
; ANSWER: 52.14.23.10 (us-east) TTL=12
; 10:01:13.456 QUERY example.api.redwood.ai A from 203.0.113.45
; ANSWER: 52.120.7.99 (eu-central) TTL=360
```

Maria: small TTLs then longer one — could be our authoritative returning mixed records (split-horizon) during a rollout? or an upstream resolver cache poisoning?

Jon: checked our authoritative logs — no config pushes at that minute. but we did have a transient failover of the eu-pop-anycast pair at 10:00:57 which shifted health checks to a backup that advertises a different egress ASN. that could cause the ISP resolver to see different nearest anycast instance and get a state where the returned A record was us-east.

Sam: customer is impacted, asking for mitigation. recommended quick fixes?

Jon: immediate mitigations: 1) add a temporary DNS override in the eu-central authoritative zone to strongly prefer eu IPs for that customer (short term), 2) rollback the anycast failover if safe, 3) ask ISP to flush cache (lee), 4) put a routing policy to prefer eu-egress for eu prefix.

Lee: I can request ISP cache flush but won't be instant. I'll also add the customer tag and escalate support SLA (we're in enterprise plan).

Maria: ops decision: do a targeted DNS override for hostnames used by this customer + add a temporary geo-affinity policy for their tenant while we root cause. Jon, can you prepare the override? include a TTL of 60s.

Jon: preparing override now. snippet I'm about to push to auth-dns: 
```
A record example.customerX.api.redwood.ai -> 52.120.7.99 TTL=60
```
Pushing in 30s. will monitor p99.

ops-bot: Change recorded: auth-dns override applied for example.customerX.api.redwood.ai by Jon at 2026-03-17T10:07:12Z.

Sam: customer reports partial improvement ~10:09 UTC, p99 down to ~180ms but some requests still hit us-east for older resolver caches.

Lee: updated ticket with mitigation steps and ETA for full resolution. also opening a JIRA to investigate why anycast failover exposed differing egress IP sets (NETENG-4821).

Jon: follow-ups: 1) validate anycast health-check logic (why backup announced different egress set), 2) add monitoring for small-TTL churn on authoritative responses from regional resolvers, 3) plan a fix so failover preserves geo-affinity.

Maria: thanks team. assigning oncall rotation to Jon for deep-dive; set postmortem flag if we hit SLO breach. tagging @networking and @dns. :white_check_mark:

Sam: closing loop with customer now. thanks everyone.

title: ops-bridge-comm-protocols-and-template-bundle
author: Jordan Lee
text:
Purpose and scope:
This is a lightweight pocket playbook for the on-call bridge lead and SRE responders focused exclusively on communications: status page messages, customer-facing messages (two tones), and the internal war-room checklist.

How to use:
- Use the three-tier status templates below (Initial / Ongoing / Resolved) verbatim for the status page; edit placeholders only.
- Pick the customer-facing template that matches the customer tier (Enterprise or Self-serve).
- Follow the internal war-room checklist immediately after bridge creation to stabilize the signal and coordinate updates.
- Use Slack templates for quick pings to owners and execs.

Severity buckets and comm expectations:
- Sev 1 (P0): Customer-facing within 10 minutes; status page up within 15 minutes; cadence: 15m updates.
- Sev 2 (P1): Status page within 30 minutes; cadence: 30–60m updates.
- Sev 3 (P2): Status page optional; one initial update and a final resolution note.

Status page templates (copy/paste and replace names/times):
1) INITIAL — short, public, plain-language
Status: Investigating
Summary: We are investigating reports of increased error rates for the Redwood hosted inference API in us-west-2. Some requests are failing with 5xx errors.
Impact: Some customers may see increased latency or failed requests for text generation endpoints. We are actively investigating and will provide an update within 15 minutes.
Next update: <HH:MM UTC>
Incident ID: <INCIDENT-YYYY-MM-DD-#>

2) ONGOING — factual, progress-oriented
Status: Partial degradation
Summary: Our engineering team has isolated the issue to a degraded routing layer affecting a subset of inference workers. We have routed traffic away from affected pools and are validating fallbacks.
Impact: Approximately X% of requests to models in the us-west-2 region are impacted; customers using pinned Dedicated pools are unaffected.
What we are doing: Rebalancing traffic, restarting affected hosts, and running a targeted KV cache flush to restore steady-state.
Next update: <HH:MM UTC> or sooner if there is a material change.
Mitigation: Automatic fallback to compatible model variants is active for most customers; if you still experience failures, please contact support with your request IDs.

3) RESOLVED — concise, root-cause direction optional
Status: Resolved
Summary: The routing layer degradation was caused by an incremental control-plane rollout. Rolling back the rollout and rebalancing hosts restored service.
Impact: Customers in us-west-2 experienced elevated failure rates between <start> and <end>. No data loss.
What we did: Rolled back the rollout, restarted affected workers, verified request success rates, and monitored KPIs for 2 hours post-fix.
Follow-up: A post-incident review (PIR) is scheduled. Affected customers will receive an email summary within 48 hours.

Customer-facing templates
- Enterprise (formal, empathetic, actionable):
Subject: Incident update — Redwood inference service (region: us-west-2)
Hi <Customer Name>,
We wanted to let you know that we recently experienced an interruption affecting inference requests in us-west-2. Our operations team investigated and deployed mitigations that restored service at <end time UTC>.
Impact: You may have observed increased latency or failed requests between <start time> and <end time>.
Action for you: No action required unless you continue to observe errors. If you do, please reply to this message with sample request IDs and timestamps and we will prioritize a review.
Our commitment: We understand this may have affected production traffic and we apologize for the disruption. We are performing a full post-incident review and will share findings and any recommended changes within 48 hours.
Sincerely,
Redwood Inference — Customer Reliability Team

- Self-serve / Developer (short, frank, pragmatic):
Subject: Service interruption — Redwood API (us-west-2)
Quick note: We experienced increased failures for some API requests in us-west-2 between <start> and <end>. We rolled back the change and traffic is healthy now.
If you saw errors: retrying should succeed; consider increasing client-side retries for transient 5xx in the short term. If you have persistent problems, paste request IDs into a support ticket.
Thanks for bearing with us — we’ll post a brief PIR soon.

Internal war-room checklist (first 30 minutes) — bridge leader responsibilities:
1) Bridge and context
- Create a dedicated bridge channel (zoom/meet + private Slack channel).
- Summon on-call owners: serving-runtime lead, infra owner, routing engineer, SRE on-call, and the on-call support rep.
- Tag exec-oncall only after first 15 minutes unless customer impact escalates.

2) Triage snapshot (collect and share on the bridge):
- Key metrics: error-rate (5xx), p50/p95 latency, success-rate by model, percent of traffic routed to fallback.
- Example query lines (share raw IDs): latest 50 failed request IDs and sample stack traces.
- Known changes: any recent rollouts, infra changes, config pushes in last 60 minutes.

3) Immediate mitigations (pick one):
- Rollback the last control-plane rollout.
- Route traffic away from affected availability zones or hosts.
- Apply circuit-breaker to degraded model variant.
- Increase autoscale/burst capacity as emergency buffer.

4) Communications cadence (delegate):
- Scribe: document actions and timestamps in the incident doc live.
- Public comm: post initial status page item (bridge lead).
- Customer comm: assign owner for enterprise customers (account rep + solutions eng).
- Engineering updates: every 15m for P0, 30–60m for P1.

5) Stabilization checklist (first 2 hours):
- Verify end-to-end success rates across models and regions.
- Confirm fallback behaviors and cache consistency.
- Run synthetic smoke tests from multiple regions.

Slack quick-templates (paste into bridge channel):
- Ping to owner: @owner — incident <INCID> created for elevated 5xx in us-west-2. Can you validate whether the last control-plane rollout touched routing service?
- Exec ping (use sparingly): @exec-oncall — P0 in us-west-2, impact on hosted API. Initial mitigation: rollback initiated. Next update in 15m.

Post-incident review prompts (to include in PIR):
- Timeline: minute-by-minute timeline from alert -> detection -> mitigation -> resolution.
- Detection gap: how long between first error and on-call awareness?
- RCA focus: causal chain (change -> failure mode -> why safeguards failed).
- Action items: owner, target date, verification steps, and risk mitigation plan to prevent recurrence.
- Customer outreach: list of customers contacted and draft copies of emails sent.

Comms hygiene rules (do not forget):
- Never speculate about unconfirmed root causes in public messages.
- If there is possible customer data impact, escalate immediately to legal/compliance and security.
- Keep status page language simple, avoid technical acronyms without brief explanation.

Templates repository and ownership:
- This doc is intentionally compact; canonical templates live in Confluence: confluence://sre/incident-comm-templates.
- Ops-bridge comms ownership: eng-sre (on-call rotation). PRs for templates: open a PR against the canonical Confluence page and notify eng-sre.

Appendix: quick checklist for support engineers handling inbound tickets:
- Ask for request ID, timestamp, model, and region.
- Verify whether the request timestamp falls inside the incident window.
- If inside window, create a high-priority follow-up and add to incident doc. Provide ETA for customer response.
- If outside, escalate to normal support flow and close with reproduction steps.

Notes and open questions:
- Consider adding a one-click status page composer in the console to reduce cadence friction.
- Discuss retention window for incident emails: 48 hours for initial summary, 7 days for follow-up PIR notification.

End of doc.

title: API Triage Cheatsheet — observable signatures & first-response workflow
author: Ava Chen
text:
Purpose:
Quick triage guide for on-call SREs and devs to identify "observable signatures" of common API failure modes and take fast mitigations while we investigate root cause. This is intentionally terse — keep as a checklist during pager events.

Scope:
- High-level symptoms covered: request timeouts, 429 rate-limits, degraded streaming (partial frames / stalls), and spikes in 5xx / client error rates.
- Assumes access to Console dashboards, request traces, request logs, and the usual k8s / autoscaler metrics.

Quick signposting (signals to look at immediately):
1) Timeouts (client-facing request deadlines hit)
 - Sudden jump in latency P95/P99 and a corresponding increase in request.duration > app_deadline.
 - Traces show a heavy tail on inference step or KV cache step (longest spans).
 - Backends: CPU/GPU saturation? look at host_gpu_util, process_blocked, and container OOM counts.
 - Quick checks: `kubectl top pods -n inference | sort -k3 -nr` and `nvidia-smi` on dedicated nodes.

Immediate mitigations for timeouts:
 - Temporarily lower concurrency (route traffic to lower-concurrency pool) or enable fallback model variant with smaller sequence length/quantized weights.
 - If autoscaler lagging: manual scale up of node pool (increase replicas), or enable burst capacity (if configured).
 - If storage/networking (e.g., S3) is slow: switch to cached model variant or bump local cache replicas.

2) 429s (throttling / upstream rate-limits)
 - Pattern: uniform increases in 429 responses across many clients vs narrow (single key).
 - Check token/billing quotas, per-customer rate-limits, and per-route rate-limiters.
 - Look at request_id patterns: are we seeing token bucket fills or sudden traffic spikes?

Immediate mitigations for 429s:
 - Identify offending API keys -> temporarily increase quota for internal/prod-critical keys only.
 - Apply lightweight global backoff header to clients, or flip on soft-limits that return Retry-After instead of hard 429.
 - If due to upstream capacity, route a fraction of traffic to lower-cost model variant as fallback.

3) Degraded streaming (partial frames, stalls, or truncated SSE/chunked responses)
 - Symptoms: streaming metric shows high stream-terminate events, client-side partial payloads, or long idle times between chunks in traces.
 - Correlated server logs: ‘write timeout’ on response socket, or kernel-level send buffer pressure.

Immediate mitigations for streaming issues:
 - Reduce chunk size / flush frequency in runtime config (short-term).
 - If network nodes show packet drops or high TCP retransmits, move streams to nodes with lower network contention.
 - Consider toggling streaming-to-buffered endpoint (convert to non-streaming) for highest-value flows.

4) Elevated error rates (5xx spiky or sustained)
 - Distinguish: 5xx internal server errors vs 502/504 gateway timeouts vs runtime exceptions.
 - Use trace sampling to find top failing endpoints and common error messages.

Immediate mitigations for elevated 5xx:
 - Roll back the most recent deployment if correlated with a release (use canary logs).
 - Circuit-break top noisy downstream calls (database, KV store, model-loading) and route to cached responses.
 - If memory pressure -> restart pods in a staggered fashion to avoid cascade.

Investigation checklist (after immediate mitigation):
- Short-term telemetry queries to run (examples):
 - Errors by endpoint: `sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{job="api",status=~"5.."}[5m])) by (handler)`
 - Latency heatmap: `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_bucket[5m])) by (le, handler))`
 - 429 attribution by api_key: `sum(rate(http_requests_total{status="429"}[5m])) by (api_key)`
- Correlate with infra metrics: host_cpu, gpu_util, io_wait, network_errors, pod_restarts.
- Look for config changes: recent feature flags, rate-limit rule updates, or rollout configs.
- Check linked PRs / deploys in last 60 minutes.
- Search Slack alert channel for repeat signals from other teams.

Escalation matrix (who to call, in order):
- Primary on-call SRE -> handles initial mitigations.
- Serving runtime lead: Marcus Rivera (if model execution or kv cache implicated).
- Infra / k8s lead: Sophie Kline (if autoscaler or node-level issues).
- Product owner / oncall PM for critical customer-facing regressions.

Post-incident notes to capture for PG (postmortem):
- Root-cause hypothesis and evidence mapping (logs, traces, host metrics).
- What mitigations were applied and their effectiveness (include timestamps).
- Action items (owner + due date): config changes, improved alerts (reduce noise, add more attribution), runbook gaps.
- Customer impact summary and communication timeline.

Open TODOs (draft-level items we should formalize):
- Add sample Grafana dashboard panels and alert thresholds here (TODO: capture panel urls).
- Define per-endpoint SLOs -> tie to automated rollback thresholds.
- Automate diagnostic scripts for `kubectl`/GPU checks and publish as `sre-tools triage-api` command.

Notes / heuristics (helpful rules-of-thumb):
- If P99 latency rises but tail CPU/GPU is not saturated -> probable queuing in request router or network blips.
- If 429s are concentrated by api_key -> consider client-side misconfiguration or test harness runaway.
- When enabling fallbacks, limit to a small percentage (5-15%) first, monitor quality regressions.

Slack snippets to post during incident (copy/paste):
- Short status: `INCIDENT: elevated 5xx on /v1/generate — mitigation: partial rollback applied at 15:02 UTC, monitoring.`
- Request for help: `Seeking serving-runtime lead: traces show 30s span in kv-fetch step on node i-0abc. Can you check model cache health?`

References/links:
- Add console dashboard links here (TODO).
- Related runbooks: ops-rate-limit-handling, model-fallback-playbook (references to be added).

End of draft — additions welcome.

title: Elysian Commerce - Search precision playthrough (hosted API)
author: Maya Chen
text:
Hosted API walkthrough focused on embeddings + reranking endpoints. Demonstrated Redwood hosted embeddings endpoint, a two-stage retrieval + rerank flow, and console traces. Discussed evaluation metrics (MRR/NDCG), latency vs cost tradeoffs, prefix/KV caching, batching recommendations, and security/compliance concerns. Customer interested in a 1-week pilot to validate search relevance for product search along with SLA targets and security docs.

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-07
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rafael Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Elysian Head of Search), Tom Adler (Elysian Lead ML Eng), Zoe Park (Elysian PM)

Summary (auto): Quick hosted API demo of embeddings + reranker, followed by Q&A on performance and security. Action items captured.

00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call?
00:06 Priya Nair: Priya here, hi.
00:08 Tom Adler: Tom on the line.
00:11 Zoe Park: Zoe, hi all.
00:13 Maya Chen: Great, I'm Maya from Redwood, and Rafael is my SE, he'll drive the deep bits. Rafael, you want to intro?
00:18 Rafael Ortiz: Yeah hi, Rafael Ortiz, I'm the solutions engineer, I work on retrieval/rerank patterns and infra. We'll show a hosted flow — embeddings + reranker — and then the console traces and Optimize suggestions.
00:30 Priya Nair: High level goal: improve product search relevancy — particularly long-tail queries and new SKUs. We're seeing poor ordering for intent queries and we want better MRR and fewer zero-clicks.
00:40 Maya Chen: Perfect. Quick qualification: current infra?
00:43 Tom Adler: We're running an ES cluster for indexing, some Redis for sessions. We tested Pinecone for vectors but latency was variable and cost spiked. We have a batch job to index products nightly.
00:56 Rafael Ortiz: Good context. We'll demo two-stage: 1) embeddings search via hosted API for vector retrieve, 2) call to our reranker endpoint to rescore top-k. We'll show trade-offs: reranker length/size impacts latency.
01:12 Rafael Ortiz: I'll share my screen now — can you see the console? (screen share)
01:18 Zoe Park: Yep, seeing it.
01:20 Rafael Ortiz: Right, on the left is the hosted embeddings API playground. We're using a 'smallish' embedding model for this demo — that gives you good economy. For high precision you can pick a larger encoding.
01:36 Tom Adler: Do you expose model sizes and tokenization? We need to know dimension sizes for our vector DB.
01:41 Rafael Ortiz: Yes, the API returns dims in the model catalog. For the model I'm using today it's 1536 dims, so that matches many vector DBs. Sometimes the catalog label gets mis-typed in the export (we saw one as 1,536 in a prior CSV) — minor thing.
01:57 Priya Nair: Walk us through the end-to-end latency contribution from each stage?
02:02 Rafael Ortiz: Sure — embedding inference is usually ~20-40ms on hosted depending on model. Vector retrieval latency is your DB's concern — but we usually target top-100 retrieval within 20-60ms. Reranker call latency depends on model size and input length; for our production reranker a common SLO is 80-150ms for k=10 reranks using a 6B-class model on the hosted tier. Keep in mind continuous batching and our smart routing can reduce per-request cost.
02:30 Zoe Park: Smart routing as in fallback to smaller model when under load?
02:33 Rafael Ortiz: Exactly. Policy-based: cost-first or latency-first. You can pin a model version for consistency or allow fallbacks.
02:40 Priya Nair: Can we see the reranker request/response?
02:43 Rafael Ortiz: Sure — switching to the reranker endpoint tab. Example payload: query + candidate snippets + doc metadata. The response is a score + optional structured explanation tokens if you enable structured output.
02:58 Rafael Ortiz: Note: sometimes the transcript generator shows 'kay v cache' instead of 'KV cache' in logs — don't be surprised.
03:05 Tom Adler: ha, yep. On the candidate side, do you accept BM25+vector hybrid?
03:09 Rafael Ortiz: You can combine signals. Many customers run a hybrid: BM25 for recall, vector for semantic match; then reranker uses both the document text and BM25 score as features. We also have a built-in reranker feature store you can forward features to.
03:25 Priya Nair: What metrics should we track to measure improvement?
03:28 Rafael Ortiz: NDCG@10, MRR@5, recall@100 are standard. For ecomm we also monitor purchase-through-query and time-to-click; Redwood Console can surface per-route MRR and regression alerts tied to prompt sets or evals.
03:42 Zoe Park: show the Optimize tab?
03:44 Rafael Ortiz: Yep, coming up — Optimize suggests batching config, quantization profile recommendations, and prefix/KV cache settings based on observed sequence length distribution. Here is a recommendation we ran against a synthetic workload: batch size 8 for lower latency 90th pct, enable 4-bit quantization on the reranker for 2–3x token cost reduction with marginal score delta.
04:09 Priya Nair: Any quality drop with 4-bit?
04:12 Rafael Ortiz: Slight, you should run an eval on your ground-truth. For many rerankers 4-bit is fine; for top-of-funnel generation we usually avoid aggressive quant. The Console includes regression alerts if NDCG dips beyond threshold.
04:28 Tom Adler: Security: we need SOC2 docs, SSO, and KMS integration for keys. How do you handle customer data in hosted?
04:36 Maya Chen: Good question — hosted includes tenant isolation, optional VPC peering for private networking, and we support KMS/HSM for model keys and payload encryption at rest. We can share our SOC2 Type II report, and SAML SSO is supported; audit logs are available via the console. Rafael, anything more?
04:50 Rafael Ortiz: For extra-sensitive workloads we recommend Redwood Private. Hosted still supports strict retention policies and encryption. We'll share the security packet, and we can set up a call with security if needed.
05:02 Priya Nair: That helps. What about data residency? We need EU region hosting for part of our catalog.
05:08 Maya Chen: We have regional endpoints — you can pin routing to eu-west for specific customers or routes.
05:13 Zoe Park: show a live rerank example end-to-end?
05:16 Rafael Ortiz: Yep. I'll call embeddings endpoint with a long-tail query "women's waterproof running shoes size 9 wide".
05:23 Rafael Ortiz: // request sent // 00:05 response for embedding vector...
05:30 Rafael Ortiz: Pass top-200 to your vector DB (here simulated), then fetch top-10 candidates and call reranker. Reranker call payload — notice we include product metadata fields (brand, price, availability) as additional context.
05:48 Rafael Ortiz: Here is the reranker response — scores and the top re-ordered list. The console trace shows a 132ms reranker latency, embedding 28ms. 160ms end-to-end for k=10.
06:03 Tom Adler: 132ms seems a bit high for our SLA (aiming <120ms for UX). Any levers?
06:08 Rafael Ortiz: You can: reduce model size for reranker (e.g., Distil or 3B variant), shrink input length by truncating less-relevant doc fields, or enable batching at the edge which amortizes some cost. Also consider prefix/KV caching if queries include common prefixes.
06:22 Priya Nair: Do you do prefix caching automatically?
06:24 Rafael Ortiz: We have automatic prefix caching for repeated session prefixes and optional KV cache for chat-like flows; Optimize will recommend enabling it when it detects repetition patterns. For search queries it's more about deduplicating similar candidate contexts.
06:36 Zoe Park: What about cost modeling?
06:38 Maya Chen: The Console gives per-token cost breakdown by route and model. Also our billing export includes per-request cost attribution. For the pilot we can provide evaluation credits so you can run a benchmark without immediate spend.
06:51 Tom Adler: On retraining reranker: do you host fine-tuned weights or do we upload and serve?
06:55 Rafael Ortiz: Two patterns: 1) you provide a fine-tuned reranker and we host it (private or hosted depending on security), or 2) you host weights in your VPC and we provide serving glue. For hosted pilots many customers let Redwood host the reranker under an NDA and SOC2 boundary.
07:12 Priya Nair: Whoosh — earlier you mentioned fallback models. If we pin to a 6B reranker and that node goes offline, what's the graceful degradation?
07:20 Rafael Ortiz: The routing layer can fallback to a 3B variant in the same family and maintain output format; you can set a degradation budget so we only fallback when latency would otherwise breach SLO. We also support region failover.
07:33 Zoe Park: Any caveats about determinism between model versions?
07:36 Rafael Ortiz: Slight variability; that's why rollouts and A/Bs are important — Redwood supports canary rollouts and auto rollback on regression signals.
07:46 Priya Nair: Are there any customers in retail space you can reference?
07:49 Maya Chen: We can share case studies — several retail customers improved MRR by mid-single digits after rerankers and Optimize tuning. We'll include anonymized benchmarks.
07:58 Tom Adler: demo more of the Console traces — the token breakdown and per-route latency?
08:02 Rafael Ortiz: Scrolling. Here is token-level: embedding token counts are low, reranker is dominated by doc length. You can set per-route max_input_tokens in the API to limit cost.
08:19 Priya Nair: Show the eval UI?
08:21 Rafael Ortiz: Yep — this is Redwood Evals. You can upload labeled queries and candidates; it will run batch scoring and surface NDCG/MRR, and then tie alerts. We also keep historical baselines so you can see regressions over time.
08:38 Zoe Park: If we wanted to test the reranker only, can we pass precomputed embeddings?
08:41 Rafael Ortiz: Yes, reranker can accept precomputed vector features or raw text candidates. Many teams precompute embeddings offline and pass cached results to save embedding inference cost.
08:50 Tom Adler: For our pilot we'll likely do precompute + rerank on the hosted tier. What about payload size limits? We're shipping product descriptions that include HTML.
08:59 Rafael Ortiz: We suggest stripping HTML and sending cleaned text to the reranker; there is a payload limit (document length caps) — the console warns on truncation. For large docs we recommend indexing only description + top bullet points.
09:15 Priya Nair: On evaluation, how can we ensure annotation quality matters? We have sparse labels and ephemeral user signals.
09:21 Rafael Ortiz: You can weight queries or bootstrap via interleaving online A/B tests; Redwood supports evaluation weights per-query and combining offline and online metrics.
09:34 Zoe Park: any gotchas with vector DB connectors?
09:36 Rafael Ortiz: Connectors are straightforward; however, keep an eye on vector distance metric alignment (cosine vs euclidean) and normalization. We'll share a vector DB integration primer.
09:48 Priya Nair: Let's talk about latency tail — 95/99 percentiles — how do you help with that?
09:53 Rafael Ortiz: Autoscaling plus continuous batching helps; also reranker warm pools and pre-warming nodes for peak windows. For strict tails we recommend Dedicated or Private where we can reserve capacity.
10:06 Tom Adler: Dedicated capacity pricing — is that a separate contract?
10:09 Maya Chen: Yes, Dedicated is a reserved capacity product with commit terms. For pilot hosted is easiest; if you need guaranteed p99 you can opt into Dedicated. We'll include pricing options.
10:19 Priya Nair: How long to ramp from pilot to production? We're concerned about engineering lift.
10:23 Maya Chen: Many teams ship in 4–8 weeks from pilot start depending on dataset and integrations. Redwood SDKs and connector templates reduce friction. Rafael: we typically run a sprint — smoke tests, evaluation, and then a production rollout with canary.
10:36 Rafael Ortiz: For the pilot we can provide a sample repo: a retrieval + rerank pipeline with S3 ingestion, a vector db connector, and dashboard dashboards.
10:45 Zoe Park: Let's get more concrete — do you have a sample notebook you can share?
10:48 Rafael Ortiz: Yes, will share the notebook containing calls to embeddings endpoint, candidate construction, reranker call, and evaluation. It includes code to replay a batch job for 20k items.
10:58 Priya Nair: On the console, can we export traces to our APM?
11:01 Rafael Ortiz: Yes — traces can be exported to Datadog or Splunk; we also provide raw logs via retention export.
11:09 Tom Adler: Any limitation on request rate for hosted?
11:13 Maya Chen: Hosted has rate limits by default but you can request higher throughput; for high sustained QPS we recommend Dedicated.
11:21 Priya Nair: How do we instrument end-to-end user latency (client to final rerank) in Redwood?
11:26 Rafael Ortiz: We recommend adding a small client header and Redwood injects a trace id. Console maps per-route latency and spans so you can see embedding vs network vs rerank.
11:37 Zoe Park: Are there costs for trace retention and long-term observability?
11:40 Maya Chen: Yes, observability retention is an add-on; by default we retain 30 days and you can increase. We'll include details in the pricing doc.
11:51 Priya Nair: Let's talk about A/B testing with rerankers — do you handle traffic split?
11:55 Rafael Ortiz: Yes, canary and A/B split by percentage, user segment, or query type. We also do automatic regression detection and can auto rollback.
12:06 Tom Adler: Suppose we run reranker hosted but keep embeddings precomputed in our infra. Is that supported?
12:09 Rafael Ortiz: Yes, hybrid ops are common. You can push candidate payloads and skip embedding call. We also accept feature fields if you want to include offline signals.
12:18 Priya Nair: Any recommendations for cold-start SKUs?
12:21 Rafael Ortiz: Incorporate metadata signals (category, brand, price), use augmentation (title synonyms) and consider mixing generation for suggested keywords. The reranker can learn to prefer freshness signals if you include them as features.
12:34 Zoe Park: sample SLA numbers for hosted?
12:36 Maya Chen: Hosted SLAs are lower than Dedicated; we guarantee multi-regional availability and provide response time targets for paid tiers. We'll include exact numbers in the SLA packet.
12:47 Priya Nair: Security follow-up: can we get an architecture diagram for hosted network flow?
12:51 Maya Chen: We'll attach an architecture diagram and networking notes in the security pack.
12:58 Tom Adler: Are there known issues with common HTML sanitizers? We use some custom markups.
13:02 Rafael Ortiz: Our ingestion examples show standard sanitizer libs; for edge cases we recommend pre-cleaning. We'll include sample cleaning code.
13:10 Zoe Park: Can we do a short live benchmark run now? Maybe 1k queries?
13:14 Priya Nair: We have only 30 mins today, but a quick smoke would be nice.
13:18 Rafael Ortiz: We can run a small synthetic evaluation against a subset. I'll switch to the eval runner and upload a 200-query set.
13:26 Rafael Ortiz: Running... this will take ~2 minutes. Console shows running eval job — progress 30%... 60%...
13:45 Rafael Ortiz: Results: NDCG@10 improved from 0.42 baseline to 0.51 with reranker + hybrid retrieval. MRR@5 up from 0.34 to 0.44. Those numbers are synthetic but directionally promising.
14:02 Priya Nair: That's encouraging. Can you export the per-query diffs?
14:05 Rafael Ortiz: Yes, you can download CSV with per-query before/after ranks and model explanations.
14:12 Tom Adler: For the pilot we'll want to run your benchmark scripts against our labeled set; can we get the script?
14:16 Rafael Ortiz: Absolutely — will include it in the notebook.
14:22 Zoe Park: Any limitations on the reranker input format for multilingual titles? We have some EU locales.
14:26 Rafael Ortiz: Reranker supports unicode and multilingual encodings; we recommend running locale-specific embedding models for best results.
14:33 Priya Nair: Ok we're about halfway through — let's fast-forward Q&A items.
14:38 Tom Adler: Deployment question: for Dedicated, do you ship a config for autoscaling?
14:41 Maya Chen: Yes, Dedicated gives you more control: reserved GPU pools and autoscale policies tailored to workload. We usually do a sizing workshop.
14:50 Zoe Park: Pricing ask: can you provide an estimate for 2M queries/month with 10k product corpus?
14:55 Maya Chen: We'll model it with assumptions (embedding dims, reranker model, average tokens). I'll send an estimate in the pricing doc.
15:04 Priya Nair: Anything else on security?
15:07 Maya Chen: We'll attach SOC2, pen test summary, and KMS integration docs.
15:12 Tom Adler: Great. Next steps?
15:15 Maya Chen: Recap and next actions: Maya will send pricing + credits, Rafael will share notebook and eval scripts, Tom will send sample dataset and labels, and we'll schedule pilot kick-off.
15:28 Priya Nair: Sounds good. Thanks Rafael and Maya.
15:31 Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links to the notebook, security pack, and next calendar invite.
15:38 Zoe Park: Thanks. Bye.

Auto-generated action items in transcript:

title: Smeared-slot scheduler: simulator notes & ops checklist
author: Priya Nair
text:
Purpose and rough summary:

This is a working note describing the "smeared-slot" scheduling idea, the simulator we should build to evaluate it, and an ops checklist for spinning up a prototype in the lab. The core idea: instead of fixed token-window coalescing or pure request-level batching we 'smear' token service opportunities probabilistically across lightweight slots so that short and long requests both make forward progress and KV cache warmup costs remain bounded. The smear is a tunable distribution that spreads tokens from oversized requests across upcoming slots to reduce tail interference for short, latency-sensitive requests while preserving kernel-friendly batch sizes.

Why try this (motivation):
- Observed issue: long-token requests (LLR) dominate slots, causing short requests to queue and suffer P95+/tail latency inflation.
- Pure token-level fairness (strict per-token round robin) yields excessive kernel churn and harms batching affinity (small kernels per slot).
- Pure request-level fairness (serve whole request when scheduled) causes starvation and poor fairness for high-arrival-rate short requests.
- Need middle ground that: (a) protects short request latency, (b) maintains decent average batch sizes for kernel throughput, (c) controls KV cache churn/cold misses.

Design sketch (behavioral):
- Time is divided into scheduling ticks (slots). Each slot can trigger an inference kernel with a target token budget T_slot (configurable).
- Incoming requests are classified into types: Short (S, <= 64 tokens), Medium (M, 65-512), Long (L, >512). We keep queue per client or per request-class depending on policy.
- For each long request, rather than enqueuing the entire token tail, we maintain a pending-token counter and place it into a smear queue with a probabilistic release schedule.
- Smearing distribution: geometric or truncated Poisson with mean mu; each slot we sample how many tokens to release from each smeared long request up to T_slot remaining capacity. This spreads service over N slots so that any single slot isn't overwhelmed.
- Admission priority: Short requests get strict low-latency lanes (token budget reserve), medium requests share a middle lane, smeared long requests fill leftover capacity but cannot evict reserved capacity.

KV cache & kernel affinity considerations:
- We add a warmup bias: prefer to complete at least R_warmup tokens from a given model stream before switching to another model/sequence to reduce KV thrash. This bias interacts with smear by ensuring any smear release contains a minimum contiguous prefix length (min_chunk), otherwise skip and postpone release to next slot.
- Kernel affinity score = alpha * contiguous_prefix + beta * batch_size + gamma * model_switch_penalty. Scheduler tries to maximize score under latency constraints. alpha/beta/gamma are tunables exposed to tuning framework.

Fairness objectives (what we measure):
- Latency fairness: per-client P50/P95/P99 for short-requests vs baseline; fairness measured with Jain's index over per-client mean latency.
- Token fairness: fraction of tokens served per client normalized by traffic demand; compute Jain's on tokens/sec per client over a window.
- Starvation windows: max time any request waits before first token served.
- Throughput cost: effective tokens/sec and kernel utilization.
- KV miss rate: fraction of requests that experience cold KV miss on first generation after model or sequence context switch.

Simulator design (event-driven):
- Inputs: real trace snippets (chatty short-request heavy, mixed enterprise long-completion heavy), synthetic bursty and steady-state profiles, model catalog (seq-len distribution, kv-warmup cost, kernel latency curve as function of batch size and prefix length).
- State: queue per priority lane; smeared-token ledger per long-request; current slot clock; KV cache state (per-model per-worker recent-key set, TTL).
- Events: arrival, slot-trigger, kernel-complete, kv-evict, sample-release.
- Outputs: time-series of latencies, slot batch sizes, kernel runtimes, KV misses.

Pseudocode (high level):
- On arrival(request r):
 if r.len <= short_threshold: enqueue(short_lane, r)
 else if r.len <= medium_threshold: enqueue(medium_lane, r)
 else: create smeared_ledger[r.id] = r.len; enqueue(smear_pool, r.id)

- On slot_tick():
 allocate reserved capacity R_short, R_med; remaining_capacity = T_slot - R_short - R_med
 form batch = drain(short_lane, R_short) + drain(medium_lane, R_med)
 for each smeared_id in smear_pool in round-robin:
 x = sample_smear(smeared_id, remaining_capacity)
 if x >= min_chunk and remaining_capacity >= x:
 attach x tokens from smeared_id to batch
 smeared_ledger[smeared_id] -= x
 remaining_capacity -= x
 if smeared_ledger[smeared_id] == 0: remove from smear_pool
 if kernel_affinity_score(batch) below threshold and remaining_capacity > 0: try to merge adjacent small batches (prefetch from next slot)
 submit_kernel(batch)

Key knobs to sweep in simulation:
- T_slot (token capacity per slot): 64/128/256/512
- smear mean (mu) and distribution (geometric vs truncated-normal)
- min_chunk (minimum contiguous tokens when releasing from smear)
- R_short reserve fraction (0-30%)
- KV warmup bias (R_warmup contiguous tokens preferred)
- affinity weights alpha/beta/gamma

Experiment matrix (initial):
- Traces: short-heavy_2023-chat, mixed-enterprise-v2, long-burst
- Sweep T_slot x smear_mu x R_short x min_chunk
- Baselines: pure request-level FIFO, token-RR, existing continuous-batcher (current mainline)
- Metrics: P50/P95/P99 latency short & medium, Jain(token fairness), average kernel throughput, KV miss rate, overall cost estimate (tokens/second * kernel-ms cost function)

Operational considerations for prototype (ops checklist):
- Simulator infra:
 - Dockerized simulator with config yaml for trace & model profiles
 - Log outputs: per-slot CSV (timestamp,batch_size,kernel_ms,kv_misses), per-request csv (arrival,first_token_ts,completion_ts)
 - Visualization: quick Grafana dashboard from CSVs or use Jupyter notebooks
- Lab deployment for A/B:
 - Implement smeared-slot scheduler as a pluggable strategy behind the runtime scheduler interface (flag: SCHED_STRATEGY=smeared_slot)
 - Add feature flag gating + Canary route in console for internal test org
 - Canary pods set to low capacity and synthetic traffic generator to replay traces
 - Instrumentation: add per-request telemetry for "tokens_released_by_smear" and "kv_warmup_hits"
- Safety knobs:
 - global throughput cap to avoid oversubmitting kernels during misconfiguration
 - watchdog that disables smear if observed P99 short-request exceeds threshold

Open questions and risks:
- Does smear add unacceptable head-of-line splitting complexity to response reassembly (ordering/streaming)? Need to prototype streaming handler that stitches partial outputs in-order with minimal jitter.
- Interaction with function/tool-calls and multi-turn chat where context must be contiguous: smear may harm coherence. Consider per-conversation affinity exemption or require min_chunk equal to conversational boundary.
- Multi-model workload: smear across different model families may cause KV thrash; require smear pool partitioned by model family and per-worker affinity enforcement.
- Fairness across tenants where tenants have very different request length distributions: need per-tenant smear policies or budgeted token quotas. Explore credit-based smear where long-tenants accrue smear debt.

Next steps / short-term plan:
- Week 0-1: implement small event-driven simulator, validate with short-heavy and mixed traces. Target: reproducible CSVs. (Owners: Priya, Ethan)
- Week 1-2: run sweep for T_slot x smear_mu x R_short, produce comparison plots vs baseline. (Owners: Sofia)
- Week 2-3: prototype in runtime as feature-flagged scheduler; route limited internal traffic and run canary. (Owners: Liam)
- Week 3: gather metrics, decide whether smear provides a Pareto improvement (tail latency down, kernel throughput comparable).

Notes to self / heuristics learned while sketching:
- Keep smear mean small relative to expected request lengths; too large smear ~ request-level behavior, too small smear ~ token RR.
- min_chunk helps maintain kernel affinity; tune against kernel latency curves.
- Reserve a small fraction for extremely short requests; this avoids worst-case tail behavior with minimal throughput loss.

Appendix: useful traces / primitives to add to corpus:
- reply-heavy-concise-chat-2023-12 (lots of 8-20 token responses),
- enterprise-qa-longform (1-2k tokens monthly batch jobs),
- bursty-bot-surge (bursts of short requests at 10k rps for 1s every 30s).

TODO (short):
- [ ] Create minimal trace DSL and loader for simulator
- [ ] Implement KV cache model (cost per context-switch)
- [ ] Hook in kernel cost curves from bench harness
- [ ] Draft canary run playbook and Slack alert thresholds

If this approach looks promising after simulation we should write a compact design doc (2-pager) for product/console folks showing tradeoffs and config knobs they can expose in the Console. For now this is a lightweight working doc — please add comments or drop JIRA links to specific tickets you want me to pull into the experiment plan.

title: Mariposa Health - POC Weekly Benchmark Triage & Routing Decision
author: Marcus Bell
text:
Weekly POC sync to review last 48h of benchmark data: latency and throughput compared to incumbent. Triage on high tail latency spikes, discuss routing policy changes, and confirm experiment to enable prefix KV caching and quantized fallback variants. Action items: share full CSV, run 1h focused tail-latency test, SE to provide routing config and cost estimate, schedule security review for VPC/SSO requirements.

Latency vs baseline provider
Throughput tuning and batching
Routing fallbacks and canary policy
Data residency / VPC and SOC2 questions
Next steps and action owners

Sofia to share raw benchmark CSV and annotated runbook by 2027-07-02
Mariposa to run 1h tail-latency test with production traffic window on 2027-07-05
Redwood to propose routing policy YAML + cost delta by 2027-07-06
Schedule security deep dive for VPC/SAML on 2027-07-08

Sofia Alvarez: upload full CSV + raw logs to shared GDrive (due 2027-07-02)
Rahul Menon: run 1h tail latency test and share results (due 2027-07-05)
Marcus Bell: send pricing delta and dedicated slot sizing calc (due 2027-07-06)
Ethan Park: prepare routing policy snippet with fallback to quantized-variant (due 2027-07-06)

Meeting header: date 2027-06-30 14:00 PDT, duration ~55m. Attendees: Marcus (Redwood AE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Lena, Rahul, Karen, Derek.

[00:00] Marcus: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I want to run through the last two days of bench results and focus on the tail latencies that popped up. Is this still a good time?
[00:18] Lena: Yep this is good. We just pulled the latest. Quick note: some of the numbers are from night batch traffic and might skew throughput.
[00:32] Sofia: got it. I'll call out which runs were steady-state vs burst. We saw a couple of 95th/99th spikes around the 10k token window.
[00:45] Rahul: the spikes correlate with KV cache misses — maybe the K V cache warmup[] -- our cache hit ratio fell to about 68% for a short period.
[00:58] Ethan: interesting, did you see those on the incumbernt runs too or just on Redwood?
[01:06] Rahul: both but more pronounced on Redwood in two runs, about +35ms at p95 and +110ms at p99 vs baseline.
[01:18] Marcus: ok let's unpack. Sofia, can you summarize which configs produced the best steady-state throughput?
[01:27] Sofia: sure — the q4_0 quantized variant shaved unit cost but increased median by 5ms. The fp16 variant with aggressive batching and dynamic batching set to 64 tokens had best throughput — 420 rps on our test rig — compared to incumbent ~330 rps. But the tail was worse when cache heat was low.
[01:50] Karen: wait, so throughput is better overall but tail latency worse in cold cache scenarios? that matches our user complaints where rare slow responses break UX flows.
[02:03] Derek: yep - the issue is the long-tail timeouts in our orchestration; we have 3s frontend timeout and anything above 1.8s causes retries.
[02:14] Marcus: ok risk is real. Two levers: routing policy to prefer warm-cached instances and fallback to a quantized lower-cost variant for overloaded nodes. Also consider prefix caching at the edge — we've seen good wins.
[02:26] Lena: can you explain prefix caching? in our stack it sounds like extra infra.
[02:32] Sofia: sure. Essentially we keep hot KV cache entries for common prefixes in the serving pool. So many requests reuse a cached K V — sorry K V cash — uh K V cache entry and avoid repeated key lookup. It saves ~50-70ms on the long tail if hit ratio >80%.
[02:48] Rahul: earlier you mentioned automatic batching. Our traffic is spiky and client bursts vary - dynamic batching helps but increases per-request latency on small messages.
[02:58] Ethan: yes that's the tradeoff. We tune per-route batching thresholds; for short prompts you set smaller batch_size/latency-window. For your high-throughput route we can use continuous batching with a 8ms window to keep latency low and still aggregate.
[03:18] Marcus: let's go through a concrete experiment plan. First: enable prefix/KV cache for the top-10 prompt templates for 24h and measure p95/p99. Second: implement routing rule to prefer cached pool, otherwise fallback to q4_0 quantized variant after 900ms. Third: run 1h tail-latency test in production-like window.
[03:37] Lena: sounds reasonable. What's the risk of degraded quality with q4_0 fallback?
[03:42] Sofia: in our internal evals quality drop is small for classification and short or structured prompts, but generative open-ended tasks show divergence. We can restrict fallback to non-generative routes.
[03:54] Rahul: also need to know cost delta. If we keep a dedicated small warm pool that adds egress cost but reduces retries maybe net win.
[04:03] Marcus: I'll share a cost calc. Ethan will propose dedicated pool sizing.
[04:10] Ethan: for your current qps, a warm pool of 4 slots (A100 equivalent) should handle spikes with 99% of requests warm, keeping p99 under 400ms — rough numbers, will firm up after data.
[04:26] Karen: on security — we need to confirm VPC peering and SAML SSO support before we move to any dedicated private deployment. Also SOC2 docs.
[04:37] Marcus: yes we'll share the SOC2 and SAML design. That security deep dive is a separate session. We'll provision a stub VPC diagram.
[04:45] Derek: on deployment, our infra team needs a simple routing YAML to plug into our ingress. Any chance you can give us a sample?
[04:53] Sofia: yes, I'll send a sample routing policy snippet. It will include priority rules: prefer cached pool, then pooled capacity, then quantized fallback with a max percentage of traffic. We'll include canary weights.
[05:04] Lena: canary weights — how are rollouts controlled? we want gradual ramp and immediate rollback if latency regresses.
[05:11] Ethan: Redwood's console supports canary thresholds and automatic fallback on latency SLO breaches. We'll show a sample: start 5% -> 25% -> 50% with automated rollback at >2% error.
[05:23] Rahul: curious — what's the granularity of metrics? per-route per-token breakdown?
[05:28] Marcus: token-level breakdowns are in Console: latency by token bucket, cost per token, and traces for specific requests. We'll give you a short recording of that view.
[05:40] Marcus: ok let's look briefly at the CSV you sent — Sofia, you flagged run #17 as the worst offender. Can you walk us through the timestamps?
[05:48] Sofia: sure. run17 was at 02:20 UTC, concurrent load ramped from 120 to 420 rps in 60s. The cache hit dropped due to an upstream purge, then the p99 hit 1.6s. The baseline vendor had p99 of ~1.2s same window. So Redwood did better median but worse tail.
[06:10] Lena: was there any hardware eviction or compaction going on?
[06:14] Sofia: we saw a background compaction job in the host (noisy neighbor) affecting memory bandwidth — we annotated that in the logs. Ethan: we can try isolating the dedicated slots to prevent noisy neighbor.
[06:25] Ethan: yes, that was our test rig's hypervisor doing cleanup. In Dedicated we'd put these on isolated GPU hosts to avoid this.
[06:33] Marcus: good. So to summarize technical path: 1) enable prefix caching for top templates 2) spin up small dedicated warm pool 3) routing policy with fallback to q4_0 for specific routes 4) measure 1h tail-latency test and compare to incumbent.
[06:48] Karen: timeline?
[06:51] Marcus: Sofia will push config and CSV by 7/2; Rahul runs the 1h by 7/5; Ethan and I will send routing and cost by 7/6. Security deep dive 7/8.
[07:00] Derek: one practical Q — will enabling caching require any SDK changes on our side or just server-side config?
[07:05] Sofia: purely server side for prefix cache. But for client-side dedup you might add a small header to prefer cached responses. We'll doc that.
[07:14] Rahul: also we need to validate audit logs — if we move to dedicated we need audit trail retention for 2 years.
[07:21] Marcus: note taken. We'll include audit log retention options and an estimate.
[07:27] (cross talk) Lena: cool, thanks.
[07:30] Marcus: ok final quick Q from me — any blockers on your side to run the 1h test?
[07:34] Lena: nothing blocking, we'll pick production-like window and notify Redwood.
[07:38] Marcus: perfect. we'll follow up in the email thread with links.
[07:42] (end of main transcript).

Post-call notes: there were a few mis-transcribed technical terms (K V cache -> K V cash in auto transcript) and short crosstalk segments. Full logs and CSVs referenced in action items.
