title: Console: Latency dashboard missing eu-west region breakdown (region filter + charts)
text:
Issue summary
- Customer reports the Console > Observability > Latency dashboard does not show eu-west as a selectable region, and charts appear to be missing eu-west series (no breakdown / only us-east/us-west).
- Customer expectation: ability to view p50/p95 latency and error rate by region, including eu-west, for the last 24h/7d.

Impact
- Customer cannot self-serve latency reporting for eu-west via Console (blocks weekly internal reporting and incident triage correlation).
- No evidence of inference degradation itself; appears to be a Console data completeness/metadata issue.

Customer / context
- Company: Aurora Search
- Tier: self_serve
- Customer reports active traffic in eu-west (they are in EU business hours).

Environment
- Console: prod
- Affected area: Latency dashboard region filter + breakdown charts
- Region: eu-west

What we see internally
- Support can reproduce in their own Console account: eu-west missing from region dropdown on Latency dashboard.
- Related: we have other eu-west symptoms in Support queue (SUP-1850 embeddings timeouts) but this ticket is specifically Console visibility, not endpoint performance.

Steps to reproduce
1) Log into Console (prod)
2) Navigate to Observability > Latency
3) Open Region filter dropdown
4) Observe eu-west absent
5) Switch timeframe to 7d; still absent

Expected result
- Region dropdown includes eu-west
- Charts render data for eu-west when selected

Actual result
- eu-west not present in region filter
- Charts show other regions only

Initial triage / hypotheses
- Console region list is populated from telemetry metadata (distinct region values) rather than a static enum; if telemetry ingestion is dropping the region label, eu-west will not appear.
- Possible pipeline issue: region label normalization ("eu-west" vs "eu-west-1" vs "euw1") causing aggregation under an unexpected value that the UI intentionally hides.
- Possible UI issue: hardcoded allowlist of regions not updated for eu-west in this view (less likely, but consistent with "missing from dropdown").

Evidence collected
- Screenshot (redacted) from customer showing region dropdown missing eu-west.
- Support reproduction screenshot (internal).

Support guidance requested
- Provide an interim reporting path for eu-west latency (customer needs numbers now).
- Determine whether data is truly missing vs only missing from UI filter.

Next actions
- Observability: verify whether eu-west latency metrics exist in metrics store / dashboards.
- Console: verify region list source for the latency view and whether eu-west is filtered out.
- If data exists: fix UI/metadata to surface eu-west.
- If data missing: identify ingestion break, backfill if possible, and provide customer interim reporting instructions.

Customer-safe interim workaround (draft)
- Use the API request logs export (Console > Usage > Exports) filtered by region=eu-west to compute latency percentiles, OR
- Use the Support-provided “Support-safe quick view” dashboard link once confirmed (see ENG-4823), with eu-west preselected.

Notes / constraints
- Do not share internal dashboard links that expose other customers or non-support-safe data.
- Keep language clear that the workaround is temporary and the Console view will be corrected.

2026-02-13 09:22Z — Priya Shah (Support) — Customer report from Aurora Search: latency dashboard missing eu-west. They say they are actively serving in eu-west and need p95 latency for weekly reporting. Marking P2 since it blocks operational visibility but not an outage. Requesting Observability/Console triage to confirm if this is data pipeline vs UI allowlist.
2026-02-13 09:40Z — Priya Shah (Support) — Repro’d internally on my Support test org: eu-west not in region dropdown on Observability > Latency. Switching to other dashboards (Errors) does show eu-west, which suggests view-specific filtering or view-specific dataset.
2026-02-13 10:05Z — Allison Grant (Observability) — Acknowledged. I’ll check metrics cardinality and the dimension mapping for region in the latency dataset used by Console. Quick question: does the customer see eu-west in any other Console views (Usage, Errors, Traces)?
2026-02-13 10:12Z — Priya Shah (Support) — Customer says they see eu-west in Usage export filters but not in Latency dashboard. I can confirm I see eu-west in Usage exports (region filter) but not in Latency view.
2026-02-13 11:00Z — Allison Grant (Observability) — Initial finding: eu-west exists in raw request metrics, but the Console latency view reads from an aggregated table that is missing eu-west partitions for the last ~10 days. This looks like an ETL job config issue (region mapping) rather than the inference metrics emitter. Looping in Platform for pipeline owner.
2026-02-13 11:18Z — Ethan Park (Platform) — Thanks. We recently changed region normalization in the aggregator to map cloud regions; eu-west might be emitting as "eu-west" while the aggregator expects "eu-west-1". We’ll confirm the distinct values and patch the normalization rule. Can Observability share the exact distinct region strings present in raw vs agg?
2026-02-13 11:35Z — Allison Grant (Observability) — Raw has "eu-west"; aggregated table expects allowlisted values and currently only recognizes "eu-west-1" (which has near-zero rows). This explains why the UI dropdown never sees "eu-west" and doesn’t show it.
2026-02-13 12:10Z — Priya Shah (Support) — Interim customer guidance proposal:
1) Use Console > Usage > Exports (CSV) filtered to region=eu-west and compute p50/p95 locally (we can provide a short snippet).
2) If they can share a handful of request IDs, Support can pull latency percentiles for a defined window and send back a one-time report.
Please confirm this is OK + customer-safe.
2026-02-13 12:22Z — Allison Grant (Observability) — Approved. For self_serve, steer them to Usage export as primary workaround. If they need immediate numbers, Support can do a one-time internal pull as long as you only report their org’s data and keep the query window/timezone explicit.
2026-02-14 09:05Z — Ethan Park (Platform) — Patch in progress: update aggregator normalization to treat "eu-west" as canonical and backfill last 14 days into the aggregated latency table. ETA: patch deploy today; backfill finishes by end of day UTC barring queue delays.
2026-02-14 10:30Z — Priya Shah (Support) — Sent customer update: confirmed it’s a Console aggregation/normalization issue (not service degradation), provided interim export-based reporting steps, and set expectation that Console eu-west breakdown will return after backfill. Customer asked if historical 30d will be restored; I told them we’re targeting 14d backfill pending confirmation.
2026-02-17 16:15Z — Allison Grant (Observability) — Backfill completed for 14d. Confirmed eu-west appears in aggregated table and should be available to the Console dropdown after cache refresh. If Support still doesn’t see it, we may need a cache bust / redeploy of the Console service that serves filter options.
2026-02-18 08:50Z — Priya Shah (Support) — I now see eu-west in the Latency region dropdown on my test org. Asking customer to confirm on their side. Leaving ticket In Progress until customer confirms and we document the interim workaround as a short internal macro (so we have it if this recurs).
2026-02-18 15:40Z — Priya Shah (Support) — Follow-up: also recommending we add a lightweight pipeline check to alert Support when a region disappears from the aggregated dataset (prevents silent UI gaps). Not sure if this folds into ENG-4823 or needs separate Eng task.

title: Axial Shelf Nexus: Compact workspace switcher + contextual sidebar proposal
author: Aisha Patel
text:
Problem: Customers report confusion when switching workspaces and losing contextual dashboards or rollout state. The current left rail is dense and forces users to navigate multiple flyouts to reach model rollouts, cost breakdowns, and per-route dashboards. Goal: design a compact, discoverable workspace switcher that surfaces contextual navigation (dashboards, rollouts, cost views) and preserves user state during route changes. Deliver a Figma prototype, annotated decision log, and a small usability test script.

This ticket synthesizes prior IA audits and telemetry showing high bounce rates from dashboard pages when users change workspaces. Engineering constraints include a single-page routing model, persisted query params for rollouts, and an existing permission matrix for private deployments. We must preserve keyboard nav and ARIA semantics.

Make workspace switching non-destructive: keep open dashboard/rollout context where possible
Surface cost and rollback affordances directly in the sidebar without adding visual clutter
Offer a collapsed axial shelf mode for tight viewports that expands on hover or keyboard focus
Ensure keyboard-first accessibility and clear feedback for cross-workspace permissions
Minimize additional API bandwidth by reusing runtime metadata and existing console endpoints

Introduce an Axial Shelf component: a two-state left rail that compresses to icon-only tiles and expands into a contextual nexus when activated. The nexus contains workspace switcher at top, followed by route-aware quick links: Dashboards, Rollouts, Cost Lens, Traces. Quick links load via client-side routing; if the target belongs to a different workspace we provide a non-destructive preview panel before committing the switch.

https://www.figma.com/file/ExampleRedwood/Axial-Shelf-Nexus-Prototype
https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/Redwood/Console/Prototypes/AxialShelfNexus
https://www.invisionapp.com/share/Redwood-Axial-Shelf-Nexus-Flow

Reuse /workspaces/:id/meta endpoint for name + role to avoid extra roundtrips
Client should persist query params: ?dashboard=summary&rollout_view=canary across switches when compatible
Fallback behaviour: if model/route not available in target workspace, show 'Unavailable in target' state and guidance
Performance constraint: expanded nexus must render < 120ms on warm cache (use skeletons for remote fragments)

All interactive elements must be reachable via tab/shift-tab and have aria-labels
Collapsed mode should provide a visible focus ring and accessible tooltip with workspace name
Preview panel must be announced to screen readers when visible
Color contrast checks for new cost lens badges (WCAG AA)

Preview-on-switch adds complexity to routing and requires tight coordination with Dedicated/Private RBAC checks
Compact mode may hide discoverability for occasional users — mitigated with a first-run spotlight tour
Expanding nexus introduces more DOM nodes; may affect initial paint on low-end devices
Non-destructive switch semantics complicate analytics for 'active workspace' — require explicit events

Figma prototype covers collapsed and expanded states, workspace preview flow, and route-aware quick links
Usability test (n=8) shows 90% success on switching to a workspace while retaining dashboard context
Engineering acceptance PR adds a feature-flagged Axial Shelf component and passes perf gating (<120ms for nexus open) and automated keyboard tests
Telemetry emits events: workspace_switch_initiated, workspace_switch_previewed, workspace_switch_committed
Documentation updated in Console help center and a short in-app tour created

Create Figma screens: collapsed rail, nexus expanded, workspace preview, unavailable state
Annotate component behavior + accessibility in the spec doc
Run 5 quick guerrilla usability sessions and synthesize feedback
Sync with Eng: API contract for /workspaces/:id/meta and preview payloads
Prototype small E2E using existing console routing and expose behind feature flag

2025-02-11 — Aisha Patel: Initial designs uploaded to Figma. Focused on reducing clicks to reach rollouts and cost views. Left a TODO to check KB shortcuts with platform team.
2025-02-12 — Marco Sanchez: Reviewed constraints; noted that Dedicated's permission model requires an extra check before preview. Filed ENG-73291 as a dependency.
2025-02-14 — Jenna Liu (PM): Confirmed success metrics and customer ask from ACME Corp pilot. Suggested adding a compact cost-badge for quick spend signal.
2025-02-15 — Accessibility review (Liam O'Connor): Requested ARIA announcement pattern for preview pane and clarified tooltip timing (200ms).
2025-02-17 — Marco Sanchez: Engineering spike concluded. Prototype clients can reuse meta endpoint; added performance caveat about initial paint. Patch PR: github.com/redwood/repo/pull/1426
2025-02-18 — Design review: core team approved visuals with minor tweaks to badge contrast and micro-interaction timing. Moving to implement phase behind FF: axial-shelf-nexus

PM: Add a way to 'pin' previewed dashboard into the target workspace when switching
Eng: Avoid fetching large dashboard payloads during preview; use a compact summary API
Security: Ensure audit logs capture preview actions (sensitive ops) — security to confirm
Research: Suggest A/B test comparing collapsed default vs expanded default for new users

Create feature flag and instrumentation plan with infra

title: Compatibility: Chat Completions request shaper with SSE streaming & function-call coalescing
author: Maya Chen
text:
Implement a compatibility layer that maps legacy OpenAI Chat Completions (v1) request/response semantics onto Redwood's streaming-first runtime while preserving expected tool/function-calling behavior and structured outputs. This includes: SSE framing (data: chunks + [DONE]), partial function call deltas, role/metadata preservation, idempotency hints, and deterministic ordering for mixed streaming & non-streaming clients.

SSE stream framing conforms to OpenAI clients: initial data chunks contain incremental "
All function call invocations can start streaming partial args and finish with a final function call event; clients expecting a single final function call object receive an equivalent assembled object.
Non-streaming requests receive identical aggregated JSON response shape to legacy API for a broad set of test prompts (n=250), including tool calls and structured outputs.
Telemetry emitted for each compatibility transformation (request_shaper.v1, function_coalesce.v1) and no >1% error-rate regression after rollout.
Backward-compat regression tests added to CI and a canary rollout plan defined in the rollout notes.

2026-02-10 — Triage: Identified customer reports where legacy clients expect a single final function_call object but new runtime streams partial function args as deltas; causes client-side JSON parse errors.
2026-02-15 — Spec drafted: three-mode shaper (strict, permissive, streaming-first). Document: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/compat/cc-request-shaper (internal).
2026-02-22 — Design review: decided to implement server-side coalescer that buffers function-call deltas up to N ms or until completion marker; default N=150ms. Trade-off: small added latency for deterministic compatibility vs. complexity managing backpressure.
2026-02-28 — Implementation started: core transforms in gateway (request normalization, role mapping, tool_call hooks). PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/3421
2026-03-03 — QA: added fuzz tests for mixed streaming + tool-call sequences; discovered edge case where two concurrent function calls interleave — added per-conversation function-call namespace to avoid cross-talk.
2026-03-07 — Performance: bench shows 2-4% p99 latency delta under heavy batching when coalescing enabled; added opt-out flag for dedicated customers (compat.mode=strict) and runtime telemetry.
2026-03-10 — In Progress: finishing integration tests and adding canary rollout steps. Next: security review if customers request KMS-backed tool-call payloads.
Implementation notes: use event types 'delta', 'func_start', 'func_arg', 'func_end' in internal stream; transform to OpenAI SSE by emitting 'data: {"choices":[{"delta":...}]}' chunks, and a final 'data: [DONE]'. Buffering is bounded and fallbacks to passthrough under heavy backpressure.
Rollout plan: canary 1% of hosted traffic for 48h, monitor compatibility-errors, p99 latency, and function_call assembly rate. If errors < 0.5% and latency < +5%, expand to 25% then 100%.
Related artifacts: design mockups (Drive): https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/cc-compat-designs, PR for telemetry enums: https://github.com/redwood-inference/observability/pull/187

domain: 日常协作与非结构化讨论
title: eng-runtime
text:
maria: Quick nsys run to investigate weird latency spikes when concurrent small batches trigger KV eviction. Dropping flags + notes below.

ashok: please paste the exact command you used. :eyes:

maria: ```
nsys profile \
 --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt \
 --output=kv-evict-2245 \
 --capture-range=nvtx:kv_start,nvtx:kv_end \
 --duration=20 \
 --sample=cpu \
 --force-overwrite \
 python -m infra.infer_runner --model x --concurrency 8 --batch_schedule dynamic
```

kevin: try bracketed osrt too, e.g. `--capture-range=osrt:begin,osrt:end` and bump sampling interval to reduce noise (or disable sampling for full timeline).

infra-bot: nsys profiler finished: kv-evict-2245.qdrep (42MB) -> /artifacts/kv-evict-2245.qdrep

maria: quick summary: saw a ~80ms gap where `kv_cache_evict` runs, followed by an attention kernel spike ~120ms. eviction seems to preempt prefetch kernels.

selena: are you using nvtx markers around the user request? bracketed captures are best for these rare evict events.

maria: yes — I NVTX push/pop around request start/end but my sample window was only 200ms so I missed the prefetch that happens slightly earlier. Extended to 4s and now we see prefetch + eviction overlap.

ashok: recommended flags for this pattern: `--trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt` + sampling disabled or long interval to avoid aliasing. Example: `nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=none --output=... --capture-range=nvtx:start,nvtx:stop --stop-delay=2`

kevin: alternatively capture full kernel timeline (no sampling) for a short period, then run a longer bracketed sampled capture to get statistical view. Both are cheap if you keep duration small.

maria: experiment result: when I forced the batcher to prefer larger batches, eviction events dropped ~70% but p99 for short prompts increased. classic tradeoff. :thinking_face:

selena: can you paste the small timeline snippet (time | kernel | dur)?

maria: ```
0.001s | prefetch_kernel | 12.4ms
0.020s | kv_cache_evict | 82.1ms <-- overlaps with next
0.105s | attention_fwd | 120.9ms
0.230s | postprocess | 3.2ms
```

ashok: I'll run a follow-up capture with your config + `--sample=none` and compare. /assign @ashok

kevin: also check GPU busy % and OSRT wait events in the trace to see if CPU stalls line up with eviction.

maria: thanks — will upload the full qdrep and a perfetto timeline link once I have both captures. :thumbsup:

title: Customer sees credits applied twice on March invoice after regional postback failover
text:
Issue summary:
Customer LumenLogic reports that their March invoice (invoice_id: INV-2026-03-07-LL) has two near-identical credit line items totaling $12,400, which produce a negative balance. The credits are labeled as 'hourly-smoothing-credit' and 'promotional-rate-override-credit' but each appears twice with the same amounts and reference metadata.

Impact:
- Customer billing shows negative line item; finance cannot finalize month-end.
- Customer is on Dedicated and expects predictable reserved-rate billing.
- Customer requests immediate explanation and provisional reversal to finalize their internal accounting.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: redwood-dedicated-us-east-2 (LumenLogic org id: org_0xLL)
- Billing pipeline: postback-ingest -> postback-processor -> charge-apply job -> invoice-generator
- Peak activity window: 2026-03-07 01:47:00 - 01:59:00 UTC (microburst batch embed job resumed)

Steps to reproduce (as reported by customer):
1) Resume previously paused batch embedding job at 2026-03-07T01:47:12Z.
2) Job emits burst of 130k tokens and multiple postbacks.
3) At 01:48:20 UTC their reserved pool experienced a brief failover to eu-west for some routing requests.
4) Invoice generated on 2026-03-07 contains duplicate credit lines.

Customer-provided evidence:
- Invoice excerpt (sanitized): two entries each 'hourly-smoothing-credit' $6,200 and two 'promo-rate-override' $0.00 (promo displayed but duplicate credit applied).
- Postback ids (sample): pb_9a1f7c_01, pb_9a1f7c_02, pb_9a1f7c_02-replay
- Slack thread: #support-lumenlogic (link provided in private)

Requested outcome:
1) Explanation for why credits were duplicated.
2) Immediate provisional correction or invoice adjustment to allow customer to close month-end.
3) Permanent fix to prevent repeat occurrences and a timeline for reconciliation.

2026-03-10 - Maya Patel: Created ticket after customer uploaded invoice PDF and sample postback logs. Asking for provisional credit reversal. Assigned to Billing team.
2026-03-10 - Ethan Ross (Support): Acknowledged receipt, requested raw postback payloads and message digests. Escalated to SRE and Billing for triage. SLA first response target set to 2026-03-13.
2026-03-11 - Priya Sharma (SRE): Initial triage shows repeated postbacks with different region tags within 18s window. We see event_id duplicate but dedup-key in processor is org_id + request_timestamp (not event_id). Attaching query results to internal INT ticket.
2026-03-11 - Carlos Medina (Billing): Correlated credits in charge-apply logs for org_0xLL: two successful charge reversal runs for the same logical event. Candidate cause: replayed postback (pb_9a1f7c_02-replay) bypassed dedupe and triggered credit path twice.
2026-03-12 - Ethan Ross (Support): Informed customer we have a provisional plan: apply an interim invoice adjustment to neutralize duplicate credits while we complete a full reconciliation. Requested explicit approval to issue a provisional debit to balance invoice.
2026-03-12 - LumenLogic Billing Contact: Approved provisional adjustment; asked for permanent fix ETA and assurance this won't reoccur during their next batch window.

Query of postback-ingest table (producer_ts between 2026-03-07T01:46:50Z and 2026-03-07T01:49:00Z) returned three distinct records with identical event_id but different region_tag fields (us-east, eu-west, us-east-replay).
postback-processor logs show dedupe check used key: concat(org_id, '|', floor(request_timestamp/60)) which groups by minute bucket and misses exact event_id collisions when replays shift timestamps by <60s.
charge-apply job is idempotent when presented with same postback_id; however, replayed messages used a suffixed postback_id (pb_..._replay) and bypassed idempotency, re-triggering credit path.
Billing code path: promotional-rate-override logic applied after smoothing-credit calculation; the second run re-evaluated smoothing and issued another credit because the first credit had been marked 'applied' but not yet reconciled to invoice when replay arrived.
Reproduction locally: simulated a replay with modified region_tag and postback_id variation results in duplicate credit generation. Patch hypothesis: strengthen dedupe key to include event_id and idempotency token (postback_id canonicalization).

2026-03-12 - Provisional action: Billing created manual adjustment invoice line (ADJ-642579) reversing the duplicate credits totaling $12,400 so the customer's invoice is balanced. Customer notified and provided adjusted PDF.
2026-03-12 - Hotfix deployed (billing-recon v1.2.3): postback-processor dedupe now uses canonical_event_id + org_id + region_shard to avoid minute-bucket collisions and normalizes postback_id suffixes to respect idempotency. Patch merged: github.com/redwood-inference/postback-processor/pull/745
Permanent reconciliation plan (next steps): Run full retro reconciliation for 2026-03-07 across affected dedicated pools and generate converse adjustments for any other orgs impacted. Billing to run job by 2026-03-15 and publish report to linked Confluence page.
Monitoring: Added a transient alert that triggers when more than one credit of the same type and amount is applied to the same org within a 2-minute window. Alert routed to #billing and on-call SRE.
Customer follow-up: LumenLogic confirmed adjusted invoice and accepted provisional reversal. They requested confirmation after retro reconciliation that there will be no net unexpected debit.

raw_metadata.summary: Customer sees credits applied twice on March invoice after regional postback failover

title: Pilot surge playbook runbook review
author: Sara Kim
text:
Weekly POC check-in focused on Dedicated sizing and the surge/runbook for an upcoming pilot. Reviewed results from initial warm-up tests, discussed autoscale policy parameters (min/max, ramp, pre-warm), burst capacity options and billing implications, and compliance concerns around audit logs and KMS. Agreed on a 1-hour burst simulation run by Redwood SE and follow-up SOC2/KMS walkthrough.

Dedicated sizing and autoscale policy
Burst capacity & pre-warm strategy
KV cache / prefix caching effects
Latency vs cost tradeoffs (batching, quantization)
Compliance: SOC2, KMS, audit logs, retention

[00:00] Sara Kim: okay everyone thanks for joining, we're gonna run 45 minutes, quick agenda is dedicated sizing, runbook review for the pilot surge, and then next steps. Priya, you wanna kick with what changed since last week?
[00:12] Priya Nair: yeah thanks Sara. Uh we've got a refined traffic trace from the staging gateway, the p95 is about 2.1k tok/s and p99 spikes to 7.4k for short bursts, also saw a 30s spike pattern tied to batch jobs. We want to validate the burst plan doesn't blow the budget.
[00:28] Miguel Ortega: mm-hmm, got it. Did you attach the trace? I pulled the csv but there's some tokenization mapping differences - looks like token counts are slightly higher because of the tokenizer mismatch.
[00:37] Daniel Cho: right that was my bad, I used the upstream tokenizer in staging which adds ~8% tokens. We'll normalize and re-upload.
[00:45] Sara Kim: cool. So today's focus — runbook walk-through. I put a draft at link: https://redwood.runbooks/bluewave-burst-playbook-v2.pdf and also small spreadsheet with sizing. Anyone not have access?
[00:58] Marcus Li: I have access. Quick Q: the min pool size in the doc is 2x A40, is that still the recommendation?
[01:07] Miguel Ortega: yeah for your workloads the baseline min is 2 A40s to keep latency stable for regular traffic. For burst we recommend a burst pool of up to 8 GPUs with a pre-warm window. The autoscale policy we propose is min:2, target_util: 65%, max:8, cooldown: 90s, ramp: 60s. That gives room for short spikes without cold starts.
[01:30] Priya Nair: when you say pre-warm window — do you mean we pre-allocate GPUs before traffic or we just pin weight to a warm cache?
[01:37] Miguel Ortega: both options. Pre-warm means spin up instances ahead of an expected surge (we'll do a timezone-based scheduling or webhook to trigger). We also use prefix/KV cache — keep hot KV shards resident so the decoder warm hits and reduces initial latency. Note: long sequences may still require KV builds.
[01:55] Daniel Cho: there was one test where the KV cache was recorded as K V cask in the logs, so the auto-detection didn't flag cache hits properly. Could be a naming mismatch in the metric tags.
[02:06] Miguel Ortega: yeah that's a tagging issue, we'll push a fix to the metric exporter.
[02:10] Leah Park: from the CSM side we want to make sure the runbook has clear rollback steps — what to do if p99 exceeds SLO for 3 consecutive minutes.
[02:21] Sara Kim: good call. Runbook section 4.2 covers fallback: route to smaller model variant or degrade to single-turn compressive mode and enable early-stop to trim tokens. We'll add explicit thresholds and an on-call alert play.
[02:36] Amira Farid: on the compliance side, I'm worried about burst logs. During a burst, we generate lots of request traces — what's retained, who can access, and are they encrypted at rest with customer-managed keys?
[02:48] Miguel Ortega: yes — Dedicated supports KMS. We can configure customer-managed keys and have audit logs forwarded to your SIEM via an S3 sink. Retention is configurable; by default we keep 90 days in the platform but can export to long-term archive.
[03:02] Amira Farid: do you support HSM-backed keys?
[03:06] Miguel Ortega: yes, HSM/KMS via the cloud provider is supported in the Private deployment; for Dedicated we integrate with your KMS—if you require HSM we can validate with infra. We'll put a compliance checklist in the runbook.
[03:18] Sara Kim: note — action item to schedule SOC2 + KMS walkthrough with Amira.
[03:22] Priya Nair: another question — billing during burst: is it per-minute allocated GPU, or do you bill per-second for the extra capacity? We need clear line for forecasting.
[03:32] Sara Kim: good question. For Dedicated base reservation we bill monthly committed. Burst usage is billed hourly for added capacity in the addendum — we're proposing a per-minute metered model in the spreadsheet to match your usage shape. I'll send a version with a minute granularity example.
[03:49] Daniel Cho: hmm, need to model worst-case — 10k tok/s sustained for 1 hour, what would that look like?
[03:57] Miguel Ortega: rough calc — with our current profiling a A40 at 4-bit quant gives ~1.2k tok/s for your model at 512 seq with continuous batching. So to hit 10k you'd need about 9 GPUs; we recommend 10 for headroom. We'll run the sim to confirm.
[04:14] Priya Nair: what about batching effects? If we tune batch size larger we might get cost savings but risk tail latency.
[04:21] Miguel Ortega: exactly. Batching reduces tokens-per-second cost but increases p99 unless the request patterns align. Our policy suggestion: dynamic batching with max_batch=64 and per-model latency SLO override — keep max_latency 250ms. For critical routes you can pin small batch sizes.
[04:37] Marcus Li: I'd like to see the p99 vs batch-size curve from the lab tests.
[04:41] Miguel Ortega: I'll attach the benchmark plots from yesterday — link to s3: s3://redwood-bench/bluewave/bench-2026-09-14.png. There was a small transcription glitch in the test logs where "quantize" came out as "can ties" in the exporter. Ignore that field.
[04:57] Sara Kim: the runbook also suggests a canary for the burst add: start with 20% traffic to burst pool, monitor errors and latency for 30m, then increment 50% then 100%. Any objections?
[05:09] Daniel Cho: sounds fine. How do we route requests for canary? Path-based? Token-level?
[05:15] Miguel Ortega: we recommend header-based routing at the gateway so you can flip easily. Also have a fallback route to hosted Redwood model in case Dedicated saturates — configured in policy chain.
[05:27] Priya Nair: what about fallback model quality? The hosted model is a different checkpoint and we need to avoid hallucinations for certain clinical prompts.
[05:36] Sara Kim: put that in the risk section — we'll run an eval set of clinical prompts as a pre-flight. If fallback quality is unacceptable, we will disable auto-fallback and only do manual failover.
[05:48] Amira Farid: on audit retention again — what about PII redaction in logs? During debugging we sometimes see PHI tokens in traces. Can Redwood redact before storing?
[05:58] Miguel Ortega: we have a post-processing hook — you can enable automated redaction filters that mask PHI patterns before logs hit S3. We'll include recommended regex and examples in the runbook.
[06:10] Marcus Li: ok good. Back to capacity — is there support for burst across regions? If east coast saturates can we spill to europe pool?
[06:20] Miguel Ortega: cross-region spill is supported but with higher latency. We advise local region first, then cross-region as last result; you'll need data residency guardrails. Also billing and egress considerations.
[06:30] Priya Nair: bluewave has a 0.5% allowed cross-region requests for privacy -- we need that enforced.
[06:36] Sara Kim: add to runbook: cross-region spill disabled by default; require explicit flag per deployment.
[06:41] Daniel Cho: anything about kernel selection and quantization? We saw weird perf differences between int8 and 4-bit quant.
[06:49] Miguel Ortega: right — kernel selection is auto but for your model the 4-bit path is generally best cost/perf. There are some sequences where int8 wins for tail latency on longer contexts. We'll include a recommendation matrix per sequence length.
[07:03] Priya Nair: can we pin kernel selection for a deployment?
[07:06] Miguel Ortega: yes we can force kernel profiles in the model config. We'll add that to the runbook.
[07:10] Leah Park: users often want an escalation path during the pilot — add Redwoods on-call and SRE contacts and hours.
[07:17] Sara Kim: done. Section 6 lists 24/7 on-call and 12-hr daytime ops contact.
[07:22] Marcus Li: I want to call out warmup cost — if we pre-warm 8 GPUs for every expected surge window, that's a lot of standing cost. Can we pre-warm the model binary but not fully allocate GPU memory until traffic arrives?
[07:36] Miguel Ortega: there is a partial pre-warm option — keep a lightweight container with model weights on disk and then do a rapid load into memory on trigger; reduces full allocation time but still has a cold-start delta. For very short spikes we'd rely on KV cache and a small burst headroom.
[07:52] Priya Nair: interesting. For our 30s spikes that might be the sweet spot.
[07:56] Daniel Cho: ok what about the telemetry during the burst run — we need per-token breakdowns, tail latency, CPU/GPU temp, queue depth.
[08:05] Miguel Ortega: the dashboard includes token-level cost and queue depth; we can add a high-frequency trace for the simulation run and export csv.
[08:12] Sara Kim: recap of decisions: Redwood will run the 1h burst sim, attach metrics & plots; BlueWave to normalize traffic trace and confirm allowed cross-region percent; Redwood to update runbook with explicit rollback thresholds, canary steps, KMS/HSM checklist, redaction regex, and updated pricing.
[08:29] Priya Nair: yep, and please call out worst-case cost example in the pricing spreadsheet.
[08:34] Sara Kim: will do. Any other Qs?
[08:36] Amira Farid: just one — data in-flight encryption for cross-region spill?
[08:40] Miguel Ortega: TLS 1.3 yes, and you can enforce mTLS between your gateway and our endpoints. We'll include sample cert rotation steps.
[08:49] Daniel Cho: that's it from infra.
[08:51] Leah Park: next sync same time next week?
[08:54] Sara Kim: yes same time. I'll create calendar invite after we update the runbook.
[08:58] Priya Nair: thanks all.
[09:00] Sara Kim: thanks, meeting adjourned.

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-words (e.g., "K V cask" for KV cache, "can ties" for quantize). Several links/resources referenced in chat: runbook: https://redwood.runbooks/bluewave-burst-playbook-v2.pdf, bench png: s3://redwood-bench/bluewave/bench-2026-09-14.png, artifact: https://redwood.pricing/bluewave-dedicated-pricing-2026-09-15.xlsx

Miguel to run 1-hour burst simulation (10k token/s sustained) on Dedicated test pool and share metrics (2026-09-17)
Sara to send updated Dedicated pricing tiers and burst addendum (2026-09-16)
BlueWave to review runbook and confirm production cutover window (2026-09-20)
Schedule SOC2 + KMS walkthrough with Compliance (Amira + Redwood Security) (2026-09-22)

Miguel Ortega: execute burst run and attach log export to SharePoint (due: 2026-09-17)
Sara Kim: update pricing spreadsheet with burst billing model (due: 2026-09-16)
Priya Nair: provide sample traffic shape (p95/p99 token rates) and business RPS expectations (due: 2026-09-18)
Amira Farid: confirm required audit retention window for logs (due: 2026-09-18)

title: Mini SDK Pod Connector — Quickstart and Canonical Fallbacks
author: Ava Patel
text:
Overview

This page describes a compact, production-minded quickstart for the "Mini SDK Pod Connector" — a small, well-instrumented SDK-side adapter designed for constrained or ephemeral compute (edge VMs, IoT gateways, mobile background workers). The connector provides:

- A lightweight HTTP/WebSocket facade to Redwood's API that enforces local telemetry and retry contracts.
- Deterministic fallbacks: local cache, synchronous stub, and degraded-mode output (short responses).
- Packaging guidance for serverless/ephemeral runtimes (single binary or minimal container).
- Docs site and snippet lifecycle guidance so examples remain runnable in our docs playground.

Goals

1. Make it easy to run a small SDK integration in low-memory/low-network environments.
2. Provide canonical retry/telemetry contracts for support teams to debug quickly.
3. Ship examples that are testable by docs automation and maintained with the docs pipeline.

Who should use this

- Integrations engineers building small adapters for customer environments (edge, on-prem gateways).
- SDK maintainers who need a reproducible lightweight runtime to run integration tests.
- Support engineers who want a deterministic set of fallbacks to reproduce customer issues.

Prerequisites

- Redwood API key with read/write generation scopes (dev key OK for local testing).
- Docker (for local container quickstart) or Go 1.20+ / Rust 1.70+ toolchain if building native binary.
- Optional: docs-playground VM access for automated snippet testing.

Quickstart: Containerized connector (recommended)

1) Clone the template repo

 git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/mini-pod-connector-template.git
 cd mini-pod-connector-template

2) Copy credentials for local testing (dev only)

 export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-dev-xxx

3) Build and run the container

 docker build -t mini-pod-connector:local .
 docker run -p 8080:8080 -e REDWOOD_API_KEY -e ENV=local mini-pod-connector:local

4) Healthcheck and sample request

 curl http://localhost:8080/health
 # expected: {"status":"ok","uptime":"PT0S"}

 curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/generate -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"prompt":"Summarize: Redwood Inference","max_tokens":40}'

Architecture and responsibilities

- HTTP facade (port 8080): handles auth, local cache, telemetry, and request shaping.
- Upstream client: handles calls to Redwood API with batching awareness.
- Telemetry agent: emits per-request events to our telemetry sink and local file for offline debugging.
- Fallback engine: ordered list — 1) cached KV prefix; 2) local stub JSON; 3) short canned summary.

API examples (connector facade)

1) Generation POST (simple)

 POST /v1/generate
 Body: {"prompt":"string","max_tokens":int,"temperature":float}

 Sample response: {"id":"conn-req-01","status":"ok","tokens":33,"result":"..."}

2) Streaming via WebSocket (forwarding mode)

 ws://localhost:8080/v1/stream?session=abc123
 - Client sends single JSON open frame with {"prompt":"...","mode":"stream"}
 - Connector upgrades, streams events from Redwood's streaming endpoint and emits standard events: event: token, event: end, event: error

Implementation snippets

- Outbound request example (pseudo-shell):

 curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
 -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \
 -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
 -d '{"prompt":"%PROMPT%","max_tokens":%MAX%}'

- Local cache policy (YAML example inserted into connector config):

 cache:
 type: lru
 size: 1000
 ttl_seconds: 3600

Telemetry contract (canonical fields)

We standardize the local telemetry emitted by the connector so support and docs pipelines can rely on fixed keys. The connector must emit the following JSON-lines to STDOUT and to the telemetry sink (when available):

| field | type | description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| trace_id | string | UUID V4 per external request |
| connector_id | string | pod instance id (hostname or generated id) |
| upstream_model | string | model name used upstream (e.g., redwood/gpt-8-small) |
| phase | string | one of [incoming, cache_hit, upstream_call, fallback, stream_chunk, completed, error] |
| latency_ms | integer | round-trip time for upstream call (ms), present when phase=upstream_call |
| error_code | string | structured error tag for canonical fixes (optional) |

Packaging and runtime guidance

- Single-binary preference: static linking (Go/Rust) reduces cold-starts. Keep image base minimal (distroless).
- Memory target: <=150MB resident for default config. Use streaming to avoid buffering.
- Configuration precedence: env vars > mounted config file > built-in defaults.

Docs site integration and snippet lifecycle

- All code snippets used on the public docs site must be runnable by the docs playground harness. To achieve this:
 1. Keep snippets under 200 lines and avoid local secrets.
 2. Provide a minimal Dockerfile and a Health endpoint for the playground to validate.
 3. Include a small test YAML manifest: tests/doc-playground.yml that runs a simple generate request.

- When updating connector examples, add an entry to docs-site/snippet-registry with: snippet id, Docker image tag, healthcheck path, and test command. The CI docs job will run the snippet and report failures.

Canonical support issues and fixes (top patterns)

1) Symptom: Connector returns 503 with error_code "upstream_backpressure"
 - Root cause: connector batch queue is full because the upstream client has slow tokens.
 - Canonical fix: increase local batch_size (config) OR enable direct-pass-through mode for latency-sensitive routes.
 - Command to gather logs: 
 journalctl -u mini-pod-connector --since "1 hour ago" | grep "trace_id=<TRACE>"

2) Symptom: Local stub returned instead of upstream content (phase=fallback)
 - Root cause: upstream auth failed (expired key) or networking egress blocked.
 - Canonical fix: validate REDWOOD_API_KEY env var and test direct curl to api.redwood.ai.
 - Diagnostic curl: 
 curl -I -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/models

3) Symptom: Streaming stops mid-response (phase=stream_chunk, then error)
 - Root cause: idle timeouts on intermediary proxies or keepalive not negotiated.
 - Canonical fix: enable ping frames on client websocket; set connector keepalive to 30s; set proxy max idle to 90s.

4) Symptom: High token counts and cost anomalies
 - Root cause: client sent unbounded prompts or connector failed to enforce per-request max_tokens.
 - Canonical fix: set per-route max_tokens and enable token-usage tracing.
 - Config sample: {"routes":{"/v1/generate":{"max_tokens":256}}}

Debugging checklist (ordered)

1. Reproduce locally with the provided mini-pod-connector:local image and the failing input.
2. Collect connector logs for trace_id and telemetry lines.
3. Run upstream curl test to validate egress and credentials.
4. If streaming issue, capture pcap of websocket frames between client and connector.
5. If cost spike, query token summary from connector telemetry and cross-check with usage dashboard in Redwood Console.

Rollout and upgrade guidance

- Canary deploy: deploy 5% of connectors to new image tag with a traffic mirror. Observe: 95th percentile latency, cache hit rate, and fallback rate for 48 hours.
- Auto-rollback: trigger when fallback_rate > 0.5% for the canary slice or when error budget breaches for >30 minutes.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: eng-developer-experience (sdk-integration team) — contact: Ava Patel (ava@redwood.ai)
- Support escalation: customer-success (level-1) -> eng-sre (level-2).

Appendix A — Example connector config (minimal)

 connector_id: mini-1
 listen_port: 8080
 upstream_url: https://api.redwood.ai
 cache:
 enabled: true
 type: lru
 ttl_seconds: 3600
 routes:
 "/v1/generate":
 max_tokens: 256
 allow_streaming: true

Appendix B — Test commands for docs CI

- Healthcheck: 
 curl -sf http://mini-pod-connector:8080/health || exit 1

- Smoke generate test: 
 curl -s -X POST http://mini-pod-connector:8080/v1/generate -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"prompt":"hello","max_tokens":10}' | jq '.status=="ok"'

Notes and follow-ups

- We keep the connector intentionally small to make debugging repeatable. For heavy workloads prefer Redwood Dedicated or a full SDK.
- Consider adding an integration test that replays captured telemetry traces against new connector releases.

If you have questions or need a walkthrough for a specific customer environment, contact the owner listed above.

title: Dequant shadow allocator and token-aware kernel routing for low-overhead INT8/FP8 paths
author: Liam Ortega
text:
Context: dequantization overhead is a persistent contributor to decode latency in mixed-precision paths (INT8/FP8). Current runtime performs eager dequant into working tensors inside the main execution arena which causes extra copies, memory pressure on prefill, and contention during decode when KV cache hits are high. This ticket proposes a lightweight 'dequant shadow allocator' + token-aware routing policy so we can minimize copies, enable zero-copy decode in common cases, and make kernel selection decisions that include per-request sequence-length and cache-warmth heuristics.

Microbenchmark: reduce per-token dequant copy costs by >=40% for 2048-context GPT-like models on A100 baseline compared to current master
End-to-end: median decode latency for 8-token responses with cold KV cache improves by >=8% on INT8 path (95th percentile should not regress >5%)
Memory: peak working set during large-batch prefill reduces by at least 6% in representative workload (batch sizes 8-32, seq len distribution matching production traces)
No functional regressions: numeric outputs match INT8/FP8 reference within existing tolerances; unit tests for kernel fallbacks added
Rollout: feature gated behind runtime flag and can be disabled per-customer route; automatic fallback to existing dequant path on assertion failures

2025-01-15 - Liam Ortega: initial spike and prototype of shadow allocator done. Measured a 35% copy-time reduction in synthetic kernel-only test. Wrote design doc (link below).
2025-01-22 - Priya Desai: design review with runtime team; decided on two-stage allocator: ephemeral shadow buffers shared across microbatches + optional pinned page fallback for large prefill windows. Action: add safety checks for buffer aliasing.
2025-01-29 - Miguel Alvarez: implemented token-aware routing hook (estimator) that annotates requests with expected KV cache hit % and avg seq len. Needs calibration with production traces.
2025-02-02 - Priya Desai: ran end-to-end perf suite on dedicated cluster. Observed 12% median improvement for short responses, 4% for longer decodes. 95th percentile regressed 2% in one shard — investigating scheduling microburst in prefill overlap.
2025-02-04 - QA: added unit tests for allocator double-free and tensor aliasing. Preparing canary rollout plan.

title: Continual delta scanner: multi-slice rehearse for PR perf gating
author: Asha Nair
text:
Build a continuous delta-scanner harness that runs lightweight, reproducible perf rehearsals in CI for every PR. The harness will: 1) run stratified micro-slices (short, medium, long seq) seeded with realistic prefix traffic and optional synthetic microbursts; 2) measure throughput (tokens/sec) and latency quantiles (p50/p95/p99) with per-run bootstrap confidence intervals; 3) compute a delta profile against a rolling canonical baseline using quantile-fusion and bootstrap hypothesis testing (CI overlap + minimum detectable effect guard); 4) apply a gating policy that annotates the PR with PASS/WARN/FAIL and blocks merges on sustained regressions beyond configured thresholds. The design emphasizes low cost per-PR (aim <= 2s GPU-seconds equivalent), reproducibility across hardware (calibration step), and minimizing flakiness via repeat sampling, sample-size checks, and a small randomized control group for variance estimation. Integration points: GitHub PR status checks, Redwood Console perf dashboards (per-model/per-route views), Slack/ops alerts for P0 regressions, and a runbook link for triage. Deliverables: harness code (Go + python runner), CI orb/job templates, dashboard tiles, docs and runbook, a migration script to convert existing canonical baselines to the rolling anchor model.

2025-02-12 - Asha Nair: Initial ticket created after perf retro; current pain points: sporadic p95 regressions in PRs, noisy baselines, and expensive full-load benchmarks blocking merges.
2025-02-13 - Marco V.: Spike done - small-scale harness prototype runs locally; bootstrap CIs look stable with 10 repeats per slice. Observed per-slice variance correlates with KV cache warmup pattern.
2025-02-15 - Priya R. (SRE): Recommended adding a hardware-calibration step to normalize tokens/sec across runner types. Also suggested an early-exit when variance is too high to avoid wasting credits.
2025-02-16 - Design review notes (Jacob L.): UX for PR annotations should include compact histograms and a link to a deterministic rerun button in Console.
2025-02-18 - Marco V.: Implemented CI job template and GitHub check reporter; opened draft PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/perf-harness/pull/214
2025-02-20 - Asha Nair: Policy draft for gating: FAIL if p95 degrade > 10% with >95% bootstrap CI; WARN if 5-10%; PASS otherwise. Need PM sign-off on thresholds and escalation flow.

title: 2025-06-04-sprint-3-quality-check-and-prompt-recalibration-with-novahealth
author: Jordan Lee
text:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-04
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Sam Torres (Redwood CSM); Maya Patel (NovaHealth - Head of Data), Carlos Ruiz (NovaHealth - ML Eng), Leah Simmons (NovaHealth - Product), Dr. Omar H (clinical advisor)
Shared artifacts: sprint-3 results sheet (link: drive.redwood/nova/sprint3_results.csv), prompt set v3 (link: drive.redwood/nova/prompt_set_v3.md)

Auto-summary (auto-generated):
- Quick review of sprint-3 quality metrics; identified regressions on rare PHI prompts (1.8% hallucination increase).
- SE proposed two prompt recalibrations + updated guardrail rules; agreed to run 1k regression and share results.
- Agreed next steps: regression run, SOW draft, PHI whitelist completion, infra deep-dive.

Topics: quality metrics, prompt variants, guardrails, scoring rubric, rollout canary strategy, latency impact of guardrails

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um, quick roll call — Priya, Sam — you good?
[00:06] Priya: Yep hi all, ready.
[00:08] Maya: Hi, thanks. Umm we pushed the sprint updates and seen the sheet, gave it a look.
[00:15] Jordan: Great. Carlos, Leah — anything to call out before we jump in?
[00:18] Carlos: Just that we did a small manual review on 200 samples and noticed a couple fuzzy outputs on the PHI edge cases.
[00:24] Leah: And the product team is worried about user-facing hallucinations for those clinical notes.
[00:29] Priya: ok, so the sprint-3 report, top-line: overall QA scores held steady — precision around 0.93 for structured extraction — but we did see a bump in hallucination when prompts included obfuscated identifiers and nested temporals, so likely prompting failure rather than model drift.
[00:45] Maya: Can you — sorry — break down "hallucination" metric for us? I think our PMs interpret that differently.
[00:50] Priya: Sure. Our rubric flags answers with unsupported assertions or invented med dosages as hallucinations; the scoring is binary per example, then we report rate. For sprint-3 baseline we saw 2.6% and the flagged subset for PHI edge cases moved to 4.4% — so about +1.8 percent points.
[01:06] Jordan: Worth calling out we also changed the prompt template in v3 — the new system instruction tightened the persona but unfortunately made some idiosyncratic completions for nested ask.
[01:16] Carlos: Right, that matches what we saw. The new prompt does better on extraction but worse on ambiguous phrasing.
[01:22] Priya: So proposal — two parallel mitigations: (A) prompt recalibration (three variants: v3a conservative, v3b constrained-extraction, v3c context-window emphasis), and (B) rule-based guardrails that run post-generation to detect likely PHI hallucinations using a lightweight regex + medical-entity model.
[01:42] Leah: How much latency does the post-gen guardrail add? Our SLO is 600ms p95 for interactive flow.
[01:48] Priya: Good question. For the rule-only path it's negligible, but for ML-based entity check it's ~40-70ms extra at p95 on our dedicated infra. If you want zero impact, we can run the guardrail async and redact after — but UX tradeoff.
[02:02] Jordan: Also note that we can canary the guardrail on 10% traffic to measure false positives.
[02:08] Maya: That's sensible. I want to avoid redacting legitimate content too aggressively.
[02:11] Carlos: One more — when you say "dedicated infra" is that Redwood Dedicated? We're currently on hosted API pilot, right?
[02:17] Jordan: Yes hosted for pilot, but the dedicated numbers are just to give an idea of runtime overhead. The canary and rollout policies can be applied in-hosted too; it just impacts how quickly we can iterate.
[02:26] Priya: Back to scoring: we recommend using a composite score for the regression: 60% accuracy/precision on extraction, 25% hallucination penalty, 15% safety/TOX. We'll export the script we use to compute that so scoring is reproducible.
[02:40] Maya: Can the scoring script handle multi-turn context? Some of our prompts use conversation history.
[02:45] Priya: Yes — it strips history to the minimal prefix per your config; for evaluation we run both single-turn and full-context variants.
[02:52] Dr. Omar H: quick clinical note — some of the obfuscated ids mimic real lookups; if you're using simple regex we might need to add a couple of patterns.
[02:58] Priya: noted, we'll add those patterns as part of the guardrail.
[03:01] Jordan: I opened the sprint3_results.csv earlier; let's pull a couple examples. Priya, would you read sample 37?
[03:06] Priya: Sure — sample 37: prompt included "patient x with hx of CAD, med list shows Lipitor and lis" — expected: list of meds; model returned a plausible drug plus an invented dosage. Marked hallucination.
[03:20] Carlos: That's the one. We flagged that.
[03:22] Priya: Ok action: we'll add an instruction to not invent dosages and to respond with "unknown" if not certain — that's one heuristic in v3a.
[03:31] Leah: Will that reduce helpfulness in some cases? If the model says unknown too often, clinicians get frustrated.
[03:36] Priya: Right — hence v3b which focuses on constrained extraction only — force the model to output structured JSON with keys present/absent, and v3c which increases context window emphasis to disambiguate. We'll run all three and compare.
[03:49] Jordan: And we'll measure tradeoffs: extraction F1 vs hallucination rate and a simple utility score combining them.
[03:55] Maya: What's the plan for regression? Timing?
[03:58] Priya: We'll run the 1k-run across the three variants plus baseline — so 4k evals — should complete in ~48 hours on our test infra. Deliverable: CSV with per-prompt scores, aggregated metrics, and examples for manual review. Target share date 2025-06-09.
[04:14] Carlos: Also can you include the original prompt ID so we can trace in logging?
[04:18] Priya: Yes we'll include a mapping id and the request hash.
[04:22] Sam: Quick note on costs — running all four variants in parallel will bump the test cost; Jordan will include a rough cost estimate in SOW.
[04:29] Jordan: Yep will do.
[04:31] Maya: On compliance: we need to capture audit logs for any redaction or guardrail action for SOC2. Does Redwood produce that?
[04:38] Priya: Yes; we log guardrail triggers and the redaction event as part of the audit trail. Those logs can be shipped to your SIEM; we have S3 and Splunk integrations.
[04:46] Carlos: Do you support KMS key handling for any redacted content?
[04:50] Jordan: For the hosted pilot we offer envelope encryption and integration with customer-managed KMS for Private/Dedicated deployments; for this pilot we can add a pseudo-KMS flow for testing.
[04:59] Leah: We also had a question about model rollbacks — if one of the prompt variants causes regression, can we auto-fallback?
[05:05] Priya: Yes — Redwood has route-level fallback policies. You can map percentage traffic to fallback model or fallback behavior. We also support canary with automatic rollback if latency or error rate crosses threshold.
[05:15] Maya: Great. Could we get a runbook for that?
[05:18] Jordan: We'll attach the rollback/runbook to the SOW package.
[05:21] [06:00] (middle of call, screen share) Priya: I'm uploading the filter patterns now, see prompt_set_v3.md. There's a table showing the three variants and example tokens.
[06:30] Maya: Looking at examples — sample 412 is interesting: nested temporals — model inserted a future date that wasn't in context.
[06:38] Priya: That's likely due to system instruction ambiguity. We'll add an explicit "do not infer dates" constraint.
[06:44] Carlos: One more ask — can Redwood run the regression with the same random seed and beam settings as prod so it's apples-to-apples?
[06:50] Priya: We'll match the sampling parameters exactly for the baseline; the constrained variants may change decoding to beam=1 or temperature=0.0 for deterministic extraction. We'll note those differences.
[06:58] Jordan: On guardrails: team prefers a two-layer approach — fast regex for clear cases, then ML-based detector for fuzzy cases; we can tune thresholds to hit your desired FP/TP.
[07:09] Maya: What's the expected false-positive rate at current thresholds?
[07:12] Priya: For regex alone low FP but misses some; for ML-detector tuned to 0.85 threshold we saw TP 0.92, FP 0.12 on our validation slice. We can move threshold toward lower FP but lose some TP.
[07:25] Leah: Ok so we want a conservative FP < 0.10 if possible.
[07:29] Priya: We'll run threshold sweeps and include ROC curves in the report.
[07:34] Jordan: Any competitor concerns? Maya?
[07:36] Maya: We looked briefly at Anthropic's approach — they have stronger instruction-following on some long-form, but cost and latency were higher; we wanted Redwood for the better unit economics.
[07:47] Jordan: Good context.
[07:48] Priya: Any other technical blockers?
[07:50] Carlos: One: our logging currently scrubs a lot of PII before sharing. For the regression we can provide syntheticized logs; just need to map back.
[07:59] Jordan: That's fine — include mapping file.
[08:02] Maya: Quick question about evaluation rubric — can we add a "clinical harm" bucket? Something beyond hallucination that flags potentially dangerous misstatements?
[08:10] Priya: Yes, we already added a harm severity label on examples (none/minor/major) and will surface examples labeled major.
[08:17] Dr. Omar H: I'll help annotate a small sample for the severity labeling so thresholds are clinically meaningful.
[08:22] Priya: Appreciate that.
[08:24] Jordan: Ok wrap up time: Priya will run regression and share by 6/9; Jordan to send SOW by 6/11; customer to finalize whitelist by 6/8; infra deep-dive planned week of 6/16. Any other blockers?
[08:36] Maya: None from me.
[08:38] Carlos: All good.
[08:39] Leah: Thanks everyone.
[08:40] Jordan: Thanks — we'll follow up in email with links and the runbook.
[08:43] (call ends)

title: StoneCove Private Onramp and Region Constraints - Discovery
author: Maya Chen
text:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-05-19 15:30 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (StoneCove), Elena Morales (StoneCove), Tomás Ruiz (StoneCove)

Summary: quick discovery focused on private onramp to Redwood Private, VPC peering, private endpoints, and regional restrictions for EU data residency. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private; leaning to Private due to regulated workloads and internal SSO/KMS needs.

Topics: private endpoints, transit gateway, egress controls, KMS/HSM integration, SOC2/ISO evidence, pilot timeline, latency/cost tradeoffs

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm maya from redwood, ill kick us off. quick intro round?
[00:12] Raj (StoneCove): yeah hi, raj here, head of platform at stonecove. we've got compliance and some networking constraints so figured we should talk private onramp.
[00:18] Elena (StoneCove): elena, security architect; i'm mainly concerned about key management and auditability.
[00:22] Tomás (StoneCove): tomás, networking, i'll be the one poking at routing.
[00:27] Liam (Redwood SE): liam here, se — i'll cover the technical bits, latency, peering, etc.
[00:33] Maya (Redwood): great. objective for today — map your constraints and see how redwood private can fit: peering options, private endpoints, region gating, and the typical trade offs.
[00:45] Raj: yes, we have three must-haves: 1) EU-only data residency for inference payloads, 2) KMS integration with customer-managed keys, 3) no public egress from our VPC for model payloads.
[00:58] Maya (Redwood): makes sense. liam, can you talk through the private connectivity options?
[01:05] Liam (Redwood SE): sure. we generally support two patterns for private: VPC peering / transit via a transit-gateway, and private endpoint (privatelink style) where traffic terminates in our private plane. for larger scale, we recommend dedicated private deployments inside your account or a customer-managed VPC peering to our private endpoint.
[01:28] Tomás (StoneCove): when you say "private endpoint" do you expose an NLB inside our VPC or is it reverse? we can't accept inbound from public internet.
[01:35] Liam (Redwood SE): good question. for cloud providers we set up an interface endpoint inside your VPC — effectively a privatelink — so traffic stays within the backbone. there is no public ingress from the internet to that endpoint. for on-prem we provide a VPN/DirectConnect pattern.
[01:49] Elena (StoneCove): we need assurance that audit logs and request traces are preserved in our logging stack. can we push logs to our splunk or a SIEM?
[01:57] Maya (Redwood): yes, we have log forwarding integrations and can ship audit logs to your S3 or to a SIEM via a dedicated forwarder. we'll include details in the security pack.
[02:06] Raj: good. question on model KV cache and session state — does any customer data persist on the Redwood side? we need to know what touches redwood storage.
[02:16] Liam (Redwood SE): by default the runtime uses ephemeral memory and KV cache per model process; we don't persist raw user PII unless you opt into long-term storage like embeddings or metrics. for private deployments you can configure log retention and disable embeddings persistence; we can also run with customer-managed storage in your cloud account for some pieces.
[02:36] Speaker 1: mhm, okay.
[02:40] Raj: about regions — our EU legal requires that inference and ephemeral caches remain in eu-west-1 and eu-central-1 only. can you pin the model runner to specific regions?
[02:52] Liam (Redwood SE): yes, you can pin to region groups. in our Private product we can instantiate model shards in specific regions only. there are some caveats: if you request autoscaling we will only scale within pinned regions, which can affect burst capacity; we can discuss burst to dedicated in a secondary region if you need fallback.
[03:12] Elena: fallback is tricky because of legal. fallback to another EU region is okay but not to us-east.
[03:18] Maya (Redwood): noted, we can document the region gating policy in the SLOs.
[03:22] Tomás: what's the networking setup for NAT/egress? we're required to egress through our egress firewall for outbound calls, e.g., to a license server, and we need to control egress IPs.
[03:33] Liam (Redwood SE): for outbound egress from model containers you can route through your NAT gateway. in the privatelink pattern, most traffic is inbound from your VPC to redwood's endpoint, but any callbacks or external calls can be routed via your VPC egress if you host the model inside your account; if redwood hosts it in our infra we can offer static egress IPs via egress proxies located in the same region.
[03:56] Raj: static egress IPs are helpful. we also need TLS with client certs for mutual TLS to the endpoint. is that supported?
[04:03] Maya (Redwood): we support mTLS in Private via customer certs; we'll capture the cert rotation and CA process in the integration doc.
[04:10] Elena: KMS — can we use our AWS KMS or something on-prem HSM to wrap model keys?
[04:17] Liam: yes, customer-managed KMS is supported. for the most secure posture we recommend you keep root keys in your KMS/HSM and we use envelope encryption when we need to persist anything. we'll need an IAM role with kms:Decrypt permission for the service account.
[04:33] Raj: how about SSO and RBAC integration? we need SCIM and SAML + role mapping to separate dev/test from prod access.
[04:41] Maya (Redwood): we support SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning. RBAC can be tied to your groups; we will share the mapping guide.
[04:49] Tomás: latency — if we pin to eu-central, what network latency should we expect for typical 2-4k token responses?
[04:58] Liam: for models like our 13B quantized variants you should see p95 token latencies in the 70-120ms per-token range depending on batch size; network RTT will add so from inside eu-central you might add 5-15ms. we'll capture realistic perf numbers in the benchmark during the pilot.
[05:18] Raj: cost considerations, we're trying to decide between Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity vs Private in our VPC. what's the rough delta?
[05:27] Maya (Redwood): generally Dedicated is simpler operationally and cheaper per-token because we control the infra; Private has higher onboarding and egress considerations but gives you data isolation and control. pricing is dependent on commit levels; we'll surface a comparison sheet.
[05:39] Elena: security checklist — we need SOC2 type II report, encryption at rest, key rotation logs, and penetration test results.
[05:47] Maya (Redwood): yes we will include SOC2 and our pen test summary in the pack. some redwood infra references may be redacted for security.
[05:56] Raj: can we run a short pilot that only routes traffic from our non-prod env first?
[06:02] Maya (Redwood): absolutely. typical pilot is 1 week baseline benchmarks + a week of functional testing. we can do dev -> private endpoint first.
[06:11] Tomás: on the peering CIDR — our VPC is 10.10.0.0/16, we run a transit gateway; how does routing for keyboards — sorry for the phrase — for the endpoint look?
[06:23] Liam (Redwood SE): for privatelink we'll create interface endpoints in your subnets, so you won't need peering routes; for peering/transit you'll add a route to the model subnet pointing to our peer. with transit we just need the TGW attachment and prefix lists; we'll ask for your exact CIDRs.
[06:43] Speaker 2: quick interjection, do you support multi-tenant models in private?
[06:48] Liam (Redwood SE): yes but we strongly recommend single-tenant model runners for regulated data to avoid any co-tenancy surface. single-tenant has higher cost but better isolation.
[06:59] Raj: what about backups, are there any persisted checkpoints that could leave the region?
[07:05] Liam: backups are optional. if you enable them we will keep them in the pinned region or in your own S3 bucket if you prefer. we'll make sure any persisted artifacts are subject to the region policy.
[07:18] Maya: i'm going to note the risk areas: egress IPs, cert rotation, kms roles, and fallback region policy. we'll follow up with the security pack covering these.
[07:28] Elena: can you share the network diagram for the privatelink flow? we'd like to run a quick tabletop.
[07:35] Maya: yes — we'll share a diagram and a step-by-step onboarding checklist.
[07:40] Raj: how long to get a dev pilot up and running? assuming we give you the necessary IAM roles and CIDRs.
[07:47] Liam: typically 3-7 business days for a dev pilot if we have all the info: CIDRs, subnets, IAM role, and certs. production onboarding takes longer.
[07:58] Tomás: we have a transit gateway + VPN to our on-prem. if we do private endpoints in the cloud, will on-prem traffic be able to reach the endpoint through the transit?
[08:07] Liam: yes, as long as your transit routes advertise the subnets where the interface endpoints are. it's a standard TGW routing config. we'll include a sample route table.
[08:19] Raj: can we do a quick risk scenario — if one region suffers an outage, what's the degrade path?
[08:25] Liam: by default we don't fail over outside pinned regions; we can configure cross-region failover within EU to another pinned region. fallback outside EU is disallowed per your legal constraint. we can automate canary routing to test failover if you want.
[08:40] Elena: logging — request-level logs should not include raw inputs, we need redaction rules.
[08:47] Liam: we provide configurable logging at request granularity and can apply redaction rules or hashing before storage. for high security we do not store full prompts unless you opt in.
[08:59] Maya: customer question — how does billing and metering work for private?
[09:04] Maya (Redwood): metering is per-token or vcpu-minute depending on model; for private we can also do a reserved capacity contract. we'll send a pricing sheet.
[09:12] Raj: any required firewall rules on our side?
[09:15] Liam: for interface endpoints you need to allow outbound HTTPS traffic to the endpoint ENIs; for peering we need routes. we'll send a checklist.
[09:24] Tomás: what about DNS? we don't want public DNS leaking.
[09:27] Liam: you can use private hosted zones or set up split-horizon DNS. interface endpoints are reachable via private DNS names; we can provide the zone names.
[09:36] Raj: are there any known limitations with GPU model sizes or sequence lengths when running in-region?
[09:42] Liam: larger model families require specific GPU SKUs; we will surface compatible instance types for each model. sequence length: typical support up to 8k tokens for some variants, but we will confirm per-model.
[09:55] Elena: pen test evidence — can you provide a summary and contacts?
[09:59] Maya: yes we'll include sanitized reports and a contact for security_questions@redwood.example (note: placeholder) in the pack.
[10:08] Raj: ok next steps?
[10:11] Maya: summarize: 1) we'll send security pack + SOC2 docs 2) liam will prepare perf checklist and recommended instance types 3) stonecove to send CIDRs, TGW info, and a list of required subnets 4) schedule a pilot kickoff for early june.
[10:28] Tomás: i'll throw in the CIDR details by friday.
[10:31] Elena: i'll review the security pack and follow up with questions.
[10:35] Raj: sounds good.
[10:37] Maya: awesome, thanks all. we'll follow up with calendar invite for the pilot kickoff and the security bundle.
[10:45] Speaker 3: small note — we might want a demo of the console for RBAC before pilot.
[10:50] Maya: we can do a short console demo in the kickoff.
[10:55] -- End of meeting --

Notes on transcription: some names may have been mis-tagged by the transcription engine; there are a few overlaps/crosstalks where speakers interrupted each other. references to internal product names may be slightly garbled (e.g., privatelink spelled as private link, redwood dedicate instead of dedicated).
